text: Avocado tree (*Persea gratíssima*, Gartn

). A tree of the laurel family (Lauraceae), cultivated in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira. It is native to tropical America and bears large fruits, obovate or pear-shaped and purplish or green, with a rather pleasant flavour. These fruits are known by the name of ‘*peras abacates*’.

Water supply of the city

The first studies for distributing drinking water to supply the city date from 1890. Although the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) resolved at its meeting of 9 July 1891 to invite tenders for the works needed to secure this supply, it was only much later, after further painstaking studies, that contractors came forward for the works, which unfortunately are still not finished.

On 22 May 1900, in a proposal submitted to the Council under the terms of a notice dated 8 February, Luiz da Rocha Machado undertook to carry out all the works needed to supply drinking water and lay sewers in the city of Funchal for the sum of 359,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). On 16 June following, the works were awarded to him, and the deed of award of the contract was signed on the 25th.

The decree of 14 August 1900 approved all the clauses of the contract concluded with Luiz da Rocha Machado except the one stipulating that the contractor would be the supplier of water to ships. Considering his interests harmed, he therefore asked for the contract to be rescinded, and the Council granted this before any work had been carried out.

Despite this setback, the Council did not give up on providing Funchal with an improvement that hygiene and public convenience demanded. On 19 July 1908 it resolved to take out a loan of 400 *contos* from the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos, at 5% interest, for the planned works; the sum was to be paid to the municipality in instalments of 50 *contos* as the works required. Half of the said 400 *contos*, with the corresponding interest, would be borne by the State and the other half by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), all in accordance with the ministerial order of 25 January 1906 and the resolution passed by the General Council at its meeting of 4 July 1908.

The contract between the Council and the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos for this loan is dated 22 August 1908. On 17 October following, tenders were invited for the works to capture the water of the Tornos (‘water turns’) springs and pipe it to a reservoir to be built in the locality (*sítio*) of Caminho dos Saltos (‘road of the falls’), with a reserve price of 32,030,000 réis.

At the council meeting of 22 December 1908 the two bidders, Luiz da Rocha Machado and João Albino Rodrigues de Sousa, undertook to carry out the said works for 24,380,000 réis, and the contract was awarded to them by a *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) drawn up in the Council's secretariat on 23 January of the following year.

The works were completed on 22 October 1910, and on 22 November 1911 the Council put out to tender the complete execution of all the works for supplying drinking water and laying sewers in the city of Funchal, setting the base price for bids at 263,460 escudos.

No bids were received in this tender, so two more were opened, with a new base price of 276,633 escudos. The contract was finally awarded on 21 October 1912 to João Pinto Correia, who had undertaken to carry out all the works for 316,000,000 réis.

The District Commission (*Comissão Distrital*) did not approve this award of the contract, and so on 14 June 1913 the Council announced that a public tender for the said works was open once again. The contract went on 26 July of the same year to the commercial firm Luiz da Rocha Machado & C.ª, which had offered a bid 24,650,000 réis below the base price. That base price was 323,500,000 réis, of which 161,400,000 réis was for the water-supply works and 162,100,000 réis for the sewerage works.

The Council’s resolution awarding the contract to this firm was confirmed by the District Commission on 8 August 1913, and on the 23rd of the same month and year the contract was signed. It was later amended by the terms set out in the instrument drawn up on 22 September 1914.

The Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s channel’) tried on several occasions to obstruct the use of the waters of Tornos for the city’s supply, but the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) at last reached an agreement with it. A deed was signed on 3 July 1912 recognising the Municipality’s right to draw from those same springs, for that purpose, a continuous flow of 18 litres of water per second. This deed, under which the Council also made some concessions to the said levada (irrigation channel), was published in nos 11,291, 11,292 and 11,293 of the Funchal newspaper *Diário de Notícias* (‘Daily News’). Now that the Council had the means and resources needed to provide the city with drinking water and a good sewer network, it seemed impossible that any obstacle could arise to the completion of so important an improvement, above all once the works had been awarded. Neither the Council nor the public, however, had reckoned with the European war, which was to drive up the price of building materials extraordinarily and make it impossible to carry out the works on the terms of the award.

On 29 November 1916 the Council granted a petition from the contractor, dated the 20th of the same month, requesting the rescission of the contract for the water supply and sewerage of Funchal. On 25 July of the following year the contractor received 80,029,468 réis as the balance of the price of the work he had carried out. Before this he had received 20,814,918 réis on 22 April 1915 and 8,041,805 réis on 8 April 1916, so that the total sum paid to him by the Council was 108,886,191 réis.

The contractor laid water and sewer pipes in Avenida Manuel de Arriaga and Rua da Imperatriz, and sewer pipes only in Rua das Hortas, from Avenida de João de Deus to Avenida de Pedro José de Ornelas, etc. Besides these pipelines, when the contract was rescinded the Council received various machinery, tools, equipment and materials. Later, and now at its own expense, it replaced the water mains from Saltos (‘falls’) to Torreão (‘turret’), and from there to the fountain of the College (*Colégio*). As can be seen from the above, much remains to be done to provide Funchal with good drinking water and a modern sewerage system. However, now that the European war is over and the main obstacles to continuing the works have gone, it is reasonable to hope that they will soon resume. This is essential to strengthen the reputation of a city visited by foreigners, whose climate has earned the highest praise from many distinguished physicians. On 18 March 1929 the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) resolved that its chairman, Captain Francisco Silvestre Varela, should go to Lisbon to take up with the central government various matters of great concern to the municipality, above all the city’s sanitation works. On 14 June of that year Decree no. 16,956 was published, authorising the Council to borrow seven thousand *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos) from the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos, to be used solely for carrying out those works.

On 3 November 1931 the engineer Rodrigo Guimarães was commissioned to update the drinking-water supply project drawn up by the engineers João Von Hafe and Adriano Trigo. On 19 January 1932 the laying of water mains in the lower part of the city, bounded by the sea to the south and by the 60-metre contour line to the north, was put out to award by public auction (*arrematação*) for the sum of 209,250.00 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis). These works began in February 1932 and were completed on 3 November 1933.

At the council meeting of 13 November 1932 the Municipal Services (*Serviços Municipalizados*) were created, charged in particular with overseeing the sanitation works and the distribution of drinking water to homes. The tender for the award of the contract for the pipework in the middle and upper parts of the city twice attracted no bidders, so the Municipal Services took on these works themselves, estimated at 552,259.00 escudos, ‘a short section fed by a siphon to be built in the Ribeira de Santa Luzia still remaining to be completed’, and 3,700 metres of piping having already been laid.

The immediate construction of a large concrete reservoir on the Levada de Santa Luzia, with a capacity of 7,000 cubic metres, had become essential. The contract was awarded for 753,640.00 escudos, and the reservoir was inaugurated with great ceremony on 27 May 1934.
Bee (Apis mellifica)

An insect of the order Hymenoptera. In the account of Barrow’s travels we read: ‘in the pleasant valleys of Madeira, where the most varied wild flowers abound, the honey from the hives is extraordinarily delicious, and it is sent to Portugal as one of the most prized of gifts’. An old warrant (*provisão*) of the captains-general forbade the hives to be robbed of their honey before the grape harvest.
Abóboras (peak)
A mountain height in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha, reaching an altitude of 1,453 metres.
Pumpkin plant

Two kinds of pumpkin plant exist in Madeira and are grown there on a large scale: the one that produces the pumpkins Madeirans call black or Guinea pumpkins (*Cucurbita moschata*), and the one that produces the *abóbora machado* (a local squash, Cucurbita pepo) (*C. Pepo*). The first, which appears to originate in the West Indies, is the more common and is easily recognised by its white-spotted leaves. The second, grown chiefly above 200 or 300 metres, comes from southern Asia and has leaves without white spots. It is the *abóbora machado* that yields the seeds used against tapeworm and roundworms. The plants that produce the orange pumpkin, the warty pumpkin and the crown pumpkin are mere varieties of *C. Pepo*. The black or Guinea pumpkin, which varies greatly in shape, has, when it comes from selected plants, a much better flavour than the *abóbora machado* or the *abóbora menina* of Portugal (*C. maxima*).
Abra (cove, landing place, point and locality)

This term is used only as a place name in Madeira. At the eastern end of the island, near Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’), between the Abra (‘bay’) and Furado (‘pierced’) points, lies the cove of Abra. Of all the small coves of Madeira it is the widest and the most deeply indented, forming a relatively spacious bay with a good anchorage. During the Pombaline administration there was a plan to build a military port and its arsenal in this cove, and in the first quarter of the 19th century the idea of establishing a small harbour of refuge there was also raised. Besides a beach or pebble beach (calhau), there is a privately owned landing quay. Bounding the cove to the west is a projection of the coastline called Ponta de Abra, and the name Abra is also kept by the locality (*sítio*) which, with its high peaks, curves round the cove and its adjoining landing place.

*Helichrysum devium*, a composite peculiar to Madeira, has so far been found only on the high rocks of the locality of Abra, whereas *H. abconicum* occurs near the sea along almost the whole of the island’s south coast.
Abreu (family)

The first person on this island who appears to have used this surname was Brites or Beatriz de Abreu, daughter of Rui de Abreu, *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) of Elvas. She married João Fernandes do Arco, so called because he held extensive *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), and of whom we shall speak in a separate article. Their sons took their mother’s surname, and some of them distinguished themselves in Africa and India. Among the daughters were the celebrated Isabel de Abreu (see that entry) and Águeda de Abreu, wife of João Esmeraldo, the owner of the Lombada da Ponta do Sol (‘ridge of Ponta do Sol’). To this family belonged António de Abreu, the discoverer of the Moluccas (see that entry).
Abreu (Aleixo de)

He was the son of João Fernandes de Andrade (see Andrade). Henriques de Noronha says that he ‘was a very great soldier in Africa and in India, and, going to the said state, he was captain of a carrack that was lost at sea, where he died’.
Abreu (Aleixo de)

Aleixo de Abreu, or Aleixo de Abreu de Melo, was the grandson of the preceding and the son of António de Abreu. All we know of him is that he was a doctor of medicine and that he was summoned to the court of Spain to hold the important post of physician to Philip III.
Abreu (António de)

This Madeiran was one of the Portuguese who most distinguished themselves in the lands of the East in the work of conquest and discovery, having already given signal proof of his remarkable courage and valour in Morocco. He was the son of João Fernandes de Andrade, who became known as João Fernandes do Arco because he held a great deal of land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) and had been the first settler of this parish (*freguesia*).

After serving in Morocco, he went to India in 1511 and accompanied Afonso de Albuquerque on an expedition to the Red Sea, where he distinguished himself greatly. He was wounded there, and when Albuquerque wished to have him replaced in the post he held, he retorted to the great captain that, if he had lost the strength to fight and his tongue was hindered from giving orders, he still had his life left to lose, and until that happened he would not leave the place he held.

Having been present at the taking of Malacca, says Pinheiro Chagas, he was entrusted by the great Portuguese general with reconnoitring and exploring the Moluccas, islands whose great riches were the subject of marvellous tales. António de Abreu set out with three ships: the commander of the small squadron himself captained one of them, Francisco Serrão another, and Diogo Afonso the third. Well armed, and carrying 120 men on board, António de Abreu’s three ships left Malacca in November 1515. António de Abreu and his companions followed the coast of the island of Sumatra and then passed on to Java, continuing by way of Madeira, Bali, Sumbawa, Solor and even New Guinea. Finally António de Abreu reached Ambon, while Francisco Serrão lost his ship at Ternate but was saved together with his crew, and was very well received by the natives. António de Abreu thus visited the principal Moluccas, and returned with an extremely rich cargo.

Richard Henry Major, however, in the remarkable work on the Portuguese voyages that he published under the title *Vida do Infante D. Henrique*, goes further and supposes that António de Abreu reached the coasts of Australia. There is indeed a map of around 1530 that marks a large territory named Great Java, lying opposite Sumatra, which incorporates many of the islands we know António de Abreu visited, such as Sumbawa, and this territory extends to latitudes and longitudes that already belong to Australia. Richard Henry Major says that before 1530 no one could have given information about the distant lands of Oceania except António de Abreu, who visited them. He supposes, with considerable plausibility, that many of the islands scattered across the Indian Ocean and the South Sea, together with the Australian continent, which Abreu seems to have sighted, were taken to form a single, unbroken territory.

Thus António de Abreu would not only have discovered the Moluccas but would also have been the first Portuguese to visit Australia, which was positively identified a century later by another Portuguese navigator, Heredia.

On his return from the Moluccas, António de Abreu remained in Malacca as sea captain, and gave effective help to the Portuguese in defending themselves against attempts by the former holders of that territory, who had been expelled by Afonso de Albuquerque, to reclaim it.

Shortly afterwards he returned to the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and went back to India in 1526, appointed captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of Malacca. He had to winter in Mozambique and reached Goa the following year, where he found the quarrels that had broken out between Lopo Vaz de Sampaio and Pedro de Mascarenhas. He took the side of the former, and even assisted him with State money that he was carrying in his carrack. He was, however, among the most moderate members of that party, and strongly urged Lopo Vaz de Sampaio not to set aside the forms of justice in his dispute with his rival. When it was resolved that twelve noblemen, six appointed by each contender, should decide the matter, António de Abreu was one of the judges chosen by Lopo Vaz. He distinguished himself greatly in Malacca when Dom Estêvão da Gama was governor of India.

António de Abreu was the only Madeiran who truly distinguished himself as a navigator and discoverer, leaving a name crowned with glory in the history of our maritime discoveries. And yet that name is almost unknown in this archipelago, and it is much to be lamented that nothing here commemorates the existence of this illustrious son of Madeira. It is to be supposed that justice will still be done, and that an omission going back centuries will be put right.

This, then, is a summary of what various writers have set out about the warrior and navigator António de Abreu, corroborated by the statements of some old Madeiran books of nobility, which regard him as born on this island and as belonging to the noble families of the ‘Andrades’ and ‘Abreus’. In volumes I and IV of the important publication *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (‘Historical Archive of Madeira’), the certainty of this birthplace is contested with weighty arguments that raise doubts in the reader’s mind. We record it here simply as a pointer for those who may wish to investigate the truth of this claim more fully.
Abreu (Councillor Francisco António de Freitas e)

). Descended from old and distinguished Madeiran families, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Francisco António de Freitas e Abreu was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) on 3 May 1826, the son of Francisco António de Freitas e Abreu and Dona Matilde de Freitas e Abreu.

After completing his course at the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city, he was appointed copying clerk in the civil government of the district and later an official of the same department, on several occasions serving as acting secretary-general. An intelligent and cultured public servant, he was repeatedly entrusted by his superiors with important special assignments, in which he always amply displayed the remarkable gifts of his mind. Particular mention is due to his work in regulating the services for foundlings, on which he wrote an important report, and to the services he rendered on the death of Princess Maria Amélia in 1854, during the cholera morbus epidemic of 1856, and on other occasions.

Among the various public commissions he held were those of president of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Poorhouse (*Asilo de Mendicidade*), and that of vice-president of the Administrative Committee of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*).

His name became very well known here in Madeira, chiefly because he was a persevering investigator of Madeiran history. He not only published numerous unpublished documents, commenting on them with great judgement, but also clarified various points in the history of our archipelago whenever circumstances called for it. Over many years he gathered an abundant store of documents, notes and information, as well as a copious collection of books and pamphlets, Portuguese and foreign, all of great interest for the history of Madeira. The collection of Madeiran newspapers he managed to assemble was remarkable and valuable, and these papers are indispensable sources for the contemporary history of this island. All that painstaking work of a collector, all that bibliographical wealth, printed and manuscript – a treasure for us Madeirans – was unfortunately dispersed at an auction held shortly after the death of Councillor Abreu. And not a single administrative body was willing to save that abundant repository of such precious material for Madeiran history!
Despite his learning and the vast and valuable store of documents he possessed, Councillor Freitas e Abreu left no work of note on the history of this archipelago.

For the highly important work of the Baron of São Clemente, *Documentos para a história das cortes gerais*, Councillor Abreu supplied many interesting documents, which fill several dozen pages of volume 51 of that work. He also contributed some material to Henrique Seco’s work *Memórias do Tempo Passado e Presente*.

Councillor Francisco António de Freitas e Abreu died in this city on 17 November 1913, having shown to the end of his life a great love of historical studies, to which he was especially devoted. The *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) of 18 November 1913 carried a lengthy biographical article on this distinguished Madeiran.
Abreu (Dona Isabel de)

Dona Isabel de Abreu was the daughter of João Fernandes do Arco and Dona Beatriz de Abreu, who were among the first settlers of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) and held a great deal of land there by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). They came from mainland Portugal and held the rank of *fidalgos*, which they passed on to their descendants.

The old Madeiran chronicles devote attention to Dona Isabel de Abreu because she was the chief protagonist of a drama that must have caused the most extraordinary sensation in its day, for her contemporaries and later generations alike to have written about it at such length. The facts are these. Dona Isabel de Abreu, widow of João Rodrigues de Noronha, son of the third captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, was living in her house at Arco da Calheta, the owner of a considerable fortune. António Gonçalves da Câmara, a nephew of the same captain-donatary, who lived nearby, then forced his way into Dona Isabel’s house at an unseemly hour, intending to make her marry him. Dona Isabel managed to convince António Gonçalves da Câmara that a proposal of marriage made in such circumstances was improper, and invited him to return the following day, when the formalities of the marriage could be arranged, to which she would gladly consent. António da Câmara set out with a retinue of some fifty horsemen from Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and made for Dona Isabel’s house. In the words of one chronicler, however, she ‘made herself strong in her houses with her people, of whom she had many, and António Gonçalves, finding himself mocked, insulted and affronted, returned to his estate, embarking a few days later for Lisbon’.

Some years later António Gonçalves da Câmara returned to his house in Madeira, still bent on his old aim of marrying Dona Isabel de Abreu. One day, as she was riding to the town (*vila*) of Calheta (‘small cove’) with some relatives and passed in front of António Gonçalves’s residence, he seized the reins of her horse and, helped by armed men, forced her into his house. News of this extraordinary affair was brought to the *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) of Funchal, since the captain-donatary was absent. The *ouvidor* arrived with a large armed force, which was to face the resistance António Gonçalves meant to offer, for he was preparing to defy the *ouvidor*’s orders and keep Dona Isabel de Abreu captive in his house. A fierce fight was imminent, with supporters, relatives and friends on both sides, when António Gonçalves da Câmara and Isabel de Abreu appeared on a balcony of the residence. They declared that they had reached an amicable agreement and that the *ouvidor* and the force with him could withdraw.

As these men were preparing to leave, Dona Isabel de Abreu let her intended husband know that, ‘since many of his relatives and friends had come with the Ouvidor, it was not right that they should go back so long a way without eating and, now that all was at peace, he should invite them’. Heeding Dona Isabel de Abreu’s wishes, António Gonçalves ordered ‘the ouvidor with his men, the alcaides, bailiffs and judges of all the towns and places of that captaincy to enter the hall; and Dona Isabel rushed forward and clung to him, saying and complaining that António Gonçalves was holding her by force in that house and that he should aid her with justice’. In the company of the *ouvidor* and the one hundred and fifty men who made up the armed force, Dona Isabel de Abreu set out for Funchal. Because of the late hour, however, she went to spend the night in the houses of her brother-in-law João Esmeraldo, which stood on the Lombada da Ponta do Sol (‘ridge of Ponta do Sol’), the seat of the said Esmeraldo’s entailed estate (*morgadio*).

António Gonçalves da Câmara was not a man to resign himself to a fresh humiliation, which he considered the greatest of affronts, at the hands of the woman he wished to win. Driven by the violence of love, by wounded pride or by the ambition to possess her fortune, he at once prepared his revenge, this time resolved on the most extreme violence. He immediately gathered several relatives and friends and many armed men from the neighbouring parishes, not excluding thieves and murderers who were hiding out in the area. He also equipped himself with two falcons, artillery pieces of the time, in order to attack the houses where Dona Isabel de Abreu was staying with the officers of justice. He laid close siege to them until, after eight days, Dona Isabel’s relatives, considering the harm that might come of this bloody struggle, decided that the marriage should take place. This put an end to a quarrel involving, among many others, four brothers, two on each side, who were perhaps ready to kill one another.

‘When Dona Isabel de Abreu and António Gonçalves da Câmara had arrived at his estate, says Gaspar Frutuoso, and the two had been wed, great festivities and wedding celebrations were held, at which all those who had accompanied them dined. In the first hall of his residence (*passos*) stood four pots of fine silver, one in each of its four corners, each holding three *almudes* of water, with four silver cups, one for each pot, fastened to them by chains of the same metal. And all the honourable people present at that banquet, who would have numbered more than two hundred, not counting others, and servants who were as many again, all ate from silver plate, with no piece of earthenware or pewter mixed into the service. Rich and exquisite dishes of every kind were consumed there, such as the refined women of the island of Madeira know how to make; for besides being very comely, most beautiful, discreet and virtuous, they excel in the perfection of these dishes and in all the inventions of rich things they make, not only in cloth with polished needlework, but also in sugar with delicate fruits’.

Águeda de Abreu, sister of Isabel de Abreu, would not accept either the marriage or the violence that had preceded it, and she laid her complaints before the monarch. He sent the high court judge (*desembargador*) Gaspar Vaz to Madeira to investigate this strange affair, as a result of which some were sentenced to death and others to banishment. António Gonçalves da Câmara went into hiding and later fled to the Canary Islands, while his wife withdrew to the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*). From the Canaries he went on to Africa, where he rendered valuable service and distinguished himself by his bravery and courage. This, and still more, no doubt, the intercession with the monarch of his mother, Dona Joana de Eça, who was chief lady of the bedchamber to the queen, won him a pardon, and he was able to return to his homeland, where he lived for some years more with his wife, Dona Isabel de Abreu.
Anyone wishing to know this affair in more detail than the very brief account we have given here should read the description of it in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), pp. 197 ff.
The episode has been used for several narratives, notably one by the esteemed writer Silva Leal, published in volume 71 of the *Panorama* under the title ‘Bem querer e mal querer’.
On this subject, see the pamphlet *A Lombada dos Esmeraldos na Ilha da Madeira* by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva, co-author of this *Elucidário*.
Abreu (Francisco Ferreira de)

In 1828 he was judge of orphans of the captaincy of Machico, having previously served as shipping factor (*feitor*), clerk (*escrivão*) of overseas executions and clerk of India and Mina. Arrested as a liberal on the orders of the special judicial commission (alçada) sent to this island under the government of Miguel I, he was taken to Lisbon aboard the brig *S. Boaventura* and was sentenced, on 3 August 1830, not to return to Madeira for 3 years. On 23 June 1838 he was appointed notary of the mortgage registry of the western judicial district (*comarca*), and on 11 June 1841 clerk of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of Funchal. He resigned this last post in order to go to Cape Verde, and died in that archipelago in 1842, at no great age. He served as secretary of the Sociedade dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes, and translated the *Compêndio Elementar de Economia Política* by Adolphe Blanqui and the *Discurso sobre as revoluções da superfície do globo* by Baron Cuvier.
Abreu (Francisco Jorge de)

He was born in Funchal on 23 April 1878 and attended the lyceum (state secondary school) and the first three years of the Medical and Surgical School of this city. He contributed to the old Funchal newspaper *Diário Popular* (‘The People’s Daily’), and was editor of *O Século* of Lisbon and of *O Primeiro de Janeiro* of Porto, having earlier been one of the writers on *A Capital*. Besides many articles scattered through these newspapers, he translated several novels, published as serials, and various plays.

He published in separate volumes *A Revolução Portuguesa, a 31 de Janeiro (Porto 1891)*, Lisbon, 1912, 178 pp.; *A Revolução Portuguesa, o 5 de Outubro (Lisboa 1910)*, Lisbon, 1912, 208 pp.; and *A Boémia Jornalística*. He died in Porto on 7 June 1932.
Abreu (João de)

Gaspar Correia, in the *Lendas da Índia*, mentions the Madeiran João de Abreu, who reached the bar of Goa in September 1513 with the fleet commanded by João de Sousa Lima. In the lands of the East he distinguished himself in several encounters with the Indians, leaving an illustrious name in the annals of our struggles overseas.
Abreu (João Gomes de)

He was known as João Gomes de Abreu da Ilha. He was captain of a carrack in the fleet that sailed for India in 1506. He took part in the fighting against the Moors of the city of Brava and the island of Socotra, and then went on to Cannanore, where he gave proof of extreme valour, according to the testimony of Gaspar Correia in the *Lendas da Índia*.
Abreu (Lopo de)
This Madeiran went to India in 1504, in the fleet commanded by Lopo Soares, and there performed deeds of valour.
Abrotea de Poça (Motella tricirrata)
A gadid fish, caught from time to time in coastal waters and in the rock pools left cut off from the sea at low tide. It has little commercial value.
Abrotea do Alto (Phycis blennioides)

A fish of the gadid family, rarely found in the seas of the archipelago. It is caught in deep water with hook tackle and is rightly prized for its delicate flavour. The same name is applied to the very rare *Phycis Yarrellii*.
See Buzia.
Abrotea do Baixo (Phycis mediterranea)

The *abrotea do Baixo*, or simply *abrotea*, is a fish of the seas of Madeira, of the gadid family. It is common, appearing in the markets throughout the year. It is solitary in habit, living on rocky bottoms, where it is usually caught with the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing). It is esteemed for its white, delicate and easily digestible flesh.
Abrotona (Teucrium betonicum, Herit.)

A woody plant of the Labiatae family, easy to recognise by its purple flowers arranged in verticillasters gathered into racemes, and by its crenate or serrate leaves, almost white on the underside. It is frequent on the north coast and in many inland valleys of Madeira. In some parts of the island it is credited with medicinal properties, and it may be of benefit as a tonic and stomachic. The *abrotona* is also known as *herva branca*.
Abruzzi (Duke of the)

He was last in Madeira in 1907, as commander of the cruiser *Etna*. On Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’) he was given a shooting party by the owners of that island, and in Funchal an official ball by the governor, Dom Bernardo da Costa. The Duke of the Abruzzi refers to Madeira several times in some of his published writings.
Abundância (Eupatorium adenophorum)

A perennial species of the Compositae family, subfamily Tubuliflorae, very common in Madeira, where it is thoroughly naturalised. It is native to Mexico and was introduced to the island as an ornamental plant shortly before 1840. It has opposite leaves, ovate-triangular or rhomboidal, and flower heads of white flowers, but with lilac styles.
Acacia

This genus of the Leguminosae family, subfamily Mimosoideae, is represented in Madeira by many species, some with bipinnate leaves, others with the leaves reduced to phyllodes (petioles shaped like leaves). To the first group belong *Acacia dealbata* (white acacia), very common at Monte, Choupana (‘hut’), etc.; *A. Farnesiana* (*aroma amarelo*), grown in gardens and subspontaneous at various places near the coast; *A. Leucocephala* (*aroma branco*), a subspontaneous shrub at Gorgulho (‘weevil’) and Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’); and *A. (Albizzia) lophantha*, an almost always shrubby species, naturalised chiefly at Monte. To the second group belong *A. Melanoxylon*, grown in *quintas*, squares and some streets; and *A. retinoides*, *A. Sophorae* and *A. longifolia*, common in the *quintas* and gardens of Madeira. Acacias are native to Australia and the warm regions of America, Asia and Africa, and many other species besides those we have mentioned may be found on the island. *Robinia pseudo Acacia*, wrongly known in Madeira as *acácia*, is a thorny tree belonging to the subfamily Papilionaceae and native to North America; it is easy to recognise by its imparipinnate leaves and its white, fragrant flowers borne in clusters.
Academia
Under this title a newspaper written by the pupils of the lyceum (state secondary school) was published in this city; the 1st issue appeared on 4 December 1910 and the last, no. 8, on 16 March 1911.
Academia (A)
). Twenty-nine issues were published, the 1st on 28 October 1900 and the last on 2 June 1901.
Academies

The taste for academies, so fashionable in mainland Portugal in the 18th century, also made itself felt in Madeira, although some of them were of very minor importance and even of manifest uselessness. In this city there was one called the Assembleia dos Únicos do Funchal, which existed in 1746, as can be seen from the autograph manuscript owned by Dr Álvaro de Azevedo entitled *Oração Académica*, which Francisco João de Vasconcelos Bettencourt recited on 15 May 1746, the day on which he took up the place of Academician in the Assembleia dos Únicos do Funchal to which he had been appointed. The end of this speech is published on page 787 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). There was another academy, devoted to the cultivation of poetry, called the Arcadia Funchalense, to which we have found only two references. One is in the epicedium, on page 80 of the second volume of the *Colecção Poética* of Francisco Manuel de Oliveira, dedicated to the death of Valisio Alceo, a member of the Arcadia Funchalense. The other is in the sonnet published on p. 31 of the *Obras* of Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, dedicated to Francisco Xavier de Ornelas, a founding member of the same Arcadia. We cannot establish exactly when the Arcadia Funchalense existed. We know only that Oliveira’s *Collecção* was published in 1794 and that Francisco Xavier de Ornelas was born in 1748. Its foundation must be later than 1770, given the sonnet’s reference to the ‘profound learning’ of Francisco de Ornelas, who ‘was surpassing the Tullies’. The Funchal Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts (*Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciências e Artes*), established in this city in 1821, was also a kind of academy; it was short-lived because of the political events of 1823. It held many meetings, at which a number of speeches were given and various papers on literary and historical subjects were read. *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’) of 7 September 1822 gives an interesting, if brief, account of it. See also ‘Longing for the Homeland’, p. 794.
Académica (square)

This was the name of a large open space now occupied by the Campo do Almirante Reis (formerly Campo de Dom Carlos). The square took its name from having been built with the proceeds of ticket sales from a performance given by the Funchal student body at the Teatro do Bom Gosto to celebrate the marriage of Queen Maria II, in 1837. The space was recently embellished with a small pond, a garden, seating, etc., and there the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had a building put up for a children’s park for poor children, which was opened in 1939 under the name of Dona Maria Lívia Nosolini.
Académico (O)
A fortnightly publication by the pupils of our lyceum (state secondary school). It appeared from 1 December 1884 to 22 December 1887, and 75 issues were published.
Acciaioly

We have found this surname written in various ways; here we follow the form currently adopted by the representatives of the family that bears it. The first person of this surname to come to this island was Simão Acciaioly, who, of all the foreigners brought to Madeira by the vagaries of fortune, seems to have been one of the most authentically noble. He was a native of the city of Florence and the son of Zenobio Acciaioly, to whom the Emperor Charles V had granted great privileges and prerogatives. He belonged to a most distinguished family and is said to have descended in the male line from the ancient Dukes of Athens. Many members of this family achieved great distinction in arms, the sciences and letters, and it had illustrious representatives in many countries of Europe. Henriques de Noronha quotes passages from various Portuguese and foreign authors who deal with the Acciaioly family.

When the illustrious annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) discusses the origin of Madeira wine, he includes the following passage, which bears closely on the subject of this article: ‘Between Malmsey wine and the Acciaiuoli family, one of the most distinguished on this island, there is a remarkable historical coincidence. This family is of Florentine origin and derives its surname from steel (*acciaio*, in Italian), the object of the trade that had made it wealthy. From it descended Reniero Acciaiuoli, on whom the titular Empress of Constantinople, Maria de Bourbon, conferred in 1364 the lordships of Vestitza and Corinth, which he took possession of, as he did of the duchy of Athens, with Thebes, Argos, Megara and Sparta, forming the principality of Acciaiuoli. Increasingly harassed by the Turks, it was finally destroyed in 1456 by Mehmed II. The island of Minoa, where the Malvasia wines come from, if not part of that principality, bordered on it or lay close by. It is therefore not only possible but natural that the Acciaiuolis, coming, as they did, to settle on the island of Madeira (the first of whom we have record was Simão Acciaiuoli, 1515), should have brought the Malvasia vine here, out of their own curiosity or for some reason now unknown’.

Arms: ‘On a field argent a lion azure, langued and armed gules; an open helm argent garnished or; mantling argent and azure; and for crest the same as the arms’. We are informed that the *Boletim da Sociedade de Bibliophilos Barbosa Machado*, vol. III, p. 27, mentions a manuscript belonging to the House of Cadaval with the following title: *Achaioli Genealogia por Miguel Achaioli, 1661, fol.* This manuscript may provide new information on the Acciaioli family on the island of Madeira.
Acciaioly (Filipe Joaquim)

Colonel and aide-de-camp to the Governor and Captain-General of Madeira, José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, when the latter took refuge aboard the warship corvette *Alligator*. He was indicted in his absence by the special judicial commission (alçada) that came to Madeira in 1828.
Acciaioly (Gaspar)
He fought valiantly in the war in Brazil, at great expense to his house. He died in Funchal on 4 May 1668. He belonged to the ancient and noble Acciaioly family of this island.
Acciaioly (Father Carlos)

His name was Carlos Acciaioly Ferraz de Noronha. He was born in the parish of Santana (‘St Anne’) on 15 July 1845 and died in Funchal on 1 February 1924. He served as a parish priest in several parishes of this island and for many years taught at the Diocesan seminary (*Seminário*), distinguishing himself as a notable preacher. He cultivated prose and poetry with brilliance, especially in the humorous and satirical genre, and his writings were read with the greatest appreciation. He became very well known here and is well remembered by his contemporaries, particularly for his witticisms, in which he achieved real celebrity; even today the stories and anecdotes featuring his phrases, full of the most spontaneous and sparkling wit, are frequently retold.
Acciaioly (Simão)

). As already stated in the article Acciaily, Simão Acciaioly was the first to come to Madeira bearing this surname. He belonged to one of the most distinguished families of Florence and was the son of Zenóbio Acciaioly and Dona Catarina Delfina. He arrived on this island in the first quarter of the 15th century, and in 1529 he was granted a coat of arms and confirmation of his nobility. Noronha says that Simão Acciaioly married Dona Maria Pimentel and that he died on 15 February 1544. He founded the entail (*morgado*) known as that of Nossa Senhora do Faial or da Natividade, and his son Zenóbio Acciaioly succeeded him in the administration of the entailed estate (*vínculo*). Simão Acciaioly owned sugar mills and a large house in Funchal, and here he held the post of *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper). He had the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*) built in the old chapter house of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), and he was buried there.
Acciaioly (Zenobio)

He was the son of Simão Acciaioly, the first to come to this island bearing that surname. Referring to the Rua Direita (‘straight street’), which then ran along the bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) perhaps as far as the present Ponte do Torreão (‘turret’), Gaspar Frutuoso says ‘that the generous and wealthy Zenobio Acciaioly had a sugar mill (engenho) there’. Was this Zenobio the same Zenobio who was the son of Simão Acciaioly, or another? We do not know.

The present Rua do Bettencourt and a small part of the adjoining Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’) once bore the name Acciaioly, and it may be presumed that the Acciaioly family’s sugar mills stood near them, on the banks of the stream.
Account
*of the discovery of the Madeira Island, letter to a friend*; pamphlet, n.d.
Chard

A subspecies of *Beta vulgaris*, cultivated and growing semi-wild in Madeira. It is native to Europe and has large leaves and greenish flowers gathered in long spikes. The leaves of this member of the Chenopodiaceae are used for purées and go into herb broth.
Achada

This archaic word (*chada* or *chaada*), meaning a small area of level ground or plain, usually lying amid rough terrain, gave its name by analogy to many places in this archipelago that still keep it today. The *achada* (small plateau) survives only in its toponymic sense (Achada de…).
Achada (Camacha)

A small plateau in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha, near the parish church. Within its bounds stand a free-standing tower with its clock and a small chapel dedicated to São José (St Joseph), built in 1924. It is a picturesque spot, much visited by people who come to that parish. In former times it was well known among the foreigners resident in Madeira by the name of Jogo da Bola, and it was used for various sports. It gives access to the old and pleasant Quinta Grabham, which houses the local hotel.
Achada de Gaula

A picturesque inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Gaula, comprising the hamlets of Achada de Cima (‘upper plateau’) and Achada de Baixo (‘lower plateau’), which are well worth a visit. It has a state primary school.
Achada de Santo António

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’) there is a locality (*sítio*) of this name, where there is a chapel dedicated to St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*), founded around the middle of the 16th century and rebuilt in 1730.
Achadas da Cruz (parish)

This small parish (*freguesia*) lies wedged between the parishes of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) and Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), and its coastline is almost equidistant from the points of Pargo and Tristão. The latter, as is well known, marked the end of the first exploration along the coast made by the discoverers João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira, and also the boundary between the two captaincies into which Madeira was divided, the other boundary being Ponta da Oliveira (‘olive-tree point’). That point was given the name of the second of the discoverers. The land that was to form the future parish of Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’) therefore belonged to the captaincy of Funchal.

It is bounded to the north by the Ribeira do Tristão (‘Tristão’s stream’), which separates it from the parish of Porto Moniz; to the south by the Ribeira da Cruz (‘stream of the cross’), which divides it from the parish of Ponta do Pargo; to the east by the mountains of the parish of Porto Moniz; and to the west by the ocean.

It belongs to the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto Moniz and to the judicial district (*comarca*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). It lies approximately 8 kilometres from the seat of the former and about 40 kilometres from that of the latter, by the road through Ponta do Pargo, Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’), etc. It is divided into the following inhabited localities (*sítios*): Pinheiro, Achada da Arruda, Igreja, Cova, Lombo do Simão, Achada de Castro and Terça. Other localities of lesser importance are Quebrada Nova, Quebrada do Negro, Fajã das Malvas, Fajã Nova, Pomar Velho, Risco, Pico da Azeveda etc. It has a post box installed in the locality of Igreja. There are no state schools, but the parish priest runs two primary education courses, one by day and one in the evening, for boys and adult men. The parish is irrigated by the levadas (irrigation channels) of the Ribeira dos Moinhos (‘mills’ stream’), of Lagos and of Pico da Arruda. It has no harbour, only a small pebble beach (*calhau*) that is difficult to reach.

Its population is about 600 inhabitants, living in 150 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’). Picturesque spots with fine views include Pico das Mós, Cabeço do Facho and Pico do Fogo. The cultivation of a climbing plant of the family Dioscoreaceae, known as *norça* (climbing plant of the yam family, *Tamus edulis*, with edible tubers), is almost confined to the area of this parish; it produces a tuber widely used as food.

As already stated, this parish belongs to the municipality of Porto Moniz. However, when that municipality was twice abolished, in 1849 and in 1895, the parish became part of the municipality of Calheta (‘small cove’). When the municipality of Porto Moniz was restored again in 1855 and 1898, the parish of Achadas da Cruz was once more included within its area.

We do not know whether the name goes back to the earliest days of colonisation. We do know, however, that in the third or last quarter of the 16th century a small chapel was built there with the dedication of the True Cross (*Vera Cruz*). It is possible that the common people’s tendency to simplify language shortened the longer expression Vera Cruz to the single syllable Cruz, and that in this way the chapel of the Cruz gave its name to the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) or *achada* (small plateau) near which it was built. That is, unless we accept that the present name of the parish existed before the small chapel was built, which would not be easy to establish today. It was certainly in this chapel of the True Cross that, in the third quarter of the 16th century, a curacy (*curato*) dependent on the collegiate church of Calheta was established. It was short-lived, however, and was abolished in 1577 by Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto. Its abolition was due to the slow growth of the population, which at that time must have been very small and which, over the years, has still developed little. The abolition of this curacy and of three or four others in similar circumstances led to the creation and funding of a new canonry in Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*).

Around 1587, as can be seen from a visitation decree (*provimento*) issued by Bishop Dom Luís Figueiredo de Lemos during a pastoral visitation to the church of Porto Moniz, that chapel was in a lamentable state of repair and cleanliness: its roof was of thatch and the altar lacked the painting of the patron saint. On this occasion the prelate acknowledged that the so-called administrator of the chapel, Gaspar da Costa, was under no obligation to see to its repairs, because his forebears had sold it to the king. The duty of keeping it properly repaired, so that divine worship could be celebrated there with due decency, fell to the inhabitants of the village. It seems that the inhabitants of the Achadas originally belonged to the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo, for in 1592 the diocesan bishop ordered that they should become parishioners of Porto Moniz and fulfil their religious obligations there.

In 1611 the prelate requested the restoration of the old curacy, in view of the difficulty the 84 residents of the Achada had in getting to Porto Moniz, and the people made the same request in 1638, on the grounds that there were already some 18 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) there. These efforts always proved fruitless. Only a century after the abolition of the original curacy was Bishop Dom António Teles da Silva authorised, by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 28 December 1676, ‘to create the curacy of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) of Porto Moniz, with the obligation of residence at Achadas da Cruz and to receive its salary from the tithe portion of the same parish’. The royal decree of 5 March 1680 set the curate’s annual salary at twelve thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. The first curate appointed was Father Manuel Ferreira da Silva, on 20 July 1677.

Achadas da Cruz was always a curacy subordinate to Porto Moniz, with varying degrees of dependence on that parish, until, by the law (*carta de lei*) of 24 July 1848, it became an independent parish, or an autonomous curacy with its own civil and religious life.

The old chapel of the True Cross, which stood near the locality (*sítio*) of Calvário (‘Calvary’), did not give the name of its dedication to the patron saint of the parish. The patron became Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*) in the new chapel that was later built, in a year we cannot determine. This chapel was enlarged a few years ago and was considerably improved thanks to the substantial *donativo* (nominally a ‘gift’ to the Crown; a compulsory war levy) that Manuel de Pontes Câmara, a native of this parish, bequeathed to it for the purpose.

We have found somewhere that João Gonçalves Zarco granted his son Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara extensive lands at the western end of his captaincy, part of which later came to form the parish of the Achadas. This grant included various lands at Ponta do Pargo and extended to the limit of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), which lay at the stream or at Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’). There is no basis for the claim that Garcia da Câmara settled on the lands of the Achadas and, with his family and servants, formed the original nucleus of whatever population there was there. Old genealogies state that Garcia da Câmara died without issue, but it is conjectured that the entailed estate (*morgadio*) that existed at Achadas da Cruz was founded by one of his heirs; its last representative died there a few years ago and was called Luís Isidoro Carvalho Drumond.

A distinguished son of this parish was Commander Manuel de Pontes Câmara, who made an enormous fortune in Brazil and performed acts of the most notable benevolence there. At the same time he earned a lofty and never-contradicted reputation for unsurpassed probity and a character of the most proven austerity. Born in 1815, he sailed at a tender age for the Brazilian empire and within a few years was able to acquire a small fortune. This grew steadily and became considerable as, with intelligent initiative and persevering work, he devoted himself to large commercial transactions, constantly widening the sphere of his activity and so acquiring the substantial wealth he left at his death. Although his commercial activity absorbed his time, he did not neglect the cultivation of his mind: he spoke foreign languages, possessed uncommon learning and was widely read in the best-known authors, which lent particular distinction and charm to his extremely unaffected, welcoming and affable manner. He visited his homeland only once, in 1881, but on his return to his home in Rio de Janeiro aboard the steamer *Douro* he died in a shipwreck off Cape Finisterre on 2 April 1882. It is said that on reaching Brazil he intended to alter his testamentary dispositions considerably and to leave substantial legacies to the charitable institutions of Madeira, which he was unable to do because of the disastrous death that unexpectedly overtook him. Nevertheless, he left generous alms here, and among his legacies was one of five *contos* (one million réis) de réis to the Misericórdia of Funchal. He left almost the whole of the disposable third (*terça*) of the estate to charitable houses, especially to the Misericórdia of the city of Rio de Janeiro, while his children received the remainder of his great fortune.

A truly sensational event for this and the neighbouring parishes was the wreck of the American yacht *Varuna*. The vessel had left Bermuda on 7 November 1909, bound for Madeira, with her owner, the American millionaire Eugene Higgins, on board, and she was wrecked on the coast of the parish of Achadas da Cruz in the early hours of the 16th of that month. The sea was calm; the disaster was attributed to the thick fog, and it seems in large part to the carelessness of the helmsman and the lookouts. The owner of the *Varuna* and three ladies accompanying him were saved, as were the captain and the other officers; only one sailor died. She was a luxurious vessel that had visited our port several times, with a crew of about 50 and a capacity of approximately 1600 tons. Shortly after she ran aground the sea became very rough, preventing the orderly salvage of the ship’s fittings and the valuable objects on board. The violence of the waves gradually destroyed the yacht, casting the precious wreckage onto the nearby coasts and carrying it out to the open sea. It is said that the American millionaire lost in this disaster a magnificent necklace of pearls of the purest water, and various inventions and fantasies have been woven around the supposed finding of this precious jewel, which seem to us to lack any serious foundation.
Ackermann (Eugène)

This author wrote the book *L'Ile de Madère considerée au point de vue scientifique et économique*, Rixheim (Alsace) 1910, 145 pp., which deals with the geological formation of our island, the composition of its soils, its mineral resources and their exploitation, the customs of its inhabitants, etc.
Acclamations of monarchs

According to the *Livro de Exéquias e Aclamações*, held in the archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), Joseph I was acclaimed king in the city of Funchal on 4 January 1751; Maria I on 29 June 1777; John VI on 7 April 1818; Pedro V on 7 September 1855; Luís I on 20 January 1862; Carlos I on 28 December 1889; and Manuel II on 6 May 1908. The said book does not record the day on which Maria II was proclaimed queen in the city of Funchal, but it is known that this ceremony, together with the recognition of the Constitution, took place at the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) on 6 June 1834. As we shall see in the article Restoration of Portugal, the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of John IV took place on 11 January 1641.
In 1855 a pamphlet entitled *Aclamação de S. M. F. o Sr. D. Pedro V, no Funchal* was published in this city, describing the festivities held on that occasion.

For the acclamation of kings a procession was organised, joined by all the official bodies. It passed through various streets of the city, stopping at several points so that the councillors (*vereadores*) could announce there, with the customary ceremonial, the name of the new reigning monarch. This procession was discontinued only at the acclamation of Manuel II.
See Funeral rites.
Açougue (stream)
A small watercourse in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), which flows into the ocean.
Acre
Around 1640 Guilherme Acre was living on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). From him descends this family surname, which we believe to be extinct.
Minutes of the District General Council of Funchal

Under this title several folio pamphlets were published covering the years 1837–1848, containing the minutes and resolutions of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district. Some of them are very rare today, and they contain interesting information about the administration of this district during that period.
Sugar

The sugar industry flourished greatly here in the 15th and 17th centuries, despite the harassment and very heavy taxes to which it was subject. Madeiran sugar was then known in the principal European markets. Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, well known for his generosity, once sent Pope Leo X several valuable gifts, the most notable of which were the Sacred College, made of that product, and the cardinals at life size, all fashioned from *alfenim* (white sugar paste for modelling figures).

In early times the canes were pressed in *alçapremas* (hand-operated lever press) – hand presses – or in very rudimentary sugar mills (*engenhos*). The rollers of these mills were sometimes made from thick trunks of til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), suitably prepared.

In 1496 there was sugar of one boiling and sugar of two boilings, the latter priced at 600 réis and the former at 350 réis per *arroba* (weight of about 15 kg). Before that, the price of each *arroba* of sugar, probably of the second quality, was 339 réis.
The owner of a sugar mill gave the Infante, Lord of the Island, a third of the sugar produced; the owner of an *alçaprema* gave only an *arroba* and a half of that product each month.
Shortly after 1452 there was only one water-powered sugar mill in Funchal, whereas the number of *alçapremas* was considerable, because the tax levied on them was lighter.
The original charter (*foral*), granted perhaps by Afonso V, besides requiring the third from the sugar mills, obliged growers to give half of any cane that was not made into sugar.

Over time the area given over to sugar cultivation grew, thanks to the building of levadas (irrigation channel) to water the land, while the mills’ contribution fell to a quarter and then to a fifth of the sugar. As a result the number of these establishments increased, and together with the *alçapremas* they were producing, around 1498, more than 120,000 *arrobas*, and by the middle of the 16th century more than 300,000 *arrobas* of sugar.

This sugar was consumed in Madeira, in Portugal and in many foreign countries, the royal decree (*alvará*) of 26 August 1503 having abolished the restrictions to which its export had previously been subject.

The royal decree of 22 March 1498 allowed foreigners permanent residence on the island, which had been denied them by the regulations (*regimento*) of 7 October 1496, and the letter of 21 January 1511 granted these same foreigners the right to load sugar for export.
This sugar paid duty at the customs houses; from 1512 onwards this clearance was carried out solely at the Funchal customs house.

In 1507 sugar sold for 315 réis per *arroba*, and in 1511 for 300 réis. The main cause of the decline of the sugar industry in Madeira was the flood of sugar from Brazil and from the Spanish colonies in America into European markets. In 1612 Madeira was still exporting some sugar, but by 1649 many of its mills were already in ruins, and few remained in 1730.

In 1736 Madeira began to import this commodity from abroad. It never stopped doing so, on a larger or smaller scale, until sugar-cane growing was re-established after *Oidium Tuckery* had destroyed the vineyards.

Between 1823 and 1826 Madeira produced an insignificant quantity of sugar, but in 1861 production stood at 275,802 kilograms. Between 1870 and 1873 it rose to between 800,000 and 900,000 kilograms a year. In more recent times sugar production has been as follows:

These figures do not include the colonial sugar that the island imported. Local consumption of sugar was 1,102,545 kilograms in 1908; 837,500 in 1912; 1,656,310 kilograms in 1916, when the surplus production was exported to Portugal; and 3,069,143 kilograms in 1938, when 399,780 kilograms were exported to the mainland.

According to Dr Azevedo, the export of Madeiran sugar in modern times began in 1854. It grew rapidly from 1858 and reached its peak in 1871 and 1872, amounting to 561,837 kilograms in the first of these years and 567,526 kilograms in the second. It then fell by half in 1873 and declined further and further until 1881. The old manufacturers used to say that 100 kilograms of Bourbon cane, a very rich cane, yielded about 7 to 9 kilograms of sugar, even though the manufacturing methods then in use were very rudimentary. Today it is known that the average sugar yield of Yuba cane varies between 9 and 101, a fact to be attributed chiefly to the improvement of the manufacturing methods employed.

Under Madeira’s sugar regime (*regime sacarino*, the legal framework governing sugar production), the price of sugar is set according to the price of cane. First-quality sugar, which in 1914 sold at 29 centavos, rose the following year to 31 centavos and then rose step by step until it reached 36 centavos per kilogram. In 1900 this sugar sold at 26.5 to 27.5 centavos, and many years earlier its price had ranged between 20 and 24 centavos per kilogram. In 1939 it costs 4.20 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) at the factory and 4.40 escudos in the retail trade.

Second-quality sugar, which sold at 24 and 25 centavos per kilogram in 1910, stood at 28 centavos in 1914, then rose to 30 and finally to 33 centavos. Before the war this sugar was sold to the Lisbon refineries at 18 and 19 centavos per kilogram.

Sugar is made by the Fábrica do Torreão (‘turret’). Decree no. 23,847 of 14 May 1934, with reference to Decree no. 16,003 of 29 October 1928, lays down that until 1953, or for as long as a rise in consumption does not justify it, no new sugar and alcohol factories may be built, the productive capacity of the existing one may not be increased, and a factory that is only a distillery may not be adapted to make sugar. All of them may, however, make the necessary improvements to their machinery under the terms of the law.

Since 1935 sugar production has in principle been restricted to local consumption. Because this limitation is combined with the obligation to buy all cane of a certain grade, the current regime guarantees the industry the Madeiran market. If there is surplus sugar in any industrial year, up to a maximum of 200 tonnes may be shipped to mainland Portugal without payment of duties, although larger exports have exceptionally been permitted for special reasons in the interest of agriculture and industry.
See Aguardente, Alcohol, Sugar Cane and Sugar Protectionism.
Madonna lily
Common name of *Lilium candidum* L. and *L. longiflorum* Thunb., plants of the lily family (Liliaceae) cultivated in Madeira.
Adams (J.)

English physician who in 1802 obtained permission from the governor and captain-general to vaccinate 4 to 6 foundlings every week; for this purpose they were to be brought to his house. He was, it seems, the first physician to apply vaccination in Madeira. Works: *A Guide to Madeira with an account of the Climate* (London 1901).
Adelaide of England (Queen)
Princess Adelaide, daughter of the Duke of Saxe-Meiningen, married William IV, King of England, in 1818, and was widowed in 1837.

In 1847, in view of her precarious health, her physicians advised her to spend the winter in a temperate climate. The widowed queen chose Madeira as the resort in which to shelter from the rigours of the English winter.

The civil governor of this district at the time was Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, who prepared a fitting reception for the illustrious visitor, which greatly touched both her and the English colony resident here.

The British warship, the frigate *Howe*, anchored in our harbour on the morning of 2 November 1847, carrying Queen Adelaide. She came ashore at two o’clock in the afternoon to visit the house prepared for her lodging, returning on board the same day; only on the following day did she disembark and settle at the Quinta Vigia (‘lookout’), temporarily transformed into a royal palace. The queen landed at the Pontinha (‘little point’), where she received the homage of all the local authorities, who accompanied her to her residence.

The queen’s retinue consisted of her sister and brother-in-law, the Duke and Duchess of Saxe-Weimar, and their four children; the maid of honour Miss Seymour; the chamberlains Colonel Cornawall and his wife; the chaplain, the Revd G. F. Hudson; the physician Dr David Davis; the secretary and almoner (*esmoler*) T. T. Bedford; the duke’s secretary M. Hartey; and 32 servants.

After 5 months’ stay on this island, Queen Adelaide embarked on 11 April 1848 on the same ship that had brought her to Madeira. She had not only experienced a considerable improvement, thanks to the mildness of the climate, but also kept the fondest memories of the tranquil days she had spent on the island.

In 1849 the queen sent Councillor José Silvestre a magnificent silver piece in the form of a serpentine, exquisitely worked and engraved with the following words: ‘-Presented to his Excellency Senhor José Silvestre Ribeiro H. M. Majesty's Counsellor and Civil Governor of the Province of Madeira-’. ‘In grateful recollection of his civility and kind attention during her residence in Madeira by A. R.’ On one side it bears the English royal crown and, on the other, the name of Queen Adelaide.
Aderno (Ardisia excelsa)

A native tree of the family Myrsinaceae, found in the mountains of São Vicente, Ribeira da Janela, Porto da Cruz, etc. It has leathery, entire, translucent leaves dotted with red at the margins, and small green or greenish flowers gathered in clusters that are almost always extra-axillary. Its fruits are small, globular and red, and its wood is white or slightly pinkish, wavy-grained and hard. This wood was formerly used for the keels of boats.
Judicial administration

In Madeira, at least in the early days of colonisation, all civil and criminal jurisdiction lay with the donataries (*donatários*). Their powers in the administration of all public affairs, and even in the trial of criminal cases, were very broad, except for serious offences punishable by death or the cutting off of a limb, in which case the imposition of the corresponding penalty belonged to the king or to the higher courts of the royal court. These wide powers were gradually curtailed as time went on. The kings’ assumption of the privileges that the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) held in this archipelago, the creation of the municipalities, the institution of *sesmarias* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and entailed estates, the various agrarian laws, above all those concerning water, timber, livestock and sugar, and still other measures of the central power contributed powerfully to the gradual curtailment of the civil, military and judicial powers that the captains-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) had widely enjoyed in this archipelago. Abuses of jurisdiction by the donataries, which sometimes went as far as encroaching on royal power, were not rare. On many occasions this led to the dispatch to this island of *ouvidores* and *corregedores* (royal district magistrate), invested with almost discretionary powers, whose special mission was to investigate and judge these excesses of jurisdiction. It was these magistrates, sent at first in extraordinary cases and later in more normal circumstances, who mitigated and corrected those encroachments of power. Conflicts sometimes arose between them and the captains-donatary, and the central government always put an end to them in the appeals lodged before the Crown.

We have several examples of this, especially the arrival in Madeira, in the last quarter of the 15th century, of the *corregedor* Álvaro Fernandes with ‘jurisdiction on the king’s behalf throughout the island’, and later that of the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) Rui Pires, also with judicial jurisdiction over the whole archipelago.

In the first quarter of the 16th century Manuel I sent the *corregedor* Dr Diogo Taveira to this island ‘for certain reasons that moved him to it, with regard to the captain Simão Gonçalves’, says Gaspar Frutuoso. This greatly angered the captain-donatary, so much so that he resolved to abandon the captaincy. He went as far as embarking in two caravels with his family and the best of his household goods, bound for Spain. He did not carry this out, because he put in at the Algarve and the king gave him satisfaction for the affront, ‘because’, as the cited chronicler states, ‘for the services he had done the king he did not deserve to have a *corregedor* sent in’.

Later, around 1579, the Cardinal-King considerably curtailed the power and jurisdiction of the donataries, ordering in particular that offices and posts in the administration of justice should be filled by royal appointment, a right that had previously belonged to the captains-donatary. Under Philippine rule the donataries’ power was restricted still further. The Spanish government created the posts of governors-general for the administration of our possessions and sent to this archipelago the high court judge (*desembargador*) Dr João Leitão, who was also charged with conducting a judicial inquiry (*devassa*) into the political events that had taken place on this island at the proclamation of Philip II. From then on the captains-donatary ceased to reside here and exercised their jurisdictional powers through their *ouvidores*, whom they appointed and on whom they conferred all the powers they enjoyed. It is easy to presume, however, that the absence of the donataries from their captaincies, and the authority wielded with real despotism by the representatives of the Spanish government, must have contributed immensely to reducing the power of these donataries in the government of these islands to paltry proportions. Although from this time on the donataries’ powers in local administration and the administration of justice were almost merely honorary, they nevertheless continued to receive substantial revenues from the various taxes levied in the archipelago. Around the middle of the 18th century they were generously compensated for the loss of these revenues and taxes, which they then began to suffer.

It would be difficult today, and perhaps even impossible, to determine precisely the sphere of powers, at the time the Castilian occupation began, both of the captains-donatary and of the various magistrates sent to this archipelago by the monarchs. We would say the same of the period of Spanish rule and of the time from 1640 until the days of the Marquis of Pombal.

The decree of 2 August 1766 created the posts of *corregedor* and *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) for the Azores. The following year the decree was applied to Madeira, and Dr Francisco de Matos Correia and Dr António de Abreu were appointed to them respectively, taking up their posts on 15 October 1767. With the appointment of these magistrates, judicial administration in this archipelago entered a regular and normal period. Until then, the duties of *corregedor* and *juiz de fora* had been combined in a single person and were exercised rather irregularly, chiefly to meet the needs of the moment. Justice continued to be administered in this way for 68 years, counted day by day, until 15 October 1835.

The judicial reform of 16 May 1832 was not implemented in Madeira until 1835. Thus, despite the proclamation of constitutional government on this island on 5 June 1834, justice continued to be administered by the *juiz de fora* and *corregedor* or their legal substitutes until 15 October 1835, when the two judicial districts (*julgados*) were installed, both with their seat in Funchal.

Dr Manuel Cirilo Esperança Freire, the last *juiz de fora* to hold the post substantively, served until 14 June 1834, and Dr Francisco António Rodrigues Nogueira, likewise the last substantive *corregedor*, left office on the 23rd of the same month and year. They were replaced on an interim basis by the most senior members of the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council), in accordance with the legal provisions then in force. Then, on 13 October 1834, acting on orders from above, the governor and captain-general Luiz da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque appointed the law graduates Daniel de Ornelas e Vasconcelos and João José Vitorino Duarte e Silva as *juiz de fora* and *corregedor*.

On 15 October 1835, as already stated, the old judicial system came to an end and the two judicial districts were installed, with their seat in Funchal. In 1838 a new judicial reform divided the archipelago into two judicial districts (*comarcas*), western and eastern, both with their seat in this city; they were established on 7 May of that year.

The first magistrate to serve in the eastern *julgado* and judicial district was Dr Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, and the first judge to serve in the western *julgado* and judicial district was Dr José Pereira Leite Pita Ortigueira Negrão.

The decree of 12 November 1875 altered the division of this archipelago into judicial districts, and from then on there have been the judicial districts of Funchal, Ponta do Sol, Santa Cruz and São Vicente.

The judicial district of Santa Cruz was installed on 17 June 1876, the day on which its first judge, Dr Manuel Inácio Rum do Canto, took office. Its first deputy crown prosecutor was Dr Bernardo Vieira Pinto de Andrade, appointed by decree of 17 February 1876.

The judicial district of São Vicente was installed on 16 November 1876. On that same day the same judge and the first deputy, Dr João Pereira dos Ramos e Silveira and Dr Aníbal Correia Taborda, took office. The judicial district of Ponta do Sol was installed on 28 April 1876. Its first judge and its first deputy were, respectively, Dr Martinho da Rocha Guimarães Camões and Dr António Augusto Freire Ribeiro de Campos, who took office on the day of the district’s installation.
Municipal administrators

The first municipal administrators (*administradores do concelho*) were appointed in 1835, but before them there were the *provedores*, who performed the same duties as the administrators. The first municipal overseer (*provedor do concelho*, government-appointed head of a municipality, 1834–35) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal was Januário Cardoso de Melo, who took up the post on 16 August 1834.
Administrators General

In 1837 António de Gamboa e Lis was civil governor of Funchal, when an administrative reform gave the governors of the districts the title of Administrators General (*Administradores Gerais*). After António de Gamboa e Lis, the administrators general of this district were the Baron of Lordelo and Dr Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo.
See Civil Governors.
Affecting. (The)

*Story of Lionel and Arabella who first discovered of Island of Madeira and perished there; with the voyage of Juan Gonzalves Zarco, who completed the discovery of the Island.* ‘From the Portuguese’. London, 1756.
Afonseca (Dr Luís Vicente de)

Although he was a contemporary, we have little information for his biography. He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’) on 21 July 1803 and died in Lisbon in December 1878.

He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in medicine of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and practised medicine with great success and skill. The most important part of the biography of this illustrious Madeiran lies, without doubt, in the way he championed the interests of this archipelago in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament). Without offence to anyone, it can be said that few men have represented their homeland in parliament with greater disinterest and self-denial than he did. That is why here in Madeira his name acquired such extraordinary prestige, amounting to true veneration, and why for many years he held an undisputed political supremacy on this island, which even his fiercest enemies acknowledged. He was deputy for Madeira for the long period of 34 years, something no one here has yet achieved, being first elected for the legislature of 1840 to 1842.

His great austerity of character, the proven self-denial and disinterest with which he handled questions in parliament, his personal qualities and his reputation as an intelligent and learned man earned him a remarkable and well-deserved standing among the politicians and parliamentarians of his time. They held Dr Afonseca in a regard and esteem that cannot be won without possessing the qualities that everyone recognised in him.
