Despite all this, he had to wage bitter struggles against political enemies who did not hesitate to distort his noblest and purest intentions, and he even suffered humiliations and outrages that only the excesses of a narrow and factious partisanship can fully explain.

He always led a simple and modest life, dying poor and in almost complete obscurity. His long political career served him only to defend, with true self-denial, the interests of Madeira and of his fellow countrymen.
At a time we cannot determine, Dr Afonseca travelled to Brazil, where he stayed for some time. There he had a son, Len de Afonseca, who became highly distinguished as a poet and journalist.
Afonseca (José de)
A distinguished engineer who, at the beginning of the 19th century, drew up and carried out the plan for building a network of roads across the whole island.
Afonso

A very old family surname here in Madeira. João Afonso, of whom we speak below, was one of the earliest settlers of this island. At the beginning of the 16th century, Martim Afonso and his wife Isabel Afonso founded the chapel of Anjos (Angels) in the parish of Canhas. Earlier still, in 1483, one Álvaro Afonso had donated the land for the building of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood).
Afonso da Ilha (Friar)

Under this name there was a religious of the Franciscan order, a native of this island, who was a writer esteemed in his day. In 1543 he published a book entitled *Tesouro da Virtude*, which was translated into Italian.
Afonso (João)

Of Zarco’s companions on the voyage of the discovery of Madeira, besides Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the chronicles have preserved the names of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, João Lourenço, Rui Pais and João Afonso, who belonged to noble families and on this island founded large lines of descendants. Having reached the bay of Machico and made the first landing there, they went on the next day to explore the coast, leaving the ships anchored at that landing place. Frutuoso mentions the boats led by Gonçalves Zarco, Tristão Vaz Teixeira and João Afonso, which left the bay of Machico and sailed along the whole south of Madeira on a voyage of exploration. The frequent references to João Afonso seem to suggest that he stood out from his companions through some ascendancy or prestige he held over them.

João Afonso held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and on them founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*), to which he attached the chantry (*capela*) of Espírito Santo (‘Holy Spirit’) in the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), where he was buried in the last quarter of the 15th century. He is the progenitor and founder of the house of Torre Bela, one of the oldest and most important in Madeira. On this island he held the office of *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper) of Prince Henry the Navigator, collecting the revenues and taxes due to him.
Agostinho (islet)

The three islets known as Agostinho, Desembarcadouros and Fora are regarded as an extension of the Ponta de São Lourenço (see that entry). The first is the one nearest the Point proper and is separated from it by a small channel (*boqueirão*). Next comes the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros (see that entry) and then the Ilhéu de Fora (see that entry). Agostinho is the smallest in area and the least important of the three islets adjoining the Ponta de São Lourenço. At low tide it is possible to ford the narrow channel that separates the little islet from the said Point.
Agrela

The first person recorded as having come to this island bearing this surname was Fernão Álvaro de Agrela, a native of Alenquer, who moved to Madeira around 1480 and is mentioned by Manuel Ferraz in the poem ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*).
Agrela (João Agostinho Pereira de)

He was born in Funchal in May 1777 and belonged to an old and noble family that held, as its property, the office of clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*) of Funchal, granted by John IV in 1645 to one of Pereira de Agrela’s forebears. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says that he was one of the most learned Madeirans of his time. It was he who, at the beginning of the 19th century, had the copy of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) made that served as the text for Dr Azevedo’s edition of the work in 1873. See the article ‘Longing for the Homeland’. ‘He was a very well-read man, says the *Diccionário Popular*, and a great investigator of antiquities; he wrote a collection of genealogical memoirs, which remain unpublished in 5 thick volumes in the possession of his heirs, and which deal with all the noble families that settled on the island of Madeira and their descendants, with a good many curiosities concerning some of them. This work reveals the painstaking study of an inquiring mind and an enlightened critical sense, and it is certainly the most free of errors and the most complete to be found in this branch of the history of that island.

Because he professed liberal ideas, he was arrested in 1828 and sent to Lisbon, where he spent a year aboard the frigate *D. Pedro* and another year in Limoeiro prison (*Cadeia do Limoeiro*), and was finally sentenced to stay away from Madeira for a further year. He returned to his homeland in 1834 and died here the following year, in February.
Watercress (Nasturtium officinale)
A perennial plant of the family Cruciferae, very common in the streams, levadas (irrigation channels) and damp places of Madeira. It is a food plant and an excellent antiscorbutic.
Agricultor Madeirense (O
). It was published from 26 March to 29 December 1851, and only 9 issues appeared.
Água de Mel (stream)

A small watercourse that crosses the locality (*sítio*) of the same name in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Roque (‘St Roch’) and flows into the left bank of the Ribeira de Santo António (‘St Anthony’) at the locality of Penteada (‘combed’).
Água de Pena (parish)

On 2 July 1419, according to the most probable date, João Gonçalves Zarco landed on the beaches of Machico. At nightfall he withdrew to the ships, so as to continue exploring the unknown coast the following day.

‘And on the next day,’ says Gaspar Frutuoso, ‘sailing further along, always keeping close to the land, they found in a cool valley and pleasant meadow a brook of water that flowed out into the sea with great freshness. He sent some men there, and those who went found another spring, which issued from beneath a large, ancient and smooth boulder, and was so precious and cold that he ordered another vessel to be filled with it to take to the Infante; and he gave this landing place the name (because of what he found in it) of Porto do Seixo (‘pebble harbour’), as it is called today’. This small landing place belonged to the lands that made up the future parish of Água de Pena. It was the second parish (*freguesia*) on which the discoverers set foot when they put in at this island, then unknown. Porto do Seixo has gone down in the history of the discovery as the first spot visited by the discoverers on the second day of their exploration along the coast.

We do not know the origin of the name of this parish, and various hypotheses have been put forward to explain it. Some have claimed that the original name was Água de Penha and not Pena, a name that would have come from water springing from a crag or living cliff, *Penha* being corrupted to *Pena* over time. To justify this explanation conclusively, there would have to be, somewhere within the area of the parish, a spring issuing from the rock, and this, it seems to us, is not the case there. It is certain, however, that in an old nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) we read that the name ‘derives from a crystalline spring of continuous flow in the *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) of Henrique Teixeira, who held extensive lands to the west of the town of Machico’. Is this the Seixo spring or another that has since disappeared? It is not easy to tell today. It may be presumed that there was some locality (*sítio*) or village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) there called Água de Pena from the earliest days of colonisation, and that this gave rise to the name of the parish. In some old documents the name is found spelt Água de Pena.

The illustrious annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that Henrique Teixeira, second son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, one of the discoverers of Madeira and first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico, held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in Água de Pena. Of him Gaspar Frutuoso says that ‘he was much given to agriculture and through this inclination became very rich, and he ennobled the town of Machico with many sugar mills as well as cane fields, cattle and grain, and upland commons (montados) which he had cleared and put to use’. We have seen in an old book of lineages that Hirão Teixeira, grandson of Henrique Teixeira, made his residence in Água de Pena; he died in 1551 and was buried in the chapel of Conceição (‘Conception’) in Machico.

It is probable that these Teixeiras were the first settlers, or at least among the earliest colonists, of Água de Pena, many years before it was constituted as a parish. The parish was created around 1560, making it one of the oldest of Madeira’s small parishes. Perhaps it originated in a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*), as happened with so many others that became the nucleus of future and important parishes. Some of these estates had small chapels, which became the seats of the parishes then created. With regard to Água de Pena, we can state nothing positive on this point.

Whether in a chapel already standing there or in a small church built at the time, the new parish began to function in 1561. Its first pastor was Father Tomé Gomes, who was followed in succession by the parish priests Manuel de Carvalho, João Ferreira Baptista, Pedro Ferreira, António do Canto, Pedro Gonçalves Ciebra, Manuel da Silva Boim, Duarte Mendes, Dr Estevão Lomelino de Vasconcelos, etc. The original annual stipend (*côngrua*) was raised in 1572 to 9,000 réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto), and increased by 3,000 réis by royal decree (*alvará*) of 14 December 1588. The royal decree of 5 February 1592 raised the stipend to an annual salary of 19,000 réis in cash, plus 1 *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine.

The general index of the books of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) of this archipelago shows that an order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 13 March 1694 authorised an expenditure of 651,000 réis ‘to put the masonry and carpentry work of the new church up for auction’. The same index records another order of the said Council, dated 2 April 1745, ‘for the work on the new church to be put up for auction at the price of 4,000,000, or at any lower bid (branch (*lanço*, *ramal*)) there may be, since the move that is intended is to a more convenient and less windy spot’. Only 50 years separate the two orders, and it is not very likely that within half a century the church would have needed to be rebuilt. We presume that the order of 1694 was never carried out. We are confirmed in this conjecture by the *Anais de Machico*, written around the middle of the 19th century, which say that about a hundred years earlier, that is, around 1745, a church was built anew in Água de Pena because the first had collapsed. The 4,000,000 réis were allocated to this construction, and the new church was built on a site somewhat removed from the first, which then stood at the far end of the glebe (*passal*).
The fabric fund of this church received 3,000 réis a year under the royal decree of 22 March 1574, to which a further 1,000 réis a year was added by the royal decree of 15 June 1598.

While the vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence) António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga was staying at Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), he issued from there a warrant (*provisão*), dated 13 June 1836, abolishing the parish (*freguesia*) of Água de Pena and creating that of Santo – or rather, annexing the former to the curacy (*curato*) of Santo da Serra and making the latter the seat of the new parish, under the name of the parish of Santo da Serra e Água de Pena. Santo da Serra was a subsidiary curacy of the parish of Machico, created in 1813, but its curate did not normally reside there. With the annexation of the parish of Água de Pena to the curacy of Santo da Serra, the latter became the seat of the parish, and the parish priest took up permanent residence there. The measure taken so arbitrarily by the vicar capitular António Alfredo did not last long. By the law (*carta de lei*) of 24 July 1848 this parish was restored once more. It lost the locality (*sítio*) of Achada do Barro (‘clay plateau’) from its former area, which remained part of Santo da Serra, but it gained the localities of Torre and Ventrecha, which had belonged to the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).

The locality of Bemposta (see that entry) was the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) dating from the first quarter of the 16th century. João Afonso Escudeiro, a man of noble descent, came from mainland Portugal to Madeira around 1450 and held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in Água de Pena. There, by his will made on 21 June 1512, the year of his death, he founded the entail (*morgado*) of Bemposta, as well as that of São Lázaro in Santa Cruz. His daughter and heiress Catarina Anes Escudeiro, the first administrator of this entailed estate (*vínculo*), married Lopo Franco de Monção. From this marriage was born João Franco, who succeeded to the entailed estate and died without issue, so that the administration of the Bemposta entail passed to a nephew of his named Diogo Lopes Tavares. Squeezed between the parishes of Santa Cruz and Machico, the parish is bounded to the north by the latter and by that of Santo da Serra, to the south by that of Santa Cruz, to the east by the Atlantic Ocean and to the west by the parishes of Santa Cruz and Santo da Serra. It forms part of the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico: the inhabited localities of Torre and Ventrecha belong to the former, and those of Bemposta, Lombo, Logarinho, Igreja and Queimada to the latter. Its patron saint is the Roman virgin and martyr St Beatrice, and its parish church stands in the locality called Igreja. Besides this church, it has the chapel of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*) in the locality of Cardiais (‘thistle patches’), founded in 1907 by Canon Henrique Modesto de Betencourt, and that of Nossa Senhora do Perpétuo Socorro (Our Lady of Perpetual Help), built by Francisco de Freitas Correia in 1924 in the locality of Queimada. The post box and the telephone booth are in the locality of Igreja, where the parish cemetery is also found. The towns of Santa Cruz and Machico lie about eight kilometres apart, and the most central part of the parish of Água de Pena is roughly equidistant from those two towns and some 20 kilometres from the city of Funchal. It belongs to the judicial district (*comarca*) of Santa Cruz and, as stated above, to the municipality of that name and to that of Machico. Since a fair stretch of it is washed by the sea, it is served by a small landing place with a beach of rounded pebbles known as the Calhau do Seixo (‘pebble shore of the flint’), at the mouth of the stream of the same name. The land of this parish is watered by the Levada do Juncal and the Levada Nova do Furado (‘new channel of the tunnel’), which rise in the north of the island, and also by the Levada do Moinho da Serra, which rises in the parish of Santa Cruz, the Levada Nova (‘new channel’), which draws from the Machico stream, and the Levada do Logarinho, whose flow starts in the locality of the same name within this parish. Some have asserted that the illustrious Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira, who distinguished himself so notably in Brazil in the war against the Dutch, was born in this parish. However, according to investigations made there some years ago, his baptismal record is not to be found in the parish archive. Today it seems established that he was born in the parish of Faial, as will be explained more fully later. A native of the parish of Água de Pena is Canon Francisco Fulgêncio de Andrade, a doctor of the Pontifical University of Rome and currently a professor at the seminary of this city.
Portuguese man-of-war (Physalia Caravella)

A floating colony of marine polyps of the class Hydrozoa and the order Siphonophora, washed up from time to time on the beaches of these islands, especially when the wind blows from the open sea. It stings extremely severely, and is known among the English as the Portuguese man-of-war and in Italy as *Vascello portoghese*. Portuguese sailors call it *Nau da Índia* (‘India carrack’).

The name *água-mar* is also applied to other hydrozoans in this part of the ocean, such as the *alforrecas* or scyphomedusae. The expression is a variant of *água-má*, used on the coasts of Portugal. The *água-mar* is also known as *água-viva*.
Água (point)

This point, or projection of the coast, lies on the shore of the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), near Cabo Girão, and midway between the Fajã das Pedras (‘stony flat’) and the Fajã dos Asnos (‘donkeys’ flat’).
Aguagem
The old-fashioned word *aguage*, which ordinary people corrupted into *augage*, means on this island a small cascade or waterfall, found especially in the stony beds of streams.
Aguardente (cane spirit)

There are at present 40 factories in Madeira producing spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) at 26 degrees Cartier (an old hydrometer scale of alcoholic strength), though some of them do not operate regularly. In the period from 1911 to 1917 these factories produced the following quantities of spirit:

Before the decree of 11 March 1911, spirit production in the whole district amounted to around 1,200,000 litres, not counting pomace spirits, which are obtained by passing the cane a second time through the rollers of the sugar mill (*engenho*) after some water has been added to it.

The decree of 11 March 1911 established a tax of 100 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for the first three years, and of 150 *réis* for the following years up to 1918, on all spirits produced in unregistered factories. From the third year, however, the maximum tax began to be collected – at the request, it is said, of the registered factories (*fábricas matriculadas*). All the spirit produced by the unregistered factories stays in the archipelago, and part of it is used in treating wines not intended for shipment. It has been calculated that 30 kilos of cane produce on average 2 litres of spirit.

The registered factories were formerly obliged to buy, at the price of 930 *réis* per *galão* (Portuguese gallon, about 3.16 litres) (3.16), the surplus spirit at 26 degrees Cartier that the unregistered factories distilled each year for consumption in Madeira, but they fulfilled this obligation in full only in 1904 and 1905.

The tax on the resale of spirit, authorised by the law of 2 May 1919 and the regulations of 25 May 1920, yielded 82,434.87 escudos in 1920. Of this, 79,137.48 escudos was shared among the Municipal Councils, with the Council of Funchal receiving 39,518.64 escudos. The sum of 3,297.39 escudos was set aside to pay the staff involved in collecting the tax.

The decree of 11 March 1911 cited above contained one of the most important measures that the governments of mainland Portugal have taken concerning this archipelago in the long span of five centuries: the expropriation of the spirit factories. In connection with this salutary measure, we wish to reproduce here some passages of what we wrote on the subject when the idea of re-establishing those same factories arose.

‘Everyone knows that one of the greatest scourges that has afflicted Madeira, and to a large extent afflicts it still, especially in its sad and baleful consequences, is that well-known and terrible social cancer which bears the dreadful name of alcoholism. Although it is vigorously fought everywhere as a true measure of public salvation, it pitched its camp among us with the manifest consent of the laws, which indirectly protected it, and it was even regarded as one of the sources of the common wealth of the whole district!

The Madeiran was thus placed on a far lower footing than the African Black! Let there be no suspicion of exaggeration in the comparison. By international measures, the traffic in alcoholic drinks on the African continent was prohibited, in order to safeguard the integrity of the native race and spare it the ravages of that great evil. What was, as a matter of course, considered a saving provision for the African savages was not considered a necessary measure of genuine social importance for the poor inhabitants of this remote archipelago.

Madeira even came to be known as the island of Spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine), a name given to it in a legislative instrument because of the huge consumption of that poison, which reached almost incredible proportions, and because of the truly appalling damage it caused, as the same decree states. A former minister, a professor of medicine and distinguished man of science, on whom the municipality of this city conferred the title of meritorious citizen of Funchal, had the courage, in a public lecture held in the city of Porto that became famous, to call the Madeirans drunkards and alcoholics. This was certainly a great discourtesy to the inhabitants of this island, but not far removed from the sad and acknowledged reality of the facts. It is known, although the general public has not yet become aware of it, that in recent decades a notable decline of the race has been occurring on this island. In stature, in bodily constitution, in muscular strength, etc. etc., a marked physiological decadence can be seen, which has not escaped the observation of several physicians, and especially of some army doctors employed for many years in examining the young men liable to army conscription. Alcoholism is identified as one of the main causes of this alarming fact. There are, however, still graver and more frightening signs, which threaten the complete annihilation of a population unless some of the measures already taken are maintained and others with more immediate and effective results are adopted. This is the astonishing percentage of cases of insanity that the population of this island keeps supplying. In addition, the cases of idiocy, epilepsy, nervous convulsions and other more or less proven degenerative conditions are countless and multiply prodigiously, giving cause for the greatest wonder and dismay if we compare them with similar cases in other populous centres. Let a few of the physicians who have particularly devoted themselves to the study of these diseases be consulted, and let the doors of our asylums be crossed, and we shall without effort be convinced of the sad truth of these assertions. Eighty per cent of the poor patients confined there are victims of alcoholism! And if to this dreadful picture we add those whom that terrible cancer has sacrificed to tuberculosis and to many other diseases, we shall form an approximate idea of the harm caused by fifty laboratories of toxic substances which for many years went on poisoning, brutalising and driving mad the unwary population of an entire district!

The lowering of the intellectual level is also notable. Among other facts, there is one that proves it. The present author, and many other people who have stayed for a longer or shorter time in the parishes of the north of the island, have noted the marked mental difference between the inhabitants of certain localities in the northern and southern parts of Madeira, to the disadvantage of the south-coast parishes. It is known that the production and consumption of spirit was almost nil in the northern parishes, where the planting of sugar cane began only a few years ago and is now spreading, whereas its cultivation in the southern region of our island goes back centuries.

The sad situation that alcoholism has created in Madeira, which we have lightly sketched, is defined in lapidary fashion by the following words taken from the report cited above: “The prosperity of the archipelago is indissolubly bound up with the physical, intellectual and moral worth of its population, and that worth diminishes in the same proportion as the consumption of spirit increases, so that, unless a prompt remedy is provided for so great an evil, there is legitimate fear that the degeneration may reach irremediable extremes.

The decree of 11 March 1911, countersigned by Brito Camacho, established the saving measure of expropriating the spirit distilleries, which several legal provisions decreed later altered in essential points. This was a very grave error, and it was cause enough for regret that so salutary and necessary a provision had not been maintained in full and was not observed in all its comprehensive scope.

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that the restrictions placed on the production of this terrible poison and the suspension imposed on the operation of the distilleries represent a great and inestimable service to the whole population of the archipelago, whose beneficial results are already markedly felt everywhere. To complete a great humanitarian work, however, a more radical and more definitive measure must be decreed, one that absolutely rules out any return to the manufacture of any quantity, however small, of that poison which gave our land the pejorative name of the Island of Spirit.’
See Álcool, Garupa, Proteccionismo, Sacarina and Junta Agrícola.
Water

The use of water, as the primary element of agriculture, was from the outset one of the greatest concerns and labours of the first settlers of Madeiran soil. These concerns have been handed down without interruption from generation to generation, taking the most varied forms and creating a vast web of economic and social interests that would merit a thorough and extensive study, which unfortunately has yet to be made.

The gigantic task of building the levadas (irrigation channels), which lasted for centuries; the struggles to acquire and hold their flows of water; the popular uprisings that broke out several times for this reason; the formation of associations of *heréus* (co-owners of the water rights of a levada) to exploit and distribute the water; the frequent lawsuits; the many laws enacted to regulate these matters; the customs and practices that took root, etc., would provide ample material for such a broad and interesting study.

The first settlers readily saw that Madeira’s particular conditions – the make-up of its soils, the ruggedness of its slopes and hillsides, the shelter the coast enjoyed under the protection of the high mountains, etc. – marked out the land along the ocean as the most suitable for profitable crops, which soon became considerable sources of wealth and prosperity. Without delay, abundant springs began to be channelled through long aqueducts, which grew in number and improved in construction from year to year as the sugar-making and wine industries also developed more widely and more efficiently.

So began the greatest undertaking ever carried out for the benefit of Madeiran agriculture, and one of the most important factors in the public wealth of the archipelago: the building of the Levadas (‘irrigation channels’).

Several legislative measures issued by the central government were soon adopted, laying down certain principles of law and establishing essential rules that came to regulate the use of water intended for irrigating the land. The oldest known are the royal letters (*carta régia*) of John II of 7 March and 7 May 1493, which contain very important provisions on this question and are transcribed on p. 673 ff. of the annotations to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), 1873.

‘Before these salutary provisions,’ Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo informs us, ‘there were already levadas (irrigation channels) and allocations of irrigation water. On fol. 270 of vol. 1 of the *Archivo da Câmara do Funchal* there is registered a letter from the Infante Ferdinand, issued in 1461, ordering that there should be two sworn men charged with sharing out the water, and on fol. 222 of the same volume one reads a chapter of another letter, of 1485, which ordered the water to be released on Sundays to all the heirs...’

These wise measures by the government of mainland Portugal were followed by others no less wise, most notably the royal letter of Manuel I of 9 February 1505 (*Saud*, 688), which confirmed, extended and regulated anew the provisions of the earlier decrees. To it the illustrious annotator of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso adds this judicious comment: this legislation produced excellent results, especially in the irrigation of the land. In that period the principal general or common levadas of the island of Madeira were built – arteries through which, from then until now, although the institution has since been distorted, there flows in abundance the blood of its agricultural life, the precious filter of its prosperity and constant rejuvenation’.

Over time, further legislative provisions came to promote and improve the management of irrigation water. Among them we should cite the royal letters of 6 March 1563 and 18 August of the same year, 20 July 1579, 26 April 1587, 13 September 1644, 7 April 1655, 10 October 1663 and 5 March 1770.

During the first four centuries after the beginning of the colonisation of Madeira, the laborious work of harnessing the water, carrying it through long aqueducts and distributing it over the cultivated land was mainly in the hands of private initiative. It was, however, greatly assisted by the State, which enacted the most effective legislative measures to protect these important services. It was a little over a century ago that the central government, responding to the urgent and forceful requests of the farmers and rural landowners of this island, undertook to begin building some levadas which, had they been left to the private initiative of the farmers, could perhaps never have been built.

The area of arable land was growing considerably, and the efforts of the cultivators could no longer meet the needs that arose, since almost all of them lacked the means to meet the enormous cost of cutting new levadas. In this way the State carried out a great work of protection for Madeiran agriculture: it fostered public wealth, raised the value of the cultivated land and greatly increased its taxable income for the benefit of the State itself, as a return on the capital invested. This most remarkable work is one of the greatest, if not the greatest of all, that the government of the mainland has carried out on this island over the long span of five centuries.
Águas Doces
This name is given to a small beach and stretch of coastline lying between the Ilhéu da Pontinha (‘islet of the little point’) and the mouth of the Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’).
Iron-bearing waters

Of the various iron-bearing springs in Madeira, the best known is the Jamboto spring, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António. Mr Carlos Lepierre, who analysed the waters of this spring on 4 June 1900, states that they belong to the group of hyposaline, chlorinated and ferruginous waters. Their most important mineral constituent, he says, is sodium chloride, followed by iron bicarbonate, which is present in a relatively large quantity (36 milligrams, corresponding to 12.6 milligrams of iron). Mr Lepierre also found bicarbonates of magnesia and lime in the same waters, with small quantities of sulphates and nitrates.

According to the same analyst, the Jamboto waters are very pure from a bacteriological point of view. The results of Mr Lepierre’s investigations appear in a pamphlet published by order of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), with the following title: *Analyse Chimica e Bacteriologica da Água da Fonte Férrea-Jamboto, Santo Antonio- Funchal, Madeira . . .* (Funchal, 1900).
Aguiar

This is a very old surname on this island. The first to bear it here was Diogo Afonso de Aguiar, one of the four noblemen sent by Afonso V to marry the daughters of João Gonçalves Zarco. Some genealogists say he was the son of José Afonso de Aguiar, first treasurer of the Lisbon mint, and others that he was the son of Pedro de Aguiar. One of his brothers, named Pedro Afonso de Aguiar, was chief outfitter of the fleet of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) and a commander of the Order of Christ. Diogo Afonso de Aguiar married Dona Isabel Gonçalves da Câmara, Zarco’s third daughter; Henrique Henriques de Noronha states in the nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) that ‘the dowry that I saw was drawn up in the year 1439’. He was the father of Rui Dias de Aguiar and of Dom Nuno de Aguiar, Bishop of Ceuta and Tangier (see those entries). The Aguiars bore as their arms an eagle displayed on a red field ornamented with black, and also another eagle.
Aguiar (Dom Nuno)

Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo calls him Dom Martinho de Aguiar, but in various chronicles and nobiliaries, and in Paiva Manso’s interesting memoir on the *Esquadras de Marrocos*, his name is generally given as Dom Nuno de Aguiar. He is said to have been born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho, the son of Diogo de Aguiar and grandson of João Gonçalves Zarco, the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. He was a Cistercian monk and held important ecclesiastical offices. He accompanied King Afonso V to Africa for the conquest of Asilah and Tangier, and when the latter diocese was created he secured his appointment as its prelate. He sought to annex the Madeira archipelago to his bishopric, but this was vigorously opposed by the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son Diogo, Duke of Viseu, Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), who was supported by the monarch and by the donataries (*donatário*) of this island. Dom Nuno de Aguiar spent little time in his diocese, and after twenty years as bishop he died in mainland Portugal in 1491.
Aguiar (Joaquim Nunes de)

This distinguished engineer was born in Funchal towards the end of the first quarter of the 19th century, the natural son of Diogo Teles de Meneses, director of our customs house. After his preparatory studies he began his course in civil engineering in Lisbon, and later completed it with great distinction in Paris in 1848. He was engineer to the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) from 1849 to 1850, and in 1852 was called to work on the Northern Railway, where he gave notable proof of his talent and love of work. He then held important posts: director of public works in Viana, Braga and Porto, member of the Public Works Council, director of the Eastern Railway and inspector of the northern lines. He travelled abroad several times on missions entrusted to him by our government. He was a man of great aptitude and remarkable energy, and died in Funchal, from overwork, on 14 November 1877.
Aguiar (Manuel Caetano Pimenta de)

His name is all but unknown here in Madeira. Some years ago Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), wishing to save the memory of this distinguished Madeiran from complete oblivion, gave his name to the lane that links Rua da Carreira (‘track’) and Rua das Cruzes. Even so, the great majority of the people of Funchal have not come to know any better the qualities or merits that may have made him illustrious.

Pimenta de Aguiar was not one of those writers who mark an era or remain immortal in the annals of a country’s literature. Nevertheless, he left a quite distinguished name in the pages of our literary history, and some even regard him as the true precursor of Almeida Garrett in the creation of a national theatre. He did not possess the prodigious and versatile talent of the author of *Frei Luiz de Sousa*, nor the inimitable beauty of his language, nor his rare and exceptional gifts as a dramatist. Yet he had the insight to see that we had no true theatre in Portugal, and he tried to awaken a taste for this kind of literature, following chiefly the lead of the French tragedians. He wrote many tragedies, which were greatly in vogue in their day and which revealed his remarkable aptitude as a dramatic writer. His literary works had the faults typical of the period, but they undeniably showed great originality, departing from the models followed until then. For this reason, despite all their imperfections, the public flocked to hear the tragedies of Pimenta de Aguiar and enthusiastically acclaimed their author.

With his admirable dramatic works, which created the true national theatre, Viscount Almeida Garrett consigned the undeniable merits of our illustrious fellow countryman to oblivion. Critics have nonetheless recognised that Pimenta de Aguiar deserves a distinguished place in our literary annals.

Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar was born in this city on 16 May 1765, the son of Bartolomeu Luís Pimenta de Aguiar and Dona Maria Felícia de Carvalho. His father, a doctor of law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), came to this island to hold the post of general guardian of orphans, and here he administered an entailed house (*casa vinculada*).

In 1778, aged 13, Pimenta de Aguiar left for Lisbon to enrol at the Colégio dos Nobres; it is not known whether or not he completed his studies there. In 1785 he went to Paris, where for some years he followed the course in arts and sciences. He later abandoned his studies to take his chances in war, taking part in the country’s internal revolts around 1790 or 1791. He always showed great daring and courage, and for this he attained the rank of captain and the Cross of the Legion of Honour. When the war was over and he had obtained his discharge from military service, he returned to his homeland and devoted himself chiefly to study and to his literary interests. In 1816 he published his first tragedy, which he entitled *Virgínia*, and he brought out his last work in 1820. He was remarkably prolific, for in so short a period he printed ten tragedies, all of them of some length. In order of publication, they are entitled *Virginia*, *Os Dois Irmãos Inimigos*, *D. João I*, *Arria*, *Destruição de Jerusalém*, *D. Sebastião em Africa*, *Conquista do Peru*, *Eudoxia Liciana*, *Morte de Socrates* and *Carácter dos Lusitanos*. After 1820, following a period of such literary activity, there is no record of his publishing any further writings, and we do not know to what to attribute this sudden and complete break in his work. We do not know whether he devoted himself to other literary genres besides tragedy; it is recorded only, on the testimony of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, that he left some unpublished works. As befits tragedy, and in imitation of the Greek and French tragedians, Pimenta de Aguiar wrote all his compositions in verse, revealing himself as an inspired poet who combined loftiness of thought with beauty of form.

Although he had lived away from Madeira for most of his life, Pimenta de Aguiar’s rare gifts of talent and learning were not unknown to his fellow Madeirans, and they therefore chose him as their representative in the general Cortes (Portuguese parliament) that sat from 1822 to 1823. He was also elected deputy for this island for the legislative session of 1826 to 1828. Of his work as a parliamentarian and representative of this archipelago in the Cortes, we know only what the *Actas das sessões públicas* of the first extraordinary annual session of the first legislature of the Chamber of Deputies record: in the session of 1826 to 1828 he attended the meetings assiduously, sat on some parliamentary committees and presented a bill permitting the free export of Madeira wine.

The establishment of absolute government forced him into hiding to escape persecution by Miguelist agents, who could not spare a man who had been an enthusiastic supporter of the Constitution of 1820 and of the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) of 1826.

Pimenta de Aguiar married Dona Micaela Antónia de Sá Betencourt, by whom he had seven children. One of them, Luís Pimenta de Aguiar, was exiled to Mozambique as a liberal and died there; another, Dona Isabel Betencourt de Aguiar, married António João da Silva Betencourt Favila, holder of the entail (*morgado*).

Pimenta de Aguiar lived in the house in the old Rua da Carreira where the respected Vieira family lives today, a little below the lane (Travessa, ‘crossing’) that bears the name of the distinguished poet and dramatist. In that house, according to information we consider reliable, he wrote some of his tragedies.

Struck down by an apoplectic fit, he died in Lisbon, in the Rua Direita (‘straight street’) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Paulo, on 19 February 1832, and was buried in the parish church of that same parish. He died just short of 67 years of age.

Dr Ernesto Gonçalves published two articles in the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (‘Historical Archive of Madeira’) on Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar, which provide new and interesting information for the biography of this illustrious Madeiran.
Aguiar (Father Dr José Gonçalves de)

José Gonçalves de Aguiar was born of humble parents in the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) on 8 October 1831, the legitimate son of Vitorino Gonçalves Rocha and Vitorina Rosa de Jesus. Like some of his brothers, he used the surname Aguiar, which was that of his maternal grandfather. He was a student at the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*) when, thanks to the patronage of the Russian Waxel family, who were then in Madeira, he went to study in the faculty of theology at the University, where he graduated in a year we cannot establish. Shortly afterwards he settled in Lisbon and remained there until his death. In the capital he held, among other posts, those of high court judge (*desembargador*) of the patriarchal curia and prosynodal examiner (diocesan examiner of clergy).

He was a man much devoted to study and of wide learning, and for this reason was highly regarded in the capital, and no less for his qualities of character and his conduct as a citizen and as a priest. He contributed to various newspapers and, as far as we know, published separately *O Dogma da Imaculada Conceição de Maria Santíssima*, Lisbon, 1880, 40 pp., and *Tratado da Penitência*, Lisbon, 1888, XVI-849 pp.
It is recorded that he was invited more than once to accept a mitre, but he always refused to enter the episcopate.
We do not know the date of his death, which occurred in Lisbon, nor any other details of his life.
Aguiar (Pedro Afonso)

He was the son of Diogo Afonso de Aguiar and the brother of Rui de Aguiar. He distinguished himself greatly as a soldier and seaman. He went to India as captain of a carrack and was present at the taking of Gran Canaria. He accompanied Jaime, Duke of Braganza, on the expedition to Azemmour, where he showed great heroism.
Aguiar (Rui Dias de)

He was the son of Diogo Afonso de Aguiar and of Dona Isabel Gonçalves da Câmara, third daughter of Zarco. He married Leonor Homem de Sousa, daughter of Garcia Homem de Sousa and of Catarina Gonçalves da Câmara, daughter of the discoverer of Madeira. He served for a long time in Africa, where he distinguished himself by his bravery. He died valiantly in the fortress of Gué, defending it against an attack by the natives. Manuel Tomás mentions him in his poem, ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*).
Garfish (Belone vulgaris)
A teleost fish of the suborder Malacopterygii, family Scombresocidae, which passes through Madeiran waters. Its body is eel-shaped, and it can reach at most 1 metre in length.

It is often seen in the company of the mackerel (*cavala*) and other migratory fish, but it is not a common species in the markets. Its dry, tough flesh does not recommend it as a delicate food. See Peixe Agulha.
Agulha (point)
It is the southernmost point of the Madeira archipelago. It lies at the southern tip of Bugio, the southernmost of the three islands that make up the group of the Desertas (‘deserted islands’).
Agulha (Scandix pecten-veneris)

An annual plant of the family Umbelliferae, frequent in Madeira and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Its fruits end in a very long point or beak, hence the name *agulha* (‘needle’) by which the plant is known, mainly on Porto Santo.
Agulheira

A very simple fishing tackle, usually intended for surface fish or those that swim in mid-water. It consists merely of a line with a hook fixed to its free end, and at the other end a small square board on which the line is wound. It is sometimes used for bottom fish, and a weight is then added near the hook.
Agulheta

The common Madeiran name for *Erodium botrys*, Bert., an annual plant of the family Geraniaceae, easily recognised by its fruits, which bear a very long point or beak that can sometimes reach 12 centimetres.
Celery (Apium graveolens)

An annual or biennial plant of the family Umbelliferae, frequent in Madeira and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Its basal leaves are pinnatisect or 3-sect, with broad segments, and the stem leaves 3-sect or entire; its umbels are sessile or short-stalked, without involucre or involucel, and its fruits are subglobose. The root and fruits of celery are diuretic and stimulant, and the leaves and stalks can be eaten in soup or salad. Garden celery is not found in the archipelago.
Alabama

This famous privateer, in the service of the insurgents of the South of the Republic of the United States of America during the civil war that broke out in that country, called at the port of Funchal and then sheltered off the coast of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) to repair damage, having fled the relentless pursuit of several ships loyal to the Northern government.
Alagoa (landing place)

A landing place on the west side of Bugio (the Desertas), not far from its southern tip. The coast there forms a natural quay sheltered from the north-east breezes, giving easy access to the crumbling cliffs that rise sheer from the sea.
Alagoas
A small plateau in the Serra do Poiso (‘resting place’), a short distance from its mountain shelter.
Álamo

Three trees of the family Salicaceae go by this name in Madeira: *Populus alba*, with leaves white-tomentose on the underside and often palmately lobed; *P. nigra* var. *italica*, with a pyramidal crown and triangular-ovate leaves; and *P. monilifera*, with a broad crown and leaves similar to those of the preceding species. The first, native to Europe, is frequent in Ribeira Brava, Machico, etc.; the second, native to the East, is also called *choupo* and is found in Camacha; the third, from North America, is grown in some squares and *quintas* and is a good shade tree. Poplars are easily propagated from cuttings, and their wood has various uses.
Álamos

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish of Santo António, Funchal. It is the site of the chapel of Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*), built in 1698 by Bartolomeu de Sá Machado; together with its manor house and adjoining lands, it formed the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Água de Mel (‘honey water’), one of the oldest entails (*instituições vinculares*) in Madeira, whose last representative was the 2nd Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). In this locality, at the spot called Til, there were entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*) under the direct administration of a Velosa family.
Alarcão (Dom João de)

Dom João de Alarcão Vellasques Sarmento Osorio was appointed civil governor of Madeira by decree of 5 April 1885 and took up the post on 8 May of the same year. He was deputy for Madeira in the legislative session of 1894–1895. He held high offices, among them that of minister of justice. He died on 13 September 1918. He was the founder of the Sopa Económica (see that entry).
Muster
An old review or parade of armed men, which in Madeira was customarily inspected by the captains-donatary before militia troops were created.
Albafar (Notidanus griseus)

A deep-sea shark of the family Notidanidae, very voracious, of which only the liver is used, to extract so-called fish oil. Some individuals yield as much as 10 gallons of oil. The flesh is rejected as among the worst the shark group can offer.
Hostel and Chapel of St Bartholomew

It adjoined the church of the same name and was founded by Gonçalo Anes de Velosa in 1497 for poor clergy. The first Jesuits stayed there before the College (*Colégio*) was founded. It was visited by the Blessed martyr Friar Inácio de Azevedo. It stood in Rua Direita (‘straight street’), which then ran along the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) to near the present Ponte do Torreão (‘turret bridge’).
See Anes (Gonçalo).
Albergaria (Manuel José Soares de Lobão e)
He was *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) in Madeira, and on 5 December 1823 he sent the Count of Subserra a memorandum on the state of the island and the improvements it needed.
Albers (Joan. Christ.)
A German naturalist who stayed in Madeira from October 1850 to June 1851. Works: *Malacographia maderensis*, Berolini, 1854.
Albertis (Captain Enrico Alberto d')
He collected algae on the island of Madeira in 1882. His collections were studied by Piccone two years later.
Albizzi (Marquis de gli)
Works: *Six mois à Madère* (*Tour du monde*, LVII, 1465 and 1566 *livraisons*); and *Madère, guide pratique pour malades et touristes* (Zurich, 1891).
Álbum Literário
A volume of 200 pages, published in Funchal in 1885, containing various writings in prose and verse.
Álbum Madeirense
Poems by various Madeiran authors, collected by Vieira Portuense. Funchal, 1884, 1 vol., 225 pp.
Albuquerque

This is a noble and ancient family surname on this island. It derives from Dona Sebastiana de Albuquerque, who married Jacinto de Freitas, of the house of the Freitas da Madalena (‘Magdalene’), around 1570. This Dona Sebastiana descended from Dom Afonso Teles de Meneses, settler of the town (*vila*) of Albuquerque in Spain.
Albuquerque (Alexandre de Moura e)
He was appointed governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira on 21 April 1676 and took office on 9 June of the same year.
Albuquerque (Diogo Vieira de Tóvar e)
Works: *Descripção Política e Económica da Ilha da Madeira* (1807). This work was never published.
Albuquerque (João Saldanha de)

In July 1672 he was appointed governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago, and took office on 20 October of the same year. Following accusations made to the government in mainland Portugal, the high court judge (*desembargador*) Manuel Soares Dourado came to Madeira to investigate his conduct.
Albuquerque (Luís da Silva Mousinho de)

This illustrious man of letters and of science, who greatly distinguished himself in politics and in our civil conflicts, was the first governor of this archipelago after the establishment of constitutional government. Under the new administrative division, Madeira became a prefecture (*prefeitura*), and Mousinho de Albuquerque was appointed prefect (*prefeito*) by decree of 30 June 1834, taking office on 6 August of the same year. His administration was short: he left the government of Madeira on 30 September 1835 and departed for Lisbon on 11 November of that year to take up a ministerial portfolio.

In the meantime he left his mark on this island through the impartiality and justice with which he exercised his high office, the reforms he introduced in many public services and the strong support he gave to the founding of an orphanage, which did not last long after his departure from Madeira. He was deputy for this island in the legislatures from 1834 to 1840.
In 1837 he published an interesting memoir entitled *Observações para servirem para a história geológica das ilhas da Madeira, Porto Santo e Desertas*.

Mousinho de Albuquerque came to Madeira by order of Pedro IV in 1832 to occupy this island, then in the hands of the Miguelites. Unable to do so, he landed on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and there made use of his leisure by writing the poem *Ruy o Escudeiro*, which he published some years later. (See Occupation of Porto Santo by the constitutional troops.)
As is well known, Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque died in 1846 of a wound received in the clash at Torres Vedras, during the civil war then ravaging the country.
Albuquerque (Major Joaquim Mousinho de)

He arrived in Funchal on 7 December 1897 from Mozambique, where he had served as royal commissioner, and was given a splendid reception here. In his honour there was a dinner at the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’), music and illuminations in the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’), and a *marche aux flambeaux* organised by the students. He left for Lisbon on 12 December.
Albuquerque (Manuel Saldanha da Gama)

He was appointed governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira on 6 March 1754 and took office on 16 May of the same year. Summoned to Lisbon in February 1757 to hold an important office, he was made Count of Ega and then appointed viceroy of India. Accused of abuses in the exercise of that office, he was imprisoned, and only after his death did a court sentence rehabilitate his memory. He died on 6 December 1771. When he left this island for Lisbon he was replaced in the government of Madeira by the diocesan bishop, Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão, in accordance with the laws then in force.
Artichoke (Cynara Cardunculus subsp. Scolymus)

A plant of the family Compositae, cultivated in some vegetable gardens in Madeira. The receptacle of its very large flower heads and the fleshy part of the bracts of the involucre are eaten cooked and have a pleasant flavour.
Alçadas (special tribunals)

Extraordinary events, generally of a political nature, that were regarded as attacks on the laws or institutions in force led to the creation of special tribunals. Armed with powers that were at times discretionary, these tribunals conducted rigorous inquiries and passed their sentences in the very places where the abuses or the offences had occurred. These improvised but fearsome tribunals came to Madeira several times; on some occasions only magistrates came, with wider powers than ordinary ones, to investigate and judge crimes or events that the central government considered deserving of more effective and exemplary punishment. ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) mentions some of these *alçadas* and several magistrates who came here invested with extraordinary powers to try certain cases, and we have already referred to this in the article Judicial Administration.

It seems that until Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) the sphere of action of these magistrates was not so broad, nor were their powers so unlimited. They were hampered and obstructed by the extraordinary, almost sovereign prerogatives and privileges enjoyed by the donataries, who often imposed their interference despotically, curtailing the jurisdiction of the *alçadas* through violence and harassment. It is true that royal power and other circumstances, as we have already pointed out, had gradually and considerably reduced the power of the captain-donataries. Nevertheless, traditional usages and customs, the old privileges and perhaps above all the distance from the central government encouraged the abuse of authority, which showed itself from time to time.

We shall give a brief account of some of the *alçadas*, or magistrates with equal powers, that came to this archipelago from the time of the Spanish yoke onwards, dwelling in particular on the ominous *alçadas* of 1823 and 1828, which inflicted on us the greatest harassment and the most unspeakable reprisals.

The high court judge (*desembargador*) João Leitão (see that entry), the first governor of Madeira under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640), came with discretionary powers to try those who had shown themselves hostile to Philip II, but we do not know how he carried out this mission or what sentences, if any, he passed. Elsewhere we shall say something about Philippine government on this island, a very interesting period of our history; it is certain, however, that the material for a complete study of the subject is scarce, beginning with the acts of the special judicial commission (alçada) entrusted to Dr João Leitão.

It was again because of demonstrations hostile to the rule of the Philips that the high court judge Francisco Cardoso was sent to Funchal in 1611. The outcome of the special judicial commission with which he came invested is not known. All that is known is that the governor-general of the time was reprimanded by higher authority for meddling in the commission’s powers.

In 1614, and already before then, serious accusations had been made about the poor administration of public affairs on this island, some cases of killing and other grave abuses and scandals. This led Philip III, by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 29 November of that year, to appoint Dr Gonçalo de Sousa, a high court judge of the Casa da Suplicação (supreme court of appeal in Lisbon), to come to Madeira with the powers of a special judicial commission, in order to try and pass sentence on those accusations and punish the criminals. The work of the judicial inquiry (*devassa*) was in vain, because those it targeted fled and went into hiding, escaping the reach of justice.

It seems that these crimes were of the utmost gravity, because, since they had gone unpunished, a new special judicial commission came to this island 13 years later to carry out the sentences passed by the high court judge Gonçalo de Sousa. By royal letter of 13 October 1627 this commission was entrusted to Dr Estêvão Coelho de Meireles, who also came to investigate other crimes committed after 1614. This magistrate had very broad powers; only death sentences had to be confirmed by the Casa da Suplicação. In the proceedings of the judicial inquiry he was assisted by the judge of pious bequests (*juiz dos resíduos*) of this archipelago. We do not know the nature of the sentences passed or whether they were ever carried out.

Shortly after Portugal was freed from the Castilian yoke, the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*), Gaspar Mousinho, was murdered on this island; we know none of the detailed circumstances of this sad event. For this reason the high court judge Jorge da Costa Osório came to Madeira in 1644 to hold a judicial inquiry. He passed sentence, but we do not know what it was.

The popular sedition of 1668, which deposed the governor and captain-general Dom Francisco de Mascarenhas, arrested him and subjected him to the greatest humiliations, brought to this island a special judicial commission invested with extraordinary powers, presided over by Dr João de Meneses Coutinho, which conducted the judicial inquiry in 1669. To avoid needless repetition, we refer the reader to the article Sedition of 1668, where this subject is set out at greater length.

With special jurisdiction, in the form of a special judicial commission, the high court judge Domingos de Matos Cerveira was in Madeira in 1683, having come to investigate the serious accusations made against the superintendent (provedor) and other officials of the royal treasury.

Serious conflicts arose between the diocesan prelate Dom Friar José de Sousa Castelo Branco on one side and the governor and captain-general João da Costa e Ataíde and the superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*) Manuel Mexia Galvão on the other. In 1702 the central government had the case investigated by the high court judge Diogo Sálter de Macedo, who passed sentence, ordering that the superintendent be ‘harshly reprimanded’ in the Council chamber, in the presence of its officers, and then sent away from the city for a period we cannot specify.
Special judicial commission of 1823

The revolution that broke out in Porto on 24 August 1820 established representative government, and the constituent Cortes (Portuguese parliament), which sat from 1821 to 1822, drew up and decreed the so-called Constitution of 1822. In the Madeira archipelago the new government was proclaimed on 28 January 1821. In June 1823 the Cortes were dissolved, the Constitution was revoked and absolute government was restored. On 26 August 1823 the frigate *Amazonas* reached Madeira, carrying the archipelago’s new governor, Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro. He was accompanied by the 7th Infantry Regiment, an artillery detachment and a special judicial commission (alçada) of six magistrates, which had come to investigate the conduct of those who had shown themselves hostile to absolute government and had supported the constitutional government.

The governor and the troops landed on the day of their arrival, but the judges of the special judicial commission, fearing some hostile demonstration by the population, put off their landing until the following day. That night, however, a sudden storm blew up and forced the frigate to weigh anchor; it returned to the landing place three days later.

The special judicial commission consisted of the high court judge (*desembargador*) Dr José de Melo Freire, who acted as president, and the judges Dr José Fernandes da Silva Geraldes Quelhas, Dr Luís de Paula Furtado de Castro do Rio e Mendonça, Dr José Freire de Andrade, Dr Francisco António de Castro and Dr José Peixoto Sarmento de Queiroz. They were assisted by the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) and the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*). They set up their court in the town hall and remained there, conducting their rigorous inquiry, from 30 August until the first days of November 1823.

The wide-ranging judicial inquiry (*devassa*) that they carried out drew in a considerable number of people. Fear gripped public opinion, and many dreaded a severe sentence. Many dozens of witnesses gave evidence, and a long and voluminous case file was compiled. Sentence was pronounced on 26 October: 24 individuals were condemned, almost all of them from the highest ranks of Madeiran society. Various penalties were imposed, most notably penal exile (degredo) and banishment to our overseas possessions.

Among those sentenced by this special judicial commission (alçada) we shall mention the illustrious author of ‘The Zarco Epic’ (*Zargueida*), Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos, condemned to eight years of penal exile in Angola; the eminent physician Nicolau Caetano Betencourt Pita, editor of *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’), the first newspaper published in Funchal, condemned to four years of banishment to the island of Terceira, where he died in 1857; the distinguished lawyer and canon of our Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), Dr Gregório Nazianzeno de Medina e Vasconcelos, condemned to ten years of penal exile in Angola; the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*), Dr Francisco de Assis Saldanha, condemned to imprisonment in São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) in Lisbon; the vicar of Campanário (‘bell tower’), Tomé Pestana Homem de El-Rei; and the captains Joaquim M. Gonçalves, João José de Sá Betencourt and António João Favila, condemned to various penalties; as well as other individuals.
The sentence of the special judicial commission, a lengthy document, was published as a pamphlet and is also printed in the *Archivo de Marinha e Ultramar*, vol. II, pp. 98 ff.
Alçada of 1828

The governor and captain-general of Madeira, José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, was a supporter of constitutional principles and used every means within his reach to promote their establishment here. On 22 June 1828, disregarding the threats of Miguel I’s government, he had the rights of Pedro IV and of his daughter Maria II proclaimed with great official ceremony and various public festivities, which greatly angered the supporters of absolute government. Valdez’s stance led to the dispatch to Madeira of a squadron carrying the new governor, José Maria Monteiro. The squadron attacked the island and surrendered it to the Miguelist forces, as we shall relate elsewhere (see Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelist troops).

By a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 6 August 1828, the central government instructed Francisco Antonio Maciel Monteiro, high court judge (*desembargador*) of the Casa da Suplicação (supreme court of appeal in Lisbon), to come to this island and conduct a rigorous judicial inquiry (*devassa*) into the political events that had taken place here, and to punish severely those who had shown themselves hostile to the principles of absolute government. The clerk (*escrivão*) assigned to this inquiry was not just any court official but Dr Manuel Luciano Abreu de Figueiredo, a high court judge of the High Court of Appeal (*Relação*) of Porto. The two high court judges came with the squadron and landed in Funchal on 25 August.

The work of the judicial inquiry (*devassa*) began on 30 August and continued for several months. By 6 September, that is, 8 days after the special judicial commission (alçada) had begun its judicial investigation, 51 people were already being held in the city gaol, 15 in the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater), 16 in the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*), 4 in the Forte do Ilhéu (Islet Fort), 45 aboard the frigate *Príncipe D. Pedro*, 15 aboard the corvette *Princesa Real*, and 21 clergymen in the ecclesiastical prison (*Aljube*). The number of people in hiding throughout the island was considerable. Some sought refuge in remote places, entirely lacking in comforts, until many were able to find in exile a relative peace from the dangers that threatened them. The governor and captain-general Travassos Valdez, the officers who had come from England and several Madeirans took refuge aboard the British warship, the corvette *Alligator* (see that entry). The special judicial commission indicted about 220 people, some of whom were released because nothing had been proved against them. Of those indicted, 77 were sent as prisoners to Lisbon to have their fate decided there, and they were sentenced to various terms of imprisonment and penal exile (*degredo*).
Alcaide-mor

The donatary of Funchal was the *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) in the captaincy, but the Philippine government entrusted the guarding of the castle to its delegates in the archipelago, who for this reason came to use that title. The powers of these new *alcaides* (town officer with police and jail duties) were laid down by the regulations (*regimento*) of 5 December 1603, registered in the Archive of the Council. The governor-general João Fogaça was the first *alcaide-mor* appointed by that government.

The *alcaides* received the gaol fees (*carceragem*) of prisoners and half of the fines, besides other revenues set out in the regulations. From the abolition of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*) in 1766, the donatary of Funchal became a mere *alcaide-mor* in the captaincy, but his rights and powers were very different from those of the *alcaides-mores* created by the Castilian government.
See Municipalities and Donataries.
Alcaide (brook)
A small brook in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), which flows into the Ocean.
Alcaides

The *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties) of Funchal was appointed by the Council, but while the captaincies existed the appointment could only fall on one of three individuals proposed by the donatary. For many years the donatary was the *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town), and for this reason the officer appointed by the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) was often called the *alcaide-menor* (lesser alcaide, an officer appointed by the council). This officer combined functions that are today divided between the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) and the Police Commissioner. There were *alcaides* in Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava and Caniço at the time when these localities belonged to the municipality of Funchal, but the powers of these officers, who were also appointed by the Council, must have been similar to those of the present-day parish officers (*regedores de paróquia*). The last *alcaide* of Funchal was José Luís Brandão, appointed in 1832.
Alcoforado

It is an old and noble surname, but one long extinct in Madeira. The first to bear it here was Gonçalo Pinto Alcoforado, who came to the island around 1500 and settled in Machico, where he died, having founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) there.
Alcoforado (Francisco)

Squire to Prince Henry the Navigator. He wrote the *Relação do Descobrimento da Ilha da Madeira*, which was never printed and whose original Francisco Manuel de Melo claimed to possess, as a precious jewel. There is a French translation of this work under the following title: *Relation historique de la découverte de l'isle de Madère*, Paris 1671. It was also translated into English under the following title: *The First discovery of the island of Madeira*, London, 1675.
The French translation of 1671 was reproduced in an edition published in Paris some 50 years ago, which by an evident mistake bears the date 1671, when it must be from eighteen-sixty-something.

Inocêncio Francisco da Silva reports another English translation, held in the British Museum and different from the one mentioned above, entitled *An Historical Account of the discovery of the Island of Madeira abridged from the Portuguese original, to which is added an Account of the present state of the Island, in a Letter to a Friend*. London, 1750. This version is attributed, on very good grounds, to Dr Johns.
Alcohol

The alcohol used since early times in treating the traditional wines of Madeira, and which gives them the special flavour and ‘bouquet’ that have characterised them, came mainly from the direct distillation of sugar cane or of the molasses left over from sugar-making. Every 34 kilograms of Bourbon cane yielded one *galão* (Portuguese gallon, about 3.16 litres) of cane spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) at 30 degrees Cartier (an old hydrometer scale of alcoholic strength). This spirit sold at 1,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) the *galão* for use in the wines, many of which were exported abroad. Some alcohol was also extracted from imported molasses, which was subject to a duty of 23 *réis* per kilogram.

When sugar cane disappeared from Madeira, the island began to import alcohol from the Azores, although it continued to bring in a great deal of molasses from abroad for the purpose described. In 1900 Madeira was still importing some 2,000 *ponches* (puncheon, cask of 100–120 gallons, c. 450–550 l) of molasses (the *ponche* holds 100 to 120 *galões*), each of which produced 40 to 50 *galões* of alcohol at 40 degrees (*restilo*). The decree of 24 September 1903 reduced to 6 *réis* the duty of 30 *réis* that the decree of 30 September 1895 had levied on each kilogram of foreign molasses imported for alcohol. The decree of 11 March 1911 maintained this reduction whenever cane alcohol was lacking, or whenever the residues of sugar-making were insufficient to extract the alcohol needed for seasoning the wines. This last decree further laid down that the price of alcohol intended for treating wines could not exceed 2,60 *réis* per centesimal degree and per litre at a temperature of 15 degrees.

Under the regime now in force, only the companies engaged in the sugar and alcohol industry in Madeira are permitted to produce alcohol for winemaking and for pharmaceutical use. The product is distinguished by its exceptional purity.

‘Decree no. 23,847 of 14 May 1934 permits alcohol to be distilled directly from cane juice only when there are no residues from sugar manufacture, or none are expected, to supply the alcohol required. Decree no. 27,912 of 31 July 1937, seeking to strike a fair balance between the prices of sugar cane and those of alcohol and spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), fixed a price of 7.50 escudos for each litre of alcohol sold by the factory to the central warehouse of the customs house (*Alfândega*), which in turn will supply it to wine growers, wine exporters and pharmacies at an increase of 50 centavos per litre.

It should be noted, however, that wine not intended for export is often only partially fortified, and in some cases no alcohol at all is added to it.
