Aldeia da Rainha
A settlement founded in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António da Serra in the reign of Maria I, with families who came from the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It was not long-lived.
See Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’).
Aldonça (beach and landing place)
A small landing place served by a short beach on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Gaula.
Aldromar

The Basque João Martins de Aldromar, who was living in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) in 1500, is the first person recorded as having borne this surname in Madeira. It seems to us that the surname is now extinct in this archipelago.
Alealdador
An office created by Manuel I. Its holder was a kind of judge in matters concerning sugar. He had under his orders the assessors of cane fields and the assessors of sugar.
Alecrim da Serra (Thymus caespititius)
A woody, prostrate plant of the mint family (Labiatae), very common on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’). It has almost linear leaves and pink corollas, occasionally white.
Alecrim de Nossa Senhora (Eriocephalus sericeus)

A small shrub of the daisy family (Compositae), cultivated in Madeira. It is native to the Cape of Good Hope, and its branches, furnished with linear leaves that are sometimes three-cleft, are used to prepare aromatic baths.
Rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis)

A shrub of the mint family (Labiatae), widely grown in Madeiran gardens. It is highly aromatic, and an infusion of its leaves is much used in baths and poultices; taken internally, it can also serve to combat loss of appetite, coughs and chlorosis. Among poor people it is customary to burn sprigs of rosemary to freshen the air in their homes.
Alecrins

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António in Funchal, where there once stood the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Quietação (Our Lady of Quietude), built in 1670 by Lourenço de Matos Coutinho. He made it the seat of the Alecrins (‘rosemary bushes’) entailed estate (*morgadio*), instituted in 1577. Today Dr Rui Betencourt da Câmara is the representative of this entailed house (*casa vinculada*).
Alegra-campo (Semele androgyna

). A shrub of the lily family (Liliaceae), subfamily Asparagoideae, widely grown in the *quintas* and gardens of Madeira and found growing wild in some ravines of the interior. Its long branches, abundantly furnished with branchlets bearing large ovate, ovate-lanceolate or lanceolate cladodes, are highly ornamental. They are used to decorate the walls of churches at religious festivals, and for some other purposes as well. The small-leaved *alegra-campo* is *Asparagus asparagoides*, a plant native to the Cape of Good Hope and belonging to the same family and subfamily.
Alegria

In this locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Roque (‘St Roch’) in Funchal stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Alegria (Our Lady of Joy), founded in 1609 by Francisco de Abreu. It was incorporated into the Torre Bela house, to which it still belongs today.
Alemanio Fino
He wrote a work with the following title: *Descritione dell Isola d'illa Madera scrita nella lingua latina del Conte Giulio Landi*, Piacenza, 1574.
Alemão (Henrique)

The surname Alemão, now extinct, ‘derives’, says the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), following the genealogies, ‘from Henrique Alemão, a legendary figure from the earliest days of the colonisation of this island of Madeira. It was said of him that he was a Polish prince and that, after the battle of Varna was lost in 1444 by Władysław IV against Murad II, he vowed to go on pilgrimage to the Holy Land and was dubbed a knight of St Catherine of Mount Sinai. When he came to the island of Madeira, João Gonçalves Zarco granted him, at the locality (*sítio*) later called Madalena do Mar, a large tract of land as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), by a charter confirmed by Prince Henry the Navigator on 29 April 1457 and by Afonso V on 18 May of the same year. Henrique Alemão did indeed found a large settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) there, with a chapel dedicated to St Mary Magdalene, from which the place took its name. He married Senhorina Anes and died a dreadful death, crushed by a landslide (*quebrada*) that fell from Cabo Girão onto the boat in which he was travelling from the city of Funchal to Madalena. His widow later married João Rodrigues de Freitas. Even now there is, above the town of Ponta do Sol, the Fajã do Alemão, which the common people corruptly call “do Limão”.’
Alencastre (Dona Mariana de Vasconcelos e Câmara)

She was donatary of Funchal in 1666 and styled herself Marchioness and Countess of Castelo Melhor and of Vila Nova da Calheta, Lady of the towns (*vilas*) of Figueiró and Pedrógão Grande, and Governor of Justice and the Exchequer of the Island of Madeira and the city of Funchal. She married João Rodrigues de Vasconcelos, 2nd Count of Castelo Melhor.
See Castelo Melhor.
Alexander (Prince)

Prince Alexander of the Netherlands arrived in Madeira aboard the Dutch frigate *Príncipe de Orange* on 20 November 1847. He died here at Tomaz Burnett’s *quinta* (country estate) in Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) on 20 February 1848. On 3 April of the same year his body was taken aboard the Dutch steamer *Phoenix*, which carried it to Holland.
Lettuce (Lactuca sativa)

A liguliflorous composite widely grown in Madeiran kitchen gardens. The juice obtained from transverse incisions made in lettuce stems at flowering time is known in pharmacies as lactucarium, and in some cases it can be used as a substitute for opium. Distilled lettuce water is used as a vehicle for certain calming potions.
Customs houses

The rapid commercial and agricultural growth that Madeira enjoyed soon after its discovery quickly led to the establishment of customs houses or revenue posts in several settlements of the archipelago, whose importance and traffic made their creation a necessity.

Around the middle of the second quarter of the 15th century the first customs duties or levies began to be collected in Funchal, although the customs house itself was not created until the beginning of the last quarter of that century. Collection was entrusted to an *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper), who gathered the taxes of the Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*). He had four assistants, then known as king’s men (*homens del-rei*), each of whom received an annual salary of 20,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

The instrument that established the Funchal customs house is dated 15 March 1477, which makes it the oldest public department of the whole archipelago. It was Dona Beatriz, mother of Dom Manuel, Duke of Beja and Grand Master of the Order of Christ, to which this island belonged, who, as her son’s guardian and in view of the remarkable growth of what was then the town (*vila*) of Funchal, decided to create the customs house. We do not know the terms on which it was created, as regards the scope of its fiscal powers, its staff and operation, or its import and export revenues. We do know that, to carry out the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 15 March 1477, the Infanta Dona Beatriz sent her accountant Luís de Atouguia to this island with the necessary powers and instructions to rent suitable premises, appoint the essential staff and organise the various services needed for the customs house to function properly. We also know that the *almoxarife* and the four king’s men were incorporated into its staff.

We have little information on this revenue office in the early days after its creation. We know only that in 1481, four years after it began to operate, the inhabitants of Funchal were exempted from paying the duty levied on certain goods.

The most important office was that of judge, and the first to hold it was Francisco Álvares, appointed in 1494. In a year we cannot determine precisely, this office became that of superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*) for the whole archipelago, or was held jointly with it, and it was one of the most important posts then existing on this island. The high court judge (*desembargador*) Dr João Leitão (see that entry), the first governor-general sent to this archipelago by the Philippine government, took up the office of superintendent of the royal treasury when he left that post in 1582, under the royal decree (alvará régio) of 5 January 1582. In 1597 Philip II combined the office of superintendent with that of *corregedor* (royal district magistrate), and the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) André Lobo was then appointed to it. By 1650 the two offices were once again being held separately.

By royal decree of 6 April 1775, Joseph I abolished the office of superintendent of the royal treasury and replaced it with the Royal Treasury Board (*Junta da Real Fazenda*). At the same time the post of customs judge (*juiz da alfândega*, head of the customs house) was established, and Domingo Afonso Barroso, who had previously served as superintendent, was appointed to it.

We give below the complete list of the judges of our customs house, from Francisco Álvares, mentioned above, to Domingo Afonso Barroso, just named, with the dates of their respective appointments. They are: Francisco Álvares (1494), João Rodrigues Parada (1498), João Leite (1508), Cristóvão Esmeraldo (1550), Pedro Fernandes (1555), Lourenço Correia (1559), Diogo Luís (1560), Leoniz Simões (1563), Luís Preto (1567), Pedro de Castilho (1577), António de Carvalho (1579), João Leitão (1582), Domingos Vaz (1585), António de Melo (1590), Bernardo Fernandes Tinoco (1596), André Lobo (1597), Baltazar Fróis (1599), Manuel Araújo de Carvalho (1606), António Gomes Rodovalho (1615), António Antunes Leite (1618), Luís da Cunha (1621), Manuel Dias de Andrade (1628), Manuel Rodrigues Pereira (1634), João Rodrigues de Teive (1638), Manuel Vieira Cardoso (1639), Marcos Correia de Mesquita (1643), Francisco de Andrade (1647), Ambrósio Vieira de Andrade (1683), Manuel Mexias Galvão (1700), Francisco Torres Pinheiro (1703), Luís de França Pimentel (1707), João de Aguiar (1710), José de Sequeira (1715), José Rebelo de Vadre (1727), Jorge Vieira de Andrade (1731), Manuel Teixeira de Castro (1745), Domingos Afonso Barroso (1757–1768).

We know of other offices, but not the dates on which they were created. By 1752 there was already the post of doorkeeper, then an office of some importance, to which that of bookkeeper was attached. The latter was separated from it in 1741 and has formed a separate post ever since. The post of clerk of the Mesa Grande (*escrivão da Mesa Grande*, the main customs table) already existed in 1526, and that of first factor (*feitor*) in 1592. There were also the posts of clerk of the marks, sealer, harbour master of the Ribeira and captain of the frigate, second clerk of the Mesa Grande, ship’s mooring man, collector of the sugar fifth (*quintador do açúcar*) and others besides. From the end of the 15th century it had eight guards, whose number was raised to 12 in 1763.

‘We hold it beyond doubt,’ says the illustrious annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), ‘that tax farming was the first system of fiscal collection adopted in these islands, and consequently overseas. We are persuaded of this not only by the above-mentioned letter of 15 March 1477, which twice refers to tax farmers – once in relation to the court (*juízo*) hearing their cases, and once so that they should not oppress the inhabitants – but also by the explicit references to contracts of this kind found in the first book of the council sessions (*vereações*) of the Council of Funchal (1471 and 1472): for the sugar duties, whose contractors at the time were the Genoese Micer Leão, Martim Annes, Álvaro Esteves and Fernão Nunes; for the tithe on timber, farmed by João Garcia; for wheat, which Martim Luís held by agreement; for the revenue from green produce; and others.’

This system of tax farming continued, albeit with some variations, even after the reform carried out by Manuel I at the beginning of the 16th century. The Funchal customs house (*Alfândega do Funchal*) became the main centre for collecting the dues of the Royal Treasury (*Real Fazenda*): other taxes and contributions were collected there that had until then been gathered by various official bodies and that were not strictly customs duties in the sense in which we understand them today, as can be seen in the charter (foral) granted by Manuel I to the city of Funchal and the towns of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Calheta (‘small cove’) on 6 August 1515.

We do not know how long this system of farming out the duties collected at the customs house lasted, but we believe it continued for a long time, although within that period collection was on several occasions carried out directly by the customs officials or by the collectors of the royal revenues. Thus we have seen somewhere that in 1772 Inácio Pedro Quintela ‘won the bid for the customs revenues for a term of six years, for forty *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis), and the same happened on other occasions.

The royal decree (alvará régio) of 15 January 1512 considerably increased the business of the Funchal customs house and markedly curtailed that of the other customs houses, for it expressly prohibited the export of sugar – then the most important and valuable product of the whole island – except through the customs house of this city. The reason for this prohibition is clearly stated in the said royal letter (*carta régia*): ‘...we suffer much loss, and our dues are stolen and concealed because goods are cleared in many remote places and by many officials, and it is not right that we should lose by it...’

Only a lengthy study – for which we have no time to spare, and for which the essential material is also lacking – could give a detailed picture of the vicissitudes our customs house has undergone in its internal workings, the manner of collecting its revenues, the way these were levied on goods, etc., above all in the period before the introduction of constitutional government, when legislation was not uniform throughout the country. Nevertheless, we transcribe the following interesting passage, which we found in the manuscript of Father António Gomes Neto, which Dr Álvaro de Azevedo cites from time to time in his notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’:

‘The superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*), Manuel Mexias Galvão, by his public notice (*edital*) of 18 July 1700, in consequence of the royal orders and other provisions recorded in Book 9, fol. 392, ordered that the loading and unloading of any goods should take place beside the redoubt (*reduto*) of the Customs House, on pain (*pena*) of forfeiting all goods landed at any other locality (*sítio*). That no person of whatever quality, estate or condition might go aboard ships with goods without the superintendent’s licence, on pain of having the boat burnt and paying a fine of six thousand réis, in gaol (*cadeia*), to the Royal Treasury, besides the penalty of penal exile (degredo) imposed by the law of 12 August 1722, and the forfeiture of half their property, Book 15, fol. 61 v., and the ordinances of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), Book 5, fol. 714, one third going to the harbour constable (*alcaide do mar*) or the informer. That the same precautions should be observed with respect to the launches of foreign ships once they had made their entry at the health office, in accordance also with the letter of the Council of Funchal of 12 February 1742, Book 8, fol. 103, the respective consuls being charged with warning those they represented, so that they could not plead ignorance and the guards could carry out their duties. It also forbids boatmen to carry cargo or goods to or from ships other than in the capstan (*cabrestante*) boats or in those appointed by the master of the pebble beach (calhau), and forbids them to go to or come from ships after nightfall. The customs factors are responsible for taking every care and vigilance in placing the guards in the manner laid down in the charter, and the said guards may not leave the ships until these have been unloaded and inspected for departure, on pain, if not found aboard, of being arrested and held until His Majesty’s royal grant (*mercê*). Guards on the establishment are to be punished with 15 days in gaol and dismissed for ever; those not on the establishment, and both alike if not found aboard, shall pay from their property for the damage to the Royal Treasury resulting from any embezzlement, Book 9, fol. 392’.

On various occasions the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of Funchal, claiming supposed privileges, sought to interfere in matters that fell exclusively within the competence (special judicial commission, alçada) of the superintendent and the other customs officials. In 1742 it was compelled by royal order to acknowledge ‘the incompetence of its authority to go or send aboard without the superintendent’s licence, and to return to the customs house the provisions it had ordered to be taken from on board’.

The governors-general and captains-general of the archipelago also at times attempted to intervene officially in customs matters, and various royal provisions were issued, chiefly by John IV, forbidding the higher authorities of this island to meddle in affairs of this kind. Immediately after the constitutional system was established here, several government measures were taken concerning our customs house. The decree of 23 June 1834 established the Funchal customs house on the same terms as those of the mainland; the law of 20 February 1835 introduced notable changes in its working and staff; and the decree of 14 June 1836 fixed the number and salaries of its employees.

Up to the end of the first half of the 19th century, the government and legislative measures published concerning our customs house included the ministerial order (*portaria*) of 13 January 1837, the decree of 14 May 1837, the ministerial order of 8 May 1837, the three decrees of 30 June 1837, the ministerial order of 30 June 1837, the ministerial order of 25 August 1837, the ministerial order of 12 January 1838, the ministerial order of 14 May 1838, the ministerial order of 4 November 1838, the ministerial order of 2 July 1839, the laws of 2, 16 and 21 August 1839, the decrees of 4 and 24 May 1842, the decree of 27 May 1843, the ministerial orders of 25 and 26 September 1843 and the ministerial order of 29 November 1849.

The royal letter (*carta régia*) of 15 March 1477 that created the Funchal customs house directed that a suitable house be rented for the purpose. It is not known precisely, however, where this fiscal house was first established. It has been claimed, and the illustrious annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ echoed the claim, that the Funchal customs house was first installed in Rua do Esmeraldo, in the building known as the granary of the pool, or in its immediate vicinity. It is also stated elsewhere, as information drawn from local tradition, that the customs house was set up somewhere in the area of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). This is not at all surprising, and it is even very likely that this was so. The first nucleus of population settled mainly to the east of the stream later called Ribeira de João Gomes, and it was there that the young settlement of Funchal grew most. This was despite the fact that the discoverer and first donatary had made his residence on the heights of Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’), which certainly would not yet have borne that name.

It also appears that the customs house operated in a house in Rua Direita (‘straight street’), which was one of the most important streets of old Funchal. A book of the cathedral chapter of our Cathedral, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), records a deed of sale, dated 18 May 1557, of ‘the houses of master Gabriel, which now belong to Duarte Rodrigues, held in quit-rent from the Fabric of the Sé, situated in Rua Direita, which run down to the sea and were the old customs house’.

It is even possible that the customs department was housed successively in the places mentioned, although the chronological order in which these moves may have taken place is unknown. ‘The customs house’, says Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘which Manuel I ordered to be built is the one that still exists in Funchal today; there are good reasons to prove it. The site that Gaspar Frutuoso, in ‘Longing for the Homeland’, gives for the Manueline building is the same as that of the present building; the interior arcades and doorways still bear the indelible architectural stamp of the period; and at the top of one of these doorways is the following inscription:
In the year 1620 this door was moved here

These words clearly show that the original building was much older than the year 1620. And, finally, as can be seen from volume VI, fol. 60, of the Archive of the Funchal Council, John IV ordered in the year 1644 that a redoubt be built there, to serve as a platform in view of the distance between the one fortress and the other, and that a gate be opened for the loading and unloading of goods; and this redoubt and gate were built, and they stand beside the present customs house, authenticated by the following inscription, which can be read engraved above the outer gate that opens onto Rua dos Mercadores:

Manuel de Sousa Meneses, being governor and captain-general of this island of Madeira, had this redoubt and its gates built by order of His Majesty in the year 1645, the superintendent being Manuel Vieira Cardoso
There is, therefore, no doubt whatever that the old building and the existing one are the same.’

The building, which could be called grand for the time and place in which it was built, has undergone various alterations and adaptations to meet the ever-growing needs of the customs establishment. It nevertheless keeps the characteristic stamp of the original Manueline construction, above all in some interior doorways and in the purity of its pointed-arch lines. Its principal floor was the part of the original building that underwent the most thorough alterations. The Order of the Treasury Council of 30 July 1733 called for major works there, and the upper part of the building facing Rua da Alfândega and the inner courtyard, with its adjoining staircase, dates from this time. In 1590 Gaspar Frutuoso said of this building: ‘the customs house, more prosperous and with better offices than that of the city of Lisbon, well walled in dressed stone (*cantaria*), and closed off from the land and from the sea, which lies beside it and often beats against it when there is a swell’.

The great earthquake that struck this island (see Earthquakes) on 1 April 1748 caused considerable damage to the customs buildings, which a contemporary account of the event describes as follows: ‘Although its walls are very strong, thirty-two cracks can be seen in them, one from top to bottom and others running across; some corners have come apart, wall plates have shifted from their places and everything else is in need of prompt repair...’

The principal floor of this building once served as the residence of the superintendents, and not long ago some public departments were still housed there. The civil government building and its offices remained and functioned there for a long time, until they were moved in 1890 to a house in Rua de João Gago.

In front of the customs building and very close to it, a small fort was built in 1644, in accordance with the plan drawn up for the maritime defence of the city. The wall that still stands there today is the only remaining trace of the old fort, or Reducto da Alfândega (Customs Redoubt), as it was then called.

The redoubt had a gate opening onto the customs courtyard, and the royal decree (*alvará régio*) of 11 August 1644 laid down that through it ‘all goods should enter, those landed at any other place being deemed forfeit’.

Beside the building there was, and still is, a small chapel, now put to uses other than those for which it was built. It was dedicated to St Anthony and was built around 1714 by the superintendent and judge of the customs house, Dr João de Aguiar. Above the portico of this chapel can be read the Latin inscription *Ad salem sol*, which has given rise to various translations and has been interpreted in different ways.

It is impossible for us to give here a complete account of the revenue of the Funchal customs house and of the other customs houses of the archipelago over successive periods from their creation to the present day, and we must confine ourselves to brief, scattered notes relating to periods very far apart from one another. Thus a ‘point [statement] taken of the revenue of the customs houses of the two captaincies of this island and of Porto Santo from the year 1581 to 1587’, cited by Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, shows that over that seven-year period the combined revenue of the customs houses was, respectively, 28,925,275, 26,619,769, 26,013,590, 29,592,155, 28,277,791, 31,206,013 and 16,368,257 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). A narrative contemporary with the earthquake of 1748 states that the customs house ‘… yields, one year with another, 27 *contos de réis* in export duties and 11 *contos* in import duties, because foodstuffs are exempt by virtue of a monopoly lease (*contracto*) concluded between His Majesty and the People of this Island’.
The revenue of our customs house was 228 and 230 *contos* in 1812 and 1813 respectively. In the financial years from 1828–1829 to 1839–1840 it yielded, in *réis*:

Nevertheless, the revenue of 21,252,161.84 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) for the calendar year 1932 (devaluation coefficient 24.45) corresponds to 869,209.97 gold escudos (*escudos ouro*: escudos at their pre-war value; 1 gold escudo = 24.45 escudos of 1932), a revenue never reached before the Great War.

The customs revenue given above does not include the municipal taxes collected together with the State’s customs duties. Below we give a statement of the taxes collected over the last fifteen years at our customs house and intended solely for distribution among the eleven Municipal Councils of the district.

The revenue of the Funchal customs house exceeds the combined revenue of the three Azorean customs houses. Over the last 30 years the directors of our customs house have been the following customs officials: José Pais de Vasconcelos, head of the Funchal customs delegation, who took office on 22 November 1889; Guilherme Read Cabral, who, when the Funchal customs delegation was abolished and raised to the rank of customs house by decree of 21 April 1892, took office as director on 7 May 1892; Carlos Maria de Vasconcelos Sobral, who took office on 9 November 1895; Francisco Xavier Teixeira, who took office on 26 April 1907; António Augusto Curson, who took office on 3 August 1908; Afonso Vieira de Andrade, who took office on 6 September 1911; and Adolfo João Sarmento Figueiredo, who took office on 23 October 1916.

We are aware that the following pamphlets have been published on the customs house of this city or on matters closely related to it: *Moção feita na Sociedade Patriótica Madeirense por um de seus membros*, Lisbon, 1835, 16 pp.; *Regulamento dos guardas da Alfândega do Funchal*, Funchal, 1856, 10 pp.; *Recurso interposto para o Illmo e Ex.mo Ministro e Secretario de Estado dos Negócios da Fazenda em Lisboa por Blandy & C1 negociantes estabelecidos no Funchal como agentes da companhia dos paquetes a vapor denominada African Steam Ship Company na ilha da Madeira da decisão proferida pelo Sr. director da alfândega da dita cidade em 17 de Abril de 1866, na qual multou o capitão do vapor Lagos...*, Funchal, 1866, 28 pp.; *Regulamento da cobrança fiscalização do imposto indirecto municipal lançado sobre os artigos importados pela Alfândega do Funchal*, Funchal, 1878, 8 pp.; *Relatório apresentado pela direcção da Associação Comercial do Funchal da sua gerência no anno findo em 30 de Junho de 1883*, Funchal, 1884, 24 pp.; *Breves considerações sobre as Alfândegas*, by ‘um curioso’, 1884, 53 pp., with no place of printing given; *A Madeira e as Canárias*, by João Augusto de Ornelas, Funchal, 1884, 28 pp.; *Representação da Câmara Municipal da cidade do Funchal, sobre diversas medidas tendentes a animar a navegação...dos paquetes transatlânticos*, Funchal, 1884, 4 pp.; *Tabella do lançamento de contribuições Municipais indirectas cobradas na alfândega do Funchal*, Funchal, 1896, 38 pp., several pamphlets with the same title having been published for various years; *Representação da Câmara Municipal do Funchal sobre a importação do vinho na Russia*, Funchal, 1906, 7 pp.

A volume has been published every year under the title *Ordens da Direcção da Alfândega do Funchal*, containing the various service orders issued by the director of that customs establishment, together with other data and information of great importance for the orderly running of the house. Many volumes have already appeared, the first covering the year 1907.

In 1824 António Marcelino Gomes, unloading clerk (*escrivão da descarga*) of the customs house, wrote a *Projecto de Regulamento da alfândega da ilha da Madeira*, which he presented to John VI but which was never published.
Machico customs house

Like the customs houses of Funchal and Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), it was created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 15 March 1477. We have already noted that although this customs house was located at the seat of the captaincy, it had less traffic and less importance than that of Santa Cruz, perhaps because more sugar was produced in Santa Cruz and the neighbouring settlements than in Machico.

We do not know when it began to operate, and we have found few references to the number of its staff. In 1486 the Machico customs house was again ordered to operate, either because it had not yet been set up or because the collection of the duties levied there had been interrupted. We do know, however, that it had a judge, the first to hold this office being António Alves Uzadamar, in 1557, and the posts of *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper) and harbour bailiff (*alcaide de mar*), created in 1550.

Even after it was abolished, the remains of the building that had housed it survived for many years in the town (*vila*) of Machico. Until very recently a stretch of wall, blackened by time, could still be seen in Rua da Árvore. A small pointed doorway opened in it, already half buried because the bed of the adjoining street had been raised. It was the only remaining trace of the old customs house and also the only example there of Manueline architecture, which has been disappearing throughout the island. These ruins ought to have been preserved with reverent care. The municipality of Machico either would not or could not preserve them, and in 1916 it allowed the demolition hammer to bring them vandalously to the ground. They formed an eloquent commemorative pillar (padrão) of the former prosperity of the town and captaincy of Machico, and no cultivated visitor who went there would fail to look with devoted interest at that strip of black wall and at the small pointed doorway that opened in it, in the reddish *pedra mole* (‘soft stone’: soft yellowish tuff and its soil) of the old Madeiran buildings.
Santa Cruz customs house

The importance and commercial traffic of the settlement of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) earned it a customs house long before it was raised to the rank of town (*vila*). Thus we find that the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 15 March 1477 – that is, 38 years before the municipality was created – ordered a revenue house to be established there for collecting taxes and royal dues. We do not know whether it began to operate immediately; the oldest document concerning it that we know of dates from 1549.

From the many references to it that we have found, from the number and standing of its posts, and also from the registers of various documents entered in the books of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) of Funchal, we can see that the customs house of Santa Cruz was more important and busier than that of Machico, even though the latter stood at the seat of the captaincy.

This revenue house had the posts of judge, *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper), clerk (*escrivão*), factor (*feitor*), doorkeeper, harbour constable (*alcaide do mar*) and four guards. Not all these posts were created when it was established, but at long intervals, as the needs of the service perhaps required. The oldest post must have been that of *almoxarife*, but the only record we know of is the warrant of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 12 March 1614, which appointed António Pimentel to that post, with the privilege that ‘he be given the houses of the Customs House to live in and to store His Majesty’s royal fifth on sugar (quintos do açúcar)’.

The post of judge, which was the highest in rank, was created by royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 August 1563, and Tomé Alves was appointed to it. The royal decree of 11 August 1644 ordered that the ‘customs judge of Santa Cruz should serve as superintendent of the Funchal customs house whenever that superintendent was unable to act, and not the clerks of the Main Board’.

The post of clerk already existed in 1551 and that of doorkeeper in 1550, but the dates of their creation are unknown. The office of factor was established by the royal letter of 10 May 1549, and Domingos Fernandes was the first to be appointed to it. The post of harbour constable, which already existed in 1600, was abolished in 1744.

When the customs house was established, four posts of guard were created. In 1682, by order of the Council of Finance (*Conselho de Fazenda*), these guards were transferred to serve in the Funchal customs house.

We do not know when the customs house of Santa Cruz was abolished. We know only of a petition made in 1768 by António João Nunes Pereira, requesting ownership of the office of factor of this customs house, by then already abolished, so that he might exercise the post in the Funchal customs house. The abolition cannot have taken place very long before 1768, and António João Nunes Pereira was perhaps a descendant and heir of the last holder of that office. In 1502 several residents of Funchal had requested the abolition of the customs houses of Santa Cruz and Machico, but their petition was rejected.

The building of the Santa Cruz customs house must have been demolished towards the end of the second quarter of the 19th century. Some people still alive today remember it. It stood in the centre of the town, at the beginning of the street that now bears the name of Dr Pinga and leads to the public promenade. It had a certain air of grandeur and was built in the Manueline style of the period, with pointed-arch windows and doors, in every respect similar to those of the building of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). It was a pity that it was not preserved with the respect owed to the venerable relics of the past. It was a monument bearing witness to the prosperity of the old town of Santa Cruz, which lost its former importance as Funchal grew and prospered.
Porto Santo customs house

As the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) judiciously observes, the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) had a station or revenue guard post (*posto fiscal*) rather than a customs house in the proper sense. We do not know the date of its creation, but it already existed in 1556, because the royal decree (alvará régio) of 8 April of that year appointed Gaspar Calaça to the post of *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper), the most important office of that customs house, with an annual salary of two thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, two *moios* of wheat and two *pipas* of wine. The last appointment of an *almoxarife* of which we have record is that of Diogo Luís Drumond, made by the royal decree of 22 July 1768. The office of clerk (*escrivão*) predates 1556, for in that year Diogo Delgado was appointed to it on the death of his predecessor, Rodrigo Anes. There was also the post of harbour constable (*alcaide do mar*), created well before 1642. We do not know when the Porto Santo customs house ceased to exist.

Revenue guard posts. Revenue guard posts were ordered to be set up at the landing places of Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Madalena do Mar and Calheta for the collection of certain duties, but we do not know whether they were ever actually created or how they operated.

‘In the ports of this archipelago, says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, there were also the *vigias*, that is, stations at once military and fiscal, which kept watch over the sea, the coasts and the beaches in order to raise the alarm against corsairs or any other enemy ships, and to prevent smuggling. The watches were kept by the local people, in small strong houses built on purpose to withstand the sea and prevent surprise attacks. King Sebastian gave them regulations (*regimento*) in 1567, which are registered in volume V, fol. 105, of the Archive of the Funchal Council, and by a royal decree of 1569 he ordered that no one “should be exempt from this service”.’
Carob tree (Ceratonia siliqua, L.)

A tree of the family Leguminosae, subfamily Caesalpinioideae, grown in a few places on the outskirts of Funchal. Its flowers are dioecious, and its fruits have a slightly laxative pulp that is sweet and pleasant-tasting. Madeiran carobs are of poor quality and have little pulp. The carob tree is also found on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Pellitory-of-the-wall (Parietaria officinalis)

A perennial plant, with stems sometimes woody at the base and pubescent leaves that are ovate or lanceolate, tapering or rounded at the base. It is common on walls, rocks and stony places, and contains a notable quantity of potassium nitrate. An infusion of the leaves and tender stems of this plant is widely used in Madeira against bleeding caused by haemorrhoidal complaints.
Alfinetes de Senhora
See Artemija.
Splendid alfonsino (Beryx splendens)
A teleost fish of the family Berycidae, which frequently appears at market. It is of excellent quality.
Alfôrra

This name is given to a *Dactylopius* and a *Tetrachynus* that appear on green plants, and to a mite that lives mainly on dry wheat straw. This last species causes itching when it gets under the skin.
Algae

In Madeira, Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) 373 species of algae have been found to date, 211 of which belong to the diatom group (Diatomaceae). Of the remaining 162 species, 127 are marine and 35 live in streams, tanks, damp places and levadas (irrigation channels); for many of them only the names of their genera are known. *Enteromorpha compressa* is extremely common on the stones uncovered at low tide, and *Ulva Lactuca*, *Padina Pavonia*, *Cystoseira ericoides*, etc., are also rare at certain points of the coast that are covered or washed by the sea.

*Laminaria saccharina*, which grows to a large size, occurs near Ponta de São Lourenço, where *Sargassum bacciferam* and two species of the genus *Liagora*, one of them *L. pulverulenta*, have also been found.
*Corallina officinalis*, *Jannia rubens*, *Gelidium corneum* and other Rhodophyceae are not rare at Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) and at some points on the south coast.

In the streams, levadas and pools of Madeira a species of *Oedogonium* (perhaps *O. capilliforme*) is abundant, and on damp rocks and near waterfalls the globular *Nostoc verrucosum* is common, sometimes associated with *Anabaena flos-asquae* and other Myxophyceae.

In the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’), under the bridge at Curral dos Romeiros (‘pilgrims’ fold’), lives the very rare *Lemanea fluviatilis*, a filamentous, leathery alga, and in the nearby pools the following Desmidiaceae have been found: *Staurastrum muticum*, *Cosmarium Botrytis*, *C. margaritiferum* and *Closterium acerosum*. The Seminary Museum (Museu do Seminário) holds a collection of marine algae identified by Professor Ernst Schmitz of the University of Greifswald, and in 1910 the Revd Schodduyn, of Pas-de-Calais, identified several freshwater algae sent to him by the present author.
See Borge, Gain, Piccone and Zimmermann.
Cotton plant

The cultivation of *Gossypium herbaceum* was attempted in Madeira at the beginning of the 19th century. In an official letter of 20 March 1802, the then minister Dom Rodrigo de Sousa Coutinho informed the captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) Dom José Manuel da Câmara that the Prince Regent, the future John VI, had learnt with great satisfaction of the progress of this crop on the island. In 1863 fresh cotton seed was brought to Madeira, but few farmers took an interest in growing the plant at that time. *Gossypium arboreum* also thrives in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira, but both this species and *G. herbaceum* now appear to be completely extinct on the island.
Garlic

Garlic belongs to the family Liliaceae, and the best-known kinds in Madeira are common garlic (*Allium sativum*), leek-garlic (*A. ampeloprasum*) and wild or American garlic (*Nothoscordum inodorum*). In common garlic the bulb is made up of bulblets (cloves) enclosed in a common skin. This species is widely grown in Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) for culinary purposes, and it has diuretic, vermifuge and antiseptic properties. Wild garlic, native to subtropical America, is a plant that spreads with extreme ease both by its bulbs and by its seeds.
Madeiran Alliance

The Madeiran Alliance insurance company (*Companhia de Seguros Aliança Madeirense*) was founded by a deed of 2 April 1891 with a capital of 200,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), divided into 2,000 shares of 100,000 *réis* each. Its principal promoters on this island were João Joaquim Mendes, now deceased, and Júlio César de Nóbrega Pereira.

It was formed exclusively with Madeiran capital belonging to merchants, landowners, industrialists, etc. Its first Board of Directors consisted of João Joaquim Mendes, João Bernardino Gomes and Júlio César de Nóbrega Pereira, and its first Supervisory Board of Luís Gomes da Conceição, now deceased, Alfredo Guilherme Rodrigues and the Viscount of Vale Paraíso. Its first bookkeeper was the late João Onofre da Gama.

By a deed of 15 May 1893 the share capital was raised from 200,000,000 *réis* to 300,000,000 *réis*, divided into 3,000 shares of 100,000 *réis* each, in accordance with the resolution of the General Meeting of 7 April of the same year.

The Company at present has a reserve fund of 831,801.40 escudos, and enjoys the highest reputation both in Madeira, where it has its head office, and in mainland Portugal. There it has been warmly praised by some of the most eminent figures in the insurance business, notably by the late actuary and director of the important insurance company ‘A Nacional’, Fernando de Brederode, a former Minister of Labour regarded as one of the greatest authorities in the field. The current chairman of the General Meeting is Manuel Maria Ribeiro; the Board of Directors consists of Dr Juvenal Henriques de Araújo and Tristão Pedro Bettencourt da Câmara, and the Supervisory Board of Francisco Dias Tavares, Vicente Ângelo Gomes da Silva and Augusto Sérvulo Ferreira. Its present bookkeeper is Abel Caires Soares.
In 1935, in accordance with the resolutions passed at the general meetings of 20 February 1931 and 18 March 1932, the Company carried out a large-scale operation to pay up its shares in full.
Alincourt (Francisco de)

He was an engineer sergeant-major (*sargento-mor engenheiro*, a field-officer rank equivalent to major), a professed knight of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) and a professor at the Royal Academy. He drew up the general map of Madeira in 1769, and in the same year he went to Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) to study the needs of that island, on which he wrote a dissertation. Arrested in 1770 as a freemason on the orders of the governor João António de Sá Pereira, he was released shortly afterwards and restored to his post under instructions sent by the Marquis of Pombal to his representative on this island.
Alindres
See Figueira do Inferno.
Aljube

When churchmen had their own separate jurisdiction, they also had their own prisons or special gaol, known as the ecclesiastical prison (*Aljube*). The old Aljube of Funchal stood in the area bounded by the Travessa da Sacristia (‘sacristy lane’), Rua de João Gago and Rua do Aljube. The post of gaoler (*aljubeiro*) of the Aljube of this city was created by King Sebastian by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 6 July 1562. The founding of the Aljube must date from this period or a little before it, and it was still in existence in 1834. During the political struggles between Miguelists and Constitutionalists, and at the time of the special tribunals that then came to this island, many priests were held in the Aljube because of their party sympathies, some of them being sent on to the Limoeiro and to the penal settlements of Africa.
Alligator (corvette)

The British warship *Alligator*, a corvette, came to Madeira in August 1828 to protect the British subjects living here, amid a well-founded fear that the political events of the time might force them to take refuge aboard a ship of their own nation. That protection proved unnecessary for the British subjects, but it served the governor and captain-general of this archipelago, Travassos Baldes, and other persons – which seems to have been the main purpose of the corvette’s visit to our harbour. Having capitulated to the invading forces that had landed at Machico (see Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelite troops), Travassos Valdez took refuge on the afternoon of 23 August 1828 aboard the corvette *Alligator*. He was accompanied by his wife, six children, two servants and other persons, among them some of the highest social standing in Madeira.

An interesting correspondence passed between M. G. Canning, commander of the *Alligator*, and Vice-Admiral Fonseca de Sousa Prego, commander of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) squadron, and José Maria Monteiro, governor and captain-general. In it the representatives of Miguel I demanded the immediate surrender of the refugees aboard that ship, but the British commander flatly refused.

After several meetings between the British consul in Funchal, Henrique Veitch, and Governor José Maria Monteiro, the matter was settled as set out in the following passage of the letter which the consul addressed to the said governor and captain-general: ‘In consequence of the wish Your Excellency has expressed that the refugees aboard the frigate *Alligator* should leave this port as soon as possible, and of the conference I had with Your Excellency a few days ago on this subject, I, in agreement with Captain Canning, have chartered, on account of the government of His Britannic Majesty, the English brig *Jane*. As a transport commanded by a naval officer, she is to sail tomorrow, the 6th of this month, taking the said refugees on board out of sight of land and beyond the range of the batteries, and to proceed with them directly to Plymouth’.

On 6 September 1828, that is, 15 days after the *Alligator* had taken Travassos Valdez and the other political refugees on board, she weighed anchor from our harbour and set course for England. On the high seas the refugees were transferred to the brig *Jane*, which headed for St Ives, a small seaport on the coast of Great Britain, arriving there on 18 September after a voyage of 12 days. We give below the complete list of the persons who left Madeira on the *Alligator* and landed at St Ives. The list was first published in the 5th volume of the work of the Baron of São Clemente, but it is known to few:

José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, former governor of Madeira and later Count of Bonfim, his wife, six children, the eldest of whom was 14, and two servants; Luís Godinho Valdez, the governor’s brother and aide-de-camp; João do Carvalhal, later Count of Carvalhal; the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) Dr José Duarte Machado Ferraz; the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) Dr Manuel Ferreira de Seabra da Mota e Silva; Lieutenant-Colonel Filipe Joaquim Aciaioly; Captain Joaquim Carlos Fernandes de Couto; the dean of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), Januário Vicente Camacho; Canon Sebastião Casimiro de Vasconcelos; Colonel Francisco Manuel Patrone; Lieutenant-Colonel António Fernandes Camacho; Major Joaquim Guilherme da Costa; Captain Pedro Cipriano de Ornelas; Major Luís António Figueiroa; Major Jerónimo Martins Salgado; the militia colonel J. A. Freitas Albuquerque; the sergeant-major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major) Francisco Moniz Escórcio; the volunteers of Dom Pedro, Luís Sauvaire and Luís Monteiro; Captain João de Betencourt; Lieutenant António José Gonçalves de Ornelas; Júlio da Câmara Leme; the ordinary judge (*juiz ordinário*, locally elected lay judge) António Joaquim Moderno; Friar António das Dores, provincial of the Franciscans; Domingos Alexandre da Silva; Miguel Ferreira Jardim; and Vicente de Sousa, servant of João do Carvalhal.

Three days before Madeira surrendered to the Miguelist troops, a number of officers had arrived in Funchal from England, sent by the Count of Palmela to help Governor Travassos Valdez in the resistance he was preparing against the absolutist forces. After three days ashore and fifteen days aboard the corvette *Alligator*, these officers went on to England and landed at St Ives with the other émigrés. They were Lieutenant-Colonel João Schwalbach; Major Francisco Xavier da Silva Pereira, later Count of Antas; Captain Tomás Carcy de Araújo; the Madeiran captain and professor at the Naval Academy (*Academia de Marinha*) António Aloísio Jervis de Atouguia, later Viscount of Atouguia; Lieutenant Francisco José da Mota; the Madeiran second lieutenant Dom Diogo da Câmara Leme; Lieutenant Francisco de Paula Lima; and the quartermaster-sergeant (*furriel*) Francisco Pacheco Guimarães.

The corvette *Alligator* did not accompany the *Jane* and returned to Funchal. On 24 September the commander of the *Alligator*, M. G. Canning, drowned while bathing in the tank (irrigation reservoir) of a *quinta* (country estate) belonging to a fellow countryman on the outskirts of Funchal. He was the son of the well-known English statesman Canning.

Bulwer’s petrel (Bulweria bulweri)

A web-footed bird. It breeds during the summer on the sea cliffs of all the islands of the archipelago and migrates away at the end of autumn, returning in the first weeks of spring. Its clutch consists of a single egg laid on the ground or in holes in the rocks.
Alma Nova
The 1st issue appeared on 1 December 1913 and the last, the 6th, on 15 February 1914.
Almada (family)

The first bearer of this surname to come to Madeira was Pedro Álvares de Almada, a native of Guimarães, son of Álvaro Vaz de Almada and nephew of the celebrated Count of Avranches, Dom Álvaro Vaz de Almada. Pedro de Almada lived in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and was one of the leading officers of the Council there. The illustrious annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says that he founded the church of Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*) in Santa Cruz, of which we have no information whatsoever.

Some genealogies state that one of the first to use the surname Almada was António de Almada, who around the middle of the 16th century married Isabel Rodrigues Leal, of the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’).
Almada (António José de Sousa)

We know of this Madeiran from what is said of him in the *Diccionario Popular* of Pinheiro Chagas and in the dictionary *Portugal*. He was born on this island in 1824 and died in Benfica in 1874. He courted the Muses, but seems not to have been a poet of great inspiration.

Marrying a very wealthy lady in Lisbon, he squandered a considerable fortune within a short time. He then turned to various industrial ventures, in which fortune did not greatly favour him. Under Marshal Saldanha’s Hundred Days government, Sousa Almada was civil governor of Castelo Branco. He was a man of the most refined manners, spoke several languages with ease and possessed uncommon strength and courage, all of which he turned to good advantage at various moments of his eventful life.
Almada (Dom Lourenço de)

This governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira was appointed on 4 August 1687 and took office on 13 April 1688. He was also governor-general of Angola and of one of the provinces of Brazil. He was a descendant of Dom Álvaro Vaz de Almada and died on 2 May 1729.
Almada (Dr José António de)

He was born in the town (*vila*) of Machico on 7 March 1843, the son of José António de Almada. After attending the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city and completing his degree at the Faculty of Law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), he set up practice as a lawyer in Funchal. There he earned the reputation of a distinguished jurist and was highly regarded in his profession. In this city he held the highest offices, such as deputy crown prosecutor, civil governor and others, and he was also deputy for Madeira in the legislature of 1900. The decree appointing him civil governor of this district is dated 15 February 1897, and he took up the post on the 18th of the same month and year.

As head of the district from 1897 to 1898, and as representative of this archipelago in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), he championed the interests of his homeland with the utmost dedication. He secured several important improvements for it, such as the creation of the forest police corps, the demolition of the city’s curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city), the abolition of the tax on fresh meat (*carnes verdes*), the start of work on the bridges of São Vicente and Santo António, and others besides.
A few years before his death he had settled in the capital, where he served as judge advocate of the army and navy courts martial; he died there on 21 March 1905.

He was active in politics and contributed to several newspapers, being an editor of the *Revista Jurídica* (‘Legal Review’), published in Funchal from 1870 to 1871. Together with J. R. da Trindade e Vasconcelos he wrote a pamphlet entitled *Projecto de lei regulamentar do contracto de colonia*; Funchal, 1867.
Almada (Dr José de)

He is the son of Dr José António de Almada, discussed above, and of Dona Margarida de Ornelas de Almada, and was born in Funchal on 23 February 1880. He completed his secondary studies in this city and in Switzerland and took his law degree at the University of Coimbra in 1903.

He is deputy director-general of Political and Civil Administration at the Ministry of the Colonies and serves as Colonial Adviser at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. His fruitful activity has been distinguished above all by important public-service commissions at home and abroad. Particularly notable are the missions on which our governments have repeatedly sent him to London, to the Union of South Africa, to Geneva at the League of Nations, etc., defending Portugal’s interests in lengthy negotiations with the governments of various foreign countries. In the course of these missions he has published many reports and studies written in French and English, and he has also published a book entitled *Impressões da Africa do Sul*.

He came to Madeira in 1927 to study the so-called Lombada da Ponta do Sol (‘ridge of Ponta do Sol’) question, as can be seen in more detail in the pamphlet entitled *A Lombada dos Esmeraldos na Ilha da Madeira*, published in 1933 by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva.
Almada (José António de)

He was born in Machico on 19 April 1813. During the blockade of Madeira in May 1832 he fled to the Queen’s naval division. In 1833 he was promoted to sergeant, having landed on the beaches of Mindelo as a soldier of the expedition commanded by Pedro IV. He was present at the siege of Porto, served at the Serra do Pilar and took part in various actions and battles of the liberal campaigns, being wounded at Asseiceira on 16 May 1834. By decree of 8 September 1834, Queen Maria II was pleased to make him a knight of the Order of the Tower and Sword. He died in Funchal on 2 May 1885.
Almanach Ecclesiasticum

There is an annual ecclesiastical calendar specific to this diocese, intended to guide priests in reciting the divine office and celebrating Mass, to indicate the feasts, etc. It has been printed in Coimbra for many years. The compiler of the liturgical calendar for this diocese was Dr António Rodrigues Porfírio Ribeiro de Vasconcelos, a distinguished professor of theology at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). The oldest printed almanac of this diocese known to us dates from 1858. Since 1927 the *Almanach Ecclesiasticum* (‘Church Almanac’) has been edited by Father José Augusto Rodrigues Amado.

Holy Souls (chapels)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), at a locality (*sítio*) that is now unknown, the cooper António Rodrigues Jardim founded a small chapel dedicated to the Souls in Purgatory in 1652.

At the locality of Vargem (‘meadow’) in the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’) there is a chantry (capela) of the same dedication, whose founder and year of construction are unknown.
There is a chantry of the Souls in the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’), but nothing else is known about it.
Around 1710 the people built a small chantry of the Souls in the churchyard of the parish church of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos; it has since been demolished.

A chantry of the same dedication was also built next to the parish church of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). Around 1925 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had it demolished to widen Rua Dr. João Augusto Teixeira.
Poor Souls (chapels)

In the angle formed halfway along the street that runs from the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) to the site where the convent of Our Lady of Ransom (*Nossa Senhora das Mercês*) once stood, a small and unusual chapel opens into the living rock. It is known as the Capela or Capelinha das Almas. That mass of basalt probably offered a hollow, or there may even have been a small grotto or cave there, which gave rise to the idea of building the chapel. Local tradition, however, tells a legend which, it seems to us, has also been used to explain similar buildings in other places and localities. It is said that a man sought a safe hiding place in a dense cane field that grew there, intending to murder a bitter enemy who was in the habit of passing that way at late hours. Night after night, and on successive days, he failed to carry out his wicked plan, because the intended victim always passed by in the company of other people. In the end the would-be killer resolved to abandon the idea that had obsessed him for so many days. When the man thus spared from his enemy’s savage fury later learned of the planned murder, he saw in it a clear miracle, since he had always passed that spot alone and entirely unaccompanied. He attributed his escape from becoming the innocent victim of that attack to the intervention of the souls in purgatory, to whom he had the most fervent devotion. From this arose the idea of building the chapel on the very spot where he believed the miracle had taken place. Major A. A. Sarmento used the subject of this legend for one of the chapters of his book *Migalhas*, introducing variants and episodes better suited to a romanticised treatment of the scene.

What we know for certain is that Roque José de Araujo, a native of Viana de Caminha who had lived in Funchal for many years, had the small chapel built in 1781. He dedicated it to the souls in purgatory and gave it the name of Almas Pobres (Poor Souls). As was customary, it was inspected by the competent ecclesiastical authority, and the corresponding record (*auto*) contains the following words: ‘... it measures from the door to the altar six *palmos* in depth and span, and in width nine *palmos* of span, and the length of the altar is the whole of it without a credence, the height is proportionate, covered with a vault. . and situated beneath the cliff and to all appearances sound’.

To provide for the upkeep of worship and the maintenance of the chapel, Roque José de Araujo granted it, by a public deed of 25 August 1781, a perpetual annual pension of five thousand réis, charged on a property he owned in Beco do Gongorra (‘Gongorra’s alley’), at Ponte Nova (‘new bridge’).
The chapel was blessed by the vicar of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro, Francisco Xavier da Cunha, on [day missing] December 1783.

There was also a chapel called Almas Pobres in the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), founded by Gonçalo Diniz da Silva around 1470. It no longer exists, and we do not know where it had been built.
Almeida

‘The wife of João Gonçalves Zarco, Constança Rodrigues,’ says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, ‘is called de Sá by some and de Almeida by others; and indeed the house of Abrantes, which springs from the same ancestry, bears the arms of the Almeidas. After Constança Rodrigues, the first person we find with this surname is Amador de Almeida, to whom John III granted a coat of arms in 1538’.
Almeida (António de Carvalho e)
Portuguese naturalist who came to Madeira in June 1784 in order to assemble a collection of the island’s natural products.
Almeida (Boaventura Mendes de)

He was appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 13 June 1907 and took up office on 3 August of the same year. In August 1907 a suspicious disease appeared in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António and within a few days killed 14 people, for that was the number struck by it. This disease, which caused extreme alarm among the population of Funchal, did not spread further thanks to the vigorous measures that were adopted. The speed and effectiveness of those measures were due chiefly to Governor Boaventura de Almeida, whose name thus became linked to the eradication of the terrible disease. He died in Lisbon on 11 August 1934.
Almeida (Dona Constança Rodrigues de)
Wife of Zarco. She had the chantry (capela) and shelter of St Catherine (*Santa Catarina*) built.
Almeida (Dom Friar Gabriel de)

After Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) had been vacant for 20 years, the prelate Dom Jerónimo Fernando was succeeded in the government of this diocese by Bishop Dom Friar Gabriel de Almeida. His episcopate was short: he was consecrated in 1671 and took possession of the bishopric on 4 March of the same year, and he died in this city on 12 July 1674.
He belonged to the Order of St Bernard and was abbot general of Alcobaça and professor of theology at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), and he held other important posts.

Although he took charge of this diocese at a fairly advanced age, he was always zealous in fulfilling his duties as prelate, making pastoral visitations to many parish churches, among them that of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Nevertheless, his episcopal administration was interrupted by serious difficulties arising from the disputes between him and the governor and captain-general. The same happened with the Franciscan friars and some members of the secular clergy, and this is said to have helped to shorten his life.

If we are to believe the author of the curious work *Monstruosidades do Tempo e da Fortuna*, written two centuries ago and published a few years ago, Dom Friar Gabriel de Almeida was harsh and brusque by nature and failed to win the sympathy of those who approached him. This, together with his advanced age and the ailments from which he suffered, sufficiently explains the friction he caused in governing the bishopric and the sorrows that troubled the last years of his life.
After a short illness he died in Funchal on 12 July 1674 and lies buried in the choir of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral). He was the second bishop to die in Madeira and be buried there.
Almeida (Dona Maria Helena Jervis de Atouguia e)
She was born in Funchal in 1847 and belonged to an old Madeiran family.

In 1907 she collected some of her poems and published them in a volume of 114 pages under the pseudonym Bertha de Ataíde, with the title *Mosaicos*. This book, of which a 2nd edition appeared in 1909, has a preface by the distinguished writer Father Sena Freitas. The book *Poetisas Portuguesas*, published in 1917, which contains some poems by Dona Maria Helena de Atouguia, states that the 3rd edition of *Mosaicos* was soon to appear. She died in Lisbon in May 1928.
Almeida (Januário Correia de)
This civil governor of Madeira was appointed to the post by decree of 15 January 1862 and took up office on the 19th of the same month and year.

He later played an important part in the country’s politics, serving as deputy, peer of the realm and minister of state. He was granted the title of viscount and later of Count of São Januário, the name by which he came to be known in Portuguese politics.

João de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos was appointed civil governor of this district and took up office in mid-January 1862. On the very day he took office, the 1st Viscount of Nogueiras, the new governor’s brother-in-law, gave a splendid ball in his honour, attended by the most distinguished people of Funchal. When the party was at its liveliest and merriest, word was brought to the Viscount of Nogueiras that a warship had just anchored in our harbour carrying a new governor for Madeira, and that Governor Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos was therefore dismissed. Care was prudently and discreetly taken to hide the news of the new governor’s arrival from the guests – the new governor was Januário Correia de Almeida – and the party continued to the end with the same enthusiasm and gaiety. The political opponents of Governor Sant’Ana, who was then municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government’s representative) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), made mocking comments on the affair, one newspaper saying that he had been so absorbed in the administration of the district that he had not even had time to sleep while it lasted, since he was governor for only a few hours.
Almeida (Luís Beltrão de Gouveia e)

He was appointed governor and captain-general of this archipelago on 13 February 1813 and took up the post on 10 August of the same year. He clashed with General Gordon, commander of the British troops occupying Madeira, who among other arbitrary acts had an English soldier hanged for killing a sergeant of his own nationality, thereby gravely offending the sovereign rights of the King of Portugal. He made every effort to secure the withdrawal of those troops and was always zealous in running the public services. He wrote a long and remarkable report on the development of Madeiran agriculture, road building and other indispensable public improvements. He died suddenly in Funchal on 1 July 1814 and was buried in the Capela do Santíssimo Sacramento (Chapel of the Blessed Sacrament) of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral).

On his death, in accordance with the legal provisions then in force, the supreme government of the archipelago passed to the diocesan bishop, Dom Friar Joaquim de Meneses Ataíde, the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*), Dr Manuel C. de Almeida e Albuquerque, and the senior officer, António Alberto de Andrade Perdigão.
The commander of the British forces claimed a place in this government, but the other members opposed it, and their stand was approved by the central government.
Almeida (Paulo Dias de)

An engineer and corresponding member of the Funchal Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts (*Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes*). Because he belonged to the constitutional party, he was arrested and sent aboard the frigate *Príncipe D. Pedro* as soon as the governor José Maria Monteiro arrived on the island. He was later sent to Lisbon aboard the storeship *Orestes* as a political prisoner, indicted by the special judicial commission (alçada) that came to the island in 1828.

He drew up the general map of the island of Madeira at the beginning of the 19th century and left a manuscript entitled *Descripção da Ilha da Madeira em geral e de cada huma das suas freguesias, villas e logares em particular, suas producções, numero de fogos e seus habitantes; e estado actual das suas fortificações*; 1817. This manuscript was published in the Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*), vol. II, with drawings of the fortifications, figures of the militia troops and popular costumes.
Sentenced for political reasons to penal exile (degredo) in Africa, he died there shortly before 1834.
Almeida (Vasco de)
He was born in Funchal. Works: *Arte de criar os bichos de seda...*, translated from French and Italian, Funchal, 1870, 61 pp.
Almeirão (*Cichorium Endivia*)
A liguliflorous composite, common in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira. It has almost bare branches and heads of blue flowers.
Almotacés
They were officials elected by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) who supervised weights, measures, the prices of goods, the cleanliness of the city and various matters of policing.
Almude

This old measure, although illegal, is still used in Madeira, chiefly for measuring musts and cane juice (*garapa*). It varies from municipality (*concelho*) to municipality. According to the tables officially published in 1868, the *almude* (old liquid measure, about 17.5 litres) of the municipality of Funchal is equivalent to 17,520; in the municipality of Câmara de Lobos, to 17,580; in the municipality of Ponta do Sol, to 17,400; in the municipality of Calheta, to 17,352; in the municipality of Santa Cruz, to 17,328; in the municipality of Machico, to 17,568; in the municipality of Porto Santo, to 17,556; in the municipality of Sant'Ana, to 17,604; in the municipality of São Vicente, to 20,538; and in the municipality of Porto Moniz, to 20,272. The average is 18 071, but in the municipality of Funchal the *almude* is generally considered equivalent to 17 litres.
Alpires

A locality (*sítio*) high up in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), where there is a small mountain shelter near the levada path (*esplanada*) of the Levada da Serra (‘upland channel’).
Alpiste (*Phalaris canariensis*)
This grass is not cultivated in Madeira, but it grows subspontaneously near dwellings.

Flash floods

The list published below records every flash flood (*aluvião*) that has occurred in Madeira and about which we have been able to obtain some information. It should be noted, however, that the flood of 1724 was not the first to cause damage: Mouquet, who was here in 1601, says, though without giving dates, ‘that the waters that come down from the mountains sometimes destroy bridges and houses throughout the island’.
18 November 1724

The damage from this flash flood was felt above all in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, where 26 people died and more than 80 dwellings collapsed. In the *Anno Histórico*, Father Francisco de Santa Maria, referring to the flood of 1724, says that ‘the island of Madeira suffered a storm and deluge so great that it destroyed the town (*vila*) of Machico, part of that of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and many other places and localities of the same island, and the city of Funchal also suffered great damage and much ruin, both to its walls and to the settlement, from the flooding of the Ribeira do Pinheiro (Santa Luzia) that divides it’.
18 November 1765

Heavy rain swelled the streams that cross Funchal on this day, destroying the Ponte da Praça (‘square bridge’) and causing considerable damage to other bridges in the city. The waters of the Ribeira da Praça, or Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’), swept the Englishman Moita (?) out to sea, and he was never seen again.
9 October 1803

On this sadly memorable day a great flood swept across the fields of Madeira and destroyed a considerable part of the city, causing not only enormous material damage but also the loss of several hundred lives. It may without doubt be regarded as the greatest calamity to have struck this island in the long span of five centuries. We would stray too far if we attempted a detailed description of this terrible catastrophe, and so we confine ourselves to a few brief notes, hastily gathered from the chronicles of the time.

Some rain had fallen, on and off, in the ten or twelve days before 9 October 1803. On that day, at about 8 in the morning, rain that was not especially heavy began to fall in Funchal. It kept up steadily until 8 in the evening, yet nothing suggested that so terrible a flood was imminent. Then the rumble of thunder began to be heard, and the rain, accompanied by some wind, was now falling in veritable torrents. By half past 8 the waters of the streams were overflowing their banks and spreading with a great roar through the neighbouring streets, beginning their work of destruction and death. It was a true deluge.

The terror that seized the inhabitants is beyond description. It was made all the greater by the suddenness of the event, which caught a great many by surprise, with no chance of sheltering from the danger that threatened everyone. Death overtook many as they fled: they were swept away by the violence of the currents or struck by the collapsing houses and walls.

The district of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) suffered most from the storm. The João Gomes stream, swollen by the abundance and violence of its waters, burst its banks at three different points, forming as many raging currents that caused the greatest damage and claimed several dozen lives. Whole streets and countless dwellings and other buildings were swept into the sea, including the parish church, known as the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), which stood on the left bank of the stream, between the present Rua de Santa Maria and Rua Nova de Santa Maria (‘new street of St Mary’). In one house in this street 21 people were buried alive, and in a building on the Pelourinho (‘pillory’) a British subject and 15 members of his household died. It is estimated that in the district of Santa Maria Maior alone about 200 people perished in the flood.

The buildings along the Santa Luzia stream also suffered badly. Above the Ponte do Bom Jesus the waters cut new courses along both banks, and caused considerable damage, above all in Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), where several dwellings and shops collapsed. The same happened in Rua dos Tanoeiros and to various buildings on the left bank of that stream which formed Rua Direita (‘straight street’); these were swept away by the violence of the current. A contemporary account of the event says: ‘Whole streets disappeared with their inhabitants, and others, flooded with water and mud, left owners and tenants reduced to extreme destitution. A large part of the parish of Santa Maria Maior, together with its church, the oldest in the city, no longer exists, along with a good many of its unfortunate inhabitants; the rest, scattered here and there, flooded and abandoned, presents to the eyes of the feeling man a spectacle of grief, ruin and dismay. The streets called Direita, Tanoeiros, Valverde, Santa Maria, Hospital Velho and others were carried into the sea with an incredible multitude of inhabitants.’

Outside Funchal, the places that suffered most from the dreadful flood were Machico, Santa Cruz, Campanário, Ribeira Brava and Calheta, while the damage in the parishes of the north of the island was relatively slight.

Of the town (*vila*) of Machico, the archive of its parish church records the following: ‘…it demolished the wall of the stream, brought down the bridge and invaded the town so that the waters rose to a height of three *côvados* in the church and in all the streets. This flood threatened everyone with death; but an evident miracle saved them all, except fourteen people who perished, swept away by the waters or buried in their houses.’ It also demolished the ancient and historic chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*). Its image was found some days later on the high seas by an American full-rigged ship, which had it placed in Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*).
The damage the flood caused in the other parishes mentioned was equally considerable, and there too many lives were lost.

Contemporary reports of the events differ considerably on the number of people who died as victims of these floods; one account of the terrible event puts the dead and missing at about a thousand. Anyone who sets the approximate number of the dead at six hundred seems not to be far from the truth, most of them in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal.

The governor and captain-general at the time was Dom José Manuel da Câmara, who promptly issued a public notice (*edital*) ordering the immediate measures that the circumstances called for. The authorities’ first concern was to find shelter for those left homeless, who were very numerous. Public buildings, various government offices, many outbuildings of churches, barracks and fortresses, and also a good number of private houses were set aside as temporary lodging for them. Among the measures taken by the governor, the most notable was an absolute ban on raising the prices of foodstuffs, under threat of severe punishment for offenders.

The main cause of the harm done by the flood was the lack of channelling of the streams. Belatedly, the government in mainland Portugal resolved to carry out this long-desired improvement, sending to Madeira Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot to direct the works; he arrived here on 19 February 1804. He showed the greatest competence in the post entrusted to him and worked in it with astonishing energy, managing within a relatively short time to channel the three streams that run through Funchal. In December 1800 he reported to the central government that, despite the great storms and severe winter weather there had been shortly before, the walls had withstood the violent impact of the waters and given clear proof of the solidity of their construction. Oudinot died in this city on 11 February 1807, and in memory of his services his name was given to the street on the left bank of the João Gomes stream, between Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) and Praça dos Lavradores.

One interesting detail: since the chancel of the church of Our Lady of Calhau had been left standing, the royal warrant (*provisão régia*) of 12 March 1805 ordered that it be preserved in the state in which the flash flood had left it, as a reminder for future generations of the event that had been the most calamitous ever to befall the inhabitants of this island. In December 1835 the part of the church that the flash flood had spared was demolished, and the União market was built on the site.
