The market was recently pulled down to widen the street that runs past it.
26 October 1815

After the great flash flood of 9 October 1803, this was perhaps the greatest to have ravaged the island. A representation on the damage caused by this flood of 26 October 1815, addressed by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal to the Prince Regent, the future John VI, states that it was *incomparably greater than the flood of 1803*. Yet neither in the number of its victims nor in the damage it caused did it reach the scale of the earlier one, despite the enormous losses it brought upon the inhabitants of Funchal.

As had happened on other occasions, it was the raging currents of the streams that caused the greatest damage. Especially at certain points along the banks where there were no walls to contain and direct the flow, the waters burst out of their beds, swept over the adjoining land and cut a new course through streets and houses. They caused not only incalculable damage but also the utmost panic among the inhabitants, some of whom fell victim to the untameable force of the current. This is what happened with the waters of the Ribeira de São João, which, seeking a new course, violently swept away some twenty houses between the Ponte de São Paulo, at the end of Rua da Carreira (‘track’), and the mouth of the stream.
In the streets along the Ribeira de Santa Luzia the damage was also great: some houses were damaged, and so, at several points, were the stream’s walls.
Throughout the island there was considerable damage, and several people died, swept away by the force of the currents.

The horrors of the great flood of 1803, still vivid in everyone’s memory, heightened the panic among the inhabitants, the great majority of whom believed there was no possibility of escaping a death that seemed to them inevitable.
28 October 1842

For fifteen days a light drizzle had been falling almost without interruption. By 9 a.m. on 24 October the rain was already heavy, and by 3 p.m. it was pouring down in torrents. The streams burst their beds and spread violently over the adjoining land, causing great damage.

The streets of the district of Santa Maria Maior, the Pelourinho, Rua dos Medinas and others besides were completely flooded, the water reaching the second and third floors of the houses. In many streets of the city boats sailed about to rescue, with great difficulty, the many families who were crying out for mercy from the top floors and rooftops. Screams of terror could be heard everywhere. One of the men to whom many of the unfortunate flood victims owed their lives was the citizen Joaquim Dias de Almeida, but many others also distinguished themselves, as the Funchal newspapers *Imparcial* and *Defensor* recorded at the time. The steep paved streets of Santa Clara, Pico, Bela Vista and Incarnação were turned into torrential streams. The district of the English Cemetery was emptied of people, all its residents being taken in and sheltered, with every comfort, by a wealthy landowner who lived at the end of Rua da Bela Vista. A large part of the city was destroyed and houses were ruined to their foundations.
Many families of modest means were left poor. The losses amounted to hundreds of *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis).

On the 26th, two days later, the south wind unleashed a fearful storm in the harbour of Funchal. The raging waves leapt over the walls of the Pontinha and at times lapped the levada path (*esplanada*) of the Ilhéu. During the afternoon ten or eleven vessels were dashed to pieces on the rocks of the beach at Funchal. The crews and watchmen who were on board were miraculously rescued by the customs house guard Carvalho and by some exceptionally daring seamen, Joaquim Dias de Almeida distinguishing himself, as always, in these disasters. 17, 18, 19 and 20 November 1848. On these days there were great floods, chiefly in the municipality (*concelho*) of Santana, where many productive and valuable improvements (*benfeitorias*, tenant-made works on the land) were swept away by the waters. In Funchal the streams ran violently but, although extremely full, caused no appreciable damage.
5 and 6 January 1856

After exceptionally heavy rain, the current of the Ribeira de João Gomes brought down a great deal of debris, which rose above the retaining walls between the mouth of the stream and the Campo da Barca. Unable to flow freely, the waters flooded the Rua de Santa Maria, the side streets that cross it, the Rua do Ribeirinho de Baixo and the square known as the Largo do Pelourinho, causing great destruction at all these points. The Ribeira de Santa Luzia did no damage, although it too became choked with debris, but the Ribeira de São João caused no small damage, especially near the chapel. At Ribeira Brava, Tabua, Serra de Água, Ponta do Sol, Paul do Mar and other places the waters also caused great devastation. 1 January 1876. The floods of this day caused notable damage only in the parish (*freguesia*) of Madalena. 2 and 3 October 1895. The flash flood (*aluvião*) of these two days caused great damage in the parishes of São Vicente, Faial, Ponta Delgada, Boa Ventura and Seixal. In the last of these parishes the landowner Manoel Inisio da Costa Lira died. The streams of Funchal carried a great deal of water.
8 and 9 November 1901

The exceptionally heavy rain that fell on Funchal on these two days flooded the streets and roads, damaged many of the latter and caused several landslips, especially along the Levada de Santa Luzia. 25 and 26 February 1920. On these two days a violent storm of wind and rain struck, causing countless losses across the whole island. The streams that run through the city carried a great deal of water but did not overflow. There was, however, flooding in several places, owing to the heavy rain and to the blocking of the Nora, Til and Louros brooks. In the Santa Maria quarter boats even moved through the streets to carry people from one place to another, and it is said that more than 500 people were left homeless across the island. The damage done by the north-westerly wind to trees, cane fields and many other crops was incalculable. On the Lazareto road a man died while making his way home at night, and on the Pontinha mole another man died who was working at the capstan (*cabrestante*). Such was the force of the wind on the 25th and part of the 26th that it was dangerous to go out even in the streets of the city. On the afternoon of the 25th the motor-car service in Funchal was suspended because of the wind.

The town (*vila*) of Ribeira Brava was in great danger of being destroyed by the waters. The image of St Benedict was carried out in procession, and prayers were afterwards offered in the parish church. At Machico, Santa Cruz, São Vicente and Camacha very serious damage was recorded, and a woman and a child died in the last of these parishes. Several fishing boats from Câmara de Lobos disappeared with their crews. The boat *Arriaga*, from Porto Santo, carrying 16 passengers, was driven southwards by the storm; it was found by the British steamer *Andorinha*, which took the passengers aboard, while the boat put in at the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*). On the 28th torrential rain fell again, and on 2 March the north-westerly wind blew once more with great violence, with heavy showers that lasted until the early hours of the 3rd.
5 and 6 March 1921

On these days heavy rain, accompanied by thunderstorms, fell throughout the island, causing flooding and damage at Machico, Ribeira Brava, etc., etc. At Machico the waters rose in some places almost to the first floor of the houses, and at Ribeira Brava four children died, three when a building collapsed and one swept away by the waters.

Besides the twelve flash floods mentioned above, we have found a record in an old manuscript that in 1611 there was a great flood in Funchal. Among the notable damage it caused, it largely destroyed the parish church of Santa Maria Maior, which then stood in the street now called Hospital Velho. A new church was afterwards built near the present public fountain known as the Calhau fountain, and this church was swept into the sea by the flash flood of 1803. We also have a record of another flash flood, in 1707, which caused considerable damage throughout the island.
Alvarenga
It was André Gonçalves Alvarenga who introduced this surname to the island. He was a native of Beira and came with his family to settle in Funchal around 1500.
Alvares

Several people bearing this surname are found, but one of the first settlers was Antão Alvares de Carvalho, who held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and later founded on it the entail (*morgado*) of São Gil. Luís Alvares da Costa founded the original convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) in Funchal in 1473. In 1523 Pedro Alvares was judge of the Council (*juiz da câmara*) of Funchal. In the last quarter of the 15th century João Alvares, an ancestor of the celebrated grammarian Father Manuel Álvares, was living in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’).
Álvares da Silva (Aníbal)
He was born in Funchal on 29 May 1819, the son of Vitorino Álvares da Silva.
He settled early in what was then the town (*vila*) of Setúbal, where his father held the post of chief customs guard (*guarda-mor da Alfândega*).

Having completed his law degree with remarkable distinction, he set up as a lawyer in his adopted homeland. Through his rare talent, austerity of character and other admirable qualities, he became the greatest influence in Setúbal. He was president of the Council there and was elected deputy several times. The services he rendered to that town were of the utmost importance; it regards him as a great benefactor, and there are plans to raise a monument to his memory there.
He died on 8 December 1908 in Lisbon, where he had practised law for many years with great renown.
Álvares da Silva (Lieutenant Luís)

This Madeiran belonged to the military garrison of our colony of Timor when, on 24 December 1912, the natives rose up against the Portuguese authorities. Overrunning the fortified post of Manufai, they murdered our fellow countryman, the commander of that post, who, abandoned by the troops under his command, could offer no serious resistance to the rebels’ attack. The gallant officer fell victim to the fulfilment of his duty and to his wish to uphold the prestige of the Portuguese name in such distant lands.
Alvares de Nobrega (Francisco)

Francisco Alvares de Nobrega is today an almost entirely forgotten name, yet in his own time he enjoyed great renown as a poet and was even known by the epithet of Camões Pequeno (‘Little Camões’). Misfortune pursued him mercilessly from his earliest years to the tragic end of his troubled life. He was, in all truth, what is usually called an unhappy man, and it seems that not the faintest gleam of good fortune ever shone on him. Francisco Alvares de Nobrega was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, ‘in a poor, yes, but paternal home’, as he himself tells us in one of his sonnets. The distinguished Madeiran Jaime Moniz states that he discovered the certain date of the poet’s birth, which was 30 November 1772, while Januario de Nobrega assigns him the year 1773, without indication of the month and year. From an enrolment record (*termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca)) at the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*), which we had occasion to examine, we see that he was born on 30 November 1772, which corroborates the date given by Jaime Moniz; the record also states that he was the son of Domingos de Nobrega. Leaving his native parish, he came to this city, where he found employment in the drapery business of Marcos João de Ornelas, in whose house he received his first education, as he himself relates in one of his poems. It was there that his poetic gift revealed itself and he began to become known as an admired devotee of the Muses.

Through the patronage of Marcos de Ornelas, he was admitted as a pupil to the Diocesan Seminary, which was then housed in the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*). ‘There, as we have read somewhere, giving little attention to practical religious studies, he went on writing poems, some of them satirical, above all against Bishop Dom José da Costa Torres. By this way of life he earned the enmity of the prelate and of his superiors, and, caught up in the persecution the bishop waged against freemasonry, he was expelled from the seminary, taken to a dungeon and then sent to Lisbon, where he lay in prison for some time longer’.

It is known that Bishop Torres, acting on the instructions of the central government and backed by the governor of Madeira, waged a relentless persecution of the secret societies that had been organised in Madeira in the last quarter of the 18th century. This resulted in many arrests and in the clandestine embarkation of several individuals and their families on the night of 19 July 1792. The prelate went too far and committed acts of violence and arbitrariness, which forced him to leave this island in circumstances most humiliating to him. Francisco Alvares de Nobrega was caught in the meshes of this persecution, and even in Lisbon he continued to feel the persecuting hand of the Bishop weighing upon him.

The passage we have transcribed above seems to contradict what Januario de Nobrega writes, when he states that the poet completed his studies in Funchal and then went to Lisbon to pursue his career, and that he was imprisoned there as a result of the persecution that Dom José Torres continued to wage against him.

When he was transferred to Elvas, he was succeeded in this diocese by Bishop Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares, who became a devoted protector of Alvares de Nobrega and went to rescue him from the dungeons of the Limoeiro, where he lay. The poet refers to this with eloquent and heartfelt words on page eleven of his *Rimas*. We transcribe what his nephew says in the passage already cited:

‘He was set free, but the rest of his life, save for brief intervals in which, as a poet, he went on gaining fame, was one long chain of misfortunes. An opponent of the fanaticism that then prevailed, he was persecuted by the Inquisition, languishing, like Bocage, in its prisons, and for a second time in the Limoeiro, from which he was released thanks to the fifteen famous sonnets with which he knew how to move the heart of the monarch. By this time he was already afflicted by the fatal disease that forbids its sufferer to offer a friend his hand or to mix with his fellow men. Weary of life, tired of struggling against adversity, enduring bitter anguish far from his own people amid painful privations, at the age of 34 he decided that he must cut the thread of his existence, carrying out what he had already revealed to his friend and benefactor Manuel José Moreira Pinto Baptista. In the silence of the night he raised his own bier; he surrounded himself with the books to which he devoted his long sleepless hours, placed his writings at his bedside and, drinking the fatal draught like Socrates, fell asleep in the bosom of the Creator’.

Speaking of Francisco Alvares de Nobrega, Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says in his *Diccionario Bibliographico*: ‘This poet, who cannot be denied happy gifts and a natural talent for poetry, followed no particular school, for some of his verses recall the manner of Bocage, others that of Francisco Manuel. In the sonnet few among us have equalled him, except Bocage himself, who never knew a rival in this kind of composition. Nobrega’s language, though not excessively abundant, is pure and correct, and his verses are on the whole fluent and harmonious. He undoubtedly deserved a better fate’. In volume IX of the important review *O Instituto*, Jaime Constantino de Freitas Moniz wrote an extensive appraisal of the poetic works of Francisco Alvares de Nobrega, which also contains some biographical notes.

The ‘Camões Pequeno’ published the *Rimas de Francisco Alvares da Nobrega, natural da ilha da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1804, and the *Rimas offerecidas em sinal de reconhecimento ao Sr. Manuel José Moreira Pinto Baptista*, Lisbon, 1804, which were reprinted in Funchal in 1850 by his nephew, the esteemed poet and journalist Januario Justiniano de Nobrega.

When, in 1806, the familiars of the Inquisition entered the room in which Alvares de Nobrega’s body lay, they found many of his writings there, and these were completely destroyed. It is said that he had a new collection of poetic works ready for printing when he sought in death rest from the tribulations of earthly life.
Alvares (Joaquim de Oliveira)

He was born in Madeira on 16 November 1776 and graduated in mathematics and philosophy from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). In 1798 he was appointed 2nd lieutenant in the navy, and two years later he distinguished himself in an engagement off the coast of the Algarve between a small Portuguese caique under his command and a French privateer. Although he emerged from the fight defeated, he was recommended for promotion for the bravery he had shown in it. He then served in the squadron of the Marquis of Nisa, and in 1804 we find him in Brazil, having exchanged the navy for the army, holding the rank of captain of artillery in the São Paulo volunteer legion.

He took part in the Montevideo campaigns, defeated the forces of the famous Artigas at the battle of Carumbé on 27 October 1816, and on 4 January of the following year distinguished himself at the battle of Catalán. In reward for these services he was given the substantive rank of brigadier, the commandery of the Order of Avis and, in 1816, the brevet rank of field marshal.
After Brazilian independence he remained in that empire, where he became minister of war, substantive field marshal, officer of the Order of the Southern Cross and lieutenant general.

He lived in London from 1830 to 1835. Having received a very large inheritance there, he placed his wealth at the disposal of the Brazilian government so that, at a time of financial difficulty, it could pay the interest on its bonds. He went to Paris in 1835 in search of relief from his ailments and died there at the age of 59. He is buried in the Père Lachaise cemetery.

He was a man of wide learning and left unpublished a substantial work entitled *Estatística do Brasil*. Volume 2 of the *Dicionário Popular* contains interesting biographical details of Marshal Joaquim de Oliveira Alvares, who was the brother of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) João Francisco de Oliveira, another illustrious son of our land.
Álvares (Father Manuel)

Old Madeiran books of genealogy say that Afonso Álvares Columbreiro, a native of a settlement on the outskirts of Seville, was one of the first and noble settlers of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). They add that he founded there the chantries (capela) of St Catherine (*Santa Catarina*) and São Bento (St Benedict of Nursia) within the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he had established, whose seat lay in that parish (*freguesia*). One of his granddaughters, named Brígida Gonçalves, and her husband João Mealheiro or Malheiro, who held the rank of noblemen, were the ancestors of Father Manuel Álvares. He therefore came of noble lineage, which in any case adds little to his undeniable merits and virtues. His parents were Sebastião Gonçalves and Beatriz Álvares, who retained the privileges of nobility inherited from their forebears.

All his biographers, including the author of the *Synopsis Annalium Societatis Jesu in Lusitania*, state that he entered the Society of Jesus on 4 July 1546, at the age of 20, and that he died in Évora on 30 December 1583, aged 57. He must therefore have been born in 1526, at a time when births were not yet regularly registered in this diocese. For that reason his baptismal entry is not to be found in the parish archive of Ribeira Brava, as we have more than once had occasion to confirm.

His vocation for the Church had dawned early, for as early as 1538 he had received the so-called minor orders from Dom Ambrósio Brandão, titular bishop of Rocina, who had come to this island to perform the episcopal functions temporarily. Father António Franco relates that a carrack bound for India put in at Funchal and, because of illness, landed a member of the Society of Jesus, who took refuge in the hospital to be treated for the sickness that had struck him. Manuel Álvares went to visit him to obtain news and information about an old friend and fellow student of his. From his dealings with the religious grew the desire to embrace the order of St Ignatius, which since its foundation in 1540 had enjoyed extraordinary renown and attracted many vocations to the Church. He soon left his father’s house and entered the congregation of the Jesuits in 1546, as already mentioned.

During his studies, in which he proved a student of extraordinary talent, he showed a special fondness for the dead languages – Latin, Greek and Hebrew. In the first of these he soon became a true authority, and he was regarded as one of the most notable Latinists of his time. He also had a thorough knowledge of Syro-Chaldaic and Arabic, and was acquainted with other oriental languages as well.

Of the works he wrote, it was his Latin grammar, *De Institutione Grammatica*, that brought him worldwide renown. To appreciate its worth, it is enough to say that, besides the countless editions made of it in Latin, it was translated into French, English, German, Spanish, Italian, Bohemian, Croatian, Flemish, Hungarian, Polish, Chinese and Japanese.

After *Os Lusíadas* (*The Lusiads*), no work by a Portuguese author has been translated and reprinted so many times. Edgard Prestage, in his study of Francisco Manuel de Melo, published a few years ago, says: ‘this work... has gone through more than 400 editions, being translated into every language, and a Chinese version was published in Shanghai in 1869. Very few scientific books have thus enjoyed three centuries of life’. José Silvestre Ribeiro, in his *Curso de Litteratura Portuguesa*, states ‘that this illustrious Madeiran is one of the pedagogical glories of Portugal and that his book is the most extensively and intensively disseminated work that Portuguese literature has had’. To conclude these quotations, the celebrated and learned Bishop of Viseu, Dom Francisco Alexandre Lobo, adds: ‘either in the ecclesiastical estate or in the republic of letters I see no other Portuguese who can be preferred to Jerónimo Osório. In the union of the one and the other I see no Portuguese who can equal him’.

For two hundred years the books of Manuel Alvares were the standard treatises for teaching Latin in almost the whole of Europe. However, the appearance of the works of António Pereira de Figueiredo and Luís António Verney, around the middle of the 18th century, gave rise in Portugal to much criticism and debate about the value of the celebrated Jesuit’s work. With the progress of the science of language over the long period of two centuries, his books began to lose the authority they had enjoyed, a decline to which the Marquis of Pombal’s ban on their adoption in public or private teaching also contributed considerably. Nevertheless, as late as the second quarter of the 19th century some twenty editions of his grammar were published in various European countries.

Besides his method for teaching Latin, Manuel Alvares wrote other works, some of which remained unpublished. The fame that crowned his name as a writer and scholar, together with the great prestige he enjoyed among his fellow religious, had marked him out for high office in his order. He thus served as rector of the renowned colleges of Lisbon, Évora and Coimbra, always showing the superiority of his talent and his eminent qualities of tact in government.

We shall close this biographical note with the very words of the author of the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’): ‘He was an exemplary model of all the religious virtues, earning for them the praise of his holy patriarch. His forbearance having been tried by a long illness, he died with great piety in the College of Évora on 30 December 1583, aged 57 and after 37 years in religion. Some years later, when his tomb was opened, his body was found incorrupt’.
In August 1917 Dr Urbano Canuto Soares came to Funchal, by order of the Ministry of Public Instruction, to carry out research on the life and works of Father Manuel Alvares.
Alvenaria (compact basalt)
This name is given to compact basalt, a rock very common in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira. See Basalts.
Alverca (Baron of)
See Pereira (João António de Sá).
Alves da Silva (Dr António)
Dr António Alves da Silva was a distinguished Madeiran whose persistent illness and premature death prevented him from revealing the full strength of his extraordinary talent.
He was born in this city on 13 September 1822 and died here on 19 January 1854, aged only 31.

He enrolled in the medical course at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), but broke it off in 1846, at the end of his fourth year, because of the political events then taking place in the country. He went to complete his doctorate in Paris. Both in Coimbra, where he won prizes every year, and in the French capital, he gave proof of a brilliant intellect and a remarkable capacity for work, which earned him the admiration and esteem of all his professors and fellow students.
Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says ‘that in Paris he obtained the degree of doctor free of charge, on 29 December 1848, as a token of the esteem due to the great talent he had shown there’.
By decree of 11 March 1850 he was appointed professor at the Funchal Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica*), a post he filled with notable distinction.

In Funchal he gave two public lectures on medicine and hygiene, which Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo describes as most remarkable, both for the way he treated the subject and for the beauty of his language. At that time the most distinguished men of our land, such as Marceliano Ribeiro and others, gave public lectures for the instruction of the people of Funchal, and these were extremely popular.
Alves da Silva was a member of the Instituto de Coimbra, a corresponding member of the Academia Real das Ciências (Royal Academy of Sciences) and of other literary and scientific bodies.

The terrible tuberculosis that had long been undermining his life did not allow him to devote himself to great exertions and intellectual labours. Even so, he was a most distinguished physician in his practice, and in the cultivation of letters he showed enviable gifts, which death did not allow him to display more brilliantly.
Alves Martins (Father Luís)

He was born in Cardigos, in the municipality (*concelho*) of Mação, on 23 December 1873, and came to Madeira in 1905 as chaplain of the 27th Infantry Regiment. In 1908 he was appointed royal preacher.

He is the author of the following publications: *A Bandeira Portuguesa*, Funchal, 1907; *Oração Fúnebre nas Exéquias de Hintze Ribeiro*, Funchal, 1907; and *Brevi vivens tempore discurso fúnebre nas exéquias d'El-Rei D. Carlos e Príncipe Real D. Luiz Filipe*, Funchal, 1908.
Alvim
See Alvino.
Alvino
This surname appeared here with the arrival on this island of the licentiate Manuel Camilo de Melo e Alvino around 1500.
Alvino is a corruption of Alvim, this surname deriving from Manuel Carrilho de Melo e Alvim (*Saud.* 846). The surname Alvim, which is old and noble, also exists in Portugal and the Azores.
Amaral (José Cabral Correia do)

He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law and held the office of Treasury Delegate (*delegado do tesouro*) here. He was elected deputy for this archipelago for the legislature of 1905 to 1906.
He was also elected deputy for Madeira in August 1910, but the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) never met.
Amaral (José Júlio do)
This distinguished army officer (1801–1876) was military commander of this archipelago in 1861.
Amaro (Padre)

*Padre Amaro* was the name of a celebrated periodical published in London, in Portuguese, from 1820 to 1830. Its chief editor was the illustrious Madeiran Joaquim José Ferreira de Freitas, who is also known by the name of Padre Amaro and whom we shall discuss in the appropriate place.
Ambrósio (Dom)

Dom Martinho de Portugal, the first and only Archbishop of Funchal, never came to his diocese, but he sent to this island the titular bishop of Rocina, Dom Ambrósio, to perform here the functions proper to the episcopal ministry. Dom Ambrósio stayed in Madeira for about a year, from 1538 to 1539, and when his ministry was over he returned to the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). Discipline and the observance of canon law had been entrusted to the two visitors Jordão Jorge and Álvaro Dias, who remained on the island after Bishop Dom Ambrósio’s departure.
Madeiran barberry (Berberis maderensis)

A shrub of the family Berberidaceae, 1 m to 1.5 m tall, with three-parted spines and fascicled leaves, subspatulate or subobovate, entire or serrate-spiny; yellow flowers gathered in racemes. In modern times it has been found only in the Serra dos Balcões (‘uplands of the balconies’). The wood of this shrub, called *fustete*, has a beautiful yellow colour and is much prized in cabinet-making, especially for inlaid work (*embutidos*).
Plum tree (Prunus domestica)

A tree of the family Rosaceae, subfamily Prunoideae, widely cultivated in Madeira. It originates in the East and produces oblong or globular fruits, usually of excellent quality. The green plum or greengage (*Rainha Cláudia*) is one of the tastiest on the island. Dried plums are slightly laxative.
Ameixoeira

This is the name of a parish (*freguesia*) about 6 kilometres from Lisbon, in the municipality (*concelho*) of Olivais. In his dictionary *Portugal Antigo e Moderno*, vol. I, p. 195, Pinho Leal says that this parish once belonged to the parish of Lumiar and bore the name of Funchal. He adds that the old chapel of Nossa Senhora do Funchal (Our Lady of Funchal) served as the mother church (*igreja matriz*) until it was rebuilt and enlarged in 1664. Pinho Leal further states, word for word: ‘It is said that the original chapel was founded in memory of a great victory won here by the Christians over the Moors. It is also said that this chaplaincy (capelania) already existed in the time of the Goths, and that a Moor called Mixo or Mixio gave his name to this settlement (which until the 17th century was called Mixoeira, having earlier been called Funchal, as I have already said)’. Pinho Leal also reports that ‘Ameixoeira, under the name of Funchal, was a hamlet of the parish of Lumiar; but on 6 June 1536 it became independent...’

Could there be some connection between the ancient village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Funchal in Amendoeira and the early settlement, later town (*vila*) and then city, of Funchal? We do not know.
Amélia (Empress Dona)

The Empress of Brazil, Dona Amélia, widow of Pedro IV, and her daughter Princess Maria Amélia arrived in Funchal on 28 August 1852 aboard the naval frigate *D. Fernando*, escorted by the corvette *D. João I* and the steam warship *D. Luiz*. The squadron was commanded by Captain José Maria de Sousa Soares, and the frigate *D. Fernando* served as flagship.

The reception was magnificent and deeply moved the empress and the princess. Although gravely ill, the princess remained cheerful and smiling all the way from her landing at the Pontinha (‘little point’) to the Quinta das Angústias (‘estate of the Sorrows’), where she took up residence, at the sight of so many demonstrations of esteem and affection lavished on her by the inhabitants of this city.

Everyone knows that Princess Maria Amélia did not find in Madeira’s balmy air and mild climate the relief that had been hoped for. After a stay of five months and a few days among us, she succumbed to the ravages of terrible pulmonary tuberculosis in the early hours of 4 February 1853.

The princess, according to trustworthy contemporary witnesses, was of unequalled kindness and aroused the liveliest and most ardent affection in all who saw her or came near her. Her death therefore caused the whole population of Funchal the deepest grief, which endured among us for many years. The empress embarked on her return to Lisbon, accompanying the coffin that held the mortal remains of her daughter, on 6 May 1853. It was an imposing procession, in which not a dry eye was to be seen. From the humblest townsman to the desolate empress, all wept copiously. It seemed as if a great calamity had occurred. This death, as everyone knows, led to the founding of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*), of which we shall speak on another occasion. The Empress Dona Amélia died in Lisbon on 26 January 1873.
See Princess Maria Amélia Hospice.
Almond tree (Amygdalus communis)

A tree native to Mesopotamia, cultivated in Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Sweet almonds are edible, as is well known, and are used to prepare an oil with various applications. Bitter almonds yield a similar oil by cold pressing, but if this oil is obtained by distillation with water it becomes extremely poisonous. Distilled bitter-almond water is also poisonous, owing to the presence of hydrocyanic acid.
Amendoeira (peak)

This hill, which commands a fine view, lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), on the Lombada dos Esmeraldos (‘the Esmeraldos’ ridge’), not far from the chapel and manor house of the Counts of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’).
Amigo do Povo (O)
It was published from 26 January 1850 to 27 April 1854, running to 178 issues.
Amor-de-burro (Bidens pilosa)

An annual tubuliflorous composite, native to South America and fully naturalised in Madeira. Its upper leaves are usually 3-sect and its fruits bear 2–4 rigid, retrorsely ciliate awns. It is widely used in the countryside as an emmenagogue, and is also known as *setas* and *malpica*.
Pansy
This name is given to various hybrids of *Viola tricolor* with several closely related species. An infusion of pansies is recommended for skin diseases.
Mulberry

Madeira has *Morus nigra* (black mulberry), whose sorosis fruits are edible and are used to prepare the mulberry rob employed as a gargle for quinsy, and *M. multicaulis* (white mulberry), whose leaves serve as food for silkworms. In May 1877 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) granted the Praça da Rainha (today Praça do Marquês de Pombal) for a nursery of white mulberries, and the late Count of Canavial went so far as to establish the nursery there, but it was short-lived. The cultivation of these mulberries is at present utterly abandoned. The black mulberry is widely grown on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Amoreiras

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), where stands the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), founded in 1911 by Father José Marcelino de Freitas. On the same spot there once stood a chapel of the same dedication, built at the behest of Isabel de Abreu in the early 16th century.
Agrimony (Agrimonia eupatoria)

A perennial plant of the family Rosaceae, subfamily Rosoideae, very common in Madeira. Its leaves are pinnatisect, with distinct segments, and its yellow flowers are arranged in long, narrow racemes. An infusion of the leaves and flowers of this plant may be used as a gargle for quinsy.
Amparo

In this locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’) stands the chapel of Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*), which belonged to the former entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Sauvaire family and was founded by Dona Luísa de Mendonça in 1712.
Amparo

The chapel of Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*) gave its name to this locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo. Crowds flock to it from the surrounding parishes on the feast day of its patron saint.
Ana Ferreira (peak)
This peak rises in the south-south-east of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), reaching an altitude of 278 metres.
Annals of the Municipality

The ministerial order (*portaria*) of 8 November 1848 required the Municipal Councils to keep a book entitled ‘Annals of the Municipality’ (*Anais do Município*) and to have entered in it, in the month of March each year, a summary of all the events, notes and information that might be of interest to the history of the municipality concerned. The illustrious civil governor of this archipelago, José Silvestre Ribeiro, who never neglected any matter that might contribute to the material and intellectual progress of the people under his administration, called for compliance with that order in his circulars to the councils and to the municipal administrators (*administradores do concelho*) of the district, dated 3 January 1848 and 22 January 1850. In them he set out, with the most persuasive arguments, the advantages and the necessity of carrying out that government measure. Few municipal councils, starting with that of the district capital, complied with so useful and necessary a directive.

We know only that the councils of Porto Santo, Machico and Calheta compiled their annals, although in the following years they failed to continue them. They thus did not comply with the law in full, and so made their compliance almost entirely useless.

On Porto Santo it was the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative), João de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, who in 1848 gathered the necessary notes and gave the annals of that municipality (*concelho*) their final form. It is a valuable work and may be regarded as an interesting monograph on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), both from the historical point of view and for its description of the island and its statistics of produce, population, customs, etc. Despite its shortcomings, it is a work that does great honour to its author's memory. It was published in full in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) in January, February and March 1906, and some passages had already appeared long before in the *Diário de Notícias* of this city.

Less complete, but also interesting and containing valuable material for the history of the municipality, are the annals of Machico. They seem to us to have been written by José António de Almada, a native of that town (*vila*), who was clerk (*escrivão*) of the court of law in the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal. They remained unpublished until 1906, when, in November, they were published in full in the *Heraldo da Madeira*. Mention must also be made of the annals of the municipality of Calheta (‘small cove’), which remain unpublished and contain some valuable material for the history of that municipality.

The Funchal Council entrusted the writing of its annals first to Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça, then to Francisco de Andrade and finally to Augusto César Barjona de Freitas. The second refused to write them, while the first and third did nothing, although there is no record that they had declined to perform the task.

At its meeting of 7 October 1897 the Council approved a proposal by its president that the municipal archive should keep a book recording in detail the history of all the major works, resolutions and improvements carried out by the Municipality. This decision, however, was never put into effect, for reasons unknown to us. The book intended for the annals ordered by Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Silvestre Ribeiro still exists today in the Municipal Archive, completely blank.
Water analyses
The results of the analyses of the various waters of Madeira are recorded in the following pamphlets: 1. *Analyse chimica e bacteriologica da Fonte Férrea do Jamboto* (Funchal, 1900).

2. *Analyse chimica de águas potáveis de várias fontes da cidade do Funchal* (Funchal, 1900). This contains the analyses of the springs of João Diniz, Campo da Barca, Ribeira de Santa Luzia and Corujeira de Baixo. 3. *Analyse chimica e bacteriologica das águas das nascentes dos Tornos* (Funchal, 1900). The waters of São Roque, in Machico, and of Fontinha (‘little spring’), on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), were also analysed, and the results of these analyses were published in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’).
Pineapple (Ananassa vulgaris)

Two varieties of pineapple exist in Madeira, one with leaves almost free of spines and the other with leaves bearing strong spines along the margins. The former is grown only in a few glasshouses and is identical to the Azorean pineapple, known in England as ‘Smooth-leaved Cayenne’. The latter flowers and fruits well in the open air in various parts of the island, although its fruits, or soroses, are smaller and more acid than those of the other variety.

The spiny-leaved pineapple, which is said to have been imported from Africa but which also exists in Brazil and other countries, is found at Ribeira Brava, Porto da Cruz, Funchal, etc. Its leaves are long and often spotted with red, and its spikes are oblong-cylindrical, borne on a peduncle or stem furnished with short, reddish leaves. The perianth has 6 divisions: the three outer ones are red and short, and the three inner ones lilac, erect, narrow and a little shorter than the bracts.
The pineapple generally fruits from November to January and flowers in March and April.
Anatole France
This eminent French writer, a member of the Académie Française, called at Funchal on 25 August 1909 on his return from South America, leaving for his own country the same day.
Andaluz (Dr António J. de Santa Marta)

(See Mesquita e Melo, 3rd Viscount of.) He was secretary-general of the district when he was appointed civil governor of Madeira by decree of 4 September 1869. He took office on the 18th of the same month and year, but held the post for only a few months. He married on this island a Madeiran lady, daughter of the Barons of Conceição (‘Conception’), and had been born on 12 April 1833.
Swallow

A name improperly given to two birds native to Madeira, *Micropus apus* and *M. unicolor*. The first is called *andorinha do mar* (‘sea swallow’), the second *andorinha da serra* (‘mountain swallow’). The true swallows, *Hirundo rustica* and *Chelidonaria urbica*, which visit these islands regularly without breeding, are known on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) as *andorinhas de fora* (‘swallows from outside’) and in some parishes in the north of Madeira as *andorinhas do Porto Santo* (‘Porto Santo swallows’), perhaps because on reaching the northern coast of Madeira they arrive from the north-east, that is, from the direction of Porto Santo.
Andrade

The brothers João Fernandes de Andrade and Diogo Fernandes de Andrade, noblemen of Galicia, were the first to come to this island bearing this surname. They obtained many lands as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) and settled there. John II, by royal decree (*alvará*) of 20 February 1485, granted the first of the two the use of the following arms: ‘on a field of gold a sagittarius, half man and half horse, the man naked in his natural colour, the horse between bay and dark chestnut, with a bow drawn in its hands, of red, and the string of silver, the arrow fletched with green; a closed helm of silver, mantling of gold and green, and for crest the demi-sagittarius with its bow’.

Diogo Fernandes de Andrade sold the lands he held at Arco to his brother and went to Galicia to claim an inheritance that had belonged to his mother. He could not obtain it, because it had been incorporated into the Crown estates.

João Fernandes de Andrade, later known as João Fernandes do Arco because he lived in this parish (*freguesia*) and owned much land there, founded an entailed estate whose seat was the chapel of Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*). He died on 9 April 1527 and was buried there; his tomb bore the following epitaph: ‘Here lie João Fernandes and Beatriz de Abreu, his wife, who were the first founders of this Arco’. To his nephew, Fernão Dias de Andrade, son of his brother Diogo, John III confirmed by royal decree of 17 April 1528 the coat of arms granted to his uncle. It is transcribed in full in the *Nobiliario* of Henriques de Noronha, of which a copy exists in the Funchal library.
Andrade (Canon Dr João Jacinto Gonçalves de)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’) on 10 February 1825, the son of Lieutenant Francisco Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade and Dona Caetana Maria de Macedo. He attended the Funchal seminary and was ordained priest. Shortly afterwards he sailed for Brazil, where his uncle Dom Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade was a bishop and where his brother, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade, was a distinguished professor at the University of São Paulo. He settled in Vassouras and was carrying out his ministry there when, on the advice of Dr Francisco Justino, he enrolled in the Faculty of Law of the University of São Paulo and took his doctorate there. Shortly afterwards he sat a competitive examination for one of its chairs and was appointed professor, a post he held until 1891, when he retired.

He was a man of broad learning and taught at the university with distinction, although he could not match the high intellectual gifts and profound knowledge, above all in the legal sciences, of his brother Dr Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade, whom we have already discussed on p. 68 of this *Elucidario*. Dr João Jacinto de Andrade never gave up his ecclesiastical duties, to which he always devoted himself with deep love. He was an exemplary priest and as such enjoyed remarkable prestige in the city of São Paulo, where he lived for many years and where he died on 16 January 1898.
Andrade Corvo (João de)

This distinguished writer and man of science was in Madeira in 1853, commissioned by the Royal Academy of Sciences of Lisbon (*Academia Real das Sciencias de Lisboa*) to study the disease called *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium), which was then invading the vineyards of this island and destroyed a large part of them. As a result of his work he published the *Memórias sobre as Ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo*.
In the first memoir he promised the publication of two more, which never appeared. Andrade Corvo arrived on this island on 29 July 1853 and stayed here until the middle of the following September.
See Mangra of the vine.
Andrade (Dom Francisco José Rodrigues de)

He was the 22nd prelate of this diocese. Born in 1761, he was already 60 years old when he was called to the episcopate. At the time he was parish priest of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Nicolau in the city of Lisbon. He was presented as bishop of Funchal in 1821 and confirmed by Pope Pius VII on 21 September of the same year. He took possession of the bishopric by proxy on 1 March 1822 and assumed the government of the diocese on 1 May of the same year.

His episcopate was a highly turbulent one, beset with difficulties, because he headed this diocese during the troubled period that runs from the revolution of 1820 to the establishment of constitutional government in 1834. He could not, or did not know how to, hold a position of absolute impartiality between the two political currents that were clashing so violently. More than once, leaning now to one side and now to the other, he drew upon himself the ill will of opponents, who waged a relentless war against him and spared no means of discrediting him and belittling him before the public. Amid the political struggles that were fought, the deep hatreds and the designs of revenge that showed themselves day after day, it became impossible to follow the straight line of duty without equivocation or devious steps.

In the clash of party passions, he published one pastoral letter dated 28 June 1828 and another dated 13 September of the same year, in which the most contradictory political principles are defended and applauded. The first advocates the representative system and praises Dom Pedro; the second defends the system of absolute government and applauds the work of Miguel I. Despite the publication of his first pastoral letter, Dom Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade, fearful of the political events then unfolding, left Madeira on 10 July 1828, accompanied by many clergymen. In Lisbon he published his second pastoral letter, of 13 September of the same year, printed as a pamphlet of 27 pages, which is today very rare throughout the country.

After a few months he returned to his diocese, but the struggles and dissensions continued, and they truly ended only with his final departure from Madeira in 1834. On 5 June of that year the constitutional government was proclaimed in Madeira, and on the 12th of the same month Bishop Dom Francisco de Andrade entrusted the administration of the diocese to the cathedral chapter. On the following day he left the island for Italy.

Several clergymen went with him, among them Fathers António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Zeferino de Sant'Ana, António Alexandrino de Vasconcelos and António Gomes Neto. He chose the city of Genoa as his residence and, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Promontório, took refuge in the convent of San Bartolomeo del Fossato, there to endure the bitter days of exile. Not quite four years later he died there, on 2 May 1838, and was buried in the parish church of Promontório.

In 1891, a little over half a century later, the parish priest of Promontório was carrying out major repairs to his church. He thought of placing over the plain grave of Dom Francisco de Andrade a tombstone with an epitaph marking the place where the mortal remains of the Portuguese bishop lay. To this end he approached the illustrious prelate of this diocese, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who, with the help of some Madeiran priests, sent to Italy the necessary sum, amounting to some hundreds of mil-réis, for placing the stone on the tomb of Dom Francisco de Andrade. The stone, of fine marble, bears the prelate’s arms carved upon it and an inscription in bronze letters, which reads as follows:

*Franciscus Josephus Rodrigues d'Andrade / Domo Olisipone / Funchalensis in Madeira insula Pontifex / Lusitania civico turbata motu / extorris / a proximum S. Bartholo. monasterium - viribus. non animo fractus/in pace Requievit/Kal. Mai. Anno 1838/An. natus 77/Ne tanti viri pro patria sibi optatissima tanta heri perpessi / excederet memoria Emanuel Augustinus Barreto vir excellentis decessori suo / An. 1891.* (Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade, a native of Lisbon, Bishop of Funchal in the island of Madeira, exiled when Portugal was troubled by civil strife, broken in strength but not in spirit, rested in peace near the monastery of St Bartholomew on the Kalends of May in the year 1838, aged 77. Lest the memory of so great a man, who suffered so much for the homeland he so dearly loved, should fade, Manuel Agostinho Barreto dedicated this to his excellent predecessor, in the year 1891.)
Andrade (Dom Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de)

This prelate of the diocese of São Paulo (Brazil) was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’) on 14 March 1767, the son of Nicolau Gonçalves de Andrade and Maria de Andrade. In October 1826 he was confirmed as bishop of that diocese, and he was consecrated on 28 October of the following year. He died on 26 May 1847. We know of no other circumstances of this prelate’s life. He was the uncle of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade, whom we have already discussed in this work.
Andrade (Dean António Joaquim Gonçalves de)

This distinguished Madeiran was born in Funchal on 7 December 1795 and was ordained priest in 1821. We believe that he held a doctorate in canon law or in theology, but we cannot state this with certainty. He was a canon of our Cathedral, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and in 1834 he was secretary to Dom Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade when this prelate left Madeira and went into exile in Italy. Together with other clergy he accompanied his hierarchical superior, and they all took up residence on the outskirts of the city of Genoa.

On the death of Bishop Dom Francisco he settled in Lisbon, and from there he was summoned to Madeira in 1844 by the prelate of this diocese, Dom José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa. Protestant proselytism was then very active on the island, and the prelate was waging a fierce struggle against the propagandist Roberto Kalley and his followers. He needed at his side a man of prestige, prudence and learning to assist him in the arduous undertaking to which he was committed. Gonçalves de Andrade gave up the cultivation of letters, to which he was then actively devoting himself, and the close companionship he enjoyed with our leading men of letters, and came to live beside the prelate, to whom he rendered the most important and distinguished services. In 1846 he was appointed vicar general of this bishopric, and in 1853 dean of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*). When Empress Dona Amélia and her daughter, Princess Dona Maria Amélia, arrived in Madeira in 1852, Canon Andrade was appointed their chaplain and confessor, and he also served them as secretary. He was present at the last moments of the ill-fated princess, who held him in the highest regard and the deepest and most respectful esteem. Together with Dr António da Luz Pita, he was one of Empress Dona Amélia’s most devoted helpers in the definitive foundation of the Hospice, the hospice (*hospício*), and in the provisional installation of the hospital for tuberculosis patients, before the construction of the sumptuous building where it is housed today.
In 1853 Dean Andrade accompanied the mortal remains of Princess Dona Maria Amélia to Lisbon, and he settled there, remaining in the empress’s service.

António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade was a man of rare talent and wide intellectual culture. He enjoyed great prestige and esteem, not only for his gifts of mind but also for the eminent qualities of his character. In Lisbon he had been on terms of close friendship with the most prominent figures in letters and politics, who greatly valued his virtues, his learning and the charming simplicity of his manner.

He proved himself a writer of considerable merit in the learned notes he wrote for Castilho’s translation of Ovid’s *Fastos*, and in the annotations he added to the edition of António Cordeiro’s ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), published in 1862.
It is recorded that he left valuable unpublished writings, and it is also said that he possessed extremely valuable documents for the history of this archipelago, which have been entirely lost.

At the seminary (*seminário*) of this city he taught Latin, philosophy and theology, and he was a corresponding member of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Lisbon (*Academia Real das Sciencias de Lisboa*) and of other literary bodies in Portugal and abroad. He died in Lisbon on 16 January 1868 and lies buried in his own family vault (*jazigo*) in the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery in Funchal.
Andrade (Francisco de)

He was the son of Francisco de Andrade and was born in Funchal on 6 June 1806. He completed in this city all the studies that were available here in his day. By decree of 4 September 1838 he was appointed permanent holder of the chair of Portuguese and Latin grammar, and Portuguese and Latin classics, at the national lyceum (state secondary school) of Funchal. He had previously held the same post on an interim basis, by virtue of a letter from the Provincial Council of Public Instruction (*Conselho Provincial de Instrução Pública*) of 23 March of the same year. Works: *Princípios de Gramática Portuguesa* (Funchal, 1844); *Grammatica Portuguesa das Escholas Primarias*, a work that ran to five editions, the first in 1849 and the last in 1879; and *Relatório sobre as escholas municipaes de instrução primaria do concelho do Funchal...* (Funchal, 1849). He was a councillor (*vereador*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), secretary and rector of the lyceum, and one of the most distinguished teachers this secondary school ever had. He left some works in manuscript. He died in Funchal on 23 February 1881.
Andrade (Dr Francisco Justino Gonçalves de)

Among the Madeirans who achieved notable distinction abroad and brought great honour to their native land, one who stands out is Dr Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade. He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’) on 18 February 1821 and died in the city of São Paulo on 25 July 1902, the son of Lieutenant Francisco Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade and Dona Caetana Maria de Macedo.

At the age of 18, after studying at the Funchal Lyceum (*Liceu do Funchal*), he sailed for Brazil to seek his fortune. Recognising, however, that his vocation did not lie in the commercial life to which he had devoted himself, he enrolled in the Faculty of Law of the University of São Paulo, thereby following the advice he had received from his uncle, Dom Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, bishop of that diocese.

His university career revealed an extraordinary talent, and in it he won the most brilliant academic triumphs, completing his degree in juridical and social sciences in 1850. The following year he defended his theses and received his doctorate. Shortly afterwards, in a public competitive examination that became famous and in which he was placed first, he was appointed substitute professor (*lente substituto*) and later full professor (*lente catedrático*) at the University where he had been one of the most studious and distinguished students.

It was as professor of the chair of Civil Law that he truly made his name, and he was regarded as the foremost Brazilian civil lawyer of his time. As happened with those distinguished Madeirans Dr Patrício Moniz, Ferreira de Freitas and others besides, he left no work that matched his great merits or bore witness to his profound knowledge and vast erudition in the difficult and thorny speciality to which he devoted his whole life. Nevertheless, his lectures as a professor, the consultations sent to him from every part of Brazil, the high regard in which the most eminent Brazilian jurists held him, and the fact that he was appointed a member of the commission charged with reporting on the draft Civil Code (*Código Civil*) drawn up by the illustrious jurist Dr Felicio dos Santos amply prove that Dr Justino de Andrade possessed the talent and learning needed to have left an enduring work, one that would have displayed more eloquently the remarkable gifts of his privileged mind and his immense erudition.

He seldom took on court cases and almost entirely confined himself to answering the consultations frequently addressed to him; his opinions were respected as those of a great authority on the various questions of Brazilian civil law. He devoted all his time to study, leading a life of retirement and silence, wholly removed from politics and from anything that might disturb that thirst for knowledge which in him seemed to take the form of an almost morbid preoccupation.

Dr Justino de Andrade had no political or party leanings, but he was a devoted personal friend of Emperor Peter II, and that alone was enough for him to be dismissed as director of the Faculty of Law; retirement from his professorship was later imposed on him as a result of a conflict that arose within the Academy. We shall close this brief biographical sketch by saying that, if Dr Justino de Andrade commanded respect through the breadth of his knowledge, his brilliant talent and his rare capacity for work, he was no less esteemed for the unbending austerity of his character and his remarkable firmness of principle, which made him a great moral figure, deeply esteemed and admired throughout the Brazilian empire.
Andrade (Manuel Dias de)

He was born around 1585, the son of Francisco de Andrade and Dona Constança de Atouguia. He was the great-grandson and great-great-grandson respectively of Fernão Dias de Andrade and Diogo Fernandes de Andrade, to whom we refer in the article Andrade. He distinguished himself greatly as a soldier and took part in the recapture of Bahia, in which he commanded a galleon. He fought in other battles, in which he gave proof of his courage. He was a commander of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) and held the post of *mestre de campo* (colonel commanding a *terço*) in Brazil. He died in 1638 in the Cape Verde Islands, while serving as *mestre de campo* of a fleet bound for the recapture of Pernambuco.
Andrew (Robert Mc.)

Works: *On the geographical distribution of Testaceous Mollusca in the North Atlantic and neighbouring seas*, Liverpool, 1854. This work mentions 156 species of marine molluscs found by the author in Madeiran waters.
Sea anemones
Eleven species of these zoophytes are known in Madeiran waters, the commonest of which is *Anthus cereus*.
Anes (Gonçalo)

Gonçalo Anes, or Gonçalo Anes de Velosa, was one of the first settlers of this island. He was born in Celorico and had been a squire of Infante Ferdinand, son of King Duarte. He founded the church of São Bartolomeu, beside which he established a hospice (*hospício*) for poor clergy, which, it seems, never actually functioned. It served to lodge missionaries who called at Madeira on their way to India and Brazil. It was in this house and church that the Jesuits settled when they came to Madeira in 1570, and they remained there until the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*) was built. Gonçalo Anes founded an entail with the obligation of having a Mass celebrated in the said church every Friday for the soul of Infante Ferdinand. Gonçalo Anes died in 1497 and was buried in the church he had founded.

The chapel of São Bartolomeu (St Bartholomew) stood on the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’), in the Rua Direita (‘straight street’), which in former times extended as far as the present-day Ponte do Torreão (‘turret bridge’).
Angústias (cemetery)

In 1662 Diogo da Costa Quintal founded, on land belonging to his entailed estate (*morgadio*), the chapel of Our Lady of Sorrows (*Nossa Senhora das Angústias*), which gave its name to the street that ran close by and also to the surrounding locality (*sítio*). We cannot say today with certainty whether the chapel of Our Lady of Sorrows that stands on the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name (Quinta Lambert) is a reconstruction of the old chapel of the same dedication, nor whether the entailed property of Diogo da Costa Quintal perhaps lay there. We are, however, inclined to think so. It was in this locality of Angústias that the bishop of this diocese, Dom Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, while president (provedor) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), to which he rendered the most distinguished services, had a small cemetery built in 1818. It was intended exclusively for the burial of the bodies of those who died in the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal, and stood on land belonging to João de Carvalhal, who had given it free of charge for this purpose. When a law prohibited burials in churches, the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) obtained from the Holy House of Mercy the transfer of the small Angústias cemetery and asked João de Carvalhal, by then a count, to sell the adjoining land so that the cemetery could be enlarged. This nobleman promptly and generously offered the municipality all the land that might be needed for the planned enlargement, and informed the Council of this in a letter dated 8 July 1836.

Work on building the new cemetery began at once and was completed in May 1838. On 8 July of that year the cemetery was solemnly blessed by the vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence), António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga, in a ceremony of the greatest splendour and solemnity. The chapel was built some years later. The work of construction and decoration was completed in November 1844, and the chapel was blessed on 15 December of that year by the diocesan bishop, Dom José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa.

The cemetery’s paths were laid out later and in successive stages, the most recent having been made only a few years ago. The oldest, planned from the outset, is the one that runs round the whole cemetery alongside the boundary walls, with the exception of the central walk, which belongs to the original construction. The wooden door that closes the inner entrance of the cemetery came from the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi).

The church of this convent was the true necropolis of the old Madeiran nobility. Many families had their family vaults there, some of them of fine and costly marble. When the convent and church were demolished in 1865 so that a building intended as the town hall could be put up on the site, the tombstone covering the mortal remains of the founder was removed from inside the church and placed in the Angústias cemetery, and many bones exhumed during that demolition were laid beneath it. In the centre of the tombstone this epitaph was written: ‘Vault of the bones exhumed from the former convent and church of São Francisco (to which the original inscription refers), transferred on 2 May 1865.’ The original inscription carved around the edge of the stone reads: ‘Here lies Lois Álvares da Costa, who founded this house in the year 1473, and his son Francisco Álvares da Costa, first *ouvidor* and overseer of the royal treasury (*vedor da fazenda*) in these islands of Madeira.’ There are many private vaults and mausoleums in this cemetery, the most prominent being the one belonging to the Carvalhal family. When a man took his own life in this city on 4 March 1877, the episcopal authority – at that time the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who had arrived in Funchal and taken over the government of the diocese only a few days earlier – refused him church burial. Despite the prelate’s ruling, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) ordered the suicide to be buried in the section reserved for Catholics, whereupon the diocesan bishop placed the cemetery under interdict by a warrant (*provisão*) of 16 March 1877. The prelate addressed the matter with remarkable boldness from the pulpit of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) in a vehement sermon that became memorable. The affair was taken up by the press, which discussed it at length, each paper according to its own opinions. On this subject an interesting pamphlet entitled *A Sepultura Eclesiástica e os Suicidas*, written by Dr Cassiano Neves, was published in Porto; its chief aim was to rebut the claims of the newspaper *A Lei* (‘The Law’), then published in Funchal.

The Angústias cemetery holds the mortal remains of many distinguished Madeirans and also of others born outside Madeira, among whom we may mention Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça, Dean António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Dr António da Luz Pita, José António Monteiro Teixeira, the Count of Canavial, the Viscountess of Nogueiras, the Count and Countess of Carvalhal, Bishop Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, Canon Dr Augusto Frederico Castilho, etc., etc.

Within the grounds of this cemetery a fine monument was recently erected to commemorate the barbarous attack by German submarines, which bombarded the city of Funchal. It is dedicated in a very special way to perpetuating the memory of the dozens of victims of German ferocity who rest there, and whom a happy and pious initiative did not wish future generations to forget. On 3 December 1917, the first anniversary of that sorrowful and tragic event, the monument was unveiled after a religious service in the Cathedral. The ceremony was particularly splendid, and several speakers gave eloquent and patriotic speeches on the tribute about to be paid to those poor victims of German barbarity. The monument, which stands to the right of the cemetery entrance, is the work of the chisel of the prize-winning sculptor Francisco Franco and owes its existence to the praiseworthy initiative of the banker Henrique Vieira de Castro. He not only opened the subscription to pay for it with a generous *donativo* (nominally a ‘gift’ to the Crown; a compulsory war levy), but also promoted all the work from the start of construction to its final unveiling. The tomb-monument, which was entrusted to the care and upkeep of the Funchal Municipal Council, cost approximately two *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis) (see Bombardment of Funchal).
Bulwer’s petrel (Balweria bulweri)

A web-footed seabird of the family Procellariidae. It has dark plumage, and its clutch consists of a single egg, laid in crevices in the rocks. It lives and nests on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) and on the rocks of Ponta de São Lourenço and the islets of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Anjos

This locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas takes its name from the chapel of Our Lady of the Angels (*Nossa Senhora dos Anjos*). The chapel is of considerable age and was built, according to some, by order of the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son, the Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which Madeira belonged in spiritual matters; according to others, it was built by Martins Afonso in 1508. The image venerated in this chapel was the object of great devotion, and Friar Agostinho de Santa Maria discusses it in vol. X of his *Santuário Mariano*. The locality of Anjos, which is exceptionally fertile and forms the coastal strip of the parish of Canhas, was once part of the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’).
Cherimoya tree (Anona Cherimolia)

A tree native to Peru and New Granada, frequently grown in Madeira up to an altitude of 300 metres. Two varieties of cherimoya tree (*anoneira*) are known on the island: one with almost smooth fruit and one with fruit covered in protuberances of varying length. The first is the more highly prized. *Anona muricata* and *A. reticulata* are also grown in Madeira, but merely as curiosities.
Anson (Jorge)
This celebrated English privateer and voyager called at Madeira in September 1740, in command of a squadron of 8 ships bound to capture and plunder Spanish vessels in the Pacific Ocean.
Antas (Count of)

Major Francisco Xavier Pereira da Silva, later Count of Antas, who won great distinction in the campaigns for liberty, was in Madeira in 1828 to assist the governor and captain-general José Lúcio Travassos Valdez in the defence he was preparing against the attack of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) squadron. Pereira da Silva had arrived in Funchal from England on 20 August 1828 and was at once placed in charge of defending several strategic points on the heights of Caniço (‘reed’). The liberal forces, however, were compelled to yield to the invading troops, and this officer, together with Valdez and others, boarded the English corvette *Alligator* and sailed for England.
See Alligator (corvette) and Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelite troops.
Anthony Epic

By the Sociedade da Primeira Gente do Mundo. Funchal, 1879. It is the work of Messrs João José Vieira, Luís de Betencourt Miranda, Francisco João Moniz, Afonso Dias de Vasconcelos, João Silvestre Moniz and Pedro Cândido da Silveira, of whom only the first two are still alive. The Sociedade da Primeira Gente do Mundo met on a property in the locality (*sítio*) of Desterro (‘exile’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, belonging to the late Madeiran naturalist João Maria Moniz.
António Alfredo

António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga, a Franciscan ex-friar (*egresso*), was born in the city of Porto in the last quarter of the 18th century. Around 1820 he left the convent and became a secular priest. In the houses of his order he taught philosophy and theology with distinction, and in his day he was a notable and renowned preacher. Persecuted for his liberal ideas, he was deported to Cape Verde and then went on to Brazil. He returned to his homeland when constitutional government was established, and was then appointed canon of Évora Cathedral (*Sé de Évora*) and later governor of the dioceses of Bragança and Funchal; he also carried out other important public commissions.

By decree of 7 November 1834 António Alfredo was appointed temporal governor of the diocese of Funchal, a post he held until April 1840; by decree of 25 February of that year he was relieved of it and entrusted with another commission. He was a man of rare talent and wide learning, as his contemporaries testify, as do the speeches, pastoral letters and other occasional writings he left us. Nevertheless, his time at the head of this diocese was not marked by the most austere probity and scrupulous conduct. He became notorious, causing grave scandal, for the showy and solemn act of going in person to the Convent of São Bernardino (St Bernardino of Siena) in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) at the beginning of June 1835 to forbid the cult paid there to Friar Pedro da Guarda, known as the Holy Servant of God. In his presence he had the statue of the humble friar, which was venerated in a chapel beside the convent, burnt. He then published a pastoral letter condemning and forbidding any cult that anyone might seek to pay to Friar Pedro da Guarda.
He left this island for Lisbon on 14 April 1840, and in the same year was appointed governor of the diocese of Bragança. He died a few years later in the city of Porto.
In 1849, through the efforts of a relative, his *Miscellanea ou colecção de vários escritos* was published posthumously; only the first volume appeared.
Anthozoans

These marine animals, also called coralliaria, have been studied by the following authors. James Yate Johnson wrote, among other works: *Notes of the Sea-Anemones of Madeira, With Descriptions of New Species* (*Proceedings of the Zoological Society of London*, 1861); *Description of a Second Species of Acanthagorgia from Madeira* (ibid., 1861); *Descriptions of some New Corals from Madeira* (ibid., 1862); *Description of Two Corals from Madeira, belonging to the genera Trimnoa and Mopsea* (ibid., 1862); *Description of a New Species of Flexible Coral belonging to the Genus Juncella obtained at Madeira* (ibid., 1863); *Notes on the Coralliidae of Madeira, With Descriptions of two new Species* (ibid., 1899). John Edward Gray published *Notice of a Second Species of Paragorgia discovered in Madeira by James Yate Johnson* (*Annals and Magasine of Natural History*, 1862). P. Martin Duncan wrote *On some recent Corals from Madeira* (*Proceedings of the Zoological Society of London*, 1882).
Anthropology
See Madeira.
Apresentação

In the locality (*sítio*) of Lombo da Apresentação (‘ridge of the Presentation’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), there was a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Presentation (*Nossa Senhora da Apresentação*). It was founded in 1524 by João Mendes de Brito and was later incorporated into the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of the Heredia family, whose last representative was the Viscount of Ribeira Brava.
Araçá

Two species known as *araçás* are frequently grown in Funchal: *Psidium littorale* (yellow *araçá*) and *P. Cattheyanum* (purple *araçá*). Both are native to Brazil and belong to the myrtle family (Myrtaceae). Their fruit is tasty, and an infusion of their leaves can be used to treat diarrhoea.
Aragon

Aragão is an old and noble surname in Madeira, although the genealogists do not agree about the individuals who first bore it among us. It is said that the first person here to bear the name was António de Aragão e Teive, who settled on this island around 1500 and was married to Dona Helena de Atouguia. The distinguished Madeiran genealogist José Betencourt da Câmara states that ‘there are two branches of Aragão in Madeira: one descends from Henrique Aragão, who settled in Funchal around 1480; the other comes from Dom Afonso de Aragão, a Neapolitan knight whose real name is unknown, and who, either as a fugitive or as a pilgrim, reached this island around 1470. He lived at Calheta (‘small cove’), at the locality (*sítio*) that came to be called after him the Volta do Cavaleiro; he went on to the archipelago of the Azores and died there, having directed that the epitaph placed on his tomb should read: “Here lies the troubled Neapolitan”. He came already married, or married in Madeira, Teresa de Lira: his son, Lopo Dias de Lira Varela, knighted in Africa, was a *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the royal household in 1515, and a professed knight of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*)’.
Aragão (Dr João José de Freitas)

He was born in Funchal on 5 February 1777, and we believe that he belonged to the old and distinguished Aragão family of this island. We know little of his life. In 1821 he was practising law with skill in Lisbon when he was elected substitute deputy for Madeira to the Constituent Cortes (Portuguese parliament), which sat from 1821 to 1822. As the elected deputy, Dr António João Rodrigues Garcez, died before his credentials were verified, Freitas Aragão was called to fill the vacancy. He spoke several times in the Cortes, both on matters of general concern and on some relating to Madeira. The *Galeria dos Deputados das Cortes Constituintes. . . de 1821* says that João José de Freitas Aragão ‘spoke little, voted well, has constantly shown the best intentions and has given ample proof of wishing to fulfil the duties entrusted to him’. He died in Lisbon on 20 September 1842. An obituary of Freitas Aragão appears in no. 197 of the *Gazeta dos Tribunaes*.
Aragonite

Calcium carbonate; orthorhombic system. It occurs on the basalts of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). On Madeira it is found in several forms: in geodes; in transparent twinned crystals resembling hexagonal prisms, but with re-entrant angles between the prism faces; in groups of needle-shaped crystals (acicular form), etc.
Aranha

Among us this surname originates with Brás Dias Aranha, who lived in Funchal around 1600. There is a street in the city that was named after the Aranhas, because a family of that surname lived there; this was perhaps the family of Brás Dias himself or of his descendants.
Aranha (weever)

Name given to two fish of the weever family (Trachinidae), *Trachinus vipera* and *T. draco*. They do not live in deep water but are found close to the shore, preferring sandy places. They have the habit of burying themselves in the sand, leaving only the head uncovered. A sting from the opercular spines, and above all from the rays of the first dorsal fin, is highly venomous and can cause, besides terrible pain, violent inflammation, sometimes accompanied by fever. Fishermen and bathers have suffered serious accidents of this kind on the great beach of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where the two species are not rare.
Aranha do mar (Plagusia clavimanus)
