A decapod crustacean of the shores of these islands, which lives under the stones exposed at low tide. It is a bait much sought after by fishermen for catching wrasse (*bodião*). The name ‘sea spiders’ is also given to certain triangular crustaceans of the genus *Stenorynchus*, which live in deeper water and are vomited up by the *garoupa*, the *requeime* and other fish at the moment the fisherman frees them from the hook of his tackle.
Spiders

Ninety-nine species of spider are known in the Madeira archipelago, the largest of which is *Lycosa (Trochosa) ingens*, which lives on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’). The large black spider of Madeira is *Lycosa (Trochosa) Blackwallii*, and that of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is *L. tarentuloides maderiana*. *Epeira aurelia* (the ‘tarântula’ of the Madeirans) lives on spurge bushes (*tabaibeiras*) and other plants, fixing the threads of its webs to them; the country people say that in these webs it writes the name by which it is known. There is no record of the bite of *Epeira* producing notable swelling or inflammation; the bite of the *Lycosa* species, spiders that prefer dark places and holes and crevices in the rocks, is perhaps more dangerous. *Cyrtophora citricola*, recently introduced into Madeira by an English lady, is now found on trees, telephone wires, etc., etc. The spiders of the Madeira archipelago were recorded or described in a work published by Mr Władysław Kulczyński, of Kraków, in 1899. See Władysław Kulczyński, Fauvel and Ernst Schmitz.
Arrowroot (Maranta arundinacea)

A species of the family Zingiberaceae, cultivated at Madalena (‘Magdalene’). The method used there to extract the starch is to crush the roots in tubs and then wash the resulting pulp; this pulp is passed through sieves and finally put out in the sun to dry. Arrowroot, or *farinha de substância*, is widely used in broths as a restorative.
Araucaria

The tree that Madeirans call by this name is *Araucaria excelsa* of Norfolk Island, distinguished by its pyramidal shape and its whorled, horizontal branches. It belongs to the family Pinaceae and is grown in many *quintas* and gardens of Funchal.
Araújo

One branch of the family of this surname descends from Gonçalo Alves de Araújo, who came to this island at the end of the 15th century and held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’), for which reason he was known as Gonçalo Alves do Jardim. Another branch comes from Afonso Enes de Araújo.
Araújo (Dr Juvenal Henriques de)

He was born in Funchal on 21 November 1892, the son of João Isidoro de Araújo Figueira and Dona Virgínia Henriques de Araújo. He completed the course at our lyceum (state secondary school) in 1909 and graduated from the Faculty of Law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1914. While a student at the University he contributed extensively to various newspapers on the mainland and was one of the founders of the *Imparcial*, published in Coimbra. For some years he was on the editorial board of the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’), and he has contributed to other Madeiran newspapers. He practises law and published a pamphlet entitled *Acção de expropriação do Montado do Barreiro requerida pela Câmara Municipal do Funchal contra os proprietários do mesmo Montado*, Funchal, 1917, 19 pp. He is a permanent teacher at the ‘António Augusto de Aguiar’ Industrial and Commercial School and has carried out various public service commissions, being at present (1939) president of the board of the Funchal Commercial Association (*Associação Comercial do Funchal*). He was elected deputy for Madeira in 1922 and in successive legislatures, and is a member of the present Chamber of Deputies. In 1928 he published in a volume some of the speeches he had made in Parliament, under the title *Trabalhos Parlamentares*.
Araújo e Sousa (Manuel de)
). This Madeiran served in Brazil in the wars against the Dutch, distinguishing himself by his strenuous valour.
Afforestation

From 1562, the year in which this island was given its second Timber Regulations (*Regimento das Madeiras*), to the present day, governments and Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*) have often sought to promote the afforestation of our mountains and to prevent the destruction of woodland. The regulations (*regimento*) of 27 August 1562 – known to have been preceded by earlier ones dated 15 January 1515, of which no record survives in the municipal archives – recommended planting chestnut and pine trees on land suited to these species. They forbade the felling of trees without the Council’s licence, and such felling could in no case be permitted in places where there were springs or running water.

The archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) records many official acts showing that in the 17th and 18th centuries more care was taken over the conservation of the woods than today. In 1799 a nursery was established in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) which, according to a report submitted to the proper authorities by the inspector of agriculture, had distributed more than 20,000 trees between then and 10 August 1823.

The royal letter (*carta régia*) of 14 May 1804, calling for observance of that of 17 June 1800, ordered the sowing and planting on the mountain tops, on both Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), of whatever tree species the ground proved suited to. Unfortunately, of the seeds the government sent us on that occasion, very few belonged to species easily adapted to our soil and climate. *Abies canadensis* and *Robinia Pseudacacia* – the former grown on some *quintas*, the latter naturalised in many places around Funchal – were introduced into Madeira on 29 October 1800, the seeds having been sent by the government of John VI.

The said royal letter of 1804 also ordered the Councils to plant trees on municipal land and to proceed severely and without remission, in accordance with the Ordinances, Book 51, Titles 75 and 76, against those who set fire to the woods or cut down trees, while likewise observing the Timber Regulations of 1562.

The instructions of 18 October 1792 that Dr António Rodrigues Veloso de Oliveira left to the Council of the town (*vila*) of Calheta (‘small cove’) when he was there on circuit (*em correição*, the corregedor’s inspection tour) also contain some proposals concerning tree planting. On 15 October 1804 the governor Ascenso de Oliveira Freire urged the Councils of Ponta do Sol, Calheta and São Vicente to see to the afforestation of their municipalities and to the clearing of the streams. This governor also attended to the afforestation of the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal and to ways of raising livestock without harming the plantations.

On 3 May 1812 a communication was read at a session of the Funchal Municipal Council from the inspector of agriculture in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), reporting that 9,233 trees, including 4,795 mulberries, had been planted in his district.

On 9 November 1814 the interim government of Madeira ordered pine seed to be sown, and the Funchal Municipal Council did the same on the 14th of the same month and year, using for this purpose some land in the parishes of Santo António and São Martinho.

Around 1821 new stands of pines were created, the stone pine being the species most sought after for planting at that time. In 1840 the government ordered the fulfilment of a request, made the previous year by the Funchal Municipal Council, for twenty *moios* of pine seed.

It was during the period in which the benevolent Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro governed Madeira (1846–1852) that the cultivation of the maritime pine increased greatly here. The correspondence on the reforestation of the mountains exchanged between José Silvestre and the Municipal Councils and municipal administrators of the whole island deserves to be read by all who wish to form an exact and clear idea of the zeal and outstanding competence with which this official handled a matter so closely bound up with the prosperity of the land entrusted to his administration, as can be seen at length in the three volumes of the work *Uma Época Administrativa*.

From 1852 onwards, the only afforestation worth noting is the planting of a large number of trees along the banks of the State levadas (irrigation channels), ordered not many years ago by the District Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas*); the creation, after 1897, of some pine woods inside the old hedge (*bardo*) of the municipality of Funchal; and the consignment of various exotic and native species sent to the island of Porto Santo by the forestry services department, some of which are thriving there.

The tamarisk and *Myoporum accuminatum* are two species very well suited to the soils of Porto Santo. The first was introduced to that island by João António Pedroso in 1834, and the second by the distinguished botanist João Maria Moniz in 1893. If this latter species were properly exploited, large masses of greenery could be established within a few years on the treeless island of Porto Santo. As regards Madeira, we hold that it is the native flora that should supply the species needed to reforest the mountains. To prefer exotic trees to native ones for this reforestation, as has unfortunately been advised, is not only to set aside, without good reason, the forest wealth with which nature endowed the island, but also to hinder an improvement whose usefulness needs no demonstration.

We do not doubt that there are species from other regions capable of acclimatising in the mountainous parts of Madeira, and especially in the valleys of the interior. What we do not see is the need to rely solely on such species to restore our forests, when we have no fewer than thirty-two trees and shrubs suited to clothing the most varied terrains and altitudes of the island. Even if it were not our duty to preserve religiously the wild species that remain to us, the mere fact that all of them are better adapted to the island’s soil and climate would be reason enough to give them preference in the planting to be carried out.

Our woodlands have two implacable enemies: the shepherd and the charcoal burner. It is essential to put an end, in the most absolute manner, to the grazing of livestock and the making of charcoal. There must not be a single exception, either as to season or as to place. Only a radical measure of this kind, and only a prohibition extended without restriction to all cases and circumstances, will provide a wholesome and effective remedy for the great evil that must be fought. Let no one point to the existence of the decrees of 23 July 1913 and 22 September 1917. They were never enforced in full, and they no longer entirely serve their purpose.

It is a serious error to suppose that the raising of sheep, goats and pigs sustains a significant industry whose suppression might in any way harm the economy of the district. Suffice it to say that only a limited number of individuals engage in it, and for them it is not their sole livelihood, since they combine it with work as farmers or as simple rural labourers. In general the livestock graze freely, without herdsmen or shepherds, and are exposed to every kind of bad weather. There are no suitable pens or shelters to protect them from the harsh winters, and for this reason a very considerable number of animals always die every year. This weighty circumstance would in itself be enough, in any country, to justify an absolute ban on the free grazing of livestock on exposed mountains.

It is well known that livestock do great damage to plants that are still young and in full growth, but the luxuriant vigour of our forest vegetation largely overcomes the attack of the strong jaws of these ruminants. What the native abundance of our woodlands cannot overcome, however, is the harmful and criminal action of the shepherd.

Flocks do not find favourable pasture on land covered with dense forest. They need ground where fodder and low-growing plants predominate, as these are essential to the diet best suited to them. The shepherd therefore promptly prepares this desired pasture in a more or less extensive clearing, which the destructive force of the flames readily provides. This is usually how the great fires in our forests begin. Herdsmen do not hesitate for a moment to turn a forest of fine, stout trees, which took centuries to grow, into a barren expanse scorched by the devouring fire, so that it may soon become a grazing field to feed a meagre few dozen goats and sheep.

The damage caused by charcoal-making is so evident – not only through the countless fine trees lost to obtain this fuel, but also through the ever-present danger of starting a violent fire, as has so often happened – that there is no need to put forward a long train of arguments to condemn outright any permission for such a practice, whatever safety conditions might perhaps be invoked for that purpose.

We know that some felling of trees in the State forests is permitted, under conditions unknown to us. The most scrupulous care should be taken in granting such licences and, above all, the strictest supervision in carrying them out.

Given the favourable climatic conditions of our environment, if these measures are adopted and forest species for replanting are chosen with judicious selection, no one will doubt that within two or three decades this island may rightly regain the name of Madeira, ‘which from its many woods is so called’, in the hallowed phrase of the immortal singer of the *Lusiadas*.
See Livestock and Forest Police (*Polícia Florestal*).
Archdiocese of Funchal

Everyone knows that our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) was honoured as a metropolitan see and that it was the seat of an archdiocese. Its existence, however, was short-lived. Created in 1533, it had already been abolished by 1551. Our ever-growing colonial and maritime expansion from the beginning of the 15th century, together with the settlement and exploitation of the newly discovered lands, led first to the establishment of the bishopric of Funchal in 1514 and, twenty years later, to the creation of the dioceses of Angra, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Goa. Before these latter bishoprics were created, the idea arose of establishing an archdiocese to serve as the seat of an ecclesiastical province, with those dioceses, and any others that might later be created, as its suffragans. Funchal, as the first bishopric established outside mainland Portugal, was chosen as the seat of the new archdiocese, which comprised the aforementioned dioceses of Angra, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Goa. The Archbishop of Funchal extended his spiritual jurisdiction from the Madeiran archipelago to the farthest reaches of the East.

We do not know the date of the papal bull creating the archdiocese. In the ‘Portuguese Diplomatic Corpus’ (*Corpo Diplomático Português*) we find the consistorial schedules of 31 January and 11 February 1533: the first communicates to John III the establishment of the archdiocese, and the second concerns the appointment of the first archbishop, who was Dom Martinho de Portugal. The bull of creation is not included there. However, since the consistorial schedules announcing such an event generally bore the date of the creation itself, we shall not stray far from the truth in stating that the archdiocese was established by a bull of 31 January 1533 and that Dom Martinho de Portugal was appointed archbishop by a bull of 11 February of the same year.

Only six years after the archdiocese was established, a bull of 8 July 1539 stripped it of its four suffragan bishoprics, which passed to the jurisdiction of the Archbishop of Lisbon. The first and only Archbishop of Funchal, Dom Martinho de Portugal, died in 1547, but the archbishopric was not filled. It was abolished in 1551, four years after his death, by the bull *Super universis*.

The circumstances surrounding the creation, dismemberment and later abolition of the archbishopric lead us to share the opinion of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, who asserts that the elevation of the bishopric of Funchal to an archdiocese was a personal favour from John III to a close relative and friend, and perhaps a reward for the services that Dom Martinho de Portugal had rendered the monarch as his ambassador in Rome.

‘Dom Martinho de Portugal, by divine mercy Archbishop of Funchal, Primate of the Indies and of all the new lands discovered and yet to be discovered’: this was how the new archbishop styled himself in the documents he issued in the exercise of his office.

The four ‘maces’ that, even today, are carried by clerics before the prelate at great ceremonies in our Cathedral are the only trace that the archdiocese has left here. These ‘maces’ symbolised the four suffragan bishoprics that belonged to the archbishopric of Funchal. Once the archdiocese was abolished, Funchal reverted to the simple status of a bishopric. To its jurisdiction over the Madeira archipelago was added the castle of Arguin, on the coast of Senegal, which some years later ceased to belong to this diocese.

We shall deal with Archbishop Dom Martinho de Portugal in a separate article. The bull of 8 July 1539 cited above, which is of great interest to the ecclesiastical history of Madeira, was translated in full into Portuguese and published in several issues of the newspaper *O Correio do Funchal* (‘Funchal Courier’) in March 1898.
Archivista (O)
The first issue appeared on 7 December 1850 and the last on 27 December 1851; 56 issues were published in all.
Navy and Overseas Archive

Until 1834 the Madeira archipelago was an overseas province and colony whose administration came chiefly under the Navy Ministry. In that year, with the creation of the island districts, it became part of the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes), with an administration entirely identical to that of the mainland districts. The official correspondence sent from Madeira at that time was addressed mainly to the Minister of the Navy and to the Overseas Council (*Conselho Ultramarino*), which handled a large part of the business concerning the administration of our overseas provinces. The valuable and extremely numerous documents on our colonial administration held at the Ministry of the Navy and Overseas were moved a few years ago to the National Library in Lisbon (*Biblioteca Nacional de Lisboa*), where they were duly arranged and catalogued. The worth of this priceless treasure then became better known, as did the outstanding service these papers could render to any studies that might be undertaken on the whole of our colonial and maritime life. When the National Library created the Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*) section, which comprises some thousands of codices and a countless number of loose documents, Dr Eduardo de Castro e Almeida was entrusted with inventorying and cataloguing them. He began his arduous and most useful task by arranging the loose manuscripts relating to Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), which cover the period from 1613 to 1833. Under the title *Biblioteca Nacional de Lisboa. Archivo da Marinha e Ultramar. inventario . . . Madeira e Porto Santo, I, 1613-1819*, he published in 1907 a volume of 402 pages in folio, and in 1909 volume II, of 487 pages in the same format. Together they form a rich and most valuable repository of news and information, absolutely indispensable to anyone wishing to study the history of this archipelago in the period to which those documents refer.

Dr Castro e Almeida did not confine himself to a simple inventory, as he modestly titles his important work. Besides cataloguing the various documents in chronological order, with a brief indication of their subjects, he gives several extracts of their most interesting passages, according to the nature and importance of the matter, always chosen with the soundest and most discerning judgement. As we were able to verify in person, these documents relating to Madeira, numbering more than ten thousand, are carefully kept in sheet-iron boxes, duly numbered and placed on shelves, so that with the inventory in hand it is extremely easy to find the manuscript one wishes to consult.

In the two volumes of the Navy and Overseas Archive containing the inventory and catalogue of the documents concerning our archipelago, we found many notes and details that served as a valuable aid for some of the articles in this *Elucidario*.

Among the hundreds of codices belonging to the Navy Ministry and now deposited in the Public Library of Lisbon, many valuable documents concerning Madeira will undoubtedly be found; but only a lengthy search of an official character could bring them to light and give them the due and indispensable publicity.
Archivo Literario (O)
The first issue was published on 15 April 1863 and no. 241, the last, on 2 November of the same year. João de Nobrega Soares was its principal editor.
Deaneries

A few years ago the Diocese of Funchal was divided, for the purposes of its ecclesiastical administration, into four deaneries (*arciprestado*, group of parishes under an archpriest), or groups of parishes. They are: that of Funchal, which comprises the parishes of the municipalities of Funchal, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava and Porto Santo; that of Calheta (‘small cove’), covering the parishes of the municipalities of Calheta and Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’); that of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), made up of the parishes of the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico; and that of São Jorge (‘St George’), comprising the parishes of the municipalities of Santana, São Vicente and Porto Moniz. The office of archpriest is filled by episcopal appointment and held by one of the parish priests of the deanery.
Arco da Calheta (parish)

Calheta (‘small cove’) was an important settlement from the earliest days of colonisation, and it lent its name to other localities that grew up in its immediate vicinity. Such were Estreito and Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). The name Arco (‘arc’) comes from the distinctive semicircular shape of its hills. These orographic features, as also happens elsewhere on the island, fully explain the name the first settlers gave it. This parish (*freguesia*) was created in 1572. Its seat was established in the chapel of São Brás (St Blaise), although it should be noted that religious services had already been held there before that year by its own original chaplain, as in other places, for Arco was then a settlement of some importance with a sizeable number of inhabitants. Brás Ferreira, one of the oldest settlers of this parish, is named as the founder of the chapel of São Brás, as he himself states in his will made in 1493; but João Fernandes de Andrade is also regarded as the man who had it built, for his wills made in 1520 and 1523 refer clearly to this. João Pedro de Freitas Drumond and the annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) note this glaring discrepancy, the latter saying that Brás Ferreira had left a bequest for the building of the chapel, but that it was actually built only by João Fernandes de Andrade. He died on 9 April 1527 and was buried in the said chapel, and it is recorded somewhere that the following epitaph could be read on his tomb: ‘Here lie João Fernandes and Beatriz de Abreu his wife, who were the first founders of this Arco.’

It was the royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 June 1572 that authorised the creation of a curacy (*curato*) held by a beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) with the powers of a vicar, with an annual salary set at 13,000 réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto). The royal decree of 10 July of the same year added 110,000 réis on the appointment of the first parish priest, Friar Pedro Delgado, and the royal decree of 20 April 1589 made a further addition of half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine. It seems that other royal instruments later increased the stipend (*côngrua*) of the parish priest still further. The diocesan prelate, Dom Friar António Teles da Silva, under the authority granted by the royal decree of 28 December 1676, created a curacy in this parish with an annual salary of 12,000 réis in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine, paid for by the ‘third superfluous beneficed cleric of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’)’. An old book in the parish archive states that this curacy was one of the best in the whole bishopric.

Before this parish was created, its inhabitants belonged to the parish of Calheta, where they fulfilled their religious obligations; some of these came to be observed in the chapel of São Brás once it had its own chaplain. At a date we cannot determine, a nave was added to the chapel of São Brás, which became the chancel of the new church. As the population grew, the church became too cramped, and the diocesan prelate ordered that the king be petitioned to build a new one. By order of the Treasury Council (*Conselho de Fazenda*) of 30 October 1744, the building of a new church was awarded by public auction (*arrematação*) to Cristóvão Gomes for the sum of 9,350,000 réis. We do not know when construction began, but it was declared complete in December 1754. The solemn blessing of the new church took place on 1 January 1755. Other additional works were carried out over time, and its tower was built in 1830.

Arco da Calheta was one of the first places on this island to be farmed on a large scale after the discovery. Its first settlers included João Fernandes de Andrade (see Andrade), who added the name ‘do Arco’ to his own because of the vast lands he held here as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation); his brother Diogo Fernandes de Andrade; Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, grandson of João Gonçalves Zarco; Gonçalo Fernandes; and others besides. Large “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*) grew up there, with their manor houses, chapels, sugar mills (engenho) and cultivated land.

Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘A quarter of a *légua* from Madalena (‘Magdalene’) lies the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) that belonged to Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, husband of Dona Joana de Eça, chief lady of the bedchamber to the queen: it is a very rich estate, with a sugar mill and much land under cane, large ranges of houses, and a church with its chaplain. A quarter of a *légua* from this *lombada*... lies another, called the Arco or Lombada do Arco, which belonged to João Fernandes, brother of Gonçalo Fernandes, likewise a very rich estate, with a sugar mill and much land under cane, large ranges of houses, a church and a chaplain.’

João Fernandes do Arco left many descendants. Particularly worthy of mention is António de Abreu, the discoverer of the Moluccas, of whom we have already spoken above and who was probably born in this parish (*freguesia*). Also a daughter of João Fernandes was the celebrated heroine of the abduction carried out by António Gonçalves da Câmara, to whom we have already referred under the name of Isabel de Abreu.

Gonçalo Fernandes, a mysterious figure mentioned in the old Madeiran chronicles, of whom we shall speak in a separate article, had a residence and a *sesmaria* in this parish. The parish has the chapels of Our Lady of Loreto, Our Lady of Nazaré, the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*), Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) and Nossa Senhora da Vida. Of the old chapels of Our Lady of the Flight into Egypt (*Nossa Senhora do Desterro*) and Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora only a few heaps of rubble remain today. Other chapels once existed that have vanished completely: those of Our Lady of Ransom (*Nossa Senhora das Mercês*), Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*), Nossa Senhora da Visitação, Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, Santo António and Santa Maria Madalena.

Almost all these chapels were entailed foundations (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela), and some of them were the head and seat of various entailed estates (*morgadio*), of which there were not a few in this parish. Among them we shall mention that of Píncaro (‘pinnacle’), founded by Braz Ferreira, the original founder of the chapel of São Braz, which, says an old manuscript, ‘began at the estate surrounding the parish church and continued along this line straight from the sea to the uplands, as far as the Pinheiro. . .’; the entailed estate founded by Iria Pires, later enlarged by its administrator Pedro Barreto, ‘which lies along the line of the Ribeira do Ledo, which bounds it to the north, and so continues as far as the Cova do Arco’; the entail of Consolação (‘consolation’), which today belongs to the house of Torre Bela and seems to have been joined to that of Píncaro; the important entailed estate founded by Gonçalo Fernandes, headed in the chapel of Conceição (‘Conception’) at Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’); that of Loreto, created by Dona Joana de Eça; the entail (*morgado*) whose seat was the chapel of Nazaré (‘Nazareth’), founded by Antónia de Cristo and her sister Leonarda do Horto; that of Florenças, founded by João Homem de El-Rei; and others besides.

The popular uprising that broke out in 1834 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta, with such grievous consequences (see Calheta), also spread to the parish of Arco: the people rioted and joined those of that parish, though we cannot say whether any parishioner of Arco da Calheta was among the victims. In 1887 the sad and notorious events surrounding the parish councils (*juntas de paróquia*) (see that entry), which in many parts of the island drove the people to the most extreme violence, also found a loud echo in the parish of Arco. The people rose up, threatening to break out into deplorable excesses, and seized the opportunity to demand the right to pay the landlords a third of the harvest instead of the half-share (*dimídia*, half of the harvest owed to the landlord) that they then paid, and which, despite everything, they continued to pay. The intervention of armed forces was needed, and they seem to have committed reprehensible excesses there. This parish has three state schools: one for boys, in the locality (*sítio*) of Ledo; one for girls, in the locality of Ladeira (‘slope’) e Lamaceiros (‘mud flats’); and one mixed school, in the locality of Lombada (‘long ridge’).
Arco da Calheta is irrigated mainly by a branch channel of the important Levada do Rabaçal and by the levada known as the Levada da Madre Grande, which rises in the Paul da Serra.

It borders the parishes of Madalena do Mar, Canhas and Calheta. It lies about 4 kilometres from Calheta, the seat of the municipality (*concelho*), approximately 7 kilometres from Ponta do Sol, the seat of the judicial district (*comarca*), and 34 from Funchal.

Its principal localities are Fajã, Ledo e Vinhatico, Fonte da Bugia e Luzirão, Ladeira e Lamaceiros, Fonte do Til, Fajã do Mar, Pombal e Fazenda Grande, Chada, Palheiros, Amoreiras, Paredes, Cova do Arco, Corujeira, Pomar Velho, Bagaceiro, Maçapez, Cales e Chada, Lombada do Loreto, Florenças and Pinheiro. The last three are extremely picturesque and command beautiful panoramas. Special mention must also be made of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Rochão, which offers the visitor an enchanting landscape and one of the widest and most striking views in the whole municipality.

Its patron saint is St Blaise, whose feast the Church celebrates on 3 February. There is an annual pilgrimage to the chapel of Loreto, with a large and well-attended *arraial* (open-air popular festival at a church feast), held on 7 and 8 September. The population of this parish is 4,639 inhabitants.
Arco de São Jorge (parish)

This small parish lies between the parishes (*freguesias*) of São Jorge (‘St George’) and Boaventura (‘good fortune’), about six kilometres from the parish church of the former and roughly two from the parish church of the latter.

The shape of the hills that surround it is explanation enough of the name it still bears. It belonged to the parish of São Jorge from the latter’s creation in 1517 until it was separated from it in 1676, and so it quite naturally took the name of Arco de São Jorge (‘arc of São Jorge’), which is much older than the date of its creation.

One of the first settlers of Madeira was Pedro Gomes Galdo, who held extensive lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in São Jorge and Boaventura, and it may be presumed that these included the land that later formed the parish of Arco de São Jorge. We cannot know when Arco began to be settled or when the clearing of its land began, but it seems to us that this would have been towards the end of the 15th century or in the first quarter of the 16th, and long before the creation of the parish of São Jorge.

On the spot now occupied by the locality (*sítio*) of Casais (‘hamlets’) there once stood a small chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*). The year of its foundation is unknown, but we presume that it must date from the third or last quarter of the 16th century. It had its own chaplain, who performed the religious services there under the authority of the vicar of São Jorge. It was this chapel that served as the seat of the new parish, created by the diocesan prelate Dom António Teles da Silva under the authority granted by the royal decree (alvará régio) of Peter II of 28 December 1676.

Long before the parish was created, the chapel of Our Lady of Pity was already in a lamentable state of repair and threatening imminent ruin. Only ten years after the parish seat had been installed there, Bishop Dom Estêvão Brioso de Figueiredo, who visited it in person, ordered that the immediate construction of a new church be requested, because of the cramped dimensions of the small chapel, which he considered unfit to serve as the parish church. It was only half a century later, by order of the Council of the Exchequer (*Conselho de Fazenda*) of 18 January 1740, that the building of the new church was ordered. It was blessed on 19 March 1744 by the vicar of the time, Father Manuel da Costa.

We know that Fathers João Batista and José de Andrade were chaplains of the chapel of Our Lady of Pity before the parish was created, the latter priest being the first to serve there as parish priest. He was succeeded, as curates of souls, by Fathers Francisco da Costa, Francisco Manuel Pereira, Bartolomeu Marques Caldeira, Joaquim Baptista Catanho, Bernardo Ribeiro, etc.

This small parish is perhaps the most fertile in the whole of the north of the island. It produces every kind of crop, and its land is especially well suited to growing sugar cane. Its output would be greater, however, were it not short of irrigation water: a considerable part of its land is cultivated only with cereals and vegetables, and even then is left at the mercy of the rains. To remedy these drawbacks, it is essential to build a levada (irrigation channel) which, drawing its water at the locality (*sítio*) of Falca in the parish of Boaventura, would irrigate much land in this parish and also in Arco de São Jorge. The surveys and plans were drawn up more than thirty years ago, when the works were estimated at about thirty *contos* (one million réis) de réis. In the legislative session of 1890 the deputy Canon Feliciano João Teixeira championed this important improvement in the national parliament, but work never began, and the construction of the levada remained no more than a plan.

The fertility of the soil in this parish goes hand in hand with its healthiness and the mildness of its climate. The mortality rate is low, and there have been epidemics on this island, such as the cholera of 1856, that never reached it. The climate is among the gentlest and most temperate of the whole north coast; high mountains shelter the settlement from the harsh, biting winds of winter. This does not, however, rule out the appearance in this parish of common illnesses and even epidemic diseases, as happens everywhere. Thus we know that in 1768 a disease of an epidemic character raged there and claimed many victims. On that occasion the surgeon of the parish of Boaventura, António Rodrigues Seabra, rendered outstanding services, and the fabric fund of the parish church contributed substantial donations to combat the epidemic. In 1849, too, a disease then classified as diarrhoea broke out in this parish, killing many people, while countless individuals fell ill. The civil governor of the district at the time, the public-spirited Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, went there in person, accompanied by two physicians and the necessary means to treat the sick, and the disease died out within a short time. (See *Epocha Administrativa*, vol. 2, p. 506 ff.)

The principal localities (*sítios*) of this parish are Igreja, Casais, Lagoa, Poços, Arco Pequeno and Quebrada. The last owes its name to the great landslide (*quebrada*) that came down there more than two centuries ago, when a great deal of land broke away, chiefly from Arco Pequeno, and gave rise to that locality. Such events are common in Madeira: the parish of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’), part of the parish of Paul, the locality of Lugar de Baixo (‘lower place’) and others besides were formed in the same way. At the Quebrada of Arco de São Jorge, however, a most singular circumstance occurred which deserves special mention. We have found several references to it, for instance in the *Noticias Mineralogicas da Ilha da Madeira* by Dr Pereira Drumond, published in 1818 in the *Investigador Portuguez*, and in other Portuguese and foreign authors, and these references tally perfectly with local tradition, which still preserves the account of the event intact. Interesting details of this extraordinary occurrence are found in a letter discovered in 1848 in the Public Library of Lisbon (*Biblioteca Pública de Lisboa*) by General António Pedro de Azevedo, of which some years ago a Funchal newspaper published the curious extract that we reproduce below (see *Verdade*, no. 944): ‘I send Your Honour this news because it is a marvellous event. Behind the island, at Arco de São Jorge, the greater part of which is an estate of my entail (*morgado*), the ground had for many years been split open by a great fissure. The land being very steep, with the heavy winter rains of this year, at midnight on Easter Day the earth slid in great quantity into the sea for about half a *légua*, pushing the boulders and shoals before it so gently that the houses, trees and vine trellises remained standing. In one house two casks of wine on their supports (*canteiro*, natural ageing of the wine in casks on wooden supports, without artificial heating) did not overturn, a beehive on a stone slab did not fall, and a hen sitting on her eggs, tied to the foot of a fig tree – all were found there with no change and no disturbance of the ground. It formed an island in the sea of some twenty *moios* of sowing land, which is joining up with this one. It made a beach with two fine harbours, which that part needed, for being a shoal nothing could be shipped there. Where the land slid away there remained a hollow, with a sheer cliff above and below a *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) of excellent new land reaching down to join the part in the sea, where before there had been a very high cliff dropping to the sea. And it slid without a crash and without being felt, except by one man who, seeing it moving in the night, was struck by a seizure; it went like a boat being launched into the sea running over its slipway timbers. And the marvel is that for some days before, along the whole width of the land that slid, the tide neither rose nor fell for three days, and the sea lay as if dead, while on either side it ebbed and flowed with the usual waves of the northern sea.’
This took place in the year 1689, and if it occurred on Easter Sunday, as the letter states, it must have been on 20 April of that year.

The most distinguished son of this parish was António Gil Gomes, whom we shall discuss at greater length in the appropriate place. Also a native of the parish was António Januário Moderno, born on 25 February 1789, the son of Captain João Rodrigues Moderno and Dona Antónia da Incarnação Moderno. He was superintendent (*provedor*) of Machico, which then included the municipality (*concelho*) of Sant’Ana, and held other public offices. In his day he was famous throughout the island, not only for the gallant and hospitable way in which he received guests at his house in Arco, but above all for the herculean strength with which he was endowed; the many remarkable feats of strength and daring he performed made him feared and respected. In London, where he lived as a political exile, he also became known among his compatriots for his courage and the might of his arm. He died in Funchal on 11 October 1864. His son was Dr António Januário Moderno, who graduated in medicine from a foreign university and practised with great success and skill in the United States of America, where he made a large fortune. He too was a native of the parish of Arco de São Jorge. He spent almost his entire life away from Madeira, but died in this city some thirty years ago, shortly after returning to his native land. He had earned a reputation as a man of exceptional talent and an eminent physician. He died in Funchal, aged 67, on 11 February 1885.

The distinguished priest António Alexandrino de Vasconcelos was born in the parish of Boaventura in 1791, but lived for more than forty consecutive years in Arco de São Jorge, where he died in 1884. He was vicar general of the bishopric and held other important posts. In 1834 he accompanied the prelate Dom Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade when the latter was forced into exile and set out for Italy. He was a churchman of remarkable intelligence and learning, and was regarded as a great authority on the various branches of Catholic liturgy.

The patron saint of this parish was Our Lady of Pity until 1744, when it became St Joseph, at the time the new church was built. By the papal briefs of 24 and 26 August 1784 the altar of the chancel was declared a privileged altar, and a plenary indulgence was granted, to be gained on the feast of St Joseph. We have found somewhere the curious information that the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Francisco Aurélio da Câmara Leme charged the third of his estate with a perpetual obligation to supply the oil needed to light the Blessed Sacrament in the church of Arco de São Jorge. His son and heir, the holder of the entail Francisco António da Câmara Leme, ratified and took on this obligation by a public deed executed on 18 February 1766, the charge falling ‘on the *quinta* (country estate) before Santo Amaro’.

Among the rural parishes of this island outside the municipal seats, Arco de São Jorge was until a few years ago the one with the lowest rate of illiteracy, which, as is well known, is so deeply and lamentably rooted here. This is owed to the zeal with which some parish priests provided primary teaching there. Special mention is due to Father Isílio Joaquim Vares, in the second quarter of the 19th century, and later to Fathers Emílio Marques da Silva, Francisco Manuel de Sousa, Francisco António de Abreu and Casimiro Augusto de Freitas. On 16 January 1886 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Sant’Ana founded an official boys’ school in Arco de São Jorge, which has rendered valuable service there. Some years later this school was turned into a mixed school.

This parish belongs to the municipality of Sant’Ana and the judicial district (*comarca*) of São Vicente, whose seats lie about twelve and a half kilometres away. It is some forty-one kilometres from Funchal by the Poiso road, and thirty-seven by way of Curral das Freiras and Boaventura. Its population is 167 inhabitants. We cannot fail to mention that this parish was the birthplace of the celebrated popular troubadour Manuel Gonçalves, known as Manuel Feiticeiro, who died a few years ago. He travelled the whole island singing his naive poetic compositions, much loved by the crowds, who listened to him eagerly and enraptured and bought the dozens of pamphlets in which he collected and printed his countless, faulty songs.
See Popular poetry.
Arco de São Jorge (peak)
This lofty height, 837 metres above sea level, towers over the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name.
Arco de São Jorge (landing place and beach)
On the coast of this parish (*freguesia*) there is a small, poor landing place, served by a short beach where disembarking is difficult.
Areeiro

Not far from the well-known locality (*sítio*) of Poiso (‘resting place’), but already within the mountains of the island’s interior, stands the Pico do Areeiro (‘sand-pit peak’), which reaches an altitude of very nearly 1,800 metres above sea level.

Meteorological and climatological studies had not yet reached the level of development of our own time when, half a century ago, the idea arose here in Madeira of setting up one or more weather stations on the highest points of our mountains. Their observations, combined with those of the Funchal Meteorological Station (*Posto Meteorológico do Funchal*), would provide valuable material for the study of the Madeiran climate, and especially for comparing the climate of our island with that of other renowned health resorts.

In 1895 the central government had some houses built on the slopes of the Pico do Areeiro to accommodate a weather station and to serve as the residence of its staff. About five *contos* de réis (*conto* (one million réis)) were spent on them, and the upkeep of the buildings was entrusted to the district Public Works Department (*Direcção das Obras Públicas*). When the Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) was created in 1911, the Areeiro (‘sand pit’) Meteorological Station passed to this administrative body. In 1919 it came into the possession of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), when the Agricultural Board was abolished, leaving a sorry memory in the pages of Madeiran history.

Once those buildings were finished, however, what many had already predicted came to pass: the station had not been supplied with the essential instruments, and the staff needed to run it properly had never been appointed. Exposed to every kind of weather and to the frequent gales that sweep the area in winter, the building soon began to suffer extensive damage and quickly fell into an advanced state of ruin. The vandalism of the woodcutter and the cattle-herder completed the destruction that the storms had begun, and the supervising authorities made no beneficial effort to put an end to such criminal neglect. Thus the former Public Works Directorate (*Direcção das Obras Públicas*), the Agricultural Board and the District General Council not only always showed the utmost indifference to the operation of the Meteorological Station created by the government of mainland Portugal, but also allowed the buildings erected for that purpose on one of the slopes of Pico do Areeiro to collapse and disappear.

Neither the protests of the press nor even the good offices of certain official bodies could save them. The matter became the subject of bitter irony in various foreign publications, notably a scientific journal in Middelburg, which remarked that more attention was paid to the study of meteorology in Turkey than in Portugal, since there was no record there of observatories without instruments or observers, as was the case in the Portuguese possession of the island of Madeira.

The distinguished Madeiran Guilherme Teles de Menezes, who for health reasons lived for some months in 1894 and 1895 in the localities (*sítios*) of Poiso and Areeiro, made a number of meteorological observations there. These were published in the press and received the most complimentary remarks from people versed in the subject.
Areias

This is the name given to the central part of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), which is covered by a thick layer of sand. The sand came from some small dunes in the north-west of the island, and to stop it advancing, windbreaks of pines, *canas de roca* and *árvores do paraíso* were planted. In the locality (*sítio*) of Areias there are large vineyards.
Areias (Calhau das)
A small landing place on Deserta Grande (the Desertas).
Madeiran herring (Clupea maderensis)

A fish common in the coastal waters of the archipelago. It is sometimes caught in large quantities in drag nets or set nets. It is not considered one of the best edible species and is in fact inferior to its counterpart in the seas of northern Europe.
Areusco

The name given on Porto Santo to poor land of calcareous sand, partly mixed with more or less clayey soil. The more demanding crops grow in it only with difficulty, and so it is usually used only for growing rye.
Arfet (Ana de)
See Robert Machin.
Arguin

On the edge of the coasts of the Sahara and Senegal, at about latitude 22° N and longitude 7° W, there is a cove, an archipelago, a bank and a strip of the African mainland coast, all bearing the name of Arguin. The largest and most important of the islands of this small archipelago, which is also called Arguin, is the one that concerns the history of Madeira, for it belonged to the ecclesiastical jurisdiction of the diocese of Funchal. The island of Arguin, which lies only about one *légua* (league, about 5 km) from the African coast, was discovered by Nuno Tristão around 1443. Trade with the natives of the mainland began at once, and it was soon recognised that, to ensure the success of this trade and Portuguese dominion in those parts, a fortress was absolutely necessary; its construction began around 1450. With the new discoveries and the great centres of trade established everywhere, Arguin gradually lost its importance, above all after the appearance of the colonies and trading posts of Senegal. Arguin had mixed fortunes, passing successively under the rule of the English, the Dutch and the French, and today it is completely abandoned. After the fortress had been built and Portuguese dominion secured, priests went there from Funchal to perform their religious services. We do not know when Arguin ceased to belong to the Portuguese, nor at what time the bishops of this diocese also ceased to have real jurisdiction over those parts, a jurisdiction that long ago became merely honorary. For more than forty years the prelates of Funchal have no longer styled themselves bishops of Arguin.
Arja
See Darja.
Arms
The following municipalities of the archipelago have their own arms: Funchal, Machico, Porto Santo, Ponta do Sol, Santa Cruz, Calheta, São Vicente and Câmara de Lobos.

The original arms of the municipality of Funchal consisted of five sugar loaves on a field of silver, arranged in a cross, with a sugar cane on each side of the shield. Later one of the canes was replaced by a vine branch. The old arms, however, appear on a bronze *quintal* (old weight of four arrobas, c. 59 kg) weight dated 1580, which served as the standard weight in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal, and also on the copper coins struck in 1750 for circulation solely in the archipelagos of Madeira and the Azores.

The arms of the municipality of Machico are the armillary sphere; those of Porto Santo, the dragon tree; those of Ponta do Sol, the sun; those of Santa Cruz, five castles, and above the shield, beneath which is the date 1515, a small escutcheon bearing the *quinas* of Portugal; those of Calheta (‘small cove’), the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove; those of São Vicente, the saint of that name; and those of Câmara de Lobos, two wolves, between which appear the shield with the castles and the small escutcheon with the *quinas* of Portugal.

Dr Azevedo says in his notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) that everything suggests the original arms of Funchal were granted by Manuel I. This is partly because that king ennobled the city as much as he could, and partly because the arms themselves show that they date from the time when the growing of sugar cane and the making of sugar were the wealth of the island of Madeira and its sole claim to fame.

In 1750 one of the canes had not yet been replaced by a vine branch, since, as we have already said, the original arms appear on the Madeiran coins struck in that year. In 1798 the two sugar canes still featured in the arms of the municipality of Funchal, as can be seen on a silver inkstand in the old chamber where the council sessions were held. By 1837, however, one of the canes had been replaced by a vine branch, although no resolution authorising this change is recorded in the minute books. The presence of the Council’s arms, already modified, on the spines of many old books in the municipal archive means nothing, for everything suggests that these books were bound only in the 19th century. The record (*auto*) of a vow transcribed on p. 726 of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ shows that in 1523 it was resolved that the image of St James the Less should be painted ‘na bamdeyra & sello da çidade’ (on the banner and seal of the city), but we have no proof whatever that this resolution was ever carried out.

After the proclamation of the Republic, the ducal coronet that crowned the arms of the city of Funchal was replaced by a star on the Council’s stamps. This change, which no serious reason could justify, lasted only a very short time.

The sphere in the arms of Machico was the emblem of Manuel I, and this monarch presented the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of that town (*vila*) with a silver signet bearing the said sphere, which is still in use today. As for the arms of the other municipalities, we can only say that those of Câmara de Lobos were adopted recently, and that the two wolves shown in them appear to be an emblem taken from the coat of arms of the Câmara family.

To shed further light on this matter, we shall transcribe an article by Mr Armando de Matos, published on p. 54 ff. of vol. IV of the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (‘Historical Archive of Madeira’) under the title ‘Uma nótula sôbre as Armas do Funchal’, although we may disagree with some of the distinguished writer’s assertions. ‘I know of no printed or manuscript text that refers to the composition or symbolism of the insignia of municipal autonomy of the city of Funchal. There is neither a written document nor a sigillographic specimen old enough to allow us, as would be desirable, to base a series of comments on it. Nevertheless, with the little that remains to us, the question of revising the seal of the municipality of Funchal must be addressed.’

‘…The shape of the shield, the coronet that surmounts it and the ornaments that surround it are inappropriate. There is no need to repeat the reasons why, for they have been stated so many times already. And this applies both to the embossed seal and to the oil-ink stamp.

‘The oldest iconographic evidence to which we can turn is found on a 17th-century salver kept in the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of that city. It is the oldest, and indeed the only, example we have to draw on. The others are merely variants of it, and distort it.’

‘The first charter (foral) of Funchal dates from 1451 and was granted by Afonso V. That is to say, only after this date, the beginning of the second half of the 15th century, can the seal of the municipality of Funchal have been created.’ ‘The oldest record, as I have said, belongs to the 17th century.

On it we find five cones arranged in a cross, their tips pointing towards the base of the shield. Placed palewise, between the central and the side cones, are two sugar canes.’ As for the identification of the cones, it is generally said that they represent either sugar-loaf moulds or the loaves themselves. This primitive arrangement, set in a fanciful shield, is surmounted by a cross pattée, certainly a poor representation of the Cross of Christ.

Let us first examine the cones. We see that there are five of them, arranged in a cross. This arrangement recalls that of the small shields of the Portuguese *quinas*. The fact that their bases face the chief of the shield possibly suggests that they are nothing more than those very small shields, incoherently stylised and carelessly represented on the salver that serves as our starting point. At the same time, it is unusual, not to say unprecedented, for the arms of a lordship of the mid-15th century to display as their main symbols the same ones as the central power. If they are not small shields, we must adopt the idea of sugar-loaf moulds. Were they the loaves themselves, it would be logical for the cones to appear base downwards, and not inverted. Yet this is seen only in the later iconographic evidence, which seems to tell us that their being taken for loaves had an influence. This idea naturally arose after their meaning had been lost. What is beyond doubt in this case is that the oldest is the one most worth weighing.’ There is yet another fact, slighter though it is, which I must not forget. The cones depicted on the salver clearly show the outline of the base, which is no longer seen in the later drawings. These charges clearly give the idea of vessels or containers.’

‘…The cones, which to me are sugar-loaf moulds and which I shall call such from now on, together with the sugar canes, represent the great wealth of Funchal, the reason for its progress, owed to the beneficent interest of Henry the Navigator, who had sugar cane acclimatised on the island. Spreading extraordinarily in the island’s most fertile soil, the cane brought Funchal such importance, and so spurred its growth, that in 1508 King Manuel raised Funchal to the rank of city.’
‘The meaning of the moulds and the canes is thus well combined in a complete symbolism, whose principal fact to be commemorated was the wealth of the island, arising from the sugar trade.’

‘The good men (*homens bons*, local notables eligible for municipal office) of Funchal chose these motifs wisely. Having no feats of arms or military or naval exploits to record in the collective memory, they turned to another subject, the chief reason for their common pride and for the growing importance of their municipality (*concelho*): the economic value of sugar. It was this that had to represent their prosperous municipality. Was the Cross of Christ part of the composition proper? I cannot say. Nevertheless, its appearance is reasonable and logical, for it recalls Prince Henry, to whose will the island owes its becoming part of the Portuguese world. And he was the master of the Order of Christ, whose revenues drove the caravels along the glorious path of the discoveries.’ ‘This is what the oldest iconographic document of the arms of Funchal suggests.’
Let us now see how, within the tradition, a solution can be devised for settling the definitive arrangement of the arms of Funchal.

‘Being of the opinion that the form and arrangement of the arms engraved on the 17th-century salver should be preserved, I would suggest that the sugar loaves should remain set in a cross, but flanked by the two sugar canes. It seems to us that the aesthetic effect is better this way than if they alternated with one another. In this way, too, the cross formed by the small escutcheons of the *quinas* stands out more clearly, and it can never be marked too well.’ ‘In a chief I would place the Cross of Christ, which I believe ought to appear in all the arms of the dominions of the adjacent archipelagos of Madeira and the Azores. This feature would carry the same spirit of difference as the crowned heads in the arms of the Algarve municipalities, the star in those of the Serra da Estrela region, or the bordure in the arms of our overseas dominions. It would be the way to set the lands of the Islands clearly apart. Even without a motto they would be recognised.’

‘It remains to speak of the colours that should adorn the component charges of these arms.’ The sugar loaves in sable, representing the abundance derived from the sugar trade. The canes should be proper, that is, vert. The chief, charged with the Cross of Christ, argent. He would thus present the following as the design for the arms of Funchal: ‘Argent, five sugar loaves sable, set in a cross, and flanked by two sugar canes vert, couped. On a chief argent, a Cross of Christ, and a mural crown argent of five towers, as a city. Motto in black on a white scroll: CIDADE DO FUNCHAL. Flag white, gyronny of green.’ ‘As has been seen, the absence of documents is almost total; it comes down to a single trace, which is the salver of the Council of Funchal.’ ‘Any solution put forward must therefore seek to explain the tradition as far as possible and to respect it. Nor can the general heraldic rules be forgotten, or those already laid down for the modern revision of the arms of dominion.’ ‘The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, at its ordinary session of 6 February 1936, in compliance with instructions from higher authority, resolved to reform its arms, flag and city seal, adopting for this purpose the design drawn up by Mr Afonso de Ornelas, which had received the full approval of the Heraldry Section of the Association of Archaeologists (*Associação dos Arqueólogos*) at its meeting of 20 December 1935.

From that report, published in the press, the following is transcribed: ‘Arms – Vert, five sugar loaves Or, heightened in spiral, with bases purpure, set in a cross, cantoned by four bunches of grapes Or, stalked and leaved of the same metal, each bunch charged with a *quina* azure charged with five bezants argent in saltire. Mural crown argent of five towers. White scroll bearing the words Cidade do Funchal in black.

‘Flag – Quartered in four pieces of yellow and four of purple, with the words Cidade do Funchal. Cords and tassels of gold and purple. Spearhead and staff gilt. ‘Seal – Circular, bearing in the centre the charges of the arms without indication of the tinctures. Around them, within concentric circles, the words Câmara Municipal do Funchal.’ The report of Mr Afonso de Ornelas, which because of its length we cannot transcribe here, contains valuable material for the study of this subject and was published in the *Diário de Noticias* of Funchal of 7 February 1936.
See Bandeira da Cidade.
Armitage (Eleonora)

English botanist who collected plants on Madeira in early 1909. She made a collection of mosses, which was studied by H. N. Dixon, and wrote the following works: *Some Madeira Hepaticae* (*Journ. of Botany*, 1910); *Intensive Cultivation in Madeira* (*Journ. of Royal Hortic. Soc.*, 1910); and *On the Habitats and frequencies of some Madeira Bryophytes* (*Journ. of Ecology*, VI, 1918).
Arnao

The surname Arnao or Arnau appears to derive from the Englishman Guilherme Arnau, who in 1378 accompanied Philippa of Lancaster, wife of John I, to Portugal. We do not know, however, when this surname appeared in Madeira, and we believe that it is now completely extinct here.
Aroma
See Acacia.
Arquimbau (Ramon Masferrer y)

Physician trained at the Barcelona school, born in Vic on 15 May 1850 and died in the Philippines on 5 April 1884. Works: *Catalogo razonado de la Flora de Tenerife y notas sobre la Flora de todo el arquipélago Canario, Madeira e demais islas de aquela región botánica* (no place or date of printing).
Madeira archipelago

The importance of this archipelago is set out concisely but strikingly in the following words from the authoritative pen of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the learned annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*): ‘This archipelago has been the object of study by learned naturalists, both foreign and Portuguese. It is celebrated, especially the island of Madeira, for the fertility of its soil, its excellent wines, the breathtaking beauty of its landscape and the healthiness of its climate. It is historically notable as the first of the Portuguese discoveries in the 15th century and, afterwards, until the close of the 16th century, as the secular and ecclesiastical metropolis of our overseas dominions and the emporium of our colonial navigation and commerce. For this reason the Madeiran archives, especially those of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, of Machico, of the former and now extinct Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) and of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) of Funchal, hold precious documents and records, perhaps not to be found elsewhere, for the history of the institutions and government of our possessions beyond the sea’.

The archipelago lies between Western Europe, which faces it to the north-east, the Moroccan coast of West Africa, which runs from east to south-east of it, the Azores archipelago to the north-west, and that of the Canary Islands to the south. The nearest point of the Moroccan west coast to the Madeiran archipelago is Cape Cantin, which lies at roughly the same latitude as Madeira and is equidistant, about 60 miles, from the cities of Mazagan to the north and Mogadouro to the south. The archipelago is approximately 500 miles from mainland Portugal and 350 from Cape Cantin, on the west coast of Africa. The relative positions of the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) group form a scalene triangle. Its shortest side is the channel between Ilhéu de Fora (‘outer islet’), at the eastern tip of Madeira (Ponta de São Lourenço), and the Prego do Mar (‘sea nail’) or Ilhéu do Navio (‘ship islet’), near Ilhéu Chão (‘flat islet’) in the Desertas. The next longest side is formed by the channel (Travessa) running from the said Ilhéu de Fora (Ponta de São Lourenço) to Ilhéu de Baixo (‘lower islet’) or da Cal (Porto Santo). The longest side is the channel stretching from the aforementioned Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal (Porto Santo) to the Prego do Mar or Ilhéu Chão (Desertas). The channels measure 11, 27 and 32 miles respectively, which are the distances separating Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas group from one another.

The extreme points of this archipelago are generally given as follows: to the north, the Rocha do Nordeste or Ilhéu de Fora (Porto Santo); to the south, Ponta da Agulha (‘needle point’) or Ponta do Sul, at the southern tip of Bugio (Desertas); to the east, Ilhéu de Cima or dos Dragoeiros (Porto Santo); and to the west, Ponta do Pargo (Madeira).

The Madeira archipelago is washed by the Atlantic Ocean and, according to Captain Vidal, lies between the parallels 32° 22′ 20″ and 33° 7′ 50″ north latitude and between the meridians 16° 16′ 30″ and 17° 16′ 38″ longitude west of Greenwich.
According to the most recent calculations, the area of the whole archipelago is 560 square kilometres, though some have raised that figure to more than a thousand kilometres.

Its population, spread over fifty parishes, is 211,000 inhabitants according to the 1930 census. The Madeira archipelago and the small group of the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) form the administrative district of Funchal, whose capital is the city of the same name. See the various articles under the headings Madeira, Porto Santo, Desertas, the Savage Islands and Funchal.
Archives
See Elements for Madeiran history.
Arrebentão (peak and locality)

This peak lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) and rises to a height of 1171 metres. Close by is the locality (*sítio*) of the same name, which is crossed by the road leading to the Poiso (‘resting place’) shelter houses.
Arriaga (Dr Manuel de)

The name of the illustrious Dr Manuel de Arriaga is bound up with the history of Madeira, for he represented this archipelago in parliament during the legislative session of 1882 to 1884. On the death of the deputy for the Funchal constituency, our distinguished fellow Madeiran Dr Luís de Freitas Branco, an election to fill the vacancy was held on 5 November 1882. Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Anselmo José Braancamp came first, but he did not obtain an absolute majority of the votes, so the election was repeated on 26 November of the same year. This time Dr Manuel de Arriaga was elected.

On 28 April 1911 the Madeirans again chose him as their representative in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), but when he was elected President of the Republic on 24 August of that year, he left his seat as deputy vacant.

Dr Manuel de Arriaga was one of the deputies for Madeira who championed the interests of their constituents in the national parliament with the greatest dedication and selflessness, and with even more remarkable brilliance, delivering speeches that became famous in the annals of parliamentary eloquence.

At the invitation of his fellow party members and friends in Madeira, the illustrious advocate first visited the island on 8 September 1883, when he was given one of the most enthusiastic and brilliant receptions that Funchal has ever prepared for its most distinguished visitors. He toured the parishes bordering the city and the parishes of the municipalities of Sant'Ana and Machico, and everywhere he was the object of the most rapturous demonstrations of esteem and sympathy from his personal and political friends. He left Madeira on 15 September 1883, receiving the most affectionate and moving farewell. In 1884 he visited Madeira again, accompanied by the illustrious professor Dr Consiglieri Pedroso, and he was on the island for the last time in 1885.

Dr Arriaga won a large number of votes in the parliamentary elections held in 1884, but he failed to be elected because of the way the poll was conducted in some of the polling assemblies. The armed force stationed at Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) even opened fire on the people on 29 June, leaving some dead and wounded.

When several republicans were prosecuted over the events at Ribeira Brava, they were defended by Dr Arriaga and Dr José de Castro at the trial held in the judicial district (*comarca*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) in April 1885. Of the twenty-eight defendants who appeared to answer the charges, twenty-two were acquitted and six convicted, but the latter merely for having assaulted the factor (*feitor*) of the late Russel Gordon.
Dr Arriaga was born in the city of Horta, on the island of Faial, in 1841, and died in Lisbon on 5 March 1917.
Rice

We are not aware that any attempt to grow rice was ever made on this island at an earlier time. We do know, however, that in 1918 a grower of that cereal, a native of mainland Portugal, who was then living in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), carried out a trial of the crop there. It was crowned with the greatest success, yielding an excellent and abundant harvest. For this reason a petition signed by several landowners of that parish was addressed to the Madeira Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola da Madeira*), asking for special protection for the cultivation of this cereal. It seems to us, however, that no further trials were made to develop this industry.
Arruda (Friar Pedro de)

Guardian of the Franciscan community of São João da Ribeira, who built the original church of the convent of São Francisco in this city. It was consecrated in 1554 by Bishop Dom Sancho Truxillo, who was passing through Madeira.
Rue (Ruta chalepensis)
A woody plant of the family Rutaceae, common in Madeira. It has a characteristic smell, and its leaves and flowers are widely used, especially as an infusion, to treat uterine complaints.
Art of Stealing

The author of this work seems to have been in Madeira, for he mentions several events that took place here while Bishop Dom Jerónimo Fernando was governor-general of the archipelago, that is, between 1624 and 1634.

‘The Art of Stealing’ (*Arte de Furtar*), which many have sought to attribute to Father António Vieira, is not his work, but that of a writer of merit who knew how to imitate the style and phrasing of the celebrated Portuguese Jesuit.
Artemija

The common Madeiran name for *Chrysanthemum parthenium*, a perennial plant of the family Compositae. It is easily recognised by its pinnatisect leaves, with more or less deeply cut segments, and by its medium-sized flower heads, in which the florets are all tubular or the outer ones ligulate. The *artemija* (a corruption of *artemisia*) is also known as *alfinetes de senhora*; it has a strong, penetrating smell and a bitter taste. The flowering tops are stimulant, tonic, emmenagogue and diuretic.
Auxiliary Artillery

The auxiliary artillery corps of Madeira, established in 1805, had a staff and fifteen companies under the regulations given to it by Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque on 12 November 1834. The staff consisted of a lieutenant-colonel or major in command, a captain or subaltern as adjutant, and a sergeant-adjutant. Fourteen of these companies belonged to Madeira and one to Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and four of the Madeiran companies had their quarters in Funchal.
The chief duty of the auxiliary artillery was to garrison, guard and watch over the batteries, forts, lookout posts and accessible points of the archipelago's coast.

In the days of absolute government it was customary for young men of the leading families of Funchal to enlist as cadets in the auxiliary artillery corps. Its commander at that time was an officer of the regular army, while the lieutenants and second lieutenants were all militiamen.
The auxiliary artillery corps, or corps of the *papoilas* (‘poppies’), was abolished by the ministerial order (*portaria*) of 3 February 1868.
Arvelos

The first people known to have borne this surname in Madeira are Diogo de Arvelos, who settled in Machico around 1490, and Pedro Gonçalves de Arvelos, who around 1569 held the office of judge in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). Both were persons of noble rank.
Silk tree (Gonphocarpus fruticosus)
A small milky shrub of the family Asclepiadaceae, fairly common in the lower zones of Madeira. It produces large, swollen, finely spiny follicles, with seeds bearing a pappus of long, silky hairs.
Incense tree (Pitiosporum undulatum)
A tree of the family Pittosporaceae, cultivated and naturalised in Madeira. It is common in Funchal and in the *quintas* of Monte (‘hill’).
Tree of Paradise (Elaeagnus hortensis)

A tree of the family Elaeagnaceae, cultivated in Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It has silvery foliage and yellow, fragrant flowers, and on the island of Porto Santo it serves to protect the vineyards from encroaching sand.
Arvoredo
A hill and picturesque locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’).
Sea trees
A common term for anthozoans with tree-like polyp colonies.
Trees and shrubs

The trees and principal shrubs growing wild in Madeira are the following: the *ameixieira de espinho* or *fustete*, the two *mocanos*, the holly, the *perado*, the *sanguinho*, the two wild cherries (one of which is also known as *tintureira*), the brooms (*piornos*), the *tramazeira*(?), the myrtle, the elder, the *codesso*, the Madeira blueberry (uveira, Vaccinium padifolium), the *urze molar*, the broom heath (*urze das vassouras*), the folhado (Clethra arborea, a native tree), the *aderno*, the *marmulano* (Sideroxylon marmulano, a shrub), the olive, the *pau branco*, the Madeira mahogany (vinhático, Persea indica), the *barbuzano*, the til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), the laurel, the *figueira do inferno* or *alindres*, the *faia*, the *seixo*, the dragon tree, the cedar, the juniper (*zimbreiro*) and the yew.

These species, which we shall deal with in their proper places, are for the most part rather rare, and some are even extinct or almost extinct. This is owing to the little care taken to propagate them and to the devastation wrought for many years in our mountains by woodcutters, charcoal burners, timber dealers and grazing livestock.

The owners of the coastal steamers were a cruel enemy of our woodlands between 1916 and 1918. During that period their agents cut down many thousands of trees to feed the boilers of those steamers, because the war had driven the price of coal to fabulous heights. The authorities made no attempt to prevent such abuse or to punish those responsible.
See *Arvores e Arbustos Madeirenses* by Carlos Azevedo de Meneses. Funchal, 1904, 17 pp.
Infant Asylum

The establishment of an asylum, which seems to have been the second of its kind founded in our country, is owed to the first governor of Madeira in the constitutional period, the illustrious Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque. Although his term of office was very short, lasting only from August 1834 to September 1835, he neglected no essential point of public administration. He also took the initiative of creating an asylum for the destitute orphans of Funchal, and in his wife, Dona Ana Mascarenhas de Ataíde, he found the most active and effective collaborator in the charitable work he had undertaken. The idea, which was new and met a great public need, won the widest acceptance and was greeted by the whole population of Funchal with the most enthusiastic excitement, which unfortunately did not last long.

Four months after Luís Mousinho’s arrival on this island, that is, around the middle of December 1834, the new charitable establishment began to operate. It was provisionally housed in some of the outbuildings of the Palácio de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’), under the direct supervision and the solicitous and loving direction of its founders themselves. It came to shelter 120 children and remained in a state of relative prosperity for as long as its founders stayed on this island. It was still thanks to that initial impetus that, by a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 13 January 1836, a house in the Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) belonging to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*) was obtained for the asylum to move into. It operated there for some years and ceased to exist at a date we cannot establish with complete accuracy. After the departure of Luís Mousinho de Albuquerque and his devoted and charitable wife, the work they had created with such dedication and affection began slowly to decline, until it died out completely, leaving behind only the blessed memory of its illustrious founders.

José Silvestre Ribeiro regarded himself, in founding the Funchal Beggars’ Asylum (*Asilo da Mendicidade do Funchal*), as merely the continuer of Mousinho’s work. Even today, in the entrance hall of that asylum’s building, there are two canvases, already badly damaged by time, depicting Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque and his wife, Dona Ana de Mascarenhas e Ataíde; they ought to be scrupulously preserved there and also suitably restored.

Planned asylum at the Angústias (‘sorrows’). In 1837 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) once again resolved to found an asylum to take in the old and infirm who begged in the streets of the city. It informed the central government of this resolution, which the government praised in a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 7 June 1838. To carry out this lofty and humane idea, the councillors lost no time in arranging the construction of a suitable building.
