The site chosen was the land where the Asilo da Mendicidade e Orfãos now stands, which the first Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’) had given for that purpose shortly before his death. Construction work, carried out to the plan and design drawn up by the director of public works, the engineer Vicente de Paula Teixeira, began on 8 August 1837, and the municipality spent approximately thirteen *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis) on the building. The building was almost completed, but it was never put to the use for which it had originally been intended. It never opened its doors to inmates, because the councillors who had taken that initiative, or those who succeeded them on the Council, abandoned the idea of creating the asylum, for reasons entirely unknown to us.
Asylum of Arts and Trades

When the cholera epidemic raged in Madeira at the end of 1910 and the beginning of 1911, the idea arose of founding an Asylum of Arts and Trades (*Asilo de Artes e Ofícios*), intended especially to house the children whom the epidemic had left orphaned and destitute. It was Dr José Alfredo Mendes de Magalhães, then serving here as High Commissioner (*alto comissário*) of the Republic, who conceived this generous initiative and went so far as to lay the first foundations for it. A public subscription and other donations provided the funds raised for the project. These reached the sum of 16,995,120 réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto) and, with accumulated interest, amounted to 22,000,000 réis by June 1917. At that time the very grave crisis caused by the European war led the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of these funds to give their income to the Asilo da Mendicidade e Órfãos do Funchal, to relieve the distressing situation of that most worthy and useful institution. The Asylum of Arts and Trades was never founded. The Administrative Committee of its funds, made up of the civil governor, General Norberto Teles and Major J. Reis Gomes, considered handing them over to the Asilo da Mendicidade e Órfãos to build a pavilion for workshops, with the remainder going to increase that asylum’s funds, and received the favourable opinion of Dr Alfredo de Magalhães for this.
Funchal Poorhouse

Several months of 1846 and 1847 became known as the ‘year of hunger’, a time when the island was ravaged by a terrible commercial and agricultural crisis and famine was felt acutely in many parishes of Madeira. The memory of that calamitous period is still vivid in local tradition. A book of 300 pages, published in 1848 under the title *Collecção de documentos relativos á crise da fome por que passaram as Ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo no anno de 1847*, gives us a detailed account of the calamity that then struck the archipelago. (See Famine in Madeira in 1847.)

The poor and the beggars swarmed through the most central and busiest streets of the city, a sad and dispiriting sight for Portuguese and foreigners alike. Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, who had taken over the government of the district in October 1846, found himself confronting this fearful crisis, which little by little took on the most distressing and threatening proportions. What that public-spirited governor then did is eloquently attested by the pages of the book cited above.

One of the means Silvestre Ribeiro used to ease the gravity of the crisis was the creation of an asylum. Happily it still exists, and as one of our most valuable charitable institutions it is also a commemorative pillar (padrão) of undying glory, bearing witness to the benevolence of its founder. On 10 March 1847 the illustrious governor had a considerable number of beggars of both sexes and various ages taken into a warehouse belonging to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*), which faces the former Rua do Mosteiro Novo and Rua dos Medinas, after the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had carried out the essential repairs there for a temporary installation. An asylum had been founded which, unlike the similar establishments previously founded here, did not share their fate, and which already counts sixty-two years of fruitful and beneficial existence.

Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro entrusted the provisional direction and administration of the new asylum to the Committee of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), which was also charged with drawing up draft statutes for the internal running of the institution; the public-spirited governor had already secured the means of maintaining the inmates. It soon became clear that the house in Rua do Mosteiro Novo did not serve the purpose for which it had been adapted. Silvestre Ribeiro promptly obtained from the Council the transfer of the suppressed Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) and, with astonishing energy, turned the former conventual building within a few days into a house fit to shelter several hundred paupers and beggars.

On 27 March, a few days after the asylum was founded, the civil governor, accompanied by various authorities and other official figures in a splendid procession, personally conducted about 400 inmates to the new premises prepared in the convent of São Francisco. In the former Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’) an abundant dinner was served to all the poor, at which José Silvestre gave a heartfelt and eloquent speech that deeply moved the large audience listening to him. The Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the new asylum was then appointed, made up of the diocesan bishop Dom José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa, Fidelio de Freitas Branco, Severiano Alberto Ferraz, Vicente de Brito Correia, António Machado Cota, Dom Jorge da Câmara Leme and Carlos Blandy.

The asylum remained in the Convent of São Francisco for only a few months. Everything pointed to installing it permanently in the house that the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had had built expressly for that purpose in 1837. The move took place in December 1847, to the great material benefit of the inmates and of the orderly running of all the services of this charitable institution. This is the moment to give a brief account of the history of the building. As we said above, it was built in 1837, but was never put to the use for which it had originally been erected. At a council meeting on 2 July 1841 it was resolved that the Casa das Angústias (‘house of the Sorrows’) should serve as the public gaol, house of correction and law courts, if the central government approved; the government, however, took no decision on the matter. The flash flood (*aluvião*) of 24 October 1842 caused serious damage to the building in the Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory square’) that housed the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), the municipal library and the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office). The Council therefore decided to move these offices to the Casa das Angústias once the necessary alterations had been made, and the move took place around the middle of 1843. Barely two years later the Municipal Council took a new decision: to move its offices to the house in the Largo da Sé (‘cathedral square’), where the gaol then was, and to transfer the gaol to the Casa das Angústias. Very substantial works were carried out on the building for this new arrangement, and large sums were spent on them.

As a result of the political events brought about by the Maria da Fonte revolution, the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) was dissolved on 25 June 1846 and replaced by an administrative committee. This committee did not abide by the decisions of the previous Council, and in July of the same year it resolved that the Casa das Angústias should be used not as a gaol but to house the town hall, which was moved there for the second time and remained there until November 1847.

On 3 December of that year the Council resolved to cede the Casa das Angústias provisionally to the administrative committee of the Poorhouse (*Asilo de Mendicidade*), which was installed there permanently on the 8th of the same month and year.

The cession of 1848 was declared definitive at a meeting of the Municipal Council on 29 May 1913, and this decision was confirmed by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) in an official letter of 21 June of the same year.

The cholera epidemic of 1856, which killed some ten thousand people in Madeira, left many hundreds of children orphaned and destitute, and suitable shelter and care had to be found for them. Governor Gromicho Couceiro, who rendered such distinguished services to Madeira in that calamitous period, had some outbuildings of the former convent of São Francisco repaired and adapted to house an asylum intended solely for children. Its management was entrusted to the administrative committee of the Poorhouse. The two asylums (*Asilos*) were later joined, and this is the origin of the name given to the establishment at Angústias (‘sorrows’): the Asilo da Mendicidade e Órfãos do Funchal (Funchal Asylum for Beggars and Orphans).
The two asylums were merged around the middle of 1862, chiefly because there were not enough resources to maintain the two charitable institutions separately.

The asylum owed very distinguished services to the civil governor Jacinto António Perdigão, which make him one of its most illustrious benefactors after Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Silvestre Ribeiro. This charitable institution had no property of its own and lived solely on public charity, which made its administration difficult and full of dangers for its future existence. By bringing together various revenues of dissolved confraternities and compelling the Council of Funchal to pay a debt owed to the asylum, Governor Perdigão created a permanent fund for it. First, however, it had to be given legal capacity, through the drafting of statutes and their approval by the central government; these were its first organic law and are dated 24 March 1866. This first core of the asylum’s funds, created in 1864 by Perdigão, amounted to five *contos* (one million réis) de réis in government bonds. Shortly afterwards he added the ownership of a large number of water hours (*horas de água*, irrigation rights measured in hours of flow) on the Levada da Cruzinha, the Levada da Serra and the Levada de São Jorge. Thanks to the diligent efforts of the same governor, in 1866 the asylum held 7,250,000 réis in bonds, yielding an annual income of 239,250 réis. By 1870 this fund in government bonds had risen to 9,450,000 réis.
The asylum’s revenue for the financial year 1869–1870 was 3,250,000 réis, and for the following year 4,142,000 réis; over the next ten years it did not increase, and at times it fell.

Among the asylum’s great benefactors, the Countess of Ribeiro Real should not be forgotten either. She bequeathed to this charitable institution the Quinta Esmeraldo, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho, and part of the furniture of the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace), amounting in all to some 300 *contos*. The Countess of Ribeiro Real, daughter of the 2nd Count of Carvalhal (see that entry), died in this city on 29 July 1921.
Asylum for Invalids

In 1842 a modest charitable establishment, then given the name of Asylum for Invalids (*Asilo dos Inválidos*), was set up in some of the ground-floor rooms of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) building in this city. It was an adjunct of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) and was run by its governing bodies, but the asylum had been founded by the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*). The Council was the official body that paid for the upkeep of the inmates, under a contract concluded between it and the administration of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia). We do not know when it ceased to operate, but its existence was short-lived. Project for a beggars’ asylum. By a royal decree (*alvará*) of 22 March 1844, the civil governor of the district, Dr Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, appointed a commission, chaired by Dr António da Luz Pita and with Maurício Castelo Branco as secretary, to propose the most suitable means of creating an asylum to house beggars. We do not know what work this commission may have presented, but we do know that the asylum project never became more than a happy and generous idea, and nothing more.
Old People’s Home

It was founded in August 1900 through the efforts of the late diocesan prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto and Father António José de Macedo. It was first housed in a building on the Calçada do Socorro (‘Succour causeway’), but as this could hold no more than forty old people, the home moved to a large house in Rua das Hortas (‘street of the kitchen gardens’), where it remains today.

At first the Old People’s Home (*Asilo dos Velhinhos*) sheltered twenty-five poor people, but by 1910 it had seventy-five residents, twenty-five men and fifty women. The work of the house was done by six nuns, two Portuguese and four foreign, who were helped by some of the more vigorous residents.

When the expulsion of the Little Sisters of the Poor (*Irmãzinhas dos Pobres*) was ordered after the proclamation of the Republic, the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) resolved to take over the running costs of the home, whose services are now in the hands of staff paid by that body.
All the furniture found in the home in 1910 was sold at public auction. Part of it was bought by the General Council, which put it to the same use as before.
Asylums

The first attempt made here to create a home for orphans and invalids predates the establishment of constitutional government on this island. In a year we cannot determine, the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) resolved to set up a charitable house to shelter destitute orphans, and this resolution earned the support and praise of the government in mainland Portugal. Some efforts and steps were taken, but this generous and selfless idea never became a reality.
Assembleia dos Únicos do Funchal

See Academies (*Academias*). Assistência a Crianças Fracas (Aid for Weak Children). This association was founded in 1908 on the initiative of some ladies of Funchal, and its statutes were approved by royal decree (*alvará*) of the Civil Governor of the District of 24 October 1908. Its aims are to set up dispensaries supplying milk and medicines to poor and sick children no older than twelve, to board such children when they have no mothers or when their mothers cannot raise them, to promote child hygiene, etc.

In the financial year 1916–1917 this charitable institution spent 1,090,220 réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto). Its board was striving to create a Jardim da Infância (kindergarten) to take in children left abandoned in the streets or shut up at home while their mothers went about their daily work away from home.
Assobiadouro
A rise on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), near which the springs of Rabaçal have their source.
Funchal Students’ Association

This defunct student society was inaugurated on 1 December 1884 in one of the rooms of the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’), with a speech on the occasion by the late Marcelino Ribeiro de Mendonça, then a pupil at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school). The newspaper *O Académico* (‘The Student’) was the society’s organ.
Catholic Association of Funchal

It was founded in 1874. Its statutes were approved by the chief officer of the district by royal decree (*alvará*) of 10 August 1874 and received the approval of the diocesan ecclesiastical authority by warrant (*provisão*) of 21 August of the same year. After the Associação Comercial and the Associação de Socorros Mútuos 4 de Setembro de 1862, it is at present the oldest of the societies existing in this city.
Funchal Commercial Association

The Funchal Commercial Association (*Associação Comercial do Funchal*) is one of the most important bodies in this city, and also the oldest of all those in existence here. The history of this worthy association is likewise the history of our economic life over the long span of eighty-four years, for the matters of closest concern to Madeiran commerce and industry have found in it their most strenuous champion. It has placed unconditionally at the service of this archipelago all the prestige, influence and credit that it deservedly enjoys in our community. There may have been some rare exception, which will serve only to confirm the general rule.

On 7 July 1835 the governor of Madeira, Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, appointed the commission charged with organising and formally installing the Commercial Association. It was made up of João Shortridge, João Coelho de Meireles, Roque Caetano de Araújo, José Phelps and Dr Alexandre de Oliveira. The commission met on 10 July, elected João Shortridge as its president and set about its task without delay. It found the most resolute support among the whole merchant community for an idea that dated back to the days of absolutism.

The association was not formally installed until 20 January 1836, in a house in Rua da Alfândega, which then bore the street number 18. On that same day its board of directors was elected: João Shortridge, president; Roque Caetano de Araújo, vice-president; and the members José Maria Bernes, João António de Gouveia Rego, Joaquim Monteiro de Afonseca, Guilherme Grant, João Coelho de Meireles and João Crisóstomo Ferreira Usel. Its first secretary was Alexandre Luís da Cunha, a language teacher and a well-known journalist in his day.

On the very day of its formal installation and the election of the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*), the statutes were discussed and approved; they received the approval of the central government by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 12 March 1836. These statutes underwent some modifications, and at the general meeting of 15 December 1887 they were thoroughly revised, receiving approval by royal decree (alvará régio) of 11 May 1888. These statutes are at present the constitution of this estimable association.

The following is the list of the gentlemen who, since its foundation, have presided over the fortunes of the Funchal Commercial Association. They are: João Shortridge (1835–1839), João A. de Gouveia Rego (1839–1841), Roque Caetano de Araújo (1841–1842), João Coelho de Meireles (1842–1843), Guilherme Grant (1843–1845), Dr Alexandre de Oliveira (1845–1847), Edmond Ellicot (1847–1850), Roque Caetano de Araújo (1850–1852), Guilherme Grant (1852–1853), João António de Gouveia Rego (1853–1856), António J. Marques Bastos (1856–1857), Carlos Blandy (1857–1875), Silvano de Freitas Branco (1875–1883), Dr George Sattler (1883–1886), Dr Manuel José Vieira (1886–1888), João B. Blandy (1888–1889), Carlos Bianchi (1889–1892), Dr Manuel José Vieira (1892–1893), Francisco José Nogueira Guimarãis (1893–1895), Manuel António da Silva Passos (1895–1897), Henrique A. Vieira de Castro (1897–1900), Jacob Abudarham (1900–1904), Luís Gomes da Conceição (1904–1911), Luís Fialho de Alvelos (1911–1916), Francisco Meira (1916–1919), Lieutenant Colonel António Bettencourt da Câmara (1919–1920), Dr Rui Bettencourt da Câmara (1920–1922), Henrique Augusto Vieira de Castro (1922–1926), José Quirino de Castro (1926–1934) and Dr Juvenal Henriques de Araújo, the present President.

In 1936 the Funchal Commercial Association celebrated the 1st centenary of its foundation with a variety of splendid commemorations held from 26 to 30 May of that year. The programme included a formal session at the Associação Comercial, a fellowship gathering in aid of the Escola de Artes e Ofícios, lectures on the principal regional industries, and exhibitions of flowers, embroidery, wines, inlaid work (*embutidos*), butter, cement goods, etc. An issue of four commemorative stamps was also made.

For the occasion the president of the Associação Industrial Portuguesa, José Maria Álvares, came to the island expressly. He also represented the Associação Comercial de Lisboa and the Associação Comercial do Porto, and delivered special messages of greeting. Also coming to Madeira on that occasion was Mr Luís Teixeira, an editor of the Lisbon *Diário de Notícias*.
The press, both in Funchal and in Lisbon, referred to this anniversary and to the manner in which it was celebrated in the most laudatory terms.
Association of Ladies of Charity

The association was founded in January 1876 on the initiative of the chaplain of the church of São Luís dos Franceses (St Louis of the French), Lisbon, and the Mother Superior of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*) in Funchal. Its chief aims are to protect and assist the sick poor in their own homes, and in particular mothers who lack the means to nurse their children.
Association for the Protection and Education of the Women of Funchal

In 1878 the distinguished writer Dom António da Costa published a pamphlet entitled *Instituição de Ouro*, which he later included in his notable work *Auroras de Instrução em Portugal*. In it he describes in broad strokes, and with well-deserved praise, the foundation and humanitarian aims of the Association for the Protection and Education of the Women of Funchal (*Associação de Protecção e Instrução do Sexo Feminino Funchalense*), which was established in Funchal on 10 March 1875.

It was a mutual-aid society, founded on the initiative of Dr João da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, later Count of Canavial. Unfortunately it did not last long, but it was the first attempt to establish a body intended to help Madeiran women in sickness or old age.

A year later the association opened a model school with classes and workshops, which the aforementioned writer Dom António da Costa, one of the men who fought and worked hardest for the advancement of education in Portugal, describes with genuine admiration and enthusiasm. By the end of a year it already had eight hundred members and had collected 2,500,000 réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto) in revenue. It had distributed allowances and medicines and maintained a truly exemplary school, where elementary industrial and vocational training was given in addition to primary teaching.
This was a great deal for so brief an existence, and it was partly for this reason that the association, deserving of praise on so many counts, did not endure for long.

The statutes were drawn up by Dr Câmara Leme and approved by the senior authority of the district by royal decree (*alvará*) of 14 April 1875. By a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 30 August 1876, the central government commended Dr Câmara for his happy initiative; rarely has an official document borne such public and well-deserved witness to truth and justice as on this occasion.
4 September 1862 Mutual Aid Association

Until quite recently, it was an established truth that no one could seriously dispute that our society suffered from an utter lack of associative spirit and of any effective initiative to organise associations of any kind, and most particularly to found benevolent or mutual-aid societies. It was a stock theme of the old local press, which from time to time strove in vain to stir public opinion, combating the ignorance, routine and reprehensible mistrust with which our fellow Madeirans met every new idea, even the most philanthropic and altruistic. Fortunately, public feeling allowed itself to be influenced by these ideas, above all those concerning the principles of mutualism, which have now put down deep roots among us and have even produced the most beneficial and valued results. We would like to believe that the rest of the country has not advanced much further than we have in this respect, but it is certain that our backwardness was manifest when set against what was happening abroad.

The attempts go back a long way, but for many years they always proved fruitless or, what amounts to the same thing, yielded meagre or almost nil results. It is true that various scientific, literary and artistic societies were organised among us at relatively distant periods, and some of them left honourable traditions behind them. In the article Academies (*Academias*) we have already referred to the Assembleia dos Únicos do Funchal and the Arcadia Funchalense, which were active in the third and last quarter of the 18th century, and we shall still have to make special mention of the Sociedade Patriótica that existed in 1834, the Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes founded in 1821, and others besides. None of these societies, however, pursued a purely humanitarian aim or the practice of benevolence among its members, of the kind that has recently, and more properly, come to be called mutual aid.

We believe that around 1840, or shortly afterwards, some efforts were made to found an association to assist its members in sickness and infirmity, but it seems to us that it never achieved a proper organisation, still less began to operate.

On page 500 of the second volume of the *Epocha Administrativa* we read that in 1850 the illustrious civil governor of this district, José Silvestre Ribeiro, launched among us, perhaps for the first time, the idea of true mutualism. He inspired and demonstrated the need for an association intended especially for the craftsmen and workers of Funchal, and set out at once the general principles on which it should be founded. Some attempts were made to turn this idea into reality, and a large meeting was even held for the purpose, but for reasons unknown to us the efforts then made came to nothing.

The cholera epidemic which, in the third and last quarter of 1856, killed some six thousand people on this island according to official figures – though information from other sources raised the toll to ten thousand – gave rise, once the panic of that great public calamity had passed, to the idea of founding a society that would not only practise mutual aid among its members but also assist the widows and orphaned children of deceased members. According to issue 13 of the newspaper *A Madeira* (‘Madeira’), published in this city from April 1857 to January 1858, the society was inaugurated on 17 December 1856 under the name Sociedade de Beneficência do Funchal. We do not know on what basis its statutes were framed; we know only that it did not last long. A new attempt, though once again without appreciable results, was made to found a mutual-aid society. It was inaugurated on 29 December 1858 under the name Associação dos Artistas Madeirenses, in the presence of some four hundred workers and many persons of standing in Funchal society, and on that occasion the distinguished teacher and illustrious Madeiran Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça delivered a most remarkable speech.

At last the ideas scattered over many years across the thankless and barren ground of the Madeiran archipelago were to bear blessed fruit. The principles of mutualism germinated, developed and flourished under the creative drive of a few men full of faith and enthusiasm who, sparing no sacrifice and facing almost insurmountable difficulties, succeeded in founding a society that is not only a genuine source of pride for our island but also one of the most flourishing and important mutual-aid associations in our country. It was on 4 September 1862, in a house in Rua da Bela Vista, the residence of the merchant and property owner Henrique José Maria Camacho, that the foundations were laid of a body originally called the Associação de Beneficência do Funchal, and later given the name it still bears, Associação de Socorros Mútuos 4 de Setembro de 1862. It was Henrique Camacho who conceived the idea of this foundation and who set its establishment in motion. He was ably and devotedly assisted by others, among whom it is only just to single out Fernando José Rodrigues, an employee of our customs house, and Pedro Júlio de Gouveia, an intelligent and energetic workman who rendered the most signal and valuable services to the nascent society. There were twenty-seven founding members, almost all of them artisans. Their portraits are still kept today in the meeting room, where they were hung in 1872 as a fitting tribute to the founders of so useful and meritorious an association.

The direction and management of this society’s affairs have met with varying fortune, especially in times not very recent, but the establishment of the savings bank (Caixa Económica) and the zeal of the governing bodies of recent years have overcome and neutralised the earlier errors and shortcomings. In 1872, ten years after its foundation, the society had one thousand seven hundred and thirty members and about 15 *contos* (one million réis) *de réis* in funds. Ten years later, in 1882, membership had risen to two thousand four hundred and sixty-one and its funds had reached 31 *contos de réis*. By 1890 these funds had fallen to 21 *contos de réis*, because the careless and less than zealous management of the previous six years had allowed expenditure to exceed income. This created an awkward and perilous situation for the association, which was fortunately averted by the vigorous measures then adopted.

Forty years after its foundation, in 1902, the society had one thousand four hundred and seventy members and approximately 104 *contos de réis* in funds, which ten years later, in 1912, had reached the considerable sum of 182 *contos de réis*. According to the latest published report, covering the year 1918, the funds of this flourishing society stand at 248 *contos de réis*.

Besides the zeal and dedication that many of the governing bodies have shown on the association’s behalf, there is no doubt that its prosperity and comfortable position are due chiefly to the Caixa Económica, which has operated alongside it since 1878. This has been the most powerful factor in its progress in recent years. Today it is a reputable credit institution, enjoying the greatest prestige and confidence in our community. The initiative for its foundation is owed to the distinguished Madeiran Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira, who, in this as in other matters of the greatest weight and importance to the association, rendered it the most valuable and disinterested services, and was one of its most meritorious and helpful members. The hanging of his portrait in the association’s main hall is perhaps the most fitting act of justice ever paid there to the members who have rendered the society the finest and most signal services. In 1918 the Caixa Económica yielded approximately 20 *contos de réis*, a very large sum for our community, where there are several highly respectable credit establishments in which the public places the fullest confidence. It is worth noting here that the creation of this savings bank was the first attempt of its kind made among us, and that it was crowned with the greatest success, although in its early years its business was small and many people were reluctant to transact business with it. It was a new institution, hence the reserve and the unfounded doubts that part of the public expressed about the confidence it inspired.

The building that houses the offices, medical consulting rooms and other premises of this worthy society stands in Rua de João Tavira and is owned by the association itself. It was acquired in December 1889 for the sum of 6,562,377 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

In the general assembly’s meeting room hang, as we mentioned above, the portraits of the founders, together with those of the members Manuel José Vieira, João da Silva, Guilherme Pedro de Melim and José Augusto da Silva, in recognition of the outstanding services they rendered to the association.

For thirty-three years it kept the name of Associação de Beneficência do Funchal (Funchal Benevolent Association). In 1895, under the provisions of the statutes of 21 December 1894, it took the name Associação 4 de Setembro de 1862, after the date of its foundation.

The association’s first statutes were approved by royal decree (alvará régio) of 5 January 1863. They have since been revised several times, in keeping with the progress of mutualist principles and the changing needs of the society. The instruments approving the various revisions of the statutes are dated 1 February 1879, 2 May 1888, 21 December 1894 and 9 October 1907 respectively.
Philanthropic Association of the Students of Funchal
Its statutes were approved by the chief authority of the district by royal decree (*alvará*) of 13 May 1892.
Madeiran Association for the Public Good and Mutual Aid
It was founded in 1877 on the initiative of Dr João da Câmara Leme, later Count of Canavial, and was short-lived.
Under its draft statutes, members were entitled to borrow money from the association's funds at an interest rate of five per cent.
Association for the Protection of Poor Students

It was formed in 1894, and its statutes were approved by the Civil Governor on 26 April 1897. Its purpose is to provide grants, books and enrolment fees to poor students attending the lyceum (state secondary school) or the special or higher schools.
Associação Protectora dos Estudantes Pobres
A single issue of a newspaper published in July 1907 to commemorate the anniversary of the founding of this benevolent association.
Association for the Protection of the Poor

It was founded in 1889 on the initiative of the then Civil Governor, Dom João de Alarcão Velasques Osório, and its chief purpose is to distribute food to the poor and the sick. The association’s statutes were approved by the same governor by royal decree (*alvará*) of 2 May 1880.
Royal Wine Association of Madeira
This association, founded in 1900, did not last long. At its meeting of 11 October of that year, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) granted it an annual subsidy of 100,000 réis.

On 12 July 1909 a meeting was held to discuss organising a wine company or association in Madeira. Despite the goodwill shown by some proprietors, however, the company was never established, and so the island continued to suffer the grievous effects of the disastrous fall in the price of its wines.

As early as 6 May 1774 the creation of a wine company in Madeira was being considered, for on that date an official letter was read at a meeting of the Council referring to the advantages our island would gain from the formation of a firm or society to champion the interests of Madeiran viticulture.
Trade associations

We know of the following, all based in Funchal: Associação Comercial (Commercial Association). It was founded in 1835 by the merchant João Shortridge, had its first statutes approved on 12 March 1836, and is at present governed by new statutes approved on 11 May 1888.

Mutual aid associations

We know of the following in Funchal, besides the Associação de Socorros Mútuos ‘4 de Setembro de 1862’, which we have already discussed in the proper place: 1. Associação de Socorros Mútuos dos Sapateiros Funchalenses. It was founded on 5 May 1895, and its statutes were approved by royal decree (*alvará*) of 16 July 1896. 2. Associação de Socorros Mútuos ‘Monte-Pio Marítimo Funchalense’. It was founded in 1900, and its statutes were approved by decree of 24 December 1901. 3. Associação de Socorros Mútuos do Sexo Feminino do Funchal ‘15 de Setembro de 1901’. It was founded on 15 September 1901, and the decree approving its statutes is dated 15 January 1903. These statutes were revised and approved by royal decree of 26 December 1905. 4. Associação de Socorros Mútuos ‘Monte-Pio Madeirense’. It was founded on 28 March 1904 by twenty-eight members of various social classes, and its statutes were approved by decree of 23 January 1905. The statutes were revised and approved by decree of 31 May 1913. It has an attached savings bank, whose creation was approved by decree of 7 September 1907. 5. Associação de Socorros Mútuos ‘Reforma dos Operários Madeirenses’. It was organised on 31 July 1904 and legalised by decree of 16 March 1905. It admits persons of both sexes. 6. Associação de Socorros Mútuos ‘Pedro Álvares Cabral’. It was established in 1916 and legalised by decree of 13 January 1917. It admits persons of both sexes.
See Associação Filantrópica dos Estudantes do Funchal, Associação Madeirense promotora do Bem Público and Associação de Protecção e Instrução do Sexo Feminino.
Assomadouro

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Prazeres (‘joys’), which commands a fine view of the coastline stretching from Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’) to the parish of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’).
Assunção (Dr Manuel da)

This well-known politician and statesman was elected deputy for Madeira for the parliamentary session of 1892–1893. As he died in office on 23 March 1893, the candidate with the next highest number of votes, Dr António Vicente Varela, was called to fill the vacancy. Manuel da Assunção was born in Vila Real on 10 May 1844.
Assunção (Friar Remígio da)

He was a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), and we believe that he belonged to the noble Freitas family, whose founder on this island was Gonçalo de Freitas. We know little of his life, but from the important offices he held we must suppose that he was a man of undeniable merit. He was a monk of the Benedictine order and held the high office of general of Alcobaça Monastery, which at that time was entrusted only to a person distinguished in learning and virtue. Special privileges and prerogatives went with this post, as did jurisdiction over all the religious houses of that order in Portugal. He was a deputy of the Inquisition at Coimbra and wrote several works in Latin and Portuguese, which are listed in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’). He died in 1654.
French astronomers

At the end of 1753 or the beginning of 1754 a commission of French astronomers was in Funchal, charged with making observations for the correction of hydrographic charts. The governor treated the astronomers with courtesy, but the people received them aggressively, and force had to be used to restore order.
Atafona (donkey mill)
A domestic mill used until a few years ago on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It was installed in the kitchen of the house, and a small donkey supplied the driving power.
Ataíde

This was an old surname in Madeira, but today it seems to us extinct or nearly extinct. It descended from Mem Moniz, who was the son of Egas Moniz. The original manor house of this family was in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ataíde, in the diocese of Porto.
Ataíde (Berta de)
See Almeida (Dona Maria Helena Jervis de Atouguia e).
Ataíde (Dr Joaquim de Menezes e)

This prelate was born in the city of Porto on 20 September 1765 and took his vows in the order of St Augustine in 1781. In his studies he showed exceptional talent, with a remarkable aptitude for letters. He was appointed in turn chronicler of the Infantado, rector of the college of Santo Agostinho in Lisbon, titular archbishop of Meliapor, and vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) and governor of the diocese of Funchal.

His appointment as vicar capitular and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence) of Funchal in July 1811 gave rise to a conflict between the chapter of our Cathedral, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and the central government. The way he ran the affairs of this diocese was judged in different ways, not least because he became actively involved in political questions and waged a stubborn struggle with the then governor and captain-general of Madeira, Sebastião Xavier Botelho.

He rendered notable services to the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of Funchal. It was to him that the construction of the Fundoa aqueduct, from São Roque to Funchal, was owed, as was the drafting of the hospital’s regulations, which in his time were held to be the most complete and perfect in the country. It was for this and other notable services that a life-size oil portrait of him was hung in the meeting room of the Holy House, where it still hangs today.
In 1821 he had to leave this diocese hurriedly, never to return, and in that same year he was appointed bishop of Elvas. In 1826 he was made a peer of the realm.

Fearing persecution by the government of Miguel I, he left Portugal to travel abroad in 1828, and died of the plague in Gibraltar on 5 November of that same year. He was a distinguished musician, whose compositions are still greatly appreciated today, and also a distinguished writer, as can be seen in the *Diccionario Bibliographico* of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva.
Almost all the poetic and dramatic compositions published by Luís José Baiardo, who served for some years as his secretary, are attributed to him.
*O Jornal* (‘The Newspaper’), of this city, published an interesting biography of Bishop Dom Friar Joaquim de Menezes e Ataíde.
Atalaia
88 issues were published, from 5 May 1892 to 15 April 1893.
Atalaia da Liberdade (A)

Its first issue appeared on 24 April 1823 and its sixth on 29 May of the same year. It was a weekly, and its chief editor was the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Diogo Dias de Ornelas e Vasconcelos. It was the third periodical published in this city.
Atalaia (peak)

The highest eminence on Selvagem Grande (‘great wild island’), rising one hundred and fifty metres above the sea and falling sheer to the island’s western coast. It is a volcanic cone cut open on the west side. According to recent observations, its geological make-up includes various rocks. At the base, decomposed phonolites, overlain by compact basalts, stand out on one side, and on the other perfect phonolites, supporting horizontal strata of volcanic tuffs. On top of this assemblage lie masses of more or less scoriaceous, reddish limburgite, which form the summit of Pico (‘peak’). The appearance of this cone, much of it already collapsed, seems to lead to the conclusion that in very remote ages it was one of the craters from which the materials that now form Selvagem Grande were ejected.
Atanásio (shoal)
A reef (restinga) or shoal lying near the cove of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’).
Athenista (O)
Published fortnightly from 29 May 1913 to 30 August 1914, with thirty issues appearing.
Athias (Dr Marck)

He was born on 11 December 1876. Atlantis (island)

According to Plato, the celebrated Greek philosopher of antiquity, Atlantis lay on this side of the Pillars of Hercules, was larger than Africa and Asia combined, and vanished in the space of a day and a night as the result of a tremendous convulsion of the globe.

For a long time Plato’s account was regarded as pure fable. Today, however, when science seeks to extend its reach even to the most remote corners of the globe, it may be said that, although the existence of Atlantis has not yet been established as fact, it cannot be considered impossible either.

Mr Termier reports in number 256 of the *Boletim do Instituto Oceanografico de Mónaco* that when the telegraph cable running from Brest to Cape Cod broke in the summer of 1898, the men charged with raising it from the sea bed noticed that it frequently caught on sharp-pointed rocks with keen edges, fragments of which the grapnels brought up. When these fragments were collected and studied, they were found to belong to a glassy lava called tachylite, with the chemical composition of basalts, which, in the state in which it appeared, could only have solidified under atmospheric pressure.

Since the rocks we have referred to were found at a depth of three thousand metres and nine hundred kilometres north of the archipelago of the Azores, Mr Termier concluded from these facts that a continent must once have existed in that region of the globe and later sunk beneath the sea. The archipelago itself, which lies, as is well known, in the Atlantic volcanic zone, may well have formed part of that continent. Only a short time can have elapsed between the eruption of the lavas and the submersion of the continent, for otherwise atmospheric erosion would have levelled and smoothed the surface of the rocks.

In the view of Professor Eduardo Forbes, all the islands of the Atlantic must have been joined to Europe or Africa at a recent epoch. For Unger and Dr Oswald Heer, the hypothesis that Atlantis existed was in no way extraordinary, since it alone could satisfactorily explain the affinities naturalists had observed between the natural productions of these islands and those of the nearby continents.

However, since the remarkable work of Darwin has demonstrated that not only many plant seeds but also certain animal species can be carried great distances by the winds, by birds and even by ocean currents, it seems to us unnecessary to resort to these hypotheses to explain the presence of a varied fauna and flora in the archipelagos of the Atlantic.

Plato’s Atlantis seems to us to differ somewhat from the Atlantis conceived by the naturalists. Yet whether we regard that real or fabled region as an island or as an extension of the present continents, what seems certain is that Madeira and the nearby islands have nothing to do with it. The geological structure of these islands, the great depth of the sea surrounding them and the absence from all of them of the small quadrupeds that abound on the nearby continents lead us to believe that our archipelago is an independent creation, and not a relic of vast territories now submerged.

What we say about Madeira may perhaps apply to the neighbouring archipelagos, notwithstanding the opinion expressed by Mr Termier on the origin of the islands of the Azores. This geologist states that, before one would be entitled to assert that the Canary Islands are fragments of a submerged continent, certain local observations would be needed, which have not been carried out to date.

In our humble opinion, the hypothesis put forward by some geologists that the archipelagos of the Atlantic Ocean were joined to Europe, Africa and perhaps America in a recent geological period does not accord with what is known about these archipelagos. This is so even though it is reasonable to believe that this sea once washed vast lands, which sank in an age of ruin and cataclysm whose beginning and duration cannot be determined.
Atouguia

Luís de Atouguia was one of the first settlers of this island and perhaps the first here to bear this surname. He was a native of Beja, the son of Luís Afonso de Atouguia and Dona Isabel Telo. In Madeira he served as treasurer to Dom Manuel, the future Manuel I, when he was Duke of Beja and Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*). This Luís de Atouguia, or one of his close descendants, held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), at the locality (*sítio*) still called the Lombo do Atouguia today, to which he gave his name. Arms: ‘On a field gules, quartered by a cross of gold voided of the field, and in each quarter a fleur-de-lis of gold; a bordure of the same; crest, a demi-lion rampant of gold.’
Atouguia (Lino Nicolau)

A Madeiran poet who flourished in the first quarter of the 19th century. Poems of his are found in the *Collecção d'algumas obras poeticas offerecidas ao Ill.mo e Exmo Snr. Sebastiao Xavier Botelho* (Funchal, 1821).
Atouguia (Viscount of)

António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia, 1st Viscount of Atouguia, belonged to a noble Madeiran family. He was born on 7 July 1797 in the locality (*sítio*) of São Francisco das Furnas (St Francis of Assisi), on the Estrada de Santo António, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro in this city, in the house of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) that his parents owned there. He was the son of Manuel Atouguia Jervis and Dona Antónia Joana Carvalhal Esmeraldo. He was baptised on the 13th of the same month and year in the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), at Cruz do Carvalho (‘oak cross’) in the parish of São Pedro, by the distinguished Madeiran Dean João Francisco Lopes Rocha, whom we discuss elsewhere in this *Elucidário*.

Near London there was a college of European reputation, known by the name of ‘Old Hall Green’, where many sons of the most illustrious families of this island were educated at that time and for a good many years afterwards. Having learnt to read and write, Jervis de Atouguia left for England at the age of 14 to enter this renowned college, where some of his relatives and fellow islanders had also been pupils. After completing what we would today call his secondary studies there, he returned to his homeland and set out for Coimbra, where he enrolled in the faculty of mathematics. Of his diligence as a student we know only that he completed his degree in that faculty on 29 July 1822, having won a prize in the first year of the course.

In the October immediately following he was appointed substitute professor (*lente substituto*) at the Naval Academy (*Academia de Marinha*), later reformed under the name of Naval School (*Escola Naval*), and he was promoted to full professor by decree of 1 February 1834.

The liberal ideas he professed made him unsafe in Portugal. Fearing the persecution suffered by many of his fellow countrymen and friends, he resolved to seek the warm hospitality of the country he knew so well, where he had spent some years of his youth. He emigrated to England in June 1828, and in August of the same year sailed for this island with other Portuguese, to join the governor and captain-general José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, later Count of Bonfim, and to help him in the resistance he was preparing against the attack of the absolutist forces. It is well known that this resistance never took place, and that the troops commanded by General Lemos bombarded the town (*vila*) of Machico, took it without difficulty and set off for Funchal. Captain José Maria Monteiro, who had come aboard Miguel I’s fleet, was then installed in the government of the island.

The captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) Travassos Valdez, accompanied by Jervis de Atouguia, by the Portuguese who had arrived from England and by other Madeirans, took refuge aboard the British warship *Alligator*, which was then lying at anchor in our harbour. A few days later they all left for England.

He remained there until the end of 1831, when he left for Terceira to join the movement that had begun on that island to free Portugal from the clutches of absolutism. Shortly after his arrival, in March 1832, an expedition was organised against Madeira to free it from the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) yoke. This expedition, commanded by Luiz Mousinho de Albuquerque and in which Jervis de Athouguia took part, proved fruitless: the liberal forces did not even attempt an attack on this archipelago, in view of the superiority of the enemy troops defending it. Only Mousinho de Albuquerque and the officers of his party stayed for some weeks on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), before returning to the island of Terceira.

In June 1832 Jervis de Atouguia was appointed secretary-general of the province of the Azores, a post he did not hold for long. His ardent wish to join those fighting for liberty on the lines of Porto led him to resign that honourable office and present himself to Pedro IV, offering his services. He was at once given a place on the imperial general staff as a captain, was later transferred to the Royal Corps of Engineers, and was then appointed military and civil secretary of Porto, an office he filled with great distinction.

As aide-de-camp to General Valdez and later to General Saldanha, António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia took part in almost every engagement fought until the end of the civil war. He distinguished himself by his daring and bravery, notably at the battle of Almoster, for which he was decorated with three grades of the Order of the Tower and Sword.

Once constitutional government had been established, he threw himself into politics. While still holding his chair at the Royal Naval Academy (*Academia Real de Marinha*), he was elected deputy for Madeira in 1834, and on 25 July 1835 he was called to the councils of the Crown, running the navy ministry until 18 July of that year.

In 1836 he was appointed civil governor of Porto, and in the same year he was elected deputy both for that city and for Madeira. He also represented his native island in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in 1837, 1842 and 1851.
Jervis de Athouguia took part in the so-called Marshals’ Revolt. When it failed, he went into exile in England, but on returning to Portugal in 1838 he gave his support to the new constitution.
In 1841 he was chosen as president of the Chamber of Deputies, and the following year he joined the cabinet headed by the Duke of Palmela, in charge of the navy ministry.
Between 1851 and 1856 he was several times a minister of state, holding the portfolios of the navy and of foreign affairs.
On 5 January 1853 he was raised to the peerage, and on 15 March of the following year he was granted the title of Viscount of Atouguia.

Jervis de Atouguia served as director of the Polytechnic School (*Escola Politécnica*), was a councillor of the Court of Auditors (*Tribunal de Contas*) and reached the rank of brevet brigadier of engineers. He died in Lisbon on 17 May 1861.
Tuna

Four tunas are known in Madeira: the atlantic bluefin, *atum rabil* (*Thynnus thynnus*), the *atum albacora* (*T. albacora*), the bigeye, *atum patudo* (*T. obesus*), and the albacore (*Thunnus alalunga*; Portuguese *atum voador*) (*T. alalonga*). Of these species, only the first and the last have been recorded in Portuguese waters. *T. thynnus* is known to Portuguese fishermen as *atum*, *atum de direito* and *atum de revés*, and *T. alalonga* as *atum galha comprida*, *alvacora* and *albacora*. Tuna was once called ‘the meat of the poor’ because this fairly substantial fish sold so cheaply at market (25 to 80 réis a kilo, depending on the catch), but today the same fish can hardly be had for less than 300 réis a kilo.
The *atum voador*, or simply *voador*, is more highly prized than the other species because its flesh is tastier and paler, sometimes turning almost white when cooked.

Tunas, teleost fishes of the family Scombridae, are caught by line and not in nets, as they are in the Mediterranean. The bluefin, the largest, appears mainly from March to May, the *albacora* from August to October, the bigeye from March to May and the albacore from November to January.
See Skipjack tuna.
Atum de cacho (surface-shoaling tuna)

The expression is used of any species of tuna that appears in large shoals at the surface of the sea. It is applied in particular to the bigeye and the albacore (*Thunnus alalunga*; Portuguese *atum voador*), but above all to young bigeye, which pass through Madeiran waters in greatest numbers in the spring months.
Administrative auditor
The posts of administrative auditor were created by the codes of 1895 and 1896, which restored the special courts of first instance for administrative litigation.

The District Commission (*Comissão Distrital*), which was one of these courts, ceased to exist in that capacity in the district of Funchal (*Distrito do Funchal*) under the Decree of 8 August 1901, which applied to the district the special organisation allowed to the Azorean districts. The judges of law and the auditor remained, however. This magistrate now holds not only the powers conferred on him by the code of 1895 and by that of 1896, but also the litigious and advisory powers which under both codes belonged to the said Commission, now abolished.
The laws of 7 August 1913 and 23 June 1916 did not alter the jurisdiction and powers of the administrative courts to which we refer.
The secretary-general acts as public prosecutor before the administrative auditor.
See District Commission and Administrative Court.

See Industrial School. Secondary classes. Before the lyceum (state secondary school) of Funchal was founded, the following public classes (*aula*) were held in the city: mathematics, philosophy, rhetoric, French and English, Latin grammar, and Latinity. In 1821 the mathematics teacher had an annual salary of 500,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis); the philosophy teacher 460,000 réis; the rhetoric teacher 440,000 réis; the Latin grammar teacher 400,000 réis; and the Latinity teacher 400,000 réis. The substitute for the first of these chairs received a salary of 250,000 réis; that of the second, 230,000 réis; and those of the third and fifth, 200,000 réis each. The Latin grammar teacher, it seems, had no substitute. All these classes, except French and English, were established under the law of 6 November 1772, which also created a Greek class that never actually opened. The French and English class was created in the time of Governor Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro. There was also a special chair of drawing, created in 1810, whose teacher received 600,000 réis a year.

Austria (Empress of)

Empress Elisabeth, wife of Franz Joseph, Emperor of Austria, who on 10 September 1898 fell dead under the treacherous dagger blow of the anarchist Lucheni, first visited Madeira in 1860 and stayed on the island for about five months. Her doctors had advised her to seek a temperate climate in which to spend the winter, where she could also escape for a while the burdens of the demanding etiquette of the court and so make a complete recovery of her shaken health. Funchal was the resort chosen for this purpose, and the house preferred for her residence was the Quinta Vigia (‘lookout estate’). With its enviable situation, beautiful gardens, commanding position above the sea and fine view over the whole amphitheatre of the city, it was considered one of the most splendid residences in Madeira.
On 29 November 1860, at about six in the morning, the steamer *Victoria & Albert*, the property of Queen Victoria of England, entered the harbour of Funchal with the Empress of Austria on board.

As she had expressed the wish that her landing should take place without any ceremony, it lacked the brilliance and grandeur that the local authorities had wished to give it. Even so, the illustrious visitor received all the military honours and the other official marks of respect required on such occasions. The senior authorities of the district went aboard the *Victoria & Albert* to present their compliments and welcome to the empress, and they accompanied her to her residence. The landing took place at the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’).

The empress was only 23 years old and was then in the full splendour of her great beauty and most radiant youth. This, together with her sublime virtues and her kind heart, deeply compassionate towards the unfortunate, aroused the greatest enthusiasm everywhere, and she was always the object of great demonstrations of esteem and affection.
On 7 December 1860 the Portuguese corvette *Sagres* anchored in our harbour, bringing the Count of Linhares, who had come to Madeira on behalf of Pedro V to greet the illustrious visitor.

On 17 April 1861 Prince Dom Luís, later King of Portugal, arrived in Funchal, charged by the monarch with accompanying the Empress on her departure from Portuguese territory. Dom Luís had come in the corvette *Bartolomeu Dias*, which he commanded, and on the 21st he gave a magnificent luncheon on board for Her Imperial Majesty.

Elisabeth of Austria embarked on 28 April on the same steamer that had brought her to this island. The *Bartolomeu Dias*, the steamer *Osborne* and an English warship sailed in company, escorting the *Victoria & Albert* as far as the port of Gibraltar.

Emperor Franz Joseph thanked the diocesan prelate, the civil governor, the president of the Council, the harbour master and the Austrian consul for the honours and other marks of esteem shown to his wife. A few years before her death, Empress Elisabeth visited this island again, by then already suffering from the mental disturbances that stayed with her to the end of her life.

Administrative autonomy

The 8th of August 1901 stands as a memorable date in the annals of this archipelago. On that day Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Ernesto Hintze Ribeiro, then President of the Council of Ministers and Minister of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), countersigned a decree granting Madeira administrative autonomy on the same terms on which it had previously been granted to the Azorean districts. It is admittedly not an autonomy with wide powers of local administration. Yet it represents one of the most valuable benefits bestowed on Madeira over a long span of centuries, and certainly the greatest of all as regards the grant of the means indispensable for readily carrying out important material improvements.

The decree of 2 March 1895, countersigned by Hintze Ribeiro, João Franco and the other ministers who then formed the government, gave the districts of the Azores the right to adopt the administrative autonomy granted within the limits of that decree, whenever two thirds of the citizens eligible for administrative office so requested. The law (*carta de lei*) of 22 May 1901 modified some of those provisions and authorised the government to extend them to Madeira. It was, however, the decree of 8 August 1901 that truly established administrative autonomy in the district of Funchal, with the powers and functions laid down in the decree of 2 March 1895. These powers and functions are vested in an administrative body called the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), whose organisation and working differ from those of its counterparts in the rest of the country. When it was created, it had fifteen popularly elected members representing the various municipalities, and they met in ordinary sessions in April and November. The General Council elected an executive committee of three members, which, at the ordinary sessions of all the members, presented reports on the decisions taken in the intervals between those sessions.

The first president of the General Council of Funchal, who rendered it most outstanding services, was Councillor José Leite Monteiro. Its first head of secretariat was Dr Manuel dos Passos Freitas, who has shown great zeal and competence in the discharge of his office.

It was from 1902, when collection of the revenues granted to the General Council began, that this administrative body started to carry out a great number of public improvements, especially the construction of the road network. The General Council’s administrative action also extended to many other public services, some already existing and others newly created, and the inestimable benefits that the grant of ‘administrative autonomy’ had brought to this district became ever more evident. Later decrees sanctioned certain services of the General Council and gave them legal standing, but they did not essentially alter its economic and administrative life. Besides its own departments of secretariat, treasury and public works, the General Council was given particular charge of the services for the maintenance and upkeep of the Asylum, the Foundlings and Destitute Children, the Land Disinfection Station, the Laboratory of Bacteriology and Hygiene, the police for the suppression of clandestine emigration, the agricultural and livestock services, and others besides.

The decree of 31 July 1928 considerably enlarged the sphere of administrative autonomy, greatly widening its powers and functions, but it also burdened it with new and heavy charges without granting it the compensating revenues needed to meet them in full. These included the services of the ministries of Commerce and Communications, Agriculture and Education, as well as those of the civil government, the civil police, public health, welfare and social insurance that depended on the Ministry of the Interior and Finance.

It was then, as stated above, that important public improvements began to be carried out, especially the building of new roads.

Communications in Madeira were, beyond any possible dispute, the worst in the whole of our country. This was due to various causes, above all the almost unbelievably rugged terrain, and also to other unfavourable local conditions. Most of them did not deserve the name of roads, for in general they were narrow paths trodden into the ground, hard and extremely difficult underfoot, overhanging bottomless chasms and skirting the flanks of high mountains, and they almost always exposed travellers to the gravest discomforts and dangers. Until 1901, when administrative autonomy was granted to this district, there were only nine kilometres of good road, linking the city of Funchal with the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). The construction of an extensive network of roads then began and is still continuing; within a few years it will make it easy to travel the whole island by fast transport and to visit its main localities quickly and comfortably.

The offices of the General Council were housed in various buildings. By the decree of 12 August 1919 the building of the former Seminary of the Incarnation (*Seminário da Encarnação*) was ceded to this administrative body for the sum of 7,500.00 escudos (escudo: Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis), and most of the Council’s departments were installed there. When the decree of 25 April 1927 restored possession of the said Seminary building to the Commission for Worship of the Diocese of Funchal, the General Council moved its offices to the old premises of St Elizabeth’s Hospital (*Hospital de Santa Isabel*), where they have been amply accommodated since October 1933.
See General Councils (*Juntas Gerais*) and Public Roads.
Chief authorities of the archipelago

The secretary to the government of this archipelago, Joaquim Pedro Cardoso Casado Giraldes (see that entry), published in Paris, in the first quarter of the 19th century, in Portuguese and French, an *Estatística Historico-Geographica das Ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo*. It contains the list of the donataries of Funchal and governors of Madeira, with the designation of the decrees of their appointment, their taking of office and the duration of their governments. The list runs from the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco to the governor and captain-general Florencio José de Melo, who began to administer this archipelago in April 1815. The French and Portuguese editions of this *Estatística*, which differ from each other in the nature of their information, are, despite their shortcomings, an extremely valuable and almost unique document for drawing up the list of the governors of Madeira. They served as the main basis for the list that Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo published in the notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) in 1873. The meritorious civil governor of this district, José Silvestre Ribeiro, continued Casado Geraldes’s list up to the time of his own government. It covers 1815 to 1847 and is published in the second volume of the *Epocha Administrativa*, on page 141 and following.

The illustrious annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ made use of the work of Casado Geraldes and Silvestre Ribeiro, completing it up to the time his notes on Gaspar Frutuoso’s work were published, that is, for the period from 1847 to 1872; this appears on pages 823 and following.
One of the editors of the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’), in articles published in issues 1594 and 1596 of that newspaper, completed the list for the period between 1872 and 1910.

The superintendence of the archipelago lay with the governors-general from 1582 to 1640 and with the captains-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) from 1640 to 1834. The first constitutional administrative authority was Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, who bore the title of prefect (*prefeito*) under the decree of 16 May 1832. This office was short-lived, however: it was replaced by that of civil governor by the decree of 18 July 1835, and later by that of administrator-general (*administrador geral*) as a result of the political events of 9 September 1836. With the restoration of the Charter in 1842, the chief authority of the province again took the title of civil governor, which it still bears today.

See Donataries, Governors-General, Governors and Captains-General, Civil Governors and Military Commanders. Auxílio Maternal. This Funchal institution was founded on 3 April 1902 on the initiative of the physician and surgeon José Joaquim de Freitas, and its statutes were approved by a royal decree (*alvará*) of the civil government of 4 July of the same year. Its main purpose is to provide suitable food for children whose mothers, through illness or hardship, are unable to nurse them.

Birds
The work by the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz entitled *Die Vögel Madeira's* records thirty-eight birds that nest in the archipelago and one hundred and fifty-seven that are migrants.

The birds that nest in the archipelago are mostly European species, whereas the migrants generally come from the African coast. Of the latter, those that appear most often are, according to J. Y. Johnson, the following: *Accipter nisus*, *Fringilla chloris*, *Upupa epops*, *Ardea cinerea*, *A. nycticorax*, *Limosa melanura*, *Numenius arquata*, *Gallinago major*, *Gallinula chloropus*, *Fulica atra*, *Mareca penelope*, *Larus tridactylus* and *Sula alba*. *Cegialitis vociferus*, an American species, has been recorded several times in Madeira, and *Phyloscosus superciliosus*, from Asia, was collected some years ago on Porto Santo. Of the native species, the canary, the *corre-caminho*, the *andorinha da serra*, the *pombo trocaz* and the *anjinho* are common to Madeira and the Canary Islands and have not been found elsewhere. The *tintilhão* occurs only in Madeira, the Canary Islands and the Azores, and the *bisbis* is a species peculiar to our island. The *toutinegra de capelo* is a curious variety which we suppose has not been found outside Madeira.
Avezac

The distinguished geographer and historian Pascoal Avezac Macaya (1799–1875), in his highly reputed work *Iles d'Afrique*, dealt at some length with the Madeira archipelago, giving a brief description of its discovery, geological structure, waters, climate, vegetation, fauna, inhabitants, industry, commerce, customs, etc. Despite its shortcomings and its sometimes less than reliable judgements about things and facts, it is undoubtedly a very interesting study, and one that cannot be read without considerable profit. P. de Avezac had Gabriel de Gorat and Oscar Marc Carthy as collaborators on his work. A translation of Avezac’s study was published in nineteen issues of the former *Diario do Comercio*, from January to April 1909.

Ávila (Carlos Lôbo de)

Ávila e Bolama (Duke of)

António José de Ávila, later Duke of Ávila e Bolama, a well-known Portuguese statesman, was appointed royal commissioner with discretionary powers by decree of 5 September 1846. He was to come to the island of Madeira to investigate the grave events that had taken place here because of the Protestant proselytism of Dr Roberto Kalley, and to take whatever measures the abnormal situation of the district might advise. António José de Ávila left Lisbon on 9 September, accompanied by José Silvestre Ribeiro, who had been appointed civil governor. On the 21st of the same month he suspended the acting civil governor and the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of Funchal, and took other administrative measures. He left for Lisbon on 10 October, José Silvestre having taken office on the 7th of that month.

Azeda

The first of these species is taken internally, as an infusion, to purify the blood, and can be used in salads, purée of greens, etc.; the second is good-quality fodder. *Scorpiurus sulcata* is frequent in Madeira, where it is known as *cabreira*.

Azeredo

Manuel de Faria Azeredo, who was shipwrecked on Madeira around the middle of the 16th century while bound for India, married on this island, settled here and left descendants. His surname (*apelido*), however, which is in fact that of a noble family of Portugal, did not spread among us, because his son Manuel de Faria took the surname Almeida, perhaps his mother’s, instead of the name Azeredo that he had inherited from his father.
Azevedo
A family originating from Besteiros. Pedro Gonçalves de Azevedo proved his noble status in 1585 as a descendant of João Nunes Cardoso, lord of Besteiros.
Azevedo (Américo Olavo Correia de)

He was born in Funchal on 16 December 1881 and, as an infantry captain, served with the Portuguese troops who fought in France alongside the Allies. He was awarded the War Cross and the 3rd class of the Order of the Tower and Sword for acts of bravery during the campaign. Taken prisoner by the Germans in the great battle of 9 April 1918, he did not return to Portugal until early 1919, and was elected deputy for Funchal in the elections held on 11 May of that year.
Azevedo (António Pedro de)

He was born in Caminha on 7 February 1814 and first visited Madeira at the time of the usurpation, when he was a second lieutenant of infantry. After completing the engineering course following the restoration of the Charter, he returned to this island, where for many years he held the post of director of Public Works of the District. In 1842 and 1843, together with the officers of the British steam warship *Styx*, he surveyed the charts of Porto Santo, Madeira and the Desertas, published in 1877, 1879 and 1886 respectively. He died in Lisbon on 10 August 1889, by then a retired divisional general.
See Geographical charts.
Azevedo (Blessed Inácio de)

On 13 June 1570 a fleet under the command of Luís de Vasconcelos anchored in the harbour of Funchal, coming from Lisbon and bound for Brazil. Besides its crews and various passengers, it carried forty religious of the Society of Jesus. Their superior was Father Inácio de Azevedo, and they were bound for the Brazilian missions run by the Jesuits. The fleet left Madeira on 30 June, and on 15 July following, off the Canary Islands and within sight of the island of La Palma, it was attacked by Huguenot corsairs, who plundered the Portuguese ships and slaughtered the forty religious, throwing their bodies into the sea. They were entered in the martyrology of the Catholic Church and granted the honour of the altars. Their passage through Madeira, and especially their stay in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, was commemorated by a stone tablet which until a few years ago was still in the chapel of the locality (*sítio*) of Pico do Cardo (‘thistle peak’) in the same parish, bearing the following inscription:

IN MEMORY OF THE GLORIOUS MARTYRS OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS, FATHER INÁCIO DE AZEVEDO AND HIS 39 COMPANIONS, WHO, SAILING FOR BRAZIL IN THE YEAR 1570, ON 15 JULY, WITHIN SIGHT OF THE ISLAND OF LA PALMA, EARNED THE CROWN OF MARTYRDOM FOR THE FAITH OF CHRIST, BEING THROWN INTO THE SEA BY THE HERETICS; AND WHO, HAVING STAYED ON THIS *QUINTA* (country estate) OF PICO DO CARDO, CAME TO THIS PLACE WITH THEIR CROSS AND HERE PERFORMED THEIR DEVOTIONS, THIS WAS ERECTED FOR THE GREATER GLORY OF GOD. YEAR 1745.
See *Paroquia de Santo Antonio do Funchal*, of 8 October 1915, where this event is narrated at greater length.
Azevedo (Carlos Olavo Correia de)
He was elected deputy for Madeira to the Constituent Cortes (Portuguese parliament) on 28 May 1911. He was again chosen as our representative in the Cortes, being elected on 13 June 1915.

He is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law and was born in Funchal on 7 July 1880. He was serving as secretary-general of the Civil Government of Lisbon when he was mobilised to join the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps; he went to France and was taken prisoner by the Germans in the battle of 9 April 1918.

He is a descendant of Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, who was Civil Governor of this district in 1841, and the brother of Captain Américo Olavo de Azevedo, whom we have already discussed in this *Elucidário*. Works: *Jornal de um prisioneiro de guerra na Alemanha*, Lisbon, 1919, 204 pp.
Azevedo Castelo Branco (José de)
See Castelo Branco (José de Azevedo).
Azevedo (Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de)

He was born in Vila Franca de Xira on 20 March 1825, the son of António Plácido de Azevedo, a native of Benavente, and Dona Maria Amélia Ribeiro de Azevedo. Originally named José Rodrigues de Azevedo, he changed his name on entering the University, where he studied in the faculty of law, completing the course in 1849.

He then went to Lisbon, where he spent about six years, before moving to this island to take up the chair of oratory, poetics and literature at our lyceum (state secondary school), which he had won in a public competition. Before this he had sought, without success, to be appointed to a post in the judiciary.

Dr Azevedo held this chair with the greatest proficiency and distinction for twenty-six years, retiring in January 1881 to Lisbon, where he settled. For some years he was also teacher of Portuguese and recitation at our lyceum, and in 1856, during the cholera epidemic, he rendered notable services to the city as municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative).

He was also a representative (*procurador*) to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and a member of the District Council (*Conselho de Distrito*) and of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of Funchal. In 1870 he declined the post of secretary-general of the district and the commandery of the Order of Conceição (‘Conception’).

As a member of the Reformist party, Dr Azevedo took an active part in the political struggles in Madeira in 1868, proving himself on that occasion a skilful, tolerant politician of liberal aspirations.

He contributed to many newspapers and was one of the editors of *A Discussão* and *A Madeira*. In the first of these periodicals he published a piece of literary criticism on the *Bosquejo Histórico de literatura classica, grega, latina e portuguesa* by António Cardoso Borges de Figueiredo. He also published, in issues 181 to 183 of this city’s *Diário de Noticias*, an interesting study entitled *A Casa em que Christovâo Colombo habitou na Ilha da Madeira*.

His works are the following: *O Livro d'um Democrata* (Coimbra, 1848); *Esboço critico-literario* (Funchal, 1866); *Curso Elementar de Recitação* (Funchal, 1869); and ‘Ballad Collection of the Madeira Archipelago’ (*Romanceiro do Archipelago da Madeira*) (Funchal, 1880). He also published the part of Gaspar Frutuoso’s manuscript entitled ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) that concerns the Madeira archipelago, enriching it with many notes intended to shed light on certain points of our history. These notes, the fruit of most patient study and research, are in our view Dr Azevedo’s most valuable work.
