The articles ‘Machico’, ‘Machim’, ‘Madeira’ and ‘Maçonaria na Madeira’, published in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguêz* edited by Fernandes Costa, are by Dr Azevedo. While still quite young he also wrote a drama entitled *Miguel de Vasconcellos*. Because of this drama, which was never published, he had to carry on a somewhat bitter controversy in the press with the distinguished bibliographer and writer, the late Inocêncio Francisco da Silva.

Dr Azevedo was a distinguished jurist, and in court he often proved an eloquent speaker and a shrewd and skilful debater. His voice was poorly pitched, but he made up for this defect with his fluent command of words and his great knowledge of legal matters.

As a teacher, he was one of the most distinguished and dedicated our lyceum (state secondary school) has ever had, and as a writer he always stood out for his pure, idiomatic prose and the ease with which he handled the language.

Dr Álvaro de Azevedo’s name is inseparably linked with the history of Madeira through the notable and never sufficiently praised service he rendered this archipelago by publishing ‘Longing for the Homeland’, and especially through the learned and most valuable annotations with which he enriched Gaspar Frutuoso’s text (see ‘Longing for the Homeland’). The ‘Ballad Collection of the Madeira Archipelago’ (see that entry), the articles already mentioned, which fill some 100 pages of the great *Diccionario Universal Português Ilustrado*, the comedy of Madeiran manners *A familia do Demerarista* and the *Almanach para a Ilha da Madeira* for the years 1867 and 1868 are further powerful reasons that fully justify this land’s gratitude to the memory of the distinguished lawyer and teacher. Apart from his important and valuable works on Madeira, there is nothing here to recall his cherished memory to future generations. It would be only just for his worthy name to be perpetuated at least on a street corner, since it is not easy, and perhaps not possible, to pay him a more fitting and deserved tribute and homage.
Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo died in Lisbon on 6 January 1898. See Koebel.
Azevedo (Dr Domingos Olavo Correia de)

He was a magistrate in one of the judicial districts of Funchal when, by decree of 26 March 1841, he was appointed Administrador Geral of Madeira, administrator-general (*administrador geral*) being the title then held by district governors; he was the third and last to hold that office here under that name. He took office on 2 April 1841. He was elected substitute deputy for Madeira, and also substitute senator, for the legislative session of 1838 to 1840.

John Adams Dix, in his work entitled *Um inverno na Madeira* (A Winter in Madeira), speaks of Dr Domingos Olavo in the most complimentary terms and states that he was a native of Madeira, which does not seem to us to be accurate.
During his administration an incident occurred that forms an interesting episode in Madeiran history and should not be entirely forgotten.

Having been caught smuggling in Madeiran waters, the *patacho* (small two-masted merchant vessel) *Bernarda* was seized by the maritime customs service, forced to put in at the landing place of Funchal and sold here at public auction under the customs laws of the time. Shortly afterwards, on 8 August 1841, the English war brig *Savage*, commanded by Lieutenant Bowquer, entered our bay. In the name of Admiral Walpole, commander of the British forces at Gibraltar, he demanded the immediate surrender of the *patacho* *Bernarda*, threatening reprisals if his demand were not promptly met. The authorities maintained an absolute refusal, and their firm stance was praised by the government in Lisbon.
Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo died in Lisbon on 9 March 1855.
Azevedo (João da Costa de Ataíde e)

He was appointed governor and captain-general of this archipelago on 1 March 1701 and took up the post on 12 June of that year. He died in Funchal on 8 March 1704, by which time his successor, Duarte Sodré Pereira, had already been appointed.
Azevedo Júnior (Dr Correia de)

The *Diccionario Bibliographico* states that this Madeiran took his doctorate at the faculty of medicine of Rio de Janeiro, where he defended theses in 1852, publishing them in that city in a pamphlet of XII-68-II pp. We know nothing more about him.
Azevedo Lemos (José António de)

Colonel commanding the military expedition that came to Madeira in 1828. He had serious disagreements with the governor and captain-general, the notorious José Maria Monteiro, going so far as to try to assault him inside the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) and to denounce him to the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government as a man who listened only to ‘a vile circle of individuals abominable for their vices and bad habits’.
Azevedo (Maximiliano Eugénio de)

He was born in Funchal on 16 February 1850, the son of António Pedro de Azevedo and Dona Teresa Rosa Bernes de Azevedo. He attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and then the Polytechnic School and the Army School, completing the artillery course in 1875. He served as second lieutenant in Santarém and then in the Azores, returning to Lisbon in 1881, which he did not leave again except for the journeys he made to various foreign countries in 1889, 1893 and 1900.

He was on the editorial staff of the *Jornal da Noite* from 1882 to 1884, chiefly in charge of the theatre criticism section, and contributed to the *Discussão*, *Occidente*, *Jornal do Domingo*, *Atlantico*, *Diário Manhã*, *Revista de Sciencias Militares*, *Contemporâneo*, *Illustração de Portugal e Brazil*, etc. For more than 10 years he assisted Latino Coelho in preparing the materials for the *Historia politica e militar de Portugal nos fins do seculo XVIII e princípios do seculo XIX*, and he wrote and translated many plays, whose titles are listed in the *Diccionario Bibliographico* of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, continued by Brito Aranha. He also wrote *Tiro das boccas de fogo* (Lisbon, 1899) and *Marchas e Estacionamentos* (Lisbon, 1892), both in collaboration with Captain Artur Perdigão, and two books of short stories entitled *Historias das Ilhas* (Lisbon 1899) and *Em Campanha e no Quartel* (Lisbon, 1900).

Towards the end of his life Maximiliano de Azevedo managed the Teatro Normal as royal commissioner. Few could rival him in matters of stagecraft or in deep knowledge of our theatrical, literary and artistic history.
He died in a nursing home in Lisbon on 4 December 1911, being at the time colonel commanding the 1st Artillery Regiment.
Maximiliano de Azevedo’s godfather was Prince Maximilian, Duke of Leuchtenberg, who was in Madeira at the time of his baptism.
Azevedo Ramos (Nicásio de)

He was born in Tondela on 2 October 1862 and arrived in Madeira on 23 January 1885. He was chief editor of the republican newspaper *A Lucta* and qualified as a dental surgeon at the Lisbon medical school, practising this profession in Funchal for many years. Works: *Discurso proferido nas solemnes exequias de Elias Garcia, celebradas no templo da loja Liberdade, aos 18 de Julho de 1891* (Funchal, 1891, pamphlet).
He died in Funchal on 8 January 1927.
Italian ryegrass (Lolium multiflorum, Lam.)
A European grass introduced to Madeira in the last quarter of the 18th century, which quickly became naturalised over almost the whole island. It is a good fodder plant.
Canary holly (Ilex canariensis)

A native shrub or small tree of the family Aquifoliaceae, found in the Ribeira de João Gomes and Ribeira de Machico, at Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’), etc. It has glabrous leaves, smooth-edged or spiny, white flowers gathered in axillary cymes, and round red fruits. The wood of this species is white and is used in some small joinery work. During the Christmas festivities it is customary to decorate cribs, or *lapinhas*, with holly branches bearing fruit.
Azinhal

We believe this surname is now extinct here. One of the first settlers of Madeira was Estêvão do Azinhal, who in 1471 was a member of the governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office) of what was then the town (*vila*) of Funchal.
Holm oak (Quercus Ilex)
This tree is cultivated in some *quintas* on the outskirts of Funchal. It is easily distinguished from the cork oak, which it resembles, by its trunk, which has no cork.
Zurara (Gomes Eanes de)

This distinguished chronicler of ours from the 15th century dealt with the discovery of the Madeira archipelago in his *Chronica do Descobrimento e Conquista da Guiné*. He was almost contemporary with the events he narrated, spoke with people who had lived through them, and had at his disposal the documents that could enable him to write history with complete truthfulness and with direct knowledge of the facts. His testimony in narrating the events recorded in his *Chronica* therefore has great value and unquestionable authority. The circumstances of the discovery of Madeira that he describes, albeit briefly, offer the conscientious researcher the surest material for reconstructing the historical truth on this very interesting and crucial point of the discovery of our archipelago. On this subject, see note III to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). The *Chronica da Guiné* remained unpublished for about four hundred years, until it was published in Paris in 1841 by the Viscount of Santarém.
Babosa
The common name of *Aloe vera*, a perennial plant of the family Liliaceae, native to southern Europe. *Babosa* is frequent in hedges near Funchal.
Babosas

A locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), with a small square or viewpoint that has been called Conceição since 1906, when a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) was built there. It is a much-frequented spot (*lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish)), and from it there is a fine view over the picturesque locality of Curral dos Romeiros (‘pilgrims’ fold’).
Badajeira

A shoal south-east of the Ilhéu de Fora (a short distance from the Ponta de São Lourenço), where the steamer *Forerunner* was wrecked in October 1854 and the steamer *Newton* on 12 April 1881. Both wrecks occurred while the sea was calm, and a great number of people perished in the first.
Badejo (Epinephelus ruber)

A fish of the family Percidae, seldom caught in Madeiran waters. It lives on rocky bottoms between the coast and a depth of about 150 *braças* (fathoms). It does not migrate, and its young have been found near the coast in shallow water. It is taken on hook gear, with the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) and the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream). Although its flavour is not especially delicate, the less demanding palates do not consider it unpleasant.
Baião

This is an old family surname in the archipelago, particularly on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), although it is almost extinct today. Belchior Baião, of noble lineage, was the first of this name to settle in Madeira. The family held an entailed estate (*morgadio*) on Porto Santo and was patron of a chapel in the parish church that is still known at present as the Capela da Morgada. Until a few years ago this chapel kept the characteristic stamp of Manueline buildings, and it was certainly the only part of the parish church that remained from the original construction.
Baiardo (Luís José)

The *Portugal* dictionary states that he was born in this city on 30 April 1775, but we have serious reasons for believing that he was a native of mainland Portugal, although he lived for some years in Madeira. In his day he won renown as a dramatist, but his plays later fell into complete oblivion. He was private secretary to the bishop of this diocese, Dom Friar Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, and this prelate is credited, on good grounds, with the authorship of some of the works that Baiardo presented as his own. In Funchal he held the post of clerk (*escrivão*) of the ecclesiastical court. In 1821 he left for Lisbon, where he devoted himself exclusively to writing, translating and adapting various works for the theatre. His literary works are listed in the *Diccionario Bibliographico* of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva. Among them is one of interest to the history of this island, entitled *Carta escripta a um sujeito da provincia da ilha da Madeira ou o landum dos bordões, que tocou Sebastião Xavier Botelho, com variações compostas por Luis José Baiardo; ou desforra das invectivas que contra ele escreveu o dito Botelho na sua “Historia verdadeira dos acontecimentos da ilha da Madeira”*. It is a pamphlet of 33 pages, published in Lisbon in 1821.
Bays

It does not seem easy to draw an exact and rigorous distinction between the meanings of such terms as *golfo*, *baía*, *enseada*, *angra*, *abra*, *calheta*, etc. Dictionaries and geographical treatises reveal this difficulty, for they disagree when they try to fix the meaning of these words. Differing in part from the classification adopted for Madeira by various authors (Frutuoso, Azevedo, Nóbrega Soares, Sarmento, Loureiro, Meneses etc.), we shall say that, of the inlets along the coast of the whole archipelago, only those of Funchal and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) deserve in our view the name of bays, and we give the rest the generic name of coves (*enseadas*).
See Madeira (coves), Funchal (bay) and Porto Santo (bay and coves).
Baixas
Along the coast of this archipelago, many reefs or shoals break the surface or lie at shallow depths; locally they are known as *Baixas*.
See Madeira (shoals).
Baixo (islet)

This islet, also known as the Ilhéu da Cal (‘lime islet’), lies next to the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), from which it is separated by a channel, the Boqueirão de Baixo (‘lower gap’). It stands at the southern tip of the island, at the western end of the wide bay, opposite the locality of Calheta (‘small cove’). For centuries all the limestone that supplies the raw material for the lime used in Madeiran building has been quarried on this islet, and it still is. The quarrying follows the seam, forming long galleries with tall columns or pillars to prevent collapses. It is carried out at several points, and each group of workers employed at the various quarrying sites is called a band (*rancho*). The stone is taxed on export to Madeira, the duty being collected at the Funchal customs house, and it is one of the most valuable sources of revenue of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Porto Santo. The islet is fairly large, and rabbits are still plentiful there, despite the constant poaching of these rodents.

The islet’s ground has been uplifted, as shown by the limestone lying far above sea level and by the sea shells, corals and beach-like stones found in the formation. The fossils date from the Upper Miocene. About fifty species have been found, both in the limestone and in the adjacent tuffs, among them bryozoans, corals, sea urchins, lamellibranch molluscs and gastropods; they were described by Carlos Mayer in Hartung’s work on the geology of the archipelago. The limestone formation is covered by subaerial lavas.

On the islet’s coasts there are some caves with salt stalactites, and at Portinho (‘little harbour’) there are large excavations cut by man in the tuffs, together with a cistern whose water is strongly salty because the rock is permeable.
Baixo (peak)
In the northern part of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), towards the east-south-east, stands a hill known as Pico de Baixo (‘lower peak’).
Baker (Alice)
Works: *A Summer in the Azores With a Glimpse of Madeira*, Boston, 1882.
Balancal

A *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), bordering the southern end of the Quinta do Palheiro Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s barn’), from which there is a striking panorama over the amphitheatre of the city of Funchal and its suburbs.
Balcões

At the locality of Ribeiro Frio (see that entry), beside the levada (irrigation channel) path (*esplanada*), there is a spot with a small belvedere (*mirante*) called Balcão or Balcões (‘balconies’). From it one enjoys one of the most striking panoramas of the island’s interior, taking in the highest summits of our mountains.
Balcões (street)
See Rua dos Balcões (‘street of the balconies’).
Common lands

The common lands (*baldios*), or uncultivated and unused land of Madeira, lie for the most part more than 800 or 900 metres above sea level. Almost all of them are privately owned, although more often than not this ownership cannot be proved by legal title. It is said that the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) and a small part of the uplands of São Jorge, Boaventura (‘good fortune’) and Poiso (‘resting place’) belong to the State, while all the other land in the island’s mountainous region belongs to private owners, except for the Montado do Barreiro (‘clay-pit wooded pasture’), recently acquired by the Municipal Council of Funchal, and the upland commons (montados) bought by the Agricultural Council of Madeira (*Junta Agrícola da Madeira*).

There are about 30,000 hectares of uncultivated land on the island. Some former common lands in the Serra do Monte are now covered with pines, and it would be well if the planting of these trees were extended to other parts of the mountainous region, to guard against the danger that threatens us of one day running short of firewood for the needs of the population. The Paul da Serra, which the people were given leave to use in the time of the government of John VI, could grow the Canary pine, a species which in the view of Dr Jorge Perez is very well suited to afforesting the upper zone of our island.

In former times the common lands were, for the most part, separated from the cultivated land by hedges or fences made of stakes and tree branches, known as *bardos*, chiefly intended to stop livestock from getting into the crops. See Barreiro.
Baldy (Dr José Maria)

He was appointed civil governor and military commander of Madeira on 9 March 1858, while he was serving here as director of Public Works, and took office on 26 April following. Despite the short period of his government, he left an honourable record in the senior administration of this district.

He was a doctor and professor of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), a field marshal and a peer of the realm. He was born in Lisbon on 16 May 1800 and died in Coimbra on 4 September 1870. He was the son of the distinguished musician and composer João José Baldy.
Whales

From time to time enormous cetaceans pass off the islands of this archipelago. They are commonly called whales, but they may be either true whales or their close relatives, the sperm whales. Although the passage of these mammals is not very rare, especially in summer, there is no whaling industry in these islands, nor any hunting of any other cetacean. Now and then half-rotten carcasses are washed ashore; the last on record ran aground some years ago at Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), in the north-west of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). These remains still included much of the spinal column, some ribs and part of the ventral and pectoral regions. The deep folds observed on the abdomen seemed to indicate a species of the rorqual group.

In May 1905 a young whale, perhaps still inexperienced, found itself trapped between a sandbank and the shore, near the great beach of Porto Santo and opposite Campo de Baixo (‘lower field’). The inhabitants of the locality easily captured the animal, whose blubber yielded dozens of gallons of oil.
The large vertebrae of these animals sometimes form part of the household furniture of poor people, who use them as benches or stools once the edges have been trimmed.

Floating on the surface of the sea, congealed by cooling, one occasionally finds the white, oily substance that fills the cranial cavity of sperm whales. This substance, known everywhere as spermaceti, is called by Madeiran fishermen by the curious expression *gomito de baleia* (‘whale vomit’), because they suppose it to be a product of the vomit of the great marine mammals.
Baleira (town)

The municipality (*concelho*) and island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) have as their seat, or capital, the town (*vila*) of the same name, which is also known as Vila Baleira. This name is certainly very old, but it seems to have been little used, even in the earliest days of colonisation. From the rare references to it that we have found in old documents, we believe that this strange name gradually fell out of use and so, little by little, sank into complete oblivion. Only now and then, and only in official documents written on the island, does one still come across Vila Baleira, perhaps as a vestige of the ancient lineage of its inhabitants and of the old noble traditions of the descendants of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary of Porto Santo.

What is the origin of this name? We do not know. Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, in note XII to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), says the following on the subject, word for word: ‘The name Vila Baleira is of unknown origin: but, reflecting that Baleira has the same root, *bal*, as the first form of the surname Perestrello, and combining this element with the ending *eira*, one readily recognises that Villa Baleira is a name signifying that the town of Porto Sancto was founded by Perestrello: it is as if we were to say Villa de Perestrello. The name of the town kept the letters of the original form, whereas the family surname replaced them in the manner we have already seen when we dealt with Bartholomeu Perestrello (note X, p. 446): and they became so different that they seem words foreign to one another, though they are in fact cognate, as has been said. This is a strong presumption that the said town was founded by Bartholomeu Perestrello.’

This explanation is very strange, and it undoubtedly takes too far the rapid transformation of a word which, within a short time, passed as if by magic from Perestrello to Baleira. Despite the great erudition of Gaspar Frutuoso’s annotator and the considerable philological knowledge he possessed, we may apply here the well-known saying: *aliquando dormitat Homerus*. Someone has already put forward the idea that the word Baleira was very dear to the Perestrelo family because it designated the place where they owned a manor house, or perhaps the cradle of their forebears. We cannot deny it, but neither have we any serious grounds for asserting it.

Various names of localities and settlements are found in Madeira that were, and still are, names of towns and villages in Portugal, chiefly in the Algarve, whence came the largest number of the first colonisers of this archipelago. Thus the locality of Boliqueme, in the parish of Santo António, bears the name of a parish (*freguesia*) in that province. In the Algarve there is a village called Baleeira, which could easily be corrupted into Baleira. It is Dr Azevedo himself who points this out, perhaps as penance for the bold explanation he had given earlier. Baleeira, or Baleira, in the Algarve is a seaside village, and moreover lies near Sagres, where Henry the Navigator lived and had his school of navigation. To his household belonged Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary of Porto Santo and the founder of the original settlement established there.

The royal decree (*alvará*) that raised the settlement of Porto Santo to the status of a town (*vila*) is not known. On this point, note XVI to the *Saudades* contains the following: ‘...we infer, in the absence of the respective charters, that the settlement on the island of Porto Santo, later called Vila Baleira, and that of Machico were likewise raised to towns and municipalities around the same year, 1452, in which the grant of the latter received royal confirmation: and it is certain that tradition points to these towns as the earliest.’

The settlement, and later town, of Porto Santo or Baleira progressed and developed in the early days of colonisation. However, little more than a century after the discovery it began to decline, and it has remained in an almost stagnant state ever since. This is despite the adoption of certain government measures intended to help it progress and lift it out of the decline in which it has languished for centuries, notably those of the Marquis of Pombal (see Fifths and eighths). This town is the seat of the municipality and of the only parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Santo.
See Porto Santo (municipality), Porto Santo (parish) and Porto Santo (island).
Balsamo de canudo (Kleinia repens)

A perennial plant of the family Compositae, widely cultivated in various parts of Madeira. It has fleshy, glaucous leaves, whose resinous sap is much used in the treatment of wounds, and it originates from the Cape of Good Hope.
Balsamo de cheiro (Heliotropium peruvianum)
A shrubby member of the borage family (Boraginaceae) with fragrant blue flowers, grown in almost every garden in Madeira.
Balsamo (Mesembrianthemum edule)

A perennial plant from the Cape of Good Hope, introduced in 1834 to the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it is now very common. It has opposite, fleshy, three-angled leaves and yellowish flowers. It is also found in the gardens of Madeira.
Balseira (vines trained on trees)

This was the association of the vine with certain trees, usually chestnuts. The system of supporting the vine on trees or twining it around them is abandoned today, but it existed along the whole north coast before *Oidium Tuckery* appeared in the island’s vineyards.
Bamboos

This name covers the following species, belonging to the grass family (Gramineae): *Bambusa arundinacea*, *B. nana*, *B. mitis*, *Phyllostachys nigra*, *Arundinaria falcata* and *A. metake*. The first is recognised by its thick, tall culms, sometimes used as hammock poles (*pau de rede*); the second, extremely common in *quintas* (country estates) and gardens, by its lanceolate, somewhat glaucous leaves; the third by its green, striated leaves; the fourth by its black culms; the fifth by its culms bearing elongated branches, with linear-lanceolate, very sharp-pointed leaves; and the sixth by its lanceolate, dark green leaves with very sharp points.

Bamboos, almost all of them native to India, China or Japan, are highly ornamental and are commonly used for hedges within *quintas*. *Bambusa nana* (*B. viridi glaucescens*) provides good fishing rods.
Banana plant

The dwarf banana and the silver banana are the varieties most widely grown in Madeira; the first is *Musa Cavendishii* and the second a variety of *M. Sapientum*. Bananas for export are produced solely by the dwarf banana, which is easily recognised by its stems, 1.30 to 1.70 m tall, and by its very large bunches, which sometimes carry more than two hundred fruits.
This banana plant, also known as the Demerara banana because it was imported from that country, originates from China and has been grown on the island since 1842 or 1843.

The silver banana, far less common than the dwarf, began to be grown in Madeira towards the end of the second quarter of the 19th century. It is recognised by its stems of three to four metres and by its smaller bunches, bearing fifty to one hundred and thirty fruits of a lovely yellow on the outside.
These fruits are delicious and slightly acid, but they have the drawback of coming away easily from the stalk, which makes them unsuitable for export.

Banana cultivation already existed on the island in 1552, for it is mentioned by Nichols, an English traveller who was here in that year. The banana then growing on the island was probably the so-called *bananeira da terra* (local banana), which is also a variety of *Musa sapientum*. It differs from the silver banana in its fruits, which are somewhat firm inside and less tasty and aromatic.

The *bananeira da terra* is today very rare in Madeira, and the same may be said of the *plantina* banana (*Musa paradisiaca*), whose very large fruits are eaten fried or boiled. The purple-fruited banana, the apple banana and the lady banana are varieties of *Musa sapientum* that have not become widespread.

Madeira exported 550,000 kilograms of bananas in 1911, 493,990 in 1912 and 619,790 in 1913, worth 27,000, 24,703 and 30,000 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) respectively. It is thought that in those years banana exports amounted to about two-thirds of production.
Once cut and chopped into small pieces, the stems of the banana plant make good fodder, to which bran is added. Cowshed owners usually buy them to feed their oxen.

Like sugar cane, the banana plant should be grown only in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira. Above 200 or 300 metres its fruit is smaller than that produced on the coast, and at an altitude of 600 metres it bears fruit only with difficulty, as we have had occasion to observe more than once.

Banana growing is one of the most valuable sources of public wealth in Madeira, and its fruit is widely exported to mainland Portugal and to various foreign countries. The superiority of its native qualities over similar produce from other regions is already earning it an almost universal reputation, which over time is bound to spread and grow ever stronger everywhere. A scientific monograph was much to be desired, one that would highlight the history of the Madeiran banana, its composition, its physiological action, its therapeutic virtues, its nutritional value, the most rational way of using it, etc., with the proven competence and due integrity that the nature of the subject imperatively demanded. This aim has just been fulfilled by the work, valuable on many counts, which Dr Vicente Henriques de Gouveia published in a second edition in 1939 under the title *A Banana/Fruto de Todo o Ano/Alimento Medicamento*. It is a book to be read and duly appreciated, and its author deserves thanks for the notable service he has rendered to his homeland.
Banks

The following mainland credit institutions have agencies in Madeira: the Banco de Portugal, the Banco Nacional Ultramarino and the Companhia Geral de Crédito Predial Português. No bank currently has its head office in Madeira, but besides these agencies there are several houses in Funchal that carry out, on a larger or smaller scale, the operations proper to banking establishments.

The agency of the Banco de Portugal already existed in 1876, when it was in the charge of the merchant João José Rodrigues Leitão, who had come to Madeira in 1853. However, as this merchant went bankrupt in 1878, the agency was handed over to Tomás António Gomes, who took up the post on 15 July of that year.

Because of the bankruptcy of João José Rodrigues Leitão, the Director of the Banco de Portugal, Henrique de Barros Gomes, came to Madeira and secured an agreement between the bankrupt merchant and his creditors that was highly favourable to that credit institution. Under this agreement all the bankrupt merchant’s property was mortgaged to the Bank, which in turn guaranteed the other creditors repayment of 50 per cent of their claims, paid in three instalments. Before the bankruptcy, the Bank’s security consisted chiefly of wines, which had been valued at 102,464,408 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

Since the beginning of 1888 the agency of the Banco de Portugal on this island has acted as treasury cashier for transactions with the State, in accordance with the provisions of the contract of 10 December 1887. In the early period, that is, before the agency was definitively constituted with the powers given to it by that contract, the former paying treasurer Raimundo Sieuve de Meneses served as the Bank’s provisional agent on this island.

From 1904 to the present the following officials have served as agents of the Banco de Portugal on this island: Commander Luís de Freitas Branco, Henrique Augusto Vieira de Castro, Eduardo Martins da Silveira, Fernando Ferro, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Henrique de Sá Nogueira, Francisco Camilo Meira, Raul Rodrigues Cohen and António Noronha de Barros. For many years the Bank has kept two of its agents in charge of the business of its Madeira agency.

Besides acting as the Government’s cashier, the agency of the Banco de Portugal in Funchal makes loans on securities, buys and sells foreign exchange, draws and discounts bills, issues letters of credit, etc. It also accepts deposits, but pays no interest on them.

The branch of the Banco Nacional Ultramarino was opened on 10 February 1919. It carries out the same banking operations as the agency of the Banco de Portugal, the only difference being that it pays a certain interest on the time and demand deposits it receives. At both these agencies the rate of interest is 6 per cent.

The Banco Comercial de Lisboa was formerly represented on this island by the trading firm Freitas & Macedo, which went bankrupt in 1881, and the first agent of the Companhia Geral de Crédito Predial Português was the aforementioned João José Rodrigues Leitão. The Banco Nacional Ultramarino had a representative in Madeira before the creation of the branch mentioned above; the first to hold this post here was the late merchant Luís Gomes da Conceição.

On 1 June 1875 the Banco Commercial da Madeira, a limited liability joint-stock company whose statutes were dated 25 April 1875, was established in Funchal. Under these statutes, the bank’s purposes were: to issue bearer notes, payable in gold or silver; to receive deposits on current account and for fixed terms, paying interest to depositors; to discount bills of exchange and local bills, commercial and order instruments, and securities of the state and of any public institutions; to make loans on mortgages, government bonds, shares in banks and companies, and objects of gold and silver; to take up bills of exchange and maritime risk bills; and to settle estates and carry out agricultural and industrial credit operations, etc., etc.

According to the same statutes, the share capital was 1,200 *contos*, divided into shares of 100,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The capital was to be issued in two series of 600 *contos* each, the first series, already issued on 24 April 1875, forming the initial fund for the bank’s operations. Most of the shares had been taken up in the city of Porto.

The bank’s first board of directors consisted of João de Sales Caldeira, Carlos Bianchi and José Paulo dos Santos, and its first board of inspectors of William Hinton, Manuel Inisio da Costa Lira, Roberto Wilkinson, António Caetano Aragão and Manuel Figueira de Chaves. The first chairman of the general meeting was Severiano Alberto de Freitas Ferraz.
The reports we have before us on the management of the Banco Commercial da Madeira show that the assets and liabilities of this institution in the years listed below were as follows:

The bank made profits of 39,942,732 *réis* in 1877 and 32,851,757 *réis* in 1879, distributing 36,000,000 *réis* to the shareholders in the first of these years and 28,125,000 *réis* in the second. In 1884, 1885 and 1886 the bank no longer paid a dividend; in the second of these years 6,000 shares had been issued, 3,197 registered and 2,803 to bearer.

The Banco Commercial da Madeira was dissolved in 1887, with losses to the shareholders, a result to which the poor security of much of its capital contributed considerably. The fall in property values caused by the disease that devastated the cane fields made the bank’s position considerably worse. As the report presented to the general meeting of 29 January 1880 shows, that position was already not very prosperous in 1879, owing to the withdrawal of capital brought about by the law unifying the currency. As early as 1878 the extraordinary rise in exchange rates had prevented the transfer of funds, an operation that had previously brought the bank excellent returns.

In 1800 the government in Lisbon, in instructions addressed to the governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara, recommended the creation of a credit fund in Madeira. On 1 July 1824 the governor and captain-general Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro sent a petition to the central government asking for a bank to be founded in Funchal. Neither establishment was ever created, and the same happened with other institutions of the same kind that people later sought to found in this city. Issue no. 169 of the *Imparcial*, of 1843, published in full a draft set of regulations for the creation of a bank in Madeira, and issue no. 145 and following of the newspaper *A Ordem* (‘Order’), of 1854, contain the project submitted to the government for the creation of a commercial and agricultural bank on the island.

In 1873 the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) of the Misericórdia resolved, in accordance with the law of 22 June 1867, to found in this city a bank of agricultural and industrial credit with the sum of its loaned capital, admitting shareholders so as to increase the bank’s capital with the proceeds of the shares. A meeting was held for this purpose in the Palácio de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’) on 10 July of the same year, at which it was agreed that the shares should be of 20,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) each and that subscription should open immediately. Nevertheless, the institution never became a reality, for reasons wholly unknown to us.

In 1886 the late Count of Canavial advised the creation of an industrial bank in Madeira to lend money at moderate interest to industry and agriculture. This idea, which the same nobleman had already put forward in 1879, was not taken up, and our island suffered greatly as a result. Money was then very scarce here, owing to the bankruptcy of five of the most important commercial houses, with losses of about 1,600 *contos*, and to the agricultural crisis caused by the disappearance of sugar cane.

There was a time when the Holy House of the Misericórdia and the Orphans’ Fund (*Caixa dos Orfãos*) lent money at 5 per cent interest. The sums these institutions had at their disposal were so small, however, that very few people managed to obtain capital for their business on such favourable terms. Private lenders almost always demanded 12 and 15 per cent, and there was no shortage of people who borrowed money at *vintém por pataca* (one vintém per pataca a month, i.e. about 24% a year) a month, a rate equivalent to 24 per cent a year.

Forty years ago the banks lent money at 8 per cent, having previously lent it at 12 per cent. Loans and discounts on the first of these terms are still frequent today, even though the agencies of the Banco de Portugal and the Banco Nacional Ultramarino long ago set a rate of 6 per cent for their transactions. Certain formalities required by the agencies of these banks, together with other circumstances, mean that not everyone can take advantage of what they offer. The lack of cheap capital is one of the reasons why our industry and agriculture sometimes struggle with serious difficulties, and why certain useful initiatives that appear from time to time are not always crowned with success.

The banking houses now established in Funchal are Blandy Brothers & C., Henrique Figueira da Silva, Reid Castro & C.a, Rocha Machado & Ca and Sardinha & C.a. These houses, which carry out the banking operations required by the commerce of Funchal, and others besides, are all in a very prosperous state, thanks to their excellent management and the confidence they enjoy in the market (1922).

We can say nothing definite about how, in former times, funds were transferred or money borrowed to meet commercial obligations. It is reasonable to suppose, however, that the Flemish were the first to engage in banking operations here, followed by the English, who, as is well known, acquired great predominance in the island’s business from the middle of the 17th century onwards.

The various attempts made between 1800 and 1873 to found credit institutions in Madeira show that there was a desire to provide Madeiran commerce, industry and agriculture with advantages they did not enjoy. It is indeed strange that none of these attempts succeeded, given that the moneylenders who then abounded on the island rarely lent money at less than 10, 12 and 15 per cent interest, an exploitation that ought to have been ended.

On 23 June 1920 the Banco da Madeira opened, provisionally housed on the ground floor of a building in Rua do Comércio. Its capital, initially 1,000,000 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis), was later raised to 2,000,000 escudos and finally to 4,000,000 escudos. The decree authorising the definitive constitution of the bank is dated 7 January 1921.
Banda de Além

A populous locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, occupying a considerable part of the town (*vila*) of the same name and lying on the left bank of the stream, near its mouth. Most of the people of the place who make their living from fishing live here, and it is one of the most important fishing centres in the archipelago. In this locality stands the historic chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*), whose foundation is bound up with the discovery and first colonisation of this island. It is the centre of the best-attended pilgrimage in Madeira, held on 9 October each year, when several thousand people flock there. From this locality a fine road runs, partly skirting the picturesque cove, and leads directly to the landing quay. It has 243 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) and 1,090 inhabitants.
Banda de Além

In this locality, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Madalena do Mar (‘Magdalene by the sea’), there once stood an old chapel dedicated to Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria), whose ruins can still be seen there. It was founded by Father Diogo de Freitas Faria, in a year that is not known.
Bandeira Coelho (José)

José Bandeira Coelho de Melo represented Madeira as an elective peer of the realm (*par do reino electivo*, elected member of the upper chamber) in the parliamentary session of 1894–1895. He died in November 1897.
Bandeira Coelho (Luiz)
He was elected deputy for this archipelago for the legislature of 1890.
City flag

Carlos Azevedo de Meneses, co-author of this *Elucidário*, wrote an excellent article on the city flag shortly before his death, and we wish to preserve it here because it contains interesting information, some of it unpublished and little known. He gathered it in the archives of the Municipal Council, where for many years he was a zealous and distinguished official, which gives it a special authority worthy of the greatest credit. This piece adds new material to what has already been said in the article headed Arms, to which we refer the reader. ‘From some notes and articles dated 1461 and recorded in the volume of the Archive of the Municipal Council, it can be seen that the first flag Funchal had, in the days when the captaincy existed, was sent by Infante Ferdinand, who, as is well known, received the lordship of the archipelago after the death of Henry the Navigator.

What colour and what emblems that flag bore we cannot say. What we do know is that later, in 1563, the image of the apostle St James appeared on the city flag, and that from the 17th century until the proclamation of the Constitution in 1834 the flag was always white, with the royal arms on one side and the city arms on the other.

The municipal standard was carried by the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*). At funeral rites or at the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of monarchs he rode on horseback, bearing the staff of the standard on his right shoulder, with two servants behind him.

At the funeral rites of the former kings a black flag was displayed, bearing the royal arms on one side and the municipal arms on the other. In more recent times, however, this flag ceased to appear on occasions of national mourning, and in its place the white flag of the municipality was shown, with the arms covered in crêpe. In 1815 the Funchal Council ordered a standard from Lisbon which cost 524,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), because it had been made from the finest silk fabrics to be found in the capital. So as not to strain the municipal finances, it was resolved that the councillors (*vereadores*) should pay 174,000 *réis* of that sum, the Council bearing the remainder. In the end, however, the price of the standard was paid entirely out of the assets of the municipality (*concelho*), as a later resolution of the Council shows.

With the establishment of constitutional government and the adoption of blue and white as the colours of the national flag, the city standard ceased to be white. The arms on it, however, were not altered, for it was after 1834, in all probability, that one of the sugar canes in those arms was replaced by a vine branch.

We have sometimes heard a former municipal employee say that the flag which for many years appeared at the official ceremonies the Council had to attend had belonged to the National Guard. What we have not been able to establish, however, is whether the vine branch that could be seen on it belonged to the original flag or was some replacement made in more recent times.
The flag to which we refer, and which we ourselves knew, has gone astray, when it ought surely to have been religiously preserved so that it might one day be displayed in some municipal museum.

The blue-and-white flag that replaced the old National Guard flag is very well preserved and is kept in the Council’s archive. As is customary, it bears the royal arms on one side and the arms of the city on the other. The shield of the city arms is greenish, while the border, crown, vine branch and sugarloaves are silver.

After the Republic was proclaimed, the Council had a flag made in the national colours, but bearing only the arms of the city, on one of its sides; the other side has no ornament at all. The shield is a very dark green, the border, sugarloaves and crown are silver, and the cane is green, though clearly distinguishable from the green of the flag on which it rests. The vine branch is also green. It seems that the flag we have just mentioned, which the Council of Funchal had made, was fit to be adopted by the municipality, needing only the addition of the national arms, since these had always appeared on the Council’s standard. The councillors who ran the municipality’s affairs until 31 December 1922 did not see it that way, however, and so they had a new standard made. Its predecessor was put away in the same cupboard in which the last municipal flag from the time of the monarchy is kept.

The standard that now appears at the ceremonies the Council has to attend is white, as in the days of absolutism, and bears the arms of the municipality on both sides, which runs counter not only to ancient practice but perhaps even to the orders issued by the central government. The shield is green with a yellow border, the crown is also yellow and the sugarloaves are white. The cane and the vine branch, both green, are joined at the base by a red-and-green ribbon on which is [written] ‘to the noble and loyal city of Funchal’, which is also an innovation.

Besides the standard we have just described, the Council has a large flag that is flown at the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) on public holidays and days of national rejoicing. This flag, which is white, was also commissioned by the same councillors. It is a valuable work of art, but one in which respectable rules laid down in former times, and for whose rejection there was no reason whatsoever, were not observed. The municipality’s two present flags were ordered at the Council session of 2 October 1919.

We said above that it was formerly the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) who carried the municipal standard. After that office disappeared, however, the flag-bearer became the youngest councillor (*vereador*), a custom that has lasted to our own day. If the secretary of the Council, known today as the head of the secretariat, has on occasion carried the municipal standard, it is not because he has any right to do so. It is because, even in the days of the monarchy, it became necessary to authorise this abuse in order to avoid disputes between young councillors eager to stand out as bearers of that standard at the official ceremonies in which the Funchal municipality took part’.
To clarify the passage transcribed above, it should be added that this article was published in the *Diario da Madeira* of 27 March 1927.
See Armas.
Bando (public proclamation)

The public proclamation (*bando*) was the public announcement by which the people were informed of the orders of the Government and of the municipalities. The town crier, who in the case of municipal orders was the Council usher (*porteiro da câmara*), went out accompanied by a bugler from the regiment, who sounded his bugle through the streets of the city to call the people to come and hear these orders. The public notice (*edital*) was read aloud by the usher and then posted up in the customary places. The last time a public proclamation was made in Funchal was on the occasion of the funeral rites of Luís I.
Bang Up

The name of a yacht that visited Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) in 1829. The owner of this vessel wrote an account of his voyage to the second of these islands, which was translated and published in the *Diário do Comercio*, a former Funchal newspaper.
Banger (John Light)

An English merchant who had a tall column built on the beach of this city; it came to be known as Banger’s pillar. In 1801 he was granted a privilege by the Council to use an *estufa* (heated store for ageing Madeira wine) intended for purifying grain.

The construction of Banger’s pillar was completed in 1798 and cost 1,350 pounds sterling. In its early days the pillar carried cranes that were used to transfer goods from the boats to the shore; at present it serves as a signal post for the firm of Blandy.

The Pilar de Banger (‘Banger’s pillar’), so much appreciated by Madeirans and so well known to all who landed at the quay of the Entrada da Cidade (‘entrance to the city’), was demolished in 1939, despite protests from the local press and without any weighty reasons that could fully justify its demolition.

A few days before this outrage was carried out, a newspaper in this city published the following words, which we wish to preserve here for the record: The outrage is about to be consummated. The death sentence has been decreed. The typical, original and characteristic obelisk of Rua da Praia must vanish from the face of the earth. Within a few days it will be inexorably cast into the deepest pits of oblivion. So the lofty destinies of human affairs have decided. No stay, no pardon, no commutation of sentence can be obtained. Let this most fateful sentence be carried out without delay and without the slightest recourse, appeal or plea.

It is clearly not a work of art that ought to be religiously respected, nor a historical memento that would need defending, nor an archaeological object worthy of study that it would be proper to preserve. Everyone knows this and everyone acknowledges it.

But, as has been said again and again, the truth is that the old and interesting pillar has created an atmosphere of its own in the spot where it proudly rises, giving it a very special and very characteristic appearance that deserved to be reverently preserved with the greatest affection, respect and esteem. Everyone knows that for more than a century (the old column has existed for 49 years) engravings, lithographs, oil paintings and, in our own day, photographs have endlessly reproduced this spot and its surroundings. It forms an integral part of our magnificent landscape as seen from the sea, and it never fails to be admired and appreciated by the hundred thousand visitors who come to us every year.
Banks (Joseph)

A distinguished English botanist who died in London, aged 80, on 19 May 1820. He was in Madeira from 12 to 18 September 1768 as botanist to the first expedition commanded by Captain James Cook, and took from this island a large number of flowering plants, as well as a variety of information on matters of natural history. Joseph Banks’s manuscripts show that he and his companion Dr Daniel Solander collected 255 species in Madeira, even though the season was not among the best suited to botanical exploration. The small herbarium of the two naturalists is deposited in the Museum.
Baraço

This is the name given in Madeira to a cutting of any plant of the family Cucurbitaceae. A *baraço* (stem cutting of a cucurbit used for propagation) of a pumpkin plant, for example, is a shoot cut from the parent plant for the propagation of the species.
Cockroaches
Of these orthopterous insects, the following two species are common in Madeira: *Blatta Maderae* and *B. decipiens*. The first species is the household cockroach.
Water beetles
Coleopterous insects of the genera *Colymbetes* and *Agabus*, common in pools and running water, especially in the interior of Madeira.
Baratissimo (O)
Thirteen issues were published, from 17 July to 9 October 1852; it was then suspended for abuse of the freedom of the press.
Barba de bode (Deschampsia argentia)
A perennial grass, very common on rocks and in damp places in the interior of Madeira. It has little value as a fodder plant.
Barbeiros (shoal, cove and landing place)

On the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), between Ponta da Cruz and Ponta do Ninho do Guincho, lies the Barbeiros shoal (*baixio*), which extends into the cove (*enseada*) of the same name, also known as Enseada de Guilherme; there is also a small landing place (*desembarcadouro*) bearing the same name, Porto dos Barbeiros (‘barbers’ harbour’).
Barbeito da Silva (João)

This army officer was born in Funchal on 3 August 1855. In 1889 he published in Lisbon two pamphlets entitled *Escola Pratica de Infantaria e Cavalaria; secção de infantaria, acantonamento* and *Escola Pratica de Infantaria e Cavalaria; secção de infantaria, bivaques*. He died in Lisbon in 1932.
Barbosa

The annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that the use of this family surname here in Madeira derives from Pedro Barbosa, a native of Viana do Castelo, who was one of the early settlers of this island.
Barbosa de Matos e Câmara (João)

He was born on this island and graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He represented Madeira in parliament in the legislative sessions from 1858 to 1869, and died in Funchal on 28 May 1906.
Barbosa du Bocage (José Vicente)
José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage is one of the most distinguished Madeirans and the most illustrious man of science ever born in this archipelago.

He was the son of João José Barbosa du Bocage, a close relative of the great poet Bocage, and of Dona Josefa Ferreira Pestana, sister of the illustrious Madeiran Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Ferreira Pestana. He was born in this city on 2 May 1823. When he was only 5 years old he went with his parents to Brazil, fleeing the political persecution that the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government was waging on this island against those who showed sympathy for liberal ideas. Returning to Madeira in 1834, he studied at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), and in 1839 he enrolled at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), where he graduated from the faculty of medicine.

He devoted little time to the practice of medicine, dedicating himself instead almost exclusively to the study of zoology, in which he was an authoritative master. He sat the competitive examination for the chair at the Polytechnic School (*Escola Politécnica*) where that subject was taught and was appointed to it. He gave zoological studies a wholly new direction in Portugal and is regarded as the true founder of that branch of science in our country, from a rigorously scientific standpoint and in keeping with the advances made by distinguished foreign scholars. He gave these studies an essentially practical character, as the magnificent collections he organised most eloquently prove; that of the natural history cabinet of the Polytechnic School deserves special mention. His scientific output is vast and valuable: it opened the doors of many foreign academies to him and won him, abroad, the reputation of a most distinguished man of science. We would go too far if we tried to give a detailed account of his scientific works, many of which are mentioned in Inocêncio Francisco da Silva’s *Diccionario Bibliographico*. Nevertheless, we will say that he wrote and published about 200 works on mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, fishes, invertebrates, zoological philosophy, etc., among which the following stand out: *Memória sobre a cabra montez* (*Mem. da Ac. das Sc. de Lisboa*, 1857); *Noticias sobre os Arvicolas de Portugal* (Id., 1864); *Peixes plagiostomos*, Part 1 (Lisbon 1866); *A Ornithologia dos Açores* (*Jorn. da Ac. Sc. Lisboa*, 1866); *Aves das Possessões Portuguesas d'Africa Occidental* (24 lists, Id., 1867 1882); *A Vida Animal nas grandes profundidades do Oceano* (Id., 1870); *Liste des Mammifères et Reptiles observés en Portugal* (*Rev. et Mag. de Zool.*, 1863); *Liste des Antilopes d'Angola* (*Proc. Zool. Soc.*, 1878); *Subsidios para a fauna das Possessões Portuguesas d'Africa Occidental, S. Thomé e Angola* (*Jorn. da Ac. Sc. Lisboa*, 1879); *Mammifères d'Angola et du Congo* (Id., 1889 1892); *Mammiferos, Aves e Reptis da Hanha* (Id., 1896); and *Contribution à la faune des quatre iles du Golfe de Guinée* (Id., 1904). On our archipelago he wrote only *Noticia sobre uma collecção de conchas das ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo* (*Ann. das Sc. e Let.*, 1857).

In his mature years he entered politics, where he rendered his country distinguished services, always displaying the most austere integrity of character as a statesman and as a parliamentarian. He was a deputy and a peer of the realm, and he made his name above all as minister of foreign affairs. In charge of this ministry he proved himself a consummate statesman. In the very grave matters debated at that time – among which the Congo question, the business of the Berlin Conference, a treaty with England on the rights of our sovereignty in West Africa and others deserve special mention – he always showed himself a remarkable statesman. He was considered by all to be one of the men who have held the foreign affairs portfolio in our country with the greatest zeal and competence.

He died in Lisbon on 3 November 1907. Volume 2 of the *Boletim da Sociedade Portuguesa de Sciencias Naturais* contains a detailed biography of Barbosa du Bocage and a complete account of all his works.
Barbosa (Pedro Correia)

He was born in Madeira and was a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), vicar general and governor of this diocese. At the end of the 16th century and the beginning of the 17th he enjoyed the reputation of one of the most notable preachers of his time. In 1699 he published a pamphlet entitled *Sermão panegyrico em a solemnissima e anniversaria festa, que o reverendo cabido da Sé do Funchal da ilha da Madeira fez na tarde do dia oitavo do Corpo de Deus ao glorioso S. Antonio, em 13 de Junho de 1697*.

In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro, on the Caminho de Santo António, there stood the chapel of São Francisco, better known as São Francisco das Furnas (St Francis of Assisi). It was founded by Canon Pedro Correia Barbosa in 1697. It belonged to the entail (*morgado*) of Jervis de Atouguia. In the house adjoining it the Viscount of Atouguia (see that entry) was born on 7 July 1797.
Barbosa (Rui)

This distinguished Brazilian politician and journalist was in Madeira on 19 December 1907. Senhor António Eusébio dos Santos, then commercial agent of the United States of Brazil, gave a luncheon for him at the Infante Palace Hotel, which was also attended by the politician’s wife and children, the civil governor, the Secretary General and the Military Commander. Rui Barbosa left for Brazil that same day aboard the *Araguaya*.
Barbot
He visited Madeira in 1681, and his impressions of the island were published in *Churchill’s Collection*.
Barbuzano
A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Tabua (‘bulrush’).
Barbuzano (Apollonias canariensis)

A tree of the laurel family (Lauraceae), found mainly in the north of Madeira, where it grows down almost to the sea. It can reach more than twenty metres in height and has leathery, hairless leaves, sometimes almost opposite, and small flowers arranged in panicles shorter than the leaves. The protuberances often seen on the upper surface of the leaves of this tree are a gall of the *Erineum* type. Barbuzano wood is very little used by cabinet-makers because it is extremely hard. On the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) the name barbuzano is given to *Sideroxylon Marmulano*, a species known in Madeira as *marmulano* (Sideroxylon marmulano, a shrub).
Barca (square)

The original Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) had its northern boundary at the ramp that now leads to the Estrada do Conde do Carvalhal (‘Count of Carvalhal road’). It was built on the orders of the governor and captain-general Florencio José Correia de Melo, on land given free of charge by João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo and Miguel Carvalho. Once ceded, it was handed over to the Council on 21 January 1818 by a ministerial order (*portaria*) of the same governor.

The part of the Campo da Barca north of this ramp was handed over to the municipality under the law (*carta de lei*) of 13 September 1897. The land now occupied by the Disinfection Station was given free of charge by the Council to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) at its session of 12 March 1903.

The Campo da Barca is, and always will be, known by this name, even though it has officially been called Campo de Miguel Bombarda since 1911. Before that, in 1897, the Council had resolved that it should be called Campo do Conselheiro José Luciano de Castro, but the public did not accept this decision either, being on the whole little inclined to respect the political sympathies of its councillors (*vereadores*).

The square we are describing was originally called Campo do Conde da Barca, but the people, with their tendency to simplify, turned that name into Campo da Barca. The Count of Barca whom Florencio José Correia de Melo wished to honour was, as is well known, António de Araújo e Azevedo, who was our minister at The Hague and later Portuguese plenipotentiary in France at the time of the negotiation of the treaty of 10 August 1797.

The Campo da Barca lies on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’). Its southern boundary was the Larguinho de São João (‘little St John square’), where the Rua do Oudinot, the Rua da Infância and the Rua do Ornelas come out. The street that continues the Avenida de João de Deus and crosses this square has divided it into two quite distinct parts. The southern part has been turned into a square named after Tenerife, the Praça de Tenerife. The northern part holds the Land Disinfection Station (*Posto de Desinfecção Terrestre*), opened to the public in 1905, and the District Anti-Tuberculosis Dispensary (*Dispensário Anti Tuberculoso Distrital*), built in 1933. In front of this dispensary stands the monument to the Count of Canavial, which formerly stood on the Avenida do Doutor Manuel de Arriaga.
Barcelos (Pico dos)

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, Funchal. On it stands a small hill known by the same name, which is today an obligatory attraction for every tourist visiting Madeira. The land stretching far from Ponta do Garajau (‘tern point’) to Cabo Girão forms a vast semicircle, and at the centre of its diameter rises the eminence of Pico dos Barcelos (‘the Barcelos’ peak’). From this point one of the most attractive and beautiful panoramas that could perhaps be offered to the eyes of any visitor can be enjoyed. The road leading there, built in 1917, makes the spot easy to reach, and it is frequented almost at all hours by countless visitors, Portuguese and foreign. It seems that this locality took its name from Diogo Barcelos, one of the early settlers, who owned several tracts of land in the area.
Bardo
See Barreira.
Barradas (Diogo)

Speaking of the daughters of Tristão Teixeira, first captain-donatary of Machico, Gaspar Frutuoso adds the following, without it seeming closely related to what precedes it: ‘And this captain Tristão, because of a misfortune that befell a certain Tristão Barradas in his house, a man held to be a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility), whom this captain punished by keeping him bolted in a fetter, grinding flour at a mill. The King ordered him to come to court and to bring with him his daughter Catarina Teixeira (as has been said): he was imprisoned in Lisbon for the punishment he had inflicted on Barradas, and by sentence he was exiled to the island of Príncipe; and before he went, the King married his daughter most honourably. He spent some years in this banishment, at the end of which the King summoned him back and restored him once more to the captaincy, and he governed for many years after that.’

It is a curious episode in the customs of the age, and it gives the measure of the despotic power of the donataries in the early days of colonisation. Their civil and criminal powers were so broad that they excluded only the trial of cases involving the death penalty or the cutting off of a limb, as may be read in the article Judicial Administration.

On the episode briefly narrated here, the reader should consult the document transcribed on p. 138 of the 1925 edition of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). It is exceptionally interesting and gives us an approximate idea of how justice was administered in the time of the donataries.
Barradas (Dr Francisco da Silva)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He won great renown in Lisbon as a lawyer and especially as a notary, and for some years he edited a legal review which dealt very particularly with notarial matters and enjoyed high esteem in its day. He died in Lisbon in the last decade of the 19th century.
Barral (Dr Francisco António)

This distinguished physician and professor at the Lisbon Medical School accompanied Empress Amélie to Madeira in 1852, as attending physician to the ill-fated Princess Maria Amélia, who died in this city on 4 February 1853 (see Amélia (Empress Dona) and Hospices of Princess Dona Maria Amélia).
Dr Barral was one of the most devoted helpers of Empress Amélie in the provisional foundation of the hospice (*hospício*), which began operating in a house on Rua do Castanheiro.

In 1854 Dr Barral published in Lisbon, in a volume of 347 pages, the work entitled *Noticia sobre o clima do Funchal e sua influencia do tratamento da phthisica pulmonar*, which is regarded as a very valuable study of the subject. It was translated into French by Dr P. Garnier and published in Paris in 1858 under the title *Climat de Madère et son influence thérapeutique sur la pthisie pulmonaire*.
Barredo (António Pereira)
He succeeded Tristão Vaz da Veiga (see that entry) as governor-general of Madeira, having been appointed on 30 December 1590 and having taken office on 21 August 1591. He served until 20 April 1595.
Barreira

What should properly be called a *barreira* (barrier) the people of this island call a hedge (*bardo*): the fence or palisade made of stakes and tree branches, intended to stop the livestock that grazed freely on the mountains and common lands (*baldios*) from coming down into the settlements and cultivated land. These hedges were, and still are, common here, and they generally formed the dividing line between cultivated land and the common grounds used for grazing livestock and gathering firewood and brushwood. The old municipal bylaws (*posturas*) of some of the councils of this archipelago contained various provisions concerning hedges, the grazing of livestock, etc. Current legislation has profoundly altered those municipal laws and established other provisions, chiefly those concerning the freedom of sheep, goats and pigs to graze on the so-called common grounds.
Barreirinha

A small beach east of the Santiago fortress (*Fortaleza de Santiago*) and below the parish church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major). It lent itself to use as a bathing beach, and in 1939 the Funchal Council made it easily accessible by improving the site and the path leading to it.
Barreiro (spring)

A small spring near the foot of Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’), at about 1870 metres above sea level. In summer it yields very little water. We believe there is no other spring in Madeira situated as high as that of Barreiro. Its water, which we had occasion to drink in the months of July and August, is clear and very cold.
Barreiro (Montado do)

It extends from the Ribeiro do Pisão (‘fulling-mill brook’) to the Terreiro das Águas (‘ground of the waters’), and it contains land for pines and wild trees and land for pasture. There are some woods of laurel and tree heath. The Montado do Barreiro (‘clay-pit wooded pasture’) is extremely rich in water: the Levada do Barreiro rises here, as do some of the springs that help feed the levadas (irrigation channels) of Santa Luzia das Hortas, of Empress Elisabeth, etc. The Tornos (‘water turns’) springs, overlooking the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’), lie within this upland woodland (*montado*). According to the experts who measured them a few years ago, the total flow of the waters of the Montado do Barreiro is 4,140 litres per minute: 512 litres belong to the Levada do Barreiro, 2,728 litres to the Ribeira de Santa Luzia and the levadas that rise in it, and 900 litres to the Tornos springs, these last waters being assigned by the Council to the city’s water supply. The works channelling the Tornos waters to a reservoir at the locality (*sítio*) of Saltos (‘falls’) were completed on 22 October 1910, while the remaining works, which consist of bringing the same waters to the city, have only just begun. The owners of the Montado do Barreiro claimed that the Council should pay them compensation of 387,517.00 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) for the expropriation of the land of the montado and its waters, excepting those of the Levada do Barreiro. By court judgment, however, this sum was reduced to 42,163.07 escudos, which, as far as we know, has not yet been paid in full. Of particular interest on this subject are the pamphlets *A Expropriação do Montado do Barreiro . . .* by Pedro de Góis Pita and *Acção de expropriação do Montado do Barreiro requerida pela Câmara do Funchal* by Juvenal Henriques de Araújo.
(See
Water supply).
Barreiros (stadium)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), in the locality (*sítio*) of Ribeiro Seco de Cima (‘upper dry brook’), at the spot known as Barreiros (‘clay pits’), lies an excellent sports ground known as the Barreiros Stadium (*Estádio dos Barreiros*). It covers an area of approximately 18,000 square metres and was formally inaugurated in 1927.
Barreto (Dom Jerónimo)
Dom Jerónimo Barreto was the sixth bishop of Funchal. He governed this diocese from 1574 to 1585, and in that year he was transferred to the bishopric of the Algarve.
He came from noble and distinguished families, being the son of Gaspar Nunes Barreto and Dona Isabel Cardoso, lords of Farreriz and Penagate. He was born in the archdiocese of Braga in 1543.

After completing his course in theology at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), and before he had yet reached the lawful age to exercise the episcopate, he was appointed bishop of Madeira in 1572. For that reason he could receive episcopal consecration only in 1573, when he reached the age required by canon law.

On 31 October 1574 he arrived in Funchal to take up the government of this diocese. He left behind him the most honourable of traditions, and his name is bound to the notable service of drawing up and publishing the Diocesan Constitutions, which had become indispensable for the proper conduct of the bishopric’s various religious affairs.

To this end he convened, for the first time on this island, a diocesan synod attended by the cathedral chapter, the parish clergy and other priests. In successive sessions the Constitutions were debated and drawn up, and they were solemnly promulgated in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) on 18 October 1578, the anniversary of the consecration of that same Cathedral. These Constitutions were printed in Lisbon in 1585 in a volume of 188 pages. Bishop Dom Luiz Figueiredo de Lemos promulgated a set of supplementary constitutions (*Constituições Extravagantes*) in 1579, which were printed in 1601. Both sets still form today the particular canon law by which this diocese is governed in applying the general laws of the Church. Dom Jerónimo Barreto was extremely zealous in the discharge of his episcopal duties. Among the other measures he adopted in governing his diocese, mention should be made of the creation of several parishes and curacies and of the reform he introduced in the Chapter and the collegiate churches, in particular by reviving the observance of many points of ecclesiastical discipline that had fallen into disuse. Dom Jerónimo Barreto was transferred to the diocese of Silves in 1585 and died there in 1589, aged only 45.
Barreto (Dom Manuel Agostinho)

He was the penultimate and 26th bishop of this diocese. From what we know of the ecclesiastical chronicles of Madeira, we can state that he was the most illustrious prelate ever to occupy the episcopal throne of Funchal. He was born on 7 December 1835 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Coentral, in the bishopric of Coimbra, the son of José Agostinho Barreto and Dona Maria Barreto. He graduated in theology from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1858, and in 1864 he was appointed a canon of Lamego Cathedral. There he held important offices, among them professor at the seminary (*Seminário*), vicar general, provisor (diocesan judicial and administrative officer) and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence). Throughout mainland Portugal he enjoyed a reputation as a remarkable preacher, and some of his sermons became memorable. In the diocese of Lamego his name was surrounded by a true aura of veneration and the most respectful esteem, owing to his virtues, austerity of character, talent, learning and ardent zeal in the ecclesiastical duties he performed there for some years.

On 8 June 1876 he was presented as bishop of Funchal, and he was confirmed by the Holy See on 29 September of the same year. By a warrant (*provisão*) of 16 December he appointed Canon João Frederico Nunes, who was then serving as vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter), as governor of the diocese of Funchal. He took possession of the diocese on the 26th of that month, through a power of attorney granted to Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira.

His episcopal consecration took place in the Basílica da Estrela (‘star’) in Lisbon on 4 February 1877. The consecrating bishop was the Archbishop of Mitylene, Dom António José de Freitas Honorato, who had been his professor at Coimbra, and the assisting prelates were Dom José Maria Ferrão de Carvalho Martens, Bishop of Bragança, and Dom José Lino de Oliveira, the retired Bishop of Angola. On the 22nd of the same month Dom Manuel Barreto arrived in this city, and on the 25th he made his solemn entry into the Cathedral, delivering on that occasion an eloquent address that deeply impressed his audience.

A month after his arrival in this city, a serious conflict arose between the prelate and the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) over the burial of a suicide in the Angústias cemetery, as already mentioned above (see Angústias). He then showed the greatest independence of character, both in the way he settled the question and in the boldness with which he addressed it from the pulpit of the Cathedral in a sermon that became unforgettable. Even so, there were those who described the act as reckless and ill-considered courage, and even as a challenge thrown down to the liberal classes of Madeira. The prelate upheld the canon laws and faced squarely all the consequences of doing his duty.

Once that stormy tempest had passed, he devoted himself entirely to the administration of his diocese, which absorbed the whole activity of his mind until the last moments of his long episcopal career, a mind ever filled with the greatest dedication and the purest zeal and solicitude for the welfare of the flock entrusted to him. Seeking a quiet and peaceful refuge, he withdrew to the modest residence of the chapel of Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*), and there he spent 34 years in retirement and work. He left his hermitage only when the unavoidable obligations of his ministry, his official duties or his shaken health forcibly compelled him to do so. Before long, his great qualities as an apostle, his rare administrative tact, his unbending energy in upholding ecclesiastical discipline, his most remarkable reform of the seminary, his unsurpassed zeal in propagating and developing religious feeling, the austerity of his ever modest life, stripped of all pomp, his ardent and proverbial charity, his active and never interrupted evangelisation through the spoken and written word, the founding of schools and of various social works, his frequent pastoral visitations throughout the diocese, etc., etc., won for his name the highest prestige, the loftiest esteem and the deepest respect that few Portuguese prelates can have attained in the last 50 years. If we further add the brilliant oratorical gifts that made him a born orator, his notable learning, his qualities as a writer and the charming conversation that so captivated and attracted, we shall see converging in a single man a series of such rare and extraordinary attributes as we could otherwise find only scattered among many individuals. For all these reasons he was considered the foremost Portuguese bishop of his time.

His first and most devoted measures were directed at the diocesan seminary. He arrived in Funchal at the end of February 1877, and by the beginning of the following October a complete course of preparatory studies, which had not previously existed, was already running there. Its boarding facilities were enlarged and its internal organisation completely remodelled, the whole establishment undergoing a radical transformation.
