Having succeeded in placing Father Ernst Schmitz at the head of this house of religious instruction and education, he saw this clergyman render the most signal and outstanding services there, not only in the formation and preparation of the future clergy but also in the establishment of a regional zoological museum. This was a truly exemplary creation of its kind, spoken of with high praise by several distinguished foreign naturalists who visited it, and it had an attached physics laboratory for the practical teaching of that science. The greatest ambition of Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto was to provide the diocese with a building fit to house the seminary, in which the various services of an establishment of this nature would be amply accommodated and could fully serve their purpose. This ardent wish was fulfilled through the inheritance left to him by Dona Maria Leopoldina de Oliveira. On the convent grounds (*cerca*) of the former convent of the Incarnação he had a fine and spacious building erected, on which he spent his entire fortune, both inherited and acquired. Although it was never entirely completed, it had the capacity and the essential requirements to house the diocesan seminary, which operated there for some years until it was abolished by the decree of 20 April 1911, the building passing immediately into the possession of the State. (See seminary).

We should go too far if we had to describe in detail every act of the episcopal administration of Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto. Anyone wishing for a more detailed knowledge of his biography as bishop of this diocese should read no. 168 of the *Quinzena Religiosa* (‘Religious Fortnightly’), of 1 February 1908, and no. 2008 of the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’), of 27 June 1911.

Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto died at the residence attached to the chapel of Our Lady of the Peña de Francia on 26 June 1911 and was buried in the Angústias cemetery. Among his last wishes was this humble and pious detail: ‘he asks that, after five years have passed, his bones be moved in a small urn to the churchyard of the Penha chapel, in front of and next to the main door, covered by a plain stone bearing his name and the dates of his birth and death, with a cross at the top and the letters P. N. A. M. at the bottom, to beg the faithful who pass by for a devout *Requiem aeternam*’. Twelve years later, on 26 June 1923, the remains of the eminent prelate were solemnly transferred. They were covered with a small gravestone bearing this modest epitaph: Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, Bishop of Funchal. Born on 7 December 1835, died on 26 June 1911, aged 76, in the 34th year of his episcopate. P. A. H. M.

From Part IV of Volume IV of the notable work *Historia da Igreja em Portugal*, by the illustrious writer Fortunato de Almeida, we transcribe a summary of the principal biographical facts about the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto: ‘He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Pedrógão Grande on 7 December 1835 and graduated in theology at the University of Coimbra in 1858. He was professor of ecclesiastical sciences at the seminary of Lamego from 1864, canon of the cathedral of that city from 1866, provisor (diocesan judicial and administrative officer) and vicar general of the bishopric from 1868, and domestic prelate to His Holiness from 1870. Presented to the see of Funchal by decree of 8 June 1876, he was confirmed in the consistory of 29 September of the same year. He took possession through his representative (*procurador*), Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira, on 26 December. On 4 February 1877 he was consecrated in the basilica of the Coração de Jesus (Heart of Jesus), at Estrela, in Lisbon, by the Archbishop of Mitylene, Dom António José de Freitas Honorato, assisted by Dom José Maria Ferrão de Carvalho Martens, Bishop of Bragança, and Dom José Lino de Oliveira, retired Bishop of Angola. He left Lisbon on 20 February and landed at Funchal on the afternoon of the 22nd. On the following Sunday, the 25th, he made his solemn entry, and on 2 March he issued his first pastoral letter. “Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto was a most remarkable bishop for his talents and virtues. A distinguished orator, he also proved a writer of great merit in his pastoral letters; some of these are models of their kind, for their doctrinal substance and their literary craftsmanship. Charity, humility and a spirit of justice were virtues in which he always excelled, and his pastoral zeal, his dedication to the affairs of his diocese and his detachment from all personal interest recall the most virtuous Portuguese prelates of former times. From the outset this brilliant combination of qualities earned him the veneration of his flock. Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, says one of his biographers, was a model priest and bishop. Although he had received substantial legacies that would have allowed him ample comfort and even luxury, he lived in his most modest residence with the simplicity of an ascetic. A poor bed and a poor table met the material needs of an existence wholly devoted to the spiritual life. In his view those revenues were better employed in founding schools, relieving widowers, protecting orphans and helping all those whom fortune had forsaken.”’

‘The favourite work of Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto was the diocesan seminary, which he reformed and improved remarkably. Besides creating several new chairs, he founded a cabinet of physical and natural sciences under the direction of Father Ernst Schmitz; so notable was this achievement that it won the praise of specialists at home and abroad. Later, recognising that the old building in Rua do Mosteiro Novo was in poor condition, he had the new seminary of the Incarnação built at his own expense and at great personal sacrifice, and it became a shining crown of glory for the great prelate’.
Barreto (Father Jaime de Gouveia)

He was born in Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) on 13 May 1887 and attended the Episcopal Seminary of Funchal (*Seminário Episcopal do Funchal*), being ordained priest (*presbítero*) in 1910. Having assisted the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz in preparing and identifying the natural history specimens in the Seminary museum, he developed a certain fondness for this kind of work, and for that reason he was later put in charge of the museum when that priest left for Jerusalem. He collected a large number of Madeiran lichens and fungi; the former were studied by Professor Navas and the latter by Professor Torrend. He is a member of the Natural Sciences Society of Saragossa. Called up to attend the school for militia officers (*oficiais milicianos*) in Lisbon during the state of war between Portugal and Germany, he succeeded in being appointed army chaplain with the rank of second lieutenant (*alferes capelão*) to the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps in France. He left for that country on 23 May 1918 and returned home in June 1919.
He is a professor at the Diocesan Seminary and director of its natural science collections. He was granted the title of monsignor and is a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé).
Barreto (Remígio António Gil Spínola)

By decree of 1 May 1913 he was appointed substitute civil governor of this district, taking office on the 10th of the same month and year. He was elected senator for Madeira on 13 July 1915. He is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law and a notary in the city of Funchal, and was born in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) on 24 February 1870.
Barilla

Throughout the Madeira archipelago this name is given to *Mesembrianthemum nodiflorum*, *M. crystallinum* and *Suaeda fruticosa*. The first two plants belong to the family *Aizoaceas*, while the last, which is woody, belongs to the *Quenopodeaceas*. Soda was formerly extracted from these plants by drying them in the sun and then burning them in pits dug in the ground. Once the materials making up the barilla (saltwort burned for soda; *barrilha*) had been burned, a hard, alkaline substance remained on cooling, called crude soda, which Madeirans called *pedra de barrilha* (barilla stone) or *pedra de fazer sabão* (soap-making stone). The crude soda was decarbonated with lime.
Barros

The first among them to use this surname was Vasco Delgado, who came to this island in the earliest days of its colonisation. He settled in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’), where he held a great deal of land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), chiefly along the Ribeira dos Melões, and also kept a splendid household, according to an old nobiliary. The family bore the following coat of arms: on a field gules three bends argent, and over the field nine mullets or – one on the first in chief, three on the second, three on the third and two on the fourth; and for difference a black *morlota* on one of the bends; the helm argent, open and garnished or; the mantling or, gules and argent; and for crest a saltire gules charged with five mullets of the arms.

Diogo de Barros and Pedro Gonçalves de Barros, who belonged to this family, distinguished themselves in Africa, particularly in the conquest of Azemmour. Of the former, Gaspar Frutuoso says that this Diogo de Barros was so well known to the Moors, and had such a name among them as a fine horseman, that they feared him as they feared death itself. Once, he relates, Diogo was with other horsemen at the taking of some encampments (*aduares*) where the Moors kept their cattle safe from the Christians, surrounded by ditches, irrigation channels and pits covered over with earth. The Christians nevertheless fell upon them, and this Diogo de Barros, from his experience of such pits, realised that they were there and leapt them on his horse. Seeing that his elder brother, Pedro Gonçalves de Barros, hesitated to do the same, he turned back, being of a hot temper and a fine horseman, and forced him to leap, telling him ‘that if he did not do so he would couch his lance against him, for it was in the perils of war that horsemen were to be known; and however great those perils were, the Barros must stand out and distinguish themselves in them’. And with these words both leapt the ditches, charging the Moors with the cry of ‘Santiago’ in great fury and wreaking great havoc among them, whereupon they routed them’.
Barros (Diogo de)

He was a valiant Madeiran knight who greatly distinguished himself in our campaigns in Morocco, above all at the taking of Azemmour, where he accompanied the fourth captain-donatary of Funchal, João Gonçalves da Câmara. (See Barros.)
Barros Gomes (Henrique de)
He stayed in Funchal from 8 July to 2 September 1878 as Director of the Bank of Portugal, following the bankruptcy of João José Rodrigues Leitão, the bank’s agent on this island. (See Banks.)
Barros (João de)
In his well-known work *Asia*, decade 10, this notable historian of ours (1496–1570) deals with the discovery of the Madeira archipelago.
Barros (Vasco Delgado de)
He was one of the first settlers, and founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’) on his lands at Ribeira dos Melões (‘melons’ stream’).
Barrow (John)

This well-known English traveller and orientalist was in Madeira in 1792, and published a description of his visit to the island in the work entitled *Voyage to Cochin China*. A translation of this description exists, published in nos 290 to 292 and 297 to 298 of the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’).
Barruncho (José Maria Smith)

According to the dictionary *Portugal*, this distinguished officer of our army was of English descent and had been born in Funchal in 1839. He died in Lisbon, with the rank of general, on 26 July 1898.
Bartolomeu (João)

By royal decree (*alvará*) of 10 November 1618 he was appointed engineer-director of the fortifications then being built on this island. Manuel Tomás refers to him in very laudatory terms in book X of ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*). (See *Diccionario dos Arch. e Eng. Port.*, vol. 2, p. 34.)
Basalts
Dark, compact and hard volcanic rocks, formed of labradorite feldspar and augite. They are relatively poor in silica but contain more lime and magnesia than trachyte, which is rich in silica.

According to the geologist James Smith, of Jordan Hill, three kinds are known in Madeira: compact basalt (*pedra viva* (‘live stone’: compact basalt used for building) or *alvenaria* (local name for compact basalt used as building stone)), vesicular basalt (*cantaria rija* (hard dressed stone of vesicular basalt)) and scoriaceous basalt. Tuffs often alternate with the basalts, and compact basalts are frequently seen resting on layers of scoriaceous basalt. When it occurs in thick layers, compact basalt often splits vertically into columns of polygonal section, as is often seen in quarries and can also be observed near Gorgulho (‘weevil’), at Tem-te não Caias (Porto da Cruz) and at Faial.
Compact basalt is used in every kind of building, although the hardness of its grain means it cannot be dressed.
Vesicular basalt is found mainly in the neighbourhood of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), and is used throughout the island for door jambs, cornerstones, steps, etc.
Scoriaceous basalt occurs everywhere, often interspersed with compact basalt, but it is not used in building.

The basalts, very common in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira and also found on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), generally contain crystals of augite and olivine, the former black, the latter greenish. They often occur as dykes, vertical or oblique, cutting through layers of conglomerate or of basaltic rocks that have split.
Batalha Reis (António)
He was in Madeira in 1905 and gave a lecture on oenology in the rooms of the Associação Comercial on 11 October 1905. A summary of this lecture has been published.
Artillery battery

Since 23 June 1877 there has been a permanent artillery force in Madeira. Its first commander was Captain Henrique de Lima e Cunha, who held the post until 20 January 1878. Before then the island was garrisoned by artillery detachments sent from Portugal.

The original No. 3 Garrison Artillery Company was renamed No. 3 Garrison Artillery Battery (*Bataria n.º 3 de Artilharia de Guarnição*) on 1 January 1902, and No. 3 Mountain Artillery Battery (*Bataria n.º 3 de Artilharia de Montanha*) on 30 June 1911.
Sweet potato (Ipomaea Batatas)

A member of the Convolvulaceae native to South America and common in Madeira. The cut-leaved sweet potato was introduced to the island in the mid-17th century; the form with entire or angular leaves did not begin to be cultivated until 1845, the first specimens to appear here having come from Demerara.
Madeirans call the aerial part of the sweet potato plant *rama* (vine), and it is by means of this that the plant is propagated.
Sweet potatoes are one of the staple foods of the Madeiran population, and they can also be made into a very tasty preserve.

On the subject of the sweet potato, which is grown on a large scale in Madeira and eaten in such great quantities by the inhabitants of the rural parishes, we shall transcribe an article published some years ago in *Portugal Agrícola*. It contains interesting information that may be of use to Madeirans who grow this tuber.

The sweet potato (*Batata edulis*), a plant of the Convolvulaceae family introduced to Madeira in the mid-17th century, thrives on this island from close to the sea up to the limits of the cultivated zone. In Madeira it is propagated from cuttings, which are planted all year round in the low-lying zone and from May to July at higher elevations.

Some farmers take two or even three harvests of sweet potatoes from their land each year, but this happens only in warm, low-lying places where rainfall is less abundant. On high ground only one crop of these roots is obtained each year, and it is generally harvested before the rainiest season, to prevent the damp from making the tubers watery and hard to keep. The sweet potato is not demanding as to the quality of the soil, but it gives more abundant yields in dry, deep soils of medium consistency.

Two quite distinct varieties of *Batata edulis* exist in Madeira: the variety *cordifolia*, with entire or almost entire leaves, and the variety *digitata*, with leaves more or less deeply lobed. The latter is the older on the island; the variety *cordifolia* was introduced in 1845, the first specimens grown here having come from Demerara.

Madeirans give no particular names to the tubers of the sweet potato plant, but the *rama* (the aerial part of the plant) receives various names according to its colour and appearance. In the variety *cordifolia* the following two sub-varieties are common: *rama inglesa* and *rama de São Martinho*, both of which produce white potatoes.

In the variety *digitata*, much richer in forms than the preceding one, the following sub-varieties may be noted as common: *rama Machiqueira* or *de Sandwich*, *da Magdalena*, *frizada*, *de graveto*, *braço de rei*, *brazileira*, *feiticeira* and *de Cayenna*. The tubers of the first four are white, those of the next two reddish, those of the penultimate somewhat violet and those of the last yellow. The *rama da terra*, introduced in the 18th century and today very rare on the island, also belongs to this variety.

‘The *rama da terra* usually produces larger, sweeter and floorier potatoes than a great many of the modern sub-varieties; it has, however, the drawback of needing more time to form roots and of giving only one harvest each year, which makes it unprofitable and therefore less valued by Madeiran farmers. Its roots are white, rarely yellow.

‘The roots of the sweet potato are starchy, sugary, pleasant to the taste and more easily digested than the tubers of the solanaceous plant known on the island by the name of potato (Madeiran *semilha*). Madeirans eat them on a large scale, and also give them to their domestic animals, which devour them greedily. From them a preserve much prized by foreigners is made.

The vines of the sweet potato make excellent food for livestock. In Madeira it is customary to give them to animals only when green, but they could also be used as dry fodder, provided care is taken to gather and prepare them before the rains.

The sweet potato, which, as we have said, is propagated on the island only by cuttings, is grown in furrows, usually together with other plants such as cabbages, maize, beans, peas, etc. The sweet potato plants usually occupy one side of the furrows, often spreading over the ridges.
Batista

This surname derives from Misser João Batista, who came of the noble Genoese family of Usodimare and settled on this island in the last quarter of the 15th century. He made his home in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), where he held a great deal of land in *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). In that parish there is a locality (*sítio*) called Terra Batista (‘Batista’s land’), which belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by Misser João Batista and passed down among his descendants. He married Tristoa Teixeira, daughter of the discoverer Tristão Vaz Teixeira, first captain-donatary of Machico.
Batista de Sousa (Dr António)

He was deputy for this archipelago in the legislature of 1892–1893, and also elective peer of the realm (*par do reino electivo*, elected member of the upper chamber) for Madeira in the parliamentary session of 1894–1895.
Batista (Friar Gregório)

A native of Funchal, he is conjectured to have been born in the last quarter of the 16th century. He was a member of the Seraphic Order (the Franciscans) and belonged to the province of Catalonia. Some years later he entered the Benedictine order, in a convent in the city of Bahia, later returning to the Order of St Francis, which he had originally embraced. In the latter he held important offices, among them professor of Scripture and examiner of the military orders, as well as others. He published several sermons, which were translated into Spanish and Italian, which proves their worth. Some are listed in the *Diccionario Bibliographico* of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva. That work also mentions this author’s book *Completas da Vida de Cristo. . .*, published in 1623. The *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’) cites two works of his written in Latin, published in 1621 and 1638. He died after the year 1640. We know nothing more about this Madeiran, who seems to have been a man of undeniable merit.
Batista Santos (José da Cruz)

Madeiran poet and journalist, born in Funchal on 24 November 1887. He contributed to the republican newspaper *O Povo* (‘The People’) and is at present one of the editors of the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’). Works: *Horas de inspiração*, Funchal, 1906, 102 pp., and *Rosas e Jasmins*, Funchal, 1913, 55 pp.
Battenberg (Prince of)

In January 1896 the British cruiser *Blonde* lay in the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal), carrying the body of the Prince of Battenberg. The prince, who had accompanied the British expedition to the Ashanti country, died on the voyage to this island, where he had intended to spend some time recovering his failing health. He was married to Princess Beatrice, granddaughter of Queen Victoria of England.
Beatriz (Dona)

She was married to the Infante Ferdinand, brother of Afonso V, and after being widowed she governed the Madeira archipelago for as long as the minority of her son Diogo, Duke of Viseu, Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), lasted.
Becker (Th.)
Works: *Dipteren der Kanarischen Inseln und der Insel Madeira* (Mitt. Zool. Museum Berlin, vol. IV, part 10, 1908). This work records 212 species of Diptera, 14 of them new.
Bédmar (Count of Vargas de)

Danish geologist who studied the geology of the Madeira archipelago. Works: *Resumo das observações geológica feitas em uma viagem ás ilhas da Madeira, Porto Santo e Açores nos annos de 1835 e 1836* (Lisbon, 1837). A second edition of this work was published on the island of São Miguel in 1857.
Begonia

A genus of the family Begoniaceae, with a great many representatives in the gardens of Funchal. *Begonia fuchsioides*, *B. semperflorens*, *B. rex* and *B. maculata* seem to be common, as do various hybrids notable chiefly for the beauty of their foliage. Madeirans also give the name *begónia* to *Farfugium grande*, a composite with spotted, somewhat fleshy leaves.
Beija Flõr (O)
The first issue is dated 7 April 1842 and the last 29 September of the same year; 26 issues appeared. Its editor was Sérvulo de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos.
Belas Donas (Amaryllis belladonna)

A member of the Amaryllidaceae, common at Monte, Camacha, etc., which flowers in autumn, when it is leafless. It is native to Southern Africa. The medicinal belladonna (*Atropa Belladona*) does not occur in Madeira, not even in cultivation.
Belas Noites (Cestrum vespertinum)
A shrub or small tree of the family Solanaceae, cultivated in Funchal and in Machico.
Purslane (Portulaca oleracea)

A plant of the family Portulacaceae, very common in the streets of Funchal. It is not used in Madeira, but it could serve as a salad, although its leaves have a purgative effect when eaten in large quantities.
Belgium (King of)

King Leopold II of Belgium visited Funchal in 1897, landing on 17 September and leaving for the Canary Islands on the 19th of the same month. He went to Monte (‘hill’), to the Eira do Serrado (‘threshing floor of the ridge’) and to a few other spots near the city.

Prince Albert, later Albert I, King of the Belgians, visited Madeira on 30 April 1909 on his voyage to the Cape of Good Hope and the Congo Free State, and was received by the senior authorities of the district.
Belisqueiro

A length of wire, single or doubled, which fishermen attach to the end of their lines and to which the hook is fixed. The *belisqueiro* is used to stop fishing lines from being cut by the sharp teeth of the fish being caught.
Belle Poule

The French frigate *Belle Poule* and the corvette *Favorite* anchored in the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal) on 24 July 1840. On board was the mission, headed by the Prince of Joinville, bound for the island of St Helena to exhume the remains of the Emperor Napoleon and carry them to France. As is well known, Napoleon passed Madeira aboard the British ship of the line *Northumberland* on 24 August 1815, when he was being taken prisoner into exile on St Helena (see Napoleon). The expedition commanded by the Prince of Joinville did not call at Madeira on its return to Europe. The head and other members of this mission attended several festivities given in their honour in Funchal. The *Belle Poule* left Madeira on 27 July, bound for the Canary Islands.
See Joinville (Prince of).
Bemposta

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Água de Pena. It was the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by João Afonso Escudeiro in 1512. He was a native of mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and came to this island around 1450. He was of noble descent, and his rank as a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) was recognised here. He died in 1512 at an advanced age, and by a will made on 21 June of that year he founded the entail of Bemposta (‘well placed’), in the parish of Água de Pena, and that of São Lázaro, in the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). The first administrator of the entailed estate of Bemposta was Dona Catarina Anes Escudeiro, daughter of José Afonso, who married Lopo Franco de Monção, so called because he was a native of the town (*vila*) of that name. He came to Madeira around 1480, and in 1515 he was the first judge of the Council (*juiz da câmara*) of Santa Cruz. He was succeeded in the administration of the entailed estate of Bemposta by his son João Franco, and in the *quinta* (country estate) and chantry (capela) of São Lázaro by a daughter named Maria Franco. The third administrator of the entailed estate of Bemposta was Diogo Lopes Tavares, who also inherited the entail of São Lázaro, because Dona Maria Franco had died without issue. This family had a family vault in the old convent of Santa Cruz, where until not many years ago its tombstone could still be seen, bearing a shield with the arms of the Tavares and Borralho families.
Beneden (Baron Charles Van)

This Belgian subject took up residence in this archipelago long ago. For many years he lived at the Quinta dos Cedros in Santo António, and more recently on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). He is regarded in his own country as a distinguished writer, with a notable body of literary work already to his name. Among his works that may interest Madeirans is the study entitled *Au Nord Ouest de l'Afrique/Madère, les iles Canaries, le Maroc*, published in Brussels in 1882. In the Belgian review *La Jeune Wallonie* he published the interesting narrative *Voyage aux iles Salvages*, which fills 50 pages of that review and is accompanied by excellent engravings. Some claim that in this author’s comedies *Les Titularisés* and *Le Mariagicide* several of the characters embody certain well-known figures of Funchal society.
He was born in Belgium on 4 July 1854 and died in the same country in December 1929.
Berenguer

‘Above the town,’ says Frutuoso, ‘a quarter of a *légua* inland, stands the sugar mill (engenho) of the Cabrais; and near it is another belonging to the Doctor of Calheta (‘small cove’), a physician named Pedro Berenguer de Lemilhana, *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) and knight of the Order of Christ.’ It is from him that the surname Berenguer derives, and even today a considerable part of the *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands that Pedro de Berenguer held in Calheta still bears the name Lombo do Doutor (‘the doctor’s ridge’). He was a native of Valencia, in Spain, a doctor of medicine and a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*). He came to Madeira in the last quarter of the 16th century and settled in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta, where he founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*), which he passed on to his descendants. A grant of a coat of arms was issued to him or to one of his successors by royal decree (alvará régio) of 5 November 1524. The arms are: on a field gules, a bend azure edged or, charged with three fleurs-de-lis argent; an open helm argent; mantling argent and gules; and for crest an arm vested gules holding one of the fleurs-de-lis in the hand.
Dr Pedro de Berenguer Lemilhana died in Calheta and was buried at the crossing before the chancel of the parish church of this parish.

One of the administrators of this entailed estate was Gaspar Berenguer de Andrade, who distinguished himself in the war in Brazil and was therefore granted the habit of Christ and noble rank (*foro de fidalgo*). With his wife, Dona Isabel de França, he founded the Convent of Our Lady of Ransom (see that entry), of which they were patrons and where they were buried. Gaspar Berenguer was born in 1603 and died in 1691.

Members of this family included Francisco Berenguer de Lemilhana, who took part in the wars of Pernambuco for 22 years and was awarded the habit of Christ; António de Andrade Berenguer, who distinguished himself in the wars of the Restoration; and Bartolomeu de Melo Berenguer, who served with valour and courage in the campaigns of Maranhão.
Beresford (William Carr)

This well-known general of the British army, who won such distinction in the Peninsular War, commanded the English troops that occupied this island for the second time on 24 December 1807. Beresford left Madeira for Portugal on 17 August 1808, accompanied by half the forces under his command, and was replaced on the island by the English colonel Mead.
See Occupation of Madeira by English troops.
Berkeley Cotter (J.C.)

In the offprint of the *Comunicações da Comissão de Trabalhos Geológicos*, vol. II, fasc. II, a study was published with the following title: *Noticia de alguns fosseis terciarios do archipelago da Madeira* by J. C. Berkeley Cotter, accompanied by another note on some fossil land molluscs of the same archipelago by Alberto A. Girard. The preface to this work reads as follows: ‘The materials submitted for our examination are not sufficient to determine precisely the subdivision of the stratigraphic system to which the deposits containing them belong; but they serve, we believe, to confirm in general the conclusions reached by the learned Zurich professor (Karl Mayer) that the fossiliferous strata of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and neighbouring islands, which Thomas Edward Bowdich had already identified as Tertiary in 1823, belong to the Helvetian stage, though the possibility should not be excluded that part of these deposits belongs to the Tortonian, or higher stage of the Miocene system.’ The materials mentioned in the passage of the preface quoted above were supplied by the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz, then a professor at the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*). Berkeley died in December 1919.
Bertrand (Arthur)

In 1841 he published in Paris a book entitled *Lettres sur l'expedition de Sainte Hélène*, which deals with the expedition commanded by the Prince of Joinville that went to the island of St Helena in 1840 to bring the mortal remains of Napoleon back to Europe. He devotes eight pages to the expedition’s call at Madeira in July 1840.
Bertrand (Henrique de Price)

Naval captain and commander of the frigate *D. Pedro*, which was lying in the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal) when the liberal government was proclaimed on this island on 5 June 1834. He was a member of Madeira’s interim government after Dom Álvaro da Costa de Macedo left for the city of Lisbon.
Besouro (hummingbird hawk-moth)

The insect known in Madeira as the *besouro* is *Macroglossa stellatarum*, of the order Lepidoptera. It appears in the afternoon to suck nectar from flowers, thereby becoming an unwitting agent in the fertilisation of various species. In its size, its manner of flight and the noise it makes when visiting flowers, it so closely resembles the hummingbird that one English traveller believed he had seen that little bird in Madeira.

The caterpillar of the Madeiran *besouro* feeds on a species of the genus *Galium*, and therefore does no damage to the plants of kitchen gardens and flower gardens. When fully fed, it burrows into the ground and there turns into a brownish chrysalis.

Following an article that Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira, a distinguished Funchal physician, published in the *Diário de Noticias* some 25 years ago, describing certain extravagant habits of European beetles (*besouros*), Madeirans took to calling *besouros* those individuals whose habits matched those the said physician attributed to these insects. The Madeiran *besouro*, although it also occurs in Europe, bears no resemblance or affinity whatever to the European *besouro*.

At nightfall another lepidopteran appears very frequently in gardens, much larger and sturdier than the *Macroglossa*, which Madeirans call *borboletão* or *besouro*. This insect, which also belongs to the Sphingidae, is *Sphinx Convolvuli*, whose larvae feed on potato leaves etc., etc. Boys often catch the *borboletões* when they settle on flowers to suck the nectar on which they feed.
Besugos (Pagellus acarne)

A fish of the family Sparidae, common in Madeiran waters, where it is fished from the shore down to about 200 *braças* (fathoms). It lives in large shoals and its young grow up in rock pools by the sea. Its flavour is reminiscent of shellfish.
Beetroot (Beta vulgaris subsp. esculenta)

A plant of the family Chenopodiaceae, grown in some Madeiran kitchen gardens. The late Conde do Canavial sought to spread the cultivation of beetroot on the island so that the plant could be used for sugar production.
Bettencourt

This is the most usual way of writing this well-known family surname, which over the years has appeared among its bearers in various spellings, according to the whim or fancy of the individuals who used it.

Some even went so far as to harbour the ridiculous notion that writing it with an h after the t denoted a genealogical branch of purer and more authentic nobility. In Madeira there was a titled nobleman who refused to sign a public deed in which his name appeared, because the notary, little versed in these heraldic subtleties, had left out the h, a consonant indispensable to the ancestral lineage of this illustrious and ridiculous *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility).

Jean de Béthencourt, who was king and lord of the Canary Islands, belonged to an ancient and noble family of France, where the rights and privileges of the highest nobility were upheld and recognised for him. A nephew of his, named Meciot de Bettencourt, who succeeded his uncle, came to this island in the early days of colonisation, having exchanged the island of Lanzarote with Prince Henry the Navigator for substantial revenues here on Madeira.

A daughter of Meciot de Bettencourt, Dona Maria de Bettencourt, who accompanied her father from the Canaries, founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Água de Mel (‘honey water’), in the parishes of Santo António and São Roque, in favour of Gaspar de Bettencourt, son of her brother Henrique de Bettencourt. Henrique and his brother João de Bettencourt were the first individuals in this archipelago to use this family surname.

Dona Maria de Bettencourt married Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, second son of João Gonçalves Zarco, who was captain-donatary of the island of São Miguel. Gaspar Bettencourt accompanied his aunt, Dona Maria Bettencourt, to the Azores. There he married and became the founder of a large line of descendants. A detailed account of the entailed estate of Água de Mel, of which he was the first administrator, and of all his successors in the administration of this important entailed estate down to the last Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’) appears in the review *Paróquia de Santo Antonio do Funchal*, in issue no. 9 and the following issues of 1915.

Henrique Bettencourt settled in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), where he held a great deal of land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and there he founded an entailed estate.
Coat of arms of this family: on a field argent a lion rampant sable, armed gules, with the same lion as in the arms for a crest.

Many members of this family distinguished themselves notably in Africa, India and Brazil. Special mention is due to Henrique de Bettencourt, who gave great proof of his valour in the East as general of the Malabar sea. He died in a shipwreck while serving as captain-major of a fleet of ships, on his way to the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) to join the expedition that King Sebastian led to Africa.
Bettencourt (Anastacio Moniz de)

A Madeiran poet who died on the island of Terceira, where he lived for many years. On 18 May 1801 he was appointed substitute teacher of the chairs of rhetoric and philosophy that then existed in Funchal, and on 30 March 1803 teacher of the chair of rational philosophy. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in canon law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), and was the father of Dr Nicolau Anastacio de Bettencourt, who also died on Terceira.
Bettencourt (Dona Maria do Monte de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos Moniz de)

She was one of the most distinguished Madeiran women of her day for her virtue, intelligence and learning. She was born in Funchal around 1809, the daughter of Pedro de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Bettencourt, and died in the same city on 12 August 1884. She contributed to several Madeiran newspapers and published two novels in book form: *o Cura de São Lourenço*, Lisbon, 1855, 183 pp., and *Bernardo e a mesa de prata de D. Diniz*, Funchal, 1879, 249 pp.
Although she was a contemporary, we have been unable to obtain any further biographical details about her.
Bettencourt de Vasconcellos (João)
He went with his father to the island of Terceira, where he was beheaded in 1582 on the orders of Manuel da Silva, Count of Torres Vedras, for being a supporter of Philip II of Castile.
Bettencourt (Dr António João de França)

This professor at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) was born in Calheta (‘small cove’) on 19 October 1827, the son of António João de França Bettencourt and Dona Ana Rita Telo de Meneses. He came from old and noble families of that town (*vila*).

After attending the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), he enrolled in the Faculty of Theology of our University, where he won the highest distinctions. He took his doctorate there and received the doctoral hood (*capelo*) on 27 July 1862.

Only ten years later did he sit the competitive examination for a professorship of Theology. He was placed first, his rival being Dr Luís Maria da Silva Ramos, who later became one of the most distinguished professors of that faculty. For this examination Dr Bettencourt submitted a study on the *Verdade philosophica do mysterio da Incarnação*, which was published as a book and ran to two successive editions; it is considered a very valuable work of its kind.

He taught theology at the seminary (*Seminário*) of Coimbra, and history and Hebrew at the lyceum of the same city. He belonged to several learned societies and to the Instituto de Coimbra, to whose journal he contributed. He was the founder and one of the most brilliant editors of the *Revista de Theologia*, which enjoyed great renown in its day. He was one of the most active and zealous *provedores* of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of Coimbra, and his name remains bound to the important services he rendered there.

According to the *Esboço Historico Literario da faculdade de theologia da Universidade de Coimbra* by Dr M. Eduardo da Mota Veiga, Dr França Bettencourt was the first Madeiran to teach in the Faculty of Theology there since the Marquis of Pombal’s reform of 1772, and the second to take a doctorate in that faculty, the first having been Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, a former bishop of this diocese.
Dr António João de França Bettencourt died in Coimbra on 29 October 1882, at the age of 55.
Bettencourt (E. A.)
In 1875 he published in Porto a pamphlet entitled *Memória sobre a descoberta das ilhas do Porto Santo e Madeira*.
Bettencourt (Friar Pedro de)

He belonged to the Bettencourt family of this island, where he was born around the middle of the 16th century. He entered the Seraphic Order of St Francis, taking the name of Friar Pedro de São Bartolomeu. He went to India, where he founded a convent of nuns of his order. He is discussed in the *Historia Seraphica* of Friar Manuel da Esperança.
Bettencourt (Nicolau Anastácio de)
This distinguished Madeiran was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’) in this city on 7 February 1810, the son of Dr Anastácio Moniz de Bettencourt and Dona Ana Rosa Bettencourt.

The father of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Nicolau Anastácio was a highly distinguished physician and a man of letters well known and admired in his day. The author of ‘The Zarco Epic’ (*Zargueida*) dedicated a sonnet to him in the introduction to his poem *Georgeida*. Whatever hyperbole there may be in those verses, they nonetheless show the esteem in which he was held and the good name he enjoyed among his contemporaries.

The subject of this biography inherited a brilliant talent from his father. He revealed it at a very early age and later gave clear proof of it as a student at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*).
Having lost his father at a tender age, he went to Coimbra in 1825, accompanied by his mother, to enrol in the faculty of philosophy and then follow the medical course.

In 1827 he abandoned his studies to enlist in the academic battalion under the command of the Count of Vila Flor, and, fighting against the royalist forces, he took a heroic part in the actions of Cruz de Alvoroços and Ponte de Vouga. Sharing the fate of his comrades in arms, he had to leave Portugal and went into exile in England in 1828. It was there that he received the news of his mother’s death, which struck his devoted son’s heart a cruel blow.

On 14 February 1829 he arrived on the island of Terceira, enlisted in the Queen’s Volunteers Battalion, and on 11 August of the same year he took part in the action at the town (*vila*) of Praia between a Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) squadron and the liberals, in which the latter were victorious.

He was not indifferent to the expedition prepared on Terceira to free the other Azorean islands still subject to the yoke of absolutism. He joined it as a volunteer, always conducting himself with courage, and was present at the action of Ladeira Velha, on São Miguel, on 2 August 1831.

Nicolau Anastácio de Bettencourt was on the island of Terceira when Pedro IV, Emperor of Brazil, landed there on 3 March 1832 to organise the liberal army that was to fight the absolutist forces and then establish the constitutional system in our country.

The liberating army landed on the beaches of Mindelo on 8 July 1832. Our illustrious subject was part of it, and during the memorable siege of Porto he gave proof of his great daring and valour. Above all, in the celebrated action of the Serra do Pilar on 13 August 1832, Nicolau Anastácio showed his courage and worth: a detachment of volunteers to which he belonged earned the highest praise from General Torres, who recommended these bold volunteers to the government for reward. There he fought with true heroism alongside José Estêvão Coelho de Magalhães, Júlio Máximo de Oliveira Pimentel, José Silvestre Ribeiro and others, who later distinguished themselves so greatly among us in various fields of human endeavour.

Once constitutional government had been established, Nicolau Bettencourt was appointed secretary-general of the prefecture (*prefeitura*) of Angra and later transferred to the same post in the district of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’). There he also served for seven years as administrator-general (*administrador geral*) and civil governor, winning the deepest esteem of those he governed by the way in which he carried out the duties of his high office.

After serving for some time as civil governor of Aveiro, to which he had been appointed by decree of 23 November 1843, he was placed at the head of the district of Angra do Heroísmo on 1 December 1844. He rendered the most signal and valuable services to the island of Terceira, which he regarded as his second homeland.

It was there that his administrative judgement and enterprising genius shone most brilliantly, as the Caixa Económica (savings bank) and the Infant Asylum (*Asilo da Infância*) that he founded in the capital of that district eloquently show.

On the occasion of his death, an Azorean newspaper wrote of these two institutions: ‘His name is today blessed for the benefits and most useful effects that generally flow from them, so much so that, a few months ago, the Caixa Económica of Angra offered the hospital of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) about two *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis) for a model ward, which is to bear the name of that benefactor, while the municipality gave the same name to one of the city’s streets, out of the pressing duty to commend him to public gratitude and respect.

The foundation of that house of charity and that credit establishment alone would suffice to make him unforgettable. The laborious effort it required can be judged from the fact that, at the time they were founded (1844-53), the scope of public assistance, of charitable and relief associations, and of the morally uplifting popular savings banks was still scarcely understood.

During the twelve years in which he administered the district of Angra almost without interruption, he never ceased to work devotedly and persistently for the advancement and prosperity of his adopted homeland. He gave a great impetus to education, founding schools, contributing much to the organisation of the national lyceum (state secondary school) and encouraging with his inspiring words all those who devoted themselves to literary pursuits.
It was during his governorship, and owing to his influence, that the customs house, the national lyceum, the law courts, the public prisons, etc., were properly established.

One of the enduring monuments to his glory is the foundation of the Asilo da Infância Desvalida (asylum for destitute children), to which he left his name indissolubly linked, endowing the city of Angra with a most important charitable establishment that spreads countless benefits there.
He was then civil governor of the district of Horta, and was elected deputy for it in 1853 in recognition of the services he had rendered to its inhabitants.

Declining the seat, he nevertheless accepted the post of civil governor of Aveiro, leaving entailed to his governorship the creation of a savings bank, which is a flourishing institution and has rendered valuable services to that city.
He was also civil governor of Portalegre, where he ended his administrative career, retiring in July 1862 and settling in Angra do Heroísmo.

Although not a writer of renown, Anastácio Bettencourt did have considerable literary gifts, which he displayed brilliantly in various writings scattered through the newspapers and in his speeches, which remained unpublished and were distinguished by the purity and elegance of their language. He is also known to have been an esteemed poet, writing inspired and beautiful verse. In 1848 he published a collection of various administrative writings, and Inocêncio Francisco da Silva attributes to him the volume published in 1857 under the title *Esposição de factos que se deram no districto de Angra do Heroísmo* etc.

He held the title of Councillor (*carta de conselho*), was a fidalgo-knight of the Royal Household (*fidalgo cavaleiro da Casa Real*) and a commander of various orders. He died in the city of Angra do Heroísmo on 7 March 1874.
Bettencourt Pita (Nicolau Caetano)

Nicolau Caetano de Bettencourt Pita, doctor of medicine of the University of Edinburgh, member of the Royal Physical Society and of the Royal Medical and Natural History Society of the same city, and professed knight of the Order of Christ, was born in Funchal on 6 December 1788.
Intending to follow a medical career, he went to the Scottish capital and enrolled at its university, receiving the degree of doctor of medicine on 24 June 1812.

‘So brilliant were the academic exercises that preceded the conferring of the degree’, says Dr Rodrigues de Gusmão in the *Memórias biográficas dos médicos e cirurgiões portugueses*, ‘that, in reward for his distinguished merit, he was elected president of the Royal Physical Society that year. This is a just and respectful tribute which, by praiseworthy and ancient custom, the University of Edinburgh pays to the talent of the member of that Royal Society who surpasses the other doctoral candidates in distinction.’

In that same year of 1812, Dr Nicolau Pita published in London a work in English, to which he gave the following title: *Account of the Island of Madeira*. The respected Portuguese physician Dr F. A. Barral refers to this work in these terms: ‘This production of a young talent, who was later to make a distinguished mark in the profession, was a descriptive account of the island’s climate and of its physical geography; it was the most important work written up to that time on the island of Madeira that could serve as a foundation for its medical topography. The *Investigador Português* of September 1813 also spoke of this work with praise.

When Dr Pita returned to Portugal, the Prince Regent Dom João, later John VI, in recognition of his talent and merits, granted him by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 8 March 1814 all the privileges, rights and honours that at that time were granted only to physicians who had graduated from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*).

When the liberal principles of the Porto revolution of 24 August 1820 were proclaimed in Funchal on 28 January 1821, Dr Pita was one of the first to embrace them, and from then on he was always a fierce opponent of the old institutions. Believing that a newspaper was the best means of spreading constitutional ideas among his fellow islanders, he had a printing press brought from Lisbon, and on 2 July 1821 he began publishing *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’). This was the first periodical Madeira ever had, and its contributors included the men best known on the island for their advanced opinions.

When the absolutist regime was restored in 1823, one of the government’s first acts was to send to Madeira a special judicial commission (alçada) to try and punish those implicated in a conspiracy, real or supposed. According to the sentence passed on the defendants named in that commission’s judicial inquiry (*devassa*), its aim was to carry out the audacious plan of restoring the outlawed constitution on this island.

Dr Pita, well known for his outspokenly liberal opinions and, moreover, editor of a constitutional periodical, could not fail to arouse the suspicion of the dreaded judges of the commission. Guilty or not, he was therefore confined in the prisons of the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater), where he lay for some time. He was finally sentenced on 24 October 1823 to four years’ penal exile (degredo) on the island of Terceira and to a fine of 50,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), payable to the treasury and the royal chamber.

Our fellow Madeiran was well received when he reached that island, and soon afterwards he was entrusted with the post of physician at the military hospital of Angra, which he held until 1834. In reward for his services as a military doctor, the regent, Infanta Isabel Maria, granted him the commission and rank of major by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 19 July 1827.

Dr Pita was one of the editors of the periodical *O Liberal* (‘The Liberal’), which began publication in Angra on 29 March 1835. This newspaper was the organ of the political tendency then called reformist, later Septembrist and finally Progressive, and it waged constant polemics with the *Sentinella*, which represented the conservative party, known as the Devourists, and with the *Angrense*.

In that city our fellow Madeiran also held the posts of physician at the civil hospital and municipal doctor to the Council, as well as that of delegate of the Public Health Council of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). His name appears among those of the citizens who signed in Angra the record (*auto*) of the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of Pedro IV and Maria II on 22 June 1828. He died on 20 May 1857, shortly before his 69th birthday.

He was a full member of the former Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts of Funchal (*Sociedade dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes do Funchal*) and one of the citizens elected in 1820 to the first constitutional council of this city. It was he who proposed erecting a monument in Funchal to commemorate the day on which liberal principles were proclaimed in Madeira. The foundation stone of this monument was actually laid with great ceremony and pomp in the square in front of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) on 28 January 1822. However, the work never got beyond the foundations, and even these were destroyed on 1 September 1823, after absolute government had been restored on this island.
Bianchi
This surname descends from João António Bianchi, a merchant of Italian origin who was already living in Funchal by 1822.
Bibliography

The body of writing devoted to this archipelago is extensive and very important, but a complete survey of Madeiran bibliography has yet to be made. The Azoreans, who are so far and so indescribably ahead of us in so many fields of human endeavour, possess a very valuable work on the subject: their *Bibliotheca Açoreana*, in two volumes of some 900 pages, the fruit of the painstaking study and diligent research of Dr Ernesto do Canto. In the article ‘Madeira’, included in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Ilustrado*, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo made a creditable attempt at a Madeiran bibliography, listing some 150 works written in Portuguese and 80 in foreign languages; it is, however, very far from being a complete study of the subject. For the bibliography of the press we have the *Resenha do Jornalismo da Madeira*, published by the company that owns the *Diário de Notícias* of Funchal, which is as complete a work as possible on the newspapers published on this island. Throughout this *Elucidário*, whenever the nature of the subject requires it, and particularly when we deal with the authors concerned, we always mention the works devoted to this archipelago, which are very considerable in number. In this way, references to the most valuable and authoritative works for the study of Madeiran events, people and things are widely scattered through these pages. Wherever possible they give the bibliographical details – year and place of publication, authors’ names, number of pages, etc. – that may be of use to any studious researcher. Nevertheless, in the article ‘Elementos para a historia madeirense’ we shall present a brief survey of the works that offer the richest store of news and information on the history of this archipelago.

This article, then, lists only various bibliographical items that have no place elsewhere in this *Elucidário*. They are certainly not the most valuable or interesting, but they may nonetheless provide useful notes for the study of certain aspects of our history, and especially of our scientific and literary activity. Libraries

The only public library in Funchal is that of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), created by a resolution of 12 January 1838. It began with 193 volumes of the *Enciclopédia Metódica*, bought from the heirs of the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), and numbered 2,000 volumes in 1850, 2,096 in 1851, 2,496 in 1863, 10,351 in 1889, 10,812 in 1902, 10,929 in 1904, 11,035 in 1908, 21,641 in 1915, 21,786 in 1916 and 21,874 in 1917. In 1913 the Library received a gift of 9,863 volumes from the British subjects Mr William and Mr Alfredo Reid. These volumes had formed the book collection of the late municipal librarian João Joaquim de Freitas, and the two gentlemen had acquired them for the express purpose of enriching that municipal institution.

In 1863 the Funchal library received 21 crates containing 3,050 volumes from the Depository of the Libraries of the Convents abolished by the Decree of 28 May 1834. Before that it had received a large number of volumes from the library of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). Most of these last are in a very poor state of preservation.

There are no incunabula in the Funchal Library. As for manuscripts, the only ones held there are the copies of the *Nobiliario* of Henriques de Noronha and of book 2.1 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) by Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, and the originals of the *Documentos Históricos e Geográficas sobre a ilha da Madeira* by Dr João Pedro de Freitas Pereira Drumond and of the *Apontamentos para a Genealogia de diversas Famílias Madeirenses* by Felisberto Bettencourt Miranda.

The creation of the Municipal Library is due chiefly to the illustrious Madeiran Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses, who, as president of the Funchal Council, made the most praiseworthy efforts to that end. It opened to the public on 8 December 1838, and its Regulations were published in the newspaper *A Flor* of the 7th of the same month and year. For seven years the library was run by the secretary of the Council. In 1845 the post of librarian was created, which was held in succession by António Joaquim Teles, Joaquim António de Sá, José Joaquim de Freitas, Carlos Azevedo de Meneses and Adolfo César de Noronha.

The library of the former Medical and Surgical School is housed in the building of the Misericórdia Hospital (*Hospital da Misericórdia*) and comprises some 600 volumes. Of these, 140 were donated by Dr Nathaniel Lister of London, on condition that they should pass to the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) if the school were abolished. The Government approved this condition by a ministerial order (*portaria*) of the Ministry of the Kingdom dated 17 December 1844.

In 1913 the Government authorised the incorporation of the Medical School’s library into the Funchal Municipal Library (*Biblioteca Municipal do Funchal*), but the books were never actually transferred, for lack of space to house them.
The Episcopal Seminary has a library consisting chiefly of works of theology, and the English club holds some 4,000 volumes, many of them works about Madeira.

There are also libraries in the barracks of the 27th Infantry Regiment and at the Liceu Central do Funchal (Funchal Central Lyceum, a state secondary school). A private individual, Mr João Eleutério Martins, owner of the *Diário de Notícias*, possesses the finest known collections of newspapers published in Madeira and of foreign books relating to this island. The Utile Dulci library, housed in a building in Rua do Dr. Vieira, has some 1700 volumes that anyone may read on payment of two centavos a week and a deposit of thirty centavos, which is returned when the borrowed book is handed back.

Some new information must be added to what has been said in this short article. The library of the defunct Medical and Surgical School of Funchal has been incorporated into the Municipal Library, and in recent years many bibliographical items have been acquired, so that the library at present (1938) holds 31,000 printed volumes.

In 1938 daytime reading was attended by 2,304 readers, who consulted 2,480 volumes, while evening reading in the same year drew 2,086 readers, who consulted 2,225 volumes. In that year, too, home reading amounted to 151 readers, who borrowed 313 volumes.
Evening reading, which is arousing considerable public interest, was introduced in July 1934.
Bica da Cana

On the plateau of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), about 10 kilometres from Rabaçal and 4 from the Lombo do Mouro shelter (*Casa de Abrigo do Lombo do Mouro*), lies the locality (*sítio*) of Bica da Cana (‘reed spout’). Here, around 1914, the now defunct Junta Agrícola da Madeira (Madeira Agricultural Board) set up an Experimental Agricultural Station and carried out trials of various crops, on which large sums were spent without appreciable results.

The station established there lay abandoned for some years, but the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), through its agricultural department, has devoted its solicitous attention to it. Important work has been done on the upkeep and repair of the buildings, the fencing of the arable land, various agricultural experiments, etc. Nevertheless, it must be admitted that the success of this work does not match the expense and effort put into it. The unfavourable climatic conditions, the altitude of the region, the frequent gales that break out there and the complete lack of shelter to which the crops are exposed are enough to explain the failure of the experiments carried out there. Only with the indispensable hedges, formed of dense stands of trees – which would take many years to achieve – might a somewhat worthwhile result perhaps be obtained, but never a richly rewarding one, as was once claimed in an official document.
Bica (Pagellus erythrinus)

A fish of the family Sparidae with a pleasant flavour, common in the markets of Madeira. It is caught over rocky bottoms or loose stones with gear such as the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream), the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) and the drag net.
See Correcaminho.
Bicheiro

A rudimentary, rough implement for hunting and fishing, whose name derives from the word *bicho* (creature). It consists of a pole with a hook or gaff at the end and is used to pull seabirds, such as *cagarras*, *anjinhos*, etc., out of their burrows; in this case a slender quince-wood pole makes up the whole implement. In other cases, made of a sturdy shaft fitted with a strong hook, it works as a true boathook, and fishermen use it to haul aboard the large fish brought alongside the boat.
See Embicheirar.
Bicho conta

A small crustacean of the order Isopoda and the genus *Armadillium*, living under stones and in shady places. It feeds on decaying plant and animal matter, and when touched it rolls up into the shape of a small ball or bead (*conta*). It is very common in Madeira.
Sugar-cane borer

It is the larva of *Nonagria sacchari*, an insect of the order Lepidoptera. As early as 1502 this larva was devastating Madeira’s sugar plantations: on 15 November of that year a royal letter (*carta régia*) was sent to the judges and councillors (*vereadores*) of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), recommending the use of ash to destroy the cane borer. On 29 June 1509 a further royal letter announced the arrival on this island of one Fernão Rodrigues, charged with providing a remedy ‘to kill the grub that infests the canes... from which so much loss and damage follows’, and recommending that this Fernão Rodrigues be lodged and rewarded as the services he came to render deserved.

Despite these measures, it was only around 1887 that the cane borer began to disappear, owing to the relentless war waged on it by *Iridomyrmex humilis*, a species of ant imported from Demerara. Before this ant was introduced to Madeira, purely by chance, growers used to light torches and walk with them at night through the land planted with cane, so that the insect would fall onto the flame and die.

The larva of *Nonagria sacchari* lives inside the cane stalks, where it bores galleries that open to the outside. The walls of the galleries harden, and the adjacent tissues turn reddish and quickly begin to ferment. It appears mainly in summer, but since the introduction of the ant it has been rare on the island of Madeira.
Bicho do lameiro (Ophion obscurus)

A hymenopterous insect found in the lowlands of Madeira. It builds a nest of mud, sheltering it in a window recess or under the eaves of a roof, and habitually feeds its larvae with spiders that it carries to the nest.
Bicho vaca

This name is given to two millipedes of the genus *Julus*, both characterised by an almost cylindrical body that sometimes coils into a spiral. They are found in the soil, in plant pots and in damp walls.
Bicuda (Sphyraena spet

). A migratory fish in Madeiran waters. It is elongated and almost cylindrical in shape and can reach a little over 1 metre. It travels in shoals, is very voracious and preys chiefly on sardines, horse mackerel and in general on the fish that the fishermen of these islands call *ruama* (fishermen's name for small shoaling fish such as mackerel and horse mackerel). It is caught at night by the method known as trolling. Its flavour, though not very fine, is not among the most unpleasant.
Biddle (Anthony J. Drexel)
Works: *The Madeira Island*, London, 1900, 2 vols.; *The island of the Wine*, Philadelphia and San Francisco, 1901, 2 vols.

We have not read the first of these works, but the second is particularly curious for the series of errors and absurdities it contains. If Mr Biddle, who styles himself a member of three American scientific associations, had also belonged to one of the many temperance societies of his country, he might perhaps have produced a more honest and accurate work than the one he dared to publish about our island.
The first edition of the book *The Madeira Island* was published in the city of Philadelphia in 1896 and contains the same errors and absurdities as the second edition, which dates from 1900.
Bignonia

In Madeira this name is given to several species of the genera *Bignonia* and *Tecoma*, among which we shall mention the following: *Tecoma australis* and *T. jasminoides*, from Australia; *T. radicans*, from North America; *T. capensis*, from the Cape of Good Hope; *Bignonia venusta* and *B. chamberlaynii*, from Brazil; *B. charere*, from Guiana; and *B. lindley*, from Buenos Aires. All these species are used to cover walls, belvederes, etc.
Madeira firecrest (Regulus maderensis)

The smallest of Madeira’s birds and the only one peculiar to it. It frequents the heath and laurel woods of the interior and skilfully builds an ovoid nest of moss. Egg-laying generally takes place from May to July, and the clutch may number up to 7 eggs of a reddish brown, with reddish dots or blotches.
Bispo (street)

The former name of the present Rua de Gomes Freire. The name comes from the fact that the prelates of Funchal had their official residence in it. The Bishop’s Palace (*Paço Episcopal*) (see that entry) has housed our lyceum (state secondary school) since January 1914. In this street stands the old manor house of the Ornelas family, whose present representative is Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos; it was built in the last quarter of the 17th century by Aires de Ornelas, holder of the entail (*morgado*). The important and flourishing mutual-aid society 4 de Setembro de 1863 (see that entry) also has its headquarters here. The chapel of São Luís (St Louis) (see that entry) is likewise in this street.
Bishops of Funchal

In this *Elucidário* we devote a separate article to each of the prelates who have guided the destinies of this diocese, but we think it useful to give here the complete list of them all, in chronological order and with the years in which they headed the episcopal administration of the archipelago. The first bishop was Dom Diogo Pinheiro (1514–1526); 2nd, and first and only archbishop, Martinho de Portugal (1533–1547); 3rd, Dom Friar Gaspar do Casal (1551–1556); 4th, Dom Jorge de Lemos (1556–1569); 5th, Dom Friar Fernando de Távora (1570–1573); 6th, Dom Jerónimo Barreto (1574–1585); 7th, Dom Luís Figueiredo de Lemos (1586–1608); 8th, Dom Friar Lourenço de Távora (1610–1617); 9th, Dom Jerónimo Fernando (1618–1650); 10th, Dom Friar Gabriel de Almeida (1672–1674); 11th, Dom Friar António Teles da Silva (1675–1682); 12th, Dom Estêvão Brioso de Figueiredo (1681–1689); 13th, Dom Friar José de Santa Maria (1690–1696); 14th, Dom José de Sousa Castelo Branco (1698–1721); 15th, Dom Friar Manuel Coutinho (1725–1738); 16th, Dom Friar João do Nascimento (1711–1753); 17th, Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão (1757–1784); 18th, Dom José da Costa Torres (1786–1796); 19th, Dom Luís Rodrigues Vilares (1797–1810); 20th, Dom João Joaquim Bernardino de Brito (1819–1820); 21st, Dom Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade (1821–1834); 22nd, Dom José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa (1844–1848); 23rd, Dom Manuel Martins Manso (1850–1858); 24th, Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura (1859–1872); 25th, Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (1871–1874); 26th, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto (1877–1911); and 27th, Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro (1914).
Madeiran bishops

We know that the following prelates were natives of Madeira: Dom Nuno de Aguiar, Bishop of Tangier; Dom Sebastião de Morais, Bishop of Japan; Dom Friar Miguel dos Santos, Bishop of São Tomé in India; Dom Mateus de Abreu Pereira, Bishop of São Paulo; Dom Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Bishop of São Paulo; Dom João Henriques Moniz, Bishop of Cape Verde; Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, Bishop of Funchal and Archbishop of Goa; Dom Ernesto Sena de Oliveira, Archbishop of Mytilene; Dom Estêvão Pedro de Alencastre, Bishop of Hawaii (Sandwich); and Dom Teodósio Clemente de Gouveia, prelate of Mozambique (see those entries).
Blandy

This family of English subjects and merchants settled on this island more than a century ago. During the first occupation of Madeira by British troops, in July 1801, the garrison included a junior officer named John Blandy, who became the founder of the family of that name on the island. By 1808, when Madeira was occupied by British troops for the second time, this English subject had already set up the trading house that he passed on to his descendants. He died on 14 January 1855 and was succeeded in the firm by his son Charles Ridpath Blandy, who died in 1878. His son was João Blandy, who raised the trading house to a remarkable degree of prosperity, leaving a very large fortune when he died on 7 December 1912. His heir and successor was João Ernesto Blandy, who died in 1930.

For many years the offices of this important firm were in Rua de São Francisco, in the premises now occupied by the firm’s wine trading department. They were later moved to Rua da Alfândega, where they are at present.
Bloxam (James Mackenzie)
