Boa Nova (A)
The 1st issue of this newspaper appeared on 2 February 1912, and no. 171, the last, on 10 July of the same year.
Boaventura (parish)

Despite all our efforts, the origin of this parish’s name has remained entirely unknown to us. If we were at least to establish its probable origin, it would be necessary to determine precisely the true spelling of this strange name, and this seems to us to present no small difficulty. Boaventura or Boa Ventura? We cannot say, because the name appears written in both forms. The first seems to be the older and is undoubtedly the more common and usual, but we know of no particular reason to prefer either of them. We can only lose ourselves in mere conjecture or in more or less ingenious hypotheses, which may well be far removed from the truth.

Nothing about the origin of this name is recorded in the parish archive of this parish (*freguesia*), in any old documents or even in local tradition. Was there perhaps some village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) or settlement on the mainland whose name the first colonists borrowed, as often happened, to give it to that locality (*sítio*), which later became a parish? The hypothesis would be no more than a mere possibility, and one without the slightest foundation, since, according to the investigations we have carried out, there is no parish, locality or village in Portugal that bears that name.

The lands that make up the parish of Boaventura belonged for almost three centuries to the parish of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), from which they were separated in 1836. Boaventura has borne this name since the middle of the 16th century, and even before that time, and therefore long before the creation of the curacy (*curato*) and before it became an independent parish. In the early days of colonisation, Pedro Gomes Galdo was one of the first settlers to hold extensive lands there by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). He is regarded as one of the earliest colonists of this parish, which at that time, as already stated, belonged to the parish of Ponta Delgada. The foundation of the chantry (capela) of São Cristóvão (St Christopher), in the locality that still bears this name today, is attributed to this Pedro Galdo or to one of his descendants.

As the population grew and spread inland, the inhabitants of Boaventura sought the creation of a curacy (*curato*) that would make it easier for them to carry out their religious duties. They took advantage of the stay of the diocesan bishop, Dom Manuel Coutinho, at the parish church of Ponta Delgada to put before the prelate the distance at which they lived from the mother church (*igreja matriz*), the difficulty of the paths, above all in the winter season, and the grave dangers to which they were exposed. Since the reasons given by the petitioners were entirely acceptable, the prelate ordered the parish priest of the time, Luís Gonçalves Caldeira, to apply for the creation of a curacy in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada, based in Boaventura.

By royal decree (alvará régio) of 4 February 1733, John V authorised the diocesan prelate to create this curacy. We do not know when it was finally filled, nor what jurisdiction or powers were conferred on it. In the meantime it remained dependent on the parish of Ponta Delgada, from which it gradually freed itself until it became an independent parish. Baptisms began to be performed there in 1790, but marriages were celebrated in Boaventura only after its elevation to a parish. The seat of the curacy was the chapel of Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria), built by the people in 1731. The curates lived there permanently and gave spiritual assistance to the inhabitants of the place, though some acts of worship were celebrated in the mother church of Ponta Delgada. Under the said decree of 4 February 1733, the curate originally received a stipend (*côngrua*) of one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine; this stipend was later increased.

The governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence) and vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter), António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga, raised the curacy of Boaventura to a parish by decree of 18 November 1836, freeing it entirely from the jurisdiction of the parish of Ponta Delgada. The priests who served there continued for some time to call themselves curates, but this curacy, like others that existed in the diocese, was autonomous, with its own civil and religious life and no dependence on any other parish. The prior (title of the parish priest) and parish priest was Joaquim Gomes Lume, and the first collated vicar (*vigário colado*, permanently instituted in the benefice) was Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade, in 1843.

As already mentioned, the curacy was established in the chapel of Santa Quitéria, built in 1731. It was enlarged, or rather rebuilt, in 1835, and became the seat of the new parish created the following year. It stands in the locality (*sítio*) of Serrão, the most central and most pleasant spot in the parish. The image of St Quiteria was given to the church of Ponta Delgada in 1721 by Manuel de Freitas Vasconcelos, a resident of Funchal, and was taken to the new chapel shortly after it was built. Boaventura had the chapels of São Cristóvão and Sant'Ana, which no longer exist, and in 1918 work began on a chapel in the locality of Fajã do Penedo, dedicated to the Immaculate Heart. We shall deal with them in the articles devoted to chapels.

The parish has several levadas (irrigation channels): the levadas of Achada (‘plateau’) Grande, built mainly through the efforts of Policarpo José de Abreu and Manuel João de Freitas Galdo; the Levada Grande (‘great channel’), whose irrigation extends as far as Ponta Delgada; the Levada das Faias (‘faya-tree channel’), which owes much of its course to João Pedro de Andrade; the Levada da Achada dos Alves e Pastel, whose construction was begun by the same Policarpo José de Abreu; and also the levada of Achada or of Serrão. All of them rise in the Ribeira dos Moinhos (‘mills’). As we have already said in the article devoted to the parish of Arco de São Jorge (‘arc of São Jorge’), many years ago a levada was planned that would draw its water from the Ribeira do Porco, at the locality (*sítio*) of Falca, and serve to irrigate both parishes; the necessary surveys and estimates were even carried out at the beginning of the last quarter of the 19th century. It never went beyond the planning stage, although Canon Feliciano João Teixeira, deputy for Madeira, championed the idea in parliament during the legislative session of 1890.

On the road linking this parish with that of Arco de São Jorge, there is a stretch on the right bank of the Ribeira do Porco, overlooking the sea, known as Engrosa because it winds its way along the sheer face of a high cliff. From the cracks in this cliff grows in abundance the plant known as *ensaião* (*Sempervivum glandulosum*, of the family *Crassulaceae*), of which William Longman wrote the following in *Frazer's Magazine* of August 1875: ‘...they grow in such profusion that they overlap one another, and reach such a size that they surpass anything of the kind to be seen at Kew or in other botanical gardens. The commonest ones are larger than a hat. At the edges they are a reddish-brown colour, shading gradually to a light green at the centre’.

At the locality of São Cristóvão there was once a small tile works. The tiles were made from a dense, reddish clay found nearby, which gave a very hard-wearing product that the salt air did not damage in the least. We have read somewhere that ‘...other kinds of clay are to be seen interbedded with the basalts, some of them whitish in colour, which could be used to advantage in the ceramics industry’.

The Lício family, holders of the entail (*morgado*) of Lagos, had entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*) in this parish, and in the locality (*sítio*) of Silveira (‘bramble patch’) they built a large house, which was never entirely finished. It was with the factor (*feitor*) of these holders of the entail and of these lands, who lived in Boaventura, that the following interesting and picturesque incident is said to have occurred. General Beresford had arrived in Madeira in December 1807, in command of the British troops that occupied Madeira for the second time. All the authorities and commissioned officers went to pay their respects to the English general. Colonel Lício, holder of the entail, could be no exception to the rule: he commanded the militia regiment of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) and was then staying on his lands at Boaventura. The factor, who happened to be in Funchal and was the lieutenant adjutant of that regiment, persuaded the lady of the entail (*morgada*), Colonel Lício’s wife, that it would be wise to spare her husband the discomforts of a journey. He put forward the sensible suggestion that he himself should don the colonel’s uniform and present himself to the English general as the commander of the militia regiment of the town (*vila*) of São Vicente! The idea, promptly conceived and accepted without reluctance by the lady of the entail, was put into effect without delay by the good and simple-minded factor. When Beresford learnt that before him stood a raw adjutant disguised as a colonel, he curtly uttered what were perhaps the only words of Portuguese he then knew: ‘Para o Pico’ (To the Pico). And off went our poor lieutenant and factor, led under guard to the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*), no doubt cursing the hour he had the unhappy idea of donning the uniform belonging to his chief, the owner of the lands he managed. As he turned his back on General Beresford, however, he came out with a phrase that became famous and, to some extent, immortalised him in local tradition. When he realised the mistake he had made, he let slip, half rueful and half ironic, this inspired remark: ‘I could see straight away this would end in a blunder!’ That was the epilogue to his sad and unfortunate adventure.

The main localities of this parish are: Igreja, Pastel, Pomar, Ribeira do Moinho, Roçada, Cabo da Ribeira, Achada do Castanheiro, Levada, Lombadinha, São Cristóvão, Serrão, Achada do Pereira, Travessa, Achada Grande, Falca, Achada da Madeira, Lombo do Urzal, Serra de Água, Quebradas, Lamaceiros, Achada do Moledo, Fajã do Penedo, Fajã Grande, Sabugueiros and Silveira. The parish is crossed by the Porco and Moinhos streams. At the mouth of the former lies the beach of the small landing place known as Porto da Boaventura, where boats anchor and where coastal steamers land cargo and passengers.

This parish belongs to the municipality (*concelho*) and judicial district (*comarca*) of São Vicente, whose seats lie approximately 9 and a half kilometres away. It borders the parishes of Arco de São Jorge, Ponta Delgada, São Vicente and Curral das Freiras.

There are two schools, one for each sex, both in the locality of Igreja. Father António Alexandrino de Vasconcelos, whom we have already mentioned in the article on the parish of Arco de São Jorge, was born in this parish. When the great poet Antero de Quental was in Madeira some years ago, he spent a period in the parish of Boaventura. Its population is 3,900 inhabitants. The well-known Serra das Torrinhas lies within the parish (see that entry).
Boaventura (islets)
These islets, also known as Ilhéu Porco (Pig Islet) and Ilhéu Vermelho (Red Islet), lie off the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Boaventura (‘good fortune’), not far from its shore.
Boaventura (landing place)

At the mouth of the Ribeira do Porco, or Boaventura (‘good fortune’) stream, there is a stony beach adjoining the small landing place of that name. It lies near Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), less than a mile away.
Boca das Torrinhas

It separates the Boaventura (‘good fortune’) uplands from those of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’). *Sedum farinosum*, a plant of the family Crassulaceae, and *Isoplexis sceptrum*, a shrub of the family Scrophulariaceae, are common at the Boca das Torrinhas (‘pass of the little towers’) and in its vicinity.
See Torrinhas (pass).
Boca das Voltas

A locality (*sítio*) between Pico do Arco (‘peak of the arc’) and Pico do Canário, from which a path leads to Ribeira da Boaventura (‘Boaventura stream’). The Boca das Voltas lies at about 750 metres above sea level.
Boca de Panela

A large marine animal, intensely hated by Madeiran fishermen and a relentless enemy of the tuna, which it hunts ferociously, at times closely encircling them and at others scattering them in flight, according to fishermen who have observed it at close quarters. The passage of such animals through the fishing grounds naturally gives the fisherman just cause for annoyance, and can even cause him enormous losses, for it is from tuna fishing that he hopes to draw the best reward for the toil and dangers of his hazardous life.

To this day it has not been possible to identify this species with certainty. It is supposed, however, that it is not a fish but a cetacean, *Orca gladiator*, which the fishermen of the Algarve call *ruaz de bandeira*, and which is no less feared there for the serious damage it does to the tuna traps.
Boca de Peixe
Common name of *Antirrhinum orontium* and *A. majus*. The first of these Scrophulariaceae is native and very common; the second is a plant found mainly in gardens.
Boca do Buraco
A locality (*sítio*) to the east of Pico do Areeiro (‘sand-pit peak’), from which a majestic panorama can be enjoyed on clear days.
Boca dos Corregos
A locality (*sítio*) near Pico Grande (‘great peak’), from which Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) and the Serra de Água valley can be seen. It lies at about 1300 metres above sea level.
Boca dos Namorados

In the uplands of the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), overlooking the pleasant locality (*sítio*) of Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’), stands Pico dos Bodes (‘billy-goats’ peak’). Close by is the Boca dos Namorados (‘lovers’ pass’), one of the places in Madeira that command the finest and most extensive panoramas. The spot became very well known because in former times it was much visited by Portuguese and foreigners alike.
Boca Negra (Sebastes dactylopterus)

A fish of pleasant flavour of the family Triglidae, caught over rocky bottoms at depths of roughly 80 to 250 *braças*. It is sedentary and owes its name to the fact that the inside of its mouth is lined with a very dark membrane. The tackle used to catch it is the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) and the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream).
Bodes (peak)

This lofty height in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’) stands at about 1135 metres above sea level, near the Boca dos Namorados (‘lovers’ pass’).
See Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’).
Bodes (peak)
There is a mountain elevation of this name in the uplands of Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’), at an altitude of 1300 metres.
Parrotfish (Scarus cretensis)

). A fish of the family Labridae, common on the coasts of all the islands of this archipelago, including the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*), and rightly prized for its delicate flavour. It is a handsome species whose colour, which varies greatly, can range from dark slate flecked with lighter tones to brilliant red, while some individuals are red and grey at the same time. Hence the distinction that some fishing communities make between the brown, the red and the *cardão* parrotfish. It is not a migratory fish, but its somewhat nomadic habits lead it to move about the shallows near the coast. Although it is not as common as it once was, it is nevertheless one of the few coastal species that have managed to escape relatively lightly from the destructive effects of the senseless and ruinous practice of fishing with explosives.

It is caught from the water’s edge down to 30 *braças*, using, besides hook tackle, drag nets and set nets, the scoop net (*peneiro*) and the fish trap (*covo*); the rod, however, is the tackle preferred by amateur anglers and professional fishermen alike. As bait they usually use the *jaca* (local name for small shore crabs) or the *aranha*, crustaceans found under the stones of the shore between the tide marks.

Off the coast of the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), the fishermen of Caniçal (‘reed bed’) sometimes make large catches of this fish, which, after being split and salted, is brought to the Funchal market, though somewhat lowered in value by the salting.
Bodioa
Said of a grey hen speckled light and dark, recalling the parrotfish (*bodião*), whose scales often show those colours.
Bogue (Box boops)

A fish of the family Sparidae, native and very common in the waters of this archipelago. It is caught in large quantities mainly in late spring and early summer, together with the mackerel and the horse mackerel, which reach us in abundance from elsewhere at that season. It is one of the species included in the group that fishermen call *ruama* (fishermen’s name for small shoaling fish such as mackerel and horse mackerel). Hook tackle is used, but the method that yields the richest catch is the conical, bag-shaped net called the *rede da ruama*. Its value is low and its taste mediocre.
Bogalho
This surname derives from Pedro Bogalho, a native of the city of Guarda, who settled on this island at the beginning of the 16th century.
Boganga

The plant known here by the names *boganga*, *bogangueira* and *abóbora de Tenerife* is *Curcubita ficifolia*, a native of China. Its fruits (*bogangas*) are used for soup and to make the preserve known as *chila* (sweet made from gourd seed filaments), which uses only the filaments or funicles of fully ripe seeds.

The plant known in Portugal as *moganga* is, according to Brotero, a variety of *Cucurbita pepo*, a species represented in Madeira by the squash plant that produces the *abóbora machado* (a local squash, Cucurbita pepo); it is therefore a mistake to give that name to the Madeiran *boganga*. The latter, according to Mr Pereira Coutinho, is called *chila caioto* or *abóbora chila* in Portugal.
The weak white wine produced on the north coast of the island is known as *bogangueira*.
Bohm (Dr Joannes)

Works: *Einige Fossilien aus den Salvages Inseln*. (Abdruck a. d. Zeitschr. d. Deutsche Geol. Gesellschaft, Jahr 1898). This work records 7 species, 2 of them new: *Nerita salvagensis* and *Cabralia schmitzii*.
Manx shearwater (Puffinus anglorum)

A marine web-footed bird, not very common in these islands. It frequents the open sea by day, returning to land late at night. As a day bird it is called *boieiro* by seafarers; as a night bird it is known throughout Madeira as *estrapagado*, *papagarro* or *patagarro*, onomatopoeic names that imitate its characteristic call fairly well. It breeds on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) and on the less accessible cliffs of Madeira, such as Curral das Freiras, Areeiro and Penha de Águia. The clutch is a single pure white egg, laid in a hole in the rocks. Many people regard it as a bird of ill omen. According to popular belief, a death will soon occur among the occupants of a house whenever a *patagarro* alights on it during its nocturnal flight from the mountains to the sea, or vice versa. It migrates, leaving the archipelago during the winter and returning at the end of February or the beginning of March.

Boliqueme

It is one of the most important localities (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António. Since there is a parish of this name in the province of the Algarve, and most of the first settlers of this island were from the Algarve, it is not surprising that they gave this locality the name of that parish. It is also possible that the orographic features of the Algarve parish and of this locality, together with other points of resemblance, gave rise to the name. Examples of this are frequent in the history of our discoveries, and they are not rare even in Madeira.
Bolsa de pastor (Oxalis corniculata

). A plant of the family Oxalidaceae, very common in Madeira. Its stems and its trifoliate leaves contain oxalic acid, and for this reason they are used to remove ink stains. An infusion of *bolsa de pastor* is widely used in Madeira to purify the blood.
Retreat House of the Good Jesus

This *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) was known as Bom Jesus da Ribeira because the ground on which it was built stretched as far as the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). Its founder was Dr Simão Gonçalves Cidrão, archdeacon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), who made it important grants. With a number of donations, and above all with the valuable help of Father Pascoal Ferreira de Sousa, chapel master of the Cathedral, he succeeded in building that modest religious house and the church attached to it, which was later considerably enlarged.

The first deed of grant of certain properties for the foundation of this *recolhimento*, made by Simão Gonçalves Cidrão, is dated 20 December 1655. Building work began in that same year or the next. It seems that the first women did not enter the house until 1666. This leads us to suppose either that the building took a long time to complete or that difficulties, unknown to us, prevented the *recolhimento* from opening. On 9 October 1673 further grants were made to the house by the same Archdeacon Dr Cidrão or by his heirs.

The *recolhimento* was intended to take in 25 to 30 lay sisters, a number that included some poor maidens who could prove that their conduct was blameless. From the outset the women gave proof of the strictest observance of their rule or statutes, and became an entirely exemplary community. This led many people of austere life to seek admission to that religious institution. Although it was not a monastic order, the daily choir service was held there and other practices proper to convents of nuns were observed.

We do not know whether the original discipline and fervour were always maintained there over the course of time. We do know, however, that for many years now the house has been a purely secular *recolhimento*, with no obligation on the women living there to observe any acts of a religious character.

The *recolhimento* of Bom Jesus was approved by Bishop Dom Gabriel de Almeida, who governed this diocese from March 1671 until his death on 13 July 1674. It was therefore within this period that the house acquired its canonical and legal existence, and it may be presumed that its foundation was preceded by a licence from the diocesan authority. We have record that, at a date we cannot determine, some of the *recolhidas* (women living in a religious retreat house) asked the Holy See for permission to take vows and thus turn the *recolhimento* into a regular religious congregation. This permission was refused, for reasons unknown to us.

According to its founder’s intentions, the *recolhimento* of Bom Jesus was subject solely to the prelate of the diocese, both in its internal direction and in the administration of its property. It was the ecclesiastical authority that appointed the chaplain of the house and an administrator of its property, who was known as the syndic (*síndico*, lay agent managing a religious house’s property) and was always a person of integrity and standing.

Despite the donations of Dr Cidrão, the *recolhimento* had no great resources, and so from a certain time onwards a dowry of 300 escudos was required for the admission of each *recolhida*. At the beginning of the 19th century this was raised to 400,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).
In 1811 the income of the house was 1,367,000 *réis* and its expenditure 2,007,000 *réis*. In the same year it had 42 *recolhidas*.

Since 1910 the *recolhimento* has been administered and run by a commission appointed by the civil governor. The commission that relinquished the administration of the house in April 1919 handed over 437.15 escudos to its successor, while the bonds belonging to the *recolhimento* yielded 931.11 escudos a year.
Bombardment of Funchal

The city of Funchal was bombarded twice by German submarines while the state of war between Portugal and Germany lasted. The first bombardment took place on 3 December 1916 and the second on 12 December of the following year.

The first bombardment was preceded by the torpedoing of the gunboat *La Surprise*, of the French navy, the *Kanguroo*, a steamer of the same nationality, and the *Dacia*, a British merchant steamer in the service of the French government. These vessels, which lay at anchor in our harbour, were torpedoed a short distance from the shore, the pirate having managed to approach them without being seen by their crews. The American yacht *Eleanor A. Percy*, which was also in the waters of our bay, was spared by the submarine, because Germany was not yet at war with the United States of America at that time.

The first ship to be hit was the gunboat *La Surprise*. After an explosion in her magazine she sank in about 2 minutes, dragging down with her a barge, crewed by Madeiran workers of the firm of Blandy, which was supplying her with coal. Of the gunboat’s crew 33 died, including Commander Ladonne, 2 officers and 7 petty officers; of the barge’s crew, Manuel Rodrigues Teixeira, Manuel Rodrigues Vieira, José Gomes Camacho, Augusto Garcês, Manuel Rodrigues, Francisco Franco and Frederico Vieira died. Manuel Rodrigues Teixeira, an employee of the firm of Blandy, had gone aboard the gunboat to direct the coaling.

The crews of the other ships managed to save themselves by swimming and in boats. Mr Bernard, captain of the *Kanguroo*, helped by two Frenchmen and a Madeiran, succeeded in firing 25 rounds from his gun at the submarine when his ship was already on the point of sinking. The brave men who helped Mr Bernard were the Madeiran José Alexandre Gomes, skipper (*arrais*) of a steam launch, and the gunner Tonnerre and the apprentice Provenzalé, crew members of the *Kanguroo*.

The explosion aboard *La Surprise* shook the houses of the city and was at first taken to be accidental. But when two more followed and the small steamers of the coaling firms began to sound their whistles insistently, everyone realised what was happening. A veritable panic then seized the population, a panic that grew still worse when the shells fired by the submarine’s two guns began to fall on the city.

Having escaped the fire of the *Kanguroo* and of the shore batteries, the pirates’ boat took up a position some 12 kilometres away, beyond the range of our artillery, and from there it bombarded the city without running any risk.

The bombardment lasted from 9 to 11 in the morning; *La Surprise* had been torpedoed at about half past eight. The Vigia (‘lookout’) battery fired 34 rounds and the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) 18, none of which hit the submarine. The submarine fired some 50 shells at the city. Some burst in the air, and the rest fell at the following points: 2 in Rua Júlio da Silva Carvalho, 1 in Rua das Queimadas de Cima, 1 in Rua do Bispo, 2 in Calçada de Santa Clara, 1 in Rua Direita, 1 on the Pelourinho factory, 1 on the Quinta Vigia, 1 in the Jardim Municipal and 1 in the Angústias cemetery.

No one died in the city, and the material damage caused by the shells was not great. Only at sea were there dead and wounded. The wounded were taken to the Civil Hospital (*Hospital Civil*) by the staff of the Red Cross (*Cruz Vermelha*) delegation in Funchal, who gave excellent service.

As soon as the first explosion occurred, Mr Carlos Pio de França and Mr Afonso Coelho had two boats launched, which picked up 15 survivors, some of them wounded. The seaman João de Gouveia, known as ‘o Gordo’ (the Fat One), a crew member of one of these boats, gave valuable service, rescuing 8 of the gunboat’s crew and 2 Madeiran workers.

In the Angústias cemetery stands a small monument, commissioned by Mr Henrique Augusto Vieira de Castro, to perpetuate the memory of the French sailors and the Portuguese workers who perished in the bay of Funchal on the tragic morning of 3 December 1916. This monument, the work of the chisel of the prize-winning sculptor Mr Francisco Franco, was unveiled on 3 December 1917.

Lieutenant Max Valentiner, commander of the submarine that committed the cowardly act of torpedoing three ships inside our harbour and bombarding the city from beyond the range of the shore batteries, was decorated by the Kaiser, and Sonderburg, his home town, named him its ‘beloved son’!!!

The second bombardment of Funchal took place on 12 December 1917. The submarine fired its first shots at 6.20 in the morning, when the first light of day was barely beginning to show. It had been sighted by the crew of a fishing boat, who at once warned the crew of the *Dekade I* of what they had just discovered. That steamer, and later the *Mariano de Carvalho*, set out to meet the enemy and give battle.

The *Dekade I* and the *Mariano de Carvalho* were two small steamers, each armed with a small gun and crewed by sailors of the navy, which served as patrol boats in the port of Funchal. The former was the first to open fire on the submarine, which, as it drew away to place itself out of range of our boats’ guns, kept raining shells on them and on the city.

The steamers suffered no damage, but in the city there was considerable destruction: 5 people were killed and some 30-odd wounded, some slightly, others seriously. Shells fell at the following points: in front of the fortress of São Tiago; 1 in Rua de São Filipe; 1 on the Lombo da Boa Vista; 1 at the Quinta Mãe dos Homens (Mother of Mankind); 1 on the Levada do Bom Sucesso; 2 on the Lombo do Terço; 1 in Rua do Dr. Juvenal; 1 at Choupana; 1 in the Jardim Municipal; 1 in Travessa de Santa Catarina; 1 in Rua dos Aranhas; 1 at the Fortress of São Lourenço; 1 at the Convent of St Clare; 3 on the beach, 1 of them in front of the customs house and 2 beside the Funchal Harbour Master’s Office (*Capitania do Porto do Funchal*); 1 in Rua da Bela Vista; 1 near the Torreão factory (this one did not explode); 1 near the Pico de São João; 1 in Rua 5 de Junho; 1 near the Jewish Cemetery; 1 near the Hotel Jones; 1 near the Castelo do Pico; 1 in the sea, opposite the point where the submarine cable comes ashore; and 1 near Travessa do Pasto. Other shells burst over the city, but caused no damage.

This second bombardment lasted only 30 minutes, during which the submarine fired some 50 rounds and the patrol boats 40-odd. The batteries of Vigia and São Gonçalo never opened fire on the submarine, because, pursued by the patrol boats, it quickly moved out of their range.

Those killed on the day of the bombardment were: Augusto Teles de Vilhena, aged 25; Carolina Adelaide Rodrigues, aged 50; Firmina Augusta Figueira, of the same age; Maria José de Mendonça, aged 45; and Emília Augusta, aged 40.

The wounded were treated at the Civil Hospital and at the branch of the Portuguese Red Cross Society, where both the branch’s physician, Dr João Albino de Sousa, and its stretcher-bearers gave good service. At the Hospital the wounded were attended by Dr Álvaro Tertuliano da Silva and Dr José Joaquim de Freitas.

The shell that burst in the Convent of St Clare wounded Father Manuel da Silva Branco, who was celebrating Mass there, the sacristan and two women, one of whom died shortly afterwards at the Red Cross branch in Rua dos Netos.
For the bravery they showed during the submarine attack, the crews of the *Dekade I* and the *Mariano de Carvalho* were commended by the harbour master in an order of the day.

Because of the bombardment, a large part of the population of Funchal left for Monte, Santo António, São Martinho and other places, and many people rented houses on the outskirts of the city, supposing that they would be better protected there against the dangers of a fresh attack by the pirates. The panic lasted a long time, and on several occasions we saw people of all ages and social conditions fleeing in terror in every direction, merely because they had heard that a new submarine had been sighted near our port or that the Germans had landed somewhere on the coast. There were nights when cars and carriages had not a moment’s rest, so great was the number of people seeking to escape the danger they believed they faced if they stayed in the city.

Some people had trenches dug inside their houses and gardens, into which they retreated whenever some ill-humoured individual took it into his head to announce a new bombardment as imminent. Street lighting was banned as a defence measure on the day of the second bombardment, and was restored only on 11 November 1918, when the first news of the cessation of hostilities between the belligerents reached Madeira. After the first bombardment, lighting had been banned for only a few days, after which the lamps were lit again in the streets that could not be seen from the sea.

To protect Madeira against any attempted German landing, the government sent us, after the events of 12 December, a company of position artillery with its guns, which was quartered in Rua do Carmo. What we never had was the artillery needed to respond effectively to a bombardment carried out at long range. It was for lack of it, both on land and at sea, that the pirates were able to carry out, without any risk, the two acts of brutal aggression recorded here. The only large-calibre gun at our disposal, mounted at São Gonçalo, could not be used on 12 December 1917 because the submarine, it is said, had placed itself out of its range when carrying out the bombardment.
Volcanic bombs

Bodies of basaltic nature, sometimes rounded, sometimes oblong and tapering at the ends, and almost always marked with parallel longitudinal grooves. They are projectiles hurled into the air long ago by volcanic activity that ceased many centuries ago. They are commonly found, sometimes loose and sometimes embedded, on the slopes of the most recent volcanic cones in the low-lying parts of Madeira and on the other islands of the archipelago. Lodged in the tuffs of these slopes, alongside the volcanic bombs, are other basalt bodies, elongated and twisted like ropes. Although these share the same volcanic origin, they were perhaps formed in a different way from the bombs proper. Characteristic specimens of both appear in many localities, among them Porto Moniz, São Martinho, Garajau, Caniçal, Porto Santo and Selvagem Grande.
Fire brigade

The company was organised at a session of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) on 24 September 1888, and its personnel were appointed on 11 April 1889. Its regulations were approved by the Council on 4 April 1889. To train Funchal’s first firemen, Luís da Terra Viana, a fireman from Porto, came to Madeira and stayed at the Hotel do Carmo (‘Carmel’) at the Council’s expense. The original company was dissolved in 1906, but by 20 September of that year a new company had already been formed, organised by Alfredo Jorge Ferraz, an employee of the postal telegraph service.
Bomboteiro

This is the name given in Madeira to a person who goes aboard the steamers calling at the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal) to sell photographs, postcards and various articles produced or made on the island. According to Cândido de Figueiredo, the word derives from the English *bumboat*.
Bonina (Mirabilis divaricata)
A plant of the family Nyctaginaceae, cultivated and naturalised in Madeira.

Its flowers are very variable in colour, but usually purplish violet, and its leaves are ovate-lanceolate or ovate, subcordate at the base. The root of this plant is purgative, but it is not used in Madeira.
Boqueirão de Baixo
A small channel or passage between the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the islet adjacent to it, called Ilhéu de Baixo (‘lower islet’) or Ilhéu da Cal.
Boqueirão de Cima
A narrow passage between the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’) or Ilhéu do Farol.
Boqueirão de São Lourenço
The same as Boqueirão Grande (‘great gap’).
Boqueirão do Furado
A small channel (*boqueirão*) separating the tip of Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’) from the Ilhéu de Agostinho (see that entry). At low tide it can be crossed on foot.
Boqueirão Grande

This is the channel or sea passage between the Ilhéu Vermelho, or Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros (see that entry), and the Ilhéu de Fora, at Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’). In calm seas, the so-called scheduled boats (*barcos de carreira*) and the coastal steamers often pass through this channel.
Boqueirão (Smaris insidiator)

A small fish of the family Maenidae, caught in Madeiran waters. Once very common, it is today a rarity in the markets, and it is not a fish of great value. It is caught from the shoreline to the open sea, and from the surface down to a depth of about 150 *braças* (fathoms). It is sometimes seen far from land, mixed with sardines, herring, horse mackerel and mackerel.
Butterflies

Some 120 species of Lepidoptera are known in Madeira, many of which go by the name of butterflies. In gardens and fields a number of day-flying species are common, notable for the colouring of their wings, such as *Pieris brassicae*, *Colias edusa*, *Lycaena baetica*, *Vanessa atalanta*, *V. callirhoe*, *V. cardui*, etc. It is *Pieris brassicae*, with its almost white wings, that produces the caterpillar which destroys cabbages.
Embroidery

The foreigners who wrote about Madeira at the beginning of the second quarter of the 19th century make no mention of the embroidery industry. This seems to mean that either it did not exist at that time or it was still of no importance at all on the island. In 1850 some Madeiran embroidery appeared at an industrial exhibition held in Funchal, but it was only between 1854 and 1856 that this work began to be produced on a large scale on the island. This was owing to the demand it already enjoyed in the markets of England, where Miss Phelps had made it known through some of her acquaintances. After Miss Phelps came the English merchants Roberto and Franck Wilkinson, who began exporting Madeiran embroidery to England on a larger scale. In this way an industry gradually developed for which the women of our countryside showed a decided aptitude, and which some 60 years ago was already an important source of wealth for our island. In 1862, according to the *Estatística Industrial do Districto do Funchal* by Francisco de Paula de Campos e Oliveira, there were 1029 embroiderers in Madeira. Sales of embroidery across the whole island amounted to some 100 *contos* (one million réis) of island *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), and nearly 15 kilograms of thread were used in this work every day. The same *Estatística* adds that most of the embroidery was sold to foreigners, who took it away in their luggage; the embroidery exported directly through the customs house was worth no more than 6 or 7 *contos de réis*. Embroiderers’ wages at that time were around 100 to 150 *réis* a day.

Exports of embroidery grew steadily, we believe, until 1878, when they were estimated at 55,252,000 *réis*. By 1880, however, they had fallen to 12,937,000 *réis*, because luxury embroidery had gone somewhat out of fashion in England. Large sums nevertheless remained on the island from sales of embroidery to the many foreigners who visited us. It was this that sustained and encouraged an industry which, although it brought no great profit to the women who practised it, did in some measure help to improve the situation of many families. Madame Counis’s shop in Rua de João Tavira made more sales than any other in the city at that time. It offered work of the most varied kinds, from white embroidery of simple design to silk embroidery and tapestry work in single or double stitch. It was a little over 50 years ago, around 1890, that the first German embroidery export houses established themselves in Funchal. This was of clear benefit to an industry that had long stood still for lack of consumer markets. Our embroidery, until then well known only in England, began to spread not only to Germany but also to the United States of America and other countries. The result was a considerable increase in production, greatly benefiting not only the rural economy but the economy of the whole district. The sum required to pay for labour across the whole archipelago, which was 200 *contos* in 1893, rose to 461 *contos* in 1906. This was due to greater exports and to a considerable increase in sales within Funchal, thanks to the arrival in our harbour of a larger number of steamers carrying passengers in transit.

‘In Madeira,’ says Vitorino José dos Santos in no. 5 of the *Boletim do Trabalho*, ‘there are two perfectly distinct classes of embroiderers: rural embroiderers and professional embroiderers. The former are found scattered throughout the district, though far more densely on the south coast of Madeira and on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). The latter live mainly in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal, and above all in the parishes of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) and São Gonçalo, where the finest embroidery in the whole district is produced.

The earnings of the two classes of embroiderers also differ greatly. Some professional embroiderers manage to earn two or three times as much a day as the best of the rural embroiderers. This result is always achieved at the cost of steady application over an excessive number of working hours, and of the consequent perfection of the embroidery produced.

The embroidery industry does not, however, offer these embroiderers the advantages we have pointed out for rural embroiderers. The rural women, through the variety of the work they do, the more carefree life of the countryside and the lower intensity of their labour, carry on an activity in reasonably healthy conditions that does not wear them out. The professional embroiderers, by contrast, most of whom suffer from an inordinate love of luxury, and who live in the municipality of Funchal, where such luxury is very widespread among the less well-off classes, work more than they should, day and night, with exhausting intensity. They almost always take very little care to eat nourishing food, and so they soon wear themselves out and contract serious illnesses, such as tuberculosis, which causes great havoc in this class of embroiderers.’

Mr Santos supposes that in 1906 there were 30,000 rural embroiderers and 2,000 professional ones in the whole district, the former earning an average wage of 70 réis and the latter 200 réis. The firms that gave these workers employment, not counting a few small Portuguese traders, numbered 8, of which 2 were Portuguese and 6 German, and the sum they set aside for paying labour amounted to 461,000,000 réis across the district. Estimating at 151,000,000 réis what these same firms spent on staff salaries, the distribution of fabrics, the collection of finished work and various other charges, Mr Santos concluded that about 596,000,000 réis were paid into the district’s economy every year, not counting, of course, what also remained here from the profits of the export trade.

‘Madeira embroidery,’ Mr Vitorino José dos Santos goes on, ‘was formerly almost all worked in blue thread on calico or cambric, first fitted and tacked over special designs (*riscos*) and carefully warped. These operations were fundamental to making good, strong and lasting embroidery.’ ‘Embroidery is still done this way in Madeira today when it is called for, but that rarely happens. Since the German firms set up in Funchal, the practice of embroidering in white thread directly onto fabrics already printed with the designs has become general, and the demand for lower prices has made quantity prevail over quality, while the warping, which was one of the main requirements for the durability of the embroidery, has also almost disappeared.’

The European war in which Portugal found itself involved at first did serious damage to the embroidery industry. The German markets, says Mr Vitorino José dos Santos in issue 97 of the *Boletim do Trabalho Industrial*, closed, and even in America the contingencies of an uncertain future soon reduced orders, forcing a cut in work and the dismissal of employees and female workers in the head houses and workshops. The crisis, terrible as it was, did not last long, however, and at the end of 1918 there were 34 embroidery export houses in Funchal, which spent about 1,500 *contos* on labour and staff salaries. On 31 December 1912, that is, before the war began, these houses numbered 19 and spent about 600 *contos* on labour.

Mr Vitorino José dos Santos supposes that on 31 December 1912 there were 32,000 rural embroiderers and 2,500 professional embroiderers in the whole district, and that by 31 December 1914 the work produced by these embroiderers had fallen by half, owing to the crisis that resulted from the European conflagration.

The embroidery industry is now (1923) flourishing in Madeira and no longer seems to feel the losses it suffered when the European war closed the German markets to the island’s products. The United States is the country that imports the largest quantity of Madeiran embroidery, and England, despite the restrictions it has placed on the import of luxury goods, remains an important market for it. Many women of Funchal live solely from the embroidery industry, and in the countryside the earnings that many female workers draw from it do a great deal to make life easier for many families.

If an industry that brings so many benefits to the great majority of the Madeiran population, and is today the most important on the island, is to survive, however, its products must be of a kind that finds wide demand in the consuming centres. To sacrifice quality to quantity, as has often been done when meeting orders from abroad, is to bring our embroidery into discredit and to provoke a future crisis that will cause incalculable harm to the economic life of our land.

At the end of 1923 there were some 100 embroidery houses in Funchal, and the value of exports to America, England, South Africa, Canada, France, etc., was estimated at about 70,000 *contos*. At the same period the embroidery industry employed about 70,000 people of both sexes, some working in the export houses and others at home. Some women earned 8, 9, 10 and 12 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) a day in this industry, and some men had salaries ranging from 200 to 1,500 escudos a month.

The expansion of the embroidery industry has brought profound changes to our social life, and it is much to be wished that the industry should always remain flourishing, so that many households do not come to feel wants and hardships unknown there at present (1923). The large profits that part of the population draws directly or indirectly from the industry we are discussing have created, for many people, needs that must be satisfied. So if tomorrow this industry, which has brought plenty and in some cases wealth to many homes, were to lose its importance, the result would be a crisis that could give rise to great evils.

The devaluation of our currency is the main cause of the expansion of the embroidery industry. It should be pointed out, however, that while this expansion has softened the effects of the economic crisis the country is going through, it has also done much, through higher wages and business profits, to give part of our people a taste for pleasure and spendthrift habits that were not seen in the past.

Since the embroidery industry does not enjoy the conditions for permanent prosperity, prudence advises those who live from it not to grow used to needless or useless spending, for if such spending is possible today, it may not be tomorrow, should the conditions under which the industry operates on our island change (1923).
At the end of this volume of the *Elucidário* we shall give further information and various statistics on this important Madeiran industry for recent years.
Bordalo (Francisco Maria)

This distinguished naval officer and writer (1821–1861) commanded the frigate *Diana*, which in 1844 carried a number of political deportees to Madeira. In 1861 he stayed on the island in search of better health, but on returning to the capital he died there shortly afterwards. One of his books contains several references to Madeira.
Borge (O.)
He identified the algae collected by Dr Lindman in 1885 and wrote a short paper on them entitled *Algologische Notizen Susswasseralgen aus Madeira* (*Botaniske Notizer*, 1911).
Borges (Gaspar)

‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) devotes eight long pages to one Gaspar Borges who, after the sack by the French pirates, unspiked the artillery pieces. These had been judged completely useless, and to everyone’s great amazement he managed to restore them to their original use. Judging by the detail into which Frutuoso goes and the praise with which he extols Gaspar Borges’s work, he must indeed have been a most skilful mechanic of uncommon competence, whatever hyperbole there may be in the chronicler’s account. To us it seems very strange that Gaspar Frutuoso should have taken the detailing of the affair so far and become so enthusiastic a eulogist of the unspiking of those guns! (Anyone wishing to learn in detail of the strange skill of the notorious Borges should read ‘Longing for the Homeland’ from page 283 onwards. Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça published an interesting historical novel entitled *Gaspar Borges*, whose main protagonist is the skilful craftsman to whom ‘Longing for the Homeland’ refers at such length.
Borges (Vasco)
He was appointed civil governor of Madeira by decree of 4 April 1914 and took up the post on the 27th of the same month and year.
Bornmuller (P.)
German botanist who collected plants in Madeira in 1900. Works: *Ergebnisse zweier botanischer Reisen nach Madeira und den Canarischen Inseln* (*Bot. Jahrb.*, 1903).
Rubber tree

Of the species that yield rubber, only *Ficus elastica*, of the family Urticaceae, and *Manihot Glaziovii*, of the family Euphorbiaceae, exist in Madeira. The first is found in several *quintas* of Funchal; the second exists, as far as we know, only in the grounds attached to the Disinfection Station (*Posto de Desinfecção*), at Campo da Barca (‘boat field’), where it thrives. In many places on the island there grows a composite, called *visco*, whose latex solidifies into a whitish, elastic mass, but which has no industrial applications.
Borracho

A goatskin used to carry grape must. The *borracheiros* are the men who carry the *borrachos* from the wine press to the establishment that buys the must for winemaking; as they march they sing a rhythmic, mournful chant which is sometimes pleasant to hear.
Borage (Borago officinalis)

An emollient, sudorific and diuretic plant, cultivated and naturalised in São Martinho, São Roque, Caniço, etc. This member of the Boraginaceae, native to Europe, is recognisable by its large blue or white flowers, which eventually droop, and by its hirsute leaves with coarse hairs.
Bory (De)
He described his voyage to Madeira in the *Histoire et Mémoires de l'Academie Royale des Sciences pour l'an 1772* (Paris, 1776).
Bosenberg (W.)
Works: *Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Arachniden Fauna von Madeira und den Canarischen Inseln*. (*Abhand Gebiete der Naturwiss.*, 1895, Hamburg).
Botelho (Alberto de Sousa)
He represented this archipelago in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the parliamentary sessions of 1901 and of 1902–1904.
He was an artillery officer and professor at the former Army School.
He died in Funchal on 28 December 1903.
Botelho (Sebastião Xavier)

This governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira was appointed on 15 June 1818, arrived in Funchal on 12 May 1819 and took office on the 15th of the same month.
He travelled throughout his captaincy and informed the central government of the most urgent improvements to be made.
It was during his rule that the Porto revolution broke out, overthrowing absolute government and establishing the representative system; in Madeira the Constitution was proclaimed on 28 January 1821.

He fought bitter political battles, and in his own defence he published a pamphlet entitled *Historia verdadeira dos acontecimentos da ilha da Madeira depois do memorável dia 28 de Janeiro ...* (Lisbon, 1821). Sebastião Botelho was gifted with rare intelligence and wide learning, and was considered one of the most esteemed writers of his time; Alexandre Herculano wrote and delivered his historical eulogy.
Besides serving as governor and captain-general of Madeira, the Azores, Mozambique and Angola, he held other important posts.
He was born on 8 March 1768 and died on 21 May 1840. He belonged to the family of the Counts of São Miguel and was the grandfather of the 2nd Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’).
Botha (General Louis)
He passed through Funchal in May 1907 on his way to London to take part in the South African Congress.
Harbour porpoise (Phocaena communis)
A cetacean of Madeiran seas. When young it is called *toninha* (local name for a young porpoise, also the common dolphin), a name also given to another cetacean, *Dellphinus delphis*.
Bowdich (T. E.)

English naturalist and traveller who was in Madeira in 1823, staying from 14 to 26 October. The results of Bowdich’s studies of the fauna, flora, geology and meteorology of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) are set out in a work published only after his death, entitled *Excursions in Madeira and Porto Santo, during the autumn of 1823* (London, 1825). This work, curious for many reasons but containing many inaccuracies, was translated into French and published in Paris in 1826. Bowdich died on 10 January 1824.
Braça
It measures ten *palmos* of nine inches, each inch corresponding to 2 1/2 centimetres. The *braça* (fathom, about 2.2 m) is used in Madeira to measure stone intended for building.
Brado d'Oeste

The third newspaper published in Madeira outside Funchal and the first published in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). The first issue appeared on 2 June 1909 and the last, no. 858, on 24 January 1918.
Braga (family)

Around 1460 João de Braga, a rich nobleman, came from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) to this island of Madeira, and was given lands as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish of Santo António, at the locality (*sítio*) called Laranjal (‘orange grove’). He was the father of the celebrated Marcos de Braga, whom the old Madeiran chronicles praise highly for his deeds of bravery and courage. João de Braga married a daughter of Nuno Gonçalves, and from this union was born Domingos de Braga, who founded the entail (*morgado*) of Laranjal on the lands his grandfather had obtained as a *sesmaria*.

This entailed estate (*morgadio*) passed to a great-grandson of his sister Dona Maria Gonçalves de Braga, named Manuel Ferreira Drumond de Vasconcelos, and from him to his son João Drumond de Vasconcelos, and then successively, by inheritance from parents to children, to Manuel Ferreira Drumond, Rafael Drumond de Vasconcelos, Francisco Moniz Drumond, João Ferreira Drumond Henriques, Dona Maria Hilaria Ferreira Drumond, António Sebastião Spinola Ferreira de Carvalho, Dona Matilde Augusta Spinola and António Sebastião Spinola Ferreira de Carvalho Barreto. The last was the final administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of this entailed estate, owing to the law abolishing entails, and his representative is his son, Dr Remígio António Gil de Spinola Barreto.
The introduction of this surname to the island is owed to João de Braga.
Braga (Gaspar de)
He distinguished himself greatly during the sack of this island by French pirates in 1566, putting up a stubborn resistance to the attackers and dying heroically in the fight.
Braga (Marcos de)

The old Madeiran chronicles speak of Marcos de Braga, praising the feats of courage and valour he performed thanks to his extraordinary physical strength. He gave great proof of this strength on many occasions, and Gaspar Frutuoso cites several curious examples of it. This chronicler says that Marcos de Braga ‘was so hairy that even the backs of his nails were covered with hair, and his face right up to his eyes...’. A son of his of the same name inherited his father’s valour and likewise performed several acts of great bravery and courage, which Frutuoso did not forget to record.
Braga (Teófilo)

In his book *Poetas Palacianos*, this illustrious writer devotes a chapter to this archipelago, which he entitled *Cyclo Poético da ilha da Madeira*. In it he mentions the Madeiran poets whose compositions appear in the ‘General Songbook’ (*Cancioneiro Geral*) of Garcia de Resende. This chapter is transcribed, with learned commentary, on p. 765 ff. of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), from the authoritative pen of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo.

The same author’s work *Quarenta anos de vida literaria* contains, on pp. 109–118, twelve letters from the illustrious annotator of the *Saudades*. They deal with the publication of that work and of the *Romanceiro e Cancioneiro da Madeira*, and contain very interesting material for the literary history of this island.
Braguinha

A wooden musical instrument shaped like a small viola (Portuguese wire-strung folk guitar), peculiar to these islands. It has 17 frets and is fitted with 4 gut strings. These are tuned not in fifths, like the violin or the mandolin, as some authors claim, but as follows: D 3, G 3, B 3, D 2, that is, with an interval of a fourth and two of a third. Sometimes, especially in the countryside, the gut first string is replaced by a metal string, which gives it a shrill sound more to the liking of the country player. Its range barely exceeds two octaves, and it can play chords in the keys of G, C, F, D and A, its easiest key being G major. Its high, sprightly and cheerful sound allows it to stand out in a characteristic way among similar instruments. It is used almost exclusively by ordinary people and lends itself to a wide variety of melodies, which are often accompanied by the *rajão* (Madeiran five-string guitar) and the viola. It forms part of popular musical groups, sometimes taking the main or melodic part in unison with other instruments such as the guitar and the fiddle, and at other times providing a simple accompaniment in chords. When playing a melody, the folk player uses only the thumb. The instrument is, however, capable of greater effect in the hands of a skilled and knowledgeable performer who plays the melody with the thumb and intersperses it with chords of three and four notes struck with the other fingers, which gives the music of this instrument an entirely distinctive character.
The popular expression *tocar a ponteado* means to play a melody, because in that case, unlike in accompaniments, the player uses most of the frets.

Funchal had several teachers of the braguinha (small Madeiran four-string guitar, ancestor of the ukulele), among them Manuel Cabral, António José Barbosa and Agostinho Martins. Some pieces of music survive in manuscript, as well as the rudiments of the instrument, whose study was pursued with particular fondness by many of the foreigners who in former times called at Madeira.

Some years ago an orchestra of braguinhas, *rajões* (Madeiran five-string guitar) and *violas* was formed in Funchal under the direction of Agostinho Martins. Playing popular and even classical music suited to the resources of these instruments, it made a strong impression through the originality and well-constructed nature of its musical arrangements.
Today the braguinha is found in the Sandwich Islands and other parts of the world to which the emigration of the Madeiran tenant farmer (*colono*, under the *colonia* contract) has been directed.

Called *cavaquinho* in Lisbon, it is also known in the Madeira archipelago as the *machete* (small Madeiran four-stringed guitar) *de braga*, or simply *braga*. Although these last names suggest an origin in the Minho, it is certain that there is at present no record of its having been found on the Portuguese mainland. Whether it was imported from other regions or is a Madeiran creation, the expression *machete de braga* may perhaps indicate that it was once played by common people, of the kind who wore the old breeches called *bragas*; or by convicts, of the kind who wore a ring on the leg known as a *braga*; or else by people who rested it against the waist, since *braga* once meant girdle, fly or waist.
Of all these hypotheses, the first is perhaps the most acceptable. Be that as it may, the question requires extensive study before sound conclusions can be reached.

It should be stressed that the simple name *machete* formerly belonged to this instrument, as the corresponding manuscript music shows. Today, however, the people use the name *machete* simply for that other native instrument, the *rajão*.
The so-called *requinta de braga*, modelled entirely on the braguinha, is still made in Funchal.
See Rajão and Requinta de braga.
Bramão (Dr Alberto Allen Pereira de Sequeira)
He was deputy for Madeira in the 1901 legislature. He was born in 1866. He is an acclaimed poet, and his volume of poems *Illusões Perdidas* has been translated into French and Italian.
Branca (islet)
A small islet close to the northern shore of the Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’).
Branca (point)
It is also known as Ponta de Nordeste (‘north-east point’). It lies on the north-east of the coast of the island of Porto Santo.
Branco (Alfredo de Castro de Freitas)

He was born in Funchal on 1 January 1890, the son of Luís de Freitas Branco and Dona Ana Augusta de Castro de Freitas Leal Branco. Besides various contributions to several newspapers, he has published: *O Destino*, 1916, 63 pp.; *Antiga Clara*, 1916, 31 pp.; *No Exílio. Scenas da vida dos conspiradores monarchicos*, 1917, 77 pp.; *Charcos*, 1917, 46 pp.; *A acção do estado nas suas relações com a egreja catholica. Conferencia*, 1917, 16 pp.; *Res Lusitanae*, a translation, 1914; *Auto da Primavera*, 1919, 22 pp.; *Madrinha de Guerra*, 1919, 44 pp.; *A Confidencia*, 1919; *A Flora Madeirense na Medicina Popular*, 1935; *A Estada de Cristovam Colombo na Madeira*, 1936; and *Os Lusiadas e a Madeira*.
Branco (Councillor Luís de Freitas)

He was born in Funchal on 19 August 1819 and studied with distinction at our lyceum (state secondary school) and at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), where he obtained high marks, graduating in law in 1852. He set up as a lawyer in Funchal and held several important offices here. He was deputy for Madeira in the legislative sessions of 1858–1859, 1860–1861, 1861–1864, 1865, 1865–1868 and 1882–1884. In the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) he proved a distinguished parliamentarian, serving as rapporteur on several bills. In 1862 he was appointed director-general of ecclesiastical affairs in the Ministry of Justice, a post he held until his death. He carried out important public-service assignments and enjoyed great influence and prestige in politics. He held several Portuguese and foreign decorations. This distinguished Madeiran died in Lisbon at the beginning of November 1884.
Branco (Dr Fidelio de Freitas)

He was born in Funchal on 16 June 1861, the son of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Silvano de Freitas Branco and Dona Maria Cândida de Sant'Ana Branco. He graduated in law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1884 and then practised as a lawyer in Lisbon for some time, but gave up this career to devote himself to agriculture and the management of his estate. He represented Madeira in parliament in the legislatures of 1887–1889, 1890–1892, 1894–1895 and 1895–1897. He was also deputy for a constituency on the mainland, and among the public-service posts he held was that of civil governor of one of the mainland districts. He died in Sintra on 29 October 1918.
Branco (João de Freitas)

He was born in this city on 5 August 1854, the son of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Silvano de Freitas Branco and Dona Maria Cândida de Sant'Ana Branco. He attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and enrolled in the faculty of mathematics of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), which he left in order to complete his education abroad and give his studies a new direction. It was in England, France and above all Austria that he acquired a profound knowledge of several foreign languages, and he was considered one of our most distinguished polyglots. He devoted himself particularly to the study of the literatures of northern Europe and wrote several highly regarded works of literary criticism on Ibsen, Rudyord, Kipling, Maeterlinck, etc. In the last years of his life he dedicated himself above all to the theatre, not only writing some original plays but also translating and adapting for the Portuguese stage many of the most acclaimed foreign dramas and comedies. He translated *Casa da Boneca* and *Esteio da Sociedade* by Ibsen, *Uma Fallencia* by Bjornson, *Penedos do Inferno* by Blumenthal, *O Fim de Sodoma* by Sudermann, etc. He also translated *Aranha d'Ouro*, *Festa da Inauguração*, *O Califa Harum Al Rachid*, *Os Innocentes*, *O Gatuno*, *O Homem das Mangas*, etc. It was he who made known in Portugal the leading dramatists of northern Europe, chiefly of Sweden, Denmark and Germany, who had been almost unknown among us.

His fondness for the theatre did not lead him to abandon the study of other literary and scientific subjects, and he was regarded as a man of deep learning in many branches of human knowledge. He died in Lisbon on 27 May 1910, aged 55.
Branco (João Soares)
The decree appointing him civil governor of Madeira dates from January 1906, and he took office on the 30th of that month and year.
He was deputy for Madeira in the legislative session of 1908–1910.

In 1915 he published in Lisbon a pamphlet of 103 pages entitled *A Nova Questão Hinton*, containing a collection of articles published in the newspaper *O Paiz*. He was a minister and a professor at the Army School (*Escola do Exército*). He died in Lisbon on 4 February 1927.
Branco (Father João Manuel de Freitas)

This priest, ‘one of the greatest talents of the province of Madeira’, as *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’) called him in 1822, was born in Funchal in 1773, or shortly after, and died in Rio de Janeiro in 1831.

For 24 consecutive years he served as a priest in various parishes far from Funchal, and in 1822 he was collated vicar (*vigário colado*, permanently instituted in the benefice) of São Jorge when he was elected deputy to the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) for the island of Madeira.
Having left for Lisbon that year, he took his seat in parliament, where he defended the interests of his homeland with considerable intelligence and judgement.

When absolute government was restored in Portugal and the Cortes were dissolved, Freitas Branco returned to Madeira. In 1826 he was appointed teacher of Latin grammar and Latinity in Funchal, and in September 1827 a member of the censorship board.
He was an ardent constitutionalist, and during Valdez’s government he used the pulpit several times to urge the people to respect the rights of Dom Pedro.
He was indicted by the special judicial commission (alçada) that the government of Miguel I sent to Madeira in 1828, but he escaped arrest because he had emigrated to Brazil.

He contributed to *O Patriota Funchalense* and was a corresponding member of the Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts (*Sociedade dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes*). Of Vicar Freitas Branco’s many sermons, the only one ever published was the one he preached in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) on 28 January 1822, the first anniversary of the proclamation of constitutional government on this island, entitled ‘*Oração de acção de graças que na solemnidade do anniversario do faustissimo dia 28 de Janeiro de 1821 pregou na Sé Catedral do Funchal em o anno de 1822*’.
Branco (peak)
In the northern part of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), to the north-east, rises the mountain of Pico Branco (‘white peak’), whose summit stands at an altitude of 420 m.
Brandão (Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa)

For the long period of 26 years, from 1757 to 1784, Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão guided the destinies of this diocese, of which he was the 17th bishop. Although we do not know the acts of his episcopate in detail, we do know that he was a distinguished prelate and that his episcopal administration left the most honourable traditions. It is true that his attitude at the time of the expulsion of the Society of Jesus from this island was bitterly censured by Catholics and, it seems, even by the Roman Curia. Particular notice was taken of the violent language of the pastoral letter he then published against the members of that religious order. The prelate did not stray from the path followed by the higher Portuguese clergy, who had neither the strength nor the courage to resist the despotic impositions of the Marquis of Pombal.

Dom Gaspar Brandão was born at Vila Cova de Subavô, in the judicial district (*comarca*) of Arganil and the diocese of Coimbra. He was the son of Bento de Figueiredo, who belonged to old families of that locality.

He was a secular priest, and in 1756 Joseph I presented him as bishop of Funchal. He was confirmed by Benedict XIV in the consistory of 19 July of that year. He received episcopal consecration the following year and arrived in this city on 5 August 1757.

He arrived accompanied by Fathers Alasia and Reis, members of the Congregation of the Mission. During the ten years they spent in this diocese, they were his most valuable helpers in the reforms he undertook, above all in enforcing discipline in the convents of both monks and nuns. Long-ingrained abuses had crept into these houses, and they could hardly be corrected entirely. In the evangelical missions held in the parishes, in the spiritual exercises of the clergy and ordinands, and in other works of a religious and ecclesiastical nature, the two priests Alasia and Reis rendered outstanding services, which are recorded in the annals of this diocese.

In the churchyards of some parish churches there still stand today crosses on modest plinths, commemorating the passage of those clergymen through these parishes as they preached the Gospel. Dom Gaspar Brandão was a most zealous shepherd of his flock. This showed above all in his visitations of the parishes, in the pastoral letters he wrote, in his preaching, in his reform of the seminary, in the missions and in his strict enforcement of ecclesiastical discipline.
He served as governor and captain-general from 1758 to 1759, and his time at the head of the archipelago’s government was marked by an administration of the utmost zeal and honesty.

For reasons we have not been able to establish, the prelate ordered the imprisonment in the Aljube (‘bishop’s prison’) of the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) António Xavier Pimentel. This led to a bitter conflict with the governor and captain-general João Gonçalves da Câmara Coutinho, and the two authorities exchanged a lengthy correspondence. It was ended by the intervention of the government in mainland Portugal, to which Dom Gaspar Brandão then appealed. Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão died in this city on 14 January 1784 and was buried in the chancel of our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*).
Brandão (José António Ferreira)
He translated Richard Henry Major’s work *The Life of Prince Henry of Portugal*, which is of considerable interest for the history of the Madeira archipelago in the early days of its colonisation.
Brandão (Pedro de Lima)
He was appointed to the office of Governor and Captain-General (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira on 29 May 1683 and took office on 18 April 1684.
Coats of arms

The work of the distinguished genealogist the Viscount of Sanches de Baena, published in 1872 under the title *Archivo Heraldico Genealogico*, contains summary accounts of several thousand royal warrants (*alvarás*) by which many individuals were granted the right to bear a coat of arms. Each account gives the date of the grant, some genealogical details of the recipient and a brief description of the coat of arms itself. For a number of people who were natives of this island or resident here, the work records many warrants granting them the privilege of a coat of arms. We shall give only their names and the dates of the favours granted, leaving out the remaining information so as not to make this article excessively long. Those interested may consult the extracts of the warrants in the work cited. The individuals mentioned there are as follows:

Aires de Ornelas, royal decree (*alvará*) of 1613; Aires Fernandes de Lordelo, royal decree of 1514; António Alberto de Andrade Perdigão, royal decree of 15 June 1790; António Doria Teixeira, 13 November 1788; António de Espíndola, a Genoese, son of Micer Cliam de Espíndola, 1513; António de Espíndola, son of Leonardo de Espíndola, 27 February 1535; António Fernandes Correia Jervis de Atouguia, 30 September 1780 and 5 May 1781; António João de Freitas de Carvalho Drumond, 20 October 1756; António Leme, 12 November 1471; António Manuel Teixeira Lomelino de Vasconcelos Caiado, 3 August 1796; António Teixeira de Vasconcelos, 17 November 1779; Baltasar Gonçalves Pereira de Drumond, 12 March 1538; Bernardino Henriques de Ornelas Vasconcelos, 29 October 1790; Brás Luís de Freitas Drumond de Aragão, 10 February 1751; Brás de Espíndola, 27 January 1572; Diogo Pires de Drumond, 19 March 1538; Estêvão de Bettencourt Perestrelo, 18 July 1734; Fernando Dias, 17 April 1528; Francisco Álvares Camelo, 8 October 1756; Francisco Homem, 23 April 1535; Francisco João Escórcio Drumond Moniz e Meneses da Câmara, 12 November 1778; Francisco João Moniz Barreto Cabral de Ornelas, 5 June 1780; Gaspar Berenguer César Bettencourt, 23 April and 8 July 1768; Gaspar Homem, 29 April 1535; João António Vasques de Araújo Neto, 5 July 1780; João Esmeraldo, 16 May 1520; João Fernandes do Arco, 28 February 1485; Dr João Francisco de Oliveira Álvares, 26 July 1790; João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos, 4 July 1460; João Gualberto Pinto, 11 July 1825; João Lombardo, 1503; Joaquim Pedro de Castelo Branco, 15 June 1857; José de Freitas Teixeira Espínola Castel-Branco, 3 April 1807; José João Cardoso de Vasconcelos, 29 July 1772; José Leão Drumond de Vasconcelos, 18 July 1770; Leandro Dias de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 27 July 1801; Lopo Machado, 1537; Lucano de Espínola, 1513; Luís Doria Veloso, 22 November 1547; Manuel Afonso Ferreira de Drumond, 2 August 1536; Manuel de Couto Cardoso, 12 June 1561; Manuel Mendes Pereira, 18 March 1538; Manuel Vogado, 21 February 1538; Miguel de Carvalho, 18 January 1544; Nicolau de Barros, 3 July 1563; Pedro Pacheco, 22 May 1535; Pedro Vaz Borges, 30 March 1556; Sebastião Coelho, 22 May 1540; Simão Acioli, 27 October 1529; Valentim de Freitas Leal, 15 November 1852.
Bravos do Mindelo (the Heroes of Mindelo)

Many Madeirans fought for the cause of liberty in the long and bloody civil war that ended with the Convention of Évora Monte, signed on 26 May 1834. Of these worthy men, many of whom were part of the expedition of 7,500 men with which Dom Pedro landed on the beaches of Mindelo on 8 July 1832, only the following names have come down to us: Dom Jorge da Câmara Leme (see that entry). He rose to the rank of lieutenant and died in Funchal on 8 July 1889.
Henrique João Fernandes. He was a native of Machico and was killed in the action of 25 July 1833 on the Porto lines, while on campaign.
Cristóvão Lomelino de Carvalho. He was a native of Machico and was killed in the action of 5 September 1833 on the Lisbon lines.

José António de Almada (see that entry). He was made a knight of the Order of the Tower and Sword for distinguishing himself at the battle of Asseiceira, in which he was wounded. He was a native of Machico and died in Funchal on 2 May 1885.
Cândido de Freitas Cabeça. He distinguished himself in many engagements and died, at no great age, in Funchal, his native town.

Francisco de Freitas Broegas. He won renown for his bravery in many engagements, but died poor in the city of Funchal, where he worked as a bailiff (*oficial de diligências*). Januário dos Ramos. After returning from Portugal, he was a customs house guard and an employee of the Municipal Slaughterhouse (*Matadouro Municipal*). He died around 1888.

Tertuliano Toribio de Freitas. He was condemned by the special judicial commission (alçada) that came to Madeira in 1828, and later rendered good service in the campaigns for liberty. He nevertheless died poor, the victim of most ungrateful neglect.
Manuel (?) Camacho. He appears to have been a native of Santo António, and died in that parish (*freguesia*) around 1880.
Luís Vicente da Silva. He was a customs house guard and died around 1880.
Atanásio Herculano Nunes. He was an employee of the Funchal customs house (*Alfândega do Funchal*) and died in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) in September 1887.

António Xavier da Costa. He was also a customs house employee, and died around 1879. Nicolau Anastácio de Bettencourt (see that entry). He was civil governor in Angra, Ponta Delgada, Portalegre and Aveiro, and died on 7 March 1874 in Angra, where he had lived for most of his life.

Jacinto Augusto Camacho (see that entry). He rose to the rank of brigadier general and, while a colonel, was acting commander of the Military Division (*Divisão Militar*, a territorial army command) of Madeira. He died in Porto on 7 June 1885. José Camacho. He was killed on the Lisbon lines.
Roberto Joaquim Cuibém. He fled to England and went on from there to the Azores. He attained the highest rank in the army, and died in Funchal around 1870.

Luís Albino Gonçalves. He reached the rank of colonel surgeon in the army without any formal medical training, and rendered good service during the cholera epidemic of 1856. He died in Funchal in March 1882.
Joaquim António de Carvalho. He commanded the corps of auxiliary artillerymen of Madeira.

Joaquim Pedro Castelo Branco. He later became harbour master of Funchal, rising to the rank of rear admiral. He died on 17 June 1884, and we believe that his only service to the cause of liberty was as a naval officer.
João Correia. He later became a second lieutenant in the 5th Infantry Regiment (*Infantaria n.º 5*).
José Bettencourt de Abreu. He reached the rank of second lieutenant in the Liberating Army.
António José de Meneses. He reached the rank of cavalry major.
António Teixeira Dória. He served only as a naval officer.
António Aluísio Jérvis de Atouguia (see Atouguia), later Viscount of Atouguia. He rose to the rank of brevet brigadier of engineers and died in Lisbon on 17 May 1861.
Francisco Venâncio de Mendonça. He held the post of clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*) of Machico and died in Funchal in 1856.
