Bertoldo Francisco Gomes. He later became a lieutenant of artillery in Funchal and died in May 1855. Paulo Manuel Ferreira Ferro. He was a native of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) and died in Funchal at the end of 1894.
Francisco Correia Herédia (see that entry). He died in Lisbon in 1880.
Francisco Alexandrino da Costa Lira. He reached the rank of brigade sergeant and later became a wealthy landowner. He died in Funchal on 21 January 1877, aged 72.
Júlio Berenguer. He died in Funchal after 1880.

José de Freitas Teixeira Espínola de Castelo Branco. He reached the rank of field marshal. Francisco António Rodrigues da Silva. He fought at the battle of Asseiceira and in many other engagements, and was made a knight of the Order of the Tower and Sword. He held the post (*lugar*) of bailiff (*oficial de diligências*) of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office), and on 29 January 1839 he was appointed keeper of the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery. João de Azevedo. He was a native of Seixal (‘pebble shore’) and served aboard the war brig *Vinte e três de Julho* throughout the siege of Porto, taking part in the action off Cape St Vincent. He was awarded the insignia of the Tower and Sword and, after his discharge from military service, held the post of keeper of the União market and of the Praça Académica.
Sebastião de Abreu. He was a customs guard and died on 15 September 1855.

António Francisco da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, holder of the entail (*morgado*), who left Madeira for England and from there went to the island of Terceira, where he joined the expedition commanded by Dom Pedro. He died in Porto at no great age and was the father of the Count of Canavial.

Of the thirty-four Liberals whose names are given above, we believe that only the first seventeen or eighteen took part in the expedition of 7,500 brave men with which Dom Pedro landed on the beaches of Mindelo on 8 July 1832. As for the rest, we have no proof that they joined that expedition, although we know that they too were devoted soldiers of liberty, for which they fought throughout the whole campaign or a large part of it. About a hundred Madeirans landed with Dom Pedro in Portugal, and many of them, perhaps most, lost their lives on the battlefield.

On 4 April 1832 the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) was occupied by a force of 60 men under the command of Captain Bento José de Oliveira, which had come from the Azores in the war brig *Conde de Vila Flôr* and the schooner *Terceira*. On the 7th the frigate *D. Maria II* put in at the same island, carrying on board Admiral George Rose Sartorius, General Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, the dean of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), Januário Vicente Camacho, and other Constitutionalists.

The occupation lasted until 25 May, when the force embarked for the Azores, accompanied by 104 volunteers who had fled from Madeira to Porto Santo in order to join the troops that Dom Pedro was organising to fight the harsh tyranny of Miguel I.

The annals of the Municipality of Machico record that these volunteers included José de Almada, Lomelino de Carvalho, Henrique Fernandes and Venâncio de Mendonça. It may also be presumed that the Madeirans Cândido Cabeça, Broegas, Ramos, Toríbio de Freitas, J. and M. Camacho, Luís V. da Silva, Atanásio Nunes and Xavier da Costa belonged to this group of Liberals, although the newspapers and official documents we have consulted give no information on the matter.
Bredos
This name is given to several species of the genus *Amarantus*, some wild and others naturalised on the island of Madeira.
Brioso (Dom Estêvão)

Dom Estêvão Brioso, or Dom Estêvão Brioso de Figueiredo, as we also find his name written, was the 121st bishop of Funchal, in the period from 1685 to 1689. He was born in the city of Évora, the son of Manuel Martins and Catarina de Figueiredo. He was a secular priest and a graduate in canon law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He was serving as vicar general of the archdiocese of Lisbon when the diocese of Pernambuco was created in 1676; he was presented as its bishop and took possession in 1678. The difficulties he struggled with in his bishopric in enforcing ecclesiastical discipline forced him to give up the office, and a few years later he returned to mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*). In 1684 he was appointed bishop of Funchal, assuming the government of the diocese in April 1685. Four years later, for reasons of health, he had to leave for the capital, where he died on 20 May 1689. He was buried in the church of the Colégio de São Patrício (St Patrick's College). We know of no facts or circumstances that marked his time in the diocese of Funchal.
Bryozoans

The bryozoans of Madeira studied to date are all of marine origin, and the following naturalists have worked on them: Professor G. Busk, the Revd Thomas Hincks, Artur W. Waters, James Yate Johnson and, recently, Dr Alfred Merle Norman. The last of these lists in his work 130 species from Madeira, Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*), of which 7 are new to science and 39 had not previously been found in the waters of this archipelago.
Briqueira

A fishing rig consisting of two slender quince rods, joined at their thicker ends and carrying at their thinner ends one or two lines one *braça* (fathom, about 2.2 m) long, to which the hooks are attached. At the point where the two rods meet there is a loop or eye, to which the line holding the rig is tied; the rig is sunk by a weight fastened to the rods just below the loop. This weight may be a piece of lead, in which case it is called a lead sinker (*chumbada*); or it may be a simple rounded stone, and then it is called a stone sinker (*pandulho*). On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) the quince rods are sometimes replaced by tamarisk stems. This rig is generally used for the fine fish that live on rocky bottoms, such as groupers, pargos, *requemes*, alfonsinos, etc.
Brisa

Madeirans give the name *brisa* to the prevailing north-east wind that blows mainly during the summer. Because of the direction it follows, this wind is generally not felt beyond Ponta da Oliveira (‘olive-tree point’).
See Embate.
Brito (family)

The surname Brito, or Brito de Oliveira, was introduced to this island by Pedro de Brito de Oliveira Pestana, who settled in Madeira towards the end of the third quarter of the 15th century with his brother João Mendo or Mendes de Brito. Both founded entails (*instituições vinculares*). According to Henriques de Noronha, the arms of this family are: on a field gules nine lozenges in three pales, each charged with a lion purpure; and as crest, a lion of the arms with lozenges argent.
Brito (Dom João Joaquim Bernardino de)

He was the 201st bishop of Funchal, and died before taking up the government of his diocese in person. He was confirmed by the Holy See on 28 August 1819 and took possession of the office by proxy on 14 May 1820. He then entrusted the government of the bishopric to Dr João Manuel da Costa e Andrade, a canon of our Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and died shortly afterwards in Lisbon on 26 July 1820.
Brito e Nobrega (Ciriaco)

He was born in Funchal on 16 March 1856 and is one of the longest-serving Madeiran journalists, being at present (1923) an editor of the *Diário de Noticias*. In 1875 he translated and published the novel *Jorge* by F. Arnault, and he is the author of *A visita de S. S. Magestades os Reis de Portugal ao arquipelago madeirense* (Funchal, 1901) and of *o Perdão do Marido* (Funchal, 1901). In collaboration with Oscar Leal he wrote *um Marinheiro do Século XV* (Funchal, 1898). Ciriaco de Brito e Nobrega was a knight of the Order of St James and 11th officer of the Finance Department of the District of Funchal (*Repartição da Fazenda do Distrito do Funchal*).
Brito (João de)
His appointment as governor and captain-general of Madeira is dated 2 February 1680, and he took up the post on 10 April of that year.
Brito Rebelo (General Jacinto Inácio de)

). He is a native of São Miguel and wrote, among other works, the following: *Casa dos Esmeraldos na ilha da Madeira* (*Ocidente*, vol. II, no. 75); *D. Ayres de Ornelas e Vasconcelos* (ibid., vol. III, p. 3); and *The Discovery of Madeira*, which serves as the introduction to Dr Alberto Figueira Jardim’s work entitled *Madeira* (Lisbon, 1914).

This last work contains some curious information on certain points of our history. Speaking of the origin of the name Machico, given to a place on the east coast of Madeira, Mr Brito Rebêlo says: In 1894, on the occasion of the 5th centenary of the birth of Prince Henry the Navigator, I discovered the name of a sailor called Machico, captain of the ship of Infante Ferdinand, to whom this king gave some houses... The sailor Machico, or one of his descendants, happened to give his name to that part of Madeira (Machico), and this name gave rise to a thousand conjectures, all equally unfounded. With the disclosure of the fact I have just mentioned, it was established that Machico was the name of a sailor, and so all the disputes over the name ceased, after having given rise to numerous dissertations and lectures in foreign geographical societies and in the Lisbon Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*).

We do not know whether Machico was the first to discover or to land at that landing place. . . but what we can establish is that Machico was the owner of a ship that lay at anchor in Lisbon and was moored to the city walls when King Henry II of Castile besieged that city. He must have made several voyages to various parts of the world, for ships are made to sail, and Machico, the owner of the ship, was a seaman of standing.

Mr Brito Rebelo supposes that Tristão Vaz Teixeira was a knight of foreign origin, perhaps of nobler birth than Zarco. When he turns to Christopher Columbus, he says that Columbus’s stay in Madeira is highly questionable, above all if we take it to have lasted a long time.

Mr Rebelo further declares that what Frutuoso relates on p. 166 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) about the punishment inflicted on Tristão Barradas, a man held to be a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility), is false. He states that this man was called Diogo, not Tristão, and that he was not shackled with a fetter and set to grind in a flour mill, but seized by the hands and mutilated on the orders of Tristão Vaz, for having abused the hospitality Tristão Vaz had shown him. Tristão Vaz was not deported to the island of Príncipe, but was simply obliged to pay 40,000 réis, a very considerable sum for the period, for the barbarous punishment inflicted on Barradas.
Britten (James)
Works: *R. Brown's List of Madeira Plants* (*Journ. of Bot. British and Foreign*, XLII, 1904.
Our Lady of Brotas (chapels)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Quinta das Freiras (‘nuns’ estate’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, on the right bank of the stream of the same name, stands the chapel known as Nossa Senhora das Brotas. In trying to trace the origin of this name, which strikes us as so strange, we have been able, despite our best efforts, to arrive only at mere presumptions and conjectures, which may perhaps be very far from the truth. We first supposed that the name came not from the dedication or patron saint of the chapel but from the place where it had been built. Since there is a medicinal herb of that name, it is possible that the plant grew there and gave its name to the spot and later to the chapel. We then conjectured that, since the province of the Alentejo has a parish called Brotas, with a notable shrine dedicated to Nossa Senhora das Brotas, the chapel might perhaps have been given that name for reasons now unknown. Both hypotheses hold true in various parts of this island. It was common for the first colonists, who came from Portugal, to give the names of their home districts or favourite spots to many of the places where they settled here or held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation).

In support of the first hypothesis, we must mention that in former times, and still at present, Our Lady of Brotas has been venerated under the dedication of Our Lady of Light (*Nossa Senhora da Luz*). This leads us to presume that the name refers to the place and not to the patron saint of the chapel.

This chapel was founded in 1678 by Manuel Martins Brandão, and the royal decree (*alvará*) licensing it to be opened for worship dates from July of that year. It was built on the *quinta* (country estate) that its founder owned there; of it there remain only the portico, almost all of the façade and part of the side walls. Tradition records that the waters of the stream, diverted from their natural course by the violence of the current, destroyed a considerable part of the churchyard, leaving the building in danger of imminent ruin.

It was the seat of an entail (*morgado*), which seems to us to have been founded by the said Manuel Martins Brandão. In 1736 the administrator of this entailed estate was the holder of the entail Pedro José de Faria Bettencourt.
Brown (A. Samler)
Works: *Madeira, Canary Islands and Açores, a pratical and complete guide for the use of tourists and invalids*, London).

This guide, one of the most accomplished ever published, contains a wealth of useful information not only on the history, geology, climate, etc. of the main islands of the archipelagos of Madeira, the Canary Islands and the Azores, but also on the places in those islands most worth visiting by foreigners. The 100th edition, published in 1910, contains 20 maps and plans and a greater abundance of useful information than the earlier editions.
Only from 1901 onwards did Mr Samler Brown begin to deal with the islands of the Azores, the work having first appeared in 1889 under the following title: *Madeira and Canary Islands, etc.* (London).
Brown (Robert)

A distinguished English botanist, born in Montrose in 1773 and died in London in 1858. He was in Madeira from 4 to 7 August 1802 and later compiled a list of Madeiran plants, which was included in the work by Von Buch entitled *Physicalische Beschreibung der Canarischen Inseln* (Berlin, 1825). This list is based chiefly on the herbaria and manuscripts of Francis Masson, Joseph Banks and Dr Daniel Solander, for Robert Brown collected few plants during his short stay on this island.
Brown (T. Kenworthy)
Works: *The Madeira Chaplaincy* (London, 1848).
Bruce (James)

A celebrated English traveller, born in 1730 and died in 1794. He deals with the discovery of the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) in the work that was translated into French by J. H. Castera under the following title: *Voyage aux sources du Nil en Nubie et en Abyssinie pendant les annés de 1768, 1769, 1770, 1771 et 1772* (London, 1791).
Brucker (M. Raynold)
He wrote an article in the *Musée des Familles* for the year 1834 with the following title: *La Chapelle des Crânes dans l'Ile de Madère*.
Brum do Canto (Dr Salvador Manuel)

Deputy for Madeira in the legislative session of 1906 to 1907. As counsel in lawsuits concerning this island he published: *Acção de processo cível ordinário. Autores Anthero da Costa Lyra e mulher e réus A Companhia de Credito Predial e outros*, 1905, and *Acção de processo cível ordinário. Autores Anthero da Costa Lyra e mulher e reus a Companhia de Credito Predial Português e outros*, 1907. He died in Lisbon on 3 November 1918, aged 33. He was the son of the high court judge (*desembargador*) Dr Manuel Inácio Brum do Canto and the great-grandson of Dr Luís Henriques, the first director of our Medical School. He had been born in the Azores.
Buarcos
The family surname Buarcos, which through corruption was also pronounced Barcos, originates here with António Buarcos, one of the first settlers of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Buch (Leopold von)

A learned German geologist and botanist, born in Stolp, in the Uckermark, on 25 April 1774 and died in Berlin on 4 March 1853. He visited Madeira in 1811 in the company of the Norwegian botanist Chetien Smith; the two naturalists landed in Funchal on 26 April and left for the Canary Islands on the 2nd of the following month.

The observations made by Buch and Smith on our island were recorded in the *Narrative of an Expedition to explore the River Zaire... in 1816, under the direction of Captain J. K Tuckey* (London, 1818).

The work entitled *Verzeichniss der auf Madeira wildwachsenden Pflanzen*, which almost all botanists attribute to Leopold von Buch because it was included in the work he published in 1825 under the title *Physicalische Beschreibung der Canarischen Inseln*, is by Robert Brown, not by von Buch.
Bucho encostado

The ailment known in Madeira by this name seems to be due to a torsion or a spasmodic contraction of the intestine. Folk healers usually treat it by repeatedly rubbing the belly with a hand smeared with olive oil, accompanying the rubbing with the following words, which must be said nine times: ‘as the myrtle opened and closed again, so this is true. May Our Lord be pleased to put this *bucho*, this belly, this *coelheira* back in its place.’ After a short rest, the healer says 9 more times: ‘little *coelheira*, go to your place; *bucho*, go to your place.’ The patient lies on his back while being rubbed. The healer ends the treatment by pouring olive oil or lard on two cabbage leaves warmed by the fire, placing one on the patient’s belly and the other on the opposite side, usually a little above the coccyx. If on the day after the treatment the leaves are dry, the *bucho* was ‘encostado’ (displaced); if they are green or wilted, the *bucho* was in its right place, and the patient must then turn to other means to seek relief from his sufferings.

What is ridiculous in the treatment we have described are the words the healer utters, apparently in order to force the *bucho* back into its place. As for the rubbing or massage, we dare not dispute its effectiveness, both because numerous cases of cure obtained by it are cited and because medicine also considers it useful in ailments arising from the causes we indicated above.
Thorn-apple (*Datura stramonium*)

A plant of the family Solanaceae, with funnel-shaped blue or white corollas and capsules covered in numerous prickles. It grows semi-wild in many parts of Funchal and is highly poisonous if swallowed in a large dose. Internally, it must be used with great caution; externally it can be used in baths to combat rheumatic pain. The thorn-apple contains an alkaloid called daturine.
Bougainvillea (*Bougainvillea spectabilis*)

A woody plant native to South America, much used in Madeira to cover walls, belvederes, galleries, etc. The branches are thorny and the flowers are surrounded by large bracts, usually pink or pinkish violet. It belongs to the family Nyctaginaceae.
Bugio

Bugio is one of the three Desertas (‘deserted islands’) and one of the five islands that make up the Madeira archipelago. According to the *Dic. Univ. Port.* II, its name derives from its resemblance to the monkey known by that name. It is five miles, or a little over nine kilometres, long and half a mile, or 926 metres, across at its widest point. To the south it ends at Ponta da Agulha (‘needle point’), one of the extreme points of the archipelago. The island is made up of high rocks and is almost inaccessible, but it has good pasture. The highest peak on Bugio stands 411 metres above sea level.

Bugio is uncultivated and has neither water nor any house. It produces poppies, clover, horehound and other plants, some of them good for fodder. On the top of the island, near its southern end, some fossil shells are found, and on the sea cliffs grows the extremely rare *Chrysanthemum haematomma*, a distinctive member of the daisy family, remarkable for its lovely flower heads, with purplish-black disc florets and white or pink ray florets.

The records of the land registry (*Conservatória*) of the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal show that on 3 October 1867 Bugio belonged to João de Vasconcelos de Sousa Câmara Caminha Faro e Veiga, Marquis of Castelo Melhor. On his death it was bought at auction by Alexandre Fernandes Camacho Júnior. Today it belongs to Carlos Cossart and Henrique Hinton, who bought it, together with the other two Desertas, on 24 November 1894, when the property of the said Alexandre Camacho was put up for auction.
Bugio belongs to the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé and has a small natural landing place on the west side, called the Alagoa (‘the pond’).
Bulhão Pato

The well-known writer and poet Bulhão Pato was a close friend of the 2nd Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), and in his company spent several seasons on this island. He refers to this in some of his books with the most vivid and fond recollection. In the book *Sob os Ciprestes* and in the three volumes of his *Memórias* he writes about a number of Madeiran people and things. They contain extensive references to the Count of Carvalhal, Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, the Viscountess of Nogueiras, Jaime Moniz, Luís da Costa Pereira and others. In cantos VI and VII of his poem *Paquita*, Bulhão Pato gives a fine poetic description of Madeira. Bulhão Pato stayed on this island from 7 August 1850 to 6 March 1851.
Bulwer (Revd James)
In 1827 he published twenty-six superb engravings of various places on the island of Madeira.
Bunbury (Charles J. F.)

English botanist and palaeontologist who studied the Madeiran flora and the fossil plants of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge in 1853. Works: *Remarks on the Botany of Madeira and Teneriffe* (*Journ. of the Proceed. of the Linn. Soc.*, 1856); and *On Some Vegetable Remains from Madeira* (*Geological Journ.*, 1859).
Buraco (point)
A small headland on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Seixal (‘pebble shore’).
Burgess (Dr)

He wrote an article in the *Association Medical Journal* in which, without ever having visited Madeira, he sought to deny the effectiveness of the island’s climate in treating lung diseases. James Mackenzie Bloxam replied to this article in two pamphlets, written as letters addressed to Dr Lund.
Busk (George)

Professor and naturalist who studied the polyzoans of Madeira, basing his work on material supplied to him from here by James Yate Johnson. These studies, the earliest known on this branch of Madeira’s natural history, list 45 species in all and were published under the following titles: *Zoophytology* (*Quart. Journ. Micros Sc.* VI 1858); *On Some Madeiran Polyzoa* (*Ibid.*, VI and VII, 1858 and 1859); and *Catalogue of the Polyzoa collected by J. Y. Johnson, Esq. at Madeira, in the years 1859 and 1860* (*Ibid.*, VIII and IX, 1860 and 1861).
See Bryozoans.
Box (Buxus sempervirens)

A European shrub of the family Buxaceae, widely cultivated in Madeira. A decoction of the roots, their bark and the leaves is recommended for rheumatism. Box wood is prized by turners for its great hardness.
Buxo da Rocha

Madeirans give this name to *Catha dryandri*, a shrub of the family Celastraceae, and to *Chamaemeles coriacea*, a shrub of the family Rosaceae. The first is found at São Gonçalo, at Seixal (‘pebble shore’), etc.; the second near the Câmara Pestana Asylum (*Manicómio Câmara Pestana*), at Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’), etc.
Búzia (Mora mediterranea)

A gadoid fish often caught in the waters off Madeira on hook lines. Apart from the black scabbardfish, it is, among the fine species, the one fished at the greatest depth. It is also called, though incorrectly, *abrótea do alto* (‘deep-sea forkbeard’, a local name for the common mora), and sometimes *robalo branco*.
Búzio

The shell of a gastropod mollusc of the genus *Triton*, often caught on shallow bottoms with drag nets. It is the largest of the univalve shells of our seas. Coastal boatmen use it as a sounding horn to announce the departure or arrival of boats, the receiving of cargo, etc. Peasants also use it on certain occasions to call their companions to revolt. In a general sense, the word is used for any shell of the genus *Triton*, however small, and also for any univalve whose shape resembles that genus.

On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) small *búzios* of the genera *Columbella*, *Murex* and *Ranella* are found, *Columbella rustica* being extremely abundant on the beach. On Madeira *Purpura hoemmastoma*, 4 to 5 centimetres long, *Mitra cornicula*, *Murex corallinus*, *Bittium reticulatum*, *Rissoa violacea*, *Mitra zebrina* and *Cypraea spurca* are not rare.
Byron (Commodore John)

He was in Madeira from 13 to 19 July 1764, in command of the British warship *Dolphin*, which was accompanied by the *Tamar*, commanded by Captain Mouat. Byron was well received by the governor and merely took on some provisions here. The aim of the expedition was to discover new lands and above all to explore the Atlantic Ocean, in the area between the Cape of Good Hope and the Strait of Magellan.
Bottle gourd (Lagenaria vulgaris)

A cucurbit native to the tropics and widely cultivated in Madeira. Its fruits are used to make soup, and once fully ripe and dried they can be used to hold liquids, since in that state it is easy to empty them of their pulp and seeds. The small gourd (var. *pusilla*), filled with wine or spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), was once the constant companion of our country folk on their outings and pilgrimages.
Caballero di Gracia (El)
Single issue of a newspaper, published on 5 March 1889.
Cabeço da Roseira
A village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) and mountain elevation in the uplands of the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’).
Cabedo (João Octávio da Costa)

He was a native of Funchal and contributed to *Direito*, a former Funchal newspaper, to *Povo de Aveiro* and to *Intransigente*, eventually joining the editorial staff of the last of these. He left it on being appointed municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Moita. Savagely attacked with an axe on 12 January 1912, during a strike that had broken out in that town, he died in St Joseph's Hospital (*Hospital de São José*), in Lisbon, on the 4th of the following month, aged only 26.
Cabeleira (Lotus macranthus)
A legume found at Cabo Garajau (‘tern cape’) and on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
On the latter island the name *cabeleira de coquinho* is given to *Lotus loweanus*, a plant not found on Madeira.
Cathedral chapter

By the bull (papal bull) *Pro excellenti praeeminentia* of 12 June 1514, Leo X created the diocese of Funchal and, together with it, the cathedral chapter of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*). By the express wording of that papal document, the chapter consisted of the dignities of Dean, Archdeacon, Precentor and Chief Treasurer, together with twelve prebendary canons. Only later was the dignity of Schoolmaster (mestre-escola, dignitary of the chapter) created, and four half-prebend canonries were also created afterwards, so that the Funchal chapter came to number twenty-one councillors (capitulares). Later still, the office of doctoral or theological canon was created, filled from one of the twelve canonries already in existence. The Funchal chapter remained so constituted until a concordat concluded between the Holy See and the Portuguese government, some decades ago, reduced it to twelve members, including three dignities – a number undoubtedly sufficient for the full discharge of all the duties entrusted to this capitular body.

The bull in question expressly refers to Nuno Cão (see that entry), naming him as the priest who was to be invested with the office of dean. It also orders that, among the fifteen beneficiaries of the collegiate church existing in the parish (*freguesia*) that later took the name of Sé, the three most senior should be appointed to the other three dignities, and the remaining twelve should fill the places of the twelve canonries then created.

The office of dean was, and still is today, the highest dignity of the cathedral chapter. Under a law of our country that remained in force until the proclamation of the Republic, it could be filled only by a cleric holding a degree in law or theology. Nuno Cão was the first to hold this office here, followed by Filipe Rebelo and then by Dr António da Costa. The last priests to occupy the deanery (office of dean of the cathedral chapter) at Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) were, in order, António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos and João Joaquim Pinto (see those entries). The office originally carried a salary of 7,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year, later 15,000 *réis*, rising to 25,000 *réis* in 1527 and to 45,000 *réis* in 1563. Latterly it carried an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of 772,680 *réis*. The first two priests to serve as dean were responsible for parish duties; on the death of the second, the two posts of curate of the Cathedral were created, and the dean was thereby relieved of pastoral ministry.

As already stated, the dignities of the Funchal Chapter were, besides the dean, those of archdeacon, precentor and schoolmaster, latterly reduced to the first three. The dignities of archdeacon and precentor have not been filled for many years; the last archdeacon was Canon José Joaquim de Sá, who died around 1869.
To the twelve canonries of the Chapter’s original constitution, two half-prebend canonries were added in 1536 and another two in 1577.

Among the clergy who were members of the Funchal Chapter were Jerónimo Dias Leite, António Veloso de Lira, Pedro Correia Barbosa, João Francisco Lopes Rocha, Gregório Nanzianzeno de Medina e Vasconcelos, António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, Alfredo César de Oliveira and António Aires Pacheco (see those entries).
Cabo

A picturesque inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), where there is a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Good Death (*Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte*), built by Custódio Nunes da Costa in the year 1666.
Cabo do Calhau
A former locality (*sítio*) beside the chapel of St Elmo (*Corpo Santo*), up to which the city of Funchal extended at the end of the 16th century.
Submarine cable

It was on 26 September 1874 that this archipelago was at last endowed with a most important and long-desired improvement: its connection to mainland Portugal by electric telegraph. An English company, under a contract concluded with our government, laid the cable and set up the telegraph installations, with the right to operate them for a period of 99 years at no cost whatsoever to the Portuguese state. The contract was signed on 12 November 1872 between the Portuguese government and Mr Jules Despecher, representative of the Mainteneuse and Falmouth and Malte companies. The cable was to be landed near the mouth of the Tagus, in the city of Funchal and on one of the islands of Cape Verde, and was to begin operating before 30 September 1873.

On 22 August 1874 the English steamer *Seine* left Lisbon, charged with laying across the ocean the submarine cable that was to link this island to the European continent. After 11 days at sea spent laying the cable, it broke some 100 miles from Madeira. The steamer then headed for Funchal to land some passengers and take on coal and provisions, arriving in our harbour on 3 September. After the necessary delay, the *Seine* sailed out to resume the interrupted work, returning to Funchal a few days later and at once landing the cable ashore.

On 24 September a few private telegrams were exchanged with the capital, but the public service began on the 26th, when the first telegraphic dispatch was sent to King Luís I. The first telegram received in this city was the monarch’s message to the civil governor of the district, congratulating him on the completion of so important an improvement.
That day saw various celebrations, with brilliant illuminations at the entrance to the city and in the former Praça da Constituição, music, fireworks, etc.
Capes

There are two capes on Madeira: Cabo Garajau (‘tern cape’) and Cabo Girão. The first juts some 120 metres out into the sea; the second projects very little and has at its base a shelf, or erosion platform, on which one can walk at low tide.

Cabo Girão, so called because it was the point at which the boats ended their rotation (giro) on the first voyage of reconnaissance around the island, is one of the highest sea cliffs in the world. Cabo Garajau, which takes its name from the great number of common terns (*garajau*) (*Sterna hirundo*) that the first explorers found there, is much lower, its crest standing 126 metres above sea level.

At Cabo Girão numerous dykes cut through the tuffs, scoriae and lavas, and at Cabo Garajau there is a quite remarkable basalt dyke; numerous basalt inclusions can also be seen in the yellow tuff of the ground.
The land near the beach to the west of Garajau, and the ravines and heights to the east of Cabo Girão, are rich in botanical species, some of which are not found anywhere else on the island.
Caboz
Common name for several Madeiran fishes of the families Blenniida and Gobiida.
Cabra (fish)

Common name of two species of Madeiran fish of the family Tríglida: *Trigla lineata* and *T. pini*. Neither is common. The few specimens brought to market are almost always caught in trawl nets. The flesh is white, but not among the most delicate.
See Caranguejo Judeu.
Cabral

One of the four noblemen whom Dom Afonso sent to Madeira to marry the daughters of the discoverer was Diogo Cabral, son of Fernão Álvares Cabral, chief health officer (*guarda-mor*) of Prince Henry the Navigator. He was one of the first settlers of this island, and here he married Brites Gonçalves da Câmara, the second daughter of João Gonçalves Zarco. Diogo Cabral had the chapel of Our Lady of the Star (*Nossa Senhora da Estrela*) built at Calheta (‘small cove’); it had been designed by Zarco, who had earnestly urged its construction on his children. Cabral held extensive lands there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), granted to him by his father-in-law. He died on 15 December 1486 and lies buried in the chapel he built. He was the grandfather of Tristão Vaz da Veiga. He was the first on this island to bear the surname Cabral.
Arms of the Cabrals: two goats passant, adorned with purple and black; crest: one of the goats of the shield.
Cabral (Henrique Read)

He was born in the Azores and for some years was director of the Funchal customs house, taking office in May 1892. He wrote various works, and in this city he published in 1895 a pamphlet entitled *Um Novo Mundo*, 56 pp., and in the same year a novel which he called historical and to which he gave the title *Angela Santa Clara*, 201 pp., a work of pure fiction containing many anachronisms and several historical inaccuracies. Its action takes place in Madeira. Cabralia. A genus of bivalve shells peculiar to Selvagem Grande (‘great wild island’). It was found in a fossil-bearing layer of the Miocene Tertiary.

The species *Cabralia Schmitzii* recalls the names of the late João Cabral de Noronha, former owner of the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*), and of the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz, a distinguished ornithologist who for many years taught at the Funchal seminary.
Cabreira
See Azeda.
Capstan

The records of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) contain three deeds of emphyteutic lease (*aforamento*, perpetual lease for an annual quit-rent) of land beside the sea for the building of capstans (*cabrestante*): the first dates from 1600, the second from 1635 and the last from 1642. The first capstan in Funchal belonged to Manuel Cabral, the second to the Castilian Lopo Pardo de Luna and the third to Bartolomeu Dias.

In February 1848 the *Correio da Madeira* (‘Madeira Courier’) published the following report on the capstan on the city beach: ‘The establishment responsible for landing export and import goods on this island, known as the administration of the Funchal Capstan, was founded more than two centuries ago and carried out its functions as a privileged royal concession (patronado), by royal order, until 1807. At that time General Beresford, then governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this island, heeding the representations made to him by the Portuguese and foreign merchants of this stronghold, abolished the said Patronado, ordering that the ownership and management of that establishment should pass into the possession and administration of merchants, who bought all the Proprietor’s boats and equipment. By a royal notice dated Rio de Janeiro, 25 July 1808, His Royal Highness the Prince Regent ordered that the establishment for the business of the pebble beach (calhau), as General Beresford had shaped it, should be provisionally maintained until His Royal Highness decided what he judged most suitable to his royal service and to the public. The capstan establishment of the Calhau has thus continued from 1808 until now, with no other contrary provision by the government of which the petitioners are aware.’

The capstan referred to by the *Correio da Madeira* still exists today. It is said, however, that only the representative of one of the former owners takes part in its administration, all the other persons with rights to the ownership of the establishment having ceased to assert those rights, for reasons that are unknown. It is said that in former times, perhaps in 1807 or 1808, shares were issued for the purchase of the capstan, and some of them are still held by a very few people.
Not many years ago there were still three capstans in Funchal, but today only two remain, both run by the managers of the old capstan, which has been greatly improved in recent times.
This information goes no further than the year 1922.
Cabrinha (Davallia canariensis)
A fern of the family Polypodiaceae, very common in Madeira. An infusion of *cabrinhas* is used for skin diseases.
Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) No. 12. See Military garrison.
Cação (Galeus canis)

A cartilaginous fish of the family Carchariidae, somewhat rare in the seas around Madeira. It is usually caught in the coastal zone and, like the great majority of dogfish and sharks, is considered of mediocre quality. On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) it is called *bico doce do baixo*.
The *cação* of the fishermen of Portugal is the shark that in Madeira is given the name *caneja*.
Cacho Roxo

The vernacular name of *Wistaria sinensis*, a leguminous plant native to China that is common in Funchal, where it is used to cover walls, pergolas, etc. It is prized for its large flowers, borne in hanging clusters.
Cacongo (Viscount of)

This titled nobleman was not born in Madeira, but he regards it as his adopted homeland. He is bound to the island by ties of kinship, settled here many years ago and is one of the wealthiest landowners among us. He follows closely every matter that concerns the prosperity of this archipelago, and his shrewd counsel and authoritative opinion have helped to resolve many problems closely bearing on the economy of the district. The Viscount of Cacongo is a devoted protector of those whom fortune has left unprotected, whom he helps generously, and he never refuses his ample contribution to any work of philanthropy and charity organised among us. Among the services he has rendered to this land, his valuable part in founding the Manicómio Câmara Pestana (Câmara Pestana Asylum) and in building a quay in the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial, which bears his name, stands out.

The Viscount of Cacongo became a benefactor of his country through the notable services he rendered in Africa, where he lived for many years. On his work in our province of Angola, we shall transcribe the following passages from volume IX of the *Encyclopedia Portuguesa Illustrada*, by Maximiliano de Lemos:

‘The prestige and great ascendancy he won among the local people, through the kind and just way in which he always treated them, is clearly shown by what happened in 1883, when Cacongo and Massabi were occupied.

‘It was in that year that Rodrigues Leitão, seeing that France intended to take possession of the whole coast from its colony of Gabon to the northern bank of the Zaire, having already occupied Loango and Ponta Negra despite the protests of the commanders of the Portuguese warships, resolved to oppose this plan.

‘To achieve this, he asked the then governor-general of Angola, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Ferreira do Amaral, to order the occupation of Cacongo and Massabi. It was owing to his repeated entreaties that the governor sent the corvette *Rainha de Portugal* to Luanda to carry it out, under the command of the distinguished officer Guilherme de Brito Capelo, then a lieutenant-commander.
‘For the occupation to take place, the Black inhabitants had to request our protectorate, and it was Rodrigues Leitão’s enormous prestige that induced them to do so in the most solemn manner.

‘To him, therefore, is owed the occupation of Cacongo and Massabi and, as a consequence, Portugal’s possession of the enclave of Cabinda, north of the Zaire, which the Congress of Berlin granted us because Cacongo was already Portuguese. ‘For this great service to his country he was awarded the title of Viscount of Cacongo, by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 1 August 1884.

The Viscount of Cacongo was born in 1843 in Ponte da Barca, the son of Manuel António Rodrigues Leitão and Dona Maria Joaquina de Oliveira. He came to Madeira at a very young age with his uncle, João José Rodrigues Leitão, who had a banking house in this city, and it was from here that he set out for West Africa, where he made a great fortune. He died in Funchal on 15 June 1925.
Cadamosto (Luiz)

Luiz Cadamosto (Alvise Cadamosto) was a celebrated Venetian navigator in the service of Portugal. He made two voyages to the western coasts of Africa and wrote an account of them, which is regarded as a valuable source for the history of our maritime discoveries. The *Navegações* of Cadamosto were first published in Italian in 1507, and later in Latin. The Portuguese translation was first published in 1812 in the *colecção de noticias para a historia e geographia...* of the Royal Academy of Sciences (*Academia Real das Ciências*). Pinheiro Chagas discusses the worth and importance of these *Navegações* at length. They matter to the history of Madeira because Cadamosto devotes several pages to this archipelago, and his is the oldest account by any of the many navigators who have written about Madeira. The *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) of 5, 9 and 11 January 1906 reproduced the passages of the *Navegações* in which Cadamosto describes his stay on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). He anchored at the landing place of the latter island on 25 March 1445, and on the 28th of the same month in the bay of Machico. Pinheiro Chagas gives 1455 as the year of the Venetian navigator’s voyage, while Dr Azevedo, in a note to his article ‘Madeira’ in the *Dicc. Port. Univ.* III, adopts the date of 1445 on the basis of arguments that he sets out. Dr Pestana Júnior, in his valuable study on the *Reconhecimento do Arquipelago da Madeira*, places Cadamosto’s voyages in the years 1449 and 1450.
Prison

The old gaol of the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal stood at the southern end of the street now called Rua da Cadeia Velha, in a small house that was sold in 1824 to José António Monteiro for the sum of 3,600,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). As early as 1768 this house was already in a fairly ruinous state, as can be seen from an official letter that the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) Francisco Maria da Mota addressed to Francisco Xavier Furtado on 31 May of that year. Nevertheless, the prisoners were still held there in 1811, for on 15 November of that year the *corregedor* Manuel Caetano de Albuquerque stated that it was urgent to move the gaol to a more spacious and more secure house.

At its session of 30 June 1803 the municipal senate (*Senado da Câmara*, historic title of the Council) took possession of the house on the Largo da Sé (‘cathedral square’), where it had been holding its meetings for some time. The house had belonged to the farmstead (*casal*) of Dona Guiomar Madalena Acciaioly and had been put up for public auction because of debts to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*). Only some years later, certainly after 1813, was the lower part of the house turned into a gaol, while the upper part continued to serve as the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*).

At its session of 20 December 1813 the Council resolved that the gaol building should be paid for with the proceeds of the sale of the house then serving that purpose and that, should this not suffice, the *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) should contribute the remainder of the costs. This resolution could not be carried out, however, because the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties) refused to contribute to these costs, claiming that he was no longer obliged to do so after the abolition of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*).

On 28 July 1827 the *Defensor da Liberdade* stated that the prisoners were extremely badly accommodated in the gaol on the Largo da Sé. It was perhaps to improve their conditions that, after the abolition of the religious orders in Portugal, they were transferred to the building of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). They remained there only until 1836, however, when they returned to the house they had left a short time before, which, we believe, ceased from then on to serve as the town hall.

Although the building on the Largo da Sé now served exclusively as a gaol, this did nothing to improve the conditions of the prisoners who could not pay the gaol fee (*carceragem*). They continued to be shut up in damp ground-floor rooms without air or light.
On 2 July 1841 the Council resolved to move the gaol to the building where the Asylum now stands, but the

Government did not approve this transfer. An identical resolution was passed at the session of 6 February 1845, but the prisoners were never moved, because the Council was dissolved in 1846 and the new councillors (*vereadores*) did not agree with the use that was intended for the house of the Angústias (‘sorrows’).

In an official letter addressed to the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) on 31 March 1847, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, that benevolent civil governor, proposed that the gaol be set up in the former convent of São Francisco, that the town hall move into the house then serving as the gaol, and that the *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) for beggars be transferred to the house of the Angústias. These suggestions were not taken up. Much later, following a petition made on 17 May 1888, the Council obtained the use of the Fortress of the Pico (‘peak’) for 10 years for the provisional installation of the prisons. It never took advantage of this favour from the Government, however, because it lacked the means needed to build a structure fit to serve as the gaol of the judicial district (*comarca*).

Later it was proposed to move the gaol to the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (1897), to the Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation) (1897), to the Fortress of the Pico (1909) and to the Seminary of Bom Despacho (*Seminário do Bom Despacho*) (1910). Obstacles arose to the realisation of all these projects, however, and so the prisoners remained in the house on the Largo da Sé, ‘that terrible focus of infection, that cemetery of living creatures, as Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro called it in 1847.

Only after the closure of St Lazarus’s Hospital (*Hospital de São Lázaro*) on 5 June 1912 could the old project of giving Funchal a gaol in good condition finally be carried out. The Municipal Council resolved that the new establishment should be built on the land occupied by that hospital, and it pressed ahead with this decision so vigorously – towards the end work even went on at night to hasten completion – that on 29 November 1913 the prisoners were transferred to the new building intended for them. On that same day demolition began of the old building on the Largo da Sé, where the gaol of the judicial district had been housed for nearly a century.

It was Dr Fernando Tolentino da Costa, a member and later president of Funchal Municipal Council, who took the greatest interest in the building of the São Lázaro gaol and the demolition of the Largo da Sé building. It was thanks to his efforts and acknowledged zeal that these two improvements were carried out so quickly. The public celebrated the fall of the first stones of the old gaol with a few sprays of rockets, and everyone rejoiced at the disappearance of a building which not only failed to serve the purposes for which it had been intended but also considerably disfigured one of the most central spots in the city.
Cadeia Velha (street)

This is the street that runs directly from Rua Direita (‘straight street’) to the small square (*largo*) of the church of Carmo (Carmelite church); Rua dos Medinas and Rua do Monteiro lead into it. Its name comes from the old city gaol (*cadeia*) that once stood there, at the corner formed by this street and Rua Direita, on the right as one walks from the church of Carmo towards the latter street. In Rua da Cadeia Velha stands the house that belonged to the Oliveira family, whose members included João Francisco de Oliveira, Joaquim de Oliveira Alvares and Benjamim de Oliveira (see those entries), among others. Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara states that it was one of the largest town houses in Funchal, and its construction must date from the beginning of the 18th century.
Coffee shrub (Coffea arabica)

A shrub of the family Rubiaceae, now extinct in Madeira, but still common some 25 years ago in the low-lying region of the south of the island. Madeiran coffee was of excellent quality and rivalled that of Mocha.
Cory’s shearwater (Puffinus kuhli)

A native web-footed bird of the family Procellariidae. It is a seabird that migrates between October and November, returning at the end of February or the beginning of March, and breeds in June. It then lays a single, entirely white egg on the steep coastal cliffs, which is ready to hatch after a month. It is hunted on all the islands, but it is chiefly on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) and the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) that its capture becomes profitable. At present the number of young birds taken each year on the Savage Islands by men from São Gonçalo and Caniço (‘reed’), who go there for that particular purpose, averages 18,000. Once salted, the *cagarra* is brought to Madeira, where it is sold mainly to the poorer classes, who value it highly despite the marked fishy aftertaste and oily character of its flesh. The hunters of the Savage Islands also call it *pardela*, as do the Spaniards of the Canary Islands.
Cagarras (landing place)
To the east-north-east of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) there is a small landing place (*porto*) of this name.
Cahus

This is a family surname (*apelido*) of French origin which, says Dr Pereira Drumond, descends from João Cahus, a native of the city of Rouen, in France, who settled in Funchal around 1580 as a merchant. The surname is now extinct.
Caires

In the poem ‘The Island Epic’ (*A Insulana*), Manuel Tomás extols the deeds that Constantino de Caires, a native of this island, valiantly performed in India. It is an old and noble surname (*apelido*), which became widespread in the parishes of Caniço, Camacha and others besides.
Quays

There are twenty-six quays (*cais*) in Madeira, spread along the north and south coasts, almost all of them built or improved by order of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) between 1905 and 1916. Thanks to these quays, it is now fairly easy to embark and land at many points on the island. It is much to be wished that others will be built, not only in Madeira but also on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), so as to end the inconvenience suffered by those who visit certain parts of the coast of the two islands. These works, although sometimes costly, amply repay the sacrifices they require, because they bring great benefits to the people by easing communications between the various parishes of the archipelago.
The information we give below is a brief account of all that we know about the quays of Madeira.
Campanário quay
The small landing place in this parish (*freguesia*) was built on the orders of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) in 1908.
Ponta da Cruz quay

It has an old part which is, we believe, the work of the Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas*), and a modern part built around 1910 on the orders of the owners of the cannery at Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’).
Ponta da Oliveira quay

The small landing place at this locality (*sítio*) was built by the same body in 1909. Cais do Lazareto (‘lazaretto quay’). It was probably built between 1866 and 1874, that is, while the works on the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’) were in progress.
Ponta do Sol quay
Its construction began on 8 May 1848 and it appears to have been completed in 1850, the costs being borne by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’).
Cais da Pontinha

It was built from 1876 to 1878 and improved at the time of the works on the mole (breakwater). Near the Pontinha fort (*Forte da Pontinha*) there were once some steps cut into the cliff (*rocha*) and a long footing of *alvenaria* (local name for compact basalt used as building stone), where it was possible to land in calm weather. These steps may have belonged to the stairway that existed there in 1817, to which Paulo Dias de Almeida refers in a work he wrote on Madeira.

At Pontinha there was also a wooden stairway for passengers embarking and landing, which was replaced in 1850 or 1851 by a stairway cut into the cliff; and beside the Ilhéu (‘islet’) there is a stairway for the use of the soldiers and the lighthouse staff.

A little short of the passenger landing quay (*cais*) at the locality (*sítio*) of Pontinha stands another, built some 20 years ago for the use of the Blandy firm (*Casa Blandy*). This firm had originally had a wooden quay for the same purposes as the present one near the old Fort of São José (St Joseph), now demolished.
Ribeira Brava quay
It was built on the orders of the same body from 1904 to 1908.
Câmara de Lobos quay
Work on this quay, undertaken by the government, began in 1876; it was, however, improved and enlarged by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) in 1903.
Machico quay

The first quay at Machico was built on the orders of the Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas*) under a project dated 9 July 1869, and it was completed around 1874. The present quay was built on the orders of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) from 1904 to 1905.
São Jorge quay
Work on this quay began in 1904 and ended in 1910. It was the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) that had it carried out.
Pedra da Pescaria (‘fishing rock’) quay, at Faial. It was built on the orders of the same body, from 1903 to 1905. (See Cacongo.)
Santa Cruz quay

Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) once had a small landing place, built in 1845, and later a quay built on the orders of the Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas*) in 1870 or shortly afterwards. The present quay is the work of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) and was built from 1908 to 1909. Porto Novo (‘new harbour’) quay. The small landing place in this locality was built by the General Council in 1904, 1905 and 1908.
Ilhéu de Fora quay

It was built in 1870 for the use of the lighthouse staff. Abra (‘bay’) quay. It was built on the orders of Mr Manuel Bettencourt Sardinha in 1905. Caniçal (‘reed bed’) quay. The small landing place of this parish (*freguesia*) was built on the orders of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) in 1909.
‘Palace Hotel’ quay

It was built on the orders of the late Dr Antas, and was improved and enlarged by Messrs W. and A. Reid, owners of the ‘Palace Hotel’ on the Estrada Monumental (‘monumental road’). ‘Wilson Company’ quay. It lies near the *quinta* (country estate) of Calaça and was built in 1903 or shortly afterwards. At the locality (*sítio*) of Gorgulho (‘weevil’) there are an inclined plane and an iron ladder built on the orders of the same company.
Pesqueiro quay
The landing place in this locality was built on the orders of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) in 1916.
Porto da Cruz quay
It was built by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) in 1903.
Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’) quay, on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It was built around 1902 and serves the lighthouse staff.
Porto do Moniz quay

It was built by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) in 1916. Before that, Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) had a natural landing place, and later a ladder, built on the orders of the same body, for passengers to embark and disembark at high tide.
Salto do Cavalo quay
It was built on the orders of the industrialist Mr Pedro da Cunha Pires.
Seixal quay
Work on this quay, carried out on the orders of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), began in 1903 and was finished in 1916.
Quay opposite the Entrance to the City

On 23 April 1843 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) resolved to build a stone quay in front of the Entrada da Cidade (‘entrance to the city’), voting the sum of 1,200,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for the purpose. After this expenditure had been authorised by the District Council (*Conselho de Districto*) on 6 May following, Major of Engineers Manuel José Júlio Guerra was put in charge of the construction. On the 24th of the same month he declared that he needed a further 1,000,000 *réis* to protect the works from the winter, a sum which the Council likewise voted.

By February 1844, 4,120,000 *réis* had already been spent on the quay, in addition to a large quantity of stone and worked dressed stone (*cantaria*) supplied by the Government. Major Guerra’s latest estimate asked the Council for a further 18 *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis), which it could not afford to spend.

At a council meeting on 6 March 1844 a proposal was discussed to appoint a committee to direct the works on the quay. It was to consist of Major Manuel José Júlio Guerra as chairman, Dr Manuel Joaquim Moniz, Captain António Pedro de Azevedo, Captain Vicente de Paula Teixeira and Lieutenant Tibério Augusto Blanc. The proposal was rejected, however, and the works continued under the direction of Major Guerra, whose incompetence the Council recognised only when it was already impossible to remedy all the mistakes he had made.

The total sum spent on the quay at the Entrada da Cidade rose to 20,390,000 *réis*. The Council finally resolved to abandon the works, having recognised that they were already threatening ruin long before they were finished.

In 1889, when work began on the present quay, some remains of the quay begun in 1843 still existed, though already much reduced. We ourselves knew one of the flights of steps of this quay, which the sea had not yet entirely destroyed in 1870.

Thirty or forty years ago the ruins of the old quay were the meeting place of many Funchal families on summer afternoons and evenings, even though there were no seats there other than a few stones still coated with cement, and the ground was very uneven because of the damage done by the sea.

By a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 17 September 1879, the Government ordered a study for a new quay in Funchal. The task was entrusted to the artillery officer Henrique de Lima e Cunha, who drew up a project that was approved, with modifications, by the Higher Council of Public Works and Mines (*Conselho Superior de Obras Públicas e Minas*) on 17 June 1881. Under this project, the quay was to be built at the Entrada da Cidade, on the same alignment as the old one.

The process for the Funchal quay made no progress, and only in 1886, when the construction of the Molhe da Pontinha (‘little point breakwater’) had already been approved, was the carrying out of the work taken up. For this purpose, the project drawn up by Captain Lima e Cunha was used, with some modifications introduced by the engineer José Bernardo Lopes de Andrade. This project was submitted on 27 April 1887 and, after being suitably modified by the Higher Council of Public Works and Mines on 27 July of the same year, was approved by a ministerial order of 5 December.

The work was put out to public tender and, on 18 January 1889, awarded to the French engineers Combemale, Michelon and Maurie for the sum of 87,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). When the accounts were settled, however, these contractors were recognised as entitled to receive the sum of 92,005,485 *réis*, on account of additional work carried out.

The work was completed on 27 April 1892 and provisionally accepted on that date, but final acceptance took place only on 27 April 1895. On the opinion of the Consultative Board of Public Works (*Junta Consultiva de Obras Públicas*) of 30 May of the same year, the contractors were judged to have discharged all the obligations they had contracted towards the State, as recorded in the ministerial order of 10 July 1895.

The extension of the Entrada da Cidade quay had become an urgent necessity. The Autonomous Board of Harbour Works (*Junta Autónoma das Obras do Porto*) opened a tender for this important improvement, which closed on 30 October 1930, and the construction was awarded to the firm Nederlandsche Maatschappij Voor Havenwerken for the sum of 4,763,000 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis). The extension of the quay was to be 80 metres long and 16.4 m wide, and would be formed of five large blocks with a total volume of 3,337 cubic metres. The first block was set in place on 25 June 1932 and the fifth and last in January 1933. On 28 May 1933 the official inauguration of this improvement took place in the presence of the authorities.
The quay is 82 m long and 16.80 m wide, and ends in a circular platform 20.66 m in diameter.
See the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*) and Molhe da Pontinha.
Quays on the island of Porto Santo

The neighbouring island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is today served by a pier, which renders excellent service to the traffic of that port and which we shall discuss later. (See Porto Santo (island).)

In former times there were plans to build a quay in front of the Funchal customs house (*Alfândega do Funchal*), and in 1824 Brigadier Raposo and Major Sant’Ana came to Madeira to choose a site for the construction of a mole (breakwater) and a quay. The site chosen was the Baixas de São Tiago, but although the considerable sum of 37 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos) was spent on acquiring and preparing materials for the works, these were never begun.
Calaça

It is the surname of some of the first settlers of this archipelago, especially on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). West of the Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’) and close to the sea there is a property, with land and buildings, called Quinta do Calaça (‘Calaça’s estate’).
Calaça de Viveiros (Canon Henrique)
He founded the Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation) in fulfilment of a vow he had made that Portugal would be freed from the Castilian yoke.
He died aged 73 on 25 May 1662. The seminary library held a life-size portrait of Canon Calaça.
Calçada (Count of)

Diogo de Ornelas de França Carvalhal Frazão Figueiroa, 1st Viscount and 1st Count of Calçada (‘paved way’), came from old and noble families of this island and was born on 29 August 1812. He was administrator and holder of several entailed estates, among them that of Gaula and that of Conceição (‘Conception’) in Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). He was appointed substitute civil governor of Funchal by decree of 4 October 1882 and took office on the 10th of the same month and year, later serving several times when the incumbents were unable to act or absent. He died on 18 September 1906.
White-faced storm petrel (Pelagodroma marina)

A web-footed seabird of the family Procellariidae which comes to breed in the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) during the spring. This elegant little bird appears there at the end of winter and stays until July or August, when it heads back south. The egg is laid at the end of a winding underground burrow; there is a single white egg with small purplish spots, which sometimes cover the whole surface and at other times cluster around the broader end. On Selvagem Grande (‘great wild island’) its enemy is a mouse that abounds there, which not only attacks the bird but also devours its egg. The breeding of this bird has been found at only two almost diametrically opposite points of the earth: the Selvagens and the west coast of Australia.
Chalcedony
It is made up of crystallised quartz and amorphous silica. It has been found in basalt cavities at certain places in Madeira.
Caldeira (Gaspar)

This name became sadly notorious as that of the man who guided the French corsairs in the terrible sack they inflicted on the city of Funchal in October 1566. See what we say about him in the article Saque dos franceses.
Caldeira (João da Silveira)

We have scant information for the biography of this Madeiran. We conjecture that he was born in the third quarter of the 18th century. He was a physician, but we do not know at which school or faculty he graduated. He devoted himself especially to the study of chemistry, in which he gained distinction, spending some years abroad on work and research in this science. Years later we find him in Rio de Janeiro as professor of chemistry at the Military School of that city, where he also held the post of superintendent of the Mint. In 1826 he published an annotated translation of Vauquelin’s *Manual do ensaiador*, and around 1843 a work of his entitled *Nova nomenclatura portuguesa, latina e francesa, etc.* was printed in Rio de Janeiro.

In the *Memória Histórica da Faculdade de Philosophia da Universidade de Coimbra*, by Joaquim Augusto Simões de Carvalho, we find the following about him: ‘... a highly esteemed chemist, who studied in England and France. He is the author of the memoir on metallic watering, published in the *Annaes das Sciências e Artes*, and of other work carried out in the chemical laboratory of Paris. Vauquelin and Laugier considered themselves greatly honoured by the friendship of this Portuguese chemist.’ It appears that he took his own life around 1828.
Caldeirão Verde

A locality (*sítio*) in the mountains of the parish (*freguesia*) of Sant’Ana, remarkable for the majestic views it commands and for the enchanting picturesqueness of the spot. In recent years the road leading there has been improved, and it is frequently visited in the hot season.
Calhau (pebble beach)

In Madeira, people give the name *calhau* – pebble beach (*calhau*) – to a stony beach, taking the part for the whole. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo writes in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*: ‘... beaches which are called *Calhao* because they are made not of sand but of loose stones or pebbles (*calháos*), which, black, rounded, many of them large, of an inhospitable and sombre appearance, produce, when the undertow churns them, a dreadful roar, never drowned by the thunderous howling of the gales...’
Calhau (Nossa Senhora do)
See Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*).
Calheta

A picturesque *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) and small beach at the far western end of the southern coast of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). They adjoin the island’s great beach directly and are separated from the Ilhéu de Baixo (‘lower islet’), or Ilhéu da Cal, by a narrow channel.
Calheta (counts of)

In the article devoted to the municipality of Calheta (‘small cove’), we referred to the creation of the countship (*condado*) that had its seat in this town (*vila*), and to the reasons that led King Sebastian to establish it in the person of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara (see that entry), 5th captain-donatary of Funchal, by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 20 August 1576. This donatary styled himself: Count Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, of the council of the King Our Lord, captain and governor of justice in the island of Madeira, in the jurisdiction of Funchal, overseer of his treasury throughout the island and that of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), lord of the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), etc. Dr Gaspar Frutuoso adds that ‘the king in his Provisions styled him Dom (noble honorific) Simão Gonçalves, but he would not accept the Dom, nor allow it to his sons, who have it by right.

The second Count of Calheta was João Gonçalves da Câmara, 6th captain and donatary of Funchal, son of the first count, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara. João Gonçalves da Câmara was succeeded in the countship by his son Simão Gonçalves, who was born in Lisbon and never came to Madeira. He was the third count, and through his marriage to Dona Maria de Vasconcelos, heiress daughter of the first Count of Castelo Melhor, the countship of Calheta was thereby merged into the countship of Castelo Melhor.

From this marriage was born João Gonçalves da Câmara, who was the fourth Count of Calheta and who did not use the title of Count of Castelo Melhor, for a reason unknown to us. His sister, Dona Mariana de Vasconcelos e Alencastre, was the fifth Countess of Calheta and married the second Count of Castelo Melhor, her kinsman; the couple are considered the 9th captain-donataries of Funchal.

They were succeeded by their son Luiz de Vasconcelos (1636–1720), 6th Count of Calheta and 3rd Count of Castelo Melhor, the statesman and diplomat who rendered such important and distinguished services to our country. He was succeeded by Afonso de Vasconcelos, whose successor was José de Vasconcelos (1706–1769), 8th Count of Calheta, 4th Count and 1st Marquis of Castelo Melhor.

The immediate successors in the countship of Calheta and the marquisate of Castelo Melhor were António José de Vasconcelos e Câmara (1738–1801), Afonso de Vasconcelos (1783–1827), Antonio de Vasconcelos (1816–1858), João de Vasconcelos de Sousa e Câmara (1841–1878) and Dona Helena de Vasconcelos (1836–1900). She was the 13th Countess of Calheta and 6th Marchioness of Castelo Melhor, and may be regarded, albeit only honorifically, as the 17th donatary of Funchal.
Calheta (parish)

It is very likely that the name of this parish (*freguesia*) derives from the small bay or cove that serves as its landing place, for that is the true meaning of the word *calheta*. The *Encyclopedia Portuguesa* of Maximiliano de Lemos, referring to this parish, says that it has an unsheltered beach or cove (*calheta*) which gives it its name. Gaspar Frutuoso, describing the first exploration of the coast made by Zarco, states that ‘having run along the coast a good two *léguas* without finding anywhere to land, they came upon a large inlet where, eager to know the land, they went ashore among some rocks, building a landing place there by hand, to which the captain gave the name Calheta’. In an old manuscript we found the following information, which we consider interesting: ‘running along the coast without finding anywhere to land, they came upon a large inlet and there went ashore, making a landing place by hand among some rocks, and to this channel they had made the captain gave the name of Calheta’. The word has fallen out of use, but it was frequently employed in the time of our maritime discoveries. In the archipelagos of the Azores and Cape Verde there are various landing places and coves called *calheta*, and the name also extended to the settlements adjoining them. This, then, must be the true origin of the name of this parish.

It is one of the oldest parishes on the island and one of the first to be worked by the earliest colonists. Here the discoverer took a great *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) for his son João Gonçalves da Câmara, and extensive lands on the right bank of the stream for his daughter Dona Beatriz Gonçalves, who married Diogo Cabral. Cabral was granted further lands by his father-in-law as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and on them he had the chapel of Our Lady of the Star (*Nossa Senhora da Estrela*) built, where he founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) and where he was buried (see Cabral and Nossa Senhora da Estrela).

Among the earliest settlers of this parish were Dr Pedro Berenguer de Lemilhana (see Berenguer), who gave his name to the locality (*sítio*) still called Lombo do Doutor today; Luís de Atouguia, who held *sesmaria* lands on the *lombo* (ridge between valleys) that came to be called Atouguia’s; João Rodrigues Mondragão (see Mondragão), a native of Biscay; and Francisco Homem de Gouveia, founder of the entailed estate of Reis Magos (see that entry) in Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). There were also others who founded chantries (capela) there with entails (*instituições vinculares*) attached. Other early settlers of this parish were the Neapolitan knight Afonso de Aragão, to whom we have already referred in the article Aragão, and João Assuna Teixeira and João Salviato, who held a great deal of *sesmaria* land there. Gaspar Frutuoso also mentions João Rodrigues Castelhano, of whom he says: ‘... who was so called because he spoke Castilian, though he was Genoese by birth; his is a rich estate of sugar cane, with its own chaplain. This João Rodrigues married off two very rich daughters in Funchal, and the finest estates on the island now belong to them: he had many slaves, five of whom killed a factor (*feitor*) of his; he handed them over to the law, and they were hanged in the town of Calheta.

The parish (*freguesia*) was created in 1430. It was first seated at the Capela da Estrela, where it seems not to have remained for many years. Its patron saint then became the Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), in the church of that name. We have found no reference to the year in which that church was first built, and know only that it was rebuilt in 1639.

From the creation of the parish, the parish priest received an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of 8,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). Successive royal decrees (alvará régio) gradually increased it; the last of which we have knowledge, dated 20 April 1626, fixed this salary at 18,000 *réis* in cash, four *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. The curacy (*curato*) was created by royal decree of 27 August 1589, with a stipend of 20,000 *réis* a year.

The parish once had a collegiate church with 4 beneficed clergy, a treasurer and a preacher, besides the parish priest and the curate. If we are to believe what we read not long ago in a newspaper, this collegiate chapter spent some years in constant wandering, moving at short intervals from church to church and from chapel to chapel. From 1811 to 1815 it was seated in the church of the Franciscan convent, from 1815 to 1821 in the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), for some months of that last year in the chapel of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), and from 1821 to 1834 in the mother church (*igreja matriz*).

Two features deserve special mention: the ceiling of the chancel of the parish church, built like that of our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), and above all the tabernacle, a work of rare artistic value made of ebony with exquisite silver inlays, which was a gift of King Manuel I. It is a pity that this precious piece of 16th-century religious art has been somewhat neglected in its state of preservation. Its antiquity, its historical value and the remarkable artistic refinements it contains demanded the most careful and attentive effort to prevent and avert, as far as possible, the corrosive and destructive action of time.

It was one of the parishes of Madeira with the greatest number of chapels, among which we can list the following: São José, Santa Quitéria, Jesus-Maria-José, São Pedro de Alcântara, Our Lady of Pity, São João Baptista, Our Lady of the Good Death, São Francisco Xavier, Our Lady of the Peña de Francia, Our Lady of the Star, Nossa Senhora da Vida, Nossa Senhora de Monserrate, Almas, Our Lady of Good Success, Our Lady of Nazaré and St Catherine. Few of them still exist, and almost all were entailed foundations (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). We shall deal with them in the articles devoted to chapels.
The parish had the convent of São Francisco, of the Seraphic Order, which we shall deal with in a separate article.
There was a Misericórdia here, with its house and chapel, which we shall discuss in the article devoted to the Misericórdias of this archipelago.
Among the most distinguished sons of this parish were the priests Dr António Veloso de Lira and Dr António João de França Bettencourt, whom we discuss at greater length in their respective places.

On 10 July 1834, little more than a month after constitutional government was established in Madeira, serious disturbances broke out in this parish. Their hidden cause was a protest against the new public order, although outwardly this did not appear to be so. On the pretext that the people were about to be oppressed with heavy taxes, a large number of individuals rioted, causing disorder and committing acts of violence, as a result of which three men were killed and others suffered more or less serious injuries. The uprising threatened to spread, and the authorities set about crushing it firmly, sending to this parish a detachment of infantry and a naval force from the frigate *D. Pedro*, which was then lying at anchor in our harbour. The people were not intimidated by the presence of the armed force and even offered it some resistance, so that the troops were compelled to act with extreme severity, and a number of men of the people fell, shot through by bullets – how many, we cannot say precisely. An extensive judicial inquiry (*devassa*) followed and numerous arrests were made. The trial took place in January 1836: seven defendants were sentenced to perpetual penal exile (degredo) in Angola, some to temporary penal exile, and Father João
Rodrigues Pestana to perpetual penal exile in Mozambique, where he died.

The mining engineer Eugène Arckermann, in his book *L’Ile de Madère considerée au point de vue scientifique*, p. 60 ff., discusses at some length the traces of petroleum found in the locality (*sítio*) of Vila in this parish, approximately 300 metres from the coastal steamer agency. Some exploratory work was carried out on the site, but it produced no appreciable result.
