The main localities of this parish are Lombo da Estrela, Lombo do Salão, Lombo do Brasil, Lombo do Doutor, Lombo do Atouguia and Vila.
It has two state schools, one for each sex.

This parish lies approximately 38 kilometres from the city by the coast road, and by the same road it is about 11 kilometres from Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), seat of the judicial district (*comarca*). It has 4,665 inhabitants.
Calheta (point)
A headland on the coast of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), next to the locality (*sítio*) and small beach of the same name.
Calheta (landing place)

The landing place serving this parish and other neighbouring parishes (*freguesias*) handles a relatively large amount of traffic. It is much to be regretted that no small quay has yet been built there, given the difficulty of access to the narrow cove bordering the locality (*sítio*) of Vila (‘town’), the only point where passengers and goods may be landed and embarked. Adjoining the town (*vila*) is a beach of large rounded boulders, which bounds the same landing place. All this traffic takes place chiefly at two points: the main one is the so-called Rampa (‘ramp’), and the other is in the locality of Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’), near the mouth of the stream of that name. The steamers of the coastal shipping service call there regularly. The landing place lies 2.3 miles from Fajã do Mar (‘flat by the sea’) and 2.1 from Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’) respectively, these being the nearest landing places to it.
Calheta (stream)

This watercourse, also known as the Ribeira da Vila da Calheta, is fed by the small streams of Cutileiro, Convento, Lombo do Brasil and Fonte de Nossa Senhora, and flows into the sea at the town (*vila*) of Calheta (‘small cove’).
Calheta (town and municipality)

The creation of the towns and municipalities of Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) dates from the middle of the 15th century, these places being the capitals of the three captaincies into which the Madeiran archipelago was divided. The captaincy of Funchal, and particularly its seat, the town (*vila*) of the same name, grew remarkably from the earliest days of colonisation and quickly prospered. Important settlements formed within it and soon reached a high level of development, so that autonomous municipalities (*concelho*) became necessary, for the convenience of the inhabitants and the sound administration of public affairs. This is what happened with the establishment of the towns and municipalities of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Calheta (‘small cove’).

The former was created in 1501, and there are good grounds for conjecturing that the latter was created at roughly the same time. It is regrettable that no record survives of the instrument that raised the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta to the rank of town. The royal decree (*alvará*) that created the town of Ponta do Sol is recorded in the municipal archive of Funchal, and a copy of it also exists in the archive of the Council of that town.

On the instrument concerning Calheta, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo says: ‘Of the charter that raised the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Calheta to Villa Nova da Calheta there is no record in the Council concerned, because the old town hall and original archive were destroyed by the sea, as the President of that Council reports in an official letter of 30 October of this year 1871. Nor is it recorded in the archive of the Council of Funchal, and it is not copied in any of the manuscripts we possess. Only in the *Breve Noticia* of Paulo Perestrello, p. 54, do we find a note that Calheta was made a town in 1511, which is a manifest error, perhaps a typographical one, because the instrument below shows that Villa Nova da Calheta was already a town in August 1502’.
The instrument ‘below’ referred to here is a reply, dated 16 August 1502, containing certain instructions addressed by the monarch to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal.

Several writings allude to the phrase, which became quite well known, ‘to his much beloved town of Calheta’, attributed to King Manuel I in a letter addressed to the Council of this municipality. We do not know the document in which this phrase is recorded, nor can we vouch for its genuine authenticity. If it is true, the Fortunate King must surely have been referring to the distinguished nobility of this town or municipality, for it is well known that a large galaxy of noble knights lived there, many of whom distinguished themselves valiantly in Africa, India and Brazil. Eloquent proof of Manuel I’s fondness for the town of Calheta survives in the rich tabernacle he presented to its mother church (*igreja matriz*), to which we have already referred in the article devoted to this parish.

Wishing to reward the services rendered by Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, 5th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, to honour in him the deeds and heroic actions of his forebears, and also to add lustre to the rich and important house of which he was the representative, the monarch granted him the title of count by royal decree of 20 August 1576. The town of Calheta, for its importance and noble traditions, was chosen as the seat of the new countship. This title, as will be explained elsewhere, was incorporated into the marquisate of Castelo Melhor, and the holders of that title were also counts of Calheta until the decree of 15 October 1910 abolished all titles of nobility.
The following passage by Gaspar Frutuoso, which we transcribe below, is of interest regarding the points we have mentioned:

‘In this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Calheta, further down, close to a beautiful stream, the town was founded, which took the name of Calheta, the most fertile of all those of the island, because it has the largest district. This town is as noble in its inhabitants as it is well supplied with the many cheap provisions to be found in it. From it there went forth, in the company of the captains of Funchal, many noble knights to serve the King at their own expense in the strongholds of Africa, and in the relief expeditions that the captains led: where all of them, besides giving proof of their persons, spent much of their own wealth, for they were rich, owing to the great estates in this *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca), such as the much-famed estate of Arco, and others, which are now divided among various heirs. This town of Calheta and its *termo* formed the countship of the Most Illustrious Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of this Vila Nova da Calheta, as will be told in its place’.

As we have already seen in the article on customs houses (*Alfândegas*), this town was the seat of a small customs office, or revenue guard post (*posto fiscal*), as it was then called, and the duty on sugar was originally collected there, later being collected at the Funchal customs house. Calheta had the offices of collector of the fifths (quintador), the officer levying the one-fifth duty on sugar, and clerk (*escrivão*) of the fifths (*quintos*, levy of one fifth on sugar), whose duties consisted in applying the taxes levied on the sugar produced there. These posts were abolished by royal decree of 30 July 1686.

In the Council of this town the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) Dr António Rodrigues Veloso de Oliveira left on record some instructions on agricultural matters, truly remarkable for their time, of which various extracts have been published in several Madeiran newspapers. ‘They deal’, it is said somewhere, ‘with the cultivation of the vine and other plants – the chestnut on the common lands (*baldios*), fruit trees in sheltered places, cotton plants near the sea, mulberries along roads and in public places, pine woods on land unfit for any other crop, plants used in pharmacies, fields of maize, the raising of livestock, artificial meadows, sheltering hedges and other suggestions’. These instructions can still be read today with some profit.
Within this municipality lies the well-known and much-visited locality (*sítio*) of Rabaçal, to which we shall devote a full article.

The present municipality (*concelho*) of Calheta, created in 1835, and the former municipality or town do not differ very markedly in the extent of their areas. Since 1835, however, it has undergone some changes, some of which we can record here. In 1849 the municipality of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), which had also been created in 1835, was suppressed, and the parishes (*freguesias*) of Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’) and Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) became part of the municipality of Calheta. These parishes were, however, reincorporated into the municipality of Porto Moniz when it was restored in 1855. The decree of 26 June 1871 detached the parish of Ponta do Pargo from the municipality of Porto Moniz and annexed it to that of Calheta. In 1895 the municipality of Porto Moniz was suppressed once more and annexed to the municipalities of Calheta and São Vicente, only to be restored again in 1898.
This municipality comprises the parishes of Calheta, Estreito da Calheta, Arco da Calheta, Prazeres, Jardim do Mar, Paul do Mar, Fajã da Ovelha and Ponta do Pargo.

As stated above, the town of Ponta do Sol was created in 1501, and the illustrious commentator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) conjectured that Calheta had been created at about the same time. Today the exact date of its creation can be established, since in 1900 Dr Damião Peres published a second edition of the work of Gaspar Frutuoso, enriching it with a number of valuable annotations. In one of these, on p. 118 ff., the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 1 July 1502 that created the town of Calheta is transcribed in full; it is an exceptionally interesting document.
Callejon (Dom Ventura de)
Spanish consul on the island of Madeira. He wrote an account of Columbus’s stay on this island in the *Ilustracion Espanola y Americana* (no. 38, 15 October 1878).
Camacha (parish)

Camacha belonged to the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’) until the year of its own creation. It was the high, mountainous part of that parish and came to form its northern boundary. The name Camacha seems to be quite old, and it is without any doubt much older than the time when the area was separated from Caniço. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo conjectures that the name may come from some *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) or settler with the surname Camacho, who perhaps owned land or had his residence there. We do not consider plausible the idea of attributing the origin of the name to an early colonist who, in memory of his distant homeland, gave this place the same name as some *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) or village on the mainland. As far as we have been able to ascertain, the name is not found in Portuguese territory, except for a small locality (*sítio*) on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).

We do not know when the clearing and settlement of the lands of Camacha began, but we must suppose that it did not take place in the first years after the discovery of the island, because the land of the interior was not immediately brought under cultivation. Nevertheless, by the beginning of the last quarter of the 16th century there must certainly already have been a very sizeable population here, enough to justify its separation from Caniço and its establishment as an independent parish. It is recorded that at this time the residents of Camacha included Captain António Figueira, married to Dona Maria Henriques Figueira, Bartolomeu de Freitas, Brás de Freitas, Domingos da Mota, Francisco de Sousa, Inácio de Caires Caldeira, José de Lamego and João de Freitas Belchior, among others.

It was the royal decree (alvará régio) of Peter II, dated 28 December 1676, that authorised the diocesan bishop, Dom António Teles da Silva, to create this parish, which seems to have been definitively constituted only in 1680. Gaspar Correia was its first parish priest, from 1680 to 1699. He was immediately succeeded by Fathers Manuel Simão de Gouveia, António Gomes Germano and Manuel João

Barreto, up to the middle of the 18th century. From its creation to the present, thirty-one priests have served this parish as its incumbent parish priests. The vicar’s original stipend was 10,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year, one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine; over time, and as the number of households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) grew, it received several increases. The growth of the population, which seems to have been rapid, led the prelate of the diocese, Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares, to request the creation of a curacy (*curato*). This came about in 1801, and the first curate was Father Inácio Cristóvão da Silva. Several curates lived permanently in the parish, but for some decades now they have not resided there.

The seat of the parish was established in the chapel dedicated to São Lourenço (St Lawrence), who became the patron saint of the new parish; we are told that it was built by Francisco Gonçalves Salgado. We know nothing of the year or the site in which the little church was built, but we conjecture that it did not stand on the same spot where the present parish church was later erected. By 1746 this chapel was already in an advanced state of ruin.

There is a vague tradition that a small chapel once stood in the locality of Salgados (‘salt marshes’), and we do not know whether it was perhaps in this chapel that the parish was installed at the time of its creation. The foundation stone of the present church was laid on 30 September 1783. Around 1886 the side walls, which were in imminent danger of collapse, were rebuilt. In recent years the church and its churchyard have undergone major repairs and have been considerably improved in their embellishment and decoration, thanks to the zeal of several parish priests.

When, on 23 August 1828, the absolutist forces landed at Machico and took this island (see Occupation of Madeira by Miguelist troops), the governor and captain-general, José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, ordered Major Francisco Xavier Pereira da Silva, later Count of Antas, to occupy the heights of Camacha. This is recorded in the following report, sent by this officer to the governor of Madeira:

‘I have the honour to inform Your Excellency that, in compliance with the order I received from Your Excellency at Porto Novo (‘new harbour’), I marched at midnight last night to take command of this post, which I reached at four o’clock in the morning. The position is very strong, and with the three hundred men and two pieces of artillery that garrison it I am quite certain of defending it, provided the soldiers do not refuse to fight, as they did yesterday to Lieutenant-Colonel Schwalback.’ Pereira da Silva detached part of these forces to Palheiro Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s barn’), and later had to withdraw to Funchal when his soldiers, on learning of the disaster at Porto Novo, began shamefully to desert. The Miguelist forces that advanced as far as the heights of Camacha no longer found the constitutional troops, who, as already said, had fled in disorder to the city.
This is one of the most picturesque parishes (*freguesias*) in Madeira. A distinguished poet who lived here and composed some of his most inspired verses in the parish wrote of it:

‘In its general appearance, in the rich tree species that people it, in the fine *quintas* (country estates) that adorn it, and in the freshness and purity of the air that persists at that altitude, Camacha is the place – perhaps the only one – that bears the greatest resemblance to, and has most in common with, the parish of Monte (‘hill’), known as the Madeiran Sintra.

It is Monte seen through a magnifying lens, its panoramas enlarged in scale, with broader and flatter roads and finer, wider horizons, taking in the coastal parishes of Caniço and Gaula, which unfold at its feet in a gradual, step-by-step descent of the land, bounded by the ocean.
The contrast between these latter places and the former is most striking, both in its flora and in its climatic conditions.

Below, on the coast, there are no forest trees, but crops of sugar cane, vines and a variety of market-garden produce; up above, reaching to the uplands, lies Camacha, with its vast pine woods and its groves of leafy oaks, where there grow side by side the oak, the chestnut, the cedar, the til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), the folhado (*Clethra arborea*, a native tree), the laurel, the beech, the lime, the cork oak, the *pau de mil homens*, the silver tree and various other native and exotic species, probably planted there by the first founders of *quintas*, for the most part wealthy foreigners, who in former times held that picturesque place in the highest favour.’

Outside Funchal, this is the parish with the finest and most numerous *quintas*. Among them the Quinta do Vale Paraíso (‘paradise valley’) stands out; it belongs to the viscounts of the same title and is a charming residence, well worth a visit. The former summer residence of the Ornelas family is also a fine and pleasant country house; its owner today is Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, who was born there in March 1866. The old Grabham, Taylor, Bean, Hinton and Francisco Nunes *quintas* also deserve special mention, besides others of lesser importance. Apart from the Ornelas *quinta*, all the others were built by British subjects, who had a great and well-founded fondness for Camacha.

One of the attractions for visitors to this parish is the well-known Achada (‘plateau’), a square of some size and perfectly flat, which causes Madeirans a certain wonder and surprise, since they live in a very mountainous region where the relief and ruggedness of the land show themselves everywhere, except on the plateau of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’). On entering this square, the visitor’s attention is at once caught by the tower rising at one end of it, within the bounds of the *quinta* that belonged to Dr Miguel Grabham. It was this English physician who, some 40 years ago, had the tower built and placed in it an excellent, finely made clock, which is certainly one of the best on this island. Inside the tower is a marble tablet bearing the following inscription: The Clock And Bell Here Placed, Were Brought From the Parish Church of Wolton Near Liverpool By Michel C. Grabham, M. D. F. L. S. E. R. C. P.-Who built this Tower For their Reception, And the Clock Was Set Going By Mary Anne Grabham (Wife of the above) On Easter Monday 6.th April 1896. The building of this tower and clock was an excellent service that Dr Miguel C. Grabham rendered to the inhabitants of this parish.

Camacha is crossed along most of its length by the rich and abundant stream of water called the Levada da Serra (‘upland channel’), to which we shall refer in the appropriate place. When this levada (irrigation channel) was planned and dug, many landowners gave the land for its construction and for the footpath alongside it free of charge, convinced that it would benefit this parish through irrigation. When the works were finished and the water was shared out, however, they saw with deep sorrow that Camacha had been entirely forgotten and had no share in the benefits granted to other parishes. A walk along the levada path (*esplanada*) of this levada is truly delightful for the varied and surprising views it offers. The footpath beside this aqueduct, level and easy underfoot, is passable from Choupana (‘hut’) to Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), a distance of more than 40 kilometres.

The Levada da Azenha and the Levada do Pico do Arvoredo are two important water sources, intended chiefly to irrigate the parish of Caniço, which also irrigate the parish of Camacha, though for only a small part of their rotation (giro). The first rises at Pico da Silva and the second in the uplands of Poiso. In the locality (*sítio*) of Salgados, fed by the Ribeira do Porto Novo, rises the so-called Levada de Baixo, which waters the land of this parish and also of Caniço.

The house at the locality of Poiso lies within the bounds of this parish. The public-spirited civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro, recognising the need for a house high in the uplands to give shelter and help to travellers passing between the municipalities of Funchal and Sant’Ana, had a house built at Poiso. Its construction cost about one *conto* (one million réis; from 1911, 1,000 escudos) and five hundred thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), and it was completed early in 1852. In the illustrious governor’s own words, a man or a family was to be stationed there permanently, ‘ready at all hours to receive travellers – to have water heated for them, if need be – to keep always a good store of firewood, so that in winter the comfort of a good fire may be found there – to give all those in need whatever help is possible’. The upkeep of this excellent service, which has continued to the present day, was entrusted to the municipal councils of Funchal and Sant’Ana, and there are officially approved instructions governing how the house is to be kept running.

Camacha’s well-known wickerwork, which is truly important and deserves a study of its own, is an industry almost exclusive to this parish. Although wicker goods are also made elsewhere, it is certain that the industry spread from here to other places, and it is here that its largest production centre lies. It is a very important source of income, and the rapid growth of the population is due chiefly to it, since the parish has no other appreciable sources of wealth: its land is suitable only for the so-called poor crops. The workers, however, do not earn from their products a sufficient reward for the labour they put in, whereas the exporting houses, it is said, make very considerable profits, and several fortunes have been made in a few years on the back of this trade. Everything points to the need for the Camacha workers to form a union, cooperative or special association, intended not only to develop and improve this industry but also to promote the sale of its products in our colonies and abroad.

The engineer Senhor Vitorino José dos Santos, head of the industrial labour section in Madeira, published in no. 4 of the *Boletim do Trabalho Industrial* for 1907 an excellent and detailed monograph on the wicker goods industry in Madeira. From it we shall transcribe a few passages on the industry’s probable origin and early development in the parish of Camacha.

‘The wicker furniture industry appeared approximately 60 years ago. It began with work on chairs, copying the methods used to make other chairs then produced in Madeira from rye straw by prisoners in the Funchal gaol. It is supposed that some prisoner from the parish of Camacha, on his release, took back to this parish the knowledge he had acquired during his apprenticeship in the gaol. In this way the industry slowly and progressively developed in that setting, which for many years was the only place where it was practised. An English subject named William Hinton, a prominent industrialist who died in Madeira a few years ago at an advanced age, also seems to have influenced the first attempts at this industry. He helped the first craftsmen with his knowledge of the manufacture of such furniture, already made in England and Germany from rattan canes, which in their flexibility and other properties closely resemble Madeiran wicker.’

Information received directly from this parish, from a person there who has carried out some research on the subject, does not in essence contradict the account given by the author of the monograph cited. It merely adds that ‘It was António Caldeira who introduced wickerwork. He took apart a mat that had come from abroad through a member of the Hinton family and studied its form and manufacture, taking the flexibility of the osier as his starting point for achieving his aim.’

It is said that this industry, albeit in a very rudimentary state, began in this parish around 1812. It was after 1870 that it began to grow markedly, and over the last 40 years it has developed extraordinarily. The monograph we have cited contains very interesting information on the cultivation of the osier, the methods of making wickerwork, its development, exports, etc.

This parish has an official school for each sex: the boys’ school was created in 1862 and the girls’ school by decree of 12 August 1914. Since its creation the former has had as teachers Miguel Luís Valério, Luís Teixeira de Vasconcelos, Constâncio Figueira da Silva and Manuel de Jesus de Antas e Almeida. The first teacher of the girls’ school was Dona Maria das Mercês Lopes de Faria.
The parish cemetery was built in 1856, at the time of the cholera epidemic, on land offered for the purpose by the Count of Carvalhal, who was one of the largest landowners in this parish.
The main localities (*sítios*) of this parish are: Igreja, Rochão, Achadinha, Casais de Além, Vale Paraíso, Ribeiro Fernando, Nogueira, Ribeirinha, Salgados and Ribeiro Serrão.
Some localities or places deserve special mention for the picturesque landscape or the fine, wide panoramas they offer, such as Poiso, Pico do Infante, Pico da Silva, Mirante do
Marcado, on the Salgados road, Eira de Fora, etc.

Camacha borders the parishes of São Roque do Faial and Porto da Cruz to the north, Caniço to the south, Santo António da Serra, Santa Cruz and Gaula to the east, and Santa Maria Maior and Monte to the west. It lies 9 and a half kilometres from the seat of the district, approximately 12 from the seat of the municipality (*concelho*) and of the judicial district (*comarca*), 6 from the parish of Caniço and 9 from Santo António da Serra.

We do not wish to close this brief article without mentioning the well-liked and helpful citizen Manuel Filipe Gomes, a native of the parish of São Roque, who died in Camacha at a very advanced age approximately 40 years ago, having lived there for more than half a century. He was a man of great austerity of character and of the most upright and unshakeable honesty. His name remains bound to the history of this parish through the selfless services he rendered it, notably in building and improving various roads and paths, in building the public fountain in the locality of Igreja, in acquiring land at Achada as common land (logradouro comum), etc. All this earned him high esteem and well-deserved prestige among the inhabitants of this parish. His personal qualities and his relations with the foreigners who frequented Camacha contributed considerably to the improvements he carried out there, some of which he undertook and completed at great and evident cost to his own fortune.
Councillor Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelos, whom we shall discuss in a separate article, was a native of this parish.
Camacho

This is a family surname that is very widespread on this island and certainly has several origins. The annotator of the *Saudades*, however, says that ‘it is of Spanish origin and seems to derive from Dom Fernando Camacho, who served on this island in the Spanish garrison, according to oral information we have obtained. In the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), where some of the earliest settlers in Madeira lived, this surname is still common. The name Camacha, borne by the parish so called, which was separated from Caniço in 1679, leads one to presume that some early *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) with the surname Camacho may have lived there.
Camacho (Jacinto Augusto)

He was the son of Colonel António Fernandes Camacho and was born in Funchal on 3 January 1815. Having emigrated with his family to the Azores to escape persecution by the Miguelists, he enlisted there as a cadet in the 3rd Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) Battalion and accompanied the expedition that landed on the beaches of Mindelo. He distinguished himself in several engagements and formed part of the forces sent to the Algarve under the command of the Duke of Terceira. He held the medal of the Liberal campaigns, the commandery of the Order of Aviz and the insignia of the Order of the Conception. Promoted to second lieutenant in 1832, he reached the rank of brigadier general on 8 May 1877, and died in the city of Porto on 7 June 1885.
Camacho (Januário Vicente)
This distinguished Madeiran was born in Funchal in 1792, the son of the artillery colonel António Fernandes Camacho and Dona Bárbara Junqueiro Camacho.

Ordained priest in 1815, he then served as parish priest in the parishes of Serra de Água, Ribeira Brava and Santo António, in Funchal. It is said – on what grounds we do not know – that, having been passed over in the competition he had entered for the vicarage of Santo António, he complained to John VI of the injustice done to him. The king, recognising that the complainant was in the right, asked him whether there was not some other vacant post in Madeira that would suit him. Januário Camacho promptly replied: ‘In Funchal the only vacancy is the deanery.’ The anecdote, for we take it as such, goes on to say that John VI, not knowing what the deanery (office of dean of the cathedral chapter) was, at once gave the important post of dean of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) to Januário Vicente Camacho.

The central government nominated him bishop of the diocese of Castelo Branco, but he was not confirmed by the Holy See, nor did he ever receive episcopal consecration. By decree of 26 February 1840 he was appointed governor of the diocese of Funchal and was elected vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) on 27 March of the same year. He later held the same office in the bishopric of Angra, styling himself in official documents bishop-elect of Castelo Branco and always placing before his name the title Dom (noble honorific), which Portuguese prelates were by custom and right entitled to adopt. It seems that his episcopal administration in the diocese of the Azores was not among the most exemplary.

He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislature of 1848 to 1851, and had previously been elected several times as deputy and substitute senator for this archipelago. In 1851 he was raised to the peerage, a dignity not easily attained at that time unless the recipient was recognised as having indisputable merits. He died in Lisbon on 22 December 1872.
Camacho (João Inocêncio)

He was a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and died in Funchal in the last quarter of the 19th century. He distinguished himself as a journalist and was the founder and chief editor of the newspaper *Religião e Progresso*, published in this city in 1879 and 1880.
Camacho (Jorge Perestrelo Velosa)

He was born in Funchal on 23 May 1870, the son of Colonel Augusto Maria Camacho and Dona Maria Iria Perestrelo Velosa Camacho. His paternal grandfather and great-grandfather were distinguished officers of our army. His great-uncle Dom Januário Vicente Camacho (see that entry) was bishop-elect of Castelo Branco, deputy for Madeira and peer of the realm.

His name gained great prestige through his military service in Africa. He took an active part in the Niassa campaign against the chief Mataca and was particularly prominent in the operations at Metauculo. For these services he was made an officer of the Order of the Tower and Sword. He was also a knight of the Legion of Honour and held the Spanish Cross of Military Merit.

In 1902 he took part in the Barué operations and commanded the Macequece military column, which earned him the gold medal for distinguished service overseas. He held the rank of infantry captain when he was dismissed for joining the royalist forces that attempted to invade Portugal, being at the time chief of staff to Paiva Couceiro.

In Funchal he served as police commissioner and as municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative), and became actively involved in the party struggles of the day.
Like his father, he devoted himself to genealogical studies, on which he wrote several articles, and he published a pamphlet on the military organisation of the overseas territories.

At the time of the monarchist uprising at the beginning of 1919, Jorge Camacho was arrested in Beja and taken to Lisbon. On landing in the capital, as he was crossing the Terreiro do Paço (‘palace square’) in the midst of a military escort, he was murdered by a civilian on 7 February 1919.
Câmara

Câmara is a very old family surname here in Madeira. The first to bear it on the island was João Gonçalves da Câmara, eldest son of the discoverer and 21. captain-donatary of Funchal. Even so, it can be said that the name derives from João Gonçalves Zarco, although he himself may perhaps never have used it. This claim rests on the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 4 July 1460, which in more than one place calls the discoverer of Madeira João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), when conferring on him his title of nobility and granting him the corresponding coat of arms. This document of Afonso V, an interesting one, was first published on p. 836 ff. of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).

Madeiran genealogists generally attribute the origin of this surname to a well-known episode of the discovery of Madeira, which Gaspar Frutuoso describes in the following terms: ‘…here they entered with the boats, and found so many sea wolves that it was a wonder; and it was no small refreshment and pastime for the men, for they killed many of them and took great pleasure and made merry in the slaughter. For this reason Captain João Gonçalves gave this sheltered cove the name Câmara de Lobos, from which he took his surname, it being the last place he discovered on this circuit and journey he made; and from this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) he took his arms, which the King gave him…’ Earlier still, João de Barros had said in greater detail in the *Decadas* that ‘a great cave, like a vaulted chamber, lay beneath a lofty stretch of land above the sea, and its floor was much trodden by the feet of the sea wolves that came there to frolic: this place he (Zarco) called Câmara de Lobos, and he took this surname in memory, since that place was the first landing of his settlement; and this surname passed to all his heirs’.

In ‘Longing for the Homeland’, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo transcribes a genealogical work by José Freire Monterroio Mascarenhas, which remains unpublished in the Public Library of Lisbon and contains the words we reproduce below: ‘There is no ground for saying that his descendants took the surname Câmara because of the chamber of sea wolves that João Gonçalves Zarco found on that island; for this was not a deed worthy of being perpetuated in memory and remaining as a surname…’. This statement by Mascarenhas flatly contradicts the origin that the books of nobility and the old chronicles of this archipelago assign to that surname. This statement by Mascarenhas flatly contradicts the origin that the books of nobility and the old chronicles of this archipelago assign to that surname. It is also in plain contradiction with the heraldic indications of the coat of arms itself, and with the words of the royal letter cited above. The way in which that letter calls the discoverer of Madeira João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos shows us that these words contain an evident reference to the episode of the sea wolves found at the place that later took the name Câmara de Lobos. It is true that the deeds of João Gonçalves Zarco as a warrior at Ceuta and a distinguished navigator, and above all the discovery of Madeira itself, would have given the kings of arms and the heraldry of the time precious material for a coat of arms of loftier significance and more ostentatious ancestral lineage for Zarco’s descendants. But it is equally beyond doubt that in matters of this kind whim and fancy sometimes won the day, leaving in a very secondary place memorable facts and heroic actions that deserved to be set in brilliant and marked relief.

The royal letter (*carta régia*) of 4 July 1460 mentioned above sets out the composition of João Gonçalves Zarco’s coat of arms in the following exact words: ‘a black shield, and at its foot a green mountain upon which stands, firmly set, a tower of silver between two wolves of gold’. Gaspar Frutuoso, however, says that John I gave Zarco ‘as his coat of arms, on a shield with a green field, a keep, with a cross of gold on its summit, richer than that on the tomb of Robert Machin, and with two sea wolves leaning against it, which seem to want to climb to the top of the tower, with its mantling and foliage of red and green; and as the crest of the arms a wolf, also a sea wolf, seated on top of the mantling. The annotator of the *Saudades* describes this information of Frutuoso’s as inaccurate.

It seems that this original coat of arms later underwent some slight modifications. Henrique Henriques de Noronha, the most distinguished and respected of genealogists, describes it as follows: ‘On a green field a tower of silver, with battlements and a spire ending in a cross of gold, and two wolves of their natural colour, rampant against the tower: crest, one of the wolves’.

From what has been set out above, and especially from the letter of Afonso V, it can be seen that the genealogical branch of the Câmaras of Madeira had João Gonçalves Zarco as its origin and stock, and is not connected with the families of the same surname on the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, the second son of João Gonçalves Zarco and 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of the island of São Miguel, moved from Madeira to the Azores, where he left a large and illustrious line of descendants. From him descend the Counts of Vila Franca and the Marquises of Ribeira Grande, as well as other distinguished families. On the mainland of the Kingdom, too, there are many noble houses descended from the Câmaras of Madeira.

João Gonçalves da Câmara, 2nd captain-donatary of Funchal and Zarco’s successor, still used the surname Lobos, because it is said that the monarch had threatened to deprive him of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*) if he did not. It is certain, however, that his successors used only the surname Câmara, and the surname Lobos, which appears in the letter of Afonso V, fell entirely out of use.

This is the moment to point out the evident error of the king of arms in drawing and composing the arms of the Câmaras: he placed a wolf (*lupus*) on each side of the tower, when it should have been a seal or monk seal (*lobo marinho*, literally ‘sea wolf’), so as to perpetuate the fact to which the arms are meant to refer. This error was never corrected, and so it was passed down to all of Zarco’s descendants who have used this coat of arms.
Câmara (Alfredo Bettencourt da)

He was born in Funchal on 21 April 1857 and for many years was a private primary-school teacher. Works: *Gramatica Portuguesa, em harmonia com a reforma ortografica ultimamente publicada*, Funchal, 1912, 240 pp.; and *Exercícios sobre a conjugação dos verbos regulares e irregulares...*, part 1, Funchal, 1915, 64 pp., part 2, Funchal, 1915, 64 pp. He died in Funchal on 26 January 1921.
Câmara (António Gonçalves da)

He was a great-grandson of the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco and a grandson of the 2nd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) João Gonçalves da Câmara. He distinguished himself greatly in Africa by his bravery and rendered good service to his country there. What truly made him famous, however, and why all the old Madeiran chronicles speak of him, was the violent and spectacular manner in which he abducted Isabel de Abreu, together with the sensational episodes and circumstances that followed. The abduction became a fertile subject for the chroniclers of the time and for other writers who have since dealt with it. We have already discussed it at some length in the article devoted to Isabel de Abreu, to which we refer the reader.

António Gonçalves da Câmara, the son of Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara and Dona Joana de Eça, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine, held various court offices, among them that of Master of the Royal Hunt to King John I.
Câmara (António Rodrigues da)

He was born in Madeira, the natural son of Luís Gonçalves da Câmara. He accompanied his father to São Miguel when the latter bought the captaincy of that island. He distinguished himself in Africa, and António Cordeiro, in the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), says that he was a great horseman, citing in this connection an incident that was much talked about at the time it happened.
Câmara (Dom José Manuel da)

On 8 May 1800 he was appointed governor and captain-general of this archipelago, taking up office on 4 December of the same year. Two important events occurred during his rule: the occupation of this island by British troops (see Occupation of Madeira by British troops) and the terrible flood of 9 October 1803 (see Floods).

He quarrelled with the prelate Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares and banished him to the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (see the article on this prelate). Among the accusations made against the bishop, the most notable was that he was a freemason and held frequent secret meetings with various members of the secret societies. The prelate and the governor were both summoned to Lisbon: Dom José Manuel da Câmara was dismissed, while Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares continued in the exercise of his ministry. The high court judge (*desembargador*) Dr Joaquim António de Araújo came to Madeira to investigate the governor’s actions.
He left Madeira on 10 December 1803, his successor Ascenso de Sequeira Freire having already arrived on the island.
Câmara (Dona Mariana de Alencastre e)

She was also called Dona Mariana de Vasconcelos e Câmara Alencastre, and was the daughter of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd Count of Calheta (‘small cove’) and 7th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. When her brother João Gonçalves da Câmara, 8th donatary, died without issue, Dona Mariana de Alencastre succeeded to the house of the countship of Calheta and was regarded as the 9th donatary of Funchal. She was lady of the bedchamber to Queen Maria Francisca of Savoy, and an old manuscript says that she was zealous in defending and supporting the natives of the island, treating them all with special affection. She died on 15 April 1689 (see Alencastre and Calheta (Counts of)).
Câmara (Dona Marta Celina Sauvayre da)

She belongs to a noble and distinguished Madeiran family and is the daughter of João Sauvayre da Câmara and Dona Matilde Lúcia de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Bettencourt. She is the granddaughter of the illustrious Madeiran writer the Viscountess of Nogueiras, and the niece of our distinguished fellow countryman Jacinto de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos, 21. viscount of the same title, both of whom we shall deal with in this *Elucidario*. Dona Marta Celina da Câmara was born in Funchal on 1 September 1857 and received a careful education, largely given by her illustrious grandmother, a lady of vast learning, who wrote for the use of her granddaughters an interesting and valuable work entitled *Diálogos entre uma avó e suas netas*, published in 1862. After a long journey through Europe and parts of Asia and Africa, Dona Marta Celina wrote a book which she entitled *De Napoles a Jerusalem* and which in
1889 was published in Funchal, in a volume of 196 pages. Dona Marta Celina Sauvayre da Câmara died in Portugal on 21 February 1929.
Câmara de Lobos (parish)

When the discoverers of Madeira, leaving their ships at anchor in the bay of Machico, began to explore the coast, they reached on the first day the point of the shore to which they later gave the name Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). This is what Gaspar Frutuoso says on the matter, word for word:

‘As João Gonçalves continued his discovery in the manner described above, going in his ship’s boats with his company, they saw between two headlands a mighty and great stream flowing into the sea. Some young men from Lagos asked leave to go ashore and see the stream, which seemed wide and pleasant. The captain stayed in the boat with the others and had them put ashore by the boat of Álvaro Afonso. Once on land, they attempted to cross the stream by swimming; but it was swollen with water and ran to the sea with such force and fury that they fell into the current and the stream carried them away. They would have been in grave danger had the captain not shouted from the sea to the boat of Álvaro Afonso, in which they had gone and which was at the shore with its men, telling them to hurry to the young men’s aid. At his cries the young men were rescued and freed from the danger of the water, which pleased the captain, for he held them dear. And from this came the name by which it is called to this day, Ribeira dos Socorridos [the Stream of the Rescued], which seemed worse to those young men close at hand than it had first seemed to them from afar.','

‘From here they went further on until they came upon a slender cliff, like a low point, which runs far out into the sea; and between this cliff and another lies an arm of calm sea, where nature has made a great cave, like a chamber of stone and living rock. Here they went in with the boats and found so many sea wolves that it was a wonder; and it was no small refreshment and pastime for the men, for they killed many of them and had great pleasure and merriment in the slaughter. For this reason Captain João Gonçalves named this cove Câmara de Lobos [Chamber of Wolves], from which he took his surname, as it was the last part he discovered on this round and journey that he made; and from this place he took his arms, which the King gave him on his return to the kingdom, as I shall relate further on.’
To the statement in the *Saudades* that they attempted to cross the stream by swimming, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo very judiciously observes:

‘The Ribeira dos Socorridos cannot be crossed by swimming, because in summer it has too little water, and when it is full, in the winter storms, it is so violent and carries so many and such large stones that no one would dare to face its current, and anyone who tried would die there. In the season to which the text refers, this stream could have been forded. Might the autograph, then, have the word *nado* (*vado*, in the Latin manner) for *vau*? [TN: *nado* means ‘swimming’; *vau* and Latin *vadum* mean ‘ford’.]
One cannot but accept the explanation of this learned annotator, which seems to be the only true one.
The origin of the name of this parish, on which all the old chronicles agree, lies in the encounter with the seals, or sea wolves, as Frutuoso relates in the words transcribed above.

When João Gonçalves Zarco, having settled in Funchal, undertook a fresh exploration of the lands of his captaincy, he came to a small rise overlooking the bay of Câmara de Lobos. There he marked out the foundation of a church dedicated to the Holy Spirit, which he had built at his own expense.

The parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos is one of the oldest on this island, and its creation dates back to the beginning of the second quarter of the 15th century, around 1430. The seat of the new parish was the chapel of Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), and it was later transferred to the church of St Sebastian. Around 1720 the chapel founded by Zargo, which was then in an advanced state of ruin, was rebuilt, and in 1908 major repairs were carried out there, as well as on the small house adjoining it. Although perhaps nothing now remains of the original building, this chapel is nonetheless a small historic monument for the municipality (*concelho*) and parish of Câmara de Lobos. It recalls the name of the discoverer of Madeira, who had it built, and it was also the seat where the parish was established at the time of its creation. We do not know when the church of St Sebastian was built, nor when the seat of the parish was transferred to it. We believe, however, that we are not far from the truth in stating that both took place at the beginning of the 16th century, and that in the last quarter of the following century the church was enlarged and the bell tower built. Around the middle of the 18th century very important works were carried out on the same church by order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*), which on this occasion contributed 291,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) towards a bell of 24 *arrobas* and 620,000 *réis* for vestments.

The parish priest originally received an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of 3,300 *réis* in cash, 4 *moios* of wheat and 2 *pipas* of wine. Under the royal decree (*alvará*) of 8 May 1591 this became 11,000 *réis* in cash, 4 *moios* of wheat and 2 *pipas* of wine, a salary that in the course of time received further and larger increases. We have been unable to obtain any information about the first priests who performed parish duties there, but we know that in the period from 1570 to 1680 the parish priests of Câmara de Lobos were Fathers Manuel Rodrigues, Belchior Drumond, Diogo Nunes, Gaspar Luís, Francisco de Aguiar, Pero Ferreira, Luís da Cunha, António de Novais Ferreira, Bernardino Teles de Meneses, Pedro do Rego Machado, José Pinheiro Taveira and Inácio Alves de Carvalho.

By a royal letter (*carta régia*) of King Sebastian dated 5 November 1576, the bishop of this diocese, Dom Jerónimo Barreto, was authorised to create a curacy (*curato*) in the parish church of Câmara de Lobos. At first it was a confirmed post, but by a royal decree of 26 February 1577 it became removable ‘because it is expedient to the service of God’. It carried an annual stipend of 18,000 *réis*, with the obligation of serving as a beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) of the collegiate church.

The parish of Câmara de Lobos was the seat of one of the nine collegiate churches (see that entry) in this diocese, all of which were abolished shortly before 1834. The collegiate church of this parish was created in the third quarter of the 16th century and had, besides the vicar and the assistant priest (*coadjutor*), three beneficed clerics, a treasurer and a preacher. In 1676 the three posts of beneficed clerics were abolished, and their revenues were assigned to fund the vicarage of Serra de Água and the curacies of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos and Arco da Calheta, which were created in the same year.

Câmara de Lobos was one of the first places in Madeira to be put under cultivation immediately after the discovery. Many people from mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), settled there, raised families and founded large lines of descendants. Several people of noble origin held extensive lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and founded their entails and entailed estates there. Among them we may mention João Afonso (see that entry), a companion of Zarco, and João Caldeira the Elder, who gave his name to the locality still called Caldeira (‘cauldron’) today. Later João Salviati (see that entry), the founder of the Florença family, also held *sesmaria* grants there, as did João Saraiva, who gave his name to the locality that still bears his surname; Brás Gil de Faria, who had lands on the right bank of the Ribeira da Caixa (‘box stream’); Diogo Lopes da Estacada, who owned much land in the locality of Torre (‘tower’) that passed to the Correia family; and also Álvaro Figueira, among others. When we deal specifically with the chapels of this diocese, we shall name the founders of the many that existed in this parish, almost all of which were entailed foundations (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) and the seats of various entailed estates.

It was perhaps the parish in Madeira with the greatest number of chapels. Those of São Bernardino, Espírito Santo, Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora, Jesus-Maria-José, Our Lady of Nazaré, Our Lady of Prayers, Our Lady of the Good Death, Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, São Francisco, Our Lady of Pity, Nossa Senhora da Fátima and Nossa Senhora das Dores in the cemetery still exist today, while those of Our Lady of Bethlehem, São João and São Cândido, and others besides, have disappeared.

This parish was once home to the convent of Franciscan nuns of St Bernardino (*São Bernardino*). What remains is the old church, completely restored a few years ago, and some outbuildings, which housed a Minor Diocesan Seminary in the academic years from 1831 to 1833. It was then closed and incorporated into the Seminary of the Encarnação (*Seminário da Encarnação*; Incarnation).

On 4 March 1929, near the mouth of the Ribeira do Vigário, a great landslide fell into the sea. As the waves drew back, they violently swept away twenty people who were in the bed of the stream, and they lost their lives there.

Natives of this parish included Henrique Henriques de Noronha, genealogist (1667–1730); João Pedro de Freitas Pereira Drumond, lawyer and journalist (1760–1825); Francisco da Silva Barradas, lawyer and writer (1835–....); Father Dr José Gonçalves de Aguiar, theologian (1831–1895); and Joaquim Pestana, poet (1840–1909).

The convent of São Bernardino, to which we shall devote a separate article, stood in this parish. In it lived, in an eminent degree of holiness, the Franciscan friar Friar Pedro da Guarda, known as the Holy Servant of God, of whom we shall speak at greater length in the proper place.

This parish is one of the most important fishing centres in the archipelago, with some hundreds of people engaged in the arduous work of fishing. A considerable number of them live in a small quarter commonly known as Ilhéu, in sanitary conditions that leave much to be desired. Nevertheless, it is said that during the cholera epidemic of 1856 the disease never reached Ilhéu, which led the parish priest of the time to remark that the epidemic could not contend with the lack of cleanliness and hygiene in that quarter. Worship in the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception was maintained by the fishermen, and an old set of statutes (*compromisso*) of their confraternity contained certain clauses on the assistance to be given to its members in sickness and infirmity, amounting to a kind of mutual aid, which was highly praiseworthy.

If Madeira produces the most precious and celebrated wine in the world, it is in Câmara de Lobos that the vineyards supplying the raw material for that wine are found. It is one of the areas of the island where the land is best used for farming, and viticulture stands out above all other crops. The particular qualities of the soil, the climate, the good exposure and the shelter from the winds certainly contribute greatly to the wine of this parish being generally regarded as superior to that of the island’s other parishes, and to its fetching a more rewarding price on the market.

The mining engineer Eugenio Ackermann, in his book entitled *L’ile de Madère considerée au point de vue scientifique et economique*, published in 1910, states that he found in the locality of Ribeira da Alforra in this parish an iron ore of some importance, of which he made a summary analysis and to which he devotes several pages. Although E. Ackermann does not enjoy great scientific standing, what he says on this subject in the said work is nonetheless of interest.

The porous basalt that lends itself to working by the stonemason, known here as *cantaria rija* (hard dressed stone of vesicular basalt), is plentiful in some parts of this parish. It is widely quarried to make jambs, lintels and sills for doors and windows, stair treads, cornerstones, etc., which are extensively used in Madeiran buildings and houses.

The most notable localities of this parish are: Vila, Ilhéu, Espírito Santo e Calçada, Palmeira e Voltas, Pé do Pico, Serrado da Adega, Torre, Aldeia, Quinta do Leme, Saraiva, Jesus-Maria-José, Ribeiro Leal, Lourencinha, Panasqueira, Fajã, Caminho Grande e Preces, Ribeira da Caixa, Heras, Garachico, Nogueira, Caminho Grande e Ribeiro da Alforra, Pedregal, Ribeiro da Alforra e Fonte do Garcia, Rancho, Caldeira, Cruz da Caldeira e Facho and Fontainhas do Mar.

The parish of Câmara de Lobos is bounded to the north by the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, to the south by the ocean, to the east by the parishes of São Martinho and Santo António, and to the west by the parish of Quinta Grande.

Four main levadas (irrigation channels) water this parish: the Levada das Preces, the Levada do Castanheiro and the Levada da Serra, which rise in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, and the Levada Nova, which has its source in Curral das Freiras.

This parish has more than 9,000 inhabitants, although the last census (that of 1911) records only 7,810. Despite this population, it has only two state schools, one for each sex. The parish is linked to the city of Funchal by the best road on the island, a little over 9 kilometres long.
The poet Joaquim Pestana, whom we shall discuss elsewhere, was born in this parish.
Câmara de Lobos (municipality)

Although the cluster of houses that forms the most central and important part of the parish (*freguesia*) is commonly called the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), the truth is that the seat of this municipality (*concelho*) was never a town. It was simply a *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), the name formerly given to a settlement intermediate between a town and a parish. Madeira had the *lugares* of Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Faial, São Jorge, São Vicente, Porto Moniz and Caniço.

It was to the *lugar* of Câmara de Lobos that Gaspar Frutuoso was referring when he wrote: ‘Going a quarter of a *légua* west from the stream of Socorridos, there is a village called Câmara de Lobos, near the sea, which has a small cove and a cave where sea wolves slept and still sleep, from which the *lugar* took its name; and the captains of the island took that of Câmara, because the first captain, João Gonçalves Zarco, found them there when he first landed, as I have already said.

This village has some two hundred households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) and a single main street, very long, and at the end of it a very fine and well-kept church. It also has two sugar mills, one which belonged to António Correia and the other to Duarte Mendes, and many canes and vines of good Malmsey, and plenty of fruit of every kind, and much water’.

The municipality (*concelho*) of the same name, with its seat in the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Câmara de Lobos, was created in 1832, but it was never actually installed. Only after the establishment of constitutional government, in 1835, was this municipality created, and it was finally installed on 16 October of the same year. From its creation it comprised the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Lobos, Curral das Freiras and Campanário. In 1848 the new parish of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’) was formed from several localities detached from the parishes of Câmara de Lobos and Campanário, and the municipality of Câmara de Lobos gained this further parish, although its total area did not change at all. When the recent municipality of Ribeira Brava was created in 1914, the parish of Campanário became part of the new municipality and was detached from that of Câmara de Lobos. The coat of arms of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this municipality shows two seals, or monk seals, between which appears the shield of the arms of Portugal.
The municipal offices are housed in the Council’s buildings, in the locality known as Vila (‘town’).
Câmara de Lobos (landing place, quay and cove)

The so-called town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), seat of the parish (*freguesia*) and municipality (*concelho*) of the same name, faces a cove that is not very large but picturesque. It is bounded by a small beach of rounded pebbles and served by a landing quay, which was built in 1876 and considerably improved in 1903. This landing place sees relatively heavy traffic, because Câmara de Lobos is an important fishing centre, whose industry employs several hundred people. The steamers of the coastal shipping service call here. It lies 4 miles from the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal) and 3 from that of Campanário (‘bell tower’).
Ecclesiastical Chamber

This is the department through which all the religious and ecclesiastical business of this diocese passes. It must have been created in the very year the bishopric was created, that is, in 1514, and, after the customs house, it is the oldest public office existing in this archipelago.

The original salary of its clerk (*escrivão*) was three thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year. By royal decree (*alvará*) of 28 October 1564 it was raised to eight thousand *réis*, to which the department’s customary fees must certainly be added. We believe that its organisation was once very different from what it is today.

The archive of the ecclesiastical chamber held very valuable documents, not only for the history of the diocese but also for that of the Madeiran archipelago. A fire that broke out there towards the end of the 17th century destroyed almost all of these documents.

This ecclesiastical department has always been attached to the bishop’s residence. When, under the provisions of the Law of Separation, the lyceum (state secondary school) was installed in the bishop’s palace (*Paço Episcopal*) in January 1914, the ecclesiastical chamber had moved a few months earlier to a house opposite the former Seminary (*Seminário*), in Rua Júlio da Silva Carvalho, which belonged to the Seminary. In May 1918 it was installed in one of the outbuildings of the new bishop’s palace, on Largo do Ribeiro Real, next to the British cemetery.
Câmara (Francisco Gonçalves da)

He was the natural son of the third captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara. In the absence of his nephew Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, fifth donatary of this island, who lived at court most of the time, Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara governed the captaincy. His name remains tied to the weak defence and resistance he put up against the French attack on this island in 1566.

The author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) refers to him in the following laudatory terms: ‘he is a man most skilful in all his exercises of war, very temperate, of great virtue and little given to softness: he was brought up in hardship, away from the pleasures of his brethren, for which reason he endures toil well, and is a most valiant knight, as he showed when the French entered the city of Funchal, where, serving as Captain-General (as he then served and serves now) in the absence, and later upon the death, of his nephew, he most honourably wounded the French captain the Viscount of Pompador at the entrance to the Fortress, where he showed the spirit of a valiant captain; and for this the king gave him the habit with a certain pension (*tença*), and exempted him for eight years from paying the fifth and the tithe on his estate, a good part of which he holds in the *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) of Funchal, in sugars and wines. The learned annotator of the *Saudades* does not share Gaspar Frutuoso’s opinion, stating that Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, ‘in whose charge was the government of the island of Madeira, far from attacking, did not even know how to defend it from the aggressors: there was only, at the entrance to the city of Funchal and at the gate of the fortress of São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’), a clash of desperate defence and some illustrious feats of individual valour, which redeemed the good name of Madeira...’ The same annotator further adds that there were ‘rewards for the faint-hearted captain Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, who, in the moment of danger, went to take refuge among the women...’ Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara owned the *quinta* (country estate) now called Quinta das Cruzes, and lived there ‘in great and sumptuous halls’, in the words of Frutuoso.
Câmara (Jaime Sanches)

He was born in Funchal on 13 March 1881, the son of José António da Câmara and Dona Helena Celisa Gomes Câmara. He is assistant to the land registrar (*conservador do registo predial*) of the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal and has contributed a great deal of verse to various periodicals. For some years he was one of the directors of the *Almanach de Lembranças Madeirense*, and he has published the following books: *Poema Antigo*, Lisbon, 1907, 235 pp.; *Satyra, o funeral do Cyriaco*, Funchal, 1910, 15 pp.; *O Rufo*, Lisbon, 1914, 16 pp.; *Junia*, Lisbon, 1918, 22 pp.; *Fructos*, 1920; *Carta em prosa*, 1921; *Auto de Villões*, 1927.
Câmara (João Gonçalves da)

When João Gonçalves Zarco came to settle on this island soon after the discovery of Madeira, he brought with him, as members of his family, his wife, Dona Constança Rodrigues de Almeida, his eldest son, João Gonçalves da Câmara, and his daughter, Dona Helena Gonçalves da Câmara, both still of tender age.

The discoverer and 1st captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) died around 1467 and was succeeded in the captaincy of Funchal by his son João Gonçalves da Câmara. He must have been born in 1414, for Frutuoso states that he died in 1501 at the age of 87. While his father was still alive he fought valiantly in Africa, and was present at the siege of Asilah when this Moroccan stronghold was taken by Afonso V. On other occasions he went there to aid our fortresses when they were threatened by attacks from the Moors, rendering notable services and always giving proof of strenuous valour. He distinguished himself remarkably, together with his brother Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, in the defence of Ceuta, when the town was under siege and in danger of falling into the hands of the besiegers. When an expedition was organised to relieve the stronghold of Larache, to be led by John II, João Gonçalves da Câmara fitted out a fleet on this island at his own expense, which went to the Algarve to join the main body of the army. There the second captain-donatary of Funchal was received by the monarch with marks of such particular esteem and regard that, says an old chronicler, he even wished ‘that he should pour water over his hands at table, which at that time was one of the highest marks of consideration bestowed on a vassal’.

Shortly after he took over the government of his captaincy, while our country was at war with Spain, Madeira was attacked by a Spanish fleet of a good many ships carrying large numbers of armed men. Despite the scant means of defence at his disposal, João Gonçalves displayed such energy and gave such examples of extraordinary valour that he succeeded in putting the Castilians to flight. They then went on to attack the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), which they seized without the slightest resistance from its inhabitants. The captain-donatary went to Porto Santo to dislodge the Spaniards, who suffered considerable losses, hastily withdrew to their ships and sought, in headlong flight, to escape pursuit by the forces that had come from Madeira.

João Gonçalves da Câmara devoted himself tirelessly to the progress and prosperity of his donatary captaincy (*donataria*), and especially of its capital. Raised to the status of town (*vila*) in the last years of his father’s government or already during his own administration, it rapidly gained importance and grew, and soon became a notable centre of trade. It attracted a considerable number of foreigners, drawn to the young town of Funchal by the fame of its commercial and agricultural wealth.

The surname Câmara, used by the second donatary, derives from the well-known fact that the discoverer of Madeira found, on the coast of what later became the settlement and parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), a cave of sea wolves [monk seals], which gave their name to the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) and which strikingly marked Zarco’s first voyage of exploration along the island’s south coast. In 1460 Afonso V granted João Gonçalves da Câmara the following coat of arms: on a green field a silver tower with two merlons and a spire topped by a gold cross, and two wolves in their natural colour standing upright and rearing against the tower, with one of the wolves as the crest. The second captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) was thereafter called João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos, a surname his successors were also to use, but ‘this addition of the Lobos to the surname, as we read in an old manuscript, was gradually dropped over time, and only that of Câmara remained’.

He built up a great house, and on this subject we read somewhere ‘that it was a remarkable thing among the splendours of this magnificent man that, having spent great sums in the King’s service in the garrisons of Africa, on himself, on his sons and on the large reinforcements he sent there, on the marriages of his sons and daughters, on continual journeys to court, on the foundation of the monastery and on other works, he should be found at his death with twenty-two thousand seven hundred *cruzados* in unencumbered property, seven *contos* and four hundred thousand réis in real estate and two *contos* in movable goods...’, all of which represented, four centuries ago, a considerable fortune.

This second donatary of Funchal was the founder of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), begun in 1492. It was attached to the church of Conceição de Cima, later called Santa Clara, which the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco had ordered to be built as a family vault for himself and his descendants. Referring to the building of the convent, we find in an old manuscript, published a few years ago in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’), ‘that the work was so arranged that Zargo’s grave lay in the middle of the chancel, with a stone tomb above it so tall that it makes it singularly venerable and worthy of respect’.

It was also in the centre of the chapel, beside the steps of the high altar, that in March 1919 the grave of the second captain-donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara was discovered. Its dark marble tombstone bears in the centre this brief epitaph: ‘Grave of João Gonçalves da Câmara, second captain of this Island.’ He died in what was then the town of Funchal on 26 March 1501.
Câmara (João Gonçalves da)

He was the 4th captain-donatary of Funchal. He was born in that city in 1489, the son of the third donatary, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, and his first wife, Dona Joana Valente Castelo Branco. Like his parents and grandparents, João Gonçalves da Câmara distinguished himself remarkably in our campaigns in Morocco, in which so many Madeirans proved their valour and courage, and contributed, perhaps like no other Portuguese, to the expansion of our colonial dominion in North Africa. While his father was still alive he went to Africa several times, always giving proof of his bravery. Particular mention is due to the aid he gave to the expedition commanded by Jaime, Duke of Braganza, which, by order of King Manuel I, was bound for the taking of Azemmour. ‘And when four hundred sail were being fitted out in the Tagus for this expedition,’ says an old manuscript, ‘João Gonçalves da Câmara came in over the bar, sent by his father to take part in it with 800 men, 200 horse and 600 foot, in twenty-one ships. And because many retainers and kinsmen joined him in Lisbon to accompany him, the King, who had received him with great rejoicing and esteem, ordered him to be given two more ships and four caravels, with which he made up twenty-seven vessels of men at his own expense. Once the stronghold was taken, in which João Gonçalves da Câmara and the Madeiran noblemen Gaspar and Francisco Bettencourt, Pedro Gonçalves de Barros, Diogo de Barros and others performed prodigies of valour, the 4th captain-donatary of Funchal remained in Africa for some time, fighting the Moors and rendering to Dom

João de Meneses, commander of Azemmour, the most notable and distinguished services. In the following year, 1514, João Gonçalves returned once more to Africa with several hundred men, where he again proved his valour and gave important support to the attacks and raids that our men undertook against the Moors of Morocco. Besides the great services he rendered in person in our battles in Africa, he sent other aid there, such as the relief he dispatched to the stronghold of Mazagan in two ships commanded by Luís de Noronha, with fighting men, provisions and munitions, all fitted out and maintained at his own expense.

When Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, renounced the government of his captaincy in 1528 and withdrew to the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Matosinhos, where he died, his son João Gonçalves da Câmara took over its administration. He governed it through his *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) and representative, Francisco Jorge, until 1530, when, on his father’s death, he assumed the government of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*) in person. He ruled it for only a brief six years.

João Gonçalves da Câmara married Dona Leonor de Vilhena, daughter of Dom João de Meneses, Count of Tarouca. From this marriage were born Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, who succeeded to the donatary captaincy of Funchal; Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, the celebrated tutor of King Sebastian; and Martim Gonçalves da Câmara, minister of the same king, who held such great sway in affairs of state. We deal with each of them in this *Elucidário*.

‘Captain João Gonçalves da Câmara, says the manuscript already cited, was a man of sincere character, kindly, affable, charitable and most virtuous, and therefore much loved by all the people. He enjoyed the gentleness of his rule only briefly, for God took him at the age of 47, in the year 1536, and he died, as it was understood, of the plague, which was then raging most fiercely on the island.

As we say elsewhere, two tombstones were recently found in the chancel of the church of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*). The one in the middle of the chancel bears the epitaph of the 2nd captain-donatary of Funchal, and the one on the Epistle side carries two funerary inscriptions relating to the 3rd and 5th donataries (*donatário*), with some struck-through lines between them whose letters are completely illegible. It is very strange that, although the 4th captain-donatary died in Funchal and was buried in the church of the Convent of St Clare, the family vault of the captains-donatary, the stone that should cover his grave is not to be found there, nor can his epitaph be read on the tombstones of his father and grandfather.
Câmara (João Gonçalves da)

The 6th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, João Gonçalves da Câmara, was born in Lisbon in 1541, the son of the 5th donatary, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, and Dona Isabel de Mendonça. He came to Madeira with his parents when he was only a year old and returned to the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) at the age of fourteen. He came back to this island in 1566, only to leave at once for the mainland, from where he never returned and where he died in 1580.

In 1566 French corsairs attacked this island, causing the terrible plunder and slaughter that the Madeiran chronicles describe with such horror (see Sack of the French). The government in mainland Portugal then sent a fleet to Madeira to punish the pirates, but it reached Funchal a few days after they had sailed away, their ships crammed with the finest treasures they had found in the city. João Gonçalves da Câmara came with the fleet in command of a ship, without having been able to avenge the damage done to his captaincy by the corsairs’ sack. On the first expedition that King Sebastian made to Africa, João Gonçalves was one of the noblemen who accompanied him most closely, ‘with many tents, horses and servants, and he spent much of his own on it, wishing that an occasion might arise in which he could show the valour of his person’, as a chronicler of his own time states.

João Gonçalves da Câmara never assumed the government of his captaincy personally and directly. He was in Lisbon when his father died in Madeira on 4 March 1580, and he himself died three months later at Almeirim without having returned to the island. He had appointed as his lieutenant (*lugar-tenente*) and representative in the archipelago his uncle Rui Dias da Câmara, son of the 5th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) Simão Gonçalves da Câmara.

João Gonçalves da Câmara was the last captain-donatary of Funchal. His successors kept the honours of the office and continued to receive the substantial revenues from the privileges and prerogatives they enjoyed on the island, but they no longer had any direct say in most matters of public administration. Castilian rule, by appointing governors-general, reduced the jurisdiction and powers of the donataries to very limited proportions. It is true that for some time the donataries continued to appoint their own magistrates (*ouvidores*), but these did little more than collect the revenues, which were considerable. Among other things, these revenues included the rights over water and wind, which King Sebastian confirmed in 1576. An old manuscript states that the exclusive privilege over mills alone made the house of the donataries of Funchal one of the finest in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal).

We do not know whether Rui Dias da Câmara, or some other representative of the 6th donatary João Gonçalves, remained in charge of the captaincy after the latter’s death on 4 June 1580, until in 1582 the governor-general João Leitão, appointed by Philip II, took over the government and administration of the whole archipelago. It is really from this time that the power of the donataries was reduced to an almost honorary role, which Philippine despotism curtailed more and more until it abolished it completely.
Câmara (João Gonçalves da)

He was born in Portugal, the son of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara (see that entry), 3rd Count of Calheta (‘small cove’), and of Dona Maria de Vasconcelos. João Gonçalves da Câmara was the 4th Count of Calheta and is regarded as the 8th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. His possession of the captaincy was confirmed on 29 July 1623.
Câmara (João Rodrigues da)

In vol. II of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), 1866 edition, p. 227 ff., António Cordeiro writes at length about João Rodrigues da Câmara, eldest son of Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd captain-donatary of the island of São Miguel.
