João Rodrigues was born in Madeira and accompanied his father to São Miguel. He became the 4th captain of that island, succeeding Luís Gonçalves da Câmara in its donatary captaincy (*donataria*).
Câmara (Jorge da)

He was known as ‘the Poet’, but we do not know whether he actually wrote poetry. He was appointed governor-general of this archipelago on 18 January 1614 and took up the post on 17 December of the same year.
Câmara (José Bettencourt da)

He was born on 19 April 1844 at the Quinta do Descanso (‘estate of rest’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia, which belonged to his paternal grandfather, the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Tristão Joaquim Bettencourt da Câmara. He died in the parish of Câmara de Lobos on 19 October 1875, while travelling from Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) to this city, aged only 31. He contributed valuably to several newspapers and showed a remarkable talent for letters. He devoted himself above all to genealogical and heraldic studies and had a wide knowledge of the lineages of the old Madeiran families. Some of the notes in the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) dealing with genealogical subjects are his. He was preparing a valuable work on this subject, which he never completed.
Câmara Leme (Dom João Frederico da)
He was born in this city and belonged to one of the oldest and noblest families of Madeira, being the son of Dom João Frederico da Câmara Leme and Dona Maria Carolina Correia Pinto.

He followed a military career and held the rank of captain in the now-disbanded 12th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) Battalion, quartered in this city, when he was appointed civil governor of this archipelago on 25 January 1868. He took office on 10 February of the same year.

It was on the following 8 March that the regrettable popular riots broke out on the beach and around the customs house of this city, aimed at violently preventing the landing of the parliamentary candidate Jacinto de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos; we refer to them at greater length in a special article of this *Elucidário*.

He remained at the head of the district’s administration for only a few months, because when the ministry led by the Marquis of Loulé came to power, Câmara Leme was transferred to the civil government of Santarém, a post he did not accept.

By decree of 21 May 1870, Dom João Frederico da Câmara Leme was appointed civil governor of Madeira for the second time, taking office on the 27th of the same month and year. He left the administration of this district at the end of March 1876. He died in the city of Tomar on 6 February 1878. He was the brother of General Dom Luís da Câmara Leme and of Dom Jorge da Câmara Leme.
Câmara Leme (Dom Jorge da)

He was born in Funchal on 13 March 1807, and on 2 December 1826 he enlisted as a volunteer in the 1st Grenadier Company of the 4th Infantry Regiment. He was, however, discharged from the service shortly after the restoration of absolute government in Portugal. Having emigrated to England because of his liberal ideas, he went from there to the island of Terceira, where he enlisted in the 5th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) Battalion, which landed on the beaches of Mindelo on 8 July 1832. He served throughout the whole campaign for liberty, up to the Convention of Évora-Monte, by which time he held the rank of second lieutenant. He died on 8 July 1889, then a retired army lieutenant.
Câmara Leme (Dom Luís da)

Dom Luís da Câmara Leme, one of the most illustrious Madeirans of the 19th century, was born in this city on 26 March 1817, the son of Dom João Frederico da Câmara Leme and Dona Maria Carolina Correia Pinto. He belonged to an old and noble family of this archipelago and descended in a direct line from Garcia Homem de Sousa, one of the four noblemen whom Afonso V sent to Madeira to marry the daughters of the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco.

He enlisted in 1836 and was promoted to second lieutenant (*alferes*) the following year. In 1883 he reached the high rank of general of division, in which he retired in June 1884. He was one of the most distinguished army officers of his time. As head of department (*repartição*) at the Ministry of War, as a military writer and as the officer entrusted with important missions abroad, he rendered the most notable services to the Portuguese army. He took part in the reform and reorganisation of many military services, and his opinion on such matters was always heeded as that of a consummate authority on the subject.

He wrote *Elementos da Arte Militar*, in two volumes, which ran to two editions; *Considerações gerais ácerca da reorganização militar de Portugal*; *Relatorio apresentado ao ministro da guerra ácerca da aquisição de novas armas portateis*; and *Relatorio ácerca dos objectos militares mais notaveis apresentados na exposição universal de Paris de 1867*, besides other works and reports that he drafted but that were never published. *Elementos da Arte Militar* was regarded as a work of extraordinary merit, which at once earned him the standing of a distinguished military writer, not only in our country but also abroad.

Although his career as an army officer was remarkably distinguished, it seems that the most marked feature of his personality was that of the parliamentarian and politician. He was elected deputy without interruption for various constituencies from 1857 until 1878, when, by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 2 December of that year, he took his seat in the upper house as a life peer. He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislatures from 1857 to 1864 and in the legislative session from 1875 to 1878, always defending the most vital interests of his homeland with unalloyed dedication.
In 1870 he was minister of the navy and public works, and he later refused several times to join certain ministries.

Although he did not possess the gifts of a great tribune, he was nonetheless a speaker of easy and correct diction and sober language, with a profound knowledge of the subjects he addressed, and his words were always heard in the national assembly with the respect usually paid to great politicians and parliamentarians. The campaign he launched in parliament on ministerial responsibility, and sustained for years on end, became well known and notable. In it he displayed the lofty qualities of his exceptional intelligence and, perhaps even more, the dauntless independence of his character. For years in succession, bowed under the weight of advanced age and tormenting ailments, the old general and peer of the realm would still go to the upper house to defend his bill on ministerial responsibility, delivering speeches that became celebrated, some of which were published in a volume entitled *Incompatibilidades Politicas*.

Dom Luís da Câmara Leme received many Portuguese and foreign honours, and was a corresponding member of the Royal Academy of Sciences (*Academia Real das Sciencias*) and a member of various literary and scientific societies. Besides the writings listed above and his contributions to various reviews, he wrote an interesting monograph on the district of Lourenço Marques, which he entitled *Lourenço Marques. Estudo syntetico sobre o aspecto historico, politico e moral*.

As a tribute to his merits and in recognition of his services to the country and especially to the army, a subscription was opened among the military officers to acquire a commandery insignia or decoration to be presented to General Dom Luís da Câmara Leme in the name of the Portuguese army. The subscription raised eight *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis), and Câmara Leme asked that only half of this sum be applied to the purchase of the decoration and that the other half be used to help the poor widows of army officers.

As is well known, General Câmara Leme married first the celebrated actress Emília das Neves, whose fortune he inherited, and secondly Dona Ana de Albuquerque, a writer and also an actress. He died in Lisbon on 27 January 1904, at the advanced age of 86.
Câmara (Luís de Vasconcelos e)

Luís de Vasconcelos Câmara e Sousa was the 3rd Count of Castelo Melhor and the 6th Count of Calheta (‘small cove’). He was the son of Dona Mariana de Alencastre e Câmara, who is regarded as the 9th donatary of Funchal and who had married João Rodrigues de Vasconcelos, 2nd Count of Castelo Melhor. Luís de Vasconcelos should be regarded as the 10th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal.
Câmara (Martim Gonçalves da)

He was the son of João Gonçalves da Câmara, 4th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, and of Dona Leonor de Vilhena, and the brother of Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, whom we discuss elsewhere in this *Elucidário*. He must have been born at the beginning of the second quarter of the 16th century. We know nothing of his early years: the first acts of his public life of which we have any knowledge date from when he was about forty, with his appointment as rector of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*).

He was the Madeiran who attained the greatest influence and prestige in the sphere of public government. He was also one of the men in our country who enjoyed the widest powers and achieved the most absolute ascendancy over the mind of the monarch. It has been said that, apart from the Marquis of Pombal, perhaps no other public figure in Portugal had ever wielded his influence with the king, in his capacity as minister, as absolutely and despotically as Martim Gonçalves da Câmara.

Historians are almost unanimous in stating that he abused the power and prestige he held over the restless and fickle mind of King Sebastian. Pinheiro Chagas, who deals with him at length in vol. 4 of his *Historia de Portugal*, describes him as an extremely proud and despotic man and highlights his baneful role in many matters of public administration.

He was nonetheless a man of great intellectual stature, who knew how to command the admiration of his contemporaries. He held the highest offices, among them those of rector of the University, president of the
Board of Conscience and of the Desembargo (*Mesa da Consciência e do Desembargo*), overseer of justice (*vedor da justiça*) and others besides.

The post that won him great prestige and influence was that of king’s private secretary (*escrivão da puridade*, in effect chief minister), which was then the office of highest responsibility in the government of the state. Having fallen from the favour of King Sebastian, he withdrew to the house of the Society of Jesus, the Casa de São Roque (House of St Roch), in Lisbon, and there ended his days. He was a secular priest and a doctor of theology of the University of Coimbra.
Câmara (Father Luís Gonçalves da)

This Madeiran is the well-known and celebrated tutor of King Sebastian, whose qualities of character – and, in particular, the ascendancy he gained over the young monarch’s mind – have been judged in such different ways by our critics and historians. The enemies of the Society of Jesus, of which he was one of the most illustrious members, portray him as an unscrupulous and ambitious man who thought only of the aggrandisement of his order. They accuse him of having sought to encourage the excessively adventurous leanings of his pupil, which had as their sad epilogue the loss of Portuguese independence. There are others, among them the unimpeachable Manuel Bento de Sousa, who hold an entirely contrary opinion and do not blame the influence of Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara for the risky enterprises on which King Sebastian embarked. The author just cited says: ‘Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara was a good man. His gaze was turned to heaven, his thoughts to God, his inclinations to virtue. He was a believer, a saint, a mystic. In the higher offices of the Society he governed the fathers by peace and directed everything with gentleness, moving others by his sincere detachment from this world. As rector of the college of Coimbra he showed his subordinates nothing but meekness, and when, through discipline or as a test, he was lowered from rector to cook of the house, he bore the change with the most angelic patience. In the lands of the Moors he sacrificed his time, his rest and his health to the comfort of the captives. He lived in the dungeons and was adored by the prisoners, who prostrated themselves as he passed, kissing his habit and earnestly begging the solace of his presence. At court he gave rise to no complaint, requested no favour and found employment for no relative; and although it is said that it was he who introduced his brother Martim, and perhaps he did, it is certain that he left not a single proof of sharing in the latter’s ambitions and misgovernment. His disinterestedness went so far that he would neither eat nor sleep in the palace, so that the queen had to oblige him to do so...’
Luís Gonçalves da Câmara was born on this island in 1518, the son of João Gonçalves da Câmara, 4th

captain-donatary of Funchal, and of Dona Leonor de Vilhena, daughter of the Count of Tarouca. In a year we cannot now determine, he enrolled at the University of Paris, which was then a very important centre of European intellectual life and drew a considerable number of students from every country to its celebrated courses, whose reputation at that time was universal. There Luís da Câmara proved a student of extraordinary talent, not only in Latin, Greek and Hebrew but also in the courses of philosophy and theology, in which he distinguished himself remarkably. When John III reformed the University of Coimbra and brought several professors from France to teach in our universities, Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara was one of those chosen to join the teaching staff of our foremost seat of learning, where he held various chairs.

He resolved to join the Society of Jesus, and within this order he held high offices. He had known the founder of the Society personally in Paris and later formed the closest friendship with him; but it was in Coimbra, while teaching at the university, that he entered the Jesuit congregation, making his profession on 2 April 1546. The following year he was appointed rector of the College of Coimbra, and three years later he went to Rome on business for his order. There, in the company of Ignatius of Loyola and other important figures, he gained great prestige and displayed his rare gifts of intellect. In the capital of the Catholic world he was chosen as superior of the Jesuits’ professed house and as visitor (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) of the order in Portugal and Spain.

On returning to his homeland he was appointed confessor to Prince João, father of King Sebastião, and later tutor to that monarch, a post he held for some years. On this subject the author already cited says: ‘His qualities as a virtuous priest were, in the time of Sebastião, the same that everyone had recognised in him when they had earlier sought him out as confessor to John III, overriding his wishes, which were only to live in the seclusion of his cell. His pupil grew so attached to him that losing him was the greatest sorrow of his life. That king without affections, who esteemed no one in this world with sincerity of heart, wept for only two people: Father Câmara and Dom Álvaro de Castro... Great must have been the master’s gifts to achieve this wholly moral seduction, which lacked even the aid of physical attractions, which help so much. Father Câmara was exceedingly ugly, a stammerer and blind in one eye.’ It was doubtless for this reason that Pinheiro Chagas asserts that he prevailed through the power of his intellect alone. The affection, however, that he inspired in his royal pupil, in his subordinates at Coimbra and in the captives in Morocco cannot in any way have been won by the force of intellect alone.

Historical works, including those of Pinheiro Chagas, commonly assert that Luís Gonçalves da Câmara exercised a baleful influence on the mind of Sebastião. Manuel Bento de Sousa contradicts this in the following terms: ‘it was the great Marquis of Pombal... who in his indictment of the Jesuits heaped up every fault that imagination could invent..., it was he who gave most currency to this inaccuracy, making Father Câmara a corrupter of the young king in the interests of the order.’ Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara died in Lisbon on 15 March 1575, aged 57.
Câmara (Paulo Perestrelo da)

He was born in Funchal in 1810 and died in the city of Rio de Janeiro on 4 February 1854. We have little information for his biography. We know only, from the testimony of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, who dealt with Perestrelo da Câmara in person for years, that he lived for a long time in Lisbon and that in 1841 he sailed for Brazil. He returned from there in 1853 and, after a short stay in Europe, went back once more to Rio de Janeiro, where he died a few months later.

He devoted himself to a literary career and, as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo observes, ‘wrote no little, but in haste and perhaps from memory; for that reason the form of his works is neglected and inaccuracies are frequent. The author of the *Diccionario Bibliographico Portuguez*, in many places in his work, points out numerous errors and shortcomings in the writings of Perestrelo da Câmara, especially in the *Diccionario geographico, historico, politico, etc.*, which would have been a very useful work had its compilation shown more diligence and more care in the study of the subjects it treats.

Nevertheless, Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara cannot be denied talent, learning, a capacity for work and a clear aptitude for literary pursuits. Among the works he published are the following: *Descripção Geral de Lisboa...*, Lisbon, 1839, iv + 190 pp.; *Breve Noticia sobre a Ilha da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1841, 136 pp.; *Novo tratado de arithmetica comercial...*, Rio de Janeiro, 1846, vi + 324 pp.; *Collecção de proverbios, adagios, anexins, sentenças moraes e idiotismos da lingua portugueza*, Rio de Janeiro, 1848, vi + 288 pp.; *Grammatica das grammaticas da lingua Portuguêza*, Rio de Janeiro; *Diccionario geographico, historico, politico...*, Rio de Janeiro, 1850, vols I and II, 495 and 612 pp.; and others besides.
Câmara Pestana (Dr Luís da)

He was born in Funchal on 28 October 1863, in the street that now bears his name, in the part of it that belongs to the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé. He was the son of Jacinto Augusto Pestana, former chief officer of the department of the secretariat of the civil government of this district, and of Dona Helena Ana da Câmara Pestana, who belonged to an old and distinguished Madeiran family.

He attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city and, after completing his preparatory studies at the Polytechnic School, enrolled in 1884 at the Medical-Surgical School of Lisbon, which he was later to honour so greatly as one of its most eminent professors.

A talented and most diligent student, he enjoyed the highest regard of professors and fellow students alike. Through his extreme kindness and remarkable qualities of character, he gathered around his name a true aura of esteem and affection, which time only increased, until it reached the proportions of genuine adoration.

The thesis he chose to defend at the end of his medical course was entitled *O microbio do carcinoma*. This study already revealed his inclination towards laboratory work, in which he was later to distinguish himself so notably.

Having completed his studies on 24 July 1889, he at once began various investigations in the speciality to which he later devoted himself entirely, and which remained, to the end of his life, the most absorbing aspiration of his mind.

Shortly afterwards, when the great parliamentarian António Cândido was Minister of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), the government decided to send a physician abroad to study the much-vaunted results of Robert Koch’s tuberculin, which had even been called the greatest discovery of recent centuries. Let us see what a newspaper of the time said on the matter: ‘Here, the excitement had spread with an intensity proportional to the large number of consumptives who loom so large in our pathology; and so great and so intense was the stir that it reached even the highest spheres of the state, as a rule indifferent to these petty matters of life or death. It must be said that the emotion of so many people condemned to death could not have found a better conductor to those high spheres than the artistic spirit of the then Minister of the Kingdom. António Cândido was the very negation of the politician, the finest praise that can be given to anyone who has ever taken part in our politics. It had been decided to send someone to Paris or Berlin to establish what was positive in the announced marvel. On the appointment, António Cândido consulted two men eminent for their standing in our medical world and for their worthy and respected characters, Professors Sousa Martins and Ferraz de Macedo. Only one name was put forward: that of Pestana. And despite the friction that arose, in January 1891 Pestana left for Paris, charged with studying bacteriology wherever and however he wished, and with establishing what was known of Robert Koch’s alleged discovery.

In Paris, Pestana hardly left the laboratories and hospitals. In the mornings he followed Potain’s clinic, then moved on to Cornil’s laboratory, where he attended Chantemesse’s course in bacteriology. When this course ended, he went to the Pasteur Institute, where he learned the methods of anti-rabies inoculation from the great master, completing his training in the laboratory of Strauss, where he began his work on tetanus toxins’.

Such was the importance of this work that on 27 June 1891 Professor Strauss, of the Paris faculty of medicine, presented Pestana at a session of the Society of Biology, where he delivered his paper, which was unanimously applauded and praised. It remains to be said that, although the Portuguese government subsidised him for only 4 months, Pestana stayed on in Paris, completing at his own expense and personal sacrifice the studies he considered indispensable for his professional training.

On returning from his mission abroad, Câmara Pestana thought only of devoting himself entirely to the work for which he had a decided vocation. From the outset he conceived the idea of bringing his country, albeit on a modest scale, into the extensive research being carried out everywhere in the new science of bacteriology. In Portugal this research was known only through foreign treatises and journals, and no laboratory work of any note had yet been done here.

He had talent, aptitude and an enthusiasm bordering on fanaticism in abundance, enough to devote himself to serious bacteriological research and draw the most fruitful results from it. Alone and without any official support, however, he could not even begin small experiments, which still required various instruments, microscopes, incubators, etc., without which no attempt could possibly succeed.

It was the Lisbon Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica de Lisboa*), aware of Dr Câmara Pestana’s rare merits and specialist knowledge, that persuaded the government to appoint him bacteriology demonstrator at the School. This came only after various official bodies had raised the greatest difficulties, which were finally overcome by the tenacity of the teaching staff of that institution of higher education.

The means given to Câmara Pestana and the instruments at his disposal were inadequate for the important research to which he wished to devote himself. Yet his iron will and his intense, persevering work meant that in a single year six inaugural theses inspired by him were prepared, in addition to other notable original work of his own.

To close the year of his research and analyses at the Medical School, Câmara Pestana gave a lecture at the Society of Medical Sciences (*Sociedade das Ciências Médicas*) reporting on his work, particularly on tetanus, which he had begun in Paris and continued in Lisbon.

That lecture, a fine study in general pathology, brings to the fore the creation of a new therapeutic method, allowing the cure of diseases which, like tetanus, are caused by poisoning of the organism by the products of microbes. Pestana turned this dreamed-of fantasy into reality, presenting at his lecture a rabbit that withstood the most violent inoculations of the tetanus bacillus.

The Bacteriological Institute was about to be created in Lisbon, where our illustrious fellow countryman achieved his greatest triumphs and succeeded in inscribing his name in letters of gold in the annals of medical science.
We shall draw on what a journal of the time published on the matter, which relates with complete fidelity the circumstances of the institute’s foundation.

‘The happiest day of Pestana’s life was drawing near; destiny was about to give him a complete laboratory, where he could live for his microbes and his work. He owed it to the waters of Lisbon and to the initiative, irreproachable in this respect, of Mr José Dias Ferreira. The alarm caused in Lisbon by reports that the water was contaminated with virulent agents, the sudden rise in cases of typhoid fever in Lisbon and its surroundings, and the urging of the public health board and the press led the Minister of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) to conclude that a rigorous scientific examination of Lisbon’s water was indispensable.
The analyst was self-evident; the minister already knew him from the petition he had read, and the medical public named him without dissent.

By a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 21 October 1892, Pestana was charged with analysing the water in Lisbon. There was nothing that could serve for this research: no assistants, no premises, no apparatus, no materials. In 15 days everything was ready. The laboratory was improvised in a building of the Hospital de São José (St Joseph), adjoining the old ward of Santo Onofre and rapidly adapted to its new purpose. The apparatus ordered from abroad at great speed arrived in successive consignments; the last, of course, were those that had come through official channels, and the first those ordered by private individuals. The assistant was chosen by Pestana, who knew him from his work at the Medical School: Mr Aníbal Bettencourt, a Pestana of sorts, a gifted microbe-maniac, as modest and disinterested as his director. To say that in all these installations Pestana, who had carte blanche for expenses, confined himself to what was strictly indispensable would be to suppose that the joy of owning a laboratory could cloud his generous faculties and lead him to act otherwise.’

The Bacteriological Institute of Lisbon was created by decree of 29 December 1892, and our illustrious fellow countryman Dr Luís da Câmara Pestana was appointed its director. He devoted his laborious life entirely to the progress and good name of that scientific establishment. The work done there was soon highly praised abroad, and the eminent physician gained standing as one of the most distinguished practitioners of bacteriology. His research and laboratory work were always the chief preoccupation of his mind, so much so that in him it became true fanaticism, of which he gave the most eloquent proof until a few moments before he lost his life.

On this research and work, much of it of great scientific value, he published various articles and papers in *Medicina Contemporânea*, the *Revista de Medicina e Cirurgia*, the *Archivo de Medicina* and other journals, which earned him the highest praise. Among them we single out *Etiologia da febre typhoide*, *Considerações sobre o diagnostico da diphtheria* and *Sorotherapia da diphtheria*.

In collaboration with Dr Aníbal Bettencourt he wrote *Contribuição para o estudo bacteriologico da epidemia de Lisboa* and *Tratamento da raiva em Portugal pelo systema Pasteur*, in the *Revista de Medicina e Cirurgia*; *Duas pequenas epidemias de febre typhoide*, in the same journal; and various works in German on the Lisbon epidemic of 1894, the leprosy bacillus, etc., as well as, in Portuguese, the report on the bacteriological analysis of Lisbon’s drinking water. He also published as separate pamphlets his inaugural and competition dissertations at the Lisbon Medical School and a study on tetanus.

His work earned him a great reputation abroad. He was elected a member of important scientific societies and was honoured with the particular esteem and regard of several foreign scholars, who referred to him in the most laudatory terms in various writings. The name he had won in the annals of science through his studies and persevering work naturally marked him out for university teaching, and he entered the competitive examination for the post left vacant at the Lisbon Medical School by the death of the eminent professor Sousa Martins. This examination, which was a brilliant one, amply confirmed the fame that preceded him; he presented as his thesis a remarkable study entitled *Sorotherapia*, and was then appointed substitute professor (*lente substituto*) of the School by decree of 12 May 1898. There he taught the chairs of pathological anatomy and forensic medicine with great proficiency, and his death deprived this institution of higher education of one of its most distinguished professors.

Dr Luís da Câmara Pestana was a physician at the Hospital de São José, where he rendered excellent service. On 17 December 1899 he began to serve there on an interim basis as duty surgeon, and he was appointed to the post permanently, by competitive examination, on 4 December 1890; in May 1895 he moved to the staff of supernumerary surgeons of the same hospital.

Besides his scientific mission abroad, to which we have already referred, he carried out various public service assignments. The last of these was to go to Porto to study, with the director of the municipal station and some foreign physicians, the value of sera against plague. It was in that city, while devoting himself to these studies, that he contracted the germ of the fatal disease.

It was after his return to Lisbon from his journey to Porto that the symptoms of the terrible disease appeared. The efforts of science and of his devoted colleagues and friends were powerless to overcome it, and he died at the Hospital de Arroios, where he had been isolated, on 15 November 1899, at about midday. He had been killed by his love of science and his devotion to humanity.

The tragic circumstances of his premature death, which echoed mournfully throughout the country and caused the deepest emotion, are still too fresh in everyone’s memory for us to attempt to describe them now, as we set down the principal biographical notes on our ill-fated fellow countryman, former schoolfellow and friend.

This was done, eloquently and movingly, in words reproduced by all the newspapers of the day, by his devoted friend and fellow worker Dr Belo de Morais. Becoming the ‘panegyrist of death’, he drew heartfelt tears from those who read those stirring pages, filled with the most vivid and striking reality.
The expressions of grief were extraordinary everywhere, and many official bodies and countless private individuals joined in them, from the humblest citizen to the supreme head of the State.

A few moments after Câmara Pestana’s death, Carlos I wrote the following letter to the then President of the Council of Ministers: ‘My dear José Luciano. I have this very moment learnt the most sad news of Pestana’s death. It is my wish that, as soon as the chambers meet, my government should present to the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) a bill granting a pension to the mother and daughter of the learned professor Pestana, glorious victim of his arduous duty.
And I wish it to be so, because it is for the Nation to pay homage to the memory of one who, in life, did it so much honour. Your true friend, THE KING’.

Among the tributes paid to the memory of the illustrious physician was the naming of the Lisbon Bacteriological Institute, by decree of 10 August 1902, as the ‘Real Instituto Bacteriológico Câmara Pestana’.

Here in Madeira, the memory of this distinguished man of science is happily perpetuated in the ‘Manicómio Câmara Pestana’ (Câmara Pestana Asylum), whose foundation is due to the initiative and diligent efforts of various gentlemen of this city, who wished the name of the illustrious Madeiran to be inseparably linked with the existence of that hospital (see Manicómio Câmara Pestana). In the garden, in front of the building, stands a bronze bust of Câmara Pestana on a marble column; he gave his name to that mental hospital. The Municipal Council of Funchal renamed the street containing the house where he was born from Pretas to Câmara Pestana.

A marble plaque was placed on this house, bearing the following inscription recording the fact: House where the eminent Portuguese bacteriologist Dr Luís da Câmara Pestana was born on 28 October 1863 (XXVIII October MDCCCLXIII); he died in Lisbon on 15 November 1899 (the XV day of November MDCCCXCIX), a victim of the bubonic plague that infested the city of Porto, to whose study he devoted himself with the greatest self-sacrifice and humanitarian altruism. Tribute of the medical profession of Madeira. 1913.

The unveiling of this plaque, a particularly splendid occasion, took place on 15 November 1913, the fourteenth anniversary of Câmara Pestana’s death. It was the Madeiran physicians who took the initiative for this tribute to their distinguished colleague and illustrious, ill-fated fellow countryman.
It is the only inscribed stone plaque in the streets of this city.
Camara Pestana (João da)

He is the brother of the late bacteriologist Dr Luís da Camara Pestana and was born in Funchal on 17 October 1871. An agronomist, he has held the post of Director-General of Agriculture. He was elected deputy for Madeira on 13 November 1913, but resigned his seat in May of the following year, having been elected senator for another constituency. He has contributed to various agricultural journals and is a member of the Portuguese Society of Natural Sciences (*Sociedade Portuguesa de Sciencias Naturais*), in whose bulletin he wrote the following articles: *La Gangrène humide de la racine du Chataignier* (vol. II, 1907) and *Destruction du Lecanium hesperidum L. par le Sporotrichum globuliferum Spegazzini* (vol. 2, 1908).
Regional Chamber of Agriculture

It was created by article 145 of the law of 9 July 1913 and abolished when the agricultural services were reorganised in May 1918. It held its first session (the inaugural one) on 16 February 1914 and its last on 16 June 1917.
Câmara (Rui Gonçalves da)

He appears to have been the first of João Gonçalves Zarco’s children to be born in Madeira, and he was the second son of the illustrious discoverer of this archipelago. He must have been born at the end of the first or the beginning of the second quarter of the 15th century. He is therefore the earliest of all the Madeirans whose names shine in the chronicles of this island. Rui Gonçalves da Câmara accompanied his brother João Gonçalves, the 2nd donatary of Funchal, to Africa, where he greatly distinguished himself as a valiant knight in the various skirmishes and encounters in which he took part. Accompanying Henry the Navigator and the Infante Ferdinand at the sieges of Asilah and Tangier, he likewise proved his valour, becoming widely known for his many acts of bravery and courage.

Rui Gonçalves da Câmara owned one of the largest properties on this island, if not the largest: the Lombada da Ponta do Sol (see that entry), which ran from the sea to the uplands and stretched from the Ribeira da Caixa (‘box stream’) to the Ribeira da Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). In 1473 he leased this property to João Esmeraldo for six hundred thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash and a perpetual quit-rent (*foro*) of one hundred and fifty thousand *réis* a year.

João Soares de Albergaria, 2nd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of the island of São Miguel, accompanied his wife to Madeira, where she died. According to Father António Cordeiro, he wished to thank João Gonçalves Zarco and his son Rui Gonçalves da Câmara for the generous hospitality they had shown him, and so resolved to sell his donatary captaincy (*donataria*) to Rui Gonçalves. He sold it so cheaply, Frutuoso adds, that he let it go for ‘eight hundred thousand réis in money and four thousand *arrobas* of sugar’.
It appears that the sale of the Lombada was intended to fund the purchase of the captaincy of São Miguel, where Rui Gonçalves da Câmara took up residence in 1474.

Rui Gonçalves, says the author of ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), ‘was a tall man, stout of body, yet discreet, and most diligent in having the land settled and cared for, going out in person to visit it... and he divided the greater part of the lands under the pact or title of *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation)’. After twenty-two years governing his donatary captaincy, he made his will in 1497, naming as his successor his natural son João Gonçalves da Câmara. He died shortly afterwards and was buried in the mother church (*igreja matriz*) of Vila Franca.

Rui Gonçalves da Câmara married Dona Maria de Bettencourt in Madeira. She founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Água de Mel (see Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*)), and he had no children by her. He took to São Miguel three natural sons he had fathered in Madeira. The eldest, who succeeded to the donatary captaincy, was the founder of the families of the counts of Vila Franca and of the counts and marquises of Ribeira Grande.
Câmara (Rui Gonçalves da)

He was one of the most distinguished of our soldiers who served in India. The chronicles that deal with our struggles in the East speak of him in the highest terms of praise. He was captain of the stronghold of Hormuz and distinguished himself remarkably at the taking of Cahul. In ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), Gaspar Frutuoso recounts some of his most notable feats of arms.

This Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, who should not be confused with the son of João Gonçalves Zarco and captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of the island of São Miguel, was a son of João Gonçalves da Câmara, 4th donatary of Funchal, and a brother of Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara and of Martim Gonçalves da Câmara.
Câmara (Simão Gonçalves da)

Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, was born in the old town (*vila*) of the same name. He was the son of the second donatary, João Gonçalves da Câmara, and of Maria de Noronha, and the grandson of the illustrious discoverer of Madeira. As a second son who took his mother’s surname, he was known as Simão de Noronha, a name he changed to Simão Gonçalves da Câmara when he assumed the government of the captaincy, on pain of losing it, by the express order of the monarch. In the books of nobility and the old Madeiran chronicles he is commonly called Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the Magnificent, for his liberality, the lavish life he led and the generosity with which he rewarded the services rendered to him.

Following the example of his father and grandfather, he showed the most outstanding valour and courage in our long campaigns in Morocco, and he was certainly the Madeiran who distinguished himself most notably in the frequent and fierce encounters with the Moors. His part was not limited to joining expeditions and fighting actively in battles and skirmishes. By fitting out many ships, raising numerous armed men on foot and on horseback, and sending abundant supplies of war, provisions and other aid, all at his own expense, he contributed, as perhaps no other subject of the time did, to upholding the prestige of the Portuguese name in Africa.

Some of the actions in which he made his name through his bravery and military genius deserve special mention, as does the aid he promptly gave to various African strongholds that were in danger of falling to the Moors. It was in performing these signal services that he went to North Africa nine times, always with the greatest disinterest and self-denial, neither seeking nor demanding any royal grant or reward, as was so usual in those times. John II and Manuel I, says Pinho Leal, owed him in large part the preservation of the Portuguese strongholds in Africa.

While his father was still alive, and when he was in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), John II asked him to relieve the stronghold of Asilah. He responded promptly with a force of three hundred men, armed, equipped and maintained at his own expense during the six months they remained in Africa. Another important relief was the one he gave to Diogo de Azambuja, governor of Safi, who, after taking that stronghold, found himself in imminent danger of losing it. When Azambuja turned to Simão Gonçalves, the latter sent him three hundred armed men within three days, and shortly afterwards went in person at the head of another nine hundred, whom he maintained and provisioned during the three months they stayed there. The help he gave in the capture of Azemmour was also considerable. For this great expedition, commanded by Jaime, Duke of Braganza, Simão Gonçalves sent his son João Gonçalves da Câmara with 600 foot soldiers and 200 horsemen. Among them was a large number of Madeiran noblemen, who were among those who most distinguished themselves in the celebrated capture of Azemmour.

We would go too far if we tried to describe in detail the various battles in which Simão Gonçalves da Câmara fought on the fields of Morocco, and the great deeds of bravery and heroism he performed there. Frutuoso and several other chroniclers recount some of these glorious actions minutely. We shall say only that at Safi, Azemmour, Asilah, Castelo Real, Cape Ghir, Mazagan, Ceuta and Tangier he always boldly showed the strength of his arm and the unbreakable courage of his spirit.

Among the displays of pomp and grandeur that adorned the ostentatious life of Simão Gonçalves, one stands out, not so much for its intrinsic value as for its singular originality: the gift he made to Pope Leo X. This illustrious pontiff, who gave his name to his century, had as his private secretary Bishop Dom Manuel de Noronha, son of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, who enjoyed great prestige and influence in Rome. The offering could be regarded as an embassy, and it was presented to the pontiff by Dom Manuel de Noronha. The ambassador, or bearer of the gift, was a Madeiran *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) named João de Leiria. He was accompanied by Vicente Martins, a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), who, being deeply versed in Latin, delivered a brilliant oration in that language in the presence of the great pontiff. Other persons, and many servants dressed in the Portuguese fashion in black velvet, made up this remarkable retinue.

Besides a costly Persian horse, ‘many fuchsias and trinkets from the island’ and other objects, the offering consisted chiefly of the Sacred College, made entirely of *alfenim* (white sugar paste for modelling figures) and life-size, which aroused the most extraordinary admiration in the capital of the Catholic world. We cannot now establish with complete accuracy how many cardinals the Sacred College then comprised; at present, and since the end of the 16th century, it numbers 72. At the time of Simão Gonçalves’s embassy, which took place in the first quarter of that same century, it cannot have been much smaller. The sugar industry had by then reached a very great development here, and it seems also a remarkable and rare perfection. This allowed Simão Gonçalves to have so many graceful figures made, which, the chronicles say, suffered not the slightest damage and arrived ‘unbroken right into Rome’.

It was under the government of this third captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) that Madeira reached a high degree of prosperity. It became a notable commercial and agricultural emporium, attracting many outsiders, who settled on the island in large numbers, founded families there and grew rich. The importance and growth of what was then the town (*vila*) of Funchal led to its elevation to the rank of city, a privilege granted by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 17 August 1508. The diocese was also created in 1514, by the papal bull of 12 June of that year.

It was in this period that King Manuel I had the magnificent Cathedral (the Sé) built, today a National Monument (*monumento nacional*), and presented to it the precious cross still preserved there. Also by order of the same monarch, the building of our customs house was erected, whose ground floor displays the characteristic lines of Manueline architecture.

When the king sent the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) Diogo Taveira to Madeira to investigate certain irregularities committed in the government of the captaincy, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara considered himself gravely injured in the privileges and exemptions he enjoyed as donatary of Funchal. He resolved to leave the country and settle in Spain. Forced by the hazards of the voyage to put in at the Algarve, he learned there of the perilous straits in which our African stronghold of Asilah found itself, and at once went to its relief, compelling the besiegers to raise the siege. As he was preparing to continue towards his destination, he received from the monarch the satisfaction that his offended dignity demanded, and returned without delay to the government of his donatary captaincy (*donataria*). This episode, set out in great detail, provided the subject of one of the chapters of the interesting book by Inácio de Vilhena Barbosa entitled
*Virtudes Civicas e Domesticas.*

Feeling old and weary, Simão Gonçalves gave up the government of his captaincy, which passed to his son and successor João Gonçalves da Câmara, and retired to the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Matosinhos, near Porto. There he died at the beginning of 1530, having directed in his will that his mortal remains be taken to this island and laid in the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), in the family vault of his parents and grandparents. ‘Not many years passed, says an old book of Madeiran historical matters, before this clause of his will was fulfilled, and when the coffin with his bones was landed in Funchal, a most solemn funeral procession was made for him from the beach to the said Convent, accompanied by the cathedral chapter of canons, the clergy and the religious who were in the land, and his obsequies were held with the greatest solemnity, the whole people accompanying and attending with many tears, for he was much loved by all.

The mortal remains of Simão Gonçalves were laid in the chancel of the church of the Convent of St Clare. There, in March 1919, on the Epistle side, the tombstone covering them was discovered, and in the centre of its dark marble this epitaph can be read: Tomb of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara.......3rd captain of this island. Here lies Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of Calheta (‘small cove’) and fifth captain of this island.

The inscription shows that beneath this gravestone lie the remains of the 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, and also those of the 5th captain of the same name and 1st Count of Calheta, whom we discuss in this *Elucidário*. We should note that two lines of the transcribed epitaph are marked off in quotation marks, a circumstance for which we cannot give a full explanation.

The 2nd and 3rd captains-donatary of Funchal appear as important characters in the historical novel *A Filha de Tristão das Damas* and in the play *Guiomar Teixeira*, by the Madeiran writer Major J. Reis Gomes.
Câmara (Simão Gonçalves da)

Simão Gonçalves da Câmara was the 5th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. He was born in that town (*vila*) on 2 September 1512, the son of the 4th donatary, João Gonçalves, and of Dona Leonor de Vilhena, daughter of Dom João de Meneses, Count of Tarouca.

Before taking over the government of his captaincy, he performed various feats of arms, which the chronicles of the time record with praise. Special mention is due to the relief he brought in 1533 to our fortress of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), at Cape Ghir in Africa.

The fortress was besieged by the Moors and in danger of being taken, and its defenders asked for prompt help to be sent to them from Madeira. Simão Gonçalves, with his father’s permission, at once invited the leading noblemen of the island and organised an expeditionary force of 600 men. He embarked without delay in six ships with all the munitions of war and provisions he could quickly gather, and he did all this at his own expense, without asking for any reward. The stronghold was in its last extremity when Simão Gonçalves da Câmara arrived there, and he succeeded in routing the Moors and inflicting a complete defeat on them. His stay in the fortress did not end there, for he also had the walls repaired and other important defensive works carried out, to guard against future assaults by the Moors. King John III wrote a most honourable letter to Simão Gonçalves, thanking him for the notable services he had rendered and praising him for the feat of arms he had performed in the defence of the castle of Santa Cruz.

Shortly after the death of his father, and after inheriting the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), Simão Gonçalves da Câmara left for Lisbon, where he stayed for some years. He returned to Madeira already married and with his eldest son, still of tender age, who was to succeed him in the captaincy. On the subject of the marriage, Gaspar Frutuoso relates that he wished to marry only with the monarch’s approval, and that he did so with Dona Isabel de Mendonça, of the household of Queen Catherine. He adds ‘that on the last day of September the contracts were drawn up, and with her went a great dowry estimated at eighty thousand *cruzados*, which the king gave him in annuities, in ready money and in offices; and besides this the captain’s house was twice exempted from the Mental Law (Lei Mental, restricting inheritance of crown grants to male heirs), a thing rarely granted; and on the fourth day of the month of October the captain was married to her, and he brought her to his house accompanied by the whole court, with Prince Dom Luís on her right and the Archbishop of Lisbon on her left, together with all the noblemen of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) who were present’. In 1555 he returned to the Kingdom with his whole family ‘for certain reasons that moved him to it’, in the words of the chronicler already cited, leaving his uncle Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara as captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal.

It was during the interim government of this captain-donatary that French corsairs attacked and sacked the city of Funchal in 1566, perpetrating the terrible slaughter of which the old Madeiran chronicles speak with such horror. Simão Gonçalves da Câmara at once sent his son and successor to Madeira with prompt relief, accompanying the fleet that the government in Lisbon dispatched in pursuit of the French. By the time they reached Funchal, however, the corsairs had already left, taking with them sixteen ships laden with the richest treasures they had found here.

Simão Gonçalves spent most of his time at court, where he was held in great esteem, and in 1574 he accompanied King Sebastian on his first expedition to Africa. By a royal decree (*alvará*) of 20 August 1576 he was granted the title of Count of Calheta (‘small cove’), not only in recognition of his own services but chiefly of those rendered by his forebears, and also because he was the head of so great and important a house. He styled himself: Count Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, of the Council of the King Our Lord, Captain and Governor of Justice in the island of Madeira and in the jurisdiction of Funchal, Overseer of His Majesty’s revenues throughout that island and in Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), Lord of the Desertas Islands, etc. ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that, besides various rights and exemptions, he had an income of four *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos), which, four centuries later, would today correspond to a very considerable sum.

He returned to Madeira, in what year is not known, and was in Funchal in 1578 when he suffered a stroke; he died on 4 March 1580. He was buried in the chancel of the church of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), as the tombstone recently discovered shows: ‘Tomb of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara.......3rd captain of this island. Here lies Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of Calheta and fifth captain of this island.’

João Gonçalves da Câmara, whom his father had sent to Madeira at the time of the sack by the French corsairs, was the 2nd Count of Calheta. He enjoyed this honour only briefly, however, for he died three months after his father. The countship and the rights of donatary of Funchal passed to his son, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, seventh captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) and 3rd Count of Calheta. He married Dona Maria de Vasconcelos e Meneses, lady-in-waiting to the queen and heiress daughter of Rui Mendes de Vasconcelos, 1st Count of Castelo Melhor. In this way the countship of Calheta was incorporated into the house of Castelo Melhor.
Câmara (Simão Gonçalves da)

He was the son of João Gonçalves da Câmara, 6th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, and of Dona Maria de Alencastre. He was born in Lisbon and never came to this island. His father died in Almeirim at the beginning of June 1580, when he was only six months old. He may be regarded as the 7th captain-donatary of Funchal, although he never took up the government of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), which from 1582 was administered by governors-general under Philippine rule. Nevertheless, he retained the title of captain-donatary of Funchal, as did many of his successors, as the warrant (*provisão*) of 10 October 1585 shows, and he enjoyed a considerable share of the substantial revenues that the donataries held in this archipelago. Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, who was the 3rd Count of Calheta (‘small cove’), married Dona Maria de Vasconcelos, daughter and heiress of the 1st Count of Castelo Melhor. For this reason the countship of Calheta was incorporated into the house of Castelo Melhor, which was later raised to a marquisate.
Shrimp (*camarão*)
A name given to various macruran crustaceans, among which *Grangon vulgaris* and *Palaemon squilla* may be mentioned as being among the most common.
Municipal councils

The original charter (foral) of the Municipality of Funchal is not in the Council archive, but the first book of council sessions, which dates from 1470, shows that the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) was then made up of individuals drawn from the class of good men (*homens bons*, local notables eligible for municipal office). Besides the councillors (*vereadores*), there were guild representatives (*mesteres*), that is, representatives of the manual trades, but these men were viewed with disfavour by the other members of the Senate, who not infrequently mistreated and insulted them. The Senate was presided over by the ordinary judge, and there was a municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) chosen from among the councillors, who collected the municipality’s revenues and paid its expenses, and was also responsible for petitioning on any matter of general interest.

Both the judges and the councillors were elected and took their oath before the captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*). The Senate of Funchal appointed the market inspectors (almotacés), the bailiffs, the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties) of the city, the *alcaides* of Ribeira Brava, Câmara de Lobos and Caniço, the local petty judges of these last three places and of Calheta, etc.

The regulations (*regimento*) of 11 February 1505 gave the Funchal Council, in addition to the judge, three councillors, a municipal procurator, a clerk (*escrivão*) and a treasurer, the last not being one of the councillors. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 17 August 1508 laid down that from then on only *fidalgos* (noblemen of the lesser nobility) could be councillors, and that the Council was to be ruled and governed in the manner of that of Lisbon. Under this last enactment, elections were to be held every 3 years, their approval resting with the king.

In the first quarter of the 17th century the councillors still took their oath before the donatary, represented by his *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown), and the citizens who were to hold municipal office were chosen by indirect election. Once the choice had been made, the names of those elected were placed in wax ballot balls (*pelouros*), which were kept in a chest with three keys, each held by a councillor. A child of 6 or 7 drew the ballot balls from the chest when lots were cast for the citizens who were to serve that year as judges, councillors and treasurer of the Senate.
The Council’s treasurer was as a rule a merchant, but the clerk had to be a *fidalgo*, and was entitled to ride a mule with a saddle, in accordance with the warrant (*provisão*) of 1538.

The Municipal Council of Funchal, better known in the past as the Senado da Câmara, always had four councillors (*vereadores*), one of whom served as municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) until constitutional government was established on this island in 1834. In the 18th century and the early 19th, however, these councillors were appointed by the Desembargo do Paço (the king's supreme court of justice), on the basis of lists of the members of the governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office) drawn up by the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*) or by the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district). The presidency of the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council), which in Funchal had at first belonged to the ordinary judge, passed from the middle of the 17th century onwards to the *juiz de fora*, an official appointed by the crown.
The Senate also included four guild representatives (*mesteres*), elected every year by the House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds).

At the council sessions of old, the *juiz de fora* sat at one end of the council board (*mesa*) and the clerk (*escrivão*) at the other. To the left of the former sat the three councillors, in order of age, and in the last place (*lugar*) the municipal procurator. These members of the Senate were entitled to high-backed chairs, whereas the four guild representatives sat on low chairs without backs beside the clerk's seat, but set apart from the council board. When members of the nobility happened to attend the sessions, they sat in high-backed chairs to the right of the *juiz de fora*.

In 1803 there was a rather stormy council session in Funchal because the *juiz de fora* had allowed the guild representatives to sit at the council board. As a result of this incident, these representatives of the people stayed away from council sessions for a long time.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of 2 April 1763 granted the council of Funchal the right to walk behind the canopy in the Corpus Christi procession, and both in processions and in churches it was customary for the guild representatives to line up behind the rest of the Senate.

The first municipal elections held in the archipelago after the restoration of liberal government took place on 2 October 1835, in the manner laid down by the decree of 18 July of the same year. On that occasion 7 councillors were elected for the council of Funchal, 3 for that of Porto Santo and 5 for each of the other councils of the province. The elections passed off peacefully everywhere, since the political parties that were later to be so hostile to one another had not yet been organised at that time. The municipality of Funchal was governed by councils of 7 councillors while the administrative codes of 1842 and 1878 were in force, but the code of 1886 raised the number of councillors to 9, and this figure was kept in the codes of 1895 and 1896. Under the law of 7 August 1913 the councils were to consist of 32 councillors in 1st-class municipalities, 25 in 2nd-class and 16 in 3rd-class ones; these numbers were reduced to 24, 16 and 12 respectively by the law of 23 June 1916, now in force. The executive committees of the municipalities consist of 9 councillors in 1st-class municipalities, 7 in 2nd-class and 5 in 3rd-class ones (article 98 of the Law of 7 August 1913).

The former clerks of the councils, who became secretaries of these bodies under the code of 1886, are now called heads of the secretariat. These officials attend the sessions of the executive committees, draw up the minutes and direct the work of their departments, in accordance with the laws and the resolutions of the council.

The present municipal system, organised on the principles of the broadest decentralisation, has restored to the councils the freedoms and prerogatives of which the constitutional governments had stripped them in recent years. The outcry raised on all sides against the tutelage that weighed on the municipal administrations was heeded by the government of the Republic. One of its first acts was to put into effect the Administrative Code of 1878, the code which, through its decentralising provisions, best allowed the people of the municipalities a free existence in fair proportion to their resources.
See Administrative organisation.
Camellia (Camellia japonica)

A shrub or small tree of the family Ternstroemiaceae, very common in Madeira. It is native to Japan and one of the loveliest ornaments of the *quintas* of Monte (‘hill’) and Camacha. It is also known by the name *japonesa*.
American railway

There was one running between the former Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’) and Pombal, set up under a licence granted by the Municipal Council to José Ribeiro de Almeida and João Aluísio Virissimo to operate this means of transport in the city. The rails, whose laying had begun in 1896, were torn up in 1915. The cars had stopped running some time before, as a result of the losses suffered by the Monte Railway (*Caminho de Ferro do Monte*) company, to which the Council had granted a licence to operate the line at its session of 7 April 1902.

The equipment of the original American Railway company was bought at auction by Manuel Betencourt Sardinha on 20 August 1900 and later transferred to the Monte Railway Company, to which the Council granted an annual subsidy of 300:00 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), paid until 31 March 1909.

The decree of 2 August 1902 approved the resolution of the Funchal Municipal Council on the conditions of the public tender it intended to open for the concession to build and operate the American railways. Under Article 6 of the terms for the award of the contract that accompany the decree, the successful bidder was free to choose the traction system to be used, and could opt equally for animal traction, electric locomotion or even compressed air.
Monte Railway

It was António Joaquim Marques, of Lisbon, who first thought of building a lift, or rack railway, between Funchal and Monte (‘hill’), and the proposal he submitted to that effect to the Municipal Council was accepted at its session of 17 February 1887. The engineer Raul Mesnier carried out some studies from 1886 onwards in order to settle the best plan to follow in carrying out the work. However, unforeseen difficulties arose, so Marques decided to transfer the concession he had obtained to Captain Manuel Alexandre de Sousa, a native of Madeira; the Council permitted this at its session of 24 July 1890.

On 22 January 1891 the Council approved the plan for building the lift. By then the Railway Company had already been formed, under a contract concluded with the concessionaire, and a short time later work began at the locality of Confeiteira (‘confectioner’), where large retaining walls had to be built. Under the contract between the Council and the Railway company, the expropriation of the land needed for the railway line was to be carried out by the Municipality, but at the company's expense. The line would belong to the company for 99 years and would then become public.

The first section of the railway, between Pombal and the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s channel’), was opened on 16 July 1893, and on 5 August 1894 services began between Pombal and Atalhinho (‘little shortcut’), an occasion marked by boisterous celebrations in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte. The works were at first directed by Captain Manuel Alexandre de Sousa, the Company's technical inspector. When this officer's services were dispensed with on 29 August 1893, however, the supervision of the works passed to the civil engineers Messrs Aníbal and Adriano Trigo, who had to correct some errors made by their predecessor.

The report and accounts of the Railway Board for the year 1894 show that the works as far as the locality of Atalhinho cost the considerable sum of 44,899,679 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). Of this, 2,229,210 *réis* went on lowering part of the road, whose gradient was steeper than the locomotives could climb.

At a meeting of the general assembly of the Monte Railway Company (*Companhia do Caminho de Ferro do Monte*) on 12 July 1910, it was resolved to extend the railway line to the Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’). The Council sanctioned this decision on 4 August of the same year, and this section of the line, together with the large restaurant built at that spot, was opened on 24 June 1912.
Between Pombal and Monte there are 2,500 metres of railway line, and between Pombal and the Terreiro da Luta 3850.

The financial difficulties that the Railway Company faced when the road was opened and the railway line laid as far as Monte forced it to borrow twice and to pay no dividend to its shareholders for a long time. For many years now, however, the Company has had its affairs in order, despite the considerable losses it suffered during the war, when shipping stayed away from our port and the price of coal rose to exorbitant levels (1923).

The line runs from Pombal, where the main station and the Company’s offices are located, to the Terreiro da Luta, its ‘terminus’. This point lies about one thousand five hundred metres from the Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’) of Monte, at an altitude of 850 metres above sea level. The whole line is approximately four kilometres long, with several halts along the route and a station at the locality (*sítio*) of Fonte. The Company runs a service of cars to the various stations and halts, which becomes more frequent on certain days when tourists arrive in greater numbers. At the Terreiro da Luta, at the end of the line, which commands one of the most marvellous panoramas, the Railway Company maintains an excellent restaurant, magnificently appointed, which rivals the best of its kind abroad.

On 10 September 1919, shortly after 6 p.m., the boiler of one of the Monte Railway’s locomotives exploded violently as the train was passing between Levada (‘irrigation channel’) and Livramento (‘deliverance’) on its way up. Of the approximately 56 people carried by the car and the locomotive, 4 died at the moment of the explosion, and many were injured, some of them seriously. Because of this disaster, journeys to Monte were suspended until 1 February 1920, which did considerable harm to the Company’s interests.
Camões

As is well known, our great epic poet refers to Madeira in his immortal poem *Os Lusíadas* (*The Lusiads*). This fine and laudatory reference is contained in the following lines, which form the 5th stanza of Canto V: ‘We passed the great island of Madeira, / which is so called from its abundant woods; / the first of those that we settled, / more celebrated for its name than for its fame; / yet, though it is the last in the world, / none of those that Venus loves surpasses it; / rather, were it hers, she would forget / Cyprus, Guido, Paphos and Cythera.’ (*Passamos a grande ilha da Madeira, / Que do muito arvoredo assi se chama; / Das que nós povoámos a primeira, / Mais celebre por nome, que por fama; / Mas nem por ser do mundo a derradeira, / Se lhe avantajam quantas Venus ama; / Antes, sendo esta sua, se esquecera, / De Cypro, Guido, Paphos e Cythera.*)
Various educational works give the following paraphrase of this stanza:

‘We passed the great island called Madeira from the many trees it has, the first that we colonised, and one better known by its name than by great deeds performed there; but although it is the last in the world, it is not inferior to all the islands that Venus loved; on the contrary, if Venus possessed it, she would forsake for it the islands of Cyprus, Guido, Paphos and Cythera.’ As *Os Lusíadas* was published in 1572, Luís de Camões’s reference to Madeira was made about 150 years after the colonisation of Madeira began.

One of the authors of this *Elucidário Madeirense* dealt with the subject at length in the pamphlet *Camões e a Madeira*, published in 1934, which covered the following points: 1. the interpretation of the well-known stanza 50 of Canto V, and particularly of lines 41 and 51; 2. the controversy between Dr José Maria Rodrigues and Admiral Gago Coutinho over the single or double route described by Camões from Lisbon to the Cape Verde islands; 3. the hypothetical location or geographical position of the so-called Isle of Love (*Ilha dos Amores*); 4. the supposed or real criticisms the poet directed at the illustrious Madeirans Luís and Martim Gonçalves da Câmara.
Campanário (parish)

‘Bell tower’ or ‘belfry’ is the meaning of the word *campanário*, which seems an odd name for a parish. In trying to trace the origin of this name, as applied to the parish (*freguesia*) with which we are now concerned, we have found only one explanation, in some notes by Dr João Pedro de Freitas Drumond held in the municipal library of this city. It is by no means implausible, but neither can we affirm that it rests entirely on the truth. We shall nevertheless accept it as genuine and as coming from a good source, since the author of the notes cited gives us no reason to suspect any lack of probity in his reports and historical statements.

When the discoverers, on their first exploration along the coast, rounded Cabo Girão, they came upon a small islet close to the shore which, from a distance, seemed to them to have the shape of a belfry or bell tower (*campanário*). They gave this name to that stretch of coast, and it was later extended to the surrounding land. ‘It resembled a belfry, says Freitas Drumond, having two tall legs, one of which the sea threw down on 1 November 1798.’ Once the ‘bell tower’ had been destroyed by the pounding and violence of the waves, it is not surprising that the origin of the name should gradually have fallen into oblivion.

Referring to the exploration that João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira made in order to fix the boundary between the two captaincies into which Madeira was divided, Frutuoso says the following: ‘Arriving at Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). . going further on to some very high lands, there he laid out another church of the True Cross (*Vera Cruz*), and all these heights he took for his heirs...’. This chapel and the lands taken by Zarco lay within the boundaries of the parish of Campanário, and today they belong to the parish of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’), which was separated from it in 1848. Elsewhere the same Frutuoso also says: ‘half a *légua* to the west there is a *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of a hundred scattered households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) (he is referring to the end of the 16th century), which they call Campanário... these are lands of livestock and of wheat and rye growing, the people being highland folk, more given to raising cattle than to cultivating vines or other fruit trees; but for all this it must be understood that in these and in all the places of the island there have always been, and are today, honourable and noble people of lofty thoughts’.

We cannot determine precisely when this parish was created, but it existed before 1556, because a royal decree (*alvará*) of 28 August of that year added one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine to the 10,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) of the vicar’s stipend (*côngrua*). This salary was increased by the royal decrees of 9 June 1581, 18 January 1589 and 19 January 1674, and then stood at 19,000 *réis* in cash, one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine.

It is recorded that a curacy (*curato*) was created there in 1698, but it seems there was a delay in filling this post. Only with the royal decree of 9 May 1727 was the curate’s stipend fixed, at 20,000 *réis* a year, and the appointment to the office was then made.

We do not know when the present parish church was built. Its façade bears the date 1683, which must be that of its reconstruction, unless one accepts that another church existed on a different site before the present building. We are aware that in 1677 the Council of Finance (*Conselho da Fazenda*) ordered the work of building the chancel to be put out to auction.

This parish has the chapels of Nossa Senhora do Bom Despacho and Nossa Senhora da Glória. The chapels of Our Lady of Mount Carmel (*Nossa Senhora do Carmo*), Nossa Senhora do Rosário, São João Baptista and Nossa Senhora dos Remédios no longer exist. We shall deal with all of them in the appropriate place.

Among its early grantees of land (*sesmeiros*) and settlers were Manuel de Noronha, son of the second captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, who held vast tracts of land that today belong to Quinta Grande; Vasco Delgado, who established himself on the banks of the Ribeira dos Melões (‘melons’ stream’), where he founded an entail (*morgado*); Pedro Enes; and others. The largest properties that the Jesuits owned on this island lay within the bounds of Campanário, and they made up chiefly the so-called Quinta Grande, which later gave its name to this parish. This rural estate yielded, 160 years ago, more than two *contos* (one million réis) *de réis*, which today would correspond to a very considerable income.

It is in this parish that the locality of Fajã dos Padres (‘the priests’ flat’) lies, so called because it belonged to the fathers of the Society of Jesus. It is a *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) beside the sea, beneath towering rocks. It is carefully cultivated and produces the finest and most celebrated Malmsey in Madeira. This locality was sacked more than once by pirates, who in January 1625 destroyed the chapel that the Jesuits had there.

In 1825 serious disturbances of public order broke out in Campanário for political reasons, and the armed forces had to intervene. At the time these events caused a great sensation because of the special circumstances surrounding them.

With the creation of the municipality (*concelho*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) in 1914, the parish of Campanário ceased to belong to the municipality of Câmara de Lobos and was included in the area of the new municipality. Born here were the bishop of São Paulo, Dom Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade (1767–1847), the distinguished jurist Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade (1821–1902) and Canon João Jacinto Gonçalves de Andrade (1825–1894), both eminent professors at the law faculty of that Brazilian city (see those entries).

In former times there were many chestnut groves in this parish. One chestnut tree of gigantic proportions became well known to Portuguese and foreigners alike, and its engraving is reproduced in many works dealing with Madeira. It stood in the locality of Achada (‘plateau’) and measured 10 metres in circumference. Partly eaten away by time, it had at its base a door-shaped opening that gave access to a hollow able to hold several people.
The most notable localities of this parish are Fajã dos Padres, Tranqual, Quebrada, São João, Pinheiro,

Lugar da Ribeira, Voltas, Pedregal, Achada, Terreiros, Lugar da Serra, Cova da Velha, Adega, Corujeira, Longueira, Rhodes, Carmo, Serrado, Chapim, Calçada, Lombo do Romão, Igreja, Lapa e Maçapez, Furnas e Amoreiras, Fajã Velha, Vigia, Porta Nova, Chamorra, Jardim, Palmeira, Roda e Maçapez, Pôrto da Ribeira, Pedra de Nossa Senhora and Nossa Senhora da Glória. The state boys’ school is in the locality of Carmo, and the state girls’ school in Furnas e Amoreira.

The parish has a small port and a stony beach where landing is difficult. A few years ago a small landing place was built there, which serves well when the sea is calm. Above the port, at different heights, several cavities with wooden doors have been dug into the tuff of a sheer cliff. They serve as storehouses for various goods, agricultural produce, firewood, fishing gear, etc.
It lies approximately 18 kilometres from Funchal, 8 from Câmara de Lobos (the church) and 4½ from Ribeira Brava.
Campanário (islet)
Off the coast of this parish, close to the shore, lies a small islet that bears this name and is also called Ilhéu da Lapa (‘grotto islet’).
Campanário (landing place and quay)
On the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of this name there is a small, poor landing place, where an insignificant landing stage was built in 1909.
It is also known as Porto da Lapa. It lies 3 miles from the landing place of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and 1.7 from that of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’).
Campanário (stream)

Also known as Ribeira da Lapa (‘stream of the rock shelter’), this stream rises at Pico dos Terreiros (‘peak of the clearings’), crosses the parish of Campanário and flows into the sea at the landing place of the same name.
Campo da Barca
See Barca (Campo da).
Campo de Baixo

An inhabited locality on the island of Porto Santo, where there is a chapel dedicated to the Divino Espírito Santo (Divine Holy Spirit). It is of quite ancient construction but was rebuilt in the first quarter of the 19th century by Captain Sebastião António Drumond. It has 35 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) and inhabitants.
Campo do Duque
The Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) (see

that entry). After Prince Henry the Navigator and his immediate successor, the Infante Ferdinand, its Grand Masters were Dom João, Duke of Viseu, Diogo, Duke of Viseu, and Manuel, Duke of Beja, who succeeded to the crown. Since Madeira belonged to the mastership of that Order, these dukes held wide jurisdiction over the spiritual, and also the temporal, affairs of this archipelago. At the centre of its most important settlement lay a vast square or open ground, which belonged to the Grand Master of the Order and was called the Campo do Duque (the Duke’s Field) in his honour. Referring to this ground, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says:
