‘The Campo do Duque was the land on which, in the city of Funchal, stand the public gaol and its square; the Sé, its churchyard and open square; and the Largo de São Sebastião, in which the chapel of that saint was built... Various documents refer to this ground, notably the letters of the Infante Ferdinand by which, in 1470, he ordered the municipal fold of the municipality (*concelho*) to be made, and granted the land “next to the great church”, that is, the Sé, for the town hall to be built... ’

Some have claimed that the Campo do Duque extended between the two banks of the streams that today bear the names of Santa Luzia and São João. It seems that it at least reached the vicinity of the grounds of the future Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi).
In the manuscript *Noticias das cousas da ilha da Madeira desde o segundo descobrimento pelo Zarco* we find the following:

‘To test whether the said canes would thrive, they first planted them in the field that was called the Duke’s, where the Church of São Sebastião now stands, which is in the middle of the city; this field was closed with a gate where the Rua do Sabão now runs. The whole of this field belonged to Francisco de Carvalhal, companion of Zargo in the discovery of this island; afterwards it belonged to his brother João Manuel, and it still belongs to his heirs. From here the cultivation of cane spread throughout the island, and they took it to Machico, where the first sugar refined on the island was made. In this Campo do Duque the first two-storey house in this town (*vila*) of Funchal, and in the whole island, was built, and the said João Manuel had it made of worked cedar wood. This two-storey house was held at that time to be so novel and marvellous a thing – all the other houses then standing being single-storey and built of planks – that articles of complaint were laid before the King against the said João Manuel, accusing him of building a tower, as though he meant to fortify himself and rise up against Funchal and against the Crown. The said house still stands today (mid-18th century) and is owned by António de Carvalhal, and it is the lowest two-storey house in Funchal’.

In the letter of 5 November 1485 that Manuel I, then Duke of Beja and Grand Master of the Order of Christ, addressed to the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of Funchal, he granted the land needed in the Campo do Duque for the building of the Cathedral (the Sé) and of the town hall.
The old Campo do Duque was the most central part of the early settlement, then town and later city of Funchal, as it may be said still to be, in the streets and squares that roughly correspond to it.
Campo Neutro (O)
Eighteen issues were published, from 31 August 1861 to 13 January 1862.
Experimental fields

The Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) set up an experimental field in each of the following localities: Louros (Funchal), Ribeira Brava, the Paul da Serra and Porto da Cruz. The experimental field at the last of these did not last long. Of the others, the one that gave the best results was at Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), which distributed a very large number of selected specimens of fruit trees to farmers. On the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) good crops were obtained of potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word), cabbages, turnips, carrots, cucumbers, lettuces, beans, peas, beetroot, etc.
Cana

A unit of area formerly used in Madeira, equal to 30 square metres. In many parts of the island an *alqueire* (dry measure for grain; as a land measure c. 900 m²) of land is 30 *canas*, or 900 square metres, but in Funchal it is only 756,225 square metres.
Sugar cane

Sugar cane was introduced to Madeira, it seems, in 1425. The first cuttings of the plant, which are said to have come from Sicily on the orders of Prince Henry the Navigator, were planted in the Campo do Duque (‘duke’s field’), the ground in the city of Funchal now occupied by the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), its churchyard and open square, the Largo da Sé (‘cathedral square’), the Rua do Aljube (‘bishop’s prison street’) and the Largo do Comércio, formerly Largo de São Sebastião. From the Campo do Duque the cane passed to Machico, where its cultivation prospered so greatly that it yielded thirteen *arrobas* of sugar, which was the first sugar sold on the island.

From Madeira sugar cane passed to the Canary Islands, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, and Angola and Benguela. It may be supposed that this useful plant also spread from our island to the Portuguese and Spanish colonies of America, where there still exists today a variety of cane called *crioula*, perfectly identical to the old local cane grown here.

Cane cultivation prospered and expanded in Madeira until the middle of the 16th century, when the island came to produce 300,000 *arrobas* of sugar. By 1590, however, when Gaspar Frutuoso wrote the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), the once flourishing sugar industry was already tending to decline, owing to the influx of sugar from Brazil and the Spanish colonies into European markets, although valuable plantations of the grass still existed here.

To avert the crisis that was beginning to appear, the Funchal Council requested and obtained in 1598 a royal decree (*alvará*) forbidding any ship to load sugar from elsewhere here. This measure brought the island no benefit, and nor did a contract made in 1608 between the city’s residents and the same Council, under which sugar imported from Brazil was not to be sold to foreigners until they had made up a third of their cargoes with local sugar.

‘By a royal decree of 1649’, says Dr Azevedo, ‘rewards and loans were promised to those who rebuilt the old sugar mills (engenho), by then already in ruins, or built new ones. However, the sugar industry on the island of Madeira had been mortally wounded ever since, from the end of the 16th century onwards, American sugar came to supply the European markets at prices with which it could not compete. Competition had indeed become impossible for it, both because America was made fruitful by the almost unpaid labour of the slave, whereas Madeira was worked for the most part by the free tenant farmer (*colono*, under the *colonia* contract); and because in America the land, the cultivation, the manufacture and perhaps the capital as well formed a single interest, a single force, a single enterprise, whereas here they did not. The ill-matched duality of landlord and tenant farmer, or holder of the entail and peasant, long dormant in its mutual jealousies in the shade of an opulence to which it had given no impulse, awoke, self-destructive, as soon as the sheltering tree split and fell under the axe of adversity.’

The illustrious annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ gives the year 1748 as marking the end of the sugar period on this island. It should be noted, however, that only the industry of processing sugar disappeared almost entirely at that time, for the cultivation of cane continued, albeit on a much smaller scale than before.

‘From the middle of the 18th century onwards’, says Dr Azevedo, ‘Madeira was reduced to a mere consumer of American sugar, with which it kept up its confectionery. This, it may well be said, had been raised here since the 16th century to a true art and a valuable export industry, as is shown by certain documents... and by various passages of the *Saudades da Serra*, especially the one which says that Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara sent to Rome to visit the Pope with a great service... many trinkets and delicacies of the island in preserves, and the Sacred Palace made entirely of sugar, and the cardinals all made of *alfenim* (white sugar paste for modelling figures)... of the height of a man.’
Few sugar mills existed on the island in 1730, and in 1736, 1739, 1741, 1748, 1758 and 1765 royal decrees were requested for the import of sugar from Brazil.

Thomas Edward Bowdich, who was in Madeira in 1823, says that an insignificant quantity of sugar was made here, and the author of *Rambles in Madeira*, who visited us in 1826, says much the same about this product, adding that there was then only one mill for crushing sugar cane on the whole island. In 1827, according to a newspaper of the time, Madeira had one more mill for the same purpose, but by 1851 the number of these establishments had risen to four, all driven by oxen, as Eduardo Harcourt attests in his *Sketch of Madeira*.

‘The manufacture of sugar and of spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine)’, states Dr Azevedo, ‘revived almost immediately after the destruction of the vineyards between 1846 and 1852. Spirit came first, in 1847, with a distillery set up in Câmara de Lobos; there followed another in Ribeira Brava in 1853; another in Câmara de Lobos in 1854; another in Canhas in 1855; two in 1857, one in Arco da Calheta and another in Câmara de Lobos; nine in 1858, namely two in Machico, two in Porto da Cruz, one in São Jorge, one in Ponta Delgada, one in Paul do Mar, one in Madalena and one in Câmara de Lobos; two in 1859, one in São Jorge and another in Faial; one in São Vicente in 1860; and lastly one in Ponta Delgada in 1861.

Then came the sugar factories: that of Ferraz Irmãos, begun some years earlier, and that of William Hinton & Son, both in Funchal, and that of Ferreira Nogueira in São Martinho, all in 1856; in 1858, that of Ornelas Frazão in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’); in 1859, that of Joaquim da Silva in Funchal; between then and 1866, that of Diogo Frazão in Arco da Calheta and that of Wilbraham in Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’); and lastly the great São João (‘St John’) factory, some of the last seven also making spirit.’

The quantity of cane juice (*garapa*) obtained in 1855 was 311,500 gallons, according to White in the book entitled *Madeira its climate and scenery*. The report presented by the agronomist Eduardo Dias Grande to the Funchal Agricultural Society (*Sociedade Agrícola do Funchal*) in 1865 shows that the island produced 14,688,043 kilograms of cane that year, the area under this crop then being about 357 hectares. According to the same agronomist, these 14,688,043 kilograms should have yielded 84:218,98 hectolitres of cane juice, representing a capital of 175,039,550 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

Sugar cultivation remained flourishing in Madeira until 1881, but in 1882 a disease hitherto completely unknown on the island began to attack the canefields, ending by destroying them almost completely in 1884, 1885 and 1886.

This disease, caused by a fungus, *Conyothyrium melasporum*, in the opinion of the distinguished agricultural engineer Mr Alfredo de Fraga Gomes, did very great damage to the island, and every treatment employed to combat it proved fruitless.

The Bourbon cane, imported from Cayenne at the beginning of the 19th century and from Cape Verde in the middle of that century, was the variety destroyed by *Conyothyrium*. However, the introduction from 1833 of new, selected varieties from Mauritius and other countries allowed the canefields to be rapidly re-established. By 1890 they had already spread across almost the whole of the island’s lower zone, and there was even one variety, the bamboo cane, which had been found to grow at altitudes that sugar cane had never before reached.

The native or Creole cane, short and green, was, as we have already said, the first to exist in Madeira. It was followed by the Bourbon cane, with taller and sometimes slightly reddish stalks, introduced in the 19th century. In 1861, or a little earlier, the Antilles cane, with violet leaves and stalks, was introduced to the island, but this variety, which grew poorly in our climate, never formed large plantations.

The varieties of cane on the island in 1890 were chiefly the Otaheite, the crystalline Haiti, the elephant and the bamboo, all with green, yellowish or greenish-yellow stalks; the violet, the light violet and the dark violet, with violet stalks and green leaves; the red, with stalks of the same colour; the Port Mackay, with russet stalks and striped leaves, already somewhat attacked by the disease; and the striped and the striped crystalline, with thick, striped stalks. These last two varieties, the violet and the Otaheite or white cane, dominated the plantations, being also the hardiest and the richest in cane juice (*garapa*). The Yuba cane, one of the most widely cultivated, has greater vitality than any of the other varieties and also outyields them, owing to the abundance of its stalks. The average yield per hectare, which in former times was 20, 25 and 30,000 kilograms, now reaches 30, 35 and 50,000 kilograms, the largest yields always coming from land eminently suited to cane growing and properly fertilised with manure and chemical fertilisers.

Although sugar cane is grown successfully in Málaga and Motril, in Spain, experience shows that in Madeira it should not go above an altitude of 250 to 300 metres on the south coast, or 150 to 200 metres on the north. At an altitude of 450 metres the cane juice registers only 4 to 6 degrees Baumé, so that the cane produced there never fetches the prices paid for cane from the lower zone (coastal belt). According to the analyses made in 1911 by Dr Otto Klein, the juice of Yuba cane grown in the island’s lower zone reaches as much as 10.46 Baumé, whereas that of the old Bourbon cane sometimes registered 11.05.

Mr Luiz de Castilho states in a work entitled *A Fabricação do Assucar de Canna* (Rio de Janeiro, 1892) that in Guadeloupe analyses of cane showed an average of 12.29 per cent sucrose, in Cuba 12.5 to 14 per cent, depending on the season, and in Brazil, on the lands of Bracuhy, 14.86 per cent. In seventy-one analyses of Yuba cane stalks made by Dr Otto Klein, the average obtained was only 11.7. It should be noted, however, that much of the cane sent to this chemist came from land situated about 350 metres above sea level.

In Madeira, before the Yuba cane, the sucrose content of the various varieties then grown was 11%, and their yield of crystallised sugar ranged between 6 and 7 kilograms per hundred. Now, thanks to better varieties and the gradual improvement of manufacturing processes, the cane’s yield of crystallised sugar is 9 to 10 per cent. According to published technical information, ‘every 100 kilograms of Yuba cane contain 78 litres of cane juice or *jus* with a purity of 86’, which leads us to consider this variety as valuable, or almost as valuable, as the varieties grown in the West Indies, ‘whose juices have 84 to 88 purity’, as stated by the author of a pamphlet published in 1910 under the title *A Questão Sacarina da Madeira*.

The price of cane has varied considerably in Madeira. In 1872 the Companhia Fabril de Assucar Madeirense paid 55 centavos for every 30 kilograms of cane of 9 to 10 degrees Baumé, 60 for cane of 10 to 11 degrees and 65 for cane of over 11 degrees. These prices did not last long, however: as soon as the enemies of the São João factory succeeded in destroying it, the price of the product fell quite markedly. In 1881 the Torreão (‘turret’) factory paid 45 centavos for cane, but this price, which was still profitable, did not hold either, and shortly afterwards the canefields disappeared because of the disease we have already mentioned. Around 1862 the factories paid 30 centavos for cane; later they sometimes paid 32 and 35 centavos. Finally came the decree of 30 December 1895, which set prices of 40 to 45 centavos per 30 kilograms for the product, and the decree of 24 September 1903, by which Madeira obtained a further 5 centavos on the minimum cane prices, an increase that the decree of 18 March 1911 left unchanged.

At present, under the provisions of decree no. 27,912 of 31 July 1937, the price set for cane in legal condition is 7.60 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) per 30 kilograms.

In 1918 some spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) factories paid prices for cane higher than those set in the 1911 decree, but the government, on the grounds of protecting the district against the danger of alcoholism, ordered these factories to cease operating, and from then on the registered factories could buy the rest of the crop at the legal prices.

It should be pointed out that, for various technical reasons, the quantity of commercial sugar obtained does not correspond exactly to the sugar content of the cane, but the difference is much smaller today than formerly, thanks to the manufacturing and maximum-extraction processes recently adopted on the island.

Before the 1895 decree, farmers could have sugar made on their own account, paying the agreed price for its manufacture with part of the product or with a certain sum of money. This right, however, was not recognised by the Torreão factory once it had been allowed to monopolise sugar production for the island’s consumption.

Cane growing, which covered 1,000 hectares in 1906, 1,100 hectares in 1911, 1,800 hectares in 1915 and 1,500 hectares in 1918, is, according to the agronomist Senhor João da Mota Prego, more profitable than viticulture, given the state of the trade in our wines, but less so than banana growing. In the same agronomist’s view, this crop ‘cannot extend over an area much greater than it has occupied in recent years; what may increase is the intensity of production per unit of area, though this increase in production will in any case be very slow, since it depends on more intensive cultivation, that is, cultivation consuming more capital, and it is therefore hampered by the present system of farming, sharecropping (*parceria*).

Sugar cane is usually propagated from the tops of the stalks, which are much cheaper than the other parts of the plant, and it is customary to plant them at a slant to encourage the growth of ratoons.

In the hot season the canefields are irrigated every 15 or 17 days, which does not mean that they cannot withstand longer dry spells. In certain places where water is scarce, the cane sometimes goes unwatered for as long as a month. Of the varieties grown in Madeira, Yuba cane resists drought best, owing to its hardy nature.

The building of levadas (irrigation channels) began in Madeira in the 15th century, and it was thanks to them that cane growing, which started in the Campo do Duque, was able to spread to new places, first in the south and later in the north of the island. The 300,000 *arrobas* of sugar produced on the island in the mid-16th century lead us to suppose that some two thousand hectares were then under cane. It is also possible that the water of many springs, which no longer exist because of the folly with which the people destroyed the old Madeiran forests, was used to irrigate the land. The Levada de Santa Luzia, the Levada do Castelejo and the levada of the Ribeira dos Socorridos had already been built in the 16th century. By the royal decree (*alvará*) of 19 October 1562, the queen regent, Queen Catherine, acting in the name of King Sebastian, ordered that these and other channels be cleaned, ‘bisto se perderem muytas canas daçucar & deixarem de se prantar outras por se nom tirarem e limparem as levadas em tempo’ (since many sugar canes are being lost and others are not being planted because the levadas are not cleared and cleaned in time).

‘The oldest document relating to the sugar industry in the archive of the Funchal Council dates from 1562, as can be seen from the notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, and it shows that the first advances of this industry in Madeira date from that time: it authorises the building of the first water-driven mill for making sugar that existed here, and its wording makes clear that before it there was no other here, powered by any means whatsoever. Until that time, therefore, sugar production could only have been scanty and a purely domestic activity.’

In 1900 there were 49 cane-crushing mills in Madeira, 16 of them driven by steam and 33 by water. Today these establishments number 51, of which only one, that of H. Hinton, makes all the sugar consumed in the archipelago or exported to Portugal. The capacity of this factory, one of the largest and most perfect known, today reaches 500 tonnes of cane in twenty-four hours, whereas from 1895 to 1900 it did not exceed 150 tonnes in the same period.

Sugar cane is useful not only as an industrial plant but also as a fodder plant, since cattle eat its leaves readily while they are green. The cane is generally stripped of its leaves twice, once between July and October and again before the harvest.

The legislation published on the Madeiran sugar regime (*regime sacarino*, the legal framework governing sugar production) is varied and abundant. The fundamental law that governs sugar growing and the sugar industry today is Decree no. 3,847 of 14 May 1934. Under this law, cane growing is limited to cane of at least 9 Baumé that is indispensable for the sugar consumed in Madeira and, additionally, for the alcohol and spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) consumed in the archipelago. This cane output is guaranteed compulsory purchase by the sugar factory at the legal price, and if in any industrial year the sugar made from it exceeds local consumption, the factory may ship the surplus to mainland Portugal, up to a maximum of 200 tonnes, exempt from duties and taxes.

To achieve this balance, the decree stipulates that the directorate of the Funchal Customs House shall determine, through appropriate prior investigation and analysis, the localities and plots distant from the sugar and alcohol factories or from the sea where the cane has less than 9 Baumé. If even so normal cane output exceeds the anticipated requirements, the Government may order the measures needed to end cultivation where it is least suitable.

The varieties that replaced Bourbon cane are extinct or nearly extinct on the island, and Madeiran canefields now consist mainly of Yuba cane, imported from Natal around 1897, and of some P.O.J. varieties, imported chiefly from the province of Angola from 1933 onwards. Yuba cane, considered of inferior quality in Brazil, Mauritius, Louisiana and other countries where it is or has been grown, has adapted so well to the soils and climate of our island that it is rightly regarded as one of the hardiest and most profitable ever grown here.

Since 1934 planting sugar cane has been prohibited on land that did not carry it at that date, and also on land where it is replaced by another crop. Later, Decree no. 25,437 of 31 May 1935 established that, when it becomes necessary to replace or renew cane plantings in order to keep the canefields economically viable, the owners may, with prior authorisation from the directorate of the Funchal Customs House, carry out such replacement or renewal up to a limit of 80 per cent of the plants replaced and 80 per cent of the area occupied.
Giant reed (Arundo donax)

A grass with tall, woody stems that are hollow between the nodes, widely grown on Madeira and Porto Santo. The stems are used for distaffs, fishing rods and supports for climbing plants, and for other purposes. The leaves make a mediocre fodder. It is also called giant reed (*cana de roca*).
Lava tubes

In various parts of Madeira there are caves hollowed out of basaltic lava, generally of the most recent date. They formed by a mechanism identical to the one that gave rise to similar formations in certain volcanic regions of the globe, such as the Azores and the Sandwich Islands.

A narrow stream of still-fluid lava, hemmed in by mud or scoria, slid down a slope or a ravine. Meanwhile its exterior, losing much of its heat by radiation, solidified, leaving the core at a temperature still high enough for its fluidity to let it keep moving.

The result was a channel in which container and contents were of the same nature, with the one essential difference of their unequal temperature. Once the pasty core had drained away, there remained this kind of volcanic conduit. The most perfect example in Madeira is the cave near the mouth of the Ribeira de São Vicente, which may measure some 80 metres in length and some 4 to 5 in width.

At Montado dos Pessegueiros (‘peach-tree pasture’), a locality in the same parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente, and at Porto Moniz there are also channels of this kind, in flows of recent lava. On the south coast, both to the east and to the west of Funchal, traces of tunnels of this nature can be seen, most of them at sea level.

The Fojo, a deep chasm hollowed out of friable tuff behind the coastline and a little to the east of Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), appears to be the result of the erosion and collapse of a volcanic channel that ran there in remote ages and opened into the sea. Its ruins, now piled up in confusion as blocks of blackened lava, show smoothed surfaces with the long, parallel striations that characterise the walls of lava tunnels. The sea water, having passed through a nearby cave formed by marine erosion and having eaten away the rocks beneath the channel, is thought to have caused this collapse, helped by the rainwater that flows into the pit, wearing away the tuff and widening its extent.

Between the Fojo and Ponta Gorda (‘broad point’), not far from the Muralha dos Franceses (‘Frenchmen’s wall’), similar traces of other collapsed channels can be seen, surrounded, like that of the Fojo, by yellow tuff of volcanic mud.

Hanging from the roofs of some of these tunnels, like stalactites or resembling Prince Rupert’s drops, are curious excrescences of vitrified lava, testifying to the fluidity of the rock under the action of a very high temperature. Specimens of these excrescences, remarkable for their size and bizarre shape, were found in a cave at Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’).
Canary Islands

Opinions vary on the discovery of the Canary Islands archipelago. Some authors state that these islands were discovered three times, the last at the end of the 14th century or the beginning of the 15th. Father António Cordeiro says in the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) that they were discovered ‘for the third time in the year 1417 by their Betencor kings; and the island of Madeira having been discovered and settled in 1420, and great fame of it spreading at once, this finally moved the aforesaid second king of the Canaries to sell the four over which he reigned to our Lusitanian and Most Serene Henry the Navigator..., and indeed he sold them to him for certain estates which the Infante gave him on the said island of Madeira, to which (and near which) the said king of the Canaries moved, now at last without a kingdom, and on Madeira he remained, and the descendants of the Betencores endure there even today...’.

There is already an extensive literature on the discovery of this archipelago, its early colonisation, the rights the Portuguese claimed to its possession and the disputes that arose on that account between Portugal and Castile.
Despite the difficulties of communication, relations between the neighbouring archipelagos of the Canaries and Madeira were relatively frequent in the 17th and 18th centuries.
See Bettencourt.
Wild canary (*Serinus canaria*)

A bird of the finch family (Fringillidae), common throughout these islands. It does not migrate on long voyages over the open sea, but moves according to the seasons and other circumstances within a single island or between two neighbouring islands. It is a bird peculiar to the archipelagos of the Macaronesian Sea, that is, the Azores, Madeira and the Canary Islands, and from it derives the highly prized *canário de fora* (domestic canary); it is not recorded, however, that it has been observed on the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*). The clutch consists of 3 to 5 eggs, speckled with more or less dark violet on a greenish-blue ground. It is easily tamed, and it is on some islets or uninhabited islands of the archipelago that the forms most remarkable for the brilliant yellow of their plumage are found.
Domestic canary (*Canário de Fora*)
The domestic variety of the wild canary (*canário da terra*), originally imported from Europe. It is traded by the bird-dealers of Funchal.
Canavial (Count of)

João da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, 1st Viscount and 1st Count of Canavial, was one of the most distinguished Madeirans of the 19th century. He was born in this city on 22 June 1829, the son of António Francisco da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, holder of an entail (*morgado*), and of Dona Carolina Moniz de Ornelas Barreto Cabral, both of whom belonged to old and noble families of this island.

Having completed his secondary studies in Funchal, he went to Montpellier, where he took the degree of bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in science in 1852 and that of doctor of medicine in 1857, proving himself throughout a most diligent student of exceptional intelligence. His astonishing energy, which remained one of the hallmarks of his character until his death, allowed him, while still a student in both Madeira and France, to devote himself to various literary and scientific works. Eloquent proof of this lies in his regular contributions to several reviews and newspapers, in his translation of Alexandre Dumas’s drama *O Conde de Herman*, published in a volume of 250 pages, and in the *Etudes sur les ombellifères venéneuses*, 1 volume of 218 pages, which earned a favourable report from the Academy of Sciences and Letters of Montpellier and a place as a member of that Academy.

After completing his doctorate he continued his scientific studies. In 1858, in an international competition and despite being a foreigner, he won fourth prize for the long memoir he wrote on the subject *Des rapports de l’alimentation avec la respiration. Existe-t-il des aliments qui méritent le nom de respiratoires?* He also wrote a substantial study entitled *De la température de l’homme et des animaux*, which received an honourable mention from the Imperial Academy of Medicine in Paris; a detailed memoir entitled *Quelques considérations ayant pour but de démontrer que la théorie des combustions jette un grand jour sur plusieurs points du domaine de la pathologie*, which remained in manuscript but served as his qualifying work for admission to a scientific society; and a valuable prize-winning work under the heading *De la chaleur animale*. There were also other studies scattered through the specialist journals. All of this opened the doors of many academies and scientific societies, both in our country and abroad.

In 1859 he revalidated his degree by examination at the Lisbon Medical School. The following year he was appointed demonstrator of anatomy at our own Medical School, and in 1867 full professor. As professor and director of that School he had to sustain several disputes with his teaching colleagues, and he published two large volumes on the matter which, however partial they may perhaps be, are works of undeniable value. As a practitioner he enjoyed a great reputation and was regarded by all as an eminent physician. He and Dr Luz Pita were, with no offence to anyone, the two great medical celebrities of Madeira in the 19th century. The breadth of his learning and his great clinical tact earned him the standing of a man of superior calibre in the field of medicine. The Count of Canavial repeatedly engaged in press controversies with some of his colleagues, writing various pamphlets, all of which reveal rare talent and vast erudition.

Like other outstanding men, he also trod the tortuous paths of politics, rendering fruitless so many admirable gifts of talent and learning that, in another field, would have been of great benefit and consequence to all. A considerable part of his life was absorbed by barren parochial politics, which drew him into fierce battles in the press. He edited many newspapers and published various pamphlets, in which he showed himself a polemicist of tough temper and an astonishingly prolific writer. In this respect his output is vast, and his language was always correct and elegant, though devoid of great refinements of style.

As head of the district, he was among the most active and zealous of those who have led the administration of this archipelago. He worked, and worked tirelessly, for the advancement and prosperity of his homeland, although he did not achieve as much as his efforts and endeavours might have led one to expect. While governor of Madeira he wrote a book entitled *Apontamentos para o estudo da crise agricola no distrito do Funchal*, which can still be read and consulted with profit today.

The great energy of his mind also showed itself in his work as an intelligent industrialist. He promoted and directed the founding of the ‘Companhia Fabril de Assucar Madeirense’ and introduced a notable improvement in the processes for making spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), so that the raw material used could be better exploited. This improvement, for which he obtained a patent, gave rise to disputes and controversies, and he published several pamphlets on the subject. He also carried out useful studies on the treatment and refining of wines, and on this subject too he wrote an interesting book and published long articles in the newspapers.

The ‘Companhia Fabril de Assucar Madeirense’ would have been a great source of prosperity for our island had it not been for the unfair and spiteful war waged against it. This remarkable man – at once practitioner, professor, public servant, man of science, journalist and writer, politician and industrialist, who in all these spheres of human activity displayed the qualities of an exceptionally gifted mind – might have been great among the great had petty and sterile political and personal quarrels not, at times, taken up too much of his vast and robust intellect.
The Count of Canavial died in this city on 13 February 1902, not quite 73 years of age.

Bibliography – By far the greater part of his writings, which would fill many volumes, lies scattered through the newspapers of the day and deals largely with sterile parish-pump politics, on which he spent the most vital energies of his great talent and his astonishing activity. These journalistic writings also include the countless articles he wrote about his inventions and industrial improvements, and on medical subjects, some of which were later published as pamphlets. To this end he was the editor and proprietor of several periodicals, such as *A Liberdade* (‘Liberty’), *O Distrito do Funchal* (‘The District of Funchal’), *A Luz* (‘Light’) and others besides.

Of his literary works published as volumes and pamphlets, we may mention the following: *O Conde Herman, drama, por Alexandre Dumas. . ., traduzido por J. C. L.*, Funchal, 1850, 250 pp.; *Etudes sur les ombellifères venéneuses . .* Montpellier, 1857, 218 pp.; *Relatorio e projecto de regulamento para a Escola-Medico-Cirurgica do Funchal. . .* Funchal, 1868, 123 pp. in folio; *Breves consideracões sobre uma laqueação da arteria illiaca*, 1868, 23 pp.; *Uma lição de clinica cirurgica*, 27 pp., 1878; *O dr. Antonio da Luz Pitta o Pharmaceutico Francisco Xavier de Sousa e o Dr. João da Camara Leme*, 88 pp. in folio, 1869; *Uma ophtalmia traumatica, lição de clinica. . .*, 1868, 29 pp.; *Discurso pronunciado... na reunião do partido progressista*, 1870, 18 pp.; *João Augusto d’Ornellas e a Nova Fabrica de Assucar*, 1871, 28 pp.; *Breves instruções sobre a cultura da beterraba de assucar*, 1871, 16 pp.; *Relatorio da Direcção da Companhia Fabril de Assucar Madeirense*, 70 pp. in folio, 1871; *Companhia Fabril de Assucar Madeirense, relatorio da direcção*, 1872, 24 pp.; *Carta sobre a nova molestia da vinha na Madeira*, 1872, 21 pp.;

*Guia do sericultor Madeirense*, 1874, 32 pp.; *Uma crise agricola, um caminho aereo e uma sociedade anonyma*, 1876, 146 pp.; *Discurso pronunciado em 20 de março de 1876 na sessao da abertura da Eschola Central da Associação de Protecção e Instrução do Sexo Feminino Funchalense*, Funchal, 1876, 56 pp.; *Apontamentos para o estudo da crise agricola no Funchal*, Funchal, 1879, 110 pp.; *A Companhia Fabril de Assucar Madeirense, Roberto Leal e o Dr. Tarquinio T. da Camara Lomelino*, 1879, 40 pp.; *Breve noticia sobre o tratamento do vinho pelo calor*, 1882, 12 pp.; *Um privilegio industrial*, 1883, 93 pp.; *Um governador civil, um delegado de saude e um ex-governador civil substituto*, 1883, 24 pp.; *Uma acção civel contra o snr. W. Hinton.*, 1884, 79 pp.; *A resposta do snr. Dr. Vicente Candido Machado*, 1884, 112 pp.; *Um alvitre para a solução da crise por que está passando o país*, 1884, 71 pp.; *Breves considerações sobre os direitos do assucar estrangeiro*, 1885, 16 pp.; *A cultura da canna de assucar e os direitos sobre o assucar*, 1885; *Felicitação aos illustres exploradores portuguezes, Hermenegildo Capello e Roberto Ivens*, 1885, 7 pp.; *Esboço de uma ideia sobre credito industrial*, 1886, 9 pp.; *Os vinhos da Madeira e o seu descredito pelas estufas*, 1889, 91 pp.; *Noticia sobre o vinho Cannavial*, 1882, 23 pp.; *Resposta á critica que fez o Ex.m Snr. Dr. João Augusto Teixeira... á “Noticia sobre o vinho Cannavial”*, 1892, 90 pp.; *Os tres systemas de tratamento dos Vinhos da Madeira*, 1900, 22 pp.

The idea of raising a monument to the Count of Canavial in this city emerged recently (1921). To that end a meeting was held in the first days of October 1920 to agree on how to pay a public and fitting tribute to our illustrious fellow countryman and to perpetuate the memory of his name among us. The initiative came from our compatriot Dr Abel Capitolino Baptista.

At the end of the avenue named after ‘Dr. Manuel de Arriaga’, opposite the churchyard of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), there stands (1923), on a finely worked marble pedestal, the bronze bust of the Count of Canavial. It was unveiled on 2 March 1922, the ceremony of laying the monument’s foundation stone having taken place on 1
December of the previous year.
A few years ago this monument was moved to Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) and placed near the Disinfection Station.

To complement what has been said above, see the articles Association for the Protection and Education of the Women of Funchal (*Associação de Protecção e Instrução do Sexo Feminino Funchalense*), Companhia Fabril de Assucar Madeirense and Estufas in this *Elucidário*.
Cancioneiro de Resende (Madeira in the)

In his book *Poetas Palacianos*, which deals at length with the ‘Cancioneiro de Resende’, Teófilo Braga includes a chapter entitled ‘El-Rei D. Duarte e o cyclo poético da Madeira’. There, for the first time, he sets out the idea that there existed a group of devotees of poetry, natives of Madeira or residents of the island, who were amply represented in that same songbook and who, by their undeniable literary merit, could form a cycle or school of their own amid the numerous phalanx of poets who appear in that celebrated collection. It seems to us that the illustrious writer carried too far the favourable view he so generously formed of this Madeiran Cycle or School.

Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the authoritative commentator on the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and also a distinguished literary critic, disagrees with Teófilo Braga’s opinion and makes the following sensible observations: ‘We hold that the group of Madeiran poets of this period does not constitute a distinct cycle but merely a branch of the mainland cycle, because it has no character of its own; the nature and form of these poets’ productions are shared with those of the other court poets of the same school, collected in the ‘General Songbook’ (*Cancioneiro Geral*). But that most notable group is nonetheless sufficient grounds for the island of Madeira to have an honourable share in the pre-classical history of the national literature, a share that T. Braga claimed for it.’

We shall now attempt a brief inventory or survey of these poetic compositions included in the ‘Cancioneiro Geral de Garcia de Resende’, going through the pages of its five volumes (1910–1918 edition) and at the same time offering some brief personal notes that may better identify the authors to whom they relate.

The first volume of the *Cancioneiro* opens with the celebrated poetic contest on ‘O Cuydar e o Sospirar’, to which many works make frequent reference and in which various court poets took part; this whole elegant debate fills more than a hundred pages of the edition we are consulting. The Madeira cycle is worthily represented in it by the compositions of the troubadour João Gomes, of whom we have already said elsewhere: ‘It has not been established whether he came to this archipelago as one of its early settlers or whether he was born in Madeira. In various writings he is cited as João Gomes da Ilha and also as João Gomes the Troubadour, for he cultivated poetry with distinction, and thirteen of his compositions are found in the “Cancioneiro de Garcia de Resende”.’

He married Dona Guiomar Ferreira in Funchal, daughter of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, the well-known companion of João Gonçalves Zarco. He held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands on the banks of the stream that took, and still keeps, the name of João Gomes. He was a page to Prince Henry the Navigator and died around 1495. Besides the verses cited above and included in the dispute of ‘O Cuydar e o Sospirar’, the *Cancioneiro* contains another twenty poetic compositions, all under the title ‘De Joham Gomez da Ylha’, though with some variants in the way these headings are spelt. As Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo has already noted, João Gomes was the most prolific of the poets of the Madeira cycle; to which we may add that he was also the most distinguished of them all.

He is followed immediately in the *Cancioneiro* by the name of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, who appears there under the heading *De Tristam teyxeyra capitãao de Machyco*. He was the second captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico and son of the first donatary (*donatário*), Tristão Vaz Teixeira. He was born in mainland Portugal and died in the capital of his donatary captaincy (*donataria*), where he was buried in the chapel of São João (St John the Baptist) in the church of Machico, which he had founded and built in the parish church of the town (*vila*) of Machico. He became better known as Tristão das Damas (‘Tristão of the Ladies’) because, says Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, he was a great courtier and a fine talker, composed many verses for the ladies and was very eloquent in speech. He appears as one of the most important characters in the interesting Madeiran novel *A Filha de Tristão das Damas*, by the illustrious writer and academician Mr J. Reis Gomes, which reproduces one of his poems included in the second volume of the *Cancioneiro*.

João Gonçalves da Câmara, son of João Gonçalves Zarco and second captain-donatary of Funchal, appears in Garcia de Resende’s collection with three poetic compositions under the heading *Joham Gonçalves capytão da ilha*. From the information given by Frutuoso, he must have been born around 1414; he died in Funchal on 25 March 1501 and was buried in the church of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), beside the steps of the high altar, where the stone covering his grave was discovered a few years ago. He greatly advanced the work of colonisation begun by his father and contributed considerably to the progress and growth of the old town of Funchal. In our hard-fought struggles in Morocco against the Moors he stood out for his fearless courage, and also for the material aid with which he several times helped to relieve the imminent danger facing the Portuguese possessions in that region. He founded the Convent of St Clare, to which he gave the large property of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) in 1492. He also appears as a notable character in the novel *A Filha de Tristão das Damas* mentioned above.

Manuel de Noronha is another court poet of the ‘Madeira cycle’ with some compositions in the *Cancioneiro*. He was born in Funchal and was the son of the second captain-donatary, João Gonçalves da Câmara. The old Madeiran chronicles speak in glowing terms of the services he rendered in North Africa and of his great bravery as a soldier, referring in particular to an encounter ‘in which, at the head of a hundred and fifty horsemen, almost all from the island, he performed prodigies of valour.’

With a small output of eight lines we come upon the name of Pero Correia, or rather Pedro Correia, as it appears in various writings on Madeiran matters. He was the second captain-donatary of Porto Santo, although Gaspar Frutuoso does not regard him as such. On the death of his father-in-law Bartolomeu Perestrelo, first donatary of that island, Pedro Correia bought the captaincy of Porto Santo, which he administered for some years. When Bartolomeu Perestrelo’s son and heir came of age, he contested possession of the donatary captaincy of which he had been unjustly deprived, and succeeded in recovering it by order of the monarch and taking possession of it. Pedro Correia was captain-donatary of the island of Graciosa, which he had to give up when he settled on Porto Santo.
Teófilo Braga and Rodrigues de Azevedo also include in the Madeira Cycle the poets of the *Cancioneiro*

Duarte de Brito, Rui de Sousa and Rui Gomes da Gran, who, as the historian of the islands tells us (*Saud.*, 156), were married to granddaughters of João Gonçalves Zargo, and also João de Abreu, who was married to a granddaughter of Tristão Vaz, first donatary (*donatário*) of Machico. Some compositions by these poets are found in the first and fourth volumes of the *Cancioneiro*.

The following words of Teófilo Braga also seem to refer to a Madeiran poet: ‘In some verses by Francisco da Silveira, written in 1498, mocking a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) from the island of Madeira who was living in Castile, he refers to the Count of Tendilla as a poet, father of the head of the Seville school, Diego Hurtado de Mendoza: “Let the Count of Tendilla and the lady Bobadilla say whether from the island of Funchal a man ever went to Castile so much to his misfortune”’

This composition is a long one and bears the title (*Canc.*, IV-230): ‘*Do coudel moor Francisco da Sylveira estando em Portugal a estas ceroylas de Manuel de Noronha, as quaes mandou a Castela*’ (By the chief cavalry magistrate Francisco da Silveira, being in Portugal, on these drawers of Manuel de Noronha, which he sent to Castile). The comment made by T. Braga cannot be clearly deduced from it; he must surely have had some other source of information besides what the context of this poem provided.
Cane (Ella and Florence du)
Works: *The Flowers and Gardens of Madeira*, London, 1909, 1 vol.
Smooth-hound (Mustelus laevis)

A cartilaginous fish of the family Carchariidae, found fairly often in these seas. It is caught near the coast, with nets or with hook tackle such as the longline and others. Of the so-called ‘leather fish’, it is one of the most pleasant-tasting.
Cinnamon tree (Cinnamomum zeylanicun)

A tree of the laurel family (Lauraceae), widely grown in the *quintas* and gardens of Madeira. It is highly ornamental and a good evergreen shade tree, but its bark has little aroma and no commercial value whatsoever. On the island we have seen only the Cassia variety.
Camphor tree (Cinnamomum Camphora)

A tree of the laurel family (Lauraceae), native to Japan and widely grown in the *quintas* and gardens of Funchal. It yields the camphor of commerce, which is obtained by placing small pieces of the trunk and branches of the tree in an iron vessel whose lid must be pierced with rice straws. When heated, the camphor volatilises and adheres to the straw, producing crude camphor, which is greyish in colour. Sublimation of this product in a sand bath yields the camphor sold by pharmacies. The camphor tree is a good evergreen shade tree.
Canhas (parish)

‘... and crossing a stream that lies beyond this Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), he marked out on a slope a church of the apostle St James, and further on he found the fire that he had ordered to be set along the coast; for which reason they could not pass, the woodland being very dense and a great fire burning in part of it. So they went down to a stream and, always following the sound of the water, came out at the sea, where they found the boats.’ This passage from Frutuoso, which refers to the first exploration made by Zarco and some of his companions in the discovery, tells us of their passage through the lands that later formed the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas, and therefore of the people who first crossed the virgin forests that covered those lands.

The origin of this parish’s name is well known. A family with the surname Canha, which settled there in the earliest days of colonisation, gave its lands the name Canhas. The name later passed to the future parish, of which those same lands were the ancient, original nucleus. Some assert, among them the authoritative commentator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), that João de Canha, squire to the Diogo, Duke of Viseu, was one of the first settlers of Canhas. He held lands there by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), which he leased on a perpetual tenure to Dona Constança Rodrigues de Almeida, widow of João Gonçalves Zarco; and his son Rui Pires de Canha founded the chantry (capela) of São Tiago, where the seat of the parish was later established. The illustrious annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), however, holds that Rui Pires de Canha was an earlier settler than João de Canha, without indicating what degree of kinship there may have been between the two men. The more common view, shared by several genealogies we have consulted, is that João de Canha settled there first, and that Rui Pires de Canha was one of his descendants who also acquired various lands within the bounds of this future parish.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of 30 January 1577 gave the diocesan bishop, Dom Jerónimo Barreto, the power to create this parish, which was only definitively constituted some years later, having been separated from the parish of Ponta do Sol. The first vicar appointed to it was Father Diogo da Silva, with an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of 20,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). By the royal decree of 10 July 1653 this became 19,000 *réis* in cash, one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. Diogo da Silva was succeeded as parish priests of this parish by Belchior Álvares de Araújo, António Fernandes, Amaro de Freitas, Francisco Rodrigues and António Novais Ferreira, in the period from its foundation up to the year 1647.

The new parish was established in the chapel of São Tiago, founded, as we have said, by Rui Pires de Canha, although others certainly attribute it to Braz da Camara or even to Rafael Castanho. We do not know when the seat of the parish was moved from this chapel to the new church, nor in what year the church was built. We conjecture that the new church went up in the first quarter of the 16th century. We do know, however, that in 1676 the Treasury Council (*Conselho de Fazenda*) ordered major repairs to its chancel, and that Joseph I, by a royal decree of 1752, ordered the parish church to be rebuilt. The foundation stone was solemnly laid on 22 July 1753, and on 4 March 1756 the episcopal decree was issued authorising its blessing and its opening for worship, which took place shortly afterwards.

During a pastoral visitation the diocesan prelate ordered the parish priest, Antonio de Caires, to petition for the creation of a curacy (*curato*), in view of the growth the population had already reached. The post of assistant priest (*coadjutor*) was created by the royal decree of 7 December 1731, with an annual stipend of one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine.

This parish has the chapels of St Andrew Avellino, Our Lady of the Angels and the Sacred Heart of Jesus. It once had the chapels of São Tiago, Our Lady of the Mount e Sant’Ana, Nossa Senhora da Anunciação and Our Lady of Succour, but these have now disappeared. We shall refer to each of them specifically in the appropriate place.

This parish still preserves some of the old ways and typical customs of the Madeiran peasantry, which are everywhere disappearing altogether. The home-made skirts, woven in stripes of bright and varied colours and so picturesque in appearance, and likewise the short capes of dark cloth, with bands at the points and edged with blue silk ribbon, are still commonly worn in this parish. At festivals and popular gatherings they lend a characteristically regional and exceedingly interesting air, and it is a pity to see them replaced by ridiculous fashions that suit so poorly the simple and modest women of our countryside. An old usage that still prevails here in the manner of address, in which the second person plural is always employed, deserves due mention at this point. *Podeis ajudar-me?* (can you help me?), *ide lá* (go there), *vinde cá* (come here) and a great many others are phrases in common, everyday use when the inhabitants of this parish address one another familiarly.

Its principal localities are Lombo da Piedade, Achada and Levada do Poiso, Anjos, Barreiro and Feiteiras, Carvalhal and Carreira, Serrado and Cova, Cruz, Fajã and Eiras, Lombo dos Canhas, Outeiro, Poiso, Salões and Levada da Madalena, Socorro, and Vale and Cova do Pico.

There is a small landing place there, called the Porto dos Anjos (‘angels’ landing’) because it lies in the locality of that name, and in this locality stands a chapel known by its dedication to Our Lady of the Angels. The parish’s trade and passenger traffic pass mainly through the town (*vila*) and landing place of Ponta do Sol. Although it may be considered an inland settlement, since the sea washes only a very insignificant part of its coast, it is nevertheless a manufacturing centre of some importance, far ahead of a great many other coastal parishes. There are four butter factories, one cheese factory, two spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) distilleries, one sawmill and one pasta factory.
It has a boys’ school, founded about 50 years ago, and a girls’ school of recent foundation.
The levadas (irrigation channels) of Pico and Cruzes rise in this parish and serve to irrigate it.

Canhas is bounded to the north by the uplands that adjoin the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), to the south by the ocean and Madalena do Mar (‘Magdalene by the sea’), to the east by Ponta do Sol and to the west by Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). It has 3,882 inhabitants.
Caniçal (parish)

This small and solitary parish (*freguesia*) lies at the far eastern end of Madeira. It is a village of poor fishermen, set between the sheer cliffs that separate it from Machico and the capriciously indented, rugged ground that forms the point of São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’). It may be said to be cut off from the rest of the island, even though the ocean does not divide it, because communications are so difficult. Only in cases of extreme necessity, and only when the state of the sea rules out the sea route, do people travel to the neighbouring parish of Machico, along a narrow footpath cut into the cliff, which is at times sheer and always strewn with the most hazardous and imminent dangers. The inhabitants spend their lives between the toil of fishing, their chief occupation, and the tilling and cultivation of a few plots of land. They live far below even a modest level of comfort, and when a storm breaks and towering waves lash the coast, preventing work at sea, poverty and hunger enter many households and parade there their whole train of horrors. They are a peaceful and orderly people, accustomed to the happy calm of that isolation and tranquillity. They know nothing of the comforts and conveniences of populous centres and so do not envy the pleasures and attractions that such places, where bustle and pleasure hold sway, offer to fortune’s favoured few.

The origin of its name must be the same as the one we have suggested for the parish of Caniço (‘reed’), and in adopting it we do not think we stray far from the truth. The original nucleus of settlement in this parish ‘comes’, says Dr Azevedo, ‘from the settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) in the locality so called (of Caniçal), which belonged to Vasco Martins Moniz, who died in 1510; by his will of 5 September 1489 he made it an entail (*morgado*) in favour of his eldest son Garcia Moniz, who was lord of Caniçal and founder of the church of the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), in the first quarter of the 16th century’.

Older than Vasco Martins Moniz, but perhaps still his contemporary, was João Teixeira, third son of the discoverer Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the first donatary of Machico. Of him Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘... he was a great hunter and fond of the chase, and for that reason he had in the town of Machico a hunting reserve (coutada) of his own at Caniçal (‘reed bed’), so full of game – rabbits, partridges, peacocks and many wild boar – that it is said to have been the best hunting reserve in all Portugal. This is suggested by a letter which is still kept today in the Council of Machico, written by King Manuel I to its officers, in which he earnestly charges them to keep strict watch over the hunting reserve of the sons of the first captain, and to let no one enter it, because he had been told and assured that, should he happen to come to the island, there were no other lands in which he could hunt and chase game but this one of Caniçal and the fields of Santa Catarina’.

Although the chronicler’s words seem to us somewhat exaggerated, we must nonetheless believe that the hunting reserve was of some importance, and the lands that made it up still bear the name of Terras de João Teixeira (‘João Teixeira’s lands’) today.

Caniçal is the oldest of the small parishes on this island. Its isolation and the difficulty of communication with the neighbouring settlements, even more than the number of its inhabitants, made the creation of the parish (*freguesia*) advisable. This took place around 1561, for at that time the couples living there would not even have numbered 15. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 12 September 1564 set the annual salary of the parish priest at 14,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). It was successively increased by the decrees of 24 November 1572, 10 September 1589, 22 October 1592 and 31 August 1609, after which he received an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of 24,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. Given the population, this was a higher salary than that of other vicars, which was justified by the poverty and isolation of the place. We know that between 1590 and 1660 the parish priests here were Fathers Amador Caldeira, António Ferreira de Quental, Matias Catanho and Vicente Luís.

The seat of the new parish was established in the chapel of São Sebastião (St Sebastian), founded by Garcia Moniz in the first quarter of the 16th century. Around 1594 the same chapel was enlarged or rebuilt, but the earthquake of 1748 left it in such a state of ruin that a contemporary witness says that *there is no remedy but a new building*. The foundation stone of the new church, the present one, was laid on 9 June 1749, and it was solemnly blessed on 13 December 1750. It was built on a site some distance from that of the first church, which still keeps the name of Sítio da Igreja Velha (‘old church’).

This parish has the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), picturesquely set on top of a hill and leaning out over the waters of the ocean. It was built on Monte Gordo (‘fat one’), or Monte da Piedade, 4 kilometres from the parish church. This is the moment to mention the unusual procession that is held every year to this chapel. The religious procession leaves the parish church and heads for the beach, where it boards several brightly decorated boats. Closely followed by a considerable number of small sailing craft, it sails to the foot of the hill, where it lands; then comes the arduous climb up the steep slope, ending finally with entry into the small, solitary chapel.

Much of the land in this parish (*freguesia*) lies uncultivated because irrigation water is scarce. It lacks springs of drinking water and no streams cross it. The author of the *Saudades*, doubtless referring to a period long before the one in which that book was written (1590), says the following:

‘To water the sugar cane in this town (*vila*) (Machico) and for Caniçal, a levada (irrigation channel) was brought from so far away that from the place where the water rises to the town it is four and a half leagues or nearly five, on which more than a hundred thousand *cruzados* were spent, because it comes through great mountains and deep ravines; and they say that in building it two peaks of hard rock were bored through, there being no other remedy. Raphael Catanho, a Genoese, with the great spirit he has, like almost all foreigners and above all those of that nation, was the first to begin bringing this water, and afterwards the King ordered it to be completed: and, because of the great cost it entailed, it is no longer used. To this passage of Frutuoso, Father Fernando Augusto de Pontes adds, in his interesting book *Excursões na Madeira*: “this is the very levada that supplies water to the *quinta* (country estate) of Palheiro Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s barn’)”. It seems that in former times this parish was notably wooded, and even today, to the north of it, some woods are found, perhaps remnants of the ancient forests.

Within the bounds of this parish lie the well-known Fossils, one of the places of greatest interest that this island offers to the observations of naturalists. We refer to them elsewhere (see Corpos Calcareos da Piedade).
São Lourenço point, with its adjacent islet, where a lighthouse and a telegraph and semaphore station are installed, deserves fuller treatment, which we shall give in a separate article.

Between the village and São Lourenço point lies the interesting and picturesque bay of Abra (‘bay’), no less extensive than that of Machico and very rich in fish. There was once a plan to build a harbour of refuge and a naval arsenal there, and some studies to that end were actually carried out in the first quarter of the 19th century.

On this side of the bay, that is, between it and the village, lies a small beach called Prainha, much visited by holidaymakers who spend the hot season in the town of Machico. It is the only sandy beach on this island, and lies at the head of a small, picturesque cove. The old church stood near it, and today preparations are being made to build salt pans there.

Apart from the inhabited part, this parish is in general very mountainous and its terrain is extremely rugged. Among its hills or peaks are Penedo do Saco, Junqueiro, Lagedo, Cancela, Judeu, Dragoal, Tojal, Facho and Castanho, the summit of the last rising to more than 600 metres above sea level. Pico da Cancela is an extinct crater, and from its surroundings one can see Ponta de São Jorge and the island of Porto Santo; it is on this height that the cape or point of São Lourenço truly begins.
The main localities are Banda do Silva, Serrado do Marmeleiro, Entre as Aguas and Banda de Além.
Caniço (chestnut-drying rack)

A rack made of canes or thin rods on which chestnuts are laid out to dry. In the room where the drying takes place, a small pit is dug in the floor and firewood is placed in it and set alight; the fire must not be allowed to go out while the process lasts. Only the smoke should reach the chestnuts, and when they are dry they are trodden underfoot in baskets so that they shed their shells.
Caniço (parish)

*Phragmites communis* is the scientific name of the common reed (*carriço*), also called *caniço*, a plant that grew there in great abundance at the time of the discovery. Frutuoso says: ‘...Ponta de Oliveira... lies seaward of some places called Caniço (‘reed’), because the land there was covered with a reed like slender canes, from which it took its name, albeit in corrupted form, for this plant, which they call *carriço*, has shoots like long canes. This place of Caniço is the end of the jurisdiction of Machico and the beginning of the jurisdiction of Funchal.’ As Manuel Tomás says in ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*):
A place hereafter in this reed-bed / By corruption shall be called Canisso. (*Hum logar depois neste carriço / Por corrupção se chamará Canisso.*)

After the discovery, and to begin the work of colonisation, João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira divided the lands of Madeira into two captaincies (see Captaincies), setting their limits and marking out the areas of their jurisdiction. A dividing line running from Ponta de Oliveira to Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’) separated the domains of the two captains-donatary. Caniço’s name is therefore linked to this drawing of boundaries, and later the parish (*freguesia*) had the peculiarity of belonging to the jurisdiction of both captaincies.

Apart from Funchal and Machico, Caniço was one of the first places on this island to be settled, and there the clearing and cultivation of the land began without delay. It had several “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*), one of them with a chantry (capela) and its own private chaplain, even before the parish was created. Some of the first colonists settled here and held much land as *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and others came later to establish themselves, widening the populated area and the cultivation and working of uncultivated ground. Among the early settlers and grantees were Álvaro de Ornelas, the Genoese Lucas Salvago, João Gavião, Gaspar do Rêgo and Vasco Fernandes Rêgo, Vasco Martins Moniz, Afonso de Viena and others, some of whom we shall discuss individually.

Some of these settlers were of noble origin. They kept their privileges of nobility and founded several entailed houses here. Particularly notable are that of Consolação (‘consolation’), instituted by Álvaro de Ornelas, one of the oldest in Madeira, dating from the end of the 15th century; the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by Vasco Martins Moniz; that of Matos Coutinho; and that of João Afonso.

Within a few years the growing number of new settlers and their immediate descendants formed a very substantial nucleus of population, which soon made the creation of a parish advisable. The densest settlement stretched along both banks of the stream, which was the boundary between the two captaincies. On either side of this watercourse two parish churches were built: the one on the right bank had the Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit) as its patron saint, and the one on the left bank St Anthony the Great. The lands around the first were called Caniço para a Cidade (‘Caniço towards the city’), and those around the second Caniço para Machico (‘Caniço towards Machico’). These names clearly indicated the captaincies to which they belonged.

We have good grounds to suppose that rivalries over jurisdiction, or disagreements between the inhabitants of the two banks of the stream, led to the building of the two churches so short a distance apart, since no plausible reason is known that would justify their construction. They implied the creation of two parishes (*freguesias*), which existed only in name, for they were always served by a single parish priest, although for some years services were held alternately in the two churches. The various references we have found to the creation of the parish, the stipends (*côngruas*) of the parish priests, the building and repair of the church, etc., do not refer specifically to either of the two churches, but only to one, without identifying which. This further confirms our view that there was only ever one parish, although its lands belonged to both captaincies. In 1538 the parish priest wrote in official documents: ‘Friar António Pires Cabral, vicar that I am of the churches of Caniço’. So it had been before, and so it remained afterwards, until religious services came to be held permanently in only one of the churches. It seems that the church of St Anthony the Great, on the left bank of the stream, gradually gained a certain pre-eminence over that of Espírito
Santo, the latter being the first to fall into ruin and be entirely abandoned.

Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo gives 1440 as the year in which this parish was created, and it is certainly one of the oldest on the island. The learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) places the church of Espírito Santo in the captaincy of Machico and that of St Anthony the Great in the captaincy of Funchal, which is not correct, as we were able to establish from documents in the archive of this parish. Did parish services begin in both churches at the same time? And if not, which of the two took precedence in the celebration of worship? We cannot say.

As noted above, services were already being held in both churches in 1538. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 21 February 1558 increased the parish priest’s stipend, which was then set at 8,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year. The *Indice Geral do Registo da Antiga Provedoria da Real Fazenda da Ilha da Madeira* reads: ‘royal decree of 25 November 1572 in favour of the vicar Belchior Mourato, granting an increase of 2,200 *réis*, two *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine on top of the 8,300 he already had, so as to have the full salary of 25,000 *réis* fixed by the Board of Conscience (*Mesa da Consciência*) for vicars with more than 100 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), the *moio* of wheat being valued at 6,000 *réis* and the *pipa* of wine at 2,500 *réis*’.

Between 1538 and the end of the 18th century the parish priests of this parish were António Pires Cabral, Belchior Mourato, Francisco de Sousa, Jerónimo Teixeira de Góis, Vicente Luís, Jerónimo Gomes de Agrela, André Moniz de Meneses, Manuel Gomes Jardim, João Baptista Spínola, Pedro Pereira da Silva, José Lomelino Barreto and António Francisco Spínola. Father José Lomelino Barreto, who worked so hard for the building of the new church and donated the land needed for it, served as parish priest of Caniço for more than 40 years.

The parish church of Caniço had the office of treasurer, a priest charged with assisting the vicar in the services of worship and especially in their administration. This office was created before 1550, for a royal decree of 6 February of that year increased its salary and fixed it at 6,000 *réis* in cash and thirty *alqueires* of wheat a year. By further instruments dated 18 September 1608, 4 July 1653 and 28 September 1668 this stipend was increased again, finally reaching 10,000 *réis* a year in cash, one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine. The office was abolished by royal decree of 27 December 1676.

The curacy (*curato*) of this parish was created by royal decree of 20 October 1605 and coexisted for some years with the office of treasurer; its annual stipend was 20,000 *réis*. Lopo Gomes Vieira, Vicente Luís and Jerónimo Gomes de Agrela were the first priests to hold this office here.
This church also had the office of organist, which received a salary of alqueires of wheat a year.

Of the chapel that stood here, with its own private chaplain, before the parish was created, we can say nothing regarding the year of its construction or the site on which it was built. Nor do we know whether it was turned into the parish church when the parish (*freguesia*) was created. We are equally ignorant about the building of the churches of Espírito Santo and St Anthony the Great, which stood one on each bank of the stream that divided the two captaincies.

By 1778 the first of these two churches had been completely destroyed and the second was far gone in ruin. Before this time, strenuous efforts had been made to build a new church, but they always came to nothing, and serious disagreements had also arisen over the preferred site, some wanting it on the left bank of the stream and others on the right. The old rivalries were resurfacing. The good offices of the vicar of the time, Father José Lomelino Barreto, who enlisted the support and influence of certain official figures, succeeded in removing every obstacle, and by her order of 3 March the queen commanded the building of the new church, which is the present parish church. The land for it was generously given by Father José Lomelino Barreto; the foundation stone was blessed on 2 August 1779, and the new church was solemnly blessed on 28 October 1783. On a stone tablet on its façade the following inscription can be read: *Sancto Spiritui Paraclito atque divo Antonio abbati sacrum Maria 1º. Lusitan. regina fideliss. equestris D. N. J. C. ordinis gubernat aedificavit: insulano tribunali regio curante. Anno )I). IDCCLXXX regni autem IIII.* (Sacred to the Holy Spirit the Paraclete and to St Anthony the Abbot: Maria I, Most Faithful Queen of Portugal, governor of the Order of Knighthood of Our Lord Jesus Christ, built it under the care of the island’s royal tribunal, in the year 1780, the fourth of her reign.)

The parish at present has the chapels of Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*) and Madre de Deus (Mother of God); those of Our Lady of Deliverance, Nossa Senhora da Salvação (Our Lady of Salvation) and Our Lady of Succour no longer exist. We refer to all of them in the appropriate place. Gaspar Frutuoso, writing of Caniço as it was in 1590, the year in which he wrote the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, says the following:

‘Almost half a *légua* further on there is a village of two hundred households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), with a church dedicated to the Holy Spirit, which is called Caniço, on a stream that runs from north to south, surrounded by many vineyards of many vine varieties and good Malmsey. Seaward of this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) lies Ponta de Oliveira, where an olive tree was planted as a boundary mark for the division of the two captaincies, which are divided by this stream, that of Machico lying to the east and that of Funchal to the west; and along it, they say, runs the boundary from the southern shore to the other side in the north. For from this Caniço down to the sea it is about a quarter of a *légua*, where lies the landing place at which everything in this area is loaded. And it is called Caniço de Baixo, in relation to the other, which is called Caniço de Cima.

Around the middle of the 15th century, when the towns (*vilas*) of Funchal and Machico were created, some ten *lugares* were also created on this island. These were settlements intermediate between the parish and the town, and the parish of Caniço was among them, which proves its relative importance even at that time. Camacha was separated from Caniço in 1676.

In former times there was a great deal of contact between the Desertas and Caniço, perhaps because the fishermen of this parish frequented the waters around those islands. Although the Desertas were not part of this parish, it was nevertheless at Caniço that boats from the Desertas most often put in, and they even brought there the bodies of those who died on those lonely islands. Until not many years ago, the workers employed there in hunting and fishing were recruited in the parish of Caniço.

Manuel do Nascimento Nóbrega, to whom we shall devote a separate entry, was a native of this parish. Father Jerónimo de Nóbrega was also born here; he sailed for North America and made a considerable fortune there. On several occasions he sent to this island very substantial sums for charitable institutions, amounting to many *contos* (one million réis) *de réis*. He also presented the church of his native parish with some rich church furnishings.

Among the events of greatest interest to the history of Caniço are the incidents involving the Liberal and Miguelist troops when they crossed this parish in 1828, and the regrettable episodes that occurred at the time of the supposed meetings of the Parish Council (*Junta de Paróquia*). As these matters will be the subject of separate entries, we shall not deal with them here.

Among the privileges and rights granted to João Gonçalves Zarco was that ‘ninguem nom faça y moynhos, soomente elle ou quem lhe prouuer’ (no one shall build mills there but he or whom he pleases). It is said that the first mill in Madeira was built in this parish, and there is still a locality there called Azenha (‘water mill’), although we cannot be sure that the name refers to that early and doubtless very rudimentary mill for grinding grain.

Onion growing in Madeira was almost confined to this parish, where the crop was cultivated on a very large scale. It is still the place that produces this crop most abundantly, but its cultivation is at present much reduced. It once produced 30,000 *pesos*, worth approximately thirty *contos de réis*, almost all of it for export.

There is a small local industry, which may be considered peculiar to this parish: the making of hats from palm leaves, worn by working men. What they lack in elegance and suppleness they make up for in sturdiness and durability.
There are two schools: one for boys, founded around 1821, and one for girls, of more recent foundation.

Besides the Levada da Serra, Caniço is irrigated by the Levada do Pico do Arvoredo, the Levada de Baixo and the Levada da Azenha. Each is run by an association of *heréus* (co-owners of the water rights of a levada), and the statutes of the first were published in the *Diário do Governo* of 31 October 1877. All these water sources rise in Camacha.
The parish is crossed by a stream which rises in the parish of Camacha and takes various names according to the places or localities through which it passes.
It has a passable harbour, Porto dos Reis Magos, where there are about 20 fishing boats. There is a small landing place at Ponta da Oliveira.

The principal localities of this parish are: Tendeira, Moinhos, Assomada, Atalaia e Portinho, Madre de Deus, Zimbreiros, Caniço para Machico, Barreiros, Pedra Mole, Castelo, Serralhal e Amoreiras, Caniço para a Cidade, Vargem, Azenha, Ribeira dos Pertetes, Livramento, Vale, Quinta, Abegoaria and Palheiro do Ferreiro.
In the locality of Barreiros stands the so-called Pico do Telégrafo, which commands fine views; on clear days the channel and the island of Porto Santo can be seen from it.
Caniço is bounded to the north, east, west and south respectively by São Gonçalo and the ocean.

The most central part of this parish is 9 kilometres from the centre of the city and 8 from the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz.
