It belongs to the municipality (*concelho*) and judicial district (*comarca*) of Santa Cruz, although the inhabitants have on several occasions sought to have their parish incorporated into the municipality and judicial district of Funchal. Its population is 4,697 inhabitants.
Canning (W. P.)

Commander of the English frigate *Alligator*, on which Governor Valdez and other constitutionalists took refuge when Miguelist troops seized Madeira in 1828. He drowned in the tank (irrigation reservoir) of a *quinta* (country estate) belonging to an English merchant, on the afternoon of 24 September 1828.
Soft cut stone
A conglomerate of black ash, made compact by pressure. It is used for ovens, braziers, basins, filters etc.
The name soft cut stone (*cantaria mole*) is also given to compact red scoria, used for door frames in country houses.

It was widely used in the construction of all kinds of buildings in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries, before the use of ‘*cantaria rija*’ (hard dressed stone of vesicular basalt), or porous basalt, became general.
Cantaria rija
This name is given to the porous basalt used for door frames, steps, corner stones, etc. *Cantaria rija* (hard dressed stone of vesicular basalt) is abundant in the vicinity of Câmara de Lobos.
See Basalts.
Cantin

Cape Cantin lies on the coast of Morocco, between two well-known points on the littoral: Mazagan to the north and Mogadouro to the south. It is roughly equidistant from these two coastal towns, about 60 miles from each. This is the point of the African continent whose latitude corresponds most closely to that of the island of Madeira. Cape Cantin lies at 32 33’ N and bears some 47 miles SW. ¼ S. of Cape Blanc. It rises steeply to 60 metres above the sea, and on its summit stands a small chapel. It is also the point on the African coast nearest to our archipelago, from which it is about 350 miles distant.
Cão (Friar Nuno)

He was a brother (*freire*) of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which the Madeira archipelago belonged in spiritual matters (see Order of Christ). He was one of the first priests whom the Order of Christ sent to this island at the request of Prince Henry the Navigator, and he held wider powers of canonical jurisdiction than the other clergy then in Madeira. He exercised parochial duties at the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*) and was later parish priest of the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé, being invested as dean of the Cathedral when this diocese was created in 1514. He was the representative of the Order of Christ and therefore carried out duties of inspection and superintendence over various branches of public administration. He left an honoured memory.
Chapel of Christ see Lord of Miracles of Machico (Chapel of the)
Capela Monumento see Nossa Senhora da Conceição (Capela de)
Chantries

They differed from entailed estates in that the property was subject to pious obligations. Chantries (*capelas*) could not be alienated, and their holders received only part of the income from the property, the remainder being set aside to fulfil the said obligations. There was a court called the ‘Juízo dos Resíduos e Capelas’ (see that entry), which oversaw the fulfilment of all pious obligations and imposed penalties on defaulters.
Capelo and Ivens (the explorers)

Among the brilliant receptions that Madeira has prepared for some of its most illustrious visitors, one stands out: that given on 12 September 1885 to the African explorers and our compatriots, the naval officers Hermenegildo Capelo and Roberto Ivens.

At a meeting held a few days earlier in the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), chaired by the civil governor Vasco Guedes, the final programme of festivities was settled and committees were appointed to carry out every item of it.

At the entrance to the city a temporary wooden quay was built and colourfully decked out. There the explorers landed, awaited by the authorities, public officials, committee members and all the most distinguished people of the city, as well as a large crowd. The city entrance and the former Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’) were magnificently decorated, and at night they were illuminated with great brilliance and profusion.

After the landing, a formal reception was held at the Palácio de São Lourenço, where several speakers greeted the explorers with enthusiastic addresses, and the explorers received the tributes of the large and select gathering present.

In the afternoon a splendid banquet for 60 guests was given in the rooms of the former Funchal Club (*Club Funchalense*), presided over by the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). Several speeches were made, which Roberto Ivens movingly acknowledged in his own name and in that of his companion.

The explorers then toured the illuminated streets and squares. Entering the building of the Funchal Commercial Association (*Associação Comercial do Funchal*), Roberto Ivens drew on a map of Africa a quick sketch of the exploratory journey they had just completed across the dark continent. For many years the sketch was kept in the association’s office, and it is surely still there, religiously preserved.

The spacious and elegant rooms of the Funchal Club opened again on the following night for a splendid ball, a magnificent occasion that greatly impressed the illustrious explorers and touched them deeply.
They sailed on 14 September for Lisbon, where a brilliant and enthusiastic reception awaited them.
The streets flanking the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’) to the south and north were named after Hermenegildo Capelo and Roberto Ivens respectively.
Capelo (Félix de Brito)

Portuguese naturalist, born in Peniche on 4 March 1838 and died on 16 April 1879. Works: *Peixes da ilha da Madeira, Açores e das Possessões Portuguezas d’Africa, que existem no Museu de Lisboa* (*Jorn. de Sc. Mat., Phys. e Nat*, vol. III, pp. 194 and 280, and vol. IV, p. 83).
Capim (Panicum barbinode)
A grass native to Brazil, widely cultivated in the surroundings of Funchal.
It is a perennial plant with sturdy stems that are very hairy at the nodes, and it is much liked by livestock.
Captains-donatary
See Donataries.
Captains-general
See Governors and Captains-General.
Capitães-mores

They were abolished on this island by the decree of 20 July 1832, which did away with the territorial militia (*ordenanças*), or third line, ‘with all their posts of whatever denomination’. The *capitães-mores*, who had the *sargentos-mores* as their subordinates, left a sad memory for the arbitrary acts they committed and the oppression and humiliation to which they subjected the people.
See Ordinance Militia (*Ordenanças*).
Captaincies

Under the original system of colonisation, our overseas dominions were divided, for the purposes of public administration, into provinces of greater or lesser extent, which were then called captaincies. Each was headed by a captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), its supreme local authority, who generally enjoyed wide powers in the conduct of the various public affairs. The first captaincies of our discoveries and conquests were those of the Madeira archipelago: one had its seat on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and the other two in Machico and in Funchal.

The first comprised only the small island of Porto Santo. Its first donatary was Bartolomeu Perestrelo, who was one of its earliest settlers and, it may be said, the founder of the town (*vila*) of Baleira, capital of that captaincy. Some authors have fallen into the error of regarding Perestrelo as a navigator and even as the discoverer of Porto Santo, misled by the fact that he was its first donatary, a position that did not always go with the act of discovery. The letter of Prince Henry the Navigator granting the island of Porto Santo to Bartolomeu Perestrelo is dated 1 November 1446, that is, more than twenty years after the colonisation of the archipelago began. We must suppose that Perestrelo had settled on Porto Santo with all the privileges and prerogatives granted to donataries, and that Prince Henry’s letter was merely the legal and authentic confirmation of those privileges. The same must be believed of the other two captaincies of Madeira. In the letter of grant (carta de doação) Prince Henry says: ‘I give charge of my island of Porto Santo to Bartolomeu Perestrelo, *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of my household, so that the said Bartolomeu Perestrelo may maintain it for me in justice and right; and should he die, it pleases me that his first son, or any other if such there be, shall hold this charge in the manner aforesaid, and so from descendant to descendant in direct line... shall have... jurisdiction... civil and criminal, save death or the cutting off of a limb...’ This letter mentions various rights, prerogatives and exemptions granted to the first donatary, including the collection of various contributions and taxes. The captaincy of Porto Santo remained in the possession and under the superintendence of Bartolomeu Perestrelo’s descendants until Philippine rule, with the appointment of governors-general, reduced the donataries of the archipelago to a very subordinate and almost purely honorary position, though they continued to collect substantial revenues from the original privileges granted to them. When Portugal fell under the Castilian yoke, Diogo Perestrelo Bisforte was the 6th captain-donatary of the island of Porto Santo.

The island of Madeira was divided into two captaincies, with their seats in Funchal and Machico. After the discovery, in order to begin the colonisation and settlement of its lands, the two discoverers lost no time in dividing and demarcating them, fixing a dividing line that ran from Ponta da Oliveira (‘olive-tree point’) to Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’). Frutuoso says: ‘... Ponta de Oliveira, where a boundary mark was planted for the division of the two captaincies, which are divided by this stream, that of Machico lying to the east and that of Funchal to the west, and along it, they say, runs the demarcation from the seashore in the south to the other side in the north’, adding elsewhere: ‘...it comes out at the other point on the southern side, where a branch or stake of olive wood, which had come from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), was driven in as a boundary mark of this jurisdiction, whence the point took the name Ponta da Oliveira ... ’

The letter of grant (carta de doação) of the captaincy of Machico to Tristão Vaz Teixeira by Prince Henry the Navigator is dated 8 May 1440. In it the grantor states: ‘dou carreguo a Tristão caballeyro de minha casa na minha ylha da madeyra de a terra dees de além da ribeyra do Caniço dez passos como se bay pella ribeyra acima & de hi atrabeçar a serra ate a ponta de Tristam... ’ (I give charge to Tristão, knight of my household, in my island of Madeira, of the land from ten paces beyond the Ribeira do Caniço (‘reed’), going up the stream, and from there across the uplands as far as the point of Tristão...). This document is couched in terms identical to the letter of concession issued in favour of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, and is six years older than the latter. The observation we have already made about the grant of Porto Santo applies here too: it must be supposed that in 1440 only the confirmation in law took place, but that the grant had existed in fact long before. Tristão Vaz Teixeira’s son, grandson and great-grandson succeeded to the captaincy. The last of them, named Diogo Teixeira, was removed from it for lack of the ability to govern it, and died much later in Funchal, in the year 1540. In 1541 the monarch gave the captaincy to António da Silveira, who greatly distinguished himself in India. Some years later he sold it to the Count of Vimioso, and it then passed to his son Francisco de Portugal, who died in a naval battle in the seas of the Azores, after which this donatary captaincy (*donataria*) reverted to the Crown. Under Castilian rule Tristão Vaz da Veiga (see that entry) was invested in the office of captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico.

It is in the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 16 August 1461, in which Afonso V confirms the grant of the Madeira archipelago to his uncle Prince Henry, published on p. 451 ff. of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), that the document granting the captaincy of Funchal to João Gonçalves Zarco, dated 1 November 1450, is inserted. The grants of the captaincies of Porto Santo, Machico and Funchal date respectively from 1446, 1440 and 1450. It is rather strange that the most recent should be that of Funchal, later even than that of Porto Santo, when there are many reasons to suppose that the concession made to Gonçalves Zarco was the oldest of all. We cannot explain this fact, about which the learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ keeps the most complete silence.

The privileges and prerogatives granted to João Gonçalves Zarco by the grant of the captaincy of Funchal do not differ essentially from those of the other captaincies. As regards the taxes and dues that the donataries (*donatário*) could collect for their own profit, the letters of grant mention the following: only they could own mills or watermills for grinding cereals; every water-powered sawmill was to pay them one mark of silver (*marco de prata*, c. 230 g of silver) a year; the donataries held the monopoly on the sale of salt; nobody could have ovens or bakeries except for domestic use; the tithe of the royal revenues belonged to them; and they could grant land in *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) on conditions that the letters of grant do not specify. In addition, they had oversight of all matters of public administration, and they tried and sentenced all crimes, except cases involving the death penalty or the cutting off of limbs. (see Donataries).

The captaincy of Porto Santo never attained a high degree of prosperity. The smallness of the island, the neglect to which the mother country consigned it from the earliest days of colonisation, the frequent pirate raids, the poor administration of some donataries and governors, the conceited pride of many of its inhabitants, who scorned work because they were descended from old noble families, and the indolence of its residents, brought about by climatic conditions and by other causes besides – all this contributed markedly to the slight development of this donatary captaincy (*donataria*) (see Fifths and eighths).

The captaincy of Machico, in conditions very different from those of Porto Santo, developed rapidly and grew remarkably prosperous, but this prosperity did not last long. Funchal gradually became the great commercial emporium of the archipelago, the centre of its inhabitants’ bustling activity, the magnet for so many visitors from Portugal and abroad, and the court of the Madeiran nobility, who abandoned their lands and manor houses to lead the coveted and enervating life of the populous towns, etc. It was then that the donatary captaincy of Machico began to fall from the prosperity it had reached, and before long it lost all the importance it had once had as a commercial, industrial and agricultural centre. What Gaspar Frutuoso says on this subject is highly expressive and eloquent:

‘…and also on his death (the donatary Dom Francisco de Portugal, who died shortly after 1580) this captaincy fell vacant and reverted to the Crown, and it came to such a state that in this populous jurisdiction of Machico there was hardly anyone who could readily keep a horse, save two or three persons. All this grandeur was turned into poverty; and it was a dream that passed away before the hardships later suffered by all the people of this so noble lineage and so prosperous Captaincy: and if the forebears had everything in abundance, their descendants paid dearly for it afterwards, being reduced to the utmost degree of poverty, for there was never anything in abundance that in time did not come to be wanting. Such are the turns of the world, in which we place so much trust, without ever being fully undeceived of its deceptions.’

Only the captaincy of Funchal developed rapidly and steadily, with remarkable growth, and within a short time it reached a truly extraordinary degree of prosperity. Its capital was made a town (*vila*) in 1451, a city in 1508 and the seat of a bishopric in 1514.
Capitão (street)

The stretch of Rua dos Murças between the Avenida de João Gonçalves Zarco and the Largo da Sé was called Rua do Capitão, a name it kept until not so many years ago. In earlier times the whole of Rua dos Murças was known as Rua do Capitão. Frutuoso says: ‘From this Rua do Sabão there rises one that is called do Capitam, because it is the most direct way to his house....’ The captain to whom the *Saudades* refer was the captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, who had his residence in the Fort of São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’).
Snails
In general, this name is given to the land molluscs of the family Helicidae, or even to others, including freshwater species, whose shells resemble those of that family.

The natural history of the Madeiran pulmonates has been carefully investigated by various malacologists, such as Richard Thomas Lowe, the Baron of Castelo de Paiva and others, but no two authors agree on the number of species recorded. If one holds that certain forms deserve the rank of species, another asserts that they are no more than mere varieties, and sometimes the reverse view is taken of other forms.

If we accept the opinion of Thomas Vernon Wollaston, the most recent of the authors to have dealt with the subject at length, there are 176 species, of which 131, counting only the land species, are peculiar to these islands.

Our archipelago is therefore a centre of origin for many species of pulmonates. What makes this part of the fauna still more remarkable is that, of these 131 species, 61 are peculiar to Madeira, 44 to Porto Santo and 10 to the Desertas, while only 16 are common to all the islands. In this count the Desertas are taken as a whole; if we consider them as what they really are, namely three islands, it follows that only 5 species can be regarded as belonging to all the islands of the archipelago. It is clear, then, that each island has in turn given rise to forms entirely its own, and that distribution has taken place over areas so limited that even small islets, isolated rocky outcrops in the sea, have seen forms arise among their rocks that have never been found outside so restricted a habitat.

Thus the islets of Cal, Fora and Fonte, off Porto Santo, have forms of *Helix* and *Pupa* found nowhere else. In other cases the habitat is confined to the crests of neighbouring hills or to the slope of a ravine, as happens both on Porto Santo and on Madeira. The genus *Helix* has the greatest number of representatives, followed by *Pupa*, *Lovea*, *Patula* and

*Clausilia*, with successively fewer species, besides other genera of lesser importance. The slugs are divided among 10 species, and 4 species are recorded in the operculate genus *Craspedopoma*, one of which, *C. trochoideum*, has been found only in certain valleys in the north of Madeira. The freshwater species include the genera *Limnaea*, *Physa*, *Planorbis* and *Ancylus*, all of whose members are European; they are common in the levadas (irrigation channels), streams and tanks, where an operculate of the order of prosobranchs, *Hydrobia similis*, also occurs. On the coastal rocks washed by the tide, endemic species of the genera *Melampus* and *Auricula* have been collected, as well as other African or European species of the genera *Pedipes*, *Truncatella* and *Assiminea*.

Many of the Madeiran pulmonates have been observed in the sub-fossil state in prodigious quantities, their dense aggregation sometimes giving them the appearance of conglomerates. The deposits of these fossils consist either of calcareous sand, sometimes compacted as if it were sandstone, or of clay mixed with angular stones; in the latter case they are clastic rocks or transported ground, almost always formed on the flanks of certain hills. Such deposits exist on Madeira, east of Caniçal (‘reed bed’); on the summit of Bugio, one of the Desertas; and on Porto Santo at various places, such as Ilhéu de Baixo, Ilhote, Vigia da Ponta, Campo de Baixo, Ribeiro da Vigia, Penedo, Mornos and Zimbral da Areia.

Of the 176 species of pulmonates – a figure established according to Thomas Vernon Wollaston’s criteria, as already stated – 82 have been found in the fossil state, and of these only 12 have not been observed living, so they may be considered extinct. *Helix Lowei*, peculiar to Porto Santo and the largest of all the snails of the archipelago, measuring 5 centimetres or more in diameter, was long considered extinct. However, the botanist J. M. Moniz succeeded in discovering a living specimen on the rocks of Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’), and the English naturalist Dr Alfred Merle Norman obtained from a shell dealer in Frankfurt a recent, well-preserved specimen which had evidently left these islands by unknown means and ended up in the German dealer’s shop.
Caracol da Vinha (Helix pisana)

A gastropod mollusc found in the far eastern part of Madeira, in the low-lying part of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and also on the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*). On Porto Santo, where it was once very abundant, it is used to feed domestic ducks.
Caramanchão

An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico. Here stands the chapel of São Cristóvão (St Christopher), which the sons of Cristóvão Moniz de Meneses, holder of the entail (*morgado*), had built in 1690 under a provision of their father’s will that obliged them to do so.
Caramelo

This is the name given to certain fragments of fossil corals of the genus *Danaia* and others, which occur in the limestone deposits of Porto Santo. *Caramelo*, which consists of carbonate of lime, was used to counter the acidity of wines, and also in the preparation of fizzy drinks such as lemonades, Porto Santo mineral water, etc.
Caramujo

A locality in the municipality (*concelho*) and parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente, 1325 metres above sea level. It has a mountain shelter built by the District Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas do Distrito*), and close by are the springs of the Levada da Ribeira do Inferno (‘hell’s stream’), a levada (irrigation channel) that irrigates land in the parish of São Vicente. Following this levada to its source, one enjoys views of astonishing beauty.

Caramujo (‘sea snail’), or Chão do Caramujo, lies a short distance from the northern edge of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) and appears once to have been the crater of a volcano. It is a spot much visited by Portuguese and foreigners alike.
Caramujo Caiado
The name given to very large, old specimens of the edible *caramujo* whose shells show whitish patches.
Caramujo de Dona (Littorina striata)

A gastropod mollusc of the family Trochidae, very common at the level of the highest high tides and even above that line. It is the sea mollusc living farthest from the water’s edge here. It is not edible and is found on all the islands of the archipelago, including the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*).
The expression *caramujo de dona* is peculiar to the island of Porto Santo.
Caramujo (Trochus colubrinus)

A gastropod mollusc of the family Trochidae. It is edible and is found in the intertidal zone of all the islands. Salted or pickled, it is imported from the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) in relatively large quantities.
Caranguejo Judeu (Grapsus webbi)

A decapod crustacean of the family Grapsidae, common on certain rocks along the coast. It is not usually eaten, although it has a pleasant taste, but once crushed or chewed it is used as groundbait for catching certain fish.
It is also called *cabra*.
Caranguejo Moiro (Plagusia squamosa)
A decapod crustacean of the family Grapsidae. In summer it frequents the coastal rocks and is a shellfish enjoyed by many people. It is also called *caranguejo de comer*.
Caranguejola

A name applied to decapod crustaceans of various families, among which the genera *Maia*, *Eriphia*, *Calappa* and *Pagurus* may be cited. The only edible *caranguejola* (local name for various crabs, chiefly spider crabs) is *Maia squinado*, rarely taken in trawl nets.
Caranguejola de Natura (Homola cuvieri)
A species of decapod crustacean, caught from time to time in the seas of Madeira.
Carcinology
The crustaceans of this archipelago are far from having been fully studied; only one group or another has received a little attention from a few naturalists.

The Decapods are represented by a few dozen species in the private collections in Funchal. These species can be roughly divided as follows: 40 among the Brachyura, 15 among the Anomura and 30 among the Macrura.

Among the Brachyura, or short-tailed Decapods, we shall mention the following as the best known or the most notable for their shape or food value. There is the edible *caranguejola* (local name for various crabs, chiefly spider crabs) (*Maia squinado*), sometimes taken in nets close to the coast; and the triangular crustaceans of the genera *Leptopodia*, *Stenorynchus*, *Amathia*, *Pisa* and others, among which the interesting *Leptopodia sagittaria* deserves mention; it frequents the bay of Funchal at depths of 20 to 40 *braças* and more. The cliff *caranguejola* (*Eriphia spinifrons*) is not common and lives in small holes dug into the rock, with an opening so narrow that it seems to live imprisoned there, catching the food that passes near the entrance of its hiding place. A large crab (*Cancer Bellianus*) is caught from time to time in coastal waters. The mild *jacas* (*jaca*: local name for small shore crabs) (*Xantho floridus* and *X rivulosus*) and the wild *jaca* (*Grapsus marmoratus*) are sought as bait and are frequent on stretches of coast covered with sand or fine gravel. The elegant *Lupea hastata*, whose hind legs are adapted for swimming, is also called *jaca*; it is common on sandy bottoms from the bay of Machico to the Ponta de São Lourenço and on the southern coast of Porto Santo. The driftwood *jaca* (*Grapsus minutus*) is common on floating timber and on the shells of turtles or other objects that the current carries into these seas. This is the crab that some claim Christopher Columbus took as a sure sign that land was near, when the navigator glimpsed it in the open ocean, clinging to masses of sargassum weed or some piece of wood carried along by the waters. Then there are the Jew crab, also known as *cabra* (*Grapsus Webbi*), suitable as bait and groundbait for fish, and the Moorish or eating crab (*Plagusia squamosa*), which is boiled before being put on sale and, like the preceding one, is not rare above the shoreline at certain points where the coast is rocky; the spider (*Plagusia clavimana*), frequent in some places among the stones left uncovered by the tide and valued as bait for certain fish; and finally the bashful *caranguejola* (*Calappa granulata*), interesting for the domed shape of its carapace and for its greatly enlarged pincers, which allow it to hide much of its face. It is not very rare in the bay of Porto Santo, on whose beach it becomes stranded during heavy swells.

Of the Anomura, or Decapods with anomalous tails, mention should be made of *Dromia vulgaris* and *Homala spinifrons*, which live in the bay of Funchal and in many other places beyond a depth of 15 *braças*; the *caranguejola de natura* (*Homola Cuvieri*), the largest crustacean known in Madeira, rarely caught on deep bottoms; and finally the genus *Pagurus*, represented by several species, some belonging to the shore and others to deeper water. Among the latter, *P. callidus* and *P. striatus* deserve mention for their great size.

Crustaceans of the genus *Pagurus* are known as *caranguejolas*, which is in fact what fishermen generally call crustaceans that are of no use at all. In certain localities these *Pagurus* are extremely abundant in rock pools at the water’s edge. As their abdomen is soft, they slip into a mollusc shell, one of the many to be found empty. This shell usually belongs to the genera *Trochus*, *Columbella*, *Mitra*, *Nassa* and *Murex*, and less often to *Bittium*, *Triton*, *Cassis*, *Ranella*, *Natica*, *Pleurotona*, *Cypriaea* or *Scalaria*; even land snails (*Helix*, *Bulimus*) will serve them, or the loose tubes of molluscs of the genus *Vermetus* and of worms of the genus *Serpula*.

The Macrura, or long-tailed decapods, include among others the genus *Galathea*, found on both shallow and deep bottoms; the lobster with broad, short, leaf-like antennae (*Scyllarus latus*), highly prized for its fine flavour and relatively frequent in shallow places such as the waters off Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’), where the fisherman gathers it by diving to the bottom and taking it directly by hand; *Arctus ursus*, allied to the preceding species but not edible, sometimes dredged at about 20 *braças* (fathoms) off Funchal and at 90 off Porto Santo; the lobster with long, thick antennae (*Palinurus vulgaris*), also called *lagostim* or *lagostão*, less common than the flat-antennaed lobster already mentioned, and caught like it, either by diving or accidentally on hook tackle or in nets; the beautiful and rare *Nephrops norvegicus*; and finally the shrimps and prawns, among them the interesting and rare *Funchalia Woodwardi*, *Penaeus Edwardsiannu*, *Palaemon squilla* and
*Crangon vulgaris*, some of which are caught in rush pots as bait for choice fish, or very rarely for sale at the market.

James Yate Johnson wrote on three decapods: *Description of a New Species of Cancer obtained at Madeira* (*Proceedings of the Zoological Society of London*, 1861) and *Description of a New Genus and a New Species of Macrurous Decapod Crustacean belonging to the Penaeidae discovered at Madeira* (ibid., 1867).
In the order Stomatopoda the sea around Madeira offers us, among others, the elegant species of the genus *Squilla*, such as *S. mantis*, *S. Desmarestii*, etc.
The order Cumacea, which is also represented, would deserve investigation by competent specialists.

The marine isopods comprise several genera that live on fish, on the rocks of the shore or in other situations, but none of them has yet been the subject of detailed study. Only the terrestrial isopods have been dealt with, by Dr Alfred M. Norman, who published *The Land Isopoda of Madeira*, 1899.
Many forms of amphipods exist in the sea, on the beaches and in freshwater streams, but the group lacks thorough investigation.
This is what we have to say about the great division of the Malacostraca. On the Entomostraca, the following occurs to us:

The marine copepods were studied in part by Isaac C. Thompson, who, in the plankton he collected in the bay of Funchal and in the Canary Islands, was able to record 64 species, 6 of them new to science. He wrote on the subject *Copepoda of Madeira and the Canary Islands, with description of New Genera and Species* (*Linnean Society Journal, Zoology*, 1887). There are, however, many others, above all fish parasites, that have yet to be recorded. Representatives of this group, such as the curious *Cyclops* and others, are also found in certain fresh waters, particularly in water held in tanks.

There are several freshwater ostracods, among which the *Cypris*, at times abundant on Madeira and Porto Santo, may be cited; among the marine forms is the remarkable *Laura Gerardiae*, a parasite of the luminous coral *Gerardia*
*Lamarckii*, which was so admirably studied by Lacaze-Duthiers in a masterly monograph.
In inland waters the order of the cladocerans is also in evidence, and probably that of the phyllopods.
Finally, of the barnacles (Cirripedia), 13 species were mentioned by Darwin in his work on this order, but the number collected is already higher at present.

Besides the scant literature cited, 8 species of the great division of the Entomostraca were described in 1855 by Dr S. Fischer in the proceedings of the Royal Bavarian Academy (*Academia Real da Baviera*).
Cardais

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Água de Pena. Here, on land he owned, Canon Henrique Modesto de Betencourt built a chapel dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*) in 1907.
Thistle

The Madeiran plants known by this name belong to the daisy family (Compositae) and to the genera *Cynara*, *Silybum*, *Galactites*, *Carthamus*, *Centaurea* and *Scolymus*. While young, or after suitable preparation, thistles serve as fodder for livestock.
See Pencas.
Cardo (peak)
A hill in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, at an altitude of 438 m.
Cardoso (Simão Nunes)

The annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says the following of him: ‘Simão Nunes Cardoso, who was surely of the family of the Cardosos of Gaula, in the captaincy of Machico, since there were no others of that surname, was alive in 1566, for he wrote the *Relação do saco que os franceses fizeram na ilha da Madeira* (Account of the sack the French made of the island of Madeira), which took place in that year. This account was never printed; but probably from it','

Jerónimo Dias Leite copied the narrative of the event for his *Historia da Madeira*, and from this it would have passed into chapters XLIV–XLVI of ‘Longing for the Homeland’. We are persuaded of this because there is no record of any other account of the event, and because those found in the *Saudades* are plainly inspired by the rivalry between the captaincy of Machico and that of Funchal, and to the discredit of the latter.’
Cardot (J.)
*On some Mosses collected in Madeira by William Trelease* (*Eight Annual Report of Missouri Bot. Gard.* 1897).
Carlos (Campo de D.)

The former Campo de Dom Carlos (‘King Carlos square’), today Campo do Almirante Reis (‘Admiral Reis field’), was begun in 1898 and completed in 1901. It cost the Municipality more than 24 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos) and was conceived to improve the sanitation of the Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) district. Towards its construction the Government contributed the land of the old Fort of São Pedro (St Peter), part of the city’s curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city) and perhaps the Campo das Loucas (‘madwomen’s field’) or de Challons; the Municipality contributed the land of the Praça Académica and of the streets bordering it to the south and east, together with that of the Rua dos Balcões (‘street of the balconies’) and of the hovels of this old street, now demolished.

The Campo de Dom Carlos is used for military exercises, and the Municipality’s rights over it are set out in the public deed concluded on 4 September 1897 between the Ministry of War and the Municipal Council.

The request for permission to give the name of the late King Carlos I to the square that the Council intended to build is dated 6 September 1897. The new name of Campo do Almirante Reis, by which the ground is now known, was given to it in 1911 by the first commission to occupy the seats of the Funchal councillors after the republican government was proclaimed in the country.
Carmo

An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário. There was once a chapel here consecrated to Our Lady of Mount Carmel (*Nossa Senhora do Carmo*), which gave the locality its name. It was founded in 1658 by Domingos Rodrigues as an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) and was the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). The locality has 15 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) and 73 inhabitants.
Carneiro

The common name of three species of coleopteran insects of the family Bruchidae: *Bruchus pisi*, *B. rufimanus* and *B. subellipticus*. They are found where peas, broad beans and other legumes are grown, and also in dwelling houses and granaries, where they do great damage.
Carneiro (shoal)
A shoal, already partly destroyed, near the Ilhéu do Gorgulho (‘weevil islet’), to the west of the city of Funchal.
Carocha

This name is given to the following two shrubs, grown in the *quintas* and gardens of Madeira: *Magnolia fuscata*, of the family Magnoliaceae, and *Calycanthus floridus*, of the family Calycanthaceae.
Carocha (Blaps gages)

A coleopteran insect of the family Tentyriidae, common on Madeira, Porto Santo and the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*). It lives in the dark corners of houses, under stones and in caves, especially in the lower zone (coastal belt) of the first two islands.
*Carocha* is often used as a general name for certain beetles of a particular shape.
Carpo (Arsénio Pompílio Pompeu do)
What we know of the life of this Madeiran is almost limited to what Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says on p. 806 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), which we transcribe below:

‘Born in the city of Funchal in 1792, he worked here as a stonemason and was an actor, until the special judicial commission (alçada) that came to the island of Madeira in 1823 condemned him as a liberal to five years of penal exile (degredo) in Angola, where he went to serve his sentence. From the parts he played in the theatre he took the grandiose surnames he used. He was a shrewd and adventurous man; for this reason he became not only a wealthy merchant in the city of São Paulo de Luanda but a leading figure in that overseas possession, a commander of the Order of Christ and a colonel. Brought under arrest to São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) in Lisbon in 1846 on serious charges, he succeeded in clearing himself. He died some years later, having written and published, under the title *Dedo de Pigmeu* (Lisbon, 1843), a collection of intimate poems, as well as some pamphlets on his personal quarrels.’

The *Diccionario Bibliographico* of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, which supplied Dr Azevedo with almost all these notes, lists the pamphlets published by Arsénio Pompílio and states that he was born on 20 February 1792. In the *Notas para um diccionario dos portugueses notaveis do meu tempo*, written by Júlio César Machado, there is a long and most interesting article on Pompeu do Carpo.
Gorse (Ulex europaeus)

A European plant introduced by the 1st Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’) to his *quinta* (country estate), the Quinta do Palheiro, in the first quarter of the 19th century. It is now very widespread in the middle zone of the island, where, often together with broom, it forms extensive thickets. The young shoots of this plant, once suitably crushed because of the spines, make excellent fodder for livestock. Gorse (*carqueja*) is known in mainland Portugal by the name *tojo*.
Castor-oil plant

The common name of *Ricinus communis*, a plant native to tropical Africa. It has palmately cleft leaves and large capsules covered with long soft spines, and it is common in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira, where it grows as a shrub or almost as a tree. Castor oil, widely used as a purgative, is extracted from the seeds of this member of the Euphorbiaceae. Castor-oil plants drive away flies.
Ticks

Parasitic arachnids of the family Ixodidae, genus *Ixodes*, which live on sheep, goats and cattle, and sometimes on dogs. Ticks are especially abundant in the mountain pastures of Madeira and are parasitic for only part of their life: for the rest they usually cling to shrubs, bracken and other plants, then pass on to animals and sometimes even to humans. Some parasitic arachnids are also known as *carraça* or *carrasca*.
Rifle range

The need for a rifle range had long been recognised. It would serve at once to give recruits of the garrison of this district preliminary instruction in target shooting, to perfect the training of those who had already been enlisted, and also to train the members of any civilian rifle associations that might come to be organised here. Several attempts were made, but they proved entirely fruitless. The rugged terrain, the intensive cultivation of the land and the difficulties raised by certain influential parties were by no means minor obstacles to the realisation of this important improvement, not to mention the hindrances raised at the Ministry of War to the granting of the funds it required.

The engineer captain Carlos Roma e Maia, and later Captain Eduardo Pereira together with Lieutenant Jorge Camacho, drew up two projects for a rifle range and carried out various field surveys, but both attempts produced no appreciable results.

Around 1904 the military commander, Colonel Joaquim Maria Alves, obtained a subsidy of three *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis) from the District General Council (*Junta Geral*). Later, at that officer’s urging, the War Office ordered a study for a rifle range and appointed a special commission for the purpose, made up of the engineer colonel Abreu Nunes, Colonel Bernardino Pereira, Lieutenant-Colonel Eduardo Pereira, Captains Cândido Gomes and Ricardo de Andrade, Lieutenant Alberto Sarmento and the artillery lieutenant

António Joaquim dos Santos Pimenta. After various studies and surveys, this commission decided definitively that the rifle range should be built at the locality of Várzea in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’). It never carried out any significant works, however, still less drew up the plans and estimates, because of the obstacles that various local interests then placed in the way of this long-desired improvement. This was in 1909. In June 1911 the Minister of War ordered an urgent study of the construction of the rifle range. A commission was then appointed, made up of Captains Cândido Gomes and Ricardo de Andrade and Lieutenant José Betencourt da Câmara, which at once set to work with the greatest zeal and energy. It chose the site of Várzea in the parish of São Martinho as suitable for the purpose and, without much delay, drew up the corresponding project, which won the approval of the higher authorities.
In October 1912 the Ministry of War authorised work to begin, and Madeira was at last to have a rifle range for the military training of its garrison.

As it was recognised that the project drawn up needed some modifications, a new commission was appointed, consisting of Major Ricardo de Andrade, Captain António Agostinho Câmara and Lieutenant Carlos Ribeiro Pestana. They prepared the final and definitive project and estimate on which the construction was based, with the costs then calculated at 18,739,000 *réis*.

This is the moment to highlight the fact that this improvement is due above all to the distinguished officer and fellow Madeiran Cândido Gomes. Serving at the War Office and well acquainted with the need for the rifle range, whose planning he had devoted himself to with great energy, he secured the funds needed to purchase and expropriate the land required before construction could begin. He never ceased to lend his valuable cooperation and good offices to the creation and operation of this military establishment.
Construction work began in March 1917 under the skilled direction of the infantry captain António Agostinho Câmara, and it has continued as actively as possible; it should be completed shortly.

The rifle range is 450 metres long, with targets at distances of a hundred, two hundred, three hundred and four hundred metres. It has firing lines, and fire is directed from south to north. It stands on the site chosen at the Várzea in the parish of São Martinho. Because the locality is quite densely populated, many engineering works had to be built to keep the surrounding population entirely safe from any danger that might arise during target practice. We are informed that it will be one of the best rifle ranges in the country.
Carreira (street)

Its modern name is Rua do Dr. Vieira, but ordinary people know it only by its old name. ‘It is called’, say the *Saudades*, ‘the Carreira dos Cavalos [horse run] because horses were customarily raced there’. It is one of the oldest streets in the city, and in former times many of the noblest and most distinguished families of Funchal had their residences there. At present it runs from the Largo do Colégio to the Ponte de São João. Before the demolition of the Portão de São Paulo (St Paul’s Gate), near the chapel of the same name, that point was one of the limits of this street, the other being Rua de São Francisco. Besides the general name of Carreira, it bore the names Rua da Igrejinha, Rua dos Pintos, Rua de São Paulo and Rua de Manuel da Grã, each of these names corresponding to one part of the present street. The small square still called Igrejinha today, which marks the intersection of Rua das Pretas (now Câmara Pestana) and Rua da Carreira, keeps this name because a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), commonly known as the Igrejinha (‘little church’), once stood there. Rua da Carreira is home to the old chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception and the private cemetery of the British community.
Common reed (Phragmites communis)

). A grass common on coastal ground, both on Madeira and on Porto Santo. Its stems can sometimes reach 2 metres in height. Frutuoso says that the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço derives its name from ‘the land there being covered with a common reed (*carriço*), like slender canes’.
Monte toboggan-cars

The Monte (‘hill’) toboggan-cars, in the form they have today, appeared in 1849 or 1850. The travellers who visited Madeira in the first quarter of the 19th century make no reference to these cars in the writings they left us. Before the cars appeared, there were small sledges on which travellers visiting the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte sometimes descended.
Geographical Maps

We know of the following maps of the islands of the Madeira archipelago: 1. *Mappa geographico particular da ilha da Madeira*, surveyed by order of His Excellency the present governor and captain-general João António de Sá Pereira (later Baron of Alverca), partly by Sergeant-Major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major) Francisco d’Alincourt and partly by Faustino Salustiano da Costa, infantry adjutant serving as engineer, in the year 1771. (A copy, or perhaps the original, of this map existed in the Ministry of Public Works in Lisbon.) 2. *Geo-Hydrographic survey of the Isle of Madeira with the Dezertas and Porto Santo Islands geometrically taken in the year 1788. By William Johnston. . . With the plan of the town of Funchal, by capt. Skinner, 1775.* 3. *Mappa geral da ilha da Madeira, levantado por ordem d’El-Rei nosso senhor D. João VI* (General map of the island of Madeira, surveyed by order of the King our lord John VI), 1817, by Paulo Dias d’Almeida, sergeant-major of engineers. (It existed in the Ministry of Public Works in Lisbon, and there is a copy in the Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas*) in Funchal.) 4. *A Survey of the Island of Porto Santo, by Lieut. William Mudge, by order of Cap. D. E. Bartholomew. Published by Captain Hurd... July 10, 1820.*

5. *Geo-Hydrographic Survey of the Island of Madeira and its Dependencies*, by James Wild (1835). 6. *The Islands of Madeira, Porto Santo and Desertas surveyed by capt. A. T. E. Vidal in H. M. S. Styx*, 1843, London. Published... 4 October 1847. 7. *Funchal Bay surveyed by capt. A. T. E. Vidal, 1843, additional soundings by H. M. S. Challanger, 1873*. 8. *Mappa da ilha da Madeira mandado publicar por J. A. L.* (Júlio Augusto Leiria), 1871. 9. *Physical Map of the Island of Madeira constructed by J. M. Ziegler*. 10. *Carta geo-hydrographica da ilha do Porto Santo e dos ilheus baixos adjacentes*, surveyed jointly in 1842–43 by the officers of the British steam warship *Styx* and Captain António Pedro d’Azevedo of the Corps of Engineers (today a brigadier general); corrected and published with various enlargements in 1877. 11. *Carta geo-hydrographica da ilha da Madeira e dos ilheus baixos adjacentes*, surveyed jointly in 1842–43 by the officers of the British steam warship *Styx* and Captain António Pedro d’Azevedo of the Corps of Engineers, today a retired major general. Corrected and published with various enlargements in 1879. 12. *Carta geo-hydrographica das ilhas Desertas*, surveyed jointly in 1842–43 by the officers of the British steam warship *Styx* and Captain António Pedro d’Azevedo of the Corps of Engineers, today a retired major general (1886). 13. *Carta geographica da ilha da Madeira*, a free gift from the *Diário Popular* in the year 1898. (It is the work of the engineers Adriano and Aníbal Trigo.)

There are also two relief maps of the island of Madeira. One was made by the German geologist A. Stubel, and a copy of it is held in the Seminary Museum (Museu do Seminário); the other was made by Captain Vitoria Pereira. This second map was commissioned by the Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) to publicise and advertise Madeira. The map of Madeira surveyed by the Geodetic Commission, chaired by Colonel Alfredo Durão, has not yet been published, but the work on it was completed in 1915. This map, it is said, is far more complete and accurate than any published so far. The chorographic map surveyed by the commission chaired by Colonel Alfredo Durão, which is said to be a very valuable work and the most accurate yet published of this island, was made public in 1937 under the title *Carta Corografica da Ilha da Madeira levantada pela Direcção Geral dos Trabalhos Geodesicos e Topograficos em 1915 e revista e actualizada pelo Instituto Geografico e Cadastral em 1934*.
See ‘Town Plans’ (*Plantas da Cidade*).
Carteret (Philip)
Commander of the *Swallow*, an English ship that carried out important explorations in the South Seas and the Pacific Ocean. He was in Madeira from 7 to 12 September 1766.
See Wallis.
Caruncho

Among the insects that gnaw wood, and whose excrement is called *caruncho*, the one that stands out in these islands for the damage it causes is a beetle, *Stromatium unicolor*. It is characteristic of inhabited places, and its larva lives in the timber of buildings and furniture.
Carvalhal (1st Count of)

João José Xavier de Carvalhal Esmeraldo Vasconcelos de Atouguia Bettencourt Sá Machado, 1st Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), was born in this city on 7 March 1778, the son of João do Carvalhal Esmeraldo Albuquerque e Câmara and Dona Isabel Maria de Sá Acciaioly. He was a fidalgo-knight of the Royal Household (*fidalgo cavaleiro da Casa Real*), colonel of the militia regiment of Calheta (‘small cove’) and administrator of several entailed estates (*morgadios*), the most notable of which were those of Santo Espírito in the Lombada dos Esmeraldos, Ponta Delgada, Água de Mel and Paul do Mar.

He succeeded to the great house of his brother Luís Vicente do Carvalhal Esmeraldo de Sá Machado, who, according to a distinguished genealogist, ‘was lord of more than twelve large entailed estates, which made him the richest subject in Portugal in patrimonial property. The Count of Carvalhal was not only the wealthiest proprietor in Madeira; his house was also one of the foremost in the country, having brought together many entails and entailed estates. He owned vast properties in almost every parish of this island, as well as in mainland Portugal and in the Azores, and on his death he left, besides, a thousand and some *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis) in various English credit institutions. A curious official document, sent by the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of this judicial district (*comarca*) to the government in Lisbon in 1823, states that the Count of Carvalhal has very great capital in the bank of London and in cash, and an enormous annual income which, even in the island’s present penury, amounts to two to three hundred thousand *cruzados*; for the period this represented a truly colossal income for this archipelago.

Although he lived without pomp or ostentation, he was nonetheless a man of generous and liberal spirit. He gave ample proof of this above all during some of the crises Madeira went through, proving a true providence for this land: with the force of his prestige, his influence and his great fortune, he did much to overcome those crises. At times he stood up to the boundless greed of the wine merchants, chiefly foreigners, who colluded to drive down the price of must, to the great loss of the poor farmers.

A supporter of liberal ideas, he was forced to emigrate to England aboard the British warship, the corvette *Alligator*, on 22 August 1828, when Madeira was occupied by Miguelist troops. In London he was not only the devoted protector of the Madeirans who had emigrated there, but also gave generous help to all his compatriots who turned to him, and it is said that he spent many tens of *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis) in doing so.

Once constitutional government had been established, he returned to this island at the end of 1834, and by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 13 September 1835 he was appointed civil governor of this archipelago, having shortly before, on the 5th of the same month and year, been granted the title of Count of Carvalhal da Lombada. The cares of administering his great household and, still more, the illnesses from which he had long suffered took him away within a few months from the government of the district, a post he had accepted very reluctantly and solely to accede to the wishes of the leading landowners and men of influence on this island.

He died on 11 November 1837 at his Quinta do Palheiro do Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s hayloft estate’) and was buried in the chapel that still stands there today. Some forty years later, his nephew and heir, the 2nd Count of Carvalhal, had his mortal remains transferred to the mausoleum he had built in the Angústias cemetery, where they lie buried.
Carvalhal (2nd Count of)

António Leandro da Câmara Carvalhal Esmeraldo Atouguia Bettencourt de Sá Machado, 2nd Count of Carvalhal da Lombada, was the representative of the oldest and noblest families of Madeira. He was born in Funchal on 6 October 1831, the son of João Francisco da Câmara Carvalhal Esmeraldo de Atouguia Bettencourt de Sá Machado, nephew and heir of the first Count of Carvalhal, and of Dona Tereza Xavier Botelho, daughter of Sebastião Xavier Botelho, governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira.

He did not distinguish himself in any branch of human knowledge, nor did he play a prominent part in events recorded by history. Yet he was, in the words of an admirer and friend, ‘a man who in life had been the most likeable and most finely characteristic figure of the Madeiran aristocracy; whose name had been known abroad, in the high society of the great capitals, among the most illustrious personages, and whose existence, now tranquil and prudent, now storm-tossed and shaken by the follies of the age, always kept the correct line of a nobleman’s courtesy, the great brilliant outpourings of a fine mind, served by the temperament of an impressionable, ardent, nervous, generous and good-hearted artist. In Paris, in Madrid, in Lisbon, at splendid festivities, at princely balls, at the races, at sporting contests, at the Opéra, in the private rooms of the Maison Dorée and the Café Anglais, in the Bois, on the Prado, at the bullfights, at premières, he was the correct and brilliant *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility), the tireless waltzer, the daring sportsman, the prodigal, the adventurous *viveur*, living life *à grand train*, distinguished among the most distinguished, amiable, elegant and renowned. One day the curtain fell on that dazzling scene. Inexorable, fatal reality extinguished that constellation of false and dangerous pleasures. Cold, grave reason came to sit upon the ruins of that dizzying, intoxicating existence of high society, full of illusions and follies, in which life and fortune ebb away like a thin trickle of water in the arid, bare desert. And he who had been the hero of that ephemeral epic, made of fleeting brilliance, splendid illusions and mad extravagance, came to sit in the shade of his hearth, until then silent and sad, abandoned and forgotten. He brought with him the same innate distinction, the same natural elegance, the gentle and courteous nobility of name and rank, but many fewer illusions, many more disappointments, and his fortune, which he had thoughtlessly flung into that enormous and insatiable vortex, squandered for ever. Reality weighed upon him, fatal, terrible and pitiless’.

Such pomp and display, which brought him to a prominent place in those capitals, could scarcely be met by the annual income of a hundred *contos* (one million réis) *de réis* that his great house yielded. In Madrid, to attend a princess’s wedding, he had a carriage built that cost a dozen *contos de réis*; in Lisbon he built a theatre beside his house, where celebrated performers acted and the best society of the capital gathered. In Paris he spent fortunes on the dazzle of his sumptuous and spendthrift life... The brilliant festivities at Palheiro do Ferreiro became famous, combining the highest and most refined distinction with the lavishness of a mighty nabob. The Count of Carvalhal came to Madeira expressly to receive the Infante, later King, Luís, and both at the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace) and at the Quinta do Palheiro the future King of Portugal admired the consummate nobility and unsurpassed distinction of a genuine representative of the old Madeiran aristocracy.

Several entails (*vínculos* or *morgadios*) had come together in the Carvalhal house. The most important was that of Santo Espírito at Lombada da Ponta do Sol (‘ridge of Ponta do Sol’), founded in 1511 by the Flemish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) João Esmeraldo on the vast property he had bought from Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, 2nd son of João Gonçalves Zarco, the discoverer of Madeira. The 2nd Count of Carvalhal was the 13th and last administrator of this entail (*morgado*). He had also inherited the entailed estate founded in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) by Manuel Afonso Sanha and his wife Dona Mécia de Carvalhal at the beginning of the 15th century, as well as the entails of Água de Mel, Paul do Mar, the Lemes, etc., not counting others situated in various parts of the island and also in the Azores and on the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). He owned vast properties in every parish of Madeira, and the Carvalhal house came to be the second or third in the country in landed wealth.

Among other public duties, the Count of Carvalhal held the post of president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, and he held the Grand Cross of the Order of Isabella the Catholic and other foreign decorations. In 1854 he had married Dona Matilde Montúfar Infante, daughter of the Marquises of Selva Alegre, in Spain. From this marriage were born Dona Maria da Câmara, who married the Count of Resende, and Senhora Dona Teresa da Câmara, Countess of Ribeiro Real.

After so turbulent a life, ruin, misfortune, longing and illness came to confront the hero of so many adventures. He fought, and fought nobly, but… death struck him down while he was still in the vigorous age of 56.
He died in this city on 4 February 1888 and was buried in the family vault he had had built in the Angústias cemetery.
Carvalhal (António do)

The old Madeiran chronicles deal at length with the deeds of bravery and muscular strength of António do Carvalhal, and Gaspar Frutuoso recounts in detail many of his acts of valour, which long survived in local tradition. ‘António de Carvalhal, say the *Saudades*, a man as knightly as he was personally valiant, noble, and magnificent in his nature and great virtue, through which, by his magnificence, he has acquired such fame and won such a name in the hearts of men that they obey him for it: and should it be necessary to raise a cry, he will gather five hundred men of the North side into his service, for any deed of war, as has already happened to him, or for any other; and not without reason, for his house is a hospital and shelter for every poor person, a lodging for travellers, and, in short, a refuge for the needy. Thus he spends his whole estate (of which he possesses much on this side) on these works, so that every year thirty *moios* of wheat are consumed in his house, besides many others that he lends, and with it he succours whoever is in need, all of which he gathers from his own farming.
He lived in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) and was the son of Pedro Ribeiro and Dona Ana Esmeraldo, both of noble descent.
Carvalhal e Carreira

An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas, where the chapel of Santo André Avelino (St Andrew Avellino) stands. It was built in 1776 by Carlos Nunes de Freitas da Silva and belonged to the house of the Lomelino entail holders. A few years ago the following inscription was placed on one of the chapel’s interior walls: ‘Given by Jacinto Fernandes and completed by José dos Reis and the people’. The locality has 89 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) and 378 inhabitants.
Carvalhal Esmeraldo (João da Câmara)
He was elected senator for Madeira for the legislative session of 1838 to 1840, and was elected deputy for the legislature of 1842 to 1845.

He was the nephew of the 1st Count of Carvalhal and the successor and heir to his great house. On 24 June 1822 he married Dona Teresa Xavier Botelho, daughter of the governor and captain-general of Madeira, Sebastião Xavier Botelho. They were the parents of the 2nd Count of Carvalhal.

João Francisco da Câmara Carvalhal Esmeraldo de Atouguia Betencourt Sá Machado was an army officer, a *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) and a commander of the Order of St James. He died in April 1844.
Carvalho de Araújo (street)
At the session of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Municipal Council of

Funchal on 8 May 1919, it was resolved to give the name of Lieutenant-Commander Carvalho de Araújo to the former Rua do Aljube (‘bishop’s prison street’). This illustrious officer of our navy commanded the minesweeper *Augusto de Castilho*, which in October 1918 escorted the steamer *San Miguel* on her voyage to the Azores. He died heroically at his post on the 15th of that month, in the engagement the ship had to fight against a German submarine near that archipelago. The minesweeper was sunk, having no guns to match the submarine’s, but the *San Miguel* was saved, and with her all the passengers travelling from Madeira to the Azores.
Carvalho (Duarte de Melo Ponces de)
He was elected deputy for Madeira on 28 April 1918.
Carvalho (João da Silva)

He was born in Funchal on 16 October 1821 and for nearly 60 years taught primary school in this city with great proficiency. On 2 October 1845 he founded his first school in partnership with Augusto Correia de Sampaio, also now deceased. In recognition of his services, the Municipal Council granted him, in the last years of his life, an annual pension of 240,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). He contributed to *O Estudo*, *A Ordem* and other periodicals, was a member of the Municipal Council and of the District Commission (*Comissão Distrital*), and in 1867 published, with his own preface, Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega’s work on the visit of the Empress of Brazil to Madeira. He died in Funchal on 9 July 1903.
Carvalho (Mariano de)

He arrived in Funchal on 6 December 1890 and left for Lisbon on the 8th of the same month. He was lavishly entertained here, attending a ball at the Funchal Club (*Club Funchalense*) and a dinner given in his honour in the great hall of the former Teatro D. Maria Pia.
Oak (Quercus robur)

A European tree, very widespread throughout the island, where it was introduced in 1803 by the 1st Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). It yields good timber, and its fruit is used to advantage as cattle fodder. The shoots and young leaves of the oak, suitably crushed, are widely used on the island to treat whitlows. Roasted and ground acorns make a drink useful to people who are forbidden coffee.
Charcoal

Charcoal for ordinary uses is obtained by the incomplete combustion of wood. Pits are dug in the ground and a few logs or pieces of wood are thrown in and set alight. As fresh logs are laid on top of the first so as to fill the pit, the combustion soon spreads, and a great quantity of smoke then pours from every part of the stack. When the charcoal burner judges the operation complete, he covers everything with branches, brushwood and earth; the charcoal is later taken from the pit and carried in sacks to the villages. Some charcoal burners pour a little water on the charcoal before covering the pit with earth. In certain parts of the island it is not the custom to dig pits, but the other stages of charcoal-making follow the process already described. The method with chimneys in the centre of the stack, used in Portugal, is unknown in Madeira.
Heathers produce the best charcoal, but it is also made from the wood of *uveiras*, laurels and other species.
Coal
It was the English merchants Jacob Ruffy and Diogo Taylor who in 1838 set up the first coal depot in Funchal, shortly after the Royal Mail began its steamship service from England to the West Indies.
Nursing Home

This was the name formerly given to the small house at the Entrada da Cidade (‘entrance to the city’) where the Port Captaincy and the Commercial Association were housed for many years. When the house was built is unknown, but it is known that on 15 June 1771 the Council contributed 100,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) towards building a new house next to the health house, as the residence of the standard-bearer, and that on 13 July of the same year it gave a further 100,000 réis for the same work.

In former times it was the custom for the chief health guards to wait at the nursing home (*Casa da Saúde*) for the papers of ships arriving in our port to be presented to them. The chief health guards were appointed by the Council and, unlike today, were not required to have medical training. Besides the chief health guards, the nursing home had an interpreter, also appointed by the Council, who received a salary of 17 réis a year.

The nursing home served as the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) from 1784 until the end of the 18th century or the beginning of the 19th. Although it was a municipal building, it was ceded by the government to the Council, which sold it in 1914; it was bought at auction by the firms Luiz da Rocha Machado & C.º and W. Winton for the sum of 22,800,000 réis.
Casa dos Cônsules

An urban building on Rua da Conceição (‘Conception’), at the corner of Rua da Figueira Preta (‘black fig-tree street’), was long known as the Casa dos Cônsules (‘consuls’ house’). It seems to have been an old manor house. It dates from the 18th century and has a certain architectural grandeur. In the past various consulates were housed there, hence the name Casa dos Cônsules. Even at the beginning of the 19th century some consulates still had their seat in this house.

We read in the valuable book *Casas Madeirenses*: ‘It is a most interesting example, worth considering for the originality of certain elements well worthy of being adopted, for greater variety, in the design of other buildings. An asymmetrical but balanced and noble whole, with a grand, lordly air. It has a broad triple eave, and the upper windows are highly original in the shape of the pediments that crown their lintels’.
House of the Destitute Poor

It was a private asylum, run by its founder, José Fernandes Velosa. Its purpose was to take in and support a certain number of poor people of both sexes, and it existed from 1897; alms, legacies and the proceeds of certain festivities were its main sources of income.

The establishment, which at first admitted only men, began in 1895 under the name ‘Albergue Nocturno’ (Night Shelter). The first poor man to whom Mr Velosa gave protection was taken in by him at his own house one night in December 1894. Its founder died on 30 January 1934.
House of the Twenty-Four
This was the name of an association made up of delegates of the mechanical trades and presided over by the people's judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds).

On 21 January 1812 a royal letter (*carta régia*) was addressed to the judge, councillors (*vereadores*) and other officers of the Council of the City of Funchal, ordering ‘that, until a new building with the necessary accommodation is constructed, the Council shall allow the corporation of the board of the Twenty-Four the use of the council sessions chamber’.

The House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds) elected the people's judge and also the four guild representatives (*mesteres*) who sat in the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council). It was abolished by the decree of 7 May 1834.
Casal (Dom Friar Gaspar do)

He was the 3rd Bishop of Funchal and one of the most illustrious prelates of his time. The contemporary Madeiran chronicles tell us nothing worth mentioning about this head of the Funchal church, because he never came to his bishopric, owing to the high offices he held in mainland Portugal, such as professor at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), president of the Board of Conscience and Orders (*Mesa da Consciência e Ordens*), theologian of John III at the famous Council of Trent, etc. He was one of the most learned Portuguese of his age and left many printed works, almost all written in Latin.

He was appointed bishop of this diocese by Pope Julius II in 1551, and took possession the following year through the vicar general and provisor (diocesan judicial and administrative officer), Dr António da Costa, who was also the governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence). A few years later he obtained a transfer to the diocese of Leiria and then to that of Coimbra, and in both these bishoprics he was an eminent prelate. He was born in Santarém in 1512 and died in Coimbra on 9 August 1584.
Many works deal at length with Friar Gaspar do Casal, who was unquestionably one of the most illustrious men of his age.
Mountain shelters

Because of their great altitude and their distance from inhabited centres, the mountains of Madeira always pose a serious danger to travellers who must cross them when storms break over them, especially torrential rain accompanied by strong gales and hail. Few winters pass without the death of several people who succumb to the violence of the storms. To help these wayfarers, who are at times imprudent and unaware of the danger to which they so easily expose themselves, small houses have been built at the most exposed points of our mountains. Some of them are already quite old, and they have rendered notable service, saving from certain death many people who have sought shelter in them, even though they lack the most rudimentary means of warmth and comfort for those who arrive there driven by the storms. We give below a list of the mountain shelters (*Casas de Abrigo*) existing in our mountains, some of which also serve the upkeep of the levadas (irrigation channels) and forestry inspection. It is much to be regretted that not all of them have the staff needed to fulfil their purpose effectively, and that their state of repair leaves so much to be desired. They are: Casa do Caramujo (see that entry), in the mountains of São Vicente; the Lombo do Mouro house (see that entry), in the mountains of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava; the Monte Medonho house (see that entry), in the mountains of the parish of São Vicente; the Casas do Rabaçal, at the well-known locality of the same name; Casa da Bica da Cana, on the plateau of the Paul da Serra; Casa da Fajã das Nogueiras (see that entry), in the mountains of Faial; Casa das Queimadas (see that entry), in the mountains of the parish of Santana; the Ribeiro Frio house (see that entry), in the parish of São Roque do Faial; Casa dos Alpires (see that entry), not very far from the locality of Choupana, in Funchal; and the one at Poiso, at the locality of that name, in the mountains of the parish of Camacha. This last is perhaps the only one that truly deserves the name of mountain shelter, for its size, its good state of repair and the relative comfort it offers to those who seek it. At other points in the mountains there were once some small shelters, long since destroyed by time and human neglect.

The British subject Roberto Page had two mountain shelters built at the beginning of the 19th century, one on the Paul da Serra and the other at Ribeira das Cales (‘stream of the channels’). The first of these has long ceased to exist, and the second, after suitable repairs, now serves as a shelter for forest guards.
At Lombo da Raiz (‘root ridge’) and at Lamaceiros (‘mud flats’) there are small shelters built by the Funchal Public Works Department (*Direcção das Obras Públicas do Funchal*).
Casinhas e Pico

An inhabited locality on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). At the spot in this locality called Graça (‘grace’) there stood an old chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*), which gave the place its name. As it was badly ruined, its rebuilding on a larger scale was undertaken at the beginning of the 19th century, but the construction was never completed, and today only some ruins remain. It had a certain architectural pretension and an octagonal interior, and it is said somewhere that it is a miniature reproduction of a famous sanctuary in Italy. It has 16 households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths') and 70 inhabitants.
Castanheira (landing place)
A small landing place on the west side of Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’).
Sweet chestnut (Castanea sativa)

A member of the Cupuliferae, cultivated in Madeira since the island began to be settled. Some years ago a chestnut tree could be seen at Achada do Campanário whose trunk measured 10.50 m in circumference, and at the locality of Fontes (‘springs’), in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), we believe another still exists whose trunk measures 11.30 m, also in circumference. The chestnut, much less common today than formerly, produces besides its nuts, which are eaten locally, a good timber with many uses. Although it is characteristic of the 2nd botanical zone of Madeira, which runs from 150 to 200 metres, it can also grow near the coast: for many years a specimen stood in the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) that never failed to bear fruit in due season. Annual chestnut production in Madeira is around 4,000 hectolitres.
Castanheiro (street)
It links Largo do Colégio with Rua de São Pedro and Rua das Mercês.

Its name comes from a gigantic chestnut tree that stood in more remote times at the northern end of the street, which as recently as 70 years ago was a narrow, winding lane. It seems that it was at one time called João Castanheiro.

It was on the initiative and at the urging of the civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro that the Municipal Council had it widened and given the alignment it keeps today. By decree of 10 January 1847 the central government authorised the ceding, from the convent grounds of the former Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), which then as now served as barracks, of the land needed for the widening. Only after this improvement were the present entrance and main gate of the barracks built; previously they had been in Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), roughly where the old lyceum (state secondary school) was once housed. In this street stands the characteristic house known as that of Dona Guiomar, now considerably altered, which once served as military quarters. It was also in a building in this street that the Hospice of Princess Dona Maria Amélia (*Hospício da Princesa D. Maria Amélia*) was provisionally installed in 1853.
Castanheta baia (Heliastes limbatus)

A bony fish of the family Pomacentridae, caught abundantly in summer off the south coast of Madeira. It is taken at shallow depth, which may vary between 7 and 12 *braças*, preferably with a suitable circular net. Although a small species, it is nonetheless prized for its pleasant flavour. It is also called *castanheta branca*.
Castanheta do alto

Madeirans apply this name to the following two fishes, both of the family Percidae: *Anthias sacer* and *Callanthias peloritanus*. They are caught on rocky bottoms between 60 and 150 *braças*, with the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream) or the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing), the latter species being much rarer than the former.

*Anthias sacer* is also known by the name *imperador*, and *Calanthias peloritanus* by that of *imperador de natura*. Some 60 years ago the latter species was also called *castanheta* or *imperador da moda* (‘fashionable emperor’), perhaps in allusion to the fashion for narrow waists among ladies, since this species is noticeably slenderer than the common *imperador*. Today, however, this name seems to be completely forgotten.
Castanheta ferreira (Glyphidodon luridus)

A small fish of the family Pomacentridae, native to the tropics, whose range extends northwards as far as these seas. In summer it frequents the water’s edge along the rocky coasts, where amateurs go to catch it with a rod or take it with a scoop net (*peneiro*). It is also called *castanheta preta*.
Castanho (peak)
The peak of this name stands on the northern coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), at an altitude of 628 m.
Castanho (peak)

A hill in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, from whose summit there are fine views stretching from the parish of Caniço (‘reed’) to the eastern tip of the island. It was on the slopes of this hill that the rebel troops and the government forces met and exchanged fire on 2 May 1931, as will be described more fully in the article on popular uprisings.
Castelo Branco (Camilo)

Our great novelist, in his book *Eusebio Macario* (we refer to the 3rd edition), added some pages on various points of poetic history; pages 245 to 275 contain an interesting chapter entitled *A Lenda de Machim. Reflexões á vida do infante D. Henrique, por Mr. Richard Henry Major*. This article includes the polemic between Camilo and Pinheiro Chagas over the legend of Robert Machin and, in particular, over the origin of the name Machico, which is exceptionally interesting.

The action of the novel *O Santo da Montanha* takes place largely in Funchal and refers to Madeiran people and things. The novel *O Regicida* contains a curious note on the ancestry of the Bishop of Funchal, Dom Jerónimo Fernando, who was a great-great-grandson of Infante Ferdinand, father of King Manuel I.
Castelo Branco (Dona Joana de)

She is the most distinguished woman poet of Madeira. She was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial on 23 June 1856, the daughter of Caetano Velosa de Ornelas Castelo Branco and Dona Maria Rosa de Freitas. She has lived in Lisbon for many years now. She has contributed prose and verse to various newspapers. In book form she published *As Minhas Flores*, Lisbon, 1905, 94 pp., and *Fluctuaçôes*, Lisbon, 1910, 88 pp. She died in Lisbon in 1920.
Castelo Branco (Dom José de Sousa)
