This worthy and zealous prelate of Funchal was born in the city of Leiria, the son of Heitor Vaz de Castelo Branco and Dona Luzia Maria da Silva e Ataíde, who belonged to old and noble families of that city.

After holding several important posts, he was appointed prelate of Funchal by Peter II in 1697. He received his episcopal consecration in Lisbon on 29 June 1698 at the hands of the bishop and inquisitor-general, Dom Friar José de Lencastre.

He did not delay long in setting out for his bishopric. First, however, at the monarch’s request, he went to Mazagan, where he arrived on 10 August 1698 to carry out the duties of the episcopal ministry there. In that stronghold, where many Portuguese scattered across various parts of the Moroccan mainland had then gathered, he was received with the greatest demonstrations of esteem and rejoicing. After staying a few days, he set course for his diocese, arriving in this city on 29 August of that year.

During the 19 years he resided in this bishopric, he always gave proof of irreproachable conduct and was extremely zealous in fulfilling his episcopal duties. He made several pastoral visitations of his entire diocese and adopted strict measures to maintain ecclesiastical discipline and to correct certain serious abuses then being committed.

A strenuous defender of the privileges and prerogatives enjoyed by the Church, he had to wage struggles with the governor and captain-general João da Costa e Ataíde and with the superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*) Manuel Mexia Galvão. The government in Lisbon sent the high court judge (*desembargador*) Diogo Salter de Macedo to Madeira to investigate the conflict that had arisen between these authorities. The result was a judgment in the prelate’s favour and a harsh censure of the acts of the governor and the superintendent of the royal treasury.
He devoted himself to genealogical studies and left several unpublished works, which are listed in the *Biblioteca Lusitana*.

On account of illness he sailed for the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) on 16 July 1717 and never returned to the diocese; four years later he resigned the mitre. He died in 1746, having been the 14th bishop of this diocese.
Castelo Branco (Eduardo Ernesto de)

He was born in Funchal on 17 March 1840 and died in Lisbon on 4 February 1905, the son of Rear-Admiral Joaquim Pedro de Castelo Branco. He enlisted in 1857, served in the artillery and rose to the rank of general. His great achievement was the founding of the Artillery Museum, to which he devoted all the energy of his mind, raising it to the level of similar institutions elsewhere in Europe. To this end he worked tirelessly and even spent considerable sums from his own pocket when the public treasury grew miserly towards the improvements he considered indispensable. He wrote the *Catalogo do Museu de Artilharia de Lisboa*.
Castelo Branco (João de Abreu)
He was governor and captain-general of Madeira. His appointment dates from 7 August 1733, and he took up the post on 21 April 1734.
Castelo Branco (José de Azevedo)

The decree appointing him civil governor of this district is dated 24 January 1890, and he took office on the 30th of the same month and year. He was born in Vila Real on 5 October 1852 and graduated in medicine in 1878.
Castelo Branco (José de Freitas Teixeira Spínola de)

He was born in Funchal on 7 January 1801, the son of Dr Maurício José de Castelo Branco Manuel (see that entry) and Dona Maria Dionísia de Freitas Abreu Castelo Branco. He followed a military career and rose to the rank of field marshal. He was a professor and director of the Escola Politécnica and a member of the Royal Academy of Sciences (*Academia Real das Sciencias*). He published *Elementos de algebra superior*, 1843, *Applicação da algebra à geometria*, 1847, and *Noções de calculo differencial*, 1838. He took part in the Liberal campaigns.
Castelo Branco Manuel (Maurício José de)

He was a native of Valezim and belonged to an old and noble family of that town (*vila*). He graduated in law and pursued a career in the magistracy, serving on this island as *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) in the first quarter of the 19th century. When representative government was proclaimed in the country, Dr Maurício Castelo Branco was elected deputy for Madeira to the Constituent Cortes (constituent parliament), which sat from 1821 to 1822. The other two representatives of this archipelago in the Cortes were Francisco João Moniz and Dr João José de Freitas Aragão.

The work *Galeria dos deputados das cortes gerais e constituintes... de 1821* shows that Maurício José Castelo Branco championed Madeira’s affairs with dedication and dealt quite boldly with various matters of general interest, revealing himself a very liberal mind of great independence of character.
He married a Madeiran lady in Funchal and on this island was the founder of the distinguished Castelo Branco family.
Castelo Branco (Maurício José de)

He was born in Funchal around 1842 and attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city and that of Coimbra. For some years he held the post of treasury clerk in Funchal, and he contributed to the *Direito*, *Recreio*, *Crepusculo*, *Diario Popular* and other local newspapers. He died in this city on 6 September 1910.
Castelo Branco (Pedro de)

Pedro de Castelo Branco, Baron of São Pedro, was born in Funchal on 19 April 1837, the son of Rear-Admiral Joaquim Pedro de Castelo Branco. He was a doctor of medicine of the University of Paris and for some years was a senior official of the postal service. He then moved to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and entered the diplomatic service. He served as secretary of legation in various European capitals and as chargé d’affaires in Berlin and The Hague, and in 1891 he was appointed minister plenipotentiary in Constantinople. He later served as head of the private office of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, and died in Lisbon on 14 December 1911.
Castelo de Paiva (António da Costa Paiva, Baron of)

This distinguished physician and naturalist was born in Porto on 12 October 1806 and died in Funchal on 4 June 1879. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in philosophy of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), a doctor of medicine of the Paris faculty, a professor at the Porto Polytechnic Academy (*Academia Politécnica do Porto*) and a member of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Sciencias de Lisboa*).

In 1855 the Portuguese Government commissioned him to study the island of Madeira from an agricultural and economic point of view. He took the opportunity to carry out numerous botanical and zoological investigations throughout the archipelago, assembling a herbarium of 515 species, which he presented in 1863 to the Lisbon Academy of Sciences, and an excellent collection of land shells. His *Monographia Molluscorum terrestrium, fluvialium, lacustrium insularum Maderensium* (Lisbon, 1867) is, in the opinion of distinguished specialists, the most accurate and conscientious work yet published on the malacology of our archipelago.

The Baron of Castelo de Paiva also visited the Canary Islands, where he made various botanical, malacological and entomological observations. The herbarium he assembled in those islands is at present, like the Madeiran one, in the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Lisbon (*Universidade de Lisboa*).

Besides the Monographia mentioned above, he wrote an 11-page report dealing with Madeira from an agricultural and economic point of view (Lisbon, 1855), and the following scientific works: *Noticia da descoberta de dois molluscos novos e tambem dos typos vivos de duas especies fosseis do archipelago madeirense* (*Annals and Mag. of Nat. Hist*, 1862), *Description of a new Sempervivum from the Salvage Island* (*Seeman’s Journ. Bot.*, 1866), *Description de deux espèces nouvelles de mollusques terrestres de l’archipel de Madère* (*Journ. de Conchyl*, VI, 1866), etc.
Castelo-Melhor (Count of)

This title was granted by Philip II to Rui Mendes de Vasconcelos on 21 March 1611. Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, 7th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, married a daughter of this count, Dona Maria de Vasconcelos, by whom he had João Gonçalves da Câmara, 8th captain-donatary, and Dona Mariana de Alencastre. She inherited the captaincy from her brother, who died without issue, although he had been married to Dona Inês de Meneses. Dona Mariana de Alencastre, 9th holder of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), married the 2nd Count of Castelo-Melhor, João Rodrigues de Vasconcelos, son of Luís de Sousa e Vasconcelos and Dona Maria de Sousa. In this way the captaincy passed into the possession of the counts, later marquises, of Castelo-Melhor, who held it until it was abolished.
Castelo (peak)

This is the best-known height on the island of Porto Santo, not far from the town (*vila*), and on its crest lie the ruins of an old fort, which gave the peak its name. Its highest point stands 440 metres above sea level, and its slopes are very steep. It therefore served as a safe refuge for the island’s inhabitants when the island was attacked by French and Moroccan corsairs, who frequently laid it waste. Before the fort was built, defence was carried out by means of boulders rolled down the slopes of the peak, which made its summit almost inaccessible. Approximately 30 years ago the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) attempted to afforest the slopes of this peak, with the forestry officer António Schiappa de Azevedo directing the work. Today there is a luxuriant growth of tree species there which, even from the sea and at a great distance, draws the admiration of the observer, in striking contrast to the aridity of the other hills.
Castilho (Alexandre Magno de)

This naval officer and writer visited Madeira several times and married a Madeiran lady here, Dona Carlota de Almeida Afonseca. He died in Funchal on 19 January 1871. His book *Roteiro da Costa Africa Occidental* contains some material of use to the history of our archipelago.
Castilho (José de)

The illustrious writer Dom António da Costa wrote a book entitled *José de Castilho, o Heroe do Brigue Mondego*, published in Lisbon in 1874. It deals with the young and distinguished naval officer José de Castilho, son of José Feliciano de Castilho and nephew of the great poet António Feliciano de Castilho, Viscount of Castilho. For health reasons José de Castilho came to Madeira with his mother, and he died here of pulmonary tuberculosis on 10 December 1864. Dom António da Costa devotes some brilliant pages of his book to the island of Madeira.
Castilho (Viscount of)

On the afternoon of 27 November 1840 the brigantine-schooner *Funchal*, then the ship that ran regular voyages between Lisbon and Madeira, dropped anchor in the harbour of Funchal. She carried a number of passengers, among them the great poet and eminent man of letters António Feliciano de Castilho. He was accompanying his brother, Dr Augusto Frederico de Castilho, who was suffering from a serious lung disease and had come to this island to seek relief in the mildness of our climate.

Dr Frederico de Castilho was a canon of Lisbon Cathedral (*Sé de Lisboa*) and a high court judge (*desembargador*) of the patriarchal curia, as well as a poet and prose writer of rare merit. For many years he served as secretary to his illustrious brother, and he did much to bring some of the writer’s works of poetic genius to light.

Castilho felt the purest brotherly love for him, as many pages of his works show: he calls him ‘the best of brothers’ and refers to him with the utmost tenderness and affection. It was this deep attachment that led him, despite his blindness, to undertake so arduous a journey, never leaving his beloved brother’s side for a single moment.

The distinguished Madeiran Januário Vicente Camacho, governor of this diocese and bishop-elect of Castelo Branco, placed the residence of the chapel of Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*), where the late prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto lived for many years, at António Feliciano de Castilho’s disposal. Standing above the sea on the outskirts of the city, the residence was considered to meet the conditions required by the illness from which the illustrious patient was suffering.

There the great master of our language received the most notable marks of esteem from all the people of high social standing in our island, who shared deeply in the immense grief that so cruelly pierced his brother’s heart and his passionate poet’s soul.

Augusto Frederico de Castilho reached Funchal with his strength so depleted, and his illness so far advanced, that neither the healthful air of this favoured land nor the efforts of medicine, combined with his brother’s utmost devotion, could save him from death, which everyone in the city at once considered inevitable. A little over a month later, on 31 December, at one o’clock in the afternoon, Augusto Castilho succumbed to the ravages of the dreadful pulmonary tuberculosis. He died in the arms of his beloved brother, surrounded by a few people who sought to make the last moments of the ill-fated invalid as painless as possible.

His body was laid in the Colégio church (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), and from there the funeral procession set out for the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), where the office of the dead was sung. It then continued to the Angústias cemetery, where the mortal remains of the illustrious priest were buried in a family vault of his own. Everyone of the greatest distinction in our land joined the funeral, beginning with the highest authorities of the district. It was a great tribute of respect to the dead man and of esteem and admiration for the great man of letters who was our illustrious guest. Having lost his brother, Castilho thought only of returning to the bosom of his family. He took with him the precious treasure of his brother’s heart: by his last wishes, Augusto had asked that it be removed from his breast, so that it could be buried together with the mortal remains of his dear and inseparable companion of so many years.

António Feliciano de Castilho left Madeira on 9 January 1841. In the same year he delivered at the Royal Conservatory of Lisbon (*Conservatório Real de Lisboa*) the historical eulogy of his brother Augusto Frederico de Castilho, which is one of his finest literary works. This eulogy contains some deeply felt pages in which Castilho describes his brother’s illness and death in Madeira.

The Castilho family had a small marble monument erected over the grave of Dr Augusto Castilho in the Angústias cemetery. It is surmounted by his coat of arms and bears this epitaph: ‘To the memory of Dr Augusto Frederico de Castilho, knight of various orders, former prior (title of the parish priest) of Castanheiro, candidate for a chair at the University of Coimbra, governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop’s absence) of Beja and deputy of the Portuguese nation, archpriest of the Metropolitan Cathedral of Lisbon and member of many literary societies; born in Lisbon on 4 September 1802 and died in Funchal on 31 December 1840.’
Castrioto Lusitano
See Fernandes Vieira (João).
Castro (Afonso de)

Appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 14 May 1870, he took up the post on the 19th of that month and year. He was the effective governor of Madeira who held this office for the shortest time: only eight days. His dismissal was brought about by the revolution of May 1870, in which Saldanha seized the government by force, taking all the ministerial portfolios himself. Afonso de Castro was succeeded by Dom João Frederico da Câmara Leme.

Afonso de Castro was appointed civil governor of Funchal a second time by decree of 24 November 1877, and took office on 24 December of the same year. He left the administration of this district in June 1879.

He was governor of several of our colonies, civil governor of various districts on the mainland and in the islands, and a deputy to the national parliament in several legislatures. He was born in Lamego in 1824 and died in Leiria in 1885, while serving there as civil governor. He wrote and published several works.
Castro (Dom Manuel de Portugal e)

He was the governor and captain-general chosen for Madeira after John VI proclaimed himself absolute king. His appointment dates from July 1823, and he took office on 28 August following. On the 26th of that month he arrived in Funchal, accompanied by the 7th Infantry Regiment, a detachment of artillery and a special judicial commission (alçada) of six magistrates, which had come to investigate the conduct of persons hostile to absolute government. With great ceremony he had the foundations demolished of the monument that had been laid on 28 January 1822 in front of the church of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral. Yet in August 1826 he also celebrated the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) and representative government with great solemnity and pomp. His administration was good, and he did all in his power to restrain the excesses of the ministers of the commission, who committed no small number of arbitrary and oppressive acts in the exercise of their office.
The Ponte e Rampa de D. Manuel (Bridge and Ramp of King Manuel) were given his name because they were built during his governorship. He left Madeira on 6 May 1828.

In 1827 he was appointed viceroy of India, where he governed excellently. He left this island shortly after 27 April of that year, the day on which his successor, José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, arrived in Funchal.

In 1853 the naval steamer *Infante D. Luiz* brought to Madeira Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro, as representative of Maria II, and the Baron of Foz, as representative of King Ferdinand. They came, in the name of Their Majesties, to offer their condolences to the Empress Dona Amélia on the death of Princess Dona Maria Amélia and to accompany the mortal remains of the ill-fated princess to Lisbon.

Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro, son of the Marquis of Valença, was born on 5 November 1787 and died on 13 July 1854. He was a minister of state and a peer of the realm, and held other important posts.
Castro (Dr José de)

This well-known politician, who only a few years ago was President of the Council of Ministers, stayed in Madeira from 8 October 1884 until 2 June 1885. He was one of the defence counsel for the republicans prosecuted in the judicial district (*comarca*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) over the events that took place in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) on 29 July 1884, which resulted in the deaths of several local people. He wrote a pamphlet recounting these events, entitled *As Victimas d’ElRey, Historia dos processos movidos contra os perseguidos politicos da ilha da Madeira, desde 29 de junho de 1884 ate o ano de 1885*.
See Arriaga (Dr Manuel de).
Castro (Father Francisco de)

He was a celebrated preacher in his day and held several important posts. Diogo Barbosa Machado says of him in the *Biblioteca Lusitana*: ‘Francisco de Castro, a native of the city of Funchal, capital of the island of Madeira, a priest of blameless life, master of arts, doctor of Theology from the University of Évora, where he was a fellow of the college of the Purificação. He was vicar of the collegiate church of São Pedro (St Peter) in the city of Funchal, whence, going to Cape Verde to seek a cure for the disease of leprosy, he passed to a better life in the year 1665. Of the many sermons he preached, only the *Sermão da Conceição de Nossa Senhora*, La Rochelle, 1656, and the *Sermão da Visitação da Mãe de Deus*, La Rochelle, 1655, were published.’ Inocêncio Francisco da Silva states in his *Diccionario Bibliographico* that these sermons are extremely rare, since he never came across a single copy of them. He was also parish priest of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António in Funchal.
Catanho
Here in Madeira this surname descends from the brothers Kirio and Rafael Catanho, natives of Genoa.

They proved their noble ancestry and enjoyed great prestige on this island. Kirio married Dona Maria Cabral, daughter of the third donatary of Machico. Rafael Catanho was a knight of the Order of Christ and held the rank of fidalgo of the Royal Household (*foro de fidalgo da casa real*).
Catanho de Meneses (Dr João)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial on 17 April 1854 and in 1874 enrolled in the Faculty of Law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), completing the course in 1879. He then moved to Lisbon, where he set up practice as a lawyer. He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislatures of 1890, 1897–1899, 1900 and 1905–1906. At that time he belonged to the Progressive Party, but after the establishment of republican institutions in the country he joined the Democratic Party, becoming Minister of Justice in 1915 in the government headed by Dr José de Castro. He left the government when Germany declared war on Portugal.
Mackerel (Scomber scomber)
A fish of the family Scombridae, at times abundant in the seas around Madeira. Another species of mackerel (*Scomber colias*) also occurs in this part of the Atlantic.
See Chicharro.
Cavalinha
See Pinheirinho.
Seahorse
This is the name given to two small fishes of the family Syngnathidae (*Hippocampus brevirostris* and *H. ramulosus*), which live in the shallow waters of the archipelago.
Cavalum (cave)

Hartung gives the following description of this cave: ‘It is 2 metres wide, 1.2 m high and some 30 metres long, narrowing at the far end. From there on the floor descends, and only at the beginning must one pass stooping. The air is damp and stifling, and the darkness so intense that only the light of many torches relieves it. A corridor follows, then a vast, high and wide chamber, then another corridor, and at the end an opening and a *profundidade* (deep, roughly circular mountain basin). Along this route one covers some 92 metres between rough, uneven walls and beneath projections that break out from the vault, which is coated with a shiny black crust.’
The Furna do Cavalum lies near the Quinta de Sant’Ana, in Machico.
Cazella
This distinguished musician, who was the teacher of King Luís I, was in Madeira in 1850 and gave several concerts here.
Onion (Allium cepa)
A member of the lily family native to Turkestan, widely grown in Madeira.

Madeirans call the young plants and the seeds *cebolinho*. Besides its culinary uses, the onion is used in medicine: raw and mixed with cold milk it can serve in the treatment of dropsy, and boiled or roasted as a poultice in the treatment of neuralgia and certain tumours. Madeira exported 1,171,678 kg of onions in 1911, 899,895 kg in 1912, 874,385 kg in 1913 and 861,697 in 1914. The exports go almost exclusively to Demerara and the British West Indies.
Cedar
Several resinous trees of the family Pinaceae go by this name in Madeira. The most common of them is *Juniperus glauca*, popularly known as the *cedro de Goa* or *cedro das barracas*.

The island cedar is *Juniperus Oxycedrus* subspecies *madeirensis*, a shrub or small tree 4–7 metres tall, with dioecious flowers, drooping branchlets, linear or linear-lanceolate leaves in whorls of three with 2 white stripes on the upper surface, and subglobose galbuli that are usually yellow. This cedar, cultivated on the *quintas* of Monte, Camacha and Santo da Serra but almost extinct in the uplands of Madeira, yields a light, aromatic wood much prized by cabinetmakers. The ceiling of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) was built of this wood and, if what Manuel Tomás says in ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*) is true, it was also used to build the first two-storey house in Funchal. Oil of cade is produced from *J. Oxycedrus*.
Cedro (peak)
It is one of the highest peaks surrounding the inhabited localities of the parish (*freguesia*) of Serra de Água.
Cephalopods
There are several species of this class of molluscs, coastal as well as pelagic or abyssal.

The most common are the octopus (*Octopus vulgaris*), the squid (*Loligo vulgaris*) and the cuttlefish (*Sepia officinalis*), all of them edible; *Spirula Peronii*, which is stranded in large numbers on beaches such as Caniçal, Porto da Cruz and Porto Santo; and the *pota* (*Ommastrephes sagittatus*), pelagic and edible, common a few miles off the coast. Among the rarer species is *Argonauta argo*, which has been seen at Porto Santo.
Alexandre A. Girard listed 11 species of these molluscs, some of them doubtful, while Robert Boog Watson mentions only the first four referred to above, together with the last.
Celestino Emídio (Manuel)

He was for some years judge of the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal and represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislative session of 1880–1881. He was born in 1812 and died in 1898.
It was Celestino Emídio who, as judge, presided at the celebrated trial of the notorious outlaw João Brandão.
Greater celandine (Chelidonium majus)
A plant of the family Papaveraceae that produces a yellow, caustic sap, used externally to treat warts, tetters, etc. It is common in and around Funchal.
Black slickhead (Alepocephalus rostratus)
A fish of the great depths, of the family

Alepocephalidae, black in colour with large, loosely attached scales, caught from time to time in Madeiran waters. It takes the hook on black scabbardfish lines, and although its flesh is very white and its appearance pleasant, it is not used as food.
Cemitério (alley)

It stood where Rua 5 de Junho (‘5 June street’) now runs, and had adjoining it the lanes of Violetas, Malvas, Alecrim, Papoilas and Aldeia. Demolition of the hovels in the alley and in the last four of these lanes began in 1887, but the works on Rua 5 de Junho were not completed until 1892. Both the alley and these lanes were mere passageways, lined with small, insanitary and unsightly dwellings.
British Cemetery

The original British cemetery stood where the Largo do Conde do Ribeiro Real (‘Count of Ribeiro Real square’) now is, at the end of Rua 5 de Junho (‘5 June street’). The ministerial order (*portaria*) granting British subjects the necessary licence to build a cemetery for burying their dead is dated 3 January 1761, but it was not until 10 September 1767 that land was acquired for the purpose. Before this cemetery was built, the bodies of non-Catholic foreigners who died in Funchal were thrown into the sea. The present British cemetery was built in 1808 and enlarged in 1852 and 1889. The oldest part of this cemetery was acquired for the burial of British soldiers who died in Funchal while Madeira was occupied by British troops, whereas the newest part only began to be used when the Municipal Council of Funchal needed to demolish the original cemetery in order to connect Rua 5 de Junho with Rua da Carreira (‘track’). The administrators of the British Chapel and Cemetery (*Capela e Cemitério Britânicos*) ceded this old cemetery in August 1888. The Council undertook to make the necessary efforts to facilitate the removal of the remains in that ground to a plot adjoining the present cemetery, which the administrators had until then been unable to use to enlarge the cemetery for lack of the necessary licences. The last burial in the cemetery where the Largo do Conde do Ribeiro Real now stands took place in July 1885.
Jewish Cemetery

It lies in the eastern part of the city, on the road to the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’). Its entrance bears an inscription in Hebrew meaning ‘house of life’ and the date 5,611, corresponding to the year 1851 of the Christian era.
Cemeteries

The oldest cemetery in Funchal for the burial of Catholics is that of São Roque, built in 1836. Work on the Angústias cemetery also began that year, but was not completed until 1838. The Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) cemetery dates from 1840 and the São Gonçalo cemetery from 1841. Before cemeteries were established, Catholics were buried in churches or in their churchyards. There was, however, at the locality of Angústias a small plot called the cemetery of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), which received the bodies of those who died in the hospital.

The establishment of cemeteries in some rural municipalities was slow: a newspaper of the time reports that in 1862 the parishes of São Jorge and Arco de São Jorge still had no grounds set aside for burial. On 19 August and 26 October 1850 Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro urged the Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*) to build cemeteries, since in many parts of the district there existed ‘the superstitious practice of burying the dead inside churches’.
The cemetery of Porto Santo was completed in 1838 and is therefore one of the oldest in the archipelago.
See Angústias (cemetery).
Cenoura da rocha (Monizia edulis)

A plant with a thick underground stem and flowering stems 3 to 8 decimetres tall, with triangular leaves, the lower ones 3–4 times pinnatisect; umbels with 20–25 rays; petals white or violet. This umbellifer, which is highly ornamental, has been found in

Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), on Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’) and on the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*); its underground stems are edible and have a flavour somewhat reminiscent of chestnuts. The *cenoura da rocha* is also known as *nozelha*.
Carrot (Daucus carota)
An umbellifer grown in Madeiran vegetable gardens for its edible roots. The pulp of these roots is used in poultices to treat tumours, burns and skin diseases, and its juice serves to colour butter.
Cenouras (islet)
A small islet off the island of Porto Santo, not far from Ponta Branca (‘white point’) or Ponta do Nordeste.
Rye (Secale cereale)

An annual grass grown in Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Rye flour, alone or mixed with wheat flour, is used to make a dark but tasty bread, and the straw of the plant is used in hat-making. The archipelago produces around 2,500 hectolitres of rye a year.
House centipede (Cermatia coleoptrata)
A harmless myriapod that sometimes appears at night on bedroom walls. It is also found in cracks and holes in rocks.
American seine net
A seine net tried out a few years ago in Madeiran waters, without profitable results.
Cherry tree (*Prunus Avium* var. *Juliana*)

A European tree of the family Rosaceae, subfamily Prunoideae, cultivated at Serra de Água, Curral, Ponta do Pargo, etc. Madeiran cherries are subglobose, red or black, and pleasant in flavour; they ripen in June and July. Cherry stalks are widely used in infusion as a diuretic. The cultivation of the black cherry tree was prohibited in 1788 by the governor Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho, on the grounds that the fruit of this tree was being used to colour wines.
Ceroulas (islets)
Off the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Seixal (‘pebble shore’) lie two small islets, called do Guincho and das Ceroulas, also known as the Seixal islets.
Cerveira e Sousa (Dom José Xavier de)

The political upheavals that swept the country when constitutional government was established led to a breach in relations between the Portuguese government and the Roman Curia. Among other drawbacks, this delayed the filling of vacant episcopal sees.

The prelate Dom Francisco José Rodrigues de Andrade had left Madeira in May 1834 and, resigning the bishopric, settled in the city of Genoa, where he died and where he lies buried. Only ten years later, once diplomatic relations between Portugal and the Holy See had been restored, was the vacant office of prelate of the diocese of Funchal filled.

The man presented by the Portuguese government and confirmed by the Roman Curia was Dom José Xavier Cerveira e Sousa. He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Mogofores, in the municipality (*concelho*) of Anadia, on 27 November 1797, the son of Dr José Xavier Cerveira, a former magistrate, and of Dona Rosa Joaquina Cerveira de Sousa. He studied in the Faculty of Theology of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), took his doctorate there and was teaching at the university when he was called to guide the destinies of the Church of Funchal. He was confirmed as bishop on 14 June 1843 and received episcopal consecration on 2 June of the following year.

He arrived in Madeira on 8 July 1844 and governed this bishopric until the beginning of 1848, when he was transferred to the diocese of Beja by decree of 18 April of the same year. He left behind him here the most honourable memories of his diocesan administration, despite the struggles he had to sustain and the great difficulties that beset his episcopate. It was in his time that Protestant proselytism rose at its most tenacious and threatening. Its bold leader, a propagandist of talent and learning, was Dr Roberto Kalley, a most distinguished physician and a born orator who drew the crowds after him. Much was written in the press, in pamphlets and in books about the Calvinist propaganda in Madeira, whose chief promoter was Dr Kalley, but the history of that agitated and tumultuous period of Madeiran history has yet to be written. To escape the people’s fury, the celebrated Scottish physician had to embark in secret, carried to the beach in a hammock (*rede*, slung from a pole and carried by two bearers) and dressed in women’s clothes. When his flight was discovered, his furniture and his choice library were set on fire at his residence at Vale Formoso (‘beautiful valley’), for which our government had to pay compensation of several *contos* (one million réis) de réis.

Dom José Xavier de Cerveira e Sousa, after serving as bishop of Beja and of Viseu, retired to Mogofores, where he died, in the very house in which he had been born, on 15 March 1862. He is buried in the parish church of that parish (*freguesia*).
Barley

The barley grown on a large scale in Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is *Hordeum vulgare*, subspecies *hexastichum*; the subspecies *distichum*, known as *cevada trigo* (‘wheat barley’), occurs only in a few localities on the first of these islands.

Barley is grown mainly in the low-lying part of Madeira, but in some places it reaches almost to the uplands, where it is generally harvested in August and sown in February. In the lower zone (coastal belt) it is sown in December and January and harvested in June and July.

Barley soup is one of the staple foods of Madeira’s country people, and the flour is used to make *rosquilhas* (ring-shaped rolls) and biscuits, particularly on the island of Porto Santo. The straw is used to thatch huts and to feed stalled cattle.
The archipelago produces some 6,000 hectolitres of barley a year.
Cevadilha (Nerium odorum)
A tree of the Apocynaceae family, grown in the *quintas* of Funchal. It is native to India and has large, fragrant flowers that are purple, pink or white. The leaves are poisonous.
Cezimbra (Marquis of)

He was appointed civil governor by decree of 9 September 1868 and took office on 18 October following. He left the governorship in September 1869. He was the son of the Duke of Palmela and father-in-law of the Madeiran Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas.
Chá Bravo

This name is given in Madeira to the following two subshrubs, both of the Malvaceae family and native to America: *Sida carpinifolia* and *S. rhombifolia*. Both have small serrated leaves and small yellow flowers, but the peduncles, which in the first species are very short and bear 1–4 flowers, are relatively long in the second and bear a single flower. An infusion of *chá bravo* can be used as an emollient.
Tea (Thea sinensis)

This plant, of the Ternstroemiaceae family, was introduced to Madeira in the first quarter of the 19th century by the English consul Henrique Veitch, who grew it for as long as he lived on his *quinta* (country estate) at Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’). Thirty years ago there were still a few tea plants on this *quinta*.

Consul Veitch made only black tea. The difference between black and green teas arises because, in preparing the former, the leaves are finally dried in sieves over a charcoal fire, whereas for the latter the drying is done in an iron vessel. According to Mr Gabriel de Almeida, the most suitable ground for growing the tea shrub is on mountain slopes that are steep, moist, cool and rich in humus. It is best if they lie away from the coast, because the shrub is very sensitive to the sea salt carried by the winds.
Chacota (A)
It was published from 9 December 1906 to 3 September 1907, with 25 issues appearing.
Chagas (Friar Damião das)

He was born in Funchal and died in 1600 on the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). He was an Arrábida friar, an order whose seat was in the Serra da Arrábida. He held important offices in his congregation, and Diogo Barbosa Machado says that he wrote an ascetic work in two volumes, which was never published.
Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus)

A plant of the Tropaeolaceae family, fully naturalised in Funchal and its outskirts. It is native to America, and its fruits, picked young and put in vinegar, can replace capers. The English make a salad of its flowers and tender leaves, and these parts of the plant can also be used as an antiscorbutic remedy. True capers are the flower buds of *Capparis spinosa*, a species unknown in Madeira.
Chão (islet)

The group of small islands called the Desertas (Ilhéu Chão, Deserta Grande and Bugio) lies on a north-north-west to south-south-east line with Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’), Ilhéu Chão being the one nearest to that point. ‘Ilhéu Chão,’ says Dr A. Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘so called because it is flat, is the smallest of the three islands; it is one mile or 1852 metres long by a third of a mile or 617 metres at its greatest width; its coasts are of steep rock, but it is level and of good soil; it is separated from Ponta de São Lourenço by a channel of 11 miles or a little over 20 kilometres, through which ships of every size pass. Its greatest height is 98 metres. To the south of Ilhéu Chão lies Deserta Grande, from which it is separated by a passage or channel navigable only by small boats. To the north of Ilhéu Chão lies the small Ilhéu do Navio (‘ship islet’), also called Prego do Mar (‘sea nail’).
Chapéu (street)
This was the part of the present Rua Correia Heredia, formerly Rua da Conceição (‘Conception’), between Rua da Figueira Preta and Rua do Bom Jesus.
Chapouto

Madeiran fishermen give this name to an extremely rare fish. It is a species of the mackerel family (Scombridae), which in Porto Santo and the Algarve is called *merma*. In Portugal the name *chaputa* is given to *Brama raii* and to *Centrophorus lusitanicus*.
Charamba

A folk song frequently heard in Madeira, above all among country people. It is a simple, unassuming melody made up of eight bars in triple time at a slow pace, alternating with a lively ritornello in duple time. It is usually played in G on the braguinha (small Madeiran four-string guitar, ancestor of the ukulele), accompanied by the viola de arame (wire-strung folk guitar) and the *rajão* (Madeiran five-string guitar).

The charamba (Madeiran improvised folk song) is most often sung as a contest between two or more people, who trade improvised quatrains and take as their theme the lives of those present, with allusions that may be friendly, or barbed, or even offensive. If tempers are already frayed by frequent drinking and the verses are too provocative, the song may end in a brawl, with the instruments themselves broken over the singers’ heads.
The interesting book by Carlos Santos entitled *Tocares e Cantares da Ilha*, published in Funchal in 1937, contains a chapter headed ‘O Charamba’, which deals at length with this Madeiran folk song.
Charcot (Jean)
He arrived in Funchal on 12 September 1908. He commanded the expedition that explored the Antarctic regions aboard the *Pourquoi pas?*.
Chaves (Dr, street)

This is the former Rua dos Aranhas (see that entry). Dr Chaves, who had completed the course of the old Funchal medical-surgical school, sat on the Municipal Council of Funchal, but did not distinguish himself in any branch of human knowledge.
Cheiros
See Savory.
Cherne (Polyprion cernium)

A fish of Madeira’s marine fauna, belonging to the family Serranidae, which local people consider one of the best-tasting fish to appear on the market. Once common, it is now becoming rarer because of the intensive fishing to which it has been subjected. Besides being abundant, specimens weighing 25 kilograms were not uncommon, and there were some, though rare, that weighed 50 and even more. It is the fishermen of Machico who chiefly devote themselves to this fishery, using the *cherriola* (vertical multi-hook deep-water line), which they lower to a great depth – from some 150 to 450 *braças*. The adults live exclusively in the abyssal zone; the young, however, roam the surface of the sea in shoals, often following a floating wooden beam or the wreckage of some shipwreck. That is why these young fish are usually called *cherna de pau*, and they are known as *charnota* if they weigh less than about 5 kilograms. In Madeira this fish is generally called *cherna*, a name given to another species on the coasts of Portugal, where the Madeiran *cherne* also exists and is known there by this latter name.
Cherriola

A fishing rig much used by the fishermen of Machico. It consists of a central line or main line (*madre*), which hangs vertically and to which 4 or 5 small rods of quince or osier are fixed horizontally, 3 *palmos* apart; from their ends hang small lines or snoods (*loros*) with their hooks. At its lower end the central line carries a stone sinker (*pandulho*), which makes the rig descend, and at its upper end it is tied to an ordinary fishing line. It is used mainly to catch adult wreckfish (*chernes*), working in depths of 200 and 300 *braças*, where hake, *gata*, *ramudo*, *xara* and other oily fish may also be taken. The rig resembles what in Portugal is called the *barqueira de arame*, and like it is let down vertically until the sinker touches the sea floor. The *cherriola* (vertical multi-hook deep-water line) of the Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) fishermen differs somewhat from the one described above. As to the origin of the term, it is not unreasonable to suppose that the rig, because the arrangement of its rods bears a certain resemblance to the *surriola* booms – which are rigged perpendicular to the side of certain ships and from which ropes hang for mooring the boats – received the name *surriola*, which was corrupted into *cherriola*.
Chicharos

In Madeira this name is given to *Lathyrus stativus* and *L. Cicera*, plants of the family Leguminosae grown in some kitchen gardens. Both plants have leaves with 2 narrow leaflets, but the upper edge of the pods, which is winged in the first, is merely channelled in the second. Some authors attribute poisonous properties to the seeds of the *chicharos*, but in Madeira, where *L. stativus* is frequently grown for food, we are not aware that such properties have been noticed. The seeds of the *chicharos* are used for soup, and the stems and leaves make good fodder and can also be used as green manure.
Chicharos (locality)
A locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial.
Chicharro

According to some authors, two species of fish of the family Carangidae go by this name in the seas of Madeira: *Trachurus trachurus* and *T. Cuvieri*. They seem to arrive irregularly: if there are seasons of great scarcity, there are others when the shoals are very numerous. They are sought sometimes on the bottom of the littoral zone with the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream), or in mid-water with the *agulheira* (mid-water line for garfish), and sometimes at the surface with the rod or the circular net; this last method is very profitable when the run is abundant. At other times they are caught in trawl nets, which can also yield a plentiful haul.

Bottom fishing is done by day, while surface fishing may be by day or by night. In the latter case a fishing lamp (*candeio*) is used, known as *griseta*, *cão* or *maçarico* depending on the locality; with its intense light it is a powerful aid to the fisherman, drawing the fish to the surface of the sea. The pursuit of the *chicharro* by tuna, the *bicuda* and other migratory species often drives it to seek shelter in coastal waters, and the same happens with the mackerel (*cavala*), which is caught by the same methods and is likewise irregular in its passage. As bait, fishermen prefer both to many other species.
Chicote (O)
Only one issue was published, on 27 August 1916.
Chocalheira (Briza maxima)

A native grass, common on Madeira and Porto Santo. It is a fodder plant easily recognised by its large, ovoid spikelets, white or reddish. The *chocalheirinha* (*Briza minor*) differs from the *chocalheira* in its very small, triangular spikelets. It too is common on Madeira and in the hills of Porto Santo.
Chôco (Sepia officinalis)

A cephalopod mollusc that is not rare in Madeiran coastal waters, especially in summer. It is edible and tastes good; it is caught on hook rigs, but more commonly in trawl nets. Its internal shell, which is called *silba* (a corruption of *siba*), often turns up on the beaches, pecked by seabirds. The gull is one of this animal’s enemies, watching for it in flight and swooping swiftly on it when it approaches the surface of the sea. The black liquid which the cuttlefish squirts out, clouding the water and so hiding itself from its enemies, is called *ferral* by the fishermen, no doubt because of its dark rust colour. This is the same liquid that elsewhere is used to make a brown ink used in painting under the name of sepia. Sometimes, when hauling in the boat’s mooring stone (*poita*), the fisherman finds it wrapped in a strange object resembling a bunch of grapes, whose black, soft and somewhat pear-shaped berries have the limpness of rubber: these are the cuttlefish’s eggs, called *uvas do mar* (sea grapes) and stained by the *ferral* itself. They were laid around the mooring rope while the boat was at anchor – or *apoitado*, in the characteristic phrase of seafaring men.
Choupa (Cantharus griseus)
A fish of the family Sparidae, not very common in the coastal waters of this archipelago.

It has a shellfish-like flavour and is almost always caught on hook rigs, sometimes letting itself be taken in the scoop net (*peneiro*) or in trawl nets, but always in small numbers, which is perhaps due to its solitary habits and its aversion to life in shoals.
Christmann (Dr Fr.)
A German physician who spent three winters in Madeira and made some meteorological studies here. Works: *Funchal auf Madeira und seine Klima*: Zabern. 1889.
Chronica
The 1st issue was published on 31 October 1840, and 44 issues appeared in all.
Chronica (A)
The 1st issue appeared on 3 March 1838 and the last, no. 96, on 28 December 1839.
Chronica Official (A)
It was published from 7 November to 12 December 1840, producing 6 issues.
Chumbada

A lead weight attached to the lower part of the fishing rigs known as the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) and the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream), serving to sink them. It also denotes the set of weights of the same metal fitted to the foot rope of trawl nets or set nets, and to that of the net called the cast net (*tarrafa*).
Chupa Sangue (Lepadogaster Gouani)

A small Madeiran fish of the family Gobiesocidae, common in the intertidal zone under the loose, smooth stones that the sea leaves uncovered. It is interesting for its form, which, among other peculiarities, includes a ventral disc shaped like a sucker that allows it to cling to the rounded pebbles of the shore. It has no use whatsoever.
Poetic cycle

In the book *Poetas Palacianos*, Teófilo Braga devoted some pages to various Madeiran poets of the 15th century, whom the illustrious writer believed could constitute a poetic cycle distinct from that of the mainland poets. The distinguished annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) disagrees with this assertion, for the learned and weighty reasons he sets out on p. 770 ff. of that work. It is an interesting question, which deserves to be read and weighed by those who devote themselves to history and literary criticism.
Cidrão (peak)
Overlooking the parish (*freguesia*) of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), and not very far from Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’), stands Pico do Cidrão (‘citron peak’), at an altitude of 1676 metres.
Cidrão (brook)
A brook in the parish (*freguesia*) of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), a tributary of the full-flowing Ribeira dos
Socorridos.
Citron (Citrus medica)

A shrub, rarely a tree, from 1.50 m to 3 metres tall, with thorny branches, blunt leaves (in the lemon and orange trees they are pointed) and large, more or less oblong fruits. These fruits never show the nipple or protuberance seen in those of Portugal. The citron, a native of Asia, is grown chiefly in Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), from where large numbers of citrons are sent to Funchal every year for the confectioners.
Gypsies

On 9 and 22 May 1912 several Gypsy families landed in Funchal and settled in huts on the Campo da Barca (‘boat field’). The men were coppersmiths, and the women practised fortune-telling (*ler a buena dicha*); some of them had quite regular features. They stayed in Madeira for about two months, and their dress and way of life aroused considerable interest among the Madeirans.
Grasshoppers

Grasshoppers or locusts are orthopteran insects known in Madeira by the name of *cigarros*. The common green grasshopper (Madeiran *cigarro*) is *Phaneroptera-4-punctata*; the grey *cigarro*, frequent in the fields, is *Pachytilus danicus*. It was *Dectycus albifrons* that caused great devastation to the crops of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) in 1844. It appears from time to time on the first of these islands, carried by winds from the coast of Africa, but since that year it has never again caused significant damage to crops.
Cigerão
Vernacular name of *Vicia hirsuta* and *V. gracilis*, plants of the family Leguminosae, very common in Madeira.
Cima (islet)
An islet east-south-east of Porto Santo, with a lighthouse installed in 1900. It is separated from the island by the channel known as Boqueirão de Cima (‘upper gap’).

Some fossil shells are found on it, and it is also known as Ilhéu dos Dragoeiros, although these trees (dragon trees) have disappeared completely not only from the islet but from the whole island of Porto Santo.
Cinco de Junho
See Proclamation of Constitutional Government.
Cinco de Junho (street)

This public thoroughfare, which links Rua dos Aranhas (today Rua do Dr. Chaves) directly with Largo do Ribeiro Real, was opened a few years ago, when the old alleys known as the cemetery alleys, which lay near the two British cemeteries, were demolished and repaired.
5 June 1834 is the date of the proclamation of constitutional government in Madeira, and the new street was given this name to commemorate that auspicious event.
Cintra (Diogo Gomes de)

This 15th-century Portuguese navigator wrote a narrative of his voyages in Latin, and in it he refers to the discovery of the Madeira archipelago. What is said on this subject on p. 905 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) is well worth reading. Diogo Gomes’s narrative was translated by Gabriel Pereira and published in the *Boletim da Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*, no. 5 of series 170., covering the years 1898 and 1899.
Cinzeiro

This was formerly the name of a disease that frequently attacked Madeiran vines. Some have sought to identify this disease, whose characteristics are not well known today, with *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium), but this opinion does not seem justified to us. If *Oidium Tuckeri* had existed on the island since remote times, it is not credible that our vineyards could have withstood it, since the effectiveness of sulphur against that parasite was only discovered after 1850. It is more natural to suppose that the *cinzeiro* was caused by *Botrytis cinerea*, *Fumago vagans*, *Pestalozzia Menezesiana* or one of the other fungi that still appear on the vine today, though without doing it great harm.
Cypress (Cupressus sempervirens, L.)

A tree of the family Pinaceae, native to Asia Minor and cultivated in the cemeteries of Madeira. It is a species with a narrow, pointed crown, monoecious flowers and relatively large galbuli. It produces good timber.
Cirripedes
Darwin’s monograph on the cirripedes lists Madeiran species: 6 balanids, 1 verrucid and 6 lepadids.
See Carcinology.
Ciúmes

Vernacular name of various species of the genus *Delphinium* (family Ranunculaceae). *Delphinium Ajacis*, L. is frequent at Monte (‘hill’), and *D. orientale*, Gay is grown in some gardens. These species have deeply cut leaves and spurred blue, violet or white flowers.
Clairouin (Hector)

He was born in France and came to Funchal in 1857, where for many years he taught French, and he died here on 20 November 1882. Works: *Methodo Michaelense para o ensino da lingua francesa*, Funchal, 1861. There is a second edition of this work entitled *O Nec Plus Ultra das Grammaticas Methodicas para o ensino da Lingua Francesa*, Lisbon, 1874.
Clamor Popular (O)
It ran from 19 March to 19 July 1892, publishing 32 issues.
Clamor Publico (O)

Its first issue appeared on 22 May 1854 and its last, no. 170, on 20 January 1858. Its editors were the Madeirans António Correia Heredia, Dr António Gonçalves de Freitas and Dr Luís de Freitas Branco.
Clarke (James)

He dealt with the climate of Madeira in his work entitled *The Influence of Climate in the prevention and cure of chronic Diseases, more particulary of the Chest and Digestive Organs*, London, 2nd edition, 1830.

Clarke never visited Madeira, but the English physicians Heineken and Renton supplied him with the information and data he needed to write the chapter of that work devoted to the climate of this island.
Clementina (Maria)

A nun of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), much admired by Portuguese and foreigners alike for her extraordinary beauty. Henry Nelson Coleridge, in his book *Six months in the West Indies in 1826*, speaks with enthusiasm of the charms of Maria Clementina, and other foreigners also mention them in the books they published about Madeira.

The author of *Rambles in Madeira*, who saw Maria Clementina in 1826, tells us that she had fair hair and a captivating expression, a type of beauty uncommon on the island, which explained the admiration the Madeirans felt for it.

In 1854, according to Lady Wortley, the Madeiran nun still revealed in her eyes and finely drawn features ‘how perfect her beauty must have been in the days of her youth’. Maria Clementina was the daughter of Pedro Agostinho de Vasconcelos, and she took her vows in the Convent of St Clare towards the end of the first quarter of the 19th century, to satisfy her father’s wishes. She died in the same convent, aged over 60, on 16 May 1867.
See the interesting article on page 104 of volume IV of the *Arquivo Historico da Madeira*.
Climate

Many physicians have considered the climate of Funchal capable of exerting a beneficial effect in the treatment of pulmonary diseases. Sir James Clark said that of all the climates known to him, that of Madeira was the best for persons suffering from pulmonary consumption. Dr Barral, in a work he wrote about this island, did not hesitate to recommend residence in Funchal *to individuals who, having a hereditary predisposition to tuberculosis, begin to suffer from a cough, or haemoptysis, or fatigue, or loss of weight, or any symptom that might give reason to fear the onset of that disease. According to the same physician, the climate of Funchal should also be recommended to all those suffering from incipient consumption or consumption in its first stage, and it may even be useful when the disease has reached the so-called second stage, provided that the patient feels strong and in good spirits. It was Dr Heberden who first gave a favourable account of the climate of Madeira, in 1751. He was followed by Dr Fothergill in 1755, Dr Adams in 1801, Dr Gourlay in 1811, Dr Nicolau Pita in 1812, Dr Heineken in 1824, Dr Sousa Vaz in 1832, Sir James Clark in 1835 and 1842, Dr Kampfer in 1847, Roberto White in 1851, Eduardo Harcourt in the same year, Dr Lund in 1853, Dr Barral in 1854, Dr Mittermayer in 1855, Dr Garnier in 1858, Dr Acursio G. Ramos in 1880, Dr Jacoud in 1881, Dr Embleton in 1882, Dr C. Taylor in 1889 and Dr Mourão Pita in 1859 and 1889.

It is true that Dr Mason did not approve of residence in Funchal for consumptives, and even sought to prove that the air here was more humid than in London. However, if we bear in mind that this physician’s observations were made in an exceptionally rainy year, and at one of the points in the city where the atmosphere is always more laden with water vapour, we are naturally led to conclude that such observations cannot be used to discredit our climate.

The frequency of tuberculosis among the natives is an argument often used by the detractors of our climate to drive away not only invalids but also those who visit us for other reasons. Yet although this frequency is a fact borne out by statistics, it does not seem to us that it can carry the significance some have sought to attribute to it. Alcoholism and other excesses, lack of hygiene and privation predispose people to tuberculosis here as everywhere else, and these are the chief reasons why one of the worst diseases afflicting humanity is so common on the island.

Dr Gourlay, in a work he published in 1811, advised consumptives to seek in Funchal a refuge from the winter of their own countries, even though he knew very well how much tuberculosis afflicted the natives. Dr Barral, whose integrity and knowledge of the subject no one can doubt, expressed himself as follows when speaking of the climate of the capital of Madeira: ‘the impression it makes on the traveller is of a gentleness and mildness so agreeable that it seems the most delicate and impaired constitutions could live there in the open air. In general, an almost uniform temperature, always moderate during the day; little wind, and that not troublesome; the hot hours tempered by a few clouds that soften the sun’s rays, and by the sea breeze (*viração*); never any notable cold; rains that are sometimes heavy but brief, soon leaving the ground fit for walking; an atmosphere in which one feels no humidity, nor dust, nor troublesome effluvia. All this at once shows the measure of an exceptional climate, suited to the treatment of chronic ailments in delicate constitutions. And on the man of the north who, fleeing the rigour of an inhospitable climate, lands there in winter and finds an extensive vegetation in full vigour, including many of the most beautiful and useful plants of every climate, it produces the marvellous effect of one of those paradises imagined and described by the poets. . . ’.

The data we present below sum up what is known about the climate of Madeira and confirm what has been said about the climate of Funchal. These data are indispensable to the physician and the physiologist, and may also be useful to the farmer and to those who intend to visit our country, whether for the benefit of their health or for any other reason.

Temperature. As a rule, Funchal has neither excessive cold nor excessive heat. The temperature in the shade rarely falls below 8 °C or rises above 26 °C, and only on days of *leste* (hot, dry easterly wind from Africa) does the thermometer here record somewhat high temperatures. The slight variation in warmth from month to month and from season to season is one of the characteristics of Funchal's climate; it should also be noted that the temperature does not change greatly during the day. Humidity. In Funchal humidity is so closely bound up with temperature that it never appears as mist, nor is it troublesome to those exposed to it. Invisible as it is, this humidity nevertheless plays an important part in the island’s climatic conditions, since it tempers the harshness of the air and prevents the extremes of temperature to which regions in the interior of continents are subject.

Between 800 and 1000 metres on the south side of Madeira, and between 700 and 800 on the north side, dense fogs are often seen wrapping the mountains, chiefly during the day, because thermal conditions there become unfavourable to keeping water in a clear vapour state. Above and below these altitudes, however, humidity changes gradually, and at an altitude of 1700 metres it is already slight.

The greatest dryness is observed when the *leste* (hot, dry easterly wind from Africa) blows; relative humidity may then fall as low as 18 per cent, as Mac Euen noted on 17 February 1849 at Quinta Holloway (‘Holloway estate’), about 85 metres above sea level.

Rain. Rain falls in every month of the year in the uplands of Madeira, but in Funchal it is sometimes absent, especially during the summer. The first heavy rains generally arrive in October, and from then until April it rains more or less abundantly in Funchal, although the precipitation does not follow a clearly marked periodic pattern. In May and June there is sometimes a lack of rain, and in July and August, in certain years, not a single drop of water falls in Funchal. The autumn rains are as a rule heavier and more violent than those of winter.

It is rare, Dr Barral reports, for it to rain in the city all day or all night; there are generally intervals in which no rain falls at all, and the weather may even turn clear during these intervals. Torrential rains are brought by the south-west, north-east and west winds, and sometimes last several days, though with varying intensity.
The averages we give below refer to the quantity of rain, in millimetres, collected by the rain gauge of the Funchal Meteorological Station in the period from 1901 to 1909:

In 1901, a very wet year, 1138 mm of rain fell in Funchal; in 1906, a very dry year, only 488 mm. In June 1904, in July 1903, 1905 and 1909, and in August 1901, 1903, 1905, 1906, 1908 and 1909, no rain at all fell in Funchal. The greatest daily rainfall was 155.1 mm, on 10 November 1901.

In Funchal it rains on average on 79 days a year; the largest number of rainy days recorded to date in a single year is 101, and the smallest 52. From December 1900 to November 1901 Porto Santo had 40 days of heavy rain and 84 of light rain, or drizzle.
Snow, frost and hail. These forms of precipitation occur in the uplands of Madeira, as we shall describe elsewhere.

*Dente de cão* (‘dog’s tooth’, popular name for crystalline hoar frost), Hail and Snow)

Clouds and fogs. ‘In Madeira,’ says Dr Barral, ‘there are a good number of clear days on which the sky is pure and almost cloudless; but there is a greater number of clear days, with excellent weather, on which clouds appear during the day in greater or lesser numbers – cumulus and cirrus – showing themselves now, then vanishing at once, cooling the temperature and blocking the sunlight for short spells… There are not many days on which the sky stays overcast without the sun being visible at any time of the day, but there are many on which the sun is not seen for hours, the day being clear and the weather fine before and after… A clear and serene atmosphere, with a resplendent, luminous and pure sky, such as is often seen in the climates of Italy, especially southern Italy, is very seldom observed in Madeira…’

‘In the morning,’ the same author goes on, ‘the mountain tops appear clear, while the horizon over the sea is laden with heavy, thick, dark clouds, *nimbus*, or else white, towering clouds, more or less separate from one another, *cirrus*, *cumulus*, rise above the Ocean. The sea breeze drives them over the land for part of the day, cooling the air and tempering the heat of the sun’s rays; towards evening the sky is overcast. The wind then shifts to the northern quarter, usually between north and north-east, and carries the clouds out to sea; many of them spread out and disperse with the wind. The nights are very often clear, especially until midnight, and the stars shine with a tropical brilliance: and this is repeated for many days, the said changes taking place at almost the same hour every day. On some nights, too, a light mist can be seen over the sea or over the mountains, and the lunar rainbow is not a very rare phenomenon there. By day it is a frequent phenomenon, and sometimes one of great beauty.

The fogs that girdle the mountains in the condensation zone, which we have already discussed above, come from the vapour carried by the rising air currents that form along the slopes during the day. These fogs often disappear at nightfall, leaving the nights clear and starry. In summer the fogs form lower down than in winter, so that the zone of greatest humidity lies higher in winter than in summer.
Winds

Observations of wind direction made at Ponta de São Lourenço from 1901 to 1909 show that the wind that prevails there most throughout the year is the NE, followed by the NNE, N, NW, SW and E. The first of these winds blows from mid-April until the end of October, although it may also appear at other times. It is generally not felt directly in the city, though its presence can be recognised by the disturbance it produces on the surface of the sea outside the bay.

The N wind sometimes blows with great force in winter, and it is this wind that brings the snow and hail that appear in the mountains during that season. The W, NW and SW winds bring a large proportion of the rain, the last two being sometimes very violent in the first months of the year. Winds from the quadrants between SW and SE by way of S sometimes cause heavy seas in the bay, and the humidity of the atmosphere in Funchal is then higher.

Dr Barral says that if we examine what happens in the different seasons, we find winds from N to E prevailing in summer and autumn, and less so in winter, and winds from SW to NW more in spring and autumn, and also in winter, though no very fixed rule can be laid down on this point.

Madeira sometimes experiences, particularly in summer, a hot, dry wind which the inhabitants call the *leste* (hot, dry easterly wind from Africa), and which generally lasts from 1 to 3 days. We shall speak of this wind, which appears to originate on the coast of Africa, in the appropriate place, as well as of the land and sea breezes (land breeze (*terral*) and *embate* (daytime sea breeze)), which follow one another every day at almost regular hours.

At Poiso (‘resting place’), according to Mr Teles de Meneses, the NE, N and NW winds prevailed from July to November 1894, and at Areeiro (‘sand pit’) the N, NNE and NW winds from June to October 1895.

The NE also prevails on Porto Santo, followed by the N, ENE, NNE and E. In 1901 the NE was the most frequent wind from May to October, and the ENE blew from March to November, even becoming dominant in that month and in April, July and August. The N was very frequent from February to July and in November, while the E prevailed in December and January. The NW blew mainly from December to March, in November, and from January to May.
See Adams, Barral, Bloxam Mackenzie, Burguess, Christmann, Clarke, Grabham, Gourlay Goldschmit, Harcourt, Heineken, Kampfer, Lund, Mason, Mittermayer, Pita, Sousa Vaz, Smyth and White.

By consulting the articles cited above, one can compile a long list of the authors who, at various times, have written on the climate of Madeira. This already vast bibliography was recently enriched by a remarkable study by the illustrious naval officer and academician Hugo de Lacerda. Written in French, it was published in 1936 by order of the Autonomous General Council (*Junta Geral Autónoma*) of Funchal under the title *Le Climat de Madère, ébauche d’une étude comparative*, and it is the most valuable work on the subject ever to have appeared in print. The island’s delegation of the tourism department very wisely had this study translated into English. The task was entrusted to the learned teacher Dr Alberto Figueira Jardim, and the translation appeared in 1938 under the title *The Climate of Madeira With a comparative study*.

We do not wish to close these lines on the climate of Madeira without placing on record here a remarkable article by Dr Armindo Narciso. In it this distinguished practitioner of the medical sciences addresses some new aspects of a subject that is always of great moment for our archipelago. He clears up doubts and lays down principles that should be of the greatest use to all who wish to find their way with complete confidence in any discussion of the matter, or in whatever publicity may be undertaken concerning the mildness and therapeutic qualities of this island’s incomparable climate.

‘Writers on the subject, even the most learned and respected, do not agree on the therapeutic action of oceanic climates, that is, the climates of the open sea, also called pelagic climates. This disagreement is more marked among continental authors than among the English. The English, being islanders and well travelled, know the sea better.

The main cause of this disagreement is that a great many climatologists regard these climates as all alike, when in truth they are influenced by local factors, just as coastal and inland climates are, and these factors vary the meteorological formula of the climate.

From what has been set out, it follows that the climate of Madeira is a special oceanic climate, for it has Mediterranean characteristics even though the island lies in the middle of the Atlantic. Yet this climate with Mediterranean characteristics has its own local ‘nuance’. The winter there is even milder than on the European Mediterranean coast, with an equally temperate and luminous atmosphere, but with slightly higher humidity.

There, the cold, damp and stormy north winds break against and are dried out by the mountains that shelter the city of Funchal. The hot, dry winds from North Africa arrive cooled and moistened by their passage over a stretch of sea, short though it is, and they are one of the factors that make the island winter so mild.

Only in summer do these African winds reach the island dry and hot, and even then only intermittently; one need only climb into the mountains, or cross to the island’s other coast, to escape their assault.

Thus this climate lacks the most exciting factors of the Mediterranean climate: dry air currents, at times violent and of extreme temperature, now extremely cold, now extremely hot, such as the Mistral and the Sirocco, and all the winds of the same origin and kinship.

In Madeira there are only factors of gentle stimulation: a pure, very transparent atmosphere and great luminosity. Moreover, the gentle stimulation of these factors is further softened by factors with a sedative effect, such as the great calm, the uniform warmth and the humidity which, though low, is nonetheless slightly higher than that of most Mediterranean climatic resorts.

This climate of Madeira is therefore not one of marked stimulation but of slight stimulation, indeed more tonic than stimulating. Its stimulating action is felt on the vegetative functions, its tonic action on the nervous functions. Thus, there, digestion and nutrition are stimulated and the nervous system is toned.

The well-being and relief that the patient feels on arriving in Madeira is a kind of euphoria, but a gentle euphoria, without excitement, without insomnia, without fever. So, rather than being excited, the patient feels calm and regains the joy of living he had lost. He puts on weight, gains strength and enters upon a new life.

The British were the first to take advantage of this climate, finding that it has considerable therapeutic properties in the treatment of the overworked, the exhausted, the weak and debilitated, the undernourished, those entering upon consumption, convalescents and those with tuberculosis, not excluding pulmonary cases. And so, for more than a century, a great multitude of invalids from all over Europe, but chiefly from the British Isles, has flocked to Madeira every winter.

The proportion of pulmonary tuberculosis sufferers among these invalids was very large, and the results they obtained were so beneficial that throughout the 19th century Madeira was the great resort for lung patients.

The offensive that the continental phthisiologists launched against the sea at the beginning of the present century drove the tuberculous away from that island. Today Madeira has ceased to be a sanatorium resort and has become a resort for rest, where the English, sick and healthy alike, spend the winter.

But is there any reason for this to be so? Is the climate of Madeira really harmful to lung patients? Clearly not. This prohibition arose from a misunderstanding that began on the European continent and later spread even to the British Isles, although some English phthisiologists still advise their lung patients to go to Madeira, as was common practice in the 19th century.

This misunderstanding stemmed from the confusion that has generally been made between the coastal maritime climate and the oceanic climate, and from the belief, as I have already said, that all maritime climates are alike. Now, in the coastal maritime climate as in the oceanic maritime climate, the elements harmful to pulmonary tuberculosis sufferers are high humidity and violent wind. It is from these that the lively, violent maritime climate derives. When these elements are joined by the alternation of sea winds with land winds, which are dry and of very variable temperature, the maritime climate becomes more violent still.

The climate of Madeira is entirely free of these aggressive factors, and so nothing prevents its use in the treatment of lung patients. It is true, and not surprising, that not all pulmonary tuberculosis sufferers are in a condition to benefit from a stay on that island. But the same is true of going to the mountains. The climate of Madeira, like the Alpine climate, is contraindicated for lung patients in advanced consumption with inadequate circulatory and digestive systems: highly feverish patients, those with diarrhoea, those with tachycardia.

But it is indicated for patients who are still vigorous, with a sound heart and digestive tract, able to bear its tonic, mildly stimulating action. And while the mountain climate, with its cold, dry, rarefied atmosphere, is preferable for patients with softening lesions and cavities, because it dries the lesions and reduces expectoration, the Madeiran climate, with its mild, slightly humid atmosphere, is superior to that of the mountains for patients with a heavy cough, congestion, and respiratory capacity reduced by extensive fibrous lesions, who are very sensitive to chills and to changes in temperature: it calms the cough and the dyspnoea and reduces congestion and the frequency of haemoptysis.

It is evident that patients sent to Madeira must still have the reserve of energy needed to benefit from the action of that island climate. But it should be noted that this reserve of energy need not be greater than in patients who go to high-altitude resorts; indeed, children and adults over 40 years of age who can benefit from a climatic cure tolerate the climate of Madeira better than the altitude climate.

There is therefore no reason to exclude all tuberculosis patients, absolutely, from the climate of Madeira. What is needed is to know how to choose those who can benefit there and to exclude the rest. This, moreover, is the secret of success in all therapy, whether surgical, medicinal, hydrological or climatic.
Madeiran Naval Club
Its statutes are dated 20 July 1917, and notice that it had been constituted was given to the competent authority on 17 May 1918.

The Clube Funchalense, to which we referred above, lasted almost 60 years. It was established in a house at Carmo (‘Carmel’), from where it moved to the mansion in Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), which it occupied until it was dissolved. Only people of a certain social standing belonged to it, whereas the Clube Unido, founded at almost the same time and dissolved early in 1879, was less demanding in the requirements it set for its members, who in any case had to be of good conduct and hold a respectable position in society. The great merchants were admitted to the Clube Funchalense, but shopkeepers and other traders with retail establishments could not join as members. When a certain British merchant, highly esteemed and respected in Funchal but the owner of a drapery shop, sought to join the club, some members who were his friends warned him that the vote of the general assembly would go against him unless he first sold or transferred the shop!

The Clube Funchalense became well known for its balls and soirées, which were almost always attended by large numbers of ladies, both Portuguese and foreign. Almost every distinguished figure who visited this island was honoured with festivities in that house, and many of these left a lasting memory, for the luxury and splendour with which they were staged and for the gallant and noble manner in which these guests were received there.

See Freemasonry (*Maçonaria*). Cochineal (*Cocus cacti*). A homopterous insect of the family Coccidae, imported from the Canary Islands in the second quarter of the 19th century, the female of which yielded the scarlet used in dyeing. It was bred on the cactus called prickly pear (*tabaibeira*) (*Opunti tuna*), but the industry never managed to flourish, despite the persistent efforts of some Funchal merchants. Its failure was due in part to the opposition of the peasants, who preferred the prickly pear (*tabaibo*) to the insect that spoiled this much-prized fruit for them, even though it was a colouring matter of high value at that time.

The term *cochonilha* has a very narrow meaning in Madeira, as indeed elsewhere, serving only to designate the dye insect of the prickly pear, whereas the *cochonilhas*, *cochenilhas* or *cochinilhas* of the naturalists are all the Coccidae, a family that includes, besides the insect mentioned, many others called *lapas* and *alforras*.

Cochineal still appears on the leaves of prickly pears at São Gonçalo and at Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’), and it is easily recognised by the patches it forms on the plant. If the tip of a walking stick is passed over these patches, it comes away more or less stained with scarlet.

It was Miguel de Carvalho e Almeida who introduced cochineal to Madeira, and the pharmacist Gerardo José de Nóbrega published a short work on this insect entitled *The Cultivation of Cochineal* (*Pharmaceutic Journal*, 1849).
