Coelho

This family surname derives from Rodrigo Anes Coelho, one of the first settlers of Madeira, who held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) land at Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), apparently at Lombo de São João.
Porto Santo rabbit

According to the zoologist Carlos França, the Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) rabbit has the characteristics and appearance of the common wild rabbit of southern Europe, differing from it only in the shape and dimensions of the skull. For this zoologist, the rabbit – of which Haeckel gave a description as fanciful as it was inaccurate in his *Historia da Criação Natural* – is a subspecies of *Oryctolagus cuniculus*, *O. cuniculus Huxleyi*, peculiar to Porto Santo and impossible to distinguish by its external characteristics from the *meridionalis* form of the European rabbit.

Darwin, who had the opportunity to examine and study seven Porto Santo rabbits, two of them alive, noted that they differed from the common English rabbit in both colour and size. It was perhaps this circumstance that led Haeckel to create his *Lepus Huxleyi*, to which he attributed ‘a particular colour, a shape approaching that of the rat, nocturnal habits and an extraordinary wildness’.

It is not only in the colour of their fur that the Porto Santo rabbits are identical to those of the Mediterranean region; they are also identical in other easily observed external characteristics. For Miller, the rabbits of that region, those of the Madeira archipelago and those of the Azores form a single subspecies – the subspecies *Haxleyi* – a view we would have no hesitation in accepting, were it not for the osteological differences pointed out by Carlos França.

The Porto Santo rabbit is, as a rule, somewhat smaller than the rabbit of other countries. This may perhaps be attributed to lack of space, as Professor Delage says: that is, to the difficulty that species confined within certain limits have in strengthening their stock through crossing between varied and numerous individuals.

Professor Camilo Torrend says that on Porto Santo rabbits, like cattle and certain molluscs, present typical examples of dwarfism. We may add that certain plant species, such as mistletoe, the wild olive, cliff box (*buxo da rocha*), etc., also reach smaller dimensions on that island than on Madeira, owing to environmental influences.

Crosses between Porto Santo rabbits and European ones are not only possible but are in use as a means of strengthening and restoring the stock. As for wild habits, it seems to us that there is no reason to attribute them solely to the animals of that island. The rabbits of Madeira are just as shy and untameable as those of Porto Santo when caught after a certain age.

Azurara relates that a friend of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary of Porto Santo, had given him a doe rabbit which bore young during the voyage. On reaching the island, Perestrelo released the mother and her litter, but within a short time these animals multiplied so greatly that nothing could be sown or planted without being at once devoured or spoiled by them. The first settlers tried in vain to wipe out the rabbits; the animals survived everything, so that the new colony had to be abandoned, since it brought nothing but losses to those who were settling it.

João de Barros, Gaspar Frutuoso, António Cordeiro and Cadamosto tell the story of the doe brought by Bartolomeu Perestrelo in almost identical terms, and it is from this doe, beyond dispute, that the present-day rabbits of Porto Santo descend.

In our view, the creation of the subspecies *huxleyi* by the Portuguese zoologist Carlos França is fully justified by the cranial characters of the animals it includes. External characters are of little importance in the case in question, all the more so as it is known that the two rabbits examined by Darwin acquired, within very few years and under the influence of new climatic conditions, the colour of the common English rabbit. The internal characters already noted, however, cannot be lightly dismissed, for they represent profound modifications undergone by the species.

The distinctive build of the Porto Santo rabbit seems, says Carlos França, to accord with the animal’s conditions of life. Living on a very small island with rather sparse vegetation, the rabbit could not thrive without well-developed sense organs, and its skull consequently underwent marked modifications, such as to characterise the subspecies *huxleyi*.
We set out below the characters that Dr Carlos França found in the four specimens on which he based his study of the Porto Santo rabbit:

‘Back chestnut, nape reddish, belly light grey in three specimens and dull grey in the fourth. The upper side of the tail is leaden grey, with a few rare hairs with yellowish tips; the hairs on the underside of the tail are white. The ears do not have darker tips, and the chest region is light chestnut...

The length of the four Porto Santo rabbits kept in captivity, measured from the incisors to the anus, was 32, 35.5, 36 and 37 centimetres respectively, that is, 35.5 centimetres on average. The smallest of all these rabbits was a male, which was rather poorly nourished.
The weight of these specimens, three of which were fat, was 815, 755, 745 and 650 grams, that is, an average weight of 741 grams’.

Although Haeckel visited Madeira in 1866, he neither saw nor studied the Porto Santo rabbit, and almost everything he says about this rodent is pure fantasy. It would indeed be curious if an animal carried to a small island had changed there within the space of 4 or 5 centuries to the point of producing a new species. Such facts, and others like them, are recorded only by naturalists of little seriousness, or by those who study superficially certain complex biological problems that deserve the most careful consideration.

Coelho Machado (Rafael)

He was born on this island in 1814 and in 1838 left for Brazil, where he died. He made his name as a composer and writer on music. We know of his works only from the list of them given by Joaquim de Vasconcelos in his esteemed book *Musicos Portugueses*. Coelho Machado wrote a *Diccionario Musical*, the first work of its kind to appear in the Portuguese language. His writings include: *Methodo de musica ou Principios de musica pratica para uso dos principiantes*, 1842; *Breve tratado de Harmonia*, 1851; *Melodias originaes*, some of which were translated into Italian; *Diccionario musical. . .* Rio de Janeiro, 1842, 275 pp. He left many compositions of sacred music, and translated and published various methods for the study of the piano, flute, fiddle, etc.
Coriander (Coriandrum sativum)

An annual umbellifer, widely grown in Madeiran kitchen gardens. It originates from the East and has pinnatisect leaves, the lower ones less deeply cut than the upper, and umbels with short peduncles, lacking or almost lacking an involucre. Its semi-globose fruits are stimulant and carminative and are used in cookery.
Mushrooms

Some 340 species of Madeiran mushrooms or fungi have been identified, 31 of which have not yet been found in any other region of the globe. Some of these species are edible, such as *Ammanita vaginata*, *Lactarius deliciosus*, *Cantharellus cibarius*, *Psaliotta campestris* (*champignon de couche*), *Boletus edulis*, *B. bovinus*, etc. Madeirans are not in the habit of eating mushrooms, and in the countryside people often destroy them, believing them to be the work of witches.
See Torrend.
Collegiate Churches

In some parishes, besides the clergy assigned to parish duties, there was a chapter made up of a small number of clerics, who recited the divine office in common and performed other functions of worship. It was in the parish churches of the most important and most densely populated parishes that the collegiate chapters were established. Like the chapters of the cathedrals, they lent greater splendour to worship, and their members were valuable helpers in all the religious services of the parishes.
This diocese had collegiate chapters in the parishes of Santa Maria Maior, São Pedro, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Porto Santo, Santa Cruz and Machico.

In the churches of the last two, the choir stalls used for reciting the divine offices are still preserved today beside the high altar. The chapters were founded in the second half of the 16th century, except for those of Ribeira Brava, Machico and Santa Cruz, which are older; the last two had six beneficiaries. They were generally made up of the parish priest, the assistant priest (*coadjutor*), three or four beneficiaries, a preacher and a treasurer, although some had a smaller staff. Each had its own regulations (*regimento*), which governed how the duties entrusted to it were to be performed.
All the collegiate chapters of Madeira were abolished before 1834.
College
See São João Evangelista (college and church).
Cholera morbus in 1856 and 1910

The horrific calamity that ravaged this archipelago from July to October 1856, taking the lives of some ten thousand of its inhabitants, is still remembered by many and remains vivid in local tradition.

Cholera was raging in Lisbon, and in the district of Belém the epidemic had broken out with extraordinary virulence. The 1st Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.º 1*) was quartered in that district, and the central government, with criminal lack of foresight, had sent it to Madeira. It arrived on the afternoon of 28 June, disembarked at once and occupied the former Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). On 2 July the regiment moved its quarters to the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*), where the bales and baggage were opened; it was then that the first cases of cholera appeared among some of the regiment’s other ranks. The first Madeiran to fall ill was a seaman named Manuel Rodrigues, who lived near the Convent of São Francisco and had been in contact with some soldiers of the 1st Infantry.

The epidemic began to spread with great intensity, above all in the district of Santa Maria, then extended to the whole city and rapidly reached the suburban and rural parishes (*freguesias*). It was by now a fire burning everywhere. It reached the height of its violence on 31 July, when within the city alone it took the lives of 162 of our fellow countrymen in the space of 24 hours.

Outside Funchal, the epidemic first appeared in the parish of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) on 11 July and in Machico on the 14th, and then successively in the remaining parishes, in some of which the mortality rate was very low. The heaviest influx of patients was at the Misericórdia hospital, where on some days it was impossible to admit cholera patients, so great was the number of sufferers filling the wards and every room with space to lay a straw mattress. The military hospital and the building of the Poorhouse (*Asilo de Mendicidade*) were adapted to take cholera patients, and makeshift hospitals were set up in the parishes of Santo António, Ribeira Brava, Machico, Ponta do Sol and others.

‘If the epidemic’, says an official report, ‘had proved terrifying in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal through the havoc it wrought, in the rural municipalities its horrors were redoubled, for besides the large number of victims, the population was also struggling with hunger and had neither physicians nor medicines to help the sick. The state of despondency, distress and misery these municipalities reached was truly indescribable. Many patients died for complete want of medical aid; others perished from lack of food. Most of the makeshift hospitals were in dreadful condition, and all lacked the most basic supplies. The sick lay on the floor on wretched straw mattresses, and men and women, and the living and the dead, were often found there together.’ In view of this, the authorities decided that the medical sub-delegates Branco (‘white’) and Brand should travel round the island, taking medicines and other aid to the cholera sufferers. No more could have been done than was done. According to the official figures, cholera killed 7,041 people, but it has always been claimed that the number who succumbed to the epidemic was about ten thousand. In the municipality of Funchal 2,014 people died: 311 in the parish of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*)), 519 in São Pedro, 376 in Santa Maria Maior, 69 in São Roque, 129 in São Martinho, 315 in Santa Luzia, 214 in Santo António, 83 in Monte and 88 in São Gonçalo.

The rural parishes with the highest mortality were Ponta do Pargo with 328 deaths, Machico 319, Câmara de Lobos 393, Campanário 206, Ponta do Sol 281, Tabua 161, Serra de Água 143, Ponta Delgada 409, São Vicente 307, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos 139, etc. In the Misericórdia hospital 619 people died, in that of Santo António 119 and in that of the Poorhouse 63.

In the article devoted to the civil governor António Rogério Gromicho Couceiro we shall highlight the truly providential work that this official carried out here, and the great gratitude Madeira owes him for the outstanding services he rendered to the whole archipelago. We also wish to mention here Dr António da Luz Pita, the delegate of the Health Council of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). He was in Lisbon at the time as deputy for this island, and at once left for Funchal on the warship *Mindelo*, bringing the relief that the central government had sent without delay and accompanying several doctors who came from the mainland to provide medical services on the island. This first relief consisted of a large quantity of medicines, a great deal of clothing, beds, straw mattresses, etc., and a credit of six *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis), and fresh and abundant consignments of relief were later sent. The medical profession distinguished itself by its extraordinary devotion: three Madeiran doctors and one Englishman, Dr Ross, fell victim to the disease.
We should go too far if we wished to enter into further details and more particular notes on the terrible epidemic that ravaged this archipelago in 1856.

Anyone wishing for a fuller account of the subject may consult the second part of the official report published in 1866 and the articles printed in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) in October 1908.

Cholera in 1910. The cholera epidemic that broke out in Funchal in October 1910 did not even remotely reach the proportions of the cholera morbus of 1856. Although the two lasted roughly the same length of time, the number of people who fell ill and of those who died was very different. According to official figures, the 1856 epidemic claimed 7,041 victims, and that of 1910 to 1911 only 556. The disease may perhaps have been less virulent, but the difference in mortality must be attributed chiefly to the means used to overcome the epidemic. Times have changed greatly, and the resources available to science in the two periods are entirely different, admitting not the slightest comparison. Today both officials and rural populations have a more exact understanding of their duties; hygiene is no longer an empty word, above all in the larger towns, and it is observed with some rigour, especially during epidemics. All this contributed powerfully to making the cholera of 1856, still remembered with such horror, and that of 1910 so unequal in their contagion, their spread and the havoc they caused. We also had the good fortune to have at the head of the various services fighting the epidemic a most remarkable physician. A man of science and a very distinguished bacteriologist, he had an essentially organising mind, a rare and prudent energy, boundless self-sacrifice and zeal, and the most proven strength of character. In so calamitous a time and in such difficult and distressing circumstances, he rendered this land services that can never be forgotten, and his distinguished name is indissolubly linked to the history of our archipelago, placed alongside those who have most deserved the recognition and gratitude of its inhabitants.

The first cases to attract the attention of doctors were those of two sisters who lived near the Paiol (‘powder magazine’). One fell ill on 20 October 1910 and the other on the 23rd of the same month, and the latter died on 4 November following. The proper precautions were taken at once: the house was isolated, disinfection was carried out, contacts were medically examined, etc. Two more cases then appeared in the Rua da Imperatriz Dona Amélia, and others were soon recorded in various parts of the city. Before long the disease appeared in Câmara de Lobos, Machico and other places. The population began to grow alarmed. The chief authority of the district, deeply concerned at the spread of the disease, convened the Consultative Board of Hygiene (*Junta Consultiva de Higiene*) on 17 November, and more vigorous and effective measures were then taken. At the same time he pressed the central government to adopt extraordinary measures and to send indispensable resources that could not be found in Madeira.

The central government sent to Madeira, with extraordinary powers, Dr José Alfredo Mendes de Magalhãis as High Commissioner of the Republic. He rendered excellent services and, throughout his stay among us, always showed the greatest willingness to cooperate effectively in stamping out the epidemic. As a well-deserved tribute to these services, a formal session was held in his honour at the Municipal Council of this municipality (*concelho*). On that occasion he was made an honorary burgess and citizen of Funchal, and his portrait was unveiled in the state room of the town hall. Besides extraordinary credits to meet the heavy costs of fighting the epidemic, the government also sent a contingent of troops, owing to well-founded fears of public disorder.

The wisest measure taken by the government in Lisbon, however, was to send Dr Carlos França. He arrived in Funchal on 22 November and, after some days of laboratory work and other essential studies, took over the entire direction of the sanitary services and of the fight against the scourge that threatened to ravage the whole island. From the outset he showed not only the surest judgement and the most proven competence, but also ardent zeal and the most fervent dedication in carrying out the many functions he had to perform in so laborious and hazardous a mission. Seven doctors, several nurses and an analyst from the Câmara Pestana Bacteriological Institute came from the mainland. Together with the doctors of Madeira, they rendered good service and showed true self-sacrifice in the duties assigned to them.
Cholera hospitals operated in the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’) and in the parishes of Santo António, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Santa Cruz and Machico.

The epidemic raged in the municipalities of Funchal, Santa Cruz, Machico, Câmara de Lobos, Ponta do Sol and Porto Santo. It did not affect the parishes of Madalena, Serra de Água, Curral das Freiras and Santo da Serra, nor the whole municipality of Calheta (‘small cove’), with the exception of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’), where there were only two cases. The thirteen parishes of the whole north coast of Madeira were also spared. Deaths by municipality numbered 210 in Funchal, 161 in Câmara de Lobos, 71 in Ponta do Sol, 75 in Machico, 26 in Santa Cruz, and Porto Santo, making a total of 556.

We would go too far if we attempted to give details of how the various sanitary services were organised and run, and further still if we wished to describe the many episodes and circumstances worthy of special record that do not fit within the limits of this article. Anyone wishing to do so need only consult the brilliant and detailed work written by Dr Carlos França, entitled *A Epidemia Cholerica da Madeira 1910-1911. Relatorio apresentado ao ministro do interior*, where they will find everything of interest concerning this calamitous period in Madeiran history.
Coleridge (Henry Nelson)
He wrote about Madeira and about Maria Clementina, a nun of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), in his book *Six Months in West Indias* 1825.

Columbus (Christopher)

A long-standing tradition holds that the illustrious navigator lived for some time in this archipelago and that it was here that he conceived his grand plan for the discovery of the New World. His stay in Madeira is positively affirmed by Las Casas in the *Historia de las Indias*, who says that he obtained this information from the very lips of Diogo Colombo, son of the great navigator and his father’s successor in the office of admiral of the Sea of the Indies. News of fresh discoveries was then constantly reaching this island, and ‘this was the beginning of the discovery of the new world’. Agostinho de Ornelas, in his *Memoria sobre a residencia de Christovão Colombo na Ilha da Madeira*, published in 1892, puts forward valuable arguments in support of that assertion, which is in any case followed by various historians and many biographers of Columbus. The discoverer of America married Dona Filipa Moniz, daughter of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, first donatary of the island of Porto Santo, but authors disagree about the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) where the marriage took place. The author of the interesting booklet *A Mulher de Colombo* states that the wedding was celebrated in the town (*vila*) of Machico. Serious presumptions and probabilities of some weight support this opinion, although one may dispute the truth of the claim. The Las Casas already cited, and others too, give Diogo Colombo as born on Porto Santo. There is also a constant tradition on this small island that the great navigator lived there, and the site of the house he occupied is even pointed out: it is that of the parish priest’s residence, near the mother church (*igreja matriz*).

A good deal has already been written about the building that tradition has always identified as the residence of Christopher Columbus in Funchal. It stood on the spot now occupied by the lane that bears the navigator’s name and links Rua do Sabão and Rua do Esmeraldo. The memoir by Agostinho de Ornelas already cited, a valuable study by Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, a detailed account published in 1878 in the *Illustracion Espanola y Americana* and still other writings have dealt with the subject at some length. The Madeiran writer J. Reis Gomes also treated it with great expertise in the notes to his book *A Filha de Tristão das Damas*, and we shall transcribe some passages from it that bear very closely on the subject of this article:

‘The building that tradition has always pointed to as Columbus’s dwelling in Madeira, and which had belonged to the Fleming João Esmeraldo, was a large two-storey building with a broad roof terrace on top. It was later reduced to a granary and was therefore known as the granel do Poço, in this quarter set aside almost exclusively for merchants.

We would lengthen this note too much if we tried to relate here how this aristocratic residence passed from the heirs of its owner into the possession of the Council, which razed it. Issue no. 55 of the *Revista Illustrada* (1892) carries an article by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo entitled ‘Era inscripcional da casa memorada como da habitação de Colombo na Ilha da Madeira’, whose first part gives us reliable and precise information on this point.

The architecture of the building was originally Gothic, as shown by the pointed-arched section facing Rua do Sabão, which *O Ocidente* reproduced as an engraving in its no. 34 of May 1879, traced from one of the various photographs of the house taken by the distinguished Madeiran photographer João Camacho. It later underwent a restoration in which the forms of Renaissance architecture appear, more or less characteristically.

The date inscribed on the capital of the small column of the lovely two-light window shown in the accompanying plate has been read in three different ways. These varying readings led to diverse hypotheses about who built the house, about the likelihood that Columbus lived in it, and even to some digressions on the architectural style displayed on the façade facing Rua do Esmeraldo! It was first read – we have never quite understood how – as 1457, while the house was still standing. This date, strikingly at odds with the style, went round the world, and Henry Harrisse himself accepted it, referring to it in a note in his book *Christophe Colomb*.

That reading was plainly mistaken. Once the window had been taken down, it was seen that the last digit was a 4, clear and perfect, and doubt remained only over the third, which some read as a 7 and others as a 9. Was the inscribed date 1474 or 1494? For Agostinho de Ornelas, owner of the stones that made up the precious window, the third digit was a 7, since ‘the crossbar, though slightly curved, does not close with the upright’, as he states in his *Memoria*, which we have already cited in another note. For Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, who saw the date with his own eyes, took a tracing of it and made enquiries among scholars, the disputed digit was a 9, exactly as it was written and engraved at the end of the 15th century.

We too went recently to see these stones, which remain the property of the Ornelas family. All the digits were clear, and the only one that left us in doubt was that third one, with its unclosed head, which suggests a seven but, by its rounded shape and curved stem, points to a 9. We traced it and made the necessary enquiries on our own account. Through a friend, himself competent in the matter, we consulted those in the capital best able to enlighten us on the subject. We were satisfied that the doubtful digit was a 9 and the date of the inscription 1494. Among various supporting documents, absolute certainty came from a date printed in the *Ephemerides* of Regiomontanus, Venice edition of 1492. There, plain to see, was a nine of the same design: the head unclosed and the stem curved back.

The date 1494, on a window that in all probability had been pointed-arched but in fact displayed the characteristic form of our Renaissance architecture, which appeared in Portugal only in the 16th century, was truly puzzling to anyone who paid attention to this strange case.

The restoration belonged squarely to the reign of John II, a year before his death, yet it had the architectural character that appeared here only much later – albeit marked more specifically by maritime attributes drawn from the discoveries and conquests – and that came to be called the Manueline style!...

The fact, however, will not seem so remarkable once one considers that the building belonged to a foreigner, noble and rich, living in a land, Madeira, which through the currents of immigration had far closer ties with the rest of Europe, where Renaissance architecture was already flourishing, especially in Italy and France, than with the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), which that style had not yet reached at that date.

The building belonged to a private individual who, by his origins and his circle, was well placed to be seduced by the art form then triumphantly establishing itself in almost all of Europe. It is no wonder, then, that João Esmeraldo’s house long preceded, in this Portuguese land, the first Manueline forms of the buildings of the mainland.

Given the scarcity of good native artists and craftsmen at this period of island life, it is natural to suppose that the restoration of the house was necessarily entrusted to Italian or Flemish workmen, from the foreign colonies then most numerous in Madeira. This may well have led to the very suggestion of the architectural style that these workmen brought with them, as the most beautiful and most modern, from their countries of origin.

The fact that 1494 is the number carved at the top of the handsome two-light window does not contradict the long-standing and well-founded assertion that Columbus lived in Esmeraldo’s house as his guest, for the discoverer of America left Funchal years before that date. It simply means that he knew the building only in its original Gothic style, and that he certainly did not lean, in his meditations, on those basalt stones later worked by the Renaissance chisel. João Esmeraldo’s near-fanatical devotion to the great Italian, his guest – if one accepts the tradition, fully justified in our view by the author of the ‘Memoria sobre a residencia de Colombo na ilha da Madeira’ – explains even better the rich Flemish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility)’s predilection for the elegant artistic form whose true cradle was Columbus’s homeland.

Did João Esmeraldo himself have the building constructed from the start, or did he buy it from its original owner? This point, of minor importance to us, does not seem to have been fully cleared up, despite what Agostinho de Ornelas and Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo wrote about it. We are inclined, however, in view of the text of the Madeiran genealogies and the words of Frutuoso, to believe that it was the Fleming who had the house built, and that it passed to his descendants as their manor house. The genealogies, without referring specifically to this dwelling, state that Esmeraldo built large houses in the street that took its name from him, and the author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says that Rua do Esmeraldo was so called because the Fleming ‘had his old dwelling there, with a house of two storeys, marble pillars in the windows and terraces on top’.

This building, about which a good deal has already been written both in Portugal and abroad, above all because, according to the most persistent tradition, it was Columbus’s residence in Madeira, ought for this and other reasons to be held in still greater respect and cherished with still greater care for its preservation. It deserves this as an example, as beautiful as it is rare from the artistic point of view, of the great aristocratic palaces of the 15th century; as a monument, on Portuguese soil, of a clearly marked transition between the Gothic style and our Manueline, displaying the general form of that style even before it became established in Portugal; and, further, as irrefutable proof, through its sumptuousness and architectural refinement, of the rapid development and progress of Madeira within the first eighty years after its discovery, bearing out what the chroniclers relate about this truly remarkable period of Madeiran history.’

The protest against the demolition of this building, which ought to have been reverently preserved, is made by the author of the passages quoted above, in the words that we reproduce below. They are full of irony but entirely just, and they express our own true feelings on the matter:

‘The monument was pulled down; but the Council, in homage to the man who, according to tradition, had been its illustrious occupant, christened the insignificant thoroughfare, barely 30 metres long, with the pompous name of *Rua de Christovão Colombo*, and everything was thus entirely put right. More than that: the Council rejoiced at its decision. It could pride itself on the glory of having endowed the city with one more public street at a relatively low price; it had met a need of the local merchants, sparing them a few more steps in going from one street to the other; and it had done away with that blackened, irritating eyesore, which served only to astonish a few Yankees passing through Madeira, flanking the empty space with fresh, well-whitewashed walls, symmetrically pierced by the ventilators of two grain warehouses.

The bourgeois spirit of the Funchal councillors was rightly radiant. And so that no one could say it did not know how to honour great men, there on the whitewash of the granary wall stood the name of the discoverer of America: it is not quite clear whether because he had lived in the demolished house, or because he had The distinguished writer and journalist the Viscount of Meireles, who visited this island in 1913, published several articles in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) in March and April of that year, eloquently advocating the idea of rebuilding the house where Christopher Columbus lived on the very spot where it once stood. The lane that now bears the great navigator’s name would disappear, and the Rua do Sabão would be renamed after Cristóvão Colombo. The rebuilt house would be devoted to a regional museum and would become a centre of attraction for foreign visitors, especially North Americans, who would not fail to visit and examine with reverent affection the place where the grand plan for the discovery of their America was perhaps conceived and developed. This would be nothing new, for various historic buildings have been rebuilt abroad to perpetuate the memory of notable events or persons that it was fitting to make more memorable and enduring. Of the old house of Columbus, as we might call it, some photographs fortunately survive, and, what is more, the famous Gothic window, widely reproduced in engravings in numerous books, publications and magazines. Architecture and art would do the rest. We record here the idea of the Viscount of Meireles, which may perhaps, in the near future, yet become an eloquent reality.

This interesting window stands today (1940), artistically and lovingly placed, in the gardens of the magnificent Quinta da Palmeira (‘palm-tree estate’), on the Caminho da Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy levada road’). The estate belongs to the intelligent and public-spirited industrialist Henrique Hinton, who preserves that precious relic of the past there with the greatest veneration and esteem.

The connection between the life of Christopher Columbus and the history of Madeira, particularly regarding the great navigator’s marriage and his stay in this archipelago, has been briefly set out above. In recent years, however, new works of historical research have drawn this connection closer and offered material for interesting and lengthy studies, which the limited space at our disposal and a proven lack of competence entirely prevent us from undertaking.

Nevertheless, we shall say this. In 1928 and 1929 two curious books by Patrocínio Ribeiro and Pestana Júnior appeared, entitled *A Nacionalidade Portuguesa de Christovam Colombo* and *Cristóbal Colom ou Simão Palha*, in which their distinguished authors seek to prove that the illustrious discoverer of America was Portuguese. They were followed by two no less curious volumes under the titles *Salvador Gonçalves Zarco (Cristóbal Colon)* and *Cristobal Colon Salvador Gonçalves Zarco Infante de Portugal*, written respectively by G. L. dos Santos Ferreira and António Ferreira de Serpa, and by Artur Lobo de Ávila and Saul dos Santos Ferreira. These attempt to demonstrate, with skilful reasoning but unconvincing arguments, that the great navigator was the illegitimate son of Infante Ferdinand and of a granddaughter of João Gonçalves Zarco. It is well known that Ferdinand, heir and successor of Henry the Navigator in the grand mastership of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), took a very direct part in the government of our archipelago, which ‘in spiritual matters’ belonged to that order. Needless to say, the Gonçalves Zarco to whom those authors refer is the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal and the most illustrious pioneer of the early colonisation of Madeira.

Although one may disagree with the conclusions these authors reached, it is only fair to admit that their books make most agreeable reading, and that they contain some material that may be of considerable use to the history of this archipelago.
Colonia (contract)

When the owner or ‘landlord’ (*senhorio*) of a piece of land cannot or will not farm it himself, he hands it over to another person on condition that this person gives him a half-share (*demidia*) of the land’s produce. In this contract, widely used on the island of Madeira, the tenant farmer (*colono*, under the *colonia* contract) – that is, the agricultural partner who works the land – also receives half of this produce or income, but all the expenses the crops require are borne by him. When the tenant farmer and the landlord are on good terms, the landlord generally contributes half of the irrigation water, fertiliser and sulphur; this, however, is a concession, not an obligation imposed on him by the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant).

The houses, huts, paved paths, walls, vine trellises, useful plants and trees on the property are called improvements (*benfeitorias*, buildings and walls made by the tenant, which remained his property). These improvements may belong either to the landlord or to the tenant farmer, and for this reason deeds of agricultural sharecropping (*parceria*) always state what the tenant farmer receives when he takes over the property. If there is a house on the landlord’s land, the tenant farmer is called a resident tenant (*caseiro*); if there is none, he is called a sharecropper (*meeiro*, without a house on the land).

The owner may remove the tenant farmer by paying him in advance for the duly authorised improvements, and also for those made solely to increase or enhance the property’s yield. The tenant farmer may sell or mortgage these improvements without needing the landowner’s permission to do so.

No tenant farmer may put up buildings or make any other substantial improvements without the landlord’s written permission. Nor may he gather the harvest without first notifying the landlord or his lawful representative. Some owners merely require the sugar production, the wine, etc. to be shared, leasing to the tenant farmer the portion of the minor crops that would otherwise fall to them.
The *colonia* contract is not extinguished by the death of the contracting parties, nor by the sale of the property or of the improvements to other persons.

On Porto Santo there are lands that pay fifths and eighths (*quintos e oitavos*: rent of a fifth or an eighth of the produce) to their landlords under the royal decree (*alvará*) of 13 October 1770. This privilege is not general, however, for there are other lands on that island that are subject to the half-share, as happens in Madeira.

The *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant), peculiar to the Madeira archipelago, is in the view of Dr Azevedo a corruption of the *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) contract (see that entry). It arose in the 16th century, subordinate to the entailed estate (*morgadio*). ‘The wealthy *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*), says the same author, grew weary of country life, took pride in his ancestral nobility and craved a residence of greater show and bustle. He therefore scorned the land and entailed it, with a view to securing its revenues; he contracted out its cultivation to free tenant farmers in return for half, or in some places a third, of the produce, so as to live in idle pleasure; he abandoned his estates and came to settle, in luxury and extravagance, in the towns, chiefly Funchal, Machico, Santa Cruz, Calheta, Ponta do Sol and Ribeira Brava. Such is the historical origin of that fatal contract which was given the name of *colonia*: a leonine contract which, through the enormous injury it inflicts, exhausted the productive strength of the farmer and, combined with the entailment of the land, later came to impoverish the former *sesmeiro* too, now holder of the entail (*morgado*) upon it’.

Military commanders

The captain-donataries (1420–1580), the governors-general (1580–1640) and the captains-general (1640–1834), who were the highest authorities of the archipelago, held civil and military powers together. From 1834 these became two independent offices with entirely distinct functions, although they were sometimes held by the same individual, in which case one of the two posts was filled on a brief interim basis. We give below the list of military commanders, with the year in which each took up command. For the sake of brevity, we omit the names of the many army officers who held this post temporarily and on an interim basis:

District Commission

The District Committees (*Comissões Distritais*) replaced the General Councils (*Juntas Gerais*) when these were abolished by the Decree of 6 August 1892. Under the codes of 1895 and 1896 they had powers of administrative litigation, and they were made up of the civil governor, as president, the Administrative Auditor and three members elected by delegates of the Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*).

The District Commission of Funchal ceased to exist with the organisation and powers described in the code of 1896 after the decree of 8 August 1901 applied to this district the special organisation granted to the Azorean districts by the law of 12 June 1901.

‘The District Committees referred to in the administrative codes of 1878 and 1886 were made up of three representatives appointed by the General Councils at their first meeting after election, and were therefore no more than mere delegates of these bodies.’

The law of 7 August 1913 gave the Executive Committees (formerly the District Committees), as delegates of the General Councils, the power to audit the management accounts of brotherhoods, confraternities, etc., and to approve the budgets of these bodies.
Constitutional Municipal Commission

On 5 July 1834 the members of the governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office) met in the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) to elect a commission to replace the councillors (*vereadores*) appointed during the usurpation. The citizens elected were: Luís Teixeira Dória, president; Valentim Leal, vice-president; João Francisco de Florença; Luís de Ornelas e Vasconcelos; and Tristão Joaquim Bettencourt da Câmara. This commission held office until 20 October 1834.

Companions of Zarco

It would be of interest to give an account, however brief, of those who, sharing the risks and dangers of settling distant lands in unknown circumstances, left their homeland, crossed the ocean and came to begin the arduous colonisation of the Madeiran archipelago. From information gathered in old books of noble lineage and other manuscript sources, Dr João Pedro de Freitas Drumond compiled in the first quarter of the 19th century a list of some of the individuals who accompanied João Gonçalves Zarco, or were at least his contemporaries in the work of that first settlement. Among them may be named Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, Francisco Carvalhal, João Lourenço, Rui Pais, João Afonso, António Gago, Lourenço Gomes, Francisco Alcoforado, Vasco Delgado, Álvaro Afonso, Aires Lordelo, Vasco Esteves, Manuel Afonso de Sanha and João do Prado. Many of these men obtained lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), which were later entailed and formed the patrimony of a large part of the many entailed estates established on this island. They were the founders of old families which in the course of time grew rich and acquired noble status.
Fisheries Company

One existed in Funchal in 1792, founded on the initiative of Eduardo Watts, but we suppose that it was short-lived. On 21 November 1822 a fishing society was founded in this city; it disappeared two years later, having caused losses to its members.
Madeiran Sugar Manufacturing Company

Only in the last thirty years has the spirit of association put down a few feeble roots in this ungrateful soil of Madeira, where major industrial, commercial and agricultural ventures have likewise failed or dragged out an existence almost always beset by difficulties of every kind. There are many examples, and among them the foundation of the Madeiran Sugar Manufacturing Company (*Companhia Fabril de Açúcar Madeirense*) stands out conspicuously.

In 1852 *Oidium Tuckeri* had wrought the greatest havoc in the Madeiran vineyards and reduced wine production to very limited proportions. A terrible economic crisis followed, which is regarded as one of the greatest calamities ever to have struck this archipelago. Thoughts soon turned to trying new crops. Sugar cane, which had ceased to be grown in Madeira only temporarily and which in past ages had been one of the island’s best sources of revenue, came to be cultivated more intensively, and within a short time it became a new and powerful source of wealth.

The development of this important and profitable crop called for a matching industry for the manufacture of sugar and the distillation of spirits. Here in Madeira this industry had always been very deficient, and at the time we are referring to it was wholly unfit to meet the needs of the moment. It was then that Dr João da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, perhaps Madeira’s most illustrious son, came forward with the bold initiative of founding a large industrial establishment designed to convert the raw material of sugar cane into sugars and spirits, using the best processes then in use, especially in France.

It was on 27 June 1866 that the foundations were laid for the company that was to carry out this worthy enterprise. A decree of 10 April 1867 approved the statutes of the Madeiran Sugar Manufacturing Company and authorised the establishment of its manufacturing and industrial plant. Various and at times insurmountable difficulties arose, and only on 20 July 1870 did Dr Câmara

Leme leave Madeira to commission the construction of the apparatus and machinery for the new factory. On 23 March 1873 the great industrial establishment was solemnly and definitively inaugurated, with the utmost pomp, in a ceremony presided over by the diocesan prelate and our illustrious fellow countryman Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos.

The new enterprise did not live up to general expectations. Serious errors of administration, and still more a disloyal and relentless war waged against the company’s management, in which local politics played its part, brought down within a few years the grand initiative of Dr João da Câmara Leme, later Count of Canavial. It is well to stress here that, despite everything that was said in the press and outside it, Dr Câmara Leme emerged unscathed from the quagmire of accusations and slanders into which some sought to drag the integrity of his distinguished name.
Several pamphlets were published, and many questions relating to the operation and administration of the Madeiran Sugar Manufacturing Company were debated in the newspapers.
Insurance Companies

Several attempts were made to found an insurance company in this city, but all of them failed. Only in 1891 was the idea realised, with the founding of the Madeiran Alliance (*Aliança Madeirense*) company, which we have already discussed in a separate article in this *Elucidário*, since it was the first that could be successfully organised here in Madeira.

A pamphlet printed in 1877 under the title *Companhia de Seguros Madeirense* gives us news of one of these fruitless attempts. An organising committee was actually formed and carried out various tasks to fulfil the mandate entrusted to it, but the company could not be established, for reasons wholly unknown to us. Later, and before 1891, further attempts were made, which also failed.
In 1906 a new insurance company, named the Funchal Guarantee (*Garantia Funchalense*), was founded in Funchal. It has made appreciable progress and is in a prosperous state.

Communications with mainland Portugal

In the first years after the discovery of the archipelago, and in the early days of colonisation, communications with mainland Portugal were infrequent. A manuscript article states ‘that the King and the Infante (Henry the Navigator) had news of the island from year to year in the summer, because in those early days no one sailed in winter.’ Improvements in the art of navigation and the rapid commercial and agricultural development of Madeira made these communications less rare, not only with the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) but, very particularly, with certain ports of Europe. A considerable number of outsiders, Portuguese and foreign, were drawn here by the fame of the soil’s great fertility; they settled in Funchal and amassed substantial fortunes. This helped to widen and multiply these communications, which were no longer very rare by the middle of the 15th century and could be called frequent by the beginning of the following century. The sugar trade, and later the export of our wines, which soon acquired a worldwide reputation, made Madeira an important commercial emporium and, consequently, made Funchal a port frequently sought by many vessels to carry those products. The same was not true of maritime relations between this archipelago and the mainland. Although less rare than in the early days of colonisation, they never became very frequent. The prelates of this diocese and the governors and captains-general almost always travelled to Madeira in state ships, not so much because of the rank of their office as because of the scarcity of vessels to carry them.

In the mid-19th century only one Portuguese vessel, the *Galgo*, made regular voyages between Madeira and Lisbon, but by that time the steamers of the Royal Mail Steam Company, the Compagnie Franco-Americaine and the Peninsular Steam Navegation Company were already calling both here and at the capital. The *Galgo* was a sailing ship of 250 tons with excellent passenger accommodation. It visited Madeira every month, taking 4 to 5 days on the voyage.

The *Comet*, of 260 tons, and the *Eclipse*, of 246, were two English sailing ships that visited Madeira regularly and had been built expressly to sail between England and this island. Besides them, the sailing ships of the African Steam Ship Company, which made voyages between Plymouth or Liverpool and the West Coast of Africa, also called here. The Royal Mail steamers were already calling at Madeira in 1838 (see Coal).

In 1858 there was an English steamer, the *Barão de Catters*, that made regular voyages solely between Lisbon and Madeira. The following year these voyages began to be made by the Portuguese steamer *Visconde de Atoguia*, which was followed by the *Lusitania*, the *Lisboa* in 1862 and the *Maria Pia* in 1863. By 1862 the steamers of the Africa line were already calling regularly at Funchal.

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’), where there is a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), built in 1673 by André de França e Andrade.
