Near the Ilhéu da Lapa (‘grotto islet’), off the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário, lies a shoal known by that name.
Conceição de Cima (church)
See church of St Clare (*Santa Clara*).
Conceição e Sousa (José Elias da)

An infantry officer, born in India, who spent some time in Madeira. He died in Portugal in 1918. Works: *Descripção geral do Archipelago da Madeira e noticia sobre as instituições de beneficencia do Funchal... para commemorar a visita de Suas Magestades os Reis de Portugal a esta ilha*, Funchal, 1901, 56 pp. Only the first part of this work appeared.
Conceição (square)

It is commonly called Largo das Babosas (‘aloe square’). Its new name comes from the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) built there in 1906, intended specifically to commemorate the fiftieth anniversary of the definition of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception, and which came to be known as the Capela-Monumento. The building of this chapel is due chiefly to Commander Luís Betencourt Miranda, secretary of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal. From this square there is a striking view over the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’) and Curral dos Romeiros (‘pilgrims’ fold’).
Concelho (peak)
It lies in the northern part of the island of Porto Santo, towards the east, and its highest point does not reach 300 metres.
Municipalities

The three captaincies into which the Madeira archipelago was divided had as their highest authority in the administration of public affairs the captains-donatary, who wielded almost absolute power and judged all criminal cases, ‘saluo em semtemcia de morte ou talhamento de membro’ (save in sentences of death or loss of limb). The curtailment of their jurisdiction and of the wide privileges they enjoyed (see Donataries) began with the creation of the municipalities. The first to be created were those of the seats of the three captaincies, Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo, around 1451. Within the captaincy and municipality of Funchal, the town (*vila*) and municipality of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) was created in 1501, and at almost the same time the municipality and town of Calheta (‘small cove’). Within the captaincy and municipality of Machico, the town and municipality of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) was created in 1515. At the beginning of the 16th century, therefore, this archipelago had the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Funchal, Machico, Porto Santo, Ponta do Sol, Calheta and Santa Cruz, which were at the same time towns, except for the first, which had been raised to the status of city in 1508. More than a century later, in 1743, a new municipality was created: São Vicente (‘St Vincent’). In 1832 the municipalities of Santana, Câmara de Lobos and Porto Moniz were created, but they were only definitively established after constitutional government was introduced. Finally, in 1914, the municipality of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) was created. There are thus eleven municipalities in this district:
Funchal, Machico, Porto Santo, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Santa Cruz, São Vicente, Câmara de Lobos, Santana, Porto Moniz and Ribeira Brava.

The old terms town, municipality and *concelho* were synonyms in our former legislation, at least as applied to Madeira. This is not so in the modern law of the constitutional period, in which town and *concelho* or municipality are very different things. Thus Câmara de Lobos, Santana and Porto Moniz are merely municipalities, not towns, since no law or special decree has raised them to that status; meanwhile, on the mainland there are several towns that are not heads or seats of a municipality.
See Administrative organisation.
Concharéu (Patella vulgata, var. Candei)

This is the limpet that is abundant today in the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) and is almost extinct on Madeira. It is so called by fishermen and by the shearwater hunter, who uses its shell, with its large size and sharp edges, to scrape pig skins. It serves the same purpose as the so-called *pedra de porco* ('pig stone': rough vesicular basalt used to scrape pig hides), a highly vesicular basalt pebble whose roughness also makes it suitable for scraping those animals. This limpet is shaped like a traveller's helmet, and its interior is often lined with a lovely egg-yolk yellow.
Shells

In Madeira, as indeed elsewhere, this word has a restricted meaning: it denotes only the calcareous shells of two-valved marine molluscs, known to specialists as lamellibranchs or pelecypods. Those with a single valve, or gastropods, are generally called *búzios* if they are marine and not very small; if they are terrestrial or freshwater, they are mostly called *caracóis*. (See Búzio and Caracóis.)

Of the sea molluscs, some live in the tidal zone; others, the great majority, live in more or less deep water, on sand or mud, or on beds where corallines abound – those strange forms of calcareous algae that look more like stones than plants.

Bivalves are rare in the first of these zones. Nevertheless, *Cardita caliculata*, *Lasaea rubra* and a few other small species are found there, living in recesses of the rock or covered by algae. In this same region live, among the univalves, two or three species of *Littorina* and four species of *Patella*, the latter all edible (see Limpets); *Haliotis tuberculata*, beautifully lined with mother-of-pearl; several species of *Trochus*, one of which, the *caramujo* (*Trochus colubrinus*), is edible and sought as bait for fish; *Mitra cornicula*, *M. zebrina*, *Columbella cribaria* and *C. rustica*. In the rock pools, the small *Fossarus ambiguus* and the tiny *Rissoa picta* are sometimes abundant at certain spots, such as Baixa Larga (‘broad shoal’) and Pôça do Governador, east of Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’).

Among the gastropods of this level, a humble-looking whelk deserves special mention: *Purpura haemastoma*, or the *búzio de marcar roupa* (linen-marking whelk). Ordinary people eat it as shellfish, and it is remarkable for possessing a gland that secretes a dye capable of giving a beautiful purple colour. Because this gland is foul-smelling, caustic and very bitter, it is called *fel de búzio* (whelk’s gall). This mollusc is known to have been used by the ancient Romans and other peoples to dye that rich and famous fabric, purple, but it ceased long ago to have any industrial use. Even so, in these islands the odd individual still uses its dyeing property to mark white linen, perhaps out of an old traditional custom that is, moreover, dying out day by day. The process simply consists of dipping the tip of a small stick in the viscous substance of the gland, drawing the desired marks or letters on the fabric and then exposing them to the direct rays of the sun. The colour, at first a citrine yellow, turns green through various shades and finally to a reddish or blackish violet, depending on the thickness of the layer applied, leaving the stroke indelibly printed. *Fel de búzio* is also used to treat impetigo.

In the coastal zone immediately beyond the tidal zone one may find the elegant *Pinna rudis*, commonly called *leque* (fan), which is the largest bivalve known in these islands; or the large, thick *Spondylus Powellii*, firmly attached to the rocks by one of its valves. There are also many whelks, among them the genera *Triton*, *Cypraea*, *Pleurotoma*, *Nassa*, *Columbella* and *Murex*, not to mention the minute forms of the genus *Rissoa*, the most widely represented in these seas, of which some 30 species have been recorded.

Moving into deeper water, one can gather on the nullipore beds, which are abundant in the bay of Porto Santo, near Caniçal (‘reed bed’) and Garajau (‘tern’), and at other points on the south and north of Madeira, various graceful species of *Pecten*, such as *P. pusio*, *P. Jacobaeus*, *P. corallinoides* and *P. pes felis*; the lovely shells of the genus *Venus*, among them *V. casina*, *V. verrucosa* and *V. chione*; the velvety *Pectunculus glycimeris*; the snow-white *Lima squamosa*; *Cardium tuberculatum*, *C. norvegicum*, *C. aculeatum* and many others, which are not hard to obtain where the bottom is flat and suitable for working a dredge. Among the numerous univalves, besides those already mentioned, are the genera *Trochus* (*Zizyphinus*), *Turbo*, *Bittium*, *Cerithiopsis*, *Scalaria* with 15 recorded species, *Aclis* with 6, *Odostomia* with 22, *Eulima* with 12, *Ranella*, *Natica*, *Ringicula*, *Bulla*, *Philine*, *Limacina* and many others, some of which are not rare on the muddy bottom of Funchal harbour.

Further out, in the coral zone, an inedible species of oyster is abundant: *Ostra cochlear*, with its variously coloured shell. There, together with *Chama gryphoides*, lives *Avicula hirundo*, with its graceful outline and pearly interior, a close relative of the pearl oyster, which hangs like a strange fruit from the branches of the so-called sea trees (*Gorgonia verrucosa*). At depths of about 90 *braças* the curious *Venus effossa* is found, at such various places as the Ponta de São Lourenço and Ponta do Garajau and the waters around the Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’), off Porto Santo. Among the univalves of this deeper zone, mention should be made of the rare *Mitra exilima*, dredged west of Garajau, *Trophon Lowei*, *Murex babelis* and the pelagic species of the genera *Atlanta*, *Limacina*, *Cavolina* and *Clio*, whose skeletons settle in myriads on the ocean floor, besides many others that it would take too long to list.

The sea casts countless shells onto the great beach of Porto Santo, above all during the high spring tides of the equinoxes. Women and children gather them in small quantities, which are pooled and sold by the *alqueire* (dry measure for grain; as a land measure c. 900 m²) to the trinket dealers of Funchal. These dealers resell them by weight for decorating brooches, small baskets, flower vases, garden grottoes, etc.

Throughout the year the pelecypods are found in great quantity on that beach: *Tellina*, *incarnata*, *Cardium tuberculatum*, *Diplodonta trigonula*, *Donax venustus*, *Anphidesma*, *castanea*; and, less numerous, *Arca tetagrona*, *Pecten pusio*, *Thracia papyracea*, *Diplodonta rotundata*, *Lucina divaricata* and *L. reticulata*. The mussel (*Mytilus edulis*), an exotic species, also reaches that island, though rarely, carried from afar by the ocean current on pieces of wood or cork. The gastropods rolled on the sand are no more numerous; among the more or less interesting ones recorded are *Emarginula fissura*, *Trochus Bertheloti*, *Rissoa cancellata*, *Bittium depauperatum* and *B. incile*; the pelagic species *Janthina commnunis* and *J. pallida*, often attached to the hydromedusa *Velella limbosa*, particularly when a strong wind blows from the open sea; various species of *Solarium*;

*Triton reticulatus*, *Ranella marginata*, *R. scrobiculator*, *R. Thomae*; and finally the beautiful and rare *Cassis crumena* and the common *C. sulcosa*. The latter is called the *búzio de chave* (key shell) on Porto Santo, because the islanders tie it to the keys they carry in their pockets, evidently to keep them from going astray.

Besides the two classes mentioned, the amphineurans and cephalopods have representatives in these seas. Among the latter appears *Spirula Peronii*, whose shell the sea at certain times deposits by the thousand on the beach of Porto Santo. Yet not once has the animal itself been found: it is so rare that the museums of the whole world hold only a very small number of specimens, although the species is spread through all the oceans. Rarely, on that same island, the beautiful shell of the female *Argonauta argo* is also found. (See Cephalopods.)
In Madeira no native bivalve mollusc is used as food, although many of them are tasty. On the other hand, certain univalves and cephalopods are eaten.

For the study of Porto Santo folklore, the names used on that island, above all by children, for the commonest shells or those they like best may perhaps be of some interest. They are indeed attractive and cheap toys, costing only the effort – itself an amusement – of searching for them along the wide sands of the beach.

The names are as follows: *Pinna rudis* = *Leque* (fan). *Pecten flexuosus*, *P. corrallinoides*, *P. Jacobaeus*, *P. pes-felis* and *P. solidulus* = *Leque*. *Pecten pusio* = *Cabra*, *Cabrinha* (goat, little goat), *Leque*. *Lima squamosa* = *Joeira* (winnowing sieve). *Cardium tuberculatum* and *C. papillosum* = *Concha* (shell). *Venus verrucosa* = *Raposa* (fox). *Venus chione* = *Lapa* (limpet). *Haliotis tuberculata* = *Peneira* (sieve). *Trochus (Zizyphinus) zizyphinus* and *T. (Z.) conulus* = *Vilão*, *Vilãozinho* (peasant, little peasant). *Triton olearium*, *T. corrugatus*, *T. chlorostoma* and *T. cutaceus* = *Buzio*, *Burro* or *Burrinho* (whelk, donkey or little donkey).

*Triton nodiferus* and *T. tritonis* = *Buzio grande*, *Buzio de tocar* (big whelk, whelk for blowing). *Cassis sulcosa* = *Boi* or *Boizinho de chave* (ox or little key ox). *Natica porcelana* = *Ovelhinha* (little sheep). *Natica variabilis* and *N. Dillwynii* = *Caracol* (snail). *Cyparea spurca*, *C. lurida* and *C. pyrum* = *Cachorro* or *Cachorrinho* (puppy or little puppy). *Mitra cornicula* = *Egua*, *Eguinha* (mare, little mare). *Nassa limata* = *Porquinho* (piglet). *Columbella rustica* = *Boizinho* (little ox). *Murex erinaceus* = *Buzio*, *Burro* or *Burrinho*. *Purpura haemastona* = *Burra* (she-donkey). *Bulla punctata* = *Boizinho de freira* (nun’s little ox). *Spirula Peronii* = *Rosquilhinha* (little ring-shaped biscuit).

These picturesque, childlike names are based on a likeness of shape or colour to domestic animals or everyday objects. *Zizyphinus*, for example, with its tall conical shape, calls to mind the old *carapuça* (traditional Madeiran cap shaped like an inverted funnel) of the Madeiran peasant or countryman; the various shades of *Columbella rustica*, in which orange predominates, recall the oxen of that island; the spotless white *Natica porcellana* and the perforated *Haliotis tuberculata* have been likened to a sheep and a sieve respectively; and so on. It should also be noted that the words *concha* and *buzio* here have a meaning restricted to particular species.

All this, however, like many other expressions of regional character, is fading day by day, owing to the inevitable change that is bringing the island into closer contact with outside civilisation, and which will end by destroying the original things its isolation had produced.
Confectionery

The sugar industry in Madeira, which reached a high level of development and a remarkable degree of perfection in the 15th and 16th centuries, gave rise to the confectionery industry. This seems to have been very important here, both for the quantity and above all for the quality of its products. Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo states that from the 16th century onwards it was raised to a true art and a valuable export industry, as shown by many documents transcribed in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and by various passages mentioned there. In support of this statement, we cite the gift of the Sacred College, made entirely of *alfenim* (white sugar paste for modelling figures), which the 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal presented to Pope Leo X, as described on p. 208 of this *Elucidário*. The learned annotator of Frutuoso’s work returns to the subject in the article ‘Madeira’ of the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, and we transcribe his words:

‘... the confectionery industry, created there, chiefly in the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), greatly developed in the course of the 16th century and finally made a true art, whose products came to be a valuable branch of exports, as some documents and ‘Longing for the Homeland’ attest’.
Conferences of St Vincent de Paul

The Conferences of St Vincent de Paul are societies or associations of a small number of individuals, devoted exclusively to helping the shamefaced poor in their own homes. This city has three conferences: that of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro, established on 10 January 1875; that of Santa Maria Maior, set up on 19 July 1908; and that of Santa Luzia, on 8 December 1911. In 1913 Conferences were founded in the suburban parishes of São Martinho, Santo António, São Roque, Nossa Senhora do Monte and São Gonçalo, and in the rural parishes of Machico and Santa Cruz. In 1914 Conferences were established in the parishes of Câmara de Lobos, Arco da Calheta, Porto do Moniz and Serra de Água; in 1915 in the parishes of Porto da Cruz, Santana, Ponta do Sol, Gaula, Camacha and Caniço; and in 1916 in those of Campanário and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.

Printed reports of the activity of these Conferences exist for various years, the one for 1916 being the last we have been able to examine. The total receipts and expenses of these Conferences for that year, 1916, were 5,974.50 and 4,760.37 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) respectively.

To bring the information set out above up to date, we would add that this city has 6 conferences: that of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro, established on 17 January 1875; that of Santa Maria Maior, set up on 19 July 1908; that of Santa Luzia, founded on 8 December 1911; that of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*)), established on 8 December 1927; and those of São Luís de Gonzaga and São João Evangelista, organised respectively by the Catholic Youth and by the students of the Lyceum (*Liceu*).

Besides those listed above, there are conferences in the parishes of Santo António (4 conferences: two parish conferences and two in the localities of Trapiche and Alecrins), São Martinho, São Roque, São Gonçalo, Monte, Santa Cruz, Gaula, Camacha, Caniço, Machico, Porto da Cruz, Câmara de Lobos, Calheta, Porto Moniz, Ribeira Brava, Campanário, Serra de Água, Prazeres, Paul do Mar, Santana, Faial, São Roque do Faial, São Jorge, São Vicente, Ponta do Sol and Porto Santo.

The Central Council of the Society of St Vincent de Paul has its seat in Funchal and consists of seven members; every year it publishes a report on the activity of all the conferences in Madeira. From the report for 1939 we have taken the following statistics: number of conferences in the Madeira archipelago, 36. There are 842 active members, 19 aspirants and 730 subscribers. Every year 671 poor families are visited. During 1939 the conferences distributed 80,507.50 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis).

On 8 December 1939 the Central Council of Women’s Conferences was likewise set up. There are 10 women’s conferences, at the Colégio de São Luís (Funchal), Santa Luzia, Santa Maria Maior, Santo António, Camacha, São Martinho, Santana, Machico, Arco da Calheta and Faial respectively.

They have 150 active members, 20 aspirants and 267 subscribers, and 164 poor families were visited during 1939, the last year covered by the report we consulted. During that year these conferences distributed the sum of 10,483.65 escudos.
Conger eel (Conger vulgaris)

A fish of the eel family that frequents the sea around these islands. It is generally fished at night with hook gear, either fixed or drifting, such as the longline and others. It is also known as *safio*, and among the common people generally by the corrupted forms *congro* and *seifio*.
Congro de Natura (Conger macrops)

A fish of the eel family, very rare in Madeiran waters, where it has been caught on the line in deep water. Among other characteristics, it is distinguished from the common conger by the great size of its eyes and by its less firm, almost watery flesh. In Machico it is called *congra*, or rather *cronga*, by corruption.
Connaught (Duke of)
Brother of Edward VII, King of England. He visited Madeira, accompanied by his wife and daughter, in December 1905.
Conselheiro (street)

The full name of this street is Rua do Conselheiro José Silvestre Ribeiro. It was opened at the time when this benevolent governor was at the head of the administration of this district, and it was given his name as a tribute to the outstanding services he rendered to this archipelago. It is the street that runs along the west side of the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’). A few years ago it was extended as far as Rua das Fontes (‘springs’), passing beside the ‘Teatro Manuel de Arriaga’ (‘Manuel de Arriaga Theatre’).
District Council

This was a tribunal composed of the civil governor, as president, and four members appointed by the Government from a list of three names for each seat proposed by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*). It had advisory and contentious powers, and was abolished by the Administrative Code of 17 July 1886.

The members of the District Council received an annual allowance of 240,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), paid from the District Treasury.
Prefecture Council

It was created by the decree of 6 May 1832 and operated alongside the prefect (*prefeito*) of the Province. The administrative code of 1836, which created the district council, did away with the old prefecture (*prefeitura*) council.
District Council of Agriculture

It was created by decree of 24 December 1901, held its first session (the inaugural one) on 16 July 1904 and its last on 1 August 1910. This Council, which dealt especially with the promotion of agriculture in the Madeira region, was abolished by article 289 of the Law of 9 July 1913.
Municipal Board

There was one attached to each municipal council, made up of as many members as there were councillors (*vereadores*). The members of the municipal council were the electors who paid the largest share of the tithe tax (*décima*) in the municipality (*concelho*).
The municipal councils were abolished by the administrative code of 1878.
Judge conservator of the English

Under an old treaty, British subjects resident in Madeira enjoyed the right to choose a judge to try them whenever they had to answer for any disputes or quarrels arising between them and the Portuguese. This judge, whom they called the judge conservator (*conservador*, special judge for British subjects) of the English, had to hold a law degree, and the choice was subject to confirmation by the Portuguese government. According to an old English work, the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) was always the judge chosen, and his impartiality was customarily rewarded with an allowance of 400 dollars a year. This right of the English ended with the treaty of 20 July 1842, although it was established that, should any of them have to be tried in the Portuguese courts, the jury would be made up of British and Portuguese subjects. This provision has long since ceased to apply.
Land Registry Offices

There are four land registry offices (*conservatórias do registo predial*) in the Madeira archipelago: that of Funchal, established on 30 September 1880; that of Ponta do Sol, created in the same year; that of Santa Cruz, established on 7 September 1910; and that of São Vicente, established on 24 November 1909.

The Funchal registry office covered the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Funchal, Câmara de Lobos, Porto Santo, Santa Cruz, Machico and Santana, but with the establishment of the São Vicente and Santa Cruz registry offices it was reduced to the first three. The Ponta do Sol office covered the municipalities of Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Porto Moniz and São Vicente; with the establishment of the São Vicente office it was left with the first two. The Santa Cruz office covers the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico, and, finally, the São Vicente office covers the municipalities of São Vicente, Porto Moniz and Santana.
The municipality of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), created on 16 August 1914, belongs to the Ponta do Sol registry office.

Before 1880 there were two registry offices in Madeira, the eastern and the western. The former covered the area of the judicial district (*comarca*) of the same name and took in the whole municipality of Funchal; the latter was made up of the remaining municipalities of the western judicial district.

The Eastern and Western Registry Offices were established under the Land Registry Regulations of 28 April 1870, approved by decree of the same date. They were preceded by the registry offices that had been set up – one in each municipality – on 1 April 1867, in accordance with the decree of 13 February of that year. These were in the charge of the municipal administrators, and were deemed abolished by the decree of 17 December 1869, which created dedicated registry offices in every judicial district.

The registry offices were created by the law (*carta de lei*) of 1 July 1863, but they were not actually set up until 1 April 1867. Before 1863 the municipal administrations kept the mortgage registers and other registers established by the decrees of 26 October 1836 and 3 January 1837, together with other related measures.
Constantino (Father Manuel)

He was born in Madeira and died in the city of Rome on 28 November 1614. He graduated in philosophy at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and received the degree of doctor of theology at the University of Salamanca. In Rome he was a professor at the celebrated University of the Sapienza, and in that city his extraordinary talent and vast learning won him the applause and admiration of the leading figures of the Curia.

He wrote and published various works, which are mentioned in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’) and of which we shall cite the following: *Oratio in funere Philippi II*, Romae 1599; *De profectione Pontificis in Ferraricus. Civitatem...*, Romae, 1598; *Historia de origine et principio atque vita omnium regum Lusitaniae...*, Romae, 1601; *In funere Seraphinae a Portugalia Joannis Brigantiae Ducis filiae...*, Romae, 1604; *Gratulatio de S. Pontif. Paulo V...*, Romae, 1607; *Votum primum ad S. S. Virginem pro salute Scipionis Cardinalis...*, Romae, 1610.

Among the works he published, one is of interest to this archipelago: it is entitled *Insulae Materiae...* and was published in Rome in 1599. It is a history, written in Latin, of the discovery of this archipelago, and Dr Álvaro de Azevedo refers to it in his notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).

The *Insulae Materiae*, which appeared in Rome in 1599, became a great bibliographical rarity. A copy was acquired by the public-spirited industrialist Henrique Hinton, who arranged for its translation into Portuguese and had it published in an elegant edition in 1930. It was translated by Father João Baptista de Afonseca, with a preface and extensive notes by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva, co-author of this *Elucidário*.
Constitution of 1821 (The)

It is common knowledge that on 24 August 1820 a revolution broke out in the city of Porto with the aim of establishing a system of representative government in our country, and that this revolution found its echo in Lisbon on 15 September following, later spreading to other parts of mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal).
It was only around the middle of September that Madeira learned of the political events that had taken place in

Portugal, through the call at our landing place of an English ship bound from London for Rio de Janeiro. On the 25th of the same month the Portuguese brig *Providencia* brought letters and newspapers giving a detailed account of the events. In an official communication addressed to the Count of Arcos, the governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago, Sebastião Xavier Botelho, stated that these events had ‘caused no sensation or popular commotion, and that he had taken the necessary measures to prevent any disturbance of public order’.

Towards the end of September Xavier Botelho received an official communication from the Provisional Government about the new political order that had come about in the country. Although he showed no hostility towards it, he maintained a prudent reserve, perhaps fearing a counter-revolutionary movement on the mainland of the Kingdom. When the Count, later Duke, of Palmela called at Madeira around the middle of November, on his way from London to Lisbon, the governor of this archipelago asked him to inform the government in the metropole about affairs on this island, stressing that order was complete and that no disturbance was feared of the peace we then enjoyed here.

Meanwhile, the governor’s attitude was increasingly displeasing the supporters of the Porto revolution, who secretly had lampoons posted on the walls of the city’s most central streets, inciting the people to revolt and to the violence that would follow. All Xavier Botelho’s hesitation ended on 23 January 1821 with the arrival of a mail sent directly from the court in Rio de Janeiro, from which he learned that John VI had recognised the new state of affairs and, in particular, had accepted the representative system established by the revolution. Rejoicing was given free rein, and preparations began at once for the solemn proclamation, which was to take place on the 28th of that month.

On that day an enormous crowd gathered in the Largo da Fortaleza (‘fortress square’), joined by the troops of the city garrison, calling on the governor to give his solemn adhesion to the principles proclaimed by the Porto revolution. Meanwhile, the captain-general’s residence was invaded by many members of the nobility and the most prominent people of Funchal, supporting the people’s demand. Xavier Botelho gave way, though not without recording his token protest, and appeared on the Bastion overlooking the square, cheering the King, the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), the Constitution and the Supreme Government of the Kingdom. Lively enthusiasm then spread through the crowd, which burst into frenzied cheering.

The governor and captain-general, followed by a great many people, the authorities, civil and military officials and a large number of persons of distinction, then went to the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), where a solemn Te Deum was sung in the presence of the diocesan prelate and many members of the clergy. Everyone then made their way to the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), which at that time stood in the building that until recently served as the gaol. There the new system of government was solemnly proclaimed, and a record (*auto*) was drawn up and signed by a considerable number of those present.

The celebrations of that happy event continued over the following days with remarkable enthusiasm, without the slightest disturbance of public order. To the Constituent Cortes (constituent parliament), which sat from 1821 to 1822, Madeira elected as deputies Francisco João Moniz, Dr Maurício José de Castelo Branco and Dr António João Rodrigues Garcez; the last died and was replaced by Dr João José de Freitas Aragão. Once the Constitution had been drawn up and promulgated, general elections were held under it in 1822, and this archipelago elected as deputies Dr João Francisco de Oliveira, Father João Manuel de Freitas Branco and Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar.

A year has passed since the events briefly narrated above, and all Funchal is celebrating. It is 28 January 1822, and the anniversary of the proclamation of the Constitution on this island is being solemnly marked. The aim is not only to commemorate the event but also to perpetuate it through time. Once the idea of erecting a monument had been put forward, the Terreiro da Sé (Cathedral Square) was chosen as the most suitable site for it, and 28 January as the day for laying the foundation stone, since it was the first anniversary of Madeira’s solemn adhesion to the principles proclaimed by the Porto revolution.

The ceremony was conducted with the utmost solemnity and splendour, and countless people of every social class took part in it, including the official and military establishment, which was represented in strength. The ceremony was presided over by the governor and captain-general Dom Rodrigo António de Melo, who, in a report to the government in Lisbon, writes as follows:

‘The city council, wishing to immortalise that same day by erecting a monument and pedestal that would carry the memory of so auspicious an epoch to the remotest ages, had officially invited me to lay, at that same ceremony, the first foundation stone of that memorial, to which I most cordially agreed. Judging that I ought to lend my military authority to the tranquillity and brilliance of the occasion, I therefore gave orders for the aforementioned disposition of troops and invited all the officers of the Province to accompany me, including the second-line troops (*segunda linha*, reserve militia) and the disbanded corps of territorial militia (*ordenanças*)...’

A splendid procession formed and, leaving the town hall, made its way to the Largo da Sé (‘cathedral square’), where the trench to receive the cornerstone and the first foundations of the intended monument had already been prepared. This passage from the record (*auto*) drawn up on the occasion and placed in the foundations is of considerable interest: ‘the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate), Dr ..., carried a basket of wedges and chips of stone, the *juiz de fora* Dr the level, the senior councillor (*vereador*) the trowel and float, the second councillor the broom and bucket, the third councillor the lime trough, the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) the medals, and I, clerk (*escrivão*) of the council, the mallet, while the people’s judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds) bore a silver casket containing the record, and the representatives (*procuradores*) of the master craftsmen a handbarrow with the stone’. When the laying of the foundation stone was over, a solemn Te Deum was celebrated in the Cathedral (the Sé), on which occasion the distinguished preacher Father João Manuel de Freitas Branco delivered an eloquent sermon. It was published as a pamphlet, today extremely rare, with the title *Oração de acção de graças que na solemnidade do anniversario do faustissimo dia 28 de janeiro de 1821 pregou na igreja da Sé do Funchal*. . .

Next the civil and military authorities, public officials and a large number of Funchal’s most distinguished people went to the governor’s palace, where Dr João Pedro de Freitas Drumond gave an enthusiastic address that was loudly applauded.
All the forts fired salutes, there were lavish and brilliant illuminations, and other celebrations were held, in which the inhabitants of the city joyfully took part.
The monument, whose cornerstone was laid in front of the door of the Cathedral, a few metres from the steps leading up to the churchyard, never rose above its foundations.

The Terreiro da Sé, or Passeio, which formed part of the old Campo do Duque (‘duke’s field’), was renamed Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’) in 1821, a name it kept until a few years ago. The following pamphlets were published on the Constitution in Madeira and on some of the questions its proclamation raised here: • *Historia verdadeira dos acontecimentos da ilha da Madeira depois do memoravel dia 28 de janeiro, escrita por ordem chronologica por Sebastião Xavier Botelho e comprovada com testemunhas da melhor fé, por seus empregos, gerarchia e independencia, para destruir um libello famoso impresso em Londres por um Cidadão Funchalense*, Lisbon, 1821, 61 pp.;

• *Noticias officiais recebidas da ilha da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1821, 20 pp.; • *Relação circunstanciada do modo com que se desenvolveu, se promoveu e se proclamou a Constituição da ilha da Madeira no memoravel dia 28 de janeiro de 1821*, Lisbon, 1821, 12 pp.; • *Carta escrita a um sujeito da provincia da ilha da Madeira, ou o lundum dos bordões que tocou Sebastião Xavier Botelho*, by Luís José Baiardo, in retaliation for the attacks that the said Botelho wrote against him in his *historia verdadeira da ilha da Madeira*... Lisbon, 1821; • *Parabens poetico-politicos á grandiosa regeneração portuguesa na congratulante adherencia da ilha da Madeira em 28 de Janeiro de 1821 no theatro grande do Funchal*, by Luís António Jardim, graduate of the faculty of law, Funchal, 1822, 29 pp.; • *Sentença proferida contra os reos comprehendidos na devassa da alçada que Sua Magestade foi servido mandar á ilha da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1823, 47 pp.
On 17 June 1823 the restoration of absolute government was proclaimed in Madeira, amid various demonstrations of rejoicing.
See Proclamation of absolute government.
Constitution of 1838

The revolution that broke out in the country in 1836, with the aim of abolishing the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) promulgated in 1826, brought back the Constitution of 1820, which the queen swore to uphold on 10 September 1836. In Madeira the solemn oath to this Constitution was taken on 25 September of the same year. Once elected, the Constituent Cortes (constituent parliament) drew up a new constitution in 1838, which was solemnly sworn on this island on 6 May of that year. This Constitution remained in force only until 1842, when the Constitutional Charter of 1826 was restored once more.
Constituição (square)

This square bore this name from 28 January 1821, because the constitution – that is, the liberal principles of 1820 – was proclaimed there on that day. Before then it was known as the Passeio Público, a name that was still often given to it in our own day.

The Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’) was renamed Praça da República in 1911, and it disappeared in 1914, when construction began on the Avenida Oeste, today the Avenida do Dr. Manuel de Arriaga, which also takes in the site of the old Jardim Pequeno (‘small garden’).
The Praça da Constituição was a shady enclosure where the regimental band used to play in former times. It had fine specimens of Indian fig trees, magnolias, *sementeiras* and grevilleas.
Constitutions of the bishopric

Diocesan constitutions are the laws and instructions peculiar to each diocese, intended to implement and regulate the general laws of the Church. The bishopric of Funchal also has its Constitutions, very old and entirely obsolete, which today have merely historical value. Copies are rare nowadays, but they are highly prized for the study of the religious customs of the time when these Constitutions were drawn up. The first edition is entitled *Constituiçôes Synodaes do Bispado do Funchal. Feitas e ordenadas por D. Jeronimo Barreto, Bispo do dito Bispado*, Lisboa, por Antonio Ribeiro, 1585, folio, XVI-188 pp. They were drawn up at the diocesan council held in our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) on 13 October 1578, under the presidency of Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto, and were approved and ordered to be put into effect by a decree (*alvará*) of the same prelate, dated 4 May 1579.

Bishop Dom Luís Figueiredo de Lemos convened and presided over a diocesan synod, held in the Cathedral on 29 June 1597, at which supplementary constitutions (*Constituições Extravagantes*) were made. These were appended to the existing Constitutions and received episcopal approval by a warrant (*provisão*) of 15 August 1597. Dom Luís de Figueiredo had the new Constitutions printed and the old ones reprinted under the title *Constituições synodaes do Bispado do Funchal, com as extravagantes novamente impressas, por mandado de D. Luiz de Figueiredo de Lemos, Bispo do dito Bispado*, Lisboa, por Pedro Craesbeeck, 1601, folio, XX-188 pp. At the end come the supplementary constitutions, with a new title page and new pagination, under the title *Constituições Extravagantes do Bispado do Funchal, feitas e ordenadas por D. Luiz Figueiredo de Lemos*, Lisboa, impresso por Pedro Craeesbeck, Ano X, folio, 54 pp.
Consulates

The first consulate in Madeira was the Belgian one, or that of the Flemings, established in 1608. It was followed by the French, English and Spanish consulates, established in 1626, 1658 and 1667 respectively. The consulate of the United States of North America was established in 1791, that of Sweden in 1796, that of Denmark in 1804, that of Russia in 1812 and that of Sardinia in 1826 or 1827. All the other consulates that now exist in Madeira were, we believe, established after 1834, although we cannot give the dates on which they were set up. As early as 1783 the Republic of Venice already had a consulate in Funchal.

In the mid-19th century the following had consular representation in Madeira: the United States of America, Austria, Belgium, Brazil, the Hanseatic Cities, Denmark, England, France, Greece, the Papal States, Holland, Naples, Turkey, Prussia, Russia, Sardinia, Spain, Sweden and Tuscany. The consulates of Italy and Germany were created later to replace those of the states incorporated into these two countries. In 1885 there was a consulate of the Hawaiian Islands, now abolished.

The consulates of the republics of Central and South America, with the exception of that of Brazil, were all created after 1882; by 1888 Uruguay and the Argentine Republic already had consular representation in Funchal.
In 1827 a vice-consulate of Brazil was created in Madeira, and the following year a vice-consulate of the Two Sicilies.
See Casa dos Cônsules (‘consuls’ house’).
Revenue accountant (contador de fazenda)
This office replaced that of district receiver (*recebedor de distrito*) under the Decree of 12 September 1846, which was put into effect in Madeira on 28 November of the same year.

Taxes

Madeirans have been liable to taxes since early times, as the charter (foral) of the city of Funchal and of the towns of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Calheta (‘small cove’) shows, together with various documents recorded in the municipal archives. When King Duarte granted his brother, Prince Henry the Navigator, the lordship of the islands of the archipelago, he gave him ‘all the rights and revenues thereof’. From the grants of the three captaincies of Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo, we know that the prince authorised their respective donataries to receive ‘one in ten of everything he should have in revenue, according to the charter, in the said captaincies. The charter of 1515, transcribed on p. 494 ff. of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), contains a reference to Prince Henry’s charter, which shows that the tax burdens he imposed on the people of this archipelago were heavy indeed.

In the articles Sugar and Customs Houses in this *Elucidário* we have already referred to some of the taxes that Madeirans paid in former times. We shall now give a brief account of other tax burdens that also weighed on the population of the archipelago. Some of them, such as the tithes, the property *décima*, the fifth, the literary subsidy and the *finto* (war tax apportioned among residents), survived into our own day, until they were abolished by the law of 11 September 1861. It was this law that brought the Madeira archipelago into the tax system adopted in Portugal, since it provided that from 1 January 1863 the legislation governing property, industrial and personal taxes in mainland Portugal should apply to the archipelago.

The tithes, which we suppose to be the oldest tax known to Madeirans, date from the first years of settlement. Prince Henry’s charter laid down that they were to be deducted from wages, services, day-labourers’ pay, the earnings of merchants and craftsmen, sales of new crops, leases and rents, and from all things grown and bred on the island.

The charter of 6 August 1515 abolished some of these tithes, for example those taken from wages of any kind and from the earnings of merchants and craftsmen, etc. It kept the tax, however, on cereals, livestock, wool, wine, fruit, vegetables, cheese, eggs, butter, milk, honey and countless other things produced on the island.

The same charter further provided that a tithe be paid at the customs house on sugar and on all other goods exported outside the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). Of the goods exported to the Kingdom, only those destined for foreigners or carried in foreign ships were to pay the tax.

Many goods imported from outside the Kingdom paid a tithe, but those coming from the Kingdom paid it only when brought by foreigners or carried in foreign ships. Cereals, olive oil, chestnuts, peas, cheese and all other goods imported to feed the public never paid a tithe, whereas silver, arms, horses, books and clothing were exempt only when they were not for sale. Firewood could be imported freely.

Most of the tithes belonged to the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), but after the mastership of the Order was incorporated into the Crown they were collected by the Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*). The costs of worship were paid from them, and in 1626 they were not enough to cover the stipends of the dignitaries, canons and other staff of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), as the royal decree (*alvará*) of 10 June of that year shows.

The royal decree of 1 August 1752 secularised the portion of the tithes exceeding what was needed to maintain the clergy. By royal grant, the Jesuit and Franciscan religious orders and the secular clergy were exempt from paying this tax, at least in the early period.
For a long time the tithes were collected by leasing them out, and there was even a period when they were leased as a single block.

The property *décima* (*décima predial*), as its name suggests, was levied on buildings and land; it has now been replaced by the property tax. Before the property *décima*, Madeirans paid the urban *décima* (*décima urbana*), created by the law of 10 June 1808.

The fifth, abolished together with the tithes and the property *décima* by the law of 11 September 1861, consisted of payment of one fifth of all the property known as Crown property. The literary subsidy (*subsídio literário*), created by the law of 10 November 1772, was a tax levied on spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), wine, vinegar, etc., and was intended solely for the upkeep of schools and the payment of teachers.

The fifth was paid by the chantries (capela) and by the donataries’ *redízima* (a tenth of the Crown’s revenues due to the donatary). In 1836 the administrator-general (*administrador geral*) ruled that the Marquis of Castelo Melhor should be assessed for the said *redízima* from 1831 until the abolition of the chief castellanship (*alcaidaria-mor*) of Funchal. In former times the fifth was assessed on donataries who held Crown property and chantries before the *corregedores* (royal magistrates), but the law of 24 April 1835 required the Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*) to appoint, for each parish (*freguesia*), a board of six citizens charged with apportioning this levy. On folio 31 verso of volume XVIII of the General Register of the Municipal Council of Funchal there is a list of the chantry properties in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal that were subject to the fifth.

The *finto* (war tax apportioned among residents), or *décima*, decreed for three years by the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) of 1641, was a war tax. At first levied at a variable rate, it was fixed by the regulations (*regimento*) of 10 April 1646 and the royal decree of 26 September 1762 at 10 per cent of all income from property, capital, industries and trades. From the regulations of 9 May 1654 onwards nobody was exempt from paying this tax. It amounted to 8,600,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in the first assessment and was later reduced to 4½%, or 3,600,000 *réis*.

The *finto* belonged to the State, but before 1834 its proceeds were collected by the Municipal Council and then handed over to the Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*). The Council appointed the individuals who apportioned the tax among the taxpayers.

The *finto* of 3,600,000 *réis*, or 9,000 *cruzados* a year, was not always paid punctually. By a royal decree of 1 April 1749 John V remitted the amount of this tax for the years 1739 to 1749, because of the damage the earthquake of 1748 had caused the island. In 1799 the people owed the Treasury Board 162,000 *cruzados*, arising from 18 years of the same tax, which the government ordered to be collected.
Besides the tributes we have just discussed, Madeirans paid others, some for the costs of war and fortifications, others for different purposes.

The first war contribution imposed on Madeira appeared in 1478. It was followed by that of 1493, which was never actually paid, and by those for doublets and cuirass corps, the former established in 1497 and the latter in the following year. There were later other war contributions, or *fintos*, the heaviest of which was that of 10,000 *cruzados* (old Portuguese coin worth 400 réis) a year, from 1637, for the fleet to recover Pernambuco. It was then, in the opinion of Dr Azevedo, that the Madeiran clergy were for the first time obliged to share the tax burdens of the population. The nobles, who had rebelled against the contributions of 1478 and 1493, afterwards paid without resistance all the other taxes levied by the central government.

The contribution known as the *donativo* (nominally a ‘gift’ to the Crown; a compulsory war levy) fell on produce and was likewise intended for war expenses. The first enactment referring to it that is recorded in the archive of the Council dates from 1635, and the last from 1691.

The municipal levies (*imposição*) on fresh meat (*carnes verdes*) and on wine sold retail, which date from the period immediately after the settlement of the archipelago, were sometimes applied to the costs of fortification, even though they were exclusively municipal revenues.

Among the taxes not specifically intended for military expenses, we shall also mention the following: the half-annate (*meia anata*, half a year’s income paid on an appointment or honour) (Law of 31 May 1631); the tax on stamped paper (*papel selado*) and tobacco, which seems to date from the first years of the reign of John IV; the funeral *décima* (Law of 27 June 1809); the labour contribution (royal letter (*carta régia*) of 1 October 1801); and the *sisa* (property transfer tax) (Law of 3 June 1809). The funeral *décima*, or inheritance stamp duty, and the *sisa* are today included in the so-called registration contribution, whereas the old half-annate tax, established by the Castilian government, has long ceased to exist, having even been temporarily abolished by the government of John IV.

This tax, which was a kind of royal grant duty, was levied on all honorific favours, both civil and military, salaries, allowances, etc. It spared only the pay of the other ranks and seamen of the army and navy and emoluments not exceeding 50 *cruzados* a year.

From the earliest days of settlement Madeirans paid customs duties. Both before and after 1834, the calculations of the State’s resources on this island include the revenue from the two indirect contributions of the *real de água* on wine and on meat, and from the following direct contributions: royal grant duties, the eighth (*oitavo*, a tax of one eighth of the produce) on sugar and the tax on *estufas* (heated store for ageing Madeira wine). In 1646 a tax of one *cruzado* was established on every *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine exported; this was the starting point of the duties on wine exports collected at the Funchal Customs House.

Madeira yielded 25,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) to the State in 1628, but the work from which we have taken this information does not say where this sum came from. In 1806, according to Tovar de Albuquerque, the tithes yielded 65,000,000 *réis*, the *subsídio literário* 7,000,000 *réis*, the wine levy (imposição do vinho) 15,000,000 *réis*, of which, however, only half belonged to the State, the *fintos* 3,600,000 *réis*, the wine *estufas* 2,000,000 *réis*, fish and meat 3,500,000 *réis*, the customs house 180,000,000 *réis* and other taxes 20,000,000 *réis*. In the financial year 1848–1849, on the other hand, as we read in vol. II of the *Epocha Administrativa*, the tithes produced 18,030,126 *réis*, the *subsídio literário* 6,202,386 *réis*, the *real de água* on wine 5,093,764, the *finto* 1,386,756 *réis*, the tax on fish 907,060 *réis*, the *real de água* on meat 1,805,751 *réis*, the tax of 3 *réis* on each *libra* (Portuguese pound, c. 459 g) of meat 3,477,351 *réis*, the customs house 109,276,641 *réis*, the *sisas* 5,553,802 *réis*, royal grant duties 863,709 *réis* and other taxes and duties 11,490,219 *réis*. We read somewhere that in 1820 Madeira yielded 529,462,215 *réis*, the revenue from the *subsídio literário* being 4,840,680 *réis*.

We lack the data to expand this account of the contributions formerly paid in Madeira any further. From what has been said above, however, it is abundantly clear that, however overburdened with taxes we may be now, our situation is incomparably better than that of the first inhabitants of Madeira. The present industrial, land, sumptuary and registration contributions, and today’s indirect taxes, almost amount to a kindness on the part of governments when compared with the tithes and the thousand other imposts with which Prince Henry the Navigator and the monarchs of old saw fit to burden the people of this island.
See Sugar, Customs Houses, Administrative Autonomy, Captaincies, Cortina da Cidade, Donataries and District General Council.
Convent of the Incarnation

The foundation of the convent of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação was inspired by the purest and most ardent patriotism. Canon Henrique Calaça de Viveiros had vowed to build a convent in honour and praise of the Virgin of the Incarnation, to whom he was deeply devoted, once his country had wholly freed itself from the iron Castilian yoke and regained its former independence. He faithfully kept his vow, having the modest convent built in the year 1650. Canon Calaça was born around 1589 and died on 25 May 1662. His life-size portrait, which until a few years ago still hung in the choir of the convent, bore in one corner of the canvas the following words: ‘Portrait from life of Canon Henrique Calaça de Viveiros, founder of this convent. He died on 25 May 1662, aged 73.’

Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says: ‘…it began as a chantry (capela), which is presumed to have been founded by António Mialheiro, who died in 1565; Dona Isabel Maria Acciaioli had the chancel built; and then, in 1650, Canon Henrique Calaça de Viveiros founded the convent…’. From these words it follows that the foundation of the convent belongs to Canon Calaça, although he made use of the chapel that already stood there. The extensive convent grounds were part of a fine *quinta* (country estate) that the founder owned at that spot.

It seems to have begun as a *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) under the name of Santa Teresa de Jesus, whose inmates followed the Third Order of Carmel and entered it in the year 1652. Only in 1660 was it turned into a convent, under the Franciscan rule of St Clare. Its first abbess was a nun from the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), chosen by the ecclesiastical authority. It was in that same year of 1660, that is, two years before his death, that Canon Calaça de Viveiros gave all his property to the convent he had founded. The convent and church underwent major repairs around the middle of the 18th century, when a new and spacious choir was built to replace the old one, which was cramped. The Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*) contributed one *conto* (one million réis) de réis to these works, as granted by the royal decree (*alvará*) of 10 February 1750. The following year the Royal Treasury also contributed 750,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) towards building the great wall that flanks the road leading to the church of St Lucy (*Santa Luzia*).

The nuns of the Incarnação had to abandon their convent when the British occupied this island for the second time, in the period from December 1807 to October 1814. The British troops were quartered mainly in the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), which was then serving as a seminary, and in the convent of the Incarnação; the nuns left for the Convent of St Clare on 7 January 1808. Various works were carried out there to lodge and quarter the British forces suitably, and they did the building considerable damage; the church was turned into an Anglican place of worship. Henrique Calaça’s patriotic and genuinely Catholic foundation was occupied by foreign troops and given over to a heretical cult! For the purpose of enforcing the laws of disentailment (*desamortização*, the sale of Church property by the State), this convent was valued by order of the government in August 1862, the valuation putting the worth of the building, church, convent grounds, chaplain’s house, etc., at 10,320,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

By a ministerial order (*portaria*) of June 1895, the Incarnação building was provisionally granted for the installation of a workshop of St Joseph, which led a precarious, lingering existence there and lasted only a very short time.

By decree of 11 July 1905, the building, church and convent grounds of the Incarnação were granted to the bishop of this diocese, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, so that a house could be built there to accommodate the Diocesan Seminary. The seminary began operating in October 1909 in the vast and handsome building that the illustrious prelate had built at his own expense on the site of the old convent (see Seminary).

The law of 20 April 1911 abolished the seminary of Funchal, and a few years later a School of Useful and Fine Arts (*Escola de Utilidades e Belas Artes*) was set up in this building; it existed for only a few years (see School of Useful and Fine Arts).

In September 1919 the various departments of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) were installed in the building that had housed the Seminary and the School of Fine Arts; the Council had acquired it for this purpose by purchase from the State.

The decree of 25 April 1927 ordered the building of the Incarnação Seminary to be handed over to the Diocesan Commission for Worship, but the General Council stubbornly opposed the handover, which did not take place until October 1933, after a hard-fought struggle of six years. In that year the diocesan seminary, with its many services of classes and boarding for pupils, once again began operating in the building that the eminent prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto had built.

On the foundation of this convent, the reader should consult the booklet published by the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* under the title *A Restauração de Portugal e o Convento da Incarnação*, Lisbon, MCMXL, 50 pp. The last nun of the convent of the Incarnação, Madre Vicência Violante do Céu, died on 20 April 1890.
Convent of Our Lady of Ransom

This convent began as a house for women living in retreat, with no religious character and no observance of canonical rules for its inmates. It was founded in 1654 by Gaspar Berenguer de Andrade and his wife, Dona Isabel de França Andrade. In 1658 the founders turned this house into a religious *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women), whose residents submitted to a rule or statute modelled on those of certain monastic houses. Finally, by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 1663, confirmed in 1665 by Pope Alexander VII, this *recolhimento* was raised to a monastery of the First Order of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), of severe and strict observance, and so it remained through the ages until the moment of its suppression. We have read somewhere that the founder was granted the right of patronage over this convent, undertaking to endow it with one hundred and sixty thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) every year, an obligation attached to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Lombo do Doutor (‘the doctor’s ridge’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta. For the period in which it was made, this endowment seems to us greatly exaggerated; today it would correspond to a very considerable sum.

If the Convent of St Clare was no model of rigid observance of its rules, it can nevertheless be said that the convent of Mercês gave the most vivid and eloquent example of the practice of all the Christian virtues, carried to the most heroic austerity and to severe and unceasing penance. It was a true cenacle of prayer, seclusion and sacrifice, to which those who went there gave themselves up willingly, seeking, as in a harsh and remote desert, complete withdrawal from the world and from all its coveted and enchanting attractions. Some nuns of this monastery won a reputation for great virtue, notably Mother Brites da Paixão, to whom we shall devote a separate article in its proper place.

The original building, which was a modest structure and remained so until its demolition, nevertheless underwent some major repairs over the years, especially in 1746 and 1752, when the sum of 1,200,000 réis was spent, already a considerable amount for that period. It was demolished in 1911.

On the origins of the foundation of this convent, ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) includes, on p. 591 and following, an interesting legend that deserves to be read as a record of the state of mind of that age.
Our Lady of the Portiuncula (convent)

This convent of Franciscan friars stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), a short distance from the parish church. It was built by the Franciscan friars in a year we cannot determine. As recently as ten years ago some ruins of the conventual buildings could still be seen, and the façade and part of the nave of the church, which was of no very modest size, were still standing. Above the portico could be read the date 1730; we do not know whether it represents the year the convent was founded or the year the church was built, which seems to us more probable.
Our Lady of Pity (convent)

Around 1476 the brothers João Baptista and Urbano Lomelino, who belonged to one of the oldest and most distinguished families of Genoa (see Lomelino), arrived on this island. It was the second of these brothers who founded this convent and began the building work, which death prevented him from completing. When he died in 1518, he entailed his property by will in favour of his nephew Jorge Lomelino and his descendants, with the obligation of completing the building of the convent, maintaining it and also supporting six friars whenever alms failed them. Joana Lopes and Isabel Correia, the wife and mother-in-law of Urbano Lomelino, built the chantry (*capela*) of Sant’Ana (St Anne) in the church of this monastery, which served the community as its chapter house, and they were buried in it. Jorge Lomelino died on 9 December 1548 and was buried in the church of the same convent.

‘Once the religious orders had been abolished,’ wrote the annotator of the *Saudades* in 1873, ‘and after a bitter lawsuit lasting several years, the convent was restored to the successors of the founder, because he, with a foresight of which this is perhaps the only example, had so provided in the relevant clause of his will, should the convent ever be abolished in the future.’
Of the convent and church, which did indeed pass into the possession of the founder’s descendants, no trace remains today.
Convent of St Clare

This convent was built beside the church of Conceição de Cima, which João Gonçalves Zarco had ordered to be built and near which he then lived. It was João Gonçalves da Câmara, son of the discoverer and second captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, who took the initiative in founding this monastery. He intended it as a retreat not only for his own daughters but also for others who wished to follow the monastic life, which they could not then do in Funchal for lack of a religious house for that purpose.

Construction of the convent began in 1492, but the first nuns did not enter it until 1497. By a deed of 11 September 1480 the founder, João Gonçalves da Câmara, bought from Rui Teixeira and Branca Ferreira, residents of Campanário, the Curral estate, later known as Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), for the sum ‘of 23,500 réis at five *ceitis* to the *real* (pl. *réis*; old Portuguese money unit, 1,000 réis = 1 milréis) and 50 gold *cruzados*... its area extended from the Passo da Cruz (‘pass of the cross’) and the Ribeira dos Socorridos (‘stream of the rescued’) up to where the stream rises, from rocky crest to rocky crest, on either side’. This rural property, the largest and most important the convent ever owned, was what the founder gave to the monastery when his daughters were admitted to it as nuns. Even earlier, the Infante Dom Manuel, Duke of Beja and later king, had urged and stressed the need to found a convent of nuns on this island. He did so in the letter which, as Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which this archipelago belonged, he had addressed to its inhabitants on 17 July 1488. In this curious document, which we first came across in the newspaper *O Reclame* of 26 November 1890, he says that the Supreme Pontiff had written to him asking for a monastery to be founded at the church of Conceição de Cima, and adds that ‘as soon as you see this, gather at once in council with the captain and discuss it all very well, and may it please you that it be so done... it will please me to give for this such alms as seem good to me, and henceforth for the maintenance of the nuns I shall always be glad to give all the alms I well can...’. We do not know whether it was the Grand Master’s request that led João Gonçalves da Câmara to found the convent four years later, and still less do we know whether Manuel I, who came to the throne in 1495, contributed to the building of the monastery.

As already stated, building work began in 1492 but was not declared complete until 1497. This slow progress must be attributed partly to the absence of the founder and captain-donatary. Having ordered and arranged everything for the building, and perhaps even begun it, he later left for mainland Portugal, where stays were always long, chiefly because of the difficulty of communications. The building was later enlarged several times as the number of nuns grew. Along the cloister, to satisfy the devotion of the nuns and of other people, many chapels and oratories were built, which were quite unnecessary for the community’s religious services. The original church, dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) and known as Conceição de Cima, came to be dedicated to St Clare (see that entry), who was the patron of the monastery. This church also underwent considerable changes over time, being almost entirely rebuilt in the first half of the 17th century.

The founder’s descendants – the captains-donatary of Funchal and later the Counts and Marquises of Castelo Melhor – always regarded themselves not only as patrons of this church and convent but also as their rightful lords and owners. As late as October 1867 they claimed possession and ownership of them, registering them at the land registry of this judicial district (*comarca*), after a lawsuit brought in 1862 in which they proved their right to the ownership of the convent. On the death of the last nun, the Marquises of Castelo Melhor could lawfully have taken possession of the building, but they did not do so, for reasons unknown to us.

The first abbess of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) was Dona Isabel de Noronha, daughter of the aforementioned João Gonçalves da Câmara. She had been a nun in the convent of Conceição in Beja and was transferred to Funchal with four other professed nuns, once the necessary licences had been obtained from the pontiff. With these mothers there entered the new convent Dona Elvira and Dona Constança, likewise daughters of the donatary, who later took their vows. After his death, which occurred in 1501, another daughter of his, also named Dona Constança, was admitted there as well; according to Frutuoso, she ‘always lived a holy life, not wishing to be a professed nun because she was always ill’.

Of the daughters of the third captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Dona Beatriz, Dona Isabel and Dona Maria de Noronha became nuns there, ‘where their father placed them with good revenues that he assigned to them for the purpose, and they always lived most virtuously and saintly’. The other donataries and the richest and noblest gentlemen of Madeira had many of their daughters as nuns of this convent.

The community was originally made up of a small number of nuns, which grew appreciably, reaching about seventy by the end of the 16th century. Around the middle of the 18th century the number of nuns rose to 130, 70 of them supernumeraries, many of whom were not professed and had not taken vows. In the first quarter of the 19th century this number had fallen to about 70. The dowry each nun brought on admission was 800,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), besides other expenses, the whole amounting to roughly one *conto* (one million réis) de réis, so that it was not easy for people of modest means to join this religious community.

The original fervour in observing the monastic rules and the former austerity of the nuns’ life in this convent gradually cooled, and serious and reprehensible abuses crept in. Truly scandalous acts were even committed, in which the ecclesiastical authority was forced to intervene by imposing the severest canonical penalties. Around the middle of the 18th century there were thirty servants in the convent, and several nuns each had a servant solely for her private use, which, in a house of strict and austere life such as a convent should be, was an unpardonable abuse. There was a time when the nuns’ way of life differed from that of the rest of the society to which they belonged only in the enclosure they kept, living shut within the walls of a convent. On one occasion the entire community even broke its own enclosure for a moment – the strictest and gravest point of discipline in monastic houses – and the diocesan prelate and the Supreme Pontiff hurled the most rigorous penalties of the Church at the nuns. Serious abuses did occur, and were afterwards severely curbed, but the events narrated in the novel *Angela Santa Clara* by Henrique Read Cabral are nonetheless without foundation.

One of the most important events in the history of this convent took place during the sack of this city by French corsairs in 1566. The nuns were forced to abandon their convent so as not to fall victim to that horde of savages and, as G. Frutuoso says, ‘they went out through the canefields, and took refuge, and did not stop until they reached their Curral, which lies a good distance from the city, and so they went, without saving any ornament, leaving everything in the convent except the monstrance of the Most Holy Sacrament. . . . The French remained in Funchal, busy with destruction and slaughter, from 3 to 17 October, and immediately after they left this island the nuns left the Curral and returned to their convent in the city. The corsairs carried out the greatest plunder there and caused great damage to the church and convent, committing every kind of vandalism.

The civil and ecclesiastical authorities of this archipelago tried on several occasions to unite the two communities of Santa Clara and Encarnação into one, on the grounds that the former had ample means to support itself while the latter was a poor convent with scant revenues. They never managed to carry out the planned union of the two convents, however, despite having obtained a papal brief authorising it, owing, no doubt, to powerful influences that intervened and blocked it entirely.

By the middle of the 18th century the Convent of St Clare had an annual income of more than seven *contos* (*conto*: one million réis), and in 1821 its revenues rose to 14 *contos*. That year, however, it ran a deficit of two *contos de réis*, owing to the lack of careful and diligent administration. Under the disentailment (*desamortização*, the sale of Church property by the State) laws, all the property of this convent, which was considerable, was sold by the public treasury; the sum raised by the sale is not known. When the religious orders were abolished, the convent had little more than sixty nuns. The last survivor was Maria Amalia do Patrocinio, who died in November 1890.

By decrees of 26 October 1912 and 17 December 1914 the convent, church and convent grounds of Santa Clara were granted to the Municipal Council of Funchal, the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) of the Misericórdia and the Auxilio Maternal, so that these bodies could build an avenue, a hospital and a ‘crèche’. The Council was to keep possession of the church and the choirs, which were intended for a regional museum.

By the decree of 12 March 1896 the old convent was handed over to the Congregation of the Franciscan Missionaries of Mary, so that an institute could be established there to train women for the religious missions in our colonies, and also to house a school of elementary and secondary education for girls, of which there was a great lack in our community. The political events that took place in our country in 1910 led to the expulsion of these nuns, who left Madeira at once, and the excellent services they had been providing here were interrupted.

The decrees of 31 October 1912 and 22 September 1913 granted the convent buildings to the Municipal Council of Funchal, the Holy House of the Misericórdia and the charitable association ‘Auxilio Maternal’, for the purposes set out in those decrees. A considerable part of the old monastery was actually demolished, and acts of real destruction and vandalism were then committed in all the buildings. The buildings reverted to the State, because the planned works had not been carried out and the specific purpose of the grant had not been fulfilled.

The decree of 25 January 1927 and the ministerial order (*portaria*) of 12 June of the same year authorised the Ministry of Finance to transfer the various premises of the former convent to the Ministry of the Colonies, for the benefit of the Associação Auxiliar das Missões Ultramarinas, with the specific purpose of establishing there a missionary training college for nuns who were to serve in the missions of our overseas colonies. The running of this college was entrusted to the Franciscan Sisters already mentioned, who also set up a *crèche* in the same convent, where some 400 children are taken in, fed and educated during the day. This is one of the most notable services being rendered to the poor of Madeira here.
St Bernardino (convent)

This was the first convent founded on this island outside Funchal. It belonged to the Franciscan order and was dedicated to St Bernardine of Siena, one of the order's great saints. It stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), in a remote and solitary *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), some distance from the mother church (*igreja matriz*). Its origins were humble and obscure, but it later became celebrated and renowned throughout the island, and it seems even in mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), because a man of outstanding virtue named Friar Pedro da Guarda lived and died there, whom the people called, and still call, the Holy Servant of God. For this reason it became a magnet for many devotees and pilgrims, who came from the most distant places on the island to invoke the intercession of the saintly and humble Franciscan. With the extinction of the religious orders and the stance taken by the vicar capitular and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence), António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga, these acts of devotion and piety cooled and dwindled. They did not die out entirely, however, for every year a considerable number of people still visit the grave in which the mortal remains of Friar Pedro da Guarda were laid. We say nothing more here about his life, his virtues and the veneration paid to him, since we shall devote a separate article to him.

Friar Gil de Carvalho, a humble Franciscan friar, came to Madeira from mainland Portugal just as the religious who had occupied the Hospício de São João (St John's Hospice) were leaving the island to establish a community near Lisbon. According to the annotator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), Friar Gil, wishing to live as a hermit in a deserted place, built a small cenobium with two cells, occupied by João Afonso and Martinho Afonso, who went begging among the settlements to support all three.

As the number of religious grew, they set about building a small convent on land donated to them by João Afonso Correia, squire to Prince Henry the Navigator, and his wife Inês Lopes, who on this island were the founders of the house of Torre Bela. The new house stood in a spot far from the settlement, bounded on one side by the stream and on the other by a cliff, and it was well suited to the way of life to which they had devoted themselves. Some years later other religious joined them, forming a community under the direction of Friar Gil de Carvalho.

Many years later, Friar Gil handed over the governance of his monastery to Friar Jorge de Sousa, who did much to enlarge it. Some years earlier a flood of the stream had destroyed the small church and part of the convent. Friar Jorge built a new and larger church, sheltered from the stream's torrents, and, after considerably improving the monastery's material conditions, gave the community the canonical organisation of a true monastic house.

The chancel of the new church was founded by Rui Mendes de Vasconcelos, son of Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos and of Helena Gonçalves, Zarco’s daughter, together with his wife Isabel Correia, daughter of the donors of the land on which the original convent had stood. João Bettencourt de Vasconcelos, grandson of the founder of this chancel and its patron, entailed the disposable third (*terça*) of the estate of his property to meet the needs of the convent, by a will approved on 12 December 1607. Of him we read in an old nobiliary: ‘…they called him the Cavalleiro [the Knight] by nickname; he was born in the year 1535 and went to India in 1580 as captain of the carrack *São Gregorio*; he succeeded to the thirds of his grandparents on the death of his brother Ruy Mendes, and made a will approved on 12 December 1607, in which he left his third entailed on the lands above Camara de Lobos and below the Quinta da Torre, and left it to the friars of São Bernardino, of whose chancel he was patron, as heir to the entail (*morgado*) of his said maternal grandparents, its founders; he died on 12 July 1615’.
