The chancel of this convent’s church was the private family vault of the descendants of its founders and patrons, and many of them were buried there, above all the successors to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*).
The convent church, which still stands, although badly ruined, bears the date 1763 carved high on its façade; this is certainly the date on which the church was rebuilt.

As already stated, the church was enlarged and rebuilt in 1763. Left utterly abandoned after the expulsion of the religious orders, however, it fell rapidly into ruin, and it was completely restored a few years ago thanks to the diligent efforts of the parish priest of Câmara de Lobos, João Joaquim de Carvalho. The outbuildings of the former conventual house were also restored at the same time, and from 1931 to 1933 they housed the classes of the first years of the preparatory course of the minor diocesan seminary, which was later abolished and incorporated into the Seminary of the Encarnação (*Seminário da Encarnação*; Incarnation).
Convent of St Francis in Calheta

‘The convent of the Franciscan friars of São Francisco, at Calheta (‘small cove’),’ says a note in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), ‘was built from alms around the year 1670, on land bought by the devout Pedro Bettencourt de Athouguia, who later took the habit of a lay brother in the Convent of São Bernardino (St Bernardino of Siena). It is private property because it was sold by the Public Treasury.’
It was the most modest of the convents of Madeira and always had a very small number of friars. The building was small, and the church, too, was of cramped dimensions.
St Francis in Funchal (convent)

The Franciscan friars first settled in modest lodgings with a small adjoining chapel, which they built on the spot where the chapel of São João (‘St John’) now stands, on the right bank of the stream of the same name. They remained there for some years until, around 1459, they abandoned the site and left for mainland Portugal, where they established a community at Xabregas, on the outskirts of Lisbon. (See Seraphic Order).

Around 1476 the Franciscan Friar Rodrigo de Arruda arrived in Funchal with some companions. They occupied the hospice of São João and organised a small religious community there, under a brief granted by Pope Sixtus IV in 1476. Taking advantage of the goodwill of the inhabitants of the town (*vila*), Friar Rodrigo set about building a convent in the centre of the settlement, on land belonging to Clara Esteves, who in her will had entailed it in favour of her kinsman João do Porto. In exchange, the friars gave up their hospice of São João and also undertook to celebrate an annual sung Mass on All Saints’ Day. All this was authorised by the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son Diogo, Duke of Viseu, Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which this island belonged. ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that the reason for the move was ‘because the place was deserted and in it a friar, at the prompting of the Devil, who always weaves such webs, hanged himself, these friars established a house below, in the town of Funchal, on grounds and lands opposite Santa Catarina, beyond the stream, where now (1590) stands one of the finest houses of this order that the Province has in Portugal; which convent is of the Observance, as sumptuous as it is cool, in which there are always nearly fifty friars, very learned, religious men of virtue and example, as much as can be found in the world’.

Clara Esteves was not the foundress of this convent, as some have wrongly supposed, for she had already died by the date of its foundation. It was the first administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of the entail she had established who made the exchange with the Franciscans, and he too contributed nothing whatever to the foundation. The true founders of this monastic house, modest in its origins and only later an important friary, were Luís Álvares da Costa and his son Álvaro da Costa, in the year 1473. This is shown by the inscription in Gothic letters on their tombstone, which was removed in 1865 to the Angústias cemetery (see that entry), where it still lies today. On this gravestone one reads: Here lies Luís Álvares da Costa, who founded this house in the year 1473, and his son Francisco Álvares da Costa, first magistrate (*ouvidor*) and overseer of the royal treasury (*vedor da fazenda*) in these islands of Madeira.
The land that had belonged to Clara Esteves was enlarged by a large kitchen garden which Maria de Atouguia, the founder’s granddaughter, had left to the Franciscan friars in her will.

The convent originally had a small church, which was later enlarged and rebuilt. The rebuilt church was consecrated on 4 March 1554 by the Spanish bishop Dom Sancho Truxillo, who had come to exercise episcopal functions temporarily on this island. Around 1578 the convent and church underwent further major repairs and new additions, when the Franciscan Friar Diogo Nabo was guardian. It is to this period that the following words of Frutuoso refer: ‘... it has a very splendid church... in which there are eight very rich chapels and... large convent grounds... ’.

Although this church was not small, it was considered too cramped for the religious life of the community, which had grown considerably, for the great numbers of the faithful and also for the building of new mausoleums and private tombs. It was therefore demolished in 1780, and a new and spacious church was raised on the same site.

The church was a large building of fine and solid construction, whose interior had not yet been entirely finished. It had stood for only three-quarters of a century when the demolition hammer brought it to the ground, and it was still in an excellent state of preservation, apart from the damage that the weather and the neglect it had suffered since 1834 would inevitably have caused.

Its preservation was imperative. If there was no need to use it for worship, it ought to have been given over to our art museum. Small provincial towns, far inferior to ours in population and in importance of every kind, have one. Modest, certainly, but it would have been the little museum of an island lost in the middle of the ocean. Countless objects that could and should have been displayed there have gone astray and been lost. The church of São Francisco was, as is well known, the true pantheon of a large number of the most distinguished and ancient families of this archipelago. Almost all of them had their burial vaults and mausoleums there, some of them of rich and beautiful marble. Today it fills us with real astonishment, and with a legitimate indignation, that the representatives of those families, and therefore the owners of those sarcophagi, allowed the destruction of what should have been, for them, a sacred necropolis.

The convent, which was old and badly dilapidated, and the church attached to it served as a hospital, a prison, a barracks, a court and an asylum. By decree of 7 November 1844 they were granted to the Municipal Council of Funchal (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) for the construction of a building to house the law courts. At the time, not even an attempt was made to carry out this idea.

In 1864 the Funchal Council resolved to hold a competition for the design and estimate of a building to accommodate the courts of justice, the municipal offices, and the administration and tax office of the municipality (*concelho*). It chose the convent grounds of São Francisco as the most suitable site for its construction.

The laying of the foundation stone of the new town hall was an occasion of the greatest solemnity. On 11 March 1866 a splendid procession left the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), headed by Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura, the diocesan prelate, and joined by the Municipal Council, the senior authorities of the district, public officials and other official bodies. All made their way to the convent grounds of São Francisco, where, before an enormous crowd, the cornerstone was laid of the building, whose construction would never rise above its foundations. Besides coins of the day, a metal plaque was placed in the cornerstone, engraved with the following inscription: *Senatus Funchalensis Hanc Sibi Curam Suis Sumptibus Aedificavit Qua in Eademn et Jus Dicatur Hunc Lapidem in Hujus Optatissimi Operis Auspicium D. Patritius Xavier de Moura regnante Ludovic. I Die Quinto Idus Martius Anno MDCCCLXVI Adstante Eodem Senatu et omnibus Provinciae Magistra Magnae Civium Corona Deum Rite Precatus* (The Senate of Funchal built this house for itself at its own expense, in which justice might also be administered. Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura, in the reign of Luís I, on the fifth day before the Ides of March in the year 1866, in the presence of the same Senate and all the magistrates of the province and a great crowd of citizens, having duly prayed to God, laid this stone as an auspice of this most desired work)
*Posuit.*

The church and the convent were demolished. The people of Madeira did not look kindly on the razing of the church, and at times the political parties exploited this, waving it as a political banner against their opponents.
As we have already said, and as everyone knows, the planned town hall never rose above its foundations, and several *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis) were buried there to no purpose.

The council house could have been built, standing near the church, and the church too could have been preserved to serve as a Catholic place of worship or as a museum, for there was ample room for these and yet other buildings.

As is well known, the former convent and church of São Francisco occupied the ground that today forms the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’), the streets Rua Hermenegildo Capelo, Rua Serpa Pinto and Rua Conselheiro José Silvestre Ribeiro, and the space on which the Teatro Manuel de Arriaga (‘Manuel de Arriaga Theatre’) stands. The streets flanking the Jardim Municipal, with the exception of Rua de São Francisco, were built after the suppression of the religious orders, that is, after 1834.
Convents

As described in earlier entries, there were four friaries of the Seraphic or Franciscan order in Madeira: São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) of Funchal, São Francisco of Calheta, Our Lady of Pity of Santa Cruz, and Nossa Senhora da Porciúncula (Our Lady of the Angels of the Portiuncula) of Ribeira Brava. The same order also had three convents of nuns, all in Funchal: Convent of St Clare, Our Lady of Ransom and Nossa Senhora da Encarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation). Of these religious houses, only the church and part of the Convent of St Clare and the church of the Encarnação survive.
The Jesuits also had a religious house or college in Funchal, now used as a barracks, which still stands together with its adjoining church (see Colégio).
Cook (James)

After the first circumnavigation of the globe, made by our illustrious compatriot Ferdinand Magellan, it was the second voyage around the world, that of the great English navigator James Cook, that rendered the most signal services to science and did most to widen geographical knowledge.

On his first voyage of circumnavigation, Cook left the coast of England on 26 August 1768 in command of the English Royal Navy ship *Endeavour*. On 13 September following she anchored in the harbour of Funchal, setting sail on the 19th for Rio de Janeiro.
Captain Cook was shown great hospitality in this city by the English consul Cheap and by the governor and captain-general João António de Sá Pereira.

Aboard the *Endeavour* were the naturalists Joseph Banks and Dr Daniel Solander, who were charged with carrying out various scientific studies. During the few days they spent in Madeira they conducted a number of investigations into several branches of natural history, assisted by Dr Heberden, a distinguished English physician then living in Funchal.

The account of this voyage of Cook’s refers to various interesting aspects of our customs, convents and churches, means of transport, wine trade, etc. Cook and the two scholars of the expedition were greatly struck by a chapel they visited in the Convent of St Francis (*São Francisco*), whose walls were literally covered with human shin bones, thigh bones and skulls. Other visitors also refer to this macabre chapel with great astonishment, but it was not a unique case, for in other convents in Europe there were likewise chapels whose walls were lined with human remains.
Issues 462, 463 and 466 of the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) printed a translation of the account of Cook’s voyage, which is well worth reading.

Cook returned to Madeira in 1772, on his second voyage to the southern seas, this time in command of the *Resolution*, and reached the port of Funchal on 29 July. The expedition’s naturalists were Johann Reinhold Forster and his son João Jorge, who observed 96 plants, some of them cultivated, during the three days they spent on the island. The narrative of this expedition records that there was at that time a prodigious number of Black and mixed-race people in Madeira, some free, others slaves.

Forster relates that the ships of Captain Cook’s first expedition bombarded the Ilhéu fortress (*Fortaleza do Ilhéu*) in 1768 over an insult to the British flag. However, neither Hawkesworth’s narrative nor the official documents of the time mention this incident, which, if it did occur, did not affect the good relations then existing between Portugal and England.
Captain Cook made a third voyage in 1776, but without calling at Madeira, and died on one of the islands of the Sandwich archipelago in a fight with the islanders.
Cooper (William White)
Works: *the Invalid’s Guide to Madeira...* London, 1840, 1 vol.
Cooperatives

Of three cooperative societies established in Funchal many years ago to supply their members with grocery goods on favourable terms, only that of the 27th Infantry Regiment still exists at present. It was set up in January 1892, and its statutes are dated 30 September 1891. The other two disappeared long ago. The older of them, called the Sociedade Cooperativa de Consumo e Credito do Funchal, whose statutes were approved on 29 April 1875, bought an excellent building in Rua do Esmeraldo, opposite Rua de Cristóvão Colombo, where it opened a well-stocked grocery.

This grocery, which closed in 1880 because it brought the shareholders nothing but losses, reopened shortly afterwards under the management of two merchants. They ran it for 5 years, receiving half the profits of the business, and it finally passed to another merchant, who kept it until 1888 or 1889, when the grocery was closed as a result of the Society’s liquidation. As the shares of the Cooperativa de Consumo e Credito do Funchal had been bought cheaply by one of the shareholders, he became, without spending any large sum, the owner of the Society’s excellent building, which he managed to sell many years later for about 40 *contos*.
The other cooperative referred to above was established around 1893 and lasted only some two or three years. It opened a grocery in the former Rua do Capitão, but never owned a building of its own.
A fourth cooperative must also be mentioned, the Cooperativa Popular, whose statutes were approved on 6 March 1919 and which opened its premises on 8 April 1920.
Copepods
See Carcinology.
Coquinho
Common name of *Cyperus rotundus* and *C. esculentus*, plants of the family Cyperaceae, very common in Madeira. These plants produce small underground tubers, which can be eaten without ill effect.
Corals

Coral, or coral tree, is the name by which various zoophytes of the seas of Madeira are known. Among them we shall mention *Dendrophyllea ramea*, or red coral, *Acanthagorgia Grayi*, or black coral, and *Hemicorallium Johnsoni*, or white coral.
Madeiran corals are well represented in the British Museum, the Liverpool Museum and the Museum of the Funchal Seminary.
Coraliarios
See Anthozoans.
Cordeiro (Father António)

He was born in the city of Angra in 1641 and died in Lisbon on 2 February 1722. He entered the Society of Jesus and held very important posts in his order. He wrote and published various books in Latin and Portuguese, which are listed in the *Bibliotheca lusitana*. He is the author of the well-known work ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), which is of great interest for the history of our archipelago and which we shall discuss in a separate article.
Coroa de Henrique (Agapanthus umbellatus)
A lily widely grown in the gardens and *quintas* of Funchal, Monte etc. It is native to the Cape of Good Hope and produces numerous blue, scentless flowers gathered in umbels.
Chorography

For the study of the chorography of this archipelago and of each of its islands, besides the material scattered through various works, notably the *Diccionario Universal Portugues illustrado*, the following booklets have been published: *Chorographia da Madeira*, by João de Nobrega Soares, first published in 1862, with the fourth and last edition in 1882; *Chorographia do Archipelago da Madeira*, by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, 1873; and *Corografia Elementar do Arquipelago da Madeira*, by Major Alberto Artur Sarmento, 1912. The last is the most complete study we have on the subject.

As was done in years gone by, some elementary notions of the region’s chorography ought once again to be taught in the schools of this district. This teaching was at one time compulsory here: four editions of a regional chorography were produced within 20 years, for a population of little more than a hundred thousand inhabitants, among whom the rate of illiteracy was very high.

To serve as a textbook for teaching the chorography of Madeira in the schools of this archipelago, the Autonomous District General Council (*Junta Geral*) published in 1937 a new edition, much improved and adapted to that purpose, of the booklet by Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento, a most valuable work that well deserved to be reissued.

On the same subject, the co-author of this *Elucidario*, Father Fernando A. Silva, had published in 1934 a detailed study entitled *Dicionario Corografico do Arquipelago da Madeira*, in a volume of 310 pages.
St Elmo (chapel)

It is one of the oldest chapels in this diocese and one of the few 15th-century buildings still surviving here, although over time it has undergone profound alterations. It was built through the devotion of seafarers and dedicated to their patron saint, Saint Peter

González Telmo, more commonly known by the name of St Elmo (*Corpo Santo*). Worship at this chapel is maintained by the fishing community of Funchal, and it was once the seat of a kind of relief society intended to support seafarers in sickness or disability. It is still not known at present whether the confraternity keeps this charitable character among its members. We shall transcribe what we found on the matter in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, which is truly interesting: ‘confraternities... there are two notable ones, both because they date from the time of the first settlement of the archipelago and because they form true mutual-aid associations: the confraternity of St Elmo, with its Manueline chapel at the eastern end of Funchal, and that of São Pedro Telmo, in the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Câmara de Lobos. Both belong to seafarers and clearly derive from the famous statutes (*compromisso*) of the Algarve seafarers, and, like these, they connect, in religious form, with the nautical institutions of the time of King Denis. The statutes of these two Madeiran confraternities, of which we possess a copy, are, like the Algarve one, precious documents for the history, obscure but glorious, not of princes nor of the navigators in their service, but of the pilots and sailors, the seafaring men properly so called, who had no small share in the discoveries’.
Calcareous bodies of Piedade

At the locality (*sítio*) of Piedade (‘pity’), on the Ponta de São Lourenço, there are numerous calcareous bodies that look like petrified tree trunks and branches. Many of them show concentric layers similar to those seen in certain woody plants. Some of these bodies extend at their lower end into a kind of root, with the shape and direction of the roots of dicotyledonous plants.

The naturalists who have visited Piedade do not agree on how to explain the origin of these bodies. The botanist Richard Thomas Lowe regarded them as sandy-calcareous concretions; Macaulay as a coral formation of the family Alcyonidae; the geologist Smith as mere casts formed in spaces once occupied by plants; and Mousinho de Albuquerque and Thomas Edward Bowdich as the petrified remains of an ancient forest.

This last explanation is the only one that seems acceptable to us, given the shape and appearance of the bodies in question. As for the process of mineralisation, it must have consisted of a simple exchange of organic for inorganic matter, with particles of carbonate of lime taking the place of the plant particles as these decayed. Water, dissolving part of the limestone, would have brought about this exchange by seeping into the cavities left by the decomposing wood.

If we accept that in remote ages the north coast at Piedade extended out into the sea in a gentle slope, bounded by a beach covered with calcareous sand, we may well accept too that the winds, carrying this sand along little by little, spread it over the land of the interior and of the south coast, thus supplying the material needed for this mineralisation.
The ground at Piedade is volcanic in origin, and tuffs and basalt are found in the adjacent cliffs.
In the north-west of Porto Santo there are calcareous bodies of the same nature as those of Piedade.
Berthelot’s pipit (Anthus Bertheloti)

A small bird of the family Anthidae that frequents open places on all the islands of the archipelago. It is not migratory, and its range is limited to the islands of the Macaronesian Sea (the Azores, Madeira, the Savage Islands and the Canary Islands). It nests on the ground from February to August, usually laying four grey eggs with irregular dark markings. In certain parts of Madeira it is also called *carreiró*, *carreirote*, *melrinho de Nosso Senhor* and *melrinho de Nossa Senhora*, and on Porto Santo it is known as *bica*.
Corregedor

There had been *corregedores* (royal district magistrates) in Madeira since the time of the donataries, but only from 1767 onwards was there a permanent *corregedor* here. He was the senior judicial officer, and his jurisdiction extended over the whole archipelago. He received a lodging allowance provided by the Council, and when he was unable to act he was replaced by the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) or, failing him, by the most senior of the councillors (*vereadores*).
When the judicial reform of 16 May 1832 was put into effect in this district on 15 October 1835, the *corregedores* disappeared and were replaced by the *juízes de direito*.
Correia

We have already devoted a short article to João Afonso, companion of Zarco, who became the founder of a noble and distinguished family on this island. He also bore the surname Correia, which he passed on to his descendants, and they were the first to use it on this island. João Afonso had a son named António Correia, who was born in Madeira in 1457 and who, several genealogists state, died in 1572, at the age of about 115. This António Correia was a valiant knight who fought bravely in Africa, chiefly at Asilah and Safi, where he maintained a large number of men and horses at his own expense. The old Madeiran chronicles speak of him in terms of high praise.
Correia Henriques (José Anselmo)

José Anselmo Correia Henriques was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) around 1777. He belonged, albeit through illegitimacy, to an old and noble family of this island, being the natural son of António João Correia Bettencourt Henriques and the brother of Fernando José Correia Brandão Bettencourt Henriques, Viscount of Torre Bela and Portugal’s minister in Prussia and Sweden.

We do not know what academic qualifications José Anselmo Correia Henriques possessed, but to hold the posts he filled and to write the books he published, he must certainly have been a man of uncommon talent and rare intellectual culture. Since he followed a diplomatic career and was a devoted cultivator of letters, he no doubt received his training in some course of higher education, or at least at the Colégio dos Nobres. There the dead languages, Greek and Latin, were then taught, along with the living languages French, English and Italian, and history, mathematics, physics, drawing, architecture, horsemanship, fencing, etc.

He pursued a career in diplomacy, and the only post we know him to have held in it is that of Portugal’s representative to the Hanseatic cities. As is generally known, these were Hamburg, Bremen and others, which formed a kind of confederation with diplomatic representation in almost the whole of Europe. Many of his literary works were printed in various European cities, and from this it may perhaps be inferred that he resided in some of them as a member of the diplomatic corps and belonged to Portugal’s legations at various foreign courts. It is very likely that the works published in Paris, London, Hamburg, Venice and Christiania indicate that their author stayed for longer or shorter periods in those cities, carrying out consular or diplomatic duties.
He was in Rio de Janeiro when the Portuguese court and government were established there, holding several posts of trust under the Prince Regent, Dom João.

Among the works of Correia Henriques mentioned by Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, we would single out his *Obras Poeticas*, of which he appears to have published only the first volume; the mock-heroic poems *A Padeira de Aljubarrota* and *Perodana*; the tragedy *Revolução de Portugal*; the comedy *Escola de Escandalo*; and many others. If these are not masterpieces of their kind, they nonetheless reveal considerable literary ability and great intellectual culture. He translated the poem *Arte da guerra* by Frederick, King of Prussia, as well as other works, and in 1821 he also published in London a political journal to which he gave the title *O Zorragar das côrtes novas*. He died in Lisbon in 1831 and was the father of the 1st Count of Seixal (‘pebble shore’).
Correio da Madeira
The first issue appeared on 3 February 1849 and the last on 9 August 1851. In all, 132 issues were published.
Correio da Manhã (O)
It began publication on 31 August 1884 and ceased on 14 March 1886, by which time 502 issues had appeared.
Correio da Tarde
It was published from 9 January 1901 to 17 January 1911, and 1294 issues appeared.
Correio do Funchal
Twenty-five issues were published, from 5 June 1867 to 10 January 1868.
Correio do Funchal
It began publication on 2 January 1897 and was suspended on 2 January 1899, by which time 587 issues had appeared.
Post Office

Regular postal service in Funchal appears to date from 1662, the year in which a deputy chief postmaster (*tenente correio-mor*) was appointed for Madeira, charged with the ‘regulation and execution of the carriage of letters’. It is to be believed that this official was subordinate to the chief postmaster (*correio-mor*) of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) and took orders from him alone, since at that time the administration of the postal services was not in the hands of the government.

The office of chief postmaster was abolished in 1797, and on 13 May 1798 the Madeira post office was created and placed under an administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality). It yielded 251,630 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in that year, 312,500 in 1800, 381,550 in 1810, 691,120 in 1820 and 1,160,830 in 1823. From 1798 to 1824 the post office yielded a total of 14,606,066 *réis*.

On 8 April 1805 a decree ordered that the post offices of Madeira and the Azores be annexed to the General Postal Administration (*Administração Geral dos Correios*). This annexation, however, apparently did not take place, since on 18 April 1838 a new decree appeared calling for full compliance with what had been laid down in the earlier enactment.

For many years the postal services in Funchal were in the charge of an assistant postmaster (*correio assistente*), subordinate to the General Postal Administration, but we cannot state precisely the year in which this post was created.
The post of assistant postmaster was awarded to whoever would fill it on terms most advantageous to the State. The appointee held office for three years, after which a new tender was opened.

The assistant postmaster lodged a surety with the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). He collected the legal postage on all correspondence and the premiums on items he insured against the risk of loss, and he was obliged to set up subordinate post offices as the service required. In all other respects he was governed by the provisions of the regulations (*regimento*) of 5 April 1805 and the instructions annexed to them.

The highest bid (*lanço*) offered in 1839 for the post of assistant postmaster of Funchal was 1,030,000 *réis* a year in strong currency (moeda forte, i.e. mainland coinage), this sum to be paid quarterly in arrears at the General Postal Administration in Lisbon.

The decree of 27 October 1852 abolished the posts of deputy postmaster and placed all postal establishments under the direct administration of the State; it was then that the post of director of the Funchal post office was created.

The same decree introduced postage stamps, but made this method of prepayment optional for internal correspondence exchanged between the mainland of the Kingdom and the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes), or between the islands and the mainland. Stamped letters paid 25 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for up to 3 *oitavas* in weight; printed matter paid 10 or 20 *réis* for up to 1 ounce in weight, depending on whether or not it was prepaid with stamps. Mail for England was formerly dispatched through the British consulate on this island, which was also responsible for receiving the mail that arrived from that country and forwarding it to the Funchal post office, once the letters had been separated from the newspapers and other printed matter. The British consulate took charge of delivering the printed matter and the Portuguese post office of delivering the letters. It should be noted that these letters paid nothing in Funchal, since the senders had already paid the postage at the British post offices. The postage on letters to England was paid at the British post offices, not at the British consulate in Funchal.
The postal convention concluded with England on 5 June 1859 regularised the service for correspondence exchanged with that country and reduced the postage charged for carrying letters.

Home delivery of mail in the city of Funchal began in 1877. In Lisbon this service already existed in 1805, when the postage on letters was paid by the recipient. Since 1866 the Funchal post office has issued money orders payable on the mainland, and since 1852 it has had branch offices in the seats of the municipalities (*concelhos*). For some time the Municipal Council of Funchal subsidised the carriage of mail between the city and certain places on the island.

On 7 July 1880 the telegraph and postal services were reorganised, and the posts, telegraphs and lighthouses were then brought together. In each administrative district the service was run by a department called the Telegraph and Postal Directorate (*Direcção Telegrafo-Postal*), and offices were set up in the localities that were not district seats.
The telegraph and postal services underwent further changes in 1886, 1892 and 1899, but the reform of 7 July 1880 is without doubt the most valuable and important carried out to date.
The revenue of the Madeira post office in the financial year 1921–1922 was 832,043.00 escudos and its expenditure 268,083.37 escudos.
Lava flows

At Porto Moniz, on the north coast of Madeira, and at Gorgulho (‘weevil’), near Funchal, there are lava flows of very curious appearance. The Porto Moniz flows, a drawing of which appears in Charles Lyell’s *Elements of Geology*, look particularly recent. One of them forms a mass bristling with jagged points that extends beyond the coastline. The Gorgulho lavas lie on the shore, close to the spot where a small fort once stood, and contain various hollows in which seawater collects.
Ocean currents
See Gulf Stream.
Corricar
Among Madeiran fishermen it means to fish by trolling. In colloquial speech it also means to make short, quick trips in various directions.
See Corrico.
Corrico

A fishing method used in Madeira in which a boat is kept moving while it tows one or two lines, each with a hook at the end carrying the bait. The movement forces the bait to glide not far below the surface of the water. The species best suited to this kind of fishing, which is carried out at night, are the *bicuda*, the *enchova* and the *serralhão*, but exceptionally the *caneja* and other fish that habitually roam the surface are also caught. The bait is almost always a small whole fish, a *chicharro*. In this it differs from the *corripo*, the method adopted in Portugal, where a piece of white rag, called the *amostra*, is fastened to the hook and the deceived fish takes it for tempting bait.
Corsa

A rudimentary drag vehicle used in Madeira solely for carrying loads. It is drawn by oxen, contrary to the claims of Portuguese lexicographers, who describe it as pulled by people and used to carry passengers. It consists simply of a wooden plank ten *palmos* long and two wide. At its front end there is an opening through which passes a strap that ties it to the pole, which is known by the extravagant name of *solas*. The plank is almost always of til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) wood and sometimes of loquat or mulberry; the pole, or *solas*, is made of pine, and the yoke and its bows of loquat or til. The edges of the plank’s upper surface are fitted with strips of wood, while the underside, which drags along the ground, is sometimes lined with two iron plates.
It is used in the Canary Islands under the same name, an interesting fact that bears witness to the exchange of customs between the peoples of the two archipelagos in times long past.

The term is perhaps, it may be said, the only genuinely Portuguese word for a drag vehicle. We believe it worthy of acceptance as standard Portuguese, all the more so because it seems to derive from the Latin *cursus*. There is therefore no reason to spurn it and replace it, as is often done in Madeira itself, with the word *zorra*, which should in general be applied to a certain wheeled vehicle and only in a very restricted sense to a drag cart.
Nor can it be replaced by the word *trenó*, of French origin, which means a wheelless vehicle for travelling on ice, an object that in any case does not exist in the climate of Portuguese lands.

The regional word *corsa* (wheelless wooden sledge), which seems to have no equivalent in the language, should perhaps be granted national standing and raised to the rank of standard Portuguese, subject to the opinion of the proper authorities.
Dr Hans Sloane, who visited Madeira in 1687, mentions the *corsa*, and it is likely that this vehicle already existed on the island in the early days of colonisation.
Corsão

A large *corsa* (wheelless wooden sledge) in which the plank is replaced by four beams arranged in a very elongated rectangle. Sometimes a wide grating-like platform rests on this rectangle, allowing very bulky loads to be carried, such as pine brushwood for bakers’ ovens, casks, furniture, etc.
French corsairs
See Sack by the French.
Cortado

A locality between Santana and Faial, from which there are superb views over the latter parish (*freguesia*) and the Penha de Águia. Anyone who climbs the steep slope leading to Cortado (‘cut’) and passes through the cutting or gap at its top has the impression of entering a *quinta* (country estate), so green and wooded are the sides of the road that leads from there to Santana.
Cortado (peak)
A mountain height in the locality (*sítio*) of the same name, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana, at an altitude of 527 metres.
Cortado (point)

On the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana, not far from the place called Rocha do Navio (‘ship cliff’) and the islet of that name, lies the Ponta do Cortado (‘cut-off point’), near the peak of the same name.
Cortez
This family surname derives from Manuel Afonso Cortez, a citizen of Porto, who married Ourana Lopes of Câmara de Lobos, where he died in 1615.
Cortina da Cidade (city walls)

This was the name given to the walls that protected Funchal against any enemy attack, from both the landward and the seaward side. On the east, the walls ran from the pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction) to the Pena (‘crag’), following the right bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’); on the west, from the mouth of the Ribeira de São João (formerly the Ribeira Grande) to the cliff of Pico dos Frias (‘the Frias’ peak’), following the left bank of the same stream; and on the south, from the mouth of the Ribeira de São João to the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater).

The curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city) of the city was begun, it seems, in the reign of King Sebastian. However, the regulations (*regimento*) for the fortifications that this monarch gave to Madeira make no mention of the walls east of the Ribeira de João Gomes. These walls were built during the period of Castilian rule: by a royal decree (*alvará*) issued in 1618, Philip III assigned substantial funds to the work, which was not completed until 1637.

According to an inscription on the parade ground and arms of the Fort of São João do Pico (*Castelo de São João do Pico*), which Dr Azevedo transcribed on p. 625 of his notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), almost all of the curtain wall joining that fort was built by the governor Luís de Miranda Henriques, who was on this island from 1636 to 1640. This part of the wall had, however, already been designated in King Sebastian’s regulations as necessary for the landward defence of the city.

João da Costa e Brito, governor-general of the archipelago from 1680 to 1684, seems to have improved the city walls. Yet an inscription that stood on the now demolished Varadouros (‘slipways’) gate, which Dr Azevedo also transcribed on p. 628 of the same work, shows that the walls were not completed until 1689, in the time of the governor Dom Lourenço de Almeida.

There is a letter from Duke Manuel I, dated 21 June 1493, ordering an enclosure and walls to be built in the town (*vila*) of Funchal. On 9 January 1494, however, a royal letter (*carta régia*) appeared revoking that order and directing that only a few bastions be built and some gateways blocked up for the proper defence and protection of the island. After this, Vicente Sodré came to Madeira on the orders of the same duke to deal with the said enclosure and walls. But, as Dr Azevedo says, this mission achieved nothing, for the island only acquired fortifications once royal power had been consolidated there through the Manueline reforms.

The Fort of São Filipe, the redoubt of Santo António da Alfândega, the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) and the battery of Fontes (‘springs’) lay within the old walled enclosure, although all these fortifications, except that of São Lourenço, were built after the walls. ‘The Alfândega redoubt,’ says Dr Azevedo, ‘was the first excrescence on Funchal’s belt of walls; it was the first blow to the system of circumvallation, and the first deliberate step towards a system of maritime defence based on the range and crossfire of cannon.’

In 1557 the government levied a contribution of 7,000 *cruzados* on the properties of the captaincy of Funchal for the fortification works; in 1576 another of 100,000 *cruzados*, likewise for the same works; and in 1617 the government demanded payment of whatever sum might be needed for the walls and other military works that Madeira required. Earlier, in 1493, a war contribution had been imposed on the island for building the enclosure and walls of the town of Funchal. This contribution had no effect, because the work was never carried out, owing to the royal letter of 9 January 1494 to which we referred above.

Of the old city wall only a few remnants still stand, more or less hidden among the houses, and the gates and gateways that once pierced it have also disappeared. The redan at the entrance to the city and the walls near the present São Pedro Market and between the Fortress and the fort of Fontes disappeared in 1839; in 1888 the gun emplacement near the old British cemetery, by the Ribeiro Real, disappeared; on 20 September 1897 demolition began of the branch (*lanço*, *ramal*) of the city wall adjoining the Fort of São Pedro (St Peter), north of the old Praça Académica; and finally, in May 1911, the part of the wall beside the chapel of the Varadouros was removed. Following representations made to the Government in August 1895 and February 1896, the Council now owns the branch of the old walls that can be seen near the spot where the Avenida de João de Deus comes out. On 29 May 1914 the same body resolved to acquire the part of the city wall needed to extend the Largo da Sé (‘cathedral square’) down to the beach, since it had been authorised to do so by a note from the War Ministry. Demolition of this part of the city wall began in March 1920 to open the Avenida António José de Almeida. On 15 October 1896 the Council ordered a halt to the demolition of the part of the city wall bordering Rua Pimenta de Aguiar, because of a complaint from the head of the engineering section on this island. That wall still stands today, perfectly useless, although the said official attributed military importance to it, so we believe.

Of the old gates and gateways of the city wall only two exist today: that of the Customs House and the one near the fortress of São Tiago. Besides these, however, there were also the following, which were demolished to improve the city: that of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), between the Fort of São Pedro and the Pelourinho, almost opposite Rua da Boa Viagem, demolished in 1836 when work began on the Praça Académica; that of Rua do Sabão, demolished in the same year; that of Saúde, near the old nursing home (*Casa da Saúde*) or Commercial Association building, demolished in 1839; that of São Lázaro, at the point where the old Rua dos Aranhas meets Rua da Ponte de São Lázaro, demolished in 1904; that of São Paulo, beside the chapel of the same name, demolished in 1839; that of Carreira (‘track’), beside Rua Pimenta de Aguiar, and that of Pico (‘peak’), in Rua das Cruzes (‘street of the crosses’) or Rua de João Joaquim de Freitas, both demolished in 1865; and that of the Varadouros, demolished in 1911.

This last gateway, which before 1839 was the main entrance to the city, was distinguished by the elegance of its architecture. When it was demolished, its stones were numbered on the orders of the municipal engineer, Mr Aníbal Augusto Trigo, so that the structure could easily be reassembled should a museum of Madeiran antiquities one day be created.

On the gateway, above which the Council’s arms could be seen, was the following Latin inscription, to which we referred above: *Perfecta haec varii praefecti moenia frustra “ praeterito cupiunt tempore quisque suo “ sed Domino Laurento ea est servata voluptas Dalmada qui istud fine coronat opus “ anno “ 1689.* (Various governors, each in his own time, vainly longed to see these walls completed; but that pleasure was reserved for Dom Lourenço de Almada, who crowns this work with its completion, in the year 1689.)

Although the city wall had long ceased to have any military importance, the Council obtained the necessary permission from the War Ministry to demolish some branches of it only with difficulty. Without the intervention of high political influence, some improvements that depended on removing the wall might still be waiting to be carried out, such was the importance that, until not many years ago, the Ministry attached to preserving a system of fortifications whose only purpose was to show that the defence and protection of the island were not, in former times, the matter neglected by those in government that they are today.
See Fortifications.
Barn owl (*Strix flammea*)
A nocturnal bird of prey of the family Bubonidea, native to Madeira. It lays its eggs in rock crevices, where it lives during the day.
Corujeira

In this well-known locality of the parish (*freguesia*) of Tabua stands an old chantry (capela) with the dedication to the Mãe de Deus (Mother of God); neither the year of its foundation nor the names of its founders are known. Destroyed by the violence of the torrential waters of the stream, it was rebuilt in 1767 on the bank opposite the site of its first construction.
Crow
Three species of the genus *Corvus* have been recorded as passage migrants in these islands: *Corvus corone*, *C. Corax* and *C. leptonix*.
Cossart

This family surname derives from William Cossart, who as early as 1809 had some interests connected with the export trade in wines from this island, carried on by the English firm of Newton, Gordon, Murdoch & Scott.

The firm now (1920) belonging to Cossart, Gordon & C.º was founded in 1745 and has since traded under the following names: Francisco Newton (1745–1748), Newton & Spence (1748–1758), Newton & Gordon (1758–1775), Newton, Gordon & Johnston (1775–1791), Newton, Gordon & Murdoch (1791–1802), Newton, Gordon, Murdoch & C.º (1802–1805), Newton, Gordon, Murdoch & Scott (1805–1834), Newton, Gordon Murdoch & C.º (1834–1839), Newton, Gordon, Cossart & C.º (1839–1861) and Cossart, Gordon & C.º (1861).
Cosson (E.)
Works: *Catalogue des plantes recueillies por G. Mandon en 1865 et 1866 dans les iles de Madère et de Porto Santo*. (*Bull. de la Soc. Bot. de France*, vol. XV, 1868).
Costa

There are two branches of this family, one descended from Luís Álvares da Costa and the other from Nuno da Costa. Luís Álvares da Costa came to Madeira in the time of Afonso V; here he served as overseer (*vedor*) and superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*), and he founded the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), Funchal. Nuno da Costa was one of the first settlers of Machico and one of the representatives of this town (*vila*) and of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) before the king for the granting of the charter (foral) of Machico in 1515.
Costa (Dom Rodrigo da)
His appointment as governor and captain-general of this archipelago dates from 2 December 1689, and he took office on 20 October 1690.
In 1702 he was appointed governor of Bahia and in 1707 viceroy of India. He was the son of the Count of Soure and died in 1722.
Costa (Daniel da)

Speaking of the Bishop of Funchal, Dom Luís Figueiredo de Lemos, Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘Of his illustrious lineage I shall set down a chapter, which the most learned Doctor Daniel da Costa, Physician to His Majesty, a noble person of great learning and virtue, residing in the city of Funchal, later composed about him in lofty style, for the greater illumination of the nobility, life, virtues and manners of the same Lord.’ Diogo Barbosa Machado says that the said work was entitled *Contra ponto, ou Vida do VII Bispo do Funchal*, and was included in the *Historia das Ilhas*.
Costa de Baixo

The coast of Madeira lying west of Funchal is commonly called the Costa de Baixo (‘lower slope’). This name covers all the parishes on that coast, namely those that make up the municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol and Calheta.
Costa de Cima

This name is given to the southern coast of Madeira lying east of Funchal. It covers all the parishes (*freguesias*) that form the municipalities of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and Machico, with the exception of the parish of Porto da Cruz, which lies on the island’s north coast.
Costa Dias (Manuel da)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) on 18 October 1883 and attended the diocesan seminary, the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), the industrial institute and the Army School. He spent some time in Brazil before enrolling at the lyceum, and while a pupil there he edited the republican newspaper *O Democrata* (‘The Democrat’). He served in Africa soon after completing his military studies, was a professor at the Escola de Guerra and represented Madeira in Parliament in the legislative session of 1915 to 1917. Works: *As subsistencias no exercito aliado anglo-luso*, Lisbon, 1909; *Colonizaçao dos Planaltos de Angola*, Lisbon, 1913; *Guerra Peninsular, 1808-1811*; *O Serviço de Subsistencias no Exercito Anglo-Luso*, 1 vol., 1913; *Administração Militar*, 1 vol., 3rd edn, 1918; *Flandres*, 1 vol., 1920. He died in Lisbon in 1930, holding the rank of major in the Military Administration.
The *Diario da Madeira* of 12 October 1930 published a detailed biographical article about this distinguished Madeiran.
Costa do Norte

The northern coast of Madeira, generally known as the north coast (*Costa do Norte*), stretches from Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’), where it meets the western region of the island, to the tip of the northern slope of Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’), which extends along the eastern side. It has been said somewhere, and with every justification, that it is an alpine, craggy coast, forming a line of high rocks like an enormous wall of cliff, its base lashed by the waves and its summit crowned with the luxuriant greenery of a native forest. Because beaches and coves are so rare, and because of the violence of the northerly winds that blow there for most of the year, it is utterly inhospitable to ships and unsafe for boats. It has only two harbours of refuge from bad weather, Porto da Cruz and Porto Moniz, lying roughly at the eastern and western ends of the coast. The coast takes in the parishes of the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Porto Moniz, São Vicente and Santana, as well as the parish of Porto da Cruz and the northern shore of the parish of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), both of which belong to the municipality of Machico.

The outline of the shoreline of the north coast is described by Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque in the following terms: ‘From Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) northwards, the coast first runs north-east as far as Ponta do Tristão, where the northern coast of the island begins. It then runs roughly east-south-east as far as São Vicente, and from there east-north-east as far as Ponta de São Jorge (‘St George Point’), whence it returns to its general south-easterly direction as far as Porto da Cruz, almost at the northern root of Ponta de São Lourenço. This point closes the island at its eastern extremity, stretching out into the sea, very narrow, for roughly three miles, in a west–east direction. Along almost the whole length of this shoreline the sea is deep and free of reefs, with these exceptions only: 1. in the recessed part of this coast, where there are some shoals and isolated rocks, among which the Ilhéu da Ribeira da Janela (‘islet of the window stream’) and the Ilhéu (‘islet’) and shoal of Porto Moniz stand out; 2. Ponta do Pargo, where a shoal stretches out into the sea, on which the waves break even in moderate winds, forcing boats to keep well away from the land in order to round it’.
Costa do Sul (southern coast)

The southern coast of Madeira, commonly called the Costa do Sul (‘south coast’), stretches from the sharp projection of the shoreline known as Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) to the tip of Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’). The southern region is very mild and picturesque, with more inlets and landing places. This, together with the shelter that the general mass of the island provides against the prevailing winds, means that ships and boats find on this coast the safety that the northern coast denies them, as in the bay of Funchal. This southern coast contains the parishes (*freguesias*) of the municipalities of Calheta, Ponta do Sol, Ribeira Brava, Câmara de Lobos, Funchal, Santa Cruz and Machico, with the exception of the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) and the northern shore of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), which belong to the last of those municipalities.

Mousinho de Albuquerque, already cited, says of the seaboard of the south coast (*Costa Sul*): ‘Starting from Ponta do Pargo, the southern coast of the island runs SE as far as Ponta do Jardim (‘garden point’), presenting along this stretch some small shoals and rocks very close to the coast, particularly off Paul do Mar and Jardim itself. The coast then follows an ESE direction as far as Ponta do Sol, and from there to Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), the southernmost point of the island, it runs in general, disregarding the lesser bends and points, in the direction ESE ¼ E. From Ponta da Cruz to Cabo Garajau (‘tern cape’), where the bay of Funchal lies, the direction of the coast is approximately E ¼ N; past this cape and as far as Ponta dos Picos da Atalaia (‘point of the watchtower peaks’) it becomes roughly ENE, and from there to Caniçal, at the root of Ponta de São Lourenço, the general direction of the coast is NNE ¼ E. Along almost the whole length of this coast the sea is deep and free of shoals, with the exception of the Ilhéu do Gorgulho (‘weevil islet’), the Baixa do Carneiro (‘ram shoal’), the fortified islet and the tip of Ponta de São Lourenço, which is surrounded by a number of isolated rocks and small rocky heads that the waters cover.’
Costa Ferreira (Dr António Aurélio da)

He was born in Funchal on 18 January 1879, the son of Francisco Joaquim da Costa Ferreira and Dona Teodolinda Augusta de Freitas da Costa Ferreira. He holds a licentiate in philosophy and is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in medicine of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He has been assistant in anatomy at the Lisbon Medical School (*Escola Médica de Lisboa*), supernumerary professor at one of the secondary schools (*liceus*) of the same city, director of the Casa Pia, and professor of general pedagogy and the history of education at the Teacher Training School (*Escola Normal*). He is a member of the Anthropological Society of Paris, the Portuguese Society of Natural Sciences, the Lisbon Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*), the Academy of Sciences of Portugal, the Institute of Coimbra, etc. He belongs to the Evolutionist Party and was minister of finance in the government headed by Duarte Leite. From a very early age he has devoted himself to anthropological studies, and he is today the Portuguese who best knows the branch of the natural sciences that deals with man and the human races. He has published various works in this field, among which we shall mention *Cranios Portugueses* (1898–1899), *La Capacité du Crâne et la Composition Ethnique probable du Peuple Portugais* (a paper presented to the Anthropological Society of Paris in 1895) and *O Povo Português sob o ponto de vista antropologico* (a lecture given at the Lisbon Geographical Society on 6 March 1909).

Dr Costa Ferreira has contributed to the *Jornal dos Medicos e Farmaceuticos*, the *Clinique Infantile*, the *Medicina Moderna*, the *Movimento Medico*, the *Anais da Academia Politecnica do Porto*, the *Boletim da Sociedade Portuguesa de Sciencias Naturais*, etc. He is one of the Madeirans who have rendered the finest service to science and who most adorn the gallery of Portuguese naturalists.

Dr Costa Ferreira was in Funchal in June 1922, travelling on from here to the Cape of Good Hope and then to Lourenço Marques, where he intended to organise the Anthropological Museum and carry out various studies in the province. He never began this work and these studies, however, for he took his own life in that Portuguese city in Africa on 15 July 1922, that is, only a very few days after arriving there. Parliament granted Costa Ferreira’s widow an annual pension of 3,600 escudos (written 3:600$00), and the Municipal Council of Funchal, at its meeting of 21 September 1922, gave the name of our ill-fated fellow countryman to the former Rua do Carmo (‘Carmel’).
Costa (João Sabino da)

He was born in Funchal on 14 October 1886 and was killed by the police of the capital on 1 February 1908, on suspicion of having been involved in the assassination of King Carlos I and the Crown Prince Louis Philippe, a crime in which it was later proved he had taken no part whatsoever.
He had been a soldier in the 5th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.º 5*), and at the time of his death was a shop worker.
The former ramp and paved lane of Cidrão now (1920) bear the name of João Sabino da Costa.
Costa (José Miguel Lamartine Prazeres da)
He was elected deputy for Madeira on 11 May 1919.
Costa (José Simão da)

He was born in Funchal and has lived in Brazil for many years. He completed a course at a higher institute in the United States of America and is a member of the Academia Latina das Ciencias, Artes e Belas Letras of Paris and of various literary societies in Brazil. Besides contributing to various newspapers, he published *Cultura intensiva do coqueiro. Seu valor economico*, Rio de Janeiro, 1913, and *A região Amazonica. Seu presente, passado e futuro*, Rio de Janeiro, 1913. He died in Brazil in June 1923.
Costa (Monsignor Hipólito da Purificação das Angústias e)

This Brazilian priest, who possessed a considerable fortune, died in Funchal on 9 January 1912. Shortly before his death he disposed verbally of the property he owned in Brazil and in Goa. His last wishes were contested, and a lawsuit on the matter went before the Brazilian courts. This case is the subject of the pamphlet *Uma questão de direito internacional*, published in Lisbon in 1913 by its author, Dr Vicente Ferrer, which refers to the stay and death of Monsignor Hipólito Costa in Funchal.
Costa Pereira (Luiz da)

Luiz da Costa Pereira was an illustrious Madeiran who distinguished himself in several fields of human endeavour, yet his name is almost entirely unknown here, although only 26 years have passed since his death. Cruelly stricken by adversity, he spent his last years in an obscure and forgotten existence, locked in a dreadful struggle with illness, poverty and old age.

Luiz da Costa was born in Funchal on 17 August 1818, and in this city he took the preparatory courses required for enrolment at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). After a brilliant course of study, in which he won several prizes, he graduated from the faculty of mathematics in 1844. His name was mentioned alongside those of Teixeira de Vasconcelos, João de Lemos, José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage, Casal Ribeiro, Couto Monteiro, Gonçalves Lima, Xavier Monteiro, etc., his contemporaries at the University, with whom he stood shoulder to shoulder in the cultivation of the sciences and letters.

In 1851 he was appointed a teacher at the Funchal Lyceum (*Liceu do Funchal*), a post he held for only a few years. He then served as schools commissioner in the district of Braga, where he likewise did not stay long. A fickle and restless spirit, he failed to make use of the gifts with which nature had enriched his exceptional intellect. That is why Bulhão Pato said of him, with complete justice: ‘I never knew anyone who combined so many faculties, nor anyone who strove more doggedly to destroy them. It was not mere aptitude that he possessed; they were lofty faculties. A blessed constitution, powerful in everything, even in the strength with which it managed to hide in the shadows a light that should have shone among the most brilliant.’

Luiz da Costa Pereira settled in Lisbon and for many years devoted himself almost exclusively to the theatre, for which he had a decided vocation. There he revealed the brilliant gifts of his extraordinary talent as actor and author, rehearsal director, technical director and royal commissioner of the Teatro Maria II, and as professor of declamation and the art of acting at the Royal Conservatory of Lisbon (*Real Conservatório de Lisboa*). Camilo Castelo Branco said: ‘This is that Luiz da Costa who in my youth was the symbol, the master of the stage; in this brain pulsed all the talents that create the relentless passions of tragedy; from this man’s breast burst the cries that lifted audiences into a frenzy of triumph’.

Luiz da Costa translated and adapted several foreign plays for the Portuguese stage and wrote the book *Rudimentos da arte dramatica*, of which he published only the first part, in a volume of 240 pages.

In his youth he cultivated poetry with extraordinary success and was one of the contributors to the well-known and brilliant review *O Trovador*, where his colleagues included João de Lemos and other poets of equal stature. The great Castilho refers to him in the loftiest terms of praise. In the literary traditions of Coimbra, the gathering known as the S. João Poético became famous. It was later immortalised by João de Lemos’s inimitable description of it: six poets met in intimate company and recited the poems they had written beforehand for the occasion. It was there that, impromptu and in homage to Castilho, they composed a sextain, which later became very well known, in which each poet wrote one line:
On the wings of poetry / Friendship brought us here. / We sang on lyres of gold / The hopes of youth, / And to the cries of ‘Spring’ / We sent a fond remembrance.
Among these acclaimed poets was Luiz da Costa Pereira, who, immediately after João de Lemos, recited the poem *Branca Alvarinho*.

Besides the works already mentioned, Costa Pereira wrote the novel *Misterios de Almas*, the book *Reflexos* (‘Reflections’), in prose and verse, and the scientific work *Leituras sobre astronomia*, and he contributed extensively to the leading literary and scientific reviews of his time. It is recorded that his unpublished papers included two works of merit: *A Natureza* and *A Religião Democratica*.
He died in Lisbon, poor and in the most complete obscurity, on 18 January 1893.
Costa Torres (Dom José da)
Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão was succeeded in the episcopal chair of Funchal by the prelate Dom José da Costa Torres.
He was born in the city of Setúbal on 11 August 1741 and held a doctorate in canon law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*).
He was confirmed as Bishop of Madeira by Pius VI in November 1786 and took possession of this diocese on 18 September 1787.

As prelate of Funchal, he marked his time on the island by the persecution he waged against freemasonry, in agreement with the governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) and under orders issued by the central government. It is nevertheless claimed that he exceeded the orders he had received, so that the government in Lisbon itself had to intervene against the excesses committed by the prelate. Among those persecuted was the dean of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), Dr João Francisco Lopes Rocha, who wrote a long letter on the matter to the minister José Seabra da Silva, complaining of the abuses of power committed by Dom José Torres. The letter is a document of interest on many counts and was published in 1822, in London, in the *Campeão Portuguez*. On 22 June 1796 he was transferred to the see of Elvas. When he was already preparing to leave Madeira, he had to bring forward his departure in haste and abandon the island, as a document of the time says, ‘on the night of 6 October 1796, without taking leave of anyone, nor of the Most Holy Sacrament: and to this day the reason for this contrived embarkation by night and by back ways is unknown’.
In 1806 he was appointed Archbishop of Braga, and he died there some years later, at the age of 72.
See Álvares de Nóbrega (Francisco).
Coasts

The mountain range which, with lofty summits and without a break, runs the length of Madeira from east to west, clearly divides the northern coast, better known as the north coast (*Costa do Norte*), from the southern coast, commonly called the Costa do Sul. Between these two coasts lies the interior, an extremely mountainous region of very broken terrain, with the exception of the plateau of the Paul da Serra.
Old customs

The old customs and ancient usages of Madeira call for long and careful study, which will receive our particular attention in various articles of this *Elucidário*. Here we shall merely give a brief account of some facts that characterise many of these customs and that show us, above all, the clear traces of the old feudalism which, in some of its nuances, long survived among the old nobility of this archipelago. Our conquests in Morocco and the holding of the cities and strongholds we had taken had a great influence on the customs of our country and on the private lives of its inhabitants. They bred an exaggerated taste for risky enterprises and for unknown and unforeseen adventures, which showed itself in territorial expansion and the enlargement of the overseas dominions, in the quest for unknown regions and ‘seas never sailed before’, in the hallowed phrase of our epic poet. In proportion to its size, no Portuguese land contributed to our struggles in North Africa as much as the Madeiran archipelago. Its donataries organised great expeditions, with fleets of dozens of ships and many hundreds of men and horses, in which a considerable number of noblemen and knights took a very active part. All this was at the expense of the expeditionaries themselves, without the least cost to the mother country, and often lasted for months on end, during which they performed the most valiant deeds, reaching the point of heroism and recklessness. The Madeiran nobility gained a reputation for courage and daring, while at the same time growing vain of its noble origins and of the independence it enjoyed on its manorial lands. It committed abuses and excesses which the almost unlimited power of the donataries had failed to curb, and which even the authority of the monarch could not correct or restrain, because of the distance between this island and the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). All this had a decisive influence on local customs, as some of the facts we are about to cite, recorded in the old chronicles of this archipelago, eloquently testify: the castellated manor house that the turbulent Garcia Homem de Sousa, Zarco’s son-in-law, built on his lands at Santo António, of which traces still remain, for the bloody struggles he waged against his brothers-in-law; the barbarous and cruel revenge that the first donatary of Machico, Tristão Vaz Teixeira, took on Diogo Barradas to avenge an affront to his house; the tragic death of Dona Aldonça Delgado, murdered by her husband Bartolomeu Perestrelo, fourth captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Porto Santo, so that he could marry his cousin Dona Solanda, with whom he was having a love affair; the murder committed by Garcia Perestrelo, who was beheaded for it; the violent and spectacular abduction of Dona Isabel de Abreu by António Gonçalves da Câmara and the struggles and quarrels that followed; and the cases of murder and scandalous rape that Dr Álvaro de Azevedo relates in note XXIV to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), adding ‘that here too there were curious types of swaggering noblemen, whose lewd adventures, brutal pranks and shameless crimes tradition has not yet forgotten’. Also characteristic of these old customs were the cavalcades, cane games (*jogos de canas*, equestrian tournament with thrown canes) and showy skirmishes of Lançarote Teixeira, the hunting reserve (coutada) of João Teixeira and his lavish hunts, the adventures and feats of muscular strength of Marcos Braga and António de Carvalhal, the contests and challenges between Pedro Ribeiro and Domingos de Braga, etc. The donataries of Funchal, seemingly wishing to rival the luxury and magnificence of the court, lived in refined pomp and showy grandeur. They organised costly military expeditions and sent the richest gifts to monarchs and pontiffs, as Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the Magnificent, did in the embassy to Leo X, and they appeared at the festivities of the royal palace and at princely weddings with such luxury and display that they dazzled everyone, etc. This excessive love of luxury and grandeur was reflected in the Madeiran nobility, leading it into a useless and idle life spent in Funchal or at court, leaving its lands and manor houses in the care and management of none too scrupulous stewards. Striking examples of this are the games, hunts and cavalcades, the skirmishes, contests and fights, and the showy festivities, typified by the banquet at the wedding of António Gonçalves da Câmara and Isabel de Abreu, etc., etc. Before long a large number of houses were ruined and their revenues mortgaged, reducing many to a shameful and wretched existence. Madeira had a considerable number of entailed estates and entails (*morgado*), as no other region of the country did, and so the number of families leading an almost useless and always unproductive life multiplied; it was even claimed that two-thirds of the land of this archipelago was subject to this extensive and harmful entailment. The original *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) evolved and was transformed into the well-known *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant), which gave Madeiran customs a very distinctive character, above all in the private lives of the tenants and farmhands. The former *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) became lord of the land and holder of an entail, acquiring, in enforced idleness, habits and tendencies that did little credit to his ancestral lineage. Towards the end of the 16th century a transformation in Madeiran life and customs began. More frequent communication with the mother country and with foreign lands, the growth of trade with many outsiders residing on this island, the departure of countless noblemen and commoners for the wars and adventurous life of India and Brazil, from which they returned with profound changes in their private way of life, the influence of Spanish rule and yet other causes contributed notably to this transformation, which became more marked in the course of the 17th and 18th centuries.
Couceiro (António Rogério Gromicho)

On 1 June 1856 Brigadier António Rogério Gromicho Couceiro took office as civil governor of this district. A month later the first cases appeared of the terrible cholera epidemic that, in four months, killed about ten thousand Madeirans. Gromicho Couceiro was a true Providence for Madeira in the most anguished trials this island has ever endured. A man of rare energy, of intelligent and fruitful initiative, and of prompt and immediate decision at the most critical and awkward moments, he managed as far as possible to ward off the evils that overwhelmed the unfortunate inhabitants of this archipelago. He won the admiration of his contemporaries and a name crowned by so many good works that the fame of the outstanding services he rendered selflessly to Madeira still lives on in tradition today. Justice requires us to recall that Couceiro had a valuable helper, among others, in the illustrious Madeiran Dr António da Luz Pita, then deputy for this island. Being in Lisbon when the epidemic broke out, he obtained substantial relief from the central government, which he himself accompanied to Madeira. Here, as a distinguished physician and a man of great prestige and influence, he rendered his fellow islanders the most notable services, particularly in organising the clinical and hospital work. The history of that calamitous period, which left in popular tradition the memory of the most Dantesque horrors, has still to be written; nor has the tribute due to Couceiro’s memory for the great services he rendered to this island yet been paid. (See Cholera in 1856 and 1910.)

Couceiro was born in Elvas on 13 March 1807 and died in Lisbon, with the rank of field marshal, on 22 June 1862. He graduated in mathematics from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), was a professor at the Polytechnic Academy of Porto and was minister of war in 1859.

He also held the post of military commander of Madeira, which he combined with the office of civil governor. He left this island on 3 September 1857, and represented this archipelago in parliament in the legislature of 1858–1859.
Coutinho (family)
This family surname derives from Luís Fernandes de Matos Coutinho, who came to Madeira around 1580 and had a large trading house here. This Luís Coutinho was the son of the knight
António Vaz de Matos, who accompanied Afonso de Albuquerque to India.
The chapel of Our Lady of Quietude (*Nossa Senhora da Quietação*), in Santo António, was founded in 1670 by Lourenço de Matos Coutinho, who was probably descended from the said Luís Coutinho.
Coutinho (Dom Manuel)

The diocesan prelate Dom José de Sousa de Castelo Branco having left Madeira in June 1715 and resigned the bishopric in 1721, John V appointed Dom Manuel Coutinho Bishop of Funchal on 25 November 1722. He was confirmed by the Holy See only on 19 February 1725, however, because of the disagreements then arising between the Portuguese government and the Roman Curia.

Dom Manuel Coutinho was born in Vila Nova de Anços in 1671, the son of Nuno Álvares Pereira and Dona Inês Micaela Pereira, wealthy people of noble rank who had the seat of their entailed estate (*morgadio*) there. He took his doctorate in theology at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1699 and received episcopal consecration from the Patriarch Dom Tomás de Almeida on 13 May 1725.

He left Lisbon at the beginning of June 1725, but as the warship carrying him called at Mazagan, he performed episcopal functions there for a few days. He reached Funchal only on 22 July of that year, when he took charge of the affairs of this diocese.

In the Madeiran chronicles we were able to consult, we found few references to his episcopal work among us. After 15 years as bishop he was appointed Bishop of Lamego, but he remained in Madeira until 25 February 1741, when he left for the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). He never took possession of his new diocese: on his way to the city of Lamego, death overtook him in the town (*vila*) of Soure, on 7 August 1742.
Coutinho (Dom Manuel Pereira)
). He was appointed governor-general of this archipelago on 22 November 1609. When his term ended, the diocesan bishop, Dom Friar Lourenço de Távora, acted as interim governor-general.
Coutinho, however, later became governor-general of Angola.
Coutinho (Francisco de Vasconcelos)

We know of this Madeiran poet through the references to him in Inocêncio Francisco da Silva’s *Diccionario Bibliographico* and in one of Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo’s notes to the *Saudades*. There we read that he was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in canon law and that he was born towards the end of the 17th century, since he wrote sonnets on the death of Peter II, which occurred in 1706, and a dramatic eulogy in honour of the governor and captain-general of the island of Madeira, João de Saldanha da Gama, when the latter’s term ended in 1718. He died after 1729, for in that year he published the following two works: *Feudo do Parnaso*, dedicated to John V, and *Hecatombe metrico*, consecrated to the Virgin, a short religious poem in a hundred sonnets, both printed in Lisbon, 1729. He also composed eight more sonnets on the death of Peter II, one to John V and four to various personages; *Effeitos de hum arrependimento*, in tercets; and the eulogy already mentioned, entitled *Residencia do Governador e Capitão General da Ilha da Madeira João de Saldanha da Gama*, performed by the nuns of Santa Clara on his departure. These works were published with the second edition of *Feudo do Parnaso* and *Hecatombe metrico* in a single volume (Lisbon, 1773). Before all of these, other poems of his had been collected in the *Fenix renascida*, vol. 1, pp. 1–32, and vol. II, pp. 220–251 (Lisbon 1716 and 1717)’.
We can add that he was the son of Lourenço de Matos Coutinho, a licentiate in law known as the Knight, and of Dona Mariana de Ornelas e Vasconcelos.
On pp. 52 ff. of vol. II of the *Arquivo Historico da Madeira* there is an interesting article containing new and valuable biographical data on Francisco de Vasconcelos Coutinho.
Coutinho (João Gonçalves da Câmara)

His appointment as governor and captain-general of Madeira dates from 19 August 1777, and he took up the post on 15 September of the same year. He sent the central government several interesting reports on the indiscipline of the garrison troops, the state of the fortifications, the administration of justice and other public services. He had a serious conflict with Bishop Dom Gaspar Brandão over the imprisonment of the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) António Xavier Pimentel, which was ended by the intervention of the government in Lisbon. Extensive correspondence was exchanged on this matter between the minister
Martinho de Melo, the governor and the prelate.

As some of his predecessors had already done, he insistently asked the home government to define with complete precision the powers and jurisdiction of the captains-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira), in order to avoid the conflicts that sometimes arose between certain authorities of this archipelago.
Couto (family)

This family surname probably derives from Joane Anes de Couto Cardoso, who held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands at Paul and Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’), and founded the chapel of St Maurus (*Santo Amaro*) in the latter place.
Cabbage (Brassica oleracea)

This crucifer, which is thought to have originated on the sea cliffs of England and the French coast of the Channel, is widely cultivated everywhere as a food plant, and is represented in Madeira by the varieties *acephala*, *capitata* and *Botrytis*. The first variety includes the *couve rinchão* or *vaqueira* and the *couve tronchuda*, both without a head; the second, the *couve murciana*, the headed cabbage, the *imperial*, the *alcanhão*, the *pão de açúcar*, etc.; and the third, the cauliflower and broccoli. The cabbages of the first variety and the headed cabbage are grown from seed produced on the island, whereas the other forms always come from seed brought from Portugal and abroad. In the cauliflower it is not the leaves that are used but the more or less fleshy inflorescences, whose flowers are almost always abortive.
The cabbages of the first and second varieties are used not only to make soup but also for cooking, cut into small pieces, with maize flour, to which they give a pleasant flavour.
