Couve da Rocha
Vernacular name of *Sinapidendron rupestre*, a crucifer peculiar to Madeira that grows on the cliffs between Entroza and Seixal (‘pebble shore’).
Covões (peak)
A small mountain elevation and picturesque village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas.
Fish traps
Traps designed to catch fish or crustaceans in the shallower waters of the Madeiran sea.
The various forms in use at present can be reduced to four main types: the red mullet fish trap (*covo*), the moray trap, the shrimp trap and the *mujona* for fish and lobsters.

The first is made of giant reed (*cana de roca*) and is polyhedral in shape; it is customary to put fragments of white, shiny crockery inside it, which easily deceive and attract the red mullet. The second is cylindrical and built of wooden laths, with openings at both ends, and catches all four species of moray of the Madeiran coast without distinction.

The shrimp trap, which is set farther from the coast than any of the others, is made of rush and is roughly the shape of a truncated cone, with the opening for the crustaceans in its larger base. Finally there is the *mujona*, introduced to Porto Santo under that name by fishermen from the Algarve who came in 1910 to set up a tuna trap (armação, a fixed trap-net) on that island. It is used for inshore fish and lobsters, is made of iron rod or cane and has the shape of a half-spheroid.
Craca (Balanus tintinnabulum)

A cirripede crustacean of the family Balanidae, relatively common on the coastal rocks of the islands of Madeira and the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*). It is found in certain spots and lives at the low-tide line, preferring places exposed to the heavy pounding of the waves. Although it very rarely appears in the market, it is edible and is rightly prized as a tasty shellfish. To gather it, people use a striking tool called a *craqueira* (iron tool for prising barnacles off rocks), since the shell that covers it is firmly attached to the rock on which it lives.
It is one of the 13 cirripedes recorded by C. Darwin as Madeiran in his monograph on this order of crustaceans.
Craqueira
An iron tool with a wooden handle, used to gather the shellfish called *craca*.
Crater
The few easily recognisable craters in Madeira are not found in the highest parts of the island, where they certainly once existed, but in the middle and lower regions.

The best known of the Madeiran craters is that of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), about 600 metres above sea level, whose highest point stands 60 or 70 metres above the surrounding land. It is shallow, holds water in winter, and some plants typical of waterlogged places grow inside it.

There is also a crater at Porto Moniz, near Terra Chã (‘flat land’), and another at Fanal (‘beacon’), the latter being a double crater. The Porto Moniz crater, like that of Santo António da Serra, has a cone, a feature not found at Fanal.

Near Caniço (‘reed’) there are three cones with imperfect craters, and at Caniçal (‘reed bed’) there is a cone with a crater on one side. On the Pico da Irandaia, west of Funchal and near the church of São Roque (St Roch), traces of craters are also found.
The craters of Santo António da Serra, Porto Moniz and Fanal are known as *lagoas* (lagoons).

Some geologists regard the Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) as a crater, others as an erosion valley. Charles Lyell, who holds the latter view, states in his *Elements of Geology* that he found no signs of volcanic action in the Curral, and that this locality, like the Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’) and the Serra de Água, is one of the deep valleys radiating from the most mountainous region of the island.
Carnation (Dianthus caryophyllus)

A plant of the family Caryophyllaceae, widely cultivated in Madeiran gardens, of which there are many varieties. In dry places at Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and in Funchal, *Dianthus prolifer* is not uncommon; it is a wild plant whose flowers look rather like small carnations.
Cravo de Burro
Vernacular name of *Tagetes patulus* and *T. erectus*, tubuliflorous Compositae native to Mexico and cultivated in the gardens of Funchal.
Cravo (fish)
See Peixe cravo.
Popular beliefs

Although civilisation has swept away many popular beliefs once common in Madeira, some still survive among us today, and they seem to us worth mentioning because they are deeply rooted in the minds of our people. Belief in sorceresses, in witches, in the evil eye, in bad air (*ar mau*) and in the power that certain individuals have to heal with words or to foretell the future by means of cards is found not only in the countryside but also in the city. It is worth noting that there are people considered educated who have not yet entirely abandoned certain superstitions handed down to us by the past.

In the popular view, sorceresses make it their business to work every kind of evil spell. They sometimes appear in the form of a stone jar rolling along the paths; if anyone touches it, it turns into a woman, who forces the person who caused the transformation to carry her home on their back. The chief task of witches is to suck the blood of children at night, although this evil can be prevented by placing an open pair of scissors under the pillow of the person one wishes to protect.

Campo Grande (‘great field’), on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), is one of the places chosen for the gatherings of the sorceresses, over which the devil presides, often taking the form of a goat. The sign of the cross, made with devotion, is enough, they say, to drive off the king of hell should we have the misfortune to meet him on our way, whatever form he may take. The words ‘tosca, marrosca, olhos na cara e freio na bôca’ [TN: a charm; roughly ‘tosca, marrosca, eyes in the face and bit in the mouth’], spoken aloud, are said to be extraordinarily effective in warding off any sorceress or sorceresses who seek to harm us or amuse themselves at our expense.

The will-o’-the-wisps that appear over ground containing rotting matter are, the people say, the work of sorceresses, who have no fear of revealing their presence anywhere, especially at night. Sorceresses are as a rule old and ugly women, and it is believed in Madeira, as in Portugal, that their power lies chiefly in a ball of thread that the devil gives each of them at her initiation. The case of the prophets of Porto Santo, related in all seriousness on p. 55 of Gaspar Frutuoso’s ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), is attributed by that writer to ‘deceptions or wiles of Satan’. On p. 180 of the same work we read the account of a struggle that a cleric had with the devil near the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Neves (Our Lady of the Snows), a struggle from which the devil would have emerged victorious had the cleric not crossed himself or invoked the name of Jesus on realising that his life was in danger.

The belief that certain people have the power, or the knowledge, to foretell the future or uncover hidden things using nothing but playing cards is perhaps the most widespread on the island. Not a few women take up the trade of telling fortunes to satisfy the curiosity of the simpletons who believe their deceptions.

Elsewhere in this Elucidário we give some information on the art of healing with words (see Bucho encostado, Evil eye and Folk medicine). As for the bad air, all we can say is that it makes itself felt chiefly at night and has the property of harming any people and animals exposed to it. If, out in the countryside, you hear dogs howling at night for no apparent reason, it is because the bad air is passing, bringing on the evil eye’s wasting spell (*quebranto*) and various diseases.

Of the superstitions of our people we will add that a broken mirror foretells misfortune. Lending a sieve, or selling salt or yeast after sunset; kissing someone who is holding a lighted candle; staying at table while a funeral passes; and starting a job on a Tuesday or a Friday: these are things that many people, not only in the countryside but also in Funchal, refrain from doing, supposing that harm might come to them from it. Many people consider the number thirteen ill-fated, and if that number of people sit down at a table, it is said that one of them will die within the year. The owl and the *patagarro* are birds of ill omen, and so is a hen that has the bad habit of crowing like a cockerel.

It is on the eves of St John and St Peter that anyone may learn part of the destiny in store for them. An unmarried young man or woman who, at the hour of the Ave Marias, fills their mouth with water and listens will learn, from the first man’s or woman’s name they hear, the name of the person to whom they are one day to join their fate. The same result can be obtained by lots cast into water, if one of them opens during the night. An egg dropped into a glass can also tell a great deal if we leave it exposed to the air on St John’s night; and if on that night the water reflects the image of a person as the clock strikes 12, it is because that person’s life is assured until the feast of the same saint the following year!

The *beatas* are branches of trees and shrubs gathered on the morning of St John’s Day, when, so the people say, every plant has virtue except the *malfurada*. Placed at the door or inside the house, they cancel the effects of the evil eye and ward off many of the spells to which humanity is subject. Of all the plants found in Madeira, rosemary is the one most used to combat the devil’s wiles.

Besides the superstitions we have just mentioned, there are others that still people the imagination of our islanders, but for brevity’s sake we do not record them here. In any case, it cannot be said that the Madeiran people are among the most superstitious, or that their credulity is in direct proportion to their ignorance.

In Europe, even in the most advanced countries, there are more superstitions and popular credulities than in Madeira, as can be seen from several works on the occult sciences and popular beliefs published in the 19th century by various Portuguese and foreign authors.
Crepusculo (O)
A literary newspaper published from 15 February to 31 July 1865, running to 12 issues. It was written by pupils of the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city.
*Crista de galo* (*Amarantus caudalus*)

A plant of the family Amaranthaceae, cultivated in the gardens of Funchal and growing wild in Câmara de Lobos and other localities. It is native to tropical Africa and America, and has drooping scarlet spikes, the terminal one very long. The name *crista de galo* is also sometimes given to *Amarantus paniculatus* and *Celosia cristata*.
Christ (chapel)

In the town (*vila*) of Machico, on the left bank of the stream that runs through it and a short distance from the parish church, stands the old chapel of Cristo (Christ). It is known today as the chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*), and it was also called the chapel of the Misericórdia, because it once belonged to that charitable institution, which had its seat in the town. It is one of the oldest chapels in

Madeira, and some claim that it was the first place of worship built on this island. The legend of Machim, which we shall deal with elsewhere, tells that when the discoverers landed on the beaches of Machico they found the graves of Robert Machin and Anne Arfet, together with a simple epitaph that recounted the adventure of the unhappy lovers and asked that a chapel dedicated to Christ be built on that spot. If we were to believe this romantic legend, the origin of the chapel’s foundation would lie in that ill-fated adventure. In his learned and most interesting notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo reduced the Machim affair to its proper proportions, and after this exhaustive study it is no longer permissible to accept the possibility of the legend, as various authors, according to Francisco Manuel de Melo, seek to describe it in poetic terms.

What seems to be established is that on the very day they first set foot on the virgin soil of this island, the discoverers had a makeshift altar put up, and one of the Franciscan friars who sailed in Zarco’s fleet celebrated the sacrifice of the Mass there, in thanksgiving for the important discovery they had just made. The discoverers vowed to build a church on this spot, and this is the true origin of the foundation of the chapel of Cristo. ‘And since,’ says Frutuoso, ‘the first Mass said in this place was that of the Visitation, which falls on 2 July, this church became a house of the Misericórdia’.

Simple and modest as it is, this small church is a true historic monument commemorating the discovery. It must be regarded and venerated as such by the inhabitants of this island, and its preservation through the ages is a sacred and patriotic duty for every Madeiran who cherishes the good name of his homeland.

Of the original building perhaps only the pointed doorway and the crosses on the façade survive, and these form the characteristic part of the little church. The great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803 left it in complete ruin, and in the following year it was almost entirely rebuilt by the brethren of the Misericórdia. Care was taken to preserve its original architectural character, as was also done when it was rebuilt once more about half a century ago.

‘Not only was what remained of the original preserved’, says the annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘but in the new work the old design has also been followed. The portico is the original one, with some new stones carved like the old; the only ornament on them is a row of crosses of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), which garland the doorway and are incontrovertible proof that the church was built by that Order’. This second rebuilding, however, was only completed in the period from 1880 to 1883, and in that year the solemn blessing of the chapel took place, the building having then been completely restored both inside and out.

The chapel houses the venerated image of the Lord of Miracles, the object of a great pilgrimage held on 9 October, to which thousands of people flock from every part of the island. This revered image was swept away by the torrent in the flash flood of 1803 and carried out to the open sea. There it was found by an American full-rigged ship bound for our port, which took it on board; it was later handed over to Funchal Cathedral (Sé Catedral do Funchal). It remained there until 15 April 1813, when it was taken to its small sanctuary in Machico, which had just then been restored.

Cruz do Carvalho (chapel)

We have found somewhere a reference to a chapel ‘situated at the spot of Cruz do Carvalho (‘oak cross’), so called, on a property named Quintinha (‘little estate’), and built in 1767 by order of Captain João Francisco de Freitas Esmeraldo, professed knight of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*). Cruz (peak)
A peak 936 m high, lying between the parishes of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and Estreito. From its summit the eye takes in a broad and beautiful panorama over several parishes.
Cruz (peak)
A hill in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’), about a hundred metres high.
Cruz (peak)

A mountainous height close to the coast, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), about 263 metres high, from which there is a striking view over the seaboard and the amphitheatre of Funchal. Cruz (point)

A little to the east of Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’) and to the west of the Ilhéu do Gorgulho (‘weevil islet’), on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), lies the so-called Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), which many regard as the western limit of the bay of Funchal. A small redoubt once stood there; it is now dismantled. In its vicinity there is an important fish-canning factory.

Red Cross

The creation of a delegation of the Red Cross (*Cruz Vermelha*) in this city was due to the initiative of the late Madeiran physician Eliseu de Sousa Drumond. Funchal is indebted to him not only for this initiative but also for the diligent and persevering efforts he selflessly devoted to setting up the delegation, and for the excellent direction he gave to all its first services.

The first meeting of the organising committee took place on 14 November 1914. Shortly afterwards the Viscount (*visconde*) of Geraz de Lima was elected president of the board, and he always showed the greatest zeal and dedication to the society’s progress.

The first physicians appointed to direct the medical and surgical services of the Red Cross delegation were Dr Eliseu de Sousa Drumond and Dr Nuno de Vasconcelos Pôrto. They at once opened elementary nursing courses to teach and train nurses of both sexes, and within a short time they had prepared staff qualified enough to carry out the most urgent and basic services required. Some stretchers were then obtained and the first stretcher-bearers enlisted, and these received suitable instruction.

It had become essential to house the delegation in suitable premises, where all its services could be centralised and accommodated and where a permanent medical first-aid post could be set up. The Society achieved this legitimate aim by renting a building in the Rua dos Netos, and the delegation is housed there today. Its first-aid post, where surgical operations, dressings, various medical treatments, etc., are carried out every day, has rendered valuable services, and the public flocks there to take advantage of the benefits offered by this worthy Society. It is only right to highlight the way in which the whole staff of the first-aid post – the nurses and the medical director – have carried out the duties so selflessly entrusted to them. It is to Dr João Albino Rodrigues de Sousa, head of these services, that the first-aid post owes the good name it has earned here in Madeira since it opened at the beginning of 1917.
Cuckoo (Cuculus canorus)
A climbing bird that occasionally reaches these islands, almost always in spring.
Useful cucurbits

Despite its length, we have thought it right to reproduce in full the excellent article on the cucurbits cultivated on this island which C. A. de Meneses, co-author of this *Elucidario*, published in an agricultural journal. It contains curious and interesting information that may be of considerable use to Madeiran farmers, since this group of plants is widely grown in every parish of the archipelago.

‘The useful cucurbits grown on a large scale in Madeira are six in number, namely: the bottle gourd, the cucumber, the black squash, the Machado squash, the *boganga* and the chayote. Because they grow so quickly, need so little care and adapt so readily to the great majority of soils, all these plants are rightly prized by the island’s inhabitants, who find in their fruits a source of income and a substantial and abundant food for a good part of the year. Although these plants are known outside the country, we shall give some information about each of them, in order gradually to make known the principal products of Madeira and the methods adopted here in growing the various useful plants.

The bottle gourd (*Lagenaria vulgaris*), native to tropical Asia and Africa, is an annual, pubescent plant with soft, flaccid, musk-scented leaves and white, monoecious, star-shaped flowers. Botanists distinguish different varieties within this species, all based on the shape or size of the fruit, and the following three occur in Madeira: var. *Gourda*, with large fruits (30 to 60 centimetres), broader at the top than at the bottom and somewhat approaching the shape of an hourglass; var. *pusilla*, with fruits of the same shape but smaller (8 to 18 centimetres); and var. *clavata*, with very large fruits, which may exceed 1 metre in length and are generally club-shaped.

The gourds are used for soup and sometimes for preserves. Once ripe, thoroughly dried and properly cleaned inside, they can serve to hold liquids. Gourds are fit for this last use when, on being shaken, the seeds are found to be perfectly loose inside the fruit. The fruits of the *pusilla* variety are much used by country people to carry wine and brandy on pilgrimages.

The bottle gourd is propagated solely from seed, sown from January to March. Some farmers dig trenches, which they call *caseiras*, into which they drop the seeds and where only the plants worth keeping are left. Others simply dig small holes for the same purpose, but only when the soil has been worked some time before to receive some other crop. The plants remain in the very place where they come up, unless there is some advantage in transplanting them to a better spot because the soil has not been properly prepared, or for any other reason.

Layering is not practised with the cucurbit we are discussing, which needs trees, pergolas or some other supports to grow well. The fruits appear from September to October in each of the varieties we have described.

The cucumber (*Cucumis sativus*), a native of north-western India, has been known in southern Europe since remote times. In Madeira, where it is widely grown, it is sown in March and April, and in some places from January to May. Sowing is done in seedbeds (*mantas* or *caseiras*), in which only the plants to be kept are left standing. When these reach a certain size, cane trellises or other supports are built so that the stems do not trail along the ground. If sowing is done outside the seedbeds, it is best for the young plants to be transplanted with their clod of soil, a precaution that should also be taken with the other cucurbits found on the island when they undergo the same operation.

The species we are discussing is annual, like the preceding one. It is seldom layered, and it bears fruit from May to September. Madeiran cucumbers are oblong, large and sometimes slightly curved; their flesh is greenish and their skin turns yellow when ripe, so the plant belongs to the variety *flavus*.

The black squash (*Cucurbita moschata*), which seems to have originated in the East, is easily recognised by its very rough leaves, blotched with white and bearing 5 pointed lobes. Its large fruits, dark green and finally yellow, vary greatly in shape and have blunt longitudinal ridges, more or less pronounced.

This cucurbit is usually propagated by cuttings, or *baraços* as the Madeirans call them, which are generally planted in March and April in trenches or seedbeds (*caseiras*) of varying depth. The *baraços* are layered by bending them at the base and making them grow in the direction opposite to the one they had before. Propagation by seed is also practised, and the plants may either remain where they came up or be moved to a more suitable place. If the soil has been properly worked, trenches are sometimes unnecessary.

Black squashes, also known as Guinea squashes (*aboboras da Guiné*), are normally spherical, but there are also elliptical, obovate and pear-shaped ones (*abobora cabeça*, ‘head squash’), as well as club-shaped ones (*abobora da rocha*, ‘cliff squash’). In some of these fruits the ridges that characterise the typical form are only very slightly pronounced.

If it is true, as Madeiran farmers say, that the squash plants with pear-shaped and club-shaped fruits reproduce their characters from seed, they ought to be treated as a variety, rather than as mere variations of the spherical-fruited form, as we believe they have been regarded until now. Naudin’s *Courge berbère* or *bédouine* corresponds to the club-shaped form, while the *Melonée* or *Courge muscade des Marseillais* seems to correspond to the obovate form.

The black squash needs pergolas to grow well, but here and there we see it growing and fruiting without any support. When properly selected, it produces delicious fruits, which are eaten boiled in salted water when young, or in soup once fully grown. Yellow squash cooked with rice is a dish much enjoyed by Madeirans. Although the squash fruits mainly in September and October, it can be said that there is no shortage of squashes for the population from August to January.

As the squash is a monoecious plant, some farmers pollinate the female flowers by hand to increase the yield. Squashes intended to be eaten once yellow are picked when the yellowing is already clearly visible and placed in sunny spots. If care is taken to turn them every few days, they will keep for a long time.
The cucurbit we are describing is an annual, like the preceding ones, but it can exceptionally last two years without fresh layering, as we have had occasion to observe.

The Machado squash (*Cucurbita Pepo*), which is thought to originate from the Caspian Sea region, differs from the previous species in having leaves without white blotches and fruits with ten well-marked ridges. The Madeiran specimens belong to the artificial group created by Naudin, the *Citrouilles proprement dites*, which is characterised by large or medium-sized fruits that are ovate, obovate or elliptical.

This species is propagated solely by seed, which is sown from January to March. Only exceptionally are the plants layered. The fruits are most plentiful from August to October, and their flavour is much less pleasant than that of the black squashes.

The Machado squash, which some call *Catôa*, is rare in the low-lying parts of the island and only becomes abundant above 150 or 200 metres. It is grown in *caseiras* or outside them, and it grows among the cane plantations, over walls or supported on trellises. According to Brotero, the *abóbora porqueira*, the *abóbora menina*, the *abóbora moganga* and the *abóbora chita* or *chilacaiota*, cultivated in Portugal, are varieties of *Cucurbita Pepo*.

The *bogangueira* (*cucurbita melanosperma*), native to Asia and introduced from Tenerife in 1836 or 1837, is an extremely common species in both the north and the south of the island. Its leaves are 5-lobed, sometimes somewhat rough, with shallow, rounded lobes; its flowers are yellow and its fruits large and elliptical, without any ridges. Richard Thomas Lowe recognised two varieties of this species: the variety *picta*, with fruits speckled green and white, and the variety *lactea*, with entirely white fruits. The Madeirans call the fruits of the first variety *bogangas rajadas* (striped bogangas) and those of the second *bogangas brancas* (white bogangas).

The word *boganga*, from which *bogangueira* derives, is exclusively Madeiran and seems to be a corruption of *moganga*, a name applied in Portugal to a kind of squash. However, since the *mogangas*, as we saw above, are produced by *Cucurbita Pepo*, whereas the *bogangas* come from *Cucurbita melanosperma*, as we have also said, it seems to us that the Madeiran term should be accepted, since this avoids confusing species that are perfectly distinct from one another. In some parts of Madeira the *bogangas* are called *abóboras moiras* (Moorish squashes) and *abóbora de Tenerife* (Tenerife squash).

The *bogangueira* is very hardy. It is propagated by seed or by cuttings and can be grown in *caseiras* or in any other suitable place. It needs no supports, as it does perfectly well on the ground, but it requires layering, just like the black squash. It can be planted or sown all year round, but the best time for this is from March to October. The fruits are most abundant from June to November, but they also appear in other months of the year.

*Boganga* soup is considered an insipid food, or perhaps even unpleasant in taste, by the great majority of foreigners and of people from Portugal who visit the island. The inhabitants, however, and especially the lower classes, eat it with pleasure, above all when broad beans, beans or any other vegetables are added. The preserve that the Madeirans call *chila* (sweet made from gourd seed filaments) or *chilacaiota* is made from the filaments (funicles) of the seeds when the fruits are fully ripe.

The chayote (*Sechium edule*), *caiota* in Portuguese, is native to Central America and is the only perennial cucurbit grown in Madeira. It is monoecious, with glabrous stems, leaves rough on the upper surface and divided into 5–7 lobules, white, greenish-white or yellow flowers, and obovate or obovate-claviform fruits with a single seed, generally somewhat compressed. These fruits, known by the same name as the plant and also as *pepinelas*, are sometimes green and sometimes white, more or less prickly on the outside, and appear during the autumn and part of the winter. Their flavour is pleasant, especially in the green variety, and they can be eaten in soup or boiled in salted water; they are also made into a preserve very similar to that made from the boganga.

The chayote is propagated from whole fruits, which are planted in small pits in January and February. Some growers set them in their natural position, but more often they are laid in the ground on their side, or else with the shoot pointing downwards, because it is said that the root, which is tuberous and very rich in starch, then grows larger. This root, although edible, is little used in Madeira.

The plant we are discussing is better known on the island as *pepinela* than as *caiota*. In Central America and the West Indies it is given the latter name, and also that of *chocho*. Because the word *pepinela*, which is genuinely Madeiran, does not appear in dictionaries of the language, some people call the fruits of the chayote *pimpinelas*. This is plainly a mistake, since the *pepinela* belongs to the cucurbit family and the *pimpinela* to the umbellifers, and there are no affinities or similarities of any kind between the two plants.

The chayote seldom bears fruit in its first year, but from the second year onwards it fruits abundantly. In some cases it can live for more than 10 years, and it needs trellises or other supports to grow well. Before planting, the fruits are left to sprout, and it is customary to put them in the ground only when the stems have reached a length of 20 to 30 centimetres, and sometimes more. When the fruits are planted upside down, these stems should be bent so that part of them stays above ground.

Of the cucurbits we have mentioned, only the black squash is widely grown on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’); there are, however, melons there, which are rare in Madeira, and watermelons, which are almost unknown on this island.

In some places around Funchal one finds *Cucurbita Pepo aurantia*, with spherical fruits resembling oranges, and a variety of *Cucurbita maxima* improperly called *abóbora menina*, which is characterised by small, flattened pepos of a very curious shape.

The bottle gourd, the cucumber, the two squashes and the boganga are always grown in ground that has been properly manured. Fold (*curral*) manure or brushwood is put into the trenches or beds, and only then are the seeds sown or the cuttings planted. The layering of the squash and the boganga, generally done two months after planting, is also accompanied by manuring.

Some farmers pinch out the main stems once they have reached a certain growth, in order to obtain stronger and more productive side branches. Third-order branches, known as *netos* (‘grandchildren’), are removed on a large scale, especially on squashes, to strengthen the plants and make them bear more fruit. On the cucumber this thinning is not always done, since some consider it harmful to the plant.

The black squash, the boganga and the cucumber are sometimes sown in unmanured ground, the manure being applied only at the time of layering. In species propagated by cuttings, these should be protected by coverings until they take root. Frequent watering is very useful during the hot season, but it can spoil the quality of the fruits as they approach ripeness. When two fruits appear close together on a squash branch, it is customary to remove one so that the remaining one grows more vigorously. The topping of fruit-bearing branches, however, is not practised on any Madeiran cucurbit; growers confine their care to removing useless shoots as they appear.

The chayote needs no manuring in the gardens of Funchal, but the same is not always true in the exhausted soils of the countryside. Once the pits have been fertilised, however, the plant can be said to need no further care, provided there are trellises or supports on which to spread its branches.
Cuibém

This family surname comes from Antónia Jaime Cuibém, who came to Madeira in 1590 with her husband, the Englishman Roberto Vizovi, a knight of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*). Vizovi set up a business house in Funchal.
Pot marigold (Calendula officinalis)

A tubuliflorous composite native to Italy and Greece, easy to recognise by its large flower heads with orange ligules and by its markedly curved achenes, which are slightly spiny on the back. It is grown in gardens and has become naturalised in some parts of Madeira. It was formerly used as a stimulant, tonic and emmenagogue medicine.
Cumiada Alta

It lies near Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’), a short distance from the famous column of basalt blocks known as the Homem em Pé (‘standing man’). It stands more than 1700 metres above sea level and is one of the few places where the rare *Pyrus Aucuparia* and *Bunium brevifolium*, two rare species of the Madeiran flora, have been found.
Cumiada de São Vicente

It stands 1000 metres above sea level, and on clear days both the north and the south of Madeira can be seen from it. The road leading from Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) to the Cumiada, by way of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), was opened in 1916. Near the Cumeada de São Vicente (‘ridge of São Vicente’) grows *Lycopodium complanatum*, a clubmoss that is extremely rare in Madeira.
Cunha

This family surname derives from Martim Afonso da Cunha, who was one of the first settlers of the island and held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands at Anjos (‘angels’) and Canhas.
Cunha (Alexandre Luís da)

He was a teacher at the Lancasterian School (*Escola Lancasteriana*) and owner and editor of the periodicals *O Defensor da Liberdade*, *O Defensor* and *Correio da Madeira*. By a sentence of 26 February 1828 he served thirty days in prison for abuse of the freedom of the press. Having left that year for the United States, he went on from there to Brazil, returning to Madeira only after constitutional government had been restored. On 28 September 1835 he was appointed teacher of French and English in Funchal, and by decree of 4 September 1838 he took up the same post at the lyceum (state secondary school). He died in the Civil Hospital (*Hospital Civil*) on 14 October 1852, at the age of 49. Works: *Os Estados Unidos da America Septentrional em 1830 e 1831*, Rio de Janeiro, 1832.
Cunha (Augusto José da)
This politician and statesman represented Madeira in parliament as a deputy in the legislature of 1897 to 1899. He died in June 1919.
Cunha (Bartolomeu de Vasconcelos da)
He was appointed governor and captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira on 21 August 1651, and took office on 16 October of the same year.
Diogo Barbosa Machado says that he wrote various sonnets on the birth of the Infante Dom Pedro, on the death of Dona Maria de Ataíde and to Manuel de Galhegos.
He was the father of the distinguished poet and writer Troilo de Vasconcelos da Cunha, who was born in Funchal in 1654 (see that entry).
Cunha (Dom Pedro Álvares da)
He was governor and captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira. His appointment dates from 30 March 1711, and he took office on 1 October 1712.
Cunha (João Severo)

He was born in Funchal on 6 November 1856. He is a colonel of engineers and was president of the Lisbon Municipal Council under the political regime of Pimenta de Castro. Besides his contributions to several reviews, he published *Espessura das abobadas*, 1895, *Estudos sobre abobadas*, 1897, and
*Esclarecimentos uteis aos mutuarios e pretendentes de mutuos da Companhia Geral do Credito Predial Portugues*, 1912.
Cunha (José Ribeiro da)
The decree appointing him civil governor of this district is dated 9 April 1896, and he took office on 23 May of that year.

By decree of 13 June 1901 he was appointed civil governor of Madeira for the second time, and took up the post on the 15th of the same month and year. During this term of office he received the visit of the King and Queen of Portugal, Carlos I and Dona Maria Amélia, and on that occasion was awarded the Grand Cross of the Order of the Conception.
He held the same office for the third time, having been appointed by decree of 22 May 1906, and took office on the 29th of that month and year.
He was appointed civil governor of Madeira for the fourth time by decree of 27 June 1910 and took office on 13 July following.
He was the last substantive civil governor under the monarchy, and represented Madeira in parliament in the legislature of 1908 to 1910.
He died in Lisbon on 14 May 1915, a victim of the revolution that broke out in that city on that day.
Cunha (Pedro da Silva da)
This governor and captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira was appointed on 16 January 1655 and took office on 22 April of the same year.
Cunha (Troilo de Vasconcelos da)

His name is today entirely unknown here, but in his own time he won considerable renown as a poet and writer. Those who make deeper studies of our literary history know the pages devoted to him by Diogo Barbosa Machado in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’) and by Costa e Silva in the *Ensaio Critico dos Poetas Portugueses*. He was born in Funchal in 1654, when his father Bartolomeu de Vasconcelos held the office of governor and captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago. He devoted himself to the thorough study of the humanities, displaying his vast learning above all in languages, especially Greek and Latin. He also applied himself to the study of various theological questions, which he chose to treat in his poetry, particularly in the work entitled *O Espelho do Invisivel*. In it he shows great poetic qualities, but its subject, unsuited to treatment in verse, made the poem difficult to understand and stripped it of the graces that should adorn compositions of this kind. This is so despite, as Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says, the purity of its style and its being little tainted by the faults of the Gongorist school that then dominated our literature.
He rendered into Portuguese the Latin poem of Justin, under the title *Justino Lusitano*, and left many unpublished works in prose and verse.
He held very important posts, such as that of secretary of the Council of the Three Estates (*Junta dos Tres Estados*), among others. He died in Lisbon on 4 August 1729.
Cupertino (Friar José)

He was a friar of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) in Funchal and in his day enjoyed great renown here as a preacher and a man of wide learning. We know of two discourses he published in Funchal in 1823: one preached in the church of São Martinho (St Martin of Tours), and the other entitled *Oração de acção de graças prégada na igreja cathedral da Sé do Funchal em 8 de Julho de 1823 por ocasião da solene festividade... pela feliz restauração de el-rei N. S. ao throno de seus augustos maiores...*, Funchal, 1823. These discourses are extremely rare.
Curral das Freiras (parish)

This small parish lies in the interior of the island, on the floor of the crater of an extinct volcano, as several geologists affirm. To reach this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), one must climb high, steep mountains and descend the sloping ravines that ring the deep valley, which, seen from the mountain peaks, appears to us as a dreadful and fathomless abyss. It is perhaps the spot in Madeira where nature shows itself at its most remarkably grand and most surprising. This is owed to the great height and fanciful shapes of the mountains, the towering, sheer slopes, the gorges and chasms scattered everywhere, and the rugged, wild tone of the landscape. All this gives the whole such an air of grandeur and majesty, and of such extraordinary and enchanting beauty, that the visitor, even the least observant and sensitive, is astonished and entranced on coming upon this scene of so many incomparable wonders. ‘We saw a channel,’ says a distinguished writer, ‘many metres wide and cut almost sheer, a fearsome gulf, an immense hollow around which, except to the south, rise titanic peaks of fantastic outline, and, at the bottom of the abyss... the rustic miniature of a paradise...’ Above Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) rise some of the highest peaks in Madeira, foremost among them the well-known Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’), which reaches an altitude of approximately two thousand metres above sea level. Numerous Portuguese and foreign works contain extensive references to the Curral, and this *lugar* has been much visited by many illustrious men, among them some who achieved distinction in the fields of science and letters.

In the earliest days of colonisation it was called simply Curral (fold), a name that came from its being a centre of abundant pasture for sheep and goats, where shepherds, living an almost nomadic life, grazed their flocks freely. Some slaves gathered there who, fleeing the settled areas, gained what amounted to their letter of manumission there, as did various criminals who had escaped the hand of justice. In this way a small nucleus of settlement formed in that remote and isolated wilderness, which distance and the difficulty of communications, across mountains thick with woodland and strewn with perilous chasms, made almost inaccessible. The clearing and cultivation of the land then began, and by the end of the 15th century there was already a small centre of population there, with inhabitants in fixed residence, lawfully established. It then ceased to be a haunt of fugitives and criminals. This early nucleus of population grew little, for in 1794 its inhabitants numbered only one hundred and ten.

In 1480 the Curral belonged to Rui Teixeira and his wife Branca Ferreira, who lived in Campanário. On 11 September of that year they signed the deed of sale of this vast property to the second captain-donatary of Funchal, João Gonçalves da Câmara. The estate stretched ‘from the Passo da Cruz (‘pass of the cross’) and the Ribeirão dos Socorridos up to where it rises, from rocky crest (*arrife*) to rocky crest, on either side’. The purchase price was ‘23,500 réis at five *ceitis* to the *real* (pl. *réis*; old Portuguese money unit, 1,000 réis = 1 milréis) and 50 gold *cruzados*, each worth 380 réis’. The captain-donatary intended this land for the endowment he made to his daughters, Dona Elvira and Dona Joana, when they took their vows at the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), the convent that he himself had founded in 1492 and which the first nuns entered in 1497. The endowment of the Curral must have been made at some point between 1492 and 1497, and from that time onwards it became known as Curral das Freiras (the Nuns’ Fold).

In 1560 the city of Funchal was sacked by French Lutheran corsairs, of whom the old Madeiran chronicles speak with such horror. The nuns of St Clare were forced to abandon their convent so as not to fall victim to that horde of savages and, as Frutuoso says, ‘they went out through the cane fields and took refuge, and did not stop until they reached their Curral, which lies a good distance from the city, and so they departed without saving any ornament, leaving everything in the convent except the monstrance of the Most Blessed Sacrament...’. The French remained in Funchal, busy with destruction and slaughter, from 3 to 17 October. Soon after they left the island, the nuns left the Curral and returned to their convent in the city. We do not know whether the nuns of St Clare had by then already built in the Curral the chapel of St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*), which stood there until the middle of the 19th century and belonged to the same convent.

Before it was raised to a parish (*freguesia*), Curral das Freiras belonged to the parish of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), from which it was separated in 1790. The Curral nevertheless had its own chaplains, who lived there more or less permanently; in 1678 a chaplain’s licence was issued to Father Cristóvão Vieira. Services were held in the chapel of St Anthony. When it was inspected in 1756 by the episcopal visitor (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) Dr António Mendes de Almeida, he ordered, in a visitation decree (*provimento*) recorded in the archive of the parish of Santo António, that the abbess of the Convent of St Clare be told to supply the chapel with the objects needed for worship, as she was obliged to do, on pain (*pena*) of further proceedings.

For the building of a new church and a residence for the chaplain – no doubt already with the coming foundation of the parish in view – the Convent of St Clare, by a deed executed on 24 July 1784, gave the mitre of this diocese six *alqueires* of land, subject only to an annual quit-rent (*foro*) of one pullet, payable on 12 August each year. The buildings were to be for the use of the chaplains and their successors.

The learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says that the parish of Curral das Freiras had its seat in the chapel of Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria), founded by Simão de Nóbrega. This is a plain mistake, for that chapel stood in the parish of Santo António, at the locality (*sítio*) that still bears that name today. It is an established fact that the small chapel of St Anthony, which stood in the Curral and belonged to the Convent of St Clare, served as the base and seat of the new parish when it was created by royal decree (alvará régio) of 17 March 1790.

We cannot state exactly when the new church was built, nor the year in which the parish seat was transferred to it. We do know, from the inscription in the church itself, that it was built in the reign of Maria I, and we conjecture that the work was carried out in the first years of the 19th century. Its patron saint is Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*), in whose honour a pilgrimage festival is held on the last Sunday of August. Its interior underwent considerable repairs in 1917 and 1918.

The centre of the parish lies 14 kilometres from the parish church of Santo António and 17½ kilometres from the city of Funchal. After crossing the Ribeira de Vasco Gil and climbing the slope of the *lombo* (ridge between valleys) of Empress Elisabeth, one joins a level road that runs as far as the Eira do Serrado (‘threshing floor of the ridge’), at an altitude of 1026 metres, from where the whole settlement of the Curral can be seen far below. There begins the steep, winding descent known as the Passo da Chave (‘key pass’), which leads to the centre of the parish.
Besides wine, the Curral had an abundant production of cherries, chestnuts and citrons; the last was very important and almost exclusive to this parish.

On the rugged slopes of this parish rises the Ribeira dos Socorridos (‘stream of the rescued’), the most important watercourse in the south of the island. The important Levada dos Piornais (‘broom thickets’) and Levada Nova do Castelejo (levada: irrigation channel) have their intakes on this stream.

For some years now Curral das Freiras has had an official boys’ school, yet in 1846, on a visit there, the worthy civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro found that only the parish priest and the *regedor* (parish administrative officer) could read and write!

Its principal localities are Lombo Chão, Serra Velha, Balseiras, Terra-Chã, Capela, Murteira, Casas Próximas, Achada, Ribeira do Cidrão, Fajã dos Cardos, Pico do Furão, Colmeal and Fajã Escura. It has a population of 1430 inhabitants.
Curral dos Romeiros

A locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), crossed by the road that leads to Choupana (‘hut’). Above the Ponte do Curral, on the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’), there is a small but pretty waterfall, which can be reached by following the levada (irrigation channel) that runs beside the bridge.
Curral dos Romeiros (‘pilgrims’ fold’) is a locality much visited by Portuguese and foreigners alike. It lies at the bottom of a large valley, where visitors come away with pleasant impressions.
Drawing Course

Funchal once had a drawing course maintained by the Municipal Council, which opened on 1 October 1877 and was abolished at a council meeting on 1 September 1892. The course was taught by the director of municipal works of the municipality (*concelho*), the late José Maria Teixeira de Agrela.
D'Orsey (Alexander J. D.)

He was an Anglican chaplain and head of a school in Funchal. Works: *Colloquial Portuguese, or the Words and Phrases of every day*, which ran to six editions, the first in 1854 and the last in 1891, and *A Pratical Grammar of Portuguese and English*, which ran to three editions. Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça, rector of the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), collaborated on the latter work.
Dahlia (Dhalia variabilis)
A composite native to Mexico, widely grown in the gardens of Funchal.
Apricot tree (Prunus Armeniaca)
A tree native to China, widely grown in Madeira.
Its fruit, which appears in June and July, varies greatly in size and even in colour. There is one variety of apricot known as ‘black’, whose skin has the colour of certain plums.
The main varieties of apricot found in Madeira are the following: *legítimos*, *franceses*, *brancos*, *churros*, *alperches*, ‘pêches’ and *maracotões*.
Dana (J. D.)
An American geologist who visited Madeira in September 1838. The results of his work were published in vol. X of the *United States Exploring Expedition*.
Dantas

The chapel of Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*) was founded by António Dantas in 1622. It is to be believed that the family surname Dantas, Antas or Antes derives from Mem Afonso de Antas, a native of the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Antes, in the former municipality (*concelho*) of Coura, in the Minho.
Darja
This family surname, now extinct in Madeira, derives from Simão Darja, who at the end of the 16th century owned a sugar mill (engenho) for crushing sugar cane in Funchal.
Darwin (Charles)

This learned English naturalist refers to Madeira several times in his works on the origin of species and on the variation of animals and plants. In his monograph on the cirripedes, he mentions 13 Madeiran species.
Historical dates

We shall list some of the principal dates in the history of Madeira, pointing out especially those that mark the most important events of a long period of five centuries. The first date to be noted here must be that of the discovery of the archipelago (see Discovery of the archipelago). Some place it in 1419, with the discovery of Porto Santo, and others in the following year. According to these two opinions, the island of Madeira would have been discovered in 1419 or in 1420 respectively. It should be noted, however, that the more widely held opinion is the first, which thus gives the islands of Porto Santo and Madeira as discovered in 1418 and 1419.

Deanery

The office of dean (*deão*) of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) was created by the very papal bull that established the diocese, and the bull expressly named the priest who was to hold the post. Nuno Cão (see that entry), whom the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) sent to Madeira with special powers, was the first parish priest of the Cathedral when this parish (*freguesia*) was created, and also the first dean; in the early days both offices were held jointly by the same man. Nuno Cão was succeeded by Filipe Rebelo, and on the latter’s death the post of dean was separated from that of parish priest, two curacies being created at that time exclusively for parish duties. The last clergymen to hold the deanery (office of dean of the cathedral chapter) of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) were António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos and João Joaquim Pinto (see those entries). Until the establishment of the Republic, a degree in law or theology was required for appointment to this post. On the deanery of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) and the priests who held this high ecclesiastical office, see the series of articles published in *O Jornal* (‘The Newspaper’) in December 1935 and January 1936.

Magnetic declination

This is the angle between the magnetic meridian and the astronomical meridian. In Funchal the angle was 15° 30′ W. in 1768 (Dr Heberden); 21° 32′ W. in 1829 (*Penny Cyclop.*); 21° W. in 1835 (Wyld); 21° W. in 1843 (Vidal); 20° 57 1/2′ W. in 1851 (A. P. de Azevedo); 20° 56′ W. in 1861 (Friesach); 19° 55′ W. in 1885 (Admiralty chart); and 19° W. in 1892 (idem). According to the officers of the *Challenger*, the declination was 18° 25′ W. on 4 February 1872 and 20° 33′ W. on 17 July 1873. Colonel Francisco Afonso de Chaves, who also made magnetic observations in Funchal in 1903 (22 June) and in 1906 (4 June), found that in the first of these years the declination was 20° 31′ 30″ W. and in the second 20° 36′ 55″ W.
On 14 November 1842 the magnetic variation on Porto Santo was 24° 38′ 12″, according to the chart of that island by the late General António Pedro de Azevedo.

Bory, who visited Madeira in 1755 and published the account of his voyage in the *Histoire et Mémoires de L’Académie Royale des Sciences pour l’an 1772*, says that ‘the variation of the magnetic needle, which our position and the lack of a meridian line prevented us from determining on land, was often observed aboard the *Cometa*; it ranged between 10° 35′ W. and 11° 55″, which gives a mean result of 11° 3/4.’
Foxglove (Digitalis purpurea)

A biennial plant of the family Scrophulariaceae, very common in Madeira. Its flowers, which hang in an elongated raceme, have large, tubular-bell-shaped, purplish-pink corollas, marked inside with darker spots ringed with white.

Foxglove is highly poisonous and in a large dose causes death; in a moderate dose it is useful in diseases of the heart, asthma, rheumatism, etc. Digitalin is the active principle of foxglove. Madeirans sometimes call foxglove *teijeira*, but the true *teijeira* (lesser burdock) is *Lappa minor*, a plant of the family Compositae, which is also found on the island.

Exiled convicts

In the days of absolute government it was customary to exile to Madeira certain criminals whose offences the courts did not regard as very serious. Joaquim Pedro Cardoso Casado Giraldes (see that entry) was exiled to Madeira for having served as interpreter to the French and Spanish generals during the Peninsular War. There is also an official letter from José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, dated 25 May 1827, in which this governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) points out the drawbacks of sending to this island exiled convicts (*degredados*) sentenced to public works.
Delgado

This family surname derives from Pedro Delgado, known as ‘o Nabo’, who, according to Dr Azevedo, married Isabel Fernandes, known as ‘a Velha da Serra’; both were of noble birth and came from the town (*vila*) of Arruda, in Portugal. They were among the first settlers of the island of Madeira and held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), apparently at Lombo das Adegas (‘ridge of the wine cellars’).

Dendrites

They are common in the trachytes of the Serra de Nossa Senhora (‘Our Lady’s upland’), on Porto Santo, and rare in the basalt slabs of São Martinho. S.

Dente de cão

In Madeira this name, *dente de cão* (‘dog’s tooth’, popular name for crystalline hoar frost), is given to the thin layers of crystalline snow that appear in the mountains after severe cold. These layers of snow result from the rapid freezing of water vapour on contact with the objects on which they appear. Frosts or *dente de cão* usually appear on the north coast above 600 or 700 metres, but on the south coast we believe they are unknown within the limits of the cultivated zone. When there is biting and prolonged cold, country people are wont to say that *dente de cão* is falling.
Political deportees

During the revolt that broke out in Torres Vedras on 4 February 1844, with the aim of bringing down the government of Costa Cabral, 23 insurgents were arrested and sent to Madeira. Among them were the lawyers António Maria Ribeiro da Costa Holtreman and Leonel Tavares Cabral, the judge of the Commercial Court Lourenço de Oliveira Grijó, Canon Dr Manuel Joaquim Cardoso Castelo Branco and eight army officers.

Some of these political prisoners came on the brig *Douro*, which reached Funchal on 20 April, and were admitted to the Ilhéu fortress (*Fortaleza do Ilhéu*); the rest came on the cutter *Andorinha*, which arrived here on the 28th of the same month, and were lodged in the Pico (‘peak’) fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*). They were all set free as soon as the unofficial news of the failure of the Torres Vedras revolution reached Madeira.

In 1919, after the monarchist revolution at the beginning of that year, new political prisoners came to Funchal. They arrived on the steamer *Africa*, of the Empresa Nacional de Navegação, which had been commissioned as a troop transport. These prisoners, 289 in number, were accompanied by a naval force and landed on 8 May, three days after the *Africa* arrived. They were housed in the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’). Among the prisoners were the former minister João de Azevedo Coutinho, the former colonel João de Almeida, the Count of Sucena, the Count of Arrochela, the Viscount of Siqueira and João Moreira de Almeida. A force of 30 naval men and 1 sergeant remained in Funchal to guard the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’), and an infantry detachment commanded by a second lieutenant joined this force for the same purpose. By order of the harbour master, all vessels were forbidden to pass through or remain in the sea area bounded by the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) and Cabo Garajau (‘tern’).

Despite these precautions, on 3 June it was discovered that 8 prisoners had disappeared, among them the Count of Sucena. It later emerged that all of them had reached Las Palmas on the motor launch *Glafiberta*, belonging to the sportsman Humberto dos Passos, who had organised the escape. On how the escape took place, we read the following in a newspaper: ‘One fine afternoon, almost all the political prisoners held in the Lazareto do Funchal (‘Funchal quarantine hospital’) left the building on the pretext of taking the air and gathered on the strip of beach immediately below it. The guards merely watched them from the windows of the Lazareto. For a while they sang, frolicked and cheered, and when the uproar was at its height and the guards were distracted by the merriment, a boat sent from the *Glafiberta* approached the beach and unhurriedly picked up the 8 prisoners... Hours later, the motor launch, towed by the *Milano*, belonging to the Blandy firm (which did not know what kind of service had been asked of its tug), sailed towards the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), and later turned south, on course for the Canary Islands’.
The owner of the *Glafiberta* went with the eight prisoners. A few days earlier he had asked the harbour master for permission to make a voyage round the island in his boat.

Of the remaining prisoners who had been held in the Lazareto, 7 were released following a telegram received from the Minister of War on 13 May, and all the others left for Lisbon on various mail steamers that called at Funchal between June and August. The steamer *Moçambique* carried the last of the 280 prisoners who had landed in Funchal on 8 May.
