Sacrilege and robbery in the church of Estreito

On the night of 6–7 November 1829 the church of Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*) in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) was broken into. Various sacred vessels were stolen from it, together with some silver crowns, 1 gold chain bearing the image of Our Lady, 1 silver flower set with red stones, 1 processional cross, 2 silver lamps, etc. The consecrated hosts kept in the tabernacle were consumed by the thieves.

Of those responsible for this crime, 6 were sentenced by the High Court of Appeal (*Relação*) of Lisbon, in a judgment of 6 March 1830, to be garrotted at Cais do Sodré, and 2 to perpetual penal exile (*degredo*) in Africa. The defendants sentenced to the ultimate penalty were the following: José Marreiros, a lance-corporal of the 2nd Infantry; Jacinto Fernandes, labourer; Manuel de Sequeira, labourer; Januário Soares, a soldier of the 13th Infantry; João Rodrigues, known as ‘o Espera Diabos’, labourer; and José de Andrade, known as ‘o Rangido’, a constable (*quadrilheiro*). The first and fourth were natives of Portugal and the rest of Madeira.

In addition to death by garrotte, the last three defendants were sentenced to be dragged from the gaol to the scaffold and, once dead, to have their heads cut off and displayed on posts for three days.

The defendants sentenced to perpetual penal exile were Francisco de Sales Rodrigues, goldsmith, and Timóteo da Graça, labourer, both natives of Madeira. The High Court later commuted the death sentence passed on the defendant José Marreiros to one of penal exile in Africa.
Discovery of the archipelago

Much has already been written about the discovery of the Madeira archipelago, yet the precise date of this happy and momentous event remains shrouded in deep darkness. The question matters not only to Madeira but equally to the history of our maritime discoveries, for it marks the glorious beginning of our Homeric deeds across continents and oceans. The discovery of Madeira is the great, undying commemorative pillar (padrão) that truly marks the auspicious start of our odyssey as navigators. Before the Portuguese put in at these unknown shores, they had undertaken only bold but almost entirely fruitless ventures; it was afterwards that they discovered the Azores, Guinea, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, Angola, the Cape of Good Hope, India, Brazil and the countless islands scattered across the vastness of the Atlantic and the Pacific. The discovery of this archipelago represents not only a notable territorial expansion of our dominions as a nation but, above all, our first great conquest as navigators and future masters of the seas. For a nation whose chief role in history was that of voyages and maritime conquests, the first important discovery we made cannot but be regarded as a great and glorious event, and the utmost zeal ought to be shown in establishing, with complete and absolute precision, the date on which this remarkable event took place. The truth is that nothing whatever has been done to this end. Although the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Sciencias de Lisboa*) has a commission specially charged with promoting the commemoration of our conquests and discoveries, we are not aware that it has undertaken any historical research aimed at determining precisely the date of any of these discoveries and conquests, as the sound and indispensable basis for holding those very commemorations.

Various legends, conjectures and hypotheses trace knowledge of Madeira and other islands of the Atlantic Ocean back to very remote times, but nothing definite has been established on the matter. In the article Atlantis we have already referred to the possible existence of that island, of which the philosopher Plato speaks, reproducing ancient Egyptian traditions, and of which Madeira might perhaps be a small fragment left by the great cataclysm that buried the perhaps mythical Atlantis in the depths of the Ocean.

Around the supposed or real existence of this island many hypotheses have been constructed and varied conjectures invented, which are of particular interest only to those who wish to study the subject in greater depth. Another legend, mentioned by some authors, is that of the islands of St Brendan, an Irish monk who is supposed to have travelled to various islands of the Atlantic, one of which would have been Madeira. Others further assert that the Phoenicians, the Arabs, the Carthaginians and the Normans, at different periods, sailed along the western coasts of Africa and visited many of the islands scattered across the Atlantic, leaving traces of their passage on some of them. Many writers have dealt in particular with the Carthaginian Hanno and his *Periplus*, or description of his sea route, and some authors of good repute and sound critical judgement regard this voyage as genuine. This would allow for the possibility that the Madeira archipelago was a point of passage on one or more of these doubtful and problematic voyages. It is generally believed, and on the firmest grounds, that such voyages were made only along the coasts. This was owing to the backward state of the art of navigation, the small size of the vessels, the terror inspired by the vastness of the ocean, the belief in sea creatures of enormous bulk capable of swallowing ships or sinking them, and yet other legends and superstitions. The chief beacons and points of reference were the most prominent capes, promontories and headlands of the land, and navigators did not then venture on voyages on the high seas or on long, distant runs that would take them too far out of sight of the mainland. It is for these weighty reasons that, although the possibility of these remote voyages is admitted, all the probabilities favour the generally accepted and acknowledged fact that the Madeira archipelago was not visited before João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira made for these unknown waters. The distinguished geographer and historian M. d’Avezac, in the second part of his notable work *Iles de l’Afrique*, pp. 2 to 41, deals at length with the legends and traditions to which we make only a brief reference here; they are also dealt with by the illustrious annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), in one of his learned notes to the work of Gaspar Frutuoso. We do not refer here to the well-known legend of Robert Machin, because we shall deal with it in a separate article.

Leaving these legends and traditions aside, some authors have claimed that Portuguese ships were not the first to make for the shores of this archipelago. This view was echoed by our learned fellow Madeiran and distinguished researcher Dr Jordão de Freitas in his interesting pamphlet *Quando foi descoberta a Madeira?* He states that a Spanish mendicant friar of the 14th century made a voyage to this island, and that his account of it, published in 1877 in the bulletin of the Geographical Society of Madrid, clearly mentions the islands Salvage, Desierta, Lecname and Puerto Santo. Seventy years earlier the Viscount of Santarém had already referred to this voyage of the Spanish monk, but without giving it any credence, and indeed regarding it as of no historical or geographical value. Others again, relying chiefly on the historical memoirs of the academician Joaquim José da Costa de Macedo, included in the *Memórias da Academia de Lisboa* and published in 1816 and 1835, believed it had been proved in the most conclusive manner that the Portuguese discovered the Canary Islands in the second quarter of the 14th century. They therefore asserted that the Madeiran archipelago must have been discovered at about that time, so that the Infante’s caravels, commanded by Zarco and Tristão Vaz, were not the first to put in at Madeira. The illustrious writer Dr Teófilo Braga, seeking to strip Henry the Navigator of the glory of having been the true initiator of our great maritime discoveries, also shared that opinion, but without bringing forward decisive arguments, or even acceptable probabilities, that might lend his bold assertion at least an appearance of truth. Costa de Macedo’s argument rests above all on a letter addressed by Afonso IV to Pope Clement VI, a letter copied from a foreign author and offering no sure guarantee of authenticity. These various historical problems, to which we refer here only briefly, were dealt with by Aires de Sá in his notable work on Gonçalo Velho Cabral, and later by João da Rocha in the work entitled *Lenda Infantista*, published in 1916. This last study proves abundantly, and without fear of any well-founded rebuttal, that the Portuguese were not in the Canaries in the second quarter of the 14th century, and that the Madeiran archipelago was discovered by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz at the time commonly given by historians, having been unknown before then to other navigators, Portuguese or foreign. The *Lenda Infantista* is, on this subject, a complete and exhaustive work, as people nowadays like to say, not only for its tireless and extensive historical research but above all for the impartial and fair criticism with which it is written, and also for the sure and tight reasoning that guides its author’s entire argument.

It appears to be established that João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz were driven by a violent storm onto the shores of the island of Porto Santo. So say the oldest chroniclers who deal with the discovery of this island. These navigators had set out in search of discoveries, to explore the unknown, making especially for the lands of Guinea, which was then the goal of the Portuguese’s daring voyages, when the tempest unexpectedly carried them to the coasts of an unknown island. Gomes Eanes de Zurara (see that entry), the earliest narrator of these events, says that ‘the Infante, seeing their good will (that of Zarco and Tristão), ordered a *barcha* to be fitted out for them, in which they might go armed against the Moors, directing them to go in search of the land of Guinea... and as God wished to bring so much good to this kingdom... He guided them so that with contrary weather they arrived at the island which is now called Porto Santo... for which reason they left that island and crossed over to the other, Madeira... ’. To shed fuller light on this text of Zurara, we transcribe the judicious commentary that Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo made on it in one of his annotations to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’:

‘In view of the preceding text of Zurara, it is clear that when Zargo and Tristão Vaz first appeared in the waters of this archipelago of Madeira, no report of it, whether of Castilian, English or other origin, had brought them here; they were going “in search of the Land of Guinea”, which was the constant aim of Dom Henrique, and according to which he had given regulations (*regimento*) to his navigators: no one but “GOD GUIDED THEM”, driving them with contrary weather” off the course they were following, until “THUS they arrived at the island which is now called Porto Santo” and “in the following year” the same discoverers “CROSSED OVER” from the island of Porto Santo “to the other island, Madeira”.','cells':null}

‘“They crossed over”, Zurara put it very well; for in this single word the whole history of the discovery of this island is perfectly contained – a history far more artless and sound than all those that have since been dreamed up; for it is physically impossible to spend any time on the island of Porto Santo and, on clear days, not plainly see the land of Madeira, lofty as it is. On this point Zurara has on his side the unanimous testimony of all who live here, confirmed by that of every generation that has lived here from Zargo’s day to ours. The discovery of the one necessarily entailed that of the other. – “They crossed over”, yes, the Portuguese discoverers, and of their own accord, without any adventure of Machim or tip-off from a Castilian, simply and plainly, over a sea of roses; and so the discovery was accomplished.','cells':null}

‘In the light of the evidence from examining the place itself, Zurara was scrupulously truthful. Let no one charge him with being deficient; for he wrote the precise words needed to relate and affirm the fact. “God guided them by the hand of the tempest to the island of Porto Santo; and from there Zargo and Tristão Vaz crossed over to Madeira: all is said.”’

The chroniclers who, immediately after Zurara, dealt with the discovery of Madeira were João de Barros and Damião de Góis, whose narratives do not differ essentially from the account given by the author of the *Chronica da Guiné*. Before Barros and Góis, it is true, Diogo Gomes and Alvise Cadamosto referred in their narratives to the discovery of this archipelago, not as historians or chroniclers but simply as seafarers. Nothing is found in their accounts, however, that contradicts the categorical assertions of the historians cited, particularly Eanes de Zurara, who was a contemporary of the events he narrated.
In what year was the island of Porto Santo discovered? As we have already noted above, the precise date of that event has not yet been established. Meanwhile, let us hear Gaspar Frutuoso’s account:

‘Arriving within a few days at Porto Santo... they at once saw from the sea that darkness... And so they stayed some days... One Sunday before dawn, three hours before sunrise, he had the ships set sail... They ran a good while to approach the darkness... And it being already midday... having gone but a short distance... they saw... land... and because it was already very late they did not go ashore that day... On the next day... having landed... he took possession... on the day of the Visitation of St Elizabeth of Portugal, the second of July of the aforesaid year of 1419’. The passages from Dr Gaspar Frutuoso transcribed above are commented upon by the illustrious annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, in the following terms:

‘As to 1 July, given by Dr Frutuoso, having been the day on which Zargo first reached this island, we have no objections to raise; on the contrary, the wealth of detail about what preceded, accompanied and followed it leads us to presume that this passage is one of those preserved from the old manuscript attributed to Gonçalo Aires, which was later corrected and enlarged by Canon Leite’.

For those less versed in Madeiran history, it should be recalled that Gonçalo Aires Ferreira was one of Zarco’s companions. He is credited with the authorship of a writing entitled *Descobrimento da Ilha da Madeira*, whose original passed down by inheritance, from father to son, among the captains-donatary of Funchal. Then, in the time of the sixth captain and second Count of Calheta, João Gonçalves da Câmara, Jerónimo Dias Leite, a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé), made use of this manuscript to write the notes he sent to Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, who drew on them for his important work ‘Longing for the Homeland’.

If we were to take Frutuoso’s account as absolutely certain, Madeira would have been discovered on Sunday 1 July 1419, with the first landing made on the beach at Machico the following day, that is, on Monday 2 July of the same year. Against this categorical assertion by the author of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, Dr Manuel Sardinha, in an article published in the *Diário de Notícias* of this city, of which he is an editor, sets out the following judicious reflections:

‘Since the distinguished Azorean writes in his “*Descobrimento das Ilhas ou Saudades da Terra*” that the navigators Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira reached Madeira in their carrack “*São Lourenço*” on a Sunday, the first day of the month of July, this discovery could only have taken place in 1414 or 1425, the years closest to those claimed in which 1 July fell on a Sunday. In 1420, 1 July was a Monday. Frutuoso’s statement certainly contains an error: either of the day of the week or of the day of the month. Whereas 2 July 1419 was a Sunday!’ Dr M. Sardinha reached these conclusions, which are entirely correct, after serious research and study, so it may be stated peremptorily that 1 July 1420 fell on a Monday and 2 July 1419 fell on a Sunday.

There is evidently a clear mistake on the part of the historian of the islands in seeking to fix the day of Madeira’s discovery with such precision. Subject to better-informed opinion, we are inclined to believe that the caravel *São Lourenço* rounded the point that later took this name and approached the bay of Machico on the afternoon of 1 July 1419, and that the landing took place on Sunday 2 July of the same year, the day of the Visitation of St Elizabeth of Portugal.

In the article transcribed above, written many years ago, we set down the ideas then current and generally accepted about the discovery of our archipelago. In the time that has passed since, many articles have appeared scattered through the newspapers and several pamphlets have been published. None of them settled the matter definitively, particularly with regard to the reliable dating of the event, the names of the true discoverers and other incidental circumstances that may have accompanied it. It is nevertheless beyond doubt that new and valuable evidence has been brought to bear on this interesting problem, raising weighty doubts and giving rise to conflicting opinions born of the discussion and study that this much-debated subject has prompted. In this way certain principles have been established and highly probable conjectures have gradually been formed which, placed at the service of more rigorous historical research, may lead to the truth.

In the light of what we know today, no one can maintain as an undisputed fact that the island of Porto Santo was discovered in 1418 or 1419 and Madeira in one of the years immediately following, 1419 or 1420, as has generally always been asserted, invariably repeating what some of our oldest chroniclers said on the subject. The only exception would be if we give the word ‘discover’ the meaning it once had of ‘reconnoitre’ or ‘find again’, and also of ‘visit’, as some have already judiciously observed.

Those who have studied this subject in recent years hold the view that, by the date to which the discovery of the archipelago is generally attributed, it was already known to Portuguese navigators, as various reasons lead them to believe. It is well known that a degree of secrecy was then kept about the early maritime explorations, as regards dates and places. It is even claimed that some rutters and accounts of these voyages contain deliberate errors, intended to conceal, as circumstances advised, the discoveries that were being made across the unknown seas.

It is hard to accept that the royal charters of grant (*doação*) issued to João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the two appointments as heads of the captaincies, and other official documents of the period make no reference whatever to the fact of the discovery. These documents do allude to personal circumstances of little importance compared with so remarkable and honourable an event. It should also be noted that they were issued when the work of settlement was already well advanced, so there was then no longer any need to keep the recommended silence about the discoveries that had been made. What appears to be established, and is steadily gaining the standing of historical truth, is that João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira, shortly before beginning the arduous work of colonising Madeira, carried out a ‘reconnaissance’ of this archipelago. This was done in preparation for its forthcoming settlement and under orders and instructions issued by Prince Henry the Navigator himself.

For fuller and more reliable information on this subject, and to understand the legendary and historical phases through which it has passed, one must consult the most remarkable study by Dr Alvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in notes III–IV (pp. 329–432) of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, as well as the articles ‘Machico’, ‘Machim’ and ‘Madeira’ in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, written by the same author. Some of his conclusions must nevertheless be disputed in the light of the important work of historical research and criticism carried out in recent years. Besides those learned notes and the works cited in them, it is absolutely essential to consult the following writings, which we list here simply as aids for the reader who wishes to gain a fuller knowledge of this subject: *Memoria sobre a descoberta das ilhas de Porto Santo e Madeira* by E. A. de Bettencourt, Lisbon, 1875; *Desenvolvimentos, guerras e conquistas dos portugueses em terras do ultramar nos seculos XV e XVI* by the same author, Lisbon, 1882; *As relações do descobrimento da Guiné e das ilhas dos Açores, Madeira e Cabo Verde* by Diogo Gomes, written in Latin at the beginning of the 16th century, translated into Portuguese by Gabriel de Almeida in 1899 and published in the *Boletim da Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa* (17th series, 1898–1899, no. 5); *Quando foi descoberta a Madeira* by Jordão de Freitas, Lisbon, 1911; *A Lenda Infantista* by João da Rocha, 1916; *O Reconhecimento do Arquipelago da Madeira* by Pestana Júnior, Funchal, 1920; *Apontamentos de Historia Insular* by João Cabral do Nascimento, Funchal, 1927; *O Arquipelago da Madeira nos mapas e portulanos do século XIV* by António Ferreira de Serpa, in *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* I-125 ff.; *D. Francisco Manuel de Melo e o descobrimento da Madeira* by Antonio Gonçalves Rodrigues, Lisbon, 1935; ‘Francisco Alcoforado’s Account’ by João Franco Machado, Lisbon, 1936; *Origens e evolução da cartografia náutica portuguesa, na época dos descobrimentos* by Antonio Barbosa, published in the review *Ocidente* (no. 8, 1938); *Zarco ou os efeitos da publicidade* by João Cabral do Nascimento, in *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* V-81; *O Problema do descobrimento da Madeira* by Antonio Alvaro Doria, published in the review *Ocidente* (no. 19, 1939 and no. 27, 1940); *Quem descobriu o arquipelago da Madeira* by Duarte Leite, articles published in the *Primeiro de Janeiro* of Porto on 28 March and 4 April 1939 and reprinted in the Funchal daily newspapers; *O Descobrimento do Arquipelago da Madeira* by M. Higino Vieira, Lisbon, 1939. On the basis of what is known to date about this much-debated subject, which is of such interest to the history of Madeira, we may perhaps reach the following conclusions: 1. This archipelago was already known to Portuguese navigators before 1418; 2. The year of the original discovery and the names of the first discoverers are unknown; 3. The ‘reconnaissance’ carried out by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira may be placed in the last years of the first quarter of the 16th century, that is, around 1418 to 1425; 4. The work of settlement undertaken by those two first donataries must have begun in the first years of the second quarter of the 15th century, that is, in 1425 or shortly afterwards.

We would go too far if we tried to reproduce here the long series of arguments that have been put forward in support of these probable conjectures, but the brevity we must strictly observe in writing these pages obliges us to bring this already long and tedious article to a close.
Desembarcadouro

On a small projection of the coastline, west of the beach and cove of Machico, there is a village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) that bears this name and which tradition holds to be the spot where the first discoverers or settlers of Madeira came ashore. It would be fitting to raise a small commemorative pillar (*padrão*) there, marking the historic event of the discovery of Madeira or the beginning of its colonisation.
Desembarcadouros (islet)

The *Carta Geo-Hydrographica da ilha da Madeira* by General A. Pedro de Azevedo marks this islet with the name of Ilhéu Vermelho or de Ametade; it is also known as the Ilhéu da Cevada or dos Embarcadouros, as other sources record. The Ilhéu de Agostinho, this Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros and the Ilhéu de Fora are regarded as part of the Ponta de São Lourenço (see that entry) and lie in line with its extension. The smallest, and the closest to the point proper, from which it is separated by a narrow channel, is the Ilhéu de Agostinho (see that entry); next comes the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros and, to the east of it, the Ilhéu de Fora or do Farol. The Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros thus lies between the Ilhéu de Agostinho and the Ilhéu de Fora. These two islets, dos Desembarcadouros and de Fora, are separated from each other by a channel called the Boqueirão Grande (‘great gap’), which is 180 metres wide and about 8 metres deep. It is therefore navigable for the ‘barcos de carreira’ and coastal steamers, which frequently pass through it. The Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros has a height of about 100 m, known as the Pico Vermelho (‘red peak’), and a small beach that gives access to the upper part of the islet. Of these three islets, known as the Islets of the Ponta de São Lourenço, the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros has the largest area, and its terrain is quite rugged.

The upper part of the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros is hard to reach, but once the coastal rocks have been climbed it is easy to walk over it in every direction. The naturalist Richard Thomas Lowe called it the botanical garden of the Ponta de São Lourenço, because many rare species, hard to find elsewhere on the island, grow together there. *Beta patuta*, *Crepis divaricata*, *Asphodelus fistolosus* and *Phalaris maderensis* are plants which, in Madeira, have not been found outside the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros.

This islet is also known as the Ilhéu da Metade, Vermelho, da Cevada and dos Embarcadouros, and is separated from the Ilhéu de Fora by the so-called Boqueirão Grande. On its west side it has a beach or pebble beach (*calhau*), which is covered by the water in two places at high tide.
Deserta Grande or simply Deserta (island)

Of the three small islands that make up the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) group, the most important and the largest in area is the one called Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’), or simply Deserta. Running roughly north to south lie the Ilhéu Chão (‘flat islet’), the Deserta Grande and the Bugio, separated from one another by narrow channels navigable only by small boats. ‘The Deserta Grande (*Dic. Univ. Port.* II), so called because it is the largest of them, measures seven and a third miles, or thirteen and a half kilometres, in length by one and a third miles, or almost two and a half kilometres, in width. It is separated from each of those two islets by narrow straits or channels through which only boats can pass. All around it... steep rocks rise from the sea, and it is accessible only at a small landing place to the west, from which a narrow, winding gully climbs to the top, which is almost flat. Of the three Desertas, this is the only one that has drinking water, though brackish, and that from a single, meagre spring.’ On this upland there is a small plain, crossed in part by a valley called Pedregal (‘stony ground’), and there a rise of about 480 m in altitude stands out.
The Deserta Grande never had a permanent population, only a temporary one, and then only during the hunting season and the orchil (a dye lichen) harvest.

The Deserta Grande once had a tiled house and two thatched huts, but at present we believe that only the former still exists. There was also a chantry (capela) there, built by order of Henry the Navigator, where a cleric was obliged to stay during Holy Week and in the months of November and December, paid from the island’s tithes.

When Frutuoso wrote the *Saudades da Terra*, there were 8 men and 1 factor (*feitor*) on the Deserta, charged with gathering orchil and tending the livestock and some crops of wheat and barley grown there. Later, however, as many as 20 to 30 men came to be employed in this work. For a long time a small military force was also stationed there, responsible for the defence and guarding of the island.

Visitors to the Deserta Grande generally land at Porto da Castanheira or to the west of Ponta do Norte (‘north point’). From either of these points it is not difficult to reach the interior of the island, which is more or less flat on top, but where, because of the livestock and the lack of water, no cereals or other useful plants are now grown. In 1823 potatoes (Madeiran *semilha*), tobacco and vines were tried there, but without success.

The Deserta has goats, rabbits and a few feral cats; the cats were taken there in the 19th century to destroy the rodents that were ravaging the cereal crops. Orchil, once gathered for export, abounds on the island’s rocks, and barilla (saltwort burned for soda; *barrilha*) grows in many places, as do various plants suitable as fodder for livestock.

The population that M. d’Avezac supposes the Deserta to have, says Dr Azevedo, the convents surrounded by orange groves that Bouillet imagined there, and the prized wines that he attributes to the Ilhéu Chão, as Dezobry and Bachelet do to the whole group, are mere dreams of frivolous tourists, whose writings these authors incautiously trusted, thereby leading others, even Portuguese ones, to fall into such absurdities’.

In 1503 a few shepherds on the Deserta Grande fought off an attack by some 80 Englishmen led by the Portuguese corsair Penteado, ‘rolling stones down the stream bed, says Frutuoso, and the rocks, as they broke, helped them with earth and other stones that they shook loose, so that the enemy re-embarked in greater haste than they had climbed up; and when the shepherds came down after the enemy had embarked, they found a mastiff and many arrows, which had been left behind in the hurry, and on the pebble beach (calhau) much blood from wounded enemies’. Near the house on the Deserta Grande there are two reservoirs of murky water and a spring that yields little more than a barrel of water over several hours. Some water is also found at the locality (*sítio*) of Eirinha.

In 1894 a great landslide occurred on the coast of the Deserta Grande, as a result of which the sea advanced and then retreated at several points along the south coast of Madeira. Some attributed this landslide to an earthquake, which, if it did occur, was not felt in Funchal.

The Deserta Grande belonged to the captaincy of Funchal until the time of the 3rd captain-donatary, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, but on his death it passed to Luiz Gonçalves de Ataíde, son of that captain and his second wife, Dona Isabel da Silva, as his mother’s dowry and marriage settlement. At that time the island yielded about 200$00 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year. Monk seals (*Monachus albiventer*) appear in the caves of the Deserta Grande, but they are now scarce.

In September 1930 a small religious monument was inaugurated on a height overlooking the Praia da Lapa (‘beach of the grotto’) on the Deserta Grande. It consists of a modest plinth bearing an image of Nossa Senhora das Graças, and it was erected on the initiative of the Madeiran Rui da Silva.
Desertas (islands)

This group consists of three small islands known as Ilhéu Chão (‘flat islet’), Deserta Grande, or simply Deserta, and Bugio. They lie in a north-north-west to south-south-east line with the Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’), south-east of Madeira, and are closer to that point. To the north of the three islets lies a small islet known as Furilhão, or more properly Farilhão (‘sea stack’), as Ilhéu (‘islet’) or Rocha do Navio (‘ship cliff’), and also as Prego do Mar (see that entry); it is separated from Ilhéu Chão by a narrow channel. Running roughly north to south, Ilhéu Chão is followed by Deserta Grande and that in turn by Bugio, separated from one another by narrow straits navigable only by vessels of very small tonnage. The extreme points of this small group of islands, or tiny archipelago, as it has been called, are: to the north, the said Furilhão islet; to the south, the Ponta das Agulhas (‘needles point’), at the southern tip of Bugio; to the east, the same point; and to the west, the Ponta do Pedregal (‘stony ground point’), on the western coast of Deserta Grande. The geographical position of the three islands, taken together, is as follows: they lie between 32° 35′ and 32° 22′ 20″ N and between 16° 27′ 25″ and 16° 32′ W (Greenwich). The group is about eleven miles, or roughly twenty kilometres, from the Ponta de São Lourenço. The Desertas (‘deserted islands’) are regarded as belonging to the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé – Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) – but it seems that they were once incorporated in the parish of Caniço (‘reed’), and those who died on the islands were generally buried there.

Ilhéu Chão (Porto de Santa Maria) lies about 19 miles from the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*), 15.5 from Caniço, 14 from Santa Cruz, 14.5 from Machico and 11 from the Ponta de São Lourenço. Deserta Grande (Carga da Lapa) is approximately 22 miles from Funchal. The Ponta da Agulha (‘needle point’), on Ilhéu Chão, which is the southernmost point of the Desertas group and of the Madeiran archipelago, is almost 27 miles from the harbour of Funchal.

The sighting of this group is bound up with the discovery of Madeira, since it is impossible to approach the south coast of the island without clearly seeing the Desertas. It seems that some attempts at colonisation were made, but above all the lack of water, together with other local circumstances, never allowed a settlement in the strict sense of the word. In the seasons best suited to hunting, fishing and the gathering of orchil (a dye lichen), a few men would stay on Deserta Grande for those purposes, but there were never any permanent residents there. The Desertas Islands belonged to the captain-donataries of Funchal. They passed from the third donatary (*donatário*), Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, to his son Luís Gonçalves de Ataíde, and then to the latter’s son João Gonçalves de Ataíde, 6th Count of Atouguia, in whose house the islands were incorporated. Ownership then passed to the Counts of Taipa. The representative of that house, Gastão da Câmara Coutinho, 12th Lord of the Desertas, sold the property in 1864 to Alexandre Fernandes Camacho, and it later passed to his son of the same name. In 1894 the islands were sold at public auction to Henrique Hinton and Carlos Cossart.

Under the title *As Desertas*, Mr Alberto Artur Sarmento published a pamphlet containing valuable information on Deserta Grande, Bugio and Ilhéu Chão, and in the book entitled *La carrière d'un navigateur* the Prince of Monaco devoted the chapter *La Chasse* to an engaging description of a hunt on the Desertas. Some further information on the same group of islands can also be found in the French review *Le Cosmos* of 1902, in the *Diário do Comercio* of March 1903, in the bulletin of the Portuguese Society of Natural Sciences (*Sociedade Portuguesa de Sciencias Naturais*) of 1911, and in the *Revista Semanal* of 1861, p. 108.
See the articles the Madeira archipelago, Deserta Grande, Bugio and Ilhéu Chão.
Desertas (headlands)

The largest headlands on the coast of the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) group are Ponta de Santa Maria, on the western shore of Ilhéu Chão (Flat Islet); those of Castanheira and Pedregal, on the west coast of Deserta Grande; and Ponta das Agulhas, at the southern tip of Bugio (see those entries).
Disinfections see Disinfection Station and Maritime Disinfection Station
Desporto (O)
Its 1st issue appeared on 17 April 1918, and it is published fortnightly.
Desterro

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), where there is a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Flight into Egypt (*Nossa Senhora do Desterro*). It was founded in 1625 by Canon Jorge Furtado de Sousa and recently restored by Dr Juvenal de Araújo, its present owner.
Diabelha (Plantago coronopus)

A plant of the family Plantaginaceae, common on Madeira, Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’). Its leaves are arranged in a rosette, elongated, hairy or almost glabrous, usually 1–2-pinnatipartite, and its spikes are narrow, with basal peduncles. An infusion of its leaves is used as a gargle for diseases of the throat. The name *diabelha* is better known on Porto Santo than on Madeira.
Diabinho (João Nunes)

He was born in Funchal on 16 March 1850. For many years he worked at the Ilhéu Semaphore Station (*Estação Semafórica do Ilhéu*), a post from which he retired, and he is well known as a setter of charades, having contributed to the *Almanach de Lembranças* and other publications. He invented and built an apparatus that he called the ‘despertador-translator’, and he is a man of undeniable artistic gifts, as several other works he has made bear witness. He died on 11 January 1927.
Diário da Madeira
It was published from 3 November 1880 to 15 December 1881, with 281 issues appearing.

Another newspaper with the same title began to appear on 1 January 1912 and is still published at present. Its first editor was Francisco Bento de Gouveia, followed by Dr Juvenal Henriques de Araújo and Major J. Reis Gomes.
Diário da Manhã
The first issue was published on 8 July 1882, and the last, number 129, on 7 December of the same year.
Diário da Tarde
This newspaper issued 305 numbers, the first on 17 December 1881 and the last on 30 December 1882.
Diário de Notícias

The first periodical published in this city was *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’), in 1821, which appeared twice weekly. Fifty-five years later came the first daily newspaper, the *Diário de Notícias*, whose first issue appeared on 11 October 1876.

In a narrow milieu such as Madeira, where love of letters was never great, the decision to publish a daily newspaper was a risky undertaking, but one worthy of the highest praise. That date marks a glorious stage in the history of local journalism, and the name of this paper’s founder is engraved in letters of gold in the annals of our literary life.

The illustrious Madeiran Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira, a poet, journalist and orator of rare merit, launched this daily paper, which to many seemed an unattainable utopia and to most an enterprise whose life would last little longer than Malherbe’s roses... For some years he sustained it with the force of his talent, prestige and influence. To do so he had to struggle against enormous difficulties, which the tenacity and energy of his will overcame entirely.
In editing and running the *Diário de Notícias*, Canon Alfredo de Oliveira had the valuable assistance of the distinguished Madeiran writer João de Nóbrega Soares.

Besides Canon Alfredo C. de Oliveira and João de Nóbrega Soares, the following writers and journalists successively served as editors of this paper: Francisco Clementino de Sousa, João José Vieira, Captain António Alves Conti, Second Lieutenant Augusto César de Morais, Captain José Augusto Pereira Ramalho, Lieutenant João Augusto César de Freitas, Father João Maurício Henriques, Lieutenant João José de Freitas, João José de Macedo Júnior, Luís de Ornelas Pinto Coelho, Ciríaco de Brito e Nóbrega, Father Fernando Augusto da Silva, Dr Manuel Sardinha, Francisco da Conceição Rodrigues, José da Silva Coelho, Dr Domingos dos Reis Costa, Feliciano Soares and Dr Alberto de Araújo.

Ownership of the paper passed from Canon Alfredo de Oliveira to Alexandre Fernandes Camacho, and then to the Baron of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’) and João Eleutério Martins; today its owners are Blandy Brothers.

The first 24 issues were published in Calçada do Cidrão (‘citron causeway’). The paper then began to appear from the mezzanine of the building in Rua de João Tavira that housed the civil government until a few years ago. Later all its premises moved to the building on the corner of the same street and the beginning of Avenida do Dr. Manuel de Arriaga.
It is the oldest newspaper in Madeira and the one that has had the longest and most prosperous existence here.
Diário do Commercio
The first issue was published on 1 October 1891 and the last on 8 September 1896, 8 issues having appeared.
Diário do Commercio (O)
The first issue appeared on 9 September 1896, and the last, number 4023, on 12 May 1911.
For many years Francisco António Ferreira was the chief editor of this newspaper.
Diário do Funchal
It began publication on 5 November 1877 and ended with no. 200, on 14 July 1878.
Diário Popular
It began publication on 18 December 1882 and ceased on 25 November 1888, 282 issues having appeared.
Another newspaper of the same name appeared on 1 July 1897; its publication ceased on 24 December 1911, after 137 issues.
Dias
This family surname is very old here. One of the first to bear it on this island was Rui Dias de Aguiar, son of Diogo de Aguiar and grandson of Zarco.
See Aguiar.
Dias (Baltasar)

Little is known of the personal circumstances of this Madeiran, although in his day he enjoyed great renown as a poet and as the author of several plays (*autos*), which the common people read avidly and which went through many editions. It is vaguely recorded that he was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Sant’Ana, and it is presumed that he spent a considerable part of his life on the mainland, in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), where he died in a year we cannot determine. Diogo Barbosa Machado says in his *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’) ‘that he was one of the celebrated poets who flourished in the reign of King Sebastian, chiefly in the composition of *autos*, with the circumstance of being blind from birth’. The *Diccionario Bibliographico* of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, in volume 1, merely reproduces the brief notice given by Diogo Barbosa Machado.

Inocêncio Francisco da Silva records the following compositions by Baltasar Dias: *Auto d'el-rei Salomão*, 1613; *Auto da Paixão de Christo*, in verse, 1613; *Auto de Santo Aleixo*, 1613, 1616, 1638, 1749 and 1791; *Auto de Santa Catharina Virgem e Martyr*, 1616, 1638, 1659, 1727 and 1786; *Auto da Feira da Ladra*, 1613; *Conselhos para bem casar*, 1638, 1659 and 1680; *Auto da milicia das mulheres*, 1640 and 1793; *Historia da Imperatriz Porcina, mulher do Imperador Lodonio de Roma*, 1660, which has been reprinted many times; *Auto do Nascimento de Christo*, 1665; *Trovas de arte maior sobre a morte de D. João de Castro*...; *Tragédia do Marquez de Mantua*, 1665. The following explanations are by Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, and we transcribe them verbatim:

‘This tragedy (that of the Marquis of Mantua), of which there are several later reprints, was recently included by Viscount de Almeida Garrett in volume III of his *Romanceiro* (vol. XV of his *Works*), from page 195 to 296, where readers may see it. There the opinion is expressed that this Portuguese version of a ballad originally French or Provençal dates from the end of the 14th century, or at the latest from the beginning of the 15th. If so, it would certainly not be by Balthasar Dias, and it had been wrongly attributed to him by our bibliographers; the illustrious critic, however, seems unaware of this, for he says not a word about Balthasar Dias, nor that the work ever circulated under his name.

‘I should dearly have liked to shed more light on what concerns this old poet, whose productions, whether his own or attributed to him, are as well known and widespread as his personal circumstances and the precise and certain period in which he lived are unknown. I should also have liked to verify whether, besides the editions listed above, taken from the *Bibl. Lus.* and repeated in the Academy’s *Catalogo*, there are other, earlier ones, as seems probable if the author lived in the period claimed. I cannot yet satisfy this wish, however, since the investigations made so far have produced no satisfactory result.

‘If, as I hope, I obtain further information, I shall set out in the *Supplemento* whatever has been added. What is undeniable, whether or not the works that circulate under his name are by Balthasar Dias, is that they (if not all, then most of them) have been reprinted again and again; and that, despite the errors with which they are riddled, which often distort the sense, they have touches so national and so pleasing to the people that even today they are sought after and read both in Lisbon and in the provinces. “Go round (says one of our most eminent modern authors) the cottages in the villages and the workshops and craftsmen’s stores in the towns, and in almost all of them you will find one or another of the many editions of the *autos* of St Alexis, St Catherine, the Empress Porcina, the Malice of Women, etc.”','

In volume VIII of his *Diccionario*, Inocêncio adds the following: ‘Concerning this poet of ours, the certain period in which he lived and the time when the productions whose authorship is attributed to him were first printed, there remains the same scarcity of information that makes everything relating to him obscure and doubtful.’ In Teófilo Braga’s *Recapitulação da Historia da Litteratura Portuguesa II. Renascença*, on p. 308, the following interesting information is found:

‘Of all the poets of the school of Gil Vicente he was the people’s favourite, and their affection for him endures still: he is read and performed in the villages. “A man lacking sight”, a 17th-century manuscript says of him, and this is confirmed by the royal decree (*alvará*) of 29 February 1537 granting the privilege for the publication of his works: “I make known that Baltazar Dias, blind, of the island of Madeira, told me by his petition that he has written certain works, both in prose and in verse, which have already been seen and approved, and some of them printed, as I could see from a public instrument that he presented before me. And since he wishes to have the said works that he has written printed, and others that he hopes to write, being a poor man with no other means of living, owing to the lack of his sight, than selling the said works, he asked me that I be pleased, as an act of charity, to grant him a privilege so that no person may print or sell his works without his licence, under a certain penalty.” The privilege was granted and a fine of thirty *cruzados* imposed on any counterfeiter, and the following condition was laid upon him: “if he should write any works touching on matters of our holy faith, they shall not be printed without first being seen and examined by Master Pedro Margualho; and once they have been seen by him and he finds that they speak of nothing that ought not to be spoken of, he shall issue him a certificate to that effect, with which certificate I am pleased that such works be printed, and not otherwise.”

These rigours of ecclesiastical censorship were systematised in the first Index of condemned *autos* issued by the Cardinal Infante Dom Henrique in 1551, and in those that banned *autos* on subjects taken from the Bible and the Gospels. The *Auto del rei Salomão*, the versified *Auto da Paixão de Christo* and the *Auto da Feira da Ladra* have been lost. Still very much alive today are the *Auto de Santo Aleixo* and the *Auto de Santa Catherina*, drawn from the narratives of the *Legenda Aurea*, and the tragedy of the *Marquez de Mantua*. He had a lively poetic sense, which is why the *Historia da Imperatriz Porcina*, the *Malicia das Mulheres* and the *Conselhos para bem casar* are still read in the villages. From a stanza of this popular satire we know that he spent his last years in Beira:

Your heralding fame moves me to send you this, although I am here in this Beira, so far removed from versifying that I cannot make a whole verse. All these works of classical stamp, scattered in loose sheets, well deserve to be gathered in one volume with a careful literary edition. He is supposed to have died towards the end of the reign of King Sebastian.’
Dias e Sousa (Bartolomeu dos Mártires)
He was deputy for Madeira in the legislative sessions of 1842 to 1845 and of 1846.

He was a graduate in canon law and took part in the campaigns for liberty. He distinguished himself as a politician and journalist. He was said to be a man of profound intellectual culture. He was born on 27 July 1806 and died on 7 January 1872.
Dias Ferreira (Dr Augusto)
He was deputy for Madeira in the legislative session of 1892 to 1893. He was the son of the great jurist and statesman José Dias Ferreira.
Dias Ferreira (José)

This distinguished politician and jurist arrived in Funchal on 7 March 1873 and stayed there for some months. He lived at the Quinta Bianchi, a *quinta* (country estate) in the locality (*sítio*) of Nazaré (‘Nazareth’), in São Martinho. The property today belongs to the heirs of Manuel José de Favila Vieira; at that time it belonged to the late merchant Augusto César de Bianchi, later Viscount of Bianchi.
Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Dias Ferreira was born on 30 November 1837 and died in Vidago on 9 September 1907.
Dias Leite (Canon Jerónimo)

He was a half-prebendary canon (*cónego de meia prebenda*) of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), a position he took up in 1572, and in 1590 he was appointed a canon with a full prebend. We do not know where he was born, nor any other personal details concerning him. His name is well known to those engaged in research into Madeiran history, because he was perhaps the first person here in Madeira to devote himself to studies of this kind. Taking as the basis of his work a short account of the discovery of Madeira left by Gonçalo Aires (see that entry), a companion of Zarco, and ‘drawing, says Frutuoso, on the registers of the councils of the whole island (all of which were handed over to him)’, he wrote the *História e Informação dos ilustres capitães da ilha da Madeira*.

The author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) acknowledges in more than one place that it was Dias Leite who supplied him with the main material for the work he wrote in 1590 on the island of São Miguel. Referring to the manuscript of Gonçalo Aires, he says that Dias Leite ‘compiled it, added to it and polished it in his grave and refined style, written on eleven sheets of paper, and sent it to me’.

Was the work of Canon Jerónimo Dias Leite lost? Referring to the authors who deal with the Robert Machin affair, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that he owns an anonymous manuscript entitled *Historia do descobrimento da ilha da Madeira e da descendência nobilissima dos seus valerosos Capitães*. He presumes it to be the original written by Dias Leite shortly before 1590, and adds elsewhere that it is ‘written on 22 small quarto leaves and a few lines more, that is, eleven sheets of paper’. This seems to indicate that it is the very original manuscript of which Gaspar Frutuoso speaks.

In the library of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) there is a manuscript that some have regarded as the historical work of Jerónimo Dias Leite, although it is perhaps a copy and not the true original. A few pages of this curious text were published around the middle of the 19th century, and a copy of that edition is held in the same library, the only one whose existence we know of. Among the old manuscripts dealing with Madeiran matters, this should be one of the first to be honoured with publication, even though it may not be possible to establish whether or not Canon Dias Leite was its author. Quite apart from that question, it contains interesting and curious information and is undoubtedly a valuable contribution to the history of this archipelago.
On this subject, it is worth reading the chapter ‘O manuscrito de Gonçalaires’ in João Cabral do Nascimento’s book *Apontamentos de Historia Insular*.
Dibblee (Harrison)

Representative of the American Red Cross (*Cruz Vermelha*), who arrived in Madeira on 6 November 1918 aboard the transport *Lake Forest*. The ship brought to this island 1465 sacks of potatoes (Madeiran *semilha*), 1047 of beans, 3,000 of maize flour and 10,628 of maize grain, sent by that charitable society at the request of Mr Kemper, the American consul in Funchal. This substantial supply of provisions was a great benefit to the Madeiran population, which was already struggling with hunger because the foodstuffs needed for its subsistence were almost exhausted.

In honour of Mr Dibblee and the American consul, a dinner attended by 76 guests was held on 9 November at the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’). Two popular demonstrations also took place, one organised by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) and the other by the working classes, both intended to thank those two foreign benefactors for having supplied our market with the grain needed for our public consumption.
Mr Dibblee left for Norfolk (Virginia) on 17 November. While in Funchal he stayed at the Palácio de São Lourenço.
Diferença

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish of Faial, where Manuel Carvalho Valdavesso, son-in-law of Valentim de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 7th holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Penha de Águia (‘eagle crag’), built in 1725 a chantry (capela) with the dedication of São Luís (St Louis).
Dillon (Frank)
He made various views of Madeira in 1848 and 1849, which were later published in London under the following title: *A Series of Views of Funchal and its Neighbourhood*.
Dinis (Júlio)

Joaquim Guilherme Gomes Coelho, the eminent novelist who adopted the pseudonym Júlio Dinis in all his writings, has a life bound up with the history of this island, for he visited it several times and wrote one of his best-known and most exquisite books here.

Stricken by a stubborn lung disease, he came to seek from the kindness of our climate some relief for his sufferings, and to look here for that ideal called health, in his own already disheartened words.

He first arrived in Funchal on 8 February 1869 and returned in 1870 and 1871. According to some notes published in the former magazine *Serões*, which we consider reliable, Júlio Dinis lived, if only briefly, in a house at the Ilhéus (islets), where the distinguished lawyer Nuno Ferreira Jardim once resided, and for longer in a building on Rua da Carreira (‘track’) belonging to the family of the late merchant António Pinto Correia. A pharmacy is now installed on its ground floor, and it stands almost opposite Rua de São Francisco (St Francis). The Funchal Council would perform an act that all its citizens would regard with grateful praise if it had a simple metal plaque placed on that house, if nothing more could be done, commemorating the stay in our land of one of the greatest figures of our contemporary literature.

It was in this city that Júlio Dinis wrote his remarkable novel *Os Fidalgos da Casa Mourisca*, which some consider superior to, and many place on the same level as, *As Pupilas do Senhor Reitor* and *A Morgadinha dos Cannaviaes*. For thirty-odd years a long letter he wrote from Madeira remained unpublished. In it he describes the island’s incomparable beauties in broad strokes, sharing with a friend the personal impressions he received on arriving at the lovely island that rises from the foam of the sea like the mythological Cytherea... to borrow a phrase of the great writer. It is a passage of fine, evocative prose, first published in the aforementioned review *Serões* and reproduced in the book of Júlio Dinis’s unpublished writings entitled *Ineditos e Esparsos*. This work published 17 letters by Júlio Dinis written in Funchal, the last dated 20 February 1870. The 1919 edition of this work includes 31 letters written in Funchal, omitting 7 from the earlier edition, making a total of 38. The *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) of 24 August 1919 published two further unpublished letters by the great novelist, also dated from Madeira.

The great novelist stayed on this island from March to May 1869, from October 1869 to May 1870 and from October 1870 to May 1871. During his time in Funchal he was on the closest terms with his fellow countryman and friend, Canon Dr Custódio de Morais e Brito, a man of uncommon talent and rare learning.

The following words, in his own hand, were found in a manuscript book belonging to the illustrious writer: ‘I began writing *Os Fidalgos da Casa Mourisca* in Funchal in March 1869. I was in the middle of chapter 8 when I returned to Porto in May of the same year. I worked in Porto and wrote up to the beginning of chapter 17, from June to October, when I went back to Madeira. I finished it in Funchal on 11 April 1870’.
Júlio Dinis died in Porto on 12 September 1871, four months after leaving Madeira, aged only 31.
Diocese (creation of the)

The first diocese created in the lands of our conquests and discoveries was that of Funchal. Our ever-growing colonial and maritime expansion from the beginning of the 15th century, together with the settlement and exploitation of the newly discovered lands, led to the creation of several bishoprics outside mainland Portugal, and the Madeiran archipelago had the honour of being the first to receive one of these dioceses. When the bishoprics of Angra, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Goa were later created, that of Funchal was raised to the rank of archbishopric and became the seat of an ecclesiastical province, with those dioceses as its suffragans (see Archbishopric).

The steady growth of the population and the remarkable importance that Funchal gradually acquired led Afonso V to raise the settlement to the rank of town (*vila*) around 1451, and Manuel I later to grant it the status of a city by royal decree (*alvará*) of 21 August 1508.

It was also essential to put the religious affairs of the archipelago on a more satisfactory footing. Madeira belonged to the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), which had its seat in Tomar, and it was therefore the Order’s task to oversee matters of ecclesiastical jurisdiction; to this end it had delegated the direction of all religious questions on this island to the vicar of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*). The creation of an autonomous diocese was thus imperative, headed by a prelate who could perform all acts of worship and freely oversee every matter of church discipline. King Manuel I understood this and requested the creation of the Funchal diocese, which Pope Leo X established by a bull (papal bull) of 12 June 1514, freeing the new bishopric from the jurisdiction of the mastership of the Order of Christ.

The first bishop of this diocese was Dom Diogo Pinheiro, who held a high office in the Order of Christ, to which Madeira belonged in spiritual matters. We shall deal with him in a separate article. The main purpose of creating the diocese was to place the personal and immediate direction of religious affairs in this archipelago in the hands of a prelate who could also perform all the acts of worship and canonical jurisdiction reserved to the ecclesiastical rank to which bishops belong. This, however, did not happen. Only fifty-two years after the creation of the Funchal diocese did its fourth bishop, Dom Jorge de Lemos, come in person to take possession of his office, which he held for some years.

On page 568 of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) there is the Latin text of a bull, which is described there as the one that created this diocese. This is not correct. It is the bull *Pro excellenti praeeminentia*, cited under this title in various places, that is the papal instrument establishing the bishopric of Funchal. It is transcribed in full on p. 257 of vol. 1 of the *Corpo Diplomatico Portuguez*, edited by Rebêlo da Silva and published in 1862, and it had already appeared, at least in part, in other, older works. Rebêlo da Silva’s edition is a copy taken directly from the Torre do Tombo (national archives), where the original and authentic record are kept in the Bundle of Bulls (*Maço das Bulas*), under no. 34. This document, which is fairly long, was translated into Portuguese some years ago by Father Ricardo Augusto de Sequeira, a distinguished teacher at our lyceum (state secondary school), and published in several issues of the *Correio do Funchal* (‘Funchal Courier’) in November 1897.

In the same volume of the *Corpo diplomático*, already cited, there is on p. 261 another bull, beginning with the words *Gratiae divinae praemium*, addressed to King Manuel I, which officially announces the creation of the diocese of Funchal and the appointment of Dom Diogo Pinheiro as its bishop. The one transcribed in the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ is addressed to the faithful and clergy of Madeira. All of them bear the date 12 June 1514. In the old Bishop’s Palace of Funchal (*Paço Episcopal do Funchal*), framed and hanging on one of the walls of the palace’s main hall, was the parchment containing the actual original of a bull concerning the creation of this bishopric, which we believe to be the one transcribed in the notes to the *Saudades*.
See cathedral chapter (*Cabido*).
Diogo (Duke Dom)

He inherited the lordship (*senhorio*) of the Madeira archipelago from his father, the Infante Ferdinand, and was Duke of Viseu. He was murdered by his brother-in-law, King John II, on 23 August 1481. On his death the lordship of the archipelago passed to his brother Manuel I, who later became King of Portugal.
Diplomats

The following Madeirans followed a diplomatic career and represented Portugal in various countries: the Count of Torre Bela, José Anselmo Correia Henriques, João Francisco de Oliveira, the Viscount (*visconde*) of Nogueiras, Agostinho de Ornelas, the Baron of São Pedro, João de Oliveira Sá Camelo Lampreia and Jorge Santos (see those entries).
Diptera
See Insects.
Dykes

Dykes (*diques*) are walls of volcanic rock formed when molten material penetrated fissures opened by earthquakes in pre-existing ground. Where dykes are abundant in a locality, this shows that volcanic activity was felt there with great intensity.
In Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) and other valleys of the interior of Madeira there are a great number of dykes, and at Cabo Girão there are both vertical and horizontal dykes.

Dykes sometimes taper to a point at the top. There are also some, such as the one at the hillock of Piedade (‘pity’) on the Ponta de São Lourenço, that are cut off or intercepted at the base by horizontal strata.

The basalt dyke that forms a knoll (*cabeço*) or nipple at the top of Garajau (‘tern’) can be made out on either side of this cape, and is double on its eastern side. There are also double dykes at Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’), on the seaward side of Penha de Águia (‘eagle crag’) and elsewhere, which probably result from a fresh penetration of lava into the same fissures.

Some dykes stand isolated because the surrounding ground has been destroyed by denudation. The peaks of Empinos, near Curral, are formed of isolated dykes, and at Ribeiro do Juncal (‘rush-bed brook’), at the head of the Ribeira da Metade (‘halfway stream’), there is a dyke in the same condition, about 45 metres high and 18 wide.

It is supposed that in most of Madeira’s dykes the molten material was forced upwards from below. In the Piedade dyke already mentioned, however, and in another at Ribeiro dos Piornais (‘broom-thicket brook’), between Caniço (‘reed’) and Funchal, the opposite seems to have occurred, since both are interrupted or cut off at the base.
Public Works Department

A Public Works Directorate existed in Funchal from the creation of the Ministry of Public Works in 1852. Before that there was a department (*repartição*) here called the Civil Engineering Archive, run by officers of the Royal Corps of Engineers. These services are today handled by the technical department of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*).
Direita (street)
It lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé and links the Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory’) with Rua 31 de Janeiro, formerly Rua da Princesa.

It is an old public thoroughfare, short and of secondary importance compared with other streets of this city. Among the streets of old Funchal, however, it was one of the most important and also one of the longest, beginning at the Pelourinho and running along the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’) to the vicinity of the Torreão (‘turret’). Gaspar Frutuoso, writing of it in 1590, says that it was ‘a great, wide street and the largest in the city’, adding that Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto (1574–1585) had there ‘his very rich lodgings, with their cool gardens’. In this old street stood the church of St Bartholomew (*São Bartolomeu*) and its hospice (*albergaria*), and some of the most distinguished people of Funchal had their residences there.
Direito (O)
The first issue appeared on 21 October 1857 and the last, no. 93, on 7 August 1859. Its editor was Pedro Maria Gonçalves de Freitas.

Another newspaper of the same title appeared, published with various interruptions over several decades; its founder and chief editor was the Madeiran writer João Augusto de Ornelas. The 1st issue came out on 2 November 1859.
Another series of the same newspaper, which we believe to be the fourth, was published from 20 April 1902 (no. 2,511) to 11 January 1911 (no. 5,060).
Speeches

So as not to make the article Bibliography too long, we have reserved for this place a brief enumeration of various oratorical pieces published by natives of this archipelago, or whose subject may in any way be of interest to the history of these islands. Although very incomplete, this list may serve as an aid to the study of Madeiran bibliography. The various items of which we have been able to obtain notice are given here without regard to subject or even to chronological order. They are: *Oratio in funere Philippi II*, Rome, 1599, *Gratulatio de S. Pontif. Sea distances
The distance between the ports of Lisbon and Funchal is generally reckoned at 520 nautical miles.
The point on the African coast closest to Madeira is Cape Cantin, and the distance separating the two is 350 miles.

The stretch of sea that separates the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), known as the Travessa (‘crossing’), measures 21 and a half miles between the Ilhéu de Fora (Ponta de São Lourenço) and the Ilhéu de Baixo (Porto Santo). The distance between the harbour of the city of Funchal and that of the town (*vila*) of Porto Santo is approximately 41 miles.

Grant of the Island of Madeira to Catherine of Braganza

Eager for firm support, so that Portugal would not succumb in the War of Independence, the country stood ready to make a great sacrifice that could be thrown promptly into the scales of our concessions to attract England’s help. The dearest jewel of Portugal was to be granted to the Infanta Queen Catherine, daughter of John IV and future Queen of England: among the bride’s gifts, if need be, would figure the flowering bouquet of the island of Madeira.

The queen regent, Dona Luísa, beset by bitterness under the weight of government, faced with an incapable heir and a court that was like a backstage of tangled political intrigues, did not wish to take upon herself the responsibility of alienating Madeira, nor to incur the curse of God invoked in the letter of Manuel I when he made the island Crown land (*realenga*) (vol. 1 of the Archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal). She therefore had a grant from the late king to his daughter forged, and sent it to the councils (*Senados*) of Funchal and Machico so that the documents might be registered. This curious point of history is discussed by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in the notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), p. 384.
These were precautionary documents, for the text states that they were to be used ‘when the time comes’, in order to overcome any obstacle that might arise in the diplomatic negotiations.

In the Archive of the Municipal Council of Machico, curious documents on this subject are registered under the headings of Book 3, Part 1 (fol. 158 v.: copy of His Majesty’s royal decree (*alvará*) of the royal grant made to the Lady Infanta Dona Catharina, 23 November 1660; fol. 261: copy of the power of attorney of the Lady Infanta Dona Catharina, 18 November 1660; royal decree declaring the manner in which the Lady Infanta Dona Catharina is to use the grants made to her by His Majesty her august father).

At that time the legend of the English lovers who had landed on this island was also revived, in order to lend colour to a supposed English priority in the discovery and so to soften the pain of losing Madeira, should that prove necessary. (See Robert Machin)

So great a sacrifice was not needed. Freedom of English trade in Brazil and the East Indies, together with Tangier and Bombay, ‘keys of the Mediterranean and of India’, satisfied British diplomacy, which remained unaware of the documents mentioned above, since they were of a somewhat confidential nature.

There is a pamphlet entitled *Um Ponto de Historia Pátria* (Funchal, 1914), an offprint of articles published in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’), nos 2815–16 and 2823–24, which deals with this subject. S.
See Melo.
Grants

It is very likely, although the chroniclers do not say so and no document is known that proves it, that it was John I himself who granted – or, rather, confirmed – possession of the Madeira archipelago to his son Prince Henry the Navigator, to whose bold initiative the discovery of the archipelago was chiefly owed.

Bernardo de Brito tells us in the *Monarchia Lusitana* that in 1433, the year in which Dom Duarte began his reign, his brother Dom Henrique had made him a ‘grant of these three islands to the crown of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and for that reason the king at once gave them back to him, reserving to himself the minting of coin and cases of death and the cutting off of limbs; and, to restore his dominion to him, he granted them to the Order (of Christ) in the said year’. This should not strictly be understood as a grant made by Prince Henry to the king, since he could not make one, but merely as his recognition that the new monarch, as head of the nation, held the primordial and fundamental right to the newly discovered lands, which formed an integral part of that nation.

Volume I of the Archive of the Municipal Council, and the transcription in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) on p. 325, contain the royal letter (*carta régia*) of Dom Duarte dated 26 September 1433, granting to the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) ‘for ever and ever all the spiritual jurisdiction of our islands of Madeira and Porto Santo and of the Deserta island...’ Bearing the same date and issued by the same monarch, another letter, included in the work *Alguns documentos do Arquivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo acerca da avançada e conquistas dos portugueses*, bestows the said islands on Prince Henry as a royal grant.

The grant to the Order of Christ should be understood to concern spiritual jurisdiction, and the one made to Dom Henrique the temporal dominion of the archipelago. Since, however, the Prince was Grand Master of the Order, it follows from reading that letter that he would have held the most absolute dominion over the islands of the archipelago; this did not prevent royal interference from sometimes being felt in the administration of the affairs of these islands. ‘It is to be noted, however,’ continues the aforementioned Bernardo de Brito, ‘that the Prince, knowing that after his death the conquests could not be continued with the resources of the Order, and that the arm of the king was needed, divided everything he had discovered in such a way as to leave the Order enlarged and ennobled and the Crown of the Kingdom extended. And so he granted the temporal rule of those islands and of the mainland of Guinea to the kings of Portugal and reserved the spiritual rule for the Order, which is what the kings enjoy today as Masters, for which reason they hold the tithes and the presentations of those churches. Already in the year 1439, when King Duarte was in possession of the temporal rule of the islands of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), which the Prince had once again granted to him, their spiritual jurisdiction was conceded to the Order by a letter drawn up in Lisbon on 20 May of that year...’ By royal letters of 11 March 1449 and 17 August 1459, Afonso V confirmed the grant made to Prince Henry by King Duarte on 26 September 1433.

The work *Alguns documentos do Arquivo Nacional* etc., already cited, transcribes a letter from Prince Henry the Navigator dated 18 September 1460, making a fresh grant of these islands, in spiritual matters, to the Order of Christ. We cannot adequately explain this, since the earlier grants cited above were already in existence. Prince Henry died on 13 November 1460, and as early as 3 December of the same year Afonso V signed a royal letter (*carta régia*) granting the Madeira archipelago to his brother, Infante Ferdinand. Ferdinand succeeded Henry in the grand mastership of the Order of Christ and therefore in the privileges that Henry had held over the discovered lands.

In the office of Grand Master of the Order of Christ, Ferdinand was succeeded by his son, the Infante Dom João, Duke of Viseu, and João in turn by his brother Diogo, Duke of Viseu, who was murdered by John II. We do not know the letters granting these islands that would have been issued to him, if indeed any were.

The Infante Diogo, Duke of Viseu, was succeeded in that grand mastership by his brother Dom Manuel, later king as Manuel I. The position of head of this powerful Order, which rendered such distinguished services to our country, passed to the Crown, to be held by the monarch with all the privileges, prerogatives and exemptions that belonged to it.

The grants had come to an end and Madeira had become Crown land (*realenga*). The document that attests to this, transcribed on p. 479 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’, is of great interest. It is the royal letter (*carta régia*) of Manuel I, dated 27 April 1497, in which he states that ‘it seems to us a just and necessary thing that the said island, with its lordship, revenues and jurisdiction, should belong solely to our said Crown for ever, and to the kings our heirs and successors... that neither the said island nor any part of it shall ever be given by us or our successors, whether as a favour, for life, in perpetuity or in any other manner whatsoever, to any person of whatever estate, condition and eminence... we swear upon the sign of the cross and upon the holy Gospels, on which we bodily lay our hands, to fulfil and maintain this wholly... and we beg and earnestly charge the kings our heirs and successors, by our blessing and under pain of the curse of God and of ourselves, always so to fulfil and preserve it for ever...’. With the incorporation of the grand mastership of the Order of Christ into the Crown in 1497 and the creation of the diocese of Funchal in 1514, the jurisdiction of that Order in this archipelago became almost nil.

Although we have said above that the grants ceased, there was certainly a sham grant made by John IV, five days before his death, in favour of his daughter Queen Catherine, who married Charles II of England. This grant served purposes that have never been properly established, but it was utterly illegal and never truly took effect. We deal with it in a separate article.
We do not deal here with the grants made to the donataries, since we have already referred to them in the articles Captaincies and Donataries.
