Old Buildings

Besides the customs house (*Alfândega*) building, whose arcades and interior doorways bear, as Dr Azevedo puts it, the indelible architectural stamp of the Manueline style, there stood in Funchal some half a century ago four buildings whose Gothic twin-light windows likewise suggested considerable antiquity. These buildings drew the attention of everyone versed in architecture. Three of them vanished many years ago beneath the destructive sledgehammer, which in our land generally respects nothing, and only one now remains standing. It must be regarded as a true relic of the times when the Gothic architectural style was still used in the buildings of Funchal.

The building to which we refer, which belonged to the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Pedro Cipriano de Ornelas, stands in Rua dos Aranhas, or Rua do Dr. Chaves, at the far end of an enclosure whose gateway bears the arms of the Ornelas family and the date 1606. In this building, in 1693, ‘a most noble woman, by the name of Dona Mécia’ was killed by a musket shot fired from the convent grounds of the former Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), as she stood at a window overlooking those grounds. The incident, which Camilo Castelo Branco romanticised in his book *O Santo da Montanha*, was related by António Vanguerve Cabral in a work entitled *Epilogo juridico de varios casos civeis e crimes*.

According to Vanguerve Cabral, who in 1693 was commissary judge of the bishopric of Funchal and assessor to the bishop, the killing was accidental, ‘its author being a religious who took up a musket loaded with quarter-shot, saying that he wished to shoot at a kestrel, and indeed he fired and missed his shot’.

When we wrote about Columbus, on p. 286 of this *Elucidario*, we referred to one of the three old buildings since demolished. Of the other two, one stood in the former Rua do Peru, now Rua do Comércio, and the other in Rua da Boa Viagem. Both of them likewise had twin-light windows, marking the transition from Gothic to Renaissance.

The house in Rua da Boa Viagem, which belonged to the chantry (*capela*) founded by Bento da Veiga, had two windows, whose stones were sold to a British subject, who had them shipped to his own country. The house in Rua do Peru, belonging to the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), had only one window, and we do not know what became of its stones. The stones of the window of Columbus’s house were in the possession of the heirs of the late Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Agostinho de Ornelas, and the window itself was photographed by the photographer João Camacho at the time of the demolition.

Apart from the buildings mentioned, we know of no other civil construction notable for its age and architectural type. Among the religious buildings, however, there are some that Dr Neale singled out, in a paper read before the Cambridge Camdem Society in 1844, as showing more or less distinctly the tertiary Gothic or Flamboyant style, which appeared in Europe in the 14th and 15th centuries.

The churches mentioned by Dr Neale were the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), the church of Machico, the chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*), the church of Santa Cruz, the chapel of Our Lady of the Snows, the churches of the Incarnation and of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), the church of São Bernardino (St Bernardino of Siena) in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), the church of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’), the church of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), the chapel of São Sebastião on the same island, etc. It should be noted, however, that many of these buildings underwent more or less considerable alterations after 1844, which gave them a somewhat different appearance from the one they had before.

Dr Neale gave a fairly extensive description of Funchal Cathedral, whose interior beauties he admires, though he adds that on the outside only the chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento has work and ornament worthy of note.
Funchal Cathedral (the Sé), as is well known, is classed as a National Monument (*monumento nacional*). Its architecture is Manueline, and its construction began shortly after 1493.
See ‘Casas Madeirenses’ by J. Reis Gomes.
Ega (Count of)

Aires José Maria de Saldanha Albuquerque Matos e Noronha, 2nd Count of Ega, was the son of Manuel de Saldanha de Albuquerque. He was born in Funchal on 29 March 1755, while his father was serving here as governor and captain-general of this archipelago, and was baptised in the chantry (*capela*) of the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace) on 27 May of the same year. He held high public office, including that of Portuguese ambassador in Madrid, but his name became better known because he was the husband of the celebrated Countess of Ega, who was the mistress of General Junot when the latter entered Portugal at the head of the troops of the first French invasion. When Napoleon’s troops left Portugal in 1811, the whole family of the Count of Ega went to France, where the count received from the emperor a pension of sixty thousand francs a year, which he enjoyed until Napoleon’s fall. Our government then took proceedings against the Portuguese who had been in France, and the Count of Ega was sentenced to death. This sentence was never carried out, however, and in 1823 he was acquitted of the crimes imputed to him.
Eira do Serrado

At the top of the steep ascent of the Passo da Chave (‘key pass’), which leads from the bottom of the settlement of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) to the road towards Funchal, lies the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of that name. It offers a surprising view over the parish (*freguesia*) of Curral and the towering mountains that surround it.
Eirinha
A locality (*sítio*) on Deserta Grande (the Desertas), where there is a small spring of drinking water.
European eel (Anguila vulgaris)

A fish of the family Leptocephalidae, common in the lower reaches of some streams and pools of Madeira. Although it tastes pleasant, it is not traded at all, and fishing for it is at most a mere pastime for boys.

The eel breeds in the sea, to which it withdraws at certain times of year. After passing through the leptocephalus stage, the young eels still live for some time in salt water, returning to the pools and streams only once they have reached a certain size.
Eirós (peak)
This mountain peak lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Gaula, and from its summit there is a vast and surprising view.
Elections
Under the absolute monarchy, elections were indirect and were held in accordance with Title 67 of Book 1 of the Ordinances. Those who held municipal office were elected as follows:

The good men (*homens bons*, local notables eligible for municipal office) and the people met in the Council house during the octave of Christmas. There, in the presence of the senior judge and the clerk (*escrivão*), each elector voted, orally and in secret, for six citizens, since this was the number of individuals whose duty it was to elect the members of the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council). From the record of the vote, drawn up by the clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*), the judges and the councillors (*vereadores*) chose the six citizens with the most votes. These were then paired off, two by two, so that each pair could vote for the various offices of the municipality (*concelho*). The electors could not be related by blood or by marriage within the fourth degree.

Once the lists had been gathered – three for each office – the senior judge, ‘reconciling them one with another’, drew up in his own hand the roll with the names of those elected, which he signed, closed and sealed. The names of those elected were then distributed among three ballot balls (*pelouro*), one for each year of the coming three-year term. The ballot balls, which were made of wax, were placed in a bag divided into as many compartments as there were offices. The roll and the lists were also to be kept in the same bag, so that at the end of the three years it could be checked whether any irregularity had been committed in the drawing.

The bag of ballot balls was kept in a chest with three keys, each held by one of the previous year’s councillors, and chance decided the order in which those elected to municipal office were called. The ballot balls were drawn from the bag by a child no older than seven.
The judges supervised the elections only when the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) was absent or unable to act.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of 12 November 1611, registered in volume V of the Council Archive, laid down that the *corregedores* or *ouvidores*, when holding elections, should choose two or three of the oldest and most honourable persons, ‘zealous for the public good and of sound conscience’, and ask them which persons had the qualities to enter the offices of the governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office), etc. Proclamations were to be made that anyone who canvassed for votes or tried to bribe the electors would be exiled to Africa for two years and would pay 50 *cruzados* towards the ransom of captives. Once the people had been summoned, they were to elect, from among the most noble persons and those of the governing body of the land, six citizens of the eldest and most zealous for the public good, and those elected were to vote for persons ‘without any taint of race’ for the municipal offices. In all other respects the electoral proceedings were to follow the Ordinance.

According to a warrant (*provisão*) issued in 1613 – almost identical to another published in 1803, and, like it, registered in the Archive of the Council of Funchal – the *corregedor* was to take up to three men of the oldest and most noble, whom he knew to be ‘of good conscience, zealous for the public good and natives of the land’. They were to name the persons who customarily served in the governing body, or whose fathers or grandfathers had served in it, and those who possessed the requirements to hold municipal office. The *corregedor* was to have ‘a separate entry made in a register, with all the declarations referred to above’, for each of these persons. Once the register was complete, the *corregedor* was to note in his own hand, in the margin of each entry, the qualities of each person, and then have the proclamations made in the manner already described.

The *corregedor* was to have the noblemen and members of the governing body appear before the Council to choose the six citizens charged with electing the councillors. Once elected, these citizens had to swear an oath ‘that according to their consciences they would vote for the persons who seemed fit to them’. The said warrant also contains some provisions on how copies of the elections were to be made and kept in the Council chest, etc., etc.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of 13 August 1508 laid down that the Council of Funchal should be ‘regida & gobernada por maneyra que se rrege a de Lisboa’ (governed and administered in the manner in which that of Lisbon is governed), that henceforth only noblemen (*fidalgos*) could be councillors (*vereadores*), and that the result of the elections, which were to be held every three years, should be sent to the monarch for his confirmation. Earlier, in 1461, Infante Ferdinand had ordered that the offices of the Council be filled by election and that two ballot balls (*pelouros*) be made each year, one for the judges and the other for the councillors and the representative (*procurador*). The captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) was to administer the oath to those elected, but without interfering in the electoral proceedings.

In 1471 a letter from the Infanta was issued requiring everyone to serve in the offices of the municipality (*concelho*), even if they held decrees of exemption, and in 1534 a fine of 20 *cruzados* was established for anyone who solicited votes or sought to bribe the electors.

John IV, by a decree of 6 July 1654, gave Funchal representation in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), but a document cited by Dr Azevedo on p. 635 of his notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) shows that as early as 1479 Madeira was already sending its own representatives to the Cortes. It should be pointed out, however, that our island is not included in the list of places that supplied representatives in 1535, which is held in the archive of the Torre do Tombo (national archives) and was published by Mr António de Sousa Júnior in the *Censo da metropole*. Nor is any reference to the election of these representatives to be found in the books of the Council of Funchal, although it was customary for the royal letters convening the Cortes to be sent to the municipalities.

Under the constitutional monarchy, Madeira’s deputies were chosen sometimes by indirect and sometimes by direct election. The first system was adopted in the elections of 1821 and 1826 and in those preceding the September Revolution; the second in 1822 and in those following the triumph of that Revolution. In 1842 indirect election was restored, and it lasted until the publication of the Additional Act of 5 July 1852, except in 1846 and 1847, while the decree of 27 July 1846 was in force.

The election of the peers of the Kingdom provided for by the law of 24 July 1885 was indirect, but the election of deputies was always direct after 1852. The senators provided for in the Constitution of 4 April 1838 were chosen by direct election.

As regards the local administrative bodies, after the restoration of constitutional government in Madeira the Councils were always elected directly by the municipalities, whereas the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) ceased to be chosen by indirect election only in 1878. The codes of 1895 and 1896 laid down that the District Commissions which replaced the General Councils (*Juntas Gerais*) should be elected by delegates of the Municipal Councils, presided over by the Administrative Auditor. However, the decree of 8 August 1901, which granted administrative autonomy to the district of Funchal (*Distrito do Funchal*), once again created a General Council chosen directly by the municipalities.
See the article ‘Representation in the Cortes’.
Materials for Madeiran History

The most important and abundant repository of information and records bearing on the history of this archipelago is the archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*). It holds a great many extremely valuable documents, above all from the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries, and it is much to be regretted that almost all of them remain unpublished, except for those that Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo published in his learned annotations to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). Referring to this archive in the article ‘Madeira’ of the *Diccionario Universal Português Illustrado*, this distinguished teacher and lawyer says the following:

‘The richest is that of the Municipal Council of Funchal, which has a well-compiled index in two large folio volumes entitled *Indice Allphabetico dos tombos do Senado da Camara do Funchal*, the work of António José de Jesus Lamedo (see that entry), doorkeeper and bookkeeper of the same Council, which runs up to 1794. This index is fundamental to the study of island history – not only Madeiran but also Azorean and Cape Verdean – and indeed of overseas history in general. The obscure author of this article has many times asked the said Council, in vain, to publish this precious and little-known manuscript, and he now takes the opportunity to repeat the request to the same Council and to make it to the government, to the Royal Academy of Sciences of Lisbon and to the worthy Geographical Society’.

The publication of the index compiled by Lamedo would no doubt be a valuable service to scholars and researchers of Madeiran history. The administrative bodies of this archipelago, however, ought to undertake a more complete work: the full publication of the oldest volumes of the Funchal Council archive, of many documents held in other archives, and also of various manuscripts in the hands of private individuals, some of which we shall mention in this article. Following the example of the Azoreans, we in Madeira should long ago have thought of publishing a journal of an essentially regional character, in which every item that could be gathered as indispensable material for the history of our archipelago would be recorded. Twelve thick volumes of the *Archivo dos Açores* were published between 1878 and 1894; publication resumed in 1906 and still continues, under the direction of the illustrious Azorean Colonel Francisco Afonso de Chaves. We should have done as much, if Madeirans had a clearer understanding of the value and usefulness of work of this kind.

Of the other municipal councils of the archipelago, that of Machico has the richest and most valuable archive, because it was the seat of a captaincy which, in the early days of colonisation, rivalled that of Funchal in importance and prosperity and, according to some, even surpassed it. The first volume of this archive is missing. According to Dr Rodrigues Azevedo it was the most precious, and after being officially requested many years ago by the civil government it never returned to where it came from. It has surely been lost for ever, for it could not be found in that department when the Machico Council reclaimed it, despite the efforts made to that end. The Municipal Council of Calheta (‘small cove’) also held important documents, among which there would certainly have been the record of the decree raising this place to the status of town (*vila*), whose exact date is unknown. However, a flood there around the middle of the 18th century completely destroyed the whole archive, and so the most precious materials for the history of that town and municipality were lost. We have not had the opportunity to examine the archives of the Councils of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), but we are told that they contain documents worth consulting, of interest not only to the history of those places but to that of the whole archipelago. The archive of the Captaincy of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and of its parish must also have been valuable, but the various pirate raids on that island, which more than once set fire to the council house and the parish church, completely destroyed all the documents there. The *Anais* of that municipality (*concelho*) record that the Council’s books were destroyed at the beginning of the 17th century and those of the parish archive in 1690.

The archive of the Civil Government of this district is also important and rich in documents of the 18th and 19th centuries. It seems to be a vein still little explored, and the annotator of the *Saudades* already cited said of it: ‘Some years ago it lay in a heap in an attic of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) itself; the author of this article went there twice and, picking up some documents at random, saw that they dated from the reign of Maria I and concerned measures of importance for Madeiran history. Besides this old archive, the secretariat of the said government holds some register books from the mid-18th century, books in perfect condition, containing copies and extracts of interesting documents, of some of which the author of this article also obtained transcripts’.

The archive that lay in a heap in an attic, when the Civil Government department was still housed on the north floor of the customs house building, is undoubtedly the same one, or a considerable part of it, that the secretary-general Curado de Campos removed to the beach some thirty years ago. There he made an *auto-da-fé* of it, destroying in a few minutes many hundreds of documents that must have been of great interest to the history of our archipelago!

The archive of the episcopal chamber of this diocese ought to be very important, not only for the history of this bishopric but also for the history of our Church overseas. Funchal was the seat of our first overseas bishopric and also of our first archbishopric, which had four suffragan dioceses and whose jurisdiction extended as far as the Far East. Valuable documents must certainly have been archived there, but a fire in the bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*) in the third or last quarter of the 17th century destroyed them entirely.

Dr Azevedo described the archive of the cathedral chapter (*Cabido*) of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) as rich, but today it has been stripped of its oldest and most important documents. Some twenty years ago a senior official of the Torre do Tombo (national archives) (*Torre do Tombo*) removed them to that institution on the orders of the central government. There they lie in a *mare magnum* of thousands of codices and loose documents, with no order or cataloguing whatsoever, and today it is absolutely impossible to consult them. It would have been better had they remained in the archive of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), where they had been carefully kept for several hundred years.

The archives of the Military Command (*Comando Militar*) and of the customs house are worth consulting, although they lack the importance of those above and are confined to very narrow aspects of Madeiran history.

The old Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) dated from the 15th century and, together with the customs house, formed a single department. Almost all matters concerning the supervision of taxes, the collection of many public levies and revenues, the creation of various posts and the appointment of officials, etc., passed through it. This department held a large and valuable register of thousands of documents, especially royal decrees and orders issued by the government in mainland Portugal. Today it would be a precious source of sound and authentic information on the public administration of this archipelago, and it is greatly to be regretted that it has been lost altogether. We know of it from the folio volume, which still exists, entitled *Índex Geral do Registo da antiga Provedoria da Real Fazenda... desde o anno de 1419 até o de 1775, da extinção da mesma Provedoria*. It shows that the register comprised twenty-four volumes of general records, besides the volumes of *Titulos Reaes*, *Ordens do Erário* and others. Reading this Index, which is useful and still provides quite valuable material for the history of this island, shows us the importance of that register and the irreparable gap its disappearance leaves today. The old Crown Revenue Office was replaced by the Royal Treasury Board (*Junta da Real Fazenda*), and of its archive Dr Azevedo reports that it ‘was some years ago, and we believe still is, in deplorable neglect; it was kept in a hovel, from which many *arrobas* of papers went astray’. Is this the archive of the old Crown Revenue Office referred to above? And where was it kept? We know nothing on the matter.

Also lost, or at least their fate is unknown to us, are the books of the Court of Residues and Chantries (*Juízo dos Resíduos e Capelas*). They contained the records of the old entails (*instituições vinculares*) with their pious obligations, the foundation of chantries (*capelas*), descriptions of the entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*), etc. All this would surely have made an abundant and most interesting store of information on a very important aspect of our history, especially as roughly two-thirds of the land of Madeira belonged to the countless entails and entailed estates that existed here.

The *Anais do Municipio*, which ought to be mentioned here, have already been dealt with in a separate article of this *Elucidário*. Likewise, under the title Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar, we gave a detailed account of the precious collection of countless documents sent from Madeira to the government in mainland Portugal over a period of roughly two centuries.
Outside the public archives, the following manuscripts deserve special mention here as very valuable sources for the history of this archipelago:

1. *Noticia das cousas da Ilha da Madeira desde o seu segundo descobrimento pelo Zargo*; 2. *Memorias sobre a criação e augmento do Estado Eclesiastico na Ilha da Madeira*; 3. *Índex Geral do Registo da Antiga Provedoria*, which we have already mentioned above; 4. a volume kept in the bishop’s palace, which deals with the bishops of this diocese; 5. a manuscript by Father António Gomes Neto; 6. *Memorias seculares e eclesiásticas para a composição da Historia da diocese do Funchal*, attributed to Henrique Henriques de Noronha.

The first is an 18th-century manuscript by an anonymous author, found among the papers of the late bishop of this diocese, Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura. It contains interesting information on the discovery, the early colonisation, the first donataries, etc., and ends with a detailed account of the descendants of João Gonçalves Zarco. The second, which dates from the beginning of the 19th century, was kept in the former secretariat of the seminary of this diocese. It deals chiefly with the creation of the diocese and of the various parishes, naming the enactments that established them, the stipends of the parish priests, ecclesiastical salaries, etc. It was one of the most valuable sources used by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in writing note XIX of ‘Longing for the Homeland’. The third, which we have already mentioned, was the work that supplied the most data for the preparation of the previous one, and the annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso seems not to have known of it. The fourth deals briefly with the bishops of this diocese and at considerable length with the episcopal administration of the prelate Dom João do Nascimento, who died in 1753; the information in this manuscript ends in that year. The fifth came from the pen of the learned priest Father António Gomes Neto and was written around the middle of the 19th century. It holds interesting information of an ecclesiastical nature, and also contains much information on the customs house, the creation of various public offices, etc., with valuable comments, though not always acceptable ones, shaped by the political ideas the author professed. It seems to us to be a different work from those cited in the notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’. All these manuscripts were published in large part in the former *Heraldo da Madeira*, thanks to the efforts of one of the authors of this *Elucidário*, who was then an editor of that newspaper. However, not only did the proofreading leave much to be desired, with many errors and slips, above all in dates and personal names, that need correcting, but there are also great gaps and shortcomings in the transcriptions made there, in the division of the material, etc. All this calls for a new and more careful publication, to which some explanatory notes on the text should be added.

The sixth and last manuscript is the work of Henrique Henriques de Noronha, of which the *Diccionario Bibliographico* says the following: ‘Manuscript in folio of 225 leaves, with an additional Appendix of 34 leaves. This autograph manuscript, said to be a complete work of Madeiran History, was bought some years ago in Lisbon, by weight, by a person who keeps it in his possession.’ Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo refers several times to Henriques de Noronha’s study. At first he supposed it to be the same as the work we have listed above as number 2, but later he stated that the two manuscripts were entirely different; and finally, in the article in the *Diccionario Universal Português Illustrado*, he again maintained that the *Memorias sobre a criação e augmento do Estado Eclesiastico* and Noronha’s *Memórias...* are one and the same work. Some years ago the distinguished researcher and our fellow Madeiran Dr Jordão de Freitas told us that he had had occasion to examine Henrique Henriques’s manuscript in Lisbon. We have just been informed that Dr Manuel Monteiro Velho Arruda, who lives in Vila Franca do Campo on the island of São Miguel, owns this much-vaunted historical work and will shortly publish it; that will be the moment for all the doubts raised about it to be entirely dispelled. Among the old writings that have been lost altogether, special mention is due to the one cited in no. 2 of the newspaper *Flor do Oceano*, of the year 1834: ‘The second most important work of which we have knowledge is the one entitled *Memorias authenticas e curiosas da ilha da Madeira*, a manuscript in seven large folio volumes, composed by Father Manuel Carlos de Vasconcellos, beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) of the parish of Nossa Senhora do Calhau. This interesting collection passed, so we are told, together with Canon Leite’s pamphlet, into the hands of Father J. L. de N., and contains interesting documents relating to the island, from its discovery up to the period when the British troops under the command of Marshal Beresford took possession of it.’ It seems to us that the initials J. L. N. are meant to designate the canon and archdeacon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé), José Luís de Nóbrega, who died around the middle of the 19th century. Another writing that has likewise gone astray is the one mentioned in the already cited article ‘Madeira’ in the *Diccionario Universal Português*, in the following terms: ‘The same happened with the manuscript of a historical and statistical work on the island of Madeira by the ill-fated and talented Madeiran writer Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega, for which he was paid from the funds of the Council of Funchal, to which it therefore belongs: the writer of these lines possesses fragments of the draft of the work and the authentic document of the payment order for its price.’
The Madeiran books of nobility also provide some information that may be of interest to the history of the archipelago, but we shall deal with them in a separate article.

Of the printed works, by far the most important and valuable is the well-known work of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, which Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo enriched with the learned annotations he added to it, turning it into a truly monumental work. It will be the subject of an article at the appropriate place in this *Elucidário*.
See Bibliography.

It is worth mentioning here that the Historical Archive of Madeira (*Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*) was created in July 1931. The following year it was provisionally housed in one of the rooms of the palace of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), where the various departments of the Diocesan Seminary operate today (1940). In 1933 the Historical Archive was transferred to the Palácio de São Pedro (‘St Peter’), where it is now permanently established, answering technically and administratively to the Directorate-General of Archives and Libraries (*Direcção Geral dos Arquivos e Bibliotecas*). Several thousand codices and documents scattered among various archives and public offices have been incorporated into it, making it the richest and most valuable repository of material for the history of this archipelago. It directs the important publication *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (‘Historical Archive of Madeira’), of which six volumes have already appeared; it contains valuable material and most interesting information, and has today become indispensable to researchers of Madeiran history. It is regrettable that publication has not begun of the index of the documents in the municipal archive compiled by António José de Lamedo, to which we refer above. This publication has long been desired, and as early as 1873 the illustrious commentator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ considered it absolutely essential that it be carried out without delay.

Prominent among this valuable documentation are the precious holdings of the Funchal municipal archive, referred to above, of which a brief but interesting catalogue or inventory, well worth consulting by scholars, can be found in the six published volumes of the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*. It hardly needs saying that the National Archive of the Torre do Tombo, the richest, most abundant and most select collection of manuscripts in our country, also holds a vast and valuable body of documents concerning every subject that may be of interest to the Madeira archipelago. This precious seam remains almost entirely unexplored, and there is not yet even a brief inventory of the documents relating to this island that might guide any scholar wishing to undertake particular historical research. Meanwhile, we note here an article published in the *Diário da Madeira* of 21 December 1933, which gives a detailed account of many collections of documents of great use to researchers. No less useful is a reading of the articles in the aforementioned volumes of the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* on the manuscripts in the Torre do Tombo (national archives) relating to the affairs of the Madeiran archipelago.

We should record here the welcome news that a manuscript copy of the *Memórias* of Henrique Henriques de Noronha, referred to above, exists in the Municipal Library. It was taken from the original, which is kept in the Public Library (*Biblioteca Pública de Ponta Delgada*) of the city of Ponta Delgada.
Embate

Madeirans call the wind that blows from the sea during the day the *embate* (daytime sea breeze), and the wind that blows from the land at night the land breeze (*terral*). The *embate* usually begins between 8 and 9 in the morning and dies away in the afternoon; the land breeze sets in between 9 and 10 at night and lasts until the early hours of the following day. Between the appearance of these two winds there is always an interval during which the air is calm. In winter the winds we are referring to are highly irregular, but in summer they blow with great regularity. They are caused by the difference in temperature between land and sea, by night and by day. By day, the sun’s rays warm the air over the land, which becomes lighter and rises to the upper regions, so the breeze blows from the sea; at night, since the air over the land is cooler than that over the sea, the reverse occurs.

The *embate* generally comes from the south-west, owing to the strength of the north-east breeze, and that is why sailing vessels passing between the Ponta de São Lourenço and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) take that course to enter the harbour of Funchal. The land breeze blows from the north or north-east and is a beneficial wind, for it carries the city’s exhalations out over the ocean and disperses them.
Embicheirar
To land a large fish with the gaff (*bicheiro*) (see that entry) and then haul it into the boat.

Inlaid work

Madeiran inlaid work (*embutidos*) is made by carefully cutting small pieces of wood and inserting and gluing them into openings of the same dimensions made in other woods. The woods of the til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), the *barbusano* (Apollonias barbujana, a laurel-forest tree), the *fustete*, the heath, the myrtle, the *perado*, the *piorno*, the *massaroco*, the walnut, the orange tree, the box, the Brazilian Madeira mahogany (vinhático, Persea indica), the cedar and the yew are the most widely used in the inlay industry, and with them designs of varied colours and considerable ornamental effect can be obtained.
All these woods are generally used in their natural colour; only *perado* wood is sometimes soaked in urine to give it a bluish colour, much used in composing flowers.

‘There are already in Madeira,’ says Vitorino José dos Santos in no. 5 of the *Boletim do Trabalho Industrial*, ‘some inlay workers, properly guided by technical training and gifted for artistic composition, who produce work of recognised merit, sought after and appreciated by connoisseurs. In general, however, Madeiran workers lack intellectual culture and artistic taste, and this leaves them indifferent to the idea of progressing by varying and improving the composition of their work. As a result, most of the inlaid work produced still follows the same models as a matter of routine, almost always depicting the traditional “Madeiran peasants”, the ox-sledges, the hammocks and the Monte (‘hill’) toboggans, framed with borders of symmetrical and little-varied designs.

‘This inlay as a rule decorates small tables, the so-called “bell tables”, card tables, trays and a variety of small boxes for sewing, paper, handkerchiefs, gloves, stamps, needles and pins, etc., etc. Of these products, those of inferior quality are the most numerous. It is these that, displayed daily on the “spardecks” of the steamers lying in the harbour of Funchal, go, mixed with other products of local industry, to make up an important sea-borne trade, that of the class of “bumboatmen”, who live from it exclusively.’

Among the finest pieces of inlaid work made in Madeira mention must be made of a table presented in 1918 to the late President of the Republic, Dr Sidónio Pais, and of two tables ordered by King Luís, while still a prince, during his stay in Madeira in 1858, intended as gifts for King Pedro V and Queen Stephanie. These last two pieces were cited with great esteem and praise by the connoisseurs of that time.
Emigration

Emigration from Madeira was already taking place in the 16th century, for Friar Gaspar da Madre de Deus, in his *Memórias para a Historia da Capitania de S. Vicente do Estado do Brasil*, refers to many married couples from this island going to that captaincy. Emigration to Brazil continued in the 17th and 18th centuries, and among the many Madeirans who went there in search of fortune during Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) was the celebrated João Fernandes Vieira, the liberator of Pernambuco. By 1676, says Dr Azevedo, the decline of the sugar trade on this island had reached such a point that emigration to the lands of the Holy Cross (*Santa Cruz*), until then a mere expedient or private venture, came to be promoted by the government. In 1747 a royal letter (*carta régia*) was issued instructing the governor-general of Madeira to assist this emigration.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of 4 July 1758 required passports of anyone who henceforth wished to leave the island, and in 1779 the governor-general ordered a judicial inquiry (*devassa*) ‘to discover the recruiters of emigration and the ships employed in transporting emigrants’. At that time there was emigration both to Brazil and to foreign countries. It was chiefly against the latter that the governor protested, and he even proposed to the government that agriculture be developed as a means of preventing the depopulation of the island.

In 1792 many Madeiran families emigrated to the United States of America because of the persecution suffered by Freemasons that year, and it is known that as early as 1753 many people were leaving for that country, almost always clandestinely, to escape the poverty that afflicted the island’s population.
Emigration to Demerara and the British colonies of the West Indies seems to have begun on a large scale only around 1840.

In 1841 the number of emigrants rose to 4,045, in 1846 to 4945, in 1847 to 4,720 and in 1853 to 3060. A good many of these people went to those countries, where from 1842 the British government paid for their passage because of the shortage of labour there. In 1847 a Portuguese warship was stationed for some time in our waters to assist the local authorities in the repression of clandestine emigration.

Of the thousands of Madeirans who left for Guiana and other British colonies in search of riches, some were favoured by fortune, and today their descendants live both in those countries and here in Madeira. The *demerarista* (emigrant returned from Demerara, British Guiana) who, through the most arduous labour and hardships of every kind, managed to amass capital did not, as a rule, forget his homeland. It was here that he liked to come to spend the rest of his life, surrounded by comforts and conveniences he had not known in his youth. It was he who, in the parishes, most zealously organised the feasts of the Senhor (the Lord), feasts that always featured an abundance of gunfire and rockets, things greatly to the liking of the simple country folk of our island.

From 1835 to 1855 about 40,000 people left Madeira, of whom only some 20,000 carried passports. Many of them went to Brazil and the United States of America, where at that time some of our compatriots also managed to make their fortunes. On 18 June 1854 the Portuguese yacht *Experiência* sailed for Rio de Janeiro carrying 188 settlers, and in the same year 104 people left Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) bound for public works in Portugal, as recorded in the *Anais* of that island’s municipality.

Emigration to the Sandwich Islands began in 1878, the first emigrants leaving here on a large full-rigged ship which took about 6 months to carry them to their port of destination. From 1883 to 1887 further waves of emigrants left for those islands, as happened again in 1909 and 1911, and in other years as well. In 1884, 232 people left for Africa, 210 of them engaged by the government to go to Moçâmedes. In 1889 and 1890, 1338 left for the same continent, most of them settling in Angola and Lourenço Marques, towards which the authorities sought to divert the emigrant current that had previously flowed mainly to America and Oceania.

Modern emigration statistics show that North America and Brazil were the countries that received the largest numbers of Madeiran emigrants in the period from 1903 to 1913. The first of these countries admitted 195 Madeirans in 1903, 218 in 1905, 874 in 1909, 1064 in 1910, 1051 in 1912 and 1491 in 1913; the second admitted 377 in 1903, 1198 in 1905, 839 in 1909, 985 in 1910, 2,059 in 1912 and 1522 in 1913. In 1915, 1114 emigrants left for North America and only 62 for Brazil.

Every year large sums arrive in Madeira, sent by Madeirans living in the United States of America. Many of these Madeirans have already returned home, bringing capital that they almost always invest in buying property.

In Brazil few Madeirans have managed to make their fortune in recent times, and in Portuguese Africa we believe that only the colony established on the plateau of Mossamedes is flourishing today. Some settlers also went to East Africa in 1889 or 1890; at first they led a life of hardship and misery, because they did not find there the resources that the government had promised to provide. There are Madeiran colonies at the Cape of Good Hope and in the Argentine Republic, and about 250 people emigrated to the latter country in 1905. Spanish émigrés

When the revolution that broke out in Spain in early 1866 failed, many revolutionaries took refuge in Portugal. Seventy of them came to this island – 46 officers and 24 soldiers – arriving here on 1 July of the same year. These Spanish émigrés, some of whom married on the island, left after the triumph of the revolution of 1868, which dethroned Isabella II. They went by night to Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’) to embark, without the authorities learning of their departure.
Encharéu (Caranx dentex)

A fish of the family Carangidae, common in the seas of Madeira. It sometimes appears in large shoals and is usually caught with the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) or the *agulheira* (mid-water line for garfish), and more rarely with the longline or the rod (*cana*).
Bluefish (Temnodon saltator)

A fish of the family Carangidae, an irregular visitor to Madeira. It is very voracious and destroys a large proportion of the coastal species. It is caught with nets close to the shore, or with a line, and in the latter case often by the method known as trolling.
Encumeada

In Madeira this noun is used only in place names, where it designates the summit of certain mountains and heights from which wide horizons open up all around the observer. The best known is the so-called Encumeada de São Vicente (‘São Vicente ridge pass’).
Encumeada de São Vicente

This high ridge lies between the parishes (*freguesias*) of Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’) and São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), at an altitude of over a thousand metres, on the crest of the mountain range that runs lengthwise through the interior of Madeira. The road from Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) to São Vicente passes here, and from this point both the northern and southern coasts of the island can be seen – or, as the local people say, ‘you can see the north sea and the south sea’, which is indeed the case on days with clear horizons. In 1939 the Madeira Tourism Delegation had a comfortable rest house and shelter built in the parish of Serra de Água; it is much to be regretted that this building was not put up closer to that height.
Sugar-cane mills

There are at present 51 factories for crushing sugar cane in Madeira: 10 in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal, 3 in that of Câmara de Lobos, 2 in that of Ribeira Brava, 7 in that of Ponta do Sol, 8 in that of Calheta, 1 in that of Porto Moniz, 6 in that of São Vicente, 7 in that of Sant’Ana, 4 in that of Machico and 3 in that of Santa Cruz. Of these factories, only two are equipped to produce sugar on a large scale, and the installation of one of them was completed this year.

Of the 51 factories that operated while the sugar regime (*regime sacarino*, the legal framework governing sugar production) established by the law of 24 November 1904 and the decree of 11 March 1911 was in force, 49 distilled only spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) at 26° Cartier, all of it intended for public consumption in Madeira. The remaining two, the only registered ones, were responsible for making sugar and the alcohol at 40° used in the treatment of wines.

The first sugar mill (engenho) for crushing sugar cane in Madeira was built in 1452. By 1590, when Frutuoso wrote the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), there were more than 30 mills scattered across the island, even though the sugar industry here was already showing signs of decline at that time. In 1730, according to Soares da Silva in the *Memorias para a historia del-rei D. João o I*, there were few mills in Madeira, and Dr Azevedo reckoned that the sugar industry disappeared from the island entirely in 1748, because it could no longer withstand the competition of American sugars, which had long been flooding the European markets, where they were sold at low prices.

When Thomas Edward Bowdich visited Madeira in 1823, only an insignificant quantity of sugar was being made here, and in 1826 there was a single mill on the whole island. Severiano Ferraz (see that entry) set about building another the following year, and it was completed in 1828. In 1851 there were four factories in Madeira (Harcourt, *Sketch of Madeira*), and in 1856 there were ten in Funchal and 18 on the whole island, all for distilling spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) (White, *Madeira its climate and scenery*). In 1861 there were twenty-nine factories on the whole island, five of which processed sugar. In 1872 Dr Azevedo stated in his notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ that there were known here ‘seven steam factories, five of them in operation and one about to begin; nine water-driven mills; and some driven by oxen’. The first of these produced sugar and spirit, the latter almost all consumed within the country.

In 1900 the number of factories had risen to 49, distributed as follows: 11 in Funchal, 2 in Câmara de Lobos, 10 in Ponta do Sol, 7 in Calheta, 5 in São Vicente, 7 in Sant'Ana, 4 in Machico and 3 in Santa Cruz. Of these factories, however, only three processed sugar: that of W. Hinton at Torreão (‘turret’), that of Silva Manique (formerly Severiano Ferraz) at Ponte Nova (‘new bridge’), and that of José de Faria & C.ª at São Martinho. Previously some sugar had also been produced by the factories of Vitorino Ferreira Nogueira at São Martinho, of Wilbraham at Ponta do Sol, of Diogo Frasão at Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), and of Ornelas Frasão at Santa Cruz.

Having bought the Ponte Nova factory and the machinery of others intended for sugar production, W. Hinton thus became the absolute master of one of the island’s richest industries. He eventually obtained from the Government the publication of a law under which only registered factories were permitted to process that product and the alcohol used for fortifying wines.

Although there were two registered factories, that of W. Hinton and that of José Júlio de Lemos, the latter was always, so to speak, a dependency of the former. Its present owners eventually leased it to Hinton for twenty-five *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos) a year until 31 March 1919, with a clause for extension should the Government also extend the sugar regime (*regime sacarino*, the legal framework governing sugar production) of 1911.

Of the factories now in operation, the Torreão factory is the most remarkable. Indeed, it may be called the most important industrial establishment in the district of Funchal and, of its kind, one of the most perfect in the whole world, since it can process 500 tonnes of cane in twenty-four hours.

The José Julio de Lemos factory has a much smaller capacity than the Torreão and has produced only alcohol, but it too is an important establishment: it has improved its installations and has powerful steam boilers of the Babcock & Wilcox type.

As for the spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) distilleries, they offer nothing remarkable. The engineer Mr Vitorino José dos Santos noted in the *Boletim do Trabalho Industrial* of 1913 that distillation in them is generally carried out in continuous stills, and that these factories are ‘in their great majority powered, for motion and distillation, by steam boilers, with the exception of 5 factories in the municipality (*concelho*) of Ponta do Sol, 4 in that of São Vicente and 5 in that of Santana, where distillation is carried out over a direct fire’.

As we said on p. 262 of this *Elucidário*, the factory known as São João, belonging to the Companhia Fabril de Açúcar Madeirense, was inaugurated on 23 March 1873. Although equipped with the best apparatus then obtainable, this establishment always had a troubled existence and eventually foundered, owing to the unfair and shameful war waged on it by its enemies. To give an idea of how this war was conducted, it is enough to say that in one year a good part of the cane juice (*garapa*) produced at the factory ended up in the bed of the Ribeira de São João, and that several attempts were made to wreck the rollers that crushed the cane by inserting pieces of iron and lumps of *cantaria rija* (hard dressed stone of vesicular basalt) into them!

Older than the São João factory, but excellent for its time, was the factory founded in 1856 by Severiano Alberto Ferraz, on which he spent some twenty-five *contos*. Improved by the founder’s sons, the Ponte Nova factory had by 1862 steam clarifiers, Bour concentrators, centrifugal machines for extracting the molasses, etc., etc. It was regarded as a first-class establishment and the best then existing in Funchal. It was driven by steam, the power being distributed by a ten-horsepower engine to the various other manufacturing machines.
The Torreão factory was founded by William Hinton & Co., also in 1856, and was driven by water; when water ran short in summer, however, power was supplied by a twelve-horsepower steam engine.

The island’s early mills were all driven by water or by oxen, and the rollers were sometimes made of the wood of the *til* (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), once very common. Besides the mills there were also the *alçapremas*, or hand presses, which we have already had occasion to discuss elsewhere in this *Elucidário*.

The old documents do not say what process the owners of mills and *alçapremas* used to make sugar. It is likely, however, that it consisted of boiling the cane juice in cauldrons to the consistency of a thick syrup and then transferring it to vessels pierced at the bottom, where the crystals would settle while the liquid drained through the holes. It may also be supposed that lime water and animal charcoal, products that modern industry likewise uses, were employed to purify the sugar.

Sugar refining flourished in Madeira in the 15th century, and it was from here that it passed to Lisbon, where, as Dr Azevedo says, it ‘created so many private fortunes, to the detriment of the colonies and of the sugar industry itself’.
Dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus)

A plant of the honeysuckle family (*Caprifoliaceae*), found at Ponta do Pargo, Porto Novo, Funchal, etc. It has unpleasant-smelling, odd-pinnatisect leaves with oblong-lanceolate, serrated segments, and white or reddish flowers with purple anthers. The crushed leaves of this plant are used in the treatment of bruises.
Foundlings

In 1583 the care of foundlings was entrusted to the Bishop, but a royal warrant (*provisão*) of 1685 transferred it to the Governor-General. Since 1693 the supervision of foundlings has been the responsibility of the Council. For many years, however, the wet nurses were paid by a treasurer elected annually by the House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds). For this purpose, and for the maintenance of the lepers, he collected a third of the revenue from the wine levy (imposição do vinho). On 7 May 1761 the Funchal Council resolved to consult the Government on whether it should continue to allow this treasurer to collect the third of the municipal levy (*imposição*), since the collection of municipal revenues fell to the treasurer of the municipality (*concelho*).
A royal decree (alvará régio) of 1752 granted the wet nurses of foundlings in this archipelago the same privileges enjoyed by those of Lisbon.

Old documents show that in 1811 the Funchal Council was struggling with a lack of funds to support the foundlings. Even in the third quarter of the 19th century the wet nurses were not paid their wages on time, which led many of them to sell their claims cheaply to certain speculators, who made considerable sums from these transactions.

The old foundling wheel (revolving hatch where infants could be left anonymously) was in the building of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*). It was there that many mothers abandoned their children when, through lack of means or for any other reason, they could not raise them.
Ensaião
See Saião.
Entrada da Cidade

As its very name indicates, this is truly the entrance to the capital of Madeira for those who come from outside the island and wish to enter the city. It was built about 80 years ago. The old entrance to the city was the Varadouros gate (see that entry), which was demolished in 1911. It was through this gate that the prelates and the former governors and captains-general made their official entry, always an occasion of great and solemn ceremony.

The present city entrance was formerly called Porto da Saúde, and since 27 October 1910 it has been named Avenida João Gonçalves Zarco. A small, narrow street once stood there, closed at its southern end by a redan and one of the city gates. Beside the gate, or very close to it, stood the so-called nursing home (*Casa da Saúde*) (see that entry), which was rebuilt or considerably enlarged in the last quarter of the 18th century. This is the building that for many years housed the Commercial Association, the Health Station and the Harbour Master's Office (*Capitania do Porto*). It belonged to the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), which sold it at public auction in 1914.

On 12 January 1838 the central government authorised the Council of this city to demolish the gate and widen the alley there. The gate was pulled down the following year and the street was then built, using for the purpose some land belonging to the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) and some hovels to the east of the fort. For the time in which it was built, it was a broad street, to which its avenues of plane trees, the nearness and view of the sea and its connection with the public promenade gave a particular beauty.
In 1843 work began on a quay as an extension of the Entrada da Cidade (‘entrance to the city’), but it was never completed. The present quay was built between 1889 and 1892. See Cais.
Entrosa

This is the name of a sheer escarpment which rises from the right bank, near the mouth of the Ribeira do Porco in Boaventura (‘good fortune’), and meets the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco de São Jorge (‘arc of São Jorge’). This ravine is crossed by a zigzag path that links the two parishes and forms a stretch of the road that runs around Madeira close to its coast.
Epanaphoras
See Melo (Dom Francisco Manuel de).
Epidemics

The epidemics that left the saddest memories in Madeira, because of the deaths they caused, were the following: plague, which began before 1521 and lasted until 1538; measles, in 1751; smallpox, in 1815 and in 1873; and cholera morbus, in 1856 and in 1910 and 1911.

Since we deal with the plague and cholera morbus epidemics in separate articles, we shall speak here only of the measles and smallpox epidemics mentioned above. We do not refer to others that have also occurred on this island because, besides being less important, they have already been noted in the article Diseases, published in this *Elucidário*.

The book by Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva entitled *Carta critica sobre o método curativo dos médicos funchalenses* contains valuable information on the measles epidemic that raged in Madeira in the year 1751. ‘All was weeping,’ wrote Dr Fernandes da Silva, ‘where hearts were most tender; all was dread where danger was uncertain; and all was funeral spectacle in the pious bearing of the corpses to their graves’.

While some physicians applied bloodletting and cold medicines and allowed those stricken with measles to drink water, others prescribed the opposite treatment. According to Dr Fernandes da Silva, it turned out that mortality was lower among the patients subjected to the former regimen.

The only physicians who favoured bloodletting were Dr Silva and the celebrated Dr Heberden, who was living in Madeira at the time. If what the said author asserts is accurate, the latter cured more than two hundred people stricken with measles without a single patient being endangered. The stubbornness of some physicians in refusing to give water to the sick, Dr Silva adds, was the sole cause of the many deaths on the island. Of the smallpox epidemic of 1815, Dr Heineken says that it was brought by a ship from Cape Verde and that it claimed about 2,000 lives. At that time, and indeed long afterwards, the value of vaccination was still little known among our people, and this was surely the main reason why the epidemic proved so deadly here. (See Adams and Vaccine.)

The epidemic of 1872 and 1873 claimed 1007 lives; after that of 1815, it was the one that did the most damage on this island. The disease was brought to Madeira by a passenger on the *Maria Pia*, who had come from Lisbon in October 1872 and was admitted to the Civil Hospital (*Hospital Civil*). It lasted until the end of 1873 or the beginning of 1874, and wrought great havoc, especially in the municipalities of Funchal, Santa Cruz, Calheta and Câmara de Lobos. Smallpox appeared in Madeira on several occasions after 1873, but thanks to the spread of vaccination and to certain sound measures adopted by the authorities, it never again reached the scale of the earlier epidemics. In 1907 many smallpox patients died in Funchal, but the epidemic was short-lived and never attained the intensity of those of 1815 and 1873. This was because, from a certain point onwards, patients who could not be isolated in their homes were admitted to the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’), where physicians and devoted nurses who knew their work gave them care and attention they would not have received at home.
See Cholera morbus in 1876 and 1910, Diseases and Plague.
Administrative Period

This is a valuable collection of the principal documents relating to the exemplary administration of Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro as civil governor of the district of Funchal in the period from 1846 to 1852. It consists of three volumes of 636, 659 and 706 pages, published in 1849, 1850 and 1852, which can still be read with appreciation today and consulted with great profit for the history of Madeira, especially of that period.
Moreover, they offer a lofty lesson and the most wholesome example to all who wish to conduct themselves wisely in the administration of public affairs.
Epocha (A)
The first periodical of this title to be published in Funchal appeared on 6 September 1886 and ended on the 30th of the same month and year, after eight issues.
Another newspaper with the same title appeared in 1895 and ran to six issues, the first on 14 January and the last on 21 February.
On 16 June 1912 yet another periodical with the same title appeared in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’); it was the third newspaper to be published in that town.
Echinoderms
This group of animals includes starfish, sea urchins and sea cucumbers (holothurians), which occur close to the coast or in the rock pools of Madeira’s shoreline.
See Starfish and Sea urchins.
Horsetails (Equisetaceae)
They are represented in Madeira by a single species, *Equisetum maximum*, a plant found in waterlogged places at São Vicente, Ribeira de Santa Luzia, Ribeira de São João, etc.
Ermida

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’). At this spot, known as Alcoforado, Gil de Carvalho built a small chapel in the second quarter of the 16th century, which gave its name to the locality; it is conjectured that it was dedicated to the miracle-worker St Anthony. It belongs to the municipality (*concelho*) of Machico.
Erva Arroz

Vernacular name of *Sedum farinosum* and *S. nudum*, native plants of the family Crassulaceae. The first species is found at the Torrinhas (‘little towers’), near the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), etc.; the second is common along the whole north coast.
Pea (Pisum sativum)
A legume native to western Asia, widely grown in Madeiran vegetable gardens.
Common vetch
Vernacular name of *Vicia sativa*, a plant of the family Leguminosae, common in Madeira.
Johnson grass (Andropogon halepensis)

A perennial grass, 3–15 decimetres tall, with its spikelets gathered in a broad, pyramidal panicle, usually violet in colour. This plant is considered harmful and even poisonous to livestock before it is fully mature. It is possible that, while young, it contains some prussic acid.
Escarpiada
The inhabitants of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) give this name to bread made from maize flour. The *escarpiada* of Portugal is a kind of *pão de rala*.
Escola (A)
A fortnightly publication of which 12 issues appeared, the first on 1 May and the last on 15 October 1912.
School of Geometry and Trigonometry

At the end of 1760 a School of Geometry and Trigonometry (*Escola de Geometria e Trigonometria*), intended especially for those following a military career, was established in Funchal. It was housed in the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), today the barracks of the 19th Infantry Battalion, and its first teachers were the sergeant-major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major) Francisco de Alincourt and the engineer Francisco Salustiano da Costa. Nine years later, that is, in 1769, the governor and captain-general João António de Sá Pereira reported to the government in mainland Portugal the good results obtained from the school. We do not know when it ceased to exist, nor any other circumstances concerning it.
School of Navigation

Attached to the Harbour Master’s Office (*Capitania do Porto*) of this city there is a School of Navigation (*Escola de Pilotagem*), created by decree of 14 November 1917, when the commander Arantes Pedroso was Minister of the Navy. The school owes its creation to the persistent and diligent efforts of the harbour master of Funchal, Commander Artur de Sales Henriques, who was entrusted with setting it up and has been its only teacher. Like other schools of this kind, its course lasts two years. The first year comprises arithmetic, elementary algebra, plane and solid geometry, plane trigonometry, general geography, compasses and dead reckoning; the second comprises spherical trigonometry, general astronomy, nautical calculations, astronomical navigation, handling under sail and steam, signals and meteorology.
The school’s course qualifies students as merchant navy officers, conferring a pilot’s certificate once the candidates have completed a certain period at sea as apprentices.

In the academic year 1917–1918, 17 students enrolled, of whom 4 passed into the second year. In 1919, 3 students completed the course, the first at this school to qualify for a pilot’s certificate. The school was abolished.
School of Useful and Fine Arts

It was intended for the education of girls and was established under a resolution of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) passed on 12 February 1913; it began operating in February of the following year.
It taught music, painting, drawing, languages, hygiene, gymnastics, dance, needlework, cookery, gardening and horticulture, arithmetic, geography, etc.

The School of Useful and Fine Arts (*Escola de Utilidades e Belas Artes*) was housed in the building of the former seminary (*Seminário*) at the Encarnação, and was abolished by resolution of the General Council of 13 September 1919, the building itself having been transferred to that body in August 1919 for the sum of 9 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos). Since September of that year the offices of the General Council have been housed there.
