Elementary School of Commerce

In the former building of this city’s Commercial Association, on the Avenida de João Gonçalves Zarco, an elementary commercial school operated for some years and rendered good and acknowledged services in our community. Young men going into commerce were taught French and English there, as well as commercial bookkeeping and accounting. They completed their studies at the Industrial School with courses in Portuguese, arithmetic and geometry, and also drawing, thereby gaining the qualifications they needed to embark boldly and confidently on a commercial career.

This educational establishment, which had the character of a private course, was created by the Commercial Association at the time when Mr Henrique Vieira de Castro, who contributed greatly to its establishment, was its president.

It was maintained by the same association, which received a modest subsidy for the purpose from the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this municipality (*concelho*). The course consisted of classes in French, English and commercial bookkeeping, with examinations at the end of each academic year, although these lacked official formalities. French was taught by Jacinto Augusto Pereira Brasão, English by Archibald Clode, and commercial bookkeeping by Abraão Atias and later A. C. Coutinho Gorjão.
The course began in 1897, but it did not last long, despite the good services it rendered.
António Augusto de Aguiar Industrial School

The painter Joaquim Leonardo da Rocha came to this island in 1807, seeking refuge from the horrors that mainland Portugal suffered during the first Napoleonic invasion. His stay here gave rise to the idea of creating a public class (*aula*) in drawing and painting. Early in 1809 a group of the most distinguished people of this city addressed a petition to the government in Lisbon, setting out the advantages and the necessity of such a class. The then governor and captain-general of the archipelago, Pedro Fagundes Bacelar, not only reported favourably on the petition but also used his best offices to have the proposed class, or school, of drawing and painting established in Funchal without delay.

The class was created by the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 7 July 1809. It opened in March 1810, and its direction was entrusted to the painter Joaquim Leonardo da Rocha. In the same year this teacher wrote a pamphlet entitled *Medidas gerais do corpo humano arranjadas em dialogo, e metodo fácil para uso da real aula de desenho e pintura da ilha da Madeira em 1810*, which was published in Lisbon in 1813. It is a small booklet of 14 pages, which our distinguished bibliographers Figanière and Inocêncio Francisco da Silva describe as extremely rare, but which seems to us to have little value from a strictly technical or scientific point of view. The library of the Industrial School holds a copy of this bibliographical rarity, donated by one of the establishment’s teachers.

Shortly after the drawing class opened, the central government sent, on 10 April 1810, a set of *Instruções* to regulate its operation. These no doubt constituted the class’s founding statute and must have contained the teaching methods or the syllabus of the subjects taught there. We have no knowledge of these *Instruções*, nor do we know where the class was held or how long it lasted. It may have formed part of the group of chairs that made up the so-called *Aulas do Pátio* (‘Courtyard Classes’, the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), but we can state nothing definite on this point. We know only that in 1812 L. Rocha obtained an increase in salary as teacher of the drawing and painting class, and that in 1818 he was still alive and living in this city, for in that year he painted a portrait of the 1st Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), which hangs in the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace).

Although the Funchal Lyceum (*Liceu do Funchal*), founded in 1837, had a chair of drawing in its curriculum, it was always considered necessary here to have a class in that subject separate from the lyceum (state secondary school). There, workers in particular could acquire the knowledge indispensable to their arts and trades, with teaching geared to the needs of the professions to which they were chiefly devoted. It was in keeping with this aim that the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) created and maintained a chair of drawing. In the last years of its existence its teacher was the head of the Council’s technical department, José Maria Teixeira de Agrela.

The need for a drawing school in this city had long been recognised when, by decree of 10 January 1889, countersigned by Emídio Navarro – the minister to whom the country truly owes the creation and development of its industrial education – the Josefa de Óbidos Industrial Drawing School was established in Funchal. Its founding decree stated that its purpose would be ‘to provide instruction in drawing as applied to the industry or industries predominant in the locality’. This foundation had been made in accordance with the decrees of 30 December 1886 and 23 February 1888.

The school was first named after Josefa de Óbidos; under the decree of 8 October 1891, which reorganised industrial education, it took the name of António Augusto de Aguiar. Under this reform, the curriculum of our School comprised courses in elementary drawing (preparatory and advanced classes), architectural drawing (artistic drawing, modelling and technical drawing) and ornamental drawing (ornament drawing, modelling and ornamental composition).

The decree of 5 October 1893, which brought profound changes to industrial education, raised the António Augusto de Aguiar Industrial Drawing School to the rank of Industrial School, while keeping the same name. Workshops for cabinetmaking and carpentry and for women’s needlework were then created. The decree of 14 December 1897 thoroughly reorganised industrial education in our country, and the Funchal Industrial School (*Escola Industrial do Funchal*) benefited from this reform through the creation of three theory classes: Portuguese language, arithmetic and geometry, and principles of physics and chemistry. These posts, with the exception of the last, which was never actually created, were not filled, however, until early December 1901, and they began to operate in the 1902–1903 academic year.

The law of 1 December 1918 reformed the services of the industrial schools and altered the range of subjects taught in Funchal, which was then organised as follows: the mother tongue, arithmetic and geometry, principles of physics and chemistry and elements of terminology, geography and history, French, general drawing, specialised drawing and workshop practice. It was in September 1889, in a building on Rua de Santa Maria, that the new school was installed; 260 pupils enrolled, and classes began the following October. Its first teacher and director was Cândido Pereira, and the Austrian subject Hans Nowach was a contracted teacher. The former served until the end of the 1903 academic year and the latter until 1895. Nowach was temporarily replaced by the engineering officer Carlos Roma Machado de Faria e Maia, who served until July 1897. From the 1897–1898 academic year until March 1903 the Spanish subject Dom Manuel de la Cuadra, a native of the city of Seville, was a contracted teacher at this School; he died in Funchal on 3 April 1903, aged about 60.

The teachers of this School have been: Cândido Pereira (1889–1903), Hans Nowach (1889–1895), Dom Manuel de la Cuadra (1897–1903), Vitorino José dos Santos (1902), Father Fernando A. Silva (1902), Augusto Pascoal Correia Brandão (1903–1908), Joaquim Porfírio (1909–1910), João Gomes Correia Faria (1911–1912), José Pedro Nolasco (1914–1915), Emanuel Paulo Vitorino Ribeiro (1914–1917), Alfredo Vital Miguéis (1917), Dona Maria Emília Arroja (1919) and Abel Tiago de Sousa e Vasconcelos (1919). Carlos Roma Machado de Faria e Maia, João dos Reis Gomes, Henrique Franco de Sousa and, on several occasions, the workshop master Francisco Franco also served as temporary teachers.

The first director of this industrial school was Cândido Pereira, now a teacher at the Afonso Domingues School in Xabregas, who served from 1889 to 1903; from that year to the present the director has been the civil engineer Vitorino José dos Santos.

As already stated, the reform of 5 October 1893 created the cabinetmaking, carpentry and women’s needlework workshops, whose masters have been Manuel Rodrigues Gaspar, who died in 1900, Francisco Franco, Manuel Dias da Costa and Dona Augusta das Dores Ornelas. The law of 1 December 1918 created the workshop for inlaid work (*embutidos*) and inlays, which began operating in October 1919 and whose master is Manuel dos Passos Aguiar.
The Escola Industrial Antonio Augusto de Aguiar was converted into an industrial and commercial school by the decree of 11 September 1925, and its courses were organised as follows:

Industrial Section: cabinetmaker, inlayer, embroidery and dressmaking pattern designer, and cutting and embroidery, all of four years; and the Commercial Section: Elementary Commercial Course, also of four years. The decree of 20 October 1931 reorganised these courses, which then became the following: cabinetmaker, carpenter, inlayer, locksmith (later converted into locksmith-mechanic), dressmaking and embroidery, embroiderer, master builder, and supplementary commercial course. The subjects that make up each of these courses are distributed as follows:

Cabinetmaker (five years): comprises classes in Portuguese, French, mathematics, physics and chemistry, technology, general and vocational drawing, and workshop practice; Inlaid work (*embutidos*) (five years): Portuguese, mathematics, general and vocational drawing, and workshop practice; Locksmith-mechanic (five years): Portuguese, mathematics, physics and chemistry, technical mechanics, technology, general and vocational drawing, and workshop practice; Embroidery pattern designer (three years): general drawing and vocational drawing (pattern design), reserved for employees of the embroidery industry; Master builder (five years): Portuguese, mathematics, physics and chemistry, technology, general drawing, projection drawing, construction drawing, measurements and estimates, and legislation. Dressmaking and Embroidery (five years): Portuguese, mathematics, general and vocational drawing, and workshop practice; Advanced course (four years): general drawing and vocational drawing suited to the pupils’ trades.
Commercial course (four years)

Portuguese, French, English, commercial arithmetic and geometry, commercial geography, communications and transport, elements of commercial law and political economy, general principles of commerce, commercial bookkeeping and accounting, elements of physics and chemistry and of natural history, basic commodity technology, and practical classes in handwriting, typing and shorthand. Supplementary Qualification (one year): in addition to the commercial course, it comprises the subjects of algebra and physics and chemistry, and serves as the qualification for entry to the Commercial Institutes of Lisbon. Attendance at this school has risen considerably year by year, as this brief statistical note on the number of enrolments in the following academic years shows:

Besides the teachers Cândido Pereira, who died in Lisbon on 15 April 1935, and Vitorino José dos Santos, who died in Funchal on 1 October 1928, to whom this technical school owes its most outstanding services, its permanent directors have been the teachers Major João dos Reis Gomes, from 1929 to 1939, and Dr Álvaro de Meneses Alves Reis Gomes, since 1939.

In November 1938 the Industrial and Commercial School was installed in the spacious building on Rua das Hortas and Avenida Elias Garcia that had housed the Old People’s Home (*Asilo dos Velhinhos*), after major repairs carried out there by order of the General Council of the Autonomous District (*Junta Geral do Distrito Autónomo*), which is responsible for maintaining this secondary school.
Lancasterian School
It was the English subject José Phelps who introduced mutual instruction (*ensino mútuo*, the monitorial system) to Madeira, using Lancaster’s system.

The Lancasterian School (*Escola Lancasteriana*), founded in 1819, was first housed in a building at Ribeirinho (‘little brook’). From there it moved to Travessa do Surdo (‘deaf man’s lane’) and then to the building on Rua da Princesa (‘Princess street’), today Rua 31 de Janeiro, which now houses the boys’ school of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). This building was commissioned by the Associação Funchalense, which existed to promote mutual instruction; the association had acquired the land at the end of 1822.

The Associação Funchalense for the promotion of mutual instruction was founded on 21 December 1821. Its first treasurer was the aforementioned José Phelps and its first president was Canon Lúcio António Lopes Rocha. The association organised balls and subscriptions to raise the funds it needed to maintain the school.

On 25 July 1827 the director of the mutual-instruction public class (*aula*) belonging to the association that promoted this teaching wrote: ‘Since its opening on 1 December 1823 this class has had 275 pupils up to the present; it now has 78, with room for 305. It should be noted that the terrible instrument called the *palmatória* is banned in this class, where the same or better results are achieved by gentler means, which at the same time appeal more to the pupils’ self-esteem.’

The school we have been describing was intended for boys. There was, however, another for girls, set up by Mrs Blackburn and Mrs Phelps. In 1850 this girls’ school was maintained by a society of Portuguese and foreign ladies, with the Government contributing part of the schoolmistress’s salary, whereas the boys’ school was then the responsibility of the State, which paid its teacher’s salary.

We do not know in which year the Lancaster system ceased to be used at the old school on Rua da Princesa, but it may be supposed that it was abandoned there in 1828, when the teacher Alexandre Luís da Cunha left for America.

The building on the former Rua da Princesa, today Rua 31 de Janeiro, was repaired at the expense of the State in 1850. The State also paid for the works on the building’s entrance, carried out in 1851 on the orders of the governor José Silvestre Ribeiro. In 1912 and 1914 the Council had various repairs made to the school. There is a publication entitled *Relatório dos progressos da Escola Lancasteriana na Província da Madeira*, dated at the end 6 February 1823, which contains interesting information on Lancaster’s teaching method and the way in which it was introduced to the island.
Medical-Surgical School

The regulations (*regimento*) of St Elizabeth’s Hospital (*Hospital de Santa Isabel*) in this city, approved by the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) on 10 August 1816 and confirmed by royal warrant (*provisão régia*) of 19 October 1819, created, in the nineteen articles that make up Title V, a medical-surgical public class (*aula*) attached to the hospital. Its purpose was ‘to prevent the ruin of humanity in this Colony through the ignorance of the Barbers, who without the proper knowledge go about the countryside treating people, bringing to the grave those who would still be alive if they were treated by skilled practitioners, or by men less ignorant than such quacks’.

We do not know when this class began to operate or how long it lasted, but we know that it had a short existence, for in 1824 the governor and captain-general informed the government in mainland Portugal of the urgent need to create a Class of Operative Surgery. He pointed out that on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and in the Madeiran countryside there was not a single operating surgeon, and that ‘one found only the odd wretched bloodletter, of whose competence many of those who called him in for the treatment and cure of their diseases have been victims’. The same governor took up this weighty matter again the following year, without his efforts and endeavours producing the slightest practical result.

The distinguished Madeiran and eminent physician Dr João Francisco de Oliveira, while president (*provedor*) of the Holy House of Mercy of this city in 1825, created a class in surgery in the hospital attached to it. He taught it himself, without payment, for some time, and later entrusted its teaching to the surgeon of that hospital, Dr Joaquim de Oliveira Simões. It was around this time that Dr João Francisco de Oliveira presented to the government a plan for the creation of a medical school, setting out the bases of its operation, teaching method, etc. Although it met with the approval of the higher authorities, it was not granted.

From what has been set out, one can see clearly how medicine and surgery were practised in this archipelago, and the need to create a scientific establishment that would train individuals sufficiently qualified to practise them is eloquently demonstrated.

The decree of 29 December 1836 created a medical-surgical school in each of the capitals of the overseas districts. Each school was to have two chairs: the first would teach anatomy, physiology, surgical operations and the art of obstetrics, and the second pathology, materia medica and therapeutics. They were to be held respectively by the principal physician and the principal surgeon of the hospital to which the school was attached. The first chair would have an assistant demonstrator, who would prepare the anatomical work, and the hospital's pharmacist would give lessons in pharmacy in the hospital dispensary. The ministerial order (*portaria*) of 16 January 1837, addressed to the administrator-general (*administrador geral*) of this district, ordered the provisions of that decree to be carried out in full in Madeira. The Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica*) of Funchal had been created.

The Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), then chaired by João Agostinho Jervis de Atouguia, set about carrying out the orders issued by the central government. Without delay it adapted the former ward for British subjects and two adjoining rooms to house the new School, which thus became the highest-ranking educational establishment here in Madeira. The surgeon, physician and apothecary of St Elizabeth’s Hospital at the time were, respectively, Dr Luís Henriques, Dr Lourenço José Moniz and the pharmacist Nicandio Joaquim de Azevedo. In accordance with the express wording of the decree, they were entrusted with teaching the chairs that made up the new School's course. Because the illustrious Madeiran Dr Lourenço Moniz was a deputy for this island and had given up his post as professor at the School, he was replaced in this office by Dr António da Luz Pita. The Funchal medical school had the good fortune to begin its work under the direction of two eminent physicians, who brought great honour to this new establishment of higher education. From the outset it began to earn the good reputation it always enjoyed, not only in our country but also in some foreign lands.

On 2 May 1837 the school council met for the first time. It was made up of Dr Luís Pita, president, Dr Luís Henriques, member, and Nicandio de Azevedo, secretary. This was also the day on which the School was definitively installed, and the first classes began in the following October. The post of assistant demonstrator was only filled the next year, by Dr Juvenal Honório de Ornelas. The appointments to these four posts only became definitive by the decree of 8 September 1838. Dr Luís Henriques and the pharmacist Nicandio Joaquim de Azevedo served until 1845, the year in which they died, and Dr Luz Pita until 1866, when he obtained his retirement.

In 1850 Dr António Alves da Silva was appointed professor at the School; he died in office in 1854. Dr João da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, later Viscount and Count of Canavial, held the same post from 1861 until 1883, the year in which he retired.

Dr João Augusto Teixeira and Dr Maurício Augusto Sequeira joined the teaching staff of the Medical School in 1874 and taught their chairs until 1907 and 1910 respectively, the years in which they died. Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira was appointed professor in 1883 and remained in this post until the School was abolished in 1910.

Francisco de Paula Drolhe, Manuel Figueira de Chaves and Francisco Clementino de Sousa, who had taken their medical course at the Funchal School, each served twice as interim professors at the same School. Drs Cândido Joaquim da Silva, Acúrsio Garcia Ramos, Carlos Leite Monteiro and Fortunato Alfredo Pita also taught chairs there.

Nicandio Joaquim de Azevedo, the first secretary and first professor of pharmacy, died in 1845. José Figueira da Silva was then appointed to this post; he died in 1858 and was followed by Francisco Xavier de Sousa and then by Abílio Augusto Martins, appointed in 1880. Vasco da Silva Pereira, who succeeded him, was the last secretary and professor of pharmacy of our Medical School.

Its directors were Dr Luís Henriques (1838–1845), Dr António da Luz Pita (1845–1866), Dr João da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, later Count of Canavial (1866–1883), Dr João Augusto Teixeira (1883–1907) and Dr Maurício Augusto Sequeira (1907–1910).

The course lasted three years until 1842 and four years from 1843, and it remained so until the school’s abolition. The first doctors trained at this School were Valentim Maximiano de Sousa, António José da Silva, João Luís Monteiro Júnior, Francisco Simplício de Vasconcelos Lomelino and João Augusto de Oliveira, who completed their course in 1840. Of the four-year course, the first doctors to qualify there were Crispiniano Evangelista da Silva, Manuel Lúcio de Freitas, António Manuel da Silva and Teófilo Joaquim Vieira.
In 1902 Dona Palmira Conceição de Sousa and Dona Henriqueta Gabriela de Sousa completed the course at this School, the first and only women doctors ever to qualify there.

In its 73 years of existence the Funchal School qualified about 250 doctors. They have practised medicine freely, and often with real brilliance and remarkable skill, not only throughout the Madeiran archipelago but also in many places in mainland Portugal, the Azores and the overseas colonies, and even in some foreign countries. To speak only of the dead, we must mention the names of Manuel Figueira de Chaves, Henrique Crawford Rodrigues, João Crawford Rodrigues, António Augusto de Santa Clara, Gabriel Franco de Castro, Luís Augusto Rodrigues, João de Deus Vieira, Henrique José Vera Cruz, Francisco Clementino de Sousa and Henrique Venâncio de Ornelas, who brought great honour to the school that had trained them.

Our Medical School had a library of some two thousand volumes, which was kept in the building of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) and is today in the Municipal Library.

Of the inaugural theses or dissertations presented by students on completing their courses, we know of only one that was printed: that of the student António Francisco da Silva Ramos, a native of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). It dealt with fibrinous pneumonia and with the aetiology and treatment of carcinoma, and was defended in 1895.

Under the School’s original organisation, those who completed its course could receive only the licence of *cirurgião ministrante* (practising surgeon). This was later modified, and subsequently the decree of 22 June 1870 granted its students advantages and privileges they had not previously enjoyed, allowing them to compete for municipal medical posts and for others dependent on administrative bodies. This matter has given rise to various debates in the press, among which the series of articles published in the *Diário de Notícias* of Funchal in January and February 1896 deserves special mention. Doctors trained at our School have always practised freely in many places on the mainland, in the Azores and in the overseas provinces, and also in foreign countries. Many of them not only obtained municipal medical posts but also found positions in the army and navy, bringing no discredit on the School that trained them and standing shoulder to shoulder with doctors trained at the higher schools of our country. Various attempts were made at different times to abolish the Funchal Medical School, all of them fruitless, until it was finally abolished by the following decree:

‘Article 1. The Medical-Surgical School of Funchal is abolished. Sole paragraph: the staff of the School thus abolished shall be placed on the supernumerary list. Article 2. All legislation to the contrary is revoked. Given at the Palace of the Republic on 11 November 1910. António José de Almeida.’
Teacher Training School

The district school for training primary teachers was established by the decree of 10 May 1900. The need for an educational institution of this kind had been recognised in an island district (*distrito*) such as ours, at a time when there was already a shortage of adequately qualified teachers to take charge of the schools then vacant and of any that might fall vacant in future. In October 1900, 37 students enrolled, and the School began its work on the 10th of that month and year. In July of the following year the examinations for passing from the 1st year of the course were held, and 26 students passed. The first and only director of the institution was Dr Pedro José Lomelino, and its first teachers were Constantino Silvano Pereira, Francisco Augusto da Silva, Manuel José Varela, Dona Maria da Piedade Oliveira and the director already mentioned. The School was housed in a building on Rua dos Aranhas and always remained there; the Higher Primary School (*Escola de Ensino Primário Superior*) now (1922) also operates in this same building.

By the decree of 24 December 1901 the district schools for training primary teachers were abolished and converted into teacher-training colleges (*Escola Normal*). The course, which had lasted two years, was extended to three, and the Funchal School kept the same teaching staff and the same number of subjects as before.

The decree of 10 May 1919 abolished all the teacher-training colleges in the country, except those of Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra, and transformed them into Higher Primary Schools, one of which had its seat in Funchal.
In its nineteen years of existence, the teacher-training college of this city qualified 172 primary-school teachers of both sexes.
Higher Primary School

The decree of 10 May 1919 abolished, or rather transformed, the Teacher Training School (*Escola Normal*) of this city into a Higher Primary School (*Escola Primária Superior*). The teachers of the Teacher Training School became part of the teaching staff of the new institution, whose establishment was completed with eight more teachers, so that it was made up as follows: Pedro José Lomelino, director, Constantino Silvano Pereira, Francisco Augusto da Silva, Manuel José Varela, Jordão Maurício Henriques, Adolfo de Sousa Brasão, Jorge Sílvio Pélico de Oliveira Neto, Francisco dos Anjos França, Domingos dos Reis Costa, Manuel José da Fonseca, Dona Maria Clara do Monte Falco Brito Figueiroa and Dona Maria Julieta de Brito Figueiroa. The new school began work in October 1919. It was abolished by the decree of 15 June 1926.
Escolar de natura (*Tetragonurus cuvieri*)

A fish of little or no food value, very rarely observed in the seas of this archipelago. It appears to be a pelagic species; nevertheless, one specimen was taken near the beach of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Escolar (*Thyrsites pretiosus*)

A fish of the family Trichiuridae, which seldom appears in the markets of Madeira. It grows to a large size and is generally considered tasty, but because of its excessive fat it has very marked laxative properties, which make it intolerable to many people.
Primary Schools

The constitutions of the Bishopric of Funchal, promulgated by Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto on 4 May 1579, show that reading and writing were already being taught in Madeira at that time. Those who followed this calling were also obliged to teach Christian doctrine from the newly printed *Cartilha* (primer), and in their schools they could use only ‘papers & books of sound doctrine’ conducive to the good morals of the children.

Primary education, as can be seen, was then directly or indirectly in the hands of the clergy. Secular teaching was established only much later, and it was the Marquis of Pombal who introduced it on this island.

The law of 6 November 1772 established six primary schools in Madeira: two in Funchal and one in each of the towns of Machico, Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol and Calheta. Around 1793 a primary school was founded in Campanário (‘bell tower’), and the towns of São Vicente and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) later received the same benefit.

In 1821, when liberal principles were proclaimed in Madeira, Funchal had 4 public elementary schools and 2 private schools of mutual instruction (*ensino mútuo*, the monitorial system), one for boys and the other for girls. In the other places of the archipelago the number of public primary schools had not increased.

By its resolution of 28 June 1821 the Constituent Congress guaranteed primary education to all citizens, and the law (*carta de lei*) of the 30th of the same month and year allowed any citizen to teach and to open primary schools. The revolution of 1820 was so short-lived, however, that public education in Madeira was never improved. Nor is there anything to record during the absolutist regime that followed, except that, under the government of Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro, one of the old elementary schools was abolished and its teacher’s salary applied to the upkeep of a public class (*aula*) in English and French created in Funchal. Primary education began to make progress in Madeira only after the restoration of constitutional government in 1834. From then until 1848, 33 public schools were founded in Madeira, 4 of them by the State in 1838 and the rest by the Municipal Councils. Many private schools also appeared, because the freedom of teaching, abolished by the absolute government, had been restored by the constitutional government.

The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal founded the boys’ schools of São Roque, São Martinho and São Gonçalo on 14 May 1841; the girls’ school of Santo António on 12 May 1845; the girls’ school of São Roque on 2 October of the same year; and the girls’ schools of São Martinho, Monte, São Gonçalo and Santa Maria Maior on 2 December 1846.

The School for Destitute Children (*Escola da Infância Desvalida*), founded by the Society of Infant Schools (*Sociedade das Escolas Infantis*), whose president was Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, opened in 1834 or shortly afterwards. The Lancasterian School (*Escola Lancasteriana*), or school of mutual instruction, for girls, which we have already mentioned above, still existed in 1856, maintained and inspected by a society of Portuguese and foreign ladies. This last school, at least in its final years, was intended to equip poor girls to earn their living as teachers, seamstresses or domestic servants.

In 1837, at the request of the deputy Lourenço José Moniz, the Government granted the Society of Infant Schools a house in Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) belonging to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*). It was there that the so-called School for Destitute Children operated for many years. It should not be confused with another school of the same name, founded in 1882 by Freemasonry (*Maçonaria*) of Funchal, which occupied a building in Rua Nova de São Pedro.

In the 1848–1849 school year the archipelago had 42 primary schools paid for by the treasury or by the municipalities, and 30 maintained by private individuals. Of the former, 29 were for boys and 13 for girls; of the latter, 10 were for boys and 20 for girls. In the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal there were 20 public schools, 9 for boys and 11 for girls, and 26 private schools, 8 for boys and 18 for girls.

In 1855 the District had 47 public and 24 private schools. In 1863 there were 34 state schools, 25 for boys and 9 for girls, attended by 950 and 370 pupils respectively, and 17 municipal schools, 8 for boys and 9 for girls, the former with 412 and the latter with 489 pupils. In the same year there were 16 private schools, 4 for boys and 12 for girls, attended by 225 and 374 pupils respectively.

In 1870 there were 36 state schools (27 for boys and 9 for girls), 17 municipal schools (9 for boys and 8 for girls) and 48 private schools (15 for boys and 33 for girls), all of them attended by 1732 boys and 1515 girls. By the 1882–1883 school year the number of public schools (state and municipal) had risen to 65, and there were also 44 independent schools. Of the public schools, 1 was mixed, 42 were for boys, 21 for girls and 1 for the teaching of linear drawing; of the private schools, 7 were for boys and 37 for girls.

The Decree of 7 May 1856 created boys’ schools in the parishes of Camacha, Caniço, Gaula, Porto da Cruz, Santa Torre, Boaventura, Fajã da Ovelha, Ponta do Pargo, Tabua, Canhas, Ribeira Brava and Serra de Água, and girls’ schools in Santa Cruz, Machico, Sant’Ana, São Vicente, Porto Moniz, Calheta, Câmara de Lobos and Porto Santo.
In 1904 the archipelago had 73 public schools, 42 for boys, 29 for girls and 2 mixed; in 1905 there were 2 more, one for boys and the other for girls.

In August 1918 there were 108 public schools in the whole District, 104 state and 4 municipal, the latter for girls. There were also 11 evening classes, all in the municipality of Funchal, 3 state and 8 municipal. Of the state schools, 12 were mixed, 48 for boys and 44 for girls. The municipality of Funchal had 4 municipal girls’ schools and 33 state schools; of these, 16 were for boys, 14 for girls and 3 mixed. Outside this municipality there were no evening classes for males.

At the same time there were 40 private schools for girls and 11 for boys in the whole archipelago. According to the best estimates, these schools together with the state and municipal ones were attended by 6,956 pupils (3,912 girls and 3,044 boys). In 1849, 3,304 pupils of both sexes were being taught in the District’s primary schools, and in 1883 the same schools were attended by 2,500 boys and 2,407 girls.

At the end of 1918, 4 central schools were created in Funchal, 2 for each sex. A report sent by the School Inspectorate of the District (*Inspecção Escolar do Círculo*) to the Secretary of State for Education (*Instrução*) on 10 October 1918 states that in the previous school year the city’s state schools had been attended by 570 pupils, of whom only 189 had mastered arithmetic, writing and fluent reading. According to the same report, the latest census of Funchal’s school-age population recorded 5,816 children aged 7 to 14 (2,929 boys and 2,887 girls), while the school-age population of the whole school district reached 19,290.

At present (1922) there are 11 mobile schools in the whole District: 2 in São Roque, 2 in Santo António, 1 in Ponta do Pargo, 1 in Madalena, 1 in Canhas, 3 in Ponta do Sol and 1 on Porto Santo. In September 1919 there were 9 such schools.

The District has (1922) two school districts – the eastern and the western – both based in Funchal. The first comprises the municipalities of Funchal, Santa Cruz, Machico, Sant’Ana and Porto Santo; the second, those of Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Porto Moniz and São Vicente. Before September 1919 the western district was based in Ribeira Brava; originally there had been a single school district for the whole District, directed sometimes by an inspector and sometimes by a school sub-inspector.

The Ministry of Finance publication entitled *Analfabetismo em Portugal* (popular leaflet no. 5) shows that the overall illiteracy rate for both sexes in the district of Funchal (*Distrito do Funchal*) was 88.4 per cent in 1864, 90.1 in 1878, 84.5 in 1890, 90.0 in 1900 and 82.7 in 1911. We do not know the present rate, but it is likely to have fallen since 1911, although people of the poorer classes do not always take care to make their children attend school.

Slaves

For centuries the soil of Madeira was abundantly watered by the sweat of slaves. In the early days of colonisation, the hard and gruelling work of clearing the land of this island was done by Black slaves, captive Moors and Canary Islanders. Slavery, which had begun at Río de Oro (Rio do Ouro) around the middle of the 15th century, grew steadily with the exploitation and cultivation of the land of the recently discovered islands, that is, the archipelagos of Madeira, the Azores and Cape Verde.

At the end of the 15th century and the beginning of the next, the Fleming João Esmeraldo had eighty slaves – Moors, Black Africans and mulattoes – on his estate of Lombada da Ponta do Sol (‘ridge of Ponta do Sol’) alone. Frutuoso says that in 1552 the confession rolls recorded 2,700 slaves in Funchal, and that in the same year their number rose to 3000, because four ships brought another 300 to this island. If we bear in mind that the total population of the archipelago at that time was around twenty thousand inhabitants, we must conclude that the number of slaves here was considerable, and it is worth noting that three hundred were imported within a single year! Half a century later, when French corsairs sacked the city of Funchal in 1566, they carried off only three hundred Black captives, because the capacity of their ships allowed no more.

The parish archives of all or almost all the parishes contain many records of baptisms and marriages of Black and mulatto slaves. Slaves came even from India: Tristão Vaz da Veiga, who was governor-general of the archipelago in 1582, kept twelve Indian slaves for the private service of his household.

Slavery seems to have grown further as time went on, but we lack reliable evidence on which to judge, even approximately, the number of slaves and the periods when they were brought to this island. To them is owed in large part the rapid and remarkable growth of the sugar industry, which was the most important source of the wealth and prosperity of this archipelago in the 15th and 16th centuries. The settler who came from the mainland became a *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*), then made himself lord of the land and in many cases turned it into an entail (*morgado*). He left the cultivation and tilling of his rural properties to the slaves and went off to the city or the court to enjoy the income from his fields and estates. The slaves gradually freed themselves from their master’s tutelage. By cultivating the *sesmaria* lands on their own account and loading them with houses, walls and other improvements (*benfeitorias*, buildings and walls made by the tenant, which remained his property), they considerably increased their value. In this way they contributed to the creation of the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant) and very nearly became co-owners of those same lands and properties. It seems that slaves in this archipelago were treated with somewhat more humanity, and that their material situation was less to be lamented than in other Portuguese colonies. This may perhaps have been due to the natural fertility of the soil, the various military expeditions to Morocco, the considerable number of foreigners who landed on this island, with gentler customs and more civilising tendencies, and still other causes unknown to us. Writing of Machico, Frutuoso records ‘that in this town (*vila*) there are many mulatto women, very well treated and with rich voices, which is a sign of the ancient nobility of its inhabitants, for in all great and wealthy houses there is this multiplication of those who serve them’. It is certain, however, that in 1505 the donataries obtained the royal decree (alvará régio), recorded in volume 1 of the archive of the Council of Funchal, at fol. 111, under which they could have the ears cut off slaves who deserved it by law. And at about this time, when some slaves of João Rodrigues Castelhano murdered a factor (*feitor*) of the same Castelhano, five of them were hanged in the town of Calheta (‘small cove’).

Social conditions gradually changed, and the slave trade came to be regarded as a reprehensible act, punished by law. ‘By the royal decree (*alvará*) of 19 September 1761,’ says Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘it had been forbidden to transport slaves to the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and any who did arrive there were to be held freed and emancipated; and on 7 July 1768 a letter from the Secretary of State to the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) Dr Francisco Correia de Mattos was published in the city of Funchal by public proclamation (bando), ordering the provisions of that decree to be applied to this archipelago. The gradual extinction of slavery in Madeira then began. Another royal decree, of 16 January 1773, completed the humanitarian purpose of that of 1768’.

Although slaves were scattered across the whole island, it seems that in certain places, notably Funchal, Ponta do Sol, Machico and Curral das Freiras, sizeable communities of Black and Moorish people formed. These intermarried among themselves and also mixed with the inhabitants descended from the settlers from the mainland, so that the characteristic features of those races were diluted and merged into the Madeiran population. A considerable number of Black, mulatto and Moorish individuals nevertheless retained, until only a few years ago, the facial features that distinguish the peoples from whom they descended. It is still not rare to meet individuals with the features of the Black race very clearly marked.

The names of Rua da Mouraria (‘Moorish quarter’) and Rua das Pretas still bear witness to the presence of Moors and Black people in Funchal. The eighty slaves of João Esmeraldo on the Lombada da Ponta do Sol, and the many others there on various “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*), show us that a large number of people of African descent lived in that parish (*freguesia*). Curral das Freiras (see that entry), as we have already said, was in the earliest days of colonisation a refuge for criminals and runaway slaves, who in this remote and almost inaccessible *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) found their true letter of manumission. They formed a centre of population, which later merged with the settlers who established themselves there.

Under an ordinance of 1483, slaves who fled to the mountains could be sold by whoever caught them, provided their lawful owners did not seek them or have them arrested within four months of their flight. In the same year an order came to inquire into the slaves’ way of life, and they were not allowed to rent houses without prior licence; earlier still, in 1474, the Infante had ordered that no slave might keep a house ‘on his own’ (*per si*).

In 1490 people from Gran Canaria, La Palma, Tenerife and La Gomera were forbidden to reside in Madeira, but in 1515 this order was revoked for those who worked as sugar masters. In November 1767 a ship carrying slaves arrived in Madeira, but their sale was forbidden by the *corregedor* of the judicial district (*comarca*), even though, as we said above, the letter ordering the provisions of the royal decree of 19 September 1761 to be applied to this archipelago was published here by public proclamation only on 7 July of the following year.
Escudeiro (João)
He was the first person in Madeira to bear this surname.

National Scout Corps

Founded in Braga in 1923 by the late lamented Archbishop Primate Dom Manuel Vieira de Matos, the National Scout Corps (*Corpo Nacional de Escutas*) grew rapidly and spread across the country. It met with great devotion from Catholics, who very rightly saw in a scout movement organised on Christian and Catholic foundations an ideal training school for Portuguese youth, which until then had been almost entirely neglected by the ruling classes.

The idea of founding a Region of the C. N. E. on our island arose in 1926. After a long period of training and preparation, the C. N. E. was founded in Madeira with members of the former Catholic Youth of Funchal, who made their solemn vow on 8 December 1928 in the Colégio church (*Igreja do Colégio*). The governing body, the Regional Board (Junta Regional), was constituted as follows: Regional Commissioner: Captain Eduardo dos Santos Pereira; Director: Father Jorge de Faria e Castro; Secretary: António Henriques de Araújo, engineer; Medical Officer: Dr José da Cunha Tavares da Silva; Head of the Instructors’ School: José Vieira da Luz Júnior.
The first group to be founded was No. 5 (Infante Dom Henrique), whose leader was António J. de Caires.

Since then the scout movement has grown, with new units founded in Santa Maria Maior (Group 88, Santiago), São Roque (Group 55, São Roque), São Gonçalo (Group 76, São Gonçalo), Caniço (Andorinha and Oliveira Salazar Patrols) and Porto Santo (Nun’Álvares Patrol); in the city centre there are Group 5 (Baden Powel) and Group 72 (Afonso de Albuquerque).
Since then the C. N. E. has carried out a variety of collective activities, above all camps, whose organisation has been regarded as truly exemplary.
Nor has it neglected religious practice: it regularly gives its members instruction in religion and has already organised several spiritual retreats.

The C. N. E. in Madeira has taken part in major national and foreign camps, always sending hand-picked delegations. The national camps were those of Cacia (1928), Braga (1932) and Lisbon (1934), and the international ones (known as jamborees) were held in England (1929), Hungary (1933) and Holland (1937), together with the rover moot in Switzerland (1932).
In Madeira, too, the C. N. E. held the 1st Regional Camp in 1938, and in 1939 a Leaders’ Congress was organised at Camacha, in which numerous Scouts from mainland Portugal took part.
To commemorate the Centenaries of the Foundation and Restoration of Portugal, the Scouts of Madeira organised a Scouting Exhibition, which was open from 1 to 8 December 1940.

The Regional Board of the C. N. E. in Madeira is at present made up as follows: Major Eduardo dos Santos Pereira, Regional Commissioner; Father Jorge de Faria e Castro, Regional Chaplain; António de Santa Clara Gomes, Regional Secretary; João Virissimo Nunes, Deputy Regional Secretary; and Dr Agostinho Cardoso as Regional Medical Officer.
The C. N. E. in Madeira currently has a membership of approximately 160.
Esmeraldo (João)

Among the outsiders of noble birth whom the hazards of fortune brought to this island in the days of colonisation, one stands out: the Flemish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) João de Esmenaut, whose name was Portuguesised as João de Esmeraldo and who seems to have landed in Funchal around 1480. He proved his noble descent, and by a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 13 August 1511 Manuel I ordered that the privileges of a *fidalgo* be upheld for him, since he was one in Picardy, the land of his birth. Later, by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 16 May 1520, which is transcribed in the nobiliary of H. Henriques de Noronha, he was granted a coat of arms and made a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*), an honour that Carlos I of Spain had already conferred on him earlier. This coat of arms comprises, besides the arms proper to the Esmenauts, the arms of Piennes, Hallwin and Nedenchel, families allied to the former and among the most illustrious in the north of France.

João Esmeraldo held a great deal of land on this island by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and by a deed of 28 January 1498 he bought, or took on quit-rent, from Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, son of João Gonçalves Zarco, the great property called Lombada da Ponta do Sol (‘ridge of Ponta do Sol’). It later took the name of Lombada dos Esmeraldos (‘the Esmeraldos’ ridge’), and we shall deal with it in a separate article. There he founded the entail (*morgado*) of Santo Espírito (‘Holy Spirit’). By a deed of 12 June 1522, with the consent of his second wife, Agueda de Abreu, of his son by his first marriage, João Esmeraldo, and of his son by his second marriage, Cristovão Esmeraldo, he divided it into two entailed estates (*morgadio*), called Santo Espírito and Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’). By lot, the first fell to Cristovão and the second to João Esmeraldo, and all this was confirmed by John III by royal decree (alvará régio) of 13 November of that year.

Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘The Lombada of João Esmeraldo, a Genoese by nation, which reaches from the sea to the uplands, has many sugar canes, and is so rich an estate that João Esmeraldo once came to produce twenty thousand *arrobas* from his own cultivation each year; and he had some eighty souls as his slaves, among them Moors, mulatto men and women, black men and women, and Canary Islanders. This was the greatest house on the island, and it has large residential buildings, sugar mills, purging houses and a church. And after the death of João Esmeraldo, everything passed to his son Christovão Esmeraldo, who spent most of his time in the city of Funchal riding a very handsome mule, with eight men behind him, four in cloaks and four young men without cloaks, sons of honourable men... ’

Despite its size and the 80 slaves it held, we find a production of twenty thousand *arrobas* on a single property excessive, especially at a time when a considerable part of the land was still uncultivated and its difficult clearing proceeded very slowly, owing chiefly to the relief and ruggedness of the terrain. It should also be noted that João Esmeraldo was Flemish or French, and not Genoese as Frutuoso asserts. Although we consider the chronicler’s words somewhat hyperbolic, we cannot help believing in the wealth and prosperity of the Lombada, if we bear in mind the importance it still has today, the large dwelling house and handsome church that Esmeraldo built there, and the many references we have found to this property, which was regarded as the most important entailed estate of the opulent house of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’).
The church was consecrated in 1508 by Bishop Dom João Lobo, and its founder, who died on 19 June 1536, was buried there.

The name of João Esmeraldo is inseparably linked with the stay of Christopher Columbus on this island, and to avoid needless repetition we refer the reader to the article we have devoted to the great navigator. João Esmeraldo was the first on this island to bear this surname, and the coat of arms granted to him and his descendants is described by Noronha as follows: ‘The field quartered: the first argent, with a bend sable; the second azure, with a fess of gold camelia; the third argent, with a lion sable, and above it a red fillet with bend, and around it billets sable; the fourth azure and a bend sable fimbriated gules: helm of silver, open, garnished with gold, mantling of gold and azure, and for crest a lion sable’. This description differs somewhat from the one found in volume 3 of the dictionary *Portugal*, on p. 184.
See the pamphlet *A Lombada dos Esmeraldos na Ilha da Madeira* by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva.
Esmeraldo (street)

The street takes its name from João Esmeraldo (see that entry), who had large dwelling houses there. It runs parallel to Rua do Sabão, with which it is connected by Travessa de Cristóvão Colombo, and extends from Rua da Alfândega to Rua do Comércio.
Silver scabbardfish (Lepidopus argyreus)
A fish of the family Trichiuridae, a visitor to Madeira, in whose waters it appears irregularly. It is caught on lines, often at a depth of 100 *braças*.
Black scabbardfish (Aphanopus carbo)

A fish of the family Trichiuridae, almost peculiar to the deep seas of Madeira, where it lives in great numbers. Caught exclusively by the fishermen of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), it is a tasty fish that supplies the Funchal market on a large scale. It is fished at a depth of about 1000 *braças*, which makes this one of the deepest fisheries in the whole world. The scabbardfish, once very cheap, now sells for as much as 60, 70 and 80 centavos each in the Funchal market.
New Zealand flax (Phormium tenax)

A member of the lily family native to New Zealand, cultivated at Monte, Santana and in some gardens in Funchal. The long, glaucous leaves of this plant, cut into strips once they have wilted, serve as ties in place of osier. A fibre can also be extracted from them, which in some countries is used to make ropes and a strong, durable fabric. The juice of *espadana* leaves has been recommended against cancerous diseases.
Esparto

Common name of *Asparagus lowei*, a plant of the Liliaceae-Asparagoideae widely cultivated in the gardens and *quintas* of Madeira, which also grows wild at Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) and between São Jorge and Santana. It has woody, sarmentose or twining stems, fasciculate, bristle-like cladodes and white flowers, with jointed peduncles shorter than the cladodes. The fine-leaved *esparto*, much grown in gardens, is *Asparagus plumosus*, and near Gorgulho (‘weevil’) *H. scoparius* has been found, a pretty plant now almost extinct on the island.
Esperança
Monthly magazine of the students of the Diocesan seminary (*Seminário*). The first issue appeared in December 1907 and the last in November 1908.
Esperança (A)
Eleven issues appeared, from 7 March to 8 June 1914.
Esperança (theatre)
See Theatres.
New Zealand spinach (Tetragonia expansa)

A plant from Australia and Japan, cultivated and naturalised in Madeira. Its leaves are used for purée of greens (*esparregado*). The spinach known by the botanical name *Spinacea oleracea* is common in Portugal but unknown in Madeira.
Espinal
A fishing gear made up of lines and hooks. It is little used in Madeira.
Espinheiro (Lycium europaeum)
A shrub growing wild on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It is found at Calheta (‘small cove’), at Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), etc. An infusion of its leaves is diuretic.
Espínola

This is a noble and very old surname here in Madeira. It descends from António and Leonardo Espínola, close relatives, who came to this island in the first quarter of the 16th century. They were natives of Genoa and sprang from an old and noble family of that city.

There are two branches. The first is the Espínolas de Adorno or Aderno, whose coat of arms, granted in 1513, consists of ‘a field of gold and a fess chequy of silver and red, and on it a red branch of thorns, and for difference a blue *marlota*, a silver helm open and for crest the same branch, mantling of gold and red’. The other branch, known by the name of Rosa or de la Rosa, has a coat of arms conferred on 27 February 1535, whose description in no way differs from the former.

António Espínola held much land in *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). On 30 April 1524 he donated a plot at the edge of the city, on which the chapel of São Tiago (St James the Greater) was built, on condition that members of his family be buried there and that the chaplain ask for an Our Father and a Hail Mary for his soul, according to the annotator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*).
Holy Spirit (chapels)

Describing the exploration of the island made by the discoverers in order to divide it into captaincies, Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘... João Gonsalves Zarco... reaching a height above Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), marked out there where a church of the Holy Spirit should be built... and all these heights he took for his heirs.’ This chapel, rebuilt more than once, still exists and is in a good state of repair. It was founded by the discoverer of Madeira himself and served for many years as the parish church when the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos was created in 1430. Around 1720 it was rebuilt because of the advanced state of ruin it was in, and in 1908 major repairs were also carried out on it and on the small house attached to it. Although perhaps nothing remains of the original building, the chapel is nonetheless a small historic monument for the municipality (*concelho*) and parish of Câmara de Lobos, recalling the name of the discoverer of Madeira who had it built, and also because it housed the parish when the parish was created, as already stated. In the locality (*sítio*) of Campo de Baixo (‘lower field’) on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) stands the chapel of Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), which is well preserved and where services are held. It is not of recent construction and was completely restored in the first quarter of the 19th century by Captain Sebastião António Drumond.
Espírito Santo (festivities)

The great festivities once held on Whit Sunday (the Sunday of the Espírito Santo, the Holy Spirit) have been much reduced. Nevertheless, in many parishes (*freguesias*) they still retain a certain splendour: the *impérios* are showily decorated, and after the religious ceremonies a meal and a complete suit of clothes are given to twelve poor people. If the gifts of the faithful for the festivities have been plentiful, other poor people also receive alms, often in the form of cotton cloth, chintz, etc. Each parish has a committee, always appointed in agreement with the parish priest, whose task is to raise the means needed to hold the festivities of the Espírito Santo.

The committee we have mentioned can be recognised, when on duty, by the red capes of its members, one of whom carries the crown, another the sceptre, another the flag and a fourth the processional banner. A few players of the *machete* (small Madeiran four-stringed guitar) and the viola (Portuguese wire-strung folk guitar) accompany the committee, and it is often joined by several girls dressed in a special way, who are called *saloias*. The men and girls sing religious hymns in the houses they enter to ask for alms, and it is not unusual for the committee members to finish their day’s work somewhat drunk, owing to the generous way in which the faithful of the parish usually receive them.

In the *impérios* of former times there was always an emperor, or divine emperor, who was crowned on Trinity Sunday. This figure, however, disappeared throughout the island about forty years ago, although the crown still features in the festivities of the Espírito Santo. The emperor was the man who had carried the sceptre the previous year, and after his election it was the custom, at least in certain places, for those present to address to him the following quatrain, which had its own music:
Crowned he is, and well crowned, Our Emperor. Crowned he was, and well crowned, By the hands of Our Lord.

In some parishes it is the custom for the organisers of the festivities to send tickets to the wealthier or more prominent people of the locality. If they accept and pay for them, they have the right to distribute them afterwards to the poor under their protection, so that these may receive alms on the day of the *Império* or after it has taken place.

Many gifts in kind obtained by the committees we have spoken of are usually sold or raffled, so that the proceeds can go towards the expenses of the *império* and the festivities. The carrying of the bread and produce to the site of the *império* is a ceremony that in some places has a certain splendour, and on the day of the festival it is customary for the celebrant to bless the bread for the meal that is served to the poor shortly afterwards.

In the *Fastos Açoreanos* of Mr José de Torres we read the following on the subject of the festivities of the Holy Spirit (Espírito Santo): ‘No one is a better custodian of good things than the common people, just as no one is more inclined to corrupt or distort many things that were excellent in their beginnings. There is no institution that does not tend to be corrupted by abuse. So it was with the brotherhoods known as those of the Holy Spirit, and with the public festivities they promote, once they passed into the hands of the people.’

‘Severe famines in the German states led one of the emperors of the dynasty, Otto, to lay the foundations of this institution as a bank formed from alms to relieve the poor in years of want. From the divinity they invoked and from the ruler who had taken the initiative arose the religious festivities which the imperial confraternity (*confraria*) dedicated to the worship of the Holy Spirit at this season of the year. This devotion and custom spread from there through the states of Christian Europe, whose kings led the work, civilising and humanitarian in its way, until the people usurped their privilege and seized the pious institution... ’

The festivities of the Holy Spirit, although far less showy in Madeira than in the Azores, still have a certain splendour in some parishes. The people never refuse their mite for these festivities, in which, alongside the edifying splendour of the religious ceremonies, there appear the *impérios* and the *bodos* (communal meals), from which the poor of the locality always benefit.

In the 18th century, as we read in the *Breve e verdadeira demonstração dos princípios e progressos do governo que João Antonio de Pereira fez na Ilha da Madeira*, *impérios* were held ‘in every street of the city’, with ‘gluttony and drunkenness’. Today, however, such festivities take place only near the parish churches, and they have largely lost the carnivalesque and at times rather unseemly character they showed in other periods.
Espírito Santo (Friar João do)

A Portuguese friar who was hanged in Funchal, dressed in the garb of a lay brother, in 1582 or shortly afterwards, for having incited the people of this island to take the side of Dom António, prior (title of the parish priest) of Crato. Friar João do Espírito Santo was in Angra before coming to Funchal, and he is mentioned in the *Relação das coisas que aconteceram na cidade d'Angra, ilha Terceira, depois que se perdeu el-rei D. Sebastião em Africa*. This account was published in vol. XIII, p. 159, of the *Panorama*.
Espírito Santo (João Gomes do)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’) in this municipality (*concelho*) and died in the city of Porto on 16 December 1839, at about eighty years of age. He was a distinguished artillery officer and for some years commanded the battery quartered in the fortress of São Tiago. A man of upright character, he made his name as a journalist, having been editor of a political newspaper published in Funchal that enjoyed great renown in its day. (He contributed to many periodicals on the mainland, having withdrawn from journalistic work many years earlier.
Sponges

About 70 species of sponges have been collected in the seas of Madeira, many of them siliceous or calcareous. Among the latter is *Melia Normani*, discovered by Mr Adolfo César de Noronha in the waters off Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and described by Mr Randolph Kirkpatrick, a naturalist at the British Museum. The largest species found so far in the seas of the archipelago measures about 60 centimetres, is somewhat bowl-shaped and consists of tightly interwoven glassy threads. When fishermen’s lines reach great depths, they sometimes bring up sponges of the same kind as the one just described, caught on the hooks. At Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’) we have seen small fibrous sponges floating near the coast, which certainly came from the nearby depths.
Issue no. 1289 of the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) contains some curious information about *Melia Normani*, the Porto Santo sponge.
Espora (A)
This newspaper began publication on 5 June 1891 and ended on 22 February 1892, after 72 issues.
Espranger

This family surname, of noble origin, descends from Adrião Basali Espranger, who held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands at Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) and left descendants there. He proved his noble lineage and bore a coat of arms.
Establishment of the port

At the syzygies, high water does not coincide with the moon’s passage across the meridian, because the waters go on rising after that passage by virtue of the momentum they have acquired. The establishment of the port (time of high water at full and new moon), or the time of high water at spring tides, is 12h48' at Funchal, according to the chart of General António Pedro de Azevedo, and the tidal rise is 2m, 28.
Telegraph and post offices

There are twelve combined telegraph and post offices in Madeira: one of the first class, in Funchal; two of the second class, in Santa Cruz and Calheta; six of the third class, in Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Sant'Ana and Machico; and three of the fourth class, in Câmara de Lobos, Ponta Delgada and Porto da Cruz. At Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) there is a telegraph, post and semaphore station, at Ponta de São Lourenço a telegraph and semaphore station, and on the Ilhéu a semaphore post.
Estanquinhos

A locality (*sítio*) at the northern end of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), about 1500 metres above sea level, where there is a mountain shelter. The Estanquinhos (‘little ponds’) spring is well known to everyone who crosses the Paul, because of the low temperature and excellent quality of its water. On the rocks beside this spring grows the rare *Sedum farinosum*, peculiar to Madeira.

Steppe

Dr Martin Vahl, the well-known botanist and biologist of Copenhagen, in an interesting work entitled *Zonas e biochoros geograficos*, included within the domain of the steppes the plant community that covers a good part of the dry land of the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira, and in which *Andropogon hirtum* appears to be the most frequent species.

Although we recognise that the shortage of rainfall is in certain years very marked on Madeira, we cannot share Dr Vahl’s opinion. To delimit the steppe, it is necessary not to lose sight of certain climatic influences, some of them entirely local.

It is well known that, as a result of the nearness of the sea and of the currents set up between it and the land, there is almost always a considerable quantity of water vapour in the low-lying zone of Madeira. Owing to the thermal conditions of that zone, this vapour seldom appears in the form of mist, but it cannot fail to be regarded as an aid to vegetation at times when rainfall is lacking. Since all soils are hygroscopic, though to differing degrees, it is evident that they can take directly from the atmosphere the moisture it contains, and this, once absorbed, must contribute in some measure to sustaining plant life. Dr Mason reports that by leaving a plate exposed to the open air on clear nights he managed to collect a considerable quantity of dew within a few hours. As other observers have noted, however, this is by no means general in the low-lying region of Madeira, although it cannot be denied that on many nights a certain amount of water vapour condenses on the soil and on the organs of plants, and that some benefit to vegetation must result from this.

By reducing the intensity of transpiration, atmospheric humidity causes plants to consume less of the water they store or draw from the soil through their roots. Even in dry climates plants can conserve their fluids, either by slowing their growth or by avoiding in other ways the losses to which this function gives rise.

There are various types of steppe, but it is probably grass steppe that Dr Vahl supposes to exist in the lowland zone of Madeira. According to Dr Drude, this steppe is characterised by formations subject to winter dormancy, in which the plants dry out during the period of greatest heat. Its accessory elements include large herbaceous plants, sometimes markedly tomentose, plants furnished with bulbs or tubers, and thickets of species with little succulence.

In the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira there are some grasses and other plants which, whether from the length of their roots or rhizomes or from the appearance and form of their stems and leaves, seem adapted to withstand a high degree of dryness. However, if we consider that such plants can exist both inside and outside the steppe, and that bulbous forms are not found in this zone, whereas succulent forms are abundant there, it is impossible not to see in these facts proof that the plant associations dominated by *Andropogon* belong to a domain different from the one in which Dr Vahl sought to include them. The first settlers, felling the forests in order to clear the land for cultivation, perhaps brought about appreciable changes both in the climate and soils of the lowland zone of Madeira and in the distribution and appearance of its flora. What they did not manage to do, as we have seen, was to cancel out the influences arising from the nearness of the sea and from the position and shape of the island. It is owing to these influences that steppe does not exist on Madeira, although it cannot be denied that in certain years the rainfall regime of the island’s lower zone shows remarkable analogies with that of countries endowed with a flora adapted to withstand a high degree of dryness.
Starling (Sturnus vulgaris)
A bird of the starling family (Sturnidae), it visits the islands of this archipelago without fail during the winter season. It is a sociable bird, seen in flocks that are at times very large.
Monumental Road and Bridge

The bridge over the Ribeiro Seco and the road that begins at it and leads to the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) are generally known as the Ponte Monumental and the Estrada Monumental (the Monumental Bridge and Monumental Road), because the original plan for their construction conceived of them as a monument raised to the memory of the King of Portugal Pedro IV. They were to bear his name and were intended to commemorate here his achievements as the liberator king. It was his comrade-in-arms and devoted friend, Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, the first governor of Madeira in the constitutional period, who conceived this project in 1835; his short stay at the head of the administration of this district left it barely begun. Writing on this subject, Servulo Drumond de Meneses says: ‘Immediately on leaving the city towards the west, one comes upon a great landslide (*quebrada*) formed by the torrents, at the bottom of which runs the Ribeiro Seco. Mr Mousinho de Albuquerque intended to cross this landslide by means of a suspension bridge, and to that end he began by having two gigantic pillars built, besides the very strong abutments on each edge of the landslide. The plan included the idea of raising a monument to the memory of the Immortal Duke of Braganza, Magnanimous Liberator of the Portuguese, and accordingly the work was to be magnificent and grandiose. It happened, however, that when Mr Mousinho de Albuquerque left the island, the works already begun made no further progress. Thus the laudable and patriotic designs of the illustrious governor of Madeira were frustrated for a long time, although, tireless and persevering, he had not only already given a great impetus to the work but had also gathered many materials, which in the end were gradually lost.’

The civil governor, the Baron of Lordelo (1838–1840), made a praiseworthy attempt to continue the work already begun, but he could not overcome the difficulties that stood in the way of its execution. That glory fell to the most distinguished and deserving governor this archipelago has had, Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, who, after persistent efforts, managed to bring this great undertaking to completion. Construction began on 6 March 1848, and the work was almost finished by the end of the same year.
For this purpose Councillor José Silvestre opened a public subscription, which raised more than three *contos* (one million réis) de réis, and the Funchal Council contributed about two *contos*.

In 1848 the secretary-general of the civil government of Funchal, Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses, published a pamphlet entitled *Colecção de documentos relativos á construçao da Ponte do Ribeiro Secco*, which contains very interesting information about this work. Although it did not deserve the name ‘monumental’, the bridge was nonetheless an important improvement, long called for, which met a great public need. The road that continues from the bridge had then only just been begun, and it advanced rather slowly until its final completion. The *alvenaria* (local name for compact basalt used as building stone) bridge over the Ribeira dos Socorridos was begun on 5 June 1848.
Roads

Writing of the year in which the first edition of this work was published, we stated, with complete truth, that road transport in Madeira was still very backward. Most of the island’s roads were unsuited to certain comfortable and rapid means of transport because of their steepness and very poor paving, and others, though flatter, were no more than mere paths, which could be travelled only on foot or in a hammock (*rede*, slung from a pole and carried by two bearers). In recent years the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) has sought to remedy this problem, improving certain routes and establishing others between various localities. There is, however, still much to be done to give this island a good road network, and it is no exaggeration to say that at many points on the north coast, and even on the south, road transport is in the same state as it was in the time of the donataries (1922).

The roads of Madeira were, beyond any possible dispute, the worst in the whole of our country. This was due to various causes, above all the almost unbelievably rugged terrain and other unavoidable conditions of the environment. Most of them did not deserve the name of roads, for in general they were narrow paths cut into ground that was arduous and extremely difficult underfoot, overhanging unfathomable chasms and skirting the flanks of high mountains, almost always subjecting travellers to the gravest discomforts and dangers. Until 1901, when administrative autonomy was granted to this district, there were only nine kilometres of good road, linking the city of Funchal with the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). Then began, and still continues, the construction of an extensive road network which, within a few years, will make it easy to travel the whole island by fast transport and to visit its principal localities quickly and comfortably.

In addition to its own revenues, the District General Council was authorised by the decree of 12 July 1912 to raise a loan intended exclusively for the construction of roads. The decree of 25 June 1935 ordered a technical mission to come to this archipelago, charged with studying and proposing the measures needed to complete the road network, and the decree of 14 April 1938 approved the plan submitted by this study commission, whereupon the corresponding construction work was diligently carried out.

Because of their very great importance, and as an indispensable explanation of the grand project to complete our road network, we shall transcribe some articles of the decree cited above: ‘Article 1. The plan of work for the completion of the supplementary road network of the island of Madeira, amounting to a total of 44.000.000$, is that set out in the schedule annexed to this decree. Art. 2. The work under this plan shall be carried out in three phases, namely: a) the first, amounting to 15.000.000$, shall be carried out over a period of three years, corresponding to an annual endowment of 5.000.000$; b) the other two phases, amounting to a total of 29.000.000$, shall be carried out over periods of five years each, corresponding to an annual endowment of 3.000.000$ in the first nine years and of 2.000.000$ in the final year.

Art. 3. The works included in this plan shall be subsidised by the Government in the proportion of 75 per cent of their cost, the remaining 25 per cent being borne by the Autonomous General Council (*Junta Geral Autónoma*) of the district of Funchal. Sole paragraph. The Government may authorise this General Council to raise a loan to meet the charges that will fall to it.’

After the establishment of the Republic in the country, the former royal roads became known as national roads. The most important are those numbered 23, 24, 25, 26, 27 and 28 on the district road map, both because of their length and because they link the principal localities of the island. These roads, which as a rule have a poor surface and are at times dangerous to travellers, as already mentioned, have lost their former importance. They are no longer so heavily used at the points where the new, recent roads have replaced them to great advantage. Nevertheless they continue to render excellent service as means of communication between various localities, and they are the true local roads for the inhabitants whose homes lie near them. They should not, therefore, be left to fall into neglect, but deserve continual repairs for their upkeep and improvement.

As stated above, it was after the granting of administrative autonomy in 1901 that construction began on the important road network, and it is still going on today. The network is gradually spreading across the whole island and already allows quick and comfortable visits to more than twenty rural parishes. It is to be hoped that within a few years easy communications can be established between all the parishes of Madeira.
