Foreigners

The conquests and discoveries that the Portuguese began at the dawn of the 15th century awakened the interest and curiosity of all Europe. There was no shortage of restless and ambitious spirits who left their native lands and took their chances with fortune, seeking in the distant newly discovered lands the glory and riches that their homelands could not give them. If some were driven only by love of adventure, by the desire for the unforeseen and the unknown, and by ardour for daring enterprises and heroic deeds, it is certain that most went out drawn by a thirst for riches, by the quest for the golden fleece, which once again stirred the ambitions of so great a number of bold adventurers. Madeira was the first and most important commercial emporium to arise in our colonial domains, and therefore also the first and most coveted point of attraction for the outsiders who made for the newly discovered shores. Their number was considerable, although we cannot determine, even approximately, how many they were, the qualities and social position that distinguished them, the precise times at which they landed here, or other general circumstances that might give us reliable evidence of their activity or influence in the community in which they settled. It is true that certain personal circumstances are known about various foreigners, which speak highly of their origins and admirable qualities of character, but these form a rather small number compared with the countless outsiders who settled on this island in the early days of colonisation. The names of Simão Acciaioly, João Esmeraldo, João Bettencourt, Pedro de Lemilhana Berenguer, João Drumond, António Espinola, António Leme, Urbano Lomelino, João Rodrigues Mondragão, João Salviati, Adriano Espranger, João Valdavesso and still others who settled in this archipelago became known through the distinguished families they founded, and they proved their noble descent; many of them were granted the status of *fidalgos*, with the privileges belonging to the most authentic nobility. We do not mean by this that the outsiders whose names remain unknown to us, who are the greater number, did not have qualities equal or superior to those of the men we have mentioned; we merely wish to record here the surnames of some families that we frequently find cited in old documents and in the old Madeiran genealogies.

The foreigners contributed considerably, though to their own profit, to the prosperity this island attained from the end of the 15th century to the middle of the following one. They engaged in various branches of trade, set up many sugar mills, and a good part of the export of that product to foreign countries passed through their hands. Gaspar Frutuoso asserts, though perhaps with some exaggeration, that João Esmeraldo produced twenty thousand *arrobas* of sugar a year on his properties at the Lombada (‘long ridge’). Many of them were at once farmers, manufacturers and merchants. By the middle of the 15th century there were already many foreigners on this island, living on good terms with the natives, most of them engaged in the sugar trade. At first the remarkable fertility of the soil and the rewarding price of the cane fields fully satisfied the tenant farmer (*colono*, under the *colonia* contract), the landlord and the merchant. Later, however, came the fall in prices, brought about by various causes, which roused the distrust and hostility of the producers of the raw material for sugar against the merchants, especially the foreign ones. The Funchal Council even took repressive measures against them, going so far as to order their expulsion from this island.

‘Among them, says Dr Azevedo, soon at odds, there at once arrived the speculation and capital of the foreign merchants, who, resentful of the fortune that had granted so many and such rich colonies to Portugal and Spain, did not miss the chance to take swift revenge, through usury, on this distracted population. Advances on account delivered it into their hands, subdued by the want of some and the extravagance of others. They had already taken possession of the future produce of the land, and were gradually becoming masters of the land itself. And, as if this internal crisis were not alarming enough in itself, it was aggravated by the slow but continuous decline in the price of sugar, a commodity still limited at that time to use in pharmacy and confectionery. Thus, on top of the constant conflict between the tenant farmer, who produced, and the landlord, who spent, came the unrelenting and merciless pressure of outside capital or cash, at once fertilising and destructive, coveted and cursed by both.

This turn of events, gradually building up and now coming to a head, had its effect on public opinion and transformed it. As early as 1486 the Council of Funchal, lacking the tact to diagnose the true causes of the harm, or blinded by them, had turned against these foreigners resident on the island, who only a few years before had been well liked and fêted. By a municipal by-law (*postura*) it ordered them to leave the island by September of that year, but the Duke, jealous of his privileges and resentful, prevented this by a letter of 7 August’.

Although the annotator of the *Saudades* does not say so, and even seems to wish to justify the conduct of the foreigners, we must believe that the drastic measure adopted by the Funchal Senate (*senado*, the municipal council), requiring their immediate departure from this archipelago in 1486, was based on very grave and weighty reasons, arising from the excesses committed by the merchants in their unbridled speculation on the price of sugar. We do not know whether the measures taken by the Council of Funchal were ever fully carried out. However, the regulations (*regimento*) of 7 October, issued by the central government to overcome the crisis then facing the sugar industry, allowed foreigners only a temporary stay on this island each year and, among other restrictive measures, forbade them to lease land planted with sugar cane. We likewise do not know whether the regulations of 7 October were faithfully observed. What is certain is that the royal decree (alvará régio) of 22 March 1498 allowed foreigners to reside freely on this island, King Manuel I declaring in it that ‘we deem it good & it pleases us that any foreigners whatsoever who wish may stay & trade on it (the island) permanently & as best suits them.

Although vine-growing in Madeira is old, it seems certain, according to Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, that it became more intensive, and the wines of this island began to be known and esteemed in Europe, around the middle of the 16th century. Foreigners contributed greatly to this, since they were the first here to take up this branch of trade, which came to reach a great scale. In the last quarter of the 17th century there were twenty-seven commercial houses in Funchal dealing in the purchase and export of wine, twenty of them foreign. From the end of the 18th century until the first twenty years of the following century, the island’s wine production was truly extraordinary. Its export, carried on chiefly through English commercial houses, reached an annual average of over twenty thousand *pipas*, and growers continued to receive a very rewarding price. When, at the beginning of the 19th century, the foreign exporting houses conspired to force a sharp fall in wine prices, the great landowner João de Carvalhal thwarted them by buying the musts at fair prices. This obliged the English merchants to turn to Carvalhal himself and buy the wines on terms quite advantageous to the farmers.

We have no knowledge of benefactions by foreigners on this island in times more remote from our own. In the first half of the 19th century, we know of the notable services rendered by the foreigners John March and Roberto Page, to whom we refer specifically elsewhere in this work. Everyone knows that in recent times some foreigners have amassed large fortunes in Madeira, running into millions. However, we are not aware that their humanitarian feelings, or even ordinary gratitude towards the land that enriched them, have found expression in any works or deeds worth recording here, except the one we have mentioned in the article Libraries (*Bibliotecas*). Estreito da Calheta (parish)

We have read somewhere that there is no plausible explanation for the use of the word Estreito, applied to the parishes (*freguesias*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’). We share this opinion. Even if we give the word the meaning of gorge, valley or *profundidade* (deep, roughly circular mountain basin), as some lexicographers would have it, it does not seem to us that the relief of those parishes, taken as a whole, justifies such a name. It is possible that a small locality (*sítio*) or village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town), with more or less aptness in the use of the term, originally bore the name Estreito, which then spread to the surrounding land and was later extended to designate an entire parish, as happened with other parishes of Madeira. Moreover, in the earliest days of colonisation the naming of the various localities must have been highly arbitrary. In many cases it would have followed only the whim and preference of the early settlers, without regard to the relief and watercourses of the places, or to any other weighty circumstances that might perhaps have arisen. An event of no importance, and sometimes even a minor episode, was reason enough for the name given to a particular locality or village, as certainly happened with the parishes of Fajã da Ovelha, Campanário, Curral das Freiras, etc.

As we have already noted, Calheta (‘small cove’) was one of the oldest places outside Funchal to be subject to early colonisation and farming. We must suppose that the settlement and clearing of the land that later made up the parish of Estreito did not take long. There were one or more “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*) there, which formed the original nucleus of the settlement established in this village.

The annotator of the *Saudades*, following the old Madeiran genealogies, says that this parish originated in the settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) begun there by André Gonçalves de França, known as the Pole because he was a native of the kingdom of Poland. He came from there to this island around the middle of the 15th century and obtained a great deal of land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in what was then the parish of Calheta, land that later belonged to the future parish of Estreito. It was his son João de França who further enlarged the already vast property and, in the words of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, ‘enhanced it with fine houses and a chapel’. He had the chapel of Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*) built, in which the new parish was later created and installed. It was also the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he founded in 1503, one of the oldest entails (*instituições vinculares*) in Madeira. João de França died around 1511 and was buried in the chapel he had founded.

Gaspar Frutuoso, giving a brief description of the parishes (*freguesias*) of this island as they were at the time he wrote the *Saudades* and even earlier, says of Estreito da Calheta: ‘And then, about a league from Calheta, lies the estate of João Rodrigues Castelhano, who was so called because he spoke Castilian, though he was a Genoese by nation; it is a large estate of sugar cane, with its own chaplain. This João Rodrigues begot in Funchal two very rich daughters, and the best estates on the island now belong to them. He had many slaves, five of whom killed a factor of his; he handed them over to Justice, and they were hanged in the Vila da Calheta (‘town of Calheta’). About half a league from the estate of this João Rodrigues Castelhano stands another sugar mill, belonging to Diogo de França, who had twelve noble and rich children, and a good estate of cane and vines, waters and fruit.’ Perhaps earlier than this João Rodrigues Castelhano is Francisco Homem de Gouveia, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) who settled in Calheta at the beginning of the 16th century. With his wife, Dona Isabel Afonso, he founded the chapel and entail (*morgado*) of the Magi (*Reis Magos*) in this parish of Estreito. One of the editors of this *Elucidário* published a detailed article on them in the *Brado d'Oeste* (‘Cry from the West’) of 2 September 1916, from which we extract the following passages:

‘Francisco Homem de Gouveia acquired in the parish of Estreito da Calheta the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) that bore his name and that, after the chapel was built, came to be called Lombo dos Reis (‘kings’ ridge’), a name it still keeps today. It was by a deed of 4 August 1529 that he and his wife established the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Reis on the thirds of their property, with perpetual succession to his firstborn son. We do not know whether the chapel is a building contemporary with the entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela), but we believe it was not built much later than that time. This entailed estate carried the obligation of a daily Mass in the same chapel, where its founders lie buried, the wife of Francisco Homem having died on 5 March 1554.’ This entail was incorporated into the house of the donataries of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) because a granddaughter and heiress of the founder, Dona Maria da Câmara, was married to Diogo Perestrelo de Bisforte, 5th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) and governor of that island.

Around the middle of the 18th century António João de França Andrade and João António Cardoso Belzago had residences in this parish, and, we believe, entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*) as well. In 1750 and 1753 they were granted papal briefs to set up oratories in the houses they owned there and to have the sacrifice of the Mass celebrated in them.

The parish was created before 1562, because the royal decree (*alvará régio*) of 12 January of that year raised the stipend (*côngrua*) of its parish priest to 17,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year, where it had previously been only 13,300 *réis*. Successive royal decrees (*alvarás*) of 30 March and 22 June 1572, 20 April 1589, 17 November 1591, 30 May 1624 and 5 March 1641 increased the vicar’s stipend as the population grew and parish work became more arduous.

The royal decree of Philip II of 20 October 1602 created a curacy (*curato*) in this parish. The chapel of Our Lady of Grace, later converted into the parish church, was built at the end of the 15th century or the beginning of the 16th, and was enlarged, or rather rebuilt, in a year we cannot state precisely. An order of the Council of the Exchequer (*Conselho de Fazenda*) of 20 July 1690 directed that a new church be built; the works were contracted to Salvador Lopes for the sum of 1,395,000 *réis*. The royal decree of the Infanta Queen Catherine, regent of the Kingdom, of 27 June 1705, approved the transfer of the new church to another site, as ordered by the diocesan bishop, Dom José de Sousa de Castelo Branco. But was the new church actually built at that time? It is certain that the present church was built in 1791 and blessed in 1793. Is it likely that two churches were built within less than a century? We do not think so. Above the portico of the present church is a stone tablet bearing the following inscription: *Mariae Patris Filiae Filii Matri Spiritus Sancti Sponsae hoc templum consecravit Aug. Reg. Maria Prima suae piae liberalitatis regio erario administro. Anno MDCCLXXXXI.* (To Mary, Daughter of the Father, Mother of the Son, Spouse of the Holy Spirit, the August Queen Maria I consecrated this church out of her pious liberality, the royal treasury administering it. In the year 1791.)

The patron saint of this parish is Our Lady of Grace. Her image, venerated at the high altar of the parish church, is an exquisite sculpture, to whose cult and veneration Friar Agostinho de Santa Maria devotes a chapter in volume X of his *Santuário Mariano*.
The parish has the chapels of the Magi, Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, Our Lady of Pity and Our Lady of Deliverance, which we shall discuss elsewhere.
The present parish of Prazeres was once part of the parish of Estreito and was separated from it in 1733, when an independent curacy was created there by royal decree of 12 November of that year.

At the beginning of the 19th century the brothers Ricardo José de França and José Sebastião de França, sons of the captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) José António de França, began to tap the waters of the Fontes dos Balcões, Água Negra and Assobiadores springs, intended to feed the levada (irrigation channel) they planned to build to irrigate the land of this and other parishes. In February 1811 they formed a company with other individuals to exploit and capture these waters, and petitioned the government in mainland Portugal for the concession, obtaining a favourable opinion from the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*), Dr António Rodrigues Veloso de Oliveira.

The main localities (*sítios*) of this parish are Lombo dos Castanheiros, Lombo do Lameiro, Lombo dos Reis, Lombo dos Serrões, Lombo da Igreja, Lombo dos Moinhos, Lombo do Girão, Lombo da Fazendinha and Lombo da Ribeira Funda. The Ribeira de São Bartolomeu, to the east, separates this parish from that of Calheta, and the Ribeira Funda, to the west, separates it from the parish of Prazeres.

Besides the Levada do Rabaçal, Estreito da Calheta is irrigated by the Levada dos Moinhos, Levada Nova, Levada do Ribeiro do Farrobo and Levada dos Ferreiros. It has a state school for boys, founded around 1879, and one for girls, founded in 1911.
It has 2,300 inhabitants.
Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (parish)

There are good grounds for believing that, outside Funchal, Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) was one of the first places where the land was settled and cultivated, and that a sizeable population centre formed there from the outset. Before long this clearing of uncultivated land would have spread and extended up to the heights of the present parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito, at least in its southern part and in the areas that border the parish of Câmara de Lobos.

As to the origin of the name of the parish of Estreito, we can only refer to what we have already set out in the article devoted to the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’), since we can add nothing, and know nothing further, to what is said there on this point. Referring to this parish in the last quarter of the 16th century, Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘Above it (the Convent of São Bernardino (St Bernardino of Siena)) lie the orchards of Estreito, which have many chestnuts and walnuts, and very sweet apples of every kind, and wines and livestock, and a parish called Estreito, of up to thirty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’)...’

We do not know the date of the decree that established this parish, but we know that its creation goes back to the first years of the 16th century, the annotator of the *Saudades* assigning it to the year 1509. We believe that it had previously been the seat of a curacy (*curato*) in the chapel of Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*), which stood there and was later turned into the parish church. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that three deeds drawn up in the old notary’s office of Câmara de Lobos show that in 1539 Father Sebastião Vaz was vicar of Estreito.

The oldest decree we have found cited concerning this parish is that of 20 January 1572, which granted Father Gonçalo de Aguiar, the parish priest at the time, an increase of 9,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) on the stipend (*côngrua*) he had previously received. The royal decrees (*alvará*) of 18 January 1582 and 15 November 1591 increased and restructured the annual salary of the vicar, which became 16,000 *réis* in cash, one and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat.

The royal decree of Peter II of 28 December 1676 abolished one of the posts of beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) in the collegiate church of Câmara de Lobos, applying its stipend to the curacy of Estreito, which the same royal decree created. Another royal decree, of 9 May 1688, set the annual salary of the assistant priest (*coadjutor*) at 120,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine.

We do not know when the chapel of Our Lady of Grace was built. It gave its name to the new parish (*freguesia*), and the parish seat was established in it. The small church underwent major repairs at roughly the time the parish was created, and important works were also carried out there in the last quarter of the 17th century. We know of the following instruments, which we found noted in the General Index of the register of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*): an order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*), dated 23 September 1692, for the work on the new church, bought at auction by Francisco Rodrigues for 811,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis); an order of the same Council, dated 5 March 1748, for the building of the church, and for 194,000 *réis* to pay for one *alqueire* (dry measure for grain; as a land measure c. 900 m²) and half a *quarta* of the land needed for the said work, and for 551,662 *réis* for the vicar’s house, which was to be pulled down for the same purpose; and an order of 15 February 1764 for the work on the high altar to be awarded at auction to the master woodcarver Julião Francisco, for 2,000 *réis*. Beyond what the documents cited say, we were able to establish from a reliable source that around the middle of the 18th century the old church was demolished, leaving the chancel standing, which went on serving as the parish church for some years. On 3 February 1753 the foundation stone of the new church was laid and blessed. On 18 January 1756 the chancel was blessed and the Blessed Sacrament was carried into it, after which the rest of the building work continued. This church was consecrated in 1814 by the diocesan prelate Dom Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde.

It was in this church that, a few years later, on 6 November 1829, a great sacrilege took place, which we have already described at greater length elsewhere in this *Elucidário*. On this case, which seems to have caused a great sensation, a pamphlet of 13 pages was published, which the *Diccionario Bibliographico Português* cites under the following title: *Sentença da Relação de Lisboa contra Jacinto Fernandes e mais septe reos, culpados do roubo e desacato na egreja da Graça do Funchal. Morreram seis enforcados e o ultimo foi degolado.* (Dated 6 March 1830). Printed in Lisbon by the Typ. de J. B. Morando.

Among the earliest priests who performed parish duties in this parish we can cite the names of Fathers Sebastião Vaz (1539), Gonçalo de Aguiar (1563), Sebastião Gonçalves (1586), João Gonçalves Evangelho (1607), Matias Lopes (1620), Manuel Lopes (1631) and Luís Gonçalves Velho (1643).

The parish has the chapels of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation), Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*), Santo António and Our Lady of Good Success (*Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso*), which we shall discuss at greater length in the articles devoted to chapels. In the locality (*sítio*) of Ribeira da Fazenda (‘farm stream’) there was once the chapel of Sant’Ana.

The principal localities are: Vizinhanças da Igreja, Caminho do Concelho para a Ribeira da Caixa, Pico e Salões, Caminho do Concelho para a Ribeira da Fernanda, Vargem, Barreiros, Covão e Panasqueira, Castelejo, Fajã das Galinhas, Quinta de Santo António, Romeiras, Foro, Fonte do Frade e Cruz dos Pomares, Serra, Cabo do Podão, Marco e Fonte da Pedra, Fontes, Casa Caída, Marinheira, Pomar do Meio, Garachico, Furneira and Jardim da Serra. We shall deal with this last locality, and with the house and grave of H. Veitch that are found there, in a separate article (see Jardim da Serra).

Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca and João Augusto de Ornelas were natives of this parish (see those entries). The parish has a small straw-hat industry, almost entirely confined to this place, and there is also a butter factory.
The so-called Boca dos Namorados (‘lovers’ pass’) is the most picturesque spot in this parish. It commands vast and astonishing views and is much visited, especially by foreigners.

The neighbouring parishes are Serra de Água and Curral das Freiras to the north, Câmara de Lobos to the south, the Ribeira dos Socorridos to the east, which separates it from Santo António and Curral, and Quinta Grande and Câmara de Lobos to the west.

It has one state school for each sex, and its population is 6,200 inhabitants. On 22 May 1927 a lamentable tragedy occurred in this parish: Father André dos Passos was murdered by a madman as he left the chapel of Our Lady of Good Success, in the locality of Garachico, where he had just celebrated the sacrifice of the Mass. This most grievous event caused the deepest emotion throughout the island, and above all in this parish.

Estrelas
Common name of *Chrysanthemum frutescens*, a composite native to the Canary Islands and widely grown in the gardens of Funchal. This plant is also known as *ovos fritos* (‘fried eggs’).
Starfish

This name is given to several echinoderms of Madeira, most notably *Uraster glacialis*, with bluish spines; *Ophidiaster attenuatus*, red and spineless; *Ophiocoma nigra*, black in colour; *Ophiolepis squamata*, small and white; and *O. siliata*, with rigid spines. This last species is common at depths of 20 to 30 *braças*. The largest of the starfish is *Astropecton aurantiacus*, a red Mediterranean species which sometimes reaches a great size.

Estufas

*Estufas* (heated stores for ageing Madeira wine) first appeared on this island in 1794. They were banned by edicts of the governor and captain-general of 13 August 1802 and 6 November 1803, but resumed operation under a royal order dated 7 May 1804.

*Estufas* are intended to give wines an appearance of age that they do not have. Those of the original system, which still exist on the island today, are heated either by hot air or by the sun. The hot-air *estufas* are stone buildings divided into compartments heated by pipes carrying air from one or more furnaces, and the new wine is kept in contact with the air of the *estufa* through a hole opened in the *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres). The air temperature in the *estufa* is kept between 60 and 70 °C, but it may fall to 54 °C, or even lower, in the case of good-quality wines.

The wines remain in the *estufas* for four to six months, in order to hasten their development and at the same time prevent them from fermenting. However, they almost always acquire a toasted taste, sometimes very pronounced, which the cellarman manages to reduce, though not to remove entirely, by subsequently using charcoal.
In sun *estufas*, the walls and roof of the building are made of glass.

In an establishment founded in 1889 by the late Count of Canavial, the wine, before going into the heating rooms (*estâncias*) or *estufas* (heated store for ageing Madeira wine), where it remains for weeks or months, enters a reservoir. From there it descends slowly through a tin pipe, in which it is heated in a bain-marie, sealed from the air, to a temperature of 70 to 80 degrees centigrade. It is at this temperature that the wine is received into the cask in which it goes to the heating rooms, where the temperature is 50 degrees. The temperature then falls slowly, with suitable pauses, until the end of the maturing process.

In this improved system the wine is sterilised by raising its temperature to 70 or 80 degrees. However, since this is the temperature at which the wine comes into contact with the air, it oxidises as a result and acquires a certain cooked taste.

This taste disappears almost entirely in another improved heating system, in which the wine is poured into a tank of *alvenaria* (local name for compact basalt used as building stone) that can be hermetically sealed and through which runs a coil carrying steam. The wine is drawn off only once it has cooled. The heating begins by raising the temperature to 80 degrees centigrade; fresh steam is then passed through the coil from time to time, so as to keep the wine at an almost constant temperature, or at varying temperatures, as required.

The system of improving wines in *estufas*, today much refined, had some detractors in former times. The preamble to the decree of 23 June 1834 states that it is ‘the principal cause of the present discredit of Madeiran wines, once highly esteemed’. Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara, however, defends the system in his *Breve Noticia sobre a ilha da Madeira*, and the decree of 20 February 1835 also considerably modified the doctrine of the earlier enactment regarding *estufas*.

There is no doubt that the *estufas* were much abused, and that by means of them many ordinary wines were prepared for sale in European markets at low prices, to the discredit of the fortified wines. Nevertheless, there were always good reasons not to abandon these establishments. If on the one hand they encouraged fraud, on the other they helped the honest merchant to raise the value of new wines from good grape varieties quickly, developing in them qualities that would otherwise have emerged only late.
See Wines, Canteiro wines and Vinho de roda.
Eucalyptus

*Eucalyptus globulus*, a native of Australia, is the only species of the genus *Eucalyptus* commonly found in Madeira, where it grows at Monte (‘hill’), at Choupana (‘hut’) and in various other places on the island. It reaches great size and grows very rapidly. It should not, however, be planted near springs, because its roots draw up a great quantity of water.

According to Dr Jorge Perez, a distinguished physician and naturalist of Tenerife, it is *E. globulus*, and not *E. collossea* as some newspapers have stated, that acts on the nervous system and stops the secretion of glucose in diabetes. The first of these species is richer in essential oil than the second, and this is why its leaves should be preferred in preparing the infusion used to treat that disease. The same physician also says that eucalyptus infusion is a medicine to be administered with caution, since cases of poisoning caused by it have been reported when it is taken in excess.

*Eucalyptus robusta* is also cultivated in Madeira, and on the *quinta* (country estate) of Mr Luís da Rocha Machado, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, there are three species of *Eucalyptus*, one of which appears to be *E. longifolia*. We are told that *E. collossea* has recently been sown in Madeira.
Eugénie (Empress)

Empress Eugénie, widow of Napoleon III, called at Madeira aboard the English steamer *German* on 30 March 1880. She was following the same route as her son, the Prince Imperial, who died in South Africa in the war against the Zulus, all the way to the very spot where he met his death. The prince had landed in Funchal on 4 March 1879, while passing through our port aboard the English steamer *Danube*.

Capital executions

We have scant information about capital executions carried out in this archipelago by public sentence. It has been suggested that the locality (*sítio*) known as Forca (‘gallows’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), was the place where a death sentence was once carried out, with the gallows as the instrument of punishment applied to the criminal. We do not know, and we are even inclined to believe that the explanation given for the name of that locality has no serious foundation.

Speaking of João Rodrigues Castelhano, who held lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’), Dr Gaspar Frutuoso says the following: ‘he had many slaves, five of whom killed a factor (*feitor*) of his; he handed them over to justice and they were hanged in the town of Calheta’.

Under Philippine rule, around 1582, according to Rebêlo da Silva, the friar João do Espírito Santo was hanged in Funchal, accused of inciting the people to take the side of Dom António, Prior of Crato.

In December 1813, when this island was occupied by British troops, an English soldier was hanged in this city for murdering a sergeant, a fellow countryman of his. Luís Beltrão, then governor and captain-general of the archipelago, protested against this execution as an offence against the rights of Portuguese sovereignty, but General Gordon, commander of the English forces, did not heed his complaint.

At the dawn of the 17th century a man named Francisco Rodrigues Jardim, of plebeian origin, was hanged in effigy in the Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory’) of this city for abducting a lady named Dona Maria de Ornelas, who belonged to old and noble Madeiran families. Had he not escaped the reach of justice by flight, he would have paid for the audacity of his crime on the gallows.
Funeral rites

The *Livro de Acclamações e Exequias*, in the archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), records that solemn funeral rites were held in the Cathedral of this city on the deaths of the following monarchs: John V, on 19 December 1753; Joseph I, on 28 June 1777; Maria I, on 17 December 1816; John VI, on 10 May 1826; Maria II, on 26 January 1854; Pedro V, on 19 January 1862; Luís I, on 29 November 1889; and Carlos I and Prince Louis Philippe, on 31 March 1908.

The said book does not record any funeral rites in Funchal on the death of Pedro IV. The *Indice Alphabetico* of the Council’s registers states that in 1495 Manuel I sent a letter to the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) instructing it to acclaim him and to hold the funeral of John II; that in 1656 a letter came from the queen announcing the death of John IV; that in 1666 a letter came from the king reporting the death of the queen; and finally that in 1683 Prince Pedro sent a letter to the Council informing it of the death of King Afonso VI. The same book also states that 192,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) were spent on the funeral rites of Queen Luisa de Guzmán in 1666, and that 100,000 *réis* from the municipal levy (*imposição*) were spent on those of Afonso VI. The funeral rites of the kings were preceded by the ceremony of the breaking of the shields, performed by the councillors (*vereadores*) at various points in the city; for this purpose a procession was organised in which the authorities, the officials and all other persons of standing in the city took part. The last time the ceremony of the breaking of the shields took place in Funchal was at the funeral rites of Luís I.

When Joseph I died, every member of the chapter of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) refused to deliver that monarch’s funeral oration, pleading ‘lack of strength for so lofty a task’. It was the Franciscan friar José Faustino who saved the situation, giving a speech fitting for the occasion.

The funeral orations for Luís I and for Carlos I and his son Louis Philippe have been published. The former was delivered by Canon António Aires Pacheco, and the latter by the chaplain of the 27th Infantry Regiment, Father Luís Alves Martins.

Bound together with the regulations (*regimento*) of the councillors and the charter (foral) of the Municipal Council of Lisbon, the archive of the Funchal Council holds a document entitled *Dos estilos que ha nas exéquias de hum Rey defunto e na acclamaçãao do vivo em as cidades e pouos*, which sets out all the ceremonies held in Funchal on the death of the former monarchs.
Scientific expeditions

Of the many scientific expeditions that have come to Madeira, whether to take on fresh provisions for their voyages or to carry out studies on this island, the most important and best known are those listed below:

1755. Bory came to Madeira in this year aboard the *Comète*, and made some observations here on the variation of the compass needle. 1764. On 13 July of this year the ships *Dolphin* and *Tamar* arrived in the harbour of Funchal, carrying the expedition led by Commodore John Byron, which set out to discover new lands between the Cape of Good Hope and the Strait of Magellan. The expedition merely took on some fresh provisions. 1766. On 7 September the *Dolphin*, the *Swallow* and the *Prince Frederick* anchored in the harbour of Funchal, carrying the expedition commanded by Captain Samuel Wallis, which included among its officers Philip Carteret, a companion of Byron. The expedition merely replaced here the provisions it had already used up. 1768. It was on 13 September of this year that the scientific expedition commanded by the celebrated English navigator James Cook reached Madeira, on its way to observe the transit of Venus across the disc of the Sun on the island of Tahiti. The expedition included the naturalists Joseph Banks and Dr Daniel Solander and the astronomer Charles Green, and the first two carried out various scientific studies on this island. The *Endeavour*, which carried the expedition, left the harbour of Funchal on 19 September. 1772. On the second voyage that Captain Cook made in the southern seas, he called at Madeira on 19 July of this year aboard the *Resolution*. The naturalists Johann Reinhold Forster and his son Georg, who were members of the expedition, made some botanical observations here. 1785. The scientific expedition commanded by Jean-François Galaup de La Pérouse arrived in Funchal aboard the *Boussole* and the *Astrolabe* on 13 August of this year, leaving three days later for the Canary Islands. The expedition included the engineer Monneron, the geographer Bernizet, the surgeon Rollin, the astronomer Lepaute-Dagelet, the physicist Lamanon, the botanist Collignon and the illustrious Monge. The last of these escaped the unhappy fate of his fellow travellers, having gone ashore on Tenerife on 29 August 1785. 1792. The illustrious orientalist Sir John Barrow visited Madeira in this year on his voyage to Cochinchina. 1816. The English scientific expedition under the command of Captain James Kingston Tuckey came within sight of Madeira on 31 March of this year, and encountered a great number of turtles (*Testudo caretta*) sleeping on the surface of the water. 1838. On 16 September of this year a small American squadron arrived in Funchal, made up of the *Porpoise*, the sloops *Vincennes* and *Peacock* and the schooners *Sea-Gull* and *Flying-Fish*, under the command of Lieutenant Charles Wilkes. The scientists aboard these ships measured the height of Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) and made some geological observations here, leaving Madeira on 25 September. 1839. The English ships *Erebus* and *Terror*, under the command of James Clark Ross and Francis Rawdon Crozier, visited Madeira in October of this year. Their officers measured the height of Pico Ruivo and made magnetic observations at Cape Verde, St Helena and the Cape of Good Hope before heading for the Antarctic regions and the other countries they explored. 1857. In June of this year the Austrian frigate *Novara*, commanded by Commodore Bernhard von Wüllerstorf-Urbair, was at Madeira on a voyage round the world. The expedition’s scientists measured the height of Pico Ruivo and received a great deal of information from the physician Dr António da Luz Pita, the military engineer Major António Pedro de Azevedo, the botanist João Maria Moniz and the Austrian consul Carlos Bianchi. 1883. In this year a French scientific expedition led by Alphonse Milne-Edwards, charged with carrying out oceanographic studies in the Atlantic, was in Madeiran waters aboard the *Talisman*. According to Milne-Edwards, there is in this sea an immense volcanic chain parallel to the coast of Africa, of which the islands of Cape Verde, the Canaries, Madeira and the Azores may be the only points not now covered by the waters. (See Atlantis.) 1897. On 12 September of this year the barque *Belgica* arrived in the harbour of Funchal from Ostend, carrying the Belgian scientific expedition that, under the command of Lieutenant Commander Adrien Gerlache, was bound for the Antarctic regions. The members of the expedition visited Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’); among them were Lieutenant Danco, in charge of magnetic observations, Dr Artoski, in charge of meteorology and oceanography, and Dr Emil Racoviță, responsible for botany and zoology.

1901. On 15 and 16 August of this year the British steamer *Discovery* lay at anchor in the harbour of Funchal, bound on a voyage of exploration to the Antarctic regions under the direction of Roberto Scott. As is well known, this navigator was assisted by Wilson and Shackleton in some of the studies and investigations he carried out in those waters.

On 30 August of the same year the German Antarctic expedition, led by Dr Erich von Drygalski, passed within sight of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) aboard the steamer *Gauss*. The report of this expedition, published in part in the *Boletim da Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*, states ‘that on 31 August, as Madeira was slowly disappearing from view, a splendid firework display rose over Funchal; and we supposed that it was in honour of the English ship *Discovery* of the South Pole expedition, which had called there that day’. We find this supposition curious, all the more so since the *Discovery*, as already stated, was not here on 1 August but on the date mentioned above.

1902. In July of this year the ship *Morning*, commanded by Captain Colbeck, was in the harbour of Funchal. This ship, which carried Dr Wilson, was bound for the Antarctic regions to bring assistance to the *Discovery*, commanded by Roberto F. Scott.

1903. On 10 September of this year the steamer *Le Français* arrived in the harbour of Funchal from Brest, carrying the celebrated French navigator Jean-Baptiste Charcot, who, like those before him, intended to explore the Antarctic regions. Jean-Baptiste Charcot remained in those regions until 1905, and the results of the natural history work carried out by the members of the expedition were published by specialists under the direction of L. Joubin.
1908. On 12 September of this year the explorer Jean-Baptiste Charcot passed through Madeira for the second time, bound for the Antarctic regions aboard the *Pourquoi Pas*.

1910. On 23 June 1910 the ship *Terra Nova* anchored in the harbour of Funchal, carrying the second expedition to explore the Antarctic regions under the direction of Roberto Scott. This explorer, who had been in Madeira some years earlier, was not aboard the *Terra Nova*, which he joined only later. The *Terra Nova*, equipped with the best apparatus and supplies required for polar navigation, left the harbour of Funchal on 26 June.

On 6 September of the same year the Norwegian ship *Fram* anchored in the harbour of Funchal to take on various goods brought by the German steamer *Hans Hoermann*. The *Fram*, bound for the Antarctic regions under the direction of Captain Amundsen, left our harbour on the 10th of that month. 1911. During the scientific campaign carried out this year by Prince Albert of Monaco aboard the *Hirondelle II*, Dr Luís Gain made some collections of marine algae along the coasts of the archipelago. Prince Albert also visited the waters of the archipelago in 1901, 1904, 1912 and in other years, aboard either the *Hirondelle* or the *Princesa Alice*, and on one of his voyages he visited Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’), which he described in his book entitled *La Carrière d'un navigateur*.

1914. On 27 June of this year the sloop *Armaner-Hansen* arrived in the harbour of Funchal; aboard it the illustrious Norwegian scientist Fridtjof Nansen made soundings and various oceanographic studies in the Atlantic. The small vessel left Madeira on 28 June, bound for the Azores.

In the same year the British exploration ship *Endurance*, under the command of Captain Worsley, called at Madeira. It was bound for the South Pole and was to take on board, at Buenos Aires, the well-known man of science Ernest Shackleton. The *Endurance*, which arrived on 21 August and left on the 25th, spent the 24th at the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), where the expedition’s scientists and the Madeiran naturalist Mr Adolfo César de Noronha carried out various scientific investigations.

1920. On 6 April of this year the Danish yacht *Dana* entered the harbour of Funchal to take on board Dr Johannes Schmidt, well known for his biological and ichthyological studies, who had arrived in Madeira the previous day on the *Almanzora*. The *Dana* left for Tenerife on the 7th, carrying the apparatus and supplies needed for the scientific exploration of the Ocean.

1921. On 16 October of this year the yachts *Dana* and *Quest* arrived in the harbour of Funchal. The latter carried the new British expedition, led by Shackleton, bound for the Antarctic; the former carried Dr Johannes Schmidt, director of the ‘Laboratorio Carlesberg’ of Copenhagen, who intended to study the biology and physics of the Ocean north of the Equator.

The scientific staff of the *Dana* carried out oceanographic explorations north of Porto Santo on the 15th and visited Deserta Grande on the 18th, while those of the *Quest* made thermometric observations in the sea south of Funchal, at a depth of about 1500 metres, corresponding to the habitat of our black scabbardfish (*espada preta*).
The *Dana* left our harbour on the night of the 18th, and the *Quest* on the 19th, at about half past one in the afternoon.

The scientists of the Danish expedition were accompanied on their trip to the Deserta by the Madeiran naturalist Adolfo de Noronha, and it was at the request of this fellow countryman of ours that the staff of the *Quest* made the thermometric observations referred to above.

1922. On 6 June of this year the Norwegian ship *Harmaner Hansen* was in Funchal, carrying a scientific expedition organised by the University of Bergen, whose members included Professors H. Hansen and Damas. The expedition was intended for oceanographic studies.

1923. On 17 May of this year the small French steamer *La Tanche*, of the scientific and technical fisheries service, arrived in Funchal carrying the scientist Gerard Belloc, of the Lafaille museum in La Rochelle, who intended to carry out research on tuna and tuna fishing. He stayed here for a few days.

1924. At the end of February 1924 the British zoologist James Hornell, former director of the fisheries service of Madras, in India, arrived in Funchal and made various ethnographic studies. He left Madeira on 1 May aboard the ship *St. George*, which carried a scientific expedition that went on from here to Trinidad and Panama.
Exhibitions

During the first four days of April 1850 an exhibition of Madeiran industry was held in the three main rooms of the Civil Government Palace (*Palácio do Governo Civil*). On display were textiles, goldsmiths’ work, cabinetwork, plaster and straw work, paintings, embroidery, needlework, etc., as well as some agricultural produce. Seventeen silver medals were awarded to those who presented the best objects. The originator of this exhibition was Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro.

On 29 April 1854 an agricultural exhibition promoted by the botanist João Maria Moniz was held in the courtyard and rooms of the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace). On 20, 21, 22 and 23 April 1861 the same palace hosted the first exhibition promoted by the Agricultural Society of Madeira (*Sociedade Agrícola da Madeira*).

This exhibition, the most brilliant ever held in Funchal, featured trees and shrubs, industrial, forage and ornamental plants, cereals, vegetables, tubers and roots, a herbarium and a collection of Madeiran shells, livestock, etc.
On 25 May 1861 the Agricultural Society held a meeting chaired by the civil governor, at which 12 first-class prizes, 18 second-class prizes and 20 honourable mentions were awarded to the exhibitors.

The members of the said society whom it charged with obtaining and classifying the objects shown at the exhibition were Major António Pedro de Azevedo, João Maria Moniz and Dr João Perestrelo de Vasconcelos.
In 1863 and 1864 two insignificant livestock shows were held in Funchal. Only nine head of cattle appeared at the first, and attendance was no greater the following year.

The last exhibition held in Funchal took place at the end of June 1901, on the occasion of the royal visit to the island. It featured wines, brandies, photographs, paintings, various textiles, embroidery, parquet and inlaid work (*embutidos*), wickerwork and straw work, etc. The exhibition was held in the Praça Académica (‘academic square’), today Campo do Almirante Reis (‘Admiral Reis field’), in huts and pavilions put up there for the purpose.
See Fairs.
Beacon-keeper

The early military system of coastal defence included the office of beacon-keeper (*facheiro*), whose duty was to light fires on the summits of the peaks to warn the settlements that enemy sails were in sight. This practice lasted until the governorship of Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho, and it is recalled by the name Pico do Facho (‘beacon peak’), in Machico and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Facho da Malhada (peak)
In the southern part of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), towards the south-south-west, stands the hill of this name, at an altitude of 265 m.
Facho (peak)

This mountain rises above the town (*vila*) of Machico at an altitude of 330 m. Its summit overlooks the land that forms the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’) and the beautiful valley through which that town’s stream flows. There was once a semaphore station here, which communicated with another set up on the so-called Pico do Telégrafo (‘telegraph peak’), in the parish of Caniço (‘reed’).

It is said in some quarters that at the top of the Pico (‘peak’) there is a small spring whose waters rise when the tide rises and fall when it falls. This phenomenon seems to be due to an internal channel between the spring’s reservoir and the coast, into which the sea penetrates further as the tide rises. It is probably the air in this channel, flowing into the spring’s reservoir, that causes the rise in water level observed at high tide on the coast of Machico (see Picos).
Facho (peak)
It is the highest mountain on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and lies in the northern part of the island, at an altitude of 500 m.
Fagundes (Pedro)
See Meneses (Pedro Fagundes Bacelar de Antas e).
Faia (Myrica faya)

A tree or shrub of the family *Myricaceae*, common in Madeira. It has glabrous leaves, obovate-lanceolate or oblong-lanceolate and usually serrated, dioecious flowers and drupaceous fruits, red at first and later black, gathered in small clusters because the female flowers adhere to one another. The *faia* yields good firewood, and its stems are used for stakes in many places on the north coast. Its bark is rich in tannin, its wood is dull in colour, sometimes tending to pink, and its fruits, apparently many-seeded and granular, taste pleasant when fully ripe. The European beech (*Fagus silvatica*, L.) is grown in some *quintas* in Monte (‘hill’).
Faial

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), where stands the chapel of the Nativity of Our Lady (*Nossa Senhora da Natividade*), known as the chapel of Faial. It was founded by Zenobio Acciaioli in 1582 and was the seat of a former entailed estate (*morgadio*).
Faial (parish)

The parish takes its name from the *faia* (*Myrica Faya*). There was once a locality (*sítio*) there where this member of the Myricaceae grew in abundance; it took the name *faial*, which later spread to the surrounding land and eventually to the whole parish. Referring to the origin of the name, Frutuoso says that this parish (*freguesia*) bears it because a great many *faias* grow there. One might perhaps say of this parish, allowing for the difference in scale, what António Cordeiro says in ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*) of the island of Faial: ‘it was called Faial because the said island was entirely full of many large *faias*’.

The lands that made up this parish and those of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) were the first on the north side to be worked and settled in the days of the earliest colonisation. One of the oldest settlers was Lançarote Teixeira, fourth son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the first donatary of Machico, whom the *Saudades* praise as follows: ‘he was one of the finest horsemen of the island; for besides being by inclination a very good rider, he had a great hand at breaking horses and was much given to it, so much so that in his time sixty knights with gilded spurs gathered in the town of Machico, very well turned out and mounted through the efforts of this Lançarote Teixeira, so that when St John’s Day or Corpus Christi came round, there were so many horsemen for the cane games (*jogos de canas*, equestrian tournament with thrown canes) and skirmishes that it looked more like an army at war than a festive pastime; and though all were very skilled in this art, he nonetheless stood out among them, so that it may rightly be said that he was the light and ornament of Machico’. This Lançarote Teixeira held much land in Faial by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), including the lands stretching from Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’) to Ribeira da Metade (‘halfway stream’) and taking in the Penha de Águia (‘eagle crag’), and there he founded a numerous line of descendants.

The parish originated in the settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) that existed there, with its chantry (capela) dedicated to the Nativity of the Virgin, or Nossa Senhora do Faial (Our Lady of Faial), which served as the seat of the new parish. Father João Soares was chaplain of this chapel from 1531, having previously been a beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) in our African stronghold of Asilah.

When the royal decree (alvará régio) of 20 February 1550 created this parish, this priest was appointed its first parish priest, with an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of 6,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), in addition to the 8,000 *réis* he already received as chaplain of the chapel. The royal decrees of 30 May 1572 and 20 June of the same year raised the vicar’s annual salary to 20,000 *réis* and 25,000 *réis* respectively, and the decree of 15 November 1591 set his stipend at 19,000 *réis* in cash and one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. Later, by royal decree of 17 April 1780, this salary was raised again, to 22,000 *réis* in cash, two *moios* of wheat and two *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. As stated, Father João Soares was the first vicar of this parish; he was succeeded in turn by Fathers Bernardo de Quintal, Sebastião Gonçalves, Cristóvão Ferreira, Francisco José, Valentim José, Pedro Catanho de Meneses, etc.

The growth of the population led to the creation of a curacy (*curato*), authorised by the royal decree of 11 February 1746. Father Pedro Catanho was the first to hold this post, with an annual salary of one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine.

The chapel of Nossa Senhora do Faial, which became the seat of the parish, stood on the left bank of the stream and in the harshest winters was often in danger of being swept away by the violence of the current. In 1699, through the efforts of the vicar of the time, Father Manuel Catanho de Meneses, a wall was ordered to be built to protect the church. This did not prevent the waters, which some years later grew more torrential, from almost entirely destroying the old chapel, so that a new church had to be built as a matter of urgency.

This need had long been recognised, not only because of the danger to which the chapel’s site was exposed whenever the torrent swelled and flooded the land along its banks, but also because of the chapel’s cramped size and the advanced state of ruin it had long been in. We do not know whether the following passage, which we found in volume X of the *Santuario Marianno* by Friar Agostinho de Santa Maria, refers to the old chapel or to the new church: ‘the church, very large and of great length and breadth, is nevertheless said to have been timbered entirely with the wood yielded by a single cedar trunk, a sign that it must have been very large or enormous, which was found close to that same chapel of Our Lady...’ Elsewhere we also found a certain detail of construction, but referring to the old chapel, as the author of the *Santuário Marianno* himself seems to suggest at the end of the passage we have quoted. By order of the Treasury Council (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 20 November 1744, the building of the new church was granted by award by public auction (*arrematação*) to Cristóvão Gomes for the sum of 7,980,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The church was put up on the slope above the stream, safe at last from the headlong violence of the current. The first stone was laid and blessed on 5 August 1745; it is not known when the building work was declared complete. It is a spacious and elegant church with excellent carved woodwork, the high altar standing out for the refined good taste of its workmanship. A papal brief of 30 August 1785 granted a plenary indulgence to those who visit this church at the feast of its patron saint, held on 8 September, the day of the Nativity of the Most Holy Virgin.

This parish also had the chapel of São Roque (St Roch), which became the seat of a new parish in 1848, and the chapel of São Luís, of which not a trace remains. There is still the chapel of Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*), in the locality (*sítio*) of Diferença (‘difference’). We shall deal with all of them elsewhere in this work.

Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, writing about this parish in 1590, says the following: ‘This parish will have some hundred households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’). The church stands between two streams with very high rock walls. It has much citrus fruit, citrons and lemons; pears, apples of two kinds, and walnuts. The church being of good size, they say it was timbered from one enormous cedar trunk found close by. On its feast day, which falls on the eighth of September, people gather in pilgrimage from the whole island, more than eight thousand souls, and a rich fair of provisions is held there, with much pork, beef and kid, the last of which is an exceptionally tasty meat on that island, although in many other lands and islands it is the worst of all. Many young goats and fruits and other things to eat are brought together there for the pilgrims to buy; and they often stay two, three or more days at Our Lady, resting from the labour of the road, for they come ten and twelve *léguas* over very rugged country. Together they hold many festivities of plays, dances and music on many instruments – violas, guitars, flutes, rebecs and bagpipes; and on the lower slopes of the streams, which have great open fields, on Our Lady’s day and during its octave, the pilgrims camp in various bands, lighting great bonfires among those mountains. They say that Our Lady appeared there where her church stands.

‘This parish has two sugar mills (engenho), one belonging to António Fernandes das Covas, which is near Our Lady, and another belonging to Luís Doria. At the end of the streams (which both come together at a sea landing) there is a good landing place. In this parish there is a water-powered saw, which was a great and profitable contrivance: two or three men bring up to the saw, by machinery, a trunk twenty *palmos* long and two or three wide, and by skill a single man, the sawyer, with one foot alone (as the potter does when he makes his ware), drives the trunk forward while the saw keeps cutting; and when it reaches the end with the cut, with the same foot he pushes back, making the whole trunk return, and the saw takes up another cut. So whoever sees this work will judge the water saw a very great and necessary invention on that island, where it would not be possible to saw such great trunks as there are there with a hand saw, nor so great a quantity of planking as is made for sugar chests, of which many are made, and for other chests for other uses, which comes to a very great sum each year. This parish has great upland commons (montados) for livestock, profitable to many.’

Even at present this church is the object of a well-attended pilgrimage on 7 and 8 September each year. After the great pilgrimages of Our Lady of the Mount, of the Milagres at Machico and of the Lord Jesus (*Senhor Jesus*) at Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), it is one of those that draw the greatest crowds of pilgrims from every part of the island, and it offers the observer one of the most interesting and picturesque sights. Frutuoso’s testimony shows that it is quite ancient and has always been remarkably well attended, and so it has remained through several centuries.

One of this parish’s most pressing needs, and the subject of long-standing demands, was the building of bridges to link it with the neighbouring parishes and with the south of the island. The hopes of the people of that region were met in 1904, when work began on that truly remarkable undertaking, which was entirely completed within a few years.

The parish has a small landing place and a quay built at Pedra da Pescaria, from which the quay took its name. Adolfo Loureiro’s work *Os portos maritimos de Portugal e Ilhas Adjacentes* contains the following: ‘The design of this quay was drawn up by Mr J. Maria Fragoso and carried out from 1903 to 1905. The Viscount of Cacongo generously contributed the sum of 1,000,000 réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto) to this work, on which 5,478,000 réis was spent.’ The District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), which had ordered the quay to be built, resolved at its session of 21 June 1904 to name it Cais do Visconde de Cacongo, granting a request made to it by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Sant’Ana.

The parish is bounded by the parish of Sant’Ana and the Atlantic Ocean to the north, the parish of São Roque do Faial to the south, that of Porto da Cruz to the east and that of Sant’Ana to the west. Its inhabited localities are Guindaste, Pico do Guindaste, Covas, Igreja, Tajal, Lombo do Lourenço, Chicharos, Diferença, Fazenda, Pinheiro, Corujeira de Baixo, Corujeira de Cima, Ressoca, Serra de Água, Água de Alto, Quebrada, Lombo do Galego, Pico do Lombo do Galego, Fajã da Murta, Alhendros, Limoeiro, Cruzinha, Fajã Grande, Lombo de Cima, Lombo de Baixo, Lugar, Longueira, Moinhos, Penha de Águia and Fajã, and there are other, less important localities, such as Pedregal, Cerrado, Fajã do Mar, etc. Picturesque spots commanding wide views include Vigia, Cortado, Portela, Cova da Roda, Penha de Águia, Ponta de Catarina Pires, etc.
In 1848 the present parish of São Roque do Faial was separated from Faial, and it has been an independent parish ever since.
Natives of this parish include Dr João Catanho de Meneses and Dona Joana de Castelo Branco (see those entries).
Faial (islets)

Not far from the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial lie the small islets of Faial, Pedra do Canto, Pedra Francesa and Pedra da Galé, together with various adjacent shoals, generally known as the Ilhéus do Faial.
Faial (landing place)
A small landing place on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of that name. See Pedra da Pescaria (quay).
Faial (stream)

It rises near Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) and receives as tributaries the Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’) and Metade streams, crossing the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial and reaching the sea there. Between 1907 and 1910 the longest bridge in Madeira was built over this stream; it had long been regarded as one of the most pressing needs to be met by the district’s public works. Its deck rests on several arches and it measures about 130 metres in length.
Faiscas (As)
A monthly publication of which four issues appeared, from March to September 1883. Its editor was Ciriaco de Brito e Nobrega.
Fajã

In Madeira the name ‘Fajãs’ is given to certain tracts of land, of greater or lesser extent, formed by the collapse of ground lying further upslope, and generally making up soil of remarkable fertility. ‘Fajãs’ form both in the interior of the island, through landslides of earth detached from the mountain slopes, and all along the coast. Striking examples of the latter are a considerable part of the parish (*freguesia*) of Jardim do Mar, Lugar de Baixo, Fajã dos Padres, Fajã da Areia and others besides. The term ‘*fajã*’ (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) is generally used as a place-name element, and there are dozens of localities called Fajã de…
See Fajãs.
Fajã

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). There was once a chapel there dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora (Our Lady of the Good Hour), of which only a few ruins remain; its founders and the year it was built are unknown.
Fajã

An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António. It lies on the left bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos (‘stream of the rescued’), and there the tributaries of Vasco Gil and Lapa flow into that same stream.
Fajã da Areia (landing place)

In the locality (*sítio*) of this name, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), there is a landing place served by a small beach. It is preferable to that of the town (*vila*) of São Vicente, from which it is not far away.
Fajã da Ovelha (parish)

In this parish there is a locality (*sítio*) that has kept the name Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) since the earliest days of colonisation; the name later spread to the surrounding land and eventually to the whole parish (*freguesia*). It is common for a simple episode, a chance circumstance or a minor event to have given rise to the name of a particular locality or village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town), which later grows into a populous centre or an important settlement. The same would have happened with the name of this parish, as we have already pointed out in the article devoted to the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’).

The learned annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that this parish only began to be called Fajã da Ovelha when, at the beginning of the 18th century, permission was given to build a new church, which was put up a few years later at the locality that then bore, and still bears today, that name. We disagree with this opinion, authoritative though it is, for the reasons we shall briefly set out. It is true that for almost two centuries this parish had its seat in the chapel of São Lourenço (St Lawrence), at the locality of that name, and that around the middle of the 18th century it moved to the new church built at the locality of Fajã da Ovelha. Yet it was never known as the parish of São Lourenço, as it naturally would have been had it not had another name, which in fact it did. The oldest document relating to this parish, cited in the *Índex Geral* of the register of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*) and in the *Memorias sobre a creaçâo e augmento do estado eclesiástico na ilha da Madeira*, dates from 1553, and it already refers to the church of the parish of Fajã da Ovelha, the name by which it was then known. If it was called neither São Lourenço nor Fajã da Ovelha, what name could it have had before the 18th century? None is known. From this we logically infer that this parish always bore the name Fajã da Ovelha, from the earliest days of colonisation or, more precisely still, from the time when the seat of a new parish was established there.

Like almost all the parishes of this island, Fajã da Ovelha had its beginnings in a fairly old chapel that stood there, around which a sizeable core of population gradually formed. This was the chapel of São Lourenço, which already had its own chaplain before the parish was created; its last chaplain and first parish priest was Father António Enes.

This parish was created as a curacy (*curato*) before 1553, for the royal decree (alvará régio) of 11 April of that year added to the original stipend (*côngrua*) of the curate or curate chaplain (*capelão-curado*), which was 9,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a month, one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine. The royal decree of 26 July 1559 made a further increase to the salary of the priest who performed the parochial duties there. It was only shortly before 1573 that Fajã da Ovelha truly became an autonomous parish and the curate chaplain came to enjoy the honours and privileges of a vicar. A decree of 6 July of that year set the parish priest’s annual stipend at 20,000 *réis*, and another of 3 June 1687 raised it to 25,000 *réis* in cash, one and a half *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine.
As the population grew, a curacy was created in this parish towards the end of the 18th century.

The chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, and the parish had their seat, as already stated, in the chapel of São Lourenço, and remained there until the second quarter of the 18th century. The royal decree of Queen Catherine, regent of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), dated 27 June 1705, authorised the building of a new church and its transfer to whatever site was judged most suitable for the purpose and in keeping with the wishes expressed by the people, after the most repeated entreaties of the parish priest of the time. Despite this, the new church was not built until some years later, the locality (*sítio*) of Fajã da Ovelha being chosen as the place that best met the conditions required for its construction. The order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 24 January 1747 (and not 1737, as the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ says) awarded the work by public auction (*arrematação*) to the carpenter Francisco Gomes for the sum of 6,350,000 *réis*. We do not know when the work was completed or when the new church was blessed.

While this parish was still a chaplaincy with cure of souls, the parish of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) was separated from it, and later that of Prazeres (‘joys’), formed partly from land belonging to Fajã da Ovelha and partly from Estreito da Calheta.
Main localities

Lombada dos Marinheiros, Lombo dos Falcões, Eirinhas, Farrobo, Massapês, Fajã da Ovelha, São João, Casais da Serra, São Lourenço, Lombada dos Cedros, Raposeira do Serrado, Raposeira do Logarinho and Maloeira.

The Pico da Maloeira, the cliff of Raposeira do Logarinho and the Ribeira dos Cedros and Ribeira dos Marinheiros deserve special mention for the picturesque scenery they offer the visitor and the fine views to be enjoyed from them.

The parish (*freguesia*) is crossed by the Ribeira da Inês, which separates it from Prazeres, and by the Ribeira da Cova, Ribeira da Chã, Ribeira dos Cedros, Ribeira de São João, Ribeira dos Falcões and Ribeira dos Marinheiros. Some of these streams feed the Levada da Cova, Levada do Ribeiro Chão, Levada dos Moinhos and Levada da Fonte do Folhado, which irrigate the parish, as does the Levada do Rabaçal. There are well-founded hopes that within a few years a long and abundant levada (irrigation channel) will be built, intended to irrigate this and other parishes of the municipality (*concelho*) of Calheta (‘small cove’).

The book by the mining engineer Eugenio Ackermann, entitled *L'Ile Madère considerée au point de vue scientifique*, refers to the manganese ore found in this parish and gives a short analysis of the proportions of its constituent elements. It seems to have little industrial value.
The parish has 2,757 inhabitants, and St John is the patron saint of its parish church. The new cemetery was blessed and opened in March 1910.
The parish has one state school for each sex and is the seat of a medical district covering this parish and those of Ponta do Pargo, Paul do Mar and Prazeres.

Natives of this parish include Father António Gomes Neto (see that entry); Canon António Joaquim Jardim, who won great distinction as a preacher and, as a supporter of liberal ideas, spent some years in prison under the absolutist government; and Augusto César de Gouveia, who, through his selflessness, prestige, learning and enterprising spirit, rendered notable and widely acknowledged services to this parish.
Fajã da Ovelha (peak)
This mountain peak stands in the uplands (*serra*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name, not far from the Pico da Fonte do Bispo (‘peak of the bishop’s spring’).
Fajã da Ovelha (point)
A projection of the coastline in the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name.
Fajã das Nogueiras
A locality (*sítio*) in the uplands of the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial, where there is a small house to shelter travellers.
Fajã do Manuel

A locality (*sítio*) on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), where an English full-rigged ship was wrecked in 1856. Fifteen of the twenty-one people on board died.
Fajã do Mar

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). Here, on a small rise overlooking the sea, stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Vida (Our Lady of Life), founded in 1663 by Inez Teixeira and rebuilt a few years ago.
Fajã do Mar (landing place)

The locality (*sítio*) of this name, in Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), has a small landing place, also called Nossa Senhora da Vida, which lies 2.4 miles from the landing place of the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and 2.3 miles from that of Calheta (‘small cove’).
Fajã do Penedo

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Boaventura (‘good fortune’). A small chapel dedicated to Sant'Ana once stood here; it was built in 1768 by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António Francisco de Caires and demolished shortly after 1840. In 1919 Dona Maria dos Anjos Ribeiro had a chapel consecrated to the Immaculate Heart of Mary built in this locality.
Fajã dos Asnos

It lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), on the near side of Cabo Girão, and is also known as Fajã do Gregório. It is partly cultivated, and on the cliffs bounding it to the north *Helichrysum monizii* grows in abundance, a species hard to find elsewhere on the island.
Fajã dos Padres

This small *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) lies on the south coast of Madeira, a little beyond Cabo Girão. At its back rises a great bare, barren cliff about 300 metres high. Its population numbers some 50 inhabitants, who are subject in spiritual matters to the church of São Brás (St Blaise) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’).

The Fajã dos Padres (‘the priests’ flat’), which in former times belonged to the priests of the Society of Jesus and where traces remain of a chapel perhaps built at their behest, was the property of Colonel Manuel J. de França Dória. After growing sugar cane on his land without much success, he re-established the cultivation of the vine there, which seems to be the crop best suited to the local soil.
The Fajã dos Padres once produced the best Malmsey wine on the island, and Sercial (white grape variety) and other excellent vine varieties were also grown there.
Fajãs

There is a parish (*freguesia*) known as Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’), and in the parishes of São Gonçalo, Faial, São Jorge, São Vicente, Porto Moniz, Ponta do Pargo, Arco da Calheta, Estreito da Calheta, Canhas, Ribeira Brava, Campanário, Curral, etc., there are *fajãs* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff) of greater or lesser extent and age.

The Fajã da Ovelha, in the parish of that name, the Fajã dos Padres (‘the priests’ flat’) (Campanário), the Fajã dos Asnos or do Gregório (Câmara de Lobos) and the Fajã da Areia (São Vicente) are the best known on the island.

On the subject of landslips, we may say that Lugar de Baixo (‘lower place’) has been much larger since 1804 than before, because in that year a large part of the land of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) fell towards the sea and formed an extensive, productive plain there. The shock of the fall, says Dr Azevedo, was such that the sea rose above its level along the whole adjacent coast, and the tremor was felt both on land and at sea more than 10 kilometres away. The sea surged far into the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’).

The late António Pedro de Azevedo found a letter written in 1689 that speaks of the displacement of a tract of land about half a *légua* (league, about 5 km) long, which had occurred a short time before at Arco de São Jorge (see that entry). If what the author of the letter says is true, the movement was so slow and gentle that the buildings standing on the land suffered nothing from their change of position.

In April 1856 a considerable tract of land shifted at Machico, and all the huts built on it collapsed. In 1894 a great landslide (*quebrada*) occurred on Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’), as a result of which the sea advanced and retreated noticeably at several points on the south coast of Madeira, much as it had at the time of the earthquake of 1755.

*Fajãs* are common in certain ravines of the interior, and some of them have caused more or less considerable diversions in the original course of the waters. When these *fajãs* lie near settlements, people usually farm them, since they are generally very productive. However, torrents sometimes ravage and erode them during the winter season, and may even destroy them if they are very low-lying or imperfectly consolidated.
Fajãzinha de Bento

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Serra de Água, where the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) owned a small property, which was sold with the Government’s authorisation on 25 April 1918.
Falcão

It was the first steamer to run regular voyages between various ports on the south coast of Madeira. It arrived at the port of Funchal on 27 February 1881. It was a vessel of 40 tons and 22 horsepower, ordered by the firm of Blandy Brothers & C.ª
Falcão e Sousa (Cristóvão)

On 20 April 1600 Cristóvão Falcão e Sousa was appointed governor-general of the Madeira archipelago. Some have wrongly believed him to be the celebrated author of the *Crisfal*, while others claim he was that author’s son; the point is disputed.
