Falgairolle (Edmond)

In 1895 he published in Paris a pamphlet of 31 pages entitled *Une expedition française à l'ile de Madère en 1566*. With evident partiality, it deals with the terrible attack that French corsairs made on this island in October 1566, which Gaspar Frutuoso treats at length in chapters XL, XLI and XLII of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).
See Sack of Funchal by the French.
Familiars of the Holy Office

The books of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) record the following individuals as familiars of the Holy Office: Manuel Mendes Serrão (1697), Father Augusto de Góis (1739) and Father António Ribeiro de Sousa (1741). The last two were notaries of that tribunal.
In 1551 the king granted a son of João Rodrigues Cavaleiro, clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*), the office of notary of the Holy Office as a royal grant.
Fanal

A locality (*sítio*) in the uplands of Seixal (‘pebble shore’) and Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’), where there is a crater that turns into a lake in winter. Beside this crater grows luxuriant vegetation of native trees and shrubs, notably *adernos* and other rare species. Ferns, grasses and mosses abound throughout Fanal (‘beacon’), which is one of the places on the island most worth visiting for the beautiful views it commands.
Phanerogams

Of the 907 phanerogams (flowering plants) recorded to date in the Madeira archipelago, 635 are native or apparently native, and 272 are naturalised or frequently cultivated. The group of native species comprises 505 dicotyledons, 126 monocotyledons and 4 gymnosperms; the group of evidently introduced species comprises 218 dicotyledons, 53 monocotyledons and 1 gymnosperm.

The archipelago has 443 annual phanerogams, of which 374 are dicotyledons and 69 monocotyledons. The native phanerogams among them are represented by 289 dicotyledons and 51 monocotyledons, and the introduced ones by 85 dicotyledons and 18 monocotyledons. Of the 464 perennial phanerogams, 205 are native and 169 introduced; the native phanerogams comprise 216 dicotyledons, 75 monocotyledons and 4 gymnosperms, and the introduced ones 133 dicotyledons, 35 monocotyledons and 1 gymnosperm. Among the native perennial phanerogams there are 106 species of trees, shrubs and subshrubs.

Among the 272 introduced phanerogams, 80 dicotyledons, 18 monocotyledons and 1 gymnosperm are well naturalised; all the remaining species are cultivated on a large scale, adventive, or still poorly established in the archipelago. Among the naturalised dicotyledons there are 34 annual and 46 perennial species; among the monocotyledons, 7 annual and 11 perennial; and among the gymnosperms, 1 perennial.

Our region has 102 endemic species and 54 that are shared between the Madeira archipelago and other groups of islands in the Atlantic. Of the former, 70 are Madeiran, 5 belong to Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), 1 to Ilhéu Chão (‘flat islet’), 1 to Bugio, 10 to Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, 10 to Madeira and Porto Santo, and 5 to Madeira and the Desertas. Of the latter, 3 occur in the archipelagos of Madeira, the Canary Islands and the Azores, 41 in the archipelagos of Madeira and the Canary Islands, 9 in the archipelagos of Madeira and the Azores, and 1 in the archipelagos of Madeira, the Canary Islands and Cape Verde. All these species, whose native status is beyond any dispute, are genuine representatives of the primitive flora of Madeira. This flora, it is to be believed, became established in our region during the Tertiary period, carried by birds, by the winds, by ocean currents and even by certain insects.

The study of Madeiran plant fossils shows no evidence of any local floristic evolution. Many of the plants found in the fossil deposit of São Jorge, on the northern coast of Madeira, are represented in the native flora of the present day. And if there were changes in the morphological characters of other species of our primitive vegetation, it is not credible that those changes were so profound as to give rise to new specific forms of an endemic or peculiar character.

These forms, in our view, did not arise from the slow or sudden transformation of other species. If they now characterise the Madeira archipelago, it is because the conditions compatible with their existence, once found over large areas, continued from a certain period onwards to survive only within the narrow limits of our floral region.

The most complete list of the phanerogams of the Madeira region was published by Carlos A. Meneses in 1914 under the title *Flora do Arquipelago da Madeira*. However, owing to the little care taken over its revision, this work contains a number of errors that considerably mar it. The description accompanying *Thlaspi arvense* does not refer to that species but to *Draba muralis*; in *Lotus argenteus* the leaflets are not always notched; in *Lotus Loweanus* the leaflets are villous rather than pubescent; and in *Senecio incrassatus* the leaves are deeply pinnatifid. The plane tree cultivated in Madeira is *Platanus orientalis*, not *P. occidentalis*, and as regards the genus *Scrophularia*, the number of species recorded in the said work may have to be reduced. *Sambucus Ebulus* is not a subshrub, although its annual stems are sometimes almost woody.

The phanerogams of Madeira were also studied by the botanists Bornmuller, Britten, Brown, Cosson, Holl, Richard Thomas Lowe and Vahl. Among those who made collections of plants here, now distributed among several European museums, the names of Joseph Banks, the Baron of Castelo de Paiva, Lemann, Lippold, Gilbert Mandon, Francis Masson, Moniz, Norman and Webb should not be forgotten.
Faria

This surname seems to have been introduced into Madeira by Braz Gil de Faria, who held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) land on the right bank of the Ribeira da Caixa (‘box stream’), in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’).
Faria e Castro (José Carlos de)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) on 9 December 1835, the son of José Carlos de Faria e Castro and Dona Amélia de Faria e Castro. He was attending the Episcopal Seminary of Funchal (*Seminário Episcopal do Funchal*), intended for the Church, when he met the writer Platão de Vaksel, who invited him to visit Russia in his company. Vaksel had come to Madeira to accompany a sister, who was suffering from a lung disease and died here.

Having accepted the invitation, Faria e Castro went to the Muscovite empire, where some time later he married another sister of his friend Vaksel. From then on he lived at the castle of Raudamy, on the banks of the Neman, which belonged to his wife’s family.

Faria e Castro was in Madeira in 1898 and 1903, and in both years he also visited several European cities. He was a corresponding member of the Lisbon Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*), a knight of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) and a *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the Royal Household. Besides many newspaper articles, he wrote the following works: *O Estado e o seu âmbito*, Lisbon, 1878; *L'Epopée maritime des Portugais, Vasco da Gama et le Camoens*, Brussels, 1898; *L'Ouverture de la grande navigation a travers l'Océan au quinzième siècle*, Paris, 1902; and *Les Jesuites et Camoens sous le roi D. Sebastiâo*. He died at the castle of Raudamy in April 1910.
Faria (João Alfredo de)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, the son of José de Faria and Cláudia Matilde de Faria. He attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and had completed the infantry course of the former Army School. His military career, in which he truly distinguished himself as one of the most eminent officers in the army, was spent not only in the ranks and in the internal services of the barracks, but chiefly in the courts and senior departments. He had been called to these by his brilliant gifts of intelligence, by the proven competence he had shown in posts he had held before and by a remarkable and widely recognised integrity of character. He was public prosecutor in the military courts and a deputy in several legislatures. In these posts he proved a very fluent speaker, carefully correct in form and with a deep knowledge of the matters he dealt with. His easy, correct and incisive speech aroused particular interest in his audiences and was always heard with the most devoted esteem. In some celebrated cases in which he had to take part as public prosecutor, he delivered speeches that were judged true models of forensic eloquence. Since he was no specialist in financial matters, his appointment as Inspector-General of Taxes caused surprise. Yet he carried out this important commission with such proficiency that he drew spontaneous and fervent praise even from people hostile to the political regime then in power. The extensive report on this work, which he published in two volumes, was the subject of conflicting judgements in the press. But no one could deny the author of so valuable a work a conscientious and thorough study of the subject, the purest desire to serve his country well and the brilliance of a lofty mind, which that very document profoundly revealed. He had risen to the rank of general shortly before his death, which occurred on 24 January 1921.
Faria (José Cupertino de)

He was born in Funchal around 1866 and is the son of Manuel de Faria and Dona Maria Isabel Fernandes de Faria. He attended the seminary (*Seminário*) of this diocese, but did not complete its preparatory studies, and afterwards enlisted in the army. He left this island long ago and lived for many years in the city of Setúbal. It was there that in 1901 he published a volume of 202 pages entitled *O Arquipelago da Madeira*, which contains many errors and inaccuracies.
Lighthouses

Only around the middle of the third quarter of the 19th century was serious thought given to lighting the coasts of our archipelago. Several attempts had been made before, but without appreciable results.

On 25 June 1861 the deputies for Madeira António Gonçalves de Freitas, Luís de Freitas Branco and Dom Luís da Câmara Leme introduced a bill in parliament authorising the construction of a revolving lighthouse on Ponta de São Lourenço and a fixed light on the Ilhéu da Pontinha (‘islet of the little point’). This new attempt, too, proved fruitless.
Ponta do Pargo lighthouse

Lighting the other end of Madeira’s south coast is also a recognised need, with the São Lourenço lighthouse (*Farol de São Lourenço*) to the east and the projected Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) lighthouse to the west. The building and other premises intended to house the lighthouse and its staff were built some years ago, and all the work has been completed. All that remains is the purchase of the lantern and the other apparatus needed to fit out the lighthouse, which the European conflict prevented from being in operation already. The continuation of the building is owed to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district, which will shortly acquire the light and install it. (1921).

The Ponta do Pargo lighthouse was inaugurated on 5 June 1922. It stands on the Ponta da Vigia (‘lookout’), some 375 metres above sea level, at the locality (*sítio*) where there was once a telegraph station and which was known as Casa do Rei (‘the king’s house’). We have read somewhere that this lighthouse ‘emits three successive beams of white light with a power of 5,500 carcels, each lasting 0.5 of a second, at intervals of 3.5 seconds’.
São Lourenço lighthouse

As is well known, the ship that João Gonçalves Zarco commanded at the discovery of Madeira was called the São Lourenço, and when he first approached that tongue of land he gave it the name of the caravel that carried him. The tip of this point, or rather a small isolated rock lying opposite it, was always considered the most suitable site for a lighthouse, since its light would reach a considerable part of the north and south of the island, as well as the crossing that separates Madeira from Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). This rock is an islet next to the point, from which it is separated by a narrow channel navigable only by small vessels.
In 1867 the final plan and estimate for the works on this lighthouse were drawn up. Construction of the keeper’s house and its outbuildings began in 1868 and was completed early in 1870.

The lighthouse is dioptric, or lenticular, of the second order. It emits a white light with intermittent flashes every 30 seconds and can be seen 25 miles away. It was built by the French firm Saulter, and the engineer Charles Trepardoux came to install it. Its cost, including transport and installation, was 8,370.00 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis).
The lantern stands 140 metres above sea level and lies at 32° 41′ north latitude and 16° 39′ west longitude from the Greenwich observatory.
It came into service, lighting those waters for the first time, on 30 September 1870.

A great public need had been met. Complaints from shipping had been constant, and claims for compensation had even been made for damage caused to many vessels. Several ships were wrecked in those waters, most notably the *Forerunner*, which ran aground in October 1854.
Porto Santo lighthouse

After the São Lourenço lighthouse (*Farol de São Lourenço*), the building of a lighthouse on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) was always recognised as the first and most urgent need. The lack of lighting on those coasts caused several disasters, with loss of lives and vessels, which are recorded in the Annals of that island. Some studies were carried out and projects and estimates drawn up, but it was only forty years after the São Lourenço lighthouse began operating that the lighthouse on the neighbouring island of Porto Santo began to light those waters, over a radius of eleven miles. The site chosen was a small islet known as Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’), separated from the island of Porto Santo by a narrow and short channel. The lantern stands 118 metres above sea level. It was a fixed white light, visible at a distance of 11 miles. It began operating in 1901. It has rendered valuable service to shipping, and especially to vessels making for the port of Funchal.
Islet beacon

This was a small fixed-light lighthouse of little illuminating power, which not so long ago was often called *a brasa do ilhéu* (‘the ember of the islet’). It served as a landmark for vessels making for the port of Funchal and came into service on 18 May 1866.
It was replaced by a new lighthouse on 1 August 1931.
Farrobo

This name was formerly given in the archipelago to *Sempervivum glutinosum*, a member of the Crassulaceae now known as *saião* or *ensaião*. ‘Less than half a *légua* (league, about 5 km) beyond the Ilhéu da Fonte da Areia (‘sand spring’),’ says Frutuoso, ‘towards the east on the northern side, there is a settlement of up to fifteen inhabitants, which is called Farrobo because there grows there this herb so called, with which the fishermen dye their lines.’

*Sempervivum glutinosum* has disappeared from Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), but it is quite common on the rocks of Madeira, where it is still used to dye fishing lines and make them tougher and stronger. The lines are rubbed with the crushed bark of the plant and then soaked in urine, a process that gives them a black colour, making them barely visible to the fish.

The term *alfarroba* or *farroba* is used on the island of Lanzarote, in the Canary Islands, to designate *Sempervivum balsamiferum*, a member of the Crassulaceae with the same uses as the *S. glutinosum* of Madeira.

In Madeira, *ferrobar* the lines means rubbing them with *saião*, as described above, *ferrobar* being a corruption of *alfarrobar*. The herb formerly called *farrobo* and today *saião* gave its name to a locality (*sítio*) on Porto Santo and to several localities on the island of Madeira.
Farrobo (Joaquim Pedro Quintela, 2nd Count of)

He was born in Lisbon on 18 May 1823 and died there on 28 July 1882. He was appointed civil governor of Funchal on 1 February 1860 and took office on the 29th of that month and year. He headed the administration of this district for little more than a year. Local tradition still preserves the memory of the brilliant and lavish parties that the Counts of Farrobo (‘carob tree’) gave at the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace).
Fasciation

A teratological phenomenon characterised by the fusing and flattening of the stems or branches of a plant. Fasciation is frequently observed in *Echium plantagineum* on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and in the specimens of *Euphorbia exigua* growing between Machico and Água de Pena, and it has also been noted in the vine, in pumpkin plants, etc.
Fauna
Like most island faunas, the Madeiran fauna is marked by the absence of land mammals and by a poverty of species in many groups that are widely represented in continental faunas.

Madeira received its native fauna and flora from Europe, and birds, winds and sea currents were the chief carriers of the animal and plant species that inhabit it. After what Darwin wrote on the origin of island faunas, no one dares to doubt that land molluscs and other animals can be carried by birds and even by sea currents, or that the wind is in many cases the carrier of certain insects, as it is of plants whose fruits or seeds are equipped with appendages suited to aiding their dispersal.

The presence of many endemic species in the Madeira archipelago may be attributed either to changes undergone here by the ancestral types of those species, or to the disappearance on the continent of forms identical to those that still inhabit our region. As we saw in the article Land snails, the archipelago has 131 species of pulmonates peculiar to it, and there are also other groups rich in species of their own, most notably the insects, which unfortunately have not yet been properly studied.

More than 3,100 animal species are known in the archipelago, and they may be divided, without great error, as follows: Protozoa, 70 species; Coelenterates, 111; Echinoderms, 19; Worms, 250; Arthropods, 1621; Molluscs, 476; Molluscoids, 130; and Vertebrates, 451. The best zoological collections from the Madeira archipelago are in the British Museum, but the Funchal Seminary Museum (Museu do Seminário do Funchal) also holds some valuable collections, most notably those of birds, fishes, shells and corals.

The land mammals found in Madeira were all introduced by man. The first settlers found only one mammal – the seal – which is still frequent on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) but now rarely appears on the coasts of this island.

Birds, being capable of flight and finding it no hard task to cross the roughly 350 miles that separate us from the Moroccan coast, are well represented in the fauna of the archipelago. Altogether, very nearly 200 species have been observed, more than in the Canary Islands and far more than in the Azores, despite the greater extent of those two archipelagos. According to Father Ernst Schmitz, the number of species confirmed as breeding here is 36, with 12 peculiar forms. Of these, 3 – the *bisbis* (*Regulus madeirensis*), the chaffinch (*Fringilla Madeirensis*) and the long-toed black trocaz pigeon (*Columba Trocaz*) – are regarded by some as good species, while the remaining 9 are mere local varieties. Among the birds, some are regular passage migrants, others occasional visitors and still others vagrants. Notable for its commercial value is the *cagarra*, a native but not resident bird, which arrives in these seas in spring and leaves in autumn after each pair has laid a single egg in the crevices of the sea cliffs, chiefly on the Desertas and in the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) group.

Among the invertebrates we find many arthropods, such as coleopteran insects, arachnids and other groups of that vast sub-kingdom, represented by species clearly distinct from their congeners in other regions. The same must be said of the land molluscs. Indeed, it may be stated of these islands, and of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) in particular, that few or no parts of the world contain so large a number of endemic species of pulmonate gastropods in so limited a space.

The marine fauna of Madeira is abundant and varied: some 250 species of fish have been collected in the seas around this island, many of them remarkable for the brilliance of their colours and the singularity of their form or structure. Among these species, the tuna and the black scabbardfish (*espada preta*) deserve special mention for their great commercial value; we shall deal with them in particular in the article devoted to the fishing industry.

The naturalists who, through their studies or explorations, have helped to make Madeira’s zoological riches known are the following: Richard Thomas Lowe, E. V. Harcourt, J. Y. Johnson, C. Azevedo de Meneses, J. M. Moniz, Thomas Vernon Wollaston, Dr Oswald Heer, Dr Auguste Forel, Becker, Father Ernst Schmitz, M. Andrew, the Baron of Castelo de Paiva, Dr Augusto Nobre, Adolfo de Noronha, Father J. G. Barreto, R. B. Watson, G. Busk, T. Hinks, A. T. Waters, Dr Alfred Merle Norman, Dr Albers, J. Gray, P. M. Duncan, I. C. Thompson, C. Darwin, Dr Fisher, A. Girard, Father J. da S. Tavares, Father Longino Navas, H. Hempel, Dr Langerhans, M. Lachlan, A. Fauvel, Alberto Artur Sarmento, etc.

In the appropriate places we shall endeavour to give an account both of the nature of the research carried out by many of these naturalists and of the works that some of them have published on the fauna of our archipelago.
Fauvel (Alberto)
Works:

*Catalogue des Coléoptères des Iles de Madère, Porto Santo, et Desertas*; *Catalogue des Coléoptères des Iles Selvages*; and *Arachnides recueillis à l'Ile de Madère en 1896*. The first two works were published in the *Revue d'Entomologie*, 1897; the last in the *Bulletin de la Societe Entomologique de France*, 1897.
Broad bean (Vicia Faba)
An annual papilionaceous legume widely cultivated on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It is native to the Caspian region and North Africa.
Sea beans

These are the seeds of leguminous plants which are carried by the ocean current to the north coast of Madeira, especially at Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’). The seeds most often found there are those of *Guillandina Bonduc* and of two species of the genera *Entada* and *Mucuna*.
Some suppose that Columbus, who perhaps did not fail to notice the arrival of such seeds, saw in them proof that unknown lands existed towards the west.
The seeds we refer to are also known as *castanhas do mar* (sea chestnuts).
Favila

This surname was originally spelt Favela and belongs to an old and noble family that settled on this island at the end of the 15th century. The first to bear it here was Fernão Favela, known as the Elder, who had served valiantly in Africa and had been a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*). He married Beatriz Pires in Madeira and founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Piornais (‘broom thickets’), centred on the chapel of Our Lady of Help (*Nossa Senhora da Ajuda*), which he had founded and where he was buried. He died in 1545, according to Henriques de Noronha, or in 1537, according to the date given by Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo. His son and successor was António Favila, who died in 1601 and lies buried in the Ajuda chapel. Dona Inês Moniz, who was born in 1553 and died in 1589, was the daughter of António Favila. She founded an entailed estate in favour of her niece Dona Isabel Acciaioli de Vasconcelos, with the clause that it should pass in perpetuity to the eldest daughter – an extremely curious circumstance and, we believe, a very rare one, at least here in Madeira.
Fazenda (Canon Manuel Esteves)

He was a native of the city of Covilhã and died in Lisbon on 13 March 1903, aged 58. In 1899 he was appointed canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), and in this city he made his name as a politician and journalist, holding several political posts here.
Fedegoso
Madeiran vernacular name for *Psoralea bituminosa*, a plant of the family Leguminosae.
On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) the name *fedegoso* is given to *Chenopodium album*, a member of the goosefoot family common both there and in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira.
Rocket (Eruca sativa)
An annual crucifer, very common on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Feijoa

Madeiran vernacular name for *Phaseolus multiflorus*, a legume native to tropical America. The *feijoa* is grown chiefly at Monte (‘hill’) and Camacha, where its roots are said to last 7 years. Its seeds are 20 to 30 millimetres long by 12 to 16 wide, and its pods are downy, especially when young, and sickle-shaped or slightly curved.
Common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris)
A papilionaceous legume widely grown in Madeiran vegetable gardens. It seems to be native to America.

The bush or dwarf bean is simply a form of the common bean. Green beans, known as *vaginha*, are a Madeiran export; before the war some 1800 to 2,000 baskets of *vaginha* left the island every week during the peak season.
Feio (Dr Carlos José Barata Pinto)
He was appointed civil governor of Funchal by decree of 18 December 1917 and took office on the day he arrived on this island, 5 February 1918.
He left for Lisbon on 12 March of the same year and shortly afterwards requested to be relieved of his post.
Fairs

On 19 July 1839 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) resolved to establish an annual fair and a weekly one in the city. The decision was approved by the District General Council (*Junta*), which left the choice of a site for the fair to the Council itself.

Despite the good intentions the Council had expressed, its decision was never carried out. Only later, on 29 and 30 June 1850, and on the initiative of the public-spirited Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, could a fair be held in Funchal, ‘with the aim of promoting Commerce and strengthening relations between the different settlements of the island’.
The fair was set up in the Praça Académica (‘academic square’), and over those two days it was visited by no fewer than fifteen thousand people, who left a considerable sum of money there.

‘The booths of the fair,’ we read in a dispatch sent by Councillor J. Silvestre Ribeiro to the Minister of the Kingdom, ‘were laid out in the best of order, and as the Praça is very spacious, some of its long avenues were left clear for the passage of the immense crowd. In the middle of the Praça a large stage was raised, and beside it a bandstand for the band of the 6th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) Battalion. Towards the afternoon of the 29th, thirteen country people from the parish of São Martinho, dressed in the costumes peculiar to this land, mounted the stage and performed exquisitely a dance particular to Madeira, known by the name of “A la moda”. That dance was followed by a masked dance, which stood out for the rich old costumes worn by the performers. The band of the 6th Caçadores Battalion, which the worthy commander of that corps obligingly lent me, entertained the spectators until late at night on both days, playing the loveliest pieces.’

Other fairs were held later in the Praça Académica, after Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro had left this island, but none of them displayed the brilliance or the extraordinary liveliness of the fair held on 29 and 30 June 1850 on the initiative of that illustrious civil governor.

At a session of the Funchal Municipal Council on 3 February 1768, orders were given to carry out a warrant (*provisão*) by which the Monarch, at the Council’s own request, had allowed a public fair to be held in the Terreiro da Sé (‘cathedral square’) on Tuesdays. If such a fair ever took place, however, it did not last long, nor did it produce the results that might reasonably have been expected of it.

On Wednesdays and Saturdays the sellers of *botas chãs* (traditional flat-soled leather boots) gather in the Largo do Comércio, or Largo do Chafariz, to ply their trade there. On Saturdays the cattle dealers flock to the Campo da Barca, or Campo de Miguel Bombarda, and the dealers in poles to the Praça dos Lavradores (‘farmers’ market’), and a great deal of business is done there. Pigs are sold on Fridays, next to the old petroleum warehouse.
See Mercado de Dom Sebastião.
Bracken (Pteridium aquilinum)
A fern that is very common in Madeira and also grows in the non-calcareous parts of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Near Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) it can reach 2 metres in height.
Bracken is used as manure and as bedding for animals.
Feiteiras (Chão das)

A nearly flat locality (*sítio*) a short distance from the Poiso (‘resting place’) mountain shelter, crossed by the road that leads from the shelter to Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’). Bracken (*Pteridium aquilinum*) is very abundant there.
Feiticeiro do Norte

Manuel Gonçalves, born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco de São Jorge (‘arc of São Jorge’) in eighteen sixty-something and better known by the nickname of Feiticeiro do Norte (‘the Sorcerer of the North’), is an illiterate peasant without any degree of education. At about the age of forty he began to show an extraordinary aptitude for composing and improvising popular verses and songs, which soon won great renown among the country people of this island. To the sound of a *rajão* (Madeiran five-string guitar), in a monotonous chant, the Feiticeiro sang his verses. For their originality and picturesqueness, and above all for the interest their subjects aroused, they were eagerly listened to and were one of the great attractions at the various festivals (*arraiais*) of Madeira. From short verses and light recitatives he moved on to more elaborate compositions, many of which were printed as separate pamphlets. Among these we may mention: *Santo Antonio*, *Chegada de Suas Magestades*, *As Raparigas dos bordados*, *O Lavrador*, *A Cidade do Funchal*, *As Inundações*, *O meu galo preto*, *A antiguidade de meu pae*, *A vida do Feiticeiro do Norte escrita por ele mesmo*, *A Madeira*, etc. etc. Encouraged by the success of his compositions, Manuel Gonçalves went to Brazil, where he stayed for some time, and among the pamphlets he printed there is one entitled *Pedro Alvares Cabral*.
He died in the parish of Arco de São Jorge in April 1927.
British Factory

It was founded before 1774 and dissolved on 31 December 1838. It maintained a special ward for the English in the Hospital of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), and while it existed it rendered various other services to the British colony on this island.
Felner (Rodrigo José de Lima)

We owe to this well-known writer and academic the memoir *Nome verdadeiro do portuguez João Fernandes Vieira*, published in 1873. In it he stated and proved for the first time that the illustrious Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira (see that entry), on leaving this island in 1624, exchanged the name Francisco de Ornelas Moniz for the one he adopted and used until his death. Lima Felner died in Lisbon in November 1877.
Hay

This name is given to grasses that are eaten by animals after they have been dried. The time for cutting hay is chosen to obtain fodder that is both plentiful and of good quality. On the coast the plants are harvested in May; in the uplands the work takes place in July.

The hay from Ponta de São Lourenço is among the best Madeira produces, but a great deal of dried grass also comes to Funchal from Caniço, São Gonçalo, Camacha, etc., for stall-fed cattle. About 500,000 kilos of Madeiran hay, generally made up of species of the grass family (Gramineae), enter the city every year. Much wheat straw comes from Portugal as animal feed.
Formerly the average price of every 15 kilograms of Madeiran hay was about 30 centavos, but this year the hay from Ponta de São Lourenço sold at 150 centavos.
*Andropogon hirtus* and *Agrostis castellana*, grasses very common in Madeira, are known by the name of hay (*feno*) even while still green.
Phenology

Madeiran phenology was studied by Dr Oswald Heer in 1851 and by C. A. Meneses from 1903 to 1912. See the articles published by the latter in the *Boletim da Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa* of 1910 and in the *Bolletin de l'Académie Internationale de Geographie Botanique* of 1905, 1908 and 1912. Besides much useful information, they contain the list of works to be consulted by anyone wishing to know the times of leaf discoloration and leafing of some woody species cultivated on the island.
Carlos A. de Meneses published a series of articles on this subject in the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) in June 1910.
Fernandes (Dona Olímpia Pio)

This Madeiran lady, who has long lived away from this island, cultivated letters here with brilliance and a well-deserved reputation. She contributed to various newspapers, and around 1877 wrote a drama entitled *Aldo ou a Filha do Mar*, which was staged in this city and won the greatest applause from the audience. The principal scenes of this drama were published in a Funchal newspaper. Speaking of Dona Olímpia Fernandes, a brilliant woman of letters said: ‘I have read with interest all the other works of this distinguished writer, and either I am much mistaken or she will one day occupy one of the foremost places among the ladies who cultivate letters’.
We do not know whether Dona Olímpia Fernandes continued to cultivate letters or whether she may have published other writings, as her talent and learning would lead one to expect.
Fernandes da Silva (Dr Julião)

*Carta critica sobre o método curativo dos medicos funchalenses. MDCCLXI* is the title of a volume of 310 pages, published in the form of a letter that ends with these words: ‘O seu mais dependente e intimo venerador I. F. D. S., Madeira 7 de Setembro de 1755’ (Your most dependent and intimate admirer I. F. D. S., Madeira, 7 September 1755). It gives neither the place (*lugar*) of publication nor the name of the printer.

As its title clearly indicates, this work is a lengthy critique – at times severe and biting, but very judicious and always well grounded by the knowledge of the time – of the way in which physicians practised medicine in Madeira in the mid-18th century. Although the author was young in years, as he himself admits in the letter, he displays an abundant store of knowledge of the healing art and was well versed in the works of the great masters, who at that time held full authority in medical matters.

On the value of the book from a strictly scientific point of view we can say nothing, since we entirely lack the competence to do so. The distinguished annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says of it ‘that it is curious and even useful, not only for the medical history of this archipelago but also for the study of the customs of the period. The phonetic spelling and aggressive diction of this letter reveal it to be the work of some bold innovator of the school of Luís António Verney’.

This important work treats several subjects with great interest and undoubtedly with remarkable proficiency, such as the measles epidemic, which claims so many victims here in Madeira, the illness and death of Bishop Dom João do Nascimento, and the causes of elephantiasis and the way to cure it. The book is altogether very curious and worth reading even by those outside medical science.

Who wrote this interesting book? Neither Inocêncio Francisco da Silva in the *Diccionario Bibliographico* nor Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in his valuable annotations to the work of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso gives us the slightest indication on this point. It was pure chance that allowed the distinguished Madeiran Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira to discover the name, hidden perhaps for more than a century, of the talented and learned author of the *Carta critica*. Among the papers left by the late physician César A. Mourão Pita (see that entry), Councillor Vieira found a printed copy of the work and a manuscript copy, both of which we presume belonged to the illustrious Madeiran and eminent physician Dr António da Luz Pita (see that entry). A quick and simple comparison of the two volumes at once revealed that they were one and the same work. The manuscript, which appears to be the author’s own autograph, contains something the printed copies lack: an excessively laudatory letter dated 28 August 1755 from the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) in this city, written by Friar João de São José and addressed to the author of the book. For reasons unknown to us, this letter did not accompany the printed edition of the work. The manuscript names Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva as its author, and his name matches the initials found at the end of the printed volume perfectly. This interesting manuscript was discovered in July 1907 and promptly acquired by the Funchal Municipal Library (*Biblioteca Municipal do Funchal*), where it is at present. Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva was the son of Manuel da Silva and was born in Funchal between 1723 and 1726. He graduated in medicine from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), completing the course on 17 November 1748. Besides the *Carta Critica*, he wrote a work entitled *Exame de Sangradores*, which is mentioned in the *Diccionario Bibliographico Portuguez*.
The *Diário do Commercio* (‘Commercial Daily’) of 12 December 1909 published a detailed article on this subject, written by one of the editors of this *Elucidario*.

The illustrious professor and academician Dr Augusto da Silva Carvalho, who has published such valuable works on the history of medicine in Portugal, intended to deal at length with the *Carta Critica…* of Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva cited above, since it is a work of great scientific value for the period in which it was written, and so to rescue the name of its distinguished author from undeserved oblivion. He communicated this a few years ago to one of the editors of the *Elucidario Madeirense*, but as far as we know this promised and undoubtedly interesting study has not been published to date.
Fernandes de Sant'Ana (Father Manuel)

Father Manuel Fernandes de Sant'Ana was born on 14 May 1864 in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo, the son of Francisco Fernandes and Dona Ana Pereira Fernandes de Sant'Ana. In 1881 he abandoned the preparatory course at the seminary (*Seminário*) of this diocese to enter the Society of Jesus, in which he took his vows and remained until his death. Giving his schooling a new direction, he began his studies in Portugal, continued them in Spain, Germany and England, and completed them in Holland. At Oña, in Spain, on a philosophy course for aspirants to the Society, he was judged the most talented of ninety select students, with the sharpest and most penetrating intellect. His academic triumphs were as many as the subjects and disciplines he studied. He distinguished himself in oriental languages – Greek, it is said, was as familiar to him as his own mother tongue – and in mathematics, biology and the social sciences; in theology he had a profound knowledge of everything connected with the vast field of Holy Scripture studies.

He was a tireless worker. Besides the most scrupulous performance of his own duties as a priest, all the time he could spare was devoted entirely to study and to works of Catholic apostolate. He seems to have had a burning, insatiable thirst for knowledge, and the further he opened new horizons in the field of his scientific work, the more he was consumed by an impatient longing to extend his already vast and profound learning. Study absorbed him so completely, and he was so miserly with his time, that he denied himself all rest, and even the small pastimes and recreations that his rule imposed on him, always seeking to justify the omission by the need to carry out without delay the most urgent and pressing tasks. It was in this way, together with his exceptional talent and the quick and ready perception with which his mind was gifted, that he enriched his intellect with the astonishing store of knowledge that amazed those who heard him or read his writings. Father Sant'Ana was not merely a scholar but a philosopher and a true man of science, as he eloquently showed in the work he wrote refuting the doctrines of Dr Miguel Bombarda.

Father Fernandes de Sant'Ana’s apostolate of Catholic action was truly remarkable. Perhaps never before in Portugal had religious ideals been promoted with such ardent zeal, such self-denial and such a spirit of sacrifice and selflessness as in the campaign of which he was the soul and the valiant, fearless leader. For some time the work of the Catholic press claimed the full attention of his enlightened zeal, and he devoted to it all the energy of his astonishing activity. He founded a widely circulated newspaper, wrote pamphlets, became a dauntless champion of journalism by both the spoken and the written word, created several associations and formed various centres of propaganda, all aimed at advancing Catholic action through the press.

Father Sant'Ana’s literary and scientific output is very significant, but it would have been greater still had he not died in the prime of life, before reaching the age of 46, his last years spent in the torment of a cruel illness. His frail constitution, the excessive apostolic labours to which he devoted himself for many years, the time given to teaching and many other cares and exertions all did much to cut short his active and industrious life.

Besides his extensive contributions to various reviews and newspapers and a number of pamphlets, he published the following works: *Questões de Biologia. O materialismo em face da sciencia*, 1900, 2 volumes of 489 and 567 pp.; *Curso de Religião. Apologetica*, 1901, 317 pp., of which only the 1st volume appeared; and *O Evangelho segundo S. Matheus*, 1909, LVII-325 pp. Under the title *P. Manuel Fernandes de Santanna, Gotas Biographicas*, his fellow Jesuit A. de Meneses published a pamphlet of 36 pages containing very interesting and valuable material for the biography of this distinguished fellow Madeiran of ours.
Father Fernandes de Sant'Ana, one of the most illustrious Madeirans of recent times, died in Lisbon on 3 May 1910.
Fernandes (Gonçalo)

He was an early settler of this island, whose identity the old Madeiran genealogies shroud in mystery, although he appears to have been a son of King Afonso V and of the king’s niece Dona Joana, the ‘Excelente Senhora’. The annotator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), following several genealogists, says that ‘this man has glimmerings of the Man in the Iron Mask, in Paris, and came to Madeira expressly forbidden to leave this island. He lived in grand style, and every year the royal household sent him in abundance all that he needed, yet it was never known who his parents were. When he died on 13 July 1539, he was buried in his chapel, on which he had placed as arms the Portuguese *quinas* in saltire over the cross of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*). His name is inscribed on the marble tombstone, which bears in half-relief the figure of a boy with his face resting on his left hand and his elbow on a skull, pointing with his right hand to this maxim from the Book of Wisdom: *Sic et nos nati continuo desivimus esse*. His arrival in Madeira after the peace concluded between Afonso V and Empress Elisabeth led to the conjecture that he was that king’s son and that reasons of state prevented his being acknowledged.’ The chapel referred to here is the one that stood near the sea, on the bank of the stream of Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta; we shall deal with it in a separate article. It was the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by Gonçalo Fernandes, to which his son Pedro Gonçalves de Andrade succeeded. This entailed house (*casa vinculada*) later passed to the Freitas da Madalena family, whose last representative was the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Nuno de Freitas Lomelino.

On this legendary figure we find the following further interesting details in the *Dicionário Portugal*, volume VI, p. 373: ‘. . . Gonçalo Fernandes, whose real name was Dom Gonçalo Afonso de Aviz Transtamara Fernandes, son of Afonso V and of the unhappy queen Dona Joana of Castile, the Excelente Senhora, who was forced to take the veil at Santa Clara in Coimbra. It was he who should have succeeded John II on the throne, had his birth not been concealed, for reasons of political expediency with Spain and for fear that he would be killed. He was exiled to the island of Madeira and forbidden to leave it, although he lived there the life of a prince, which was his by right. The Royal Household let him lack nothing needed to display that grandeur, sending him every year caravels laden with everything he required. With the death of John II and the confinement of Dom Gonçalo, the royal line was broken; for this reason Manuel I came to occupy the throne of Portugal unlawfully, and the succession of the Braganças was more irregular still.’
Fernandes (Valentim)

Valentim Fernandes, also known as Valentim Fernandes Alemão, was a German printer and publisher who settled in Lisbon towards the end of the 15th century. He earned a place in the history of our maritime discoveries by collecting a number of unpublished writings of interest to the history of those same discoveries. In 1845 Dr Johann Andreas Schmeller published a curious memoir on these unpublished texts, of which Richard Henry Major gives a detailed account in his work on Prince Henry the Navigator. These narratives of certain maritime discoveries made by the Portuguese in the 15th century bear on the history of the discovery of this archipelago, and for that reason Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo deals with them at length on pp. 366–372 and 905 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). Part of these narratives, concerning the Azores, was published in volume 1 of the *Archivo Açoreano*. It seems to us that the remaining manuscripts of Valentim Fernandes’s collection are still unpublished.
Fernandes Vieira (João)
Francisco de Ornelas Moniz Júnior – who later changed his name to João Fernandes Vieira – was born in the captaincy of Machico in 1613, in a time of oppression and poverty under Castilian rule.

His father, Francisco de Ornelas Moniz, was a great-grandson of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the first donatary of Machico, and a grandson of Lançarote Teixeira, the great horseman; his mother, Antónia Mendes, was a great-grandson of Pedro Vieira, the great holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Ribeira de Machico (‘Machico stream’). Among his great-grandparents was António Fernandes, a *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) at Covas do Faial (‘hollows of Faial’), in the north of the island.

It was from the Fernandes branch, linked to the Vieira line, that the young Francisco de Ornelas Moniz took an assumed name when he joined the stream of emigrants to Brazil. He wished to work as an unknown man so as not to sully the ancestral honours of the Teixeiras, Ornelas, Monizes, Saavedras, Mendonças and Vasconcelos, at a time when work was a disgrace and the oppressive burden of the lower classes. The nobility of Machico was among the proudest: it was starving, yet still flaunting its coats of arms.

Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640), which abolished certain prerogatives of the donataries in the captaincies, ordered a review of entailed estates and dissolved many of them as unsustainable and absurd. At that time, in the populous jurisdiction of Machico, there was hardly anyone who could comfortably keep a horse, except two or three people, as the historian of the islands puts it. Then came crises in the crops, and the holders of entails, dreaming of grandeur and lolling in idleness, fell little by little into ruin and into the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant), under which they handed their lands over to tenants and received from them a half-share (*demidia*) of the produce.

In this way the eldest sons of the entail holders still managed to get by, living on their rents. Their younger brethren, however, starving and resentful of their lot, would submit to work only in a foreign land, and even then only after exchanging their noble name for another. This can be seen in various Madeiran genealogies, in the entries for families of the 16th and 17th centuries, some of whose members went to Brazil.

Once sugar had declined in Madeira, the lands discovered by Pedro Álvares Cabral produced it in abundance from canes imported there, and some men skilled in growing and making Madeira’s sweet products had already gone there in the time of Martim Afonso de Sousa, the governor of Portuguese America. Those who had stayed behind in poverty heard of the good results obtained and of the lands being lavishly distributed under the broad system of *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). So they began to leave for Brazil on a promising adventure – hence a great stream of emigration – to try their fortune far from their oppressed homeland, free of alien prejudices.
João Fernandes Vieira, the descendant of the discoverer and 1st donatary, was a clerk in Pernambuco when the Dutch invaded the province in 1630.

Having taken Olinda, the enemy marched on Recife, which was poorly defended on the landward side and lacked the strength for effective resistance, its defence having been entrusted to hastily raised territorial militia (*ordenanças*). Undisciplined, these abandoned their position, leaving garrisons only in the forts of São Francisco and São Jorge.

It was in the latter that the young hero began his career, performing prodigies of valour. He wrapped himself in the Portuguese flag so that it should not fall into the hands of the enemy, who granted an honourable capitulation.

With the sea open to them, the Dutch poured continual reinforcements into Recife. They lacked no resources and strove to extend their dominion, while the Portuguese, in difficult circumstances, struggled to bar their way.

The young Fernandes Vieira, chivalrous and adventurous, commanded the scouts in the field when the enemy attacked the camp in 1634. Matias de Albuquerque, the Portuguese governor, would not risk battle, because he knew well the nature of his forces. He abandoned the fortress, losing the fruit of four years of relentless labour on the long line of entrenchments around Pernambuco. Vieira shut himself in the fortress, determined, fearless as he was, to defend it, but he was taken prisoner and ransomed himself for a weight of gold.

After this fresh setback João Fernandes Vieira appears to have settled down. He fell in love with Dona Maria César, daughter of his fellow countryman Francisco Berenguer de Andrade, who was also committed to the same cause of defending Portugal’s patrimony, and married her, now turning to commerce with a view to growing rich.

The news of the revolution of 1 December 1640 resounded through Brazil, and a year later that of John IV’s treaty with the Netherlands, a policy of alliance with the enemies of Castile, which heartened the defenders of Brazil. The Dutch, however, unscrupulously and on frivolous pretexts, went on with their work of conquest.

João Fernandes Vieira had a sudden resolve: he would restore Pernambuco, using the same cunning tactics as the enemy. The Dutch called him into their service, and he accepted the posts of business agent of the Company and member of its supreme council, thereby learning all their schemes and resources. He wrote to John IV asking leave to rescue the country from the hands of the usurpers, and the monarch refused!

The Dutch discovered his intentions and dissembled in turn, seeking to lure him to Recife, but Vieira outwitted them and took the field, raising the banner of Liberty in Pernambuco. From estate to estate, from sugar mill (engenho) to sugar mill, he stirred up the Revolution.

The Dutch issued a public proclamation (bando) promising an amnesty to rebels who surrendered within a set time. Vieira declared traitors all who did not follow his cause. The council of Pernambuco put a price on his head. Vieira put a price on the heads of the members of the Council of Pernambuco!
His lucky star protected him at Tabocas and Guararapes. This last battle is compared to Aljubarrota, for it decided the independence of the country.

He triumphed. Favours were heaped upon him. Such is the law of fortune. He was governor of Paraíba and then of Angola, nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*), *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) of the town (*vila*) of Pinhel and commander of many commanderies, of the kind that yielded good money.
João Fernandes Vieira died in Olinda on 10 January 1681, aged 85, leaving a curious will.

Anyone wanting fuller information about this distinguished Madeiran should read the weighty volume by Friar Rafael de Jesus, the *Castrioto Luzitano*, or the lighter French edition of 1842; *O Valoroso Lucideno* by Manuel Calado; the memoir by Lima Felner presented to the Academy of Sciences in 1873; and the monograph *Ascendência, naturalidade & mudança de nome de João Fernandes Vieira* by the author of this article. S.

Issue no. 152 of the *Correio da Madeira* (‘Madeira Courier’), in September 1922, published an interesting document taken from a copy of Book I of Baptisms and Marriages of the parish of Faial, which reads as follows: ‘On the twenty-ninth day of the month of June of . . . I [baptised] in this Church Fran[cisco], son of Francisco dor Nellas and of Ant[óni]a Mendes, and the godparents were Braz P[erei]ra and … of Beatriz oriz, and thus the godparents with the baptised are parishioners of this Church of N[ossa] S[enhora]... I made this *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) this day, month, year as above—Sebastião Gonsalves=and Braz P[erei]ra’. Since this record lies between two others from the year 1596, it seems evident that it was made in that year. There are also strong reasons to believe that the individual to whom the record refers is the celebrated João Fernandes Vieira, whose real name was Francisco de Ornelas Moniz and whose parents were Francisco de Ornelas Moniz and Antónia Mendes. If Fernandes Vieira was born on 29 June 1596, he died short of his 85th birthday, and not at 68, as was stated in the 1st edition of this work.

The copy of Book I of Baptisms and Marriages of the parish of Faial was made in 1766 because the original book was in very poor condition. The work was ordered by the Bishop of the diocese in June of that year, as certified by the present vicar of the parish (*freguesia*), the Revd Dr Francisco Fulgêncio de Andrade. (1921).

On the initiative of Dr Abel Capitolino Baptista, a modest monument to the memory of João Fernandes Vieira was erected on Avenida Manuel de Arriaga. It was solemnly inaugurated on 11 May 1924 and in 1933 was moved to the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’).
Fernando (Prince)
He was the son of King Duarte and in 1460 inherited from his uncle, Prince Henry the Navigator, the lordship of the Madeira archipelago. He married his cousin Dona Beatriz, daughter of Prince John.
Ferraz (Francisco João de Freitas)

The annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) mentions this priest as one of the most distinguished preachers of this diocese in the 19th century. He was born in Funchal in 1823 and died in Lisbon on 31 July 1859. Illness and an early death prevented him from revealing the full power of his talent and his remarkable gift for preaching. Even so, in his day he was regarded as a brilliant ornament of the pulpit, not only in Madeira but throughout the country. He held the honours of a canon and was curate of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) of this city. He died in Lisbon, where he had gone in search of better health, a victim of pulmonary tuberculosis.
Ferraz (Ricardo Júlio)

He was born in this city on 26 May 1824, the son of Severiano Alberto de Freitas Ferraz and Dona Leonor Filomena Ferraz. He completed the course of a higher school of engineering in Paris. In the practice of his profession as an engineer he left his name attached to works of great scale, such as the artificial harbour of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) and the building of Lisbon Penitentiary (*Penitenciária de Lisboa*). From 1866 to 1870 he directed the works on that harbour, and he wrote a report on the way he had directed its construction. He went abroad to make special studies of the various penitentiary systems and of prisons for offenders sentenced to major penalties, in order to guide the construction of Lisbon Penitentiary. He designed, planned and directed that work until this great building was almost finished. The way he carried out these important works provoked some debate in the press. Among the posts he held in Lisbon was that of director of the Water Company (*Companhia das Águas*).
He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislative session of 1879.
He died in Funchal on 24 December 1880.
Ferraz (Severiano Alberto de Freitas)

A distinguished Madeiran craftsman and industrialist, he died in Funchal on 24 August 1856, aged 64. In 1822 he built a new steam still, very simple and with excellent practical results. In March 1828 he set up a sugar factory in Funchal, the first in Madeira since the collapse of the Madeiran sugar industry in the mid-18th century. The factory was greatly improved in 1856, shortly before its owner’s death. He was a corresponding member of the Funchal Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts (*Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes*) and a member of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), and he wrote an article on precious stones in no. 50 of *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’). He suffered persecution under the government of Miguel I because of his liberal ideas.
Ferreira (Alípio Augusto)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) on 27 December 1837. He studied at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and became a primary-school teacher, later holding the post of revenue clerk (*escrivão de fazenda*) in several municipalities of this district. He contributed extensively, in prose and verse, to various Madeiran newspapers and was principal editor of *A Pátria*. According to Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, he wrote the novellas *Um Sacrilegio* and *Romance em seis capítulos*, which he had ready for printing but which were never published in book form; only a few extracts appeared in various newspapers. He lived for many years in Demerara, where he was editor of the newspaper *O Portuguez*. He became a merchant but had little success in his business dealings, and he died in New York, on a hospital cot, on 3 August 1915, destitute and in the most complete obscurity.
Ferreira da Silva (Dr António Joaquim)

This distinguished man of science, whose works are well known and highly regarded abroad, wrote two pamphlets of considerable interest to Madeiran viticulture: *Sur les vins de Madère*, 1896, and *La vinification des vins de Madère et leur composition*, 1911. The latter work was published in the *Annales des falsifications*, pp. 4–59.
Ferreira de Freitas (Joaquim José)

All of Joaquim José Ferreira de Freitas’s biographers state that he was born in Madeira, but every effort made by the late Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Freitas e Abreu and by the present author to discover the parish (*freguesia*) of his birth, or any other personal circumstances of interest to his biography, has proved fruitless. We suppose that he left this island at an early age, perhaps to pursue studies that could not be undertaken in Funchal in that setting and at that time. We also suspect that he never returned to his native soil, which is easily explained by the eventful life he led across Europe.

In the history of the political upheavals that our country went through in the turbulent period from 1820 to 1834, Ferreira de Freitas became known as Padre Amaro, although he was not a priest. The name came from a periodical of that strange title which he published in London; it enjoyed a European reputation, and it was there above all that he displayed his great gifts as a writer.

A restless and adventurous spirit, we see him travel the length and breadth of Europe: now fighting in Napoleon’s armies, now the confidant of Joseph Bonaparte; here a merchant and manufacturer, there a supplier of provisions to the troops; one day the director of a reading room in Paris, and the next the distinguished and vigorous journalist and pamphleteer who rendered such notable services in London to the cause of Portuguese liberty.

All agree that Ferreira de Freitas would have left a great name in the literary history of our country had his life passed serenely and quietly in the calm of a study, devoted to reflection and learning. Instead, he led an extremely eventful existence of struggles and passions, of hatreds and despair, with strokes of fortune and also the distressing ordeals of poverty. The glaring inconsistencies and contradictions of his character contributed greatly to this, for unfortunately it did not always allow itself to be guided by the rules of the strictest probity or by the most impartial principles of justice.

Meanwhile, besides his vast and brilliant work as a journalist, he wrote several volumes that are incontestable evidence of his prodigious talent and his rare qualities as a writer. In 1822 he published in London the *Memória sobre a conspiração de Gomes Freire*, in which he seeks to clear Marshal Beresford of the responsibility attributed to him for the death of the Portuguese general. For this work Ferreira de Freitas is said to have received the sum of 300 pounds, which was a considerable amount for the time. Shortly afterwards he published the *Coup d'oeil sur l'état politique du Brésil*. When he was contradicted by the distinguished French writer Afonso de Bauchamp in the work entitled *Historia do Brasil*, Ferreira de Freitas replied with such spirit and wealth of argument that he earned the praise of his opponent himself. He undertook the publication of a larger work entitled *Bibliotheca Histórica, Política e Diplomatica da Nação Portuguesa*, of which only the first volume appeared, in London, in 1830. Attacking the distinguished jurist Ferreira Borges, he wrote the pamphlet *O Bota-Fora do catavento ou a cabeça de bacalhau fresco*, which has been attributed to Garrett; the prose and verse compositions it contains would not shame the author of *Fr. Luiz de Sousa*. He wrote various pieces in Portuguese, French and English, intended chiefly to promote the independence of Brazil and later the establishment of constitutional government in Portugal.

He worked tirelessly as a journalist and pamphleteer almost until his death, which came in London on 20 July 1831, when he was little more than 50 years old. The costs of his funeral were paid by the wealthy Madeiran, his fellow countryman and friend, the 1st Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), who was then living in exile in that capital.
Ferreira (Francisco António)

He began as a typesetter, and his only formal qualification was the primary-school examination. Although he himself regretted the gaps in a broader and more solid education, it is nonetheless certain that in journalism he made up for this original lack with the exuberance of an exceptional talent, with a superficial and fleeting reading of some contemporary prose writers and poets, and with a light study of a few textbooks. In various newspapers, and notably in the *Diário do Commercio* (‘Commercial Daily’), of which he was principal editor for some years, he revealed his remarkable literary aptitude and his marked qualities as a journalist. The characteristic feature of his writing, to which he always gave an unmistakable note, was biting irony, scathing satire and irreverent mockery. In it, wit, talent, art, literary flavour, perfect metre and pointed phrasing amply redeemed the excesses of thought and the not always pure or praiseworthy intentions of their author. His impulsive, fickle and restless temperament sometimes led him into regrettable excesses, which he was the first to acknowledge once reflection and calm replaced the enthusiasms of his combative and ardent nature. In the *gazetilha* (satirical verse column in a newspaper) Francisco António may be said to have been unsurpassed, and in another setting he would have won well-deserved fame. It is a pity that some of these literary gems have not been collected in a volume.

Francisco António Ferreira was born in Funchal on 25 November 1870, the son of Francisco António Ferreira and Dona Maria Cândida Ferreira, and died in this city on 24 October 1912. He held the post of copying clerk of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) and used to sign his poems with the pseudonym Campos Verde.
Ferreira (Gonçalo Aires)

In the short article devoted to João Afonso, we have already touched briefly on the companions of João Gonçalves Zarco in the hazardous enterprise of discovering and settling this archipelago. Although João Afonso stood out among the seamen who manned the caravels commanded by Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira, it is nevertheless certain that Gonçalo Aires Ferreira was the most distinguished companion of the first discoverer. This was due not only to his noble ancestry but also to his learning, compared with that of the other men who made up the crew of the small fleet that first sailed to this island. Some genealogists have highlighted the fact that Gonçalo Aires was the most dedicated companion and most devoted friend of João Gonçalves Zarco in the labours of the expedition and discovery, and also in the early settlement of the captaincy of Funchal.
Gaspar Frutuoso, referring to the first expedition made along the coast by the discoverers, says the following:

‘Before they reached this delightful valley, they sailed along the coast, which was of high cliffs, without finding any place to go ashore, except at a stream that thrusts a rock out into the sea, where they could land as at a quay. There the captain ordered his friend Gonçalo Aires to go ashore at this stream with certain companions and to walk inland some distance, to see whether there were any animals or creatures, serpents or venomous snakes, and not to stray from the watercourse, so that they would know how to return to the boats they had left at sea. Gonçalo Aires went with his companions, ranging over the land for the space of three hours, at the end of which the captain was already growing vexed at their delay, when lo, they appeared coming down the stream with garlands on their heads, decked with branches, talking with great delight, for they had found no living thing but birds; and from this the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires took its name.’

Elsewhere, speaking of some of Zarco’s companions, he says ‘that came in his company. . . had children, many lands and properties which they acquired, and a most noble lineage, as was that of Gonçalo Aires, from whom descends the family that on the island of Madeira is called the great’.

Gonçalo Aires held vast lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), stretching from the stream that came to bear his name as far as the Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) stream and reaching up to the ridges of the uplands. Besides giving his name to that stream, he also gave it to the street now known as Rua do Carmo (‘Carmel’), which then ran from the church to the bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’).

In the article on Canon Jerónimo Dias Leite we have already referred to the account of the discovery of this archipelago attributed to Gonçalo Aires. On this subject the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says: ‘He (the sixth captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal) kept in his study the Discovery of the Island of Madeira, the most truthful yet found, which they say was written by Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, who went to discover that same island with the first Captain, João Gonçalves Zargo; and since this Discovery belonged to the Captains of the same island, they kept it in their studies as a thing inherited from descendant to descendant. And when information about this island of Madeira was requested, on my behalf, from the Reverend Canon of the Cathedral of Funchal, Jerónimo Dias Leite, he, having seen it in the possession of the said Captain João Gonçalves da Câmara, sent to ask him for it in Lisbon, where he then was; and the Captain had it copied by his chamberlain Lucas de Sá, and sent it to him written on three sheets of paper in the said chamberlain’s hand; and by his letter (because the discovery makes no mention of this) he sent word that Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, who had been one of the servants whom Zargo, the first Captain, took there with him, wrote down all that he saw with his own eyes, and, as he was neither a learned nor a lettered man, set it down in a rough style, with nothing else added’.

Gonçalo Aires was the son of Gomes Ferreira and Isabel Pereira de Lacerda. He came to this island already married at the beginning of the colonisation, and from his marriage he had twin children, who were the first people born on Madeira and were therefore named Adão and Eva (Adam and Eve). For this reason the name of Gonçalo Aires is bound up with the earliest settlement of the archipelago, and he was also the founder of a distinguished and numerous line of descendants. He was the first here to bear the surname Ferreira, and he and his descendants used the following arms: ‘on a field gules four bars or; crest, an emu proper holding a horseshoe or in its beak’.

In the manuscript *Noticias das cousas da Ilha da Madeira desde o seu segundo descobrimento pelo Zarco* (see Elements for Madeiran History) we read the following, which we hold to be true: ‘Gonçalo Aires had many lands in Funchal and the best valleys there, such as the whole of Vale Formoso. He was much loved and cherished by Captain Zargo, being a person of standing and a knight of the Infante’s household; and when he died, Zargo had him buried in Nossa Senhora de Cima, in the chancel, which was the family vault he had made for himself, his wife and children’.

The surname was also used by Brás Ferreira, to whom we have already referred in the article on the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), and of whom we do not know whether he was a descendant of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira.
Ferreira (Nicolau)

Several canvases bearing the signature of the painter Nicolau Ferreira can be found in some churches of this diocese, but we have been unable to find any information about him. We have reason to believe that these paintings were made on this island and that they date from the end of the 17th century.
Ferreira Passos (José Gerardo)
On 14 June 1854 he was appointed civil governor of this district, taking office on the 25th of the same month and year, and he served at the same time as military commander of Madeira.
He served in the liberating army and greatly distinguished himself in many engagements. He held the rank of divisional general, was a peer of the realm and held the portfolio of war.
He was born in Elvas on 11 November 1801 and died in Lisbon on 12 April 1870.
Ferreira Pestana (Daniel)

He was born in Funchal on 13 October 1824 and died in the city of Nova Goa in November 1906, the son of Manuel Ferreira Pestana and Dona Vicência Rosa de Jesus Guedes Pestana. His first wife was the mother of the Count of Nova Goa, and his second the Countess of Torres Novas. In 1845 he accompanied his uncle, Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Ferreira Pestana (see that entry), to India as his aide-de-camp, and he spent a considerable part of his life there. He followed a military career: he was commissioned second lieutenant (*alferes*) in 1844 and died with the rank of general. In Portuguese India, where he was held in the highest regard and where his qualities of character and intelligence were much appreciated, he carried out various important public-service assignments. In the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) he also held some distinguished posts, such as that of aide-de-camp to Marshal Saldanha, whose well-known martial bearing he is said to have imitated. He contributed to several newspapers and published in India a grammar textbook, which is listed in the *Diccionario Bibliographico Portuguez* under the title *Principios de grammatica geral applicada á lingua portuguesa, publicados e offerecidos á mocidade de Nova Goa*, Nova Goa, 1848, XII-196 pp. Not long ago an educated person who had lived for some years in Portuguese India informed us that this work was a slavish imitation of the work of Francisco de Andrade, published in Funchal in 1844, but we have not had the opportunity to verify this.

Pestana was one of the most illustrious Madeirans of the 19th century. He distinguished himself remarkably as a soldier, as a teacher and man of science, as a politician and statesman, and no less as a man of the most austere integrity, bequeathing to his descendants a prestigious name that fully commanded the regard of all his compatriots. His biography is long, and we shall try to condense it into a few lines so as not to give this article excessive breadth.

He was the son of Manuel Ferreira Pestana, captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), and of his wife Dona Ana Teresa Sousa Pestana, and was born there on 26 March 1795. After completing his preparatory studies in Funchal and enlisting in the artillery battalion of that city, he left for Coimbra in 1815 to enrol in the faculties of philosophy and mathematics of the University. Ferreira Pestana’s academic life was an unbroken series of triumphs, which earned him a proposal from the university congregation concerned to receive the degrees of licentiate and doctor free of charge; he received the doctoral hood (*capelo*) in the faculty of mathematics on 3 July 1820. Returning to his native island, where he spent some time teaching a chair of mathematics, he later settled in Coimbra to serve as assistant at the astronomical observatory and to prepare for the competitive examination for a university teaching post. The civil conflicts forced him to leave Coimbra, and it was only in 1834, by decree of 14 July of that year, that he was appointed professor in the faculty of mathematics.

As soon as the movement of reaction against the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government took shape, Dr Ferreira Pestana, as a lieutenant of the academic corps, joined it. He thereby exposed himself to persecution by the followers of absolutism, and was arrested and taken to the prisons of the city of Porto, where he remained for a long time. Caught in the net of the special judicial commission (*alçada*) that the Count of Basto sent there, he was sentenced on 9 April 1829 to perpetual penal exile (*degredo*), with the death penalty should he ever attempt to return to Portugal. By the same sentence ten of Ferreira Pestana’s fellow prisoners were condemned to death, and by order of the judges of the commission he was also made to witness the execution of the unfortunate condemned men in the Praça Nova. The sentence was carried out on 9 May 1829. Dressed in the white robe of the condemned and with the rope around his neck, Ferreira Pestana walked three times around the gallows and witnessed the death of the ten wretched men, victims of the tyranny of Miguel I. A witness of the time relates that Dr Ferreira Pestana, not wishing to watch the horrible spectacle of the execution, lowered his head and closed his eyes, but one of the executioner’s assistants struck him a violent blow across the face and forced him to look at the scaffold.

Ferreira Pestana was not executed in the Praça Nova, as his fellow countryman and friend Dr José Martiniano da Fonseca and the other condemned men were, because the boundless devotion of his wife, Dona Maria Lecor, carried to the point of heroism, succeeded in freeing him from the bloodthirsty hands of the executioners. She went to Lisbon to implore the clemency of the king and his ministers on her husband’s behalf. She could not obtain an audience with Miguel I, but she managed to have the Infanta Dona Maria da Assunção receive her kindly and yield to her pleas and her tears. Through the Infanta’s intervention, Dona Maria Lecor was able to approach various authorities and obtain from them several letters of recommendation to the judges of the commission. Some received her kindly, but others were filled with indignation, telling her that her husband was a great *malhado* (derogatory nickname for a liberal under the Miguelist regime), deserving of the severest punishment. Her tears and heroic devotion were not in vain, however, for the sentence spared Dr Ferreira Pestana from climbing the steps of the gallows. His devoted wife accompanied her husband as he walked around the scaffold, and afterwards followed him into exile.

After the execution of his companions, Ferreira Pestana was returned to the prisons of Porto, and shortly afterwards was sent to Lisbon, where he was committed to the notorious dungeons of São Julião da Barra. He remained there for some time, suffering the horrors that the notorious Teles Jordão inflicted on the prisoners of those cells. In 1829 he left Lisbon for Luanda to serve the sentence of penal exile imposed on him by the Porto commission. In Angola, Ferreira Pestana and other political deportees managed to charter a ship secretly, which, despite the risk of the undertaking, succeeded in carrying them to the city of Rio de Janeiro. In the capital of Brazil, to earn his living, he founded a school, of which he was director and which gained great renown there.

When constitutional government was restored, Ferreira Pestana returned home and resumed his place in the army. He also began teaching his chair in the Faculty of Mathematics, to which he had been appointed by decree of 14 July 1834. He seems not to have been very assiduous as a professor, because active political life and the various posts he held did not allow him to stay long in Coimbra. In 1834, while still in Rio de Janeiro, he was elected deputy for Estremadura. He represented Madeira in the legislative sessions of 1836, 1837–1838, 1838–1840, 1840–1842 and 1851–1852, and was also deputy for Coimbra. At a time when only men of recognised merit held the office of civil governor, Ferreira Pestana headed the districts of Vila Real, Leiria and Coimbra. In 1841 he was called to the councils of the Crown, serving as Minister of the Navy from July of that year to February of the following year. He returned to the ministry in 1851, holding the portfolio of the Kingdom. From then on he always refused to join the government, despite the many appeals made to him on various occasions. By royal letter (*carta régia*) of 30 December 1862 he was appointed a peer of the realm.
