Ferreira Pestana’s administration of the districts in which he served as civil governor was brief and passed unnoticed. The same was not true in India, where he was governor-general of that state at a time when the traditions of the viceroys, and the honours and privileges they had enjoyed, were still very much alive. Although the office had already been abolished, Ferreira Pestana was widely known, and particularly on this island, as the Viceroy of India. He twice held that office, then so exalted, and showed not only the qualities of a true statesman but also his eminent gifts of character, above all the impartiality and justice with which he shaped every act of his administration. It is impossible here to go into details and recount facts that would take us very far. We cannot, however, resist mentioning an event that occurred during his second government of India, which won great renown at the time and whose echoes resounded with great admiration in Europe. Near Goa, but in British territory, the *fondus* rose in insurrection against English rule. The revolt was crushed after a hard-fought struggle lasting many months, in which the British troops suffered serious reverses. A considerable number of rebels and their families took refuge in Portuguese territory, laying down their arms and asking for the protection of our flag. The protests and demands of the Governor of Bombay and the Governor-General in Calcutta for the surrender of the insurgents were forceful and full of threats. Ferreira Pestana, however, invoking the law of nations and moved by the most just and elementary feelings of humanity, flatly refused to hand them over. The negotiations lasted some months. In the end, the dispatch of British troops to the Portuguese frontier, and an English warship anchored at Goa with its gunports open and its guns trained on the governor’s palace, made it plain that the matter was to be settled by force and that Portugal would once again suffer humiliation and affront at the hands of her faithful ally. Meanwhile Colonel Ontiani appeared in Goa and, in the name of the Governor-General of British India, demanded the immediate surrender of the refugees. Ferreira Pestana simply replied that he would not hand over the insurgents who had sheltered under the Portuguese flag, and that if they were seized and taken by force to English territory, the governor and representative of Portugal would go among them. In this way he highlighted, and set in sharp relief, the violence that the government of British India intended to commit. This firmness and pride, which neither threats nor dangers could bend, daunted the English, and the matter was later settled amicably between the governments of the two home countries.
Councillor José Ferreira Pestana, who had retired in 1875 with the rank of general, died in Lisbon on 12 June 1885, at the full age of 90.

For the biography of this illustrious Madeiran, the pamphlets *José Ferreira Pestana, apontamentos biográficos*, by V. Esteves, Nova Goa, 1855, and *Duas palavras sobre a India Portuguesa em relação ao Sr. conselheiro José Ferreira Pestana, ao Sr. conselheiro José Joaquim Lopes Lima e a Custódio M. Gomes*, Lisbon, 1848, may be consulted.
Ferreiro de Fora (peak)
A height close to the preceding one.
Ferreiro (peak)
The Pico do Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s peak’) lies not far from the Encumeada de São Vicente (‘São Vicente ridge pass’).
Ferreiros

A small locality (*sítio*), also called Quinta dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’ estate’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), where there was a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Penha (Our Lady of Penha), built in 1682 by Dr Manuel Fernandes Gomes.
Ferreiros (street)

This is one of the busiest streets in Funchal, running from Rua 5 de Outubro to the Ponte do Torreão (‘turret’). In former times the name Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’) applied only to the part of the street running from its beginning to the so-called Largo do Chafariz, or Largo de São Sebastião. In relatively recent times, the section between the Largo do Chafariz and the Largo do Colégio (*Colégio*, ‘College’) was still called Rua do Peru; the section between the College and Rua dos Netos was called Rua do Estudo; and the section from Rua dos Netos to the Torreão was called Rua do Pinheiro (‘pine tree’). The name Ferreiros must certainly have come from the presence there of a number of blacksmiths’ workshops. ‘Christovão Martim de Agrinhão,’ says an old nobiliary, ‘was a *fidalgo* of the Household of Jaime, Duke of Braganza, and came to this island from Peru, in the Spanish Indies, and was therefore called o Peru, a name he gave to the street where he lived.’ For many years the Jesuits held their classes in Rua dos Ferreiros, and after their expulsion the so-called Aulas do Pátio continued there; the lyceum (state secondary school) was also installed there in 1837. This amply explains the name Estudo (‘Study’) given to part of the street. Frutuoso, speaking of Rua Direita (‘straight street’), says that ‘it is the largest in the city, and leads to the Pinheiro, which is a tree standing at its end, the largest and most beautiful in the city’. It should be noted that, although the Pinheiro stood on the left bank of the stream, the place known by that name extended to the right bank. It should also be borne in mind that a considerable part of the present Rua dos Ferreiros ran alongside the stream, rather than at a distance from it as it does today.
In more remote times, a part of this street near the former Largo do Chafariz bore the names of Simão Acciaioly and of Pedro or Pero Bettencourt.
On 19 November 1915 Rua dos Ferreiros was renamed Rua do Comércio.
Iron

Large quantities of this mineral are found in the archipelago, but in compounds not worth mining. Where it occurs in higher concentrations, it is only in tiny veins, such as the beautiful plates of specular iron in the cliff overlooking the Cais da Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), and in the inner linings of lava tubes, as in the caves of Cavalum, in Machico, and the cave of Cardais (‘thistle patches’), in São Vicente.

It is owing to iron salts that most of the rocks on our slopes break down. This is how new soils (*poios*) are prepared: the rocks are left to crumble under the action of natural agents, and the soil is then retained in small cultivation terraces.

Iron gives the greyish-brown colour to the coatings of basalt blocks and the red colour to the soils known as *massapês* (red clayey soil), and it also produces the laterites that streak the rocks, especially along the coast, sandwiched between two basalt layers.

It is found in granular form among the tuffs at Canhas, in cellular form at Madalena do Mar (‘Magdalene by the sea’), and in lamellar form over clays at Sant’Ana and São Jorge, looking like scrap iron, and dissolved in the water of some springs, such as the Jamboto spring in Santo António. S.
Ferro (islet)
The Ilhéu de Ferro (‘iron islet’) lies to the south-west of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), from which it is separated by a narrow channel. Altitude 115 m.
Wheat rust

Yellow and eventually black spots that appear on the leaves of wheat and other cereals. These spots are produced by the spores of *Puccinia rubigo-vera* breaking through the leaf tissue. Rust impairs the functions of the leaves and can reduce harvests.
Arbour Day

The first Arbour Day held in Funchal was organised by the Primary Education Inspectorate and took place on 29 March 1914, at 11 a.m. The procession set out from the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’) for the Campo da Barca (‘boat field’), or Campo de Miguel Bombarda, where some exotic tree species were ceremonially planted. Several speeches were made on the occasion, in which the speakers urged those present, and the children in particular, to regard trees as sacred objects because of the great benefits they bring us.

The trees solemnly planted on 29 March 1914 had withered a few months later, for nobody gave them another thought once the organisers of the festival and the people who had graced it with their presence had left the Campo da Barca!
Feto abrum (Dicksonia culcita)

A very rare fern in Madeira, now found only in the Montado dos Pessegueiros (‘peach-tree pasture’) and in the uplands of Boaventura. Its rhizomes are covered with soft, rust-coloured hairs, which were used in former times to stuff mattresses and pillows.
Feto de botão (Woodwardia radicans)
A common fern in the valleys and ravines of the north and interior of Madeira. Near the tips of its fronds it produces rooting buds.
Ferns

Forty-one native ferns and 4 naturalised ones are known in the Madeira archipelago; these 45 species comprise 1 Cyatheacea, 3 Hymenophyllaceae, 40 Polypodiaceae and 1 Ophioglossacea. Of the 40 Polypodiaceae, 36 are native and 4 naturalised. *Dicksonia culcita*, Herit. (*feto abrum*), is a beautiful Cyatheacea that is common only in the Montado dos Pessegueiros (‘peach-tree pasture’); *Davallia canariensis* (*cabrinha*), *Adiantum reniforme*, *Pteris arguta*, *Pteridium aquilinum* (bracken), *Woodwardia radicans* (*feto de botão*), *Athyrium Filix-foemina*, *Asplenium Adianthum-nigrum*, *Polystichum aculeatum*, *Nephrodium Filix-mas*, etc. etc., are Polypodiaceae common in Madeira. Complete lists of the ferns of the Madeira archipelago are given in the *Flora do Arquipelago da Madeira* by C. A. Meneses (Funchal, 1914) and in *Madeira Ferns* by the same author (Funchal, 1906).
*Few (A) plain words to visitors to the Island of Madeira on the present position of the English Church there. . . by a visitor.* Funchal, 1848, 19 pp.
Tokens

The *Almanach de lembranças Madeirense* for the year 1908 published an article entitled ‘Fichas Madeirenses’, written by our fellow Madeiran Dr Carlos da Silva Carvalho, an official of the Lisbon Customs House (*Alfândega de Lisboa*). With due acknowledgement we transcribe it below, since it is the most complete work on the subject known to us:

‘Tokens (*fichas* or *tentos*) are so closely bound up with the commercial development of this island – whether used to make change easier at times when small coin was scarce, or to pay the ox-cart drivers and wine-skin carriers for their haulage, who at the end of each week exchanged them for current money – that we consider a brief account of those substitutes now known to be of some interest. It enlarges a survey published some time ago in the *Diario de Noticias* of this city.

The earliest known tokens date from the end of the 18th century, and, it is to his credit, it was a Madeiran, the merchant J. F. Esmeraldo, who first introduced them into fiduciary circulation. Other commercial houses subsequently took advantage of the same benefits, such as Vicente d'Oliveira & Companhia, Phelps, Page & C.°, Colson, Smith & Robinson, Diogo Adams, etc.

Little by little their use became widespread, and today it is rare to find a commercial house of any importance, or a club where gambling takes place, that has not struck them. The public places such confidence in these little pieces of brass, copper, zinc and even tinplate that almost everyone accepts them, sure that they represent money. Witness the curious tokens of the Count of Calçada (‘paved way’), Diogo d'Ornelas Frazão (a seal on sealing wax, D. O. F., and the value), which circulate among the numerous stewards of that same opulent house in the town (*vila*) of Calheta (‘small cove’).
Besides the list we publish below, we know that many other houses struck them, but neglect and the greedy crucibles of the foundries have left us no trace of them.

In the German newspaper *Munz Blatter* the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz published a short note on Madeiran tokens, and Major Alberto Altur Sarmento also dealt with the same subject in an article that appeared in the now-defunct *Diário do Commercio* (‘Commercial Daily’) of Funchal.
Figueira

Pedro Figueira, a native of the island of Faial and son of João Figueira and Aldonça Fernandes, was one of the first on this island to bear this surname, having settled here around 1500. One of his sons, named Manuel Figueira, founded an entail on this island. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo gives these men the name Figueiró, but in various books of nobility we have found the surname Figueira applied to the individuals mentioned above; the same commentator on the *Saudades* adds that he does not know who first introduced this surname to the island. It is certain that Álvaro Figueira was also one of the first settlers of Madeira and held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’).
Indian fig (Ficus comosa)

A handsome tree cultivated in the *quintas* (country estate) and in some of the squares of Funchal. It belongs to the family Urticaceae and has evergreen leaves of a lovely green, and small syconia that never fully ripen.

It is said that the first Indian fig tree in Madeira came on a ship bound for Europe that was wrecked in the harbour of Funchal at the end of the 18th century. A sailor from that ship managed to bring the fig tree ashore, and it was planted in the grounds of Quinta Vigia (‘lookout’), where it lived for many years and became the parent stock of all the specimens of the same species that later appeared on the island.
Figueira do Inferno

Three species are known by this name in Madeira, two of them native and one cultivated. The native species are *Euphorbia mellifera* and *E. piscatoria*, the latter always shrubby, the former sometimes tree-like; the cultivated species is *Ficus stipulata*, much used to cover walls, which is also known as *figueira do diabo* (devil’s fig). *Euphorbia mellifera*, known in some parts of the island as *alindres* or *alhendros*, is found at Achadas da Cruz, Seixal, Ribeiro Frio, etc.; *E. piscatoria* is common on coastal ground. The latex produced by the cut branches of this last species is used by fishermen to blind or stun the fish found in rock pools by the sea.
Figueira (Dr João Joaquim)
He graduated in 1837 from the faculty of medicine at Montpellier, defending the thesis *Etude de l'accouchement premature artificiel*, which he printed as a pamphlet of 59 pp.

He rendered notable services in France during an epidemic of cholera morbus, for which he was awarded a medal of honour. In Madeira, where he practised medicine for many years, he was municipal physician to the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*). He died in 1859 or shortly afterwards.
Fig tree (Ficus carica)

A tree native to the Mediterranean region, widely cultivated in Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). The most prized Madeiran figs are the *doces*, the *martinhos*, the *brancos*, the *cotios* and the *beberas*, the last being distinguished from the rest by their black colour and elongated shape. Figs that pass the winter in a rudimentary state and develop early the following year are called *lampos*.

At Serra de Dentro (‘inner upland’), on the island of Porto Santo, there is a large fig tree which is said to have been planted by the early colonists. It is without any doubt the oldest tree on the neighbouring island.
Figueira (Father António da Silva)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) on 13 June 1887. After completing his studies at the seminary (*Seminário*) of this diocese, he was ordained priest in the bishopric of Portalegre in November 1912, and has since carried out parish duties in several parishes of this island. Besides various contributions in prose and verse to a number of newspapers, in 1914 he published a volume of poems entitled *Columbario*, of 89 pp.
Figueiredo
This surname derives from Pedro Lopes de Figueiredo, who lived in Machico and Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) at the beginning of the 16th century.
Figueiredo e Lemos (Dom Luís de)

Among the prelates who distinguished themselves in the episcopal government of this diocese, the name of Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos, 7th bishop of Madeira, Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and Arguin, stands out.
He was born on the small island of Santa Maria in the Azores archipelago on 21 August 1544, the son of Miguel Figueiredo de Lemos and Dona Luiz Nunes Velho, who were highly respected people there.

After his first studies on his native island, he went to the city of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), where he devoted himself to the humanities and preparatory studies so that he could take a university course at Coimbra. He studied in the faculties of canon law and civil law, graduating as bachelor in both, and in one of them he sat the licentiate examination.

He returned to the island of São Miguel, already ordained priest and preceded by a reputation as a learned and virtuous man. There he held the post of ecclesiastical judge (*ouvidor eclesiástico*), and he was later appointed dean of Angra Cathedral (*Sé de Angra*) and later still vicar general and governor of that bishopric.
In 1585 he was presented as bishop of Funchal, and he was confirmed by the Holy See early in 1586, arriving in Madeira on 4 August of the same year.

His episcopate was highly fruitful, thanks to the many reforms he introduced into numerous church services, above all in the administration of the parishes. Abuses there were widespread: pastors abandoned their parishes, there were no parish houses, the registers of religious events were not properly kept, many churches were in an advanced state of ruin, etc. He dealt with all these ills energetically and effectively, and he achieved this chiefly through the pastoral visitations he made to every church in the diocese.

The old bishop’s palace, a considerable part of which still survives, and the adjoining chapel of São Luís (St Louis), now deconsecrated, were built through his efforts and diligence. Next to the palace, and also in its outbuildings, he established the diocesan seminary, whose direction and growth received his special care.

He convened a diocesan synod in 1587, at which new diocesan constitutions were promulgated, to be joined to the Constitutions ordered by Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto; they were printed in Lisbon in 1601.

He re-established the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), which had been abolished, gave new regulations (*regimento*) to the cathedral chapter of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), increased the parish stipends, entirely reformed the episcopal chancery and reorganised many other church services. All this earned him the title of an eminently reforming prelate, and he left the most honourable traditions in the chronicles of this bishopric. It should be added that he led a life of great austerity, that his conduct was impeccable, and that he was irreproachable in the administration of all the affairs of his diocese.

He died in this city on 26 November 1608 and was buried in the chapel of São Luís, which he had built next to the bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*). As this chapel had been deconsecrated, the late lamented Bishop Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto had the prelate’s remains transferred to the Cathedral in 1903. They were interred inside the draught porch and covered with the carved marble slab that had lain over his tomb in the said chapel of São Luís.
Figueiroa de Albuquerque (Luís)

He was born in this city on 4 February 1828 and died in Caniço (‘reed’) on 13 December 1904, the son of Lieutenant-Colonel Luís Agostinho Figueiroa de Albuquerque and Dona Maria Vicência de Freitas Bettencourt. He was a man of uncommon learning, acquired chiefly during his long residence abroad, and especially in the French capital. He devoted himself above all to economic studies, publishing a volume on the subject and many articles scattered through the newspapers. He held the posts of president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, secretary-general of this district and of that of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Misericórdia of this city and member of the former District Council (*Conselho de Distrito*), and he also served for a time as acting civil governor of this archipelago. He contributed to the former newspaper *O Povo* and to other periodicals, and published separately the two volumes *Tratado Elementar de Economia Politica*, 171 pp., and *Compêndio Elementar do Novo Systema Geral de Pesos e Medidas*, 166 pp.
Figueiroa (Francisco Anacleto de)

He was a colonel of the militia (*milícias*) and died in Funchal in 1810. We know nothing about him that would make him worthy of mention, but the horrible death he met at the bottom of a tomb deserves special record here. In an official document we came across the following information: ‘Francisco Anacleto de Figueiroa, colonel of the militia, was taken for dead in Funchal, where he lived. He was carried to the burial vault (*carneiro*) of João Gonçalves Zarco in the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*). Years later, another death in the family made it necessary to open the vault, and there, beside the heavy iron grille at the entrance, at the gloomy foot of the stairway, lay the skeleton of Figueiroa, clutching the bars in a last despair of atrocious agony.’
Sons and sons-in-law of Zarco

The old Madeiran books of nobility state that the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco had three sons and four daughters: João Gonçalves da Câmara, Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara, Helena Gonçalves da Câmara, Beatriz Gonçalves da Câmara, Isabel Gonçalves da Câmara and Catarina Gonçalves da Câmara. The genealogists do not agree, however, on where some of these children were born. Several assert – and this is the most widely held opinion – that when Gonçalves Zarco settled in Madeira with his wife, Dona Constança de Sá, he brought with him his eldest son, who was heir to the house, and his daughter Dona Helena Gonçalves da Câmara. It seems that the first child born on this island was Rui Gonçalves da Câmara. We have already dealt with him and with João Gonçalves da Câmara, the second donatary of Funchal, in this *Elucidário*. The books of lineages give Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara as a natural son of the discoverer. He always enjoyed his father’s most particular affection and was a wealthy heir of his. He married the daughter of Nuno Cardoso, founder of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of São João de Latrão, in Gaula, and succeeded to the administration of this entailed house (*casa vinculada*).

From the two legitimate sons, João Gonçalves da Câmara, 2nd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, and Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd captain-donatary of the island of São Miguel, descend some of the most distinguished families of Portugal, such as the Counts of Vila Franca and of Atouguia, the Marquises of Ribeira Grande, the Counts of Tarouca, the Marquises of Castelo Melhor and others.

When Gonçalves Zarco asked Afonso V to send him some persons of quality to marry his daughters, the monarch replied in the following terms: ‘Herewith I send you four noblemen to marry your daughters; and if you endow them according to their qualities, I shall hold you much honoured and them well endowed.’ These noblemen, marrying the daughters of the illustrious discoverer, became the founders of numerous lines of descendants, and all of them established important entailed houses on this island.

Helena da Câmara, the eldest daughter, married Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, who settled in São Martinho (‘St Martin’), on the left bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos, where he held a great deal of land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and also in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’). He was buried in the church of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), and the learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says of this: ‘in the church of the convent of Santa Clara in Funchal, at the entrance on the right-hand side, stands the sarcophagus of this Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, with an inscription in Gothic capitals, illegible from wear; but in the adjoining pavilion there is a large marble slab bearing the following epitaph:

Tomb of Captain Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcelos, which he had made for himself and his heirs, because the first gravestone placed here was removed, as a descendant of the first Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, who lies here and came to this island to marry Helena Gonçalves da Câmara, daughter of João Gonçalves Zarco, its discoverer. It was made in the year 1710

This is the tomb said to be that of João Gonçalves Zarco, and it is reproduced as such in engravings in many works, chiefly foreign ones. It is worth mentioning here that the discoverer was buried beside the altar steps of the chancel. An old manuscript states ‘that the work was so arranged that Zarco’s grave lay in the middle of the chancel, with a stone tomb above it so tall that it made it singularly venerable and imposing’. It is said that many years later the nuns obtained the removal of the showy mausoleum, which blocked their view of the altar, and it was perhaps on that occasion that the ashes of the discoverer of Madeira were transferred to the family vault of his son-in-law Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos. It is certain that in March 1919, when the floorboards of the chancel of the church of the Convent of St Clare were lifted, only the tombstones of the second, third and fifth captain-donataries of Funchal were found. Had the mortal remains of Gonçalves Zarco lain there, the gravestone of his tomb would probably have been discovered. But was the transfer really made? And when did it take place? We do not know.

Dona Brites or Beatriz Gonçalves da Câmara, Zarco’s second daughter, married Diogo Cabral, son of Fernão Alves Cabral, chief health officer (*guarda-mor*) to Prince Henry the Navigator. Diogo Cabral held vast lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Calheta (‘small cove’), granted to him by his father-in-law. He fulfilled Zarco’s vows and wishes by building in that parish (*freguesia*) the chapel of Our Lady of the Star (*Nossa Senhora da Estrela*) (see that entry). He died on 15 December 1486 and was buried in the chapel he had founded, which he made the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). The discoverer’s third daughter was Isabel Gonçalves da Câmara, who married Diogo Afonso de Aguiar; Henriques de Noronha says ‘that the dowry which I saw was drawn up in the year 1439’. According to some, he was the son of José Afonso de Aguiar, first treasurer of the Lisbon mint, and according to others, of Pedro de Aguiar, who belonged to an old and noble family of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). He held many lands by *sesmaria* on this island. His son, Dom Martinho de Aguiar, was Bishop of Ceuta and Tangier.

Garcia Homem de Sousa was the *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) who married Catarina Gonçalves da Câmara, Zarco’s fourth daughter. Old chronicles say that he was a turbulent man and that he had waged bloody feuds with his brothers-in-law. In the locality (*sítio*) of Santo Amaro (‘St Maurus’), in the parish of Santo António, he had a large settled estate (*fazenda povoada*), and there he built a chapel with that dedication (see Santo Amaro).
Phylloxera

The phylloxera invasion of Madeira, says F. de Almeida e Brito in a report published in 1883, was confirmed in 1872. By then many vineyards had already been lost and land laid completely waste in the municipalities of Funchal and Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), which suggests that the disease had been present here since 1865 at least. According to the same agronomist, the pest was brought to Madeira in cuttings of the Isabella, or American vine, which had been admitted to cultivation because of its proven resistance to oidium or *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium). This opinion was shared by many of the island’s winegrowers, who had closely followed the course and development of the new disease.

Madeirans had several times asked the government to provide them with the means to resist the terrible scourge that was devastating the island’s vineyards, but only in 1883 were these requests partly granted. In June of that year inspector Almeida e Brito was sent here, and he immediately launched a campaign against phylloxera, assisted by some landowners, by the livestock intendant (*intendente de pecuária*) Salvador Gamito de Oliveira and by the president of the District Anti-Phylloxera Committee (Comissão Distrital), the late João de Sales Caldeira.

In 1873 a British subject had applied resin and oil of turpentine, dissolved in hot water, to the roots of many diseased vines. Although this treatment, aided by generous manuring, produced results, it could not be adopted generally because of what it cost the landowners.

In February 1883 carbon disulphide was applied for the first time in some Madeiran vineyards, and this method of treatment was afterwards adopted throughout the island in order to save the plantations that still survived. On the recommendation of the said inspector, a treatment post was set up on a property at the top of São João, with an attached store of carbon disulphide and injectors. It was found that vines which still showed considerable vigour always improved with the use of this insecticide, which was applied at doses of 28 and 24 grams per square metre in simple treatment.

To make it possible to replant the devastated land with reliable American hybrids and stocks, two nurseries of cuttings and rooted vines were set up, one at Ribeirinho (‘little brook’) and the other at Torreão (‘turret’), and as early as 1883 some 60,000 young vines were distributed among the island’s landowners. Riparia, Jacquez, Herbemont, Rupestris, Solonis, Taylor, Clinton, Elsimbro and York Madeira were the first stocks grown in these nurseries; they were followed by Cunningham, Viala, Elvira, Othello, Cinerea, Black Pearl and Gaston Bazile. According to Inspector Almeida e Brito in his report, Taylor was the stock that could be used with greatest confidence in Madeira, since it had ‘already seven years of trial, growing admirably in phylloxera-infested soils’.

Experience showed that this stock did not adapt as well as others to the island’s soils, and so it was gradually replaced by Riparia, Herbemont, Cunningham and Jacquez. The last of these has long been the preferred rootstock for grafting scions of the European vine.

On examining some very well-made preparations of phylloxera in its various stages, made by the British subject Leacock, Inspector Almeida e Brito found no hibernating insects among them, as there are on the mainland. This led him to conclude that the parasite leads a life of constant activity in Madeira, and that this was why it destroyed the island’s beautiful vineyards with such intensity and speed.

Phylloxera was not known on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) until around 1895, and the stocks on clay soils were the ones it devastated most. On sandy soils few vineyards were attacked by the insect, which was doubtless carried to that island in young vines from Madeira.

According to Inspector Almeida e Brito, the area under vines in 1883 did not exceed 500 hectares, and the harvest could be estimated at 3,500 *pipas*, whereas before the appearance of phylloxera the area had been 2,500 hectares, with production reaching 16,000 *pipas*.

Phylloxera and the galls it produces have long ceased to be observed in Madeiran vineyards, but this does not mean that the dreadful hemipteran has entirely disappeared from our island. The great difficulty of preserving or propagating the old grape varieties, except by grafting them on to resistant hybrids or American stocks, and the appearance of the insect on Porto Santo many years after it had ceased to be recorded in Madeira, lead us to believe that *Phylloxera vastatrix* is not wholly extinct here. It is the cruellest enemy of *Vitis vinifera*, the plant which from the 16th century contributed so much, through its abundant and excellent yields, to fostering the island’s wealth and securing the well-being of many of its inhabitants.

Fischer (Dr S.)
He wrote on the entomostracans of Madeira in the Transactions of the Royal Bavarian Academy of Sciences, 1855.

Flor do Oceano (A)

The first issue appeared on 22 June 1828 and the last on 22 August of the same year. Its editors were Dr Manuel Ferreira de Seabra da Mota e Silva, then *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) on this island, Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses (see that entry) and the lawyer Jean de Béthencourt.

Another newspaper appeared under the same title; it was the first to be published here after the establishment of constitutional government. The first issue is dated 9 November 1834 and the last 29 October 1840. The issues were numbered consecutively up to no. 108, of 23 December 1836. In the following years the numbering was annual.
On 1 September 1860 another newspaper was published under the title *Flor do Oceano*; its last issue, the 353rd, appeared on 31 August 1867.
Flora

As is generally known, plants from almost every country in the world grow side by side in Madeira in close and agreeable company, breathing the same air and lit by the same sun, and the great majority of them need no shelters or greenhouses – a circumstance that at once conveys the excellence of the climate and the kindness of the sky that covers and protects it. The island represents a gathered fragment of the flora of widely differing latitudes: beside the tall, majestic tree species of the tropics grow the humble, low-lying plants of northern regions. In Madeira, as in all mountainous countries with varied climatic conditions, plants are distributed in a more or less characteristic way into distinct zones. In Lowe’s opinion, these zones can be reduced to four. The 1st zone, that of cacti and banana plants, extends from the edge of the ocean to about 200 metres above sea level; the 2nd zone, that of the vine and chestnut trees, covers land at altitudes of 150 to 750 metres; the 3rd zone, that of laurels and heaths, runs from 750 to 1,650 metres; and the 4th zone, that of the high summits, takes in all the elevated points from 1,650 to 1,850 metres. This classification does not exclude other plants that are widespread and predominant within each of these zones. Thus we have sugar cane, whose cultivation is very widespread within the first and part of the second of these zones; the same is true of the vine and of many other plants widely cultivated here. In defining these zones, the role of temperature in the distribution of plants is easily recognised, although numerous facts show that it is not always the only factor fixing the vegetation limits of certain species.

It is beyond dispute that fires and farming have caused the disappearance of many plant species, perhaps abundant before the island was settled. In compensation, however, numerous plants from other countries have become naturalised or acclimatised in Madeira, and some of them have brought changes to its flora that in many cases do not accord with the island’s geographical position. Sugar cane from the East Indies, the vine from Europe and Central Asia, the maritime pine from Europe, the acacias from Australia and the *abundância* from Mexico are species more or less acclimatised or naturalised, and in many places they give the vegetation of our island a character quite at odds with its original one.

The flora of the Madeira archipelago as known today comprises 931 phanerogams, 50 vascular cryptogams, 265 bryophytes and 916 thallophytes. If we set aside the naturalised plants, however, the group or division of the phanerogams is left with only 641 species and that of the vascular cryptogams with 45. Among the phanerogams there are 104 species that we regard as endemic and 55 that are common to the Madeira archipelago and to other groups of Atlantic islands. In other words, of the 641 species that we usually call native, 159 are not found in the nearby continental regions, although they are probably genuine representatives of a flora that once existed there.

In our archipelago 106 native woody plants are known, comprising trees, shrubs and subshrubs. The first two groups, which are the most important, are represented by 34 species: 10 of these are European, 1 is found in Madeira and the Azores, 3 in Madeira, the Azores and the Canary Islands, 11 in Madeira and the Canary Islands, and 9 are peculiar to Madeira, or endemic. These species are distributed among 22 families, 4 of which are not found in Europe, although one of them is represented in the neighbouring empire of Morocco.

While the Madeiran phanerogams and vascular cryptogams can be considered well studied, thanks to the patient research of the Baron of Castelo de Paiva, João M. Moniz, Gilbert Mandon, Lowe, Carlos de Menezes, Father Gonçalves da Costa and others, the same cannot be said of the cellular cryptogams, even though for some of their groups there are works worthy of the highest esteem that greatly ease the identification of species. Mosses, lichens and fungi are the cellular plants that have drawn most attention from collectors. This does not mean, however, that methodical and careful exploration of many parts of the island would not one day lead to the discovery of many species of these same groups not so far recorded in our land.

The distinguished men of science Richard Thomas Lowe, a British subject, and Carlos Azevedo de Meneses, an illustrious Madeiran, were the botanists who studied the flora of this island most extensively. They left substantial and notable works, which have been duly appreciated and praised by the scholars who pursue this scientific speciality.
See Algae, Equisetaceae, Ferns, Fungi, Liverworts, Mosses, Lichens, Lycopodiaceae, Selaginellaceae and Phanerogams.
Florence

This surname descends from João Salviati, a native of Florence who, with several members of his family and other compatriots, joined in defending his homeland against the oppression and tyranny of the Medici around the middle of the 15th century. When they failed, some of them were hanged, while others had to seek safe refuge in exile and flight from the persecution of the Medici’s supporters. An archbishop, João Salviati’s uncle, was hanged from one of the battlements of his palace, while João Salviati found asylum in Madeira from the persecution directed against him. Here he was received with distinction, in recognition of the noble cause he had defended and of his aristocratic descent, and he retained the privileges of nobility he had enjoyed in his homeland. He held lands as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) on the bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), where he settled, and also in the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears the name Florenças today. There one of his descendants, named João Homem de El-Rei, founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*).
Flowers of Madeira

Dr José Leite Monteiro and Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira (see those entries) published two volumes, of 210 and 190 pages, in 1871 and 1872, in which they collected about a hundred poems by Madeiran poets of their own day, under the title ‘Flowers of Madeira’ (*Flores da Madeira*). This collection, a valuable resource for the study of our literature, earned the highest praise from the eminent writer Teófilo Braga in an article reprinted in no. 5 of the newspaper *A lâmpada*, which was published in this city in 1872.
Florosa
In Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and other parishes this name is given to the *papinho* (robin).
Seals

Seals are generally called *lobos marinhos* (‘sea wolves’), and the article on the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (p. 210, vol. 1) explains the reason for the name given to that parish. These amphibious mammals, which once abounded in the seas of our archipelago, have almost entirely disappeared from these waters, and only a few of them have been caught at long intervals. As recently as a few decades ago it was not rare to see them on the neighbouring Desertas (‘deserted islands’), where fishermen hunted them. On this subject it is worth reading p. 79 onwards of A. Artur Sarmento’s book *Mamíferos do Arquipelago da Madeira*.
Focinho de burro (Bellardia trixago)

A plant of the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae), common on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), which has also been found in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana, on Madeira. Its scientific name is *Bellardia trixago*.
Fire from Heaven
On 26 July 1593 this island witnessed a phenomenon of atmospheric incandescence which became known in the Madeiran chronicles as the Fogo do Céu (‘Fire from Heaven’).

On the 24th and 25th of that month the well-known ‘east wind’ – the *leste* (hot, dry easterly wind from Africa) – had blown violently, bringing such intense heat that, in the words of a contemporary witness, ‘there was no living person who . . . would leave the house or open a window, nor could it be endured inside the houses, nor could one stay in them, for the air was so hot that all believed they would perish, and the wind was such that it seemed to burn the very bones, a thing that men had never seen in these parts’.

The heat grew ever more intense, and by nightfall on the 26th the rare but known phenomenon of atmospheric incandescence was clearly visible. At around 11 o’clock it turned into a terrifying fire, which burned all the vegetation and reduced a considerable number of dwellings to a vast mass of embers.

The fire broke out in the houses of Tristão Gomes de Castro; it cannot be determined precisely whether it was caused by the incandescence of the air or by a lightning strike. Within four hours one hundred and fifty dwelling houses burned down, among them those of some of the richest and most important residents of the city. The damage was considerable, above all to crops: the grape harvest was destroyed, the sugar cane fields were also damaged and all the green vegetables were devastated, which together raised the losses to many hundreds of thousands of *cruzados*. Most of the burned houses were of wood, but many held great wealth, and several warehouses also burned, in which thousands of *arrobas* of sugar awaiting shipment were stored.

This was undoubtedly one of the greatest calamities ever to strike Madeira. It occurred only twenty-seven years after the terrible sack and massacre by the French Huguenots, whose consequences were even sadder and more lamentable than those of the dreadful Fire from Heaven.
Fojo

An excavation west of Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), which we have already discussed on p. 230 of vol. 1 of this Elucidário. The sea is visible at the bottom of this excavation, which connects with it through an underground channel.
Folklore

A study of Madeiran folklore, even an elementary one, has yet to be written – one that would bring the beliefs, traditions and popular customs of this archipelago into sharp relief, not only from the narrow viewpoint of the simple songs sung by the people but also in a broader perspective, thus embracing the old regional customs in their most varied and characteristic forms. Meanwhile, we would say that various scattered writings by Adolfo César de Noronha, A. Artur Sarmento, Carlos Santos, E. Antonino Pestana, J. Reis Gomes and the Viscount of Porto da Cruz provide valuable material for such a study. The articles Bucho Encostado, Old Customs, Popular Beliefs, Dress, Legends, Rural Medicine, Evil Eye, Christmas, Processions and Pilgrimage Festivals in this Elucidário also contain a variety of notes and information that could serve the same study.
Folhado (Clethra arborea)

A small tree of the family Ericaceae, common in Camacha and in many other parts of Madeira. It has oblong or oblong-lanceolate leaves, rusty-pubescent on the petioles and on the veins of the underside, and white, fragrant flowers borne in racemes forming a panicle. The young stems and shoots of this tree make excellent walking sticks or staves, much used on the island, and its wood is made into spoons, spindles, etc.
The folhado (Clethra arborea, a native tree) is a tree peculiar to Madeira and is the only species of the genus *Clethra* that grows wild outside the Americas.
Famine in Madeira in 1757

In September 1757 there was famine in Madeira because bread had run short. According to a dispatch from the governor Manuel Saldanha da Gama to Tomé Joaquim da Costa Corte Real, in some parts of the island the people lived only on roots, broom flowers and fruit, but the crisis was short-lived, for by the following November the island was already supplied with cereals. It is curious that the people ate broom flowers when they had many plants, such as watercress, sorrel, *rabaças*, docks and even nettles and sow-thistles, which taste more pleasant than those flowers.
In 1757 potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word) had not yet been introduced to Madeira, but the sweet potato was already grown here, though we do not know whether on as large a scale as at present.
Famine in Madeira in 1846 and 1847

A large part of the Madeiran population died in the horrors of famine during the last three months of 1846 and the first months of 1847. The cause was the failure of the potato (Madeiran *semilha*), then the staple food of the poor, which was destroyed by a disease previously quite unknown on the island. Had the rural population possessed the means to buy other provisions, and had these been plentiful on the island, the crisis that afflicted it would have been less terrible. Unfortunately, however, the potato disease was compounded by a marked fall in the price of wine. This brought destitution to the farmers and smallholders, whose cash income came almost exclusively from selling their must to the merchants.

Fortunately, since the beginning of October 1846 Madeira had been governed by Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, a man who attended to everything with truly remarkable zeal and dedication. It was thanks to the sound measures he adopted at once that the violence of the calamity could be lessened and its duration shortened.

On 15 October 1846 a meeting of the principal authorities and officials of the district, called by the governor, was held in the offices of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*). It was resolved that the three key-holders (*claviculário*, one of the officials each holding a key to the strongbox) of the central treasury should advance up to 1 500$000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for clearing debris from the watercourses. Shortly afterwards the Governor persuaded the Central Relief Committee (*Comissão Central de Auxílios*), set up at the time of the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1842, to apply to the same works the sum of 282,000 *réis* that it still held in its coffers. This made it possible to give work, and therefore a cash income, to a great many men struggling with destitution.

As there was a severe shortage of foodstuffs on the market, Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro had the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of the city authorised to draw from the central treasury the sum needed to buy a large quantity of maize held in store by an English merchant and to distribute it to the people at cost price. At the same time he induced several merchants and some landowners to contribute, each according to his means, to a special fund for buying provisions in countries that could supply them on favourable terms. On that occasion, again at the Governor’s instigation, a committee of 7 members, Portuguese and foreign, was formed in Funchal under the presidency of the Bishop to solicit donations for the destitute. It was agreed that this committee should set up branch committees in every parish to obtain relief in money and in kind and distribute it among the poor.

By 25 May 1847 the city’s merchants and some landowners had raised a fund of 32,500,000 *réis* for the purchase of food. By that date the committee in charge of the fund had brought in the following provisions: in March, 2 *moios* of beans; in April, 100 *moios* of maize, 100 of wheat, 1250 barrels of flour and 194 sacks of rice; and in May, 557.5 *quintais* of maize. Other provisions also reached the city, though not ordered by this committee.

When this committee wound up the sale of the provisions it had acquired, it not only reimbursed the merchants for the sums they had contributed but even realised a surplus of 1,755.55 escudos, which the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) applied in 1848 to the building of the Ponte do Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’).

At the end of February 1847, when food shortages were at their worst, there were even fears of serious unrest, for popular anger ran high against the merchants, who were branded monopolists and enemies of the poor. Fortunately, however, public order was never actually disturbed. A considerable part in this was played by the fact that some of those merchants, fearful of what might befall them, decided to put the maize and wheat they held in store on sale on terms favourable to the public.

On some days in February a large part of the population lived on sugar cane, and steps were taken to stop the mills from crushing it for spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) and molasses.

The treasurers of the parish branch committees often found it difficult to put the money they received to use, because they could find no foodstuffs on sale, or came across only small quantities. It became necessary to distribute rations of meat and fresh fish to those for whom the relief was intended, so that they would not die of hunger.

The extraordinary measures taken by the Governor in drawing money from the central treasury to bring prompt relief to the ills afflicting the people of the archipelago won the Government’s approval. However, when the Governor requested a credit of 30 *contos* (one million réis) for public works in the district, he was allowed to spend only 2,500,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), in addition to the sum already authorised for those works under the credit of the financial year.

To benefit the people of the archipelago, the Government reduced the import duty on foreign-grown wheat to 25 *réis*, and exempted all other cereals, whether as grain or as flour, from payment of the third required for municipal levies by the law of 2 August 1839. These provisions, however, remained in force only until harvest time in the archipelago.

On 1 March the Governor had a further 3 *contos de réis* released from the public treasury for the purchase of food for the truly needy in the various parishes who were unable to work or had no work. On the night of 17 April, at the same Governor’s request, a charity performance was given in the city’s small theatre: the drama by Ducange and Dinaux *Trinta anos ou a vida de um jogador* (‘Thirty Years, or the Life of a Gambler’), which had been rehearsed by Dr Luís da Costa Pereira. On the night of 26 April the same drama was staged again, and on both occasions all the actors gladly agreed to play the parts assigned to them without payment, and even at their own expense.

‘During the famine crisis,’ says Dr Azevedo in the notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), ‘a committee made up of Messrs George Stoddart, John Howard March, George Hasch and Richard Davies raised subscriptions abroad, which produced the following: from Hamburg, 556,520 réis in cash; from Russia, 873,600 réis in cash; from the United States of America, 19,660,780 réis in provisions and 3,215,190 réis in cash; from England and Ireland, 48,000 réis in provisions and 10,073,080 réis in cash. In the British chantry on this island, after a sermon on charity by the Revd T. K. Brown, 464,000 réis in cash were then offered. The committee also asked the English, Americans and Germans on this island for a subscription, which, including the individual gifts of the four members named, produced 2,536,600 réis in cash. The total of these donations, including 54,554 réis in premium on the sovereigns imported, came to 37,482,324 réis.’

Thanks to the outstanding services of Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro, and to the loyal assistance given to this illustrious official by the municipal councils, the administrators of the municipality (*concelho*), the relief committees, various foreigners and even some merchants, the situation of the Madeiran people had already improved considerably by the end of April 1847. Everything returned to normal only later, however, when the subsistence of the population was fully secured by the spread of sweet potato cultivation, the disappearance of the potato disease and the arrival of large quantities of cereals from abroad and from some Portuguese colonies.

The first three months of 1847 were a season of misery and desolation for the Madeirans. Nevertheless, there is no record that anyone managed to amass great wealth at the expense of the people’s misfortunes, as has happened in more recent times, nor that any authority or official failed to do his duty honestly. The right of property was respected, and if some goods rose in price, this was not for want of provident measures taken by the authorities.

On 1 March 1847 the Governor told the Administrators of the Municipality that if the inhabitants of the country parishes dared to come to the city with the criminal intention of forcing the merchants to put on sale maize they supposed was still in the warehouses, ‘he was prepared to punish them very severely, and in such a way that they would remember the lesson for many years’. Yet while he sought to enforce respect for the right of property, he also issued a public notice (*edital*) inviting all cereal merchants who had any maize stored to declare it immediately before the Council, so that it could be ground into flour and put on sale on the terms previously laid down.

Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro showed no indulgence towards anyone where the people’s interests were concerned. It was owing to this that complete calm always prevailed, and that everyone endured without any protest worth mentioning the misfortunes that afflicted Madeira in 1846 and 1847.

The *Collecção de documentos relativos á crise da fome*, published by Servulo Drumond de Meneses in 1848, records all the measures taken by José Silvestre Ribeiro to relieve the people’s sufferings for as long as the crisis lasted. Scholars should turn to that work if they wish to learn in more detail of the benefits the Madeirans owed to that official during the calamitous period the island went through.
See Diseases.
Famine on Porto Santo

The crisis that Madeira went through in 1847 was also felt on the neighbouring island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Relief in kind and in money had to be sent there on several occasions, but even so, ‘the people could certainly not have withstood so great a scourge’, say the *Annais do Porto Santo*, ‘had it not been for the very great abundance of fish, chiefly mackerel, which came to be sold at 50 for half a *tostão* (coin of 100 *réis*)’. There was also famine on Porto Santo in 1802, in 1806, in 1815, in 1816 and in 1829, when relief in kind had to be sent there, and after 1847 the scourge struck the island several more times, for example in 1850, in 1854, in 1855 and in 1883.

During the famine of 1850 the Governor, José Silvestre Ribeiro, took upon himself the responsibility of ordering the money needed to buy 75 *moios* of cereals for the people of the neighbouring island to be drawn from the public coffers. He also persuaded two American warships that had called at the port of Funchal to contribute 8 *moios* of maize for the same purpose.

The prolonged droughts to which Porto Santo is subject are the main cause of the poverty and shortage of food seen there in certain years. When the drought is severe, the harvests are negligible, and this is the greatest of misfortunes in a land where a large part of the population lives solely on what the soil provides.
Fonseca (Dr Augusto de Arzila)

He was born in Funchal on 21 October 1853. In 1883 he graduated in philosophy and mathematics from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), and in 1884 he took his doctorate in the latter of these faculties, having previously completed the infantry course at the Army School (*Escola do Exército*), where he graduated first in his class. On the occasion of his doctorate he published his *These de mathematica pura e applicada*. In 1885 he was appointed substitute professor (*lente substituto*) at the University. He published *Princípios elementares de quaterniões à mecanica*. He died on 17 February 1912.
Fonseca (Dr José Maria Martiniano da)

Anyone moderately versed in the history of our country knows that on 7 May 1829 ten men, victims of the intolerance of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government, were executed in the Praça Nova of the city of Porto. Among them was the Madeiran Dr José Maria Martiniano da Fonseca, as we have already mentioned in the article devoted to Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Ferreira Pestana.

We know little of the life of Dr Martiniano da Fonseca, and had it not been for his tragic death, his name might well have remained entirely unknown to us. He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé in this city on 16 October 1794, the son of José Maria da Fonseca, inspector-general of Agriculture, and of Dona Ricarda Umbelina Spinosa. He graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and practised as a lawyer in Funchal.

A revolutionary junta had been formed in the city of Porto to fight the Miguelite usurpation, and the governor and captain-general of Madeira, José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, wished to join the movement it had launched and to communicate with it directly. For this he needed a capable and wholly trustworthy person who could fully carry out the important and dangerous mission he was about to entrust to him. The choice fell on Dr José Maria da Fonseca, who left Funchal aboard an American ship on 30 June 1829 and entered Porto on the 13th of the following month, by which time the government of Miguel I had already been recognised in that city. The position of the Madeiran governor’s emissary was critical. When he tried to approach the high court judge (*desembargador*) Caldeira Velez, secretary of the revolutionary Junta, he was arrested on suspicion and taken to the prisons of the High Court of Appeal (*Relação*). A search of his lodgings and the papers found there, which were the correspondence of Travassos Valdez, turned those suspicions into certainty.

Dr José Martiniano da Fonseca was now irretrievably lost. After nine months in prison he was tried together with other defendants, and on 9 April 1829 sentence was pronounced, condemning ten of them to the ultimate penalty and others to various punishments. The iniquitous and revolting sentence was carried out on 7 May of that year. Two gallows were erected in the square of the Praça Nova, and there the ten defendants suffered capital punishment, Dr José Martiniano da Fonseca being the eighth to climb the steps of the gallows. To carry out the sentence in full, the victims’ heads were cut off and placed at various points in the city. That of Dr Fonseca was exposed for three days at São João da Foz, and on 12 May the brotherhood of the Misericórdia (the charitable Holy House of Mercy) took it to its chapel and had it buried there together with the mortal remains of the other defendants sacrificed to the ferocity of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government. Seven years later, on 6 February 1836, the ashes of those victims were exhumed; they were all gathered into an urn and reburied in the church of the Misericórdia, awaiting the opportunity of a more fitting and appropriate tomb. It was in 1875 that an elegant mausoleum was raised in the Prado do Repouso (‘meadow of rest’) Cemetery, within the precinct belonging to the Misericórdia of Porto, to hold the mortal remains of the men executed on 7 May 1829 and of two more who suffered the same penalty on 9 October of the same year. The translation of the last remains of these victims, who became known as the Twelve Martyrs of the Fatherland, was marked by an unusual and most brilliant grandeur. A funeral procession was formed in which thousands of people and the entire Porto garrison took part, making it one of the most splendid and significant processions ever organised in the country, as may be seen in the pamphlet *Memória Descriptiva da trasladação das ossadas dos Doze Martyres da Pátria*, published in 1878.
Fontainhas
A small hill on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), not far from Pico do Facho (‘beacon peak’).
Fonte Arcada (Pedro Joaquim de Magalhãis, 1st Viscount of)

He was a distinguished soldier and married, on this island, Dona Luíza da Silva, daughter of Manuel Dias de Andrade, who was the administrator of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Andrade family. Fonte Arcada, who died in 1688, inherited this entailed estate. A descendant of his and his wife’s, Francisco Joaquim de Magalhãis, 4th Viscount of Fonte Arcada, a distinguished diplomat and peer of the realm, administered this important entailed estate. He was on this island in 1865, visiting his properties, and while here contributed to one of the Funchal newspapers. A descendant and heir of his sold all the properties he owned in Madeira some twenty years ago.
Fonte da Areia

A locality (*sítio*) on the north coast of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where the point of the same name is found. It has a public fountain with good drinking water and is a place much frequented by visitors to the island, with many excursions made there in the traditional wheeled carts of Porto Santo.
Fonte da Areia (islet)

or simply the islet of Fonte (‘spring’). It lies off the north-west of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), not far from the coast and facing the place known as Fonte da Areia (‘sand spring’). Altitude 82 m.
Fonte da Areia (point)
or simply Ponta da Fonte. A small projection of the coastline in the north-west of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), in the locality (*sítio*) of that name.
Fonte da Bica (peak)
A hill on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), at an altitude of 1,560 metres.
Fonte do Bispo (peak)
A height of about 1,300 m in altitude, in the uplands of the parish (*freguesia*) of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’).
Fonte do Norte (peak)
This hill stands at an altitude of 1540 metres on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), near the place called Casa Queimada (‘burnt house’).
Fonte dos Ingleses

In the locality (*sítio*) of Fanal (‘beacon’), in the uplands of Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’), there is a small spot known as Fonte dos Ingleses (‘Englishmen’s spring’), which is notable for its pleasantness and for a spring of crystal-clear water.
Fonte Vermelha

Beside the road linking the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’) with that of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), not far from the locality (*sítio*) of Eira do Cerrado (‘threshing floor of the enclosure’), there is a place of that name, with a drinking fountain built in 1847.
Fontes (battery)

It was handed over to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) in March 1898 and demolished by order to improve the land west of the former Praça da Rainha (‘Queen’s Square’), today Praça do Marquês de Pombal (‘Marquis of Pombal Square’). (1921).

João Diniz (springs)

The oldest reference we have found to the Fontes de João Diniz (‘João Diniz’s springs’) is in a document recorded in the 3rd volume of the archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) and published in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), under the title *Apontamentos & Regimento que se ha de ter nas obras de forteficaçâo que ellRey nosso senhor mâdou fazer na cidade do Funchal*. It reads: ‘And that from the springs of the fortress such part of their water as seems fit be collected in a fountain to be made in the open square outside the fortress, as His Highness had ordered through Pero da Sylva; and from the rest of the said water two spouts, or as many as seem fit, shall be made for the ships to take on water, which spouts shall be placed along the shingle shore.’ The document refers to the sack by the French corsairs, which took place in 1566, and seems to us to date from shortly after that time.
The name of João Diniz that these springs preserve must come from their original owner or from some individual who had worked them. Gaspar Frutuoso was already calling them by this name in 1590.
Dr F. A. Barral extols the good qualities of the water from these springs and devotes several pages to them in his book *Noticia sobre o Clima do Funchal* (pp. 139–141).

At its session of 7 April 1784 the Municipal Council resolved ‘to build a defence or a wall capable of preventing the sea, in wintry weather, from continuing to choke the city’s springs with debris’. The work was estimated at 1 082$500 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). In 1841 the present public fountain was built, and at that time the embrasures of the battery that stood on the seaward side of the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) disappeared.

In March 1896 the waters of the João Diniz springs were declared suspect by the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative), Guilherme Teles de Meneses. This did not stop the public from continuing to draw water from them with as much confidence as before. Meanwhile, some works were carried out at that time on the pipes of the São Lourenço palace to prevent possible seepage that might impair the purity of the water.
With the major repair works carried out on the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’), the well-known Fontes de João Diniz disappeared in November 1939.
Fontes Pereira de Melo (António Maria de)
This notable Portuguese statesman was in Madeira in 1858. He arrived here on 10 September aboard the brig *Mariana* and left for Cape Verde on the same ship on the 26th.
Fontes Pereira de Melo, who was then a lieutenant of engineers, visited the works on the Rabaçal levada (irrigation channel).
Fontinha

A locality (*sítio*) in the town (*vila*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where there is a public fountain whose waters were analysed in 1893 at the École Nationale des Mines de Paris. The residue found in one litre of these waters weighed 1.728 g, of which silica accounted for 0.048 g, sodium carbonate, including the alkaline-earth carbonates, for 0.891 g, sodium sulphate for 0.290 g and sodium chloride for 0.490 g. According to the analyst of that school, the mineral water of Porto Santo may be classed among the bicarbonated and sodium-sulphated waters. The analysis revealed very little lime and magnesia, and also showed that almost all the carbonic acid of the bicarbonates is combined with the alkalis.

They are undisputedly regarded as excellent table waters, and today they are widely drunk in Madeira and also exported beyond the archipelago. In this locality there is a public fountain that supplies these waters to the public, as well as the building of the concessionary company, which prepares them and exports them from that island.
Fora (islet)

It is also known as the Ilhéu do Farol (Lighthouse Islet). Next to the Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’), and separated from it only by a narrow channel, lies the small islet called Agostinho. Very close to it is the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros, and a short distance away the Ilhéu de Fora, or do Farol. The last two are separated from each other by a channel known as the Boqueirão Grande (‘great gap’), which is about 180 metres wide and 8 deep and gives easy passage to the coastal steamers that frequently pass that way. This islet is the easternmost point of Madeira, and since September 1870 it has had a working lighthouse, which has rendered valuable service to shipping. Its lantern stands about 100 m above sea level and is situated at 32° 41' north latitude and 16° 39' west longitude (Greenwich). It is a white light with intermittent flashes, visible from 25 miles away. There is also a telegraph station there, linked to the central station in Funchal. To the south-west of the Ilhéu de Fora lies the dangerous shoal of Badajeira (see that entry). The altitude of this islet is 107 m.
Fora (islet)
To the north-east of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), close to its coast, lies the so-called Ilhéu de Fora (‘outer islet’), also known as the Rocha de Nordeste. Altitude: 100 metres.
Charters

Madeira had several charters, but the oldest are known only from mentions in certain later documents and in the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso. In the letters granting the captaincies of Funchal and Machico to João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira, transcribed on pp. 453 and 456 of the notes to Frutuoso’s work, Prince Henry the Navigator refers to the charter (foral) that he had ordered to be drawn up for the island. However, neither this charter nor the one that Afonso V gave in 1452 to what was then the town (*vila*) of Funchal is recorded in the municipal archives.

An anonymous manuscript *Miscelânea*, cited by Dr Azevedo and held in the National Library in Lisbon, states that ‘in 1452 Dom Afonso V gave a charter to the town of Funchal with many privileges, exempting the inhabitants of the whole island from paying excise, tolls or any of the levies that existed at that time in the Kingdom’. Dr Gaspar Frutuoso gives 1472 as the year in which this charter was granted, but Dr Azevedo believes this to be an error on the part of either the author of the *Saudades* or the copyist, since several documents recorded in the archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) show that the Funchal municipality already existed before that year.

The charter of the city of Funchal (see that entry) and of the towns of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Calheta (‘small cove’) is dated 6 August 1515. A certified copy of it, taken from the *Livro das Ilhas* on 2 May 1736, is kept in a special book in the archive of this city’s Municipal Council. It is a document of interest for many reasons, and Dr Azevedo transcribes it on p. 494 of the notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’. Its forty-one chapters set out the taxes to which the people of the captaincy of Funchal were subject, the formalities required for the manufacture, transport and export of sugar, and the fines incurred by gamblers, the excommunicated and persons found carrying or using weapons, etc., etc.

On p. 507 of the same notes Dr Azevedo transcribes the charter of the towns of Machico and Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), whose chapters differ little from those of the charter of Funchal and the towns of Ponta do Sol and Calheta. It is dated 15 December 1515, and in its 2nd chapter it ordered that there should be a customs house in the captaincy of Machico, which could be established in Machico or Santa Cruz, ‘wherever His Highness shall later declare’.

The village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of São Vicente was made a town and separated from the jurisdiction of Machico by a royal decree (alvará régio) of 23 August 1743, but whether it was granted a charter we do not know. This decree and the letter of grant (carta de mercê) of 25 August 1744 allowed the *lugares* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Porto Moniz, Seixal, Ponta Delgada, Arco de São Jorge and São Jorge to be attached to the new town, ‘all of which were far from the town of Machico, for which reason their inhabitants suffered the same oppressions as those of the village of São Vicente’.

By a royal decree (*alvará*) of 17 August 1508, Manuel I ordered that the Council of the town (*vila*) of Funchal should be governed in the same way as that of the city of Lisbon. As a result, many provisions of the regulations (*regimento*) of the Lisbon Council were adopted here from the outset. The archive of the Funchal Municipal Council holds a fairly old book, written by one of the finest calligraphers of the day, containing the regulations and charter of the Municipal Council of Lisbon. Certain changes were gradually introduced into it, some of which appear in notes written in the margins of the book.

According to these regulations and charter, the board (*mesa*) of the council sessions was to be ten *palmos* long and six wide, and the councillors (*vereadores*) were all to sit three ‘on one side and unencumbered, facing the people’. The councillor in the middle was charged with answering ‘all parties that which had been determined and agreed by all’, but this duty lasted only one month, after which another councillor took over those functions. The clerk (*escrivão*) was ‘seated on the bench at the head of the table’, and opposite him sat the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) when he attended the Council, as did the civil and criminal judges, the market inspectors (almotacés), the city procurator, the judge of orphans, etc., etc., when they came ‘to dispatch the parties’ cases’ or were summoned. The steward (*viador*) of works or the city accountant, when he attended the Council, sat ‘on the bench and at the end of the clerk’. There was no bench ‘on the other side of the table, facing the people’, but a railing that was to be no higher than the table and was not to ‘obstruct the councillors’ view of the people’.

It is likely that at the meetings of the Municipal Council of Funchal, at least those attended only by members of that body, the ordinary judge (*juiz ordinário*, locally elected lay judge), later replaced by the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), sat at one end of the table, with the councillors and the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) on his left, and the clerk opposite him. The regulations in question, whose wording is not always clear, raise many doubts. It is reasonable to suppose that they underwent various modifications so that they could be applied to the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of Funchal, since certain official bodies mentioned in them never existed here.

At a council meeting on 22 December 1802 it was resolved that from then on the president, that is, the *juiz de fora*, ‘should sit at the head of the table, with the clerk facing him and the councillors on his left side in order of age, the last place being occupied by the municipal procurator’, and that the guild representatives (*mesteres*) should sit at the foot of the table, ‘in such a position that they would not be hampered by the clerk’s chair’. The guild representatives were entitled only to ‘plain chairs’, while the other members of the Senate were to sit in high-backed chairs, a privilege also granted to members of the nobility when they attended council meetings. The nobles’ place was opposite the councillors, and the people’s judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds), when he came to the Council, ‘sat above the eldest of the guild representatives’.

The regulations and charter of the Municipal Council of Lisbon also contain provisions on the Council’s accounts, public works, the manner of accompanying the king, processions, the appointment of the market inspectors and the treasurer, etc., etc., the latter to be ‘a faithful and prudent person’. In the Corpus Christi procession (see Processions) the councillors, with their red staves, were to walk ‘on the right-hand side of the king and behind him, so as not to be level with him’, and no other person could go ‘ahead of him, except on the other, left-hand side’.

Since in Funchal the king could not accompany the Corpus Christi procession, it was the Council that held first place in this religious cortège, following immediately behind the canopy. This same place was guaranteed to it by the royal decree of 2 April 1763, which did not prevent a governor and captain-general from later trying to dispute it, without having any right to do so.

On some occasions in this procession the governor placed himself between the first and second councillors, and the *corregedor* between the procurator of the Senate and the clerk, although this was permitted neither by the charter nor by the warrant (*provisão*) of 1763. In our own day we have seen the Council always yield its place to the authorities, whether out of excessive courtesy or through ignorance of the enactments that entitled it to walk behind the canopy in that religious procession.
See ‘Longing for the Homeland’, p. 888.
Foraminifera

About 70 species of these protozoa were collected in Madeira by the English naturalist H. B. Brady. They are found in sand, among seaweed, etc., and have a small shell or case with either a single opening or numerous pores.
Forel (Dr)
He wrote on the ants of the Madeira archipelago in the *Mittheilungen der Schweiz Entom Gesellschaft*.
The species studied by Dr Auguste Forel were collected by the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz.
Forerunner

On the afternoon of 25 October 1854 the British steamer *Forerunner* left the port of Funchal. Coming from the coast of Africa and bound for England, she was carrying many officers of the British army and the governor of Sierra Leone. Off Ponta de São Lourenço, after nightfall, the steamer struck a shoal there called the Badajeira and sank completely; three passengers and eleven crew members died in the wreck. A boat from Machico that happened to be passing the scene of the disaster gave the most valuable service in rescuing the passengers and crew. Its men were commended by the Portuguese Government in a ministerial order (*portaria*) and decorated with the medal of the Royal Humane Society (*Real Sociedade Humanistica*).
Forjaz Coutinho (Dom Diogo Pereira)

By royal letter (*carta régia*) of 26 September 1781 Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho was appointed governor and captain-general of this archipelago, and he took office on 15 November of the same year.

He was one of the governors of Madeira who, through his zeal and uprightness in managing public affairs, left the most honourable memory among us. He was reappointed to his post several times at the request of the Funchal Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) and of petitions from the people and the nobility. His government made itself felt in every branch of public administration: he corrected many abuses, introduced reforms and improvements in many services, and very frequently pointed out to the government in mainland Portugal the wisest and most indispensable measures for the advancement and prosperity of this archipelago.

He was one of the most deserving purveyors of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of this city, to which he rendered outstanding services. His life-size portrait is still kept today in the meeting room of the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of that institution. In the vestibule of the building there is a stone tablet bearing his name and the year in which he had a new entrance built giving access to the wards.
