Prompted by instructions from the central government and assisting the diocesan bishop, Dom José da Costa Torres, he pursued a relentless persecution of the secret societies that had been organised in Madeira in the last quarter of the 18th century. This led to many arrests and to the clandestine embarkation of several individuals and their families on the night of 19 July 1792.
He was what we would today call a man of wit, skilfully wielding satire and irony, and local tradition still preserves accounts of several episodes in which he was the witty protagonist.
He left the government of the archipelago through illness on 26 March 1798 and died in this city on the 30th of the same month. He was buried in the church of Carmo (Carmelite church).
Ants

Seven species of ants have been found in Madeira. The commonest is *Iridomyrmex humilis*, native to the tropical regions of America and introduced from Demerara in 1886 or 1887. This species, which first appeared in Funchal, is now spread over all or almost all of the low-lying part of the island, reaching altitudes of more than 500 metres in some places. The old Madeiran ant, *Pheidole megacephala* or *Oecophthora pusilla*, which is also found in Europe, has gradually disappeared from the island since it was invaded by *Iridomyrmex humilis*.

No species peculiar to Madeira or Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is known, but there are two varieties that appear to be confined to the former island: *Plagiolepis pygmaea* var. *Schmitzii* and *Tepinoma erraticum* var. *maderense*. *Stenamma structor*, found more than 40 years ago in the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’), appears to be an introduced species.
*Monomorium Salomonis*, found in the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*), does not occur in Madeira, whereas *M. carbonarium* has been found on this island, at spots not very far from the coast.

Although Dr Oswald Heer published a curious description of *Oecophthora pusilla* around the middle of the 19th century, it was only much later, thanks to the research of the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz, that the ants of Madeira became properly known. The species collected in our archipelago were dealt with first by Dr Forel (see that entry) and then by the Revd Schmitz, in an article published in the *Annaes de Sciencias Naturaes* of Porto and reproduced in nos 5,709 and 5,713 of the *Diário de Noticias* of Funchal in March 1896.
See *Subsidio para o estudo das formigas da Madeira* by Alberto Artur Sarmento, 1937.
Fornos de Algodres (João Maria de Abreu Castelo Branco Cardoso e Melo, 1st Viscount and 1st Count of)
He was born in 1789 and died on 7 January 1878. On 13 November 1852, while Viscount of Fornos de Algodres, he was appointed civil governor of this district, and he held the post for about a year.
Forster (Johann Reinhold)

This German botanist and his son Johann Georg Adam Forster accompanied Captain James Cook on his second voyage to the southern seas, arriving at the port of Funchal on 29 July 1772. Specimens of the plants they collected on this island are in the herbaria of the University of Kiel and of the Natural History Museum in Paris. The younger Forster discusses some Madeiran plants in two works entitled *Plantae Atlanticae* (Goetting, 1787) and *Herbarium Australe* (Goetting, 1797).
São Francisco (fort)

It was built in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) by order of the bishop-governor Dom Friar João do Nascimento in 1749, who applied to the work the money from the fines paid by the territorial militia (*ordenanças*) for failing to perform lookout duty.
St Joseph, Porto Santo (fort)
Built under Pombal’s government inside the town (*vila*), with a house for the governors’ residence. It is at present (1921) ceded to the Revenue Guard (*Guarda Fiscal*, customs and excise corps).
Fortifications

The seats of Madeira’s two captaincies, Funchal and Machico, were important centres of trade and shipping from the very beginning, with Funchal predominating thanks to its spacious harbour. João Gonçalves da Câmara, 2nd donatary of Funchal, knew of the damage the Moors were doing to merchant ships on the high seas and feared an attack on the flourishing town (*vila*). He therefore asked the Infanta Dona Beatriz, guardian of her son Diogo, Duke of Viseu, and administrator of the mastership of the Order of Christ, to have a fortress built to defend the harbour. The Infanta, however, pleading the heavy expenses already incurred, kept postponing the work.

Manuel I, while still duke, arranged for a wall to be built around the town of Funchal, promising that once it was finished a similar fortification would be undertaken in the town of Machico. Considering the costs this would entail, however, he gradually reduced his plan to a single bastion in Funchal. This was to be paid for by an increase in the sugar tax, reckoned at 1,266,000 réis a year – a large sum at that time – together with one day of compulsory labour, from which only the nobility were exempt.

Work on the fortifications began only in the reign of Manuel I, with the bastion and tower being started. The new contributions levied in the reign of John III, especially the meat levy (*imposição das carnes*), gave it fresh impetus. The defence plan was later modified in 1572. It ordered that a fortress with three bastions be built, that the houses standing in its way be demolished, and that the balconies on the frontage facing the pebble beach (calhau) be cut back. There the city walls were to be built with five gates: two to the south, facing the sea, one to the east and two to the west. The walls were to run between the Ribeira de João Gomes and the Ribeira de São Francisco (today the Ribeira de São João), abutting on the hills of Pena (‘crag’) and Pico dos Frias (‘the Frias’ peak’).

The corsair attack on the city in 1566, made by way of Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’), turned attention to the defence of the coast. Entrenchments were built at points commanding the sea, on the rocks overlooking the settlements; these were called *fortes roqueiros* (rock forts) and were placed under the watch and supervision of the captain-corporals, ‘& os portos se empossebillytaram asy & da maneyra que se fez de camara dellobos atee a cidade’ (and the landing places were made impassable in this way and manner, as was done from Câmara de Lobos to the city).

Under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) the rules of defence were changed to follow the polygonal layout. The forts of São Tiago (St James the Greater), São Felipe, Loures and Our Lady of the Peña de Francia were completed, and work began on the Fortress of the Pico (‘peak’) in Funchal, on São Roque in Machico and on the Castelo do Pico (‘castle of the peak’) on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).

During the period of the Restoration and in the 17th century, the redoubt of Santo António da Alfândega, Santa Catarina and the Fortress of Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu (‘Our Lady of the Conception of the Islet’) were built, and the city walls were extended eastwards to meet the fortress of São Tiago.

In the 18th century the forts of São Pedro and São José da Pontinha (St Joseph) were built in Funchal. Along the coast as far as Câmara de Lobos came those of Gorgulho, Engenhoca, Nossa Senhora da Ajuda, Praia Formosa, Nossa Senhora da Vitória and Pastel, and São Sebastião in Câmara de Lobos. There followed the fort of São Bento in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’); those of Madalena do Mar, Ponta do Sol and Calheta; the fortress of Santo António in Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’); the fort of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’); that of Faial, that of Entroza in Boaventura (‘good fortune’), that of Terrachã in São Vicente, that of São Jorge and that of Arco de São Jorge; that of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’); the redoubt of Caniçal (‘reed bed’); the forts of São João Baptista and Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*) in Machico; those of São Francisco, São Lázaro and Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*) in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’); the small fort at the mouth of the Ribeira do Porto Novo (‘new harbour stream’); that of Reis Magos and that of the Ribeira do Caniço (‘Caniço stream’); and the fort of São José on the island of Porto Santo.

In the 19th century the battery of Fontes (‘springs’), opposite São Lourenço, the redoubt of Seixo (‘pebble’) in Água de Pena, the Fort of Porto Novo (‘new harbour’) in Caniço (‘reed’) and the redoubt of Pico de São João were built.
Finally, in 1916 the Quinta Vigia (‘lookout estate’) battery was built, and in 1917 that of Montanha (‘mountain’), to defend the city against submarines.
Fortress of São Lourenço

Begun in the reign of Manuel I as a simple bastion, the fortress was successively altered in the reigns of John III and King Sebastian and completed under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640). In 1566 it was stormed by pirates from the north side, where the wall rose only 12 *palmos* high. Montluc seized a house opposite and from there had the turret and other parts of the fort raked with fire. The gate of the bastion was then forced, and 250 people, both defenders and others who had taken refuge there, were put to the sword.

The east tower bears, in carved dressed stone (*cantaria*), the arms of Portugal, the ducal crown, two armillary spheres, the emblem of Manuel I, and a Cross of the Order of Christ. The north bastion bore, in white marble, the arms of Castile, onto which those of Portugal were later grafted; its projecting section was cut back in 1917 to align the Avenida Dr Manuel de Arriaga.
The chapel of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) was built within the precinct of the Old Fortress in 1635, and from then on the fortress was called the Fortress of São Lourenço.

The royal decree (*alvará*) appointing the 1st constable is dated 20 June 1566 and was issued in favour of Gonçalo Fernandes, who came from Lisbon. The fortress was garrisoned by 24 gunners at 30 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a day, rising in 1753 to 80 *réis*.

The 1st chaplain was Father José da Costa, in 1641. He was ordered to be given 44, as was done for any soldier on enlisting, and he drew a gunner’s pay, with the obligation of saying Mass there on Sundays and holy days.
Various public buildings were constructed in the Fortress of São Lourenço, around the large square inner courtyard and the north bastion. (See the São Lourenço Palace.)
Fortress of São Tiago

It was built under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) on a rocky point east of the landing place, and the original portico bears the date 1614. Enlarged after the Restoration, it was given a new wall and outer gate, forming the end of the city walls. In 1697 Manuel Telo Catanho de Meneses was honorary captain (*capitão ad honorem*) of this fortress, with the obligation of keeping it clean and supplied with lookouts. In 1767 it underwent further alterations, as an inscription there shows: ‘This fortress was rebuilt and enlarged when José Correia de Sá was governor and captain-general of this island, and he had fifty pieces of artillery, with all their equipment, brought from London for the same fortress in the year 1767’.

When British troops occupied Madeira at the beginning of the 19th century, this fortress was garrisoned by British gunners. In 1803 the holder of the entail (*morgado*) João de Freitas da Silva was imprisoned here after fleeing the convent of São Bernardino, ‘to which he had been sent until he was instructed in the rudiments of Christian doctrine’ – a curious document published by the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’), no. 441.
It currently serves as the barracks of No. 3 Mountain Artillery Battery (*Bataria n.º 3 de Artilharia de Montanha*). (1921).
Fortaleza do Pico

Under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640), a castle was begun on the Pico dos Frias (‘the Frias’ peak’) for maritime defence and to command the city. The first works were completed in 1632, as the date above the outer gate shows, and building continued until 1640, as a stone tablet records: ‘The governor Luís de Miranda Henriques Pinto built the third of the bastion of São Paulo and almost all of the curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city) that joins the bastion of São João, and the cistern with its rooms and guardhouse cut into the cliff, and the ravelin of the gate and the four houses’.
The bastions were completed in the period of the Restoration, as was the chantry (capela) of São João Baptista in the first stronghold, which gave the castle its name.
The 1st master gunner (*condestável*) of this fortress was Francisco de Sousa, in 1624, with an annual salary of 24$ and two *pipas* of wine.

John IV created the post of lieutenant of the Fortress of the Pico (‘peak’), to which Benedito Catalão was appointed, and in 1751 there was also the post of *capitão-cabo* (local militia commander responsible for coastal defence), held by Rodrigo da Costa Almeida.

In 1770 the vagrant boys of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) were sent to learn trades in the workshops of this fortress, which included tinsmithing, blacksmithing, Flanders tinplate work, gunsmithing and gunstock-making. These workshops expanded greatly in 1802 under the supervision of the sergeant-major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major), and three muskets were made there with stocks of different woods from the island, for the instruction of Their Royal Highnesses. (*Livro das ordens*, fol. 6.) In the great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803 all the families left homeless were sent to the Fortress of the Pico, which filled with campaign tents pitched on the esplanades.
In 1833 it was renamed Forte de São Miguel, but in 1834 it took back its old name as soon as the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government was overthrown.
The fortress enclosure, in the form of a citadel, covers an area of 2,750 square metres and stands at an altitude of 111 m.
It has a large vaulted cistern cut into the rock above the main battery, measuring 18 m long by 6 wide and 10 high to the crown of the vault.
The Fortress of the Pico is one of the places from which the majestic panorama of the city and harbour of Funchal can most easily be enjoyed.

The Fortress of Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu (‘Our Lady of the Conception of the Islet’). The Governor’s order to build this fortress, on an isolated rock to the west of Funchal bay, dates from 1642 (Archive of the Municipal Council, vol. 6, fol. 66), but building did not begin until 1656. In 1670 it had a captain of gunners, who was ordered to be paid 10$ a year for oil to light the soldiers’ quarters.
In 1682 the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição was ordered to be built, and we have a record of the 1st chaplain, a post held by Father Manuel de Andrade at a salary of 18$ a year.

In 1698 Simão Fernandes Forte was appointed the first master gunner (*condestável*), the garrison consisting of 12 gunners paid 30 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a day. At that time the fishermen were obliged to carry provisions to the Islet without any payment; but if the sea prevented them, in extreme cases a rope was thrown ashore to relieve those cut off.

It bears the following inscription: ‘This fortress was built by the governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Bartolomeu de Vasconcelos da Cunha... 1654. At this time the superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*) was Francisco de Andrade, who oversaw the expenses of the fortification and greatly assisted this work’.
It ceased to be isolated when the Molhe da Pontinha (‘little point breakwater’) was built, which abuts on it.
It has a signal station and a harbour light. (See Molhe da Pontinha.)

The Castelo do Pico (‘castle of the peak’), Porto Santo. Repeated pirate raids on the island of Porto Santo led Philip II to see to its resettlement. The worst was the raid of 1619, in which almost the entire population perished or was carried off into captivity, leaving only 18 men and 7 women. He ordered a fortress to be built on the steep, stony Pico (‘peak’) that overlooks the town (*vila*), and had residential houses, storehouses and a cistern put up on the small plateau of the knoll. It was a place of refuge rather than of war, although it was suitably armed with artillery.
The post of constable was created in 1624 and given to Francisco de Sousa, with an annual salary of 24$ and two *pipas* of wine, paid by the royal revenue office (*almoxarifado*) of Porto Santo.
Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, governor of the island, took a keen interest in the revival of Porto Santo, and the bricks from which the vaults of the Castle were made were produced on that island.
Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (fort)

It was an outwork defending the cove of Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’), built in 1712; its 1st master gunner was Manuel de Ceia. In 1801 part of the British troops under Colonel Clinton were quartered there.
Loures (fort)

Tradition has it that the fort was built by a private individual in the 17th century. It covered the cove of Gonçalo Aires and the mouth of the stream. By the time of the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Dom Diogo Coutinho it had lost its importance, and he intended to set up a silk factory there.
Nossa Senhora do Amparo (fort)
Triangular in plan, it was built in 1706 at no expense to the Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*).
According to an inscription, the work was directed by Francisco Franco, who was its first captain.
It stands beside the Machico promenade and was the last to surrender when the Miguelist troops landed in 1828.
São Bento da Ribeira Brava (fort)
Built by order of Governor Duarte Sodré Pereira to defend the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town).
São Filipe da Praça (fort)

The fort was built by order of the bishop-governor Dom Jerónimo Fernando in 1628, between the mouths of the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’) and the Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), south of the pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction), on the spot where there once stood a great *til* (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) whose timber was used in a Castilian war carrack. In 1754 its master gunner was Captain Roque João Acciaioly. Sold by the Ministry of War, it made way for a large warehouse.
São João Baptista (fort)
Also called the fort of the Anchorage and of Desembarcadouro (‘landing place’). It was built on a rocky point east of Machico bay in 1708.
On 22 August 1828 it fired on the war brig *Infante D. Sebastião* of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) squadron, damaging it slightly.
In 1910 wooden houses were built on the esplanade and the fort was adapted as a hospital for cholera patients.
São Jorge da Calheta (fort)
In 1751 the captain of this fort was Bernardo da Gama.
São Pedro (fort)

It is also called the New Fort (*Forte Novo*). It stood on the curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city) of the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), by Corpo Santo (‘St Elmo’). It had a Renaissance-style gorge doorway, topped by an inscription and surmounted by an ornate, finely worked crown in white marble, which showed that the fortification works ordered on the island by the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Duarte Sodré Pereira were completed in 1707. The fort had a furnace for heated shot: the balls were taken out with iron tongs and inserted through the muzzle of the already loaded gun, with a wad of dampened tow. The heat set off the gun, and the red-hot ball reached the decks of wooden ships, where it holed them and set them on fire. The fort was demolished in 1897.
São Roque de Machico (fort)

Built under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640), at the mouth of the Ribeirinho (‘little brook’) inside Machico bay. It stood beside the São Roque parade ground. In 1695 its master gunner (*condestável*) was Pedro de Sousa Maciel. Only a few blocks of its walls remain on the beach.
St Anthony da Alfândega (fort)

The order to build a salient in the enclosing walls and in the courtyard of the Alfândega Grande (Great Customs House) dates from 1644. Its purpose was to sweep the beach with crossfire, and the customs-house gate was opened for greater convenience ‘in the loading and unloading of goods’.
This fort had 11 embrasures; the site was later turned into warehouses. It bore the following inscription:

‘Manuel de Sousa Mascarenhas, being governor and captain-general of this Island of Madeira, had this redoubt and its gates made by order of His Majesty in the year 1645, Manuel Vieira Cardoso being superintendent.’
Caniçal (fort)
Built in the 1st quarter of the 18th century, after a pirate landing at that settlement. In 1758 the captain of this fort was João de Morais Perestrelo. It stood above the cove.
Porto da Cruz (fort)
It dates from 1708 and was built above the bay. In 1804 it was dismantled, and its garrison was sent to work on clearing the Ribeira de Machico (‘Machico stream’).
In 1713 João de Vasconcelos Uzel was appointed captain of this fort.

Fort of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua) at Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’). It was built in 1754. A warrant (*provisão*) of the Council of War of 1761 ordered one more *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine to be added for the master gunner (*condestável*) to the annual salary of 12$ set when the post was created.
Porto Novo (fort)

It was begun in 1827 by Governor José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, on the right bank of the Ribeira do Porto Novo (‘new harbour’). It was still unfinished when Miguelist troops took the island in 1828, and a chest of munitions exploded there. The fort was completed by order of Dom Álvaro da Costa and was served by the old Caniço road (*Estrada velha do Caniço*).
There was also a small fort on the beach, already in ruins by this time and of no importance.
São Jorge (redoubt)
In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge. In 1785 its captain was Francisco Manuel Jardim Telo de Meneses.
Fortifications

The first master of fortifications (*fortificador*) was João de Carceres, a well-regarded mason living in Funchal. The royal letter (*carta régia*) of 13 May 1513 directs that ‘no person of whatever estate or condition shall do him any harm, injury or wrong, but that he shall receive honour and favour from all’, for he was in charge of building the bastion and the first defensive walls.
In 1595 the architect Jerónimo Jorge, a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*), was appointed master of fortifications of the Ilha da Madeira, with a salary of 100$ a year.

The two sons of Jerónimo Jorge – Bartolomeu João and João Falcato – practised their father’s craft during Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640). The former distinguished himself at the Fortress of the Pico (*Fortaleza do Pico*), and his merits were sung by Manuel Tomás in ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*), book X, stanza 57.

In 1602 Mateus Fernandes held a letter of appointment as master of fortifications, with the grandiose title of engineer and master of the royal works. In 1617 Bartolomeu Arias was sent to fortify Madeira because of the damage done by corsairs to the small settlements along the coast.

At the time of the Restoration we find Bartolomeu João as master of fortifications, and a son of his, Bartolomeu João de Abreu, inherited the office from him, receiving it as a royal grant in 1660. It is a family of masters of fortifications.

Most curious of all, a lady, Dona Mariana da Câmara, obtained the office in 1664 because she was the widow of a master of fortifications (*fortificador*), on behalf of whoever should marry her daughter. The future son-in-law, as acting holder, was to receive only a third of the income until a son, who was then away in Brazil and was due to inherit the office on his father’s death, returned to take it up.
The works suffered as a result. Manuel Gomes Ferreira, master of fortifications at Setúbal, was therefore brought over from mainland Portugal in 1699, on the same salary that he had received there.

In 1711 Inácio Gomes Fragoso held a patent as engineer of fortifications, and no work of the Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*) could be carried out without his involvement; his monthly pay was 8,000 réis.
In 1744 the Treasury Council (*Conselho da Fazenda*) engaged João Moniz de Abreu, for 100,000 réis a year, to hold the same office; he was followed in 1748 by Domingos Rodrigues Martins.

From 1756 onwards the post was held by military officers with special training in engineering, among whom Francisco Tossi Columbina, Francisco de Alincourt, Faustino Sebastiano da Costa and Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot stand out.
Fortification and military engineering work is at present the responsibility of a section of the Military Command (*Comando Militar*) of Madeira. S.
Phosphorescence of the sea

The phosphorescence of the coastal waters of Madeira is produced by myriads of cystoflagellates belonging to *Noctiluca miliaris*. It was already noted by La Pérouse during the visit he made to this island at the end of the 18th century.
Many dinoflagellates are also phosphorescent, and some may well be discovered once the plankton of Madeira has been properly studied.
Fossils
See Calcareous bodies of Piedade, Phanerogams, Leaf deposit and Lignite.
Fothergill (Dr)
He advised people suffering from lung diseases to seek out the climate of Madeira, in a work entitled *On consumption medical observations*, 1775.
Photography

The first photographic experiments on Portuguese soil were made in Madeira by Vicente Gomes da Silva in 1848, when he studied the daguerreotype on silvered copper plate. José António Monteiro Teixeira later brought him a camera and plate holder from France, and Teixeira was the first person to be photographed on this island. The ‘Vicente’ studio opened in Rua João Tavira, on the southern corner of Rua do Bispo, producing hand-coloured positives on glass. In 1856 many people already stricken by the terrible cholera epidemic hurried there to have themselves photographed, so as to leave their portrait to their families.

When the widowed Empress of Brazil, Empress Amélie, was in Madeira, she sent João Francisco Camacho, who kept a bookbinder’s workshop in the same street, to Paris at her own expense to perfect his craft. While staying in that capital, however, he set about learning the art of photography, and on his return to Madeira in 1864 he set up a photographic studio in the street east of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). It was the second studio to exist here. S.

In 1867 there was a photographic studio in a house next to the old Mercado de São João (St John's Market), belonging to Jacinto A. de Freitas and Aluísio Betencourt. Before that, around 1863, a lady born on this island, the daughter of the military engineer António Pedro de Azevedo (see that entry), produced various photographic works that were much admired here. This lady was Dona Amélia Augusta de Azevedo; she died at Idanha, near Lisbon, on 20 November 1914, aged 70.
See Silva (Vicente Gomes da) and Torre Bela (Count of).
Fowler (R.)
Works:

*Hither and thither, or sketches of a travel on both sides of Atlantic, containing notes of a visit to Madeira, Lisbon; Gibraltar, etc.*, London. We do not know the year in which this work was published.
Frade (fish)
The name formerly given in Madeira to *Blennius palmicornis*, a fish known today as the *caboz*. It lives along the coast and is common in rock pools.

The fish known in Portugal as the *frade* is *Selache maxima*, which appears from time to time in Madeiran waters. It is a very large shark that comes from the cold northern seas and is sometimes found already dead, floating on the surface of the ocean.
Fradesso Bello (João)

A musician born in Portugal who lived for many years in Funchal, where he raised a family and died on 15 May 1861. He was a pupil of the celebrated musician Friar José Marques, and left musical works of great merit that enjoyed wide popularity and received special praise from noted music critics.
Fraga Gomes (Alfredo de)

He was born in Funchal on 21 April 1873 and is agronomist of this district and a member of the Society of Agronomic Sciences of Lisbon (*Sociedade de Sciencias Agronomicas de Lisboa*). He wrote an interesting monograph on the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), published in the *Boletim da Direcção Geral da Agricultura*, and a pamphlet entitled *A doença da canna d'assucar pelo Conyothyrium melasporum na Ilha da Madeira*, Lisbon 1900. He has published numerous articles on agricultural subjects in the Funchal newspapers, and is known throughout the district as a most zealous, distinguished and learned official. (1921)
Fragoso (Joaquim Maria)

He was born on the mainland and has lived in this city for many years. As an official of the Ministry of Public Works he has carried out various public service assignments here, among them that of director of the technical department of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*). In no. 1 of vol. X of the *Boletim da Associação dos Condutores de Obras Publicas* he published a study of the roads of this island, entitled *Duas palavras sobre a viação da Ilha da Madeira*, which fills 28 pages of that journal. (1921). He died on 17 May 1923.
França (family)

Shortly after the discovery, André Gonçalves, known as ‘Polonês’, came to this island; he settled in Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) and held land there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). His son João de França, who introduced this surname to the island, owned a great deal of land and a fine house in Estreito. He founded the original church of this parish (*freguesia*), where he established the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he created. He died in 1511 and was buried in the church of which he was founder and patron. The last holder of this entailed estate, one of the largest on the island, was the Count of Calçada (‘paved way’), who died in 1906.
França (Alfredo de)

He belongs to an old family of the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial, where he was born on 14 December 1883, the son of Alfredo Abel de França. He studied at the Faculty of Law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) but did not take the degree of bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate). While still a student he published the verse pamphlets *Poema Rubro*, *A Imagem* and *o Pagem*. He has contributed to many newspapers and is at present an editor of *O Século*, of Lisbon. He is a senior official of the Ministry of the Colonies. (1921).
França (Dr Carlos)

A military physician and distinguished bacteriologist, sent to Madeira by the government during the cholera epidemic of 1910. He rendered this island outstanding services as head of the sanitary services throughout the epidemic, consistently showing uncommon professional skill and great self-sacrifice in carrying out the many duties entrusted to him.

On 5 March 1911 a formal session was held in honour of Dr Carlos França at the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*). On that occasion the president of the Council presented him with an elegant, finely ornamented silver cup and a portfolio with allegorical inlaid work (*embutidos*) in native woods, containing the address the president had read at the session.
Dr Carlos França’s wife attended the ceremony, and the Council presented her with a beautiful *corbeille* of fresh flowers, decorated with ribbons in the national colours.

Dr França wrote the following works relating to Madeira: *A Epidemia colérica da Madeira, 1910-1911*, a report submitted to the Ministry of the Interior, Lisbon, 1911, 91 pp.; *Le Cholera à Madère* (*Bullet. de la Soc. de Pathologie Exotique*, vol. IV, 1911); and *Contribution à l'étude du Lapin de Porto Santo* (*Bullet. de la Soc. Port. de Sc. Natur*, VI, 1913).
França e Vasconcelos (José Júlio de)

He was born in Boaventura (‘good fortune’) in 1776, graduated in law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and practised as a lawyer in Funchal, where he died on 22 April 1859. He left a manuscript *Nobiliario Madeirense*.
France (Anatole)

It has already been stated in this *Elucidário* (I-66) that the eminent French writer Anatole France called at Madeira on his way to the Argentine Republic in 1909, accompanied on the voyage by his private secretary, himself a man of letters, Jean Jacques Brousson. In 1927 Brousson published a book entitled *Itenerario de Paris a Buenos Aires*, in which he deals with their stay on this island. In it he gives free rein to the most fervent imagination, attributing to Anatole France ideas and opinions about what the writer saw and heard in Funchal that are far removed from the truth and must be the pure invention of his imaginative secretary. On this subject, it is worth reading the article in the *Diário de Notícias* of Funchal of 23 June 1929.
Kestrel (Cerchneis tinnunculus)

A bird of the family Falconidae which nests in Madeira and can sometimes be seen over the rooftops of houses, even in the centre of Funchal. It is much less common today than it once was, owing to the war waged on it by certain hunters.
It feeds mainly on lizards, crickets and mice, but when the opportunity arises it also devours small birds, such as canaries, goldfinches, etc.
Its clutch often consists of five or six eggs, of variable shape and colour, generally laid in the crevices of inaccessible rocks.
Franco de Castro (Alfredo César)

We know nothing of his circumstances, and know only that in 1865 he published in Lisbon a volume of 144 pp. entitled *Julia ou Recordações da Ilha da Madeira*. It is a novel dedicated to Vasco Tristão da Câmara, whose plot is set on this island, where the author spent some months for reasons of health. It contains descriptions of several buildings in Funchal and deals briefly with some points of the history of this archipelago.
Franco de Sousa (Francisco)

Francisco Franco de Sousa Júnior was born in Funchal on 9 October 1885, the son of Francisco Franco de Sousa and Dona Maria Carolina de Sousa. He began his studies in drawing under his father at the Funchal Industrial School (*Escola Industrial do Funchal*) and then enrolled at the former Royal Academy of Fine Arts (*Academia Real de Belas-Artes*), now the School of Fine Arts (*Escola de Belas Artes*), where he completed a brilliant course in sculpture under the distinguished master Simões de Almeida.

While still at the School of Fine Arts, he entered the competitions for the Peninsular War monument and the Barahona monument, receiving an honourable mention in each. Around the same time he made the bust of Manuel II, which was acquired for the Artillery Museum in Lisbon, as well as another work commissioned by the Grémio Literário of Lisbon.

In 1910 he passed the practical competitive examination for a scholarship of the Valmor Bequest (*Legado Valmor*) in Paris; his test piece, a bas-relief on a classical theme, was remarkable. That same year he left for Paris, where he studied under the French sculptor A. Mercier at the School of Fine Arts, and he made a study tour of Spain, Belgium and Holland.

He returned to his homeland in 1911, but three years later he went back to Paris because of the war. Among the many works he has produced in Funchal from 1911 to the present, we shall mention the following: the busts of the Viscount of Cacongo, Mr H. Vieira de Castro and Mr Rocha Machado; the bronze monument to the discoverer of Madeira, placed on the esplanade of Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’); the monumental statue for the tomb of the Rocha Machado family; the bronze monument for the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery, dedicated to the victims of the torpedo attacks of 3 December 1916; the maquette for the monument to Gonçalves Zarco, commissioned by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*); the maquette for the monument to Christopher Columbus; the bust of the President of the Republic, Sidónio Pais; and the bronze monument dedicated to the aviators, for the Jardim Municipal do Funchal (1921).
Franco de Sousa (Henrique)

He is the brother of the preceding subject and was born in Funchal on 3 March 1883. In 1892 he began studying drawing at the Funchal Industrial School (*Escola Industrial do Funchal*), and then went to Lisbon to enrol at what was then the Royal Academy of Fine Arts (*Academia Real de Belas-Artes*). There he completed his course in history painting under the eminent painter Columbano Bordalo Pinheiro in 1911. During his studies he won several bronze and silver medals, honourable mentions and the ‘Lupi’ and ‘Anunciação’ prizes.

In 1910 he exhibited for the first time at the National Society of Fine Arts (*Sociedade Nacional de Belas-Artes*), showing three paintings and five drawings, and on that occasion was awarded 2nd- and 3rd-class medals in painting and drawing. In 1911 he exhibited seven paintings and three drawings, and the State then acquired his painting *Outros Tempos* for the Museum of Contemporary Art (*Museu de Arte Contemporânea*). In 1912 he passed the competition for the Valmor Grant (*Pensão Valmor*) for artists to study abroad, leaving that same year for Madrid and later settling in Paris, where he painted *Ar livre* as proof of his progress abroad.
He returned to his native island in 1914, where he has continued to display his remarkable artistic gifts in many works of merit (1921).
Frangolho

A porridge made from barley or wheat flour. The barley and wheat intended for this porridge are ground in hand mills and the flour is sifted; when barley is used, however, the grain is lightly dried over the heat of the fire before it goes to the mill.
Frasão (family)

‘The family descends,’ say the notes to the *Saudades*, ‘from Pedro Frazão, who was living on the island of Madeira around 1532 and married Maria de Gouveia, by whom he had Dona Francisca Frazão, who in 1581 married Diogo de Ornelas e Vasconcelos.’ The name Frasão was the characteristic surname of the Count of Calçada (‘paved way’) and of many of his ancestors.
Frasão (steamship)

This was the name of the first steam vessel built in Madeira. It belonged to the late Frasão, holder of the entail (*morgado*), later Viscount and Count of Calçada (‘paved way’), and it was launched in 1870 or shortly afterwards.
Frederick Charles

Prince Frederick Charles Christian, who in 1848 succeeded his father on the throne of Denmark as Frederick VII, visited Madeira in 1846 aboard the Danish frigate *Glefioar*, staying in this city from 25 to 30 May of that year. He was warmly received by the local authorities, and the prince gave a gala dinner on board for the principal officials of Funchal.
Parishes

The Franciscan friars who accompanied João Gonçalves Zarco when he began the settlement and colonisation of Funchal were the first priests to perform ecclesiastical and parochial duties on this island, in the chapels of St Catherine, São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), Conceição de Cima, São Sebastião (St Sebastian), São João, etc. The first parish (*freguesia*) to be created was undoubtedly in Funchal, but it is difficult today to determine precisely where its first seat was. It is probable that the seat was not always the same, and even that parish duties were performed in more than one chapel at the same time. The annotator of the *Saudades* says that the first parish was perhaps established in the chapel of São Sebastião, but this is no more than a simple conjecture. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo asserts that the first church built in Funchal was that of São Sebastião, which seems to us not to be true, as we shall see elsewhere, and from this he deduces that the first parish was probably created in that chapel. The discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco first set up his residence on the height of Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’) and later at São Paulo. It is certain, however, that the first and most important nucleus of population grew up not far from the beach, along the left bank of the stream that later came to be called Ribeira de João Gomes. It is therefore more likely that the seat of the first parish was established there, at least once the parish took on a more permanent character and a more definite organisation.

The original chapel of Our Lady of Calhau dates from the second quarter of the 15th century, having been built around 1438. The creation of the parish that had its first seat there must date from this time or shortly afterwards.

The Order of Christ, ever jealous of its privileges and prerogatives, feared that the Franciscan friars would claim for themselves the rights that belonged to the Order by the grant of spiritual jurisdiction over this archipelago that had been made to it. It therefore sent to this island a qualified member of the Order, Friar Nuno Cão (see that entry), to oversee all religious services and to uphold the rights and exemptions that King Duarte had granted to the Order by the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 26 September 1433. Friar Nuno Cão took charge of the parish of Our Lady of Calhau. When the parish moved its seat in 1508 to the church that later became the cathedral, he remained parish priest until 1514, when he was appointed dean on the creation of the diocese.

The first parish, both while its seat was at the church of Our Lady of Calhau and after it was transferred to the Igreja Grande, covered a very large area, and new parishes were gradually carved out of it, as happened in many other parts of the island. Around 1558 Funchal was divided into two parishes, with their seats in the churches of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) and of Our Lady of Calhau. By then the chapels of São Martinho, Santo António, São Roque, Nossa Senhora do Monte and Nossa Senhora das Neves each formed a centre of population and constituted “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*) of some importance. They were soon turned into autonomous parishes or curacies and became the seats of new parishes. The parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’) had been created in 1566, but it was short-lived: it was abolished in 1579 and restored again in 1589.

Outside Funchal, Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) seems to have been the first parish created, in the year 1430, followed perhaps at the same time or shortly afterwards by that of Calheta (‘small cove’). Both are considered older than Machico, even though Machico was the seat of a captaincy. Around 1440 the parishes of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and Caniço (‘reed’) were created, and after them those of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). New parishes were carved out of all of these as the population spread out and climbed the mountains and ridges of the interior.
We devote a separate article to each of the parishes of this archipelago, giving a brief account of the facts of greatest interest to its history.
There follows the complete list of all the parishes.

Municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal: Sé, São Pedro, Santa Maria Maior and Santa Luzia (urban parishes); São Martinho, Santo António, São Roque, Nossa Senhora do Monte and São Gonçalo (suburban parishes). Municipality of Câmara de Lobos: Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Quinta Grande and Curral das Freiras. Municipality of Ribeira Brava: Ribeira Brava, Campanário, Serra de Água and Tabua. Municipality of Ponta do Sol: Ponta do Sol, Canhas and Madalena do Mar. Municipality of Calheta: Calheta, Arco da Calheta, Estreito da Calheta, Prazeres, Jardim do Mar, Paul do Mar, Fajã da Ovelha and Ponta do Pargo. Municipality of Porto Moniz: Porto Moniz, Achadas da Cruz, Ribeira da Janela and Seixal. Municipality of São Vicente: São Vicente, Ponta Delgada and Boaventura. Municipality of Sant’Ana: Sant’Ana, São Jorge, Arco de São Jorge, Faial and São Roque do Faial. Municipality of Machico: Machico, Porto da Cruz, Caniçal, Santo António da Serra (part) and Água de Pena (part). Municipality of Santa Cruz: Santa Cruz, Água de Pena (part), Santo António da Serra (part), Gaula, Camacha and Caniço. Municipality and island of Porto Santo: a single parish, Porto Santo.

Of these municipalities, Porto Moniz, São Vicente and Sant’Ana lie on the north coast of Madeira and the rest on the south coast, apart from that of Porto Santo, which lies on the island of the same name.
Freira

In Madeira this name is given to *Brama raii*, a pelagic fish of the mackerel family (scombrids), and to *Ostrellata mollis*, a web-footed seabird of the petrel family (procellariids) native to the archipelago. *Brama raii* is eaten, but its flesh is of poor quality. *Ostrellata mollis* is a rare species, known to nest in the mountains near Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) and on the sea cliffs of the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), where it has been observed in the summer and autumn months.
Freire (Ascenso de Sequeira)

He was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira on 15 October 1803. He arrived in Funchal on 5 December following and took office on the 8th of the same month and year, while his predecessor, Dom José Manuel da Câmara, was still in the city.

He was accompanied by the high court judge (*desembargador*) Dr Joaquim António de Araújo, who had been charged with conducting an official inquiry into the serious disagreements that had arisen between the governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara and the bishop Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares (see those entries).
During his term of office, because of the European wars, British warships frequently entered our harbour, bringing in various vessels, mainly Spanish, which they had captured on the high seas.

In 1804 and 1805 the important improvement of channelling and walling the three streams that run through the city was carried out, under the direction of the distinguished engineer Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot (see that entry).
Ascenso de Sequeira Freire left Madeira after the arrival of his successor, Pedro Fagundes Bacelar de Antas e Meneses, who took up the post at the end of July 1807.
Freire de Carvalho (José Liberato)
In September 1834 this well-known and distinguished writer became a deputy for Madeira for the legislative session of 1834–1836.

Together with Lourenço José Moniz, António Aluísio Jérvis de Atouguia and João de Oliveira, he was among the first representatives of this archipelago in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) after the establishment of constitutional government.
Freire (Francisco da Costa)
He was governor and captain-general of this archipelago. His appointment is dated 6 June 1724, and he took office on 27 July of the same year.

As president (*provedor*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), he rendered excellent service to this charitable institution. He linked his name to Madeiran history by founding the Orphan Girls’ Retreat (*Recolhimento das Órfãs*) in 1724 (see that entry).
Freire (Nuno Pereira)
He was the first governor and captain-general of Madeira appointed after Portugal’s liberation from the Castilian yoke. His appointment is dated 9 August 1641, and he took office on 20 March 1642.
Freitas

This is a very old surname among us. One of the first to bear it was Gonçalo de Freitas, who settled in the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and had his residence there, on the *quinta* (country estate) called da Torre (‘tower’). He was a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and Master of the Royal Hunt to Infante Ferdinand. His daughter Catarina de Freitas founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) on the land she inherited from her father, in the locality (*sítio*) that later took the name of Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’). Gonçalo de Freitas’s son was João de Freitas, who enjoyed the privileges of nobility inherited from his father. An old nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) says that he built the church of Salvador (the Saviour) in Santa Cruz by order of the king, and for this received the royal grant of the chantry (capela) of that church as his family vault, in recognition of his services and of the expenses he had incurred on the church. One of his sons, named Jordão de Freitas, distinguished himself valiantly in India, where he was lord of an island and captain of the Moluccas. A member of this family was João de Freitas da Silva, who in 1631 raised on this island a company of 100 men at his own expense and went with it to serve in Pernambuco, where the Dutch killed him.

There was another family of the same surname on this island, also very old, descended from João Rodrigues de Freitas, a native of the Algarve. He held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Madalena (‘Magdalene’) and died there in 1523. He was buried in the church that Henry the German had founded there, whose widow, named Isabel Lopes, he had married. They founded an entailed estate there, which later became an important house; its last representative was the holder of the entail Nuno de Freitas Lomelino.
Freitas (Augusto César de)

He was a man of rare talent and remarkable literary gifts, whom adversity struck hard, never allowing his intellectual gifts to shine and be appreciated as they truly deserved. We know little of his life, although he was our contemporary. We know that he was a primary-school teacher and that he took up journalism, showing remarkable qualities as a writer. In Funchal he was an editor of *O Noticioso* and *O Paiz*, and in Lisbon he contributed to *O Parlamento*, *O Conservador* and *O Monitor Portuguez*, on a par with the leading journalists, according to a witness of the time. On the editorial staff of *A Revolução de Setembro* he was a colleague of our foremost journalist, António Rodrigues Sampaio, who thought very highly of him. He died abandoned on a straw pallet in a hospital on 21 December 1874.
Freitas da Silva (Dr João de)

He was born in Lisbon in 1842 and is the 1st Viscount of Monte Belo. He qualified as a physician and surgeon at the former medical school of Funchal, took a doctorate in medicine at the faculty of Montpellier (1863) and is chief officer of the Port Health Station (*guarda-mor da Estação de Saúde*). He was director of the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’) and representative (*procurador*) to the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*). Works: *De l'Affection bilieuse, thèse présentée et publiquement soutenue à la faculté de médicine de Montpellier*. (1921).
Freitas (Dr Justino António de)

This illustrious Madeiran was born on 13 September 1804. He was studying in the faculty of law of our University when the civil war broke out, forcing him to interrupt his studies, so that he was able to complete his academic career only late. As he professed liberal ideas, he suffered persecution at the hands of the absolutist government: he spent many months imprisoned in the gaols of Coimbra and also some time as a fugitive.

He had a most distinguished course of studies, completing his degree in 1836 and taking his doctorate in April 1837. He joined the teaching staff of the University in 1840 as a substitute professor (*lente substituto*), and was promoted to full professor (lente catedrático) by decree of 4 November 1852. As a professor at our foremost educational establishment, he was noted above all for the reform he introduced in the teaching of a branch of the legal sciences hitherto little cultivated in Portugal: administrative law. He organised the study of this discipline on sound foundations and along truly scientific lines, whereas until then it had been taught at the University in a very antiquated manner that left much to be desired. To serve as the textbook for this chair, he published a valuable work entitled *Instituições de Direito Administrativo Portuguez*, of which two editions appeared within a few years. Besides his important contributions to specialist journals, he wrote the *Manual dos Juizes eleitos*, which ran to seven editions, and the *Manual do Rendeiro*, which was reissued twice.

Dr Justino de Freitas was one of the ablest advocates of his time. In Coimbra, where so many distinguished jurists devoted themselves to a career at the bar, he was then considered the most illustrious lawyer in the city. He carried on these honourable traditions in Lisbon when he practised law in the capital, having settled there to serve as a member of the Higher Council of Public Instruction and to take a more active part in political struggles and, in particular, in parliamentary work.

In the national assembly, where he sat as a deputy for many years, he brilliantly upheld the reputation as a distinguished jurist and orator that had preceded him. It was perhaps, however, as a member of various parliamentary committees and as rapporteur of countless bills that he revealed his qualities as a distinguished parliamentarian. He would several times have held a ministerial portfolio had he not always sought to avoid joining any cabinet. The work of his law office, which frequently handled cases of great importance, some of them notoriously celebrated, his regular attendance at the sessions of the Higher Council of Education (*Instrução*) and his work on parliamentary committees systematically kept him away from the grave concerns and heavy responsibilities that a minister’s portfolio would have brought him. ‘It was for this reason,’ we read somewhere, ‘that in Justino de Freitas, besides remarkable talent, served by an uncommon learning in forensic matters, there was something like the artistic inspiration of advocacy; and in the last years of his life, more than the interests of that honourable and glorious profession, it was a fanatical love of the practice of jurisprudence that kept him at the advocate’s bench.’

Dr Justino António de Freitas was actively involved in politics from his student days. He followed liberal ideas during our civil wars, for which he was imprisoned and persecuted. He later took a very active part in the revolutionary movement of 1846 and became a member of the provisional government formed at that time. Despite this, he asked politics for neither sinecures nor honours: he never accepted or sought public posts, and he always disdained the titles and honorary offices with which others at times wished to distinguish him.
He died in Lisbon on 28 November 1865. He was the father of the well-known statesman Augusto César Barjona de Freitas.
Freitas (João Joaquim de)

He was born in Machico on 5 October 1832 and died in Funchal on 1 April 1910. For more than thirty years he served as librarian of the Funchal municipal library, and he was also acting teacher of Portuguese language and literature at the central lyceum (state secondary school) of this city. Although he died almost forgotten, he was a distinguished educator and a man of uncommon talent and great learning. He assisted the distinguished jurist Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo (see that entry) in interpreting and correcting Frutuoso’s manuscript entitled ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*As Saudades da Terra*), and he contributed to several of the island’s newspapers. He left a rich library, which the British subjects W. and A. Reid bought for two thousand escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) and presented to the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*). The former Rua das Cruzes in Funchal now bears the name of João Joaquim de Freitas. (1921).
Freitas (Jordão Apolinário de)

He was born in this city on 23 July 1866, the son of Luís M. de Freitas and Dona Ana Fortunata de Sousa e Freitas. After completing the theology course at the seminary (*Seminário*) of this diocese, he took the course of the Funchal Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica do Funchal*). He settled in Lisbon many years ago, and there he at present (1921) holds the post of director of the Ajuda public library, having previously been librarian of the Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia*). He has devoted himself especially to historical research, and his literary output in books and pamphlets is already considerable, besides his contributions to various reviews and newspapers.

His publications include: *Subsídios para a bibliografia portugueza relativa ao estudo da língua japoneza e para a biografia de Fernão Mendes Pinto* 1905; *Fernão Mendes Pinto e a sua ultima viagem á China*, 1905; *A Inquisição em Goa*, 1907; *O 2.° visconde de Santarém e os seus atlas geographicos*, 1909; *Capela Real a Egreja Patriarchal na Ajuda*, 1909; *O Marquez de Pombal*, 1910; *Francisco Moraes o ‘Palmeirim’*, 1910; *Quando foi descoberta a Madeira*, 1911; *Camões em Macau*, 1911; *Onde nasceu o 2.° visconde de Santarém?*, 1913; *O Naufragio de Camões e os Lusiadas*, 1915; *A imprensa de tipos moveis em Macau e no Japão nos fins do seculo XVI*, 1916; *Cervantes e Argensola*, 1916; *O Marquez de Pombal e o Santo Oficio da Inquisição*, 1916; *Dom Bento de Camões e o Príncipe dos poetas Lusitanos*, 1917, besides other works. He compiled and annotated the works of the Viscount of Santarém, *Opúsculos e Esparsos*, 2 volumes, and *Inéditos*, 1 volume, and wrote their prologue.
Freitas (José Vicente de)

He was born in Calheta (‘small cove’) on 22 January 1869 and belongs to an old family of that town (*vila*). He is a lieutenant-colonel of infantry and served in the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps that fought in France. (1921)

He was appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 9 February 1915, took office on the 22nd of the same month and served until 15 May of that year. On 28 April 1918 he was elected deputy for Madeira.

He published the following works: *Atlas de desenho, geometria descritiva e noções de arte*, Lisboa 1908; *Atlas de desenho, organizado em harmonia com os programmas de 1905*, Lisboa, 1908, 2 volumes, the first for the 1st, 2nd and 3rd forms and the second for the 4th and 5th forms of the lyceums; *Compendio de Desenho para a instrução primaria*, Lisboa, 1903, 2 volumes, the first for the 1st and 2nd forms and the second for the 3rd and 4th; *Roteiro e planta de Lisboa* on a scale of 1/7,500, 1906 edition; and *Livro de Leitura para 4ª. classe das escolas primarias*, in collaboration with F. Veyrier, Lisboa, 1910.
He was president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Lisbon and head of the government for some years.
Freitas Vale (Henrique Félix)

He belongs to an old Madeiran family and was born in this city around 1840. He was a licensed advocate (*advogado provisionista*, practising by licence without a law degree) and municipal receiver (*recebedor do concelho*) of Funchal, and carried out various public-service commissions. He contributed widely to several newspapers and was chief editor of *A Lei* and the *Diário do Funchal* (‘Funchal Daily’). He published the pamphlets *A Crise Agrícola da Madeira, suas causas e efeitos*, 1887, and *A Revolta da Madeira e a comissão de inquérito*, 1888. He settled on the mainland many years ago, where he has held various administrative posts. (1921).
Ash (Fraxinus excelsior)

This member of the olive family, which now occurs only in some *quintas* (country estates), seems once to have formed part of Madeira’s forest flora. A letter issued by John II in 1493 ‘pera confirmaçom & firmidom da merçee das auguas & outras cousas’ (for the confirmation and ratification of the grant of the waters and other things) reads as follows: ‘… we see fit and are pleased to confirm, as by this letter we confirm and hold confirmed, the said chapter containing the said things, with this declaration: that the ash trees and cedars which we reserve for ourselves they shall not use or cut, except for some church or council house…’
Frias

The peak on which construction of the castle of São João Baptista, better known as the Fort of the Pico (*fortaleza do Pico*), began in 1622 was and still is called Pico dos Frias. The name was given to it by Romeu Frias, an Italian by nationality, who lived there and held land there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and who was one of the earliest settlers of this island.
Friderichsen (K.)
Danish batologist who identified the species of the genus *Rubus* collected by Dr Vahl in Madeira. Works: *Rubi fra Madeira* (*Bot. Tidsskrift*, 1905).
Cold store

The now defunct Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) sought to establish a cold store in Funchal, and for this purpose bought a plot of land between the former Rua da Conceição (‘Conception’) and Rua das Hortas, today Rua Correia Heredia and Rua do Alferes Veiga Pestana, for the sum of 10,500.00 escudos. The machinery for the establishment cost 6,000.00 escudos, and by 1915 about 5,000.00 escudos had been spent on installations, walls, opening the connection between the two streets mentioned, etc.

Although the cold store was an establishment capable of rendering good service, it never went into operation, and at a meeting of the Agricultural Board on 23 August 1918 it was resolved to hand over to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) the street on which the buildings intended for it had been constructed. (1921).
Fritze (R.)
German botanist who collected plants in Madeira in 1879 and 1880. Works: *Ueber die Farnvegetation der Insel Madeira* (*Jahresbericht der schlesischen Ges. fur vaterl. Kultur*, (1881).
[Front matter]

This work was intended to mark the fifth centenary of the discovery of Madeira, as one of the commemorations with which that remarkable and auspicious event ought to have been celebrated in our country. For the reasons we have briefly set out in the article Discovery of the Archipelago, we took the view that, to be complete, such a celebration would have to take on a national character and not be confined to the narrow limits of a regional tribute, within the isolation and distance of these remote islands. The words with which the press of the capital recalled the duty of holding this commemoration were lost or entirely forgotten. They drew the attention in particular of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Sciencias de Lisboa*), and most especially of the Commission charged with promoting the celebration of the centenaries of our conquests and discoveries, which exists and operates within that same Academy. If the conquest of Ceuta, as the first to be achieved beyond the frontiers of the mainland, deserved a fitting and solemn commemoration, the discovery of this archipelago could not be forgotten either, for it truly marks the beginning of our brilliant odyssey as navigators and future masters of the seas.

It is no cause for surprise that this should have happened, given that this glorious date passed unnoticed in the capital of this archipelago itself, apart from a few brief and fleeting references in the daily press of Funchal. The honour of commemorating the quincentenary of the discovery of Madeira fell solely to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district. It commissioned the model of the monument to be erected to the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco and arranged for the publication of the work to which these words serve as an introduction. It was at the ordinary session of May 1917 that Mr João Augusto de Pina, a member of that administrative body, put forward the proposal for the publication of this work, which was to be shaped according to the principles set out in that proposal, in the following words:

‘.... I wish to refer to a literary work, historical in character but popular in style, intended chiefly for the less learned classes and easy and quick to consult, in which the whole life of this archipelago, in its many manifestations and varied aspects, is brought into sharp relief, albeit in a condensed picture, so as not to give the work excessively large proportions. This does not remove the need for the work to deal with the principal events that have taken place in Madeira over the long span of five centuries; with the biographies of its most notable men; with its usages, customs and traditions; with its literary, scientific, artistic, industrial, agricultural and commercial activity; with the mildness of its climate, the richness of its fauna and flora, the incomparable beauty of its landscape, etc., etc. In this way the work should become an abundant repository of information and news, of particular interest to all those who, for lack of time or of specialised training, are unable to devote themselves to lengthy studies and wider research’.

Within the sphere of our modest resources and the limited space at our disposal, we have sought to discharge with the most scrupulous diligence the heavy task we took on voluntarily and without reward. We have aimed to write a book that would not only meet the needs of the popular classes, for whom it was especially intended, but would also be of profitable use to educated readers, pointing to the fullest and most authoritative sources that those wishing for a more complete and detailed account of some of the subjects treated in the present work should consult. And despite the elementary character of the *Elucidário Madeirense*, we did not consider ourselves excused from studying certain points of the history of this archipelago in greater depth. To this end we drew on some lengthy research of our own carried out in years past, and undertook fresh research recently, thereby gathering some valuable material for the history of these islands, as we have noted in the article Madeiran History. Only one clause of the undertaking we gave was not observed, because of circumstances entirely beyond our control: the publication of this book within the time originally allotted to it. This work of ours was enriched by the valuable collaboration of our distinguished friends Adolfo César de Noronha and Major Alberto Artur Sarmento, so well known here for their rare talents and wide learning, and especially for their profound knowledge of Madeiran matters. While thanking them for that collaboration, we sincerely regret that it was limited to only part of the first volume, so that the rest of this work has been deprived of the great deal that could have been expected from the proven competence of these illustrious collaborators of ours.

We must point out here that a number of our own writings on various Madeiran subjects, published in several Funchal newspapers, notably the former *Heraldo da Madeira*, the *Diário da Madeira* and the *Diário de Notícias*, have been drawn on extensively in preparing this work, many of those articles being reproduced in part or in full, as the requirements of the subjects we had to deal with demanded.
[Front matter]
O
Fruit

Apart from the careful and methodical cultivation of the vine and the banana, it may be said in general terms that fruit trees are not grown as a crop in this archipelago. This is so even though the special climatic conditions would allow an excellent and abundant yield, and Madeira's geographical position favours the easy export of fruit to various foreign countries and Portuguese colonies. It is true that many fruit-bearing trees are found here, of varied kinds and from almost every region, including tropical climates, but they are generally left to grow as nature itself dictates, without the proper care that experience and science could provide. The true orchard is almost entirely unknown here in Madeira: fruit trees appear scattered among other crops, as though they had sprung up spontaneously, and most farmers give them neither attention nor care.

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that this situation has changed considerably in recent years, and the growing of fruit trees can now be regarded as a significant factor in the economy of the district.
Some legislative measures have been enacted, prompted above all by the cultivation and export of the banana, which at present is one of the most important sources of Madeira's public wealth.

The Decree of 5 June 1935 created in Funchal the Guild of Fruit and Horticultural Produce Exporters (*Grémio de Exportadores de Frutas e Produtos Hortícolas*); another decree of the same date established in this city a Delegation of the National Fruit Board (*Junta Nacional de Frutas*); and the decrees of 21 August 1938 and 16 May 1939 adopted certain measures to protect the export of these products.
Frutuoso (Doctor Gaspar)

Gaspar Frutuoso, the celebrated author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), was born in 1522 in the capital of the island of São Miguel. He was the son of noble and wealthy parents, who gave him every means of acquiring a sound and wide-ranging education.

He went to Salamanca at a tender age, and there he completed the preparatory studies for enrolment at that city’s famous university. He took his doctorate in its faculty of theology, where he was a most distinguished student and revealed an exceptional intellect. Having obtained the doctor’s laurel, he went to the diocese of Braga, but stayed there only a short time, because the repeated entreaties of his relatives, friends and admirers compelled him to return to his native city. While passing through Lisbon he was strongly urged to accept a mitre, which he firmly refused on this and on other occasions in his life.

The fame of his merits and virtues had preceded him to Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), and Dr Gaspar Frutuoso was therefore the natural choice for the highest offices in his diocese. He always sought to excuse himself from them, content to serve as parish priest in the parish (*freguesia*) of the town (*vila*) of Ribeira Grande, where he lived for many years, where he died and where he lies buried.

He was of truly remarkable modesty and simplicity of manner, ‘preferring an obscure and tranquil life, devoted to work and study, to the brilliant and showy positions to which his talent, his vast learning and his eminent virtues could undoubtedly have entitled him.

He died in the town of Ribeira Grande on 24 August 1591, aged 69, and was buried in its parish church, where the following epitaph could be read on his tombstone: ‘Here lies Doctor Gaspar Frutuoso, who was Vicar and Preacher of this Church, *vere* a truly Apostolic man, distinguished in letters and virtues.’

It was in the peaceful retreat of his presbytery at Ribeira Grande that he wrote the vast work ‘Longing for the Homeland’, which was followed by the *Saudades do Céo*, which it seems he never completed.

The year 1922 marked the fifth centenary of the birth of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, and a commission was formed in the city of Ponta Delgada to commemorate the date in fitting style. It also took the opportunity to give due prominence to the eminent qualities as prose writer, historian and humanist that had made this illustrious native of São Miguel famous. To the warmest applause of all, the Centenary Promotion Committee decided that the greatest tribute it could pay to the author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ would be to publish his vast work in full. In this way it would strengthen his memory and make it endure through the ages, while giving his contemporaries and future generations knowledge of the history of the eastern group of the Azorean islands in the 15th and 16th centuries. For weighty reasons, the commission did not carry out its original plan, but it succeeded in publishing the third and fourth books of the *Saudades*, which cover the history of the islands of São Miguel and Santa Maria, which form the administrative district of Ponta Delgada.

They make up four large volumes, whose value and interest are enriched by an extensive study of the historian of the islands, in which the subject is entirely exhausted, whatever the many aspects from which we might judge and appreciate him. The learned *Noticia Bibliográfica das Saudades da Terra* by Mr João Simas and, above all, the biography and appraisal of Gaspar Frutuoso and his work by Mr Rodrigo Rodrigues are studies that reveal not only patient and conscientious historical research combined with the most refined and rigorous critical spirit, but also a profound understanding of the gifts and qualities that should characterise the work of the writer, the scholar and the historian, taking into account the conditions of the time, the environment and the other special circumstances in which the work was produced. Of Mr R. Rodrigues’s masterly study, chapter III deserves particular mention. Entitled *O Humanista, o Historiador, e o Valor da sua Obra* (pp. XXXIX–LV), it can, without any exaggeration, be placed on the same level as similar works by Dona Carolina Michaelis, Teófilo Braga, Mendes dos Remédios and Fidelino de Figueiredo, the most authoritative masters of literary historiography in our country.

In 1866 the mortal remains of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, which lay in the parish church of the town (*vila*) of Ribeira Grande, were transferred to the municipal cemetery of the same town. They were interred in a modest mausoleum that the town’s Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had erected to the memory of the illustrious historian of the islands.
Funchal (Agostinho de Sousa Coutinho, Marquis of)

He is the son of the Count of Linhares and belongs to the family of the 1st Count and 1st Marquis of Funchal, whom we discuss in this *Elucidário*. He was born on 3 March 1866. He was governor of this district (*distrito*) from 23 December 1899 to 25 June 1900.
He held the same office a second time, to which he was appointed by decree of 22 October 1904, taking office on 10 December of the same year.
Old Funchal

In the short article devoted specifically to the raising of the old town (*vila*) of Funchal to the rank of city, we transcribed the royal decree (alvará régio) of 21 August 1508 that brought this about. Here we now wish to give a brief idea of what Funchal must have been like at that time, as regards the few narrow streets that then made up its limited extent. Since this is not easy to do with great topographical precision, we shall confine ourselves to a light sketch, presenting the scant material available for the purpose.

The church whose patron saint was Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), commonly known as Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), and which was destroyed by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803, was already built by 1508 on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, near the spot where the so-called Poço do Calhau (‘well of the pebble shore’) stands today. To the east of this church lay Rua dos Balcões (‘balconies’) and Rua de Santa Maria. The latter was probably shorter than it is now, but it had many large, well-built houses in which a number of noblemen and wealthy men lived.

The Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory’), Rua Direita (‘straight street’) and Rua dos Mercadores existed in 1508, though certainly with a very different appearance from the one they present now. The Largo do Pelourinho was planted with trees, probably native species, and on the site where Rua da Cadeia Velha now runs stood an enormous til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) which, in the words of Manuel Tomaz, ‘embraced two streams with its outstretched branches’: the Ribeira de João Gomes and the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’).

By that time Rua do Sabão and Rua do Esmeraldo also existed. In the latter stood the noble house of João Esmeraldo, a Flemish knight who had come to Madeira in 1480, and near it the granary of the Poço, which had been the residence of Christopher Columbus and where, according to tradition, the original customs house of Funchal was housed.

The Chapel of Varadouros (‘slipways’), demolished in 1911, already existed in 1508. Of the present customs house building, however, if anything existed at all, it can only have been the foundations, for it was in that year that the order came from mainland Portugal for it to be built.

The first parish church was the church of Our Lady of Calhau, but in 1508 the parish was transferred to the so-called great church, whose patron saint is Nossa Senhora da Assunção (Our Lady of the Assumption). Its construction had begun in 1493, funded by the revenues of the wine levy (imposição do vinho), and after the bishopric of Funchal was created in 1514 it became, as it still is, the Cathedral. Only in 1558 was the city divided into two parishes, that of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral) and that of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), and from then on the church of Our Lady of Calhau became a parish church once again.

Beyond Rua dos Mercadores, at the point where the entrance to the city now stands, there were a few houses, but the place looked very different from how it does at present. The Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) had not yet been built, and on the ground now occupied by Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’) there were plantations of sugar cane. These probably extended to somewhere near Rua da Carreira (‘track’), since the building of the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal was begun only after 1686.

When Funchal was raised to the status of a city, there was a small hospital in the street now called Rua do Hospital Velho. Before that there had been another establishment of the same kind beside the chapel of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle), already outside the settlement, on land granted by the donatary (*donatário*) of the island on 25 March 1454.

The Council’s house, then known as the Curral do Concelho, stood in the locality (*sítio*) where Avenida António José de Almeida now meets Rua da Alfândega, and in Largo de São Sebastião stood the chapel dedicated to this saint, which was one of the first churches built on the island. Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’) ran to a little above the Colégio church (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), which was built after the period we are describing. Near the present-day Travessa de João de Oliveira there stood for many years a building that we ourselves knew, whose construction must have dated back to the reign of Manuel I.

The *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) of Bom Jesus (Retreat of the Good Jesus) did not yet exist in 1508, nor did the street in which it stands, nor Rua das Hortas. The church of Carmo (‘Carmel’) had not yet been built either, but the street that took its name from that church must have existed at the time. It connected with Rua Direita by the street later called Rua da Cadeia Velha and by Rua da Margem da Ribeira. It is likely that a wooden bridge at the end of Rua Direita linked the two banks of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia.

Rua da Carreira, the widest street in the settlement, though very different in appearance from today, probably did not extend beyond Rua dos Aranhas, which was built later. Close by lay the Mouraria (‘Moorish quarter’), where the captive Moors lived. Rua das Pretas also existed in 1508, but the church of São Pedro was begun only later.

Outside the city stood the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), built in 1492 near the residence of the donatary, which was probably on the *quinta* (country estate) now called Quinta das Cruzes. There were also the chapels of São Paulo and of St Catherine, the latter with an attached hospice (*hospício*) where poor women lived. It is possible that the Hospital de São Lázaro (St Lazarus) had already been built by 1508.
