Where Rua 5 de Junho and the lanes that run into it now lie, there were a great many hovels in which the poorest people of the settlement lived. To the west stretched extensive plantations of vines and sugar cane, which must have covered the ground now crossed by Rua da Imperatriz, Calçada da Cabouqueira and part of Rua da Carreira. The churches of Santa Luzia and Santa Maria Maior, the Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation), the convent of the Mercês and the curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city) were all built after 1508. By that time, however, the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) already existed, on the site where the Jardim de São Francisco is today, as did the chapel of São João.

At that time, although they looked different from today, the little streets of João Tavira, Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’), Cidrão and Hospital Velho already existed, as did the squares of Corpo Santo and São Paulo, besides other squares and streets whose names have not survived in local tradition.

From what has been said, then, it is clear that although the Funchal of 1508 was much smaller than the present city, it nonetheless covered an area large enough to form a city. To the west it extended a little beyond the convent of São Francisco, without, however, reaching the Ribeira de São João. To the east it reached as far as the chapel of St Elmo (*Corpo Santo*), which even in Frutuoso’s time adjoined the first houses of the city. Finally, to the north its limits were the Rua do Hospital Velho, the Rua do Carmo – which probably did not go beyond the point where the church stands – the Rua da Carreira, the Rua das Pretas and the Mouraria.

But it was not only its size that commended the foremost settlement of Madeira in the time of King Manuel I. It was also commended by its climate, by its landing place and by being the centre of the industry and shipping of the whole archipelago. It is possible that all these circumstances contributed, more or less directly, to leading the monarch to sign the decree that raised the town (*vila*) founded by Zargo to the rank of city.
Funchal (bay)

The bay of Funchal is the widest in the archipelago, bounded by Ponta do Garajau (‘tern point’) to the east and Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’) to the west. It forms a fairly regular curve and inlet between those two headlands and is sheltered from winds from every quarter except the wind that blows from SSE to SSW by way of S. Its breadth makes it a vast anchorage, but communication with the land can be established with relative ease only at the most accessible points of the shore. These stretch from the Ilhéu da Pontinha (‘islet of the little point’) in the west to the vicinity of the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) in the east, some two thousand metres apart. All the traffic and movement of the landing place takes place within these limits. It is bounded by a beach of rounded boulders, with deep water and free of reefs or shoals that might hinder access. High water, or the establishment of the port (time of high water at full and new moon), according to the geographical map of Madeira by General A. P. de Azevedo, is at 12 h 48 min, with a tidal rise of 2.28 m; the engineer Mariano F. Faria e Maia, however, states that the tidal range reaches 2.80 m. With regard to the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*) and the tides of the Madeiran coast, the illustrious engineer Adolfo Loureiro says that little is known about the lunar influences on spring and neap tides, about their propagation, velocity and direction, about the height and force of the waves according to the direction of the wind, their thrust, duration, etc. The temperature of the waters and its distribution at the surface, and their periodic movements and conditions, which follow a law that seemed constant, ought to have become the subject of very interesting oceanographic studies, which unfortunately were never carried out.
See Cais, Autonomous Board of Harbour Works, Molhe da Pontinha, the harbour of Funchal and Tides.
Funchal (judicial district)

Only in 1767, when *juízes de fora* (crown-appointed judges) and *corregedores* (royal magistrates) began to be appointed on a permanent basis, did the administration of justice in this archipelago take on a regular form in keeping with the nature of the important services it performed. This situation lasted until 1838, when two judicial districts (*comarcas*) were created, both with their seat in the city of Funchal. They were named the western judicial district and the eastern judicial district. The first comprised the parishes (*freguesias*) of the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Funchal, Câmara de Lobos, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Porto Moniz and São Vicente, with the exception of the parish of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral); the second covered the parish of the Sé and the parishes of the municipalities of Santa Cruz, Machico, Sant’Ana and Porto Santo.

The decree of 12 November 1875 profoundly altered the judicial division by creating the judicial districts of Funchal, Ponta do Sol, Santa Cruz and São Vicente. That of Funchal was installed on 16 November 1876 and was divided into nine *julgados* (lower court divisions), comprising the parishes of the municipalities of Funchal and Câmara de Lobos.

The decree of 22 June 1927, which abolished the judicial district (*comarca*) of São Vicente, altered the division of the *julgados*, or justice-of-the-peace districts, of the Funchal judicial district. These were thereafter made up of the parishes (*freguesias*) of Arco de São Jorge, Câmara de Lobos, Campanário, Curral das Freiras, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Faial, Santa Luzia, Santa Maria Maior, São Pedro, São Roque, Monte, Porto Santo, Quinta Grande, Sant'Ana, Santo António, São Jorge, São Martinho and São Gonçalo, each of these parishes forming a *julgado* of its own.

The extraordinary volume of business in this judicial district led to the creation of a further court, so that there came to be a Civil and Commercial Court (*Juízo Cível e Comercial*) and a Criminal Court (*Juízo Criminal*), each of the two courts headed by a judge. All this was regulated by the Decree of 22 June 1927, which thus rendered a notable service to the orderly and effective administration of justice. The Decree of 29 June 1933 recast the provisions of the earlier decree, establishing two courts (*varas*) of mixed jurisdiction, named the Court of Law of the First Division of the Funchal Judicial District (*Juízo de Direito da Primeira Vara da Comarca do Funchal*) and the Court of Law of the Second Division (*Juízo de Direito da Segunda Vara*). The same decree created the Judicial Secretariat (*Secretaria Judicial*). Each court consisted of three sections, each section of a head and a clerk, and there was also a central section common to both courts with two heads, known as heads of the secretariat, one of them being a deputy.
The complete list of the magistrates who have served as judges of law in the judicial districts of Funchal from 1835 to the present day will be published in the articles under the heading Judges.
See Judicial Administration and Judicial Organisation.
Diocese of Funchal

To the article on the creation of this diocese (1-363) it should be added that it is the Portuguese ecclesiastical circumscription with the smallest area, covering only the territory of the Madeiran archipelago; the small island of Arguin once also belonged to its jurisdiction. It comprises 50 parishes, which correspond exactly to the 50 civil parishes into which the district is divided. For the purposes of ecclesiastical administration these parishes are grouped into four archpriest districts (see that entry). Its seat is the city of Funchal, with its Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) and cathedral chapter (*Cabido*), the bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*), the seminary (*Seminário*), ecclesiastical offices and various religious services, all under the direct supervision of the diocesan prelate, who actually resides in the same city.

The first to exercise ecclesiastical functions here were the Franciscan friars and, after them, the priests sent by the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which the archipelago belonged in spiritual matters. The rapid growth of the population led to the creation of a diocese, in which its prelate could freely perform all the acts of worship proper to his episcopal rank. The bull (papal bull) *Pro excellenti praeeminentia* of 12 June 1514 established the Diocese of Funchal, and on the same date Diogo Pinheiro, one of the highest-ranking members of the Order of Christ, was appointed its first prelate, though he never came to his diocese.

At that time it covered a vast area, extending over most of the islands and lands discovered or conquered by the Portuguese. In 1533 it was raised to the rank of an archbishopric, with the newly created bishoprics of Angra, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Goa as its suffragan dioceses; the archbishopric was abolished in 1551. Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto promulgated and published the Constitutions of the Bishopric in 1581, which the prelate Dom Luís de Figueiredo had reprinted in 1601, publishing in the same year the supplementary constitutions (*Constituições Extravagantes*), which he added to them. The apostle Saint James the Less is the patron saint of the diocese of Funchal; his feast is celebrated every year on the first day of May.

The Cathedral is a fine and spacious church, classified as a National Monument (*monumento nacional*), and it well deserves an unhurried visit. The pure Gothic of its architectural lines, the slender columns of its naves, the ceiling made of native cedar in the Moorish style and inlaid with ivory, the magnificent chapel of the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*), the sumptuous processional cross of silver gilt presented by Manuel I, a number of excellent paintings and other exquisite works of art are objects of admiration and esteem for all who visit this church. Its construction began in the last years of the 15th century and it was consecrated in 1516, although the ornamental work and interior decoration of the church as a whole had not yet been entirely completed.
See the pamphlet *Sé Catedral do Funchal* by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva.

The old bishop's palace, which now houses the lyceum (state secondary school), was built in 1751. Despite its heavy façade, devoid of any architectural refinement, it nevertheless retains a certain air of grandeur and did no discredit to the high rank of its occupants. The present episcopal residence stands in Largo do Ribeiro Real, and its outbuildings house the various ecclesiastical offices.
Closely related to this subject are the articles Archbishopric, Bishops of Funchal, cathedral chapter, Deanery, bishop's palace, Cathedral and Seminary, included in this Elucidário.
Funchal – I. Origin of the name

It is commonly stated that the umbellifer *Foeniculum vulgare*, known as *funcho* (fennel), gave Funchal its name, and no reasons or facts are known that contradict this. On landing at this spot, which later became a town (*vila*) and later still a city, the discoverers or first settlers came upon the plant growing abundantly in the valley, and the place quickly and naturally began to be called Funchal. As Frutuoso says: ‘. . .Funchal, a que o capitam deo este nome, por se fundar em hum valle fermoso de singular arvoredo, cheyo de funcho até o mar’ (Funchal, to which the captain gave this name because it was founded in a beautiful valley of remarkable trees, full of fennel down to the sea). According to the author of the *Saudades*, it was João Gonçalves Zarco himself who gave the name Funchal to the place that later became the capital of this archipelago.

One question arises, however, and it is not the first time it has been asked. Since this valley was certainly home to trees and large plants, why would the discoverers have preferred to name it after a plant that is not even a shrub? It is possible that amid the mass of trees filling the valley there was a clearing where fennel abounded, making it stand out from the surrounding vegetation. It is also said that the discoverers found fennel in abundance in the immediate vicinity of the landing place, hence the easy christening of the spot as Funchal.

A settlement named Funchal existed – and we do not know whether it still exists – in the parish (*freguesia*) of Lumiar, on the outskirts of Lisbon, as we have already noted in the article Ameixoeira (see that entry). According to what we read in the *Encyclopedia Portuguesa* of Maximiliano de Lemos, there are also settlements named Funchal in the parishes of Aldoar and Igreja Nova, in the municipality (*concelho*) of Mafra, in Terrugem, in the municipality of Sintra, and in Vilar de Mouros. Might there perhaps be some connection between the name of Funchal and any of these settlements?

On this subject, it is worth reading the short article entitled Ameixoeira on p. 63 of the first volume of this *Elucidário*. Only recently, in the *Dicionário Corografico de Portugal Continental e Insular*, we saw some twenty localities and settlements named Funchal mentioned.
II – Creation of the town and municipality

The earliest settlement may well have begun at the same time in more than one place. It has been established that one of the first population centres formed on the left bank of the João Gomes stream, not far from its mouth, and soon spread widely into the surrounding area. This spot and its immediate surroundings certainly offered considerable advantages for extensive settlement: its size, the shelter given by the high mountains that encircled it, a good seaport, the plentiful watercourses that crossed it and its temperate climate, besides many other circumstances worthy of the greatest consideration. Yet it also presented serious dangers, because it was exposed to the constant threat of floods whenever the swollen streams burst their beds and overran their banks, becoming terrible agents of destruction and death. This happened more than once, above all in 1803, when a considerable part of the city and several hundred of its inhabitants were swept into the ocean.

Meanwhile this centre of population developed rapidly and soon reached a remarkable degree of prosperity. At the same time, important groups of settlers were forming in other parts of the island, and these were quickly turned into independent parishes and later into towns and municipalities.

The illustrious annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) tells us that the first parish (*freguesia*) on this island was established in 1430, with its seat at the locality (*sítio*) of Nossa Senhora da Calheta, in the settlement that had grown up there. This seems to us unlikely if we give that word the meaning of a community of settlers with a life of its own, independent from the social and religious point of view. It was perhaps a chaplaincy (capelania), like those set up in various places, which later became so many parishes.

As colonisation spread widely, the settlement grew rapidly in importance, and before long there arose the legitimate aspiration to have it raised to the rank of town (*vila*), enjoying the privileges and rights that charters granted to municipalities.

Despite his diligent research, the learned annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ was unable to find the document that raised the early settlement of Funchal to a town. On the strength of the weighty arguments he puts forward, based on various documents, 1451 can nevertheless be given as the year of its creation. The same annotator says he examined a manuscript miscellany in the Public Library of Lisbon, in which he found the following: ‘In 1452 Afonso V gave a charter (foral) to the town of Funchal with many privileges, exempting the inhabitants of the whole island from paying excise (*siza*), tolls, produce dues or any of the taxes then levied in the Kingdom’. This transcription corroborates the conclusions reached by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo.

The document creating a town either included or had attached to it a charter, which formed the organic law of the municipality, setting out the rights and exemptions granted to it and also the obligations imposed on it. The record of the charter of the town of Funchal has not yet been found, and it is known only through references to it in various official documents and other sources, such as the one quoted above.

The town and original municipality of Funchal took in the former captaincy of the same name and stretched from Ponta da Oliveira (‘olive-tree point’) along the south and west coasts of Madeira to Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’). Half a century later this area was greatly reduced by the creation of the towns and municipalities of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Calheta (‘small cove’), the first in 1501 and the second at roughly the same time, as we have noted elsewhere in this *Elucidário*. A little over 50 years after the town of Funchal was created, it was raised to the rank of city, in 1508.

As late as 1834 the municipality of Funchal still stretched from the eastern part of the parish of Ponta do Sol to Caniço (‘reed’); only in 1835 did it acquire its present area. By the royal decree (*alvará*) of the prefect (*prefeito*) of the Province of 20 January 1835, it lost the part of the parish of Ponta do Sol that had been left to it by the letter of King Manuel I of 2 December 1501, in which he made ‘the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Ponta do Sol a town’. At the end of that same year, 1835, it lost Caniço, which was annexed to the municipality (*concelho*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), together with the parishes of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and those that follow it westwards as far as the *lugar* of Ponta do Sol. The old town of Funchal originally covered a very small area. Even at the end of the 15th century it was bounded to the south, by the beach, by a dry-stone wall fitted with small turrets a crossbow shot apart and by a solid wooden stockade; to the west by the São João (‘St John’) or São Paulo stream; to the north by the lands of Pico dos Frias (‘the Frias’ peak’) and Valverde (‘green valley’); and to the east it came close to the right bank of the Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) stream. The large population centre that had formed from the earliest times on the left bank of the João Gomes stream and near the beach lay outside the area originally called the town, and was later incorporated into it.
See Charters.
III – Creation of the city

The natural and ever-increasing growth of Funchal in former times, which made it an important commercial emporium and a centre of great industrial and mercantile activity, fully justifies the measure taken by King Manuel I in his royal letter (*carta régia*) of 21 August 1508, raising the town (*vila*) of Funchal to the rank of city. It had become a town from a simple settlement 50 years earlier, and after only half a century it gained the privileges of a city, the first to be created in our overseas domains. Despite the concision we have given to the subjects covered in this work, which has forced us to omit all documentation, we shall, by way of exception, transcribe the royal instrument that created this city, which is the capital of the archipelago, the principal centre of its intellectual life and the seat of its commerce and industries. Here it is:

‘Dom (noble honorific) Manuel, by the grace of God King of Portugal and of the Algarves on this side of and beyond the sea in Africa, Lord of Guinea and of the conquest, navigation and commerce of Ethiopia, Arabia, Persia and India. To all who see this our letter we make known that, considering, with praise to Our Lord, how the town of Funchal on our island of Madeira has grown into a very great settlement, and how many noblemen, knights and honourable persons of great wealth live there, through whom, and through the great trade of the said island, we hope with the help of Our Lord that the said town will be much further ennobled and increased; and having regard to the great service we have received from its inhabitants and hope to receive in the future; and because we are pleased to do honour and favour to the said noblemen, knights, squires and people of the town, without their or anyone on their behalf asking or requesting it of us, we, of our own motion and royal and absolute power, with that good will which we have always had and have for all the good and greater increase of the affairs of the said town, by this present letter are pleased to make it, and do in fact make it, a city. And we wish and are pleased that from now on it be entitled and called a city, and have all the insignia that belong to the cities of our kingdoms, and use and enjoy all the privileges, pre-eminences, liberties, favours, graces and franchises that the cities of our said kingdoms enjoy and use and ought to enjoy and use, and that have been granted to them by the kings our predecessors and by us. We therefore so notify all in general, and command all our magistrates (*corregedores*), high judges, judges, justices, officials and persons to whom this our letter is shown and to whom knowledge of it pertains in any way and manner whatsoever, that in all matters of the said city they fulfil and keep, and cause to be very fully fulfilled and kept, the privileges, liberties, graces, pre-eminences, honours and favours granted to the cities of our kingdoms, which they are to enjoy and use, together with the insignia that belong to them as aforesaid, without going or allowing anyone to go, in part or in whole, against any of the above, for it is our favour and will that all be very fully kept for it without any contradiction. And in certification thereof we order this letter to be given to them, signed by us and sealed with our pendent seal. Given at Sintra on the 21st day of the month of August. In the year of our Lord Jesus Christ one thousand five hundred and eight. And these privileges which we are thus pleased that the said city of Funchal shall enjoy shall not be those granted specially to certain cities of our kingdoms, for it shall only use and enjoy those which are given and granted in general to the cities of our kingdoms. The King.’

A few days before this royal letter was issued, King Manuel had sent, dated 17 August 1508, a royal decree (*alvará*) ordering that the council of Funchal ‘be ruled and governed in the manner in which the council of our city of Lisbon is ruled’. This instrument, which preceded by only a few days the one raising the town to the rank of city, was an act of special deference by the monarch towards the inhabitants of Funchal, and was complemented by the royal letter of 21 August 1508.
See the articles Coat of arms (I-85 ff.), City flag (I-123 ff.) and Charters.
IV – Captaincy

For the purposes of public administration, this archipelago was divided into the three captaincies, or donataries, of Porto Santo, Machico and Funchal. At their head were the captains-donatary, invested with almost unlimited powers by virtue of the respective grants conferred on them by the royal charters of 1440, 1446 and 1450. The detailed articles under the headings Captaincies (I-244) and Donataries (I-373) have said all that is needed to give an adequate account of the captaincy of Funchal.
V – Administrative district

The district of Funchal consists of the islands that make up the Madeira archipelago (see Madeira Archipelago). Before the establishment of constitutional government, the Madeiran archipelago was an overseas province and colony whose administration came chiefly under the Ministry of the Navy. Around 1834, with the creation of the four island districts, three in the Azores and one in Madeira, this archipelago received an administration entirely identical to that of the other districts, governed by the same laws as the whole of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal).

The donataries were succeeded in 1580 by the governors-general, and these in turn, in 1640, by the governors and captains-general, who lasted until 1834 (see Senior Authorities of the Archipelago). With the creation of the district, the senior authority bore the title of prefect (*prefeito*), an office first held in 1834 by Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque. In 1835 the post was renamed civil governor, in 1836 administrator-general (*administrador geral*), and in 1846 civil governor once more, the title it still holds.

From its creation this district comprised the ten municipalities (*concelhos*) of Funchal, Machico, Porto Santo, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Santa Cruz, São Vicente, Câmara de Lobos, Sant’Ana and Porto Moniz; in 1914 the municipality of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) was created (see Municipalities). The municipality of Sant’Ana was abolished in a year we cannot now determine and restored shortly afterwards, and the municipality of Porto Moniz was likewise suppressed in 1849 and in 1896 and restored again in 1855 and in 1898.
See Administrative Organisation.
VI – Municipality

Since the end of 1835 the boundaries of the municipality of Funchal have remained unchanged. The people of Camacha and Caniço, especially those of the latter parish (*freguesia*), have made more than one attempt, petitioning the head of the district to be detached from the municipality of Santa Cruz. However, political influence in the seat of that municipality entirely thwarted the wishes and efforts of the inhabitants of those parishes. One civil governor put forward in an official report the idea of abolishing the municipality of Câmara de Lobos, but the proposal found no echo in higher quarters.

As already stated in the article Parishes, the municipality of Funchal consists of the parishes of Sé, São Pedro, Santa Maria Maior, Santa Luzia, Monte, São Martinho, Santo António, São Roque and São Gonçalo. In 1834, however, when the constitutional privileges were proclaimed in the archipelago, it still included the parishes of Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Nossa Senhora da Graça, Curral das Freiras, Campanário, Ribeira Brava, Serra de Água, Tabua and Caniço.

The boundaries of the municipality of Funchal are: to the north, the central summits of the mountains that divide the slopes of the north and south coasts; to the south, the ocean; to the west, the Ribeira dos Socorridos; and to the east, the Ribeira da Quinta, which separates the parish of São Gonçalo from that of Caniço.
VII – The city

The Madeiran archipelago, which forms the Administrative District of Funchal, has as its capital the city of that name. It lies on the south coast of Madeira and stretches along the foot of high mountains, climbing rapidly up the slopes from the edge of the ocean to an altitude of roughly two hundred metres. It forms a considerable part of a vast and exceedingly beautiful amphitheatre, spread across a broad valley, which as a whole presents itself as one of the most astonishing wonders the eye is granted to behold. As if serving as a backrest to the city and overlooking it along almost its entire length, there rises an unbroken mountain range of hills and heights, covered with the most opulent and varied vegetation and sprinkled with the most picturesque dwellings, which lend still greater distinction, greater charm and greater splendour to so marvellous a scene. It is no wonder that visitors entering the landing place of Funchal, whether they round Cabo do Garajau (‘tern cape’) or Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’) or arrive from the south, should find themselves before a genuine counterpart of the bay and hillsides of the city of Naples, feel their spirits captivated and overwhelmed at the sight of this unequalled panorama, and keep the deepest and most grateful impressions of it for ever. The settlement that served as the nucleus of the future city has existed for five centuries. It was built on very irregular and broken ground, without following any preconceived ideas or plans, in a setting far removed from populous centres, by settlers who came from poor lands and villages and were entirely cut off from what world civilisation could have offered them at that time. The islanders of those days, our ancestors and forebears, left to their own efforts and without effective help from the metropolitan government, gradually built in this isolation of the ocean many settlements, several towns and a city, spurred on above all by the remarkable fertility of the soil and the gentle mildness of the climate. And yet, although the city of Funchal, considered in itself, has no dazzling beauties or charms, it keeps a marked and interesting regional character of its own, and presents distinctive features, shaped by its environmental conditions, that deserve the attentive observer’s notice. It offers the rich produce of its vines, of worldwide reputation, its incomparable embroidery, its fruit and its matchless flowers all year round, its highly original sledges, the typical Monte toboggans, the most enchanting landscape in creation, the mildest and most temperate climate on this planet, etc., etc., and, gilding all of this, an eternal spring and the ever-affectionate hospitality of its inhabitants, which has never been belied.

‘Funchal’, say Messrs Adriano and Aníbal Trigo in the work to which we have already referred, ‘is not a modern city that commends itself by broad avenues, great monuments, varied entertainments and the other attractions that distinguish the most important cities of Europe. There is, however, a combination of natural circumstances here, true privileges of creation, a way of life so particular and typical, a comfort so pleasant and a hospitality on the part of its inhabitants so attractive, that they give the city a very distinctive character and recommend it as a health resort par excellence, especially to the foreigners who flock here in very great numbers, chiefly in the winter season, to enjoy the delights of this unrivalled climate or to seek relief from their ailments.’

‘The impression of the traveller who lands in Funchal for the first time’, says Mr Alberto Artur Sarmento in an interesting work he published in 1908, ‘is always marked by a pleasant surprise, whether at the clarity of objects and the limpidity of the air, or at the original display, so simple and so grand, that springs as much from little Art as from abundant Nature. Wherever tourists come from and whatever season of the year they pass through, they cannot fail to feel a particular emotion, arising from the sweet temperature that governs this matchless climate. And if it happens to be winter and they have fled the heavy mists of the north, their admiration knows almost no bounds, seeing the scene so swiftly changed, the unbroken mantle of ice transformed into carpets of greenery, dappled with flowers.’

As may easily be supposed, it is chiefly in the city of Funchal that all the manifestations of human activity, in their many and varied forms, are concentrated; they have only a faint reflection in the other settlements of the district. Thus tourism, commerce and industry – apart from agriculture and some industries derived from it – the life of the mind expressed through the press and literary publications, and even the rare achievements recorded in the field of the arts . . . all of this appears and develops in the centre of Madeiran civilisation, which is the small city of Funchal.
VIII – Area of the city

The city’s limits steadily expanded as the industrial and commercial activity of the archipelago, which was felt entirely within it, grew in scale, soon reaching a high degree of prosperity. In 1809, 1863 and 1909 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) defined these limits precisely, in keeping with the growth of the population. In the last of these resolutions they were fixed as follows: the area of the city ‘shall be the perimeter formed by the angles whose vertices rest on the following points: 1. Reid’s Hotel, on the Estrada Monumental; 2. the Old Bridge of Ribeiro Seco; 3. the intersection of Rua do Arcebispo D. Aires with the Estrada da Levada de Santa Luzia; 4. the intersection of the said road with Avenida Pedro José de Ornelas; 5. the intersection of Caminho do Palheiro Ferreiro with Caminho do Terço; and 6. the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires, it being understood that the link between the 3rd and 4th vertices is to be taken as made by the polygonal line following all the windings of the Estrada da Levada de Santa Luzia’.

At its ordinary session of 17 October 1927, the Municipal Council resolved to give the city an excessively vast area, extending it deep into the suburban parishes and fixing its limits in the following terms, which, moreover, are not remarkable for their clarity: ‘From the sea in a straight line to the road linking National Road no. 23 with the Caminho Velho de São Gonçalo, the road to the church of São Gonçalo, Caminho do Palheiro Ferreiro, Caminho do Terço, Caminho da Levada do Bom Sucesso in a straight line to the Estrada da Levada de Santa Luzia, from there in a straight line to the Muro da Coelha (north of Quinta Drolhe), Caminho da Água de Mel, Álamos, Ponte da Ribeira Grande, Quinta do Leme, Pilar, Avista-Navios, Caminho de São Martinho and Caminho do Amparo to the Estrada Monumental, and in a straight line down to the sea’. With these new limits the city came to cover an area almost twice as large, taking on truly exaggerated proportions. Under the Council’s resolution of 1909, the parishes of the Sé and Santa Luzia, almost the whole of São Pedro and a considerable part of Santa Maria formed an integral part of the city, and for that reason were called urban parishes. Under the new division of the city in 1927, the district capital came to comprise the area established in 1909, plus the territory added by the suburban parishes of São Martinho, Santo António, São Roque and São Gonçalo; the parish of Monte is the only one that has no share in the perimeter recently fixed for the city limits. Its former area, which was estimated at about five hundred hectares, must at present reach approximately 750. The truth is that this excessive enlargement of the city has not caught the attention of the population, which continues to regard as the boundaries of urban Funchal the limits that were logically and rightly fixed for it in 1909.
Funchal (Marquis of)

Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho was one of the most distinguished Portuguese diplomats. In various European capitals, and especially in London, he represented his country with the greatest brilliance and selflessness, rendering outstanding services at a time of great upheaval throughout Europe.

It is well known that Madeira was twice occupied by English troops, ostensibly for its protection and defence against supposed attacks by Napoleonic forces. These occupations amounted to a genuine conquest, as is proved not only by many diplomatic documents of the period but also by the way the English ran the public affairs of this archipelago: the Portuguese authorities kept only a semblance of power, which in reality lay solely with the commander-in-chief of the British forces (see Occupation of Madeira by English troops). The Madeirans suffered every kind of humiliation during the eight years these occupations lasted. Despite the resolutions adopted at the Congress of Vienna, under which England was to evacuate this island without delay, it is certain that many European chancelleries, and even the highest circles of the Portuguese government, believed that the occupation of Madeira amounted to absolute and permanent possession. It is to the distinguished diplomat Dom Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho, then Portugal’s representative in London, that the evacuation of this archipelago and its return to the Portuguese nation are owed. Through his eminent qualities as a statesman and his numerous writings published abroad, he rendered so many outstanding services to his country. Our government honoured him with the title of Count and later Marquis of Funchal, a title still borne today by the representatives of his family. If we are still Portuguese, it is chiefly to him that we owe it; and yet nothing exists in this city to commemorate this fact or to serve as even a small tribute to the memory of the illustrious diplomat. He died in London in 1832.

A genus of crustaceans dedicated by the late English naturalist James Yate Johnson to the city of Funchal, where he lived for many years. *Funchalia Woodwardi* is the only species so far recorded in this genus, which was published in the *Proceedings of the Zoological Society* of 28 November 1867.
Fennel (Foeniculum vulgare)
An umbellifer common in the low-lying region of Madeira’s south coast. Its fruits are stimulant and carminative. See what we have said about the origin of the name of Funchal.
Funcho (peak)
It lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), at an altitude of 255 m.
Funda (stream)
It rises at the Picos da Silva and da Relva and separates the parishes of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) and Prazeres (‘joys’). Its tributary is the Mendes brook.
Funda (stream)
The parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge (‘St George’) is crossed by a stream of that name.
Fundoa

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Roque (‘St Roch’), Funchal. In this locality, on the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’), stands the chapel of Our Lady of the Rosary (*Nossa Senhora do Rosário*), built by João da Paz de Castro in 1668. The Jesuits had a residence there, with a private chapel and surrounding land.

This locality was also the site of an important reservoir of drinking water, which an extensive aqueduct carried to the centre of the city, chiefly to supply the old Misericórdia Hospital (Hospital da Misericórdia) and other buildings. It was built in 1817 on the orders of the then president (*provedor*) of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), Bishop Dom Friar Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, under the direction of the engineer Paulo Dias de Almeida, and at the time it was considered a valuable work from a technical point of view.
Fura-Vasos

A fish of the perch family (Percidae) that frequents the coastal waters of the archipelago in summer. It is rare and is almost always caught in drift nets (*redes de atravessar*). Its flavour is delicate and its colour a brilliant crimson.
It is also called *alfonsim do rolo*, and was formerly known as *alfaraz* and *realista*.
Furado (shoal)
It is a shoal off the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’).
Furado (shoal)
See Nariz (shoal).
Furado (point)
This point lies on the south-western coast of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It is also called Ponta da Cana Vieira.
Furado (projection)
It is the projection of the coastline that bounds the Abra inlet (see that entry) on its eastern side, near Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’).
Furão (peak)
This mountain peak stands in the mountains of the parish (*freguesia*) of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’).
Furilhão
The Furilhão, or Prego do Mar (‘sea nail’), is a rock 49 metres high, rising a very short distance from Ilhéu Chão (Flat Islet).
According to Madeiran tradition, this rock was once shelled by an English frigate, which had mistaken it for a suspicious vessel. English sailors know the Furilhão as Sail Rock.
Furna da Mulher
This is the name of a hollow or cave on the western coast of Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’), in the Desertas (‘deserted islands’).
Furtado (family)

The Furtado surname descends from Rodrigo Enes Furtado, one of the earliest settlers of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). There he founded a chantry (*capela*) in the parish church, where he lies buried; he died in 1486.
Furtado (Diogo de Mendonça)
He was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira on 17 December 1659 and took office on 2 December 1660.

Five days later he went to the council house of this city and presented to the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) the deed of grant by which John IV had given this archipelago to Queen Catherine, so that it might be duly registered. See Grant of the island of Madeira to Catherine of Braganza.
Fusão (A)
The first issue was published on 21 January 1868 and the last around the middle of July of the same year; twenty-four issues appeared in all.
Fustete
See Ameixieira de Espinho.
Old Natural History Cabinet

This establishment, intended to collect the most notable natural products and curiosities of the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), began to be organised on 4 April 1850. Several rooms of the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’) were set aside to house it.

The natural history cabinet was one of the many improvements owed to the initiative and energetic will of Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro when he was civil governor of the District. It was always very poorly equipped, and the collections it came to hold were all lost or stolen after that governor left the island in 1852.
See Museums.
Livestock

‘All the breeds of domestic animal found in mainland Portugal’, said the agronomist Eduardo Dias Grande in 1865, ‘are present in Madeiran agriculture, with cattle forming the most important capital of the district’s livestock farming.’ According to the same agronomist, there were then 25,338 head of cattle in the whole archipelago, each weighing on average 238 kilograms live weight.

‘There are good reasons to believe’, we read in the report Eduardo Grande presented to the Funchal Agricultural Society, ‘that the first cattle came from the Minho (Zarco’s homeland), and it may also be supposed that others came from the Algarve, from where a great number of settlers arrived in the earliest times. If so, the island breed would have arisen from the union of these two branches, and the bulk of the northern oxen, tempered by the lighter build of those from the Algarve, must have continued to shrink in size from generation to generation, coming to resemble the small breeds of hot countries with fine pastures and such capriciously mountainous terrain. Strength in work, moderate milk yield and abundant butter production are the characteristics of these breeds.’

In 1802 Miguel Fitzgerald brought the first cattle of English breeds to Madeira, and shortly afterwards he asked the Portuguese government for help in establishing a model farm on this island. The help was granted, and a contract was even concluded between Fitzgerald and the governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara for establishing the farm, but the enterprise came to nothing, for reasons entirely unknown to us.

After Fitzgerald, others introduced cattle from England and elsewhere to Madeira. Crossed with the island’s animals, these gave rise to a breed of medium build, but larger than the local breed. The crossbreds predominate today among Madeiran cattle and are generally known as ‘English cattle’, whereas on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) the local breed predominates, having become smaller there than on Madeira.

On Porto Santo, oxen, like rabbits and certain plants, are typical examples of dwarfism. This phenomenon may well be attributed to the difficulty that species confined to a limited space have in strengthening their stock through crossing among varied and numerous individuals.

It is recorded that some Ayrshire Dairy cows were introduced to Madeira between 1830 and 1840, and later an English breeder brought over the first Durhams. Then came Dutch cattle, Jerseys, Schwyz, Alderneys and Taurinas. All these, mixing with the local breed in repeated crosses, gave rise to the new type that, as we have said, now predominates in Madeira.

Within the local breed two sub-breeds may be distinguished: the red and the *alvaçã* (whitish). The first, the more common, is found in every parish of Madeira and is recognised by its red or dark yellow coat. The second is confined to the municipalities of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) and Calheta (‘small cove’) and is characterised mainly by its white or whitish coat. Cattle of the red sub-breed are also known as *profetas* or ‘Porto Santo cattle’, while those of the *alvaçã* sub-breed are often called *gado maneiro* or ‘Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) cattle’.

The working oxen used in Funchal are almost all from Porto Santo. Although small, these animals are excellently suited to the hard work demanded of them and show a vigour rarely seen in cattle from elsewhere. In the rest of the island work is often done by cows of the local breed, which are not, for that reason, any less used for breeding.

Cattle born on Porto Santo grow somewhat taller when fed in the stalls of Funchal and its surroundings, but their offspring lose some of the hardness of hoof that makes the cattle of the neighbouring island so prized for work on steep or stony ground.

Also valued as working animals are the oxen sometimes imported from the Azores, which are larger than those of the local breed. The Corvina cows imported from that archipelago seem to have lost a good part of their milking ability in Madeira.

Crossbreeding increased the milk yield of the native breed, but weakened its spirit for work and its ability to haul heavy loads over the rugged terrain of our island. Crossbred cows are said to give between 900 and 1500 litres of milk a year, but the agronomist Eduardo Grande allows that the yield may reach 1770 litres in the parishes from Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’) to Canhas, owing to the atmospheric humidity, the quality of the grazing and other conditions found there. Daily yield at the peak of lactation does not generally exceed 6 to 8 litres, although cases of 14 and 15 litres are cited.

Formerly numerous cattle of the archipelago’s breed were raised in the uplands, but at present almost all these animals are kept in stalls or under a mixed regime of grazing and stall-feeding. On the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), at Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’) and in a few other places, some free-ranging cattle are still found, generally destined for slaughter.

Horse breeding is of far less importance in Madeira than cattle breeding. A distinction must be drawn between animals born on the island and those imported from Portugal, England and other countries, almost always by the livery-stable keepers. The native breed is strong, active, frugal and remarkably spirited, but there is little demand for it today because of its small stature.

Around 1891 a stallion of good breed was brought to Madeira to improve the quality of the local animals. No benefit came of this introduction, however, perhaps because of the great difference in size between the breeding stallion and the island’s mares. After spending some time in Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’), the horse came to Funchal, where it was kept for a while by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), and it finally went on to Lisbon, to return to the stud or establishment that had lent it.

Horse breeding, which is of no importance on the island at present, is confined to the Paul da Serra and Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’). The animals are generally raised in the open, but when they are two or three years old the breeder brings them in to sell them if they have reached a certain size; those of inferior quality are sent back to the uplands if they can be put to no use. Very small colts are usually castrated to prevent them from breeding.

Mules and donkeys are also found in Madeira, the former imported from Portugal, Andalusia and Morocco, the latter from Porto Santo. Mule breeding once existed on Porto Santo, but today it has died out there completely.

As for sheep, goats and pigs, they are raised everywhere in Madeira, and many goats and pigs are still found in the uplands, although this is prohibited by law. These animals have done great damage to our forests, and it would be an act of great public benefit to enforce everywhere the so-called ‘law on the grazing of livestock in the uplands of the island of Madeira’, published on 23 July 1913.

Madeiran sheep are almost all of the native breed, which is quite hardy and is generally raised in the mountains. Besides these animals, however, there are some merino sheep and sheep of English breeds, kept under a system of full or partial stall-feeding.

According to Eduardo Grande, in 1802 the regent sent a dispatch to the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Dom José Manuel da Câmara, congratulating him ‘on the good result of the introduction of long-woolled sheep’. This stock degenerated on the island, however, as did other well-bred animals introduced later. Eduardo Grande found documents in the archive of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) showing that in that same year of 1802 the Irishman Fitzgerald offered the Government a pair of wool-bearing sheep of the finest breed in England.
White wool predominates in the district. It is used to stuff mattresses and to make certain coarse fabrics worn by the country people.

Goats, which until quite recently lived in great numbers in the uplands, are now beginning to be brought down to the farms. Yet it will be hard to end the bad habit of letting them graze freely in the high parts of the island, even though everyone recognises that they are the worst scourge of trees and of every kind of crop. The fires that destroyed many of Madeira’s valuable forests between 21 and 28 August 1919 were caused by livestock breeders, who were deeply angered at having been forced to obey the provisions of the law on grazing in the uplands of the island of Madeira, published on 23 July 1913.

The milk of the goats that graze in the mountains goes unused, but these animals are useful nonetheless, for they supply the skins from which the so-called *borrachos* (see that entry) are made, as well as *botas chãs* (traditional flat-soled leather boots), or peasant boots. Goat meat is little prized, but that of young kids is tasty and appears on many tables, especially at Easter.

It is customary for goat breeders to gather in the uplands on a day in August to round up the animals intended for sale or slaughter. With the help of dogs, the breeders drive the goats into a piece of ground they call a *falso*, which they enclose with interwoven staves and heather, on which they lay their waistcoats; it is there that the selection is made. The animals brought down to the villages are most often destined for milk production, and milk is consumed in large quantities throughout the district.
The females of the native breed produce 200 to 250 litres of milk a year, not counting what their young consume, but there are goats of other origins with greater milking capacity.

The Desertas (‘deserted islands’) goat, descended from animals released on those islands from time to time, is smaller than the Madeiran goat, and differs from it also in its sturdier limbs and straighter horns. The billy goats’ horns are stout and twisted at the tip. Among the goats brought into Funchal every day to supply milk, many belong to the breed of the neighbouring archipelago of the Canary Islands; they differ from the local goats in their thicker muzzle, much longer hair, large drooping ears and some other features.

As regards pigs, the only livestock that remains for us to discuss, a distinction is made between the local breed, descended from animals brought from Portugal in the days of settlement, and the breeds imported in modern times, chief among them the English and Alentejo breeds. The Alentejo pigs have degenerated somewhat in the district, but the Berkshire, Yorkshire and other breeds from England produce excellent specimens, whether of medium or large build. The Poland-China breed, of American origin and also introduced into Madeira, is less highly regarded than the Berkshire and Yorkshire, because it puts on too much fat.

The local pigs that roam free in the mountains sometimes show features that distinguish them from sty-kept pigs, and the finest specimens of the Madeiran variety are found above all at Fanal. The boars of this variety have strong tusks, equal in size to those of *Sus scrofa*.

‘The pig,’ says Eduardo Grande in his report, already cited, ‘is the animal of poor countries and of small holdings. Voracious and omnivorous, its ease of breeding and its low price make it precious and almost indispensable to the poor inhabitants of our countryside, and the only animal compatible with the narrowness of their means.’

Indeed, few peasants do not raise one or more pigs on the plots they cultivate. These animals supply a good part of the manure with which they fertilise the land, and the meat they eat at Christmas and through the rest of the year.

Raising pigs at complete liberty in the mountains is prohibited, as we have already said, by the grazing law, but it will be hard to stamp out, although something has been done recently to put an end to an abuse that has contributed considerably to the destruction of our forests.

The main pig-producing centres are Sant'Ana and Ponta do Sol, but pigs, of immense use to the peasant, are raised all over the island. Males and females intended for fattening are castrated from two months of age onwards, and three or four months before slaughter their feed is improved: they receive a daily ration of maize or wheat bran so that they fatten quickly. Before concluding this brief account of the different species making up the archipelago’s livestock, we should say that although the number of cattle and pigs has not risen since 1893 as considerably as certain circumstances might suggest, their value today is vastly greater than it was then. A yoke of working oxen, which shortly after the outbreak of the European war could be bought for 200 and 250 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis), today costs from 800 to 1200 escudos. A milk cow that 20 years ago was bought for 50 and 60 escudos, and not long ago for 100 and 120 escudos, now fetches prices ranging between 200 and 300 escudos. A piglet now costs 30 and 40 escudos, whereas only a few years ago its price was around 5 and 6 escudos.

The enormous demand for milk at present, owing to the growth of the butter-making industry, is one of the main causes of the prices reached by cattle. It should be noted that in some localities the rearing of calves has been almost entirely abandoned: they are killed a few days after birth so that the cows’ milk yield can be devoted exclusively to industrial purposes.

In our view, the livestock population cannot be significantly increased until the district’s fodder resources are improved. According to the best estimates, there are today only 3,480 more head of cattle in the archipelago than in 1893. This truly insignificant increase, for a country that has in livestock rearing and butter-making extremely important sources of revenue, shows that these industries have already reached all the development compatible with local resources.

The livestock farmer who sets fire to the forests of our mountains is generally aiming to enlarge the district’s grazing land. To achieve this *desideratum*, however, what he ought to do is make proper use of the existing meadows and pastures and introduce and spread new fodder species suited to the soils and climate of the island. No serious effort has ever been made to improve the country’s fodder resources, and our land now feels the effects of this neglect more than ever, for its rural economy would gain a great deal from an increase in the cattle population and the rational use of dairy breeds.

Anyone wishing for a more detailed account of the livestock of this archipelago must consult the important and extensive study devoted to it by the distinguished veterinary surgeon João Tierno. It forms part of the report which, some forty years ago, he addressed to the higher authorities in his capacity as livestock intendant (*intendente de pecuária*) of the district of Funchal. Although it does not refer to a very recent period, its statistics and its interesting information remain highly relevant today and can be consulted with the greatest benefit. It deals with the livestock census, the areas the animals occupy, the numbers of each species in relation to land area and population, their breeds and sub-breeds, their anatomical characteristics, their importance in the district’s economy, the causes of their limited expansion, etc., etc., all of which undoubtedly makes up a broad and expert study.

Among the interesting sections on bovines, equines, ovines, caprines and swine, the first deserves particular mention: its author gave it an extensive exposition, making it, as far as possible, entirely complete of its kind.
On this subject, it is also very rewarding to read the interesting book *Mamíferos do Arquipélago Madeirense* by Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento.

As the observations on livestock development that the *Diário de Notícias* of Funchal published in one of its editorials in January of the present year, 1941, seem to us very sound and useful, we shall, with due acknowledgement, reproduce them in these pages, convinced that they may serve as guidance and encouragement for those in this archipelago who devote themselves in particular to cattle breeding.
‘In Madeira, an essentially agricultural land, the livestock question is of special interest from the point of view of farming, of dairy products and of the public food supply itself.
Unfortunately, livestock is bred on this island without any rational criterion, and the result is that stock farming does not yield all the income it is capable of.

In every country where an intelligent approach to this matter exists, efforts are made to determine the purpose of stock farming, and the breeds or animals for breeding are chosen according to whether it aims at producing milk or meat.

In the areas close to the city, preference is given to the breeds that yield large quantities of milk, as these are the most profitable. In the more distant areas, where the milk produced goes to the dairy products industry, the breeds chosen are those which, although they produce less milk, give a product better suited to making cheese or butter.

In Madeira, unfortunately, our farmers have no sound guidance on this matter. Not only are there no defined types or varieties, but what remains of imports made years ago tends to degenerate more and more, through mixing and crossbreeding governed by no rational criterion whatsoever.

Cattle breeding here does not follow principles that are elementary in animal husbandry. The health of the animals is neglected, and they often live without enough air and light. When the slaughterhouse condemns an animal as diseased or unfit for consumption, there is a great outcry, as if the public were obliged to buy everything intended for it.

In truth, cattle are rarely raised here for slaughter. Most of the beasts that come to the slaughterhouse are cows that have spent years as dairy animals and are killed because keeping them no longer pays.

We believe that our farmers should be encouraged to select their cattle on the basis set out above. In the suburban parishes – São Roque, São Martinho, Monte, etc. – the cattle raised should be chiefly high-yielding dairy stock. In the more distant parishes – Santa Cruz, Sant'Ana, Fajã da Ovelha – there should be cows whose milk, being rich in cream, is best suited to making cheese or butter.

Among the local varieties, adapted to the environment, to its climate and to the system of stall-feeding, usable types could be found, capable of improvement through rational selection and through new blood, which is always advisable and beneficial.

Beef cattle are not raised in Madeira. Yet this too is an aspect worth considering and a goal worth pursuing, provided that meat were paid for according to the quality of the animals presented. Admittedly, this criterion is already partly followed today, with the slaughtered cattle graded into categories. But it should go further still, making it quite clear that the breeder who selects and treats his animals rationally deserves greater reward.

The instability seen in the post of livestock intendant (*intendente de pecuária*) has hindered the adoption of a plan of action in a matter of such great importance to Madeiran rural life. But now that this office depends on the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), this administrative body will certainly set a policy of its own that is stable, all the more so as its interest in farming matters and problems fully guarantees the soundness and judgement of that policy.
Locusts

Every so often a few locusts from the African coast appear in Madeira, but the only real damage these insects have caused on record was in October 1844. For two or three days the locusts traced an ellipse in the air 5 to 6 kilometres across, settling in the afternoon on the trees and other plants, whose foliage they destroyed.

The locusts vanished as quickly as they had come, but for several days large numbers of them could be seen floating in the waters of the bay of Funchal and off Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). ‘The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Porto Santo,’ say the *Anais* of that island, ‘passed a resolution (acordam) ordering each inhabitant to deliver one *alqueire* (dry measure for grain; as a land measure c. 900 m²) of those insects to the secretary of the said Council, João António Pedroso, and in this way within a few days 360 *alqueires* of that monstrous plague were buried.’
The locusts that invaded Madeira and Porto Santo at the end of October 1844 belonged to the species *Dectycus albifrons*, which has since been seen several times in Funchal.

Gago (António)

In the article Afonso (João) we did not mention another companion of João Gonçalves Zarco on his first voyage of discovery to the archipelago, named António Gago, whom Frutuoso describes as ‘a nobleman of the Gagos of the Algarve’.

Skipjack tuna (Thynnus pelamys)

A fish of the family Scombridae, a seasonal visitor to Madeira, chiefly in summer and autumn. It is extremely abundant in some years and is generally eaten after being salted and dried in the sun. It is caught with a line and, like the other species of the genus *Thynnus*, is used to prepare so-called tuna conserve, which Madeira exports in large quantities to Portugal. In some parts of Portugal the skipjack tuna (*gaiado*) is also known as *bonito*.
See Tuna.
Gaias

Towards the end of the 15th century Braz Gonçalves de Gaias, a member of the king’s household, lived in Machico. He was one of the early settlers of this island and introduced this surname here; it has since died out.
Gain (Dr L.)

He collected some seaweeds on the beaches and sea rocks of Madeira and Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’) on 11 and 12 August 1911. Works: *Algues provenant des campagnes de l'Hirondelle II–1911 à 1912* (*Bullet de l'Institut Océanographique*, no. 279, January 1914, Monaco). Gaio
See Gull.
Gull (Larus cachinnans)

A bird of the family Laridae, resident in the archipelago. Egg-laying takes place on the sea cliffs in April and May, the clutch consisting of three eggs of variable colour. The nest is built of dry, interwoven plants.
Madeirans call young gulls *gaio* or *gaivoto*; they are distinguished from the adults by their dark plumage, which is replaced by the definitive plumage only after three years.
Gallon
A measure of capacity equal to 3.5 or 3.6 litres. It is widely used on this island for measuring wines and spirits.
Galdo

In the article on the parish (*freguesia*) of Boaventura (‘good fortune’) we have already mentioned Pedro Gomes Galdo, one of the first settlers to bear this surname here. He held much land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Boaventura and São Jorge. The foundation of the chapel of São Cristóvão (St Christopher) in the parish of Boaventura, long before the creation of the parish itself, is attributed to this Pedro Galdo or to one of his descendants.
Galé (shoal)
On the coast of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), not far from the Boqueirão de Cima (‘upper gap’), lies a shoal called Galé.
Galé (point)

This small projection of the coastline of the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) is also called Galera by some; it lies between the mouth of the Ribeira de São Bartolomeu (‘St Bartholomew’s stream’) and that of the Ribeira Funda (‘deep stream’).
Galeão (shoal)
East of the landing place of the town (*vila*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), and not far from the coast, lies a reef (restinga) that bears this name.
Galhardo
The annotator of the *Saudades* says that the name Galhardo originates in the surname Gaillard; who introduced it to this island is not known.
Galinhas (stream)

This watercourse rises in the parish (*freguesia*) of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) and reaches the sea on the coast of the parish of Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’), where there is a small landing place at its mouth called Porto das Galinhas (‘hens’ harbour’).
Woodcock (Scolopax rusticula)

A bird of the family Charadriidae, subfamily Scolopacinae, which breeds in Madeira, preferring the wooded valleys of the interior, such as Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’), etc. It is much pursued by hunters.
Galo (fish)
See Galo (fish).
Galo (peak)

A hill in the locality (*sítio*) of Cruz da Caldeira (‘cross of the cauldron’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), not far from Cabo Girão. See Pico do Galo (‘cockerel peak’).
Galvão (António)
In his *Tratado dos descobrimentos antigos e modernos*, written in 1550, this well-known writer deals with the discovery of this archipelago.
