Gama

Dr Lourenço Vaz Pereira da Gama appears to have been the first on this island to use this family surname. He came to Madeira at the beginning of the 16th century to hold the post of commissioner for the estates of the dead and absent (*provedor de defuntos e ausentes*). He was the father of Dr António da Gama, whom we discuss in this *Elucidário*.
Gama (Arnaldo)

The well-known novelist Arnaldo Gama (1828–1869) wrote, among other books, the novel *A Caldeira de Pêro Botelho*, whose plot is largely set on this island; some of its characters are also natives of Madeira, notably the noblemen Diogo and Pêro Botelho. On the sources he used for weaving this historical novel, Arnaldo Gama says in a final note to his book: ‘In closing, I must say that the story of the love of Diogo Botelho and Dona Beatriz, as well as that of the Caldeira de Pêro Botelho, were taken from the *Relação de uma viagem a Espanha*, written by Tomé Pinheiro da Veiga, who is said to be the author of the famous ‘The Art of Stealing’ (*Arte de Furtar*); the manuscript of this account is owned by Mr António Rodrigues da Cruz Coutinho, proprietor and publisher of this book.’
Gama (Dr António da)

António da Gama is doubtless a name unknown to most Madeirans, even though he flourished in the 16th century as an eminent jurist who enjoyed a great reputation in his day throughout the learned world of Europe.

His writings, and the fame he had won as a professor at a foreign university, earned him standing in our country as one of the foremost jurists of his age. He held the highest offices in the Casa da Suplicação (supreme court of appeal in Lisbon), the Chancery and the Desembargo do Paço (the king's supreme court of justice), chiefly in recognition of his vast knowledge of jurisprudence. His work *De Juribus, quibus Lusitanum imperium in Africa, Índia ac Guinea. Decisiones supremi senati regni Lusitanae* was published successively in Lisbon, Frankfurt, Cremona, Venice and Antwerp. It went through six editions in the last of these cities, the final one in 1735, a hundred and forty years after its author’s death.

The vogue that some of his writings enjoyed throughout Europe over so long a period can be attributed only to their intrinsic merit, especially since he was a foreigner, a native of a country that had not greatly distinguished itself by its intellectual culture.

António da Gama, or António da Gama Pereira, as he also signed some of his works, was born in this city in 1520. He was the son of Dr Lourenço Vaz da Gama Pereira, who held the office of commissioner for the estates of the deceased and absent (provedor dos defuntos e ausentes) in this archipelago, and of his wife, Dona Branca Homem de Gouveia.

From an early age he showed a marked inclination for letters. After studying the humanities, in which he revealed a great aptitude for Latin, he went in 1537 to the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), where he studied civil (Roman) law and was the most distinguished pupil of the celebrated professor and jurist Gonçalo Vaz Pinto. Barbosa Machado says of him ‘that, envying none of his fellow students, he was envied by them all’.
In 1543 he took the degree of bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate), and on 23 February 1546 he competed for one of the university’s chairs, to great applause from masters and students alike.

Wishing to broaden his learning, he went to the University of Bologna, perhaps the most renowned of its day. There he gave brilliant proof of his talent and knowledge and was admitted to the teaching staff of that famous institution, then regarded as one of the great centres of European learning.

John III, drawn by the fame of his name, invited him to return to Portugal and then appointed him professor of a chair at our university. He was later summoned to court, where he remained until his death, holding high offices in which his vast intelligence and the depth of his knowledge shone out remarkably. He was a high court judge (*desembargador*) of appeals of the Casa da Suplicação (supreme court of appeal in Lisbon), then became Chancellor, and afterwards rose to the Desembargo do Paço (the king’s supreme court of justice); he also held other important offices. He not only distinguished himself as a magistrate and always proved an outstanding jurist, but was also greatly revered for his eminent qualities of character, so that his name commanded the highest regard of all.

For more than 40 years he devoted himself entirely to the duties of his various offices, never abandoning the study of jurisprudence, of which he was a consummate master. His opinion was always highly respected and sought on the most difficult questions.

Besides the work mentioned above, he left other writings, all in Latin, which are listed in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’); some of them went through several editions. He also left various unpublished works. He died in Lisbon on 30 March 1595 and was buried in the Convent of Santo Elói (St Eligius), where his tomb bears the following inscription: ‘Tomb of Doctor António da Gama Pereira, of the Council of the King Our Lord, his Judge of the Desembargo do Paço and Chancellor of the Casa da Suplicação, in which Courts he served 49 years. He lived 75. He died on 30 March 1595.’
Gamboa

This surname ‘derives,’ says the annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘from António Garcia Gamboa, a native of the town (*vila*) of Almeida and a knight of the Order of Christ, who was commander of the small tithes (*miunças*) of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and of the fish tithe of the towns of Machico and Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). He also held noble rank (*foro de fidalgo*) and the proprietary post of sergeant-major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major) of the island of Madeira in the time of King Sebastian.’
Gamboa e Liz (António de)

He was appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 7 December 1835 and took office on 14 May of the following year. During his term the post of head of the district came to be called administrator-general (*administrador geral*), and he was the first to hold this office here. In 1838 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) sent a petition to the government on the mainland protesting against this governor’s poor administration. He was born in Arruda dos Vinhos on 10 January 1778 and died on 26 March 1870.
Migratory geese

Among the birds that come to the archipelago, several species of geese have been observed, such as *Anser cinereus* and *A. segetum*. The first inhabits northern and eastern Europe, the second the regions of the Arctic Circle.
Garajau (cape)

Referring to the discovery of this island and the first exploration along its coast, Gaspar Frutuoso says the following: ‘Having come to a high, great point, which the land thrust out, massive and sheer, into the sea, they found there so many common terns (*garajaus*) (sea birds), which without any fear settled on their heads and on the oars, that they took them by hand, at which they were much pleased and made great merriment. And for this reason the name Ponta do Garajau remained. . .’ This point forms the eastern end of the bay of Funchal. On rounding it, heading from east to west, the enchanting panorama of the city suddenly appears, climbing like an amphitheatre up the green slopes, the whole forming one of the most marvellous stretches of landscape a traveller could eagerly hope for. . . Ponta do Garajau rises 126 metres above sea level.

On one of its highest spots, at an altitude of about 120 metres and still within the bounds of the property that Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas owned in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), this distinguished Madeiran had a large statue dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*) erected in 1927. Vessels sight it from a great distance as they make for the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal).

On this web-footed bird and the coastal point to which it gave its name, it is worth reading the series of articles that the distinguished naturalist Adolfo César de Noronha published in the *Diario de Noticias* of Funchal in December 1927.
See Cabos (‘capes’).
Common tern (Sterna hirundo)
A bird of the tern family, common in the seas around Madeira. It breeds on rocks overlooking the sea, laying on the bare ground the three eggs, of variable colour and shape, that make up its clutch.
The common tern (*garajau*) leaves these islands in October and November and returns in the first months of spring. See Cabos (‘capes’).
Funchal Guarantee

The Funchal Guarantee insurance company (*Companhia de Seguros Garantia Funchalense*) was founded in this city on 6 January 1907, with a share capital of 200,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), for the purpose of providing land and marine insurance.
Cane juice (garapa)

Cane juice (*garapa*) is the juice produced by pressing sugar cane. In the factories that produce spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) it is reckoned that 30 kilograms of cane are needed to obtain one *almude* (old liquid measure, about 17.5 litres) (171) of cane juice, and that this *almude* of cane juice produces 5 to 6 *quartilhas* of spirit at 26 degrees Cartier (an old hydrometer scale of alcoholic strength).
See Sugar cane.
Garapau

This name is applied both on Madeira and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) to the young of the *goraz* and sometimes of the *besugo* (see those entries). When the first of these fish reaches a certain size it is called *peixe anique*, and only as an adult does it receive the name *goraz*. The adult *goraz* seeks the depths, while the young, the *garapaus*, live close to the coast, where they are caught with hand lines by simple amateurs.

As is well known, there is no resemblance whatever between the *garapaus* of Madeira and the *carapaus* of Portugal. The latter name designates the young of the *chicharro* (see that entry), a species also found in the seas around the Peninsula.
Herons

*Ardea purpurea* and *A. cinerea* are two species of heron that visit the archipelago, the latter being called *garça real*. The former appears mainly in the autumn, winter and spring months. They belong to the family Ardeidae.
Garcez (Dr António João Rodrigues)

He was a physician in Funchal when, in 1821, he was elected deputy for Madeira to the Constituent Cortes (Portuguese parliament), which sat from 1821 to 1822. He never took his seat in the Cortes, having died in Lisbon before his credentials were verified. The substitute deputy, Dr João José de Freitas Aragão, was called to fill the vacancy (see that entry).
Garcia Ramos (Acursio)

He was born on the island of Terceira in 1834. For some years he lived in Funchal, serving as a military physician. In 1872 he was appointed acting professor at the Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica*) of this city and physician of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) hospital. A serious conflict arose between him and the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia). For this reason Dr Acursio Ramos published in 1874 a pamphlet entitled *O Hospital de Santa Isabel da cidade do Funchal visto á luz da hygiene*. In 1880 he published in Lisbon the work *A Ilha da Madeira* (‘The Island of Madeira’), in two volumes of 276 and 200 pp. He left other printed works.

Having become involved in Madeira’s political struggles, his enemies prevailed on Colonel António Augusto de Macedo e Couto to have him imprisoned in the Forte do Ilhéu (Islet Fort). He was accused of seeking to stir anarchy in the 12th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) Battalion (*batalhão de caçadores n.° 12*) and of being the soul of a Masonic plot to hand the island over to the Americans. From there he was sent to Lisbon, where he was confined in São Jorge Castle (Castelo de São Jorge) and then in the tower of the Fort of São Julião da Barra (St Julian's Fort). Arrested on 19 April 1874, Dr Acursio regained his freedom only on 8 December of the same year, after the board of inquiry into the ridiculous case brought against him by the said Colonel Macedo e Couto declared that there were no grounds for a court martial. He died in Lisbon on 14 September 1892.
Gardner
Works: *The Geology of Madeira* (*Quart. Journ. of Geol. Soc. of London*), XXXVIII, 1882.
Garnier (Dr P.)

French physician who in 1858 published a translation of Dr Barral’s work on the climate of Madeira. This translation is entitled *Le Climat de Madère et son influence thérapeutique sur la phthisie pulmonaire*, and several important changes were introduced into it with the author’s consent.
Dr Garnier, who was in Madeira at the end of October 1850, also wrote a pamphlet with the following title: *Itinéraire de Paris à Madère* (*Union Médicale*, October, 1859).
Garoto (O)
A clandestine publication of which only one issue appeared, numbered 0 and marked as the 5th year of publication, on 28 October 1912.
Another clandestine and irregular publication appeared under the same title and ran to four issues, the 1st on 23 September 1906 and the last in January 1907.
Garoupa (Serranus cabrilla)

A fish of the family Percidae that lives on shallow rocky bottoms from the coast out to a little beyond 100 *braças*. The *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) is the tackle generally used to catch it.
Besides being common, the *garoupa* is one of the finest fish in the seas of Madeira.
Garreta (Léon)

A young French naturalist who carried out a scientific exploration of the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) in June 1911 and also visited Madeira, where he stayed for a few days. He was travelling in the small sloop *Adolphe Marie*, which very nearly foundered on his return to Europe.
Garreta met his death on the battlefields of France, in 1914 or shortly afterwards.
Garro
This family surname was borne by Afonso Garro, one of the earliest settlers of Funchal. We believe that the family has long been extinct.
Gaspar (Alfredo Rodrigues)

He was born in this city on 8 August 1865, the son of Manuel Rodrigues Gaspar and Dona Maria Augusta Gaspar. He completed the course in marine engineering in 1885 and that for naval officers in 1888; he holds the rank of captain in the navy (*capitão de mar e guerra*) and has been a professor at the Naval School since 1898. He has devoted himself in particular to the study of ballistics and explosives, which he teaches, and is regarded as a true authority on these subjects. He represented our country at the congress of applied chemistry held in London in 1909, where he presented an important paper on the comparative study of some of the stability tests for explosives.

In 1911 he was elected a deputy to the Constituent Assembly, and in 1913 a senator. He was minister of the colonies in 1914 and 1915, and returned to head the same ministry in 1919, in the government led by Mr Sá Cardoso. He was president of the council of ministers in 1924. He died in Lisbon on 30 November 1938.
Gata (Scymnus lichia)

A shark of the deep seas of Madeira, which has been caught at between 150 and 900 *braças*. It is of industrial value for the oil extracted from its liver and for the abrasive its skin provides, which is used in cabinet-making under the name of *lixa de gata* (‘gata sandpaper’).
Gaula (parish)

Anyone moderately versed in the history of Portuguese literature knows the celebrated romance of chivalry *Amadis de Gaula*, attributed to Vasco de Lobeira. Its origin, the language in which it was written, the period of its composition, etc., have been the subject of various works of literary criticism and historical research, especially the books of Teófilo Braga: *Introdução e Theoria da Historia da Literatura Portugueza*, *Poetas Palacianos* and *Amadis de Gaula*. Is there any connection between the name given to this parish and that of the famous romance? Dr Álvaro de Azevedo neither denies nor affirms it, making a vague and ambiguous reference to the parish (*freguesia*) of Gaula when he deals with the narrative romance and its devotees in this archipelago. He seems to have deliberately avoided giving an opinion that might perhaps have been called risky or rash. Meanwhile, let us transcribe the words of the annotator of the *Saudades*: ‘Tristan of Léonois, Lancelot of the Lake and Yseult are among these characters; Gaula is the homeland of the protagonist of one of them; *Amadis de Gaula* is the title of the celebrated romance attributed to our Vasco de Lobeira, a contemporary of John I. And in these islands, at the beginning of this period, Tristãos abounded, from Tristão Vaz Teixeira, or simply Tristão, Tristão da Ilha, first captain-donatary of Machico, so called, not because of any inferiority with respect to Zargo, but on the contrary, through a kind of poetic celebrity of the name, in honour of his singular chivalry and nobility,” as Frutuoso writes, copied by António Cordeiro in the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), book III, ch. IX, § 54: there was also in these islands more than one *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) named Lançarote, a manifest corruption of Lancelot; Bartolomeu Perestrelo, first donatary of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), gave his second daughter the name Yseu, or Hiseua, also a clear corruption of Yseult; and, finally, Gaula was the name then given to the vast lands west of the town of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) which, since 1558, have formed the parish of Gaula.’

Dr Teófilo Braga refers to the subject in almost the same terms as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo in his book *Amadis de Gaula*, from which we transcribe the following passages: ‘It is worth noting that the only place where Portuguese tradition preserves the romance of Lancelot is where there are the most traces of a knowledge of the *Amadis* in aristocratic society: the name of Grimanesa, lover of Apolidão, lord of the Firm Island, was also that of the wife of Tristão Teixeira, third captain of Machico. “The fourth and last son of Captain Tristão was called Lançarote Teixeira: he was one of the best horsemen of the island; for besides being by inclination a very good rider, he had a great hand at taming horses and was much given to it, so much so that in his time sixty well-appointed knights with golden spurs gathered in the town of Machico, mounted through the efforts of this Lançarote Teixeira; and when a feast of St John the Baptist or of Corpus Christi came round, there were so many knights for the cane games (*jogos de canas*, equestrian tournament with thrown canes) and skirmishes that it looked more like an army at war than a festive pastime; and though all were very skilled in this art, he nevertheless stood out so much among them that it may rightly be said he was the light and ornament of Machico.” Of this Lançarote Teixeira were born, besides other children, a son called Lançarote Teixeira de Gaula and a daughter who married Fernão Nunes de Gaula. Gaspar Frutuoso describes this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) at some distance from Machico: “Going on from this stream (the Boaventura) almost a *légua*, there is a settlement of thirty households of the same *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) of Santa Cruz, called Gaula, and it has many vineyards of Malmsey and many vineyards of other varieties.” The influence of the romance of *Amadis de Gaula* in this very place is easily proved, knowing that this Lançarote Teixeira de Gaula was the grandson of Tristão Teixeira das Damas, a love poet of the Songbook of Resende (*Cancioneiro de Resende*): “He was called ‘das Damas’ [of the Ladies] because he was a great courtier, a fine speaker, composed many verses for the ladies and was very eloquent in speech. This poet, married to Dona Guiomar de Lordelo, lady-in-waiting to the Excellent Lady, was a contemporary of Zurara, and his character and taste would necessarily have made him acquainted with the adventures of *Amadis de Gaula*.”’

From what has been transcribed, it cannot logically be inferred that there is any connection between the name given to this parish and the existence of the celebrated romance of chivalry. Although Teófilo Braga asserts that the influence of the *Amadis de Gaula* in this very place is easily proved, the truth is that the presence in Gaula of a Lançarote and of the granddaughter of a Tristão, characters of the chivalric romances of the *Amadis* cycle, is not an argument that leads us to identify the name of the parish with that of the romance. It should be noted here that in the oldest entries of the parish register, beginning in the mid-16th century, the name of this parish is always spelt Guaula. This seems to be the original name, which a popular corruption turned into Gaula. This removes still further the idea of any close affinity between the two names.

This parish (*freguesia*) was formed from land that belonged to the parish and town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz, from which it was separated around 1558. We have found no record of a chapel existing there that might have served as the seat of the new parish. Its parish priest originally received an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of 12,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), which the royal decree (*alvará*) of King Sebastian of 9 June 1572 raised to 20,000 *réis*; the vicar at the time was Friar Diogo Moreno. The subsequent royal decrees of 9 June 1581, 20 January 1589 and 4 July 1592 successively increased the parish priest’s pay, which the last of them fixed at 16,000 *réis* in cash, one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. Jorge Rodrigues, Diogo Fernandes and Friar Diogo Moreno were among the earliest priests to serve in this parish.

The seat of the parish was established in a chapel that either already existed there or was built when the parish was created; it stood to the east of the present parish church, not far from it. Although it was a building of cramped dimensions, it served as the parish seat for roughly two centuries. An order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 17 October 1753 authorised the building of a new church, the works for which were contracted to the stonemason Manuel Rodrigues for the sum of 3,400,000 *réis*. We do not know when the building works were completed or in what year the new church was blessed. The bell tower was built in 1915 at a cost of 1,800.00 escudos.

This parish church possesses a finely wrought silver cross, which in 1882 was shown at the Retrospective Exhibition of Ornamental Art (*Exposição Retrospectiva de Arte Ornamental*) held in Lisbon, and which is described in its catalogue as follows: ‘Processional cross of silver gilt with a figure in white silver, its arms ending in the shape of a fleur-de-lis. It rests on a hexagonal base representing a castle, defended by six giants with Gothic-style pinnacles. Height, 0.70 m. 15th century’.

This parish had the chantries (capela) of São João de Latrão (‘St John Lateran’), in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears that name today, and of São Marcos (St Mark), in the locality of Porto Novo (‘new harbour’), which we shall discuss elsewhere.

The main localities (*sítios*) are Porto Novo, Fazenda, Levadas, Achada de Baixo, Achada de Cima, Achada da Rocha, Salgados, Pico, Cova do Moinho, Faia, Lombo, Fonte, Povo, Lobos, Furtados, Salão, Torre, Fonte do Lopo, Fazendinha São João, Castelejo, Aldonça, Beatas, Lombadinha, Lajeas, Farrobo and Contenda.

Among the localities, special mention is due to that of Achada, known as the Achada de Gaula (‘plateau of Gaula’), where there is a large cluster of dwellings. Many of them are surrounded by tall box hedges, which shelter them from the winds and give the place a rather interesting and picturesque appearance. The spot bears a strong resemblance to the charming parish of Sant'Ana, even in the make-up of the soil itself. From the Pico dos Eirós, which overlooks the parishes of Camacha, Santo da Serra and Caniço, a vast and astonishing panorama opens out, stretching eastwards as far as the Ponta de São Lourenço. The locality of Lombadinha deserves particular mention because it was once almost entirely held by quit-rent (*foreiro*) from the Captives’ Fund (*Cofre de Cativos*). The Fund had its seat in Lisbon and was intended for ransoming Portuguese taken prisoner by the Moors in Morocco, where they suffered the greatest outrages and the harshest cruelties.

This parish is irrigated by the Levada do Pico dos Eirós, the most important, which rises within the parish boundaries; by the Levada da Ribeira da Metade, which has its source in the brook of Junça in the parish of Camacha; and by the Levada da Roda, whose water comes from the parish of Santa Cruz.

The parish is separated from the parishes of Caniço and Camacha by the Ribeira do Porto Novo. At its mouth lies a small landing place of the same name, the most important in the parish, where the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) had a small quay or landing place built some fifteen years ago. In September 1873 the American corvette *Supply* arrived at Funchal and was refused pratique because she came from a port where cholera morbus was raging. Two boats from this warship attempted to land people at Porto Novo, but the local inhabitants vigorously opposed them, and this stand by the people of Gaula forced the American sailors to abandon their attempt. The parish also has the insignificant landing place of Aldonça; on a spot overlooking it, the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Sebastião Botelho had a small fort built in 1820.

It is said that in former times, when an inhabitant of this parish was asked where he came from, he invariably replied ‘I am from Gaula, what is it to you?’ if the question was put in the season of the blackberries, which grew there in abundance, or else ‘I am from Gaula for my sins’ if the answer was given after that fruit had been gathered. The question is still frequently and pointedly repeated today, but it generally gets no answer, because the man from Gaula sees in it an insult, or a cause for ridicule or scorn of his native parish.

Nuno Fernandes Cardoso, son of Fernão Nunes Cardoso, ‘a man of lineage’ in the words of the genealogies, came to this island towards the end of the 15th century and held extensive lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish of Gaula, where in 1511 he founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of São João de Latrão. His eldest son, Pedro Nunes Cardoso, was, according to H. H. de Noronha, criminal *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the court and high court judge (*desembargador*) of the Casa do Porto. He inherited his parents’ entail (*morgado*) on this island, died at Gaula on 17 May 1552 and was buried in the chapel of São João de Latrão. His brother, Diogo Nunes Cardoso, studied at Coimbra and in Italy, where he took his doctorate, and became a judge of the Desembargo do Paço (the royal supreme court; *desembargador do paço*). This Diogo Cardoso was the father of Tomaz Nunes de Afonseca, who, says an old genealogy, ‘studied at Coimbra and was criminal *corregedor* at court, and after serving the King in matters of great importance came to this island, where he had inherited the entail of Gaula from his grandfather, for want of issue from his uncle Pedro Nunes Cardoso’. The last representative of this entailed house (*casa vinculada*) was Nuno Fernandes Cardoso e Vasconcelos, grandfather of Luís Cardoso de Castro e Abreu, the present schoolteacher of this parish of Gaula. (See São João de Latrão.)

The patron saint of this parish is Nossa Senhora da Luz (Our Lady of Light), and the parish has 3,120 inhabitants. On 28 March 1932 Father João Jorge Bettencourt died in this parish, where he had been born and served as parish priest. A priest of the most refined virtues, he distinguished himself as a journalist, having for some years been the chief editor of a daily newspaper published in this city.

Recently the idea has arisen of attributing the origin of the parish’s name to a family with the surname Gaula, which might have settled there in the early days of colonisation. The truth, however, is that this name left no trace among the population, nor was it recorded in the books of the parish archive.

See *Diário de Notícias* of 19 May 1929. Gavião. ‘João Gavião, says a distinguished genealogist, belonged to the King’s household; coming to the island of Madeira, he was shipwrecked on that of Porto Santo, and went to live at Caniço, where he died, leaving a will, in 1555.’ He was one of the first on this island to bear the surname Gavião.
Sparrowhawk (Accipiter nisus)
A bird of the falcon family that builds its nest in trees. It is native, but uncommon, and was not mentioned in Harcourt’s list. It is also known by the name *fura-bardos*.
Kittiwake (Rissa tridactyla)

A bird of the family Laridae, originating in the Arctic regions, which comes to winter in the Madeira archipelago. In the bay of Funchal it is a common sight in winter, now rocking on the swell, now perched on the gunwales of the coal lighters.
Gazeta da Madeira (A)
It was published from 1 February 1866 to 27 February 1869, and 101 issues appeared.
Geheeb (A.)
Works: *Bryologische Fragment E. Madeira Moose* (*Flora*, 1886). He died on 13 September 1909.
Gente Nova

Its first issue appeared on 15 October 1919 and its last, the tenth, on 20 March 1920. It resumed publication in February 1921. It was a newspaper written by pupils of the lyceum (state secondary school).
Geodesy

Under the general heading of Geodesy and the subtitle *Localização das Cartas Hidrográficas do Arquipélago da Madeira no Elipsóide Internacional*, Mr Pires de Matos, a distinguished officer of the Portuguese navy, published a long and valuable article in the *Anais do Club Militar Naval* (Jan.–Feb., 1940). Its length does not allow us to reproduce it in full in these pages, so we shall transcribe only a few brief passages, in order to acquaint our readers with this subject, to whom it may perhaps be of some interest.

‘In 1914 the Directorate of Geodetic and Topographical Works (*Direcção dos Trabalhos Geodésicos e Topográficos*) established a triangulation on the island of Madeira. Its main use and immediate purpose was the survey of the island’s chorographic map, carried out in 1915, revised and updated by the Geographical and Cadastral Institute (*Instituto Geográfico e Cadastral*) in 1934 and published in 1938 at a scale of 1/50 000.

The base of the triangulation was measured on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), and the survey marker of the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) was taken as the origin of coordinates. This marker was built near the spot where an American Mission made observations of astronomical latitude and longitude in 1892, and the Directorate of Geodetic and Topographical Works observed the astronomical azimuth of one of the sides of the triangulation at the Fort of São Tiago.
With the exception of the azimuth, therefore, it was the astronomical observations of the American Mission that were used to calculate the geographical coordinates of the island of Madeira.

In 1936 the need was recognised to revise the 1914 triangulation, rebuild some destroyed survey markers, triangulate Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) and link the islands of the archipelago, with the immediate aim of a chorographic survey of Porto Santo and the Desertas and a hydrographic survey of the Madeira archipelago. In this new work, carried out in 1936 by the Geographical and Cadastral Institute, some vertices of the old 1914 triangulation were abandoned. At the same time, working in parallel with the Institute, the Hydrographic Mission extended the triangulation to the cliff line and to the landing places where hydrographic plans were surveyed.

The Geographical and Cadastral Institute abandoned the old origin at the Fort of São Tiago and made astronomical observations – latitude, longitude and azimuth – at the astronomical marker on the island of Porto Santo.

Although this marker is better placed than that of São Tiago, at least as regards latitude, everything suggested that the observations would still be affected by a considerable deflection of the vertical, and that consequently, if the astronomical observations of this new origin were adopted, appreciable errors would be made in placing the whole on the ellipsoid.

If we had as the origin of coordinates a marker at which the effect of the deflection of the vertical was not felt, if the triangulations were rigorously measured and calculated, if the surfaces of the geoid and the international ellipsoid fitted perfectly, and if there were no disturbing causes or observational errors, the geographical coordinates of any vertex carried over geodetically would always equal the astronomical coordinates observed directly at it.

This is not the case, however, and differences, sometimes considerable, are found. They are explained by the following causes: a) attributing to the origin marker astronomical coordinates affected by deflection of the vertical and by observational errors; b) geodetic observations not free of observational errors; c) carrying geographical coordinates over a reference ellipsoid that departs from the geoid more or less irregularly and according to unknown laws; d) local disturbing influences, due to imbalance in the distribution of masses around the astronomical stations, which are difficult to calculate because the densities of the various geological layers below the earth’s surface are unknown.

A single astronomical station would give us particular geographical latitudes, longitudes and azimuths for the geodetic vertices and sides. Each vertex will then have as many systems of coordinates as there are origins chosen.

The Hydrographic Mission had two systems of geographical coordinates at its disposal: the first corresponding to the 1914 triangulation, with its origin at São Tiago, and the second to the 1936 triangulation, with its origin on Porto Santo. Although the first of these two systems was used provisionally, neither was adopted in the definitive publication of the charts.
To shed more light on this problem and solve it, the Hydrographic Mission decided to make astronomical observations at the following survey marks:

PICO RÁDIO–FUNCHAL, in the south of the island of Madeira; MONTADO, in the north; PONTA DO PARGO, in the west; CANCELA, in the east; POISO and BICA DA CANA, in the interior of the island, at altitudes of 1,414 and 1,621 metres respectively; ILHÉU CHÃO (Flat Islet), on the Desertas.

The astronomical observations at these marks were made with a universal theodolite acquired in 1937 from the German firm Askania Werk A. G. Bambergwerk, listed in its catalogues as Universal Instrument A. U. Z. 21 C.

The Talcott method was adopted for observing latitude; with some 15 pairs of fundamental stars from the Eichelberger catalogue, probable errors of less than 0".10 were achieved. Longitude was obtained by comparing the chronometer states referred to Greenwich, received by radiotelegraphy and calculated by timing the chronometer at the coincidences of the rhythmic signals and the exact seconds of the chronometer, with the states referred to local time. These were obtained from about 6 series of 12 stars, 6 in each series being observed with the eyepiece to the east and 6 with the eyepiece to the west. The azimuth was obtained by observing circumpolar stars at elongation.

Once these astronomical data had been gathered, the problem was to adopt methods of calculation by which all the astronomical stations listed above could help us assign the most probable geographical coordinates to the vertices of the geodetic network under study.

In the present state of geodesy the problem, in its absolute form, cannot be solved, but that circumstance is no argument against adopting one of the various existing methods to reach the desired end. While recognising the force of the criticisms made of the hypothesis of isostasy formulated by Pratt and adopted by Faye, Airy and other scientists, we nevertheless decided to follow Hayford’s method, which rests on the hypothesis of isostatic compensation and which served to define the international ellipsoid.
Although the results obtained cannot legitimately be presented as definitive, they are undeniably of interest. Since some of the charts used for Madeira give heights and depths in metres, we have:
D = 0"000328 times the height in metres; D = 0.000202 times the depth in metres. The charts used to calculate the topographic deflections were as follows:

1) HYDROGRAPHIC PLAN OF FUNCHAL BAY – scale 1/7,500; 2) CHOROGRAPHIC MAP OF THE ISLAND OF MADEIRA – scale 1/25,000; 3) CHOROGRAPHIC MAP OF THE ISLAND OF MADEIRA – scale 1/50,000; 4) HYDROGRAPHIC PLAN OF PORTO SANTO BAY – scale 1/15,000; 5) CHOROGRAPHIC MAP OF THE ISLAND OF PORTO SANTO – scale 1/25,000; 6) HYDROGRAPHIC CHART OF THE ISLAND OF MADEIRA – scale 1/75,000; 7) HYDROGRAPHIC CHART OF THE ISLAND OF PORTO SANTO – scale 1/50,000; 8) HYDROGRAPHIC CHART OF THE DESERTAS – scale 1/50,000; 9) HYDROGRAPHIC CHART OF THE MADEIRA ARCHIPELAGO – scale 1/150,000; 10) BRITISH ADMIRALTY HYDROGRAPHIC CHART NUMBER 1:226 – scale at the mean parallel 1/3181400.
These charts required the construction of compartment-distribution diagrams at the respective scales, taking into account the projection used.
From the established ratio r'/r1 = 1.426, it can be seen that the radius bounding a compartment on the outside is obtained by multiplying the inner radius by 1.426.
Each pair of consecutive circles forms a ring comprising 16 compartments.

Given the scale of the charts, the innermost ring we used was number 30, bounded on the outside by a radius of 134.2 m. The outermost ring reached by the compensation was number 6, with an outer radius of 670.8 km.

From the results obtained in the Madeira archipelago we can conclude that, where astronomical data cannot be obtained at a large number of stations, it is highly advantageous to choose stations on ground that is topographically not very rugged. It should not be forgotten that rugged topography very close to a station calls for sufficiently detailed charts, which cannot always be obtained easily. The more extensive the level area around the station, the smaller the scales of the charts needed to achieve a given degree of accuracy.
On a very rugged island, the astronomical survey marker should be placed in a high area, preferably on a plateau, around which the distribution of masses is as symmetrical as possible.
In an archipelago, the island with the least rugged relief should be chosen for astronomical observations.
Under the conditions defined above, the correction applied to the observations at the origin marker seems to us sufficient.

Because the reference axes are unstable and difficult to relate to one another – which is possible only approximately, and after a great deal of work – astronomical traverses can serve us well only in mere reconnaissance work.

Variations in the deflection of the vertical are greatest in coastal regions. This shows us how dangerous it is to use an astronomical traverse in such regions to produce charts that are meant to represent the topography of the ground with a certain care and accuracy. Over distances of two hundred kilometres we may make errors sometimes exceeding 500 metres on coasts such as those of Angola and Mozambique.

The astronomical vertices could be corrected for the effects of the deflection of the vertical, but even in regions where sufficient charts are available, the method is so laborious that it is not to be recommended.

If adjustment makes us lose part of the accuracy achieved thanks to the modern instruments employed and to lengthier observations and calculations, then, according to some opinions, substantial spending on good instruments and the greater loss of time on better methods of observation and calculation are not justified.
I disagree entirely, because I believe we must not lose sight of the fact that in work of this kind there are two aims to be achieved:

First – to place the charts as accurately as possible on the international ellipsoid, in the light of the methods of investigation known at present. Second – to gather an ever larger body of data for the present and, above all, future study of the shape of the Earth.

While any modest theodolite is sufficient for the first aim, the second can be fully achieved only if we use in our work the best modern instruments possible and good methods of observation and calculation.

In my humble view, those to whom the State entrusts posts of scientific research must never forget that their services contribute to the growth of human knowledge not only through the immediate, practical purpose of their work, but also through its more distant purpose, sometimes less apparent but of great future importance.
And, besides, the truth is that the small increase in expenditure involved is no obstacle, even when the services have modest budgets.
Geology

The formation of the islands that make up the Madeira archipelago goes back to the Tertiary era, in the Miocene. Submarine uplifts formed columns of emergence, in which volcanic activity continued into the earliest Quaternary. In successive periods of upheaval these altered the islands’ outline, Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) branching apart at a depth of 2,000 m and surfacing in the Atlantic 21 miles apart.
The absence of well-defined craters, long since collapsed or reshaped by natural agents, is a characteristic proof of their long period of formation.

On Madeira the main eruptive focus lay in the central part of the island, at Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’). It was immense and violent, producing partial reliefs in stages that rose from 300 m to 600 m and from there to 1,200 m in a great deluge of lava. This marked and defined the backbone of the central chain, piling up scoria engulfed in fresh torrents and rising progressively to altitudes greater than those the island shows today.

Adventitious and secondary vents opened, some partly within the central massif, others breaking out at points far distant from it. The outer slope of the cones is at times very steep, so that the lavas do not always solidify in regular layers, and instead scatter as blocks and fragments.

Long periods of quiescence were followed by greater paroxysms. During one of the spells of calm, soils formed through the natural breakdown of the rocks, and some plants were thus able to grow: this early flora was discovered in the lignite of São Jorge, buried by later volcanic emissions. In one of the periods of upheaval came the uplift marked by the marine fossils of São Vicente, lodged at the head of an erosion valley at an altitude of 360 m, where they form an enclave.

The first subaerial formations appear in the Pliocene, with a great outpouring of basaltic lavas radiating from the original focus. Sometimes denser, sometimes more fluid, they solidified more quickly at the surface and were covered with scoria in a flexible crust that cracked and bristled. They spread further to the north and were more broken up to the south, running and flowing down different gradients that tend towards the horizontal near the sea.
A new basaltic period followed, with a great projection of scoria and the formation of conglomerates, which blocked and diverted the lava flows discharged irregularly in every direction.

The trachytic lavas followed the basaltic ones after Madeira had reached a moderate relief. Fissures and vents opened in them, determining the mountain chain along the island’s spine. North of the Curral these lavas rose with a high proportion of alumina, covering depressions and accumulating between obstacles.

Trachydolerites alternate with trachytes and extend chiefly to the west and north. It is worth noting that lavas of this kind in the Boaventura (‘good fortune’) valley are younger than those of the upper formation of the Curral.

The essexites, which welled up from adventitious fissures and were forced out by pressure from great depths, look like ancient rocks but are recent in formation. They are found embedded at Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), the Curral and Ponta do Sol.

Many peaks in the interior of the island are embedded in lavas younger than those that formed them, which run along their feet and slopes. Others were drowned in lavas and in blocks fallen from the nearest calderas, as can be seen in the sections cut by the Socorridos and Boaventura streams.

The main crater of formation, which at its widest measures 2,500 metres in diameter and is broken in its collapsed southern segment, arched from west to east through the peaks Grande, Empinos, Arranhamento, Jorge, Casado, Torrinhas, Lage, Eirinhas, Coelho, Ruivo, Torres and Cidrãos Cedro. The adventitious vents within the same crater gave rise to the peaks of Roda, Meio and Cerro, and to the upland commons (montados) of Cidrão and Paredão.

The Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), considered until recently to be a crater choked by internal collapse (the opinion of Stuebel), is seen in the most recent studies as a lava bank, with tuffs and scoria identical to those of the Lombo Gordo (‘broad ridge’) formation in the Curral (the opinion of Gagel).
Indeed, a line of heights with small depressions carved by erosion links these two points by way of Bica da Cana, Pináculo, Monte Medonho, Rocha Negra and Pico do Ferreiro.
Had all the volcanic activity been concentrated in the central caldera, Madeira’s highest point would rise, at Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) or another peak, to an altitude of 2,500 metres.

The last volcanic surge appears outside the central zone: at the ends of the island (Porto Moniz and Caniçal), after the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) had already separated, and in the southern region, at Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), Funchal and Caniço, where the most recent cones are found.
Basalts
Basalt is a rock of uniform appearance, blackish, heavy and hard.

Its variations in colour and hardness depend on its accessory elements and on its former state of fluidity. It occurs in large beds, ranging from thin layers to enormous rock masses, lavas from different periods of formation, and it predominates in the lower region.

Basalts show contraction cracks caused by cooling, and they break into large prismatic blocks of polygonal section, mostly irregular hexagons, as can be seen in quarry workings. These masses, stacked in long prisms, form handsome walls of columnar basalt, which are common on the banks of deep streams; the most typical face is that of Tem-te-não-caias (‘hold on, don’t fall’), in the valley of Porto da Cruz.

Where the flow is thinner and gently sloping, lamellar basalt is found, contracted into parallel faces that come apart under the violent blow of the pick. Columnar basalt is called *pedra viva* (‘live stone’: compact basalt used for building). Its density varies, so it needs different charges of explosive to be split into blocks, which are then partly dressed for use as building material. Lamellar basalt yields the slabs used for kerbs, levadas (irrigation channels), washing places, paving, etc. The flagstones of the churchyard at Monte were taken from a quarry, now worked out, which, from the nature of its rock, gave its name to the locality (*sítio*) of Lajinhas (‘little flagstones’). These basalts cannot be carved.

When basalt is fractured, it is sometimes found to be covered by a coating or thin greyish layer, caused by the alteration of iron salts. This creates a line of least resistance, the *casco* (‘shell’), which masons strip off, and they reject such basalt for more important work, such as tanks, etc.

Basalts contain small bubbles formed by gases, whose arrangement and shape indicate the direction and speed of the flow. In larger, egg-shaped bubbles, geodes sometimes form, in which aragonite, exuded from the basaltic mass as it cooled, crystallises. It is known as *madre de pedra* (‘mother of stone’) because it is found inside the rock.

When it is full of a great number of vesicles, basalt is known as *pedra favada* and *pedra de porco* (‘pig stone’: rough vesicular basalt used to scrape pig hides), from the use made of it at pig-killing time to scrub the animal’s hide after singeing and strip it of its bristles.

Fine-grained, somewhat vesicular basalt forms the hard dressed stone, which can be worked well and is widely used in buildings, coats of arms, bridge voussoirs, millstones, hand mills, large troughs, etc. Fine carved work can be seen on the façade of the chapel of São Luís (St Louis), in the old Rua do Bispo, and on the portico of the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery.
Trachytes

These are rough rocks of microlitic texture and a certain fluidity. They sometimes look like spheroids decomposed in concentric layers, like a tunicate bulb, and are dirty brown or greyish in colour. They form an amorphous matter of feldspathic elements and contain, visible to the eye, small scattered crystals of sanidine and magnetite.

Trachytes have been confused with porphyry and, when truncated, with volcanic bombs. In Madeira, trachytes are found in the zone above 300 m in altitude, where they decompose, as can be seen in road cuttings, showing a darker nodule.
Trachydolerites

They show a very characteristic appearance of former fluidity, as can be observed in a lava flow in the valley of Boaventura. They are richer in alkalis than trachytes and sometimes contain granules of peridot.

Their colour varies from light to dark grey, passing through yellowish tones, speckled with lighter dots. Trachydolerites alternate with trachytes at some points in the high region and on the slopes of Pico do Serrado, Rabaçal and Porto da Cruz.
Essexites

These are plutonic rocks, composed mainly of plagioclase, olivine and magnetite. Two kinds are distinguished: porphyritic essexite, dark grey to brownish, dotted with magnetite and diopside of greasy vitreous lustre, as at Penha de Águia (‘eagle crag’), the Massapez brook and Ponta do Sol; and melaphyric essexite, grey, porous and fine-grained, with relatively large crystals of augite and microliths of olivine, as at Ponta Delgada, Ribeira Brava and the stream of São Vicente.

In the Soca brook, at Porto da Cruz, the first bed of essexite looks different from other rocks of the same nature, not only those found in Madeira but all others known. For this reason Dr Gagel, in view of the quantitative and qualitative analysis of this rock, and having consulted the greatest authorities on the subject, gave it the name madeirite, and included a fine colour microphotograph of it in his valuable work *Studien über den Aufbau und die Gesteine Madeiras*.
Dykes

During the period of upheaval the rocks cracked, and fresh lavas and scoria filled the open fissures, forming veins between the walls of the fracture. Where these walls were less resistant than the intruded mass, they broke down under the action of the weather, leaving the vein unsupported and exposed.

Exposed dykes predominate in the central region. The jagged outline of the Torres (‘towers’) and Torrinhas (‘little towers’) resembles the ruins of fantastic castles, an immense curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city) toppled by the forces of nature. Like a lone sentinel, on the way up to Pico Ruivo, one comes upon the picturesque dyke known as the Homem em Pé on the Achada do Ferreiro (‘the blacksmith’s plateau’), at an altitude of 1522 m; it seems to grow taller as the ground at its base erodes.
Among the many dykes that cut through the coastal rocks, those set into the sheer walls of Cabo Girão deserve notice, among them the Poço do Eiró, which is perfectly vertical.

The arrangement of the dykes and their transverse, convergent and even intersecting directions reflect the effect of different centres of disturbance at widely separated times, which often had their foci at points now submerged beneath the sea.
Lava channels

The lavas cooled more quickly at the surface, and where they touched the walls and bed over which they flowed, than in the interior, which therefore stayed fluid for longer. As a result they became hollow when the flow ended, forming underground channels. The most characteristic lava channels are the Fojo (a collapsed channel), near Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’); those of Cavalum, on the Ribeira de Machico (‘Machico stream’); and that of Cardal, beside the bridge of the town (*vila*) of São Vicente.
Volcanic bombs

These are contorted pieces of lava, either hurled out by the calderas, in which case they are pear-shaped or lenticular, or forced through fissures, in which case they look like dough pressed through a strainer. They occur among conglomerates and, singly, near the most recently formed cones. Olivine bombs are fragments of a peridotitic rock lying at depth and torn loose under pressure in volcanic explosions; they are bound up with basalts or form conglomerates, as is most often found at Porto Moniz.
Tuffs
These are consolidated volcanic muds, highly variable according to the nature of the materials that formed them, and generally scoriaceous.

The commonest tuffs yield *pedra mole* ('soft stone': soft yellowish tuff and its soil), yellowish in colour; lime predominates in the paler kinds, while the darker ones contain oxidised iron salts. It is used only for rough infill and retaining walls.

Soft cut stone (cantaria mole) is coarse-grained, heterogeneous, and greyish-brown or dark magenta. Filter stone (*cantaria de filtro*) is dark grey and used for filtering water in wells and basins. Oven stone (*cantaria de forno*), reddish-brown, is used to make braziers and the lining of ovens. These soft stones are also used as building material, although they are eroded by time and the action of natural agents.
Scoria

Scoria derives from volcanic froth that solidified rough, rugged and vesicular. It sometimes settled in layers, or built up mounds, cones and humps on the mountain spurs; in that case it consists of masses thrown out of the caldera in an explosive surge.

Its colours vary widely, blackish tones predominating. It is used as an outer facing for garden tanks and cascades and, in recent times, inside the partition walls of houses, in place of wood shavings.
Volcanic ash

Volcanic ash consists of lava very finely divided by pulverisation during explosions. It forms microlithic aggregates of amorphous appearance, which nevertheless contain countless small dark crystals rich in augite and iron oxides, and, in the more recent ashes, concretionary aragonite – Ribeiro Seco, Gorgulho, etc.

Sometimes carried by water down gentle slopes, the ashes lie in black layers between the tuffs and are deposited in cavities, forming cave sand (*areia de furna*), which is used in the mortar for the interior rendering of some dwelling houses. Ashes also occur in the matrix of the tuffs as an integral part of the soft stones. The so-called Monte sand (*areia do Monte*) is a purplish aggregate of ash which, once mechanically ground to particles, is used in the same way as cave sand.
Pumice

Pumice is a spongy obsidian lying over the volcanic muds and forming aggregates with them where they flowed viscously – Santa Luzia, Pilar, etc. – or bedded in layers parallel to those of the tuffs, as can be seen in orderly sequence on the coast at Penha de França, at the mouth of the Ribeiro Seco.
Greenish pumice of recent appearance is found at Porto dos Frades, on Porto Santo, and seems to have been carried there by ocean currents.
Clays

Clays form a mass made up of a great variety of earthy products derived from the decomposition of the aluminium silicates in the rocks, especially the trachytes. Old, hardened clays containing ferric hydroxides and carbonates lie interbedded and baked between layers of volcanic products; these are called laterites.

Clays containing sand form the *barros* (loams), a type of ground that gives its name to several localities called Barreiros. Some clays are coated with a layer of iron hydroxides that looks like scrap iron – São Jorge, Santana, etc. – and others with carbonates and sulphates – Porto Santo.

*Massapez* (heavy ferruginous clay soil) is an earth containing a large quantity of brownish ferruginous clay, which retains the water it absorbs for a long time, while *salão* (reddish clay soil of volcanic origin) is reddish and less dense. These terms likewise give their names to several localities where the two earths are found. The purplish earths derive from the decomposition of trachytoids at high altitudes, and the yellowish earths from the disintegration of the tuffs called *pedra mole* (‘soft stone’: soft yellowish tuff and its soil).

On the colouring mineral earths and clays there are two curious reports from the time of the captains-general Dom Diogo Coutinho and Dom José da Câmara, concerning the use of red ochre (*almagre*), ochres and pozzolana, and proposing their application and industrial development.
Alagoas

This name is given to several localities where the ground is marshy and forms ponds (*alagoa*, seasonally flooded hollow) in the rainy season. They arise either from depressions caused by erosion in low-lying places or from the remains of old secondary eruptive centres found at high altitudes. To this latter cause belong the ponds of Porto Moniz, Fanal de Cima and Fanal de Baixo, and that of Santo da Serra. On the Pico da Cancela, at Caniçal, there is one in the shape of a horseshoe, and therefore an old breached pond.
Limestones
They derive from the remains of submarine life, the shells and carapaces of small animals, mechanically and chemically transformed into rocks that surfaced or were torn loose by volcanic action.
Calcareous products ejected by the craters in the form of muds are often found – Ponta da Cruz, Queimadas de Machico, etc.

The limestones at present worked for the kilns are found on the Ilhéu da Cal (Lime Islet), on the island of Porto Santo, on Selvagem Grande and, in the north of Madeira, at São Vicente. From some unworked deposits stone could be obtained for other industrial purposes.
Calcium carbonates in concretionary forms and stalactites line the walls of some caves, especially on the Ilhéu da Cal.

Calcite in the form of rhombohedra, pure white, or in yellowish granular varieties, is found at São Vicente; aragonite, of the orthorhombic system, in needles and diverging sheaves and in beautiful columnar and acicular forms, occurs at Madalena do Mar and Boaventura.

The ancient action of waters charged with dissolved sulphates on the limestones produced gypsum, interbedded in layers of sediment or in concretions: compact in some places, coarsely crystalline in others. In its pure form it constitutes the selenite found on Selvagem Grande.
Concretions

Rainwater, charged with carbonic anhydride and dissolving the calcium carbonates, penetrates the tuffs and loose sands, forming little channels through shrinkage, which branch according to the direction of infiltration.

This is how the curious calcareous-sandy arborescent formations of Piedade, at Caniçal, and of Mornos, on Porto Santo, were formed, as well as those in some tuffs at Covões, in Caniço, and among tuffs and ashes at Fojo and Praia Formosa.
The fanciful shapes into which the calcareous sands have sometimes cemented, especially at Piedade, earned them the popular name of *bonecos* (dolls).
Other views hold that the Piedade and Mornos deposits are of plant origin, classing them as fossils. (See Calcareous bodies.)
Erosion

Over time the relief of the Madeira group has been considerably altered. The chief agent has been the action of rainwater and the sea, whose sometimes prodigious work wears away the different materials, mechanically and chemically, and carries them off to the sea.

The rocks gradually decompose, lose their balance, lean and collapse, turning into successive debris, transitory deposits governed by the weight and speed of the currents. The torrential rains that accompanied the various periods of volcanic formation caused progressive erosion and carved out the valleys with varying degrees of energy, according to the nature of the bed. Meanwhile the currents – now squeezed between the cliffs, now dropping from one level to another in falls that scoured deep rock pools at their base, now overflowing and then spreading out to form the flats and the meadowlands – went on depositing and removing their load according to the contributions of their confluences, their flow and the obstacles they met.

The varying severity of the winters, which sometimes causes floods, twists and diverts the course of the waters, as shown by old beds and traced on the high banks of the cliffs by the remains of transported material.

Our valleys are magnificent sections that show the order in which the layers forming them were laid down, the irregularities of their arrangement and the influence of the causes of unconformity that produced their present shape.

The action of the sea has greatly reduced the outline of the shore and shifted the coastline, which in some places has been cut almost sheer. It has opened small bays, inlets and coves, enlarged and diminished the beaches, and opened up rocks and cut them off as islets. Even in historical times the north coast has been visibly eaten away, while the south coast has grown appreciably.
The trachytic rocks of the Ilhéu da Fonte da Areia, on Porto Santo, are hollowed out into bowl shapes, in which sea salt and sands of various debris are sometimes deposited.

In the 16th century the springs of João Diniz gushed out onto the pebble beach (*calhau*). The Bânger pillar was built on a shoal, and in the 18th century people crossed by canoe between it and the city’s defensive wall. The chapel of the Misericórdia of Machico stood at the mouth of the stream and is now about 200 metres from the sea. The Ribeira de São João is gradually silting up the cove of Pontinha. One need only see how the streams become choked in the winter floods, and look at the muddy fringe of the sea, to understand readily the work done by the waters.
Fajãs

When rock faces collapse through denudation, they form heaps, terraces or aprons (*pataréus*, *poios* or *sapatas*) at the base of the fall. When these are large, they make up land with a natural slope, inland or on the coast: Fajã Escura, Fajã das Galinhas, Fajã dos Padres, Fajã do Mar, etc.

Lugar de Baixo, in Ponta do Sol, is a growing *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff), much enlarged by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803. When rock faces fall into the streams, they force them to twist and divert their beds.

In the 17th century, water seeping between gently sloping sedimentary layers of different kinds caused a slow landslide, or avalanche, of ground that pushed out into the sea in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge.
Sands

Sands come from the crushing and rolling of different materials. Their colour and nature reveal their origin: black sand comes from basalt; greyish-brown sand from trachytes; dark yellow sand from tuffs; and pale yellow sand from shelly limestones. The sands contain microlithic crystals from the decomposed rocks, and olivine crystals are abundant during the great high tides at Praia Formosa.

Calcareous sands sometimes form a sandstone, a hardened aggregate, or are cemented together with particles of different materials, and are then called *ariusco* (cemented calcareous sandstone of Porto Santo) – Porto Santo. S.
