II, 1940, include a detailed study of the geology of the Savage Islands (Selvagens) entitled *Uma Missão Geológica a bordo do navio Hidrográfico Carvalho de Araújo*, from the pen of Dr J. C. de Morais, director of that museum.
See Thomas Edward Bowdich, Dana, Albuquerque, Hartung, Lyell, Smith, Macaulay.
Germinal (O)
Its first issue appeared on 8 January 1919.
Broom (Cytisus scoparius)

A very common shrub on Madeira, which also occurs on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It belongs to the family Leguminosae, subfamily Papilionaceae, and has trifoliate leaves with very small leaflets, yellow flowers and strongly compressed pods, ciliate along the margins. Broom is widely used to manure the land, and its branches are made into baskets, hampers (*gigos*) and other small articles. This craft already existed on the island at the time when ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) was written.
Gil

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António there is the locality (*sítio*) of Vasco Gil, where a man of that name, one of the first settlers of this island, held land as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and was one of the good men (*homens bons*, local notables eligible for municipal office) of the old governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office) of Funchal. He was perhaps the first person in this archipelago to bear the surname Gil.
Gil (Emílio A. Santos)
He was elected deputy for Madeira in August 1910, but the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) never met.
Ginjeira brava (Prunus Lusitanica, var. Hixa)

An evergreen tree with narrow, oblong, acuminate, serrate, glabrous leaves and white flowers borne in long axillary racemes. It has only recently been found, in the Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’). It yields a yellowish-pink or reddish-brown wood that is very durable.
See Tintureira.
Sour cherry (Prunus Cerasus)

A tree or shrub of the family Rosaceae, subfamily Prunoideae, cultivated and naturalised on Madeira. It originates in the East and is easily distinguished from the sweet cherry by its leaves, which are glabrous on the underside. Madeiran sour cherries are dark red, only slightly acidic and juicy.
Gypsum
Hydrated calcium sulphide; monoclinic system. It occurs in crystalline and lamellar form on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Giraldes

‘This surname was brought by the Florentine Dr Pedro Giraldes, who lived in Calheta (‘small cove’) from around 1500 to 1535, and in that last year founded the Misericórdia there, of which he was the first president (*provedor*).’
Giraldes (Joaquim Pedro Cardoso Casado)

At the time of the French invasions, the army officer Casado Giraldes was sentenced to deportation to this island on suspicion of having supplied information to Napoleon’s troops when they invaded our country. Once the charge was proved false, Geraldes went on living in Madeira, where he held the important post of secretary-general of the government. He was a patient researcher into Madeiran matters, and it is said that his papers were found to contain many documents of considerable interest for the history of this archipelago. In the first quarter of the 19th century he published in Paris the *Estatística Historico-Geographica das ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo*, of which a French-language edition appeared in the same city (see Superior Authorities of the Archipelago). He wrote various works, among them a compendium of geography in four volumes that was very popular in its day. He died in the city of Genoa, where he was Portuguese consul, on 3 September 1845.
Girão (cape)

Some have remarked how inappropriate it is to use the word ‘cape’ (*cabo*) for this towering cliff, which drops sheer into the ocean. Looking at the map of this island, we can make out no projection or tongue of land there that would justify the name, and this becomes still clearer when one travels along the coast, or even when one takes in the cliff along its greatest extent from its highest and most prominent point. Frutuoso seems to give it the name *cabo* to signify the end (*termo*) of the first stage of the original maritime exploration, and the name Girão because the circuit (*giro*) of the first day of that same exploration ended there. To justify the name *cabo* further, the chronicler refers to a point that the cliff formed below, a point that almost escapes the observer’s notice and can in no way deserve the name of cape. The *Saudades* say: ‘…they saw a very high cliff close by, and the sea breaking upon a point which it formed below, which became for them the goal and end of their discovery, and they gave it the name of Cabo de Gyrão, because it was on that occasion the last part and end [*cabo*] of the circuit [*gyro*] of their course’.

As a cliff overlooking the sea, several authors state that it is among the highest and sheerest to be found anywhere in the world. From some of the highest and most prominent points of that gigantic escarpment, one sees the ocean waves breaking at the foot of the sheer cliff some 600 metres below. That is why countless Portuguese and foreign works contain frequent references to the cliffs of Cabo Girão, which amply reward the scholar and the tourist with a subject for close and lengthy observation. Access to the highest points of the cliff is neither easy nor comfortable, for want of a good road leading there. A branch road 800 metres long is planned, to link these points with the national road that crosses the parishes of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’) and Campanário (‘bell tower’). (1921)

Around 1935 or shortly afterwards, the road was connected to the top of the cliff of Cabo Girão, and a fine viewpoint was built there, which has been widely visited by Portuguese and foreigners alike. From this spot a vast and astonishing panorama unfolds, in which the enraptured eye ranges from the beautiful amphitheatre of Funchal to the parishes of the municipality (*concelho*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’).

In the report of a former director of district public works in Madeira we came across a curious account of this well-known point on our coast. We transcribe part of it here, for the interest it may perhaps hold for some of our readers.

‘At Cabo Girão there is a sheer drop to the sea of 633 metres, a magnificent height not easily found anywhere else on the globe. While surveying the royal road from Funchal to São Vicente, I passed along the top of Cabo Girão and confirmed by levelling that this altitude was true. I wanted to experience the impression I would feel on contemplating the spectacle of so great a height, for I had heard it said, with astonishment, that English tourists would sit there on a projection of the ground, dangling their legs over the abyss. I timidly approached the edge of the cliff and noticed that the sight of such a height made no impression on me at all! The reason was simple: below lay the sea… the sea stretching as far as the eye could see, an immense plain without a single point of reference to make me aware of the great height at which I stood. My fellow workers doubted that the height could be so great, when a chance occurrence allowed me to prove to them that I had not misled them. Directly below that height, down on the sea, was a boat fishing close to the shore. The boat could be seen, very small and completely empty. I had found a point of reference. In the boat there were men who could not be seen, because at a vertical distance of 633 metres it is difficult, if not impossible, to see with the naked eye the horizontal projection of a man, which is little more than the surface of a hat…’.
See Cabos (‘capes’) and Geology.
Girard (Alberto A.)

A naturalist who accompanied the late King Carlos I on many of his oceanographic explorations. He was a French citizen but became a naturalised Portuguese, and had a degree in civil engineering obtained in Portugal. He was born in 1860 and died on 2 September 1914. Works: *Les Céphalopodes des Iles Açores et de l'Ile Madère* (*Jorn. das Sc. Math, Phys. e Nat.*, 1892). He also dealt with some fossil molluscs of the Madeira archipelago in the *Extracto das communicações da Commissão de trabalhos Geológicos*, vol. II, fasc. II.
Sunflower (Heliantus annuus)

An annual plant widely cultivated in Madeira. It belongs to the family Compositae, is native to Peru and produces flower heads one to two decimetres in diameter. Its achenes serve as food for poultry, and the leaves are eaten with relish by sheep and cows.
Godman (Frederic du Cane)

In his book entitled *Natural History of the Asores* (London, 1870), he published a list, compiled by W. Mitten, of the mosses of Madeira, the Canary Islands and the Azores, together with a work by Hewett Cottrell Watson on Azorean botany, which contains some observations that may be of use to those who study the flora of our archipelago.
Gofe
A porridge made on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) from tender green barley, crushed after being lightly toasted.

When the Canary Islands were conquered by the Spaniards, they noticed that the inhabitants ‘ate *gofio* of toasted barley’. It is likely that *gofe* is a corruption of *gofio*, and that this term was brought to the Madeira archipelago by people from Gran Canaria, La Palma, Tenerife and La Gomera who came to our island in the 15th century (see Slaves).
Élisée Reclus says that *gofio*, the national dish of the Canaries, is a paste made from the flour of various grains, popped over the fire.
See Frangolho.
Guava tree (Psidium pyriferum)

A small tree native to the West Indies, cultivated and naturalised in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira. The fruits (guavas) of this member of the Myrtaceae are made into a very tasty preserve. The guava tree is much less common today than it once was.
Goimpy (Comte François Louis Edmond Gabriel Martz de)

The Naval Academy in Paris holds a manuscript entitled *Observations faites à Aveiro et à Funchal*, whose author is the Count Francisco L. E. G. M. de Goimpy. We do not know when these observations were made, nor their nature.
Góis (Damião de)

This illustrious chronicler, who lived in the first half of the 16th century, was, after Gomes Eanes de Zurara, one of the earliest historians to write about the discovery of Madeira. On the value of his statements, see what the annotations to the *Saudades* say, on p. 338 of that work.
Goivo
Common name of *Matthiola maderensis* and *M. incana*, plants of the family Cruciferae. The first is native and grows on coastal rocks; the second is cultivated in gardens.
Goldschmidt (Julius)

This German physician, who lived in Funchal for many years, was living in Paris, where he had a large practice, when war broke out in 1914. Writing on Madeiran subjects, he published the pamphlets *Die lepra auf Madeira*, 1891, *Madère Étudiée comme station d'hiver*, 1880, and *Madère étudiée comme station d'hiver et d'été*, 1884. He died in 1924.
Gomes (António Gil)

António Gil Gomes was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco de São Jorge on 23 June 1803 and died in Funchal on 3 July 1868. He was the son of Captain João José Gil Gomes and Dona Maria Justina Gil Gomes. His liberal ideas forced him to leave Madeira in 1828, escaping the persecution and harassment suffered by some of his friends and relatives. In Rio de Janeiro, where he settled, he devoted himself to teaching and contributed regularly to various newspapers; he also wrote some pamphlets, which he published in that city. Once representative government had been established, he returned without delay to his native land, arriving in August 1834. Here he devoted himself to study and letters, keeping entirely aloof from party struggles and almost wholly withdrawn from social life. In Funchal he contributed extensively to many of the city’s newspapers, preferably on economic subjects, and also published here a pamphlet on customs reform and a book entitled *Compilação de Elementos de Filosofia Racional*. In his day he enjoyed a reputation as a man of uncommon intelligence and wide learning.
Gomes de Castro (Tristão)

He was born on this island in 1543, the son of Cristovam Martins de Agrinhão and Dona Joana Gomes de Castro. He was a descendant of João Gomes, the Troubadour, and administered the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) that he inherited from his parents. He studied away from the island and was reputed among his contemporaries to be a man of wide learning. He cultivated poetry, and several genealogies say that he was an excellent Latin poet. Diogo Barbosa Machado, in the *Biblioteca Lusitana*, deals with Tristão Gomes de Castro and cites the work he wrote in two volumes, *Argonautica da Cavallaria, Façanhas de Lesmundo*, which remained unpublished. He died in 1611.
Gomes de Cintra (Diogo)
See Cintra (Diogo Gomes de) and Discovery.
Gomes (Francisco Luiz)

This distinguished writer (1829–1869), author of *Os Brahamanes* and other works of undeniable merit, was struck by a serious lung disease and came to this island seeking relief from his sufferings. He did not, however, find in the mildness of our climate the cure he so longed for. The great novelist Júlio Dinis (see that entry), who met Francisco Luiz Gomes in Funchal, refers to him in a letter dated 5 April 1869 in the following terms: ‘Francisco Luiz Gomes is here in Funchal. I was disappointed when I saw him. He is a figure no one can see without turning round after he has passed. Imagine a skeleton in the strict sense of the word, tall and lanky; his legs bending under the weight of his body; his clothes hanging on him as if from a nail; the copper colour typical of Indians; his teeth bare and protruding. He is frightening, poor man! No one would say there is a man of intelligence there!’

Shortly after this meeting with Júlio Dinis, Francisco Luiz Gomes left Madeira and set out for Portuguese India, his native land, but succumbed during the voyage to the ravages of pulmonary tuberculosis in the first days of October 1869.
Gomes (João)

It has not been established whether he came to this archipelago as one of its early settlers or was born on this island. In various places he is cited as João Gomes da Ilha and also as João Gomes o Trovador (the Troubadour), for he cultivated poetry with distinction, and thirteen of his compositions are found in the *Cancioneiro* of Garcia de Resende. In Funchal he married Dona Guiomar Ferreira, daughter of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, the well-known companion of Gonçalves Zarco. He held land as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) on the banks of the stream that took, and still bears today, the name of João Gomes. He was a page of Prince Henry the Navigator and died in 1495. He was one of the first in this archipelago to use a surname.
See Cancioneiro de Resende (Madeira in the).
Gomes Leal

This distinguished poet lived in Funchal for some time, when his father was an official at the customs house of this city. The *Diario da Madeira* of 7 July 1923 published an interesting letter by Gomes Leal, written in Madeira and addressed to Albano Coutinho, dated 25 April 1868, in which he refers to various Madeiran matters.
Gomes (M. Teixeira)

He is Portugal’s current representative in England (1921). Some years ago he visited Madeira and travelled through part of the island, describing his excursions in the second edition of his book *Cartas sem moral nenhuma*, pp. 159–239. He speaks with great enthusiasm of the triptych in the sacristy of the church of São Pedro (St Peter), saying that ‘as types I know nothing superior in any painting, and the composition, the colouring and the drawing are certainly those of a most powerful artist’. The Viscount of Meireles, in articles published in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’), discussed Manuel Teixeira Gomes’s remarks, bringing out brilliantly the beauty of those paintings. Manuel Teixeira Gomes claims to have discovered this marvel, and indeed we know of no one before him who had referred to these unknown canvases.
Gomes (Romano de Santa Clara)

He holds a law degree as a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and is the registrar of the Land Registry for the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal. (1921) He represented Madeira in parliament as a deputy in the legislative session of 1895 to 1897. He was born in Funchal on 12 August 1869.
Gomito de Baleia
See Whales.
Gonçalo Aires (stream)

Gaspar Frutuoso, referring to the first exploratory work when the settlement of this island began, relates, among other episodes, the following: ‘Gonçalo Ayres went with his companions over the land for the space of three hours, at the end of which the captain was already growing vexed at their delay, when, behold, they appeared coming down the stream with garlands on their heads, and decked with branches they came talking with great pleasure, saying that they had found no living thing but birds; and hence the name “Ribeira de Gonçalayres” remained.’ This stream crosses the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), and at its mouth stands the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’) known as Gonçalo Aires.
See Ferreira (Gonçalo Aires) and Lazareto.
Gonçalves (Commander Manuel)

He was an intelligent and active Funchal merchant whose enterprising spirit and bold initiative rendered excellent services to his homeland. His work would have been still broader and more valuable had a spiteful campaign against him not hindered the realisation of his projects. Great and fruitful were the efforts he made to free local trade from the influence of certain foreign houses, which were stifling the commercial and industrial activities of the island’s native merchants. The organisation of the Companhia dos Sanatórios is due chiefly to his efforts, as will be seen more fully in the article devoted to it.

As director of the Companhia de Ferro do Monte, he carried out the important improvement of extending the railway from Monte (‘hill’) to Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), and had an excellent restaurant built there, which rivalled similar establishments abroad.
Commander Gonçalves was born in Funchal around 1867 and died in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte on 18 August 1916.
Gonçalves de Freitas (Councillor António)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) on 5 December 1827, the son of Captain António Joaquim Gonçalves de Freitas and Eulália Cândida de Freitas, and died in Lisbon on 14 July 1875. He graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1848, having earned several distinctions and shown himself a highly talented and diligent student. From 1852 to 1860 he practised as a lawyer in Funchal and devoted himself to politics and journalism. He was deputy for Madeira in the three legislatures from 1860 to 1865. Settling in the capital, he held several public offices there, among them that of director-general of direct taxation. He was regarded as a great authority on the administration of public finance, in which he specialised. More than once he was invited to take a ministerial portfolio, at a time when not everyone could aspire to one, but he always refused to accept a post of such great responsibility. He enjoyed great prestige in Lisbon, not only for his intellectual gifts and acknowledged competence but also for the austere qualities of character that ennobled his spirit. He was one of the most distinguished Madeirans of the 19th century.
Gonçalves de Freitas (Luís António)

He was the son of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) António Gonçalves de Freitas (see that entry) and Dona Júlia de Abreu Gonçalves de Freitas, and was born on 23 February 1858. He completed his law degree at Coimbra in 1880. He began cultivating letters very early and published several volumes of verse while still a student at the University. His literary output, in both prose and verse, is substantial. After bringing out a number of volumes, he undertook the publication of all his writings under the title *Obras Completas de Luiz António Gonçalves*; death prevented him from finishing it, but nineteen volumes nevertheless appeared. Among his works we may cite *Impressões*, *Phantasias*, *A Pupila de Beltrão*, *Oscillações*, *Mavalen*, *Reminescências*, *Discursos e Trabalhos Parlamentares*, *Artigos Políticos*, *Das Galerias*, *Expansões*, *Respigas*, *Humorismos*, *Discussão e Controvérsias*, *Mescla de Assumptos*, *Rachel*, *Horas de Paz*, *Noite de Nupcias* and *Os Pecados da Mocidade*.

He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislative session of 1882 to 1884, and the speeches he delivered in parliament in defence of the interests of this archipelago are published in his book *Discursos e Trabalhos Parlamentares*.
He was head of department in the civil government of Lisbon and carried out various public-service commissions.

Some months before his death, Dr Luís Gonçalves de Freitas suffered the great sorrow of losing his fine library, consumed by fire. The blow was so violent that he came close to succumbing. Some time later he was struck down by a cerebral congestion, on 28 October 1904, at only 46 years of age.

He was a distinguished and admired poet, and also wrote several plays in both prose and verse. He contributed widely to many magazines and newspapers, and a large number of these writings were collected in the edition of his *Obras Completas*.
Gonçalves de Freitas (Viscount of)

Pedro Maria Gonçalves de Freitas, Viscount of Gonçalves de Freitas, was born on this island on 17 March 1836, the son of Captain António Joaquim Gonçalves de Freitas and Dona Eulália Cândida Gonçalves de Freitas. He took up the legal profession early, as a licensed advocate (*advogado provisionista*, practising by licence without a law degree), and in it he won the reputation of a distinguished and brilliant pleader. He acted in several cases that became famous, always displaying the force of his extraordinary talent, the acuity of his mind and the ingenious dialectic of his reasoning, together with fluent, imaginative language full of warmth and enthusiasm that deeply impressed his audiences.

As a politician he enjoyed extraordinary prestige here, and there was a time when he was the most influential party figure in the whole archipelago. He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) as a deputy in the legislatures of 1884 and 1887 and from 1894 to 1895, and as an elective peer of the realm (*par do reino electivo*, elected member of the upper chamber) in the legislative session of 1887 to 1889. He was also deputy for the archipelago of Cape Verde, where he lived for some years practising law.
He was a senior customs official and served as director of the Funchal customs house, and also held other public-service commissions, such as that of civil governor of this district.

He edited the former periodical *O Direito* and contributed to other publications, proving himself a distinguished journalist. In the national parliament he displayed his brilliant qualities as a parliamentarian, both as an orator and as a profound expert on the matters he dealt with there. He died in this city on 6 July 1915, aged 79.
Gonçalves (Francisco Mendes)

Around the middle of the 19th century a boy of tender age, a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’), left Madeira and settled in the Argentine Republic. There, after some years, he acquired a great fortune, and he later became one of the richest men in that prosperous South American nation. What deserves special mention here, however, is the astonishing energy and enterprising spirit of this Madeiran. As a merchant, coloniser of vast uncultivated territories, director of banking houses and negotiator of high-finance operations, he attained the greatest prestige and influence. He extended the network of his dealings to the whole of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay, and it was not unusual for the governments of those countries to turn to his experience and knowledge to solve many problems closely bearing on the highest interests of the state. He died in the city of Buenos Aires, at an advanced age and possessed of great wealth, on 28 December 1930, known as ‘Gonçalves the millionaire’.
It is regrettable that he did not heed any of the appeals sent to him from Madeira to help with some small improvements needed in his native parish, which it urgently required.
Gonçalves (Joaquim Melchior)

He was a member of the first Constitutional Council of Funchal, a captain of the territorial militia (*ordenanças*) and a corresponding member of the Sociedade dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes. Sentenced by the special judicial commission (alçada) that came to Madeira in 1823 to four years of penal exile (degredo) in the Cape Verde islands, he went there, but returned home in 1826. A most ardent constitutionalist, he was indicted by the special judicial commission sent to Madeira in 1828, but this time he escaped arrest by going into hiding.

It is said that one night, when Melchior Gonçalves had gone out to visit some friends, he met in the Largo da Sé (‘cathedral square’) a band of constables (*quadrilheiros*) led by Governor José Maria Monteiro. Realising that he could not escape, he resolved to approach the governor. Declaring that he had been looking for him to make a communication that only he should hear, he asked him to have the constables withdraw some distance so that they could speak freely.

The request was granted, and the governor was preparing to hear what Melchior Gonçalves had to tell him when the latter swiftly dealt him several punches that knocked him down. He then fled, and the constables, who at once ran after him, failed to catch him.

We do not know the dates of birth and death of Francisco Melchior Gonçalves, but a member of his family tells us that he was a native of Campanário (‘bell tower’) and that before 1834 he emigrated to Brazil, where he died.
Gonçalves Marques (Vasco)
See Marques (Vasco Gonçalves).
Gonçalves (Moisés)

He was a dental surgeon trained at a school in New York, and for many years practised dentistry in the city of Lisbon with a large clientele, being considered at the time the most distinguished member of his profession. In 1895 he published the important work *Os Dentes Humanos*, in one volume of 198 pages. He was a native of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).
Blackspot seabream (Pagellus centrodontus)

A fish of the family Sparidae, common in Madeira and among the most highly prized for its delicate flavour. The *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream) and the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) are the preferred tackle for catching it.
Gorazeira

A fishing tackle widely used in Madeira. It consists of a main line and small secondary lines attached to it, each ending in a hook. A weight is fixed at the end of the main line to make the tackle sink.
Gorda (point)
A small projection of the coastline, not far from the Ilhéu do Gorgulho (‘weevil’) and Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’).
Gorda (point)
On the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge (‘St George’). See São Jorge (point).
Gordo (mount)
See Piedade (‘pity’).
Gordo (peak)
A mountain peak in the uplands of the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), near Monte das Estrebarias (‘hill of the stables’), at an altitude of 1200 metres.
Gordon (C. A.)
*The Flower of the Ocean, the Island of Madeira*. London, 1894, 1 vol.
Grain weevil

The name *gorgulho* is applied to *Sitophilus granarius* and *S. Orizae*, species of beetles that attack grain and flour and are frequent in houses and storehouses throughout the island. The second species, which seems to be commoner than the first, is easily distinguished by its darker colour.
Gorgulho (locality and islet)
A coastal locality (*sítio*) west of the city, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho, where there was once a small fort, now in complete ruin.
Gorgulho (‘weevil’) is of geological interest because of the lava flows that can be seen beside this fort.
There is an iron stairway and an inclined plane there, built by order of the Wilson Company.
In 1932 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) had a public pool for bathing and swimming built at this locality, supplied with seawater.
At this locality, a short distance from the shore, lies a small islet named Gorgulho.
Gorjão (Francisco Pedro de Meneses)

He was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira on 18 May 1737 and took office on 16 July of the same year. He held this post until 27 May 1747, when he left the island directly for Maranhão to govern that province, aboard the fleet bound there that called at Funchal carrying the new bishop of that diocese, Dom Friar Francisco de São Tiago.
He was succeeded as governor of Madeira by the diocesan bishop, Dom João do Nascimento, who was appointed on 5 May 1747 and held the post until 1751.

We have read somewhere that Francisco Pedro de Meneses Gorjão ‘died at the age of 83, full of services to his country, as recorded on the stone of his tomb in the chapel of the *quinta* (country estate) of São Lourenço.
Gourlay (Dr William)

English physician who came to Madeira in 1792 and lived here for 18 years. Works: *Observations on the Natural History, climate and diseases of Madeira during a period of eighteen years*, London, 1811. The accuracy of the meteorological observations published in Gourlay’s work, covering the period from 1793 to 1803, has been questioned by several authors, among them the distinguished Portuguese physician Dr Barral.
Gouveia (Canon António Homem de)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) on 17 December 1869. He studied at the seminary (*Seminário*) of this Diocese and was ordained priest in 1893. By royal letter (*carta régia*) of 30 November 1899 he was appointed canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*). He was clerk of the Diocesan Chancery (*Câmara Eclesiástica*) and has carried out various public-service commissions. He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislative sessions of 1905–1906, 1906 and 1906–1907. Of the speeches he delivered in parliament, three were published as pamphlets under the titles *A Escravidão da Igreja em Portugal*, Lisbon, 1905, of which another edition was produced in Funchal the same year, *Necessidade do Descanso Dominical*, Lisbon, 1907, and *A Situação da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1907.
Gouveia (Francisco Bento de)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) on 16 July 1874 and has devoted himself to industrial studies and research, succeeding in making paper from sugar-cane straw and in extracting from Madeiran trachytes the silica needed to make glass. Some years ago he also took up oenological studies, going so far as to produce a type of table wine from the Jacquez grape, which won the approval of the late Batalha Reis. He was one of the editors of the former *Diário Popular* (‘The People’s Daily’), collaborated on a revue staged at the Teatro Manuel de Arriaga, and is a first-class inspector of agricultural products, although he has been absent from the service for some time now. (1921)
Gouveia (João)

He was born in this city on 8 February 1880, the son of Colonel José Maria de Gouveia and Dona Elisa Camacho de Gouveia. His poetic gift awoke early, but he also soon stopped cultivating poetry. We do not know what led him to abandon the literary career he had begun so auspiciously. He published the volumes *Breviário*, Funchal, 1900, 112 pp., and *Atlante*, Lisbon, 1903, 108 pp.

It seems that João Gouveia closed his soul to the inspiration of the Muses in order to devote himself more fully to the study of mechanics, and especially to building the aeroplane he had invented. The newspapers wrote at length and with the highest praise about this invention, but it seems that serious and insurmountable difficulties arose in its construction.

João Gouveia has lived in Lisbon for many years, and has lately turned his attention to building a poultry apparatus that has aroused great interest among all those engaged in the artificial rearing of chickens. (1921).
Gouveia (José Maria de)

He was born in Funchal on 13 March 1856 and had long since settled on the mainland. He was a colonel of infantry, and in 1895 published in this city a pamphlet entitled *Serviço de Campanha, Instrução Pratica de secção para uso dos oficiais inferiores da arma de infantaria*. He died in Lisbon in November 1930.
Gouveia Júnior (Francisco Gomes de)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’) on 12 April 1864, the son of Francisco Gomes de Gouveia and Dona Antónia de Jesus de Gouveia. After studying at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), he attended the former postal school in Lisbon and completed its course. He was a retired postal officer and held various public-service posts, among them vice-president of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) and president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*). He contributed widely to various Funchal newspapers and other publications, and was chief editor of the newspaper *A Madeira* (‘Madeira’). He died on 11 August 1926.

Governors General

With Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) the government of the captain-donataries came to an end (see Donataries), and this archipelago came to be administered by Governors General, appointed directly by the Spanish government. The administration of the Governors General lasted throughout the whole period of Castilian rule. They were:

The governors and captains-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira), and after them the first civil governors, took office in the session hall of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), in the presence of the assembled councillors. Such was the respect that the former captain-lieutenants inspired that, when they went out, all men stopped and doffed their hats as they approached, and horsemen had to dismount as they passed. On 3 September 1803 a certain Henrique Correia, of noble family, was committed to the prison of the islet because he had not dismounted as the governor Dom José Manuel da Câmara passed, and had answered this authority somewhat rudely when admonished for his discourtesy. The late holder of the entail (*morgado*) António João da Silva Betencourt Favila was likewise arrested on one occasion for failing to salute a governor and captain-general! *Quantum matatus ab illo!*

Dr Damião Peres, a distinguished professor at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and former rector of the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), whose name is linked to valuable works on the history of our country, published in 1924 and 1925 two interesting pamphlets entitled *O Desembargador João Leitão Governador Geral da Madeira* and *O Problema dos Governadores Gerais da Madeira*. In them he set out to show that there was no basis for the generic title of governors-general given by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the learned commentator on ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), to the highest authorities of this archipelago during Castilian rule, and that they were entitled only to the name of captains-general, as can be read in some official documents of the period. The co-author of this *Elucidário*, C. A. de Meneses, in a series of articles published in the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) in September 1925, explains and justifies the title used by Dr A. R. de Azevedo, putting forward weighty arguments that invalidate Dr Damião Peres’s assertion. It is worth noting that this is a matter of secondary importance, of no great interest to the history of this island.

Grabham (Dr Michael)

English physician, born on 11 January 1840, who lived for many years in Funchal. Works: *The Climate and resources of Madeira*, London, 1870, and *Materia Atlantica*, London, 1901. The latter work, written in Portuguese, was intended as a guide for people coming to this island on the occasion of the visit of the King and Queen of Portugal. Graça

A locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, near the town (*vila*), where the chapel of Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*) stands. When it was built is not known. It is known to be quite old and to have been rebuilt by its brotherhood in 1750.
Graça

A locality (*sítio*) on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). An old chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Graça (Our Lady of Grace) once stood here and gave the place its name. As it was badly ruined, its reconstruction on a larger scale than the original was begun in the early 19th century, on the initiative of the governor of that island, Manuel Inácio de Avelar Brotero. The rebuilding was never completed, however, and today the chapel is reduced to a heap of ruins. It was unusual in being octagonal, and it is said to have reproduced in miniature a famous church in Italy.

Bermuda grass (Cynodon Dactylon)
A rhizomatous grass with linear spikes, green or violet, clustered 3 to 7 together at the top of the stems. It is very common in Madeira, and its rhizomes are emollient and diuretic.
Gramacho

The origin of this family surname here in Madeira, which we believe is now extinct, seems to have been the *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) Rui Gramacho, who was one of the first settlers and held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). In the parish (*freguesia*) of Sant'Ana there is a locality (*sítio*) called Achada do Gramacho (‘Gramacho’s plateau’).
Grande (Eduardo)

He was a native of Portalegre and served as agronomist attached to the Civil Government of the district of Funchal (*Distrito do Funchal*), later becoming secretary-general of the same Civil Government. He was also a member of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*). He wrote a report that was presented to the board of the former Agricultural Society of Funchal and published in 1865. Although it has some shortcomings, this report contains a good deal of curious information on the state of agriculture in Madeira at the time of its publication. Eduardo Grande died in Lisbon around 1881.

Hail

This watery meteor, known in Madeira as snow, forms the broad white sheets that in winter sometimes cover the island’s mountains for days on end. Hail falling on the mountains is often accompanied or preceded by thunderstorms, and it always brings a marked drop in temperature along the whole coast.

In the island’s upper region, hail always takes the form of small, irregular, angular lumps. The rounded form, which seems to be due to the lumps beginning to melt as they pass through a thicker layer of the atmosphere, appears only in the middle region, and now and then on the coast. At an altitude of 1,500 metres hail sometimes forms layers more than a metre thick. When it appears between 600 and 800 metres, which is rare, it usually melts within a few hours.

Hail is almost unknown on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Nevertheless, on 4 February 1860 it fell on that island in such abundance that the hills and valleys were covered with it. ‘In the town (*vila*) there was so much of it’, say the *Anais do Porto Santo*, ‘that many people filled plates and tubs, and even made sorbet; a thing unheard of among these people’. In our climate hail appears only from the end of autumn to the beginning of spring, and it contributes notably to increasing the volume of water in the springs and streams. It is said that nearly 60 years ago a hailstorm caused great damage to the crops of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), and it is also recorded that some years ago hail destroyed a good part of the foliage of the fruit trees and other plants in the parish of Canhas. Fortunately, however, such cases are so rare that the Madeiran farmer, when cultivating his land, does not even think of this enemy, so much to be feared in more northerly latitudes.

So as to record in these pages a fuller account of the nature of the meteorological phenomena of snow, frost and hail in the islands of our archipelago, we shall transcribe a few passages from an article on this interesting subject which the co-author of this *Elucidário*, the distinguished naturalist C. Azevedo de Meneses, published many years ago in the former *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’).

‘The information on these meteors provided by the various works dealing with the climatology and meteorology of Madeira is so meagre that the few data we now present on them, nearly all the fruit of our own observation, may perhaps be of some interest.

As a rule, snow falls in Madeira only from January to early March, that is, in the period when the cold is most intense, and, we believe, it is never seen below 1200 or 1000 metres. Madeirans who visit or cross the mountains during the winter months call snowflakes *folhelho* (popular name for snowflakes), reserving the word *neve* (snow) for hail, which is far more frequent on the island and is also seen at lower altitudes.

During the coldest season, the centigrade thermometer in Funchal sometimes falls to 8 and 7 degrees. If, then, we accept that heat decreases by one degree for every 180 metres of elevation, it follows that on the same occasions the thermometer should read temperatures slightly below zero at altitudes above 1300 metres, which, as is well known, are enough to bring about snowfalls. In our climate snow does not last long, generally melting within a few hours.

Guilherme Teles de Meneses, who made some meteorological observations at the station on the Pico do Arieiro (1700 metres), saw the thermometer there register 2 degrees below zero in November. It is therefore reasonable to suppose that still lower temperatures occur at the same spot in January and February, which in Madeira are the coldest months of the year. In the opinion of the late English naturalist James Yate Johnson, the limit of perpetual snow at the latitude of Madeira must lie at 3,450 metres, an altitude that our Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) does not even approach…

During the winter months frosts also sometimes appear on the high points of the island. The crystalline layers of ice that form on certain objects are known to the common people as *dente de cão* (‘dog’s tooth’, popular name for crystalline hoar frost). We are told that on the north coast frosts usually appear above 600 or 700 metres, but on the south coast we believe they are unknown within the limits of the cultivated region, which only at a few points rises above 800 metres.

Hail is far more frequent on the island than flake snow or *folhelho* and frosts or *dente de cão*. It falls most abundantly from November to March, but also appears occasionally in October and April. It is hail that forms those broad white sheets which in the winter season sometimes cover a good part of our mountains for days on end (3 to 15, rarely more).

Hail falls in the mountains every year, but it is not always visible from Funchal. Hailfalls are often accompanied or preceded by thunderstorms, and always bring a drop in temperature in the city. When this meteor appears between 600 and 800 metres, which is rare, it generally melts within a few hours.

Hail in the mountains of Madeira always takes the form of small, irregular, angular pieces, similar in shape to the basaltic sand of the beaches. The rounded form, which is much less frequent, appears only at middle altitudes on the southern and northern slopes, and now and then near the coast. At an altitude of 1500 metres, hail in some years builds up layers more than a metre thick.

Because of the altitudes at which they appear, snow and frost do no damage to the island’s crops; hail, however, can sometimes be harmful, though never as much as in the countries of Europe. It is said that more than 50 years ago a hailstorm caused great damage to the crops of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal, and Guilherme Teles de Meneses told us that some nine or ten years ago he saw hail destroy a good part of the foliage of the fruit trees in other areas of the parish of Canhas. These cases, however, are fortunately so rare that the Madeiran farmer, when cultivating his land, as stated above, never even thinks of this enemy, so much to be feared in more northerly latitudes. He fears droughts far more, and their effects are indeed much more disastrous for agriculture, especially in places that irrigation water does not reach.’
See Snow and Dente de Cão.

Guarda (Friar Pedro da)

Friar Pedro da Guarda was a poor and humble Franciscan. He was born in 1435 in the city from which he took his surname, and he died in the convent of St Bernardino (*São Bernardino*), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), in the year 1505. The austerity of his life, the harsh penances to which he gave himself and his most exemplary practice of all the Christian virtues won him a reputation for sanctity even during his earthly pilgrimage. After his death many miraculous events were attributed to his intercession, and several beatification processes were set in motion so that he might canonically receive the veneration of the altars. The last was some 32 years ago, and various extracts from the principal documents of the process were published in a folio volume of 163 pages. The Holy See never pronounced on the canonisation, but the prelates of this diocese allowed a certain public cult, which for centuries never waned but instead grew more fervent with time. The Holy Servant of God, the name by which he was known and still is today, had countless fervent devotees, who flocked from all over the island to his burial place to implore his protection and help for the ills from which they suffered.

In the city of Guarda lived João Luís, a weaver, and his wife Águeda Gonçalves, and of their marriage Pedro was born in the year 1435. At the age of twenty he entered the Franciscan order, where he took his vows as a lay brother. For thirty years he lived in convents on the mainland, where the austerity of his life became well known and some prodigious events were attributed to him. Wishing to escape the admiration that his virtues aroused, he asked to withdraw to a convent of his order in Madeira, which he did around 1485. Seeking an obscure refuge in the convent of St Bernardino, in the parish of Câmara de Lobos, he lived there for about twenty years, and died on 27 July 1505. The penitent life he led in this retreat, and above all the miraculous events attributed to his intercession, drew the attention of his contemporaries, as we have already noted. A true halo of sanctity formed around his name, and it grew and swelled still further after his death.

No sooner had the governor of this bishopric, António Alfredo Santa Catarina Braga, arrived on the island in 1835 than he set about erasing the traces of the influence exercised by the religious orders, which had been expelled the year before. Bound up with that influence was the cult paid to the Santo Servo de Deus, and he moved without delay to prohibit every manifestation of a religious character in honour of the humble Franciscan. On 2 June 1835 António Alfredo went to the convent of St Bernardino, accompanied by several clergymen and some persons of social standing, and conducted a summary inquiry into the miraculous deeds attributed to Friar Pedro da Guarda. He then ordered that the statue of this religious, which was venerated there, be publicly burnt in his presence, together with other objects used in the ceremonies of worship offered to that humble lay brother of the Franciscan order. He had a record (*auto*) of the whole proceedings drawn up on the spot, a document full of rancour, even though it displays the greatest zeal for the integrity of Catholic doctrine and the prestige of religion. The following day he had a warrant (*provisão*) published in which the cult of the Santo Servo de Deus was utterly condemned and prohibited, imposing severe penalties on any clergy who failed to obey the orders contained in that warrant.

The act of the ecclesiastical authority caused great indignation and scandal throughout the island. This was not so much because of the prohibition of the cult, which could be justified under canon law, as because of the pomp and solemnity with which it was carried out, and above all because of the auto-da-fé performed on the image of the poor friar, whose memory certainly did not deserve to be exposed to such public execration.

It appears that the beatification process opened a few years ago is to go forward once more. It is possible that the Holy See will, in the near future, decree public veneration of Friar Pedro da Guarda, whom the people know only by the name of Santo Servo de Deus.

As stated above, several efforts were made to obtain the decree of beatification of the humble Franciscan Friar Pedro da Guarda. The most important of them all was the one undertaken around 1623, whose case file is still in Rome and which reached an advanced stage. In 1905 a new process was opened in the episcopal curia of Funchal and continued in Rome before the tribunals of the Holy See; in 1905 various separate documents from it were published in a folio volume of 180 pages. For reasons unknown to us, this process was not carried forward, and the investigations into the matter that had begun there, in the secretariat of the ecclesiastical congregations, remain suspended.
In 1864 a pamphlet (*opúsculo*) was published in Funchal containing a biography of Friar Pedro da Guarda, taken from the chronicles of the Seraphic Order in Portugal.
National Guard

By a royal decree (*alvará*) of the Prefect and Military Governor of Madeira, dated 1 September 1834, a commission was appointed to carry out the census and nominal enrolment of all individuals who, under the decree of 29 March of the same year, were to serve in the National Guard. By the end of 1835, however, this guard had still not been properly organised, even though its officers had already been elected and approved by the competent authorities.

It seems that in the early days there was a certain reluctance to supply arms to the members of the National Guard (*Guarda Nacional*), because it was suspected that not all of them were loyal to the constitutional cause.

The ministerial order (*portaria*) of 19 March 1835 ordered the formation in Madeira of a battalion of Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) of the National Guard. It was definitively constituted in 1836, its officers and non-commissioned officers having been elected on 10 January of that year at a meeting held in the Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’).

The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) sent the Governor the list of elected officers so that he could submit it to the Government for approval. Elections were held every two years, and the first commander of the battalion of Caçadores of the National Guard was Valentim de Freitas Leal.
The National Guard of Funchal had a flag presented by Dona Ana Mascarenhas e Ataíde on 14 January 1835.
The national guards were dissolved by the law of 7 October 1846.
Republican Guard

Independent Company no. 1 of the Republican Guard (*Guarda Republicana*), today (1921) Mixed Company no. 1, was created by decree of 10 May 1919. On 3 December 1919, 2 sergeants, 3 corporals and 21 soldiers of this guard arrived in Funchal aboard the *Quelimane*; 11 of the men belonged to the cavalry and 15 to the infantry. The force has since been enlarged and at present numbers 3 sergeants, 8 corporals, 1 bugler corporal and 66 soldiers, under a captain commanding the company and 1 subaltern commanding the mixed section of Funchal. The force includes 16 Madeirans, discharged soldiers of the infantry and artillery.
The strength of the Company has not yet been firmly settled, as it depends on the number of posts that come to be established on the island. (1921)

The Republican Guard withdrew to Lisbon in 1922, on the April and May sailings of the steamer *São Miguel*. In its last period it had its barracks at the Quinta Vigia (‘lookout estate’), which belongs to the State and where, in former times, the Empress of Austria and Archduke Maximilian, later Emperor of Mexico, resided.
Guarnição de jardim

Madeirans give this name to several species of the genus *Verbena*, the commonest of which is *V. bonariensis*, fully naturalised in various parts of Funchal. This species is also known by the names *jarvão* (popular name for vervain) or *urgebão* and, like *V. officinalis*, is regarded by country people as a stimulant and tonic. It has lilac flowers arranged in spikes and very rough, incised-serrate leaves.
Military garrison

The military garrison of Madeira consists of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*Infantaria n.º 27*), No. 3 Mountain Artillery Battery, a company of the Republican Guard and No. 1 Company of the Revenue Guard (*Guarda Fiscal*, customs and excise corps) (1921). Before this garrison was assigned to the island, however, other military forces were stationed here, many of which appear in the list we publish below:
Infantry No. 5
The 5th Infantry Regiment was organised by the decree of 21 July 1834 for the defence of Madeira.
Infantry No. 11

The 11th Infantry Battalion garrisoned Madeira from 1837 to 1847, although part of it left for Portugal in 1843. It was forces of the 11th Infantry and the 4th Artillery that staged the pronouncement of 29 April 1847. For this reason they left the island in August of the same year, once the queen’s government had been restored.
Caçadores No. 6

The 6th Battalion of Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry), 400 men strong, arrived in Madeira in 1847. However, having mutinied on the night of 30–31 July 1852, it was immediately transferred to Lisbon, where it arrived on 15 August. It was disarmed on board, the other ranks being sent to the frigate *Diana* and the officers to the frigate *D. Fernando*. (See Lapierre.)
Infantry No.
7. The 2nd Battalion of the 7th Infantry, 241 men strong, arrived in Funchal on 29 August 1852 and remained here until 19 April 1853.
Infantry No. 13

The 2nd Battalion of the 7th Infantry was relieved by a force of 250 men of the 13th Infantry, which remained in Madeira until 27 July 1854. The steamer *Duque da Terceira*, which carried this force to Portugal, was wrecked near Aveiro.
Caçadores No. 2
From 24 July 1854 to August 1855 four companies of the 2nd Battalion of Caçadores were stationed in Madeira.
Infantry No. 4
The 2nd Battalion of the 4th Infantry Regiment was stationed in Madeira from 24 August 1855 until July 1856.
Infantry no.

1. The 1st Battalion of the 1st Infantry Regiment (*Infantaria n.º 1*) arrived in Madeira on 28 June 1856 and left for Portugal on 6 August 1858. It was this force that brought us the epidemic of cholera morbus, which was then raging with great intensity in Portugal. Infantry no. 16. A force of 306 men of the 16th Infantry Regiment relieved the preceding force, remaining in Madeira until 17 August 1859.
Infantry no. 10
Madeira was garrisoned by forces of this regiment from the time the 16th Infantry left the island until 1860.
Infantry no. 2
It replaced the 10th Infantry and remained in Madeira until 19 June 1861.
Caçadores no. 1
It arrived on 16 June 1861 and left for Portugal in July 1862.
Caçadores no. 5
A force of 218 men of the 5th Caçadores Battalion arrived in Madeira on 17 July 1862 and left for Portugal on 1 August 1864.
Caçadores no. 12

In July 1864, 10 officers and 72 other ranks came to Madeira to form the new 12th Caçadores Battalion, which, according to the plan published on 23 June 1864, was to have its barracks in Funchal. The new battalion was brought up to strength with men recruited on the island.

The 12th Caçadores Battalion was intended to be stationed in Funchal. However, because it was transferred to Tomar in December 1869 as a result of political intrigues, the 5th Caçadores Battalion came to replace it. The 12th did not return to the island until 1870, and it has never left since.
Under the military reorganisation of 30 November 1884, the 12th Caçadores Battalion became a regiment.
Caçadores no. 5

The 5th Caçadores Battalion arrived in Madeira in December 1869. However, because two of its companies mutinied on 2 August 1870, following an inspection of arms, the entire battalion was transferred to Portugal, and the aforementioned 12th Caçadores Battalion was ordered back to the island.
Infantry no. 27
Since 9 October 1899 the 12th Caçadores Regiment has been called the 27th Infantry Regiment, in accordance with the provisions of the decree of 14 September of the same year. (1921).

Besides the forces we have just mentioned, there are others to record, but these came to this island only temporarily, to reinforce the troops serving here. Thus in 1847 the 4th Caçadores Battalion (Portuguese light infantry) and a detachment of the 2nd Artillery were in Madeira, brought from the Azores by the governing board (junta governativa). In 1887 the 1st Infantry Regiment and a company of the 5th Caçadores were sent to this island because of the popular riots provoked by the elections to the parish councils (*juntas de paróquia*). And in 1911 the 6th Caçadores Battalion was charged by the Government of the Republic with keeping order in Madeira, together with the garrison troops, for as long as the cholera epidemic lasted here. From the beginning of 1918 to March 1919 a company of position artillery was stationed in Funchal to defend this island against any German attack.

Before the proclamation of the Constitution on 5 June 1834, we know of only the following regular army forces having been in Madeira: the 7th Infantry Regiment and a detachment of the 2nd Artillery, which arrived here on 23 August 1823, the former returning to Lisbon in 1826 after provoking several conflicts in Funchal; a force of the 7th Artillery, which was in Madeira in 1823; a battalion of the 1st Infantry, another of the 2nd Infantry, a contingent of the 11th Caçadores, a detachment of artillery and another of engineer artificers, which garrisoned the island during the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government; the 13th Infantry Regiment, which was also here during the same government and left for Lisbon at the end of 1829 after mutinying; and finally four companies of the Beira Alta Caçadores Regiment and the 1st Battalion of the Lagos Infantry Regiment, which were on this island in 1831.

In 1815 there was in Madeira a battalion of first-line artillery with six companies, as recorded in the *Estatística Histórico-geográfico da ilha da Madeira* by Casado Giraldes. During the rule of the Philips there was in Madeira the so-called Spanish garrison, made up of permanent, paid troops whose purpose was to secure possession of this island and the authority of the governor-general of war. ‘The said garrison,’ says Dr Azevedo, ‘was composed of four companies, each with its captain, the captain of the first being commander of the whole garrison, and in his authority independent of the Portuguese governor.’

As regards second- and third-line troops, it is known that Madeira had the militia, the territorial militia (*ordenanças*), the lookouts (*vigias*), the auxiliary artillery and the National Guard (see those entries), as well as the auxiliary *terços*, approved by the royal resolution of 27 November 1784; the Volunteer Battalion of Pedro IV and the Battalion of Urban Royalist Volunteers, the latter created in the time of Miguel I and the former during the government of José Lúcio Travassos Valdez; the National Battalion of Funchal Volunteers, established on 28 August 1836; the National Caçadores Battalion of the Prince Royal, created on 6 March 1847 and dissolved on 29 April of the same year; the National Battalion of Funchal, organised by the governing board in 1847, etc., etc.

In the time of Peter II an artillery company was instituted, and a building was begun to house it, but it was consumed by fire before it was finished. On 5 September 1661 the creation of a corps of 100 gunners to defend the fortresses was ordered, each of them earning 50 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a day. In 1762 there was a cavalry company in Madeira, in 1780 an infantry company of the governor’s guard, and in 1799 there were infantry troops receiving pay, although it is to be believed that all these forces belonged to the second line.

Major Alberto Artur Sarmento, in his *Alicerces para a historia militar*, in various articles published in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) and in other writings, provides valuable information on the military forces that have garrisoned this island at different times.
Guedes (Vasco)

Vasco Guedes de Carvalho e Meneses, who was then military commander of Madeira, was appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 14 August 1884, and took office on the 18th of the same month.

He had been governor-general of Angola. To defend himself against the accusations made against him while he was administering that overseas possession, he published in Funchal in 1882 a pamphlet entitled *Apontamentos para a Historia de Angola*. He died in April 1915.
Guelro (Atherina presbyter)

A small fish of the family Atherinidae, common in the seas of the archipelago. In the hot season it gathers in dense shoals in coastal waters and in the rock pools along the shore. It is a tasty fish but seldom appears at market, as fishermen usually use it as bait and groundbait. Its chief use is in fishing for skipjack tuna (*gaiado*).
Great War

This was the name given to the tremendous conflict that began in Europe in 1914, provoked by Germany, and that for four long years convulsed the whole civilised world, forcing the belligerent countries into efforts and sacrifices that no earlier war had ever demanded. Portugal also entered the struggle, at the request of her old ally, England, and her troops, though few in number, gave excellent service wherever they were called upon to fight. In Europe and in Africa alike, Portuguese soldiers made the name of our country shine in all its brilliance, and the way their services during the campaign were appreciated by the foreign press, especially the French, is highly honourable to our national pride.

The list we publish below gives the names of the sons of our land who died in combat or were taken prisoner by the enemy, together with those who were decorated or commended for good service during the campaign. It does not include the names of all the Madeirans who belonged to the expeditionary forces and were in the war zone, because we found it impossible to obtain complete and reliable information on the matter:

1. Ernesto de França Mendes, major on the Army General Staff. He was awarded the Grand Cross of the Legion of Honour by the French Government and the Distinguished Service Order by the British Government.
2. João Nepomuceno de Freitas, infantry major and commander of the 2nd Infantry Battalion. He was taken prisoner in the battle of 9 April 1918.

3. Américo Olavo Correia de Azevedo (see that entry), infantry captain. He was taken prisoner by the Germans in the same battle and was decorated with the War Cross and the Order of the Tower and Sword.

4. Jaime César Nunes de Oliveira, infantry captain and commander of the 4th company of the 35th Infantry Battalion of the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps (C. E. P.). He was decorated with the medal for Distinguished Service in the field and with the campaign medal bearing the legend ‘Crossing of the Scheldt and pursuit of the enemy’; he also received three commendations, two from the General Commanding the C. E. P. and one from the Minister of War.
5. Francisco Silvestre Varela, infantry captain and commander of the 1st company of the 35th Infantry Battalion. Honourable mention.
6. Jaime Pereira Rodrigues Baptista, infantry captain. He was taken prisoner in the battle of 9 April 1918.
7. António Eduardo Gonçalves Henriques, infantry lieutenant. Commended.
8. Carlos José Machado dos Santos, medical lieutenant. Commended.

9. João Paulo da Veiga Pestana, militia second lieutenant of infantry. He was 20 years old and studying engineering in Portugal when he was called up to attend the school for militia officers. Shortly afterwards he left for France, where he met a glorious death in the battle of 9 April 1918. At a session of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) on 10 April 1919, councillor (*vereador*) Francisco Gomes de Gouveia proposed that Rua das Hortas be renamed Alferes Veiga Pestana, and the proposal was approved unanimously.
10. Gabriel Rocha de Gouveia, militia second lieutenant of infantry. He was a native of Calheta (‘small cove’) and died in France on 13 October 1917, aged about 30.

11. Alfredo de França Dória Nóbrega, militia second lieutenant of infantry. He was decorated with the War Cross and later made a Knight of the Order of Christ, with palms, for having helped the 15th Infantry Battalion, after the battle of 9 April 1918, to resume its place at the front, incorporated as a fighting unit in a British brigade. 12. Henrique Ernesto Teixeira Moniz, militia second lieutenant of infantry. He was first commended and later received the War Cross, 3rd Class, for the courage and composure he showed in the battle of 23 November 1917.
13. Américo Aldónio de Meneses, militia second lieutenant of infantry. He was taken prisoner in the battle of 9 April 1918.
14. Artur de Brito Figueiroa, militia second lieutenant of infantry. He was taken prisoner in the battle of 9 April 1918.
15. Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo (see that entry), militia second lieutenant. He was taken prisoner on 9 April 1918.
16. Osvaldo de Andrade, artillery second lieutenant. Commended.
17. Armando Pinto Correia, infantry second lieutenant. He was twice commended for acts of courage and devotion during the campaign. He left for France in August 1918.
18. José Maria da Conceição Macedo, militia second lieutenant. He holds the War Cross, 3rd Class, for distinguished service in the field.
19. João da Silva Júnior, militia second lieutenant. He was decorated with the War Cross, 2nd Class, for distinguished service in the battle of 9 April 1918.

20. Daniel Fernandes de Aguiar, infantry lieutenant. He holds the War Cross, 3rd Class, and the silver military medal for good service, and was commended for the daring and fighting spirit he showed in many battles and for the dangerous missions he carried out during the campaign.

21. António Martins Ferreira Júnior, second lieutenant in the 2nd Infantry Regiment (*Infantaria 2*). He was commended for the courage with which he led his men and for his efforts to recover the wounded during the raid carried out on the night of 2–3 April 1918, although he himself was also wounded. He holds the War Cross and was taken prisoner by the Germans at the Battle of the Lys on 9 April 1918.

22. Carlos Elói da Mota Freitas. He was killed in the naval action fought by the minesweeper *Augusto de Castilho* against a German submarine on 15 October 1918. The Government awarded him the War Cross, 1st Class, and the certificate of this decoration was sent by the Secretariat of State for the Navy to the midshipman’s father. At its session of 8 May 1919, the Funchal Municipal Council resolved to give the name of Midshipman Mota e Freitas to the Travessa da Sacristia (Sacristy Lane), in Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’).
23. João Augusto de Sousa, chaplain with the rank of second lieutenant. Honourable mention.
24. Jaime de Gouveia Barreto, chaplain with the rank of second lieutenant. Commended.
25. Eduardo Rodrigues, 2nd sergeant. He was taken prisoner in the battle of 9 April 1918.
26. Pedro da Silva, a volunteer private in the American army, born in Madeira. He died in France in the battle of 12 April 1918.
27. Luís Baptista, a volunteer private in the American army, born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro, in Funchal. He was wounded in action and decorated by the American Government.
28. Henrique José de Sousa, lieutenant of infantry. He was killed in action in East Africa.

29. João de Andrade, corporal and bugle-major, born in Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’). He died on 24 August 1918 in the hospital at Lourenço Marques from wounds received in action. He had been commended in the expedition’s orders of the day of 9 April 1918.
30. Júlio Teodoro Betencourt, lieutenant of infantry. He holds the War Cross, 3rd Class, for distinguished service in West Africa in the campaign against the Germans.
31. Alberto de Sena Mendes, 1st sergeant of the battalion of the 1st machine-gun group. He died in the battle of Naulila, after checking the German advance with the fire of his gun.
32. Álvaro Teles de Azevedo, captain (now major) of infantry. He commanded a machine-gun battery in southern Angola and holds the War Cross and the silver medal for military valour.

33. Manuel da Costa Dias, lieutenant (now major) in the military administration. He served in southern Angola in 1915 and in France from 1917 to 1918. He holds the War Cross and two medals for good service.

34. Bráulio Ludgero de Freitas, lieutenant (now captain) in the military administration. He served in Angola in 1915 and in France from 1917 to 1918. He was commended and holds the silver medal for good service.
35. Dr João Francisco de Sousa. See that entry.

Of the Madeirans killed in action, only Corporal João de Andrade belonged to the 2nd Infantry Regiment (*Infantaria n.º 2*), and a simple plaque in the barracks of the College (*Colégio*) preserves his memory. The plaque was inaugurated on 10 June 1920; it was unveiled by the dead man’s father, and the regiment attended the ceremony at full strength.

Besides making itself felt in Madeira through the grievous consequences that struck the whole world, the Great War also echoed ominously and bloodily in the capital of this archipelago, when German submarines bombarded our harbour on 3 December 1916 and 12 December 1917, as we have already related in the article Bombardment of Funchal. Enemy submarines frequently roamed the waters of this archipelago, and the crews of many steamers and sailing vessels sunk by them sought safety on the shores of these islands. We shall mention some of these vessels, as well as others that were torpedoed or attacked on voyages to Madeira. Our list may well contain significant gaps, above all for the period in which the press was obliged to omit accounts of certain wartime events.

The schooner *Senhora da Conceição* was sunk by a German submarine off the coast of France; she belonged to the Funchal shipping community (*praça*) and was bringing a cargo of sulphur to this island. She had a crew of seven and an apprentice pilot, a native of Madeira, all of whom landed at the port of Gijón in Spain. The torpedoing took place in April 1916.

In July of the same year the Danish steamer *Moskow* left Funchal with a cargo of wine bound for several ports in northern Europe. She was captured and sunk by the Germans, and the insurance company Madeiran Alliance (*Aliança Madeirense*) paid the value of the cargo.
The Italian steamer *Etna* was torpedoed 150 miles from Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and her 44 crew reached that island on 2 April 1917.

On 17 July 1917 the seamen of the Greek steamer *Chalkidom*, which had been sunk by a submarine 80 miles from Madeira, landed in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). She had a crew of 23 and was bound from New York for Marseilles.

The Portuguese barque *Viajante*, bringing general cargo to Madeira, was sunk about 150 miles from the island of Porto Santo. After three days of exhausting travel, her crew reached Funchal on 5 October, leaving for Portugal a few days later.

On 22 October of the same year, fifty crew members, officers included, of the Japanese steamer *Ikoma Maru* landed on the neighbouring island of Porto Santo. The ship had been sailing from Marseilles to Chile to take on a cargo of saltpetre. The *Ikoma Maru* fought the German submarine without success 170 miles from that island and was sunk there. The men were Japanese, except for two gunners and a wireless operator, who were French, and they reached Funchal on 24 October.

The American yacht *Margaret S. Roberts*, which had left New York on 6 October of that year with a cargo of wheat for Madeira, was torpedoed on 15 November between the Azores and this island; her six crew reached Funchal on the 19th of the same month. A German submarine, with two captured Norwegian steamers in tow, came upon the French full-rigged ship *Tijuca* on 22 November 1917, about 240 miles north-east of Madeira, and sank the steamers, the ship and the Portuguese yacht *Trombeta*, which was sailing in the same waters. The crews of the Norwegian ships and of the Portuguese yacht headed for the Azores, while the *Tijuca*’s crew, 36 in number, made for Funchal, where they landed on 27 November.

On the 17th of that month and year the Portuguese lugger *Açoreano* was torpedoed 250 miles from this island. Her crew of 12 landed at Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on the 19th and went on to Funchal the same day.

On 4 June 1917 the Norwegian steamer *Kaggefos* anchored in our harbour, carrying the 23-man crew of the *Sorland*, a steamer of the same nationality that had been sunk by a German submarine off the coast of France while bound from Saint-Nazaire for Baltimore. These seamen landed in Funchal and a few days later left for England.
On 30 January 1918 the small steamer *Neptuno* (formerly the *Maria*), belonging to the Funchal shipping community, was torpedoed. She had left Lisbon the day before, bound for this island.

In the first fortnight of February 1918 the crews of a British, a Greek and an Italian ship, torpedoed in the waters of this archipelago, landed in Funchal. An Italian barque was sunk 250 miles from our shores, between the Azores and Madeira, and the twenty men of her crew reached Funchal on 15 March 1918.

On the 30th of the same month and year the Portuguese schooner *Beira Alta* was sunk 100 miles from Porto Santo; she was bringing 20 tonnes of potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word) from Lisbon to Madeira, besides other cargo.
In the first days of April 1918 the crew of a Portuguese sailing vessel, bound from the Azores for Lisbon, which had been torpedoed by a submarine, landed in Funchal.

The decree authorising the seizure of enemy ships lying in Portuguese ports is dated 24 February 1916. At that time the German steamers *Colmar*, *Petropolis*, *Guahyba* and *Hochfeld* were at anchor in the bay of Funchal. On orders from above, the captain of our port, Sales Henriques, accompanied by the commander of the Revenue Guard (*Guarda Fiscal*, customs and excise corps), Lieutenant Leovegildo Rodrigues, occupied those vessels on 2 March 1916, and their crews, numbering 100, left their ships without delay. According to statements by some of these crew members, the German government had ordered various parts of the machinery to be destroyed and disabled, so that the ships could not sail. The crews carried out these orders, but after suitable repairs the steamers were in good seagoing condition, and all of them sailed for mainland Portugal. The ships were renamed *Madeira*, *Porto Santo*, *Machico* and *Desertas*.

German subjects resident in Madeira were interned in the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’), and from there they were sent on to the island of Terceira. The captain of the steamer *Colmar* escaped from the lazaretto, and various accounts circulated among the public of how this escape was carried out.

On 30 March 1921, shortly after 8 o’clock in the evening, the mortal remains of an unknown soldier were landed at the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’). He had fallen, giving his life for his country, on the distant shores of East Africa in the struggle against the Germans. The urn containing the remains, which had come on the steamer *Briton* of the Union Castle Mail, spent the night at the Maritime Disinfection Station (*Posto de Desinfecção Marítima*). At around 1 p.m. the following day it was taken to the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), where it remained until 3 April, when it was embarked on the cruiser *Republica*, charged with carrying it to Lisbon. Both when the urn was brought to the town hall, where it lay in state, and when it was taken back to the quay for embarkation, splendid and imposing processions were formed. On 1 April these were joined by the civil and military authorities, the consular corps, some British officers, representatives of the various schools and associations, contingents of the military forces of the Funchal garrison, etc. etc. In the article Unknown Soldier we shall endeavour to describe the spectacular demonstrations held in this city from 1 to 3 April 1921 to glorify the humble soldier, whose remains now rest in the majestic Batalha Monastery, built by order of King John I after the heroic battle of Aljubarrota.

For a fuller understanding of what we have said, the article Bombardment of Funchal, on p. 159 of vol. I of this *Elucidário*, should be read. As further information of considerable interest on this subject, we would add that the *Diário da Madeira* of 9 January 1919 contains a detailed account of the first bombardment of Funchal, on 3 December 1916, written by Max Valentiner himself, commander of the submarine U 38; an editor of the *Seculo* made lengthy extracts from it and commented on it judiciously. The *Diário do Governo* of 14 April 1938 published a list of 62 people resident in Funchal who had suffered losses caused by a German submarine and who were recognised as entitled to certain compensation totalling 46,451.04 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis).
Guerra Júnior (Manuel José Júlio)

He was the son of the engineering officer Manuel José Júlio Guerra and was born in Funchal in 1845. Although he did not complete the course in civil engineering, he devoted himself to that field and carried out several works that were well regarded. He wrote the *Diccionario Topographico para uso dos engenheiros civis e seus auxiliares*, of which he published only the first part, in 1872. He was a distinguished amateur photographer and made several improvements in that art. For his work he was deservedly awarded a grade of the Order of St James.
Guillin
He made some geological observations in Funchal, which were published in the appendix to the work of Bory Saint Vincent.
Guincho (shoal)
It lies off the north coast of the Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’).
Guincho (islet)
Not far from the landing place of Pesqueiro (‘fishing spot’), on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), lies a small islet that bears this name.
Guincho (islet)
See Seixal (islets).
Guindaste (point)
This projection of the coast lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Gaula, not far from the small landing place of Porto Novo (‘new harbour’).
Guiomar (Belvedere of Dona)
