The old instructions on how to anchor in the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal) mark the belvedere (*mirante*) of Dona Guiomar, because it was a point easy to pick out and recognise from on board ship. It stands on the *quinta* (country estate) of Angústias (‘sorrows’), which belonged to Count Alexandre Carlos de Lambert (see that entry) and was sold to Dr Júlio Paulo de Freitas by deed of 19 August 1903.

Dona Guiomar, or more precisely Dona Guiomar Madalena Acciaioly, the lady who gave her name to the belvedere of the former Quinta das Angústias, lived at the end of the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th, and had her goods seized for debts to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*). She owned the house on the Largo da Sé, now demolished, which housed the gaol (see that entry), and she possessed other buildings in the city. The Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*) refers to an official letter from the governor Dom José Manuel da Câmara to Dom Rodrigo de Sousa Coutinho concerning the dispatch of bills of exchange from the Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) to the Royal Exchequer, and of jewels, silverware and tapestries belonging to the estate of Dona Guiomar Madalena.
Gulf Stream

This ocean current, which rises in the Gulf of Mexico and reaches as far as the North Cape and Spitsbergen, divides into several branches. One of them, larger than all the others, runs down along the west coast of Africa. After heading E., this branch flows S.S.W. between Madeira and the Canary Islands at a speed of 12 to 16 miles a day.

The Gulf Stream raises the temperature of the sea and is the main cause of the large quantity of water vapour contained in the atmosphere of our archipelago. It is this current that carries the seeds of *Guilandina*, *Mucuna* and *Entada* (sea beans (*favas do mar*, tropical drift seeds) or sea chestnuts) which sometimes appear at Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) and on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
See Sea beans.
Günther (Albert)

Ichthyologist at the British Museum who described several new species of Madeiran fish, among them *Melanocetus Jahnsonii*, a fish of the great ocean depths, which was the subject of a paper to the Zoological Society of London entitled *On a new genus of Pediculate Fish from the sea of Madeira*.
Guiana Epic

About eight years ago there was a great emigration of Madeirans to British Guiana. This extraordinary exodus, which threatened to leave the island depleted, inspired some talented and good-humoured young men to write a mock-heroic poem. Although it was never printed, it was popular in its day and much admired at the time. Its subject was the emigration, and it featured some of the most prominent individuals in Funchal society. The poem was extremely caustic and biting, at times even irreverent and perhaps aggressive. It had, however, not the slightest intention to offend, and was simply the frank and cheerful outpouring of young men enjoying themselves while training their hand at poetry. This highly amusing satire was written by several men who later distinguished themselves in various fields of human endeavour. They were Francisco Clementino de Sousa, Maurício Castelo Branco, Gabriel Franco de Castro, Matias Figueira, João José Vieira and Carlos Acciaioli Ferraz de Noronha.
Several manuscript copies of this satire exist, and it would be worth publishing, even though few people are alive today who were contemporaries of those who appear in the poem.
Early dwellings

Since forest species abounded on this island at the time of its discovery, they supplied the main raw material for building the first dwellings. The earliest dwelling houses were all built of wood taken from that dense woodland, and it may be presumed that many of them used the native cedar and other species best suited to the purpose.

João Gonçalves Zarco had his first home on the heights of Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’), built perhaps of the rich, fragrant cedars that grew in thick forests everywhere. It must without doubt have been a more than modest and uncomfortable dwelling, of a single storey and devoid of all architectural display. Also of wood was the small chapel of St Catherine, which the discoverer’s wife had built beside their home.

Only some years later was the first two-storey house built, and an old manuscript gives the following interesting information on the subject: ‘In this Campo do Duque (see vol. 1, p. 22) was built the first two-storey house in this town of Funchal and in the whole island, and João Manuel had it made of dressed cedar wood. This two-storey house was held at that time to be so novel and wondrous a thing, all the other houses being single-storey and of planking, that articles of complaint (*capítulos*) were brought before the King against the said João Manuel, charging him with building a tower, where it seemed he meant to fortify himself and rise up against Funchal and against the Crown.
The said house still stands today (mid-18th century) and is owned by António de Carvalhal, and it is the lowest two-storey house in Funchal.’

As we see in various places, tradition records that the first stone house built on this island was the one João Gonçalves Zarco raised as his residence beside the chapel of St Paul (see Moradias de Zargo). It is also said that one of the oldest buildings of this kind was the one intended as a hospital, likewise built near the same chapel of St Paul.
Hadfield (William)
Works: *Brazil, the River Plate and the Falkland Island..., including notices of Lisbon, Madeira, etc.*, London, 1854.
Haeckel (Ernst)

German biologist, born in 1834 and died on 10 August 1919. He was in Madeira in 1866, and in his *Natural History of Creation* he deals with the Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) rabbit, regarding it as a species distinct from the European rabbit. On p. 283 of this *Elucidário* we have already had occasion to say that this opinion has not the slightest foundation. We must now add that the doctrines of the learned professor of the University of Jena are discredited among all men of science, Professor Yves Delage going so far as to declare that they are nothing but ‘an execrable hotchpotch, unworthy of the naturalists of our time’.
Hagen (Dr O.)
*Notiz uber eine aufserordentliche Lufttrockenheit in Madeira* (1861, pamphlet of 5 pp.).
Hann
*Klima der Azoren und der Madeira* (*Meteor. Zeitschr.*, 1871).
Harcourt (Eduardo Vernon)
Works:
*A Sketch of Madeira, with maps and views* (London, 1850). This work contains a list of Madeiran birds and various meteorological notes, among them those of W. V. Harcourt.
Hartung (Dr George)
A distinguished German geologist who visited the Madeira archipelago in the winter of 1853 to 1854. Works: *Geologische Beschreibung der Inseln Madeira und Porto Santo*, Leipzig, 1864.

This is the most complete work yet published on the geology of the archipelago. It also includes an account of the Madeiran fossils studied by Professor Carlos Mayer, some of which were previously unknown to science.
Hartwig (W.)

*Die Vogel Madeira's* (*Cab. Journ. f. Ornith*, 1896, pp. 452–485). The Vienna journal *Ornis* contains a note on some species of birds published by Hartwig, and the already cited journal *Cab. Journ. fur Ornith.* for the year 1893 contains an addendum to the list of the birds of the archipelago.
Heberden (Dr Thomas)

He was the brother of the well-known William Heberden and practised medicine in Funchal, where he rendered excellent service during the measles epidemic of 1751. When Joseph Banks and Dr Daniel Solander visited Madeira in 1768, he supplied them with many natural history specimens, as well as a copy of his observations on the island’s flora. The two naturalists named the genus *Heberdenia* after him; Aiton later merged it into the genus *Ardisia*. The meteorological observations made by Dr Herberden in Funchal from 1747 to 1751 were the first carried out on this island, and they were published in vol. X of the *Philosophical Transactions*.

Dr Heberden also made some astronomical studies in Madeira, and a work of his appeared in the *Philosophical Transactions* under the following title: *Observations of immersions and emersions of Jupiter's first Satellite made at Funchal, in Madeira, 1763-1768*. See Diseases and Epidemics.
Heer (Dr Osvaldo)

A Swiss botanist and palaeontologist who stayed in Madeira from the winter of 1850 to the spring of 1851. Works: *Remarques sur la manière de végéter des arbres de l'Europe et des Etats Unis transportés à Madère* (*Bot. Zeitung* 1853); *Ueber die fossilen Pflanzen von St. George in Madeira* (Zurich, 1855); and *Der Renton-Garten in Funchal* (*Gartenflora Deutschlands und der Schweiz*). He died in Lausanne in 1883.
Heineken (Dr Carlos)

An English physician who lived in Funchal for 9 years and died here on 4 January 1830. In an article published in vol. XII (1824) of the *Medical Repository*, and in another piece that appeared in the *Rambles in Madeira*, he recommends the climate of Funchal for the treatment of lung diseases.
During his residence on the island he made many meteorological observations, which are of great value for the knowledge of our climatology.
Henry (Prince), the Navigator

The name of Prince Henry the Navigator is inseparably bound up with the discovery and early colonisation of this archipelago. He was the initiator and promoter of our maritime discoveries, and Madeira is the great, undying commemorative pillar (*padrão*) that truly marks the auspicious beginning of our odyssey as navigators. If a monument ought long ago to have been raised here to João Gonçalves Zarco, to remind Portuguese and foreigners alike of the discoverer’s distinguished personality, the glorious figure of the illustrious prince should not be forgotten either. It was he who opened a new era of prosperity for Portugal, setting in motion the one enterprise that truly made us great in the eyes of the whole world. Madeira owes his memory a worthy tribute, which future generations will know how to pay him in full justice, when the time comes for the future to make good the errors and failings of the past.

We have already referred in another article to the grants of this archipelago made to Prince Henry. It is to be presumed, although the chroniclers do not say so and no known document proves it, that it was John I himself who first granted this island to his son and recognised him as the true lord of the whole archipelago. The later grants that are known (see Grants) would merely have confirmed, in a more solemn and more authentic manner, those already made earlier. They would also be proof that Duarte, without wishing to give up his rights of sovereignty, recognised in his brother the privileges and prerogatives that the monarch, their father and his predecessor, had conferred on the prince.

The proof of the sweeping grant obtained by Prince Henry lies in the donations he made to the discoverers João Gonçalves Zargo and Tristão Vaz Teixeira, in which, referring to this island, he speaks of ‘my island of Madeira’ (*minha ylha da Madeyra*). We are convinced that the king granted this archipelago to the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) chiefly because Prince Henry was Grand Master of that Order, besides other weighty reasons that may have recommended the grant.

It may be said that Prince Henry held the most absolute dominion over this archipelago and exercised true sovereign rights over it. The kings gradually curtailed the privileges that he had granted to the recipients of his donations, and these came almost entirely to an end under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640).

In various places in this work we refer to the part played by Prince Henry in the discovery, early colonisation, administration and development of this archipelago, and for that reason we omit here various facts and circumstances that might be relevant to the subject of this article. Prince Henry was born in 1394 and died in 1460.
Henriques

This family surname derives from Dom João Henriques, third son of Dom Henrique Henriques, who was royal harbinger (aposentador) and Master of the Hunt to Afonso V, John II and Manuel I. There are other Henriques who descend from Henry the German, and the Henriques de Noronha, who descend from Dom João and Dom Diogo Henriques and from Dom João and Dom Garcia de Noronha, all sons of Dom Garcia Henriques of Seville.
Henriques (Dom Francisco)

He was appointed governor-general of Madeira on 20 July 1622 and took office on 28 October of the same year. He was a native of this island and died here while serving as governor, on 27 June 1624; he lies buried in the church of the College (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church). On his death the diocesan bishop, Dom Jerónimo Fernando, took over the duties of governor-general on an interim basis, and he was confirmed in the post by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 3 August 1624.
Henriques de Noronha (Henrique)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) on 1 March 1667, the son of Pedro Bettencourt Henriques and Dona Maria de Meneses, and succeeded to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of his uncle, the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Inácio de Bettencourt e Câmara. He was a highly cultivated mind and devoted himself especially to historical and genealogical studies, in which he had acquired a great wealth of knowledge, and he was regarded as a true authority on matters of Madeiran history. He sent several manuscript works to the Royal Academy of Portuguese History, and was consequently admitted to its membership. Diogo Barbosa Machado in the *Biliotheca Lusitana* and António Caetano de Sousa in the *Historia Genealogica da Casa Real Portuguesa* write approvingly of Henriques de Noronha’s works and refer to him in highly complimentary terms. He is credited with the *Memorias seculares e eclesiásticas para a composição da historia da diocese do Funchal*, mentioned in the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) on page 786, which we have also discussed at some length on pp. 389 and 390 of vol. I of this *Elucidário*. He wrote a *Nobiliário Genealógico* of Madeiran families, a nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) of which a three-volume copy exists in the library of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this municipality (*concelho*), and which is held to be one of the most authoritative writings on the subject (see Nobiliaries).
Henrique Henriques de Noronha died on 26 April 1730. An oil portrait of him exists in the mansion of the Counts of Torre Bela.
Henriques (Dr Júlio Augusto)

He was in Madeira on 25 June 1903, during the scientific voyage he made to the island of São Tomé, and visited Monte (‘hill’) and various parts of the city. Dr Júlio A. Henriques was born in Cabeceiras de Basto on 17 January 1838. He was a professor of botany at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), retired on a pension from his chair, and one of the most distinguished naturalists of our country.
Henriques (Dr Luiz)

Towards the end of the 18th century, a violent storm drove a Norwegian vessel onto the rocks of the coast, near the Pontinha (‘little point’). João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, later Count of Carvalhal, arrived near the scene of the disaster. As he looked on at the sad plight of the poor castaways, his attention was caught by a child of about twelve, the cabin boy of the wrecked ship, whose engaging features, lively expression and intelligent, searching gaze aroused his keen interest and moved him to the tenderest compassion. The wealthy *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) took the child under his protection and, some years later, sent him to England to attend the University of Edinburgh. Having completed his medical studies, with the most brilliant results, he returned to Madeira, where he settled and raised a family, and he died in this city in 1845. He was Dr Luiz Henriques.

We do not know what led him to adopt a genuinely Portuguese name and abandon the one he had borne in his native country. Nevertheless, he was always regarded as a foreigner, and when he sought to hold public office he had to become a naturalised Portuguese citizen, which he did by decree of 22 December 1821.

Dr Luiz Henriques was an eminent physician and a most distinguished surgeon. He is said to have been the first to perform an extremely difficult surgical operation that only began to be carried out in London some time later, and we have been told that the case is described in several medical books written in English. We are also informed that he was the first physician on this island, and perhaps in Portugal, to use the then recent discovery of chloroform in surgical operations. That first operation was attended by our great statesman and diplomat the Count, later Duke, of Palmela, who happened to be in Funchal at the time.

When the Funchal Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica do Funchal*) was founded in 1837, Dr Luiz Henriques was appointed professor (*lente*) there and its first director. He held both posts until 1845, while also serving as chief surgeon of the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal (*Santa Isabel*).
Dr Henriques took his own life in this city on 18 July 1845 by swallowing a large dose of opium, a drug he frequently abused.

His portrait in oils hung in the main hall of the Medical School. It had been presented to the institution by his great-grandson Dr Salvador Brun do Canto (see that entry), who was a member of parliament for this island.
Henriques (Jordão Maurício)

The son of António Maria Henriques, he was born in Funchal on 15 October 1880 and attended the Lyceum (*Liceu*) and the Curso Superior de Letras. He was clerk (*escrivão*) and interpreter of the Health Station and a teacher at the Higher Primary School (*Escola Primária Superior*), and he was also an acting teacher at the Lyceum. He was an editor of the former *Diário Popular* (‘The People’s Daily’) and contributed extensively and valuably to other Madeiran newspapers, his writings being distinguished by their refined literary style.

In 1922 he published a book entitled *Da Pátria e da Escola*. Having taken up a diplomatic career, he served for some years at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and he is at present consul-general of Portugal in the city of Rio de Janeiro.
Henriques (Manuel António de Azevedo)

We know of this Madeiran only from the little that the author of the *Diccionario Bibliographico Portuguez* tells us about him. In Lisbon, in 1778, he published a 47-page pamphlet entitled *Reino de Deus ou Reino de Portugal, Panegyrico Funchalense, oferecido. .. a D. Maria I e D. Pedro III*.
Henriques (Father João Maurício)

He was born in this city on 22 March 1852, the son of António Gomes Henriques and Dona Ana Rosa de Sousa Henriques, and died in Lisbon on 16 December 1901. He studied at the lyceum (state secondary school) and the seminary of Funchal, and was ordained priest in 1877. After serving in church posts as curate of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and parish priest of Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’) and of Santana (‘St Anne’), he was appointed military chaplain by decree of 2 March 1885. He served for some time in the Algarve and in 1887 moved to Funchal, serving in the 12th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) regiment and later in the 27th Infantry. He contributed to several Madeiran newspapers and was an editor of the *Diário de Noticias* of this city. In 1909 he published in Funchal a 104-page pamphlet entitled *Breve Noticia historica e descriptiva do extinto regimento de caçadores n.° 12*.
Henriques (Father Leão)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) in the first quarter of the 16th century, the son of Dom João Henriques and Dona Filipa de Noronha. He was a close relative of Father Luís Gonçalves da Câmara (see that entry), the celebrated tutor of King Sebastian, and was descended from João Gonçalves Zarco, the illustrious discoverer of Madeira. He studied canon law in Paris and Coimbra, and was the first rector of the University of Évora. He joined the Society of Jesus while its founder was still alive, maintaining close ties of friendship with him and receiving from him directly marks of the highest regard and esteem. Within his order he held the most senior posts, such as rector of the colleges of Coimbra and Évora, provincial, delegate in Rome, etc. For many years he was confessor and counsellor to the Cardinal-King Henrique, with whom he enjoyed great prestige and influence. In his day he was widely renowned as a man of vast learning and extraordinary talent. His biographers dwell particularly on the most generous and ardent charity with which he was endowed, showing the poor and unfortunate the most exquisite displays of affection and tenderness of which the human heart is capable. He died in Lisbon on 8 April 1589.
Henriques Pinto (Luís de Miranda)

He was appointed governor-general of this archipelago on 18 November 1635 and took office on 6 June 1636, his term ending on 6 June 1640. He was the last governor-general of Madeira, his successor being styled governor and captain-general.
Henriques Pinto (Luiz de Miranda)

He succeeded his father, Luiz M. Henriques Pinto, and was the first governor of this archipelago to bear the title of governor and captain-general, a title retained until 1834; he was also the last to govern Madeira under Castilian rule. His appointment, made by the vicereine of Portugal Margaret of Savoy, Duchess of Mantua, is dated 22 May 1640, and he took office on 6 June of the same year. It was he who, on 11 January 1641, proclaimed John IV on this island. See Restoration of Portugal.
Henry (Paul)

An officer of the French navy, killed in Beijing on 30 July 1900, when the allied armies entered the city. He was in Madeira in October 1895, aboard the ship *Iphigénie*, and in October 1896 and June 1897 aboard the *Melpomène*.
R. Bazin writes about this officer’s stay in Madeira in his book entitled *L'enseigne de vaisseau Paul Henry*.
Liverworts

These Muscineae are represented in the Madeira archipelago by 76 species, according to Miss Armitage in her work entitled *Some Madeira Hepaticae*. They are small plants that live in damp places, on tree trunks, on the ground, on walls and on rocks, and they appear sometimes with a stem and leaves, sometimes entirely without these organs. Among the Madeiran liverworts we shall mention *Madotheca canariensis*, *M. Thuja*, *Frullania polysticta*, *F. Teneriffae*, *Anthocerus dichotomus*, *Aitonia rupestris*, *Saccogyna viticulosa*, *Plagiochila spinulosa*, *Lunularia cruciata* and *Marchantia polymorpha*. See Armitage, Mitten, Godman and Luisier.
Ivy (Hedera Helix subsp. canariensis)

A plant that climbs by means of short lateral roots. It belongs to the family Araliaceae and is very common in Madeira, where it is used for hedges and to cover walls. Ivy water is used for washing and dyeing black fabrics. The so-called ivy ropes are made not from the fibres but from the slender, flexible branches of the plant. It is with these ropes that the grape pomace is customarily bound in the wine presses.
Hera-terrestre (Sibthorpia peregrina)

A plant of the Scrophulariaceae, subfamily Antirrhinoideae, with stems that root at the nodes; hairy, orbicular-reniform leaves; and small yellow or white corollas with 5 to 8 lobes. It is very common in Madeira, where it is frequently used as an expectorant. In Seixal (‘pebble shore’) this plant is called *herva redonda*. True ground ivy (*Glechoma hederacea*) is a plant of the Labiatae family which is not found in Madeira, not even in cultivation.
Heraldo da Madeira

This daily newspaper began publication on 14 August 1904 and ceased on 14 August 1915, after 3,218 issues. In its early years it ran to eight pages and printed illustrations on Sundays. For some time an English-language edition was also published, intended especially for the passengers of the foreign steamers calling at the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal); this edition appeared irregularly.

Its director was Captain J. Reis Gomes, its editor-in-chief Father Fernando A. Silva, and its editors Lieutenants A. Artur Sarmento and Jaime de Campos Ramalho. It published a considerable number of unpublished writings and valuable documents of great interest to the history of this archipelago.
Herbaria

Madeiran herbaria are not rare in Europe, owing to the large number of botanical expeditions carried out here in the 18th and 19th centuries, chiefly by foreign naturalists. The British Museum and Kew Gardens hold the collections of Richard Thomas Lowe. The first of these institutions also possesses the herbaria of Joseph Banks, Dr Daniel Solander, Francis Masson and Downe, and the second holds the valuable herbarium of our late fellow countryman João Maria Moniz and part of that of Dr Carlos Lemann. Cambridge University has numerous specimens collected in Madeira by the latter naturalist, and Kew Gardens, already mentioned, has many specimens from the collections of the French botanist Gilbert Mandon, who travelled through the archipelago in 1865 and 1866.

It may be supposed that the Madeiran herbarium that belonged to Dr Oswald Heer is in the Zurich Botanical Garden, since many of his botanical collections were deposited there. Forster’s herbarium is presumably at the University of Kiel or in the Natural History Museum in Paris, where, according to Alphonse De Candolle, the botanical collections obtained on James Cook’s second voyage round the world were sent.

The herbaria of Franqueville and Cosson in France, those of Boissier, Candolle and Delessert in Switzerland, and that of the Palatine Museum in Vienna contain many specimens of Madeiran plants collected by Mandon, and the Botanical Museum in Florence holds many of the collections that the English botanist Webb assembled on this island in 1828. The herbaria of M. Gandoger and O. Debeaux in France contain rich collections from this island, donated by one of the authors of this *Elucidário*. At the universities of Coimbra, Lisbon and Porto numerous dried plants from our region can be seen, sent by the same collector, who also sent complete collections of the Madeiran Ranunculaceae, Onagraceae and Cyperaceae to the former International Academy of Botanical Geography of Le Mans, and collections of the native ferns to the same Academy and to Prince Bonaparte, the distinguished French pteridologist.

We do not know what became of the collections of Holl, Lippold, Schacht and Captain Norman. As for those of Bornmüller, Trelease and Dr Vahl, everything suggests that they remain in the hands of those who assembled them. Many of the plants collected in Madeira by Nathaniel Mason are in the Palatine Museum mentioned above, while the collections of the distinguished Portuguese botanist the Baron of Castelo de Paiva were donated by him to the Lisbon Academy of Sciences, and passed from there to the Faculty of Sciences of the same city.

James Yate Johnson assembled a small herbarium of Madeiran plants, which is held in the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*) Museum. Although fairly incomplete, this collection is notable for containing most of the island’s rare species. The last time we saw it (1921) it was well preserved, thanks to the care taken to expose it from time to time to carbon disulphide vapour.

Thanks to the plant-collecting of the young Madeiran botanist José Gonçalves da Costa, a 3rd-year theology student at the Episcopal Seminary of Funchal (*Seminário Episcopal do Funchal*), the herbarium of that seminary is today (1921) one of the richest known in plants of the Madeira archipelago. Mr Costa has collected chiefly in Funchal, Porto Moniz, Achadas da Cruz, Ribeira da Janela and Porto Santo, and his work has yielded material of great value, including some new species and varieties.

We have so far referred to collections of Phanerogams and Vascular Cryptogams. As for collections of Cellular Cryptogams, the most valuable assembled to date are, we believe, those of Kny, Johnson, Mandon, Winter, Miss Armitage, Castelo de Paiva, Bornmüller and Father J. Barreto: the first five of Madeiran mosses and the rest of Madeiran lichens. Some years ago the Revd Father Jaime Barreto made abundant collections of Madeiran fungi, while Dr Liebetruth, Captain Albertis, the Revd Ernst Schmitz and Dr Gain collected the marine algae of the archipelago. Dr Lindman collected the freshwater algae of Madeira, as did one of the authors of this *Elucidário*; his specimens were identified for the most part by the Revds Zimmermann, a Swiss botanist, and Schodduyn, a French botanist.

Besides Johnson’s herbarium, already mentioned, the Funchal Seminary Museum holds the excellent collection of mosses that belonged to the same botanist, the lichen and fungus collections of the Revd Father Jaime Barreto and the marine algae collections of the Revd Father Ernst Schmitz. It also contains a notebook of lichens gathered on this island many years ago by the late Madeiran naturalist João Maria Moniz, as well as other material of lesser value.

The botanical collections in the seminary (*Seminário*) are the only ones that can guide the foreign naturalist visiting Madeira in the study of the native flora, for neither the government nor the administrative bodies have yet thought of creating a regional museum to house the products of the three kingdoms of nature, which are extremely varied and interesting in many parts of the archipelago. See Natural history cabinet and Museums.
Heredia (family)

The Spanish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) Dom Antonio Herédia served in the army that entered Portugal under the command of the Duke of Alba in 1580. In 1602 he came to Madeira as captain of the Company of the Castilian Garrison (*Companhia do Presídio Castelhano*), later becoming commander of that garrison, and afterwards he governed the whole archipelago in the absence of the governor in office. He was the founder of the Herédia family in Madeira, whose last representatives were Francisco Correia Herédia, António Correia Herédia and Francisco Correia Herédia, Viscount of Ribeira Brava (see those entries). Dom Antonio Herédia and his descendants married into the most distinguished Madeiran families. The Heredia family absorbed the important entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Britos, whose principal seat was in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, at the chantry (capela) of Our Lady of the Presentation (*Nossa Senhora da Apresentação*), in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears this name today. Attached to it was a large manor house, one of the biggest residences outside Funchal. House and chapel were demolished long ago.
Heredia (António Correia)

This illustrious Madeiran was born on 2 March 1822 and died in Lisbon on 23 June 1899. He was the son of Francisco Correia Herédia (see that entry) and Dona Ana Margarida de Bettencourt Acciaioly e Sá Escórcio Drumond, and descended from old and noble families of this island. We do not know whether he held any formal academic qualifications, but his lack of higher or university education did not prevent him from being a skilful and talented journalist. He might perhaps have become a distinguished writer, had his many occupations not wholly absorbed the great energy of his mind. The writings he left prove it. He held many public offices: he was president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), representative (*procurador*) on the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), secretary-general (*secretário geral*), civil governor, director of the customs houses (*Alfândegas*) of Funchal, Porto and Lisbon, director-general of customs, deputy, peer of the realm, and president of many commissions for the reform of various public services, etc. In the course of some of these offices he wrote several reports, regulations and bills that amply prove his learning, his competence and his great capacity for work. Besides his journalism, which is extensive, he published: *Breves reflexões sobre a abolição dos morgados na Madeira*, Lisbon, 1849; *As contradições imaculadas*, Funchal, 1850; *A Boa Fé do «Archivista»*, Funchal, 1852; *Observações sobre a situação económica da ilha da Madeira e sobre a reforma das Alfândegas*, Lisbon, 1888, 96 pp.; *Relatório do Projecto do Regulamento Geral das Alfândegas*, Lisbon, 1876, 129 pp.; *Exposição e Documentos enviados à Câmara dos Dignos Pares*, Lisbon, 1886; *António Correia Herédia — Ao Público*, Lisbon, 1885, 235 pp.

António Correia Herédia was secretary-general of this district and also served as civil governor, and he represented Madeira in parliament in the legislative sessions of 1857–1858, 1858–1859 and 1865–1868.

During the provisional government of the Porto Junta in 1847, António Correia Herédia was secretary of the governing board (junta governativa) of Madeira – or rather, he was the soul of that revolutionary movement in this city. See Junta Governativa.
Heredia (Councillor Francisco Correia)

He belonged to the old and noble Herédia family of this island. One of the direct representatives of this family, and administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of several entails, was Dom José de Brito Heredia, whose daughter and sole heiress, Dona Antonia Basilia Heredia de Bettencourt, married in 1801 the well-known and distinguished diplomat and statesman António de Saldanha da Gama, who was granted the title of Count of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). As the Count and Countess of Porto Santo died without issue, the important house passed to their nearest relative, Francisco Correia Herédia, father of António Correia Herédia and grandfather of the Viscount of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’).

Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Francisco Correia Heredia was born on this island on 4 July 1793 and died in Lisbon on 27 July 1880. He was the son of Dom Francisco Moniz de Aragão e Melo de Heredia. The persecution that he and his family suffered at the hands of the Miguelites forced him to emigrate to Brazil. He then went on to France and England, and later joined the liberating army, in whose ranks he served, distinguishing himself by his valour, above all at the siege of Porto.

He was deputy for this district in the legislative session of 1842–1845, and president of the governing board (junta governativa) set up in Madeira at the time of the Maria da Fonte revolutionary movement.
The services he rendered during the cholera epidemic that ravaged this island in 1856 were outstanding and remained memorable.

Here in Madeira he held various public offices, such as president of the Funchal Council, receiver-general (recebedor geral, head of the district revenue office), acting civil governor, president of the Junta Governativa, etc.
*A Religião e Progresso* (‘Religion and Progress’) of 20 August 1880 reprinted a long biographical article on Councillor Herédia published in the *Diário de Noticias* of Lisbon.
Herédia (Francisco Correia)
See Ribeira Brava (Viscount of).
Herédia (Sebastião de)
By decree of 30 December 1914 he was appointed civil governor of Madeira, taking office on 8 January 1915.
He was civil governor of this district for a second time by decree of 24 May 1915, and took up the post on 22 July of the same year.
Heréus
See Levadas (‘irrigation channels’).
Hermenegildo Capelo (street)

The land that now forms the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’), Rua Hermenegildo Capelo and the site of the Teatro Manuel de Arriaga once made up the grounds of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). Despite the opposition of the Franciscan friars, the street was opened there in 1814 and was given the name Rua dos Frades. In 1823 the market built by order of the city Council (*Câmara Municipal*) opened to the public on the site later set aside for the theatre, and the adjoining street became known as Rua do Mercado de São João. In 1885, when the explorers Hermenegildo Capelo and Roberto Ivens called at this island (see those entries), the Municipal Council resolved to give their names to the streets bordering the Jardim Municipal on the south and north.
Herrera (Dom Agostinho)

Lord of Fuerteventura and Count of Lanzarote, he was appointed governor-general of Madeira on 12 November 1582. He came to this archipelago on the special mission of preparing the military defence of the island against the expected invasion by the French fleet which, under the orders of António, Prior of Crato, was attacking Portuguese ships and preparing to assault several ports, as later happened in the archipelago of the Azores. Once the fear of this expected attack had passed, Herrera left Madeira, and João Leitão resumed the post of governor-general (see that entry).
Herva-Branca
See Abrotona and Selvageira.
Lemon balm (Melissa officinalis)
A European plant of the family Labiatae, grown in Madeiran kitchen gardens. It is used as an infusion to induce sweating, and for sluggish digestion and nervous complaints.
Guinea grass
A fodder grass, cultivated and naturalised in Funchal and Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). It has tall culms that are hairy at the nodes, and narrow, loose, elongated racemes gathered into a panicle.
It is a long-established plant in the island, for it was found by Francis Masson in 1776. Its scientific name is *Panicum Maximum*.
Black nightshade (Solanum nigrum)

A member of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) with ovate or rhomboidal leaves, usually sinuate-toothed; white flowers gathered in corymb-like cymes; and berries that turn black when ripe. It grows on rubble, on walls, in cultivated places, etc., in Funchal and its surroundings. The leaves of this plant are used as an anodyne; when they are cut and crushed and olive oil is added, they form the so-called plaster or *unguento das Aires* (folk ointment of nightshade leaves and olive oil), which is very useful in treating wounds and inflammations.
Herva-de-São-João
See Hipericão.
Self-heal (Brunella vulgaris)

A member of the mint family (Labiatae), generally prostrate-ascending, with its verticillasters gathered in a compact terminal spike furnished with large bracts. It is an astringent plant, and its juice is sometimes used in treating sores and inflammations.
Bear’s breech (Acanthus mollis)
A member of the acanthus family (Acanthaceae) from southern Europe, cultivated in Madeira. The large, irregularly lobed leaves of this plant are used in treating wounds.
Herva-Menina (Commelina agraria)
A plant of the family Commelinaceae, common in damp places in the lower zone of Madeira. It is native to South America and has small blue flowers inside a heart-shaped, spathe-like involucre.
Redshank

A member of the knotweed family (Polygonaceae), very abundant in the pools and damp places of Madeira. Its leaves are spotted and its flowers are small, pink and gathered in a cylindrical or elongated spike. The scientific name of this plant is *Polygonum Persicaria*.
Herva-Pombinha
See Molarinha.
Hydrography
See Geodesy.
Hinks (Revd Thomas)
Works: *The Madeiran Polyzoa* (Ann. & Mag. Nat. Hist., ser. 5, Vol. VI).
Hinton

The Hinton family, English by nationality, settled in Madeira more than 90 years ago. In 1838 William Hinton, then a student at the University of Oxford, came to this island for the sake of his health. At that time the British subject Robert Wallas was living in Funchal; he owned a steam-powered flour mill, set up on the same site where the Torreão (‘turret’) Factory (*Fábrica do Torreão*) stands today. In 1839 William Hinton married Mary Wallas, daughter of Roberto Wallas and Mary Wallas. He sold the properties he owned in England and settled permanently in Madeira in 1841. Some years later he founded the Torreão sugar factory. William Hinton, who was the representative of an entailed house (*casa vinculada*) (esquire) at Greenhill House, in the county of Wiltshire, England, was born in Naples in 1817 and died in Funchal on 15 June 1904. He was the father of Harry Hinton, the present owner of the Torreão Factory.

In the article on the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha, on p. 196 of volume I, we set out the origin of the important wickerwork industry. We must add here that it is due chiefly to William Hinton, who had a skilled craftsman from that parish build a piece of furniture using Madeiran osier, taking as his model a chair of English make that this British subject and energetic industrialist had brought from England.

This is a fitting occasion to present a brief profile of the present representative of this distinguished family, whose name is closely linked with Madeira through the great development it has given to the sugar industries, through the many generous acts of benevolence it has performed here, and above all through the devoted support it has given to every charitable institution on this island. To this end we shall reproduce some passages from an article published in a Funchal daily newspaper when Henrique Hinton was honoured by the Portuguese government in just recognition of the services he had rendered to this land.

‘Today we have news for our readers that is, in every respect, particularly pleasing: our well-loved friend Mr Henrique Hinton, who was already, by his high merits, a Commander of the ancient Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), has been proposed for the rank of Grand Officer of the Order of Agricultural and Industrial Merit.

Seldom have we felt such satisfaction as today in making news of this kind public, for we need not strain our conscience and our mind in search of merits, so often fictitious, with which to gild the proposed royal grant. They are there, plain to see before our eyes and in the minds of all who know the agricultural and industrial life of Madeira. Upholding the traditions of his distinguished family, which settled on this island exactly a century ago this year, as one may read in the *Elucidário Madeirense*, and adding lustre to that tradition with constant, intelligent and honest work towards the development and improvement of his great industry, the present head and soul of the Torreão Factory is to receive the new honour conferred on him by the Portuguese Government as a tribute of the clearest and most absolute justice. For some years now Madeiran agriculture, prey to various vicissitudes, has lived chiefly through the mechanism that the factory of the firm William Hinton & Sons represents in our economy.

English in name, the firm has at its head that noble and manly figure of a gentleman, Mr Harry Hinton, born on this island, married here and residing here, who holds for the land of his birth a love and affection shown hour by hour in many expressions of the heart. These range from works of charity, many of them hidden, to a bibliographical and artistic interest in every publication, Portuguese and foreign, old and modern, that concerns Madeira. But this, though very important to our feelings and to our gratitude, is not the aspect we must focus on especially at this moment, when speaking of the high honorific distinction proposed for Mr Harry Hinton’s breast by the Minister of Commerce and Industry.

That aspect is his industrial activity among us. By stimulating and developing sugar-cane growing, it has considerably increased the value of Madeiran land and given farmers a sure return for their produce – which did not and does not happen with any other crop. It has also made it possible to maintain cattle-rearing and the production of the milk from which one of the most reputable, if not the most preferred, brands of Portuguese butter is made. And all this goes hand in hand with the production of one of the finest sugars in the world, and of the alcohol used to fortify our precious wines, under conditions of such rare manufacturing perfection that they have always earned the most honourable awards at the exhibitions in which they have competed.

Mr Hinton owns and equips the most advanced factory of its kind in the world: so say those who know; and with it he is able to develop, for its raw material, a form of agriculture that is the best source of Madeiran wealth.

We may further add that large-scale Madeiran banana growing, as we all know, owes much to the initiative and efforts of this public-spirited industrialist, who in this respect is also a great and intelligent farmer.

The proposed decoration, the Grand Officership of the Order of Agricultural and Industrial Merit, is therefore his with every propriety and every justice. Applying the English expression to the occasion, we may well say that, in this honorific rank, Mr Hinton will truly be “the right man in the right place”.
Hinton (question)

The so-called Hinton question, which has often been stirred up in the press, in parliament, within the administrative bodies, in diplomatic circles, in cabinet meetings and even at public rallies, had its origin in the regime of privilege granted by the governments of mainland Portugal to the industrialist Henrique Hinton, owner of the Torreão Factory (*Fábrica do Torreão*). It gave him the exclusive right to manufacture sugar and alcohol, subject to certain conditions, the chief of which was the obligation to buy the sugar cane grown on the south coast of the island at a price fixed beforehand by law. This regime was granted through various laws and decrees, almost identical in their fundamental provisions, although they differ from one another on some points of secondary importance.

The sugar regime (*regímen sacarino*, the legal regime governing sugar and alcohol production), which was in force in Madeira for nearly a quarter of a century, was a remarkable source of prosperity for this archipelago. The consistently rewarding price of sugar cane led farmers to grow this crop on a large scale. Rural property thus rose considerably in value, and this had a very beneficial effect on the economic life of the district.

The first period of the sugar regime (*regímen sacarino*, the legal regime governing sugar and alcohol production) began with the decree of 30 December 1895, which created the optional registration (*matrícula facultativa*) of sugar and alcohol factories. The decree of 24 September 1903 and its regulations of 24 December 1904 introduced various changes to the regime of 1895. The law of 24 November 1904 strengthened the provisions of the regime then in force, while amending some of them. Less than four years later, parliament enacted a new sugar regime with the law of 9 September 1908. This was replaced by the decree of 11 March 1911, and finally came the decrees of 12 April and 2 May 1919, which put an end to the sugar monopoly. This last enactment contains certain provisions that are generally considered harmful to the interests of the cane growers, but which the decree of 12 April 1920, now in force, has not repealed.

The articles published in the periodical press, the individual pamphlets, the petitions and complaints addressed to the government and the speeches delivered in parliament on the Hinton question would be enough to fill several volumes. In addition, we know of the publication of the following pamphlets: *O alcool do continente na Madeira*, Lisbon, 1908, 10 pp.; *A questão saccharina da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1910, 50 pp. (Dr Quirino de Jesus); *Bases para a solução da questão saccharina e meios de combater o alcoolismo na Madeira*, by Henrique A. Vieira de Castro, Funchal, 1911, 12 pp.; *A nova questão Hinton*, Lisbon, 1915, 65 pp. (Dr Quirino de Jesus); *A Nova Questão Hinton*, Lisbon, 1915, 137 pp.; *A nova questão Hinton*, Lisbon, 1915, 103 pp. (João Soares Branco); *O problema sacarino da Madeira*, by Pestana Júnior, Funchal, 51 pp.; *Os Direitos de W.m Hinton & Son* by Quirino de Jesus and *a Questão Sacarina*, by Julio do Amaral, 1918, 22 pp.
St John’s wort

This name is given to *Hypericum perforatum* and *H. humifusum*, perennial plants of the family Hypericaceae, with yellow flowers and small translucent dots on the leaves. The first of these species, which is also called *herva-de-São João* and *malfurada*, has firm, often erect stems and narrow leaves, linear-oblong or elliptical and distinctly pointed. The second has thread-like, prostrate stems and small leaves, ovate or oblong and more or less blunt. Both species are common in Madeira, and an infusion of their leaves is recommended for diseases of the kidneys and bladder. *Hypericum androsaemum* does not occur in Madeira.
Hypersthenite

Johnson records this rock, which belongs to the diabase group, at Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), but his discovery does not appear to have been confirmed by the observations of the modern geologists who have visited the locality. In Gagel’s view, essexite and madeirite occur there, rocks which probably correspond to Johnson’s hypersthenite. See Geology.
Hissopo (Satureja thymoides)

A small woody labiate with sessile or almost sessile leaves, which look linear because their margins are rolled, and small purplish corollas whose tube is enclosed, or almost enclosed, in the calyx. It is very common across almost the whole archipelago, where it is used as an expectorant. The hyssop of the pharmacies (*Hyssopus officinalis*) is not found in Madeira, not even in cultivation.
Island History

The full title of this work is ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana das Ilhas a Portugal sugeitas no Oceano Occidental*). Its author was Father António Cordeiro (see that entry), and it appeared in two editions, in 1717 and 1866. Until 1873 it was a very well-known work, highly regarded by everyone interested in the history of the Madeiran archipelago. With the publication that year of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and the extremely valuable notes that accompany them, however, Father Cordeiro’s work came to be of very secondary value, chiefly because it is a summary, not always free of defects, of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso’s extensive manuscript. Apart from the few pages that some chroniclers had devoted to the history of Madeira, nothing else in print was known on the subject, and for that reason the appearance of Father António Cordeiro’s book aroused genuine interest. As Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo points out in the preface to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, the ‘Island History’ neither replaces Frutuoso’s work nor surpasses it in any respect, because Cordeiro’s work is a summary of the *Saudades* and goes no further than 1590, the year in which they were written, even though the ‘Island History’ was published in 1717. While Book II of the *Saudades* fills 300 printed pages, Book III of the ‘Island History’, which deals with Madeira, runs to no more than 44 pages of text in the second edition of this work.

The ‘Island History’ consists of nine books. The first deals with the various peoples who occupied ancient Lusitania, the second with the Canary Islands and Cape Verde, the third with Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and Madeira, and the remaining six with the islands of the Azores, to which Cordeiro devotes the greater part of his work. The ‘Island History’ had long been out of print and was already quite rare when a second edition appeared in 1866. It was identical to the first in every respect except for an addendum entitled *Algumas notas e adições á História Insulana do padre Antonio Cordeiro na parte relativa á ilha da Madeira*, by A. J. G. A. In a brief introduction the annotator, referring to the vast work of Gaspar Frutuoso, says, if somewhat exaggeratedly: ‘this work contained materials gathered without critical judgement, heaps of genealogies, in which its author was strong, set down without order, which called for a man of another calibre, capable of writing a continuous history, free of the many defects that Gaspar Frutuoso himself would perhaps have avoided had he been granted more years of life. Such a man Father Cordeiro was not! He did not undertake this task, nor did he seek to verify the facts related by his predecessor; rather, content to compile them, as Justin had done with the history of Trogus Pompeius, he fell into the same faults as his original, and the ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*) is still far from perfect’.

In the second volume of the third edition of his *Historia de Portugal*, Pinheiro Chagas wrongly attributes these notes to the writer Guião. It is beyond doubt, however, that they are the work of the distinguished Madeiran António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade (see that entry), dean of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), who was living in Lisbon when the second edition of the ‘The Island Epic’ was published. These notes, which fill only thirty pages of text, are very interesting and valuable, and show the author’s profound knowledge of the history of this archipelago.
Island History (commission)

By a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 17 March 1911, a commission of distinguished men of letters was appointed, some of whom had made their names through their writings on the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes). Its special task was to collect and publish, in a series entitled *Arquivo Insular*, all the documents that might be of interest to the history of the archipelagos of Madeira and the Azores. The commission set to work without delay and met several times, taking various decisions on the important work to be done. Foremost among these tasks were the publication of old manuscripts and unpublished documents and the reissue of rare and hard-to-obtain works, which would have rendered a notable service to Portuguese culture, and particularly to those who devoted themselves to the study of our early discoveries and the first ventures of our overseas colonisation. For reasons unknown to us, the commission was short-lived and produced no work worthy of esteem, despite its official character and the competence that distinguished every one of its members.
Madeiran history

A great deal of scattered material exists for the history of this archipelago, gathered by a few patient researchers, but the architect and builder of the edifice has yet to appear. A conscientious study of Madeira, one that does not confine itself to a tedious list of names and dates, remains entirely to be done. We mean a modern work of historical criticism, in which the ideas of the time, the customs, the individuals, the setting in which events unfolded, etc., are presented in a brilliant and evocative synthesis, giving us, in one swift overview, a complete vision of the whole of Madeiran life over the long span of five centuries. In that panoramic picture, several things would stand out in sharp relief: the early colonisation, which soon took the form of the old *sesmarias* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and later turned into the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant); the relations between the landlords, who had become holders of entails, and the serfs bound to the soil who broke the ground; the despotic and almost arbitrary conduct of the donataries; the influence exerted in this society by settlers from the mainland and by countless foreigners; the expeditions to Africa; the early emigrations to Brazil; the sources of wealth brought by the making of sugar and wine, and the export trade that went with them; and the changes that all these and still other factors must have produced in local customs, etc., etc.

All this laborious study still awaits a powerful intellect and a conscientious researcher who, with a remarkable gift for generalisation, will carry out this longed-for work, drawing on the fragmentary and scattered material to be found in various places. The learned and valuable notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) are indisputable proof that their talented and most erudite author had ample breadth and a sure sense of direction for so great an undertaking. However, his modest aim of acting simply as annotator of the work of Gaspar Frutuoso did not allow him to leave us the work that he could have produced without effort, and perhaps even with great pleasure to his mind. There are points of our history that Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo treats with the necessary fullness and with all the rigour of historical criticism. Others he left only in outline, without the commentary the subject demanded, because they lay outside the plan he had drawn up and would have forced him to give the notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ an excessive scope. In spite of everything, it is above all in this valuable and abundant storehouse of news and information, of appraisals and criticism, of observations and philosophical reflections, that the future author of the history of Madeira will find his richest treasure when he sets out to prepare and write his work.

Some twelve years after the notes were printed, Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo published a substantial article on Madeira in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*. It is a most interesting monograph on this archipelago and deals, albeit in summary form, with every subject that might bear on the various spheres of its activity from the earliest days of the discovery onwards. In it he masterfully traces a remarkable sketch of Madeiran history, which he divides into four periods and prefaces with the following words:

‘And this is no easy undertaking, above all in the part concerning the crisis from the discovery to the final consolidation of this archipelago with mainland Portugal. It was a hidden crisis, not investigated even to this day, which surely later had repercussions in the archipelago of the Azores and, to a greater or lesser degree, throughout our overseas territories. Its effects might perhaps have been utterly fatal to Portugal’s colonial power had the monarchical element not averted it, as it gallantly knew how to do and succeeded in doing. It was aided in this by the jurist magistrates and supported by the bourgeois municipal element in the struggle that it waged, from the mainland all the way to the island, against the aristocratic element strongly entrenched on the island of Madeira – an element that was perhaps, at the outset, the unwitting instrument of a personal design. But even apart from this delicate part, Madeiran history is of interest both for its local autonomy and for its relations with the mainland and with the other Portuguese colonies, especially those of West Africa and America. For the island of Madeira, and on it the town, later city, of Funchal, were for a time the centre of the once most important ecclesiastical government and the principal hub of all Portuguese shipping and trade in the Atlantic. The island first stood out in the export of timber for building, then in the cultivation, manufacture and trade of sugar, next in that of its excellent wines, and lastly in both these products, besides others of lesser importance. Finally it became a health resort, owing to its beautiful and celebrated climate and picturesque scenery, for which it is beloved by all the foreigners who visit it, above all the English. They twice occupied it militarily in the first quarter of the present century [TN: the 19th century, when Azevedo wrote.] and gave up possession of it only reluctantly, and many of them still make it their favourite residence, especially in the winter season. As a result of the particular circumstances indicated above, anyone who wishes to study the institutions and history of overseas Portugal must of necessity investigate them largely in the archives and history of Madeira, the land where Columbus stayed and where he perhaps received the first rays of light that revealed to him the existence of the New World. This history is therefore undoubtedly useful and curious. Let us add to the very brief synthesis set out above some of the more important or more characteristic features of the picture.’

The four periods into which Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo divides his sketch of the history of the archipelago run as follows: the 1st from the discovery to the death of John I in 1433; the 2nd from that year to the liberation from the Spanish yoke in 1640; the 3rd extends to the establishment of constitutional government in 1834; and the 4th runs from that year to the present day. In the article Bibliography we said that in the article Sources for Madeiran History we would give a short survey of the works offering the richest store of news and information on the history of this archipelago. In that article we dealt at some length with the public archives and other manuscript sources, but through a mere oversight we did not include a brief list of printed works, which we shall now do in this place. As we have said more than once, and as everyone generally knows, the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, and above all its valuable and abundant notes, are the richest, fullest and most reliable repository of material we possess for the history of our archipelago. We shall deal with that monumental work at the appropriate point in this *Elucidário*. Next in importance and value come the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) and the Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*), to which we have already devoted separate articles in this *Elucidário*. Of more secondary importance, but still offering valuable information and news, we may mention the *Epocha Administrativa* (3 vols, 1849, 1850, 1852) and the other pamphlets by Sérvulo de Meneses on the model administration of Governor Silvestre Ribeiro; *Breve Noticia sobre a Ilha da Madeira*, by Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara (1841); *Catalogo dos Bispos da Igreja do Funchal*, by Dom António Caetano de Sousa (1721), in the *Colecção dos Documentos e Memórias da Academia Real de Historia Portugueza*, vol. 1; *As Dezertas* and *As Selvagens*, by A. Artur Sarmento (1903 and 1906); *Os Portos Marítimos de Portugal e Ilhas Adjacentes*, by Adolfo Loureiro (1910, vol. V); various pamphlets on the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant) (see the bibliography of the article *Colonia* contract); *Documentos para a Historia das cortes geraes da nação portugueza*, by the Baron of São Clemente (1888, vol. V); *Constituições Sinodais do Bispado do Funchal* (see the article Constitutions of the Bishopric); various works on the discovery of this archipelago, cited on pp. 330, 349, 350 and 906 of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, to which we must add *Memória sobre a descoberta das ilhas do Porto Santo e Madeira*, by E. A. Betencourt (1875), *Quando foi descoberta a Madeira?*, by Jordão de Freitas (1911), and *O Reconhecimento do Arquipelago da Madeira*, by Manuel Gregório Pestana Júnior (1920); some pamphlets on the entailed estates of Madeira and their abolition (see the article Entails); various leaflets on the proclamation of the Constitution of 1821 in this archipelago (see the article Constitution of 1821); three pamphlets on Madeiran chorography (see the article Chorography); *Statistica Historico-Geografica das ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo*, by Joaquim Pedro Cardoso Casado Giraldes (Paris, 1815); *A Ilha da Madeira* (‘The Island of Madeira’), by Acúrsio Garcia Ramos (2 vols, 1879 and 1880); some leaflets on the Protestant proselytism of Dr Robert Kalley (see the article Kalley); and the precious collection of Madeiran newspapers belonging to the company of the *Diário de Notícias* of Funchal, which is the subject of the pamphlet *Resenha Chronologica do Jornalismo Madeirense* (1908). The article Madeira in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, which devotes several pages to Madeiran bibliography, the article Bibliography in this *Elucidário*, and the whole course of this work mention many bibliographical items of interest for the history of our archipelago.

May we be permitted the satisfaction – not vanity – of saying here that, over the long course of this work, we too have gathered some valuable material for the history of our archipelago. That satisfaction is all the greater because we can affirm, without fear of contradiction, that we did so with complete disinterest, placing at the service of this modest undertaking several years of persevering and conscientious research and enquiry in public and private archives, and in many dozens of printed and manuscript works, both Portuguese and foreign. It seems to us that we have sufficiently clarified various points of Madeiran history and contributed many indispensable materials for those who, after us, attempt to write that history, or at least carry on this worthless but painstaking work of ours.

*Sketch of the Island of Madeira, with a coloured view of the Island*. London, 1819, 1 vol.
