*of Madeira, with a series of twenty seven coloured engravings illustrative of the costums, manners and occupations of the Inhabitants of that Island*. London, 1821. The work is by William Combe (1741–1823).
Hochstetter (Dr Ferd. von)

An Austrian geologist who visited Madeira in July 1857 as a member of the scientific expedition led by Commodore Bernhard von Wüllerstorf-Urbair, commander of the frigate *Novara*. He measured the height of Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) and wrote a pamphlet entitled *Madeira* (Vienna, 1861).
Holl (Frederico)
A German botanist who stayed in Madeira from June to August 1827. Works: *Verzeichniss der auf der Insel Madeira beobachteten Pflanzen* (*Flora oder Bot. Zeitung*, 1830).
Holothurian
A genus of holothurian echinoderms comprising a large number of species. *Holothuria tubulosa*, with its elongated, soft body, is common near the coast in Madeira. See Echinoderms.
Homem

This family surname derives from: Garcia Homem de Sousa, who married Catarina Gonçalves da Câmara, daughter of Zargo; Francisco Homem de Gouveia, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of the household of Manuel I, who lived in Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’), where he founded an entail (*morgado*) in 1529; Francisco Homem d’El-Rei, who lived in Calheta (‘small cove’) at the beginning of the 16th century; and Rui Fernandes Homem, natural son of Fernão Homem and nephew of the aforementioned Garcia Homem de Sousa.
Homem em Pé
A column of lava about 12 metres high, standing isolated near Cumeada Alta (‘high ridge’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana. See Geology.
Homage of Reparation to the Redeemer of the World
Single issue of a newspaper published on 26 October 1913 by the Catholic Youth of Funchal (*Juventude Católica do Funchal*), in large format and 24 pages long.
Hooker (William)

His work entitled *Niger-Flora* contains a list of Madeiran plants compiled by him, followed by another by Dr C. Lemann, also dealing with plants of this island. Volume VI (1847) of the *Journal of Botany* published an article by W. Hooker entitled *Notes on Madeira Plants*.
Official time

It was established by Decree no. 2,922 of 30 December 1916. On 31 January of the following year the military authorities asked the Council to put the clock of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) forward by one hour at 11 p.m. The request was granted, but the president, Dr Fernando Tolentino da Costa, declared that he saw no benefit whatever in the measure for Madeira.
Hortas (street)

It is now (1921) called Rua do Alferes Veiga Pestana, following a resolution passed by the Council on 10 April 1919. It links Rua do Carmo (‘Carmel’) with the avenues of Pedro José de Ornelas and Elias Garcia, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’).
Second Lieutenant João Paulo da Veiga Pestana died in France, in the battle of 9 April 1918.
Mint

The common name of *Mentha viridis* and *M. silvestris*, plants of the family Labiatae, the first of which appears to be native. Leaves of *M. viridis* steeped in milk give it a distinctive flavour. Both species are grown in Madeiran vegetable gardens, although *M. silvestres* is much less common than *M. virídis*.
Hortelã de burro (Cedronella triphylla)

A labiate subshrub with a strong, unpleasant smell; leaves with 3 lanceolate, crenate segments; corollas large, violet, veined and dilated at the throat. It is common at Monte, Ribeiro Frio, Camacha, Jardim da Serra, etc.
Peppermint (Mentha aquatica-viridis f. piperita)

A highly aromatic labiate with a peppery taste, glabrous or almost glabrous, with lanceolate or oblong-lanceolate, serrate leaves. It is widely grown in vegetable gardens, and an infusion of its leaves is useful for intestinal pains, colic and spasmodic coughs. The essential oil of peppermint is highly caustic.
Princess Maria Amélia Hospice

In the article devoted to the Empress Amélie of Leuchtenberg (see that entry) we have already said that the widow of Pedro IV, accompanying her daughter Princess Maria Amélia, arrived in Madeira on 28 August 1852, and that the princess died in this city on 4 February of the following year. Two months later, on 6 May 1853, the empress left the island, accompanying the mortal remains of the lamented and ill-fated princess.

Before leaving Madeira, however, she addressed a letter to Queen Maria II on 13 April 1853, which contains the following passage: ‘Wishing to leave on this island, for the benefit of the destitute afflicted by the cruel disease to which Princess Maria Amélia, My Most Beloved and Lamented Daughter, succumbed, some trace of Our Stay in Madeira that will recall the tokens of esteem that We Both received from its good inhabitants, I conceived the idea of establishing in Funchal, for the present solely by way of trial, and later, as experience may show me, in the form of a pious foundation, a hospice or house of charity, where twenty-four poor persons suffering from pulmonary consumption may be received and treated, under the direction of a committee.’ The Queen of Portugal replied with another letter, from which the following words are taken: ‘The attempt at a foundation which expresses in a manner so worthy of Your Imperial Majesty the enlightened virtue that inspires it could not fail to arouse my sympathy and merit my full approval, and I am pleased to assure Your Imperial Majesty that I shall endeavour to lend you all the cooperation and assistance that depends on me for the realisation of Your Imperial Majesty’s generous purpose.’

Wishing to carry out her most noble idea without delay, the empress had a building in the Rua do Castanheiro rented from the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António Caetano Moniz de Aragão, and ordered that the hospice (*hospício*) be installed there provisionally; it opened on 10 July 1853. Before leaving Madeira, the illustrious foundress visited all the premises and outbuildings of the new hospital, and on that occasion gave it the regulations and instructions needed for its proper running. The distinguished Madeiran and eminent physician Dr António da Luz Pita was appointed its medical director, and she entrusted the administration of the establishment to a committee made up of Canon Dr António Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, Dom Jorge da Câmara Leme, José Phelps, Joaquim Pedro de Castelbranco and Jacinto de Freitas Lomelino. As Canon Andrade accompanied the empress as her chaplain, and Dom Jorge da Câmara Leme asked to be excused from the committee, António Gonçalves de Almeida and Diogo Guilherme Selby were nominated to replace them.

In the founding of the new hospital the most outstanding services were rendered by Canon Gonçalves de Andrade and Dr Luz Pita. The latter, later the establishment’s physician, devoted to it the most fruitful activity and unsurpassed zeal, of which the report he wrote on the hospice’s activity and on the clinical observations he made in its first year is eloquent proof. Particular mention must also be made here of the devoted service of the first matron, Dona Amália Cândida Teixeira, above all during the calamitous period when cholera morbus raged severely in this city. For this the empress presented her with a magnificent gold watch, as a memento of the excessive labour she had expended during the terrible epidemic. It was this exhausting work that gravely sapped her strength, and she died in the hospice on 23 January 1867.

The empress wished to perpetuate the memory of her beloved daughter on this island in a more lasting way, and at the same time to give more effective expression to the charity she felt towards the plight of the unfortunates stricken by terrible pulmonary consumption. At once the idea took shape in her mind of building a suitable edifice which, by its situation, its size, the pleasantness of the site and every requirement of comfort, could fully serve the purpose she had in view. The idea grew and within a short time became a happy and eloquent reality.

The law (*carta de lei*) of 19 July 1853 authorised the foundation of the Hospice with the powers and privileges set out in it. It could acquire property without any licence or grant, have an administration subordinate only to the foundress or her heirs, and not be dependent on or supervised by any official department or body. Dr António da Luz Pita, as representative (*procurador*) and agent of the empress, bought the land, water rights and improvements (*benfeitorias*, buildings and walls made by the tenant, which remained his property) intended for the building of the new hospital.

On 4 February 1856 the cornerstone, or first stone, of the grand building was laid. The ceremony, presided over by the diocesan prelate, Dom Manuel Martins Manso, was one of imposing solemnity, attended by all the most distinguished people of Funchal and a great crowd of ordinary people. The building site and the adjoining land had been prepared beforehand, and important works had already been carried out there for their intended purpose. The designs and plans of the building were drawn up by the English architect E. B. Lamb, with notable modifications proposed by the distinguished Madeiran engineer and architect João de Figueiroa de Freitas e Albuquerque, under whose direction the whole work was built and to which he rendered the most valuable services.

Owing to insurmountable difficulties, the construction did not proceed as swiftly as the august foundress wished, and it was declared complete only six years after it began. We would have to go far if we wished to give a detailed description of the sumptuous building and its many outbuildings and rooms. We find in it no great architectural refinements, nor the strict features of a well-defined style, and it does not have the proportions of a vast and grand palace. It is nevertheless an elegant building, full of stateliness and majesty, though severe in line. Much of this is due to the black basalt of its doors, windows, quoins, cornices and ornaments, which stand out against the pure whiteness of the walls. It is what anywhere could be called a large and handsome building, in no way unworthy of the social standing of its illustrious and virtuous foundress.

Among the rooms of the Hospice the chapel stands out: small but most elegant, with sober yet exquisite ornament. Above the altar is a lovely image of Our Lady of Sorrows (*Nossa Senhora das Dores*), the gift of the ill-fated Prince Ferdinand Maximilian, later Emperor of Mexico.

It would be an interesting detail to know the cost of buying the land, constructing the building, and the various installations and furniture, but we do not know whether reliable data on the matter exist, or whether the empress deliberately concealed how far the generosity of her heart extended.

The illustrious foundress entrusted the running of the Hospice and the care of the patients to the religious institute of the Sisters of Charity, founded by St Vincent de Paul and based in the city of Paris. The chaplain of the establishment was to be a priest of the Congregation of the Mission, also founded by that model of Christian charity. The first chaplain, Carlos Francisco Bertrand by name, and the first Sisters of Charity arrived in Madeira at the beginning of 1862. On 4 February of that year, nine years after the princess’s death, the first patients, twelve in number, were admitted, and the new hospital began its work.

At the far end of the spacious entrance hall, between the two flights of the staircase, is a black marble tablet bearing the following inscription, which sums up the history of that house of charity: ‘Hospice of Princess Dona Maria Amélia, daughter of Dom Pedro I, Emperor of Brazil and King of Portugal, 4th of the same name, and Duke of Braganza, and of Dona Amélia, Empress of Brazil and Duchess of Braganza. She arrived on this island on 20 August 1852. She died on 4 February 1853, aged 21 years, 2 months and three days. In memory of so beloved and lamented a daughter, her grieving mother raised this building for the treatment of poor sufferers from diseases of the chest. The first stone was laid on 4 February 1856 and the work was completed in the year 1859. The first patients were admitted on 4 February 1862.’

The Hospice remained open for only a few months, closing its doors around the middle of July 1862. The Sisters of Charity had been ordered by the Portuguese government to leave our country, and on 9 June of that year they sailed for France aboard the French naval frigate *Arenoque*, which had come to the Tagus expressly to collect them. An exception had been made for Madeira, but M. Etienne, superior general of the congregation, ordered the Sisters of Charity to give up the running of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*) and return to their own country without delay; they left Funchal on 2 August 1862. The Empress then ordered that the house she had founded be closed provisionally, pending a further decision.

Only nine years later, in November 1871, did the Hospice reopen its doors and admit its first patients for the second time. The Sisters of Charity returned and took charge of the administration and nursing services, as they had done before.

A little over a year after the reopening, on 26 January 1873, the Empress Dona Amélia died: the illustrious and generous founder of that model hospital, to whose cherished and saintly memory the poor of our land owe so much. She never visited her great work, which she had so longed to see at first hand, nor had she secured its future existence definitively. She left to her sister Josephine of Leuchtenberg, Queen of Sweden, the task of placing on firm foundations the perpetuity of the monument she had dedicated to the memory of her daughter, Princess Dona Maria Amélia.

The Empress’s will contains the following words: ‘Knowing my sister Josephine’s affection for me, and our hearts having always understood each other, I earnestly commend to her the permanent foundation of the small hospital for sufferers from diseases of the chest, “Hospicio da Princesa D. Maria Amelia”, which I had built in Funchal, on the island of Madeira, to perpetuate there the memory of my beloved daughter, so that, should I die before the said foundation is completed, everything may be done according to my intentions. Baroness Carolina de Stengel, my lady-in-waiting, Mr Primislao Sperling, my secretary, and the good and most devoted Doctor Barral can give my sister all the information she may wish on this matter; they know my plans for the endowment and administration of the said hospital, and Dr Barral, through his special knowledge, will be of very good counsel.’

Queen Josephine then became the devoted protector of the work her sister had founded, and it was she who truly secured its future, adding to its funds and giving it a sounder organisation. On 5 June 1876, a few days before her death, she laid down in a testamentary disposition how the work was to be made stable, and ordered that a public instrument should give the Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amelia the official and definitive character of a perpetual foundation. Her son, King Oscar II of Sweden, carried out the queen’s wishes in 1877, when several documents were drawn up that secured the Hospice’s existence and regulated how it was to operate. M. Primislao Sperling, former secretary to the Empress Dona Amélia, contributed greatly to this through his intelligent and effective cooperation.

The way in which the direction and administration of the Hospice was organised is interesting and ingenious. In 1877 King Oscar appointed a council of three members, each of whom in turn appointed a deputy. If a full member is absent or dies, his deputy is called upon and at once appoints his own substitute. If all are lacking, Queen Josephine’s representative appoints one member of the council and the Mother Superior of the Sisters of Charity another, and the two appoint the third. Full members of the board of administration have included the Viscount of Aljezuar, who was chamberlain to the Empress, Father Emilio Eugenio Miel, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Augusto Maria Quintela Emauz, Bernardino de Barros Gomes, José Franco de Sousa, Dr Luís Filipe de Abreu, Vitor Boulard, the Marquis of Pombal, the Count of Oeiras, José Quintela, Desiré Caulet, Alfredo Fragues, Dr Lino Neto and others. The council has its seat in Lisbon, and each year it must send to Queen Josephine’s representative, the King of Portugal, the Emperor of Brazil and the Mother Superior of the congregation of the Sisters of Charity a report on its administration and on the financial state of the establishment; many of these reports have been printed. Its funds were constituted in 1877 by one million francs in French government bonds, which were later, on King Oscar’s advice, converted into shares of a Swedish railway company. These funds have grown steadily, if slowly, because rising expenditure does not allow the growth to be large. At the end of 1914 they had reached the value of 261,055.98 escudos. The members of the board of administration have always shown the greatest zeal and disinterestedness in managing the affairs of this establishment, and so they deserve the gratitude of the Madeirans, whom alone this hospital concerns and benefits.

By a contract concluded in Paris on 20 May 1877 between the board of administration and the Mother Superior of the Sisters of Charity, in accordance with the wishes of the founder and of Queen Josephine, the Sisters were entrusted with the running of the Hospice as regards internal administration, nursing, etc., and they report to the same council on how they manage these services.

The hospital’s religious services were entrusted to the priests of the Congregation of the Mission, and at least one clergyman lives there permanently to serve as chaplain. Since the foundation the post has been held by Fathers Carlos Francisco Bertrand, in 1862; Francisco Fougeray, 1862; João Baptista Pémartin, 1871; Ernst Schmitz, 1874; Alberto Docet, 1875; Jorge Luiz Monteiro, 1875; Ernst Schmitz, 1878; Pedro Varet, 1881; Leão Xavier Prévot, 1892; Pedro Pinto Leitão, 1895; José Maria Garcia, 1897; Vitor Maria Boulard, 1898; Fernando Aliot, 1900; Sebastião Mendes, 1908; José Maria Garcia, 1909; and Henrique Jansen, 1920.

The direction of the Hospice’s various clinical services has almost always been entrusted to a single physician, although for a short time they were in the charge of two, one serving as principal physician and the other as his assistant. The distinguished physician António da Luz Pita was the first to perform clinical duties there. He was followed, briefly, by Dr Pedro Júlio Vieira, and then by Dr César Augusto Mourão Pita, over a long period of several decades. On the latter’s death in 1907, Dr João Francisco de Almada was appointed, and he is the present physician. Besides the report by Dr Luz Pita, we understand that Dr Mourão Pita printed some reports on the hospital’s clinical services, but we have no knowledge of them. Every year the physician in office sends the board of administration a detailed report on the hospital’s activity and the clinical service carried out there.

Few illustrious and distinguished persons have passed through Madeira without visiting that house of charity. Its visitors’ books are full of the names of people from every social rank, from kings and princes, scholars and men eminent in science and letters, to obscure sailors from ships that had put in at Funchal. King Carlos I and Queen Amélie, King Oscar of Sweden and various princes and princesses signed their names there. Among the men of science, Dr Sigismond Jaccoud stands out, a great medical authority and specialist in pulmonary diseases, who in a few brief lines paid that establishment the loftiest tribute.

In the visitors’ room hang two magnificent canvases, depicting the Empress Dona Amélia and her daughter, Princess Dona Maria Amélia. When King Oscar visited the building, he noticed that the portrait of Queen Josefina, his mother, was missing, and later had it placed there, which was simply an act of complete justice.

The number of patients at present in the hospice is twenty-four. The board of administration intends to increase this number, but has been prevented by the dreadful crisis brought about by the war. (1921).

The Empress conceived the idea, which she set down in one of her dispositions, of creating near the Hospice an orphanage with attached schools for poor children. The Mother Superior of the house, Madame Rolland, was able in May 1878, after first building premises that were later enlarged, to carry out the foundress’s noble intention, taking in twelve children at the outset. That number grew considerably, reaching many dozens. However, the political events in our country brought about the almost complete disappearance of this work, one of the most remarkable and most beneficial that the spirit of charity has inspired among us. The orphanage in no way affected the Hospice’s finances, since it was maintained entirely by the generosity of many people, Portuguese and foreign, who saw in it a true instrument of social regeneration and a safe refuge for so many unfortunate children whom orphanhood had cast into poverty, and many of them on to the road to perdition.

The excessive length already given to this article obliges us to leave out other circumstances and details that might perhaps be of use to the history of this truly model establishment, which our land has the glory of possessing.
St Lazarus’s Hospital

We do not know the year in which this hospital was established, but everything suggests that its foundation dates back to the end of the 15th century. On 25 July 1512 permission was given for the ‘house of the leper hospital to move to Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’) and Santa Catarina to it. . . . , safeguarding what pertains to the charges of the said house of Santa Catarina’. It seems, however, that St Lazarus’s Hospital (*Hospital de São Lázaro*) remained where it had been established, since there was no further mention of its transfer.

In 1515 the Council of Funchal resolved ‘that all who are sick with the disease of St Lazarus shall go to the house of São Lázaro...... & that the officers shall go through the streets & all whom they find to be sick with the said disease they shall at once make go to São Lázaro or leave the city’. The same Council further resolved that those who served the lepers should carry small wooden tablets so that they could be recognised, and that lepers found in the city after they had been assigned a place should be publicly flogged.

At first the lepers received 30 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a day for their food. On 26 January 1641, however, they began to receive an allowance of 40 *réis* paid by the Council, which was raised to 80 *réis* in the 18th century and to 100 *réis* on 4 September 1801.

On 24 April 1835 the Council resolved to supply the patients of St Lazarus’s Hospital with food directly, and the councillor (*vereador*) holding the relevant portfolio (ballot ball (*pelouro*)) was to present a monthly account of the expenses incurred on that food. In 1910 the patients’ diets were costed at 145 *réis* a day, and at its session of 17 November the Municipality resolved to grant up to 200 *réis* a day for that purpose.

A royal warrant (*provisão régia*) of 1685 entrusted the administration of the lepers, previously in the hands of the bishop, to the governor-general. By the warrant (*provisão*) of 1693, however, the supervision of these patients passed to the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), while their expenses continued to be met by the Council of Funchal. An old decree ordered that the lepers ‘should be sent to the island of Maio’.

Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva, author of the *Carta Critica sobre o metodo curativo dos médicos funchalenses*, attributed the cases of elephantiasis that have appeared on the island since the 15th century to the eating of salted fish, broad beans, sour wine and yams. He added that badly cured venereal diseases and the suppression of haemorrhoids could also give rise to the disease. For that distinguished 18th-century physician, elephantiasis was contagious, and there ought therefore to be ‘enclosure for those who suffer from the disease’. Dr Barral, however, writing in 1853, says that although the disease is hereditary in a good many cases, it never appeared to be contagious on the island. Many modern doctors regard elephantiasis as a contagious disease, but we have known several male and female nurses of the now closed hospital of São Lázaro who, after living in close contact for years with patients suffering from that terrible illness, never had even the slightest skin eruption.

‘St Lazarus’s Hospital,’ says Dr Barral, ‘situated in the locality (*sítio*) of Santa Catarina, to the west of the city, is a small, old house intended to take in patients afflicted with elephantiasis, and maintained by the municipality. It holds more or less twenty-six patients, of both sexes and of different ages, and has at times sheltered more than thirty-four. There they find a home, a bed, food, a physician’s care and medicines. As a work of art the building, although it was intended for this purpose from the outset, is of very poor and insignificant construction. It is well ventilated, because it is always possible to keep the windows open, small though they are, and it meets the principal conditions of healthiness. We found no foul smell there, although in the women’s ward the partitions and curtains, of which we disapprove, could well contribute to one. The patients sheltered there receive sufficient and wholesome food and some palliative or other remedies to combat the more troublesome symptoms of the disease, or of intercurrent illnesses.’

On 5 June 1912, on the proposal of Dr Fernando Tolentino da Costa, the Council resolved to close St Lazarus’s Hospital, which then held only four patients, two belonging to the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal and two to that of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). On 19 June of the following year the same Council decided that the Civil Gaol should be installed in the building of the closed hospital, since the terms on which the Government was provisionally lending the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*) to house the prisoners were very costly.

On 28 December 1912 the President of the Council drew up an inventory of all the furniture and utensils at São Lázaro. However, it was only in February of the following year that the two lepers still in the hospital at that time were moved to a hovel in the Travessa do Cascalho, after thought had been given to sending them to the hospital of São José or to that of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). The last hospital pay-sheets of São Lázaro settled by the Council were for expenses incurred in that month of February.

Besides the subsidy of 10,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a month granted by the Government, the hospital of São Lázaro had the income of two legacies, one from António Ferreira de Araújo Guimarães of the city of Porto and the other from the Baron of Castelo de Paiva. In 1912 the Council was spending 1,693,000 *réis* on the establishment, a sum that included the employees’ salaries, amounting to 693,600 *réis*. There is a warrant (*provisão*) from Bishop Dom João do Nascimento, dated 16 December 1748, authorising the creation of a confraternity, based in the church of São Pedro (St Peter), to help maintain the hospital of São Lázaro.

The land for the new church of the Lepers was bought for 8,000 in 1665, and on 17 May 1779 a cemetery was completed for the burial of patients who died in the hospital, since it had been recognised that the church itself could not provide graves for all of them. The prisoners were installed in the São Lázaro gaol on 29 November 1913, even though the contract for the works to complete the building was not awarded until February 1915.

At the end of 1890 and the beginning of 1891 Dr Julio Goldschmidt administered Robert Koch’s tuberculin to several patients at the hospital of São Lázaro, but in none of them did it halt the course of the disease, from which all of them eventually died. The consumptive patients inoculated with the same tuberculin at that time likewise obtained no satisfactory results from this method of treatment.

Over the last 30 years St Lazarus’s Hospital rarely housed more than ten lepers, most of them natives of the municipalities of Ponta do Sol and Calheta (‘small cove’). Elephantiasis of the Greeks is the most common form on the island. Those who suffer from it show tubercles or ulcerations on the face, hands, legs, etc., have difficulty breathing and seldom reach the age of 50; the disease almost always appears between the ages of 15 and 25. Of the patients we knew in the hospital, almost all died suddenly, from suffocation caused by oedema of the respiratory organs.

Of particular interest on the subject of this article are Dr Augusto da Silva Carvalho’s book *Historia da Lepra em Portugal*, which contains a chapter on the hospital of São Lázaro in Funchal; Dr Julio Goldschmidt’s pamphlet *La Lèpre*, which includes the lengthy clinical observations that this physician made in the said hospital; and the *Arquivo Historico da Madeira*, vol. I, pp. 107 ff., which contains some valuable notes on its history.

In the *Diário de Noticias* of Funchal of 12 March 1937, Dr Vicente Henriques de Gouveia published a substantial article entitled ‘Haverá alguma relação entre o inhame e a elefantiase?’ (‘Is there any connection between the yam and elephantiasis?’), which is of particular interest to those who wish to gain a broader knowledge of the subject.

Marmeleiros Hospital

St Elizabeth’s Hospital (*Hospital de Santa Isabel*), which belongs to the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of Funchal, operated for 244 years in the building now occupied by the offices of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this autonomous district. It began to be known as Marmeleiros Hospital (*Hospital dos Marmeleiros*) in 1931, when the various hospital services moved to the large new building in the locality (*sítio*) of Marmeleiros (‘quince trees’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (‘Our Lady of the Mount’).

As will be explained at greater length in the article Sanatoria, in 1903 the Portuguese government granted the German prince Frederico Hohenlohe a concession to establish seaside and mountain sanatoria in Madeira for the treatment of lung diseases. In return, he was obliged to admit to them a certain number of poor patients of Portuguese nationality suffering from diseases of that kind. Among these establishments was the hospital in the locality of Marmeleiros, begun in 1905 and intended particularly for the destitute, which is why it came to be called the Sanatório dos Pobres (Sanatorium of the Poor). The decree of 3 November 1909 authorised the cancellation of the contract between the Portuguese government and Prince Hohenlohe, who was awarded compensation of 4,425,000 marks, plus 328,541 marks in accrued interest.

The Marmeleiros building, whose construction had never been entirely completed, stood there utterly abandoned and exposed to every kind of weather until the central government, in a most praiseworthy and beneficial act of public administration, ceded it to the Holy House of Mercy (*Misericórdia*) of Funchal for the installation of its hospital, by the decrees of 9 and 29 March 1928. The first patients were transferred there in November 1930 and the rest the following year. The building was then fully completed and suitably adapted for that purpose, and it is one of the foremost hospitals of its kind in the country, not only as an appropriate facility but also for the way in which all its clinical and nursing services are provided. To this end, the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) was authorised by the decree of 17 January 1930 to raise a loan of five hundred *contos* (one million réis) *de réis* from the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos, giving as security the proceeds of the 4% surcharge on the duties collected at the Funchal customs house, which had been created by the decree of 28 November 1927.

In all fairness it must be recorded here that the most notable benefit received by the Misericórdia of Funchal over its long history of four centuries was the installation of its hospital in the building of the Marmeleiros Sanatorium (*Sanatório dos Marmeleiros*). This invaluable and never sufficiently praised improvement is due chiefly to the diligent efforts and boundless dedication of the Managing Board presided over by Canon Manuel Francisco Camacho in the period from 1930 to 1933.

The hospital facilities, however, were insufficient for the ever-growing number of patients, and it became urgently necessary both to enlarge the building and to create new sources of revenue to improve the financial position of that charitable institution. Despite the pressing representations of its successive Managing Boards to the higher authorities, it took Dr José Nosolini’s assumption of the office of civil governor of this district to bring about the great benefit of building several new wards, able to accommodate a further 120 patients, and three operating theatres, besides other improvements. These new hospital services were formally inaugurated on 10 August 1940. See Misericórdias.
Military Hospital

More than a century ago, when other ranks of the Madeira military garrison fell ill, they were taken into the hospital of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of this city. Pleading a shortage of resources and the lack of a suitable ward in which to maintain an infirmary set aside for that purpose, the board of that institution more than once put to the higher authorities the need for a small hospital, independent and separate from that of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) and subject only to the military authorities of what was then an overseas province. For their part, the governors and captains-general supported the proposals of the Holy House and pressed for the creation of a modest hospital.

The exact year of its establishment is not known, but it is known to have been created in the period between 1820 and 1824. From January of the former year there survives an official letter sent by the governor and captain-general Sebastião Xavier Botelho to the government in mainland Portugal, pressing for its creation. From 1824 there is a known official document containing various references to the activity of the new hospital, which would have been established shortly before that year of 1824.

It is recorded that it was first housed in a town building in Rua do Castanheiro known as Dona Guiomar’s house (*Casa de D. Guiomar*), a fairly spacious building whose construction had not been fully completed, and where the hospital did not remain for long. It then moved to a house ‘in Rua das Mercês, above the chapel of the same name’, that is, near the present building of the public welfare institution known as the Auxílio Maternal.

A ministerial order (*portaria*) dated 14 February 1849 authorised the hospital’s move to the house in Rua da Rochinha de Baixo, with a right of way to Rua de Santiago, where it operated until last year, 1938. The house had been private property and had passed into the possession of the State Treasury (*Fazenda Pública*) for non-payment of the taxes due on it.

Once the idea of using the various premises of the old military hospital had been definitively accepted, as the most suitable site for the construction of the building to house our lyceum (state secondary school), the necessary steps were at once taken to acquire the old mansion in Rua da Rochinha. For that purpose it was ceded to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district by the decree of 5 September 1936, which empowered this administrative body to expropriate the surrounding land that might prove indispensable for the planned building.

The Directorate-General of Public Assistance (*Direcção Geral da Assistência Pública*), acting on behalf of the Ministry of War, proposed to the Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of Funchal that other ranks and officers requiring hospital treatment be admitted to the Marmeleiros Hospital (*Hospital dos Marmeleiros*). The Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of the Holy House promptly agreed, subject to certain conditions, which the Directorate-General of Public Assistance accepted.

In September and October 1938, through official correspondence between the Military Command (*Comando Militar*) of Madeira and the Managing Board of the Holy House of Mercy, the conditions for admitting patients from the island’s military garrison to the Marmeleiros Hospital were finally settled. The first patients were admitted there on 22 November of that year.
Hospital Velho (street)

The street runs from the Praça dos Lavradores until it meets the southern end of Rua da Rochinha and the Travessa do Arcipreste. It is one of the oldest streets in Funchal and was once called Diogo Afonso. Its name comes from the fact that the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal (*Santa Isabel*) stood in it for many years, before it moved to the building it occupies at present. Later it was also called Rua de Santo António, a name many people still use today, because a chapel with that dedication was built there; its ruins lie on the south side of the street. Next to the hospital stood the old parish church of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’).
Hughes (T. M.)

English poet who visited Madeira in 1845. He was the author of *Ocean Flower*, a poem in ten cantos, preceded by a brief historical and descriptive study of the island and a sketch of Portuguese literature.

The poet Hughes is one of the few Englishmen who regard the story of Robert Machin and Ana de Arfet as pure invention, ‘probably arising from the close relations between Portugal and England. “I would gladly, says the poet, have left the touching fiction (of Machin) undisturbed; few fables are as poetic as the legend I am now dealing with. However, to my regret, I find it rests only on the fragile basis of vague tradition, so much so that, although I spent three days in Machico making careful enquiries, I could not find there the slightest trace confirming that the story was true”’.
Eça (João Fogaça de). Under Castilian rule João Fogaça de Eça was governor-general of Madeira; his appointment dates from 14 August 1603.
Cottony cushion scale (Icerya purchasi)

An insect of the order Hemiptera, first recorded in Funchal about 40 years ago and since found also in São Vicente and other places on the island. It lives on many species of forest and fruit trees, as well as on various garden plants.

*Vedalia cardinalis*, very similar to the small insect known in Madeira as the *rã-rã*, is the worst enemy of the cottony cushion scale, so it is advisable to release it on trees attacked by this hemipteran. *Vedalia* lays its eggs inside the egg sac of the scale insect, and the scale’s larvae serve as food for those of *Vedalia* as they emerge.
Each female scale insect can lay 1000 eggs or even more. These remain inside a sac of waxy matter that she secretes and deposits in filaments laid side by side.

Ielinek
In collaboration with the Baron of Castelo de Paiva, he wrote the following work: *Reise S. Magestat Fregate «Novara» um die Erde (Botanischer Theil I. Wien)*.
See Novara.
Igreja

In this locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (‘Our Lady of the Mount’) stand the parish church dedicated to this patron saint, where Emperor Charles of Austria lies buried – he died at the *quinta* (country estate) of Monte on 1 April 1922 – and the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), founded a few years ago by Captain José Sotero da Silva and today the property of José de Freitas Belmonte.
Igreja
See Achada, I–II.
Igreja

In the locality (*sítio*) of this name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’), on the *quinta* (country estate) of Pombal, stands the chapel of St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*). It was built at the behest of Father António Silvino Gonçalves de Andrade in 1884, and its present owner is Dr João Francisco de Almada.
Igreja Velha

In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Roque in Funchal there is a locality (*sítio*) of this name, and there was once an old chapel dedicated to St Roch, which served as the parish church from 1579 to 1790. In that year it collapsed, being by then already in an advanced state of ruin.
English churches

The land on which the Anglican church in Rua da Bela Vista stands was bought by the British Factory (trading establishment of foreign merchants) in 1810 for 5,435 dollars. Some years later the Factory acquired, for 840 dollars, another plot in the same street, adjoining the first. The church was completed in March 1822 at a cost of 40,000 dollars, a sum raised through subscriptions and a voluntary contribution of 2 shillings and 6 pence on every *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine exported by the British merchants.

In 1848 another Anglican church was established in Rua dos Aranhas, with the botanist Richard Thomas Lowe as its chaplain. Religious disagreements among the British subjects living in Madeira led to the opening of this church, where services were held for 33 years. The Scottish church, opened in 1842 in a house in the Travessa do Surdo, now has its own building in Rua do Conselheiro, next to the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’).
Igrejinha (street)

It ran between the Largo of the College (*Colégio*) and Rua das Pretas. At its end, in the locality (*sítio*) now occupied by the Largo da Igrejinha, stood the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*) – or, as it was commonly called, the Igrejinha (‘little church’) – founded in 1613 by Domingos Rodrigues Garcez and demolished by the Council in 1836.
Ilha

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge. There was once a small chapel there dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Piedade, built in the last quarter of the 18th century by Father Matias Jorge Jardim. The locality formed part of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by Jorge Pinto in 1559. Its last administrator was the Azorean Laureano da Câmara Falcão, known as the *morgado* of Ilha (‘island’), who some decades ago sold these lands to their tenant farmers. The locality takes its name from the fact that it is encircled by the stream, which forks and then rejoins itself at a single point.

This periodical issued four numbers, the first on 7 September and the last on 3 October 1878.
Ilhéu

This is the name by which we know the islet that lies at the western end of the harbour of Funchal and that today (1921) forms one of the limits of the Pontinha (‘little point’) mole (breakwater), or harbour of refuge. On it stood the small Fortress of Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu (‘Our Lady of the Conception of the Islet’), a red light that marked the harbour entrance, and a signal station. It has been reproduced in engravings in countless Portuguese and foreign works, in many magazines, on postcards, etc., and it also frequently appears as a design in Madeiran inlaid work (*embutidos*), on sewing boxes and other products of local cabinet-making.

Referring to the first exploration along the coast, made by the discoverers, Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘at the end of which (the valley of Funchal) there are two islets, where they went to shelter because it was already late’. The two islets were the one now called the Ilhéu (‘islet’), although today it is joined to the land by the mole, and the one that ceased to bear that name when the small Fort of São João da Pontinha (St John the Baptist) was built at the end of the 18th century, and which has since also been connected to the land. Anyone who knows the place is aware that the two small islets lay a short distance from each other.

In his *Epanaphoras de Varia Historia Portuguesa*, where he deals with the supposed story of Robert Machin, Francisco Manuel de Melo makes some mistaken references to these islets, to which the illustrious annotator of the *Saudades* responds with the following words:

‘On a par with this runs the fiction, no lesser in its way, that Zarco “took on water and wood” at the two islets, which, in Melo’s picturesque phrase, are the windbreaks of the harbour of Funchal. Of these two islets, the one further out to sea is still surrounded by water as before (this was in 1873), and so keeps the name Ilheo; the other, joined for a long time to the island’s shore by strong walls, is for that reason called Pontinha. Both are bare crags, lashed and swept by the waves in the swells and storms from the south, which are unfortunately not rare at this spot; both, therefore, bear only the vegetation of marine slime and moss; both are without any spring of drinking water; both are unshakeable witnesses, testifying with their eternal nakedness against the assertion that they gave water and wood to Zarco and his companions.’

The Fortress of Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu was built around the middle of the 17th century (see fortifications (*Fortificações*)), and its chapel was built by royal decree (alvará régio) of 9 November 1682, with its own chaplain. See chapel of the Immaculate Conception of the Islet (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu*).

The harbour light on the islet came into operation on 18 May 1866 (see Faróis (‘lighthouses’)). In 1890 the islet was permanently joined to the shore by a breakwater linking the two points, which forms the most substantial part of the Pontinha mole (breakwater).
Ilhéu Chão

It is 1,852 metres long and 617 metres across at its widest point, and it owes its name, Ilhéu Chão (Flat Islet), to its flat top. Like the other two Desertas (‘deserted islands’), it is uninhabited, and its highest point stands 98 metres above sea level. It is separated from the Ponta de São Lourenço by a channel a little over twenty kilometres wide, through which ships of every size can sail.
*Lolium lowei*, a grass peculiar to the archipelago, has so far been found only on the Ilhéu Chão.

The three Desertas ‘are all an entail (*morgado*) of the Captains of the Jurisdiction of Funchal, says Frutuoso, from which it may be gathered that the glory of this discovery is owed to them; for although these islands lie opposite Machico, and very close to it compared with Funchal, the captains of Machico never had jurisdiction, possession or ownership of them, for they all belong to the Captains of Funchal: for which reason their descendants style themselves lords of them, as I have already said’. See Chão (islet), I-269, and Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’) and Desertas, I-356 and 357.

Islets

The main islets off the coast of Madeira are, on the south coast: Agostinho, Desembarcadouros and de Fora (Ponta de São Lourenço), Santa Catarina (Santa Cruz), Ilhéu (bay of Funchal), Gorgulho and Praia (São Martinho), Campanário or Lapa (Campanário) and Guincho (Ponta do Pargo); and on the north coast, those of Porto Moniz, called Mole and Negro (Porto Moniz), those of Ribeira da Janela (Ribeira da Janela), those of Seixal, known as Ceroulas and Guincho (Seixal), those of Boaventura, or Preto and Vermelho (Boaventura), São Jorge (São Jorge), Rocha do Navio (Santana), those of Faial, the chief of which is the Ilhéu do Faial (Faial), and Porto da Cruz (Porto da Cruz). See those entries. The main islets surrounding the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), not far from its coast, are these: the Ilhéu das Cenouras, the Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal, the Ilhéu de Cima or dos Dragoeiros, today also called the Ilhéu do Farol, the Ilhéu de Fora or Rocha do Nordeste, the Ilhéu da Fonte or Fonte da Areia, and the Ilhéu de Ferro (see each of these entries).
In the Desertas group lies the islet of Furilhão or Prego do Mar (see those entries), also known as the Ilhéu do Navio.
Street lighting

Anyone walking the streets of Funchal at night a little over ninety years ago would have found them in complete darkness. Only now and then did a gleam of light filtering through the windows of houses, or a lantern guiding some late passer-by, briefly break the gloom in which the city lay buried.

The public-spirited Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro took office as civil governor on 7 October 1846, and as early as the 23rd of the same month he had a few lamps, though not many, set up at the most central points of the city. The great improvement of Funchal’s public lighting had begun.

Private citizens came to the aid of the illustrious governor’s initiative, and some of the wealthiest people also had lamps placed on the buildings they lived in. By December of that year the city already had several dozen public lights. Only later, after repeated urging by Silvestre Ribeiro, did the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) resolve to extend the lit area and take on the costs of this important service. On 22 August 1849 the same governor informed the central government that the city was lit by 70 lamps, and expressed the hope that this number would gradually be increased.
The lamps were fuelled by oil until 1870; shortly afterwards they switched to petroleum, which remained in use until electric light was installed.

The lamps hung from the end of horizontal iron rods a little over a metre long. The oldest were tied to a chain which ran along the rod and down the wall to a lock; this was opened to raise or lower the fuel reservoir so that it could be cleaned, and also to light or extinguish the lamp. Later the lamps were fixed to the ends of iron poles, and ladders were needed for all the work of lighting.

Silvestre Ribeiro made several further attempts to light the city by gas, but his efforts and endeavours came to nothing. At the council meeting of 14 July 1858 some resolutions were passed to this end, but they met with no greater success. A public tender was even opened, and its terms were published in a pamphlet, but without any appreciable result.

On 4 January 1884 the Council of Funchal signed a contract with the engineer Eduardo Augusto Kopke to light Funchal by gas, which could be replaced by electric light. The contract was never carried out.

On 22 May 1895 a new contract for electric lighting, which is still in force, was concluded between the same engineer and the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this city. On 20 April 1896 A. Kopke transferred the concession granted to him to ‘The Madeira Electric Lighting Company Limited’, and the Council authorised this transfer at its meeting of 25 May 1896. Electric light was inaugurated in the city of Funchal on 19 May 1897. By 28 December of the following year the 500 lamps and 8 arc lamps specified in article 4 of the contract were already in operation, and this last date was taken as the end of the 24-month period allowed to the company for installing the public street lights.

On 5 January 1899 the Municipal Council approved a proposal to raise the number of public street lamps from 500 to 701. At present there are 14 arc lamps and 1400 lamps across the whole city and its suburbs, and the lighting extends as far as the Lazareto, Quinta Reid on the Caminho do Meio, Conceição in São Roque, Quinta do Leme in Santo António, Nazaré in São Martinho, and Confeiteira in Monte.

In 1821 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) attempted to introduce public lighting in the city, resolving at its meeting of 26 February ‘to have 1, 2 or 3 lanterns placed in each street, the residents to contribute in turn to the expenses of this lighting’.
At the end of February 1821 some of the city’s streets appeared lit, but this improvement was short-lived, despite its usefulness.
Immaculate Heart of Mary (chapel)

In 1918 construction began on a chapel with this dedication in the locality (*sítio*) of Fajã do Penedo (‘boulder flat’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Boaventura (‘good fortune’), thanks to the initiative and persevering efforts of Dona Maria Margarida dos Anjos Ribeiro, who lives in the same locality. Imports and exports

The island of Madeira imports cereals, woollen, linen and cotton fabrics, olive oil, paraffin, salt, sulphur, grocery and café goods, barrel staves, chemical fertilisers, crockery, glassware, tobacco, machinery, cutlery, etc., and exports wine, sugar, embroidery, wickerwork, butter, eggs, onions, fruit, etc. It re-exports coal.

The values of imports, exports and re-exports through the Funchal customs house (*Alfândega do Funchal*) in 1908 were 2,012,000 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis), 750,000 escudos and 1,215,000 escudos respectively.

A substantial item among the imports is coal, intended chiefly for supplying the steamships that call at our port. In that same year, 1908, 167,682,031 tonnes of coal were imported and 150,617,881 re-exported.
See customs houses (*Alfândegas*).

Fire-fighting

The municipal fire-fighting service in the city began in 1837, when the Council spent 460,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) on a pump ordered from London through the firm of João de Oliveira & C.ª.

Before 1837, fires were fought with pumps belonging to private individuals, and the men who operated them were exempted from service in the National Guard so that their help could be counted on when needed.

Only in 1889 did the fire service begin to be run properly, thanks to the creation of the Companhia de Bombeiros Voluntários do Funchal (Funchal Volunteer Fire Brigade). Before then, the wildest follies were committed during fires: mirrors and crockery were even thrown from the windows of burning buildings to prevent the fire from destroying them!

In August 1878, during a fire in a building on Rua da Alfândega that housed the bakery and confectioner’s of the Englishman Payne, so much glass and crockery was hurled into the street that some supposed the damage done to the building by human hands had been greater than that caused by the fire.

At the end of the volume, or in a supplement to this work, we shall give a more detailed account of the improvements made to the fire service, and in particular we shall discuss the Volunteer and Municipal Fire Brigades that have been organised in this city for that purpose.
Forest fires
Of the many fires that have broken out in the forests of the island of Madeira, the most important are unquestionably the two we mention here:
Fire of 1919

After the burning of Madeira’s forests in the lifetime of Gonçalves Zargo, the fire that reached the greatest proportions and caused the most damage was unquestionably the one of August 1919, set by criminal hands. For eight days people worked vigorously to put it out. It began on the 21st in the western part of Madeira and then spread rapidly to other localities on the island. However, the extraordinarily dry, hot wind that the islanders call the *leste* (hot, dry easterly wind from Africa), which blew with unusual violence from that day until 27 August, repeatedly thwarted the efforts of those who, with the greatest courage and devotion, strove in a fiery atmosphere to halt the advance of the terrible destroying element. Several times it was feared that the fires would reach the villages, some of which, as is well known, lie near the middle region of the island. Fortunately this was avoided, even though the wind greatly hampered the work of containing the fire’s devastation. In the upland region some small buildings were consumed by the flames, many livestock were lost and many crops were ruined, but there were no serious casualties, although some people were slightly injured while fighting the fires. On 28 and 29 August some rain fell in the mountains, and this did much to put out completely the fires that in the preceding days had destroyed many of our finest forests, causing losses of more than 2,000 *contos* across the whole island.

In the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto Moniz, the woods around Ribeira da Janela and Fanal suffered badly; in that of São Vicente, those on the edge of the Paul, at Lombada das Vacas, Lombo da Palha and the uplands of Ponta Delgada (Serra da Ponta Delgada); in that of Sant'Ana, those of Arco de São Jorge and Faial; in that of Machico, those of Pico da Suna and Lamaceiros; in that of Funchal, those of São Roque and Monte; in that of Câmara de Lobos, those of Ribeiro Garcia and Fontainhas; in that of Ribeira Brava, those of Serra de Água; and in that of Calheta, those of Lombada Gorda, Ribeira dos Moinhos, Rabaçal and the edge of the Paul da Serra.

At Rabaçal, the locality (*sítio*) that travellers explore so enthusiastically for the superb scenery it offers, the damage was not total, and the houses suffered nothing, thanks to the effort and dedication devoted to saving them. At Monte and São Roque the fire took on truly frightening proportions, covering an area of several kilometres and threatening to destroy a great number of dwellings. At Bica da Cana (‘reed spout’), on the Paul da Serra, the plantations laid out there by the Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) were badly damaged.

In the grave crisis the island went through, good service was rendered by the civil governor, General Simões Soares, the Military Commander, Colonel Veiga, the forestry officer (regente silvícola) Schiappa de Azevedo, the forestry staff and various detachments of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*Infantaria 27*). All of them, within the limits of their duties, worked with perseverance and used every means available to contain and put out the fires. Where there was little zeal and energy was in seeking out the arsonists and handing them over to the judicial authorities, so that they might be punished without leniency. The indulgence with which the enemies of our forests have always been treated is the main cause of the stripping of the mountains, and of the island having suffered on various occasions the damage caused by torrents and floods.
Fire in the time of Zargo

The burning of Madeira’s forests in the time of Zargo, the first donatary (*donatário*) of Funchal, is an event mentioned by João de Barros, Frutuoso, António Cordeiro, Manuel Tomás and other authors, and one that tradition has also kept alive. Ferdinand Denis relates that an early French traveller met an old sailor to whom an eyewitness had described the burning of the island of Madeira. According to the learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), the Torre do Tombo (national archives), in the *Livro das Ilhas*, folio 84, holds a certified copy of an apostolic brief of Pope Paul II, dated 1469, which clearly alludes to this same fire. Gaspar Frutuoso, the historian of the islands, describes the fire in the interior of Madeira in the following terms: ‘Hence the captain (João Gonçalves Zarco) resolved, seeing that the labour of men could not clear so many trees as had stood on this island since the beginning of the world or of its making, that in order to consume them, so that the land might be tilled and put to use, it was necessary to set fire to them. And since, with the great mass of trees and their great age, some lay felled on the ground and some stood dead and dry, the fire took hold in this valley of Funchal in such a way, and was so fierce, that when the wind blew off the land its flames and heat could not be endured, and the people often took refuge on the islets and in the ships until the weather changed. And because the valley was very thick both with much fennel and with trees, the fire was so stoked that it burned for seven years in the trees, and in the trunks and roots below ground, so that it could not be put out. It did great destruction to the timber both in Funchal and in most of the island along the sea on the southern coast, where it had been decided to clear and cultivate the land.’

Francisco Manuel de Melo, referring to the Madeira fire, says the following in *Epanaphora III*: ‘I cannot but doubt the fire which (Barros) affirms lasted seven years throughout the island. Against this, it seems, stand the woods that have always remained there, from which timber has been cut for so many years for the making of sugar; of which, they say, there came to be a hundred and fifty mills on the island. These could hardly have been continuously sustained after so universal a fire, still less have grown up after it: but let the credit of such an Author always be preserved.’

Melo’s arguments carry some weight in showing that the Madeira fire neither lasted seven years nor spread to every part of the island. It should be added, moreover, that had the fire been general, as some writers claim, Cadamosto, who also refers to the disaster, could not have said in 1455 (?) that our country produced highly prized timbers, among which cedar and yew stood out. It must also be noted that, for the fire to have burned for seven consecutive years in forests made up chiefly of broadleaved species, not one of those violent downpours would have had to fall on the island throughout that long period – downpours which even today, although rainfall is far less abundant than it once was, flood the inland valleys and give rise to torrents that plunge in cascades from the heights of the mountains.

There is no doubt that many forests in the Funchal valley and in other parts of the island’s south coast were destroyed by the fire that João Gonçalves Zargo imprudently ordered to be set in order to clear the land. But to accept that this fire, spreading rapidly and leaping from tree to tree, came to engulf the whole island seems to us a fantasy born of the rich imagination of Manuel Tomás and other early writers. Nothing in the passage from ‘Longing for the Homeland’ that we have transcribed suggests that the fire was general. João de Barros, the first historian to record the disaster, confines it to the part of the island of Madeira ‘where it is now called Funchal’, adding, however, ‘that the fire took hold of the clearing and of the rest of the woodland, and that for seven years it burned alive in the wilds of those great forests which nature had raised over so many hundreds of years’.

Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo states that, since the south of the island was ‘precisely the part cultivated and inhabited immediately after the discovery, it is possible not only that the land there was gradually cleared by burning the virgin forests – a method still used today in the American backlands, for want of labour, for other agricultural and economic reasons, and out of immediate necessity – but also that such clearing by fire continued to be resorted to during the first seven years, without any traces of it being found a short time afterwards. The south of the island of Madeira was the first to be exploited and inhabited, and it is the most productive zone. Only a short period would have been needed for human labour to erase the signs of devastation there. And if the fire is confined to only one part of the island, the arguments to the contrary lose their force. Mello himself doubts not so much the fire as that it was so universal’.

Once the disaster is reduced to the proportions that Dr Azevedo assigns to it, there is no reason for us not to accept it as historical truth, all the more so because, as the same writer says, it is authenticated by the clear allusion in the Apostolic Brief, which is almost contemporary. It was undoubtedly a mistake to order the woods to be set on fire instead of felling them with the axe, but fortunately that mistake did not lead to the complete annihilation of those forests, as has already been seen above.

The fire increased the fertility of Madeira’s soil, which was still marvellous when Cadamosto visited the island. It did not, however, win the approval of Prince Henry the Navigator, who in the early days of settlement drew, it seems, a considerable income from the timber shipped to Portugal.

Frutuoso records that the island had such a quantity of fine, hard timber that great numbers of planks, beams and masts were carried to many places, all of it cut with water-driven mills or saws, ‘of which there are still many today on the north side of the same island: and at this time, because of the great quantity of timber taken from there to the Kingdom, they began to build with it ships with topsails and forecastles, for before there were none in the Kingdom, nor had they anywhere to sail to, nor were there any ships other than the caravels of the Algarve and the *barinéis* in Lisbon and Porto’.

Zurara, discussing the benefits that flowed from the discoveries made on the initiative of Prince Henry the Navigator, mentions ‘the great heights of the houses that reach to the sky, which were and are built with the timber of those parts’. To this the Viscount of Santarém adds the following note, which Pinheiro Chagas reproduces in his *Historia de Portugal*:

‘This interesting detail shows that the timber carried to Portugal from the islands newly discovered by Prince Henry, chiefly from the island of Madeira, came in such quantity that its abundance changed the method of building town houses: storeys were added and the houses thus raised, and in this way it replaced the Roman and Arab method that had probably been used until then. This probability carries more weight in view of the system of lighting in Lisbon ordered by King Ferdinand, as recorded in certain documents in the archive of the Lisbon Municipal Council.’

Zurara, who is extremely laconic about everything concerning the islands, says nothing about the Madeira fire in the *Chronica do Descobrimento da Guiné*. From what he notes about the height of the houses, however, it can be deduced that, however long-lasting and extensive the fire may have been, enough woodland still remained for the island to export a great quantity of timber to Portugal.

Magnetic inclination

It was measured by A. P. de Azevedo and Soulier de Sauve on 25 April 1839, and by the same A. P. de Azevedo together with the officers of the *Rattermaker* on 20 December 1846. The first observations, made in the Praça Académica (‘academic square’) with the Gambey compass, showed an inclination of 59° 30; the second, made in the churchyard (*adro*) of the College (*Colégio*) with the ‘Fox’s Dipping’ and the ‘Intensity Instrument’, gave an inclination of 60º 40.

On 4 February 1872 and 17 July 1873 the officers of the *Challenger* found inclinations of 56° 14' 1 N. and 55° 12 5 N. respectively. More recently, the distinguished Azorean meteorologist Colonel Francisco Afonso Chaves recorded the following magnetic inclinations: 54° 32' 5 N. on 22 June 1903, and 54° 22'7 N. on 4 June 1906. All these observations were made on the parade ground of the College barracks, and Colonel Chaves used the Abbadie-Brunner compass to determine the inclination.
