Dress

The dress of the Madeiran peasant has nothing remarkable about it today. It generally consists of trousers of linen, *seriguilha* (homespun linen-and-wool cloth), *marafuz* (coarse homespun linen-and-wool cloth) or some other fabric, a linen or cotton shirt, and a waistcoat and jacket, often made of the same fabric as the trousers. In some parts of the island a sleeveless jacket of *marafuz* or *seriguilha* is widely worn, leaving the arms covered only by the shirtsleeves. While at work, the farmer usually takes off his waistcoat and jacket but keeps on his hat or cap, which protects his head from the heat of the sun.

The peasant’s cap bears no resemblance whatever to the old *carapuças*. It is made of wool, fits the head closely and has a small tassel on top and two flaps at the sides, which are either let down over the ears or turned up, sometimes fastened to a button. This cap, known as the eared cap, appears to be a Madeiran creation and was already being worn in 1857.

The old costumes of the countrywomen have almost disappeared, replaced by dresses and bodices or polka jackets of chintz or wool, exactly like those worn by lower-class women in Funchal. In Camacha and some other places the women tie a roll of cloth round the waist and put on several skirts over it. As a result their hips take on a rounded shape, and the dress, which is rather short, sways from side to side as they walk. This movement is not without grace when the woman is tall and elegant and walks with an easy step.

The headscarf, its ends tied under the chin, is the head covering most worn by countrywomen, but there are parishes where the mantilla and the hat are becoming general, above all among women who come often to Funchal. A shawl thrown over the shoulders often completes the dress of the women of our countryside.

The old costumes of our peasants were unquestionably far more charming and picturesque than those of today. The men wore wide linen breeches ending at the knee, where they were gathered, with a shirt and a jacket of the same cloth. The women wore a striped skirt of a linen-and-wool fabric made on the island, a linen shirt and a cape of blue or red baize reaching to below the waist; this cape had pointed scallops, sometimes edged with ribbon. Many men owned coats or cloaks of coarse wool, which they wrapped around themselves on cold days.

For feast days the men had their waistcoats and coats of blue cloth, and the women pretty bodices or stays in bright colours, sometimes ingeniously embroidered, which they wore over their shirts. Men and women alike fastened their fine linen shirts with yellow buttons, sometimes of gold, and covered their heads with a small cap of blue cloth (*carapuça* (traditional Madeiran cap shaped like an inverted funnel)), lined with red, which had the shape of an inverted funnel. Well-to-do women could be recognised by the gold chains with which they adorned themselves; these were wound twice around the neck and then fastened to the lower part of the bodice.

It is likely that the striped skirts and embroidered bodices derived from old Moorish costumes, all the more so as it is known that there were once many Moors, chiefly in Funchal and Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). As for the *carapuça*, however, it is hard to guess its origin, although White tells us that in some of Rubens’s paintings an object very similar to this old Madeiran cap can be seen on ladies’ heads. The *carapuça* protected the head so poorly that it is surprising the people of this island wore it at all.

Hans Sloane, Ovington, Captain James Cook, Forster and Barrow make no mention of the *carapuça* in the accounts of their voyages, which leads us to believe that this cap only began to be worn in Madeira in the first quarter of the 19th century. Paulo Dias de Almeida, in his *Descrição da ilha da Madeira*, written in 1817 and published in the Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*), includes two plates showing *carapuças*, but without the long points that gave these caps the shape of inverted funnels.

Before they knew the funnel-shaped *carapuça*, the peasants wore a cap of red or blue wool, whose shape can be seen in the plate accompanying the work on the climate of Madeira published by Dr Nicolau Caetano Pita in 1812. This cap fitted closely to the head and was certainly far more comfortable than the pointed *carapuça* that became widespread on the island shortly afterwards.

Diogo Vieira de Tovar e Albuquerque, in an unpublished work written in 1807 entitled *Descripçâo política e económica da ilha da Madeira*, tells us the following about the costumes worn on the island: ‘Working men always wear a cloth *carapuça*, fitting close to the head, with two small ear-flaps, a long coat, wide linen drawers, short to the knee, where they are fastened, and close-fitting boots in the natural colour of the leather from which they are made. I believe this custom has perhaps been preserved from the usage of the first Portuguese inhabitants of the island, for the Portuguese of that time dressed in almost the same way, at least in form. I also believe that the use of long coats among working people is encouraged and maintained by the English, in order to promote greater consumption of their cloth, for the whole island is supplied with cloth from England. The women wear the same *carapuças*, skirts of cotton or chintz, and boots. Polite society dresses entirely in the Portuguese manner.’

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’) the men wear hats made of palm leaf which, although very durable, have nothing to recommend them in elegance or suppleness. We do not know when these hats first came into use.

The *carapuças* shaped like an inverted funnel were worn in certain parishes until 1870; nevertheless, around 1880 and even later, a few old peasants could still occasionally be seen in Funchal wearing these extravagant caps. Some *carapuças* had two flaps at the sides, while others had none.

Of the old Madeiran costumes all that remains today are the boots of white or yellowish leather, without heels and with the leg turned down in the middle, and the blue baize capes with pointed scallops, which are still worn by some peasant women, even in the parishes bordering the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal.

Barrow, who was in Madeira in 1792, says that the middle class, that is, shopkeepers and artisans, wore hats, shoes and stockings, with a long coat to hide the patches on their trousers, and that the women of the same class invariably dressed in black and wore a *capacete* on their heads. Ovington, who visited the island in 1689, noted that the people affected a certain gravity in their dress, wearing black in imitation of the clergy, and that the sword was so widely carried that even servants wore one while waiting at table.

Men of a certain social standing once wore embroidered silk waistcoats, and as late as 1870 physicians could almost always be recognised by their long black frock coats and top hats. During Holy Week and in the season of confession, ladies replaced their hats with black veils that covered their heads and sometimes their faces. This fashion, which went back to ancient times, began to fall out of use shortly after 1880.

Around the middle of the 19th century the councillors (*vereadores*) of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) wore capes, breeches and stockings at official ceremonies. It was still in this dress, together with the obsolete plumed hats, that the members of the municipality appeared at the funeral rites of Luís I and at the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of Carlos I, both held in 1889, even though the municipal uniform had by then been reduced to the said capes, which were of black silk lined with white.
At the beginning of the 20th century these capes were replaced by sashes of blue and white silk, which were worn until the proclamation of the Republic on this island.

Apart from minor local peculiarities, the dress of the inhabitants of Madeira today differs in no way from that worn in Europe. The fashions of Paris are strictly followed in Funchal, and it is above all the fair sex that pays them the most faithful homage, sometimes at the cost of great sacrifices.

If in Barrow’s time the women of the middle classes always dressed in black, heaven knows how things stand today, when it is they who most worship fashion and show the greatest inclination towards luxury, despite the high price of fabrics of every kind, and of fine fabrics in particular. It is the nouveaux riches of both sexes, generally vain and ill-bred people, who display the finest clothes, while the upper classes sometimes dress modestly, whether for lack of means or so as not to be confused with those who, by means not always lawful, have managed to increase their capital astonishingly.

Anyone walking through the streets of the city on feast days notices the greatest luxury everywhere and gains the impression that the great majority of the people of Funchal have the means to sustain it. Unfortunately, however, this is not so, and if we could enter many homes, we might perhaps find poverty and disorder there, in contrast to the costly finery their occupants display in public. (1921).

The truth is that the old and characteristic dress, especially that worn by the countrywomen of Madeira, has disappeared entirely, although some claim to find traces of it in certain localities far from the centre of Funchal.

For a fuller study of this subject, besides the authors cited in this article, the following writings should be consulted, as they provide curious and interesting information: *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) of 7, 8 and 13 March 1938; *Arquivo Historico da Madeira*, vol. IV, pp. 178 ff.; and ‘Zargo’s Islands’ (*Ilhas de Zargo*), pp. 683 ff.
Agriculture

Agriculture is the oldest and most widespread industry in the Madeira archipelago, occupying some seventy-five per cent of its inhabitants. The arable land can scarcely exceed an area of 300 square kilometres, that is, 30,000 hectares. The uncultivated land, which includes the highest and most rugged ground, must cover an area of more than 200 square kilometres. Cultivation does not generally extend above 700 to 750 metres. The land lying immediately above that is reserved for gathering firewood, brushwood and broom, and also for rearing and grazing livestock, with the exception of cattle.

It is both interesting and useful to reproduce here what the distinguished Madeiran botanist Carlos Azevedo de Meneses wrote in one of his works on the distribution of plants according to the altitudes at which they can become acclimatised and thrive.

Four agricultural zones may be recognised in Madeira, corresponding to the four botanical zones into which the island is customarily divided. The first extends from the seashore up to 200 or 300 metres, the second up to 700 or 750 metres, the third up to 1,600 metres and the fourth up to 1,850 metres.

Sugar cane, the banana plant and cacti characterise the first zone, which, adopting Koppen’s classification, we may call subtropical. Besides these plants, however, it is also home to the vine, wheat, barley, maize, cabbages, turnips, the black or Guinea pumpkin, the Tenerife pumpkin or *chilacaiota*, the gourd, the chayote, broad beans, beans, peas, sweet potatoes, potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word), etc., etc. Among the fruit trees common below 200 or 300 metres we may mention the cherimoya tree (*anoneira*), the mango, the guava, the Surinam cherry, the papaya and the avocado, species that originate in hot countries and need a certain degree of warmth to live and flourish.

The species characteristic of the second zone are the vine and the chestnut, although in many places one also sees the same vegetables as in the lower zone, as well as various fruit trees that grow there too, such as orange, pear, apple, plum, peach, apricot, loquat, walnut, fig and mulberry trees, etc., etc. Cereals, and wheat in particular, are grown abundantly, above all on land without artificial irrigation, whereas from 300 or 400 metres upwards sugar cane is a poorly rewarding plant, because of the low sugar content of its juice. Cherry trees are grown in the damp, cool valleys of the upper part of the second zone, sometimes living alongside the laurel, the *til* and the *vinhático*, magnificent members of the laurel family that belong to the native forest flora.

The third zone is almost entirely given over to fodder, brushwood and wild trees. Here and there, however, it still has a few cultivated fields of wheat and rye, and some small plots where cabbages, beans, potatoes, etc. grow. But there the sweet potato no longer yields usable tubers, the banana plant and the cherimoya tree bear no fruit, and the vine ripens its grapes only in a few places less visited by mist. It is in the third zone that the *bardos* are found, separating the uncultivated region from the cultivated one.

The fourth zone, which takes in the peaks of the highest mountains, has remained uncultivated to the present day. We do not believe that it will ever be put to profitable agricultural use, since it is inhospitable for most of the year and its soils are scoriaceous and shallow.

Of the useful species we have noted in the four zones into which Madeira is subdivided, the most important, whether for their yield or for the area they occupy, are sugar cane, the vine, the banana plant and wheat. Cane growing, which now covers an area of about 2,000 hectares, was until recently, and still remains, one of the most profitable crops on the island, far more lucrative than the vine and on a par with the banana. The banana covers an area of 150 to 200 hectares, while the vine and wheat must each cover some 2,000 to 2,200 hectares.

Land in Madeira is worked with the hoe; only in very few localities is the plough used, where the ground allows this agricultural implement. For various reasons Madeiran rural property is extremely subdivided, and its small plots generally combine several crops together. Curious though this association of crops is, it does not always seem to us to serve the farmer’s interests.

It should be said here that, from an agricultural point of view, our island is not as backward as is generally supposed. If farm work is done by hand almost everywhere, it is because the lie of the land does not lend itself to ploughing machinery. And if crop rotation, so necessary for good harvests, is not practised, it is because it runs counter to the extraordinary subdivision of property and sometimes also to the farmer’s interests. On the sloping land of the southern and northern flanks, it is the water that carries the main fertilising elements down from the heights. This is why many soils, neither manured nor improved by rotation, constantly maintain a certain degree of productivity.

Terracing (*sorribas*), manuring, the clearing and improvement of land, etc., are almost always carried out rationally in Madeira. If anything seems to us to deserve criticism, it is chiefly the little care usually given to the selection of seed and the preservation of good varieties, and the injudicious way in which the growing of trees is often managed. The poor quality of many of our fruits and the sorry appearance of many of the trees in our orchards are almost always the result of absent or badly executed pruning and of the excessive yields that fruit trees are forced to bear on the island.

It is in this industry that the most important elements of the public wealth and prosperity of the whole archipelago are to be found. The economic life of its population and its relative well-being depend largely on the progress and development of agriculture.

The two principal crops, which on account of their rewarding profits occupy the most fertile land and the largest area, are sugar cane and the vine, both almost as old as the first work of colonisation. In the last three decades banana growing has developed extraordinarily, and together with the two preceding crops it makes up what are called the three rich crops of Madeira.

The oldest is the cultivation of sugar cane, which was the main factor in the rapid growth of the population in various parts of the island after its discovery. Its production has not held steady over time, because of the diseases that at times attacked the canefields and also because of economic causes of a local nature. At present this crop is perhaps the most considerable source of public wealth, above all in the southern region of Madeira nearest the coast. This is not only because of its remunerative price but also because of the fodder it provides for raising livestock and the raw material it supplies for preparing the manures known as fold manures (*adubos de curral*). The area under sugar cane must be approximately two thousand hectares. The yield per hectare has varied, ranging from twenty to thirty-five tonnes, with the average at present being approximately thirty. Over the last four years its average total output across the whole archipelago was forty-six million four hundred and forty thousand kilos each year.

The cultivation of the vine is also today a considerable source of wealth and prosperity. Like sugar cane, it has had mixed fortunes, depending on the period, on particular local circumstances and above all on diseases, which have already once caused the complete extinction of the crop, as happened around the middle of the 19th century. Little by little the vineyards were replanted, and for some decades now the production of must throughout the archipelago has been remarkable. We have seen elsewhere that the area under this crop is about two thousand hectares, with an average yield of six to seven *pipas* of wine per hectare. Vines normally grow from the coast up to an altitude of 500 metres, some reaching 600 and even 700 metres.

For various reasons, the work of the wine growers in recent years was barely rewarding, or rather ruinous, because of the low price at which their musts were sold. Wine production in the period from 1910 to 1930 was as follows:

In the five years 1918–1922, average annual production was about 6 230.000 litres. It did not fall in the decade from 1923 to 1931, so it may be conjectured that over the last ten years the archipelago produced an annual average of approximately 6,500,000 litres of wine, that is, 1,300 *pipas* of five hundred litres.

The municipalities of Funchal and Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) have the largest wine production, followed by those of São Vicente, Porto Moniz, Porto Santo and Calheta. It is on the southern coast of Madeira that the vines are found which supply the raw material for the fortified wines of worldwide reputation, and the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos deserves special mention as the place where the finest musts of the archipelago are produced. The principal and most celebrated varieties grown were Sercial (white grape variety), Malmsey, Boal and Verdelho, from which specialised types of wine were made; the first two, once aged, were the most precious kinds of fortified wine in the whole world. With the phylloxera invasion, new resistant rootstocks were introduced onto which the old varieties were grafted, but the specialised selection for making the different kinds has been maintained only on a very limited scale.

The richest aid to agriculture is the distinctive irrigation system formed by the numerous and important aqueducts known as levadas (irrigation channel), which are spread through every parish of Madeira. We shall deal with them in due detail. The articles Banana, Sugar Cane, Wines and Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) are relevant to this subject of agriculture.
Wickerwork industry

The wickerwork industry, or the making of osier goods, chiefly pieces of furniture, has its main centre of production in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha. We have already given a brief account of it on pp. 195 ff. of volume I, in the article devoted to that parish.
In 1912 the head of the section of technical industrial services in Funchal wrote:

‘The manufacture of wickerwork is at present making great progress, both through the expansion and improvement of the corresponding crops and through the value of exports of wicker and of finished goods, which is growing and gaining in worth thanks also to more careful workmanship and better taste in design.

Work of good taste and careful finish in this speciality is now frequently to be found. All that the Madeiran worker achieves with a complete lack of vocational training leaves us with the vivid impression of how much better he would be able to produce if guided by artistic instruction.

Given the way this industry operates here, almost exclusively located in the parish of Camacha, from which it has not been possible to move it, it is easy to see that only vocational teaching given in a school in that same locality could be put to proper use.

The Funchal Industrial School (*Escola Industrial do Funchal*) could contribute to the education of this worker, but he does not attend it because he lives too far away. Moreover, the conditions of the industry, long bound up with local customs and working habits, do not in most cases offer enough pay for someone who would have to live away from home and from the other small interests he needs in order to make a living.

The price of labour has fallen recently. As with embroidery, it is certainly also owing to a certain home-industry character that the payment for labour can be reduced to rates that would be utterly unacceptable in workshop employment.
Exports of wicker in 1911 may be assumed to have been 900 tonnes, and it is no exaggeration to suppose that as much again was consumed in local manufacture.
The commercial value of exports should be reckoned at no less than 180 *contos* (one million réis) de réis a year, in osier goods alone.
This industry may be assumed at present to occupy more than 600 people, including over 300 men, 200 women and 100 minors.’

From the same source we obtained the following information in 1921: ‘This industry is in decline today, while it is expanding in other countries, and above all in South Africa, to which the island exports its wicker. The rising cost of the raw material, which prevents some manufacturers who are short of capital from buying it at the right season; the departure abroad of many workers formerly employed in the industry, while others on the island turn to other, more profitable work; the heavier freight charges on finished wicker goods, because they take up more space in ships’ holds; and the local duties and taxes, which weigh more heavily on wickerwork articles than on the raw material: these, in the view of that enlightened manufacturer, are the main reasons why the industry has lost a large part of its former importance.

Madeira produces 700 to 800 tonnes of wicker a year, perhaps half of which is shipped off the island. At the Cape of Good Hope, once an important market for Madeira’s wickerwork, many of the same articles are now made with wicker imported from our island, and the same is happening in Brazil. England is at present the country that imports the largest quantities of wickerwork made in Madeira, and, we are told, it also receives large amounts of raw wicker.’

We have been unable to gather any further information for the years after that, but we believe that the industry long ago entered a phase of steep decline, owing to the causes set out above and particularly to the competition from other centres of production that have since emerged.
Embroidery industry

This industry contributed considerably to the prosperity of the archipelago and was regarded by everyone as a great source of wealth. Because it was a home-based occupation, in which Madeiran women could devote themselves to its work within their own homes while carrying out their domestic duties, it spread to every poor and modestly off household and became one of the most significant factors in family prosperity. Children of eight and ten and women in their eighties worked busily at the tasks of this industry when it reached a very flourishing state that was highly rewarding for all. Then came its decline and ruin. At present the work of those who engage in it is poorly paid, and there is even a very large number of women workers who cannot find employment in the industry. Nevertheless, many thousands of people scattered throughout the archipelago still devote themselves to making embroidery, despite the ruinous state to which the industry has fallen. It is still a small resource for the poor and a relief from the crisis that overwhelms everyone.

In 1920, when the industry was very prosperous, there were as many as 60 commercial houses in the city of Funchal, most of them foreign, which dealt exclusively in the purchase, finishing and export of embroidery. At that time there were more than 35,000 embroiderers spread across all the parishes of this island and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). By the end of 1923 the number of exporting houses had risen to 100, and the value of the goods exported, chiefly to North America, was then estimated at 70,000 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos). See what we have already said about this industry at some length on pp. 162 ff. of vol. I of this work, under the heading Embroidery.
Dairy industry

Butter has long been made in Madeira, but at first the way it was prepared was quite rudimentary. Milk, which was scarce, was almost always left standing in the vessels until enough cream had accumulated to bring about the coagulation of the butterfat. This, together with a lack of cleanliness and ignorance of the proper method of salting, meant that the product was generally of poor quality.

In any case, as early as 1870 some butter was being made in Madeira that rivalled the butter imported from abroad, which was usually sold in Funchal at 300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a *libra* (Portuguese pound, c. 459 g). The price of second-quality butter ranged between 180 and 240 *réis* a *libra* (459 grams). At the beginning of the second quarter of the 19th century almost all the butter consumed in Funchal came from England, but forty years later the island was already producing all the butter it needed and could even export some to Lisbon. Butter exports, which in 1881 amounted to only 129 kilograms, rose to 1932 kilograms in 1885, 9 897 in 1887, 25,554 in 1889 and 42,476 in 1890. In the following two years they fell to 1775 and 2,580 kilograms, before rising again in 1893 to 48,124.

Around 1895 Adolfo Burnay set up a dairy-products factory at Santo António da Serra (‘St Anthony of the uplands’). It began rather modestly, using only the milk produced by his own cows, but it later widened the scope of its operations, buying all the milk that the local cattle breeders could supply and paying 20 *réis* a litre for it.

The breeders were entitled to keep the whey, which was a great advantage to them: thanks to the rapid skimming processes, this product had no time to ferment and could therefore be used as food for people.

Besides excellent butter, which was sold on the island and exported to Lisbon, the Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) factory also produced cheeses, but these met with little favour because they were made with little care. Only many years later was this latter industry able to improve and achieve a certain growth in Madeira, thanks to the studies and experiments of the agronomist João da Mota Prego.

In 1920 there were 22 factories and some thirty-odd skimming stations scattered across the island, paying about 600 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos) for the 11 to 12 million litres of milk bought each year from farmers. The price of milk, formerly 2 centavos a litre, was fixed in 1919 at 5 centavos and, more recently, on 4 January 1921, at 10 centavos for butter making and 14 centavos for cheese making.

In 1920 Madeira exported about 450,000 kilograms of butter to mainland Portugal and Africa, while local consumption was about 110,000 kilograms. The price of butter at the Funchal depot, which was at first 72 and 80 centavos, rose to 1.20 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) in December 1919, under a ministerial order (*portaria*) requested by the exporters, then to 3.00 escudos in September 1920 and to 4.00 escudos in November 1921. Yet consumers are often unable to obtain this staple there, because the exporters do not always keep properly supplied the only establishment where the public can buy it on favourable terms.

Since on average 23 litres of milk are needed to make one kilogram of butter, it is clear that the dealers’ profit lies mainly in exports, as butter fetches far higher prices in Lisbon and Africa than in Funchal. Butter intended for industrial use, on which part of the population of Funchal nevertheless sometimes relies, is sold (1921) at 8.00 escudos a kilogram, having previously been sold at 7.00, 5.00, 4.80 and 1.80 escudos. This last price remained in force until August 1920.

Under an undertaking signed very recently (1921) by the representatives of several butter factories, the depot was to be supplied daily with 400 kilograms of butter, that is, 2,800 kilograms a week, to be sold to the public at 4.00 escudos. Before going on sale the butter was to be examined by the deputy health officer (*sub-delegado de saúde*), and the manufacturers kept the right to sell privately, at whatever price they set, any butter in excess of the quantities they were required to supply to the depot.

No one who was not a supplier of the depot was allowed to sell butter at more than 4.00 escudos a kilogram. Manufacturers who broke the terms of the agreement by failing to deliver to the depot the quantities apportioned to them were barred from obtaining permission to export any butter until they proved that their deliveries were up to date.

Before the agreement to which we refer, manufacturers were obliged to supply 10 per cent of the butter they exported for public consumption in Funchal. At the end of 1919 there were ten factories required to contribute 40 per cent of their output to the depot, under an apportionment made by the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office).

As the manufacturers were as a rule far from punctual in sending the required quantities of butter to the depot beside the Market, the public was often unable to obtain this staple at the prices set in the agreement and had to buy it at exorbitant prices from a private depot in Rua Direita (‘straight street’). If the authorities had always exercised strict supervision over the supply of butter, instead of resorting to the so-called *bicas* (queues), which served only to drive away many consumers and to protect the manufacturers, a good many abuses would have been avoided, and order would have been brought to a service which, though it has improved lately, is still very far from meeting the needs of the public.

What has been said above about the dairy industry goes no further than the year 1921. After that date the industry continued to make considerable progress and to develop, and it is a significant factor in the public wealth of this archipelago. Various legislative instruments were enacted to promote its prosperity. The most notable of these are the decree of 4 June 1936, which created the National Dairy Board of Madeira (*Junta Nacional de Lacticínios da Madeira*), and the decrees of 22 September and 24 November 1938 and of 24 November 1939, which regulate the workings of this Board.

A considerable part of the rural population did not willingly accept the provisions of these decrees, which it judged to be an attack on its legitimate interests. It pressed its protests to the point of committing the gravest excesses, invading public offices and perpetrating other deplorable acts of disorder. Armed forces sent from the mainland had to intervene, and some of the local people lost their lives. Countless arrests were made, and many individuals suffered the penalty of exile to the Azores and Cape Verde.

Today everyone recognises the advantages of the legislative measures that were adopted, and the successive boards of the National Dairy Board have fully discharged the thorny task entrusted to them. Its *Boletins de Informação e Publicidade* are valuable documents that deserve careful reading by all who take an interest in these matters.
Livestock farming

Agriculture, as is well known, has in livestock farming one of its most valuable aids, especially in cattle, which supply the raw material for making cheese and butter. Since all the cattle in Madeira are kept in stalls, it is chiefly they that provide the farmer with the manure indispensable for fertilising the land given over to the various crops.

What we might say here about livestock farming has already been set out at some length in the article Livestock, on pp. 70–75 of this volume of the *Elucidário*, to which we refer the reader. Nevertheless, we do not wish to omit recording here an interesting particularity of the horses and other equines of the Madeiran region, as a clarification of, or supplement to, what was said in the article devoted to Livestock. This information is taken from an article published in the former *Diário Popular* (‘The People’s Daily’) of 2 July 1902, which may be read with considerable profit on this subject.

‘Livestock needed to feed the settlers and to work alongside them was taken from Portugal to Madeira. However, as the clearing of the land gradually reduced the pastures, the size of the animals also gradually diminished for lack of food.
Today the descendants of the horses that first populated the island form a variety marked by its small stature: on average Madeiran horses stand 1.22 m high, never exceeding a maximum of 1.30 m.
This is how the variety was described by Mr João Tierno, formerly livestock intendant (*intendente de pecuária*) of Madeira.

‘In general the horses of this variety have a long, slender, lean head; the face straight, or sometimes slightly arched; short ears; prominent orbital arches; a neck of moderate thickness with a fair mane; flat sides; a saddle back; a sloping croup; a large, thick tail; a small, drawn-in belly; and straight limbs with slender bones. They are hardy and frugal, with that enforced frugality imposed by meagre grazing; and the functional exercise to which grazing on steep mountains has accustomed them has given them well-set limbs and hard hooves. These qualities, together with the natural spirit of their mountain temperament, make them fit for work on the island’s rough paths.

This shows that the Madeira pony is the Portuguese horse with a convex profile, the Betic-Lusitanian type, which, despite the smallness to which its scanty diet has reduced it, still retains the elegance of its original forms.

Horses in Madeira are kept on pasture. Even mares far advanced in pregnancy are kept this way, grazing in the mountains, where the foals are born and follow their mothers, with no shelter to protect them from the vagaries of the weather.

Under such conditions it is easy to understand how the Betic-Lusitanian breed, brought to the island, gradually lost its original morphology over five centuries, until it became what is now the Madeiran variety.

Madeira’s horse population has no economic importance. The few good horses seen on the island were brought from the mainland and are used for riding or to draw the very small number of wheeled carriages in the city of Funchal, where urban transport is preferably by luxurious sledges drawn by oxen.

More than once Madeirans have attempted the venture of crossbreeding, with the aim of increasing the size of their ponies; the regime imposed on the animals by the island’s agricultural situation has always frustrated these attempts.’
Fishing industry

This industry is carried on in the two main islands of the archipelago, and it is at Funchal, Caniço, Machico, Câmara de Lobos and Paul do Mar, on the south coast of Madeira, that it is most important. In 1914 there were 537 registered boats, with a tonnage of 1,222.17, expressly designated for fishing in our waters, and in the same year there were 519 boats employed in other maritime services, such as carrying passengers, bumboats, and transporting cargo between the various ports of the archipelago, etc., etc. The fishermen registered as such, who paid their poll tax and contributed to the Shipwreck Relief Institute (*Instituto de Socorros a Náufragos*), numbered 893, of whom 835 were adults and 58 minors. There were, however, other individuals licensed to carry on the fishing industry who took it up only when other work was lacking. With these added, the total of registered fishermen rose to 1648, of whom 1585 were adults and 63 minors.

The main fishing gear used in Madeira comprises nets, rods, the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing), the *agulheira* (mid-water line for garfish), the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream), the cherriola (vertical multi-hook deep-water line), the scoop net (*peneiro*), the jumping poles (*varas de salto*) and fish traps (*covos*) (see those entries). The fishing carried out farthest from the coast is for tuna and for scabbardfish (*espadas*). For the latter a very long line is used, from which short side lines or *chambions* branch off, each ending in a piece of wire that holds the hook. By fastening one or more of these rigs to the gunwale of the boat, a large quantity of scabbardfish can sometimes be taken in a short time. The scabbardfish generally lives at a depth of about a thousand *braças*.

Nets are used to catch *chicharro*, mackerel, *sargos*, *pargos* and other species that come to the surface of the water; the *briqueira* takes grouper, *peixe-rei*, *pargo*, *alfonsim*, *bôca-negra*, *goraz*, *castanheta-do-alto*, etc.; the *agulheira*, *pargos*, *chicharros*, mackerel, etc.; the *gorazeira*, deep-water *salmonete*, hake, *pargo*, *bôca-negra*, *goraz*, *castanheta-do-alto*, etc.; the cherriola, hake, wreckfish (*cherne*), etc.; the scoop net, *castanheta*, *roncador* and other small fish; and the fish traps, moray eels, *salmonetes de rolo*, octopuses, etc. The jumping poles are intended for fishing tuna and skipjack tuna (*gaiado*), which can also be caught with a line when they do not appear at the surface, and fishing rods serve to catch wrasse (*bodiões*), bogue (*bogas*), *douradas*, *dobradas* and many other species that do not grow large. Mackerel, *chicharro*, crab, limpet, squid (*pota*) and spider crab (*aranha do mar*) are widely used as bait, which often varies with the species being sought.

The so-called drag nets (*redes de arrasto*), which have lead weights along one side to make them hang vertically, are used with good results in fishing for species that live near the coast. Some fishermen give the improper name of *peneiros* to the small conical nets sometimes used in fishing for mackerel, *chicharro*, sardine and *guelro* (see that entry).

There is a fishing lamp (*candeio*), which the fishermen call *griseta-cão*, that is often used in night fishing (see Chicharro), and to deceive the fish there is the method of fishing known as *de corrido*, which we have already discussed on p. 320 of volume I of this *Elucidário*.

In 1910 Judice Fialho set up a tuna trap (*armação*, a fixed trap-net) on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), but it produced no results – because, it is said, the waters around that island are very clear. Some time before, in 1903, the late Commanders Manuel Gonçalves and Francisco de Araújo Figueira had tried to establish fixed traps for catching pelagic species, but they too were unsuccessful. This was despite the fact that a specialist and two trap foremen had come to Madeira to study the fishing conditions of our seas, and that a report submitted by the same specialist in October 1903 stated that large-scale fishing in the archipelago, using tuna traps, would be advantageous, naming the Ilhéu de Cima, off Porto Santo, and Machico as the best sites for placing gear for tuna fishing.

The Companhia Atlântica de Pescarias, which sought to exploit the fishing industry in the waters of the archipelago using gear unknown in Portugal, likewise obtained no encouraging results from its operations, and in early December 1921 the Government withdrew the licence it had granted the company for this purpose. In 1792 and 1802 there were two attempts to establish fishing companies in Madeira, but neither was crowned with success. In 1822 experienced fishermen even came from Sesimbra to direct the fishing operations, but this did not prevent the company founded that year from dissolving a short time later.

In 1909 a tuna cannery was established at Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), and in 1912 another at Paul do Mar. These ventures certainly benefited the fishing industry in Madeira, but they caused the price of tuna to rise, and the fish, formerly plentiful, often became scarce in the market. It should be noted, however, that if tuna has lately sold at 2, 3 and even 4 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) a kilo, this is due more to the greed and lack of scruple of the dealers than to the constant demand from the fish-canning industry for the various species of the genus *Thynnus* found in the seas of the archipelago. (1921)

The fishing boats sometimes belong to the crews themselves, and sometimes to merchants with whom the fishermen share the income they earn from the sea. As for the fishing gear, it always, or almost always, belongs to the owner or owners of the boats.

Madeira’s fishermen are known not only for their daring and fearlessness at sea but also for the skill they show in their trade. Poorly favoured by fortune until only a few years ago, they now form a class that lives in relative independence, thanks to the excessive profit they make from selling fish and to their needs being few and easily met. (1921). The income of the fishing industry, which came to about 110 *contos* in 1914, 434 *contos* in 1920 and 977 *contos* in 1921, rose to over 1,155 *contos* between January and November 1922. This was not because the quantities of fish caught were much greater than in 1921 or earlier years, but because sale prices were much higher. Some fishing boats can bring back fish worth more than 3 *contos* in a single trip.

The tax on fish yielded 22,252.65 escudos in 1920, 50,080.94 escudos in 1921 and 59,257.96 escudos from January to November 1922, and the quantity of fish caught each year in the seas of the archipelago is probably between 1,500,000 and 1,800,000 kilograms.

Worship in the chapel of St Elmo (*Corpo Santo*) in Funchal and in the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) in Câmara de Lobos is maintained chiefly by members of the fishing community. In 1769 the fishermen of Câmara de Lobos founded a mutual benefit society under the dedication of Saint Peter González, whose image stands on the altar of the said chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception.

Among the fish caught in Madeiran waters, the finest are the *cherne*, the *alfonsim*, the *salmonete-do-alto*, the *tainha*, the *peixe-galo* and the *abrótea*. They are followed by the *garoupa*, the *salmonete*, the *sargo*, the *goraz*, the *pargo*, the *boqueirão*, the *bodião*, the *atum avoador*, the garfish (*agulha*), the *espada*, the *cavala*, the *chicharro* and the *sardinha*, which are also much sought after and appreciated.

The scarcity or abundance of certain species at certain times of year is explained by changes in the plankton (see Oceanography) due to little-understood causes. Just as grazing animals seek out green pastures because that is where they find their food, so fish seek the places where the organisms they feed on are plentiful. If the plankton fails, the fish that feed directly on it migrate to other regions, since without suitable food no species can live, whether on land or in the ocean.

We lack reliable and recent data on the activity of this industry here in Madeira. We shall present the statistics for the year 1909 offered by the illustrious engineer Adolfo Loureiro in his important work *Portos Maritimos de Portugal*, which were gathered at the Funchal Harbour Master's Office (*Capitania do Porto do Funchal*). The ports where the fishing industry is carried on are the following: Funchal, Caniço, Porto Novo, Aldonça, Santa Cruz, Seixo, Machico, Caniçal, Porto da Cruz, Faial, São Jorge, Ponta Delgada, São Vicente, Seixal, Porto Moniz, Ponta do Pargo, Paul do Mar, Jardim do Mar, Calheta, Fajã do Mar, Madalena do Mar, Anjos, Lugar de Baixo, Tabua, Ribeira Brava, Campanário, Câmara de Lobos and Porto Santo. It should be noted, however, that a large number of these ports are fishing centres of little importance, and some of none at all. The total number of fishermen then reached 2,482, of whom 1,566 were over 18 years of age, 726 were between 12 and 18, and 190 were under 10. The ports of Câmara de Lobos, Paul do Mar and Machico are comparatively very busy and the most important of all, with 575, 336 and 244 people respectively employed in the fishing trades. In number of fishermen these are followed by the ports of Funchal with 153, Porto Santo 156, Caniço 95, Caniçal 90, Santa Cruz 88, Calheta 82, etc. The boats engaged in this industry numbered 509, with a capacity of 1,268 tonnes and a value of 29,113,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The value of the catch was estimated at 126 523$265 *réis*, on which 5,696,572 *réis* was paid in tax.

Somewhat at odds with this information, the *Elucidário Madeirense* gives some official data for the year 1914. It states that the number of fishermen was then 893, 835 adults and 58 minors. There were, however, other individuals licensed to engage in this industry who did so only occasionally, giving a total of 1648 registered fishermen, of whom 1,585 were adults and 63 minors.

The tax levied throughout the archipelago on fish offered for sale produced 4,346.48 escudos in 1930, 3,040.40 escudos in 1931, 2,308.52 escudos in 1932 and 1,259.52 escudos in the first half of 1933.

In the important publication *Estatística das Pescas Maritimas no Continente e Ilhas Adjacentes no ano de 1931....*», we find the following data on our archipelago. In 1927 there were 446 sailing or rowing boats employed in this industry, with 1427 fishermen; in 1928 there were 481 sailing or rowing boats with 1735 fishermen; in 1929 the number of boats was 490, with 1,547 fishermen; in 1930 there were 21 motor boats and 519 sailing or rowing boats with 1,416 fishermen; and in 1931 there were 24 motor boats and 1444 sailing or rowing boats.
Sugar industry

The raw materials supplied by the cultivation of sugar cane and the vine inevitably gave rise to the industries producing sugar, alcohol, spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) and wine. The sugar industry, under the protectionist regime in which it currently operates, is the most important of them all and the one that renders the greatest services to agriculture, as has already been stated above. Sugar production, which in the earliest days of colonisation was the chief source of wealth and prosperity, has varied greatly over the long span of five centuries. This is because it is closely bound up with the flourishing or declining state of the cane fields, which disease at certain times wiped out completely. The sugar consumed in the archipelago, which is of superior quality, is all made in Funchal, and its production in 1932 amounted to four thousand one hundred and seventy-three tonnes.

The alcohol produced is used exclusively for seasoning and fortifying the fortified wines, and without it the proper preparation of wines destined for export would be impossible. In 1932 the alcohol industry produced eight hundred and twelve thousand seven hundred and seventy-seven litres.

The making of spirit, which for many years was the greatest scourge afflicting Madeira, was very considerable and was consumed here at an alarming rate. Fortunately, over the last twenty years it has been cut back to quite modest proportions, which has contributed notably and effectively to combating alcoholism and improving public health. For every reason, it is to be hoped that the prohibitive measures in force will be maintained absolutely and inexorably. At one time as much as two million litres of spirit were produced, although part of it was used to season wines consumed in the archipelago. In 1927 this production was reduced by law to five hundred thousand litres a year, almost all of which was drunk by devotees of this coveted poison, and today production is quite small.

Below we give a note of the total production of sugar cane throughout the archipelago over a number of years, together with the production of sugar and alcohol over the same period. It should be noted that the total cane production also includes the cane used in making spirit (*aguardente*).

Wine industry

Because of its remarkable importance and the particular characteristics that set it apart, this industry has been, through the ages, not only one of the greatest sources of public wealth in this archipelago but also, together with the mildness of the climate and the enchanting landscape, one of the most notable factors in the widespread fame that the name of Madeira enjoys.

A few years after its settlement this island was already producing some wines, for Cadamosto, who was here around 1450, refers to them and to the cultivation of the vine. A warrant (*provisão*) of 1485 authorised the imposition of the wine levy (imposição do vinho) to meet the expenses of the municipality (*concelho*), and the charters of 1515 ordered that tithes be paid on the island’s wine.

According to Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara, Madeira exported its Malmsey and dry wines to the court of Francis I of France, who came to the throne in 1515 and died in 1547, at the time of the wars in which that sovereign had embroiled his realms; and Rebelo da Silva says in the *Historia de Portugal* that Belgium was already importing the island’s wines in 1567. We have read somewhere that an old register of this city’s customs house records that in 1566 Madeira exported some wines and that the price of a *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine then stood at 3,200 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). There is also the account of Lopes’s voyage, written in 1588 and published in *Purchas’ Pilgrinages*, and Frutuoso’s ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), written in 1590, both of which refer to the export of our wines in the 16th century. On p. 113 of the latter work we read that ‘Malmsey wine is the best to be found in the universe, and is taken to India and to many parts of the world’.

However, although it is well established that Madeira produced wines in the 15th century and that they were already being exported in the 16th, it is the opinion of Dr Azevedo, borne out by various facts, that exports began on a large scale only after 1640, and especially after the close alliance between Portugal and England sealed by the marriage of the Infanta Queen Catherine to Charles II in 1660. This was because many English merchants had settled in Madeira to take up this line of business, and our government heaped privileges and exemptions upon them.

In 1621 the Council and the inhabitants of Funchal requested a royal warrant admitting only Portuguese wines into Brazil, so that those of this island could easily be exported there. It seems, however, that nothing was done to protect our viticulture until 1643, when John IV sent a letter to the superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*) instructing him to obtain wines here for the fleets.

In 1646, says the annotator of the *Saudades*, Madeira exported some 2,000 *pipas* of wine. Christopher Jeaffreson, who called at this island in 1676 on his voyage to the West Indies, states that he was told that in some years wine production amounted to 25,000 *pipas*, and he lists the imported goods that were bartered for these wines and for the sweetmeats made here. Jeaffreson had a quantity of wine loaded on to his ship bound for St Kitts.

Around 1680, according to Paulo Perestrelo, there were in the city of Funchal some ten English trading houses, another ten belonging to various other foreigners and six or eight Portuguese ones. They bought the wines ready-made and exported them, taking consumer goods in return. Some merchants began to distil the lower-grade wines into spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), which they shipped to Brazil and the coast of Africa together with other imported goods, receiving slaves and gold in exchange.

The English traveller Atkins, who visited Funchal in 1720, says that he managed to acquire two *pipas* of wine here, giving two used suits for one and three second-hand wigs for the other. This report can be trusted only if we accept that the traveller confused *pipas* with gallons. What cannot be doubted, however, is that in olden times the barter of certain objects for wine was very common on the island: the Englishman Paterson, leader of an expedition that visited Madeira in 1698, relates that some of its members traded certain braided or embroidered articles of clothing here for wine and other provisions.

An article published in 1882 in the *Wine and Spirits News* states that Madeira wine had become very well known in England in the 18th century, and that in 1799, on 14 October, a convoy of 96 ships anchored in the harbour of Funchal to load 3,041 *pipas* of wine for the West Indies, part of which was then to go on to England.

José Soares da Silva, who around 1730 wrote the *Memorias para a historia do governo de D. João o I*, states there that Madeira ‘exported more than 20,000 *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine every year, besides spirits’. An old set of statistics records that exports stood at 7,073 *pipas* in 1774, 10,819 in 1788, 13,713 in 1790, 16,891 in 1800, 22,000 in 1813, 18,000 in 1818, 10,115 in 1821 and 14,432 in 1825.
By 1830 exports had fallen to 5,994 *pipas*, but they later recovered markedly: 8,875 *pipas* left the island in 1834, 9,782 in 1840, 7,054 in 1844, 14,445 in 1849, 13,875 in 1850 and 12,356 in 1851.

In 1852 only 5,676 *pipas* were exported, already as a result of the *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium) that was then devastating the island’s vineyards. Between 1853 and 1881 the largest quantity of wine exported was 4,204 *pipas*, in 1853, and the smallest 536, in 1865.
Exports of Madeira wine from 1910 to 1932 are shown in the following table. The quantities are easily converted into *pipas*, since each shipping *pipa* (see that entry) corresponds to 418 litres:

In 1920, 1921 and 1922 France imported 413,343, 95,458 and 1,705,187 litres of Madeira wines respectively; Germany 9,703,000, 72,381 and 348,428; England 304,437, 419,594 and 217,800; Sweden 1,111,033, 189,108 and 371,403; Denmark 297,465, 337,169 and 872,925; and Brazil 208,570, 33,923 and 68,740. In the days of the Empire, Russia was one of the chief importers of Madeira wines, receiving 770,840 litres in 1899, 674,600 in 1900, 491,420 in 1901 and 239,710 in 1902.

France was the country that imported the largest quantities of Madeira wine in 1922. However, the lack of a trade agreement with that country, based on the reform of our tariffs, meant that, after twelve years under a *modus vivendi* – with numerous short-term extensions obtained in recent times – the entry of our fortified wines was banned there in 1923, to the grave detriment of Madeiran and Portuguese wine-growing.
Our finest wines are today exported mainly to Sweden, Denmark and Norway, where they are consumed in large quantities (1921).

The wars between France and England, the American War of Independence and the campaigns of France against Europe, and especially against England (1754-1761, 1775-1783 and 1793-1815), gave rise, says Dr Azevedo, to a great demand for our wines. From 1810 to 1815 exports reached an average of some 20,000 *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) a year. However, the adulteration or counterfeiting of these wines, carried out not only abroad but even on the island itself, gradually brought about the decline of a branch of trade that had remained fairly prosperous for more than half a century.

In 1809 7,000 to 8,500 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) was paid for a barrel of must, and the merchant sold the wine at 250,000 to 400,000 *réis* a *pipa*. In 1922 and 1923 the price of must ranged, respectively, between 30 and 35 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) and between 85 and 110 escudos, while a *pipa* of wine fetched an average price of 30 pounds abroad. If one considers the value of our currency at the beginning of the 19th century and at present, it is easy to see that, although the conditions of our viticulture and winemaking have improved remarkably in recent years, they are nevertheless not as prosperous now as they were in times long past.

In earlier times, to prevent winegrowers from adulterating their wines, whether by fortifying them with low-quality brandies or by blending them with weak wines, a series of measures appeared: the decree of 22 December 1800, regulating and policing the marks on casks; the decree of 22 July 1801, prohibiting the admission of wines from the Azores into Madeira; the orders of the Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) barring wines from mainland Portugal from entering this island; and finally the municipal by-law (*postura*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of 27 May 1837, which sought to prevent the wines of the northern parishes (*freguesia*) from passing to those of the south. ‘But counterfeiting,’ says Dr Azevedo, ‘especially abroad, continued on a large scale, and the discredit and competition it brought upon the genuine wines of Madeira greatly harmed the esteem, value and consumption they had enjoyed.’

‘At the same time,’ the same author says further, ‘other wines, such as port, sherry, the wines of Sicily and of France, and, from 1815, that of the Cape of Good Hope, flooded into the English market, and some of them became favourites of the palates of the wealthy. Thus, with Europe at peace in that year of 1825, and as agriculture developed, the then new generation grew accustomed to those other wines, to the detriment of those of Madeira, especially from 1825 onwards. This is shown by the interesting table of wines imported from various countries for consumption in England from 1784 to 1842, included in the article “Wine” of the *Dictionary. . . of commerce. . .*, by J. R. Mc. Cullosh. For the year 1784 this table records no import at all of Madeira wine; for the period 1786 to 1794 it gives 196,140 gallons; for 1805 to 1814, 354,050; for 1815 to 1820, 353,940; for the year 1821, 400,476; for 1825, 372,504; and then, in gradual decline, it reaches 1842, a year in which England imported only 65,509 gallons. *Quantum mutatus ab illo!* – Under the converging blows of fraud, competition and fashion, the trade in Madeira wines in the British markets therefore went into decline.','

‘In compensation, however, though not a complete one, in the decade from 1830 to 1840 these wines gained ever greater standing in the markets of the Hanseatic cities, Russia, Holland and other parts of Europe, and in the United States of America. The United States of America imported some 4,200 *pipas* annually; the Muscovite empire, 2,000; the other countries, about 3000. As a result, the export of wine from this island, which in 1830 had fallen, as we have already said, to 5,994 *pipas*, steadily increased, reaching 9,782 in 1840, at a price of 30 to 44 pounds sterling per *pipa*.’

To prevent grapes of inferior varieties being mixed in the wine presses with those that produce the fortified wines of Madeira, there was formerly in each parish a general inspector chosen by the Municipal Council, with authority to appoint sub-inspectors charged with ‘supervising the purity of the grape harvests and the proper selection of the grapes, and all else concerning the quality of the crop’.

The first appointment of inspectors for the grape harvests was made, we believe, at the council meeting of 21 August 1820, and at the meeting of 3 September 1836 those appointed to these posts were urged to avoid mixing ‘the grapes of bad wine, such as those called *cachudo*, *malvazião*, *carão de dama*, *maroto*, etc., with grapes of good quality’.

We said earlier that it was around 1660 that the export of Madeira wines began to grow, thanks to the impetus given to it by British merchants. Yet these merchants, whom our monarchs showered with privileges, even exempting them from the tax of 400 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) on every *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine exported, introduced in 1646, later became the cruellest enemies of Madeiran viticulture.

Since they were almost the only buyers of wine, the British merchants became, as Dr Azevedo says, the supreme arbiters of its price, and everyone was left in complete subjection to them. At the end of the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th this subjection was hardly apparent, because the wines, thanks to their high price, paid owners and farmers a decent return. But as soon as those same wines began to decline, a long era of misery and privation began for many Madeirans, bringing profound changes to the economic situation of our island. ‘Before the abominable treaty of 1810,’ says Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara, ‘the English were forbidden to buy wine as must; but once this was permitted them, they became the arbiters of this commodity and the true masters of the land.’

Had it not been for a few respectable Portuguese trading houses on the island, foremost among them that of the holder of the entail (*morgado*) João da Câmara de Carvalhal, later Count of Carvalhal, the British merchants would have exercised the most deplorable tyranny here unchecked, while abroad they reaped the still considerable profits of exporting our wines. Several times these houses set remunerative prices for the must, to prevent it being bought at the derisory prices the English merchants established here sought to pay.

In 1852 *Oidium Tuckeri* appeared on the island and destroyed most of its vineyards, bringing poverty to many homes and forcing many Madeirans to emigrate to Brazil and other countries. Yet the dreadful crisis that then ravaged our land regenerated it, as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo judiciously remarks in his notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’. ‘With the wine gone, the English merchant wound up his affairs as best he could and withdrew; of the old British houses there remained only those of Newton Gordon & Comp.ª, J. W. & T. Selby, Blandy, and Rutterford & Grant, the last two sustained chiefly by the valuable coal trade. Thus Madeira was freed from its capitalist masters. The peasant, spurred by necessity, devoted himself to the lands he farmed, working them not with a single crop, as the vine had been until then, but with several: sugar cane, which soon gave him more and quicker money than wine had in recent times; and cereals, pulses, sweet and ordinary potatoes, yams and vegetables, which soon brought back to his home the prosperity and joy that had so long eluded it.’

From 1872 to 1883 Madeira suffered fresh devastation, this time from the phylloxera invasion. Once its vineyards had been reconstituted by introducing resistant rootstocks, onto which the old varieties were grafted, the island again produced its delicious and celebrated wines. Unfortunately, however, the methods of adulteration we have already mentioned had not been forgotten. The way they were abused, chiefly abroad, where the labels of reputable exporting houses were even imitated to ease the acceptance of the commonest concoctions, did much to devalue our island’s principal product. It also made the grower’s position very critical, since merchants paid him derisory prices for his must, because they had difficulty finding buyers for their wines.

By exhausting the stocks of genuine Madeira wine, the Great War helped to raise the value of the harvests and stimulate exports. But if exports are to be maintained and developed, as is in the island’s interest, it is necessary, as everyone knows, that the flavour, body and aroma of the wine are not altered by adulteration. Blending our wines with weak wines from Portugal, or adulterating them in any other way, even one not harmful to health, is a mistake, or rather a crime, that could seriously damage the economy of this island, which has already suffered so many upheavals through the greed and lack of scruple of certain merchants.

In some foreign markets the abuse is quite often committed of presenting wines produced in Spain, Greece and other countries as coming from Madeira. This abuse must also be stopped. To that end it is necessary to enforce and extend the clauses of the Washington convention of 2 June 1911 and the provisions of articles 274 and 275 of the peace treaty signed at Versailles on 28 June 1919 between Germany on the one side and 27 powers on the other, one of them Portugal.

It is claimed that some wine-growers, in order to obtain more alcohol than they need and are entitled to, submit exaggerated returns of the must produced on their properties. If this is true, it is an abuse that certainly harms the interests of the island, since the surplus alcohol can be used in adulteration. On 15 October 1919 an attempt was made to obtain a law in Parliament authorising our wine-makers to use in preparing Madeira wines the same quantities of alcohol as are applied to port wines. Such a law, which would only have served to encourage fraud, was never approved. With alcohol and sugar in abundance, some merchants would have no need to buy from the farmer the wine required to fill the orders arriving from abroad.

Using grapes suited to making table wines in the preparation of fortified wines, although not a genuine fraud, should nevertheless be avoided, by creating special Madeiran types of table wine, as the regulations of 1913 permit. Some years ago a well-known oenologist succeeded in making a type of Madeiran table wine which some tasters considered of excellent quality.

Among the present (1921) exporters of Madeira wine we shall mention the following: Companhia Vinícola da Madeira; António Isidro Gonçalves; Tarquínio Torquato da Câmara Lomelino; Freitas Martins, Caldeira & C.ª; Júlio A. Cunha, Sucessores; Portugal, Santos & C.ª; F. F. Ferraz & C.ª; Luís Gomes da Conceição & Filhos; João Carlos de Aguiar & C.ª; Artur Barros Sousa; F. M. Sardinha & C.ª; João Teodoro Figueira; The Madeira Wine Association; Cossart, Gordon & C.ª; Blandy Brothers & C.ª; Leacock & C.ª; Henrique P. Miles; and Power, Drury & C.ª. Our wines are sold abroad through agents whom the exporting houses maintain there for that purpose.

We have dealt with the export of Madeira wines and with the need to restore to them the well-deserved reputation they once enjoyed in many foreign countries. We shall now present some data on the production, the principal types and the making of these wines, in order to complete the account we set out to write of one of the chief sources of wealth of our island.

Wine production, which stood at 25,440 *pipas* (wine casks) in 1813, had fallen to 20,986 *pipas* in 1847, to 11,140 in 1850, to 2,277 in 1852, to 660 in 1853, to 138 in 1854 and to 38 in 1855. From 1856 onwards a small increase in production can be seen compared with those last two years, but in 1858 it still did not exceed 197 *pipas*, and it fell to 162 the following year. In 1861 and 1865 production was 400 and 5,000 *pipas* respectively. In 1882, when phylloxera (see that entry) was still wreaking great havoc in the island’s vineyards, it was about 4,500 *pipas*, dropping to 3,500 in 1883.

The grafting of the old grape varieties onto resistant rootstocks and the large-scale use of Jacquez as a direct producer greatly improved the island’s situation in the following years. Production reached some 8,000 *pipas* in 1895, 9,200 in 1900 and 11,401 in 1909.

Funchal and Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) are the municipalities with the largest wine production, followed by the municipalities of São Vicente, Porto Moniz, Porto Santo and Calheta. The fortified wines come from the south coast of Madeira, especially from Câmara de Lobos and Funchal, but the wines of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), on the north coast, are as a rule of very good quality.

The principal Madeiran wines are the following: Malmsey, Boal, Sercial (white grape variety), Verdelho, Tinta and Madeira. The first four take their names from the grapes that produce them; the last comes from blending various Madeiran grape varieties in the wine press.

Malmsey is sweet and aromatic and, in the view of Frutuoso and of modern English consumers, the most valuable of the Madeira wines. Boal is also aromatic and ‘excellent for the table or toast’. Sercial is dry and cannot be drunk before eight or ten years; at that age, however, it is regarded ‘as one of the most delicate and wholesome wines of the island’. Verdelho is strong and aromatic and ‘is of great value for the table’; and Tinta is sweet and aromatic, especially while young, and owes its colour to the grape skins left in the wine during fermentation. Madeira, the most common of the island’s wines, comes from grapes of various varieties pressed together in the wine presses, and may be more or less strong and more or less aromatic according to its age and composition.

It is Madeira that the island exported, and still exports, on a large scale. In the English markets this wine was once known as East or West India Madeira when it had been sent out to those countries to improve through the action of the heat, and as London Particular when it had not made such a voyage.

In Madeira a wine called *surdo* is made by adding large quantities of alcohol to the musts. This wine, which retains part of its sugar, is used to give body to other wines and also to sweeten them. It was once known in England, to which small quantities of it were exported, as Nuns’s wine.

We said earlier that the present average price of a *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine was 30 pounds, but we are told that some old wines have lately been sold at 100 pounds. Johnson, who wrote his *Handbook* in 1885, states there that the price of Madeira wine ranges from 25 to 300 pounds per *pipa*, and at the beginning of the 19th century, in the period of great exports, the price varied between 55 and 90 pounds. A *pipa* of wine cost 15, 18 and 20 pounds before the last war (1914-1918), about 40 pounds in 1878 (average price), 50 to 80 pounds in 1856, 25 to 50 some years earlier and 30 to 44 in 1840.

The grape harvest takes place in September, but in warm, sunny spots it can begin at the end of August, and in high, cold places it can last until the middle of October. The grapes are crushed in the wine press by barefoot men, and beside the press stands a vat to receive the must. Once the grapes have been pressed, the pomace is piled in the centre of the press and bound in a spiral with a thick rope. Boards are then laid on top of it, and on these the beam exerts its pressure: a thick timber tightened by means of a screw that passes through one of its ends and is fixed below to what is called the press stone.

Compressed in this way, the pomace yields a further quantity of must, which runs out through the spout of the press into the vat standing at a lower level. The work of extracting the grape juice is not yet finished, however, for there remains the second treading (*repisa*), a final crushing of the pomace, likewise carried out by barefoot men inside the press. This operation is extremely strenuous and can only be done well by young, healthy men.

Piquette (*água-pé*, thin drink made from pomace and water) is made by pouring water over the pomace and pressing it again. When alcohol is added, it gives a weak wine that is drunk in the countryside of the island.

The must is carried in barrels or in goatskins to the grower’s wine store, where it is poured into pipes or vats and ferments, as a rule for two months. When fermentation is over, the wines are drawn off the lees and transferred to other casks, previously washed, disinfected with lime and finally sulphured. There they are clarified with eggs, milk, ox blood or clay.

After clarification the wines are sent to the *estufas* (heated store for ageing Madeira wine), unless they are being matured by the canteiro system (natural ageing of the wine in casks on wooden supports, without artificial heating). It was once the custom to add alcohol to the wine before heating, but today the most common practice is to add none until afterwards. Alcohol distilled from sugar cane is now used in treating our wines. Around the middle of the 19th century, however, the alcohol used for this purpose was made from the wines of the north, and at the beginning of that century foreign brandies were often used to treat the island’s wines. The records of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) contain several petitions from the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) asking for the import of these brandies into Madeira to be banned.

To weak Madeiran wines 10 to 11 per cent of alcohol is generally added, to better wines 6 per cent, and to *vinho surdo* (sweet must fortified to stop fermentation, used for sweetening) 30 per cent. This last wine serves, as we have already said, to improve other wines and give them body, and its use is preferable to that of sugar syrup, which growers once used widely. Boiled must (*arrobe*) is little used today in treating wines.

According to Dr Ferreira da Silva, Madeiran musts have a sugar content of 19 to 28 per cent. Kickton and Murdfield state that, to prepare the fortified wines of Madeira, ‘it is necessary to increase the noble and vinous quality by adding musts that have been made *surdo* (*abafado* or *surdo* wines, *jeropigas*), and liquids distilled from wine’. They go on to add, however, that alcohol, as a rectified product of sugar cane, is also used on a large scale on the island to season the wines. The same authors further state that Madeira wine is a dessert wine of a distinctive character, prepared exclusively on the Portuguese island of Madeira, and that its composition varies considerably across analytical results. This is due not only to the sugar content, which differs among the various base wines, but above all to the variety of sweetening methods employed.

The decree regulating the trade in and production of Madeira wines dates from 8 November 1913. Another, which appeared in 1915, failed to gain approval after the press, the administrative bodies and the people of the island rose up against it. The main provisions of this latter decree, and what was said and written about it, are set out in a publication entitled *A Imprensa, as Colectividades do Distrito e o Projecto de Regulamentação da Produção, Fiscalização e comercio dos Vinhos da Madeira* (Funchal), (1916).

From the middle of January 1924 a commission sat in Funchal, charged by the Ministry of Agriculture with proposing to the Government the amendments to be made to the regulation of 8 November 1913, so that wines might be inspected as strictly as possible and adulteration prevented.

On the purchase of musts from growers and the export of wines, the civil governor José Nosolini issued a Regulation dated 18 October 1939, which lays down the conditions under which such purchases and exports must be made.

The following writings provide valuable information on the subject of this article: *Os vinhos da Madeira e o seu descredito pelas estufas*, 1889, *Noticia sobre o vinho Canavial*, 1882, and *Os tres sistemas de tratamento dos vinhos da Madeira*, 1900, all by the Count of Canavial; *O Vinho da Madeira. Como se prepara um nectar*, 1937, by J. Reis Gomes; *Os Vinhos da Madeira*, 1935, by Nuno Simões; *Acção Bactericida do Vinho Madeira* by Dr Vicente Henriques de Gouveia, 1930; and *Vinho da Madeira* by Ferreira da Silva.
See Alcohol, Estufas, Vineyards, Vinho de roda and Vinho de canteiro.
Industries

In the preceding pages we gave an overview of industrial activity in this archipelago in its principal aspects. In this article we give a brief account of other industries which, although of lesser importance, deserve a place here for the information of some of the readers of this work.

At present (1921) Madeira has 2 fish canneries, 1 tobacco factory (see that entry), 1 stearin candle factory, 2 wax candle factories, 1 brewery, 2 soft-drink factories, 2 soap factories (see Soap works), 2 nail factories, 1 factory of cement roof tiles and floor tiles, 6 sawmills, 5 factories of biscuits and crackers, 7 pasta factories, 1 chemical fertiliser factory and 1 paint factory. There are also a foundry, several small butter factories (see that entry), 7 cheese factories, 5 potteries, 6 mills and about 300 watermills for grinding cereals, and various cabinet-making workshops, some of which make very elegant furniture that rivals what comes from Portugal. There are small tanneries and a great number of wine presses where the grapes that yield the island’s delicious wines are pressed (see Wines), *estufas* (heated store for ageing Madeira wine) (see that entry) for treating those same wines, 2 workshops for minor ship repairs and shipbuilding, various fireworks workshops, several lime kilns, many looms, etc., etc. Embroiderers (see Embroidery) are spread throughout the island, and there are also makers of botas chãs (traditional flat-soled leather boots), or potato-skin boots, of rye-straw hats and of wickerwork (see Camacha, Broom and Osier), as well as people engaged in dyeing, although this industry is still very backward here. Special mention is also due to the industry of wood inlay which, though little developed, has a characteristic regional character and is much appreciated by foreigners (see Inlaid work).

The industries of stearin candles, nails, cheese, chemical fertilisers, paints, cement tiles, biscuits and crackers, and tuna canning are modern on the island. Tuna canning is carried on at the Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’) factory, founded in 1909, and at the Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’) factory, founded in 1912. All the remaining industries are more or less old, some dating back to the 15th and 16th centuries, such as sugar, milling, soap, sawmilling, broom wares, etc., etc.

The Ponta da Cruz cannery exported 557,085 kilos of tuna to Portugal in 1910, the year in which it prepared the largest quantity of fish. The stearin candle factory referred to above came to supply more than 60,000 packets a year, but it has now reduced its production for reasons unknown to us.
