Many tallow candles were once made in Funchal, but this industry began to disappear around 1878, when stearin candles from England, sold at very modest prices, flooded our market. In earlier times tallow candles were found in the homes of rich and poor alike, and were sold at 20 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) each.

Before the war, the mills and watermills of Madeira and the windmills of Porto Santo ground 9 to 10 million kilograms of wheat, of which 7 to 8 million were imported; 11 to 12 million kilograms of maize, almost all of it imported; and about 350 thousand kilograms of barley and rye, grown on the island. In the time of the donataries only they could own cereal mills and public ovens, although anyone was permitted to have a hand mill, provided he did not grind for others.

The sawing of timber is, like milling, a fairly old industry. Frutuoso refers to it, as does the letter of grant (carta de doação) of the captaincy of Funchal made by Prince Henry the Navigator to João Gonçalves Zarco. According to that chronicler, ‘on the island there was so great a quantity of timber, so fine and hard, that an abundance of boards, beams and masts was carried to many parts, all of which was sawn with engines or water-powered saws, of which there are still many today on the north side of the same island.’ On this subject it is worth reading the pamphlet *Serras de Agua na Ilha da Madeira e Porto Santo* (‘Water Saws on the Island of Madeira and Porto Santo’), published in 1937 by Dr Jordão de Freitas.
Instead of the water-powered saws, there are now several sawmills driven by steam power, six of them the principal ones, as stated above.

Frutuoso mentions the soap and wickerwork industries. The former was a monopoly until the publication of the law of 25 April 1857. By 1860 there were already two soap factories, and two exist at present too, although large quantities of soap are nevertheless imported from Portugal for consumption on the island.

In 1856 there was a brewery in Funchal, and metal founding perhaps dates from 1834. Eighty years ago iron, tin, copper and zinc were already being cast in the workshops of José Pires Soares and William Hinton, using blast furnaces, with the bellows worked by hand or by horses. If this industry did not grow at once here, it was because large quantities of metal goods of various kinds came from England and were sold here at low prices. Besides the foundry now (1921) established in Rua 5 de Junho, there was until a few years ago another in the former Rua da Princesa.

Although rye-straw plaiting for hat-making is carried out in Funchal and Camacha, it is in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’) that this industry is most developed and the finest work is done. The weavers of this last parish (*freguesia*) also plait the straw from which openwork hats for ladies are made.

Cheese-making, stagnant for years but now apparently making progress, is carried on in Faial, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Ponta do Sol and Canhas. Adolfo Burnay made the first cheeses in Madeira, in a dairy he set up in Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) in 1895. That attempt was unsuccessful, however, and only fifteen years later did some cheeses begin to appear in the municipality (*concelho*) of Ponta do Sol which, thanks to their pleasant flavour and good preparation, won public favour.

Looms are widespread across the island, weaving linen, tow cloth and mixed fabrics of linen and wool (*seriguilha* (homespun linen-and-wool cloth), *marafuz* (coarse homespun linen-and-wool cloth), etc.). According to a set of statistics before us, about eighty years ago the whole district produced 143,000 metres of linen, 3,300 of tow cloth and 7,800 of mixed fabrics. Today, however, this output has fallen perhaps by half, because homespun cloth is less in demand for household use. The municipalities of Calheta, Sant’Ana and Ponta do Sol produce the greatest quantity of linen and linen-and-wool fabrics.

Not only the sailing and rowing boats that serve the waters of the archipelago are built in Madeira, but also the small steamer *Vitoria*, which used to sail along the south coast of Madeira. This steamer was built in Machico. More than fifty years ago, to the east of the former Praça Académica (‘academic square’), Madeiran workmen built the small but excellent steamer *Queen*, which, after sailing in our waters, went on to serve on the Tagus. In 1920 the yacht *Gonçalves Zargo* was built in the Cabrestante (‘capstan’) enclosure, and another vessel of greater tonnage than that one – the yacht *Anfitrite*, likewise intended for voyages on the high seas – is now (1921) under construction in the Campo do Almirante Reis (‘Admiral Reis field’).

There are three potteries in Funchal, the most important of which is the Funchalense, on the Estrada do Conde de Carvalhal. It is expected that a first-class establishment for the manufacture of glass (see Trachytes) and of roof tiles, bricks, etc. will shortly be set up in the locality (*sítio*) of Gorgulho (1921). The raw materials used in the island’s ceramics are red clay, white sand and saltpetre from Portugal, and *massapez* (heavy ferruginous clay soil) clay from Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’); the latter, however, has the drawback of sometimes cracking when not combined with another clay, owing to an excess of ferric oxide. At Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) curved roof tiles, jugs and other objects are made using only the local clay.

Frutuoso says that on Porto Santo there were many dragon trees, from whose trunks a great deal of ware was made. Today, however, these trees are extinct on that island, and in Madeira, where they are very rare, they are not used for anything at all. Spoons and other objects are made from the wood of heath and *folhado* (Clethra arborea, a native tree) in Camacha and other parishes.

In the countryside of Madeira, and especially in Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), pasta is made by means of very rudimentary machines built on the island. Establishments equipped with improved machinery for the same purpose exist only in Funchal and Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).

The confectionery industry was of some importance in Funchal, as we saw on p. 298 of volume I of this *Elucidario*. Among Madeira’s small cottage industries, mention should be made of feather and paper flowers, birdcages, palm-leaf hats (see Caniço) and ginger beer. The women of Madeira, says Frutuoso, ‘besides being very well favoured, very beautiful, discreet and virtuous, are outstanding in the perfection of rich and exquisite dishes of every kind, and in all the inventions of rich things they make, not only on cloth with polished needlework, but also in sugar with delicate fruits.’

At the end of 1912 there were 494 registered industrial establishments in the whole district, and the industrial workforce numbered 3,547 persons: 209 employees, 287 masters and foremen, and 3,051 workers. The last class comprised 2,042 men, 426 women, 288 boys and 295 girls.

Although Madeira is a more agricultural than industrial country, there are nonetheless industries that may be considered vigorous here, and others that hold out promise and are already more or less profitable today. The workforce is as a rule active and intelligent, and if it does not always produce work free of certain defects, this is because its limited education, not only literary but also artistic, does not allow it to advance as it should.

The industry processing the products of sugar cane is among the most valuable on the island; also very important are embroidery, butter, milling, soap, foundry work and beer. These last two industries, which were carried on by Portuguese, are now in the hands of foreigners, and it was likewise an English industrialist who for many years held the monopoly of sugar manufacture throughout the district.
Infante (peak)
A mountain peak in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), north of the locality (*sítio*) of Choupana (‘hut’).
Inferno (stream)

It rises in the mountains of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) and separates that parish from the parish of Seixal (‘pebble shore’) before flowing into the ocean. Along the banks of this stream and in its inner reaches lie some of the most breathtaking scenery in our island, where one frequently comes upon the most fearsome and deepest precipices. The water of this stream feeds a levada (irrigation channel), which irrigates the land of the parish of São Vicente.
Ethnic influences

The first groups of settlers who came to colonise this archipelago in the second quarter of the 15th century were made up of inhabitants of mainland Portugal, especially from the provinces of Minho and the Algarve. Most of them were recruited from among farmers and field labourers, but there were also a good many craftsmen, who practised the so-called mechanical arts.

The captain-donataries brought with them some relatives and other people from their close circle. Earlier in this work (vol. I, p. 293) we gave the names of fourteen individuals, some of noble origin, who shared with João Gonçalves Zarco the labours of the first settlement. The same would have happened with the donataries Tristão Vaz Teixeira in Machico and Bartolomeu Perestrelo on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).

Dr Gaspar Frutuoso gives us this curious piece of information, which various reasons persuade us is not without foundation: ‘. . . the King gave leave to any person who wished to come with him (Zargo) to settle the said islands, both Porto Santo and Madeira. He ordered that the murderers and convicts in the prisons and throughout the Kingdom be handed over, and of these João Gonçalves would take none who were guilty of crimes against the faith, or of treason, or of theft; of those guilty of other crimes and homicides he took all there were, and they were well treated by him; and of the other people, those who of their own will sought a living and fortune, there were many, most of them from the Algarve’.

It is not surprising that this should have happened, given the shortage of people for an attempt at colonisation in so remote a region and under entirely unknown conditions. It should also be noted that at all times and in all places criminals and convicts have always supplied a large contingent to fledgling settlements. This circumstance could have had no influence on the ethnic purity of the population, nor even on its customs and traits of character, because that small batch of convicts was relatively insignificant compared with the great number of colonists who came from many parts of Portugal.

It cannot be denied, however, that the great multitude of Moors, Black Africans and mulattoes brought to these islands in the early days of colonisation, and in later periods too, markedly adulterated the native purity of the Portuguese race. They imprinted on it certain characteristics of the ethnic origins from which they came, and these can still be seen at present in many inhabitants of some rural localities. We have already pointed this out in the extended article on Slaves (I-407), and we shall return to the subject in the article we shall devote to the Moors.

The number of foreigners from various European countries who settled in Madeira at the beginning of colonisation, and particularly in the 16th and 17th centuries, was also quite considerable. It is therefore not surprising that their intermarriage with the natives should have produced, in some centres of population, certain facial features characteristic of other European races. Several visitors have observed this in their travel narratives, and it can still be seen among us today. On this point, the reader should consult the article Foreigners, on p. 419 of the 1st volume of this work.

Although one may disagree with some of the assertions made in the chapters ‘Povoadores’ and ‘Origem Étnica’ of the esteemed work ‘Zargo’s Islands’ (*Ilhas de Zargo*), there is no doubt that it contains valuable information and material for the study of the subject that heads this short article.
The English

In the article on the grant (*doação*) of the island of Madeira to the Infanta Dona Catarina we have already referred to the attempts said to have been made by the English government to obtain possession of this archipelago at the time of the marriage of the Portuguese infanta Queen Catherine to Charles II, King of England. The question was treated at length by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in one of the notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). Although he does not prove conclusively there that negotiations were opened between the two governments for the cession of Madeira, there can be no doubt that on this and other occasions British diplomacy sought to seize the opportunity to voice these aspirations, which are believed to go back a long way. After that period there are positive and eloquent facts that clearly demonstrate the wishes of our old ally. The two occupations of Madeira by English troops, carried out in the name of protection and defence against supposed attacks by Napoleonic forces, amounted to a genuine conquest. This is proved not only by many diplomatic documents of the time but also by the way the British administered the public affairs of this archipelago: the Portuguese authorities kept only a semblance of power, which in reality lay solely with the commander-in-chief of the British forces (see Occupation of Madeira by English troops). The Madeirans suffered every kind of humiliation during the eight years that these occupations lasted. Despite the resolutions adopted at the Congress of Vienna, under which England was to evacuate this island without delay, it is certain that in many European chancelleries, and even in the highest circles of the Portuguese government, the occupation of Madeira was thought to amount to absolute and permanent possession. It is to the distinguished diplomat then representing Portugal in London, Dom Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho, that the evacuation of this archipelago and its return to the Portuguese nation are owed. Through his eminent qualities as a statesman and his numerous writings published abroad, he rendered many signal services to his country. Our government honoured him with the title of Count, and later Marquis, of Funchal, a title still borne today by the representatives of his family. If we are still Portuguese, it is chiefly to him that we owe it; and yet there is nothing in this city to commemorate this fact or to pay even a small tribute to the memory of the illustrious diplomat.

During the period of our civil wars, when British diplomacy interfered so much in our internal affairs, England once again hinted at its old and never-forgotten desires. It always did so in a veiled manner, however, which was never confirmed by facts leaving any trace in the diplomatic relations between the two countries. It is certain, nonetheless, that in the political circles of the time the matter was sometimes discussed with a certain insistence, above all at the moments when England’s help was most needed.

In 1897 the English newspaper *The Empire* put forward the idea that the Madeiran archipelago should be ceded to England, or else purchased. The suggestion was taken up by other British papers, although it is true that some important, widely read London newspapers rejected outright what seemed to be the start of a deliberately prepared campaign.

In the article Foreigners we made no special reference to the English or to subjects of any other nationality. The British colony in Madeira, however, deserves a short article of its own at this point in the *Elucidário*, on account of its age, the number of its members, the importance it enjoys among us and other particular circumstances.

The number of English people who came to these parts does not seem to have been large in the early days of colonisation, nor during the 15th century and the beginning of the 16th. In those times the foreigners who landed on this island in the greatest numbers were many from northern Europe, notably Flemings, and also from the south, especially Genoese, drawn by the spirit of adventure and still more by industrial and commercial trade (see Foreigners). Only towards the end of the 16th century did the English colony grow and begin to gain real importance, and Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo states ‘that their settlement in Madeira in greater numbers than before dates from 1640.’
The English consulate on this island was created in 1658, and João Cater was the first to hold it. We can present a list, which we do not consider complete, of other individuals who held this office:

Richard Milty, João Arls and Guilherme Bolton (all in 1691), Benjamin Henrique (1705), Thomás Morgan (1709), Diogo Clarque (1726), Ricardo Baker (1734), Matheus Itnox (1738), Carlos Chambres (1750), Guilherme Naich (1756), Carlos Murray (1787), José Pringle (1803), Archibald Brown (1805), Henrique Veitch (1813), George Stoddart, G. Hayward and W. Keen.

We have a record that in 1754 the English subjects Guilherme Naich, João Catanach, Gul Mundach, Richard Hill, Thomas Lamar, Richard Hill Jnr., João Scot, João Pringle, Matheus Hiccox, Carlos Chamber, Diogo Gordo, João Searte and Francisco Newton, among others, were merchants in Funchal. Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara, in his book *Breve Noticia sobre a ilha da Madeira*, says that in 1840 there were twenty-odd English commercial houses in this city. He names twelve of them, which he calls rich and reputable, and Dr Azevedo transcribes their firm names on p. 721 of the *Saudades*.

From 1640 the British colony took hold of almost all trade, above all the wine trade, which came to be entirely in the hands of English merchants. As a result of this veritable monopoly, as the annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso says, these merchants built up large fortunes for themselves, while the landowners and vine-growing farmers grew poorer. Some Portuguese wine-exporting houses later emerged, but they could not compete with the English giants. They lacked capital, they could not easily find outlets for their products abroad, and besides there were the privileges and exemptions those foreign merchants enjoyed. The administrators of entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*), who generally led idle lives, and many rural landowners too, not excluding the tenant farmers themselves, would draw large sums from the English houses in the course of the year, to be repaid at harvest time. Those houses thus became the creditors of the poor vine-growers, who were left at the mercy of the whims and greed of the wine merchants. On one of these occasions, when the exporting houses set an unprofitable price for the must, João de Carvalhal, later Count of Carvalhal, rescued the farmers from their distress by buying the wine at remunerative prices and forcing the English merchants to follow his salutary example. But João de Carvalhal enjoyed the greatest prestige and influence here in Madeira. He was an extremely rich landowner in every parish of the island and, what is more, held some three million *cruzados* in banks in England. From note XXVIII of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ we transcribe a few passages that bear closely on the subject of this article:

‘After the revolution of 1 December 1640, Portugal, in order to sustain the war of independence against Spain, had to secure the good offices of France, and especially of England, and obtained them only at the price of painful sacrifices, as we have already had occasion to note on p. 378. One of the favours granted to British subjects was permission, in 1654, to bring in their goods on payment of a small duty. By 1658 there was already an English consul on the island of Madeira. From 1660 to 1662 the English merchants here already enjoyed a special tax exemption on the export of wine. By 1680 they already had powerful trading houses here, which supplied the population at large with basic necessities, and the farming and landowning class with goods of every kind, luxuries included; that class, unfortunately, with honourable exceptions, had grown accustomed to idleness and dissipation. – From this dates English preponderance on the island of Madeira’.

This preponderance became further rooted and extended through the privileges granted to the English by the famous Methuen Treaty, which, says the note cited, tightened still further Madeira’s vassalage to British mercantilism. That vassalage turned into complete and absolute domination when this archipelago was occupied by troops sent from England.

We do not know whether it was to soften somewhat the excesses of this acknowledged dominance, and to forestall any protests or complaints about it from the archipelago’s highest authority, that the English government had decided to offer the governor and captain-general of Madeira an annual sum – no small gift for the time. The legality of accepting it, or the propriety of doing so, gave pause to Governor João António de Sá Pereira, who, in a submission to the government of the Marquis of Pombal dated 30 April 1768, wrote the following curious words:

‘The English Nation, wishing to oblige the Governors so as always to keep them favourable, the better to pursue the great profits it draws from this island, and seeing that its vessels paid nothing to the Government, imposed, with the permission of its Court, a levy on the captains of its ships of 240 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for each *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine or spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), 300 for each chest of sugar, 150 for each *arroba* (weight of about 15 kg) of cinnamon bark and 200 for each sack of orchil exported from here in their vessels, which they came to call – nation’s dues (*direitos de nação*, export levies collected by the British community) – and which are paid by the shippers, be they Portuguese, English or of any other nation; to collect them they appoint every year a treasurer and a clerk (*escrivão*), and it amounts to a great sum; from it they meet all the expenses which the community of the nation incurs here, among which is this. . . ’. The gift was 600,000 *réis* a year, which 150 years ago represented a considerable sum. We do not know when it began to be paid, nor whether it continued to be paid after Sá Pereira’s submission. What we find rather curious, but utterly degrading to our pride as a free nation, was the privilege granted to England of collecting taxes and customs duties on this island, as if it were an English colony!

Another privilege enjoyed by the British colony on this island is the one we have already described in the article Judge-conservator of the English (see that entry). Under it, English subjects had the right to choose a judge to try cases in which disputes or questions between them and the Portuguese had to be settled. The English residents here also had a land registry (*Conservatória*) of their own for registering their properties and certain commercial transactions, but we cannot determine precisely what this privilege consisted of or how the department concerned operated. British subjects had several places of worship in Funchal for Protestant services. At present there is the Anglican church in Rua da Bela Vista, built in the first quarter of the 19th century, and the Calvinist church in Rua Conselheiro José Silvestre Ribeiro. Not many years ago there was another church in Rua dos Aranhas, which we believe belonged to the sect known as the Ritualists (see English churches). We have vague information that, before these churches were built, there were other Protestant churches in this city, but we cannot specify when they were built or where they stood. At various times some British subjects unconnected with the English colony have appeared among us and devoted themselves to propaganda and proselytising for the Calvinist religion, notably the distinguished physician Dr Roberto Kalley, of whom we shall treat in a separate article.
The English colony has its own cemetery, and it had another near the present one, as can be seen in more detail in the article British Cemetery.

At the beginning of the 19th century a ward known as the British Ward was set up in the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal (*Santa Isabel*) in this city, intended chiefly for the treatment of the crews of English ships calling at our port. It did not last many years, because in 1837 the Funchal Medical-Surgical School was installed in the rooms occupied by the ward. We know nothing of the circumstances of this ward’s foundation, its upkeep and operation, the reasons for its closure, etc.

The exceptional mildness of our climate (see Climate) has drawn an extraordinary number of foreigners to this island, first and foremost among them the English. Many illustrious figures from England, such as Queen Adelaide (see that entry) and other princes, statesmen, men of science, writers, etc., have sought in Madeira relief from their ailments or a place of rest in which to restore strength drained by exhausting labours, sheltering in a climate of eternal spring and in a region overflowing with the most enchanting and astonishing natural beauties.

This is the place to say that the study of certain branches of the natural history of this archipelago is owed to a relatively large number of English subjects. There are very valuable works, the fruit of deep and lengthy scientific research, which cannot and must not be forgotten by Madeirans. In this Elucidário we have tried to bring out the names of the authors of these works, giving, however briefly, an account of the nature of their studies and of the services they rendered to the natural sciences. The distinguished men of science Richard Thomas Lowe, Thomas Vernon Wollaston, James Yate Johnson, Dr Alfred Merle Norman, etc., etc., will always be remembered by all who devote themselves to the study of Madeiran matters, and their names are inseparably linked with the history of our archipelago. If, as someone has already suggested, a gallery of marble or bronze busts were opened in our public garden, representing some of the most distinguished sons of Madeira or those who had rendered notable services to this land, two or three of the most illustrious English naturalists who studied the flora and fauna of the islands of the archipelago would certainly, and with complete justice, have their place there.

Referring to the influence exerted by the English in our midst, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo wrote the following: Madeira is to a great extent anglicised, in race, in customs, in property, in commerce and in currency; and the English language is the most widely spoken here after our own. If we are imprudent in saying this, what are the governments, if they are unaware of it, since they do not prevent it – what will they be? Only Portuguese pride keeps us Portuguese. These words, although they refer to 1873, the year in which they were written, are not entirely true to the facts. Yet they undoubtedly contain some assertions that we fully endorse and that seem to us to correspond to reality. The English colony built up remarkable influence and dominance here, owing largely to its monopoly of several important branches of trade. The purchase and export of wine lay entirely in its hands, as did the agencies for the ships that called at our port, the supply of coal and of the provisions and refreshments those ships needed, foreign exchange and the transfer of funds abroad, the import and sale of the main foodstuffs and clothing that the island required, the running of various industries, etc. In this way almost an entire population came to depend on a few dozen foreign subjects. And as the English houses expanded their trade and swelled their capital, their dominance grew in step, helped greatly by the innate haughtiness of their race and the natural and well-known timidity of the Madeirans. In these circumstances it was not difficult for the English to impose themselves as masters, abusing in a truly despotic and cruel manner the sad and distressing situation in which the inhabitants of this island sometimes found themselves. Nor is it surprising that poor islanders, living in the isolation of the ocean and with no spirit of resistance to outside influences, should have let themselves be seduced by the customs, tendencies and tastes of foreigners who came from the great European centres and were regarded as the very models of a civilised people. It is certain, moreover, that in some respects these influences had a very beneficial effect in our midst, especially on social relations and on the elegant society of the so-called people of fashion.

To go from this, however, to asserting that Madeira is anglicised, and that British influence has made itself felt in the race and very profoundly in the customs and habits of the natives, is certainly an exaggeration, which should not pass without the brief remarks we make here. And if we were to apply Dr Álvaro de Azevedo’s words to present circumstances, they would fall even further short of reality (1921). The dominance of the English colony in Madeira has weakened considerably over the last two decades, thanks to the effective initiative and energetic stance of some Portuguese merchants, and especially of the late lamented merchant Commander (*comendador*) Manuel Gonçalves. Trade has freed itself from local British influence, and this emancipation is making itself markedly felt, day by day, in many branches of our industrial and commercial activity.

This is a fitting moment to say that the English colony never succeeded in winning the affection of Madeiran society, despite the dominance and influence it enjoyed. Racial pride, the isolation it almost always sought to maintain, the haughtiness with which it generally treated the islanders, and its rare displays of philanthropy or charity towards the land that had made it rich are the main reasons why it never created a favourable climate or made itself well liked in the eyes of the Madeirans. There are, however, rare and honourable exceptions, and where acts of notable philanthropy are concerned we shall not forget, in the appropriate places, the names of Roberto Page, J. Phelps and Harry Hinton (see Foreigners).

In 1920 the number of British nationals permanently resident in Funchal was 50 to 60, whereas in 1845 there had been 293 people of that nationality here, 280 in 1855 and 200 in 1885. From 1845 to 1855 English visitors averaged 342, and from 1880 to 1885, 200. There are now some 250 English people in Funchal who intend to spend the winter here (1921).

Although English is the foreign language best known among the commercial class, and many seamen and bumboat men who are illiterate or almost illiterate speak it with a certain practical fluency, it is nonetheless true that the great majority of educated people in Funchal either do not know the language or know it poorly. French is the only language whose study receives the attention of everyone who wishes to be educated. A great many Madeirans speak it with elegance and perfection, and still more, though they do not speak it, are able to read and understand the best that has been written in it.

In March and April 1930 the *Diário de Notícias* of Funchal published a series of articles under the title *Ingleses na Madeira*, from the pen of Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento, which contain extensive and interesting information about the British colony in Madeira over a long period of three centuries.
Taro

Of the five or six species of the family Araceae known in Madeira by the name of *inhames* (taro), says the distinguished botanist Carlos Azevedo de Meneses, only two seem to us to deserve special mention, because of how common they are and the benefits the inhabitants derive from growing them. They are *Colocasia antiquorum* and *C. esculenta*.

The first species, which is said to have been introduced to Madeira in 1640, has been valued as a food plant since the most remote times. The peoples of Egypt and ancient Greece already made wide use of its elongated, tuberous, starchy rhizomes at their tables, and even exported them to other Mediterranean countries.

Madeirans distinguish two varieties of *Colocasia antiquorum*, calling one white taro (*inhame branco*) and the other red taro (*inhame vermelho*). The red variety differs from the white in that the veins on the underside of its leaves are slightly reddish and the inside of its rhizomes is pink or pale red, a colour that becomes more pronounced after cooking.
White taro is found in waterlogged places; red taro needs less moisture and can even grow in dry places, provided care is taken to water it frequently.

The taro that in some parts of the island is called ‘of the woods’ or ‘of the bracken’ (*do mato*, *da feiteira*) belongs to the red variety. It comes from land at high altitude that receives irrigation water only every 8 or every 15 days.

Taro (*inhame*) is generally harvested in March and April, and the plant is propagated from small fragments of its tubers, each of which must have an aerial shoot attached, stripped of its leaves. Whenever possible, the ground intended for planting is manured with farmyard dung or with vegetable matter.
The taro can be lifted once a year has passed since planting, but some people are in the habit of leaving it in the ground longer, sometimes for two years, so as to obtain larger rhizomes.

Red taro cooks more easily than white. White taro should only be considered fit for eating once it has been over the fire for at least five hours. Some physicians have sought to attribute the cases of elephantiasis observed in certain parts of the island to the heavy consumption of undercooked taro there.

To date, as far as we are aware, no naturalist has yet observed flowers on the white and red taro of Madeira. This should perhaps be attributed to the fact that these plants are pulled up very young, or before the flowering season. In the Algarve, according to Brotero, taro flowers during the summer.
The inhabitants of Funchal seek out red taro more than white, because it is tastier, less acrid and easier to cook. White taro is eaten almost exclusively by the rural population.

Taro cultivation covers a large area in both the north and the south of Madeira, but it is less important than that of potatoes and sweet potatoes. It is grown on the largest scale on the low-lying land bordering the rivers and streams, and over a good part of their beds.

*Colocasia esculenta*, commonly known as *inhame de enxerto* (‘grafted taro’), is far less cultivated than *C. antiquorum*, although its rhizomes are tastier and richer in starch than those of that species.

Grafted taro, like red taro, needs damp or frequently irrigated ground, though not waterlogged, and it too is propagated from fragments of the rhizomes, each of which must have a stem or aerial shoot attached.
Inhame de lagartixa (Cotyledon Umbilicus)

A small, succulent plant with peltate-suborbicular basal leaves on long stalks. This member of the Crassulaceae is common on walls and rocks at Monte, São Martinho, Santo António, etc., and its juice has been recommended against epilepsy and against sores and wounds of the legs, etc.
Inquisition

The Tribunal of the Inquisition never existed in Madeira, but it is known to have had familiars here, and the names of some of them are recorded in the books of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) (see Familiars of the Holy Office).

By a warrant (*provisão*) of 20 July 1612 the visitor (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) Francisco Cardoso de Cernejo was instructed to come to this island, but we do not know whether that mission led to any sons of Madeira being thrown into the dungeons of the Holy Office in Lisbon, or handed over to the flames.

The warrant enjoined the island’s officials to give the said Cernejo all the support and help he required, even ordering that the best buildings in the places he was to visit be vacated for his residence!

Of the Madeirans persecuted by the Inquisition, the best known is the poet Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega (see that entry). Like Bocage, he languished in the dungeons of the Holy Office, and even after his death the room in which he had lived was invaded by the familiars of that tribunal, who destroyed many of his writings (see Jews).
Insects

According to the late English naturalist James Yate Johnson, there are 1,331 species of insects in the Madeira archipelago, distributed as follows: Coleoptera, 695; Euplexoptera, 4; Orthoptera, 19; Thysanoptera, 6; Neuroptera, 37; Trichoptera, 10; Hymenoptera, 217; Lepidoptera, 112; Hemiptera, 54; Homoptera, 14; Aphaniptera, 3; and Diptera, 160.

It should be noted, however, that since these figures were published new studies have been made of some groups: Professor Teodoro Becker has recorded 212 Madeiran species of Diptera, and Malcolm Burr 29 of Orthoptera. Perhaps we shall not stray far from the truth if we say that there are some 2,000 species of insects in the archipelago, the Coleoptera, Hymenoptera and Diptera being the most widely represented groups in our region.

Thomas Vernon Wollaston, the author of *Insecta Maderensia*, found 629 Coleoptera on Madeira, 163 on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and 89 on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), and noted that many of these species have no wings or only very imperfectly developed ones. In Darwin’s view, this is a consequence of natural selection, probably combined with the disuse of those organs. Insects that do not feed on the ground but, like certain Coleoptera and Lepidoptera, feed on flowers, and must therefore use their wings to find food, have, as Thomas Vernon Wollaston observed, well-developed wings rather than rudimentary ones, the same naturalist adds.
Philosophical and Mechanical Institution

Under this title a society was founded in Funchal in 1840 with the aim of carrying out scientific studies of Madeira. The society was short-lived; one of its members, the military engineer António Pedro de Azevedo, published in the *Flor do Oceano* a translation of James Smith’s memoir on Madeiran geology.
Charitable institutions

Around 1425 Constança Rodrigues de Almeida, wife of the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco, founded the chapel of St Catherine (*Santa Catarina*) (see that entry), and ‘beside it, says Frutuoso, she built many houses to shelter women of good life, poor *mercieiras* (almswomen: poor women kept on alms in return for serving a chapel), to whom she left alms so that they should always take care to clean and serve that house (the chapel), as is still the custom today’. Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo comments on these words as follows: ‘The Mercearia de Santa Catharina.... was a kind of hospice (*hospício*), where poor women of good morals lived on alms and were responsible for keeping the saint’s chapel clean. Both have been preserved to the present day. They are the property of the Count of Castello-Melhor’.

We can add nothing to what has been transcribed above, and we also do not know whether Constança de Almeida’s foundation really survived until 1873, although doubtless with a purpose different from that of the original institution. What we can now affirm is that the institution disappeared long ago and that the houses and the chapel passed to other owners. This was certainly the first charitable institution in Madeira, and it lasted some four and a half centuries.

Around the middle of the 15th century João Gonçalves Zarco donated some land beside the chapel of St Paul (*São Paulo*) for the foundation of a hospital, which was built at the people’s expense around 1469. It was the second charitable institution the archipelago had. This hospital remained there only a few years before it was moved to the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) and placed in the care of the confraternity of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), which was then founded in this city and later established itself in the towns of Machico, Santa Cruz, Calheta and Porto Santo. We shall deal more fully with the hospital, which later moved to the building it occupies today, and with the Misericórdias of Funchal and of the towns in the article Misericórdias. We have already devoted a separate article in this Elucidário to the hospital of São Lázaro, whose foundation dates from the beginning of the 16th century. The mental hospital, the Manicómio Câmara Pestana, will be dealt with elsewhere in this work.

In the last quarter of the 15th century Gonçalo Aires founded the chapel of São Bartolomeu (St Bartholomew) and, attached to it, a hospice (*albergaria*) intended for poor clergy, but it seems that it never came to be used for the purpose for which it was founded. (See the article Gonçalo Aires.)

On the *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) of Bom Jesus, which also had, and still retains, the character of a charitable institution, we have already said all that is necessary in the entry devoted to it in its proper place. Something will also be said, at the appropriate point in this work, about the Recolhimento das Órfãs, founded in 1725.
In the entry asylums (*Asilos*) we dealt at some length with these houses of charity, both those now extinct and those that still exist, and we refer the reader to it.

To the fine charitable institution known as the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*) we have already devoted a detailed entry, in which we also referred to the Orphanage attached to it.

Although constituted as associations, the Association for the Protection of the Poor (*Associação Protectora dos Pobres*), the Associação Protectora dos Estudantes Pobres, the Assistência a Crianças Fracas and the Auxílio Maternal are true charitable institutions; we have already referred to them elsewhere.
Entailed foundations

It has been asserted that the Madeiran archipelago, in proportion to its area and population, was the region of the country with the greatest number of entails (*morgados*), or entailed leaseholds. Judging by the number of chantries (capela), most of which were entailed foundations (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela), scattered across every parish of the island, it can safely be said that entails abounded in Madeira. Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro stated in an official document that two-thirds of the land in the whole archipelago was entailed. Madeira was a land of entails, although some of them dragged out a wretched existence that did little credit to their ancestral pretensions.

In the early days of colonisation many noblemen, both Portuguese and foreign, came to this island, together with an even larger number of merchants and adventurers. They came to seek their fortune, drawn by the fame of the remarkable fertility of the soil, by the spirit of adventure and also by the lack of resources in the lands they came from. These men were given large tracts of land in *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), which they had cleared by Black and Moorish slaves imported from Africa and by free tenant farmers (*colono*, under the *colonia* contract) from mainland Portugal. Many of these *sesmeiros* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) built up fine houses with the large income that the exuberant fertility of the soil gave them, above all from the production of sugar, which was exported on a large scale. Then ‘the rich *sesmeiro*, in the words of the annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), grew weary of country life, took pride in his original nobility and craved a residence of greater display and bustle; he therefore scorned the land and entailed it, with the aim of securing its revenues; he contracted its cultivation to the free tenant farmers for a half-share (*demidia*) or, in some parts, a third of the produce, and, to maintain himself in idle enjoyment, abandoned his estates and came to set up a luxurious and wasteful residence in the towns, chiefly in Funchal, Machico, Santa Cruz, Calheta, Ponta do Sol and Ribeira Brava.’

Although Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo lays on the colours thickly, as he generally does when referring to monarchy, the nobility and the clergy, the passage we have transcribed above nonetheless contains great truths. It highlights some of the local causes behind the creation of entails on this island. These causes must be taken together with others that were common to the whole country, which Gama Barros identifies in his monumental work *historia da Administração Publica em Portugal*. We have already said elsewhere that the settler who came from the mainland became a *sesmeiro*, then lord of the land, and in many cases turned into the holder of an entail, leaving the cultivation and tending of his rural properties to slaves while he went to enjoy the income of his fields and estates in the city or at court.

It seems that some entailed estates (*morgadio*) were already being founded in Madeira in the second quarter of the 15th century. Gaspar Frutuoso implies as much, although he does not say so clearly and conclusively. Of entails created in the last quarter of the same century there is reliable record, such as that of Água de Mel (‘honey water’), in Santo António (‘St Anthony’), which was incorporated into the house of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’); that of Consolação (‘consolation’), in Caniço (‘reed’), whose last representative was Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas; that of João Afonso in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), which passed to the house of Torre Bela; that of Vasco Moniz, in Machico, whose last administrator was José de Betencourt e Freitas; those founded by João Gomes, beside the stream that took his name; that of Rodrigo Aires Furtado, in Ponta do Sol; and many others besides.

It was in the first half of the 16th century that many entails were founded, some of which later grew into important houses. Among them were the entailed estate of Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry), in Ponta do Sol, founded in 1512 by the Flemish *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) João Esmeraldo (see that entry) on lands he held on lease from Luís Gonçalves da Câmara; that of the Lomelinos, in Santa Cruz, founded by Urbano Lomelino in 1518; that of the Franças, in Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’), in 1503, by João de França; that of São João de Latrão, in Gaula, by Nuno Fernandes Cardoso, in 1511; that of Penha de Águia (‘eagle crag’), in Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), by António Teixeira, in 1535; that of São Gil (‘St Giles’), in Santa Cruz, by Dona Brites Escórcio, daughter of João Drumond; that of Ribeira dos Melões (‘melons’ stream’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário, by Pedro Gonçalves de Clara; and that of Reis Magos (‘the Magi’), in Estreito da Calheta, in 1529, by Francisco Homem de Gouveia, besides others that we omit for the sake of brevity.

Among the entailed estates mentioned above, and others created over the course of time, some became very wealthy houses that have remained prosperous and opulent to our own day. We shall mention, among others, the house of the Count of Carvalhal, one of the richest in our country in landed property, which seventy years ago had an annual income of one hundred *contos* (one million réis) de réis; that of the Count of Calçada (‘paved way’); that of the Countess of Torre Bela; that of the holder of the entail Nuno de Freitas Lomelino; that of Councillor Agostinho de Ornelas; that of the Viscount of São João; and that of the holder of the entail Bettencourt e Freitas.

As we have already had occasion to say in the article Elementos para a historia madeirense, the books of the old Court of Residues and Chantries (*Juízo dos Resíduos e Capellas*) have been lost, or we do not know what became of them. They held the records of the old entails (*instituições vinculares*), with their pious obligations, foundations of chantries, descriptions of the entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*), etc. It is there that valuable data could have been gathered for an interesting and complete study of the entails and entailed properties that existed in this archipelago.

This large number of entails was reduced by the Marquis of Pombal’s law of 9 September 1769, which abolished many of the small entailed estates (*morgadios*), and further by the law of 3 August 1770, which reorganised the entails then in existence and, above all, restricted the creation of new ones.

Even so, many entailed houses survived here in Madeira, and they struggled with great economic difficulties. Some even went so far as to request the commutation of the pious obligations to which they were bound, on the grounds that the income from their lands was insufficient to meet those obligations; we have found this in documents from the early 19th century, and we do not know whether it happened even earlier. On 17 February 1849 the Madeiran peer of the realm Dr Daniel de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 1st Baron of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), presented to the upper chamber a bill abolishing all the entails existing in this archipelago, considering them not only useless but actually harmful, above all because they were a great obstacle to agricultural progress. The bill caused a great stir in Madeira and gave rise to extensive debate in the press. Thirty-odd representatives of old entailed houses addressed a petition to parliament, refuting the principles of the bill and asking for its rejection. It is an exceptionally interesting document that still deserves to be read today. Besides this petition and the debate in the local press, the following pamphlets were published on the subject: *Breves reflexões sobre a abolição dos morgados na Madeira*, by António Correia Heredia; *As contradições vinculadas*, by the author of *Breves reflexões sobre a abolição dos morgados na Madeira*; and *Resposta ao folheto «Breves reflexões sobre a abolição dos morgados na Madeira, pelo Sr. A. C. Heredia»*, whose author we do not know.

The Baron of São Pedro’s bill was not approved by the chambers, but the law of 11 May 1863, which decreed the complete abolition of entails throughout the country, dealt a heavy blow to Madeira’s entails and brought an end to old and wealthy houses of this island. Little by little they were divided and subdivided, and today not one of these houses remains intact.

In Alfredo Pimenta’s book *Vínculos Portugueses* we found some information about various entailed houses or estates based in Madeira. Particular mention should be made of the one whose last administrator was the 2nd Viscount of Torre Bela, João Correia Brandão Henriques de Noronha: it comprised 26 entails, and its first founder was João Afonso Correia, in 1490. Others were the house of the Counts of Calheta, incorporated into the marquisate of Castelo-Melhor and originally founded by João Gonçalves Zarco in 1450; that of the entailed lords of Ilha (‘island’) – a locality (*sítio*) in the parish of São Jorge –, founded by Jorge Pinto in 1559; and that of the Savage Islands (Selvagens), founded in 1717 by Manuel Ferreira Teixeira.

Fortunately, a considerable part of the documents that made up the important archive of the Court of Pious Bequests and Chantries (*Juízo dos Resíduos e Capelas*) mentioned above, which were held in the former department of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government’s local civil office) of Funchal, was incorporated into the Funchal District Archive (see Judge of Pious Bequests and Chantries).
Education

As was only natural and logical, public education in this archipelago followed roughly the same phases as in mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). In its essential lines, the history of the one is the history of the other.

Higher education was represented here by the creation of the Funchal Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica do Funchal*) in 1837, which came to an end in 1910 (see Medical-Surgical School). In some localities of Madeira a shortage of doctors is already being felt (1921), and it will soon be severe. Before very long, no doubt, it may again be said, as the governor and captain-general of this archipelago told the government of mainland Portugal in 1824, that on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and in the Madeiran countryside there was no operating surgeon at all and that ‘one found only some wretched bloodletter, of whose competence many of those who called him to treat and cure their diseases have been the victims’. Our Medical School ought to have been reorganised in its original structure and in the range of its classes, making the teaching of the subjects taught there more effective; but the needs of the island districts did not warrant its abolition, which was due mainly, it is said, to the insistence of the director of public health, Dr Ricardo Jorge. Special education was provided here through the teaching of theology at the Diocesan Seminary, from its foundation in the last quarter of the 16th century (see seminary (*Seminário*)). There were also special courses in theology at the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) and at the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), for the exclusive use of their respective religious. The following may be regarded as special courses: the public class (*aula*) in drawing and painting, created in 1810; the drawing class that ran in this city for some years, maintained by the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*); and the Industrial School, established in 1889. We have already given a detailed account of all of these in the article António Augusto de Aguiar Industrial School (*Escola Industrial António Augusto de Aguiar*). In the first quarter of the 19th century there was a course of military studies in this city, whose organisation, workings and period of existence are entirely unknown to us. Among the courses of special education we must also mention the Teacher Training School (*Escola Normal*) (see that entry), which lasted from 1900 to 1910, the Higher Primary School (*Escola Primária Superior*) (see that entry), created in 1919, and the School of Navigation (*Escola de Pilotagem*) (see that entry), which opened in 1914.

The first public secondary classes held here in Madeira were those the Jesuits taught at their College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*), covering Latin, philosophy, rhetoric and literature. We do not know when they began, but they already existed in 1590, for the author of the *Saudades* refers to them, and they ended with the expulsion of the Jesuits in 1759. This secondary course was known as the *Aulas do Pátio* ('Courtyard Classes', the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), because it was held in an inner courtyard that formed part of the college. The college stood in Rua do Estudo, and after the expulsion of the Jesuits some secondary classes continued to be taught in the same building under the same name of *Aulas do Pátio*. It was also in this building that the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city was established in 1837 (see the Lyceum (*Liceu*)), and it remained there for about 50 years. We cannot say exactly how much time passed between the expulsion of the Jesuits and the resumption of the *Aulas do Pátio*, nor can we tell whether these courses ran without interruption until our lyceum was established. In 1772 public classes in philosophy, Latin, mathematics and rhetoric were created, and around 1825 classes in French and English (see Secondary classes). Everything suggests that these were created to make up for the loss of the classes taught by the Jesuits, and it must then be accepted that there was a break in these courses in the period from 1759 to 1772.
For primary education, see the article primary schools (*Escolas Primárias*), where the subject is dealt with in some detail.
Military mutinies

We know only of the following mutinies to have occurred on the island of Madeira: that of July 1829, in the 13th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.º 13*), because an officer from outside the unit had been appointed acting commander; that of 30 July 1852, in the 6th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) Battalion (*batalhão de caçadores n.º 6*), during which Lieutenant Lapierre was killed; and that of 2 August 1870, in the 5th Caçadores Battalion (*batalhão de caçadores n.º 5*), following an inspection of weapons.
See military garrison (*Guarnição Militar*) and Lapierre.
Island Epic
We shall deal with this poem when we speak of its author. See Tomás (Manuel).
Invejosa
On the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) this name is given to *Echium plantagineum*, a plant of the family Boraginaceae, which is also found on Madeira and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’).
Winter in Funchal

In his highly regarded work *Noticia sobre o clima do Funchal*, Dr F. A. Barral gives a most curious and interesting account of the winter season in this city. We record it in these columns, although we have already touched on the subject in the article Climate:

‘The climate of Funchal has a warmer season and a colder one; it has rain, thunderstorms, sometimes strong winds, storms, floods and the *leste* (hot, dry easterly wind from Africa); and all of this, which does not come every year at a fixed time and season, and does not always last the same length of time, produces notable variations and breaks that supposed uniformity and monotony. The years 1749 and 1750 were extremely dry, according to Heberden. In 1826 it rained much more than in other years. In the year 1834 to 1835 there were more days of rain than is usual, although no proportionally greater quantity of water fell; the rain was finer and more persistent, as in the countries of the North. In 1803 and 1842 there were terrible floods.

In some years the summer is hotter: in 1852 the thermometer in the shade rose in the month of September to 83° (Fahrenheit scale), and in some places to 85°, which is rare. In almost every winter there are days when snow falls in the uplands and some cold is felt. In the winter of 1851 to 1852 no snow fell, while in that of 1852 to 1853 more snow fell than in many previous winters; it was cold, the thermometer dropped below 50° on some nights, and once or twice reached 45°, which is also rare.

It is true that there the seasons do not show the great differences and striking contrasts of climates in higher latitudes, which give a country very different aspects. Madeira, or rather the southern part of Madeira, where Funchal lies, is always a garden. Neither the cold of winter nor the heat of summer withers or dries its luxuriant vegetation. Even so, something happens in those different periods of the year called seasons that marks them out clearly: phenomena less pronounced than in other countries, but easily felt by the natives. The Funchal winter may be the London summer, yet the resident there perceives the difference between the two seasons: a lower temperature, colder nights, greater humidity and more frequent rain. For him, all these changes characterise winter, even though the season may seem to the newly arrived Englishman to be his summer, and to the Portuguese from the mainland to be his autumn.

Winter in Funchal is a beautiful season. The temperature is pleasant during the day, and the sky is for the most part clear or only lightly clouded; wind and rain are moderate. The weather is so ordered that it leaves intervals in the day when everyone, even invalids, can go out without discomfort, since the streets dry easily. It is in winter that the excellence of this climate is best appreciated, above all when it is compared with all the other better-known and more sought-after climates. In our opinion, this is the season that gives the island’s climate its great superiority over the others, which in summer could better dispute Madeira’s pre-eminence. If one ever feels cold, it is at dawn or at night, and out of doors, at hours when invalids should not be out walking. Even the days reputed to be the coldest in some years always have many hours of pleasant temperature when invalids can go out. There are houses in Funchal which, because of their exposure or construction, have on those few cold days a lower temperature than one would wish or than is advisable. On such days a fire lit for a few hours with a low flame, especially at night, is pleasant, above all for people from the north. A fire also has the advantage of reducing and dispelling the damp that some houses may have in winter. In this season there is sometimes a north-easterly wind, less humid and of a cool temperature, which gives people a certain degree of useful vigour and energy.

The transition from winter to spring is usually imperceptible and seems a continuation of the same season. Sometimes, however, there are heavy rains in March, lasting for days, with winds from the western quarter. This season is extremely pleasant until the end of May, with the temperature still remaining very moderate. In general it is only in July that a certain number of invalids, mainly English, think they ought to leave the island and return to England; before that time the change may be very strange and harmful’.
Little Sisters of the Poor

These nuns came to Madeira in 1900 and at once founded an asylum for the elderly, to which the diocesan prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto and Father António José de Macedo contributed a great deal, as already mentioned in the article asylums (*Asilos*), on p. 94 of the 1st volume of this work. With the decree expelling the religious orders from our country, the Little Sisters of the Poor (*Irmãzinhas dos Pobres*) had to abandon the asylum they had founded. Twelve of them left Madeira on 18 April 1911, bound for the French town of Latour.
Isabel (Empress)
See Austria (Empress of), on p. 106 of the 1st volume of this *Elucidário*.
Isabel (Princess)

Queen Elisabeth of Belgium visited Madeira while she was still a princess. She arrived on the British steamer *Araguaya* on 28 July 1909 and left for the Canary Islands on the German steamer *Kamerun* on the 6th of the following August. She stayed at the Monte Palace Hotel, where her husband Prince Albert, now King of the Belgians (1921), had stayed a few months earlier. She visited many parts of the city and its surroundings and also made two journeys by sea: one to Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), landing at Madalena (‘Magdalene’), and another to Machico, where she went ashore and made an excursion to the locality (*sítio*) of Portela (‘mountain pass’).
The princess travelled under the name of Countess of Rethy and was greeted by the civil governor and the military commander, the former of whom accompanied her on some of her outings.
See Belgium (King of).
Isca (Phagnalon saxatile)

A small subshrub of the family Compositae, very common on all the islands of the archipelago. On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) its branches, once crushed, are made into a very coarse tinder, which is nevertheless widely used by the inhabitants of that island, especially the fishermen.
In former times a great deal of tinder was also made from *Phagnalon* in Madeira, and the uses to which this plant can be put are still known to many people today.
Isopods
See Woodlouse and Carcinology.
Ivo (Pedro)

This writer from Porto, who left his mark on the literature of our country with a well-known and admired book of short stories, visited Madeira in 1867. Captivated by the natural beauty of this island, he wrote an inspired poem entitled *Adeus à Madeira*, which was published in the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) of 19 June 1924.
Jaca brava (Grapsus marmoratus)

A decapod brachyuran crustacean, common along the shores of the islands of the archipelago. It prefers to live in the zone between high-water and low-water marks, and is sought after as bait for certain species of fish.
Jaca de pau (Grapsus minutus)

A brachyuran crustacean carried to this island by ocean currents, usually attached to wooden objects such as beams, casks, etc. It also lives on the shells of the turtles that come into Madeiran waters.
Jacaranda (Jacaranda mimosifolia)

A tree of the family Bignoniaceae, grown in the *quintas*, avenues and gardens of Funchal. It flowers in spring, when its blue flowers, gathered in panicles, make a lovely effect. It remains bare or sparsely leaved until the beginning of summer, which makes it little valued as a shade tree and therefore unsuitable for lining streets and public squares, at least in our climate.
Jacas mansas (Xantho floridus and X. rivulosus)
Decapod brachyuran crustaceans that live on the Madeiran coasts, in the part uncovered at low tide. They are used as bait.
Jaccoud (Dr)

This eminent French physician, a well-known specialist in lung diseases, was in Madeira in September and October 1881. He came expressly to study our climate from a therapeutic point of view, and concluded that the superiority of this island’s climate over that of other health resorts was beyond dispute. In his notable work *Curabilité et traitement de la phthisie pulmonaire* he deals at length with Madeira as a winter resort for the treatment of lung diseases. These pages, which are of the greatest importance given the undisputed authority of the name that signs them, should be read and weighed by all who wish to concern themselves with the climate of this archipelago.
Hyacinth (Hyacinthus orientalis)
A blue-flowered member of the lily family, grown in some Funchal gardens. It was found naturalised near Santa (‘saint’), in Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), by Mr J. G. da Costa.
Rose apple (Eugenia Jambos)

A tree of the family Myrtaceae, grown in some gardens and *quintas* in Madeira. It is native to India and bears subglobose, fragrant fruits with a pleasant taste. An infusion of rose-apple leaves has been recommended against diabetes.
Jamboto

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, Funchal. The name is a corruption of João Boto, an early settler. In this locality there is a chalybeate spring which at one time gained considerable fame because certain therapeutic qualities were attributed to it. For this reason the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) had the water chemically and bacteriologically analysed. The result of the analysis was published in a pamphlet in 1900 and reproduced on pp. 119 ff. of the book *Paroquia de Santo Antonio da Ilha da Madeira*, by one of the authors of this *Elucidário*.
Janela (stream)

This is the longest and fullest watercourse in Madeira. It rises on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) and, crossing the parish (*freguesia*) that bears the same name, flows into the ocean there. A short distance from its mouth lies an islet that also bears the same name. The well-known Rabaçal levadas (irrigation channels) draw much of their water from the springs of this stream, captured at its sources.
See Ribeira da Janela (parish).
Jangão

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). It was the seat of the former entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’), founded in 1522 by João Esmeraldo, whose last representative was the distinguished Madeiran Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas. Here stands the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), which belonged to this entailed house (*casa vinculada*). It was founded by António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo around 1670 and restored in 1777 and in 1879 by the respective administrators, Francisco de Ornelas de Vasconcelos and Councillor Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos.
See Lombada dos Esmeraldos (‘the Esmeraldos’ ridge’).
Jardim Botânico
A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), where in the early 19th century there was a plant nursery known as the Jardim Botânico (‘botanical garden’).
Jardim da Serra

At the northern end of the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’) lies the charming and delightful spot known as Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’). The pleasantness and beauty of the place justify the name. It consists largely of a picturesque valley set deep among rugged mountains and surrounded by dense, luxuriant vegetation. It is unquestionably one of the most enchanting spots in Madeira, and from its heights some of the broadest and most astonishing panoramas of the whole island can be seen. On the Pico dos Bodes (‘billy-goats’ peak’) and the Boca dos Namorados (‘lovers’ pass’), which overlook it, we are above all enraptured by the sight of the abyss of the Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) and the mountains that surround it. As we have already noted, this is one of the places in Madeira where nature appears at its most grandiose and striking, because of the great height and fanciful shapes of the mountains, the steepness and sheer drop of the slopes, the ravines scattered everywhere and the rugged, wild character of the landscape. All this gives the whole such grandeur and majesty, and such extraordinary and enchanting beauty, that even the least prepared and least sensitive traveller is astonished and spellbound on beholding this scene of so many incomparable wonders. And it is from the heights of Jardim da Serra that these astonishing panoramic views can best be observed, drawing a considerable number of Portuguese and foreign visitors to the spot.

It was surely the charm of these natural beauties and the delightful pleasantness of the place that led the English consul Henrique Veitch to build a fine country house in this locality (*sítio*). He was buried close by, in a mausoleum that stands there in the midst of the mountains (see Veitch).

It was in this locality that the cultivation of tea was first attempted here in Madeira, in the early 19th century, under the direction of H. Veitch, who, it is said somewhere, managed ‘to offer a genuine Madeira tea, which was much appreciated by all his guests’. We believe that not a single specimen of *Thea sinensis* now survives there. We know that recently (1921) the learned farmer Augusto César de Gouveia tried planting tea on his properties at Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) with the greatest success, obtaining an excellent product that rivals the best tea imported here from England. It seems to us that, besides the attempts at Jardim da Serra and Fajã da Ovelha, others were made on this island to grow the plant.
Acclimatisation Garden

On 23 September 1852 the Austrian botanist Friedrich Welwitsch proposed the creation of two acclimatisation gardens, one in São Paulo de Luanda (Luanda) and the other in Funchal. ‘The Funchal garden’, the botanist wrote, ‘would form a subtropical garden, receiving tropical plants already accustomed to a certain regular cultivation and naturalising them there, so that they could later be grown with better results in less hot climates; it would likewise accustom plants sent there from colder countries to grow at a higher temperature, thereby adapting them so that they would not find cultivation in regions of the tropical zone so strange... The scientific gardens of Lisbon, Coimbra and Porto would receive from the Funchal garden the tropical and subtropical plants acclimatised there, and would send it useful plants from colder countries to be acclimatised there.’
The Funchal acclimatisation garden was never created, despite the great advantages it would have brought not only to our island but also to Portugal and various foreign countries.
See Smith.
Jardim de Oliveira (António)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente on 7 June 1858 and graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1883. For some years he practised as a lawyer in Funchal and held various public-service appointments here in Madeira. He also taught law at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school).
On 30 March 1890 he was elected to represent Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) for the legislative session of 1890 to 1892.

Appointed Secretary-General of the Civil Government of Funchal in 1890, he gave up active practice as a lawyer and devoted himself almost exclusively to his official duties. Until 1919, the year in which he retired, he was called upon countless times to act as head of the district in the absence, unavailability or incapacity of the civil governors.

Although we have made it our rule to refrain from praising the living, we cannot fail to mention the distinguished services that Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Dr Jardim de Oliveira rendered to Madeira, above all during the grave food-supply crisis that this island suffered as a result of the European war. To ward off the spectre of famine, he ordered several tonnes of maize to be unloaded from a Portuguese vessel that had arrived at our port in early August 1917. This act was not approved by the higher authorities, and Colonel Sousa Rosa was at once appointed Civil Governor and Military Commander, so that Councillor Jardim de Oliveira gave up the leadership of the district. The affair caused the deepest displeasure among all the inhabitants of this island, and on 7 and 9 August two imposing demonstrations of esteem and sympathy were held for Councillor Jardim de Oliveira. They carried the highest significance, because countless people of every social class joyfully took part in them, without distinction of sect or party.

After obtaining his retirement, Councillor Jardim de Oliveira lived for some time in Lisbon. Having returned to Funchal in 1921, however, he practised here as a lawyer, a profession from which his official duties had kept him somewhat apart. He died in Funchal on 31 May 1926.
Jardim do Mar (parish)

Set amid the bare cliffs that make up part of the coastline of the parishes (*freguesias*) of Calheta (‘small cove’) and Paul lies the tiny parish of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’). The abrupt change from sheer slopes stripped of vegetation to a cheerful, green spot that leans picturesquely out over the ocean amply explains the name that the first settlers gave to this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish). It is also said that various wild flowers grew there in abundance, wild roses foremost among them, and there is still today a locality (*sítio*) called Roseiras (‘rose bushes’), which seems to confirm the tradition.

In his brief description of the more important parishes and settlements on the south-west coast of this island, Gaspar Frutuoso refers to the localities of Jardim do Mar and Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’), calling them simply Jardim and Paul. We do not know whether they were known by these names in the earliest days of colonisation, perhaps without the added designation ‘do Mar’ (‘of the Sea’) that they bear today and have long borne. Nor do we know whether the places called Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) and Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’) received these names to distinguish them from those localities, the one pair being washed by the sea and the other lying in the interior of the island. It is perhaps impossible today to establish this.

Between the coasts of Calheta and Paul a projection of the shore stands out; it is called Ponta do Jardim (‘garden point’) and makes up a considerable part of this parish. The parish is also formed by a *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff), which broke away from the higher ground above it. There is no record of its formation, and it is conjectured that it already existed before the discovery.

Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘Half a *légua* from here is a parish called Jardim, of forty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), with a church dedicated to Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*). It also has a sugar mill (*engenho*), grain land and vineyards.’ The annotator of the *Saudades* corrects this information in the following words: ‘There is a manifest error in this account because, as the above-cited documents concerning the parishes of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) and Jardim do Mar show, Our Lady of Grace was already then the patron saint of the former, and at the time when Gaspar Frutuoso himself wrote the *Saudades* (1590) the latter had not yet been established: the author was therefore referring to the former and not to the latter, as the local circumstances he mentions confirm.’

As the soil of Jardim do Mar is quite fertile, it may be presumed that its land was cleared among the earliest agricultural ventures, albeit by people whose permanent residence was in the neighbouring locality of Paul, to which Jardim originally belonged. It may also be presumed that its settled population dates from a fairly early period, even though the parish was created more recently; this is fully explained by the very small number of its inhabitants.

Among the earliest inhabitants of Jardim do Mar, Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo mentions Gonçalo Alves de Araújo, who came to Madeira from mainland Portugal at the end of the 15th century and held land there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation); he was known as Gonçalo Alves do Jardim. The wealthiest *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) here and in Paul do Mar, however, was Joanes de Couto Cardoso, whose first and second sons founded two entails (*morgados*) with their seats in Paul and in Jardim. Their representative today (1921) is Francisco João Vasconcelos de Couto Cardoso, a leading landowner in the latter of these parishes.

Jardim do Mar began as a curacy (*curato*) dependent on Prazeres (‘joys’) or on Paul – which of the two we have not been able to establish. It seems that it was first a daughter curacy of Prazeres and later of Paul do Mar, and that it was created in the second quarter of the 18th century. In the *Índice Geral do Registo da Provedoria da Real Fazenda* (general index of the register of the Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*)) we read on p. 132: ‘Royal decree (*alvará*) of the Lord King John V, of 15 November 1734, creating the curate of Jardim do Mar, with a salary of one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine, in view of the grave inconvenience suffered by the inhabitants of this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) in going to hear Mass in the parish (*freguesia*) of Prazeres or Paul, as a result of which they not only missed Mass but also died without the sacraments.’ And in the *Memorias sobre a criação e augmento do Estado Eclesiástico na Ilha da Madeira* we find the following further instrument cited: ‘Royal decree of the said Lord, of 12 March 1736, granting the respective salary of one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine to the said curate of Jardim do Mar, Father Manuel do Nascimento, with the certificate of the vicar of Prazeres that he fulfils his obligations.’

The curacy was created at the end of 1734, and religious services seem to have begun at the start of the following year with the appointment of the curate Manuel do Nascimento.
