There was a small chapel there, which served as the seat of the curacy. It was rebuilt in 1786, for on 9 December of that year permission was granted for it to be blessed. The petition requesting this permission was made by Francisco Manuel da Silva, curate of Jardim do Mar, and it states that ‘by order of Her Majesty.... the chapel of Our Lady of the Rosary (*Nossa Senhora do Rosário*), to which that curacy is attached, has been built anew, for it had fallen into ruin, with only the altar left standing, and all the walls of its nave have been built anew...’

It is probable that Jardim formed a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) with a chantry (*capela*), as happened in so many other parts of Madeira, the estates and chantries having been the original nucleus and centre of future parishes.

The curate did not reside permanently in Jardim do Mar. A warrant (*provisão*) of the diocesan prelate dated 20 July 1809 ordered the priest holding that post to take up residence there, so that he could promptly attend to all the duties of his office. This was observed only after 1836, when the vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence), by a warrant of 28 September of that year, released Jardim from its dependence on Paul do Mar. He was granting a petition addressed to him by the inhabitants, who by then numbered about 300. Only with the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 24 June 1848, however, was Jardim raised to the status of a parish, wholly independent, in its civil and religious life, of the neighbouring parish of Paul do Mar.
The old chapel served as the parish church until it was replaced by the present building, about which we shall transcribe the following passages from *O Jornal* of 28 May 1909:

‘On 3 May 1906 the then vicar of this parish (*freguesia*), the Revd Father César Martinho Fernandes, began demolishing the cramped, ancient and half-ruined little church of Our Lady of the Rosary, in order to raise in its place an elegant, beautiful and artistic building for divine worship.

Hintze Ribeiro was then Minister of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and the civil governor of Funchal was Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Ribeiro da Cunha. This official had promised a *conto* (one million réis) de réis to help rebuild the church; meanwhile, however, the ministry fell, the vow faltered, and Jardim do Mar no longer had a church. And no money at all!

It was a tiny settlement, with a mere 420 inhabitants that year. How, then, could a church be rebuilt without resources? It was a children’s dream or a visionary’s fancy... But it was neither dream nor fancy; very soon it became a reality.
The most heartfelt generosity and the most devoted dedication to religious worship led the people of this parish to achieve truly sublime feats of thrift! They set to work.

The parish priest, a shrewd and daring spirit, drew the plan of the new church, bought part of the land, contracted with builders, summoned his people, collected their contributions for the contracted works and set everything in motion.
Many of the parishioners, having no money to pay their contributions, borrowed it at interest, and some of them still owe it today.

The parish priest was not only the architect; he was also the builder, the master mason and the labourer: he directed all the work, measured, aligned, squared, mixed the lime and dropped the plumb line.

The women groaned and sweated under the weight of sacks of sand and loads of stone, which, like their husbands, fathers and sons, they carried up from the beach to the building site, all for the love of God! Our distinguished friend Mr Francisco João de Vasconcelos not only placed his chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*) at the disposal of the Revd parish priest for the celebration of divine services, but also gave land and large sums of money, and on a single day fed at his own expense ninety-odd men who, at his request, carried stone free of charge.
There were also others who, besides the contributions due from them, spontaneously gave further sums.
When the emigrants from this parish heard abroad of this enormous undertaking, they sent the precious fruit of their toil to be spent on this work of religious zeal.

And the combination of all these efforts and sacrifices soon raised from the ground a building constructed strictly according to the rules of the art, the only one in Madeira that displays the true, pure Gothic style.

In the building of this church three benefactors stood out and deserve to be singled out: the then parish priest, the Revd Father César Martinho Fernandes, Mr Francisco de Vasconcelos, and the people as a whole, whose names will be bound for ever to the history of this parish, and will remain alive and remembered for as long as the church stands, with its elegant and graceful bell tower smiling on future generations.

Jardim do Mar is rightly proud (1921) of having been the only settlement in the whole diocese to have built a parish church. Its chief pride, however, lies in the hope of future reward, for which so many feats of self-denial were accomplished.’

The new church was solemnly blessed by the diocesan prelate, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, on 19 October 1907. The occasion was marked by various festivities of great splendour, attended by countless people from the surrounding parishes.

The Revd Father César Martinho Fernandes left this parish shortly afterwards, serving as a priest in other parishes and then going to North America, where he stayed for some years. On returning to his homeland he again became parish priest of the small parish of Jardim, and died there on 1 November 1920, aged only 42. He rests in the shadow of the church that he succeeded in raising through so much labour and toil, and it would be entirely just for the people of this parish to erect a modest mausoleum over the seven *palmos* of earth that cover his body.

The *Diário da Madeira* of 20 November 1920 published a short biography of this most worthy and well-loved priest, to whom this parish owes the most outstanding and notable services, which well deserve to be remembered.

Once the diocesan prelate had obliged the curates of Jardim do Mar to keep a fixed residence within the bounds of their curacy, priests did indeed live there more or less permanently in the period from 1837 to 1848, the year in which the parish was definitively created. They were Francisco José Nunes, João José Lucio Gonçalves, Manuel da Purificação, Manuel Joaquim de Sena, Francisco Gomes da Silva and Manuel Rodrigues Correia.

Beside the manor house of the Coutos Cardosos, holders of the entailed estates, stands the chapel of Our Lady of Pity, which served as the parish church while the new church was being built. We shall deal with it in the article devoted to chapels.

This parish is bounded by the parishes of Paul, Prazeres and Estreito da Calheta. It communicates with the first across a beach of large boulders, exposed to the danger of stones that crash violently down from the overhanging cliffs. The other two parishes are reached by mere apologies for roads, narrow tracks cut into sheer slopes, which in recent years have undergone major and much-needed repairs. The landing place and the path leading to Paul do Mar have also been properly repaired. All these improvements were due to the initiative and diligent efforts of Francisco João de Vasconcelos, who was a major landowner there and lived there almost all year round. The building of the new church is also largely owed to the same gentleman, as already mentioned, for he was Father Martinho Fernandes’s most powerful helper in raising it. João Francisco de Vasconcelos died in Lisbon on 13 April 1928. The patron saint of the parish church is Our Lady of the Rosary. The parish has an official mixed school, established in 1914.

Tristão Vaz Teixeira Bettencourt da Câmara, brother of José Bettencourt da Câmara, whom we have already dealt with in this *Elucidário* (see vol. I, p. 204), married a lady of the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of the Coutos Cardosos mentioned above, and in 1896 was granted the title of Baron of Jardim do Mar. He was owner and editor of the *Diário de Noticias* of Funchal and died in this city on 20 October 1903. He was the uncle of Francisco João de Vasconcelos, of whom we spoke above.
Jardim (Dr Alberto Figueira)

He was born in this city on 10 April 1882, the son of the lawyer Dr Nuno Ferreira Jardim and Dona Isabel Figueira Jardim. He is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and a permanent teacher at the Funchal Lyceum (state secondary school). The public offices he has held include those of member of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), president of the executive committee of the same Council, member of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) and substitute judge of this judicial district (*comarca*). Besides various contributions to some newspapers, he wrote in English the pamphlet *Madeira, the Pearl of the Atlantic*, Lisbon, 1914, and in Portuguese the book of poems *Amostras*, Funchal, 1915, and the verse tragedy *Galateia*, Funchal, 1920.
Jardim (Dr Manuel Gomes)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) on 9 January 1881. After completing his studies at the Diocesan Seminary, he attended the Gregorian University in Rome and was ordained priest in 1904. In 1921 he was appointed canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*). For some years he has been a professor at the seminary of this diocese. He has contributed to various newspapers and is at present (1921) the editor of *Vida Diocesana* (‘Diocesan Life’). Of his sacred orations, some have been published as pamphlets – *Sermão ao Santíssimo Sacramento*, Funchal, 1912, and *Oração Fúnebre nas exéquias do S. Pontífice Pio X*, Lisbon, 1915 – and others in a volume, *A Aurora da Redenção*. He is the author of the notable works of religious polemic *As Razões do Protestantismo*, *A Existencia de Deus á luz da sciencia e da razão* and *A Igreja e o Protestantismo*. In defence of the return of the building of the Seminary of the Incarnation (*Seminário da Encarnação*) to the Diocesan Worship Commission of Funchal, he wrote the pamphlet *A Legalidade do Decreto n.° 13.514*.
Jardim (Dr Nuno Ferreira)

He was born in Funchal on 27 January 1851 and graduated from the faculty of law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1874. He has practised as a lawyer in the courts of Madeira with notable brilliance and skill, and has published some of the legal pleadings in which he was involved as a distinguished advocate.
Jardim (Lino Cassiano)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’) and qualified as a physician and surgeon at the Medical School of this city. To be able to practise medicine freely in Brazil, he defended a thesis before the faculty of medicine of Rio de Janeiro, publishing his dissertation under the title *Da Febre Biliosa. . .*, Rio de Janeiro, 1871.
Jardim (Luiz António)

He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), a member of the Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts (*Sociedade dos Amigos das Sciencias e Artes*) and a lawyer in Funchal, where, we presume, he was born around 1780. He was a member of the first Constitutional Council of Funchal, and in 1822 he was elected by this island substitute deputy to the ordinary Cortes (Portuguese parliament). At the press of *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’) he published a *Colecção Poética*, a volume of 122 pages, and, under the title *Parabéns poetico-politicos*, an *oitava*, eighteen sonnets and an ode, in a pamphlet of 29 pages. He died in Funchal on 14 February 1825.
Jardim Municipal (Municipal Garden)

On 21 February 1878 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) appointed a committee of councillors (*vereadores*) charged with promoting, under the supervision of the civil governor, the laying out of gardens on the convent grounds of the former Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) and on the land between those grounds and the Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’). The land to the west of the Praça da Constituição was laid out as a garden shortly afterwards, but work on the São Francisco convent grounds did not begin until August 1880; the design and plan of the garden that exists there were approved by the Council on 15 September 1881. To meet the costs of this work, the Council first allocated the sum of 15 *contos*, diverted from the loan of 69,980,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) taken out in 1883 with the Companhia Geral do Credito Predial, and then the sum of 19,980,000 *réis*, from another loan taken out the following year with the same company.

In October 1880, while the first work was being carried out on the site of the former convent of São Francisco, there was found, according to a document of the time, ‘a stone serving as the lid of a small cavity cut into another stone, in which were found some remains that appeared to be of rotted parchment’. The stone, or lid, was ordered to be deposited in the Municipal Archive, where, however, it is not to be found. It bore the following inscription in gilt letters: D. Ma. Iª. Rainha de P. Pio VI, P. M. Fr. Bernardo N. E. P. D. U. S. C. ‘Julho 1780’.

On 1 October 1885 the Council gave the new garden the name Jardim Municipal, but on 6 September 1897 this name was replaced by Jardim D. Amélia, which it kept until 27 October 1910, when it was resolved to restore the name given to the grounds in 1885. Electric lighting was inaugurated there on 21 March 1902, and in 1916 this lighting was improved, since it had already been recognised in 1911 that the wires carrying the power were in poor condition.

On 28 March 1921, at 5 p.m., before an enormous crowd, the ceremony was held of laying the foundation stone of the monument that Mr Henrique Vieira de Castro is to have erected in the Jardim Municipal in honour of the aviators who first made the Lisbon–Madeira flight. After being signed by the authorities present at the ceremony, the minutes were sealed, together with some coins, in an iron casket, which the civil governor placed in the foundations of the work (1921).

The first plants introduced into the Jardim Municipal came from Paris, and others later arrived from Porto and a few other places. Among the species growing there at present, the following deserve special mention: *Pritchardia filifera*, *Phoenix canariensis* and *Trachycarpus excelsus*, highly ornamental palms; *Dammara australis* and *Ginkgo biloba*, broad-leaved conifers; and *Wigandia macrophylla*, *Astrapaea Wallichii*, *Jossinia tinifolia*, *Plumiera lutea*, *Pterocarya japonica*, *Negundo fraxinifolium* and *Alsophila excelsa*. On 29 August 1888 the Council resolved to buy twenty-nine panes of glass to build a greenhouse, which still exists today in the Jardim Municipal. Some curious species grow in it, chiefly begonias and maidenhair ferns.
The land and building of the convent of São Francisco, where the Jardim Municipal stands, were ceded to the Council by decree of 7 November 1844.
Jardim Pequeno

This was the name of a small garden laid out in 1878 between the old Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’) and the convent grounds of the former convent of São Francisco, now the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’). The garden, which had a few benches and fine vegetation, disappeared in 1914, when work began on the Avenida Oeste, now Avenida do Dr. Manuel de Arriaga.

On the site of the garden there was once a public fountain, whose water the governor Dom Álvaro da Costa de Macedo had diverted to the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence). Before 1878 the same site was occupied by a square, around which stood a few trees. The Council requested the basins of the fountain from the administrator-general (*administrador geral*) in 1838, and they are at present in the Largo de São Sebastião, or Largo do Comércio.
When telegraphic communications with mainland Portugal were inaugurated in 1874, the old Largo de São Francisco was splendidly illuminated.
Jardin (Sir W.)
He wrote on the birds of Madeira in the *Edin. Journ. of Nat. and Geogr. Science* of January 1830, p. 245.

Gardens of Madeira

It is not only the wild plants that interest the naturalists who visit Madeira. The plants cultivated in the *quintas* and gardens also deserve attention, whether for their variety, for the vigour of their growth or, finally, for the brilliance and splendour of their foliage or flowers. Alongside the plants of central Europe, many tropical species grow in the open air in Madeiran gardens, and this mingling of forms from the most varied latitudes makes a strange impression on the educated visitor who travels round this island for the first time to admire its natural beauties. The floras of the most varied zones of the globe have representatives here. Only the breadfruit tree, the *cavaleiro*, the cashew tree, the baobab and a few other species do not grow in Madeira’s climate, certainly because they do not find here the amount of heat they need to pass through all the phases of their growth.

In every backyard in Funchal there are always a few plots of ground set aside for growing flowers, and few people in the city do not own at least a few pots of ornamental plants, to which they devote the greatest care. In the countryside the same inclination can be seen to adorn the surroundings of houses with lovely and varied plants. Among them the naturalist recognises various forms that, in more northerly latitudes, can survive only in greenhouses or under shelters, things that are almost unknown here.

In almost all the small country gardens of Madeira one finds fuchsias, *martírios*, carnations (*craveiros*), *urze-de-cheiro*, *malvas* (*Pelargonium*), *maravilhas*, *goivos*, *saudades-de-inverno*, *não-me-deixes*, *losna*, *alfinetes-de-senhora*, the dahlia, *cuidados*, *pampilios*, *mãozinhas-de-nossa-senhora*, *madre-silva*, *saudade*, *bôca-de-peixe*, *manjericão*, *alecrim*, *salva*, *rosmaninho*, *pessegueiro-inglês* or verbena, *erva-gigante*, *amores-perfeitos*, *lírios*, *beladonas*, *açucenas*, *coroa-de-henrique*, *junquilos*, *esparto* and *alegra-campo* (see those entries), *amores-de-rapazes* (*Mesembrianthemum conspicuum*), *amores-escondidos* (*Grazania rigens*), *Lobelia Erinus*, *Vinca rosea*, *Epiphyllum truncatum*, etc. These species, more or less ornamental, cannot, however, rival either in brilliance or in magnificence certain forms that fill the island’s *quintas* and give them a distinctive character.

The Quinta Vigia, the Quinta do Deão, the Jardim Municipal and the garden of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*) are the grounds within Funchal most notable for the luxuriance and variety of their trees. Here one sees fine specimens of the flora of many latitudes of the globe, alongside native types with tough, evergreen foliage. *Liriodendron tulipiferum*, *Bombax ceiba*, *Astrapaea Wallichii*, *Mammea americana*, *Euphoria Lit-chi*, *Pachira aquatica*, *Spondias lutea*, *Podocarpus neriifolius* and *Taxodium distichum* are trees growing in the Quinta Vigia. In the nearby gardens of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice, meanwhile, the woody species include, among others, *Pittosporum Tobira*, *P. eigenioides*, *Brachychiton populneum*, *Erythrina senegalensis*, *E. poianthes*, *E. Caffra*, *Schotia brachyata*, *Acacia Julibrissin*, *Aleurites triloba* and *Gingko biloba*. *Crescentia cucurbitina* is one of the chief ornaments of the Quinta do Deão, while in the Jardim Municipal the principal adornment consists of the palms, prominent among them *Phoenix canariensis*, together with *Pandanus odoratissimus* and *Dammara australis*.

With the exception of three or four, the trees listed above are quite rare on the island. Among the common ones, the following seem to us worth mentioning: the magnolia, the incense tree, various acacias, the cherry laurel, the Indian pepper tree (*Schinus*), the *louro-régio*, the privet, the *cevadilha*, the jacaranda, the duranta, the camphor tree, the cinnamon tree, the oak, the plane, the nettle tree (*Celtis*), the Indian fig, the cedar of Goa and the araucaria. These trees, together with the native *barbusano*, til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), Madeira mahogany (vinhático, *Persea indica*) and dragon tree, and various exotic shrubs, among which we shall note the camellia, the *cardiais* (*Hibiscus*), the *manhã-de-páscoa*, the angel’s trumpet and various roses and fuchsias, are the principal representatives of the woody flora of Madeiran *quintas* (country estates) and gardens.

The camellia, although cultivated in Funchal, does not reach its full development here. The same is true of *Kalmia*, *Rhododendron arboreum X ponticum*, *Prunus lauro-cerasus*, *Viburnum Opulus*, *Syringa vulgaris*, *Ribes Grossularia*, *R. rubra* and *Betula Alba*: they thrive in the gardens of Camacha, but often languish and die at altitudes below 400 or 500 metres. Madeira mahogany, a native tree, grows poorly below 150 or 200 metres.

Covering the walls and railings of the *quintas* and gardens of Funchal are numerous plants, such as *Ampelopsis*, *Quisqualis indica*, *Tacsonia manicata*, *Wistaria sinensis*, the *Allamandas*, the *Bignonias* (see that entry), *Stephanotis floribunda* (*jasmim-do-cabo*), *Cobaea scandens*, *Plumbago capensis*, *Jasminum grandiflorum*, *Thunbergia Harrisii*, *Solandra macrantha*, *Lantana Camara*, *Bougainvillea spectabilis*, *Ficus stipulata* and *Asparagus Lowei* (growing wild). Meanwhile, in the flower beds, which often take up a good part of these same gardens, one sees, mixed with the shrubs we mentioned earlier, coleuses, chrysanthemums, pelargoniums, gladioli, bamboos, *Lathyrus odoratus*, *Russelia juncea*, *Salvia eriocalyx*, *Libonia floribunda*, *Cyrthanthera Pohliana*, *Zinnia elegans*, *Heliotropium peruvianum*, *Acalipha musaica*, *Iresine Verschaffelti*, *Dichorisandra thyrsiflora*, *Iris biflora*, *Canna indica* (*conteira*), *Globba nutans* (*flor-de-espírito*), *Imantophyllum miniatum*, *Crinum Moorei*, *C. Amabile* and various other plants besides. Lovely azaleas and begonias, as well as the large *Farfugium*, orchids of the genera *Sobralea*, *Stanhopea* and *Cypripedium*, some palms and numerous native and exotic ferns are grown in pots and tubs to adorn the gardens and the entrances of houses.

Madeira has no gardens that can rival certain gardens of southern Europe or of the island of São Miguel, in the Azores, in extent or in the richness of their flora. There is, however, in these enclosures of our island a character so peculiar, born both of the varied aspects of its vegetation and of the way in which the life of nature manifests itself there, that the foreigner who visits them always finds a great deal to admire and to learn, especially if he is endowed with the spirit of observation that the study of the natural sciences imparts. Whatever the season of his visit, he always encounters a multitude of plants in the full vigour of their growth. This cannot fail to make a vivid impression on him, for it reveals that this island enjoys a constant spring, unknown in more northerly countries.

‘Extraordinarily delightful and magnificent,’ says Commodore Bernhard von Wüllerstorf-Urbair, commander of the Austrian frigate *Novara*, ‘is the first impression that the sight of Funchal makes on the traveller, with the prospect of its gardens and flowers and the opulent vegetation that garlands and crowns the hills rising from the shore. There is not, it is true, the wild majesty or the colossal forms of vegetation proper to tropical countries. One senses there the features of an island of southern Italy rather than the splendours of an equatorial landscape. Yet there unfolds before the observer’s eyes so pleasing a picture, in which the life of nature appears in such rich variety and beauty, that the most inventive imagination could conceive nothing more lovely and enchanting. The most beautiful plants of the temperate and subtropical zones delight the eye there in their full development, while some of the finest representatives of the tropical flora also appear in the luxuriant splendour of this marvellous vegetation, which a German naturalist recently compared to the fabled hanging gardens of Semiramis.’

The passages we have transcribed, elegantly translated by Latino Coelho, express the admiration and delight of a man of science contemplating the luxuriant vegetation of our island for the first time. Other travellers speak as the Austrian scholar does, and their writings show no disagreement in how they judge the appearance and richness of the flora of Madeira’s *quintas* and gardens.
Arum lily
Common name of *Richardia aethiopica*, a plant of the arum family (Araceae) naturalised in Madeira.
Jarvão
See Urgebão.
Jasmineiro-do-cabo

This name is given to *Gardenia florida*, a shrub of the madder family (Rubiaceae) native to the Indies, and to *Stephanotis floribunda*, a climbing plant of the milkweed family (Asclepiadaceae) native to Madagascar.
Jasmines

Several species of the genus *Jasminum* occur in Madeira, two of which – *J. odoratissimum* and *J. azoricum* – are native. The first of these Oleaceae, which generally has trifoliate leaves and yellow flowers, is found at São Gonçalo, at Caniço (‘reed’), etc. The second, which also has trifoliate leaves but with larger leaflets, and white flowers, has been found only in the vicinity of Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’). *J. grandiflorum*, from Malabar, and *J. revolutum*, from India, are grown in gardens, the former with white flowers and the latter with yellow.
*Trachelospermum jasminoides* is also known in Madeira as jasmine (*jasmineiro*), although it belongs to the dogbane family (Apocynaceae).
Jasper
It is a mixture of opaque quartz with variously coloured hydrates. It is found on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it is pale yellow and brownish in colour.
Fossil leaf beds

Many years ago, at Ribeiro do Meio (‘middle brook’), on a slope of the São Jorge valley, at the same spot where lignite occurs, various layers of tuff and clay were found, one of which contained numerous leaves of dicotyledons and ferns. Dr Oswald Heer, who studied these leaves, recognised that they belonged to 25 species, among them the til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), the folhado (*Clethra arborea*, a native tree), the tree heath (*urze molar*), the Madeira blueberry (*uveira*, *Vaccinium padifolium*), the *tintureira* and the myrtle.

In a light-coloured tuff to the west of the village of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) there are also some leaves and leaf impressions, perhaps belonging to *Rubus Bollei* and *Carex pendula*, as well as pieces of a soft, spongy wood.

When we come to speak of lignite, we shall return to the São Jorge deposit. As for the Porto da Cruz deposit, it may be supposed that it formed in an ancient lake, perhaps bounded by the islet in the bay, where the tuffs and sands accumulated that erosion later exposed.
Jerónimo Fernando (Dom)

When the bishopric of Funchal fell vacant in 1617 on the transfer of the prelate Dom Lourenço de Távora to Elvas, the secular priest Jerónimo Fernando was presented as bishop of our diocese in 1619, and he took office in 1621. He was a native of Santarém, the son of Cristóvão Dias de Figueiroa and Dona Maria de Basto, and descended through illegitimacy from King Duarte, as can be read in his epitaph in the cloister of the Convento da Graça (Convent of Our Lady of Grace), Lisbon. In a note to his novel *o Regicida*, Camilo Castelo Branco says the following about this prelate’s ancestry:

‘The Infante Ferdinand, father of King Manuel I, had an illegitimate daughter named Leonor. Queen Eleanor, wife of John II and half-sister of that girl, took her into the palace and brought her up with a sister’s care and affection. The lady grew up very flirtatious and wayward, to the great displeasure of the queen, who reproved her repeatedly, to no avail. Then one day, when the court was at Santarém, the queen caught the illegitimate girl by surprise flirting from the window with a knight in the street, who spurred his horse away on sensing the queen’s presence. A fierce quarrel broke out between the two Leonores, and the illegitimate girl, in a fit of defiance, declared that she would marry whomever she pleased. “Not that!” replied the wife of John II. “You shall marry whomever I see fit, and it shall be the first man who passes in the street, if he is unmarried.” At that moment an ordinary man named Álvaro Fernandes, a harness-maker by trade, appeared at the end of the street. The queen called him over, gave him a dowry and ordered the chaplain to marry them. They had children. Father Jerónimo Fernandes of Santarém was the great-grandson of this coquette, daughter of the Infante Ferdinand and sister of King Manuel I, and therefore also the great-grandson of the said Fernandes the harness-maker. The priest claimed and proved to Philip II that he was a great-great-grandson of the Infante Ferdinand, and obtained the mitre of Funchal.’

Dom Jerónimo Fernando was the ninth prelate of this diocese, which he governed for the long period of thirty years. Ungracious in manner and by nature harsh and brusque, he was nicknamed ‘Bravo’ (the Fierce) as a result. He was nevertheless able to soften the meaning of that word through the impeccable correctness of his conduct and the irreproachable way in which he discharged the high duties of his office. A serious accusation was, however, made against him, though a political one: that he had supported Spanish rule and had not joined in the demonstrations held here at the time of the Restoration. It was Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo who echoed this accusation in one of his notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). Yet a manuscript from the middle of the 18th century certainly states that ‘when Luís de Miranda Henriques was governor of this island, and this news (that of the Restoration) arrived on the tenth of January, the said lord was at once acclaimed king throughout the island, the bishop playing a great part in calming the tumult of the people, to whom the governor had become suspect because of the homage he had paid to King Philip II’. This statement contradicts the assertion of the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’, and today it is not very easy to establish on which side the historical truth lies.
Dom Jerónimo Fernando was very zealous in preaching and in his pastoral visitations, and he was the first prelate to confirm and preach on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).

He was assiduous in the religious services of the cathedral, to which he gave new regulations (*regimento*), and at his own expense he had the great organ built that is still there in the choir, beside the main entrance of the church. He reformed various church services, curbing many abuses and imposing strict observance of canonical discipline, though at times with excessive severity, which drew outcries and protests from those under his authority. He was indeed accused of appointing some priests from the mainland to various church posts, disregarding long-standing custom and even existing royal orders in favour of Madeiran clergy. However, he cleared himself of this charge, and his appointments were later upheld and confirmed by the higher authorities.

Three times, in the absence of the respective governors, he headed the administration of the archipelago, and the governments of mainland Portugal praised him for the impartial way in which he conducted himself in that office.

Towards the end of 1641 he withdrew to the mainland and never returned to the diocese. He died on 2 May 1650 and was buried in the church of the convent of Graça, in Lisbon. His tombstone bears the following epitaph: Tomb of Dom Jerónimo Fernando, bishop of Funchal for more than thirty years, great-great-grandson of King Duarte of Portugal through the most serene Infante Dom Fernando, his son; he died on 2 May 1650.
Jérvis
This family surname derives from Ricardo Jarvis, an English merchant who settled in Funchal around 1660.

Jesuits

João Gonçalves da Câmara, the sixth captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, was in Lisbon when, in the first days of October 1566, French corsairs attacked this city and carried out the terrible sack of which the old Madeiran chronicles speak with such horror. The donatary came to the rescue at once, but the help brought by his fleet arrived too late, for the French had already left the island after several days of destruction and slaughter. In this fleet the captain-donatary brought the Portuguese Jesuit Francisco Varca, whose companion was a Castilian religious of the same order, surnamed Naxera. The preaching and religious services of these two members of the Society of Jesus pleased people enormously, so much so that the author of the *Saudades* went as far as to say, in a grossly exaggerated hyperbole, ‘that he did not know which of these things had been greater for this island, what it lost with the arrival of the corsairs or what it gained with the coming of these religious’.

Three years later, at the urgent request of the inhabitants of Funchal, King Sebastian founded a college of the Society in this city by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 20 August 1569, which is transcribed in full on p. 738 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). This document fixed the annual endowment at 600$00 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), ‘paid in produce of the best quality and that with which the Rector and fathers of the said College are most content’. This endowment, for the year 1569, that is, three and a half centuries ago, was not small, but it grew considerably through many private donations and various privileges granted by the monarchs.

To form the new community, the following left Lisbon on 9 March 1570 and reached Madeira on the 18th of the same month: Father Manuel de Sequeira, rector of the College; Father Pedro Quaresma, professor of moral theology; Father Belchior de Oliveira, to perform the religious duties; the deacon Vasco Baptista, professor of Latin and rhetoric; and two further religious. Because plague was raging in the capital, they did not enter this city but settled provisionally in some houses belonging to Fernão Favila next to the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Ajuda (Our Lady of Help), where they stayed for little more than a month.

The Jesuits then moved their residence to the hospice (*albergaria*) of St Bartholomew, founded by Gonçalo Anes Velosa (see vol. 1, pp. 30 and 70), and remained there for some years. Less than two months after their arrival, they opened their classes in theology, philosophy, Latin and rhetoric in some houses next to the old chapel of São Sebastião (St Sebastian), on the site now called Largo do Comércio. The solemn opening took place on 6 May, and on that occasion Professor Vasco Baptista delivered a speech in Latin befitting the event.

From 13 to 30 June 1570, that is, a few months after the religious of the Society had settled in Funchal, the forty Jesuits who were martyred by French Huguenots off the Canary Islands stayed in this city; they were later canonised, as stated in the article devoted to Blessed Inácio de Azevedo (see vol. I, p. 110).
We shall deal with the Jesuits’ College and Church in a separate article.

The royal decree establishing the college states that the religious would reside there ‘studying and reading Latin and cases of conscience’, but it is known that they also taught logic and rhetoric, which made up an abridged course in the old humanities. When the members of the Society settled into the new College, they opened their courses there. These were called the *Aulas do Pátio* (‘Courtyard Classes’, the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), because they were held in an inner courtyard that formed part of the College, as has already been described in the article Education.

Besides the church of the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*), the Jesuits owned the residences of Pico dos Frias (‘the Frias’ peak’), near the Pico (‘peak’) fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*), of Pico do Cardo (‘thistle peak’), in Santo António (‘St Anthony’), of Our Lady of Succour (*Nossa Senhora do Socorro*), in Caniço (‘reed’), and of Fundoa, in São Roque, on the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). They were country houses with chapels attached, where the Jesuits took turns to carry out the various religious services.

The upkeep of the community, the religious solemnities and other acts of worship, the pious obligations imposed by the benefactors and donors of the college and church, and the other obligations inherent in the religious orders all called for great expense. This was met from the substantial revenues the Jesuits held on this island. If we give full credence to the documents published on p. 747 and following of the *Saudades*, we see that the Society of Jesus had an income in Madeira of 10,808,049 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). Of this, 5,670,000 *réis* came from public taxes, 4,028,783 *réis* from the revenues of the estates of the College, Church and Chancel, and 1,109,266 *réis* from the revenues of the estates of the chantries of Our Lady of Succour, St Anthony, São Miguel, São Francisco Xavier and Cem Mil Virgens. Besides these revenues, the community of the College of São João Evangelista had others, from capital lent at interest, etc.

According to the same documents, the public taxes collected by the Jesuits were the revenue from bread and wine in the parishes (*freguesias*) of Campanário, Ribeira Brava, Tabua and Serra de Água; that from fish and small tithes (*miunças*) in the parish of Campanário (‘bell tower’); that from fish, vegetables and small tithes in the parish of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’); that from small tithes and vegetables in the parishes of Tabua (‘bulrush’) and Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’); and that from fish in the parish of Tabua.

When the Marquis of Pombal ordered the expulsion of the Jesuits throughout the country, the members of the Society living on this island had to abandon their College, after being held there as prisoners, cut off from all contact, for more than a year. On 29 May 1759 the College and the Church were unexpectedly surrounded, and the imprisonment and isolation continued until 16 July 1760, when the religious embarked for Lisbon. The carrack the Nativity of Our Lady (*Nossa Senhora da Natividade*), commanded by the Count of São Vicente, came to Funchal; he was charged with conveying to the capital the eighteen Jesuits who were in Madeira.

During the imprisonment all their movable and immovable property was sequestrated. An inventory was drawn up of the rural and urban properties, the furniture, the objects of worship, the silver, the money, etc., and all the documents and papers found in the various residences were carefully collected. The Church and the College were placed in the keeping of the diocesan prelate. The properties were let and later sold at public auction. The Quinta Grande (‘large estate’), which is today a parish (*freguesia*) and was the largest of the Jesuits’ properties, was sold for 140,000 *cruzados*; the *quinta* (country estate) of Pico do Cardo fetched 7 *contos*, and the residence of Pico dos Frias 9 *contos*.
Among the Madeiran Jesuits we must mention here Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, Manuel Álvares and Sebastião de Morais, with whom we deal elsewhere in this *Elucidário*.
Jesus (Dr Quirino Avelino de)

He was born in Funchal on 10 November 1865, the son of Manuel de Jesus and Dona Quirina Augusta de Jesus. After attending the preparatory classes of the seminary (*Seminário*) of this diocese and completing the second year of the theology course, he enrolled in 1887 in the Faculty of Law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), graduating in 1892. While still a university student he contributed to various newspapers; the series of articles he wrote on the economic situation of Madeira became very well known, and at once revealed his future qualities as a writer and journalist.

Having graduated in law, he settled in the capital and devoted himself ardently to journalism, to legal practice and to the study of various social, religious and economic questions. He specialised in colonial affairs, on which he soon became a genuine and undisputed authority. In 1893 he published the book *As Ordens Religiosas e as Misões Ultramarinas*, and in the legislative session of 1897, as a deputy, he delivered a speech on the overseas question that established his standing as a distinguished colonial expert. This reputation was further strengthened by the publication of the remarkable review *Portugal em Africa*, of which he was for some years director and chief editor.

He devoted himself actively to journalism: he was director of the *Correio Nacional* and a regular contributor to, and later chief editor of, *A Tarde*, and in both these periodicals he waged campaigns that have left their mark on the chronicles of Portuguese journalism. His contributions to many newspapers and reviews are extensive and valuable. Most recently he has been director of the *Economista Português*, dealing at length with economic and financial questions, which at present (1921) constitute one of the facets of his intellect.

Although he never devoted himself professionally to the practice of law, he has nonetheless produced several legal works, among which one on the levadas (irrigation channels) of Madeira deserves special mention; it has been published as a pamphlet. As lawyer to the Funchal trading house of Hinton Sons, he wrote and published several pamphlets, which have already been mentioned in the article Hinton Question. Once a fierce and enthusiastic defender of the sugar regime (*regímen sacarino*, the legal regime governing sugar and alcohol production), both as a lawyer and as a publicist, he soon became, with equal ardour and conviction, an avowed enemy of that same regime.

Dr Quirino A. de Jesus was a head of department at the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos, a post to which he was appointed in 1890. He was elected deputy for Madeira on 25 November 1900, having previously represented the district of Braga in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament). At first a member of the Regenerator Party, he later joined the Nationalist Party, which he left because of disagreements with its leaders.

Besides being a distinguished prose writer, as the countless articles he has written on economic and colonial questions, public administration, jurisprudence, etc., etc., prove, he is also a poet of merit, having published an epic poem entitled *Lusa Epopeia*, which is little known in Madeira. He died in Lisbon on 3 April 1935.
Jesus (Friar Rafael de)

He was born in 1614 and died in 1693. Despite his shortcomings as a man of letters and as a historian, he enjoyed renown in his day. Among other works, he wrote one that concerns the history of this archipelago and that ran to two editions. The 1st edition is entitled: *Castrioto Lusitano. Entrepresa e restauração de Pernambuco e das capitanias confinantes. Vários e bellicos successos entre portuguezes e belgas, acontecidos pelo decurso de 24 anos, tirados de noticias, relações e memórias certas. Oferecidos a João Fernandes Vieira, Castrioto Lusitano*; Lisbon, 1679. It describes the life and heroic deeds of the illustrious Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira, whom we have already discussed in this *Elucidário*.
Jesus, Mary and Joseph (chapel)

Sebastião Gonçalves Cordeiro and his wife Luzia de Ornelas founded the chapel of Jesus-Maria-José in 1694 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), at the locality (*sítio*) that still bears that name today. Its deed of endowment is dated 10 May 1694.

At the locality of Lombo do Doutor (‘the doctor’s ridge’), in the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’), there was also a chapel of Jesus-Maria-José. It was founded in 1708 by João de Andrade Berenguer Neto and his wife Dona Tomásia de França Andrade, who endowed it by public deed on 30 October of that year.

A chapel with the same dedication existed in the parish of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral), at a site we cannot determine; it was founded in 1626 by Canon Manuel Afonso. Mateus da Gama Ferreira also founded a chapel dedicated to Jesus-Maria-José in the parish of Monte (‘hill’), on land that later came to belong to the parish of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). It must have been built before 1676, the year in which the parish of Santa Luzia was created.
João de Deus (method)

On 1 September 1879 the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), president of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), sent an official letter to Dr João de Deus introducing the teacher Teodoro João Henriques, whom the Council had commissioned to study the new method of teaching children to read devised by that distinguished poet and zealous apostle of popular education. Henriques spent some months in Lisbon. On his return to Madeira it was he who spread among state and private teachers the teaching method he had learned from the illustrious author of the *Cartilha Maternal*.
João Diniz (springs)
See Fontes de João Diniz (‘João Diniz’s springs’).
Game of canes

The game was very popular in Madeira in the time of the donataries, and Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of Calheta (‘small cove’), was particularly fond of it. We read on p. 202 of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) that in 1555, when António Gonçalves da Câmara returned to Madeira with his second wife, Dona Margarida de Vila-Verde, a lady-in-waiting to the queen, many festivities were held here. Francisco Leomelim shone at them, being so skilled at the game of canes ‘and dodging so well that no cane touched him, not even the hooves of his horse’.

The Moorish game of canes consisted, says Pinheiro Chagas, ‘in lightly hurling, at the swift gallop of a horse accustomed to this kind of exercise, a light cane which the opponent had to avoid while at the same time hurling his own’.
The novel *A Filha de Tristão das Damas*, by J. Reis Gomes, contains an interesting account of the ‘game of canes’ on this island.
Johnson (James Yate)

A distinguished English naturalist, who died in Funchal on 3 February 1900, aged about 80. He came to Madeira shortly after 1850, having previously visited Algeria and Sicily, in search of relief from his lung complaints. He published a large number of works on Madeiran ichthyology and also devoted himself to the study of the shells, bryozoans, crustaceans, zoophytes and flora of the archipelago. He left a herbarium of flowering plants that is rather incomplete but rich in rare species, now in the Funchal Seminary Museum (*Museu do Seminário do Funchal*). He collected a large number of Madeiran mosses, which were studied by the English bryologist William Mitten. He was also a distinguished jurist and a great friend of Madeira. It was on this island, where at first he lived only during the winter, that he managed to recover considerably from his long-standing lung complaints.

He published the second and third editions of the work entitled *Madeira its climate and scenery* (see White), the former in 1857 and the latter in 1885. He wrote several works on the island’s natural history, among which we mention the following: *Description of some new genera and species of fishes obtained at Madeira* (Proc. Zool. Soc., 1863); *Description of three new genera of marine fishes obtained at Madeira* (ibid., 1863); *Description of a new genus of Trichiuroid Fishes obtained at Madeira* (ibid., 1865); *Description of Trachichthys darwinii* (ibid., 1866); *Description of a new genus of Spinacidae* (ibid., 1867); *Description of a new species of Cancer obtained at Madeira* (ibid., 1861); *Description of a new genus and a new species of Macrurous Decapod Crustaceans... discovered at Madeira* (ibid., 1867); and *Notes on some rare and little known plants of Madeira* (Hooker’s Journ. Botany, 1857).
See Anthozoans.
Johnston (William)
See Geographical maps.
Joinville (Prince of)

He was born in 1818 and died in 1900. He was the son of Louis Philippe, King of France, and had married the Portuguese infanta Princess Francisca, sister of Pedro II of Brazil and of Queen Maria II of Portugal. He was a distinguished officer of the French navy and in that capacity visited Madeira several times in command of warships. In 1840 the French naval frigates *La Belle Poule* and *La Favorite* lay in our harbour, carrying the mission charged with exhuming the body of Napoleon I on St Helena and bringing it back to French soil; the Prince of Joinville was the head of this important and honourable mission. We shall refer to this event at greater length in the article Napoleon in Madeira.
Joksimowitsch (Ziwko)

A Serbian palaeontologist who studied the fossils of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) in a work entitled *Die Zweite Mediterranstufe von Porto Santo und Selvagem*. Published in Berlin in the *Memoirs of the Geological Society*, this work records 106 distinct forms, species and varieties, all collected on those islands by the Madeiran naturalist Adolfo César de Noronha.
Jones (Eugene F. G.)
Works: *A Handy Guide to Madeira*, 1895, pamphlet.
Jorge (Francisco)

By royal decree (alvará régio) of 10 February 1595, this architect and engineer was charged with directing the fortification works on this island. He was the father of João Bartolomeu, whom we have already discussed in this *Elucidário*. (See *Disc. dos Arch. e Eng. Port.*, vol. 2, p. 38.)
Jornal da Manhã
One hundred and twenty-eight issues of this newspaper were published, the first on 6 February and the last on 22 August 1887.
Jornal de Notícias
One hundred and eight issues appeared, from 31 March to 23 August 1886.
Jornal do Commercio do Funchal
It was published from 15 July to 18 November 1878, running to one hundred and five issues.
Jornal do Funchal
The first issue appeared on 31 October 1878 and the last, the 73rd, on 31 January 1879.
Jornal do Povo
It began publication on 22 January 1888 and ceased on 10 January 1890, after one hundred and seventeen issues.

It began publication on 27 March 1906 and ceased on 31 December 1910, after one thousand three hundred and ninety-seven issues.
Journalism

Some years ago our fellow Madeiran Dr Jordão Apolinário de Freitas published, as a loose sheet, an alphabetical list of Madeiran newspapers. The company that publishes this city’s *Diário de Noticias* corrected and enlarged it in the pamphlet ‘Chronological Survey of Madeiran Journalism’ (*Resenha Cronológica do Jornalismo Madeirense*), which we shall use to compile the list that follows, adding the names of the newspapers that have appeared here since 1908, the year in which that *Resenha* was published.

In the Portuguese colonial domains, that is, outside the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), it was on this island that the first newspaper saw the light of day: *O Patriota Funchalense* (see that entry), which appeared in 1821. By the time the first periodical came out in the Azores, in 1830, eight newspapers had already been published in Funchal.

‘Once the revolution had taken place in Funchal, says Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, on 28 January 1821, Dr Nicolau Caetano Bettencourt Pitta planned to set up a printing press and publish a periodical. The press was sent for from Lisbon, together with the printer Alexandre Gervasio Ferreira; and on 2 July of the same year, a day chosen because it was held to be the day of the island’s discovery, no. 1 of *O Patriota Funchalense* came out, edited by the said Dr Pitta’.

*O Patriota Funchalense* ceased publication in August 1823. In February of that year the *Pregador Imparcial da Verdade, da Justiça e da Lei* began to appear, in April the *Regedor*, and in the same month the *Atalaia da Liberdade*. Jews

There were Jews in Madeira in the 15th century, and many of them, willingly or not, embraced Christianity after the barbarous decree expelling the children of Israel, issued by Manuel I in December 1496.

This conversion did not, however, shield the old Hebrew families from harshness and persecution. Long before 1547, the year in which the Tribunal of the Holy Office was definitively established in Portugal, the New Christians (*cristãos-novos*) of this island suffered many wrongs and acts of violence, owing to the spirit of intolerance that then reigned in our country.

‘In the islands of the Azores and Madeira,’ says Alexandre Herculano in the *Origem e Estabelecimento da Inquisição em Portugal*, ‘in those small tracts of land, lost as it were in the solitudes of the Atlantic, insults and accusations of Judaism were repeated, and witnesses were easily found to support them, who were afterwards proved to be false.’ ‘This is attested,’ the same author adds in a note, ‘by the judicial instruments presented by the New Christians in Rome in 1544, which are to be found in the *Symicta*, vol. 31, fol. 137 et seq.’

It should be noted that Dom Diogo Pinheiro, Bishop of Funchal, always upheld in the councils of King Manuel I the true principles of evangelical tolerance in everything concerning the unfortunate Hebrews. ‘Trials for crimes of Judaism,’ says Herculano, ‘which apparently fell under his jurisdiction, or which he was sent to judge, ended as a rule with the release of the accused. Knowing thoroughly the history of the conversion of the Jews, which he had witnessed, he was profoundly convinced that such a conversion had been nothing but brutal violence. For him the fact of an imposed baptism had no validity whatsoever, and the converts had remained as Jewish as they had been before.’

In the ‘Notes and Articles of Complaint’ which Infante Ferdinand sent in 1461 to João Gonçalves da Câmara and to the knights, squires, judges, procurators and good men (*homens bons*, local notables eligible for municipal office) of the captaincy of Funchal, the following is found: ‘As to your request that neither Jews nor Genoese should trade in that island as buyers and farmers of revenues, because of the ruin that is wrought in the lands where they are active, I say that it pleases me to keep in this the practice that the said lord Infante my father kept.’

The petition addressed to the Infante reveals that as early as 1461 there was a certain ill will in Madeira against the Israelites. This ill will only showed itself very clearly later, when the intolerance and fanaticism of Manuel I opened the way to the persecutions suffered by the members of that proscribed race, even when they accepted baptism to avoid expulsion from the country.
Júdice de Vasconcelos (João Frederico)
He was a deputy for Madeira in the parliamentary session of 1904.
Judge conservator of the British nation
See Judge-conservator of the English.
Judge of the customs house

This was the most important office of this revenue house, and its holder later came to be called superintendent (*provedor*). Besides directing the customs house, he was responsible for collecting other revenues and various taxes, as we mentioned in the article Customs Houses (see vol. I, p. 36).
On 20 February 1494 Manuel I appointed Francisco Alvares judge of the Funchal customs house, because he had married a daughter of the previous judge. The office survived until the 19th century.
People’s judge

The people’s judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds) was elected by the House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds) (see that entry). He represented the popular classes before various corporations and official bodies and had certain administrative duties. He acted unofficially as intermediary between the people and the local authorities, chiefly in cases where the legal provisions were not entirely clear, and he could not be elected without at least six years’ service in the House of the Twenty-Four.

Under a resolution passed by the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of the City of Funchal on 22 December 1802, the people’s judge, when he came to the Council ‘to make a petition on some matter’, sat on a low chair (chairs with backs were reserved for the councillors (*vereadores*) and the clerk (*escrivão*)) above the eldest of the guild representatives (*mesteres*).
We do not know when the office of people’s judge was created here; it lasted until 1834.
Judge of Pious Bequests and Chantries

The office was originally called Judge of Pious Bequests and Superintendent of Chantries, Hospices, Hostels, Leper Houses and Orphans of the Island of Madeira. In 1486 João do Porto was appointed to this post (*lugar*); he is the earliest holder of whom we have found any record. The office, whose powers later became less extensive, served chiefly to oversee the fulfilment of pious legacies and of the obligations attached to many chantries (*capelas*) and churches, and the registration of the properties burdened with those obligations, etc.

In 1763 the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*) complained to the governor and captain-general about the abuses committed in this court, and pointed to the need to create a Superintendent of Chantries and Bequests to put an end to such misconduct and excesses. He referred to the register (*tombo*) begun in 1590, comprising eight volumes, stating that it showed that many chantries had been usurped from the Crown or from their lawful holders. We do not know what measures were taken regarding the serious wrongdoing that had occurred. We do know, however, that in 1800 fresh abuses were discovered, committed by João Luís Pestana da Silva, clerk (*escrivão*) of the court, who had appropriated a considerable sum derived from various legacies, forging several documents to do so.

The Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*) records the individuals who held the important office of Judge of Residues and Chapels over the long period from 1493 to 1767. Their names are given below: Pedro Quaresma (1493), the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) João Fernandes (1501), Afonso Costa (1535), Luís da Guarda (1546), the licentiate José Jorge (1555), Jácome Dias, Simão Cabral and the licentiate Gonçalo Mendes (1560), Liones Simões Homem and the licentiate Luís Preto (1566), Manuel Rodrigues Pereira (1593), the high court judge (*desembargador*) André Lobo and the bachelor Pedro Fernandes Tinoco (1597), the high court judge Baltasar Fróis (1599); Belchior Tavares de Sousa (1639), António Tavares de Sousa (1682–1699), Francisco Moniz de Meneses (1705), António da Cunha Franco (1714), Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (1718), Sebastião Mendes de Carvalho (1731), Pedro Nicolau Betencourt de Freitas (1752), António Dionísio da Silva Conde (1761), João José Betencourt de Freitas (1767), José Vicente Lopes de Macedo (1769), Pedro Nicolau de Betencourt e Freitas (1797).

As entails and entailed estates multiplied, the number of legacies and pious obligations burdening rural and urban properties grew very considerable, and it was not uncommon for the holders of the usufruct to try to evade those obligations. The court, especially in matters of a religious nature, did not always act with due impartiality and in accordance with the law. At times serious conflicts arose between its judges and the ecclesiastical authorities, and the latter were forced to appeal to higher authorities to have the provisions of the pious legacies carried out, which ought to have been the most sacred of duties and from which no one could in conscience exempt himself. On occasion the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*) and the governor and captain-general intervened in these conflicts to compel the court to observe the laws in force.

Since most of the property in Madeira became entailed, and all the documents relating to the entails (*instituições vinculares*), to their rights of possession of the properties and to the privileges attached to them were registered and filed in the registry of this court, it is easy to appreciate how important that registry was and the interest it may still hold for the detailed study of these institutions.

This valuable collection of documents was thought to be entirely lost, but not many years ago it was found in the former office of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of Funchal, and today it is properly catalogued in the Madeira District Archive (*Arquivo Distrital da Madeira*). This corrects what was said about this court on p. 388 of vol. I of the *Elucidário* (2nd edition).

We do not know when this court was abolished in Madeira, but we know that it was still functioning in 1829. With the introduction of the constitutional system, many of the functions peculiar to this court, which have long since lapsed, were exercised by the administrations of the municipalities (*concelho*).
Judges (juízes de direito)

Professional judges have served in Madeira since 15 October 1835, the day on which the judicial reform decreed on 16 May 1832 came into force on this island. From then until 1876, that is, for as long as the western and eastern comarcas (originally *julgados*) operated here, the following magistrates came to Funchal, many of whom served in both comarcas:

Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo (1835), José Pereira Leite Pita Ortigueira Negrão (1835), Francisco Jerónimo Coelho de Sousa (1838), Francisco Leite Pereira da Costa Bernardes (1846), Dom João Correia Portugal da Silveira (1847), José Afonso Botelha (1849), António Magalhães Mexia Baião de Lança Salema (1852), José Pereira Sanches de Castro (1855), Augusto das Neves Sousa Pimenta (1861), Caetano José Gomes Monteiro (1862), António Bernardo de Amorim de Guerra Quaresma (1863), Francisco José Monteiro Tavares (1869), Cassiano Sepúlveda Teixeira (1869) and Francisco António da Silva Seide.

The present judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal was established on 16 November 1876, and the aforementioned Francisco António da Silva Seide, previously district judge (*juiz de direito*) of the western judicial district, took office as its district judge. Since then the judicial district has had the following judges:

As stated in the article Funchal (judicial district), a second court was added to the judicial district of the district capital, so that there came to be two courts, each with its own judges. These posts have been held by Drs Joaquim Crisóstomo da Silveira Júnior (1925), Albano de Gusmão Tavares do Canto Taveira (1929), Pedro de Melo Coutinho de Albuquerque (1929), Luís Afonso Viana de Lemos (1932), Augusto Simões Cantante (1935), António Magalhães Barros Araújo Queirós, Viscount of Cortegaça (1935), Tomás António Bandeira da Gama Pessanha Faria Coutinho Vilhegas do Casal (1938), José Ferreira Machado (1939) and José Pinto Magalhães (1940).
