Juízes de fora

In the entry Judicial Administration we stated that in 1767 the decree of 2 August 1766, which had created the offices of *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) and *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) in the Azores, was applied to Madeira. From then on these posts were held in the Madeiran archipelago by two magistrates, whereas before that date they had been filled by a single individual. The application of the decree of 2 August 1766 merely made the exercise of the two offices permanent, and they also came to be held definitively by two magistrates.

The two offices of *juiz de fora* and *corregedor* are very old here, but they were not permanent and were sometimes held together by the same individual. The archives of the Council of Funchal record many letters of appointment to one or the other office. The oldest are that of 1512, issued in favour of Rui Pires as *juiz de fora*, and that of 1466 in favour of Denis Anes de Aragão as *corregedor*. Thereafter, though with some interruptions in the exercise of the office, the following served as *juiz de fora*: Pedro Fernandes (1554), Lourenço Correia (1558), Pedro Anes (1566), Pedro Barbosa (1567), Lourenço da Cunha Macedo (1573), Francisco de Sousa (1645), António de Sousa Galvão (1649), Manuel de Sena Tenreiro (1657), António Freire Cardoso (1657), Manuel Soares Monteiro (1662), António Martins Machado (1681), Manuel de Sequeira e Gouveia (1685), Manuel Viegas (1689), Francisco Gomes de Góis (1691), Manuel de Sousa Teixeira (1695), Nuno de Afonseca Homem (1698), António de Macedo (1702), Vital Casado Rotier (1705), António da Costa Maciel (1709), António da Cunha Franco (1714), João de Andrade Albuquerque (1717), Feliciano Prestes de Gouveia (1722), Sebastião Mendes de Carvalho (1730), Manuel Vieira Cardoso (1733), José Barquette de Oliveira (1739), Miguel de Arriaga Brun Silveira (1747), Luís António de Sousa Tavares e Abreu (1763), António Felipe Bulhões (1766), Francisco Álvares de Andrade (1770), Bernardo José de Oliveira Perdigão (1779), António Rodrigues Veloso de Oliveira (1784), José Maria Cardoso Soeiro (1790), António Felipe Ferreira Cabral (1798), José Júlio Henriques Gordilho (1802), Manuel Caetano de Almeida Albuquerque (1808), José Joaquim Nabuco de Araújo (1812), Luís Ribeiro de Sousa Saraiva (1819), Joaquim de Assis Saldanha (1821), António Joaquim de Carvalho (1823), Manuel Ferreira Seabra da Mota (1826) and Manuel Cirilo Esperança Freire (1828), who was the last and served until 14 June 1834.

The *juiz de fora* was the *ex officio* president of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) and exercised his functions only within the *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca), which was a subdivision of the judicial district (*comarca*). When he was unable to act, he was replaced by the eldest councillor (*vereador*), who was then called the judge by operation of law (*juiz por bem da lei*), and his lodging allowance was paid by the Council. Both he and the *corregedor* were required to hold a degree in law.
See Judicial Administration.
Justices of the peace

The decree of 16 May 1832 created a justice of the peace in each of the parishes that made up the jurisdictions, the judge to be elected by the people. The justices of the peace were intended to reconcile the parties, and from 1835 to 1840 they carried out duties that had previously belonged to the judges of orphans.

The decree of 29 March 1890 laid down that justices of the peace should be appointed by the Government, and that of 5 June 1905 fixed the composition of the justice-of-the-peace districts of Funchal, Ponta do Sol, Santa Cruz and São Vicente.
Judges of the mechanical trades

They were elected by the guilds of the working classes in the House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds). The people's judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds) was required to inform the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of the results of the elections, so that the Council could have the respective letters of appointment issued to them. Besides the senior judge, there was sometimes a second judge, or junior judge, and in addition to these officers each trade had a clerk (*escrivão*) and a banner steward (mordomo da bandeira). The shoemakers elected one judge for black work and one for white work, and it was customary for the clerk of the blacksmiths’ trade also to serve as clerk of the locksmiths’ trade.

We know that judges existed in Funchal for the trades of stonemason, carpenter, cabinetmaker, locksmith, blacksmith, shoemaker, bootmaker, tanner, barber, miller, tailor, axe carpenter, caulker and cooper.
Judges of orphans

There was a judge of orphans (*juiz dos órfãos*) in Funchal, another in Calheta and a third in São Vicente, who ‘had jurisdiction in all civil cases in which orphans were plaintiffs or defendants, until their emancipation’. As early as the time of Manuel I there was a judge of orphans in Madeira, and the first to hold this office on the island was Fernão de Perada, appointed in 1493.

In 1835 the powers that under the old laws had belonged to the judges of orphans passed to the justices of the peace. In Funchal a commission was appointed to make an inventory of the orphans’ registries, which were handed over to the court of the *juiz de fora* under a royal decree (*alvará*) of the President of the Province.

The orphans’ inventories, after being kept in the archive of the Council, passed to the archives of the justices of the peace. At present it is the deputies of the Public Prosecutors who hold the powers that belonged to the former judges.
Elected judges

They existed in the parishes and performed functions similar to those of the pedaneous judges (*juízes pedâneos*) of the absolutist regime. They were created by the Judicial Reform of 1837 and abolished by the law of 16 April 1874. Permanent judges (*juízes efectivos*) had existed under the Constitution of 1822.
Ordinary judges

They existed under the absolute regime, and under the *Ordenações Filipinas* they held office for one year. They were judicial officers, and they preceded the *juízes de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) as presidents of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*). The other councils of the archipelago were presided over by them until liberal government was established in Madeira in 1834.

The law of 30 April 1835 abolished the ordinary judges (*juiz ordinário*, locally elected lay judge), but the New Judicial Reform of 1837 restored them, and they were finally abolished by the decree of 20 July 1886. Their powers passed to the judges of law in all jurisdictions that were the seat of a judicial district (*comarca*) or formed part of the city or town (*vila*) where the seat of a judicial district was located, and to the justices of the peace in all other jurisdictions.

In the days of absolute government there were five jurisdictions in Madeira, each with its own ordinary judge, namely Machico, Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol, Calheta and São Vicente. In Funchal, the seat of the judicial district, there was a *juiz de fora*.
Juízes pedâneos (village judges)

They existed in Madeira and were also called *juízes de vintena*. They served in villages lying one *légua* (league, about 5 km) or more from the seat of the *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca), and they judged cases of fines, damages and actions concerning movable property of small value.
Under the absolute regime the judicial district (*comarca*) was divided into *termos*, and the *termos* into *vintenas*.

There were *juízes pedâneos* in Ribeira Brava, Câmara de Lobos and Caniço, at the time when these places belonged to the municipality of Funchal, and it was the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) that appointed them.
Júlio da Silva Carvalho (street)

This street, originally named João da Mata, came to be called the New Convent (*Mosteiro Novo*) when a building intended for a small convent was built there, although it was never put to that use. It was also called Rua do Seminário, because the diocesan seminary operated in the house intended for the convent. A few years ago it was given the name Rua Júlio da Silva Carvalho (see that entry). It has since reverted to the name Rua do Seminário.
Junça (Cyperus longus)
Common name of *Cyperus longus*, a member of the sedge family (Cyperaceae) frequent in Madeira.
Junco (rush)

Among the species of the genus *Juncus* found in Madeira, the most notable are *J. acutus*, which is used for making cages, and *J. inflexus* and *J. effusus*, whose stems are used for ties and sheaf-bands.
Junquilho

Madeirans give the name *junquilhos* to certain species of the genus *Narcissus*, of the family Amaryllidaceae, whereas on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) it is *Cyperus laevigatus*, of the family Cyperaceae, that bears that name.
Agricultural Board

The Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) was created by the decree of 11 March 1911. This legislative act, which settled the so-called Hinton question (to which its preamble makes special reference), established a new sugar regime (*regímen sacarino*, the legal regime governing sugar and alcohol production). The regime was variously judged and gave rise to conflicting opinions, but it unquestionably contains principles and lays down provisions so useful and wholesome that, if observed, they would contribute greatly to the growth and prosperity of the whole Madeiran archipelago. It must never be forgotten that this decree created the Agricultural Board and the corresponding expropriation of those laboratories of toxic substances known as spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) factories.

The creation of the Agricultural Board, says the lucid report that precedes the decree, ‘will contribute in the fullest measure to the economic development of Madeira’. And so it would certainly have done, had the work of this body not at times been hampered by a mistaken approach. In an essentially agricultural country, where most of the population lives by planting and tilling the land, it is easy to judge the notable services that a body of a special technical character, with very substantial resources at its disposal, could render to our agriculture if all the provisions of the said decree had been respected and fully carried out. That did not happen, however. Before the calamitous crisis we are now going through (1921), enormous sums were spent without improving the condition of the Madeiran people by putting into effect certain wholesome measures set out in the decree.

The report accompanying the decree of 11 March 1911 refers to the name ‘Island of Spirit’ given to Madeira because of the abundant production of this poison and the excessive use made of it in the archipelago. This name was echoed, and given full currency, by a well-known politician and statesman who, in a public lecture, so ungraciously described the inhabitants of this island as drunkards and alcoholics. He did so after having received here the highest distinctions and the most elevated marks of esteem and regard, which went so far as to confer on him, at a solemn and splendid session of the Funchal Council, the titles and honours of a citizen of Funchal, with the unveiling of his portrait in the great hall of the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*).

Advocating the lofty moral principle that so preoccupies the governments of states today, that of combating alcoholism vigorously and effectively, the decree enshrines one of the most beneficial measures ever adopted in favour of this archipelago: the expropriation of the spirit factories. This mattered for the good name of our land, and above all it was to accomplish a great social and humanitarian work.

We have already said elsewhere (1921) that a marked decline of the race is becoming noticeable in Madeira. In stature, in physical constitution, in muscular strength, etc., a decline worth recording can be observed. The fact still passes unnoticed by the general public, but not by doctors, and especially not by those who have to select the young men destined for military service.

There is, however, an even more eloquent and persuasive fact: the astonishing percentage of cases of insanity that the Madeiran population is supplying, according to the authoritative testimony of science. The contingent that alcoholism supplies to tuberculosis is also considerable, not to mention the frequent cases of idiocy, epilepsy, convulsions and other more or less proven forms of degeneration. A significant part of the inhabitants of this island who give themselves over to alcoholism already carry in their cells an imperious tendency towards the vice. This tendency finds fertile ground for its development in the ease with which one can buy the terrible poison with which fifty factories flood the market, even as they are poisoning, brutalising, infecting with tuberculosis and driving mad the unwary population of an entire district.

In view of these reasons, set out here only briefly, the advisability and necessity of that great measure, the expropriation of the spirit factories, stand out clearly. Everyone knows, however, that this measure of the greatest moral and social import was never fully adopted. What was judged absolutely indispensable for the black population of Angola, with the prohibition of the manufacture of and trade in spirit, was considered of minor importance for the white inhabitants of this our archipelago of Madeira!
The Agricultural Board was created by Article 26 of the decree of 11 March 1911, which we transcribe verbatim:

Art. 26. An Agricultural Board of Madeira is hereby created, with the special task of managing the fund formed by the tax on the manufacture of spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine). The revenue of this board shall also include the fines imposed for any infringements of the present decree having the force of law, and whatever is laid down in the respective regulations.

Sole paragraph. This fund shall be applied to the economic development of Madeira. A part of it shall be reserved for the expropriation of the spirit factories, for financing the promotion of Madeira wine abroad, for meeting the costs of founding and maintaining an agricultural station that may come to be created on the island, and for promoting the regrafting or transformation of the grape varieties at present cultivated, so that, within a period set by regulation, the only vines in production shall be those that traditionally made up the type known as the vines of Madeira’.

The creation of the Agricultural Board of Madeira therefore had the following special and expressly stated aims: 1. the expropriation of the spirit factories; 2. the promotion of Madeira wines abroad; 3. the founding and maintenance of an agricultural station; 4. the transformation, by regrafting, of the grape varieties now in existence, so as to turn them into the traditional types that produce what is called Madeira wine.

As we have already said, the expropriation of the spirit factories was never even begun (1921). We must now add that the promotion of our wines abroad produced no satisfactory result at all, because of the impractical way in which it was carried out. Nor was the propagation, by grafting, of the varieties that produce traditional Madeira wine undertaken on the desirable scale, even though everyone saw in it the means of restoring to the island one of its oldest and most valuable sources of wealth. The experimental field at Bica da Cana (‘reed spout’) yielded few practical results. Fairness, however, demands that it be said that many useful selected plants came from the nurseries of Louros (‘laurels’) and Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), especially the latter. The organisation of the services for combating the insects and parasites that attack plants also left nothing to be desired: it was an excellent service to our farmers, sparing them countless losses, above all in fruit trees.

The excessive importance that the Agricultural Board attached to the tourist industry at times made it forget the purposes for which it had specifically been created, and led it to spend large sums on studies and works that it should have undertaken only later.

At Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) and on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) a great deal of money was spent with no known benefit. The purchase at high prices of several upland commons (montados) and extensive tracts of land in our uplands, although it may be justified by the need to afforest the mountainous zone of the island or to make use of waters now running uselessly into the sea, did not win the approval of the great majority of the inhabitants of Madeira.

The cold store (see that entry), an establishment that could have served the island well, never came into operation, for reasons unknown to us, and the street on which its installations had been built was finally handed over to the Council.

It is worth noting that the decree of 15 May 1912, which approved the Regulations for the implementation of the decree having the force of law of 11 March 1911, laid down new provisions on the purposes for which the Agricultural Board had been created and on its operation, altering the organic and fundamental constitution that a law had assigned and conferred on it. This decree charged the body with afforesting the mountains, establishing an effective rural police and promoting all improvements in roads, sanitation and other matters tending to develop the tourist industry on the island. It was under these provisions that some of the measures we have noted above were carried out.

It should be noted here that the regulations of 15 May 1912 place the obligation to expropriate the spirit distilleries last, and assign only a tenth of the Junta’s annual income to meeting the cost of that expropriation.

Under these regulations the Agricultural Board was composed as follows: the district agronomist or the director of the Agricultural Station, three delegates representing the Municipal Councils, two delegates of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), two delegates of the Commercial Association, one delegate of the Viticulture Commission (*Comissão de Viticultura*), and the forestry officer (regente silvícola) serving the General Council.

Article 21 of the same regulations provided that the following staff should be seconded from the tax inspection corps to supervise the spirit distilleries: one district chief 1st class, one district chief 2nd class, two chief inspectors, thirty inspectors 1st class and ninety inspectors 2nd class.

For the proper and regular operation of the Agricultural Board there are three decrees dated 28 December 1912: the first approved the Internal Regulations of the Agricultural Board, the second the Regulations for the expropriation of the spirit distilleries, and the third the Regulations for the collection of the tax on spirit.

The second set of regulations completely destroys the most important and most advantageous clause of the law that created the Agricultural Board, namely the expropriation of the distilleries. It provides that only three years after the sugar regime of 1911 has come into force, and when it is recognised that sugar-cane cultivation has disappeared in some region of the Madeiran archipelago, will the distilleries be expropriated, and even then only when they request it. And so, with a stroke of the pen in a mere set of regulations, the most useful and beneficial provisions of a law are entirely annulled!

The decree of 1 February 1913 approved the Instructions for the promotion of the products of Madeiran soil, and that of 8 March of the same year approved the Regulations for the rural and forestry service. It was not for lack of regulations that the Agricultural Board failed to fulfil its civilising mission.

The body was installed on 22 August 1912 and held nine further sessions that year. It met 40 times in 1913 and 29 times in 1914. Its revenue for the five financial years from 1910–1911 to 1914–1915 was, in round figures, 25, 64, 155, 149 and 121 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos) respectively.

By ministerial order (*portaria*) of 27 February 1915, Dr Fernando Maria Allen Urculu Vieira de Castro, judge in the judicial district (*comarca*) of Santa Cruz, was appointed to conduct an official inquiry into the acts of the Agricultural Board. He began the work but did not complete it. By ministerial order of 26 August of the same year, Dr Francisco Antunes de Mendonça was instructed to continue the inquiry, and he concluded his investigations on 4 November 1915, the date of his report to the Government.

The inquiry’s work was long and detailed, and its publication filled a hundred pages of the *Diário do Governo*. The report ends with eight conclusions, the first of which states ‘that all the members of the Agricultural Board, even those who have already left office, acted with honour and dignity’. The other conclusions mention some minor infringements of laws and regulations, which in no way affect the first conclusion.

Article 3 of the law of 31 August 1915 transferred to the Agricultural Board the administration, upkeep and repair of the state levadas (irrigation channel), and provided that the Junta should continue to operate beyond 1918 without time limit. Under Article 5 of the same law, the Junta was empowered to approve its own budget.

On 2 September 1915 a decree was issued permitting the Agricultural Board to contract with the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos a loan of 100:000$, to be applied specifically to the construction of roads and tourist hotels, in accordance with no. 4 of Article 3 of the aforementioned regulations of 15 May 1912. On 11 February 1916 a bill granting autonomy to the Junta and extending its privileges and prerogatives was presented to Parliament, but it was not approved.

The decree of 2 May 1919, which modified the sugar regime, abolished the Agricultural Board, and the decree of 12 June of the same year transferred its staff to the 9th Agricultural Region, under the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*).
Autonomous Board for the Funchal Harbour Works

This body was created by the decree of 13 August 1913. The purpose of its creation and the scope of its remit are set out in Article 1 of its founding law, as follows: ‘The indispensable repair works on the harbour of refuge at Pontinha (‘little point’), on both the inner and the outer side of the cove; the installation on the same mole (breakwater) of loading and unloading machinery; a link with the customs house by means of an electric railway line; warehouses at the terminus of the line, together with the extension and improvement of the quay at the entrance to the city; the construction of a goods quay opposite the customs house; the opening of a seafront avenue between the quay at the entrance to the city and the eastern end of Campo Almirante Reis (‘Admiral Reis square’); the construction of a small dock between the customs quay and the mouth of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’), with the necessary installations for the island’s small-scale coastal shipping; and, finally, all other complementary installations, such as a customs building, the construction of a maritime disinfection station, of a market, a fish market, a building for the Harbour Master’s Office (*Capitania do Porto*) and the health service, and likewise the maintenance, operation and use of all the installations, works and services that it may set up within the limits of its remit’. The Autonomous Harbour Board was made up of the following: the president of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), the president of the Funchal Council, the president of the Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*), the director of Public Works of the District, the director of the Customs House, the harbour master, the president of the Commercial Association (*Associação Comercial*), a member specially appointed by the Minister of Development (*Ministro do Fomento*), a member elected by the banking houses, a member elected by the trade associations of wholesale and retail merchants, and a member elected by the Councils of the various municipalities (*concelhos*) of the district. The deputies and senators elected for the constituency of Funchal were also members of this body.

The revenues of the Autonomous Board are expressly laid down in Article 11 of its founding law, and were as follows: a) a surcharge of 3 per cent on import duties and on the municipal taxes collected by the Funchal customs house (*Alfândega do Funchal*), foodstuffs excepted; b) 6 per cent of the annual yield of the production tax on spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) collected by the Agricultural Board of Madeira; c) 50 per cent of any increase in the collection of direct taxes paid by taxpayers of the municipality of Funchal that are revenue of the District General Council, from the second half of the financial year in which the Board is instituted, relative to the highest amount reached by that collection in the same period of the three previous financial years; d) 30 per cent of the yield of the municipal tax on domestic and foreign tobacco; e) the revenue from the commercial operation of the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*), the sale of land reclaimed from the sea, and the leasing of warehouses and of the said land or of other land that the Government or any other bodies may cede to the Board.

By a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 27 November 1915, the internal rules of the Autonomous Board, consisting of 25 articles, were approved. The Board also has internal regulations (*regimento*) for its Secretariat.

The works foreman (*condutor*) Furtado de Mendonça, who served on the staff of the Board, published in 1915 a pamphlet entitled *Junta Autónoma das Obras do Porto do Funchal. Memória descritiva e justificativa das obras projectadas*, which contains the plans and designs for the works to be carried out in our harbour. This work, however, did not win the approval of the higher authorities.

Later the engineer Francisco Soares Júnior drew up a new project, which was submitted for assessment to the relevant technical department of the Ministry of Public Works (*Ministério do Fomento*) and which is said to be a study showing a special knowledge of the subject. It was published under the following title: *Junta Autonoma das Obras do Porto do Funchal. Novo projecto das obras do porto artificial do Funchal. Memoria descritiva e justificativa.* (Lisbon, 1921, 19 pp.).

Before this Autonomous Board was set up, a commission for the improvement of Funchal harbour had been appointed by the ministerial order (*portaria*) of 8 December 1911, and on 29 April 1912 it drew up a report on the works to be carried out. A member of this commission, the engineer Adriano Augusto Trigo, submitted an important study, which was published as a pamphlet under the title *Breves Considerações sobre os melhoramentos de que carece o porto do Funchal*. The commission was short-lived and, apart from the reports it presented, carried out no other work of note.

As already stated, the Junta Autónoma das Obras do Porto was created by the Decree of 13 August 1913. The decrees of 27 November 1915, 2 July 1926, 6 February 1934 and 5 September 1936 modified its original organisation and regulated the way it operated. This body was granted broader powers and new sources of revenue so that it could fulfil the purposes for which it had been created. In its first years of existence the Junta Autónoma confined itself to collecting its revenues, which served as the basis for the tender opened in March 1922 for the award of the contract, thus making a start on the works previously planned. This tender attracted no bidders, and a second was opened in January 1923; the contract for this construction was awarded to the firm ‘Fumasil Company Limited’, which was then formed in London. After lengthy debate in the press, petitions addressed to the central government, appeals to the courts, an opinion from the Office of the Attorney General of the Republic, etc., the contract between the Junta Autónoma and the ‘Fumasil Company’ was deemed rescinded in 1928, leaving the Junta free to open a new tender for the award of the contract for those works.

With the appointment of a technical director for the works to be carried out in the harbour of Funchal, the Autonomous Board for the Funchal Harbour Works (*Junta Autónoma das Obras do Porto do Funchal*) became far more productive. This was soon shown by the reinforcement of the breakwater protecting the mole (breakwater) between the islet and the Pontinha: between April 1930 and March 1931, 239 blocks with a volume of 4,784 m³ were built, at a cost of 590,000 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis). This improvement had to be carried out at once, because the great storm of 15 December 1926 had caused serious damage to the mole, putting it at risk of imminent and total destruction. Another improvement that local circumstances demanded even more urgently was the extension of the Cais da Entrada da Cidade (City Entrance Quay). A tender for the contract was opened and closed on 30 October 1930, and the construction was awarded to the firm Nederlandsche Maatschappij Voor Havenwerken for the sum of 4,763,000 escudos. The addition to the quay was to be 80 metres long and 16.4 metres wide, and to consist of five large blocks with a total volume of 3,337 cubic metres. The first block was set in place on 25 June 1932 and the fifth and last in January 1933. (See Cais (‘quay’)).

The Autonomous Board for the Funchal Harbour Works’s main source of revenue is the tax levied on imported tobacco, collected at the Funchal customs house. We give a summary of it for the years 1923 to 1932:

The staff of the Autonomous Board for the Funchal Harbour Works consists of an engineer-director, a head of accounts, a head of the secretariat, a clerk, a ‘foreman’ of the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point quay’), a timekeeper, a warehouse inspector and an office messenger. For a fuller account of this subject, readers should consult the articles Cais, Molhe da Pontinha and the harbour of Funchal in this *Elucidário*, as well as the following writings: *Breves considerações sôbre os melhoramentos de que carece o porto do Funchal* by the engineer Adriano Trigo, 1912; *Lei Organica da Junta*, 1914; *Memória descritiva e justificativa das obras projectadas. . .* by the engineer Furtado de Mendonça, 1915; *Lei Organica e Regulamento da Junta Autonoma*, 1917; *Novo Projecto das obras do porto artificial do Funchal* by Francisco António Soares, 1921; *Obras do Pôrto do Funchal*, published by the Companhia das Obras do Porto, 1926; *Obras do Porto do Funchal*, an opinion by three professors of the University, 1926; *A Questão do Porto do Funchal*, a petition to the government, 1927; *Documentos relativos á questão do porto do Funchal*, 1928; *Construção do prolongamento do cais da Entrada da Cidade*, by the engineer Rodrigo António Machado Guimarães, 1933; *Protecção do quebra-mar da Pontinha*, by the same, 1931; *Os Portos Maritimos de Portugal e Ilhas Adjacentes*, vol. 5, by Adolfo Loureiro, 1910; and *Dicionário Corografico do Arquipelago da Madeira* by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva.
Junta da Justiça (criminal justice board)

It was created in this archipelago by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 26 October 1803 and consisted of the Governor and Captain-General, the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*), the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) and the Judge or Superintendent of Bequests and Chantries (*provedor dos resíduos e capelas*). We do not know how far its powers extended, but we have read somewhere that it was intended ‘to try the crimes committed in the judicial district, and that its decisions could be appealed to the Casa da Suplicação (supreme court of appeal in Lisbon), in Lisbon. For reasons unknown to us, the Governor and Captain-General informed the government in mainland Portugal in 1809 that it would be advisable to exclude the judge of pious bequests and chantries from the Junta da Justiça. And in 1824 the Governor complained to the higher authorities of the excesses committed by the said Junta, proposing that the royal decree of 15 October 1810, which had created the Junta da Justiça Criminal in the Azores, be extended to this archipelago. We do not know when it was abolished, but it was still operating here in 1830.
Royal Treasury Board of the Island of Madeira

The Governor and Captain-General of this archipelago, João António de Sá Pereira, pointed out to the government in mainland Portugal how carelessly various public revenues were being collected on this island, some of them having even ceased to be collected at all. In consequence, the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 6 April 1775 created the Royal Treasury Board of the Island of Madeira (*Junta da Real Fazenda da Ilha da Madeira*), whose specific purpose was to oversee the collection of all taxes and levies. It was composed of the Governor, as president, a clerk (*escrivão*), the Treasurer, the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) and the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district).

The Royal Treasury Board replaced the former Treasury Superintendency (Provedoria da Fazenda) and operated until 6 August 1834. From then until 30 June 1835, treasury business was administered by an interim commission established by the decree of 23 June 1834, which also abolished the Board.

On 1 July 1835 treasury business passed into the charge of a receiver-general (recebedor geral, head of the district revenue office), the first to hold this post in Funchal being Francisco Correia Heredia.
Board for Agricultural Improvement of Madeira and Porto Santo

This body was created by the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 20 July 1810. Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo states that its creation was inspired by the Instructions on agriculture which the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) Dr Veloso de Oliveira (see that entry) left recorded at the Council of Calheta (‘small cove’). Its purpose was not only to protect and develop farming in general but also, in particular, to promote the cultivation of the common lands (*baldios*) by dividing them into leaseholds, thereby extending the area of arable land and making productive the many plots that lay waste and barren. This measure, which was reinforced by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 September 1811, was also intended to remedy some of the damage that the terrible flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803 had caused to Madeiran agriculture.

Despite the well-founded hopes that the creation of the Junta raised in many people, and the pressing ills it had been called upon to combat, the Governor and Captain-General Luís Beltrão de Gouveia e Almeida did not convene the first meeting of this body until early December 1813, that is, three years after it had been created! We do not know how long it operated, and we believe that the services it rendered to Madeiran agriculture were nil. This Junta was abolished in 1821.
Junta do Desembargo do Paço

This body was established in Madeira on 10 September 1811. One of its duties was to name the members of the governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office) who were to serve on the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council). For the warrant (*provisão*) appointing the councillors (*vereadores*), the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) paid the secretary of the Junta a fee of 6,400 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).
Governing Junta of Madeira in 1847

The popular revolt that broke out in the province of Minho in 1846 and spread rapidly to other parts of the country became known in our history as the Maria da Fonte revolution. After a provisional government was set up in the city of Porto under the name of the Governing Junta of Porto (*Junta Governativa do Porto*), other juntas acting as its delegates were organised in various towns and cities. Their aim was to support the revolutionary movement, which sought to overthrow the government of the Cabrais and to cancel the great influence it enjoyed in the spheres of power. There followed a truly calamitous period of civil war, which threatened to drag on indefinitely had it not been for the intervention of certain foreign powers.

The revolution found its echo in Madeira in the early hours of 29 April 1847, when the troops of the garrison rose and, on the old public promenade, solemnly declared their adherence to the revolution and to the Governing Junta of Porto. At five o’clock that morning, in the courtyard of the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), various officials, some persons of standing and a good number of ordinary people gathered, with the armed force posted a few metres away. They proclaimed the principles of the revolution, declared their adherence to the Junta of Porto and named the Governing Junta of Madeira. It was made up of Luís de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, president; Francisco Correia Heredia, vice-president; Diogo Berenguer; Luís Agostinho de Figueiroa; Dr José Júlio Rodrigues; and António Correia Heredia, secretary. As Luís de Ornelas e Vasconcelos withdrew from the Junta’s work at once, its presidency was assumed, until its dissolution, by Francisco Correia Heredia, holder of an entail (*morgado*). The civil governor of the district at the time was the meritorious Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro. Refusing to join the revolutionary movement, he immediately left office and withdrew to the Quinta do Pico de São João and later to the Quinta do Deão, placing himself under the hospitality offered to him by two British subjects living there.

From the very first moments of its formation the Governing Junta of Madeira displayed an astonishing energy, which seems to have surpassed the labours of its counterparts organised in many parts of Portugal. It appointed Manuel Joaquim da Costa Andrade, a teacher at the Lyceum (*Liceu*), as civil governor. He resigned shortly after taking up the post and was replaced by Lieutenant-Colonel Manuel José Júlio Guerra, who had also been appointed military commander of Madeira. Dr António Ribeiro Pacheco Nunes, Dr Luís da Costa Pereira and Dr Juvenal Honório de Ornelas were appointed deputy crown prosecutor, president of the Council and health officer (*delegado de saúde*) respectively. Many public officials were dismissed and replaced by individuals who had joined the revolutionary movement or embraced the principles proclaimed by the Junta of Porto. Some officers of the garrison were advanced in rank, and several sergeants were promoted to second lieutenant. The governing action of the Madeira Junta was at times felt in a truly arbitrary manner in many branches of public administration, provoking vigorous protests from the people, despite the discretionary powers with which the Junta had invested itself. According to a document of the period, it left the public coffers of the district completely exhausted.

As the civil war dragged on, England, Spain and France resolved to intervene in the internal affairs of our country, putting an end to the anarchy that was spreading everywhere. On 23 June the English frigate of war *Thetis* appeared in the port of Funchal, and her commander demanded the immediate dissolution of the Governing Junta of Madeira. The Junta dissolved itself on 14 July 1847, addressing a proclamation on that occasion to all the inhabitants of this archipelago.

On 21 July the English warships *Terrible* and *Recruit* and the French frigate *Armide* anchored in our harbour. On the 26th of the same month their commanders handed over the government of the district to Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro. The ceremony, held in the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), was conducted with the greatest solemnity, and there were various demonstrations of rejoicing on that occasion.

On 11 August, the revolutionary movement having already ended, the steam warship *D. Luiz* anchored in the bay of Funchal from the city of Porto, carrying on board the 6th Battalion of Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel José Marques Salgueiral.
On this subject, see the pamphlet by Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento entitled *Maria da Fonte na Madeira*.
Governing Board of the Diocese in 1869

Although this diocese was on several occasions governed by governing boards (junta governativa) following the death or absence of its prelates, there was one that caused a great stir by the way it managed the affairs of the bishopric. The press of this city, and of the capital too, took up its actions, which went so far as to earn the formal condemnation of the Portuguese episcopate and even of the Holy See. Owing to the absence of Bishop Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura in 1869, the diocese was administered by a governing board of three clerics. Departing from canon law and established practice, this board aroused the ill will of the clergy and the faithful, and its conduct was censured by the nunciature in Lisbon. The most prominent and scandalous act of its administration was the circular of 26 January 1870, which condemned various practices of piety and religion in the most diametrical opposition to the teachings of the Church and the doctrines of its most authoritative doctors and theologians. The distinguished writer and great Catholic polemicist Sousa Monteiro dealt with the matter in the *Bem Publico*, and in 1870 a pamphlet was published in Lisbon under the title *Breves reflexões acerca da Circular de 26 de Janeiro de 1870 do presidente da Junta Governativa do Bispado do Funchal*.
Parish councils

The decree of 18 July 1835 created parish councils (*juntas de paróquia*) in the Madeira archipelago. They were actually set up in some parishes, but in a great many parishes they never functioned. We do not know whether these administrative bodies did any good in some of the localities where they were elected. We believe that their operation was wholly useless and fruitless, and we have found no trace of their parish administration. It can be said that they were short-lived and that their activity here in Madeira amounted to nothing at all.

After the promulgation of the Administrative Code (*Código Administrativo*) of 1886, which retained the old parish councils and granted them wider powers, an attempt was made, in compliance with the law, to set up these administrative bodies in Madeira.

The parish councils would have been installed and would even have carried out their administrative functions, had petty parish-pump politics not seized the welcome opportunity to stir up old hatreds and carry out the most reprehensible reprisals. A sustained and stubborn opposition then arose to the operation of these administrative bodies, and it soon degenerated into serious violence and the most deplorable excesses.

Above all, it was the fear that the parish councils would have to levy taxes, and could not function without doing so because they had no revenues of their own, that roused popular indignation. A general outcry soon went up across the whole island against the ‘Juntas de Parreca’, or simply the *Parreca* (popular name for the 1887 parish councils and the riots against them), as the people called those administrative bodies.

A revolt then spread like wildfire through the whole district. It did not always show itself in public, but it lay latent in people’s minds. We know of no other event that produced such intense and widespread indignation here, except perhaps the plague epidemic of 1907. We are convinced that, even today, if ill-intentioned people were to raise the question of the *Parreca* as a banner of revolt, they would once again succeed in stirring people up and might well cause serious disturbances of public order (1921).

For this reason nobody has thought, or thinks even now, of electing parish councils. For us they are bodies that exist only in the pages of the Administrative Code. A long period of thirty years has already passed, and another of equal length will pass, without their becoming a true reality for this archipelago. And truth obliges us to say that they would bring no benefit to the people – given what some rural municipal councils, and even those of district capitals, have done, as we well know.

The situation of Madeira at that time was quite critical. Sugar cane had almost completely disappeared, and the vineyards produced little and were also gravely threatened. The departure of shipping from our port and the ills afflicting the whole country made the archipelago’s economic situation even worse. The ground could not have been more fertile for public indignation to take root at the idea of new taxes being levied. The installation of the parish councils, cleverly but maliciously exploited by unscrupulous political schemers, was the fuse that lit the fire, which soon spread everywhere.

In many parishes (*freguesias*) of Madeira very grave events took place, and at times public order broke down. In some of them these events took on a character of open hostility towards everyone who held a position of authority or performed any public function, not excepting the most eminent and most respected people who lived there. It was a time of real terror, and many found themselves forced to leave their homes and seek safe refuge in Funchal from the excesses of the rebellious populace.

In the municipality (*concelho*) of Sant'Ana, and especially in the parish of Faial, the population rioted and committed many outrages: the parish priest and some of the most respectable people of the locality were humiliated, ill-treated and even beaten.

In Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) the people came down to the town (*vila*) in a threatening mood and would certainly have committed the most reprehensible excesses had the troops not barred their way. The soldiers were attacked and threatened with being violently driven off with stones, and they had to use their carbines; five of the populace were killed and others wounded.

In the parish of Caniço (‘reed’), the disturbances provoked by the supposed meeting of the parish council (*junta de paróquia*) also reached the gravest proportions, with the most tragic consequences. On 22 November 1887 a considerable number of the parish’s inhabitants invaded the parish priest’s house, on the pretext that the parish council was meeting there. After a thorough search of the whole dwelling and of all the church buildings, which they occupied entirely, together with the surrounding area, they remained there for many hours in a threatening and hostile attitude, and it was feared at every moment that this attitude would break out into a terrible storm.

At nightfall a force from Funchal commanded by Captain Luís Maria dos Reis arrived near the parish church of Caniço. He at once sought to have the church cleared, which he achieved only with difficulty. The troops were then violently stoned, and a soldier fell dead, struck by a large stone thrown from the church roof. The armed force, which had acted with every caution, found itself thus attacked; it defended itself and repelled the assault, and four of the populace fell, pierced by bullets, while many were wounded, some of them mortally.

From the mainland came contingents of the 5th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) and the 16th Infantry Regiment, commanded by Lieutenant-Colonel Cibrão, to support the military forces quartered here, and they gave good service.

The events found an echo in the mainland press and in the highest circles of power. Our representatives in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) and some Madeirans living in Lisbon impressed upon the central government that the events in Madeira had their origin chiefly in the distressing situation in which the island found itself. The revolt, they argued, was in essence a vigorous protest against the neglect to which the public authorities had abandoned the archipelago.
The government immediately adopted various measures and later took some far-reaching steps with regard to public works, the suspension of coastal shipping dues, etc.

By decree of 31 December 1887 the government appointed a large commission, chaired by Colonel of Engineers Manuel Raimundo Valadas and made up of various official bodies of this district and some landowners and merchants. Its secretary was Dr Gaspar Malheiro Pereira Peixoto, secretary-general of the civil government of Funchal.

Colonel Valadas showed the greatest zeal in carrying out the thorny mission entrusted to him. Wishing to find his bearings and to produce useful work, he heard everyone who approached him and took into account the suggestions of the press, of the administrative bodies and also of private individuals. He made a detailed study of the underlying causes of the district’s situation and, within the commission, which met countless times, he sought through discussion and close examination of the issues to reach practical and definitive conclusions on the serious matters the commission had been called upon to resolve.

The chairman of the commission wrote and submitted to the government a long and illuminating report, which is said to have been a valuable piece of work containing precious information on the causes of the revolt that had spread through Madeira and on the measures it would be advisable to adopt to overcome the crisis afflicting the district. The central government was urged to publish this report, but it never allowed it, consenting only to let Madeira’s representatives in parliament examine it at the offices of the Ministry of the Kingdom (*Ministério do Reino*), where it was kept. It was said at the time, and the press echoed it, that the report contained references to matters and persons that it was thought inadvisable to make public.
Colonel Valadas and the contingent of 250 infantrymen arrived in Funchal on 11 January 1888.
General Councils

The decree of 16 May 1832 created the Provincial General Councils (*Juntas Gerais de Província*), which never actually functioned in this archipelago. The law of 16 July 1835 established the District General Councils (*Juntas Gerais de Distrito*). An official document of 1837 states ‘that in this Province the Council has met only once, in extraordinary session, for a specific and very limited purpose, so that it may truly be said that the first ordinary session of the General Council of this district opens today’. It seems to us that this single extraordinary meeting took place in 1836, and the first ordinary session was held on 15 July 1837. It was presided over by the civil governor, António de Gamboa, and the twelve representatives were present: Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, Dr Alexandre de Oliveira, António Ferreira Nogueira, Francisco Ferreira de Abreu, João Crisóstomo Ferreira Uzel, José Joaquim Fernandes de Sousa, Manuel Joaquim da Costa Andrade, Manuel Joaquim da Trindade, Patrício Malheiro de Melo, Rufino de Carvalho Pereira, Sebastião Joaquim Rodrigues Leal and Vicente de Paula Teixeira. Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos was elected president and Francisco Ferreira de Abreu secretary. The session comprised eighteen meetings, the closing one being held on 25 August 1837.

The first members of the General Council, thirteen in number, were elected in the Council house on 11 October 1835, in the manner laid down in Article 10 of the decree of 18 July of the same year. The administrative codes of 1836 and 1842 did not change the number of representatives on the General Council, but the code of 1878 raised it to 21, and the elected representatives were to choose the District Commission (*Comissão Distrital*) at their first session. Direct election of the District General Councils was authorised by the code of 1878; the code of 1842 had laid down that these administrative bodies were to be elected by the municipal councils together with the Municipal Boards (*Conselhos Municipais*).

The administrative codes of 1895 and 1896 confirmed the provisions of the decree of 6 August 1892 abolishing the District General Councils. However, the General Council of Funchal was restored by the decree of 8 August 1901, which applied to this district the special organisation granted to the districts of the Azores by the decree of 2 March 1895, as amended by the law of 12 June 1901. With the abolition of the General Councils, a District Commission remained in existence at the seat of each district. In the mainland districts, the General Councils were not restored until the decree of 13 October 1910.

Under the law of 7 August 1913, the General Council of the autonomous regime is made up of procurators elected directly by the municipalities (*concelhos*): 7 for each 1st-class municipality, 5 for each 2nd-class municipality and 3 for each 3rd-class municipality. It has an executive committee made up of three procurators.
See Administrative Autonomy, Administrative Organisation and Revenue and Expenditure of the District.

Justiça (A)
The newspaper first appeared on 27 March 1858 and ceased publication on 26 June 1861 with issue no. 166. Its editor was Bernardo Francisco Lobato Machado.
Kalley (Dr Robert Reid)

He was born at Mont Floridan, near Glasgow, in Scotland, on 6 September 1809, the son of Roberto Kalley and Joana R. Kalley, and he died in the city of Edinburgh on 17 January 1888. In 1832 he completed his degree in medicine at one of the British universities.

Some six years later, on 2 October 1838, Dr Kalley arrived in Funchal, where, apart from short intervals, he lived until 9 August 1846. He became famous for the Protestant proselytism he carried on so widely among us and for the grave disturbances he brought into the heart of Madeiran family life. He was a man of extraordinary talent and a most distinguished physician, with the rare gift of holding crowds in thrall with his suggestive and eloquent speech, which was the chief secret of the effectiveness of his propaganda. He was no doubt a believer, but above all he was a fanatic. A fierce and hate-filled sectarianism ruled him, and he would never have yielded a single step in his bold and tireless propaganda had he not been forced to leave this island in haste.

At first he confined himself to practising medicine free of charge, in which he soon became renowned, to charity towards the poor and to founding schools. Together with his attractive personal qualities and the prestige of his words, this surrounded his name with an aura of sympathy, esteem and respect among all the social classes of our land. Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) publicly paid him a lofty tribute for his services to education and for his acts of philanthropy towards the unfortunate, and the government in mainland Portugal exempted from duty at the customs house of this city the medicines he imported for treating the poor. The benefactor later turned into a fierce propagandist, and it became clear that in him proselytism outweighed in every respect the disinterested practice of charity. This became even more marked after a journey he made to England, where he stayed from June to September 1845. It is said that the meetings he held there with the leaders of the Bible societies and with important figures interested in anti-Catholic propaganda greatly inflamed his natural sectarian ardour and gave him greater courage and boldness in spreading Protestant ideas.

On his return, Dr Kalley launched an even more intense campaign. The very patients he treated at his house were made to listen to his religious addresses, although they showed their reluctance to do so. By then the outcry against the bold propagandist was general. Yet neither the warnings and orders issued by the authorities nor the popular threats, which rumbled beneath the surface, cooled the fervour of the celebrated Scottish physician. With his house surrounded by the police and the insults hurled at him ringing in his ears, he fearlessly went on spreading his religious ideals.

The affronts to the Catholic religion turned the people of Madeira as a whole against Dr Kalley. He had come among us to tear from the people the beliefs of their forefathers and to sow the most baneful dissension within families. The reaction that such bold proselytism naturally provoked led to serious disturbances, and the local authorities had to intervene to curb the excesses of the propagandists. There followed deeply regrettable scenes, in which excesses were committed by Catholics and Protestants alike. These would have been avoided entirely had Dr Kalley not begun his campaign, or at least had he not given it so markedly fanatical a character.

Since he was a British subject, he was treated with genuine moderation and prudence. More than once the Protestant physician formally declared, before the local authorities and other persons of high social standing, that he would put an end to the evangelisation of his creed among Madeirans and confine his campaign to foreigners living in Madeira or who might chance to put in here. He broke every one of these promises, and feelings grew ever more inflamed, reaching their regrettable epilogue in the sad events of 9 August 1846.

Dr Robert Reid Kalley lived on a *quinta* (country estate) at Vale Formoso (‘beautiful valley’), and it was there that his converts held their meetings. The house had long been guarded by the police, for it was feared that popular anger would break out in reprehensible excesses. Meanwhile, the apostolic zeal of the fanatical propagandist allowed him no rest. He also worked with remarkable energy as a physician, treating the sick free of charge and distributing medicines and alms among the poor, while it was claimed that he worked wonders in the art of healing.

On 9 August 1846, in broad daylight, Dr Kalley’s house was surrounded by an enormous crowd of townspeople, which the police were powerless to hold back. Excesses of every kind were then committed. The crowd broke down the doors of the residence and, storming inside, searched every corner for Dr Kalley, who fortunately found safe refuge from the fury of the attackers in flight. He took shelter in the house of a fellow countryman, and there the British consul advised him to leave Madeira without delay. Dressed in women’s clothes and carried in a hammock (*rede*, slung from a pole and carried by two bearers) to the beach of this city, he managed to board a British ship and leave this island, to which he never returned.

Dr Robert Reid Kalley went to Illinois, in the United States of America, and called to join him many of the Madeirans who had followed his teachings. Others, fearing persecution, and an even larger number driven merely by a spirit of adventure, emigrated and swelled the Portuguese colonies of Demerara, Trinidad and the United States of America.

The Portuguese government sent António José de Ávila, later Duke of Ávila and Bolama, to Madeira to investigate these events. He came accompanied by the new civil governor, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro.

Through his government, Dr Kalley claimed compensation for the damage done to the library and furniture of his house, and the Portuguese government paid the sum of 1574 pounds sterling, or about seven *contos* (one million réis) de réis, at which this damage had been assessed. We do not know when the claim was lodged, but we know that only some years after the events that prompted it did Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro, civil governor of this district, report confidentially to the government in mainland Portugal on the claim for compensation, on 25 July 1851 and on instructions from above. In his opinion it ought to be granted on the terms in which it had been made (see Protestant Proselytism).

Besides the countless articles that the newspapers of the day printed on the Kalley Affair, the following pamphlets were also published: *Exposição de Factos*, by R. R. Kalley, Funchal, 1843, of which a 2nd edition appeared in Lisbon in 1875; *An Account of the recent persecutions in Madeira*, by Dr Kalley, London, 1844; *Revista Histórica do proselitismo protestante exercido na ilha da Madeira pelo Dr. Roberto Reid Kalley, medico escossez*, by Manuel de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos, Funchal, 1845; and *Perseguições dos Calvinistas da Madeira*, by João Fernandes da Gama, São Paulo (Brazil), 1896, 218 pp.

The claim made by Dr Kalley through his government, seeking substantial compensation for the damage done to his residence by the rioting populace, was the subject of several debates in the local and mainland press and aroused the keenest interest throughout our country and abroad as well. The diplomatic case took a long time to resolve, for only seven years after the regrettable occurrence did the Portuguese government pay the compensation demanded by Dr Roberto Kalley. Various incidents took place and a number of diplomatic notes were exchanged between the governments of Portugal and England before an amicable settlement was finally reached. The Minister of Foreign Affairs at the time was the illustrious Madeiran the Viscount of Atouguia, who set out the grounds of the claim in a detailed report; the interesting information that follows is taken from this important document:

‘The Administration of 18 June 1849 having issued a ministerial order (*portaria*) on 7 February 1851 to the Civil Governor of Funchal, instructing him to carry out every inquiry into the damage which Dr Kalley had represented as having been caused to him by a popular tumult that took place in that same city of Funchal, that Magistrate complied on 25 July 1851 with his report.

The present Administration, after a scrupulous examination of all the papers relating to this claim of the British Government, and above all in the light of the report given by the aforementioned Civil Governor (Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro), could not but recognise the right of Dr Kalley to compensation for the damage he suffered on the island of Madeira as a consequence of the said tumult, which had taken place on 9 August 1846.

Not wishing, however, to take upon itself the responsibility of fixing any sum on that account without ordering fresh inquiries, the same Administration confidentially instructed the Civil Governor to answer three questions it had sent him and at the same time to give his opinion on the claim in question. When that Magistrate sent the required reply on 3 November 1851, he added that, as regards his opinion, he referred to the last part of his report of 25 July 1851.

In that report the said Civil Governor, after assuring the Government that he had given this matter the most serious attention and had used every possible means to ascertain the truth with the greatest scruple, detail and impartiality, observed that in the tumultuous and disorderly scene of 9 August 1846, in which the house of Dr Kalley had been subjected to outright pillage, many things must necessarily have been damaged, broken, ruined and lost, besides those that fell prey to the flames.

In these circumstances, pressed by the Government of Her Britannic Majesty to pay that compensation, and not wishing to be accused of bad faith, the Government of Her Majesty agreed to pay the sum claimed of seven *contos* eighty-four thousand six hundred and thirty-one *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), equivalent to 1574,7 pounds, shillings and 3 pence at the exchange rate of 4,500 *réis* each, the amount at which the said damage was shown to have been calculated, in three instalments, which were paid at the agreed times.’
Secretariat of State for Foreign Affairs, 20 June 1853. – Viscount of Athouguia.

Kirkpatrick (R.)

Koebel (W. H.)
Works: *Madeira old and new*; London, 1909.

On p. 5 of this work we read the following: it should be noted that the notes to Frutuoso’s work published in 1873 by Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo are immensely useful to all who wish to study that old manuscript. Dr Azevedo was a lawyer in Madeira, a scholar and a freethinker, and this last circumstance brought him into disfavour with the local clergy. The most intransigent members of that body began a campaign against his way of life, promising him a dog’s funeral (*a dog's funeral*) after his death. When he died, however, the clergy suffered the bitterest of disappointments. Documents left by Dr Azevedo showed that he had obtained a papal bull guaranteeing him the greatest number of funeral rites that the Church had the power to grant. He therefore received all these rites, but the clergy who took part in them earned nothing for their services, since everything had been paid for in advance in Rome. Could one conceive of a livelier display of posthumous irony?’

What Mr Koebel relates about the papal bull obtained by Dr Azevedo is nothing but a mere fabrication. On his death this distinguished professor received the funeral rites customarily granted to all Catholics, and there is nothing strange in that, since he had been reconciled with the Church in the last 10 or 15 years of his life. Dr Azevedo was always a grave and serious man, and therefore incapable of staging the ‘display of posthumous irony’ that Mr Koebel sought to attribute to him. The assertions of this British subject enjoyed not the slightest credit.

La Pérouse (Jean-François de Galaup de)

French navigator of the 18th century. He arrived at Madeira aboard the *Boussole* on 13 August 1785 and left for the Canary Islands on the 16th of the same month. Sailing with the *Boussole* was the *Astrolabe*, commanded by Captain de Langle, on which the illustrious Monge had also embarked, although he went no further than Tenerife. La Pérouse was treated with great kindness in Funchal by the English merchant Johnston, who gave him, on his departure, 100 bottles of Malmsey wine, half a barrel of dry wine, and fruit preserved in syrup and in spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine). On 14 August he dined at the house of the Portuguese Monteiro, who was in charge of the affairs of the French consulate, having lunched that same day at the residence of the English consul Murray.
Labaça
The common name of several Polygonaceae of the genus *Rumex*. In Madeira these plants grow along streams, by the roadsides, etc.
Laboratory of Bacteriology and Hygiene

It was created by the decree of 17 May 1904, at the request of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district, which was made responsible for setting it up and for its running costs. Its staff then consisted of a chief physician, a laboratory technician and an attendant; the demands of the service later made it necessary to enlarge the staff.

Its first director was Dr António Balbino do Rego, who was forced by the regrettable events in Funchal in January 1906 to give up the post, which he had held with great zeal and recognised competence. The laboratory technician Dr António Capelo then took over the post of director on an interim basis.

By the decree of 22 December 1939 the Laboratory’s service was reorganised. It was given a section for bacteriological and clinical analyses and another for chemical and technological analyses, and its staff was made up of a medical director and bacteriologist, an analytical chemist, a laboratory technician, an assistant technician and two laboratory assistants.

The distinguished bacteriologist Dr Vicente Henriques de Gouveia, already well known for his remarkable laboratory work, was engaged as medical director in 1931 and permanently appointed to the post on 5 November 1940.
Dairy products

In the article ‘Indústria dos Lacticínios’ (p. 149) we briefly mentioned the decrees that created the Junta Nacional dos Lacticínios da Madeira (National Dairy Board of Madeira) and laid down the rules for its operation. This would be a fitting occasion to give a detailed account of how that body has carried out the duties those decrees assigned to it, if the space and material now available to us allowed it. Nevertheless, it would be a flagrant injustice if we did not at least record here, however briefly, the undeniable benefits that the said credits have brought, through that Board, to the economy of the whole district. The subject has been treated with the most careful judgement, thorough knowledge and great love of truth in the valuable and in many respects interesting *Boletins de Informação e Publicidade* published by the Junta de Lacticínios da Madeira, which may be profitably consulted and to which we draw the attention of our farmers. (See Livestock and Butter.)
Lafões (Duke of)

Queen Maria I, styling herself ‘governor and perpetual administrator of the mastership of knighthood of the Order of Our Lord Jesus Christ’, made a royal grant in 1778 to her uncle Dom João de Bragança, Duke of Lafões, of the commandery of the islands of Terceira, Madeira and São Miguel of the said Order. Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) took note of this grant, which was ordered to be entered in the appropriate register, on 15 May 1784.
Madeiran wall lizard (Lacerta Dugesii)

A small reptile, very common in Madeira, which does great damage to grapes, tomatoes, etc. It already existed on the island before the discovery, for Gaspar Frutuoso refers to it in the following terms: ‘on this fresh island no other kind of creature was found but some little lizards the size of a finger, which do no notable harm and are not venomous’. Frutuoso also recorded lizards on the island of Porto Santo (see *Saudades*, p. 50), and the naturalist Richard Thomas Lowe found among the calcareous formations of Piedade (‘pity’) the jaws of a small vertebrate which Professor Owen identified as a reptile. For lack of material for comparison, however, Owen could not state whether it was identical to the Madeiran lizard.
Lagoa

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), forming the blocked crater of a volcano, lies a small village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) known as the Lagoa (‘lake’). In the longer winters it fills with water, forming a small lake with a surface area of approximately six thousand square metres. It is a picturesque spot and was much visited in former times.
Lagoa (peak)
In the uplands of the locality (*sítio*) of Poiso (‘resting place’) stands the Pico da Lagoa (‘lagoon peak’), which reaches an altitude of 1,450 metres.
Lobsters

The name given to *Scyllarus latus* and *Palinurus vulgaris*, macruran crustaceans caught in shallow waters. The latter is distinguished by its long, thick antennae, the former by its short, leaf-like antennae. The second species, also called *lagostim* or *lagostão*, is less common than the first and is caught in the same way, either by diving or accidentally in nets and other tackle.
*Arctus ursus*, occasionally dredged up in the waters off Funchal and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), is not considered edible.

In the Funchal *Diário de Notícias* (‘Daily News’) of 26 October 1927, Adolfo César de Noronha published a detailed and interesting article on these crustaceans under the title ‘A Lagosta da Madeira’.
Laje (peak)
In the uplands of the locality (*sítio*) of Poiso (‘resting place’) stands the Pico da Laje (‘slab peak’), which reaches an altitude of 1,450 metres.
Laje (landing place)
This landing place lies on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Seixal (‘pebble shore’), and there is a small landing stage there.
Laje (stream)
This watercourse lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial, and a levada (irrigation channel) begins at it, watering some land in the municipality (*concelho*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).
Lajedo (peak)
A mountainous elevation on the northern coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’).
Lamaceiros
Several localities (*sítios*) in Madeira are known by this name, but the one most worth visiting is in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’).

The locality of Lamaceiros (‘mud flats’) in Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) is also worth a visit. From some nearby peaks part of the Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’) can be seen. There is a chapel there dedicated to St Peter (*São Pedro*), badly damaged by the earthquake of 1748 and rebuilt shortly afterwards; it was restored once again a few years ago.
Lamaceiros

A very picturesque locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), offering lovely views over the parishes of Porto da Cruz, Faial and Santana. It lies three kilometres from the parish church of Santo da Serra. As far as this locality the waters of the levadas (irrigation channels) of Furado (‘pierced’), Juncal (‘rush bed’), Nova do Furado (or the Shareholders’ Levada) and Serra do Faial (‘uplands of Faial’) flow in a shared aqueduct. There the first passes into its own channel and the second goes on to the parish of Porto da Cruz. The waters of the other two levadas continue together as far as the locality of Lombo da Raiz (see that entry).
Lambert (Count of)

General Count Alexandre Carlos de Lambert, aide-de-camp to the Empress of Russia, spent some time in Madeira, having acquired as his residence the Quinta das Angústias (‘sorrows’), on Rua da Imperatriz Dona Amélia (‘Empress Amélia street’).

It is said that in Poland the Count of Lambert had a serious quarrel with a Russian general, whose name we do not know. The two eventually agreed that whichever of them the lot fell upon should kill himself by taking a poisonous draught. The lot went against the general, who at once carried out what he had so rashly bound himself to do. Shortly afterwards the count withdrew to Madeira, deeply distressed by the outcome of the quarrel in which he had become involved.
The Count of Lambert, who was born around 1816, was in Madeira in 1863; he visited Lisbon and London that year but returned to Madeira in September. He died around 1866.
Lambert (Quinta)

In the article devoted to the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery, we stated that in 1662 Daniel da Costa Quintal founded, on land belonging to his entailed estate (*morgadio*), the chapel of Our Lady of Sorrows (*Nossa Senhora das Angústias*), which gave its name to the street running nearby and also to the localities around it. As we have also already noted, we cannot now say for certain whether the chapel of Our Lady of Sorrows that stands on the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name (Lambert) is a reconstruction of the old chapel of the same dedication, or whether Daniel da Costa Quintal’s property might have been located there. We are inclined to think so. When the Quinta das Angústias passed into the possession of Nicolau Hemiterio de la Tuelière, and later into that of the Count of Lambert, the house, the chapel and the adjoining grounds were greatly improved, and it became one of the most pleasant and comfortable residences in Funchal. Queen Adelaide of England (see that entry) lived on this *quinta* from 3 November 1847 to 11 April 1848, and the Duke of Leuchtenberg (see that entry) also lived there from 27 August 1849 to 23 April 1850. The widowed Empress of Brazil, Empress Amélie (see that entry), accompanied by her daughter Princess Maria Amélia (see that entry), took up residence there on 28 August 1852. The ill-fated princess died in this house on 4 February 1853. Three months later, on 6 May, the coffin containing the princess’s mortal remains left the chapel of the *quinta*, followed by the empress, and was taken on board at the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’).

Dr Júlio Paulo de Freitas bought the *quinta* das Angústias from the Countess of Lambert, Luísa Margarida de Loucosme Bredes, and her children for the sum of 4,000 pounds on 19 August 1903. It was on this *quinta* that the well-known belvedere (*mirante*) of Dona Guiomar stood (see that entry).
Lamedo (António José de Jesus)

He was perhaps the most distinguished official the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) had in former times, although he held only the modest post, now abolished, of doorkeeper and bookkeeper to the Council.

We do not know when Lamedo was born, nor whether he was a native of this island. What we do know is that ‘not only for his conduct, truthfulness, intelligence and good handwriting, but for his experience of old scripts, which few people can read’, he was appointed to this post by the Council on 3 June 1765, an appointment confirmed by a royal warrant (*provisão*) of 17 August 1766.

Lamedo never came to hold the post of Council usher (*porteiro da câmara*) of the Funchal Municipal Council as his own property: at first because the former holder, Pedro Luís Correia, was still alive, and later for other reasons unknown to us. This is why the municipal records contain various resolutions and instruments reappointing him to the post, which he held until May 1797.

In 1781 Lamedo was appointed official reweigher (repesador) of wheat and flour, a post he thereafter combined with that of Council usher, always to the satisfaction of the various council sessions under which he served. For some time he also served as representative (*procurador*) of the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) in the court of the judicial district (*comarca*).

The most important service that António José de Jesus Lamedo rendered to the municipality was the compilation of an index, in two volumes, of the documents contained in the Council’s General Register; the first volume has 284 folios and the second 81. This most valuable work, which took ‘three years, working days’ to complete, as its author states, is in the Council’s archive and bears the following title: *Índese & dos Tombos da Camara desta Cidade mandado copiar neste livro 1.°, e no 2.° pelos Senhores D.or Juis de Fora Bernardo José de Oliveira Perdigão, e Vereadores Francisco de Ornelas de Brito Tristão Joaquim Neto, e o Procurador do Conselho Manoel Jozé de Brito, e Misteres.*

Referring to Lamedo’s work in his notes to the *Saudades*, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo says that ‘it is fundamental for the study of the history of the archipelago of Madeira’. Indeed, this work, in which all the documents scattered through the Council’s registers up to the year 1794 are clearly summarised, is an interesting and most valuable repository of immensely useful information on our history, administration and customs. The way in which the material has been arranged leaves nothing to be desired, and the whole work reveals uncommon method, patience and dedication.

António José de Jesus Lamedo died suddenly in the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé, in this city, on 24 May 1797, and was buried in the now defunct convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). He was married to Antónia Rosa, who survived him, and we calculate that he would have been about 70 years old at the time of his death.
Lâmpada (A)
The 1st issue appeared on 21 November 1872 and the 51st on 3 January 1874.
Lampreia (Francisco Joaquim de Sá Camelo)

He was born in Funchal on 27 June 1829, the son of Marshal João Lampreia, and died in Lisbon on 17 December 1876, while deputy for Moura, aged only 47.
