He graduated in medicine from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), where he always proved a student of exceptional and brilliant talent. While still very young he displayed rare gifts as an orator, which later, in Parliament, made him one of the most notable speakers of his time. He belonged to the Historic Progressive Party and was a close friend of the Duke of Loulé, the party's leader. He represented several mainland constituencies in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) and was also deputy for Madeira in the legislative session of 1865. He was a permanent teacher at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and held various public service commissions in Lisbon, in which he always revealed the high faculties of his mind.

We shall complete this brief article with the words, full of truth, that the *Diccionario Popular* devotes to this Madeiran: ‘He graduated in medicine from the University of Coimbra, where he acquired the reputation of a brilliant orator and a man of exceptional talent. And so he was indeed; and if he could not display the full greatness of his intellectual gifts on the political stage, if he did not show all that he was worth, it was because illness came to prevent him from playing the part for which his great mind had been fashioned.’

‘Instances are cited that revealed the loftiness of his intellect and, above all, his natural gift for oratory. When he sat the examination for the 4th year of medicine, one of his examiners was a most distinguished professor who had, however, fallen into the habit of not studying his students’ theses. So, whenever he began to argue, he would always declare that the proposition maintained in the thesis was perfectly self-evident and that he was going to challenge it only out of duty as an examiner. This system produced the following result. If the student defended the thesis well, the audience concluded that nothing could be easier; if he was beaten, the professor’s glory shone with all the splendour of a difficulty overcome. Lampreia went to the examination and, hearing the professor remark that the thesis upheld a self-evident doctrine, grew irritated and replied at once: “If it is as self-evident as Your Excellency supposes, then let Your Excellency defend it, and I shall proceed to attack it.”

‘Challenged in this way, the professor could not back down. With him in the singular position of opponent of his own theories, Lampreia displayed such dialectical subtlety, such skill in argument and so much natural eloquence that the victory may be said to have been his.

‘So brilliant a talent and such rare faculties could scarcely show themselves, because illness came to paralyse them. A disease of the larynx rendered his eloquence useless; his hoarse, rasping voice could barely be heard and spoiled all his oratorical effects. Even so, his talent was so great that he often wielded influence in the Chamber.’
Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Lampreia was unquestionably one of the most distinguished Madeirans of the 19th century.
Lampreia (João de Oliveira Sá Camelo)

He was born in Funchal around 1864, the son of the distinguished Madeiran Francisco Joaquim de Sá Camelo Lampreia (see that entry). He attended the former Lisbon Commercial Institute (*Instituto Comercial de Lisboa*) and pursued a diplomatic career, being appointed attaché to the legations in Stockholm and Copenhagen in 1883. In 1890 he left for Rome as secretary of embassy and remained there for some years, serving several times as chargé d’affaires. After serving at the legation in Madrid, he moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1896 as first secretary. By decree of 8 September 1900 he was appointed envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary in Brazil, a post he held for some years. There he rendered notable services to his country, while at the same time winning the warmest regard not only of the important Portuguese community but also of the most eminent figures of the Brazilian Republic. With the establishment of the new political regime, he abandoned his diplomatic career and settled in the city of Rio de Janeiro, devoting himself to the labours of an active commercial life. He died in the city of Rio de Janeiro on 11 July 1943.
Lamprey (*Petromyson marinus*)

A cyclostome fish that appears from time to time in the seas around Madeira, but to which the island’s fishermen give no name at all. Besides its worm-like shape, it has neither pectoral nor ventral fins, and it is equipped with a round, jawless mouth, with which it forms a kind of sucker that it uses to attach itself to other species. The sea lamprey usually appears in the rivers of Europe during the spring.
Landi (Count Giulio de)

When we dealt with Father Manuel Constantino on page 300 of vol. 1 (2nd ed.) of this *Elucidário*, we intended to transcribe some passages from the article we had published in *O Jornal* (‘The Newspaper’) of 29 July 1934 under the title ‘Pela História da Madeira–Notas Bibliográficas’. In that article we had revealed the plagiarism that this Manuel Constantino had committed of the book by Count Giulio de Landi, which had been published in an Italian translation by Alemanio Fino in 1574. Through a mere oversight it was not transcribed, and this is done here, as a supplement to the article on Father Manuel Constantino:

‘Certainly, from Barbosa Machado down to the present day, the wish must often have arisen for a fuller knowledge of the *Insulae Materiae historia*. . . It was the only printed work dealing exclusively with this archipelago, since no other published works existed apart from the few pages to be found in some chroniclers, such as Zurara, Barros, Galvão and Damião de Góis. It seems that Constantino’s work became very rare from the outset, perhaps because it had been printed in Rome and perhaps also owing to other unknown circumstances. We know of only two references that show an accurate knowledge of the book: that of the annotator of ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) in 1866, and that of Dr Jordão de Freitas, in 1911.

It should therefore come as no surprise that the author of this brief article advised the purchase, albeit at a high price, of an extremely rare copy that had turned up in Vienna, Austria, and promptly arranged for its translation into Portuguese. He also wrote the Preliminary Note and the copious notes that accompanied the publication of this translation, produced in this city in 1930.

What, then, was our surprise and our disappointment when, two years ago, we learnt that there existed a printed work on Madeira earlier than Constantino’s, published in the city of Piacenza in 1574 and written by Count Giulio Landi! Our surprise rose to indignation when we discovered that the work of Doctor Manuel Constantino was a slavish copy, a brazen plagiarism, of Landi’s work, apart from a few slight alterations!

It was our esteemed friend Dr Jordão de Freitas, a distinguished scholar of the historical sciences, who gave us this news in a most interesting letter received at the time. We did not publish it in full, as we had intended, because it has regrettably been lost. What had happened was this: the learned director of the Ajuda Library (*Biblioteca da Ajuda*), in connection with the printing of the *Insulae Materiae Historia*, had told our illustrious friend Mr Henrique Hinton of the existence of this work predating Constantino’s, of which he knew only the title, the author’s name and the year of publication. Mr Hinton had a search made in London, through an authorised intermediary, in the famous library of the British Museum, and there discovered the extremely rare book, perhaps the only surviving copy. He at once had a complete photographic copy made of it, which he presented to the Funchal Municipal Library (*Biblioteca Municipal do Funchal*).

When Dr Jordão de Freitas published an interesting pamphlet in 1911 entitled *Quando foi descoberta a Madegra?*, he had closely examined the copy of the *Insulae Materiae Historia* held in the National Library in Lisbon (*Biblioteca Nacional de Lisboa*). When, about two years ago, he was given access to the photographic copy of Count Giulio Landi’s work, he recognised without difficulty that the former was an outright plagiarism of the latter. From the comparison he then made, he even pointed out the small differences between the two works, as he informed us at once in the letter referred to above. The title of the work in question, which served as the text for the literal copy that is the *Insulae Materiae Historia*, is, *ipsis verbis*, as follows: ‘*La descrittione de l'Isola de la Madera, gia scritta ne la lingua latina, dal molto Ill. Signor conte Giulio Sandi, et hora tradotta dal latino ne la nostra materna lingua, dal reverendo A. Alemanio Fini, ne la quale i contengono molto belle, e deletteuoli narrationi; e massimamente l'agricoltura del Zucchero, e li costumi degli huomini di quel paese, e li nobili esercitii Cavalereschi; e particolarmente il giuoco di Canne, & il modo di lottare, e la Caccia de li Tori à piedi, & à Cavallo, V'é posta anco la Descrittione latina del primo autore di tutte le souradette cose, acciò possa il lettore leggere in quella lingua che sia piu di gusto suo. In Placenza, appresso Francesco Conti. 1574*’ (‘The description of the Island of Madeira, formerly written in Latin by the most Illustrious Count Giulio Sandi, and now translated from Latin into our mother tongue by the Reverend A. Alemanio Fini, containing very fine and delightful narratives, above all on the cultivation of sugar, the customs of the people of that country and their noble knightly exercises, and in particular the game of canes, the manner of wrestling and bullfighting on foot and on horseback; the Latin description by the original author of all the aforesaid matters is also included, so that the reader may read in whichever language is most to his taste. At Piacenza, by Francesco Conti. 1574’).

As the wording of the title transcribed above shows, the work was originally written in Latin by Count Giulio Landi and translated into Italian by Father Almenio Fini. It was published in the city of Piacenza in 1574 and contains both the original Latin text and its Italian translation. The book has 95 numbered pages, besides the title page. The first twelve are taken up by two dedications, one by Almenio Fini and the other by Giulio Landi, written in Italian and addressed to the princess of Piacenza and Parma. The Italian text follows, running from p. 13 to p. 54, and the Latin continues up to p. 95, the last page of the book.

As we have said above, we were greatly surprised, and also greatly displeased, that a man of the moral, social and intellectual standing of Dr Manuel Constantino should have committed the plagiarism which, in the light of a comparison of the works mentioned, we are bound to attribute to him. We even went so far as to suppose that we were perhaps facing an intricate bibliographical problem, which might one day be adequately cleared up by the emergence of new evidence for research and criticism, hitherto unknown.
Langerhans (Dr Paul)
He studied the worms of Madeira in the *Zeitschrift für wissenschaftliche Zoologie* (1879–84) and wrote a small book entitled *Handbuch fur Madeira* (Berlin, 1884).
Lapa da Cadela (cave)

This is a cave (*furna*) close to Pico (‘peak’) Ruivo (‘russet’), where people visiting the mountain usually spend the night. It is wide but shallow, so it gives those who shelter in it little protection from the winds and rain that come from the direction of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’). It takes about 20 minutes to walk from the cave to the summit of the peak.
In 1940 the Tourism Delegation (*Delegação de Turismo*) had a ‘pousada’ (rest house) built in its vicinity to shelter and rest those who make the ascent of that height. See Ruivo (peak).
Lapa do Sol
A picturesque spot commanding wide horizons, situated near Monte Mendonho in the Serras de São Vicente (‘St Vincent’).
Limpets

*Patella aspera*, *P. caerulea*, *P. lusitanica* and *P. vulgata* are known by the general name of limpets (*lapas*). The first is the fishermen’s *lapa branca* (white limpet), the commonest of the four species; the second is the *lapa preta* (black limpet); the third the *lapa pé de burro* (donkey’s-foot limpet); and the fourth the *concharéu* (see that entry). The white limpet lives in the deepest water; the donkey’s-foot limpet is often found above the high-water line; and the black limpet, also called the women’s limpet, is exposed as soon as the tide goes out. These three species are common to Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas.

*Patella vulgata*, which once existed on all the islands of the archipelago, is found today only on the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*). Every year a large number of salted and pickled limpets of that species and of *Patella aspera* come from these islands.

The name of limpets is also given to various homopterous insects of the family of coccids, among which we shall mention the following: *Diaspis Rosae*, on rose bushes; *Aspidiotus Lataniae*, on loquats, guavas, pear trees, vines, fennel and robinias; *Aspidiotus Hederae*, on broom, rue, vines and *taxónia*; *Lecanium haemisphericum*, on orange and custard-apple trees; *Lecanium nigrum*, on custard-apple and banana plants; *Lecanium Oleae*, on olive trees and esparto; *Ceroplastis tenuitectus*, on fig and custard-apple trees; *Ceroplastis floridensis*, on mango trees and box; *Asteroclanium variolosum*, on oaks; and *Chrysomphalus dictyospermi*, on palms, orange trees, lemon trees, incense trees, lawn grass (*Fluggea japonica*), etc.
Professor Cockerell, who travelled through the archipelago in 1920 and 1921, found thirty-odd species of coccids here. See Paoli (Guido).
Inscribed stones

As a contribution to the study of Madeiran epigraphy that may one day be undertaken, we record here a number of lapidary inscriptions. Some were already included in the first edition of this work; others we came across in the course of our research into the history of our archipelago. In this way we offer some scattered and still little-known material that may prove useful in preparing that interesting study. All of them belong to relatively recent periods and are of no particular interest for their antiquity, since the history of Madeira began some five hundred years ago and the events recorded can go back no further than the middle of the 15th century. Where the exact dates of events are not known, we have always tried to give the approximate year in which they occurred. João Gonçalves Zarco was buried in the chancel of the church of Conceição de Cima (today the Convent of St Clare), which he had founded. It is stated in some places, though there is no proof of it, that his ashes were moved to the tomb of his son-in-law Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, which stands beside the choir of the same church. We dealt with this matter at some length in the article Zargo in the first edition of this *Elucidário*, and it is very strange that this church contains no funerary inscription referring to the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. He must have died around 1467.

In 1919 a gravestone was discovered beside the high altar of this church, bearing the following inscription: Tomb of João Gonçalves da Câmara, second captain of the Island. On the same occasion and in the same place another tombstone was found, which preserves these words: Tomb of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd captain of this Island. Here lies Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of Calheta (‘small cove’) and fifth captain of this island.

Regarding the tomb of Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, mentioned above, the following is to be read on p. 594 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*): ‘... in the church of the Convent of St Clare, at the entrance, on the right-hand side, is the sarcophagus of this Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, with an inscription in Gothic capitals, illegible because worn; but in the adjacent pavement is seen a large marble slab bearing the following epitaph: “Tomb of Captain Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcellos, which he had made for himself and his heirs when the first gravestone placed here was removed, as descendant of the first Martim Mendes de Vasconcellos, who lies here and came to this island to marry Elena Gliz da Câmara, daughter of João Gonçalves Zargo, its discoverer. It was made in the year 1710”.’

Another son-in-law of João Gonçalves Zarco was Diogo Cabral, who died in 1486 and was buried in the chapel of Our Lady of the Star (*Nossa Senhora da Estrela*), which he had founded in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta, at the locality (*sítio*) that still bears that name. Twenty years ago the stone that covered the mortal remains of Diogo Cabral was removed to the parish cemetery and reused for an ordinary grave, after the coat of arms and the epitaph of Zargo’s son-in-law had been scraped off – all of which constitutes an unspeakable abuse.

Not far from there, at the locality of Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’) in the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), stood the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), founded by Gonçalo Fernandes in the first half of the 16th century. About ten years ago a fairly old tombstone was found there with this inscription: Tomb of Gil y Enes, master mason of the Sé. It is now kept in the Funchal Municipal Museum (Museu Municipal do Funchal). According to Henrique Henriques de Noronha, in his highly interesting and respected *Memorias*, Gil Enes was ‘the architect of the whole work’ of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) of Funchal.

This is the moment to mention a tomb in our Cathedral, situated beside the side door on the north side. It is covered by two cut-out bronze figures laid side by side, and the pamphlet *Laminas Sepulcrais de Bronze* by the distinguished archaeologist Pedro Vitorino says the following about it: ‘The figures measure about 0.90 in height. One is mutilated. They rest on a slab, possibly Belgian blue stone. . The very small series of sepulchral plates in our country offers us examples of the two known types: a stone to which the figure, cut out of a metal plate, is fixed (Funchal). . . and a whole sheet of metal. formed of several pieces.’

As Pedro Vitorino says, such tombs are very rare in our country, and this specimen in the Cathedral, the only one in Madeira, therefore deserves the greatest care in its conservation. It has been claimed, without foundation, that the Fleming João Esmeraldo, who died in 1536, and his wife were buried there. The date 1425 is carved on the lintel of the portal of the chapel of St Catherine (*Santa Catarina*). It is presumably meant to mark the year in which the settlement of Madeira began, and perhaps the year this chapel was built, although one may conjecture that the stone belonged not to the original building but to a rebuilding later than the date shown. It was the first church built in Madeira, and we dealt with it in a detailed article published in the *Jornal* of 27 October 1942.

In the Angústias Cemetery (‘Sorrows’) there is a marble stone that was formerly in the old Convent of St Francis (*São Francisco*), bearing this epitaph: ‘Here lies Lois Alvares da Costa, who founded this house in the year 1473, and his son Francisco Alvares da Costa, first *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) and overseer of the royal treasury (*vedor da fazenda*) in these islands of Madeira’. When the church of this convent was demolished in 1865 and many of the bones it contained were moved to the Angústias Cemetery, the stone was used to cover these mortal remains, and the following words were inscribed on it: ‘Family vault of the bones exhumed from the former convent and church of São Francisco (to which the original inscription refers), transferred on 2 May 1865’.

In 1562 Filipe Gentil de Limoges founded a chapel dedicated to St Philip in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), at the locality (*sítio*) that still bears the name of this chapel today. In it is a tombstone with this strange inscription: ‘Grave of the innocents who were tyrannically killed at the Achada of this city 1612’. The foundling nurse (*ama dos expostos*) of the time took in newborn children, killed them and buried them at the locality of the Achada (‘plateau’). Their bones were gathered some years later and laid beneath the floor of the chapel, where the stone was placed, as described above.

More than thirty years ago, during excavations at the barracks of the 25th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria n.º 25*), the former Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), a large block of dressed stone (*cantaria*) two and a half metres long was found, bearing the following Latin inscription: ‘*Altissimus creavit medicinam de terra et vir prudens non abhorrebit illam*’, which the translator Pereira de Figueiredo renders thus: ‘It is the Most High who has brought forth all medicines from the earth, and the prudent man will not oppose them’. It is verse 4 of chapter XXXVIII of the Book of Ecclesiasticus in the Old Testament, which praises medicine and those who practise that noble and beneficent profession. In the church of the same College of St John the Evangelist (*Colégio de São João Evangelista*) there are several chapels that served as mausoleums for their founders and descendants, with their tombstones and inscriptions giving the names of the patrons and the dates of their deaths.

The old chapel of the Varadouros, so called because of where it stood, was demolished around 1682 and rebuilt in 1689, when the well-known Portão dos Varadouros was built there. The gate became the main entrance to the city, through which bishops and governors made their solemn and ceremonious entry into Funchal. The chapel had been rebuilt over the arch of this gate, which bore at its top a stone with a curious Latin inscription, transcribed on page 628 of the annotations to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’.

Around the third quarter of the 15th century a small chapel is said to have been built on the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) of Lombada da Ponta do Sol, later called Lombada dos Esmeraldos. On the same site the Fleming João Esmeraldo built the chapel of the Holy Spirit (Santo Espírito), which was solemnly consecrated by the titular bishop Dom João in 1508. It was rebuilt in the first quarter of the 18th century, and on one of its interior walls there is a marble plaque with the inscription: ‘This church was consecrated by Dom João Lobo, Bishop of Tangier, on 27 August 1508’. This is perhaps the same plaque that had been in the original building.

On the façades of the parish churches of Santo António, Caniço and Estreito da Calheta there are three lapidary inscriptions bearing the dates 1783, 1789 and 1791, the years in which these churches were built. All are written in Latin and give the names of their titular saints or patrons. On the front of the parish church of Tábua can be read the words: ‘King Dom Pedro 1696’.

In the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Pópulo (Our Lady del Popolo), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, which belonged to the residence the Jesuits owned there, there was a marble stone carved with these interesting words: ‘In memory of the glorious martyrs of the Society of Jesus, Father Inácio de Azevedo and his 39 companions, who, sailing for Brazil in the year 1579, on 15 July, within sight of the island of La Palma, earned the crown of martyrdom for the faith of Christ, cast into the sea by the heretics; and who, having stayed at this *quinta* (country estate) of Pico do Cardo, came to this place with their cross and here performed their devotions. This was erected for the greater glory of God in the year 1745’. The events to which this stone refers are narrated at length on pages 125 ff. of the book *Paróquia de Santo António da Ilha da Madeira* by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva.

The church of São Tiago Menor (St James the Less), now the parish church of the parish of Santa Maria Maior, preserves on its façade a stone with a Latin inscription recording the grant made in 1803 by the Funchal Municipal Council to the State, so that the church might serve as a parish church. This was because the great flash flood (*aluvião*) of that year had destroyed the original church, which then stood between the Largo dos Lavradores and the public fountain known as the Poço de Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Well of Our Lady of Calhau).

In the vestibule of the majestic building of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice there is a black marble stone bearing a detailed inscription on the foundation and construction of this excellent hospital for tuberculosis patients, which opened in 1862.

All the fortresses and coastal defence works built in Madeira, and particularly in this city, bore curious lapidary inscriptions, of which Dr Álvaro de Azevedo’s annotations to Gaspar Frutuoso’s book give a full account.
Lapierre (Lieutenant)

An officer of the 6th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) battalion who was murdered at the barracks of the College (*Colégio*) by soldiers of that battalion on 31 July 1852. It is said that the mutineers actually meant to kill the commander, but the lieutenant stood up to them. This gave a quartermaster-sergeant (*furriel*) time to shut the door through which the soldiery had to pass to reach the commander’s room, and gave the commander, warned of what was happening, time to flee.

The quartermaster-sergeant in question was called Miguel Fernandes. For many years he was inspector of the Praça de São Pedro, and he was decorated by the government for having saved his commander from the fury of the unruly soldiery.

The newspapers of the day did not dare to comment on the excesses of the 6th Caçadores battalion, but years later a Madeiran periodical stated that these excesses had been instigated by civilians, with the aim of driving out of the island the commander, who belonged to the Regenerator party.
Lapinha

This is the word used in Madeira for the ‘presépios’ (Christmas cribs), which have been so widespread here for centuries. We believe it to be a word peculiar to this archipelago. It must be the diminutive of ‘lapa’ in the sense of a cave, grotto or hollow in a rock, by analogy or resemblance with the place where the Divine Redeemer was born. It is possible that in former times they kept this analogy or resemblance, but at present Madeiran ‘lapinhas’ are generally set up on a table. At their centre is a small stepped stand a few decimetres high, with three adjoining flights, on top of which the image of the Christ Child is placed. On all the steps and around the stand are arranged the ‘pastores’ (shepherds) and various ornaments, sometimes very odd and with little connection to the rest of the crib. In keeping with their surroundings, they have certain features of their own, such as decorations of sprigs of the ‘alegra-campo’ shrub and of ‘cabrinhas’ ferns, which give them a picturesque and cheerful look. The so-called ‘pastores’ have a certain originality: small clay figures of rough local make which almost never represent shepherds or herdsmen, but people from the various social classes.

‘Lapinhas’ with so-called ‘rochinhas’ (little rocks) are still very common. These imitate a small stretch of very rugged ground, made from sugar-cane ‘socas’ (root stumps), and usually keep at the base a small ‘furna’ (cave) representing the Nativity in tiny clay figures.

There used to be, though today they are very rare, these same ‘rochas’ on a larger scale, showing churches, roads, small villages, etc. Although the whole lacked much harmony, they had a certain original picturesqueness. See ‘Christmas’.
Laranjal

Inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), Funchal. Marcos Braga, one of the earliest settlers of Madeira, held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) land there, which his grandson Domingos Braga turned into an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). The present representative of this house is Dr Remígio Barreto.
Orange tree

A tree of the family Rutaceae, native to the Himalayas. Its botanical name is *Citrus Aurantium*, and two subspecies are grown on the island: *amara*, known as the bitter orange (*laranjeira azeda*), and *sinensis*, known as the sweet or China orange (*laranjeira doce* or *da China*). The sweet oranges produced in Madeira are almost always inferior to those that come from Portugal and São Miguel.
The leaves and flowers of orange trees are used as an infusion for nervous diseases and difficult digestion.
The bitter orange, the one most used in medicine, is little grown in Madeira, and its fruit, which used to sell very cheaply, can only be eaten as a preserve.
Tangerines, or tangerine oranges, are produced by *Citrus nobilis*, a species native to China which is grown in many gardens in Funchal.
Laranjeira (street)
This was the part of the present Rua do Carmo (‘Carmel’) between the church of Carmo (Carmelite church) and the Ponte do Ribeirinho (‘little brook’), next to the Travessa do Rego.
The chapel of St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*) stood in Rua da Laranjeira. Its founder and the year it was built are unknown, and the Council ordered its demolition on 5 February 1836.
Largo da Fonte

In the locality (*sítio*) of Fonte (‘spring’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), lies the so-called Largo da Fonte, a spot with a roofed public fountain containing a small image of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*). It is bordered by the track of the Monte Railway (*Caminho de Ferro do Monte*), and there is a station of the railway there called the Fonte station (*Estação da Fonte*). It is a very picturesque place, much frequented by visitors to the enchanting resort of Monte, especially since the site was enlarged a few years ago.
Largo dos Milagres

A locality (*sítio*) in the town (*vila*) of Machico, where the chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*) stands. It was destroyed by the great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803; it was then called the chapel of Christ (*Cristo*) or of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), to which it belonged at the time, and it was rebuilt shortly afterwards. See Cristo (chapel), p. 332 of vol. 1.
Larica (António Augusto)

The son of Fortunato Leandro Larica, he was born in Funchal in 1831 and took his doctorate in medicine at the Faculty of Montpellier in 1852. For many years he was chief officer of the Port Health Station (*guarda-mor da Estação de Saúde*) of Funchal, and he died in this city on 22 May 1903. Works: *Apprécier les méthodes opératoires de la fistule vésico-vaginale, thèse présentée et publiquement soutenue à la Faculté de Médecine de Montpellier le 26 Avril 1852* (Montpellier, 1852).
Látego (O)
Published from 12 June 1889 to 8 March 1891, running to one hundred and sixty-four issues.
Latino Coelho (street)
The former Rua Nova de Santa Maria (‘new street of St Mary’), which links the Praça or Largo dos Lavradores with the Largo das Torneiras.
It was given the name of Latino Coelho at a session of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) on 7 September 1911, but it is generally known by its old name.
Latzel (Dr)
Works: *Beitrage zur Kenntnis der Myriapoden Fauna von Madeira, den Selvages und den Canarischen Inseln* (*Jahrb. der Hamburgischen Wissenschaftlichen Anstalten*, XII (1895).
Lauraceae

Several reasons persuaded us to reproduce here in full the interesting article on the ‘lauraceae’ of Madeira that Carlos de Meneses, co-author of this *Elucidário*, published in the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) of 22 May 1909. Here it is:

‘The laurel family (Lauraceae), which comprises about 900 species, almost all of them tropical and distributed among 42 genera, has the following representatives in the Madeira archipelago: Madeira mahogany (vinhático, *Persea indica*), *barbusano* (*Apollonias barbujana*, a laurel-forest tree), til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) and *loureiro*.

Madeira mahogany (*Persea indica*), which also grows wild in the Canary Islands and the Azores, is one of the most useful and interesting forest trees of Madeira. Its leaves are large, leathery, oblong or oblong-lanceolate, light green or reddish, silky-pubescent when young and glabrous when mature. Its flowers are small, greenish-white and tomentose-pubescent, borne in axillary panicles on compressed peduncles, and its berries are ovoid or oblong and black when ripe. The wood of this species, which is reddish in colour, is highly prized on the island. It is used chiefly for making furniture, and it is hard to tell apart from mahogany, which it resembles very closely, although it is slightly inferior in quality. In furniture made of mahogany, the grain is more pronounced than in furniture made from the wood of our island’s species.

Madeira mahogany, once very common, is becoming rare because of the relentless war waged on it for its precious timber, which fetches high prices on the Funchal market. Extensive woods that we knew in the interior and the north of the island have been destroyed completely by unscrupulous individuals. They did not even trouble to sow the land again, so as not to deprive it for many years of the forest cover that is so useful in a country as rugged as Madeira.

This Madeiran laurel was still to be found in many valleys and ravines in the north and centre of the island, and it is cultivated on several *quintas* in Camacha and Santo António da Serra (‘St Anthony of the uplands’). It grows poorly in Funchal and in all places in the southern region below 150 or 200 metres. It flowers from August to November and fruits from October to April. It prefers damp places and can reach 25 metres, and in some cases even 30 or 32 metres, in height.

Madeira mahogany grows as a naturalised plant in some parts of Portugal, where, according to Brotero, it is known as *loureiro real*. On the introduction and cultivation of this tree on the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), an article by the Revd Father Manoel Narcizo Martins in vol. VI of *Broteria*, the natural sciences review of the college of São Fiel, deserves to be consulted.

During the 18th century, Madeira mahogany timber was exported to England, where it was known as Madeira mahogany. According to Professor Piazzi Smith, the largest ships of the Invincible Armada, sent by Philip II against Great Britain, were built or fitted out inside with Madeira mahogany and til wood from the island. However, since Portuguese historians, as far as we know, say nothing on the matter, it seems to us that the said professor’s revelation should not be accepted without a certain reserve.
The wood that Funchal cabinetmakers call ‘Brazilian vinhático’ comes from *Eucalyptus robusta*, a species cultivated in some parts of the island.

The *barbusano* (Apollonias barbujana, a laurel-forest tree), given here as *Apollonias canariensis* and peculiar to the archipelagos of Madeira and the Canary Islands, is a tree with leathery leaves, ovate-oblong or oblong-lanceolate, of a green noticeably darker than that of the Madeira mahogany (vinhático, Persea indica). Its greenish-white flowers are borne in panicles shorter than the leaves, and its fruits are oblong and black. On the leaves of this tree there is a very prominent gall, produced by an eriophyid mite, which was described by the distinguished cecidologist the Reverend Joaquim da Silva Tavares in vol. II of *Broteria*.

The wood of the *barbusano*, which is heavy and dark brown or dark grey, is now very little used by cabinet-makers, because it is extremely dense and hard. In the countryside excellent spindles are made from it, and in the past it was also used for the beams of houses.

The *barbusano* is found at various points on the north coast of the island between Seixal (‘pebble shore’) and Boa Ventura, at São Gonçalo, in Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), on the Levada do Bom Sucesso, etc., and it is the member of the laurel family best suited to the coastal region. Frutuoso mentions it on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it now seems to be completely extinct. It is widely cultivated in the *quintas* of Funchal and Monte (‘hill’), where it reaches 30 and 35 metres in height, whereas outside these localities it seldom exceeds 20 metres. It flowers from November to March and generally fruits from January to April.

The til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), given here as *Oreodaphne foetens*, is easily distinguished from the other Madeiran laurels because its berries are enclosed up to a certain height (sometimes up to half-way) by a kind of cup formed by the enlarging calyx. It has ovate, ovate-oblong or oblong leaves, which are glabrous but bear tufts of hairs in the axils of the veins on the underside, and small greenish-white flowers arranged in panicles longer or shorter than the leaves.

In tils of a certain age, the heartwood and the sapwood are very clearly delimited, the latter being white and the former black. When freshly cut, the wood has a strong and rather unpleasant smell, which disappears completely only after years. Today this wood is used only for making furniture, but when it was more plentiful it was also used for the beams and floors of buildings. The old chests in which country people usually store their wheat are for the most part made of til.

Madeiran cabinet-makers distinguish between white til and black til, although both belong to the same botanical species: the white wood of the til comes from young trees, the black from old trees. We believe that only after 40 years does the inner part of the wood of the species we are discussing begin to take on a markedly black colour.
Black til is the only kind truly prized in cabinet-making. White til is worth much less, although it can also be used in inlaid work (*embutidos*) and for making some utensils.

The til is a species peculiar to the Madeira and Canary Islands group. In Madeira it grows especially in the valleys of the interior and the north, where, like the Madeira mahogany, it is becoming rare because of the great demand for its timber and the high price it fetches on the market. It can reach 35 metres, and even a little more, but it usually does not exceed 25 to 30 metres in height. It flowers from November to June, and its berries, which are black and ovoid or oblong, appear irregularly for a large part of the year. The foliage of the til can be used as fodder.

The laurel (*Laurus canariensis*) is the most abundant of the Madeiran lauraceae and the one that reaches the greatest altitudes. On the high ground of the mountain region it generally grows no taller than 10 to 12 metres, but in the valleys and the low-lying parts of the island it can reach 25 to 30 metres. Its leaves, which are elliptical, ovate, oblong or lanceolate, have a pleasant and distinctive scent, and its small umbels of yellowish-white flowers, arranged in clusters, are usually shorter than the leaf stalks. It flowers at the same time as the *barbusano*, and its berries, which are ovoid and black, rarely yellow, appear from September to April.

The wood of the laurel, which is light in colour, is inferior to that of the other Madeiran lauraceae and is little used for building work. Its charcoal is soft and less sought after than that of the heaths (*Erica scoparia*) and the *uveiras* (*Vaccinium maderense*).

Laurel leaves are used as a seasoning in cooking, and an oil is extracted from the berries that was once used to light the poor houses of the countryside. To extract this oil, the berries are boiled and then pressed inside a cloth bag in small wooden presses. As the oil is lighter than the remaining liquid, it floats on top and is easily drawn off from the vessel in which the operation took place. The light obtained by burning laurel oil gives off no bad smell, but it is weak and very smoky. The tree we are describing is today completely extinct on the island of Porto Santo, where it also once grew.

On the trunks of old laurels a very curious plant gall is often found, produced by *Exobasidium Lauri*, a fungus of the family Exobasidiaceae. This gall, which can reach 20 centimetres in length and usually branches, is known by the name of ‘*madre de louro*’ (fungal gall on laurel trunks) and is held in Madeira to have emmenagogue properties.

The laurel is a species peculiar to Madeira and the Canary Islands; the Azorean tree referred to by Hewett Cottrell Watson and by Meissner as *Laurus canariensis* of Webb is *Persea azorica* of Seubert. The small laurel of Portugal and the Mediterranean region (*Laurus nobilis*) is quite close to the Madeiran tree, which today forms a species distinct from it, owing to geographical isolation and climatic influences, important factors in the separation of systematic forms.

Besides the four native lauraceae mentioned above, the following exotic species are found in Madeira: the avocado (*Persea gratissima*), the camphor tree (*Cinnamomum Camphora*) and the cinnamon tree (*C. Zeilanicum*). The camphor tree and the avocado are very common; the latter produces pear-shaped fruit, violet or green, much appreciated both by the Portuguese and by the foreigners who visit the island.

All the native lauraceae are evergreen, sprout well from the stump, grow quickly, live long and propagate perfectly from seed. The many qualities that recommend them lead us to believe that they will play an important part in reforesting the Madeiran mountains, today for the most part bare, if one day serious attention is given to carrying out this improvement. It has been talked about for so many years, and it truly deserves the attention of those whose offices allow them to promote the prosperity of the district.’
Lavadeira (Motacila boarula)

A bird of the wagtail family (Motacillidae), very common in Madeira, where it frequents streams, streets, the roofs of houses, etc. etc. It is easily recognised by the yellow colour of its breast and by the movement of its rather long tail.
It lays a clutch of 4 to 5 eggs and builds its nest on roofs and in hollows in walls, using roots, grass leaves, etc.
It is also known by the name *lavandeiral*, and in Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) it is sometimes called *papa-moscas*.
The *lavadeira de fora*, which spends the winter in Madeira and is frequent on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), is *Motacila alba*.
Lavradores (Largo or Praça dos)

This square (*largo*) lies on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, as a continuation of Rua da Infância and Rua Oudinot, both of which open into it. It also gives access to Rua do Hospital Velho. Every Saturday a fair used to be held in this square for the sale of pine poles and chestnut stakes, used for the vine trellises known in Madeira as ‘corredores’. The square is also the site of the main entrance to the city’s large market, known as the Farmers' Market (*Mercado dos Lavradores*), which was opened in 1939.
Lazaretto

At a session of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) on 1 July 1816, a ministerial order (*portaria*) from the Governor and Captain-General was read, ordering a lazaretto to be built at the expense of the municipality’s (*concelho*) property. At the session of the 11th of the same month and year, a letter from the same authority was read, suggesting that the funds needed to build the said establishment could be raised by public subscription.

Despite these instructions, and although on 8 July 1816 the Council had petitioned John VI for a loan of the sum needed to build the lazaretto, the work was never carried out. A short time afterwards the Governor ordered that ships arriving from suspect ports should anchor off Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’), and that their passengers should undergo quarantine in the house known as the Engenhoca (‘small mill’), which probably stood in that locality (*sítio*) or close by.

On 2 December 1800 the Municipal Council ordered two ships that had arrived at the port of Funchal without a bill of health to weigh anchor within 2 hours. The guards who were on board were to be put ashore at Praia Formosa, stripped there and ‘plunged in the water more than 6 times’, and were then to remain in quarantine, under the watch of a sentry, for 40 days.

In 1848, when José Silvestre Ribeiro was civil governor of Madeira, a lazaretto was established at the Quinta do Gorgulho (‘weevil estate’), a *quinta* (country estate) belonging to the British subject Henrique Veitch. The newspaper *O Madeirense* (‘The Madeiran’) published the regulations of the establishment on 11 November of the same year.

From the Quinta do Gorgulho, the lazaretto moved in 1851 to some houses that Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro had ordered to be built on land belonging to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*), at the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires’s stream’). It was on this same land that the buildings of the present lazaretto were later erected; work on them began on 22 April 1866 and ended in 1874. In 1857 one of the outbuildings of the lazaretto built on the orders of José Silvestre Ribeiro was destroyed by fire.

In building the premises at the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires, certain topographical requirements that ought to have been met were disregarded. For that reason the buildings were not used as a general lazaretto, although it is recognised that they can serve without drawback as an observation lazaretto. In 1874 Drs Craveiro and Pereira came to Madeira on the Government’s orders to examine the lazaretto building. It is curious to note that the very parties who had contributed to the construction of this establishment at the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires were the first to declare to those physicians that it did not serve the purposes for which it had been undertaken and carried out.

The lazaretto building was used in 1904 to treat people stricken with cerebrospinal meningitis, in 1905 for those stricken with bubonic plague, in 1907 for smallpox patients and in 1910 and 1911 for cholera patients. In 1897 there were plans to set up a ward for the insane in the same building. That same year the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal tried to move the gaol of the judicial district (*comarca*) there, but it was unable to do so because the Government did not grant the petition it had been sent to that effect.
In 1919, 280 political prisoners implicated in the monarchist revolution that broke out in Portugal that same year were held in the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’).

The Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’) had a director and a physician appointed in 1889, and an inspector appointed in 1890. These employees, whom the Government had engaged under article 59 of the decree with force of law of 3 December 1868, ceased to serve at the lazaretto after the publication of the Health Regulations (*Regulamento de Saúde*) of 24 December 1901, which turned the establishment into an observation post.
Lazareto (road)

The road lies in the parishes of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) and São Gonçalo and continues the Calçada do Socorro (‘succour’), bounding the grounds of the Gonçalo Aires lazaretto on the north. The lane that runs into this road, to the east of the Ribeiro do Pasto (‘pasture’), is known as the Travessa do Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’). On the southern edge of the Caminho do Lazareto, overlooking the sea, stands the Jewish cemetery. Its entrance still bears an inscription in Hebrew meaning ‘Dwelling of Life’ and the date 5,611, which corresponds to the year 1851 of our era.
Leal

Leal is an old family surname, found chiefly in Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’). António de Almada married Isabel Rodrigues Leal, of this parish (*freguesia*), around the middle of the 16th century. In 1684 Maria de Aguiar, widow of Gonçalo de Faria Leal, founded the chantry (*capela*) of Our Lady of Succour (*Nossa Senhora do Socorro*) in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’). A member of this family, João Nepomuceno de Freitas Leal, founded in 1770 a chapel dedicated to St John Nepomucene in the locality (*sítio*) of Lombo dos Leais (‘the Leals’ ridge’), in the aforementioned parish of Porto da Cruz.
Leal (Councillor João Baptista de Freitas)

Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) João Baptista Leal, who belonged to an old and distinguished Madeiran family, was born in Funchal on 24 June 1837 and died in the same city, at the age of 82, on 30 March 1920. He was the son of Commander Valentim de Freitas Leal and Dona Augusta de Freitas Abreu Leal. In 1864 he completed his law degree at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He did not take up a career at the bar, but on several occasions, always with distinction and a genuine love of justice, he held the post of substitute district judge (*juiz de direito*) of this judicial district (*comarca*). He carried out various public duties, as a member of the District Council, representative (*procurador*) on the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Asylum and of the Soup Kitchen (*Sopa Económica*), etc. His devotion to the Catholic cause and the services he rendered to the Church led Leo XIII to honour him with the high distinction of Privy Chamberlain of the Sword and Cape to the Roman Pontiff. He was one of the principal founders of the Catholic Association of this city and of the first Conference of St Vincent de Paul to be established here in Madeira.

He promoted the publication of the former newspaper *A Verdade*, whose first issue appeared on 23 January 1875 and of which he was for many years the chief editor. From 1879 to 1888 he published, in seven instalments of about 1400 pages, the account of a journey he made through several European countries, under the title *Recordações e Impressões de Viagem*. In 1894 he published in Funchal a pamphlet of 136 pages entitled *Devocionario das Almas do Purgatório*, of which in 1901 he brought out a new, considerably enlarged edition of 281 pp. He also published several pamphlets containing some of the speeches he delivered at the formal sessions of the Catholic Association of this city, in his capacity as its president. Councillor Freitas Leal was a highly cultivated gentleman and a correct and elegant writer, of the most refined and noble manners and of remarkable austerity of character.
Leal (Sebastião Frederico Rodrigues)

This Madeiran held a law degree and followed a career in the magistracy, serving as deputy crown prosecutor in one of the judicial districts of Funchal. He represented Madeira in parliament in the legislative session of 1857 to 1858 and was editor of the newspaper *O Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Citizen’), which was published in this city from 1859 to 1861.
On the island of Graciosa, a pamphlet of 58 pp. was published in 1866 under the following title: *Abusos d'autoridade praticados na ilha Graciosa pelo juiz de direito Sebastião Rodrigues Leal*.
Ledo e Vinhatico

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). João Fernandes de Andrade, one of the earliest settlers of this parish, founded in the locality of Ledo a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Lanço (Our Lady of the Lanço), which he made the seat of an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). The chapel of Our Lady of the Flight into Egypt (*Nossa Senhora do Desterro*), built by Rafael Esteves in the third quarter of the 17th century, also once stood there. A state elementary school operates in this locality.
Legislation

In the short article entitled ‘Legislation’ in the first edition of this work, we stated that we would give in the ‘Supplement’ a brief account of the legislative enactments promulgated concerning this archipelago, as a valuable aid to the study of the measures adopted by the governments of mainland Portugal in the public administration of Madeira over the long period of five centuries. The ‘Supplement’, which was to have formed the third volume of the *Elucidário Madeirense*, was never published, and in this new edition the gap cannot be filled, because a summary of that legislation would take up far too much space. The deficiency has been partly remedied by the publication of the book *O Arquipélago da Madeira na Legislação Portuguesa*, by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva. It contains a summary of these legislative enactments for the period from 1934 to 1939, accompanied by a detailed, annotated index, and occupies more than a hundred pages of the book. Should a second edition of that work be produced, it ought to add a summary of the legislation promulgated before the constitutional period. For this the learned notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) offer us an abundant repertory, as do several old collections of Portuguese legislation, and in particular the works of José Anastacio de Figueiredo and José Justino de Andrade e Silva.
Lei (A)
The first newspaper of this title published in Funchal appeared on 11 July 1861 and ran to twenty-seven issues, the last on 25 January 1862.

Two other periodicals with the same title later appeared in this city. The first ran to one hundred and thirty issues, from 6 December 1873 to 20 June 1877, and the second to ninety-seven issues, its first issue being published on 27 April 1879.
Leiria (Júlio Augusto)

A military engineer from mainland Portugal who held the posts of director of public works of the district of Funchal and teacher of the first three years of mathematics at our lyceum (state secondary school). In 1871 he published a map of the island of Madeira, to which we have already referred in this *Elucidário*, and in 1874 he wrote a pamphlet with the following title: *Duas palavras de Júlio Augusto Leiria em resposta ao folheto intitulado «O Hospital de Santa Isabel da cidade do Funchal»*. There is a road in Machico named after the engineer Leiria, since it was owing to this official’s diligent efforts that its construction was begun. He died in Coimbra in January 1878, at about 50 years of age.
Leitão

In the time of Philip I, the high court judge (*desembargador*) João Leitão came to Madeira. He was captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of War and Governor-General of the archipelago, but we do not know whether the Leitões whom Manuel Tomás, in ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*), includes among the notable families of Madeira descend from him. Around the middle of the 19th century, the merchant and banker João José Rodrigues Leitão, a native of the mainland, settled in Funchal and founded another branch of the Leitão family. See Cacongo (I-182).
Leitão (João)

When Portugal fell under Spanish rule, the captain-donataries of Madeira lost the power and importance they had enjoyed. The privileges and functions attached to their high offices, which had already been considerably reduced by 1580, as stated in the article Donataries, became almost purely honorary.

To administer our colonial possessions, the Spanish government created the post of governor-general, which carried extensive powers and whose authority extended to every branch of public administration.

Although Dom Felipe was proclaimed king of Portugal in September 1580, the first governor-general of the Madeira archipelago appointed by the usurping government did not reach Funchal until long after that proclamation. The man chosen for the post was the high court judge (*desembargador*) João Leitão, who enjoyed the full confidence of the Governor of the Kingdom. He was also charged with conducting a judicial inquiry (*devassa*) into the political events that had taken place on this island at the time of the proclamation of Philip II. His powers covered the administration of the royal treasury and the trial of criminal cases, as well as general oversight of civil and military affairs. A writ of lodging (*provisão de aposentadoria*) recorded in volume 2 of the General Register of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) shows that he was sent to Madeira on 5 January 1582.

In 1582, since it was feared that the French fleet supporting the claims of António, Prior of Crato, might invade Madeira, Dom Agostinho de Herrera was sent to the island as military commander. The high court judge João Leitão continued in charge of the civil administration, and in 1584, when Dom Agostinho de Herrera left the archipelago, he resumed full civil and military jurisdiction. João Leitão served until 1585 and was succeeded in the government by Tristão Vaz da Veiga.

On this subject, the following words were printed in the ‘Addenda and Corrigenda’ of the second volume of the 1st edition of this work, and they are worth recording here: ‘In the present year of 1924 Dr Damião Peres, former rector of our lyceum (state secondary school) and now a professor at the University of Porto, published a short pamphlet entitled *O desembargador João Leitão, primeiro governador geral da Madeira*. Its sole purpose is to show that the high court judge (*desembargador*) Leitão was governor-general of this archipelago not by law but only in fact, and that he came to Madeira in 1582 and not in 1581, as we read in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and in vol. 1 of this *Elucidário*. As for the correction of that date, it should be noted here that it was made more than a year ago, on p. 44 of this volume. As for the fact that the document appointing that magistrate to the post of governor-general is not known, this does not prove that he did not hold that office on an interim basis and in fact, as Dr Damião Peres seems to acknowledge. When Spanish rule was established in Portugal, would the government in Madrid have left an important colony such as Madeira for a long time without an official representative of its own to oversee the various affairs of public administration? That representative was João Leitão. Indeed, the proven fact that he “was invested with a multiplicity of powers and privileges”, to which must be added that he was charged with conducting a judicial inquiry (*devassa*) of a political nature, sufficiently explains why his appointment to that post was not made definitive.’ (1921)
Leite Monteiro (Councillor José)

Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Leite Monteiro was not Madeiran, but he felt for the land where he had spent most of his life the touching and tender devotion that the most loving son can feel for the beauties of his native corner of the earth. All his affections, all his aspirations, all the flights of his intellect were concentrated within the narrow bounds of this small island. A mind of eminent superiority, of the widest learning and one of the most distinguished jurists, with varied and remarkable gifts in many branches of public affairs, he could legitimately have aspired in this country to the most enviable positions in politics, at the bar, in letters and in teaching. His natural modesty, his love of seclusion and study and his innate aversion to showy display, however, firmly turned him away from the brilliant and lofty offices that generally so tempt and attract intellectuals. In another setting and under other circumstances, Councillor Leite Monteiro could easily have attained a prominent position and produced some valuable works, which the Madeiran conditions in which he lived did not allow him to produce.

He was born in the city of Porto on 27 September 1841, the son of Dr Caetano José Gomes Monteiro, who was district judge (*juiz de direito*) of one of the judicial districts of Funchal, where he died, and of Dona Margarida Fernandes Leite Monteiro.

He enrolled in the Faculty of Law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1859 and graduated in 1864. In 1863 he published a pamphlet entitled *O Ultramontanismo na Instrução Pública em Portugal* and, in 1864, the book *Estudos de Patologia Social*. These writings reveal a remarkable and precocious talent, although the doctrines they defended provoked the harshest criticism. In 1895 he began publishing the work *Elementos de Direito Civil Português*, of which only the 1st fascicle, of 244 pages, appeared.

Dr José Leite contributed extensively to the Funchal periodical press, notably to *A Lâmpada*, *O Oriente do Funchal* (‘The Funchal Orient’), *A Imprensa Livre* and *O Direito*. Many of his articles became famous for their originality and beauty of form, for the force of their argument and, perhaps even more, for the ardour and vehemence of their language. Had he worked as a journalist in the capital, it can be said without exaggeration that his name would stand alongside those of the great journalists Sampaio, António Enes, Mariano de Carvalho and Emídio Navarro.

As an advocate he produced most remarkable work, and it is a great pity that it has remained buried on the shelves of lawyers’ offices. As far as we know, only two or three short works on legal subjects were published, besides the work already cited.

The competitive examination he sat, by public trial, for the post of philosophy teacher in the lyceums was a brilliant one. Dr Teófilo Braga, an admirer of Dr Leite Monteiro, travelled from Lisbon to Porto to attend it; one of the other candidates was our distinguished fellow Madeiran Dr Manuel Joaquim Teixeira. He obtained the highest mark and in 1867 was appointed teacher at our lyceum (state secondary school). Despite the brilliant showing he made in that examination and his undeniable competence to hold the chair of philosophy, truth obliges us to say that he lacked the qualities of a true teacher, and that on the whole his pupils gained little from their master’s lessons. Among the public offices he held was that of deputy civil governor; on several occasions he actually exercised this post, to which he was appointed by the decrees of 3 February 1902 and 26 March 1906. He was also a member of the District Council (*Conselho de Distrito*) and president of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal. In this last office he showed great interest in the development of the public library. Almost all the foreign works on Madeira held there were acquired during his term of office, and he also sought to create a municipal museum.

He belonged to the former Fusionist Party and took part in the Madeiran political struggles of 1868. Later he rendered notable services to the Regenerator Party, chiefly as editor of *Direito*. He was a member of the International Law Association of Berlin, and it is to him and to the late Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira that we owe the publication of ‘Flowers of Madeira’ (*Flores da Madeira*), which brought together many valuable works by Madeiran poets. He died on 10 March 1920.
Leite Monteiro (park)

Construction of the park began in 1894 on land bought from João Baptista de Sousa for 1,640,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), following a decision taken at the council meeting of 2 August that year. Although it offers nothing out of the ordinary in the way of vegetation or ornament, it is nonetheless a place one visits with pleasure, both for its coolness and lush greenery and for the views it commands. The fountain known as the Fonte de Nossa Senhora (Our Lady’s Spring), where a small image of the Virgin can be seen, is made of marble and stands in the park. Beside it lies a spacious square, where grow the most beautiful plane trees we know of on the island.

The old fountain of Nossa Senhora, far more charming and picturesque than the present one, was destroyed in 1896 when a large chestnut tree that overhung it fell. The contract for installing the new fountain was awarded at the council meeting of 12 August 1897.

Inside the fountain there is a brass plate bearing an inscription in English, which reads as follows: ‘Charles Murray, Consul General of His Britannic Majesty in the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), founder and first owner of the *quinta* (country estate) of Belo Monte, in the year 1776 purchased the surplus water of this fountain from the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Henrique Felix de Freitas, for the sum of 5,000 *réis* a year, to be paid in perpetuity to the heirs of the said holder of the entail; and he ordered this structure to be built so that the waters might be better gathered, the fountain repaired and the aqueduct and fountain at the roadside constructed, all at his own expense, in the year of Our Lord 1778’.

At its session of 22 August 1895, the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) gave the name of its president, Dr José Leite Monteiro, to the park at Monte (‘hill’). However, the municipal administrative commission (*comissão administrativa municipal*) appointed after the proclamation of the Republic annulled this decision at its session of 27 October 1910. On 13 February 1913, when Dr Manuel Gregório Pestana Júnior was president of the municipal administrative commission, the park’s original name was restored, a decision that was very well received by the people of Funchal.
Leituga
This name is used for several Compositae found in Madeira, such as *Tolpis macrorhiza*, *Crepis laciniata*, *C. divaricata*, *Sonchus pinnatus*, etc. All these species are highly milky.
Lemann (Dr Carlos)

An English botanist who came to Madeira in 1837 and left the island for London on 19 May 1838. The plants he collected on this island and in the Canary Islands are at Kew Gardens and the University of Cambridge. See Hooker.
Lemay (Gaston)
He writes about Madeira in his book entitled *A bord de la «Junon», voyage autour du monde* (Paris, 1879).
Leme
Leme is a very old family surname here in Madeira. It derives from António de Leme, who on this island founded a large and distinguished line of descendants.

At the capture of Asilah and Tangier, two Flemish noblemen, Martim de Leme and António de Leme, natives of the city of Bruges in the former Flanders, distinguished themselves by their bravery and heroism. Their father, Martim de Leme, had sent them to fight under the orders of the King of Portugal, accompanied by a number of men-at-arms armed and equipped at their own expense. The letters patent and coat of arms of 2 November 1471, granted by Afonso V to António de Leme, who was then a knight of the household of Prince Dom João, made honourable mention of this deed. They conferred and ratified the title of nobility he already held in his native land, and gave him as arms ‘on a field of gold five black blackbirds in saltire, without feet or beaks, and for crest one of the blackbirds within a saltire of gold’.

Among other children, António de Leme had Martim de Leme, who seems to have been born, like his father, in Flanders. After serving in Portugal and holding high court offices in his homeland, he came to Madeira around 1483, bringing to the Funchal Council letters of recommendation from Infante Ferdinand, master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which the island then belonged. He was given lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), which he left to his heirs. He died in Funchal and was buried in the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi). Martim de Leme married Dona Maria Adão Ferreira, daughter of Adão Gonçalves Ferreira, the first man born on this island, who was himself the son of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, companion of Zarco in the discovery of Madeira.

It was he, or a son of the same name, who built in this parish (*freguesia*) the dwelling house still called Quinta do Leme (‘Leme’s estate’) today, together with the adjoining chapel, whose construction Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo dates to 1535. António de Leme married Dona Catarina de Barros, who founded an entail (*morgado*) from the disposable third (*terça*) of her estate, on lands she owned in the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). They lived and died at the Quinta do Leme residence and were buried, as we see in an old book of lineages, ‘in the chancel of Santo António do Campo’, which is undoubtedly the parish church of that parish.

From this marriage was born Pedro de Leme, who founded the entail (*morgado*) of the Lemes on the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name, with the express obligation that the surname Leme be perpetuated in the successor and administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of this entailed estate (*vínculo*). For reasons entirely unknown to us, and which today it will perhaps be impossible to discover, Pedro de Leme and his eldest son Cristóvão de Leme were arrested and taken to Lisbon. Both died in prison there, in the same year and a short time apart, the latter in September 1556. We are faced here with a mysterious drama, and perhaps a bloody tragedy: father and son, cast into the depths of a prison for some heinous crime, may have been put to death there by an avenging hand, for fear that a commutation of the sentence or a pardon, as easily happened to noblemen, might yet restore them to freedom.

Dona Maria de Leme, daughter of Pedro de Leme, who married Pedro Gomes Galdo, at once took over the administration of the estate she had inherited from her parents, and died without issue. A long lawsuit followed, and the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Quinta do Leme passed to Francisco de Moraes and his wife Dona Maria da Câmara, daughter and son-in-law of Dona Leonor de Leme, sister of Dona Maria de Leme, the last administrator of the entailed estate. The next to succeed to the entailed estate was their daughter, Dona Felipa da Câmara, who married António da Silva Barreto, who died in 1633. From this union was born Manuel da Silva Câmara, who immediately succeeded to the entailed estate but died shortly afterwards, in 1634.

The heir and immediate successor in the administration of this entailed house (*casa vinculada*) was Inácio da Câmara Leme, lieutenant-general in Madeira, knight of the Order of Christ and *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the Royal Household, who enjoyed considerable prestige and influence on this island. It was he who, around the middle of the 17th century, rebuilt the house and chapel of the Quinta do Leme. In 1647 he married Dona Isabel de Castelo Branco Bettencourt, and from this marriage was born, in 1649, the heir to the house, Francisco da Câmara Leme, who, like his father, was a knight of Christ and *moço fidalgo* of the Royal Household. He married Dona Francisca de Sá e Meneses, and from this marriage was born, on 25 July 1695, the eldest son and successor, Pedro Júlio da Câmara Leme, *moço fidalgo* and knight of the Royal Household like his father and grandfather. He married Dona Mariana de Meneses, daughter of Pedro de Bettencourt Henriques and Dona Mariana de Meneses.

His son and successor in the entailed estate was Francisco Aurélio da Câmara Leme, who in 1731 married Dona Antónia Maria Acciaioli de Vasconcelos Betencourt. He held the privileges of knight of Christ and *moço fidalgo* that he had inherited from his forebears. It was he who in 1748 entirely rebuilt the chapel of São Filipe (St Philip) at the Quinta do Leme, which the earthquake of that year had left in ruins, as can be seen in the article already cited.

Their son, Francisco António da Câmara Leme, then took possession and administration of the entailed estate. He married in turn Dona Anna Correia Accioli; Dona Maria Luísa Correia Accioli, sister of his first wife; and Dona Júlia da Cunha, an illegitimate daughter of the Count of Cunha, who died of cholera in Lisbon in 1832. Francisco António da Câmara Leme died without issue, and on his death the administration of this entailed estate passed to his nephew, João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo de Bettencourt de Sá Machado, 1st Count of Carvalhal. It was thus absorbed into the great house of Carvalhal, the richest and most important on this island.

On the title of Dom (noble honorific), which some members of this family used, the work *Resenha das Familias Titulares e Grandes de Portugal*, vol. 1, p. 384, states the following: ‘The Câmaras Lemes… of the island of Madeira never had the Dom. The last representative of this family began, after a certain time and arbitrarily, to place the Dom before his baptismal name; the arbitrary usage was continued by his descendants, and since it was mentioned without due verification in various royal grants that have been made to them, the Dom became legalised, His Majesty thus bestowing two favours at no cost to himself. This happens with other people too.’

This information does not contradict what an old Madeiran *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) told us to explain the use of the Dom by the last members of the Câmara Leme family. One of them, petitioning for some royal grant or other, placed a D before his name to stand for *Diz* (‘states’). When the favour requested was granted, however, the official who drew up the royal letter (*carta régia*) inadvertently took the abbreviation of *diz* for *dom*, writing: ‘we grant to Dom So-and-so’ etc. And from this, it is said, came the illegitimate use of the Dom with which the last descendants of the Câmaras Lemes paraded themselves.
Leme (João da Câmara)

He was born in Funchal in 1865 and held the post of doorkeeper of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*). In 1887 he published in this city a volume of poems of 83 pp., entitled *Amor e Pátria*. When it appeared, it was claimed in the press that the pamphlet was an outright plagiarism, pilfered from various Portuguese poets, notably Almeida Garrett.
Lemos (Colonel José António de Azevedo)

He commanded the military expedition that came to Madeira in 1828 to bring the island under the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) government. He became known for his serious disagreements with the Governor and Captain-General José Maria Monteiro, going so far as to ask the Government to replace this official because of his incompetence and his habit of listening only to ‘an infamous circle of individuals abominable for their vices and bad morals’. On one occasion he insulted the Governor in the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’), and was only prevented from striking him because several officers who were present intervened.
Colonel Lemos allowed the troops under his command to commit every kind of excess against the constitutionalists, and he consequently became unpopular with most of the population of Funchal.
Lemos (Dom Jorge de)

Before the diocese was established, Bishop João Lobo (see that entry) visited this island in 1508. After the bishopric was created, the prelates Dom Duarte, in 1516, and Dom Ambrósio, in 1538 (see those entries), came to Madeira. They performed the episcopal duties here in place of the titular bishops, Dom Diogo Pinheiro and Martinho de Portugal, who never visited the lands under their jurisdiction; nor did the third bishop, Dom Friar Gaspar do Casal. The fourth prelate, Dom Friar Jorge de Lemos, was the first to take personal charge of the episcopal government of this bishopric. He administered it from 1558 to 1569, although he resided on this island for only five years.

He came of noble families and was the son of Francisco Velho and Dona Brites de Lemos. He took his vows in the Convent of São Domingos (St Dominic), Lisbon, and among the offices he held in his order was that of professor of theology. Already advanced in years, he was confirmed as Bishop of Funchal on 9 March 1556 by Pope Paul IV, and took possession of the office in 1558. Five years later he left for the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and in 1569 he resigned the mitre. He died a short time afterwards and was buried in the church of the convent where he had taken his vows.

As the first diocesan prelate to come to this bishopric in person, he was received with special marks of regard and esteem by the clergy and by all the people of this island. More than 130 years had passed since colonisation began. Despite the special powers enjoyed by the delegate of the Vicar of Tomar (*vigário de Tomar*, head of the Order of Christ’s spiritual jurisdiction overseas), and even though a Franciscan religious community of strict observance already existed in Funchal, it is certain that some abuses had crept into ecclesiastical doctrine and into the observance of the various canon laws. Because the prelate had to correct these abuses and reform old and deep-rooted customs, he naturally incurred the displeasure of many. Serious difficulties and frictions resulted, which he nevertheless managed to smooth over through his spirit of justice and the irreproachable conduct of his actions. ‘He was’, says Dom António Caetano de Sousa, ‘of a harsh disposition, which he always tempered with prudence; magnificent in his manner of living and a great rewarder of the deserving.’

He paid particular attention to the service of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), requesting and obtaining the creation of several new posts, such as those of succentor, chapel master and choirboys, an increase in the salaries of the canons and dignitaries, the reform of the music and the creation of curacies, which relieved the dean of the burden of parish duties. In his time the single parish (*freguesia*) that existed in Funchal was divided into two parishes, with their seats in the Cathedral and in Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). Shortly afterwards he petitioned for the creation of the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), which did not last long: it was abolished in 1579 and restored again in 1587. He also worked for the creation of the diocesan seminary (*Seminário*), which was established in this city only some years later (see seminary).

In 1563 Dom Jorge de Lemos left for mainland Portugal, where he held the office of Chief Almoner (*esmoler-mor*) to King Sebastian. On 15 November 1569 the Pope accepted Dom Jorge’s resignation of this bishopric and appointed Dom Fernando de Távora, a friar of the Order of Preachers, to succeed him.
Lencastre (Dr Luís Adriano de Magalhães Meneses e)
He was elected peer of the realm for Madeira for the legislative session of 1890–1892.
Legends

The annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) refers only very briefly to the legends that took shape over time among the peoples of this archipelago. He deals at length, and with great erudition, only with the well-known legend of Robert Machin and Ana d’Arfet, which we shall discuss in its proper place in this *Elucidário*. The legend of the Hidden Island (*Ilha Encoberta*), which is not peculiar to this region and generally forms part of the beliefs of the Sebastianists, takes on a particular aspect here: the island is said to lie, if the expression may be allowed, near Madeira, and there are people who claim to have seen it distinctly on certain mornings of St John’s Day. Apart from these and some legends of a religious character, Dr Azevedo mentions no other legends that were current on this island.
