He says: ‘Religious legends abound on the island of Madeira, and we are forming a collection of them; besides the three already mentioned (that of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*), in the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), that of Friar Pedro da Guarda, in Câmara de Lobos, and that of the foundation of the Convento das Mercês (Convent of Our Lady of Mercy)), we already have the following: that of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*), that of the Lord of Miracles of Machico, that of Santo António da Serra, that of the Lord Jesus (*Senhor Jesus*) of Ponta Delgada, that of St Vincent of Saragossa of the islet (in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente), that of St Martin and that of Nossa Senhora of the Orphan Girls’ Retreat (*Recolhimento das Órfãs*). We reserve them for publication in a separate volume.’ This volume was never published.

Apart from these legends or popular tales, we know of few on this island, but we shall mention those that come to our knowledge. In vol. 1, p. 44, under the title chapel of the Poor Souls (*Almas Pobres*), we have already referred to one of them.
Firewood

The wood burnt as fuel in Funchal and the island’s other main settlements generally comes from the maritime pine, whose logs or split pieces are often sold by the *cento* (firewood unit of 1,400 sticks) or the *talha* (firewood unit of 56 sticks). Each *cento* contains 1400 sticks and each *talha* 56 sticks; the woodcutters call a *cento* of 100 sticks a ‘small *cento*’.

Firewood became enormously more expensive during the war, because of its consumption by coastal steamers and factories. Today a *cento* of firewood costs six times as much as in 1914, owing to the same causes and to the rise in value of all the produce of the land. An ordinary *cento* of firewood that cost 12 to 13 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) ten years ago now costs between 70 and 80 escudos. (1921) The inhabitants of some parishes go up into the uplands to gather firewood, and they cause great devastation among the trees to obtain the fuel they need for domestic use.
Professors
