law of 26 July 1888 permitting associations of ‘*heréus*’ to acquire real property and conferring legal capacity on them; ministerial order of 30 May 1894 appointing a commission to study regulations for the forests and waters of Madeira; decree of 9 November 1894 granting a subsidy for the construction of the Levada do Furado; law of 21 May 1896 authorising the Government to award contracts for the construction of the levadas; decree of 18 June 1896 ordering a call for tenders for the award of the contract; decrees of 13 November 1903, 3 January 1905, 24 August of the same year, 29 August 1906 and 6 November of the same year, opening various credits for the construction of new levadas; ministerial order of 14 November 1910 provisionally granting the use of those waters of the Ribeira da Janela not used by the riparian owners; law of 20 April 1914 upholding for the legal entities ‘Levadas da Madeira’ the rights acquired over certain spring waters located on the property of others; decree of 31 July 1928 authorising the sale of the levadas; decree of 14 February 1931 upholding for the ‘Levadas’ the rights they had acquired at the date of publication of the Civil Code, without prejudice to the rights under the law of 14 April 1914; decree of 26 June 1939 sending a technical mission to Madeira to survey the technical and economic possibilities in their combined hydroelectric and hydro-agricultural aspects; and Decrees nos 33,158 and 33,159, dated 21 October 1943, which authorise the construction of an important and extensive network of irrigation channels and lay down the rules to be followed in carrying out this inestimable improvement.

Of all the legislative instruments cited, the royal letters of 1493, 1515 and 1563 and the decrees of 1841, 1888, 20 April 1914, 14 February 1931 and 21 October 1943 must be regarded as the fundamental bases, constituting the true organic laws governing the levadas, although the others contain valuable material for anyone wishing to acquire a broader knowledge of this important subject.

Among the writings published on the levadas of Madeira, three stand out above the rest for their relative length, complete impartiality and acknowledged competence. None of them is a comprehensive work, for their authors, treating the matter from limited points of view, did not intend a complete study, but only to set out the particular subject with which they wished to deal. Nevertheless, all these writings certainly contain valuable data and information that are indispensable for any study one might wish to undertake. They are: *Representação dirigida ao Governo acerca das águas de irrigação na Madeira*, by the presidents of various associations of *heréus*, drafted by Dr Quirino Avelino de Jesus and published in 1897 as a pamphlet of 34 pages; *Plano Geral de distribuição das águas da Levada da Serra do Faial*, by the engineer Adriano Augusto Trigo, a volume of 138 pages, published in 1911; and *das águas no Direito Civil Português*, by Dr Guilherme Alves Moreira, published in 1920, which contains a substantial chapter, number 21, entitled ‘Os direitos adquiridos sobre as águas e levadas na Madeira’.

The concession or award of contracts for the levadas, the application of the mainland’s water regime to Madeira and the plans to sell the levadas provoked long and bitter debates in the Funchal press, in which political passions, interests and hatreds played a large and deplorable part. It is nevertheless beyond doubt that these articles, numbering about a hundred, provide valuable material for anyone wishing to write a detailed history of the phases through which the management and direction of the Madeiran levadas have passed.

One may consult in particular the *Diario do Comercio* of August and September 1896, the *Diario do Comercio* of March, April, August, September and October 1897 and April 1898, the *Diário Popular* of July, August and November 1897 and April, May and July 1898, the *Diário de Noticias* of May 1897 and April and May 1898, and the *Correio do Funchal* of January and February 1897. The numerous articles in the Funchal press on the 1916 plan to sell the levadas, published in February and March of that year, were collected in a volume of 196 pages entitled *A Imprensa e os três projectos*.

In addition to the works and newspapers already cited, we may mention the following publications on levadas: ‘Longing for the Homeland’, by Dr Gaspar Frutuoso, annotated by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo; *Apontamentos para o estado da crise agrícola no distrito do Funchal*, by Dr João da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, Funchal, 1879; *levadas da Madeira. Relatório justificativo da proposta apresentada pelo Consultorio de Engenharia e Architectura do Funchal no concurso para a adjudicação da Empresa de irrigação no arquipelago da Madeira*, by Carlos Roma Machado de Faria e Maia and Aníbal Augusto Trigo, Lisbon, 1896; *As aguas e as levadas da Madeira*, by Quirino Avelino de Jesus, an article published in no. 51 (March 1898) of the review *Portugal em Africa*, occupying pp. 81–127; and *A Empreza das Levadas nas mãos de um aventureiro... aggravo para a Relação de Lisboa em que é aggravado Manuel Alexandre de Sousa e aggravante Anibal Augusto Trigo*, Funchal, 1896, 41 pp.

In the columns of *O Jornal*, under the general title ‘Problema Máximo’ (‘The Greatest Problem’), we published a series of articles in which we argued for the need to build a few more levadas, to maintain and improve the existing ones, and to exploit new springs in order to increase the volume of their flows.
Léveillé (Hector)

A distinguished French botanist, born on 13 March 1863, who died at Le Mans on 25 November 1918. He wrote the following works on the Madeiran flora: *Les Onotheracées de Madère* (*Le Monde des Plantes*, October 1896); *A propos de deux plantes de Madere* (ibid., October 1897); and *Les Renonculacées, Geraniacées et Haloragées de Madere* (ibid., February 1898).
He never visited Madeira; the materials he needed for his studies of the island’s flora were supplied to him by one of the authors of this *Elucidário*.
Liberal (O)
Four issues of this newspaper were published, the first on 23 December 1875.
Another newspaper with the same title was published in this city from 1 May to 7 December 1913, running to 176 issues.
Liberdade (A)
Four issues of this newspaper appeared, the first on 12 March 1870 and the last on 12 April of the same year.
Another periodical with the same title was published in this city from 20 November 1878 to 5 February 1879, running to 59 issues.
Lyceum

Until 1759, the year in which they were expelled from this island, secondary education in our archipelago was entrusted chiefly to the members of the Society of Jesus. In their College (*Colégio*), where the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.º 27*) is quartered today, the Jesuits taught the humanities in the so-called *Aulas do Pátio* ('Courtyard Classes', the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), which formed part of the same College. There, besides a course in theology, they directed the subjects of Portuguese and Latin, philosophy and rhetoric (see Jesuits).

In 1772, by a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 6 November, the Marquis of Pombal established in Madeira three classes of Latin, one of Greek, one of rhetoric and one of philosophy, thus making good the gap left by the abolition of the course run by the Jesuits. At the beginning of the 19th century, classes in drawing and painting and in arithmetic and geometry were created in this city, and later classes in French and English. Some of these subjects were taught in the former Aulas do Pátio and the rest in other State buildings. These studies lacked a suitable scientific and literary organisation, nor did their direction follow definite teaching methods and syllabuses. Above all, they lacked a management that would give them unity and make of them a systematic and regular course.

The decree of 17 November 1836 established a lyceum (state secondary school) in the capital of each district of the mainland and the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes), in which ten chairs or subjects were to be taught. It thereby brought to an end the classes that had previously been held in scattered fashion throughout the country.

The governor of this archipelago, António de Gamboa e Liz, was ordered to carry out the decree and to establish the lyceum (state secondary school) in this city. The building chosen was that of the former *Aulas do Pátio* (‘Courtyard Classes’, the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college). The first council of teachers met there, and the new educational establishment was installed on 12 September 1837. Its opening, a very solemn occasion, took place on 10 October following, and regular classes began on that same day.

The first teachers, appointed provisionally, who held chairs there were Dr Manuel Joaquim Moniz, who served as acting rector, Dr João de Freitas e Almeida, Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça and Alexandre Luís da Cunha; all were made permanent by decree of 17 September 1838. By a decree of the same date, Dr Lourenço José Moniz was appointed titular professor and permanent rector of our lyceum. Francisco de Andrade began to hold a chair as a provisional teacher at the start of the 1838 academic year, and was made permanent on 19 November of the same year.

The following were successively appointed permanent teachers: Dr Luís da Costa Pereira (1850), José Camilo Delanave (1854), Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo (1855), Dr Joaquim Camelo Lampreia (1859), Dr Manuel José Vieira (1861), João Fortunato de Oliveira (1863), Dr José Leite Monteiro (1867), Daniel Simões Soares (1881), Dr Maurício Augusto Sequeira (1887), Father Ricardo Augusto Sequeira (1887), etc.

The rectors of this lyceum have been Dr Manuel Joaquim Moniz (1837), Dr Lourenço José Moniz (1838), Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça (1850), Francisco de Andrade (1866), Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira (1881), Canon Manuel Esteves Fazenda (1900), Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira (1900), Dr António Augusto Pereira da Silva (1910), Aníbal Sertório dos Santos Pereira, Dr Damião Peres, Dr Joaquim Carlos de Sousa, Dr Alberto Figueira Jardim, Dr António Luís Franco and Dr Ângelo Augusto da Silva.

Among the teachers now deceased, some were regarded as truly outstanding figures in education, not only for the brilliant way in which they held their chairs but also for the valuable works they published on the subjects they taught there: Francisco de Andrade with his grammars of the Portuguese language, Marceliano Ribeiro with a Latin grammar and his studies on philosophy, and Dr Álvaro de Azevedo with a book on literary criticism and a textbook of reading, philology and composition.

Among the reports written by the rectors, those of Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça and Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira stand out, and some of them have been printed. Special mention, however, is due to the valuable *Anuários* (yearbooks) published in recent years and compiled by the distinguished rector Dr Ângelo Augusto da Silva.

We believe that the ten chairs or subjects established by the decree of 17 November 1836 were not all taught in our lyceum from its foundation, and that they were only actually taught in the years immediately following. We cannot trace the various phases through which teaching at the lyceum of this city has passed across the many reforms of secondary education, because that would demand patient research that the shortness of time and the narrow scope of this work do not allow us to undertake. As we have said, the lyceum was installed in the former *Aulas do Pátio* (‘Courtyard Classes’, the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), which were outbuildings of the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*) with access from Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’). It remained there for more than 40 years. In January 1881 it was transferred to a house in the same street, a former manor house of the Vasconcelos de Couto Cardoso entail-holders which later belonged to the Barons of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), and there it began to operate on the 11th of the same month and year. In January 1914 it moved to the former bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*), in the old Rua do Bispo, today Rua Gomes Freire, where it is at present (1921) housed; in 1880 it had also spent some time in outbuildings of the Palácio de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’).

The pamphlet *Cem Anos de Vida Escolar*, by the teacher J. R. Basto Machado, published in 1937 to mark the first centenary of the founding of the Funchal lyceum, contains some information of interest for the history of this educational establishment.

For a long time the local press and every rector who has headed our lyceum never ceased to insist on the pressing need to build a building to house that important institution of secondary education in proper pedagogical conditions. After careful studies of the most suitable site and of how to carry out so costly a construction, the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) resolved to take the initiative in this undertaking of such remarkable social and educational significance. To that end it obtained from the central government the transfer of the former Military Hospital (Hospital Militar) of this city, which was authorised by the decree of 5 September 1936. Work on the sumptuous building began shortly afterwards and proceeded rapidly and without interruption. By October 1942 all the lyceum’s services had been installed in the new building, meeting one of the great needs of our community, and classes began on the 8th of that month and year.
Lycopodiaceae

These vascular cryptogams are represented in Madeira by the following two species: *Lycopodium complanatum* and *L. Selago*. The latter is used at Christmas time to decorate the *lapinhas*, or Nativity cribs.
Liebetruth (Dr)
Austrian botanist who collected marine algae in Madeira in 1862.
Lignite

In the Ribeiro do Meio (‘middle brook’), in the valley of São Jorge, at about 300 metres above sea level, two seams or deposits of impure lignite have been known for many years. This lignite is associated with various layers of tuff and clay, in one of which fossil leaves of dicotyledons and ferns were found in abundance. Since a thick layer of basalt and scoria, more than 300 metres high, rests on top of the deposits, it seems evident that abundant land vegetation once existed at the spot, long before the volcanic formations that now cover it.

The nature of the tuffs accompanying the lignite and of some of the nearby agglomerates justifies the assumption, says Lyell, that a series of eruptions once took place close to where the deposits lie. It is therefore not impossible that the lignite and the leaves accumulated in a crater, and that the erosion of the valley later exposed them.
It is said that an analysis of the São Jorge lignite showed 60 per cent carbon and 30 per cent ash.
This lignite, which had lain buried for many years owing to landslips from the ground above, was exposed once again in 1917. See Leaf beds and Phanerogams.
Japanese privet (Ligustrum japonicum)
A tree of the olive family (Oleaceae) seen in some streets, squares and public and private gardens. It has large, ovate-acuminate leaves and white, very fragrant flowers arranged in panicles.
Lima (Dr José L. Ávila e)
He was elected deputy for this archipelago on 28 August 1910. Parliament never met, because the Republic was proclaimed on 5 October of the same year.
Lima e Cunha (Henrique de)

He was born in Barreiro on 15 March 1843 and died in São Pedro de Sintra on 17 October 1915. An artillery officer, he commanded No. 3 Garrison Artillery Company while holding the rank of captain, taught drawing at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and served on a commission in the district’s Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas*). Works: *Plano de melhoramentos para a ilha da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1879, pamphlet.
Sweet lime (Citrus medica, subsp. Lumia)
A small tree of the rue family (Rutaceae), little cultivated in Madeira. Its fruits are known as *limas* or *limões doces* (sweet limes).
City limits

The municipal by-law of 30 December 1909, confirmed by the District Commission (*Comissão Distrital*) on 3 August 1911, established that the urban part of the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal was the perimeter formed by the angles whose vertices rest on the following points: 1. the Reid’s Hotel on the Estrada Monumental (‘monumental road’); 2. the old bridge over the Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’); 3. the intersection of Rua do Arcebispo Dom Aires with the Estrada da Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy levada road’); 4. the intersection of that road with the Avenida de Pedro José de Ornelas; 5. the intersection of the Caminho do Palheiro do Ferreiro with the Caminho do Terço (‘rosary road’); and 6. the mouth of the Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires’s stream’). The 3rd and 4th vertices are to be taken as joined by the polygonal line that follows every bend of the Estrada da Levada de Santa Luzia.

According to the royal decree (*alvará*) of 5 October 1863, the limits of the city were as follows: to the south, the beaches of the bay of Funchal; to the east, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), the localities of Louros, Forca and Rochinha de Cima; to the north, in the parish of Santa Luzia, the localities of Vale Formoso, Calçada da Torrinha and Ponte do Deão; and to the west, in the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), the localities of Pico, São João da Ribeira, Maravilhas, Ribeiro Seco and Ponte Monumental.

Before that decree, the city was bounded by the chapel of St Catherine, the Ponte de São Paulo, the Castelo do Pico (‘castle of the peak’), the Beco dos Arrifes as far as the upper mill, the church of Santa Luzia, Pena, Rochinha and the Encruzilhada da Forca. These limits had been fixed by a commission appointed at the council meeting of 19 December 1809.

The city began to spread towards Ribeiro Seco and the Caminho do Monte (‘Monte road’) after the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803, because many of the city’s buildings had been ruined and many families were left without homes. At its ordinary session of 17 October 1927, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) resolved to give the city an excessively vast area, extending it deep into the suburban parishes. It fixed the limits in the following terms, which, it must be said, are not remarkable for their clarity: ‘From the sea in a straight line to the road linking National Road no. 23 with the Caminho Velho de São Gonçalo, the Caminho da Igreja de São Gonçalo, the Caminho do Palheiro Ferreiro, the Caminho do Terço, the Caminho da Levada do Bom Sucesso, in a straight line to the Estrada da Levada de Santa Luzia, from there in a straight line to the Muro da Coelha (north of the Quinta Drolhe), the Caminho da Água de Mel, Álamos, the Ponte da Ribeira Grande, Quinta do Leme, Pilar, Avista-Navios, the Caminho de São Martinho and the Caminho do Amparo to the Estrada Monumental, and in a straight line down to the sea’.

With these new limits fixed for its area, the city almost doubled in size, taking on truly exaggerated proportions. Under the Council’s resolution of 1909, the parishes of the Sé and Santa Luzia, almost the whole of São Pedro and a considerable part of Santa Maria formed an integral part of the city, and for that reason they were called urban parishes. Under the new division of the city in 1927, the capital of the district comprised the area established in 1909, together with the territory added from the suburban parishes of São Martinho, Santo António, São Roque and São Gonçalo; the parish of Monte is the only one that has no share in the perimeter recently fixed for the city’s limits. Its former area, reckoned at about five hundred hectares, must now reach approximately 750. The truth is that this excessive enlargement of the city has not caught the attention of the population, who continue to regard as the bounds of urban Funchal the limits so logically and rightly fixed for it in 1909. The official population census for 1920 gives the city 24,284 inhabitants, a number that has grown greatly today, not only through the natural increase of the population but also through the enlargement the city underwent in 1927, as already mentioned.
Lemon tree (Citrus medica subsp. Limonium)

A member of the rue family (Rutaceae) from the Himalayas, widely cultivated in Madeira. The juice of its fruit is used to make lemonade and is helpful in certain inflammations of the throat. The lemon tree that produces the lemons known as *limões de galinha* is the acid variety of the subspecies *Limonium*.
Limoges

A family surname of French origin, now extinct in Madeira. Felipe Gentil de Limoges founded the entail (*morgado*) and chantry (*capela*) of St Philip (*São Filipe*), in Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). See São Filipe (chapels).
Limonite
Anhydrous iron oxide. It occurs in masses in the form of concretions at Ponta de São Lourenço (island of Madeira).
Lindinger (Dr Leonhard)
Works: *Die Schildlause (Coccidae) Europas, Nordafrikas und Vorderasiens, einschlisslich der Azoren, der Kanaren und Madeiras...*; Stuttgart, 1912, 388 pp.
This work records 18 Madeiran species found on 34 different species of plants.
Lindman (Dr Carlos)
A Swedish botanist who visited Madeira in 1885. The algae he collected on this island were identified by Professor Oscar Borge.
Língua cervina

The fern that Madeirans call by this name is *Elaphoglossum squamosum*, distinguished by its elongated fronds covered with rust-coloured or almost black scales. This species grows at Porto da Cruz, Boa Ventura, Lamaceiros, etc., and is widely used in Madeira as a cough remedy. The fern known in Portugal as *língua cervina* is *Scolopendrium vulgare*, a species that also occurs in Madeira but is quite rare.
Língua de vaca (Sonchus fruticosus)

A member of the daisy family (Compositae), 1 to 3 metres tall, common at Monte, Camacha and in the ravines of the interior. It has elongated leaves with broad, rounded lateral lobes, and large yellow umbellate flower heads which together form a panicle. It is also known as *serralha da rocha*.
Lignite
See Lignite.
Flax (Linum usitatissimum)

This textile plant is grown in almost every parish of Madeira, over an area of some 150 to 200 hectares. After harvesting, the flax is drawn through the teeth of the rippling comb (*ripanço*) to remove the seed bolls. It is then retted in tanks or in the waters of streams, where it stays for 8 to 10 days. After this it is set out to dry and then crushed with a flail. To separate the textile fibres from the woody matter clinging to them, the flax goes to the brake (*gramadeira*) and is then scutched. But it is only on the hackle (*sedeiro*) – a kind of comb made of metal teeth fixed to a piece of wood – that the fibre is disentangled and can be made finer, while the tow is separated at the same time.

Both the flax and the tow are spun on the distaff by women. The yarn obtained in this way is reeled into skeins, placed in the oven or in a lye wash, and then bleached in the sun. Once bleached, the yarn is wound and can finally go to the small looms scattered across various parts of the island. There the series of operations ends that country people aptly call ‘the torments of flax’.
The linen cloth made in Madeira is of excellent quality and very durable, and much of the household and body linen used by country people is made from it.
Linseed (the seed of flax) is much used in rural folk medicine, but that sold in the pharmacies comes almost entirely from outside the island.
On this subject, see the book *As pequenas Indústrias da Madeira*, in the chapter ‘O Linho na Madeira’, by Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento.
Lippold (Dr)
A German botanist who collected plants in Madeira in 1838. In the October 1838 issue of *Gardner's Magazine* he wrote a note on the gardens of Dr Renton’s house on the island of Madeira.
Lichens

The distinguished Spanish lichenologist the Revd Father Longinos Navas lists and describes, in his *Sinopsis de las Liquenes de las Islas de Madera*, 203 species of these curious cellular plants, which, as is well known, consist of an association of an alga with a fungus. The fungus takes carbohydrates from the alga; the alga receives from the fungus protection against drying out, together with a certain quantity of nitrogenous substances. This association is called symbiosis.

Among the Madeiran lichens we may mention the following: *Stiacta damaecornis*, *Pseudocyphellaria aurata*, *Lobaria pulmonaria*, *Xanthoria parietina*, *Usnea florida*, *Nemaria fuciformis*, *N. rocella*, *N. fucoides*, *Cenomyce pyxidata* and various *Lecanora*, *Parmelia*, *Lecidia*, etc. The three species of the genus *Nemaria* that we have, known as *urzelas*, were formerly much used to extract a red-violet substance, obtained by fermenting the plants with lime and urine. Lichens are found on tree bark, on rocks and walls, on the ground, etc. See August von Krempelhuber, Stein, Stizenberger, Steiner, Navas.
Lira

This surname is still common today in some parishes of this island. In Calheta (‘small cove’) there was a noble family of this surname, to which Canon António Veloso de Lira and Father Manuel de Lira belonged (see those entries). Some genealogical works state that it descends from Teresa de Lira, wife of Dom Afonso de Aragão, of the late 15th century; their son, named Lopo Dias, adopted that surname, which has survived on the island ever since.
Lira (António Veloso de)

He was one of the most distinguished Madeirans of the 17th century. He belonged to an old and noble family of the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), and he was born there on 14 June 1616, the son of Manuel Dias de Lira and Dona Mécia Rosa de Couto. After completing his studies in the humanities on this island, he enrolled at the celebrated University of Salamanca, which at that time was attended by many Portuguese. He was about to complete, or had perhaps already completed, his doctorate in theology when the revolution broke out that threw off the Castilian yoke and placed the Duke of Braganza on the throne. A considerable number of Veloso de Lira’s compatriots, almost all of them students, were then in that Spanish city. He did more than anyone to ensure that they all returned home immediately to join the movement for liberation and independence that at once spread throughout the country. Camilo Castelo Branco refers to this event in the article ‘Estudantes Portugueses em Salamanca’, included in his book *Coisas leves e pesadas*. In his work *Espelho de lusitanos*, António Veloso de Lira makes a brief reference to this episode, stating that more than four hundred Portuguese were then in Salamanca.

He devoted himself to letters and in his day enjoyed a reputation as a man of wide learning. In 1643 he published a book entitled *Espelho de Lusitanos em o cristal do psalmo 43*, which went into a second edition in 1753. Like Father António Vieira and other superior minds, he could not escape the prevailing taste of the age, and his writings are riddled with that detestable Gongorism which then infested Portuguese and Spanish literature. Despite its faults, the work reveals a superior intelligence and uncommon learning, and as late as the middle of the 19th century Alexandre Herculano published lengthy extracts from it in the review *O Panorama* (‘The Panorama’). We do not know whether he published any other works; Diogo Barbosa Machado says that he left the following unpublished: *Política Christiana*, *Zodiacus Ecclesiae*, *Stella Matutina in medio nebulae*, *Domus Sapientiae*, *Philosophia muta*, *Glosa sobre os Evangelhos* and *Antiguidades da ilha da Madeira*.

After a long stay in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), he settled in Madeira. In 1670 he was appointed canon of our Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and in 1689 he was raised to the dignity of magistral canon (*cónego magistral*, the canon charged with preaching). Among the offices he held here, the most notable was that of governor of this bishopric. He died in this city on 4 January 1691 and was buried in the chancel of the Cathedral.
Lira (Father Manuel de)

This Madeiran priest was for some time a captive in Algiers, where he rendered great services to the other captives held there, tending and helping them with the most evangelical charity. He belonged to an old family of Calheta (‘small cove’), where he was born and where he died in the first half of the 17th century. He was a relative of Canon António Veloso de Lira (see that entry).
Lírio

This name is given to all the Iridaceae of the genus *Iris* cultivated in Madeira. *Iris biflora*, which comes from Portugal and is easily recognised by its large white or purple flowers, is the commonest plant of the genus.

Madeirans also give the name *lírio* to *Reseda luteola*, a plant of the family Resedaceae that is very common on the island. This plant contains a yellow colouring principle, which Madeirans customarily use by gathering the plants in flower and boiling them with whatever they wish to dye. The dyed article is finally put through a lye wash made with ash.
The *lírio* should be gathered shortly after flowering, once some of the seeds are already ripe.
Lírio (Controlophus ovalis)
A fish of the family Scombridae, caught at some distance from the coast, both at the surface and in mid-water. It is an edible species, but little valued.
Literature
Madeiran literature followed the phases of mainland literature, although few writers from this archipelago left a name crowned with glory in the literary history of the country.

It is certain, however, that as early as the century of the discovery there appeared several poets of notable merit who feature in the *Cancioneiro* (songbook) of Garcia de Resende. In his book *Poetas Palacianos*, Teófilo Braga went so far as to regard them as a group apart, characteristic and distinct, which he called the *Cyclo Poético da Ilha da Madeira* (Poetic Cycle of the Island of Madeira), a classification with which the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) disagrees. Nevertheless, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that ‘that very notable group is none the less sufficient title for the island of Madeira to have an honourable share in the pre-classical history of national literature, a share which Senhor Teófilo Braga claimed for it.’ The chief of these poets who feature in the songbook are Tristão Teixeira, 2nd donatary of Machico, known as Tristão das Damas; João Gomes, the Troubadour; João Gonçalves da Câmara, 2nd donatary of Funchal; Rui de Sousa; João de Abreu; Manuel de Noronha, son of the 2nd captain-donatary João Gonçalves; and Rui Gomes. We know of no Madeiran prose writer who lived in the 15th century (see Cancioneiro de Resende, 1-233).

Of the Madeiran prose writers of the 16th century, Diogo Barbosa Machado, in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’), mentions Afonso da Ilha, Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, Damião das Chagas, Tristão Gomes de Castro, Manuel Álvares, António da Gama and Sebastião de Morais (see those entries). From this period the blind poet Baltasar Dias (see that entry) should also be mentioned.

In the 17th century, the writers include Luís de Morais, António da Visitação, João Pinto da Vitória, Francisco de Santa Teresa, António Veloso de Lira, Belchior de Teive, Gregório Baptista, Remígio de Assunção, Manuel Constantino, Francisco de Castro and Daniel da Costa (see all those entries). To this period belongs the poet Manuel Tomás (see that entry), who, although not a Madeiran, wrote the well-known poem ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*), which deals exclusively with matters of this island.

In the 18th century, we shall mention the writers Nicolau Francisco Xavier da Silva, Manuel Rodrigues, Henrique Henriques de Noronha and Julião Fernandes da Silva (see those entries). In this period, Troilo Vasconcelos da Cunha, Francisco de Vasconcelos Coutinho, Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega and Francisco Manuel de Oliveira (see those entries) distinguished themselves as poets.

For the first half of the 19th century we must mention the names of Dr Nicolau Caetano de Bettencourt Pita, Father João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo, João António Monteiro, Joaquim José Ferreira de Freitas, José Manuel da Veiga, Francisco Ferreira de Abreu, Justino António de Freitas, Servulo Drumond de Meneses, José Anselmo Correia Henriques, Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça, António Gil Gomes, Manuel de Santana e Vasconcelos. Paulo Perestrelo da Câmara and Francisco de Andrade as prose writers, and Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar and Francisco de Paula de Medina e Vasconcelos as poets (see those entries).

As Madeiran writers of the third quarter of the 19th century we name José António Monteiro Teixeira, the Viscountess of Nogueiras, Luís da Câmara Leme, António Correia Heredia, Patrício Moniz, José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage, Agostinho de Ornelas, Luís da Costa Pereira, Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega, João Augusto de Ornelas, João de Nóbrega Soares, Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira, the Viscount of Nogueiras and Maximiliano Eugénio de Azevedo.

From the last quarter of the 19th century we shall mention as Madeiran authors the names of Luís de Ornelas Pinto Coelho, João Baptista de Freitas Leal, Alexandre José Sarsfield, Dona Joana Castelo Branco, Father José Gonçalves de Aguiar, Father Manuel Fernandes de Santana, Ciríaco de Brito e Nóbrega, Carlos Azevedo de Meneses, António Feliciano Rodrigues and Francisco António Ferreira.
Livramento

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’). It takes its name from a chapel that once stood there, dedicated to Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*), which was the centre of a well-attended pilgrimage, now transferred to the parish church. The foundation of this chapel is attributed to Sebastião de Oliveira, around the middle of the 17th century; he held land there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation).
Livramento

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’). It takes its name from the chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance) that stands there. It was built at the behest of Inácio Ferreira Pinto in 1684 and rebuilt a century later by João José Bettencourt de Freitas, and it is an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). In the same locality there is a chapel consecrated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*), built a few years ago by Father Jorge de Faria e Castro.
Livramento

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), where there is a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance), after whom the place is named. It was built at the behest of Diogo Ferreira de Mesquita and his wife, Dona Isabel de Meneses, in 1656, as the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) that they founded. They were descendants of the German *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) Adriano Spranger, who owned land in the area as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation).
Livramento

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’). It contains a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*), which gave this place its name. It was founded by Father Manuel Gomes Garcês in 1683.
Lobato (João Carvalho)

Some years ago, several North American newspapers wrote about this Madeiran at some length and with great praise for his discoveries, particularly in the field of mechanics and electricity; he obtained a number of ‘patents of invention’ for these inventions in various European countries. The latest news of him that we have come across was published in the Madeiran periodical *O Jornal* (‘The Newspaper’) of 26 February 1932, which carries a detailed and interesting article about him.
Lobato Machado (Bernardo Francisco)

He was born on this island in 1802 and died in Funchal on 20 February 1878. He was a skilful ‘provisional’ lawyer (*provisionista*) and left several writings that enjoyed a well-deserved reputation in their day, especially a carefully prepared formulary on various legal questions. He became widely known as a journalist for the violence with which he attacked his opponents and for the abusive language he generally used, and he was forced to go into hiding to escape threats of likely reprisals. Only a few years ago people still often spoke of the bitterly scathing articles that Lobato Machado had published in the weekly newspaper *A Vergasta*, of which he was chief editor. He was a regular contributor to the newspapers *Amigo do Povo*, *Clamor Publico* and *A Justiça*.
Lobo (Dom João)

He was the first bishop to come to this island. The colonisation of the archipelago had begun more than 80 years earlier, yet no prelate had yet performed episcopal functions there. The Vicar of Tomar (*vigário de Tomar*, head of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*)'s spiritual jurisdiction overseas) – or rather the mastership of the Order of Christ, to which Madeira belonged in spiritual matters – sent Bishop João Lobo in 1508, and he visited all the churches and principal chapels of this island. The bishopric of Funchal was created in 1514, so João Lobo confined his religious mission solely to the exercise of episcopal functions: confirming, ordaining clergy, blessing vestments and liturgical vessels, consecrating churches, etc. He had no part in the administration of ecclesiastical affairs, the observance of canon discipline or the suppression of abuses. These belonged only to the diocesan bishop, who did not yet exist, and that charge therefore fell to the representative of the Order of Christ, who at that time was already Nuno Cão (see I-243), a brother (*freire*) of the Order. The first consecrated church on this island (and few are consecrated, most being merely blessed) was the chapel of the Lombada do Esmeraldo, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), and to this day the following inscription can be read on one of the interior walls of the building: ‘This church was consecrated by Dom João Lobo, Bishop of Taiere, on 27 August 1508.’ This prelate returned to Portugal after spending little more than a year on this island. It was after his visit that the need to create a diocese in this archipelago was more fully recognised; it was established only in 1514, as stated above. In Vieira Guimarães’s excellent book *A Ordem de Cristo*, published in 1901, we read the following: ‘As early as 1508, to satisfy the wishes of these petitioners (the creation of the bishopric of Funchal), the Vicar of Tomar sent them the titular bishop (*bispo de anel*) Dom João Lobo, who was awaited on the island by the master, Friar Nuno Cão, with all the clergy, and they held many celebrations for him.’
Monk seals

Frutuoso says that João Gonçalves Zarco and his companions found at the place they named Câmara de Lobos ‘so many monk seals (*lobos marinhos*, literally ‘sea wolves’) that it was a marvel; and it was no small refreshment and pastime for the men, for they killed many of them and had great pleasure and merriment in the slaughter’.

What the discoverers did was repeated countless times later, with the result that the monk seals disappeared from Câmara de Lobos, and perhaps from other points of the island where they may have existed. Today these animals appear only in the sea caves of the Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’), but since fishermen kill them whenever they find them, it is to be expected that they will disappear from that island too, as they have already disappeared from Madeira.

In the spring of 1878 eight monk seals were killed on the Deserta Grande, and after that others were destroyed or captured on that island, some of them being put on show to the curious public of Funchal. The British Museum holds several specimens of monk seal from the Deserta Grande, one of them more than a metre and a half long. The museum of the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) once had a small specimen of the same species, also captured on that island, which lived for a few days in a pond in the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’). There is a specimen in the Municipal Museum.
The monk seal of the Madeira archipelago is *Monachus albiventer*, a Mediterranean species whose southernmost habitat is the Deserta Grande.
Lombada

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). The old chapel of St Peter there was built by João Escorcio Drumond in the early 16th century and stood on the bank of the Ribeira da Boaventura (‘Boaventura stream’). Destroyed by the great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803, it was rebuilt soon afterwards on a site less exposed to the violence of the current. It is said that in this locality Dona Maria do Rosário de Arvelos built, in 1670, a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*), which disappeared long ago.
Lombada do Loreto

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), home to the old chapel of Our Lady of Loreto (*Nossa Senhora do Loreto*). It is the focus of a well-attended pilgrimage, drawing many people from several distant parishes and above all from the surrounding parishes. Although small, the chapel has a certain architectural distinction, and it is a pity that an ill-suited porch should spoil the harmony of the whole. It dates from the first years of the 16th century and was founded by Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, grandson of João Gonçalves Zarco, the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. A large manor house once adjoined it, for the founder made this the seat of the important entailed estate (*morgadio*) that he established. Others attribute the founding of the chapel and the entailed estate to Dona Joana de Eça, widow of the said Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine and patron of the Convento da Esperança (Convent of Our Lady of Hope), Lisbon, where she was buried. The nuns of this convent owned a great deal of land in the parish of Arco da Calheta, bequeathed to them by Dona Joana de Eça. In the first quarter of the 20th century the tomb of the patron, Dona Joana de Eça, was found in the ruins of the church of the Convento da Esperança.
Lombada dos Esmeraldos

It is also known as the Lombada da Ponta do Sol (‘ridge of Ponta do Sol’), because it lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of that name. This must have been its original name. Only when it passed to João Esmeraldo and his descendants, as administrators of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded there, did it take the name Lombada dos Esmeraldos (‘the Esmeraldos’ ridge’). To avoid needless repetition, we refer the reader to the article devoted to João Esmeraldo (vol. 1, p. 410), where we have already given a detailed account of this great property, which was and still is the largest on the whole island. We shall add only a few details not mentioned there. In the earliest days of the colonisation, the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco reserved for himself and his sons several *lombadas* (long ridges between valleys) and extensive tracts of land, almost all of which became important and flourishing entailed houses. Rui Gonçalves da Câmara (see vol. 1, p. 206), the second or third son of Zarco, received the great *lombada* that ran from the sea to the uplands and stretched from the Ribeira da Caixa to the Ribeira da Ponta do Sol. We do not know how long he held this property or what farming he may have carried out on it. Contrary to what is stated in the article on João Esmeraldo, it was in 1473 that Esmeraldo bought, or rather leased, that vast and highly fertile land from Rui Gonçalves da Câmara for the sum of 600,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) and a life annuity of 150,000 *réis*. This was the year before Rui Gonçalves went to settle in the Azores, for the chronicles of that archipelago give as certain his departure for the island of São Miguel in 1474.

João Soares de Albergaria, 2nd captain and donatary of São Miguel, accompanied his wife to Madeira, where she died. Father António Cordeiro, in the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), says that, wishing to thank Rui Gonçalves da Câmara for ‘the great hospitality he had shown him’, he decided to sell him his donatary captaincy (*donataria*), and at so low a price, adds Gaspar Frutuoso, ‘that he ceded it for eight hundred thousand *réis* in cash and four thousand *arrobas* of sugar’. It is said that the sale, or rather the emphyteutic lease (*aforamento*, perpetual lease for an annual quit-rent), of the *lombada* of Ponta do Sol was intended to fund the purchase of the donatary captaincy of the island of São Miguel, which seems very likely.

As already outlined in the articles cited, João Esmeraldo married twice, and in 1522 he founded two entailed estates (*morgadio*) in favour of the two sons born of these marriages. The entailed estate of Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’) comprised the eastern half of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys); that of Santo Espírito (‘Holy Spirit’) comprised the western half. The dividing line ran from Pico das Pedras (‘peak of the stones’), near the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), down the municipality (*concelho*) road to the crown of Pico da Amendoeira (‘almond-tree peak’), and from there to the sea. Once the division had been made, lots were drawn: the entail (*morgado*) of Vale da Bica fell to João Esmeraldo de Vasconcelos, son of the first marriage, and that of Santo Espírito to Cristóvão Esmeraldo, son of the second. Doubts arose over this division, and long lawsuits followed which, with intervals, were renewed over the years; these seemingly interminable legal disputes lasted for more than a century. They gave rise to curious episodes and incidents, which Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Agostinho de Ornelas, the last holder of the entailed estate of Vale da Bica, briefly describes in an interesting article published in no. 237 of the newspaper *A Verdade* (‘Truth’) of 16 October 1897.

There Esmeraldo built a chapel dedicated to the Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), also called the chapel of the Conceição (‘Conception’), which was consecrated by Bishop João Lobo in 1508 and became the seat of this entailed estate. The present church is a rebuilding from the first half of the 18th century, and it is the largest, most elegant and richest chapel in the whole diocese. Worthy of admiration and esteem is the dado of *azulejos* (painted glazed tiles) lining the lower part of the chapel’s interior walls, which depicts in symbolic figures the Gifts and the Fruits of the Holy Spirit. It has five altars and contains several exquisitely carved images. Nearby stands the vast, ruined manor house, once the most splendid country house in Madeira, rebuilt around 1679 by Luís Esmeraldo de Atouguia, holder of the entail. The last representative of this entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) was the 2nd Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), who displayed there the brilliance and magnificence with which he used to adorn his dazzling and lavish festivities. In this locality (*sítio*), at the place called Passo (‘pass’), are one of the two parish cemeteries and the ruins of an old chapel dedicated to St Maurus (*Santo Amaro*), whose construction is likewise attributed to João Esmeraldo. See *A Lombada dos Esmeraldos na Ilha da Madeira* by Father Fernando A. Silva.
Lombo da Apresentação

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). It took its name from the chapel of Our Lady of the Presentation (*Nossa Senhora da Apresentação*) that once stood here. Attached to it was a large manor house, the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded in 1524 by João Mendes de Brito and his wife Isabel Fernandes Tavares, whose last representative was the Viscount of Ribeira Brava.
Lombo da Estrela

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’). Here stands the chapel of Our Lady of Good Success (*Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso*), built by Lourenço da Costa in 1683. The old chapel of Our Lady of the Star (*Nossa Senhora da Estrela*) also stood here; the seat of the parish was established in it when the parish was created, as we noted in the article on the parish of Calheta. There was also a chapel dedicated to St Quiteria in this locality, built in 1724 by João Homem de Abreu. Moving the seat of the town (*vila*) of Calheta to this locality has often been proposed.
Lombo da Igreja

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). It is usually divided into two localities, Igreja (‘church’) Acima and Igreja Abaixo, according to their position relative to the Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’). Here stands the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), founded by André de França e Andrade around 1672. It was the seat of one of the largest entailed estates in Madeira, whose last administrator was the 1st Count of Calçada (1812–1906).
Lombo da Pereira

In the locality (*sítio*) of this name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) there is an orphanage for poor children, founded by Father José Lino da Costa and opened on 8 July 1922. It has rendered excellent service to destitute children there.
Lombo da Raiz

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’). It has a small house that can shelter those passing through, and it is also where the waters of the Levada da Serra (‘upland channel’), which irrigates the parishes of Caniço, São Gonçalo and Santa Maria Maior, are separated into their own channel. As far as Lombo da Raiz (‘root ridge’) these waters run together with those of the Levada do Juncal (‘rush-bed channel’), destined for the parishes of Santo da Serra, Água de Pena and Santa Cruz, and with those of the Levada Nova do Furado (‘new channel of the tunnel’), which waters the lands of the parish of Santa Cruz.
Lombo das Adegas

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). Pedro Delgado, an early settler, held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands here, which were later turned into an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). There was once a small oratory here dedicated to St Anthony, probably founded by this family. In 1853 it was enlarged and converted into a public chapel, the third chapel of that dedication in the parish.
Lombo das Mercês

A locality (*sítio*) incorporated into the inhabited locality of Florenças, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). It took its name from the chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom (*Nossa Senhora das Mercês*), founded in 1650 by Gaspar Homem de El-Rei and his wife Dona Isabel Florença, which was an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). It is also stated that João Portes Homem built a chapel dedicated to Santa Maria Madalena (St Mary Magdalene) in this locality in 1684.
Lombo das Têrças

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), where the chapel of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*) stands. It was built by the people in 1751 and enlarged in 1775, and in June 1810 it suffered a serious act of desecration. There was once also a chapel dedicated to São Caetano (St Cajetan), built in 1780 by António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo e Alencastre.
Lombo de Dona Isabel

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), Funchal. It borders the locality of Vasco Gil and is crossed by the road to Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’); at its top lies the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) known as Estrela (‘star’).
Lombo de São João
An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). It contains the chapel of St John the Baptist (*São João*), which gave the place its name.

Neither the year of its original construction nor the identity of its founder is known. It was an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) and belonged to Diogo Berenguer de França, holder of the entail (*morgado*), who in 1871 was granted the title of Viscount of São João, taken from this locality.
Lombo de São João

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), which took its name from the chapel there dedicated to São João Baptista (St John the Baptist). The year of its first construction is unknown, but it is known that it was rebuilt in 1750 by Second Lieutenant Tomé João Pimenta, administrator of the entail to which the chapel belonged.
Lombo do Atouguia

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), named after the early settler Luís de Atouguia, who held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands here and founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) on them. There was once a chapel here dedicated to Our Lady of the Good Death (*Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte*), founded by Francisco Homem de Couto in 1661. The chapel of São Pedro de Alcântara (St Peter of Alcántara), formerly also known as St John the Baptist, still stands here; João Baptista Teixeira had it built in 1783. In this same locality, at the place called Vargem de Baixo (‘lower meadow’), António Moniz de Meneses and his wife Dona Catarina de Meneses built a chapel consecrated to Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*) in 1657.
Lombo do Doutor

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’). It was named after Dr Pedro Berenguer de Lemilhana, who founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) here. He was a native of Spain and a *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the Royal Household. The chapel of Jesus-Maria-José once stood in this locality, founded in 1708 by João de Andrade Berenguer Neto, a descendant of Dr Pedro Berenguer. There was also a chapel of St Catherine here, built by Rodrigo Enes in 1505. The well-known village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’) lies in this locality.
Lombo do Mouro

A locality (*sítio*) high in the mountains of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). It has a small house that shelters travellers, and the projected road meant to link the Encumeada de São Vicente (‘São Vicente ridge pass’) with the parish of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) across the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) was to pass through it.
Lombo do Salão

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’). At the place called Vale dos Amores (‘valley of loves’) there is a small chapel dedicated to Santo António dos Milagres (St Anthony of Padua, Wonder-worker), which is today (1921) the property of Juvenal Raimundo de Vasconcelos. This locality was also once home to the chapel of Sts Cosmas and Damian (*Santos Cosme e Damião*), founded in 1681 by the physician António de França Gomes. At the spot known as Cadeado (‘padlock’) there is still a chapel dedicated to São Francisco Xavier (St Francis Xavier), built in 1693 by Manuel da Silva Pinheiro.
Lombo dos Aguiares

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), Funchal. Its lords were Diogo Afonso de Aguiar, son-in-law of João Gonçalves Zarco, or some of his closest descendants, and the locality took its name from its owners.
Lombo dos Canhas

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas. Here stood the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Anunciação, or da Incarnação, rebuilt in 1696 by João Rodrigues da Câmara and his wife Dona Isabel César da Câmara, which for some time served as the parish church.
Lombo dos Leais

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), incorporated into the inhabited locality of Folhadal (‘folhado grove’). Here stands the chapel of São João Nepomuceno (St John of Nepomuk), founded by João Nepomuceno de Freitas Leal in 1770. Near the chapel is a fine dwelling house belonging to the old Leal family, from which the locality took its name.
Lombo dos Reis

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). Here stands the Chapel of the Magi (*Reis Magos*), founded around 1529 by Francisco Homem de Gouveia, who made it the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he established; the estate was later incorporated into the house of the donataries of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). In the same locality is the chapel of Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*), built by Dona Inácia Betencourt Perestrelo in 1860.
Lombo Grande

A long ridge that stretches from the parish (*freguesia*) of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) to the summit of the Serra das Torrinhas (‘little towers’). It is crossed by a road leading to the parish of Boaventura. Before the road reaches the Torrinhas ridge it forks, one branch heading towards Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’); this is the preferred route for climbing that height.
Lombrigueira (Chenopodium ambrosioides)

A native member of the goosefoot family (Chenopodiaceae), also known as *formigueira*, very common both on Madeira and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Its leaves are sinuate-toothed or almost entire, with a strong and distinctive smell; they are a very effective vermifuge, and Madeirans sometimes use them as an emmenagogue.
Lomelino

This family surname was introduced into Madeira in 1476 by João Baptista Lomelino and his brother Urbano Lomelino, both Genoese and descendants of the Lomellini marquises, who were among the twenty-eight families that made up the old Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of Genoa. They came to this island with the recommendation of the Infanta Dona Beatriz, in a letter written to the Council of Funchal. Urbano Lomelino settled in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), where he acquired a great deal of land. There he married Joana Lopes, with whom he had no children, and he left his property to his nephew Jorge Lomelino, in whose favour he established an entailed estate (*morgadio*) that was among the most important on this island. As we have already said on p. 308 of volume 1, Urbano Lomelino founded the Franciscan convent in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz, which Jorge Lomelino completed because Urbano had died in 1518, before the building work was finished. (See Convent of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), p. 308 of vol. 1.) Jorge Lomelino died on 9 December 1548 and was laid to rest in the church of the Santa Cruz convent, of which he was patron. In the chantry (capela) of the Quinta das Cruzes (‘estate of the crosses’), which belonged to the Lomelino entailed estate, there is a marble burial vault containing bones said to be those of Urbano Lomelino, the founder of that entailed house (*casa vinculada*).
Family arms: ‘a shield party, with a black somewhat arched profile, the upper part purple and the lower part of the said shield gold’, according to Henriques de Noronha.
The house of the Lomelinos was one of the richest entailed estates in Madeira. Its last representative was Nuno de Freitas Lomelino, who died in Funchal on 12 January 1882.
Lomelino (Pedro José)

He was born on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) on 19 November 1864, the son of Justiniano Lomelino de Serpa and Dona Fortunata Augusta de Castro. He attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and completed the course at the Medical School of this city in 1887. He was the first director of the district school for the training of primary teachers, created in Funchal in 1900 (see Teacher Training School), and in that capacity he published in 1902 the pamphlet *Relatório da Escola Distrital do Funchal*. He is at present (1921) director of the Higher Primary School (see that entry) and municipal medical officer. He has held various public-service appointments, among them that of substitute Civil Governor of this district, to which he was appointed by decree of 22 October 1904, taking office on the 24th of the same month and year. He died on 9 November 1930 while travelling from Lisbon to Madeira.

Longman (William)
Works: *Impressions of Madeira* (with a map), 1875.
Lopes

‘Diogo Lopes, da Estacada (‘stockade’), says the annotator of the *Saudades*, was one of the first settlers of the island of Madeira: he lived in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), at the locality (*sítio*) of Torre (‘tower’), and his *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) comprised a good part of the land lying from the Pico (‘peak’) towards Funchal as far as the Covão (‘large hollow’).’
Lopes de Mendonça (António Pedro)
This well-known and distinguished writer arrived on this island, where he stayed for some time, on 3 November 1861.
Lopes Rocha (Dr Vitúrio)

He was born in this city on 5 September 1752, the son of António Lopes Rocha and brother of the dean Dr João Francisco Lopes Rocha. He studied in the Faculty of Mathematics at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), where he took the degree of doctor, receiving the doctoral hood (*capelo*) on 24 December 1777. He sat the competitive examination for professor and taught there for many years. When already retired on a pension and a member of the Royal Academy of Sciences (*Academia Real das Sciencias*), he applied for the post of prefect (*prefeito*) of the Public Schools of Madeira, an office which we do not know whether he ever held. We have been unable to obtain any further information about this Madeiran.
Lopes Rocha (João Francisco)

He was the son of António Lopes Rocha and Dona Vitória Maria Rocha, and was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé in this city on 18 July 1747. He graduated in canon law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1770 and was ordained priest in the same year. By a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 30 July 1775 he was presented as parish priest of the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), and some years later he was appointed canon of our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), in whose chapter he later held the offices of archdeacon and dean. More than once he served as governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence). Thanks to his learning and great influence, he enjoyed the highest prestige here in Madeira and was held in great esteem by all social classes of this land. He came into conflict with the diocesan prelate Dom José da Costa Torres, above all at the time of the persecution directed against the secret societies of which Lopes Rocha had been a member (see Freemasonry). He then wrote a long letter to the Minister of State José Seabra da Silva, complaining of the persecutions of which he was the victim. Regardless of whatever justice may have been on his side, the letter is a document that reveals in its author a great independence of character, uncommon learning and a remarkable beauty and correctness of style. Written in 1793, this letter was published in London in the July 1820 issue of the *Campeão Portuguez*, some time after its author’s death, and filled about forty pages of that review.
Dr João Francisco Lopes Rocha died in this city on 8 May 1819, at the age of 71.
Lordelo (José da Fonseca e Gouveia, Baron of)

This head of the district was the second here to bear the title of administrator-general (*administrador geral*). The decree appointing him is dated 28 April 1838, and he took office on 14 September of the same year, having arrived in Funchal three days earlier. He was relieved of his post, at his own request, by decree of 14 November 1840.
The Baron of Lordelo was born in 1792 and died on 30 January 1863; he had been granted the barony on 10 October 1838.
Losna (Artemisia argentea)

A native composite with woody stems, whitish leaves that are 1–2-pinnatisect with very narrow segments, and small flower heads forming a panicle. It is cultivated in kitchen gardens and gardens, and grows wild at Ponta do Sol, Calheta and Porto Santo. Although Madeirans use it only as an emmenagogue, it may also be useful as a tonic and vermifuge.
Lotteries

The Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of this city was more than once granted the right to hold a lottery to help meet the costs of maintaining this charitable house. The first of which we have knowledge was granted by the royal notice of 5 April 1803. It was for thirty *contos* (one million réis) *de réis* and was divided into six thousand tickets at five thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) each. The business of this lottery was directed by the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*), by the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) and by three other individuals appointed by the governor and captain-general. The draw was to take place several times a year, but it seems that the wheel never actually turned.

Through the efforts of the president (*provedor*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), the illustrious Madeiran Dr João Francisco de Oliveira, a new concession was made to the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) of Funchal in 1823. The proceeds of the lottery were to be applied to repairs at the Orphan Girls’ Retreat (*Recolhimento das Órfãs*) and to turning this establishment into a school for respectable girls from both the city and the distant towns.

The president’s proposal was submitted to the Government with a favourable report from the Governor, and the Holy House of Mercy easily obtained the royal licences needed to hold the said lottery. It was laid down, however, that its proceeds would be applied first to paying the debts of the Holy House and then to the repairs that the *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) required. We believe that this lottery was short-lived.

By a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 12 September 1857 the Misericórdia obtained yet another concession, from which it benefited for some years. The value of the lottery’s top prize varied greatly: it was 400,000 *réis*, 500,000 *réis*, 600,000 *réis*, 800,000 *réis* and 1,000,000 *réis*.

In May 1865 there were 2,400 tickets and 488 prizes, the three largest being of 800, 200 and 100 thousand *réis*; and in January 1868 the lottery consisted of 1800 tickets, 600 of which won prizes, with one prize of 400, another of 100 and a third of 50 thousand *réis*. Each ticket cost 1000 *réis* and the smallest prizes were of 1200 *réis*.

In the early 19th century the government assisted those rebuilding the Teatro Grande (‘great theatre’) by granting them an annual lottery, whose top prize was 3 *contos de réis*. The minutes of the meeting of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) of 12 January 1814 refer to ‘a lottery held in this city for the benefit of the lepers’, but we have been unable to gather any further information about this lottery. It seems to have been promoted by the Council in order to raise funds to improve the conditions of those sufferers.
Loucas (Campo das)

This name, or that of Campo de Challons (‘Challons square’), was formerly given to a large open ground lying to the east of the old Praça Académica (‘academic’) and now forming part of the Campo do Almirante Reis.
The troops quartered in Funchal frequently held their military exercises there.
Lounsbury (Prof. C. P.)

A naturalist who, in the gardens of the ‘Bela Vista’ hotel in Madeira, came across by chance a tiny insect about half a millimetre long, which was named *Prospatella Lounsburyi* or *Aspidiotiphagus Lounsburyi*. It destroys *Chrysomphalus dictyospermi*, a scale insect that lives on orange trees, palms, banana plants, incense trees, etc.

The little insect to which we refer was probably imported from America, where, however, it has not been found. It apparently reproduces by parthenogenesis and feeds on the larvae of *Chrysomphalus*, a scale insect that does considerable harm to our orange trees and other useful species.

In vol. XI of *Redia* (1916), p. 305, Professors Berlese and Paoli described *Prospaltella*, in a paper entitled *Un endofago esotico efficace contra il Chrysomphalus dictyospermi, Morg.* See Limpets and Paoli.
Loup (Mademoiselle)

In February 1922 the publishers of the *Comercio da Madeira* brought out, under the pseudonym Mademoiselle Loup, an 80-page pamphlet entitled *Bosquejos*, written, as was then stated, by a Madeiran woman writer. It consists of various chronicles and impressions previously published in the same newspaper.
Loureiro (Adolfo)

This distinguished engineer came to Madeira in 1898, sent by the central government to study how the water regime created for the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) by the decree of 1 December 1892 might be adapted to this archipelago. He spent several months on the island and presented the results of his work to the Government in a lengthy report. In Lisbon, at the Association of Civil Engineers (*Associação dos Engenheiros Civis*), he gave an interesting lecture on the Madeiran archipelago, which is published under the title *Breves Noticias sobre os archipelagos da Madeira, dos Açores, de Cabo Verde e das Canárias*. In his vast work entitled *Os Portos Maritimos de Portugal*, he devotes the 5th volume to the ports of Madeira. The 5th volume of the atlases that complete the work contains 16 plates, all relating to this archipelago.
The engineer Adolfo Loureiro died in Lisbon on 23 November 1911.
Laurel (Laurus canariensis)

A tree of the Lauraceae family, 6 to 20 metres tall, with persistent aromatic leaves, umbels gathered in axillary clusters, usually shorter than the petioles, and ovoid berries that are black, rarely yellow. It yields a pale timber, inferior to that of the other Madeiran Lauraceae, and its leaves are used as a seasoning in cooking.

An oil was formerly extracted from the berries and used to light the poor houses of the countryside. It was prepared by boiling the berries and then pressing them in a cloth bag in small wooden presses. Being lighter than the rest of the liquid, the oil floated on top and was easily drawn off from the vessel in which the operation was carried out.

The laurel is found in the first, second and third zones of Madeira, but in the last it is a small tree. It once grew wild on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it died out, but it is now cultivated on that island.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of 14 September 1651 laid down that only the Count of Vimioso, donatary (*donatário*) of Machico, might sell and ‘ship out of the island laurel berries and buy them from private persons. See Lauraceae and Madre de Deus (‘Mother of God’).
Lourenço (João)
He came of a noble lineage and was a companion of João Gonçalves Zarco in the discovery and settlement of this island. See Afonso (João).
Cherry laurel (Prunus Laurocerasus)

A small tree or shrub of the Rosaceae family, cultivated at Camacha, Monte, Choupana, etc. It is native to Persia and is recognised by its large, obovate-elliptic, serrated leaves, which smell of bitter almonds when crushed between the fingers. The essential oil and distilled water of cherry laurel contain prussic acid. In Madeira the cherry laurel is also known as *louro inglês*.
Laurustinus (Viburnum Tinus)

A shrub or small tree cultivated in the *quintas* and gardens of Madeira. It is native to the Iberian Peninsula and has leathery, usually ovate-elliptic leaves and white flowers arranged in corymbiform cymes.
Louros
Inhabited locality in the parish of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’)

This locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) once had a small chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Incarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation), built in 1656 by Diogo Bernardes Branco. There is an agricultural station (*posto agrário*), or experimental agricultural ground, known as the Viveiro dos Louros (‘laurel nursery’), which is maintained by the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*).
Lowe (Revd Richard Thomas)

English naturalist, born on 4 December 1802. He came to Madeira in 1826 and stayed until 1852, later returning to the island in 1855, 1860, 1863, 1865, 1867 and 1871. Wishing to visit Madeira once more, he sailed in the steamer *Liberia*, which left the landing place (*porto*) of Liverpool bound for the island on 11 April 1874. The ship, however, was wrecked in the Bay of Biscay on the second or third day of the voyage, and there Lowe met his death, together with his wife Catarina Maria, whom he had married in 1828.

During his long residence in Madeira, Lowe gathered extremely important material for the study of the fauna and flora of the archipelago. The botanical material, which, fortunately for science, had remained in England, was divided after his death between the British Museum and Kew Gardens. Duplicates of many plants from Madeira and the Canary Islands collected by Lowe are held in the Imperial Garden of Petrograd, in Webb’s herbarium in Florence, and in that of De Candolle.

In 1858 Lowe visited the Canary Islands, returning there in 1861, and in 1864 and 1866 he visited the Cape Verde islands. From 1834 to 1848 he served as chaplain (*capelão*) of the British church in Rua dos Aranhas in Funchal.

He was a Master of Arts of the University of Cambridge and a corresponding member of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences and of the Zoological Society of London. After leaving for England in 1852, he was for some time chaplain at Lea, in the countship (*condado*) of Lincoln.

In the British cemetery in Rua do Dr. Vieira there is a modest gravestone surmounted by a cross, bearing an inscription that commemorates some events in the life of Richard Thomas Lowe, the foreigner who rendered the greatest scientific services to Madeira.

Among R. T. Lowe’s many works, we shall mention the following: *A Synopsis of the Fishes of Madeira* (*Trans. of the Zool. Soc.*, II, 3, 1837); *Supplement to a Synopsis of the Fishes of Madeira* (*Idem*, III, I, 1839); *A History of the Fishes of Madeira* (London, 1843–1860, I vol.); *Primitiae Faunae et Florae Maderae et Portus Sancti* (*Trans. Cambridge Phil. Soc.* IV, 1, 1830); *Novitiae Florae Maderensis* (*Idem*, VI, 3, 1838); *A Manual Flora of Madeira and the Adjacent Islands* (London, 1868, vols I and II, part I); *Florulae Salvagicae Tentamen* (London, 1869, I sheet); *Catalogus Molluscorum Pneumatoram Insularum Maderensium* (*Proceed. Zool. Soc. of London*, 1854); and *Protest against the ministration in Madeira of the rev. T. K. Brown...*, with an appendix (Funchal, 1848).

In connection with the dispute between Lowe and Brown over the real or alleged violation of the laws and constitutions of the English Church in Madeira, the *English Review* of June 1848 published an article favourable to the former.
Lucta (A)

Two newspapers have appeared under this title. The first came out on 11 February 1888 and ceased publication on 1 July 1894, with issue no. 319. The second began on 5 January 1896 and ran to 26 issues, the last of which appeared on 28 June of the same year.
Lugar de Baixo

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), lying between the town (*vila*) and the parish of Tábua. It is one of the many *fajãs* formed along the coast by the collapse of the land that towered above them. ‘Since 1804 the *Logar de Baixo*,’ says the annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘has been much larger than before, because in that year a great part of the land of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) that overlooks it, split open by the storms of the preceding years, fell towards the sea and there formed a broad and productive plain. The shock of the fall was such that the sea rose above its level along the whole adjacent coast, and the tremor was felt both on land and at sea at a distance of more than ten kilometres: the sea came far inland into the town of Ponta do Sol.’ Lugar de Baixo (‘lower place’) formed part of the great estate of Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry). However, when, on the death of João Esmeraldo, the property was divided anew between his two sons and his widow, Águeda de Abreu, she reserved the Lugar de Baixo property for herself as an integral part of her dowry. It is possible that on her death it reverted to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Santo Espírito (‘Holy Spirit’); it is certain, at any rate, that it was incorporated into it at a date unknown to us. It was sold at public auction at about the same time as the Lombada, being bought by the English merchants A. Criorgi & C.ª. There stands the chapel of St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*), with a fine house attached, which we shall discuss elsewhere in this work.
Lugar de Baixo (cove and landing place)

At the locality (*sítio*) of this name there is a small cove bordering a beach, which serves it as a landing place; landing there is sometimes preferable to landing at the Cais da Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) or the Cais da Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). It was at this landing place that Prince Luís, later King of Portugal, came ashore on 25 October 1858, because the state of the sea did not allow him to land at the quay of the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol.
Luís (Infante Dom)

Infante Dom Luís, later King of Portugal, first visited Madeira in 1858. He was the first member of the Portuguese royal family to visit the island. Commanding the corvette *Bartolomeu Dias*, he reached our harbour on 8 October of that year, accompanied by his chamberlain, the Count of Linhares. The gunboat *Sagres* sailed in company. He landed at the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’) the following day, and the reception was of the greatest splendour and grandeur. During the twenty days that Dom Luís spent in Madeira, besides the other festivities and public demonstrations of esteem and affection held in his honour, splendid private festivities took place, whose memory lived on in local tradition for many years because of their brilliance and extraordinary pomp. Outstanding among them were the festivity at Palheiro Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s barn’) and the dinner and ball at the Palácio de São Pedro (‘St Peter’), given by the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), which greatly impressed the prince; the ball at the Funchal Club (*Club Funchalense*), given by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*); and the reception at the house of the holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Cruzes, Nuno de Freitas Lomelino. Dom Luís made lengthy visits to the Asylum for the Destitute (*Asilo de Mendicidade*), the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*), the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal (*Santa Isabel*), the military hospital, the lyceum (state secondary school) and several public offices.
