On 25 October the prince and his retinue went to the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). After landing he went straight on to the beautiful spot of Rabaçal, returning in the afternoon to the same town, where he spent the night.

On the eve of his departure, Infante Dom Luís held a reception at the Palácio de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’) and took his leave there, thanking the civil governor for the address he delivered on that occasion and the inhabitants of the island for the extraordinary proofs of esteem and affection he had received from them. He left for Lisbon on 27 October 1858.

Dom Luís returned to Madeira in 1861, coming on behalf of Pedro V to visit Empress Elisabeth of Austria and to escort her when she left the island. He arrived in Funchal on 17 April of that year and, aboard the corvette *Bartolomeu Dias*, accompanied the vessel carrying the Empress as far as Gibraltar.
Luís Miranda (road)

From 19 January 1896 until 27 October 1910 this was the name of the road between the parish church of Santo António (‘St Anthony’) and the Ribeira (‘stream’). Commander Luís de Bettencourt Miranda was born in Funchal on 16 December 1856 and died there on 17 July 1921. For more than 30 years he served first as an official and then as secretary of the Council, posts in which he rendered excellent service to the municipality.
Luisier (Father Alphonse)

A native of Switzerland, he belongs to the Society of Jesus and was for some years a teacher at the now defunct Colégio de Campolide in Lisbon. In 1907 he received a collection of Madeiran mosses assembled by one of the authors of this *Elucidário*. He was later sent the excellent bryological collection that had belonged to James Yate Johnson and is today the property of the Seminary Museum (*Museu do Seminário*). These were the main materials for his studies of Madeiran bryology, on which he has published the following works, all of great value: *Note sur quelques mousses nouvelles pour la flore de Madère* (*Bullet. Soc. Port. Sc. Nat*, 1, 2, 1907), *Deuxième note sur les mousses de Madère* (Ibid., II, I, 1908), *Contribution à l'Etude des Muscinées de Madère* (*Broteria*, vols VIII and IX, 1909 and 1910) and *Les Mousses de Madère* (Ibid., vol. XV, 1917 to 1922).

Professor A. Luisier does not study mosses alone; he has also devoted himself to the study of flowering plants, and volume XIX of the *Boletim da Sociedade Broteriana* contains a paper of his on the plants of the Setúbal region.

Deprived of his bryological collections at the time of the 1910 revolution, he later managed to recover part of them, which enabled him to continue his most valuable studies of the mosses of the Madeira archipelago.
Squid (Luligo vulgaris)

A cephalopod mollusc caught close to the coast, in trawl nets and with the *torneira*, a device introduced into the archipelago about 15 years ago. The name *lula* is also given to other cephalopods, one of which is luminous.
Lund (Dr G.)

An English physician who practised in Funchal and made meteorological observations here in 1855 and 1856. Works: *The climate of the Island of Madeira*, London, 1854. In 1853 he wrote another work under the same title, and he also wrote about Madeira in the *Association Medical Journal* of September 1853.
Hop (Humulus lupulus)

A climbing plant of the family Urticaceae, grown in São Roque, Santana, etc. Its leaves resemble those of the vine, and its flower heads, which have a very pronounced bitter taste, are used in brewing beer.
Luz
This is a fairly old family surname in Madeira. In 1513 there was a Pedro da Luz who was clerk (*escrivão*) of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) of Funchal.
Luz (A)
Seventy-six issues of this newspaper were published, from 21 May 1881 to 4 November 1882.
Another newspaper with the same title appeared on 6 February 1918 and is still published (1921).
Luz da Madrugada (A)
Seven issues appeared, the first on 27 April 1902 and the last on 7 September of the same year.
Lyell (Charles)

A distinguished English geologist, born at Kinnordy in 1797 and died in London in 1875. He spent two months of the winter of 1853–1854 in Madeira, carrying out various geological explorations here, almost always accompanied by the German geologist Hartung.

Lyell deals with the geology of Madeira in chapter XLI of his *Principles of Geology* (1868) and in chapter XXIX of the *Manual of Elementary Geology* (1855). On page 325 of the *Proceedings of the Geological Society* for March 1854 there is an article entitled *On the Geology of some parts of Madeira*, which summarises the principal observations made on this island by the learned English geologist.
Eça (João Fogaça de). Under Castilian rule João Fogaça de Eça was governor-general of Madeira; his appointment dates from 14 August 1603.
Mac Euen (Carlos)

An American, a native of Philadelphia, who made meteorological observations at the *quinta* (country estate) Hollway from December 1848 to May 1849. These observations are included in Dr Mason’s work on the climate of Madeira, published in 1850.
Maçacota (Chenolea lanata)
A whitish, woolly subshrub whose upper leaves are usually gathered in clusters. It is found on Ponta de São Lourenço, on Porto Santo and on Selvagem Pequena.
Maçarico

Madeirans know *Numenius phaeopus* by this name and *N. arquatus* by that of *maçarico real*. These species, which belong to the family Charadriidae and the subfamily Totaninae, appear on the sea cliffs of Madeira.
Maçaroco (Echium nervosum)

A shrub of the family Boraginaceae, common near the shore on the south coast of Madeira. It can reach 2 metres in height and has blue flowers arranged in ovoid, generally dense panicles. It yields a black wood that was formerly used for inlaid work (*embutidos*). *Echium candicans* is a shrub of 5 to 15 decimetres, easily distinguished from *E. nervosum* by its elongated, more or less cylindrical panicles.
Macaulay (Dr James)

A distinguished English scientist who spent part of 1839 and 1840 in Madeira. He wrote a valuable work on this island entitled *Notes on the Physical Geography, Geology and Climate of the Island of Madeira*, published in the *Edinburgh New Philosophical Journal* of October 1840, pages 1 to 39. James Macaulay was the editor of *The Stranger*, a newspaper written in English and published in Funchal, of which only the first issue appeared, in January 1840.
Macedo
This surname, says Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, comes from Martim Gonçalves de Macedo, an illustrious defender of John I at the battle of Aljubarrota.
Macedo (Dom Álvaro da Costa de Sousa)

Dom Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo was the last governor and captain-general of this archipelago, and the last representative that the absolutist government had here in Madeira. He took up office on 1 April 1830 and left Madeira on 13 July 1834.

Not only did Dom Álvaro de Macedo offer not the slightest resistance to the proclamation of constitutional government on this island, but he fully accepted the new order of things. Had he wished, he could even have remained governor of Madeira, following the invitation made to him directly by the monarch himself, Pedro IV.

Although he remained at the head of the government of this province during the turbulent period of our civil wars, when hatreds and deep dissensions divided the Madeiran family into two irreconcilable factions, he knew how to conduct himself so as not to inflame these party divisions. As far as circumstances allowed, he maintained an attitude of remarkable impartiality, which won him the esteem and regard of the people of this island.

Despite the spirit of rectitude and justice that moved him and the conciliatory tendencies that guided the acts of his administration, there came a moment when he allowed himself to be swept along by the despotic demands of party politics. Yielding to the entreaties of his fellow partisans and bad advisers, he ordered the Teatro Grande do Funchal (‘great theatre of Funchal’) to be demolished down to its foundations. It was the second-largest theatre in the country and had been built some sixty years earlier.

This theatre, of which we shall speak at greater length, stood in the square that the people still call the Largo da Fortaleza today. Its capacity and proportions exceeded what a small provincial place such as Funchal required, and as a whole it had an air of grandeur and majesty that made a most pleasing impression on visitors. On some performance nights, supporters of constitutional ideas took advantage of the large gathering of spectators to give vent to their liberal sentiments and to spread the principles they professed. This propaganda spread from the stage to the stalls, even though it constituted a sacrilege (*desacato*) against the institutions.

That was the true cause of the demolition. Simply closing the theatre would have saved it from complete destruction. Dom Álvaro de Macedo, however, claimed that the building stood next to a fortress, hindering the defence of the city, and that it also disfigured the site and the entrance to the governors’ palace. He therefore took the drastic step of having it demolished, leaving not one stone upon another.

Dom Álvaro de Macedo had been granted the title of Count of Madeira. He died in France a few years after leaving this island. He was the uncle of Dom Bernardo da Costa de Sousa Macedo, who twice served as civil governor (*governador civil*) of this district (*distrito*).
Macedo (Dom Bernardo da Costa de Sousa)
He was appointed Civil Governor of Madeira by decree of 21 February 1901 and took office on 9 May of the same year.
By decree of 6 June 1906 he was appointed Civil Governor of the district for the second time, and he took up the post on the 23rd of the same month.
Macedo (Father Dr João Crisóstomo Espínola de)

We have scant information for the biography of this Madeiran. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in theology and served as acting chaplain of the church of São Tiago Menor (St James the Less), and later as vicar in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). In 1811 he was imprisoned on the orders of the cathedral chapter of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), following a complaint brought against him by the ordinary judge (*juiz ordinário*, locally elected lay judge) of the same town. He edited the second newspaper to be published here in Madeira, the *Pregador Imparcial da Verdade, da Justiça e da Lei*, which first appeared in February 1823. Although his political ideas differed from those of José Agostinho de Macedo, he was nonetheless a distinguished disciple of his in the violence of his language and the unruliness of his phrasing, methods he knew how to imitate in the writings he left us. Prominent among these is a pamphlet printed in London in 1825, which is extremely rare and bears the following extravagant title: *O Tramista Descoberto! Converça do cónego Francisco B-r-o, da cidade do Funchal, com o seu moço Simão Caraça, que foi estudante e servio de economo, por alguns anos, em hum beneficio da Igreja da Ponta do Sol da ilha da Madeira, ouvida pelo padre João Vicente do O-v-a no pateo do mesmo cónego*. It is a booklet of 98 pages, riddled with typographical errors, which deals mainly with the governor of Madeira, Sebastião Xavier Botelho. It also contains unflattering references to the author himself, who hides behind anonymity and in this way placed himself further beyond the suspicions that might fall upon him.

He embraced the ideas proclaimed by the Porto revolution and was elected substitute deputy for this island in 1822. When absolutism was restored, however, he sent his deputy’s credentials to the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), ‘as he did not wish to keep in his possession any longer a document that he considered unseemly’.

Because of the intemperate language of his writings, and for other reasons unknown to us, he drew upon himself the hostility of powerful figures in Funchal. This culminated in a sensational incident on 9 February 1822, which caused the greatest scandal here in Madeira and even had wide repercussions in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). Some officers, cadets and sergeants of the island’s artillery battalion went to the residence of Dr Espínola de Macedo, in the old Rua da Conceição (‘Conception’), dragged him violently from it and took him to the pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction). There, in broad daylight and in view of many people, says a contemporary account, ‘they flogged him, and he was beaten and mocked’. The perpetrators of the assault were arrested and tried, and were sentenced to severe terms of imprisonment and penal exile (degredo). They were saved, however, by the advent of absolutist government, which restored them to liberty.

The minutes of the session of the Municipal Council of Funchal of 8 February 1822 record that Dr Macedo, vicar of Santa Cruz, was ‘a public insulter in his manuscripts and printed works, in which he was wont to attack honourable citizens, lawful and useful corporations and all the constituted authorities’. Nevertheless, as a lawyer in the island’s courts he left a reputation as a notable orator and polemicist, and as a journalist he was among the best of his time.

In 1823 Dr Macedo was convicted of political crimes and deported from the Kingdom, leaving Funchal for Gibraltar in May of that year aboard the English brig *Fanny*. He died in 1828, at an advanced age.
Chamomile (Anthemis nobilis)

A composite plant widely grown at Camacha and elsewhere in Madeira. An infusion of its flower heads is stimulant and tonic, and can also be used externally to treat certain inflammations of the eyes. It is not the typical form but the golden variety that occurs in Madeira. The chamomile (*macela*) used at Madalena (‘Magdalene’) and Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) is *Achillea Ageratum*, a plant that likewise belongs to the family of the Compositae.
Yarrow (Achillea Millefolium)

A composite plant, both cultivated and growing semi-wild in Madeira. It is also known as *feiteirinha*, and has properties identical to those of chamomile (*macela*), although it is less used by the people.
Maceta de Santa Cruz
It was published in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and ran to only two issues, on 10 November and 24 December 1878.
Machado

Frutuoso refers to the peak of Lopo Machado, above the chapel of Our Lady of the Snows (*Nossa Senhora das Neves*). Dr Azevedo, however, says that the surname Machado derives from João Machado de Miranda, a native of Guimarães. He came to Madeira at the call of his uncle Bartolomeu Machado, who had no heirs by his wife, Dona Francisca Velosa, and the couple together founded an entail (*morgado*) from their property in favour of the said nephew’s descendants.
Machado (Dr Vicente Cândido)

He was born in Funchal on 3 October 1855 and died in the same city on 23 November 1911. He graduated from the Faculty of Medicine in Paris in 1880. On returning to Madeira, on 2 October of the same year he performed, with complete success, a delicate surgical operation on the late prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, which at once earned him great renown as a distinguished physician and surgeon. He defended and published the thesis *E'ssai sur les oreillons sous-maxillaires*, and in 1884, in a controversy with the Count of Canavial, he published the pamphlet *Resposta ao folheto do dr. João da Camara Leme Homem de Vasconcellos. . .*
Machico (captaincy)

Acting on instructions received from Prince Henry the Navigator, as Dr Gaspar Frutuoso reports, the discoverers João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira divided up the lands that were to form the area of their jurisdictions at the very beginning of colonisation, as the starting point for the orderly administration of the domains entrusted to them. In the articles Captaincies (vol. 1, p. 244 ff.) and Donataries (vol., p. 373 ff.) we have already referred to the division of the island of Madeira into two captaincies, with their seats at Funchal and Machico, and to the way in which their boundaries were drawn, the first falling to Gonçalves Zarco and the second to Tristão Vaz Teixeira. On pp. 456 and 457 of the *Saudades* is transcribed the charter of the grant of the captaincy of Machico made by Prince Henry to Tristão Vaz Teixeira, dated 8 May 1440. It is the oldest of the grants of the three captaincies into which the archipelago was divided, and all these grants must be understood as merely the solemn and authentic confirmation of concessions made earlier.

The captaincy of Machico extended from Ponta da Oliveira (‘olive-tree point’) to Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’) and from there to Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’), taking in a considerable part of the south coast and the whole of the north coast of the island. Its area corresponded to the present municipalities of Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Santana, Machico and almost all of Santa Cruz, except for part of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’).

The captaincy of Machico was much larger in area and extent than that of Funchal, but the whole north coast, which formed part of it, was plainly inferior in its situation, climate, nature of the soil, lack of beaches and landing places, difficulty of communications, etc. As will be seen in the article Town and Municipality of Machico, the seat of this captaincy grew and developed rapidly, and it has even been claimed that it rivalled that of Funchal and even surpassed it in importance and prosperity. On this subject it is worth reading the first pages of the book *A Filha de Tristão das Damas* and the notes on pp. 254 and 255 of the same novel. This remarkable early growth, however, did not last long. The special conditions of the seat of the captaincy of Funchal – its admirable situation, the ample room for the growth of a populous settlement, the spaciousness of its harbour, the fertility of the soil, the picturesqueness of the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), the mildness of the climate, etc. – were bound to assert themselves forcefully and would soon overshadow the other places that were being established, even under the best auspices of rapid progress and development. The captaincy of Machico stagnated and later declined in prosperity, owing also to the importance soon gained by the settlement of Santa Cruz. Santa Cruz was made a town (*vila*) at the beginning of the 16th century and became a great industrial and commercial centre for the making and export of sugar, its customs house coming to handle far more trade than that of its neighbour and rival.

This is the moment to say that the administration of the donataries (*donatário*) of this captaincy, including the first, always left much to be desired. Let us hear Dr Álvaro de Azevedo in the following passages which, though somewhat long, give us a reliable idea of what that administration was: ‘The donatary captaincy (*donataria*) of Machico passed by succession from Tristão Vaz to his eldest son Tristão Vaz das Damas, so nicknamed “because (says Frutuoso) he was a great courtier, a fine talker, and composed many verses for the ladies”; his are the three songs collected in the ‘General Songbook’ (*Cancioneiro Geral*) of Resende, there attributed to “Tristão Teixeira, Captain of Machico”. He was succeeded by his son, also called Tristão Teixeira, and on his death the donatary captaincy was inherited by his son Diogo Teixeira, the fourth and last donatary descended from Tristão Vaz. The governments of these four captains were deplorable and in constant conflict with the royal power, which was severe with them. Tristão Vaz, for his despotism, especially towards Tristão Barradas, “whom he kept locked up with a shackle, grinding flour in a mill” (*Saudades*, p. 116), was summoned by the king to Lisbon and, by sentence, banished to the island of Príncipe, where he remained for some years, until, certainly in the reign of Afonso V and through the intercession of Prince Henry the Navigator, he was restored to the captaincy; he died around 1470. Tristão Teixeira das Damas, “because of charges brought against him”, was likewise summoned by the king to Lisbon, where he spent some years, with much toil and expense, seeking his acquittal and “finally clearing his honour”; but after him the king sent Dr Álvaro Fernandes and, later, Fernão de Perada as *corregedores* (royal district magistrate), with a special judicial commission (alçada) over the whole island of Madeira. Tristão Teixeira, succeeding Tristão das Damas, apparently did not take the title of captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) but simply that of governor, the capacity in which he had superintended the captaincy in his father’s absence; this reduced him, nominally at least, from holder of a right of his own to a mere royal delegate. Moreover, while he lived, the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) Rui Pires was on the island as *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) and *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) in the captaincy of Funchal, and after him Dr Diogo Taveira as *corregedor* in both captaincies; so watched, Tristão Teixeira behaved prudently. His son and successor Diogo Teixeira, however, “was a man of defective judgement… and almost feeble-minded;…. he governed so badly” that “King Manuel I and King John III… sought to take the captaincy from him, and over this he brought a lawsuit… until the year 1536”. During the suit Dr Francisco Diniz served as *corregedor* in the captaincy for nine years and, after him, the licentiate Antão Gonçalves for almost three years. Diogo Teixeira won the case, and so held the captaincy until 1538; but in the end John III took it and its revenues from him, ordering him to be placed in the custody of João Simão de Sousa, who “held him in his power until the year 1540”, in which year the captive died without a male heir or any other heir, so that “the house and inheritance passed to the Crown” (*Saudades*, pp. 117–119). Thus ended the line of Tristão Vaz. “Still in the year 1541 John III made a royal grant of this captaincy to António da Silveira, who had been captain of Diu, for services he had rendered him”; with royal licence he sold it to the Count of Vimioso, Dom Afonso de Portugal; on the latter’s death his son Dom Francisco succeeded to it, and on the death of the last it reverted to the Crown. None of these, however, governed it in person, but only through *ouvidores*, and there were always superintending *corregedores*, with whom these *ouvidores* had more or less serious conflicts.’

In the article Donataries (vol. 16, p. 373 ff.) we have already given the complete list of the captains-donatary of Machico up to the year 1775; for most of them the donatary captaincy was a merely honorary title.

The creation of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz in 1515 and that of São Vicente in 1744, with their charters and exemptions, did not strictly reduce the area of the captaincy of Machico, but they considerably restricted the jurisdiction of its donataries or their *ouvidores*.

This captaincy had *ouvidores*, who were appointed by the captain-donatary. The first to hold the office was Manuel Homem da Câmara, appointed on 4 June 1641. The captaincy had two ordinary judges, whose sentences could be appealed to the *ouvidor*. There was also a judge of orphans (*juiz dos órfãos*); the office was created on 25 September 1625 and Cristóvão Moniz Barreto was appointed to it.

According to Frutuoso, in 1590 – that is, almost three and a half centuries ago – the captaincy of Machico yielded its donatary about nine hundred thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year.
Machico (Count of)

Charles Stuart, England’s envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary in Lisbon and a member of the government of the Kingdom of Portugal during the Peninsular War, was granted the title of Count of Machico by decree of 22 November 1825 and that of Marquis of Angra by decree of 1 May of the following year. He had descendants, but we are not aware that the title of Count of Machico was carried on by them. He died in 1845.
Machico (cove, harbour and quay)

Apart from the bays of Funchal, Porto Santo and Abra, the cove of Machico is the widest and most picturesque in the archipelago. It is fringed by a fine stretch of beach and overlooked by two roads, and it opens directly onto a most beautiful valley that extends for several kilometres along the green banks of the stream. The centre of the town (*vila*) is linked to the landing quay by a handsome tree-lined road, which makes the most pleasant of walks on calm summer evenings. Many years ago a landing place was built near the southern end of the cove, beside the chapel of St Roch (*São Roque*), but it was later entirely abandoned. On the other side of the bay a quay was planned, making use of a reef (restinga) there, together with a road connecting it to the interior of the town; these works were carried out between 1870 and 1873. As that landing place was considered inadequate, a new and larger quay was built in 1905, and it was altered and improved in 1907. At the end of 1931 three harbour lights were placed at the three points marking the entrance to this bay, and they are giving excellent service to the many fishing boats that make for this cove at night. The harbour is fairly large but shallow, so vessels of large tonnage cannot enter it. Above the site of the quay stood an old fort, known as the Desembarcadouro (‘landing place’) fort or the Fort of São João Baptista (St John the Baptist), now dismantled. On its esplanade a hospital was improvised in 1910, during the cholera epidemic that ravaged Madeira at that time.
See Desembarcadouro.
Machico (health resort)

Besides the special conditions that make it a favourite place to spend the summer season, this locality should also be regarded as an excellent health resort. The mildness of a cool, temperate climate, the fine bathing beach and the much-praised São Roque waters (águas de São Roque), with their well-known therapeutic properties, commend it as the most valuable health resort in the archipelago after Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Further attractions are the natural beauty of the lovely valley in which the picturesque town (*vila*) lies; the ease of making short excursions to the charming settlement of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and the delightful parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’); boat trips to Caniçal, Prainha and Ponta de São Lourenço; a comfortable hotel open all year; houses to let; and rapid, frequent communications with the city of Funchal, etc. etc.
Machico (parish)

The oldest and most glorious traditions concerning the discovery of this island and its first settlement are inseparably bound up with the name of the place that later became the parish (*freguesia*), the town (*vila*) and the seat of the captaincy of Machico. The history of Madeira begins at the very moment when the caravels commanded by João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira dropped anchor in the picturesque and enchanting bay of this locality. At this moment the history of Machico also begins. As they rounded the promontory of São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’), which had been given that name shortly before, there opened before the enraptured eyes of the navigators a small but lovely cove, bounded by a beach of rounded pebbles, which met a smiling valley hemmed in between steep and towering mountains. Everything invited them to make their first landing. It seems that the discoverers put in here on a warm, calm July afternoon, when the sun was already sinking fast towards the horizon. Despite the eagerness that overwhelmed those spirits, hungry for adventure and the unknown, the captains did not allow anyone to set foot that day on the virgin soil of this remote and unknown island. The landing took place the following day (see Discovery of the archipelago), and the historian of the islands describes it in these terms:

‘As soon as day broke on the morrow, the captain sent a ship’s boat ashore, placing it in the charge of Rui Pais, that he might go and see the lie and situation of the land and bring him word of what he found. He went, but could not land on the beach, because of the trees that came down to the sea and the timber that they and the stream had gathered there. From there he went towards the east to land on the cliff, where there are rocks and shallows on which one can easily land, however rough the sea may be, for it is sheltered by the cliff; and this place is called today the Desembarcadouro [landing place], where Machim’s people also landed. Once ashore, they found the land very pleasing and delightful with great woods, and in places meadows, all of which could also be seen from the ships. Rui Pais went with his companions between the woods and the sea, and, finding cut wood and traces of people, they followed them and came upon the trunk of the great tree where Machim had been, and they found the table and the crucifix that the Englishmen had left, and the graves with crosses at their heads; at which they were astonished, although they had heard of all this from their pilot’.

If we were to believe the romantic legend of Robert Machin and Ana de Arfet, we would have to accept that the discoverers, on landing on the beaches of Machico, found the graves of the two ill-fated lovers, and on them the epitaph that told of their unhappy adventure and asked that a chapel dedicated to Christ be built there. What does seem established, however, is that on the very day the captains of the small fleet made their first landing, they had a makeshift altar set up, and there one of the Franciscan friars whom Gonçalves Zarco had brought with him celebrated the sacrifice of the Mass. It was an ardent expression of faith, offering Providence without delay the humblest thanks for the fortunate and momentous discovery they had just made. It is said that the discoverers vowed to build a church on that spot, and this is the true origin of the foundation of the chapel of Christ (*Cristo*), or of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*) (see Capela de Cristo, p. 332 of vol. I).

What is the true origin of this locality’s name? Nothing definite is known on the matter, although several men of great intellectual stature, such as Pinheiro Chagas, Camilo Castelo Branco, Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo and J. I. de Brito Rebêlo, have dealt with the subject at length. When we treat the legend of Machim, we shall try to summarise the opinions of those who have discussed this matter with the most recognised authority, presenting a brief outline of the various hypotheses and conjectures to which the explanation of the fact has given rise.

No one doubts that Machico was one of the first places to be settled, and that a large population centre formed there at once and grew rapidly. Detailed information on its earliest colonisation and first settlers is scarce, however, and even the exact year in which the parish (*paróquia*) was created is unknown. All that is known is that the discoverer Tristão Vaz chose this place as the seat of his captaincy and settled there in the very first days after the discovery, devoting himself zealously to peopling and cultivating his lands. Gaspar Frutuoso says that some claim the first donatary (*donatário*) settled in Machico with his wife and children in May 1425. Much land was granted in *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) to colonists and noblemen from mainland Portugal, and it soon became an important settlement that rivalled Funchal and even surpassed it, according to some old documents.

Dr Álvaro de Azevedo gives 1430 as the year in which the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and Calheta (‘small cove’) were created, and 1440 for those of Caniço (‘reed’) and Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), while fixing 1450 for Machico. This is rather surprising, considering that Machico was one of the first places settled and one of those that grew and prospered most quickly; it was, moreover, the seat of a captaincy and a very important centre of the early colonisation. We are inclined to believe that the parish of Machico was created around the middle of the 15th century, whereas the others were at first merely constituted as chaplaincies with cure of souls or autonomous curacies (*curatos*) in the years indicated. Machico must have had a more or less regular religious service from the building of the chapel that Tristão Vaz erected there at the very start of settlement and land clearance. It was in 1450 that Dom Friar Pedro Vaz, prior (title of the parish priest) of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), sent Friar João Garcia to Madeira as the first vicar of the recently created parish of Machico. A similar case occurred in Funchal with Friar Nuno Cão, also sent by the Order of Christ to serve as parish priest at the seat of the captaincy and to superintend religious services throughout the island. In the article Parishes we expressed the opinion that the first parish created in Madeira had its seat in Funchal; we now add that the foundation of the parish of Machico was probably almost contemporary with it, just as the two towns were created at the same time.

The parish, as has been said, was created around 1450 and its parochial jurisdiction extended over the whole area of the captaincy. Chaplaincies with cure of souls, dependent on the mother church (*igreja matriz*), were later established in Santa Cruz, Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Ponta Delgada, São Jorge, Santana, Faial and Porto da Cruz. That of Santa Cruz was soon made an independent parish, and the other chaplaincies gradually became autonomous parishes. The rapid growth of the population at the seat of the captaincy led to the creation of new ecclesiastical posts: a collegiate church with six beneficed clerics was established before 1572, and a curacy by royal decree (*alvará*) of 15 November 1576.

The parish church also had the posts of preacher, created by royal decree of 4 August 1590, organist, created by royal decree of 27 November 1594, and treasurer, the date of whose creation we do not know.

The *Indice Geral do Registo da Antiga Provedoria* mentions the following instruments concerning the ecclesiastical posts of this parish: a royal decree of 11 February 1560, fixing the stipend (*côngrua*) of the vicar at 12,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year in cash, 40 *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine; a royal decree of 18 June 1572, raising the whole of that stipend to 34,000 *réis*; a royal decree of 8 May 1591, adding a further 7,700 to that sum; a royal decree of 27 October 1592, changing this salary to 24,000 *réis* in cash, two *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and two *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine; a royal decree of 18 June 1572, ordering that each beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) should have an annual stipend of 12,000 *réis*; a royal decree of 8 May 1591, adding one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine to that salary; and a royal decree of 5 November 1741, commuting this stipend into 6,000 *réis* in cash, two *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine. The curate was assigned an annual stipend of 18,000 *réis* by the royal decree that created the post.

Within this parish chapels were built to the Lord of Miracles, which we have already discussed (vol. 1, p. 332), St Roch, Nossa Senhora do Rosário, Our Lady of Grace, Our Lady of Prayers, São Cristóvão, Our Lady of Protection, St Joseph, Santo António and Santana, to which we shall refer at greater length elsewhere in this work. Among the events of interest to the history of this parish, special mention should be made of the floods of 1724 and 1803 (see Floods, vol. 1, p. 54 ff.), the attack by the Miguelist squadron and troops on this town (see Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelist troops) and the killings that took place in the mother church (*igreja matriz*) of this parish in May 1870 (see Popular Riots).

In the article Geology we have already referred briefly to the lava channel on the left bank of the stream, near the Quinta Santana, and on p. 265 of vol. 1 of this *Elucidário* we transcribed the description of it that Hartung gave in his book *Geologische Beschreibung der Inseln Madeira und Porto Santo*. About this channel, or the Furna de Cavalum as it is generally known, there is a legend which Lieutenant-Colonel A. Artur Sarmento used for one of the chapters of his book *Migalhas*.

Overlooking the sea at the western end of the bay stands the old chapel of St Roch. At its foot rise the springs known by the name of the chapel’s patron saint, which issue from the cliff almost at the level of the ocean’s waterline. These waters have excellent therapeutic properties, and their use is especially recommended for certain diseases of the stomach. The statements of many patients and the testimony of physicians are irrefutable proof of their efficacy. The local Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had the waters chemically and bacteriologically analysed, and the results confirmed the opinion already held of them. They draw a considerable number of people to this town in the hot season. For this reason, and because of its bathing beach, the place is gradually becoming a popular spa and seaside resort. Another powerful attraction is the enchanting beauty of the spot and the complete absence of heat, which together make the town of Machico one of the most sought-after places in Madeira in which to spend the summer.

In the article Fortifications (p. 45) we have already referred to the forts that defended this place. The small, old and useless fortress facing the town’s finest public promenade, a handsome avenue of old and massive plane trees, ought to be demolished.

The principal localities (*sítios*) of this parish are: Vila, Pé da Ladeira, Pontinha, Estacada, Moinhos, Serra de Água, Azinhaga, Piquinho, Torre, Terça, Fazenda, Moinho da Serra, Caramanchão, Murtinhal, Landeiros, Marco, Maroços, Ribeira Grande, Ribeira Seca, Poço do Gil, Paraíso, Graça, Banda de Além and Misericórdia.
There are three state schools in this parish (1921), two in the town itself and the other in the locality of Caramanchão.
The 1930 census gives this parish 10,114 inhabitants.

Machico’s most illustrious son is Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega, known by the epithet of ‘Camões Pequeno’ (the Little Camões), who was born in the locality of Torre in this parish on 2 October 1772 and whom we have already discussed in this *Elucidário* (vol. I, p. 60). Another distinguished son of this place was Dr José António de Almada, born on 7 March 1843 (vol. I, p. 48).
Machico (parish church)

It has been claimed that the chapel of Cristo (see vol. I, p. 332), today the chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*), in the town (*vila*) of Machico, was the first place of worship built on this island. We disagree with this claim (see Santa Catarina, chapel of), and are even of the opinion that it was not the first to be built in that parish (*freguesia*). On settling in Machico, Tristão Vaz Teixeira promptly had a small chapel built, which he later enlarged and improved. It became the seat of the parish when the parish was created around the middle of the 15th century.

The present church, although very old, does not appear to be the original building in which the centre of the new parish was established. There is a constant tradition that the white marble columns of the fine side doorway were given by King Manuel I. Since he died in 1521, it may be conjectured that the building does not date from much before that year. An old manuscript places its construction in the year 1499. It is said somewhere that the massive buttresses reinforcing the outer walls appear to belong to the original building.

Over the centuries the church has undergone major repairs and some alterations to its interior, especially to the altars, while keeping the general lines of the original building. Notable repairs were carried out in 1683, 1698 and 1713, particularly those to the chancel after 1698. The bell tower was demolished in 1844 because it threatened imminent collapse, and was rebuilt in 1853. This tower once held an old clock, dating from before 1609, which stopped working in 1824.

The arch and vaults of the chapels of the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*) and of St John the Baptist are in the Gothic style, and the ceiling of the first of these chapels is of remarkable beauty and perfection. The arches of the chancel and of a chapel on the Gospel side are Manueline.

Above the altar of the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament hangs a painting on panel of the Adoration of the Magi (*Reis Magos*), which is beyond dispute a most remarkable work of art. A former and distinguished teacher at our Industrial School said of it:

‘Over the centuries this notable painting has suffered the ravages of age, and it is truly to be regretted that it could not be preserved, like so many other masterpieces of equal antiquity. Nevertheless, the flawless drawing of the figures still stands out, together with all the vigour of its colour and the whole special character that this painting displays, which brings it so close to the works of Grão Vasco, the great artist who flourished in Portugal at the beginning of the 16th century. It is undoubtedly to this painter, whose pictures are admired in the cathedral of Viseu, or to the school he created, that the Adoration of the Magi of Machico is owed. This is attested by the characteristics of the drawing and the colour, and above all by the care taken over the execution, which is most evident in the rendering of the gold embroidery, the jewels and the metal ornaments, painted with extreme precision and extraordinary truthfulness. Among the rare relics of early painting that Madeira possesses, this is without doubt the most notable. . .’ Only recently, one of the most distinguished Portuguese painters described this picture as a fine museum piece and advised that it be restored without delay, without harm to the original painting.

The chapel of the Blessed Sacrament, which houses this exquisite work of art, was founded by Dona Branca Teixeira, daughter of the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico. In her will she refers to her chapel of the Magi, to which she left substantial property for the celebration of a daily Mass. Frutuoso says that Branca Teixeira died unmarried and was commonly known as ‘the Mestra’ because of her gift of healing.

The chapel of St John the Baptist was founded by the second captain-donatary and was intended to serve as the family vault of the donataries of this captaincy; the arms of the Teixeira family appear at the top of its arch. The altars or chapels of St Francis Xavier and of the Holy Spirit (*Espírito Santo*), with their pious obligations, were founded by Canon Dr Manuel Pereira de Castro, a former vicar of Machico, and by Sebastião de Morais, as their family vaults and as the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) that the latter established.

Special mention is due to a painting of the Holy Souls, which is on the altar between the arches of the chancel and the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament. It is without doubt a work of value, which a poor restoration has considerably damaged.

Tradition not only attributes to King Manuel I the gift of the marble columns of the church’s side doorway, but also says that the same monarch presented the organ that is still in the choir of the church today. As it was badly damaged, it was repaired in 1857 on the orders of the governor António Rogério Gromicho Couceiro. It bears the following inscription: ‘Munificence of the Lord King Dom Manuel. At the request of the Municipal Council, repaired by order of His Excellency General António Rogério Gromicho Couceiro, civil and military governor of Madeira, 1857.’
Machico (origin of the name)

In the article devoted to the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, we said that the origin of this singular name was not yet known. Despite the research carried out and the various hypotheses and conjectures put forward to explain it fully, the problem remains unsolved. And although the illustrious annotator of the *Saudades* claims to have resolved it satisfactorily, it is nonetheless certain that his authoritative opinion was not accepted by the distinguished writer and historian Pinheiro Chagas, as we shall see below.

But does settling this point really have any historical importance? Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo answers this question in the following terms: ‘...it became important when, in 1868, the Englishman Richard Henry Major, in his work *The Life of Prince Henry of Portugal*, took seriously the false legend of the supposed Englishman Robert Machin and raised to the status of an argument the false etymology that derives Machico from Machim. He concluded that this legend was a real event, and that his Machim discovered the Madeira archipelago many years before Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira landed there at the end of the first quarter of the 15th century. This opinion, which Major developed with artifice, relying on writings of no historical value, may in future be invoked as grounds for leonine claims – all the more plausibly since the Portuguese government and the Royal Academy of Sciences of Lisbon heaped naive honours on the author of this learned but reserved book, the *Life of Prince Henry*, whose aim seems to be none other than, while magnifying our legitimate maritime glories, to claim for England the precedence in the actual discovery of the Madeira archipelago. It is therefore worth unravelling the origin of the name Machico, setting historical probability against the inaccuracy spread by Major’.

We cannot follow Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo in every detail of his long, learned and at times tedious account of the origin of this name. Once it is proved – and Dr Azevedo did so in the most complete and conclusive manner – that the Machim story is nothing but a pure and simple legend, it is also demonstrated that the name Machico cannot derive from the unfortunate Robert Machin, the hapless lover of the ill-fated Anne of Arfet. Dr Azevedo’s argument about this origin merely reinforces the force of his tight reasoning in proving that the legend is baseless, but it is not a new proof of the legend’s falsity. Moreover, the account of the Machim story first appears only a century after the discovery of the Madeiran archipelago, which in itself rules out even the mere probability that the name Machico could derive from Machim.

Dr Álvaro de Azevedo traces the origin of the word Machico to a corruption of Monchique, the name of a settlement in the Algarve. Many of the first settlers of this island came from that province, and in all probability so did some of the very crews of Zarco’s caravels. According to information supplied by the illustrious Algarvian Estácio da Veiga and by others who have visited the valley of Monchique, it seems that the orographic and hydrographic conditions of the two places show strong resemblances between Monchique and Machico, and from this circumstance Dr Azevedo draws an argument in support of the view he holds. Against these assertions Pinheiro Chagas sets the following reasons: ‘In the first place (*lugar*), Zurara, a contemporary of some of the discoverers, writes Machito, whereas it is Cadamosto, who as a foreigner would be expected to distort the word, who writes Monchrico, bringing it closer to the Portuguese word than the Portuguese chronicler himself – which is positively absurd. In the second place, it is no less absurd that the name of an Algarvian town should have been distorted so quickly by the Algarvians themselves. They gave it the name and they corrupted it. The islanders’ pronunciation has nothing to do with such a distortion: first, because in Zurara’s time the colonists were still men born in Portugal and had not yet had time to acquire a distinctive pronunciation; second, because Zurara was not a Madeiran writer but a mainland one, who wrote the name as the Algarvian navigators told it to him. And, we repeat, nothing is less acceptable than the supposition that men born in Monchique, having given a land they discovered the name of their homeland, should not know how to pronounce it twenty years later.’ Camilo Castelo Branco, neither accepting nor rejecting Dr Azevedo’s hypothesis, says that in his view it is superior to all the others. The annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso replied at length to Pinheiro Chagas’s criticism, but it seems to us that he did not refute the illustrious historian’s arguments.

Two years after the publication of the *Saudades*, E. A. Bettencourt writes in his booklet entitled *Memoria sobre a descoberta das ilhas de Porto Santo e Madeira*: ‘Nor, in our view, can the name Machico, given to a place on the island of Madeira, serve as an argument for a stay of Englishmen on that island before the Portuguese arrived there. We shall note in the first place, without however making this our chief objection, that the name Machico may just as well be a corruption of Machim as a diminutive of *macho* [TN: Portuguese for a male mule or male animal]. The popular character of the Portuguese language does not stand in the way of this supposition. Zurara supports it when in his *A Chronica* (‘The Chronicle’) he calls it Machito, as does Melo himself when he names it Machino. For just as in Africa the point where in 1435 the discoverers landed two horses to ride them into the interior of the country came to be called “Angra dos Cavalos (‘horses’ cove’)”, could not the name Machico, machito or machino likewise have been given to that place on Madeira for a similar reason?’ This opinion is rejected by Pinheiro Chagas and Dr Azevedo.

In 1879 the great writer Camilo Castelo Branco, in his book *Historia e Sentimentalismo*, included an article entitled *A Lenda de Machim*, in which he put forward a new origin for the word Machico. He said that it should be pronounced Maquito and that it derives from the Italian word *macchia*, which means forest, thicket, bramble, etc. This explanation by the illustrious novelist provoked an interesting controversy between him and Pinheiro Chagas, which is published in full in the aforementioned *Historia e Sentimentalismo*. The annotator of the *Saudades* does not embrace Camilo’s opinion either.

Seventeen years after the controversy between Pinheiro Chagas and Camilo Castelo Branco, General Brito Rebêlo published, in 1894, an interesting document that sheds much light on the subject with which we have been dealing, and to which we have already referred in vol. X of this work, on p. 174. If it is not decisive proof, it is without doubt the most acceptable presumption so far put forward concerning the origin of the word Machico. The document reads as follows: ‘Charter whereby the said lord gave some houses standing in the rua nova of Lisbon, bordering on houses of the captain-major and on Joham piriz canellas, to Machico, master of his barque, to dwell in for as long as it should be his pleasure, etc. At Alenquer, 12 days of April of the year one thousand and 1417 (1379).’ Archive of the Torre do Tombo (national archives), Book 2 of Ferdinand I, fol. 42. ‘From this document,’ adds General J. I. de Brito Rebelo, ‘there follows the positive fact of the existence in Portugal, in the year 1379 (1417), of a mariner of important rank named Machico; and once such a name is found, the origin of the name by which a certain spot on the island of Madeira was designated is found. Documents of this nature prove facts with complete evidence. It seems to me, therefore, that the following conjecture may be made: the Machico of whom the document speaks, or some descendant of his, went to the island of Madeira on the first or one of the first voyages; through old age, illness or some other mishap he died at a certain point on the coast; his companions buried him, marking the place with a rough wooden cross. This would be the cross that was placed in the original church when it was founded, and which legend later portrayed as taken from the grave of Machim; and the site would come to be called by the name of the first man who honoured with his remains the land until then uninhabited. However the event came about, in this way or another, a hitherto unknown document now raises from the oblivion of almost five centuries the name of the obscure mariner who, assisting in the enterprise to which Prince Henry the Navigator devoted himself, bequeathed his name to a place in one of the loveliest regions discovered through his zeal, and explains the origin of that name. Let the name of Machico, then, be inscribed on the list of the first discoverers. When, therefore, we cite and extol the names of Gonçalves Zarco and Perestrello, let us never forget that of poor Machico, who was perhaps the one who guided them on their bold and fortunate expedition.’

It is evident that Brito Rebêlo carried his conclusions much too far. There are acceptable probabilities in his conjectures, but the truth is that the document transcribed cannot demonstrate that the sailor Machico, to whom Ferdinand I granted some houses in Lisbon, took part in the expedition of João Gonçalves Zarco. It does prove that the name Machico existed in Portugal, which constitutes a new argument against the truth of the story of Robert Machin, and further confirms the account given by Azurara and other early chroniclers of the discovery of this archipelago. The document found by General Brito Rebêlo in the Torre do Tombo (national archives) is nonetheless very valuable and interesting.
Machico (town and municipality)

‘The valley of Machico, in which the town (*vila*) of the same name stands, is,’ says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘some five to six kilometres long and two to three wide. It runs from north to south between two mountain ridges. One, to the east, rises above the town to form the Pico do Facho (‘beacon peak’), then extends towards Caniçal (‘reed bed’) and, running out into the sea, forms the towering Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’), on whose furthest pinnacle there has stood for some years a good revolving lighthouse, visible from beyond the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’); the other ends in the high plateau called the Queimada (‘burnt land’), overlooking the sea. From these ridges spring and flow abundant and beautiful waters that fertilise its already exceedingly rich soil; draining through the rugged ground or feeding the lesser brooks, they form its full-flowing stream, which winds along the valley to the beach, where it empties into the Atlantic. In these conditions the valley of Machico is rich in the most varied vegetation, from grasses to fruit-bearing and non-fruit-bearing trees; picturesque and most delightful, it must have been astonishing when, still virgin forest, it was beheld by Zarco and Tristão Vaz. The vast landing place and wide cove, protected to the east by the Ponta de São Lourenço and sheltered to the west by the towering coast known as the South coast, and therefore safe in all winds except those from that quarter, complete the general panorama of the site of Machico. The town lies at the very bottom of the valley, by the sea, cut lengthwise by the stream into two parts or quarters. To the west is the old quarter, the town proper, with the houses of the nobility, the modestly Manueline mother church (*igreja matriz*), the town hall of the municipality (*concelho*) and, along the beach, the charming tree-lined promenade. To the east is the Banda de Além (‘the far side’), a suburb of poor seafaring folk, with humble dwellings and narrow, twisting alleys, but with little white houses rising in an amphitheatre, for they are already climbing the slope of the neighbouring Pico do Facho; and, on the bank of the stream, towards the sea, stands the small church of Cristo (Christ), or, more exactly, of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), as the crosses of that military order adorning its original portal still proclaim – this little church being without doubt the first built on the island of Madeira. Between these two quarters rise the thick walls within which the stream flows, gentle and clear almost always, torrential and fearsome in the winter storms: such is the town which, set in that frame, enhances its beauty..... This whole varied scene, beheld from the heights of the Queimada or of the Pico do Facho, which command the valley and the slopes, the stream and the crops, the town and the hamlets, the landing place and the cove, the sea as far as it merges with the horizon, the Ponta de São Lourenço turning blue in the haze, and the south coast fading little by little into the twilight of sunset. . is majestically beautiful. . . ’

The date on which Machico was made a town is not known. The first and oldest book in the municipal archive, in which the relevant charter may have been recorded, disappeared some decades ago, and no reference whatever to that document has been found. The *Anais do Município*, written some seventy years ago, state that ‘the creation of the town of Machico dates from the time when the town of Funchal was created’. This seems probable, if we bear in mind that in the earliest days of colonisation the two places grew in importance side by side; it has even been supposed that Machico reached a greater degree of development than the future capital of the archipelago. Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo accepts the view that the two towns were created at about the same time.

Nor is the precise date of the creation of the town of Funchal known. The annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) conjectures that it dates from the year 1451 (see Funchal (Creation of the Town and Municipality of), vol. II, p. 59), and this approximate date should likewise be adopted for the elevation of Machico to the rank of town.

The municipality of Machico corresponded in area and extent to the old captaincy. It was sharply cut back when the town and municipality of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) were created in 1515, and it suffered no lesser mutilation when the municipality and town of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) were established in 1744.

With the introduction of constitutional government and its new administrative organisation, the municipality of Machico was once again reduced to narrower dimensions when the municipality of Santana (‘St Anne’) was created in 1835. Despite the protests of the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of Machico, the new municipality was maintained. It was made up of the parishes (*freguesias*) that compose it at present, together with the parish of Porto da Cruz. By the decree of 19 October 1852 this parish was detached from the municipality of Santana and incorporated into that of Machico.

Under the same decree, certain localities in the parishes of Machico and Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) were annexed to the municipality of Santa Cruz. This provoked vigorous protests from the Municipal Council of Machico and from various official and private figures prominent in the municipality. After a series of incidents and vicissitudes that seemed endless, the secretary-general of the district, António Lopes Barbosa de Albuquerque, acting as civil governor, convened a meeting at the Casa dos Romeiros (pilgrims’ house) of Santo da Serra on 11 September 1862. Present were representatives of the municipal councils of Machico and Santa Cruz, the municipal administrators, various public officials and other persons of standing. There a new division of municipalities and parishes was definitively agreed, the one in force today, and so an end was put to the claims and protests raised on both sides.

On the arms of the municipality of Machico, the *Anais* already cited state the following: ‘A sphere in relief, like that in the arms of King Manuel I when he was Duke of Beja and Grand Master of the Order of Christ, forms the arms of the ancient town of Machico, granted by the same king in 1499 to the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of the Council. Tradition has it that the silver seal with an ivory handle which still exists in the Council is the very one with which the king ennobled this town.’

Manuel I also presented the old Senate of Machico with a bronze weights standard which, besides the royal arms, bears the following engraved inscription: ‘Dom Emanuel the first of Portugal, the most high and most excellent king, had me made, in the Year of Our Lord. J. H. P. O. D. 1499’. The same monarch likewise gave some valuable objects to the mother church (*igreja matriz*) of this town, as we shall see elsewhere.

When the Council of Machico was asked in 1780 about the privileges it enjoyed, it replied that the Senate of this town enjoyed the same prerogatives and exemptions as the Senate of the Council of Lisbon, and that the form of address due to it was as follows: Most Illustrious Senate of the Council of the ancient and noble town of Machico.

After the restoration of constitutional government, an Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Council was appointed on 16 July 1834, and the first body of councillors was elected on 20 October of the same year. The first municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) was Alberto de Oliveira, appointed on 4 October 1835.
The town of Machico was the seat of a Misericórdia, which we shall discuss at greater length in the article Misericórdias.

It had a customs house, which we have already dealt with on pp. 43 and 44 of vol. I of this work. The municipalities or towns of Machico and Santa Cruz shared a common charter (foral), dated 15 December 1515, which is transcribed on p. 507 ff. of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’. It contains interesting information for the history of public administration in these municipalities.

Since 1929 this town has had a fine building housing several municipal departments and the various services of the Council. General António Teixeira de Aguiar, an illustrious son of the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, contributed notably to the construction of this town hall.
Machim (legend)

The poetic and moving legend of Robert Machin, with its tragic twists, has been celebrated in prose and verse by Portuguese and foreign writers alike, stirring the morbid sensibility of those who believe such tales of love or are easily swayed by them. After the exhaustive work of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, who subjected the case of Robert Machin to all the rigour of historical criticism, no one may legitimately accept that this charming but fantastic invention could be true. From 1563, when António Galvão first set this legend in circulation in his *Tratado dos Descobrimentos*, down to some writers of our own day, it has been told with many variations. It takes its most interesting and attractive form, however, in the third *Epanaphora* of Francisco Manuel de Melo, above all for the beauty of its language and the vividness of its narrative. The best-known version, nevertheless, is that of Gaspar Frutuoso, which does not differ in essentials from that of Francisco de Melo. We shall transcribe the ingenuous account of the historian of the islands, so as not to commit the fault of omitting from these pages the story of the famous legend of Robert Machin and Ana de Arfet.

‘In the time of King Edward of England there was a noble Englishman, a renowned knight, known by the nickname of Machim, who, having lofty thoughts and being also a man of honourable deeds, was in love with a lady of high lineage called Anna de Arfet. As he pursued his love with great ardour, she in turn came to love dearly the one who loved her, for in the end love, if not repaid with love, has no equal reward. And since love (like fragrant things) cannot be hidden where it is enclosed, the lovers were found out through the signs and suspicions they gave of themselves, for they loved each other greatly (since the prohibition of a thing is sometimes the cause of greater desire for it, and trying to put out the fire of love is tinder for a greater blaze, for our nature is most stirred by, and most aspires to, what is most forbidden it). Just as the owners of irrigated fields, in times of great floods, dig great ditches at the head of the waters where they come in, to turn them elsewhere, and as physicians, to cure a stitch in one side, order bleeding from the opposite side, so her kinsmen, thinking to pour water on the fire and not the pitch that burns in it, acting as masters of the field and physicians of her lovesickness, sought to divert the current of love that was flooding her and to draw the blood away from the contrary stitch, as though making opposing ditches and bleedings; and with the King’s consent they married her in Bristol to a man of high estate. Machim was deeply grieved by this and she most unhappy. Finding no remedy for the passion and pain of the extremes in which both found themselves, and showing with burning tears their sorrow at this marriage, they agreed in great secrecy to flee to France, with which England was then waging great wars. Machim spoke with some aggrieved men and kinsmen, to whom he opened his heart and all his mind and treasure (which he kept locked where his heart and love were), and they pledged their faith and swore to go with him to France. To carry out this departure the better, they went secretly, a few at a time, to Bristol, where certain merchant ships lay laden for Spain, resolved to board one of them, set sail by force and cross to France. With all secrecy they informed Anna de Harfet of this plan, so that she might join them and flee. A day was fixed when the ships would be empty of their principal people, a feast day, when the master and merchants were ashore. Anna de Harfet, having been warned, rode off as secretly as she could on a palfrey and, taking a crucifix and all her precious jewels, reached the appointed place, where they were already waiting for her with a ship’s boat. She got into it with her Machim, and he, with his servants and friends, took her aboard one of the ships they had in readiness, which they at once set under sail; and, having cut the cables, they took the boat aboard. It happened, however, that a great storm blew up, churning the waves as though they envied that unrestrained love, and with it they were soon driven away from land. When night fell, reckoning that the other ships might come out after theirs, since it would be understood that they were crossing to France, they turned aside from that course, hoping to make for the furthest parts of France in Gascony, or Spain. And since the pilot and master had stayed ashore, and those aboard the ship knew neither how to make land nor how to take its latitude, finding a favourable wind they ran under full sail wherever fortune carried them, so as not to be overtaken; and within a few days they found themselves off a point of a wild land, covered all over with woods down to the sea, which left them astonished and bewildered. Just behind the point they saw a large cove; entering it, they cast anchor, put the boat out and went to see what land it was. Unable to land because of the breaking surf, they made for a cliff that jutted into the sea on the eastern side, where they landed at their ease. From there they went along the beach between the woods and the sea until they came upon a beautiful stream of good water, which flowed out to the sea through the woods. They found no animal or creature of any kind, but they did find many birds, and they saw that the woods were so dense and thick that it filled them with amazement. Among other trees, they found near the sea a very large and thick one, which from great age had a hollow at its foot that they could enter as if it were a house. Returning to the ship with this news, Machim and his companions, understanding that it was a new land, resolved to ask the Kings of Spain for it. Anna de Harfet, who was sick and seasick from the sea, begged Machim to take her ashore to see that stream and recover from her sickness for a few days. He did so: he had clothing and provisions taken ashore so as to stay there at leisure for some days while the weather allowed, taking some companions with him to keep them company on land, while others went back and forth to the ship; but when fortune runs against someone, it gives them no leisure to rest. On the third night after their arrival, so strong a wind rose over the land that the ship broke from its moorings. Those aboard set sail, unable to stop, and ran wherever the wind carried them; and within a few days, it is said, they were cast upon the coast of Barbary, where they were at once taken captive by the Moors and carried off to Morocco.’

When day broke and those who had stayed ashore could no longer see the ship, they were plunged into deep sorrow, at once giving themselves up for lost and despairing of ever being able to leave that place. Machim’s lady, seeing herself left there, was struck dumb and never spoke again, and three days later she died. Machim, for the great love he bore her, was bursting with grief; and, seeing himself banished from his homeland and his love dead, she who had been the whole comfort of his banishment, he no longer felt any longing for his country; he felt only an unbearable longing for his Anna de Harfet, whom he had so swiftly seen turned to earth before his eyes. With this grief that remained to him, and with ardent sighs and tears, he mourned her there; and in the place where they had taken shelter he had her buried, and set a wooden cross at the head of her grave, and a board (*mesa*) or slab of stone with his crucifix upon it, and at the foot of the crucifix he placed an inscription in Latin, in which he told the whole of his most sorrowful fate and all that had befallen him on that most unfortunate voyage, asking that, if Christians should ever live there, they build a church in that place with the dedication of Christ. This done, he asked his companions to take the clothing they had and such birds as they might catch, and to go wherever fortune might guide them, since he had not had the fortune to keep his beloved alive; and he said that he wished to stay there and die where he had killed Anna de Harfet, keeping company with her dead body with his longing alone, since she had kept him company while she lived. His companions, moved to pity, all told him that they would not leave him, and that they would die and remain there with him. Machim, who thanked them warmly for that love, and would have thanked them more for the cruelty of leaving him alone, lasted no more than five days, out of grief and sorrow for his beloved. His companions, who felt no small sorrow at the loss of his company, buried him beside his Anna de Harfet and placed another cross at his head; and, leaving the crucifix just as Machim had placed it, and leaving these two graves in that deserted land as a most sorrowful spectacle of longing and love, they boarded the ship’s boat in which they had come from the ship (although others would have it that they made it from the trunk of the tree, which was thick and could hold many people) and, reaching the coast of Barbary, were taken captive there by the Moors and carried off to Morocco, where the other companions from the ship were also already held captive, so joyless and unfortunate. Such are the brief, fleeting and costly pleasures of the world’s great and long-cherished hopes, whose custom, condition and nature always was and always will be to pay out very little or nothing to those who ask much.’ Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, in some of his annotations to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and in a lengthy article in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Illustrado*, deals with this subject at the greatest length, not only to show the utter falsity of the claims of those who believed they saw historical truth in the legend, but also to vindicate for the Portuguese the priority in the discovery of this archipelago. The assertions of the British writer Richard Henry Major in his monumental work on Henry the Navigator also led the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ to undertake this study, since the recognised authority of the English scholar could lead readers of his notable book on our first maritime discoveries into serious errors. Anyone wishing to gain a deeper knowledge of this subject should turn above all to Dr Azevedo’s interesting and erudite dissertation included in note V of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (pp. 340–429) and in the *Diccionario Universal Illustrado Portuguez* (volume for the letter M, p. 190), and may also consult the *Historia de Portugal* (vol. II, pp. 230 ff.) by Pinheiro Chagas, which contains laudatory references to the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’, ‘a Madeiran scholar and one of the most erudite writers that Portugal possesses’.
The most brilliant narrative of the legend, or romance, of Robert Machin and Ana de Arfet is that of Rebelo da Silva, published in vol. IX of the *Archivo Pittoresco*.
Macieira
See Pereiro.
Maclaren (Duncan)

He stayed in Madeira from October 1844 until the summer of 1845 and wrote a short work entitled *A visit to Madeira and Tenerife*. According to this work, 250 foreigners visited Madeira from 1844 to 1845, a figure that includes the invalids and the friends and servants who accompanied them. In the two preceding years the number of visitors had been between 300 and 400, and at that time some 300 English people were resident on the island.
Freemasonry

According to Dr José de Arriaga in his *Historia da revolução portuguesa de 1820*, the island of Madeira was one of the first places in Portugal where Freemasonry (*Maçonaria*) found a particularly favourable welcome. By 1770 there was already a Masonic lodge in Madeira, whose members included Aires de Ornelas Frasão, Francisco de Alincourt and Bartolomeu Andrieux, as can be seen from an official letter sent by the Governor, João António de Sá Pereira, to the Marquis of Pombal on 3 December of that year. On 14 April 1792 the Governor, Dom Diogo Forjaz Coutinho, complained to Martinho de Melo e Castro that the Frenchman João José de Orquiny had established a Masonic lodge on this island, most of whose members belonged to the nobility and the clergy.

Frasão, Alincourt and Andrieux were arrested as Freemasons in 1770 on the Governor’s orders, and the first was sent to Lisbon. A Madeiran document shows, however, that the Marquis of Pombal not only ordered the release of the second of these Masons but also restored him to his post of engineer sergeant-major (*sargento-mor engenheiro*, a field-officer rank equivalent to major), which suggests that the same happened to the other two prisoners.

As for the Frenchman Orquiny, he was a grand commander of the Grand Orient of France, and he secured an appointment from the government of Maria I to study the Madeiran flora and its therapeutic value. He arrived in Madeira in 1789, but his first concern was to transplant the French Masonic institutions to this island. In this he succeeded easily, but he was less fortunate in Lisbon, where he went in 1792: there the police discovered his designs, imprisoned him in the cells of the Inquisition and later expelled him abroad. The Madeiran Masons suffered a great persecution in 1792. As soon as Bishop Dom José da Costa Torres learned that a Masonic lodge had been formed in Funchal, and that its members included the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate), several clergymen, many sons of noble houses, men of letters, etc., he urged the Inquisitor General, says Dr José de Arriaga, ‘to publish a public notice (*edital*) against the Freemasons, inviting the citizens of the island to denounce before the Inquisition all those whom they knew to belong to the accursed sect, which had a pact with Satan and was excommunicated. The notice was not long in coming and appeared that year. There was general panic, because a large part of the island already belonged to Freemasonry, and the notice was indeed going to cause grave disturbances within families and give rise to disastrous events.’

‘The arrests followed immediately,’ the same author continues. ‘The vicar general, the judge of residues and the visitor (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) of the bishopric were dismissed from their posts and suspended from preaching and hearing confession, though they could still say Mass. Many vicars were arrested in their parishes and put on trial; others were suspended from preaching and hearing confession outside their jurisdiction. The chaplains of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) were removed from their chaplaincies, the curates from their curacies, and many clergymen were suspended from preaching and hearing confession throughout the bishopric, being branded with heresy and incurring excommunication.’
Many Masons, among them various military officers and public officials, fled Madeira at that time. Some of them went with their families to the United States, where they were well received.

The Government, considering the persecution of the Masons impolitic, put an end to it, and on 23 June 1792 a pardon reached the island for all members of secret societies, on condition that they abjured the heresies of which they were accused. The bishop refused to reinstate the priests he had dismissed or suspended, but they appealed to the Crown, which upheld their appeal.

The Madeiran poet Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega and the dean of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), João Francisco Lopes Rocha, suffered greatly during this persecution. The latter wrote a letter to the minister José de Seabra da Silva, dated 16 October 1793, in which he complained bitterly that the Bishop was keeping him suspended from the exercise of his priestly offices and from the corresponding stipends, in open violation of Portuguese law and of the express instructions of the Queen’s government. This letter, published many years later in volume III of the *Campeão Portuguez* in London, is an important document for the study of Masonic institutions in Madeira.

Four years after the persecution, on 22 June 1796, Bishop Dom José da Costa Torres was transferred to the bishopric of Elvas. A manuscript of the period, cited by Dr Azevedo, says that he ‘left (the island of Madeira) on the night of 6 October 1796, without taking leave of anyone, not even of the Most Holy Sacrament; and to this day the reason for this studied embarkation by night, and by back ways, is unknown’. Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho ceased to be captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) only on his death, on 30 March 1798.

Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, in the article ‘Madeira’ published in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez*, states that everything suggests the Masonic impulse on this island was of French origin. If the Marquis of Pombal, and later the ministers of Maria I, chose not to oppose it openly, it was because they saw in it a means of counterbalancing the all-absorbing dominance of the British merchants. If that was indeed the aim of these ministers, however, it failed.
