The British occupation, and the protection later given by various individuals of the same nationality to the Madeiran liberals, created among the latter a British party which, as the same learned investigator says, dissolved only little by little, as a result of the fall of the government of Miguel I in 1834.

Freemasonry was reorganised while Madeira was occupied by British troops (1801 to 1802 and 1807 to 1814). The founding of the Unido lodge probably dates from that period; from it sprang the Constância and Fidelidade lodges, established during the liberal period. Agostinho de Ornelas was the first Worshipful Master of this lodge, and it seems that both it and its offshoots were subordinate to the Grand Orient of Lisbon, or at least worked in agreement with it, for as long as the country was governed by liberal institutions.

The special judicial commission (alçada) that the absolutist government sent to Madeira in 1823 dispersed the masons and sentenced many of them to penal exile (degredo). Yet as early as 1825 there was here a secret society known as the Jardineiros (Gardeners), organised by graduates and students of the University. An old document shows that in 1824 the masons met at the house of the Englishman Gran, who was also a freemason.

The Masonic constitution was printed at the press of *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’) in January 1823. Prominent among the masons condemned by the special judicial commission that came to Madeira that year were Dr Nicolau Caetano Pita, editor of that newspaper; Dr Francisco de Assis Saldanha, *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district); Father Gregório Nazianzeno Medina e Vasconcelos; and Father Tomé João Pestana Homem de El-Rei, vicar of Campanário.

Freemasonry, says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in the *Diccionario Universal Portugues*, re-emerged strongly in 1826, led by João do Carvalhal. But the political events of 1828 decimated and dispersed Madeiran Freemasonry, just as, for identical causes, that of mainland Portugal had been. These were the special judicial commission that came to Madeira that year; the indictment of 216 and the imprisonment of 101 liberals and masons; the penal exile and imprisonment to which they were sentenced; the emigration and homicide (*homisio*) of those not imprisoned; the terror of the scaffolds on which so many Portuguese were put to death; and finally the five years of bloodthirsty despotism under the government of Miguel I.

‘When liberal institutions were established in Madeira on 5 June 1834, few masons remained here. It is recorded, however, that even so two lodges arose, but by then far removed from the old spirit of Masonic unity: not true lodges, but factional clubs, which were therefore soon absorbed by the party clubs proper. Foremost among them all was the celebrated Club do Carmo, where the now deceased Madeiran political leaders of the generation preceding the one that entered active life around 1846 and 1847 won their first spurs.’

In 1843 there was no Masonic lodge in Madeira, and matters remained so until 11 March 1872. On that day a group of men with no involvement in politics, led by the retired lieutenant-colonel José Paulo Vieira, set up the Liberdade chapter lodge in Funchal, whose first Worshipful Master was the said lieutenant-colonel.

On 16 April 1873 the Trabalho lodge was set up in Funchal, followed by the União Liberal lodge on 23 May 1877 and the Cinco de Junho (‘Fifth of June’) lodge on 13 April 1878. These three lodges merged shortly after 1880, however, and from then on there was a single lodge, named Trabalho, which was short-lived.

In 1872 Madeiran Freemasonry set up a printing press, on which it published first the *Madeira Liberal* and then *O Oriente do Funchal* (‘The Funchal Orient’), the latter paper being a continuation of the former. If the lodges ‘had not been abandoned’, Dr Azevedo wrote in 1882, ‘abandoned by those who had the imperative duty of giving them counsel, direction and strength, they would today be the glory of Portuguese Freemasonry’. Besides the Liberdade chapter lodge, of which we spoke above, there are today (1921) in Funchal the Trabalho lodge, the Grémio 5 de Outubro, the Britannic Lodge and the Pátria Portuguesa lodge. The first of these Masonic associations was founded in June 1901, the second on 13 October 1911, the third on 29 December 1913 and the last on 12 January 1916. The Revolução e Progresso lodge, founded in 1899, lasted only 6 or 7 months. The Britânica lodge, created, we believe, in June 1908, was replaced by the Britannic Lodge, whose members are almost all English and answer to the Grand Lodge of England.

Such, in brief, has been the history of Madeiran Freemasonry from the founding of the first lodge, towards the end of the third quarter of the 18th century, to the present day (1921). Its aims being identical to those of Portuguese Freemasonry, one of the articles of its programme is to put advanced principles into practice. For this reason it had to endure great persecution and humiliation before winning the freedoms it has long enjoyed on our island.
Madalena do Mar (parish)

This parish on the south-west coast of Madeira lies below the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas. It is bounded to the east by the locality of Anjos (‘angels’), in that same parish, and to the west by the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’).

It is conjectured that its original name was Madalesia or Santa Maria Madalena, and that the words ‘do Mar’ (of the sea) were added later because it is washed by the ocean – and perhaps still more to distinguish it from the locality and chapel of Santa Maria Madalena in the parish of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), when that place became the centre of a well-known and much-frequented pilgrimage. The hypothesis is not entirely without foundation, and there are other examples that support it. The name by which it is generally known today, even in official documents, is Madalena do Mar, although the people, with their tendency to simplify language, also call it simply Madalena.

The parish grew out of a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) that existed there from the earliest days of colonisation, with a chantry (capela) whose patron saint was, as is stated somewhere, Santa Maria Madalena; it is also claimed that the original chapel was dedicated to St Catherine. On this origin, several old books of noble lineages contain what is summarised in the notes to the *Saudades*, in the following terms: ‘... Henry the German, a legendary figure of the earliest days of the colonisation of this island of Madeira. It was said of him that he was a Polish prince, and that after Władysław III lost the battle of Varna against Murad II in 1444 he vowed to wander the earth and was dubbed a knight of St Catherine of Mount Sinai. When he came to the island of Madeira, João Gonçalves Zarco granted him, at the spot later called Madalena do Mar, a large tract of land as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), by a charter confirmed by Prince Henry the Navigator on 29 April 1457 and by Afonso V on 18 May of the same year. Henry the German did indeed found a large settled estate there, with a chapel dedicated to Santa Maria Madalena, from which the place took its name. He married Senhorinha Anes, and met a disastrous death, crushed by a landslide (*quebrada*) that fell from Cabo Girão onto the boat in which he was travelling from the city of Funchal to Madalena. His widow later married João Rodrigues de Freitas. Even now there is, above the town of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), the Fajã do Alemão, which the people corruptly call “do limão”.’

We may therefore regard the Pole Henry the German as the original founder of this settlement, and it was also he who had the first chapel built there. Senhorinha Alves, widow of Henry the German, married secondly João Rodrigues de Freitas, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) from the Algarve. Together they instituted an entailed estate (*morgadio*), seated in the said chapel, whose present representatives are the Viscounts of Geraz do Lima. A son of the founder, also named João Rodrigues de Freitas, declares in his will, made in 1520, that he was the founder of the chapel of Santa Maria Madalena, which must therefore have been built before that year. We must infer from this that Henry the German built the original chapel and that João Rodrigues de Freitas later rebuilt it, or founded the chapel of Santa Maria Madalena anew, since it was common at that time for people who had merely rebuilt churches and chapels, or carried out notable repairs to them, to be described as their founders.

Before this place became an independent parish, it had its own chaplains. In 1538 they were granted the right to administer the sacraments to the inhabitants of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town), and in 1539 the right to build a baptismal font, at the request of the patron of the chapel, then João Rodrigues, whom we believe to have been its founder or a close descendant of his.

This parish was separated from that of Ponta do Sol and made an independent parish by Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto on 1 February 1582, its first parish priest being Father João Leandro Afonso. The royal decree (alvará régio) of 22 September 1587 set the parish priest’s annual salary at 20,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The royal decree of 10 September of the following year increased it by half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine. Two years later, by a royal decree of 15 November, this stipend became 16,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine, and it was raised by 3,000 *réis* a year by the royal decree of 9 December 1611. We know of another royal decree, dated 28 July 1649, which set the parish priest’s annual salary at 19,000 *réis* in cash, one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a quarter *pipas* of wine.

The text of Gaspar Frutuoso, written in 1590, contains the following references to this parish: ‘. . . Magdalena, a thing so singular and noble for the chapel of this saint which the inhabitants built there, where much profit is gathered from sugar.’ Elsewhere in the *Saudades* we read: ‘Half a league from the town of Ponta do Sol, along the sea, lies the parish of Magdalena, of up to thirty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’). It has a sugar mill (engenho) which belonged to one Manuel Dias, and a fine estate of good land under canes, and much fresh water. In this parish there is a chapel of Our Lady of the Angels (*Nossa Senhora dos Anjos*) which, though small, is a rich house, with a small altarpiece, fresh and well adorned; beside it is a cool spring beneath some boulders, among sugar-cane plantations of very handsome canes.’ (See Anjos 1-71). This locality of Anjos now belongs to the parish of Canhas and was once part of the parish of Ponta do Sol; we do not know whether it may perhaps have belonged to the parish of Madalena, as Gaspar Frutuoso states.
In this parish stood the chapel of Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria), of which today only a heap of rubble remains. It was built at the behest of Father João da Silva Alves.

The soil of this place is remarkably fertile, and from the very first years of colonisation it was farmed extensively. Sugar cane was grown on a large scale, a sugar mill was soon set up to make sugar, and the place became an important centre of sugar production. Even today its land is very fertile for the so-called rich crops, and its production of bananas for export is also notable.

According to the 1920 census, this parish (*freguesia*) had 1,093 inhabitants, scattered across the localities of Passo, Vargem, Lombo, Banda de Além, Palmeira, Torreão, Ribeira da Madalena, Moledos, Achada and Rua.
It has an official boys’ school, founded in 1882, and a mobile mixed school, which has been running since 1919 (1921).
The parish is irrigated by the levadas (irrigation channels) of the Ribeira da Madalena and of the Nateiro, and by the Levada Nova (‘new channel’).

The physician and surgeon António Policarpo dos Passos Sousa, who for many years served as secretary of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Ponta do Sol, was a native of the parish of Madalena do Mar. According to the testimony of his fellow students and contemporaries, he was a man of extraordinary talent, which an untimely death and other special circumstances prevented from shining with the brilliance that might have been wished. He cultivated poetry with distinction, leaving several compositions that were highly regarded in their day.
Father António João de Lessa, who died in Brazil, where he achieved distinction, was also a native of this parish (see that entry).

The Ribeira da Madalena flows into the sea on the coast of this parish. In 1932, where it crosses the parish of Canhas, its left bank suffered a great landslide, which caused enormous damage and largely blocked the bed of the stream. This event contributed greatly to what happened on 30 December 1939, when, swollen by the heavy winter rains that fell at that time, the stream rose to the most frightening proportions. It swept away several dozen dwellings in its path, killed a number of people and caused incalculable damage, making it one of the greatest calamities caused by floods on this island.

Madeira (anthropology)

As is well known, ‘anthropology’, in its etymological meaning and in its most general sense, is the study of man or of humanity. Commonly, however, the term is used to designate the study of the physical characteristics of man and of the laws governing their principal variations. When this study is applied to a particular region, its essential factors include the races predominant in the original settlement and their origins, contact with other peoples over time, geographical situation, orographic and hydrographic features, landscape, climate, the productivity of the soil, social and economic conditions, local usages and customs, etc. etc. To these are added the various strictly environmental circumstances of a psychological, ethnological and religious character, which are also of valuable and indispensable help to such a study.

A work of this kind, which demands special preparation and a broad knowledge of the environment, remains entirely to be done for Madeira. There are, however, some scattered materials that could be put to good use for this purpose. The principal ones to mention are the first chapters of the second volume of the esteemed work ‘Zargo’s Islands’ (*Ilhas de Zargo*) and the information scattered through the pages of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and its learned annotations.

Throughout this *Elucidário*, and especially in the article Madeira (island), there are various notes of some value for such a study. They are also found in the articles *Colonia* (Contract of), Old Customs, Popular Beliefs, Slaves, Foreigners, Dress, Ethnological Influences, Entails, Moors, Settlement, *Rambles in Madeira*, Pilgrimages and Peasant (*Vilão*).
Madeira (archipelago)

The importance of this archipelago is set out concisely but strikingly in the following words from the authoritative pen of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*): ‘This archipelago has been the subject of study by learned naturalists, both foreign and Portuguese. It is famous, especially the island of Madeira, for the fertility of its soil, its excellent wines, the breathtaking beauty of its landscape and the healthiness of its climate. It is historically notable as the first of the Portuguese discoveries in the 15th century and, afterwards, until the close of the 16th century, as the secular and ecclesiastical metropolis of our overseas dominions and the emporium of our colonial navigation and commerce. For this reason the Madeiran archives, especially those of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, that of Machico, that of the former and now extinct Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) and that of the Civil Government of Funchal, hold precious documents and records, perhaps not to be found elsewhere, for the history of the institutions and government of our possessions beyond the sea.’

The Madeira archipelago consists of the islands of Madeira (see Madeira (island)), Porto Santo (see that entry) and the Desertas group (1-357), which comprises Deserta Grande (1-356), Ilhéu Chão (1-269) and Bugio (1 - 176). Because this archipelago lies relatively close to the European continent, and also because it is regarded as a group of ‘Adjacent Islands’ (Ilhas Adjacentes) of a country on that continent, there has been no shortage of geographers who have considered Madeira part of Europe. This opinion, however, is not followed or adopted today by any authoritative writer.

Its geographical position has been the subject of some disagreement. After an in-depth study of the question and a comparison of various charts, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo adopted the following geographical coordinates as the most reliable: the archipelago lies between the parallels 33° 7′50″ and 32° 22′20″ north latitude, and between the meridians 16° 16′30″ and 17° 16′ 38″ west longitude (Greenwich).

The archipelago lies between Western Europe, which faces it to the north-east, the Moroccan coast of West Africa, which runs from east to south-east of it, the Azores archipelago to the north-west and the Canary Islands to the south. The nearest point of the west coast of Morocco to the Madeiran archipelago is Cape Cantin, which lies at roughly the same latitude as Madeira and is about 60 miles equidistant from the towns of Mazagan to the north and Mogador to the south. Its distance from mainland Portugal is approximately 500 miles, and 350 from Cape Cantin, on the west coast of Africa.

The relative positions of the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo and the Desertas group form a scalene triangle. Its shortest side is the channel between the Ilhéu de Fora (‘outer islet’), at the eastern tip of Madeira (Ponta de São Lourenço), and the Prego do Mar (‘sea nail’) or Ilhéu do Navio (‘ship islet’), near the Ilhéu Chão (Desertas). The next longest side is formed by the channel (the Travessa) running from the same Ilhéu de Fora (Ponta de São Lourenço) to the Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal (Porto Santo). The longest side is the channel stretching from the Ilhéu de Baixo or da Cal (Porto Santo), already mentioned, to the Prego do Mar or Ilhéu Chão (Desertas). The three channels measure 11, 27 and 32 miles respectively, these being the distances that separate Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas group from one another.

The extreme points of this archipelago are generally given as follows: to the north, the Rocha do Nordeste or Ilhéu de Fora (Porto Santo); to the south, the Ponta da Agulha or Ponta do Sul, at the southern tip of the Bugio (Desertas); to the east, the Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’) or dos Dragoeiros (Porto Santo); and to the west, Ponta do Pargo (Madeira).

Estimates of the area of the whole archipelago, and especially of each of its islands, vary. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, who treated this subject at some length in his notable article in the *Dic. Univ. Port.* II, says that some authors put the total area of the archipelago at more than a thousand square kilometres, and that it was later accepted as being around 800 kilometres. He concludes by stating that the most recent calculations, which he believes to be closest to the truth, give the whole archipelago an area of 560 square kilometres: 500 kilometres for the island of Madeira, 50 for Porto Santo and 10 for the small Desertas group.
Various official documents, and more recently the ‘Censo da População’ published in 1934, state that the area of the island of Madeira is 740,k62 square kilometres and that of Porto Santo 42,k217.

Apart from the cities of Lisbon and Porto, the Madeira archipelago is the region of our country with the highest population density: the ‘Censo’ already cited gives a figure of 270 inhabitants per square kilometre at the present time. The article Population will give a detailed account, by municipality (*concelho*) and parish, of population movement throughout the archipelago. Meanwhile, we shall say here that the census taken in 1940 gives our archipelago a total of 251,798 inhabitants, 249,097 in Madeira and 2,701 on Porto Santo.

The Madeira archipelago and the small group of the Savage Islands (Selvagens) (see Selvagens) make up the administrative district of Funchal, whose capital is the city of the same name. (See the articles on the district, judicial district (*comarca*), municipality, city and diocese of Funchal, which give a brief account of the organisation of the various public services, civil, religious and military, that have their seats there.)

The surveys carried out a few years ago by the ‘Hydrographic Mission of the Adjacent Islands’ (*Missão Hidrográfica das Ilhas Adjacentes*) show that the figures for the area of the islands of this archipelago differ in part from those known until now. The special conditions under which this work was done make it entirely trustworthy, and so we shall record here some of the new data obtained by this ‘Hydrographic Mission’, transcribing them from the first volume of the work ‘Zargo’s Islands’ (*Ilhas de Zargo*).
The island of Madeira has an area of 728 square kilometres, Porto Santo 49, Deserta Grande 10, Bugio 3 and Ilhéu Chão 380 square metres.

From the same source come these figures for the length of Madeira’s coastline: from Ponta do Barlavento (‘windward point’) to Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), 37,200 metres; from Ponta da Cruz to Ponta do Pargo, 40 950; from Ponta do Pargo to Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’), 7,575; from Ponta do Tristão to Ponta de São Jorge (‘St George Point’), 32,400; and from Ponta de São Jorge to Ponta do Barlavento, 33,225, making a total of 151,350 metres. The coastline of the island of Porto Santo measures 37,800 metres, that of Deserta Grande 26,700, Bugio 17,000 and Ilhéu Chão 3,700.

The greatest length is given as follows: from Ponta de São Lourenço to Ponta do Pargo, 57,000 metres, and from Ponta de São Lourenço to Ponta do Tristão, 52,650, while the breadth between Ponta da Cruz and Ponta de São Jorge is 22,900 metres. Porto Santo measures 11,600 metres in length and 5,000 in breadth; Deserta Grande 11,000 in length and 1,900 in breadth; Bugio 7,500 in length and 700 in breadth; and Ilhéu Chão 1,600 in length and 500 in breadth.

Madeira (hydrographic features: bays, coves, landing places and beaches)

As we have already stated on page 116 of this volume, it is not easy to draw a strict distinction in meaning between the terms ‘bay’ (*baía*) and ‘cove’ (*enseada*). When referring to the inlets found along the coastline, we therefore class as ‘bays’ only those of Funchal (p. 66 of this volume) and Porto Santo (see that entry).
The small coves of Madeira are the following: Abra, Machico, Garajau, Câmara de Lobos, Lugar de Baixo, Santa Cruz, Reis Magos and Porto Moniz (see those entries).

According to an official report, the landing places (*portos*) of Madeira were until recently graded as follows. Those of Funchal (see Funchal (bay) and the harbour of Funchal) and of the south of the island of Porto Santo (see that entry) were considered good. Those of Abra, Machico, Santa Cruz, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Porto Moniz and Porto da Cruz were deemed fair. Those of Caniçal, Porto Novo, Reis Magos, Oliveira, Campanário, Lugar de Baixo, Madalena do Mar, Anjos, Fajã do Mar, Calheta, Jardim do Mar, Paul do Mar, Pesqueiro, Seixal, Fajã da Areia, Ponta Delgada, Boaventura, São Jorge and Faial were considered poor. The landing places of the parishes of Porto Moniz and Porto da Cruz are regarded as good when the winds blow from the southern quarter, for at such times no traffic at all is possible along the whole southern coast of Madeira, although this happens only a few times each year. Over the last thirty years, conditions at the landing places of these localities have improved considerably, thanks to the building of small quays and landing stages and to the extension and repair of those already in existence (see each of the entries named above).

Of considerable interest on this subject is the article Maritime Distances, on page 367 of vol. I, which gives a table of the number of miles separating the various landing places of Madeira from one another.

It has been said that Madeira has no beaches, perhaps because they are not sandy and are of limited length. Indeed, the beaches of this island, with the exception of Prainha (‘little beach’) at Caniçal, are made up of small stones or rounded pebbles of dark basalt; all of them look sombre, and walking on them is difficult and uncomfortable. By way of compensation, the neighbouring island of Porto Santo has one of the finest and longest beaches in the whole country. The principal beaches of Madeira, some of them very short, are the following: Prainha, Caniçal, Machico, Seixo, Santa Cruz, Porto Novo, Reis Magos, Funchal, Formosa (see those entries), Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Lugar de Baixo, Madalena do Mar, Calheta and Paul do Mar, on the south coast, and those of Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Fajã da Areia, Ponta Delgada, São Jorge and Porto da Cruz on the north coast. (See those entries, under the heading ‘Ports’ or ‘Beaches’, and also the article Ports.)
Madeira (hydrographic features: shoals and islets)
See the article Ilhéus (‘islets’) on p. 138 and each of the names mentioned there.

The reefs or shoals near the coast that break the surface of the ocean, or that lie only a little below it even at low tide, are generally known in Madeira as *Baixas*. Those worth mentioning are the Aguagem shoal, south of the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros (‘islet of the landing places’), near the Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’); and those of Atanásio, Badajeira, Barbeiros, Bispo, off the coast of Câmara de Lobos, Carneiro, Cesto, near the coast of Jardim do Mar, Conceição, Cotrim, off Porto Santo, Furado or Nariz, Galé, Galeão, Guincho, Junqueira, Larga, Leão, Marinheiros, Neta, Raiz, São Pedro, Três Irmãs, Machico and Pôrto do Moniz (see those entries).
Madeira (hydrographic features: streams)

These natural watercourses, which generally run along the beds of deep, narrow valleys, are very numerous on this island and carry a great volume of water in the winter season. They rise on the slopes of the central mountain range and flow into the ocean, some of them fed by tributary streams that increase their volume and the speed of their course. ‘All of them, in winter,’ says the illustrious annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘carry abundant water, often torrential: they then fill up and at times overflow, bringing down from the mountains thousands of tons of boulders of greater or lesser size, many of them so large that they can afterwards be removed only in pieces; and all of them, rolling in the torrent against one another, make a sinister noise as they collide, until, blocking the beds of these same streams, they raise them above the adjoining land, and this land, once blocked, does not remain, but is carried off by the diverted waters a great distance out to sea, dissolved into mud; in summer, however, their flow of water becomes scanty, and some streams even run dry, because the water is diverted both for irrigating the land along their banks and into the levadas (irrigation channels), which take up the running water there and carry it to fertilise distant crops across the whole coastal area of the island.’ From time to time these streams turn into raging torrents which burst their beds, flood the banks on either side and violently sweep away large stretches of cultivated land, animal pens and even dwelling houses, at times causing considerable loss of life and property to those who live nearby.

In the article Ribeiras (‘streams’) we shall give a detailed list of the streams of this island, naming the places where they rise and reach the sea and describing their course, and also indicating their tributaries and the points where they join.
See waterfalls (*Quedas de Água*).
Madeira (relief: slopes, plateaux and valleys)

The almost unbelievably rugged terrain of Madeira and the capricious, varied configuration of its relief would deserve a long and detailed description. Lack of space and of reliable data does not allow us to provide one, so we confine ourselves to a brief list of the principal mountain heights and their altitudes, and of the headlands, slopes and hillsides, valleys, plateaux, depths, etc., found across the 500 square kilometres of the whole surface of this island.

‘It consists, says the *Dicionário Universal Portuguez Ilustrado*, already cited, of a lofty range of mountains from twelve hundred to nineteen hundred metres high, from whose back a number of peaks rise. It runs from east to west from Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’) until it finally forks, extending north-westwards over Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) to form Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’), and sending out a smaller branch to the south-west, whose tip is Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’). This longitudinal range, descending with its foothills and some secondary spurs to the north, west and south along its whole length down to the sea, divides the island into three great regions, namely: the northern, from Ponta de São Lourenço to Ponta do Tristão; the western, from Ponta do Tristão to Ponta do Pargo, which covers the territory within the said fork; and the southern, which runs from Ponta do Pargo to Ponta de São Lourenço. However, as the western region slopes towards the north-west and is already largely under the influence of the northern quarter, seafarers, and with them Madeirans in general, distinguish only two regions: one, which they call the Costa do Sul (‘south coast’), being the one marked out above on this side, and the other the north coast (*Costa do Norte*), which comprises the northern and western regions mentioned’ (on these coasts, see what is said on p. 324 of vol. I).

As already stated, the mountain range that crosses Madeira lengthwise from east to west, with high summits and without a break, clearly separates the northern and southern coasts. Along its back rise many peaks of considerable height, among which stand out Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’), the highest of all, Pico do Cidrão, Torrinhas, Canário and Arieiro. Besides those already named, we shall mention the best known: Pico do Castanho, Pico da Maia, Pico do Arco de São Jorge, Pico das Torres, Pico da Neve, Pico do Poiso, Pico da Lagoa, Pico de Santo António, Pico do Arrebentão, Pico do Infante, Pico Grande, Pico dos Bodes, Pico da Urze, Pico do Gato, Pico da Amendoeira, Pico Queimado, Pico da Suna, etc. As offshoots of the mountains and peaks of the central range, many other heights also stand out, sometimes extending as far as the coastal areas. Among these we shall mention Pico dos Barcelos, Pico da Cruz, Pico do Cardo, Pico dos Eirós, Pico do Facho, Pico das Favas, Pico da Cruz, Pico da Relva, etc. (see each of these entries).

For further detail, we must draw the reader’s attention to the extensive account on p. 52 ff. of vol. I, which gives the ‘altitudes’ of a large number of mountain heights and of other points especially worth knowing. On this subject, the data supplied by the Hydrographic Mission of the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes), published on p. 95 of vol. I of the esteemed work ‘Zargo’s Islands’ (*Ilhas de Zargo*), are of particular interest.

The only stretch of ground in Madeira’s extremely rugged terrain that deserves the name of plateau is the Paul da Serra (see that entry). Nevertheless, the name plateau is commonly given to the small plains of Santo da Serra (see Lagoa), in the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name, the Achada de Santana (‘plateau of Santana’), in the parish of Santana, and the plain of Achadas, in the parish of Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’).

The principal points or projections of this island’s coastline are the following: the point of São Lourenço, the longest, which has several secondary points named Furado Abra, Dedais, Rosto, etc.; Ponta da Queimada, Ponta de Santa Catarina, Ponta do Guindaste, Ponta da Atalaia, Ponta da Oliveira, Ponta do Garajau, Ponta da Cruz, Ponta da Água, Ponta do Sol, Ponta da Galé, Ponta do Jardim, Ponta da Fajã da Ovelha, Ponta do Pargo, Ponta do Tristão, Ponta do Porto Moniz, Ponta Delgada, Ponta de São Jorge, Ponta de Santana, Ponta do Cortado and Ponta de Larano (see each of those entries).

The mountainous and extremely rugged terrain of this island gives rise to many valleys, some of remarkable depth, though in general they are of fairly limited length. The principal ones are the valley of Funchal, especially at the locality called Val Formoso; that of Machico, which stretches from the beach of the town (*vila*) of the same name between the banks of its stream; that of Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’), at the northern end of the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’); that of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), lying in the drainage basin of the stream of the same name and including the town and its surroundings; that of Penha de Águia, which curves round the cliff of that name (see Penha de Águia); that of Metade, near Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’); and that of Ribeira da Janela, between the banks of the stream of that name (see Vales). The articles Fajãs (‘coastal flats’) and Quebradas are related to this subject.

Madeira and the Isle of Love

Anyone moderately familiar with the work of Camões knows that the well-known episode of the Isle of Love (*Ilha dos Amores*) has given rise to many questions of a critical and literary nature, and that a sizeable Portuguese literature deals with them at length. Leaving aside the older authors, it is enough to name contemporaries such as Teófilo Braga, the Count of Ficalho, Epifânio Dias, José Maria Rodrigues, Ludovice de Meneses and others still to gauge the interest this subject has aroused among many commentators on *The Lusiads* (*Os Lusíadas*). One of the points most widely discussed is the ‘location’ or ‘geographical situation’ of the fantastic island. It is this point that is of particular interest to us here, because of the close or remote connection that may exist between it and the island of Madeira.

It is true that most critics and interpreters regard the episode as a product of pure poetic fiction, which Camões never deliberately placed at any particular point in the known world. On this view he either drew solely on the boldest flights of his ardent imagination, or sought inspiration in certain poems of universal renown, such as Homer’s *Odyssey* and Ariosto’s *Orlando Furioso*, or in various Arab and Indian legends whose narratives resemble the Camonian description. There is no shortage, however, of writers of recognised authority who have maintained – not, we would say, with absolutely unanswerable arguments, but certainly with very weighty and acceptable presumptions – that on his long voyage to Africa, India, China and other Eastern lands Luís de Camões found fertile ground for inspiring the invention of his episode in the countless islands that his enraptured eyes beheld across the vastness of the two oceans.

Both hypotheses have been put forward, and both have found their fervent champions. ‘The poet,’ says a notable commentator on *The Lusiads*, ‘by a graceful effort of the imagination, took a mythological island with all its features and transported it from the regions of the Mediterranean – the homeland of ancient poetry – to the seas of the East... Its true geographical situation lies in the poet’s imagination, and it is not badly placed there.’ Some interpreters, however, no less illustrious and respected, allow that the islands of Anjediva, Ceylon, Zanzibar, Ascension Island, Terceira and Madeira may each have been a stage on which the glorious poet ‘rested’ his incandescent imagination and received the first motifs of inspiration for the design of his sublime and still unsurpassed creation.
In recent years, had a kind of plebiscite been held among those who have expressed an opinion on this subject, Madeira would have gathered the largest and most authoritative number of votes.

In a pamphlet of our own, entitled *Camões e a Madeira*, we also dealt with this subject at some length, and we have just (1938) read with particular pleasure another work on the same theme, which continues to attract the attention of new and fervent devotees.

A small pamphlet entitled *Ilha dos Amores–Dados para a sua identificação* has recently been issued by the ‘Tipografia da Liga dos Combatentes da Grande Guerra’ in Lisbon. It comes from the pen of Mr Henrique Manuel Terra Negra, who has already published several studies of the work of Camões. It opens with the following dedication: *Á Flôr do Oceano–Pérola do Atlântico - Ilha Maravilhosa* (‘To the Flower of the Ocean – Pearl of the Atlantic – Marvellous Island’).

It is a curious work of literary exegesis that deserves to be read with due appreciation and is of particular interest to scholars and devotees of these subjects. It is true that we did not find in it, nor could we have expected to, conclusive proof that Camões had in mind the fame Madeira already enjoyed in his day when his imagination devised that marvellous episode of *The Lusiads*. It would not, however, be too bold to suppose so, if we consider carefully the words of praise the poet set down in the 5th stanza of Canto V of his immortal poem. Here he became a great panegyrist of this island, and he was without doubt the precursor of all those who have extolled its natural beauties.

The pamphlet we are referring to cites many passages of the poem, whose interpretations serve as the basis for various hypotheses, presumptions and conjectures. Skilfully constructed as they are, however, they do not amount to arguments proving the thesis it seeks to demonstrate. Some of these interpretations contain excessively bold assertions, as the following passage shows, which does not even approach an apparent reality:

‘The flora of the Isle of Love is the same as that of Madeira, because both are the same island. We shall say as much of the fauna, even though there are timid gazelles there (IX, 63, F), either to embellish the poetic style or because they existed on the island at that time. In Portugal there are no bears (we mean the zoological species), but there used to be. The Madeira of 1498 differs from the marvellous island of our own day. That is natural: more than 400 years have passed.’

There are, however, other interpretations which, applied to the texts of Camões with greater critical rigour and more thorough analysis, might lead to hypotheses and conjectures of sound plausibility, and possibly even to the discovery of incontrovertible truths. Meanwhile, we consider some of these interpretations quite felicitous and even ingeniously constructed; besides revealing remarkable perspicacity, they also show a deep knowledge of our national Bible.
We are pleased to record the closing words of this interesting pamphlet, which now takes its place in the already vast bibliography of Madeira:
‘As we conclude these brief notes on the fabulous episode of the Isle of Love, which is (like all fables) a mixture of truths and fictions, we joyfully salute and congratulate from here the

Fresh and lovely Flower of the Ocean, enamoured island, set there in the midst of the kingdom of liquid and gentle crystal, adorned with the gifts of Flora and Zephyr; marvellous Island of Madeira, so called from its many trees, beautiful, joyful and delightful, for whose sake the Cyprian Goddess forgot Cyprus, Cnidus, Paphos and Cythera;
divine isle, Pearl of the Atlantic, which is the angelic island painted by Camões in the epic of our famous people.’
Madeira and Afonso de Albuquerque

Anyone moderately versed in the history of Portuguese rule in the East knows that the great Afonso de Albuquerque, for political, economic and religious reasons, had conceived the bold plan of invading Egypt. Part of this plan was the intention of diverting some of the headwaters of the Nile from their true beds, perhaps by means of a series of laborious drainage works.

What not everyone may know, however, is that Afonso de Albuquerque was counting on the ‘cabouqueiros da Madeira’ (Madeiran quarrymen) to carry out this part of his audacious and perhaps unrealisable project.

It is worth recalling here what we have already said elsewhere about the colossal work of building our levadas (irrigation channels), which always deserves to be given the greatest prominence. For this hazardous and gruelling construction it was at times necessary to skirt high, craggy mountains, cross sheer ravines and tunnel through hills. It was a dangerous and titanic labour lasting many years, costing large sums of capital and even a good many lives, and it gave the land the blood that makes it fertile and the plants the sap and vitality that make them produce abundantly.

The fame of the tenacious and persistent efforts of the early Madeiran settlers in clearing the virgin land, and particularly in the difficult and hazardous construction of the aqueducts meant to irrigate it, had reached Portugal and had reached India.

It is no wonder, then, that the most distinguished governor of India should have thought of the ‘cabouqueiros da Madeira’, as he calls the rural labourers of this island in his most interesting and instructive *Cartas*, now published in several volumes, to carry out the idea he had conceived for the invasion of Egypt.

As we are unable, at the time of writing these lines, to reproduce Afonso de Albuquerque’s words verbatim, we shall transcribe from Pinheiro Chagas’s ‘History of Portugal’ (III, 322) the passages that concern this subject and fully bear out our assertion.

‘What is quite certain, and generally unknown, is that this project, soon forgotten, received, so to speak, a beginning of execution: the governor’s own son, the author of the *Commentarios*, states that his father wrote more than once to King Manuel I, begging him to send to Abyssinia a few hundred of those peasants from Madeira who were reputed to be the most persevering workers of that age at cutting through mountains, accustomed by the nature of the island’s terrain to levelling mountains and flattening valleys in order to build levadas with which to water their sugar cane more easily.’

Madeira (history)

Many valuable materials exist, scattered through various printed works and some unpublished ones, besides the documents recorded in the public archives. They would provide the essential materials for a short historical study of the Madeiran archipelago which, in a concise outline and an overall synthesis, would give an account of the main phases of its already long active life of five centuries, from the beginning of the first settlement to the present day. This interesting sketch could be drawn in little more than a hundred pages. It remains entirely to be done, and it is much to be regretted that no one has yet come forward to undertake it.

We have already outlined this subject at greater length in the article History of Madeira, on pp. 124-127 of this volume, to which we refer the reader. Closely related to this subject are the articles Bibliography and ‘Materials for Madeiran History’ (*Elementos para a História Madeirense*), on pp. 143 and 386 of vol. 1 of this work, and Madeira in the Torre do Tombo (national archives) (*Torre do Tombo*), besides many other articles.
Madeira (island)

It is the largest and most important of the islands of the archipelago. It lies between 32° 52′ 8″ and 32° 37′ 25″ north latitude, and between 16° 39′ 30″ and 17° 16′ 38″ west longitude (Greenwich). It is twenty-one and a half miles from Porto Santo (from Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’) to the Ilhéu de Baixo (‘lower islet’), or Ilhéu da Cal) and eleven miles from the Desertas (from Ponta de São Lourenço to Ilhéu Chão (‘flat islet’)). From the harbour of Funchal to the anchorage of the town (*vila*) of Porto Santo the distance is forty and a half miles. The island stretches from east to west and has a ‘shape tending towards a pentagon’, roughly defined by the points of São Lourenço to the east, Santa Cruz to the south, Pargo and Tristão to the west, and São Jorge to the north. Its greatest length, east to west, between the extreme limits of Ponta de São Lourenço and Ponta do Tristão, is 67 kilometres, and its greatest width, north to south, between the extreme limits of Ponta de São Jorge and Ponta da Cruz, is 28 kilometres. The perimeter of the coast is conjectured to be approximately 157 kilometres, and its area 500 square kilometres.

A high mountain range running from east to west divides Madeira into two coasts, the southern and the northern. In this range, whose heights rise from 1000 to 1861 metres, the island’s great streams have their source. In winter they carry large volumes of water, which have quite often caused damage in Funchal and at other points along the coast. The slopes of the central mountains are generally steeper on the north side than on the south. On the north side there are only two passable landing places, Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) and Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), whereas on the southern coast there are several coves and bays where ships and boats can find shelter from the prevailing winds. The main spurs of these mountains are the Penha de Águia (‘eagle crag’) and the Cortado de Santana (‘Santana cut’) on the north coast, and Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), Cabo Girão and Cabo Garajau (‘tern cape’) on the south coast.

The highest summits of central Madeira are Pico Ruivo, Pico das Torres, Pico do Canário, Pico do Areeiro, Pico de Santo António, Pico Grande and Pico das Torrinhas. They surround the Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), a vast *profundidade* (deep, roughly circular mountain basin) regarded by some geologists as a crater and by others as a valley of erosion. The most notable streams of the island are those of Machico, Santa Cruz, São Pedro, Porto Novo, João Gomes, Santa Luzia, São João, the Socorridos, Câmara de Lobos, the Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Madalena, São Bartolomeu, Janela, Seixal, São Vicente, the Moinhos, São Jorge and Faial.

In the bay of Funchal ships ride at anchor in complete safety in all winds except those from the quarters between south-west and south-east by way of south. Around the bay, on the lower slopes of the mountains and rising like an amphitheatre, stands the city of the same name. It is the capital of the island and of the whole archipelago, and has long been known for the mildness of its climate, the beauty of its surroundings, the lovely *quintas* (country estates) that adorn it and the courtesy of its inhabitants.
The island of Madeira has only one city, Funchal, and six towns, which, starting from the east, are Machico, Santa Cruz, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Calheta and São Vicente.

The places in the interior of the island most worth visiting for the superb panoramas they command are Rabaçal, Monte Medonho, the Fontes da Ribeira do Inferno, the Cumeada de São Vicente, Pico Ruivo, Pico do Areeiro, the Boca dos Namorados, Ribeiro Frio, the Ribeira de São Jorge, Santana, Pico da Suna, etc. On the coast, too, there are places that deserve to be seen, such as Piedade, Ponta de São Lourenço, Garajau, Praia Formosa, Fojo, Cabo Girão, the mouth of the Ribeira da Janela and that of the Ribeira do Inferno, the Ribeira de João Delgado, the chapel of São Vicente, Entroza, the Ponte de São Jorge, the Rocha do Navio and Porto da Cruz. Many streams have beautiful waterfalls, and from every high point one can admire wide and varied views of unsurpassable beauty.
The Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) is the only plain of any size on Madeira, but it is an inhospitable place in winter because of the violence of the storms that break there.

Madeira’s roads are often appalling, and on some the gradient is so steep that they can be travelled only with great effort. The visitor can reach almost every spot on the outskirts of Funchal by ox-drawn cart, but to reach certain places in the interior and climb the rugged heights that make up a large part of the island, one must resort to the horse or the hammock (*rede*, slung from a pole and carried by two bearers), the latter being the most suitable means of transport for certain kinds of journey. (1921).

Funchal is linked to the Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), above the church of Monte, by a lift or rack railway (1921), and Machico and Ribeira Brava can today be reached in reasonable comfort, since the roads now take motor traffic. The Cumeada de São Vicente, a point in the interior with astonishing views over both the north and the south of the island, has been accessible by car since 1916, and work has already begun on other roads intended to make it easier for tourists to discover the natural beauties of our land. In recent years the roads have been greatly developed, as will be seen in the article ‘Viação’.

Madeira produces vines, sugar cane, cereals, sweet potatoes, potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word), onions, various useful cucurbits and legumes, flax, sorghum, etc., and its flora is extremely rich: in the *quintas* and gardens one sees plants from almost every region of the globe, thriving as well as in their native lands. Besides all the European fruit trees, the island has custard apples, bananas, guavas, papayas, passion fruit and other species native to hot countries.

The seal, or monk seal (*lobo marinho*, literally ‘sea wolf’), and two bats are the only mammals that appear to be native, but birds, and above all molluscs and insects, are represented on the island by a great number of species. Madeiran waters yield a great number of fish species, some with very tasty flesh, and the turtle is not rare, although its eggs have never been found on Madeira or Porto Santo.

There are no metal mines or sulphur deposits on the island, but iron pyrites and specular iron have been found in small quantities near Ponta do Sol, and in Santo António and other places there are waters more or less rich in iron carbonate. Limestone is found in São Vicente, and in São Jorge there is a deposit of rather impure lignite.

Rain is scarce in the hot season, and in some years not a single drop falls in the low-lying region of Madeira during July and August. To remedy this shortage, numerous channels, or levadas (irrigation channels) (see that entry), have been built to carry water from the interior to various places. It is thanks to irrigation, practised here since very ancient times, that certain crops survive not only through the summer but also at other times when rain fails or is sparse. Some levadas were built by the State and others by private individuals, the latter being far more numerous than the former.

Madeira exports its excellent wines, wickerwork, embroidery, onions, butter, sugar, etc., and imports cereals, textiles, olive oil, paraffin, salt, grocery goods, etc. Among Madeiran industries, those deserving special mention are embroidery, the manufacture of sugar and spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine), butter-making, tuna canning, the weaving of straw for hats of various kinds, and wickerwork.

The first settlers of Madeira were the donataries and the people who accompanied them. Frutuoso relates that, when it came to settling the island, the King ‘ordered that the homicides in the kingdom’s gaols be handed over, of whom João Gonçalves Zarco would take none guilty of offences against the faith, or of treason, or of theft; of those guilty of other crimes, fugitives, he took all there were, and they were well treated by him; and of the other people, those who of their own will wished to seek a living and fortune were many, most of them from the Algarve’.

But if it is certain that the first people to colonise the lands of the archipelago came from Portugal, and especially from the Algarve, it is no less certain that this nucleus of settlers was joined over time by various elements from other parts. The sugar trade, and later the wine trade, drew numerous foreigners to Madeira in search of fortune, while many Moorish captives and Black and Canarian slaves were brought to this island to clear the land and be employed in other work.

Around 1486 there were many foreigners in Madeira who had become sugar growers and manufacturers, and for this reason they were twice ordered to leave the island and afterwards readmitted. When Frutuoso wrote ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) in 1590, there were many English and Flemish families in Funchal, who carried on their business in the Rua dos Mercadores. The Flemish colony, still important at the beginning of the 17th century, later disappeared or merged with the Madeiran population, whereas the English colony survived and even grew from 1640 onwards, coming in the 19th century to hold a real preponderance in the island’s trade.

Castilian rule, which lasted for 60 years, brought a great number of Spaniards to Madeira; and when the British troops withdrew from this island after occupying it from 1801 to 1802 and from 1807 to 1814, they left some families settled here.

From what has been said, it is clear that the population of Madeira is very far from homogeneous. Intermixing in varying proportions and in various directions over more than 4 centuries has somewhat modified the original dominant type, giving rise to variations that often do not accord with the island’s geographical position.

It is at village festivals and processions that one can best observe the traces left in the Madeiran population by the various elements that settled on this island from the middle of the 15th century. Fair skin, blond hair and blue eyes, characteristic of the peoples of northern Europe, are not rare among the women, and it may be said that 20 to 30 per cent of children are blond until the age of 6 to 8. The men are as a rule more or less dark, but the blond type is sometimes seen among them too, though much less often than among the women.

The Berber type, marked by a swarthy complexion, especially in men, a somewhat hooked nose and straight black hair, appears in a somewhat modified form at some points on the east coast, and it is natural that it should derive chiefly from the Moors who once lived on the island. ‘The city of Funchal,’ says Dr Azevedo in his notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’, ‘had its Moorish quarter, and tradition holds that many Moors lived in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol.’

It is likely that the arrival of many Castilian families in Madeira during Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) contributed somewhat to the spread of the Berber type on the island; nevertheless, it was not from Spain, where it is common, but from Morocco that this type first reached us, a type still so easy to recognise among the population of certain Madeiran localities.

In the 18th-century parish registers there are many records of baptisms, marriages and deaths of Black slaves, and the narrative of Captain Cook’s second voyage states that in 1772 there was a prodigious number of Black and mixed-race people in Madeira, some free, others slaves. Dr Azevedo, who wrote the notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ in 1870, says that people of mixed African descent were then numerous, ‘especially in Curral das Freiras and in the north of the island’.

Certain individuals, mainly from the lower classes of society, still show their affinities with the Ethiopian race in their tightly curled hair, the shape of the nose and the colour of the whites of the eyes, and sometimes of the skin; but these affinities are tending to disappear through intermixing, and it may even be said that they no longer exist in a great many localities on the island.

The country people of Madeira are as a rule of vigorous constitution and endure the greatest fatigue without feeling the effects. The sanguine temperament is common among them, whereas in the city the bilious-sanguine temperament predominates, mixed to a greater or lesser degree sometimes with the lymphatic and sometimes with the nervous.

‘Great robberies and murders,’ says Dr Barral, ‘are rare in Madeira; the studied, organised, immoral and slanderous begging of the great cities does not yet exist there; and a great number of the island’s inhabitants have no idea of the extraordinary crimes committed today in Europe, in the midst of civilisation.’

Dr Hans Sloane, who visited Madeira at the beginning of the 18th century, relates that all the merchants went about armed and that none of them dared go out at night for fear of being wounded or killed. The same physician also says that to be rid of an enemy it was enough to give a small coin to a black man, and that on one occasion he treated a priest who had been wounded at night after being mistaken for another person whom they meant to kill.

We do not know whether Dr Sloane’s account is exaggerated. What we do know is that murders are extremely rare in Madeira today, and that the streets of Funchal and its suburbs can be walked at any hour of the night without great risk, even though the police are too few to watch over the citizens’ safety. All modern writers do justice to the people of Madeira, regarding them as among the most orderly and generous in the world.

In a work entitled *Breve e verdadeira demonstração dos principios e progressos do governo que João António de Sá Pereira fez na ilha da Madeira*, we read that there was a custom, dating from ancient times, whereby women about to marry fled their parents’ houses to join their sweethearts, and that on the following day ‘the future bride and groom dressed with care to go to the houses of their friends and announce that so-and-so had left her parents’ house to marry.’ The same work adds that this practice ‘was common, with few exceptions, among the nobility’ and that when it was presumed that so-and-so wished to marry so-and-so, arrangements were made as to when the night of the flight, or of the ‘theft’, would be.

The governor João António de Sá Pereira, ‘the Madeiran Pombal’, as Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo calls him, sought to put an end to these and many other abuses practised on the island. For this reason, when he departed for Lisbon on 10 June 1777, many houses were illuminated and many fireworks were let off. He witnessed all these displays of rejoicing, because the ship on which he was to sail could not leave the port of Funchal at once for lack of wind.

The old habit, long since vanished from the island, of maidens fleeing their parents’ house before the wedding day shows us that it is a mistake to suppose that simplicity of manners always prevailed among our forebears. Reprehensible practices and customs belong to every age; and if part of the present generation shows clear signs of corruption, it must nevertheless be granted that certain social conventions are more respected today than in former times.

The common people of Madeira, almost always well disposed, today generally live carefree and happy lives. Any branch of industry or trade currently yields considerable profits, and higher wages and the rising value of the produce of the land have brought the working classes and farmers an independence and well-being they did not enjoy in other times. This state of affairs has not, however, noticeably affected the simple ways of the country people, whose aspirations remain those of their forebears. Only in the city and its surroundings does one sometimes observe among the working classes spendthrift habits and a certain taste for pleasure which certainly did not exist only a very few years ago.

The island of Madeira is unquestionably one of the most important Portuguese colonies. Remarkable for the fertility of its soil, its excellent wines, the mildness of its climate and the natural beauty with which it is endowed, it has long been known as a favoured land, thanks to the excellent descriptions of it published by many foreigners.

Much still remains to be done, however, for this island to become what it can and should be. Nature has been lavish with it, clothing it in charms that may be equalled but not surpassed; yet these charms are not always revealed to the eyes of the foreigner eager for impressions, because of the backward state of our roads.

The building of good roads fit for motor cars, linking Funchal to the places most famed for their beauty or for the superb views they offer, is an urgent necessity if we wish to draw from the visits of foreigners to this island all the benefit they can bring. If tomorrow tourists can visit the Rabaçal, the Fanal, the Paul da Serra, the Ribeiro Frio and Santo da Serra as comfortably as they visit Monte and other places around the city today, we shall have endowed the island with a great improvement and assured its inhabitants a future full of the broadest prosperity (1921).

In this article, Madeira (from the 1st edition), some general data and information are briefly set out; the articles under the same title that follow seek to provide more detailed material on all the subjects indicated.
Its capital and the centre of all its activity is the city of Funchal, with which we have already dealt at some length on pages 59–68 of this volume.

Madeira in the Torre do Tombo

Everyone knows that the National Archive of the Torre do Tombo (National Archives) is the richest and most abundant repository of original manuscript documents in our country. For that reason it is also the surest and most copious source for any historical research into mainland Portugal and into its former overseas dominions in Africa, Asia and America.

The Madeira archipelago is extensively represented in this archive, which holds a precious body of documents that it would be very worthwhile to make known to those who devote their labours specifically to the study of Madeiran history. We are not unaware of the difficulties such an undertaking would entail. Most of the documents held in the Torre do Tombo (national archives) (*Torre do Tombo*) have not been catalogued, and there would be considerable expense in employing suitably qualified staff to carry out such laborious and lengthy research.

Nevertheless, something could and should be done. Let the Azorean archipelago serve us as an example and a spur. When in 1878 the illustrious native of São Miguel Dr Ernesto do Canto began publishing the *Archivo dos Açores*, he at once commissioned the journalist José Torres to carry out an exploration, albeit a summary one, of that vast archive. It brought to light valuable documents, which were included in several volumes of that important publication. The same should be done for Madeira. The first research would be limited to a search among the documents already catalogued, and work would begin at once on compiling an inventory, as complete as possible, of the documents of interest to the history of these islands. Once this inventory had been completed and published, the most useful and necessary manuscripts could be printed little by little, after careful selection, as circumstances at the time advised. There would be no lack, in Lisbon or even in Madeira, of a person of recognised integrity and competence to be entrusted with this arduous task; what may be lacking is an administrative body or official entity willing to take the initiative in carrying out so profitable and praiseworthy an idea.

It is with great satisfaction that we see, in several issues of the *Arquivo Historico da Madeira*, a list of documents relating to this island that belong to the precious ‘Corpo Chronologico’ collection of the Torre do Tombo. It may be presumed that other documents are still contained among the eighty-three thousand documents making up that collection; to find them, one would consult the twelve volumes of Index to the said ‘Corpo Chronologico’, which fortunately survive. It is also known that extensive and valuable documentation on this archipelago is to be found in the books of the Islands (*Ilhas*), the *Misticos*, the *Ementas* and the General Confirmations (*Confirmações Gerais*), and especially in the books and bundles of the Chancery records of all the kings of the second dynasty, as well as in other collections.

As we said above, the work of research in the collections of the Torre do Tombo (national archives) relating to Madeira ought to begin with a thorough examination of the catalogues and inventory books held there, and particularly of the following, which we find cited in a short historical and descriptive study of that Archive: ‘Funchal, Alfandega, Catalogo em verbetes; Cabido da Sé, Catalogo em verbetes: Convento de Santa Clara e N. S. da Incarnação, Catalago em caderno; Relação dos livros existentes no arquivo da Alfandega, Catalogo em caderno; Relação dos livros existentes no arquivo do Cabido da Sé, Catalogo em caderno; Relação dos livros existentes na repartição de fazenda do distrito, Catalogo em caderno’ (Funchal Customs House, card catalogue; Chapter of the Cathedral, card catalogue; Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) and Nossa Senhora da Encarnação, catalogue in notebook form; lists of the books in the archives of the Customs House, of the Chapter of the Cathedral and of the district Revenue Office, catalogues in notebook form). In the same study we also read that the following documents are in the ‘Sala da Livraria’ (Library Room): ‘Receipts and Expenditure of the Works of the High Court of Appeal (*Relação*), Funchal Customs House, Azemmour and Hormuz, 10 bundles; Revenue from the fifths (*quintos*, levy of one fifth on sugar) on the sugar of the island of Madeira, single bundle; Revenue of the customs houses of the Algarve, Funchal and Marvão, bundle 7; and Register belonging to Funchal Cathedral (the Sé), single book’. And the same study further states that the ‘Sala A – Ministério do Reino’ (Room A – Ministry of the Kingdom) holds: ‘Funchal Customs House, 255 books, shelves 18 and 19; Santa Clara, 16 bundles, shelf 74, and 128 books, shelf 74; Encarnação, 46 books, shelf 75; Chapter of the Cathedral, 23 bundles and 44 books, shelf 74’.

Among the Customs House books referred to above are those of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), which was attached to that revenue house and exercised superintendence over it until 1775, when it was abolished. The enactments issued by the central government concerning the collection of certain contributions and taxes, the creation of posts and the appointment of those who were to hold them, the construction and repair of buildings, the reorganisation of various public services, etc., etc., were addressed to the Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*). This office filed and registered these enactments and partly carried them out, so its register books are of great interest and value for the history of our island. The importance of these documents becomes clear on reading the ‘*Index da antiga Provedoria da Real Fazenda. . .*’, a bulky folio volume held in this city and partly published some years ago in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’). It gives a brief, methodically arranged list of the enactments registered in twenty-four volumes, covering the long period from 1566 to 1775. This index ought to be reproduced again in some newspaper or review, since the first printing was riddled with typographical errors, and the opportunity should be taken to accompany the new publication with short explanatory notes on the text.

As for the books belonging to the archive of the cathedral chapter (*Cabido*) of Funchal Cathedral, to which we also referred above, we were given a long and interesting list of most of these books, now kept in the Torre do Tombo (national archives); it is too long to reproduce here. We shall nevertheless mention the following codices, since they belonged to an archive which the distinguished annotator of the *Saudades* described as rich: ‘Year 1525 and following – Book 1 of the rulings and resolutions of the Chapter of the Cathedral; 1538 and 1553 and following – Book dealing with the stay in Madeira of the visiting bishop Dom Ambrósio, sent by the Archbishop of Funchal Dom Martinho, and with some measures taken by this metropolitan; 1586 and following – Book of the Register; 1587 and following – Book of Visitations; 1572 – Book of the Statutes (*compromisso*); 1590 – Book of the inventory of silver and vestments; 1568 – Book of Receipts and Expenditure of the church fabric (*fábrica*), etc.’ These documents, listed in the same inventory, must also be valuable: ‘15th century onwards, written on parchment and paper, relating to the churches of the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and also to Funchal Cathedral, bundles from no. 1 to 23.

From what we have said and from the passages transcribed above, it is clear that it would not be very difficult to gather a considerable body of material for compiling a list or catalogue of the documents of interest to Madeira, making use of the inventories and indexes that already exist, in addition to the further research that should be undertaken in due course.

Some sixty years ago the Madeiran Roberto Augusto da Costa Campos, a distinguished official of the Torre do Tombo (national archives), visited the archives of several public departments in Funchal and, with official authorisation, collected some hundreds of volumes to be incorporated into the National Archive. They are there at present, awaiting patient researchers who will make these valuable codices known to those who need to consult them.
Madeira in the University of Coimbra

By a charter of 22 September 1460, Henry the Navigator made a grant to the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) of ‘twelve marks of silver’, to be paid out of the tithes that the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) collected in the Madeira archipelago and intended specifically for the professor holding the ‘prime’ chair of the faculty of theology. The deed in question is transcribed on pp. 39 ff. of the *Memoria da Faculdade de Teologia da Universidade de Coimbra* by Dr Mota Veiga. The Infante’s will contains a clause that reads: ‘I ordain that the professor of the prime chair shall have each year for ever twelve marks of silver from the first revenue of the tithes that the Order of Christ has in the Island of Madeira.’

The distinguished priest from São Miguel, Friar António do Presépio, who died in 1931, extracted from the archive of the University of Coimbra the names of all the Madeirans and Azoreans who attended that institution of higher learning over the long period from 1578 to 1730. From these names he compiled a long and interesting alphabetical list. It not only contains valuable material for the biographies of many illustrious sons of the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes), but also gives us useful information on the relatively large number of students from the Azores and Madeira who studied at the University of Coimbra in that period. The list comprises 589 names: 276 belong to Madeira, 149 to the island of São Miguel, 108 to Terceira, 24 to Faial and the remaining 32 to the other Azorean islands. It can be seen that, in proportion to the population, the number of Madeiran students who attended the University in that period was much higher than that from the various islands of the Azores archipelago.

Because it is far too long, we do not reproduce here this list of 276 names of students, covering a period of 157 years, but we have had it published in vols I and II of the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (‘Historical Archive of Madeira’), where it can be found.
See Doctors and Professors.
Madeira in the African strongholds

In the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), in various articles and chronicles and in many books of genealogy, there are countless references to Madeirans who distinguished themselves in the strongholds of Morocco in the assaults against the Moors. Particularly deserving of honourable mention is the prompt and valuable relief sent from this island when those same strongholds were threatened and in danger of being destroyed by the warlike followers of Muhammad. The donataries of Funchal organised several expeditions, some of them well equipped and supplied and at no cost to mainland Portugal, which rendered the most notable services to the Fatherland. Various items of information bearing on this subject can be found in scattered articles of this work, and especially in the pamphlet *A Madeira e as Praças de Africa* by Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento.
Madeira (origin of the name)

Speaking of the discovery, Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘… which they called Madeira because of the great, dense woodland with which it was covered…’. It may be inferred from this account that it was the discoverers themselves who gave the name Madeira to the unknown island on which they had landed. Elsewhere the same Frutuoso says: ‘The Infante, seeing the samples and hearing the account of the island that they gave him, gave it the name it now has, the island of Madeira…’ This must surely be understood to mean that Prince Henry the Navigator merely confirmed the name by which the first navigators had called the land they had discovered. Another passage of the *Saudades* states expressly that it was the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco who called this island Madeira: ‘to which the said captain gave the name of Madeira’. And he says so still more categorically in another place in the same work: ‘. its most fortunate first captain, João Gonçalves Zargo, gave it this name because of the very dense and great woodland with which it was covered, and because it was full of an infinite quantity of wood’.

Unlike what happened with other islands and lands that were discovered, this island and archipelago were never known by any name other than the one they had from the beginning. It is true that Dr Gaspar Frutuoso states ‘that, because it was so very rugged, they say its name was, or should have been, Ilha das Pedras’, but from this emphatic manner of speaking on the part of the historian of the islands it may be concluded that he did not mean to assert that the island had borne that name. Apart from this passing reference by Frutuoso, which does not amount to an assertion, that name is not known in any other writings, ancient or modern, as a designation for the island or archipelago of Madeira.

Let us hear a question put by Pinheiro Chagas: ‘Was this the name that would most naturally have occurred to him? Since the word *madeira* [TN: *madeira* is Portuguese for ‘wood’ or ‘timber’.] refers especially to the trunks of trees already felled and prepared for their proper uses, was it not strange that this should be the name that immediately served Gonçalves Zarco to designate the island, rather than Island of the Groves, Island of the Flowers or Island of the Woods?’
This question from the illustrious historian does not invalidate the simple and artless, but true, account given by Gaspar Frutuoso.

Madeira (landscape)

Countless works in prose and verse, both in Portuguese and in foreign languages, sing and extol the well-known and by now proverbial beauties of Madeira. Among them stand out admirably the marvellous ruggedness of its high mountains, the improbable steepness of its ravines and gorges, the depth of its valleys, the capricious relief of its terrain, the varied tones and hues of its rich crops, the variety and fragrance of its flowers, the eternal spring of its climate, its famous wines, fruit and embroidery, its typical and interesting regional customs, the patriarchal hospitality of its inhabitants, etc., etc. We shall not attempt even a pale description, however fleeting, of this whole array of wonders with which divine omnipotence has endowed the privileged land of our birth. We shall confine ourselves to drawing the reader’s attention to the brilliant pages that various writers have devoted to extolling these astonishing beauties, carving their enduring impressions into passages of the most beautiful and inimitable prose. In the *Dicionário Corográfico da Madeira* we recorded, over some ten pages, many extracts from these brilliant writings, which limited space does not allow us to reproduce here.

In discussing the marvellous scenery of Madeira, we cannot fail to mention, if only in passing, a number of places that deserve a special visit for the astonishing panoramas that can be enjoyed from them in rapt delight. In the interior of the island we would point to Rabaçal, Monte Medonho, the Fontes da Ribeira do Inferno, the Cumeada de São Vicente, Pico dos Barcelos, Pico Ruivo, Pico do Arieiro, Boca dos Namorados, Ribeiro Frio, the Ribeira de São Jorge at Santana, Pico da Suna and Terreiro da Luta. On the coast there are Piedade, Ponta de São Lourenço, Garajau, Praia Formosa, Fojo, Cabo Girão, the mouth of the Ribeira da Janela, that of the Ribeira do Inferno, the Ribeira de João Delgado, the chapel of São Vicente (St Vincent of Saragossa), Entroza, Ponta de São Jorge, Rocha do Navio and Porto da Cruz. Many streams have beautiful waterfalls, and from every high point one can admire wide and varied views of unsurpassable beauty.

Madeira under the Crown

The monarchs and governments of mainland Portugal, united in the same purpose, gradually restricted the original and almost discretionary powers of the first donataries of this archipelago, until they achieved a high degree of centralisation in public administration and in the collection of the various taxes and dues. We have already dealt with this point at some length in the articles Grants (vol. 1, p. 368) and Donataries (vol. I, pp. 373 and 374), recalling that the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 27 April 1497 (see *Saudades*, p. 479) was one of the first and principal blows struck against the privileges and exemptions of the old donataries. The captaincies, which had been regarded almost as the property of the donataries, gradually came to belong to the Crown and became true colonies of the central power. It should not be understood that Madeira became Crown land (*realenga*) in the sense of having been entirely withdrawn from the governing authority of the captains-donatary. Rather, the successive limits placed on the powers they enjoyed curtailed their privileges and reduced their prerogatives to such an extent that one may well say, with the author of the *Saudades*, that the archipelago passed into the possession of the State, whereas before it had been a fief and a lordship almost entirely enjoyed by the donataries.
