Timber

The name Madeira (‘wood’, ‘timber’) given to this island by its discoverers derives from the rich, luxuriant vegetation that covered its entire surface. The abundant and gigantic trees, which so amazed the first navigators to land here, stretched in dense forest from the edge of the ocean to the summits of the highest mountains. The settlement and colonisation of the island made it imperative to destroy part of these thick, impenetrable woods, and only a fire could rapidly reduce them to the necessary extent and allow farming to begin at once. (See Forest fires, vol. II, p. 140.)

It seems that the destruction caused by the fire went far beyond what would have been desirable, for the historian João de Barros stated in the mid-16th century that ‘those living now feel this damage keenly through the lack they have of timber and firewood, for that first fire burnt more than the strength of arm and axe has been able to cut down from then until now’. In our view, this assertion of Barros must refer to the first years after the fire, because the timber regulations of this island of 1515 and 1562 contradict it. Madeira was rapidly restocked with forest species, and if the fire cost it the first, native opulence of its trees, there can be no doubt that it was soon covered with extensive and abundant vegetation. Many facts prove this.

The timber trade and export were a logical consequence of the abundance of tree species that densely covered the mountains. The following interesting passage is by Gaspar Frutuoso: ‘And there was such a quantity of timber, so beautiful and hard, that they carried to many places great quantities of planks, beams and masts, all of which were sawn with water-driven mills or saws, of which there are still many today on the north side of the same island; and at this time, because of the great deal of timber they carried from there to the Kingdom, they began to build with it ships with topsails and forecastles, for before there were none in the Kingdom, nor had they anywhere to sail to, nor were there any ships other than the caravels of the Algarve and the barinels in Lisbon and Porto’.

According to the Viscount of Santarém, cited by Pinheiro Chagas, as we have already seen on page 141 of this volume of the *Elucidário*, this superabundance of timber brought about notable progress in naval architecture and in the construction of buildings.

On the abundance of forest trees, and on some of them in particular, the following passage by the historian of the islands also makes interesting reading: ‘This whole island is exceedingly rugged and covered with tall, cool woodland; it is so dense that some travellers lose their way on the paths, and some who have been lost in it have already died. And not only are there great and lofty uplands in the middle and along the *lombo* (ridge between valleys) of the land, but also great, deep hollows covered with thickets, stout timber and groves of til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), which, when it is sawn, is very black inside the heartwood and smells bad. From this wood much planking is made for sugar chests and for the flooring and beams of houses, and most of the firewood burned in the sugar mills comes from it. There is also another red wood, called *vinhatego*, from which chests for household use are made, and these are very good; but those made from it for use at sea are prized far more highly. There are other woods of *aderno*, from which a great deal of timber is made for casks for wine and honey; but they are better for honey than for wine, not because the quality of the wood spoils the wine, but because it is very hard and dry, and honey does not seep into it as wine does, which moistens it and sometimes runs out through the middle of the wood: this *aderno* wood is so hard that it is split with a wedge. There are also many *folhados*, which grow very straight and thick, from which the framing for houses is made, and often from a single trunk they make three or four rafter legs; but it is not as hard as that of this island of São Miguel; it is almost as soft to cut as cedar, and from it are made the plough-beams used in farming. There is another wood, *azevinho*, very hard, from which axe handles are made: but it is not white, as that of this island is. There are also laurel woods, and on the skirts of the uplands, on the southern side, much broom, which is low scrub like heather bearing a yellow flower, which they use in their ovens; and from it they gather the switches, which they peel like wicker, and from which are made very handsome, fresh white baskets for table service, for christening offerings and other things, because they are very white and clean: and they are sold to many places outside the island and the Kingdom of Portugal, for many ingenious and very fine and costly baskets are made, sometimes ten or twelve different ones built upon one, all together forming a single piece; and to make them whiter than the switches are by nature, although very white, they smoke them with sulphur. And there is also much *barbuzano* timber, from which they mostly make the stakes for vine trellises, because it is a very hard wood and lasts a long time in the ground. Nor is there any lack of heather, from which charcoal is made for blacksmiths and braziers.’

The name of the parish (*freguesia*) of Serra de Água, and of the various other localities and places that bear the same name, tell us that many water-driven sawing mills, or simply water-powered sawmills (*serra de água*), once stood scattered across this island, as recorded in various old documents and even in some legislative enactments.

The abundance of trees, and the abuses committed in exploiting them, led to the enactment of various legislative measures to guard against the destruction of the forest wealth that covered the uplands of this island. The most notable of these enactments is the Timber Regulations (*Regimento das Madeiras*) of 27 August 1562, which fills eight pages of one of the notes to the *Saudades*. Of it Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says that it is an important document for the agricultural history of Madeira. It constitutes the island’s own peculiar forestry legislation, still largely in force today, and is the source of the municipal bylaws (*posturas*) in all the municipalities of this island.

The woody flora of Madeira still contains today some species that yield timber of great value in cabinet-making. From the wood of the Madeira mahogany (vinhático, *Persea indica*) and the *til* (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), the latter black and the former reddish, fine furniture is made, the former closely resembling mahogany. From cedar, which is pale, light and aromatic, excellent boxes are made that, as a rule, are not attacked by moths. From *maçaroco*, *fustete*, *seixo*, *piorno*, *pau branco*, holly, *tintureira*, etc., inlaid work (*embutidos*) of various colours is made for tables, boxes, cases and other small pieces. The woods of the *faia*, *barbuzano*, laurel, *aderno*, *folhado* (*Clethra arborea*, a native tree), heath, wild cherry, *sanguinho*, *mocano*, etc., also have or could have uses in various kinds of work, but their use in cabinet-making is generally very limited, because nearly all of them are now very rare. Valuable information on this subject is given in the articles of this *Elucidário* entitled Afforestation, Fires, Forest Regime and Forestry Services (*Serviços Florestais*).

Madeirans in Angola

Despite its great importance, we have no detailed account of the colony formed by Madeirans at Lubango and on the Huíla plateau. We therefore confine ourselves to transcribing the interesting information given by Dr Leandro de Mendonça, a son of Madeira, in the speech he delivered in Sá da Bandeira at the end of 1940, when a commemorative pillar (padrão) marking the arrival of the first Madeirans in those African lands was unveiled there. After paying the highest tribute to the sons of this island for their upright habits, love of work and remarkable aptitude for colonisation, he said the following:

‘The first Madeirans destined for the colonisation of the Huíla plateau, 222 individuals of both sexes, left Funchal aboard the warship “India” on 13 October 1884 and arrived at Moçâmedes on 18 November of that same year. As the lack of means of transport did not allow all the colonists to travel up to the Plateau at the same time, they were divided into two groups. The first reached the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Barracões on 25 December 1884 and the second on 18 January of the following year, as stated in the Reports of the Director of the Colony, Dom José da Câmara Leme. On 19 January of that same year the Colony was officially established. Six months later a further 349 colonists arrived, who had embarked at Funchal on the steam warship “Africa”. Of these 349 emigrants, 44 joined some families from Humpata and, moving to the valley of Chimpumpunhime, founded the Colony of São Pedro da Chibia there. For two years, until the settlement of these two colonies was complete, the flow of emigrants ceased, resuming in 1888, the year in which a further 10 colonists settled in Huíla. In the following years, 1889 and 1890, another 704 emigrants came, making a total of 1,281 Madeirans.','cells text text_placeholder_ignore':''

It is to this handful of emigrants, little more than a thousand men, women and children, who left Madeira of their own free will, that we owe the transformation of the virgin forest that Lubango once was into the most fertile and progressive city of Sá da Bandeira.’
Madeirans in Brazil

In the article Emigration (1-391) we have already referred to the large number of emigrants who left this island for Brazil in the 16th and 17th centuries. This is an opportunity to recall what is read in many places about the planting of sugar cane in that country: it is asserted that Madeirans took the first plants there and were also the first to begin growing this rich crop, which later spread so widely and became one of the great sources of prosperity of the young colony.

It is also asserted that it was the Governor of Brazil, Martim Afonso de Sousa, who requested that these Madeirans go there and, through them, set in motion the first planting of sugar cane. The crises that afflicted Madeira at various times led large waves of emigrants to leave, and the following information, given in one of the annotations to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), is of interest: ‘By 1676 decline in this archipelago had reached such a point that emigration to Brazil, until then a mere expedient or private speculation, came to be promoted as a measure of government: in that year a royal letter (*carta régia*) was issued, and another in 1747, both recorded in the archive of the Council of Funchal. The first ordered that three hundred to four hundred couples be transported to Brazil at the expense of the state, and the second recommended that the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) give help and favour to this emigration.’

It is well known that, particularly during the period of the Restoration wars, in which the Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira (see p. 18 of vol. II) distinguished himself so brilliantly and heroically in that country, there was a large emigration of Madeirans to Brazil, encouraged by the illustrious restorer of Pernambuco. A great number of the sons of our island also won high distinction alongside their illustrious fellow countryman. The names of many of them are mentioned in the chronicles of the period and in various articles and nobiliaries, and we shall record the deeds of bravery of some of them in the article Varões Ilustres.

Not only in that period of military struggle, but also later and in various fields of human activity, many Madeirans brought great honour to their native land through their love of work, their intelligence and their initiative. Some even earned the standing of meritorious citizens and received the most laudatory mentions from the most distinguished people of that country.

As regards the 19th century, we wish to make brief mention here of the Madeirans Dom Mateus de Abreu Pereira and Dom Manuel Joaquim Gonçalves de Andrade, bishops of São Paulo; Drs Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade and João Jacinto Gonçalves de Andrade, professors at the university of the same city; Dr Patrício Moniz, a great sacred orator; Caetano Alberto Soares, a distinguished jurist; General Joaquim de Oliveira Álvares; Father João António de Lessa, a deputy; João da Silva Caldeira, professor of chemistry; and Francisco João Rossio, a military engineer, among others, of whom we have given some biographical notes scattered through the pages of this work.

It is well known that one of the most notable achievements of the Portuguese in Brazilian lands was the creation of the ‘Gabinete de Leitura do Rio de Janeiro’, which founded a rich and extensive library whose catalogue, largely printed, runs to several volumes. One of the most active and helpful promoters of this foundation was the Madeiran Francisco Eduardo Alves Viana, a merchant in the city of Rio de Janeiro.

Mother of God (chapels)

This is a small church in the typical Manueline style, which makes it of particular interest to visitors, especially for certain details of its construction. It stands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), in the locality (*sítio*) to which it gave its name. It was built in the 16th century and is said to have been founded by a Salvago family, who held land there as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). Services are still held in it, and it belongs (1921) to the heirs of João Maurício de Gouveia.

There is a chapel with the same dedication in the parish of Tabua (‘bulrush’), better known by the name of Mãe de Deus. We do not know the year it was built, but we know that around the middle of the 18th century it was completely destroyed by the violent current of the nearby stream. It was rebuilt around 1767 on the other bank of the stream, on a safer site, and was inspected on 9 December of the same year so that divine services could be celebrated there. A papal brief of 22 May 1781 grants a plenary indulgence to those who visit this chapel on the first Sunday of May.

In 1705 Inácio Uzadamor do Rêgo and his wife had a chapel built in the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Madre de Deus (Our Lady Mother of God) and to the wonder-worker St Anthony; the licence for its blessing is dated 5 December of that year.
Madre de Deus (Friar Francisco da)

He was professed in the Seraphic Order (*Ordem Seráfica*) in 1613 and was guardian of the Franciscan convent in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). Some describe him as Madeiran, but it is not certain that he was born on this island. He was a man of vast learning and wrote a mystical book that is remarkable for the beauty of its language. (See *Bib. Lusit.* II-165).
Madre de Louro

A plant gall that frequently appears on the trunks of old laurel trees. It can reach 20 centimetres in length and is produced by *Exobasidium Lauri*, a fungus of the family Thelephoraceae. Combined with spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), it is a haemostatic much used in Madeira, and it is also employed as an emmenagogue.
Honeysuckle

Common name of *Lonicera etrusca*, native to the Mediterranean region, and of *L. confusa*, native to China and Japan, plants common in Madeira and belonging to the family Caprifoliaceae. The first of these plants is fully naturalised on the island; the second occurs only in gardens. *L. longiflora* is a large-flowered honeysuckle grown in some gardens in Funchal.
Madureira
One of the first settlers of Madeira was Manuel Madureira da Maia, who lived in Gaula. João Rodrigues Madureira was a valiant Madeiran knight who fought in Africa in the early 16th century.
Magalhães (Dr José Alfredo Mendes de)

This well-known politician, a professor at the Porto Medical School and a former minister and deputy, was sent to Madeira as High Commissioner (*alto comissário*) of the Republic during the cholera epidemic that raged in this archipelago from October 1910 to February 1911.

Although he was charged specifically with matters of public health, Dr Magalhães extended his action further as the Government's delegate. Through the vigorous measures he put into practice, he succeeded in restoring public order, which had been somewhat disturbed on this island since the establishment of the republican government. His proclamation of 27 December, in which he told the Madeirans of his firm intention to have those who tried to disturb order punished by summary trial and with the utmost rigour, was received with general applause. The arrest of a sergeant identified as one of the main causes of the unrest in Madeira finally reassured those who feared that the new institutions would bring nothing but anarchy to the island.

The sergeant to whom we refer, who came to play an important role in Funchal in the early days of the Republic, was held in solitary confinement in the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater), from where he left for Lisbon; there he was dismissed from the army on account of his poor military conduct.
Dr Magalhães gave a public lecture at the Teatro Manuel de Arriaga, which was well received, and took an interest in the creation of a Children's Asylum for Arts and Crafts.

In return for the services rendered by Dr Alfredo de Magalhães, the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) awarded him the diploma of distinguished citizen of Funchal, which was presented to him in the great hall of the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) on 25 February 1911.
See Cholera Morbus in 1856 and 1910 and Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*).
Magnolia (Magnolia grandiflora)
A North American tree, widely grown in the *quintas* and gardens of Funchal. It flowers in May and June.
Madeirans also give the name magnolia to *Osmanthus fragrans*, a shrub of the family Oleaceae native to Japan, which produces small, fragrant white flowers.
The *carocha* of the gardens of Camacha and other places belongs to the genus *Magnolia* and the family Magnoliaceae, and is much prized for its scent.
Major (Richard Henry)

A contemporary English writer, who died in London in June 1901. He was a member of the Royal Geographical Society and keeper of the department of maps and charts at the British Museum. The work he published in 1868 under the title *The Life of Prince Henry of Portugal* became very well known in our country; it is a true commemorative pillar (padrão) raised to the memory of Prince Henry the Navigator, and also an unimpeachable tribute to the maritime odyssey accomplished by the Portuguese in the course of the 15th century. Richard Henry Major regards the legend of Robert Machin as historical truth, but Dr Álvaro de Azevedo triumphantly refuted the English writer's assertions, devoting to this subject some of the most interesting pages of his learned notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo's irrefutable argument reduced the Machin affair to the proportions of a charming and poetic legend without the slightest glimmer of historical foundation. Major published another work entitled *The Discoveries of Prince Henry the Navigator and their results* (London 1877), and his first work was translated into Portuguese by José António Ferreira Brandão.
Malacology

See Albers, Andrew, Snails, the Baron of Castelo de Paiva, Cephalopods, Shells, Girard, Richard Thomas Lowe, Nobre, Octopus, Squid, Hewett Cottrell Watson, Thomas Vernon Wollaston and Cockerel, the last in the Supplement.
Malcolm Burr
Works: (*The Orthoptera of Madeira* (*The Entomologist's Record*, vol. XXIV, no. 2). This work records twenty-nine Madeiran orthopterans.
Malfurada

Common name of various species of the genus *Hypericum* and of *Globularia salicina*. The latter belongs to the family Globulariaceae and is a shrub with entire, glabrous, lanceolate leaves and white or blue-and-white corollas. It is common in Madeira.
See Hipericão.
Malheiro

In the early 16th century there lived in Madeira one Bartolomeu Malheiro, who gave a plot of land for the building of a new hospital (see *Saudades*, p. 645). The present Malheiro family, however, whose representative in Funchal is Dr José Maria Malheiro (1921), the learned administrative auditor of the district, descends from Paulo Malheiro de Melo, a native of Viana do Castelo who settled on this island in the 18th century. In the first quarter of the 19th century there was in Funchal the trading house of Paulo Malheiro de Melo & Filhos, and the Malheiro family was regarded as being of noble origin.
Malheiro de Melo (Patrício)

He was born in Funchal on 17 March 1791 and died in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’) on 18 May 1842. He took an active part in the movement of 28 January 1821, which led to the proclamation of the Constitution in Madeira, and he was a member of the first Constitutional Council of Funchal and consul of Prussia. Indicted by the special judicial commission (*alçada*) that came to Madeira in 1828, he escaped arrest by going abroad, and returned only after constitutional government had been restored in the country.
Malmequer
Vernacular name of *Chrysanthemum segetum*. A composite common in Madeira and on Porto Santo.
Malpica
See Amor de burro.
Malva

Madeirans use this name both for the species of the genus *Pelargonium* grown in gardens and for the species of the genera *Lavatera* and *Malva* that grow wild or naturalised in the archipelago. *Pelargonium inquinans* is the commonest of the Geraniaceae introduced into gardens; *Lavatera cretica*, *Malva silvestris* and *M. parviflora* are the dominant Malvaceae in Madeira. All these Malvaceae are emollient and are used to treat inflammations. A decoction of their flowers or leaves is used in gargles, baths, eye lotions, etc. The inhabitants of Porto Santo make ropes from the fibres which they extract by crushing *Lavatera arborea*, a species cultivated and naturalised on that island.
Mammals
See the article Fauna; anyone wishing for a fuller knowledge of this subject should consult the pamphlet *Mamiferos do Arquipelago da Madeira* by Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento.
Coot (Fulica atra)
A bird of passage of the rail family (Rallidae) that occasionally appears in Madeira. In Portugal it is known by the names *galeirão*, *franga real*, *nagera negra* and *galo*.
Manchon (L.)
Works: *A travers Madère, onze jours en hamac* (Paris, 1888).
Mandon (G.)

A distinguished French botanist, well known for the extremely valuable botanical collections he assembled both in the Madeira archipelago and in Bolivia. He stayed on this island from 1865 to 1866, and his collections served as the basis for a work by Cosson on the flora of the Madeira archipelago.
See Cosson.
Mangas (Manuel Júlio Tôrres)

He is the son of Colonel Manuel Júlio Torres Mangas, who was civil governor and military commander of Madeira at the time of the revolutionary movement that broke out in this city on the morning of 29 April 1847, proclaiming the principles of the Junta of Porto (see Governing board). Of Manuel Júlio Torres Mangas the younger we know only what Brito Aranha tells us in vol. XVI of the *Diccionario Bibliographico*. He was born in Funchal in 1835 and held various public offices on the mainland and overseas. He was a journalist and contributed to the *Jornal do Porto*, *Verdade*, *Ecco Popular*, *Nacional*, *Alemtejano* and *Jardim Literario*. He wrote a pamphlet entitled *Vida do Visconde de Almeida Garrett, principe dos poetas no século XIX*.
Marjoram (Majorana hortensis)

An aromatic labiate, grown in some Madeiran kitchen gardens solely as a seasoning for cooking. It is native to North America and Central Asia, and is also known by the name *orégãos* (see that entry).

*Majarona paniculata*, probably a mere variety of *M. Maiorca*, also appears in some kitchen gardens and is easily told apart from *M. hortensis* by not having the lower lip of the calyx very small or absent.
Mangin (General)

General Carlos Maria Manuel Mangin, one of the defenders of Verdun, arrived in Funchal aboard the cruiser *Jules Michelet* on 26 November 1921, shortly after 9 in the morning. He was greeted on board by the Civil Governor and the Military Commander, and came ashore shortly after half past 10 at the quay at the entrance to the city. At the start of the quay stood a handsome triumphal arch made of box, bearing on its south side the words ‘Viva a França’ (Long live France), with the national flag at either end and, in the centre, a trophy formed of four French flags and one Portuguese flag.

It was beside this arch that the Civil Governor, the Military Commander, the President of the Council, the officers of the garrison and other officials received the General and escorted him to the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), where he stayed for some time. They all then set off for the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), where solemn funeral rites were to be held in honour of the French sailors killed when the gunboat *Surprise* was torpedoed in the harbour of Funchal.

Military honours were paid to the general both at the quay and as he left the fortress of São Lourenço by a detachment of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria n.º 27*) under the command of a captain. In honour of General Mangin, a dinner was given on the 26th at the palace of São Lourenço by the Civil Governor, and on the 27th a tea was held at Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), given by the Military Commander. The general made several excursions around Funchal and visited the Diocesan Prelate on the 26th, immediately after the funeral rites. On the 27th the general gave a gala dinner aboard the cruiser *Jules Michelet*, attended by the authorities and other official figures.

The general joined the procession that accompanied the remains of the sailors of the *Surprise* from the Angústias cemetery to the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’). He had come to Funchal to attend their transfer aboard the cruiser *Jules Michelet*, which left the port of Funchal for France on the 28th at 7.30 p.m.
See Surprise.
Mangra of the vine

On 29 July 1853 the agronomist João de Andrade Corvo, who later became one of our most distinguished writers and statesmen, arrived in Funchal. He had been commissioned by the central Government to make a thorough study of the disease that had attacked the vineyards of this island and to propose the measures most likely to overcome the calamities then afflicting us.

Our vines had been attacked by *Oidium Tuckeri*, to which the people had given the name *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium). The disease had appeared in Europe only a few years earlier, and it seems that its presence was first recorded in a garden in England in 1845. It was suspected that its appearance in Madeira dated from 1851, but it was in 1852 that the disease spread and began to cause its terrible damage. In February 1851 a French subject visited Funchal, and among the collection of plants he sold in this city were some varieties of vine, gathered in France in localities already invaded by the disease. A distinguished agronomist supposes that this was the cause of the invasion of *Oidium Tuckeri* in this archipelago.

To give an approximate idea of the violence of the disease and its disastrous consequences, it is enough to say that average wine production in the years 1849, 1850 and 1851 was fifty thousand hectolitres. In 1852, the first year of the general invasion of the *mangra*, it was eight thousand; in 1853 it fell to three thousand, and in 1854 to a mere six hundred hectolitres. The difference between 1851 and 1854 is roughly 80 to 1.

The economic crisis this caused throughout the district was enormous. The island was not prosperous at the time, since its only profitable crop was the vine. Sugar cane was grown on a small scale. Bananas and other fruit, and vegetables too, were not produced in sufficient quantity for export. The butter and embroidery industries existed only in a rudimentary state, and reached the development they have here today only later.

The crisis that followed the disease of the vineyards was among the most serious ever to have struck this archipelago. One of its consequences was emigration, which in some years reached alarming proportions. Famine settled among us, with all its train of horrors.

To relieve so many ills, the central Government ordered the construction and repair of various roads, thus employing some hundreds of hands who had no work. By royal decree (*alvará*) of 22 November 1852, the civil governor of the district appointed a large committee charged with promoting a subscription and the collection of donations in several foreign countries. It went on to distribute relief to the value of thirty-seven *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos), and for six months employed about three hundred men each day on the road linking Funchal with the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos.

João de Andrade Corvo stayed two months in Madeira, and in 1854 published an interesting report on the studies he had carried out in this archipelago, a work that still deserves to be read by scholars today.

The *mangra* still exists in the vineyards of the archipelago, and sulphur has long been used to combat it. It forms patches, white at first and later greyish, which appear on the leaves, shoots and bunches of the vine, and are produced by the mycelium and spores (conidia) of the fungus. The mycelium lives on the surface of the green organs of the vine and sends small suckers into them, through which it feeds.
See Cinzeiro.
Oak mildew

White patches that appear on the leaves of oaks, produced by *Oidium quercinum*, a fungus of the family Mucedinaceae. It was first observed in 1909, on the oaks at Monte (‘hill’). The species has probably been spread by conidia carried on the wind.
Mango tree (*Mangifera indica*)

A small tree of the family Anacardiaceae, widely cultivated in the lower zone of Madeira. It is native to India, and its large yellow or reddish fruits are among the best that Madeira produces. Mangoes appear from August to October.
Manhã de Páscoa
The Madeiran vernacular name for *Euphorbia pulcherrima*, a woody plant of the family Euphorbiaceae, native to Mexico. In this euphorbia the floral leaves are large and red.
Manicas
Mackerel (*cavalas*) are given this name while they are young.
See Cavala.
Asylums

In the archive of this city’s Council we found a reference to a request made by the Funchal Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) in 1493 for the construction of a *Tronco*, the name then given to the house intended for the detention of the insane. We believe that this request was not granted by the government in mainland Portugal or by the grand mastership of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*). We do not know where the unfortunates afflicted by mental illness, particularly the poor and destitute, might have been confined, if indeed a house specially devoted to that humane purpose ever existed.

The regulations (*regimento*) of this city’s Civil Hospital (*Hospital Civil*), drawn up in 1816, were an excellent piece of work for their time and extremely thorough, at times descending into unnecessary detail. Yet they make no reference at all to the hospitalisation or detention of the insane, which leads us to suppose that such people were not then admitted there. The same is true of the regulations of 1834. It is only in the Regulation of 1844 that we first find an express provision for ‘some secure rooms for the insane, which must be separate from the other wards...’. Until the Câmara Pestana Asylum (*Manicómio Câmara Pestana*) was built, the poor insane were kept in some outbuildings of the hospital, and the inhumanity with which the hospital’s nurses and servants treated them became proverbial here.

Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, who as head of the administration of this district sought to meet every public need, wrote to the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*). He set out the reasons in favour of building a suitable edifice for the hospitalisation of the insane and promised his full support for this important improvement. The founding of an asylum went the same way as the removal of the old gaol and the construction of the quay, the Pontinha (‘little point’) mole, the theatre and the fruit and vegetable market: they were stock subjects of the local press, especially at election time or when a shortage of news led the journalist to brew Tolentino’s tea once again.

What had long been regarded as an important improvement to be made, however, became the answer to a pressing and urgent need. The proportion of people afflicted by mental illness grew alarming, above all for the reasons we briefly set out in the article Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*), where we spoke of the need to curb alcoholism by the strictest restriction of the production of spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine). The press intensified its campaign in view of the well-founded refusal to admit the insane to our hospital, the repugnant crowding of these wretches in the foul cells of the police station, and the large number of them wandering the streets and roads. The public then felt a deep compassion for this human misery and, at the same time, a general indignation at the criminal neglect to which the authorities abandoned the insane who were poor and lacked the means to be placed in suitable nursing homes. Madeira contributed to the official hospitalisation of the insane, but the Rilhafoles asylum refused to admit patients sent from this island, no doubt for lack of the necessary accommodation. A distinguished alienist who passed through this city vigorously condemned the distressing situation of the poor insane, and so brought into sharper relief the need to found a hospital to house those deprived of the light of reason.

A committee was then formed to put this altruistic and humane idea into practice. It began its work at once, and its efforts were crowned with complete success. Dr António Jardim de Oliveira was one of the first here to suggest the idea and became one of its most strenuous advocates. An asylum in Madeira is today a happy reality. Although this establishment does not fully serve its purpose, above all for want of more spacious accommodation and better nursing, it is without doubt a hospital that is rendering most valuable services and has met one of the most urgent and pressing needs felt among us. (1921)

When Dr Luís da Câmara Pestana died in Lisbon on 15 November 1899, the idea immediately arose, both on this island and among the Madeiran community in the capital, of raising a monument in Funchal to perpetuate the memory of the distinguished bacteriologist and illustrious son of this land. It was the Ateneu Comercial, a society that ceased to exist long ago, that took the initiative here in Madeira to realise this idea. It delegated to its honorary members the Viscount of Cacongo, Luís de Freitas Branco, Henrique Vieira de Castro, António Rodrigues Leitão and Nicásio de Azevedo Ramos full powers to ensure that the tribute to the eminent man of science became, without delay, a deserved and tangible reality.

These gentlemen formed themselves into a committee, with the first as chairman and the last as secretary, and the Viscount of Cacongo proposed founding an establishment for the hospitalisation of the insane. This would also serve as the monument to Dr Câmara Pestana and would bear the name of our illustrious fellow countryman. Another committee was joined to this one: it had been organised in this city to collect donations for the flood victims of the Azores and was made up of Dr António Jardim de Oliveira, the Count of Ribeiro Real, Dr João Augusto Teixeira and Canon Manuel Correia de Figueiredo. That committee held about two *contos*, and this sum became the nucleus or fund of the Câmara Pestana Asylum committee.

The committee worked with great zeal and ardour, but the Madeirans failed to respond to its diligent efforts. A public subscription raised only about eight *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis), a sum far from sufficient for the undertaking, not only for constructing the building and installing the hospital but above all for running the establishment properly, even though only a small number of patients were to be admitted. Various proposals were put forward for the site of the hospital building, with particular preference for the convent grounds of the former Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation). Despite the efforts made, however, the central government could not be persuaded to cede a plot of land for the construction. Housing it in part of the Hospital dos Lázaros (lepers' hospital) was also suggested, and one of the outbuildings of the Misericórdia building was likewise considered, but it was later recognised that these premises were unsuitable for properly accommodating an asylum, even if the indispensable and costly adaptation works were carried out. In the end, after hearing the opinions of the health authorities, the committee resolved to acquire the Quinta do Rochedo (‘crag estate’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’). The purchase was completed on 28 March 1904 for the sum of five *contos*.

Shortly afterwards the committee offered the building, together with some donations it still held, to the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*). It did so not only because it was unable to meet the cost of maintaining the hospital, but also because that administrative body was responsible for the hospitalisation of the insane under the decree of 10 October 1902. The General Council accepted the grant with thanks, and this decision was confirmed by the central government on 10 May 1904. Doubts and some difficulties arose over the handover of the building at the Quinta do Rochedo because of the conditions imposed by the donor committee, and the final transfer took place only in 1907; in the meantime, however, the Council kept the hospital running normally.

Within the grounds of the Quinta do Rochedo, the founding committee had a pavilion built to house the patients and adapted the residence of the *quinta* (country estate) for the same purpose. There it set up the hospital, which it supported and maintained for some time.

The public subscription reached about ten *contos* and five hundred thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), including the accumulated interest, the two *contos* from the flood-relief committee and a legacy of one thousand five hundred escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) from Dona Júlia Maria Torres da Costa. The benevolent committee applied these sums as follows: purchase of the *quinta* and the related tax, 5,656,000 réis; construction of the first pavilion, 3,393.00 escudos; linen and furniture, 627.00 escudos; and acquisition of the bust of Dr Câmara Pestana, 402.00 escudos.

The opening of the new hospital was a particularly solemn occasion, and the bronze bust of our illustrious and ill-fated compatriot was unveiled at the same time. Its base bears the following inscription: ‘This Asylum was founded by public subscription and is dedicated to the memory of the illustrious Madeiran bacteriologist Dr Luís da Câmara Pestana.’

The committee that took the initiative in founding this hospital consisted of the Viscount of Cacongo, Dr António Jardim de Oliveira, Henrique Vieira de Castro, Nicásio de Azevedo Ramos, the Count of Ribeiro Real, Canon Manuel Correia de Figueiredo, Dr João Augusto Teixeira, M. Nascimento de Ornelas, Sabino Joaquim Rodrigues and António Rodrigues Leitão. Justice and truth require us to state here that the Viscount of Cacongo, Henrique Vieira de Castro and Nicásio de Azevedo Ramos – respectively chairman, treasurer and secretary – were the members of the committee who showed the greatest zeal and dedication in bringing so altruistic and humanitarian an idea to fruition.

In 1908 the General Council bought some land adjoining the *quinta*, belonging to Captain Cândido Gomes, and in 1913 had a new pavilion built on it. The growing number of insane patients led the Council to build a third pavilion in 1915.

The Asylum was opened on 4 April 1906, and in the following May the physician-surgeons José Joaquim Mendes and João José Maria de Oliveira were appointed acting director and acting chief nurse, respectively, of the new hospital. Its present permanent director (1921) is Dr João Francisco de Almada, who took up the post in July 1907. The Regulations of the Câmara Pestana Asylum were drawn up by a committee delegated by the General Council and received the Council’s full approval at its ordinary session of November 1906.
At the end of December 1919 and 1920 there were 54 and 54 insane patients, respectively, in the asylum, and the expenditure on the patients’ upkeep in 1920 was 28,627.00 escudos.

On 21 May 1924, 38 male patients who were in the Câmara Pestana Asylum were moved to the Trapiche Nursing Home, established at the beginning of that year by the benevolent Brothers of St John of God. The female patients remained at the Câmara Pestana asylum, and their care was entrusted to a religious order.

From what has been said, it can be seen that from 1924 onwards the hospital services for the mentally ill underwent a remarkable transformation. This was not only because the male patients were housed in the Trapiche Nursing Home, leaving the building of the Câmara Pestana Asylum reserved solely for female patients, but also because of the great improvement in the treatment of the inmates. In both establishments this treatment became truly exemplary, and it need fear no comparison with similar institutions in our country.

From the book *Paróquia de Santo António da Ilha da Madeira*, some pages will now be extracted on the history and running of the Casa de Saúde de São João de Deus, established at the locality of Trapiche.

The idea of setting up a hospital for the insane in the houses at Trapiche predates the founding of the Câmara Pestana Asylum. It came from the diocesan bishop, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who made the most diligent and persistent efforts to bring it about. He persuaded the owner to cede the *quinta* (country estate) intended for that purpose and pressed the Brothers of São João de Deus to take charge of the asylum that was to be founded. His efforts were not successful at the time, for serious difficulties arose that could not be overcome. It should be clearly stressed that he ardently wished to endow this archipelago with a model hospital for the insane, and worked towards that end with the greatest dedication and enthusiasm. This is one more title of glory adding lustre to his eminent qualities as a benefactor and apostolic prelate.

The Câmara Pestana Asylum was created in 1906, and Dom Manuel Barreto still considered the founding of the Trapiche institution necessary, foreseeing that in the near future this further hospital would become absolutely indispensable. Around that time, and perhaps even earlier, some Brothers of São João de Deus, who had come to Madeira more than once to collect alms for the hospitals they maintained on the mainland, recognised how useful and fruitful their work could be on this island. They had in mind the considerable number of patients who needed to be admitted under the conditions required by science and in keeping with the precepts of true Christian charity.

Around 1920 there was talk of handing the management of the Câmara Pestana Asylum over to the Brothers of São João de Deus, which caused a great outcry in the press and at the sessions of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*). Meanwhile, the old idea of founding the hospital at Trapiche was taking shape. The diocesan prelate, Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, gave it his most unconditional support, and the dedication and selflessness of Dr João Francisco de Almada, combined with the well-directed efforts of some Brothers of São João de Deus, did the rest. The work would soon be a tangible reality. At the beginning of June 1922 the Brothers of São João de Deus occupied the houses of the Trapiche *quinta*. The installation was more than rudimentary, with difficulties arising on every side and putting the poor brothers’ spirit of self-denial and sacrifice to a severe test. They did not lack courage, and at once took in a few patients from this parish (*freguesia*), none of them insane. Their crusade of good works had begun.

The first patients deprived of reason were not admitted there until October 1923. The period between those two dates was devoted chiefly to collecting alms in various parts of the island and to acquiring the means indispensable for adapting the building to its new purpose. A considerable part of the manor house was in an advanced state of ruin, and it was moreover difficult to fit it out so that people suffering from mental disturbances could be housed there in safety. The brothers therefore had to struggle with great labour and sacrifice to prepare the building properly and make it fit to receive the first patients. Their number grew, and the notable and never surpassed services that the new institution was rendering were recognised from the outset.

In May 1924 the question of transferring the insane from the Câmara Pestana Asylum to the Trapiche Nursing Home was raised in the General Council. Within that body attention was drawn not only to the inadequate nursing, the cramped premises and the brutal and inhuman treatment given to the patients, but also to scandals of every kind occurring inside that ‘Bastille’, as the asylum at the Quinta do Rochedo was then called. The transfer of the patients to the Trapiche hospital had become absolutely imperative. The chief champion of this idea was Dr Domingos Réis Costa. Supported by the president of the General Council, Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques, and by other members, he advocated with the greatest enthusiasm, both at the sessions of this administrative body and in the local press, the immediate admission of the asylum’s patients to the Casa de Saúde of the Brothers of São João de Deus. The transfer took place on 21 May 1924, when 38 male insane patients were moved from the Quinta do Rochedo to the Trapiche *quinta*. A great work of humanity had been accomplished.
The solemn inauguration of this asylum took place in August 1924, attended by the illustrious diocesan prelate, the provincial of the Order of São João de Deus and other persons of social standing.

For the legal maintenance of the Trapiche Nursing Home an association was formed, its statutes approved by the competent authority, named the ‘Associação dos Irmãos de São João de Deus’. From the founding of the hospital until 1928 its director was a member of the Order, Manuel Maria Gonçalves. Despite his simple manner, unaffected modesty and precarious health, he managed to guide and complete that work, which is a model institution of the purest charity towards the sick and, at the same time, a Calvary of the most heroic virtues on the part of its benevolent and unsurpassed nurses.

The valuable services rendered by the new home for the insane aroused lively enthusiasm everywhere. Alms and donations began to arrive, brought by what were called *romagens*, or pilgrimages. Very large groups of people of every age, sex and condition formed great processions, which went to lay their offerings of money, foodstuffs and household articles of every kind in the hands of those in charge. These pilgrimages began in this parish (*freguesia*) and continued here for a long time. Especially worthy of mention were those from the localities of Casas Próximas, Madalena, Preces, Três Paus and Boliqueme, which formed long and attractively picturesque processions in which the spirit of charity was admirably combined with the most interesting and typical originality. Other parishes also took the initiative of organising similar pilgrimages on an even grander scale, among which those of Monte, São Roque, Câmara de Lobos and Estreito stood out.

Of the many important improvements carried out by the Brothers of St John of God, special mention must be made of the motor road, which put the house at Trapiche in quick and direct communication with the locality of Boliqueme and therefore with the city; the connection of the house to the general telephone network; the piping of water; and the preparatory works for building new pavilions. This is without counting the adaptation of the old buildings to house the hospital, as we have already mentioned above.
The number of patients in this hospital since its foundation, as at 31 December of each year, has been as follows:

Like all similar institutions, this nursing home has a special religious service, directed by the establishment’s own chaplain. Although their religious work is intended mainly for the patients and the community that works there, the priests of the Brothers of St John of God have taken part in the various acts of worship held in this parish, proving the most excellent and selfless helpers of the parish priests. In their chapel they readily administer the sacraments to the faithful who seek them; they attend the sick in their homes with spiritual comfort, accompany the dead to their last resting place and perform in the Igreja Paroquial every service asked of them. The first chaplain was Father José Maria Antunes, who served there from February 1923 to July 1925. In August of the same year he was replaced by Father Lázaro Ribeiro, who is the present chaplain (1928).

The history of this model nursing home, from its foundation to the present day, apart from the ever-growing number of its inmates and the material improvements gradually introduced there, consists simply in this very plain thing, yet admirably beautiful and admirably holy too: always the same spirit of courage, self-denial and sacrifice on the part of the tireless nurses; always the most attentive and affectionate treatment of the patients; always the most devoted care for their material well-being. And this, likewise always, without weakness, without faltering, without discouragement, despite the difficulties, setbacks and struggles that must be faced from time to time.

The data and information transcribed above go no further than 1928. However, the progress made at that mental hospital in recent years is highly significant and deserves special record, and we shall give a brief account of it here.
Among other improvements, two large pavilions were built to house the patients, together with a spacious chapel, a residence for the staff and a dairy.

The two pavilions, that of São José for calm patients and that of São João de Deus for agitated patients, contain spacious dining rooms, recreation and games rooms, bathrooms, dormitories, private rooms, etc. Everything conforms to the rules of hygiene and to the latest findings of psychiatric science. Beside the pavilions are courtyards for the patients’ recreation, artistically laid out as gardens and planted with shade trees, from which there is a fine view over the city and much of its surroundings.

The treatment of the patients is constantly improving. Madeirans can be proud that they now have a house where our mentally ill enjoy both loving care and Christian charity and the latest requirements of psychiatry.

Anyone who ever visited the old Câmara Pestana Asylum, with its strict regime of surveillance, repressive measures and isolation, will be astonished at the life of this house, once thought impossible and unattainable.

Many patients live as if they were in good health. They no longer spend twenty, thirty or more years in a life of repression. Many work in the shoemaking, carpentry and locksmithing workshops, on the various building and repair works on the premises, in cultivating the kitchen garden and in looking after the domestic animals, such as cows, goats, pigs, rabbits and hens. It is they who clean the refectories and dormitories. The planting of the courtyards and gardens of the establishment is in their care. And everything is done as perfectly as if it were the work of people in excellent health.
In this way the worthy brethren of São João de Deus manage to occupy several hundred men who would otherwise be the cause of their own distress.

In addition, the distinguished psychiatrist Aníbal Augusto Faria and the eminent physician Dr William Clode visit the patients three times a week and apply the latest findings of psychiatric science, such as electroshock, etc.

The body known as the ‘Associação dos Irmãos de São João de Deus’, set up to provide for the legal maintenance of this mental hospital, ceased to exist in 1940. In that year the ‘Ordem Hospitalária de São João de Deus’ was granted legal personality under the Concordat concluded between the Holy See and Portugal. The house continued to be maintained by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district.

Religious services, for the private use of the community and of those patients able and willing to attend, were held in the old chapel of the *quinta* (country estate) and then took place in rooms in one of the ‘pavilions’ until 1936. In that year the new church was inaugurated, dedicated to the holy founder of the worthy hospitaller order of São João de Deus. Although it is intended principally for the purpose stated above, it gives the inhabitants of that village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) and the surrounding localities the most valuable services in every form of religious care.

The period from 1906, the year the ‘Manicómio Câmara Pestana’ was founded, to 1924, when it came to be reserved solely for the treatment of female patients and all the male patients were transferred to the Trapiche Nursing Home, has already been described at length in the opening columns of this article on ‘Asylums’.

A year later, that is, from 9 May 1925, the ‘Manicómio Câmara Pestana’, in the parish of São Gonçalo, was placed under the management of the Hospitaller Sisters of the Sacred Heart of Jesus. To the present day they have carried out their demanding and arduous hospital work there with the greatest zeal, the purest devotion and the most accomplished skill. To the performance of these services we apply, without reservation, what we said above about the way in which they have been carried out at the ‘Casa de São João de Deus’ at the Trapiche, in the parish of Santo António.

Public rejoicing

Besides music and illuminations, which have probably been part of every age, Madeirans formerly expressed their rejoicing in other ways on feast days and national holidays. Frutuoso records that among the festivities held in Funchal to celebrate the birth of Prince João, son of John III, ‘many large and fierce bulls’ were run. The bullfights took place on a square beside the churchyard of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), where cane games were also played and there were other amusements.

On 9 December 1761 Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) resolved to hold festivities on the news of the birth of Prince José, in accordance with what had already been decided at the session of 29 October of the same year, in view of an official letter from the governor and captain-general. According to the minute book of the Council’s sessions, the festivities consisted of the following: ‘Three days of public illuminations, with all the inventions of fireworks conducive to and necessary for the said celebration; and on the afternoons of the three days to be appointed, on the first there shall be cavalcades, the arena being prepared with the cleanliness necessary and proper for the occasion; on the second a duck shall be run, and on that afternoon there shall be some music carts and other festivities to fill the same afternoon; and on the third afternoon there shall be a pageant of figures on horseback, representing the four parts of the world, and with them the island of Madeira and all its other towns; and besides this celebration there shall also be ring-tilting (*argolinha*)’.

The game or pastime of ring-tilting (*argolinha*), in which the rider, at full gallop, had to thread one or more rings placed on the field with a lance, was much enjoyed by Madeirans. It was last held in Funchal a little over thirty years ago.

On days regarded as occasions of national rejoicing, such as royal anniversaries, a hand-kissing ceremony (*beija-mão*) was held at the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace) in the days of absolutism. For this purpose the portrait of the reigning monarch was displayed beneath a canopy in one of the palace’s rooms. As a curiosity, we give below the text of a notice sent in 1815 to the councillors (*vereadores*) of Funchal Municipal Council, on the eve of the anniversary of Queen Maria I, summoning them to attend the ceremony:

‘The Most Illustrious Dr *Juiz de Fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), President, directs and informs Your Honour that on Sunday, the 17th of this month, immediately after the Te Deum, Your Honour is to be present in the hall of the council sessions, so as to proceed from there with the other councillors, in the formal body of the Council, to the Palácio de São Lourenço, where His Excellency the Governor and Captain-General of this State is holding a solemn hand-kissing ceremony to celebrate the happy anniversary of the Most Serene Queen Our Lady.’

In earlier times it was customary for official festivities to last three days. There were, for example, great illuminations in Funchal on 4, 5 and 6 January 1803, for the birth of an infante; on 10, 11 and 12 February 1807, for the same reason; on 7, 8 and 9 July 1815, for a religious solemnity in honour of St James the Less; on 11, 12 and 13 October 1823, because the ‘King of Spain had been restored to the fullness of his royal powers’; at the beginning of 1826, because John VI had taken the title of Emperor of Brazil and King of Portugal; on 6, 7 and 8 August of the same year, for the proclamation of the new constitution; on 12, 13 and 14 March 1828, for the arrival of Miguel I in Lisbon; on 7, 8 and 9 February 1829, for the recovery of the same prince; and on 11, 12 and 13 December 1834, for the marriage of Queen Maria II to Prince Auguste, Duke of Leuchtenberg. When Maria II married, the national mourning decreed for the death of Pedro IV, Duke of Bragança, was suspended for three days:

The decree of 19 November 1825 ordered that courts and other public offices should use not wax but oil for their illuminations, with the lights enclosed in lanterns placed on the outside of the windows. It was during the festivities held in Funchal because John VI had taken the title of emperor and king that the Municipal Council first used, at the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), the system of illumination recommended in that decree.

The festivities held in Funchal on 28 January 1822 to mark the first anniversary of the proclamation of the Constitution were of unusual splendour, as the description of them in no. 62 of *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’) shows. There were many others that would also deserve mention, were we to set out to give an account of every celebration referred to in the newspapers and old documents we have consulted.

In the days of absolutism, failure by the so-called persons of the governance (*pessoas da governança*, notables eligible for municipal office) to attend the religious or secular ceremonies held to solemnise royal anniversaries was punished with imprisonment in the public gaol or in a fortress. This was also the penalty incurred by those who, without good reason, failed to accompany the procession of Corpus Christi. On gala days the noblemen and other persons of rank in the city were required to illuminate their buildings and to take part in the other official celebrations that it was customary to hold.

In the articles Festas do Espírito Santo, Jogo de Canas, Natal, Procissões, Rambles in Madeira, Romarias, etc., readers will find further information on the festivities, pastimes and celebrations of the Madeirans, almost all of them unofficial. To conclude this account, we shall add only that the custom of greeting the passage from the old year to the new, on the night of 31 December to 1 January, with gunshots, rockets and other fireworks is not very old. It began to become widespread only 45 to 50 years ago (1921), and it is said to have been the late merchant João José Rodrigues Leitão who introduced it to Madeira around 1860 to 1865.
Manilha

Water was formerly measured in *manilhas* (old water-flow measure: an orifice one palm in circumference, = 16 *anéis*), *anéis* (water measure: 1/16 *manilha* = 8 *penas*) and *penas* (traditional unit of water flow, roughly 1/60 litre per second), each *manilha* containing 16 *anéis* and each *anel* eight *penas*.
According to an official letter dated 8 November 1849 and published in vol. II of the *Epocha Administrativa*, the *manilha* was ‘an orifice one *palmo* (span, about 22 cm) in circumference’.
The *manilha* is little used today, but drinking water is still sold by the *pena*, half-*pena* and quarter-*pena*, as in the days before the metric decimal system came into force.
See *Pena de água*.
Basil
An aromatic plant of the Labiatae family, belonging to the genus *Ocimum*. It is widely grown, mainly in pots, in Funchal and in the countryside.
Manso (Dom Manuel Martins)
Dom Manuel Martins Manso was the 24th bishop of Funchal, heading the administration of this diocese from 16 November 1850 to 13 June 1858.
He was born in the municipality (*concelho*) of Mogadouro on 21 November 1793 and died in the city of Guarda on 1 December 1878.

In 1819 he graduated in canon law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), and he was ordained priest in 1822. In 1824 he was appointed vicar general of Bragança, where on several occasions he governed the diocese as vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter).
Presented as bishop of Funchal on 18 April 1849, he was confirmed by the Holy See on 28 May 1850 and received episcopal consecration on 8 October of the same year.

Referring to this prelate, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo says: ‘cultured and virtuous, Bishop Martins Manso was the Good Shepherd in the diocese of Funchal, and he acted in the same way in that of Guarda, to which he was transferred in 1858’. During the eight years in which he presided over the fortunes of the Funchal church, he was always most zealous in fulfilling his episcopal duties, leaving the most honourable memories here in Madeira. The prudence, gentleness and evangelical spirit with which he conducted the affairs of this bishopric are still remembered today. He won the widest sympathy, and his departure for the diocese of Guarda was therefore deeply felt.
Common buzzard (Buteo vulgaris)
A bird of the family Falconidae, found mainly in the uplands of Madeira, which builds its nests on rocks, in laurels, etc.
It seizes small birds and is less common today than formerly, because it is much persecuted by hunters. Its eggs are speckled.
Mantegazza (Paulo)

A few years ago, some time after 1905, a translation by Henrique Braga was published in Lisbon of the work by the illustrious Italian writer and psychologist Paulo Mantegazza entitled *Uma pagina de Amor (Um dia na Madeira)*. As a whole it is a work of pure fiction, but it contains some interesting pages on Madeira that deserve to be read, especially for the beauty of the language and the originality of the plot. The translation was made from the 24th Italian edition. Of all works containing references to this archipelago, it is the one that has run to the greatest number of editions, owing solely to the author’s celebrated name and to the passionate love story that unfolds throughout the book. The book closes with a short account of Madeira and a chapter reviewing various works dealing with this island. Both are of some interest, despite the inaccuracies they contain.

Maracujá

The Passifloraceae to which Madeirans give this name are the following: *Passiflora ligularis*, from Peru; *P. edulis*, from Brazil; *Tacsonia mollissima*, from Quito; *T. Van Wolxemii*, from New Granada; and *T. Parritae*, from Tolima. The genus *Passiflora* differs from the genus *Tassonia* in having a very short calyx tube. The first species (yellow or English *maracujá*) and the second (purple *maracujá*) are the most prized on the island. The juice of the fruit of *P. edulis* is said to be useful in treating cancerous diseases.

March (John Howard)

In the article Englishmen (p. 164) we made a brief reference to John Howard March, saying that he was of English nationality, whereas in fact he was born in the United States of North America and was a citizen of that country. He was a wealthy merchant in Funchal and on several occasions served as American consul. He became well known here in Madeira for his great acts of benevolence. He not only relieved the poor of this land and some of its charitable institutions with extraordinary generosity, but also contributed liberally to various public improvements, the upkeep of schools, etc. Although a Protestant, he rebuilt the church of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) and the large churchyard surrounding it. In 1828 he lent the money needed to pay the Miguelite troops who had seized Funchal, while at the same time sheltering many Constitutionalists in his house to protect them from persecution by the Absolutists. During the famine that ravaged this island in 1846 and 1847 he rendered notable services and did much to ensure the success of the subscriptions opened in this archipelago and abroad for the poor of Madeira.

Because he was a republican, the Portuguese government could not at that time honour him with any of the degrees of the military orders then existing, and so it had a special gold medal struck to reward the notable services rendered by this North American citizen.
Tides
On p. 378 of the 1st volume of the work ‘Zargo’s Islands’ (*Ilhas de Zargo*) there is the following information, which we take the liberty of transcribing word for word:
‘On the movement of the tidal currents of Madeira, the Hydrographic Mission of the Adjacent Islands (*Ilhas Adjacentes*) has kindly supplied us with these reliable notes:
During the flood tide the waters come from the southern quadrants; during the ebb, from the north-east quadrant.

The flood waters divide on the south coast of Madeira, running west and east from the stretch between Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Ponta do Jardim do Mar (‘point of the garden by the sea’). From this point to Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), the sea currents generally set from the north-west close to the coast. These currents run parallel to the coast or slightly inclined towards it, and are at times quite strong offshore (in the zone of approximately 500 m depth). Near the headlands they become stronger, sometimes producing a meeting of waters, as can be seen at Ponta do Pargo and above all at Ponta de São Lourenço, where their speeds reach about 2 miles at spring tides.

The flood currents are felt chiefly on the south coast, at Ponta do Pargo and Ponta de São Lourenço, and also on the north-west coast, at Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’) and near Ilhéu Mole (Porto Moniz).

The ebb waters produce strong currents towards the south-south-west at Ponta de São Lourenço, towards the west at Ponta de São Jorge and towards the south-west at Ilhéu Mole and Ponta do Tristão. The waters run almost parallel to the coast from Ponta de São Jorge to Ilhéu Mole, that is, on the north coast; on the north-east coast the currents are nil or very weak, except in the deep waters off Ponta do Barlavento (‘windward point’).
The ebb currents are felt chiefly on the north coast, above all at Ponta de São Lourenço and Ilhéu Mole, where at spring tides they reach speeds of 1.5 miles.
At neap tides the currents are generally nil or very weak. These currents are influenced by the prevailing winds and the barometric conditions of the North Atlantic.

At Funchal it is chiefly the flood currents that are felt; they run slightly inclined towards the coast (east-north-east) and at spring tides reach speeds of about 1.2 miles at around half-flood. The ebb currents are generally nil or very weak, the waters running east-north-east and at other times west.

At Porto Moniz, both the flood and the ebb currents are felt at spring tides, but chiefly during the flood counter-currents and surges of water arise at first inside the harbour, the waters running more directly during the ebb at a speed of 1 mile. At Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) the currents are generally quite weak or nil.

Around the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) the sea currents reach their greatest speeds at spring tides, running from the southern quadrants during the flood and from the north-east quadrant during the ebb. They are felt chiefly at the southern point of Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’), where at spring tides the waters run north-east at a speed of 1 mile during the flood and 1.5 during the ebb. At the point of Ilhéu de Baixo (‘lower islet’), during the flood, they run west or east at a speed of 1 mile, at spring tides, during the ebb.

The tides are very regular, with two high waters and two low waters every day. The values of the harmonic and non-harmonic constants are those of the tables drawn up by the Hydrographic Mission of the Adjacent Islands (*Ilhas Adjacentes*). By comparing the values of the establishments of the port (time of high water at full and new moon), one obtains the differences between the times of high and low water at the respective ports’. These tables are printed on p. 380 ff. of ‘Zargo’s Islands’.

Since 1939 the ‘Junta Autonoma dos Portos do Arquipélago da Madeira’ has published every year an interesting booklet entitled *Tabela das Marés no Porto do Funchal*, which gives precisely, from 1 January to 31 December and at stated times, the heights of the high and low waters, taken morning and afternoon within the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*). These data are preceded by the following notes: ‘This table was calculated by the Hydrological Mission of the Adjacent Islands from the records of 1937 supplied by the same Mission’s tide gauge, installed on the Molhe da Pontinha (‘little point breakwater’). The heights in the tide table refer to the plane of hydrographic zero, which lies 1.40 m below mean sea level (1937) and 4.138 m below the level mark of the Hydrographic Mission of the Adjacent Islands on the upper rim of the well of its tide gauge. – The times are Funchal legal time (Greenwich Mean Time minus one hour).

The ‘tidal elements’ for the port of Funchal given there are as follows: unit of height 1.06 m, maximum observed range 2.58 m, mean deduced range 1.53 m, minimum observed range 0.55 m, maximum diurnal inequality in height 0.25 m, and the ‘establishment of the port’ 0 h 32 min.

The establishment of the port, or the time of high water at spring tides, is at Funchal, according to the geographical map of General António Pedro de Azevedo, 12 h 48 min, the rise of the tide being 2.28 m’.
Margaça

The vernacular name of *Anthemis mixta* and *A. cotula*, annual plants of the family Compositae. The first is found in the streets of Funchal, at Rabaçal, at Ponta do Pargo, etc.; the second at Ponta de São Lourenço, on Porto Santo, etc.
Maria Amélia (Princess)

Princess Maria Amélia was the only child of the marriage of Pedro IV and the Empress Amélie. She was born in Paris on 1 December 1831 and died in Funchal on 4 February 1853. She received a refined education in Portugal and abroad, and interrupted her studies only when, in 1852, she was struck by the illness that killed her. She spoke several languages and possessed a considerable store of knowledge, which filled those who knew her closely with genuine admiration. To a lively intelligence and brilliant gifts of mind she joined the most captivating kindness and the most attractive qualities of heart.

The princess had a frail constitution, and it was in the gardens of the Necessidades Palace that a chill brought on the first signs of her illness. Once this crisis had passed, the doctors advised a voyage to Madeira. It took place in August 1852, as has already been briefly related in the article Amélia (Empress Dona) (vol. I, p. 63), to which we refer the reader.
The death of Princess Maria Amélia in this city led to the creation of the hospice (*hospício*) that bears her name, founded by her grieving mother, the Empress Dona Amélia.

To avoid needless repetition, the reader should consult the articles Amélia (Empress Dona), Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*) and Quinta Lambert. Anyone wanting a fuller account of the empress’s visit, the princess’s death and the founding of the Hospice should consult the pamphlet *Visita de sua magestade a imperatriz do Brasil, viuva, duqueza de Bragança, à ilha da Madeira, e fundação do Hospício da Serenissima Princesa D. Maria Amélia*, written by Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega and published in Funchal in 1867 by Júlio da Silva Carvalho.

In 1916 the writer Mário de Almeida was preparing the publication of a book entitled *Lisboa antes da Regeneração*, from which a Lisbon newspaper published an extract of the chapter entitled *Princesa D. Maria Amélia – Os seus derradeiros momentos – O Paço das Angustia*. It is an interesting and heartfelt description of the ill-fated princess’s stay on this island. This fine piece of prose was reprinted in the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) of 15 September 1916.

Quince (Cydonia oblonga, subspecies maliformis)

A shrub of the family Rosaceae, subfamily Pomoideae, originating, it seems, in south-west Asia. It is cultivated in Madeira, where its fruit is much sought after for making quince marmalade. Quince juice is useful against diarrhoea, and an infusion of the seeds can be used against coughs.
Marmulano (Sideroxylon Marmulano)

A shrub of the family Sapotaceae, with milky sap, large, leathery, obovate or obovate-oblong leaves, and very small flowers arranged in axillary clusters. It is found at Porto Moniz, at Ribeira da Janela, at Seixal, on Porto Santo, etc. It yields a yellowish wood, and its leaves make good fodder.
Marquis of Pombal

On 20 January 1776 religious ceremonies were celebrated with the greatest pomp in the church of the College (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), in thanksgiving for the Marquis of Pombal’s escape from the crime planned by the Genoese João Baptista Pele, who was executed in Lisbon. The sermon was preached by Friar Inácio José de Varona who, to please the Marquis – represented at the ceremony by his kinsman, Governor Sá Pereira – implied in his address that the Jesuits could not have been strangers to the said crime.
The cost of the religious celebrations was borne by the Royal Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*) of the Island of Madeira.
Marques (Dr Vasco Gonçalves)

He was born in Funchal on 29 August 1877, the son of Dr Joaquim Gonçalves Marques and Dona Maria Gonçalves Marques. He qualified as a physician and surgeon at this city’s now defunct Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica*), completing the course in 1897. For some time he was a physician in Seixal (‘pebble shore’), and later moved to Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) as the Council’s district medical officer. He remained there until 1904, when he was appointed secretary of the emigration police in Funchal, a post he held until after the establishment of the Republic in our country.

Having joined the Regenerator Party while still quite young, he always rendered it the most notable services, both in the electoral contests fought in the days of the monarchy in the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto do Moniz, where he wielded great political influence, and in the party’s press. This was especially true of *Direito*, in which for some years he wrote countless articles that revealed his much-appreciated gifts as a journalist.

When the Republic was proclaimed and the old monarchist parties dissolved, Dr Vasco Marques joined the Democratic Party, led by Dr Afonso Costa, and under the new regime he continued to display his great intellectual gifts and his tough fighting temper. He edited the *Liberal* and the *Democrata*, and was municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of Funchal in 1912 and 1913. After the death of the Viscount of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) he was elected president of the District Committee (Comissão Distrital) of that party. In 1920 he joined the Republican Party of National Reconstitution, in which he now holds a post identical to the one he last held on the district committee of the Portuguese Republican Party (1921).

Dr Vasco Marques has been elected senator for Madeira four times: on 13 June 1915, 11 May 1919, 10 July 1921 and 29 January 1922. In the national parliament he has made many speeches championing the interests of this archipelago.

As president both of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and of its executive committee, he has rendered many services to his homeland. To him is owed the great expansion of the district's roads in recent years, the acquisition of the Incarnação building, where the episcopal seminary (*Seminário*) was housed, and of the house that serves as the old people's home, the construction of a new pavilion at the Camara Pestana asylum, etc., etc. The plan of improvements that he and the executive committee of the General Council drew up and intended to carry out includes the construction of several new roads and the repairs that many existing ones need, the harnessing of water for irrigation, the reforestation of Madeira's mountains, the construction of a modern housing district, etc., etc.

Dr Vasco Marques rendered excellent services on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) during an epidemic that broke out on that island, and in Porto Moniz, where, as we have said, he spent many years, he left a great deal of goodwill through the way he carried out the duties of his post. For some time he was also a teacher of German at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), and on 4 October 1897 he enlisted in the reserve corps of medical officers; at present he holds the rank of militia captain in the army (1921).
Marquês (square)

It is also known as Moinhos (‘mills’). Near it stood several water mills belonging to the marquesses of Castelo Melhor, who also gave the place its name; the mills were demolished in 1898. See Moinhos.
Porbeagle (Lamna cornubica)

A shark of the family Lamnidae, which also lives in the waters off Setúbal, Buarcos and Sesimbra. It attacks humans and destroys various useful species, and is therefore hunted by fishermen, especially when it comes close to the coast. It is also known by the name *anequim*.
Fishermen usually catch porbeagles with the gaff (*bicheiro*) (see that entry), and then kill them by clubbing or by some other means.
White horehound (Marrubium vulgare)

A perennial labiate, common on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
