It has also been found near the chapel of Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) on the island of Madeira, and on all three of the Desertas (‘deserted islands’). Its flowers are white and its leaves ovate-suborbicular, wrinkled, and greyish or whitish. An infusion of horehound is used as a tonic, stimulant and emmenagogue medicine.
Martins

Frutuoso refers to Cristóvão Martins de Grinão, nicknamed ‘the Turkey’ (*o Peru*), and to Vasco Martins Moniz, noblemen who lived in Funchal in the 15th century, and Dr Azevedo says that there was a Spaniard named Diogo Martins, to whom Queen Catherine granted arms in 1560. At the time the French sacked Funchal, Cristóvão Martins and João Martins, clerk (*escrivão*) of the royal exchequer, were living here. Among those who signed the record (*auto*) of the vow by which St James the Less was adopted as patron saint of the city appears Fernão Martins, of whom we do not know whether he belonged to the island’s nobility.
Martins (Agostinho)

A distinguished Madeiran musician, born in 1841, who died in Funchal on 9 April 1909. He became a pupil of the celebrated violinist Agostinho Robio when he was only 10 years old, and later grew into a most distinguished musician, equal in knowledge and performance to the best Portuguese and foreign violinists.

He founded the Academia Marcos Portugal, the Sociedade de Concertos Funchalense and the local band (*filarmónica*) Restauração de Portugal, and in the last years of his life he organised the sextet that bore his name and earned a distinguished reputation here in Madeira.
Martins (Dr Frederico dos Santos)

He is the son of the wealthy landowner Manuel Martins, was born in this city on 1 November 1869, and holds a bachelor’s degree (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He settled in Lisbon many years ago and practises law there with distinction. He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislative sessions of 1902-1904 1904 and 1906. He has published some of his legal work in defence of various civil and commercial cases in several pamphlets. He is the author of the notable work *Direito Comercial Maritimo*, of which only the first part has appeared, in one volume of 383 pages, in 1932.
Martins (Dr João Augusto)

An army doctor of the overseas service, now deceased. He was a native of Cape Verde and had qualified at the Lisbon Medical School (*Escola Medica de Lisboa*). Works: *A Madeira e o seu clima*, Lisbon, 1901, 10 pp., and *Madeira, Cabo Verde e Guiné*, Lisbon, 1891, 271 pp. This last work is commendable for the correctness, elegance and spontaneous charm with which it is written.
Martins (Dr Manuel Augusto)

He was born in this city on 1 March 1867, held a bachelor’s degree (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and was one of the longest-established lawyers in Funchal. By telegram of the Provisional Government of the Republic of 5 October 1910 he was appointed Civil Governor of Madeira, taking office the following day; the office was conferred on him by an employee of the secretariat of the Civil Government.

By decree of 17 February 1919 he was again appointed Civil Governor of this district, taking office on the 19th of the same month and year and leaving it the following May, having been elected deputy for Évora.

It was during his first term as Civil Governor of Funchal that the cholera epidemic broke out in this city, and Dr José Alfredo Mendes de Magalhães (see that entry) then came to Madeira as High Commissioner (*alto comissário*) and representative of the central government. In July 1921 he was elected senator for this archipelago. He contributed widely to the local press, notably the newspaper *O Povo* (‘The People’), of which he was chief editor for some years. He died in Funchal on 4 April 1936.
Martyrs (Forty)

On the passage through Madeira of the forty members of the Society of Jesus who were massacred off the Canary Islands on 15 July 1570, see the article Azevedo (Blessed Inácio de), on p. 110 of vol. I, and the book *Paróquia de Santo António na Ilha da Madeira*.
Martírio
The vernacular name of *Passiflora caerulea*, a species of the family Passifloraceae, native to North America and widely grown in Madeira.
Martius (C. Fred. Phil. de)

A German botanist, born in Erlangen in 1794, who died in Munich in 1868. Having taken part in the scientific expedition organised in 1817 by the Austrian and Bavarian governments to explore Brazil, he visited Madeira towards the end of the first quarter of the 19th century, and in his works mentions various plant species found both in Funchal and at Nossa Senhora do Monte (‘Our Lady of the Mount’).
Mascarenhas (Dom Filipe de Alarcão e)

He succeeded Francisco da Costa Freire as Governor and Captain-General (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago; he was appointed on 13 August 1727 and took office on 27 September of the same year.
Mascarenhas (Dom Francisco de)

His appointment as Governor and Captain-General (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira dates from 31 July 1665, and he took up the post on 28 November of the same year. He faced great difficulties during his governorship, and on 18 September 1668 a popular uprising broke out which deposed him, arrested him and then forced him aboard ship, as will be told more fully in the article Popular Riots. He was replaced on an interim basis by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos.
He was the son of the Count of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and had served with valour in the War of Restoration. He died on 25 February 1699.
Mascarenhas (Manuel de Sousa)

He was appointed Governor and Captain-General (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira on 27 February 1645 and took office on 11 April of the same year. He was arrested by his successor, Manuel Lôbo da Silva, under an order the latter brought from the government in mainland Portugal, Manuel de Sousa Mascarenhas being accused of grave abuses in the exercise of his office as Governor of this archipelago.
Mason (J. A.)

He was a doctor of medicine of the University of Edinburgh, although he had begun his medical studies in Paris. He visited Madeira in 1834 because of a lung complaint from which he was suffering, but, as he did not find here the improvement he had hoped for, he moved to another climate and died in Nice the following year, at the age of 27. Works: *A Treatise on the Climate and Meteorology of Madeira*. In this work, valuable for many reasons and not published until 1850, its author sought to prove that the climate of Funchal was damper than that of London and its surroundings!
Mason (Nathaniel Haslope)

English botanist and dealer in natural-history objects who visited Madeira in 1857 and assembled here various collections of phanerogams, ferns, woods, shells, beetles and corals, which he supplied to various European scientific institutions.
Massapez
A hard clay soil, common in the cultivated zone of Madeira. When it is not irrigated frequently, it develops large cracks, which does not happen with other soils on the island.
Masson (Francis)

This English botanist arrived in Madeira in May 1776, and the following year he visited the Azores, where, we believe, he remained until October 1778. After spending time in the West Indies, England and Portugal, he returned to Madeira, which he finally left in 1785.

Masson was the first to carry out systematic botanical explorations in the Madeira archipelago, and he made known several species peculiar to this part of Portuguese territory. On several occasions he sent Joseph Banks specimens of the flora of our archipelago, and he also sent some plants to the son of Linnaeus, who described and published them.

Many of the plants sent to Joseph Banks are in the British Museum, which also holds a manuscript entitled *Massonii Flora Maderensis*; this appears to be a copy of another, now lost, compiled by Francis Masson.
On Masson’s stay in Madeira and the botanical work he carried out here, the article published in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) of 27 April 1915 should be read.
Mastruço

In Madeira this name is given to *Lepidium virginicum*, *L. sativum* and *Coronopus didymus*, plants of the family Cruciferae; the first two are naturalised and the last is native. *Coronopus didymus* and *Lepidium virginicum* are easy to recognise: the latter by its erect stems, its toothed upper leaves and its suborbicular silicles, and the former by its deeply cut leaves and its kidney-shaped silicles, broader than they are long. Both are very common in Madeira, whereas *L. sativum*, with broadly winged silicles, is found only at São Roque. All these species are antiscorbutic, and the last can be eaten in salad. The juice of the leaves of *Coronopus didymus* is used externally to treat certain skin diseases.
Municipal Slaughterhouse
The old municipal slaughterhouse was built in 1851, next to the Fish Market (Praça de São Pedro). It served its purpose well and had abundant water for cleaning.

A council resolution of 1495 ordered the butchers to slaughter and skin livestock at the Cabo do Calhau (‘end of the pebble shore’). On 20 May 1791, however, the Council decided to draw up an estimate for building a slaughterhouse next to the house of the market inspectorate (*almotaceria*), and in 1795 it asked the Royal Treasury for a loan of 400,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) to carry out the building. On 9 September 1825, by order of the municipality, the slaughterhouse was moved to the vicinity of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), and the market inspectors (almotacés) were authorised to punish ‘the slaughtermen and skinners’ who killed livestock outside the new place assigned to them.

As early as 1446 there was a public butcher’s shop (*açougue*) and a house for the sale of meat in Funchal, and the book of council sessions for 1488 shows that the butchers’ house then stood towards Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’).

The slaughterhouse of 1851 was demolished and replaced by the present Municipal Slaughterhouse (*Matadouro Municipal*), which dates from 1941. It stands on the right bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’), in the continuation of the former Beco do Cascalho (‘gravel alley’). It is a modern and spacious building, constructed not only with the room needed to carry out all the services proper to it, but also in accordance with the strictest rules of hygiene.
Forests

Our principal forests are of laurel, chestnut and pine. Laurels dominate in the valleys of Madeira’s interior; chestnuts form substantial groves below 750 or 800 metres; and pines, which today climb to an altitude of 1200 metres, cover extensive tracts of the southern and northern slopes and are one of the island’s most important sources of wealth.

The *til*, the *vinhático*, the *barbusano*, the *pau-branco*, the *aderno*, the *folhado*, the holly and other native species are tending to disappear from Madeira’s woodland. The forests of ancient tree heath that we knew 30 or 40 years ago in the upper part of the island were long ago destroyed by woodcutters and charcoal burners, without anyone thinking to call them to account for their acts of vandalism.

Madeira, which at the time of its discovery was one vast forest that had to be set on fire before the land could be cleared, has today greatly reduced its area of woodland of wild species. We suppose that this area does not exceed 15,000 hectares, which is very little in so rugged a land as ours. It is therefore desirable to plant new woods, especially along the banks of the streams and on the slopes of the central mountains, so that their roots hold the soil and the torrents do not rush down violently, causing incalculable damage. See Afforestation, Trees and Shrubs, Common Lands and Timber.
Matos

This family surname begins with Luís Fernandes de Matos Coutinho, who came to the island of Madeira around 1580 and had a large trading house in Funchal. He was the grandson of Pedro Vasques de Matos, who claimed descent from the kings of León.
Evil eye

It is still a common belief today, not only in the countryside but also in Funchal, that certain individuals are endowed with the power to cause illness through their eyes. If a child begins to lose weight for no known reason, or if the pig, the cow, the sheep or the goat falls ill with a disease that is not easy to identify, there is always someone who blames these ills on the evil eye (*mau olhado*), since it is not easy to find a better explanation for them. A tree that bears good fruit may stop bearing it because of the evil eye, and even our food is not safe from the spells of those to whom the devil has granted the power to do harm, without the law being able to hold them to account.

According to believers, no one can escape the evil eye, but curing it is an easy matter, and the sick person need not even be present for the treatment to succeed. A single item of the afflicted person’s clothing, or any other object that has touched them, is enough for the folk healer (*curandeira*) to carry out the treatment with absolute certainty of success.
To find out whether a person is afflicted by the evil eye, a drop of olive oil is dropped into water. If the oil spreads, the evil eye is present; if it stays together, it is not.

Once the evil eye has been recognised, the test is repeated as many times as necessary until the oil no longer spreads when it falls into the water. As soon as this result is achieved, the patient is cured. The treatment can sometimes last eight days, and the water used on one day must not be used in the following tests.

Each time she carries out the treatment, the folk healer speaks the following words: I cure you in the name of God and of the Virgin Mary; if they gave it to you (the evil eye) in your eating, or in your drinking, or in your laughing, or in your mocking, or in your beauty, or in your walking, may whoever gave it to you never give it to you again, and may it leave this body and go into the sea.

The belief in the evil eye is one of the few superstitions that progress and civilisation have not yet managed to destroy here in Madeira. It is so deeply rooted in the minds of the simple people of our countryside that no advice or warning can make them see how ridiculous and absurd are the methods the women healers use to cancel out the supposed harm that certain people cause their fellow beings.

The horns so often seen over pigsties are placed there by the owners of the pigs to prevent the animals from being affected by the evil eye or by bad air (*ar mau*)! Fishing boats, too, sometimes carry a few ox horns so that the evil eye does not drive away the fish, especially tuna and related species.
See Folk Medicine.
Maurice
Works: *Découverte de l'ile de Madère* (*Musée des Familles*, vol. IV, 1836, p. 90).
Maximilian of Habsburg

He is the brother of the late ex-Emperor of Austria and ex-King of Hungary, Emperor Charles I. He arrived in Madeira on 17 April 1922 aboard the British steamer *Kenilworth Castle* and went to stay at Monte (‘hill’), in the house of his sister-in-law, the ex-Empress Zita.
He left for Lisbon aboard the British steamer *Arcoma* on 26 April 1922, travelling on from there to Spain.
Maximilian (Emperor of Mexico)

On 5 July 1852 Prince Ferdinand Maximilian, who later became Emperor of Mexico, arrived in Madeira for the first time. His brief stay on the island was marked by the generous way in which he contributed to the building of the Ponte Monumental (‘monumental bridge’) and by the valuable gift he made to the Funchal Asylum for the Destitute and Orphans (*Asilo de Mendicidade e Órfãos do Funchal*).

In 1857 he married Princess Maria Carlota, daughter of Leopold I, King of the Belgians, and he arrived in Madeira with his wife on 6 December 1859 aboard the Austrian steam warship *Elisabeth*. The prince left the island on 22 December on a study voyage to South America, while the princess spent the winter in Funchal awaiting her husband’s return, which took place on 5 March 1860. On the 12th of the same month and year the prince and princess left the island for Austria.

On 10 April 1864 Prince Ferdinand Maximilian accepted the charge of becoming Emperor of Mexico, and as such he was at once proclaimed and recognised. On the 28th of that month and year he called at Madeira with his wife on the way to that country, aboard the Austrian frigate *Novara*, which was accompanied by the French frigate *Themis*. The emperor and empress were paid the honours due to their high rank, and the illustrious travellers graciously returned them by inviting to dinner aboard the *Novara* the diocesan bishop, Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura, the civil governor, the Count of Farrobo (‘carob tree’), the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), the consul Carlo de Bianchi, Dr Luís Pita, etc.

The unhappy emperor’s wretched end is well known. Unable to put down the revolutions that followed one another in the country, and abandoned by the French government, he was shot on 16 June 1867. The empress lost her mind and never recovered the use of her reason.

Everyone today acknowledges that Emperor Maximilian was the victim of the most atrocious injustice. By nature averse to violence and to all measures of excessive severity, he perhaps succumbed to the lack of energy and daring of which some of his most loyal supporters accused him.
He was a highly cultivated man and published several volumes, which were translated into French.

It seems that a marriage had been planned between Prince Maximilian and Princess Maria Amélia, daughter of Pedro IV and of Empress Amélie, who founded the hospice (*hospício*) that bears that princess’s name.

The beautiful statue of Our Lady of Sorrows (*Nossa Senhora das Dores*) that crowns the altar of the chapel of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*) was a gift from Prince Ferdinand Maximilian.
Mayer (Carlos)
See Hartung (p. 114).
House of Dona Mécia

The name ‘Casa de Dona Mécia’ is given to the old building in Funchal, in the Rua dos Aranhas, which we have already mentioned in this work (1-183). For some years it housed the Teacher Training School (*Escola de Habilitação ao Magistério*), and before that it was home to the Protestant church of the Ritualist sect. There was no shortage of people who took this house to be the setting of the tragic adventures that the distinguished Madeiran writer João Augusto de Ornelas fancifully devised in his curious novel *A mão de Sangue*. Others also gave credence to the interesting narrative by Camilo Castelo Branco in his book *O Santo da Montanha* (chs XXV–XXXI), which contains some useful details about Madeira.

Because of its old and typical construction, and certain features and peculiarities that distinguish it, the ‘Casa de Dona Mécia’ was included in September 1940, under a ministerial order (*portaria*) published in the *Diário do Govêrno*, in the list of national monuments and properties of public interest. It thus came under the direct authority of the public department that oversees these matters. The Casa de Dona Mécia was classified as a ‘property of public interest’.
See National Monuments (*Monumentos Nacionais*).
Medals
We know of the following medals, intended to reward services rendered in Madeira or to commemorate events worthy of being handed down to posterity:
Medal commemorating the defence of Funchal

Law no. 1123 of 4 March 1921 granted soldiers who served in Funchal during the war the right to wear the commemorative medal of the Campaigns of the Portuguese Army referred to in decree no. 5,086 of 3 January 1919, with the legend ‘Funchal-Defesa Maritima 1916- 1918.’
Medal commemorating the royal visit

To commemorate the visit of King Carlos I and Queen Amélia to the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes), a special medal was struck in Lisbon, of which few examples reached Madeira. One face bears the effigy of the former monarchs.
Constitutional Monument medal

It was made of silver by Severiano Alberto de Freitas Ferraz. According to no. 62 of *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’) of 1 February 1822, on one side it bore, ‘between two olive branches, the respected names of the 13 heroes who deserved well of the fatherland, and below them the following: the foundation stone of this monument was laid by the governor Dom Rodrigo António de Mello on 28 January 1822. On the other side it bore the following inscription: The Council of Funchal, acceding to the wishes of the citizens of this province, agreed to the erection of this monument to the political regeneration of the Portuguese monarchy, proclaimed in this city on 28 January 1821. Around this inscription were engraved the memorable days of 24 August, 15 September and 1 October 1820, and 26 January, 26 February and 4 July 1821. On the milled edge of the medal was engraved the following: Long live the Constitution, long live Religion and long live the dynasty of the House of Braganza.’

On 1 September 1823, by order of the absolutist authorities, the constitutional monument medal was crushed, then weighed and sold, and the proceeds went into the coffers of the municipality (*concelho*).
Exhibition medals

No. 62 of the *Correio da Madeira* (‘Madeira Courier’) reports that 17 silver medals were awarded to those who presented the most commendable products at the Madeiran Industry exhibition held from 1 to 4 April 1850. In no. 102 of the *Funchalense* we read that on 25 May 1861 the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace) was the scene of the prize-giving for the exhibitors who had earned them at the exhibition held in the same palace from 20 to 23 April; 12 first-class prizes, 18 second-class prizes and 20 honourable mentions were awarded. We have not seen any medal from the 1850 exhibition, but we have seen a second-class one from the 1861 exhibition, which reads on one side: ‘1ª. Exposição da Sociedade Agricola do Funchal–1861’, and on the other ‘*Res non verba*–Premio de 2ª. classe.’ This medal, which is silver and 40 millimetres in diameter, has various decorations in relief and was designed and made by the late Vicente Gomes da Silva (see that entry). Medal to reward the services of John March: see March.
Medeiros

This family surname appears to be almost extinct in Madeira. It descended from Rui Vaz de Medeiros, one of the first settlers who came to this island and who held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) land at Tábua.
Rural medicine

Country people in Madeira generally possess a certain amount of medical knowledge. Rare is the countrywoman who does not know how to treat herself for certain uterine complaints, and rare too is the one who does not know one or more effective remedies for various minor diseases that frequently afflict children and adults. There are women healers who can skilfully reduce a dislocation, and more than one educated person has benefited from the advice and directions of these women. They are almost always illiterate, yet some of them cannot be denied a certain skill and experience in the art of treating a number of ailments.

Below we give some information on how certain ailments are treated in the Madeiran countryside. Much remains to be said on the subject, which well deserves study by someone whose specialist knowledge makes them better placed than we are to judge the advantages or disadvantages of using particular medicinal agents.
Gravel (urinary)
An infusion of St John’s wort gives good results in treating this disease, provided the patient takes little meat, wine and spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine).
Asthma
To combat this disease, they customarily give patients a broth of slugs or of pigeon droppings.
Bronchitis, coughs and colds

They are treated with bees’ honey and hot infusions of ground ivy, sage, eucalyptus, hyssop, horehound, mullein, borage, *selvageira*, and fennel and coriander seeds (fruits). Mustard plasters on the chest, rubs with spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine) and hot foot baths are widely used for severe bronchitis, whereas simple colds usually pass without any medicine.
Watercress with sugar, warmed in the oven, is much used to combat coughs.
Sores, wounds, tumours, erysipelas and other inflammations

Plantain, *herva de Santa Maria*, *amor de burro* and *erva gigante* are applied boiled or crushed to external inflammations, and henbane (*meimendro*), generally known as *meiomento* (popular name for henbane), is used in the same way. The blood drawn from a freshly cut cockscomb is said to be useful in treating erysipelas, and it is also said that ground lupin seeds applied to the inflamed part of the body give good results.

The juice of *balsamo de canudo*, of *inhame de lagartixa* and of *formigueira* is used to heal wounds, and rubbing with the crushed leaves of dwarf elder (*engos*) is recommended for injuries caused by wounds or blows. The ointment known as the *unguento das Aires*, useful in many inflammations, is made with olive oil and the crushed leaves of *erva de Santa Maria* and plantain.

Decoctions of mallow, *chá bravo*, *amoricos* or agrimony, elder (the flowers), *diabelha* and other plants are widely used for washes, baths, gargles, eyewashes, etc. The infusion of chamomile (*macela*), besides being very useful for stomach upsets, is an effective remedy for inflammations of the eyes. Styes are treated by applying the soft inside of a loaf of bread to the inflamed part.
To treat whitlows, Madeirans use crushed oak shoots; and to help bring phlegmons to suppuration, they use poultices of linseed, potato (Madeiran *semilha*), banana and carrot.
Fainting or syncope

If fainting comes from weakness or from disorders of the digestive functions, it is customary to make the patient smell vinegar, or the boot of someone who takes little care to keep his feet clean. If it comes from more serious causes, mustard plasters on the legs and hot foot baths are resorted to until the doctor arrives. In the days when there were bloodletters in Madeira, bleeding was often practised to bring the patient round. There are women healers who know how to apply cupping glasses properly in cases of apoplexy.
Diabetes

An infusion of rose-apple leaves is recommended against this disease, which is very uncommon in the countryside. In the city, an infusion of eucalyptus leaves (see that entry) has been used with good results.
Dysentery
To treat it, the patient is given cinnamon tea and tea of *alfavaca de cobra*, vinegar lemonade, rice water, etc. In certain cases a purgative stops the evacuations.
Epistaxis or nosebleed

It often stops when a pinch of fine salt is put into the nostril from which the blood is flowing, or when the nose is washed with cold water, plain or mixed with vinegar. The bleeding can also be stopped by raising the arm on the same side as the affected nostril and holding the index finger upright.
Breathlessness
It is treated with orange-leaf or peppermint tea when it is due to nervous complaints, and with cupping glasses when it arises from disease of the respiratory organs. (See Asthma.)
Haemorrhoids
They are treated with an infusion of *alfavaca de cobra*, used internally and externally, and with cold or hot sitz baths.
Jaundice
It is treated with a decoction of the rhizomes of the strawberry plant or of couch grass, and by sucking sugar cane.
Ringworm and other skin diseases

The remedies used against skin diseases are, internally, infusions of *molarinha*, pansy, sorrel, stinging nettle, *teijeira* (lesser burdock), shepherd’s purse and walnut leaves; and, externally, paraffin, sea water and the somewhat caustic juices of celandine and *trovisco*. The use of sublimed sulphur is becoming widespread, and very hot water poured over the affected part of the body gives excellent results in soothing herpetic itching. Ash and spittle are considered useful in treating ringworm, and it is customary to accompany their application with the following words: ‘Ringworm with a tail, what have you come here to seek? Spittle from the mouth and ash from the hearth to cure you.’ (*Impigem rabicha, que vieste aqui buscar? Cuspo da boca e cinza do lar para te curar.*) Toasted flour moistened with forge oil is applied externally to eczema of the face, which Madeirans call *cobro*.
Inflammations of the liver
They are treated with purgatives and with poultices of *urgebão*. The infusion of this plant and that of horehound are also used with good results in diseases of the liver.
Stomach complaints

An infusion of chamomile (*macela*) is the remedy most used against colic, indigestion and other stomach complaints. For surfeit, an infusion of lemon balm is sometimes given, and for stomach pains an infusion of peppermint. In some cases a cup of black tea is enough to relieve disorders of the digestive functions caused by poor-quality food or by the amount eaten. A glass of very hot water, drunk on an empty stomach, is said to be very useful for dyspepsia and stomach pains. Linseed poultices are also useful for these pains, which may also disappear with the simple application of a suitably warmed baize cloth or a slice of bread soaked in hot wine.
Neuralgia

They are treated by applying a hot baize cloth or a mustard plaster to the painful spot. We are told that white onion, roasted in the embers and applied very hot to the sore spot, gives excellent results.
Uterine complaints

A remedy widely taken internally for uterine complaints is prepared from spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), *madre de louro* (fungal gall on laurel trunks), cinnamon, rue buds, aniseed and two or three cloves. An infusion of chard, basil and *amor de burro* is also used for the same purpose, as is one of wormwood and other emmenagogue plants. Rosemary, lavender, basil, *amor de burro*, *alecrim de Nossa Senhora*, etc., are used in baths or washes. With crushed rue and lavender or French lavender, a beaten egg and a little flour, a poultice is made that has a stimulating action on the uterus. Half a small glass of spirit eases the pains that often accompany menstruation.
Burns
They are treated with egg white, fresh urine, milk cream, and olive oil with a pinch of fine salt.
Rickets
Children suffering from this disease are placed in must inside the wine presses in which the grapes are trodden.
Retention of urine and other urinary complaints

Madeirans treat these diseases with warm baths, linseed poultices and infusions of *sempre-noiva*, *amor de burro*, *artemija*, couch grass, corn silk, cherry stalks, duckweed, St John’s wort, *pessegueiro inglês*, etc.
Rheumatism

Sulphur and paraffin applied externally, massage, mustard plasters, rubs with spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), warm wine or camphorated alcohol, washes with a decoction of rosemary or *trombeteira*, and salt-water baths are of some benefit in treating rheumatism. We are told that some people have cured themselves of this disease with paraffin applied with a hen’s feather. An infusion of avocado leaves is being taken internally against rheumatism, and rubs or fomentations with paraffin mixed with a well-beaten egg white are said to have given good results in treating this disease.
Intestinal worms

For tapeworm, or *solitária*, the remedies used are pumpkin seeds (those of the *abóbora machado* pumpkin being the most effective) and a decoction of the bark of the pomegranate root. For roundworms, or the small worms that often appear in children’s intestines, their expulsion is helped with peppermint tea or peppermint lozenges. Crushed garlic is sometimes used against roundworms.
Warts

Warts are removed by applying salt or the yellow, caustic sap of greater celandine, a plant that is common in Madeira. Many people suppose that, for the salt to take effect, it must be thrown into the fire after the wart has been rubbed with it.
Long after the publication (in 1921) of this note on country medicine in the archipelago, the Viscount of Porto da Cruz published a pamphlet entitled *A Flora Madeirense na Medicina Popular*.
Medicis (Dom Cosme de)

He lived in Funchal around the middle of the 18th century and was, according to tradition, a wealthy man. On one occasion he invited several friends to spend the day in a cave east of the spot where the lazaretto now stands, to enjoy various amusements. All of them met their death there when the ground above collapsed. The only survivor was a Black servant of Dom Cosme, who happened to be some distance from the cave; he brought to the city the news of the terrible catastrophe he had witnessed.
The place where the catastrophe occurred is known to seafarers as the Furna de D. Cosme.

From 1679 to 1684 Father Dom Zenóbio de Medicis, son of Dom Cosme de Medicis, attended the faculty of theology of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). It is therefore to be believed that the disaster happened long before the middle of the 18th century, since it is unlikely that this Dom Cosme de Medicis was still alive at that time.
Medina

According to Dr Álvaro R. de Azevedo, this family surname is of Spanish origin, and it may have appeared on the island during the Philippine period of Spanish rule. The Medina family of Cape Verde is of Madeiran origin.
In 1930 Dr João Cabral do Nascimento published the interesting pamphlet *Genealogia da Familia Medina da Ilha da Madeira*.
Medina e Vasconcelos (Canon Dr Gregório Nazianzeno)

He was born in Funchal in 1787 and died in that city on 23 April 1858. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), and practised as a lawyer here in Madeira with notable brilliance. He held various posts, among them judge of the British Conservatorial Court (*conservatória britânica*, special court for British subjects), representative (*procurador*) to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), vicar general of the bishopric, etc. He was a brilliant journalist and deputy for Madeira in the legislative session of 1837 to 1838. He enjoyed great prestige and influence thanks to his uncommon learning and remarkable qualities of character. He was the brother of the poet Medina e Vasconcelos, author of ‘The Zarco Epic’ (*Zargueida*).
Medina e Vasconcelos (Francisco de Paula)

The well-known author of ‘The Zarco Epic’ (*Zargueida*), who in his day enjoyed great renown as a poet, was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé in this city on 20 November 1768, the son of Teodoro Felix de Medina e Vasconcelos and Dona Ana Joaquina Rosa de Vasconcelos. He died a political exile on the island of Santiago, in the Cape Verde archipelago, in 1824, at the age of 56. We believe that the distinguished Medina e Vasconcelos family living in that archipelago descends from this illustrious fellow countryman of ours. The great Madeiran satirical poet Francisco Clementino de Sousa was also descended from Francisco de Paulo Medina.

There is little material to enable us to write a biography of the poet Medina in any detail. Some of the poems in his volume *Poesias Lyricas* show that he was twenty years old when he enrolled at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), which must have happened in 1788; he adds that ‘in the space of only two winters he heard the learned lectures of the sages who explain the mysteries of the sciences.’ Dr Azevedo says that, Medina having been ‘from his youth a follower of the ideas of the philosophers of the 18th century, this led, around 1790, to his being imprisoned for a year and a half in Coimbra, and afterwards forced to leave the city and expelled from the University for ever.’ The severity of this punishment seems to indicate that very serious charges weighed on Medina, but he utterly rejects them when he declares that it was ‘a false crime, never even conceived by me’. The poet wrote two *Epistolas* in verse to the rector of the University, Dom Francisco Rafael de Castro, one shortly after his imprisonment and the other when ‘already, sir, twelve moons have passed since I began weeping among tyrannous irons’. These letters were meant to implore the prelate’s protection and to obtain his release. It is not known whether Medina’s heartfelt poetic inspiration moved the inflexible magistrate, who was perhaps little swayed by the plaintive pleas of a poor, helpless student. It is certain, however, that he was set free a few months later, returning to his native land around 1792.

If Medina’s verses are to be believed, he led a life of bitter tribulations, both in Madeira and in mainland Portugal, which came to a sad end with his banishment to Cape Verde. Between 1792 and 1823 he made several visits to Portugal, and possibly abroad, though we do not know; on one occasion he was away from Madeira for about six years. It was surely during these more or less prolonged stays on the mainland that he published some of his volumes of verse, which appeared in Lisbon in 1797, 1805 and 1806.

Medina e Vasconcelos, who, in the words of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo already cited, showed himself from his youth a follower of the ideas of the 18th-century philosophers, was also a staunch supporter of the Constitution of 1821. For this reason he was caught in the net of the special judicial commission (alçada) that came to this island in 1823 (vol. I, p. 32) to conduct a rigorous and oppressive judicial inquiry (*devassa*) into the events that had taken place here at the proclamation of the first representative government in our country. The six magistrates who made up the commission arrived in Funchal on 26 August 1823 and delivered their sentence on 24 October of the same year. It states that Medina e Vasconcelos, ‘forgetful of the duties of honour and of a loyal subject, and of the ties that bound him most closely as a public official, had the reckless audacity to utter in public most grievous insults offensive to the decorum, veneration and respect due to the Throne and to the royal persons of Their Majesties, so grave that they are judged unworthy of being written in this judgment’. The same sentence asserts that he belonged to Freemasonry (*Maçonaria*) and took part in its work, having contributed notably to the proclamation and establishment of constitutional government in this archipelago. He was sentenced ‘to eight years of penal exile (degredo) in the State of Angola, with disqualification from offices of Justice or the Treasury, and to fifty thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) to the Exchequer’.

Medina e Vasconcelos died in the capital of the Cape Verde archipelago in 1824, that is, shortly after the sentence banishing him to Angola had been passed; the reasons for the change in the place where the penalty was to be served are unknown to us. This fellow countryman of ours held the post of notary in Funchal when he was tried by the commission and banished to Cape Verde.

Of the poetical works published by Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos, we know of the following: *Poesias Lyricas de Medina* .. Lisbon, 1797, 245 pp.; *Sextinas Elegiacas ao sempre memoravel estrago... na calamitosa aluvião do dia 9 de Outubro de 1803*, Lisbon 1805, 24 pp.; *Zargueida, Descobrimento da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1806, 254 pp.; and *Georgeida*, London, 1819, XIV-215 pp. In the *Diccionario Bibliographico Portuguez*, Inocêncio Francisco da Silva also mentions these poetical compositions: *Poesias lyricas*, Lisbon, 1793; *Noute triste a que deu logar a morte da Ex.ma Srª. D. Carlota Margarida*, Lisbon, 1792; *Noites tristes de Fileno na ausencia de Marilia*, Lisbon, 1805; and *Elegia á deploravel morte do grande e incomparável Manuel Maria Barbosa du Bocage*, Lisbon, 1806.

In a short critical appraisal of Medina’s poetry, Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says the following: ‘As a lyric poet he belonged to the French school; his verses are in general sonorous and well crafted, and he certainly did not lack naturalness. He aspired to sound the epic trumpet; but it is clear that this undertaking was far beyond his talent, and so in the two attempts he composed in that genre he never managed to rise above mediocrity. There are, however, in both of them, episodes that do not tarnish his muse and that may be read with pleasure.’

Of Medina e Vasconcelos’s compositions, it was ‘The Zarco Epic’ that brought him the greatest renown, and it is still today the best known of them all. It is an epic poem in *ottava rima*, modelled on the classical forms of the ancient epic. It is divided into ten cantos and contains more than five thousand lines. It deals with the discovery of Madeira by João Gonçalves Zarco, taking the discoverer’s surname as the title of the poem. It contains a series of interesting episodes with some felicitous poetic digressions, among which the legend of Robert Machin stands out. The actual discovery of this island is described only in Canto X. The poem is preceded by a sonnet dedicated to Bocage, to which that distinguished poet replied with another sonnet, which is without doubt the finest composition in this volume.
The *Arquivo Historico da Madeira* and the *Diário de Noticias* of 15 July 1928 contain some previously unpublished information about the poet Medina e Vasconcelos.
Medina e Vasconcelos (Sérvulo de Paula)

He was the son of the Madeiran poet Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos. He was born in Funchal around 1822 and went to the Cape Verde islands as a civil servant with the governor Dom José Miguel de Noronha in 1845, dying there around 1854. In Funchal in 1845 he published a drama entitled *Amor e Pátria*, which had been staged in this city at the Teatro Concórdia in August 1844. He was an editor of the *Beija-Flôr*, and around 1851 in Cape Verde he was editor of the *Boletim Official*, in which he published the novel *Um filho chorado*.
Medina (Friar Diogo de)

He was a monk of the Order of St Benedict and a distinguished calligrapher, who wrote most of volume I of the *Registo Geral da Camara Municipal do Funchal*, which contains documents of the 15th and 16th centuries. We do not know whether he was Madeiran, nor any other details of his life.
Medinas (street)

It is bounded by Rua da Cadeia Velha and Rua do Ribeirinho de Baixo. Its name comes from a family with the surname Medina having lived there. Before the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1856, this street was inhabited by families worthy of the greatest consideration and respect.
Medusa

The French frigate *Medusa*, well known for its wreck on the Banc d'Arguin, 40 *léguas* from the coast of Africa, and for the untold sufferings endured by many of its crew and passengers after they abandoned the ship, passed within sight of Madeira on 28 June 1816, but did not make contact with the land. The frigate was commanded by Duroy de Chaumareys, whose obstinacy and incompetence caused the deaths of more than 150 people who had embarked on it at Aix, bound for the French settlements on the west coast of Africa. The wreck occurred on 2 July 1816.
Meia Légua
To the east of the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’) lies a cliff that seafarers commonly call the Rocha da Meia Légua (‘half-league cliff’).
Henbane (Hyosciamus albus, subspecies major)

A member of the Solanaceae with incised-lobed leaves and yellow, funnel-shaped flowers, whose filaments and the inner part of the corollas are dark purple. It is found on the coast of Madeira and on Porto Santo. It is a poisonous plant, but its leaves can be used externally in the treatment of ulcers. Henbane oil can be extracted from this species as well as from *Hyosciamus niger*, a member of the Solanaceae not found in Madeira. In some parts of the island henbane is called *meiomento* (popular name for henbane).
Meireles
The first bearer of this surname we have found was Joaquim Coelho de Meireles, who in 1812 was treasurer of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*).
Meireles (Viscount of)

This distinguished writer and journalist, who died in 1915, visited this island several times and held the most devoted admiration for its natural beauty and mild climate. It was in 1913, when he spent a long stay in this city, that he argued brilliantly and with weighty arguments for the idea of rebuilding the house where Christopher Columbus lived, as we have mentioned elsewhere (vol. 1, p. 286 ff.). He also concerned himself with the triptych painted on wood in the sacristy of the parish church of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), making known to Madeirans the fine description of it by the distinguished writer Manuel Teixeira Gomes in his book *Cartas sem moral nenhuma*.
Mela
See Potato disease.
Watermelon (Citrullus vulgaris)
A member of the Cucurbitaceae grown on Porto Santo but little known in Madeira. The watermelons of Porto Santo are of good quality, though almost always small.
Melon (Cucumis Melo)

It is chiefly on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) that this member of the Cucurbitaceae is frequently seen. At the time Manuel Tomás wrote ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*), melons seem to have been abundant in Madeira, since we find them mentioned among the many fruits the island then produced. It is likely that the Ribeira dos Melões takes its name from the great abundance of melon plants once found on its banks or nearby.
Melim
It is, says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, the Portuguese form of Lomelini or Lomelino, but at present it is a separate surname borne by families of a decayed branch, if not wholly unrelated to the Lomelinos.
Melo

This family surname, says Dr Álvaro R. de Azevedo, became linked with those of the Câmaras and the Noronhas through the marriage of Dona Filipa de Noronha, second daughter of João Gonçalves da Câmara, second donatary (*donatário*) of Funchal, to Henrique Henriques, lord of Alcáçovas, son of Dom Fernando Henriques and Dona Branca de Mello.
Melo (Dom António Jorge de)
This governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of the archipelago was appointed to the post on 13 March 1689 and took office on 27 April of the same year.
Melo (Dom Francisco Manuel de)

We have already dealt with this illustrious writer in the article on Robert Machin, because it was he who, in his third *Epanaphora*, gave the widest currency to the poetic and well-known tale whose protagonist is that legendary figure. Other reasons, however, call for a fuller account of the author of the *Carta de Guia de Casados* and the *Apologos Dialogaes*, and so we return to him here.

Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, the second son of the illustrious discoverer of Madeira, was the third captain of the island of São Miguel, having bought that important donatary captaincy (*donataria*) from João Soares. Rui Gonçalves’s second son, Antão Rodrigues da Câmara, who had married a noblewoman from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), founded a great entailed estate on the island of São Miguel, whose present representative is the Count of Silvã; and it is to this distinguished family that the great writer Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo belongs.
Concerning this Antão Rodrigues da Câmara, we find the following curious episode in the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) of Father António Cordeiro:

‘. . . and he became so fine a horseman that on one occasion, when he was riding with many others escorting King Manuel I, who was also on horseback in the court city of Lisbon, an Indian happened to pass in front of them with an elephant that he was taking to show, and at that sight all the horses, even the King’s own, took fright and bolted, and some riders fell; but Antão Rodrigues so mastered his horse that, charging the elephant, he made his horse put its mouth on the elephant’s haunch, and, giving the beast a light stroke with his cutlass, he turned to the King saying that it was nothing: and the King at once ordered his master of the horse to buy that horse from Antão Rodrigues at any price; Antão Rodrigues immediately offered it, but as a gift, yes, and for no price at all; and as the King would not agree to this, nor would Antão Rodrigues sell it, he returned with the horse to the island from which he had brought it, already trained for him . . .’
Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo refers to his ancestry, tracing it back to the discoverer of Madeira:

‘. . . João Gonçalves Zarco, a man famous among our people, for, leaving aside the more ancient houses, of which no record is kept because they are uncertain, we have had few men in Portugal with such opulent descendants, to whom three counts of this surname owe their male line: Calheta (‘small cove’), Vila Franca and Atouguia. . . And through marriages 21 titles of this kingdom descend from João Gonçalves . . . And since my testimony does not seem invalid in matters concerning him, it is right that I should count myself in the very list of his successors, with no less claim than some I have mentioned; for, apart from those who hold the entails (*morgados*) of his male lines, I am the one who enjoys the greatest entail of the Câmara family, founded by António Rodrigues da Câmara, who was the maternal grandfather of my paternal grandfather and grandson of João Gonçalves da Câmara, son of his second son Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, lord of the island of São Miguel. . .’.

Among the large and brilliant progeny, spread across mainland Portugal, the Azores, Madeira and Brazil, that descends from the great navigator and discoverer of Madeira, there is certainly no figure as distinguished as Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo. According to the testimony of his contemporaries he was the greatest talent of his time, and he was also a most remarkable writer, an illustrious soldier and a skilful politician and diplomat.

Dr Azevedo notes Melo’s deliberate inaccuracy in making himself a descendant of Zarco in the legitimate male line, when it is certain that Luís Gonçalves da Câmara (see vol. 1, p. 206) had no issue from his only marriage, to Dona Maria Bettencourt.
In his notable work *D. Francisco de Mello*, Edgar Prestage, dealing with the writer’s exile to Brazil, describes the illustrious writer’s passage through this island in the following terms:

‘On Saturday, 17 April 1655, the fleet left Lisbon with thirty-six ships, and in four days it reached Madeira, where it was to take on the Company’s wines. News arrived there that an English fleet had put to sea with more than forty galleons and twelve thousand men, intending to cross to Brazil. Doubts at once arose as to whether, in view of this circumstance, the King’s regulations (*regimento*) should be obeyed, which ordered the general to proceed to Rio de Janeiro with the largest galleons, dividing the rest of the fleet into two squadrons, one bound for Pernambuco and the other for Bahia. The senior commanders, among them no doubt Dom Francisco Manuel, were called to a council. Opinions differed, but in the end it was resolved that the fleet should keep to its course for Cape Verde and gather information there about the English fleet.

‘The stay of almost a month in Madeira must have been agreeable to the writer, for it gave him the opportunity to see the natural beauties of the island. These certainly held a particular interest for him, not only because the island had been occupied by his ancestor João Gonçalves Zarco, who became its captain and the founder of the city of Funchal, but also because a year earlier he himself had recounted, in the 3rd *Epanaphora*, the supposed discovery by the runaway lovers Roberto Machim and Anna de Arfet. Leaving Madeira on 15 May, the fleet sighted the island of La Palma on the 19th and that of Cape Verde on the 26th....','

As already stated, Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo deals with the discovery of the island of Madeira in the third part of the *Epanaphoras*, which became very well known here after Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo included long extracts from it in one of his notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).

This narrative, with its florid and imaginative language, the implausibility of many of the facts and episodes it presents, and even its frequent digressions wholly unrelated to the subject, gives us the clear impression of a description of one of those fantastic love adventures with which the medieval romances of chivalry are filled. At first glance, and without any lengthy critical study of the text, it is evident that the illustrious writer did not write history but merely produced a work of pure romantic fiction. Soldier and poet, man of the world and gallant, of fiery and ardent imagination, he let himself be set alight by the lava of his fantasy. He so impressed the minds of his readers that, two and a half centuries later, his narrative still attracts, if not fervent believers, at least impressionable souls who find true allure and charm in it. Various prose writers and poets have found in it a source of inspiration for some of their finest literary compositions.

It was not Melo, however, who invented the story of Robert Machin, for before him, beginning with António Galvão (1563), several writers had referred to it. He sought to give it the standing of historical truth by basing his narrative on a manuscript which he claimed to possess, written by Francisco Alcoforado, one of the companions of João Gonçalves Zarco. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo himself, who treats Dom Francisco Manuel with so little indulgence, admits that he may have been deceived in good faith regarding the existence of this manuscript. Yet there is not the slightest doubt that he gave free rein to his ardent imagination in the account of the discovery of Madeira that he left us in his third *Epanaphora*.

As for the *Relation Historique de la découverte de l'isle de Madère*, published in Paris in 1671, whose preface claims it to be Alcoforado’s manuscript itself, it is nothing but a scandalous literary fraud, as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo amply demonstrates. Melo, however, bears not the slightest blame for it, since the illustrious writer died in 1666 and the *Relation* was published in 1671.

It is possible that, even in Melo’s time, word had spread, however vaguely, that the Madeira archipelago had been discovered in the 14th century, so that Zarco and his companions would not have been the first to land on these solitary shores. Over time this assertion has been supported by weighty arguments, without the fact diminishing the glory of Zarco as navigator, discoverer and first coloniser of Madeira.

In 1873 Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo was the first to bring to light the probable idea that the cession of Madeira to England had been contemplated, and perhaps even negotiated, as an integral part of the dowry of Queen Catherine.

In one of his annotations to the work of Gaspar Frutuoso, Dr Azevedo writes: ‘And the queen regent Dona Luísa, since any price seemed cheap to her to secure this marriage for the infanta, was secretly preparing the sacrifice of yet another valuable and coveted Portuguese colony, should it prove necessary: that of the island of Madeira… There is no record of this fact in the historians of the time, whether Portuguese or English, not even in the memoirs of Lord Clarendon, who deals at length with the said marriage and who, as chancellor to Charles II, even took an effective part in the diplomatic negotiations for it. So cautious was Queen Luísa that she managed to conceal her plan to cede the island of Madeira in this way; but, from the evidence we have found, we are convinced that such a plan really existed.’

In support of his assertion, Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo then enlarges on some extremely interesting considerations. Although they do not amount to decisive arguments or fully conclusive reasons, they are nonetheless conjectures and presumptions of great weight in favour of the idea of ceding this island, had England demanded this further sacrifice of Portugal. We do not reproduce Dr Azevedo’s sensible reflections in this place (*lugar*), because of their excessive length and because they can easily be found on p. 381 and following of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’.

The same illustrious annotator also maintains, though with less weighty arguments, that Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo collaborated with Queen Luisa de Guzmán in the plan for that cession by writing his *Epanaphora* and presenting Madeira as discovered by Englishmen, so as to make its handover to England more feasible and less odious to the Portuguese. It is only fair to hear Edgar Prestage, the learned biographer of Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo: ‘… the annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ of Gaspar Frutuoso alleges that Dom Francisco, having received the legend of the island’s discovery by the two English lovers Roberto Machim and Anna de Arfet, turned it into a romance in order to popularise this story and make the handover of Madeira to Charles II of England less hard on Portuguese pride, should that prove necessary. Now in our view this argument is somewhat forced, not to say fantastic, and Mr A. R. de Azevedo, in order to sustain it, has to press the charge further, saying that the *Epanaphora*, which in the printed book is dated from Belas in 1654, was deliberately antedated, having been written after Dom Francisco’s return from Brazil. But he forgets that he has previously stated that the *Epanaphora* shows, on its author’s part, an ignorance of the island’s topography, a circumstance that was natural in 1654 but could hardly have arisen afterwards, since, as we have already related, Dom Francisco stayed there for a month on his way into exile.

‘It was therefore Portugal’s absolute need to obtain England’s military and diplomatic support that justified the cession of Tangier and Bombay, besides an enormous dowry that was never paid in full, and the same need would have justified the cession of Madeira, had it been demanded. Whether the queen regent was ready to cede it, as Mr Azevedo argues, we cannot say, given the silence of the historians; but that Dom Francisco de Melo was Dona Luisa de Guzmán’s partner in the plot there is no proof whatever. For our part, it is a gratuitous assertion that deserves no credence. We are of the opinion that the subject of our biography genuinely believed in the original English discovery, as renowned historians before him had believed, even though he embroidered the details of the narrative’.

This is a point that may perhaps be impossible to clear up today, but it is not, in truth, of capital importance. The same cannot be said of the supposed cession of Madeira to the English, because that is of considerable interest to Madeiran history and still more to the general history of our country. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo did not settle the matter sufficiently, establishing only a probable hypothesis, and the talented author of the pamphlet *Um ponto de história pátria* added nothing essential to the considerations of the annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’.
Melo (Dom Rodrigo António de)

His appointment as Governor and Captain-General (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of the Madeiran archipelago dates from June 1821, and he took office on 2 July of the same year. He was dismissed at his own request by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 22 March 1822, but he did not leave the government until his successor, António Manuel de Noronha, had arrived and taken office on 22 April 1822. It was he who presided, on 28 January 1822, over the ceremony of laying the first stone of the Constitution monument, which was marked by the greatest solemnity.
Melo (Diogo de Azambuja de)
This governor-general of Madeira under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640) was appointed on 23 May 1594 and took office on 20 January 1595. He died in Funchal in 1600.
Melo (Florêncio José Correia de)

He was appointed governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago on 12 October 1814, arrived in Funchal on 16 April 1815 and took up his post on 22 April.

He arrived in Madeira a few months after the departure from the island of the British troops, whose presence over the long period of 7 years had brought the utmost indiscipline to the garrison forces and serious disorder and disruption to all the public services. Correia de Melo managed to correct these abuses as far as possible and rendered excellent service in the public administration of the archipelago.

During his government, Madeira saw the passage of the Emperor Napoleon, on 23 August 1815, on his way to banishment on St Helena, and of Princess Leopoldina, on 11 September of the same year, who was travelling to Brazil to marry the Prince Royal Dom Pedro and to whom Florêncio de Melo gave a splendid reception (see Napoleon in Madeira and Princess Leopoldina).
Florêncio José Correia de Melo personally handed over the government of Madeira to his successor and left the island in the second half of May 1819.
Melo (Pantaleão de Sá e)
He was appointed Governor and Captain-General (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira on 1 March 1694 and took office on 22 July of the same year.
Melo (Professor Carlos de)
Works: *Machico and the discovery of Madeira* (*The Scottish Geographical Magazine*, April 1896).
Blackbird (Turdus merula)

A bird of the thrush family (Turdidae), native to Madeira, which builds its nests in small trees, banana plants, etc. Laying generally takes place in May and June. It has been found on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), but does not breed on that island. It is the males that are noted for their strong and pleasant song. The blackbird sometimes shows white patches.
Mendes

Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, sent by John I to Madeira to marry Helena Gonçalves da Câmara, daughter of Zargo, was one of the first settlers of the island. He held large *sesmarias* (royal land grants to settlers on condition of cultivation) in São Martinho, beside the Ribeira dos Socorridos, and in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’). Joane Mendes de Brito was another early settler, who held a *sesmaria* in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário.
Mendes (Coelho)

Nearly forty years ago an Azorean with the surname Coelho Mendes lived in Funchal. Around 1885 he published in this city a volume of poems entitled *Flores Agrestes*, and he also published a short pamphlet in a controversy he carried on with Canon Aires Pacheco.

João Fortunato de Oliveira had earlier published in Funchal, in 1860, a volume of poems under the title *Flores Agrestes*, and many years later, in 1903, Manuel Ribeiro also published in this city a small volume of verse with the same title.
Mendes dos Reis (José)
In May 1919 he was elected deputy for this archipelago.
Mendonça

This family surname perhaps derives from descendants of the donataries (*donatário*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and Machico, since Bartolomeu Perestrelo, first donatary of that island, married Beatriz Furtado de Mendonça, and João Teixeira, third son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, married Filipa de Mendonça Furtado, by whom he had Tristão de Mendonça.
Mendonça (António Teixeira de)

In the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’), Diogo Barbosa Machado says that António Teixeira de Mendonça was a native of the island of Madeira and that he wrote the *Livro das Geraçoens do Reino de Portugal*. We know nothing more about him.
Meneses

This family surname derives from Vasco Martins Moniz de Meneses, nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*), who held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Caniço (‘reed’) and a large house in the town (*vila*) of Machico, and who founded an entail (*morgado*) from his disposable third (*terça*) of the estate by a will approved in 1498; and from António Telo de Meneses, or António Teles, founder of the chapel of St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). The Teles de Meneses descend through illegitimacy from the Counts of Vila Pouca, according to the late Madeiran genealogist José Bettencourt da Câmara.
Meneses (Aires de Saldanha de Sousa)

On 9 November 1668 he was appointed Governor and Captain-General (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira, and he took office on 10 April 1669. Some years later he was Governor and Captain-General of Angola.
Meneses (Carlos Azevedo de)

Few names of people born in the so-called ‘Pearl of the Ocean’ appear in the glorious annals of science. While the Azorean islands count a considerable number of their sons who achieved notable distinction in every branch of human knowledge, Madeira has not always been able to keep pace with its island brethren in cultivating the loftiest manifestations of the mind.

These words are not meant to assert that our land has not been the homeland of some distinguished practitioners of the sciences, letters and arts, who deservedly ought to be remembered and with whom we have so often concerned ourselves with the greatest admiration and esteem.

That is what we now come to do once again, as the most fitting tribute of justice and the most heartfelt and grateful acknowledgement, concerning the man who was our distinguished and devoted companion in the preparation of the thousand-odd pages of this *Elucidário Madeirense*. Since almost the entire contribution to the scientific part of this work came from the pen of Carlos Azevedo de Meneses, it falls to us to emphasise that he is the author of the most valuable and meritorious articles found throughout these pages.

Carlos de Meneses came from old and distinguished Madeiran families and was born in Funchal on 26 August 1863. He was the son of the eminent physician Dr Antero Drumond de Meneses and of Dona Elisa Azevedo de Meneses; his paternal grandfather was the illustrious Madeiran Servulo Drumund de Meneses (1-381), and his maternal grandfather the general and engineer António Pedro de Azevedo (1-113). He was also the nephew of the distinguished writer and playwright Maximiliano de Azevedo (1-113).

Through his close friendship with the late botanist João Maria Moniz, and by a natural bent of mind, Carlos Azevedo de Meneses developed an ardent passion for the study of botany, and especially of the Madeiran flora, which only death could extinguish. He never interrupted his scientific work, and as late as 1928 he published an interesting study in the respected journal *Broteria*, to which he was a distinguished and regular contributor. On the strength of his numerous works and his thorough studies, Carlos de Meneses was regarded as an authoritative botanist and counted among the most illustrious Portuguese naturalists. His work, which is vast, profound and utterly conscientious, and therefore free of all scientific charlatanism, was always highly valued and praised by the foremost authorities in that branch of the natural sciences. For this reason he was received into many scientific societies and invited to contribute to the most respected national and foreign journals, which accepted only valuable botanical work.

Among these journals we may mention *Broteria*, *Anais das Sciencias Naturais*, *Jornal das Sciencias Matematicas, Fisicas e Naturais*, *Boletim da Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*, *Academie de Geographie Botanique*, *Bulletin de Géographie Botanique*, etc., etc. He was a laureate member of the International Academy of Botanical Geography of Le Mans, a full member of the Portuguese Society of Natural Sciences of Lisbon, a provincial associate of the Academy of Sciences of the same city, a member of the Brotero Society of Coimbra, and of others still, about which we have been unable to gather more reliable information.

Among the scientific works of Carlos Azevedo de Meneses we shall mention the *Flora do Arquipélago da Madeira*, a work of 282 pages; *Fanerogamicas da Madeira e Porto Santo*; *Arvores e Arbustos Madeirenses*; *As Gramineas do Arquipelago da Madeira*; *Madeira Ferens*, translated into English by Herbert Gilbert; *Contribuição para o estudo da Flora do Arquipelago da Madeira*; *Contribuição para o estudo das Algas da Madeira*; *As Zonas botanicas da Madeira e Porto Santo*; *As Labiadas do Arquipélago da Madeira*; *A Flora dos mais altos picos da Madeira*; and many other booklets written in French, among them the *Notice sur les Phanérogames de Madère et Pôrto Santo*. There are also countless pamphlets and offprints of studies published in specialist journals, not counting the great number of articles scattered through various scientific publications.

Carlos de Meneses did not confine his scientific and literary activity to his distinctly botanical writings. He also dealt quite extensively with other subjects in the natural sciences, and in particular with historical matters, as many articles in the *Elucidário Madeirense* and in various Funchal newspapers bear witness.

After completing his secondary education, he attended the Lisbon Commercial Institute (*Instituto Comercial de Lisboa*) for some years, but did not finish the course. He served as a copying clerk in the secretariat of the Funchal Council and was later appointed director of the Municipal Library, a post he held until his death on 1 May 1928.
Meneses (Dom João de)
He was Governor-General of Madeira, taking office in January 1634. He distinguished himself in the wars of the Restoration and was Governor of Porto.

Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo says of him that he was a secret but steadfast enemy of the rule of the Philips. So much so that, being in Madrid at the time of the revolution of 1 December 1640 in Lisbon, he fled towards that city, but was arrested in Burgos. After five years he managed to escape and entered the service of John IV. He died in Holland in 1649.
Meneses e Lencastre (Dr Luís Adriano de Magalhães)
He was elective peer of the realm (*par do reino electivo*, elected member of the upper chamber) for Madeira in the legislative session of 1890–1892.
Meneses (Inácio Espinola de Castro e)
The *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’) records that he was a native of Funchal and that he wrote a work entitled *Nove Dialogos* in Castilian.
Meneses (Jorge Martins de Sousa e)

This Governor and Captain-General (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira was appointed on 1 June 1718 and took office on 5 October following. He distinguished himself as a soldier in India and gave great proof of valour in the War of the Succession. He died on 24 January 1728.
Meneses (Pedro Fagundes Bacelar de Antas e)
This Governor and Captain-General (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira was appointed to the post on 4 March 1807 and took office on 5 August of the same year.

Five months after his arrival in Funchal, the island was occupied for the second time by British troops, who arrived at the end of December 1807 and did not leave Madeira until October 1814 (see Occupation of Madeira by British troops).

In May 1813 Pedro Fagundes was struck by paralysis, which left him unable to remain at the head of the government. He withdrew to the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) and died in Lisbon on 1 November 1813. He was still in Funchal when his successor, Luís Beltrão de Gouveia, arrived on 7 August of that year.
Menezesia

A genus of Protomycetaceae (fungi) dedicated by the distinguished French mycologist the Revd C. Torrend to one of the authors of this *Elucidário*. For the present it comprises a single species, *Menezesia setulosa*, found in September 1913 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), on decaying branches of *Hedera Helix*. It was published on p. 175 of vol. XI of *Broteria* (botanical section).
Menino Jesus Perdido

This was the name of a private annual feast – private because it was not authorised by any liturgical provision – that was celebrated, sometimes with some pomp, inside nuns’ convents without the direct involvement of their chaplains. It nevertheless took an edifying form of devotion and piety that deserves particular esteem. In the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) in this city it was established around the middle of the 17th century by the pious nun Clara da Chaga; the account of this feast and its details published in *O Jornal* (‘The Newspaper’) of 6 January 1934 is of interest. The book *Ripas da Madeira* contains interesting details of the feasts of the ‘Menino de Jesus Perdido’, although these are drawn with some touches of pure fiction.
Mentastro

The vernacular name of *Cedronella triphylla*, *Mentha aquatica* and *M. rotundifolia*, plants of the family Labiatae. The last of these species, which is distinguished by its strong, unpleasant smell and its reticulate-rugose, crenate leaves, grows in stream beds and near levadas (irrigation channels).
See Sandalos and Hortelã de burro.
Mercado de São Pedro – see Praça do Peixe
Market and Chapel of St Sebastian

The square that the people commonly call ‘do Chafariz’ (of the Fountain) used to bear the name of São Sebastião, and a few years ago received from the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) its new name of Largo do Comércio. Before the square was laid out with the area it keeps today, a narrow street ran there. It was the continuation of Rua do Aljube (‘bishop’s prison’) and was also called Rua de São Sebastião. Between Rua de São Francisco and the building of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) (see Jardim Pequeno) stood a public fountain commonly known as ‘the Fonte’ (‘spring’). Its basins were requisitioned by the Council in 1838 for use in the present public fountain of Largo do Comércio, which was built in 1827.

The name of São Sebastião comes from the small chapel with this dedication that once stood there. It was one of the oldest on this island, but not the oldest of all, as the illustrious annotator of the *Saudades* seems to believe. We have already referred to this point in the article Parishes, and we shall deal with it at greater length in the article devoted to the chapel of St Catherine (*Santa Catarina*).

We do not know whether it was because this had been one of the oldest chapels in Madeira or because of a particular devotion that the people of Funchal held for its patron saint or protector, but it is certain that the inhabitants of the town (*vila*), and later of the city, always felt the deepest and most respectful veneration for the little church. After four centuries, however, on the morning of 22 January 1803, the old chapel was unexpectedly found demolished. The governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara had ordered it razed the night before, without the knowledge of the city’s inhabitants. The Governor had ordered the Council, which administered the chapel, to demolish it in a curious document dated 15 January of that year, first published in the newspaper *A Flôr do Oceano* in 1840. The reason given there for pulling down the little church and two houses adjoining it was the construction of a market, on the pretext that no other site was better suited to that purpose. The Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) was unwilling to take responsibility for so violent a measure, which it knew beforehand would provoke popular fury, and did not carry out the Governor’s order. He then wasted no time in having the chapel destroyed.

Astonishment and indignation were universal, but the Governor’s threats and the measures he had shrewdly and cautiously taken in advance managed to avert trouble and prevent the violence that everyone expected. Only the diocesan prelate, Dom Luís Rodrigues Vilares, protested against the demolition of the chapel without his prior authorisation; but that was all that came of the storm that had so justifiably been feared.

The people, however, did not forget their chapel, nor their wish to raise it again. Nineteen years pass. There is great commotion in the city and lively enthusiasm reigns among its inhabitants. The city adheres to the revolution that had broken out in Porto in August 1820, and the liberal principles it had come to establish in the country are publicly and solemnly proclaimed. Although we can find no full explanation for it, the truth is that the people, having just demonstrated enthusiastically for the ideas preached by the Porto revolution, went to the square of São Sebastião, by then turned into a market, and destroyed the work of Dom José Manuel da Câmara. They carried there all the surviving materials of the old chapel, and others they could lay hands on, and demanded the immediate rebuilding of the chapel razed in January 1803. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo relates that the governor and captain-general of the time, Sebastião Xavier Botelho, a descendant of the highest nobility of Portugal and a distinguished man of letters, also went there carrying a basket of stones for the rebuilding of the chapel that one of his predecessors had ordered demolished.

A contemporary document states that the demolition of the stalls of the São Sebastião market began at 4 p.m. on 1 February 1821 and that by 5 o’clock everything had been levelled; during the night a great deal of dressed stone (*cantaria*), stone and timber intended for the chapel was brought in. On the 7th the breaking of stone for the chapel began, ‘all of which was done amid much riot and clamour from the people, which struck fear into all the officials’, and within a few days the rebuilding was carried out, although it was never actually completed.

On 21 February 1826 the Council asked the Governor and Captain-General to order the ‘removal of the chapel of São Sebastião . . . since this building is no more than a hovel, which, most indecently, is serving as a receptacle for filth and obscenity’. On the 28th of the same month and year it renewed the request, adding that the said chapel should be moved to another place ‘more in the service of God and of His Imperial and Royal Majesty’. By January 1827 the chapel of São Sebastião had already been demolished.

By July 1827 the public fountain in the square of São Sebastião already existed, but only later was it given its elegant marble obelisk, from which four spouts of water pour into a circular tank (irrigation reservoir), also of marble, reached by a flight of steps that is likewise circular. It is the most imposing fountain structure we possess on this island.

The old market for greens and vegetables disappeared long ago, and the same square is at present (1921) the place where a kind of footwear characteristic of Madeira is sold. Made of goatskin and much worn by the common people of the rural parishes, it is chiefly produced in the parishes of the municipality (*concelho*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’).

Before the chapel was destroyed in 1803, the images of Our Lady, St Eligius and St Sebastian were carried in procession from it to the church of São Tiago (St James the Greater). This ceremony took place on 20 January of that year, attended by the clergy of the parishes of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral), São Pedro and Santa Maria Maior do Calhau, by the Franciscan community, by the nobility and by the people, the latter represented by the House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds). The work of levelling the ground and building the stalls took little time, and the market was opened on 18 June 1803.
União Market
