The market was built in 1835 on the site of the ruins of the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*). On 12 June the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) asked the prefect (*prefeito*) for permission to demolish the tower and the remains of the church, even though the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 10 March 1805 had ordered them to be preserved. To enlarge the market, the Council acquired two buildings, one belonging to Francisco João de Santa Clara e Brito and the other to the Confraternity of the Blessed Sacrament of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), and these too were ordered to be demolished.
Although the market was already operating by the end of 1835, it was not until early 1839 that it was enclosed with an iron gallery with three gates.

On 10 November 1910 the Council resolved to close the União market and demolish it at the end of the year, but it was only on 8 June 1911 that the demolition works were ordered to be put out to tender; the contract was awarded on 10 April of the same year.

The premises of the Pedro V Market (*Mercado de D. Pedro V*), intended especially for the sale of ‘greens and vegetables’, and of the Praça de São Pedro, where all the fish consumed in the city was sold, were becoming very cramped. These weighty circumstances, together with the pressing need to extend the ‘Avenida do Mar’ (‘seafront avenue’), made it advisable to build new markets in keeping with the ever-growing population, with the most modern and rigorous rules of hygiene, and with the breadth and spaciousness that these important services required. The Funchal Council ventured upon this undertaking and raised a grand building in which these many services all operated under one roof, though in separate, spacious and independent premises, meeting every condition required for the most perfect organisation of those services. It was even claimed to be the finest installation of its kind in the whole country.

The site chosen was a large polygon bounded by the Largo dos Lavradores (*largo*: square), Rua de Santo António or Rua do Hospital Velho, Rua da Boa Viagem and Rua Nova de Santa Maria or Rua Latino Coelho, with the main entrance opening on to the old Largo dos Lavradores.

As already stated, despite the diversity of the services brought together, which had previously been carried on in two different markets, the great capacity of the premises and the special, methodical organisation that governed everything allowed it all to be arranged and ordered so that no disturbance or friction arose between the various industrial and commercial sections that carry on their business there.
Markets

– Mercado de São João (St John's Market). It opened on 24 June 1823 and was to have been called the Mercado Constitucional de São João (Constitutional Market of St John). It never received that name, because news reached Madeira that the absolutist regime had been restored following the revolution of 27 May of the same year. It stood on the site now occupied by the ‘Dr. Manuel de Arriaga’ theatre, and was built with money lent by João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, president of the first Constitutional Council.

In our own day it was known as the ‘Feira Velha’ (Old Fair), and it was demolished in 1883, when the Municipality decided to build the said theatre. In 1878 the Funchal Circus (*Circo Funchalense*) was built within the market grounds, and several companies performed there.

The market known as São João was at one point to have been built between Rua do Hospital Velho and Rua Nova de Santa Maria (‘new street of St Mary’), on a square (*campo*) that existed there. The site was inspected by the Council and by the lieutenant-colonel of engineers Feliciano António de Matos on 15 May 1821.
The land on which the market was built belonged to the Franciscan friars and was leased to the Council on 24 December 1822.
It seems that the São João market was closed, or ceased to serve the public, for some time, for we have read somewhere that it was reopened on 4 April 1846.
Pedro V (market)

Work on this market began in July 1876. To carry it out, the Council raised four loans: one of 6 *contos* (one million réis) de réis in 1876; two of 10 *contos de réis* each, on 19 June and 7 November 1878; and the last of 34 *contos de réis*, of which only 4 were set aside to pay old wage bills of the same market. The sum of the first of these loans was drawn by the councillors (*vereadores*), on their own responsibility, from the banking house of João José Rodrigues Leitão.

On the site where the Pedro V Market (*Mercado de D. Pedro V*) now stands (1921), opened to the public on 19 December 1880, there was once a sawmill for timber, and later a few stalls selling fruit and vegetables. It was Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses, while serving as a councillor in 1853, who first suggested that it would be advisable to have the market built.
Mercês (street)

This street links Rua dos Netos and Rua de São Pedro with Largo do Marquês and Rua da Saúde. It takes its name from the Convento das Mercês (Convent of Our Lady of Mercy), which once stood on it and which we have already discussed in the 1st volume of this *Elucidário*. The convent grounds extended to near the chapel of the Almas (Holy Souls in Purgatory), and the Travessa das Capuchinhas was then very narrow.

The Council considered establishing the gaol in the convent of Our Lady of Ransom (*Nossa Senhora das Mercês*), whose grounds it had obtained after the proclamation of the Republic. Having abandoned this idea, however, it resolved on 22 April 1914 to cede the same grounds to the ‘Auxílio Maternal’, receiving in exchange the part of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) that had been ceded to that institution by the decrees of 31 October 1912 and 22 September 1913.

Demolition of the Convento das Mercês began in 1911 to make way for the gaol. In that same year the building served to house some of the troops who came to Madeira to maintain public order during the cholera epidemic. On 4 March 1915 the executive committee of the Council informed the Government that it would not use the convent building for the construction of the gaol.
See Our Lady of Ransom and Convents.
Merens de Távora (Luís do Canto e Castro)
On 22 June 1892 he took office as Civil Governor of this district, to which post he had been appointed by decree of the 9th of the same month and year.
Mero (Serranus fimbriatus)

A fish of the family Percidae, similar to the grouper but larger, usually caught near the coast. It lives in holes in the rocks and, although it is not among the finest fish, it nevertheless has a pleasant flavour.
Mesquita (family)

This family surname derives from Pedro Ferreira de Mesquita, who was living at Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) in 1662 and founded there the chapel of Nossa Senhora dos Milagres (Our Lady of Miracles), and from a certain António de Mesquita, a native of Majorca, who for reasons unknown to us came to this island.
See Esprânger.
Mesquita e Castro (Francisco Albuquerque de)
By decree of 1 May 1876 he was appointed Civil Governor of this district, taking office on 10 June of the same year.
Guild representatives (mesteres)

The representatives of the guilds, or guild representatives (*mesteres*) as they were also called, were the craftsmen who belonged to the so-called House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds). Every year, in January, the people’s judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds) presented to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) the list of the four guild representatives who were to take part in the work of the councillors. They could be rejected if they had not served for at least six years in the House.

In former times the guild representatives attended council sessions seated on low chairs beside a table separate from that of the councillors (*vereadores*). In 1803, however, the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) José Júlio Henriques Gordilho allowed them to sit at the council table. This prompted protests from the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) João da Câmara Leme, who considered the concession degrading to his rank as a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility).

On 7 August 1811 the Council resolved that the guild representatives should return to their former places, but they appealed against the resolution and succeeded in having it annulled. For about a year the representatives of the crafts stopped attending council meetings, because they considered themselves wronged by the decision the councillors had taken concerning them.

In former times the guild representatives were held in low regard by the councillors, who often went so far as to insult and humiliate them. At the beginning of the 19th century, however, their situation improved considerably, owing to the profound social changes that took place in our country before the liberation movement of 1820.

The guild representatives ceased to sit among the councillors after the proclamation of constitutional principles in Madeira in 1834, and the House of the Twenty-Four, which they represented, was abolished by the decree of 7 May of the same year. The Constitutional Council elected on 3 November 1822 had no guild representatives.
Metade (valley)

Seen from the belvedere (*mirante*) built by order of the Public Works Department on the Levada do Juncal (‘rush bed’), this great valley offers one of the most vast and majestic panoramas of the interior of Madeira. At the head of the valley rise Pico Ruivo (‘russet’) and Pico das Torres (‘towers’), the highest peaks on the island, and on its precipitous sides, in many places clothed with trees, grow many of the most beautiful and rare plants of Madeira. The belvedere on the Levada do Juncal is about 15 kilometres from Funchal.
Meteóro (O)
Only two issues of this newspaper appeared: on 31 October and 14 November 1856.
Mexico (Empress of)

Empress Carlota was in Madeira with her husband, Emperor Maximilian, in April 1864, on her way to Mexico aboard the *Novara*. Some years earlier she had spent some time on this island, arriving in December 1859 in the company of her husband.
According to Cesare Cantù in *Ultimos trinta anos*, Empress Carlota wrote a work entitled *Um inverno na Madeira* (‘A Winter in Madeira’).
See Maximilian (Emperor of Mexico).
Miguéis (Alfredo Vital)

He was born in this city on 28 April 1883. He began his artistic education at the Funchal Industrial School (*Escola Industrial do Funchal*) and, having enrolled at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in 1889, completed his course in history painting there under the illustrious painter Columbano Bordalo Pinheiro in 1911. During the course he won prizes several times and obtained a medal on completing it. In 1914 he sat the competitive examination for teachers of the Industrial Schools; in 1915 he was appointed teacher at the Setúbal Industrial School and in 1917 transferred to the Funchal Industrial School.

In 1912 he passed the competition for the Valmor Prize for a scholarship abroad, leaving that year for Madrid and later settling in Paris, where he remained until 1914 studying and perfecting his art.

He first showed his work at the exhibition of the National Society of Fine Arts in Lisbon in 1910, and also took part in the exhibitions of 1911, 1915, 1916, 1917 and 1919, winning an honourable mention, three third-class medals and, in 1916, the second-class medal. He was admitted to the Paris Salon in 1913, 1914 and 1922. He held exhibitions of his work in Funchal and Setúbal, and was one of the exhibitors at the First Exhibition of Painting and Sculpture held in this city in 1922.

His paintings *Jardim do Luxemburgo* (1915), *A Taça de Leite* (1916) and *Torre de Jesus em Setúbal* were acquired by the State for the National Museum of Contemporary Art. He died in Funchal on 9 July 1943.
Miguel Bombarda (Campo de) see Barca (Campo da) (vol. I, p. 127)
Milagres (chapel)
The chapel of Christ (*Cristo*), which we have already described in this *Elucidário* (vol. I, p. 332), is also known by this name.
Downy mildew

This disease, which attacks mainly the leaves and bunches of vines, began to cause appreciable damage in Madeiran vineyards only in 1912. The white, powdery patches that characterise it are caused by a fungus of the family Peronosporaceae – *Plasmopara viticola* – whose branches emerge through the stomata of the leaf and form conidia at the tips of their last ramifications. The mycelium of the fungus lives inside the green organs of the vine, and it is this that directly harms the plant. Downy mildew spreads not only by means of spores (conidia) but also by means of eggs or oospores, which result from the fusion of two dissimilar cells. Bordeaux mixture has given good results in the preventive treatment of downy mildew.
Milhã (*Setaria glauca*)
Common name of *Setaria glauca*, a grass (Gramineae) frequent in Madeira.
Maize (*Zea mays*)

A grass originating in America, introduced to the island much later than wheat, barley and rye. Porridge made from maize meal is the staple food of two-thirds of the Madeiran population, and the grain is used to feed livestock and poultry. The panicle formed by the male flowers (the maize ‘tassel’, *bandeira do milho*) and the stalks and leaves of the plant can also be fed to cattle, while the bracts surrounding the female inflorescence are usually used to stuff mattresses. This inflorescence or spadix is called the *maçaroca* (cob); the *barbas* (silk) of the maize are the long styles or filaments at the end of the ovary.

Maize has long been grown in Madeira, but it was in 1847 that Laureano da Câmara Falcão, better known as the holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Ilha (a locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Jorge), developed its cultivation in the parishes of Santana (‘St Anne’) and São Jorge. For this purpose he brought over from the Azores several farmers, who taught here the growing methods used in that archipelago. The results he obtained from his undertaking were very gratifying, and to encourage maize growing among us the law of 22 July 1853 was passed, exempting local produce from the payment of tithes.
Maize production in the archipelago does not exceed 6,000 hectolitres, and some 11 million hectolitres have to be imported to meet consumption throughout the district (1921).
Militia

When Madeira was discovered and settled, says Dr Azevedo, the feudal period of the people’s militia was still under way, though already in transition: a period ‘in which arms were the privilege of few and the subjection of almost all’. ‘Each donatary (*donatário*), the same author continues, was in his captaincy the chieftain, the captain; subordinate to him were the noblemen who had received lands from him as *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation); and subordinate to the noblemen, or lords, were the lesser settlers, who in peace were their tenants, almost bound to the land, and in the host were obliged to serve as men-at-arms.’

The feudal period was followed by what Dr Azevedo calls the monarchical period, in which the king, claiming for himself the right to demand military service from his able-bodied vassals, ‘broke with the martial pre-eminence of the donataries and noblemen, leaving them only the burdens’.

The first document in which the king directly demanded this service, from both the nobility and the people of Madeira, so that they would accompany him on an expedition to Africa, is dated 25 March 1500. However, the donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara respectfully protested against these orders from the central power, invoking ancient rights that could not be set aside. In the same year another letter appeared, revoking the earlier one in so far as it concerned this island and ordering its inhabitants not to leave it ‘unaccompanied’, so that they could guard and defend it in case of need.

The monarch temporised with the donatary, perhaps because he did not consider himself strong enough to consolidate royal power on this island. This did not last long, however, for on 12 May 1509 the king ordered, by a letter sent from Évora, that the noblemen, knights, squires, good men (*homens bons*, local notables eligible for municipal office) and people of the city of Funchal should provide themselves with arms and horses, since their services might become necessary at any moment.

The creation of the modern Madeiran militia cannot be traced to this document, since it merely ordered the people to arm themselves without giving them any military organisation. We can, however, date from its publication the subordination to royal power of the forces this island could contribute to the defence of the country.

The watch-posts, kept by the people in small fortified houses built specifically to face the sea and prevent surprise attacks, were in the view of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo more than the prelude to the militia later known as the territorial militia (*ordenanças*). They were, he held, the *ordenanças* themselves, with little difference, and their institution therefore marks the boundary between the feudal and the monarchical periods in the history of the Madeiran militia.

The watch-posts received regulations (*regimento*) in 1567, issued by King Sebastian, and long before that, in 1515, there were bombardiers here, who were then granted privileges. In 1532 an *anadel-mor* (chief commander of the musketeers or crossbowmen) of musketeers was appointed for this island, and he was later authorised to appoint musketeers for the towns and villages. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 2 March 1497 shows that even before that date Madeira had an armoury where weapons were made.

Under the regulations (*regimento*) of 10 December 1570, the territorial militia (*ordenanças*) was divided into companies, grouped into *capitanias-mores*. ‘Each *capitania-mor*,’ says Dr Azevedo, ‘had a *capitão-mor*, who was the commander; a sergeant-major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major), his second-in-command; and, later, an adjutant. Each captaincy had a captain and a second lieutenant, without royal commission, a sergeant, a bailiff (meirinho), a clerk (*escrivão*) and ten corporals. The donataries, or the *alcaides-mores* in the lands that had them, were *capitães-mores* by birthright; in other lands they were elected in the Council, as were the other officers, in all lands, until this privilege of election was reduced, for those lands that had no donatary, to a mere recommendation by the royal decree (*alvará*) of 18 October 1701. It was the king, or the donataries in their own lands, who granted the commissions, but only the former could withdraw them.’

We do not know whether all the posts that, according to the regulations, the companies of the territorial militia were supposed to have actually existed in Madeira, but several documents show that there were captains and sergeants-major here, as well as adjutants to the *capitães-mores*. The territorial militia must already have existed on the island in 1575, since there is a document of that time granting an increase in pay to the sergeant-major of Funchal. Dr Azevedo thinks that the watches we referred to earlier eventually merged into the territorial militia.

At the beginning of the 19th century the territorial militia formed a third-line corps, with the following *capitanias-mores* in Madeira: Funchal, Câmara de Lobos, Campanário, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Madalena, Calheta, Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Ponta Delgada, Porto da Cruz, Machico, Santa Cruz and Caniço. ‘After the Castilian rule,’ says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, ‘the Portuguese militia underwent four reforms or renewals up to 1809: 1st, that of John IV, decreed by resolution of the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) around 1641, with two kinds of troops, paid and auxiliary, all other men remaining in the territorial militia, which served as a kind of nursery of recruits; 2nd, that of John V, instituted by the royal decree of 15 November 1707, which was given the name of the new *ordenanças*; 3rd, that of Joseph I, set out in the regulations (1763–1766) known as those of the Count of Lippe, because the reform was inspired by that illustrious general, then commander of the Portuguese troops; and 4th, finally, that of 1806–1809.’

Besides the fourteen *capitanias-mores* mentioned above, at the beginning of the 19th century the archipelago had a first-line artillery battalion with six companies and 727 men, an auxiliary artillery battalion with fifteen companies and 2,171 men, and three militia regiments – those of Calheta, Funchal and São Vicente – each with ten companies and about 800 men. All these forces, except the first-line artillery battalion, were militia: the auxiliary artillery and the three militia regiments made up the second-line troops (*segunda linha*, reserve militia), and the territorial militia the third line of Madeira's troops.
Of the militia forces in the archipelago, Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) had only an artillery corps of four companies, created in 1805.

The territorial militia (*ordenanças*) was abolished by Philip II at the request of the Cortes of Tomar and restored in 1623. It seems, however, that the decree abolishing it was never applied to Madeira, where the territorial militia continued to exist until the decree and law (*carta de lei*) of 22 August 1821 came into force, dissolving it once again together with the militia. Both were restored by the law of 13 July 1823, and were finally abolished only by the decrees of 14 and 20 July 1832, which were not put into effect on this island until after the proclamation of the liberal government in 1834.

A report submitted to the Government in 1754 by the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Manuel Saldanha de Albuquerque, together with what has been published on the part played by the militia when the Miguelists seized Madeira in 1828, shows that in those periods these troops were commendable neither for discipline nor for military valour. Yet these were the very qualities that had so distinguished the militias which, in the time of the donataries, went to the aid of our strongholds in Africa when they were threatened by the Moors, and also those which in earlier times had several times defended the island against attacks by its foreign enemies.

Despite the show of organisation with which the militias of the 18th and 19th centuries were invested, all that reached the islands of Madeira and Porto Santo from that institution, says Dr Azevedo, was ‘the caricature and the abuses of power, ending in the swarm of gentlemen captains, lieutenants and second lieutenants whose commissions are still, in the rural settlements, vain memories and respected pretexts for distinction and esteem’.

In the first quarter of the 19th century the captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) and the sergeant-major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major), the principal commanders of the territorial militia, were appointed in the Council, being chosen ‘from among the persons of the governance (*pessoas da governança*, notables eligible for municipal office) and the nobility, well endowed with property and of sound Christian faith’. Luís Teixeira Doria, holder of an entail (*morgado*), was the last captain-major, and Aires de Ornelas Cisneiros, likewise holder of an entail, the last sergeant-major in the captaincy of Funchal; both were appointed in 1828.

Captains and sergeants-major were exempt from holding the offices of the governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office), that is, from serving as councillors (*vereadores*), market inspectors (almotacés), etc., etc.

Mimos (Fuchsia)

The common name for all plants of the family Onagraceae belonging to the genus *Fuchsia*. *Fuchsia coccinea*, which apparently originated in Brazil, is naturalised at Monte, Camacha and other places in Madeira.

Miranda

This family surname (*apelido*), says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, derives from João Lourenço de Miranda, one of the noble companions of Zarco. There are other Mirandas who descend from João Machado de Miranda.
Miranda (Felisberto de Betencourt)

He held the post of copying clerk (*amanuense*) in the secretariat of the Municipal Council, to which he was appointed on 3 November 1835. He died at over 70 years of age on 30 January 1889, having by then retired. The Council library holds a manuscript work compiled by him, bearing the following title: *Apontamentos para a genealogia de diversas familias da Madeira, colleccionados de 1887 a 1888*.
Belvederes

The astonishing beauty of the Madeiran landscape, which can never be praised enough (see Landscape of Madeira), unfolds marvellously across terrain of such rugged and capricious relief. It frequently offers many spots and places that invite rapt contemplation of the widest and most enchanting horizons. At these privileged points the need to build small viewpoints comes readily to mind, so that visitors may enjoy a welcome rest and the spiritual pleasure that nature can so lavishly afford them there. A few comfortable benches, shade trees and perhaps a ‘pergola’ clothed in some ornamental plant would serve as the simple and indispensable adornment of such places. Funchal has several of these viewpoints, such as those of ‘Montanha’, ‘Babosas’ and ‘Pico dos Barcelos’, the churchyards of the church of Monte, the church of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), the church of São Martinho (St Martin of Tours) and the church of São Gonçalo (St Gonsalo of Amarante), ‘Largo António Nobre’, ‘Largo das Cruzes’ and still others, but not all of them offer the indispensable comfort that would encourage an attractive and lingering visit.

Scattered over the whole surface of the island are many points overlooking beautiful stretches of enchanting landscape, where such viewpoints ought to be built, a task now made easier by the opening of the new roads.

On 27 July 1850 the Civil Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro recommended to the director of Public Works, Tibério Augusto Blanc, the construction of a belvedere (*mirante*) at the locality of Macelas (‘chamomiles’), in the municipality (*concelho*) of Machico, because of the astonishing view to be enjoyed from there. The belvedere was built shortly afterwards and, as is well known, still stands today. Besides the belvedere at Macelas, J. Silvestre Ribeiro recommended building a belvedere at Portela (‘mountain pass’), in the municipality of Machico, and another at Eira do Serrado (‘threshing floor of the ridge’), in the municipality of Funchal.

Near the Levada do Juncal (irrigation channel), about a quarter of an hour from the mountain shelter at Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’), there is a belvedere built by order of the Public Works Department, from which there are majestic views over the Ribeira da Metade (‘halfway stream’).
Misericórdia of Machico

– The Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) of Machico is of quite ancient foundation, but the exact date of its creation is unknown; it is conjectured to date from the first quarter of the 16th century. Tradition holds that a lady left a substantial property to the poor of the town (*vila*) of Machico, and that this bequest gave rise to the idea of founding the Misericórdia, serving as the nucleus of the assets it later came to own.

In 1803 the flash flood (*aluvião*) swept the chantry (capela) of the Misericórdia and the adjoining house into the sea, and with them its archive, so that we lack the essential material for writing a historical account of this institution. We can nevertheless say, from some data provided by the ‘Annals of the Municipality’ (*Anais do Município*), that its functioning was governed by the statutes (*compromisso*) of the Misericórdia of Lisbon. Its administration seems always to have left much to be desired, and the benefits it gave the poor were not great. It is certain, however, that besides the president (provedor) and board member it came to have two clerks, two collectors, a keeper of the strongbox, two procurators of the poor and two informants. This bureaucratic apparatus, though perhaps unpaid, did not prevent many quit-rents and properties from being lost, especially after their title deeds were destroyed by the flood at the beginning of the 19th century.

Originally it had no hospital, only a chantry that served as the seat of the brotherhood, which we have already discussed at some length (vol. 1, p. 332) and to which we shall return in the article chapel of Christ (*Cristo*). The beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) of the collegiate church of Machico, Father Inácio Barbosa da Silva, by public deed of 20 May 1748, bequeathed to the confraternity some houses he owned in the locality of Banda de Além (‘the far side’), so that a hospital could be set up in them and they could serve as the Misericórdia’s building, since the confraternity had no building intended for that purpose. We can give no information on the running of the hospital; the said ‘Annals of the Municipality’ state that those houses passed into the possession of the Confraternity of the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), for reasons unknown. In 1856 the Misericórdia leased a property to house a hospital, which played an important role during the cholera epidemic and was closed around 1862.

One of the most zealous presidents of the Holy House of Mercy (*Misericórdia*) of Machico was Captain Cristóvão Esmeraldo, elected to that office in 1810. Besides his good service in running the brotherhood, he did much to rebuild the chapel, which the flash flood of 9 October 1803 had destroyed. Another president who rendered no less notable service to this institution was the vicar of that town, Father Manuel José da Paixão. He obtained several certificates for properties and quit-rents and returned to the Misericórdia’s possession some assets already considered lost by then.

The brotherhood was abolished in 1835. By a royal decree (*alvará*) of the civil governor dated 13 June of the same year, an Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) was appointed and took over the management of this Misericórdia.

It still owns a property in the locality of Ribeira Seca (‘dry stream’), and it used to hold many quit-rents charged on various properties in the enclosed fields (*serrados*) of Isidoro and Travesso and in other localities as well.

In the *Boletim do Trabalho Industrial* cited above, we read that the revenue of this Misericórdia in 1909–1910 was 151.40 escudos, which was added to a balance of 79.51 escudos. Expenditure that year amounted to 37.75 escudos for the doctor and medicines and 71.21 escudos for invalid diets. In 1913 the revenue was 842.76 escudos, of which 81.19 escudos was the balance, 181.20 escudos rents and 508.37 escudos the rent of a pine wood. Expenditure was 271.26 escudos, leaving a balance of 571.50 escudos for 1914. The sick are helped in their own homes, because the Misericórdia has at present no premises for a hospital and, even if it had, it would not have the means to maintain one.
Misericórdia of Santa Cruz

The *Boletim do Trabalho Industrial* no. 95, which we have cited more than once already, contains a very interesting and, as far as possible, complete account of this Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), which we shall transcribe in full:

‘It appears to be established that this charitable institution was founded at the beginning of the 16th century in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), and that its own building was put up in the year 1520. Outside the city of Funchal, it is the most important establishment of its kind, and from its origin it was designed with ample accommodation in relation to the community it served.

Having been cared for and maintained, it still today (1920) provides hospital care to poor patients in reasonably comfortable conditions, something found in no other rural municipality (*concelho*) of the district.

Among the probable founders of this Hospital, established by the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of Santa Cruz, the names cited as board brothers (*irmãos mesários*) of the highest standing are Manuel da Costa Moniz, José Bettencourt de Freitas, Diogo Lopes Fernandes, António Mendes Bettencourt, António Baptista Spínola and Marcos de Aragão.

‘The building of this Misericórdia underwent major repairs in 1759, 1786 and 1892, at the expense of public charity, without which it would already have disappeared; and in 1908 it was repaired again by order and at the expense of the State.

This building consists of a two-storey house with a large chapel and many rooms, such as spacious wards, a room for the pharmacy, some other rooms, bathrooms, etc., as well as disinfection rooms and a mortuary.

Given the size and condition of the building, it could provide more and better hospital services if its income allowed. That income, however, is very meagre and goes a very short way unless public charity supplements it and comes regularly to its aid.

Thus the Misericórdia’s own income amounts to little more than 200 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) a year, and it is evident that this sum, without the addition of public charitable aid, can go only a very short way, especially in view of the heavier costs that always arise from maintaining and running a building of such ample dimensions.

‘This Misericórdia has statutes approved by the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) of Funchal in 1889. ‘In 1910 the management and performance of all internal and nursing services in the hospital of this Misericórdia were in the charge of the Franciscan hospitaller sisters, who gave good service there. They were the same sisters who improvised a hospital in the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’), in the city of Funchal, during the last smallpox epidemic that ravaged Madeira.

After the service of these nuns was discontinued, the Misericórdia Hospital (*Hospital da Misericórdia*) continued to function under the direction of a managing board (*mesa*) elected from among the brethren of the Confraternity of St Elizabeth of Portugal. It was assisted by nursing and pharmacy staff who remained partly the same as before, but secularised.
The pharmacy services, however, were leased out, although the same dispensing staff employed by the Misericórdia continued in post.

‘In 1913 the income of this Misericórdia was 1,034.68 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis), including a balance of 640 escudos from the previous year. Expenditure was of equal value and included the sum of 400 escudos spent on repairs to the Hospital chapel.
The staff of the establishment comprises a physician at 36 escudos, a clerk at 36 escudos and two nurses at 30 escudos each, all per year.

‘In 1913 the hospital treated 14 patients, 6 men and 8 women, of whom 9 improved, 3 died and 2 remained under treatment. ‘From the above it can be seen that the services this hospital, or its Misericórdia, can provide are relatively small. Given the commendable conditions of its premises, however, it would well deserve effective support that would allow it to increase its admissions and the benefits it provides, and so better meet the growing needs of the community it serves, which is today one of the most important towns of the district, seat of a municipality and of a judicial district (*comarca*).’
Misericórdia of Porto Santo

In the town (*vila*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) there is a small chapel with a little house attached, known as the Misericórdia church (*Igreja da Misericórdia*). It was the seat of an old confraternity of that name, the date of whose foundation we do not know. Although a royal decree (alvará régio) of 9 April 1767 approved its statutes (*compromisso*), it is nonetheless certain that it was created at a more remote date. It never had a hospital. We do not know what services it provided, and at present it gives no assistance of any kind to the poor.
Misericórdias

It seems that the idea of founding a hospital here arose shortly after the colonisation of this island began. It was the discoverer himself, João Gonçalves Zarco, who by public deed of 25 March 1454 granted some land beside the chapel of St Paul for the building of the new hospital. The building, which was paid for by the people, was not constructed until 1469. The hospital operated there for roughly fifteen years and was transferred to the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) around 1484. The new foundation was built on land belonging to Álvaro Afonso, who gave it for this purpose in 1483 on condition that the hospital should have six beds for poor patients.

By virtue of a papal bull obtained from Pope Alexander VI permitting the foundation of a new hospital on this island, King Manuel I ordered, by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 25 May 1507, the construction of a building specially intended for that purpose, on land belonging to one Bartolomeu Malheiro. It is presumed that the old hospital was incorporated into the new foundation and that this was built on the same site, in the street that still bears the name Hospital Velho. However, in an old register of visitation orders (*livro de provimentos*) of the parish church of Nossa Senhora do Calhau (Our Lady of Calhau, ‘pebble shore’), we find the following passages, which quite clearly refer to two hospitals, though perhaps housed in adjoining buildings and forming, as it were, a single establishment: ‘The Vicar and Beneficiaries of Nossa Senhora do Calhau shall hold and regard as their parishioners those persons who are taken into the old hospital as incurables, and when they die… shall accompany them to the grave…, and they shall do the same with those who die in the new hospital…’. It is not easy to determine with complete precision when work on the new building was completed, but it cannot have been much after 1515, for in a royal letter of 4 June of that year Manuel I pressed for the works to be finished, ordering the proceeds of the wine tax to be applied to them until they were entirely completed. We read in an old nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) that the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) João Fernandes de Amil was charged by the monarch with directing the foundation and construction of the new hospital. Nothing is known about the running of this establishment in the early years of its existence, particularly as regards the number of patients, its own revenues, the meeting of its expenses, the form of its administration, etc., for no record of any kind on the subject can be found.

Gaspar Frutuoso, referring to the new premises, says the following, perhaps with some exaggeration: ‘The House of the Misericórdia has rich workshops, and many alms and works of charity are done in it by the presidents and brethren, who cure many sick people and relieve many poor and needy, not only of this island but also those who come to it from various parts and voyages, for it is rich, well provided and compassionate, a port of call and refuge for all’. These words were written in 1590, and 45 years earlier, in a lengthy and well-argued petition addressed to the monarch on 8 March 1645 by the President (*provedor*) and Brethren of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), they had protested against the hospital remaining ‘in the worst site in the city’, citing the smallness of the building, the nearness of the stream, the cramped church, the lack of space for burials and many other drawbacks that caused ‘many patients to die’. In the register of visitation orders cited above, the church authorities also advised moving the hospital to another building, stating there that the chantries (capela) of the Espírito Santo and of the Chagas in the parish church lay beneath the floor of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), so that the cries and groans of the patients could be heard inside the church, especially when they underwent some operation or particularly painful treatment.

A warrant (*provisão*) of John IV, dated 20 April 1654, ordered the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) of Funchal to inquire into the petition of the President and Brethren of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) and to have an estimate made of the works concerned, consulting for this purpose the officers of the Council.

Earlier, in 1612 and 1638, the Holy House of Mercy (*Misericórdia*) of Funchal had petitioned Philip II and Philip III for authorisation and aid to build the new hospital. Those monarchs ordered various inquiries, but none of these proceedings brought the Holy House the slightest benefit.
On 9 November 1682 the Prince Regent, later Peter II, issued a warrant granting alms of 5,000 *cruzados*, but the works began only later.

On 22 July 1685, in the presence of the Governor and Captain-General of Madeira, Pedro de Lima Brandão, who was serving as president of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), plots of land were leased under quit-rent (*foro*) on the Terreiro da Sé (Cathedral Square), as the area now occupied by the Largo da Sé, the Avenida do Dr Arriaga and the adjoining streets was then called. The aim was to build there a large building that would meet the needs of the Misericórdia of Funchal. (See *Diário de Notícias* (‘Daily News’), 21 to 27 October 1896.)

This land consisted partly of a kitchen garden belonging to Captain Luís de Atouguia da Costa, and it adjoined his dwelling house. Under the deed drawn up on that same day, 22 July 1685, the Holy House was bound to pay an annual quit-rent of 12$00 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for the land on the Terreiro da Sé.
Only after 1686 did building work on the new house of the Misericórdia begin there.

An inspection carried out on 3 April of that year, to draw up the plans and estimate, found that the main works would cost about 8,000,000 *réis*; it was later recognised that a further forty thousand *cruzados* would be needed to finish them completely. The work seems to have proceeded rather slowly for lack of funds. Peter II, by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 9 November 1692, granted 5,000 *cruzados* for these works, and an order of the Treasury Council (*Conselho da Fazenda*) dated 19 October 1745 allotted a further 4,000 *cruzados* to them.
Meanwhile, the sick were gradually admitted to the new building, while construction moved, albeit slowly, towards its final completion.

The hospital remained in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior until the end of the 17th century or the beginning of the 18th, when the various hospital services were moved to the buildings they occupy at present (1922). In the entrance hall, above the two doors leading into the interior, are the following inscriptions, which clearly show how slowly the work proceeded: ‘This new entrance was made on 20 June 1788, the president being the Most Illustrious and Most Excellent Lord Governor and Captain-General Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho’; and on the right-hand side: ‘This new entrance to the British infirmary was made on 20 April 1807, the president being Pedro Júlio da Câmara Leme’. On the door of the meeting room one also reads: ‘This new entrance was made in the year 1790, the president being the Most Illustrious and Most Excellent Lord Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho.’

Over time various improvements and additions were made to the building, such as the church, the *Recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) das Órfãs and the house for private wards, though we cannot determine when they were built. At the beginning of the 19th century an infirmary was set up especially for British subjects, known as the British Infirmary. It must have closed before 1837, since in that year the new Medical-Surgical School began to operate in it.

What the press of this city has said about the hospital’s appalling sanitary conditions, the poor location of its building and its insufficient capacity to house all the hospital services properly would fill a good-sized volume. These claims contain no small exaggeration, which is not to say that the establishment fully met the modern demands of science. Nevertheless, it may be stated that its sanitary conditions were reasonable, according to the authoritative testimony of several eminent physicians who had visited it. With the major improvements introduced in 1922, these conditions improved markedly, and little more could then have been achieved in the circumstances.

The building is an old one, three centuries in existence, situated in the most central and low-lying part of the city. Its wards, however, are spacious, open and well ventilated, and for the time in which it was built it could be considered one of the best in the country. Indeed, even today few would surpass it in the capacity of its various departments, provided the number of patients housed there does not exceed sixty (1922).

We are, however, of the opinion that the hospital should be moved to a site and a building whose sanitary conditions fully meet the modern precepts of medical science. For many decades the press has advocated this move, citing the reasons briefly set out above. The Lazareto, Marmeleiros and the former convents (*conventos*) of the Incarnação and the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) were put forward as the preferred places for housing the hospital, once the necessary conversion work had been carried out. Among the proposals made, those considered best and most fully suited to the desired purpose were to build new buildings in the convent grounds of the Incarnação and the Convent of St Clare, reusing only some of the materials of the old, ruined monasteries. The authoritative opinion of the doctors confirmed the public’s preference for the site of the Convent of St Clare. A committee made up of Drs Nuno Silvestre Teixeira, Fortunato Pita, João Francisco de Almada, José Joaquim de Freitas and José Joaquim Mendes gave its opinion, in a long and well-argued report, that the new hospital building should be erected within the precinct of the Convent of St Clare, and it rejected the buildings of the Lazareto and Marmeleiros as unsuitable for that purpose. (See the *Diário do Comercio* for January 1910.)

The decree of 31 October 1912 ceded the former Convent of St Clare to the Holy House of Mercy, except for the church, the land needed to widen the streets bordering the convent, and the land already ceded to the Auxílio Maternal association. The decree of 22 September 1913 confirmed the cession made to the Misericórdia by the decree of 31 October 1912 for the building of the hospital, and introduced some changes to the way the land and buildings were to be divided among the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), the Auxílio Maternal and the Holy House of Mercy. The board of the Auxílio Maternal proposed to the Council that it cede the land it held within the precinct of the convent and grounds of St Clare, subject to certain conditions. Those bodies and the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House then decided to set down the terms of their agreement in a public deed, which was done on 3 March 1916.

In April 1922 the Committee of the Holy House petitioned the central government for the land that the former Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) had held at the locality (*sítio*) of Louros, on the Lazareto road, in order to build there the pavilions and other facilities for a modern hospital meeting present-day standards of hygiene.

The Confraternity of the Misericórdia of Funchal was established by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 1514, according to a record we found in the archive of this institution. By another royal letter, of 18 September of the same year, the hospital was annexed and handed over to the said Confraternity, under whose supervision and administration all the hospital services were placed, ‘provided that the poor and sick who come to the said hospital are always provided for’. The Confraternity was installed in the parish church of Santa Maria Maior, which adjoined the hospital. The annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ states that John III revoked this concession made by Manuel I, and adds the following: ‘we presume that from then on it functioned in the chapel of the Santos Reis, near the hospital, which had been donated to it in the year 1514’.

Over time the Confraternity was granted various exemptions and privileges, which contributed greatly to its growth and prosperity. Thus, by the royal letter of 23 August 1605 and by other later enactments, the Confraternity may use all the privileges granted to the Misericórdia of Lisbon, in cases where the provisions of those enactments can apply in this archipelago. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 8 June 1740 extended for ten years the privilege of collecting the alms from the tithes of ‘kids, young chickens, eggs, milk, cheese, lambs and pigeons’ in the jurisdiction of Funchal and in the towns of Ponta do Sol and Calheta. A royal letter dated 22 August 1734 allowed the Confraternity to have its own notary’s office for all the contracts it concluded. The religious services of the Confraternity and the Hospital were exempted from the jurisdiction of the prelate by royal letter of 27 March 1767, and placed under the direct authority of the chief chaplain.

The Misericórdia of Funchal was run as a brotherhood from its foundation until 1834, that is, for the long period of 320 years. We have no detailed knowledge of that administration, but it can be said that in those three centuries our first charitable institution was created, developed and prospered. The last 80 or 90 years of management by administrative committees, on the other hand, added nothing new to the greatness and prosperity of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), although some of those committees rendered notable and disinterested services to this charitable establishment.

Between 1514 and 1834 the Misericórdia of Funchal had 300 presidents (*provedores*), some of whom marked their tenure with far-reaching measures and highly effective administration. Prominent among them were the bishop of this diocese, Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos, in the late 16th and early 17th centuries; the governor and captain-general Francisco da Costa Freire, founder of the Recolhimento das Órfãs, in the second quarter of the 18th century; the governor and captain-general Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho, in the last quarter of the same century; and the diocesan bishop Dom Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, in the first quarter of the 19th century. Large painted portraits of the last two presidents hang in the meeting room of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*).

The oldest statutes (*compromisso*) of this Misericórdia were modelled on the regulations (*regimento*) of that of Lisbon. However, the royal letter of Philip III of 22 March 1631 approved separate statutes for our Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), which remained in force for many years. It was a skilfully drafted document, dealing at length with every matter concerning the life of the Holy House. It was printed in 1943, simply as a piece of historical documentation, in a pamphlet of 46 pages.

We do not know when the statutes of 1631 were revised, but we know that the president Dom Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde drew up new regulations in 1801, which were confirmed by royal warrant (*provisão*) of 19 October 1819. These regulations, said to be a work of great merit for their time, were printed in 1820 under the title *Regimento ou Regulamento do Hospital Real de Santa Isabel da Cidade do Funchal, Ilha da Madeira, sendo provedor da mesma Santa Casa o excelentissimo e reverendissimo senhor Bispo Vigario Apostolico D. Frei Joaquim de Menezes e Athaide*.

In 1906 the old Confraternity of the Misericórdia of Funchal was restored, its statutes being approved by a decree of the civil governor José Ribeiro da Cunha dated 30 April of the same year. On 17 May following, the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*), elected every two years, was chosen, with Canon António Homem de Gouveia as its first president. A few days after the proclamation of the Republic, contrary to what was done with all or almost all the Misericórdias in the country, the civil governor of the district dissolved the Confraternity of this city and appointed an Administrative Committee to manage the affairs of the Holy House.

As we said above, the rule of the confraternities in the administration of the Misericórdia ended in 1834. Management then passed to Administrative Committees appointed by the chief authority of the district, which exposed the administration to the hazards of party passions and to the swings of factional parish-pump politics, one of the greatest ills of our land.

The political events that had taken place in the country and the absence from the island of many members of the confraternity prevented the election of its managing board (*mesa*) in July 1834. The prefect (*prefeito*) of this province, Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, by decree of 16 August that year, appointed a committee to examine the accounts of the Holy House, study the causes of its decline during the period of our civil wars and propose means of remedying it. Following the committee’s recommendations, he then ordered by decree of 8 November 1834 that, on a provisional basis and until the central government reached a final decision on the matter, the Funchal Municipal Council should appoint an Administrative Committee of five members to manage the affairs of the Holy House from 1 January 1835, and that the appointment of three members should be renewed at the start of each year. He also ordered that the Council should propose six suitable persons, from whom the prefect would choose three to form a committee charged with settling the Holy House’s overdue accounts and collecting all debts owed to the establishment.

‘Since it was recognised that the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) and the Liquidating Committee were incompatible,’ we read in the statutes (*compromisso*) published in 1906, ‘the latter was dissolved by the prefect (*prefeito*) of the province by royal decree (*alvará*) of 4 May 1835. The Administrative Committee then ran the affairs of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) entirely under new regulations (*regimento*), which had been approved and put into force by the governor Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque by royal decree of 8 November 1834. These regulations were printed in 1840, and the Misericórdia was administered under them until 1843.

‘A ministerial order (*portaria*) of the Ministry of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) of 9 August 1838 declared that the administration of the Holy House belonged to the elected board (*mesa*) in accordance with its statutes (and that, if it had none, it should be governed by those of the Misericórdia of Lisbon). That administration did not fall to any committee unless the board had been dissolved, in which case an interim committee would be appointed until a new board was elected.

‘In view of so clear a ruling, the Administrative Committee was relieved of its duties, at its own request, on 27 October 1838. The administrator-general (*administrador geral*) appointed an interim committee, which was to manage the affairs of the Holy House in accordance with the provisions of the regulations drawn up in 1834 and approved on 8 November of that year.

‘On 19 October 1839 the administrator-general ordered the committee of the Holy House to draw up a draft of definitive regulations, to be submitted to the central government for approval. The committee carried out this task, presenting the basis for new regulations on 29 April 1839. On this occasion the Administrative Committee gave its opinion on how the affairs of the Misericórdia should be managed. It favoured the committee system, while recognising the need to appoint a senior official who would be responsible for the direct supervision of all the services of the Holy House, under the direction of the Administrative Committee.

This draft of the regulations was not approved, but it served as the basis for the draft sent to the government by the administrator-general on 3 January 1842, which was provisionally approved by ministerial order of 13 February 1843.

In 1854 the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) petitioned the government for the restoration of the old confraternity, convinced that this system would bring the Holy House a new era of prosperity. Consulted on the matter, the Administrative Committee took the view that reorganising the old confraternity was inadvisable and that the established system of administrative committees should remain.

‘Although provisional in character, the administrative system of committees appointed by the senior authority of the district was now established, and it remained in force until the beginning of 1906, even though other attempts were made to restore the old brotherhood or confraternity of the Misericórdia.

‘By virtue of a ministerial order of the Ministry of the Kingdom of 23 April 1855, the civil governor of the district appointed a committee to propose to the Confraternity of the Misericórdia of Funchal amendments to its statutes, based on the provisions of the statutes of the Misericórdia of Lisbon. The results of any work this committee may have carried out are not known.

Although the administration and direction of the affairs of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) lay entirely with the administrative committees, the members of the old confraternity were nevertheless convened in 1869. They met on 15 December of that year to give their opinion on whether the property owned by the Misericórdia should be converted into bonds of the Public Credit Board (*Junta de Crédito Público*). This was a measure of great importance, and the committee concerned, knowing itself to be a provisional administrative body, did not wish to bear alone the consequences and serious responsibilities of such a step. At this meeting, attended by 13 brethren while 17 stayed away, the confraternity gave its last sign of life.

In 1885 the Administrative Committee, in an official letter to the head of the district, acknowledged the need to reorganise the old brotherhood, and in 1888 the civil governor likewise recognised the same need.

‘In that year the head of the district, who was then the Viscount of Canavial, carried out a thorough study of the administration of the Holy House and wrote an interesting and detailed memorandum on the subject. In accordance with this study, and with the aim of improving the position of the Misericórdia, he drew up new regulations, approved by royal decree of 10 March 1888 and put into force on the 14th of that month. These regulations created the post of Director-General, who, under the direct authority of the Administrative Committee, oversaw all the services of the hospital.
‘These regulations remained in force only until 25 March, so that the affairs of the Holy House were run under them for the brief period of just eleven days.

‘On 17 December 1901 the civil governor of the district approved new regulations, which began to be applied on 2 January of the following year. Under them the internal running of the hospital was entrusted to the Franciscan Sisters of Mary, who entered the Misericórdia on that same 2 January. On 18 June of the same year, the regulations of 17 December 1901 having been suspended, the sisters left the hospital service.

‘On 13 March 1894, 16 citizens, among them the members of the then Administrative Committee of the Holy House, applied to the civil governor of the district for approval of draft statutes under which the old confraternity of the Misericórdia would be restored and the internal services of the hospital handed over to nursing sisters. The head of the district, not wishing to decide the matter of the petition himself, sent a lengthy report on the subject to the Ministry of the Kingdom on 21 March of that year. He received a reply dated 22 May following, which laid down that the old confraternity could be reorganised, provided certain legal formalities were observed.','

‘It was on the strength of this reply from the Ministry of the Kingdom that some years later, on 22 February 1905, the civil governor sent an official letter to the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government’s representative) of Funchal, ordering that the brethren of the old confraternity be summoned so that, together with those admitted by the Administrative Committee, they should constitute themselves within 15 days, on pain of the confraternity being abolished, in accordance with the Administrative Code then in force.

‘Once the period set in the public notice (*edital*) had expired, and since none of the former brethren answered the summons – all of them having already died – a petition from 28 citizens asking to be admitted to the confraternity was laid before the Administrative Commission on 11 March 1905, and the request was granted at once.

‘The confraternity having been deemed extinct and this having been reported to the Ministry of the Kingdom, the ministerial order (*portaria*) of 8 February 1906 was issued. It re-established the Confraternity of the Misericórdia of Funchal and brought to an end the rule of the Administrative Commissions, which had lasted for a period of 62 years, from 1834 to 1906’.

The affairs of the Holy House have been administered with varying fortune over the long span of four centuries, and we have detailed knowledge only of the period from 1812 to 1885, through the study by the Count of Canavial referred to above. At the end of 1834, that is, shortly after the civil wars had ended, the institution possessed a capital of approximately eighty *contos* (one million réis) *de réis*, which yielded an annual interest of four *contos de réis*. To this was added an income of two *contos de réis* from rural and urban properties, making a total income of about six *contos de réis*. Expenditure in the two preceding years, however, had exceeded seventeen *contos*, so that there was an annual deficit of more than two *contos de réis*. At the same period the Holy House had a debt of more than six *contos de réis* and uncollected revenues worth thirty *contos*. Eighteen years later, that is, in 1852, the financial position of this charitable establishment had worsened considerably. Its capital had fallen to 66 *contos de réis* and its debts amounted to some five *contos*, while uncollected revenues stood at 54 *contos*. In 1872 the hospital’s economic position improved markedly, thanks to the genuine zeal shown in its administration in the preceding years, and revenue was brought into balance with expenditure, which that year amounted to some twelve *contos de réis*.

We do not have the information to discuss in detail the administration of the Holy House in more recent years, but we cannot fail to mention the administrations of 1897 to 1900 and of 1906 to 1910, under the direction of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira and Canon António Homem de Gouveia, during which the affairs of this charitable establishment were conducted with the most scrupulous zeal and with the most fruitful results.

We would be guilty of an unforgivable omission if we did not record here the act of the highest benevolence performed by Henrique Vieira de Castro, a banker of this city, who offered the Holy House the substantial sum of four hundred *contos* to found a ward devoted exclusively to the treatment of cancerous diseases. That benevolent gentleman had suggested, though not imposed, that the ward would best be staffed by Portuguese hospital sisters. That alone was enough for the administrative committee then in office to refuse the offer, thus depriving the hospital of so important a *donativo* (nominally a ‘gift’ to the Crown; a compulsory war levy).

The same gentleman became chairman of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House in January 1922 and at once opened a large public subscription, which raised more than three hundred *contos*; he himself launched it with a contribution of 30 *contos*. He has devoted himself tirelessly to the administration of the hospital, to which he is rendering, and will certainly continue to render, the most outstanding and notable services. (1922).

The foregoing brief account of the history of the Misericórdia of Funchal goes no further than 1926. From the following year, however, a series of favourable circumstances arose that made it possible to carry out the most important improvements and to bring inestimable prosperity to this benevolent institution, of which we shall now give a brief account.

In 1927 the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia) began a tenacious, persistent and intelligently directed campaign to obtain from the central government the cession of the Marmeleiros Sanatorium building, with its adjoining land, water and other rights, so that the various hospital services could be properly installed there. This was achieved by the Decree of 29 March 1928, a date that deserves to be recorded as one of the most memorable in the history of the Misericórdia, for it marks the greatest benefit the institution has received in its already long existence of four centuries. To complete the building, adapt it suitably to its intended purposes and set up the new and urgently needed services, the Managing Board had to raise a loan of five hundred *contos* de réis (*conto* (one million réis)). As a result, our hospital became one of the leading establishments of its kind in our country, according to the authoritative testimony of distinguished physicians who have visited it at length. In 1931 all the hospital services were moved to the new Marmeleiros building, having been housed for 240 years in the old Santa Isabel building, which in 1933 was ceded to the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) for the sum of one thousand five hundred *contos* de réis.

This most remarkable work on behalf of our foremost charitable institution, which we have set out here only very briefly, is owed to the Managing Board of the Misericórdia under the presidency of the Very Reverend Canon Manuel Francisco Camacho, and above all to this illustrious member of the Madeiran clergy, who spared himself no hardship and no persistent effort to bring to a successful conclusion an undertaking beset with so many and such great difficulties. It is only just to record here the names of General António Teixeira de Aguiar, Dr Carlos de Melo, Dr Oscar Baltazar Gonçalves and Dr João Francisco de Almada, for the pressing and valuable help they gave the Managing Board in achieving so notable an improvement.

Another date, and one of the most memorable in the annals of the Holy House, is 10 August 1940, when various improvements were solemnly inaugurated – the most important carried out in the Marmeleiros building since its acquisition and adaptation for hospital use. A considerable enlargement of the building, with new wards, spacious and well-equipped operating theatres, piped water and drainage, better accommodation for the secretariat and administration, and many other improvements in various parts of the hospital, made it possible to admit a greater number of patients and brought an inestimable improvement to the many complex services performed there. In mentioning this work, remarkable on many counts, two names come unbidden to the tip of our pen: that of the illustrious civil governor José Nosolini Pinto Osorio da Silva Leão and that of the president (*provedor*) and distinguished churchman Father Jacinto da Conceição Nunes. To the former is owed the procurement of the funds needed for this important improvement, and to the latter the intelligent and tenacious work of initiating, directing and completing it.

A valuable benefit granted to the Holy House was the ministerial order of 10 January 1939, which charged the District General Council and the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) with covering the annual ‘deficits’ of this charitable institution, which in 1942 exceeded the very considerable sum of six hundred *contos* de réis.

As stated above, the regime of the Confraternities of the Misericórdia lasted in Madeira only until 1834, unlike on the Portuguese mainland, where it has continued to the present day. In that year an Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) was appointed for Funchal, which served until the old Confraternity was restored, the latter taking office in 1906. It was short-lived, for it was abolished in 1910 and restored again in 1927, and it continues to the present day to direct all the hospital services with the most ardent zeal and a remarkable spirit of self-denial and sacrifice.

In closing this article, we cannot fail to add to the distinguished gallery of benefactors of the Holy House, briefly mentioned above, the names of the worthy citizens António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, Bishop Dom Luís Figueiredo de Lemos, the governor and captain-general Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho, Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira and the industrialist Henrique Hinton, who likewise rendered that house of charity outstanding and disinterested services.

Attached to the hospital was the Recolhimento das Orfãs (orphan girls’ home), which we shall discuss at the appropriate place in this work; and annexed to the same hospital, for 74 years, was the Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica*), to which we have already referred at length (vol. I, p. 401 ff.). The printed writings of possible interest for the history of the Misericórdia of Funchal known to us are the following: *Regimento ou Regulamento do Hospital Real de Santa Isabel da cidade do Funchal, Ilha da Madeira, sendo provedor da mesma Santa Casa o Excelentissimo e Reverendissimo Senhor Bispo Vigario Apostolico D. Frei Joaquim de Menezes e Athaide. Ano de 1816*, Lisbon, 1820, 60 pp.; *Regimento do Hospital Nacional e Real da cidade do Funchal, Provincia da Madeira. Ano de 1834*, Funchal, 1840, 16 pp.; *Discurso de abertura pronunciado na Escola Medico-Cirurgica do Funchal no dia 15 de Maio de 1867*, by Dr João da Câmara Leme, Funchal, 1867, 15 pp.; *Relatorio e Projecto de Regulamento para a Escola Medico-Cirurgica do Funchal...*, by Dr João da Câmara Leme, Funchal, 1868, 104-XX pp.; *A Questao entre o dr. João da Camara Leme... e o pharmaceutico Francisco Xavier de Sousa...*, Funchal, 1868, 55 pp., which appeared anonymously but is attributed to the physician-surgeon Francisco Clementino de Sousa (see that entry); *O dr. Antonio da Luz Pita, o pharmaceutico Francisco Xavier de Sousa e o dr. João da Camara Leme na Escola Medico Cirurgica e na Delegação de saude*, by Dr João da Câmara Leme, 1869, 88 pp.; *Projecto de Regulamento para a Santa Casa da Misericordia e seu hospital denominado de Santa Isabel, da cidade do Funchal, no anno de 1844*, Funchal, 1871, 36 pp.; *Saudades da Terra*, Funchal, 1873 (pp. 644–646); *O Hospital de Santa Isabel da cidade do Funchal visto à luz da hygiene*, by Acúrsio Garcia Ramos, Funchal, 1874, 36 pp.; *Ilha da Madeira*, by Acúrsio Garcia Ramos, Lisbon, 2 vols, 1879 and 1880 (it deals with St Elizabeth’s Hospital on pp. 49–117 of the 1st volume, where Dr Ramos’s pamphlet cited above is reproduced in full); *Relatorio apresentado á nova comissão Administrativa de Santa Casa da Misericordia do Funchal a 2 de Janeiro de 1901*, Funchal, 1901, 22 pp.; *Compromisso da Irmandade da Santa Casa da Misericordia do Funchal*, Funchal, 1906, 27 pp., preceded by a brief historical account by one of the editors of this *Elucidário*; *Regulamento interno da Santa Casa da Misericordia do Funchal*, Funchal, 1907, 24 pp.; *Boletim do Trabalho Industrial*, no. 95, *Instituições de Beneficencia e Associações de Classe*, by Vitorino José dos Santos, Lisbon, 1914, 84 pp., dealing with the Misericórdias on pp. 14–21 and 34–37. Since 1927, when the brotherhood of the Misericórdia resumed control of all the administrative services of the Holy House of Funchal, various reports have been drawn up and published as pamphlets. They contain important information, notably that for 1933, for the valuable documentation recorded in it.

Confraternities of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), each with its attached establishments, were also founded in the towns (*vilas*) of Calheta, Machico, Santa Cruz and Porto Santo. They still exist, although the scope of their charitable work is very limited.

The Misericórdia of Calheta: – In 1815 the Misericórdia of Funchal sought to add to its own assets the properties and ground rents belonging to the four Misericórdias just mentioned, on the grounds that the sick poor of those places were treated in the city hospital. It petitioned the government of mainland Portugal to this effect, but the petition was not granted, despite the report given by the governor and captain-general Florêncio Correia de Melo. The presidents (*provedores*) of the rural Misericórdias protested jointly against the claim of the Misericórdia of Funchal. They argued that, although their institutions did not maintain hospitals for lack of means and other local circumstances, they nevertheless supported invalids in suitable houses and performed other acts of charity, and that they should continue to provide the services they were providing, with their own separate and autonomous existence, as they had done until then. From this protest, which was upheld, we quote the following passages, which concern the history of the Misericórdia of Calheta:

‘This House of Mercy was established in 1535 by royal decree (*alvará*); the papal bull was dated 7 October of the same year; and in the year 1569 another royal decree granted it the power to collect its revenues, ground rents and debts by summary process, as for the Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*), its president being the enforcement judge (*juiz executor*). It has statutes (*compromisso*) dated from the year 1616, and from its foundation to this day it has maintained poor incurables, whom the House feeds, clothes and cares for decently, as far as its income allows. . . ’

This pious institution owed its foundation to various noble and distinguished persons of that town. Over time it reached a relatively high degree of prosperity, thanks to the legacies and donations made to it, and the leaseholds it owned were very substantial. Then came the careless management of some of its brotherhoods, the various crises that struck this island, our civil wars, etc., all of which brought about its decline and ruin, and the resources of this establishment are at present reduced to very limited proportions.

From the earliest days of the confraternity it had its own building and chapel, which still exist today, although they have undergone some alterations over the years. It seems that no hospital ever existed there, except perhaps in the period closer to its foundation, which we cannot affirm. Besides the brotherhood’s own religious services, held in its chapel, the House of Mercy served to shelter invalid and incurable people, chiefly drawn from the most distinguished families of that town who had been struck by misfortune or poverty.

In recent years (1921) a more diligent administration succeeded in restoring the whole building, which showed signs of imminent collapse, and some poor people are now housed there and receive an allowance for their keep. The house owns some properties and ground rents, which in 1913 yielded about three hundred escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis).
Marquis of Pombal Mission

It was founded on 21 March 1913, and its aims are the same as those of the association ‘O Vintém das Escolas’, to which it is subordinate and which was established in Lisbon in 1901 on the initiative of the late José de Moura Barata Feio Terenas.

The statutes of ‘O Vintém das Escolas’ show that this institution is devoted to promoting liberal and civic education. Its stated aims are to spread instruction among the children of the common people, to promote the moral and intellectual development and progress of the working classes, to help and relieve children of proven poverty, to promote the federation of independent schools and to establish prizes for teachers and pupils who prove worthy of them. The same institution’s programme also includes founding labour exchanges, schools and popular libraries, and holding lectures and literary and scientific talks.

The Marquis of Pombal Mission (*Missão Marquês de Pombal*) maintains a school in Funchal, in the Rua de Santa Maria. Its attendance today (1921) is 40 pupils, although at first it had an attendance of 105 pupils of both sexes. Its income comes from members’ subscriptions and from balls, charity fairs, etc., held from time to time.
Mitten (William)

English bryologist who studied the mosses collected in Madeira by James Yate Johnson. His herbarium was acquired by the New York Botanical Garden in 1906, according to a letter written by Professor T. D. A. Cockerell to the Madeiran zoologist Adolfo de Noronha. Works: *Contributions to the cryptogamic flora of the Atlantic Islands*. (*Linnean Society's Journ. Bot.*, VIII).
See Godman.
Mittermaier (Dr Carlos)
German physician who was in Funchal from 1852 to 1854 and made valuable meteorological observations here. Works: *Madeira und seine Bedeutung als Heilungsort*; Heidelberg, 1855.
Mocano

Two species are known by this name in Madeira: *Visnea mocanera*, of the family Ternstroemiaceae, and *Pittosporum coriaceum*, of the family Pittosporaceae. The first is a shrub or small tree, with leaves that are hairy while young, chiefly on the margins and the midrib of the underside; the second is always a tree, with leaves devoid of hairs at every age. The latter species is almost extinct in the mountains of Madeira, but it is cultivated on the *quintas* of Monte (‘hill’) and Camacha; the former can be found on the rocks between Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’) and Ribeira do Inferno (‘hell’s stream’), though it is quite rare. The wood of *Visnea mocanera* is dull in colour, sometimes tending slightly towards red, and very heavy and hard; that of *Pittosporum coriaceum* is light and yellowish or greyish.
Coinage

The money in circulation in Madeira in the early days of settlement was the same as that used in Portugal, as the letter of 26 September 1433 shows, by which King Duarte granted this island to Prince Henry the Navigator. That letter forbade the prince to have coin minted, and the money of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) was to circulate on the island.

Old documents show that the mark of silver (*marco de prata*, c. 230 g of silver) and the *reais* were coins circulating in Madeira, and that there were *reais* of silver and of copper, the former minted by order of John I.
