These old *reais* or *réis* were worth far more than the *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) that have lasted to our own day, and which even today are often used as the unit for reckoning values.

The charter (foral) of the city of Funchal and of the towns of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Calheta (‘small cove’), dated 6 August 1515, speaks of *cruzados* (old Portuguese coin worth 400 réis), of *réis* and of *reais*. The Timber Regulations (*Regimento das Madeiras*) of 27 August 1562 and many other documents also refer to the first of these coins, which in the course of time became a nominal money.

The new *cruzados* were of gold or silver; the old *cruzado* was of gold and was worth 400 *réis*. Even today it is the custom in Madeira to call the sum of 40 centavos or 400 *réis* a *cruzado*, whatever coins it may be made up of.

The books of the council sessions of 1550 show that *riales*, half *riales* and quarter *riales* were already circulating on the island at that time, the first worth 36, the second 18 and the last 9,5 *réis*. Nevertheless, even under Philippine rule, it was the *réis* and *cruzados* that served as the basis for expressing values.

In 1643 there circulated in Madeira *patacas* (silver coin, worth about 75–80 réis in the 17th century), half *patacas*, *tostões*, half *tostões* and coins of 120 *réis* and of 3 and 2 *vinténs*. However, the document in which we found this information does not tell us whether this money was all Spanish or whether some of it was Portuguese.

A royal letter (*carta régia*) of 9 February 1664, addressed to the superintendent (provedor) Francisco de Andrade, permitted the minting of gold and silver coin in Madeira. On the 10th of the same month and year the regulations (*regimento*) were published for establishing a mint on this island, with a superintending judge and such other officers as might be needed. The regulations of 1640 had ordered that the money of the Kingdom should circulate in Madeira, and in 1664 instructions came for the Municipality to appoint a clerk (*escrivão*) for the Mint and to have *patacas* and half *patacas* struck.

On 15 August 1704 the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) Duarte Sodré ordered that the *rialetes* and half *rialetes*, which on this island were worth 75 and 37 and a half *réis* respectively, should henceforth be worth 80 and 40 *réis*. He also ordered that half *patacas* and double silver *riales* (quarter *patacas*) be accepted, the former at 375 *réis* and the latter at 187 *réis*, provided they had the legal weight, which was 7 and a half *oitavas* per *pataca*. It was further decided on the same occasion that the *patacas* called *Marias* and the half *patacas* or half *Marias* should continue to circulate at 600 and 300 *réis*, the former when they weighed 6 and the latter 3 *oitavas*.

In 1700 the Governor received a royal letter ordering him to withdraw clipped money, and on that occasion 80,000 *cruzados* in new coin arrived to remain in Madeira. The value of the *pataca* of 7 and a half *oitavas* was then 750 *réis*.

At the end of the 18th century and the beginning of the 19th, the coins in use in Madeira were *patacas* (silver coin, worth about 75–80 réis in the 17th century) and Spanish pesetas and half-pesetas, the first worth 1,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), the second 200 *réis* and the last 100 *réis*. In 1819 these same coins were still circulating on the island, according to an English work published in London that year. French copper coins from the time of Louis XVI have been found in the foundations of some 18th-century buildings, which seems to indicate that they circulated in Madeira.

On 27 July 1762 the superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*) complained of the difficulty of transferring money to Lisbon, because the currency in circulation was foreign. In 1819 Governor Botelho asked that, so that he should not lose out, the difference in value between Madeiran and mainland money be taken into account when his salary was paid.

English and American money, which circulated on the island for many years, was introduced long after Castilian money had arrived. The Spanish gold coins that circulated in Madeira until 1879 were worth 16,000, 8,000, 4,000 and 2,000 *réis*, and the silver ones 1,000, 200, 100 and 50 *réis*.

The American gold coins current in Madeira were the double eagle, the eagle, the half eagle and the quarter eagle, worth 20,000, 10,000, 5,000 and 2,500 *réis* respectively. The silver coins were the *pataca* or dollar (1,000 *réis*), the half dollar (500 *réis*), the dime (100 *réis*) and the half dime (50 *réis*). Gold dollars or *patacas* also appeared, but this coin was uncommon.

The English gold coins current on the island were the pound sterling or sovereign and the half pound or half sovereign, the first worth 4,800 and the second 2,400 *réis*. Silver was represented chiefly by half-crowns (600 *réis*) and shillings (240 *réis*) and their subdivisions. Before the pound sterling was given its value of 4,800 *réis* by the decrees of 7 December 1836 and 4 May 1842, it had been worth 4,600 *réis* under the decree of 10 October 1835.

Besides the coinage we have mentioned, Bolivian, Chilean, Colombian, Argentine and Mexican *patacas*, all worth 1000 *réis*, and some other foreign coins were current in Madeira. In 1887 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) was obliged to refund to some merchants a tax they had paid on importing the foreign money circulating on the island.

Alongside the foreign gold and silver coins that circulated in Madeira for many years, another coinage was in use that had no currency in Portugal. An article by Alberto Artur Sarmento in the now defunct *Diario do Commercio* states ‘that the first Portuguese coin struck exclusively for the islands is the PECUNIA INSULANA of Joseph I . . . It bears the date 1750 and comes in three copper values: 10, 5 and 3 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). On the obverse it reads *JOSEPHUS I. D. G. PORT. ET ALG. REX*; two figures II (Josephus I) in the centre support the crown, the date is split on either side, 17-50, and below is the value X, V or III, according to the coin. On the reverse is PECUNIA INSULANA with the five *quinas* in the centre, flanked by palm branches and surmounted by the royal crown. The 5-réis coin had two issues, the second in 1751’.

Manuel B. Lopes Fernandes, in the *Memoria das moedas correntes em Portugal desde os tempos dos romanos até nossos dias* (*Memorias da Ac. Real das Sciencias*, new series, vol. II, part I), states that the pecunia insulana of Joseph I was intended for the Azores; it is certain, however, that it also circulated in Madeira, even after the pecunia madeirensis (copper coins minted specially for Madeira) appeared here. On p. 85 of vol. I of the *Elucidário* (article Armas), relying on the opinion of Dr Azevedo (see *Saudades*, p. 492), we said that the copper coins struck in 1750 show five sugar moulds flanked by canes, also of sugar. According to the same Lopes Fernandes, however, what appears there, as on the coins of 1751, is the *quinas* between two palm branches. This seems more accurate to us, although the two branches could easily be taken for sugar canes. The coins of the first issue, worth 12,000 *cruzados*, still show the two sugar canes of the old arms of Funchal, whereas the 19th-century issues show a vine branch instead of the canes.

‘Maria II,’ Alberto Sarmento goes on, ‘created the coinage exclusive to Madeira, the PECUNIA MADEIRENSIS, and there are likewise three values: 20, 10 and 5 réis. The obverse reads *MARIA II. D. G. PORT. ET ALG. REGINA*, with the Portuguese crown in the centre. The reverse bears PECUNIA MADEIRENSIS and the respective value – XX, X or V – bordered by a vine branch. The *vintém* (coin of 20 réis) had only one issue, in 1842. The 10-réis coin had 3 issues: in 1842, 1850 and 1852. The 5-réis coin was issued in 1850 but never circulated in Madeira, passing from the Mint into the hands of keen collectors, and today it is highly prized.’

As regards Madeiran money, it should also be said that in 1919 the Asilo da Mendicidade e Orfãos issued notes of 1 and 2 centavos, and in 1920 of 4 centavos, to make giving change easier, since metal coins had disappeared from the market. These notes circulated only briefly, however, because some traders refused to accept them.

The law of 2 May 1879 ended the circulation of foreign money in Madeira and set a deadline for exchanging the old weak currency for Portuguese coin. The pound sterling was the only foreign coin that remained current, although its value fell from 4,800 to 4,500 réis.

In the summary we have just given of the coins known in Madeira up to the publication of the law of 1879, we have mentioned only the kinds whose existence seemed to us well established. It is likely, however, that in the 15th century *ceitis*, escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis), *espadins* and white and black *reais* circulated here, and that in the following centuries various other coins current in Portugal reached this island, even though the documents we have consulted say nothing on the matter.
Mills

Among the privileges granted to the donataries of this archipelago was the exclusive right to build mills or water mills; when they saw fit, they could license others to do so in return for a special levy. This privilege was one of the richest sources of the captain-donataries’ revenues, which were very large indeed. At the locality still called Moinhos (‘mills’) today, along the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), they owned a considerable number of water mills that have survived to our own day, many of which the Marquises of Castelo Melhor, at a time not very distant from ours, leased to various people. The square known as Largo dos Moinhos or Largo do Marquês keeps these names because there were several water mills there belonging to the house of Castelo Melhor, into which the entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) of the donataries of Funchal was incorporated.

A letter or set of instructions sent by Prince Henry the Navigator to João Gonçalves Zarco states: ‘... to order João Afonso to fit another millstone and to build a water mill like the one at Tomar’. It is said that Caniço (‘reed’), outside Funchal, was the first *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) where a mill was built, and there is still a locality there called Azenha (‘water mill’).
See Levadas.
Moinhos

An inhabited locality in the parish of Caniço (‘reed’), with 68 households and 368 inhabitants. The ruins of a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Salvação (Our Lady of Salvation), founded in 1614 by Francisco Morais de Aguiar, still stand here.
Moinhos (stream)
It crosses the parish (*freguesia*) of Boaventura (‘good fortune’) and flows into the ocean a short distance from the Ribeira do Porco, in the same parish.
Moinhos (stream)
It lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’).
Moinhos (street)

This was formerly the name of the part of Rua das Mercês between Travessa das Capuchinhas and Largo do Marquês. At the upper end of the street stood a mill, demolished some years ago. Rua dos Moinhos (‘mills’) was originally called Rua do Peso.
Molarinha (Fumaria muralis)

An annual plant of the family Fumariaceae, common on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Its corollas are irregular and spurred, pink, white or purplish, usually dark purple or greenish at the tip. An infusion of *molarinha* or *herva-pombinha* is used for skin complaints.
Mole (islet)
A small islet off the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’).
Pontinha mole (breakwater)

The contract for the Pontinha (‘little point’) mole (breakwater) was awarded to the French engineers Combemale, Michelon and Maury under an agreement of 30 June 1885. The works lasted until 1889, and their provisional acceptance was authorised by a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 16 August 1890. The design had been drawn up by the engineer Mariano Augusto de Faria e Maia, although it underwent some modifications, some proposed by the said contractors and others imposed by the Consultative Board of Public Works and Mines (*Junta Consultiva de Obras Públicas e Minas*).

The work cost 447,256,855 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). However, since a large part of it was destroyed by the storms of 28 February 1892, the Government was obliged to spend 90,000,000 *réis* on its reconstruction, which was completed in 1895. Adding to these two sums the 2,502,960 *réis* spent on supervising the works, we see that the expenditure on building the Pontinha mole rose to the considerable sum of 539,759,815 *réis*.

It is worth noting that a mole was already being considered for Funchal as early as 1823. The governor and captain-general even asked the Council for its opinion on the proposed mole, and on 13 September of the following year a royal letter (*carta régia*) was published ordering Brigadier Francisco António Raposo to travel to the island of Madeira to carry out the studies needed for its construction. It was on the shoals near the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) that the brigadier intended to build a mole and quay, and to this end the considerable sum of 37 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos) was spent on breaking and dressing stone, most of which was left to go to waste.

At a session of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) on 26 November 1824, the governor and captain-general read out, before the Council, the nobility and the body of Portuguese and foreign merchants, a royal letter concerning the quay and mole in the city’s harbour. The *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) then asked the governor to convey to His Majesty the gratitude of the Madeirans for the benefit they were about to receive.

As for the wall joining the Pontinha islet to the land, it was begun in 1757 but only completed many years later. The plan and model of the work were drawn up by the engineer Francisco Tossi Columbino under a royal letter sent on 22 May 1756 to Governor Manuel Saldanha de Albuquerque, ordering the construction of a harbour of refuge in Funchal. A gale that struck our harbour on 4 November 1757 caused considerable damage to the works on this wall, which had by then already begun.
The work by the late Adolfo Loureiro entitled *Os Portos Maritimos de Portugal e Ilhas Adjacentes* contains a detailed account of the present Pontinha mole and the quays of Funchal.
See Abra and Cais.
Mona (Pseudotriacis microdon)
A fish of the family Mitsukurinida, found in the seas around Madeira and known in Portugal as *peixe carago*.
Monaco (Prince of)

Prince Albert I of Monaco, born in 1848 and died in June 1922, visited the seas around Madeira in 1879, 1888, 1901, 1904, 1911 and 1912, and in other years as well, aboard either the *Hirondelle* or the *Princesa Alice*. On every one of these occasions he made valuable collections for the study of the hydrobiology of this part of the Atlantic. In March 1888 he was on Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’), which he discusses in his book *La Carrière d'un navigateur*; the chapter on that island was translated by Mr Alberto Sarmento and published in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’).

The Bulletin of the Zoological Society of France (1892) published a work entitled *Orthoptères provenant des voyages de S. A. le prince de Monaco dans les archipels de Madère et des Açores*, and the Bulletin of the Oceanographic Institute of Monaco (1914) contains a work by L. Gain entitled *Algues provenant des Campagnes de l'Hirondelle II (1911-1912)*.
Monarchia (A)
Ten issues were published, the first on 11 August and the last on 24 October 1884.
Moncada (Dr Francisco Xavier Cabral)
He represented Madeira in parliament in the 1906–1907 legislature.
Mondragão

This family surname, which we suppose to be extinct in Madeira, came from João Rodrigues Mondragão, a Biscayan nobleman who settled in Madeira around 1500 and founded an entail (*morgado*) in the town (*vila*) of Calheta (‘small cove’).
See Castilian rule.
Moniz

This is a very old family surname here in Madeira. Among the first settlers who came from mainland Portugal, says the annotator of the *Saudades*, Vasco Martins Moniz de Meneses established himself on this island and held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Caniço (‘reed’). He was a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and the second son of Henrique Moniz, *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) of Silves, and of his wife Dona Inês de Meneses, daughter of Gonçalo Nunes Barreto, *alcaide-mor* of Faro. Vasco Martins Moniz kept a great house in the town (*vila*) of Machico and, by a will approved in 1489, founded an entail (*morgado*) from the disposable third (*terça*) of the estate; he died in 1510 in the town of Torrão. Nicolau Florentino (António Maria de Freitas) writes at length about Vasco Martins Moniz in his pamphlet *A mulher de Colombo*, extolling his deeds and qualities. He says that in the town of Machico, where Moniz had settled, he stood out among all the Portuguese and foreigners living there for his generosity, the nobility of his manners and the princely splendour of his house. Its comforts and attractions did not make him soft; on the contrary, whenever the king and the country called for his services, he left his family to lend his arm and often his purse. Vasco Moniz’s daughter, Dona Isabel Moniz, was the wife of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary (*donatário*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and from this marriage was born Dona Filipa Moniz, wife of the great navigator Christopher Columbus. The pamphlet by Nicolau Florentino cited above also deals at length with all these figures.
Francisco Moniz, the Elder, a native of the Algarve, also came to Madeira. He gave his name to the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz, or rather Porto do Moniz, where he held *sesmaria* lands.

We do not know whether the Moniz family to which the distinguished Madeirans Lourenço José Moniz, João Henriques Moniz, Patrício Moniz, Jaime Moniz and João Maria Moniz (see those entries) belonged descends from Vasco Moniz or from the Francisco Moniz mentioned above.
Moniz (Dom João Henriques)

He was born in this city in the last quarter of the 18th century and was a close relative of Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Dr Patrício Moniz and Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Jaime Moniz, all of whom are covered in this *Elucidário*. He graduated in canon law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and was ordained priest in the first quarter of the 19th century.

He was serving in this diocese as ecclesiastical promoter (diocesan prosecutor) when he was caught up in the special judicial commission (*alçada*) that came to this island in 1828. The following year he was sent under arrest to Lisbon, and from there he was deported in 1830 to the Cape Verde archipelago. He lived for some years on the island of Brava, where he carried out parish duties and rendered notable services to education by founding two schools.

When constitutional government was restored he did not return home, and in 1835 he was appointed governor of the diocese (*governador do bispado*, administering the see in the bishop’s absence) of Cape Verde. In 1841 he was nominated bishop of that diocese, but it was only in 1844 that he came to Lisbon to receive episcopal consecration.

His episcopate was very short, for he reached Cape Verde in February 1847 and died on 1 July of the same year. It was believed at the time that the setbacks and persecution he suffered as soon as he landed on the island of Santiago swiftly drove him to the grave. The cathedral chapter, which consisted of one black canon and one mulatto canon, refused to grant him possession of the bishopric, and the Governor, in the absence of legal possession, did not recognise him as prelate and refused to pay him the corresponding emoluments. Amid these struggles and sorrows he succumbed to an attack of pernicious fever and was buried in the cemetery of Praia, without receiving the civil and ecclesiastical honours to which his high rank entitled him. There were those who claimed that the prelate had been the victim of murder by poisoning, which was then attributed to a close relative of his.
Dom João Henriques Moniz had been elected substitute senator for Madeira for the legislative session of 1840 to 1842.
Moniz (Dr Lourenço José)

He was one of the most distinguished Madeirans of the first half of the 19th century, combining a brilliant talent with a remarkable austerity of character. He and Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca, who for several decades represented Madeira in parliament, were the men who championed the needs of this archipelago with the greatest self-denial and disinterest. They sought no posts for themselves and lent their support to no scandalous claims or shady dealings; they always lived in modest circumstances and died in almost destitute poverty.

Dr Lourenço José Moniz was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) in this city on 10 August 1789. His paternal uncle, Father Filipe Gomes Moniz, curate of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), recognised in him a lively and precocious intelligence and took charge of his young nephew’s education. The boy fully lived up to the hopes that his devoted protector placed in him.

Having completed his preparatory studies in Funchal, Lourenço Moniz went to England to enrol in the faculty of medicine of the University of Edinburgh. The university enjoyed a worldwide reputation, and the physicians trained there were then highly regarded and considered very learned in their field. In England, although a foreigner with no deep knowledge of the country’s language, he fully upheld the reputation he had earned in Madeira, winning several prizes in various chairs of his university course. On 1 August 1815 he defended his inaugural thesis, *De Ictero*, written in Latin and published in London the same year.

On returning to his native land, he took up the practice of his profession with brilliant success. In 1824 he was appointed professor of a chair of humanities, which he later also taught at the lyceum (state secondary school) when it was established in 1837; he was a distinguished teacher there and its first rector. Likewise, when our Medical School was created in 1837, Lourenço José Moniz was appointed its professor and first director. He never actually held these posts, however, because they became incompatible with his seat as a deputy and the other official commissions he was then carrying out.

His austere character, his recognised talent and the high regard in which his fellow Madeirans held him naturally marked him out for high public office. Thus, in the first elections held after the promulgation of the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) in 1826, Dr Lourenço Moniz was elected deputy for Madeira to the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) that sat from 1826 to 1828.

When the Cortes were dissolved and absolute government proclaimed, Dr Moniz returned to Madeira. Soon, however, fearing the persecution that was beginning against supporters of liberal ideas, he had to leave his homeland. He sailed for the United States of America, where he stayed for some years, returning to Funchal after constitutional government had been restored.

At the very first elections, in 1834, he was elected deputy for this archipelago. In the nine following legislatures, which ran from that year until 1856, shortly before his death, he represented Madeira in parliament without interruption, except for the legislative session of 1842 to 1845. No other Madeiran has managed to represent his homeland in the Cortes for so long a period, which is eloquent proof of the selfless way in which he did so and of how hard he worked for the prosperity and advancement of his native soil.

Dr Moniz enjoyed the reputation of a distinguished parliamentarian, not only for the speeches he delivered but also as a member of various committees. He was rapporteur for many bills and reports, in which he always showed remarkable competence. On occasion he presided over the Chamber of Deputies, and he was held in high esteem by the most brilliant parliamentarians of every party faction.

He carried out important public service commissions, among them that of commissioner judge for maritime prizes at the Cape of Good Hope. In this difficult and hazardous mission, the manner in which he conducted himself before the British authorities brought great honour to the Portuguese name.

He was also civil governor of Coimbra, a member of the Overseas Council (*Conselho Ultramarino*), a member of various scientific and literary societies, etc. He died in Lisbon on 4 December 1857, at the age of 68. Here on the island a public subscription was opened to raise a mausoleum in the Alto de São João cemetery to hold his mortal remains, and on it the following epitaph can be read: HONOUR, SCIENCE, PATRIOTISM.

Here lies Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Lourenço José Moniz, doctor of medicine and member of the Overseas Council. He was a deputy of the nation, representing Madeira, his homeland, for more than twenty years in successive legislatures. He was vice-president of the elective chamber in 1841, commissioner of studies in the district of Funchal, rector and professor of rhetoric at the lyceum (state secondary school) of the same city, and judge commissioner for maritime prizes at the Cape of Good Hope, and he carried out many other public service commissions without payment. He was born on the Island of Madeira on 10 August 1789. He always lived modestly and, at the end of so long a career, died poor in Lisbon on 6 December 1857. In testimony of their gratitude for the intelligence and unsurpassed zeal with which he always championed the interests of Madeira, and in tribute to his civic and moral virtues and his high scientific merit, the Madeirans had this monument erected to him.
Moniz (Dr Patrício)

Dr Patrício Moniz was without doubt the most gifted mind our land produced in the 19th century. The vigour of his talent, eloquently displayed in a remarkable philosophical culture, and his immense learning, which made him a true sage in every sense of the word, fully bear out our assertion, bold as it may seem to many. He was an eminently superior spirit, drawn to the abstractions of the loftiest philosophy, to which he had devoted himself entirely, and he made a point of despising the Europeans of superficial, ill-founded science. Nevertheless, he was sometimes taken for a man of only middling learning by those who can judge only by appearances and who are accustomed to measure a man’s intellectual worth by an endless parade of dates, names and quotations from the most respected and fashionable authors.

He possessed the most remarkable aptitudes and merits, which aroused the admiration and astonishment of those who knew him most closely and were best able to appreciate the full range and greatness of his mental faculties. The general public could only occasionally, and always imperfectly, gauge the calibre of that splendid talent. Just as pearls hide in the depths of the ocean and diamonds in the bowels of the earth, so his vast intelligence lay buried in the deepest modesty and the most complete self-effacement, which made him simply adorable and truly delightful to those who were on intimate terms with him. And yet a man of such intellectual stature passed almost unnoticed, leaving to posterity no substantial work, which his rare faculties as a scholar, thinker and philosopher could undoubtedly have produced. This regrettable circumstance must be attributed in large part to the fickleness of his temperament and to the constantly unsettled life he led during the years when his mind was at its most vigorous. Nevertheless, anyone who consults his writings will readily recognise what his intellect would have been capable of, had various causes not prevented him from producing a work of greater scope.

Dr Patrício Moniz was a great theologian. Every branch of the vast science of theology was familiar to him, and he discoursed on all of them with remarkable proficiency. To hear him from the professor’s chair was to be enraptured by such profound knowledge, such astonishing erudition and such spontaneous and persuasive eloquence; it seemed that theology, a science so difficult in itself and so strewn with pitfalls, held no secrets for him.

If he was a most distinguished theologian, he was no less accomplished a philosopher – a philosopher in the strict and proper sense of the word, not merely an amateur or even a devoted student of philosophy. Dr Patrício Moniz wrote a book entitled *Theoria da Afirmação Pura*, which we are not competent to judge properly, but which we can confidently state bears witness to the lofty faculties of his mind. The work may have its imperfections and is evidently shot through with much obscurity; it seems rather to have been written by a German philosopher absorbed in the most abstract philosophical speculation than by a southerner who spent a large part of his life in a country such as Brazil. It is beyond dispute, however, that a mediocre intellect would have been incapable of producing a work of that kind and of delving so deeply into such lofty philosophical questions.

He enjoyed great renown as an orator, and was indeed a most distinguished one, the city of Rio de Janeiro being the chief arena of his oratorical triumphs. The Brazilians rightly took pride in their great sacred orator Mont’Alverne, who, after the great Vieira, won a prominent place among those who have preached in the Portuguese language. The Brazilian press was unanimous in proclaiming Dr Patrício Moniz the true successor of Mont’Alverne. His fame as a sacred orator crossed the ocean and resounded in the Old World. He published some sermons and funeral orations, which are true gems of their kind, but most of his discourses were not written down. Having reflected on and studied his subject, he left the delivery to the flights of improvisation. He was gifted with remarkable fluency, and words often poured from his lips in cascades of eloquence. Yet he was not, and never could be, a popular orator. The breadth of his learning, his natural bent for philosophical questions and a certain itch to tackle subjects that were inherently thorny and bristling with difficulties drew him irresistibly away from the kind of speech that moves and carries away the masses. Utterly disdaining applause, he generally chose as the subject of his orations only those matters most closely akin to his philosophical and theological predilections. Dr Patrício Moniz was one of the most notable sacred orators of our country, and unquestionably no one surpassed him in the theological sciences or in his profound knowledge of all the sources of sacred oratory.

Philosophers are generally little inclined to works of fiction and outpourings of feeling. Nevertheless, in his youth Patrício Moniz courted the Muses, adopting the Arcadian name of Cleomenes Messeide as a member of the Roman Arcadia, and he wrote two volumes of verse, which he published at the ages of 18 and 19. Later, when the study of the speculative sciences, to which he had devoted himself wholeheartedly, had taken complete hold of his mind, he ceased to be a disciple of Apollo in order to follow the path of the great philosophers. It was nonetheless clear that he could have won a distinguished place on Parnassus had he continued to play the lyre.

It remains for us to give a few biographical details of this illustrious fellow countryman of ours. He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) in this city on 2 April 1820, the son of Francisco João Moniz, a senior official of the Treasury Board (*Junta da Fazenda*), and of Dona Ana Foster Moniz. In 1828, when he was only 8 years old, he went to Rio de Janeiro with his father. His father had been elected deputy for Madeira to the constituent Cortes (Portuguese parliament) that sat from 1821 to 1822 and professed the principles of the Porto revolution, so he was forced to leave the country when Miguel I proclaimed himself absolute king in 1828.

Patrício Moniz completed his secondary education in the Brazilian capital, while at the same time devoting himself to poetry. In 1838 he published the volume entitled *Meditações Noturnas*, and in 1839 another volume of verse, to which he gave the title *Composições poéticas offerecidas ao seu querido pai Francisco João Moniz*.

Shortly afterwards he went to Paris, where he enrolled in the faculty of law and took the degree of bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate). He then made his way to Rome, and in that capital he studied at the celebrated Roman College, or Pontifical University, taking his doctorate in the faculty of theology after revealing his extraordinary talent and winning various academic distinctions. Having been ordained priest in Rome and having completed all his university work, he returned to the city of Rio de Janeiro. There he devoted himself to the service of the Church, to preaching, teaching, journalism and study, which he never abandoned.

As we have already said, the capital of the empire was the scene of his triumphs as an orator. At the Recreio Literário Português he gave remarkable and brilliant lectures, and in recognition that society had a life-size oil portrait of the illustrious Madeiran hung in its rooms. At many ceremonies, at solemn funeral rites and at other public occasions, he delivered speeches that became famous. Despite his long career as an orator, few of these speeches were published, owing to the circumstance, which we have already noted, that he rarely wrote down the orations he delivered.

Dr Patrício Moniz was a journalist and a polemicist of stern mettle. He brilliantly displayed his distinguished qualities as a writer and scholar in *Religião*, *Tribuna Catholica*, *Iris* and other newspapers, which he edited or to which he contributed with greater or lesser regularity.
He taught with great proficiency in Rio de Janeiro and in Funchal. At the seminary of this city he held the chairs of theology, philosophy, history and eloquence, as well as other subjects.

Dr Patrício Moniz was a member of various literary and scientific societies, both Portuguese and foreign, and always refused all the decorations and honorary titles with which others sometimes wished to distinguish him. In addition to the works already cited, he published five speeches as separate pamphlets and a few other booklets, among them one entitled *Reflexões sobre a carta do sr. Alexandre Herculano*.

In 1878 or 1879, after being for some time a professor at the Funchal seminary, where the breadth of his learning filled his pupils with genuine amazement, he left for mainland Portugal. There he held various ecclesiastical posts until he was appointed parish priest of Aveiras de Baixo, a humble parish of the Patriarchate (the archdiocese of Lisbon) with fewer than a thousand inhabitants. He lived there for years, close to destitution and in the most complete obscurity – perhaps the greatest luminary of the Portuguese clergy of his day.

He was a man of great austerity of character, of a lively and purified religious faith and of irreproachable conduct. Scorning all pomp and ostentation, he lived simply and modestly, and whatever was left over from his meagre means he generously shared among the poor. He had eccentricities and very personal ways of looking at things and judging people, which at times bordered on the ridiculous, but an unaffected simplicity and a sincere, artless ingenuousness always made them attractive and endearing. He died in Lisbon on 28 February 1898, at the age of 78.
Moniz (Francisco João)

He belonged to the Moniz family, which gave so many distinguished men to Madeira. In the first elections held in this archipelago for the Constituent Cortes (Portuguese parliament), which sat from 1821 to 1822 after the representative system was established, Francisco João Moniz was chosen to represent this island in the Cortes, and he championed with dedication the questions of most direct concern to Madeira.
He was a clerk and later accountant of the Royal Treasury Board (*Junta da Real Fazenda*), and in 1828 he sailed for Brazil to escape Miguelist persecution.
He held the post of Portuguese vice-consul in Rio de Janeiro and was one of the benefactors of the Beneficência Portuguesa of that city.
He was the father of the illustrious Madeiran Patrício Moniz (see that entry) and died, according to what we heard from a member of his family, around 1848.
Moniz (Jaime Constantino de Freitas)

He was one of the most distinguished sons of Madeira in the 19th century. He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Sé (Funchal Cathedral) in this city on 18 February 1837, the son of António Caetano da Costa Moniz and Dona Eufémia de Freitas Moniz.

After completing his preparatory studies at the Funchal Lyceum (state secondary school), he enrolled in the Faculty of Law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1857. He graduated in 1862, having won the first prizes in every year of his course.

He immediately took up the practice of law, but his career in the courts, though extremely brilliant, was short. During this period of his life there occurred the lamentable tragedy, which shook the whole country, in which the deputy José Cardoso Vieira de Castro murdered his own wife. The trial aroused an interest never before seen in Portugal. Jaime Moniz had taken on the defence of his unfortunate friend, a former companion from his student days. The case was one of the most celebrated ever tried in Portugal, and the defence was recorded in the annals of the Portuguese bar as one of the most brilliant oratorical triumphs of forensic eloquence. The magistrate who led the prosecution had said that Jaime Moniz was a true meteor that had appeared, shining intensely, at the bar. Moniz at once retorted that he was indeed a meteor, not for the brilliance with which he shone but for the speed with which he passed. He was thus alluding to his short career as an advocate, which he soon abandoned for good.

Pinheiro Chagas and Camilo Castelo Branco wrote of this brilliant defence in terms of the highest praise, and the Portuguese living in Rio de Janeiro sent Jaime Moniz a gold crown in homage to the author of that monumental speech. The speech and the entire proceedings of the trial were published in a volume, printed in a large edition that soon sold out.

Like most men of merit in his day, Jaime Moniz also made his way through the tortuous windings of national politics, but he emerged unscathed from that quagmire in which so many wallow away their own dignity. He was deputy for the constituency of Castelo Branco in the three legislatures that ran from 1870 to 1874, and for the constituency of Goa in the legislative session of 1871 to 1875. When a law allowed the scientific establishments and bodies to elect a representative of their own to the House of Peers, Jaime Moniz was unanimously chosen to fulfil that high and honourable mission. His debut in parliament, in 1871, was a genuine political event, and he at once won standing as a notable parliamentarian. Whenever he raised his voice within the national assembly, the whole chamber listened to him attentively, and applause broke out spontaneously, even from the opposition benches. The subjects he chose to address above all, and with unquestionable authority, concerned public education and colonial questions.

When the Marquis of Ávila e Bolama fell in 1871, Fontes Pereira de Melo was called upon to form a ministry under his own presidency, in which Jaime Moniz took the Navy portfolio. That ministry included men of the stature of Rodrigues Sampaio, Barjona de Freitas and Andrade Corvo. Although his time in the councils of the Crown was not long, our illustrious fellow countryman left his mark on the Ministry of the Navy and Overseas through far-reaching measures. His name is still cited today as one of the statesmen in our country who did not neglect colonial questions.

Abandoning the bar and politics, Jaime Moniz devoted all the faculties of his mind to teaching, to the work of the Academy and to the many services of public instruction. In 1863 he entered the competitive examination for the chair of philosophy and universal history at the Curso Superior de Letras, publishing the thesis he presented, entitled *Da natureza e extensão do progresso considerado como lei da humanidade e applicação especial dessa lei às bellas artes*. As a professor at this institution of higher education he was among the most distinguished, and his colleagues on the teaching staff included professors of the stature of Viale, Pinheiro Chagas, Adolfo Coelho and Teófilo Braga.

He was a full member of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Ciências de Lisboa*) and for many years held the post of secretary of the country’s foremost scientific and literary body, a post previously held by Latino Coelho and Pinheiro Chagas. His work within this illustrious areopagus stood out brilliantly, not only in the reports and memoirs he wrote but also in the organisation he gave to some of the Academy’s internal services; he also played a most notable part in all its most important work.

It was in the former Consultative Board of Public Instruction (*Junta Consultiva de Instrução Pública*), and later in the Superior Council of Public Instruction (*Conselho Superior de Instrução Pública*), over which Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Jaime Constantino de Freitas Moniz presided for many years, that his activity showed itself most remarkably. He had a genuine passion for every matter connected with education, to which he devoted a considerable part of his life. He wrote many reports and opinions, drafted bills, delivered speeches, went abroad on official missions, reorganised those advisory bodies, etc., creating a name that, in the history of national education, will be crowned with many claims to public gratitude.
Jaime Moniz was also director-general of the secretariat of the Chamber of Deputies and published several annual reports on the services of that department.

He belonged to many literary and scientific societies, both Portuguese and foreign, and after his death, on the proposal of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences, his name was given to the Funchal Lyceum (state secondary school). He died in Lisbon on 16 September 1917.
Moniz (João Cirilo)

We know of this Madeiran through the references to him that we have found in volumes X and XI of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva’s *Diccionario Bibliographico*. He was born in Funchal on 28 January 1818 and died in Niterói, Brazil, on 2 June 1871. In 1809 he accompanied his father to Rio de Janeiro, where he studied piano and singing. He belonged to various societies and in that city founded one devoted to providing free instruction. He published a pamphlet entitled *Breve compêndio de musica*, dedicated to Her Highness the Most Serene Imperial Princess Dona Leopoldina. It seems that he left several unpublished works intended for the study of music, but we have no knowledge of them.
Moniz (João Maria)

He was born in Funchal on 23 July 1822, the son of José Inácio Moniz and Dona Marciana Jardim Moniz. In 1849, having previously completed his secondary studies at the lyceum (state secondary school), he was admitted as a trainee clerk in the Funchal Revenue Office (*Repartição de Fazenda*). In 1860 he was appointed junior clerk in the same department, where he served until 27 June 1895, when he retired, by then holding the rank of officer, which he had attained on 22 August 1883.

He was a distinguished naturalist, and between 1848 and 1855 he assembled an excellent herbarium. Part of it, which had been lent to the botanist Richard Thomas Lowe, was lost in the shipwreck in which that English scholar lost his life. Fresh explorations in the archipelago enabled him to replace the lost specimens with others and to discover various species not previously recorded.

In 1856 Lowe created the genus *Monizia*, which he dedicated to our distinguished fellow countryman. He accompanied the description of the genus that he published in Booker’s *Jornal Botanico* with the following words: ‘this name is a tribute to Mr João M. Moniz, a distinguished botanist and successful investigator of the native flora of Madeira, and no less zealous a horticulturist, always actively engaged in introducing rare or new plants to the island and in promoting the advancement of agricultural and horticultural knowledge among his fellow countrymen’.

Three botanical species commemorate the name of J. M. Moniz – *Carex Moniziana*, *Helichrysum Monizii* and *Scrophularia Moniziana* – and two molluscs and an insect were also named after him: the insect is *Zargus Monizi* and the molluscs are *Craspedopoma Monizianum* and *Helix Moniziana*.

João Maria Moniz was the first botanist to record the presence in Madeira of *Visnea Mocanera*, a tree thought to be peculiar to the Canary Islands. It was also he who showed, by means of authentic specimens gathered on this island, that the *Euphorbia Luthyris* in the herbarium of Francis Masson, held in the British Museum, came from here and not from the Azores, as someone had supposed.

Many exotic plants now found in abundance in our *quintas* (country estates) and gardens were introduced by the subject of this entry. He grew and acclimatised them on a property in the locality (*sítio*) of Desterro, and then distributed them among his friends and acquaintances.

João Maria Moniz was a knight of the Order of St James, a provincial associate of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Ciências de Lisboa*), a corresponding member of the now defunct Geographical Society of Porto (*Sociedade de Geografia do Porto*) and a member of the former Agricultural Society of Funchal (*Sociedade Agrícola do Funchal*). He promoted an exhibition held in Funchal in 1854 and was one of the members of the committee that organised the agricultural exhibition of 1861. He owned a diamond ring given to him by the Infante Dom Luís, later King of Portugal; Empress Elisabeth of Austria and Prince Maximilian, later Emperor of Mexico, also showed him great esteem when they visited this island.

On his death he left a valuable herbarium, which was acquired by the English botanist Murray and is now at Kew; a magnificent collection of land shells, which was bought by the Englishman Blandy, now deceased; and a collection of woods, which is at present in the archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal. In the last years of his life he was trying to gather the marine shells of Madeira in order to submit them for examination to the Englishman Watson, but death overtook him before he had finished this work.

J. M. Moniz was above all a botanist and malacologist, but he knew the great majority of the fishes of Madeiran waters and was no stranger to entomology. A small collection of insects that he had put together was given during his lifetime to the distinguished French entomologist Fauvel.

He was gifted with a prodigious memory and an admirable power of observation. For this reason he seldom failed to give the name of a plant he had once studied, even many years after that study. If he could not, like Augustin de Candolle, recognise plants by their cotyledons, he could often recognise them from a mere fragment of a leaf, as we had occasion to observe more than once.

João Maria Moniz died in Funchal on 10 July 1898. He worked until the end of his life and was unquestionably one of the most distinguished men of our land, even though he left no work to bear witness to his great learning and to the interest he always devoted to the study of the natural sciences.
Monizia

A genus of the Umbelliferae family, dedicated by the English naturalist Richard Thomas Lowe to the distinguished Madeiran botanist João Maria Moniz. It was published in vol. VIII, p. 285, of Hooker’s *Journal of Botany*, and comprises a single species, *Monizia edulis*, found in June 1855 on Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’) and later in the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) and in Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’).
Monóculo (O)
Nine issues of this newspaper appeared, from 14 April to 13 June 1889.
Montado do Barreiro
See Barreiro (Montado do), I-129.
Montalembert (Charles Forbes de Tryon, Count de)

This well-known French politician and man of letters, one of the greatest orators of his day, stayed on this island from 26 January to 4 March 1844 because of his wife’s health. He landed in Funchal on a day of violent storm, and his life and those of his travelling companions were in serious danger. In this city he wrote, and later published in France, a long letter addressed to the Cambridge Camden Society, which became famous.
Monte Belo (Viscount of)
He died in Funchal on 17 February 1922.
See Freitas da Silva (João de).
Monte (parish)
See Nossa Senhora do Monte (parish).
Monte Gordo e Boa Morte

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). A chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Good Death (*Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte*) once stood there and gave the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) its name. It was built by Francisco Fernandes and Brásia Fernandes, in a year that is not known.
Monte Medonho

A locality (*sítio*) in the uplands of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), where the Levada do Monte Medonho (‘fearsome hill’) begins. Since 1908 this levada (irrigation channel) has irrigated the parishes of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and Tábua; before that it watered the land of the parish of São Vicente.
Monteiro

In Madeira this family surname descends from Pedro Jorge Monteiro, who settled in Funchal in 1763, where he came to hold the office of tobacco administrator. He was married to Dona Maria Teresa de Gusmão.
Monteiro (Dr João António)

We know of only two Madeirans who achieved notable distinction in the natural sciences – José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage (vol. I, p. 125) as a zoologist and João António Monteiro as a mineralogist. Both left us several works that bear witness to their profound knowledge of these branches of human learning.

João António Monteiro, whom several foreign authors call ‘the Portuguese savant’, was born in this city on 31 May 1769, the son of the wealthy merchant Pedro Jorge Monteiro and Dona Maria Teresa de Gusmão. He was baptised João António in honour of his godfather, João António de Sá Pereira, then governor and captain-general of this archipelago and later Baron of Alverca. The circumstances of his life are entirely unknown to us until 1791, when he received the degree of doctor in the faculty of philosophy at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). Shortly afterwards he was admitted there as professor of the chair of mineralogy. Since he received the doctoral hood (*capelo*) at so tender an age, and throughout his life gave constant proof of a most brilliant talent and the most devoted love of work, we must believe that he had been an outstanding student from his first days in primary school.

Dr João António Monteiro taught at the university with notable distinction. His name was placed alongside those of José Bonifácio de Andrade e Silva and Manuel José Barjona, who, for the new direction they gave to the teaching of the natural sciences and for the depth of their learning, are regarded as true ornaments of our foremost institution of learning.

Dr Monteiro did not remain long in his teaching career, for he was eager to broaden the range of his knowledge abroad. There he devoted himself entirely to profound studies, which earned him a great reputation in all the scientific centres of Europe. He left the country in 1804 on a long scientific journey through various European countries and never returned to Portugal, for reasons that are today wholly unknown.

By decree of 11 May 1804 he was appointed professor of one of the chairs of the recently founded chemical laboratory of Lisbon, a post which, it seems to us, he never actually took up. Shortly afterwards he was commissioned by our government to make the scientific journey mentioned above, and the corresponding royal letter (*carta régia*) guaranteed him his seniority, salary and other prerogatives, as if he were actively holding his chair at the University.

Once abroad, he devoted himself entirely to his scientific work. This is attested by the important writings he left scattered across many foreign journals and publications, which were never collected in volume form, as well as by several separate pamphlets.

On the value of Dr Monteiro’s work and his scientific merit, we shall transcribe a few passages from what Dr Joaquim Augusto Simões de Carvalho wrote about him in his *Memoria histórica da faculdade de philosophia da Universidade de Coimbra*, published in 1872:

‘This Portuguese scholar honours his homeland by the breadth of his knowledge, above all in mineralogy. He began his work in Paris, where he published interesting memoirs, and then went to Germany to attend the lectures of the celebrated Werner at Freiberg. There he distinguished himself by important scientific studies in crystallography and the natural history of minerals, so much so that he earned honourable citations from celebrated German and French mineralogists.

‘At a session of the Philomathic Society in Paris, Haüy and Binet presented a highly flattering report on a memoir by this illustrious Madeiran, which dealt with the direct determination of a new variety of the crystalline form of carbonate of lime and the remarkable properties it displays.

‘Haüy, in his treatise on mineralogy and in many memoirs, always cites Dr Monteiro’s observations and work with the highest praise. The memoir on “red sulphurated arsenic” published by the eminent French mineralogist in the *Annaes do Museu de Historia Natural* is based entirely on communications from our learned compatriot.

The memoir on many new varieties of topaz, published by Dr João António Monteiro in the collection of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Bavaria, earned him a diploma of membership of that illustrious scientific body. ‘Schrauf, in his treatise on physical mineralogy, Friedrich Mohs, in his fundamental principles of mineralogy, Haiduiger, in his manual of mineralogy, and many others among the most respected and authoritative writers of Germany, refer in honourable terms to the work of Dr Monteiro and of his illustrious contemporary José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva.’

Besides the scientific works already cited, the *Diccionario Bibliographico* of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva mentions the *Memória sobre o fluato de cal do Vesuvio* and a translation of Dr Jenner’s celebrated work on vaccination, published in Lisbon in 1803, not counting the countless writings he left in the proceedings of many foreign scientific societies.
Dr João António Monteiro, one of the most illustrious sons of this land, died in Paris in 1834, at the age of 65.
Monteiro (Dr Luciano Afonso da Silva)
This well-known statesman and parliamentarian sat as deputy for this archipelago in the legislative session of 1895 to 1897.
Monteiro (José Maria)

– He was the first Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) governor to administer this archipelago. He was appointed on 15 June 1828, and on the 25th of the same month the frigate *Príncipe Real*, which was carrying him, appeared off Funchal. However, the Governor and Captain-General José Lúcio Travassos Valdez prevented him from landing. As will be seen in the article on the Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelite troops, once the island had been taken by the royalist forces, José Maria Monteiro landed and took office on 24 August 1828.

His rule was not long, but it was sadly marked by the abuses of power he committed and the humiliations he inflicted on the inhabitants of the archipelago. The ominous special judicial commission (alçada) that came to this island in his time, presided over by the high court judge (*desembargador*) Francisco António Maciel Monteiro, committed the gravest excesses and drew hundreds of individuals into its inquisitorial judicial inquiry (*devassa*). Many of them were imprisoned and banished from this island, and not a few were sent to our overseas possessions. Emigration by people of every social class fleeing the persecutions was very heavy, chiefly to England, Brazil and North America. A considerable number of public officials were dismissed, many of them being imprisoned and sent to Lisbon. (See Alçadas.)

José Maria Monteiro became notorious not only for the persecution he waged against the liberals of this island but also for his lack of dignity and scruples; on one occasion he even went so far as to help himself to part of the money intended for paying the troops. It is said that on the frequent visits he made to the homes of the *malhados* (‘piebalds’, nickname for the Liberals), accompanied by constables (*quadrilheiros*), he seized everything he saw that had any value. Two of his sons also distinguished themselves in these exploits, and a major theft committed at the *quinta* (country estate) of Palheiro, which belonged to João de Carvalhal, was attributed to them.

José Maria Monteiro, who was a post-captain (*capitão de mar e guerra*) and held a court office in the household of Miguel I, left Madeira at the end of April 1830, after his successor, Dom Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo, had already arrived. For his biography, see what we said on p. 113 of vol. I and p. 95 of vol. II, when we discussed Colonel José António de Azevedo Lemos and Joaquim Melchior Gonçalves.
Monteiro (Luís)
He was born in Funchal on 25 August 1773, the son of Pedro Jorge Monteiro and Dona Maria Teresa de Gusmão, and the brother of the learned mineralogist Dr João António Monteiro (see that entry).

He was a wholesale merchant in Lisbon when, on 24 August 1821, the revolution broke out in Porto whose aim was to establish the representative system in the country; it found its echo in the capital on 15 September of the same year. Besides the Provisional Junta of Porto (*Junta Provisional do Porto*), a provisional government was formed in Lisbon. It was short-lived, and Luís Monteiro was a member of it as the representative of Lisbon’s leading merchants.

On the death of John VI, Dom Pedro was proclaimed King of Portugal and granted the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*). Elections of deputies followed, and Madeira returned Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar, Father Caetano Alberto Soares and Luís Monteiro. The last of these asked to be excused from the office to which he had been elected; the Chamber did not accept his request, but Luís Monteiro never took his seat in the national assembly.
Luís Monteiro carried out several public service commissions, and in 1834 he was entrusted with a mission attached to our legation in London.
Monteiro (street)

This is a short street that runs from Rua da Cadeia Velha, opposite the end of Rua dos Medinas, to Rua 31 de Janeiro, on the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). It is almost parallel to Rua do Phelps. Some members of the old Monteiro family lived there and gave the little street its name.
Monteiro Teixeira (José António)

José António Monteiro Teixeira came of an old and distinguished Madeiran family and was born in Funchal on 27 December 1795. He was the son of the wealthy landowner José António Teixeira and his wife Dona Ana dos Anjos Teixeira. They gave him a sound and varied education, which he completed over the years through constant contact with books, long travels and extended stays in the most civilised centres of Europe, and also through the close friendship he kept up with some of the most celebrated French writers of his day.

In 1808, despite the uncertainty of the times and the general alarm that the Peninsular Wars and grave political upheavals had spread throughout Europe, Monteiro Teixeira, then little more than twelve years old, was sent to a college in the city of Pau, in France. The college then enjoyed a worldwide reputation and had pupils from various foreign countries.

He himself tells us, in his flawless French, of the struggles between a misguided paternal love and the fervent wishes of his mother. She was a caring and devoted mother who, silencing the tenderness of her maternal heart, wanted above all to give her sons the education that they could in no way receive in the public or private schools of the capital of Madeira.
It is worth hearing his own eloquent words, which we translate below:

Yet, pressed ever harder by the tenacity of this maternal self-sacrifice, my father was bound to give way. Holding out in his last redoubts, he wished to attempt one final effort: to overcome this mother’s heart through the very excess of its own love. ‘So you want’, my father said to her one day when she was weeping at the mere thought of this separation, ‘to send your two sons to France, to that France which is at war with the whole world (it was in 1807), to throw them as prey to that Napoleon who respects nothing in his tyrannical fits?! Think of the bitterness you are preparing for yourself, of the tears you will still have to shed! You will never see them again; I have a presentiment of it.’

‘The answer was not long in coming, and it was impetuous. “Napoleon”, she said, “is not a wild beast, and the innocence of childhood commands respect even from the fiercest animals. On that score I am at ease. And even though I too have a presentiment that I shall never see them again (and as she said this, tears once more bedewed her cheeks), I would rather never embrace them again than see them, up there, badly brought up, uneducated, depraved and idle, like most of your friends’ sons, who dishonour them by their ignorance and bad conduct. The heart of a true mother knows how to sacrifice itself for the welfare of her children. I want for José and for António a liberal education and the lessons of the school of the world in an enlightened country such as France.” ‘And we left. ‘This mother’s heart was to be put to harsh trials! ... No news of us at all! They managed to learn only that we had arrived in France.
‘The war, ever more ferocious, had cut off all means of communication with this island.’

After their departure, two long years went by without the devoted parents having any news of their sons, because of the great turmoil raging throughout Europe as a result of the Napoleonic wars. The French invasions of Portuguese territory and France’s constant hostility towards Portugal made communications between the two countries even more difficult. It is easy to imagine the anguish suffered by those most loving parents, whose other children death had snatched away in the full bloom of life.

It was at this renowned college, where he remained until 1814, that his taste for the study of the French language was awakened. He came to know it thoroughly, to the point of writing it with the utmost correctness and elegance, according to the testimony of several notable French writers. It was also there that his poetic gift revealed itself very early, together with his marked inclination towards satire, which later made him one of the most distinguished disciples of Juvenal and Tolentino.

Having finished his schooling at the college, he stayed on in Paris for some years, devoting himself to various historical studies and to reading the French classics. At the same time he cultivated his literary inclinations with refined taste, above all poetry, in which satire and the epigram predominated. On his long visits to the French capital he formed friendships with some of the most illustrious men of letters of the day, who greatly admired the unsurpassed refinement of his manners and the flawless perfection with which he spoke and wrote French. Chateaubriand, a proud and not very approachable man, Béranger, Méry and above all Barthélemy felt a devoted admiration and the highest esteem for our illustrious fellow countryman; the last of these in particular remained on the most intimate terms with him for many years. In London too, which he visited frequently, he came to know closely some of the most notable men of the time, who likewise held Monteiro Teixeira in the regard due to the lofty qualities of his gifted mind and his uncommon learning. His close friendship with our great poet Castilho became widely known. In many places in his vast body of work Castilho refers to J. A. Monteiro Teixeira, not only with tender affection but also with the greatest admiration for the gifts of his cultivated intellect and his undeniable merits as a poet and man of letters. Our learned compatriot and great jurist Silvestre Pinheiro Ferreira, the distinguished man of letters and publicist José Liberato Freire de Carvalho and many others were also among Monteiro Teixeira’s intimates. If men of such intellectual stature, Portuguese and foreign alike, as well as others of the highest social rank, singled out our illustrious compatriot in this way – and at a time when the aristocracy of blood and of talent did not seek to place itself on a level with conceited mediocrity – we may well judge the merits of the man to whom such marks of regard, esteem and admiration were addressed.

After 14 years away in the leading cities of Europe, Monteiro Teixeira returned to his native land, where he devoted himself to literature and to his duties as consul of France on this island. He systematically refused every honour with which others sought to distinguish him, including a chair in parliament. Only to oblige some friends did he accept the post of councillor (*vereador*) of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), at a time when only men of proven worth or high social standing were called to such positions.

As France’s representative, he rendered that country such outstanding services that the French government on several occasions sought to reward him with various honours, among them the Legion of Honour. He always refused them, on the grounds that he had not accepted such honours from the government of his own country either. In 1840 the frigate *La Belle Poule* called at Madeira, carrying the French mission charged with bringing back to France the remains of Napoleon, which had lain buried on St Helena since 1821. Monteiro Teixeira showered the members of this mission with the most refined courtesies and the most charming kindnesses. The mission was headed by the Prince of Joinville and included the great General Bertrand, Bonaparte’s most faithful and devoted friend, who had accompanied him in all his battles, followed him into exile and stood by him to his last moments. Wishing to give the subject of our biography a token of its gratitude for his services and of the high esteem in which it held his personal qualities, the French government had a special gold medal struck and awarded it to him, since, as stated above, he had flatly refused to accept any decorations or honorific distinctions.

It remains for us to consider Monteiro Teixeira as a poet, which we shall do briefly so as not to make this article overly long. He cultivated above all the epigram, and his volumes of poetry written in Portuguese contain hardly any compositions outside that genre. He was a distinguished disciple of Nicolau Tolentino, and many of his verses rival the master’s finest compositions. We are convinced that had he published his books somewhere other than Madeira, he would have won great renown as a satirical poet, and his name would not lie buried in the almost complete oblivion in which it now rests.

Some believe – and this seems to have been Monteiro Teixeira’s own opinion – that his poems written in French surpass in thought and form those he wrote in his native tongue. They include compositions of various kinds, and particular mention is due to certain odes and epistles, which seem to have attained remarkable perfection both in metrical technique and in the beauty of their ideas. As for the correctness of the language, the authoritative opinion of distinguished Parisian writers is that Monteiro Teixeira wrote a pure French of rare elegance, which a foreigner could hardly surpass or even equal.

In 1848 and 1849 Monteiro Teixeira published the two volumes of the *Obras Poeticas*; in 1861, the volume *Oeuvres Poétiques*; and in 1871, the *Nouveau Récueil de poésies en français*. He also published a few pamphlets of verse. Although he wrote so great a number of poems, we are not aware that he left any prose compositions apart from the prefaces to his books.
He died there, in Funchal, on 31 May 1876, at the age of 80.
Mutual Aid Society Building
This was the name of an institution for poor and respectable widows, founded by João de Carvalhal in 1825 or 1826. The houses of the Monte Pio stood in the eastern part of Rua dos Netos.
Madeiran Mutual Aid Society

It was founded in 1900, and its first statutes were approved on 23 January of the same year. It is governed today by statutes approved by royal decree (*alvará*) of 17 January 1917; before that it had others, approved by royal decree of 31 May 1913.

Membership of the mutual-aid society is open only to persons aged from 16 to 55, of good moral and civil conduct, who may subscribe capital of 50 to 400 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis).
The Madeiran Mutual Aid Society (*Montepio Madeirense*) had 1134 members in October 1921, and since 1915 it has owned the building in which it is housed.
Funchal Maritime Mutual Aid Society

It was founded on the initiative of an employee of the Empresa dos Cabrestantes do Funchal, and its statutes were approved by royal decree (*alvará*) of 24 December 1901. Its main aims are to assist members in case of temporary illness, to arrange the defence of members when they are indicted in court, and to provide funerals for members who die. Membership is open to males employed in seafaring life who are over 12 and under 60 years of age and of good moral and civil conduct.
Medical assistance is also provided to a member’s close relatives when they live with him.
Montluc (Pedro Beltrão de)
Commander of the corsairs who sacked the city of Funchal in 1566. He died here as a result of a wound he received in one knee.
See Sack of Funchal by the French.
Monument to Câmara Pestana

– In the Jardim do Manicómio (‘asylum garden’) at São Gonçalo stands, on a marble column, the bronze bust of the distinguished bacteriologist and great martyr of science Luís da Câmara Pestana, whom we have already mentioned on p. 332 of this volume. The bust was erected in 1906.

On 15 November 1913 the physicians of Funchal had a commemorative plaque placed on the house where Dr Câmara Pestana was born, and the street was given the name of the illustrious bacteriologist. (See I-219.)
Monument to the Constitution of 1821

– This monument, which we have already discussed at some length (I-302), never rose above its foundations and was demolished on 1 September 1823. On that occasion a record (*auto*) was drawn up, stating that the following had been found in the foundations: a bottle containing seven issues of *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’); a manuscript recounting the history of the monument; and a stone box holding a silver one, which contained the record describing the ceremony of laying the monument’s foundation stone, together with a blue and white purse containing some silver coins and a medal of the same metal.
Monument to João Fernandes Vieira

– On the initiative of Dr Abel Capitolino Baptista, a modest monument to this illustrious Madeiran was raised in the former Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’), now Avenida Arriaga, and inaugurated on 11 May 1924. Nine years later the bust and its plinth were moved to the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’), where they stand at present.
Monument to João Gonçalves Zargo

– Homage should long ago have been paid to the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, worthily perpetuating his venerable memory among us. Although it can no longer be claimed today, as has so often been done, that he was the discoverer of the archipelago, it must be acknowledged that he was the most authoritative and fruitful promoter of the early colonisation of Madeira, to which his prestigious name remains indissolubly linked. His monument stands on Avenida Arriaga: a majestic bronze statue by the distinguished Madeiran sculptor Francisco Franco, formally inaugurated on 28 May 1934.
Monument to Our Lady of Peace

– On 1 November 1923 the foundation stone was laid of the grand monument erected at the Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), in honour of the Blessed Virgin (*Santíssima Virgem*) under the dedication of Nossa Senhora da Paz. It consists of an exquisite marble statue set on a plinth flanked by artistic bronze bas-reliefs, which allude to the traditional belief that the Blessed Virgin appeared on that very spot. Beside the monument stands a small and elegant chapel, where the holy sacrifice of the Mass and other acts of worship are frequently celebrated. The erection of this monument is due to the ardent zeal and untiring efforts of Father José Marques Jardim, who spared no sacrifice to give it the imposing and grand appearance that distinguishes it, even travelling abroad to collect donations to bring the work to completion. The formal inauguration, held with the greatest pomp and attended by thousands of people from every part of the island, took place under the presidency of the diocesan prelate on 14 August 1927.
Monument to the Count of Canavial
– The homage paid to this illustrious Madeiran has already been described (I-233).
Monument to Doctor Teles

– On 14 May 1939 a modest but meaningful and well-deserved monument was inaugurated with great solemnity in the gardens of the Poorhouse and Orphanage (*Asilo de Mendicidade e Órfãos*), to the memory of Dr Alexandre da Cunha Teles, who had rendered that charitable house and various welfare services the most valuable benefits through his devoted zeal, natural selflessness and boundless dedication.
See Commemorative monuments.
Monument to the Sacred Heart of Jesus

– Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos had a monument in praise of the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*) raised at Ponta do Garajau (‘tern point’), on a small height overlooking the sea at the western end of his lands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’). It is a fine and majestic statue, bearing witness to the religious piety of this illustrious Madeiran, a member of one of the oldest and noblest families of this island. The inauguration and blessing of the sacred image were held with the greatest solemnity on 30 October 1927.
Monument to the Aviators

– On 28 March 1921 the foundation stone was laid in the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’) of the monument commemorating the flight from Lisbon to Funchal made by the illustrious aviators Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral. The formal inauguration took place on 11 May 1921. See Jardim Municipal (II-182).
Monument to the dead of the Great War
– On 11 November 1935, in the Praça do Marquês de Pombal (‘Marquis of Pombal Square’), the foundation stone was laid of a small monument to those who died in the Great War.
Monument commemorating the Bombardment of Funchal
– On pp. 71 and 160 of volume I we have already given a brief account of this small monument, erected in the old Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery.
Monuments
Below we give a brief account of the few public monuments that exist here in Madeira.
National monuments

– Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) was the only building regarded as a National Monument (*monumento nacional*), although there were other buildings that ought to have been included in that category. The *Diário do Governo* of 24 September 1940 and of 18 August 1943 published the complete lists of the buildings classified as National Monuments and as ‘properties of public interest’ throughout our country. As regards this district, the following were declared National Monuments in addition to the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*): the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’), the church and outbuildings of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), the church of São Evangelista (the College) and the Customs House (*Casa da Alfândega*).

The following buildings count as ‘properties of public interest’: the houses of Dona Mécia, of the Consuls and of the Ornelas family, and the bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*) with its adjoining chapel; the chapels of Incarnação, São Paulo, Nazaré and Espírito Santo; and the forts of São João Baptista, the Ilhéu and São Tiago, all in the city of Funchal; the chapel of the Magi (*Reis Magos*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’); the parish church, the chapels of Milagres and São Roque, and the forts of Santo Amaro and São João in the parish of Machico; the parish churches of the parishes of Ponta do Sol, Ribeira Brava and Santa Cruz; and the chapel of the Mother of God (*Madre de Deus*) in the parish of Caniço (‘reed’).

The following works of art were also declared to be of public interest: a 16th-century baptismal font in the Mudéjar style, in the church of Ponta do Sol; and a wooden sculpture of the Adoration of the Magi, with thirteen figures in high relief, dating from the 16th century, in the chapel of the Magi at Estreito da Calheta.

The window of Columbus’s House, preserved in a private garden in the city of Funchal. It is a Manueline work, salvaged when the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had the property of the Fleming João Esmeraldo demolished, where Christopher Columbus is said to have lived.

Paintings on wood: the panel of St James, placed on the high altar of the church of Socorro (Our Lady of Succour), Funchal. The triptych in the sacristy of the same church. The panel of the Apostles, from the same sacristy, placed beneath the triptych. Three panels (St Paul, St Peter and St Andrew) preserved in the sacristy of the church of São Pedro (St Peter), Funchal. Three panels (the Annunciation, the Nativity, and St Anne and St Joachim) from the new church of São Martinho, Funchal (placed in a chapel on the Epistle side). A panel (emblem of Christ) from the private chapel of Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*), Funchal. A triptych (the Deposition from the Cross) from the church of Ribeira Brava, on the left side wall of the chancel. A panel (the Adoration of the Magi) on the left side wall of the nave of the same church. The panel of Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*) on the altar of the same name in Funchal Cathedral (the Sé).
Moquet
