A traveller, probably English, who visited Madeira in 1601. He wrote a work about this island which we have not seen and whose title is unknown to us.
Residences of Zarco

Pinpointing the places where João Gonçalves Zarco built his dwelling houses is certainly not essential to the history of Madeira, nor is it a central point of inquiry for the biography of the illustrious navigator and coloniser of our archipelago. Even so, there is some interest in knowing with complete accuracy where he made his home and where he spent the three or four decades of his long stay on this island. These places deserve from the public authorities, and especially from the administrative bodies based in Funchal, the respect and veneration that are everywhere paid to the objects and things closely bound up with the lives of great men. To identify with absolute precision the buildings and grounds most intimately connected with his life is to awaken in Madeirans the veneration owed to his memory, and to encourage generous initiatives that aim to perpetuate, worthily and here among us, that same glorious and unforgettable memory.

The historian of the islands relates: ‘. . . Captain João Gonçalves Zarco... sheltering the ships by the islets that lie off the cape (*cabo*) of this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish), because there was a fine cove there, resolved to build his wooden dwelling on land, which he at once built right beside the sea on a high spot, where the captain’s wife (*capitoa*, wife of the captain-donatary) Constança Rodrigues later founded a church of St Catherine.’ This was Zarco’s first settlement, and the chapel that the navigator’s wife had built was also the first place of worship erected on Madeira. The small, primitive chapel underwent several rebuildings and repairs over the centuries; the present chapel is a building of the middle or end of the 17th century. It is nonetheless the only building in Funchal that truly recalls the discovery. As such, it ought to be religiously preserved. In its smallness, its modesty and its poverty, it commemorates the beginning of our brilliant maritime discoveries, and for Madeirans it stands, besides the discovery, for the start of the settlement and colonisation of this archipelago. The chapel still bears on the threshold of its portal the date 1425, which marks the year of the original construction. It was beside this small church that João Gonçalves Zarco had his first residence for some years, built perhaps of the rich, fragrant cedars that grew everywhere in dense forests. It was no doubt a more than modest and uncomfortable dwelling, of a single storey and stripped of all architectural display, as were all the earliest houses built here. We read somewhere that only later did a man named João Manuel build in the Campo do Duque (‘duke’s field’) the first two-storey house, made of dressed cedar wood, which caused no small wonder at the time.

From the solitary retreat of Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’) – for the first and densest core of population, with its houses, took shape on the left bank of the easternmost stream (*ribeira*) of Funchal – Zarco directed the first work of colonisation and laid the foundations of the future town (*vila*), which progressed rapidly and grew extraordinarily even in his lifetime. There he would dream of the progress of the captaincy of which he was donatary (*donatário*), and of the rise of the house he had founded, glimpsing in the near future the honours and privileges that would be heaped upon his descendants and successors. Perhaps he had guessed that the monarch would reward him with the marks of nobility and the use of a coat of arms, already seeing his grandsons’ patents of nobility adorned with the coronet of count and of grandees of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), in homage to the services rendered by their grandfather. . .

A few years later Zargo moved his residence to the left bank of the stream, at the foot of the hill later known as Pico dos Frias (‘the Frias’ peak’), close to the chapel he had built there with the dedication to St Paul. This is said to have been the first stone-built dwelling house to be raised in Funchal. In this vicinity the first hospital was built, on land donated by Gonçalves Zargo in 1454. It operated there for some years, until it moved to the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes.

João Gonçalves Zargo does not seem to have stayed very long in his first two residences. He settled for good, and spent the greater part of his life, in the immediate vicinity of the spot where he built the church of Conceição de Cima. An old manuscript says: ‘he resolved also to build a dwelling for himself, as he did, on a height above the valley of Funchal: and directly opposite, a church of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) as a family vault for himself and his kin, which they began to call Nossa Senhora de Cima, because it was founded on a stump of cliff at the foot of a peak’. It is in this church, which later took the name of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), that the mortal remains of the illustrious navigator lie, and it was surely in the dwelling houses he built nearby that he ended his earthly career. We read in the manuscript already cited: ‘the great Gonçalves Zargo reached such old age that he had himself carried in men’s arms to be set in the sun, which greatly invigorated him. From there he disposed the affairs of his jurisdiction, governing and administering justice with his understanding whole, never suffering the feebleness of a decrepit man’.

On the strength of various documents that we have examined closely, we have been able to establish, for the first time, that Gonçalves Zargo’s old residence corresponds to the former manor house of the Lomelino entailed estate holders (*morgados*), which today still bears the name of Quinta das Cruzes (‘estate of the crosses’). Over the centuries, however, it has undergone such profound alterations that at present nothing of the original building is likely to remain.

It seems that this old and noble residence remained in the possession of his descendants. It is certain that a century after his death it belonged to his grandson Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, who was married to Dona Joana de Eça, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine. In 1575 it was in the usufruct and possession of a grandson of this couple, also named Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, who by public deed of 16 September of that year sold it to his close kinsman Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, grandson of João Gonçalves Zargo. It was this Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara who was governing the captaincy of Funchal, in the absence of his nephew João Gonçalves da Câmara, the sixth donatary (*donatário*), when in 1566 this city was attacked by French corsairs, who carried out a terrible sack here and massacred some three hundred people. Gaspar Frutuoso stated in 1590 that Gonçalves da Câmara lived near the convent of the Holy Cross (*Santa Cruz*) ‘in a great and sumptuous palace’.

This house passed into the possession of a daughter of Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara, named Dona Joana de Noronha, and then to her son António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, who owned it in 1624. At the end of the 17th century it belonged to Francisco Esmeraldo Henriques, who founded there the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*). The date 1692 is still visible at the top of its doorway, but the deed of grant dates from 1695, and it was in that year that religious worship began there. In this chapel there is a marble burial vault said to hold the mortal remains of Urbano Lomelino, founder of the convent that once stood in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and one of the founders of the Lomelino family on this island. The house at Cruzes was incorporated into the entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) of this important entailed estate (*morgadio*), probably through marriage, in a year we cannot determine. It remained in this family until our own day, and a few years ago became the property of the barons of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’).

This is a fitting moment to make special mention of the two-handed sword (*montante*) of João Gonçalves Zargo, which was always kept in this house. A constant tradition, handed down from generation to generation within the family that owned it, holds beyond doubt that it belonged to the illustrious coloniser. It was always regarded as such, and the deep veneration paid to that relic there at all times further confirms the truth of its origin. It is an old weapon, made to be wielded with both hands, and not remarkable for the fineness of its workmanship. It certainly has no intrinsic or artistic value, but it is worth a great deal for its five hundred and more years of existence and, above all, for having belonged to the great navigator who colonised this archipelago. It is perhaps the sword that Gonçalves Zargo wielded in Morocco in his charges against the Moors, winning fame as a brave and daring knight. This venerable relic is in this city in the hands of a foreigner, who keeps it with the esteem it truly deserves. It ought, however, to be in the possession of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this city. It is the duty of this administrative body to arrange its acquisition and keep it reverently in its archives until it can take its worthy place in the museum of art and antiquities that must one day be founded in this city (1921).
The two-handed sword attributed to João Gonçalves Zargo is today in the Municipal Museum.
Morais

This family surname derives from João de Morais, one of the first settlers of Madeira, who lived in Machico, where he held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in its fields. His eldest son, Sebastião de Morais the Elder, proved his nobility in 1508, according to the annotator of the *Saudades*.
Morais (Dom Sebastião de)

Early Portuguese colonisation in the lands discovered or occupied by conquest went hand in hand with the evangelising work of Catholic missionaries, who contributed so much to consolidating our colonial rule and to widening our sphere of action in infidel countries. From the outset it became imperative to create dioceses in the distant lands of the East. One of them, at the ends of the earth, was established in Japan, a country which in the 16th century was known in Europe only through mystery, legend and terror.

The first bishop appointed to the new diocese was the Madeiran Sebastião de Morais. He was born in Funchal in 1534 and in 1550 entered the Society of Jesus, where he stood out for his talents and exemplary conduct. He held the highest offices in his order, including those of provincial of Portugal and visitor (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) of the provinces of Rome and Milan.

He was charged with escorting Princess Dona Maria, granddaughter of Manuel I, to Italy, and in that country he held important posts at the instance of the Pope and of the general of his order. On 19 February 1587 Sixtus V confirmed him as bishop of Funai, the see of the first diocese created in Japan. He never took up the office, however, because he died in Mozambique on 19 August 1588 while travelling to his bishopric.

He wrote the work *Vita e morte della Serenissima Maria di Portogallo Principessa di Parma e Piacensia*, published in Bologna in 1578, of which editions were later printed in Rome and Madrid. He also published a volume on theological questions.
Morais (Father Luís de)

Diogo Barbosa Machado states that Father Luís de Morais, a Jesuit, was a native of this island and that he died in 1622. He wrote the *Pregaçam da Beatificação de São Francisco Xavier*, which is included in the *Relação das Festas*, published in 1621.
Strawberry plant (Fragaria vesca)

A member of the rose family (Rosaceae), growing wild and cultivated in Madeira. The strawberries produced in kitchen gardens are large and highly prized; those from the mountains are small but tasty. The stoloniferous rhizomes of the strawberry plant are used in infusion against jaundice.
Morávia (Valentim de)
See Fernandes (Valentim) (II-16).
Bats

Mammals of the order Chiroptera, of which two species are known in the archipelago: *Vesperugo madeirensis*, of Madeira and the Canary Islands, and *V. maurus*, a European species. Bats are insectivorous and come out only at night, spending the day hidden in dark places, hanging by their hind limbs.
*Vesperugo maurus* is a larger and more robust animal than *V. madeirensis*, as the specimens in the Seminary Museum (*Museu do Seminário*) show.
Moreão
This name is given to *Muraena unicolor* and *Cynaphobranchus pinnatus*. The second of these fishes is the *moreão de fundura*, or *de natura*, of Madeiran fishermen.
Morays

Fishes of the family Muraenidae. Known in Madeira are *Muraena helena* (*moreia pintada*, spotted moray), mottled with yellow; *M. anatina* (*moreia serpente*, serpent moray), also with yellow spots; and *M. augusti* (*moreia preta*, black moray). The first of these species lives in shallow waters; the second and third near the coast.
Morena (Porto or Portinho da)
A small landing place to the south-south-west of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Moreno

An inhabited and picturesque locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), where there is a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Remedies (*Nossa Senhora dos Remédios*). It was founded in 1690 by Canon Manuel Ferreira Teixeira and incorporated into the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Barreto family of Santa Cruz; its owner today is Dr Remígio Barreto. This locality is also known as Vale do Moreno.
Morgado Esmeraldo (road)

It links the church of São Martinho (St Martin of Tours) with the locality (*sítio*) of Pilar (‘pillar’). The *quinta* (country estate) at the northern end of the road that bears its name belonged to the Esmeraldo entailed estate (*morgadio*).
Entails
See Entails and Chantries.
Mortality
See Diseases.
Flies

Several species of Diptera are known by this name. The commonest is *Musca domestica*, a troublesome insect that lives mainly in and around dwellings, but whose larvae are found in dunghills and wherever there is manure. The blowfly (*Calliphora erythrocephala*) is also common, and the greenbottles (*Lucilia Caesar* and *L. sericata*) appear on trees, on human and animal excrement, etc. It is a fly of the genus *Hypoderma* that, by laying its eggs under the skin of cattle, causes through its larvae the tumours seen fairly often in these animals; the larvae are known in Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) as *berros*.
Mosquitoes

Insects of the order Diptera, some of them very abundant. The mosquito that seems commonest in Madeira is *Culex longiareolatus*, which lives near wells and tanks, where its larvae breed. It sometimes enters bedrooms, and its buzzing is quite a nuisance. *Culex pipiens* has been recorded on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), but not on Madeira.
The bite of *Culex longiareolatus* causes itching and sometimes a passing oedema.
Mustard

Two crucifers are known by this name in Madeira: *Brassica Sinapistrum* and *B. nigra*. It is the latter species that produces the seeds whose flour is used to prepare mustard plasters. *B. nigra* has siliques with 1-nerved valves; *B. Sinapistrum* has siliques with 3–5-nerved valves. Both species grow wild and are frequent in Madeira. Mustard used as a condiment comes mainly from *Sinapis alba*, a very rare species in Madeira.
New Convent

This is the building of the present Diocesan Seminary. (1921). The annotator of the *Saudades* says that it was an undertaking of Father Manuel Afonso Rocha, begun around 1654 and intended for nuns, but that it was never completed. In an old manuscript we found some further detailed references to this projected convent, which we reproduce below.

On 17 December 1638 Canon Manuel Afonso Rocha, confined to his bed by a serious illness, summoned a notary and also requested the presence of the diocesan prelate, Dom Jerónimo Fernando. He declared that he had begun a monastery, comprising houses, workshops, a church and a choir, under the dedication of São José (St Joseph), intended for monks or nuns on condition that certain Masses and offices were celebrated. As he had not yet completed it, he entrusted its government and administration to the protection of the same prelate and his successors. He asked them only to apply it to that purpose or to a *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) for ladies or women of quality; should that not be possible, the monastery with its church and houses was to be given to virtuous mendicant friars or to other religious who might render greater service to God there. Canon Rocha’s request and conditions were accepted, but because income was scarce the building was never put to the use its founder had intended for it. We also believe that the planned works were never completed, for it seems to us that there was never a church and choir there, but only a small chantry (capela) inside the house. In 1647 the diocesan prelate authorised the founder’s nephews, Canon António Espranger Rocha and his brother Father Inacio Espranger, together with some of their sisters, to live in the building. After their deaths the house was occupied by a nephew of theirs, Canon António Espranger, who died in 1691.

Some years later, around 1697, the Diocesan Seminary was installed there; until then it had operated beside the bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*). The earthquake of 1748 left the house of the New Convent (*Mosteiro Novo*) badly damaged, and it had to be abandoned. After suitable repairs, it served once more as the seminary from around 1760. In 1788 the Diocesan Seminary was transferred to the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), and from there it returned to the New Convent in 1801, when Madeira was occupied by British troops. It remained there until 1909, when it was installed in the spacious building erected in the convent grounds of the convent of the Incarnation. The seminary of this diocese was suppressed by the decree of 20 April 1911, but it has continued to operate since that year, without official status, in the old house in Rua do Mosteiro Novo. (1921).
See Diocesan Seminary.
Mota Freitas (Carlos Elói)

He was born in this city on 1 December 1894 and completed the course at the Naval School in 1917. As a naval midshipman, he was serving in the crew of the minesweeper *Augusto Castilho*, which was escorting the steamer *São Miguel* on a voyage from Madeira to the Azores, when the minesweeper was treacherously attacked and sunk by a German submarine on 14 October 1918. Among those who died were her brave commander and our fellow Madeiran Mota Freitas. The heroic resistance of the *Augusto de Castilho* shielded the steamer *São Miguel* from the German submarine’s onslaught, and the Portuguese steamer was saved with all her crew and passengers. Anyone wishing to learn more about this terrible tragedy should read the interesting pamphlet *200 milhas a remos*, written by Lieutenant Luís José Simões, an eyewitness to all those events. Another of our fellow Madeirans, Samuel da Conceição Vieira, then a naval midshipman, was among the survivors of the German submarine’s attack.

The government awarded Midshipman Mota e Freitas the War Cross, 1st Class, and the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), at its meeting of 8 May 1919, resolved to give his name to the former Travessa da Sacristia in Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). In October 1921 a committee was formed with the aim of erecting a modest monument to Midshipman Mota e Freitas; on the same occasion the insignia of the War Cross, awarded to him after his death, were put on display at the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*).
Mota Prego (João da)

An agronomist who lived for some time in Funchal. He wrote a valuable article on the agriculture, industry and trade of Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), in vol. I, pp. 377–400, of *Notas sobre Portugal*, a book that was shown at the national exhibition in Rio de Janeiro in 1908.
Popular riots

It is universally acknowledged that the people of this archipelago are essentially peaceful and orderly by nature. The great majority are devoted to farming, which in this region is extremely hard and toilsome because of the peculiar nature of the terrain. They labour from the first light of dawn until the shadows of night fall, generally untroubled and indifferent to everything but the ceaseless toil of their hard-working lives.

Whether they live in straitened circumstances or in reasonable comfort, their lives pass serenely and quietly, and no spirit of insubordination or revolt disturbs the peace they calmly enjoy. This statement should not lead one to conclude that the proverbial calm reigning among the Madeiran family has never been broken and has never burst violently into the public square. This has been witnessed only rarely, and always very briefly, and only when some vile speculators, for shameful ends, have tried to exploit the good faith or excessive credulity of populations steeped in ignorance, error and superstition.

One of the earliest popular movements known to us is the uprising of the inhabitants of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) who, in the year 1533, roused to fanaticism by the self-styled prophets Fernão Bravo and Filipa Nunes, committed highly reprehensible excesses. We shall give a fuller account of these in the article Prophets in this *Elucidário*.

A few days after the government of John IV was proclaimed on this island (see Restoration of Madeira), events of considerable gravity took place, disturbing public order. We find their main episodes narrated as follows in an old manuscript:

‘On 25 January 1641 the people went in a crowd to the Council and threw out the judge Luís Fernandes de Oliveira, because he was a Castilian. They appointed a new judge, a municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*), a councillor (*vereador*) and a market inspector (*almotacel*). From there they went to the house of Paio Rodrigues Pais da Cunha, clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*), who had been suspended for misconduct, reinstated him in his office and threw out the deputy holder, Manuel Teixeira Pereira. A certain Manuel da Ceia and a nephew of his, who had indiscreetly spoken about the new tax, would hardly have escaped death and the fury of the people but for the efforts of the governor, the bishop and the cathedral chapter, whom the people respected. From here the rioting people went on to the customs house, threw out the superintendent (*provedor*) Manuel Vicente Cardoso and put in his place João Rodrigues de Teive. He lived at Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), and they went there to fetch him; when he tried to slip away as they passed the church, the crowd, on the pretext of saying a prayer, would not let him. Thus brought to the customs house, he was acclaimed superintendent by the people, with the threat that if he refused he would be killed by them on the spot. The doorkeeper, because he had kept the doors shut, was in danger of his life. In this popular commotion great help came from the good name of Dom António Fernandes, the bishop’s nephew and an officer of the Council, and the regard in which the people held him, and above all from the prelate, who knew how to calm the people with prudence and save the lives of those pointed out as their persecutors. As soon as they had taken an inventory of the superintendent’s property, the people grew quiet, and of this whole event the necessary records and entries were made, as is recorded in Book 4, fol. 202.’ John IV ordered an official inquiry into these events and the punishment of those who had shown disrespect to the superintendent Vicente Cardoso, though it is not known whether any penalty was actually imposed on them.

The governor and captain-general of Madeira, Dom Francisco de Mascarenhas, who took office on 28 November 1665, had earned the ill will of the clergy and above all of the nobility, for reasons that have still not been properly established. The result was the deplorable popular uprising that broke out in Funchal on 18 September 1668.

Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo states that the revolt was led by the dean, Dr Pedro Moreira, and that the clergy had played a very active part in it. However, the judicial inquiry (*devassa*) conducted by the high court judge (*desembargador*) João de Moura Coutinho, an investigator sent expressly to this island by the government on the mainland, ended in sentences of penal exile (degredo), together with heavy fines, for many Madeiran *fidalgos* (noblemen of the lesser nobility) and three slaves. Not a single churchman was among those condemned, not even Dr Pedro Moreira himself.

It seems that the governor and captain-general had treated the clergy and nobility of this island with scant consideration, curtailing many privileges which they perhaps enjoyed improperly but to which they believed they had an undeniable right. This opened a serious conflict with the most disastrous consequences. Dom Francisco de Mascarenhas may perhaps have exceeded the powers the law gave him; he may have been harsh in his manner and his dealings with the fidalgos and some members of the clergy, and may even have held their prerogatives and exemptions in lofty contempt. But there is no doubt that the instigators of the uprising behaved in an unspeakable manner, and posterity cannot absolve them of what they did in resorting to violence and sanctioning the excesses then committed in this city.

On 18 September 1668 the governor, Dom Francisco de Mascarenhas, accompanied by the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), was on his way to the country house that the Jesuits owned in the locality (*sítio*) of Pico do Cardo (‘thistle peak’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), which is still known today as Quinta dos Padres (‘the priests’ estate’). On reaching the locality of Água de Mel (‘honey water’), where the manor house of the holders of the Bettencourt and Sá Machado entail (*morgado*) stood, he was confronted by a group of armed men, among them several members of that family. They violently assaulted the governor and wounded the *juiz de fora* with a sword cut.

Dom Francisco de Mascarenhas was thrown into a squalid dungeon in the company of a villainous mulatto who had once served as an executioner. From there he was taken to the prison of the Pico fortress (*Fortaleza do Pico*), where he suffered the grossest insults and humiliations at the hands of his gaoler, Dom João Heredia, and another fidalgo, who thus took ignoble revenge for the offences they supposed they had received. He was then put aboard a small cargo ship, the same train of insults following him all the way to embarkation, and the vessel set him ashore in Galicia.

The rioters released the prisoners and, gathering some of the townspeople, roamed the city committing many disorders and excesses, while the military, perhaps in league with the movement, made no attempt to put a stop to such outrages. A curious detail: the councillor (*vereador*) António Correia Henriques was hanged in effigy at his own door, after they had searched every room of his house for him in vain.

Meanwhile, they appointed the holder of the entail Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos as interim governor, and he gave no thought to punishing the guilty. He sent the fidalgo Gaspar Berenguer to Lisbon to inform the government on the mainland of what had happened here. On his return to Madeira Berenguer was greeted with great rejoicing, for he brought news that the higher authorities had approved everything done during the uprising.

Some time later the high court judge Dr João de Moura Coutinho arrived in Madeira, charged with conducting a rigorous official inquiry into those very grave events. He had to contend with serious obstacles: threats, the bribing of witnesses – every means was brought into play. The judge departed, and months later the sentence was published. Dom Gaspar de Sá, Dom José de Sá, Dom Francisco de Sá, Rui Dias de Aguiar, João Machado and Albano Veloso, all fidalgos, were condemned to perpetual penal exile in Angola and to pay several thousand *cruzados* each to the plaintiff, Dom Francisco de Mascarenhas, and towards the costs of the case. José Machado de Miranda and João Vieira Pita were sentenced to five years’ exile in Angola, and three slaves to public flogging and to serve for life in the galleys.

It caused surprise that the holder of the entail Aires de Ornelas managed to clear himself and suffered no penalty at all, although he was prosecuted, and that Dr Pedro Moreira and other priests were not caught in the net of the rigorous judicial inquiry that was held.
This curious episode in Madeiran history has still not been sufficiently clarified as regards its origins and the responsibilities involved.
In this year there were riots in the towns of Calheta, Ponta do Sol and São Vicente over a proposed grant of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’).

In the article Constitution of 1821 (Vol. I, p. 301) we have already given a brief account of the events that took place in this city when that Constitution was proclaimed. See also the article on the market and chapel of St Sebastian (*São Sebastião*).

In October and November of this year there were several popular riots in the city of Funchal, stirred up by officers and soldiers of the 2nd and 13th Infantry Regiments (*infantaria n.° 2 e 13*) after some men of the latter regiment were poisoned. In their fury, the soldiers tried to force their way into the Governor’s Palace to seize the aide-de-camp José Joaquim Januário Lopes and murder him.

From the revolution of 1820 until the establishment of constitutional government in 1834 – a period in which political struggles and civil war brought such grave upheaval to the Portuguese family – there were at times various disturbances and breaches of public order on this island. They had no very dire consequences, although feelings ran extremely high and the gravest events were expected. Although constitutional government was proclaimed in this city on 5 June 1834 without the slightest disturbance of order, it is certain that in several parishes (*freguesias*) the discontent of many found expression in acts of violence. The most important of these events took place at Calheta, as already described in the article devoted to that parish (see Vol. I, p. 190). We may add that seven individuals, besides Father Rodrigues Pestana, were sentenced to perpetual penal exile (degredo) in Angola.

Very sad events occurred in this year, caused by the Calvinist propaganda of Dr Roberto Kalley, as may be seen at greater length in the article we devote in this volume to that illustrious Scottish physician.

In the article Governing Board of Madeira in 1847 we have already dealt at some length with the events that occurred in Madeira when the echoes of what unfolded in our country after the Maria da Fonte revolution reached us here.

In our political history, the name Janeirinha was given to the popular revolt that broke out in Lisbon and Porto in January 1868 in protest against the law of 10 June 1867, which had created the consumption tax and caused such great indignation throughout the country. For this reason the ministry headed by Joaquim António de Aguiar resigned; its members had included men of the stature of Martens Ferrão, Fontes Pereira de Melo, Andrade Corvo, Casal Ribeiro and Barjona de Freitas. Its political opponents had stirred up all the fury of the people against it, waving the notorious consumption law, which never came into force, as their banner of war. Our distinguished fellow Madeiran Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos followed the ministry's policy and belonged to the Historic Party, which at that moment was struggling against the great tide of the Janeirinha parties, backed by the ministry that had then come to power under the presidency of the Count of Ávila, later Duke of Ávila e Bolama.

The supporters of the two political factions were known as *fusionistas* and *populares*. In Madeira, for reasons we cannot clearly identify, the animosity between these party groups was intense when, on 8 March 1868, the Portuguese steamer *Bengo* anchored in our harbour. Among its passengers was our fellow Madeiran Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, later viscount of Nogueiras. He had come to visit his illustrious family and to pursue his candidacy as deputy for this island, as a member of the Historic Party, or Fusion.

Of the events that took place in this archipelago in the third quarter of the 19th century, two remained indelibly engraved in the memory of contemporaries and were even passed on to later generations: the cholera epidemic of 1856 and the Pedrada movement of 8 March 1868. Seen from a distance and freed of the base passions that gave rise to it, this last episode surprises us greatly today: a mere question of electoral politics drove a population to the most deplorable excesses, with several deaths and the violent prevention of Jacinto de Sant'Ana's landing.

And yet this fellow Madeiran of ours had always behaved correctly towards all Madeirans and had never contributed to harming, morally or materially, the land of his birth. Indeed, as this island's representative in parliament across three legislatures, he had championed the most vital questions of this archipelago disinterestedly and with the purest zeal. Nothing in his conduct as deputy and politician could justify, or even explain, the strange reception he met here on 8 March 1868. He simply belonged to a political camp opposed to the one that then held the greatest sway and influence on this island, and he had had the courage to put his name forward to the popular vote and to come in person to argue the case for his candidacy.

His arrival in Madeira was known in advance. When news began to spread through the city that Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos was aboard a steamer lying in the harbour, a huge crowd, mainly of the lower classes, gradually occupied part of the beach and the surroundings of the customs house, until before long it became impossible to pass. The crowd's aim was to prevent Jacinto de Sant'Ana from landing, which posed not the slightest difficulty, since it had within reach a considerable number of projectiles that were easy and quick to throw – stones.

Sant'Ana, a brave man who had been the hero of many perilous adventures, tried to land despite the hostile attitude of the mob. Faced with the shower of stones filling the air, however, he had to give way, and he also followed the prudent advice of some of the people around him. He then went aboard the sailing ship *Galgo*, which carried cargo between Lisbon and Madeira. Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos's life was in imminent danger on this occasion, and the long-established and important merchant of our town João de Freitas Martins, better known as Papinho, did much to shelter him from the savage fury of the unbridled mob.

Tempers were already running high even before Sant'Ana's arrival, and there had been minor disturbances of public order, forewarnings of what might follow. With feelings inflamed by his arrival, the crowd broke into open violence, and several people were injured by the hail of stones hurled wildly from all sides. The armed forces had to intervene and, finding themselves defied by the crowd, resorted to their carbines, and some men of the people fell, shot through by the bullets. The civil governor at the time was our fellow Madeiran Dom João Frederico da Câmara Leme, a major of the 12th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry). Despite the prestige and popularity he enjoyed, his presence alone could not restrain the rioters, and the intervention of the public force was absolutely necessary to contain them and put an end to the excesses they were committing.

In the midst of the fighting, someone had the happy idea of faking a fire in Rua das Queimadas de Baixo by setting light to a straw mattress. The bells rang out urgently in alarm, and a considerable part of the crowd occupying the customs house courtyard and its surroundings rushed to the scene of the fire. Shortly afterwards the rest dispersed, thus ending the sad and regrettable episode that became known as the riot, or uprising, of the Pedrada.

Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos left for Lisbon and was shortly afterwards elected deputy for another constituency. In *Revolução de Setembro* he published a series of articles under the title *Cartas ao conde de Avila sobre matérias eleitorais da Ilha da Madeira*, which we have not seen, but which we are told contain exceptionally interesting material for the history of the events they deal with.

On 1 May of this year there were serious disturbances in the town (*vila*) of Machico during the elections of deputies held there, and armed force had to intervene. The townspeople defied the military detachment stationed in the town, which opened fire on the crowd inside the parish church, killing several people.

Other disturbances were also stirred up by the Popular Party, which, although in opposition, held sway on the island in 1870. The late Dr Joaquim Ricardo da Trindade e Vasconcelos, a Fusionist, was seized at Pontinha by members of the public when he landed in Funchal on his way from Machico. He was taken to the former Praça da Constituição, where he would have been murdered but for the intervention of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, one of the most prestigious figures of the Popular Party. The funeral of one of the victims of the disturbances in that town served as a pretext for fresh demonstrations hostile to the government, which neither the authorities nor the police sought to prevent.

The events at Machico caused a great sensation, not only in Madeira but also on the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and the government of the day was fiercely attacked in parliament and in the Lisbon press.

On 29 June 1884 several popular disturbances broke out at a number of polling stations or in their vicinity. The breakdown of public order was most serious in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, where it had the most tragic consequences: several local people were killed, cut down by the bullets of the armed forces. The candidate for deputy was Dr Manuel de Arriaga, who failed to be elected. The republican press of Funchal, and above all that of Lisbon, covered the matter at length, and it echoed within the national parliament. In the judicial district (*comarca*) of Ponta do Sol, several legal proceedings were brought concerning the events in the parishes of Ribeira Brava and Ponta do Sol. Drs Manuel de Arriaga and José de Castro came to this island to defend their fellow party members involved in these cases, and stayed here for some time. Under the title *Victimas d'El-Rei*, Dr José de Castro published a pamphlet of 83 pages recounting the most notable episodes and incidents of these trials. The killings at Ribeira Brava caused an extraordinary sensation.

The few months of 1887 and 1888 were a truly calamitous period for this archipelago. Serious breaches of public order took place on the pretext of the supposed organisation of the parish councils (*juntas de paróquia*): the most reprehensible acts of violence were committed, and alarm and terror spread through every parish on this island. Among the people, the movement became known as the *Parreca* (popular name for the 1887 parish councils and the riots against them). We have already dealt with it in the article Parish Councils, to which we refer the reader.

On 22 May, on the arrival of the steamer *Funchal*, riots broke out at the Entrada da Cidade, as the people sought to prevent the landing of passengers from Lisbon, where cholera was said to be raging. The troops and the police were stoned, and some of the passengers who tried to land at the quay at the Entrada da Cidade were also injured.

At the end of November 1905 a case of suspected disease appeared in the household of Leopoldo Cabral, who lived in Rua dos Ferreiros in this city, affecting a member of his family. The patient and the rest of the family were promptly removed to the Lazareto of ‘Gonçalo Aires’, which had been turned into an isolation hospital. Other people were also taken there. To stop the disease from spreading, complete isolation was certainly necessary, but it seems to have been applied with excessive rigour, if indeed there can be excess in adopting measures of this kind. From the outset the most improbable and incredible rumours began to spread among the population, arising largely from the strict isolation maintained at the Lazareto and the lack of news of the people held there. Popular imagination, aided by factional politics and an unscrupulous press, gave free rein to the most deplorable frenzy, conjuring up every sort of crime within the Lazareto, from the cruellest ill-treatment to outright murder! These rumours spread so widely, and these fanciful inventions grew so large in the public mind, that before long the great majority of the people of this island firmly believed that the isolation hospital had become a veritable public butcher’s shop (*açougue*) for human beings, far outdoing the bands of brigands that infested the passes of the Sierra Morena, Calabria and the Black Forest, of which certain more than doubtful narratives tell us with such horror.

It was undoubtedly a serious mistake, as everyone later acknowledged, to cut off all communication between those inside that enclosure and the rest of the population. The mistake was corrected, with no danger of contagion, but it was too late, and it was by then impossible to undo the deep impression that the alarming rumours had made. The wave of indignation, held back for some days, burst through the barriers that contained it and spilled violently into the public square.

On 7 January 1906, at about 11 in the morning, an enormous mass of townspeople, followed by some men of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.° 27*), set off for the Lazareto in a plainly hostile mood, ready to commit the worst excesses. Through inexcusable lack of foresight the entrances to the Lazareto had been left without any defence, so the rioting mob easily broke into the enclosure and committed the greatest and most deplorable acts of vandalism. Everything there was completely destroyed: furniture, kitchen equipment, pharmacy, surgical instruments, linen, machines, provisions etc. Nothing escaped the insane fury of the attackers. The buildings themselves suffered serious damage: every windowpane was broken, the doors were destroyed and even the floors bear clear traces of the rioters’ rage.

The people under observation in the refuge area were forced to leave it, and the crowd then invaded the treatment hospital, where there were five patients, some of them recovering. A carriage, escorted by a large number of townspeople, took the patients to their homes amid the most enthusiastic cheers along the way. The bulk of the crowd, which numbered about a thousand people on its return to the city, went by the Estrada do Conde de Carvalhal, fearing that troops sent out from the 27th Infantry barracks might surprise it on the road.

Some days earlier the Land Disinfection Station at Campo da Barca had been attacked by a large group of townspeople, who were driven back by the police and a detachment of infantry. There were also various disturbances at Bom Sucesso and in other localities, which foreshadowed the attack on the Lazareto.
On 10 January the cruiser *Dom Carlos* arrived in Funchal with an enlarged crew, to help the military forces stationed here maintain public order.

The clinical director of the ‘Gonçalo Aires’ isolation hospital was Dr António Balbino do Rego, who held the post of director of the Bacteriology and Hygiene Post in this city. It was against him that the wrath of the populace was chiefly roused, for they regarded him as the author of, or the person chiefly responsible for, the alleged crimes committed at the Lazareto. The hatred aroused here against Dr Balbino do Rego (see that entry) is truly incredible, given that it had no serious basis, and even today his name is cursed as though he had been some great scourge that had ravaged this island.

Besides numerous articles in the local press, the following pamphlets were published on this subject: *A Tragédia do Lazareto*, Funchal, 1906, 51 pp.; *A Peste bubonica na Madeira e as suas consequências*, notes by António Pedro Gomes, Lisbon, 1906, of which only one fascicle of 12 pp. appeared; *Um Ano Depois*, Porto, 1907, 63 pp.; and *Na Ilha da Madeira*, Porto, 1907, 117 pp., the last two by Dr António Balbino do Rego.

The popular muse gave free rein to its fertile inspiration, and countless pamphlets and broadsheets were published, in which lack of inspiration kept pace with faulty metre, and in which coarse language owed nothing to the lack of good sense and of the most elementary rules of grammar. (See Popular poetry.)

At the end of July 1921 the flour millers of Funchal decided to raise the price of flour to 1820, which meant that bread would go from 80 centavos, the price at which it was then being sold, to 1 escudo (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) per kilogram. A group of consumers therefore called a meeting in the Largo da Feira on 1 August, at which it was decided to close industrial and commercial establishments in protest at the unjustified rise in the price of this staple. From 1 to 3 August all establishments did indeed close, opening only in the morning, before 8 o’clock, so that the public could buy provisions. However, certain disorderly elements joined the strikers, and this led to some disturbances and riots. On the 3rd two millers were seized by the people; one of them was brought from Monte down to the city surrounded by a large crowd but protected by the police, which did not prevent him from being wounded in the head as he passed along the Rua de João Tavira on his way to the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence), where he was held in custody.

On 2 August the crowd broke into the house of the president of the Council and forced him to accompany them to the town hall to fix the price of bread. Several attempts were also made to seize the clerk of an English firm, who was held chiefly responsible for the proposed rise in the price of flour. To escape the fury of the people he hid at first in his employer’s house, and later left the island on a foreign steamer.

At first the authorities took no interest in the popular movement, but the events of the 3rd forced them to change their attitude and to order the police and the Republican Guard to keep order in the city. Once Funchal began to be properly patrolled on 4 August, the establishments reopened that same day, and the disturbances of the previous day were not repeated. Their only victims had been those whom the people, rightly or wrongly, considered responsible for the extortion that was being attempted against them.

The price of bread was not changed in August 1921, but in February of the following year the British flour mill succeeded in having it raised temporarily to 1 escudo, since it had begun selling flour at 1.10 escudos per kilogram.

A few days before the riots we have just described, others had taken place, prompted by the elections of deputies and senators at the Câmara de Lobos polling station. Captain Américo Olavo and Dr Manuel Augusto Martins, who had gone there to observe the electoral proceedings, were wounded. The riots took place on 11 July and were provoked by individuals from Funchal, with the aim of invalidating the vote in Câmara de Lobos, where the opposition could count on a large majority.

From 4 to 8 February 1931 Funchal saw disturbances of public order of the utmost gravity. They were caused by the promulgation of a decree that established a new cereals regime and restricted the free import of wheat and flour, thereby creating a ‘monopoly’ in so important a branch of the public food supply. The enforcement of the decree was suspended, but the rioters insisted on its outright repeal. Meanwhile, serious disorders broke out in various places, and for five or six days trade was completely paralysed: every shop stayed shut, and the public offices and schools were closed. On 6 February the riots took an alarming turn, with violent attacks on the Lavradores flour mill, on a large ‘wholesale’ house in Rua Cinco de Junho, on a bakery at Ponte de São João and on a shop in Rua da Alfândega, etc. etc., all of which were completely destroyed, the damage amounting to several thousand *contos* (one million réis) *de réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The police intervened; three members of the public died, and one member of the police force also lost his life. The infantry forces that left their barracks to restore order either would not or could not do so, and a large share of the responsibility for these deeply regrettable events came to be laid at their door.

The enforcement of a new decree, which created the Dairy Products Board (*Junta dos Lacticínios*) and regulated the distribution and sale of milk, aroused great indignation among the rural population. On 4 and 5 August 1936 it provoked the most serious disturbances of public order in various parts of the island; the intervention of the armed forces was required, and eight people of the popular classes died. Two warships came from Lisbon carrying contingents of troops and members of the investigative police, and a large-scale judicial inquiry (*devassa*) was held, in the course of which several hundred people were arrested. Of these, about fifty were sent to Cape Verde to be tried there. Today everyone acknowledges that the decree which had provoked these regrettable disorders contained provisions beneficial to cattle breeders and milk sellers.
Moura

António de Moura Rolim, says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo on p. 527 of the *Saudades*, is named in the roll of benefactors of the Holy House of Mercy (*Misericórdia*) of Funchal, soon after its foundation. The same work also records, on p. 851, that João de Moura Rolim founded the chantry (*capela*) of the Lord in the original church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major), where he had his tomb with this epitaph: ‘Tomb of João de Moura Rolim, founder of this chantry of the Most Holy Sacrament – 727.’
Moura (Dom Patrício Xavier de)

In volume XI of his dictionary *Portugal Antigo e Moderno*, on p. 872, Pinho Leal writes the following about José Joaquim Januário Lapa, 1st Viscount of Vila Nova de Ourém, which we transcribe word for word:

‘A remarkable thing happened between the 1st Viscount of Vila Nova de Ourém and Father Patrício de Moura e Brito, a native of Setúbal. When that titled gentleman, before he held his title, was living in Vila Franca, he was playing backgammon with the said priest, who was prior (title of the parish priest) there. The priest declared that he would inflict a *codilho* on Lapa, who for his part declared the contrary, adding that he would make that prior a bishop if he suffered a *codilho* at his hands and ever became a minister, though he said it in a tone of pure jest. Time passed, and Lapa, from the modest position he then held as administrator of the Lezírias do Tejo, rose in the social scale through his merits and the fortunes of politics, and became a minister of state. The prior of Vila Franca, following his movements, so to speak, and prompted by a happy presentiment, presented himself to the viscount as soon as he was appointed minister, congratulating him and claiming the fulfilment of the vow. The minister, who at first did not remember the vow, in the end recalled it perfectly, and gave the prior of Vila Franca the mitre of Cape Verde. Blessed *codilho*!’
This account is confirmed by the dean of the Cathedral (the Sé) of Cape Verde, Francisco Ferreira da Silva, who in his book *Diocese de Cabo Verde* adds the following interesting details.

‘Dom Friar Patrício Xavier de Moura was an Augustinian friar of the Graça, and while a brother (*freire*) of the Order he had been appointed by John VI canon of Bemposta (‘well placed’) and private chaplain to the Infanta Isabel Maria, after the king had heard the magnificent voice with which he was gifted. Being a legitimist, he withdrew to his native town, preaching from the pulpit until he was sent to serve as priest of the parish (*freguesia*) of Vila Franca de Xira. There he became acquainted with the Viscount of Villa Franca Nova de Ourém, who promised to make him a bishop when he became a minister, a vow that was kept. On leaving for Cape Verde he took with him Dom João de Noronha, already 70 years old, who had been presented as archdeacon, and three servants: Fernandes de Aguiar, who recently died in Cape Verde leaving a fortune of more than 80,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis); José Silvestre Teixeira, who did not live long; and José Maria Pinto, who at the age of 18 had been appointed to a canon’s place and remained in Cape Verde until 1880, leaving a respected name as a teacher. Dom Patrício, although more inclined to don the helmet and draw the sword than to put on the mitre and grasp the crosier, was a hard-working and zealous prelate. While he would rebuke in public and with asperity a servant who proposed a toast at a festive dinner without asking leave, and would order a priest who sat down in his presence without due reverence to stand up, he generously praised and rewarded those who did their duty and did not take such liberties. Barely restrained in his reprimands, he saw the dean of the Cathedral only once, for the dean never returned there while this prelate remained in the diocese.’ He established his residence on the island of Fogo, but made frequent and lengthy visits to the islands of Brava and Santiago. He fought battles with the governor-general, chiefly over the appointment of acting parish priests (*párocos encomendados*, appointed without tenure), and the government in mainland Portugal confirmed the prelate’s right to make such appointments. When a great food crisis struck the archipelago, he gave up in favour of the starving eighteen *contos* de réis of the mitre’s revenues that were due to him. He administered the bishopric of Cape Verde for about ten years and then, on account of illness, requested his presentation to the See of Funchal.

In July 1858 the prelate Dom Manuel Martins Manso left this diocese for Guarda, to which he had been transferred. On 20 April of the following year Pius IX confirmed the transfer of Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura from the bishopric of Cape Verde to the diocese of Funchal, and he took possession of the office by proxy on 28 May 1859. He arrived in Funchal on the 26th of the following August and made his solemn entry into the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) on the 18th of the next month, September.

Dom Patrício de Moura’s episcopate was not a happy one. The reasons given by the dean Ferreira da Silva – the prelate’s interference in local politics and the special fondness and favours he showed certain priests, to the detriment and disregard of others – raised great difficulties for him and created serious friction, which never entirely faded before his death. Less than a year after his arrival in the diocese, a 70-page pamphlet had already appeared under the title *Chronica do Bispado do Funchal nos primeiros seis meses de governo do Snr. D. Patrício Xavier de Moura*. It is a veritable indictment of the prelate’s episcopal administration, written with evident partiality and at times even with refined bad faith. Some turbulent members of the cathedral chapter (*cabido*) and certain dominant figures in local politics waged a spiteful and relentless war on Bishop Dom Patrício, which he bravely withstood despite his advanced age and well-known ailments. Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura was a prelate zealous not only for the integrity of the privileges and prerogatives of the Church, and especially for the observance of canonical discipline, but also for the propagation of Catholic doctrine, for the austere life of his clergy and for the exact fulfilment of ecclesiastical law.

During one of his absences from the island, the prelate appointed the Governing Board of the Bishopric (*Junta Governativa do Bispado*), to which we have referred elsewhere. By exceeding the powers conferred on it, this board drew the censure of the Holy See and prompted the publication of the pamphlet *Breves Reflexões acerca da circular de 26 de Janeiro de 1870 do presidente da Junta Governativa do Bispado do Funchal aos parochos desta diocese*.

In 1870 Dom Patrício de Moura asked for a coadjutor (*coadjutor*) and future successor, and in March 1871 the dean, Dr Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, was appointed titular bishop of Gerasa, with the right of succession to the diocese of Funchal.

Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura died on 19 September 1872 in the city of Lisbon, to which he had retired some years earlier, having handed over the administration of this bishopric to his successor, Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos.
Mourão Pita (Dr César Augusto)

He was born in the city of Lisbon on 21 March 1837, the son of Miguel Pinto da Silva Mourão and Dona Joana Marques. He was only three months old when the distinguished physician Dr António da Luz Pita adopted him as his son, at the time when, accompanied by his parents, he was passing through the port of Funchal on his way to Africa. He graduated in medicine from the faculty of Montpellier, defending the thesis *Du Climat de Madère...*, which he published in 1859 in a volume of 262 pp. On the same subject, and under the title *Madère, Station Médicale fixe...*, he published a pamphlet of 101 pp. in Paris in 1889. He was an army doctor, reaching the rank of brigade surgeon, and for many years held the post of clinical director of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*). He served as French consular agent on this island, as representative (*procurador*) to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), and on other public service commissions. He died in Funchal on 22 May 1906.

A volume of 234 pp. entitled *Os Acontecimentos do Theatro do Príncipe Real. Historia completa do infame trama urdido... contra João Radich* was published in Lisbon in 1870, in which the name of Dr César Mourão Pita features prominently.
Mouraria (street)

Since 8 March 1917 it has been called (1921) Rua do Dr. Sequeira, and it links Rua da Carreira (‘track’), or Rua do Dr. Vieira, with Largo de São Pedro. In this street stands the palace that once belonged to the Counts of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), which now houses the Municipal Museum, the Madeira District Archive (*Arquivo Distrital da Madeira*) and the Funchal Municipal Library (*Biblioteca Municipal do Funchal*).
In our view, the original name of the street should not have been changed, since it recalls that there was once a Moorish quarter on the site. A few years ago it regained its original name.
Moors

We have already referred, in the entry Slaves, to the Moorish captives employed in clearing the land of Madeira. Since the general term ‘slaves’ covered Black people, mulattoes, Canary Islanders and Moors, it is difficult today to determine with precision the facts or circumstances that concern any one of those groups in particular. Nevertheless, we know that there was a large number of Moors in this archipelago in the early days of colonisation, and that important communities of this population formed, notably in Funchal, Ponta do Sol, Curral das Freiras and Machico. In the first of these places there was a *mouraria* (Moorish quarter), a district of Moors, and the public still today gives one of the streets of Funchal the name of Mouraria.

Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento published in no. 1983 of the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) an interesting article on the Moors in Madeira, from which we transcribe the following passages:

‘The Moor was a harder worker than the slave from Guinea and Mina, which is why landowners preferred to import him for their farming estates. This scandalous trade, arranged between the donataries here and the governors of the strongholds in Africa, who ordered raids, provoked the outcry of the chief of the Moors, who complained in a letter to Manuel I of what Azambuja was doing: seizing people indiscriminately, of every class, to send under contract to the captains of Madeira. This is what we find in the “Documentos arabicos copiados dos originaes da Torre do Tombo, 1790.” ‘The Moors formed large communities, gathering in groups or in a separate quarter, as the Mouraria, one of the oldest streets in Funchal, bears witness, and they were heavily traded in the towns, especially in Ponta do Sol and Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). In Santa Cruz, until a few years ago, an altarpiece in the parish church could still be seen, depicting Moorish slaves wearing a small funnel-shaped turban with a drooping tip. From this derived the peasant’s *carapuça* (traditional Madeiran cap shaped like an inverted funnel) and the little cloth hanging from the head, old characteristic garments of the Madeiran countrywoman. ‘From the Moors comes the plaintive quality of the songs, though the stamping dance is a movement of the Black people. From the Moors come the rambling rhymes of the hill folk, the popular ones: *lengi lengi* the passing fog, the ant that catches its foot. Amid the mists, enchanted princesses, tales of palaces and hidden treasure, thieves and magic wands are influences and themes of the people, carried over in this current from a distant subject race. ‘From the Moors, too, comes couscous, that granulated paste of wheat flour, so prized by the poorer classes, who eat it only on solemn occasions, with a chunk of pork, at baptisms and weddings, never without the sprig of savory and coriander that crowns the dish and gives it its aroma. ‘“Vae-te p’ra Argel” (Go off to Algiers) is a popular curse that recalls the plundering and captivity in the lands of the Moors. A 15th-century episode is handled by an artist’s hand in one of the chapters of the historical novel “A Filha de Tristam das Damas”, with a vivid colouring of the golden days of the dandyish donatary of Machico. ‘That intelligent and adventurous race gave us a figure in history in the person of the Moor Barque, of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), who overthrew the false doctrine of the prophet Fernão Bravo. As in the tale of “the king is naked”, from then on everyone began to see the fraud, and the authorities took charge of the impostor who had deceived a credulous people with his tricks.’

Changes of system of government

The system of absolute government, which had prevailed in Portugal for seven centuries, was overthrown by the revolution that broke out in Porto on 24 August 1820 and established representative government. In the article Constituição de 1821 we gave a detailed account of how this new system of government was proclaimed in this archipelago.

On 3 June 1823 John VI issued a proclamation to the nation dissolving the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), abolishing the Constitution of 1821 and restoring absolute government. On the 17th of the same month the old system of government was solemnly proclaimed in Madeira, as we have already described at some length in the article Alçadas (vol. I, p. 31).

John VI died on 10 March 1826, and his son Prince Dom Pedro was recognised as king. On 29 April of the same year he granted a Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) and at once ordered the Cortes to be convened. The Charter was proclaimed in Madeira with great splendour and enthusiasm on 6, 7 and 8 August 1826, the last day being set aside for swearing the oath to it. The elections were held on 5 October following, and those elected deputies were Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar, Father Caetano Alberto Soares and Luís Monteiro.

Prince Dom Miguel, regent of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), dissolved the Cortes on 13 March 1828 and afterwards proclaimed himself absolute king, by decision of the Three Estates, which had met on 3 May of the same year. In the articles Ocupação da Madeira pelas tropas miguelistas and Proclamação do governo absoluto we shall give a more detailed account of this event, which took place here amid great commotion on 24 August 1828.

When the civil war had been ended by the Convention of Évora-Monte, Dom Pedro, by decree of 28 May 1834, ordered the electoral assemblies to be convened and restored representative government. We shall deal at length with how this event was celebrated in this archipelago in the article Proclamação do Governo Constitucional.

On 4 October 1910 a revolution broke out in Lisbon, and on the following day it proclaimed the Republic. On 6 October Dr Manuel Augusto Martins took office as civil governor of this district, and there were various public demonstrations of rejoicing on that occasion.

Município (square)

This is now the name of the former Largo do Colégio. The churchyard of the church of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist), the church of the College (*Colégio*), was partly demolished at the beginning of 1836 to make way for the Largo do Colégio.

Its considerable enlargement, the freeing of the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) from the adjoining buildings, the construction of the imposing public fountain and other notable improvements carried out there date from 1943 and 1944.
Municipalities

Of the 11 municipalities in the Madeira archipelago, 7 were established under the absolute monarchy, 3 under the constitutional government and 1 under the republican government. The first group comprises the municipalities of Funchal, Machico, Porto Santo, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Santa Cruz and São Vicente; the second those of Câmara de Lobos, Santana and Porto Moniz; and the third only that of Ribeira Brava.

The municipality of Funchal already existed in 1450, for in that year the donatary (*donatário*) was ordered to propose to the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) the persons from among whom the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties) was to be chosen. The municipalities of Machico and Porto Santo, it may be supposed, were created at about the same time or shortly afterwards, since tradition identifies their towns as among the earliest.

The municipality of Ponta do Sol was established in 1501 and that of Calheta in 1502. To this end the municipality of Funchal was divided up; in the 15th century it had stretched from Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’) to the Ribeira do Caniço (‘Caniço stream’), and was bounded inland by the mountain range running from this stream to the same point. The municipality of Machico, made up of the rest of the island, was likewise divided in 1515, the year in which the municipality of Santa Cruz was established. The municipality of São Vicente was not created until 1743.

The municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santana and Porto Moniz date from 1835. In his royal decree (*alvará*) of 10 August of that year, the prefect (*prefeito*) of the province ordered that the proceedings for the municipal elections, which were to be held throughout the archipelago on 4 October, should be presided over in the first of these municipalities by a councillor of the Funchal Council, in the second by a councillor of the Machico Council, and in the third by a councillor of the São Vicente Council. On that occasion the electors of the municipality of Funchal elected 7 councillors (*vereadores*); those of Porto Santo, 3; and those of the remaining municipalities, 5. The municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santa Cruz and Santana were abolished by the decree of 10 December 1867 and restored shortly afterwards. The municipality of Porto Moniz was abolished by this same decree, which remained in force for only a very short time, and also by the decrees of 7 November 1849 and 18 November 1895; it had already been restored by 1855 and by the beginning of 1898 respectively. The municipality of Ribeira Brava, the most recent in the archipelago, was created by the decree of 16 August 1914.

The decree of 10 December 1867 mentioned above, which abolished the municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santana, Santa Cruz and Porto Moniz, divided the archipelago into 6 municipalities, with 21 civil parishes and 50 ecclesiastical parishes. (See Administrative organisation.)

The establishment of municipal government in the archipelago in the 15th and 16th centuries was a useful provision for the people, despite the scarcely democratic character of the laws that governed the old municipalities. Under this new government the people felt stronger and happier, because they understood that above the will and whims of the donataries and the nobles stood the laws that laid down individual liberties and privileges. If the councillors (*vereadores*) did not respect the laws of the municipality, or harassed the people with their acts or resolutions, there was the right of appeal to the king, who in former times seldom failed to hear the complaints of his oppressed subjects.

It may be supposed that the donataries did not look kindly on the installation of the municipal corporations, which came to strip them of part of the jurisdiction they exercised under perfectly legal grants. However, being more prudent than the nobles of the time of John II, they offered no serious resistance to the royal will. They thus allowed a measure to be carried out that must be regarded as the first step towards the destruction of the privileges of the high nobility and the aggrandisement of monarchical power in the archipelago.

Stream walls

Walls have long existed along the banks of some streams, to prevent the water from eroding the land or flooding the settlements. On 28 June 1613 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) protested against various acts of the Governor, Dom Manuel Pereira Coutinho, and in particular against the way in which he opposed it in the direction of the works on the streams ‘in manifest violation of the royal provisions’. The charters of 4 January 1660, 9 August 1747 and 18 July 1748 ordered, respectively, the building of protective walls on the streams of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and Machico.

These walls were built, but not, it seems, with the necessary soundness, for on 24 July 1756 the superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*) wrote officially to Diogo de Mendonça Corte Real about the need to rebuild them.

On 30 May 1772 the captain of engineers Domingos Rodrigues Martins was summoned to the Funchal Municipal Council to draw up the estimate for rebuilding the walls of the streams, without which the Council could not petition the Monarch to carry out this improvement. The *Relação dos Estragos causados pela Tempestade que houve na noite do dia 9 de Outubro de 1803 na ilha da Madeira* (‘Account of the damage caused by the storm on the night of 9 October 1803 on the island of Madeira’), published on p. 723 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), refers to the destruction by the waters of ‘high and strong walls, built of stone and lime along the eastern and western banks of the three streams, for the safety of the city’. This shows that something was done in that year of 1772, or shortly afterwards, to protect Funchal against the danger of floods. The present walls of the city’s streams were begun, or greatly improved, in 1804 under the direction of Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot, who also proposed various urgent works on the streams of Santa Cruz, Machico, Porto da Cruz, Calheta, Madalena, Ponta do Sol, Ribeira Brava and Tábua, some of which were carried out. On 9 December 1804 the brigadier reported to the Viscount of Anadia ‘that the rains had produced great floods in the streams, which had demonstrated the effectiveness and solidity of the works already built both in Funchal and in Machico, Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol and in the parishes of Tábua and Madalena.’

In 1806 several houses on the banks of the Ribeira de João Gomes and the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) were demolished to make way for the new walls. A report submitted to António de Araújo e Azevedo on 28 December 1814 shows that at that date some works still remained to be done on these streams and on the Ribeira de São João before the city would be fully protected from floods.

Part of the wall of the Machico stream was raised after the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1842. In 1847 and 1848 the wall of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia beside the fish market and the walls of the Ribeira de João Gomes near its mouth and the Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) were built, although we do not know whether these works were then being carried out for the first time. In 1847 some stone was laid out along the Ribeira Brava, and more solid works have recently been carried out there to protect the town (*vila*) against the danger of floods.
Murças (street)

It is said in some quarters that the name comes from the fact that certain canons of our Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) once lived in this street. When performing their liturgical duties, canons wear the so-called *murças* (short capes), an insignia reserved for members of cathedral chapters. The street runs from Rua do Sabão to Avenida Gonçalves Zarco. Part of it was originally called Rua do Capitão (see that entry).
House mouse (Mus musculus)

A small rodent mammal, very common in Madeira but not native. It breeds very readily and feeds on whatever it finds. It gnaws floors and doors, and sometimes digs extensive tunnels inside houses. See Rats.
Barley smut (Ustilago hordei)
A smut fungus (Ustilaginaceae) that attacks and destroys barley grain; its spores give the grain a charred appearance. It occurs at São Gonçalo and in other parts of Madeira.
Wheat bunt (Tilletia laevis)

A smut fungus (Ustilaginaceae) that attacks and destroys wheat grains. The charred appearance they acquire is due to the presence of numerous spores of the fungus. Bunt (*murrão*) is frequent in Madeiran wheatfields.
Murray (Charles)

He was British consul in Madeira in the 18th century. He had the old Senhora fountain built at Monte (‘hill’), which was destroyed by the fall of a large chestnut tree in 1896. Although a Protestant, he also had the parish residence built in the same parish (*freguesia*), as well as part of the pilgrims’ house.
He helped to carry out a number of public improvements and also contributed generously to various works for the benefit of the poorest classes of Funchal.

It is of some interest to mention here that he had published at his own expense a curious pamphlet entitled *Avisos interessantes à humanidade ou Colecção de alguns artigos concernentes à restauração da vida dos afogados e outros casos de morte aparente...*, translated from English by the Madeiran poet Francisco Manuel de Oliveira and printed in Lisbon in 1788.
See Leite Monteiro (park).
Murray (Revd P.)

An English clergyman who collected plants in Madeira in 1894 and also visited Portugal and the Canary Islands. He died on 29 October 1908. His herbaria, which included that of J. M. Moniz, are today held at Kew Gardens and the British Museum. Works: *Notes on species of Lotus and Pedrosia*. (*Journ. of Botany*, 1897).
Myrtle (Myrtus communis, forma lusitanica)

A shrub or tree of the myrtle family (Myrtaceae), growing wild in Madeira. It is found at Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’), in the valley of Machico, etc., and is cultivated in many *quintas*. Myrtle branches are widely used to decorate churches for religious festivals, and are strewn in the streets on days when there are processions. Myrtle wood is reddish grey, hard and of good quality.
Archaeological Museum

On 26 January 1915 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) resolved to authorise the removal of various objects belonging to it to the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), in order to begin founding an archaeological museum that might later be greatly expanded. Following this decision, a number of valuable objects that had lain forgotten or neglected in the municipality’s storehouses and elsewhere were taken there. Among the objects moved to the convent were the marble coat of arms and crown of the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi); the turn (*roda*, revolving hatch in the convent wall) of the Convento das Mercês (Convent of Our Lady of Mercy); an inscription from the Ponte de São João; several paintings from the Bishop’s Palace (*Paço Episcopal*); the vestments of the chapel of the same palace; the marble coat of arms of the old gaol; the marble coat of arms and crown of the Varadouros (‘slipways’) arch, together with the Latin inscription, in local basalt, from the same arch; various items from the defunct Hospital de São Lázaro (St Lazarus); the old measures of the weights and measures office; the portrait of Canon Viveiros, founder of the Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation), etc., etc.

The spiteful campaign waged by the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), chaired by Francisco Gomes de Gouveia, against the establishment of the archaeological museum in the building of the former convent, together with the little energy the Council showed in asserting its rights to possession of certain parts of that building, caused the museum to stall almost from the outset, so that it failed to render the services that might reasonably have been expected of it. In January 1916 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) did resolve to petition the Government, requesting the grant of all the articles belonging to the Convent of St Clare that had any historical value, so that they might be kept in the archaeological museum. However, this show of interest in an institution which, once properly set up, could well have fed the spirit of inquiry of learned people, is the last of which we have any knowledge. Nothing more has since been said about properly housing the countless objects of value that may deteriorate or go astray, because they have been left in the most complete neglect (1921).
