Natural History Museum

The idea of establishing a Natural History Museum (*Museu de Ciências Naturais*) is a fairly old one. Nearly a century ago the civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro, a benefactor of the island, laid the foundations for such an institution: he made several rooms of the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’) available for it and gave it devoted support, both with his prestige and with the means at his disposal, towards its permanent installation. When Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Silvestre Ribeiro left the island, the Museum, which, though inadequate and of modest proportions, already represented a hope, soon disappeared entirely.

Valuable light is shed on this subject by what we briefly outlined in a newspaper of this city in 1934, which we shall partly transcribe. ‘Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), meeting a long-standing and acknowledged need, saw fit to create in this capital of the district a museum of natural-history specimens of a strictly regional character. In doing so it followed in the wake of the original initiative of the Civil Governor José Silvestre Ribeiro, which unfortunately did not last long, and it complemented the fine undertaking of Father Ernst Schmitz in setting up the Seminary Museum (*Museu do Seminário*), which has been the object of the greatest admiration and esteem on the part of distinguished naturalists, who have often referred to it in works of the highest scientific standing.

The superabundant richness of the Madeiran fauna has long attracted the attention of many men of science and prompted the thorough study of the principal branches of zoology, giving rise to several hundred bibliographical items published in Portuguese and in various foreign languages.

These facts, and other weighty reasons that could easily be adduced, fully justified the creation of a natural history museum. The seed sown by a benefactor governor and illustrious man of letters germinated and bore fruit eighty years later, full of vigour and to the great satisfaction of scholars and the general public, thanks to the happy and bold initiative of the Council of this city, which acquired a fine and spacious building for the purpose and paid the costs of the first installations. This most useful institution continues its remarkable development and is gradually being enriched with numerous rare specimens, especially of marine fauna and birds. It already forms a precious collection, one that deserves to be visited and studied with care, and it has earned the most flattering remarks from people deeply versed in the natural sciences.

It is worth recalling that the Funchal Council created a Museum that was to consist mainly of specimens of the natural history of the archipelago. Everything proves it. The extensive campaign waged in the local press at the time, the interesting interviews that a distinguished army officer held with the various official bodies and the most qualified personalities of Funchal, and the persistent and effective efforts made by various people when the museum was created all eloquently demonstrate our assertion.

The question naturally arises: should an art museum not have been created instead? The answer is this: the establishment founded by the Council would comprise various sections devoted to art, archaeology, ethnography, etc., as far as the limited conditions of our environment allowed. What was called for at the outset, therefore, was the organisation of a modest art section, attached to the Regional Museum of Natural Sciences, which would gradually be enlarged and enriched as circumstances advised. It would also be permissible to annex to this museum other sections deemed necessary, subject to local needs and to the resources the municipality (*município*) might have at its disposal.

Then came the decree of 7 March 1932, which deals only with museums of art, archaeology, etc., and makes not even a remote reference to establishments of the kind found in Funchal. But was the Council of this city obliged to adapt the conditions of its museum to the provisions of the new decree? It could no doubt do so voluntarily, but nothing in that enactment compelled it to. And since there was then no law, nor is there any yet, preventing a municipal council from establishing a museum on the terms on which Funchal’s operates, we consider that the Council acts lawfully in keeping its Regional Museum in the state in which it was created and in which it is at present. And is there any legal rule that forbids maintaining a small art section attached to a Natural History Museum?

Would it be good, would it be useful, would it be necessary to establish here a museum devoted exclusively to works of art? No moderately cultured person in our society would oppose it, and whoever could bring this praiseworthy idea to fruition would have the unconditional support and applause of everyone’.

On 5 October 1933 the Natural History Museum, attached to the Funchal Municipal Library (*Biblioteca Municipal do Funchal*), was installed in the São Pedro Palace (‘St Peter’), the former manor house (*casa solarenga*) of the Counts of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). It had supplementary sections of art, archaeology, ethnography, etc., and was regarded as meeting a cultural need of our community, a need fully justified by the words quoted above.

Its creation and installation in the handsome building it occupies are due chiefly to Adolfo César de Noronha, as will be seen in the article we shall devote further on to this distinguished man of science.
Lyceum Museum

The lyceum (state secondary school) building houses a small museum for the instruction of the school’s pupils. Besides a shell collection and a mineral collection, it contains a seal and a number of birds, fish and botanical specimens. These natural-history objects were acquired in 1913 and 1914 thanks to the efforts of Major Alberto Artur Sarmento, a distinguished teacher of natural sciences. Before then the lyceum had held a few zoological specimens, whose state of preservation was already poor some 40 years ago. (1921).
Seminary Museum

The so-called seminary (*Seminário*) museum, the only one of undisputed scientific value in Funchal, was founded in 1882 by the German priest Father Ernst Schmitz, then a teacher at that institution. For many years it was attached to the Episcopal Seminary of Funchal (*Seminário Episcopal do Funchal*). Only recently was it transferred to the house on the Largo do Visconde do Ribeiro Real, next to the residence of the diocesan prelate, where it is at present (1921).

The seminary museum is a natural-history museum, representing the fauna, flora and minerals of the archipelago. As regards the fauna, the collections of birds, fish and shells deserve mention, as do those of corals and of certain groups of insects. As regards the flora, notable for their importance are the collections of mosses and flowering plants made by the late James Yate Johnson, those of lichens and fungi made by Father Jaime de Gouveia Barreto, and the seaweed collection assembled by Father Ernst Schmitz. The collection of flowering plants has been much improved recently, thanks to the research of the young Madeiran botanist José Gonçalves da Costa.

Father Ernst Schmitz, who rendered such great services to the seminary museum, directed it until June 1908. Its present director is Father Jaime Barreto, a distinguished naturalist who has succeeded in preserving and advancing the work begun by his illustrious teacher (1921).
The natural-sciences museum of the Diocesan Seminary is currently housed in the Incarnação building, under the able direction of Canon Jaime de Gouveia Barreto, professor and rector of the Seminary.
Oceanographic Museum

On 23 December 1920 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) resolved to contribute 200 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) towards setting up an oceanographic museum, and 50 escudos a month towards its running costs. Some building work was even begun in the premises of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) to house the planned museum. It had to be abandoned, however, once it was recognised that with the meagre sum voted by the Municipal Council nothing of scientific interest could be achieved, especially where oceanography was concerned. (1921). (See that entry).
Mosses

Professor A. Luisier’s work, entitled *Les Mousses de Madère*, records 189 species of mosses in our archipelago. Some of them are common, such as *Dicranum Scottianum*, *Fissidens asplenioides*, *F. serrulatus*, *Weisia viridula*, *Trichostomum brachydontium*, *Glyphomitrium polyphyllum*, *G. nigricans*, *Funaria hygrometrica*, *Haplodontium Notarisii*, *Epipterygium Tozeri*, *Bryum capillare*, *Mnium undulatum*, *Bartramia stricta*, *Polytrichum juniperinum*, *Thamnium alopecurum*, *Scleropodium illecebrum*, etc., etc.
See Cardot, Dixon, Geheeb, Juratzka, Luisier, Mitten, Schiffner and Winter.
Music

‘The music common to the whole island of Madeira’, wrote the well-known Russian writer Platão de Vakcel in 1869, ‘comes down to two or three kinds of song, accompanied by violas (Portuguese wire-strung folk guitar), *rajões* (Madeiran five-string guitar) and *machetes* (small Madeiran four-stringed guitar), from which the same modulations are always drawn, now in single chords, now in doubled ones. In the countryside there are some songs peculiar to certain localities and suited to the various kinds of farm work: some of them bear a remarkable resemblance to Arab chants, having not only their monotony but even their ornaments, made up of successions of intervals smaller than semitones.’

Since the city of Funchal once had its Moorish quarter (*mouraria*), and tradition holds that many Moors lived at Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), it is not surprising that these people, in whom Arab blood almost always predominated, left notable traces of their stay on the island in certain songs, just as they did in the old costume and in the anthropological characteristics of part of the Madeiran population. The Arabs, one author notes, never pass from one note to another, whatever the distance between them, whether rising or falling, without running through all the intermediate intervals. These glissades, not always pleasant to a European ear, can be heard in some of the music of our countryside, probably introduced to the island during the 15th century.

‘The Madeiran people’, Platão de Vakcel says further, ‘are much inclined to adopt foreign melodies, made popular among them by military or amateur bands and by itinerant musicians. This inclination shows that the national song of the Madeirans lacks that vigorous originality which belongs to a people’s national character; a people possessing such music could never grow familiar with another whose stamp differed from its own. A Russian peasant, for example, will never keep in his memory a melody that does not have the individual character of his own music.’

The ease with which the Madeiran people learn what they hear played by the philharmonic bands, today widespread on the island, is extraordinary, and it is not rare to see boys still in early childhood reproduce, by singing or whistling, pieces of music of relative difficulty. These pieces, however, are either easily forgotten or replaced by others, whereas Madeiran songs remain unchanged, with their Moorish stamp and cadence, so much loved by the people of our land. Fados imported from Portugal are the only musical compositions unknown to our forebears that Madeirans have adopted and can no longer forget, so much do they please our people and speak to their imagination.

The braguinha (small Madeiran four-string guitar, ancestor of the ukulele) or *machete de braga*, the *requinta de braga*, the *rajão*, the French guitar (*viola francesa*), the viola de arame (wire-strung folk guitar) and the fiddle (*rabeca*) are the instruments now most common on the island, and those that always appear at the pilgrimages (*romarias*) so beloved of Madeirans. Frutuoso, referring to the pilgrimage still made today to the church of Faial, says that the pilgrims (*romeiros*) hold ‘many festivities of plays, dances and music of many instruments, violas, guitars, flutes, rebecs and bagpipes’; but these last two instruments are now unknown on the island, the *rabis* or *arrabis* of which the historian of the islands speaks being of Moorish origin.

The flute is today very little known in our countryside and, like the fiddle, is always very badly played. The concertinas that sometimes appear at the pilgrimages deserve mention only for the clumsy way in which they are played.

As regards sacred music, Platão de Vakcel says that what was sung in former times in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) ‘must have been the best there then was in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal)’. ‘In the Chapter of the Sé,’ the same writer adds, ‘there is a book of masses, printed in Antwerp in 1639, composed by the celebrated Duarte Lobo, and it was surely not the only book of music there would have been there at the time.’

Frutuoso relates that Dom Jorge de Lemos, appointed Bishop of Funchal in 1558, brought a chapel master with him, and that in his time ‘music flourished greatly in that land, because the bishop favoured the singers and musicians, being himself a man of great discernment.’ At the time ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) was written, there were in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) ‘many mulatto women, very well kept and with rich voices, which is a sign of the ancient nobility of its inhabitants.’

We also read in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ that the canons Gaspar and Francisco Coelho, natives of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), ‘were outstanding men with rich voices’, the former having been chapel master of the Sé and the latter chapel master of the royal chapel at court. It adds that Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the Magnificent, possessed ‘a chapel of many singers and chaplains, which rivalled that of the King’, whose chapel master was Diogo de Cabreira, ‘a Castilian very skilled in the art of singing and of the organ, so much so that the King himself asked him to sing in his chapel.’

The post of chapel master seems to have been created officially only in 1566, whereas that of organist, or organ player, already existed in 1554. A letter written by King Manuel I to Nuno Cão, dean of the Sé, states that the canons and choirboys should know ‘organ chant, so that on Sundays and feast days the masses might be celebrated with organ chant’.

In 1613 Philip II presented an organ to Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*). In the time of Bishop Dom Jerónimo Fernando a large organ, made in Córdoba by master João Manuel, came to the same church; it was Father António Gonçalves, beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) of São Pedro, who tuned it and directed its installation in the choir.

‘Few are the names of Madeiran musicians, says Platão de Vakcel, that have come down to us. In the second half of the 17th century Canon Manuel Fernandes was a music teacher in Funchal. His pupil, Francisco de Valhadolid, a native of this city, rose to be chapel master at the archiepiscopal seminary of Lisbon, where he died in 1770. He owned a rich registry of musical works and was a renowned composer. He wrote, for example, a piece for sixteen voices. It is a pity that none of his work was ever printed.

‘We know the names of some of the chapel masters of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé): Father Manuel de Almeida (1618–1651); his successor, Father Miguel Pereira, who died in 1682; António Pereira da Costa, a composer, by whom there are some *Concerti grossi* for bowed instruments, published in London, and who died in 1770; his successor Luís António; António José de Vasconcelos, who was living in 1800; and Pedro Correia, who died in 1840, and whose pupil is the present chapel master, Father Manuel Joaquim dos Passos, rector of the seminary and teacher of plainchant there.

‘Bishop Ataíde, a talented composer, brought many musicians with him to Madeira in 1812, among them José Joaquim de Oliveira Paixão (died 1833) and a pupil of Friar José Marques, João Fradesso Belo (1792–1861). The former was an accomplished fiddler and music master at the seminary, and the latter chapel master of the Sé and also a teacher at the seminary. Both wrote a great deal of sacred music, which reveals more knowledge of the craft of composition than true inspiration.’

After Father Manuel Joaquim dos Passos, the chapel masters of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) were Eduardo Maria Frutuoso da Silva, António de Melo, Francisco de Vila y Dalmau and Father Manuel Joaquim de Paiva. Eduardo Maria Frutuoso da Silva, who died on 4 November 1878, had one of the finest voices we have known in Funchal and left some sacred compositions of some merit (1921).

Among the authors of sacred compositions, we should also not forget Friar Manuel Gaspar, Canon Libório José Furtado, Father Barros, of Silveira (died 1864), Father Francisco Drumond de Vasconcelos (died 1864), Father José Maria de Faria and António de Melo, the last of whom left some works of merit, among them the *Miserere* and a composition dedicated to Leo XIII (1921).

In the second and third quarters of the 19th century, the following composers of secular music were known in Funchal: Rafael Coelho Machado, who left for Brazil in 1838; António Maria Frutuoso da Silva (died 1874), who directed a concert society that existed from 1840 to 1848; Duarte Joaquim dos Santos, a native of Elvas who died in Funchal on 24 May 1855, aged 54, and who wrote many pieces for piano, printed in London, and some church music, which remained in manuscript; Ricardo Porfírio da Fonseca, who died in 1855, composed a psalm for the Anglican church, where he was organist, and left various other compositions; and António José Bernes, who died in Portugal around 1880 and wrote a great deal of brilliant piano music. Of this last composer, Platão de Vakcel said in 1869 that he was the only one in Madeira who deserved, to a certain extent, the name of composer.

At the time Vakcel visited the island, the following were still held in esteem for their talent and musical knowledge: Cândido Drumond de Vasconcelos, a distinguished player of the *machete* (small Madeiran four-stringed guitar); Júlio da Silva Carvalho, violinist; Agostinho Martins, violinist; José Sarmento, pianist and organist; Artur Sarmento, concert performer; Dona Maria Paula Rego, pianist and harpist; Dona Carolina Dias de Almeida, singer; and Dona Júlia de França Neto, pianist and singer, prizewinner at the Geneva conservatoire, ‘the musical glory of Madeira and one of the musical talents who most honour Portugal’, as the same Vakcel put it in 1869. There are those who remember hearing Dona Júlia Neto sing at some concerts in aid of the poor held at the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace) in early 1866, and at other festivities held before and after.
Dona Júlia de França Neto, already known in 1855 as a most distinguished singer, died in Funchal on 14 May 1903.

Dona Amélia Augusta de Azevedo (see Photography), who completed her course at the Lisbon conservatoire and after 1885 gave some concerts in Lyon (France), was a distinguished player of the *machete de braga*, performing at many gatherings held in Funchal from 1860 to 1866. Manuel Cabral, António José Barbosa, Agostinho Martins, Dona Virgínia Baptista and Diogo Sarsfield also played that instrument, or the *machete rajão*, with the greatest precision, and many of the present-day *machete* players of our island were their pupils.

Among the good musicians of fifty or sixty years ago, we must not forget the violinists Nuno Rodrigues, Anselmo Serrão and Eduardo Gomes da Silva (who won the 1st prize of the Belgian conservatoire), and the cellist and double-bass player Miguéis. Among the moderns, we are minded to record here the names of Nuno Graciliano Lino, violinist and pianist; Guilherme Honorato Lino and António Rosa Caires, cellists; Alfredo Lino, pianist; William Carlton Wilbraham, violinist; Manuel Passos de Freitas, mandolinist; António Vieira de Castro, pianist; captain Edmundo da Conceição Lomelino, pianist and author of a waltz entitled *Desalento*; and Dona Elisa Drumond Carregal, Dona Maria Adelaide de Meneses, Dona Floripes Gomes, Dona Elisa Gorjão Caires, Dona Maria Amália Colares Mendes Rocha de Gouveia, Dona Maria da Conceição de Meneses Santos Pereira, Dona Angelina Pereira Freitas, Dona Palmira Pereira, Dona Leonor Ferraz Leça and Dona Maria Helena Portugal Azevedo Ramos, pianists (1921).

In speaking of secular music in Madeira, we cannot fail to mention the name of the artillery major João dos Reis Gomes, the distinguished author of *A Musica e o Teatro*. Major Reis Gomes is not a musician in the true sense of the word, for we are not aware that he has devoted himself diligently to the study of any instrument; but he is a theorist of great merit, a philosopher of art and a profound connoisseur of the origins and history of music.

His book, the fruit of more than ten years of conscientious observation and study, is not only a philosophical work but also a repository of varied information on the conditions of musical art, music and the life of the passions, symphonic music and art, etc., etc.

*A Musica e o Teatro* is a book that honours not only its author but also Madeira, for it is clear proof that there are those here among us who can treat the loftiest questions of art with expertise and popularise scientific principles from which musicians themselves are, more often than not, remote.

Since Platão de Vakcel wrote the article to which we have referred several times, a number of singers have distinguished themselves in sacred music. First came Canon Augusto José de Faria and Fathers António Vieira, José Dias Ferreira and Manuel Nunes, all of them basses, and António José Barbosa, tenor. Later came Jacinto Augusto Pereira Brasão, tenor; Father José Bebiano da Paixão, Father Eduardo Pereira and José Dias Ferreira, baritones; and Abel da Silva Moniz, bass, who died in 1921 aged only 46. The best singers of sacred music now on the island belong to the choirs of the Cathedral chapel (*Sé*) and of the Schola Cantorum, which is ably directed by Canon Manuel Mendes Teixeira. (1921).

There are at present 14 bands on the island of Madeira: 3 in Funchal, including the band of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria n.° 27*), 2 in Câmara de Lobos, 1 in Campanário, 2 in Ribeira Brava, 1 in Ponta do Sol, 1 in Paul do Mar, 1 in Faial, 2 in Machico and 1 in Santa Cruz. In 1869 the only bands known on the whole island, apart from that of the 12th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) Battalion, was the Filarmónica dos Artistas Funchalenses, a local band (*filarmónica*) founded on 18 February 1850 (1921).

Funchal has several musical groups made up of amateurs. The most notable is the one directed by Dr Manuel Passos de Freitas, a lawyer and a most distinguished musician. This group, which has twice visited the neighbouring archipelago of the Canary Islands, where it won well-deserved applause, has, besides its conductor, other highly accomplished members of whom our island is very proud (1921).

A few Madeiran singers of some merit are known in secular music, but vocal music has far fewer devotees on the island than instrumental music. In 1921 a choral society (*orfeão*) was formed in Funchal under the direction of Dr Manuel Passos de Freitas, and it has already performed brilliantly several times at the Teatro Manuel de Arriaga. There are also a number of ladies and gentlemen here with fine voices, among whom we shall mention the following, whom our public has had the opportunity to hear and applaud at various concerts: Dona Gabriela de Freitas Martins and Dona Matilde Pestana, sopranos; João A. Fernandes, baritone; Tristão da Câmara, tenor; Luís Pestana, baritone; and Lieutenant Carlos Silva, bass. The distinguished tenor Nuno Lomelino Silva is a Madeiran. He completed the singing course at the Milan Conservatory, in Italy, and the Italian press has praised him, highlighting his considerable artistic gifts as a singer.
Funchal once had a school of choral singing maintained by the Council, but it was short-lived. It opened in 1885, and its teacher was the late Francisco de Vila y Dalmau.

It was once believed that Madeira’s rather humid climate stood in the way of good voices. Today, however, it seems to have been shown that vocal training can be pursued here as well as anywhere else, and that only goodwill and good teachers were lacking to improve the aesthetic qualities of the voice and to develop among Madeirans certain artistic gifts that every musician must possess. Most of our present singers have taken lessons with the teacher Júlio Câmara, who has spent some time in Funchal. The way some of them have performed in public highlights the special aptitude of Madeirans for music, and shows that a constellation of fine artists could be formed here, once the vocal resources of many of our fellow islanders are properly used and guided (1921).

For the valuable information it contains, and for the undisputed authority of the illustrious professor Luís de Freitas Branco, we shall transcribe some passages from the interesting talk he gave on the microphone of the Emissora Nacional on 24 May 1937.

‘I usually speak only of my own profession, and so you, ladies and gentlemen, will not be surprised that I choose as the theme of my talk a subject relating to the art of sound. My talk is entitled “Madeiran Musicians” and, as you will see, they are more numerous than one might suppose.

I shall begin with the first years of the settlement of the island of Madeira. Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, “the Magnificent”, third captain and donatary of Madeira, who died almost in poverty at Matosinhos, in the municipality (*concelho*) of Bouças, in 1530, had in his golden days been a highly enlightened lover of music. He organised in Funchal a sumptuous chapel with a great many chaplains and singers, rivalling in quality and number those of the chapel of the Court, which were famous at that time. Under the administration of Simão Gonçalves, the notable composer and organist Diogo de Cabreira was chapel master in Funchal.

The Bishop of Funchal, Dom Jorge de Lemos, an accomplished musician, himself reorganised the chapel of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) in 1558, providing it with everything it needed to function. The post of Cathedral organist already appears in 1554, and that of chapel master first appears in 1566. At this time the master of the royal chapel at court was Canon Francisco Coelho, a native of Ribeira Brava.

In the 17th century we find two distinguished musicians on the island of Madeira: the priests Father Manuel de Almeida and Father Miguel Pereira. In 1770 the Madeiran Canon Manuel Fernandes died in Lisbon; at the time he held at court the high musical office of chapel master of the archiepiscopal seminary, where he taught the celebrated Spanish musician Francisco Valladolid. From the same period comes the celebrated chapel master of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé), António Pereira da Costa, whose ‘concertos’ for string orchestra were published in London.

I remember hearing a member of the family mention the name of José Fradesso Belo, who made his name as chapel master of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) and as a music teacher. Seeking information about this Madeiran musician, I was able to establish that he was born in 1792 and died in 1861. It can be said, broadly speaking, that the chapel masters of the Cathedral combined that post with that of music teacher at Funchal Seminary.

I shall now mention the most notable Madeiran composers of sacred music in the 19th century. They were Friar Manuel Gaspar, Canon Libório Furtado, Father Francisco Drumond de Vasconcelos and António Melo. The following composers of secular music are more recent: Rafael Coelho Machado, Ricardo Joaquim da Fonseca and José Bernes.
From 1840 to 1848 there was a ‘Concert Society’ (*Sociedade de Concertos*) in Funchal, on the lines of the one founded a few years earlier in Lisbon by João Domingos Bomtempo.
The Funchal Concert Society was founded and directed by the notable musician António Frutuoso da Silva.

In 1885 there was also a singing school in Funchal. Some years earlier an excellent Austrian violinist, Ernest Machek, had lived in Funchal for health reasons. There he gave concerts and trained pupils, among them the two amateurs João and Fidélio de Freitas Branco, the first of whom was a music critic for the Lisbon newspapers *Vanguarda* and *Luta*.

From the contemporary period I shall also mention, among professionals and amateurs, the following Madeiran musicians: Júlio da Silva Carvalho, José Sarmento, Artur Sarmento, Dona Maria Paula Rego, Dona Silvana de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, Dona Carolina de Almeida, Dona Júlia de França Neto, Dona Amélia Augusta de Azevedo, Nuno Rodrigues, Gomes da Silva, who won a prize at a conservatoire in Belgium, Nuno Graciliano Lino, Guilherme Lino, Guilherme Wilbraham, António Vieira de Castro, Captain Edmundo Lomelino, Dona Elvira Carregal, Dona Amália Rocha de Gouveia, Dona Conceição dos Santos Pereira and Dona Palmira Lomelino Pereira.

Some years before the Great War the tenor Júlio Câmara, today a singing teacher at the Porto Conservatoire, founded and directed a singing school in Funchal. Dona Angélique de Beer Lomelino also ran private courses in singing and piano in Funchal. She later became piano teacher at the Lisbon Conservatoire, a post she held until 1921.

There are numerous civilian bands in Madeira and several musical ‘groups’, the most celebrated of which is the ‘Septeto Passos de Freitas’, directed by Dr Manuel Passos de Freitas, a leading social and artistic figure in Madeira.

To close this series of contemporary Madeiran musical celebrities, I shall mention: Reis Gomes, author of notable published works of musicology; Francisco Jorge de Sousa Baía, pianist and composer, professor and director of the Music Section of the Lisbon Conservatoire; Alexandre de Bettencourt, a notable violin teacher at the Lisbon Conservatoire; Matilde de Bettencourt, a singing teacher in Paris; Nuno Lomelino Silva, a tenor with a long and acclaimed career abroad; and, finally, Maestro Pedro de Freitas Branco, a former pupil of the Funchal Lyceum, whom my distinguished listeners of the Emissora Nacional must know perfectly well.

May my distinguished listeners in Madeira, whom I greet once again, forgive the length of this talk, for the satisfaction and pride they must feel on seeing how numerous and notable Madeiran musicians are.’
Valuable material on the subject of this article is provided by the two works *Cantares e Tocares da Ilha* and *Trovas e Bailados da Ilha* by the journalist Carlos Santos.
Mutualism

In the article ‘Associado 4 de Setembro de 1862’ (I-97) we gave a brief account of the earliest efforts to establish the principles of mutualism here in Madeira. These principles have borne their valued fruit only very slowly, with the exception of the association just mentioned, which stands as an admirable commemorative pillar (*padrão*) testifying to their beneficial effect. A detailed article on this subject, published in the issue of *Trabalho e União* (‘Labour and Union’) of 1 September 1917, is well worth reading. See also the pamphlet ‘Mutualismo’ by Dr Álvaro Reis Gomes.

Napoleon

The disaster of Waterloo had forced Napoleon to abdicate and leave French soil. Despite the doubts and hesitations then troubling his mind, it seems that he had at last taken the firm decision to make for the United States of America. On 16 July 1815 he embarked at Rochefort, voluntarily going aboard the British naval ship *Bellerophon* and placing himself, trusting and resigned, under the noble and generous hospitality of the English. On reaching the coast of England on 24 July, he recognised, disillusioned but too late, the sad and cruel fate that awaited him: exile and death on the harsh and lonely rocks of St Helena.

On 7 August Napoleon transferred from the *Bellerophon* to the flagship *Northumberland*, which that same day set a southward course, accompanied by the frigates *Havannah*, *Ceylon* and *Bucephalus* and the brigs *Peruviana*, *Zephiro*, *Zenobia*, *Ferrol*, *Icarus* and *Redpole*. The squadron was commanded by George Cockburn and carried the 53rd Regiment of English infantry, which was to garrison St Helena. The emperor’s suite consisted of General Bertrand with his wife and children, the Count of Las Casas and his family, Generals Montholon and Gourgaud, a naval captain, two aides and a few servants.

On 22 August they sighted the Madeira archipelago. As they passed between Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), the *Northumberland*’s doctor pointed out to the Count of Las Casas the resemblance he saw between the latter islands and the bare, barren rocks of St Helena. Napoleon, on the ship’s deck, was gazing absorbed at the steep ravines of the Desertas when the count approached him and passed on the ship’s doctor’s remark. The same thought may well have crossed the emperor’s mind. It is also likely that, on seeing the luxuriant vegetation of Madeira, he reflected on the stark contrast between the incomparable beauty and mild climate of this island and the desolate aridity of St Helena and the conditions of so inhospitable a region. Napoleon said nothing to Las Casas, merely giving a faint smile and a disdainful shrug.

During the night of 22 August the squadron appeared off Funchal, but it seems that it did not anchor until the following day. All the ships anchored in our bay except the flagship *Northumberland*, which sailed offshore not far from the harbour. Under the strict instructions of the British Admiralty, the ship carrying the emperor was not to call at any port during its voyage, nor allow anyone outside its crew to come aboard.

23 August brought heat more intense than any the inhabitants of this island could remember. It was the familiar *leste* (hot, dry easterly wind from Africa), which this time came with a violent storm. The people, in their superstitious simplicity, attributed the phenomenon to Napoleon’s passing. The Attila who had laid Europe waste at the head of his invincible armies, though a prisoner stripped of all his power and grandeur, had still unleashed the fierce gale that did so much damage to agriculture here and harmed many buildings and dwellings!

The sea had grown rough, and communication with the ships of the squadron was difficult. An eyewitness states that the wind was strong and the swell very heavy, so that the emperor suffered considerable discomfort. Nevertheless they managed to take on provisions and refreshments, among them ‘unripe oranges, poor peaches, tasteless pears and excellent grapes’.

It is said that the British consul in Madeira, Henrique Veitch, had learned in advance that Napoleon would pass Madeira and at once resolved to do everything possible to see and speak to him. Despite the state of the sea and the distance of the *Northumberland* from land, he managed to reach the ship and speak to Admiral Sir George Cockburn, a personal friend, to whom he confided his great wish to greet the victor of Austerlitz and Marengo. The admiral tried to dissuade Veitch from any such attempt, on the pretext that Napoleon had become extremely irascible and even intractable, even towards the members of his own suite.

By good fortune for the British consul, one of Bonaparte’s aides appeared at that moment. Veitch was introduced to him and at once said that he ardently wished to offer his most respectful greetings to His Imperial Majesty. It was the first time that the title of majesty had been used for the emperor aboard the *Northumberland*, for he could only be addressed simply as General Bonaparte. This, it seems, was the talisman that broke the spell and brought Veitch into Napoleon’s presence. Napoleon received England’s representative in Madeira warmly and, when offered his services, replied that he would much appreciate some books and fruit from this beautiful island. Henrique Veitch graciously met Napoleon’s wishes, sending him a splendid gift of fruit, sweets and old wines. The emperor sent the consul some gold napoleons to pay for the boat that had carried the refreshments aboard, and tradition has it that Veitch placed them in the foundation stone of the Anglican Church (*Igreja Anglicana*) in Rua da Bela Vista when the foundations of that church were dug. On the afternoon of 24 August 1815 the whole squadron set sail for its destination, passing the Canary Islands on the 27th without calling there, and the latitude of Cape Verde on 1 September, and anchoring at St Helena on 15 October. Napoleon was born on 15 August 1769 and died on the island of his banishment on 4 May 1821.

Of particular interest is what can be found in the ‘Diary’ of J. R. Glover, secretary to Admiral Georges Cockburn, commander of the Northumberland, the ship carrying Napoleon into exile. The book was published in Oxford in 1931 by Colonel H. A. Newel, and the distinguished Madeiran writer Father J. Vieira Caetano extracted a few pages from it in summary form. We shall transcribe the main passages that concern our subject.

‘23 AUGUST. The wind veered to the east and became very hot and unpleasant. At two o’clock the island of Porto Santo was sighted, and shortly afterwards that of Madeira. That day Bonaparte did not take his walk before dinner.

At the meal he appeared pensive and out of sorts. He asked the admiral a few questions about Madeira: its size, how long ago it had been discovered and by whom. Immediately after dinner he went to the stern and watched the island, most particularly as we sailed along its coast, until we reached the bay of Funchal when it was already dark. After playing for a while with Madame Montholon, he withdrew to his “cabin”, evidently dejected. These words are translated from the Diary almost literally.

They show us the victor of Marengo and Austerlitz melancholy and dejected. This is hardly surprising in a man who had stood at the zenith of glory and was now sailing into exile, passing from the splendours of Paris and Versailles to the solitude of the remote islet of St Helena. Within sight of the Madeiran coast, Bonaparte (the ship’s secretary gives him no other title) was learning the history and geography of Madeira, of which he knew nothing, as the questions he put to His Britannic Majesty’s admiral show.
24 AUGUST: ‘We lay in the bay of Funchal, a long way off the landing place. The crew went ashore to fetch water and provisions, and I too went to buy some fruit and wine.
Mr Veitch, His Majesty’s consul, visited the ship, and Bonaparte asked him many questions about the island, its produce, its height above sea level, its population, etc.

Mr Veitch dined on board. After dinner Bonaparte walked with him and the admiral for a considerable time, talking about general topics, after which he retired to bed without stopping at the card table.’
On this second day the frigate took on provisions and the English consul, Mr Veitch, went on board. Napoleon talked and went on learning about Madeira, retiring to bed without his game of cards.

Whether it was on this day that he received the visit of the young lady of Funchal handed down by tradition, which inspired Major Reis Gomes’s fine historical tale ‘Anel do Imperador’, the secretary does not say in the ship’s diary; nor did the visit lessen the exile’s despondency.

25 AUGUST: ‘The violent and very unpleasant sirocco continued, having begun when we sighted Madeira. Such was the superstition of the inhabitants that they blamed this destructive wind on Bonaparte, who was in the harbour; they were very anxious about their crops, which, already almost ripe, would be half lost.’

The secretary, Mr Glover, goes on to state that, owing to rough seas and unpleasant weather, they spent the whole day until nightfall taking on provisions. It was already dark when they set sail for the south.

Of Bonaparte he adds: ‘The heat of the *leste* (hot, dry easterly wind from Africa), the unpleasant nature of the wind and the ship’s rolling, which was very considerable, evidently affected the General. At dinner he ate very little and was downcast.

That evening he played vingt-et-un for only about half an hour and retired to bed.’ On this day the ship left Madeira, which Napoleon saw for the first and last time. The ship’s diary makes no mention of the gold coins the Emperor left in Madeira in payment for fruit and some books he had asked for.

The author of *The English Church in Madeira*, however, mentions them and relates that Consul Veitch placed them in the foundations of the Anglican church when the building’s first stone was laid. He found this confirmed in a letter written on 5 January 1860 by Mrs Minet, of the Cossart family, to her sister Mrs Leacock.
Mrs Minet says that, as a little girl, she saw the consul, Mr Veitch, place some gold coins received from Napoleon beneath the first stone and then affix the seal.

On that afternoon of 25 August the Emperor of the French left the harbour of Funchal, whose astonishing panorama he had contemplated, for his retreat on St Helena, where he went to meditate on the vanity of worldly greatness and to exclaim, like the eloquent orator of his homeland: God alone is great!’
Of considerable interest on this subject is the book *O Anel do Imperador* by the illustrious writer and academician João dos Reis Gomes.

Nineteen years passed. On 24 July 1840 the French naval frigates *La bela Poule* and *Favorite* dropped anchor in our harbour. They were carrying to St Helena the mission that the government of Louis Philippe had charged with officially transporting the mortal remains of the Emperor Napoleon I from that island to Toulon, and from that port to the city of Paris. The mission was led by the Prince of Joinville (see that entry), and it included some of Napoleon’s former servants, among them General Bertrand, who had been the emperor’s companion in exile and had attended him in his last moments in his retreat on St Helena.

The distinguished Madeiran Monteiro Teixeira (see that entry), who was the French consul in Funchal, gave a splendid ball for the Prince of Joinville and his retinue, attended by the most eminent people of this city. It was at this party that a charming Funchal lady sang, with great accuracy and feeling, a poem in French dedicated to General Bertrand, which had enjoyed great popularity throughout Europe. It moved the illustrious soldier deeply, and he could not hide the great emotion that stirred him so keenly at that moment. Taking from his finger a precious ring, a gift from Napoleon and the dearest relic he kept of his emperor, he presented it to our distinguished compatriot, thanking her in this way for the affectionate and captivating tribute that had been paid to him. The lady graciously declined the kind offer, above all because she knew how much it must be prized and valued by General Bertrand’s heart.

The Prince of Joinville’s retinue included Artur Bertrand, son of General Bertrand, who had been born on St Helena during the exile and had received the first lessons of his education from the Emperor Napoleon himself. In the most eloquent and expressive language he described the ceremonies of the exhumation of the emperor’s body and of its transfer on board the French ships, an account that cannot be read without respectful and heartfelt emotion. This description refers to the passage of the *Belle Poule* and the *Favorite* through the port of Funchal.
Napoleon (Prince Eugène)

This prince, who died in South Africa in the war that the English waged against the Zulus, was in Funchal on 4 March 1879, having landed from the English steamer *Danube*, which was bound for the Cape of Good Hope. See Eugénie (Empress).
Sunrises and sunsets in Funchal

From the annual publication compiled and issued by the ‘Autonomous Board of the Ports of the Madeira Archipelago’ (*Junta Autónoma dos Portos do Arquipélago da Madeira*), we reproduce the table of sunrise and sunset times in Funchal for the current year, 1944. Although these figures are not a permanent guide, they are nonetheless of particular interest, because they always remain very close to reality, and they may be of considerable use to anyone who wishes to consult them. When it is not easy to obtain a calculation made with complete mathematical precision, it is often useful to arrive at an idea that comes as close to the truth as possible.

Nascimento (Dom Friar João do)

Dom João do Nascimento was one of the most distinguished prelates of this diocese. His episcopate lasted from 5 September 1741, the day he arrived in Madeira, until 6 November 1753, the day he died in the house on Rua do Bispo that later housed this city’s lyceum (state secondary school).

He was born in Lisbon, the son of Inácio Mira and Dona Garcia Ferreira de Afonseca, both of illustrious lineage and lords of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Torre da Giesteira (‘broom-thicket tower’), on the outskirts of Montemor-o-Novo. He took his doctorate in the faculty of canon law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1711. He was preparing to compete for one of the chairs of that institution when, in 1713, he felt drawn to the monastic life and entered the seminary of Varatojo, where he made his profession in the Seraphic Order of St Francis.

After some years of religious life, during which he devoted himself to missionary work in many provinces of Portugal, he was appointed bishop of Funchal by John V. He tried insistently to refuse the office, but could not escape it because his superiors imposed it on him. He was appointed on 7 November 1740 and confirmed by Benedict XIV on 5 January 1741, and received episcopal consecration on 5 May of the same year.

Throughout the twelve years he lived on this island, he showed unfailing austerity of character and the most blameless conduct, not only as head of the Funchal church but also as governor of this archipelago in the period from 1747 to 1751.

He made pastoral visits to every parish church, issuing instructions on many points of ecclesiastical discipline. He introduced notable reforms in the diocesan seminary, created several curacies and took other important measures in the exercise of his episcopal duties.

Here in Madeira his name remains linked to one notable work: the building of the bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*). Although it was a heavy structure, stripped of any architectural refinement, it was nonetheless, for this small city and for the period in which it was built, a building of some importance, and one that did no discredit to the high rank of its occupants. It was built between 1748 and 1751, at a cost of twenty *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis), a large sum for the time (see bishop's palace).

He worked hard for the construction of the parish church of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*), and the building of that church is owed in large part to him, above all through the creation, in every parish of the island, of the Confraternity of the Slaves of Our Lady (*Confraria dos Escravos de Nossa Senhora*), whose revenues were applied exclusively to the building of that church. He was bishop and governor of this archipelago when, on the night of 31 March 1748, a violent earthquake was felt in Madeira. It caused few casualties but did considerable damage to most public and private buildings. He took the measures that the circumstances called for at the time, and obtained substantial funds from the government in mainland Portugal to repair the damage caused by the earthquake, chiefly to many churches, to some fortresses and to the customs house buildings.
He died in this city on 6 November 1753 and lies buried in the chancel of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral).
Nascimento (João Cabral do)

He was born in Funchal on 22 March 1897, the son of João Crawford do Nascimento and Dona Palmira Cabral do Nascimento. He attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city and in 1922 completed his law degree at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). From an early age he showed a decided inclination for letters, making his name above all as a poet. He published the verse pamphlets *As tres Princesas mortas num Palácio em ruína*, 1916, *Além-Mar*, 1917, and *Hora de Noa*, 1917. He has contributed to various newspapers and reviews and was an editor of the *Restauração* of Coimbra (1921). When the District Archive was created in 1931, Dr Cabral do Nascimento was appointed its first director. He promptly launched the review *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (‘Historical Archive of Madeira’), of which he has been the principal contributor and of which six volumes have already appeared.

In addition to the works mentioned above, he has published in verse *Alguns Sonetos*, 1924, *Descaminho*, 1926, *Arrabalde*, 1928, and *Cancioneiro*, 1943, and in prose the following writings: *Documentos para a história das Capitanias da Madeira*, 1930, *Genealogia da Familia Medina da Ilha da Madeira*, 1930, and *Apontamentos de História Insular*, 1927.
Christmas

In Madeira the Christmas festivities last from the day on which the birth of Jesus is commemorated until Epiphany (*dia de Reis*). Throughout this time there is much merrymaking, singing and other rejoicing, which lends poetry to this lovely season of the year. Meals become more lavish, and rare is the house where *carne-de-vinho-e-alhos* and *bolos de mel* do not appear, together with other delicacies unknown during the rest of the year. The churches fill with people for Midnight Mass (*missa do galo*), at which the image of the Christ Child is often offered to be kissed. To complete the Christmas festivities and solemnities there are also the nativity scenes, the *presépios* or *lapinhas*, some of them truly remarkable for the richness and variety of their decoration. Not many years ago it was the custom in some parishes of Madeira to ‘tend’ the image of the Christ Child on Christmas night, that is, to carry it and dress it on a dais set up inside the church, a service always performed by a girl. We believe, however, that this custom has disappeared, as has another, which consisted of offering various produce of the land to the Christ Child on that same night. Young men and girls dressed in old-fashioned costume piously carried their offerings to the church, announcing in their songs, at times very harmonious, for whom the offerings were intended.

The old habit of devoting the whole of Christmas Day to quiet family life and celebration is tending to disappear, and the streets of the city, once deserted on that day, are today almost as busy as on the first, second and third days of the octave. Nevertheless, it is mainly during these three days, which the people continue to keep holy although the Church has dispensed them from doing so, that visits and season’s greetings take place. Among the common people these are almost always accompanied by abundant drinking, singing and other merrymaking, which go on until the dead of night. From Christmas Eve until Epiphany, bombs and squibs explode everywhere, gravely endangering not only passers-by but also those who throw them, many of whom have been the victims of their own folly and recklessness.

The custom of seeing out the old year and welcoming the new with every kind of firework, a custom not very old, is the one that most catches the attention of visitors. The city of Funchal and its outskirts offer a truly imposing and beautiful spectacle as midnight approaches on 31 December, when coloured flares are lit everywhere and thousands of rockets and shells rise into the air. With them the Madeirans celebrate the passing from one year to the next, in the hope that the year now beginning will bring them all the good fortune denied them by the one about to vanish into the abyss of time. The night of 31 December is very lively in Funchal. Large groups of revellers pass through the city on their way to various points in the surrounding area, to the sound of *machetes* and *violas*, to watch the midnight celebrations from there.

It is on 7 January, after Epiphany, that the *lapinhas* (Madeiran Christmas crib) are taken down and everything returns to normal. Some people, however, keep their nativity scenes set up until the 15th, the feast of St Maurus, which, in the opinion of some, is when the Christmas festivities so dear to the good people of Madeira should be considered over. See Lapinha.
Shipwrecks

Funchal bay (*baía*) is sheltered from all winds except those blowing from the quarters between south-west and south-east by way of south. Severe storms are felt there only when the wind blows violently from the south; the sea then sometimes rises in towering waves that hurl themselves violently against the beaches. On such occasions sailing vessels are no longer safe inside the bay, and if they fail to put out to sea at the first signs of the storm, they run the risk of being driven ashore and dashed to pieces there by the sea. Of the many storms that have struck our harbour, the following deserve mention because of their disastrous effects.

1757. At the end of October or the beginning of November of this year, a great storm endangered several ships and damaged the harbour works of Funchal (the link between the Pontinha (‘little point’) and the shore).

1802. On the night of 30 August 1802, at 1 a.m., a terrible explosion occurred aboard a Portuguese ship anchored in the harbour of Funchal and bound for Brazil. Thirty-two people died, 4 of them Madeirans. It was said that the explosion had been caused accidentally by a sailor who was in the ship’s powder magazine in order to steal gunpowder to sell in the city.

1804. On 8 and 11 January of this year there were violent storms, and two English full-rigged ships were wrecked. 1828. On 22 January the American brig *Calixto* was driven ashore opposite the Customs House and was completely destroyed by the sea within a few hours; on 1 March the English full-rigged ship *Britannia* was wrecked at Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’), with the loss of one crew member. 1834. This year saw the wreck of the English full-rigged ship *Greenwelle*, in which five crew members died. 1836. The great storms of 18 October drove the Portuguese barque *Maria Adelaide* and the yacht *Conceição e Almas* ashore near Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’), and one member of the latter vessel’s crew died. At the same time a boat laden with wine, coming from the north, was also wrecked there. 1842. On 26 October of this year the sea hurled five ships onto the beach, and another vanished and was never seen again. 1846. From 8 to 11 January there were great gales in the harbour of Funchal, which wrecked the works on the quay, and on the 10th of the same month the Tuscan *patacho* (small two-masted merchant vessel) *Duque de Sussex* was driven ashore at São Lázaro. 1848. On 10 December the yacht *Senhor dos Passos* and the schooner *Eugenia* were lost, and on the 31st the yachts *Fevereiro I.°* and *Boa Fé*, both Portuguese, and the patachos *Delfim* and *Levant*, the latter American and the former Portuguese. During this last storm the English warship, the corvette *Daphne*, very nearly ran aground. 1858. On 5 March of this year the English brig *Reliance* was wrecked in the harbour of Funchal as a result of a strong gale, and on the 15th of the same month the Brazilian patacho *Liberato Terceiro*, whose master was Thomás Whister, met the same fate. 1858. On 14 November the Portuguese full-rigged ship *Defensor* entered the harbour of Funchal on the point of sinking. She was on a voyage from Rio de Janeiro to one of the ports of Portugal, carrying her crew and some passengers, 23 persons in all. The vessel had come from an infected port and the sea was very rough, so that only with great difficulty could 16 people be landed; they were isolated in the old fort of Pontinha. The others stayed on board, refusing to land on that occasion, but during the night they lowered a boat and tried to reach the shore; six of them died and only one could be saved, beyond the fort of São Tiago. The ship ran aground at the mouth of the stream of Gonçalo Aires on 16 November. 1872. A violent storm on 22 December drove the English patacho *Champion* ashore near the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’), and the captain and four other crew members died. 1875. On 2 February 1875 the English steamer *Soudan* ran aground on the beach opposite the former Praça da Rainha (‘Queen’s Square’), today Praça do Marquês de Pombal (‘Marquis of Pombal Square’). The sea was calm, and the disaster was attributed to the incompetence or carelessness of those in charge of the anchoring manoeuvre. 1876. This year there were two great storms in Funchal bay, the first on 13 May and the second on 11 November. The first drove ashore the English schooner *Orphey*, the Portuguese patacho *Barbosa 2.°*, the Portuguese sloop *Moura 7.°* and the American patachos *Maurice* and *Nellieclifford*; the second brought the same end to the German boat *Fear-Not*, the Portuguese yacht *Fontes Pereira de Melo* and the English schooner *Theodosia*. During the November storms the *Valente*, a small Madeiran steamer, was flung onto the rocks below the Quinta Lambert (‘Lambert estate’), more than 15 metres above ordinary sea level; and as early as 3 January a storm less violent than the two we have mentioned had wrecked the English barque *Patagonia* near Santa Catarina. 1881. On 6 January of this year the Portuguese yacht *Aliança* was driven onto the beach by the south wind. 1884. On 26 November the sea hurled the schooner *Eulalia* and the Italian brig *Torquato* onto the beach. 1892. The storms of 28 February damaged the mole (breakwater) of Pontinha. 1896. During the night of 26 to 27 October of this year the French brig *René Adrienne* and the Portuguese brig *Comercio* came ashore, the latter at the Ribeira de São Lázaro and the former against the sea wall of Pontinha. Although Funchal bay is bounded by Cabo Garajau (‘tern cape’) and Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), which are a little more than 8 kilometres apart, it is to the east of the Ilhéu (‘islet’), opposite the city, that ships usually drop anchor, the bottom there consisting of basaltic sand and some mud. The quantity of stones, sand and mud that the waters of the streams carry down every year is considerable, and as a result the sea in the bay has become shallower and the beaches have gradually grown. Banger’s pillar, whose base was washed by the sea when it was built (1798), now stands at a distance from it, and the Rua da Praia, the fish and fruit markets and the Praça do Marquês de Pombal are built on places the waters reached in former times (1921). We shall now give a brief account of other shipwrecks that occurred at various points of this archipelago. In March 1720 a boat carrying eight people was making its way from Machico to Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) when it was caught by a violent storm and driven onto the coasts of the Canary Islands, where they were able to land. They returned to Porto Santo two months later, when everyone there believed them to have perished in the storm. Around 1730 a Swedish ship coming from India with a valuable cargo was wrecked on that island, at the locality of Pedregal (‘stony ground’), at the place called the cliff of Guilherme, and some of the crew perished. Some months later a ship of the same nationality came to the site of the disaster and managed to salvage a considerable part of the cargo, including several objects of great value and, it seems, also some chests of money. At the beginning of 1768 the French warship, the carrack *Balance*, commanded by the Baron of Arras, sank near the island of Porto Santo; her crew, numbering 239, were taken aboard by a French ship, which carried them to the harbour of Funchal. In 1790 a coastal packet boat laden with wine, bound from the north of Madeira to Funchal, sank in the channel of the Ilhéu de Baixo (‘low’), on Porto Santo, having been driven to that spot by a great storm. The whole crew died except for one man who, clinging to a wooden plank, managed to reach the Ilhéu de Ferro.

One great disaster on the Porto Santo crossing (*travessa*) occurred on the night of 11 January 1823, when nine people lost their lives; no trace of the boat or of the victims of this wreck was ever found.

On 5 December 1850 a boat belonging to João Rodrigues Rei and José Alexandre de Viveiros left Funchal for Porto Santo. Its skipper (*arrais*) was the seaman Justiniano Joaquim de Sousa, and besides its owners it carried 13 passengers and 12 crew. In the stretch known as the Travessa the vessel was caught by a fierce storm. The owners and passengers then advised, and insisted, that the crew should make for the Ilhéu de Cima or the Porto dos Frades rather than the landing place of the town (*vila*), because of the grave danger they faced in going ashore there. Unfortunately these pleas and advice went unheeded. As they tried to land, the sea grew rougher under the violent wind, and of the 27 people on board only 12 were saved; 15 met a horrible death amid the towering waves breaking violently on the beach. Among the victims were the owners of the boat and several women and children. The news of this disaster at sea caused the deepest emotion on the island of Porto Santo and in Madeira too.

At that time and in earlier periods, wrecks were frequent on the crossing between Madeira and Porto Santo, because it was made in so-called open boats (*de boca aberta*), that is, boats without a deck. The disaster of 6 December 1850 led to the regulation of that maritime service, and vessels not meeting the necessary conditions were then expressly forbidden to sail between the two islands. From that time on, accidents in navigation between Madeira and Porto Santo became rare. The Portuguese schooner *Maravilha* ran aground on the beach of that island on 7 April 1855, without loss of life. To the north-west of that island a Brazilian steamer was lost on 8 March 1882, and four of its crew died. Various vessels have been cast up on the coasts of Porto Santo at different times, some abandoned and others with their crews, as can be seen in the *Anais* of that island. Off Ponta de São Lourenço the British steamer *Forerunner* sank in 1884 with the loss of 14 lives, as we have already said on p. 44 of this volume. Two *léguas* (league, about 5 km) north of the same Ponta, a fishing boat from the landing place of Machico, crewed by six men, sank on 23 February 1838, and all of them lost their lives. Praia Formosa has been the scene of several wrecks. We may mention one on 1 March 1828, of the British full-rigged ship *Britannia*, in which one crewman died and the ship was completely destroyed, and another on 18 October 1875, of a coastal boat, in which five people perished.

A greater number of maritime disasters have occurred near the so-called Ponta da Cruz, a short distance from Praia Formosa. At the top of the cliff stands a small iron cross, replaced several times, as a sign and reminder of the disasters and loss of life that have taken place there. It is a pious custom for passengers on coastal boats passing this spot to bare their heads respectfully, and many murmur a fervent prayer in recollection. A coastal boat from Ponta do Pargo sank there on 12 March 1901, and seven people died.

Off Ponta do Pargo, a fishing boat from the landing place of Paul do Mar was wrecked on 31 March 1850, and some of its crew died. On 31 January 1857 the Portuguese brig *Triunfo*, under Captain Francisco António da Silva, sailing from Pará with cargo for Lisbon, was wrecked on the beach of the parish (*freguesia*) of Madalena do Mar; all the crew were saved. Off the landing place of the parish of Porto da Cruz, a *légua* and a half from the coast, the French brig *Homs*, under Captain F. Azemas, bound from Cette for Martinique, foundered in a violent storm on 20 September 1858. All the crew were saved and were generously assisted in that parish by Commander Valentim de Freitas Leal, a wealthy landowner there.

In the first days of December 1859 the British full-rigged ship *Flying Foame* left Cardiff bound for the British colony of Hong Kong, in China. A great storm drove it towards Madeira and hurled it violently against the coastal reefs at the locality called Fajã do Manuel, in the parish of Porto Moniz. Of the 21 people on board, 15 died, among them the ship’s captain, William Lidle, and other officers. This ship, which carried a full cargo of coal, was wrecked on 19 December 1859.

On 24 December 1860, in a great storm, the Dutch galliot *Alfa*, bound from England for the island of Haiti, was wrecked on the cliff of Ilhéu do Navio, on the coast of the parish of Santana. The crew of 7 men was saved.
On 18 August 1861 a coastal boat was wrecked at Porto Novo, in the parish of Gaula, with the loss of seven lives, passengers and crew.
The coastal boat *Bailão*, from the landing place of Calheta, sank on 3 September 1872 while sailing from that town to Funchal; three of its crew died.

On 18 October 1875 a coastal boat carrying cargo and passengers left the landing place of Anjos, in the parish of Canhas, for Funchal. It was wrecked, we do not know exactly at what point in the voyage, and four men and two women perished. In the parish of Ponta Delgada a Norwegian full-rigged ship ran ashore on 9 December 1877, and two of its crew died.
We have already given a brief account of the wreck of the yacht *Varuna*, in the parish of Achadas da Cruz, on p. 13 of vol. I of this work.
On 12 March 1901 the coastal boat *Brilhante Pargueiro* was wrecked off Ponta da Cruz, and eight passengers died.

Lighting for the Desertas has long been planned. The lack of lighthouses has led to several wrecks of ocean-going vessels in those waters, above all when the fog is thickest. There have also been various accidents there involving fishing boats which, driven by storms, sometimes meet their destruction on those steep, exposed coasts, with the loss of their crews’ lives.

Several abandoned ships have been cast up on the coasts of those islands. The British steamer *Lagos*, sailing from Liverpool to Madeira with a few passengers, ran aground on Deserta Grande on 17 January 1902, chiefly because of the thick fog.

In 1788 the English privateer *Dart* was wrecked on the coast of the same island, at a spot unknown to us. In 1804 two galleys of the same nationality were driven onto the coast, likewise at a place of which we have been unable to find any record. In many foreign ports there are small monuments or simple stone inscriptions bearing the names of those who, during shipwrecks and storms at sea, rendered outstanding service in saving their fellow men from the raging elements.

The example ought to be followed, and a Funchal newspaper (*D. da Mad.* of 11 December 1926), through the pen of one of the authors of this work, has already urged that the idea be carried out, writing the following lines.

‘A modest plaque placed somewhere near the sea, bearing the names of all those who earned the gratitude of Portuguese and foreigners alike for services rendered during storms at the landing place of Funchal, would be a simple way of showing that Madeirans, too, know how to do justice to those who, by ennobling deeds, proved that they had kept the virtues of the race intact. But until this is done, we shall try to save some of those names from complete oblivion by recording them in the columns of this newspaper.’

Forty to fifty years ago, the men we name below, by their names or nicknames, were the best known for the daring and courage with which they braved the fury of the waves whenever there were lives to be saved during shipwrecks at the landing place of Funchal: António Maria de Gouveia, António da Silva Cambé, Silvano Cardoso, Manuel Teixeira, Manuel Caramujo, João dos Passos (the mute), João Pereira (‘o Marau’), José de Sousa (‘o Patacho’), Manuel Capitão, José (‘o Gato Fardão’), Guilherme and Vitorino Pófia, the two Russos, ‘o Tigela’ and Guilherme Albuquerque de França. This last Madeiran, who was consul of Uruguay in Funchal and did not, as is well known, belong to the seafaring class, never hesitated to battle the raging waves as soon as his services were called for during storms. In earlier times the following Madeirans won great renown in Funchal for the same reason: Henrique Crawford, to whom the castaways of the English schooner *Wave*, which ran aground near São Lázaro on 26 October 1842, owed their lives; José Ferreira Ourela, Arsénio Pombo, João de Freitas, João Vieira, António Silveira and Pedro António. All these men, except the first, belonged to the seafaring class and received an honourable mention in the minutes of the session of the Royal Humanitarian Society of Porto (*Real Sociedade Humanitária do Porto*) of 14 April 1858, which also mentioned the names of Domingos Teles de Meneses, Augusto César Bianchi, Alexandre Sheffield, Roberto Taylor, Gregório Antunes dos Santos, José Francisco da Silva and Cândido Augusto de Mesquita Spranger, for the good services they rendered at the wreck of the brig *Reliance*.
At this wreck the musician Amaro José, a native of mainland Portugal, rendered most outstanding services, and for this he was awarded the first-class gold medal of the said Humanitarian Society.
Navás (Father Longinos)

A distinguished Spanish lichenologist and member of the Society of Jesus, he studied the lichens sent to him from this island by Father Jaime de Gouveia Barreto and by one of the authors of this *Elucidário*. His published work, entitled *Sinopsis de los Liquenes de las islas de Madera* (*Broteria*, vols. IX to XI, 1910–1913), lists 203 species, some of which are mentioned only in the works of other lichenologists. See Lichens.
Aviation

The first aviators to attempt the journey between Lisbon and Madeira were Captain António Jacinto de Brito Pais and Lieutenant José Manuel Sarmento de Beires. They took off from the Amadora airfield on 18 October 1920, at about 10 in the morning, but unfortunately never reached Madeira: the biplane they were using for the journey came down in the sea. It was found at midday on the 19th by the British steamer *Gamboa River*, of the port of Liverpool, which picked up the shipwrecked airmen.

More fortunate than these two aviators were Captain Gago Coutinho of the Navy, Lieutenant Commander Sacadura Cabral, 1st Lieutenant Ortins Bettencourt and the French mechanic Roger Soubiran. Leaving the Tagus in the seaplane ‘F-3’ at 9.25 a.m. on 22 March 1921, they reached the bay of Funchal that same day, shortly after 5 p.m.

No sooner had the aircraft arrived in our bay than it was surrounded by a large number of boats. It was towed to the Pontinha (‘little point’) mole (breakwater), where it remained, by a motor launch carrying the civil governor and other local authorities.

After the first official greetings, the four aviators went by car to the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), where they stayed. There they were welcomed by the civil governor, the harbour master, the Secretary-General and the Military Commander, and Lieutenant Commander Sacadura, on his own behalf and that of his companions, gave thanks for the tokens of esteem shown to them by both the authorities and the Madeiran people. A glass of champagne was then offered to the aviators and several toasts were raised, among them one to Brito Pais and Sarmento Beires.

On the morning of 28 March the seaplane performed some manoeuvres over the bay of Funchal, then flew on as far as Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’). At 5 p.m. that day, before a huge crowd, the ceremony was held of laying the foundation stone of the monument that the banker Henrique Vieira de Castro had erected in the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’) in honour of the aviators who first completed the Lisbon–Madeira raid. The record of the ceremony, after being read and signed by various dignitaries, was sealed in an iron casket together with some coins, and the casket was placed on the site intended for the monument. On 30 March, at 5.45 p.m., the seaplane took off again to meet the British steamer *Briton*, which was carrying the urn containing the remains of the Unknown Soldier. On 2 April, at 1.40 p.m., it set off for Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where the aviators intended to wait for favourable weather to return to Lisbon.

Unfortunately, however, that return could not be made in the aircraft that had brought them to the archipelago. On the morning of the 6th, as it was taking off over the bay of Porto Santo bound for the capital, it caught fire, and the aviators had to take refuge aboard the destroyer *Guadiana*, which was lying in the same bay and in which they travelled on to Lisbon.

It was said that the disaster was caused by the rupture of one of the seaplane’s smoke bombs. The four daring aviators escaped death by quickly throwing themselves into the sea, where they were promptly rescued by some fishing boats, which took them aboard the *Guadiana*.

The aircraft was completely destroyed, but its crew suffered nothing beyond the fright and the disappointment of the disaster that prevented them from completing the air journey they had set out to make.

Besides the tributes to the aviators already mentioned, there were held in their honour a tea and a dinner at the ‘Monte Palace Hotel’, the former given by the Funchal Commercial Association (*Associação Comercial do Funchal*); a ball at the Casino Pavão (‘peacock casino’), organised by the Madeira Sports Club (*Clube Sports da Madeira*); car excursions to various places around the city; a luncheon at the Quinta da Palmeira (‘palm-tree estate’), given by its owner; etc., etc. On Porto Santo, a group of ladies offered the aviators wine and sweets when the seaplane arrived on that island.

The destroyer *Guadiana*, which had arrived in Funchal on 24 March, left for Porto Santo on 2 April, before the aircraft’s departure, to carry the petrol for the journey from that island to Lisbon. The ship returned to Funchal on the 4th to take on coal and provisions, and left again for Porto Santo on the 5th, where, as we have seen, it took in the aviators after the disaster of the 6th.

The infantry captain and aviator Brito Pais and the engineering lieutenant and aviator Sarmento Beires, to whom we have already referred, were commended in the Army Order of November 1920 ‘for the magnificent proof of daring they gave in attempting an air raid to the island of Madeira, in which, though they did not achieve their objective, they nonetheless proclaimed loudly the rare qualities of intrepidity and energy that mark out aviators, and performed a feat that has brought extraordinary distinction to aviation and honour and lustre to the army.’

Although the daring aviators Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral did not touch Madeira during their glorious flight from Lisbon to Rio de Janeiro, their heroic feat was nonetheless splendidly celebrated here from 17 to 20 June 1922. When news reached Funchal, shortly before 4 p.m. on the 17th, that they had arrived in Rio de Janeiro, thousands of shells and rockets were sent up into the sky. At the same time the church bells rang out and almost all commercial and industrial establishments closed in honour of the two great Portuguese heroes.

For four days the illuminations were truly dazzling, not only on public buildings but also on many business premises. Those of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) stood out for their beauty or refined taste, as did those of various houses and establishments in Rua do Comércio, Rua do Bettencourt, Rua do Capitão-Tenente Carvalho de Araújo, Rua de João Tavira, Rua do Dr. Vieira, Rua da Alfândega, etc. The avenues of Dr. Manuel de Arriaga and Gonçalves Zarco remained lit up, with a band playing in the former, and several shop windows displayed decorations more or less alluding to the feat of the two glorious aviators. On some buildings hung banners bearing the Cross of the Order of Christ, which had accompanied the Portuguese of old on their glorious voyages, and portraits of Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral were displayed everywhere, above all on postcards, which the people of Funchal bought with enthusiasm.

On the 19th there was a night-time procession of boats, followed by a *marche aux flambeaux* that went from the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point quay’) to the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), where the tomb of the island’s discoverer lies. There Dr Juvenal de Araújo and Second Lieutenant Armando Correia gave brilliant, patriotic speeches. On the 20th, at 2 p.m., a formal session was held in the Municipal Council building, with speeches by Dr Teixeira Jardim, president of the Council, the aforementioned Dr Juvenal de Araújo and Gabriel Brasão Vieira, a student at the lyceum (state secondary school). When the portraits of the illustrious aviators were unveiled at this session, the hall rang with prolonged applause.

Besides the celebrations already mentioned, there was also a Te Deum in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), organised by the Catholic Youth of Funchal, which ended with an address by Dr Gomes Jardim; a festival at the Teatro-Circo, at which various gifts were given to the children and Dr Pestana Júnior spoke; a dinner in honour of the aviators given by the Brazilian consul for the Funchal authorities; a ball at the Casino Vitória, etc., etc. In Santo António, Ribeira Brava, Machico, Santa Cruz, São Vicente, etc., there were also various demonstrations of rejoicing to commemorate the glorious feat of the two Portuguese aviators.

Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral were given an imposing reception in Funchal on their return to Europe aboard the steamer *Porto*, after their daring flight to Brazil. They landed at the Cais da Pontinha at 10.30 a.m. on 21 October 1922, amid the liveliest and most spontaneous displays of enthusiasm. They then went to the Palace of São Lourenço, accompanied by various dignitaries, where the head of the district once again offered them his greetings of welcome. Afterwards they went to the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), where they received the diplomas conferring on them the freedom of Funchal, and then left for the Cathedral, where they attended a solemn Te Deum presided over by the diocesan prelate, who delivered an excellent patriotic address.

After the Te Deum the two heroic aviators went up to Monte (‘hill’), where a luncheon was given by the banker Luís da Rocha Machado at his *quinta* (country estate) there. In the afternoon a garden party was held for them at Reid’s Palace Hotel, attended by a large number of people. In the evening there was a performance in their honour at the Teatro-Circo, at which the film ‘Raid Lisboa-Rio de Janeiro’ was shown.

On the 22nd Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral lunched with the civil governor, took tea at 4 with the British consul and dined in the evening with the Danish consul. They also took a drive by car to Caniço (‘reed’) and attended a gala performance at the ‘Dr. Manuel de Arriaga’ theatre, at which Dr Juvenal de Araújo spoke brilliantly and Commander Sacadura Cabral replied in a warm impromptu speech that was loudly applauded.
