On the 23rd the distinguished aviators lunched at the ‘Golden Gate’ hotel at the invitation of the Brazilian consul, and in the afternoon they gave a tea aboard the steamer *Porto* for the authorities and other people of Funchal. In the evening the two aviators attended a farewell dinner given by the celebrations committee, which was very lively and ended with a photograph of the guests. At about 10.30 they went aboard the *Porto*, while countless people gathered on the quay to cheer them and bid them farewell.

While Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral were in Madeira, there were brilliant illuminations on the quay, on Avenida Gonçalves Zarco, on the Pontinha road, on all public buildings and on many private houses. The quay and the entrance to the city remained decked with flags, among them many banners bearing the Cross of the Order of Christ.

The patriotic celebrations held in Madeira from 17 to 20 June and from 21 to 23 October 1922 were truly imposing. They were joined not only by all Portuguese nationals but also by some foreigners who understood how daring and moving the achievement of the two distinguished aviators had been. During those days Madeirans showed that they too take pride in the undying glories of Portugal, and the grandeur of the demonstrations held here is eloquent proof that the feelings of patriotism that once raised our country to the height of its former opulence have not been erased among us. See Praia, Sabão and São Francisco (streets) and Pontinha (road).
Coastal navigation

The law of 27 July 1893, which authorised the government to subsidise a regular steam navigation service between Lisbon and the Adjacent Islands (*Ilhas Adjacentes*), also allowed support for a similar service between the islands of each of the two archipelagos. Under a provisional contract of 30 November of that year, concluded between the government and the trading firm Bensaúde & C.ª, regular sailings were established between Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), made by the small steamer *Falcão*, belonging to the Blandy house of Funchal. Towards the end of 1897 this firm began a coastal navigation service between Funchal and various landing places on the south and north coasts of Madeira. It was one of the most notable benefits ever conferred on the principal settlements of the whole island.
Neale (Revd J. M.)
Works: *On the Ecclesiology of Madeira*, a paper read before the Cambridge Camden Soc. (30 April 1844).
Mortuary

The mortuary of the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery, where the bodies of poor people without family found by the authorities are laid, was ordered to be built by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) at its session of 11 October 1900.
Nery da Silva (Canon Vicente)
He was born in the last quarter of the 18th century and died in this city on 3 April 1860.

He was ordained priest around 1815 and, after holding various parish posts on this island, was appointed a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*). He was a man of extraordinary talent and rare intellectual culture, qualities that showed themselves remarkably in his work as a journalist and author of several pamphlets, and also as an orator, a teacher and in the other posts he held.

He won extraordinary fame as a preacher, not only in Madeira but also on the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). This was due in good part to his rare and overwhelming eloquence, but above all to the freedom with which, from the height of the pulpit, he lashed out at the excesses of those in government and the abuses committed by the authorities, sparing not even the real or supposed excesses of his own superiors in the hierarchy. The sacred rostrum at times served him as a political stage, from which he struck at his adversaries or at those he believed to be his enemies and persecutors. It often happened that, alongside a remarkable beauty of language and passages of rapturous eloquence, his sermons revealed malicious insinuation, hostile aggression and even offence and insult aimed at persons of standing who were among the congregation. Once, in the church of Carmo (‘Carmel’), he violently attacked the governor José Silvestre Ribeiro while the governor was present, seated beside the diocesan prelate. On another occasion, in the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), he was ordered by the ecclesiastical authority to come down from the pulpit and was suspended from preaching, before he had even finished his sermon. His contemporaries state that these excesses of language stirred up against Canon Nery the ill will, and at times the persecution, of those struck by these veritable diatribes. They add, however, that the boldness and courage with which he spoke, the tribune’s eloquence with which he thundered his attacks from the pulpit, and the beauty and pithy elegance of his diction softened the effects of the orator’s errors and follies. He had many ardent defenders, who forgave him the unseemly outbursts of his fiery and aggressive eloquence.

Of his writings, the annotator of the *Saudades* says: ‘He wrote politico-ecclesiastical pamphlets, of which we have thirteen before us, the most notable being the following: *Justificação do conego Nery. . . sobre o sermão que fez na Sé, em quinta-feira santa* (Funchal, 1859); *Apontamentos para a história contemporânea do Bispado do Funchal*, 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 5th epochs of the elevation of Canon Sá, in six separate publications, printed in Funchal, 1859; and, lastly, *Os espectros de Catanea, cidade episcopal da Sicilia, ou as visões que apparecerão no século 17 ao seu vigário capitular. Por um crente nos Espectros* (Funchal, 1859).’

We possess the pamphlets cited by Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, but have no knowledge of the others, which must be extremely rare. They readily show that the pamphleteer was a match for the orator. Canon Nery was a contemporary of José Agostinho de Macedo, and it is to be supposed that *Besta Esfolada* and *Tripa virada* exerted a notable influence on the mind of our fellow Madeiran. It is hard to understand how the pen that wrote the remarkable poem *Oriente* and so many other marvels could also have produced those abominable diatribes. Allowing for the different circumstances of their surroundings, the same may be said of Canon Vicente Nery da Silva. He was a man of undeniable intellectual stature, but, carried away by his ardent and impetuous temperament, he said and wrote things that do little credit to his character, even though he was an austere priest, as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo calls him.

Vicente Nery was an enthusiastic champion of liberal ideas, and as such he was persecuted by the special judicial commission (*alçada*) that came to this island in 1828. He was arrested and sent to Lisbon, where he was held in confinement for some time.
Nery (lane)

It lay in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria and took its name from Canon Vicente Nery da Silva, who lived there. It was widened and is today a street linking Rua Bela de São Tiago with Estrada Conde de Carvalhal, under the name of Caminho do Acciaioly (‘Acciaioly road’).
Loquat (Eriobotrya japonica)

A tree of the rose family (Rosaceae), introduced to Madeira in 1846 or 1847 and today very common in the cultivated parts of the island. It fruits from February to June and is native to Japan. In some localities one also finds *Mespilus germanica*, likewise known by the name *nespereira*, whose fleshy fruits are harsh before picking but become sweet and tasty as they ripen.
Neto

This family surname derives from João Rodrigues Neto, who lived in a street that he had opened for the passage of the Corpus Christi procession and which, from his surname, came to be called Rua dos Netos. He held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in São Martinho and was the son of Rodrigo Álvaro Neto, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of Salamanca.
Netos (street)

It runs from Rua de São Pedro to the Ponte Nova (‘new bridge’) over the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). Formerly, however, it ended at Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), today Rua do Comércio, and the stretch bounded on the east by the said Ribeira de Santa Luzia was included in Rua da Ponte Nova.
This street was named after João Rodrigues Neto Calassa, who came from mainland Portugal, settled on this island and died here in 1531, having lived in the street that bears his name.
Neuville (Josefina)

Under the title *Memórias da minha vida. Recordações de minhas viagens*, a two-volume work written by Josefina Neuville was published in Lisbon in 1864. It caused a great sensation at the time, even producing a genuine and resounding scandal. Among the figures who appear at length in the work, the name of our distinguished fellow countryman Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, 2nd Viscount of Nogueiras, stands out.
Snow

Madeirans give the name *neve* (snow) to the hail that falls in the mountains during winter, but snow in flakes also appears in the high region of the island, where it is known to the people as *folhelho* (popular name for snowflakes). Snow is never seen below 1200 or 1300 metres, whereas hail has come down as far as 600 metres and may even appear at lower altitudes, although this is not frequent.
In our climate snow does not last long and generally melts after a few hours. It is hail that forms the extensive white sheets that sometimes cover the mountains for many days. See Hail.
Neves (Dr Cassiano das)

He was a lawyer in the city of Lamego when, in 1877, he published in Porto a pamphlet entitled *A sepultura Eclesiástica e os Suicidas*, which deals with the refusal of burial in the Angústias cemetery in Funchal to a man who had committed suicide in this city on 4 March 1877. It is a warm defence of the diocesan prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto. (See vol. I, pp. 71 and 130.)
Nichols (Thomas)
This Englishman, who lived in the Canary Islands around 1552 to 1561, wrote a brief description of Madeira, which was published in *Astley's General Collection of Voyages and Travels* of 1745.
Nobiliaries

Various works of genealogical research exist on the oldest and most distinguished Madeiran families, but we have no complete study of the subject. It is widely pursued today by patient and diligent researchers, and it is undoubtedly a valuable contribution to the history of a region, as well as a very considerable element in the general history of a country.

Among the Madeirans who have devoted themselves most notably to these studies, taking the families of this archipelago as the subject of their research, we must mention Henrique Henriques de Noronha, João Agostinho Pereira de Agrela and José Bettencourt da Câmara. The first is regarded as one of our most authoritative genealogists. Of José Bettencourt da Câmara, whom we have also discussed already (vol. I, p. 204), we must add that his most valuable genealogical writings, which he was preparing for the press, were regrettably lost in an unforeseen accident for which no one bears responsibility. It is said that the most extensive and complete work of this kind produced here was that of the second genealogist mentioned above (see vol. I, p. 20), the *Dicionário Popular* stating ‘that he wrote a collection of genealogical memoirs, which remain unpublished, in five volumes, in the possession of his heirs’. We recently learned with real satisfaction that this valuable manuscript was bought by the distinguished Azorean Ernesto do Canto, who donated it to the public library of the city of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), where it is at present. The publication of this work, once duly purged of the errors and gaps it contains, and also properly updated and enriched with various notes elucidating the text, would be an excellent service to the history of this archipelago and a valuable aid to those among us who devote themselves to certain kinds of historical research.

Apart from what is found on pages 514–533 and 846–851 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), in the *Attestado Genealogico dos ascendentes de José Francisco de Sant'Anna de Vasconcellos Moniz de Bettencourt*... (1857), which deals with only one Madeiran family, and in the *Noticia das cousas da ilha da Madeira desde o seu segundo descobrimento pelo Zargo*, which ends with the descendants of the discoverer and was published in the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) from December 1905 to January 1906, we know of nothing else in print on Madeiran genealogy.

The interesting work *Bibliographia Nobiliarchica Portugueza* by Eduardo Campos (Carcavelos) briefly describes almost all the genealogical works concerning this archipelago of which we are aware, as well as those mentioned by the annotator of the *Saudades*; indeed, some of them were unknown to us and are not listed in the annotations of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo. We shall transcribe verbatim the bibliographical entries from Eduardo Campos’s work, as a contribution towards a short study of this subject, which may perhaps interest some curious researcher into Madeiran genealogies and the history of our land:

‘António Bettencourt Perestrelo de Noronha. He was one of the leading noblemen of the city of Funchal. He lived in the 17th century. He wrote: *Genealogia das familias da ilha da Madeira*. MS. in folio. A copy of this work exists in the National Library in Lisbon (no. 296 of the manuscripts section, Pombaline Collection), made from the original by the author himself. MS. in folio of 178 ff., with index.

‘Diogo da Fonseca Acciaioli. He belonged to the lineage of the Acciaiolis, who in the 1st quarter of the 16th century went from Florence to the island of Madeira, where they founded the entail (*morgado*) of Nossa Senhora da Natividade (Our Lady of the Nativity), and from where they later moved to various places in Portugal. He was born in Castelo Branco, on a date I have been unable to discover. He wrote on various families, and in particular on: *Acciaiolis*. MS. in folio. ‘Henrique Henriques de Noronha … He wrote: *Nobiliario Genealogico das familias que passaram a viver na ilha da Madeira desde o tempo do seu descobrimento, que foy no anno de 1420*. MS. in folio, in 3 vols., which were owned by the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). At least two copies of this work exist (MSS. in folio): that of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), in 3 volumes, and that of the National Library in Lisbon (18th century), in 2 vols. of 280 and 283 ff., with index, nos 270 and 271 of the manuscripts section, Pombaline Collection. ‘*Árvore dos Henriques*. MS. in folio, of 7 unnumbered and 383 numbered pages. The 1st page, unnumbered, contains a frontispiece with warriors, surmounted by the coats of arms (*escudos*) of Dom Fernando Henriques and Dona Branca de Melo, 1st Counts of Alcáçovas, with the following words: *Horóscopo Genealogico da casa dos Henriques Senhores das Alcaçovas*. On the following page one reads: *Horoscopo Genealogico. Árvore da Casa de Henriques, Senhor das Alcaçovas. Em Portugal. Escripto por Henrique Henriques de Noronha, 1710*. This precious autograph, bound in crimson leather with gilt border and fillets, belongs to the library of the Count of Alcáçovas. ‘*Non plus ultra da Nobreza. Fidalgos da Ilha da Madeira, etc.*, 1717. A manuscript that belonged to the Viscount of Torre Bela, the author’s great-great-grandson (4th grandson), of which there is a copy that was owned by the genealogist João Carlos Feo Cardoso de Castelo Branco e Torres. ‘*Familia dos Freyres de Andrade, deduzida dos condes de Trava*. Dedicated to Bernardino Freire de Andrade. ‘*Memórias seculares e eclesiásticas para a composição da historia da Diocese do Funchal, na ilha da Madeira, distribuídas na forma do systema da Academia Real de Historia Portuguesa*. MS. in folio, of 255 ff. plus an appendix of 34 ff. It is considered a complete work on Madeiran history, according to p. 786 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’. ‘*Ramo da família dos Mirandas*. 1720. MS. in folio, of 14 pp. Bound. It belongs to the library of the Count of Castro. ‘João Agostinho Pereira de Agrela e Câmara. … He wrote: *Genealogia da ilha da Madeira*. MS. in folio, which covers almost all the old Madeiran families. In 1873 it was in the library of his eldest son, Pedro Agostinho de Agrela e Câmara. ‘João Pedro de Freitas Drumond … He wrote: *Arvores de Costados de Familias da ilha da Madeira*. MS. in folio, in 2 thick vols. containing 620 family trees. Unpublished autograph. It belongs to the library of Luís Ferraz de Barcelos. At least one copy of this work exists, which in 1873 was owned by Dr Gregório Francisco Perestrelo da Câmara, of the island of Madeira. ‘João Teixeira Soares de Sousa … A native of the Azores (1827–1882). He wrote: *Memórias históricas sobre os capitães-donatarios dos Açores e Madeira*. ‘José Bettencourt da Câmara. He wrote: *Famílias Madeirenses*. MS. in folio. ‘José Julião de França e Vasconcelos. Bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He was born in 1770 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Boaventura (‘good fortune’) and died in 1859 in the city of Funchal. He wrote: *Nobiliario Madeirense*. MS. in folio, owned in 1873 by the author’s heirs.’

Many books of lineages once existed here in Madeira. They dealt in particular with certain families and were kept for those families’ private use. We believe that most of these nobiliaries (book of noble genealogies) have been lost, chiefly because some of these families died out and because of the political events of 1828 to 1834, which scattered the owners and continuers of these genealogical works.

In the registry of the Ornelas family, whose present representative is Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (1921), there is a nobiliary from the first half of the 18th century entitled *Noticia breve mas verídica das ilustríssimas famílias d'Ornellas, Cabraes, Carvalhal Esmeraldo e outras a elas ligadas*, written in two folio volumes. We understand that Councillor Aires de Ornelas has already prepared for the press a genealogical work on the Madeiran Ornelas family (1921).

Father Fernando de Meneses Vaz, vicar of the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), has recently devoted himself to painstaking genealogical studies and is preparing a work for publication (1921).
Nobre (António)

Like so many other illustrious invalids, mortally stricken by advanced and incurable pulmonary tuberculosis, the poet António Nobre (1867–1900) came to Madeira in search of a miracle that the excellent mildness of the climate could no longer work for him. He died a few months after leaving this island.

António Nobre lived in Funchal from 3 February 1898 to 24 April 1899. He too sought our privileged climate, perhaps as a last resort to ease the ravages of the pulmonary tuberculosis that was mortally undermining him, after a stay in the mountains of Switzerland and a curative sea voyage to the United States of America.

Our distinguished fellow Madeiran Dr Alfredo de Freitas Leal, who died a few years ago and was a close friend of António Nobre, gives us some information about the poet’s arrival in his curious book *Coimbra nos Noventas...*, in the following expressive terms:

‘In Madeira I am going to meet an old friend, the great poet António Nobre... I then remembered that in the spring of that year, 1897, we had met in Lisbon and that he had asked me many questions about the advantages of Madeira’s climate for consumptives. And I remembered that, so as not to discourage him, I had told him of cases of cure and of the prolonged lives of consumptives who had settled in Madeira. António Nobre came to talk to me with an attempt at cheerfulness and said: “My dear Leal, I had the feeling I would never see you again. I followed your advice and here I am on your island. I have liked everyone in this land and all this lovely scenery immensely, but it seems to me that I have come to Madeira too late. You were right, if I were in the condition of those you told me about...” I felt a kind of inner tear that must not show in the eyes. . . and we went to talk at the “Casa Havanesa” (‘Havana house’)..., while I sensed that I would never see him again...’

What happened to António Nobre has happened countless times to so many other patients who, at an advanced stage of the gravest illnesses, hope to find in the mildness of our climate the miracle of a complete resurrection. On returning to Portugal, sad and disheartened, he uttered this bitter lament: ‘I come back worse than I went. A dreadful climate. Warm and humid, exactly the opposite of what my illness needs.’

With these poor, hopeless patients, doctors too bear the consequences of a delicate morbid state, which sometimes seeks revenge for the cruelty of fate in the harshest and most unwarranted reproaches. The poet’s attending physician in Madeira was Dr Vicente Cândido Machado, a distinguished clinician and a perfect gentleman, who could not entirely escape the bitter criticism of his illustrious patient, anguished by the unbearable torments of his illness and perhaps disillusioned by the deceptive hope that had fled from him for ever... He might then have written the desolate quatrain:
Various poets have come to Madeira / For the fame it has (for its sea airs) / Some soon to return to their hearths, / Others, alas for them! to remain here.

During the not quite fifteen months he lived in Funchal, António Nobre stayed at the former ‘Royal Hotel’, now the ‘Hotel Savoy’, at the ‘Pensão Almeida’, now the ‘Atlantic Hotel’, and in a house in the locality (*sítio*) of Boliqueme in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’). He may also have lived at the former ‘Pensão Scheffield’, to which he refers in a letter written in Lisbon on the eve of his departure for Madeira, or else at the ‘Quinta da Saudade’ (‘estate of longing’), where the sonnet ‘Sestança’ was written, dated 29 July 1898 and included on p. 33 of the book *Despedidas*.

In the hot season of 1899 he spent some time in the parish of Santo António, living in a small house in the locality of Boliqueme. It still stands there, with no appreciable change since the days when the illustrious and ill-starred poet lived in it.

At that time he was a frequent visitor to a house near the Quinta do Trapiche (‘sugar-mill estate’), where a family distinguished by both its virtues and its lineage was living for a time; he maintained relations of respectful and affectionate esteem with them. On the trunk of a tree in the garden of that house he carved the phrase ‘Sede de imensa luz como a dos pára-raios’ (‘A thirst for immense light, like that of lightning rods’), which survived there for some years, as we have already related at greater length in the book *Paróquia de Santo António*, published in 1929.

The eminent man of science and professor at the University of Porto, Dr Augusto de Nobre, who holds the memory of his brother, the illustrious author of *Só*, in the most fervent veneration, paid a moving visit to that modest house in September 1927, accompanied by Adolfo César de Noronha and by the writer of these unadorned lines. There he met the ‘hammock man’ who had served the poet, and learnt that the old maidservant who had looked after the invalid during the weeks he lived there was still alive. In view of her extreme poverty, he granted this former servant a monthly allowance, which on her death he transferred to one of her daughters, and which has continued unchanged to the present day over the fourteen years that have since passed.

As is well known, the only work António Nobre published in his lifetime was his principal one, *O Só*, issued in Paris in 1892; the volumes *Despedidas* (1898) and *Primeiros Versos* (1921) appeared posthumously. The second edition of *Despedidas* contains fifteen poems written in Madeira in 1897 and 1899: eleven sonnets and four other short poetic compositions.

At the session of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) on 24 October 1927, on the proposal of councillor (*vereador*) Manuel Nunes Farinha, now director of the customs house at Luanda, it was resolved that the square adjoining the Ponte Monumental (‘monumental bridge’), near the Hotel Atlântico, where the poet had lived, should be given the name of António Nobre.

In this square, known as the Jardim do Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’), the Funchal Municipal Council ceremonially unveiled a bust of the illustrious poet on 28 December 1941. On that occasion the distinguished teacher and writer Feliciano Soares delivered an exquisite speech, which has been published.

Because of the interest it holds for our subject, we shall now transcribe some passages from a fine article that the distinguished writer Dr Luís Vieira de Castro published in *O Jornal* (‘The Newspaper’) of 7 July 1936. ‘….. Among the unpublished letters to which I refer, six were written from Madeira, between 25 May 1898 and 8 April 1899 – a little less than a year before the death of the author of *Só*.

In January 1898 António Nobre declared himself ‘anxious to leave Lisbon’. His doctor sent him to Funchal. One concern held the family back: the cost of living in Madeira. To this António Nobre replied: as for the high cost of living in Madeira, the rumours spreading everywhere are little short of a crime… In Funchal one lives as in Foz, as here; there are hotels and boarding houses at every price’. And there was this detail, of great importance to a sick man: the doctors were cheap. In support of his opinion he cited an authoritative witness: ‘only yesterday I was with Dr Athias, a native of the island, who was my contemporary in Paris – and he gave me the best information. It is expensive for the English and for those who buy presents or lead a life of luxury’.

On 13 January António Nobre told his brother of his intention to come and live in an excellent boarding house – ‘on a *quinta* on the outskirts of the city of Funchal, belonging to Dona Carolina Scheffield’. That is – if he did not end up in the Canary Islands, where some believed he would do better to live.

But by May António Nobre was already in Madeira, and was even planning to visit British Guiana aboard the sailing ship *Felisberta* – of fond memory. It was a three-month voyage costing 100,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), during which, in the long calms on the high seas, the passengers would ‘have the boat lowered and go off fishing and rowing out to sea’… According to António Nobre, ‘that was how the natives of the island who fell ill were cured’.

While he had not yet sailed for Georgetown, António Nobre told his brother about the most remarkable things on the island… Thus one day he wrote: ‘In Madeira there is a kind of spider, called tarantulas, very curious, which write their name in the web they spin’. Besides the tarantulas, there were the young ladies of the island… ‘When I arrived from Portugal, a few days later almost all the Madeiran girls came here, in masks, to meet me’. And in the same letter he concluded his reflections thus: ‘This place is very curious and amusing because of the people here – young ladies whose sole existence consists of afternoon teas, lawn tennis and catching whatever fiancé comes their way’. How romantic this António Nobre was!

The young ladies of the island were, moreover, most kind to the Poet. He tells us so himself: ‘the ladies of Funchal have been very kind to me; they send me beef tea, custard, old wine, jelly, etc.’. What more could the elegant, sad recluse have wished for?… What afflicted António Nobre most, in his invalid’s despair, was the climate. ‘Madeira is dreadful for my constitution.’ He complained of everyone: ‘Only now has Dr Machado acknowledged it, after deceiving me for a year and a half’. In another letter he says further: ‘As soon as I reached the island, I fell ill. And ever since, I have been ill’. His resentment grew as his illness worsened: ‘the doctors here know how useless this climate is, but they cynically hide it from me, to keep their practice going. My doctor has been, and continues to be, my ruin’.

Finally António Nobre returned to Lisbon, because ‘it is in Madeira that he has no faith at all’. Poor poet! What remained of his life was a mixture of suffering and hopelessness. In March 1900 he wrote from Seixo (‘pebble’): ‘I am still unwell and cannot stay here any longer’. Nothing could cure his miseries any more! ‘The air is too strong. I shall die if I stay.’ The end of his life was fast approaching – and not even in the pains of his last agony could he count on the jelly and old wine of the young ladies of the island…’
Nobre da Veiga (Colonel Álvaro)

He was appointed civil governor of the district of Funchal by decree of 13 February 1922, taking up the post on 30 March of the following year and leaving for Lisbon shortly afterwards. Before becoming civil governor he was for some time Military Commander of Madeira.
Nobre (Dr Augusto)

This distinguished man of science is the brother of the poet António Nobre. He was born in Porto in 1865 and taught there as a university professor for many years. He has a large and valuable body of scientific work and has enriched the Madeiran bibliography with several notable studies, of which we shall mention ‘*Moluscos Testaceos marinhos do Arquipélago da Madeira*’, ‘*Moluscos Terrestres Fluviais e das Águas Salobras do Arquipélago da Madeira*’ and ‘*O Globicephalus nos Mares da Madeira*’.
Nóbrega

The family descends from Simão de Nóbrega, who founded the chapel of St Quiteria (*Santa Quitéria*) in Santo António (‘St Anthony’). In the time of the fifth captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, there lived in Madeira a certain Gaspar de Nóbrega, who was *ouvidor* (judicial officer of the donatary or the Crown) and lieutenant to that same donatary, and he may have given rise to another branch of the same family.
Nóbrega de Quintal (Luís de Ornelas)

He was born in Madeira on 18 June 1894 and attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), completing its course. He then went to the capital, where he was an editor of *A República*, and joined the Evolutionist Party. He was elected deputy for India in 1919, and in the same year he was appointed head of the 3rd department of the Directorate-General of Civil Administration of the Ministry of the Colonies, having previously been a 2nd officer of the same Directorate. For some time he was governor of the district of Cuanza Sul, for which he left in 1921.
Nóbrega (Januário Justiniano de)

He was born in this city on 25 February 1824 and died on 29 July 1866. He was the nephew of the distinguished poet Francisco Álvares de Nóbrega, known by the sobriquet of ‘Camões Pequeno’ (the Little Camões), with whom we have already dealt in this *Elucidário* (vol. 1, p. 53).

Januário de Nóbrega was appointed copying clerk of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government’s local civil office) on 30 June 1837 and 3rd clerk (*escrivão*) of the same Administration on 8 January 1857. In his day he enjoyed a great reputation as a journalist and showed a great aptitude for letters, in both prose and verse. On his literary work, we transcribe what the annotator of the *Saudades* says: ‘He contributed to the same periodicals as Dr António da Luz Pitta, as well as to *O Funchalense* and *Campo Neutro*, and in these, in *O Estudo* and in others he published many poems. He had the collection of his unpublished and published poems ready for the press, but destroyed it a few days before his death. He wrote a historical and statistical work on the archipelago of Madeira, of whose draft we possess fragments, given by his family, who assure us that the fair autograph copy is in the possession of Mr José Silvestre Ribeiro. The following work of his appeared posthumously: *Visita de Sua Magestade a Imperatriz do Brasil, viúva, Duqueza de Bragança, á ilha da Madeira, e fundação do Hospício da Serenissima Princesa D. Maria Amelia* (Madeira, 1867). He was endowed with uncommon talent and poetic gift, so much so that, with no more schooling than primary instruction, he was one of the best journalists of his time and an esteemed poet. In the last period of his life his natural clarity of mind became clouded; and, suspected of suicide, he died from a fall from a cliff by the sea on 28 July 1866.’

In 1860 the first part of a book entitled *Flores Agrestes, Poesias de João F. de Oliveira e Januario J. de Nobrega* was published in Funchal. The second part of this work never appeared; it certainly consisted of the collection of poems to which Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo refers, and which its author destroyed when he was seized by an attack of mental derangement that led him to suicide.
Nóbrega (João António de)

A century ago there was heavy emigration of Madeirans to British Guiana, and many settled in the city of Georgetown. Among them was João António de Nóbrega, a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), who in that city took the initiative in founding the first Catholic church built there, which was dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*). He left his name bound up with this great undertaking, earning the highest praise of the whole Portuguese colony in that British possession. João António de Nóbrega died in Georgetown on 20 March 1912.
Walnut (Juglans regia)

A tree of the family *Juglandaceae*, widely cultivated in Madeira. It is native to south-eastern Europe and Asia, and bears fruits that are green at first and later black, with a furrowed stone (the nut). The kernel is the edible part of these fruits, and in some countries a drying oil is extracted from it, used in the arts and in household economy. Walnut wood is much sought after for certain luxury work, and the bark of the tree yields a dark brown dye. An infusion of the leaves and of the outer part of the fruit (epicarp and part of the mesocarp) is taken internally to purify the blood.
Nogueiras (Viscount of)

Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Betencourt, 2nd Viscount of Nogueiras, was the son of Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Betencourt, 1st Viscount of Nogueiras, and of Dona Matilde Isabel de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Bettencourt, the distinguished writer the Viscountess of Nogueiras, whom we shall discuss in this *Elucidário*. He became very well known here, and still is, as the chief protagonist of the grave events that took place on the beach of this city on 8 March 1868, which we have already described at some length in the article Popular riots. On the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) he became even better known among his contemporaries for his acts of courage and daring, as the hero of adventurous exploits that caused a resounding stir at the time. His contemporaries and companions in carousing included the Marquis of Niza, the diplomat Soto Maior and others. Ramalho Ortigão in the *Farpas*, Bulhão Pato in his *Memórias*, Augusto Forjaz in *Livro das Feras*, Luís Palmeirim and still other authors refer to Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos at length.

Nevertheless, few people on this island perhaps know that Jacinto de Sant'Ana held a prominent place in politics as a brilliant journalist and distinguished parliamentarian; that he was an inspired and admired poet; that, as a senior official of the Ministry of Finance, he published three highly notable works on economic questions; and that, as a diplomat, he represented Portugal in the United States of America, holding a place of distinction among the foreign ministers accredited in Washington.

Jacinto de Sant'Ana was born in Funchal in 1824. After attending the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city, he went, while still very young, to Rio de Janeiro, where he stayed for some years. There he devoted himself to commerce and also cultivated letters, publishing in that city in 1848 the translation of a French novel under the title *Talismans*. Around that time he began to be known for his bohemian life and the strength of his arm.

Around 1850 he returned to his homeland and enrolled in the faculty of mathematics of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), devoting himself, it seems, more actively to politics than to study. That same year he published the pamphlet *O Grito do Povo*, a tirade against the government of the Cabrals, which won great renown throughout the country. When Marshal Saldanha raised the standard of revolt in 1851, Sant'Ana was one of the university students most enthusiastic about the movement, and one of those who did most to bring the regiments that had accompanied King Fernando to Coimbra over to the Duke of Saldanha.

When the revolution triumphed, he abandoned his course and threw himself openly into politics, fighting energetically in journalism while at the same time, as has been said somewhere, ‘he proved a fearless boxer, causing an uproar in the easy life of Lisbon with his devilry as a scatterer of crowds. For a long time in the rest of his life Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos struggled with these traditions and memories of his youth, even though he had become one of the most serious, grave and prudent men of his generation, mastering his temperament so that he should not seem to bring his old fighting habits into political debate.’

Among the various commissions and public offices he held were those of secretary-general of the districts of Aveiro and Faial, official and head of department in the Ministry of Finance, career consul, deputy and Portuguese minister in the United States of America. He devoted himself to the study of financial and economic matters, publishing in 1863 an important report on the consumption tax, and in 1870 another study on the same subject, a volume of 247 pages that was regarded at the time as a work of great value.

He was deputy for the constituencies of Viseu, the island of Pico (‘peak’) and others. In parliament he took an active part in many debates, proving a distinguished speaker who handled the subjects he addressed with great proficiency.

In the press, too, he proved a brilliant journalist, sustaining attacks and polemics that became celebrated. He was at times violent and rough in debate, which was in any case the natural consequence of his ardent and restless temperament. He contributed extensively to *O Português* and *A Revolução de Setembro*. It was one of these disputes that provoked a duel between Sant'Ana and our foremost journalist, Rodrigues de Sampaio. Sampaio, who did not practise arms, wounded his opponent, who was a great swordsman and an excellent shot.

Besides the writings already mentioned, Jacinto de Sant'Ana published a volume of verse entitled *Pátria e Amor*, with a long preface by Latino Coelho. Special mention is due to the series of articles he wrote in *A Revolução de Setembro* under the title *Cartas ao conde de Avila sobre materias eleitorais da ilha da Madeira*, articles that caused the greatest sensation.

In 1875 he was granted the title of Viscount of Nogueiras, and shortly afterwards he left for the United States as Portuguese minister. He lived there for about 12 years, never returning to his country. In Washington he won a prestigious name and was regarded as a distinguished and able diplomat. He died there on 24 January 1888 and lies buried there.

Our readers will be interested to learn of some of Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos’s adventures, and so we shall draw on what Bulhão Pato published on the subject in his *Memórias* and Augusto Forjaz in *Livres das Féras*.
The author of *Paquita* credits him with no fewer than seven duels in Paris, one of them with a fencing master, in which ‘Sant'Ana was badly wounded and the fencing master was at death’s door.’

‘After six years of a whirlwind of adventures,’ the same author continues, ‘his father’s leniency wore thin, and he sent him off to Rio de Janeiro on a little wooden horse, which, as people thought at the time, was an effective remedy. He could already have said of him what the Count of Mirabeau said of the great orator: “My son – the hurricane!”’ ‘What Jacinto de Vasconcelos did in Rio de Janeiro was extraordinary!

Once, in a café, grappling with the *capoeiras*, after hurling stone jars and bottles like cannonballs and smashing benches to splinters, he went for the stone tables and threw them at his enemies! Only a few years ago the café owner was still showing the broken stones to customers who arrived from Portugal.

‘Another time – and this was the last in Brazil – Sant'Ana was watching a bullfight. A mulatto snatched from a young Portuguese man’s hands a dart bearing our flag, threw it to the ground and trampled it as an insult. Sant'Ana leapt into the arena, felled the mulatto with a kick and cleared the ring! The police came; he routed the police! As he left the ring, a troop of cavalry fell upon him: Sant'Ana, still clutching a pitchfork, threw himself at the cavalry! The commander drew a pistol from its holster and told him he would fire. Sant'Ana replied: “That will not go off!” And it did not! More troops came, more cavalry. Sant'Ana was finally arrested and ordered to leave, in the third canto of his Odyssey! The first had taken place in Coimbra, the second in Paris, the third in the land of the Holy Cross (*Santa Cruz*)! The fourth was to take place in Lisbon. ‘This man, who could clear a fairground, was an elegant gentleman of exquisite breeding, talent and lively wit! ‘…. In June 1851 Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos was appointed secretary-general of Horta, and the following year transferred to Aveiro. ‘Before he left, one night – it was summer, and Sant'Ana was going through a period of heroic calm – we went to the Martinho for ices. We gathered round a table: Mendes Leal, A. Pedro Lopes de Mendonça, José Maria d'Andrade Ferreira, Luís de Vasconcelos, author of a drama entitled *a Cruz* which was a success at the Dona Maria II theatre, António Correia Heredia and I. The last two are still standing; the others have all fallen. ‘Shortly afterwards a ship’s captain came in at the door, a man well known at that time in the Baixa set, accompanied by a tall, broad-shouldered, strong man. He was a German. The seaman had suffered a setback at Sant'Ana’s hands in Rio de Janeiro and still had the bone stuck in his throat, but he came up very amiably and introduced the German, who spoke French fluently. Sant'Ana received him with his characteristic courtesy. I, however, noticed something constrained about him. With his lynx’s eye he saw that the seafarer, a crooked sort, had brought the other along as a mastiff. After a few words Jacinto took his leave and was about to go out when the German suddenly grabbed the collar of his frock coat and tore it! Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos took a step back and punched him: the man went down flat! He got up, his face badly swollen, and charged wildly. Another punch, and the colossus was on the ground. He got up yet again and returned to the attack… Then Sant'Ana, in a surge of fury, seized him and hurled him over the table that stood beneath the large mirror! This time the aggressor lost consciousness. When he came to, he left, staggering, on the seaman’s arm. ‘Sant'Ana sat down panting, his nose pinched, his moustache bristling and his eyes flashing. António Heredia, who had known his fellow countryman, friend and kinsman since childhood, was nonetheless astonished at this act of bull-like strength! ‘After entering politics, Sant'Ana fought two duels: one with a Frenchman named Clavel, with swords, and the other with A. Rodrigues Sampaio, with pistols. Sampaio fired first; he hit him, and Sant'Ana very nearly did not leave the field alive. ‘Rodrigues Sampaio often said in my presence: “If my bullet had gone in just a tiny bit further, Sant'Ana would have been a dead man, and I would have carried a shadow on my heart all my life.”’

In the volume *Livres das Feras* by Augusto Forjaz we read the following: ‘Another episode in which he took part occurred in December 1859. The royal commissioner of the São Carlos theatre, Dom Pedro Brito do Rio, had engaged the two rival singers Marcellina Lotti della Santa and Fortunata Tedesco de Franco. One night, when the opera *Lucrécia Bórgia* was announced, the two ladies deliberately declared themselves ill. Factions formed, and Tedesco won over most of the theatre’s regular audience and almost the entire Lisbon press. Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos took up Lotti’s defence in the *Revolução de Setembro*. On the night of the 19th Tedesco reappeared; the great majority gave her an ovation, intending to receive the rival lady with hostility. Dom Pedro do Rio and his wife, Dona Maria Krus, were in a box with Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos, who calmly went down to the stalls. Approaching the group of demonstrators, he asked them to abandon the planned hostile demonstration. Only four refused, pleading the freedom of their heels. Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos then warned them with the utmost courtesy: “You gentlemen say you are within your rights to stamp your feet in protest. That may be so. But you gentlemen express yourselves with your feet, and I am accustomed to express myself with my arms. So use your freedom, and in the first interval we shall settle accounts between feet and hands.” ‘Marcelina Lotti della Santa was not booed. ‘At that time there was also published in Lisbon a satirical newspaper called *O Asmodeu*, which spared no unpleasant remarks about Dom Pedro do Rio, an honourable man and therefore incapable of bowing to the whims of the artists and of a certain public. Some spectators in the stalls declared themselves for or against the artists according to how generously they rewarded their applause. This demand of a particular public was called the *molhadura* [TN: literally ‘wetting’, i.e. a tip or bribe], and the royal commissioner could not prevent it. The editor of *O Asmodeu*, Marciano de Azevedo, took the side of those making demands, boasting that there was no watchdog that could frighten him. Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos took the phrase as aimed at himself, linking it to the failed demonstration against Marcellina Lotti. Seeking out Marciano de Azevedo in the stalls, he demanded an explanation. In the midst of the uproar the editor of *O Asmodeu* slipped away to the stage and shut himself in the dressing room of the dancer Emilia Bellina, who was extremely ugly and was said to be his mistress. Sant’Anna broke down the door with a punch, but when that fearsome-looking woman appeared before him he burst out laughing, adding that Marciano de Azevedo was already well punished by his relations with such a scarecrow....’ ‘His consular and diplomatic career was remarkable, and the country owed him no small interest and many benefits, above all in every matter relating to commercial expansion. I believe there exist in the archives of the ministries of foreign affairs and of finance some unpublished reports which well deserved to be published, since they served as the basis for several treaties and conventions... But since it is true, as it is, that those who do most are least appreciated, the patriotic work of Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos went unrecognised, to which his withdrawal from our political world also greatly contributed. ‘So long an absence had brought oblivion. His fine athletic figure had faded from memory through his lengthy stay abroad. When one day he returned for a visit, none of the younger generation recognised the brilliant poet, the incisive journalist, the distinguished orator who from 1851 to 1872 had attracted attention by his talent, his elegance, his humour and the episodes of his bravery. Jacintho Augusto Sant’Ana e Vasconcellos, Commander of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) and of the Order of Charles III of Spain, nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and 2nd Viscount of Nogueiras since 2 July 1875, found his old companions and best friends in the peace of the grave. His hair was turning white; his body was beginning to stoop. The circles of his former society had disappeared, giving him the impression of being a stranger, sorely tried by the reverses of Fortune. One night in January, leaving the Dona Maria II theatre, he found himself alone. For him, who had known so many friends and enemies, devoted to the former and intimidating the latter, that isolation sent shivers down his spine. He went into the Rossio café, then in the former Mattos Moreira shop, in the building on the corner of Largo de Camões. He sat down and ordered tea and toast. At the table opposite, two rakes of the day, strapping, quarrelsome young men, burst out laughing. To them, knocking back glasses of cognac, that old man drinking tea and eating toast was a figure of fun. Sant’Ana e Vasconcellos smiled. Then he clapped his hands and ordered the waiter: “Bring two more teas and two more rounds of toast.” The young men’s mirth grew. What a magnificent bumpkin they had found in that bourgeois! When the waiter carried out the order and returned with the tray, Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos told him, in a loud voice, to place it on the table of the impertinent would-be dandies. In the packed room silence fell, for an imminent clash was foreseen, all the more so since the two young athletes, mocking the harmless waiter, had pushed the tray away with contempt. Sant’Ana e Vasconcellos rose and approached. His voice rang out like a bugle of war: “You gentlemen laughed because I take tea, being an old man. Now I am going to laugh at you gentlemen, who have not yet taken it, being a pair of overgrown children. My name is Sant’Anna e Vasconcellos. So, whether you like it or not, you must swallow that tea.” And under his menacing gaze the two obeyed, resigned.’
Nogueiras (Viscountess of)

Dona Matilde Isabel de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Bettencourt, Viscountess of Nogueiras, was one of the most respected Madeiran ladies, admired for her eminent virtues and priceless qualities of heart. She was also a most graceful mind, a rare and gifted talent who, in any setting other than Madeira, would surely have won an illustrious name in the literary history of our country.

She was the daughter of José Joaquim de Vasconcelos and Dona Francisca Emília Teles de Meneses, both of whom belonged to the most distinguished Madeiran families, and she was born in this city on 14 March 1805.

She showed an early talent and a remarkable inclination for study, so it was easy to give her a careful education. Over the years this was enriched by a constant love of work, which she gave up only when persistent illness and the crushing weight of her years made it wholly impossible.

She took up letters early, and they were always one of the greatest delights of her mind; her first literary works already revealed a great intelligence and a remarkable aptitude for various literary genres. She paid worthy tribute to the Muses, writing inspired verse, above all in her youth, and later devoted herself entirely to prose, in which she proved a writer of rare merit.

Besides many articles and poems published in various newspapers, she wrote the novel *Soldado de Aljubarrota* and the educational work *Diálogo entre uma avó e sua neta*, both published in Lisbon; the latter book was approved by the Higher Council of Public Instruction (*Conselho Superior de Instrução Pública*) for use in state schools. She is also the author of the *Nota ao mês de Maio* that accompanies the translation of Ovid’s *Fastos* made by the Viscount of Castilho.

The Viscountess of Nogueiras had a thorough knowledge of English and French, and from the latter she translated several works into our language. Of these, *Genoveva* by Lamartine and *As Castelãs de Roussilon* and *Vida de Santa Mónica* by Bougaud were published.

She undertook the French version of Alexandre Herculano’s well-known historical novel *Eurico o Presbítero*, which was published in Paris in 1888 on the initiative of Prince Nicholas of Oldenburg, who had had the opportunity to read the manuscript and had found the translation excellent.

She may have published other works of which we have no knowledge, and we are told that she left some valuable literary works unpublished, not counting the writings scattered through various periodicals.

The illustrious lady never gave up study, and almost to the end of her long life her literary pursuits were the dearest pastime of her enlightened mind. The translation of the *Vida de Santa Mónica*, perhaps her last literary work, was made at a very advanced age, when few are still able to devote themselves to exhausting intellectual labours. At times she suffered illnesses that forced her into inactivity, but she knew how to make use of the time, devoting herself to composing and translating her books, and so found in the work of the mind relief from her physical sufferings.

Her most kindly heart was often wrung by very cruel sorrows, and certainly not the least of them was that caused by the riotous events in this city on 8 March 1868, in which her son, Jacinto de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, later Viscount of Nogueiras, whom we have already discussed, nearly lost his life. A factious and intolerant politics inflamed passions and drove an excited crowd to the most deplorable excesses. As our distinguished fellow countryman approached the landing place, he was forced to retreat hastily to the vessel that had brought him from the capital, not without grave danger to his life, and some of the common people were killed. These were hours of terrible anguish for a considerable part of the city’s population, and many who lived through those events still keep them vivid in their memory. The Viscountess of Nogueiras, who truly adored her son, suffered this harsh blow, and afterwards that of seeing her husband succumb, unable to withstand the shock of so great a grief.

The great poet Bulhão Pato, writing about Jacinto Sant'Ana in his *Memorias*, refers to the Viscountess of Nogueiras in the following terms: ‘I met Sant'Ana’s mother, the Viscountess of Nogueiras, Dona Matilde, when I was twenty, during some months I spent in Madeira with a childhood friend, the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). ‘She was then in the prime of life. Education, character, beauty of face and grace of figure, distinction in everything, and a superior talent made this lady one of the most enchanting beings I have ever known’! ‘She composed verses of admirable delicacy and feeling. She wrote delightful prose. In a wider milieu she would have been a writer of the first rank. Sant'Ana adored his mother, and how often I saw that fearless, impetuous man weeping like a child as he read her letters, which he then kept in a sacred casket with the fervour of the purest love.’ The illustrious lady outlived by one year her son, who died as Portugal’s minister in Washington, but her granddaughters, out of compassion, hid the fatal news from her, and she died without having learnt of it, on 23 December 1888, at the advanced age of 83.
Nola (António da)

This Genoese navigator was in Madeira in 1460, according to the account of the voyages of Diogo Gomes. ‘Then,’ says Gomes, ‘we sighted one of the Canary Islands, called Palma, and from there we went to the island of Madeira. As I was anxious to return to Portugal, I set out and was driven by a contrary wind to the Azores, but António de Nola stayed behind in Madeira and, making use of a more favourable wind, reached Portugal before me.’
Street names

On 19 June 1890, on the proposal of the councillor (*vereador*) Dr José Joaquim de Freitas, the Council resolved to give the streets to be opened in future the names of various illustrious sons of this land. This resolution, sensible as it was, has seldom been obeyed, as anyone can easily see by walking through the city and reading the names with which various public thoroughfares have been christened or renamed in recent times.

For the name of a deceased citizen to appear on a street corner, something more is required, in our view, than the councillors’ fondness for his memory: he must also, while alive, have rendered some service to the country or to his homeland. Without this, such a tribute becomes ridiculous both for the person honoured and for those who pay it.

Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, the learned annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), the man whose historical works made him so worthy of the gratitude of Madeirans, has no street named after him in this city. This is despite the fact that, at the session of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of 27 January 1898, the president of that body declared his wish to confer with his colleagues on the tribute the Municipality ought to pay to that learned professor. Many other illustrious sons of this land, such as Baltasar Dias, João António Monteiro, Nicolau Bettencourt Pita, Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos, Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça, Francisco de Andrade, Justino António de Freitas, José Ferreira Pestana, Jaime Moniz, etc., etc., are likewise forgotten, through the ignorance or the lack of spirit and of justice of the administrative bodies!

It would not be advisable to undo everything deserving of criticism or ridicule that has been done over the last thirty or forty years in the naming of streets, so as not to add to the confusion that already exists on this matter today (1921). We do, however, consider it most desirable that, from now on, whatever was resolved at the council meeting of 19 June 1890 should be carried out whenever a street or public road is opened or inaugurated.

Municipal councils should exercise with the greatest circumspection the right granted to them to baptise or confirm the streets and roads of the municipality (*concelho*). They should do so not only to avoid giving an unflattering impression of their intelligence and judgement, but also to spare their residents harm; we have heard many of them complain bitterly about the arbitrary replacement of old names of public roads with others that there is no reason to adopt or perpetuate (1921).
Norborough
He was in Madeira in 1669 and discusses the island in the *Voyage to the Straits of Magellan*.
Norça (Tamus edulis)

A native climbing plant of the yam family (Dioscoreaceae), cultivated at Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’) and Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) for its edible tubers. In the wild it has been found only at Garajau (‘tern’). Frutuoso mentions it on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it is now completely extinct. It has dioecious, purple flowers and heart-shaped, acuminate leaves with 9 veins.
Norman (Captain Francisco N.)
An English botanist who collected plants in Madeira in 1860 and after whom Richard Thomas Lowe named the genus *Normania*, later included in the genus *Solanum*.
Norman (Dr Alfred Merle)

A distinguished English zoologist, now deceased, who visited Madeira in 1897 and 1908. The English naturalist Randolph Kirkpatrick (see that entry) named after him *Merlia Normani*, a curious sponge found by the Madeiran naturalist Adolfo de Noronha in the seas off Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Works: *The Land Isopoda of Madeira* (1899) and *The Polyzoa of Madeira and Neighbouring Islands* (*Linnean's Society's Journ.-Zool.*, XXX, 1909).
Noronha

There are three branches of this family in Madeira: one descended from Dom João and Dom Garcia de Noronha, sons of Dom Garcia Henriques (see Henriques); another from Dona Maria de Noronha, who was married to João Gonçalves da Câmara, second captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal; and a third descended from Dona Luísa Agostinha de Noronha, daughter of Manuel Freire de Noronha. We believe the second branch to be the most noble.

Manuel de Noronha, son of the aforementioned João Gonçalves da Câmara and Dona Maria de Noronha, received as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) the land that later became the Quinta dos Padres da Companhia (‘the Jesuit fathers’ estate’).
Noronha (Adolfo César de)

He was born in Funchal on 9 September 1873, the son of Augusto de Nóbrega Noronha and Dona Adelaide da Silva de Noronha. He attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of Funchal and took some courses at the former Polytechnic School (*Escola Politécnica*) of Lisbon and Polytechnic Academy of Porto. On 11 December 1914 he was appointed librarian of the Funchal Municipal Library (*Biblioteca Municipal do Funchal*).
He made meteorological observations on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) from 1900 to 1902, and at that time and later he also carried out various studies of natural history there.

In 1904 he sent Dr Openheim, a German palaeontologist, various fossil corals from the archipelago, and shortly afterwards he sent Dr Bohm the fossil shells of the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*). These collections were duly studied, to the great benefit of science. The Serbian palaeontologist Joksimowitsch also received a fine collection of fossils gathered on Porto Santo; in an excellent study he published on it, he recorded 106 distinct forms, counting species and varieties.

Adolfo de Noronha has also devoted himself to the study of the ichthyology, ornithology, malacology and carcinology of the archipelago. We also owe him various observations on the geology of Porto Santo and Selvagem Grande (‘great wild island’), which Dr Gagel made use of in his works on those islands. The interesting *Merlia Normani*, to which we have already referred on p. 413 of vol. I of this Elucidário, was collected by him in the seas off Porto Santo. From there, too, came many of the bryozoans he sent to Dr Norman, who recorded them in a work published in the *Journal of the Linnean Society*.

He wrote a pamphlet entitled *Carta aberta ao Ex.m° Sr. Governador Civil do Funchal* (Lisbon, 1911) and is the author of the interesting articles entitled ‘Braguinha’, ‘Canais de lava’, ‘Carcinologia’, ‘Charamba’ and ‘Conchas’, published in the 1st volume of this Elucidário, as well as of the great majority of the entries on the fishes and birds of the archipelago found up to p. 341 of the same volume.

The following species and varieties commemorate the name of Adolfo de Noronha: *Schizoporella Noronhai*, an abyssal bryozoan; *Pecten Noronhai* and *Spondylus Noronhai*, fossil shells; and *Echium candicans* var. *Noronhae*, a plant of the borage family from the interior of Madeira. When it was thought to be a coral, *Merlia Normani* bore the name *Noronha scalariformis*.

Adolfo de Noronha was appointed director of the Funchal Municipal Library in 1928 and at once began to campaign for the creation of a Natural History Museum (*Museu de Ciências Naturais*). He was its most strenuous and persevering champion, both in the press and among those who could lend their prestige and influence to the project. He always linked this idea with that of acquiring a suitable building to house the Municipal Library and the attached science museum, with sections for art, archaeology, ethnology, etc. With the authorisation of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), he spent some months in Lisbon arranging the issue of a postage stamp to pay for these planned premises. The scheme succeeded in full, and that public department is now housed in a fine, spacious building known as the São Pedro Palace (‘St Peter’), the former manor house of the Counts of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). It is beyond dispute that the realisation of this important improvement is due chiefly to Adolfo de Noronha. When he retired from his public duties, the Council paid him a well-deserved tribute, in which various official bodies joined, by unveiling a stone inscription placed in one of the rooms of the Museum.
It is only right to reproduce the words that we set down in the columns of the Funchal daily press on the occasion of this well-merited mark of esteem and high regard.

‘Despite the undeniable merits that so notably distinguish him, Mr Adolfo César de Noronha is still unknown to many Madeirans, because of the retiring modesty behind which he has sought to hide, and which a persistent illness has made more marked in recent years. Were it not so, he would have produced an important and highly regarded body of work, especially on various branches of Madeiran zoology. For this he has in abundance the most thorough knowledge of the subject, a deep love of study and scientific research, and an easy, elegant style in presenting whatever matters he might treat.

Mr Adolfo de Noronha has published several pamphlets and some dozens of articles, which excel above all in the clarity with which the subject is presented and the depth of knowledge they reveal. At the same time they show a remarkable gift for the most accessible popularisation of science.

Those who know closely the studies to which Mr Noronha has devoted himself, and who have appreciated his valuable writings, are unanimous in affirming the refined scientific integrity that marks all his work, into which he always puts the most exacting scruple and the most conscientious application.

It is no wonder that we heard a distinguished university professor, one of our most eminent men of science, say of Mr Adolfo C. de Noronha in particular these well-deserved words: “he has every qualification to hold a chair with distinction at any university in the country.

It is much to be regretted that the pressing circumstances of life did not allow this distinguished man of science to display, in fruitful and profitable work, the full breadth of his learning and the exquisite gifts of his exceptional intellect.
And gilding these priceless gifts of mind and deep scientific culture, there stand out above all the truest qualities of character, so abundantly known in Madeiran society.’
Noronha (António Manuel de)

The royal letter (*carta régia*) appointing him Governor and Captain-General of Madeira is dated 26 March 1822, and he took office on 22 April of the same year. He asked to be relieved of his post on 4 February 1823, pleading ill health. He was governor of this archipelago when John VI dissolved the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) and revoked the Constitution, proclaiming himself absolute king. He was succeeded by Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro.
In 1852 he was granted the title of Viscount of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), a parish (*freguesia*) and town (*vila*) on this island.
Noronha (Dom Manuel de)

Simão de Noronha, second son of the captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) João Gonçalves da Câmara and Dona Maria de Noronha, and grandson of the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco, took the name Simão Gonçalves da Câmara when he inherited the captaincy of Funchal on the death of his elder brother. He was the third donatary (*donatário*) of this captaincy, and we have already dealt with him at some length on p. 20 ff. of vol. I of this work. This third captain-donatary and his first wife, Dona Joana Valente, were the parents of Manuel de Noronha, who must have been born in the old town (*vila*) of Funchal in the last quarter of the 15th century.
We know nothing of his life until the moment when we find him raised to the rank of prelate and already holding important and honourable offices.

It seems that, having gone to Rome on a mission entrusted to him by the monarch, he received his investiture as a prelate there and was appointed to an important office in the Vatican. It is not to be believed that the great Leo X, at a time when so many prelates shone for their talents and virtues, would have summoned a foreigner to his side had he not recognised in him merits and qualities that set him apart from his contemporaries. One of his biographers states that Dom Manuel de Noronha even became a nuncio, an office then of the greatest responsibility because of the political role it had to play at the courts where it represented the Roman pontiff. We do not know, however, in which European capital he held this post, nor any circumstances of how he conducted himself in so difficult and delicate a mission.

We know that, on the death of the pope or for some other reason, he left the capital of the Catholic world and settled in Portugal. In 1547 he was appointed bishop of Lamego, then regarded as one of the foremost sees of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). The chroniclers of that bishopric are unanimous in counting Dom Manuel de Noronha among its most distinguished prelates. His name is linked to works of note, such as the building of several churches and above all of the chapel of São Nicolau (St Nicholas) in the cloister of the Cathedral, to which he left substantial revenues for the upkeep of daily worship, with the attached obligation of maintaining a college for eight aspirants to the ecclesiastical life. He endowed the city with various improvements, chief among them the channelling of drinking water. He reformed many points of ecclesiastical discipline and convened a diocesan council. He died on 23 September 1569 and lies buried in the chapel of São Nicolau, which he founded and where the following epitaph can be read: ‘Here lies Dom Manuel de Noronha, formerly bishop of Lamego, son of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, captain of the Island of Madeira, and of Dona Joana Valente, his wife; he died on 23 September 1569.’
Noronha (Henrique Henriques de)
See Henriques de Noronha (Henrique).
Noronha (João Rodrigues de)

He was the son of the 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, and brother of Dom Manuel de Noronha, Bishop of Lamego, whom we have dealt with in this *Elucidário*. He must have been born in the last quarter of the 15th century. The chronicles that deal with our affairs in India speak of João Rodrigues de Noronha with the highest praise for the acts of heroism he performed there. The author of the *Saudades* says of him: ‘...he was captain of Hormuz in India in the time of the governor Dom Duarte de Menezes, his brother-in-law, which was in the year 1521: and before he entered the fortress he had been captain of the sea off the coast of Diu, and served the King well until he became captain of Hormuz, where he seized the tyrant Raesxarafo and kept him under close guard in the fortress until the arrival of the Viceroy, his brother-in-law Dom Duarte de Menezes.’
Norte da Ilha

The name ‘Norte da Ilha’ (‘North of the Island’) is generally given to the northern coast of Madeira, which stretches from Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’) to Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’) – that is, from the parish (*freguesia*) of Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’) to the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’). It takes in all the parishes of the municipalities (*concelhos*) of Porto Moniz, São Vicente and Santana, together with the parish of Porto da Cruz in the municipality of Machico. See the north coast (*Costa do Norte*).
Norton de Matos (General)

General Norton de Matos, High Commissioner (*alto comissário*) of the Republic in Angola, called at Funchal on 3 April 1921 aboard the *Moçambique*. He was greeted on board by the civil governor, the military commander, the secretary-general, etc. After landing he joined the procession of the Unknown Soldier, and then travelled by special train to Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), where the deputy Captain Américo Olavo de Azevedo gave a luncheon in his honour, attended also by the civil governor and others.

The return journey was made in Monte sledges (*carros do Monte*), and the industrialist Henrique Hinton offered tea to all the guests at his residence. The general re-embarked at about half past four, when military honours were paid to General Norton de Matos by an infantry detachment under the command of a captain (1921).
Our Lady of Help (chapel)

Almost beside the road that leads from the Ponte Monumental (‘monumental bridge’) to the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) stands the chapel of Our Lady of Help (*Nossa Senhora da Ajuda*). It was built by Fernão Favila on the estate he owned in São Martinho (‘St Martin’), and he made it the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). This Fernão Favila was a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and fought valiantly in Africa, afterwards settling on this island, where he married Beatriz Pires. Other genealogists, however, state that it was António Favila, son of Fernão Favila, who founded the entail (*morgado*) of the Piornais (‘broom thickets’), with its seat in the chapel of Ajuda, where he lies buried, having died in October 1545. Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira, as owner of this chapel, carried out major restorations there in 1876, and it was blessed on 16 August of that year.

In 1916 the owner of this chapel, Manuel José de Perestrelo Favila Vieira, published a pamphlet of 15 pages entitled *A Interdição da capela de N. S. da Ajuda na freguesia de São Martinho. Antecedentes e exposição de factos.* It deals with the interdict placed on the chapel by the diocesan prelate, Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, because the prelate had been refused a visit to the chapel during the canonical visitation he made to the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho in 1916. A few months later the interdict was lifted and the chapel was restored to worship.
Our Lady of Joy (chapel)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Roque (‘St Roch’), at the locality (*sítio*) known as Alegria (‘joy’), lies the *quinta* (country estate) of the same name, with a house and a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Alegria (Our Lady of Joy), both belonging to the family of the Counts of Torre Bela. The chapel was founded in 1609 by Francisco de Abreu. A feast is held there every year and draws large numbers of people from the surrounding area.
Nossa Senhora da Anunciação (chapel)
See Lombo dos Canhas (p. 279). The seat of the parish was housed in this chapel after having been in the chapel of São Tiago.
Presentation of Our Lady (chapel)

The locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) known today as Lombo da Apresentação (‘ridge of the Presentation’) took its name from the chapel that stood there, dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Apresentação (Our Lady of the Presentation). It was founded by Isabel Fernandes Tavares in 1524 on the entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*) she owned there. The chapel later passed to the house of the Heredia family. Beside the chapel stood a sumptuous residence of which not even traces now remain.
Our Lady of the Good Hour (chapels)

The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora stands in the locality (*sítio*) of Torre (‘tower’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), and is the property of the Countess of Torre Bela (1921). It was founded by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António Correia Bettencourt Berenguer. It had its own private chaplain. A chapel of the same name, ‘above this city’, was built in 1726 by Captain António de Carvalho Drumond and his wife Dona Inácia Micaela Henriques, the deed of endowment being dated 22 May 1726.
In the locality of Fajã (‘coastal flat’), in the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora was built, of which only a few ruins remain.
Our Lady of the Good Death (chapel)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) there is a chapel with the dedication of Our Lady of the Good Death (*Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte*), which has been closed to worship for some years.

There was a chapel of the same name in the parish of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), founded by Francisco Fernandes and Brásia Fernandes in a year unknown to us. In the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’), in the locality of Atouguia, there was also a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Good Death, which we have found mentioned somewhere under the name of Nossa Senhora da Piedade. Of this last chapel, built in 1661 and founded by Francisco Homem de Couto, not even traces remain today, but the locality where it stood is still called Boa Morte.
In the parish of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), Custódio Nunes da Costa founded a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Good Death in the year 1666.
Our Lady of the Good News (chapel)
In the locality (*sítio*) of this name, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Boa Nova, founded in 1701 by Eusébio da Silva Barros.
Our Lady of the Good Voyage (chapels)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Carne Azeda (‘sour meat’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), Manuel Pestana Teixeira and his wife Francisca Xavier da Conceição founded a chapel of this dedication in 1711; it was inspected for the celebration of acts of worship on 28 June of the same year. In the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), in the street that still bears the name of Boa Viagem, stood a chapel of the same dedication, founded by Bento da Veiga. We do not know the date of its foundation, but we know that it was a very old building. We have read somewhere that it was a building of interesting and characteristic construction, as was a house adjoining it. It is said that the first customs house, and later the first public butcher’s shop (*açougue*) of the municipality (*concelho*), were installed in this house. The deconsecrated chapel that stands today in Rua da Boa Viagem is not the chapel of this dedication to which we refer here.
Our Lady of the Chair (chapel)

A chapel of this name once stood in the locality (*sítio*) of Cadeirinha (‘little chair’), within the present boundaries of the parish (*freguesia*) of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’); it would have had another dedication, since forgotten over time.
In the same parish there was also a chapel consecrated to Our Lady, known as the chapel of Porta da Quinta (Estate Gate).
Our Lady of Candlemas (chapel)

A chapel with this dedication stands in the locality (*sítio*) of the same name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Tábua. Its original construction is attributed to one of the early settlers, surnamed Medeiros, and it was rebuilt in a year unknown to us. It was the centre of an old pilgrimage.
Immaculate Conception (chapels)

There was once in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), founded by Tristão de França Bettencourt in a year unknown to us. In 1906 a chapel with the same patron saint was built in the Largo das Babosas (‘aloes’), in the same parish. It was founded to commemorate the jubilee celebrations held in Madeira to mark the fiftieth anniversary of the definition of the dogma of the Immaculate Conception. The main part of these festivities was an imposing and brilliant religious procession that set out from the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) and made its way to the Largo da Fonte (‘spring’), in the parish of Monte, where an open-air Mass was celebrated. On that occasion the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto delivered one of his most stirring and enthusiastic speeches. It was then that the idea arose of building the Chapel-Monument, which was carried out two years later; the diocesan bishop had first appointed a committee to raise the necessary donations and to direct the construction. Commander João Bernardino Gomes, vice-president of the committee, donated the land for the building of this graceful church and the image of the Virgin that stands on its altar, and there were other generous gifts for the ornamentation and decoration of the chapel.
