Justice demands that we record here that it was Commander Luís de Bettencourt Miranda who contributed most notably to the construction of the Chapel-Monument. To his diligent and persevering efforts is owed not only the completion of all the work but also the embellishment of the site, which became an exceedingly picturesque spot and an obligatory place to visit for all who go to the enchanting, paradisal resort of Monte. The pamphlet *Nossa Senhora do Monte*, by Father Joaquim Plácido Pereira, contains a detailed account of the jubilee celebrations and the founding of this chapel.

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), a short distance from the parish church, stands the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, which is very old and is presumed to have been built by the people. Over time it has undergone various repairs, and only about twelve years ago major work was carried out there for its preservation and interior decoration. This chapel, which is not particularly small, is in the care of the fishing community, which maintains and supports worship in it.

In Rua da Carreira (‘track’), in this city, between Rua do Conde de Canavial and Rua da Alegria (‘joy’), stands the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception. It was founded in 1770 by Captain Luís Bettencourt de Albuquerque e Freitas next to his residence, and was blessed on 7 December of that year. In the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), at a spot unknown to us, Rui Dias de Aguiar and his wife Leonor de Ornelas de Andrade founded in 1662 a chapel of the same dedication, whose deed of endowment was dated 11 December of the same year.

On the property he owned in the parish of São Roque (‘St Roch’), Canon António Lopes de Andrade founded in 1700 a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, its deed of endowment being dated 8 July of the same year. Diogo Afonso de Aguiar founded in 1688 a chapel in the parish of Tabua (‘bulrush’), likewise dedicated to Our Lady, which he had built very close to the shore. It was rebuilt in 1910 by José da Silva Novita and was blessed by the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto on 31 July of the same year.

The chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception in the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) was the seat of an important entailed estate (*morgadio*), which covered one of the largest properties on this island. A few years ago its last owner sold it off in plots, and the chapel and the adjoining manor house were also sold. The chapel was founded by André de França e Andrade around 1672.

The chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception in the locality (*sítio*) of Amoreiras (‘mulberry trees’), in the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), is of very recent construction. It was blessed on 27 December 1911 and was founded by the parish priest José Marcelino de Freitas with donations from the faithful.

On the bank of the Ribeira da Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’), close to its mouth, in the parish of Arco da Calheta, Gonçalo Fernandes built a chapel consecrated to Our Lady and made it the seat of an entailed estate, with the obligation of a daily Mass and the recitation of a responsory over his grave every day ‘for as long as the world shall last’, according to the relevant clause of his will.

Regarding this Gonçalo Fernandes, several genealogists say what is summarised in a note to the *Saudades*, in the following terms: ‘When peace had been made by King Afonso V and the Excellent Lady had retired to the convent, he was sent to the Island and forbidden to leave it. Every year the King sent him a ship with everything needed for his household; he was treated with great consideration, although his parents were never known. In his chapel he set up as his arms the Portuguese *quinas* in saltire, and on his tomb he had carved a boy with his face resting on his left hand and his elbow on a skull, pointing with his right hand to the following inscription taken from the Book of Wisdom: *Sic et nos nati continuo desivimus esse* (So we also, as soon as we were born, ceased to be). It is said that elsewhere he had a mule painted, kicking at Fortune.’

According to a manuscript from the beginning of the 19th century that we have seen, the chapel at Arco da Calheta ‘was an exquisite work’, and the nobiliary of H. H. de Noronha says that the founder adorned it ‘with great splendour and fine paintings’.

Gonçalo Fernandes died on 15 June 1539 and lies buried in this chapel, as already stated. He was succeeded in the entailed estate (*morgadio*) by his eldest son, Pedro Gonçalves de Andrade. This entailed house (*casa vinculada*) passed to the Freitas family of Madalena (‘Magdalene’), whose last representative was the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Nuno de Freitas de Lomelino.

Also dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception are a chapel in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), founded around 1600 by Bartolomeu Telo Moniz de Meneses, and another in the parish of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), rebuilt in 1754 by Nuno de Freitas da Silva; the year of its original construction is unknown.
In the parish of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), in the locality (*sítio*) of Conceição (‘Conception’), there is a chapel with the same dedication, of which we have no further information.

In the locality of Fajã dos Padres (‘the priests’ flat’), on the coast of the parish of Campanário (‘bell tower’), there was once a small chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, which belonged to the Jesuits and was destroyed by Algerian corsairs in 1626.

With the same dedication, the Viscount of Cacongo had a chapel built in 1930 on his *quinta* (country estate) of Choupana (‘hut’), in the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’); it was blessed on 12 October of that year.

Also with this dedication, Captain José Sotero e Silva founded a chapel in the locality of Igreja, in the parish of Monte, which its present owner, José de Freitas Belmonte, had completed and opened for worship.
Immaculate Conception of the Islet (chapel)

The Fort of Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, Fort of the Islet) had its own chapel, built by order of the royal decree (alvará régio) of 9 November 1682. Its first chaplain was Father José de Andrade, appointed by royal decree (*alvará*) of 31 July 1692. The chapel must therefore have been built between these two dates; its patron saint was Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception.
Our Lady of Consolation (chapels)

Álvaro de Ornelas, who greatly distinguished himself as a navigator and whom his contemporaries called ‘the Great’, held vast lands granted as *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’). They stretched from the brook of Garajau (‘tern’) to the Ribeira do Porto Novo (‘new harbour’), and from the sea to the uplands. It was there that in 1499 he founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*), whose administration always passed from father to son and whose present representative is Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (1921). The founder laid down as a clause that this entailed house (*casa vinculada*) ‘might be pledged only to ransom the administrator who, in the service of God and the king, should be held captive by the infidels.’ It was around 1591 that Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos founded, on lands of this entail (*morgado*), the chapel of Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*), which still exists and belongs to the founder’s family. Together with its adjoining manor house, it became the seat of this entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela). It was to this house that the governor and captain-general Sá Pereira exiled in 1774 the holder of the entail, Agostinho António de Ornelas, who died there shortly afterwards, on 5 August of the same year. He was buried in the said chapel, and the marble of his family vault bears this inscription: ‘Tomb of Agostinho António de Ornellas e Vasconcellos, *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the Royal Household, ninth lord of this entail. 1718 to 1774.’ This chapel stands in the locality (*sítio*) still called Quinta (‘estate’) today, which takes its name from the manor house adjoining the chapel, mentioned above.

Beside the road that runs alongside the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), almost at the point where it meets the Caminho da Torrinha (‘little tower’), stands the chapel of Our Lady of Consolation. Here, in the summer season, the novenas and the accompanying feast are celebrated with great splendour and draw large crowds. We do not know the year of its construction, but we presume that it dates from the end of the 16th century. It was small, and in 1861 it was suitably rebuilt and enlarged, being blessed in July of that year. The altar front, a fine old mosaic, belonged to the church of the Convent of St Francis. This chapel formed part of the parish of Monte (‘hill’) before the creation of the parish of Santa Luzia, within whose bounds it now lies.

The chapel of Our Lady of Consolation in the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’) is more commonly known as the chapel of Foro (‘ground rent’), because it stands in the locality of that name. It was entailed, and we do not know the year of its construction. On 1 November each year a feast is held there, together with a well-attended *arraial* (open-air popular festival at a church feast) for the people of the surrounding area. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says that a chapel dedicated to St James the Less once existed in the locality of Foro; we do not know whether it is the same as the one mentioned above or a different one.
Near the parish church of the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) stood the chapel of Our Lady of Consolation, founded by Isabel de Abreu at the beginning of the 16th century.
Nossa Senhora da Esperança (chapel)

In 1744 Father Manuel de Nóbrega founded a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Esperança at the locality (*sítio*) of Vale Formoso (‘beautiful valley’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’); the deed of endowment is dated 11 December of the same year. The chapel was demolished many years ago.

There was a chapel with the same dedication in the parish of São Roque (‘St Roch’). It was very old and was the focus of an ancient pilgrimage. Lieutenant-Colonel A. Artur Sarmento published a detailed historical account of this chapel in a pamphlet.
Nossa Senhora da Estrela (chapel)

‘And there, on another *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) belonging to the same daughter (Beatriz Gonçalves), on a high spot with a fine view of the sea and the land, the same captain (Zarco) traced with his own hand a church of Our Lady of the Star (*Nossa Senhora da Estrela*), and said that he would leave this church strongly commended to his children, because he had long wished to build it in a place of his liking.’ Such, as Gaspar Frutuoso describes it, is the origin of this chapel’s foundation. It was Diogo Cabral (see Cabral), husband of Dona Beatriz Gonçalves da Câmara, daughter of João Gonçalves Zarco, who fulfilled the discoverer’s wishes by having this chapel built; it was the head of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he founded. Diogo Cabral died on 15 December 1486 and was buried in the chapel he had founded. When it was already in an advanced state of ruin, some decades ago, the tombstone covering Diogo Cabral’s mortal remains was moved to the parish cemetery and placed over an ordinary grave. On that occasion the epitaph and Cabral’s coats of arms were either scratched out of the slab, or else it was laid face down, hiding the inscription from visitors. The founder’s bones, however, remained among the rubble of the chapel, and today not even traces of those ruins can be found.

The parish was installed in the Estrela (‘star’) chapel, which was not small, when it was created, and remained there for a good many years. We have found somewhere that this chapel was built in 1479 and rebuilt in 1560 by Rui de Sousa, great-grandson of its founder Diogo Cabral.

From an old register of visitation orders (*livro de provimentos*) of the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), which survived the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803, we know that in 1632 the chapel of Our Lady of the Star existed in that parish, though we do not know where it stood.
Our Lady of Fátima

At the locality (*sítio*) of Pico do Galo (‘cockerel peak’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), Father António de Abreu Vieira founded a chapel with this dedication, paid for with donations collected in the parish. It was blessed on 11 October 1931.
Our Lady of Faith (chapels)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’) stood a chapel with this dedication, founded by Manuel Gonçalves Lisboa in 1668. It gave its name to the locality (*sítio*) where it was built.

At the locality of Mirante da Terra do Baptista (‘lookout of Baptista’s land’), in the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Diogo Dias de Ornelas e Vasconcellos founded a chapel with the same dedication. The deed of endowment is dated 25 November 1825, and the inspection for the licence to hold services in it took place on 11 August 1826. It no longer exists.
Our Lady of Glory (chapel)

Henrique de Bettencourt founded this chapel in 1599 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’). In 1823 its administrator was the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Luís Correia. It was restored a few years ago by the Countess of Torre Bela, to whom it belongs (1921).
Our Lady of Grace (chapels)

The chapel of Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*) was one of the oldest on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). At the beginning of the 19th century, under the auspices of Manuel Inácio de Avelar Brotero, governor of that island, its reconstruction was begun because of its ruinous state, but it was never completed. It must have been of some size, and it is said to have been a miniature copy of a famous sanctuary in Italy. Its peculiarity was an octagonal interior. The walls still stand, partly demolished by the action of time and the vandalism of men.
In the town (*vila*) of Machico there is a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Grace. All we know of it is that it is quite old and that it was rebuilt by its confraternity in 1750.
A chapel with the same dedication existed in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), built in 1520 by Pedro Álvares de Almada.
In the parish of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral), ‘situated beside the Ribeirinho of this city’, the precentor Domingos de Andrade e Alvarenga built a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Grace in 1699.
Our Lady of the Incarnation (chapel)

According to the annotator of the *Saudades*, there was a chapel with this dedication at the locality (*sítio*) of Louros (‘laurels’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), founded by Diogo Bernardes Branco in 1656.

In the south of the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), on the boundary with the parish of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação. The date 1671 over its portico must be that of its construction. It belonged to the holder of the entail (*morgado*) João José de Ornelas Cabral and is now the property of Dona Maria Teresa Figueira. See Convent of the Incarnation (1-306).
Our Lady of Light

She was adopted as patron of studies in Madeira at the end of the third or the beginning of the last quarter of the 18th century, and for that reason the students held an annual feast in her honour which lasted, we believe, until 1855. On that occasion there was an *outeiro* (poetic gathering with improvised verse), attended by the island’s poets.

In September 1880 this feast, which had not been held for 25 years, took place in the College church (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), but without the participation of the pupils of the lyceum (state secondary school), who in earlier times had been its chief promoters.
Nossa Senhora da Madre de Deus (chapels)
See Madre de Deus (‘Mother of God’), p. 326.
Nativity of Our Lady (chapel)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Faial, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), on the *quinta* (country estate) of that name, stands the chapel of the Nativity of Our Lady (*Nossa Senhora da Natividade*), or of Faial, as it is more commonly known. It was built on the lands of the entail founded by Simão Acciaioly, who died in 1544. The chapel was built by Zenobio Acciaioly, his son and successor in the administration of the entailed estate (*morgadio*).
Our Lady of Nazaré (chapels)

There is a chapel of this name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), which was the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by the two sisters Antónia de Cristo and Leonarda do Horto in favour of their nephew Francisco Friz de Barros Maciel. It was he who built the chapel, around the third or last quarter of the 17th century. In 1694 he had the mortal remains of his uncle, Father Inácio Barbosa da Silva, moved there; he was the brother of the founders of the entail and had been one of the owners of the property on which the chapel stood. Having fallen into great ruin, the chapel was rebuilt in 1830 by António João Barbosa de Matos e Câmara, a descendant of the founders.

There is a chapel of the same name in the parish of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), founded in 1757 by Maria do Rosário Henriques, widow of Pedro Bernardes Cardeiro. Concerning her, or another owner of this chapel, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo gives the following curious information: ‘It is a tradition among the fishermen of Câmara de Lobos that at the beginning of this century the lady of the entail (*morgada*) of Nazaré, armed with a small sword, would take up her position on the height where the chapel stands; she would hail the fishing boats as they came into the landing place; and, by privilege or abuse, she would take from them whatever fish she wanted and pay for it as she saw fit.’
There is also, in the parish of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), in the locality (*sítio*) called Nazaré, a chapel with this dedication, founded by Martim Vaz in the year 1627.
Our Lady of Peace (chapel)

It was founded in 1621 by the priest Jerónimo da Silva and stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’). See Monuments (*Monumentos*) and Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’).
Our Lady of the Rock (chapel)

The chapel of this dedication was built in 1657 on land then belonging to the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’). Its founders were Duarte Mendes de Miranda and his wife Dona Beatriz de Vasconcelos, who endowed it by public deed of 20 September of the same year. The earthquake of 1748 left the chapel badly damaged, and it was soon rebuilt by António José Espínola, grandson of the founders, who moved it to a more suitable site near the original building.
Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (chapel)

The chapel of Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*) stands in Rua da Penha de França, in this city. It was founded in 1622 by António Dantas and rebuilt in 1712. It became the centre of a well-attended pilgrimage, with pilgrims coming from various parts of the island. Attached to it was a house for those who came from the more distant parishes to fulfil their vows to Our Lady of the Crag. In 1755 major repairs were carried out on it, paid for by the donations of the faithful. Around 1818 it was incorporated into national property (*bens nacionais*) and given to the diocesan bishop, and the pilgrims’ house was then turned into a summer residence for the prelates of this diocese. At that time the locality (*sítio*) was still regarded as a suburb of the city. For some time, for reasons unknown to us, it ceased to belong to the mitre; in 1838 it passed back into the possession of the prelates. Some years later repairs were made there at the expense of the State, which gave rise to a question and a debate in parliament. The Penha chapel had its own chaplain, and for many years its worship was maintained by the house of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’).

Several of the prelates have lived there for a time, and Bishop Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto made the little house his permanent home, drawn by the pleasantness of the spot, its position overlooking the sea and its distance from the centre and noise of the city. The prelate Dom José da Costa Torres was living there when, on 6 October 1796, he found the house surrounded by troops and was forced to embark at once, ‘without taking leave, says a manuscript of the time, of any person, nor of the Most Holy Sacrament; and to this day the reason for this contrived embarkation by night and by back doors is unknown’. From 27 November 1840 to 9 January 1841 our great poet Castilho (see that entry) lived in this house. He had come to the island to accompany his brother, Canon Augusto Frederico de Castilho, who died there on 30 December and lies buried in the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery. In his historical eulogy of his brother, delivered at the Royal Conservatory of Lisbon, Castilho referred to his stay in Madeira, and in particular to the house adjoining the chapel, in these terms: ‘... a dwelling in a lovely suburb of the city, the parochial residence of Nossa Senhora da Penha de França; a humble house, cheerful and solitary like that of our hermitage, and not only neighbour to its church but embraced by it, shaped as if on purpose for both kinds of health: for that of the body through the freshness of the air, the tranquillity of the spot and the nearness of the sea, which bathes the feet of its modest garden and almost mirrors its banana trees; for that of the spirit through all these same circumstances of the beauty and grandeur of creation and through the worship of the Virgin...’

The prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who lived there for more than thirty years, left as his last testamentary wish that his mortal remains be ‘transferred in a small urn to the churchyard of the Penha chapel, in front of and next to the main door, covered by a plain stone slab on which his name shall be engraved, with the dates of his birth and death, a cross at the top and below the letters P. N. A. M., to beg from the faithful who pass by at least a pious *Requiem aeternam*.’

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), Luís Gonçalves Mercador built a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Peña de Francia in 1620, and in 1685 a chapel with the same dedication was built in the locality of Fazenda (‘farm’), in the parish of Faial. This latter chapel has the peculiarity of being hollowed out and built within a single solitary block of soft cut stone (cantaria mole). The walls, the ceiling, the floor, the altar and the portico were all carved from the enormous stone, forming a single piece. It was founded by António Teixeira, 5th-generation grandson of the discoverer Tristão Vaz Teixeira, and the deed of endowment is dated 13 August 1685.

An interesting article published in the *Correio da Madeira* (‘Madeira Courier’) of 22 September 1922, which we believe to be the work of Father Fernando de Meneses Vaz, contains some curious details about this chapel. The most striking of them is that it was originally intended to serve as a small mosque for a number of Moorish slaves. The author of the article gives the chapel as founded by Irvão Teixeira in the first quarter of the 16th century, whereas the date we have recorded above was taken from an official document kept in the archives of the Diocesan Chancery (*Câmara Eclesiástica*) of the diocese.

On the *quinta* (country estate) known as Quinta dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), in the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’), the physician Manuel Fernandes Gomes had a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Peña de Francia built in 1682, endowing it by public deed of 15 June of the same year.
In 1670 Maria do Rosário Arvelos founded a chapel with the same dedication in the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).
Our Lady of Pity (chapels)

A chapel with this dedication stands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), on top of a steep cliff overlooking the sea. Anyone rounding the Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’) at once sees the little chapel gleaming white on the summit of the craggy hill. In former times it had an adjoining house to shelter the devout who came there on pilgrimage. We have read somewhere that, according to tradition, the chapel was built in fulfilment of a vow by sailors who, seeing their ship about to be dashed to pieces on the rocks of the coast, promised to raise a small chapel dedicated to the Blessed Virgin (*Santíssima Virgem*) on the crest of the hill. It is also said to have been founded by Garcia Moniz, the first administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Caniçal, or by one of his successors. Many years ago it belonged to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of São Gil (‘St Giles’), whose manor house stood at Calçada (‘paved way’), in the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).
Every year an unusual religious procession makes its way to this chapel; we have already described it in the article on the parish of Caniçal.

In 1800 Father Manuel Gonçalves Henriques built a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*) beside his residence in the locality (*sítio*) of Caldeira (‘cauldron’), in the parish of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). He endowed it, in accordance with canon law, by a public deed of 3 April of that year. It is today (1921) the property of Father António Rodrigues Diniz Henriques.

Another chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Pity once stood in the locality called Vargem de Baixo (‘lower meadow’), in the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’). It was built in 1657 by Captain António Moniz de Meneses and his wife, Dona Catarina de Meneses. Within the lands of the entailed estate of Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’), on the Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry), in the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), at the place called Jangão, a small chapel with the same dedication was built in a year we cannot establish. In 1777 the administrator of that entailed estate (*vínculo*), Francisco de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, enlarged and improved the chapel, and on 3 August of that year permission was granted for it to be blessed anew. On 12 October 1879 the Archbishop of Goa, Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, blessed the chapel again and celebrated Mass in it, after the repairs carried out at the orders of his brother, the peer of the realm Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 15th administrator of the said entailed estate of Vale da Bica.

The small square formed by Rua da Carreira (now Dr. Vieira) and Rua das Pretas (now Câmara Pestana) is still known today as Largo da Igrejinha (‘little church square’). The name comes from a chapel or small church dedicated to Our Lady of Pity that once stood there. Domingos Rodrigues Garcês had it built in 1613, and the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) demolished it in 1836.

One of the notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) mentions the chapel of Our Lady of Pity that existed in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), built in 1722 by João Rodrigues Oliva. In the parish of Monte (‘hill’), Dona Escolástica Lomelino de Vasconcelos, widow of João de Freitas da Silva, founded a chapel with the same dedication in 1728. Its deed of endowment and record of inspection are dated 6 and 25 June of that year.
Francisco Álvaro Homem built a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Pity in the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) around 1641, but it has long since disappeared.

On the *quinta* (country estate) of Cruzes, with its door opening onto the square of the same name, stands the chapel of Our Lady of Pity, founded by Francisco Esmeraldo Henriques, who owned the *quinta*. The date 1692 is carved on the portico, but the deed of endowment is dated 25 May 1695, and on 14 June of that year the chapel was inspected so that divine services could be celebrated there. It at present (1921) contains a burial vault said to hold the mortal remains of Urbano Lomelino (see Lomelino), founder of the convent of Our Lady of Pity (see that entry) in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz.

In the locality (*sítio*) of Paço (‘manor house’), in the parish of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), Father Manuel de Andrade had a chapel consecrated to Our Lady of Pity built in 1784; its deed of endowment is dated 16 December of the same year. In the parish of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’) there is also a chapel with the same dedication, founded in 1736 by João de Couto Cardoso, holder of the entail (*morgado*), next to the houses where he lived. One of his successors, Francisco João de Vasconcelos Couto Cardoso, had it rebuilt in 1825 because of its advanced state of ruin, enlarging it and moving it to the vicinity of the old chapel. It has served as the parish church. Its present owner (1921) is Francisco João de Vasconcelos, a direct descendant of its founder and restorer.

A chapel with the same dedication existed in the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’). It belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by António Teixeira, nicknamed the Rei Pequeno (‘Little King’) (see Teixeira). It was one of the oldest in the captaincy of Machico and was already badly ruined in the first quarter of the 16th century. One of the later administrators of this chapel, Manuel de Carvalho Valdavesso, had it rebuilt in 1734, and permission to bless it was granted on 8 September of the same year. In 1814, when Tristão Teixeira de Vasconcelos Saavedra was its administrator, it was closed because of its ruinous state, and its church furnishings were taken to the parish church, where the old altarpiece that stood on the chapel’s altar can still be seen.
Our Lady of Quietude (chapel)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Alecrins (‘rosemary bushes’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), stood the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Quietação, of which today not even traces remain. It was better known as the chapel of Alecrins, and in a reference to it made in 1680 it was even called the church of Alecrins, despite its cramped dimensions. The unusual name Quietação comes from the fact that the chapel’s patron saint was the mystery representing the peace and tranquillity that the Blessed Virgin (*Santíssima Virgem*) enjoyed, in the retirement of the house of Nazaré (‘Nazareth’), in the company of the Child Jesus and the patriarch St Joseph.

It was Lourenço de Matos Coutinho and his wife Dona Mariana de Ornelas de Vasconcelos who founded this chapel in 1670, in fulfilment of a vow they had made to the Blessed Virgin. They built it on the *quinta* (country estate) they owned in the locality of Alecrins, which they had inherited from his father and her father-in-law, the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Bento de Matos Coutinho, who in turn had acquired it by purchase from Simão Gonçalves da Câmara and Jorge da Câmara Esmeraldo. It was on this *quinta* and in this chapel that in 1677 its founder instituted the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Alecrins. The present representative of this entailed estate is Dr Rui Bettencourt da Câmara (1921).
Our Lady of Salvation (chapels)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Moinhos (‘mills’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), on land belonging to the Figueiroa de Albuquerque family, the ruins of the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Salvação can still be seen; we have read somewhere that it was founded in 1614 by Francisco Morais de Aguiar. In Funchal there was a chapel of the same name, ‘in a yard of their houses where they live at the fountains’, built by João de Bettencourt Henriques and his wife Dona Antónia de Castelbranco.
Our Lady of Health (chapel)

On Rua da Saúde, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), near Largo do Marquês, the chapel of this dedication still stands, although it is not open for worship. It was founded by Dr Pedro Cardoso Valdavesso and his wife Dona Maria Gondim in 1659, the deed of endowment being dated 4 January of that year.
Our Lady of Health of the Mount of Olives (chapel)

A note in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that this chapel, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), had been built on the entailed estate (*morgadio*) instituted by Pedro Lopes de Vasconcelos in 1675. It no longer exists, and we do not know where it stood.
Our Lady of Life (chapels)

In 1679 Manuel Valente founded a chantry (capela) dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Vida (Our Lady of Life) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’); we do not know where it stood. On a small rise overlooking the sea stands a chapel of the same dedication, founded by Inês Teixeira in a year unknown to us. It is in the locality (*sítio*) of Fajã do Mar (‘flat by the sea’).
Our Lady of Victory (chapel)

On the coast road that leads from Funchal to Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), on the left bank of the Ribeira dos Socorridos, stands the chantry (capela) of Nossa Senhora da Vitória (Our Lady of Victory), at the far edge of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’). The annotator of the *Saudades* gives 1594 as the year of its construction and says that it was founded by Jean de Béthencourt on the lands of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he established there. It was rebuilt in a year we cannot determine, and roughly forty years ago it was enlarged and underwent considerable repairs.
Our Lady of Sorrows (chapel)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), at the locality (*sítio*) to which it gave its name, Diogo da Costa de Quintal built a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Sorrows (*Nossa Senhora das Angústias*) in 1662. There stands the *quinta* (country estate) of Nossa Senhora das Angústias, better known as the Quinta Lambert, which has a chapel of this dedication, perhaps a rebuilding of the old chapel that existed at that locality. Princess Maria Amélia lived at this *quinta* and died there on 4 February 1853.
Nossa Senhora das Brotas (chapel)
See vol. 1, p. 174.
Our Lady of Sorrows

The parish cemeteries of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), and the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery in Funchal (now closed), each have their own chapel for the religious services held there, all dedicated to Our Lady of Sorrows (*Nossa Senhora das Dores*). The first was built in the last quarter of the 19th century and the last in 1844.

The chapel of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*), which serves the patients cared for there, is also dedicated to Our Lady of Sorrows. Its exquisite image was given by the ill-fated Prince Maximilian, later Emperor of Mexico, who was barbarously shot there in 1867.
Our Lady of Wonders (chapel)

At the *quinta* (country estate) of Maravilhas, in the square of the same name, Diogo Bettencourt Correia and his wife, Dona Catarina da Silva, founded a chapel with this dedication in 1657, with a deed of endowment dated 18 August of the same year. It was rebuilt in 1736 by Dona Mariana da Silva and was inspected so that Mass could be celebrated in it on 20 November of that year. It no longer exists.
A chapel with the same dedication once stood in the locality (*sítio*) of Passo (‘pass’) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Madalena do Mar (‘Magdalene by the sea’).
Gaspar Betencourt de Andrade founded another in 1658 in the parish of São Pedro.
Our Lady of Ransom (chapel)

In 1650 Captain Gaspar Homem de El-Rei and his wife, Dona Isabel Florença, founded a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom (*Nossa Senhora das Mercês*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’); it stood in the locality (*sítio*) called Florenças.
Our Lady of the Snows (chapel)

Referring to this chapel, Frutuoso says: ‘... there is a church of Our Lady of the Snows (*Nossa Senhora das Neves*), within sight of Funchal, on a headland called Garajau (‘tern’), one *légua* before reaching the city.’ It is very old and one of the few 16th-century chapels still standing, although it has undergone some alterations over time. It was founded by João Afonso Mealheiro and his wife Catarina de Sá. Speaking of him, Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo says: ‘... he was one of the first settlers of the island of Madeira, and held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Ribeira Seca, in São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), as far as Caniço (‘reed’). His wife Catarina de Sá, or Pires, founded the entail of Neves and left it to her nephew, the *almoxarife* João Cabral; but on behalf of the Royal Treasury the entail was sold to pay off a deficit in his accounts; it was bought by Lopo Machado de Góis, and his son Bartolomeu Machado founded it anew.’

We have read somewhere that in 1692 this chapel passed into the possession of Dona Guiomar Castelo Branco, daughter of Gaspar Vilela and wife of António Correia. In the last quarter of the 19th century the English merchant John Blandy bought this chapel and the adjoining lands, which bordered on the magnificent Palheiro Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s barn’) estate, also acquired by the same merchant. John Blandy carried out major repairs to the chapel and enlarged its churchyard.
The chapel of Neves gave its name to the locality (*sítio*), was the seat of a curacy (*curato*), and the parish of São Gonçalo was housed in it when that parish was created.

On p. 80 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), the ingenuous Gaspar Frutuoso tells of the struggle that a cleric had with the devil near this chapel, when the devil tried to hurl the churchman into the sea from the heights of the cliff of Garajau.
Our Lady of Prayers (chapels)

On the altar of the chapel of Preces (‘prayers’) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’) one can read the date 1708, which is probably that of its construction. We believe that this chapel was an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela); in 1770 its administrator was Captain Rodrigo da Costa, and in 1796 the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Joaquim Manuel de França. The chapel and the adjoining house were rebuilt in 1856 by their then owner, Dona Joana de Albuquerque e França, who died there on 12 February 1884. This chapel gave its name to the locality (*sítio*) in which it was built.

Father Francisco de Canha e Mendonça had the chapel of Our Lady of Prayers (*Nossa Senhora das Preces*) built in the parish of Câmara de Lobos, in the locality that later took this name. Its foundation dates from 1683. It still exists, but remains closed to worship.
In the parish of Machico there is another chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Prayers. We do not know when it was built; it was rebuilt by António Tiago da Silva in 1884.
Our Lady of the Virtues (chapel)

In the locality (*sítio*) and *quinta* (country estate) of Virtudes (‘virtues’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), Francisco de Vasconcelos Bettencourt built in 1661 a chantry (capela) with the dedication of Nossa Senhora das Virtudes (Our Lady of the Virtues).
Our Lady of Victories (chapel)
In the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico there was once a chantry (capela) dedicated to Nossa Senhora das Vitórias (Our Lady of Victories), built in 1749.
Our Lady of Bethlehem (chapel)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) there was a chapel, now extinct, of Our Lady of Bethlehem (*Nossa Senhora de Belém*), which stood in the locality (*sítio*) of that name. It was founded in 1649 by Gaspar Vasconcelos Henriques and his wife Dona Bernardina de Carvalho, and the deed by which they made the endowment of this chapel is dated 9 February of the same year. When it fell into ruin, it was rebuilt in 1758 by Dom Francisco Inácio Telo de Meneses, a descendant of the founders. The new chapel was built a short distance from the old one, next to the residence, with which it communicated internally. In the locality of Referta (‘refuge’), at Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), there was a chapel with the dedication of Our Lady of Bethlehem, which was later renamed Our Lady of Succour (*Nossa Senhora do Socorro*). See Our Lady of Succour (chapels).
Our Lady of Jesus (chapel)

‘The first chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora de Jesus that we have found’, says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, ‘is the one founded by João Bettencourt de Atouguia in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), in 1656.’
Our Lady of Protection (chapels)

At the locality (*sítio*) of Álamos (‘poplars’) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’) stands the chapel of Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*), which is in a fair state of repair; the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass is celebrated there from time to time. The chapel lies on the boundary between this parish and that of São Roque, at the locality known as Água de Mel (‘honey water’), a name once shared by a large tract of land belonging to both parishes. On the part of this locality within the bounds of Santo António stood the chapel, a large dwelling house and other outbuildings, which formed the seat of the old entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) known as Água de Mel.

The annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) gives 1698 as the year this chapel was founded, but we are inclined to believe that it is much older, perhaps even contemporary with the founding of the entail (*morgado*), which dates from the last quarter of the 15th century. It is certain, however, that Bartolomeu de Sá Machado, administrator of this entail, had it built – or rather, perhaps, rebuilt – in that same year of 1698. (See Bettencourt, I-139.)

Dona Luísa de Mendonça, widow of José de Seixas, had a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Protection built in 1712 in the parish of São Martinho (‘St Martin’); it belongs to the heirs of the Sauvayres entail-holders. In the parish of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) there is also a chapel of the same dedication, which gave its name to the locality where it stands. The feast celebrated there every year is very well attended. Francisco Franco also founded a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Protection in the parish of Machico in 1692.
Our Lady of Good Dispatch (chapel)

This chapel stands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’). It was founded in 1672 by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Jerónimo de Atouguia Bettencourt and his wife Dona Catarina Espranger, the deed of endowment being dated 27 June of that year. In 1762 it was rebuilt by Father Francisco Nicolau de Brito, the chapel then belonging to a brother of this priest. Today it belongs to Feliciano de Brito Correia, representative of this family (1921).
Our Lady of Good Success (chapels)

At the far western edge of the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), in the locality (*sítio*) of Garachico, stands the chapel of Our Lady of Good Success (*Nossa Senhora do Bom Sucesso*), which is considered to belong to the latter of these parishes. The chapel had the peculiarity that its altar stood within the boundaries of one of these parishes while its door opened onto land of the other, neighbouring parish. It seems that in times more remote from ours doubts arose as to which parish the chapel should belong to, and there were even conflicts of jurisdiction between the respective parish priests. It was built in the early 17th century by Manuel João Ferreira, especially so that his son, Father Francisco Luís Ferreira, could say Mass in it. Some years ago it was enlarged by the inhabitants of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town).

There is also a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Good Success in the locality of Lombo da Estrela (‘ridge of the star’), in the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’), founded in 1683 by Lourenço da Costa. In the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), beside the road known as Caminho do Meio (‘middle road’), stands another chapel of the same dedication, which belongs to the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), as does the adjoining house, where a state school is housed. We do not know the name of the founder of this last chapel, nor the year in which it was acquired by the Funchal Council.
Our Lady of Calhau (church)

This church was known by several names. It was called Conceição de Baixo (Lower Conception) to distinguish it from the chapel that Zarco had built on the site where the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) later rose, and which was known as Conceição de Cima. It was also called Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), in contrast to the small church of Conceição de Cima, which was of more modest dimensions. Finally, it took the name of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), which was the one that lasted longest, because it stood not far from the beach, in a spot commonly called the pebble beach (calhau). On this subject Dr G. Frutuoso says: ‘Having made his lodging in this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) (Santa Catarina), where he sheltered his wife and children, Captain Zargo resolved to build a church that should be the beginning and foundation of the town of Funchal. So that it should be secure and well placed, he had it laid out by the sea at the end of the valley of Funchal, along the first stream of this meadow, where the sea, next to the current of the stream, formed an inlet full of pebbles and small stones, washed by the constant waves that beat upon it. For this reason this first church of Funchal was commonly named Nossa Senhora do Calhao, its patron saint being the Nativity of the Virgin ...’

Its construction began around 1438, by which time a sizeable population had already settled beyond the left bank of the stream that later took the name of João Gomes. A great flash flood (*aluvião*) that devastated the city in 1611 destroyed much of the church and of the hospital attached to it, and a new church was then planned on a more sheltered and secure site. It seems that this building was not undertaken straight away, for a note in the *Saudades* states that the church was rebuilt between 1664 and 1688.

Another flood, in 1707, caused various damage to the new church and destroyed a considerable part of the churchyard, and major works were then carried out on the wall that protected the building from the violent current of the stream. This did not prevent the great flood of 1803 from bringing down the church, leaving only part of the chancel standing. The warrant (*provisão*) of 10 March 1805 ordered that these ruins be carefully preserved in the same state in which the flash flood (*aluvião*) had left them, as a reminder to future generations of the event that had been the most calamitous for the inhabitants of this island. This did not happen, however, for thirty-two years later, that is, in December 1835, the Council of Funchal ordered the demolition of what still remained of the old and historic church, so that a fruit and vegetable market could be built there. It was named the União Market (*Mercado União*), and its construction took place in the year 1835.

Dr Gaspar Frutuoso is not correct when he states that the church of Calhau was the first to be built in Funchal. According to the annotator of the *Saudades*, the chapel of St Sebastian (*São Sebastião*) was the first to be erected here, while others maintain that the right of priority belongs to the chapel of Santa Catarina (see that entry), built of wood beside the residence of João Gonçalves Zarco. We share this opinion, since we believe it to be the one that comes closest to the historical truth.
When the flash flood of 1803 swept the church of Our Lady of Calhau into the sea, it also destroyed the parish archive, which was important and contained valuable documents.
At the end of 1803 the seat of the parish moved to the church of St James the Less (*Santiago*), which was the property of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). See St James the Less (church).

It should be pointed out here that the church of Our Lady of Calhau stood on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, between the openings of the present Rua de Santa Maria and Rua Nova de Santa Maria (‘new street of St Mary’), or Rua Latino Coelho. On the site where the church stood, as already mentioned, a fruit and vegetable market was built, which was demolished a few years ago to widen the street that runs alongside the same stream (see Markets).

We shall also note that the old hospital, or one of its outbuildings, adjoined this church. This is clearly shown by what is recorded in a register of visitation orders (*livro de provimentos*) of the parish archive, the only one to escape the flash flood of 1803. It states that within the church, to the great disturbance of the faithful, the cries of the sick could be heard, especially during operations or the most painful dressings.
Our Lady of Mount Carmel (chapel)

In 1658 the merchant Domingos Rodrigues, a native of Guimarães, built the chapel of Our Lady of Mount Carmel (*Nossa Senhora do Carmo*) on the *quinta* (country estate) he owned in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’).
Our Lady of Mount Carmel (church)

This church, which gave its name to the street in which it stands, was built in the mid-17th century. Captain Roque Acciaioly de Vasconcelos donated the land for the church and its adjoining houses; the chancel was built at the expense of the prior of the Third Order of Carmel, Pedro Gonçalves Brandão, and the body of the building at the cost of the brethren of the same Order. Work began in 1656, and the church was only declared complete in 1660.

The Third Order of Carmel was established in this city by Father Luís do Rosário de Vila Nova, whom the provincial sent to this island for that purpose. It had its seat in the church of the Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation) and remained there until the new church was built.

The Carmo (‘Carmel’) church once had a small hospice (*hospício* or *albergaria*) attached to it, founded by Henrique Henriques de Noronha. Some Carmelite friars lived there, but we know nothing further about the existence and duration of this hospice.
On the side walls of the chancel of this church stand two fine mausoleums, the only ones of any artistic merit in the churches of this island.

A chapel with this dedication existed in the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’). It was an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) and was built in 1658 by Domingos Rodrigues.
Our Lady of Rest (chapel)

A chapel with this dedication once stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), on the property still known today as the *quinta* (country estate) of Descanso, Quinta do Descanso. It belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Tristão Bettencourt da Câmara, but we do not know when it was built.
Our Lady of the Flight into Egypt (chapel)

At the locality (*sítio*) that now bears this name, Canon Jorge Furtado de Sousa founded a chapel with the same dedication in the first quarter of the 17th century. Its present owner is the distinguished Madeiran Dr Juvenal Henriques de Araújo. It is often visited by people from various parts of the island, and in 1942 an interesting historical monograph about it was published.

In the last quarter of the 17th century, Raul Esteves had a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Flight into Egypt (*Nossa Senhora do Desterro*) built at the locality of Ledo, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). Only a few ruins of it remain.
There was also a chapel with the same dedication at the locality of Ribeira Grande, in the parish of Machico, founded in 1661 by Captain Manuel Telo de Meneses.
Our Lady of Deliverance (chapels)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’) there stood a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*), in the locality (*sítio*) that still bears this name today. It was the object of an old and well-attended pilgrimage. Since the chapel was demolished, the pilgrimage has been made to the parish church, and it still takes place at present; not even traces of the chapel remain today. It seems to have been built around the middle of the 17th century, and its foundation is attributed to Sebastião de Oliveira, who owned land in that locality.

We also know of other chapels with the same dedication: one in the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), another in the parish of Monte, another in the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) and a fourth in the parish of São Vicente.

The first of these chapels was built in 1656 at the behest of Diogo Ferreira de Mesquita and his wife, Dona Isabel de Meneses, and was endowed by a deed of 14 September of the same year. The second was built by Inácio Ferreira Pinto in 1684 and rebuilt a century later by João José Bettencourt de Freitas; the inspection allowing acts of worship to be held in it took place on 5 July 1784. The third, of recent foundation, was built at the behest of Dona Inácia Bettencourt Perestrelo in 1858; the deed of endowment dates from 11 September of the same year and the canonical inspection from 17 April 1860. The last was erected in 1685 by Father Manuel Gomes Garcês.

The chapel of Our Lady of Deliverance in the parish of Estreito da Calheta is today (1921) the property of Francisco Bettencourt Pimenta and stands on the *lombo* (ridge between valleys) known as Lombo dos Reis (‘kings’ ridge’).
Our Lady of Loreto (chapel)

About this chapel, an old book in the parish archive of the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) contains the following passage: ‘this chapel is magnificent in its architecture and workmanship; it was built in the early days of this parish... its first founder was an illustrious man of the most notable family of the Câmaras, as the escutcheon of his arms above the main door shows. . . in this chapel lies the seat of an entail (*morgado*) which the priors of the Esperança of Lisbon administered for many years... and it comprises all the properties that the Ribeiro do Ledo (‘Ledo brook’) divides on the eastern side. . . .’. Henrique Henriques de Noronha gives the following further details: ‘Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd son of the second donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara, married Dona Joana de Eça, who was a lady-in-waiting to Queen Catherine, wife of John III. . . he rebuilt the monastery of the Esperança, in Portugal, and built the chapel of Our Lady of Loreto (*Nossa Senhora do Loreto*), in Arco da Calheta, where he had noble houses, of which nothing but ruins can be seen today: his portrait can be seen in that chapel’. Dona Joana de Sá left this chapel and the lands attached to it to the nuns of the Convento da Esperança (Convent of Our Lady of Hope), Lisbon, who in turn sold them to Jean de Béthencourt, and he established there the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). We have read somewhere that it was built in the year 1510.
Our Lady of Montserrat (chapel)

Near the old pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction) of the town (*vila*) of Calheta (‘small cove’) stood the chapel of Nossa Senhora do Monserrate, which has long since ceased to exist.
Our Lady of the Mount (chapel)

In 1750 the inhabitants of the localities of Lombo das Adegas (‘ridge of the wine cellars’) and Terças (‘thirds’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), asked permission to build a chapel. They cited the distance at which they lived from the parish church and their wish to build a small sanctuary to house and venerate the revered image of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*), which stood in a small thatched oratory lacking the decorum due to the image. The chapel had a deed of endowment executed on 7 July 1750, and permission for its blessing was granted on 15 September 1751. Twenty-four years later it was enlarged, and it was blessed anew on 10 June 1775.

On the night of 1 June 1810 the doors of the chapel were forced and the image of Our Lady was taken out and set down some distance away, stripped of all the jewels that adorned it, which caused the deepest sorrow among the whole population. The image was taken to the parish church and, after various acts of reparation, was carried back in procession and with the greatest solemnity to the chapel on 6 August 1810.
Nossa Senhora do Monte (parish)

Although this is its historic and true name, and the one written in official documents, beginning with those kept in the parish archive, it has certainly become more widely known as the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’). This reflects the simplifying tendencies of popular speech, which always seeks to follow the law of least effort.

Despite the name it keeps, the parish does not lie on the summit or slopes of an isolated mount, but halfway up the high mountains that encircle the outskirts of the city. The large nucleus of population that formed in Funchal on the shores of the ocean in the very earliest times gradually spread out across the surrounding ridges and hillocks, sometimes seeking out trackless and almost inaccessible places. It was not long before the clearing of woods and thickets, and the corresponding breaking of the land for cultivation, reached the heights of this parish, at least within the limits where it bordered on the original Funchal. The homesteads slowly advanced up the steep mountainside, and higher up there already stood the small and devout chapel of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*), which lent its name to the locality (*sítio*) and later to the future parish.

This parish had its origin in the settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) that Adão Gonçalves Ferreira held there. He was the first man born on this island and the son of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira (see p. 21), the most distinguished companion of Zargo in the discovery of the archipelago. As was generally the case, a small chapel was the centre around which the first settlers gathered: around 1470 Adão Ferreira built a modest chapel there, which seems originally to have been called Nossa Senhora da Incarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation). It later came to be called Our Lady of the Mount, certainly owing to the lie of the land, which fully justified the new and fitting name. Others maintain that it was the miraculous apparition of the image of the Blessed Virgin (*Santíssima Virgem*), which people at once began to call Our Lady of the Mount, that led the chapel to take this name, which passed to the locality and later to the whole parish.

The legend of this miraculous apparition is told in the following terms on the back of the engravings depicting the tiny and venerable image: ‘More than 300 years ago, at Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), about 1 kilometre above the church of Our Lady of the Mount, a little Girl played one afternoon with a certain young shepherdess and gave her a snack. Full of joy, the shepherdess told her family of this, but they did not believe her, for it seemed impossible to them that a little Girl should appear in that lonely forest so far from the village. The following afternoon the same thing happened, and the shepherdess told of it again. The next day, at the hour the shepherdess had given, her father secretly went to watch the scene, and he saw on a stone a small Image of Most Holy Mary, and in front of it the innocent shepherdess, who, when her father unexpectedly appeared, declared that this Image was the little Girl she had spoken of. The shepherd, amazed, did not dare to touch the image, and reported the matter to the authorities, who had it placed in the chapel of the Incarnação, near the present church of “Our Lady of the Mount”, the name that has been given to that venerable Image ever since.’ This account does not differ in essentials from a manuscript description in our possession dating from the middle of the 18th century, which was itself based on an unbroken oral tradition. That description contains the following interesting detail: ‘On the following day at dawn Our Lady was found outside the Chapel, at the spring close by it, upon a stone on which some ancient characters, barely legible, may still be seen today…’ This most precious stone, says Father Joaquim Plácido Pereira, was buried at the bottom of the Ribeiro de Nossa Senhora (‘Our Lady’s brook’) when the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) had the Largo da Fonte (‘fountain square’) enlarged in 1896.

The chapel founded by Adão Gonçalves Ferreira became the seat of the parish when the parish was created by royal decree (alvará régio) of 7 March 1565. The cramped dimensions of the little church perhaps made it necessary to enlarge it shortly after the parish (*freguesia*) was created. In 1688, too, the Treasury Council (*Conselho da Fazenda*) authorised expenditure of 900,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for the construction of a new church. This seems not to have been carried out, since in 1739, that is 50 years later, the works for building a new church were put out for award by public auction (*arrematação*) for 6,742,000 *réis*.

From all this it seems that the original chapel underwent some alterations over time, but that it survived until 1741, when it was entirely demolished; the foundation stone was laid on 10 June of that year. The new building was declared complete in 1747, at a cost of 3,454,292 *réis* raised from various donations and alms from the faithful, in addition to the sum of 6,742,000 *réis* already mentioned, granted by the public treasury. The work of decoration and the construction of various outbuildings of the church and of the houses attached to it continued, however.

A year later the earthquake of 1 April 1748 (see Earthquakes), which caused so much damage on this island, left the new church badly damaged and in need of major and immediate repairs. Work began without delay, but it proceeded slowly, and its full and final completion took several years. The opportunity was taken to correct, as far as possible, some serious errors made in the construction begun in 1741, which made the cost of the repairs carried out there all the greater. According to a note entered in one of the books of the parish archive, the total cost of the works, including the church with its churchyard and flights of steps, the walls, the attached houses and various ornaments and church furnishings, was 200,445,500 *réis*, undoubtedly a very considerable sum for the time. To meet these heavy expenses, collections were made throughout the island. A large contribution also came from the Confraternity of the Slaves of Our Lady of the Mount, founded in 1750 by Bishop Dom Friar João do Nascimento. It soon spread to every parish, arousing great devotion among the faithful, and almost all its revenue was applied to this purpose.

The church of Monte was consecrated by Bishop Dom Friar Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde on 20 December 1818. In its architecture, its ornaments and decorations, its paintings or its carved woodwork it does not offer any artistic work of notable value or refined craftsmanship to catch the eye of visitors, still less of connoisseurs of art. It is nevertheless undoubtedly one of the best-proportioned churches in this diocese, and its architectural lines, some of its interior decoration, several paintings and the beauty of the whole make it well worth a visit. Since the pleasant and enchanting resort of Monte has always been visited by the most eminent personages passing through this island, its church has likewise been visited by many of them, among them the two empresses of Brazil, Leopoldina and Amélia; the Empress of Austria, Isabel; the Infante Dom Luís, later King of Portugal; King Carlos I and Queen Amélia, etc. This church holds the provisional tomb of the Emperor of Austria, Charles, who died in this parish on 1 April 1922 and of whom we shall speak elsewhere in this work.

Gaspar Frutuoso, who wrote the *Saudades* in 1590, makes no reference to the cult of Our Lady of the Mount, so widespread throughout the island, although he does mention a miraculous event (*Saudades*, p. 250) that occurred during the terrible sack of Funchal by the Huguenots on 3 October 1566. Devotion to Our Lady of Monte is nonetheless very old throughout the archipelago. From the second quarter of the 17th century onwards, the parish archive contains many references to this cult and accounts of extraordinary events attributed to the intercession of the Blessed Virgin through the devout image venerated there. Even so, it seems certain that it was only after the founding of the Confraternity of the Slaves of Our Lady of the Mount, around the middle of the 18th century, that the cult grew more intense and spread more widely through all the parishes of Madeira. It was then that pilgrimages and visits to the church began to draw larger crowds of the faithful, and these have grown steadily and considerably over the years. Today it is the most frequented pilgrimage festival on the whole island, with tens of thousands of people gathering there on 14 and 15 August each year.

After the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803 (vol. I, p. 54 ff.), the diocesan bishop, the cathedral chapter, the clergy and the faithful placed the island, and especially the city, under the protection of Our Lady of the Mount. This was confirmed by an Apostolic Rescript of Pius VII dated 21 July 1804, and the feast of the Patronage of Our Lady of the Mount was then instituted. It was celebrated on 9 October each year with a solemn procession from the Cathedral to the parish church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major). The ninth of October was formerly a holy day of obligation, preceded by its own vigil with fasting.

The chapel founded by Adão Gonçalves Ferreira had its own chaplain, and when the seat of the parish was established there in 1565, religious services had long been held in it. The first parish priest of this parish was Bento Fernandes, followed in the post by Fathers António de Amorim, Sebastião de Amorim, Pedro Nunes de Afonseca, Pedro Nunes Furtado, Pedro Noronha de Mendonça, Inácio Espinola de Castro e Meneses, etc. The first parish priest was assigned an annual salary of 12,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). By the royal decree (*alvará*) of 1 March 1577 this was increased by two thousand *réis* and one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat, the parish then having 58 households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths'), that is, fewer than 300 inhabitants. The royal decree of 9 June 1581 raised the stipend (*côngrua*) to 25,000 *réis* a year, and that of 27 April 1591 fixed it at 16,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. We do not know when the curacy (*curato*) of this parish was created, but we believe it must have been in the second half of the 18th century.

Someone once thought of calling this parish the ‘Madeiran Sintra’, and the long-serving and distinguished journalist João Augusto de Ornelas made the name widely known by popularising it in his writings. It is already cited under that name in various Portuguese and foreign works. Without seeking either to dispute or to justify this charming name, there can be no doubt that this parish is among the most beautiful and enchanting in Madeira. It owes this not only to its lush vegetation, its astonishing panoramas, the picturesque and pleasant character of the place and its admirable position overlooking the city, but also to the freshness of the locality, the clarity and purity of its waters, its fine walks, its lovely park, its excellent hotels, the lift, the Esplanade restaurant, and likewise its numerous *quintas* (country estates) and country houses, which are found everywhere. So remarkable a combination of qualities makes Monte the opulent and noble suburb of Funchal, the favourite resort for the summer season and a true and coveted Eden for the favoured of fortune (1921).

Among these *quintas* the well-known Quinta do Monte stands out as one of the most beautiful and richest in Madeira, for its sumptuous residence, opulently and artistically furnished, and its magnificent gardens, woods, vegetable plots and orchards, from which vast and astonishing panoramas can be enjoyed. It was built by the British subject James David Gordon in the second quarter of the 19th century, later passed into the possession of Leland Cossart, and is today the property of Luís da Rocha Machado (see *Almanach do Diário da Madeira*, 1915, p. 6). The Emperor Charles of Austria lived there for some months and died there in April 1922. The English consul Charles Murray built the Quinta do Belo Monte around the middle of the 18th century. In 1817 its owner was Roberto Page, who received the Empress Leopoldina of Brazil there. It later passed to the house of Calçada and today belongs to Captain Francisco W. Frasão Sardinha (1921). The Quinta do Pico da Pedra was built a few years ago by the banker Luís da Rocha Machado as his residence (1921).

We mention these *quintas* in particular only because we would have to go a long way if we tried to deal with the other summer residences scattered throughout this parish, some of which are excellent and comfortable country houses. One of the factors in the prosperity and growth of the parish of Monte was the building of the railway lift, which draws there most of the foreigners passing through our port, who number many thousands each year. The railway, from Pombal to the Terreiro da Luta, is approximately four kilometres long, and we have already dealt with it on p. 221 of the 1st volume of this work (1921).

The parish of Monte is today served by a privately owned road for motor cars, which does much to increase the number of visitors to the locality. It was built a few years ago and lies at one end of the road along the Levada de Santa Luzia, as a continuation of the Avenida Pedro José de Ornelas.

We cannot fail to give special mention to the distinctive means of transport used to carry visitors back from Monte to the city. These are small wicker cars, modelled on Russian sledges, which slide at dizzying speed down the steep slope, propelled by men long trained in this work, to which they devote themselves almost exclusively. References to this typical means of transport are countless in many Portuguese and foreign works. Despite the danger it naturally involves, accidents are rare, thanks to the drivers’ extreme skill (vol. I, p. 252).

The absence of a particular reference here to the Terreiro da Luta and its restaurant, the Parque Leite Monteiro, the Capela-Monumento and the Fonte da Senhora would be noticed, were it not that we deal specifically with these places, which are of considerable interest to the history of this parish, elsewhere in this work (see Terreiro da Luta, Parque Leite Monteiro and Capela-Monumento).

The Revd Father José Marques Jardim, the present parish priest of Monte, is engaged in the praiseworthy endeavour of raising a monument to the Blessed Virgin near the Terreiro da Luta, that is, where local tradition holds that the miraculous apparition of Our Lady took place. To this end he travelled to North America to raise donations for the construction of the great statue that will form part of the monument (1921). See Monuments.

Some of the points touched on here were treated more fully by the Revd Father Joaquim Plácido Pereira in his excellent pamphlet *Nossa Senhora do Monte, Padroeira da Ilha da Madeira*, an interesting monograph on the parish.
Our Lady of Perpetual Succour (chapel)
In the year 1244 Francisco de Freitas Correia had a chapel with this dedication built in the locality (*sítio*) of Queimada (‘burnt land’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Água de Pena.
Our Lady of the Pillar (chapel)

On the road and in the locality (*sítio*) of Pilar (‘pillar’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), stand the *quinta* (country estate) and chapel of that name, founded in 1676 by Gonçalo de Freitas Drumond. Today they are the property of Dr Romano de Santa Clara Gomes (1921).
Our Lady of the People (chapel)

It stands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’). The chapel is dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Pópulo, but nobody knows it by this name; it is commonly called the chapel of Pico do Cardo (‘thistle peak’) or of the Quinta dos Padres (‘the priests’ estate’). This name comes from its standing in that locality (*sítio*) and at the residence that the Jesuits owned there. We do not know the year of its foundation, but we presume that it is no earlier than the first quarter of the 18th century. The Jesuits acquired this property between 1635 and 1714 and built the house and chapel there, which in 1770, together with the adjoining land, were sold at public auction for seven *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis; *réis*: old Portuguese money of account). This small chapel is hexagonal in shape and stands almost adjoining the residence. It is in a good state of repair, and divine services are celebrated in it.

Fuller information on the subjects touched on in this short article can be found in the articles on Blessed Inácio de Azevedo, on the Jesuits and on the chapel of Pópulo, published in the review *Parochia de Santo António do Funchal*.
Our Lady of the Rosary (chapels)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’) a chapel of this dedication was founded in 1748 by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António Leandro da Câmara Leme. The deed of endowment is dated 18 July 1734, but the chapel was inspected only fourteen years later, so that acts of worship could be celebrated in it.

On the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), at the place called Fundoa, within the parish of São Roque (‘St Roch’), there is a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Rosary (*Nossa Senhora do Rosário*), built by João da Paz de Castro in 1668. Matias de Mendonça e Vasconcelos built a chapel of the same dedication in the parish of Machico in 1660.
In the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) there was a chapel whose patron saint was Our Lady of the Rosary, but we know nothing of its founder or the year it was built.

The chapel of Our Lady of the Rosary in the locality (*sítio*) of Vargem (‘meadow’), in the parish of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), is not small. The original chapel, instituted by José Caldeira, has undergone various alterations and additions. The curate of the parish usually lives near this chapel and conducts religious services there.

There was a chapel of the same dedication in the parish of São Jorge (‘St George’), founded in the last quarter of the 17th century by Father Matias Jorge Jardim; it stood in the locality of Ilha (‘island’).
Our Lady of Succour (chapels)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Azenha (‘water mill’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), beside a country house that belonged to former holders of an entail, stands the chapel of Our Lady of Succour (*Nossa Senhora do Socorro*). It is now far gone in ruin and put to secular uses, and neither the name of its founder nor the year of its construction is known.

A note in the *Saudades* states that there was a chapel with this dedication in the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), founded in 1684 by Maria de Aguiar, widow of Gonçalo de Faria Leal.

There was one in the parish of Canhas, in the locality of Socorro (‘succour’), founded by João Fernandes Linhares in 1665. In the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) there is a chapel with this patron saint, originally known as Our Lady of Bethlehem (*Nossa Senhora de Belém*). We do not know who its founder was, but it belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) established by Captain Manuel Telo Moniz de Meneses, of the house of Lagoa (‘lake’) in the same parish, which was later called the Torresão entailed estate. It was built around 1713 and is in a fair state of repair; it is the property of Dona Cristina de Campos Pinto Soares, who lives in Lisbon (1921).
Our Lady of the Rosary Beads (chapel)
In 1770 the people of Machico built a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Terço beside the parish church of the parish (*freguesia*).
Our Lady of the Valley (chapel)

In 1726 António Vogado founded a chapel in the locality (*sítio*) of Vale Formoso (‘beautiful valley’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). He dedicated it to Nossa Senhora do Vale and endowed it by a public deed of 4 June of that year.
Our Lady of the Angels (chapel)

‘In this parish (Madalena (‘Magdalene’))’, says Frutuoso, ‘there is a chapel of Our Lady of the Angels (*Nossa Senhora dos Anjos*) which, apart from being small, is a rich house, with a small, fresh and well-adorned altarpiece, beside which is a cool spring beneath some stones, among some sugar cane fields of very fine canes.’ Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that this chapel was founded in 1508 by Martim Afonso and his wife Isabel Afonso, who established an entailed estate (*morgadio*) there in favour of their son Diogo Martins de Canha, called the Knight. The annotator of the ‘Island History’ (*História Insulana*), however, says that the chapel of Anjos (‘angels’) was built in 1474 by order of the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her son, the Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which this archipelago belonged in spiritual matters. The image venerated in this chapel was an object of great devotion among the faithful, and Friar Agostinho de Santa Maria devoted a chapter to it in vol. X of his *Santuário Mariano*. The locality (*sítio*) where the chapel stands, called Anjos, is noted for the fertility of its soil; it belongs today to the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas, but it was once part of the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). The chapel was restored by its then owner, Dona Júlia de França Neto, in 1892 and consecrated for worship on 10 December of that year.
Our Lady of Miracles (chapels)

In 1661 Brás de Freitas da Silva built a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora dos Milagres in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), on land belonging to his entailed estate (*morgadio*). The annotator of the *Saudades* mentions a chapel with the same patron saint, founded in 1662 by Pedro Ferreira de Mesquita in the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’).
Our Lady of the Joys (chapels)

In 1611, on land in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) that later came to belong to the parish of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), Tristão Gomes de Castro founded a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Joys (*Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres*). There was a chapel of the same dedication in the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’); it was entailed, and in 1610 its administrator was João Gomes de Castro. We do not know the year of its foundation.
Our Lady of Remedies (chapel)
