In the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), in the locality (*sítio*) of Moreno, there is a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Remedies (*Nossa Senhora dos Remédios*). It was built by the vicar Manuel Ferreira Teixeira in 1690, and not in 1610, as the annotator of the *Saudades* states.
Our Lady of Remedies and Protection (chapel)

Attached to the manor house of the viscounts of São João (‘St John’), on Rua das Maravilhas, its present owner, Dr Rui Bettencourt da Câmara, founded a chapel of this dedication, which was blessed on 1 January 1940.
Our Lady of the Slipways (chapel)

Varadouros (‘slipways’) was the name given, on the beach of Funchal, to the principal point for the embarkation and landing of passengers and goods, and to the spot set aside for hauling small boats ashore. This stretch of beach must have corresponded roughly to the space occupied by the present capstans, from the waterline up to the street that today lies above them. Nearby stood the small chapel of Nossa Senhora (Our Lady), which we believe had the Assumption of the Virgin as its patron saint (*orago*), and which took the name Varadouros from its position. After the chapels of St Catherine, St Sebastian and St Paul, it was among the oldest in Funchal.

The building that many contemporaries still knew, and which was demolished in April 1911, was not the original structure. That earlier chapel stood on the same spot, but directly on the ground rather than on the arch on which it was later built. When it was decided to open the city’s main gate and entrance in its defensive curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city), the old chapel had to be demolished. Plans were then drawn up for an imposing gateway and chapel, which formed a single body and were built almost simultaneously. The chapel was therefore pulled down around 1682 and rebuilt in 1689, and at about the same time the adjoining arch and gate were built, which became the main entrance to the city. This work is owed to Dom Lourenço de Almada, who was Governor and Captain-General of Madeira from 1688 to 1690.

On this subject Dr Álvaro de Azevedo writes: ‘... having ordered the Varadouros gate to be cut through the old walls and designed with the elegance of the period and of its style, which became the principal entrance to Funchal, the following Latin inscription was placed above that gate in memory and honour of him: *PERFECTA HAEC VARII PRAEFECTI MOENIA FRUSTRA PRAETERITO CUPIUNT TEMPORE QUISQUE SUO SED DOMINO LAURENTO EA EST SERVATA VOLUPTAS DALMADA QUI ISTUD FINE CORONAT OPUS ANNO 1689*’.

This inscription, which means ‘Each of the previous governors strove in vain to complete these walls; to Senhor Lourenço de Almada was reserved the satisfaction of their completion’, was reproduced, with minor variations, in no. 5 of the newspaper *A Justiça* in 1858.

This gate ought to have been carefully preserved, and the adjoining chapel with it, had the Funchal Council of the day possessed a true idea of what the conservation of old works of this kind means. What should have been done was to clear away the hovels that surrounded them and to leave the gate and chapel standing on their own in the middle of the square, making the spot more spacious, cheerful and airy. The gate, though not a monumental work, was beyond any shadow of doubt an interesting and characteristic building of its period. It did not lack a certain architectural grandeur, and it had been admired by many Portuguese and foreigners who were genuine connoisseurs of archaeological matters.

Through this arch and gate the governors and prelates made their ceremonial entry into the city. The occasion was always one of extraordinary splendour, attended by the officials, all the troops of the garrison, the most eminent people of the island, the clergy, noblemen, knights and a great crowd of ordinary people.

When the chapel was demolished, its altar was moved to one of the sacristies of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), where it is still kept. Above the door of this sacristy a notice in English was put up, describing the Varadouros chapel as the first to be built in Funchal. This is an obvious error, and it must be accepted that not even the altar kept there belonged to the original chapel.
Our Lady Mother of Mankind
On the Caminho do Meio (‘middle road’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), there is a chapel with this dedication, which is the property of the Viscount of Cacongo.
Our Lord Jesus Christ (chapel)

In the 15th century Gil Anes founded a chantry (capela) with this dedication in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’); it later became the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*) established by one of his forebears.
Notaries

The notarial service in this archipelago must surely have followed the same stages as in mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), apart from any modifications that local circumstances made advisable. It is nevertheless interesting to note here that in 1579 Funchal had no fewer than 21 court notaries, 8 notaries of deeds and 6 inquirers – truly extraordinary for a population that, across the whole island, then amounted to some twenty-five thousand inhabitants. Let us hear Frutuoso: ‘And because in Funchal, the city that his forebears (of the 5th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*)) founded, there were twenty-one court notaries and eight notaries of deeds and six inquirers, King Henry saw fit, in the year 1579, for certain reasons that moved him to it and for the better service of God, to reduce them to ten court clerks, four notaries and three inquirers, who now serve (in 1590)....’

It should be noted that in the seats of the other captaincies and in the towns already created by then – Machico, Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol, Calheta and Porto Santo – there were also officers of justice with the same duties as those in Funchal. Within the jurisdiction of Funchal, Cardinal Henry reduced the number of clerks from 35 to 17!
Noticioso (O)
The first issue appeared on 22 October 1862 and the last on 22 January 1866. In all, 152 issues were published. Its principal editor was Augusto César Barjona de Freitas.
Nova Aldeia or Aldeia da Rainha

A settlement founded by royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 December 1768 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), made up of several couples from the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) who moved there and to whom the government in mainland Portugal granted various privileges. This new settlement, however, did not last long.
Nova de Santa Maria (street)

Roughly parallel to Rua de Santa Maria (‘St Mary’), and a short distance from it, runs Rua Nova de Santa Maria (‘new street of St Mary’), which was opened shortly after the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803; until then there was only a small alley there. Between the entrances of these two streets stood the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), or of St Mary, which gave its name to both streets. It runs from the bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes to the Largo das Bicas or Torneiras, where Rua Bela de São Tiago begins. Today it bears the name of Latino Coelho.
Novara (frigate)

This warship of the Austrian navy made a voyage of circumnavigation in the years 1857 to 1859, and lay at anchor in our harbour for several days. The account of this voyage is highly regarded. Latino Coelho translated and published in the *Revista Contemporânea* the part of it dealing with this island, which is very interesting and well worth reading. It was reprinted in no. 2,279 and following of the now defunct *Diário do Commercio* (‘Commercial Daily’) of this city.
Hydrangea (Hydrangea hortensis)
A plant of the family Saxifragaceae, widely cultivated at Monte, Santana, Camacha and various other places on the island. It has blue or pink flowers, generally sterile, arranged in broad corymbs.
Novidades (As)
A periodical with this title was published in Funchal; its first issue appeared on 26 July 1866.
Another newspaper of the same title published here appeared on 18 November 1881 and ran to twenty-six issues, the last of them on 24 December 1882.
Novos (Os)

The first issue of this newspaper appeared on 1 May 1920, and the tenth, which we suppose to be the last, in November of the same year. It was written by pupils of the Liceu do Funchal (Funchal secondary school), and replaced *Gente Nova* (‘New People’).
Nozelha
The vernacular name of *Monizia edulis* and *Bunium brevifolium*, native plants of the family Umbelliferae, the first of which is also known as *cenoura da rocha* (see that entry).
Numismatics
See Medals and Coinage.
Nuncio

On 25 July 1808 the envoy of His Holiness in Lisbon arrived in Madeira by chance, coming from London. He landed at the Pontinha (‘little point’) and went straight to the Cathedral, where he heard the ten o’clock Mass. After visiting the church, he got into a sedan chair and went on to the bishop’s palace. He left the island on the 28th. During his short stay he conferred minor orders on some students, since the bishop was not in Funchal, and gave the dean the powers needed to grant certain marriage dispensations. On his departure all the forts of the city fired salutes.
Nunes

The first person of this surname mentioned in the Madeiran chronicles was called Fernão Nunes. He lived at Gaula and married Helena de Góis, daughter of Lançarote Teixeira, fourth son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, first donatary of Machico.

In the first quarter of the 16th century a certain Bartolomeu Nunes lived on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’); he was the father of the false prophet Fernão Nunes, of whom we shall speak elsewhere in this *Elucidário*.
Nunes da Mata (José)
He was in Madeira in 1920 and in 1921 published in Lisbon a 24-page pamphlet entitled *Navegação aérea entre Portugal e a ilha da Madeira*.
Nunes (Fernão and Filipa) see Prophets
Nunes (Filipe José)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) in 1824 and died in this city around 1890. For many years he was curate of the parish of the Sé (Funchal Cathedral) and held the royal grant of honorary canon. He possessed uncommon learning and distinguished himself as a journalist, especially in the periodical *O Popular* (‘The People’s Paper’), waging fierce battles in the press in which his excesses of language at times recalled the diatribes of José Agostinho de Macedo. At the time of his death he had a collection of sermons ready for publication, but it was never printed.
Nunes (Father Manuel)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’) in 1848 and died on 28 December 1892 in the parish of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), where he was parish priest. He was one of our most distinguished preachers, his sermons being remarkable for their elegance of form and correctness of language. He cultivated poetry with brilliance, above all the satirical genre, in which he became very well known here, and some of his compositions stand comparison with those of our own Nicolau Tolentino.
District Public Works

For centuries the improvements ordered by the government in mainland Portugal – such as the building of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) and of various churches, the military fortifications, some public buildings, the roads and others besides – had no central department to supervise them and direct them properly, not only in their administration but also in the technical direction of the various works to be carried out. This work was handled through several public departments, such as the secretariat of the archipelago’s Superior Government, the local military commanders, the Treasury Superintendency (Provedoria da Fazenda) and the municipalities, while engineers or technical experts were sent from Lisbon to direct the larger works.

It was only in 1852 that a department called the ‘Direcção das Obras Públicas Distritais’ (District Public Works Directorate) was created in Funchal to direct and administer all these works. The central government granted it an annual allocation, which was always very limited and varied from year to year, despite the constant requests made from this island. The department was headed by an engineer and had the necessary staff. It was often directed by officials who left their names linked to important public improvements, such as the engineers Major Tibério Blanc, Captains Júlio Augusto de Leiria and Henrique de Lima e Cunha, and others besides.

This situation lasted until 1901, when administrative autonomy was granted to this district. All the services handled by that department then passed to the public works department of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), and the former department was abolished.
Phenological observations

On page 15 of volume II of this work, under the title ‘Phenology’, mention is made of several articles on this subject from the pen of the distinguished botanist Carlos Azevedo de Meneses. One of them, published in the former review *Portugal Agrícola*, was judged worth reproducing in these pages, and is transcribed here. ‘The little that is known about the phenology of Madeira is owed to the observations of Dr Oswald Heer, made in 1850 and 1851, and to those we have been making on this island since 1902. The observations for the period from September 1902 to early April 1905 were published in a French botanical review. Today our task is limited to presenting the data gathered after that date, with the aim of shedding a little more light on the phenological behaviour of various tree species introduced into the island that thrive in our climate. Of the four species mentioned in the *Instructions* of Hoffmann–Ihne, only the oak (*Quercus pedunculata*) is common in Funchal and its surroundings. It stands out from all the other species we have had the opportunity to observe for the truly extraordinary earliness of its leafing.

Of the many oaks planted on the left bank of the Ribeira de São João, two came into bud on 3 December 1905. By the 23rd of the same month two-thirds of these oaks had new leaves, and many of them were already fairly well in leaf. By the end of January of the following year every specimen grown in Funchal had leaves, but they did not become fully green until the first fortnight of March.

We saw the first yellow leaves on 16 September. Once yellow, the leaves remain on the trees and fall only very late, when the new leafing is already well advanced. In the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), which lies at an altitude of 600 metres, the oaks did not begin to leaf until 15 January, that is, 43 days later than in Funchal.

Of the horse chestnut (*Æsculus Hippocastanum*), also mentioned in Hoffmann–Ihne’s *Instrucções*, we were able to observe only two specimens planted in Funchal. The leaves began to lose their colour on 3 September, and the first new leaves appeared on 12 March. The flowers began to appear in the first eight days of April. In *Platanus occidentalis*, *Vitis vinifera* and *V. Labrusca*, leaf colouring set in on 14, 15 and 21 September respectively, and budding took place on 24, 22 and 20 February of the current year. The leafing of the plane trees began in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte on 6 March, that is, 12 days later than in Funchal. The leaves of the plane trees also stayed on the trees for a long time after turning yellow, but they always fall before the new leafing begins.

In *Robinia Pseudo acacia* leaf colouring began on 15 October, in *Tilia argentea* on the 18th of the same month and in *Ficus Carica* on 2 November; the leafing of these same trees began on 27 January, 12 March and 24 January respectively. All these observations refer to Funchal; in Monte the budding of the species mentioned took place on 19 February, 19 March and between 21 and 25 February.

On the cherimoya trees (*anoneira*) (*Anona cherimolia*) of Funchal, the first yellow leaves appeared on 14 February of the current year and the first new leaves on 9 April. The chestnut trees of Monte budded on 20 April and the walnut trees between 30 April and 5 May.

We were unable to gather precise data on when the leaves of the trees change colour in the surroundings of Funchal, but we have noticed more than once that this colouring comes later the higher the spot where the trees stand.

From the above, then, it can be seen that the length of winter dormancy in the period covered by our latest observations was 163 days for the plane, 160 for the vine, 152 for the Labrusca vine, 170 for the horse chestnut, 78 for the oak, 104 for the robinia, 145 for the lime, 83 for the fig and 54 for the cherimoya tree. For the period from 1903 to 1905 we found the following mean figures for the winter dormancy of the same species: plane 168 days, vine 162, Labrusca vine 156, horse chestnut 192, oak 123, robinia 112, lime 166, fig 125 and cherimoya tree 50.

According to the phenological notes published by Mr Adolpho Frederico Moller in the *Boletim da Sociedade Broteriana*, the mean length of winter dormancy in Coimbra, in the period from the end of 1903 to the beginning of 1905, was 140 days for the plane, 154 for the vine, 136 for the horse chestnut, 154 for the oak, 146 for the robinia and 156 for the lime. Comparing these figures with some of the earlier ones, one concludes that the robinia and the oak rest longer in Coimbra than in Funchal, whereas the reverse is true of the other species.

It may seem surprising at first sight that certain species at the latitude of Madeira should have a longer dormancy, and consequently shorter periods of vegetative activity, than in more northerly countries. Yet the case is in no way abnormal and is easily explained, as we shall see.

In the first place, rainfall is not distributed in Coimbra in the same way as in Funchal. While that city records on average 79 millimetres of rain during the summer months, Funchal records only 16.9. The mean rainfall measured by the rain gauge of the Coimbra observatory is 19.4 millimetres in July and 15.3 millimetres in August, whereas in Funchal it is 1.1 and 2.4 millimetres respectively. In that mainland city there are 21.5 days of rain during the summer months; in Funchal, only 4.2.

Since prolonged droughts during the hottest season of the year are therefore one of the characteristics of the climate of Funchal, and since they must bring about an early suspension of the plants’ vital activity, it is clear that leaf fall must occur here sooner than in Coimbra, and all the earlier the more sensitive the trees are to drought.

This, then, is one of the causes of the long periods of dormancy recorded in Madeira. The other lies in a peculiarity of certain trees cultivated here: they begin to bud only after receiving a sum of temperature considerably greater than that which brings them into growth in their countries of origin.

This late budding, in which A. de Candolle wished to see an adaptation of the trees to the climate and A. Grisebach the survival of habits ingrained in the species, is not, however, observed in all species. The oak, for example, seems to be an exception to the rule, and an exception all the more surprising given that it also occurs at the island’s middle altitudes.

It should be noted, however, that although the budding of the oak begins extraordinarily early in Madeira, general leafing is completed only after a fairly long interval, as we showed at the beginning of this article. This seems to indicate a certain tendency in the species, caused by hereditary habits, to resist the influence of normal leafing temperatures.

From September onwards, many premature shoots frequently appear both on the trunks of oaks and on vine canes. As these shoots are not accompanied by a general swelling of the buds, they must not be mistaken for the start of the new leafing.

Comparing the data gathered from 1903 to 1905 with those from our own observations of 1905 to 1906, we find that in the latter period many trees in Funchal budded considerably earlier, the advance being greater in the oak than in the other species. As humidity is one of the factors of periodicity, and as rainfall was extremely abundant in the last months of 1905, unlike in previous years, it may be presumed that this was the reason why these trees came into growth earlier.’
The botanical journal referred to above is the ‘*Bulletin de l'Academie Intern. de Geogr. Botanique du Mans*’, nos 189 and 190 of 1905.
Oceanography

The sea is a vast biological environment, home to the most varied forms of life, both plant and animal. While the higher plants are almost all terrestrial, countless lower plants are born, live and die within the waters of the ocean. The animal kingdom, too, has numerous representatives in sea water. They provide a good part of human food, as well as a varied number of organisms which, though of no importance to the human economy, challenge the curiosity of scientific observers.

The study of oceanography is still very backward in Madeira. Nevertheless, we already have some valuable descriptive or taxonomic works on various groups of organisms that live in the sea. Although they do not always meet the demands of modern hydrobiology, they are nonetheless very useful for understanding the composition of the fauna and flora of our waters.

The articles Algae, Carcinology, Shells, Fishes, Starfish, Sea Urchins, Worms, etc., etc., contain some information on the animal and plant life of our seas. However, the results obtained so far, chiefly through fishing and dredging, though they represent a great step forward in the investigation of the organisms living in our marine environment, shed little light on certain questions of oceanography that greatly occupy the attention of modern scientists. The plankton – the whole body of plants and animals that float passively in the water and are therefore at the mercy of the currents and of the physical and chemical conditions of their environment – has been very imperfectly studied. The same can be said of certain benthic groups, that is, those that are active near the sea floor. The study of ecological factors such as temperature, salinity, dissolved gases, pressure and the movement of the water in our seas, etc., has hardly begun. On the organisms of the plankton, or planktonts, which play a dominant role because of their abundance, only a few brief notes have been published, on the Madeiran Copepoda and Diatomaceae. Nothing is known, as far as we are aware, about the Dinoflagellata, and of the Cystoflagellata only *Noctiluca miliaris* is known, a very common organism in our waters which causes phosphorescence at night.

There has been much talk lately (1921) of establishing an oceanographic museum in Funchal. If such an institution is to be created and to prove truly useful, however, the study of the organisms of our waters must be given far wider scope than it has had until now. It is not enough for the museum’s cabinets to display fishes, crustaceans, shells, anthozoans, echinoderms and other groups whose size is enough to catch the attention of those untrained in the natural sciences. There must also be room for the bacteria, flagellates, green algae, foraminifera, ciliates, radiolarians, tunicates and other groups of plants and animals that characterise ocean waters and in many cases belong to the realm of plankton. Installing aquaria designed to reproduce the conditions of the marine environment would be highly advantageous, since it would allow observations that are difficult to make in any other way.

Equipping expeditions to study the fauna and ecological factors of the great depths is undoubtedly very costly, because of the ship, the apparatus and the men required. If our aims are more modest, however, and we wish only to study the faunal and floral composition of the waters of the bay of Funchal or of those near our coast, it is enough to turn to the fishermen’s tackle, to Muller nets improved for collecting plankton organisms at various depths, to wide-meshed nets and wide-mouthed jars for the macroplankton, and to dredges for collecting the organisms that live in contact with the bottom.

A boat, which need not be very large, and a few jars of fixative and preservative fluids complete the equipment needed for small-scale oceanographic exploration. If those who own boats and practise water sports were to spend part of their time afloat collecting marine organisms, our local oceanographic knowledge, which, as we have said, is still very limited, would advance considerably. It is plankton above all that calls for the attention of friends of the natural sciences. Although the study of the microorganisms that make it up is sometimes difficult, it must not be forgotten that many of these difficulties can be overcome with some effort and work, and others by seeking the enlightened advice of specialists, who as a rule do not refuse their help to beginners who show zeal and love for the research to which they themselves are devoted.

Because they bear closely on the subject of this article, we transcribe the following passages from the valuable work by the engineer Adolfo Loureiro, *Os Portos Marítimos de Portugal e Ilhas Adjacentes* (V-21):

‘It is known that Madeira lies in the region of the great ocean currents that flow through the liquid part of our planet. From the very beginning, ever since the discovery of Madeira, it was noticed that ships sailing from this island towards the Canaries were imperceptibly carried from N. to W. The current setting towards SSW ran at 12 to 16 miles a day, and was attributed to the action of the wind. On the north coast of Madeira, and especially at Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), the sea sometimes brought unknown fruits, which were supposed to come from the W. The temperature found in the waters seemed to follow persistent laws and phenomena. Since the inhabitants of Madeira included seafarers and men who knew the sea, these facts did not escape them, and it is even believed that Christopher Columbus was led by them to conjecture that there must be lands to the west from which those samples of fruit came.

The temperature of the waters and its distribution at the surface, their periodic movements and conditions, following a law that seemed constant, ought to have become the subject of very interesting oceanographic studies, which unfortunately were never carried out.

It was also recognised that the depth conditions of this sea were exceptional: already very great close to the coast, the depth increased rapidly towards the Azores, ranging from 1,650 to 2,675 *braças*.

To the north of Madeira, 120 miles from the coast, it was 1,650 *braças*. Between Madeira and the Canary Islands it reached 2,298 *braças*. And between Madeira and the coast of Africa, as well as between Madeira and the Canaries, it reached 2,400 *braças*, being 2,225 only a short distance from the island.

As for the daily movements of the waters, or the tides, these phenomena have not been properly studied and recorded. The charts of the engineer Azevedo, for example, confirmed by various British naval officers, state that the establishment of the port (time of high water at full and new moon) at Funchal is 12 h 48 m, and the rise of the tide 2.28 m.’
Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelite troops

As is well known, Miguel I, regent of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), dissolved the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) and convened the Three Estates on 3 May 1828, proclaiming himself absolute king. On the 12th of the same month news of these events reached Madeira, and the governor and captain-general José Lúcio Travassos Valdez at once prepared to resist and to remain loyal to the principles enshrined in the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) granted by Pedro IV.

On 25 June 1828 the Portuguese frigate *Príncipe Real* appeared off our harbour, bringing the new Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) governor, José Maria Monteiro, and a *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) for this judicial district (*comarca*), both armed with discretionary powers. On board the frigate was Vice-Admiral Prego, who was on his way to the Azores as governor and captain-general of those islands.

José Lúcio Travassos Valdez sent an emissary to the commander of the Miguelite warship, informing him of the state of feeling in this archipelago and of the resistance he would offer to the landing of the new governor, and at the same time ordering him to leave Madeiran waters immediately.

On the 27th the frigate disappeared, but on the 28th a corvette and a brig belonging to the usurping government appeared in our bay. From a communication made to the British consul, Henrique Veitch, it became known that the absolutists intended to maintain a blockade of the whole archipelago, against which the consul immediately protested in the name of his government.

The energetic and resolute stance of the governor and captain-general Travassos Valdez prevented the Miguelite forces from landing, and the squadron left Madeiran waters without achieving the aims of conquest that had driven its commander.

On 16 August 1828 the royalist squadron appeared once again off the bay of Funchal. It consisted of a carrack, two frigates, two corvettes, two brigs and two storeships. It was commanded by Vice-Admiral Henrique da Fonseca Prego and carried on board, besides the crews, about a thousand men under the command of Colonel José António de Azevedo Lemos.

At dawn on 22 August the squadron set course for the bay of Machico, and at 11 in the morning the brig *Infante D. Sebastião* opened fire on the Forte do Ancoradouro (Anchorage Fort) and then on the Amparo (‘protection’) battery. Both put up only a weak and short-lived resistance, their garrisons fleeing in disorder almost at the first shots fired by the enemy squadron. The Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) troops then landed ‘without the slightest resistance and in complete comfort’, according to the unimpeachable testimony of a contemporary of the events.

José Lúcio Travassos Valdês, who was undoubtedly a brave man with a gift for strategy, of which he gave such eloquent proof in the campaigns for liberty, had prepared the defence of Madeira. He had only weak means for it, however, not only because of the number and abilities of his officers but also because of the poorly disciplined, raw militiamen who made up the garrison of the archipelago. It is true that a few days earlier some officers, our compatriots, had arrived from England, but they came too late. Only their courage and military competence could be counted on, and that was not enough to organise a defence that had to be vigorous and perhaps prolonged, given the number and quality of the attackers. Travassos Valdês organised several centres of resistance from Machico to Funchal, especially at Seixo, Santa Cruz, Porto Novo and Palheiro do Ferreiro, under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Schwalback. At Seixo there were 200 men commanded by Captain Brito, who was the first to flee as the enemy approached, and the whole military force stationed there followed his example. In view of these successive disasters, and recognising that the resistance he had prepared at Santa Cruz was useless, Schwalback decided to concentrate his forces in the Forte do Porto Novo, which was well armed with artillery. From there, commanding the steep slopes that the enemy would have to climb, he could inflict heavy losses on the royalist troops and even force them to retreat.

While Schwalback was organising at that excellent strategic point the means of resistance at his disposal, together with others arriving from Funchal, an explosion occurred in the ammunition. That officer and other men of the garrison were seriously wounded. The soldiers then abandoned the fort in headlong flight, and Schwalback was barely able to gather a few men to carry him to Funchal.

Travassos Valdês, leaving the city to reinforce the garrison of Porto Novo, met Schwalbach on the Caniço (‘reed’) road, wounded and heading for Funchal. He could then see that all was lost: any resistance was futile, and all that remained was to spare his soldiers’ lives and shield the population from reprisals by the Miguelite troops.

The governor and captain-general José Lúcio Travassos Valdês, who so distinguished himself in the struggles for liberty and also in politics under the name of Count of Bonfim, placed himself under the protection of England. He took refuge on board the warship corvette *Alligator* (see that entry, vol. I, p. 46) on the afternoon of 22 August, and a few days later sailed for London with other émigrés.
On the morning of 23 August the royalist troops left Santa Cruz for Funchal, meeting not the slightest resistance, and entered the city on the afternoon of the same day.
José Maria Monteiro (see that entry, vol. II, p. 390), the new Miguelite governor, landed on 24 August and took up his new post that same day.
Occupation of Madeira by British troops

Anyone moderately versed in Madeiran history knows that this island was twice occupied by British troops: the first time from July 1801 to January 1802, and the second from December 1807 to October 1814.

Everyone knows that the English alliance plunged us into the hazards of the Napoleonic Wars. Yet our part in the campaigns against France brought not the slightest advantage to our country, which was not even represented at the Congress of Vienna when the terms of peace were discussed. Among the humiliations we then suffered was the first occupation of Madeira. It was carried out in the name of protection and defence, but in fact it amounted to an outright conquest, as the documents of the period clearly show; they leave not the slightest doubt about the designs behind that occupation.

On the morning of 24 July 1801 a small British squadron appeared in the harbour of Funchal. It consisted of the ship of the line *Argo*, the frigate *Carrysfort*, the brig *Falcon* and five further transport ships, under the command of Commodore Bowen, and carried some 3,500 soldiers and officers commanded by Colonel Henry Cliton. Several officers landed at once and, after a brief conference with the British consul José Pringle, the consul went straight to the Governor and Captain-General, Dom José Manuel da Câmara. He informed him of the orders he had received from the commanders of the British forces, whose sole purpose in coming to Madeira was to protect and defend it against a supposed attack by French ships.

The Governor could not have been more surprised. Not only did he consider the arrival of the squadron and the stationing of the troops among us unnecessary, but he had also known nothing whatever of their coming, and the affair caused the greatest indignation throughout the island. Dom José Manuel da Câmara nevertheless complied with the orders conveyed by the British consul, for he was convinced that the slightest resistance on his part would mean the immediate bombardment of the city. All this can be clearly inferred from the report Dom José Manuel sent to the central government.

John VI’s government was no less surprised. It gave our representative in London the necessary instructions to lodge a vigorous protest with the British government against the occupation of Madeira and to demand the immediate withdrawal of the troops, especially after Napoleon had adopted a more benevolent attitude towards Portuguese affairs.

While the negotiations dragged slowly on in London, Colonel Cliton set about finding more suitable and comfortable quarters for his troops. At first they were scattered among the various fortresses; later they occupied the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), then serving as the diocesan seminary, as well as a number of private houses, whose owners and occupants were turned out. Nor did he fail to interfere improperly in local government and administration, oppressing the inhabitants of this island with harsh measures that revealed the true tyranny of intruding masters.

After the preliminaries of the Peace of Amiens were signed on 1 October 1801, our representative in London pressed again, and more forcefully, for the evacuation of the British forces from Madeira. Only at the beginning of 1802, however, did the British government order Colonel Cliton to withdraw from this island, and the troops embarked on 25 January 1802. Seven years later the island was again occupied by British troops, and this time the occupiers’ rule here was more complete and more absolute. There can be no doubt that England proceeded to take definitive possession of the archipelago, and it is truly remarkable how our skilful diplomacy, through its efforts in London and other European centres, succeeded in restoring Madeira to Portuguese possession.

On 24 December 1807 a British squadron anchored off Funchal. Commanded by Admiral Samuel Hood, it consisted of four ships of the line, four frigates and sixteen transports, and carried two infantry regiments of a thousand men each and two companies of artillery, the troops being under the command of Major-General William Carr Beresford.

Once the troops had landed, the British general lost no time in demanding that the governor and captain-general of Madeira, Pedro Fagundes Bacelar de Antas e Meneses, immediately surrender the archipelago. Since any resistance was impossible, the governor promptly agreed, and the capitulation was drawn up without delay. Its first article contained the clause that ‘the island of Madeira and its dependencies shall be handed over to the commanders of the forces of His Britannic Majesty, to be held and governed by His said Majesty with the same rights, privileges and jurisdictions as the Crown of Portugal has enjoyed them until now.’ This deed of capitulation, consisting of 7 articles, was signed on 26 December by Pedro Fagundes and Beresford. On the 30th of the same month Beresford issued a proclamation to the inhabitants of the island, which is transcribed in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and is in many respects a most interesting document.

This time the occupation was more complete and absolute than the first. It caused great and painful surprise in Rio de Janeiro, to which the court had moved shortly before, and at our legation in London, and diplomatic efforts began at once to obtain whatever redress was possible for the harm the occupation had done to Madeira. Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho, later Count of Funchal and our representative in London, a man of talent and energy, made the most diligent efforts to have the island handed back. After a stubborn struggle he secured the return of the entire civil administration to the Portuguese Government, while Major-General Beresford kept charge of all military matters and of whatever related directly to them.

Governor Pedro Fagundes resumed his post at the end of April 1808 and reoccupied the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), from which he had been ousted. In practice, however, the British occupation continued, though softened by the diplomatic negotiations conducted by Portugal’s distinguished representative in London and set down in the convention of 16 March 1808.

On 17 August 1808 half of the British troops stationed here, namely one infantry battalion and one artillery company, left for Lisbon under Beresford’s command, and Colonel Mead came to command the British forces that remained in Funchal. In July 1812 Colonel Mead was replaced by Major-General Gordon, who stayed here in command of the British forces until they left Madeira on 3 October 1814.

During these seven years of foreign occupation there were several clashes between the senior authorities of the archipelago and the commanders of the British forces, caused by the latter’s encroachment on powers that belonged exclusively to the governors and captains-general. Prominent among them was the one provoked by a flagrant violation of our sovereignty, when General Beresford had a British soldier who had killed a fellow countryman hanged on our territory.

Even after the European war had ended, the British troops remained in Madeira, contrary to the express letter of the treaties and to the promises solemnly made to our ambassador in London. Only after repeated representations by the Portuguese Government did they embark at Funchal, on 3 October 1814, bound for England under the command of Major-General Gordon, as stated above.
As a fitting tribute to the memory of this illustrious diplomat, one of the new streets of the city of Funchal was named after him. See Funchal (Marquis of).
Occupation of Porto Santo by the Constitutional troops

On 4 April 1832 Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) was occupied by a constitutional force of 60 artillerymen, who had arrived from the island of Terceira aboard the war brig *Conde de Vila Flor* and the war schooner *Terceira*. The force was commanded by Captain Bento José de Oliveira, who at once had Queen Maria II proclaimed on the island. On the 7th of the same month the frigate *D. Maria II*, returning from the blockade of Madeira, reached Porto Santo. On board were Admiral Sartorius, the future prefect (*prefeito*) Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque, the dean of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), Januário Vicente Camacho, and other constitutionalists. The occupation lasted until 5 May, when the said force and the others who had landed on the island left for the Azores.
In addition to the force of 60 men already mentioned, 104 volunteers embarked who had fled the island of Madeira to enlist in the constitutional army.

While the expedition remained on Porto Santo, several ships were captured, and their cargo was used to supply the inhabitants. These were already suffering some hunger, both because the island’s harvest the previous year had been poor and because the blockade made it impossible for provisions to come from Madeira.
Complete calm reigned on Porto Santo throughout the occupation, thanks to the discipline of the troops and the vigilance of Mousinho de Albuquerque and the officers under his command.

On 29 May, after the constitutional troops had left, the yacht *Bomfim* arrived at Porto Santo from Madeira. On board were the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) Esperança Freire, the inspector of the Arsenal José Joaquim de Amorim, the engineer Pegado and a detachment of 30 soldiers of the 7th Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry) and the 8th Infantry, commanded by Second Lieutenant António Pedro de Azevedo. The acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of Miguel I took place at once, and all of them returned to Madeira that same night.
Maria II was proclaimed again on the island of Porto Santo on 7 June 1834.
Oldenburg (Prince of)

Prince Nicholas Frederick Augustus of Oldenburg, a lieutenant-general in the Russian army, spent about two years in Madeira (1884–1885). He became very well known here for the lavish and grand life he displayed, for the dazzling parties held at his residence and also for the acts of philanthropy he frequently performed.
It was he who had published in Paris the French translation of Herculano’s novel *Eurico, o Presbytero*, made by the Viscountess of Nogueiras.

The Prince of Oldenburg lived at the *quinta* (country estate) ‘Vigia’ (‘lookout’) and had in his service two Cossacks, excellent horsemen, who were watched with curiosity by the people of Funchal whenever they rode out. He died in Geneva in January 1886.
Oliveira

At various times several individuals bearing this surname settled on this island, founding a number of families that spread through many parishes of the archipelago. Around the middle of the 18th century Domingos de Oliveira Alvares came to Funchal and set himself up as a wine merchant. He founded a large and distinguished family whose members include Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) João Francisco de Oliveira, Joaquim de Oliveira Alvares and the Count of Tojal, all of whom we deal with in this *Elucidário*. Domingos de Oliveira had a grandson, Benjamim de Oliveira, born in England in 1806, who held high offices in that country. A biographical notice before us states that he was a member of the British Parliament, of the Royal Society and the Society of Antiquaries of London, of the Council of the Royal College of Chemistry and of the Botanical, Zoological and Horticultural Societies of the same city, vice-president of the Archaeological Society of England, director of the British Institution for the Fine Arts and of the English Painters, a member of almost all the philanthropic societies of London, etc., etc. Benjamim de Oliveira was several times entrusted by his country’s government with important missions to various European governments. He published several works.

Many of the people surnamed Oliveira in Madeira also descend from Pedro de Brito Oliveira Pestana, who came to Madeira with his brother João Mendes de Brito around 1470. Both held noble rank (*foro de fidalgo*), according to Dr Azevedo in his notes to the *Saudades*.
Oliveira (Benjamim de)
See Oliveira.
Oliveira (Canon Alfredo César de)
This illustrious Madeiran, the son of Augusto César de Oliveira, was born in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) on 22 May 1840.

After studying at the Lyceum (*Liceu*) and the seminary (*Seminário*) of this city, he was ordained priest on 30 August 1863. He held parish posts in the parishes of São Roque (‘St Roch’) and Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), and by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 15 February 1867 he was presented to a canonry of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*). He also held the ecclesiastical offices of vicar general, member and president of the governing board (*junta governativa*) of the bishopric, and deputy to the governor of the diocese. In 1880 he was transferred to the archiepiscopal cathedral of Évora, and he lived in that city until his death.

As a preacher, as a writer, poet and journalist, as a politician and parliamentarian, and as a citizen holding various important public offices, Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira always displayed the superiority of his intellect. He showed the versatility of his talent, which could deal with varied and complex questions on subjects diametrically opposed and without any affinity with one another – a gift granted only to choice minds, privileged by nature.

The most characteristic side of his mind, and the one in which he shone most brilliantly, was that of preacher, politician and journalist. In all these expressions of his intellect he showed his undeniable worth and the rare abilities he possessed.

From a very early age he devoted himself to preaching from the pulpit. He made his debut, with the most auspicious success, in his native town while still a mere deacon, at the festivities held there to celebrate the marriage of King Luís I to Dona Maria Pia.

From then on his triumphs as an orator were great. Here in Madeira he enjoyed the reputation of an accomplished preacher, and some of the sermons he delivered in the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) and in other churches of this diocese were truly remarkable. In the pulpits of the capital he confirmed the reputation as a distinguished preacher that had preceded him there, delivering several sermons in the churches of the Madalena (‘Magdalene’) and the Incarnação and in the chapel of Saúde, which earned him the most flattering mentions in the Lisbon press. He planned to publish his sermons, but as far as we know he published only two sermons as separate pamphlets and another in a newspaper of this city.

Canon Alfredo was a skilful and adroit journalist who combined ease and elegance of expression with tightly reasoned argument. This made him a formidable debater and an opponent to be feared. He was a tireless fighter who never retreated, even in the thick of combat. He took part in memorable press campaigns in which the heat of passion sometimes drove the contenders to excesses of language, but our distinguished fellow Madeiran bore no grudges and readily forgot the wrongs done to him. He wielded the weapons of irony and ridicule with rare skill and, taking aim at his adversary now in prose, now in verse, almost always emerged the victor in these often sterile battles of the pen, whose chief spurs are political partisanship, vanity and personal interest.

He contributed more or less regularly to the *Imprensa Livre*, the *Revista Semanal*, the *Aurora do Domingo* and the *Crença*, of Lisbon, as well as to other newspapers. He was the founder and chief editor of the periodical *A Lâmpada*, published in Funchal in 1872. In 1876 he undertook the publication of the first daily newspaper here in Madeira. Many at the time thought the venture impossible or bound to be very short-lived, but it overcame every obstacle and still exists today with a promising future: the *Diário de Notícias* of Funchal. In the city of Évora he also founded the *Notícias do Alentejo*, the first daily newspaper published there (see vol. I, p. 359).

He was also an inspired poet, writing a number of lyric poems that lie scattered through various newspapers. He also cultivated the satirical genre, at times showing himself a worthy disciple of Nicolau Tolentino.

Canon Alfredo and Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Leite Monteiro, wishing to save from oblivion many poetic works of undeniable merit by Madeiran poets, which remained unpublished or scattered through the newspapers, undertook the publication of ‘Flowers of Madeira’ (*Flores da Madeira*), of which two volumes appeared. The collection earned high praise from the eminent writer Teófilo Braga in a letter published in 1872 in a newspaper of this city.
Besides countless articles, he wrote the novels *Uma noite num hotel*, published in the *Revista Semanal*, and *Os Mistérios do Funchal*, published in the *Diário de Notícias*.

Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira was a passionate politician. With a prominent place on the platform of the press, and able to draw on the influence of many friends and colleagues scattered throughout the district, he wielded remarkable party ascendancy here in Madeira. This soon marked him out for elective posts and positions of political trust: he served as a representative (*procurador*) to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and as a member of the District Council (*Conselho de Distrito*).

His influence and learning had naturally marked him out to represent his fellow Madeirans in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament). On 13 October 1878 he was elected deputy for the opposition by the constituency of Ponta do Sol for the legislature of 1879, and he was elected again by the same constituency on 19 October of that year for the legislature of 1880–1881. On 6 March 1887 he was once more elected deputy for Madeira, but he withdrew his candidacy in favour of his close friend and our distinguished fellow Madeiran Henrique de Sant'Ana e Vasconcelos, who had been the candidate with the most votes after the four deputies elected.

In parliament Canon Alfredo confirmed the reputation he enjoyed as a preacher. He proved a distinguished parliamentarian, revealing considerable gifts as an orator, above all in the debate he conducted with the noted publicist Rodrigues de Freitas. He always defended the interests of his fellow Madeirans with great fervour; particular mention should be made of his speech and bill on the afforestation of the mountains of Madeira. He was president of the administrative committees of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) and of the Asilo da Mendicidade (Mendicity Asylum) of Funchal, and he also carried out other public-service commissions.
In Évora he declined the posts of civil governor and deputy with which his friends and fellow party members on several occasions wished to honour him.
He died in the capital of the Alentejo, where he enjoyed the greatest prestige and the most heartfelt esteem, on 19 April 1908.
Oliveira (Dom Francisco Júlio de)
He was appointed Bishop of Funchal in 1723, but never took possession of the office, having been transferred to another diocese.
Oliveira (Dr António Rodrigues de)

He was a native of Portugal, but lived for many years on this island while carrying out various public-service commissions. He came here appointed *corregedor* (royal district magistrate), taking up office on 4 October 1790. He later held the posts of inspector of tobacco and soap works and of judge conservator (*conservador*, special judge for British subjects) of the British Conservatorial Court (*conservatória britânica*, special court for British subjects). He also served as inspector of agriculture, and in that capacity he left on record at the Council of Calheta (‘small cove’) a set of instructions on agricultural matters, which for the time were a valuable piece of work and can still be read with interest today. Laudatory references to these instructions are found in various works and documents.
Oliveira (Dr João Francisco de)
He was born in Funchal on 9 March 1761, the son of Domingos de Oliveira Álvares and Dona Lourença Rosa Justiniana de Oliveira, wealthy property owners in this city.

He enrolled in the faculty of medicine of the University of Coimbra, where he must have been a distinguished student: not only did he receive the degree of bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate), but he also took the doctoral hood (*capelo*) and was later appointed substitute professor (*lente substituto*) in the same faculty. He received his doctorate on 3 July 1785, and in 1787 he was entrusted with deputising in one of the University’s chairs. It seems, however, that he never actually took up teaching, according to Dr Serra Mirabeau in the *Memoria Histórica e Comemorativa da Faculdade de Medicina*. The reasons that led Dr Oliveira to abandon his university career are not known.

He returned to Madeira and, after some time in this city, settled in the capital of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), where he began to practise medicine. He immediately proved himself an eminent physician and soon built up a large and select clientele. The reputation he gained as a clinician marked him out as physician to the Royal Palace, at a time when posts of this kind were held only by members of the nobility or by men who had achieved great renown in the practice of medicine. He was later appointed *físico-mor*, or chief surgeon of the army, and while holding this important post he wrote a set of regulations for the military hospitals, which was regarded at the time as a work of great value.

João Francisco de Oliveira enjoyed the highest regard at court and the particular esteem of John VI, then Prince Regent, who granted him several favours. He and his wife, Princess Carlota Joaquina, stood as godparents to some of Dr Oliveira’s children, which was then a mark of favour that the monarchs granted to few.

It was these ties of friendship, and no doubt the favours he had received, that led Dr Oliveira to stage the abduction of Dona Eugénia de Meneses, lady-in-waiting to Princess Carlota Joaquina, so as to shield the sovereign from his wife’s suspicions and from a scandal at court. He embarked secretly at Caxias bound for Cádiz and, after leaving Dona Eugénia de Meneses there in a safe refuge, went on to the United States of America, where he remained for some years. The scandalous affair, whose truth only the Prince Regent knew, took on the proportions of a great crime, and the higher courts promptly took it up. João Francisco de Oliveira was sentenced to death, and Dona Eugénia de Meneses, who belonged to the highest nobility of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), was stripped of all the honours and favours attached to her rank, expelled from court and barred from any share in the property or privileges of her family. Anyone wishing to learn more about this episode, in which João Francisco de Oliveira took part to save the sovereign’s honour and which can be explained only by the customs of the time, should consult the lengthy account of it, with the relevant documents, given by the writer Alberto Pimentel in his most interesting work *A ultima Côrte do Absolutismo em Portugal*.

During the years he spent in North America, Dr Oliveira practised medicine there with extraordinary success, according to the Italian geographer Adriano Balbi in his *Ensaio Estatístico do Reino de Portugal*, who adds that he was as distinguished a physician as he was a skilful surgeon. In this connection we may mention that a letter written by a contemporary of Oliveira calls him the greatest Portuguese physician of the last fifty years. Setting aside whatever exaggeration that claim may contain, it is proof of the rare merits of the most distinguished clinician that he was.

When the Portuguese court had already moved to Rio de Janeiro, João Francisco de Oliveira presented himself there to John VI, who not only received him kindly but also ordered the case to be reviewed. In April 1820 the *Mesa do Desembargo do Paço* (the supreme royal tribunal of petitions and pardons) acquitted Oliveira of the crimes of which he had been accused.

João Francisco de Oliveira was then appointed minister plenipotentiary in England. He discharged this office with notable distinction, winning the favour of the English court and rendering important services to his country.

Things seem to have gone less well in Paris, where Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Oliveira also represented Portugal. There he found himself caught up in legal proceedings, on the allegation that he had taken part in a conspiracy to dethrone Louis XVIII. The accusation was never proved and appears to be entirely without foundation. It is well worth reading the long statement that Dr Oliveira wrote on the matter, clearing himself of the charge made against him; it is published in the 2nd volume of the *Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*.
Dr João Francisco de Oliveira was called to the councils of the Crown in 1823, as a member of the short-lived ministry formed after the Vila-Francada, which lasted only from 31 May to 3 July 1823.

He was elected deputy for Madeira for the legislature of 1822 to 1823, and in the national assembly he championed the needs of this archipelago with the greatest zeal. Particularly notable was the speech he delivered at the session of 5 February 1823, in which he proposed important measures to combat the crisis then afflicting Madeiran trade and agriculture. Among his proposals, all of them far-reaching, were the creation of a bank in Funchal to assist merchants and farmers, the organisation of a company for the export of wines and the import of goods, and the construction of a quay in front of the customs house, extending out to where the water reached a depth of 25 feet, etc.

On leaving the embassy in Paris, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) João Francisco de Oliveira withdrew to Funchal with his wife and children. There he devoted himself entirely to study, to the management of his household and to directing the affairs of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) of this city. He was its president (provedor) for some years and rendered it very notable services, and his portrait still hangs today in the meeting room of the Managing Board (*Mesa Gerente*) of that charitable institution. It was at this time that Councillor Oliveira founded a public class (*aula*) in surgery attached to the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal (*Santa Isabel*), which he himself undertook to teach without payment. He then proposed to the central Government a plan for establishing a medical school, which received official approval but was never fully carried out. Shortly before his death he again took up residence in Lisbon, and he died there on 26 December 1829.

In April 1803 the Prince Regent granted Dr Oliveira extensive lands in São Jorge (‘St George’) and the Quinta de Sant’Ana in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), which had belonged to Pantalião Fernandes and had been incorporated into the Royal Property (*Reais Próprios*) or the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*), as it is called today. These and other properties were inherited by his son, Dr Alexandre de Oliveira, who in the middle of the 19th century built the house on the *quinta* (country estate) at São Jorge. He bequeathed the properties in that parish and the family residence in Funchal to his sister, Dona Maria Leopoldina de Oliveira, who had been born in the United States of America while Councillor Oliveira was living there. The universal heir of Dona Maria de Oliveira was the lamented and eminent Bishop of Funchal, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who applied the entire proceeds from the sale of this inheritance exclusively to building the great edifice of the Seminary of the Incarnation (*Seminário da Encarnação*). It was never entirely completed, and the offices of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) are housed (1921) there. Dona Maria Leopoldina de Oliveira died in Funchal on 3 February 1902.

We understand that the distinguished writer and man of science Dr Eduardo Burnay is working on a historical study of João Francisco de Oliveira, for which he has gathered many valuable documents, some of them found on this island and supplied by one of the authors of this *Elucidário* (1921).

Various articles have been published in newspapers and journals about the real or feigned abduction mentioned above. Worth reading is what appears in volume IV of the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (‘Historical Archive of Madeira’) and in the pamphlet *A Rua da Junqueira* by Artur Lamas, published in 1922.
Oliveira (Francisco Manuel de)

In his own day he enjoyed a certain reputation as a poet, but today his name is entirely forgotten. Inocêncio Francisco da Silva classed him as a poet of the second rank, saying that his compositions were not altogether bad and that he deserved credit for making known in Portugal the first examples of a genre until then wholly unknown there. The author of the ‘Portuguese Bibliographical Dictionary’ (*Dicionário Bibliográfico Português*) is referring to Oliveira’s translation, made from the English text, of various poems written in some of the Oriental languages of India. Francisco Manuel de Oliveira was born on this island in the second quarter of the 18th century and died shortly before 1819.

When the public chair (*aula pública*, state-funded teaching post) of philosophy was created in this city in 1772, Francisco Manuel de Oliveira was appointed to the chair, which he held for many years. He was retired on a pension by a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 3 April 1799. We believe that he also taught at the Diocesan Seminary, since he delivered an address there at the opening of classes in 1786. We know of no other details of his life.

Inocêncio da Silva gives the following list of the works published by Oliveira: *Escolha de Poesias Orientaes. . . seguidas de outras varias rimas*, Lisbon, 1793, pp. 61–138; *Colleção Poetica*, vol. II, Lisbon, 1794, 173 pp., a continuation of the preceding volume; *Oração... na inauguração do Seminário do Funchal*, Lisbon, 1787, 40 pp.; *Ensaio poetico sobre a harmonia do mundo...*, Lisbon, 1805, 120 pp.; *Princípios elementares da língua Inglesa. . .*, Lisbon, 1809, 255 pp.; and the translation of the *Avisos interessantes á humanidade ...*, Lisbon, 1788.

In the time of Governor Botelho, a daughter of Francisco Manuel de Oliveira was granted an allowance equal to a third of the salary her father had received, in recognition of his services and of the poverty to which she had been reduced.
Oliveira (João Fortunato de)

He was born in this city on 26 March 1828 and died here on 6 April 1878. He lived abroad for some years, especially in England, where he perfected his knowledge of French and English. In 1863 he was appointed teacher of these languages at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), and he taught both subjects there until his death. He contributed prose and verse to several of this city’s newspapers. A volume of poems entitled *Flores Agrestes* was published in Funchal in 1860. It is the first part of the work and contains the poetic compositions of João Fortunato de Oliveira; the second part, which was to contain the poems of Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega (see that entry), never saw publication.
Oliveira (João Nepomuceno de)

He was born in Funchal in 1783 and died in 1846. He was the son of the Madeiran writer Francisco Manuel de Oliveira. He published a small book of verse and the Portuguese version of two novels translated from French, according to the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (‘Historical Archive of Madeira’).
Olive tree (Olea europaea)

An evergreen shrub or small tree with lanceolate-linear leaves (var. *madeirensis*) or oblong, obovate, oval or rounded leaves (var. *buxifolia*), found on the coast of Madeira, on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and on Ilhéu Chão (‘flat islet’). It yields a yellowish wood with dark veins and small fruits that are not used because they have little flesh. It is also known as *zambujeiro*.

Some olive trees that we saw years ago on Porto Santo, whose fruit was used although less tasty than that of the mainland, probably came from cuttings imported from Portugal rather than from specimens native to the island (1921).
Oliveira Paixão (José Joaquim de)

He was a native of Portugal, but lived for many years in this city, having come here as violist of the Teatro Grande do Funchal, which the governor Dom Álvaro de Sousa de Macedo ordered to be demolished in 1832. Oliveira Paixão was a distinguished composer of sacred music, and until a few years ago many of his musical compositions were still performed in the churches of this diocese.
Oliveira (point)

On the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’) there is a projection, or point, called Oliveira. When the discoverers João Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira marked out the limits of their captaincies, the territory was divided by a roughly straight line running from Ponta da Oliveira to Ponta do Tristão, these points being regarded as the extremities of their donataries. At the south-eastern end an olive stake was planted as a boundary marker; it is said to have been sent from the mainland expressly for that purpose by Prince Henry the Navigator. This is why that projection of land bears the name Ponta da Oliveira.
Oliveira (landing place and quay)
At Ponta da Oliveira (‘olive-tree point’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), there is a small quay, built in 1909 and linked to the main road (Igreja) by a branch 1800 metres long.
Olivine
A silicate of magnesium and iron; orthorhombic system. It occurs in the basalts of Madeira as grains and small irregular crystals, yellowish green in colour, transparent and with a vitreous lustre.
Omboni (Tito)
Works: *Viaggi nell Africa Occidentale*, da Milano Stabilimento di Civelli (1846). This work, which is dedicated to Queen Maria II, contains various references to the island of Madeira.
Omnès (Dr Charles)
This French naval physician dealt with the climate of Madeira in his work entitled *Stations sanitaires de l'Atlantique occidental* (Montpellier, 1888).
Onda (A)
Its first issue appeared on 12 September and its last on 15 December 1871; twelve issues were published in all. It was a newspaper of instruction and recreation, edited by João de Nóbrega Soares.
Common opal
Hydrated silica. The resinous-looking, semi-translucent variety and the red variety (jasper opal) are found on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Openheim (Dr)
A German palaeontologist who studied several fossil corals from Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) found by the Madeiran naturalist Adolfo César de Noronha.
Operário (O)
This periodical, which styled itself the organ of the working classes, published its first issue on 31 January 1920 and ceased publication in June 1922.
Ordem (A)

Its first issue appeared on 5 January 1852 and its last on 1 September 1860. It had two series: the first of two hundred and thirty-five issues and the second of one hundred and ninety-eight. It was published on Saturdays.
Order of Christ

The Order of the Templars had rendered the most distinguished services in the formation and consolidation of the Portuguese nation, and afterwards in the struggles that had to be waged against the Moors and the Castilians. It passed on to its successor the same enthusiastic ardour and the same heroic self-sacrifice in defence of the homeland, and in that successor the monarchs always found their best and most powerful ally in extending our dominions and in the greatness and prosperity of our country.

Prince Henry the Navigator was the first Portuguese prince to assume the mastership (*mestrado*) of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), and it is said that he sought in that powerful body the principal support for carrying out the grand enterprise he had conceived. Diogo Lopes de Sousa, his predecessor in the mastership of the Order, had left it highly prosperous and surrounded by the greatest prestige and influence, which suited remarkably well the projects that the prince would attempt to carry out.

It was a rich and powerful order. Its members, full of faith and daring, eager for the spread and triumph of their religious ideals, hungry for adventure and irresistibly drawn to the mysterious and the unknown, could no longer be contained within the narrow limits of the mainland frontiers. They went to Ceuta in 1415, in a first and fruitful attempt, and would later go to the ends of the earth.

Prince Henry could not have found more active and devoted collaborators anywhere else. There is no doubt that the material resources at the Order’s disposal and the battle-hardened, heroic phalanx of its members, all bound by religious vows, were the principal factor in the accomplishment of his gigantic work.

The prince, and above all the highest-ranking members of the Order, did not forget the services rendered, and demanded spiritual and religious supremacy in the new dominions won from the seas and the continents. The monarchs made various grants to the Order of Christ, giving it superintendence over religious services, which it exercised chiefly through the priests it counted among its members.

The royal letter (*carta régia*) by which King Duarte granted the Madeira archipelago in spiritual matters ‘for ever’ to the Order of Christ is dated 26 September 1433. We have already dealt with this subject, albeit briefly, in the article Donations (vol. I, p. 368), and we refer the reader there. That article shows how the Order soon lost its predominance and the privileges it enjoyed, chiefly because the mastership of the Order was incorporated into the Crown (royal letter of 27 April 1497) and because the diocese of Funchal was created (papal bull of 12 June 1514).

It is not easy today to determine precisely how far the privileges and rights enjoyed by the Order extended in this archipelago. Besides its oversight of spiritual and religious matters, it collected certain taxes and levied charges on certain revenues. Of these we have only a vague knowledge, and we lack the material for a sound and detailed assessment of the subject.

In spiritual matters, the religious leadership of the Order, which was vested above all in the Vicar of Tomar (*vigário de Tomar*, head of the Order of Christ's spiritual jurisdiction overseas), always sought to maintain its supremacy in this archipelago. It sent priests to carry out ecclesiastical duties here and to oversee all religious services.

Father António Cordeiro says ‘that João Gonçalves Zarco, as soon as he had founded the town of Funchal and saw that it still had no secular priests with parish jurisdiction, wrote to Prince Henry the Navigator asking him to send some; and the Prince, as master of the Order of Christ, ordered Dom Friar Pedro Vaz, then prior (title of the parish priest) of Tomar, to remedy that want; and the said Prior at once sent to Madeira a priest with the title of vicar and others with the title of beneficiaries; and in the same manner he provided the town of Machico with others of the like kind’. João Garcia, vicar of Machico, was a knight of Christ and came to this island by order of his Order, overseeing religious services in the captaincy of Machico (*Capitania de Machico*) in the second quarter of the 15th century. The name of the churchman who may then have directed ecclesiastical affairs in the captaincy of Funchal is not known. Nuno Cao, a senior member of the Order, came to this island in the last quarter of the 15th century to take supreme charge of religious affairs in the captaincy of Funchal, and perhaps in the whole archipelago; in 1514 he became the first dean of our Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*). In 1508 the Order of Christ sent to this island Bishop Dom João Lobo, whom we have already discussed on p. 277 of the 2nd volume of this work. In 1514 this diocese was created, and Dom Diogo Pinheiro, Vicar of Tomar, was appointed to it; the Order of Christ thus lost the spiritual supremacy it had enjoyed in this archipelago.

Elsewhere (vol. I, p. 225) we have given a detailed account of the Campo do Duque (‘duke’s field’), which belonged to the grand mastership of the Order of Christ. It kept that name because its Grand Masters were the Duke of Viseu, Prince Henry the Navigator; Duke Ferdinand, the Infante Ferdinand; the Dukes of Viseu Dom João and Diogo, Duke of Viseu; and the Duke of Beja, Manuel I, later king.

It was these dukes and Grand Masters who, through their representatives, exercised the rights belonging to the Order in this archipelago, and it seems that they collected for themselves the various taxes whose usufruct belonged to the Order. They owned the Campo do Duque and made several grants on it for the building of the municipal fold of the municipality (*concelho*), the Council house and the Cathedral (Sé Catedral). It is not known whether they owned any other land. It was the Order that brought about the creation of the customs house of this city, intended especially for collecting the duties levied on the export of sugar. It was the Infanta Dona Beatriz, as guardian of her young son Diogo, the Grand Master, who sent Luís de Atouguia to this island to set up those customs services.

As we have already said, we cannot establish precisely the extent of the temporal privileges the Order enjoyed in this archipelago. It seems, however, that they were far from small, to judge by the list of commanderies that Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo transcribes from the *Definições e Estatutos* of the Order in one of the notes to the *Saudades*:
‘The commandery of the tithes of fish and the small tithes (*meunças*) of the captaincy of Machico and the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Forty *moios* of grain, that is to say, twenty of wheat and twenty of barley, which are granted with the Habit, on the island of Porto Santo.
The commandery of the tithes of all the grain revenues of the island of Madeira and of those of the Azores.

The commandery of the tithes of fish and small tithes of the captaincy of Machico and the island of Porto Santo, at thirty-five thousand réis (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto) in the year 1555.
The commandery of forty *moios* of mixed grain of the island of Porto Santo, at sixty-four thousand réis in the year 1545.
The commandery of the tithes yielded by the grain mills of the island of Madeira and the islands of the Azores, at one hundred and forty thousand réis in the year 1600.’

When the Grand Master Manuel I, Duke of Beja, succeeded John II on the throne, the principal rights and privileges that the powerful Order enjoyed on this island passed to the monarch, completing a process already begun by the kings before him. The Order of Christ was not entirely stripped of some of the dues it collected here, but once this archipelago had become crown domain (*realengo*), the rights and exemptions it enjoyed were reduced to very limited proportions.
Seraphic Order

An old chronicle of this Order states that it was the Order which spiritually discovered this archipelago, because some of its members, who accompanied the discoverers, began to perform religious duties on the very day of the first landing at Machico. There they set up an improvised altar and celebrated the holy sacrifice of the Mass, which is said to have taken place on the feast of the Visitation of Our Lady to St Elizabeth of Portugal, which the Catholic Church celebrates on the second of July. There is no reason to dispute this statement, since it is certain that in the earliest days of the settlement and colonisation of this island it was the Franciscan friars who exercised all the functions of their ministry here. In the chapels of St Catherine, St Paul, São Sebastião (St Sebastian) and Conceição de Cima (Upper Conception) they carried out all the parochial religious services, certainly until the time when the priests sent by the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which the archipelago belonged in spiritual matters, took charge of those same services.

Nuno Cão came to this island on the orders of the Order of Christ in the last quarter of the 15th century, invested with powers to superintend all religious services. Earlier still, around the middle of the same century, the Order had sent Father João Garcia to take charge of the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico and its captaincy. Even before these men, as stated in the article Order of Christ, other secular clergy had been sent to this archipelago to perform religious and, in particular, parochial duties.

The Franciscans nevertheless remained on this island, and their numbers became considerable, for we read in an old Seraphic chronicle ‘that so many friars came from Spain, Castilians, Galicians and Biscayans, that they could well fill the whole island with convents.’ These religious were drawn by the solitude of the place and the isolation in which they could live here. They sought out spots far from the centres of population and gave themselves up to the hermit’s life, like the ancient cenobites in the deserts of Egypt. It seems, however, that their stay on this island was not long.

The Seraphic Order remained here in Madeira, forming regular communities and founding several convents. Around 1430 Friar Rogério came to this island, and he seems to have established the first regular Franciscan community. The first nucleus of that community was probably formed beside the chapel of São João da Ribeira (St John the Baptist). One of the religious hanged himself there, and it seems that the remaining brethren abandoned the place.

Around 1476 a number of Franciscans led by Friar Rodrigo da Arruda arrived in Funchal and reorganised the community of São João, as set out at greater length in the article Convent of São Francisco (vol. I, p. 312), to which we refer the reader.
Several convents of this order were founded, for both friars and nuns, of which we have already given an account on pp. 306–314 of the 1st volume of this work.
Ordinance Militia
They were established in Madeira in the third quarter of the 16th century and later came to form a third-line corps, as stated in the article Militia (*Milícia*), p. 363 ff. of vol. II.
Religious Orders
