The religious orders that established themselves in this archipelago were the Seraphic or Franciscan order, as can be seen at greater length in the articles Seraphic Order (*Ordem Seráfica*) and convents (*conventos*); the order of the Jesuits, to which we have devoted a special article entitled Jesuítas; and the order of the Carmelites, which occupied the hospice (*hospício*) attached to the church of Carmo (Carmelite church). Of this order we know nothing beyond what we have said in the article devoted to that church.
*Orelha de boi* (*Silene venosa*)
Vernacular name of *Silene venosa*, a member of the Caryophyllaceae that is not rare on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
*Orelha de cabra*
See Tanchagem.
*Orelha de rato* (*Elatinodes spuria*)

Vernacular name of *Elatinodes spuria*, a glandular plant of the Scrophulariaceae family, with prostrate stems and small, spurred, yellow flowers with a purple upper lip. It grows in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira.
Orphan Girls’ Retreat House

The home was founded in 1725 by the governor and captain-general Francisco da Costa Freire, with money raised from alms. It opened with 4 orphan girls, who were given a matron, a portress and a maid from the start. The number of residents was later raised to 6, and in time other ladies were also admitted to the establishment, among them some widows and some married women. All of them came on the vow (*promessa*) to pay annual pensions of never less than 30$00 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), which were not always paid.

For a long time the establishment was governed by the so-called Compromisso de Lisboa (Lisbon statutes (*compromisso*)). Among various provisions, these allowed only orphans aged 15 to 20 to be admitted, besides as many ladies in the conditions already mentioned as could be taken. The orphans themselves, however, had to leave on coming of age, to make room for new admissions, so that the function of this *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) was kept up in this way.»
In 1849 regulations (*regimento*) of its own, with eight articles, were drawn up for the *recolhimento*, but they were never put into effect.

Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro tried to turn the Orphan Girls’ Retreat (*Recolhimento das Órfãs*) into an independent charity home (*casa pia*), but the idea came to nothing, even though many people received it favourably.

The Orphan Girls’ Retreat, also called the Orfanato or Recolhimento of St Elizabeth of Portugal, is housed in a building adjoining the old Hospital, and the Commission of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) is responsible for paying the subsidies that the residents receive. There are at present (1921) 16 residents, together with a superintendent, a doorkeeper and a servant. The superintendent receives 18 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) a month, the doorkeeper 15 and the servant 5. As for the residents, one receives 12.50 escudos and another 10.00, while the rest receive subsidies ranging from 7.50 to 5.00 escudos a month. The commission at present spends 140 escudos a month on the subsidies for the 19 people who live in the *recolhimento* (religious retreat house for women) (1921).
Expenditure on the Orphan Girls’ Retreat amounted to 631.42 escudos in 1909–1910 and 716.67 escudos in 1913.

In 1913 there were 2 orphan girls and 24 ladies living there. The orphans received 3 to 6 escudos a month, according to circumstances, for their keep, as well as diets of meat and milk. The subsidised residents received an average of 3.50 escudos a month; two of them held the posts of doorkeeper and turn-keeper (*rodeira*, in charge of the revolving hatch), and therefore received an additional monthly allowance of 1 escudo. One of the orphans was superintendent of the Recolhimento, for which she received 15 centavos a day in addition to the subsidy mentioned.
The designation of Orphans has disappeared from the subsidy roll, which now lists only 16 residents, besides the superintendent, the doorkeeper and the servant (1921).
Madeiran Choral Society
It first appeared in public at the Teatro Dr. Manuel de Arriaga on 7 and 8 July 1921. Its conductor is the distinguished musician and lawyer Dr Manuel dos Passos Freitas (1921).
It visited the Canary Islands in May 1922, where it was warmly applauded.
Administrative organisation

The province of Madeira forms a single administrative district, the district of Funchal, which is divided into 11 municipalities (*concelhos*). On the island of Madeira these are the municipalities of Funchal, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Porto Moniz, São Vicente, Santana, Machico and Santa Cruz; the municipality of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) lies on the island of that name. The Desertas (‘deserted islands’) and the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) belong to the municipality of Funchal.

The following list gives the parishes into which the municipalities of the archipelago are subdivided. Municipality of Funchal: Sé, Santa Maria Maior, São Pedro, Santa Luzia, São Gonçalo, Monte, São Roque, Santo António and São Martinho. Municipality of Câmara de Lobos: Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Quinta Grande and Curral das Freiras. Municipality of Ribeira Brava: Ribeira Brava, Campanário, Serra de Água and Tábua. Municipality of Ponta do Sol: Ponta do Sol, Canhas and Madalena. Municipality of Calheta: Calheta, Arco da Calheta, Estreito da Calheta, Prazeres, Paul, Jardim do Mar, Fajã da Ovelha and Ponta do Pargo. Municipality of Porto Moniz: Porto Moniz, Achadas da Cruz, Ribeira da Janela and Seixal. Municipality of São Vicente: São Vicente, Ponta Delgada and Boaventura. Municipality of Santana: Santana, São Jorge, Arco de São Jorge, Faial and São Roque do Faial. Municipality of Machico: Machico, Água de Pena (part), Caniçal, Santo António da Serra (part) and Porto da Cruz. Municipality of Santa Cruz: Santa Cruz, Água de Pena (part), Gaula, Caniço, Camacha and Santo António da Serra (part). Municipality of Porto Santo: Porto Santo.
Under the administrative organisation that came into force in Madeira in 1835, there were 10 municipalities, made up as follows:
Municipality of Funchal: it had the same organisation as at present.

Municipality of Câmara de Lobos: the parishes (*freguesias*) of Câmara de Lobos, Quinta Grande, Campanário, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos and Curral das Freiras. Municipality of Ponta do Sol: the parishes of Ponta do Sol, Tábua, Ribeira Brava, Serra de Água, Canhas and Madalena.

Municipality of Calheta: the parishes of Calheta, Arco da Calheta, Estreito da Calheta, Jardim do Mar, Prazeres, Paul and Fajã da Ovelha. Municipality of Porto Moniz: the parishes of Porto Moniz, Achadas da Cruz, Ribeira da Janela, Seixal and Ponta do Pargo. Municipality of São Vicente: the parishes of São Vicente, Ponta Delgada and Boaventura. Municipality of Santana: the parishes of Santana, São Roque do Faial, Faial, Porto da Cruz, São Jorge and Arco de São Jorge. Municipality of Machico: the parishes of Machico, Caniçal, Água de Pena and Santo António da Serra. Municipality of Santa Cruz: the parishes of Santa Cruz, Gaula, Caniço and Camacha. Municipality of Porto Santo: the parish of Porto Santo.

Of the 10 municipalities (*concelhos*) mentioned above, only those of Funchal, São Vicente and Porto Santo have the same extent today as they had in 1835. Part of the parishes (*freguesias*) of Água de Pena and Santo António da Serra passed long ago to the municipality of Santa Cruz, under the authority granted to the Government by the law of 29 May 1843 to alter the territorial division of the municipalities. Since 1852 the parish of Porto da Cruz, which originally belonged to the municipality of Santana, has been incorporated into the municipality of Machico, in accordance with the decree of 19 October of that year. The municipality of Porto Moniz lost the parish of Ponta do Pargo, which was definitively annexed to the municipality of Calheta by the law of 26 June 1871. The municipalities of Câmara de Lobos and Ponta do Sol also had to give up parishes when the municipality of Ribeira Brava was established on 16 August 1914: the former ceded the parish of Campanário, and the latter the parishes of Ribeira Brava, Tábua and Serra de Água.

The decrees of 7 November 1849 and 10 December 1867, which abolished the municipality of Porto Moniz, incorporated the parishes of Porto Moniz, Seixal and Ribeira da Janela into the municipality of São Vicente, and that of Ponta do Pargo into the municipality of Calheta. When the same municipality was abolished once again by the decree of 18 November 1895, all the parishes that belonged to it passed to the municipality of São Vicente, with the exception of Achadas da Cruz, which was incorporated into the municipality of Calheta, to which, as we have seen, the parish of Ponta do Pargo already belonged.

The same decree of 10 December 1867 also abolished the municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santa Cruz and Santana. It annexed the parishes of Campanário, Quinta Grande, Câmara de Lobos, Estreito, Curral, Caniço and Camacha to the municipality of Funchal; the parishes of Santa Cruz, Gaula, Água de Pena, Santo António da Serra, Faial, São Roque do Faial and Santana to the municipality of Machico; and the parishes of São Jorge and Arco de São Jorge to the municipality of São Vicente.

Under the classification established by the Ministry of the Interior in November 1920, the municipality of Funchal is of the 1st class, the municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Calheta and Ponta do Sol of the 2nd, and all the remaining municipalities of the 3rd. The law of 26 August 1922 altered what was stated on p. 219 of vol. I of this *Elucidário*: under that law, municipalities of the 1st class have 20 full councillors (*vereadores*), those of the 2nd 16, and those of the 3rd 12. The executive committees consist of 7, 5 and 3 councillors respectively.
See Administrative autonomy, Municipal Councils, District Committee, Municipalities, Governors and captains-general, Civil governors, General Councils and Municipalities.
Fiscal Organisation

The city of Funchal is home to the Finance Directorate (*Direcção de Finanças*), which consists of two departments: the District Finance Department (*Repartição Distrital de Finanças*) and the Tax Inspection Department (*Repartição da Fiscalização de Impostos*), formerly the Tax Inspectorate (*Inspecção de Impostos*). This latter department, once autonomous, now depends, like the District Department, on the Director of Finance.

The district of Funchal is of the 1st class, and the Director of Finance must therefore hold the rank of head of services. The Director of Finance has in the past been called Inspector of the Treasury (*Inspector de Fazenda*), Treasury Delegate (*delegado do tesouro*) and Inspector of Finance.

Each municipality (*concelho*) has a municipal tax office and a section of the tax inspection service. The municipality of Funchal is of the 1st class, that of Calheta of the 2nd, those of Ponta do Sol and Santa Cruz of the 3rd, and the rest of the 4th class.

The Funchal Customs House, which today reports directly to the Directorate-General of Customs (*Direcção Geral das Alfândegas*), was for some time merely a branch office of the Customs House of Ponta Delgada (the Azores) and later a branch of the Customs House of Lisbon. It was the decree of 21 April 1892 that granted it the autonomy it now enjoys. The decree of 29 December 1887, which divided the country into three districts – Lisbon, Porto and Ponta Delgada – and made Funchal a branch of the last of these, was received with general displeasure in this city, and perhaps for this reason it remained in force only briefly.
Decree no. 4560 of 8 July 1918 established clearance posts on Porto Santo, in Câmara de Lobos and in Machico, but this provision has not yet been put into effect.

The Funchal Customs House has Company no. 1 of the Revenue Guard (*Guarda Fiscal*, customs and excise corps), with the following sections: Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo. The revenue posts of the Cais do Lazareto, the Cais da Alfândega (Customs House Quay), Ponta da Cruz, the Praça de São Pedro, Ribeira Brava, Câmara de Lobos, Ponta do Sol, Calheta, Paul, Porto Moniz, São Vicente and Ajuda belong to the Funchal section; those of Machico, Reis Magos, Santa Cruz and Porto da Cruz to the Machico section; and that of Porto Santo to the Porto Santo section. See Customs Houses (*Alfândegas*) and Royal Treasury Board.
Judicial organisation

Under absolutism the whole Madeira archipelago formed a single judicial district (*comarca*), with Funchal as its seat. It had a *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) and a *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), both appointed by the Crown, and was divided into five *julgados*, each with its own ordinary judge (*juiz ordinário*, locally elected lay judge): Machico, Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol, Calheta and São Vicente. There was also a judge of pious bequests (*juiz dos resíduos*) and three judges of orphans, one in Funchal, another in Calheta and the third in São Vicente. All these magistracies were overseen by the Junta de Justiça (see that entry), which, as we have read somewhere, decided all criminal cases carrying a penalty of no more than ten years’ deportation; its decisions could be appealed to the higher courts of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), which sat in Lisbon.

On 15 October 1835 the old judicial system came to an end, and two *julgados* were set up, both seated in Funchal, each with its own district judge (*juiz de direito*). In 1838 these *julgados* came to be called judicial districts – the eastern and the western. The first comprised four *julgados* and the second five, each of them presided over by an ordinary judge. The eastern judicial district stretched from the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), to that of Arco de São Jorge, and also included the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). The western judicial district ran from the parish of São Pedro to that of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) and Boaventura (‘good fortune’), which borders on Arco de São Jorge. On 27 May 1838 the ordinary judges were elected for the newly created *julgados*; the Madeiran newspaper *A Chronica* (‘The Chronicle’), for the year 1838, records how the parishes were distributed among these *julgados*.

The decree of 12 November 1875 established four judicial districts (*comarcas*) in Funchal, and the justice-of-the-peace districts (*julgados de paz*) of these judicial districts are at present organised as follows:

Judicial district of Funchal. It has nine *julgados*: that of São Pedro, with the parishes (*freguesias*) of São Pedro and São Roque; that of the Sé, with the parishes of the Sé, Santa Luzia and Monte; that of Santa Maria Maior, with the parishes of Santa Maria Maior and São Gonçalo; that of Campanário, with the parishes of Campanário and Quinta Grande; and those of São Martinho, Santo António, Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos and Porto Santo, with the parishes of those names.

Judicial district of Ponta do Sol. It has five *julgados*: that of Ponta do Sol, with the parishes of Ponta do Sol, Canhas and Madalena do Mar; that of Ribeira Brava, with the parishes of Ribeira Brava, Tábua and Serra de Água; that of Calheta, with the parishes of Calheta and Arco da Calheta; that of Estreito da Calheta, with the parishes of Estreito da Calheta, Jardim do Mar and Prazeres; and that of Ponta do Pargo, with the parishes of Ponta do Pargo, Fajã da Ovelha, Paul do Mar and Achadas da Cruz.

Judicial district of São Vicente. It has five *julgados*: that of São Vicente, with the parish of that name; that of Porto Moniz, with the parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela and Porto Moniz; that of Ponta Delgada, with the parishes of Ponta Delgada and Boaventura; that of São Jorge, with the parishes of São Jorge and Arco de São Jorge; and that of Santana, with the parishes of Santana, Faial and São Roque do Faial.

Judicial district of Santa Cruz. It has four *julgados*: that of Caniço, with the parishes of Caniço and Camacha; that of Machico, with the parishes of Machico, Caniçal, Água de Pena (part) and Santo António da Serra (part); that of Porto da Cruz, with the parish of that name; and that of Santa Cruz, with the parishes of Santa Cruz, Gaula, Água de Pena (part) and Santo António da Serra (part).
The former ordinary judges (*juízes ordinários*) who served in the *julgados* were abolished by the decree of 29 July 1886.

The judicial organisation described above was profoundly altered when the Judicial District of São Vicente was abolished by the decree of 9 June 1927. In 1931 a municipal court district (*julgado municipal*) was created, covering the three parishes of the municipality (*concelho*). See Judicial Administration, District Judges, Ordinary Judges and Justices of the Peace.
Military Organisation
Under the military organisation of 31 October 1844, the Madeira archipelago was an autonomous Command governed by a colonel.

When the constitution was proclaimed in 1834, Madeira received a prefect (*prefeito*) and military governor: the illustrious Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque. He took up the post on 6 August and left it on 30 September 1835, and from then until 8 November of the same year he served solely as military governor.

In 1836 the 9th Military Division (*Divisão Militar*, a territorial army command) was created on the island of Madeira. Its commander was Brigadier, later Marshal, Antonio de Padua da Costa, formerly military governor, who took up the post on 30 January 1837 and held it until 12 September 1838. He returned to command the 9th Division on 23 September 1847, remaining in the post until the Division was abolished by decree of 20 December 1849. In the interval between Marshal Padua’s two terms, the Division was commanded on an interim basis by mere colonels.

After this decree the Madeira archipelago became a simple Military Command (*Comando Militar*). In February 1861, however, the Division was restored and lasted until 1868. Its commanders were first Brigadier José Julio do Amaral and then Colonel Jacinto Augusto Camacho, the latter on an interim basis.

Before the military organisation of 31 October 1884, to which we referred above, the archipelago formed a subordinate Subdivision of the 1st Division, whose headquarters were in Lisbon. See Madeira (military administration), vol. II, p. 312.
Organ of the Convent of St Clare

Under this heading, the Funchal *Diário de Notícias* of 22 November 1924 published a short article that aroused particular interest at the time; the historical claim it put forward went entirely unchallenged. We reproduce it here in full, and refer the reader to the articles Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) and Children and Sons-in-Law of Zarco, which shed useful light on the subject.

‘The old organ of the extinct Convent of St Clare, which had lain dismantled for some years, has been sent for repair. The work was entrusted to the well-known and distinguished musicians Mr César R. Nascimento and Mr Guilherme H. Lino, who have just completed their task.
As early as tomorrow the ancient instrument will be heard at the feast of St Cecilia, patron of musicians, which a group of devotees is having celebrated in that church.

Mr César Nascimento and Mr Guilherme Lino carried out investigations inside the organ and established that it had been commissioned by the children of João Gonçalves Zarco, who presented it to the convent in the reign of Manuel I, in 1498, seventy-nine years after their father had discovered Madeira.
The instrument is therefore 426 years old and is regarded as a relic on account of its age.

For this reason the restorers, conscientious artists, took a great interest in repairing it, even though they had at one point resolved to abandon the task, since the organ was badly damaged – indeed, one might say, almost beyond use.

After work that demanded great patience as well as their extensive artistic knowledge, they succeeded in bringing it to a successful conclusion, preserving all the principal parts of the old organ so as not to diminish the value its antiquity confers on it.
The holes made by woodworm were skilfully filled with inlaid work (*embutidos*). The repair, which was finished a few days ago, had begun in October 1923.

Some years ago this organ was put up for public auction together with other property belonging to religious congregations. It was bought by Dr Romano Santa Clara Gomes, who kept it for a long time in an outbuilding of that former convent.
Last year he gave it to the confraternity of St Clare so that it could be repaired and used in the religious services of that church.
It was then that Mr Raimundo de Freitas, the worthy custodian of that church, commissioned Mr César Nascimento and Mr Guilherme Lino to repair it.

Last year the same craftsmen repaired the organ of the parish church of Machico, a gift from King Manuel I made in 1499. That organ, too, had become almost unusable. It is now a fine instrument once more, and it is also of great value, being 425 years old.

As is well known, the church of St Clare, which suffered serious damage on 12 December 1917 when it was hit by a shell from the submarine that bombarded Funchal, is classed as a National Monument (*monumento nacional*), and its upkeep is the responsibility of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*).’

Origin of the Island of Madeira
This is the title of a 10-page pamphlet published in this city by Miguel Manuel de Ornelas e Vasconcelos in 1897. The merit of the work may be judged from its ‘argument’, which we transcribe below:

‘In September Bacchus and divine Ceres, joining the world, bring forth the harvest. I shall tell you what I saw in the uplands of Faial, what fired my inspiration, heart and vein, so poor, so wretched in resources, which might have been strong and full of learning, but comes chaotic, hoarse and out of tune to play upon the rough and jangling lyre.’
Miguel de Ornelas, who held the post of solicitor (*solicitador*) in the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal, died in this city on 3 October 1889.
Ornelas

The first of this surname on the island of Madeira, says the distinguished annotator of the *Saudades*, was Álvaro de Ornelas, only son of Lopo Esteves de Ornelas, head of this ancient and noble family, which is one of the principal families of this island. He belonged to the household of Prince Henry the Navigator, on whose orders he took part in the discoveries promoted by the prince. He was one of the first settlers of the island, and held as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Caniço (‘reed’) the lands from Ponta do Garajau (‘tern point’) upwards as far as the stream of Caniço, from the sea to the uplands, where his son Álvaro de Ornellas Saavedra later founded the entail (*morgado*) known as that of Caniço. – Constança de Mendonça de Vasconcellos, first wife of this Álvaro de Ornellas Saavedra, or, according to others, of Ayres de Ornellas e Vasconcellos, founded the entail of Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*), also at Caniço, in 1591.’ (See *Obras de D. Aires de Ornelas*, 1881.)
Ornelas (Baron of)

António Evaristo de Ornelas, Baron of Ornelas, was born in Funchal around 1830 and took his doctorate in medicine at the Paris faculty in 1854. His doctoral thesis is entitled *Anatomie pathologique et traitement des polypes fibreux de la base du crâne, dits mesopharyngiens* (Paris, 1854). Around 1886 he retook the examinations at the Medical-Surgical School of Porto, and the thesis he then defended is entitled *Da Dilatação do Estômago*. The Baron of Ornelas practised his profession in Paris, where he had a large clientele and where he died in the early years of the 20th century.
Ornelas de Vasconcelos (Agostinho de)

Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos Esmeraldo Rolim de Moura was a true representative of the old and legitimate Portuguese nobility, polished and enriched by all the worthy qualities of modern civilisation. Although jealous of his titles of nobility and of the aristocratic traditions of his illustrious family, he remained an eminently liberal spirit, a mind open to every manifestation of progress and a passionate devotee of the sciences and letters.

Eloquent proof of these statements lies in the consistent disdain with which he always spurned titles and honours, content with the pedigree inherited from his forebears and with the distinctions attached to the high offices he held. It lies, too, in the tireless zeal with which, day after day, he enriched his profound intellectual culture, diligently following every discovery, innovation and advance made in the various branches of human knowledge.

The subject of our biography was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé in this city on 14 March 1836. He belonged to one of the most distinguished families of Madeira, whose ancestors included several notable figures who left an illustrious name in the history of our country. His parents were Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, holder of the entail (*morgado*), who served as civil governor here, and his wife Dona Augusta Correia Vasques de Olival.

Having completed his secondary education with notable distinction at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), he enrolled in the Faculty of Law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1852, graduating in 1857 after a brilliant academic career.

Drawn by the allure of diplomacy, he embarked on this glittering career as soon as he had completed his university studies. By decree of 18 November 1857 he was appointed second attaché to the legation in Washington, taking up the post in June of the following year and remaining there until February 1859. He made use of his leisure as a young diplomat to travel through a considerable part of the country, visiting its most notable establishments and institutions. A record of this survives in the important memoir he wrote on the Philadelphia penitentiary, which is included in the work *Reforma das cadeias em Portugal*, from the pen of Dr António Aires de Gouveia, Archbishop of Chalcedon.
Transferred to the court of Berlin, he remained there until 1862, on several occasions serving as chargé d’affaires in the absence of the ambassador.

In 1862 he was promoted to first attaché and posted to Rio de Janeiro and then to St Petersburg, but illness prevented him from taking up either post. On 26 April 1865 he was appointed secretary of legation in Vienna, and was then transferred to London, where he remained until December 1867.

Placed on the inactive list, he spent some years away from the diplomatic career. He returned to it by decree of 27 September 1886, which appointed him minister plenipotentiary to Madrid, a post he never actually held: by decree of the 30th of the same month and year he was transferred to the office of director of the political department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. By decree of 17 November 1891 he was appointed director-general of political and diplomatic affairs in the same ministry. He later asked to be relieved of this post, and the decree granting his request stated that he had served with great zeal and great intelligence.
By decree of 6 September 1894 he was appointed minister plenipotentiary to Russia, taking up the post on 10 November of the same year, and he remained there almost until his death.

As a diplomat he carried out several important and thorny missions, which earned him special praise and various honours. Particular mention should be made of his work on the convention concerning the Moura dispute, for which he was awarded the Grand Cross of the Order of Charles III of Spain. In 1900 he was one of our country’s representatives at the celebrated Hague Conference.

Throughout his long career as an official of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, he gave constant and eloquent proof of the strength of his intellect, his great learning and the rare diplomatic qualities that distinguished him and made him a true statesman. For this reason he was regarded as one of the most highly esteemed members of the Portuguese diplomatic corps.

He also trod the winding paths of Portuguese politics. Yet he emerged unscathed and unblemished from that quagmire, in which so many sully the purity of their convictions and even their own dignity. He was elected deputy for Madeira for the legislatures of 1868–1869, 1869–1870, 1870–1871 and 1871–1874, and by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 16 May of that last year he was appointed a peer of the realm. In both chambers he stood out as a parliamentarian of great merit, always marked in his speeches by the most perfect courtesy, together with a remarkable correctness of form. He was certainly not a tribune who swept his listeners away in torrents of eloquence, but a fluent and correct speaker who knew the subjects he discussed, and his words were always heard with the closest attention by the whole chamber. Among the speeches he delivered in both houses of parliament, several are counted as notable, especially those he gave on the *Padroado* (Portuguese royal patronage over the Church in the East) of India and the overseas missions.

He was, as we have said, a passionate devotee of the sciences and letters, and indeed his most constant endeavour was to enrich his mind with new knowledge, drawn daily from extensive study and long hours of reading. Gifted with a brilliant intelligence, served by an astonishing memory, he possessed an uncommon erudition in every branch of human learning. His command of several languages, including Latin itself, contributed not a little to this. As a man of letters, he gave us incontestable proof of his worth in the writings he left, showing that he could have won an honourable name in the history of his country had he devoted himself entirely to a literary career.

Goethe’s masterpiece, the famous tragedy *Faust*, was all but unknown in Portugal. Councillor Agostinho de Ornelas ventured upon the hazardous enterprise of rendering the most admirable product of German literature into the vernacular. It was an arduous and difficult task for the illustrious subject of this biography, who, not being a poet, sought to translate into Portuguese verse the work of genius of Germany’s greatest poet. The version suffered from this circumstance, and it must be confessed that its poetic form was not always free of imperfections. These imperfections often arise from the desire, carried to the most exacting scruple, to render Goethe’s thought faithfully, even at the evident sacrifice of form. The translation by António Feliciano de Castilho, which appeared later, is undoubtedly most correct and adorned with true poetic splendour. However, it was made from an imperfect French version and with the boldness and liberties of the inspiration of a most exquisite poet, so it departs fairly often from the German original, and at times seems more a paraphrase than a true translation. There is no lack of critics who prefer Councillor Ornelas’s version to Castilho’s, because it was made from the German original and with unsurpassed scruple of fidelity. Despite its defects, it is without doubt a work of value, which speaks highly of his literary merits.

In 1884 a thick volume entitled *Obras de D. Ayres de Ornelas de Vasconcellos* was published in Porto, containing the various writings of the former and unforgettable bishop of this diocese, who was the brother of Councillor Agostinho de Ornelas. These fine writings are preceded by a long and exquisite biography of the illustrious prelate, which takes up nearly 200 pages of the book and which, in the words of a distinguished writer and eminent professor of the University, was written with a pen of gold. This biography, a true model of language with a marked classical flavour, was the work of Councillor Agostinho de Ornelas.

In 1892, on the occasion of the Columbus centenary, he published an interesting *Memoria sobre a residência de Cristóvão Colombo na Ilha da Madeira*, which was included in the volume *Memorias* that the Royal Academy of Sciences of Lisbon (*Academia Real das Ciências de Lisboa*) published to celebrate that centenary.
On all these grounds he was elected a member of that Academy, and was one of the members it appointed to organise the publication of the said *Memorias*.
He was also a member of other scientific and literary societies, both Portuguese and foreign.

He carried out with distinction various public missions of great importance, such as representing Portugal at the Columbus centenary celebrations in Madrid, and serving as our country’s delegate at the celebrated Hague conference held in 1898.

Among other decorations, he held the following: the grand crosses of Charles III of Spain, of St Gregory the Great of Rome, and of the Crown and of St Stanislaus of Prussia; grand officer of the Legion of Honour; commander and knight of St James; commander of the Order of Albert the Valiant of Saxony, of the Red Eagle of Prussia, and of the Imperial Order of the Rose of Brazil, etc.
He died on 6 September 1901 at Niederwalluf, Germany, while holding the important post of minister plenipotentiary of Portugal in Russia.
Ornelas e Vasconcelos (Aires de)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha on 5 March 1866, the son of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos (see that entry) and Dona Maria Joaquina Saldanha da Gama. On his father’s side he belongs to one of the oldest and most distinguished Madeiran families, and on his mother’s side he is a grandson of the Counts of Ponte. He took his preparatory studies at the Colégio de Campolide and, after attending the Polytechnic School (*Escola Politécnica*) and the Army School (*Escola do Exército*), was commissioned second lieutenant in 1889 in the General Staff.

He devoted himself from the outset to the study of military affairs, soon contributing actively to specialist reviews. In 1893 he founded the *Revista do Exercito e da Armada*, of which he was one of the most assiduous editors.

Aires de Ornelas left for East Africa in 1895, where he proved himself a most distinguished soldier and quickly won great renown throughout the country. He took part in the campaign against Gungunhana and in the preparation of the Marracuene and Inhambane columns. It was, however, in the battles of Coolela and Marracuene, where he truly displayed his courage, his competence and his unsurpassed composure, that he most firmly consolidated his existing reputation as one of the officers who had most distinguished themselves in our African wars. Mousinho de Albuquerque, the great hero of our African campaigns in the second half of the 19th century, would have no other chief of staff than Aires de Ornelas, stating in his report on the campaigns of 1896-1897 that ‘in his arm he was the most complete officer he had ever known, possessing all the qualities of a cavalry officer in the field and of a staff officer.

He devoted himself above all to the study of colonial affairs, in which his time in Africa, his administration of the district of Lourenço Marques and the various military and diplomatic missions he carried out gave him the greatest authority. In our country he was regarded as one of the public men with the broadest and deepest knowledge of our overseas questions, above all in their bearing on relations with the other colonial powers. His expertise in this field showed itself chiefly in the studies he published in various reviews, in his editorship of the *Jornal das Colónias*, in the chapters ‘Marraquene’ and ‘Coolela’ of the book *Campanha das tropas portuguesas em Lourenço Marques e Inhambane*, in the study entitled *As raças e línguas indígenas de Moçambique*, and in a number of lectures given at the Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia*) and the Naval League (*Liga Naval*). Aires de Ornelas represented the Portuguese government at the Military Congress held in Madrid on the occasion of the Columbus centenary, and later served as a technical delegate at the celebrated Hague conference. He was also chosen, together with Admiral Hermenegildo Capelo and Commander Ernesto de Vasconcelos, to form the technical commission that went to discuss with the British the question of the Barotse boundaries, which had been submitted to the arbitration of the King of Italy. Aires de Ornelas took a very active part in this mission, especially in helping to prepare the historical memorandum justifying Portugal’s rights.

When Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) João Franco was charged in 1906 with forming a government – leaving throughout the country glorious traditions that still endure – he chose Captain Aires de Ornelas to hold the portfolio of the navy and overseas. It was as holder of this portfolio that in 1907 he accompanied the Crown Prince, Louis Philippe, on a journey to our overseas colonies in West and East Africa.
When the Republic was established, Councillor Aires de Ornelas resigned his army commission and left the country, living abroad for some time.

On returning home, he took an active part in organising and leading monarchist politics, and today he is the lieutenant of Manuel II in our country (1921). Caught up in the political events of the attempts to restore the monarchy, he was arrested and spent many long months imprisoned in the Penitentiary and in the Fort of São Julião da Barra (St Julian's Fort).

He contributed widely to many newspapers and reviews, and for some years was editor of the *Diário Nacional*. Besides the writings already mentioned, we know that he published: *Mousinho de Albuquerque e a sua acção em Moçambique*, *A Expansão de Portugal*, *Politica Marítima Nacional*, *A Marinha Portuguesa*, *As doutrinas politicas de Charles Maurras*, *Um Anno de Guerra*, 285 pp., *Segundo Anno de Guerra*, 305 pp., etc.
He was deputy for Madeira in the legislative session of 1918, and in January 1922 he was also elected deputy for one of the constituencies of mainland Portugal.
He died in Lisbon on 14 December 1930, and in 1934 his remains were transferred to the Angústias cemetery in Funchal.
Ornelas de Vasconcelos (Ayres de)

Following the popular sedition that deposed and imprisoned Governor Francisco de Mascarenhas (see that entry), ‘Ayres de Ornellas was elected by the nobility and the people as governor and captain-general on 18 September 1668. The prince regent Dom Pedro confirmed him in this high office, and he remained in it until his successor, Ayres de Saldanha, took office the following year, 1669.
He was the great-great-great-great-grandfather of two distinguished Madeirans, Archbishop Dom Aires de Ornelas and Agostinho de Ornelas, peer of the realm.
Ornelas e Vasconcelos (Dom Aires de)

Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, who belonged to one of the oldest and noblest families of this island, was born in Funchal on 18 September 1837. He was the son of Aires de Ornelas de Vasconcelas, holder of the entail (*morgado*), and of Dona Augusta Correia Vasques de Olival.

Having attended secondary classes in this city, where he was an outstanding pupil, he enrolled in 1854 in the faculty of theology of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and graduated there in 1859, winning first prize in every year of his course. In 1860 he defended his *conclusões magnas* (doctoral theses), receiving the doctoral hood (*capelo*) and the degree of doctor on 29 July of the same year. His inaugural dissertation, written in Latin and later published as a volume, is entitled *De Christianae Religionis Origine*. Invited to become a professor in his faculty, he resolved to pursue a university career, but later abandoned that intention for reasons unknown to us.

Returning to Madeira already ordained a priest, he was appointed in succession professor at the seminary (*Seminário*), canon, synodal examiner, dean, vicar general and president of the governing board (junta governativa) of the bishopric. In all these posts he always showed irreproachable conduct and a charming simplicity. As a teacher in particular he revealed a profound knowledge of the theological sciences, and this, together with the way he treated his students, made every pupil an admirer and a friend.

On returning from a visit to Rome, where he had attended the sessions of the Vatican Council, he was proposed by the prelate of this diocese, Dom Patrício Xavier de Moura, as his coadjutor and future successor. He was confirmed as titular bishop of Gerasa in the consistory of 6 March 1871 and received episcopal consecration in Lisbon on 7 May of the same year.

He took over the interim administration of this diocese on 17 May 1871, but only began to govern it definitively on 27 October 1872, after the death of the incumbent bishop. His episcopate lasted only three years and was not free of serious difficulties, created in large part by some turbulent members of the cathedral chapter. Despite his great austerity of character, his zeal for the observance of church discipline, the most upright intentions that guided him in office, and his exceptional talent and profound learning, he was unable to show in his native land the worth of all these enviable qualities. He did so instead in the distant regions of Hindustan, where he displayed so brilliantly his remarkable qualities as a fearless apostle, a reforming spirit, a man of action and a highly cultivated intellect, winning the respect and admiration of millions of people scattered across the vast dioceses of which he was the metropolitan.

By royal letter (*carta régia*) of 23 July 1874, Dom Aires de Ornelas was presented as archbishop of Goa and Primate of the East, and he was confirmed by Pope Pius IX in the consistory of 19 November of that year. He left Madeira on 25 January 1875, amid the most imposing and affectionate farewell in living memory here. On 27 December of the same year he arrived in Goa and took charge of his vast archdiocese.

We would go too far if we tried to give details of his episcopal administration in the East. His episcopate lasted little more than three years, and in so short a span it would have been impossible to show greater energy and zeal in the exercise of his arduous apostolate. The reform of the seminary, the administration of the church fabrics, the religious dissensions among the various Indian castes, the direction of several charitable institutions, the observance of ecclesiastical discipline, the revival of the religious spirit, etc. etc., all received his special attention, and to these many questions he devoted the best of his ardent zeal and boundless dedication. His rule of the archdiocese of Goa was particularly marked by the pastoral visitation he made to such remote regions of the Portuguese *Padroado* (Portuguese royal patronage over the Church in the East) in the East, and by the exposition of the body of St Francis Xavier, the great apostle of the Indies. This visitation, made through foreign countries and among peoples so diverse in religion, usage and custom, was a triumph for the archbishop. More than that, it contributed notably to strengthening the prestige of the Portuguese name in the vast regions he travelled through.

The exposition of St Francis Xavier was an event for the whole of India. To the old city of Goa, so lonely and so abandoned, flocked many thousands of visitors from very distant countries, bringing to the capital of the former Portuguese empire in the East a bustle and liveliness it had never seen. It was on this occasion that the archbishop received several bishops, his suffragans, and vicars apostolic, and gathered them in a provincial synod. He then revealed to these members of the higher clergy, some of them of great intellectual stature, the gifts of his intelligence and learning, aided greatly by his knowledge of theology and of the Latin, French and English languages, which he wrote and spoke correctly.

The writings of the illustrious archbishop – pastoral letters, sermons, speeches and reports – show a shepherd full of zeal and self-denial for his flock. They are also models of the purest and most idiomatic Portuguese, with a marked classical flavour, and they both instruct and charm the reader.

It was in his laborious apostolate in India, and especially on his painful and exhausting pastoral visitations, that he contracted the serious illness that forced him to leave his archdiocese. He returned to his native island, arriving on 22 May 1879, and was given perhaps the most affectionate and enthusiastic reception this island has ever prepared for its visitors. After some months of rest he went to France to consult specialists about the illness that tormented him. It grew gradually worse until, on 28 November 1880, he died in Lisbon, in the house of his brother, the illustrious Madeiran Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Agostinho de Ornelas de Vasconcelos.

In 1903 his remains were moved to the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua) in Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), the former family vault of the Ornelas family. (See *Obras de D. Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos*, Porto, 1881, 358 pp.)
Ornelas de Vasconcelos (Daniel de)
He graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and practised as a lawyer in Funchal with great distinction and skill.
In the legislature of 1838–1840, when a seat as full senator for Madeira fell vacant, Dr Daniel de Ornelas was elected to it in April 1839.
He was later raised to the peerage and granted the title of Baron of São Pedro (‘St Peter’).

As a peer of the realm, he became known for the bill he presented in parliament on 15 February 1850, abolishing all the entails, entailed estates and annexed chantries (capela) of this archipelago. The bill was very badly received in Madeira, and more than thirty representatives of old entailed houses sent a petition to the Chambers, showing how inexpedient it was and how harmful to the interests of this island.
He died in Lisbon on 23 February 1878.
Ornelas (João Augusto de)

His is today an unjustly forgotten name, yet it once enjoyed well-deserved renown, not only in Madeira but also in mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). His literary output is vast, less because of the dozen volumes he published than because of the contributions he left scattered across various newspapers, notably the old and well-known periodical *O Direito*, of which he was for several decades the principal and most assiduous editor.

In his youth João Augusto de Ornelas contracted a terrible illness that took all movement from his legs, and he spent most of his life confined to his work desk, which he left only shortly before death overtook him. As he found it very difficult to move his pen across the paper, he took advantage of the visits of the many people who called on him to dictate his novels, his short stories, his serials, the correspondence he sent to several newspapers on the mainland and, above all, the countless articles intended for his own newspaper.

He was a tireless worker. Neither the paralysis that crippled his movements, nor the distressing privations he so often endured, nor the torments he suffered within his own home, nor the harsh battles he fought in the press, nor even the smear campaigns raised against him, dampened his spirit or weakened his will. He worked actively and courageously in a combat without truce, a fierce war against adversity, until death laid him low in the arena at the still vigorous age of 53.

His enemies and opponents not infrequently levelled a serious accusation against him – the changeability of his character. The accusation was not entirely unfounded, but it is easily explained, and even largely justified, by the circumstances that surrounded his troubled life and placed him in a tight situation from which few would have been able to emerge victorious.

According to João Augusto de Ornelas’s own statement, made in the *Direito* of 24 August 1863, he was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’) on 26 June 1833. He started out as an apprentice printer and later attended some classes at the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city. He made his literary debut with a few pieces in the *Estudo* and the *Baratíssimo*, and contributed to other newspapers. He took over the editorship of the *Direito*, where for more than twenty years he devoted himself actively to journalism. He cultivated the novel with great success, publishing several works of fiction that were much admired and received high praise from some of our most illustrious men of letters. We shall mention the following: *A Arrependida*, Funchal, 1871, 190 pp., with a letter by José Vieira de Castro and an introduction by Júlio César Machado; *Maria*, Lisbon, 1873, 200 pp., with a prologue by António Augusto Teixeira de Vasconcelos; *A Mão de Sangue*, Lisbon, 1874, 266 pp., with an introduction by Camilo Castelo Branco; *A Justiça de Deus*, Funchal, 1876, 199 pp., with a critical letter by Pinheiro Chagas; *a Victima dum Lazarista*, Porto, 1879, 266 pp.; and *O Engeitado*, Porto, 1886, with an introduction by Pinheiro Chagas.

He published other novels as serials in the *Direito*, some of which he was preparing for publication in separate volumes. He also published the pamphlets *A coroa de oiro ou a honra e a justiça; o que foi e o que é José Cardoso Vieira de Castro*, Funchal 1871, XXXVIII-23 pp., and *A Madeira e as Canárias*, Funchal 1884, 28 pp.

João Augusto de Ornelas was a knight of the Order of Nossa Senhora da Conceição de Vila Viçosa (Our Lady of the Conception of Vila Viçosa). He served as representative (*procurador*) to the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) and as a member of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Poorhouse (*Asilo de Mendicidade*). He died in Funchal on 11 July 1886.
Ornelas (Juvenal Honório de)

Doctor of medicine from the Paris school. He was born on this island and died here, at the age of 67, on 20 October 1873. He was a professor at the former medical school of Funchal. Works: *Dissertation sur le traitement des pertes de sang qui peuvent suivre l'accouchement, par la compression de l'aorte abdominale exercée sur le ventre, la position convenable du corps et l'usage du seigle ergoté et des fortifiants* (thesis); Paris, 1834.
Ornithology
See Birds, Harcourt, Jardim and Ernst Schmitz.
Orography: see Madeira (orographic aspects), II, 314

On this subject, the following articles are also of some interest: Achada, Calhau, the north coast, Costa do Sul, Costas, Encumeada, Fajã, Geologia, Massapez, Quebradas, Salão, and the ‘Dicionário Coreográfico do Arquipélago da Madeira’ by Father Fernando A. Silva.
Orchids

Of the four native orchids known in Madeira, only one – *Orchis foliosa* – is a truly ornamental plant. It does not flower in Funchal, but in the ravines of the interior it bears small, purple, scentless flowers gathered in spikes that are sometimes elongated. Salep can be extracted from the palmate tubers of this orchid, and this is why it is becoming rare in some parts of the island. Some foreigners who visited our island a few years ago took back to their country all the tubers of *Orchis foliosa* they could gather at Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’)!
Orquigny (João José de)

A French physician and naturalist who came to Madeira in 1789, commissioned by the government of Maria I to study the island’s flora and its therapeutic value. Although he lived here for some years, the services he rendered to science were, it seems, nil. See Freemasonry (*Maçonaria*).
Orthoptères
provenant des voyages de S
A. Le Prince de Monaco dans les archipels de Madère et des Açores (*Bull. de la Soc. Zool. de France*, 1892, pp. 46–49).
Dew

Dew is water vapour deposited in tiny droplets on the ground and on plants as a result of the cooling produced by radiation at night. It is seen in Funchal on certain clear, cold winter mornings, when the streets are sometimes as wet as if a fine drizzle had just fallen on them. It is in the mountainous region, however, and particularly in the valleys of the island’s interior, that dew is most abundant and noticeable. Despite what Mason wrote in his *Treatise on the climate and meteorology of Madeira* (see vol. I, p. 276 ff.), we can state without fear of contradiction that the amount of dew deposited in Funchal is notable on only very few days of the year.
Madeirans call dew *sereno*, reserving the word *orvalho* for fine drizzle. [TN: in standard Portuguese *orvalho* means dew.] The *sereno* is unknown in Funchal. (See Climate, I-273.)
Osborne (John)
Works: *Guide to the Madeiras, Azores, British and Foreign West Indias, Mexico and Northern South America*. The 2nd edition of this work was published in London in 1844.
Osga (Tarentola mauritanica var. angustimentalis)
A small reptile of the gecko family (Geconida), which does not occur in Madeira but is found on the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*). It is brown and has a short tail.
Oudinot (Reinaldo)

After the great flash flood (*aluvião*) that devastated Madeira on 9 October 1803, the government in mainland Portugal sent Brigadier Reinaldo Oudinot to the island to supervise the public works then carried out, especially the building and repair of the walls of the three streams that run through the city. He arrived in Funchal on 19 February 1804 and died here on 11 February 1807. He rendered excellent services, not only through the great energy he showed in the works he directed, but also through the proven competence he displayed in carrying out the commission he came to fulfil among us.
On 9 September 1805 he sent the Viscount of Anadia a detailed map of the city of Funchal and its bay, and he began the general map of Madeira, which was completed by Paulo Dias de Almeida.

He wrote a set of *Instructions*, of which a copy, now lost, once existed in the archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*). In 1837 the same Council supplied copies of these *Instructions* to the parish councils of the municipality (*concelho*).

In reward for the services Brigadier Oudinot had rendered to Madeira, his widow, Dona Vicência do Carmo Oudinot, was granted the chantry (capela) founded by Felipe de Barros in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’).
Oudinot (street)
This name is a tribute paid by the Council of Funchal to Brigadier Oudinot, who through his services to Madeira fully earned the gratitude of the island’s inhabitants.

Rua do Oudinot links the Praça dos Lavradores with the small square of São João. A little below it there once stood a bridge over the Ribeira de João Gomes, which we suppose collapsed or was demolished towards the end of the second quarter of the 19th century. The street gives access to the Largo dos Lavradores, where the new Market was built.
Oregano (Origanum virens)

A native labiate, very common in Madeira. It has a pleasant smell and taste, and flowers gathered in spikes, with pale green bracts larger than the calyces. It is used in cooking and can replace marjoram (see that entry).
Sea urchins

About ten species of these echinoderms have been recorded in Madeira. Two of them – *Echinus lividus* and *E. brevispinosus* – live in abundance in the pools near the coast, but they are not used as food. *Diadema europaeum*, dark purple and armed with long spines, and the small *Echinocyamus pusillus* also occur in some places. See Echinoderms and Starfish.
Outeiro
An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas. A chapel dedicated to Our Lady and St Anne once stood there, built in 1733 by Manuel Rodrigues de Canha.
A few years ago José Francisco Cabral de Noronha and his wife, Dona Maria Trindade de Noronha, had a chapel dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*) built at this locality.
Outeiros

They were held in Funchal in the 18th century, as is clearly shown by the *Colecção poética* of the teacher Francisco Manuel de Oliveira, which contains an ode and two sonnets written for *outeiros* in honour of Senhora da Luz (Our Lady of Light), patroness of learning on this island. We have heard from some elderly people that on certain occasions it was customary for the local poets to gather at the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) to gloss mottoes set by the nuns, some of whom cultivated the Muses.
Granting of the Charter
News that Pedro IV had granted a Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) to the Portuguese Monarchy on 29 April 1826 reached Madeira on 12 July of the same year.

On the night of the 14th, while several citizens were gathered at the house of Manuel José da Silveira to celebrate the restoration of constitutional monarchy, the building was stormed by a picket of the 7th Infantry Regiment, which attacked those present with fixed bayonets, even though the governor and his aides-de-camp were among them. In the fray Major Adão was wounded, as was the celebrated António Manuel Rodrigues, known as ‘o Aninhas’, an ardent constitutionalist and one of the strongest men of his day. In the end, however, the soldiers were forced to withdraw in the face of the resistance put up by the constitutionalists, who used the chairs, the tables and everything else in the house to defend themselves against their attackers.

The Minister of Justice had ordered the prelates to issue pastoral letters and to instruct parish priests to explain the Constitutional Charter to the people. According to the *Defensor da Liberdade*, however, the Bishop of Funchal did not comply with this order, and it is certain that three years earlier he had been lavish with instructions to his subordinates to speak against liberal principles.

As the soldiers of the 7th Infantry continued to insult and provoke the constitutionalists, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) resolved at its session of 22 August 1826 to ask the Infanta Regent to transfer the regiment. On 5 October of the same year it also resolved to ask the Governor that the regiment should no longer supply patrols for policing the city and that its other ranks should not leave their barracks after 7 in the evening.

On 23 November 1826 the Council resolved to thank the Infanta Regent for granting its request for the regiment’s departure. Only after the troops had withdrawn could the constitutionalists give themselves over, without risk of provocation, to public demonstrations of rejoicing at the fall of the absolutist regime.

Despite the presence of the 7th Infantry Regiment in Madeira, there were several celebrations on 6, 7 and 8 August of the granting of the Constitutional Charter. See Proclamation of the Constitutional Government.
Ouvidores

They were judges appointed by the donataries and in many cases acted as their deputies. In the donataries’ absence they received the oath of the councillors (*vereadores*), and they exercised judicial and police functions, with power to arrest persons accused of any crime. To curb the excesses of jurisdiction of the donataries and their *ouvidores*, there were already *corregedores* in Madeira in the 15th century, charged with conducting judicial inquiries and punishing judges who abused their office. The bishops also had *ouvidores*: the prelate Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos created two *ouvidorias* in Madeira and one on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). The donataries’ *ouvidores* received a lodging allowance paid by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*).
Ovington (John)

English clergyman and traveller who was chaplain to James II. In the book he published under the title *A voyage to Suratt in the year 1689* (London 1696), he deals with Madeira, giving information that would be of interest were it not for several more or less gross falsehoods among it. As a curiosity, we give below a translation of his account of a ‘mishap’ that befell the ship’s company before leaving the landing place of Funchal. ‘Some of our sailors having failed to answer the roll-call, we supposed that they had fallen into the hands of the Jesuits, who, zealous to spread their faith, seize every opportunity to convert foreigners. A letter was sent to the Governor asking for the return of our men, but it seems he had no authority over that order.
‘Our commander then resolved to land on the beach with 14 armed men, in order to replace the sailors he needed with fishermen.
A happy chance, however, brought his way a small boat carrying an abbot and a vicar to Funchal, who, to their great surprise, found themselves taken prisoner by the crew of our launch.

‘We made them write at once to the governor, telling him of the situation they were in, while at the same time a note was sent to our consul to pass on to the authorities, demanding an exchange of prisoners. ‘The affair was turning sour, because the news of the priests’ capture endangered the English merchants settled in Funchal, but happily everything was settled: we recovered our sailors and the priests were sent ashore, where they were received with great rejoicing by the people.’

If the arrest of the British ship’s crew really took place, as Ovington relates, it was most probably due not to the Jesuits’ zeal for converting foreigners but to the Englishmen’s zeal in the worship of the god Bacchus, which may have led to the intervention of the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties), who at that time was responsible for maintaining order in the city.
Sheep

To expand on and further clarify what is set out in the article Livestock (II-70 ff.), we reproduce an article by the distinguished agricultural engineer Torres Baptista. It contains some interesting details and deals in particular with the wool produced by Madeira’s sheep and its qualities.

‘On Madeira we find acid pastures, and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) basic ones. Pastures derived from the weathering of acid rocks are suited to milk production, because the females find in their fodder substances suited to that purpose.

Hence a special and highly distinctive breed of cattle has developed through adaptation to the environment, and its selection ought to receive (if it does not already) the attention of the competent official bodies.
On Porto Santo, the weathering of limestones, strongly alkaline rocks unsuited to milk production, gives us animals with a fairly robust bone structure, and therefore fit and hardy for work.
But it is not cattle that I wish to speak about, but another kind of livestock that is hardly ever mentioned in Madeira: sheep.
The island of Madeira has about 16,000 sheep. Some live in flocks at pasture, and others are kept under stall-feeding or grazed on a tether.

The island of Porto Santo has about 600 head, which live in flocks, as I have had occasion to see. We all know that wool-bearing livestock can be used for three purposes: producing meat, producing milk and producing wool.
The economic solution to the problem lies in the choice between these purposes.

Let us see which it seems to me it should be. I do not think we should opt for meat production at the expense of the other two. The islands are well supplied with beef, and the cattle are very small in stature, so they do not require, as often happens on mainland Portugal, the slaughter of a smaller animal because consumption is low. Meat production therefore is not very necessary.

Moreover, since these functions do not exclude one another, meat can be obtained without detriment to the use of the wool or the milk. I therefore believe that breeding with meat in view would not improve the breeds in the economic direction required. With this function set aside, the other two remain. For Porto Santo there is no need to hesitate: the geological make-up of the land and the method of rearing on pasture tell us that wool production is the course to take. But Madeira? Various factors must be considered, and they must be weighed with great care. The geological make-up of the land gives us pastures suited to milk production, while the system of rearing in enclosures or on a tether gives us very coarse wool. In addition, the island has a dairy products (*lacticínios*) industry, which is limited to the production of butter. What use is made of the skimmed milk? I know of no manufacture of low-fat cheese, although I am told that it exists on the island, and nor do I know of a casein industry on the island. Madeira consumes a good deal of cow’s butter and exports much more still. The failure to use the skimmed milk is a waste which, in my view, represents a great deal of value. Now, ewe’s milk is richer in fat than cow’s milk, and if it were used and added to skimmed cow’s milk, it would yield not a low-fat cheese but a good cheese for consumption by all social classes and for export. As for the wool function of the Madeiran sheep, in animals that do not live in flocks the wool, although it may improve, will always be inferior.

We must bear in mind that the upper parts of the island, almost uninhabited and unused, lend themselves to pasture, and because of their great altitude a small-scale transhumance could even be practised, which would bring great advantages. In summer, after shearing, communal flocks could be formed by parish, making use of those pastures during the hot season to the advantage of all, and even of the animals’ health and the use of breeding rams.

With these suggestions made, and given that the wool of this archipelago is of the coarsest quality there is, it is urgent to improve it with blood brought in from outside. But should we aim at the production of wool or of milk? Which will be more economical and more suitable? For Porto Santo, the merino, and among the rams of this breed the ‘Fonte Boa’, fully meets the need, so that we need not resort to the blood of foreign breeds, since only improvement in wool has to be considered. For Madeira, if we wish to go for wool, the breed recommended for Porto Santo should be used for the white ewes, or the Alentejo black for the black ones, since there is no better black breed in the world than the one we possess. If we wish to go for milk production, I recommend the French Larzac or, so as not to go outside our own country – and I see no need to – the *saloia* ewe from the outskirts of Lisbon, which fully meets the need.

Now you will ask me for what reason. I will satisfy your curiosity: because I have found that Madeiran wool is so coarse that manufacturers will not take it even in a time of crisis, and that, as it stands, it is fit only for mattress-making, the production of rugs and coarse blankets, and rough goods, while the other economic functions of the sheep are not exploited to compensate.

But a suggestion is often adopted, and I do not wish the improvement to be made in favour of the wool function, for once it has been achieved, economic interests may later tell us that this was not the course that should have been followed, but rather that of milk.

The reverse could happen in the case of the milk function. The industries derived from the products of these functions are non-existent in Madeira, because there is no woollen industry and cheese-making is extremely limited.

It is therefore urgent to improve the breeds in one direction or the other, so that Madeira may tomorrow possess good raw material, and so that its industries, if they are attempted, may establish themselves in future on foreign markets, for labour it has, and more than enough. See Pastures and Livestock.
P
Pacheco

This family surname descends from Antão Pacheco and the commander Gomes Pacheco, who came to Madeira around the middle of the 15th century. Pedro Pacheco, son of Gomes Pacheco, proved his nobility in 1535.
Pacheco (Canon António Aires)

He is a canon of Lisbon Cathedral (Sé de Lisboa) and is regarded as one of the most distinguished Portuguese preachers. He was born on 15 September 1854 in Vilarouco, in the district of Viseu. He came to Madeira in 1877 with the late prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, and took the theology course at the seminary (*Seminário*) of this city, being ordained priest in 1881. For some years he was a teacher and rector of the Diocesan Seminary. In 1888 he was presented as a canon of our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), and some years later he was transferred to the Patriarchal Cathedral of Lisbon.

As editor of the newspaper *A Verdade* (‘Truth’), which he directed for some years, he proved a brilliant and vigorous journalist, distinguishing himself in his writings above all as a skilful polemicist. In reply to the pamphlet *O Sudário Negro*, he published in 1882 a pamphlet of 54 pp. entitled *O Sudário Negro no banco dos réus*. In 1890 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) published the funeral oration that Canon Aires Pacheco delivered in the Cathedral at the funeral rites of King Luís I. He left Madeira in 1890.
Bishop’s palace

When Pope Leo X created the diocese of Funchal by the papal bull *Pro excellenti preeminentia* of 14 June 1514, the magnificent church that today serves as the Cathedral was already almost finished, its construction having begun at the end of the 15th century or in the first years of the 16th century. The same could not be said of the bishop’s palace.

The first prelate of Funchal to reside here was Dom Jorge de Lemos, and we do not know which dwelling houses he occupied in this city. Jerónimo Barreto was the second bishop to come to this island and, according to Frutuoso, he lived in Rua Direita (‘straight street’), ‘in very rich apartments, with their cool gardens’ (vol. I, p. 365).

When Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos, the seventh prelate of Funchal and the third to come in person to administer his bishopric, arrived in Madeira in 1586, he took up residence in Rua das Pretas, in some private houses that later belonged to the chief standard-bearer (*alferes-mor*) of this island, Tristão Gomes de Castro, and where his predecessors are said to have had their usual residence already. It was this prelate, one of the most illustrious of this diocese, which he governed from 1586 to 1608, who built the old bishops’ palace and also the original seminary building, which adjoined it. Of these there remain some apartments, the episcopal chapel and a kind of cloister, a structure typical of old conventual residences, which today form outbuildings of the present palace in Rua do Bispo. The chapel, which ceased to be used for worship after the new bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*) was built, was dedicated to São Luís de Tolosa (St Louis of Toulouse), and its founder, who died in this city on 26 November 1608, was buried there. In view of the state of complete neglect into which this old chapel had fallen, the prelate of this diocese, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, had the mortal remains of Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos transferred from there in 1903 to Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*). They lie just inside the entrance of the church, covered by the same white marble tombstone that could be seen on the original grave.

Bishop Dom Friar António Teles da Silva (1675–1682) enlarged the original palace, and the prelate Dom José de Sousa de Castelo Branco (1698–1721) incorporated into it the adjoining seminary, when the latter moved to the street of the New Convent (*Rua do Mosteiro Novo*). The earthquake felt in Madeira on the night of 31 March to 1 April 1748 caused considerable damage throughout the island to many public and private buildings, and the old bishops’ palace and the adjoining seminary were also badly ruined. The bishop of Funchal at the time was Dom João do Nascimento, who governed this diocese from 1741 to 1753. He proved an eminent prelate who marked his time on this island with various notable works, both in the performance of his episcopal duties and in serving for some years as acting governor and captain-general of this archipelago.

It is to him that we owe the building of the bishop's palace, where the lyceum (state secondary school) is housed today (1921). Obliged to abandon the old residence of the bishops, which the earthquake had left in ruins, he promptly set about building a new palace, which he planned to raise near the Cathedral (the Sé). The insurmountable difficulties that arose in acquiring a new site forced him to make use of that of the ruined palace, which was entirely demolished, except for the part that still stands today. There he had the new bishop's palace built from its foundations. Although it is a heavy building devoid of any architectural refinement, it is nonetheless, for this small city and for the period in which it was built, a building of some importance, and one that in no way dishonoured the rank of its occupants.

The new palace was built in the period from 1748 to 1751. Its founder spent about ten *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis) on it, and the public treasury contributed a roughly equal sum, so that the total cost of the work was twenty *contos de réis*, an amount which, spent 170 years ago, represents a considerable sum today. (1921)
To bring this work to completion, Dom João do Nascimento had to struggle against very grave difficulties, which his unshakeable tenacity was able to master and overcome.
He enjoyed his work for only a short time, for he died on 26 November 1753. He lies buried in the Cathedral of this city.

After the death of the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto in 1911, the bishop's palace passed into the possession of the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*), and the city’s lyceum was installed there in January 1914.

When the present prelate of this diocese came to take charge of the bishopric in 1915, he found a house ready to serve as the episcopal residence, which the Catholics had rented and furnished and then handed over to the head of the Funchal church. This house stands in Rua dos Netos, on the corner with Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), on the right-hand side as one goes up the latter street. The diocesan prelate’s residence did not remain there long, for, through the acquisition by grant and inheritance of an excellent dwelling house in the Largo do Ribeiro Real (‘royal’), this house was definitively made the bishop's palace. The prelate lives there at present, and the ecclesiastical offices are housed in the outbuildings of the property.
The use to which the former bishop's palace was to be put was regulated by the decrees of 5 July and 6 August 1913 and of 9 March and 24 August 1922.
Town hall

The palace on Rua do Comércio, formerly Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), which houses the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office), the police, the land registry (*Conservatória*), etc. (1921), belonged to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’) and is one of the largest buildings on the island. It was built in 1758, and it contained improvements (*benfeitorias*, buildings and walls made by the tenant, which remained his property) that formed part of the unentailed property of the holder of the entail (*morgado*) João Agostinho Figueiroa de França e Albuquerque. The part of the palace that belonged to the Count of Carvalhal was ceded by him to the trading firm Freitas & Macedo in payment of debts. The remaining parts, owned by Afonso de Albuquerque, the Count of Calçada (‘paved way’), Francisco Roque de Albuquerque, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca and others, were acquired by the same firm through purchases made at different times.

The Council rented the palace from the Count of Carvalhal in 1868, and on 4 August 1883 bought it from Freitas & Macedo for 25 *contos*, paid in bonds of the Companhia Geral de Crédito Predial Português which, reduced to their official quotation, yielded the sum of 22,423,900 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). Before this, the Council could have acquired the building for 12 *contos*, but it failed to seize the opportunity it was offered of concluding a highly profitable deal for the municipality.

The present town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) building once housed the English trading house Blackburns & Comp.ª and later the British consul George Stoddart. The Count of Carvalhal had his residence in the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace).

Before it acquired the magnificent building facing the Largo do Município, or Largo do Colégio (*Colégio*, ‘the College’), the Council met in various parts of Funchal. The first building it owned, though not the first in which it held its meetings, was built under an order of Duke Manuel I dated 1486, which directed that a ‘stronghold, council chamber, notaries’ house & pillory’ be built on the square called the Campo do Duque (‘duke’s field’), the ground on which the Cathedral (the Sé) and its adjoining squares and streets now stand. As early as 1470 a letter from Infante Ferdinand to the donatary João Gonçalves da Câmara had asked him to undertake ‘to build the council house & the council pound’ out of the money from the fines of the judge-auditor & of João Gonçalves himself’. The same Infante ordered land to be given beside the great church for this building, which was estimated at 213,096 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

Until 1784 the town hall remained in the building erected on the Campo do Duque, but in that year the Council began to hold its meetings in the Casa da Saúde, at the Entrada da Cidade (‘entrance to the city’), because that building was in a very poor state of repair. The Campo do Duque building stood on the site occupied today (1921) by house no. 61 in the street named after Lieutenant-Commander Carvalho de Araújo, formerly the Rua do Aljube (‘bishop’s prison’). Its ruins, valued at 432,000 *réis*, were sold by award by public auction (*arrematação*) to Dr António José Monteiro for 432,250 *réis* on 30 March 1805.

In 1796 the Council rented a building belonging to Fernando José Correia Brandão for 500,000 *réis* a year, but it occupied it only until 10 March 1798, since its meagre revenues did not allow it to pay so high a rent. It moved back to the Casa da Saúde, where it held its first session on the 31st of the same month and year.

On 7 January 1797 the Council, meeting with the nobility and the people in the town hall, resolved unanimously to ask the Government for a subsidy that would allow it to erect a building to house the various services in its charge. It was suggested that this building might be put up in the Rua do Cotife, the part of the present Rua da Sé lying between the Rua do Sabão and the Rua dos Capelistas. As the Council’s petition went unanswered, the building could not be carried out.

On 13 November 1802 the Council held its first session in the house on the Largo da Sé which in our own day served as the gaol of the judicial district (*comarca*).
