On 30 June 1803 it took possession of that house, having obtained it ‘by award at auction from the Royal Treasury Board (*Junta da Real Fazenda*), which had seized it from the farmstead (*casal*) of Dona Guiomar Madalena Acciaioly for debts to the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*).’ On 20 December 1813 one of the guild representatives (*mesteres*) proposed that the house on the Largo da Sé be sold and the proceeds applied to building a new town hall and a new gaol, but the proposal was rejected by the other members of the Council.

As various works were carried out on the town hall in 1824 so that the gaol could be installed there, the Municipality spent some time in a rented house, returning to the building on the Largo da Sé on 29 April 1825, once those works had been completed. In 1837 the Council again left the building ‘because of the noxious smell of the prisons, where there were 180 prisoners’. It settled first in the Casa da Saúde and then in a building belonging to Dr Daniel de Ornelas, which it resolved to leave at its session of 16 May 1838, to occupy a house on the Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory’), on the site where today (1921) stands the flour mill that belonged to the commercial firm Viúva de Romano Gomes & Filhos.

The flash flood (*aluvião*) of 24 October 1842 caused considerable damage to the building on the Largo do Pelourinho, so in 1843 the Council moved to the Asylum building in the locality of Angústias. It stayed there only two years, however, returning in 1845 to the house on the Largo da Sé. In July 1846 the Council decided once more to occupy the Angústias building, but at the beginning of 1848 it moved to a building in the Rua da Alfândega, having resolved at its session of 2 December 1847 to hand the said building over to the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Asylum.
The last building to serve as the town hall before the present one stood in the Rua do Esmeraldo, opposite the Rua de Cristóvão Colombo; the Council took it on lease at its session of 2 August 1862.

Some 80 years ago the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) sought to put up, on the site then occupied by the convent of São Francisco and now by the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’), a building to house the law courts, the town hall and the administration and tax office of the municipality (*concelho*). In 1864 it opened a competition for the design and estimate of this building. The rules laid down that the design placed first would receive a prize of 240,000 island *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) (50 pounds) and the runner-up the sum of 72,000 island *réis* (15 pounds). The ranking was to be made by a committee made up of the district judges and public prosecutors of the two judicial districts (*comarcas*) then existing on the island, the two engineers directing the public and military works of the district, and the president of the Council.

The design judged most suitable and appropriate was the one submitted by Samuel Sloan & A. Hulton, of Philadelphia, and the runner-up that of Frutuoso Abel Maria dos Santos, of Lisbon. The Council had the result of the competition published in the local newspapers on 2 March 1865. On 19 April of the same year the Council ordered the demolition of the part of the convent of São Francisco that was still standing, and on 11 March 1866, the work needed before construction could begin being already complete, the ceremony of laying the foundation stone of the building took place. Besides the Council, it was attended by the Bishop, the Civil and Military Governor and all the authorities and distinguished persons of the town.

The works on the town hall in Rua de São Francisco were estimated at 40 *contos*, but they never rose above the foundations, and even these were demolished when the Jardim Municipal was laid out (see Convent of São Francisco of Funchal, vol. I, p. 312). The building was to have a ground floor and a first floor: the former for the law courts and their offices, and the latter for the municipality and the administration and tax office of the municipality.

In 1807 the Council archive was moved to a house in Santa Luzia belonging to Dona Ana Cecília, wife of Agostinho Pedro Pereira, and in 1811 to the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, from which it did not return until 1818. These moves were prompted by fears of an enemy landing at Funchal. In 1824 the archive was kept for some months in the residence of the clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*), because the town hall building was undergoing works.

All the municipal councils of the archipelago, except those of São Vicente and Ribeira Brava, own their own buildings, but only those of Santa Cruz and Porto Santo occupy, it seems, their original premises, enlarged or improved to a greater or lesser degree. The original town hall of Machico was recently demolished, and the Council is building another on the same site (1921). That of Calheta, which stood beside the beach, was destroyed by the sea before 1871, and the municipal archive was lost on that occasion. The old council house of Ponta do Sol was destroyed by fire, and the same happened to that of Câmara de Lobos, though we are unable to establish the years in which these disasters took place.
Patron saint and *The Lusiads* (The)

It is regrettable that our greatest poet, in writing the glorious pages of *Os Lusíadas* (*The Lusiads*), should have fallen into the error, through a mere slip or misunderstanding, of confusing St James the Greater, the well-known apostle of the Spains and so deeply venerated there, with Saint James the Less, who preached the Gospel in the regions of Palestine and is the principal patron (*padroeiro*) of the Diocese of Funchal. In stanza 9 of Canto V of *Os Lusíadas* we read:
We put in at that island, which took the name of the warrior Saint James, who so greatly helped the Spaniards to wreak fierce havoc on the Moors!

‘To wreak fierce havoc on the Moors!’ (*Ao fazerem nos Mouros bravo estrago!*): in these words the poet refers to the island of Santiago, the principal island of the Cape Verde archipelago, discovered on the first of May in the year 1460. Camões’s mistake is evident, for that island, and likewise the island of Maio in the same archipelago, were found by the Portuguese on the feast of Saint James the Less, that is, on the first day of May, whereas the lines quoted concern St James the Greater, whose feast the Church celebrates on 25 July. The name given to that island by its discoverers was determined by the fact that it was found on the first of May, the day dedicated to the apostle Saint James the Less, as stated above.

Had it not been for the brilliant poet’s mistake, the passage of *Os Lusíadas* cited above might have contained a laudatory reference to the principal patron saint of our diocese, rather than to the great apostle who evangelised the ancient lands of Spain.
Patron saints

From a strictly religious point of view, every diocese has its own special patrons, and that of Funchal could not have departed from this praiseworthy custom, or rather obligatory precept, which is followed everywhere and always marked by fervent devotions on particular days of the year. It is well known that this diocese has as its first and chief patron the apostle St James the Less, and as lesser patrons St Sebastian and St Roch; and that, since 1803, the city of Funchal and its surroundings have been solemnly consecrated to the protection of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*). The ecclesiastical calendars published every year for the private use of the various churches and chantries (*capelas*) mention the two lesser patrons on 20 January and 16 August of each year.

For centuries the first of May has been solemnly celebrated on this island, and especially in this city. Long before the workers had dedicated that day to commemorating the assertion of their rights, and before the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) had resolved to adopt the first of May as the municipality’s annual public holiday, the feast of the apostle St James the Less, which the Church celebrates on the first of that month, was already solemnly observed here. The day was kept as a holy day; the feast of the patron saint was celebrated in the church that is the seat of the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’); and, above all, there was a splendid procession that set out from the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) and made its way to that church.

These festive commemorations had their origin in solemn vows made by our forebears, which the generations that succeeded them always fulfilled with the most devout commitment over a long period of almost four centuries. At present, this ancient and traditional commemoration is reduced to the feast held on the first of May in the Cathedral and the small procession that goes round the same church (1921).

Gaspar Frutuoso writes that ‘in the year 1521, when King Manuel died, there was a great mortality from plague in Funchal, from which God deliver us; and because it had been in the city for years, Captain Simão Gonçalves and the Council chose by lot as Patron of the said city the Apostle St James the Less, at the end of which they built him a fine house, to which they went in procession.’ This event is narrated in greater detail in the record (*auto*) of the vow of 1523, which reads: ‘.... on the eleventh day of the month of June of one thousand five hundred and twenty-one, this city being in great storm and tribulation of plague and famine and many other hardships, it was agreed in the Council by its officers, who were then Pero João Correia, councillor, and Vicente Gonçalves and Pero Álvares, judges, and the bachelor João de Sousa, purveyor, and the guild representatives, to take a roll of the saints, namely the name of Jesus our Lord and of the Virgin Our Lady, St John the Baptist and the twelve apostles, each by his own name; they put them in a cap, and the lot was drawn by a small boy named João, seven years of age, all first kneeling in prayer and promising to build a house in honour of whichever saint should come out; and by lot there came out the blessed apostle St James the Less, in whose honour a feast was held at once that same day throughout the city; and on the twenty-first day of July they began his house, the city and the said Chapter going in solemn procession barefoot, with the Master of the School, Gonçalo Martins, bearing the altarpiece with the image of the blessed apostle; and he struck the first blow of the hoe at the corner of the chapel on the Gospel side, which house was built on a piece of land that António Spínola gave for the said house...’

On 24 January 1523 the vow was renewed with full solemnity in the Cathedral (the Sé). Present were the captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) with its councillors (*vereadores*), various officials, the whole cathedral chapter and a great many people. All of them solemnly undertook, on behalf of the inhabitants of this municipality (*concelho*), ‘for ever, in each and every year of the world, to venerate and celebrate the feast of the said glorious saint and apostle, which is the first day of May, on which they shall hold a solemn procession, which shall leave the cathedral of the said city solemnly and go to the said house of the blessed saint, where they shall hold solemn vespers for him; and the same shall be done on the eighth day, with solemn mass and procession, which processions shall be held like that of the Lord’s Corpus Christi itself; and it further pleased the said citizens to have the said saint painted in the council chamber, on the banner and on the seal of the city, just as St Vincent is borne on the banner of the city of Lisbon; and the aforesaid vowed this into the hands of the said dean, to fulfil it all themselves and through their successors, and in witness and faith of the truth thereof they signed here...’

From the work *Alma Instruida* by Father Manuel Fernandes, the annotator of the *Saudades* transcribes the following passage: ‘And they soon recognised the Saint’s protection on this occasion; but they came to know it more fully in the year 1538, when a terrible plague was raging. During the procession, the Chief Health Officer, then a man of great standing, said in a loud voice in the middle of the Saint’s chapel: “Lord, until now I have guarded this City as best I could; I can do no more. Here is my staff: be Thou the Guardian of Health.” And he at once laid down his staff and considered himself released from the duty of guarding the City; and from that moment all the stricken grew better, and there was not a single further case of plague. From this comes the custom of the Council, as soon as it enters the church of Socorro (‘succour’), of laying down their staffs on the steps of the high altar.’

On 22 June 1632 a new record (*auto*) was solemnly drawn up before the Funchal Senate (*senado*, the municipal council), intended to display and confirm the gratitude of the Madeirans to their patron saint, St James the Less. After a reference to the plague of 1538, it contains the following words:

‘Never again has the said evil (plague) been on this island. Rather, it is true that, although many ships came to this island with men stricken by this evil, who were sent into penal exile (*degredo*) on the beaches outside this city, where some of them at times died of the said evil, it never entered nor took hold among the people of the land. And God Our Lord has miraculously defended us many times and on many occasions from being attacked by enemies, as happened at the time of the disturbances in this Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), when many fleets came towards this island, of which we had particular warnings from His Catholic Majesty; some of them came within sight of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and all were miraculously turned away by storms and other unexpected events.’

The same record deals with the raid that the Moors made on Porto Santo in 1617, ‘seizing the island and carrying off all its people into captivity’; it was considered a miracle of the saint that those pirates did not come to Madeira. It also alludes to the fact, likewise held to be miraculous, that during the octave of St James, or before or after it, ‘some ship with grain’ never failed to ‘enter this island’. ‘In the year 1632, says the record, the land being in such straits, with poor harvests. . . , there entered, by a particular royal grant of God, through the intercession of the glorious saint (for so all must believe), during the octave of his feast, into the landing place of this city, from the northern parts whence we least expected it! more than 1000 *moios* of grain, by count made, which came to avert the danger that threatened everyone of famine being felt in Madeira.

It is further recorded in the same document that, to show the gratitude of the Madeirans for the protection so often granted by their patron St James the Less, it was resolved to ask ‘the most illustrious and most reverend Bishop Dom Jerónimo Fernando, who at present is governor and captain-general. . . to be pleased to consecrate the church of the same patron.’
See São Tiago (church).

We must record here that in 1942 the Council of Funchal resolved to revive the traditional homage paid to the glorious patron saint and to join in it festively, also ordering the old vows made by the Funchal Senate in past times to be published in a pamphlet. It moved its municipal holiday to 21 August and decreed that the first day of May should be specially devoted to paying due homage to the patron saint of the city. This decision was well received by the whole population and does great honour to the body that took it.

The flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803 caused many deaths and enormous material damage in Madeira, which greatly alarmed our people. On 13 November of the same year, therefore, Bishop Dom Luís Rodrigues Vilares, the cathedral chapter (*Cabido*) and the rest of the clergy met in the choir of the Cathedral to implore divine protection for this island. It was resolved ‘by unanimous agreement’, as we read in a record drawn up on that occasion, ‘to celebrate a most solemn festival on the 9th day of the month of October each year in honour of the patronage of the Most Holy Virgin, Mother of God and of sinners, taking her as protector and special advocate before Our Lord Jesus Christ, her only-begotten Son, to obtain from Him in the first place a general pardon for all our sins, and in the second the suspension of the punishment with which He justly wished to chastise us, so that this city may not again find itself in so lamentable a crisis; on that same day the office of the patronage of the same Most Holy Virgin shall be recited with first-class rite, and a most solemn procession shall be held, attended by His Excellency the Bishop, the Chapter and the rest of the secular and regular clergy, as is customarily done at the feast and solemnity of our most amiable and most devout patron saint, St James the Less; for which the necessary licences of the Prince Regent, Our Lord, and Briefs of the Holy Apostolic See shall be sought; the procession shall go from this cathedral church to the chancel of the aforesaid church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), which was thrown to the ground, should it be preserved in memory of this fatal calamity, and, should it not survive, to the new church that is to be built, where solemn vespers shall be sung in the presence of the Chapter and Clergy, and Mass shall be celebrated on the said 9th, with a sermon, in which this dreadful night shall be commemorated, so that the peoples and future generations may always remember the fate with which we were punished, and the powerful intercession of the Most Holy Virgin, in whom we take refuge so as not to suffer a second punishment and to be preserved from similar calamities.’

The procession referred to in the record, which we have partly transcribed above and which was published in full in no. 159 of the *Correio da Madeira* (‘Madeira Courier’) of 8 October 1922, still takes place today, but only around the Cathedral (1921).

In connection with the same procession, a meeting of the nobility and people was held on 11 November of that year, 1803, in the building of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). Its purpose was to consider a letter from the diocesan prelate, addressed to the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) on the 9th of the same month, ‘concerning the proposed vow that he wishes to be made of an annual procession and festival of the patronage of Our Lady on 9 October each year, so that all the people of this colony may merit the protection of the Mother of God and may not suffer a repetition of the punishment it endured with the flood and flash flood of the said 9th...’. It was decided unanimously that the nobility and people should conform to the prelate’s intention, although this resolution was to remain suspended until the Prince Regent had pronounced on it’. After the flash flood of 9 October 1803 (vol. I, p. 54), the diocesan bishop, chapter, clergy and faithful placed the island, and especially the city, under the protection of Our Lady of the Mount. This was confirmed by an Apostolic Rescript of Pius VII dated 21 July 1804, and the feast of the Patronage of Our Lady of the Mount was then instituted. It was celebrated on 9 October each year, with a solemn procession that went from the Cathedral to the parish church of Santa Maria Maior. The ninth of October was formerly a holy day of obligation, preceded by its own vigil with fasting.
Memorable landmarks

As this subject is closely related to the articles Monuments, National Monuments, Moradias de Zargo and Artistic Heritage, we set down here a few brief notes on the places and buildings that should be regarded as Padrões Memoráveis (‘memorable monuments’) and that are of particular interest to the history of our archipelago.
Madeira

It has been said, and we have repeated it several times, that Madeira is the great undying commemorative pillar (*padrão*) that truly marks the auspicious beginning of that prodigious odyssey unfolding across unknown oceans and continents.

Before the Portuguese sought out these unknown and mysterious islands, they had carried out daring but almost entirely fruitless ventures. Only after this marvellous encounter did they discover the Azores, Cape Verde, São Tomé and Príncipe, the Cape of Good Hope, India, Brazil and the countless islands scattered across the vastness of the Atlantic and the Pacific.

The ‘discovery’ or ‘reconnaissance’ of this archipelago represents not only a notable territorial expansion of our domains as a nation, but also marks our first great achievement as navigators and future masters of the seas. For a nation whose principal role in the history of humanity was that of discoveries and maritime enterprises, the places where those glorious ventures began to unfold, and above all the eminently civilising work they represented, cannot fail to deserve the most devoted interest and the most heartfelt veneration.
Machico

This locality holds a distinguished place in the history of the Madeiran archipelago. Its name is inseparably linked with the auspicious discovery, the first landing and the beginning of the settlement of these remote and unknown regions. It may be said, without undue hyperbole, that the great colonial expansion and the remarkable work of Portuguese colonisation had their first starting point there. It is therefore greatly to be regretted that no commemorative pillar has yet been raised at the spot called the Desembarcadouro (landing place) to remind present and future generations of the glorious events that began to unfold at that memorable site more than five centuries ago.

Gaspar Frutuoso tells us, in his picturesque language, that the discoverers, or rather the first settlers, went ‘to land on the cliff, where there are stones and shallows on which one can easily land, however rough the sea may be, because it is sheltered by the cliff: and this *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) is called today (1590) the Desembarcadouro, where Robert Machin’s people also landed. . . ’.

Although no credence can be given to the well-known and celebrated legend, many weighty reasons suggest that the landing of the earliest colonisers of this island took place there, and that the spot was given the name ‘Desembarcadouro’, which tradition has preserved and the chroniclers have recorded. As stated above, it recalls the discovery, the first landing and the beginning of settlement, each of them a further reason that urges and imposes the duty of a fitting commemoration. This has long been suggested and advocated, but a favourable opportunity for carrying out this pressing task has so far been lacking.

A simple column, crowned by some emblem or patriotic trophy and set on a modest plinth rising from the living rock, would in itself be a small but expressive monument, perpetuating the memory of those events and perhaps recalling them to the many, many people who are surely unaware of them.

In Funchal there are three buildings that every Madeiran should regard as true ‘memorable landmarks’ and look upon with the deepest respect and the purest devotion: the chapel of St Catherine (*Santa Catarina*), the church of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) and the Quinta das Cruzes (‘estate of the crosses’).
Chapel of St Catherine

This small and modest chapel, built by Dona Constança de Almeida, wife of João Gonçalves Zarco, was the first place of worship raised on this island. Beside it the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) had his original residence, and from there he directed the hard and unremitting work of the fledgling colonisation of Madeira. Settlement developed rapidly, and the first towns (*vilas*) were soon created at the seats of the three captaincies, the town of Funchal becoming the most important of them.
Convent of St Clare

As the final resting place for himself and for his successors in the government of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*), João Gonçalves Zarco had the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) built. It became known as Conceição de Cima and, when the adjoining convent was founded, took the dedication to St Clare, which it still keeps today. Enlarged and later entirely rebuilt in the second half of the 17th century, nothing of the original building is likely to remain there, but within its walls it holds the venerable ashes of its founder, the first captain-donatary of Funchal. It must be regarded as our most precious and revered ‘memorable landmark’, inspiring in all the most respectful and heartfelt veneration.
Quinta das Cruzes

In the immediate vicinity of this church Gonçalves Zarco had his last residence, and there he ended his long and toilsome life. It is the manor house of the Quinta das Cruzes, which has also become a ‘landmark’ worthy of equal and well-deserved veneration.

Milagres chapel – Outside the city there still stands an old and likewise venerable chapel which, because of the spot where it was built and the various events closely linked with it, is equally a ‘memorable landmark’ deserving the highest and most considered esteem: the chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*) in the town of Machico, which we have already discussed on several occasions.
Page (Roberto)

This English subject, who so endeared himself to the people of Madeira through his acts of philanthropy and generosity, was already in Madeira in 1804. There, together with José Phelps, he ran a wine business, which still existed in 1840. He withdrew, we believe, to England around the middle of the 19th century, when many English firms wound up their affairs because of the hardship brought on the island by the devastation of its vineyards by *oidium tuckery*, and he died there some years later. Among many other things, we know that he did the following for the benefit of the island and its inhabitants, as we have already had occasion to state in an article published in January 1904 in a newspaper of this city:
Repairs to the chapel of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*) in Machico, to which he gave a fine painting for the chancel, contributing money towards the works carried out there.

A contribution in money, at the request of the then captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) and governor of Madeira, Pedro Fagundes Bacelar, towards the ransom of Portuguese sailors held captive in Algiers.

The placing of an iron marker on the shoal known as the Carneiro (‘ram’), west of Funchal, to prevent the loss of coastal boats, many people having previously perished there. A tiled house at the Ribeira das Cales (‘stream of the channels’), as a shelter for travellers. A large bridge over that same stream, which was extremely dangerous in winter. A tiled house at the Ribeira dos Boieiros, in the hills of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), as a shelter for travellers. Repairs to many public paths in the hills. The completion of the bridge and road at the Ribeira dos Frades, in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), a work considered greatly needed. A stone bridge over the Ribeira do Engenho, on the main road west of Funchal, which had been destroyed by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803. A wooden bridge over a fearsome precipice near Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’). Major repairs to the São Martinho road. Extensive repairs to the Rua da Laranjeira and Rua do Mosteiro Novo (‘New Convent’), a very necessary and useful work. A contribution towards the new fountain in Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’). A contribution towards the new fountain at the stream of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*). A contribution of 700 escudos towards the great theatre of Funchal. A contribution towards a bridge in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). A wooden bridge at Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’). A house next to the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), to shelter the poor. A contribution towards the church of São Sebastião in this city. A new bridge at Monte (‘hill’). Repairs, for the second time, to the bridge in Rua dos Ferreiros. Repairs, twice, to the upper Torreão (‘turret’) bridge. A good tiled house in the hills of the Paul, as a shelter for travellers. A public fountain on the Monte road. Another at the Fonte da Telha. Repairs to and paving of the street running from Cruzes to São Paulo. Another fountain on the Monte road. Four resting places and seats on that same road. A wooden bridge on the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s channel’). A new bridge at the Ribeira das Cales. Six plank beds for the Funchal gaol. A loan of one *conto* (one million réis) *de réis* for the completion of the Lancasterian school. 100 blankets for the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*). Six iron beds for the same Holy House. A donation of 300,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for the building of the bridge over the Ribeira dos Socorridos. A substantial donation to the inhabitants of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) during the great drought there in 1822. He organised a subscription, to which he contributed generously, in aid of the prisoners in the Funchal gaol. What is listed above, done for the inhabitants of this island, is no small thing. But there is more.

In 1816 he kept up the price of Madeira wine against a monopoly that had been formed, and thanks to his energetic stance and unfailing probity the inhabitants of this island gained many tens of *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis). So evident and so significant was this benefit that the Funchal Council sent him an official letter of sincere and affectionate thanks.

Such acts of benevolence could not go unnoticed by those in government, and Robert Page was twice honoured by John VI. At that time decorations and other royal favours still carried great value and were not squandered as they are today. One did not obtain a knighthood of the Order of Christ or a commandery of the Order of Our Lady of the Conception for trivial reasons or for unmentionable services, as happens so frequently at present.

Ninety and a hundred years ago this was not the case. Robert Page received the rank of knight of the Tower and Sword and was later made a commander of the same order. If even today its grades are among the few that carry any standing in the social market, we may judge that in those days they were held in high esteem and granted only to those who had truly earned such an honour.

It is rather surprising that Robert Page, who gave so many notable proofs of the nobility of his character and of his sympathy for the Portuguese, should have lent himself – moved, perhaps, by a misguided patriotism – to posing as the discoverer of the famous ‘relics of Robert Machin’s cross’ to which Dr Azevedo refers on p. 417 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). These ‘relics’, deposited in the mother church (*igreja matriz*) of Machico and which nobody has so far taken seriously, are kept in a wooden frame glazed on the front. The label accompanying them states that they were found in 1814 in the chapel of the Lord of Miracles in the same town (*vila*).
Powder magazine

The military powder magazine was built in 1825; the works had been estimated in 1819 at 5,358,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). Above the door are the royal arms, and beneath them the date 1825.
Before the present magazine was built, gunpowder was stored in the Fort of São João do Pico (St John the Baptist of the Pico).
The Caminho do Paiol (‘powder magazine’) was much improved in 1815, the works being carried out directly by the Council.
Pais (Rui)

He was one of the companions of João Gonçalves Zarco in the discovery of this archipelago. Referring to the first landing, made at Machico, Gaspar Frutuoso says ‘that as soon as dawn broke the next day the captain sent a ship’s boat ashore, and put Ruy Paes in charge of it, that he should go and see the lie and situation of the land...’
Landscapes
See Madeira (landscape).
Paiva (João de)
João de Paiva de Faria Leite Brandão was appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 22 February 1908, and took up the post on 9 March of the same year
Paixão (Mother Brites da)

Hers is a name almost entirely forgotten, above all since the abolition of the religious orders, and still more since the closure of the Convento das Mercês (Convent of Our Lady of Mercy) in this city, where she was a nun and where she died in the odour of sanctity. The tradition preserved in this convent and certain writings found in its archive attest the eminent degree of moral perfection this nun attained, and several miraculous acts are attributed to her, especially after her death and through her intercession. Her tomb was always the object of special veneration and was frequently visited by many people, who went there to ask God for special graces through the effective mediation of this humble nun.

Mother Brites da Paixão was the natural daughter of Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 6th holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Caniço (‘reed’), and she took her vows in the Convento das Mercês in 1673 or 1674.
We possess an interesting manuscript by Father António Gomes Neto recounting many miraculous events attributed to the nun Mother Brites da Paixão.
Paixão (Mother Virgínia da)

Crowned with a reputation for the most sublime Christian virtues, Mother Virgínia da Paixão died on 17 January 1929 in the locality of Lombo dos Aguiares (‘the Aguiars’ ridge’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’). She had been one of the last professed nuns of the former Convento das Mercês (Convent of Our Lady of Mercy), dedicated to Our Lady of Ransom (*Nossa Senhora das Mercês*), and when that religious house was demolished she withdrew to the modest home of her relatives in the same locality, where she had been born in the third quarter of the 19th century. During her lifetime, and particularly after her death, the most laudatory tributes were woven around her name, going so far as to regard her as one truly predestined, to whom heaven had granted exceptional gifts in the practice of the most heroic virtues. *O Jornal* (‘The Newspaper’) of 17 January 1941 and of 16 January 1944 wrote about this nun at some length.
Paiz (O)
Forty-one issues of this newspaper were published, from 5 January 1865 to 30 July 1866, its principal editor being Augusto César Barjona de Freitas.
Palácio de São Lourenço

Referring to the fortress of São Lourenço, Frutuoso says the following on p. 84 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*): ‘and just as it has water within, it lacks neither horse-mills, ovens nor granaries for storing provisions, and rich lodgings where the captain resides, adorned with their garden and cool greenery’.

It is therefore clear that in 1590, when ‘Longing for the Homeland’ was written, the highest authority of the archipelago – at that time Tristão Vaz da Veiga, captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of war and governor-general – resided at São Lourenço. And if we read the same Frutuoso’s description of the sack of the city of Funchal by French corsairs in 1566, it is also clear that the fortress already had rooms and other accommodation in that year.

Dr Azevedo says that the fortress of São Lourenço has been called a palace only since the end of the 18th century, because it was the residence of the highest military and civil authorities of the archipelago. It should be added that the living quarters of the building underwent more or less notable alterations at different times.

In 1689 works were carried out on the quarters of São Lourenço at a cost of 1,007,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), as shown by a warrant of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) dated 8 November of the same year. On 14 May 1699 a fire broke out in the same quarters, and the damage was repaired with money from the fortification funds, raised under the responsibility of the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) and the superintendent (provedor).

We have read in two English works on Madeira that the palace of São Lourenço underwent great alterations, being partly rebuilt, during the occupation under General Beresford in 1808. If this is true, it did not prevent Governor Botelho, twelve years later, from requesting various works on the same palace, some of them very urgent.

In 1820 the building had ‘four rooms facing a corridor that ended at the bastion on the west of the island’. In the second of these rooms an open staircase led down to a courtyard 176 *palmos* long and 86 wide, which was entered through the gate of the fortress.

An examination of the view of the São Lourenço Palace that accompanies the *Descripção da ilha da Madeira* drawn up in 1817 by Paulo Dias de Almeida shows that, on the side of the building facing the sea, there were then balcony windows only on the west side, two of them at the western end of the less projecting part of the building; the remaining windows were identical to those of the present residence of the military commanders. It was towards the end of the third quarter of the 19th century that the residence of the civil governors underwent major alterations inside and out: new balcony windows were built and the ceilings of the rooms on the seaward side were raised. We believe that the work was completed in 1873 or 1874. The residence of the military commanders was not improved at the same time, owing to obstacles raised by Colonel Macedo e Couto, then military governor of Madeira.

Before the proclamation of the Republic, one of the rooms in the part of the São Lourenço Palace occupied by the civil authority held a collection of portraits of former governors, among them that of João Gonçalves Zarco.
The building of the São Lourenço Palace once included the chapel that existed in Funchal dedicated to the same saint, which we believe disappeared in the third quarter of the 19th century.
The chapel had its own chaplains. The first of whom we have found any record is Father José da Costa de Lima, appointed in 1641, who received as his salary ‘whatever a soldier’s pay amounted to’.
‘On gala days the household service passed through the chapel, the altar being covered with a curtain.’

A document from the first quarter of the 19th century records that the governors’ residence always had a room of its own hung with crimson silk, with a canopy, and beneath it the Royal Effigy of the Kings of Portugal, where on solemn days the nobility, clergy and authorities gathered to render, in the august presence of those royal effigies, the tribute of their faithful allegiance’.

Decree no. 29,742 of 12 July 1939 granted a subsidy to the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) to carry out various repair and adaptation works, long needed, in several parts of the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’).
Palanquin

It seems to us that the palanquin, which was much used here, was an adaptation to local circumstances of the palanquin that in India and China served to carry persons of rank. The American citizen John Adams Dix, who was in Madeira in 1842, describes the palanquin in these terms: ‘Many invalids who cannot walk and lack the strength to ride have as their only resource, and one recommended solely by necessity, a palanquin: a shoe-shaped plank surrounded by a small railing 6 inches high and fitted with a backrest. It is long enough for a person to sit and stretch out the legs. It is usually carpeted and furnished with cushions, with a cloth covering the pole from which it hangs, sometimes in the form of an oriental pavilion, showing good taste in its finish and richness in its ornamentation. This is what may be called the body of the carriage. It hangs from a rod fixed to a pole 12 feet long and 4 inches in diameter, so that, when in motion, it is only a short distance from the ground.

‘It is carried on the shoulder by two men, who lean on a staff. Sometimes, to ease the shoulder, they pass this staff under the pole on the other shoulder as a lever, so that both shoulders share the weight. The ease and speed with which they travel with this weight between them is remarkable: they climb the steepest slopes without slackening their pace and descend them without slipping. Sometimes they use a litter (*maca*) instead of a palanquin; this is more common in the mountains, and not only is it lighter but, because it hangs shorter, it is carried more easily over rough ground, where the palanquin would be useless. For invalids, both these modes of transport are wretched substitutes for wheeled carriages. The palanquin has, however, one advantage over carriages: there is no danger of being thrown out of it and breaking one’s bones, as so often happens in the most modern vehicles. There can be no safer conveyance than the palanquin.’

The palanquin disappeared from Madeira long ago. Some 40 years ago it served only to carry to the churches the little ‘angels’ who took part in the Lenten processions. By that time it was no longer used to transport adults, but in the first quarter of the 19th century it was used by ladies going out for a stroll or to pay visits. They could shield themselves from the public gaze by drawing the curtains of the canopy that hung over the pole by which the two bearers carried it.
Palco (O)
Only a few issues were published, the first on 11 November 1883.
Palha-carga

The vernacular name of *Festuca donax*, a grass 5 to 15 decimetres tall, with broad leaves and spikelets gathered in ample, loose and sometimes drooping panicles. This plant is common in the ravines of the interior of Madeira. *Brachypodium silvaticum*, which has large spikelets gathered in a slightly nodding spike, is also known by the name *palha-carga* in various parts of the island.
Palheiro do Ferreiro (quinta)

It is the loveliest, the most sumptuous and the largest *quinta* (country estate) in Madeira. Set high among lofty mountains, it commands the most astonishing and sweeping panoramas, especially from the spot known as Balancal. Its woods, orchards, gardens, farmland, pastures, lakes and walks, its dwelling houses, stables and farm storehouses, in their vastness and in the meticulous care with which they are kept, give the place the proportions of an opulent, princely residence and of a grand and immense estate.

The Palheiro de Ferreiro *quinta* is the work of the 1st Count of Carvalhal, who around the beginning of the 19th century began planting many hundreds of trees there and had a small house built, which was merely a *rendez-vous de chasse*. He later built a country residence, the gardens, the walks, the chapel and the farm buildings, and had abundant water brought from high in the mountains and over great distances to fertilise the land of the *quinta*.

An old manuscript records that on 5 January 1801 the Palheiro property was visited by the governor, Dom José Manuel da Câmara, who attended the ‘laying of the thresholds of the door to the walk’. When the Empress Leopoldina (vol. II, p. 232), first wife of Pedro IV, called at Madeira in 1817, the *quinta* (country estate) of Palheiro was already admired by the princess and her retinue, and on that occasion João de Carvalhal gave a splendid entertainment in honour of the illustrious royal visitor.
The 2nd Count of Carvalhal received Prince Dom Luís, later King of Portugal, with great pomp and splendour at the *quinta* of Palheiro when he visited this island in 1858 (II-286).

Some thirty years ago (1921) this property passed into the possession of the British subject John Blandy, who in 1901 gave a brilliant entertainment there for the King and Queen of Portugal, Carlos I and Dona Maria Amélia.

Many references to the Quinta do Palheiro are to be found in various Portuguese and foreign works. We shall confine ourselves to reproducing the following description, written by an Englishman who visited it on 13 January 1826: ‘One of the best places to visit in the environs of Funchal is the Palheiro, a *quinta* (country estate), or rather a park, belonging to Mr João de Carvalhal, the richest *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) on the island and probably the richest subject, at least in landed property, of the King of Portugal. Today we visited the place. On high ground, a little to the east of Funchal, Mr João de Carvalhal has succeeded in acquiring a large expanse of relatively level land, which he has had cut through with roads and walks and where he has planted oaks and firs. Everything there is laid out and arranged as in an English park, which robs the spot of the grandeur and wild character that foreigners so admire in the scenery of Madeira. Nevertheless, it is understandable that a Madeiran should like to bring to the island what does not exist there. Owing to the altitude, the temperature at the Palheiro is lower than in Funchal, and I am sure that the beauty of the *quinta* will increase when the trees have grown larger. The house is modest both in size and in architecture, but elegant and comfortable, and the gardens surrounding it are richly clothed in flowers. Camellias are their chief ornament, the specimens being 6 to 8 feet high and bearing white or crimson flowers, which rival roses in shape and colour but lack their lovely scent.’
Palheiros
This name is given to two rocks lying near Selvagem Grande (‘great wild island’). Some seamen call one of them Palheiro de Dentro (‘inner barn’) and the other Palheiro de Fora (‘outer barn’).
Palmeira (quinta)

The well-known Quinta da Palmeira (‘palm-tree estate’), one of the most beautiful and sumptuous residences in Funchal, has access to the Estrada da Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy levada road’) and the Caminho da Torrinha (‘little tower road’). Its owner, the benevolent industrialist Henrique Hinton, lives there. When we dealt at some length with Christopher Columbus’s stay in Madeira (I-286 ff.), we referred to the house he lived in on Rua do Esmeraldo and to the celebrated window that belonged to that building. Today it has been placed, with artistry and devotion, in the garden of the Quinta Palmeira, where its present owner preserves it with the greatest veneration and esteem.
Palms

The palm family is represented in Madeira by several species, none of them native. The most widespread at present are *Phoenix dactylifera*, native to northern Africa, and *Ph. Jubae*, native to the Canary Islands. The latter has dark green, closely set leaves; the former has greyish-green leaves, usually somewhat spaced apart. The dates of the Canary Island palm are smaller than those of the desert palm, and their stones are not elongated as they are in that species. *Ph. jubae* is cultivated in the municipal garden and in the *quintas* (country estates) to the east and west of Funchal; *Ph dactylifera* appears in many localities of the lower zone of Madeira, and also on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). On this last island the fruits of the desert palm reach full ripeness only after they have fallen. Besides these two palms, Madeira also has *Trachycarpus excelsus*, *pritchardia filifera*, *Latania borbonica*, *Seaforthia elegans*, etc., etc.
Palmela (Duke of)

The Duke of Palmela, Dom Pedro de Sousa Holstein, visited Madeira in November 1820, during his voyage to Brazil. He was warmly received on the island by the governor, Sebastião Xavier Botelho, who gave a ball in honour of the illustrious diplomat that was attended by more than two hundred people.

Of the short time he spent in Funchal, he says in a letter written here: ‘there were so many visits, so much business, so many outings, etc.,... that I have no time for everything.’ He went to the Quinta do Palheiro Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s hayloft estate’), belonging ‘to the richest landowner on the island and perhaps in Portugal’, where he found ‘an English-style park of the finest kind’.
The Duke of Palmela visited Madeira again in October 1847, this time to accompany his wife, who was suffering from a serious lung disease; her condition did not improve on the island.

On 27 January 1848 the duke was still in Madeira, but shortly afterwards he left for Lisbon with his wife, whose condition had grown considerably worse. ‘On a litter (*maca*) softened with cushions and pillows,’ says Dona Maria Amália Vaz de Carvalho in *Vida do Duque de Palmella*, ‘sailors carried her from her house on the island to the ship that brought her, and from that ship to the house at Rato where she died. Beside the litter, on foot, as close to it as possible, came the duke and their youngest daughter, the only unmarried one, who had accompanied her devoted mother to Madeira. Behind them, also on foot, followed the other children, the closest relatives and the most intimate friends.’

The Duke of Palmela outlived his wife by not quite eighteen months, dying at his house at Rato on 12 April 1850. Thirty years earlier he had written to the duchess, then in the bloom of youth and exceedingly beautiful, enclosing a sprig of myrtle in the letter, ‘as a protest’, says Dona Maria Amália Vaz de Carvalho, ‘against that tropical flora whose violence of colour and perfume oppressed him without speaking to his heart.’
Pampilho

Common name of *Chrysanthemum pinnatifidum* and *C. dissectum*, shrubby Compositae of the Tubuliflorae, growing wild in Madeira. The first species is common in the north and the interior of the island; the second occurs only at Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) and Cabo Girão.
Panasco
On the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) this name is given to *Bromus madritensis*, a grass common there, which also occurs in the lower zone of Madeira.
Paoli (Dr Guido)

He is inspector of plant diseases and director of the Regional Phytopathological Observatory of Liguria (*Observatorio Regional de Fitopatologia da Liguria*). He was in Funchal from 6 to 17 March 1922, commissioned by the Italian government to study and collect *Aspidiotiphagus lounsburyi*, a small hymenopteran that parasitises *Chrysomphalus dictyospermi*, a limpet or scale insect that lives on various plant species and has caused great devastation in the orange groves of Italy. Works: *Un modo di difendere le piante contro gli assalti della formica dell' Argentina* (*La Costa Azurra Agricola–Floreale* II no. 6, 1922); *La Bianca-Rossa degli agrumi e l'introduzione del suo parassita* (*Agricoltura Ligure*, no. 6, ser. 3, anno I, 1922); *il parassita della bianca - rossa degli agrumi e la sua introduzione in Italia* (*il Coltivatore*, no. 15, 1922); *Isolator, per difendere le piante contro la formica dell' Argentina* (*Redia*, XV, 1922); and *Una missione nell' isola di Madera. . .* (*Nuovo Annali del Ministero per l'Agricoltura*, II, 3, 1922).
In all these publications Dr Paoli refers to what he saw and studied during his short stay in Funchal.
Papagarro
See Boieiro.
Papaya (Carica papaya)

A woody member of the Passifloraceae from South America, with a usually unbranched trunk and very large leaves, divided into 7 to 9 more or less deeply cut segments. Its fruits are sometimes sessile, sometimes on long stalks; the latter are found on the individuals that produce the male flowers, which in Madeira always or almost always bear a certain number of flowers provided with pistils. The fruit of the papaya is eaten raw or cooked, but its flavour is not very pleasant. When cut, the trunk yields a juice which, mixed with water, has the property of making tough meat tender within a few minutes. The same result can be obtained by wrapping the meat in the leaves of the tree.
Stamped paper

In an interesting article on the stamped paper (*papel selado*) of our island, published in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) of 1 April 1911, Mr Alberto Artur Sarmento states that the first paper used here was of fine linen. It ‘bears the date 1661 at the top and in the middle of the page, and immediately below it “fourth stamp of ten réis” (the Portuguese money of account before 1911; 1,000 réis = 1 mil-réis, 1,000,000 réis = 1 conto); on the left-hand side is the circular stamp, engraved in wood, with the Portuguese arms, and around it “stamp III (stamp III?) of ten réis, year of 1661”. Only the first sheet of each deed was on stamped paper.

‘The third stamp of forty réis, with its designation at the top of the page, has a circular die formed of 14 arcs of a circle. This paper was overstamped with a new stamp in the right-hand margin, shaped like a coin, and on some sheets one can see the initialled signature of the superintendent (*provedor*) and the new date on which it was reused.

‘In 1664 the fourth stamp of ten réis is hexagonal, with four outer fleurons, and the stamp with the new date in the right-hand margin is an armillary sphere with the Portuguese arms, with the year on the support, and the superintendent’s initialled signature placed at the top and in the middle of the page.
On paper stamped in 1665 with the circular stamp, the new date is placed beside the old one and the initialled signature is set beneath the stamp.
‘Until 1840 the stamped paper does not differ from that used in Portugal; it then bears an overprint in black beneath the right-hand margin: O. L. GOV. C. DE FUNCHAL.

‘The paper carries the watermark “Louzãa”, the date and “Credito publico” in the lower margin. ‘The embossed stamps, in white at the top of the sheet, have the arms in the centre, the value in Roman numerals on the left and the modern numbering on the right.
‘The shield is bordered by palm fronds, on other values by trophies of flags, with “Thesouro Publico” written in relief.’

‘There is a variety of this paper that has four embossed stamps, the middle one being a monogram with the initials C. P. intertwined and “Credito Publico” written beneath it. The circular stamp “Thesouro publico” is printed in the left-hand margin.

‘The last special stamped paper bears the overprint “Madeira” in red ink. The paper carries as a watermark the Portuguese arms, “imposto do sello”, “Louzãa” and the various dates. The types are white paper and bluish paper, with the overprints in the left-hand margin. The bluish paper is ruled with 25 and 30 lines, the final issue having 30 lines in blue. The overprint “Madeira” lies close to the stamp at the top of the page.
‘These overprints, which were ordered because of the difference in currency, continued for many years afterwards.’

Mr Sarmento adds that the stamped paper used in Madeira always came from mainland Portugal, and that on fol. 167v of volume VI of the *Registo Geral da Camara Municipal do Funchal* there is a letter ordering that ‘the stamped paper left over from one year to the next’ be initialled, ‘so that it may be used and circulate freely in this archipelago’.
Robin (Erithacus rubecula)
A native bird of the thrush family (Turdidae), which breeds from May to June. It lays up to seven eggs, which vary greatly in size and colour. Its song is melodious.
Poppies

The commonest species in Madeira are *Papaver rhoeas* and *P. somniferum*, the latter with white flowers and the former with red. By crushing the capsules of *P. somniferum* or making shallow incisions in them, a juice known as opium is obtained, which is one of the most precious remedies in medicine. Morphine is the most active principle of opium. The capsules of the white poppy are used in decoction as an anodyne; the petals of the red poppy are sedative, pectoral and sudorific. The extraction of opium has never been attempted in Madeira.
Paquete (O)
The 1st issue was published on 7 February 1874 and the 84th on 14 June 1876.
Skylark (Alauda arvensis)
This is the *calhandra* or *laverca* of mainland Portugal. It appears in Madeira, but only as a bird of passage.
Rock sparrow (Petronia petronia)

A bird of the finch family (Fringillidae), common on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), which feeds on seeds and insects. On the one hand it damages crops through the great quantity of grain it eats; on the other, it should be regarded as an ally of the farmer, because of the great numbers of harmful insects it destroys, especially when it has young to feed in the nest. There were once municipal bylaws (*posturas*) aimed at destroying this species. A particularly curious one was that of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Porto Santo, which obliged every head of household to present 25 sparrow heads during the whole month of June each year.

It nests from February to June, usually in holes in walls or under the roof tiles of houses. Its nests are roughly made and lined with wool, cattle hair, human hair and above all hens’ feathers. The eggs, 5 or 6 to a clutch, vary greatly in colour and markings, being whitish, greyish or yellowish.
Pardela
See Cagarra.
Paredes

An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). The chapel of Our Lady of Nazaré (*Nossa Senhora da Nazaré*) that stands there was built in the last quarter of the 17th century by Francisco de Barros Maciel. It was entirely rebuilt in 1830 by António João Barbosa de Matos e Câmara, a descendant of the founder. It is an entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela), whose first administrator was the said Francisco de Barros Maciel.
Peers of the realm

Under the constitutional regime, the Madeirans who sat in the Chamber of Peers were António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia (Viscount of Atouguia), João de Oliveira (Count of Tojal), José Ferreira Pestana, Daniel de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, Januário Vicente Camacho, Luís da Câmara Leme, Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, José Vicente Barbosa du Bocage and Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos.

While the law of 24 July 1885 was in force, the electoral college of Funchal elected two peers. Among those who then sat in the upper chamber were the Viscount of Vila Mendo, António C. Heredia, Pedro Gonçalves de Freitas, Tomás Nunes de Serra e Moura, etc.
The Madeiran Jaime Moniz was a peer of the realm elected by the scientific institutions.
Red porgy (Pagrus pagrus)

A fish of the sea bream family (Sparidae), Pagrinae group, common in the waters of the archipelago. It lives in coastal zones and ranges over all the sea bed along the coast, though it prefers rocky bottoms. It breeds close to the shore and is highly valued as food. It is caught by day and by night with various gear, such as the *brigueira*, the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream), the *agulheira* (mid-water line for garfish), the rod and the net.
Parkinson (Sydney)

English painter and draughtsman who accompanied Captain James Cook on his first voyage round the world. He drew 22 Madeiran plants during the few days he spent in Madeira. His drawings are in the British Museum; some of them were engraved, but they were never published.
Parma (Duchess of)

The Infanta Dona Maria Antónia, daughter of Miguel I and widow of Prince Robert of Bourbon, Duke of Parma, stayed in Madeira from 7 April to 22 May 1922, having come to visit her daughter, the former Empress Zita. She was accompanied by her children, Princes Sixtus, Xavier and René and Princess Isabel; the first three left for Lisbon on 12 April 1922.
Parochia de Santo Antonio do Funchal
A fortnightly publication, whose 1st issue appeared on 8 March 1914 and the last on 22 January 1916. It was the first newspaper published in Madeira intended for a single parish (*freguesia*).
Leite Monteiro Park
See Leite Monteiro (park).
Partidista
A merchant who buys wine from the grower and prepares it on his own account, selling it to the export trade when a favourable opportunity arises.
Political Parties

In the days of absolutism there were only two parties in Madeira, the Liberal and the Conservative, the former having shown the first signs of its existence soon after the French Revolution. The organisation of secret societies, which in those days lacked the anti-religious character that people have sought to give them in modern times, was the forerunner of the great movement that was later to establish liberal institutions on our island.

The Madeiran Liberals also came to be called Constitutionalists after they adhered to the constitution of the Portuguese monarchy voted and sworn in Lisbon in 1821. The absolutists or Conservatives took the name of Miguelists after the Infante Dom Miguel (later Miguel I), on returning from Vienna to Lisbon, was welcomed in the latter capital by a base mob that urged him to proclaim himself absolute king.

In Madeira, as in Portugal, the absolutists and Miguelists were nicknamed *corcundas* (‘hunchbacks’) by the Constitutionalists, who in turn received from them the epithet of *malhados* ('piebalds', nickname for the Liberals), because the mules drawing the carriage in which Dom Miguel was travelling, when he suffered the fall that for some time endangered his life, were piebald.

When the civil wars ended in 1834 there were two liberal parties in Portugal: the Cartist party, made up of the entourage of Dom Pedro, and the opposition party, which, while combating the errors and extravagance of the former, nonetheless proclaimed its love of liberty and its devotion to the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*). The first of these parties included the Madeirans João de Oliveira, later Count of Tojal, José Ferreira Pestana, Lourenço José Moniz, Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses, Luís Vicente de Afonseca, etc.; the second included António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia and the members of the former Carmo (‘Carmel’) club, who later figured in the Septembrist party. Yet despite the political differences on the island, the newspaper *A Chronica* (‘The Chronicle’) stated on 24 March 1838 that the Madeirans had until then ‘marched united and obedient to the principles of legality’, and indeed there is no record that the September Revolution of 1836 gave rise to any noteworthy hostilities between Cartists and Septembrists. *A Flor do Oceano* (‘The Flower of the Ocean’), which appeared in 1834, was the organ of the Madeiran Cartist party.
The Constitution of 1838 was solemnly sworn on this island on 6 May of the same year and remained in force until the restoration of the Charter on 10 February 1842.

It was, we believe, the violence and extreme despotism of Costa Cabral that caused the political hatreds and passions, which were later to make our land so notorious, to appear here for the first time since the proclamation of the Constitution. In 1844 the *Tribunal Secreto*, an irregular clandestine publication intended to denounce the unconstitutional acts of Cabralism, appeared in Funchal. By then the political camps on our island were already sharply divided, and the advanced party was by no means the one that gave the least proof of its vitality.

At that time the Cartist or Cabralist party included Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca, Sérvulo Drumond de Meneses, etc., and the Progressive or Septembrist party included Dr João de Freitas e Almeida, Francisco Correia Heredia, Luís de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, Luís Agostinho de Figueiroa, etc. The last three played an important part in local politics after the uprising of 29 April 1847 and the installation of the Junta Governativa, the governing board (junta governativa) (see that entry), which administered the archipelago until 14 July of the same year. This board was supported in the press by the periodicals *O Independente* and *O Madeirense* (‘The Madeiran’), which had been preceded by the *Ecco da Revolução*, which appeared in 1846 after the Patuleia insurrection against the policies of Costa Cabral.

The Convention of Gramido and the dissolution of the Junta Governativa did not bring peace to Madeira. According to the periodical *O Progressista*, which began publication on 28 August 1851 and was the organ of the Liberal party, the elections of 1847, 1848 and 1851 saw the worst acts of violence.

The Regeneration of 1851 made it its hallmark to reconcile the parties, since it had drawn the men who then formed the government from both the Cartists and the Progressives. The Cabralist party, however, though reduced, continued to show its vitality, above all while Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro governed the district. In the elections held that year Madeira still sent two Cabralist deputies to parliament, which proves that the policies of the Count of Tomar had admirers here. In the press these policies had two organs, *O Archivista* and later *A Ordem* (‘Order’), edited by the well-known Cabralists Dr António da Luz Pita and Sérvulo de Meneses.

Many politicians from our island joined the Regenerator party of 1851. Among them were Jervis de Atouguia, who served in the ministry headed by the Duke of Saldanha; Jacinto de Santana, later Viscount of Nogueiras; Luís de Freitas Branco; Diogo Berenguer, a former Cabralist; Luís da Costa Pereira, etc. Others, such as António Correia Heredia, Dr Juvenal Honório de Ornelas, Pedro José de Ornelas, etc., joined the Historical Progressive party, whose leader was the Marquis, later Duke, of Loulé.

An old newspaper claims that from 1860 to 1868 Madeira never had a parliamentary representation that faithfully and spontaneously expressed the popular vote. It is nevertheless certain that the opposition sometimes defeated the government. The election of 1860 became famous because Dr Afonseca won more votes than the Count of Carvalhal, the Historical candidate, even though that nobleman was a man of great prestige and political influence and also enjoyed the support of the local authorities.

In 1865 the Historical party, except for a small faction, merged with the Regenerator party. This union gave birth to the Fusionist party, which many Madeirans who had previously belonged to one or other of those political groups joined. Shortly afterwards, in 1868, came the political demonstration known as the *Janeirinha*. It led to the emergence of a new party, called the Popular party, the product of a fusion of heterogeneous elements. Its motto, as the press sympathetic to it proclaimed, was economy and morality in the administration of the revenues of the State.

The struggles in Madeira between the Fusionist and Popular parties became notorious for the violence committed and for the shameful scenes of which the island was the stage for about a year and a half. The leading figures of Madeiran Fusionist politics were Dr Luís de Freitas Branco, Dr António Gonçalves de Freitas, Jacinto de Santana e Vasconcelos, João de Santana e Vasconcelos and Silvano de Freitas Branco, from the former Regenerator party; António Correia Heredia, Dr Francisco Joaquim Lampreia, Dr João da Câmara Leme, Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira, Pedro José de Ornelas, Dr Manuel José Vieira, Dr José Leite Monteiro and João José Vieira, from the former Historical party; and Dr Joaquim Ricardo da Trindade e Vasconcelos, formerly a Conservative or perhaps a Legitimist. The Popular party, on the other hand, included Dom João da Câmara Leme, who served for a long time as civil governor; Dr Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos; Canon Filipe José Nunes; Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, Januário Justiniano de Nóbrega and Nuno Dias de Vasconcelos, former Regenerators; Joaquim Coelho de Meireles, once a Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel); and the former Cabralist Conservatives Dr António da Luz Pita, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca, Caetano Velosa Castelo Branco, the first Popular deputy for the Funchal constituency, and Diogo Berenguer, holder of the entail (*morgado*), in whose house the party committees met. *A Razão*, *O Popular* and *O Direito* were the organs of the Popular party in Madeira, while the *Correio do Funchal* (‘Funchal Courier’), later replaced by *A Fusão*, *A Voz do Povo* and *A Imprensa Livre* championed the opposing policy.

The summoning to the councils of the Crown of the ministry headed by the Bishop of Viseu did not end the dominance of the Popular party, which had caused the riots of 8 March 1868 (see Riots in Madeira), because that party, and Dr Álvaro de Azevedo in particular, had sponsored the so-called reformist policy. When the military sedition led by Saldanha broke out in May 1870, island politics likewise underwent no notable change, because the same party had decided to support the Government that then came to power in place of the Historical Progressive ministry dismissed a few days earlier. Dom João da Câmara Leme, who had ceased to be civil governor of the district under the governments of the Count of Ávila, the Bishop of Viseu and the Duke of Loulé, returned to that office under the ministry headed by the Duke of Saldanha.

It is curious to note that, although a Historical ministry was in power, in the elections of 1 May 1870 it was not the party supporting the government in Madeira but the opposition that triumphed in most of the polling assemblies. The men killed by the troops in the church at Machico were Popular party voters. Yet it was Popular supporters who, on the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’), seized the late Dr Ricardo da Trindade e Vasconcelos as he returned from that town and took him to the public garden of Funchal, where they meant to murder him. This shows that they were masters of the situation and free to commit the wildest excesses. It was the lack of energy of the Viscount of Andaluz, then civil governor, and the indulgence he showed towards the opposition, even keeping in office officials who were openly hostile to him, that caused the anarchy and disorder of which Madeira was the stage in May 1870.

In 1858 *A Reforma* stated that, since the Regeneration had brought together elements of every political colour, personal politics had begun to lose ground on our island. A few years later, however, the same newspaper, had it still existed, could not have expressed so optimistic a view, especially regarding the politics that prevailed here during the turbulent period from 1868 to 1870. It was not the interests of the island but those of particular individuals that drove the struggles fought at that time, which became notorious for the violence committed by the two parties contending on the island.

The summoning to the councils of the Crown, at the end of 1871, of a Regenerator ministry headed by Fontes Pereira de Melo seemed likely to calm tempers. However, the new government kept Governor Dom João da Câmara Leme at the head of the district administration, and the opposition disapproved of this, resolving to harass him by every means within its reach. The lampoons, persecutions, stoning of buildings and killings of 1868 and 1870 were followed by a regime of bombs, which mysterious hands placed at night in various parts of the city and which exploded with a great roar, sometimes causing material damage.

With the formation of a thoroughly Regenerator ministry, the party welcomed back not only the Regenerators who had taken part in the fusion of 1865 but also many of those who had joined the Popular party. João de Santana e Vasconcelos was the local leader of Regenerator politics, which before 1862 had been directed by Dr Luís de Freitas Branco.

On 7 September 1876 the modern Progressive party was organised in Lisbon from Historic and Reformist elements. Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Anselmo José Braamcamp was elected its leader, and Dr João da Câmara Leme, later Viscount and then Count of Canavial, was the party’s first leader in Madeira. The former Madeiran Historics who had belonged to the Fusionist party joined the new political grouping, with the exception of Dr Manuel José Vieira, João José Vieira and Dr José Leite Monteiro. For some time these three showed no party sympathies, but in 1882 they joined the Constituent party, together with João de Sales Caldeira, Augusto Bianchi, Dr José António de Almada, Dr Nuno Ferreira Jardim, etc. *O Direito* was this party’s organ in Madeira.

When the Constituent party broke up, Dr Manuel José Vieira, João José Vieira and Dr José António de Almada moved to the Progressive party, of which the last was elected local leader in 1885. Dr José Leite Monteiro, meanwhile, stayed at his post, and was among the last to abandon the ill-fated policy of Councillor José Dias Ferreira.

After the death of General Fontes Pereira de Melo in 1887, almost all the Madeiran Regenerators accepted the leadership of António de Serpa Pimentel. Only Dr Luís António Gonçalves de Freitas, then living in Lisbon, and a few other politicians joined the so-called Dynastic Left, founded by Barjona de Freitas.

In 1901 the local Regenerator party split. The cause was that Councillor José Ribeiro da Cunha had been charged with coming to Madeira to receive the monarchs Carlos I and Empress Amélie, which amounted to an affront to the civil governor, Dom Bernardo da Costa de Macedo. On that occasion there were some popular demonstrations in Funchal, organised by various Regenerators who were friends of Ribeiro da Cunha, in which the Progressives also had a hand, with the aim of discrediting the authorities. Among the senior members of the Regenerator party who then withdrew from party politics were Councillor Silvano de Freitas Branco, Dr João Augusto Teixeira, Dr Romano Santa Clara Gomes, Dr Júlio Paulo de Freitas and the engineer Vitorino José dos Santos. Councillor José Leite Monteiro took over the leadership of the party in Madeira.

The Progressives, who had been allies of the Regenerator faction that supported Governor Ribeiro da Cunha, afterwards became its bitterest enemies. The many incidents of the struggle between these two political groups, especially during the electoral period, are still fresh in the memory of Madeirans. Almost everywhere the freedom of the ballot box was made a mockery of, and in Machico the Progressives suffered the worst humiliations for having dared to scrutinise the election being held there. The Progressive newspapers *Diário Popular* and *Correio da Tarde*, and the Regenerator newspapers *O Direito*, *O Rebate* and *O Debate*, provide valuable, if at times impassioned, information for the history of one of the most calamitous periods in Madeira’s political life.

At that time the leading figures of the local Progressive party were Councillor Manuel José Vieira, the party’s leader in Madeira, Captain João Augusto Pereira, Canon Manuel Esteves Fazenda, Dr Pedro José Lomelino, Councillor João Baptista Leal and João José Vieira. In the Regenerator party, alongside Councillor Leite Monteiro, served various young politicians known for their liberal aspirations, prominent among them Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques, Dr José Joaquim Mendes, Dr António Capelo, António Luís Nunes Vieira, João Octávio da Costa Cabedo, etc., etc.

The creation of the so-called Henriquist group and the split between Councillors Luciano de Castro and Alpoim had no influence on Madeiran politics, although the Viscount of Ribeira Brava followed the second of these political leaders. However, the rise to power in 1907 of a government headed by Councillor João Franco led at once to the formation on the island of a well-organised group intended to promote that statesman’s policy. Its members included, among others, Luís Gomes da Conceição, Dr Júlio Paulo de Freitas, Father Fernando Augusto da Silva, Dr Romano Santa Clara Gomes, Dr Alberto Figueira Jardim, the engineer Vitorino José dos Santos, Dr Fernando Tolentino da Costa, etc., etc. The tragic death of King Carlos I on 1 February 1908 prevented the local Franquists from carrying out their programme of administration, since Councillor João Franco left office immediately after that event.

The Nationalist party, formed in 1903, also had many followers in Madeira, chiefly among the clergy. Canon António H. de Gouveia, originally elected by the Progressives, championed the interests of this party in parliament; its press organ was *O Jornal*, which appeared in 1906. Dr Quirino A. de Jesus, long resident in Lisbon, belonged to the Nationalist party, but only for a short time.

When the Republic was proclaimed on 5 October 1910, Madeira adhered to it at once. From then on the monarchist parties disappeared, though monarchist ideas did not, even if few dared to express them in the days following the establishment of the new regime. The disturbances that had occurred in Madeira in 1826, 1828 and 1834 with the change of institutions were fortunately not repeated in 1910. Despite the efforts of certain troublemakers, various irregular incidents occurred only in the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.º 27*) and in some civil services, and fortunately these did not go beyond certain limits. No public official was dismissed and property was respected, although the moment was favourable for many outrages.

At first the Madeiran republicans formed a single party, within which there seemed to be no notable differences. This state of affairs did not last long, however, and by the time the first elections of deputies were held in May 1911 the supporters of the new regime were already divided. Various irregularities and abuses were committed on that occasion, against which the parliamentary candidate Francisco Correia Heredia, Viscount of Ribeira Brava, protested at the counting assembly. The electoral trickery that tarnished our republican apprenticeship differed from that of the monarchy only in the clumsiness with which it was practised.

In 1911 the political groups known as the Democrats, the Evolutionists and the Unionists were formed in Portugal, led respectively by Dr Afonso Costa, Dr António José de Almeida and Dr Brito Camacho. Little by little several valuable figures from our island joined the first of these, some coming from the old monarchist parties and others who until then had kept aloof from politics. The republicans of the period before 5 October, whose local leader was Dr Manuel Augusto Martins, declared themselves supporters of the second group, while only a small number of politicians, almost all of them recent republicans, joined the third. In February 1913 the Democrats, as members of a political faction, entered the administration of the district’s administrative bodies. Having elected the late Viscount of Ribeira Brava as president of their District Committee (Comissão Distrital) and Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques as vice-president, they soon formed the strongest and most disciplined party on the island.

When Dr Álvaro de Castro broke away from the Democratic Party, also called the Portuguese Republican Party, in order to form the party he named National Reconstitution, the great majority of the local Democrats resolved to follow that politician and join the new republican party. The political meeting at which this was decided took place at the Quinta do Jasmineiro on 30 May 1920 and was chaired by Azevedo Ramos. Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques was elected president of the new party’s district committee, and Dr Fernando Tolentino da Costa president of its municipal committee. Parish committees were elected for the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal, and individuals were appointed to organise the party in the various municipalities.
