The Democratic group was considerably weakened by the defections we have just mentioned. In December 1921, however, both the independent republicans and the members of the Liberal Republican Party (formerly the Unionists) enlisted in its ranks. Some time before, in July 1921, Captain Manuel da Costa Dias had visited Madeira with the aim of reorganising the group, which nevertheless never again regained the importance and vitality it had shown at first.

As for the former Evolutionists, a group of no great political importance, since the fall of Sidonism they have been more or less allied with the ex-Democrats who joined the National Reconstitution party. On 8 July 1920 the Evolutionists resolved to remain united until Portuguese politics had been clearly defined. For this reason, and also because of incompatibilities with former Unionists, they took no part in forming the local political committees of the Liberal Party, despite the merger of Unionists, Evolutionists and Centrists that had taken place some time before in Portugal.

After the defeat of the monarchists at Monsanto, the republican parties, which had refrained from any public activity in Madeira during Sidonism, came to an understanding and formed a committee to direct the island’s politics. Shortly afterwards, however, the Unionists withdrew, and it was the Democrats and Evolutionists who conducted the political elections and later the administrative elections on the island. Because the Unionists formed a coalition with the monarchists after the withdrawal we have just mentioned, that group was for some time at odds with the other republican groups on the island, as stated above.

During the government of Dr Sidónio Pais it was chiefly the monarchists who held sway in Madeira. Governor Pinto Feio replaced with supporters of the old regime the republicans whom the secretary-general, acting as governor, had appointed to the administrative committees of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and the Municipal Council.

In the elections of 10 July 1921, two candidates of the Presidentialist party and one of the Popular party stood before the voters, but the small number of votes they won reveals how poorly organised their parties were in Madeira. On that occasion the Madeiran Catholic party also failed to have its candidate elected; it fared better in the elections of 29 January 1922, when it succeeded in sending a deputy to parliament. On 22 February 1919 the *Trabalho e União* reported that the Madeiran Labour party, made up of workers and others, had just been definitively organised, but as far as we know this party has not yet sought to intervene directly in the island’s political life (1921).

In January 1922 Lusitanian Integralism elected a regional committee in Madeira, with Dr Rui Bettencourt da Câmara as president and Dr Abel Capitolino Batista as vice-president. In August of the same year the elections of the Conservative Monarchist Youth (*Juventude Monárquica Conservadora*) took place in Funchal: the Viscount of Cacongo was elected honorary president, César Barbeito president of the general assembly, and Dr Nuno Porto president of the board. The Republican party was organised in Madeira in 1882, on the occasion of the election of Dr Manuel de Arriaga as our representative in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), but by the time the Republic was proclaimed in 1910 it had grown very weak on this island.

The Reconstituintes of Madeira resolved to join the Nationalist Republican party at a meeting chaired by Nicásio de Azevedo Ramos, held at the Casino Vitória on 29 April 1923. When Dr Álvaro de Castro left the Nationalist party in December of the same year, he was followed by the Madeirans Captain Américo Olavo de Azevedo and Dr Carlos Olavo de Azevedo. Almost all the other parliamentarians and politicians of our island who had joined that party on 29 April, however, remained faithful to the principles they had resolved to defend.

On 21 December 1923 the District Committee (Comissão Distrital) of the Radical party of Madeira met, with Senator César Procópio de Freitas in attendance; before then the party had given no clear proof of its existence here in Madeira.

These, very lightly sketched, are the main facts of the political history of Madeira from the last days of absolute government to the present (1922). We recognise, more than anyone, how inadequate our information is. But since we are bound to deal with every subject relating to the island, so as not to stray from the programme we set for our work, we have in many cases been obliged to turn our summary into a mere outline. Anyone who consults the collections of our island’s newspapers will find there more or less detailed reports of the political events we have treated very superficially. They are the best source available, since no published work on the subject exists (1921).
Passada da Novilha

A locality in the uplands (*serra*) of Faial, where the former forestry officer (*regente silvícola*) Júlio Carlos Etur set up a small nursery of native forest trees. The Funchal Municipal Council leased the land intended for the nursery for 6,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year, but the nursery never produced results, because the said forestry officer was transferred to the mainland.
Chapel of Christ Carrying the Cross

The Stations of the Passion (*passos*, wayside oratories depicting scenes of Christ's Passion) were oratories found at various points in the city, in which some of the torments of the Redeemer were represented. The stations that existed in Funchal in our own day stood in the following places: the north side of the Jardim Pequeno (today Avenida do Dr. Manuel de Arriaga), Rua do Aljube (today Rua do Capitão-Tenente Carvalho de Araújo), Largo do Pelourinho and Rua de Santa Maria.
The Passos procession (Lenten procession of Christ carrying the Cross) made a halt beside each of these Stations of the Passion of Christ (1921).
We have read somewhere that the governor Dom José Manuel da Câmara had a station of Jesus Christ built in the alley of Jacinto Acciaioly.
Passos (António Romão dos)

He was born in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) on 28 February 1866, but went to Portugal at a tender age, where he completed his secondary studies and attended the General Institute of Agriculture (*Instituto Geral de Agricultura*). For many years he has been agronomist to the Companhia Geral de Crédito Predial Português. He published the *Elogio do Conselheiro João Inacio Ferreira Lapa*, delivered at the solemn session of 20 May 1905 of the Sociedade de Sciencias Agronomicas de Portugal, and we are told that he also brought out a biography of the learned botanist and agronomist Dom António Xavier Pereira Coutinho (1921).
Passos de Freitas (Dr Manuel)

He was born in Calheta (‘small cove’) on 3 March 1872 and graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1896. He is retired secretary of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) and a most distinguished musician, being director of the musical group that bears his name and conductor of the Madeiran choral society (*orfeão*), which the Funchal public has on various occasions had the chance to appreciate at the Dr. Manuel de Arriaga theatre.
Passos (Francisco Carregal da Silva)

He was born around 1878, the son of Manuel António da Silva Passos and Dona Maria Teresa Bastos Carregal da Silva Passos, and served as Portuguese consul in Dakar. He had qualified as an agricultural regent and contributed extensively to many newspapers and magazines in Lisbon, and he wrote two pamphlets entitled *a Tagante* and *O Escalpello*. He died in Lisbon on 1 October 1931.
Passos Freitas (Humberto de)

He was born in Funchal and wrote ‘The Ornithological Expedition to the Delta of the Danube’ and *Vinte e um dias em bote*, 1923, an account of a sea trip round Madeira. Passos Freitas boldly assisted the escape of several political deportees held in the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’), as mentioned on p. 350 of vol. I of this *Elucidário*.
Passos (Heitor Eugénio de Magalhães)
He was inspector of the Funchal school district when, on 11 May 1919, he was elected senator for Madeira.
Passos Sousa (António Policarpo dos)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Madalena do Mar (‘Magdalene by the sea’) on 26 January 1836 and died in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on 26 May 1875. He was a surgeon trained at the Funchal School and secretary of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of Ponta do Sol. According to the testimony of his contemporaries, Policarpo dos Passos Sousa possessed a prodigious talent, which misfortune did not allow to show itself with the vigour and brilliance that might have been so much wished for. He contributed to several newspapers and was regarded in his day as an inspired poet, his verse compositions enjoying great popularity. One of his compositions appears in the 1st vol. of ‘Flowers of Madeira’ (*Flores da Madeira*).
Pastures

The decree of 23 July 1913, regulating the grazing of livestock in the mountains of Madeira, contains provisions that ought to be strictly observed, although it has become necessary to extend the scope of these legal measures and to make them more effective and easier to enforce.

The first article of this decree lays down that ‘the grazing of pigs and goats is permitted only on land belonging to the owners of those animals, and which is completely fenced so as to prevent the animals from straying onto land of other owners’.
These provisions are frequently broken, to the serious detriment of the woodland and especially of young and vigorously growing plants.
See the articles Afforestation, Livestock, Livestock industry, Levadas, Animal husbandry and Meadows.
Woad (Isatis praecox)

A glaucous annual crucifer, with the lower leaves stalked and oblong and the upper ones sessile and arrow-shaped; small yellow flowers gathered in a corymb; pendulous silicles, indistinctly winged. From the leaves of this plant a blue colouring principle is extracted, capable of replacing indigo, which was once much used by Madeiran dyers. Madeira formerly exported some woad to Portugal, as can be seen from some notes that João Gonçalves Zarco received from Prince Henry the Navigator, in which he said: ‘let it be a reminder to you to send the woad once it has been prepared, and tell João Affonso to send some if it is prepared.’ Preparing the woad probably meant simply drying it in the sun, or else crushing its leaves, letting the resulting mass lose its water and forming it into balls, after allowing it to undergo the beginnings of fermentation for 8 to 12 days. Woad is not only useful in dyeing; it is also a fodder valued by cattle and sheep. In Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) its juice is used to treat pimples and other skin complaints.
Duckweed (Lemna gibba)

A plant of the family *Lemnaceae*, common in the streams, ponds and tanks of Madeira. It has small fronds each bearing a single root, and is also known by the name *lentilha-de-água* (see that entry).
Mallard

The duck known by this name in Madeira is *Anas boschas*, a domestic bird very common on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), which nevertheless also sometimes reaches the archipelago in the wild, in which case it belongs to the group of wild ducks. Its meat is highly prized, but its eggs are less tasty than hens’ eggs.
See Wild ducks.
Wild ducks

Under this name are known in Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) a number of web-footed birds that arrive here, chiefly in winter and more or less regularly. They are: *anas boscas*, *Mareca penelope*, *Nettion crecca*, *Dafila acuta*, *Marmaronetta angustirostris*, *Nyroca ferina* and *Oedemia nigra*.

Artistic heritage

Several foreign works dealing with Madeira, the books *Cartas Sem Moral Nenhuma* by Teixeira Gomes and *Ilha da Madeira* by the Marquis of Jácome Correia, and various Funchal periodicals contain a number of laudatory references to certain works of art in some of the island’s churches, chiefly paintings of superior artistic workmanship on purely religious subjects. These references, however, were generally made in passing descriptions and not always with a thorough knowledge of the subject. They made no impression on the general public and drew the attention only of a small number of the most cultivated people in our society. It was only in 1933 and the following years that Dr Manuel de Almeida Cayola Zagalo, the distinguished curator of the Museum of Ancient Art (*Museu de Arte Antiga*) in Lisbon, revealed to us the existence of a rich heritage, remarkable both for the number of its treasures and for their artistic excellence, worthy of a place in a well-equipped museum. He did so, with the most profound knowledge of the subject, the most devoted admiration and the most disinterested affection, in various reports, in a paper given at the National Tourism Congress, in interesting articles in the *Arquivo Historico da Madeira* and above all in his valuable work *A Pintura dos Séculos XV e XVI da Ilha da Madeira*. This last work is a painstaking and highly expert historical and descriptive study, owed to the zeal and competence of Cayola Zagalo, and it deserves in particular the gratitude of all Madeirans who value the good name of their native land.

‘... What must be recorded and made known’, Cayola Zagalo tells us, ‘is that the revelation of the Artistic Heritage of Madeira forms one of the noble parts of the National Heritage.... An equal abundance is found in no less beautiful pieces of goldsmiths’ work, sculpture, ceramics, tapestry and furniture... The preponderance of the schools of Bruges and Antwerp and of the Portuguese school is such that I can point to only one exception: the small painting of St Jerome, presumably of Dutch provenance, belonging to the bishop's palace of Funchal (*Paço Episcopal do Funchal*). Gérard David, Jean Provost, Jean Gossart and other masters yet to be identified, but of equal merit, are the authors of the island’s beautiful Flemish altarpieces; some of the panels whose artistic affiliation is as yet unknown are executed in the style of great painters such as Van der Weyden, Hans Memling, Quentin Metsys, etc. The explanation for so large a percentage of paintings from Flanders and Brabant, together with many other items of similar origin, most of them now lost, among them sculptures, furniture, tapestries and most of the tombstones faced with bronze plates, rests almost exclusively on sugar cultivation...’

There are ample reasons for creating a Museum of Painting in Funchal, and it may be presumed that it will soon be set up. Meanwhile, a small museum of sacred art has been created in one of the rooms of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*). A fuller account of it and of the projected museum is given later in this article.

It would be interesting to follow *pari passu* all the research carried out by Cayola Zagalo and his critical and descriptive study of so large a number of paintings of superior artistic quality scattered throughout the island, and to give a brief account of them here, if the space, time and competence at our disposal allowed us to do so. We shall therefore confine ourselves to a summary record of the paintings reproduced in photographs in the exquisite book *A Pintura dos Seculos XV e XVI da Ilha da Madeira*, cited above:

The Cathedral: ‘Altarpiece of the High Altar’, painted on wood in fifteen panels, Portuguese School, early 16th century; four paintings on the altar of St Anthony and several paintings on the altar of Bom Jesus.

In the Sacred Art Museum, in one of the chapter rooms: ‘Our Lady of Protection’ (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*), by Jean Grossart, 1526, a notable work; a triptych showing the apostles ‘St Peter’, ‘St Paul’ and ‘St Andrew’, Netherlandish School, 16th century; ‘St Nicholas’, Portuguese School, 16th century (2nd quarter); ‘Descent from the Cross’, Portuguese School; ‘St James the Great’, 15th–16th centuries; ‘St Mary Magdalene’, Netherlandish School, 16th century; ‘Calvary’, mid-16th century; ‘St Bernardino of Siena and St Louis’, mid-16th century, Portuguese School; ‘Deposition’, first half of the 16th century.
In the church of the Retreat of the Good Jesus (*Recolhimento do Bom Jesus*): ‘Annunciation’, early 16th century, Netherlandish School.
New church of São Martinho (‘St Martin’): ‘Nossa Senhora da Incarnação’ (Our Lady of the Incarnation), ‘Nativity’ and ‘St Joachim’, a triptych, first third of the 16th century, Netherlandish School.

The church of Our Lady of Succour (*Socorro*): ‘St James’, ‘St Philip’ and the ‘donors’, a triptych, first half of the 16th century, Portuguese School; ‘Apostles’, showing six apostles, 1st third of the 16th century, Portuguese School.
Chapel of Our Lady of Consolation (*Consolação*), Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s channel’): ‘Monograph of Jesus and Angels’, early 16th century.
Bishop's palace: ‘St Jerome’, 1st half of the 16th century, Netherlandish School, and ‘St Anne and St Joachim’, first half of the 16th century, Netherlandish School.

Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*): ‘Two Angels Adoring the Cross’, first half of the 16th century, Portuguese School; ‘Birth of St John the Baptist’, second half of the 16th century, Portuguese School; ‘Appearance of Christ to the Virgin’, first half of the 16th century, Portuguese School; ‘Appearance of Christ to Mary Magdalene’, 1st half of the 16th century, Portuguese School; and ‘*Ecce Homo*’.
The church of St John the Evangelist (*São João Evangelista*), the Colégio church: ‘Appearance of Christ to St Peter’, 2nd half of the 16th century, Portuguese School.

Chapel of St Elmo (*Corpo Santo*): ‘St Peter Gonzalez Telmo’, ‘St Anthony’, ‘Our Lady’, ‘St Peter’, ‘A King and a Female Saint’, ‘St Vincent’, ‘St Paul’, ‘St Lawrence’ and others besides, all from the mid-16th century, Portuguese School.

Parish church of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’): ‘Descent from the Cross’, ‘Mary Magdalene’ and ‘Joseph of Arimathea’, a triptych from the early 16th century; ‘Adoration of the Magi’, 1st third of the 16th century; and ‘Nativity’, Netherlandish School.
Parish church of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’): ‘Santa Maria del Popolo’, ‘St Barbara’ and ‘St Catherine of Alexandria’, a triptych from the 1st third of the 16th century.

Parish church of São Brás, Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’): ‘St Blaise and the Donors’, 2nd quarter of the 16th century, Portuguese School; ‘Presentation of the Child in the Temple’, 2nd quarter of the 16th century, and other paintings besides. Chapel of the Magi (*Reis Magos*), Estreito da Calheta: ‘Adoration of the Magi’ and ‘Veronica’.

Church of Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), Calheta: ‘The Angel and the Virgin’, ‘St Anthony’ and ‘St Francis’, a triptych whose panels are described as ‘extremely valuable’, first third of the 16th century, Netherlandish School.

Chapel of the Mother of God (*Madre de Deus*), Caniço (‘reed’): an altarpiece showing ‘St James the Great’, ‘St John the Baptist’, ‘St Catherine of Alexandria’ and ‘St Anthony’, later than 1536, Portuguese School.

Igreja Paroquial of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz: six paintings adorning the chancel, showing the ‘Annunciation’, the ‘Nativity’, the ‘Adoration of the Magi’, ‘Calvary’, the ‘Descent from the Cross’ and the ‘Resurrection’, 1st half of the 16th century, Portuguese School.

Igreja Paroquial of the town of Machico: ‘Adoration of the Magi’, early 16th century, described as a splendid altarpiece that has drawn the greatest admiration from eminent art critics; and also ‘Christ and the Apostles’, 2nd quarter of the 16th century, Portuguese School.

The article ‘National Monuments’ (II-394) mentioned the buildings and works of art in this archipelago that are classified as ‘National Monuments’ (*monumentos nacionais*) and as ‘properties of public interest’, most of which are referred to in the list given above.

The revelation that this abundant and precious artistic heritage existed created a favourable climate for organising and installing a small but interesting and valuable museum of sacred art. This was due above all to the efforts of the governor José Nosolini and the unconditional support of the diocesan prelate. For this purpose two rooms of the chapter house of the Cathedral were used; they adjoin the church, which has long been classified as a National Monument. The museum was solemnly inaugurated on 6 October 1940.

We also wish to stress here that Cayola Zagalo’s work deals in some detail with the paintings listed above, not only in terms of their artistic value and the most striking features that distinguish them, but also of their history, their state of conservation and the pressing need to create a Museum of Painting. It is a valuable and highly interesting study of the rich and abundant heritage scattered across many places in our archipelago, as was briefly mentioned above.

On this important subject, and also on other interesting specimens of various artistic forms, the information gathered in the pages of the second volume of the esteemed work ‘Zargo’s Islands’ by Father Eduardo Clemente Nunes Pereira can be read with profit.
Patriota
A single-issue newspaper published on 14 February 1890.
Patriota Funchalense

Among the most important places in our country, Funchal was by no means the last to see a periodical publication appear for the first time. When the first Azorean newspaper appeared on the island of Terceira in 1830, eight Madeiran newspapers had already been published before that date. The same was true in relation to the other places outside Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra. Since the Portuguese had begun their great colonising movement in this archipelago, a movement that soon spread to the ends of the earth, it would also seem natural that the most powerful lever of modern civilisation should have been introduced here before it reached the other lands discovered or conquered. And so it turned out.

A great political event on the Portuguese mainland, which had repercussions in all the island and overseas dominions, was the immediate cause of the publication of Madeira’s oldest newspaper, which took the name *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’). The advance of the so-called liberal ideas, which brought about the Porto Revolution and the resulting Constitution of 1822, was soon felt on this island. However, it was only some months after the events in the capital of the north that the political principles which were to establish the representative system in Portugal were solemnly proclaimed in Funchal. The official consecration of these principles took place on 28 January 1831. The event was commemorated on its anniversary the following year by the laying of the foundation stone of a monument to the Constitution, in front of the churchyard of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and this commemoration was marked by extraordinary and remarkable pomp.

One of the most fervent supporters of those ideas at the time was Dr Nicolau Caetano Betencourt Pita, an eminent physician and distinguished Madeiran who enjoyed great prestige and wide influence in our society. He placed these enthusiastically at the service of a cause that he believed to be among the most beneficial for the greatness and prosperity of the nation. To promote the new political principles and consolidate the system of government that had just begun, he undertook the publication of a periodical sheet. To do so he had to struggle against almost insurmountable difficulties, which his tenacity and boundless dedication succeeded in overcoming entirely. Many will say, perhaps with some reason, that the nature of this cause did not deserve such great sacrifices, but the sincerity of his convictions will suffice to absolve him of any perhaps exaggerated positions he may have taken at that juncture.

A ‘press’, as it was then called – in fact a modest printing workshop – was bought in Lisbon and brought to Madeira. With it came the typesetter and printer Alexandre Gervásio Ferreira, who for about two years directed the composition and printing of *O Patriota Funchalense*; from no. 179 onwards he was replaced by the typesetter Inácio S. de Abreu. The workshop, management and editorial office were installed in a house in the Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), which bore the street number 7 and must have stood not far from the former editorial office of *O Jornal* (1921).

On 2 July 1821, regarded as the anniversary of the discovery of Madeira, the first issue of *O Patriota Funchalense* appeared. It was a twice-weekly publication, coming out regularly on Wednesdays and Saturdays. It had four pages of text, but many issues were accompanied by ‘supplements’ of two and sometimes four pages. It was of small format, the printed area not exceeding 23 by 16 centimetres. In all, 214 issues were published, the last on 16 August 1823.

On the plan of the subjects covered by the paper and its distribution to subscribers, the first issue carries this curious notice: ‘The plan of *O Patriota Funchalense* is as follows: this sheet will be published twice a week (Wednesdays and Saturdays) and will contain the most interesting news from the National and Foreign Gazettes – Reflections on the internal Economy and external Relations of Madeira – Politics – Miscellany – Arrivals and departures of ships, Current prices, etc. Subscribers, and those who wish to become subscribers, will send for the sheet on the said days in the afternoon.’
On every issue, at the top of the first page, the royal arms stood out, bearing as their motto these lines by Almeida Garrett:
I raise a belated voice, but I raise it free, Before you, before the Heavens, before the Universe, If the Heavens, if the World should hear my voice

The great writer, giving thanks for the tribute paid to him, sent an interesting letter to the editor of *O Patriota Funchalense*, which ends with these fiery and hyperbolic words: ‘Receive, Sir, my thanks, not as a Poet, but as a Citizen – for I prize and honour myself in the latter quality as much as I disdain the former when it is detached from it.’
On p. 142 ff. of volume I of this work we gave the main biographical details of Dr Nicolau Caetano Bettencourt Pita, founder of *O Patriota Funchalense*.
Patudo
See Tuna.
Pau branco (Notelaea excelsa)

A tree of the olive family (Oleaceae), with persistent, leathery, glabrous and entire leaves, white flowers gathered in short racemes, axillary or extra-axillary, single or paired, and elliptical fruits, red at first and later violet. It is found in the mountains of São Vicente and of Boaventura and Porto do Moniz, etc., but is almost extinct on the island. It yields a white wood, or one tending slightly towards pink, which is very hard and heavy and takes a good polish; it is still used today for the screws of wine presses and the keels of boats.
Pau do Sebastião

It lies beyond Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’), on the road to Santana (‘St Anne’). From the top of the slope there, superb views can be enjoyed, especially towards the Ribeira da Metade and the Pico do Areeiro (‘sand pit’).
Paul da Serra

This plain, the only one of any real extent on Madeira, lies 1500 metres above sea level. It measures about 5 and a half kilometres from east to west, and its greatest width is a little over 3 kilometres. It forms part of the municipalities of Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Calheta and São Vicente, between which it is enclosed, and it is a desolate place, battered by storms for most of the year. Tree heath and bilberry are the only native shrubs that form thickets there; the rest of the vegetation consists of *Pteridum aquilinum* (bracken), *Agrostis castellana*, *Hypericum linarifolium* and *Thymus caespititius* (*alecrim da serra*). This last is extremely abundant here but hard to find in other regions.

The Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) can be put to use, as Thomas Edward Bowdich said in 1823, and the former Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) trialled the growing of wheat, potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word), turnips and carrots there with good results. If stands of trees are planted to shelter the ground from the winds, the region may yet come to produce in abundance many of the foodstuffs that people need.

At the locality (*sítio*) of Estanquinhos (‘little ponds’), at an altitude of 1450 metres, there is a house that shelters travellers. The mountain shelter known as Meio Paul, which the Englishman Roberto Page had built towards the end of the first quarter of the 19th century, disappeared long ago through the action of time. This latter house stood at Campo Grande (‘great field’), a spot almost entirely bare of vegetation and the most inhospitable part of the Paul da Serra plateau.

The Paul da Serra is much visited at sheep-shearing time. Serious disturbances sometimes break out there, generally caused by the copious drinking indulged in by the people who flock there to watch the shearing, which sometimes goes on for more than three days.
The Paul da Serra is said to be one of the few places in the Madeiran uplands still owned by the State.

It is ‘common land’ (logradouro comum), and the inhabitants of the surrounding parishes (*freguesias*) make much use of it, gathering firewood for fuel and, above all, grass and brushwood for fattening livestock and as raw material. It is a very inhospitable place and much exposed to storms. As stated above, this makes cultivating the land almost impossible, unless it were broadly protected by strong hedges of dense trees able to withstand the gales that frequently break out there. It serves as pasture for many flocks of sheep. All the surrounding parishes are linked to this plateau by roads, and on some of them, poor though they are, animal-drawn wheeled carts travel to carry the firewood, grass and brushwood.

The former Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) planned a road that would cross the Paul plateau along its greatest length, running from the Encumeada de São Vicente (‘São Vicente ridge pass’) to the landing place of the parish of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), about 38 kilometres long. The sections of this road were to be: from the Encumeada (‘ridge pass’) to the locality of Lombo do Mouro (‘the Moor’s ridge’), a distance of 4,200 metres; from there to Pico da Urze (‘heather peak’), a stretch of 8,300 metres; a third section from Pico da Urze to Lamaceiros (Porto Moniz), 23 kilometres long; and the last from Lamaceiros to the seaport, measuring 3,000 metres. Work on the road began in 1914 at both ends, but only a few kilometres of it were built.
See Bica da Cana, Estanquinhos, Lombo do Mouro and Rabaçal.
Paul do Mar

We have already noted elsewhere that Gaspar Frutuoso, in his brief description, written in 1590, of the most important parishes (*freguesias*) and villages (*lugares*, settlement rank below a town) on the south-west coast of Madeira, refers to the localities of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’) and Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’) simply as Jardim and Paul. We do not know whether they were known by these names in the earliest days of colonisation, perhaps without the added designation ‘do Mar’ that they bear today and have long borne. Nor do we know whether the places called Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) and Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’) received these names to distinguish them from those localities, the former pair being washed by the ocean and the latter lying in the interior of the island.

We do not know the origin of the name Paul by which this parish is known, if we relate it to the meaning that lexicographers commonly give it [TN: *paul* means a marsh or bog in Portuguese.]. A considerable part of the parish consists of a fairly level *fajã* (strip of flat land at the foot of a cliff), to which the name Paul would be apt if waterlogged ground had once existed there, turned into a kind of bog or swamp by water coming down from the high surrounding cliffs, or even by the sea at some lower point of the beach, and if the early settlers had then called it Paul. It is also possible that some orographic or hydrographic resemblance to a locality on the mainland justified the name, something that it will probably be impossible to establish today. Dean Gonçalves de Andrade, however, finds the name very well suited to the topography of the place, for he says that it ‘forms a kind of valley beneath high cliffs, beside the sea, whence its name’. We do not see how these circumstances justify giving the name Paul to that place.

The lands that make up the present parishes of Paul do Mar, Jardim do Mar and Prazeres once belonged to the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). The first to be separated from it was Paul do Mar, created by the royal decree (*alvará*) of 28 December 1676, which then also included the future parish of Jardim do Mar. The curacy (*curato*) of Prazeres (‘joys’) was created later, as a dependency of Paul do Mar.

One of the earliest settlers of this parish was João Anes de Couto Cardoso, who held many lands here and in Jardim do Mar as *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation). Various genealogies state that he founded the chapel of St Maurus (*Santo Amaro*), which later served as the seat of the parish, and that he lies buried in it. One of his sons, Francisco de Couto Cardoso, who died in May 1542, established an entailed estate (*morgadio*) with its seat in this parish. Another member of this family also founded an entailed house (*casa vinculada*) in the neighbouring locality of Jardim do Mar.

Paul do Mar, together with the parishes (*freguesias*) of Machico and Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), forms one of the three most important fishing centres of the archipelago. In Paul some hundreds of people make their living from the toil of fishing. A fish-canning factory was set up there a few years ago and is an important industrial establishment. The salt pans established in this locality did not produce the expected results, as has happened with various attempts made elsewhere on this island. The yield at Paul was always meagre, and the salt pans were abandoned a good many years ago.

This parish produces the agricultural crops common to the whole island, and sugar cane and vines are grown here in particular. The Malmsey produced in this locality was famous, and was not inferior in quality to the well-known Malmsey of Fajã dos Padres (‘the priests’ flat’).
It has two schools, one for each sex, the girls’ school having been founded in 1912.
According to the 1911 census, its population is 1,586 inhabitants.
Its principal localities are Ribeira das Galinhas, Serrado da Cruz, Alagoa, Igreja and Quebrada.

It has been claimed that a good deal of the ground overhanging some of the most important localities of this parish is on the verge of collapsing. This would bury countless homesteads and inevitably kill hundreds of people, and it would, unhappily, be one of the most horrifying tragedies in Madeiran history.

The District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) took the praiseworthy initiative of having a fishermen’s housing estate built in this locality. A block of houses intended specifically for people employed in fishing has already been built, and it was formally opened in July 1944.
Pavia (Father Teodoro)

In 1705 the book *Il Primo Scuoprimento dell'isola di Madera fatto da Roberto Macico inglese...* was published at Tortona, Italy, translated from the Portuguese and greatly expanded by Father Teodoro de Pavia. It is a volume of 190 pages, divided into two chapters. The first, which gave the book its title, is a literal translation of the celebrated third *Epanafora* of Dom Francisco Manuel de Melo, first published in 1660 and later reissued in other editions. As is well known, it was through this narrative by Dom Francisco de Melo that the legendary adventure of Robert Machin became widely known, and even came to acquire a certain standing as historical truth among some of the more credulous writers.

The second chapter of Father Pavia’s book is of greater interest to Madeirans, because of the information it gives us about the second half of the 17th century and the beginning of the following century. The first, by contrast, is a version of a very well-known work that has been extensively discussed, especially in the learned annotations to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).
Pé de Pau

Gaspar Frutuoso gives this name to a French corsair who put in at the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*) in the time of the donatary Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of Calheta (‘small cove’). Two hundred Frenchmen landed from the corsair’s galleons, which numbered seven. They bought provisions in the city and sold many things they had with them, ‘bringing Jaques Soria as their captain to punish them should they get out of hand.’ The ships lay eight days in our port, and during that time ‘Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara watched, and had others watch, the city by night with his guard posts, notwithstanding the friendship and peace that the corsair had promised him’.
Peacock (G)

Doctor of theology, Dean of Ely and professor of astronomy at the University of Cambridge. Works: *On the Agriculture and Tenure of land in Madeira*. This work is usually appended to Dr Mason’s book on the climate of Madeira.
Livestock farming

Since agriculture on this island, together with some of the important industries derived from it, is the chief source of the public economy, the main efforts of ‘governors and governed’ alike should be directed towards protecting this so widespread industry as far as possible. In this way everyone will contribute to the greater prosperity of the population of the Madeiran archipelago. Three valuable ‘elements’, besides others of lesser importance, are most intimately bound up with this subject and at once claim our special attention: Water, Forests and Livestock.

We dealt with the first of these at length in the article Levadas (II-235-269), where we stressed the importance and necessity of the levadas (irrigation channels) and the benefits they have brought. Everyone hopes that the measures adopted by the decrees of 21 October 1943 (‘Aproveitamentos Hidraulicos da Madeira’) will complete more satisfactorily the outstanding services already rendered over the long period of several centuries.

The second valuable ‘element’ to consider is the conservation and development of the Forests. A legislative act is indispensable here. After a rigorous study has been carried out, it should mark out beyond dispute the boundaries of the ‘common lands’ (*baldios*) belonging to private individuals, to the municipal councils and to the State. It should lay down with clearly defined precision the powers of the bodies that are to oversee these services. Finally, it should provide for the creation of a ‘forestry district’ (*circunscrição florestal*), which would be empowered to enforce all the legal provisions that have been or may be published on the matter.

The third ‘element’, which is of capital importance and deserves the most devoted protection, is the livestock question. Only a few years ago did it begin to attract the careful attention of the official departments and to awaken in the public a particular interest hitherto unknown here in Madeira.

This initial movement is owed to the valuable studies carried out by the Livestock Intendancy (*Intendência de Pecuária*) of this district. On so momentous a subject, it drew up a large and substantial report, setting out the most suitable measures to adopt in our circumstances in order to achieve the most profitable results for the agricultural industry of our island.

The selection and improvement of breeds, the rearing and care of livestock, their hygienic housing, veterinary services, fodder, milk production, mutual protection and many other interesting aspects of this most useful subject are treated in that report with great clarity, with the necessary thoroughness and with the most remarkable expertise, which does great honour to the distinguished official who conceived and wrote it.
It would be most desirable for a popular edition of this valuable document to be produced, intended for distribution throughout our countryside and villages.

In referring, however briefly, to this subject, it would be a flagrant and unforgivable injustice not to mention the excellent studies published in several issues of the *Boletim de Informação e Publicidade*, issued by the National Board for Dairy Products of Madeira (*Junta Nacional dos Lacticínios da Madeira*) and edited by the distinguished engineer Luís Pedro Baptista. These studies are of particular interest for the relationship between agriculture and livestock farming through the important dairy products industry.
The articles of this *Elucidário* on Livestock, the Dairy Industry, Dairy Products and Pastures offer some useful material on this subject.
Pedra de Ferida
Jasper (see that entry) goes by this name on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) because it is sometimes used on that island to treat wounds. It is applied after being ground to a powder.
Pedra Mole

A yellowish tuff found in various parts of Madeira. When reduced to powder it is very light, and it is therefore easily washed away by the rains. Combined with *saibro* (gravelly weathered soil), it makes, says Thomas Edward Bowdich, an excellent soil for vines. According to the same author, the specific gravity of *pedra mole* (‘soft stone’: soft yellowish tuff and its soil) is 1.95.
Pedro José de Ornelas (avenue)
This is the former Caminho da Pena (‘crag’). It runs from the old Rua das Hortas, now Rua do Alferes Veiga Pestana, to the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s channel’).
Pedro José de Ornelas was president of the Municipal Council of Funchal and died on 12 January 1878, aged 59.
Pedroso (João António)

He was a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santíssimo Nome de Jesus in Odivelas, the son of Francisco António Pedroso and Inácia Joaquina. Being in Madeira in 1823, he was deported to Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) for political reasons, where he later managed to be appointed clerk (*escrivão*) of the Municipal Council. He introduced the tamarisk to that island, a tree that spread there easily and is of great service to the inhabitants. He was a close friend of the English botanist Richard Thomas Lowe, who dedicated to him his genus *Pedrosia*, which modern botanists include in the older genus *Lotus*. He contributed to several Madeiran newspapers and died on Porto Santo, aged 68, on 29 March 1869.
Remora (Echeneis remora)

A scombrid fish, rare in our seas. On its back it bears a broad disc crossed by transverse plates, which works as a sucker and allows it to attach itself to the bellies of sharks, to turtles, to the sides of ships, etc. It is also known as *chupa-sangue*.
Swordfish (Xiphias gladius)

A large fish of the family Xiphiidae, caught from time to time in the seas around Madeira. It grows up to 4 metres long. Its powerful musculature and the peculiar shape of its upper jaw, drawn out into a spur, make it a formidable enemy even of the mightiest inhabitants of the sea. Madeiran fishermen have been in danger of being lost when a swordfish drove its terrible weapon through the side of their boat. The flesh is white and of quite acceptable flavour, recalling that of tuna. See Garfish.
Peixe-cão (Crenilabus caninus)

A fish of the family Labridae, uncommon in the waters of the archipelago. Its bright red colour makes it a handsome species; its flavour, however, does not match the beauty of its scales. It prefers rocky bottoms, moving along the coast, and is caught down to about 150 *braças*.
Red scorpionfish (Scorpaena scrofa)

A fish of the family Triglidae, common in Madeiran seas. It varies greatly in colour and has an oddly shaped head that sets this species apart from all others that come to market. The skull bristles with spiny projections, some of which exude a venom secreted by special glands in the head. A prick from one of these spines can have serious consequences.
The *peixe-carneiro* is sedentary in habit and lives on rocky bottoms. Its flesh is white and somewhat tough, but pleasant in flavour.
Peixe-cavalo
In Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) this name is given to *Alepidosaurus ferox*, a scopelid fish also known as *peixe-agua*.
Peixe-coelho
See Coelho.
Opah (Lampris luna)

A fish of the family Scombridae, rare near Madeira, although some authors record it as common. Its brilliant colouring makes it one of the most beautiful species of the Atlantic; its body is compressed and it can reach a little over a metre. It is caught between 75 and 200 *braças*, generally with the tuna line. By day it stays out at sea, but at night it comes somewhat closer to the coast.
Peixe-espada
See Espada branca and Black scabbardfish.
Peixe-frade
See Frade.
John Dory (Zeus faber)

A scombrid fish that sometimes appears at the Funchal market. Its flavour is not very delicate, and it is usually caught with the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) or the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream).
Peixe-lagarto
Madeirans give this name to the following two species: *Saurus lacerta* and *Saurus griseus*. The first is also known as *lagarto-do-mar*, and the second as *lagarto-de-rôlo*.
Grey triggerfish (Balistes capriscus)

A sclerodermous fish found between the shore and a depth of about 30 *braças*. It is caught with a line, with the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) or with the *agulheira* (mid-water line for garfish). On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) it is called *peixe-burro*, the name *peixe-porco* being applied there to *Orthagoriscus mola*, of the family Gymnodontes.
Thresher shark (Alopecias vulpes)

It belongs to the family Mitsukurinidae and is one of the largest migratory sharks that appear from time to time in the seas of the archipelago. It can reach 5 metres in length and is caught in mid-water, generally far from the coast. It is said to be harmless to humans.
Peixe-rei (Coris giofredi)

A fish of the family Labridae that lives close to the coast and feeds on small molluscs, crustaceans and other shellfish. Its flavour is pleasant, although the flesh is rather soft, a characteristic of all species of the same family. It is caught with the rod, the scoop net (*peneiro*) or the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing).
Ornate wrasse (Julis pavo)

A fish of the family Labridae, common along the coast, which prefers rocky places covered with algae, where it can find small molluscs, sea urchins, crustaceans and other small hard-shelled animals that it crushes with its strong teeth. Its flesh is somewhat soft, but not unpleasant in flavour. It is also known as *cagão*.
Fish

Some 250 species of fish have been collected in the seas around Madeira, many of them remarkable for the brilliance of their colours or for the singularity of their form or structure. These species are recorded in the publications of Richard Thomas Lowe and Johnson (see those entries), and in the present work we also mention some of them, such as the *alfonsim*, the garfish (*agulha*), the *abróteas*, the tunas, the *bicuda*, the *bodião*, the *boga*, the *boqueirão*, the *cavala*, the *castanhetas*, the conger, the *chicharros*, the *cherne*, the *dourada*, the *espada*, the skipjack tuna (*gaiado*), the *garoupa*, the *goraz*, the moray, the *pargo*, the *peixe-carneiro*, the *peixe-agulha*, the *peixe-galo*, the *peixe-verde*, the *requeime*, the *salema*, the *salmonete*, the *sargo*, the *tainha*, the *urjamanta*, etc.
The only freshwater fish living in Madeira are the *eiró* (see that entry) and *Cyprinus auratus*, but the latter is not found outside the tanks of the island’s cultivated zone.

In 1934 the distinguished men of science Adolfo César de Noronha and Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento published, under the title ‘Os Peixes dos Mares da Madeira’, a long and substantial study. It will be consulted with profit by all who wish to know this interesting subject, from whatever point of view it may be considered.
See Fishing Industry and Fisheries.
Pelargoniums
See Malva.
Pelicão
See Hipericão.
Pillory

In 1486, while still Duke of Viseu, Manuel I ordered the building of ‘praça, camara, paço dos taballiães & picota no seu campo’ (a square, a council house, a notaries’ hall and a pillory (*picota*) in his field). This field, then called the Duke’s Field (Campo do Duque), was the ground now occupied by the square and the church of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), the former Praça da Constituição, the former Rua do Aljube and the Largo do Comércio, or Largo do Chafariz. We do not know whether the pillory was ever actually set up in that field, as the council house was. If it did stand there, it was only for a short time, until the jasper pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction) was built ‘na fermosa praça cercada de boas casas sobradadas’ (in the handsome square surrounded by fine houses of several storeys), to which Frutuoso refers on p. 85 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).

The pillory stood in Funchal for three and a half centuries. Its demolition was ordered at a council session on 3 November 1835, because it was ‘an emblem of feudal times and not in harmony with present-day customs, the stones removed to be kept.’

The pillory was indeed demolished, but its stone column disappeared, and its base ended up, we do not know how, at a property in the locality of Pena (‘crag’), which belonged to the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Pedro José de Ornelas, a former president of the Council.

Prisoners who were flogged or exposed at the pillory were tied to it by the waist, and it was on the same pillory that the written orders and public notices of both the Government and the Municipal Council were posted. In the early 17th century one Francisco Rodrigues Jardim, a man of humble birth, was hanged in effigy at the Funchal pillory for having abducted Dona Maria de Ornelas, a lady belonging to one of the noblest Madeiran families. We have also read in an old manuscript that on 28 March 1808 a Black man received six lashes on his bare back at the same spot, and was then led through the streets of the city, accompanied by the officers of justice and an escort of soldiers.

Calheta, Ponta do Sol, São Vicente and Porto Santo also had pillories, as the names still borne by the places where they stood reveal. In Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) the pillory seems to have stood beside the mother church (*igreja matriz*), and in Machico it stood in the square near the parish church, where there is a fountain and where vegetables are now sold.
Pena (A)
A single-issue newspaper published in May 1908 in tribute to Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Dr José Leite Monteiro.
Pena (road)
The former name of Avenida de Pedro José de Ornelas and its surroundings. The name comes from the old chapel of Nossa Senhora da Pena (Our Lady of Pena) that once stood there (see vol. II, p. 462).
Pena of water

The quantity of water needed to fill a litre, or about three *quartilhos*, in the space of one minute. Drinking water is sold by the *pena* (traditional unit of water flow, roughly 1/60 litre per second), the half-*pena* and the quarter-*pena*.
See Manilha.
Pencas

This is the name by which the highly prolific variety of *Cynara cardunculus* is known on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). The central parts of the leaves of this composite are eaten raw by the island’s inhabitants once the spines have been removed. The plant also grows at Caniçal (‘reed bed’) and Piedade (‘pity’), where it is known as *cardo-da-gente*.
Penedo do Saco
A rock near Ponta do Furado (‘pierced point’), on the Ponta de São Lourenço, from whose bare summit the surrounding beaches can be seen.
Peneiro

A fishing device consisting of an iron hoop to which a net of wire or twine is attached, forming a shallow bag. Two wires cross over the hoop, and the bait is threaded onto them. A rope used to handle the device is tied to the iron hoop by three thinner branch lines and a small wooden rod.
Penela (Jacinto do Carmo Sá)

He is a naval paymaster officer, currently holding the rank of captain (*capitão de mar e guerra*), and was born in Funchal on 7 December 1856. He is a corresponding member of the Lisbon Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*), and before joining the navy he worked in the Revenue Office (*Repartição de Fazenda*) of the district of Funchal. Works: *O Incendio da Escola Naval* (*Anais do Club Militar Naval*, 1916) and *Noticia cronologica sobre a Academia das Guardas Marinhas e a Escola Naval* (1921).
Penfold (Jane Wallas)
Works: *Madeira-flowers, fruits and ferns–a selection of the botanical productions of that Islands, foreign and indigenous, drawn and coloured from nature*; London, 1845.

In 1803 the English merchant Guilherme Penfold was living in Funchal, and in 1813 the firm of Penfold & Veitch existed here. It may be supposed that Jane Penfold was a relative of this merchant, who lived at the Quinta da Achada.
Penha de Águia

An eminence shaped like a truncated pyramid, rising at the sea’s edge between Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) and Faial, on the north coast of Madeira. It is cultivated on top, and its highest point stands 580 metres above sea level. It can be reached only from the landward side, and the footpath to the summit is not bad, although quite steep.
Penha de França (battery)

It stood near the chapel of the same name, the chapel of Penha de França (Our Lady of the Rock of France), and was definitively ceded to the Municipal Council by a deed signed in April 1902. It was apparently a fortification ordered to be built during the period of Philippine rule. It was occupied by British troops, and it is said somewhere that an English soldier was executed near it, as we have already mentioned on p. 427 of vol. I of this work. A serious affront was thus committed against the sovereignty of our country, despite the protests of the local authorities.
Penteada
A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António.
Penteado
See Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’).
Penumbra Literaria (A)
Eight issues of this newspaper were published, the first on 1 May and the last on 31 August 1877.
Cucumber (Cucumis sativus)

A cucurbit widely grown in Madeira. Its fruit is a cooling food and is used to prepare an ointment useful in treating wounds. The cucumber is sown in March and April, and in some places from January to May. It is sown in beds or seed plots, and once the plants reach a certain size, cane frames or other supports are built so that the stems do not trail on the ground.
Chayote (pepinela)

Madeirans give this name to *Sechium edule*, a plant of the family Cucurbitaceae which in Portugal is called *chuchu* or *caiota*. The latter name was once much used in Madeira, but today it has been abandoned and even forgotten by the people.

Some people unfamiliar with botany call our chayote (*pepinela*) *pimpinela*, although there is no relationship whatever between the two plants. The *pimpinela* of Portugal is a member of the rose family (*Sanguisorba minor*) which we have seen cultivated in Madeira, but which never became common. There is also a genus of umbellifers called *Pimpinella*, which includes anise (*herva doce*) and other species.

The chayote comes from Central America and bears obovate or obovate-claviform fruits, green or white, each with a single seed. The plant is propagated from whole fruits, which are set in small holes in January and February, sometimes lying flat, sometimes with the shoot pointing down; in the latter case the shoot must be bent so that part of it stays above ground.

The chayote can in some cases live for more than 10 years, and it usually bears little fruit in its first year. The fruits appear in autumn and early winter; the green ones are the tastiest and the white ones the best suited for preserves.
The chayote already existed in Madeira at the beginning of the 19th century, when many people knew its fruits by the odd name of *pepinos nelas*, from which, it seems, the word *pepinela* derived.
Pepino (pera-melão)

A solanaceous plant introduced to Madeira under the name *Solanum guatemalense*, but which should perhaps be referred to *S. muricatum*. It bears oblong yellow fruits whose flavour is somewhat like that of melon.
Perado (Ilex perado)

A shrub from 1 metre to 2.50 m tall, with thick leaves, mucronate or spinulose at the tip and generally spinulose-serrate at the margins; peduncles 1-flowered, rarely 2–3-flowered. It is a rare species, found only at Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’) and in the Serras de São Vicente, Seixal and Boa Ventura. The wood of this member of the Aquifoliaceae is white, light and takes a good polish; it is used for inlaid work (*embutidos*) and other small pieces of cabinetwork, after being boiled in two or three changes of water to remove all the sap. It can take on a bluish colour if steeped in urine or any ammoniacal solution.
Perdigão (Dr Jacinto António)

He was serving here as secretary-general of the district when, by decree of 1 July 1863, he was appointed substantive civil governor, a post he had already held on an interim basis. He took office on the 17th of that month and year.

Among the reports he wrote as civil governor, the one he presented to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) at its ordinary session of 1864 stands out: a truly remarkable piece of work that can still be read with profit today. Jacinto Perdigão was a distinguished jurist and published several works of value.
Partridge

The Madeira partridge is *Caccabis rufa*, of the family Phasianidae; that of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is *Caccabis petrosa*, of the same family. The former lives on the coastal slopes and in the interior, where nests with 17, 19 and 21 eggs are found; the latter is a species introduced in 1900, but it multiplied rapidly on Porto Santo. The Madeiran partridge can today be considered a rare species (1921).
Peregrinações Madeirenses

Under the name ‘Peregrinações Madeirenses’ (Madeiran Pilgrimages), two excursions took place in 1923 and 1926 in which several hundred people from this archipelago took part, visiting the most celebrated shrines, monuments and museums in various countries of Europe. Father Jacinto da C. Nunes published an interesting description of the first in a score of articles in the review *A Esperança* (‘Hope’) in 1924 and 1925. Of the second, the well-known writer João dos Reis Gomes published a detailed account entitled *Através da França, Suíça e Itália*, an exquisite and instructive travel book.
Pereira

Around 1460 Rui Mendes Pereira, nicknamed ‘o Tacão’, came to Madeira; according to Dr Azevedo, he married twice on this island. Many of the people who bear the family surname Pereira on our island descend from him. It is a very widespread surname, and it derives from various origins.

Issue no. 33 of the newspaper *A Informação*, of 13 August 1931 (Funchal), contains an interesting article entitled ‘Os Pereiras de D. Nuno Alvares’, which sets out to prove that the great Constable Nuno Álvares Pereira, now beatified by the Catholic Church, had a large kinship on this island, spread over various parishes. This curious passage deserves special mention: ‘we thus see that the Pereiras of the Constable mingled abundantly with the people of Madeira. In the labyrinth of genealogical connections, the blood of Nuno Álvares looms large in almost the whole population, not only in the noble families but even in those of the common people, for both gradually merged in the slow course of social evolution.’
It may be said that this phenomenon occurred intensely in Madeira with all the families, of noble and plebeian origin alike, that came from mainland Portugal.
Pereira (César Atanásio da Silva)

He was born in Funchal on 5 July 1864, the son of José Marceliano Pereira and Dona Maria de Jesus da Silva. He attended the Polytechnic School and the Army School, and was commissioned second lieutenant of artillery on 8 January 1891. He served in the 2nd Artillery Regiment, in no. 3 Garrison Artillery Company and in the 4th Artillery Regiment, and in 1896 was requested for a tour of service overseas. He left for Lourenço Marques, arriving there on 15 January 1897, and shortly afterwards volunteered for the military expedition organised in Beira to punish the Cambuenga. He fought in the battle of Gorongosa, where he proved a distinguished and brave soldier, but he had the misfortune to be struck by a bullet that fractured his lower jaw. He recovered from this wound only in Lisbon, after an operation at the hospital of São José. Having returned to Africa in 1889, after serving again in the 4th Artillery, he became secretary of the district of Manica there, and died in Macequece of a bilious fever on 27 May 1901.
He was a knight of the Order of the Tower and Sword and held the silver military medal for distinguished service overseas.
Pereira (Dom Mateus de Abreu)

We have found several references to this illustrious prelate as a native of Madeira, where he is said to have been born on 8 August 1756. We know nothing of the personal circumstances of his life until we find him, in 1794, presented as bishop of the diocese of São Paulo, in Brazil. He was confirmed by a papal bull of Pius VI dated 17 June 1795 and took possession of the bishopric on 31 May 1797. He was a prelate who rendered distinguished services to his diocese, and Cândido Mendes de Almada, in his work *Direito Civil Eclesiastico Brasileiro*, states that he contributed a great deal to the independence of Brazil. Two addresses delivered at the ceremonies held to celebrate the anniversary of this prelate’s consecration were published, one of them by the great orator Monte Alverne. He died in the city of São Paulo on 5 March 1824 and was buried in its cathedral.
Pereira da Silva (Manuel)

He was born in Madeira on 5 September 1862 and is an infantry officer; for some time he served in the now-abolished Municipal Guard. He holds the rank of Knight of the Legion of Honour of France. He published his address entitled *A preparação para a guerra* and another delivered at the ceremony presenting the national flag to the recruits of the 12th and 34th Infantry Regiments of the Guarda Military Command (*Comando Militar*) (1921).
Pereira da Silva (Father José)

He was born in Porto on 19 March 1874, entered the Congregation of the Lazarists in 1890 and was ordained priest in 1898. That same year he came to Madeira, where he was a teacher and finally vice-rector of the Seminary. He left for Hamburg and from there for Paris on 21 October 1910, and died in the latter city on 14 June 1922. Works: *Á memoria de Leão XIII*, a funeral oration delivered in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) on 12 November 1903; Funchal, 34 pp.
Pereira de Sousa (Francisco Luís)

He was born in Funchal on 28 September 1870, the son of the distinguished Madeiran writer Francisco Clementino de Sousa. Having enlisted in the army on 3 November 1888, he was commissioned second lieutenant of engineers on 25 October 1894, after studying with great distinction at the former Polytechnic and Army Schools. He was a professor in the 3rd section (natural sciences) of the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Lisbon (*Universidade de Lisboa*) and a member of the Mineralogical Society of France and other scientific bodies. He devoted himself especially to geological, mineralogical and seismological studies, and in the last of these he was the foremost authority in our country. His research on the effects of the earthquake of 1755 is truly remarkable, not only from the scientific but also from the historical point of view. Works: *Subsidios para o estudo dos calcareos do distrito de Lisboa* (1897); *Elementos de geographia physica da Europa* (1901); *Estudo Geologico do polygono de Tancos* (1902); *Idêa geral dos calcareos empregados nas construções de Lisboa* (1904); *Os calcareos do distrito de Leiria* (1905); *Os calcareos mais empregados em Portugal* (1908); *Effeitos do terremoto de 1755 nas construções de Lisboa* (1909); *Alguns trechos do relatorio do engenheiro Rego Lima sobre a sua missão ás minas de Cassinga em 1898* (1911); *Le Raz de marée du grand tremblement de terre em 1755, en Portugal* (Paris, 1911); *Ideia geral dos effeitos do megasismo de 1755 em Portugal* (1914); *O Megasismo do 1.° de Novembro de 1755 em Portugal–distrito de Faro* (1915); *O Terremoto do 1.° de Novembro de 1755 em Portugal e um estudo demografico–dos distritos de Faro, Beja e Evora* (1919). He died in Lisbon on 25 September 1931.
Pereira (Duarte Sodré)
His appointment as governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira dates from 15 November 1703; he took office on 20 April 1704.
Pereira (João António de Sá)

He was governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago in the period from 1677 to 1766. The commentator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) calls him the ‘reformer par excellence’, and he also became known as the ‘Madeiran Pombal’, both because he was appointed to this post by the Marquis of Pombal and because of the reforms he carried out in many public services during that statesman’s government. Among his services, one stands out: he went in person to the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) to enforce the famous royal decree (alvará régio) of the fifths and eighths (*quintos e oitavos*: rent of a fifth or an eighth of the produce), which caused the greatest sensation at the time.
Pereira (João Augusto)

He was born in the town (*vila*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) on 26 May 1857, the son of António de Sousa da Silva Pereira and Dona Luísa da Conceição Pereira. He attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and the former Polytechnic School and Army School, and was commissioned second lieutenant of artillery on 7 January 1885. He served at Vendas Novas, where he also taught at the Practical School of Artillery (*Escola Prática de Artilharia*), and from there he moved to Funchal. There he served as a subaltern and later, after promotion to captain, as commander of No. 3 Garrison Artillery Company. He was also commander of war material on the island of Madeira. In every military duty and commission he undertook, he proved a highly intelligent, spirited officer and a firm disciplinarian.

João Augusto Pereira represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislatures of 1900, 1902–1904, 1904, 1905–1906, 1900–1907 and 1908–1910. It was he who, on his political debut in the Chamber of Deputies in 1900, drew the government’s attention to the need to complete the irrigation levadas (irrigation channels) of our island. His speech earned words of praise from the then Minister of Public Works, the late Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Elvino de Brito.

In the same legislative session he took an active part in the debate on the bill he had introduced, co-signed by other deputies, concerning the reorganisation of the services of these levadas. It was also he who, in 1900, introduced the first bill seeking administrative autonomy for Madeira, which never came to a vote because the government fell at that time.

It was thanks to the deputy João Augusto Pereira that the Municipal Council of Funchal was authorised to raise a loan of 400 *contos* from the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos to meet the cost of the sewerage and drinking-water works of Funchal – a most important service, though some council sessions failed to make proper use of it. He was also responsible for the establishment of the telephone network in Funchal and for preserving the archipelago’s division into judicial districts (*comarca*), still in force, which someone wished to alter, etc., etc.

Of the many speeches made by the deputy João Augusto Pereira, the only one published in this city was the one he delivered at the session of 17 March 1903 on the anarchic state of the district of Funchal.

He was a provisional teacher at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and one of the editors of the former *Diario Popular* and of the *Diario da Madeira*, and he held an eminent place in the Madeiran press among the journalists of his day. The now defunct Progressive Party, in which he was always active, owed him notable services. He was one of the most valuable collaborators of his father-in-law, the late Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira, who for many years led that party here in Madeira.

João Augusto Pereira abandoned politics after the proclamation of the Republic in our country. During the last fifteen years of the monarchy he had been one of the men who enjoyed the greatest influence and prestige in this district, and one of those who defended the needs of the archipelago most selflessly. He died in this city on 22 June 1915, by then a retired major of artillery.
Pereira (Father Eduardo Clemente Nunes)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) on 23 November 1887 and was ordained priest in mainland Portugal in 1913. He taught at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and has contributed to various newspapers in this city. His works are: *Delenda est Carthago*, a speech, 1913, 37 pp.; *Golpes*, a collection of poems, 1914, 151 pp.; *Manual de Nossa Senhora do Carmo e Santa Thereza*, a translation, 323 pp.; *Como se Vence*, 1 vol.; and ‘Zargo’s Islands’ (*Ilhas de Zargo*), 2 vols.
Pereira (Father Joaquim Plácido)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Seixal (‘pebble shore’) on 10 December 1885 and was ordained priest in 1909. He has held ecclesiastical posts in various parishes of the diocese. Besides contributing to a number of newspapers, he published in Lisbon the book entitled *Nossa Senhora do Monte, Padroeira da Ilha da Madeira*.
Pear tree (Pyrus communis, subsp. sativa)

A European member of the Rosaceae-Pomoideae, widely cultivated in Madeira and also found on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Its fruits vary greatly in both shape and flavour. The best known are those usually called by the following names: *bergamotas*, *caniças*, *condes*, *flamengas*, *francesas*, *carvalhais*, *de São João*, *marmelas*, *formigas*, *brancas* and *saramanhas*. These last two pears and the *caniças* are the most sought after for preserves. On Porto Santo only the *caniça* pear exists.
Pereira Reis (António)

He was born in Funchal on 27 April 1866 and graduated in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1892, having previously taken the theology course at the Funchal Episcopal Seminary. He has practised as a lawyer in Lisbon, where he is well known, and contributed to the former newspaper *O Tempo* and to other periodicals of the capital. He belonged to the former Constituent Party and later to the Henriquista party, joining the Democratic Party after the establishment of the Republic in Portugal. In the ministry formed in March 1916, immediately after Germany’s declaration of war, he was entrusted with the portfolio of the Interior, which he left at the end of May of the same year. He has published some of his legal works.
Pereira Ribeiro (Dom António Manuel)
He is the present and 28th prelate of this diocese, which he has administered as bishop since 1915.

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Friande, in the district of Braga, on 16 February 1879, the son of Duarte Pereira Dias Ribeiro and Dona Deolinda Rosa da Silva Pereira Ribeiro. He studied at the former College of São Fiel and completed his degree in the Faculty of Theology of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1901, being ordained priest in October of the same year.

He was a teacher at the lyceum (state secondary school) of Viana do Castelo and vice-rector of the Seminary of Bragança. Presented to a canonry of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), he took possession of this post in June 1905. In this city he taught at the Diocesan Seminary and was editor of the former periodical *O Jornal* (‘The Newspaper’).

When the diocesan bishop, Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, died on 26 June 1911, Canon Pereira Ribeiro was promptly elected capitular vicar of this bishopric by the cathedral chapter, a post he held until his elevation to the episcopate.

He was appointed prelate of this diocese by the Holy See on 2 October 1914 and received episcopal consecration in the city of Viana do Castelo on 7 February 1915. He arrived in Funchal on 7 March of the same year, and on the 14th of that month he took possession of the see and made his solemn entry into the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*).
Pear tree (Pyrus Marus subsp. hortensis)

A European rosaceous plant of the Pomoideae, usually shrubby, and widely cultivated in Madeira. The apple tree is one of the many garden varieties of this species. It is easily told apart from the pear tree by its flattened fruits, which have finer flesh and a more pleasant flavour. The best apples come from Camacha, Santo António da Serra and other high-lying places on the island, whereas pears are found everywhere, some of them quite tasty once ripe. The *pêro-vime*, the *pêro-estopa*, the *pêro-doce*, the *maçã-barral*, the *maçã-reineta*, the *maçã-cara-de-cama* and the *maçã-pino-de-ouro* are the best-known varieties in Madeira.

In the past a great deal of wine was made from the juice or must of pears and apples and sold to consumers as grape wine. Today the vinification of these fruits is prohibited, but they may be used to make cider, a pleasant drink that is widely consumed in many countries.
Peres (Damião)

He was born in Lisbon on 8 July 1889. For some years he was a teacher at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school), and its rector, and he is at present a professor in the Faculty of Letters of Porto. Besides the works he published on John I and on *Portugal e o Schisma*, in 1914 he brought out in Funchal a pamphlet entitled *A Madeira sob os donatarios*, which is of considerable interest for the history of this archipelago in the period up to the beginning of Philippine rule on this island (see II-100).
He is the author of important historical studies, among which his *Historia de Portugal* stands out.
Perestrelo

This is a very old family surname here, for it descends from Bartolomeu Perestrelo, the first donatary and settler of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). He was the son of Filipone or Felipe Perestrelo, whom the genealogies record as having come to Portugal at the end of the 14th century. Filipone was a native of Piacenza, in Lombardy, and the son of Gabriel Perestrelo, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of lineage whose privileges were recognised in our country. The arms of this family are described thus: ‘shield party per pale; in the first, on a field of gold, a lion purpure armed gules; in the second, on a field of silver, a bend azure charged with three eight-pointed stars between six *tosas* gules, three and three in pale; crest the lion of the shield, with a star on its shoulder’.
Perestrelo (Bartolomeu)

He is the well-known first donatary and settler of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Some authors have made the serious mistake of regarding Bartolomeu Perestrelo as a navigator and even as the discoverer of that island. They were perhaps led to this by the fact that he was its first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), an office that was sometimes linked to the fact of discovery.

He was a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of the household of Prince João, brother of Henry the Navigator, when Prince Henry invested him with the donatary captaincy (*donataria*) of Porto Santo and entrusted him with the settlement and colonisation of the island.

The charter by which Henry the Navigator granted the island of Porto Santo is dated 1 November 1446, that is, roughly twenty years after the colonisation of the archipelago began. We must suppose that Perestrelo had already settled on Porto Santo with all the privileges and prerogatives granted to the donataries, and that the charter was merely the loyal and formal confirmation of those privileges. We must believe the same of the other two captaincies of Madeira. In the letter of grant (carta de doação), Prince Henry says: ‘I give charge of my island of Porto Santo to Bartolomeu Perestrelo, *fidalgo* of my household, so that the said Bartolomeu Perestrelo may maintain it for me in justice and right; and should he die, it pleases me that his first son, or another if such there be, shall hold this charge in the manner aforesaid, and so from descendant to descendant in the direct line... shall have... jurisdiction... in civil and criminal matters, save for death or the cutting off of a limb...’. The charter mentions various rights, prerogatives and exemptions granted to the first donatary, including the collection of various dues and taxes. The captaincy of Porto Santo remained in the possession and under the authority of Bartolomeu Perestrelo’s descendants until the period of Philippine rule. With the appointment of governors-general, that rule reduced the donataries of the archipelago to a very subordinate and almost purely honorary position, although they continued to collect substantial revenues under the original privileges granted to them. When Portugal fell under the Castilian yoke, Diogo Perestrelo Bisforte was the 6th captain-donatary of the island of Porto Santo.

The captaincy of Porto Santo never reached a high degree of prosperity. The smallness of the island, the neglect it suffered from the mother country from the earliest days of colonisation, the frequent pirate raids, the poor administration of some donataries and governors, the conceited pride of many of its inhabitants, who scorned work because they descended from old *fidalgos*, and the indolence of its people, brought about by the climate and by other causes as well: all of this contributed markedly to the meagre development of this donatary captaincy.

In his short work *A Mulher de Colombo*, the writer António Maria de Freitas (Nicolau Florentino) deals at some length with the first captain-donatary of Porto Santo. We shall transcribe a few passages from this work, which we consider extremely interesting.

‘The disappointment that the young Bartolomeu suffered on visiting his future domains was the same that befell many others, both in the islands and on the mainland. They measured the scale of royal generosity only by the much-vaunted extent of the territory, by fanciful reports of its fertility and by the grand name of the lordship. They learned the true worth of what they had petitioned for only when the obligations they had undertaken, amounting to a sum far greater than the local income, forced them either to let the land out in parcels for trifling rents or to leave it to lie abandoned, of which abundant traces could still be found until recently in many parts of the country.

‘Carried away by the much-proclaimed virtues of the newly discovered island, Bartolomeu did not know what he was asking for.
