In this he perhaps differed from Zarco and Tristão, whose second voyage is more reasonably explained by their intention, after landing the settlers on Porto Santo, to continue the enterprise they had begun, or at least to sound and explore those waters of the Atlantic, than by any wish to bury themselves on an island whose area and geological conditions, even if appraised only at a glance, ought not to have tempted them...

‘Bartolomeu soon realised that his imagination had betrayed him and that he had given too free a rein to his credulity. The comparison between Porto Santo and the new island found by Zarco and Tristão – incomparably superior to the first in its attractive appearance and in the promising vigour of its vegetation – completed his discouragement.

‘He therefore returned to the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), most probably after Madeira had been found. The cause of this withdrawal, and at the same time of the departure of his two companions for the second island, is attributed to a destructive plague of rabbits which multiplied on the island after a doe rabbit with young, born during the voyage, had been set loose there. The following year – if indeed a year passed between Bartolomeu’s departure and his return – “they had already killed a very great many, yet without making any dent” in the damage, which disheartened the settlers by ruining their agricultural labours.

This extraordinary power of procreation, before which zoology bows, powerless to explain it, causes no great astonishment to us, who are laymen in science. Our forefathers had a guileless readiness to believe without seeing or questioning, which, from the standpoint of spiritual hygiene, is simply enviable in these troubled times of malice and suspicion...

‘Porto Santo, with its neighbour Madeira beginning to prosper visibly, became more attractive and less isolated, finding close at hand many resources that its own unkind local conditions could not at first provide. Yet even with the passing of time – despite the transformations and improvements that Bartolomeu’s domains underwent thanks to relentless toil, which brought him down very early, and to financial sacrifices that were little more than futile – the island never distinguished itself by any course of economic and ethnographic autonomy that would prove sufficient material and moral progress; still less in the first years of its colonisation...

‘One of the documents on which we are working shows that Dona Margarida Martins, Perestrelo’s wife, did not live much beyond 1431. The last trace of this lady’s life in our possession is a letter from John I, dated 8 June of that year, granting her and her husband some houses subject to a quit-rent (*foro*) in the Rua Nova, next to the Porta da Erva.

‘No children were born of this marriage, as far as we know, and Bartolomeu married a second time, to Dona Brites Furtado de Mendonça, of the well-known family of that name, which also holds a distinguished place in the history of the archipelago.

‘Three daughters of the second marriage are known, all married to important men. The first, Dona Catarina Furtado de Mendonça, was the wife of Mem Rodrigues de Vasconcelos, commander of Seixo (‘pebble’); the second, Dona Filipa de Mendonça Furtado, married João Teixeira, third son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, first captain-donatary of the jurisdiction of Machico; the third, Dona Izeu Perestrelo, joined her fate to that of Pedro Correia da Cunha, captain-donatary of the island of Graciosa. ‘Widowed a second time, Bartolomeu Perestrelo, who was still a relatively young man, married for the third time, taking as his wife Dona Isabel Moniz, daughter of Vasco Martins Moniz, who at that time lived in Machico with all his great household, as was seen when we dealt with the Moniz family.

‘This new alliance, the most distinguished and the one most directly bound up with our historical purpose, reveals in a certain way Bartolomeu’s moral standing and the confidence inspired by the seriousness of his dealings and his love of work. Only those who know closely, from the old papers, the proud nobility of the Moniz family, whose alliances were sought by the best houses of Madeira and the mainland, can judge the firm conviction with which we set down this biographical note. . .

‘To ennoble Bartolomeu Perestrelo, it was invented that he came from Spain to Portugal in 1428 with the wife of Dom Duarte, and immediately afterwards that he was the companion of Zargo and Tristão in the discovery of Porto Santo in 1418 (!), when the most reliable evidence of his nobility is the proof of lineage made by his father Filippone Palestrello in 1399. To glorify him as a seaman, people have even gone so far as to imagine manuscripts he left and advice he gave to his son-in-law Christopher Columbus, although it has been proved that he never knew the man whom his little daughter Filipa, left fatherless at the age of 5, was to marry...

‘The donatary of Porto Santo is not entitled to bear the palm for having discovered his island; but on his head rightly rests the halo of a martyr to work, one of the most valuable social consecrations of all time.

‘Death came to take him at his post around 1457, when he was little more than 50 years old. He left his family in precarious financial circumstances, for his captaincy had consumed everything he had, from his wives’ dowries and the benefits he obtained by various means to his very health, without all that capital buried there yielding a tolerable income to support his widow and his two children, Bartolomeu and Filipa, left fatherless at a very tender age.

Bartolomeu Perestrelo died in the town (*vila*) of Baleira, on the island of Porto Santo, and from the most reliable evidence it appears that he was buried in the parish church of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*).’
For a fuller picture, the reader should consult what is said in vol. 1 of this work, p. 117 ff., about the town of Vila Baleira and the municipality of Porto Santo.
Perestrelo (Bartolomeu)
The second donatary of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) bore the same name as his father. He married Guiomar Teixeira, daughter of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the first donatary of Machico.
See Donataries.
Perestrelo (Bartolomeu)

He was the son of the preceding and became the third donatary of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). He married Aldonça Delgado, daughter of Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara, whom he killed so that he could marry Dona Solanda, sister of Tristão Teixeira das Damas.
Because of this crime he lived as a fugitive (*homiziado*), but in the end he ‘obtained the pardon of the parties and went to clear himself in the Kingdom’. He died in the Algarve at the age of 60.
A son of this Bartolomeu Perestrelo, named Garcia Perestrelo, also killed his wife and was beheaded for it.
See Donataries.
Pearls
Small pearls have been found in Madeira in *Haliotis tuberculata*. In 1909 a grey pearl the size of a pea was found in the fan mussel (*Pina rudis*).
Perreymond (Charles)
French man of letters who died in Funchal on 4 June 1854. He was preparing a book on Madeira, which death did not allow him to finish.
Rock samphire (Crithmum maritimum)

A glaucous umbellifer with fleshy, 2–3-pinnatisect leaves, abundant on the north coast of Madeira. It has also been found at Ponta de São Lourenço, between Gorgulho (‘weevil’) and Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’), and on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It is eaten in salads, but is little used in the archipelago.
Perry
According to Dr Azevedo, on p. 529 of the *Saudades*, the family surname (*apelido*) Perry derives from the Englishman Perry, who was a merchant in Funchal in 1650.
Fishing

In the article Fishing Industry (II-151 ff.) we have already devoted several pages of this work to the subject, and we refer the reader to them, also drawing attention to the short articles describing the various kinds of gear used in this industry. As a fine and authoritative synthesis of this interesting subject, however, we wish to record here an excellent article by the distinguished naturalist Adolfo César de Noronha, published in the *Diário de Notícias* of 1 July 1932.

‘The Madeira archipelago, as a group of essentially oceanic islands – formed by the mighty action of submarine volcanoes – does not show around the edges of its islands the broad, flat submerged shelves usually found around the continents.

The adjoining sea floor is very rugged in relief. Beyond the 100-*braça* sounding line – which around the main island lies sometimes only half a mile from the coast, as off Ponta do Garajau (‘tern point’), and at most 3 or 4 miles away, as off Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) and Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) – the floor falls rapidly towards the abysses of 2,000 *braças* and more that yawn between the Canary Islands and Madeira, or between Madeira and mainland Portugal.
With deep waters and a rough sea floor, the fisherman of these islands must favour floating hook gear, and uses more rarely the gear that requires contact with the ocean bed.

Thus steam trawlers, those modern instruments of intensive fishing that supply mainland Portugal with a great mass of fish for food, are excluded from these broken island waters by the nature and depth of the sea floor.

Like the oceanographers, this rough fisherman, brutalised by alcohol, has also marked out different bathymetric zones in the sea for his own use. It is a convention based on observed facts which does not depart from, but rather coincides with, what science has already established. It is an interesting phenomenon of the popular mind that well deserves inclusion in the study of folklore.

The natural edge of the island shelf, set by hydrographers at about 100 *braças*, is known to fishermen as the *bairil* or *bairilho*, perhaps a corruption of *beiril*, which in turn seems to derive from *beira* (edge). Some also call it the *sarrilho do baixo*, or simply the *baixo*.

Beyond this edge, they say, the sea *abica*, meaning that the floor drops away more steeply. They give the word a very Madeiran sense, for among the common people *abicar* means to hurl down from a height, to fall suddenly.
Out in the depths, beyond the rim of the *bairil*, it is customary to distinguish three zones: the *alto*, the *altura* and the *altio*.

Together these zones correspond to the upper part of the oceanographers’ abyssal region, which some place from 200 *braças* downwards. Here depths are measured in *linhas* (fishermen’s depth unit of about 23 *braças*, c. 50 m) – the fisherman’s bathymetric unit, equal to roughly 23 *braças*.

The *alto* may be defined as running from about 10 *linhas*, or 230 *braças*, to a depth of roughly 15 *linhas*. The *altura* runs from this sounding to some 25 *linhas*, or 650 *braças*, the maximum depth at which the gear is made to touch the bottom. Finally, the *altio* is the region stretching indefinitely beyond, out to sea, which they also call the *golfo*; there the fishing line often reaches a depth of 850 *braças* or even more, yet normally always stays clear of the bottom.

‘On the submarine plateau, and likewise seaward of its edge on the great slope, down to about 200 *braças*, fishermen catch the species generally called coastal. These are either sedentary, in which case they make up a large part of what is called “good fish”, or nomadic, moving from the coast to the open sea and travelling everywhere without going very deep, and so deserving the name of coastal-pelagic. These in turn are sometimes simply erratic, and at other times migratory: long-distance travellers somewhat irregular in their passage, like the tuna, which come from no one knows where and go no one knows where.

Finally, in the deepest zone the abyssal species are caught. Some of them yield a great deal, such as the black scabbardfish, and since they are not migratory they supply the markets with a reliable product on which the consumer can count all year round.

If we except the group of the dogfish – or sharks in the widest sense of the term – which are almost always species of the lowest quality and which we place in the third category, it may be said that the most delicately flavoured fish consists, in general, of the sedentary inhabitants of the coastal and abyssal zones, while second-quality fish is almost always represented by the markedly nomadic species, which travel more or less widely. The family richest in species, and one of the richest in individuals, is that of the mackerel and tuna. It is also the most important in economic value, although it does not enter the first category for flavour. Characteristically migratory, this group, represented by 15 edible species, the largest of which is the bluefin tuna, crosses the pelagic and coastal zones indifferently, as it is driven by the biological needs of the moment, determined by currents, temperature, plankton, etc.

Next in yield comes the family of the trichiurids, with the silver scabbardfish, very irregular in its passages, and the abundant black scabbardfish, a remarkable and faithful friend of the poor, a friend all year round, hauled up from the great depths. This family, however, is represented by only five species of commercial value, for all the others included in it are rare and abyssal and are of almost purely scientific interest.

Richer in species than this is the esteemed family of the *pargo* (sea bream), a sedentary group that numbers eleven members in these seas. It is followed by that of the grouper, all of it prized and likewise sedentary, which contains six, of which two, the *cherne* and the *robaldo* – not to be confused with the *robalo* of the mainland – may be considered abyssal.

With some six species, all of them wanderers within the nearby waters and of some economic importance, comes the less esteemed family of the *chicharro* (horse mackerel). With four each come that of the *requême* – which is not the *requeime*, but one of the *cantarilhos* of the fishermen of Portugal – and the hake, a species very rare in Madeiran waters; these two families are considered among the finest by general consent of consumers.

That of the *alfonsim* – or *imperador* of the mainland – a tasty family of the deep zone, numbers only three species. It includes the most delicate fish in the Lisbon market, and the tastiest of all we know: the almost despised *olho-de-vidro*, which by an irony of fate has even been given an obscene name by the foul-mouthed fishwives of Ribeira Nova!

This berycid, for such is its family name, is not entirely foreign to the seas of Madeira, but its great rarity relegates it to the field of scientific values that ichthyology prides itself on having frequently searched out in this deep zone of the Atlantic.
Other families of bony fish are represented in these seas, but as they are of lesser importance we refrain from making special mention of them.

The dogfish, or sharks, have a certain value. Being fish of inferior quality, they are eaten mostly by the poorer classes, after being salted and dried in the sun, and are sent in large quantities to the north of Madeira, where they are bought as a substitute for salt cod.

The livers of almost all the fish of this group – hence called ‘oil fish’ – yield an oil used chiefly for lighting the fishing itself. The skin of one of them, the *gata* – which should not be confused with the *gata* of Portugal, being rather identical to what is called *carocho* there – is used by cabinetmakers and carpenters for sanding wood, just as on the mainland.

Among the shellfish, limpets are prominent, gathered mainly on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) by the fishermen of the village of Caniçal (‘reed bed’). From time to time a certain sea snail appears on the market, as does a particular crab, a cosmopolitan crustacean found in almost all seas but which seems not to inhabit the coasts of Portugal. Lobster and *lagostim* are also sold, though they are not identical to their namesakes on the Portuguese mainland.

To these edible invertebrates must be added some shell-less molluscs, such as the octopus, the cuttlefish, the squid and the *pêta*. The last belongs to summer and autumn and is sought by fishermen at a high price when it grows scarce towards the end of the season, because at that time it is the preferred bait of all for catching the profitable black scabbardfish.

And to close this brief enumeration, we shall mention two animals of a higher order – two species of turtle, one of which is edible; but it is not the object of organised fishing, being simply caught by chance.’

‘The fishing gear is not especially varied; hook gear predominates here, as the physical conditions of the environment demand. In a brief classification we shall divide this gear into three groups: hook gear, nets, and pots or creels. The first either have a rod and line, or consist simply of lines.

Among those with rod and line, some carry a single hook, such as the *salto* for tuna, the rod for skipjack tuna (*gaiado*) and the fishing rod; others carry a greater or smaller number of hooks, and these are the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing) and the cherriola (vertical multi-hook deep-water line). Among the hook gear made solely of lines, a distinction must also be drawn between those fitted with a single hook, such as the *agulheira* (mid-water line for garfish) and the tuna line, and those with many hooks; in this latter group are the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream), the longline and the gear for scabbardfish.

The nets amount to a few seine nets – of the *xávega* type – which are worked from time to time on the great beach of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and in three or four open, sandy nooks on the south coast of Madeira, together with some set nets, generally without trammel. There is, however, a considerable number of bag nets (*redes-de-fole*), funnel-shaped gear used for fishing certain small species at the surface. Alongside these there is also the scoop net (*peneiro*).
In the category of pots there are three types, differing in shape and in the material of construction, which may be split cane, pine lath, rush or osier.
The fishing industry has evolved little since the last official inquiry carried out in Madeira 42 years ago.
As the most significant event, albeit a short-lived one, we should record the laying of a tuna trap (armação, a fixed trap-net) in the great bay of the island of Porto Santo.

This experiment, attempted by the industrialist J. A. Judice Fialho for three consecutive years, from 1910 to 1912, and set up in connection with a canning factory on the island of Madeira, would have brought substantial benefits to the fishing industry, had it been possible to adapt gear of that kind to the waters of the archipelago.
The factory, opened in 1909, remained. The tuna trap, however, had to go back to the Algarve, whence it had come at great expense.

In the last twenty-five years a humble implement – a lamp burning paraffin or fish oil, with a far greater illuminating power than the old lanterns – has altered established practice, to the notable advantage of the industry.

The tuna that come to Madeira in summer, especially the albacore tuna (which is not the *albacora* of the Algarve fishermen), are now, thanks to that lamp, taken on the line at night by the deep-sea fishermen while they are fishing for scabbardfish.

At the same time, fishing for *ruama* (fishermen’s name for small shoaling fish such as mackerel and horse mackerel) – the name they give to mackerel and horse mackerel together when gathered in a shoal or *ruma* – which was formerly carried out only in coastal waters with the bag net and the old lantern, is now practised by some fishermen out at sea, at the surface as always, but in the grounds of the black scabbardfish (*espada preta*) and even beyond. They travel far because the catch is sometimes rewarding, thanks to the modern strong-light lamp, however primitive it looks.
It is, in the end, genuine lamplight fishing, in which the harpoon is replaced by a line or a net.

The scabbardfish catch has intensified in recent years, and in summer this increase owes something indirectly to the fishing lamp (*candeio*), which, especially on moonless nights, draws the *pêta* – the preferred bait – to the surface of the ocean.
There are days when two to three thousand scabbardfish reach the Funchal market alone, and not long ago that number exceeded four thousand, equivalent to a weight of 7 to 8 tonnes.
In the boats used, which are nearly always very small, some slight progress must also be recorded.

Petrol motors have been fitted to some boats, but most of these craft, like all the sailing boats, are open boats, that is, without a full deck, with only a small awning forward and another aft, which they call *leitos*. With such boats, if shipwrecks are not more frequent, it is because the seas of this zone are very calm and typhoons truly rare!
‘As we write, the markets are overflowing with bigeye tuna and the cannery is at work.
This is the season when this species passes on a large scale, as the currents and the plankton bring it into the vicinity of the archipelago.

If this tuna, mixed with the albacore (Thunnus alalunga; Portuguese atum voador), arrives in numbers in Madeiran waters from spring to the beginning of summer, the year goes well for the fisherman, who draws the best of his earnings from this run.

But woe to them if the beasts pass – the *bocas-de-panela* – that mortal enemy of the tuna, which wounds, kills, scatters and puts them to flight, when it does not close tightly round them! ‘The *bocas-de-panela* have come!’ This is the cry of desolation we have often heard from the fisherman, tired, disillusioned and hungry, as he hauls his small boat up on the beach at the end of a day of toil, and at times of terrible dangers! Then he sees all his hopes dashed, above all if the tiger of the ocean, instead of merely crossing these seas, keeps attacking the passing tuna, as has been observed in certain years.

In that case there is misery in countless homes in Machico and Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’), to say nothing of the lesser fishing ports, nor indeed of Câmara de Lobos. That port, the most important of all, seeks compensation in the great depths when the tuna fails it, turning to its year-round speciality, the black scabbardfish.

The *boca-de-panela* has not yet been identified. Everything suggests, however, that it is not a fish but a mammal – the famous and ferocious cetacean which the fisherman of the Algarve unfortunately knows well by the name of *roaz de bandeira*.

It seems to us that one means of hunting and driving off so harmful an animal would be the use of firearms and explosives. Only the State, however, and no other body, could undertake the task, arranging matters in the most efficient and least costly way. And the State owes this protection to the poor fisherman, not only in his own immediate interest but also in that of the whole community.
Generally speaking, we can say that, thanks to more intensive fishing and a certain improvement in methods, output has increased in recent years.
It should be noted, however, that some coastal species are becoming rarer by the day and tending towards disappearance.

This harm is due to the explosive bomb and to the abusive and criminal reduction of the mesh of certain nets and sieve nets. Although it does not affect migratory fish or those of the great depths, it falls heavily on the native species of the shallows.
Remedying this harm is an almost impossible task. The law has foreseen everything, but its enforcement is impracticable.
The poacher who throws explosives condemns himself, risking the loss of his life, or at least of an eye, his arms or his hands, as has so often happened!’

In 1937 the ‘Casas dos Pescadores’ (Fishermen’s Houses) were created, and they have rendered such notable services to the fishing community; the decree of 20 August of that year laid down the basis of their operation. The founding of one of these ‘Casas’ in Madeira was not long in coming, thanks to the efforts of the then harbour master of the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*), Artur Barbosa Carmona. It began operating in 1939, with first-aid posts in the most important fishing centres. In Machico a house was acquired for this purpose, and it was formally inaugurated on 17 July 1943. The ‘Casas dos Pescadores’ provide medical assistance, allowances for invalids and their families, the upkeep of a school, shelter for the destitute, etc., as circumstances permit. In the parish (*freguesia*) of Paul do Mar, as already mentioned, the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) had ten blocks built containing fifty dwellings for the poorest members of this community.

The fishing industry in Madeira is of considerable importance. In the fifteen ports with customs inspection, fish of various species worth 2,725 *contos* (one million réis) *de réis* were landed in 1941, 3,614 *contos* in 1942 and 4,800 *contos* in 1943, the largest quantities being in the ports of Funchal, Câmara de Lobos and Machico.
See Fishing ports.
Hake (Merluccius merluccius)

A gadoid fish that appears only rarely in the Funchal market. It has a delicate flavour and is caught on the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream) or the cherriola (vertical multi-hook deep-water line), at depths of 200 to 400 *braças*.
Pescadores (Casa dos)
See Fishing.
Peso
A measure used to determine the weight of onions. The *peso* corresponds to 52 kilograms in Funchal and to 50 kilograms in Caniço (‘reed’).
Lemon verbena (Lippia citriodora)

A shrub from Chile, very common in the gardens of Funchal, which is also known as verbena. It belongs to the family Verbenaceae and has lanceolate, rough and highly aromatic leaves. An infusion of these leaves has diuretic properties.
Peach tree (Prunus persica)

A tree of the family Rosaceae, subfamily Prunoideae, widely cultivated in Madeira. It is native to China and Afghanistan, and produces delicious fruits that are either smooth or covered in down. The former characterise the variety *laevis* and are known as *pêssegos calvos* (‘bald peaches’); their stones may separate easily from the flesh (*pêssegos calvos molares*) or cling firmly to it. In the downy peaches, too, the stones cling to the flesh sometimes strongly, sometimes only slightly: the former are called *pêssegos burros* or *durázios*, the latter *pêssegos molares*. The skin of these fruits may be yellow or white. The best peaches in Madeira are grown in Santana, Calheta, Arco da Calheta and Fajã da Ovelha; those grown in Funchal are generally of poor quality, and many are attacked by the larvae of various Diptera. Peaches ripen from July to September.
Pestana dos Reis (Manuel)

He was born in Madeira on 1 April 1894 and is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law of the University of Lisbon (*Universidade de Lisboa*), although he began his legal studies at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He attended the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*) before enrolling in the faculty of law. As a student he devoted himself lovingly to poetry, publishing in 1913 a promising volume of verse entitled *Canções de Tristes*. This mentions the forthcoming appearance of the volumes *A avosinha* and *Canções da Ilha*, which it seems to us were never published. He has contributed extensively to various newspapers of Coimbra and Funchal (1921).
Pestana (Dr Eduardo Antonino)

He was born in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) on 8 September 1892 and graduated in letters in 1918 and in law in 1920 at the University of Lisbon (*Universidade de Lisboa*); he also completed the course of the Escola Normal Superior (higher teacher-training college) in 1919. He taught at the Pedro Nunes lyceum (state secondary school) in Lisbon, and for some time now has lived in Funchal, where he practises as a lawyer and teaches at the Jaime Moniz lyceum. While in mainland Portugal he contributed to the review *Voz da Juventude*, in which he wrote a series of thirty articles on syncretism, to the *Economista Português*, to the *Ordem*, etc., and since returning to Funchal he has published many articles in the *Diário de Notícias* and the *Comércio da Madeira*. Works: *A Egreja catolica e os operarios*, a lecture given at the ‘Círculo Católico dos Operários’ in Lisbon; *Sciencia da Linguagem*, a lecture given at the ‘Academia de Estudos Livres’ in Lisbon; and *O Estudo do Latim*, a thesis presented at the Escola Normal Superior. He is preparing a study of Madeiran folklore (1921).
Pestana (Joaquim)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) on 24 December 1840 and was a distinguished poet. His verse is scattered through several periodicals of Funchal and of the city of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), and through the annuals *Novo Almanach de Lembranças Luso-Brasileiro*, *Almanach das Senhoras*, *Almanach Madeirense* and *Almanach de Lembranças Madeirense*. He left in manuscript a book entitled *Espinhos e Flores*, in which many of his poems published in various almanacs and newspapers are said to be collected.

He died in the parish of Câmara de Lobos on 6 February 1909. The *Novo Almanach de Lembranças Luso-Brasileiro*, to which he had contributed for 38 years, published a portrait of the ill-fated Madeiran lyric poet, together with a short notice about him.
Pestana Júnior (Dr Manuel Gregório)

He was born on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) on 16 August 1886, the son of Manuel Gregório Pestana and Dona Carolina dos Ramos Pestana. He is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and practises as a lawyer in the judicial districts of this island. He has held various public service posts here in Madeira. He represented Madeira in the first Constituent Assembly, which sat from 1911 to 1915, and in the legislative session of 1915 to 1917. He has contributed widely to various newspapers and has published the pamphlets *O Problema Sacarino* and *Reconhecimento do Arquipelago da Madeira* (1921).
He was Minister of Finance, and in 1928 he published the interesting and learned historical study entitled *D. Cristobal Colom ou Symam Palha*.
Pestana Júnior (João)

He was the son of João Pestana and was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) in the last years of the 19th century. He was studying in the faculty of law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) when death struck him prematurely on 21 October 1918. He contributed to several newspapers of this city, notably the *Diário da Madeira*. His first verses revealed a promising and decided vocation for poetry. He published in Coimbra a volume of verse entitled *Nevoas de Lagrimas*.
Pestana (Luís da Câmara)
See Câmara Pestana (Luís da).
Plague

The scourge of plague, which in former times repeatedly struck Portugal, was also felt with great severity in Madeira in the first and second quarters of the 16th century. Frutuoso, the historian of the islands, refers to it in the following terms:

‘In the year 1521, when King Manuel I died, there was a great mortality from plague in Funchal, from which God deliver us; and because it had been in the city for years, Captain Simão Gonçalves and the Council chose by lot as patron of the same city the Apostle St James the Less, at the end of which they built him a fine house, to which they went in procession. And because, in spite of this, the plague did not cease, in the year of our Lord 1538 God inspired in all, as in one heart, the wish that there should be no longer any chief guards or lesser guards; and in the same procession held on his day, the first of May, they had it proclaimed that all those stricken by this sickness and the healthy should go together, mingled, to his house, where they offered him on the altar the guards’ staves, which are there today in remembrance; and when they returned, the stricken all came back healed; and from that day until today, through the merits of the Blessed St James, there has been no more plague on the island of Madeira, blessed be the Lord! Wherefore, in remembrance of this grace, a great feast is held for this saint on his day, as if it were Corpus Christi.’

From what Frutuoso says on p. 221 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), it is clear that the plague that ravaged the city of Funchal did not reach the town (*vila*) of Machico. Bishop Dom Ambrósio and two visitors stayed there until St James’s Day, in the month of May, when, ‘the danger of the contagious disease having passed, the same visitors came to the city and carried out their office throughout the island, not with that indulgence in which the bishopric had been raised, but rather with great rigour and harshness ...’

Bishop Dom Ambrósio returned to Portugal as soon as he had completed the mission entrusted to him in Madeira. The two visitors were less fortunate: having escaped the plague, they died in a shipwreck off the coast of Sines while they too were returning to the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). Before leaving, they had committed the greatest acts of violence on the island in order to remove ‘the calluses that vice had formed on the souls of the offenders’, as Dr Gaspar Frutuoso puts it.
Bubonic plague

On p. 404 of vol. II, in the article Popular riots, we have already referred to the cases of bubonic plague that broke out in Funchal in November 1905 and to the extraordinary events that followed them. These were caused by the people’s conviction not only that the disease did not exist on the island, but that the patients admitted to the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’) were being murdered by Dr Balbino do Rêgo and the nursing staff, with the consent of the local authorities. To what we said then, we need only add now that the bacteriological tests carried out in Lisbon fully confirmed Dr António Balbino do Rêgo’s statement that bubonic plague was present in Madeira. The only strange thing was the secrecy in which everything that went on inside the Lazareto was shrouded, which allowed the absurd and fanciful reports mentioned in that article to circulate in the city and beyond. Had full and precise information been given to everyone who sought news of the condition of the patients in the establishment, it may be supposed that the events of 7 January 1906 would not have taken place. Those events, however, did not bring about the harm to public health that many had predicted.

It was said that the people had killed the plague, and indeed, after 7 January no new case of the disease was recorded in Funchal, even though the patients had been carried in the arms of their liberators and many dozens of people had flocked to their homes to see them and talk to them.

It was Regenerator Party politics, seeking to prepare the ground for a future electoral victory, that did most to make the people believe that the most heinous crimes were being committed in the Lazareto. What was established after the events we have described, however, is that the patients had always been well treated there, both by the director and by the nursing staff. Their only complaints were about the strictness of the isolation and the discomfort caused by the hygiene rules they were obliged to follow.
See Diseases, Popular riots and Rêgo (Dr António Balbino do).
Peto (Tetraptures belone)
A fish often seen at the market, whose flesh, similar to that of tuna, is tasty.
Phelps (José)

English merchant who came to Madeira at the end of the 18th century. He set up a school on the Lancaster system at his own expense and contributed greatly to the founding of the Associação Funchalense do Ensino Mútuo, of which he was elected treasurer. He returned to England at the beginning of the third quarter of the 19th century and died there after 1863. See Lancasterian School (*Escola Lancasteriana*), Page and Phelps (street).
Phelps (street)

It links Rua do Bettencourt with Rua do Carmo (‘Carmel’), today Rua Costa Ferreira, and was opened in 1856 at the expense of the English merchant José Phelps. He lived in the large building that later housed the firm of Krohn Brothers & C.ª and afterwards the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) (1921).

In 1788 the firm of Phelps & C.ª existed in Madeira, and in 1804 that of Phelps, Page & C.ª. In February 1920 three descendants of the female line of the Phelps family were in Funchal, and at about the same time the building that had belonged to José Phelps was sold to Sardinha & C.ª and to Joaquim José da Silva Vieira.
Piazzi Smyth (C.)
Works: *Madeira Meteorologic*; Edinburgh, 1882, 1 vol.
Piccone (A)
Works: *Crociera del «Corsaro» alle Isola Madera e Canarie del Capitano Enrico d'Albertis*; Genoa, 1884.
Picken (Andrew)

Works: *Madeira illustrated, with a description of the Island*; London 1842. This work contains 9 magnificent plates showing various parts of the island, and is preceded by a description written by James Macaulay on the basis of information supplied by Cirilo W. Page and José Phelps.
Pico (Castle of São João do)

‘The castle of São João do Pico (‘peak’)’, says Dr Azevedo, ‘lies north-west of the city of Funchal, overlooking it and the harbour, on the height of the Pico dos Frias (‘the Frias’ peak’). This point and that of the Pena (‘crag’) were already indicated in the regulations (*regimento*) of King Sebastian as the closing points of the walls for defence by land; but the Philippine building was perhaps designed for sea defence as well. Two of the manuscripts of the history of this archipelago in our possession state that the castle of the Pico was begun by the governor-general Dom Francisco Henriques: now he took office on 28 October 1622 and died on 23 July 1624; a stone tablet in the parade ground commemorates the governor-general Luís de Miranda Henriques Pinto as the builder of the rest of the work; and he, according to those manuscripts, took office on 6 June 1636 and left it on the same day in 1640; it is therefore clear that the castle of São João do Pico was built between 1622 and 1640’.

Above the outer gate that closes off the ground adjoining the fortress, the date 1632 can be read. It is known that the Spaniard Benedicto Catalão, who for 30 years had belonged to the Castilian garrison on this island, was appointed lieutenant of the fortress by letters patent of 4 December 1655.

On p. 184 of the 1st vol. of this work we said that the Municipal Council never made use of the grant of the Pico fortress, obtained from the Government for 10 years, to house the gaol of the judicial district (*comarca*) provisionally. What we failed to say is that many years earlier, in 1821, the prisoners were transferred to the same fortress. They remained there until the work of converting into a gaol the lower part of the building, now demolished, in the Largo da Sé was completed; that building had belonged to the farmstead (*casal*) of Dona Guiomar Madalena Acciaioly.
See town hall, the prison and fortifications.
Pico dos Barcelos

As already mentioned (I.127), this hill in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António is a favourite place for visitors to go, because of the astonishing panorama it offers over the whole amphitheatre of Funchal. As a commemorative pillar (padrão) of the centenary celebrations of the Independence and Restoration of Portugal, the society ‘Juventude Antoniana’ of this parish had an attractive monumental cross erected on the spot. It was solemnly inaugurated in 1941 and has become a further attraction for visiting the site, which is linked to the city centre by an excellent and busy road.
Pico (fortress)

‘The fortress of the Pico (‘peak’), on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), was’, says Dr Azevedo in his notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), ‘more a refuge than a stronghold’. Gaspar Frutuoso, writing in 1590 about the Pico do Castelo, does not say that there was a castle on it, but that it was given this name because it was in itself ‘strong and defensible.’ The fortifications that once stood there, now destroyed, were raised during Philippine rule ‘after the terrible slaughter and pillage’, says Mr A. A. Sarmento, ‘carried out by the Moors in 1617’.

Some thirty-odd years ago there were still, on the top of the peak, remains of the old fortifications and a cistern intended to supply water to those who took refuge there during pirate raids. (1921).

The fortress of the Pico do Castelo had a constable in the time of Philip II, and in 1805 the governor Manuel Inácio de Avelar Brotero had the roof tiles that still covered the buildings brought down, to reuse them in repairing the barracks of the town (*vila*) and his own residence.
