Piedade

Overlooking the sea in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’) rises a height known as Monte Gordo (‘fat hill’) or Piedade (‘pity’). On its summit stands out the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), which ships approaching the coast can see from a great distance. It is said to have been founded in the 16th century by Garcia Moniz, the first administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of the entail (*morgado*) of Caniçal. Ownership later passed to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of São Gil (‘St Giles’), whose manor house stood in the locality of Calçada (‘paved way’), in the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’).
Piedade

An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’), where stands the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), with an adjoining manor house, belonging to the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of the Couto Cardoso family. It was founded in 1730 by João do Couto Cardoso, holder of the entail (*morgado*), and rebuilt by his successor Francisco João de Vasconcelos de Couto Cardoso in 1825.
Pimenta de Aguiar (Manuel Caetano)
See Aguiar (Manuel Caetano Pimenta de).
Pimenta de Aguiar (street)

This is the public thoroughfare linking Rua da Carreira (‘track’), or Rua do Dr. Vieira, with Rua das Cruzes, or Rua de João Joaquim de Freitas. It received the name by which it is known, in honour of the poet Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar, at a session of the Municipal Council on 24 October 1895.

The Madeiran poet Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar lived opposite Rua da Bela Vista, in the building that today belongs to the heirs of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira (1921).
Chilli pepper (Capsicum frutescens)

A shrub of the family Solanaceae, apparently native to America and widely cultivated in Madeira. Its red fruits, ovate-oblong or ovate-conical, are pungent and are used as a seasoning in cooking. *Capsicum baccatum*, with small, globular fruits, appears in some kitchen gardens in Funchal and is known on the island as *malagueta*. The round black seeds that Madeirans call *pimenta de fora* (‘foreign pepper’) come from *Piper migrum*, a climbing shrub of the family Piperaceae, unknown in Madeira but common in India, China, Java, Borneo, etc.
Peruvian pepper tree (Schinus molle)

A tree from Peru, with drooping branches and compound leaves bearing a large number of narrow leaflets that smell peppery when crushed between the fingers. Male and female specimens of *Schinus molle* grow in the *quintas* and gardens of Funchal, and they flower almost all year round.
Pina (family)
Gaspar Frutuoso, on p. 50 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), lists the Pinas among the gentle and noble families who settled Madeira.
Pinheirinho (Equisetum maximum)

A member of the Equisetaceae, easily recognised by its white stems, its sheaths with 20 to 40 teeth and the whorled branches of its sterile stems (20 to 40 in each whorl). It grows in damp places in São Vicente, São Roque, etc. An infusion of this cryptogam has diuretic properties.
Pinheiro (Dom Diogo)

The very bull (papal bull) creating this diocese, *Pro excellenti preeminentia*, of 12 June 1514 (vol. 1, p. 363), names Dom Diogo Pinheiro as the first bishop of Funchal. Since this archipelago belonged to the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), and Dom Diogo Pinheiro was one of its highest-ranking members, holding the lofty office of Dom Prior (*D. Prior*, head of the priory of Tomar or of the collegiate church of Guimarães) and Vicar of Tomar, the seat of the Order, he was the obvious choice to occupy the new episcopal throne established within that powerful body and in the area of its spiritual jurisdiction, which stretched to the furthest bounds of the East.

The first prelate of Funchal never came to his bishopric, and on being invested in the new office he had certainly not thought of crossing the ocean to tend his flock in person. The great prestige and influence he enjoyed at court, and the posts he held as councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) of state and judge of the Desembargo do Paço (the royal supreme court; *desembargador do paço*), did not allow him to take direct charge of the episcopal government of the new diocese.

He did not, however, neglect the administration of his bishopric. Little more than a year after its creation, he sent the prelate Dom Duarte (vol. I, p. 382) to this island, where he performed all the episcopal functions and consecrated our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) in 1516. He sent other visitors to this diocese, charged with watching over canonical discipline and superintending the various ecclesiastical services. He died in 1526, having governed this bishopric for 12 years.

Dom Diogo Pinheiro came from noble and distinguished families. He was the son of Dr Pedro Esteves Marques and Dona Isabel Pinheiro. He was Dom Prior of Guimarães and counsellor to Manuel I, and held the offices already mentioned. Alexandre Herculano highlights the qualities of his character: he had the courage to condemn publicly the persecution of the Jews and to defend them with all the weight of the authority and prestige he enjoyed. Still more remarkable was his stance on the condemnation of Dom Fernando, Duke of Bragança, who was executed in 1483 for conspiring against the life of John II. He maintained at court that the duke was the victim of a great injustice, and he wrote the *Manifesto da innocencia do duque de Bragança D. Fernando II*, which is included in the *Provas da Historia Genealogica* of Dom António Caetano de Sousa.

Dom Diogo Pinheiro died in Tomar in 1526 and was buried there, and ‘today he lies’, says Vieira Guimarães in his remarkable work *Ordem de Christo*, ‘in a superb and beautiful tomb in the chancel of the church of Santa Maria dos Olivais (St Mary of the Olive Groves)’.
Pine trees

The first pines grown in Madeira were stone pines (*Pinus Pinea*). Maritime pines (*Pinus Pinaster*) seem to have been introduced in the last quarter of the 18th century, and it is strange that a species so useful to man should have begun to be cultivated on the island only so late.

On 19 September 1807, it was reported at a session of the Municipal Council of Funchal that some *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of pine nuts had been given from America, though the species to which they belonged was not stated. On 29 August 1812 the same body resolved to order four *moios* of pine seed of the best varieties from Portugal.

On 26 October 1821, the guild representative (*mester*) Severiano Ferraz proposed to the Council that 100 *alqueires* of maritime pine seed and 100 of stone pine seed be ordered for sowing on the island. On 15 March 1822 the same Council resolved to announce by public notice that it had one *moio* of maritime pine nuts to share out among the farmers, and that it was awaiting two *moios* of stone pine nuts for the same purpose. On 18 September 1823, notices were posted informing the public that a quantity of pine nuts had arrived in this city for distribution among the farmers.

On 12 January 1830, the treasurer of the municipality (*concelho*) was authorised to order two *moios* of pine nuts for sowing in suitable places. At its sessions of 17 January 1837 and 20 September 1839 the Council once again showed the interest it took in the afforestation of the municipality’s mountains and common lands (*baldios*).

During the administration of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, large quantities of pine seed came to Madeira, which he had distributed among the Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*) and rural landowners. It was from then on that the cultivation of the maritime pine began to expand greatly on the island. The cultivation of this species now covers an area which we suppose to be no less than 2,000 hectares, while that of the stone pine is today abandoned or almost abandoned (1921).

Maritime pines are generally felled at 12 to 15 years, but the slender stems of these trees are already put to use at 6 years as supports for bean plants, and at 8 for building trellises or covered walkways. Because pines are generally sown very close together, they need thinning after a few years, and the poles cut at that stage are sold to farmers for these purposes.
As far as we know, tapping for resin has never been practised in the archipelago, at least not for industrial purposes.

Pine seed is customarily sown from January to March. The last two months are preferred for sowing on high ground, so that the young pines are not damaged by the hail that often falls during the winter months. Many growers sow wheat, barley, rye or broom together with the pine seed. These shelter the young pines from the sun’s rays as well as from the wind, rain and hail, which can break them or tear them up by the roots.
Besides *Pinus Pinaster*, or maritime pine, and *P. Pinea*, or stone pine, Madeira also has *Pinus halepensis* and *P. canariensis*, the latter species having been introduced from Tenerife in 1837.
The maritime pine grows on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) on non-calcareous soils, while on the calcareous soils there *Pinus halepensis* is now cultivated with good results.
Pintainho (Puffinus obscurus)

A bird of the shearwater family (Procellariidae), close to the *boieiro*, from which it differs in its smaller size and in having bluish-grey feet instead of flesh-coloured ones. It lives on all the islands of the archipelago and is common on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’). It is also known as the *pintelho*, from a particular cry it can be heard giving in flight. It is often absent during the hot season, and usually lays a single white egg in rock crevices, generally on the bare ground.
Linnet (Acanthias cannabina)

A bird of the finch family (Fringillidae) that lives in the Madeira archipelago. It forms large flocks in winter, and its clutch consists of 4 to 6 faintly bluish-white eggs with reddish spots. Its nests are made of dry roots and lined inside with animal fur and hair.
Goldfinch (Carduelis carduelis)

A bird of the finch family (Fringillidae) that nests on Madeira but has not been found on the other islands of the archipelago. Its clutch consists of 4 or 5 faintly bluish or greenish-white eggs with brick-coloured speckles. The nest is made of thin roots on the outside and wool and other soft materials inside.
Pinto (family)

This family surname derives from Lopo Fernandes Pinto and Gonçalo Pinto Alcoforado, both of noble descent. The former came to live in Madeira around the middle of the 15th century and died in 1500; the latter settled on this island around 1500 and made his home in Machico, where he died. Lopo Fernandes Pinto held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) land in Santana (‘St Anne’) and in São Jorge.
Pinto (Acácio Augusto Correia)
He was appointed civil governor of the district of Funchal by decree of 14 November 1921 and took up the post on the 23rd. He left for Lisbon on 20 February 1922.
Pinto Coelho (Frederico)
He was the son of Joaquim Pinto Coelho and Dona Maria Carlota de Ornelas Linhares Pinto Coelho, and was born in Funchal on 28 May 1851.

He was a copying clerk at the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of Funchal and secretary of the Municipal Administration of Évora. After retiring from the latter post he returned to Madeira, where for some time he served as municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Câmara de Lobos. He was an editor of and contributor to various Madeiran newspapers, and in 1881 he published in Funchal a 40-page pamphlet entitled *Sudario Negro*, a diatribe against the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto. Father António Aires Pacheco replied to it with the pamphlet *O Sudario Negro no banco dos réus*. He died in Funchal on 2 January 1916.
Pinto Coelho (Jacinto)

He was born in Funchal on 7 October 1847 and is the brother of the preceding. For many years he was a private primary-school teacher, and on 18 December 1884 he was appointed temporary junior officer of the Funchal Customs House, where he at present holds the rank of sub-inspector. He has contributed to a great number of local newspapers, and more recently to the *Diario de Noticias*; his articles are commended by the correctness and elegance with which they are always written (1921).
Pinto Coelho (Luís de Ornelas)

Luís de Ornelas Pinto Coelho was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’) in this city on 21 February 1843, the son of Joaquim Pinto Coelho and Dona Maria Carlota de Ornelas Pinto Coelho. We believe he held no academic qualification at all, not even a primary-school certificate, but he made up for that deficiency through a persevering love of reading and study, and came to hold a true pre-eminence among us in the literary and journalistic field. He contributed extensively to many Madeiran newspapers, notably the *Diario de Noticias*. It may be said that in this paper, as its editor over a period of several decades, he published many hundreds of articles, which would fill a dozen thick volumes. He rarely sent the paper anything other than the leading article or a polemical piece, and his prose had an elegant and correct form that gave particular pleasure. He fought hard battles in the press, in which, as always happened here at that time, excesses of language were not rare on either side.

Luís Pinto Coelho held first place in poetry among us. Although his lyricism was somewhat old-fashioned and perhaps out of step with his time, it is certain that no one surpassed him in the harmonious cadence of his verse and the impeccable beauty of its form. He was beyond dispute an inspired and distinguished poet. He collected some of his poems, publishing the volumes *Harpa Madeirense*, 1896, and *Folhas Dispersas*, 1899, and the verse pamphlet *a Reacção e o Progresso*.

He was in Brazil at the time of the Paraguayan War and published various poems in the *Diário do Grão Pará*; in Funchal he held for many years the post of head of the Civil Police force. Before receiving its present name, Rua João Joaquim de Freitas was called after Luís de Ornelas Pinto Coelho. He died in this city on 17 March 1920.
Pinto Correia (Armando Eduardo)

He was born in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) on 3 September 1897, the son of Guilherme Pinto Correia and Dona Inácia Augusta de Seixas Alves Correia. He attended the Faculties of Science of Lisbon and Coimbra, and then the War School (*Escola de Guerra*), and is at present a lieutenant in the machine-gun company of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.º 27*). He was mobilised for the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps (*C. E. P.*) and spent some time in the trenches at Kadingham, where a British battalion was stationed, and was commended by his superiors for the service he rendered there (1921).

Since 1911 he has contributed to various newspapers in Funchal, Ponta Delgada, Coimbra and Lisbon, always standing out for the elegance and colour of his prose. He was director of *Vida Academica* (1913) and chief editor of the *Jornal de Coimbra* (1916), and in 1921 published the pamphlet *Um Poeta em frangalhos*.

Devoting himself to colonial life, he lived for some years in our overseas province of Timor, holding public office, and rendered notable services there that were much appreciated by the higher authorities in the mother country. He published two fine books: *O Gentio de Timor* and *Timor de lés a lés*. Having recently gone to the province of Mozambique, he died in Quelimane on 29 January 1943.
Pinto (Dean Dr João Joaquim)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) on 4 March 1851. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in theology from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), completing his degree in 1879, and in that same year he was ordained priest. He was teaching at the Archiepiscopal Seminary of Évora (*Seminário Arquiepiscopal de Évora*) when, in 1888, he was presented to a canonry of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), and he was later raised to the office of dean of the same Cathedral. Here in Madeira he was professor and vice-rector of the Seminary, vicar-general and on several occasions governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop's absence). He also carried out other duties, such as president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House (*Santa Casa*, the Misericórdia), etc.

He was a man of wide learning and great application to study, especially versed in theological subjects, which he taught with distinction. To his gifts of intellect he joined a great austerity of character, which earned him the regard and esteem of his fellow countrymen.

He was editor of the newspaper *A Verdade* and published *Documentos para o subsídio ao estudo do direito civil ecclesiastico portugues*, 1894, 2 vols of 379 and 537 pp., and *Evangelho de S. Mateus*, 1901, 136 pp. He died in this city on 11 February 1919.
Pinto Feio (Dr Carlos José Baeta)
He was appointed Civil Governor of this district by decree of 18 December 1917 and took up the post on 5 February of the following year.
Pintos (street)
This name was formerly borne by the part of the present Rua da Carreira (‘track’), or Rua do Dr Vieira, lying between Largo da Igrejinha and Rua de São Francisco.
Piorno

Two species are known by this name in Madeira: *Genista maderensis* and *G. virgata*. The first is a shrub or small tree of 1.50 to 5 metres, with trifoliate leaves and small, satiny-pubescent leaflets, only rarely almost hairless on the upper surface. The second is a shrub that can reach 2.50 m in height, with very small, leafless-looking, satiny-pubescent and whitish leaves. These two Leguminosae, both belonging to the subfamily Papilionoideae, have yellow flowers arranged in racemes. *G. maderensis* occurs in some ravines of the interior and between São Vicente and São Jorge; *G. virgata* is common in the outskirts of Funchal, in the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’), at Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’), etc. The wood of the latter species, used exclusively for inlaid work (*embutidos*), is heavy, hard and compact, at first a yellowish white and later a reddish brown; that of the former, entirely unknown to cabinetmakers, is white or yellowish white. *Genista maderensis*, sometimes used as fodder for domestic animals, is, contrary to what Masferrer y Arquimbau supposed, a species quite distinct from the ‘gacia’ of the Canary Islands (*Cytisus stenopetalus*).
Pipa

The so-called shipping *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres), so named because it is the one used in exporting our wines, holds 418 litres, and the so-called *carreteira* *pipa* holds 500 litres. Decree no. 5,492 of 2 May 1919 set at 55 litres the quantity of alcohol required to treat one *pipa* of wine of 500 litres.
Pires

In 1566 a certain Gonçalo Pires was living in Funchal, where he held the office of clerk of the accounts (*escrivão dos contos*), and in 1471 Diogo Pires and Francisco Pires were resident here. It is possible that these three individuals brought the Pires family surname to Madeira.
Pires (António Augusto da Silva)
He was appointed Civil Governor of the district of Funchal by decree of 9 June 1921 and took up the post on the 19th. He left for Lisbon on 18 July of the same year.
Pita (Dr António da Luz)

Dr António da Luz Pita was perhaps the ablest physician ever born on Madeiran soil. In his day no one here disputed his intellectual supremacy in matters of medicine and surgery, and we know of no other doctor, before or after him, who showed more proven competence in clinical practice. One might perhaps cite Dr João Francisco de Oliveira, physician to John VI, Dr Julião Fernandes da Silva, author of the *Carta Critica sôbre o Metodo Curativo dos Medicos Funchalenses*, and also the Count of Canavial, all of whom left a reputation as eminent clinicians. We have no reason, however, to believe that they surpassed Dr António da Luz Pita, even allowing for the periods in which they lived, above all because he was at once a great physician and a most skilful surgeon.

Born into a humble family, Dr António da Luz Pita came into the world in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on 2 September 1802. Having completed his secondary studies in this city, he went to Montpellier, where he took the degree of bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) of letters in 1826, that of bachelor of physical sciences in 1827 and a doctorate in medicine in 1830. The following year he received the degree of doctor of surgery from the Paris faculty.

He married, in Montpellier, a lady from one of the most distinguished families of that city, and in 1833 he intended to return to his homeland with his wife. On calling at Gibraltar, however, he became convinced of the grave dangers he would face in entering a country where the civil war was then at its most acute stage. He remained in Gibraltar until the Convention of Évora-Monte and practised there with success. Against the opinion of the English doctors, he identified as cholera morbus a suspicious disease that had appeared there, and his diagnosis was later fully confirmed. He rendered notable services on that occasion, which led the British government to grant him the diploma of citizen of the 1st class, with the right of residence in Gibraltar, at that time the highest distinction that could be conferred there on a foreigner.

In Madeira he held the posts of health officer (*delegado de saúde*) and professor at our Medical School, in which he brilliantly displayed the high qualities of his mind. As teacher and director of our foremost educational establishment, he had to sustain a prolonged struggle with Dr João da Câmara Leme, later Count of Canavial, a man of character and rare merit but of a violent and quarrelsome temperament, who in various pamphlets harshly attacked Dr António da Luz Pita, both as professor at the School and as health officer of the district.

Dr Luz Pita, who enjoyed great prestige and influence here in Madeira, represented the island in parliament in the legislative sessions of 1851 to 1852 and of 1853 to 1858, championing with selfless dedication the prosperity and advancement of his homeland.

He was a deputy and was in Lisbon when word reached the capital that the terrible epidemic of cholera morbus had begun to spread in Funchal. Having requested the most immediate and urgent aid from the central government, he left without delay for Madeira aboard the steam warship *Mindelo* to take up his post as health officer. He was accompanied by several doctors and nurses, and also carried a large quantity of medicines, a great deal of clothing, beds, straw mattresses, etc., as well as an extraordinary credit of six *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis), intended to meet the initial costs of setting up the medical and hospital services. In him Gromicho Couceiro found his most valuable and effective assistant, and the name of Dr Luz Pita is closely linked to the memory of that meritorious and never-forgotten governor. In so calamitous a time he rendered the most distinguished services as a physician, as head of the health services, as a man of great prestige and influence, and also through the prompt aid he obtained from the government in the mainland. In the midst of this humanitarian campaign, in which he was wholly engaged and absorbed, he was dealt a most terrible blow: the death of his wife, Dona Ângela Delmas, a victim of the epidemic.

In the article Princess Dona Maria Amélia Hospice (vol. II, p. 128) we highlighted the services that Dr António da Luz Pita rendered to the Empress Dona Amélia in founding that charitable institution, in setting up the hospital and directing it medically, and also as the representative on this island of its august and illustrious foundress. We refer the reader there, thus avoiding needless and tedious repetition.

As a politician, he fought battles in the press against his opponents, serving as editor of and contributor to several newspapers, such as *O Archivista*, *A Ordem* and *A Razão*. He published the following pamphlets:

*Proposições sobre a vacina*, an inaugural thesis defended at the Faculty of Montpellier; *Vantagens da reunião imediata por meio da sutura depois das operações cirurgicas*, an inaugural thesis defended at the Faculty of Paris; *Excisão do colo do utero*, an operation performed in Lisbon in 1848; *Lições feitas na Escola Medica do Funchal sobre a colera-morbus*; and *Relatorio Historico e estatisco sobre a invasão, desenvolvimento e mortalidade da epidemia colerica na Madeira*.

He wrote several reports on the clinical service of the Princess Dona Maria Amélia Hospice, some of which were published, and also a *Nota sobre uma modificação do estetoscopio*, read at the Academy of Medicine in Paris, which we do not know ever saw publication.

He was one of the founding members of the Society of Medical Sciences of Lisbon (*Sociedade das Ciencias Medicas de Lisboa*) and belonged to several learned societies abroad. Besides holding the posts of professor and director of our Medical School and of health delegate, he served here in Madeira as president of the Funchal Municipal Council and as a member of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*). He held the title of Councillor (*carta de conselho*) and several Portuguese and foreign honours. He died in this city on 23 February 1870.
Pita (Dr Nicolau Caetano de Bettencourt)
See Bettencourt Pita (Dr Nicolau C.).
Pita (Dr Pedro Góis)

He was born in Funchal on 26 May 1891, the son of António Félix Pita and Dona Maria da Conceição Góis Pita. He graduated as a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). After practising as a lawyer in Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and in this city, where he also held the post of notary, he was appointed land registrar (*conservador do registo predial*) of one of the judicial districts of Lisbon, where he likewise devotes himself to life at the bar. As a deputy, he represented Madeira in Parliament in the legislatures of 1919-1921 and 1921, and he was again elected deputy for this archipelago in January 1922.

He is an officer of the Orders of St James and of Christ, has contributed to various newspapers and was one of the founders and editors of the *Revista de Direito* (‘Law Review’) in this city. In Funchal he published a pamphlet entitled *A Expropriação do Montado do Barreiro...*, and in Coimbra the volume *Pratica d'Advocacia*, with a preface by Dr José Alberto dos Reis (1921).

He was Minister of Commerce and Labour, is a full member of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Ciências de Lisboa*) and has published various legal and literary works, among which we may list the following: *Estudos de Direito*, *Na Vida do Fôro*, *Comentarios ao Codigo do Registo Predial*, *Novo Codigo do Registo Predial Anotado*, *O Direito na Pratica*, *O Contrato de Colonia na Madeira*, *A Demencia* and *Gente que passa*.
Pitanga (Eugenia brasiliana)
A small tree native to Brazil and widely cultivated in Funchal. It belongs to the myrtle family (Myrtaceae) and bears flattened, ribbed fruits with a tart flavour.
Pitão Grande
See the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*).
Pitão Pequeno
See the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*).
Agave (Agave americana)

A member of the Amaryllidaceae, cultivated and naturalised in Madeira. Its long, fleshy leaves, sometimes yellow at the edges, are steeped in water for a few days and then beaten, yielding a fairly tough fibre that is used in rope-making.
Plateaux

Plateaux, or plains lying on mountain heights, cannot be numerous or extensive, given the relatively small area of this island and the extraordinarily rugged terrain that makes up almost its entire extent. From the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Ilustrado* we transcribe: ‘This island has four principal plateaux: that of Santo António da Serra, or, popularly, Santo da Serra, which contains a lake, in the municipality (*concelho*) of Machico; that of Achada de Santa Ana, in the municipality of that name; that of the Paul da Serra, or simply the Paul, which is the largest, on the boundaries of the municipalities of São Vicente, Ponta do Sol and Porto Moniz; and lastly the plateau of Achadas da Cruz, or merely the Achadas, in the municipality of Porto Moniz, which is the smallest: the lake looks like an extinct crater; it measures 66 metres in diameter and 40 in depth. There are very beautiful meadows in the municipality’.
Town Plans

Captain Vidal’s *Funchal Bay*, published in 1843, shows the plan of Funchal at that time, and William Johnston’s map of Madeira, published in 1775, has attached to it a small-scale plan of the city surveyed by Captain Skinner. The first of these works served as the basis for all the charts of Funchal later published in various foreign works on Madeira.

On 2 April 1893 the Council opened a 60-day tender for the award by public auction (*arrematação*) of the work of surveying the city plan. The work was awarded to the Consultório de Engenharia, whose members included the engineers Carlos Roma Machado de Faria e Maia and Adriano Augusto Trigo. The plan was completed in 1895 and cost the municipality about 9 *contos* de réis (*conto*: one million réis), a sum that was finally paid off on 16 May of the same year.
The drawing boards of the city plan are kept in an iron safe bought by the Council for that purpose.

On 6 September 1897 the Council resolved to acquire, for 700,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), a reduction of the said plan made by the engineer C. Roma e Maia. A copy of this reduction was sent shortly afterwards to the engineers of the District Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas*), who were then in charge of the studies for the city’s water supply and sewerage, while the original was filed in the relevant municipal department.

Other copies were later made of this reduced plan. One of them, or its original, served as the basis for the *Guia Panoramico da Madeira*, published some years ago by Dr Luís Rodrigues Gaspar and Francisco Bento de Gouveia, and for the *Planta da cidade de Funchal contendo todos os melhoramentos realisados até 1911*, drawn up by the engineers Adriano A. Trigo and Aníbal A. Trigo
See Maps.
Plane tree

The plane tree cultivated in Madeira is *Platanus orientalis*, and not *P. occidentalis*, as all the botanists who have studied our flora have wrongly stated. It is a tree that can reach 35 metres in height, with monoecious flowers, the staminate and pistillate ones on separate branches and gathered into globular heads. Plane wood is light-coloured and wavy-grained; when well seasoned it is excellently suited to cabinet-making. We are not aware that the eye irritations mentioned by some authors, caused by the hairs of young plane leaves, have been observed in Madeira.

The plane tree thrives not only in Funchal and its surroundings, where it already grew at the end of the 17th century, but also in the ravines of the interior. High in the mountains, however, it grows poorly, apparently suffering from the strong winds that frequently blow there.
Poço (square)

This is the square beside the Campo do Almirante Reis, into which Rua de Santa Maria opens. It has a public fountain of some architectural pretension, which is at present supplied with water from the Tornos (‘water turns’) but which before 1911 provided only groundwater, drawn up from the subsoil by a pump. A short distance away stood the old church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*).
Poço Novo

(Rua do). The former name of the street now called Rua dos Tanoeiros. ‘From this Rua dos Mercadores,’ says Frutuoso, ‘beyond Rua Direita (‘straight street’), another street can be seen, not so long, with other shops of lesser trade, such as fruit, linen cloth and haberdashery goods brought from abroad; at the end of it there is a well, for which reason it is called Rua do Poço Novo (‘new well’)’.
Snow pits
These are large pits dug by man in the ground at certain points in the mountains, intended to receive the hail that falls during the winter in the high parts of the island.
The snow pits are abandoned today, but in summer they supplied the ice needed to make sorbets, before the apparatus for freezing water artificially was introduced to Madeira.
Near Pico do Areeiro (‘sand-pit peak’) and the Serra de São Roque there are several snow pits, some badly ruined, others well preserved.
Pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium)
A native member of the mint family (Labiatae), common on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It is used in infusions as an expectorant and emmenagogue.
Poems about Madeira

Countless verse compositions sing and extol the beauties of the Madeiran landscape, the marvellous ruggedness and capricious relief of its terrain, the incomparable mildness of its climate, and the variety, charm and fragrance of its flowers, etc. It would be quite impossible to gather them all, or even to make a selection of those that stand out most for the loftiness of their conception or the refinement of their form. We wish only to mention the poems devoted exclusively to this archipelago, which are the following: ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*), by Manuel Tomás. . . , Antwerp, 1635; ‘The Zarco Epic’ (*Zargueida*). . ., by Francisco de Paulo Medina e Vasconcelos, Lisbon, 1806; *The Ocean Flower*..., by T. M. Hugues, London, 1845; and *Auto da Lenda*, by J. Brito Câmara, 1943. References to these three poems, one of which is written in English, and some biographical details about their authors are to be found elsewhere in this *Elucidário*.
Popular poetry

It is not Madeiran folklore that we intend to deal with here; we hope to say something about this interesting subject in the Supplement to this work, drawing for that purpose on the studies carried out among us by Dr Eduardo Antonino Pestana. Nor do we wish at present to refer to the narratives in verse of which Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo made a large collection, publishing the precious anthology entitled ‘Ballad Collection of the Madeira Archipelago’ (*Romanceiro do Archipelago da Madeira*). On this occasion the point of view we adopt in writing this short article is a very narrow one.

When an extraordinary event stirs the soul of the people and drives it to give noisy expression to the feelings that possess it, the spontaneous, rough poetic inspiration of the common people at once makes itself felt. Artless lyres then appear, singing in laboured laments or lashing out in fiery songs of indignation at the events that provoked this passion and at the circumstances that gave it weight and prominence in the heated minds of the crowds. This has been observed here more than once, but it showed itself in a truly remarkable way at the time of the so-called Plague of the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’), to which we have already alluded on p. 224 of volume II and on p. 77 of this volume. Popular poetry – simple, artless and incorrect, but spontaneous, vehement and passionate – poured out in a profusion of compositions which, printed as small pamphlets and loose sheets, were bought and eagerly read by people of every social class. The fever of poetic inspiration set many imaginations alight, and the fertility of these verse productions was truly astonishing: the presses could not keep up with the multitude of poems written at that time.

We give below a list of some of these compositions, which was kindly supplied to us: *Farça do Lazareto*, 13 pp.; *Sonho dum Machiqueiro*, 9 pp.; *Auto da Peste*, 16 pp.; *O dr. Rego no Inferno*, 8 pp.; *O Dedo da Providencia*, 8 pp.; *A Peste no Funchal (versos do Feiticeiro)*, 7 pp.; *A Peste Balbinica*; *A Peste no Funchal*; *A Panelinha da Peste e um medroso*; *Os Primos do dr. Rego*; *O dr. Rego enforcado*; *Confissões do dr. Rego*; *Os Pestilenciais no Funchal*; *A Despedida*; *Canção da Peste*; *Má Peste dê nos Pestes*; *Farças e Farçantes*, 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th parts; *O Bicho desapareceu*; *Viva o dia 7 de Janeiro de 1906*; *O Ultimo Suspiro*; *Assalto ao Lazareto*; *A Peste no Funchal no dia 7 de Janeiro de 1906*; *Partida*, etc. etc.

As generally happens, the people, carried away and deceived by vile profiteers, committed the most deplorable excesses at this sad juncture. These excesses are eloquently reflected in the productions listed above, in which the unruliness of the language matches the excesses committed.

Prose pamphlets were also widely popular, and the campaigns in the periodical press, with rare and honourable exceptions, matched these excesses of the fervent popular lyre in both quantity and quality.
Poiso

About 10 kilometres from the city and roughly seven from the Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’) of Monte (‘hill’), but within the bounds of the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha, stands the finest mountain shelter in our uplands. It is called the Poiso house (*Casa do Poiso*), because it lies at the well-known locality of the same name. The Poiso (‘resting place’) is a much-travelled spot, since the road that crosses it links Funchal with several parishes in the north of Madeira. As the place is very exposed and subject to frequent gales, the worthy civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro had a mountain shelter for travellers built here in 1850. It has rendered the most notable services and saved many of those who passed that way from certain death. The old road across this spot, which connects it with the charming and much-visited locality of Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’) and several northern parishes, has been considerably improved, and regular motor-car services have been established between Funchal, the Poiso and Ribeiro Frio. There is also a road, already used by motor cars, between the Poiso and the pleasant resort of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), and it is believed that before long it will be possible to reach the parish of Santana (‘St Anne’). The Poiso shelter (*Casa de Abrigo do Poiso*) is equipped with a telephone booth. We have already given a detailed account of the excellent services it provides, and of its foundation, on p. 195 of vol. I of this work.
Of particular interest on this subject is the article that one of the authors of the *Elucidário Madeirense* published in the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’), which we transcribe below:
‘Anyone who has never crossed the mountains of Madeira in the winter season cannot imagine how intense the cold there is on certain days, or how violently the storms break over that region.

The temperature, which in the city of Funchal seldom falls below 7 degrees, can in some cases drop to 2 and 3 degrees below zero in the mountains. If the Areeiro (‘sand pit’) station had not, to our shame, been left in the most complete neglect, we are convinced that wind speeds of 60 and 70 kilometres an hour would often be recorded there, speeds very rarely observed in the low-lying part of the island.

It is not only hail that often falls in the mountains of Madeira during the winter season; flakes of snow are also sometimes seen in the high regions, and the cold is then extremely intense and hard to bear.

In the Poiso uplands, one of the coldest and most storm-lashed points in the mountains, many people died in former times for lack of shelter and help. The same would still happen today had the benevolent Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro, when civil governor of the district, not sought to remedy so great an evil by having a house built in those uplands, a little beyond the Fonte das Moças, to take in travellers in every season of the year and at any hour of the day or night.

The mountain shelter known as the Poiso shelter was built in 1851, and it has been open ever since to the public passing that way, who find in the building safe refuge from the cold and storms of the mountains.

In an official letter dated 6 October 1851, the late Councillor José Silvestre Ribeiro urged the Municipal Council of Funchal to reach an agreement immediately, without losing a moment, with the Council of Santana on the share each should contribute to the upkeep of a man and his family who would live in the house and take charge of giving travellers whatever help and assistance they needed.

In the same letter the governor further urged that the choice of whoever was to live in the house we refer to and carry out the duties mentioned should be made with the greatest care, so that only a person or family of recognised honesty, capable of grasping the duties incumbent on them in a *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) so lonely and so far from any inhabited place, would be placed there.

We do not know who the first keeper of the Poiso shelter was. What we do know is that the last but one keeper there was dismissed for his slovenliness and lack of care over cleanliness, and that the building then passed under the supervision of Mr Caminata, who has introduced or is about to introduce some improvements of recognised benefit to the public (1921).

Besides the ground floor, which contains the keeper’s rooms, the tavern and a large kitchen, the house has a first floor with three rooms, the one on the south side being quite spacious. In the kitchen there are some plank beds intended for the humble country folk; the first floor generally serves persons of a certain standing who wish to spend the night in the building.

Under the regulations, the keeper must always have bread, wine, spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) and coffee to supply to travellers. He is also obliged to keep a store of firewood and to give all those in need whatever help he can.

The works on the original Poiso house were contracted for the sum of 1,442,950 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), but further sums have since been spent on improvements and extensions to the building. As it stands today, it perfectly fulfils the purpose for which it is intended, and could even serve as a forest police station, if there were a will to put an end to the abuses of the woodcutters and charcoal burners who are laying waste to our mountains’ (1921).
Police

For centuries public security in Funchal was in the hands of the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties), an official who, in the time of the captaincies, was proposed by the donatary but appointed by the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council). To assist the *alcaide* in the duties and tasks he was obliged to carry out, there was at first a certain number of men appointed by the donatary, who, according to a decree of 1450, were to be ‘of good life’. At the end of the 15th century the Council appointed for each district of the town a certain number of officers, called constables (*quadrilheiros*), whose duty was to keep order and protect the property of the residents.

Despite all these police officials, public security in Funchal does not seem to have been assured. In 1489 the captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) allowed ‘merchants and men of standing’ who owned armour of ‘helmet and lance’ to carry sword and dagger, and shortly afterwards extended this permission to all married men who owned a house, but only until the ‘bell was rung’. When travelling, married men were permitted to carry sword and dagger.

Under the charter (foral) of 6 August 1515, the revenue of the alcaideship (*alcaidaria*) consisted of the gaol fees (*carceragem*) paid by prisoners and the fines paid by card players, the excommunicated, brawlers, frequenters of brothels and all persons found in the streets, armed or unarmed, after the ‘bell was rung’.

The ‘curfew bell’ (*sino de correr*) hung in the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), in Rua do Aljube (‘bishop’s prison street’), and when it rang at night the constables went out to patrol their districts or wards. Machico also had a ‘curfew bell’, which was placed beside the town hall building.
At no time was the town police so disregarded, or rather so powerless to curb the excesses of robbers and brawlers, as under Philippine rule.

As we saw when dealing with Castilian rule, the city’s streets were then frequently stained with blood from private feuds, and three judicial commissions came to Madeira to punish the criminals and restore order on the island.

The Englishman Hans Sloane, who visited Madeira in 1687, saw that businessmen carried a long sword under their cloaks and a sharp knife or dagger in their pockets. This seems to mean that even at that time little reliance was placed on the town police to defend the lives and property of citizens. Ovington, who was on this island in 1689, also observed that many of the inhabitants went about armed.

While he governed Madeira, the governor and captain-general João António de Sá Pereira showed the greatest zeal and energy in curbing the abuses committed by nobles and commoners alike. Even so, public security seems to have become known on the island only after constitutional government was established on solid foundations throughout the country.

On 20 May 1812 the Council resolved to ask the captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) to establish night-time military patrols ‘so as to put an end to the robberies committed not only in sacred places, warehouses and offices, but even in dwelling houses’. On 13 January 1814 it decided to write to the same authority asking him to place at its disposal each night 80 men of the territorial militia (*ordenanças*), in order ‘to put into effect the system of patrols newly ordered’. On 19 November 1796 the Council had ordered the constables (*quadrilheiros*) to wear a badge so that they could be recognised.

In 1826 the city was patrolled by men of the 7th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria n.º 7*). After the granting of the Charter, however, these same forces became a source of disorder, since the regiment was absolutist. This led the Council to ask the Governor to suspend the patrols and to forbid the soldiers to leave barracks after 7 in the evening.

From 1828 to 1830, that is, while the notorious José Maria Monteiro, nicknamed ‘the Baize’ (*o Baeta*), governed Madeira, the liberals suffered the harshest persecution. It was enough for someone to be accused of being a *malhado* (derogatory nickname for a liberal under the Miguelist regime) for him to be savagely beaten at once by the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) mob, with no help from the agents of authority. The constables were then a source of disorder. Egged on by the governor, who often went with them on their night patrols, they committed the worst excesses, arresting and beating every constitutionalist who dared to go out into the street. In 1830 there were also constables in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’).

The last *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties) of Funchal was appointed in 1832, so the office existed for as long as absolute government lasted. The Funchal Council also appointed *alcaides* for Caniço, Câmara de Lobos and Ribeira Brava, who carried out police duties in those places.

In 1834, after liberal principles had been proclaimed in Madeira, the prefect (*prefeito*) created the posts of commissioners of the municipal superintendents (provedor) and of police corporals in the parishes, with the direction of police services entrusted to the Superintendent. Some years later a body of 26 guards or process officers was set up in the city for public security, under the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative).

In 1838 *A Chronica* (‘The Chronicle’) called for the law of 22 February of that year, which had created municipal guards in district capitals, to be extended to Madeira. It added, however, that there was then complete calm in Funchal, even though the only patrols here were those of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office). At that time the posts of police corporal were much sought after by people of all classes, because those who held them were exempt by law from service in the National Guard.

On 14 June 1856 the civil governor reorganised the police once again. He left 3 process officers (*oficiais de diligências*) with the Municipal Administrator and placed the other 23 under the orders of an officer of the regular army (*tropa de linha*), who was given the title of police chief. Besides the chief there was a deputy chief. The force was at the disposal of the civil governor, but was bound to meet the requests of the Municipal Administrator.

The first military chief of police was Major Ascenso Elminio de Bettencourt, and the second Lieutenant Jaime Florindo Pereira. The latter was in the habit of calling the troop of 23 men under his command the municipal guard, although the police regulations did not authorise him to do so. In 1857 the police were housed in the building of the former Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), and their commander was the same Lieutenant Jaime F. Pereira.

Shortly afterwards the police were reorganised again, now with a director or chief, officers and soldiers, and the whole corps was once more placed under the Municipal Administrator. Under this new organisation there was no longer an officer of the regular army in the police, and command of the corps passed to the former deputy chief António José de Sá, who had already been director of the police before the reform of 1856. Although the policemen were called soldiers, it should be noted that these men did not answer to the military authorities.

On 3 August 1864 Pedro de Alcântara Góis was appointed process officer of the Municipal Administration and director of the police. He continued in the latter post after becoming a copying clerk in the same Administration on 2 October 1865. The law (*carta de lei*) of 2 July 1867 created the post of commissioner of the civil police of Funchal, but it was not until 1877 that Alcântara Góis was entrusted with it, in recognition of the services he had already rendered in directing the city’s public security corps.

The Funchal police were reorganised again on 21 December 1876 and 7 December 1894. The regulations of the latter date laid down that the Municipal Administrator should also become Police Commissioner as soon as that post fell vacant. The same regulations provided for 2 chiefs, 1 clerk (*escrivão*), 4 corporals and 50 guards, divided between 2 stations, each commanded by a chief.

The law of 12 June 1901 restored the posts of Police Commissioner in districts with a special organisation. The decree of 27 April 1918, which we suppose was never put into effect in Funchal, placed at the head of each district a general commissioner with oversight of all police services. As for the establishment of the rest of the commissariat’s staff, it is still today constituted as laid down in the regulations of 7 December 1894, and the division of the civil police corps into two stations also remains (1921).

Although some progress has been made since 1834 towards establishing public security in Funchal, there is no doubt that our city is still very far from being regarded as properly policed. If the grave outrages that disgraced the streets of Funchal in more or less distant times are no longer committed, countless irregularities and excesses are, and the police, few in number and almost always negligent, cannot or will not repress them (1921).

It was supposed that bringing a detachment of the Republican Guard (see that entry) to Madeira would be of great advantage. However, the constant conflicts provoked by men of that guard and the many abuses of power they committed showed that this was not the way to establish order and security on this island. After being kept away from police duties in the city for some time, the Republican Guard, which had come here in 1919, was finally ordered to leave the island, departing for Lisbon on the April and May 1922 sailings of the steamer *San Miguel*.

To establish in Funchal the order and discipline that ought to exist in every civilised land, it is essential to enlarge the district’s civil police force, as was said at the session of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of 22 December 1921, and to admit to it only robust, intelligent individuals of good conduct. A large and populous city such as ours cannot be policed with 50 men, some of them almost unfit for service, above all in an age of disrespect and social decay such as the one we are living through (1921).
Since 18 November 1934 the various police services have been housed in their own building in Rua da Carreira (‘track’).
See Comissário da Polícia.
Emigration Police

The police force for the suppression of clandestine emigration was created by decree of 11 May 1904. Its staff consisted of 1 commissioner, 1 secretary and 6 agents, paid by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) in accordance with the resolution passed by that body on 23 April of the same year.
Forest Police

It is the responsibility of the rural guards appointed and paid by the Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*) and of a special police corps of rural and forest police guards, created by the now-abolished Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) under the regulations of 8 March 1913. When at full strength, this corps is to have 3 chief guards, 5 mounted guards and 25 foot guards, under the direction of the district forestry officer.

The Timber Regulations (*Regimento das Madeiras*) of 1562 and other old enactments show that the protection and conservation of the forests was then entrusted to the judges and councillors (*vereadores*), to the bailiffs of the uplands and to the magistrates (*ouvidores*) of the island’s two jurisdictions. Each January the magistrates were required to hold inquiries to discover the authors of any damage done to the trees.

After the Agricultural Council was abolished, the rural and forest police service was provisionally placed under the Agricultural Station of the 9th Region, under article 33 of the decree of 3 April 1922 (1922).
Octopus (Octopus vulgaris)

A cephalopod mollusc found in rocky places along the coastal zone of this island. It is caught by chance on a line or in a fish trap (*covo*), and in summer it is gathered by hand by boys who dive for the purpose, taking care to ‘turn its hood inside out’ so as not to be troubled by the animal’s tentacles. The hood is the sac containing the respiratory siphon, so that once it has been turned inside out the octopus is rendered completely helpless. Like all coastal species, the octopus has fallen victim to the use of dynamite and potassium chlorate bombs, and it is therefore much less common today than in the past.

According to information given to us by Mr Adolfo César de Noronha, in November 1861 the French dispatch vessel *L’Alecton* found, between Madeira and Tenerife, a gigantic octopus 5 to 6 metres long, not counting its eight enormous arms, which proved to belong to the genus *Architeutis*. Among the rarest cephalopod species found in Madeira is also *Argonauta argo*, whose delicate shell, elegantly shaped like a volute, is used by the female to shelter her eggs. She lays them in this kind of floating cradle and settles on top as if to brood them, until the moment of hatching.
Rock dove (Columba livia)

A columbid bird found on the seaside cliffs and in the ravines throughout the island. It is sociable, forming small groups during the breeding season that settle on the inaccessible cliffs of the coast. Its nest is rough, and the clutch, of two slightly bluish-white eggs, may be laid twice a year.
It is also known as *pombo da rocha*, *pombinho* and *pombo doméstico* (domestic pigeon), the last name being used only when it is raised in the dovecotes that abound throughout the island.
Wood pigeon (Columba palumbus)

A columbid bird that lives in the mountains of Madeira. It builds its nests beneath the trees and raises two young in each brood. It is perhaps the rarest of the pigeon species that nest in Madeira, and because of its colour it is also known as *pombo branco* and *pombo claro*.
There is a variety distinguished by plumage and feet darker than in the typical form of the species.
Trocaz pigeon (Columba trocaz)

A bird of the family Columbidae that lives mainly in the interior valleys of Madeira. It is easy to recognise by the silvery ring on its neck and by the length of the middle toe. Its chief food consists of laurel berries, grasses, watercress, etc. It nests from February to June and is sometimes offered for sale in the Funchal market. Its meat is of excellent quality. Because of the colour of its plumage, the *pombo torcaz* is also known as *pombo escuro da serra* and *pombo preto*.

Ponta da Atalaia

In the locality of Atalaia (‘watchtower’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’), and roughly equidistant from Ponta da Oliveira and Ponta do Guindaste, lies the projection of coast or headland called Ponta da Atalaia. It overlooks a small landing place, Porto da Atalaia, of the same name.
Ponta da Cruz
See Ponta da Cruz.
Ponta da Oliveira
See Oliveira (Ponta da).
Ponta de Larano
At the locality of Larano, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), the projection of the coastline there bears the name Ponta de Larano (‘Larano point’).
Ponta de São Lourenço

It lies at the eastern tip of Madeira. According to Frutuoso, it received the name by which it is known because São Lourenço was the name of the ship carrying Captain João Gonçalves Zarco when the island was discovered.

‘The Ponta de São Lourenço,’ says Mousinho de Albuquerque, ‘which stretches for nearly 3 miles out to sea in a west-to-east direction and is very narrow, is made up of a succession of the remains of hills that appear to have been largely destroyed. As soon as it begins to narrow, shortly after the settlement of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), it generally shows the remains of strata dipping to the S. or SW., which on the northern side are abruptly and vertically cut away, the cut forming almost vertical cliffs above the sea.’

In summer the Ponta de São Lourenço is arid and dreary, because the heat of the sun soon scorches the vegetation covering the ground. In the first part of spring, however, the little valleys and hills are adorned in various spots with a luxuriant carpet of greenery, among which stand out several species found nowhere else on the island. The appearance of the place then changes greatly, and the life of nature lends it charms that cheer and delight the visitor.

The Ilhéu de Fora (‘outer islet’), where the lighthouse stands, is considered part of the Ponta (‘point’), although it is separated from the neighbouring land by a channel, or *boqueirão*, about 85 *braças* wide and 3 to 4 deep. To the west lie the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros (‘islet of the landing places’) and the Ilhéu do Agostinho, followed by the bay of Abra (‘bay’), where there is a quay (see that entry), and then the locality (*sítio*) of Piedade (‘pity’), with a beach of calcareous sand, the only one of its kind on the island. On a small mound beside the beach stands the little chapel of Our Lady of Pity (see that entry).

The whole of the Ponta is now entirely treeless, but near the beach just mentioned there are many calcareous bodies. If they are, as everything suggests, the petrified remains of woody plants, they show that in fairly remote ages there were once some woods at that spot. (See Calcareous bodies.)

At the locality of Piedade many land shells are found belonging to species of the upland region, few of which occur alive there. This rather curious fact has not yet received a satisfactory explanation.

Some livestock is raised in parts of the Ponta de São Lourenço, and the Ilhéu dos Desembarcadouros and the lands of Abra are renowned for the great quantity of fodder plants they produce. The best hay on the island comes from the Ponta de São Lourenço.
Springs are very scarce throughout the Ponta, but rain is abundant there from autumn to spring. The land could produce cereals if the livestock did not destroy the crops.
Of particular interest on this subject are the articles Agostinho (islet), Desembarcadoiro (islet), Lighthouses and Calcareous bodies of Piedade.
Ponta Delgada (parish)

(Parish of). It is not easy to establish the true origin of the name of this parish (*freguesia*). A learned person who lived there for some years and carried out serious research informs us that the name comes from Antónia Delgada, widow of Captain António Gonçalves de Castro, who died on 8 October 1606. Against this assertion we must set the existence of several royal decrees of the 16th century, the oldest dating from 1552, entered in the registers of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), which refer directly to the parish of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’). Gaspar Frutuoso, too, gives it the name Ponta Delgada in 1590, saying that it is ‘so called because there is a very dangerous passage there, which is crossed on top of two poles laid from one cliff to the other, and the sea lies so far below that it is lost to sight’. Nor, certainly, is it a very satisfactory explanation that a narrow and dangerous passage overhanging the sea should be called Ponta Delgada.

In the earliest days of colonisation this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) was called the Lord Jesus (*Senhor Jesus*), after the chapel of that dedication which stood there, and it was still known by that name after the parish was created. There is no doubt, however, that from the middle of the 16th century the name Ponta Delgada came into general use, and it was by this name that the place later became known.

Manuel Afonso de Sanha was one of the earliest settlers of this island, and in 1469 he obtained extensive lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), stretching from Ponta Delgada to the Ribeira das Vacas (‘cows’ stream’). He founded the chapel of Senhor Bom Jesus (Lord Good Jesus), which became the centre of a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*); this estate formed the original nucleus of inhabitants who made up the future parish.

The parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada must have been created towards the end of the second quarter of the 16th century, at least as an autonomous curacy (*curato*), and it is one of the oldest on the north coast of this island. Its seat was the chapel of Senhor Bom Jesus, the year of whose construction is unknown. It cannot, however, be much later than the first years of the 16th century, since its founder is recorded as having died in 1507. The chapel underwent some repairs and alterations in 1636 and was considerably enlarged around 1700. At the beginning of the 19th century it was repaired again, becoming one of the finest churches of the diocese; the chancel, the chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento (Most Holy Sacrament) and the sacristy deserve special mention. On 12 July 1908 this church was completely destroyed by a violent fire, which reduced it to a heap of rubble. Thanks chiefly to the diligent efforts and boundless dedication of the parish priest of the time, Father Casimiro Augusto de Freitas e Abreu, the church was rebuilt in 1910, and it was solemnly consecrated in 1919.

On the night of 30 December 1847 a major theft of a large number of silver objects was committed in this church, causing a great sensation throughout the island. The thieves were discovered, and most of the stolen objects were returned.

The curacy of Ponta Delgada, perhaps dependent on the parish of Machico, was only definitively raised to a parish around 1577. Its first vicar was Father António Lopes, who was followed in the parochial office by Fathers Belchior de Insola, Rodrigo Afonso, Aleixo, Gil, etc. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 3 February 1552 added 2,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year to the stipend of the curate, which was then 6,000 *réis* a year and 1 mark of silver (*marco de prata*, c. 230 g of silver). The vicar’s salary was raised by royal decree of 28 February 1577 to 20,000 *réis* a year, and later to 25,000 *réis* by the royal decree of 2 June 1581. The royal decree of 12 December 1588 then fixed the same salary at 16,000 *réis* a year, plus one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine.

The area of this parish comprised the land that constitutes it at present and also the present parish of Boaventura (‘good fortune’). By royal decree of 4 February 1733 a curacy was created, with its seat in the chapel of Santa Quitéria (St Quiteria) in the said parish of Boaventura, as may be seen in greater detail in the article we devote to it on p. 154 of the 1st volume of this work.

The chapel of Senhor Bom Jesus was the centre of an ancient pilgrimage, which is still today one of the best attended on the whole island. It is recorded as already taking place in 1577, which makes it the oldest pilgrimage festival held here in Madeira. The pilgrimages of the Lord Jesus of Ponta Delgada, of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*) and of the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*) at Machico are the oldest, the best attended and the most characteristic of this diocese.

This parish has the Chapel of the Magi (*Reis Magos*), which belonged to the house of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). There was formerly a chapel of Santo António at the locality of Pico (‘peak’), and another at the locality of Ladrilhos (‘tiles’); we shall deal with these elsewhere in this work.

António de Carvalhal was a former resident of this parish and died here on 15 July 1598. Of him Gaspar Frutuoso says: ‘a man as chivalrous as he was personally valiant, noble and magnificent by his station and great virtue, through which, by his magnificence, he has acquired such fame and won such renown in the hearts of men that they obey him for it; and should it be necessary to raise a cry, he will gather five hundred men from the northern side to his service, for any feat of war, as has already happened to him, or for any other purpose; and not without reason, for his house is a hospital and shelter for every poor person, a lodging for travellers and, in short, a refuge for the needy. Thus he spends all his estate (and he owns a great deal on this side) on these works, so that in his house thirty *moios* of wheat are consumed each year, besides many others that he lends, and with it he succours those in need, all of which he gathers from his own farming’. The historian of the islands then goes on to narrate in detail many feats and episodes of strength and valour performed by António de Carvalhal, as may be read on pp. 101 and 102 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).

The parish of Ponta Delgada was once called the ‘court of the north’, because it contained many houses of old and noble families, who lived there or spent a considerable part of the year there. Several entailed estates had their seat in the parish. Manuel Afonso de Sanha founded the entails of Ribeiro do Pêso and Ribeira do Inferno (‘hell’s stream’).

The idea of transferring to this parish the seat of the municipality (*concelho*) and judicial district (*comarca*), both of which are based in São Vicente, has been put forward more than once. Several judges have already represented to the central government the necessity and advantages of this change.

The principal crops are the vine and sugar cane, and there are two mills for making spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine). The main levada (irrigation channel) serving the irrigation of this parish is the one known as the Levada Grande (‘big’), which has its source in the Ribeira dos Moinhos (‘mills’) and crosses part of the parish of Boaventura.

The parish has two state primary schools, one for each sex, and a telegraph office opened in October 1905. It is also the seat of a medical district, which also includes the parish of Boaventura (1921).

Traffic through its Porto is relatively considerable, serving this parish and those of Boaventura and Arco de São Jorge. It is the terminus of the voyages that the coastal steamers, setting out from Funchal, make alternately by the east and by the west to the north of the island.
In the hills of this parish lies the enchanting locality called Topo (‘top’), from which broad and striking horizons open out.
Natives of this parish include the Viscount of Gonçalves de Freitas and Councillors António Gonçalves de Freitas and Francisco António de Abreu (see those entries).
Ponta Delgada (point and landing places)

In this parish (*freguesia*) there is a projection of the coastline called Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’). In its immediate vicinity lie a small landing place and a narrow beach, which serve this parish and those of Boaventura (‘good fortune’) and Arco de São Jorge (‘arc of São Jorge’). Around 1908 a short ramp was built there, giving access to the small beach, to make it easier to transport goods. There is also a short beach at the locality called Passo da Areia (‘sand pass’).
