Ponta do Pargo (lighthouse)

On the heights of the projection of the coastline known as Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’), at the place called Vigia (‘lookout’), stands the lighthouse building. Its construction had long been demanded, but it became a concrete reality only in 1922, when that coast began to be lit. We have read somewhere that this lighthouse ‘emits three successive flashes of white light with a power of 5,500 carcels, each of 0.5 of a second, at intervals of 3.5 seconds’.
Ponta do Pargo (parish)

This is the parish (*freguesia*) at the western extremity of the island’s south coast. It stands high on cliffs overlooking the sea and partly forms a picturesque plain, without any great unevenness of terrain except in the mountainous region that bounds it, chiefly to the north.

Gaspar Frutuoso states the origin of its name very clearly: ‘From Calheta (‘small cove’) the captain went on down to the last point above the sea, beyond which it seems there is no more land; and while he was there, the men from Tristão’s boat and from Álvaro Afonso’s boat brought him a fish that looked like a *pargo* [sea bream], of wondrous size, and the largest they had seen up to that time; on account of which fish that Point was given the name of Pargo. From this Ponta do Pargo the land turns northwards to another point, which some say lies two, others three, *léguas* from this one…’

Beyond Ponta do Pargo, continuing northwards, lies Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’), which, as is well known, formed one of the boundaries dividing the two captaincies of Funchal and Machico, the other boundary being Ponta da Oliveira (‘olive-tree point’).

The lands that now make up the parish of Ponta do Pargo originally belonged to the parish of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’), and were separated from it when Ponta do Pargo was constituted as an independent parish. The exact year of its creation is not known, but it must have been before 1560, since the royal decree (*alvará régio*) of 4 March of that year added one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter (*quarto*) of wine to the stipend (*côngrua*) of the parish priest, which was then 11,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year. The royal decree of 1 March 1577 set the parish priest’s annual salary at 20,000 *réis*, and that of 9 June 1581 raised it to 25,000 *réis*, likewise a year.

It was the chapel of St Peter (*São Pedro*), about whose founder and year of construction we have no information, that served as the seat of the new parish. It underwent enlargements and rebuildings in years we cannot specify. Its reconstruction was ordered by a warrant of the Treasury Council (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 20 July 1620, the works being estimated at 2,231,606 *réis*; it is not known whether the rebuilding was carried out immediately, which did not always happen. In 1851 major repairs were made to this church, at a cost of about 1,700,000 *réis*. We are informed that the parish church, through its successive constructions and reconstructions, has occupied three different places, though always within the same locality of Salão (‘hall’). It stood first at the spot called Pé do Pico (‘foot of the peak’), then at Achada da Igreja (‘church plateau’), and finally where it stands today.

Pedro de Couto Cardoso, André Nogueira and Duarte Mascarenhas Jaques were the first priests to exercise parish duties in this parish. A curacy (*curato*) was created here at the end of the 18th century.
This parish has the chapels of Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*) and Our Lady of the Good Death (*Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte*), which we have mentioned elsewhere.

It has two official primary schools: one for boys, established in 1850, and one for girls, established in 1910. It is only right to recall here the services rendered to this parish, and to other neighbouring parishes too, by the private teacher Dona Maria Amélia de Sousa. Over a period of roughly seventy years she gave primary instruction to many people of both sexes, with great skill and the utmost dedication, and her name deserves to live on in the memory of the children of this parish.
Three entailed houses had their seat in this parish; their last representatives were João Alves Espínola e Freitas, Francisco Freire de França e Almeida and Manuel de Ponte de Gouveia.

Cattle fattening is an important industry, as is the production of milk for butter-making. The crops are the same as in the other parishes, except for sugar cane. Special mention is due to the Sercial (white grape variety) wine produced in this area, which has always been regarded as of superior quality.

Farming here is served by the levadas (irrigation channels) of Moinhos, Cabo, Lombada da Velha, Ribeira da Vaca, Serrado, Serra, Ribeiro Velho, Lombadinha, Amparo and Lombo, as well as the Levada do Rabaçal, which also waters part of this parish. The coasts of Ponta do Pargo and Achadas da Cruz (‘plateaus of the cross’) were extremely dangerous waters for shipping. A lighthouse was therefore needed in the first of these parishes, since it forms the most prominent point of that coastline and lies at a height from which the lantern’s light could easily be cast several miles out to sea. Some years ago the building to house the lighthouse was constructed on the initiative of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), which paid all the construction costs, and the lighthouse came into operation on 5 June 1922. The parish also has a post and telegraph office and a semaphore station.

This parish belonged to the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) from the time that municipality was set up, in 1835, until 1849, when it was abolished; the parish then became part of the municipality of Calheta. When the municipality of Porto Moniz was restored in 1855, the parish of Ponta do Pargo was again incorporated into it. The law of 26 June 1871 detached it from the municipality of Porto Moniz and returned it to the municipality of Calheta, to which it belongs today. Principal localities: Cabo, Lombada Velha, Ribeira das Vacas, Serrado, Salão, Corujeira de Dentro, Corujeira de Fora, Lombadinha, Amparo and Lombo. According to the 1911 census, the population of the parish is 2,546 inhabitants.
Ponta do Pargo (point)

The westernmost point of Madeira’s coastline is formed by a rugged projection called Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’). This projection of the coast and its immediate surroundings make up a considerable part of that parish (*freguesia*), and it is there that the lighthouse referred to above stands.
Ponta do Sol (parish)

The author of the *Saudades*, summarising the first exploration carried out by the discoverers along the south coast of this island, says that João Gonçalves Zarco, setting out in the boats at Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), ‘came to a point which lies a league below, and juts far out into the sea; and, because on the cliff above the point one can make out from afar, and see clearly, a round vein in the rock itself with rays that look like the sun, the captain named it Ponta do Sol…’ Another passage of the same work reads: ‘…Ponta do Sol is so called because it has a point to the west of the town which has the appearance… where the Sun also strikes first, before it reaches the town, when it rises’. Such is the explanation the chronicler offers for the origin of the name of this place. It does indeed seem plausible, since there are no weighty reasons that entirely contradict it. We do not know whether other places with the same name, such as a locality on the island of Santo Antão, Cape Verde, derived their names from circumstances similar to those recorded by Dr Gaspar Frutuoso.

João Agostinho de Freitas, an intelligent and patient researcher into the affairs of his native corner of the island, does not depart significantly from Frutuoso’s opinion. He says that the name ‘derived from an arm or reef (*restinga*) of living rock which, because it advances out into the sea, is called a point, and from a projection with concentric veins or cracks, in the form of a halo, as the Sun is customarily depicted, which existed on the face of the rock of the Passo (‘pass’) that stands directly above the Fojo (‘pit’), beside the said point’. And he adds: ‘this rock lies to the south-east of the town and not to the west, as is stated, perhaps through a copyist’s error, in Dr Frutuoso’s manuscript, which is in the library of the Council of Funchal’.

The colonisation of Ponta do Sol began around 1440. One of its earliest settlers was Rodrigues Enes, the Lame, who obtained extensive lands there and established a large settled estate (*fazenda povoada*), which was the origin and original nucleus of the future parish (*freguesia*). It is said somewhere that the lands Rodrigo Enes began to clear, which had been granted to him as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), lay to the west of the stream and stretched from the edge of the ocean up to Arrebentão, near the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’).

It is conjectured that he settled in this place around 1450. The year of his death is not known, but some of the provisions of his will are known. They were made on 8 April 1486, in this locality, before the Funchal notary João Tavira, and among them is the following: ‘he orders that from the income of his disposable third (*terça*) of the estate a chantry (capela) be made for him in the church of Ponta do Sol, on the right-hand side facing the sea, and it shall be made like that of Clara Esteves, which is in the church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major) in Funchal, and it shall be dedicated to the Holy Spirit, and an image of the said Lord shall be placed in it, together with a silk vestment and a silver chalice of one mark’. According to a distinguished researcher who lived for many years in the parish of Ponta do Sol and died there, the chapel known as the Capela do Coxo (the Lame Man’s Chapel) is that of Nossa Senhora do Patrocínio (Our Lady of the Patronage), and there, beside the altar and beneath the wooden floorboards, lies the tomb of Rodrigo Enes. It would be worth checking whether the inscription on Rodrigo Enes’s tomb confirms these indications, for it is claimed that he expressly stipulated in his will that the epitaph should make special mention of his being the founder of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Ponta do Sol. It would indeed be fitting to uncover the tomb of the man whose name is so closely bound up with the earliest history of this locality, and to pay some other worthy tribute to his memory. It is the municipality of Ponta do Sol that has the inescapable duty of paying this well-deserved homage to the memory of the founder of this parish.
The date on which this parish was created is not known. We conjecture that it was in the third quarter of the 15th century. It is one of the oldest in this diocese.

The oldest document concerning this parish that we have found cited is the royal decree (*alvará*) of 28 August 1559, which set the parish priest’s stipend (*côngrua*) at 10,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year in cash, plus one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. The royal decrees of 23 July 1566, 13 March 1572 and 27 November 1598 raised the vicar’s annual salary to 13,300, 26,000 and 29,000 *réis* respectively, in addition to the *moio* of wheat and the *pipa* of wine.
This parish had a collegiate church (see Collegiate Churches) made up of four beneficiaries, as well as the curacy (*curato*), which was created by the royal decree of 26 August 1589.

The chapel of Our Lady of Light (*Nossa Senhora da Luz*), where the seat of the parish was established, was built before the parish was created; neither the year of its construction nor the name of its founder is known. It has undergone various alterations and seems to have been almost entirely rebuilt and enlarged in the first quarter of the 18th century, according to some *Apontamentos* (notes) that Dr Tomé Vieira Barreto recorded in one of the books of the parish church while he was parish priest there.

This church venerates the image of Our Lady of Light, its patron saint, whose particular cult was at one time very widespread in this and many other parishes. Friar Agostinho de Santa Maria, in volume X of his well-known work *Santuario Mariano*, devotes a chapter to the veneration then paid to that revered image. Father Miguel Francisco Velosa, vicar of this parish church, petitioned for and obtained from the Holy See a brief dated 30 July 1805, granting a plenary indulgence, on the occasion of the patronal feast, its novenas and the octave – that is, from 30 August to 15 September each year – to all persons who, duly prepared, visit the parish church of this parish.
This parish had many chapels, of which we shall give a brief account elsewhere in this work.

Thanks to its rapid and extensive development, the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol attracted a considerable number of people from mainland Portugal – the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) – and even from abroad. They obtained a great deal of land there as *sesmarias* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), and some of them founded important entailed houses that had their seat in this locality and have survived to our own day... Among these people we shall mention Rodrigo Enes Furtado, of whom we have already spoken above, a man of noble lineage who left numerous descendants in this parish; Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, whom we have already discussed (vol. I, p. 206, and vol. II, p. 278); Dom João Henriques, to whose family Father Leão Henriques belongs, and after whom a locality that belonged to him is still called Pomar de Dom João (‘Dom João’s orchard’); Pedro Delgado, who held a *sesmaria* at Lombo das Adegas (‘ridge of the wine cellars’); Rodrigo Anes Coelho, of the family of Rodrigo Enes Furtado, who seems to have had land at Lombo de São João (‘St John’s ridge’); Diogo Ferreira de Mesquita, who founded the Chapel of Livramento (Our Lady of Deliverance); and still others. Among the foreigners we may recall the names of João Esmeraldo, whom we have already discussed at some length; António de Lemes, of Flemish origin, whose descendants gave their name to the locality of Lemes; an individual with the surname Schomberg; and others.

Several entailed estates existed within the boundaries of this parish. Those worth mentioning are the entail of Espírito Santo and Vale da Bica, which we have already discussed in the article Lombada dos Esmeraldos; that of Fajã do Furtado, founded by a descendant of Rodrigo Enes, ‘o Coxo’; that of Lemes, founded by António Leme at the locality that bears his name; that of Anjos, with its seat in the Chapel of Anjos (Angels) and created by Martim Afonso; one founded by Diogo Ferreira Mesquita; and another by Ambrósio Berenguer in 1601.

Among the most distinguished natives of Ponta do Sol we shall mention Father Leão Henriques, Dr António da Luz Pita, Dr João Augusto Teixeira, Canon Feliciano João Teixeira and Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira, whom we shall discuss elsewhere.

It would be unjust not to recall here the name of João Agostinho de Freitas, a patient and distinguished researcher into the history of this parish, who left some valuable manuscripts. Under the title *Resumo da Hera Patriotica* he wrote a monograph on Ponta do Sol, which, through the efforts of one of the editors of this *Elucidário*, was published in nos 335 to 340 of the newspaper *Brado do Oeste*. He was born in 1827 and died in 1906. Nor do we wish to forget the name of Nuno de Freitas Pestana, who, as a licensed advocate (*advogado provisionista*, practising by licence without a law degree) and in the posts he held, displayed uncommon talent and learning.

One notable work in this parish is its landing quay, built by order of the Municipal Council in 1848. The following year, before the whole work had been finished, the head of the district, José Silvestre Ribeiro, reported the Council’s undertaking to the central government, highlighting the service it had rendered to this locality. There is no record of any municipal council having since ventured to carry out any other major improvement there.

Prince Luís, later King of Portugal, visited this parish on 25 October 1858 on his way to the picturesque resort of Rabaçal, returning to this town (*vila*) the following day. Both on his arrival and on his return from Rabaçal, he and his retinue lunched at the residence of the esteemed Ponta do Sol native Nuno de Freitas Pestana. He landed and embarked at Lugar de Baixo, because the rough sea did not allow him to do so at the town quay.

‘Ponta do Sol as a parish,’ says João Agostinho de Freitas, ‘extended over the whole territory from the Ribeira da Tabua, to the east, to the Ribeira da Madalena, to the west. Later – the precise date is not known, but it is supposed to have been around 1510 or some years later – when the parishes of Madalena and Canhas, to the west, and that of Tabua, to the east, were created, the territory of Ponta do Sol was reduced to a few kilometres of coast, that is, from the mouth of the Ribeira do Alto, the boundary with Canhas, to the mouth of the Ribeira da Caixa, the boundary with Tabua.’

The principal localities of this parish are: Vila, Ribeira da Ponta do Sol, Lombo das Terças, Lemes, Lombo das Adegas, Pomar de Dom João, Lombo de São João, Fregueses Novos, Ribeira da Lombada, Lombada, Entre Caminhos, Jangão and Lugar de Baixo. The 1920 census gives this parish 6,190 inhabitants.

The book *Na Madeira-Offerendas* by Dona Mariana Xavier da Silva, published in Lisbon in 1884, contains the narratives *O Rapazinho da Lombada*, *A Virgem das Dôres* and *Ponta do Sol*, which are of interest for the history and customs of this parish.
See the articles Isabel de Abreu, João Esmeraldo, Lombada dos Esmeraldos and Lugar de Baixo, as well as those devoted to the chapels and to the most distinguished natives of Ponta do Sol.
Ponta do Sol (headland, landing place and quay)

The stretch of coastline known by this name lies partly at the eastern end of the town (*vila*) of the same name. We have read somewhere that the name comes from the fact that, from this point, the sun can be seen all year round from the moment it rises until it sets below the horizon.

Close by lies the small landing place, facing the town and bounded in part by a short beach and by a small headland on which the quay stands, giving direct access to the centre of the town. Since the town is the seat of the municipality (*concelho*) and of the judicial district (*comarca*), and the landing place serves both it and other neighbouring settlements, this harbour handles a relatively large traffic in passengers and cargo, with frequent connections by coastal steamers to the city of Funchal and to some parishes on the west coast of Madeira. The quay, a work of some architectural pretension, was built by order of the Municipal Council of that municipality between 1848 and 1850. Several studies were made for extending the quay by making use of the reefs found at the site, and in 1880 a project and plan of works was drawn up, but the works were never carried out. The first name given to this quay was that of the Duke of Leuchtenberg, who was living in Madeira at the time of its construction.
Ponta do Sol (town and municipality)

In the early days of the colonisation of Madeira, Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) was one of the most active centres of agriculture, above all in the growing of sugar cane and the associated products of the sugar industry. Many grantees of land (*sesmeiros*) from the mainland settled here, a great number of Moorish and Black slaves worked the land, and many mills were built for making sugar. All of this contributed to the growth and prosperity of this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town). Frutuoso states that João Esmeraldo (see that entry) had some eighty slaves on his property at the Lombada (‘long ridge’) and that he came to produce twenty thousand *arrobas* of sugar a year, which seems to us an exaggeration.

As it grew in importance and population, and as it was the centre of other small settlements that gradually arose around it, it was natural that it should become a town (*vila*) and municipality with its own charter (foral), granting it the privileges and exemptions that the people of the time guarded so jealously. The government in Lisbon took this view, and in the relevant royal letter (*carta régia*) the monarch says: ‘we, of our own motion, without their requesting it, nor others in their names, see fit and do make the said *lugar* of Ponta do Sol a town...’ This document is dated 2 December 1501 and is recorded in volume 1 of the *Registo Geral da Camara do Funchal*, at fol. 67. According to the annotator of the *Saudades*, the copy held in the secretariat of the Ponta do Sol Municipal Council, which was taken from the register of the Funchal Council, contains various inaccuracies. The corresponding charter, which is shared with the municipalities of Funchal and Calheta (‘small cove’), is dated 6 August 1515 and is transcribed on p. 494 ff. of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).

The new municipality was carved out of that of Funchal, and its area and jurisdiction extended from the Ribeira da Ponta do Sol to Ponta do Tristão. The Lombada dos Esmeraldos (‘the Esmeraldos’ ridge’) belonged to the municipality of Funchal, although in ecclesiastical terms it depended on the parish church of Our Lady of Light (*Nossa Senhora da Luz*). Only in 1835, by a royal decree (*alvará*) of the prefect (*prefeito*) dated 24 January and registered in the Archive of the Funchal Council, was it incorporated into the municipality (*concelho*) of Ponta do Sol.

With the creation of the municipality of Calheta, in a year that cannot be determined precisely but was no later than 1502, the municipality of Ponta do Sol was reduced to half of the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name, to Canhas and Madalena (‘Magdalene’), which at that time were not yet independent parishes, and to the locality of Pinheiro (‘pine tree’), which now forms part of the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’).

The area of this municipality remained unchanged until 1835, when, with the creation and reorganisation of the municipalities, the municipality of Ponta do Sol was constituted with the parishes of Ponta do Sol, Madalena do Mar, Canhas, Tabua, Ribeira Brava and Serra de Água.

When the municipality of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) was created in 1914, the parishes of Tabua (‘bulrush’) and Serra de Água were detached from the municipality of Ponta do Sol and incorporated into the new municipality.

Tradition has it that when the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Ponta do Sol was raised to the rank of town, King Manuel I presented it with a weights standard and a seal bearing the arms of the Municipality. The arms consisted of a face, as the sun is customarily depicted, surrounded by the following legend: *Benedictus Dominus Deus Israel quia visitavit et fecit redemptionem* (Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed [his people]). The weights standard is of bronze and weighs 64 *arráteis*; engraved around it are the words: *Me madou fazere Dom Emânuel rei de Portugal Ano de 1499* (Dom Manuel, King of Portugal, had me made in the year 1499). An official document addressed to the central government in 1853 states that this standard is, of its kind, an archaeological piece of value.

The town of Ponta do Sol is the seat of the judicial district (*comarca*) of the same name, which covers the municipalities of Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol and Calheta. This judicial district, like those of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), was created by the decree of 12 November 1875. It was installed on 28 April 1876, its first judge and first public prosecutor being Dr Martinho da Rocha Guimarães Camões and Dr António Augusto Ribeiro de Campos, who took up their posts on the day of, and at the ceremony marking, the installation of the judicial district.
Ponta do Tristão

The headland lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), a short distance from Santa Maria Madalena (‘Magdalene’). On either side of it are some beaches of large boulders, which make very poor landing places.
Ponta do Tristão formed one of the boundary points dividing the two captaincies of Funchal and Machico, as we have already said elsewhere (1-244).

Both the headland and the neighbouring Ribeira do Tristão, which separates the parish of Porto Moniz from that of Achadas, were explored botanically only very recently. There the naturalist J. Gonçalves da Costa found *Beta vulgaris* var. *maritima*, *Ononis Costae*, *Carex pendula*, *Carex elata*, *Allium vineale*, *Polypodium drepanum*, etc. etc.
Headlands

The principal headlands are: São Lourenço, in the municipality (*concelho*) of Machico, which includes several secondary points, such as Furado, Abra, Dedais, Rosto, etc.; Queimada, in the same municipality; Santa Catarina, Guindaste, Atalaia and Oliveira, in the municipality of Santa Cruz; Cruz, in the municipality of Funchal; Água, in the municipality of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’); Sol, in the municipality of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’); Galé and Pargo, in the municipality of Calheta (‘small cove’); Tristão, in the municipality of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’); Delgada, in the municipality of São Vicente; and São Jorge, Santana and Cortado, in the municipality of Santana (see those entries).
The principal headlands of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) are: Incão, Frades, Branca, Cruz, Varadouros, Furado and Calheta (see Porto Santo).
In the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), the following deserve mention: Ponta da Agulha, on Bugio, and Boqueirão, Pedregal, Norte and Rocha Negra, on Deserta Grande (see the Desertas and Cabos).
Ponte Nova (street)

The present street of this name links the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’) with the Calçada da Incarnação, but the old street extended as far as Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), thus taking in part of the present Rua dos Netos. This part of the street was opened in 1833.

The works on the so-called Ponte Nova (New Bridge) over the Ribeira de Santa Luzia were contracted out for 890$00 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) at a session of the Municipal Council on 25 May 1768.
Pontes (Father Armando Augusto de)

He was born in Funchal on 18 May 1836 and died in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico on 3 November 1897. He studied at the lyceum (state secondary school) and the seminary of this city, and was ordained priest on 16 September 1860. He held ecclesiastical posts in various parishes of this diocese, especially in the parish of Machico, where he was parish priest for many years. He was a highly intelligent man of wide learning, and also an exemplary priest of impeccably austere character.

He contributed extensively to several periodicals, notably the former *Jornal Verdade*. He published the pamphlets *O Domingo, a Fé*, Funchal, 1895, 55 pp.; *Excursões na Madeira*, Funchal, 1891, 106 pp.; and *Um monumento Histórico*, Funchal, 1886, 27 pp.
Pontinha (locality, road, islets and mole)

The name Pontinha (‘little point’), given to the projection of the coastline that partly bounds our small harbour of refuge, has at times seemed strange. The spot was originally known as Ilhéus (islets), because two isolated rocks washed by the sea once stood there, and the name also covered the immediate surroundings of the locality (*sítio*). Even today the Rua dos Ilhéus, which lies nearby, recalls the original name.

The tiny islet that lay closer to the shore was joined to the land early in the third quarter of the 18th century by strong walls, which abutted the walls of a fortified redoubt that stood there. The other islet, which can still be clearly made out at this spot, was finally joined to the first islet and to the coast in 1889, on the completion of the great wall that forms the most important part of the Pontinha mole (breakwater).

The illustrious commentator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), though somewhat forcedly, offers this explanation of the name Pontinha given to that stretch of the coast: ‘Of these two islets, the one farther out to sea is still now (in 1873) isolated in the waters as before, and so keeps the name of Ilhéu; the other, joined long since to the shore of the island by strong walls, has therefore the name of Pontinha’.

This name, which has prevailed over time, is of quite ancient use and may go back to the mid-16th century. The soundest probabilities suggest that the colonisation of Madeira began around 1425. The historian of the islands, describing the first exploration carried out along the coast and referring in particular to the arrival of the first settlers at the locality later called Funchal, tells us that ‘as it was already late, they went to shelter at the Ilhéus, which lie at the end of it (the valley of Funchal)’. This is the earliest known reference to the Ilhéus da Pontinha (‘islets of the little point’). The locality and the neighbouring stretch of shore would from then on have been called Ilhéus, the name Pontinha later prevailing, as stated above.

In the vicinity of this locality, António Dantas founded in 1622 the chapel of Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*), with which several events of considerable interest to the history of Madeira are connected (see Penha de França). Also in the same vicinity, and taking its name from this chapel, a fortress was built in the second quarter of the 17th century. It was rebuilt in 1712 and served as quarters for detachments of English troops in 1801, when they occupied this island.

On the islet farther from the coast, the ‘Fortaleza de Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu’ was built in 1654. There, in 1682, a small chapel of the same dedication was erected, which had its own chaplain from 1692. In 1866 a tiny red-light lighthouse was installed there, commonly and ironically called ‘the ember of the Islet’ (*a braza do Ilhéu*); in 1931 it was replaced by a proper lighthouse. Until a few years ago a detachment of the Artillery Company quartered in the Fortress of São Tiago was permanently stationed at this stronghold, chiefly to return the ‘salutes’ of warships entering our harbour. A semaphore station also operated there.

The Pontinha islet, the one nearer the shore, was joined to the facing coast between 1757 and 1762 by solid walls, as already mentioned. It is conjectured that this work was carried out when the small Fort of St Joseph (*São José*), which once stood there, was built, or a little before. This link, together with the stairway cut at that time into the living rock, already formed a small landing quay, which was much used when the state of the sea did not allow landing on the beach.

Volume I of the Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*), published in 1907, cites many documents concerning the works that were to be carried out in the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*). It refers to the projects submitted by the engineer Francisco Tossi Colombina and to the works already begun under his direction, which aroused particular interest at the time and included some improvements at the Pontinha.

When one of the islets was joined to the shore around the middle of the 18th century, as already stated, a stairway cut into the cliff or a small landing quay would have been built. This was considerably improved in 1850. A quay on more advantageous lines was completed in 1878, and it received further notable improvements when the mole (breakwater) was built.

The works carried out there from the middle of the 18th century until 1878 did not make landings safe or convenient, and on several occasions makeshift wooden quays had to be built when pressing circumstances of the moment required it.

Around 1872 the construction of the pleasant ‘Estrada da Pontinha’ (‘little point road’) was planned. Especially since the completion of the works on the small harbour of refuge, this road has rendered the public the most valuable services, which will become greater still as the conditions of the harbour improve. Work did not begin at once and construction was slow; it was declared complete only in 1895, some years after the Pontinha mole. The road contributed greatly to the embellishment of the bay (*baía*), and also eased communications between the busiest part of the city and the western districts of Funchal. On top of the sheer escarpment overlooking this road stand some of the finest *quintas* in Madeira, which enjoy an enviable position with views of the harbour and of the whole amphitheatre of Funchal.

The Caminho da Pontinha (‘little point road’) runs from the western end of the Cais da Entrada da Cidade (City Entrance Quay) to the mole, and at the session of 6 July 1922 it was given the name Rua Sacadura Cabral (see Aviation).

The Caminho da Pontinha has also been called Avenida do Dr. José António de Almada and Avenida de Francisco Ferrer, making it one of the public thoroughfares most often renamed by our municipal councils. It was to have been opened at the beginning of the 19th century, but was built only much later, between 1873 and 1875, when the late engineer Júlio Augusto Leiria was director of Public Works.
The articles Cais, Ilhéu and Molhe da Pontinha contain further details relevant to this subject, and we refer the reader to them.
Population
In the article Settlement and Colonisation we give a brief account of how the population developed here in Madeira when the arduous work of the first colonisation of the island began.
The old chronicles have left us very little information about this settlement, particularly as regards the number, social position, personal qualities and places of origin of the first colonists.

It is known only vaguely that they included individuals of noble descent, others from the common classes, artisans and tillers of the soil, and also some criminals serving their sentences in prison. Gaspar Frutuoso tells us that João Gonçalves Zarco ‘had refused to bring those guilty on account of the faith, or of treason, or for theft’.

The approximate number of these individuals is not known, nor is the proportion in which the various social strata made up these first bands of settlers. It is conjectured, with good reason, that they were not few, and that their number grew soon and rapidly with the frequent arrival of other colonists and, above all, with the great legion of Moorish and black slaves, which soon became a sizeable multitude. This was demanded by the extensive and gruelling work of clearing the virgin land, the energetic cultivators being spurred on by the exuberant fertility of the soil and the exceptionally mild climate.

It was in the second half of the 15th century that settlement expanded more widely, with settlers coming from mainland Portugal, countless African slaves and also many foreigners from various European countries. Some of these came from old families and sought in this new promised land what their own homeland could not give them.

It would be of considerable interest to compile statistics of the population of this archipelago from the earliest days of its colonisation to the present, but we have little material for a complete work of this kind, especially for the 15th century and the first half of the 16th. From the middle of the 16th century onwards, however, compiling such statistics would not be impossible, with results very close to the truth, by drawing on the archives of the parish churches. In all or almost all of them, baptisms, marriages and deaths have been regularly recorded since the third quarter of that century. Such a study is not very difficult for each parish (*freguesia*), and it would then be easy to carry it out for the whole archipelago. Epidemics and other public calamities aside, a uniform proportion was generally maintained in those periods between the number of inhabitants of a given locality and the number of births and deaths occurring there, so that regular population statistics could be compiled.
Zurara relates that ‘at the time of writing’ there were ‘C L householders’ in Madeira, ‘besides other people who were there, such as merchants, and unmarried men and women, and youths’.

As for Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), the annotator of the *Saudades* states that in 1529 the island had more than 800 inhabitants, and Frutuoso asserts that in 1590 there were some 400 households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths') there, which would mean about 1600 inhabitants. On this statement of Frutuoso’s, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says: ‘although this seems an exaggeration, since the *Annais da Ilha do Porto Santo* record that in 1850 the population was 1799 persons, that is, some 450 households, and the census of 1864 that there were 363 households with 1425 inhabitants, we believe Frutuoso’s statement to be accurate; the island of Porto Santo made progress only in the first hundred and fifty years after its discovery; afterwards the scarcity of its natural means of production, the frequent raids of corsairs, and the neglect in which it was left by the donataries, by its wealthiest inhabitants and even by governments, the Marquis of Pombal excepted, condemned it to the state of decline in which it has lain until now.’

The overpopulation now observed in Madeira is not a phenomenon peculiar to our own day. At various times this excess of population has occurred and, combined with other serious circumstances of the moment, it has brought about fearful crises, forcing people to resort to emigration. It would be useful and interesting to produce a detailed study of the causes of these crises, the means adopted to combat them and the beneficial effects that resulted. There can be no doubt that these voluntary expatriations, despite the drawbacks that accompany them, generally have beneficial consequences. Special mention should be made of the large-scale emigration to British Guiana in the middle of the 19th century, which brought this island considerable elements of prosperity. See Emigration.

Of particular interest is the information supplied to us by the Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*) for the year 1762. It tells us that the then governor and captain-general José Correia de Sá, in a communication to the government in Lisbon on 23 July of that year, reported ‘the departure for Lisbon of various individuals who, owing to the excess of population, were unable to find means of subsistence’.

It is the simple mention of a fact that, over time and with greater or lesser intensity, has been recurring here in Madeira. The problem grows worse day by day and is taking on the most alarming proportions. It has prompted a well-directed campaign in the local press, which ought to command the closest attention of ‘governors and governed’ alike.

Popular (O)

It began publication on 19 February 1869 and ceased on 12 September of the same year, after 29 issues. Another periodical of the same title was published from 1874 to 1877, its first issue appearing on 16 March 1874.
City gates

Like all old cities, Funchal had its gates, which were closed at hours fixed in advance by the authorities and opened only when reveille sounded. In some cities these gates were defended by fortifications intended to keep out any enemy attackers. We do not know whether the gates of this city, apart from those next to the forts, had any elements of military defence.

At the beginning of the 19th century our city had sixteen gates, and in 1836 only eleven remained. Some were demolished in the period from 1836 to 1839, and none of them survives today apart from the Alfândega gate and perhaps an opening that still exists in the city’s curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city), near the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater). The gates still standing in 1836 are given in the following list, which is more complete than the one we published on p. 322 of volume I of this work:

The two gates between the Fort of São Tiago and the so-called New Fort (*Forte Novo*) and the Pelourinho (‘pillory’), the eastern one being the gate we have already mentioned; the Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*) gate, between the New Fort and the Pelourinho at the mouth of Rua da Boa Viagem, which was demolished in 1836 when work began on the Praça Académica; the Varadouros (‘slipways’) gate, demolished in 1911, which replaced the one taken down when the arch and chapel of the same name were built there (see p. 467 of volume II), and which continued to be one of the city gates; the gate at the southern end of Rua do Sabão, demolished in 1836; the gate of the Customs House fort (*Forte da Alfândega*); the Saúde gate, between the nursing home (*Casa da Saúde*) (see City Entrance) and the Fort of St Lawrence, pulled down in 1839 when the Entrada da Cidade (‘entrance to the city’), today Avenida João Gonçalves Zarco, was built; the São Lázaro gate, at the top of Rua dos Aranhas, which also bore this name, demolished in 1904; the St Paul gate, next to the chapel of the same name, demolished in 1839; the Carreira (‘track’) gate, below the British cemetery, which was built in 1865;
The Pico (‘peak’) gate, which stood between the chapel of St Paul and Rua da Bela Vista, likewise demolished in 1865.
Of the other five gates that existed at the beginning of the 19th century, there is no reliable information about where they stood.

A book in the archive of the Municipal Council shows that in 1597 there were the following gates on the seaward side: that of Rua do Peixe, that of the Varadouros, that of Rua do Sabão and that of the Fortress. We cannot establish exactly where the first of these gates stood, but there are strong reasons to believe that it lay near the present Praça de São Pedro and was the same gate that Frutuoso places near the butchers’ stalls.

The regulations (*regimento*) for the fortification works issued by King Sebastian refer to the opening of two gates on the seaward side, between the fortress and the church of Our Lady of Calhau. In ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), Frutuoso mentions three gates in the wall along the Ribeira de João Gomes, and also three others on the south side: one beside the said church of Our Lady of Calhau, another further towards the middle of the city, near the butchers’ stalls, and the third, ‘the most important, at the Varadouros’.
See Curtain wall and Entrada da Cidade.
Porto da Cruz (parish)

Travelling from the south of this island towards the north and rounding the Ponta de São Lourenço, we come upon the first of the parishes (*freguesia*) that make up that rugged coast. This is Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’). It takes its name from the cross that the first explorers of this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) raised at the small cove that serves it as a landing place.

The first lands brought under cultivation on the north coast were those of Porto da Cruz and Faial. It may be supposed that some of the closest descendants of the first donatary, Tristão Vaz Teixeira, held lands by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in this parish and devoted themselves to farming here. The early settlers included António de Abreu, Fernão Nunes, Simão Teixeira, Baltasar da Mata, Francisco Velosa, João Dias, António Teixeira de Mendonça and António Leal, almost all of noble descent.

The royal decree (alvará régio) of 26 September 1577 empowered the diocesan prelate, Dom Jerónimo Barreto, to erect this new parish, and the same instrument granted the parish priest a stipend (*côngrua*) of 20,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year. The royal decree of 15 November 1591 then fixed this salary at 19,000 *réis* in cash, one and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat.

It is probable that before the parish was created, as happened in almost all the parishes of this island, there was some chapel with its own chaplain who performed the ecclesiastical duties there. This may well have taken place in the very chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), where the seat of the parish was established, perhaps under the canonical authority of the parish priest of Faial. We have already given a brief account of this chapel on page 465 of volume II.

It seems that the original patron of the parish was Nossa Senhora da Piedade, the dedication of the small church that first served as the parish church. According to the parish archive, the mystery of the True Cross (*Vera Cruz*) was later given to it as its patron saint. In the deed of grant of the land for the new church, the church is called Nossa Senhora da Glória, and finally, once the new church had been built, it was consecrated to Nossa Senhora de Guadalupe, a patron saint that endured and which it still keeps today.

The seat of the parish remained in the chapel of Piedade (‘pity’) for only a few years. In 1580 Dona Guiomar Lomelino, who lived in this parish (*freguesia*), donated to the parish priest Nicolau de Abreu the land needed to build the new church, presbytery and adjoining glebe (*passal*). We do not know when the building of the church was finished or when services began to be held in it. It underwent various alterations over time, and around 1637 and 1688 major repairs were carried out. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 30 October 1748 authorised the payment of 2,450,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for the works on a new church, which turned out to be too small for the population of the parish. The chapel of the Santíssimo Sacramento (Most Holy Sacrament) was built in 1763 on the orders of Manuel Caldeira da Silva, as administrator of the entailed estate (*vínculo*) founded by Marcelino de Moura and in fulfilment of a vow the latter had made; this chapel belonged to the same entailed estate. Around 1820 the building of a new parish church was planned, estimated at twenty-six *contos* (one million réis) de réis, but the attempt never went beyond a mere project.

A papal brief of 21 April 1795 grants a plenary indulgence to those who visit this church, and another brief, of 15 August 1781, grants the favour of a special privilege to the altar of the Lord Jesus (*Senhor Jesus*) on every Monday.

The first vicar was Father Nicolau de Oliveira, who was in charge of this parish for more than forty years. He was followed by Fathers Rui Gomes de Ornelas, Manuel Fernandes Braga, Francisco Fernandes, Pedro Ferreira, Inácio Álvaro de Carvalho, Cristóvão Moniz de Meneses, etc.

In some interesting articles on this parish published in the *Correio da Madeira* (‘Madeira Courier’), we find the following lines on the creation of the curacy (*curato*): ‘As parish activity kept growing after 1700, at the request of Father Caetano Alberto de Araújo and by royal decree of Maria I dated 31 July 1797, the curacy of this parish was created, with the obligation of residence near the chapel of São João Nepomuceno (St John of Nepomuk), at Lombo dos Leais (‘the Leals’ ridge’), the curate receiving an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine. This curacy was the cause of disputes between the vicar and the owners of the chapel, which was placed under interdict for some time for that reason’.

Volume I of the Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*) cites several documents showing that in 1818 various parishioners of this parish, and especially the inhabitants of the locality of Folhadal (‘folhado grove’), asked the government in Lisbon to create a curacy based at the chapel of São João Nepomuceno or, perhaps rather, to move the seat to that chapel, which would then become the parish church. Bishop Dom Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde reported unfavourably on the petition.

Several entails (*instituições vinculares*) had their seat in this locality, and we give a brief account of some of them. The entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of the Baptistas was founded at the end of the 15th century by the Genoese Micer Baptista; its last representative was João Bettencourt Baptista, who died a few years ago (1921). The entailed estate (*morgadio*) of Referta (‘refuge’) was established by Manuel Telo Moniz de Meneses, who died in 1713; its last administrator was Manuel Raimundo Telo Moniz Torresão, and its representative today is his granddaughter Dona Cristina de Campos Soares (1921). There was also the entail founded by Father Cristóvão Moniz de Meneses, whose last representative was the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António Caetano de Aragão; and the entailed estates founded by Captain Brás Moniz Telo de Meneses and by Captain Inácio de Carvalho Favila.

The old and distinguished Leal family lived in this parish (*freguesia*). It formed one of the wealthiest houses in the north of the island, and its representative today is Dr Alfredo de Freitas Leal (1921). A member of this family was Commander Valentim de Freitas Leal, who among other offices held that of civil governor of this district, and who declined the title of Viscount of Porto da Cruz, a title that one of his great-grandsons has used for some years. He was born in 1790 and died in 1879.

Commander Valentim’s son was Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) João Baptista de Freitas Leal, whom we have already discussed in this volume. The first of this distinguished lineage recorded as having settled in this parish was António Leal, who died in 1582. His descendant in the fifth generation, João José Nepomuceno de Freitas Leal, founded the chapel of Lombo dos Leais.
A distinguished son of Porto da Cruz was Father Dr Caetano Alberto Soares, to whom we shall devote a separate article at the appropriate place in this work.

The main localities are Casas Próximas, Serrado, Fajã e Palmeira, Ribeira Tem-te-não-caias, Lombo dos Leais, Cruz da Guarda, Maiata, Larano, Achada, Achadinha, Referta, Massapês and Terra do Batista. From Portela (‘mountain pass’) and from Lombo dos Leais there are vast and striking views over the country between this parish and the parish of Faial. Overlooking the sea, at a height of nearly 600 metres, rises the well-known cliff of Penha de Águia, from whose heights broad and beautiful horizons also open out.

This parish is the seat of a medical district, and it has two schools, one for each sex, and a telegraph office created by the decree of 17 August 1888. According to the last published census it has 4,284 inhabitants (1921).

Porto da Cruz belonged to the captaincy of Machico from its creation, and in 1835 it became part of the municipality (*concelho*) of Santana (‘St Anne’). It was separated from that municipality by the decree of 19 October 1852 and annexed to the municipality of Machico, to which it still belongs.
Porto da Cruz (islet, harbour and stream)

Close to the coast of this parish (*freguesia*) lies an islet facing a small harbour, whose landing place is known by the name of Furna (‘cave’). The islet and the harbour both bear the name Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), as does the stream that flows into the sea some distance from this spot.

Harbour of Funchal

Funchal Bay is the widest bay in the archipelago. It is bounded by Ponta do Garajau (‘tern point’) to the east and Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’) to the west. Between these two points it forms a fairly regular curve and inlet, and it is sheltered from winds from every quarter except those blowing from SSE to SSW by way of S. Its breadth makes it a vast anchorage, but communication with the shore can be established with relative ease only at the most accessible points of the coastline. These stretch from the Ilhéu da Pontinha (‘islet of the little point’) in the west to the vicinity of the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) in the east, some two thousand metres apart. All the traffic and activity of the port takes place within these limits. The port is bounded by a beach of rounded pebbles, with deep water and free of reefs or shoals that might hinder access. According to General A. P. de Azevedo’s map of Madeira, high water, or the establishment of the port (time of high water at full and new moon), is at 12 h 48 min, with a tidal rise of 2.28 m; the engineer Mariano F. Faria e Maia, however, states that the tidal range reaches 2.80 m. Regarding the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*) and the tides of the Madeiran coast, the distinguished engineer Adolfo Loureiro says ‘that little is known about lunar influences on the phenomenon of spring and neap tides, or about their propagation, speed and direction, or the height and force of the waves according to the direction of the wind, their impetus, duration, etc. The temperature of the waters and its distribution at the surface, and their periodic movements and conditions, which follow a law that seemed constant, ought to become the subject of very interesting oceanographic studies, which unfortunately have never been carried out’.
The ports of Lisbon and Funchal lie 520 miles apart. Funchal is approximately 350 miles from Cape Cantin (see that entry), 1220 from Plymouth, 1330 from Southampton and 1430 from Liverpool.

It is of real interest and recognised usefulness to give here a detailed account of the shipping movements of the harbour of Funchal in recent years. This serves not only to gauge the commercial and tourist development that has taken place here, but also to provide material for study of the improvements that may perhaps still need to be made in the near future within the limits of our harbour of refuge.
The article Movimento do Porto (II-409) gives information on these movements for the period from 1901 to 1943, which complements what we have set out here.

It should be noted that the marked decline in shipping at the harbour of Funchal from 1914 onwards was due to the great European conflagration, which drove a considerable number of vessels away from Madeira. Numbers then rose gradually until, in 1937, they reached 1438 vessels. With the recent world war the decline became even greater, the number of ships entering being 389, 234, 190 and 187 in the years 1940 to 1943.

The interesting and valuable information on the harbour of Funchal that we present below is taken from the reputable periodical *Jornal do Comercio e das Colonias* and comes from the pen of Dr C. Dias de Carvalho.

‘The ports of the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes) rank, in order of importance, as follows: Funchal, Ponta Delgada, Horta and Angra. First, however, we should give an idea of their combined traffic.
The goods loaded and unloaded in these ports in 1936 amount to some 251 thousand tonnes, with a value of approximately 132 thousand *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos).

The harbour of Funchal accounts for almost all of this traffic, with 88.63% of the tonnage and 82.76% of the overall value. It is followed by Ponta Delgada, with 6.97% of the tonnage and 11.52% of the value respectively; then comes Horta, with 4.21% of the tonnage, and Angra, with 3.56% of the value; and finally Angra, with 0.19% of the total tonnage, and Horta, with 2.16% of the value.
Having thus briefly seen the position each of these ports holds in terms of the quantities of goods handled on its quays, let us move on to a more detailed analysis of each of them.
We have already said that this port is the most important in the Adjacent Islands, and it ranks fourth among all the ports of mainland Portugal and the islands, immediately after Setúbal.
Its traffic exceeded that of Leixões, and in imported tonnage the harbour of Funchal even stands above the Port of Setúbal itself.

The goods imported and exported through that port on the island of Madeira reached 222,258 tonnes in 1943, with a value of 109,203,000.00 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis).
Let us see what the figures for the import and export trade tell us.

Imports. Total imports through the harbour of Funchal in 1936 come to 95,096 tonnes, with a value of 58,652 *contos*. Below we break down these quantities and values according to the different tariff headings: Live animals – imports amount to only tonnes, with a value of 28 *contos*.
Raw materials – This class accounts for the greatest tonnage: 73,963 tonnes of various products were imported, their value rising to 16,665 *contos*.
Yarns and textiles – Of these goods, 565 tonnes were unloaded at the harbour of Funchal, but with a value of 17,096 *contos*; this is the class with the highest import value.
Foodstuffs – The products in this class rank second in quantity – 19,216 tonnes – and third in value – 14,664 *contos*.
Machinery, apparatus, etc. – Imports of these items are smaller, amounting to only 410 tonnes with a value of 5,400 *contos*.

Miscellaneous manufactures – The quantity of manufactured articles imported is also relatively small – 891 tonnes – with a value of 4,790 *contos*. We must, however, bear in mind the size of the island and the needs of its population, so as not to belittle these figures.

In summary: the imported products that generated most traffic at the harbour of Funchal (in tonnage, of course) fall into the following classes, in order of importance: 1. raw materials; 2. foodstuffs; 3. miscellaneous manufactures; 4. yarns and textiles; 5. machinery, apparatus, etc.; and 6. live animals.
In terms of value the order is different, as can easily be seen from the figures already given.
Exports – Let us now examine the export trade for 1936, which amounted to 127,162 tonnes of products valued at 50,551 *contos*.
Following the approach used for imports, we shall likewise assess this trade according to the tariff classification of the goods.
Raw materials – Exports of the articles in this class generated the greatest tonnage at the harbour of Funchal, reaching 118,649 tonnes. The value of these exports was 10,469 *contos*.

Yarns and textiles – Under this heading is classed the fine, world-famous embroidery of the island of Madeira, so it is not surprising that this class accounts for the largest sum among exports: 25,004 *contos*, for 238,000 kilos of products.
Foodstuffs – Food products rank second among exports, both in quantity – 8,207 tonnes – and in value – 14,891 *contos*. They include the celebrated Madeira wines, bananas, etc.
As for the two remaining classes, machinery, apparatus, etc., and miscellaneous manufactures, the tonnage exported in each was 3 and 65 tonnes, and the values 24 and 163 *contos*.
