Porto do Moniz (parish)

This is one of the oldest parishes (*freguesias*) in the north of Madeira. The exact period in which its first colonisation began is not known, but it cannot have been much later than the beginning of the third quarter of the 15th century. Francisco Moniz, the Elder, is named as one of its earliest settlers. This should be understood, however, to mean that he was one of the first to hold *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands there, and the first to form a substantial core of inhabitants in this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town), with the settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) he established and the chantry (capela) he founded beside it. Around the one and the other the population gradually grew denser, and a new parish soon took shape. This is what generally happened throughout the island.

This locality was first called Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’), a name which then covered the land corresponding to the present parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela, Porto Moniz, Achadas da Cruz, and perhaps also part of Ponta do Pargo. Once the chapel of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) had been founded, the place took the name of that chapel with the addition ‘da Ponta do Tristão’; the learned annotator of the *Saudades* states that the parish is so named in the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 12 March 1574. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo also says that in the letter of 1 March 1577 it is already given the name of Porto Moniz, which is the one that prevailed and endured. Francisco Moniz was of noble descent and a native of the Algarve. Some genealogists say that he married, on this island, Filipa da Câmara, daughter of Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara, who was the natural son of the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco. As we said in the article devoted to the parish of Achadas da Cruz, Garcia da Câmara owned a great deal of *sesmaria* land at Ponta do Tristão, granted to him by his father, and it is not unreasonable to conjecture that Francisco Moniz shared, by inheritance, in the ownership of those lands. The approximate period in which Francisco Moniz made his first settlement in this locality is unknown; Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo first gives 1535 as the year of his death, and later 1533.

Francisco Moniz built the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Conceição not far from the sea, and gave his surname to the nearby landing place. The name later spread to its immediate surroundings and, later still, to the neighbouring lands.

The year in which this parish was created is unknown; the royal letter of 11 March 1574 is the oldest document concerning it that we have found cited. On the evidence of similar cases, we suppose that the establishment of this settlement as an independent parish did not long precede that date, and there was no doubt a private chaplain there to perform the duties of worship, as was generally the case in large settlements that had a chapel attached.

The royal letters of 1 March 1577, 9 June 1581, 17 July 1588 and 20 February 1593 successively increased the parish priest’s stipend, which the royal decree (*alvará*) of 15 October 1650 fixed at 20,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year in cash, one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine.

Since Francisco Moniz died in 1533 or 1535, the chapel of the Immaculate Conception, which he founded, must predate that year, but the year of its construction is unknown. The chapel underwent several alterations and was demolished after the new church was built on a different site. It is said in some source, and local tradition held, that the move was made to place the church in greater safety from the raids of the corsairs who at times infested those waters. Work on the new building began in 1660, but it was only in 1668 that it was declared entirely finished. It is of simple architecture and bare of any works of art. It should be noted, however, that the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament, built later, shows good artistic taste and contrasts with the other decorations of the church. This chapel is owed to Captain Manuel Rodrigues Ferreira Ferro, who died in 1717 and was buried in it as its founder.

We shall deal with the chapels of this parish elsewhere. Meanwhile, we shall say here that in the locality (*sítio*) most commonly known by the abbreviation Santa (‘saint’) stands the chapel of Santa Maria Madalena (St Mary Magdalene). It is of no mean size and is the centre of a well-attended pilgrimage held every year in July. When the parish has its curacy (*curato*) filled, the curate usually lives near this chapel and performs his religious duties there. Besides the cemetery in the locality of Vila, there is another cemetery close to this chapel.

Referring in 1590 to the parish we are discussing, Gaspar Frutuoso says the following: ‘Half a league from Seixal lies Magdalena, which is a parish of thirty households, with much growing of grain and plenty of water. This parish lies inland, nearly half a league, at Ponta do Tristão...’ These few words contain several inaccuracies. The parish is not that of Magdalena but of Porto Moniz, the former name referring to a locality that has an old chapel dedicated to Santa Maria Madalena. Porto Moniz is not merely half a league from Seixal, nor does it lie half a league inland at Ponta do Tristão for someone coming from the Seixal side, as the author describes. The royal decrees that regulated the stipend (*côngrua*) of parish priests show that Porto Moniz could not have had only thirty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) at that time, but approximately a hundred or even more. In 1611, that is, twenty-one years later, Achadas da Cruz alone already had about twenty households.

We mentioned above that, according to tradition, the site for the parish church was chosen because it placed the church in a better position to escape the raids of corsairs, which is not hard to believe. The Moors of the Moroccan coast at times attacked the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and some settlements on the Madeiran coast. It may be presumed that Porto Moniz did not escape the corsairs’ plunder, since it was one of the places in Madeira closest to their point of departure, although we have no reliable record of these raids by Moroccan pirates. We have read somewhere (1921) that at the top of the town, in the place called Pedra Mole (‘soft stone’), one can still see today the remains of caves dug into the clay, where the wealthier inhabitants are said to have hidden their church furnishings and valuables whenever the corsairs approached the coast. To prevent these incursions and drive off the raiding ships, a fort was built in this parish; according to the annotator of the *Saudades*, it was the best on the north coast. It was Captain Manuel Rodrigues Ferreira Ferro, already referred to, who paid all the costs of building this fort, the State contributing only the guns and the rest of its artillery equipment. It bore the name of São João Baptista (St John the Baptist), and we are told that the stone tablet bearing the inscription recording the date and the founder of this small fort is kept in one of the military offices housed in the Palácio de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’).

Captain Manuel Ferreira Ferro founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*) with its seat in this parish. From the facts related about him, he was a true benefactor of this place, and we do not know whether even one of the streets of the settlement still bears his name, recalling to present and future generations the charitable deeds he performed.
The parish comprises the localities of Vila, Lamaceiros, Junqueira, Levada Grande, Batalhão, Ribeirinho, Pico Alto, Santa, Fazenda and Pombais, with 3,412 inhabitants.
Porto Moniz (municipality)

As we have already pointed out with regard to the Municipality of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), Porto Moniz was never a town (*vila*), but only the seat of the municipality (*concelho*) established there in 1835. The people of the locality and of the neighbouring parishes (*freguesias*) sought at times to have the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Porto Moniz raised to the rank of town, but these efforts came to nothing.

Porto Moniz, like all the localities in the north of the island, belonged to the town and Municipality of Machico. When the Municipality and town of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) was created in 1743, it became an integral part of the new municipality. In 1817 the engineer and inspector of public works Paulo Dias de Almeida impressed upon the government in Lisbon the need to create the Municipality of Porto Moniz. In a dispatch to the higher authorities dated 10 April 1825, the governor and captain-general Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro gave a favourable report on the petition the people had made to that end, which merely answered long-standing aspirations already voiced on other occasions. According to the request then made, the new municipality would comprise the parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela, Porto Moniz and Ponta do Pargo. Its boundaries would be the stream of João Delgado, from the sea up to the heights of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), in the parish of Seixal, and the stream of Marinheiros up to the uplands of Fonte do Bispo (‘bishop’s spring’), in the parish of Ponta do Pargo.

Only with the establishment of constitutional government and the division of this district into municipalities was the municipality (*concelho*) of Porto Moniz created. Its seat was in the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name, and it then comprised that parish together with the parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela, Achadas da Cruz and Ponta do Pargo.

The municipality was created in 1835 and installed on 31 October of the same year. Its first administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) was Captain Tomás João Perestrelo da Câmara, and the first president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Municipal Council was the naval captain Teodoro Moniz de Bettencourt.

The municipality of Porto Moniz has been abolished and restored several times. It was suppressed in 1849 and restored a few years later. The decree of 10 December 1867 abolished the municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santana and Porto Moniz, but they were re-established shortly afterwards. The decree of 18 November 1895 suppressed this municipality once again; it was restored by the decree of 13 January 1898 and reinstalled on 13 February of the same year.
The parish of Ponta do Pargo was detached from the municipality of Porto Moniz and annexed to that of Calheta (‘small cove’) by decree of 20 June 1871.
Porto do Moniz (harbour)

This harbour enjoys the reputation of being one of the best in the archipelago, and it is unquestionably the safest and most sheltered on the whole north coast of Madeira. It has even been claimed that embarking and landing are always possible there, whatever quarter the wind blows from. The truth is that, although communication with the shore is often easy, it is equally certain that at times it is genuinely impossible to make for the inner harbour, and entering it is very risky and dangerous. The coastline stretching from Ponta do Tristão (‘Tristão’s point’) to beyond the islet of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) is battered by frequent storms, especially in winter, and the sea there is not infrequently very rough and turbulent.

The harbour lies to the NW, almost at the western extremity of the island. Although it is very sheltered, it is nonetheless exposed to north-westerly winds. When winds blow on the south coast that make all movement and traffic in the ports impossible, many coastal vessels, and even ocean-going ships, seek safer shelter there.

Because of the relative safety and ease of landing that this harbour offers, there has been no shortage of people wishing to turn the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz, with its natural landing place, into a small town and port of call for times when the winds blow from SSE to SSW and the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*) and the other ports on the south of the island are sometimes closed to shipping.

In 1914 the Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) commissioned the naval lieutenant Francisco de Aragão e Melo to carry out various hydrographic studies at Porto Moniz, whose results never became widely known. We find only the following words, in the report of the inquiry that Dr Francisco António de Mendonça conducted into the actions of the Agricultural Council:

‘Once the studies had begun, difficulties of various kinds arose, chiefly in fixing the hydrographic zero, which the caprice of the waves several times tore away, so that whole nights had to be spent working in order not to prolong the studies endlessly. The solar observations with the sextant on board small boats, and the corresponding soundings, carried out with the help of inexperienced staff, were also exhausting and slow work. Once the triangulation of the land with the islets surrounding that harbour had been established, a plan of the bay was drawn up, which accompanies these lines.’

There is a natural landing place there, but it requires substantial engineering works to serve its purpose fully. Around 1901 the local Municipal Council had some essential works carried out, and in 1909 the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) had a flight of steps built giving access to the branch of the existing quay, all of which improved the natural conditions of the site. Around 1916 more substantial works were undertaken there, with the construction of a quay that serves this locality well.
Porto Novo

A hamlet at the mouth of the stream of the same name, forming part of the parish (*freguesia*) of Gaula. It is a port of call for the steamers that run services to the east coast of the island. There is a landing place there, built by order of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*); the work was completed in 1908.
See Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelist troops.
Porto Santo (waters of)

When droughts are prolonged, as happens from time to time, this island suffers the consequences of a veritable public calamity. The District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), under the presidency of Dr João Abel de Freitas, deserves great praise for ordering important agricultural water works there, in order to lessen the crises caused by these droughts and to bring considerable benefit to the farming of that whole region. The construction of a large ‘ditch’ (*vala*) was judged necessary, and in an interview given to a newspaper in 1942 the president described it in the terms we shall now reproduce.

‘The construction of a ditch to capture and distribute rainwater, now under way, is perhaps the work of greatest economic and social importance ever carried out there, not only because it comes at the right moment to provide work for hundreds of hands, but also because of the influence it should have on the agricultural development of the region.

The first function of this ditch is to capture the water which, sometimes in great volumes, runs down the slopes of Pico do Castelo (‘castle peak’) and has done so much damage to the slopes below. Once one of the main causes of the ruinous state of this land has been removed, the incentive may arise to rebuild the walls and restore the land that has been lost.

Secondly, the water thus captured will be carried, along the part of the ditch intended for distribution, across sandy ground in the localities of Camacha, Eira Velha, Areias, etc. These form a natural reservoir of great capacity, into which all the water channelled there will soak. From this great infiltration field comes the water for almost all the existing springs and wells.

The aim is thus to make use, in two ways, of water that has until now been harmful: first, directly, by irrigating the land below the ditch; and secondly, by increasing the groundwater and, consequently, the flow of the springs. This will also make it economically worthwhile to sink new wells, and so to extend the irrigated land.

A further advantage of building this ditch is that it will encourage the construction of wells or dams at the most suitable places along its course, where water can be held back for future irrigation, once a regular surplus of water is found to justify such construction.’
Porto Santo (demographic aspects)
The following passages are taken from an interesting lecture given by the Revd Father Eduardo Pereira and published in the Funchal *Diario de Noticias* of 22 and 23 July 1941.

‘The social life of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is also a subject of interest, curiosity and study, because of the striking contrast it offers with that of Madeira. The people have always kept to themselves within the island and within their own ethnic character, customs and traditions.

It is a distinctive and original land in the geological and demographic make-up of the archipelago. The people, descended directly from two races, the Portuguese and the Arab, show their influences and atavism in everything.

They are Portuguese in the sharply marked, strong features of 16th-century colonisers; they are Arab in atavistic traits of a pronounced Moorish character. The former reveal themselves in a sensitivity about lineage and in moral attributes; the latter in physical characteristics and mixed temperaments. In their moral make-up, however, they are more markedly Portuguese, and island and inhabitants show so much physical and political affinity with the Portuguese mainland that one might easily say they belong more there than here. The very upbringing of that people is another original facet of considerable psychological importance.

Their way of living and feeling, social manners, notions of hygiene, qualities of courtesy and solidarity, language, family, paternal authority, marriage, pedigrees, morals, diet, amusements, music, farming system – everything, absolutely everything, distinguishes the population of Porto Santo from that of Madeira. Out of Arab mistrust, the people do not give or open themselves at first contact to anyone, whether from within or without, wherever they may come from. First they get to know, then they study, and only then do they esteem, with Portuguese frankness and affection. Their affection is slow to come, but lasting. Let no one set out to deceive them, for they will be the first to see through the deceit. Unusually intelligent and shrewd, they do not let strangers know them without first knowing them. They are, however, of a captivating courtesy unequalled among our populations.’
Porto Santo (captaincy)

As is well known, the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) formed one of the three captaincies into which this archipelago was divided (see vol. 1, p. 244). The letter of grant (carta de doação) to its first donatary, Bartolomeu Perestrelo, is dated 1 November 1446 and is transcribed on p. 457 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). It states: ‘I give charge to Bartolomeu Perestrelo, *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of my household, of my island of Porto Santo, so that the said Bartolomeu Perestrelo may maintain it for me in justice and right; and should he die, it pleases me that his first son, or another if such there be, shall hold this charge in the manner aforesaid, and so from descendant to descendant in the direct line; and should the said son be of such an age that he cannot govern, I or my heirs shall place there someone to govern until he is of age to govern. And it pleases me that he shall hold on this aforesaid island jurisdiction, for me and in my name, in civil and criminal matters, save for death or the cutting off of a limb, from which appeal shall come before me; yet notwithstanding the said jurisdiction, it pleases me that my orders and inspection (*correição*) be carried out there as a thing of my own.’ This letter mentions various rights, privileges and exemptions granted to the first donatary, including the collection of various contributions and taxes.

The captaincy of Porto Santo remained in the possession and under the authority of Bartolomeu Perestrelo’s descendants until the time when Philippine rule, with the appointment of governors-general, reduced the donataries of the archipelago to a very subordinate and almost purely honorary position. They nevertheless continued to collect substantial revenues from the original privileges that had been granted to them.

Bartolomeu Perestrelo (see Perestrelo) was succeeded in the donatary captaincy (*donataria*) by his son of the same name, who was stripped of it during his minority when his mother sold the captaincy to Pedro Correia, brother-in-law of the second Bartolomeu Perestrelo. After a lawsuit and an appeal brought before the Crown, the donatary captaincy was restored to him with all its rights and privileges (1437). He was succeeded by his son Bartolomeu Perestrelo (1529), who killed his wife Aldonça Delgado in order to marry his cousin Solanda Teixeira. Garcia Perestrelo, son of the third Bartolomeu, killed his wife just as his father had done, and while his father was still alive; for this he was condemned to death and beheaded. The lineage of the Perestrelos of this archipelago thus counts these two notorious murderers. The captaincy was inherited by Diogo Soares Perestrelo (1545), grandson of the third Bartolomeu Perestrelo, and he was succeeded by his son Diogo Perestrelo (1576). This donatary was a valiant knight. While he lived on his island, corsairs never attacked it, as had happened on other occasions, because, despite the feeble means of defence at his disposal, he managed through his energy and astonishing activity to keep the raiders at a distance. It may fairly be said that he was truly the last donatary of Porto Santo, since with Castilian rule and the appointment of the governors-general in 1581, the superintendence of the whole archipelago passed to them, as we have already said. After the Restoration, in 1653, John IV made a royal grant of the captaincy of Porto Santo to Vitorino Bettencourt Perestrelo, who is regarded as the seventh donatary, although the rights and privileges enjoyed by the former captains-donatary were considerably curtailed. He was followed by Diogo Perestrelo, Estêvão Bettencourt Perestrelo, Vitorino Bettencourt Perestrelo and Estêvão Bettencourt Perestrelo.

The donataries were succeeded by the governors, the first to be appointed being, according to the *Anais* of that island, Nicolau Bettencourt Perestrelo. In the article Ilha do Porto Santo we give a list of all the governors who served there up to 1848, the last to hold that office on the island being José Caetano Peixoto.

The captaincy of Porto Santo progressed slowly and never attained any notable degree of prosperity. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says that it progressed during its first hundred and fifty years. These words should be taken to mean that it developed gradually from the earliest colonisation until the middle of the 16th century. That progress, however, was never great, owing to the causes already pointed out elsewhere. The chief of these were the frequent pirate raids, the droughts, the sometimes lengthy absences of the donataries, the ancestral pride of many inhabitants, which kept them away from farming, and the abandonment of their lands by a large number of the original holders of land grants, who took up residence in Funchal and some in Lisbon, etc. All these causes of decline led to the promulgation of the celebrated law of 13 October 1770, known as the Law of Fifths and Eighths (*lei dos Quintos e Oitavos*), of which we give a detailed account in another article.
See Baleira (Vila), Donataries, Captaincies and Perestrelo (Bartolomeu).
Porto Santo (Count of)

The statesman and diplomat António de Saldanha da Gama, who married a Madeiran lady, daughter and heiress of the former holder of the entail (*morgado*) José de Brito Heredia, was granted the title of Count of Porto do Santo by decree of 26 October 1823, a title that had no successors.
Porto Santo (discovery and origin of the name)

The discovery of our archipelago is the great and undying monument that truly marks the auspicious beginning of the wondrous odyssey the Portuguese undertook across unknown seas. It must therefore be especially remembered that the small island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) was the first maritime haven at which those daring navigators made landfall, the glorious starting point of one of the most remarkable events in the whole history of our country. This circumstance alone would be enough for the island to be regarded as the firstborn and beloved daughter of Portugal, deserving the most active and valuable protection from the mother country – which, in reality, has not always been forthcoming. As to its discovery, what was set out at some length on pp. 351–356 of vol. I of this *Elucidário*, in the treatment of the discovery of the archipelago, applies in full.

Dr Gaspar Frutuoso and other chroniclers, following the account João de Barros gives in his *Asia*, Década I, attribute the origin of the name Porto Santo to the fact that the first discoverers found safe shelter there from the violent storm that had beset them. We transcribe Barros’s words: ‘... For before they reached the coast of Africa, so great a storm broke upon them, with the force of winds contrary to their voyage, that they lost all hope of their lives: for the ship was so small, and the sea so heavy that it swallowed them, running under bare masts at the sea’s mercy. And since the seamen of that time were not accustomed to venture so far into the open ocean, and all their navigation was by day’s runs always within sight of land, and as it seemed to them they were very far from the coast of this Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), they were all so troubled, and so out of their wits, fear having taken hold of the greater part of them, that they could not judge at what spot they were. But it pleased the mercy of God that the weather abated, and although the winds had made them lose the course they were following according to the regulations (*regimento*) of the Infante, they did not turn them from their good fortune: for they discovered the island which we now call Porto Santo, the name they then gave it because it had kept them safe from the peril they had passed through in the days of the storm. . . ’
This is the generally accepted opinion. The only disagreements concern the time when the event took place and the navigators who were driven into the harbour of that island.
Porto Santo (development, decline and crises)
Fifths and eighths

In the early days of colonisation the settlement of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), later a town (*vila*), grew and prospered. Yet little more than a century later it began a clear decline, which has persisted through the ages and is from time to time aggravated by fearful crises, due above all to the prolonged droughts that occur there with relative frequency.

This first prosperity was neither long-lived nor especially noteworthy. Its almost immediate ruin, particularly from the end of the 16th century, was brought about not only by the serious cause already mentioned but also by the frequent attacks of pirates, the absence of the donataries, the ancestral pretensions of many of the inhabitants, who abandoned the cultivation of the land, the climatic conditions that then led to enforced idleness, and still other circumstances of a local nature that are not well known today.

Dr Álvaro de Azevedo tells us that ‘the obscure history of that island amounts simply to the neglect to which governments always consigned it. Only in the time of the Marquis of Pombal, whose representative in this archipelago was the energetic governor and captain-general João António de Sá Pereira, did mainland Portugal discover that the island was a Portuguese possession.

Porto Santo had fallen into such a state of decline that it was in danger of becoming depopulated. Various causes contributed to this, the chief ones being the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant), made worse by frequent droughts, and the foolish pride of many of its inhabitants, who disdained to devote themselves to farming or to the crafts and trades. The wealthier landowners led idle lives in Funchal or in Lisbon and received the half-share (*demidia*) of the produce of their properties, leaving the tenants in the most deplorable situation, very close to destitution. A luxury in the most flagrant contradiction with the sad circumstances of the island was rife among its inhabitants, a great many of whom believed themselves descended from illustrious ancestors.

The royal decree (alvará régio) of 13 October 1770 put an end to many of these abuses, although it did not cut the evil out at the root. Even so, only the iron hand of the Marquis and of his representative on this island – whom the annotator of the *Saudades* calls ‘the Madeiran Pombal’ – could have enforced a decree with such draconian provisions, one that would certainly have provoked vigorous protests from those whom it harmed so profoundly.

The first paragraph of this truly Pombaline enactment, and the most violent of them all, establishes that the ‘lands must be vested in their present cultivators and their families, so that they come to possess the useful domain of those same lands. . . this remaining perpetual in the same families, with the obligation of paying for the best lands the fifths of their produce and for those of second quality the eighths, without these payments being subject to alteration . . . ’. Under this provision of the decree, the landlords not only could not alienate their lands but received from them merely a simple quit-rent (*foro*); moreover, instead of half the produce of the properties, they now received a fifth or an eighth, according to the quality of the land. Hence this royal decree came to be called the Law of Fifths and Eighths (*lei dos Quintos e Oitavos*), the law of ‘fifths and eighths’, which benefited the inhabitants of Porto Santo but stripped the proprietors of their centuries-old rights, unless they chose to live on the island and personally manage the farming of their lands. Under this first paragraph, the inhabitants were also exempted for ten years from paying the tithes that belonged to the State.

The second paragraph lays down that the posts of judges, councillors (*vereadores*), procurators of the municipality (*concelho*) and other offices of justice or of the treasury, which had been held by persons of rank, could be held only by individuals who ‘farmed the land’.

The third paragraph orders the governor to have chosen, ‘from among the sons of the said idlers who do not farm the land’, six to learn the trade of shoemaker, as many again to become tailors, two potters, four carpenters, four stonemasons and two blacksmiths.

The celebrated enactment contains other interesting provisions, which we omit for the sake of brevity; it is transcribed in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), on p. 713 and following. This is the celebrated legislative enactment that became known as the ‘Law of Fifths and Eighths’, which caused the greatest sensation at the time and was the subject of the most controversial comment, even though it was promulgated under the authoritarian government of the Marquis of Pombal.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of 13 October 1770 ordered the governor and captain-general, accompanied by other officials, to go in person to Porto Santo to carry it fully into effect. João Antonio de Sá Pereira accordingly took with him the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) Dr Francisco Moreira de Matos, the superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*) Domingos Afonso Barroso, the engineer Lieutenant Francisco Salustiano da Costa e Sá and the government secretary José Anastacio da Costa. He reached the island on 28 May 1771 and remained there with the other state officials until 20 June following.

While the *corregedor* of the judicial district (*comarca*), the superintendent of the Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*) and the assistant engineer undertook the registration of holdings (*encabeçamento*), distinguishing the lands that were to pay ‘fifths’ or ‘eighths’ of their produce, the governor and his secretary set about implementing the other provisions of the decree. He left behind a set of regulations chiefly concerned with agriculture, appointing as its inspector Captain Pedro Teles de Meneses, a native and resident of Porto Santo, with an annual salary of four hundred thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

Sá Pereira assembled the Municipal Council, the authorities, the public officials and many of the common people, and there the decree of 13 October was solemnly proclaimed and its execution and observance declared to have begun.

Twenty years later the governor and captain-general Dom Diogo Pereira de Forjaz Coutinho visited the island to examine how the celebrated decree of 1770 was being carried out; with the passing years its principal provisions had fallen into disuse.

The crises that arise from time to time on the island, brought on especially by long droughts, as stated above, are a terrifying prospect for its inhabitants, who live forever under the spectre of famine with all the horrors that accompany it.
Porto Santo (health resort)

The neighbouring island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) has long been recommended as an excellent health resort for the cure of certain diseases. The number of Madeiran visitors who go there is not greater because of the lack of hotels and suitable accommodation, and also because of the complete absence of comfort, speed and safety in the vessels used to carry passengers. There is no one in Madeira who is unaware of this. Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira – who was a professor at our Medical School, served as health officer (*delegado de saúde*) of the district and was a distinguished practitioner of the medical sciences through his studies and polished writings, and who had moreover spent long periods on that island – states that a stay on Porto Santo has far more beneficial and wholesome effects than the same length of time spent taking mineral and medicinal waters at the spas where they rise.
The words of Dr Nuno Teixeira deserve to be recorded here, for in our view they constitute a complete study of the subject.

The island of Porto Santo, says this physician, is unique as a health resort, because it combines qualities and sanitary conditions that, as far as we know, are found together nowhere else, and certainly not to such an excellent degree as on that island. They allow the simultaneous use of thalassotherapy, or sea bathing, on a beach that has no rival abroad in any country; of grapes, than which none better are known; and of mineral waters that need fear no comparison with the best in Portugal and abroad. Which health resort in the world, we ask, offers the healthful and wholesome resources that characterise Porto Santo, where the invalid finds sea bathing, grapes and mineral waters all at the same time? We know of none but Porto Santo, and Porto Santo alone. Abroad, the beaches are far from the spas, and sea bathing cannot be combined with mineral waters. Treatment with grapes, it seems to us, is not practised anywhere in our country, and abroad this treatment, or ampelotherapy, stands on its own and is not used together with sea bathing and mineral waters. Porto Santo alone, therefore, offers the three great agents for restoring the body – sea, grapes and mineral waters – which can be applied at the same time, if necessary, and in conditions of unsurpassable purity and curative power.

‘As for sea bathing, Porto Santo has the finest beach known, much appreciated and even admired by foreigners. It is three *léguas* of pure, yellowish, golden sand, with no intervening boulders forming rock pools in which to bathe, as on some beaches in Portugal.

‘The sea water is exceptionally pure, with no refuse to foul it, because no sewers or industrial outflows empty into the bay. The bottom is a reef (*restinga*), very shallow for a great distance from the breakwater, so that a bather who cannot swim can go far out from the beach while still touching the bottom, which makes it very suitable for ladies. It is a beach where no bathing attendant is needed, because there are no currents that could carry non-swimmers out to the open sea, as has sometimes happened on the beaches of the mainland.

‘All these excellences and refinements of the beach of Porto Santo culminate in the uniformity of the floor of the bay, always flat, always even, with no hollows or holes into which an inexperienced bather might suddenly sink, dragged further down by the vortex of the undertow. That is a danger on every beach, but it does not exist on that of Porto Santo.

‘It is therefore an ideal beach, combining every possible perfection, and we know of none abroad that can compare with it. In former times it was used by some English families living in this city, who went to Porto Santo expressly, with their bathing tents, to bathe on the splendid beach. The beach is also the club or assembly where, in the evening, the families spending the summer on that island gather to talk, sing, play music and play games.

‘Having dealt with the beach, let us now consider the grapes. We knew a gentleman who lived in Paris with his family and with whom we were on very friendly terms. He was eighty-three years old when we were introduced to him, and he was in very good spirits for his age, despite the ailments common to all old people. He lived in Paris, as I said, and with the first heat of summer he lost all desire to eat; he had no appetite for anything except grapes. In Paris, however, grapes do not appear on the market until September, and the person of whom we speak could not wait so long, because he lost his appetite at the very beginning of July. So he came to Porto Santo to feed himself, as he put it. He was the first to begin eating grapes and the last to stop, and since the grape harvest in those days went on until the end of September, he ate grapes from mid-July to the end of September, that is, for two and a half months. He ate nothing but grapes, for no other food appealed to him. From the first year we knew him, he came to Porto Santo every year to eat grapes for as long as he lived. He told everyone that, as soon as he began his grape diet, he enjoyed far better health and saw all his usual complaints disappear, and he assured them that the grapes had prolonged his life and greatly improved his health. He died at the age of ninety-four.

‘Let us now consider the mineral waters of Porto Santo. The improvement felt by people suffering from dyspepsia who take the waters of Porto Santo is a commonplace fact, so ordinary is it, especially if the waters are taken on the island itself, at their source. We wish to relate a case known to us which is extraordinary, quite remarkable, and which proves the almost miraculous action of Porto Santo water. There was a young man here, our contemporary at the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city, very talented and one of the most distinguished poets of his time, especially in the humorous genre; his satirical verses were extremely amusing and much appreciated in this city. Sadly, he died young of pulmonary tuberculosis, from which he had suffered for several years. He was a senior employee of the now defunct Banco Comercial da Madeira and, being ill, he accompanied the director and founder of that bank, the prominent landowner and well-liked citizen João de Sales Caldeira, to Porto Santo every year. The young man of whom we speak, like all consumptives, was a dyspeptic, but his stomach was so sensitive and intolerant that everything disagreed with him. He took only liquids; his stomach would accept no food that needed chewing, for it was immediately vomited and brought on diarrhoea. His broths had to be strained; a single grain of rice or a tiny strand of vermicelli was enough to cause indigestion. Yet this poor young man, whom here in Madeira it was a real torment for his lady to feed, as we heard her say more than once, and whose stomach tolerated nothing but strained broths, ate everything on Porto Santo: cabbage soup, melons, watermelons, grapes, etc., and nothing disagreed with him. What we state is a fact, for we witnessed it many times. It is possible that this extraordinary tolerance of the stomach was the result of various factors – rest, climate, atmospheric surroundings – but the waters were surely the most important.','

‘In conclusion: sea bathing, grapes and mineral waters – such is the threefold claim that recommends Porto Santo as a health resort, one which is certainly not surpassed, nor even equalled, by any other.’
Porto Santo (flora and fauna)
The flora and fauna of this island have some peculiar features, which receive special mention where these subjects are treated in the articles on Madeira.
See Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) rabbit (I-282).
Porto Santo (parish)

Because of its small area and small population, the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) has always formed a single parish (*freguesia*). It has borne, and still bears today, the name of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), the patron saint of its parish church. Although Frutuoso stated in 1590 that the patron saint and name of the parish was the Salvador (the Saviour), the truth is that documents earlier than that date already give the patron saint as Our Lady of Pity, and we believe it was never any other.

Just as in the seats of the captaincies of Funchal and Machico the parishes were created only some years after colonisation began, the same must have happened, with all the more reason, on the island of Porto Santo. A chaplain would certainly have carried out the ecclesiastical and parochial duties there until the island was constituted as an autonomous parish.
The year of its creation is not known, but it must be roughly contemporary with the first parishes established in Madeira.

The oldest instrument we have found cited in the General Index of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*) is the royal decree (alvará régio) of 3 January 1529, which assigned the parish priest an annual salary of 11,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, four *moios* of wheat and two *pipas* of wine. By this time the collegiate church had already been established; besides the parish priest, it had a curate and four beneficiaries. The curacy (*curato*) was created by the royal decree of 27 August 1589, with a salary of 20,000 *réis* a year.

The first vicar of this parish of whom there is any record was Father Nuno Vaz, who seems to have begun his ministry in 1572. He was followed as parish priests by João Cordovil de Couto, Manuel Calaça, Jerónimo Vieira, Father Siebra, Dr Manuel Lopes da Silva, Dr Inácio Manuel da Silva, Dr Estêvão Lomelino de Vasconcelos, Domingos Ferreira de Agrela and Baltasar de Andrade, who served until the end of the 17th century.

We believe that the seat of the parish was established in the chapel of Our Lady of Pity, which already stood there before the parish was created. It underwent various repairs and extensions, and was completely rebuilt around 1667. Nothing remains of the original building except the so-called chapel of the Morgada, which belonged to an old Baião family. It still keeps its pointed arch, which, since some of the stones forming it were somewhat damaged, was rendered with a cement coating a few years ago! No church in the diocese ever suffered so many profanations and outrages as this one, owing to the raids that corsairs made on that island from time to time. As there were no defences of any kind there, the inhabitants thought only of taking refuge on the Pico do Castelo (‘castle peak’) and in other safe places whenever they sensed the pirates approaching, leaving them a free hand to carry out their work of destruction and plunder. In 1617 Porto Santo was invaded by Algerian corsairs, and the mother church (*igreja matriz*) was sacked and set on fire; the same happened again in 1667, after which the church was rebuilt. In 1556, 1690 and 1708 it was not Moors but French ships fitted out as privateers that attacked the island and thoroughly plundered it, the parish church again being a target of the attackers’ fury. It should be remembered that in those times French ships were protected by high-ranking personages – some even claim by the kings of France themselves. These ships often roamed the seas as pirates, committing the gravest crimes with impunity, slaughtering and robbing defenceless settlements. Such was the case with the French invasion of Madeira in 1556, as we shall see in its proper place.
Besides the parish church, this parish has the chapels of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy), St Catherine, Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit) and St Peter, of which we give a brief account elsewhere.

The main localities (*sítios*) of Porto Santo are: Vila, Casinhas e Pico, Serra de Fora, Serra de Dentro, Pedregal and Esmoitadas, Camacha, Farrobo, Areias, Tanque, Matas and Lombas, Fontinha, Pedras Pretas, Campo de Baixo, Campo de Cima and Ponta.
Porto Santo (hydrography)

Under this heading we give a brief account of the quays, coves, landing places, beaches, shoals, islets and streams of this island. On the southern coast of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), running almost the whole length of the island, lies the bay of the same name. It is bounded by the Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’), or Lighthouse Islet, to the east, and the Ilhéu de Baixo (‘lower islet’), or Lime Islet, to the west, and measures about four nautical miles between these two points. It forms a fairly spacious harbour and offers easy anchorage to ships of every tonnage. For most of its length the bay is edged by a most beautiful beach of fine yellow sand, free of any reefs or rocks, quite wide and approximately nine kilometres long, which is without doubt one of the finest beaches in the whole of our country. Gently sloping, washed by a sea that is always calm and crystal-clear, and free of marshes or stagnant water, this beach meets every requirement of an excellent seaside resort. The harbour of the town of Porto Santo is today served by a pier, which has proved very useful for the passengers who land there.

Besides this broad bay with its excellent and spacious beach, there are a few small landing places with narrow beaches, which serve, though rarely, as landing places. We shall mention the following: Porto dos Barreiros, to the north-north-east; Porto das Cagarras, to the east-north-east; Porto dos Frades, to the east; Porto da Morena, or Portinho da Morena, to the south-south-west; Porto Novo, to the south-south-west; Porto dos Porcos, to the west-south-west; Porto da Fonte da Areia, to the north-west; and Porto do Zimbralinho, to the east.
Of these beaches, the best known are those of Serra de Dentro (‘inner upland’) and Zimbralinho (‘little juniper grove’), which lie in the localities that still bear those names.

The only known raised beach in the Madeira archipelago is on the island of Porto Santo. The uplift seems to have occurred in a recent geological period, and the ground contains a great number of marine shells, some belonging to species still living in the archipelago, others to species that are not found in our region but live in other countries.

Numerous traces of the raised beach are found near Fontinha (‘little spring’) and at Campo de Baixo (‘lower field’), and it may well cover a much larger area than has been attributed to it so far. Mr Adolfo César de Noronha, who has made numerous studies of this beach, intends to publish a note on the species of marine shells that have been observed there (1921).

Thick layers of soil or sand now lie over the raised beach, and large excavations are needed to expose it. The beach extends far inland: traces of it have been found more than 300 metres from the shoreline of Porto Santo.

Near the coast of the island of Porto Santo lie several shoals, known by the following names: Rocha do Pescador (‘fisherman’s rock’), to the north-east and facing (*fronteiro*) Ponta Branca (‘white point’); the Meio shoal, or Rocha de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’s rock’), to the north of the Pescador; the Cotrim shoal, or Ilhéu Redondo (Round Islet), next to Ponta dos Frades (‘friars’ point’); the Galé shoal, near Ponta do Incão; and the Penedo do Sono (‘rock of sleep’) shoal, not far from the Ilhéu de Cima. Further from the shore, about five miles off the coast, there is a shoal commonly called the Baixa de Nordeste (‘north-east shoal’).

Lying next to the island of Porto Santo and very close to its coast are the ‘Ilhéu de Baixo’, or Ilhéu da Cal, and the ‘Ilhéu de Cima’, or Ilhéu do Farol. These are the largest and most important islets in the whole archipelago, and they have already been described on pp. 116 and 272 of volume I and in the article Faróis (‘lighthouses’). Mention should also be made of the small islets of ‘Fora’, or ‘Rocha Nordeste’, of ‘Fonte da Areia’ and of ‘Ferro’. Compared with the long, abundant streams of Madeira, the small watercourses that cross the neighbouring island of Porto Santo do not deserve that name. The most important of them is the so-called Ribeira da Vila (‘town stream’), which stays dry for most of the year and carries a small flow in the winter season, running into the ocean at the locality (*sítio*) of Vila. Other small brooks worth mentioning are those of Pedregal de Fora, Pedregal de Dentro and Perregil, to the north; those of Serra de Fora and Serra de Dentro, to the east; those of Santo António, Fontinha, Cochino and Salgado, to the south; and the Ribeiro Fundo (‘deep brook’), to the west.
See Porto Santo (Águas).
Porto Santo (island)

The island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) – so named, according to Frutuoso, because it was there that Gonçalves Zarco and Tristão Vaz Teixeira escaped a violent storm, as already mentioned, which had made them lose ‘all hope of their lives’ – is one of the five islands of the archipelago. It measures 11.4 kilometres in length by 7 in width, and its surface area is calculated at about 50 kilometres. Including its outlying islets, it lies between 32° 59′ 40″ and 33° 7′ 50″ north latitude, and between 16° 16′ 30″ and 16° 24′ 35″ west longitude of Greenwich. Its capital is the town (*vila*) of Baleira, or of Porto Santo, which stands at the head of a vast and beautiful bay, sheltered from the winds from SE round by W to NW (1921).
Porto Santo is much flatter than Madeira, and its highest point, Pico do Facho (‘beacon peak’), is only 507 metres above sea level.

Porto Santo has the largest beach in the archipelago. This beach, which is about 10 kilometres long and formed of calcareous sand, has a gentle slope, and the tides there do not rise more than 2.13 m. As there is as yet no quay of any kind (1921), people who wish to land on the island have to be carried on men’s backs from the boats to dry ground.

Porto Santo is very prone to droughts and poor in water. Its principal springs are the following: that of Areia, in the north; that of Tanque, which supplies water for some of the crops of the town; that of Fontinha (see that entry), known throughout the archipelago for its medicinal properties; that of Voltas; and that of Enguias. The water of the Areia spring is as good as the best in Madeira; that of the other springs generally contains certain salts that make it unpleasant to the taste of visitors to the island. (See Porto Santo (waters) and Health resort.)

Porto Santo forms a single municipality (*concelho*) with only one parish (*freguesia*), that of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (‘Our Lady of Pity’), and today belongs to the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal. It had donataries (see Porto Santo (captaincy)) until the reign of Joseph I, and thereafter the following governors: Nicolau Bettencourt Perestrelo, in the reign of Maria I; Manuel da Câmara Perestrelo de Noronha (1785); Manuel Ferreira Nobre (1797); João Baptista Rofe (1800); Joaquim Bernardino Bianchordi (1804); Manuel Inácio de Avelar Brotero (1805); João de Alvelo Leiria (1815); Joaquim de Freitas Aragão (1822); Cosme Damião da Cunha Fidié (1824); José Crisóstomo de Freitas e Sousa (1829); Francisco Ladislau Correia (1830); João Pinto Carneiro (1837) and José Caetano Peixoto (1848). Governor Leiria never actually came to the island, and Governor Peixoto lived there for only three days.

Both in the town and outside it, there are many rough hovels roofed with clay, which sometimes shelter large numbers of people. Although they offer little comfort, a certain standard of hygiene can be observed in these hovels, and this, together with the island’s healthy air, makes the population generally quite robust.

The town has no notable buildings, but its houses are as a rule of good appearance. In the Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory’), which is laid out as a garden, stands the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), and near it is the parish church.

The town also has the chapel of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy) and the chapel of St Catherine. Next to the latter lies the cemetery, one of the oldest in the archipelago, for it was opened in 1838, on the feast of Corpus Christi.

The dragon trees and junipers that covered Porto Santo at the time of its discovery are now completely extinct. The only native shrub species worthy of note that can still be found there are the hawthorn, the *marmulano* (Sideroxylon marmulano, a shrub), the *durazia* heath and the olive.

The tamarisk, introduced in 1834 by João António Pedroso, is common on Porto Santo, and the palm, the maritime pine, the tree of heaven, the poplar and the myoporum grow in some parts of the island. If proper use were made of this last species, a good part of Porto Santo could easily be afforested in a short time. On Pico do Castelo (‘castle peak’) and its surroundings there are some stands of trees planted over the last 20 years by the forestry officer (*regente silvícola*) António Schiappa de Azevedo (1921).

The island produces vines, wheat, barley, rye, lentils, broad beans, pumpkins, melons, watermelons, potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word), sweet potatoes, garlic, and some cabbages, onions, maize and sugar cane. There are also many fig and mulberry trees there, and some pear, pomegranate, almond and *tabaibeira* trees. See Porto Santo (vegetation).

The numerous soundings made by Vidal in the waters around Porto Santo seem to suggest that the island was once larger than it is today, and in some parts of its territory there are clear signs of uplift caused by volcanic action. T. D. A. Cockerell states that the oldest fossil deposits are Miocene and marine, and that shells and corals mixed with a black volcanic rock, which appears to come from a lower zone, can be found on Ponta da Calheta (‘small cove’). Between the peaks of Castelo and Facho there are whitish-grey trachytes, and on the summit of the latter height there is a rather curious dyke.

To irrigate the land of Porto Santo there are several wells sunk by private individuals, from which the water is raised by means of *noras* (water wheels). Without this resource, many plots that now yield good harvests would perhaps lie barren, since the island frequently suffers from a lack of rain.

Porto Santo, whose population is 2,701 inhabitants (1940), is an interesting and curious place from several points of view, with certain customs and practices unknown in Madeira, at least at present. If frequent steamer services were established to the island and visitors found there the amenities and comforts demanded by modern civilisation, it is to be expected that this land of the archipelago where Zarco and Tristão Vaz first landed, today almost unknown, would become at certain seasons a meeting place for Madeirans and foreigners, eager either to try the curative effects of the waters of Fontinha on stomach ailments or to enjoy the magnificent resources the island offers as a bathing resort. In 1919 Porto Santo was provided with the important improvement of a Radio-Telegraph Station, inaugurated on 17 March of that year, which broke the isolation in which the island had lived, especially in winter.
Porto Santo (orography)

For an island of such small area, Porto Santo is mountainous in appearance and made up of decidedly rugged terrain. Pico do Castelo (‘castle peak’), which we have already described on p. 259 of volume I of this work, rises to 440 metres above the sea.

The principal heights of the island’s mountain range, known by the generic name of peaks (*picos*), are the following: Ninho do Guincho, Branco (423 m), Concelho, Maçaricos, de Baixo, Juliana (455 m), Facho (509 m), Atalaia or Gandaia (492 m), Castelo, Monte Vidio, Ana Ferreira, Facho da Malhada (265 m) and Calhau da Malhada (182 m).
Despite the marked relief of its surface, two small plains stand out and deserve mention: that of the Vila and that of the Areias (‘sands’).
The principal points or headlands of the coast are those of Cruz or Santa Cruz, Ninho do Guincho, Branca or Nordeste, Frades, Incão, Calheta, Malhada, Furado, Varadouros and Fonte da Areia.
Porto Santo (population, surface area and geographical position of the island)

Gaspar Frutuoso states that in 1590 there were some 400 households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths') on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), which would mean about 1,600 inhabitants. On this statement of Frutuoso’s, Dr Alvaro de Azevedo remarks: ‘although there seems to be some exaggeration in this, since the *Annais da Ilha do Porto Santo* record that in 1850 the population was 1799 persons, that is, some 450 households, and the census taken in 1864 records 363 households with 1425 inhabitants, we believe Frutuoso’s statement to be accurate; the island of Porto Santo prospered only in the first hundred and fifty years after its discovery.’ The following figures for its population have been gathered from various sources:

The figures given for the surface area of the archipelago differ. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo set it at 500 kilometres for Madeira, 50 for Porto Santo and 10 for the Desertas (‘deserted islands’). The *Censo da População* for 1930 states that the surface area of the island of Madeira is 740.62 square kilometres and that of Porto Santo 42.17 km². We read in ‘Zargo’s Islands’ (I-59) that official studies carried out in 1937–1938 give Madeira a surface area of 728 km² and the island of Porto Santo 48.8 km².

The known calculations of its geographical position are equally at variance. The illustrious commentator on ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) presents several of them. He prefers those of the geo-hydrographic chart by General António Pedro de Azevedo, which are as follows: 33°3′30″ north latitude and 7°45′27′ west longitude of Lisbon.
Porto Santo (prophets and nobles)
In the article Prophets, the reader will find a detailed account of this curious episode in the life of Porto Santo and of the ‘nickname’ by which the inhabitants of that island are known.

The royal decree (alvará régio) of 6 November 1522, issued in favour of the donatary (*donatário*) Bartolomeu Perestrelo, grants that ‘his wife and daughters-in-law may be called and call themselves Dom (noble honorific) according to our ordinance…’. What was a privilege became a manifest abuse, and countless people committed it.
Porto Santo (raids on the island)

The small island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), isolated and undefended, was raided and sacked several times by corsairs and pirates. Although they could not hope to find rich and plentiful plunder there, they could at least count on complete impunity and on the hasty flight of the inhabitants to the mountain tops, which left the field clear for the raiders’ rapacity. It was chiefly the summit of Pico do Castelo (‘castle peak’), difficult to reach and easy to defend against anyone trying to climb it, that served as a refuge for the poor inhabitants of the neighbouring island, who sheltered there from the ferocity of the pirates. The steep mountain gained regular defences, with guns and battlements, only at the beginning of the 18th century. In earlier times the inhabitants relied solely on the sheer slopes of the peak, where plain boulders rolled freely down the sides were enough to repel any assault. The fort of the town (*vila*), which was named São José in honour of King Joseph I, was built in the time of the Marquis of Pombal. We do not know what means of defence Porto Santo had before that time in the event of an attack, but they must have been very weak and useless, for there is no record of any resistance to the various pirate raids (see Preston).

The earliest recorded raid was the one carried out there by French pirates on 2 October 1566. On the following day they landed at Funchal and made the terrible assault on the city of which the Madeiran chronicles speak with such horror.

In 1617 the Moroccans attacked Porto Santo and sacked the town (*vila*). Among other damage, they completely destroyed the archives of the municipal council and of the parish church. The same happened in 1667.

On 11 December 1690 two French corsairs ‘invaded this island, says an eyewitness, and sacked it, above all the church, which was stripped of everything, of vestments, silver and books... and the vicar, Dr Estêvão de Vasconcelos, could do nothing but consume the Most Holy Sacrament. . . and with only the ampulla in his hand he withdrew to the Pico do Castelo. . . ’ No further details of this attack are known.
In January 1708 the island was sacked again by French pirates, who, besides the plunder in which they indulged, set fire to the parish church and to some houses in the town.

Rebelo da Silva relates in his *Historia de Portugal* that in 1641 Porto Santo was all but blockaded by a squadron of twelve Ottoman sail. However, when the inhabitants learned of the revolution of 1 December 1640, they ‘greeted the news with repeated salvoes of artillery and musketry, and the Turks, alarmed by the noise and ignorant of its cause, judged it prudent to yield and disappeared’.

It is certain that Algerian pirates attacked and sacked the neighbouring island of Porto Santo on various occasions, chiefly during the 17th century, but we cannot establish the years in which these attacks took place, since we have found no detailed account of them.
Porto Santo (vegetation)

The passages that follow on the vegetation of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) are the work of the distinguished botanist Carlos de Meneses, co-author of this work. They are taken from a fine study published in the Funchal *Diario Popular* of 1 and 2 April 1908, and are reproduced here because they are judged to be of particular interest to the inhabitants of that island.

‘Phylloxera, which first appeared in Madeira in 1872, showed itself on Porto Santo only much later; yet although its introduction there is recent, the damage it has caused is already considerable. The vines most heavily attacked have been those on clay soils, but in some places, though few, where the soil is sandy, the vineyards have also been invaded by this insect. We are told that almost all the vines of the coastal strip have disappeared, and that today only two cultivated belts of vineyard remain there, one at Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit) and the other at Ponta (‘point’).

Since the low-lying land of Porto Santo is almost entirely calcareous, it might perhaps be advisable to try *Vitis monticola* there, and more particularly *V. Berlandieri*, American species that could be grafted with the grape varieties now cultivated. Unless serious attention is given to introducing resistant vines suited to the soils, the viticulture of Porto Santo may yet suffer great devastation, for experience has shown that sand does not always form a dyke against the invasion of the terrible phylloxera.

Fig trees and mulberries are the only fruit trees that are plentiful on Porto Santo. The almond, the peach, the pomegranate, the prickly pear (*tabaibeira*), the olive, the pear and the *pereiro* are also cultivated there, but all of them are more or less rare. The pears known as *caniças*, the only ones we saw on that island, are excellent, and the olives from the trees in the town, though inferior to those of Portugal, can be used for eating.

It is reasonable to believe that the olive trees growing in the gardens of the town of Porto Santo were brought from the mainland, since both the shape of their leaves and the size of their fruit differ from the varieties *madeirensis* and *buxifolia* of *Olea europea*, which grow wild in the archipelago. The latter variety occurs on the cliffs (*rochas*) of Pico de Ana Ferreira (‘Ana Ferreira’s peak’) on that island, where it is no more than a simple shrub.

The junipers (*Juniperus phoenicea*) and dragon trees (*Dracoena Draco*) that covered Porto Santo at the time of its discovery are now completely extinct. The only native shrubby species worth mentioning that are still found there are the boxthorn (*espinheiro*, *Lycium Europoeum*), the *marmulano* (Sideroxylon marmulano, a shrub) (*Sideroxylon Marmulano*), the cliff box (*buxo da rocha*, *Catha Dryandri*), the heath (*urze*, *Erica scuparia*) and the olive referred to above.

Apart from the fruit trees already mentioned, the only other woody species foreign to the island are the following: the tamarisk (*Tamarix Gallica*), introduced in 1834 by João António Pedroso and now fairly common; the white poplar (*Populus alba*), which is also frequent; the pine (*Pinus Pinaster*), grown on a very small scale at Enguias (‘eels’) and at Curral do Canário; the oleaster (*Eloeagnus angustifolia*); the date palm (*Phoenix dactylifera*); *Myoporum acuminatum*; and *Nicotiana glauca*. These last two species, which are becoming increasingly frequent, were introduced by the late botanist João Maria Moniz.

Two specimens of the Aleppo or Jerusalem pine that we saw growing on Porto Santo were felled some years ago. This species ought to adapt well to the limestone soils in the north of the island, which cannot be used for agriculture.

Counting native and naturalised plants together with those cultivated on a large scale, Porto Santo has 325 species, 317 of them phanerogams and 8 vascular cryptogams. The families most widely represented on the island are the Leguminosae with 40 species, the Compositae and the Gramineae with 38 each, the Cruciferae with 15, the Umbelliferae and Caryophyllaceae with 13, and the Labiatae and Chenopodiaceae with 11. Only two species appear to be peculiar to the island: *Cheiranthus arbuscula* and *Pedrosia porto-sanctana*.

Of the many fodder species found on Porto Santo, we shall mention only the following, because they are abundant: the *serralha* (*Lonchus oleracens*), the *leituga* (*Crepis divaricata*), various clovers, two *Melilotus*, the *azeda* (*Scorpiurus sulcata*), the *balanco* (*Avena fatua* and *A. barbata*), *Briza maxima*, *B. minor* and the *azevem* (*Lolium perenne*). Two species of *Mesembrianthemum* (*M. crystallinum* and *M. nodiflorum*) yield soda, and a textile fibre used in making ropes is extracted from *Lavatera arborea*. The white poppy, which yields opium, is very common among the cornfields’.
Porto Santo (town and municipality)

The town (*vila*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is also known by the name of Baleira, and we have already given an account of it on p. 117 of the 1st volume of this work, to which we refer the reader. As the seat of a captaincy, its donataries held the almost discretionary powers conferred on them by the letters of grant (carta de doação). But as it was also the seat of a municipality, the municipality, through its charters (foral), granted the people certain rights and privileges that tempered the powers of the captain-donataries. The letter of grant given to Bartolomeu Perestrelo on 1 November 1446, as donatary of Porto Santo, makes express reference to the charter that was to be given to the future town, which was created a few years after that date. We have found no trace of this charter, however, although one generally accompanied the establishment of new municipalities. It must nevertheless be supposed that it was modelled on the same lines as those of the other towns and municipalities of this archipelago.

In 1834 Porto Santo was treated as a Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) for administrative purposes, and João de Santana de Vasconcelos was its first superintendent (provedor), appointed by royal decree (*alvará*) of the prefect (*prefeito*) of the province dated 9 August of that year. With the administrative reform of 1835, the island of Porto Santo became a municipality (*concelho*), its first administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) being João José de Alencastre, appointed on 25 November of the same year.
Harbours of Madeira

Of the ports of the archipelago, until recently those of Funchal and of the south of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) were considered good; those of Abra, Machico, Santa Cruz, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol, Porto Moniz and Porto da Cruz were regarded as tolerable; and those of Caniçal, Porto Novo, Reis Magos, Oliveira, Campanário, Lugar de Baixo, Madalena do Mar, Anjos, Fajã do Mar, Calheta, Jardim do Mar, Paul do Mar, Pesqueiro, Seixal, Fajã da Areia, Ponta Delgada, Boaventura, São Jorge and Faial as poor. The ports of the parishes of Porto Moniz and Porto da Cruz are considered good landing places when winds blow from the southern quarter, since all traffic along the whole southern coast of Madeira is then impossible, although this happens only a few times each year. Over the last thirty years, conditions at the ports of these places have improved considerably with the building of small quays and landing places and with extension and repair work on those already existing.

In September 1944 the engineer Henrique Schreck, technical director of the Autonomous Board of the Ports of the Madeira Archipelago (*Junta Autónoma dos Portos do Arquipélago da Madeira*), acting under the measures taken by the central government concerning works to be carried out in the various ports of the mainland and the islands, presented to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district a well-prepared report on the various works to be carried out shortly in the ports of our archipelago.

Anyone wishing to acquire detailed knowledge of the ports of Madeira, and especially that of Funchal, should read the 5th volume of the important work *Os Portos Marítimos de Portugal e Ilhas Adjacentes* by the distinguished engineer Adolfo Loureiro.
See the harbour of Funchal (*Porto do Funchal*) and each of the names listed above.
Fishing ports

Listed below are the fishing ports of this archipelago. They are the principal ones, and in them customs supervision is carried out and the tax levied on the fish landed there is collected. There are other small ports where fishing is also practised, but on a very limited scale and sometimes only temporarily.

As stated above, the fishing industry is of relative importance in this archipelago, since some two thousand people are employed in it as their sole occupation, besides those who take it up only temporarily and at certain times of the year. Several thousand people, therefore, depend exclusively on it. It is regrettable that there is no industrial and commercial organisation to protect the workers of this most useful industry effectively and shield them from the unbridled greed of vile and inhuman speculators. It is also greatly to be deplored that no mutual-aid body has been created to provide for the sickness, incapacity and invalidity of these poor and unprotected fishermen.

According to information supplied by the distinguished ichthyologist Adolfo César de Noronha, the fish caught most abundantly in Madeira is the black scabbardfish (*espada preta*). Three and four thousand scabbardfish often appear in a single day in the city market alone, and it is widely eaten by all social classes. According to the same information, for some years the tuna, ‘which comes from no one knows where and goes no one knows where’, has at certain seasons been caught abundantly in our seas, and is one of the most profitable catches for the fishermen.

Portugal (newspaper)
Only a few issues of this newspaper appeared, the first on 11 January 1891.
Portugal (Dom Afonso de)

He was the 1st Count of Vimioso and fought at the battle of Alcácer Quibir, where he was taken prisoner. In 1549, with the authorisation of King John III, he bought the captaincy of Machico from António da Silveira, becoming its 6th donatary (*donatário*). He died in Africa, a captive of the Moors, but outlived his son Dom Francisco de Portugal.
See Vimioso (Counts of).
Portugal (Dom Francisco de)

He fought alongside his father at the battle of Alcácer Quibir, where he was wounded and taken prisoner. Having managed to return to his homeland, he took the side of the Prior of Crato, to whom he rendered notable services, and died gloriously at the famous naval battle of Vila Franca do Campo on 26 July 1582. He was the 7th donatary (*donatário*) of Machico and 2nd Count of Vimioso, because only long after the disaster of Alcácer Quibir was it learnt that Dom Afonso de Portugal had not died in the battle but was a prisoner of the Moors in Africa. Philip II gave the captaincy of Machico to Tristão Vaz da Veiga while the 2nd Count of Vimioso was still alive.
See Vimioso (Counts of).
Portugal (Dom Martinho de)

He was the second prelate of this diocese and the first and only archbishop of Funchal. Although through illegitimacy, he belonged to one of the oldest and noblest families of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), being a close relative of King John III, whose favourite and Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) he was. He was born in Évora in the last quarter of the 15th century and died in Lisbon on 15 November 1547.

We do not know whether it was owing to his personal connections and kinship with the royal house, or to whatever merits of his own he may have possessed, that he held the highest offices and carried out important diplomatic missions, as representative of John III in Rome and as nuncio and ambassador of the Pope in Lisbon; he was also bishop of Viseu and held other high offices at court. He was one of the diplomats whom John III charged with negotiating in Rome the establishment of the tribunal of the Inquisition, and Alexandre Herculano refers to this prelate at length in his work *Da origem e estabelecimento da inquisição em Portugal*. The great historian, who showed great partiality in this work, as almost everyone acknowledges today, holds the worst opinion of Dom Martinho de Portugal, going so far as to say of him that ‘he was a man without morals and without beliefs, for whom religion was nothing more than a political instrument.

The archbishopric of Funchal was established in 1533 and abolished in 1551. The reasons for its creation, the dates of the bulls that instituted it and the circumstances surrounding it were briefly set out in the article Archbishopric (Vol. I, p. 77), to which we refer the reader.

Dom Martinho de Portugal, occupied with other offices, never visited his archdiocese. He sent to this island Dom Ambrósio Brandão, titular bishop of Rociona, who stayed here for about a year, from 1538 to 1539, exercising his episcopal functions. He also sent the visitors Jordão Jorge and Álvaro Dias, who attended to the observance of canonical discipline.
Portugal e Castro (Dom Manuel de)
See Castro (Dom Manuel de Portugal e).
Anthropometric Office

When Dr Joaquim Crisóstomo da Silveira was representative of the Public Prosecutor's Office (*Ministério Público*) in Funchal, an anthropometric post was installed in the court of the judicial district (*comarca*). It still existed in 1915, for on 22 July of that year the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) resolved to provide it with various items of furniture that it needed.
Campo da Barca Disinfection Station

It was built in 1904, and the land it occupies was granted free of charge by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) on 12 March 1903 and 23 March 1911.

The Disinfection Station (*Posto de Desinfecção*) of Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) opened on 29 November 1905. Its staff, consisting of a medical director, an administrator, a machinist, a head disinfector, two disinfectors and an attendant, had been approved by decree of 23 May 1904.

Home disinfections have been carried out mainly in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal, including the suburban parishes. However, when their services are requested, the disinfection staff also go to parishes of other municipalities to disinfect homes where deaths from contagious diseases have occurred.
The number of home disinfections includes hospitals and charitable houses, banks, schools, pawnshops, hotels, the civil gaol, police cells and other public buildings.

The director of the Public Disinfection Station since its opening has been the distinguished physician Dr Carlos Leite Monteiro. Its administrator is Mr J. Cruz Baptista Santos, who has held this post since 3 November 1919, having been appointed to replace, on his retirement, the distinguished man of science and journalist Dr Manuel Sardinha, who had held the office since the station opened (1921).

We are pleased to record the services that the Public Disinfection Station, founded on the initiative of the late Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Dr José Leite Monteiro, then president of the District General Council, has rendered to the Madeiran population, particularly during epidemics on this island.

All the costs of maintaining the station are borne by the District General Council, and because of its public usefulness this service ought to be counted among the welfare works maintained by that Council, such as the Trapiche and Dr Câmara Pestana nursing homes, the Old People’s Home (*Asilo dos Velhinhos*), allowances to minors and the destitute, etc.
Maritime Disinfection Station

A small maritime disinfection station has existed at the Pontinha (‘little point’) since 1901. The sums raised from disinfections, after deducting the cost of buying disinfectants, form revenue of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), which pays the rent of the building where the station operates. The station's staff, an inspector and a guard, are paid by the Government (1921).
Municipal Medical Post
It began operating on 10 April 1889 and was created by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) under the presidency of the late Viscount of Ribeiro Real.
The X-ray apparatus at the medical post was acquired by the Council in 1922; there had been another there which became unusable.
See Health Services.
Areeiro meteorological station
