Meteorological stations

The Funchal meteorological station, set up in the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence), began operating in January 1865 under the direction of the late military engineer António Pedro de Azevedo. It stands at an altitude of 21.2 m and is subordinate to the Infante Dom Luís Observatory, with which it communicates by telegraph every day. Observations are made at 6 and 9 a.m., at 3 and 5 p.m. and at 9 p.m., the last of these being optional (1921).
Before this timetable came into force, observations were made at 7 and 9 a.m., at noon, at 3 p.m. and at 9 p.m.

In 1901 a room was built to house the station’s records, and in 1913 a terrace was built over the station, reached by an outside staircase. Both improvements were carried out on the recommendation of the 1st assistant, Colonel Eduardo Agostinho Pereira, who died on 22 September 1918.

The Funchal meteorological station has a barograph, a psychrograph, an anemograph, an Adie barometer, an August psychrometer, maximum and minimum thermometers, an evaporimeter, a rain gauge, etc. The station usually supplies the press each day with a bulletin giving the wind direction, the state of the sky, the pressure, the temperature and the amount of rain that has fallen in 24 hours (1921).

Near Pico do Areeiro (‘sand-pit peak’), at an altitude of 1700 metres above sea level, a wooden house was built in 1895 to serve as a meteorological station and as living quarters for the observers. This establishment, however, which cost the State some 5 *contos de réis* (*conto*: one million réis), never came into operation, owing to the indifference with which governments and administrative bodies generally regard services of a scientific nature.

The house, which was in the charge of the Public Works Department (*Direção das Obras Públicas*), was handed over to the Madeira Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) on 13 August 1913 so that a meteorological station could be installed there. When that body was abolished, it passed into the possession of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*). The ministerial order authorising the transfer of the Areeiro (‘sand pit’) building to the Agricultural Board is dated 19 April 1913.
The tower that held the compartment for the meteorological instruments, reached by an outside staircase, was blown down by the great gales of 25 and 26 February 1920.

The foregoing is a verbatim transcription of what appears on p. 326 of vol. II of the first edition of this *Elucidário*. To it we can now add the following valuable information, kindly supplied to us by the present director of the Funchal Meteorological Station, António Feliciano de Castilho, which thus expands the earlier data already known.

‘The former Post now has the status of a Meteorological Observatory. It is still housed in the São Lourenço Palace, but is on the point of being moved to a building of its own. Its equipment and functions have been considerably expanded. It is headed by a first assistant of the Infante Dom Luís Observatory and has technical oversight of all the other stations and posts in the archipelago. The present head of the Observatory is First Assistant António Feliciano de Castilho.

Its instruments today consist of an Adie barometer, a barograph, a psychrometer, a hygrograph, a thermograph, a rain gauge and a recording rain gauge, a maximum and a minimum thermometer, an ordinary thermometer and a maximum solar-temperature thermometer, an anemograph, a heliograph, two solarigraphs, a solarimeter and an evaporimeter.

Observations are made at 6 a.m., 12 noon and 5 p.m. to determine temperature, humidity, wind, pressure, sunshine, the state of the weather, etc. Besides the Funchal station, we also have the following:
Areeiro

The Areeiro meteorological station stands near Pico do Areeiro at an altitude of 1,610 metres. A house had already been built on this site in 1895 to serve as a post and as quarters for the staff in charge of the service, but for various reasons it never came into operation (see Areeiro). In November 1936 a temperature and rain-gauge post began operating there, supplying data on rainfall and temperature. In December 1939 this post was enlarged and equipped with the following instruments: a barometer, a barograph, a psychrometer, a maximum and a minimum thermometer, a rain gauge, a wind vane and an anemometer. Observations were made at 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., collecting data on pressure, temperature, humidity, wind, rainfall, visibility and the development of the weather. In January 1942 observations were changed to 6 a.m., 12 noon and 5 p.m. Because of its importance, this station is about to be installed in a building of its own and to become part of the international service.
Encumeada de São

Vicente, Santana, Lugar de Baixo and Monte Sanatorium: these stations, set up in June 1941, January 1942, June 1941 and June 1941 respectively, make three observations a day, at 6 a.m., 12 noon and 5 p.m., collecting the following data: temperature, humidity, rainfall, visibility, evaporation, and wind direction and speed. For this purpose they are equipped with maximum and minimum thermometers, a psychrometer, a thermohygrograph, a rain gauge, an evaporimeter and a wind vane. At the Monte Sanatorium there is also a heliograph, which supplies data on sunshine. Both the Encumeada and the Santana stations had already been operating as temperature and rain-gauge posts since December 1938.
Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’)

This station, on the island of the same name beside the radio-telegraph station, was set up in July 1941 by Manuel Melquíades Alarques, then in charge of the Funchal post, and initially made two observations, at 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. It has the same instruments as the preceding stations and supplies the same data. Its observation times are the same as those of the others, at 6 a.m., 12 noon and 5 p.m.
There are also the temperature and rain-gauge posts of Madalena do Mar, Queimadas, Ribeira Brava and Santo da Serra, all set up between November 1936 and December 1938.

In addition to these, we have the rain-gauge posts of Caramujo, Machico, Montado do Pereiro, Ponta do Pargo, Porto Moniz, Rabaçal, Ribeiro Frio, Santa Cruz, Santo António, Canhas, Bica da Cana, the Paul da Serra and São Vicente. Of these posts the oldest is that of Santa Cruz, set up in November 1936, and the most recent is that of São Vicente, set up in May 1945.

All the data from the meteorological services of Madeira are published monthly in the monthly summary of the Infante D. Luís Central Meteorological Observatory (*Observatório Central Meteorológico do Infante D. Luís*) in Lisbon, in the weather report of the *Jornal das Frutas da Madeira* and in the *Boletim Mensal do Funchal*. Every year, all these data appear in the *Anais do Observatório Central*. The Funchal Observatory publishes a daily bulletin containing the reports from the stations of Funchal, Arieiro, the Sanatorium, Santana, Lugar de Baixo and Porto Santo, and from the post at Santo da Serra.

All these stations and posts form part of the National Climate Service (*Serviço Nacional de Clima*), which is run by the Central Meteorological Observatory of Lisbon, attached to the Faculty of Sciences. Its Director since 1937 has been Dr Herculano Amorim Ferreira, full professor at the same Faculty.

The present state of the Meteorological Services of Madeira is owed to the great impetus given to the National Climate Service by the present Director of the Central Observatory, who came to Madeira in June 1938 solely to study the needs of this Service. With the same aim, Dr Amaro Monteiro, Head of the Climate Services of the Central Observatory, also visited Funchal in July 1941. Many of these stations are fitted with equipment bought by the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), under the distinguished presidency of Dr João Abel de Freitas, and are in the charge of the staff of the Agricultural Services, a department headed by the agronomist Maurílio Ferraz e Silva. The Delegation of the National Fruit Board (*Junta Nacional das Frutas*), then directed by the agronomist António Teixeira de Sousa, also set up some of the first temperature and rain-gauge posts, which were later handed over to the Directorate of Agriculture.
Also worthy of note is the selfless and most valuable work of Dr João d’Almada, now deceased, and Vice-Admiral Hugo C. de Lacerda Castelo Branco.’
By-laws

As is well known, Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*) have the right to lay down, within the area of their municipalities, certain legal rules of a local character in keeping with the general laws of the country. These rules must be strictly observed, and any breach of them incurs various penalties. In this archipelago, before 1834, it not infrequently happened that these particular codes of law, or municipal bylaws (*posturas*), clashed with decrees issued by the central government, prompting the higher authorities to intervene forcefully and compel the municipal council sessions to comply fully with those decrees.
All the Councils of this archipelago, at various times, established and enforced many ‘by-laws’, some of which were published in the press.

As an attempt at ‘codification’, we are aware that in 1841, 1842, 1856, 1890, 1897 and 1900 respectively, the Municipal Councils of Santana, Calheta, Machico, Porto Moniz, São Vicente and Ponta do Sol had their by-laws then in force printed as pamphlets, a sound measure for good municipal administration.

In 1912 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) published, in a volume of 245 pages, the *Código de Posturas do Município do Funchal*, a collection of the by-laws then in force, the great majority of which are still in force; the oldest dates from 1881. It is an excellent work of codification, compiled in particular by the secretary of the Council, Luís Betencourt Miranda.
Pota (Ommastrephes sagittatus)

A cephalopod mollusc that lives in depths beyond 350 *braças* (fathoms), but which in summer often appears at the surface of the ocean, especially in August and September. Some specimens weigh more than 10 kilograms. The flavour of this mollusc, when young, recalls that of the squid and the octopus. The *pota* is a valuable and much sought-after bait for fishing tuna, black scabbardfish (*espada*) and other species.
Hoopoe (Upupa epops)
A bird of the family Upupidae that visits Madeira and is said once to have formed part of the island’s native fauna.
Povo (O)
It began publication on 1 January 1883 and ceased on 4 February 1888, after 260 issues.

Another periodical with the same title began publication on 31 January 1907 and ceased on 30 September 1917, after 1248 issues. It was published weekly, but from 15 December 1910 to the end of October 1913 it was a daily newspaper.
Settlement and colonisation

In the article Discovery of the Archipelago we devoted a number of pages to the much-debated question of the first encounter with, or ‘reconnaissance’ of, these distant islands. It still awaits a sound and definitive answer, particularly as regards the date of that auspicious event, the daring navigators who undertook it and the chance circumstances that accompanied it.

What seems beyond doubt is that, once the truth of the event had been recognised and the geographical position of this unexpected find recorded, little time can have passed before active exploration and immediate settlement began, although the details of the first fruitful attempts made to that end are unknown.

Despite the extremely dense forest that covered the whole of Madeira and the incredibly rugged nature of its slopes and hillsides, the first settlers lost no time in exploring the coastline quickly. They made several landings at the most accessible points, as an essential preparation for the colonising movement that was to begin at once.

Many mountain heights, ridges and crags, valleys and ravines, streams, landing places and headlands along the coast were named at that time, and their names have remained for ever inscribed in the toponymy of Madeira. Thus words such as Seixo (‘pebble’), Oliveira, Garajau (‘tern’), Cruz, Formosa, Socorridos, Espírito Santo, Girão, Vera-Cruz, etc., etc., became proper names and came to designate things and places that have survived unchanged through five centuries to the present day.

With the extraordinary development of the various industries and the valuable means of action now so widely at our disposal, we can scarcely imagine what it meant to colonise an unknown island lost in the vastness of the ocean, five hundred miles from the mainland, which kept up communications with mainland Portugal only in the summer season. An old manuscript records ‘that the king and Prince Henry the Navigator had news of Madeira from year to year in the summer, because in those early days no one sailed in winter’.

Besides the innate worth of their race and their tenacious love of work, the early settlers could count only on the great mildness of the climate and the abundant fertility of the soil. Like forerunners of a legendary Robinson, isolated on a deserted and forsaken island, they performed true miracles of heroism in breaking the virgin ground, building their comfortless dwellings and forming small hamlets, which they came to call “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*).

When this auspicious colonisation began, the island was divided for the purposes of public administration into two distinct zones. Their limits were marked by a dividing line running between the point of Oliveira (Caniço) and the point of Tristão (Porto do Moniz). The whole northern coast and part of the southern coast formed the captaincy of Machico, and the rest the captaincy of Funchal, governed respectively by Tristão Vaz Teixeira and João Gonçalves Zarco, as already mentioned in the articles Captaincies and Donataries.

Among the companions and contemporaries of the latter captain-donatary, the names are known of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, Francisco Carvalhal, João Lourenço, Rui Pais, João Afonso, António Gago, Lourenço Gomes, Francisco Alcoforado, Vasco Delgado, Álvaro Afonso, Aires Lordelo, Vasco Esteves, Manuel Afonso de Sanha and João de Prado, preserved in old chronicles and various books of nobility. All of them obtained land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), much of which was entailed by their heirs and successors, who became the founders of the oldest and noblest Madeiran families. See Sesmarias and Entails.

Invested with the broad powers conferred on them by the ‘letters of grant’ and assuming supreme direction of all matters of public administration, the captain-donataries at once became the most eminent settlers of the nascent Madeiran colony. They acquired the greatest prestige and the most dominant influence, which some of them later managed to turn into the award of high titles of nobility and the acquisition of large landed estates.
The old chronicles have left us very little information about the first settlement, particularly regarding the number, social standing, personal qualities and places of origin of the first colonists.

It is known only vaguely that they included people of noble descent, others from the common classes, artisans and tillers of the soil, and also some criminals serving prison sentences. Gaspar Frutuoso tells us that João Gonçalves Zarco ‘had refused to bring those guilty on account of the faith, or treason, or as thieves’. The approximate number of these people is not known, nor is the proportion in which the various social strata were represented in these first waves of settlers. It is conjectured with good reason that they were not few, and that their number soon grew rapidly with the frequent arrival of other colonists and especially with the great legion of Moorish and Black slaves, which quickly became a large multitude. This was demanded by the extensive and arduous work of breaking the virgin ground, the active cultivators being spurred on by the exuberant fertility of the soil and the great mildness of the climate.

It was, however, in the period after the one we are dealing with, that is, in the second half of the 15th century, that settlement grew more substantially. It came from settlers arriving from mainland Portugal and from countless African slaves, and also from many foreigners from various European countries, some of them of old families, who came to seek in this new promised land what their own homeland could not give them.

Settlement began within the area where the city of Funchal stands today, and at the same time at various points considered most suitable for the purpose, such as Machico, Santa Cruz, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, Ponta do Sol and Calheta, as well as other places on the southern coast of the island.

The greatest obstacle to immediate and effective settlement was the dense, gigantic forest that covered the whole surface of the land judged suitable for the first agricultural ventures. A violent fire, perhaps recklessly started but also necessarily imposed by the pressing force of circumstances, opened up vast clearings suitable for bringing these wide tracts of hitherto unproductive land under the plough. How far this fire’s destruction reached, and what its immediate consequences were, is not easy to say today; of particular interest on this point is what may be read in the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and its annotations, and also in the pages of the *Elucidário Madeirense*. See Fires.

The remarkable fertility of Madeiran soil was soon recognised, but it was also readily apparent that the most profitable crops could not reach a high and rewarding level of prosperity except at the cost of a difficult and expensive system of irrigation. And so the first levadas (irrigation channels) appeared.

No Madeiran is unaware of what these aqueducts are: long, narrow channels cut into the ground and generally built of solid *alvenaria* (local name for compact basalt used as building stone). They carry the precious water that gives the land the blood that makes it fertile, and gives the plants the sap and life that make them yield abundantly.
In the article on levadas (II-235, 269) we have included a detailed study of this important subject, which so closely concerns the economy of the archipelago.

This painstaking labour spent on farming the land was regularly rewarded by the grants that the captain-donataries made to the cultivators, under the instructions they had received from Prince Henry the Navigator and by applying the system of *sesmarias* (royal land grants to settlers on condition of cultivation) already in use in mainland Portugal. These first grants were later modified with wider privileges: the right to own the improvements (*benfeitorias*, tenant-made works on the land) was established, together with the power to grant the land on perpetual lease (*aforar*) and even to sell it, subject to certain conditions that were not regarded as very burdensome or oppressive.

The number of the earliest settlers who came from the mainland was relatively large, but insufficient for farming on a large scale, above all because of the rugged terrain, the density of the forest, the heavy labour of irrigation and other local circumstances.

As stated above, the soil of Madeira was watered by the sweat of Black, Moorish and mulatto slaves, who, by intermarrying with the settlers from the mainland who held *sesmarias*, so profoundly debased the native purity of the race. At the end of the 15th century there were approximately two thousand slaves on this island, a considerable number beside the European population, which then amounted to some fifteen to eighteen thousand inhabitants.

The system of *sesmarias* already mentioned, by distributing the land advantageously, favoured the establishment of many “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*), where the first settlers lived with their families and slaves. They soon became the owners of that land and left its cultivation to tenants and slaves. Then came the entailing of land, and the wealthy grantees and the more fortunate tenants abandoned farming and sought, in the more densely populated centres, a life free of the toils of the early settlers. The so-called *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant) was born, and three-quarters of the arable land of this island had been turned into entails and entailed estates.

To determine with true precision the year in which the settlement of this island began, one would need to be able to fix the date of its discovery, which has still not been established with complete certainty. In the letter of grant (carta de doação) from Prince Henry to the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), dated 18 September 1460, to which the publication entitled *Alguns documentos do Archivo Nacional da Torre do Tombo acerca das navegações e conquistas dos portuguezes* refers, we read: ‘I began to settle my island of Madeira some thirty-five years ago now, and likewise that of Porto Santo...’ From these words it follows that colonisation began around 1425, that is, a few years after the discovery, which agrees with the indications of various chroniclers.

The first priests to perform ecclesiastical duties were the Franciscan friars who came in the fleet carrying the earliest settlers. They served in the various chapels that were soon founded, which would have been those of Santa Catarina, São Paulo and St Sebastian, and perhaps even in rustic, improvised chapels temporarily adapted for that purpose.

On the so-called ‘settled farmsteads’ (*fazendas povoadas*), established at various points on the island, many chapels were built, each with its own private chaplain. Most of them became ‘curacies’ (*curato*) and ‘chaplaincies’ (capelania) with the standing of a parish, and they were the seats of the future, legally constituted parishes (*freguesia*). For this reason, given the evidence the old chronicles provide, it is not easy to determine with complete precision the date on which some of the parishes organised in the 15th and 16th centuries were created, if we take the meaning of these groupings of inhabitants in the sense given to them today. ‘Chaplaincy’, ‘curacy’ and ‘parish’ are terms used, at times interchangeably, to designate what today we very properly call a parish. Thus these chronicles state, and the annotations to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ repeat, that the parishes of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and Calheta (‘small cove’) were created in 1430, and that the parish of Machico – capital of the captaincy and a village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) intensively settled from the beginning of colonisation – was created in 1450. It is known that this locality came to rival Funchal in its expansion and development, although only in the early days of that colonisation.

It was around 1430 that the first parish was established in Funchal, covering a vast area. Its centre was one of the chapels mentioned above, although some reasons argue in favour of the small chapel of St Sebastian. In 1438 its seat was fixed in the church of Santa Maria, or of the ‘Conceição de Baixo’, which Prince Henry the Navigator had ordered to be built on the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes, a short distance from the beach, and which took the name of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*).

In 1508 the parish moved its seat to the so-called ‘Igreja Grande’ (Great Church), which was still at a backward stage of construction. Fifty years later, that is, in 1558, the city of Funchal and its surroundings were divided into two parishes, with their respective seats in the church of the Sé – Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) – and in the church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major).

By the end of the middle years of the 15th century, the period to which we have been referring in particular, there were already ten autonomous parishes in this archipelago, in which all the religious services of independent parishes functioned regularly. Their seats were in the most central chapels existing in these settlements.

It should be remembered that, in addition to the obligatory religious services held at the parish seats, many acts of worship continued to be performed in various chapels, as mentioned above. These were led by other priests and received valuable assistance from various members of the Seraphic Order, scattered among their modest and dispersed convents.

By the end of this period (1425-1450), the work of settlement had already reached a remarkable stage of development: one or two years later, that is, in 1451 or 1452, the settlement of Funchal was raised to the rank of town (*vila*), with the privileges and prerogatives belonging to municipalities, as happened at about the same time with the seats of the captaincies of Machico and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that Madeiran settlement reached its greatest development only in the second half of the 15th century and the first half of the following one. This came with the ever-growing progress of agriculture and of the industries derived from it, such as the large-scale production of sugar and wine, and the export of timber, orchil (a dye lichen), woad and many other agricultural products. Closely bound up with this progress was a great expansion of the settlements. New parishes were created one after another, and the town of Funchal was soon raised to the rank of city. A few years later it became the seat of a diocese, the first to be founded in our overseas dominions.

Although the official grants of the captaincies of Machico, Porto Santo and Funchal to Tristão Vaz, Bartolomeu Perestrelo and João Gonçalves Zargo date from 1440, 1446 and 1450 respectively, it is certain that these first three captains-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) were invested from the outset with the direct exercise of their offices and privileges, when the settlement of the Madeiran archipelago began around 1425.

It is said that on that occasion Prince Henry the Navigator – to whom these islands had been granted by the monarch, and who was moreover Grand Master of the Order of Christ, to which they ‘belonged in spiritual matters’ – gave the donataries (*donatário*) the instructions needed to regulate the various branches of public administration, fixing the scope of their powers and perhaps specifying the authority they might use in administering and applying justice. If such instructions existed, as Gaspar Frutuoso supposes and as we are inclined to believe, they were not recorded in any known document, or all knowledge of them was lost when other provisions on the same matter were enacted.

What is known, however, is that the donataries’ powers became truly discretionary in every branch of administration. Many facts prove this, and the charters of grant themselves confirm it, stating expressly that he (the captain-donatary) ‘shall have throughout this aforesaid land jurisdiction, for me and in my name, in civil and criminal matters, saving death or the cutting-off of a limb’. It is clear that, apart from the infliction of the ‘ultimate penalty’ and of the ‘cutting-off of a limb’, which were reserved to the royal power, the governing authority of the captains-donatary extended to all the services of the State, including the collection of the various taxes and dues, the distribution of uncultivated land and the appointment to the various public offices, etc.

In the more important localities the captains-donatary had their representatives in the conduct of public affairs. These were the *ouvidores* and *alcaides*, who were specially charged with administrative duties and with collecting the various taxes and dues. Following the example of their chiefs, from whom they received their appointments in the early days of settlement, they not infrequently abused the powers vested in them, and were at times the blind instruments of the captains-donatary’s own high-handedness.

It is well known that only from 1834, when constitutional government was established, did Madeira begin to be administered entirely under the same laws that were in full force in mainland Portugal. Until then the Adjacent Islands (Ilhas Adjacentes) were regarded as overseas provinces, and their public administration was generally conducted under special laws, which often differed fundamentally from those in force on the mainland.

It is not surprising that this discrepancy was even more marked when settlement began, given the unforeseen and extraordinary circumstances of the time, and even leaving aside the arbitrary acts and excesses committed by the captains-donatary and their representatives in the various localities, as we have already pointed out above.

There are weighty reasons for believing that Prince Henry the Navigator gave the first three donataries the necessary instructions when he placed them in charge of the work of the early colonisation. The historian of the islands refers in particular to the ‘Regimento’, the regulations (*regimento*) that governed the division of this island into its two captaincies and the granting of arable land under the system of *sesmarias* (royal land grants to settlers on condition of cultivation). These are the oldest measures of government of which any record exists.

For the distribution of plots of land, the already familiar system of *sesmarias* was adopted (see Gama Barros III, p. 699 ff.), though perhaps with the modifications that local circumstances advised. A *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) who did not make proper use of the land within five years lost his right to it. These provisions were later modified, and wider privileges were granted to those who cultivated the land, such as the right of ownership of the ‘improvements’ (*benfeitorias*, tenant-made works on the land) and the power to grant on perpetual lease (*aforar*) and even to sell that same land, subject to certain conditions which were not then regarded as burdensome or oppressive, as we have already said in a previous article.

We do not know the precise date on which the ‘Regimentos’ and instructions we have been referring to were drawn up and granted, but they must predate the royal letters of King Duarte of 26 September 1433. By these letters the archipelago was granted to Prince Henry, and its spiritual jurisdiction to the Order of Christ, of which the prince was Grand Master. We believe that these royal letters were the full confirmation of grants made earlier, perhaps by John I, the prince having held the entire lordship of these islands since the beginning of settlement.

In the letters granting the three captaincies to the first donataries, the prince mentions a ‘Foral’, a charter (*foral*), and we do not know whether this was a document distinct from the instructions we have referred to. It certainly existed, however, because the ‘Foral’ granted in 1515 by King Manuel I to the municipalities of Funchal, Ponta do Sol and Calheta contains an express reference to the charter granted by Prince Henry, as can be seen on page 494 of the notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’. Elsewhere we refer at greater length to the documents cited here and to the prince’s role in the great enterprise of the early colonisation of this archipelago, and to those pages we direct the patient reader’s attention.

After the ‘Regimento’ and the ‘Foral’ granted by the prince, whose dates are unknown, and the royal decrees of King Duarte of 1433, confirmed by Afonso V, the letters of grant from Prince Henry to the first donataries, dated 1440, 1446 and 1450, are the oldest known documents of a governmental nature concerning the early public administration of this archipelago. They record important legal provisions to be observed, and they also list the high privileges the donataries might enjoy and the various dues and taxes they were entitled to collect.

The archive of the Funchal Council holds the registers of several ‘chapters’ issued by Prince Henry and by the mastership of the Order of Christ, dated 1450 and the following years, towards the close of the period we have dealt with in these articles. They concern the appointment of *alcaides*, the collection of taxes and other administrative measures, and it would take us too far afield to describe them in detail.

It was, however, in the second half of the 15th century and the first half of the next that many royal decrees on various matters of government were ‘promulgated’. We do not mention them here, as they fall outside the period within which we have set the events briefly recounted above.

Of particular relevance to this subject, we published in *O Jornal* in July and August 1943 a series of articles under the title ‘Comêço do Povoamento Madeirense – 1425-1450’, of which only a few passages are transcribed above, since it was impossible to reproduce them in full in these pages.
Praça da Rainha (square)
It was built in 1839 on land that had previously been used to store the boats and anchors belonging to the Military Train.

In May 1877 the square was granted to Dr João da Câmara Leme Homem de Vasconcelos, a physician in Funchal, as a nursery for white mulberry trees. A great many of these trees came to grow there, together with various installations for rearing and exploiting the silkworm, but these sericultural trials yielded no encouraging results.

The pavilions that stand today on the site of the former Praça da Rainha (‘Queen’s Square’) began to be built in 1897, under a concession granted by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) on 30 May 1895. The original concessionaires intended to set up a permanent bazaar of Madeiran industry and an exhibition of horticulture and floriculture there (1921).

Within the former Praça da Rainha there was once a pond (*lagoa*) built for swimming exercises, but it was never put to this use; to the west of the square there was another pond intended for the same purpose, which was likewise never used. Both ponds were filled in many years ago.
Since November 1910 the former Praça da Rainha has been called Praça do Marquês de Pombal.
The construction of the ‘Avenida do Mar’ (‘seafront avenue’) swept away the greater part of its area.
The name ‘Praça da Rainha’ was given in honour of Queen Maria II.
Praça de São João

It stood beside the Campo da Barca (‘boat field’), at the spot now called Larguinho de São João. It was demolished before 1860 and was already considered very old at the beginning of the 19th century. It is now incorporated into the Praça de Tenerife (‘Tenerife Square’).
Praça do Peixe (fish market)

Before the Praça de São Pedro (‘St Peter’s Square’) was built, fish was sold in a small market that the Council had built in 1817 for the modest sum of 159,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). This market stood on the inner side of the city’s curtain wall (*cortina*, the defensive wall of the city), to the north of the present one. The land it occupied had belonged to Diogo Berenguer, who ceded it to the Council in exchange for the site of a shop owned by the municipality (*concelho*).

The works for the present Praça do Peixe (‘fish market’), or Praça de São Pedro, were put out to tender on 8 February 1839 and the contract was awarded on the 22nd of the same month and year. Certain alterations to these works were contracted out on 17 August 1839, and the market was formally opened on 29 June 1840 (1921).

To build the Praça de São Pedro, part of the city’s curtain wall was demolished with the permission of the commander of the 9th Military Division (*Divisão Militar*, a territorial army command). The municipal butcher’s stalls and the municipal slaughterhouse, attached to the market, were not built until 1851.

It may be supposed that the place used for selling fish before 1817, which, according to the minutes of the session of 13 March of that year, was ‘most indecent and filthy’, lay close to the present São Pedro market.
The first bridge over the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’), near the Praça do Peixe, was ordered to be built by the Council on 26 August 1836. The bridge that stands there now was built in 1890.

Vicente de Paula Teixeira was the technician the Council entrusted with drawing up the plans for the works of the present Praça de São Pedro, and Vitorino Teixeira prepared the estimate for those works (1921).

Because of the construction of the ‘Avenida do Mar’ (‘seafront avenue’), this ‘Praça’ had to be demolished, and a new market was built, which we have already described on p. 361 of vol. II of this *Elucidário*.
Meadows

As is well known, there are natural meadows and artificial meadows. The former consist of various species of plants, for the most part not sown by man, while the latter are formed by a single plant that man sows and cultivates for a certain time. The meadows of Madeira belong to the first category; only a few small artificial meadows exist, at the *quinta* (country estate) of Palheiro and in a few other places.

There are natural meadows in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira, in the middle zone and in the interior. The last of these cover the largest area, although they are not always the most important as regards the quality and number of species.

In the south of Madeira, the dominant species along the whole coastal fringe is *Lotus glaucus* (*trevina*), a perennial of the family Leguminosae that grows in the driest places and is regarded by everyone as good fodder. Further inland, and common on the grassy ground of the southern lowland, are the following species: *Trifolium angustifolium*, *T. scabrum*, *Scorpiurus sulcata* (*cabreira*), *Psoralea bituminosa* (*fedegoso*), *Melilotus parviflora*, *Lotus parviflorus*, *Galactites tomentosa* (*cardo*), *Plantago lanceolata* and *P. Lagopus* (*tanchagem* or *orelha-de-cabra*), *Andropogon hirtus* (*feno*), *Avena fatua* (*balanco*), *Cynosurus echinatus*, *Cynodon Dactylon* (*grama*), *Bromus madritensis* (*panasco*), *Hordeum murinum*, *Lolium multiflorum* (*azevém*), etc.
All these plants, and many others besides, thrive in dry places; in damp places the first of the plantains mentioned, *Trifolium repens* (*trevo*), *Paspalum paspalodes*, etc., are common.

Because so much land is taken up by crops, the meadows of the lower zone cover only a limited area. Among the crops and along the edges of paths, however, many forage plants also appear, among which we shall mention *Bidens pilosa* (*amor-de-burro*), *Cichorium Endivia* (*almeirão*), *Senecio vulgaris*, *Setaria verticillata*, *Agrostis verticillata*, *Panicum sanguinale*, etc., etc. *Panicum barbinode* (*capim*) and *P. maximum* (*erva-da-Guiné*) are two thoroughly acclimatised grasses, which livestock breeders cultivate to feed their animals.

On the rocks from Seixal (‘pebble shore’) to Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) grows *Sideroxylon Marmulano* (*marmulano*), a shrub whose foliage makes good feed for livestock. Between São Vicente and Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) grows *Genista madeirensis*, a species close to the ‘gacia’ and the ‘tegasaste’ of the Canary Islands, which is also used as animal feed.

The meadows of Madeira’s lower zone (coastal belt) extend up to an altitude of 200 metres on the south coast and 150 on the north. Above that lie the meadows of the middle zone, which occupy the sides of ravines too steep to be cultivated, and various hills, peaks and other ground not yet taken over by crops. They are often cut through or bounded by pine woods, and species of the interior zone appear in them very frequently, but associated with others that only begin to dominate from a certain altitude, such as *Ornithopus perpusillus*, *O. compressus*, *Trifolium agrarium*, *Briza minor* (*chocalheirinha*), *Holcus lanatus*, *Poa trivialis*, etc. *Ulex europaeus*, gorse (*carqueja*), is abundant in Madeira’s second botanical zone, where the commonest meadow species appear to be *Vulpia bromoides* and *Andropogon hirtus*. The latter dominates on dry hills and the former in cool or damp places, where it frequently forms a dense, fine sward that livestock eat greedily.

From 750 or 800 metres upwards begin the meadows and pastures of the interior, which take in the mountain tops, the unwooded central ravines and also part of the island’s southern and northern slopes. In dry places in the mountains, *Leontodon nudicaulis*, *Aira proecox*, *Agrostis castellana*, *Lotus hispidus* and *Plantago lanceolata* are very common. On the lower ground of the slopes these plants appear alongside others already mentioned for the meadows of the middle zone, and in the ravines of the interior alongside *Deschampsia argenvea* (*barba de bode*), *Festuca Donax* (*palha carga*), *Cynosurus elegans* and various other species that are peculiar, or almost peculiar, to these places and live only in damp or shaded spots.

In the ravines of the Ribeira da Metade (‘halfway stream’) and the Boa Ventura there grows a grass with succulent leaves, unfortunately very rare, which is considered one of the best forage plants on the island. This grass, *Festuca albida*, has already been cultivated with good results on a plot on the outskirts of Funchal. In the same Ribeira da Metade there is also a legume, *Anthyllis Lemanniana*, which we regard as an excellent forage plant, worthy of cultivation. *Dactylis glomerata* and *Anthoxathum odoratum* are plants which, though not common, occur in the second and third botanical zones of Madeira (1921).

The grasses of the meadows in Madeira’s lower zone (coastal belt) spring up or revive with the October rains and disappear, scorched by the heat of the sun, between April and May, except in waterlogged spots and in places frequently reached by irrigation water. In the middle and upper parts of the island, and especially in the zone constantly visited by mists, the grasses stay green for longer, until the middle or end of June. This is an advantage even for livestock farmers near the coast, who often go up there to gather them, covering considerable distances.

When the meadow grasses are dry, the animals are generally fed on potato haulms, on the leaves of the vine, of sugar cane and of the giant reed (*cana de roca*), on the plants that grow beside watercourses and on those that appear among the crops in frequently irrigated places. Hay from the island and hay imported from Portugal, together with banana stems chopped into small pieces and mixed with bran, are widely used to feed the stall-kept livestock of Funchal.

Since Madeira’s meadows receive no treatment of any kind, harmful or useless species abound in all of them. High in the mountains the animals graze freely on the grass that grows there, whereas in the lower zones the more general rule is for the plants to be cut green, as and when they are needed for the livestock’s daily feed.

Of the 30,000 hectares of uncultivated land in Madeira (1921), it may be assumed that 10,000 produce only grasses, of good or poor quality, for feeding animals. If this vast area were properly used – that is, if efforts were made to improve its yield – Madeiran livestock farming would gain a great deal, for all it needs in order to develop is more ample forage resources than the island now offers. With a little goodwill, it might not be an extremely difficult task to turn certain parts of the mountains, where only a thin and stunted turf grows, into highly fertile pastures capable of properly feeding part of the livestock population of our island.
Praia Formosa

‘Rounding this point (Ponta da Cruz), says Frutuoso, they came upon a beautiful beach, which, for its beauty and its setting, the captain (Zargo) named Praya fermosa’ [the Beautiful Beach]. The commentator of the *Saudades* adds that it keeps this name ‘and, being sandy, it lies next to the charming panorama of the wide mouth and steep banks of the Ribeira dos Soccorridos’.

Madeirans, used to the sheer cliffs that line almost the entire coast of this island, look with a certain pride and pleasure on the relatively long stretch of this beach. It presents a delightful sight, above all to those travelling along the road that leads to the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’).
It was on this beach that the French corsairs landed when, in 1566, they subjected this city to a terrible sack.
See Sack of Funchal by the French.

A distinguished Portuguese physician, who visited Funchal several times and for long periods, had the following to say about ‘Praia Formosa’ when referring to some of the beaches of mainland Portugal, and his words deserve to be transcribed: ‘Some of them are not even beaches in the proper sense of the word. Yet the truth is that they all fill up with people, because people bathe there, because everyone takes part in water sports, because everyone swims, because everyone wants to soak up the streaming sunlight. It is interesting to see those long boardwalks crowded with people sunbathing! The adults on one side, chatting pleasantly, and the children on the other, playing in the water, leaping, jumping, breathing life. So I ask: does Madeira, an essentially maritime land with a population bowed under the weight of ancestral defects, not make use of the sea? Does Funchal, already a city with modern characteristics, progressive and rich, not use the sea as a source of health? In fact, the present beach by the quay does not, and cannot, satisfy the demands of its inhabitants and of its middle class. But I ask again: why is Praia Formosa not used? Today the regular lorry services, and tomorrow motor buses, would solve the problem of transport at modest prices. That beach is delightful in every respect: seclusion, excellent exposure, a picturesque spot, and a stretch of more than a kilometre, only some 5 to 10 minutes from the centre.

The morning or evening walk itself would in its own right be extremely beneficial to muscle and nerve. It lacks means of access, I know, but that is easily remedied. Why should the Council, through its department of hygiene, not consider creating an easy and quick route to the seafront? I am sure that all the landowners would gladly contribute to it. Once this difficulty was resolved, Funchal would have a beach enviable for its position and the gentleness of its sea.

There everything would be provided for, from water sports to sunbathing. Yes, because today local authorities evidently have to face this and other problems aimed above all at improving the living conditions of their inhabitants, at establishing means that encourage the development of the young, creating for them a sound mind in a sound body.’

Prainha

A small beach on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’). It stands apart from all the other beaches of Madeira because it is formed of sand, whereas all the others are made of rounded pebbles. It lies at the head of a picturesque cove, much visited by summer holidaymakers from the town (*vila*) of Machico.
Prazeres

A former locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), corresponding roughly to the site now occupied by the Monte Palace Hotel and its surroundings. A chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Joys (*Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres*) once stood here and gave the place its name.
Prazeres (parish)

In the early days of colonisation, and long afterwards, a good many chapels were built in various localities of this island. They generally gave their names to these places, which were often important centres of population and became the origin of future parishes. This is why every parish (*freguesia*) in Madeira that keeps a name of a religious character takes it from a chapel that already existed and was later turned into a parish church. The same is true of the parish of Prazeres (‘joys’), whose name comes from a small chapel dedicated to Our Lady of the Joys (*Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres*), built there long before the parish was created. It is to be presumed that the original chapel was known as the chapel of Prazeres, and that this name, thus simplified, became that of the new parish.

The land that makes up the greater part of the parish of Prazeres originally belonged to the parish of Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’). It was detached from that parish to form, together with a few hamlets of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’), an independent parish, created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 28 December 1676. It was only around 1684 that the new parish was established, with its seat in the chapel of Our Lady of the Joys. Its parish priests were Father Manuel Dias Pinheiro (1684–1692), Francisco Correia da Silva (1692–1693) and José Cordeiro de Andrade (1693–1700). In that year, 1700, the parish of Prazeres was abolished, or at least part of the parish services held there was suspended and transferred to the church of Estreito da Calheta, to whose parish the hamlets of Prazeres were annexed. We have not discovered the reasons behind this measure, which seems strange to us but did in fact take place. The locality did, however, have a chaplain of its own, who celebrated some acts of worship there.

Thirty-three years later, by the royal decree of 12 November 1733, the curacy (*curato*) of Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres was created, and it was then made dependent on the parish of Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’). The only parish in this diocese that we know to have been abolished and soon afterwards restored as a parish was that of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), in this city. But of an autonomous parish that was suppressed and afterwards reduced to the subordinate rank of a curacy, we know only of Prazeres.

As happened with Jardim do Mar, Achadas da Cruz and others, the curacy of Prazeres gradually freed itself from its dependence on its mother church (*igreja matriz*) and went on to become an autonomous parish, in a year we cannot determine. This is the place to say that the last parishes in this diocese to bear the name of curacies, such as those of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), Achadas da Cruz, Prazeres, etc., were in recent times genuinely autonomous parishes, independent of the parishes from which they had been separated, although they kept the traditional name of curacies. Shortly before 1880 the priests who performed parochial duties in Prazeres began to sign the relevant official documents as parish priests, and the first collated vicar, in 1881, was Father João António Marcial. The old, original chapel stood in the locality of Estacada (‘stockade’), beside the road. No trace of it remains, as it was demolished when the present parish church was built. In 1745 the works on the new church were put out for award by public auction (*arrematação*) for 4,100,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), but construction began only some years later: the foundation stone was laid and blessed on 9 September 1751, and the licence decree stated that the old church was ‘small and unfit to serve’. In 1922 the building was substantially altered: the main body was enlarged and a tower and two sacristies were added, giving it more ample proportions. It was in this church, in December 1827, that a sacrilege was committed with the theft of the sacred vessel containing the Holy Eucharist. It caused a great sensation throughout the island, and for that reason many acts of reparation were held in all the churches of the diocese.

The parish of Prazeres is one of the least known on this island, but it is undoubtedly one of the most picturesque. Father Fernando Augusto de Pontes describes this parish as follows: ‘In the distance the undulating mountains stand out against the blue of the sky, and the winding tracks and paths cut across the heights in different directions. Close at hand, the vegetation is a carpet unrolled everywhere. The roads are lined with box and laurel, and the air is very pure. One cannot pass over in silence the ravishing beauty to be enjoyed from the brow of a mountain above the sea – the Assomadouro. Down below, on the left, lies a settlement whose houses are almost hidden beneath the vegetation that smothers them: it is Jardim do Mar. On the right there is another parish – it is Paul do Mar. And how lovely are the houses clustered together at the water’s edge in Paul!’
Main localities: Lombo do Coelho, Lombo da Velha, Estacada, Picos, Lombo da Rocha, Carreira, Referta and Jardim Pelado.

The parish has the levadas (irrigation channels) of Ribeiro de Inês, Ribeira do Batel and Ribeira da Lombada, and it is crossed and irrigated by the Levada do Rabaçal. It has a state boys’ school. Its population is 1251. (1921)
Preces

A village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, set within the inhabited locality of Marco (‘boundary stone’). It takes its name from the chapel of Our Lady of Prayers (*Nossa Senhora das Preces*), founded by Canon Agostinho de Góis e Meneses in 1750 and rebuilt by António Tiago da Silva in 1884.
Preces

An inhabited locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), Funchal, where there is a chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Prayers (*Nossa Senhora das Preces*). It was built in 1768, and in 1770 its administrator, and perhaps its founder, was Captain Rodrigo da Costa. It was rebuilt in 1856 by its owner, Dona Joana de Albuquerque e França.
Preces

Caminho Grande (‘main road’) or Preces, a locality in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). Here stands the chapel of Our Lady of Prayers (*Nossa Senhora das Preces*), which gave the place its name; it was founded in 1683 by Father Francisco da Cunha e Mendonça. In the same locality is the chapel of Our Lady of Nazaré (*Nossa Senhora da Nazaré*), built in 1757 by Dona Maria do Rosário Henriques, widow of Pedro Bernardes Cordeiro. At the place known as Fonte da Rocha (‘rock spring’), the ruins can still be seen of an old chapel dedicated to São Cândido (St Candidus), which Canon Francisco Cândido Correia Henriques had built in 1732. It has 96 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’) and 516 inhabitants.
Prices of goods

etc. Below we give the prices of various foodstuffs and other goods now and before the war, so that in future it will be easy to see how much the cost of living has risen in Funchal since 1914 (1921). We believe that the greed and lack of scruple of many merchants, industrialists and farmers have done more to drive up the cost of living than the depreciation of our currency and the increases in taxes and in workers’ wages. These, however, are the causes generally put forward to explain the multiplication of household expenses and the consequent disappearance of the small savings once built up by people of modest means at the cost of great sacrifice.
