It should come as no surprise that tea and paraffin, for example, which are foreign goods, cost seven and twenty times more today (1921) than in 1914. What has no possible explanation, despite the excessive wages demanded by farm labourers, is that not only Portuguese goods but even those produced in Madeira are being sold at prices fifteen, twenty and even fifty times higher than before. If we turn from groceries to fabrics of various kinds and to articles of clothing, the discrepancies are greater still. The ever-rising cost of living has made the situation of some classes that once lived in comfort very hard indeed.
See Wages.
Preacher to the Council

The Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) once had a salaried preacher, who was required to deliver the sermons at official festivities. In 1831 Father Friar José de Jesus was appointed preacher to the Council; before him the post had been held by Friar João José da Purificação, appointed in 1829 with a salary of 24,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year.
Pregador Imparcial da Verdade, da Justiça e da Lei (O)

This was the second newspaper to appear in this city. Its first issue came out on 17 February 1823 and its last, no. 61, on 2 July 1824. It was a weekly, edited by Father João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo. (See First Publications.)
Prego do Mar (islet)

It is also known as Ilhéu do Furilhão, or more correctly Farilhão (‘sea stack’), and as Ilhéu do Navio (‘ship islet’). It lies north of Ilhéu Chão (‘flat islet’), in the Desertas (‘deserted islands’). It is a rock about 40 metres high and 8 in perimeter which, from a distance, resembles a ship under sail; hence the name Ilhéu do Navio.
See Furilhão.
Preito e Homenagem
Single issue of a newspaper published in July 1908 in tribute to the late Father Ernst Schmitz. His Excellency the military honours that were due to him.
Presado (João Maria de Santiago)
By decree of 17 February 1912 he was appointed Civil Governor of Madeira, taking office on 4 April of the same year.
In February 1920 he was declared deputy for Madeira without an election, having been the only candidate for the seat, which was then vacant.
President of the Republic

The President of the Republic, Dr António José de Almeida, was in Funchal on 9 October 1922. He arrived in our harbour at 7 o’clock in the morning aboard the British steamer *Arlanza*, on a voyage from Rio de Janeiro to Lisbon.

At 6 o’clock a salvo of shells announced that the steamer was in sight, at 7 o’clock a *girândola* (wheel of rockets) signalled that she had arrived, and at 8 o’clock the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) fired a 21-gun salute. The landing took place at about half past ten at the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’), because the sea was quite rough and it was difficult to come alongside the quay opposite the Avenida de Gonçalves Zargo. At the start of this avenue a superb triumphal arch had been raised, covered in box, bearing a double photograph of the President of the Republic and, at the top, the following motto: ‘Supreme incarnation of the Homeland’. Beside it were the *quinas* (the shields of the Portuguese arms) wrapped in green and red.

The President of the Republic received the appropriate military honours beside the Cais da Pontinha from a naval detachment of the destroyer *Guadiana*. His Excellency then travelled by car from there to the Palácio de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’), followed by the various officials who had gone to greet him.

All along the Estrada da Pontinha and at the entrance to the city an enormous crowd had gathered. Three large *girândolas* of shells and rockets were set off along the route, and the artillery battery posted near the Pilar de Banger fired a 21-gun salute when the Head of the Nation reached the triumphal arch at the start of the Avenida de Gonçalves Zargo. Before this, a detachment of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*Infantaria n.º 27*), drawn up beside the Praça do Marquês de Pombal, had rendered His Excellency the military honours due to him.

Near the quay the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) went to meet the Head of State and greet him. The President of the Council handed him the keys of the city, which he did not accept ‘because they were in good hands’. This ceremony was followed by the greetings of the diocesan prelate, the district judges, public prosecutors and other judicial officials, the Judge Advocate, etc.

When the Head of State arrived at the Palácio de São Lourenço the national anthem was played, and the civil governor gave a short speech there, for which His Excellency thanked him. The civil governor accompanied the Head of State throughout, having gone to greet him aboard the *Arlanza* as soon as she dropped anchor.

The reception at the Palácio de São Lourenço was followed by a visit to the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), where Dr Teixeira Jardim, President of the Municipal Council, read a fine address, to which the Head of State replied. The guard of honour at the building was provided by the volunteer firemen.

He then left by a train provided by the Companhia do Caminho de Ferro for Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), where he was offered a glass of champagne and another of Madeira wine. His Excellency showed himself truly delighted with the superb views to be enjoyed from that fine resort, as he made clear in a few lines he wrote on a sheet of paper presented to him, which is duly preserved in the archives.

On returning to the city, at about one o’clock in the afternoon, in wicker sledges, the President of the Republic visited the building of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), where he was offered a glass of champagne. To the greetings addressed to him by Dr Tolentino da Costa, the distinguished President of that body, His Excellency replied with a short speech in which he once again displayed his gifts as an orator and the prestige of his talent.

At about two o’clock in the afternoon a lunch was held at the Palácio de São Lourenço. Those present included, among others, the diocesan prelate, the civil governor, the two Presidents of the Municipal Council, the Military Commander, the harbour master, the President of the General Council, António Luís Gomes, former Portuguese ambassador to Brazil, Francisco António Correia, former Minister of Foreign Affairs and of Finance, General Bernardo Faria, Admiral Neuparth, Dr João de Barros, Dr Juvenal de Araújo, Dr Manuel A. Martins, the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative), and the consuls of Brazil, the United States and England, etc., etc. The civil governor and the diocesan prelate proposed toasts to the Head of State, for which His Excellency thanked them.

The lunch was followed by a drive to the locality of Cancela (‘gate’), in which 21 motor cars took part. His Excellency embarked at about 5 o’clock in the afternoon, and the launch that took him on board was accompanied by many boats full of people, who cheered him enthusiastically.
The civil governor and the diocesan prelate accompanied the Head of State on board the *Arlanza*, and the steamer left the harbour of Funchal for Lisbon at about half past five in the afternoon.

On returning from the drive to Cancela, the President of the Republic went to the Palácio de São Lourenço, where the diocesan prelate was waiting; His Excellency invited him to accompany him in his car as far as the Pontinha.

Also travelling from Brazil with the Head of State were the already mentioned António Luís Gomes, Francisco António Correia, General Bernardo de Faria, Admiral Neuparth, Dr João de Barros, etc., who took part in all the festivities held in Funchal in His Excellency’s honour.
Preston (Captain Amias)

Johnson states on p. 187 of his *Handbook for Madeira* that in 1595 some English ships under the command of Captain Amias Preston attacked and burned Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), even though the inhabitants had offered to pay a large sum to spare the island any harm.
Prim Garibaldi e Costa (João)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) on 31 August 1867, the son of António Tolentino da Costa and Dona Romana Augusta de Coito e Costa. For some years he was municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of the municipality (*concelho*) of that name, and he now holds the post of head of its telegraph and post office there. He contributed to several Funchal newspapers and was a particularly regular contributor to the *Brado de Oeste*, published in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). As president of the Associação Recreativa Porto-Monizense, he gave a speech there that was published as a pamphlet in this city under the title *Conferencia*, dedicated to Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Leite Monteiro (1921).
Primavera (A)
Only a few issues of this newspaper were published, the first on 1 October 1882.
First publications

We have already devoted an article to the first publication produced in Madeira by the art of printing – *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’) –, a twice-weekly newspaper that first saw the light of day on 2 July 1821, as stated on page 57 of this volume.

*O Patriota Funchalense* was still appearing with complete regularity when, on 17 February 1823, the second newspaper ever to exist here came out. It bore the grandiloquent title *O Prégador Imparcial da Verdade, da Justiça e da Lei*, which would amply have sufficed to christen four different periodicals. Its editor and owner was Father Dr João Crisóstomo Espínola de Macedo, a distinguished lawyer and parish priest in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). Although he possessed a lively intelligence and an uncommon culture, he wrote in language so violent and unbridled that it brought him the greatest troubles and the most outrageous humiliations. He was a worthy rival of Father José Agostinho de Macedo, even though he professed political principles diametrically opposed to those of the author of *Burros*, *Besta Esfolada* and *Tripa Virada*. *O Pregador Imparcial…* was a weekly, and 61 issues of it appeared, the last on 2 July 1824.

In the same year, 1823, two more newspapers appeared: *A Atalaia da Liberdade* and *O Regedor* (‘The Parish Magistrate’), respectively the third and fourth periodicals published in Funchal. The first, which had the ephemeral life of two months, was edited by Dr Daniel de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, a lawyer and brilliant orator who later represented Madeira in parliament and sat in the House of Peers, where he distinguished himself as a notable parliamentarian. *O Regedor*, which did not last much longer than its contemporary *Atalaia da Liberdade*, was published from April to June 1823; the names of its editors and owners are unknown.

From the middle of 1824 until 1827 no newspaper was published. Then, on 3 February and 2 June of the latter year, *O Funchalense Liberal* and *A Flor do Oceano* appeared, respectively the fifth and sixth periodicals to see the light on this island.

Outside the newspaper activity we have briefly sketched above, the press could not have much influence in a social and intellectual setting as narrow as the city of Funchal then was. Even so, considering that setting and that period, the bibliographical items published in the first years after the first printing press was set up in 1821 are quite considerable in both number and quality.

In that year a literary and scientific association called the Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciências e Artes was founded here. It had 27 full members, 45 corresponding members and 24 honorary members, and included the most distinguished Madeirans of the time. Among the full members were such eminent names as Pimenta de Aguiar, Canon Gonçalves de Andrade, Nicolau Betencourt Pita, Lourenço José Moniz, Dr Caetano Alberto Soares, Dr João Pedro de Freitas Drumond and José Marciano da Fonseca, among others, to whom the *Elucidário Madeirense* devotes detailed notices. This society was the first to publish a small work in print: its constitution, entitled *Estatutos e Regulamentos da Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciencias e Artes*. It is a small pamphlet of twenty-three pages, printed in 1822 at the press of *O Patriota Funchalense* and now extremely rare, and it enjoys the well-deserved distinction of being the first work of typography printed on this island.

In that same year, 1822, two further pamphlets were published: hymns of praise to the constitution proclaimed by the Porto Revolution, which was solemnly recognised in Madeira in January 1821. One of them is entitled *Parabens poético-politicos à grandiosa regeneração portuguesa na congratulante aderência da Ilha da Madeira em 1821 no teatro grande do Funchal*. Its author was Dr Luís António Jardim, a lawyer and deputy to the first constituent Cortes (Portuguese parliament), who died in Funchal on 14 February 1825.

The other pamphlet contains the panegyric delivered from the pulpit of our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) by Father João Manuel de Freitas Branco, and bears this title: *Oraçâo de Acção de Graças que na solenidade do aniversário do faustissimo dia 28 de Janeiro de 1821 pregou na Igreja Catedral da Sé do Funchal por convite do Ill.mo e Rev.mo Cabido o vigário de Sâo Jorge João Manuel de Freitas Branco em o anno de 1821*. It is a booklet of 43 pages and is today a great bibliographical rarity.

The following year, 1823, another hymn of praise, no less hyperbolic and excessively laudatory than that of the previous year, was heard in the principal church of this diocese. It was published in Funchal that same year under the following title: *Oraçâo de graças prègada na igreja Cathedral da Sé do Funchal em 6 de Julho de 1823 por ocasiâo da solemne festividade que fêz sua excellencia reverendissima pela feliz restauração de S. Magestade El-Rei N. S.*, by Friar José Cupertino, a Franciscan friar, professor of theology and synodal examiner of this bishopric of Funchal.

In 1823 there also appeared a small and curious volume of 60 pages, entitled *Instrucçoens para a inspecçâo ou revista de hum batalhão d'infanteria... traduzido do ingles. . .*. Its subject can arouse not the slightest interest today; it is worth noting only as an uncommon bibliographical rarity of some value for the history of printing in Madeira.

We are not aware of any books or pamphlets having been printed here in the period from 1824 to 1827, and the same is true of periodicals, as we have already noted above. We attribute this gap to the political events then taking place in our country, which were hardly conducive to maintaining the freedom the press needs to carry out its mission profitably.

In that year of 1827 three pamphlets were published in Funchal. One dealt with local political matters, and the other two contained the poems recited at the ‘Theatro Grande’ during the celebrations of the anniversary of the proclamation of the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) granted by Pedro IV.
Primeiro de Dezembro
It was published from 1 December 1907 to 3 May 1908, and twenty issues appeared.
Early dwellings

Since forest species grew in great abundance on this island at the time of its discovery, they supplied the chief raw material for building the first dwellings. The earliest dwelling houses were all built of timber taken from these dense woods, and it may be presumed that many of them used the native cedar and other species best suited to that purpose.

We have already said elsewhere that João Gonçalves Zarco had his first residence on the heights of Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’), built perhaps from the rich and fragrant cedars that grew everywhere in dense woods. It was doubtless a more than modest and uncomfortable dwelling, built on a single storey and stripped of all architectural display. Also of wood was the small chapel of St Catherine, which the discoverer’s wife had built beside her home.

Only some years later was the first two-storey house built, and an old manuscript gives the following interesting account of it: ‘In this Campo de Duque (see vol. 1, p. 225) was built the first two-storey house there was in this town of Funchal and in the whole island. João Manuel had it made of dressed cedar wood. In those days this two-storey house was thought so novel and remarkable a thing, all the other houses being single-storey and of planking, that articles of complaint were laid before the King against the said João Manuel, accusing him of building a tower, in which it seemed he wished to fortify himself and rise up against Funchal and against the Crown. The said house still stands today (mid-18th century) and is owned by António de Carvalhal, and it is the lowest two-storey house there is in Funchal.’

As we have seen in various places, tradition records that the first stone house built on this island was the one João Gonçalves Zargo put up as his residence beside the chapel of St Paul (see vol. 2, p. 395). It is also stated that one of the oldest buildings of this kind was the one intended as a hospital, likewise built near the same chapel of St Paul.
Princesa Dona Maria Amélia (street)
In 1852 the Council gave this name to the street that links Rua da Imperatriz Dona Amélia with the area near the Pontinha (‘little point’), when the Princess visited Madeira that year.
Princesa (street)

This was the name, before the proclamation of the Republic, of the street on the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’) that is known today as Rua 31 de Janeiro (‘31 January street’). It seems that it was Princess Carlota Joaquina, wife of Prince Dom João, later John VI, whom the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) wished to honour when it gave that thoroughfare the name it kept until 1910. Local people used to call Rua 31 de Janeiro the Rua das Árvores (street of the trees), because of the lovely plane trees planted along it.
Moroccan princesses

On 19 April 1793 a Moroccan brig put in to the harbour of Funchal. On board were the wife, three daughters and two sons of Prince Muley Abdessalam, together with nine of his concubines and several other persons of high rank in Morocco, among them the widow of the former emperor Muley Ismael.

The retinue of the prince’s family consisted of two ladies’ maids, a eunuch, a skipper (*arrais*) in command, a secretary, a black doorkeeper who served in place of a eunuch, seventeen female musician servants, thirty male servants, seventeen wives of the servants, one hundred and nineteen slaves, male and female, with their children, eleven Moorish passengers, a Jew and a Jewess, the latter a friend of the skipper.
Counting the crew, there were more than two hundred people aboard the brig, all of them in great discomfort, owing both to the smallness of the vessel and to the shortage of water on board.

The brig was bound for Salé, where Muley Abessalam intended to place his family out of reach of the dangers of the civil war then ravaging the empire of Morocco. However, it met contrary winds that drove it away from its port of destination, and its commander was forced to bring it into the harbour of Funchal, where he knew he would find the means to continue the voyage in better conditions.

The princesses were very well received in Funchal, both by the governor and captain-general Dom Diogo Forjaz Coutinho and by the Moroccan consul Diogo Teles. The governor had two Portuguese brigs made ready and divided the travellers between them; the consul also embarked on one of them, intending to accompany the princesses as far as Salé.

The voyage was not a happy one. After leaving the harbour of Funchal the ships were driven off their course, and the princesses had to land on the island of São Miguel. From there they went on to Lisbon, and finally returned to their own country on 8 August, aboard three vessels that the Portuguese government had placed at their disposal.
The consul Domingos Teles accompanied the princesses only as far as the island of São Miguel, abandoning them there without troubling to justify his conduct.
Príncipe (street)

Before the Republic was proclaimed on this island, this was the name of the street that runs alongside the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s stream’) and extends from the paved lane of Cidrão, or of João Sabino da Costa, to the Rua dos Netos. Today it is called Rua 5 de Outubro. We believe that the name was intended to honour the Prince Regent John VI, but we have never found any indication of this in the records of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this city.
Procession of the Bull of the Holy Crusade

This procession was already being held in Funchal at the beginning of the 19th century, and apparently with great splendour. The Council (*Câmara*) invited six persons of the governance (*pessoas da governança*, notables eligible for municipal office) to carry the poles of the canopy, after receiving a letter from the deputy of the commissary of the papal bull informing it of the day on which the procession was to take place. At the Council session of 31 January 1807 it was resolved ‘that persons who fail to attend the procession of the Bull of the Holy Crusade (Bula da Santa Cruzada) without just cause shall be punished in the manner prescribed by the latest orders of His Highness’.
The votive procession of 1 May

In the article Plague, on p. 77 of this volume, we transcribed what Frutuoso says about the origin of this procession. It set out from the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) and made its way to the church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major), originally dedicated to Saint James the Less, accompanied by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) and the principal authorities of the district. In the latter church the ceremony of the handing over of the staffs of office took place, together with a sermon on the miracle performed by the Patron Saint of the City in 1538. After the proclamation of the Republic, it was only in 1918 that the procession of 1 May followed its old route, accompanied by two members of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Municipal Council.

In former times it was the Council that directed the procession of 1 May, issued the invitations to the confraternities and authorities, and paid the preacher. Custom required that the Council be censed in the church of São Tiago by one of the three canons who said the Mass. When, in 1815, this ceremony was performed not by a canon but by a chaplain, the Council resolved to complain to the bishop, considering itself slighted by the substitution».

On 5 May 1829 the Council decided that the market inspector (juiz almotacé) should penalise, ‘in accordance with the municipal by-laws (*posturas*), the examined officers of the mechanical trades who were absent from the procession of 1 May, as well as the fishermen belonging to the confraternity of St Elmo (*Corpo Santo*) and its guild who failed to attend, also imposing the appropriate penalty on the residents of the streets through which the procession passed who had not swept the frontages of their houses and adorned their windows’.

In recent times we have often seen the Council represented by only three or four councillors (*vereadores*) in the procession of 1 May, because it is an old local custom for many people to spend this day in the countryside. We knew one president who invited almost the whole city to join the votive procession, since it was, as he put it, ‘a vow of our forefathers greatly respected by the municipality’, yet who never accompanied the procession himself, nor even took the trouble to justify his absence (1921). In the days of absolute government such an absence would probably have been punished with a fine or a few days in prison, since it was regarded as a sign of little respect for the Patron Saint of the City.

In former times the procession of 1 May, which, as we have said, set out from the Cathedral, returned to that church only eight days later. During the octave various festivities were held in the church of São Tiago Menor, which has been the parish church since the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803. The procession still takes place today, but it goes only round the churchyard of the Cathedral (the Sé), and the Council has no part in it (1921).

As we have already stated in the article Patron saints and on p. 37 of this volume, in 1942 the Municipal Council revived the old traditions of the Funchal Senate (*senado*, the municipal council), taking part in the various acts of worship held in honour of the patron saint São Tiago. (See Vow to São Tiago.)
Processions of Candlemas, the Litanies and the Way of the Cross in Ponta do Sol
The article referred to above records that these processions were formerly held in Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’).

The procession of the Litanies (*Ladainhas*, a Rogation procession) took place in May. According to a document of 1600, on the first day it went to the church of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), in Canhas; on the second, to the chapel of Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit), in Lombada (‘long ridge’); and on the third, to the chapel of São Sebastião (St Sebastian), in the town (*vila*).

In 1607 the Council ordered that on the first day the same procession should go to the chapel of Espírito Santo, on the second to that of Our Lady of Pity (Jangão?) and on the third to that of São Sebastião. The parishioners of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Canhas) and of Madalena do Mar (‘Magdalene by the sea’) were excused from attending the procession, since it was held in their own parishes.

The processions of the Way of the Cross outside the church came to an end, says the author of the article mentioned, around 1830. In the days when they were held, they set out from the parish church and passed through the streets of the town, going as far as the chapel of Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*), in Lombo das Adegas (‘ridge of the wine cellars’), and the chapel of St Maurus (*Santo Amaro*), in Lombada. Crosses stood along the streets and paths these processions followed, and on the Caminho da Lombada (‘ridge road’) there is a cave called the furna do Calvário (Calvary cave), which was one of the stations of these processions.
Processions

The account that follows gathers a number of notes on various processions, some of which are no longer held, while others still take place, though with a ceremonial different from that of the past. It is curious to note that, in the days of absolutism, the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) and the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) received perquisites (*propinas*) for the processions that went out in the city. This custom disappeared, we believe, with the establishment of constitutional government on this island.
Ash Wednesday procession

This was the name given to the procession held on Ash Wednesday, which in distant times set out from the Convent of St Francis (*São Francisco*), accompanied by friars who sang religious chants along the way. The procession always passed through the churches of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) and the Mercês, where the nuns sang religious hymns as the processional litter (*andor*) bearing the image of St Francis embracing that of Christ entered the church.

At the head of the procession went the processional banner of the Third Order of St Francis, with its coat of arms exquisitely embroidered in gold, followed immediately by the so-called tree of penance, which bore a crucifix adorned with hawthorn branches, a rosary and a set of scourges. Behind came the brotherhood of penance, with four brethren walking beside the cross: one carried a tray with two crossed bones and a skull, another a glass urn holding ashes from palm and olive branches blessed on Palm Sunday, another an hourglass with two wings, and the fourth a lamp-stand with an extinguished lamp. Next came the cross of the Order and the litter of Christ Carrying the Cross (*Senhor dos Passos*), with its confraternity, and then the litters of St Francis carrying the cross on his back; of the Confirmation of the Rule, showing the same saint, Pope Innocent III and a cardinal; of St Anthony of Noto (black); of St Lucius and St Bona (the two siblings); of St Rose of Viterbo; of St Margaret of Cortona; of St Joan; of St Elizabeth, daughter of the Queen of Hungary; of St Elizabeth, Queen of Hungary; of St Roch; of St Elzéar and St Delphine (the happily married couple); of St Henry, King of Dacia; of St Louis, King of France; of St Ivo, doctor; and of St Elizabeth of Portugal, all these images being accompanied by their respective confraternities. The religious cortège was brought up by the board (*mesa*) of the Third Order, the litter of St Francis embracing Christ, the corporation of Chaplains, and the purple canopy, beneath which walked three clergymen in copes of the same colour, the one in the middle carrying a reliquary with the Holy Wood of the Cross; and finally the Bishop of the Diocese, in his cappa magna (the bishop's long ceremonial cape with train), the train of which was held by five seminarians.

After the church of St Francis disappeared, the images that had featured in the Ash Wednesday procession passed to the church of the College (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), and in our own day it was from this church that the procession set out; it has not been held for about 25 years (1921). The capes (*opas*) worn in the procession were purple, and in olden times the professed brethren who joined it wore the habit. The place of the women penitents who accompanied the cortège was near the so-called tree of penance.

A foreign author writing in 1827 said the following about the Ash Wednesday procession: ‘The images are almost life-size and all wear religious habits, not excepting St Louis, King of France, and St Elizabeth of Portugal. One of them, representing Our Lord bowed beneath the weight of the cross, is a well-executed work which, through the expression of suffering it bears, makes an impression on those who behold it.’
The Ash Wednesday procession is still held today in the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), where many people come from Funchal to see it.
Procession of St Francis

In the early 19th century a procession was held in honour of St Francis, as can be seen from an order of the captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) instructing that ‘a salute be given from the upper stronghold of São Lourenço to the procession of St Francis... and that only those guns be fired that have been ordered, so that they do no harm to the house or the fishpond’.
It is likely that the procession left the Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi), which stood on the site now occupied by the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’).
Procession of St Barbara

It left the chapel of St Lawrence (*São Lourenço*) in the Fortress and made its way to the church of the College (*Colégio*) (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), where a feast was held in honour of the saint. According to tradition, the procession was organised by the military, and all of them, from the highest-ranking officer down to the simple soldier, contributed a certain sum towards the expenses of the feast.
In 1826 there was in Funchal an association of brethren of St Barbara, whose purpose was to distribute alms to people in need.
The image of St Barbara, which belonged to the chapel of St Lawrence, is today in the church of the College.
Procession of St Anthony

We have found references to this procession, which left the church of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), in documents from the beginning of the second quarter of the 19th century. It included three processional litters (*andores*): one with St Anthony of Padua as a canon, another with St Anthony as a friar, and a third with St Anthony as a choirboy. These litters were carried, respectively, by canons of the Sé, Franciscan friars and choirboys of the Cathedral. The minutes of the session of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) of 13 June 1815 show that the municipality accompanied the procession of St Anthony.
Corpus Christi procession

What Alexandre Herculano wrote in *O Monge de Cister* about the Corpus Christi procession in the Middle Ages applies in large part to Madeira. Here too, as old documents show, the festival had a burlesque character unbefitting religious ceremonies.

The Archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal records a ‘regimento e ordenança’ (regulations and ordinance) dated 1483, which laid down the order in which the various guilds obliged to take part in the procession were to walk.

According to this document, the crossbowmen with their crossbows were to lead the cortège, followed by the *almuinheiros* (market gardeners) with their *almuinhas*, and then the town criers, the day labourers or pack-saddle makers, the muleteers, the butchers with their emperor and king, the weavers, the furriers with the *gato paúl*, the potters, tile makers and glassmakers, the grocers, spice merchants and apothecaries, the harness makers, the shoemakers and tailors, the ropemakers, the fishermen, the masons and carpenters with the *engenhos*, the vine growers and coopers with the tower, the armourers and barbers with the Sagittarius, the carriers and candle makers, the brokers, the bell-founders, the sugar masters, the notaries and the merchants.

The ‘Resposta do Duque a alguns apontamentos’ (the Duke’s reply to certain points), also of 1483 and recorded in the same Archive, ordered that the merchants should walk with torches in the Corpus Christi procession ‘ante a gayolla’ (before the cage), and that the merchants, notaries and other craftsmen should accompany the procession with candles and banners, likewise placing themselves in front of the ‘gayolla’, under penalty of a fine of one mark of silver (*marco de prata*, c. 230 g of silver). The same fine applied to ‘as mulheres dos privilegiados que são regateiras’ (the wives of privileged men who are market hawkers) if they failed to accompany the ‘procissões regias’ (royal processions).

There is an order of 1468 requiring ‘those of the village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) to come with their trades to the Corpus Christi procession’, and in 1502 it was ordered that in the towns the procession should be held ‘on the Sunday after the day itself’. We read in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) that at the church of Lançarote Teixeira, son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, ‘sixty knights of the golden spurs, very finely turned out’ used to gather in Machico, and that ‘when St John’s Day or Corpus Christi came round, there were so many horsemen for cane games (*jogos de canas*, equestrian tournament with thrown canes) and skirmishes that it looked more like an army in the field than a festive holiday.’

So many ridiculous and perhaps even indecent acts were committed, both here and in Portugal, when the Corpus Christi procession took place that in 1565 a royal decree (alvará régio) was issued, recorded in the Archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), ordering that no profane things or masks be allowed in churches and processions, under penalty of a fine of 1,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), or of penal exile (degredo) for a repeat offence.

‘In the Corpus Christi procession held in Funchal in 1603,’ says Senhor Fortunato de Almeida in volume 3 of his *História da Igreja em Portugal*, ‘there were disorders and scandals, because the vicar-general left the place that belonged to him in order to walk in the procession with his officers, watching whether anything indecent was being done in it. When the bishop brought these events to the king’s attention so that measures might be taken for the future, the monarch decided that in processions the prelates’ vicars could concern themselves only with the government of ecclesiastical persons. If among the laity any excess were committed, or anything resulting in irreverence towards the Holy Sacrament, or towards the relics and sacred objects carried in the processions, the vicars, as the competent judges they were in law, could and should deal with such excesses and order whatever seemed fitting to them; but outside such an occasion they were not to interfere in the government of the laity, nor leave the place in which the clergy walked, even if they said they wished to do so in order to watch for and prevent such incidents.’

Pantaleão de Sá e Melo, who was appointed governor-general of Madeira in 1694, imprisoned three councillors (*vereadores*) on the occasion of a Corpus Christi procession for ‘defending the jurisdiction of His Majesty’ in that procession. In 1725 and 1726 two councillors were imprisoned for the same reason at the bishop’s request, the arrest being carried out by Governor Francisco da Costa Freire.

What the Council called ‘defending the jurisdiction of His Majesty’ was opposing, by whatever means were within its reach, any attempt by anyone to occupy in the procession the place of honour that rightfully belonged to it.

The abuses and excesses committed by the civil and ecclesiastical authorities led the Council in 1732 to petition the Government that its members should not be liable to arrest by those authorities, but we do not know what decision this request received.

An old book of official letters and representations kept in the archive of the Funchal Municipal Council contains the account of another conflict between the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) and the governor, once again over the Corpus Christi procession. We shall try to summarise that account:

‘When the governor and captain-general José Correia de Sá made known his intention of walking behind the canopy, together with the knights of the habit of Christ, in the Corpus Christi procession due to take place on 21 May 1762, the Council sent the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) to ask him “that, for the service of His Majesty, he should not seek to disturb the good harmony that ought to exist between the Senate and the governors, nor alter the legitimate custom always practised, thereby violating the regulations of the Council and the royal warrants (*provisões*); for on this island it had never been the custom for the knights of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*) to attend the said procession, but should they wish to attend, they should walk in the body of the procession, in the place belonging to the said Order; behind the canopy, however, or holding its poles, they could not walk, both because this had never been the custom and because the place behind the canopy belonged to the Senate, and it was for the Senate alone to choose who should carry the poles of the canopy, not only because the direction of the procession belonged to the Council, but also because it had always been the unalterable custom that, by order of the Senate of the Council, the poles of the canopy were carried by those of the governing body (*governança*, the notables eligible for municipal office) – from the Cathedral to the College of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) by the married men, and from the said College to the Sé by the unmarried men and those who had already served as councillors, bearing torches – and all this by order of the Senate”.’

To this representation the governor replied ‘that he would always walk with the said knights, as he had determined’. And indeed, on the said day, 21 May, the violence prepared by that authority was carried out, and the Council found itself compelled to allow others to occupy the place of honour that rightfully belonged to it.

The Council complained to the Desembargo do Paço (the king’s supreme court of justice) of the scant consideration with which the governor had treated it and of the violence he had used against it. In reply came the royal decree (*alvará*) of 2 April 1763, which established that the Municipality’s place was behind the canopy, as had already been laid down by the regulations of 18 August 1508 and confirmed by a warrant of 28 February 1755. It was further ordered on the same occasion that the councillors (capitulares) should hold the poles of the canopy as far as the door of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), the honour thereafter falling to the persons of the governance (*pessoas da governança*, notables eligible for municipal office), chosen by the Council, as has already been said above.

In the Corpus Christi procession held in Funchal in 1801, Governor Dom José Manuel da Câmara placed himself behind the canopy and in front of the Senate, which gave rise to protests from that body. The following year the same governor had the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), president of the Council, informed that he had resolved to take the first pole on the right of the canopy, next to the members of the Senate, as soon as the councillors let go of the poles, and then to follow the procession behind the canopy. In reply to this communication, the Senate once more reminded the governor of the provisions of the royal decree of 1763 already cited, adding, however, that if he wished to hold the poles with the *juiz de fora* he might do so, and likewise with the councillors or with the persons of the governance, since these were of the same standing as the councillors.

In the last years of the constitutional period the poles of the canopy were carried by the commanders and knights of the various orders, who were invited by the Municipal Council. The Council usually ceded to the authorities the right, which it held under old charters, to walk behind the canopy. The municipal standard, which after 1835 came to be carried by the youngest councillor (*vereador*), had been borne in the days of absolutism by the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*).

We do not know when the Corpus Christi procession ceased to be a burlesque ceremony – with its train of market gardeners carrying their garden produce, butchers with their emperor and king, furriers with their ‘gato paúl’, etc., etc. – and took on the decent and serious appearance proper to religious ceremonies. It may be supposed, however, that this happened at the end of the first or the beginning of the second quarter of the 18th century, after the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 27 May 1724, which ordered that games, dances and figures, even those representing saints, be removed from the procession, the only exceptions being the image of St George and some processional litters (*andores*) that the brotherhoods might wish to carry of their own accord. The royal decree (*alvará*) of 1565 seems not to have had the desired effect, for, as we have seen, as late as 1603 the vicar general still thought it necessary to watch whether ‘indecent things’ were being done in the Corpus Christi procession.

The persons of the governance (*pessoas da governança*, notables eligible for municipal office) were obliged, on pain of imprisonment, to accompany the procession. As late as June 1820, letters of notice were sent to Aires de Ornelas Cisneiros and António Venâncio de Ornelas ordering them to report to the Pico (‘peak’) fortress ‘for having failed to appear to carry the poles of the canopy’, and a warrant was later issued for their arrest for having disregarded the Council’s invitation.

The Corpus Christi procession was once accompanied by an image of St George, which is today in the building of the Funchal Municipal Museum (Museu Municipal do Funchal). The image rode on horseback and had a staff made up of members of the leading families, who joined the procession on horseback, dressed in rich costumes of velvet and silk. It was customary, a few days before the procession, for the Council to write to the market inspectors (*almotacés*) to make the horse-hirers lend their horses to accompany the saint, and at the beginning of the 19th century the bloodletters’ trade elected a steward (*mordomo*) ‘to provide the cavalry’ for the procession.

The image of St George ceased to appear in the Corpus Christi procession around 1857, and since then it has always been kept in a room of the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), stored in a cupboard. It is said that when the image was placed on the horse it did not hold a proper rider’s posture, leaning now to the right, now to the left, and that it was to avoid unpleasant remarks from the public that the bishop forbade it to appear in the procession.

The image was made in Lisbon and until 1823 was entrusted to the keeping of the Guild (*grémio*) of the Trades, which, it seems, had nowhere to house it. It was to prevent acts of disrespect or damage to it that the Council was allowed to take charge of it, ‘not as owner, but to keep it clean and decent’. It was kept in the chapel of the town hall, at the time when the latter stood in the Largo da Sé, in the building of the since-demolished gaol. The mantle in which the image appeared in the procession, and which we ourselves saw, had been presented to it by the Municipality in 1823 (1921). All the confraternities of the municipality (*concelho*) took part in the Corpus Christi procession, and the rear was brought up by the available troops, both first-line and second-line troops (*segunda linha*, reserve militia). In our own day the troops fired three volleys after the procession returned to the Cathedral, and a 21-gun salute was also fired by the Fort of Nossa Senhora da Conceição do Ilhéu (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, Fort of the Islet) as the Blessed Sacrament left the church.

An interesting article by a learned priest of this island, published in the review *A Esperança* of 15 March 1923, states that in 1578 the inhabitants and the sugar masters and refiners of the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol were obliged to accompany the Corpus Christi procession held there, carrying torches of their own and sugar canes in their hands, and that the farmers were also obliged to join the procession, bearing ears of grain, vine branches, garlands and sugar canes. At the Corpus Christi festivities held in the same town in 1599, the stewards appeared with their ‘folgares’, which, as can be gathered from a document of 1610, were ‘a sword dance with its music, of seven dancers.’

‘There was never an image of St George in the town of Ponta do Sol. The warlike saint was represented in the same procession by a master blacksmith, mounted on a horse, with two squires at his side, likewise of flesh and blood;’

On the subject of ‘saints of flesh and blood’, we may add that there are still people who remember seeing, at religious festivities held in the countryside, St John the Baptist and St Mary Magdalene represented by a boy and a girl dressed in costumes suited to the parts they had to play.
Procession of the Triumph

Nine processional litters (andores) featured in this procession. Eight bore images of the Lord (the Lord in the Garden, of Patience, at the Column, of the Cold Stone, of the Green Reed, of the Stations of the Passion (*passos*, wayside oratories depicting scenes of Christ's Passion), on the Cross and on the Bier) and one bore an image of the Virgin, and each of these images had its own brotherhood. At the head of the procession went the processional banner, followed by the cross of penance and the brotherhood of the same name, in two files, with the women penitents walking two by two between them. The cross of the Third Order of Nossa Senhora do Monte do Carmo (Our Lady of Mount Carmel) preceded the litters, and after the last litter came the confraternity of the same order, with the prior (title of the parish priest) carrying the scapulars proper to it. The prelate walked at the end of the procession, vested in the cappa magna (the bishop's long ceremonial cape with train), which was held by five seminarians.

All the litters carried cypresses, some six and others four, and it was the custom to adorn them with ranunculuses, anemones and other flowers; that of the Lord in the Garden also carried olive branches.

The processional robes were purple, except for those of the brotherhood of Nossa Senhora, which were blue and white, and those of the confraternity of the Third Order, which were brown and white. In former times the professed brethren wore a brown habit, a scapular and a white cape.
The procession of the Triumph, also called the Carmo procession because it set out from that church, ceased to be held some years before the proclamation of the Republic.
Passos procession

In times now somewhat removed from our own, the images of Christ Carrying the Cross (*Senhor dos Passos*), from the church of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), and of Nossa Senhora da Soledade (Our Lady of Solitude), from the church of the Mercês, were carried in procession on Saturday night: the latter to the Cathedral (the Sé) and the former to the church of the College (*Colégio*). The image of Our Lord was the first to leave, and the image of Our Lady then joined the cortège. Many boys bearing lighted torches went ahead of the procession, which, after passing the church of the College, made its way to the Cathedral. The Passos procession (Lenten procession of Christ carrying the Cross) left the church of the College on Sunday afternoon and went along Rua da Carreira (‘track’) and Rua de São Francisco to visit a station (of the Cross) that stood on the north side of the old Jardim Pequeno. It then proceeded to the Cathedral, where the ceremony of the encounter took place, at first inside the church and later outside it. On that occasion a sermon was preached on the event. The procession, now joined by the confraternity and the image of Nossa Senhora da Soledade, then went on to the church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major), making short halts in front of the Stations of the Passion (*passos*, wayside oratories depicting scenes of Christ's Passion) in Rua do Aljube (‘bishop’s prison’), at the Pelourinho (‘pillory’) and in Rua de Santa Maria.

The cortège was headed by the processional banner, followed by a large purple processional banner bearing the letters S. P. Q. R. There was a time when it was customary to have a man playing a trumpet march at the front of the procession; he was known as the *gajeiro*.

In the church of Santa Maria Maior the scenes of Calvary were enacted, generally at some length, and the procession returned to the church of the College only after nightfall, when the images were put back in their respective niches.

Candles were lit in the windows of the buildings, and, as on the previous evening, the cortège was preceded by many men and boys carrying large lighted torches, which gave it a strange and fantastic appearance.

Many women penitents, usually barefoot, accompanied the procession, and in remote times it also included some penitents carrying heavy iron bars or armed with scourges with which they lacerated their bodies.

It is worth mentioning here that the image that appears in the Passos procession was brought from Porto by a man named Joaquim Roque, who bequeathed it in his will to the church of the Convent of St Clare. The image of Nossa Senhora da Soledade (Our Lady of Solitude) had the same origin and was bequeathed to the convent of the Mercês. When that house ceased to exist, the image passed to the church of the College.

When the two images arrived in Madeira, they were placed, so it is said, in a private chapel in the lane of the Capuchinhas. From there they passed to the chapel of the Quinta do Til, where they remained until they were carried in procession to the two convents mentioned, following the grant made by their owner.

Before these two images were acquired, the procession we are describing featured an image of Christ Carrying the Cross belonging to a holder of the Correia entail (*morgado*), and an image of the Senhora da Soledade, which is now in the chapel of Faial.
Votive procession of 9 October

On 13 November 1803, in the presence of Bishop Dom Luís Rodrigues Vilares, the cathedral chapter and the rest of the clergy in the choir of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), it was unanimously resolved to hold a procession on 9 October each year in honour of the patronage of the Virgin, in order to obtain the protection of the Mother of God and prevent any repetition of the disasters and damage caused by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October of the same year. The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had already taken the same decision on 11 November. In accordance with these resolutions, a procession was held for many years that set out from the Sé and made its way to the church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major), accompanied by the ecclesiastical and civil authorities, the municipality and the clergy. This procession, which is often moved to the Sunday nearest to 9 October, is still held today, but it now goes only round the churchyard of the Sé, accompanied by the confraternity of the parish. (See Vow to the Blessed Virgin.)
Penitential processions
A foreign work published in 1819 describes these processions as follows:

‘In the processions of penance there appear images of the Saviour, the Virgin and various saints, carried on the shoulders of penitents clad in habits of blue cotton, with only the openings needed to allow them to see and breathe. These processions are accompanied by part of the clergy, in magnificent vestments, and by a military detachment with its band. Beside the penitents who carry the images walk others bearing heavy stones, iron bars, chains, etc., or striking their backs with bundles of wire or nettles until the blood drips.’

Penitential processions were held either to beg heaven for rain or some other favour, or to show the population’s sorrow for some offence committed against Providence. Some fifty-odd years ago the image of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*) was taken out in procession along the Caminho dos Saltos (‘falls’), across the Levada (‘irrigation channel’) and back to its church by the Caminho do Monte. Along this whole long route the image was accompanied by numerous penitents who either carried heavy loads or scourged themselves or wounded themselves with brambles (1921).

This was, we believe, the last procession of rigorous penance held in Funchal. It is said that, having been held because of a drought that had long been felt, it was already raining heavily when the image was returned to the church of Monte.

In the Passos procession (Lenten procession of Christ carrying the Cross) and the Ash Wednesday procession, men once appeared with scourges, chains or iron bars, but that custom disappeared long ago. In modern times the only practice is for a few women penitents to join the Passos procession and the Good Friday procession, usually barefoot, which is a great sacrifice only for those to whom wearing shoes is a necessity.
Proclamation of the Republican Government
See Republic (proclamation of the).
Proclamations of the absolutist government

The revolution that broke out in Porto on 24 August 1820, and was echoed in Lisbon on 15 September of the same year, established representative government, which the general Cortes (Portuguese parliament) sanctioned by promulgating the Constitution. The event was solemnly celebrated on this island, and the new system of government was proclaimed in this city on 28 January 1821, as already described on p. 301 ff. of vol. 1 of this work. Not even three years after the Porto revolution, on 3 June 1823, John VI addressed a proclamation to the country dissolving the Cortes, abolishing the Constitution and restoring absolute government. News of these extraordinary political events reached Madeira on the 16th of the same month, and the next day the establishment of the new order of things was publicly solemnised in this city. There were various demonstrations of rejoicing on that occasion, with the permission of the then governor, the captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) António Manuel de Noronha.

The new governor of the archipelago, Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro, arrived in Funchal on 26 August 1823, and on 1 September he at once ordered the destruction and levelling of the foundations of the planned monument to the Constitution, which had been laid 19 months earlier amid the greatest enthusiasm and with uncommon splendour and pomp. Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro gave the act great solemnity and ceremony, so as to make the Madeirans fully aware that any attempt to restore the principles proclaimed by the Porto revolution would be futile. He reported to the government of mainland Portugal in close detail how he had carried out the complete levelling and destruction of the foundations of the monument that was to have been erected: the foundation stone, the silver casket and what it contained – the corresponding record (*auto*), the commemorative medal and the coins of the time placed there – were all entirely ruined and destroyed. (See Constitution of 1821 and Monuments (*Monumentos*).)

Dom Manuel de Portugal e Castro also ordered that the public offices should obliterate every trace left in their books and in any other documents of the acts of public administration during the period from 1821 to 1823 (see Burning of constitutional documents).

The article Special judicial commissions (vol. I, p. 31) gives a detailed account of the first administrative acts of this governor, and especially of the special judicial commission (*alçada*) that accompanied him to this island.

Less than three years later, on the death of John VI on 10 March 1826, Dom Pedro was recognised as King of Portugal. On 29 April of that year he granted the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*), and representative government was thus restored (see Granting of the Charter).

Two years later, on 25 April 1828, Prince Miguel I, regent of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), was proclaimed absolute king after the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) had been dissolved. In Madeira absolute government was not proclaimed at once, because José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, the constitutional governor of this archipelago, remained loyal to the principles he represented and prepared to resist the attempts of the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) troops who sought to seize the island. The article Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelite troops (p. 6 of vol. III) gives a brief account of this resistance and of its failure to prevent the royalist forces from landing.

The Miguelite governor José Maria Monteiro landed in Funchal on 24 August 1828 and took office that same day, holding the post until April 1830. This governor, who became known here in Madeira by the nickname ‘Baeta’ (baize), left a far from honourable memory of his administration because of the abuses of power he committed, as we have said in the article devoted to him in this work (vol. II, p. 390). He made the action of the special judicial commission (*alçada*) that the central government sent to this island (see Alçadas, vol. I, pp. 31 ff.) still more odious and oppressive, through the partial support he gave it and his encouragement of the various excesses and abuses committed by that tribunal.
Proclamations of constitutional government
On p. 301 ff. of vol. I of this work we gave an account of how the first Constitution was proclaimed in this archipelago, and we refer readers who wish to learn about the subject to that passage.

In 1823 absolute government was restored, and on the death of John VI in March 1826 Dom Pedro granted the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*), introducing representative government. The Charter was solemnly proclaimed on this island with great splendour and enthusiasm on 6, 7 and 8 August 1826, the last day being set aside for the oath of loyalty to the Charter. In Funchal and other places there were noisy celebrations to mark the advent of constitutional government. The following October elections for deputies were held, and those elected were Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar, Dr Father Caetano Alberto Soares and Luís Monteiro.

Miguel I restored absolute government once again in 1828. In 1834, with the Convention of Évora Monte and the end of the civil war, the representative system was raised up anew, in keeping with the provisions of the Constitutional Charter of 1826. It was on 5 June 1834 that the new system of government was solemnly proclaimed in this city, and for many years its anniversary was celebrated with the most fervent enthusiasm.

In those days it was always the students of our lyceum (state secondary school) who gave these festivities their characteristic liveliness and lent them all the warmth and enthusiasm of their ardent, restless youth. With what tender longing do we old men remember the dawn serenade played at the doors of the teachers’ homes, the Te Deum in the Colégio church (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church), the procession of students led by the blue and white silk processional banner, the recitation of some stanzas of *The Lusiads* (*Os Lusíadas*) by the octogenarian Sergeant Ferro on a bandstand in the old Passeio, and our emotion on seeing the aged peer of the realm and former minister José Ferreira Pestana hoist on the mast of the Fortress the blue and white flag, by then worn to a rag, but the very one that had been unfurled there on 5 June 1834!

On the afternoon of 3 June 1834 the war schooner *Amélia*, commanded by the distinguished Madeiran naval officer António Teixeira Doria, sailed slowly into our bay with the blue-and-white ensign hoisted at the head of her mainsail. The enthusiasm this at once aroused among supporters of constitutionalism was beyond description. The schooner had brought news of the convention of Évora-Monte, concluded on 26 May, and of the immediate end of the civil war that followed it, with the complete triumph of the supporters of the liberal cause.

Pedro IV officially informed the governor and captain-general of Madeira, Dom Álvaro da Costa de Macedo, of the political events that had changed the country’s system of government. He required him to submit the archipelago completely to the new Government, on pain of being considered a rebel, and held him responsible for any consequences that might arise from whatever attempt at resistance he might perhaps wish to make.

Far from thinking of offering the slightest resistance, Dom Álvaro de Macedo was in fact preparing to declare his public support for the new order of things when he was approached by a group of citizens, representing some thousands of the island’s inhabitants. They asked that the new sovereign and the new form of government be proclaimed at once, in the most public and solemn manner.

The governor agreed to the request, and the white flag of Dom Miguel was immediately lowered on the so-called bastion of the chestnut tree (*baluarte do castanheiro*) and the two-coloured flag raised in its place. The city’s fortresses fired salutes as they hoisted the same flag, and the constitution was joyfully acclaimed everywhere. On the 6th the ceremony of swearing to the Charter and of the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of Queen Maria II took place in the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*). It was attended by the governor, the bishop, the other military and civil authorities and many citizens, and it was finally resolved to send congratulations to the regent, Dom Pedro, on the establishment of the liberal regime in the country.

The constitutionalists who went to the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace) to demand the immediate proclamation of the new government were António Barnabé Soares, Cândido de Freitas Abreu, Luís António de Ornelas, Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça and Paulo Emílio de Ornelas. A painting in the Masonic lodge Liberdade depicts the glorious part these five Madeirans played on 5 June.

As they made their way from Rua de João Tavira towards the fortress, bearing two-coloured flags, the detachment guarding the gaol formed up. It is said that it was preparing to open fire on the five constitutionalists and the people following them when the officer of the watch arrived and ordered the soldiers to withdraw, preventing the outrage from being carried out.

Near Madeira the schooner *Amélia* met the frigate *D. Pedro*, commanded by Captain Henrique de Price Bertrand, which had been blockading the island since 28 May. This officer had sent an envoy under flag of truce to Dom Álvaro on that same day, the 28th, but Dom Álvaro refused to receive him or the correspondence he carried.
The following quatrain comes from a patriotic song that was widely sung in liberal families in 1834:
Here comes the swift Amélia, / She fears not the breaking waves, / Bringing news of liberty / To Funchal, groaning in oppression.

Having sworn, and administered, the oath of loyalty to the Charter and the Queen, Dom Álvaro de Macedo continued to govern the archipelago until 13 July, when he sailed for Lisbon aboard the frigate *D. Pedro*. He was succeeded by an interim government made up of the provisor (diocesan judicial and administrative officer) of the bishopric, since the bishop was absent, the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) of the judicial district (*comarca*) and Captain Henrique de Price Bertrand. Under the terms of the royal decree (*alvará*) of 12 December 1770, this government administered the province until 6 August following, when the prefect (*prefeito*) Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque arrived from Lisbon.
Prophets

In the year 1533 there lived on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) a certain Fernando or Fernão Nunes, nicknamed o Bravo (‘the Fierce’), who had a seventeen-year-old niece named Felipa Nunes, paralysed for some years. This Fernão Nunes sought to pass himself off as a prophet. One night he came down from the hills where he lived and entered the town (*vila*) ‘to see his niece, ringing a little bell, says Frutuoso, and on reaching the place where she was, he told her that the Holy Spirit had sent him to her, so that both might preach to the people of that island and tell them their sins..... And that Philipa Nunes answered him that the Holy Spirit had revealed to her that he was coming in that manner’.

A great many people gathered to find out what was happening, and, as Frutuoso relates, Fernão Nunes pointed out to each of them the sins they had committed. For this reason the pair were readily believed, not only by the ignorant common people but also by the judges, councillors (*vereadores*) and leading men of the island. Some days later, at the orders of the prophets Fernando and Felipa, the people went in procession, with the vicar and clergy, to the chapel of Our Lady of Grace (*Nossa Senhora da Graça*). There Fernão Nunes said such things ‘that all went about confused, and astonished, and disconsolate, without eating; the women threw into the sea all their face paints, without regard for their precious garments, but rather took off the poor ones they wore, and remained in their shifts, as if doing penance, eating but little, and standing on their feet.’

One day, while this Fernão Nunes was preaching, ‘many publicly confessed grave and abominable sins that they had committed’. When a certain João Calaça, a notary, dared to pray from a book during the sermon, the prophet declared that ‘he who was praying had the devil in his body’, and at once many men fell upon Calaça and killed him. The prophet ordered the dead man to be carried to the chapel of São Sebastião (St Sebastian) and left there, because he would rise again within three days.

The population was so blinded and frightened by what the prophet said that no one looked after their estates and business, and ‘the most highborn and noble women, says Frutuoso, went to the church in their shifts, before their husbands, with large wicker baskets.... full of drained curds, cheeses and bread, and other food, for those who were in the church night and day listening to the prophet’s preaching to eat’. ‘One night the prophet Fernando was in the house of the prophetess Philippa Nunes, where there were many people, honourable women and men, all barefoot and on their knees, among them one Rodrigo Alves, a very honourable and rich man, and his wife, and Manuel de Crasto and his wife, and many other persons and noble women. Before them all, he went up to Rodrigo Alves’s wife and put his tongue in her mouth, saying to her husband: “Does it grieve you, Rodrigo?” And he answered him: “God knows.” And then he made him kneel before him and gave him two slaps. And he told Manuel de Crasto to go and fetch bread and wine for those who were there to eat. He went and brought a sack of bread and a barrel of wine, which they all ate and drank. After eating he ordered Manuel de Crasto and his wife to undress, which they did at once, remaining in their shifts, with no one looking at them or paying heed to it, as if it were the state of innocence; and thus half-naked he ordered them to go to Sancto Spirito, and said that from there they would go to Paradise. And they went unclothed, though it was winter, in February, and so they stayed in the said chapel of the Spirito Sancto until just before dawn, when they then went home, and not to Glory, as the prophet had said.’

The Prophet set men and women to threshing in a barley field, and it is asserted that the clergy, in the confession during Mass, said: ‘St Peter, St Paul and the Blessed Prophet Fernando’, and named him thus in the introit and prayers.

When word reached Madeira of the extraordinary events taking place on Porto Santo, the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) João de Afonseca set out for that island with two clerks (*escrivães*). He had the two prophets arrested and sent to the gaol at Machico. The vicar and clergy were also arrested for having taken Fernão Nunes’s deceptions seriously, as were the prophet’s town crier and doorkeeper, one Francisco Fernandes, a Castilian.

The judicial inquiry (*devassa*) conducted by the *corregedor* lasted until 10 March 1533. For eighteen days the people of Porto Santo had been subject to the influence and follies of the prophet Fernando, who was the son of an honourable man named Bartolomeu Nunes, living in the locality of Farrobo (‘carob tree’), on the north side of that island.

‘As soon as the prisoners were brought to the town of Machico, relates Frutuoso, Philipa Nunes, who had previously pretended not to eat, at once ate hastily, saying that she knew nothing of what they told her she had done. The *corregedor* sent them both as prisoners to the King, with the inquiry, which the clerk Henrique Coelho carried and delivered to His Highness, who regarded it as a great service. Under it the prophets were sentenced both to stand at the door of the Cathedral of Évora on a stairway, each with a paper mitre bearing letters that read: Prophet of Porto Santo, and each with a lighted candle in hand while the Mass of terce was said, she clothed and he naked from the waist up; and they were then to be released, since it was the work of the Devil. And as to the death of João Calaça, no proceedings were to be taken against anyone, as these too were works of the Devil, who had blinded them all. And the King fined all the inhabitants of the Island of Porto Santo, for believing the said superstitions of the false prophets, two hundred *cruzados* for a public work on the said island, namely the Judges, Councillors and persons of the governance of the island ten *cruzados* each, and the rest of the people according to their estate; and these two hundred *cruzados* were paid. And while the clerk Henrique Coelho was on the said island, they were collected and handed to Estevão Calaça, a resident there, to be spent on things needful to the land, as the King commanded. The clerics were condemned to penalties and punishments by Antonio Machado, who was then in Portugal, Provisor of the See of Funchal, since it was vacant... Of the prophet Fernando some say that he went mad or feigned madness, the better to free himself; others, that he died a prisoner in the Limoeiro; others, that after being sentenced and doing penance he went on pilgrimage to foreign lands, doing penance; and in the end he never again went to the island, nor appeared, nor was seen. But the prophetess married and lived in Portugal, without ever returning to Porto Santo, where she had done things far from holy.','cells','cells'

‘Some, on account of this deed, would mock the inhabitants of the island of Porto Santo, who bear no blame for their forebears; but even if they did, it is not the office of a humane Christian man to mock the faults of others, for he may fall into similar ones; for the cord that is twisted often untwists; and whoever has a roof of glass should not throw stones at another’s roof.’

From the book *Diocese do Funchal*, recently published, we extract the following passages: The ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) dwell at length on the strange case that occurred in 1533 on the neighbouring island of Porto Santo, in which Fernão Bravo and Filipa Nunes, uncle and niece, common folk without any education, set themselves up as ‘prophets’. They revealed the hidden acts and deepest secrets of many people with such power of suggestion that even the island’s own clergy came to believe them and to attend the ‘sermons’ that these ‘seers’ preached to a crowd gripped by fear and the greatest wonder. The extraordinary event caused a considerable sensation and even had wide repercussions in mainland Portugal. It was the Franciscan friar and celebrated preacher Friar Gaspar Gato who, going to that island and making contact with the ‘prophets’, exposed the whole cunning fraud of these deranged people, who were brought as prisoners to Madeira and tried and sentenced. The clergy of Porto Santo suffered the consequences of their extreme credulity, being likewise arrested and severely punished by the competent ecclesiastical authority, the governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop’s absence), the diocese being then vacant through the death of the prelate Dom Diogo Pinheiro.
Profundidades

Dr Álvaro R. de Azevedo gave the name *profundidades* (‘depths’) to certain places of considerable altitude, fair extent and roughly circular shape, because the generic term ‘valleys’ did not suit them. He mentions the *profundidades* of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of that name, the most remarkable of them all; that of Fanal (‘beacon’), in the mountains of the parish of Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’); that of Rabaçal, in the valley of the said stream; and that of Fõjo, near Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’), in the parish of São Martinho (‘St Martin’).
Dr Azevedo deals with all these *profundidades* at some length in the *Diccionario Universal Portuguez Ilustrado*.
