Protestant proselytism

As we have said elsewhere in this work, the English colony began to be of importance here at the end of the 16th century. From that time until the introduction of representative government, we have no record that members of that colony, or of any other Protestant nationality, tried to promote their religion among us by making converts within the Madeiran population. They had churches reserved for their own worship, attended only by their adherents, to the complete exclusion of the natives. And in fairness it must be said that, in general, the foreign subjects living in Madeira as merchants or invalids, and also the visitors who seek out our mild climate or the beauties of our privileged natural surroundings, do not devote themselves to propagating their religious ideals, nor do they try to turn Catholics away from the practice of the religion they profess. Several Protestant foreigners have even supported some Catholic works and helped to build and repair churches and chapels, as John Howard March did when he rebuilt the parish church of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’).

What has just been said does not exclude the undeniable fact that some English Protestant propagandists, acting as emissaries of the so-called Bible societies, attempted on several occasions, with greater or lesser energy, to win converts to their religion on this island, at times bringing disturbance and disorder to some of its parishes. This propaganda began chiefly in 1838. Several attempts had been made before, but they proved entirely fruitless. It was Dr Roberto Kalley who truly succeeded in conducting an effective campaign here. His personal qualities contributed powerfully to this: his captivating eloquence, his charity towards the poor and, above all, his eminent skill in the art of healing, for he was a most distinguished physician and treated everyone free of charge. It was chiefly in this that the secret of his campaign’s effectiveness lay. We have already dealt with it, and with its baleful consequences, on p. 207 ff. of volume II.

Dr Kalley’s hurried departure from this island in 1846, never to return, did not put an end to the adherents of Protestantism among the inhabitants of some Madeiran parishes, above all in Santo da Serra, Machico, São Roque and Santo António. The propaganda had taken root, and proselytising never ceased in these and other centres, though under more moderate conditions and without the enthusiastic fervour Dr Kalley had given it. The truth, however, is that the results of this propaganda are not great. More than 90 years have passed since the celebrated Scottish physician left this island, and the number of converts, far from increasing, has fallen considerably. Although the propagandists have powerful means of attraction at their disposal – the press, with the publication of a newspaper and the distribution of countless pamphlets, the maintenance of schools, and even handouts of money and clothing – it is nonetheless certain that the adherents of Protestant ideas do not exceed about a hundred individuals in a population of 169,000 inhabitants (1921). That number would be much larger if one were to believe the reports sent to the Bible societies and other foreign associations that foster this propaganda, but the truth is that such reports are written to suit the interests and convenience of those who maintain the propaganda in this archipelago.

The proselytising carried on by Dr Kalley lasted roughly eight years, from 1838 to 1846, apart from a few short journeys the celebrated propagandist made to England. With his abrupt departure from Madeira, Protestant propaganda almost disappeared among us, not only because it had lost its chief support, but also because of the well-founded fear that popular anger might again break out in violence as lamentable as that of 9 August 1846.

The propaganda became less intense and more cautious, but it never ceased, and was carried on especially in the parishes of Machico and Santo da Serra, as well as in some parts of Funchal. Shortly after Dr Kalley’s hasty flight, the Protestant minister Hewitson appeared and began a moderate campaign; or rather, he came to nourish and preserve the fruits of the Scottish physician’s proselytism. In 1850 the civil governor José Silvestre Ribeiro had to intervene in the attempts that a certain Wilkinson was making in Machico to draw various individuals into the Calvinist sect.

The ardour of the propaganda then cooled, gaining a certain momentum some years later when, around 1860, a Calvinist church was established in Funchal. A new and more active campaign took place around 1875, and it grew still further after 1894. The ministers Angus and Buchanan were the chief agents of this propaganda. It is certain, however, as we have already pointed out, that Calvinist proselytism has always had meagre results here, except for the propaganda carried on by Dr Robert Kalley, owing above all to the eminent qualities that distinguished him and to the way in which he knew how to address the people of this island.

It is a tribute owed to the truth to state here that in recent years the English colony on this island has not lent its action and influence, which are considerable, to this propaganda, and that at times it has even openly condemned the conduct of certain Calvinist ministers who sought to win over the inhabitants of this island to the practice of their religious ideals.
The article Kalley (Robert), on p. 207 of vol. II, offers further interesting information on this subject, which should be consulted.
Prostitution

Prostitution already existed in Madeira in the 15th century, as is clearly shown by various old decrees and by a petition addressed to the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) on 8 October 1495. This asked that the brothel quarter ‘be removed from beside the sea, because the men from outside went ashore with the harlots, caused disturbances and took refuge in the boats, and the law did not arrest them’. The *mancebia* was the place set aside for prostitutes to live.

The charter (foral) of the captaincy of Funchal, granted by King Manuel I on 6 August 1515, laid down that anyone found ‘in the brothel quarter with weapons, whether by day or by night, should lose the weapons and pay a penalty of 500 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), and that every married man proved to keep a mistress ‘held and maintained’ should pay the *quarentena* (fine of a fortieth part of one’s property) on half of the estate he possessed.

We do not know when syphilis appeared in Madeira, but it is reasonable to suppose that this dreadful disease was already known here at the end of the 15th century or the beginning of the 16th. If the sailors of the ships that called at our port ‘went ashore with the harlots’ and withdrew to their boats without the police being able to arrest them, nothing could be more natural than to accept the contagion and spread of an illness that, even in those times, was known and feared in Europe. Dr Hans Sloane, who visited this island in October 1687, found syphilitic symptoms in some of the people who consulted him.

At the beginning of the second quarter of the 19th century, as the records of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) show, prostitutes were living in the most central parts of the city, especially in Rua do Monteiro. A document of the period states that they caused frequent scandals there. This led the Council, at its session of 9 December 1835, to urge the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) to keep these women under the closest watch and to have them removed from those places whenever this proved necessary.

Inspection of prostitutes was introduced in Portugal by an order of the intendant Pina Manique dated 2 April 1781. In Madeira, however, it is only since 1854, we believe, that these women have been subject to medical supervision, even though Mousinho de Albuquerque in 1834 and Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro in 1846 had urged the advisability of submitting them to regular sanitary examinations.

On 5 November 1834 the Council received a letter from the prefect (*prefeito*) of the Province referring to the ‘venereal disease present in a great number of public women’. It was resolved to pay the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Misericórdia Hospital (Hospital da Misericórdia), ‘on this one and only occasion’, the expenses it had incurred in treating these women from 21 October to 4 November of that year.

On 8 March 1836 the Government ordered 1,000,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) to be given to the Committee of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) of Funchal to help with the treatment of prostitutes suffering from venereal diseases. It also urged the Committee to make every effort to treat in the hospital, and with its resources, the poor who suffered from those diseases. The ministerial order (*portaria*) that laid down these provisions suggested that the Committee should turn to public subscriptions to raise the funds needed for the treatment of these poor people.

It was after the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1856 that prostitutes began to settle in Rua do Ribeirinho de Baixo and Rua dos Medinas. Before then these streets had been inhabited only by respectable people, some of whom belonged to the leading families of the city. In 1840 there was a boys’ school in a building on the southern part of Rua do Ribeirinho de Baixo, and in 1819 the Lancasterian School (*Escola Lancasteriana*) was housed in a house in the same street, although it remained there only for a short time.
Sugar protectionism

The laws of 4 February 1876, 18 May 1881 and 22 March 1886 exempted Madeiran sugar imported into Portugal and the Azores from the payment of duties, the first two for five years and the last for three years. True sugar protectionism, however, began only with the publication of the decree of 30 December 1895. This decree obliged the factories that registered to pay farmers for their cane at the price of 400 and 450 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) per 30 kilograms. In compensation for this burden, it granted those factories the privilege of paying a duty of 30 *réis*, instead of 60 *réis* per kilogram, on molasses imported for making alcohol for wines. Madeira sugar, which under the preliminaries of the 1892 tariff paid a quarter of the rate on the mainland and in the Azores, was freed from that municipal levy (*imposição*).

The decree of 24 September 1903 added 50 *réis* to the minimum prices for 30 kilograms of cane, in exchange for new concessions to the factories. The law of 24 November 1904 then turned the sugar and alcohol industry in Madeira into a true monopoly, vesting the exercise of this industry in the registered manufacturers W. Hinton & Sons and José Júlio de Lemos.

The decree of 1903 mentioned above lowered the duty payable by the manufacturers on foreign molasses from 30 to 6 *réis* per kilo. At the same time it granted them ‘the right to extract from this raw material, before the distillation of alcohol for wines, the little sugar still usable, to be consumed in Madeira. This, however, would be deducted from the total extracted from the cane, and the deducted portion, if it were also exported instead of being sold on the island, would pay the duties and other general taxes at the customs houses of destination’.
Under this decree, Madeiran sugar lost its free entry into the Azores, to which some had been exported until 1903.

The monopoly established by the law of 24 November 1904, which the law of 9 September 1908 did not significantly alter, was to last 15 years. However, the firm of Wm Hinton & Sons lodged a complaint against a provision of the regulations of 11 March 1909 that restricted the sale of alcohol for the treatment of wines. After long and protracted negotiations, the Government was forced to publish the decree of 11 March 1911, intended to resolve the awkward situation created by that firm’s demands.

The complaint to which we refer was not the last. The one that arose from the disclosure of the provisions of clause 23 of the law of 15 August 1914 became notorious because of the stir it caused throughout the country.

The decree of 11 March 1911 established four zones based on the strength of the sugar-cane juice, kept the prices of 450 to 500 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) set by the decree of 1903, and exempted from all duties Madeiran sugar destined for mainland Portugal. It taxed foreign sugars once again and allowed the registered factories (*fábricas matriculadas*) to import up to 550 tonnes of sugar a year from the colonies with a 50 per cent reduction in the corresponding duties.

Other concessions were made to the registered factories. The same decree, which was to remain in force until 31 December 1918, also laid down, however, that the quantity of alcohol needed to fortify wines would be 55 litres per *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of 500 litres.
The regulations for implementing the decree with force of law of 11 March 1911 were approved by the decree of 15 May 1912.

Although the former Companhia Fabril de Açúcar Madeirense set prices of 550, 600 and 650 *réis* per 30 kilograms of cane in 1872, it is well known that these prices were not maintained and that, before protectionism was decreed, the product was rarely sold for more than 300 or 320 *réis*.

Under the protectionist measures we have mentioned, the situation of many landowners and farmers improved considerably, since growing cane had become much more profitable. However, as these same measures did not also fix the price of sugar, this basic necessity grew steadily dearer in Madeira. It even came to the rather curious situation that, for a long time, the refineries on the mainland bought Madeiran sugar at lower prices than consumers in Funchal paid.

The manufacture of sugar was declared free from 1 January 1920 by Decree no. 5492 of 2 May 1919. This decree contains certain provisions of evident usefulness, but, as we have already had occasion to say on p. 226 of volume 1 of this work, it also contains others that pleased neither industry nor agriculture. Decree no. 6521 of 9 April 1920 modified or eliminated some of these provisions, and finally Decree no. 8089 of 3 April 1922 entrusted the administration of Madeira’s sugar regime (*regímen sacarino*, the legal regime governing sugar and alcohol production) to the Agricultural Station of the 9th Region, except for the [functions relating to] sugar and alcohol reserved to the Ministry of Finance. Under the same decree, the technical commission for the supervision of Madeira’s sugar regime consists of the director of the Agricultural Station of the 9th Region, the engineer of the Industrial District and the head of the District Inspection Department.

In May 1922 an attempt was made to revive the protectionist regime, or at least to guarantee a remunerative price for cane, in return for authorising the old registered factories (*fábricas matriculadas*) to sell sugar at 1.65 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis). Although things seemed to be going well at first – the Government even went so far as to prohibit the clearance of about 600 tonnes of sugar arriving from Brazil – in the end nothing was decreed in the sense desired by the owners of those factories. A major contributing factor was the campaign waged against this claim by an important Lisbon newspaper and also by various classes in Madeira which, not living from agriculture, wish only that sugar should be sold at prices within the reach of every purse.

Superintendent of the Treasury

He was one of the most senior officials in Funchal, subordinate to the Treasury Council (*Conselho de Fazenda*), a tribunal created by Philip II of Spain on 20 November 1591 and confirmed by law of 22 December 1761. He was responsible for accounting for the revenue and expenditure of public money, and he ran the Funchal Customs House until 1775, as stated on p. 34 of vol. I of this *Elucidário*. The royal letter (*carta régia*) of 2 August 1641 ordered the judges and officers of the Council to assist him whenever necessary, and the warrant of the Treasury Council of 11 January 1701 laid down that he could summon any officers or soldiers of the militia to give evidence in matters concerning the Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*), without the Governor’s authorisation. He could order the arrest of any person without the leave of the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate), and have any prisoner brought from the gaol..., when this was needed for any business of the Royal Treasury, as can be seen from the warrant of the Treasury Council of 10 March 1735.

The Treasury Superintendency (Provedoria da Fazenda) was abolished by royal letter of 6 April 1775 and replaced by the Royal Treasury Board (*Junta da Real Fazenda*), to which we have already referred in this *Elucidário*.

The official who held the post of superintendent (provedor) when the office was abolished became judge of the Customs House, in accordance with the determinations of the Royal Treasury Board of 21 August 1775. See Junta da Real Fazenda.

Pterygium

This disease, also known as *unha do olho* (‘nail of the eye’), was noted as frequent in Madeira some 170 years ago by Dr Heberden, an English physician. Dr Alfredo Ernesto Rodrigues, a distinguished eye specialist, has told us that it continues to occur on a large scale on the island. It is characterised by a thickening of part of the conjunctiva, which almost always appears at the inner corner of the eye (1921).

Quebradas

It is chiefly the action of rain that causes the frequent landslides on this island commonly known as *quebradas*. It seems to us that this word has a special meaning here that is entirely unknown in other regions of our country. The remarkably rugged terrain, where deep valleys abut towering mountains, aided by various atmospheric agents, explains these falls of rock and earth. They sometimes cover a large area and in some cases cause loss of life and great material damage. Roads cut into mountainsides beneath overhanging rocks are from time to time destroyed or made impassable by *quebradas* crashing down from above. The same happens to the irrigation levadas (irrigation channel).

The so-called fajãs (Volume II, p. 7), both inland and on the coast, owe their origin to the fall of great *quebradas*. These now rarely occur, but in winter small *quebradas* are frequent and cause considerable damage. Many date from before the discovery, such as that of Jardim do Mar (‘garden by the sea’), while some are of more recent formation, such as that of Lugar de Baixo (Volume II, p. 285), and others.
Waterfalls

The best known on the island of Madeira are the following: that of Eiró, near Fajã dos Padres; that of the Ribeiro da Lombada do Esmeraldo; that of the Ribeiro de São Tiago, near Ponta do Sol; that of the Ribeiro do Ledo, near Loreto; that of Paul do Mar; that of one of the tributaries of the Ribeira do Tristão; that of the Ribeira de João Delgado, near Seixal; those of the Ribeira do Inferno; that of Água de Vento, in Seixal; those of Poço das Cales, Poço da Furna, Poço Pulido and Poço do Passassol, in the valley of São Vicente; that of Risco, in Rabaçal; those near the Serrado das Ameixieiras; that of the Madre de Água, on the Ribeira de Santa Cruz; those of Caldeirão Verde, Silveira, Lombo and others on or near the Ribeira de São Jorge; those of the Ribeira de João Gomes; those of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia, the largest of which is that of the Poço do Cabo da Ribeira; that of the Ribeiro do Pisão, in Monte; and that of the Ribeiro and Lage, beyond Ribeiro Frio.
Burning of Constitutional documents

On 29 September 1833 the people’s judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds) petitioned the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) to collect and publicly burn, ‘as unworthy and shameful acts of a loyal people’, all documents and orders issued by the Constitutional Government. The Council granted the petition, and the burning took place on 4 October of that year, at about 4 in the afternoon, in the Largo da Sé, before a large crowd and the military corps of the 1st and 2nd line. According to the *Pregador Imparcial*, the documents burnt were ‘the minutes of the elections and all the other autographs and powers of attorney of the substitute deputies’. After the ceremony the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) raised several cheers for John VI, absolute king, which the people warmly echoed.
Queimada

This is an inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Água de Pena, in the municipality (*concelho*) of Machico. Here, in 1924, Francisco de Freitas Correia had a chapel built dedicated to Nossa Senhora do Perpétuo Socorro, the first of this dedication to be built in Madeira.
Queimada de Cima (street)
This public street links Rua de João Tavira with Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), or do Comércio. It was once called Rua do Oliveira and later Rua Afonso Vaz.

Parallel to it and a short distance away lie Rua Gomes Freire (formerly Rua do Bispo) to the north and Rua da Queimada de Baixo (‘low’) to the south. In these streets are most of the stables housing the hire horses and the oxen and mules used to draw carts and sledges (*corsas*). The local press has often and at length called for these stables to be removed from the most central part of the city. Despite this, and despite the efforts of some council sessions, it has not yet been possible to remove those veritable sources of infection, which so disfigure the place and contribute greatly to the unhealthiness of those streets (1921).
Queimada (point)
This headland of the coast lies between the parishes of Machico and Água de Pena.
Queimadas

A picturesque locality (*sítio*) in the uplands of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’), where there is a small mountain shelter for travellers. It is an obligatory point of passage for those wishing to visit the astonishing and breathtaking spot of Caldeirão Verde (‘green cauldron’), in the parish of São Jorge (‘St George’).
Queimado (peak)

A village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) and mountain height roughly equidistant from Lombo do Mouro (‘the Moor’s ridge’) and Monte Medonho (‘fearsome hill’), on the boundary between the parishes (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and São Vicente.
Red cinchona (Cinchona succirubra, Pav.)

A member of the Rubiaceae from the Andes, Peru and Ecuador, introduced to Madeira in 1867 by the late botanist João Maria Moniz. Of the 20 specimens that came to the island at that time, only one survived in 1909, on a *quinta* (country estate) a little above the church of St Lucy (*Santa Luzia*), where it flowered every year without, however, producing fertile seeds. Some cinchona trees planted in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’) did not last long there. According to the late Richard Thomas Lowe, the places in Madeira where the cultivation of the red cinchona might perhaps be tried with success are the Ribeira da Metade and the Ribeira da Boaventura, the Lombada das Vacas in São Vicente, the Montado dos Pessegueiros on the Ribeira do Inferno, the Ribeira Funda near Seixal, etc., etc. *Cinchona calisaya*, mentioned in a work on the climate of Madeira as growing in the garden of the hospice (*hospício*) of Princess Maria Amélia, was never cultivated on our island.
Quincentenary of the discovery of Madeira

As we have said elsewhere (see the publication entitled *V Centenário do Descobrimento da Madeira*, p. 2), the year 1419 or 1420 had generally been adopted as the most probable date of the discovery of this archipelago. This followed the lead of the old chronicles, and in particular the period that Gaspar Frutuoso had fixed for the event, which had in turn been followed by the illustrious and learned annotator of the *Saudades da Terra*. In 1920 an interesting pamphlet appeared, entitled *O Reconhecimento da Madeira*, by the lawyer and journalist Dr Manuel Gregório Pestana Júnior, which opened a new path towards fixing the date of the discovery. According to it, this notable event would have taken place in the period from 1441 to 1425. Although one may disagree with the conclusions reached by Dr Pestana Júnior, it is nonetheless beyond dispute that his work represents a painstaking and conscientious study, which may perhaps lead to new research and possibly to firmer and more conclusive statements on the subject.

Authoritative opinions differed over the fixing of this immemorial date, and the centenary of the great event had not been commemorated in the year the old chronicles assigned to it, for reasons we refrain from characterising. Together, these circumstances left the way open for postponing the celebration of the quincentenary of the discovery, and this solemn commemoration finally took place at the end of 1922.

It was Major João dos Reis Gomes, a distinguished son of our land and the most illustrious of its writers and journalists, who launched and championed the idea of celebrating the centenary in the *Diário da Madeira*, of which he is editor (1921). He drew up the framework of the commemoration, began its preparatory work, directed many items of the programme, and constantly followed and supervised, sometimes down to the smallest details, all the work on the various festivities held in this city at the end of December 1922 and the beginning of January 1923. If it is true that Major Reis Gomes was the soul of these festive commemorations, it is equally beyond doubt that he had valuable and devoted helpers, chosen by himself, who identified with his ideas and his actions and rendered the most brilliant and notable services to the celebration of the fifth centenary of the discovery. They were the former teachers of our Industrial School, Cândido Pereira and Emanuel Ribeiro, now serving in the industrial schools of the capital. Displaying their eminent artistic gifts, their great capacity for work and their tireless energy, they gave the festivities an indelible stamp of magnificence, brilliance and originality, which aroused the greatest admiration and the warmest praise, not only from Madeirans but also from all the visitors who came to our island on that occasion (1921).

The festivities were of the utmost grandeur and unusual splendour, despite the systematic and obstinate refusal of the government of mainland Portugal and its representatives in this district to join and take part in these patriotic expressions of rejoicing. The central government had a particular duty to decree the festivities of the centenary official and to associate itself publicly with the commemorations, since above all they celebrated the glorious beginning of our maritime discoveries and conquests, the one fact that truly gives us a prominent place in the history of the civilisation of modern peoples.

As we said in the brief Preliminary Note to this work, we held that this celebration, to be complete, had to take on a national character and not be confined to the narrow limits of a regional tribute, within the isolation and distance of these remote islands. The words with which the press of the capital recalled the duty of this commemoration were lost or entirely forgotten. They had drawn the particular attention of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Ciências de Lisboa*) and, most especially, of the Committee charged with promoting the celebration of the centenaries of our conquests and discoveries, which existed and operated within that Academy. If the conquest of Ceuta, as the first achieved beyond the continental frontiers, deserved a fitting and solemn commemoration, the discovery of this archipelago, which truly marks the beginning of our brilliant odyssey as navigators and future masters of the seas in both hemispheres, could not be forgotten either.

The outline programme for the centenary celebrations, drawn up by Major J. Reis Gomes, was as follows. In its broad lines it was carried out, apart from minor changes advised by the circumstances of the moment: 1. Receptions at the Palace of the civil government, at that of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) and at that of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal.
2. Pilgrimage to the tomb of Gonçalves Zargo in the church of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*).
3. Ball at the Quinta Pavão, with dances of the late 15th century performed by couples dressed in the fashion of that period.

4. Serenade in boats decorated in the style of the same period, held in the cove of Pontinha during the interval between the two parts of the ball programme given in no. 3, with water fireworks and set-piece fireworks at the Ilhéu fortress (*Fortaleza do Ilhéu*), and illuminations outlining the contours of the Pontinha and of that fortress.

5. Gala performance at the ‘Dr. Manuel de Arriaga’ theatre, staging the regional play *Guiomar Teixeira* by Major J. dos Reis Gomes, whose action is set in the early days of the Discovery, with the auditorium decorated in medieval style.

6. Te Deum in the Cathedral and, afterwards, the laying of the first stone of the monument to J. Gonçalves Zargo on the Avenida ‘Dr. Manuel de Arriaga’. Its model, the work of the Madeiran sculptor Francisco Franco, was commissioned and paid for by the District General Council.
7. Equestrian games of the period being commemorated, on the Campo do Almirante Reis.
8. Sports games on the same square.

9. On the Campo Dr. Miguel Bombarda, a retrospective exhibition of the old Madeiran wine presses, mills and lever presses (*alçapremas*) used in the wine and sugar industries, and a fair of the island’s agricultural and industrial products, above all wines, embroidery, textiles, wickerwork and inlaid work (*embutidos*).

10. Exhibition at the António Augusto de Aguiar Industrial School (*Escola Industrial António Augusto de Aguiar*) of historical and artistic objects and of works of applied art produced at the school.
11. Illuminations and decorations of the city, in the style of the period being commemorated.

12. Grand procession with allegorical floats of a historical character: the float of the discovery (a 15th-century caravel) and the Infante’s float, besides others representing our main industries: sugar, wines, wicker, embroidery, etc., etc.

At a select meeting held in the ‘Dr. Manuel de Arriaga’ theatre, the founding committee for the centenary celebrations was appointed. It was given the powers needed to organise the various subcommittees that were to direct and carry out the many items of the brilliant programme, which won the fullest approval of that distinguished and select assembly.

Besides the Honorary Committee and the Executive Committee, the following were appointed: the Technical and Directing Committee, the Fundraising Committee, the Propaganda and Publicity Committee, the Works Committee, the Grand Historical Procession Committee, the Religious Ceremonies Committee, the Theatre Committee, the Ball Committee, the Public Decorations Committee, the Tourism and Reception of Visitors Committee, the Concerts and Musical Festivities Committee, the Industrial Exhibition and Fair Committee, the Bibliographical Exhibition and Industrial School Products Committee, the Sports Festivities Committee, the Nautical Festivities Committee and the Equestrian Games and Cavalcades Committee.

The Honorary Committee consisted of the civil governor; the military commander, Colonel João Maria Ferraz; the diocesan bishop, Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro; the senators César Procópio de Freitas, Vasco Crispiniano da Silva and Vasco Gonçalves Marques; the deputies Américo Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Juvenal Henriques de Araújo and Pedro Góis Pita; the President of the General Council, Vasco Gonçalves Marques; and the President of the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) of Funchal, João Joaquim Teixeira Jardim.

The Executive Committee comprised Adolfo João Sarmento de Figueiredo, Alberto Artur Sarmento, Ciríaco de Brito Nóbrega, Father Fernando Augusto da Silva, Fernando Tolentino da Costa, João dos Reis Gomes and Leandro António do Rêgo.

More than a hundred gentlemen and prominent figures of our community made up the various festival committees. Some of their members showed an energy that could not have been surpassed, and a zeal and devotion worthy of the highest praise. Besides Major João Reis Gomes, Cândido Pereira and Emanuel Ribeiro, whom we have already mentioned above with well-deserved praise, special mention is due to Commander Adolfo Sarmento de Figueiredo, who was one of the most valuable and helpful assistants the centenary celebrations had.

We shall give a brief review of the main items of the programme that were carried out. We cannot go into great detail or a full description, because that would take us too far and would greatly exceed the limits we can devote in this work to the various subjects it covers.
The centenary celebrations began on 29 December 1922 and ended on 4 January 1923.

A few days before the festivities began, the publication entitled *V Centenário do Descobrimento da Madeira* appeared, prepared under the responsibility of the Propaganda and Publicity Committee. It is a folio pamphlet of 60 pages, with contributions by Jordão Henriques, Father Fernando A. da Silva, Jaime Câmara, Carlos Azevedo de Meneses, Adolfo César de Noronha, Alberto Artur Sarmento, Luís de Ornelas Pinto Coelho, Manuel Ribeiro, Manuel Sardinha, Father Eduardo Pereira, Manuel Pestana dos Reis, J. Reis Gomes, Vitorino José dos Santos and Eduardo Antonino Pestana. It was published under the direction of one of the editors of this *Elucidário*, and it should be said here that some of the articles in the *V Quinto Centenário do descobrimento da Madeira* were taken from the same *Elucidário* and came from the pen of the authors of this work.

The festivities opened with a solemn Te Deum in the Cathedral, which was immensely well attended. The distinguished sacred orator the Revd Father José Marques Jardim went up to the pulpit and delivered a remarkable sermon that pleased everyone present. Among those present were many of the Tenerife visitors (see that entry) who had arrived in Funchal the day before, 28 December, the consular corps, the officers of the destroyer *Guadiana*, several officers of the city garrison, the administrative bodies, the students of Funchal, etc. The ceremony was presided over by the diocesan prelate, Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, assisted by Canons Manuel A Miranda and Manuel Mendes Teixeira, and the choral music was performed by a large *schola*, accompanied by an excellent orchestra.

After the Te Deum a procession formed and made its way to the Convent of St Clare, where the tomb of João Gonçalves Zarco lies. There Dr Antonino Pestana gave a patriotic speech in which he reminded the young of the value of heeding the lessons to be drawn from reading the biography of the great discoverer of Madeira.

On the way back from the Convent of St Clare, when the procession reached the spot opposite the former Entrada da Cidade, where the statue of Zargo is to be erected, Dr Juvenal de Araújo spoke, and in a short but brilliant address he stirred the hearts of his listeners. He was followed by the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties) of Santa Cruz de Tenerife, Don Antonio Orosco Baptista, who stressed the value of drawing the ties of friendship and trade between Portuguese and Spaniards ever closer.

When the illustrious Tenerife visitor, who is a professor in the Faculty of Law at La Laguna, had finished his speech, the prelate Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, assisted by the two canons already mentioned, blessed the stone that will be the first of the foundations of the future monument to Zargo, while the national anthem was played.

On 29, 30 and 31 December the drama *Guiomar Teixeira*, by the distinguished writer Major João dos Reis Gomes, was performed at the ‘Dr. Manuel de Arriaga’ theatre to great applause. On the 30th the fair and the agricultural exhibition were opened. They were held not on the site first chosen but in the Praça do Marquês de Pombal, and were visited by many people from every social class.

The fair offered little of interest, because of the very limited number of articles shown there. The exhibition, however, included many Madeiran agricultural products worthy of attention, though it was regrettable that they had not been scientifically classified so that foreigners could easily recognise them.

The opening of the fair and the agricultural exhibition was attended by the illustrious Tenerife visitors Don Andrés Orosco Batista and the colonel of the Tenerife garrison, Don Galdador Garcia y Rodriguez de Aumente, who spoke after the address given by the agronomist Aurelio Botelho Moniz.

The bibliographical and art exhibition, opened on 30 December at the Industrial School in Rua de João Tavira, was one of the items on the festival programme that aroused most interest among Funchal’s elite. The curious Manueline window that belonged to the house in Rua do Esmeraldo where Columbus is said to have lived was set up in the courtyard of the school building, and Zarco’s famous two-handed sword (*montante*), about a metre and a half long, lay on a table in the first room to the left of the staircase. Numerous Portuguese and foreign publications, almost all belonging to the Municipal Library, were displayed in the same room. The remaining rooms held various maps of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas; many pictures of picturesque spots on the island and of the customs and ways of its inhabitants; the portraits of Zargo, of the president (*provedor*) of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) Forjaz Coutinho, and of the founder of the convent of the Incarnação, etc.; several oil paintings by the Madeiran painters Mígueis and H. Franco; and many pieces of inlaid work (*embutidos*) of undeniable merit, etc., etc.

The historical procession held on 4 January was a most imposing spectacle and was immensely admired, not only by the people of Funchal but also by the distinguished visitors from Tenerife who spent several days among us to attend the celebrations of the fifth centenary of the discovery of the island.

This procession, said the *Diário da Madeira*, ‘was without any doubt the festivity that gave the best measure of the intense excitement that ran through the whole city, its streets packed with its inhabitants and with an enormous crowd of visitors.

‘As the allegorical floats passed by, we read further in the same newspaper, pennants and flags fluttered, handkerchiefs and hats waved, and hands clapped along the lines of spectators and at the windows, applauding the work and its designers and artists.

‘The Float of the Nations, offered by the consuls, whose moving spirit was the illustrious representative of Brazil, most closely assisted by the very worthy representative of Spain and firmly supported by the rest of the consular corps, made a truly superb effect, both as decoration and as allegory.

‘The floats of wine, sugar, wicker and embroidery, which through their regional picturesqueness or artistic line, their splash of colour or their ornamental whole, emphasised the antiquity, wealth, value and progress of their respective industries, were – some for their meaning, others for their beauty – a welcome tribute to the principal sources of Madeira’s economic life.

‘The ideal splash of colour lent to the Embroidery Float by the old costumes of our countrywomen, worn by lovely young ladies of our society who had volunteered to take the place left empty by the genuine embroiderers, was one of the most radiant blossomings of the procession and one of its most moving and charming notes...

‘Also appearing in this memorable procession was the Sports Float, which, in contrast with the ancient and more or less austere character of our industries, struck an original note of youth and strength, marking the well-developed presence in Madeira of a new source of vitality: that of physical and moral rejuvenation.

The moving pageant was opened and closed respectively by the two historical floats: the Float of the Discovery and the Float of the Infante. The first was the caravel *San Lourenço*, a replica of the one that found us and gave us to civilisation and to the world; the second was the float of the austere and wise Henry the Navigator, the initiator and driving force of the great Portuguese voyages of discovery. ‘This little vessel, built on the most exact models found in documents of the period, does not hold for us merely an allegorical meaning. In its elegant architecture, in its methods and details of construction, in the evocative power of its lines, in the charm of its proportions and in the feeling with which its frames and timbers are curved, it represents the unquestionable tradition of the ingenuity and skill of our first caulkers – those who, on this island and at the spot, a little nearer or a little farther, where the famous ship was raised, built from the primeval timber the high-sided vessels that set out on adventure from this radiant centre of the voyages of discovery.

‘Master Luís Basílio perhaps had as an ancestor one of those great master shipwrights of the adze who, in the age of the discoveries, laid keels and rounded hulls somewhere near the old Rua da Boa Viagem.

‘From the shipyard that he so ably directs today have come our best and most graceful sailing vessels. His caravel, presented in the procession as a precious and evocative historical float, is eloquent and living testimony to the perfection attained by Madeiran naval architecture, even outside modern patterns.

‘The car paying homage to the creator of the fruitful School of Sagres is, in its sculpture and decorative modelling, the work of the distinguished Portuguese sculptor Mr José Pereira, who produced both the marvellous bust of the Infante and the exquisitely beautiful statues of Navigation and History resting against the central body of the car. It is the work of a great artist and a true Portuguese.

‘By its generosity, its high artistic value and its symbolism, it fell to this car to close the splendid and patriotic procession. Its magnificence eclipses every allegorical car ever presented in our capital. Even the Caravel of the Henrician Centenary, displayed in the entrance hall of the Lisbon Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*), may fairly be considered, beside our *San Lourenço*, a mere child’s toy in its dimensions, modelling and finish.
‘At every point along the route, the passing of the Infante’s Car drew an intense chorus of exclamations born of the most heartfelt and simple admiration.’

The procession included representatives of the press, of the various branches of commerce and industry, of the administrative bodies, of the chapter of the Cathedral, of the medical profession, of the judiciary, of primary and secondary teaching, of the army and navy, etc., as well as the committee for the festivities of the Fifth Centenary of the Discovery of Madeira.

A band led the procession and another brought up the rear. The band of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*Infantaria n.° 27*) took no part in the festivities, and the state-owned buildings displayed no illuminations, even though the occasion commemorated an event that is a national glory. The Spanish ship *Viera y Clavijo* was dressed overall throughout the festivities, but the Portuguese warship *Guadiana*, which was then anchored in the Port of Funchal (Porto do Funchal), paid no such courtesy.

The fireworks let off near Reid’s Palace Hotel at the start of 1923 were truly dazzling. Equally dazzling were the illuminations in the city from 29 December to 3 January, above all those of the avenues of Gonçalves Zargo and Dr Manuel de Arriaga, of the Largo da Sé and the Largo do Comércio, and of Rua João Tavira, the street of Lieutenant-Commander Carvalho de Araújo and Rua do Comércio, etc., etc. At the start of the Avenida de Gonçalves Zargo stood a superb triumphal arch of painted wood, showing the city’s arms, caravels on a stormy sea and lions in fighting pose.

The festivities for the fifth centenary of the discovery of Madeira were unquestionably the most important and majestic ever held on the island. It may be said that they were carried out solely with local resources, for the Government, as already mentioned, did nothing to help them.

Madeirans would not take the responsibility of letting one of the most notable dates in our history pass unnoticed. It was well that they did so, for it showed Portuguese and foreigners alike that we too take pride in our country’s glories, and that there is no difficulty we cannot overcome when it comes to commemorating the events that did most to give our country the well-deserved renown it enjoyed in other ages.
Quinta

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’). There was once a *quinta* (country estate) or country house here, and the chapel of Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*) still stands. Both belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded here at the end of the 15th century by Álvaro de Ornelas, which was one of the oldest entails (*instituições vinculares*) in Madeira and whose last representative was Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Aires de Ornelas (1866-1930). The Consolação (‘consolation’) chapel was built by Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos around 1591 and rebuilt around the middle of the 18th century (see Garajau and Jangão).
Quinta

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’). The Quinta do Pomar (‘orchard estate’) lies in this locality, and on it stands a chapel dedicated to St Anthony of Padua, founded by Father António Silvino Gonçalves de Andrade in 1883; there is also a state primary school here. At the spot in this locality known as Ponta da Quinta (‘estate point’) there was once a small chapel dedicated to the Virgin, Our Lady, of which not even a trace now remains.
Quinta da Palmeira
See Palmeira (Quinta).
Quinta das Cruzes

A brief historical account of this old manor house, which is closely bound up with the history of our archipelago, has already been sketched in the articles Moradias de Zargo (‘Zargo’s dwellings’) and Padrões Memoráveis (‘memorable monuments’).

Taking up the generous offer of a well-known collector of precious antiques and valuable works of art, the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) resolved to create a Museum of Ancient Art, to be housed in this *quinta* (country estate) of such noble traditions. Our island was thus to gain a major improvement in the sphere of general culture and in the spread of worthwhile artistic knowledge, as well as a further attraction for the visitors who frequently come to us.
Quinta das Freiras

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), Funchal. This locality was the site of the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Brotas (Our Lady of Brotas), founded in 1678 by Manuel Martins Brandão, of which a heap of rubble still remains. The parish cemetery also lies here; it was built in 1839 and greatly enlarged in 1903. The cemetery has its own chapel, built in 1844 and dedicated to Our Lady of Light (*Nossa Senhora da Luz*).
Quinta de Santo António

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’). It has a chapel dedicated to St Anthony of Padua, built in 1705 by Inácio Viana do Rego, with an adjoining manor house that belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Heredia family, whose last representative was the Viscount of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’).
Quinta do Leme

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), Funchal. It has an old manor house with an adjoining chapel, which were the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Leme family, founded by Pedro de Leme before 1550. Its last direct representative was Francisco Aurélio da Câmara, who died without issue, so the administration of this entailed house (*casa vinculada*) passed to his nephew João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, 1st Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). The chapel, dedicated to the martyr St Philip, was built in 1536 by António de Leme and rebuilt in 1654 by Inácio da Câmara Leme. It was reconstructed once more in 1752, together with the adjoining manor house, because of the state of great ruin in which the earthquake of 1748 had left it. Having been deconsecrated for some years, it was restored to worship in 1942.
Quinta do Monte

In the locality (*sítio*) of Pico, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (‘Our Lady of the Mount’), stands the *quinta* (country estate) of this name, also known as Quinta Cossart. It is one of the most sumptuous residences in Madeira, and we have already given a brief account of it on page 461 of volume II of this *Elucidário*.

It became very well known, and has been much visited, since the time when Emperor Charles I lived there for some months and ended his days there on 1 April 1922. A few years ago its present owner, Luís da Rocha Machado, built in the house a beautiful chapel dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus (*Sagrado Coração de Jesus*) and consecrated to the memory of the ill-fated and much-missed emperor. He had arrived in Madeira with his wife, Empress Zita, aboard the British cruiser *Cardiff* on 10 November 1921, and took up residence at the ‘Vila Vitória’, an annexe of Reid’s Hotels. When the princes, the imperial couple’s children, arrived in Funchal on 2 February 1922, the whole imperial family moved to the Quinta do Monte (‘estate of Monte’) on the 18th of the same month. There, as already stated, the unfortunate emperor died on 1 April of that year. On the 5th he was buried in a side chapel of the Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’) of Monte, where his remains still lie. The emperor’s death and funeral stirred the deepest feelings of grief throughout the population of Funchal, which took on the character of true national mourning. Empress Zita left Madeira with her children on 19 May 1922.
Quinta do Palheiro
See Palheiro (quinta).
Quinta do Salvador

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (‘Our Lady of the Mount’). It contains the fine residence of the Quinta da Paz (‘estate of peace’), which has an adjoining chapel dedicated to Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*).
Quinta dos Reis

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’). Here, on a small hill, stands an old manor house recalling an ancient castle on a crag, with an adjoining chapel dedicated to the Holy Magi (*Reis Magos*) and built in 1554 by Duarte Mendes de Vasconcelos. This locality also has a chapel dedicated to the Menino Jesus (Child Jesus).
Quinta Grande (parish)

In ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) we read: ‘reaching (João Gonçalves Zarco) a height above Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), he marked out there where a church of the Spirito Santo should be built. Passing further down to some very high mountains, there he marked out another church, of the Vera-Cruz; and all these heights he took for his Heirs’. These high mountains and the church of Vera-Cruz (see that entry) are today an integral part of the parish (*freguesia*) of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’).

A considerable stretch of the land that makes up the present parish originally belonged to the parish of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), and the rest to the parish of Câmara de Lobos. When the parish of Campanário (‘bell tower’) was created around the middle of the 16th century, it received the part of Quinta Grande that then lay within the jurisdiction of the parish of Ribeira Brava.

Among the properties the Jesuits owned on this island, one stood out: the estate in the parish of Campanário which, because of its size and importance, was known as the Quinta Grande. As already stated, this land originally belonged to the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco and passed into the hands of some of his descendants. It is not known when they disposed of it, nor when it was granted or sold to members of the Society of Jesus. The Jesuits were dispossessed of the property when all their goods were confiscated in 1759. In the following years the rent of the estate was let by award by public auction (*arrematação*), until in 1770 it was sold at public auction and acquired by João Francisco de Freitas Esmeraldo for the sum of 140,000 *cruzados*, that is, 56,000.00 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis), a very considerable amount for the time. We suspect that this purchase included the property called Fajã dos Padres (Volume II, page 6), but we cannot state beyond doubt that this was so.

It may not be easy today to determine precisely the boundaries of the land belonging to the Jesuits that bore the name of Quinta Grande. This became the name of the future parish, whose area was considerably enlarged when the curacy (*curato*) was created. One question arises: when the Jesuits acquired this property, was it already called Quinta Grande, or was it given that name on passing into the possession of those religious, because it was one of the largest estates they held on this island? The version generally adopted is that it was the Jesuits who gave the property the name of Quinta Grande, and we know of no reasons that contradict this assertion.

A population centre of some importance had grown up between the parishes of Campanário and Câmara de Lobos, and it had become very difficult to bring spiritual assistance to that settlement. The diocesan bishop, Dom Friar Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, therefore decided, by his warrant (*provisão*) of 8 February 1820, to establish a curacy with its seat at the chapel of Our Lady of Remedies (*Nossa Senhora dos Remédios*). Its area was to take in the 93 households of the localities of Vera-Cruz and Fontainhas (‘little springs’), which belonged to Campanário, and the 41 households of the localities of Cama do Bispo (‘bishop’s bed’) and Cadeirinha (‘little chair’), which belonged to Câmara de Lobos. In the very month of its creation the curacy was filled by Father Felisberto de Gouveia. Its jurisdiction remained dependent on the parish priests of the two neighbouring parishes, which had given up their land to form this chaplaincy with cure of souls (*capelania-curada*), not yet an autonomous parish. It seems that the parish priest of Campanário always exercised the broader jurisdiction there, and in the end he took over all supervision of the curacy’s religious services.

This arrangement, however, lasted only until 1848, when a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 24 July of that year raised the curacy of Quinta Grande to the rank of an autonomous parish. The curate at the time, Manuel Joaquim Serrão, was appointed its first provisional parish priest (*pároco encomendado*). The following priests then served the parish in succession: Fathers António Silvino Gonçalves de Andrade, António Feliciano de Freitas, José Isidoro Gonçalves, João Fernandes de Freitas, Agostinho Teodoro Pita, António Rodrigues Denis Henriques, Eugénio Rodrigues Teixeira and Augusto Prazeres dos Santos. The first collated parish priest (*pároco colado*, instituted for life) was Agostinho Teodoro Pita, in 1862.

Among these parish priests, Father António Rodrigues Denis Henriques deserves special mention. He served as pastor of this parish for 46 years, always setting an example of the most austere life, the most ardent zeal and the greatest selflessness in carrying out his ministry. The rebuilding of the present church is owed to him, and he rendered other important services to the parish. He was born in the parish of Câmara de Lobos on 2 September 1833 and died there on 6 January 1922.

At Quinta Grande stood the chapel of Our Lady of Remedies, which was the seat of the curacy established in 1880 and also served as the seat of the parish. It was preferred to the chapel of Vera-Cruz because it was more central, and perhaps for other reasons unknown to us. It was built in 1601 and underwent some alterations over time, above all in 1901, when it was considerably enlarged. It is the centre of a well-attended pilgrimage in honour of Our Lady of Remedies, the patron saint of the parish. The pilgrimage festival takes place on the second Sunday of September each year, drawing enormous crowds from the surrounding parishes.
We shall discuss the chapels of this parish elsewhere in this work.

The main localities are Igreja, Aviceiro, Cama do Bispo, Ribeira do Escrivão, Quinta, Fontes, Lombo Vera-Cruz and Fontainhas. The last of these is very picturesque and well worth a visit. The parish has a state school, founded in April 1914. Its population is 996 inhabitants (1921).

Quintas

It seems to us that the word *quinta* (country estate) has a special meaning here in Madeira, one that sets it markedly apart from the sense in which it is generally understood in the rest of our country. On Madeira the term usually denotes a rural and urban property, of greater or lesser extent, walled all the way round or at least along a considerable part of its perimeter, and always containing a good dwelling house surrounded by gardens and walks shaded by clumps of trees. It is entered through a wrought-iron gate of some architectural pretension, opening onto a drive that leads straight to the residence. Many *quintas* include land cultivated with vines and sugar cane, vegetable gardens, orchards and groves of trees. Some have buildings for various farm purposes, stables and dwellings for the tenant farmers, and the oldest have, besides the main house, an adjoining chapel, formerly for the private use of their owners.

The most important and sumptuous *quinta* on this island is that of Palheiro Ferreiro (‘blacksmith’s barn’), which we have already described on page 43 of this volume. Next comes the so-called Quinta do Monte (‘estate of Monte’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of that name, which we have also dealt with elsewhere (Volume II, page 461).

After these, special mention is due to the Quinta Lambert (see that entry) and the Quinta da Vigia; the Quinta das Cruzes (see Moradias de Zargo); the Quinta de São João, in Rua das Maravilhas, the former manor house of the holders of the entail of São João, where its present owner, Dr Rui Bettencourt da Câmara, had the chapel of Our Lady of Protection and of Remedies built in 1940; the Quinta do Vale, in Rua do Vale Formoso, which at other times possessed some curious plants, studied by Dr Lippold in 1838 and by Dr Oswald Heer in 1852, its present owner being Dr Grabham (1921); the Quinta da Levada and the Quinta de Santa Luzia, the latter belonging to the Blandy family and the former to the Cossart family; the Quinta da Palmeira, belonging to H. Quinto
A tax formerly levied in Madeira, which we have already discussed on page 304 of volume I of this work, in the article Taxes.

Besides the fifth (*quinto*, levy of one fifth on sugar), abolished by the law of 11 September 1861, there was in remote times the so-called fifth of sugars, to which we referred on pages 14 ff. of the same volume. It came to an end with the royal decree (*alvará*) of 15 October 1688, and from then on an eighth (*oitavo*, a tax of one eighth of the produce) of the sugar produced on the island was levied instead.

The fifth of sugars was established by the charter (*foral*) of 6 August 1515, transcribed on page 494 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). Before that, as the same charter shows, sugar had been subject to payment of a quarter.

Under a contract concluded in 1452 and transcribed on page 665 of the same work, the Infante, Henry the Navigator, claimed for himself a third of all the sugar made in the only sugar mill (*engenho*) then existing on the island!

Rabies

Around the middle of 1892 a disease appeared in Funchal that killed many dogs, and to which some residents of the island are also said to have succumbed. The population was extremely alarmed, for this was a disease completely unknown here, and it attacked not only animals but also some human beings. This natural alarm was heightened by the indecision of Madeiran doctors, who disagreed on the diagnosis, chiefly because the necessary bacteriological tests could not possibly be carried out in Madeira.

At this juncture the local press did important service, not only by calling for vigorous and immediate measures, but also by warning the inhabitants of the dangers of dog bites and of the need to confine the dogs so that they could not pass the disease to any person or other animal.

At the urging of the civil governor of the district at the time, the engineer Luís Merens de Távora, the government in mainland Portugal sent to Madeira the distinguished veterinary surgeon António Roque da Silveira, charged with studying the disease that had appeared here and recommending a means of stamping it out. He arrived in Funchal on 8 October 1892 and began his studies at once, making use, on the very day he landed, of some work already done by inoculating rabbits with an emulsion of the medulla of dogs killed by the disease. His further inoculations, microscopic examinations, lengthy clinical study and other work diligently carried out convinced him that hydrophobia existed in Madeira, although some distinguished Madeiran doctors held that the epizootic among the island’s dogs was not rabies.

Roque da Silveira states that the rabies was imported, and accepts as probable the account of those who say that in May 1892 a foreigner landed in Funchal with two dogs and, on returning aboard a few hours later, was followed by only one of them. It is possible that the dog that went astray here was incubating rabies and that, when the disease broke out, it bit other animals and so transmitted it.
Although the number of victims was not very large, the deaths of seven people who succumbed to the terrible disease of rabies were nevertheless confirmed.
We have no knowledge of that disease having appeared here either before or after this time.

The veterinary surgeon António Roque da Silveira sent the central government a detailed report on the rabies that appeared on this island in 1892, which was published in no. 2 of the 5th year of the *Boletim da Direcção Geral da Agricultura*, pp. 29–62.

Rambles in Madeira

Under the title *Rambles in Madeira and in Portugal in the early part of M.DCCC.XXVI*, a rather curious work attributed to Mr Lyall appeared in London in 1827. It provides a great deal of information not only on various places in Madeira worth visiting, but also on the history and climate of the island and the ways and customs of its inhabitants. Speaking of the ladies of Funchal, the author says that they go out only to attend Mass or, now and then, to visit a friend, in which case they travel by palanquin and in their finest clothes. Referring to a Portuguese ball he attended, he adds that the ladies were carried in palanquins and received at the door by the master of the house and other gentlemen, who escorted them to the upper floor. To see them gathered in a drawing room is a dazzling sight for a foreigner little used to facing so many large dark eyes. The author of the *Rambles in Madeira* also refers to the habit the ladies of Funchal have of sitting at their windows, where they receive the greetings of gentlemen passing on their way to the cathedral; to the theatre that the governor Dom Álvaro ordered to be demolished; to Carnival; to the Ash Wednesday procession and that of the Stations of the Passion (*passos*, wayside oratories depicting scenes of Christ's Passion), etc., etc. He also sought to describe, as accurately as possible, the features of the nun Maria Clementina de Vasconcelos, whom we have already discussed in this *Elucidário*.

The rats known in Madeira are *Mus rattus*, *M. norwegicus* and *M. musculus*, the last of these species having already been noted on page 412 of volume II. *M. rattus*, or black rat, and *norwegicus*, or brown rat, are both common in Madeira, where they cause great damage; the Municipal Councils once adopted certain measures to destroy them.
Both the house mouse and the two species we have just mentioned are imported animals, and it is likely that they reached the archipelago at the time of colonisation.

On Selvagem Grande (‘great wild island’) there is a species of rat, perhaps *Mus bárbaros*, which destroys the eggs of the *calcamar* (see that entry) and does not hesitate to attack this bird, despite its strong beak.

Hammocks

In the article Palanquins we have already referred to a kind of litter (*maca*) used in Madeira to carry people. We must now add that it is known as the hammock (*rede*, slung from a pole and carried by two bearers). It is made of a very thick, strong cloth woven on the island, tied at both ends to a pole or *pala*, usually of *folhado* (Clethra arborea, a native tree). The hammock perhaps appeared on the island after the palanquin, but it has continued to serve for carrying people, although it is less used today than in earlier times.

The luxury hammock is fitted with an awning and curtains, and inside with a cushion and a blanket. The hammock used in the countryside, by contrast, has no awning; this is often replaced by a piece of chintz thrown over the pole to shelter the passenger from both the wind and the rays of the sun. When carried by experienced men, the hammock is an excellent means of transport for invalids.

Every hammock always has two bearers, but if the person being carried is heavy, three or even four may be needed. The pole of the hammock rests on one shoulder of each man. He also carries a staff in his hand, which is often laid across the other shoulder so as to spread the weight better. Some men rest the pole of the hammock on their bare shoulder, using the staff only now and then during long marches, to avoid the effects of prolonged friction on that part of the body.

Foreigners who use the hammock on their journeys through the interior of the island marvel at the prodigious ease with which its bearers climb or descend the steepest slopes, even during the hottest hours of the day in the hot season. On level ground or going downhill it is very hard to keep up with them, so fast do they walk and leap, and no obstacle makes them slacken their pace.

The hammock is a comfortable way of seeing the island, but today only the wealthy can use it, so exorbitant is the price the bearers ask for their work. On top of the bearers’ pay there is always what is spent on them in wine and spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine). These men drink prodigious quantities of both during the marches without seeming to suffer noticeably from such excesses. These are justified to some extent by their need to find a stimulant for the arduous and gruelling work to which they frequently devote themselves.
Fishing nets
The nets most often used by the fishing industry in Madeira are the following: the circular net, the set net (*rede de atravessar*) and the drag net.

The first, often seen hanging from the mast of fishing boats, has curved poles tied to its mouth to keep it open while it is in use. It is the most frequently used and serves not only for catching *chicharro* but also other small species. Ropes connect the net to a pole, which the fisherman holds when he works the gear, and the mesh of the net is finer or coarser according to the species to be caught.

The set net, sometimes very large, has pieces of cork along one side and lead weights along the other, which make it sink and hang vertically. It is sometimes used to encircle the fish, and it is hauled by means of ropes fastened to the net, which also serve to lift it when the catch is taken in.

The drag net, like the set net, has pieces of cork along one side and lead weights along the other, but it differs in having a large bag in the middle, designed to catch the fish that enter it. The net is usually hauled from the shore by very long ropes that run through a kind of pulley.

Besides the nets described above, trammel nets, cast nets, etc., are sometimes used in fishing. Trammel nets have three panels, the inner one of finer mesh than the outer ones, while cast nets are small nets with lead weights around the edge. Using cast nets calls for a certain skill, since they are thrown from some distance from the spot where the fish are.
Some fishermen call set nets drag nets, although, as we have seen, set nets differ from drag nets in lacking the bag designed to catch the fish.

Agricultural Region (Ninth)

The decree of 8 May 1918 established eleven agricultural regions, with Madeira forming the 9th region, based in Funchal, and divided the agricultural regions into sub-regions, Funchal’s being numbered 36. The same decree created in each region an agricultural station, in which all regional services were to be concentrated, and provided that each agricultural sub-region should have one or more agrarian posts.

The decree of 2 May 1919 laid down that the proceeds of the tax on the manufacture of spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine), the tax on molasses, etc., should form revenue of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) ‘expressly assigned to the costs of installing and running the agricultural station of the 9th Region’. However, the purposes of this station and the services entrusted to it were only clearly set out in decree no. 8089 of 3 April 1922.

Under this decree, the Agricultural Station of the 9th Region is responsible for the physico-chemical and technological services of the district, the crop-growing and biological-agricultural services, and the services of the sugar, alcohol and spirit regime. It is also charged with spreading knowledge about the best use of native plants and the eradication of harmful and poisonous weeds, as well as about the protection of useful animal species and the destruction of harmful ones.

The administration of Madeira’s sugar regime (*regímen sacarino*, the legal regime governing sugar and alcohol production), except for those fiscal functions relating to sugar and alcohol that belong exclusively to the Ministry of Finance, is the responsibility of the Agricultural Station of the 9th Region. There is a technical commission for the supervision of this regime, made up of the director of the said Station, the engineer of the Industrial District (*Circunscrição Industrial*) and the head of the District Inspection Department (*Repartição Distrital de Fiscalização*).

The decree of 3 April 1922 transferred to the Agricultural Station of the 9th Region all the rural and urban properties that had belonged to the defunct Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*), together with the materials they contained. It further laid down that the revenues previously handed over to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) for the Station's expenses should continue to be collected in the customary way, but deposited with the local branch of the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos, at the order of the Director of the Station, so that he could apply them as the law prescribed.

The Station is to have a meteorological and phenological station, experimental and demonstration plots, a chemical laboratory, a facility for the observation of plant diseases, a display collection of soils, fertilisers, etc., and a cold store.

On 7 May 1921 the agricultural engineer Sá Viana arrived in Madeira, charged with organising the 9th Agricultural Region, setting up its services and placing the staff of the defunct Agricultural Board. Only in 1922, however, was the Agricultural Station of the region definitively installed, taking over certain services that had provisionally been in the hands of the General Council.

The decree of 24 December 1901, which divided the agronomic services into three regions, placed the district of Funchal in the southern agronomic region, and the law of 9 July 1913 created 28 agricultural sections, the Funchal section being no. 25. The decree of 17 August 1912 and the decree with force of law of 26 May 1911 also deal with the agricultural organisation of the country.
See Junta Agrícola.
Cereal regime

The Madeiran cereal regime (*regímen cerealífero*), against which the population always protested, began in 1899 and ended in January 1913. It was the decree of 23 December 1899 that approved the regulations for the trade in wheat and flour in Madeira and established this regime; that decree had been preceded by the law of 14 July of the same year. The decree of 26 July 1899 approved the regulations for the trade in wheat and the products of its milling, and the decree of 28 October 1909 introduced further modifications to the island’s cereal regime. Under the enactments that established the monopoly, the import for consumption of wheat of any origin was permitted only to registered merchants and flour millers, and to farmers for seed. The managing committee of the central market was required to announce, by 5 August each year, the call for the declaration of the island wheat available for sale. Within five days at most of the close of the call, the delegation was to publish a statement of the cereal declared and of its apportionment among the said registered merchants and millers.

Law no. 960 of 24 March 1920 declared the trade in and transport of Portuguese wheat and its milled products free. It obliged the registered millers to acquire all the declared wheat and laid down that foreign wheat destined for Madeira should be apportioned among the registered merchants and millers according to the tables in force published by the Ministry of Agriculture. The purchase of this wheat and of foreign flour was to be carried out by the Government, and the price of bread outside Lisbon and Porto was to be fixed by the Municipal Councils. After this enactment came the decree of 30 November 1921, which brought only slight modifications to the previous regime. It did, however, lay down that the prices of flour and bread in Funchal should be decreed for each cereal year by the central government, after consulting a delegated committee of the Agricultural Trade (*Comércio Agrícola*), which was to sit in this city.

The people repeatedly voiced their dislike of the cereal regime, under whose cover so many abuses and extortions were committed, and several prominent figures of the Republic had pledged to secure its abolition. Even so, it was only on 22 December 1922 that the Senate was finally induced to approve the bill for the free import of flour into Madeira, which had already been debated in the Chambers in September of the previous year. The law that put an end to the odious cereal monopoly is dated 13 January 1913 and bears the number 1392. Law no. 1294 of 31 July 1922 and the regulations approved by the decree of 1 September of the same year had not freed the island from the dominance of the flour millers.

The sugar regime (*regímen sacarino*, the legal regime governing sugar and alcohol production), despite the justified protests it provoked, chiefly because of the high price at which sugar came to be sold, at least had the advantage of raising the value of much land and of greatly benefiting a very large number of the island’s landowners and farmers. The cereal regime, by contrast, served only to enrich the flour millers, and it may even be said that this was the very purpose for which it was decreed. It is true that the people are still being exploited and that bread is being sold at exorbitant prices. But if the laws prohibiting imports were still in force, we are convinced that our circumstances would be even more critical, for long years of experience have shown us that no profit could ever satisfy the greed of the millers.
See Popular riots.
Forest regime

Since it is closely related to our subject, we shall recall in passing the astonishing spectacle our island must have presented to those who first came in search of these unknown and distant parts, above all the sight of the luxuriant vegetation that so ecstatically amazed them all.

We should not be surprised, then, by what we read in many places about the ‘true astonishment’, a mixture of the most staggering surprise and the most stirring admiration, felt by the first bold navigators on facing a scene they had never beheld: a wonderful forest stretching far in a compact mass from the tranquil edge of the ocean to the summits of the loftiest mountains. Trees of gigantic size and the most exuberant growth, without a break, densely covered the slopes and hillsides. They made inaccessible the land that was soon to be brought under active cultivation.

We would go too far if we tried to reproduce here the interesting accounts that old chroniclers have left us of this rich and exceedingly abundant forest vegetation. We shall therefore confine ourselves to a brief summary of some of these historical testimonies, contemporary with the events described.

There are many passages in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) concerning the opulent forest vegetation at the time of the first settlement. Among other things, they say that the island was ‘all covered with trees down to the sea… and so even on top that it seemed made by hand, with no tree taller than another’.

The Portuguese navigator Diogo Gomes, who visited Madeira at the beginning of the 15th century, likewise refers, in no less expressive terms, to the leafy woods that covered the whole surface of the island.

The Venetian Alvise Cadamosto, who served in the Portuguese navy around the middle of the 15th century and visited this archipelago, says that at the time of the discovery ‘there was not a *palmo* (span, about 22 cm) of land that was not full of very great trees…’

Another Italian navigator, Pompeu Arditti de Pesaro, also in the service of Portugal, left in writing in 1567 this interesting account: ‘it is inhabited only along the seashore, for in the mountains, because of the thickness of the trees, which are there in very great abundance and very tall, so that, they say, because of them one walks two or three *léguas* without ever seeing the sun…’ Other testimonies could easily be added, if the space at our disposal allowed.

If nature was remarkably lavish in the abundance of these dense and vast woods, it was no less generous in the variety of forest species with which it covered all the soil of Madeira. It can truly be said that the wealth of ‘quantity’ was richly matched by the wealth of ‘quality’. To prove it, we shall recall that the existence of thick and extensive woods of cedar, *til*, *vinhático*, ash, heather, *barbusano* and other valuable tree species is an established fact. Of some of them only a… wistful memory remains.
