In view of what has so often been said, and what we have briefly repeated here once more, it is no wonder that our beloved island was given the name of Madeira [TN: *madeira* means ‘wood’ or ‘timber’ in Portuguese.], which the centuries continue to perpetuate and which fame has made universal. Through the unheard-of vandalism of men, the use of that name is becoming less exact and less justified, and a glaring contrast is arising between its true meaning and what it ought in reality to express…

When the first settlers landed on these unknown shores, they at once recognised the mildness of the climate and the fertility of the soil, which boldly encouraged them in the farming ventures they were about to begin. They faced, however, a great and almost insurmountable obstacle: the gigantic forest that stretched in a dense mass from the edge of the ocean to the mountain tops.

Fire, perhaps set rashly but also necessarily imposed by the pressing force of circumstances, opened up clearings suitable for bringing the land under cultivation. Gaspar Frutuoso says, albeit with hyperbole, that ‘because the valley was very thick with trees, the fire took hold in such a way that it went on burning for seven years through the trees, trunks and roots, both in Funchal and in most of the island...’ The learned commentator of the *Saudades*, without wholly accepting the claim of the historian of the islands, does not doubt the intensity and extent of the violent fire. It is not possible today to say what the approximate area of its destruction was, or what its immediate consequences were, but several reasons suggest that it must have reached the most alarming proportions (see II-140).
After the fire, and at the same time as the first tilling of the plots, the forest vegetation was being heavily thinned, and it also supplied the raw material for building the first dwellings.

The superabundance of timber, its prized quality and the demand for it on the mainland and abroad gave rise to the idea of large-scale export and the trade that went with it. This at once created an important source of revenue in a setting as limited as Madeira then was.
A new industry, if a rudimentary one, arose with the preparation of timber for shipment. The trees had to be felled, sawn and fitted to the particular purpose for which they were intended.

Then came the so-called ‘water saws’ (*serras de água*), which multiplied in various places; several localities in a number of parishes still bear that name. They were rather rudimentary ‘engines’ set up on the banks of fast-flowing streams, using the motive power these provided.

This passage from Dr Gaspar Frutuoso is exceedingly interesting: ‘...there was such a quantity of timber, so fine and hard, that plenty of boards, beams and masts were taken to many parts, all of it sawn with engines... and at that time they began to build with it ships with topsails and forecastles, for before there were none in the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal)’.

No less interesting is what we read in Pinheiro Chagas’s ‘History of Portugal’ (II-252), which we shall transcribe word for word: ‘Zurara, dealing with the advantages that resulted from the discoveries, mentions “the great heights of the houses that reach up to the sky and are made with the timber of those parts”. To which the Viscount of Santarém adds in a note: this interesting detail shows that the timber carried to Portugal... chiefly from the island of Madeira came in such quantity that its abundance changed the method of building town houses, increasing the number of storeys...’.

Special mention should be made of the building at that time of a large number of small-tonnage vessels, intended for fishing and the carriage of goods, which were exported to the mainland. This export had to be banned because of the abuse committed in the use of the raw material concerned.
Many other facts and circumstances concerning the density and extent of the primeval forests could still be mentioned, but an unfair need for brevity compels us to omit them.

Despite the reality of the original fire, Madeira was quickly repopulated with tree species, and it did not take many years to become covered with extensive and abundant forest vegetation. Then, however, came the felling, trade and export of timber, which was widely used and abused. This provoked vigorous protests and led to the adoption of severe repressive measures, as we shall see in a later article.

Although human vandalism was powerless to alter the climate and the vigorous fertility of the soil, men never tired of systematically and constantly destroying the unsurpassed forest wealth of the mountains. First came the violent original fire, with its great destructive effects; others of lesser scale, but always with baleful consequences, occurred over time, some of them purely accidental and most set by criminal hands, as we shall have occasion to see below.

Later came sawmilling (‘serração’) and the trade in and export of timber, but on so vast a scale and in such immoderate proportions that vigorous repression by the government of mainland Portugal became necessary. This took the form of the royal letters (*cartas régias*) of 1515 and 1562, of which only the latter is known in full; it is transcribed on pages 463–471 of the annotations to ‘Longing for the Homeland’.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of John II of 7 March 1493, which deals chiefly with various grants concerning springs and sources, contains these curious words relating to our subject: ‘... the ash trees and cedars, which we reserve for ourselves, they shall neither use nor fell... save for some church or town hall or for whomsoever we give... leave by our letter’. In this connection we may add that half a century ago or a little more there were still, in various parts of the island, many stands of our native cedar, the highly prized and fragrant wood much used in Madeiran cabinet-making. We do not know whether today, if only as a simple and nostalgic sample of the past, a few specimens still survive in some corner of the forests of the interior.

Although not all the provisions of the regulations (*regimento*) of 5 January 1515 mentioned above are known, it is known that they ordered pine and chestnut trees to be planted on the land best suited to these species, and forbade the felling of trees without a licence from the Councils. Such felling could in no case be permitted in places where there were springs or running water. The same regulations also contained other prohibitive provisions, together with the corresponding penalties for offenders, as may be inferred from scattered references found in various places.

The doctrine they contained was extended and completed by the Regulations of 27 August 1562, promulgated by the queen regent, Queen Catherine, which may truly be called the ‘Forest Code of Madeira’. Referring to them in 1873, the learned commentator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ wrote: ‘It is an important instrument for the agricultural history of this island and constitutes its particular forest legislation, still largely in force even now, and it is the source of municipal bylaws (*posturas*) in all its municipalities’.

Given the natural progress of human knowledge and present circumstances of a strictly local character, the legal provisions of this instrument cannot be accepted in their entirety. We are nevertheless bound to acknowledge its great importance, its undeniable legal value and the very sound judgement with which it treated the matter it was meant to regulate.

At the very outset these regulations (1562) refer to the need that had given rise to the earlier regulations of 1515, owing to the great abuses already being committed at that time, and they stress the still greater need to adopt more vigorous measures of repression to check the excesses that continued to be committed.

We cannot discuss the main provisions of this instrument in detail, but we shall not fail to touch, however briefly, on one or two points. We therefore note the following: a) no timber could be felled without a licence from the Councils, and these licences had to be endorsed by the donataries; b) anyone who exceeded the limits of the licences granted was to be flogged, fined and sent into exile in Africa as an exiled convict (*degredado*), and those who set fire to the uplands were likewise to be exiled; c) the cutting of tree branches to feed livestock was forbidden; d) the building of ships, and even of small boats, for export was not permitted; e) timber was not to be felled within ‘one hundred and fifty paces’ of springs and streams; f) landowners in certain localities were obliged to plant certain trees, especially chestnuts, etc.

It seems that the legal provisions of the 1515 regulations were even more draconian than those laid down in the regulations of August 1562. Both, however, remained fully in force, since the second had been intended to extend and complete the doctrines of the first, as stated above.

The *ouvidores*, the donataries’ representatives in the more important settlements, were to exercise strict supervision over compliance with the regulations and to see that the corresponding penalties were applied to offenders. It may be presumed that this supervision left a good deal to be desired.

As we have stated elsewhere, many instruments are registered in the archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), and they show ‘that in the 17th and 18th centuries great care was taken to preserve the forests, a nursery being established in 1799 in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), which from that year until 1824 distributed more than twenty thousand trees of various species for replanting.

Besides the ‘regulations’ already cited, the decree of 11 March 1796, the royal decree of 18 October 1811 and the royal letter of 14 May 1804, all expressly promulgated for Madeira, are of great relevance to our subject and contain measures that ought to have been fully adopted.
In the article ‘Arborisation’ (I-75) we mentioned other measures intended to protect and develop our forest heritage, and we draw readers’ attention to them to avoid needless and tedious repetition.

Our woods have three implacable enemies: the shepherd, the charcoal burner and the timber merchant, the last being the most dangerous and harmful. Livestock rearing, charcoal-making and timber felling ought to be banned outright. And if, under pressing circumstances and only very exceptionally, they had to be allowed, no amount of rigour would be too much in supervising them as strictly and closely as possible.

It is a serious error to suppose that the rearing of cattle, goats and pigs sustains a considerable industry whose suppression could in any way harm the economy of the district. Suffice it to say that only a limited number of people engage in it, and for them it is not their sole livelihood, since they combine it with farming or with simple work as rural labourers. As a rule, the animals graze freely without herdsmen or shepherds and are exposed to all weathers. There are no pens or suitable shelters to protect them from the harsh winters, and for this reason the number of animals that die every year is always very considerable. This weighty circumstance alone would justify, in any country, an absolute ban on the free grazing of livestock on exposed mountainsides.

It is well known that livestock cause great destruction among young plants still in full growth, but the luxuriant vigour of our vegetation largely overcomes the attack of these ruminants’ powerful jaws. What the native richness of our woods cannot overcome, however, is the harmful and criminal action of the shepherd.

Flocks do not find good grazing on land covered with dense woodland. They need ground dominated by fodder and low-growing plants, which are essential to the diet best suited to them. The shepherd therefore readily prepares this coveted pasture in a clearing of greater or lesser size, which the destructive force of the flames provides him without difficulty. The great fires in our forests usually have this origin. Herdsmen do not hesitate for a moment to turn a forest of fine, stout trees, which took centuries to grow, into a barren expanse scorched by the devouring fire, so that it may soon become a field of pasture to feed a few paltry dozen goats and sheep.

The damage caused by charcoal-making is so evident – not only through the countless fine trees lost to obtain this fuel, but also through the ever-present danger of starting a violent fire, as has so often happened – that there is no need to put forward a long train of arguments to condemn outright any permission for such a practice, whatever safety conditions might be invoked for that purpose.

The decrees of 23 July 1913 and 22 September 1917, which became known here as the ‘Law on the grazing of livestock in the mountains’, laid down certain provisions on grazing on privately owned land and on land belonging to the State or to the municipal councils, with the aim of preventing the damage caused by the free grazing of livestock. They did not, however, achieve the desired end, nor were they ever fully observed, so that their promulgation proved useless or of little benefit. We share the opinion of those who hold that these decrees must be abolished or completely recast. And what we have set out here regarding grazing applies equally to the provisions of the said decrees on the making of charcoal.

In Madeira the axe has been the great ‘arboricide’. So useful and serviceable a tool often turns into an agent of destruction and ruin. So it was in past centuries, and so, perhaps, it will continue to be in times to come.

We have already seen the use and abuse made of our primitive and abundant forest vegetation. The improvident inhabitants were not content with enjoying, however liberally, the benefits that this priceless wealth offered them as fuel and as raw material for building houses and making furniture and other household objects.

As we have already said, the large-scale export of timber created the ‘sawing’ industry and the practice of preparing the trees for shipment. At the same time, the abuses and excesses committed led to the enactment of various laws imposing severe penalties, extending to flogging and penal exile (degredo) to the coasts of Africa.

As we have already mentioned, the conservation of the woods should have found its most effective protection in the celebrated ‘regimento’ of 27 August 1562. Among other salutary provisions, it laid down those concerning the licences issued by the municipal councils and countersigned by the donataries for cutting timber in our forests. This system has survived through the ages and has now reached the venerable age of 380 years. It would be interesting and useful, if the necessary records existed, to know how it has been observed – that is, to make an approximate assessment of the benefits or harm it has brought.

It is under cover of these licences that the third implacable enemy of the leafy woods has stripped, is stripping and will go on stripping our mountains of the precious and abundant timber that is the stuff of its lucrative trade. Clearly, these frank and categorical statements of ours are not meant as a sweeping generalisation, for we know that we would commit a flagrant injustice if we ever sought to make one.

Once all the bureaucratic formalities have been observed, and they present no great difficulty, the applicants can count on their social standing, on the well-known leniency of our ways and on the shortage of inspection staff, besides the influence that is often brought to bear in favour of the interested parties.

Although perhaps not a recent development, it has happened that a penalty is imposed for the unlawful felling of a single tree, while hundreds upon hundreds are allowed to be cut down under cover of a licence that permitted no such thing. This may seem strange, but it is nonetheless a sad reality.

In 1928 the executive committee of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), recognising the plain and pressing need to remedy the damage, by then irreparable, done to the woodlands, and judging ineffective the measures being taken to avert this evil, asked the central government to send to Madeira an official specialising in forestry matters. He was to carry out a broad study and present a detailed report on the results of the work to which he would devote himself with proficiency.

This delicate mission was entrusted to the illustrious forestry engineer José Augusto Fragoso. After a lengthy study carried out *in loco*, in mid-June 1929 he presented to the General Council an extensive report setting out the plan of all the measures that ought to be adopted.

The report was at once regarded as the product of painstaking and conscientious work, in which a distinguished professional had combined the most thorough knowledge of the subjects treated with the most careful scruple in solving such delicate problems.

Its foremost measure is the need to enact a decree laying down the principles by which all forestry services are to be guided and directed, giving them complete uniformity throughout the archipelago. For it is well known that some municipal councils still claim the privileges set out in certain archaic and obsolete municipal by-laws (*posturas*), perhaps remnants of the old, abolished customary law.

The creation of a ‘forestry district’ (*circunscrição florestal*) headed by a forestry engineer is today an urgent necessity acknowledged by all. It will burden the budgets of the General Council, but the future will demonstrate the benefits that will flow from this advantageous measure. It is not surprising, therefore, that the *Organização dos Serviços Florestais e Fomento Agrícola da Madeira*, drafted by the engineer J. M. Fragoso, opens with this clause and with the staff to be assigned to the proposed ‘Forestry District’. It is incomprehensible how certain individuals, without special technical training, can be in charge of services of this kind, which demand specialised knowledge that can only be acquired in institutions properly intended for that purpose.

The report opens by devoting a most illuminating chapter to the ‘Need for the Reafforestation of Madeira’. It then sets out the six ‘Bases’ on which the services concerned should be modelled, which are amply expounded in the sub-chapters ‘Organisation of the Forestry Services (*Serviços Florestais*)’, ‘Forest Regime’, ‘Forest Police (*Polícia Florestal*)’, ‘Protection of Woodlands’, ‘Promotion of Afforestation’ and ‘General Provisions’. These are followed by a detailed justification of the ideas suggested and of the various proposals put forward throughout this remarkable study.

The report concludes by indicating the first works that should begin without delay, of which we give this brief summary: 1. to secure, by decree, the inclusion of all common lands (*baldios*) in the ‘Forest Regime’; 2. to obtain the creation of a ‘Forestry District’ provided with the necessary qualified staff; 3. to enter a substantial sum in the budget to begin the work; 4. to seek to have the central government take charge of these services and guarantee their continuity; 5. to have two houses built at the places indicated in the ‘Bases’; 6. to continue the afforestation of the Montado dos Barreiros (‘wooded pasture of the clay pits’) and of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’); 7. to establish a nursery near Funchal; and 8. to promote the enactment of a decree on the grazing regime.

It hardly needs stressing that these final recommendations of the Report refer specifically to the first works to be undertaken, and not to the whole range of services to be established, which are amply set out in the same Report.

By what we have said we do not mean to maintain that this broad and well-crafted study should be accepted in its entirety; it is even possible, indeed probable, that later circumstances will require profound and indispensable changes to its wording. What does seem established, however, according to the learned and authoritative opinion of officials versed in these matters, is that, at least in its general lines and its judicious whole, it suits the conditions of the setting for which it was prepared and can be of excellent help to the work that may be carried out.

The creation of a ‘Forestry District’, as briefly outlined in this unpretentious article, is increasingly becoming a truth acknowledged by everyone: one in which proven proficiency, the most ardent zeal and the greatest independence would guide and direct from above all the services under that department.

On this momentous subject, particular interest attaches to the observations we recently set down in a newspaper of this city, from which we shall now extract a few passages that expand upon and clarify what has been briefly outlined above.

We were deeply gratified to see that the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district, earnestly committed to the conservation and development of our woods and trees, had taken the important decision to extend its supervision and protection over what remains of the ancient and celebrated forest wealth that once thickly clothed almost the entire surface of our mountains.

A local periodical recently (1945) informed us that, to carry out this sound measure, the number of ‘forest posts’ had been raised from fourteen to nineteen, and that eleven more guards had been added to the thirty-one already serving. There is now a body of forty-two rural or forest guards, which makes it possible to provide wider and more effective supervision than has been exercised until now.

We do not know the extent of the surface or area over which this permanent supervision is to be exercised, nor the particular area assigned to each forest post, but we are convinced that this recent reorganisation of the services was drawn up on lines that will fully achieve the desired end. Since our island has a surface of approximately seventy-five thousand hectares, with land of the most rugged relief, the number of men making up this forest police cannot be considered excessive.

Numbers alone, however, are not enough for these staff to discharge their duties fully. They must also be faithful and diligent executors of the orders and instructions issued by the departments that oversee these services. It is still more important and necessary that these higher offices be guided, directed and regulated by rules with a clearly defined sphere of jurisdiction, and that they meet no obstacles in the exercise of their administrative action.

Although some would claim otherwise, the truth is that no single piece of legislation covers all the various services concerned with the conservation and development of our woodlands. It has therefore become absolutely essential to adopt a new forest regime offering more effective protection and more reliable supervision than has so far been in force here.

The management of forest affairs was originally in the hands of the captain-donataries and their ‘*ouvidores*’ (magistrates), and later in those of the Municipal Councils, while the governors of the archipelago and afterwards the civil governors of the district also intervened in some of these matters.

Since 1897 these services have been the responsibility of a department headed by a forestry officer (*regente florestal*). To this day it has confined itself to planting some exotic trees on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and to promoting the sowing of maritime pine in the mountainous region of Madeira. Nothing has yet been done to conserve and propagate the native trees, and many of them may soon disappear owing to the constant devastation wrought on them by woodcutters, charcoal-burners and livestock.

Law no. 26 of 9 July 1913 created four forest sections, which were divided into zones; that of Funchal became no. 25 and was included in the fourth section, based in Lisbon. The decree of 8 May 1918 established eight forest districts, Funchal being placed in the sixth district, based in Lisbon, and eighteen forestry offices (*regências florestais*), that of Funchal being no. 18 (1922).

The decree of 11 March 1911 and its accompanying Regulations, which created the Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) and governed its operation, established the Agricultural Station (*Estação Agrária*). Technical and administrative control of forest matters passed to this department in 1919, when the Board was abolished.

Apart from the famous ‘Timber Regulations (*Regimento das Madeiras*)’ (see *Saudades*, p. 463), decreed in 1562 and a remarkable piece of legislation for its time, it may be said that no other useful legal provisions were enacted on this matter. This is despite the various decrees and measures issued by the central government, which are cited in the *Elucidário Madeirense* but which did not produce the beneficial results expected of them.

Over time, all the Municipal Councils, believing themselves to hold inalienable rights over the forest vegetation of the mountains, drew up various ‘by-laws’ (*posturas*) to regulate its use and exploitation. These were local provisions, allowing greater or lesser administrative latitude; they lacked any real harmony of principle, and they were applied with great arbitrariness. Even today certain rural council sessions occasionally invoke ancient and obsolete municipal by-laws and try to enforce them. This is hardly surprising, since even the central department itself does not apply consistent measures across the various branches of these services.

As we shall see, a brief reference at this point to what in Madeira are called the *baldios* is closely related to our subject. These are lands not given over to farming, generally lying at an altitude of more than eight hundred or nine hundred metres. They belong to private individuals, to the Municipal Councils (*Câmaras Municipais*) and to the State, and the boundaries between the various owners are not clearly drawn. In former times the ‘baldios’ were separated from the cultivated land, as in part they still are, by hedges or fences made of stakes and tree branches, which are also called *baldios*; their main purpose was to stop livestock from getting into the crops.

Since the limits of these lands have never been precisely marked out, it is easy to imagine the abuses that must have occurred, the bold claims that surface from time to time and the frauds used by wholly unscrupulous individuals to take unlawful and permanent possession of them.

A large part of these ‘baldios’ were regarded as ‘common grounds’ (*logradouros comuns*), where the farmers, under certain conditions and under the supervision of the ‘Forestry Service’ (*Regência Florestal*), gathered fodder, material for manure and fuel. This was a valuable privilege for them, one they could not do without in the toil of their busy and modest lives. If we allow these ancient, traditional privileges to be steadily whittled away through the sale to private individuals of ‘baldios’ belonging to the State or the municipalities, we shall see the legitimate prosperity, the prized household economy and the relative well-being of thousands of people of merely modest means seriously threatened, for the benefit of a small number of well-off but unscrupulous persons.

Not long ago, at a State department in a rural municipality (*concelho*), some common lands (*baldios*) were sold at public auction for a few paltry hundreds of escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis), on the grounds of certain hypothetical property rights, although the public enjoyed their use by customary right. The Municipal Council had reported that these lands were not ‘common grounds’, yet the said department went ahead with the sale and collected the corresponding tax due to the public treasury (1944).

There is no need to stress the pressing and unshakeable necessity of delimiting these ‘baldios’ as exactly as possible, whether they belong to the State, the councils or private individuals. This is demanded by the preservation of the woodland, by the strict supervision to be exercised by the forest guards, by the policy to be adopted by the central department, and also by the need to maintain the privileges enjoyed by countless farmers, as mentioned above.

We know that in several parishes of this island there has been great surprise at the ease with which licences are granted to fell various tree species that are becoming remarkably rare and whose exploitation ought to be absolutely forbidden, as it once was. It is worth recalling here that an old municipal by-law (*postura*) contains this sensible provision: ‘It is expressly forbidden to cut timber, firewood, bark and branches from the following trees and shrubs: laurel, *til* (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), Madeira mahogany (vinhático, *Persea indica*) and any other forest species, whether trees or shrubs, native or acclimatised (the pine excepted), whatever the situation or place in which they grow. This prohibition extends to the owners themselves of the properties on which the said trees and shrubs grow, who, if they infringe this provision, incur like any other person a fine of 2,000 to 20,000 réis according to the damage caused.’ Some have given the groups or stands of these and other very rare species the name of ‘spontaneous forests’, which ought to be preserved as religiously as were, in remote times, the so-called Sacred Forests, objects of fervent worship among ancient peoples, who paid them the deepest veneration.

These precious relics of our old wealth of forest are a ‘true title of glory’ for Madeirans, for they are indissolubly bound up with the name given to this island and this archipelago, which our glorious epic poet immortalised in the well-known and so expressive phrase: ‘which from its many trees is so called…’

It is easy to suppose that acts of vandalism, and even of outright extermination, must have been committed deep in those mountains, in our already so impoverished woodlands, under the legal cover of this lavish generosity in concessions and licences – above all by those who consider themselves owners of ‘baldios’, lands that ought to be the legitimate and inalienable heritage of the poor and of those less favoured by fortune.

Until our own time, the relentless enemies of the woods and forests were held to be the ‘shepherds’, the ‘charcoal-burners’, the ‘woodcutters’ and the ‘timber merchants’. To these have recently been added new and more dangerous enemies, sheltering behind questionable rights protected by certain public departments and based on elastic, ill-defined licences…

But, as the experience of centuries has amply shown, it is still not enough… to publish a certain number of legislative decrees, with their showy train of ‘instructions’ and ‘regulations’ meant to secure the full and strict enforcement of those same laws.

It is indispensable – absolutely indispensable – that the overall direction of the various forestry services be entrusted to a department which, besides the fundamental qualities of zeal and integrity that should distinguish the exercise of public office, also possesses the full body of knowledge, theoretical and still more essentially practical, needed to carry out these important and specialised services properly. This aim can only be fully achieved by creating a Forestry District (*Circunscrição Florestal*), as we have repeated more than once in the pages of this work.
Sugar regime
See Sugar cane and Sugar protectionism.
Timber regulations
See Afforestation, Forestry regime and Timber.
Regniard (J.)

In 1895 a pamphlet of 47-VII pages entitled *No Laboratório. Psychologia e Pathologia Cerebral* was published in this city. Signed with the pseudonym J. Regniard, it caused a great sensation here, and its author is still unknown to many.
Rego (family)

According to the distinguished genealogist José Bettencourt da Câmara, now deceased, there are several branches of this family: some descend from João Rego, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) from the Algarve; others from Gaspar Rego; and others from Vasco Fernandes Rego. The last two were among the first settlers of Caniço (‘reed’).
Rego (Dona Maria Emília Acciaioly)

She belonged to an old and distinguished Madeiran family and died more than 70 years ago. According to the information we have been able to gather, she published a small volume of verse, whose title we do not know. One of her compositions is included in ‘Flowers of Madeira’ (*Flores da Madeira*). We know nothing more about her.
Rego (Dr António Balbino do)

He was a native of mainland Portugal and was born on 23 May 1874. In 1900 he completed his medical training at the Porto School, and in 1904 he was appointed director of the Laboratory of Bacteriology and Hygiene (*Laboratório de Bacteriologia e Higiene*) in Funchal, which had recently been established by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) of this district.

Dr Balbino do Rego was practising privately as a physician in this city and carrying out his official duties as director of the Bacteriology Laboratory when, towards the end of 1905, a disease of suspicious character appeared here in Madeira. The health authorities were obliged to confine those who had been struck by it in the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’), which had been turned into an isolation hospital, and the director of the Laboratory of Bacteriology and Hygiene was placed in charge of that hospital. The sad and regrettable events that followed are briefly narrated in the articles Popular Riots (Volume II, page 404), Bubonic Plague (Volume III, page 77) and Popular Poetry (Volume III, page 87), and we refer readers to them, so as to avoid needless and tedious repetition.

Dr Balbino do Rego’s error was to insist on keeping the patients in absolute isolation, cut off from all communication. This measure was necessary and fully justified in principle, but given the circumstances of the time, and in particular the reprehensible attitude of the press and of politicians, it would have been wise to relax it without harm to public health, as was eventually done, though belatedly. He committed no other fault and no other error. It must be said, however, that the nursing staff of the isolation hospital left much to be desired, and that various abuses and even excesses took place, for which its director was not responsible. The history of those events has not yet been written with complete impartiality, and so we are pleased to record in this work some material that may serve for a conscientious study of this turbulent period of Madeiran history.

After the events at the Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’), Dr Balbino do Rego had his house stoned by the populace, even though a naval detachment was posted beside it. He was forced to take refuge in the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence), from where he went aboard the *D. Carlos*, finally leaving for Lisbon on the Companhia Insulana steamer.

Dr Balbino do Rego later returned to Madeira on the orders of Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) João Franco, Minister of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), to take charge once again of the Bacteriology Laboratory. The popular demonstrations, however, took on so serious a character that they compelled the local authorities to prevent the physician from landing. He left for the capital on the very day he arrived in our port, passing directly from the vessel that had brought him from Lisbon to the one that took him back there.

Dr António Balbino do Rego was appointed, by competitive examination, physician and surgeon of the civil hospitals of Lisbon and also director of the Anthropometric Post of the Civil Police of that city (1921).

In 1907 Dr Balbino do Rego published two interesting pamphlets entitled *Um ano Depois Assumptos Madeirenses* and *Na Ilha da Madeira Hospital Improvisado*, which contain valuable material for the study of the bubonic plague epidemic on this island.
Rego (Dr José Joaquim de Abreu)

He was born on this island around 1815. In 1839 he graduated in mathematics at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), after a course in which he obtained the highest marks, and was invited to become a professor, an offer he declined. He then graduated from the faculty of medicine of the same University. He entered the competition for the post of professor of the chair of mechanics at the Polytechnic School (*Escola Politécnica*), in which, through public examinations, he showed the worth of the lofty faculties of his mind and his profound learning, and he was placed first in the competition. He was appointed professor, but we do not know whether he ever actually taught the chair. His frail constitution, utterly exhausted by the excessive labours of the competition, had forced him to give up study, and he died in this city on 22 July 1847, aged little more than 30.
Reid

A family surname descending from the Englishman William Reid, who came to Madeira in 1844 or 1845 and set up a hotel here in the old Rua do Mercado de São João. His sons William and Alfred Reid, who carried on their father’s line of business, wrote a short work in 1881 entitled *Madeira, a guide book of useful and varying information*. Their chief service to the island, however, was their gift to the Funchal Municipal Library (*Biblioteca Municipal do Funchal*) of nearly 10,000 volumes from the library of the late Madeiran João Joaquim de Freitas.
Reis Gomes (João dos)

He is a reserve major of artillery and was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’) in this city on 5 January 1869, the son of João Gomes Benta and Dona Maria Gertrudes Castro Gomes. He attended the Lyceum (*Liceu*) of Funchal and completed the courses of the Polytechnic School and the Army School with high distinction, being commissioned second lieutenant on 29 December 1892.

Besides military service at various places on the mainland, he was commander of No. 3 Battery of Garrison Artillery in this city, inspector of war matériel for this island, and a teacher at the Liceu de Jaime Moniz and at the Funchal Industrial School (*Escola Industrial do Funchal*).

He was director of the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) and is the present director of the *Diário da Madeira* (1921). Besides the numerous articles published in these newspapers, he has contributed to many other publications. His writings published in book form are: *O Theatro e o auctor*, Funchal, 1905, XIII-214 pp. (philosophical study); *Historias Simples*, Lisbon, 1907, 214 pp. (stories); *A Filha de Tristão das Damas*, Funchal, 1909, 302 pp. (novel); *Guiomar Teixeira*, Funchal, 1912, IX-90 pp. (drama); *A Musica e o Teatro*, Lisbon, 1919, XVIII-334 pp. (philosophical study); *Acustica Fusiologica. A Voz e o ouvido Musical*, Lisbon, 1922, XI-133 pp.; and *Portugal-Brasil*, Funchal, 1922, 17 pp. (speech). A second edition of *O Theatro e o auctor* was published in Lisbon in 1916, and a new edition of the drama *Guiomar Teixeira* also appeared in Funchal in 1914.
Major Reis Gomes is a member of the Academy of Sciences of Portugal, holds the Palmes Académiques of the French Academy and is a commander of the Order of St James.

He is, beyond dispute, the most distinguished Madeiran writer and journalist, and many also regard him as the foremost theatre critic in our country. It would be most desirable if, from the hundreds of theatre reviews and critical appraisals that have come from his pen, a selection of some dozens were made and gathered into a volume. This would rescue from undeserved oblivion true masterpieces, which they unquestionably are in their genre. We have already referred briefly elsewhere to Major Reis Gomes’s writings on music and the theatre, and it should be added here that, in our view, the time has not yet come for these studies to be given the assessment they deserve, bringing out the great value they contain (1921).

One of the features that distinguished some of J. dos Reis Gomes’s writings, and that made them most appreciated here, was irony and satire, handled somewhat in the manner of Ramalho and Fialho. The comic and the grotesque in people and things, caught in the act, were presented to the reader with an original and spontaneous wit, and also with rigour and fairness of judgement, although at times biting and irreverent mockery came to underline the words and ideas... (1921).

After that date, Major João dos Reis Gomes published the following further works: *Forças Psíquicas* (philosophical essay), *O Belo Natural e Artístico* (paper presented to the Academy), *Figuras de Teatro*, *Através da França, Suíça e Itália* (travel diary), *Três capitais de Espanha (Burgos, Toledo e Sevilha)*, *O Anel do Imperador* (paper presented to the Academy), *Natais* (tales and narratives), *O Vinho da Madeira* (monograph), *Casas Madeirenses*, *O Cavaleiro de Santa Catarina* (paper presented to the Academy), *De Bom Humor* (narratives) and *Casos de Tecnologia* (popular science).

As a matter of principle we have generally refrained from any assessment of our writers from a strictly literary point of view, but we may be permitted to say now that Major Reis Gomes is among those who bring the greatest honour and lustre to Madeiran letters, and that his name will remain in the history of this archipelago as that of one of its most brilliant and accomplished writers and journalists.
Reis (Luís Maria dos)

This Madeiran was born on 9 December 1846 and died on 6 December 1920 with the rank of retired general. He wrote a pamphlet, published in Funchal in 1892, entitled *Organização e Historia do Regimento de Caçadores n.° 12*.
Magi (chapel)

At Lombo dos Reis (‘kings’ ridge’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito da Calheta (‘small cove’), stands the old chapel of the Magi (*Reis Magos*). It was founded around 1529 by Francisco Homem de Gouveia and his wife, Dona Isabel Afonso, who made it the seat of an entailed estate (*morgadio*). This chapel and the entailed foundation (*instituição vincular*, a morgado or capela) attached to it were discussed at length in an article published in the *Brado d'Oeste* (‘Cry from the West’) of 2 September 1916. There is also a chapel dedicated to the Magi in the parish of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), which belonged to the house of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’). It is of very old construction, for a document of 1577 states that it was already in a poor state of repair at that time. It was rebuilt in 1778 by João de Carvalhal Esmeraldo e Câmara, administrator of the entail to which it belonged. A few years ago it was restored once more, and today it is the property of João Fidélio de Canha.
Reis Magos (cove and landing place)

On the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’) there is a cove called Reis Magos (‘the Magi’), with a beach and a small landing place of the same name. It is home to a fishing centre of some importance.
Reis Torgal (Luís Maria dos)
He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the parliamentary session of 1892–1893.
Religião e Progresso
The first issue was published on 15 November 1879 and the last, the 44th, on 17 November 1880.
Clocks

Apart from the clock of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé Catedral do Funchal*), there are clocks for telling the public the time in the following places: São Martinho, Monte, Camacha, Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol, Canhas and Estreito da Calheta (1921). The tower of the parish church of Machico once had a clock, which stopped working in 1824.

The clock of the church of São Martinho was inaugurated in 1922. That of the church of Monte was acquired by the church’s own fabric fund in the time of the late vicar, Canon Francisco José Rodrigues de Almada. The clock of Camacha (see that entry), which stands in a tower at the locality (*sítio*) of Achada (‘plateau’), and that of Santa Cruz were gifts: the latter from the late R. Blandy and the former from Dr Grabham. The clock at Canhas, installed on the Levada do Poiso (‘resting place’), belongs to the *heréus* (co-owners of the water rights of a levada) of this levada. The clock of Estreito da Calheta was given by a group of young men from that parish (*freguesia*) living away in South Africa. Since 1899 the tower of the church of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) has had a clock acquired by the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*).

The present clock of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) was offered by Dr M. Grabham to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) at its session of 3 August 1914, but it did not reach Madeira until 8 November 1921, aboard the steamer *Walmer Castle*. It was blessed by the diocesan prelate on 23 February 1922, and the late Emperor of Austria, Emperor Charles I, attended the ceremony. On 27 July of the same year the vice-president of the Council declared that the clock had already been handed over to the Municipality; the fitting of two of the hands, the last work carried out on it, had been completed on 30 June.

The old Cathedral clock, taken down on 6 December 1921 so that the clock offered by Dr Grabham could be installed, was commissioned in 1775, during the governorship of João António de Sá Pereira. Its mechanism bears the following inscription: ‘This clock was made under the administration of the Most Illustrious and Most Excellent Governor João António de Sá Pereira. Year 1775. Paulo de França *fecit*.

On 6 August 1776 the Council appointed the first employee to look after the Cathedral clock, and from then on the clock always remained in the charge of the Municipality, which appointed the clockkeepers. The Council’s records contain no note explaining how the clock came to be handed over to the Municipality.

In 1823 the Council had the clock thoroughly repaired. The work cost 85,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) and was carried out by José Pedro Pereira, a locksmith, who charged nothing for his labour ‘since it was a work for the public, to whom he wished to be useful’. ‘The clock,’ says an old document, ‘was left perfect, having been on the point of being abandoned, and in Lisbon no one would have repaired it for less than 400 *patacas*’.

The original hour bell of the Cathedral clock broke – in what circumstances we do not know – and was replaced by a bell from the former convent of São Francisco, requisitioned by the Council in 1835. Around the same time the clock’s quarter bell was exchanged for a bell from the church of the College (*Colégio*) of São João Evangelista. The broken bell was put up for public auction by the Council and sold for 2,400 *réis* per *arroba* (weight of about 15 kg).

The four stone dials of the old Cathedral clock, which were reused for the present clock, measure 2.3 m in diameter, and their numerals are 0.35 m high. The hands, which could not be reused because they did not show the minutes, were 1.35 m long.

In the days when there was no clock in the Cathedral tower, the hours were announced there by a timekeeper, who was paid at first from the revenue of the wine levy (imposição do vinho) and later from the surplus of the Customs House tithes. The oldest document we know concerning this official dates from 11 April 1713, but everything suggests that already in the 17th century someone was charged with striking the hours, or some of them. This was a necessity for bringing a certain regularity to public and private business, above all at a time when wall clocks and pocket watches were still very uncommon in Funchal.
Rendell (J. M.)
Works: *Concise Handbook of the Island of Madeira, with a plan of Funchal and map of the Island*; London, 1881, 1 vol.
Renton (Dr)

An English physician who lived in Madeira for many years and published a study of the advantages of the island’s climate in the treatment of lung diseases in the *Edinburgh Medical and Surgical Journal* (1827). In collaboration with Dr Heineken, he made various meteorological observations in Funchal from 1826 to 1831.
Representation in the Cortes

In the old General Cortes (Portuguese parliament), or Three Estates, representation belonged to those lands and towns of the country which, because of their importance or other special circumstances not yet well understood, sent their delegates to those assemblies, where they championed the interests of the people they represented. The overseas possessions, to which Madeira belonged, gained their own representatives in the old Cortes only later, and the Madeiran archipelago appears to have been the first to enjoy what was then a signal privilege.

By the decree of 6 July 1645 Madeira was given a seat in the Cortes on the first bench, and it is affirmed that John IV granted it this favour because the island had been the first possession in which he was acclaimed King of Portugal. We know nothing of how the delegates to the Cortes were chosen here, a process which in any case was not carried out uniformly throughout the country. Nor do we know the names of any individuals who represented this archipelago in the Cortes after that date. We are aware only that on 14 March 1619 Philip II addressed a letter to João Fogaça, which is recorded in the books of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), informing him that, as the Three Estates were to assemble in the town (*vila*) of Tomar to swear allegiance to Prince Dom Filipe, he was to be present in that town on ‘the 20th of the month of May, when the Cortes are to begin’.

On page 635 of the notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) we read that Madeira seems to have been sending procurators to the Cortes as early as 1479. Yet if we consult the list of places that supplied such procurators in 1535, preserved in the archive of the Torre do Tombo (national archives) and published in the *Censo Eleitoral da Metrópole* by Mr António de Sousa Júnior, we do not find our island on that list.

Once absolute government had been overthrown by the Porto revolution of 1820, which established the representative system, electoral assemblies were convened in 1821 to choose the members of the Constituent Assembly. Madeira returned as deputies Dr Maurício José Castelo Branco, Francisco João Moniz and Dr António João Rodrigues Garcês; the last died before taking his seat in Parliament and was replaced by Dr João José de Freitas Aragão. General and ordinary elections were held in 1822, in which this archipelago elected as full deputies Dr João Francisco de Oliveira, Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar and Father João Manuel de Freitas Branco, with Father Jerónimo Alvares da Silva Pinheiro, Dr Luís António Jardim and Father João Crisóstomo Espinola de Macedo as substitutes.

When absolute government was restored in 1823 the Cortes were dissolved, but on the death of John VI in 1826 the representative system was established once more, with the granting of the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) by Pedro IV. Elections were held and the Cortes convened at once, Madeira returning Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar, Father Caetano Alberto Soares and Luís Monteiro.

Miguel I, regent of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), dissolved the Cortes and proclaimed himself absolute king in 1828, and only in 1834 was the representative system of government definitively established in Portugal. In September of that year elections were held on this island and four deputies were returned.
We give below the complete list of the individuals who represented this archipelago in the various legislatures, whether as deputies, as elective peers of the realm or as senators:

When the civil war was over, Peter IV called the electoral assemblies by decree of 28 May 1834. The elections were held in Madeira the following September, and Dr Lourenço José Moniz, António Aluísio Jérvis de Atouguia, João de Oliveira and José Liberato Freire de Carvalho were returned. In November 1835 elections were held in this archipelago to fill the seat left vacant by Jérvis de Atouguia, and Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque was elected. The decree of 4 June 1836 dissolved parliament and ordered elections, and in August of the same year Dr Lourenço José Moniz, António Aluísio Jérvis de Atouguia, João de Oliveira and Dr José Ferreira Pestana were elected. The Cortes (Portuguese parliament) never met, because the Constitution of 1822 was proclaimed on 10 September 1836.

The decree of 8 October 1836 ordered the electoral colleges to be convened and granted the deputies constituent powers. In December of the same year Dr Lourenço José Moniz, João de Oliveira, Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque and Dr José Ferreira Pestana were elected as full members, with António Aluísio Jérvis de Atouguia, Dean Januário Vicente Camacho and Canon Gregório Nazianzeno de Medina e Vasconcelos as substitutes.

1838–1840 – Under the decrees of 18 and 20 June 1838, elections for senators and deputies were held in this district the following August. João da Câmara de Carvalhal Esmeraldo and the Marquis of Saldanha were elected full senators and the Duke of Terceira substitute senator; Dr Lourenço José Moniz, António Aluísio Jérvis de Atouguia, Luís da Silva Mousinho de Albuquerque and Dr José Ferreira Pestana were elected full deputies, and Dean Januário Vicente Camacho and Sebastião Xavier Botelho substitute deputies. To fill one senator’s seat and two substitute deputies’ seats, an election was held in September 1838, which returned the Baron of Tojal as substitute senator and Dr Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo and Canon Gregório Nazianzeno de Medina e Vasconcelos as substitute deputies. There was another election to fill a senatorial vacancy, and Dr Daniel de Ornelas e Vasconcelos was chosen as full senator and Dr Domingos Olavo Correia de Azevedo as substitute.

The Cortes were dissolved on 25 February 1840 and the electoral assemblies were convened by decrees of the 27th and 28th of the same month and year. The following April Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Dr José Ferreira Pestana, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca and António Aluísio Jérvis de Atouguia were elected full deputies, with Canon Dr Gregório Nazianzeno de Medina e Vasconcelos, Father Dr João Henriques Moniz and Dr José Maria Lopes Carreira as substitutes. When Senator the Baron of Tojal was appointed Minister of Finance and so vacated his seat in the upper chamber, an election was held in June 1841, and the same Baron of Tojal was elected. In June 1841 Dr José Ferreira Pestana was appointed Minister of the Navy, vacating his seat as deputy; the by-election was held the following July, and the choice again fell on Dr José Ferreira Pestana.

By decree of 10 February 1842 the Cortes were dissolved and the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) was declared in force. That decree and another of 5 March following ordered elections, and in June of that year Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca, João da Câmara Carvalhal Esmeraldo, Francisco Correia Herédia and Dr Bartolomeu dos Mártires Dias e Sousa were elected deputies.

When the legislature ended, the decree of 28 April 1845 ordered the electoral assemblies to meet, and the following August Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca and Dr Bartolomeu dos Mártires Dias e Sousa were elected.

The decree of 23 May 1846 dissolved parliament, and that of 27 July of the same year ordered elections. Because of the civil strife of the time, these were held only in November 1847, under the decree of 12 August, and the following December Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca, Dean Januário Vicente Camacho and José Silvestre Ribeiro were elected.

Parliament having been dissolved on 25 May 1851, the assemblies were convened for the election, which was held in November of that year under the decree of 16 July conferring constituent powers on the deputies. The choice fell on Dr Lourenço José Moniz, António Aluísio Jérvis de Atouguia, Dr José Ferreira Pestana and Dr António da Luz Pita.

The decree of 24 July 1852 dissolved parliament, and elections were ordered by the decree of 2 October of the same year. The following April Dr Lourenço José Moniz, Dr José Ferreira Pestana, José Silvestre Ribeiro and Dr António da Luz Pita were elected.

The legislative term having ended, the decree of 29 September 1856 ordered the assemblies to be convened for elections, and in December of the same year José Silvestre Ribeiro, Dom Luís da Câmara Leme, Dr Sebastião Frederico Rodrigues Leal and António Correia Herédia were elected.

The Cortes were dissolved on 26 March 1858 and the electoral colleges met in May under the decree of 6 April of the same year. António Correia Herédia, Dr Luís de Freitas Branco, Jacinto Augusto de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos and António Rogério Gromicho Couceiro were elected. As the last was also elected for Portalegre, he had to opt for that constituency, being his native one, so a fresh election was held in this archipelago in November 1858, which returned Dom Luís da Câmara Leme.

The decree of 23 November 1859 dissolved the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), and that of the 28th of the same month and year called the electoral assemblies. The election returned Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca (Funchal constituency), Dom Luís da Câmara Leme (Calheta), Dr Luís de Freitas Branco (Santa Cruz) and Dr António Gonçalves de Freitas (Ponta do Sol).

Parliament was dissolved by decree of 27 March 1861, and a decree of the 30th of the same month and year ordered elections to be held. They took place on 15 May following, and returned Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca (Funchal constituency), Dom Luís da Câmara Leme (Calheta), Dr Luís de Freitas Branco (Santa Cruz) and Dr António Gonçalves de Freitas (Ponta do Sol).

When the legislative session had ended, the decree of 4 August ordered the assemblies to meet for the ordinary elections. Those elected were Dr Luís de Freitas Branco, Jacinto Augusto de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos, Dr António Gonçalves de Freitas and Dr Francisco Joaquim de Sá Camelo Lampreia.

After the Cortes had been dissolved, the electoral colleges were convened by decree of 15 May 1865. The election was held on 25 July of the same year and returned Dr Luís de Freitas Branco (Santa Cruz constituency), António Correia Heredia (Ponta do Sol) and Jacinto Augusto de Santana e Vasconcelos (Funchal). António Correia Heredia resigned his seat, and another deputy was elected to fill the vacancy.

The decree of 14 January 1868 dissolved parliament, and the decree of 17 February of the same year ordered the election to be held. It took place on 19 April following and returned Caetano Velosa Carvalhal Esmeraldo Castelo Branco (Funchal constituency), Dr Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (Ponta do Sol) and Dr João Barbosa de Matos e Câmara (Santa Cruz).

The decrees of 23 January and 18 March 1869 respectively dissolved the Cortes and called the electoral assemblies. The election took place on 2 May following, and Dr Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (Ponta do Sol constituency) and Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca (Funchal) were declared deputies.

Parliament having been dissolved by decree of 2 January 1870, the decree of 3 February following ordered elections, which were held in this archipelago on 1 May of the same year. Those elected were Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca (Funchal) and Dr Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (Ponta do Sol).

The Cortes were dissolved by decree of 1 July 1870. After the electoral assemblies had been convened by the decree of 18 September of the same year, Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca (Funchal) and Dr Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (Ponta do Sol) were declared deputies.

The decree of 3 June 1871 dissolved parliament and ordered the electoral colleges to be convened on 9 July following, but in this district they met only on the 20th of the same month. Dr Luís Vicente de Afonseca (Funchal) and Dr Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (Ponta do Sol) were elected.

When the legislative term had ended, a decree of 5 June 1874 set the election for 18 July following. The election in Madeira was held on that day, and from then on it took place on the same day as in mainland Portugal. Dom Luís da Câmara Leme and Ricardo Júlio Ferraz were elected.

1879 – When the legislature had ended, the decree of 29 August 1878 set the elections for 13 October of the same year. Those elected were the engineer Ricardo Júlio Ferraz (Funchal), Dr Manuel José Vieira (Santa Cruz) and Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira (Ponta do Sol).

Parliament was dissolved by the decree of 28 August 1879, and the election was set for 19 October following by the decree of 11 September. Those elected were Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira (Ponta do Sol), Dr Manuel Celestino Emídio (Santa Cruz) and Canon Feliciano João Teixeira (Ponta do Sol).

The decrees of 4 and 30 June 1881 dissolved parliament and convened the electoral colleges. The election took place on 21 August, and Dr Luís de Freitas Branco (Funchal), Dr Manuel José Vieira (Santa Cruz) and Dr Luís António Gonçalves de Freitas (Ponta do Sol) were declared deputies. Following the death of the deputy Dr Luís de Freitas Branco, a decree of 7 September 1882 ordered an election in the Funchal constituency, and the poll was held on 5 November of the same year. The candidate Anselmo José Braamcamp received the most votes but did not obtain an absolute majority, so the election was held again on 26 November of the same year, and Dr Manuel de Arriaga was elected.

The decree of 24 May 1884 dissolved parliament and summoned the electoral assemblies for the following 29 June, granting the deputies special powers to reform the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*). Those elected were Dr Manuel José Vieira, Pedro Maria Gonçalves de Freitas, Dr João Augusto Teixeira and Henrique de Santana e Vasconcelos. Under the provisions of the decree of 8 October 1885, the election of peers of the realm took place on 2 December of the same year, and António Correia Herédia and the Viscount of Vila Mendo were elected for this district.

Parliament having been dissolved, the elections of deputies were set for 6 March 1887 and those of elective peers for the 27th of the same month. Elected as deputies were Dr Manuel José Vieira, Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira, Canon Feliciano João Teixeira and Dr Fidélio de Freitas Branco, and as peers of the realm Pedro Maria Gonçalves de Freitas and Tomás Nunes de Serra e Moura. When Canon Alfredo de Oliveira resigned his seat, the runner-up, Henrique de Santana e Vasconcelos, was called to fill the vacancy.

At the end of the legislative session, the decree of 15 September 1890 ordered ordinary elections to be held on the following 20 October. Those elected were Dr Carlos Lobo de Ávila, Luís Bandeira Coelho, Henrique de Sant’Ana e Vasconcelos and Dr João Catanho de Meneses.

The decree of 20 January 1890 dissolved the Chamber of Deputies and the elective part of the House of Peers, and the decree of 20 February of the same year set the election of members of the lower chamber for the following 30 March and the election of peers for 14 April. Elected as deputies were Dr Fidélio de Freitas Branco, Dr António Jardim de Oliveira, Dr José Júlio Rodrigues and José Maria Greenfield de Melo, and as peers of the realm the Viscount of Vila Mendo and Dr Luís Adriano de Magalhães Meneses e Lencastre.

The decree of 15 September 1892 ordered elections to be held on 23 October of the same year. Those elected were Dr Augusto Dias Ferreira, Dr Luís Maria dos Reis Torgal, Dr António Baptista de Sousa and Dr Manuel de Assunção. When the last of these died, the runner-up, Dr António Vicente Varela, was called to fill the vacancy.

The decree of 7 December 1893 dissolved parliament, and the decree of the 19th of the same month and year set the elections of deputies for the following 11 February and those of peers for the 25th. The decree of 31 January 1894 postponed the elections, which were fixed for 15 and 29 April respectively. Elected as deputies were Dr Manuel José Vieira, Pedro Maria Gonçalves de Freitas, Dr Fidélio de Freitas Branco and Dom João de Alarcão Velasques Sarmento Osório, and as peers of the realm Dr António Baptista de Sousa and José Bandeira Coelho de Melo.

The Cortes (Portuguese parliament) were dissolved by decree of 28 March 1895, and the decree of 25 September of the same year set the following 17 November for the election. Those elected were Dr Fidélio de Freitas Branco, Dr Romano de Santa Clara Gomes and Dr Luciano Afonso da Silva Monteiro.

Parliament was dissolved by decree of 8 February 1897, and, under the decree of the previous 24 March, the poll was set for 2 May of that year. Those elected were Dr João Catanho de Meneses (Santana constituency), the Viscount of Ribeira Brava (Ponta do Sol) and Augusto José da Cunha (Funchal).

The decree of 17 October 1899 ordered the poll to be held on 26 November of the same year. Elected as deputies were Dr João Catanho de Meneses (Santa Cruz), Dr José António de Almada (Funchal) and João Augusto Pereira (Ponta do Sol).

The Cortes having been dissolved by decree of 25 October 1900, another decree of the same date ordered the election to be held on 25 November of that year. Those elected were Dr Quirino Avelino de Jesus (Funchal), Alberto Botelho (Santa Cruz) and Dr Alberto Bramão (Ponta do Sol).

Parliament was dissolved by decree of 4 June 1901, and the decree of 24 August following set the elections for 6 October immediately after. João Augusto Pereira, Alberto Botelho, Alexandre José Sarsfield and Dr Frederico dos Santos Martins were elected.

Parliament having been dissolved by decree of 29 April 1904, the election took place on 26 June following, under the provisions of the decree of May of the same year. João Augusto Pereira, Alexandre José Sarsfield, Dr Frederico dos Santos Martins and João Frederico Júdice de Vasconcelos were elected.

The Cortes having been dissolved by decree of 24 December 1904, the electoral assemblies were convened for 12 February 1905, as laid down in the decree of 3 January of the same year. Dr Catanho de Meneses, João Augusto Pereira, Dr José Cabral Correia do Amaral and Canon António Homem de Gouveia were elected. Major Alexandre José Sarsfield, who was the fifth candidate by number of votes, challenged the election of Captain João Augusto Pereira on the grounds that this candidate was commander of the war matériel section on this island. The Court for the Verification of Powers (*Tribunal de Verificação de Poderes*) declared the said candidate ineligible and, by its ruling of 30 March 1905, ordered a new election to fill the vacancy. The decree of 4 April of the same year set the poll for 7 May following, and Captain João Augusto Pereira was elected once again.

1906 – The decree of 9 February 1906 dissolved parliament, and that of 24 March following ordered the poll to be held on 29 April of the same year. Dr Frederico dos Santos Martins, Alexandre José Sarsfield and Canon António Homem de Gouveia were elected deputies.

1906–1907 – The decree of 5 June 1906 having dissolved parliament, the decree of 4 July of the same year set the elections for 10 August following. João Augusto Pereira, Canon António Homem de Gouveia, Dr Salvador Brum do Canto and Dr Francisco Xavier de Oliveira Cabral Moncada were elected deputies.

1908–1910 – The Cortes were dissolved by the decree of 10 May 1907, and the decree of 24 December of the same year set the poll for 5 April 1908. João Augusto Pereira, José Ribeiro da Cunha, João Soares Branco and Ernesto Jardim de Vilhena were elected. The validity of the election of the candidate João Augusto Pereira was challenged, and the Court for the Verification of Powers, by its ruling of 27 April 1908, found the said candidate ineligible. The election of one deputy was then ordered in this district; it took place on 26 July 1908, and Captain João Augusto Pereira was elected once again. Parliament was dissolved and the poll was held on 28 August 1910, at which Alexandre José Sarsfield, José L. Ávila e Lima, Emílio A. Santos Gil and José Correia Cabral do Amaral were elected. The Cortes never met, because the Republic was proclaimed on 5 October of the same year.

1911–1915 – The decree of 28 April 1911 summoned the electoral assemblies for 28 May following, when the deputies to the new Constituent Cortes were elected. This archipelago returned Dr Manuel de Arriaga, Dr Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Francisco Correia Heredia Ribeira Brava and Dr Manuel Gregório Pestana Júnior. When Dr Manuel de Arriaga was elected President of the Republic on 24 August 1911, his seat as deputy fell vacant, but the election to fill the vacancy was not held until 16 November 1913. The agronomist João da Câmara Pestana was elected, and he resigned his seat shortly afterwards.

1915–1917 – General elections were held on 13 June 1915. The deputies returned for this archipelago were Francisco Correia Heredia Ribeira Brava, Dr Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Dr Manuel Gregório Pestana Júnior and Manuel da Costa Dias, and the senators Daniel Simões Soares, Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques and Dr Remígio Gil Espínola Barreto.

After parliament was dissolved, the election took place on 28 April 1918. Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, José Vicente de Freitas and Duarte Melo Ponce de Carvalho were elected deputies, and Alberto Correia Pinto de Almeida and Adolfo Augusto Baptista Ramires senators.

The election took place on 11 May 1919. The deputies returned were Dr Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Dr Pedro Góis Pita, Américo Olavo Correia de Azevedo and José Miguel Lamartine Prazeres da Costa, and the senators Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques, José Mendes dos Reis and Heitor Eugénio Magalhães Passos. When one of this archipelago’s seats as deputy fell vacant, João Maria de Santiago Prezado, the only candidate put forward, was declared elected.

Parliament was dissolved and the election was held on 10 July 1921. Dr Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Dr Pedro Góis Pita, Américo Olavo Correia de Azevedo and Manuel de Sousa Brasão were elected deputies, and Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques, Dr Manuel Augusto Martins and Dr José Varela senators.

The Cortes having been dissolved, the election was held on 29 January 1922. The deputies returned for Madeira were Dr Carlos Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Américo Olavo Correia de Azevedo, Dr Pedro Góis Pita and Dr Juvenal Henriques de Araújo, and the senators Dr Vasco Gonçalves Marques, Vasco Cipriano Silva and César Procópio de Freitas.

In 1911 there were no direct elections for senators. Instead, the constituent electoral assembly chose them from among its own members, in accordance with Article 84 and its paragraphs of the Political Constitution of the Portuguese Republic.
