Republic (proclamation of the)

News of the proclamation of the Republic in the capital reached Madeira on the afternoon of 5 October 1910, and shortly afterwards a telegram arrived announcing the formation of the government. On the 6th, Dr Manuel Augusto Martins, who had been invested by telegram from the new government with the highest authority in the district, conferred about the events with Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) António Jardim de Oliveira, the secretary-general acting as civil governor, and with Colonel Valeriano José da Silva, the military commander. These authorities told him that they had received no official communication that the Republic had been established in the country. He immediately telegraphed Lisbon, asking for this communication to be made so that he could take up the post to which he had been appointed and the new government could be recognised by the Madeirans.

The communication to the military commander was not long in coming. This authority then declared that he did not object to the republican flag being raised at the Fort of São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’) or to the forces rendering it the due honours. These acts took place shortly afterwards at the Fort of São Lourenço, witnessed by Dr Martins and several fellow republicans, who had stationed themselves on the balcony of the Restoration Club (*Club Restauração*), which overlooks the Avenida de Gonçalves Zargo. The new flag was given a military salute by the guard, which had formed up for the purpose, while a local band (*filarmónica*) played *A Portuguesa*, which everyone heard in silence and with the greatest respect. Dr Martins, Azevedo Ramos, Dr Pestana Júnior and Dr Gonçalves Preto spoke from the balcony, all urging the people to keep order and respect individuals.

The new civil governor had been installed before the ceremony just described. Because the secretary-general was not present, office was conferred on him by the official Octaviano Soares, and the revolutionary flag was hoisted on the flagpole of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) while *A Portuguesa* was played. Dr Martins raised cheers for the Republic, for Liberty and for the Fatherland, which were warmly returned by the people gathered in the street.

In the evening, numerous groups, accompanied by the Artístico-Madeirense and Artistas Funchalenses bands, paraded through the streets of the city, burning Bengal lights and cheering the Republic. At the end of the demonstration, Azevedo Ramos addressed the people from one of the windows of the ‘Dr. Manuel de Arriaga’ centre.

On the 7th, at half past nine in the morning, the republican flag was raised at the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater), with the battery firing a salute. At 1 p.m. an identical ceremony took place at the fortress of São Lourenço, attended by the 27th Infantry Regiment. Led by a few sergeants, the regiment had left its barracks armed with rifles and bayonets, in breach of the standby order the commander had given so that it could respond to any request from the administrative authority should public order be disturbed.

Several officers appeared in the Praça da Constituição (‘Constitution Square’), among them Captain Henrique Luís Monteiro, who tried to impose discipline on the troops but was not heeded. Dr Pestana Júnior, municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of Funchal, then climbed onto a bench in the square. He declared that no officer of the regiment would act against the new political regime, as the captain himself had assured him on his word of honour, and that in these circumstances the men should obey their officers and fall back into line. Dr Pestana Júnior added that, for his part, Captain Henrique Monteiro’s word of honour was a pledge he greatly respected.

Shortly afterwards the artillery major Goulart de Medeiros arrived at the Largo da Restauração. He was known as a republican, and everyone supposed that he had helped bring the troops out of their barracks. After conferring with the distinguished and spirited officer Captain Henrique Monteiro, he too addressed the troops gathered there, urging them to obey, since the regiment’s officers had declared their support for the new regime. He was the object of an enthusiastic demonstration of sympathy from sergeants and soldiers alike, as well as from the people.

Meanwhile, an officer of the regiment raised the republican flag at the fortress of São Lourenço. The troops presented arms to it, and Dr Pestana Júnior led several cheers, which the people returned with enthusiasm.

At the troops’ request the band of the 27th Infantry arrived, and by order of the military commander the flag was lowered and raised again to the strains of ‘A Portuguesa’, with due honours. By then the force was already under the command of its officers, as Major Medeiros had asked in his speech. On their way from the Praça da Constituição to the Largo da Restauração, where, as we have said, this officer spoke, the men had refused to be commanded by their officers, and it was the sergeant-major who led them.

The regiment then set off, accompanied by its band playing ‘A Portuguesa’ and under the command of Major Luís Correia Acciaioly. It marched through the Rua de São Francisco, Rua da Carreira, Rua de João Tavira, Rua do Aljube, Rua dos Ferreiros and Rua do Príncipe, the Rampa de Dom Manuel, the Largo do Pelourinho and the Campo de Dom Carlos, and went to salute No. 3 Garrison Artillery Battery. The battery had not joined in the infantry regiment’s demonstrations and maintained the strictest discipline throughout, under the command of Captain João Augusto Pereira.

At the artillery barracks, which many members of the public entered, several cheers were raised for the Republic. The troops and the people then continued along the Rua de Santa Maria, the Largo do Pelourinho, the Rampa de Dom Manuel, the Rua do Príncipe and Rua dos Ferreiros, the Largo do Colégio and the Rua do Castanheiro, finally entering their barracks, where there were fresh displays of rejoicing.

At the request of the infantry sergeants and men, the military commander, Colonel Valeriano José da Silva, declared the regiment’s standby at an end and had the bust and portrait of Manuel II removed from his office in the barracks. He likewise ordered that all disciplinary punishments cease to be served.

The troop movement of the 7th was called a public demonstration of support for the Republic. Those who analysed the facts dispassionately, however, regarded it as an insubordination of a serious nature, though hardly surprising in a revolutionary period, when discipline and military regulations are generally little respected.

Near the former Praça da Constituição we saw many English people, who had landed in Funchal on the morning of the 7th, flee in terror at the sight of the armed soldiers heading in disorder towards the square. Truth demands it be said, however, that apart from the indiscipline and the soldiers’ refusal to obey their officers’ orders, nothing else deserving censure occurred that day, either on the part of the troops or of the people.

The Republic was proclaimed in Madeira without any obstacle whatsoever. Despite some foolish acts later committed by partisan individuals with little respect for the opinions and beliefs of others, the new regime was well received by almost everyone. It was then supposed that under it morality would enter the administration of the State’s revenues, and that the errors and follies which had so discredited the governments of the last years of the monarchy would no longer be committed.
Requeme (Sebastes kuhlii)

A fish of the gurnard family (Triglidae), caught at depths ranging from 100 to 250 *braças* (fathoms). In Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) it is known as *chapado* and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) as *vermelho*. It is not a rare species and lives in rocky places. Its flesh has a pleasant flavour.
Requinta de Braga

A small four-stringed instrument, similar to the *braguinha* (small Madeiran four-string guitar, ancestor of the ukulele), which is said to have been created by the late Madeiran musician Agostinho Martins. Its tuning is A, D, F, A, according to information given to us by Dr Manuel dos Passos Freitas.
Chronological Survey of Madeiran Journalism

This is the title of a work compiled in 1908 under the direction of the late João Eleutério Martins, which lists every Madeiran newspaper that had appeared up to that time, giving the years in which each was published, how long it ran, the issues that came out, etc. The work was based on the extremely important newspaper collections acquired by Eleutério Martins himself, which are now the property of the company that publishes the *Diário de Notícias*.
Restoration of Portugal

Towards the end of December 1640 a ship on its way from Cádiz to the Canary Islands called at Madeira. It brought news that grave events had taken place on the mainland, but it deliberately concealed the details of the revolution of 1 December, and also the fact that the Duke of Bragança had been proclaimed King of Portugal.

It was on 8 or 9 January 1641 that a caravel reached our landing place, and from its crew the whole truth became known. The ship carried letters from the new sovereign to the governor and captain-general of Madeira, Luís Miranda Henriques, and to the bishop, Dom Jerónimo Fernando. They announced the extraordinary event of Portugal’s liberation from the Castilian yoke and ordered that the independence of the nation be proclaimed without delay. All authorities and officials, as well as the members of the clergy and nobility and the representatives of the people, were to swear oaths of vassalage and fidelity to the new king and to the lawfully constituted government.

The news spread quickly through the city and was received with immense joy by the population. The Senate (*senado*, the municipal council), in agreement with the principal authorities, at once resolved to summon all the nobility, clergy and people to a great meeting in the Council house on 11 January 1641, so that the new monarch could be acclaimed and recognised there.

On that day the following were present at the said place: the governor; the bishop; the ordinary judges Luís Francisco de Oliveira and Diogo Pereira da Silva; the councillors (*vereadores*) João Baptista Acciaioly and António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo; the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) Dom António Dias; the guild representatives (*mesteres*) Pedro Rodrigues, Simão Lopes, Francisco Gomes and Lourenço Gonçalves; the captain of the Castilian garrison, Dom Tomás Velasquez Sarmento; and the representatives of the clergy, nobility and people. The governor then declared to all those present ‘that he had a letter from the most high and most mighty lord King John IV, in which he informed him of the general accord with which he had been raised up as lawful king and lord of his realms of Portugal’.

Once the governor had read this letter, the bishop presented the one he too had received from the new king. The whole assembly then acclaimed John IV with great commotion and enthusiasm, and he was at once recognised as the true sovereign of the Portuguese. A record (*auto*) of the ceremony just held was then entered in the books of the Senate. It is an interesting document and was first published in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) of 1 December 1906.

The Church celebrated the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of John IV with a solemn *Te Deum* in the cathedral. On the night of the 11th and on the following nights the whole city was brilliantly illuminated to celebrate an event that filled the hearts of true Portuguese with joy.

The commander of the Castilian garrison, Dom Tomás Velasquez Sarmiento, although he had some forces at his disposal, did nothing to oppose the will of the Madeirans. He handed over the fortresses and accepted quarters both in them and in the towns, and calmly awaited the arrival of a ship to take him to Spain.

The clergy, nobility and people swore their oath of loyalty to the new sovereign on 13 January, in the council house. On the 25th several Portuguese citizens were called upon to take up offices of the Senate that had been held by Spaniards. Pero Catanho was elected people's judge (*juiz do povo*, elected representative of the craft guilds), Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos councillor, and Gonçalo de Freitas da Silva municipal procurator; Pedro Rodrigues Neto was appointed to the post of market inspector (almotacé).

The new sovereign had been recognised throughout the island without the slightest resistance, and the various public offices had been filled by Portuguese citizens. It remained to present John IV with the congratulations and homage of the Madeirans, and to inform him of the general acclaim with which the news had been received that a genuinely Portuguese monarch sat on the throne.

On the 26th the ship's master Francisco Rodrigues Belo was summoned to the Council. There he was ordered, on pain of a fine of 200 *cruzados* and four years' penal exile (degredo) away from the island, to make ready within eight days a caravel to carry to the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) the letters that the Senate was about to write to John IV. On 16 February the councillor Martins Mendes de Vasconcelos and the guild representative (*mester*) Pedro Rodrigues were elected to bear these letters and to kiss the monarch’s hand at court on behalf of the inhabitants of Madeira.

The councillor Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos declared that all the expenses of his journey to the capital would be met by himself and not by the Senate, ‘for all his possessions were but little to spend in the service of His Majesty’.

The caravel carrying the Senate’s two representatives did not leave for Lisbon until early March. The two councillors João Baptista Acciaioly and Antonio de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, who at first had shown such zeal and interest in the service of the new monarch, stopped attending the council sessions from a certain date onwards. Their absence held up the dispatch of the letters, which by custom had to be signed by all the members of the Senate.

The nobility, the people and the Council, meeting on 26 February, had to elect Antonio de Aragão de Teive and Baltasar de Abreu Berenguer as councillors before the letters addressed to the monarch could finally be signed and sent to the Kingdom in the ship of the master Rodrigues Belo.

On 12 April of the same year, 1641, the nobility, the representatives of the people and the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) met once more in the Council’s chambers. They resolved unanimously that, following the example of the cities, towns and localities of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), Funchal should contribute a voluntary *donativo* (nominally a ‘gift’ to the Crown; a compulsory war levy) towards the costs of the war that the nation was about to wage against Castile. Many of those present declared that they were resolved to give not only their possessions but also their lives, if need be, to defend their homeland from the Castilian yoke.

‘The island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’),’ says Rebelo da Silva, ‘followed Madeira’s example as soon as it learned of the revolution of 1 December 1640. When the despatches from Funchal arrived on 5 February, the inhabitants, whom a squadron of twelve Ottoman sails had almost blockaded, greeted the news with repeated salvoes of artillery and musketry. The Turks, startled by the noise and ignorant of its cause, thought it prudent to withdraw, and disappeared.’ The separation of the Madeira archipelago from the Castilian dominions did not cost a single drop of blood, and it was accomplished with the evident assent of every social class. The horrors of a 60-year captivity had rekindled the love of liberty in Madeiran hearts, so that as soon as news of the revolution of 1 December became known, everyone united at once to celebrate it with enthusiasm, without fear of the Castilian troops then on the island.

Madeira was the first Portuguese possession to proclaim John IV, and the patriotic fervour with which the ceremony was held shows us that hatred of the usurper and love of national independence were no less intense here than in the Kingdom.

Restauração (square)

This is the square at the main entrance of the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence). It was opened when the Teatro Grande was demolished, during the governorship of Dom Álvaro da Costa Macedo. Before this theatre disappeared, two narrow streets ran alongside part of the fortress walls and led to its main entrance. The name given to the square recalls the restoration of the Constitutional Charter (*Carta Constitucional*) on 5 June 1834.

Ribeira Brava (parish)

On the origin of the name of this parish (*freguesia*), the lineage and services of its inhabitants and the fertility of its lands, let us hear the celebrated historian of the islands, albeit with his customary hyperbole: ‘…and they spent many days on the way until, three *léguas* further on, they reached a furious stream, on whose beach the captain was waiting. He had gone ashore and had laid out a settlement there, which he named Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) after the stream that ran through this place. The settlement later founded here became so pleasant and noble, one of the best on the island, that besides having many fruits and provisions in abundance, it is and always was so generous with the inhabitants who live in it that, when it suited the captains of Funchal to go later to the relief of the strongholds of Africa with men, from this one place alone they drew such noble knights and distinguished people, who went at their own expense to serve the King, and who won such renown, as will be seen later in the course of this history; besides other noble people, retainers of the captains, who always had very knightly men of noble birth from here. This place is not a town, not because it lacks many inhabitants and a good site, nor because it is the least on the island – on the contrary, it is the best situated and most magnificent of all – but because it lies within the *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) of the City of Funchal, and is a pleasant *quinta* (country estate), from which the inhabitants of the city obtain, and where they are supplied with, the best wheat, fruit, game and meat, and in greater abundance than in the whole island; and it may rightly be called the granary of Funchal, as the Island of Sicily is called the granary of Italy.’ Elsewhere the author of the *Saudades* also says: ‘A *légua* west of Campanário (‘bell tower’) lies Ribeira Brava, which bears this name to the full: it is a village of about three hundred households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), with a church of St Benedict and a good landing place of fine shingle. Its houses stand up along the floor of the stream, and it has much sugar cane, two sugar mills and very rich orchards with many apples and pears, walnuts and plenty of chestnuts, so that it is the pleasantest village on the island. For this reason, and because it deserves it, having a good landing place and being very lush, the inhabitants have many times tried to have it made a town. It also has many vineyards, although the wine is not as good as that of Funchal. The stream is so furious when it floods that it sometimes carries away many houses and does great damage, because it comes down from great mountains and high ranges; and because it is like this, they came to call it *brava* [wild].’

It is one of the oldest parishes (*freguesia*) in Madeira, its creation being dated by Frutuoso’s annotator to the year 1440. It was perhaps not yet a parish in the strict sense that the term is meant to convey, but it already formed a sizeable centre of population, with its small church and its own chaplain, who no doubt enjoyed some of the privileges and rights granted to vicars *in solidum*. The same happened with other parishes in the earliest days of colonisation.

In the General Index of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*) we find the following instruments cited concerning the parish priests of this parish: a royal decree (alvará régio) of 28 May 1549, adding one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and one mark of silver (*marco de prata*, c. 230 g of silver) to their original salary of 8,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis); a royal decree of 28 July 1556, setting that salary at 8,000 *réis* in cash, one mark of silver, two *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine; a royal decree of 13 March 1572, raising the same salary to 34,000 *réis*; a royal decree of 8 May 1591, fixing it at 27,000 *réis* in cash, two *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine; and a royal decree of 22 October 1599, adding a further 3,000 *réis* to that salary. All these sums were annual.
The curacy (*curato*) of this parish was created by the royal decree of 30 August 1594, and the royal decree of 2 January 1606 set its annual salary at 20,000 *réis* in cash.

Because of its importance and the growth of its population, this parish became the seat of a collegiate church (vol. 1, p. 283), which was created around 1540 with four beneficiaries, each paid 8,000 *réis* a year. The royal decrees of 16 May 1549, 18 June 1572, 8 May 1591 and 13 March 1745 successively increased this salary, which the last of these instruments set at 6,000 *réis* in cash, two *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine a year. The number of beneficiaries was reduced to three by the royal decree of 5 September 1577.

Besides these clergy, the collegiate church had the office of treasurer, who under the royal decree of 10 February 1666 received an annual salary of 10,000 *réis* in cash, forty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine, with the obligation ‘to provide wax, wine and hosts for the sacristy’. It also had the offices of preacher, organist and sacristan.

We do not know the date of foundation of the old chapel of St Benedict (*São Bento*), which was the seat of the parish and of the collegiate church, though its existence must go back to the second quarter of the 15th century. This chapel underwent various alterations and repairs until the present parish church was built, which is unquestionably one of the oldest rural churches in this diocese. It has undergone various additions and modifications, but its original construction cannot be later than the second half of the 16th century.

This parish had a convent of Franciscan friars, called according to some the Convent of Nossa Senhora da Porciúncula (Our Lady of the Angels of the Portiuncula) and according to others that of São Francisco, of which we have already given a brief account (volume I, page 308).

This parish once had the chapels of Our Lady of the Presentation (*Nossa Senhora da Apresentação*), Our Lady of the Good Death (*Nossa Senhora da Boa Morte*), St Anthony of Padua and the Almas (Holy Souls in Purgatory). The chapel of São José (St Joseph) lies in ruins, while those of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception and St John the Baptist are still used for worship. We give a brief account of all of them elsewhere in this work.

Among the natives of this parish were the celebrated grammarian and humanist Father Manuel Álvares (volume I, page 59), José Anselmo Correia Henriques (volume I, page 317), José Ferreira Pestana (volume II, page 23), Belchior de Teive and the Viscount of Ribeira Brava. Also born in Ribeira Brava, says Gaspar Frutuoso, were ‘the Coelhos, canons of the Cathedral of Funchal, outstanding men with rich voices. One of them was called Gaspar Coelho; he was choirmaster of the Cathedral for many years; and Francisco Coelho, his younger brother, while a canon, was also choirmaster of the King’s chapel at Court’.

Many noble persons lived in this parish, holding a great deal of land here by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and founding several entails. Prominent among them were the Teive family (see that entry); Henrique Bettencourt, whose widow Dona Isabel Fernandes Távora founded the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of Apresentação (‘Presentation’); Lopo Vaz de Sequeira; António Vilela; and others besides.
Among the events in this parish that deserve special mention are the killings that took place there on 29 June 1884, to which we have already referred on page 403 of volume II of this work.

This locality owes much to the Viscount of Ribeira Brava. It was he who secured its elevation to the seat of the municipality (*concelho*) and of a school district, and who endowed it with important material improvements, transforming the locality (*sítio*) of Lugar (‘place’) into a pleasant settlement well worth a visit. The opening and widening of streets and roads, the building of a small theatre, the rebuilding of the small fort of São Bento and other works carried out there place the people of Ribeira Brava under a duty to be grateful to his memory and to perpetuate it in a worthy manner through the times to come.
On 10 February 1902 the virtuous priest Francisco Manuel de Sousa died in this parish. As parish priest and public-spirited citizen, he rendered notable services to this locality.

According to the 1911 census the parish has 5,339 inhabitants, and its principal localities are: Lugar, Achada, Amoreira, Barreiros e Carreira, Caminho Chão, Cova, Cruz da Caldeira, Cruz e Pico da Banda de Além, Eira do Mourão, Espigão, Fajã dos Bichos, Fajã do Cerejo, Fajã da Ortiga, Fajã da Ribeira, Fonte Cruzada, Fonte do Pinheiro, Fontes, Lombo Cesteiro, Meia Légua, Moinhos, Pedra Mole, Pomar da Rocha, Ribeira Funda, São João, Terça, Til and Vale.

Every year on 29 June the village of Ribeira Brava is visited by a very great number of people from all parts of the island, drawn by the *arraial* (open-air popular festival at a church feast) held there. The procession, with its little boat and the sword dance, was the chief attraction of the festivities in that place, but some time ago the religious cortège was at last purged of the dance, which had been much enjoyed by the pilgrims. We do not know when the little boat and the sword dance first appeared in the procession of St Peter, but it is likely that both date from early times.

The little boat, decked with flowers and carrying some fishing gear as a symbol of that industry, appears in the cortège because St Peter, whose image also features in it, was a fisherman. The sword dance, on the other hand, was apparently the last vestige of the many folk dances (*folias*) that once appeared in certain processions, and particularly in that of Corpus Christi (see Processions).

The seven men who took part in the dance wore white breeches and red waistcoats, and on their heads green caps shaped like a mitre, trimmed with plumes and long ribbons. Each held a sword by the hilt in one hand and, with the other, the point of the sword held by the man next to him. To the sound of a tambourine they performed various measured movements, passing now and then beneath the swords.

In the little boat, which still appears at the head of the procession, ride a few children dressed as fishermen, together with various offerings of local produce. The celebrated sword dance, which we had occasion to see several times more than twenty years ago, also went before the religious cortège. The men taking part in it never ceased their gestures and twirling while the cortège made its way through the streets of the village, between dense rows of people who had come from every part of the island.
Ribeira Brava (municipality and town)

As we have already noted above in connection with Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) and Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) never held the rank of town (*vila*), although it was often given that name, even before the municipality (*concelho*) was created. On page 213 of volume I of this work we stated that there were seven villages (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) in Madeira, among them that of Ribeira Brava. Even today the most important locality (*sítio*) in this place, which serves as the seat of the parish and of the municipality, is known by the name of Lugar (1921).

The municipality of Ribeira Brava is the most recently created. It has existed for only nine years (1921), for it was created in 1914. Its formal inauguration took place on 2 August of that year. It is made up of the parishes (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, Serra de Água and Tabua, detached from the municipality of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), and the parish of Campanário (‘bell tower’), separated from the municipality of Câmara de Lobos. Its population is 12,800 inhabitants. Its arms show the small fort of São Bento (‘St Benedict’), which stands at the entrance to the settlement, on the street leading to the quay.
By a decree of 31 August 1915 a school district was created with its seat in this municipality; its seat is today in the city of Funchal (1921).
The municipality of Ribeira Brava was created by the decree of 6 May 1914, and its seat was raised to the rank of town by the decree of 26 May 1928.

The locality (*sítio*) known as Lugar, being the most populous and busiest in the parish (*freguesia*), adjoining the landing place and in easy and frequent communication with the other localities, could not fail to be chosen as the seat of the new municipality (*concelho*) and the new town (*vila*). The town takes in the said locality of Lugar together with those of Calvário, Bagaceira and Moinhos. Within its area stand the town hall and the other municipal offices, the Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’), two state primary schools, one for each sex, the post and telegraph office and the telephone exchange, the civil registry office, the revenue guard post (*posto fiscal*), the seat of a medical district (*partido médico*, served by a municipal doctor), the parish cemetery, the landing quay, the small fort of São Bento, the ruins of the church of the former convent of Franciscan friars, etc. Some forty years ago the now defunct Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) set up an experimental agricultural station here; of those established in Madeira at that time, it is perhaps the only one that has been of any practical use. When this district was divided into two primary-education school districts, western and eastern, one of them had its seat at Ribeira Brava. Shortly afterwards the seat was transferred to the city of Funchal, and that district was abolished in 1923.
Ribeira Brava (landing place and quay)

The landing place of this locality is a beach of large pebbles, where embarking and landing are none too easy, especially when the waves are running high. A quay was therefore needed, and it was built between 1904 and 1908. It lies to the east of the town (*vila*), to which it is linked by a tunnel and a short road, and it serves this parish (*freguesia*) well, as well as the surrounding villages and even some localities on the north of the island. The coastal shipping steamers call at this landing place.
Ribeira Brava (Viscount of)

Francisco Correia Heredia, who after the abolition of titles of nobility took the name Francisco Correia Heredia Ribeira Brava, was born on 2 April 1852 in the parish (*freguesia*) from which he took his title. He was the son of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) António Correia Heredia (see that entry) and Dona Ana de Bettencourt Heredia, and he descended from the oldest and noblest Madeiran families (see Heredia). He was granted the title of viscount by decree of 4 May 1871.
He studied at the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city and attended the former Higher Course of Letters (*Curso Superior de Letras*).

He was active in politics and a prominent figure in the former Progressive Party. He was elected deputy several times and represented Madeira in the legislative session of 1897–1899; he was also civil governor of the districts of Bragança, Beja and Lisbon. He played a leading part in the progressive dissidence headed by Councillor Alpoim, taking part in various revolutionary movements that hastened the fall of the monarchy.

Once the republic had been established, he followed the party faction of Dr Afonso Costa, of whom he was a great admirer and friend, and came to hold a prominent place in local politics in Madeira, representing this archipelago in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislatures of 1911–1915 and 1915–1917.

For some years he was president of the Madeira Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola da Madeira*), and he launched several noteworthy undertakings, although their practical results were slight. As we have pointed out elsewhere (volume II, page 197), this administrative body did not live up to the great hopes placed in its work as the powerful force for the prosperity of this archipelago that it ought to have been.

He also sat on the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), the Autonomous Board for the Funchal Harbour Works (*Junta Autónoma das Obras do Porto do Funchal*) and the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*). Around 1893 he was in the Argentine Republic, managing the properties of the Armstrong firm (*Casa Armstrong*), and he often had occasion to assist the Viscount of Faria in receiving the distinguished persons who visited that country. He also lived for some years in Paris, where he mixed with many men of letters and moved in the best society of that capital, and as a result he had a perfect command of the French language.

The Viscount of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) was killed in Lisbon on 16 October 1918, while he was being taken, with other political prisoners, from the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) to a fortress where he was to be held. It is said that the political prisoners attacked the escort guarding them, and that the escort replied with a volley at point-blank range, killing seven of the prisoners. See Ribeira Brava (parish).
Ribeira da Janela (parish)

The most abundant and longest watercourse that rises in the interior of the island, amid towering mountains, and flows into the ocean is the one called Ribeira da Janela. Near its mouth stands a small islet, 40 metres high, with a natural hole almost at its top which, from a certain distance, readily brings to mind a window opening in the rock face. This is the origin of the name that the first settlers gave to this stream. The settlement or cluster of inhabitants that gradually grew up on its banks naturally took the name the stream already bore. Such is the origin of the name of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira da Janela.

The land that today forms this parish belonged almost entirely to the parish of Porto do Moniz, while a less considerable part of it belonged to the parish of Seixal. By the middle of the 16th century there were already inhabitants with a fixed residence on the slopes of the stream, and in the last quarter of the same century there were some homesteads on the right bank, which belonged to the parish of Porto Moniz.

The chapel of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation) is said to have been founded in 1630 by António Fernandes and Manuel Rodrigues, who lived there, and it is said that some years later it was destroyed by a great flash flood (*aluvião*). It is certain, however, from documents we have examined, that the chapel was built by the people in 1699, its endowment being dated 7 September of that year. Was this a rebuilding or the original construction? We do not know, but we are inclined to believe that 1699 is the year of its first building. In 1754 the chapel was enlarged, and licence for its blessing was granted on 28 April of that year. In 1852 the works for building a new church were put out for award by public auction (*arrematação*) for the sum of 6,100,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), but construction never began. It was only in the last quarter of the 19th century that the small church underwent a great transformation. It was converted into the chancel, and the nave of the church was added to it; the works were declared complete in 1874. Over the portico is the following inscription: ‘Built by the people and directed by Father Pombo in 1879.’ Great contributions to this important work were made by the parish priest of the time, Father Manuel da Silva Pombo, by Dr João Barbosa de Matos e Câmara and by José Teixeira Rebêlo, a landowner in this parish and representative of a noble and ancient family which owned entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*) here. In 1922 new and important repairs were carried out in this church, owing to the efforts of the present parish priest, Father Manuel Vasconcelos da Incarnação (1921).

This chapel was served by a private chaplain until the diocesan prelate, Dom Friar Manuel Coutinho, by a warrant (*provisão*) of 25 September 1726, established a provisional curacy (*curato*) in it. The curacy was formally created by royal decree (alvará régio) of 4 February 1733, which states that it had been created at the request of the vicar of Porto Moniz, Paulo Vieira Jardim, and which assigned the curate an annual stipend of one and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. It was a curacy dependent on the vicarage of Porto do Moniz, but, like other curacies of this diocese, it gradually freed itself from the mother church (*igreja matriz*) and became an autonomous parish. The first priest to exercise parochial duties here was Father Inacio de Aguiar Sequeira.

The uplands of this parish (*freguesia*) are celebrated here in Madeira for their incomparable beauty. Foremost among them is the well-known locality (*sítio*) of Fanal, which, with its wonderful pond (*lagoa*), its dense and gigantic trees, the picturesque character of the place, its astonishing landscapes and crystal-clear waters, is a spot full of the greatest attractions and the most fascinating charms. Anyone who knows the natural beauties of this island well but has not crossed the uplands of Ribeira da Janela is unaware of a new aspect of those beauties, and one of the most marvellous.

The land of this parish is remarkably fertile and yields in abundance every crop customarily grown in Madeira. It is irrigated by the Levada dos Cedros and the Levada do Lombo Gordo. A new levada (irrigation channel) is planned for the near future (1921); construction work on it began many years ago, as has been said elsewhere in this work.
The principal localities of this parish are Casais de Baixo, Penedo, Casais da Igreja, Casais de Além and Eira da Achada. It has 748 inhabitants (1921).
As a mere curiosity, we will add that someone informed us that the inhabitants of Ribeira da Janela are very hard-working, deeply religious, intelligent and... vindictive.
Ribeira da Janela (islets)

Not far off the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira da Janela (‘window stream’) lie the islets of Ruama, Comprido and Ilhéuzinho, commonly called the Ilhéus da Ribeira da Janela (‘islets of the window stream’). One of these islets gave its name to the stream and to the parish, as stated in the previous article.
Ribeira de Santa Luzia

This is one of the three streams that run through the city, and it takes its name from the chapel of this dedication, the chapel of St Lucy (*Santa Luzia*), which stood on a rise on its left bank. The land along its banks was among the first to be farmed in various ways in the earliest days of colonisation. At the end of the 17th century there were four sugar mills on its banks. Important levadas (irrigation channels) rise in the basin of this stream, the chief of them being the one called the Levada de Santa Luzia (see II-255).
Ribeira dos Socorridos

This is one of the most important watercourses on the island. It forms the boundary between the parishes (*freguesias*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’) and Santo António, on its left bank, and those of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), on its right bank. São Martinho and Câmara de Lobos flank the mouth of the stream. It rises in the interior of the island, in the locality (*sítio*) of Torrinhas (‘little towers’), and crosses the parish of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’).

During the first exploration that João Gonçalves Zarco made along the coast, some of his companions landed at the mouth of this stream and were nearly swept away by the force of the current. The captain promptly came to their aid, and ‘they were rescued and freed from danger... and hence the name... of Ribeira dos Socorridos, says the author of the *Saudades*.
Streams

These natural aqueducts, which generally run along the beds of deep, narrow valleys, are very numerous on this island and carry abundant water in the winter season. They rise on the slopes of the central mountain range and flow into the ocean, and some of them have tributaries that increase their volume and the speed of their course. ‘All of them, in winter,’ says the illustrious annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘carry abundant water, often torrential: they then fill up and at times overflow, carrying down from the mountains thousands of tonnes of boulders of varying size, many so large that they can afterwards be removed only in pieces; and all of them, tumbling in the torrent against one another, make a sinister noise as they collide, until, blocking the beds of these streams, they raise them above the land along the banks; and this land, when it is not buried, is carried off by the stray waters far out to sea, dissolved into mud. In summer, however, their flow of water becomes scant, and some streams even run dry, because of the diversions made both for irrigating the land along their banks and for the levadas (irrigation channels), which take up the running water there and carry it to fertilise distant crops across the whole coastal area of the island.’ From time to time these streams turn into raging torrents which, leaving their beds and invading the banks on either side, violently sweep away large stretches of cultivated land, animal pens and even dwelling houses, at times causing considerable loss of life and property to those living nearby. The principal streams of Madeira are the following:
Ribeira de São Bartolomeu
It rises on Pico Gordo (‘fat one’) and Pico da Silva, and its principal tributary is the Farrobo (‘carob tree’) brook.
Ribeira de São João

It rises on Pico Escalvado and Pico de Santo António, and receives the waters of the brooks of Água de Mel (‘honey water’) and Santana (‘St Anne’). In former times it bore the names Ribeira de Santa Catarina, de São Pedro, Grande and de São Francisco, and it is still known as the Ribeira de São Lázaro and the Ribeira de Santo António.
Ribeira de São Jorge
It rises on Pico do Canário and receives the waters of the brooks of Canário, Grande and Tombo da Furna.
Ribeira Brava
It rises at the Cumeada de São Vicente (‘ridge of São Vicente’), and its tributaries are the brooks of Poço, Pico, Vicente Vaz and Eira da Moura.
Ribeira da Boaventura

It rises to the west of Pico das Abóboras and receives the waters of the brooks of João Ferino and Eixo. It lies in the municipality (*concelho*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and is also known as the Ribeira de São Pedro.
Ribeira da Boaventura
It rises at the Boca das Torrinhas (‘pass of the little towers’) and is one of the fullest streams on the island. Near the village it is known as the Ribeira do Porco.
Ribeira da Calheta
It rises at the Cabeço da Levadinha (‘knoll of the little levada’), or Cabeço do Lombo do Salão (‘hall ridge’), and its tributaries are the brooks of Cutileiro and Convento.
Ribeira do Caniço
It rises at Camacha, and its tributary is the Vale Paraíso (‘paradise valley’) brook.
Ribeira da Cruz
It rises on Pico da Pedreira (‘quarry peak’) and carries little water.
Ribeira da Janela
It rises on the Paul da Serra, at the Fontes do Rabaçal and at Assobiadouro, and is one of the longest and fullest streams on the island.
Ribeira da Madalena
It rises near Pico da Urze on the Paul and receives the waters of the brooks of Pinheiro (‘pine tree’) and Amoreiras (‘mulberry trees’).
Ribeira da Ponta do Sol
It rises on Pico da Fonte do Norte.
Ribeira da Serra de Água da Calheta
It has the same source as the preceding stream and receives the waters of the brooks of Aza, Fragueiro and Meninas.
Ribeira da Tabua
It rises on Pico das Pedras and receives the waters of the Barqueiro brook.
Ribeira de Gonçalo Aires
It rises on Pico do Infante. It carries very little water.
Ribeira de João Gomes
It rises in the Serra do Poiso (‘resting place’), and the Ribeira das Cales flows into it. In former times it was also known as the Ribeira de Nossa Senhora do Calhau (‘Our Lady of Calhau’).
Ribeira de Machico

It rises at Lamaceiros (‘mud flats’) and the Portela do Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), and its principal tributaries are the Ribeira Seca and the brooks of Alcanforado, Ermida, Escuro, Cales and Cova.
Ribeira de Santa Cruz
It rises at Santo António da Serra (‘St Anthony of the uplands’), and its principal tributary is the Ribeira da Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’).
Ribeira de Santa Luzia
It rises on Pico do Areeiro (‘sand pit’) and Pico Escalvado, and its tributaries are the brooks of Cidral, Frades, Pisão and Til. It is also called the Ribeira da Praça.
Ribeira do Campanário
It rises on Pico dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’) and carries little water. It is also called the Ribeira da Lapa.
Ribeira do Faial
It rises on Pico Ruivo (‘russet’) and is also known as the Ribeira Seca (‘dry stream’). It receives the waters of the Ribeira da Metade and the Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’).
Ribeira do Porto da Cruz

It rises on Pico da Suna and is also called the Ribeira da Igreja (‘church’). The Ribeira do Tem-te-não-caias (‘hold on, don’t fall’) is better regarded as a continuation of the Ribeira do Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) than as a tributary of it.
On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), the streams worth mentioning are the Ribeira da Vila, the brooks of Salgado and Cochino, and the Ribeira da Serra de Dentro and Ribeira da Serra de Fora.
Ribeira do Porto Novo
It rises in the Serra do Poiso (‘resting place’) and on Pico da Silva, and its tributaries are the Ribeira dos Boieiros and the brooks of Pedro Lourenço and Hortas.
Ribeira do Seixal
It rises on Pico do Assobiadouro (‘whistling place’) and receives the waters of the brooks of Voltas and Quebradas.
Ribeira do Tristão
It has the same source as the preceding stream, and its tributaries are the Calvário (‘Calvary’) brook and the rivulets of Agriões and Lages.
Ribeira do Vigário

It rises at the Achada do Poiso (‘resting-place plateau’) and the nearby peaks, and the brooks of Jardim do Cabral and Frades flow into it. It is also called the Ribeira de Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’).
Ribeira dos Marinheiros
It rises on Pico da Fonte do Bispo (‘bishop’s spring’) and carries little water.
Ribeira dos Moinhos
It rises on Pico da Fonte do Barro and, like the four preceding streams, carries little water.
Ribeira dos Moinhos
It rises in the Serra da Boaventura (‘uplands of Boaventura’) and is shorter than the Ribeira do Porco.
Ribeira dos Socorridos
It rises at the Torrinhas (‘little towers’), and its principal tributaries are the Ribeira de Vasco Gil and the brooks of Cidrão, Gato and Lapa.
Ribeira Funda
It rises on Pico da Silva and Pico da Relva, and its tributary is the Mendes brook. It carries little water.
Ribeira Seca
It rises in the uplands above Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) and receives the waters of the brooks of Cedros and Meloeira.
Ribeira de São Vicente
It rises on Pico dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’) and Pico da Cumeada (‘ridge’) and receives the waters of the Ribeira Grande (‘big’), the Atalho brook, etc.
Ribeirinho (alley)

This alley links the Travessa do Rêgo with the Travessa da Conveniência, near the Avenida de João de Deus. It was once longer than it is today: at a council meeting on 12 June 1902 the owner of the *quinta* (country estate) das Rosas was permitted to close it off next to the Travessa da Conveniência, on condition, however, that he give the *levadeiro* (levada keeper who maintains the channel and distributes the water) of the Levada das Hortas, for the upkeep of the levada (irrigation channel), a key to the door that closes the entrance to the alley on the side of the said avenue.
Ribeirinho (street)

It ran from the eastern part of the Avenida Elias Garcia to the Rua do Carmo (‘Carmel’), or Rua do Dr. Costa Ferreira. Today it is called Rua do Alferes Veiga Pestana, and before it received this name it was called Rua das Hortas (see that entry).

The small brook that gave the street its name is the Ribeiro do Vale, which comes down from Pena (‘crag’) and passes along the Avenida de João de Deus and the Rua do Carmo. In the latter street, next to the Travessa do Rego, there was a bridge that formed a large hump in the ground; it was lowered in 1906.
Ribeiro

The people of this surname, says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, descend from Manuel Afonso Sanha and his wife Leonor Ribeiro, who died in 1536. There was also a Pedro Ribeiro, who married Mécia Carvalhal; both lived around 1500, and their descendants took the surname Carvalhais.
Ribeiro (Councillor José Silvestre)

Over a span of more than a century, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro was the most illustrious civil governor of this district, and the one to whom this land owes the greatest sum of outstanding services and acts of the highest and purest benevolence. This is an almost axiomatic truth, which needs no demonstration.

He was born in Idanha-a-Nova on 31 December 1807. Having completed his degree in law, he enlisted in the liberating army, and, once the war was over, he became in turn secretary-general, civil governor, deputy, peer of the realm, minister and councillor of state, and carried out many important public service commissions. He was a man of rare intellectual culture and one of the most prolific and erudite writers of his time, leaving a vast literary output.

António José de Ávila, later Duke of Ávila e Bolama, arrived in Madeira on 12 September 1846 as royal commissioner, accompanied by José Silvestre Ribeiro, in order to investigate the events that had taken place on this island because of the Calvinist proselytism of Dr Roberto Kalley. Silvestre Ribeiro came as the appointed civil governor of the district, but his appointment only became known after António José de Ávila had dismissed the governor and the municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of Funchal and taken other administrative measures that were judged indispensable.

We cannot list, even in summary, the services by which José Silvestre Ribeiro marked his time among us. Yet it is impossible not to mention, however briefly, the founding of the Asylum; the swift and salutary measures taken to overcome the terrible famine crisis of 1847; the creation of the Agricultural Society; the building of the Ponte Monumental (‘monumental bridge’); the introduction of public lighting; the exhibition of Madeiran industries; the organisation of a natural history museum; and the creation of many primary schools. Nor can we pass over his very important measures for the replanting and preservation of woodland; the major repairs to the roads and to almost all the buildings of the State, including most of the churches; and the effective and strict measures he adopted concerning the management of charitable institutions, municipal taxes, cemeteries, foundlings, council revenues, etc. We must also mention the way he defended the interests of Madeira in parliament, the great expansion of public works, the remarkable impetus given to the cutting of levadas (irrigation channel), especially that of Rabaçal, and the building of shelters in the mountains and on the ridges. There was no public need he did not seek to meet, nor any area of administration that his effective initiative and tireless energy did not reach. We would go far, very far, if we wished to descend into details and particulars, which do not fit within the narrow limits of this article, which cannot be long.
Silvestre Ribeiro represented Madeira in parliament in the legislative sessions of 1848 to 1851, 1853 to 1856 and 1857 to 1858.

The Madeirans, grateful for the most outstanding and never sufficiently praised services that José Silvestre Ribeiro had rendered to this archipelago, resolved to present him with an object that would not let him entirely forget the gratitude of its inhabitants and would at the same time remind him of his stay among us. This object, acquired by public subscription, was a rich gold collar, made up chiefly of seventeen small shields, each of which represented one of the most notable acts of his administration. From it hung a medal which, besides the dedication, bore the Latin legend taken from the verses of Virgil: *Semper honos, nomenque tuum, laudesque manebunt* (Your honour, your name and your praises shall endure for ever). The designs and moulds for this exquisite work were by the distinguished Madeiran artist Vicente Gomes da Silva, who died a few years ago (1921). On the occasion of the solemn presentation of this meaningful gift, the merchants of the British colony presented Silvestre Ribeiro with a silver salver, specially made in London, engraved with a dedication in English.

As is well known, José Silvestre Ribeiro was civil governor of the district of Angra do Heroísmo, and during his administration a violent earthquake reduced the town (*vila*) of Praia da Vitória to a heap of rubble. What Silvestre Ribeiro then achieved, raising a new settlement from the ruins in a short time, is eloquently attested by the monument that stands today in the centre of the town, an undying commemorative pillar (padrão) of his glory.

The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Angra presented Silvestre Ribeiro with a rich small sword with a gold hilt, a true artistic treasure. The benefactor governor bequeathed this sword to the Municipal Council of Funchal, where it remains, and the collar given by the Madeirans to the Municipal Council of Angra do Heroísmo, where it too is carefully kept.

On 31 December 1907 the island of Terceira marked the centenary of Silvestre Ribeiro’s birth with solemn and meaningful displays of esteem and gratitude towards his cherished and illustrious memory, among which several literary publications stood out. In articles in the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’), the present author put forward the idea of associating Madeira with those celebrations, but no one, from the civil governor down to the most remote Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), answered the call…

The name of José Silvestre Ribeiro is still well remembered here and is regarded, beyond any possible dispute, as that of the most illustrious and beneficent governor the Madeira archipelago has ever had. In Funchal, the blessed memory of José Silvestre Ribeiro has been perpetuated only by giving his name to one of the city’s thoroughfares, better known by the shortened form Rua do Conselheiro (‘Councillor’s street’); even the general public does not know that it represents a tribute to this governor. One thing could still be done, and the press has already suggested it: to give the Asilo da Mendicidade (poorhouse) the name of its founder. Anyone wishing to gain a fuller knowledge of his administration in this district should read *Uma Época Administrativa na Madeira e Porto Santo*, 3 thick volumes; *Colecção de Documentos relativos à crise da fome por que passaram as ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo no ano de 1847*; *Colecção de Documentos relativos ao Asilo da Mendicidade do Funchal*; *Colecção de Documentos relativos á construção da Ponte do Ribeiro Seco*; and *Brevíssima resenha de alguns serviços que no distrito do Funchal tem prestado o conselheiro José Silvestre Ribeiro*.

A most painful detail, but one worth recording: while in this land José Silvestre Ribeiro went through one of the most anguished ordeals of his life, losing his only son, who met a tragic death in the tank (irrigation reservoir) in the garden of the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’).
Silvestre Ribeiro left Madeira on 27 November 1852 and died in Lisbon on 9 March 1891.
Ribeiro de Mendonça (Marceliano)

Although he held no higher or university degree and never left the narrow circle in which he always lived, Marceliano Ribeiro de Mendonça achieved a true intellectual supremacy here in Madeira, which no one ever thought of disputing. He owed it to the brilliance of his outstanding talent, his vast learning and his most ardent love of study.
He was born in this city on 18 April 1805, the son of Jerónimo Ribeiro dos Santos and Dona Juliana Rita de Mendonça.

He had completed his secondary schooling – the *Aulas do Pátio* ('Courtyard Classes', the public secondary classes held in the former Jesuit college), as they were then called – when Miguel I proclaimed himself absolute king and sent to Madeira the notorious and ominous judicial inquiry (*devassa*). Its net caught so many Madeirans, forcing many of them into exile or into hiding from justice. Marceliano Ribeiro sought safe refuge in the house of a British subject and remained there as a fugitive for six long years, until constitutional government was established in this archipelago in June 1834.

In that sad and enforced retreat, which the subject of our biography put to such good use, he acquired the persevering habit of study that he kept until his death. It was above all there that he enriched his brilliant intellect with the remarkable learning he came to possess. His literary and scientific inclinations led him to the study of the Portuguese and Latin languages, of which he was a consummate master, and to philosophical studies, in which he revealed a superior mind. Ample proof of this lies in the elements of Latin grammar that he published in 1835 and the elements of philosophy that he wrote for the use of his pupils.

Marceliano Ribeiro made his name above all as a teacher, and as such he acquired a great reputation throughout the country. Besides his engaging manners and extremely affable disposition, which quickly won his pupils’ affection, he had the rare gift of knowing how to teach. His exposition was easy and clear, and it drew great brilliance and force from the tone of conviction in which he spoke and the enthusiasm he conveyed in his words. He was a speaker beyond compare with a profound knowledge of the subjects he lectured on, and his students never tired of hearing him, enraptured by the beauty of his expression and the loftiness of his ideas. He taught at the classes of the old Pátio, and when the Funchal Lyceum (*Liceu do Funchal*) was founded in 1836 he joined the teaching staff of the new establishment, teaching the Portuguese and Latin languages and later holding the chair of philosophy.

Appointed rector of the Lyceum (*Liceu*) and schools commissioner (*comissário dos estudos*), he distinguished himself remarkably in these posts, above all through the impetus he gave to the spread of primary education, the new teaching methods he introduced and the scrupulous care with which he selected teachers. His reports in this field are truly exemplary, and some were published in the scientific review *O Instituto*. To encourage primary teachers in the exercise of their calling, he founded an ‘Associação de Conferencias’ (Lecture Association), in which the subjects most closely concerning popular education were discussed. Given the great zeal and dedication he showed in extending primary education, it may without doubt be said that he was the first person in this archipelago to take a genuine interest in popular education, and this fact alone is enough to make his memory blessed among us.

Marceliano Ribeiro was an eloquent orator of polished language. Among his speeches, the academic orations delivered at the solemn opening of the Lyceum and the public lectures he gave on ‘the beautiful’ stand out.

Here in Madeira he held the posts of president of the Council of Funchal, secretary-general of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*), rector and teacher of the Lyceum, schools commissioner and member of the district council, besides other public-service commissions.

He contributed extensively and valuably to many Madeiran periodicals and left several works in manuscript. He published *Princípios de gramática geral aplicados á língua latina*, *Filosofia em Coimbra e no Funchal*, *Método paralelo de leitura e escrita* and the historical novel *Gaspar Borges*, as well as his important reports. He died in Funchal on 5 August 1866, at the age of 61.
Ribeiro (Emanuel Vitorino)

He is a native of Porto and the son of the well-known painter Joaquim Vitorino. He lived among us for some years as a teacher at the ‘António Augusto de Aguiar’ Industrial School, and at present he is a teacher and director of an industrial school in Porto (1921). He was in Madeira at the time of the celebrations of the fifth centenary of the discovery, rendering the most outstanding services, as we have already noted in the article Quincentenary of the Discovery.

In collaboration with Feliciano Soares he published in 1915 a pamphlet entitled *Terra! Terra!*, on the discovery of Madeira, written in prose (F. Soares) and verse (E. Ribeiro). Emanuel Ribeiro contributed extensively to several newspapers of this city, and he was preparing a historical and artistic monograph on our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), which he never published.
Ribeiro Frio

A locality (*sítio*) in the interior of the island, 15 kilometres from Funchal, much visited by Portuguese and foreigners alike for the enchanting landscapes it offers. It was once far more wooded than it is today, but the land nearby still has some woods, made up chiefly of laurels and heather. *Ranunculus grandifolius*, *Geranium anemonefolium*, *Carex peregrina*, *Carex elata* and *Orchis foliosa* are found at Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’), and salep can be extracted from the tubers of the last of these plants.

Following the Levada do Juncal (‘rush-bed channel’), one soon reaches a belvedere (*mirante*) with astonishing views over the Ribeira da Metade (‘halfway stream’). Further on there are some tunnels, though they are difficult to reach, because the levada wall (*mainel*) of the levada (irrigation channel) is narrow and at times unstable. The extremely rare *Goodyera macrophylla* and *Musschia Wollastoni* are found near the tunnel that follows the Quebrada da Azeda (‘sorrel slope’).

To the east of Ribeiro Frio there are also beautiful landscapes to admire, and if we head in that direction, always walking along the levada, we shall reach Lamaceiros (‘mud flats’), from where it is easy to cross to Santo António da Serra.

The locality of Ribeiro Frio is crossed by the Levada da Serra (‘upland channel’), and on the edge of the footpath that runs beside it, at the place called Balcão or Balcões (‘balconies’), there is an astonishing panorama over the Ribeira da Metade and other parts of the interior, with the basalt column of Homem-Em-Pé (see that entry) visible in the distance. There is a mountain shelter there for travellers, which is also used by the levada’s staff. Since April 1932 the locality has had a small establishment called the Casa de Chá, offering a good service of tea, food and drink. The locality of Ribeiro Frio lies about 4 kilometres from the Poiso house (*Casa do Poiso*) and 15 from the city of Funchal. The brook that crosses this locality, and from which the locality took its name, provides the source that feeds the Levada do Furado (‘pierced’).
Ribeiro (Manuel)

He was born in Lisbon on 31 August 1861 but has lived in Funchal since childhood. He has contributed to various newspapers and is a poet of merit, the author of the following slim volumes: *Flores Agrestes*, Funchal, 1903, 67 pp.; *Pyrilampos*, Funchal, 1905, 56 pp.; *Outomnaes*, Funchal, 1910, 55 pp.; and *Poentes*, Funchal, 1913, 96 pp.
The poet’s real name is Mardónio da Câmara; Manuel Ribeiro is merely a pseudonym, but one that he adopted for all his literary works.
Ribeiro Neto (Manuel)

In the *Dicionário Popular*, edited by Pinheiro Chagas, we find the following about this man: ‘Portuguese jurist, a native of Funchal, who came to Portugal to take his degree at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and, on returning to Madeira, was promoted to a canonry in the Cathedral of Angra. He wrote and printed a Latin volume of *Commentarios de Direito Civil* and various pleadings on canon law. He died in 1681, having been born at the beginning of the 17th century or the end of the 16th.’

Diogo Barbosa Machado, however, gives Ribeiro Neto as born in Angra, which we consider more probable, although we cannot state it beyond all doubt. Among the works on canon law that he published are the following, cited in the *Biblioteca Lusitana*: *Alegações de direito sobre as meias conezias do Funchal*, *Officios que tachou o cabido* and *Explicaçam do privilegio de hum altar no Funchal*, all of which appeared in one volume in 1660.
Ribeiro Real (Count of)

João Bettencourt Araújo Carvalhal Esmeraldo, 1st Viscount and 1st Count of Ribeiro Real, was born in Funchal on 21 December 1841, the son of Francisco António de Bettencourt Araújo de Carvalhal Esmeraldo and Dona Júlia Henriqueta de Freitas Esmeraldo, holders of entailed estates. He held various public offices, among them those of president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this city and of civil governor in 1879, taking up the latter post on 15 March of that year. He was granted the title of viscount by decree of 23 March 1882.

As president of the Municipal Council, he was responsible for the demolition of the old alleys between Rua dos Aranhas and the old British cemetery, and for the construction of Rua 5 de Junho. He died on 22 March 1902.
Ribeiro Seco (bridge)

When he was prefect (*prefeito*) of Madeira, the illustrious Mouzinho de Albuquerque conceived the plan of building a suspension bridge over the Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’). To this end he began the construction of two gigantic piers, besides two very strong abutments, one on each bank of the brook. ‘The plan of the work, says Sérvulo de Meneses in the *Colecção de documentos relativos á construção da ponte do Ribeiro Seco*, included the idea of raising a monument to the memory of the immortal Jaime, Duke of Braganza, the magnanimous liberator of the Portuguese, and accordingly the work was to be magnificent and grand.’

When Mouzinho left for Lisbon, work on the bridge stopped. The Baron of Lordelo later tried to resume it, but without success, after deciding that the bridge would be of stone rather than a suspension bridge. It was in this governor’s time that work began on the road linking Funchal with Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’).

At the end of 1846, when Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro had come to govern Madeira, he resolved to draw the engineers’ attention to the means of carrying out the work planned by Mousinho de Albuquerque. However, work could begin only in 1848, after the governor had obtained a vow of donations sufficient to cover a quarter of the estimated cost of the works.

The award by public auction (*arrematação*) of the bridge works took place on 27 February 1848, and work began on 6 March following; shortly before, the Governor had opened a subscription to meet the cost of the bridge. The works were awarded for the sum of 5,799,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The successful bidders were the master builder José Pereira and his partners Antonio Joaquim Marques Basto, João António Bianchi and Francisco Luis Pereira.

Through donations, the Governor managed to raise the entire price of the award. The works, however, cost 8,227,302 *réis*, so the contractors suffered a loss of 2,428,302 *réis*. According to their own statement, this loss would not have arisen had they not been so determined ‘to present a well-finished and lasting work, generously meeting every instruction of the directing engineer’.

The work on the bridge was carried out under the direction of the captain of engineers Tiberio Augusto Blanc and was finished in February 1849. In his official letter of 5 December of the same year, this officer informed the civil governor that the grand work had been completed with every solidity and perfection. The contracting partnership, he reported, had in many respects exceeded the obligations it had undertaken, moved solely by the wish that the work should fully satisfy public expectation and not belie the good name of the partners; this was the main cause of the heavy loss they suffered.

Among those who contributed gifts towards the construction of the Ribeiro Seco bridge was Queen Adelaide of England, who gave 480,000 *réis*. The civil governor thanked all the subscribers through the press for the generous help they had given him in carrying out the grand work he had undertaken.

Many people have taken their own lives at the Ribeiro Seco, exploiting the great height of the middle section of the bridge. Of all the deaths that have occurred there, however, the one that perhaps caused the greatest sensation in Funchal was that of a man from a good family who, around 1860, threw himself to the bottom of the brook because the declarations of love he had dared to address to the wife of a civil governor had been rejected. A letter that went unanswered, followed by a ban on returning to the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), where he had previously always been well received, drove the unhappy lover to end his life in the manner described. This tragic event was followed by the burlesque act of the suicide’s son, who proposed, or wished to propose, a duel with the governor, whom he held responsible for his father’s death.
See Estrada e Ponte Monumental.
Ribeiro Seco (square)

The square lies beside the Ponte Monumental (Monumental Bridge), on the left bank of the Ribeiro Seco brook, and was built shortly after 1850. Today it is called Largo de António Nobre (‘António Nobre square’).
See Nobre (António).
Richter (Johannes)
Doctor of philosophy of the University of Leipzig. Works: *Die Klimatishen Grundlagen der landwirtschaftlichen Bodenkultur auf Madeira*; Leipzig, 1909.
Risco

This is one of the spots at Rabaçal most worth visiting, for the majestic panoramas it offers. It takes its name from the risk (*risco*) run by the workmen who built the channel on the high, sheer cliff down which the waters fall. The Poço do Risco, a pool at the bottom of the ravine some 80 metres below the levada (irrigation channel), is also worth a visit, although it cannot be reached without some effort. The waters of the Risco come from a pond (*lagoa*), or excavation, on the edge of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’).
See Levadas, Paul da Serra and Rabaçal.
Risota (A)
Twelve issues appeared, from 6 August 1906 to 21 October of the same year.
Robaldo (Pomatomus telescopium)
A percoid fish that lives over rocky bottoms at depths of between 300 and 400 *braças*. Its flesh is of good quality.
Roberto Ivens (street)

This street lies north of the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’) and links Rua do Conselheiro with Rua de São Francisco. It was given the name by which it is known at the council meeting of 17 September 1885.
See Capelo and Ivens.
Roberts (Lieutenant-Colonel)
In 1802 he published the *Plan of the Island of Porto Santo*.
Roberts (Lord)

This distinguished English general, who finally secured England’s dominion over the Transvaal, received a brilliant welcome when he passed through this island on 26 December 1900, on his way home from South Africa.
Robins
English botanist who planted trees in Madeira in the year 1774.
Roca de Vénus (Hedychium gardnerianum)
A member of the ginger family (Zingiberaceae) grown in Madeiran gardens. It is native to India and has large yellow flowers arranged in a very elegant thyrse.
Rocaz (Sebastes madeirensis)

A fish of the family Triglidae that lives in the shallow waters of the Madeiran coast. It is small, and its head is armed with spines whose sting can cause inflammation. It can be found close to the shore but is not exploited, although its flesh has a pleasant flavour.
Rocha

This family surname, says the learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), begins with João Enes Rocha, squire, *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) and *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper) in Funchal in 1568.
Rocha da Meia Légua
A short distance east of the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’) there is a cliff overhanging the sea, known as Rocha de Meia Légua (‘half a league’).
Rocha de Gouveia (Gabriel)

He was born at Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) on 30 September 1887, the son of Manuel Rocha de Gouveia and Dona Maria Augusta Soares Rocha de Gouveia. He was studying agronomy in Lisbon when he was called up to the army after Germany declared war on Portugal. Commissioned as a second lieutenant, he left for France, where he met his death on 13 October 1917 while on duty in the trenches. It is said that he was chatting carelessly with other officers when he was struck by several shell splinters, which killed him instantly.
Rocha do Navio (islet)
Near the locality (*sítio*) of Rocha do Navio (‘ship cliff’), on the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’), lies the islet of that name, where a Dutch ship was wrecked in 1860.
Rocha Furada
This is a wide opening in the rocks of Ponta do Furado (‘pierced point’), at Ponta de São Lourenço. Seen from a distance, it resembles a great doorway cut into the coastal land.
Rocha (Joaquim Leonardo da)

We have already dealt with this painter in the article on the António Augusto de Aguiar Industrial School (volume I, page 398). It should be added here that he was born in Portugal in 1756 and died in Funchal some time after 1821, and that he was the son of the distinguished painter Manuel Joaquim da Rocha. He was above all a portraitist and left several canvases on this island.
Foundling wheel

On 14 January 1820 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) resolved to have a foundlings’ turn (*roda*, revolving hatch in the convent wall) installed in the house of the official wet-nurse (ama geral), since there was none in this city. Three years later it had another made at Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), in a house adjoining the chapel of Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit).

So great was the number of foundlings in the Council’s care at the beginning of the 19th century that on 20 May 1812 it resolved that the councillor-magistrate (juiz-vereador) should keep ‘a police register’ recording all the prostitutes who were pregnant, so that they would account for their children and raise them.
Road corvée

The Royal Treasury Board (*Junta da Real Fazenda*) asked the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) ‘to indicate the gentlest means of requiring the inhabitants of this island to contribute to the repair of the damage caused by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803’. At its meeting of 21 August 1804, having heard the nobility and the people, the latter represented by the House of the Twenty-Four (*Casa dos Vinte e Quatro*, assembly of the craft guilds), the Council resolved ‘that the fairest means, the least burdensome and the most in keeping with the proposed aim of having the island’s inhabitants contribute to the repair of the streams, was that all male inhabitants from the age of 16 to that of 60, without exception of any person, ecclesiastical or secular, native or foreign, *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility), noble or commoner, should be obliged to go in rotation to work at clearing and repairing the streams, not more than five times in each year, each without pay, in those of the district of the city or town (*vila*) where he lived and where such work was needed’.

Such was the origin of the road corvée (rodas de caminho), which fell into disuse in Funchal around 1880. It could be redeemed in cash according to ‘the price that each day-labourer earns daily’, as was laid down at the said council meeting of 21 August 1804 (1921).
Rodrigues

Those who bear this family surname descend from various lines: some from Mem Rodrigues de Vasconcelos, who married a daughter of Bartolomeu Perestrelo; others from Garcia Rodrigues da Câmara, father of Aldonça Delgado, wife of the 3rd donatary (*donatário*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), who murdered her; others from João Rodrigues, who lived in the 16th century and held a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) near Calheta (‘small cove’); and others, finally, from João Rodrigues Neto, who died in 1531, held a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in São Martinho and died in the street called Rua dos Netos, in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro.
Rodrigues (Adolfo de Sousa)

This distinguished painter, whom an early death and the persistent illness of his last years prevented from displaying the full strength of his talent, was born in Funchal on 13 January 1867 and died in the city of Lisbon on 9 March 1908.

He completed the course at the Academy of Fine Arts, where he always obtained high marks. He distinguished himself in history painting, in which he won first prize with the picture *Hero e Leandro*. He studied this speciality under José Ferreira Chaves and later went to Paris to perfect his skills under Paul Laurens and Benjamin Constant. In the 2nd year of the Academy course he had also won the ‘Anunciação’ prize. At the exhibition of the Grémio Artístico in Lisbon he won the third medal in 1895. He took part in various exhibitions, where his pictures shown included, among others, *Tentação de Cristo* and *Bom Samaritano*.

He painted the portrait of King Carlos I that hung in the meeting room of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), that of our illustrious fellow Madeiran Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, etc. etc. He held the academic palms of the Académie de France and the commandery of Isabella the Catholic, of Spain.
Rodrigues Ciebra (António)

Of this Madeiran we know only that he was a surgeon at the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal (*Santa Isabel*) in this city and that he wrote and published a pamphlet with the following title: *Narração cirúrgica de hum carbunculo maligno que com facilidade se curou na cara...*, Lisbon, 1760, 31 pp.
Rodrigues de Vilares (Dom Luís)
If this Funchal prelate was not born in Brazil, he at least spent part of his youth there, and it was there too that he received his literary education.
He was confirmed as Bishop of Madeira by Pope Pius VI on 29 July 1797 and took possession of his diocese at the beginning of 1798.
He was always zealous in the exercise of his episcopal duties and in the observance of church discipline.
