He waged bitter struggles with the governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara. These lasted a long time and eventually erupted into violent conflict, so that the central government had to intervene in the regrettable dispute that had arisen between the two highest authorities of the archipelago. The disagreements went back a long way. The prelate had opposed the quartering of English troops in the Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*), which Maria I had granted for use as the diocesan seminary, but he had to yield before force. When the troops withdrew to England, Dom Luís Vilares pressed for the building to be handed over. The governor refused, on the grounds that it was indispensable for quartering the garrison forces. Other causes arose that aggravated the disagreement still further. Claiming that he had been slighted by the prelate in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), Dom José Manuel da Câmara ordered him to leave the city immediately. This took place on 18 June 1803, when Dom Luís Vilares went to a property that the mitre owned in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’), where he remained for about four months.

The affair caused a great scandal, not only in Madeira but also in Portugal. The central government sent to this island the high court judge (*desembargador*) Dr Joaquim António de Araújo, charged with investigating the events. He came accompanied by the new governor, Ascenso de Sequeira Freire, and the two reached Funchal aboard the frigate *Carlota* on 5 December 1803.

On the 10th and 11th of the same month, each in his own warship, Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares and Dom José Manuel da Câmara respectively left for the capital, under the orders of the government of mainland Portugal, while the official inquiry proceeded actively in Funchal. It resulted in the immediate dismissal of the governor and captain-general, who was also censured for the arbitrary acts he had committed. For the prelate, it resulted in his continuing in the post he held in this diocese and in the restitution of the Jesuit College. He could not, however, escape a censure addressed to him by the government for the little prudence and judgement he had shown in many of his actions.

During his stay at Santo da Serra, Dom Luís de Vilares had trees planted on the glebe (*passal*) and had work continued on a public fountain that still exists there and is known as the Fonte do Bispo (‘bishop’s spring’).
He died in this city on 1 October 1810 and lies buried in the chancel of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*).
Rodrigues dos Santos (Dr António da Cruz)

He was born in this city on 14 September 1877. He completed the course at the Lisbon Medical School (*Escola Médica de Lisboa*) in 1902 and is a lieutenant-colonel in the medical corps of the Overseas medical staff. He was civil governor of this district, taking office on 14 October 1920 and holding it until 30 May of the following year. He was appointed to the same post again on 22 November 1921, but did not accept it. He is at present president of the Funchal Municipal Council (1921).
Rodrigues dos Santos (José Jorge)

He was born in Funchal on 23 April 1879 and is the brother of the preceding. He holds a higher degree in letters and followed a diplomatic career, having served in the Portuguese legations in Sweden, Denmark, etc. Works: *Caravella* (poems), and *Mar de Lagrimas*, *Festa de Actriz* and *Rosa enamorada* (plays) (1921).
Rodrigues (Dr António Feliciano)

His schoolfellows at the lyceum (state secondary school) called him Castilho, perhaps because his name resembled that of the great Castilho and also because he wrote verse. The nickname has endured, and Dr Feliciano Rodrigues himself sometimes adopts it as a pseudonym in his writings. He was born in this city on 9 June 1870. After graduating from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1897, he set up as a lawyer in Funchal, and in this judicial district (*comarca*) he has also served as acting deputy of the public prosecutor. He is secretary of the lyceum and an officer in the secretariat of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) (1921).

Besides contributing to various newspapers, in both prose and verse, he has published the short poems *A Escola*, Coimbra, 1893; *A Consciência*, Funchal 1897; *Versos da Mocidade*, Funchal, 1903, 127 pp.; *Versos para meus filhos*, Funchal, 1910, 118 pp.; *Collar de Vidrilhos*, Funchal, 1911, 54 pp.; *Canção das lágrimas*; and *Sonetos*, Lisbon, 1916. In prose he published the novels *O Cirurgião de Marinha* and *Martim de Freitas*, the latter appearing in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’). He has other works ready for the press (1921). He died in Funchal on 5 February 1925.
Rodrigues (Dr José Agostinho)

He was born in Funchal on 1 October 1864. He qualified as a physician and surgeon at the Lisbon Medical and Surgical School (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica de Lisboa*) and was appointed army medical lieutenant on 15 November 1894. He served for many years in the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.° 27*), and at present holds the rank of colonel, serving as deputy director in the Directorate-General of Medical Services (*Direcção Geral dos Serviços Médicos*) of the Ministry of War. He was in France with the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps (*C. E. P.*) and has contributed to various Madeiran newspapers. In 1890 he published the thesis he defended on completing his medical course, entitled *A opportunidade da laparotomia nas perfurações traumáticas gastro-intestinais* (1921).
Rodrigues (Dr José Júlio)

Although some biographers give Goa as his birthplace, it is certain that he was born in Funchal on 8 May 1843. He was the son of Dr José Júlio Rodrigues, a native of Goa, who was then deputy crown prosecutor in this judicial district (*comarca*), and of Dona Teresa Cristina de Sá Bettencourt, a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’) in this city of Funchal.

‘A man of study,’ says the *Encyclopedia Portugueza*, volume IX, ‘and one of the scientific luminaries of his time, he distinguished himself by extremely valuable works that earned him a well-deserved reputation and placed him in the front rank of the scholars of his generation. Having studied at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), where he graduated in mathematics, he was soon afterwards appointed teacher of the introductory course at the lyceum (state secondary school) of Lisbon. He was also professor of chemistry at the Polytechnic School (*Escola Politécnica*) and at the Industrial Institute of Lisbon, and president of the central market for agricultural produce, a commission from which he resigned when he withdrew to Brazil (1892).

He was one of the signatories and promoters, in Paris, of the 1875 agreement on international exchanges. He was the first in Portugal to carry out scientific photography of underground cavities (the lava tunnels of the island of Terceira), using magnesium light. On a scientific excursion to the Azores he also took nearly 500 snapshots, which form the most complete collection, from the technical photographic point of view, that exists of the islands of São Miguel and Terceira. He invented and improved a number of instruments for study and for technical and scientific work, and devised several new processes, for which he obtained patents in Portugal and abroad.

‘He was entrusted with organising the Portuguese forensic chemistry service for the courts, a task he did not carry out owing to subsequent political circumstances. As a deputy to the Cortes (Portuguese parliament), first for India and then for Funchal, in the legislature of 1890 to 1892, he dealt with notable proficiency with technical education and practical and general education, industries, public development, customs tariffs, the working classes, etc. Among the works he organised we shall mention: experimental teaching of the physical and natural sciences at the Lisbon lyceum (state secondary school); the photographic section of the Directorate-General of Geodetic Works, considered a model of perfection; the installation of the Portuguese section at the Paris exhibition of 1875 (geographical sciences); the chair of chemical technology at the Industrial and Commercial Institute of Lisbon; practical teaching of mineral chemistry at the Lisbon Polytechnic School; the mineral chemistry laboratory at the Lisbon Polytechnic School, considered one of the best of its kind; the laboratory of the central market for agricultural produce, etc.’

Dr José Júlio Rodrigues sought to establish or encourage various industries in Portugal. He went so far as to organise a company with a capital of 2,500 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos) to attempt the manufacture of beet sugar in the country, and to set up a depot of chemical products and a factory of printing inks. He also devoted the greatest attention to the quinine industry and its derivatives, for which reason he made a journey to São Tomé in 1885, and to the use of the sweet potato for the manufacture of alcohol and the extraction of starch.
Dr José Júlio Rodrigues was in Madeira a little before 1890, when he gave a brilliant lecture at the Teatro D. Maria Pia, attended by the elite of Funchal society.

He was a member of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences, of the Geographical Society of the same city, of the Coimbra Institute, of the French Photographic Society, of the Society of Men of Letters of France, of the Franco-Spanish Society of the same country, etc., and he held the commandery of the Order of St James and the cross of the Legion of Honour. He died in Lisbon on 29 April 1893.

Among other publications by José Júlio Rodrigues, we shall mention the following: *Estudos sobre as bases fundamentais dos novos pesos atómicos e suas relações physicas mais notáveis*; *Curso elementar de sciencias physicas e naturais* (with António Augusto de Aguiar); *Breve noticia sobre a composição chimica das águas mineraes de Pedras Salgadas*; *Breve noticia acerca d'uma nascente mineral em Traz-os-Montes*; *Coisas Portuguesas* (lectures); and *O assucar portuguez de beterraba*.
Rodrigues (Manuel)

This fellow Madeiran of ours led a rather eventful life, as we see from some of the works that deal with him. He was born in Funchal on 25 November 1697 and died in Lisbon in the second half of the 18th century, in a year we cannot determine. He was the son of Francisco Maria dos Ramos and Dona Josefa Maria Pereira. At the age of 15 he sailed for Rio de Janeiro to join his uncle, Captain Manuel Neto Barreto. He enrolled at the seminary of Cachoeira, where he proved a very talented student. In 1715 he enlisted in the regiment of the *mestre de campo* (colonel commanding a *terço*) Manuel de Almeida Castelo and went to Colónia do Sacramento. Shortly afterwards he left the army and entered the Order of St Francis, taking his vows in 1719, having studied philosophy and theology at the convent of Córdoba, in the interior of Argentina. He accompanied Friar José de Cardena on a journey to the province of Santa Fe and travelled through other countries. On learning of his father’s death and of the helpless state in which his three sisters had been left, he set off for Lisbon without delay in order to support them. As the author of the article in the *Missionário Popular* says, Manuel Rodrigues must have led a life ‘adventurous and probably stormy, for it was certainly no mere chance that made him successively a seminarian in Rio de Janeiro, a corporal at Colónia do Sacramento, a Franciscan in Buenos Aires, a student of philosophy in Córdoba and a preacher in Lisbon!’

In the capital he devoted himself to the ministry of preaching and won fame as one of the most acclaimed orators of his time. Diogo Barbosa Machado and Inocêncio Francisco da Silva list the many sermons and addresses he published between 1732 and 1757, among them the funeral oration he delivered on the death of John V.
Rodrigues (Rodrigo)

This distinguished Azorean, one of the promoters of the publication of Books III and IV of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and the author of the excellent biography of Gaspar Frutuoso that accompanies the first of those books, held the post of finance inspector in the district of Funchal, though he stayed only a very short time on this island.
The first payroll on which his name appears dates from October 1921, but no *termo* (formal record) conferring on him possession of that post was ever drawn up at the tax office.
Turtle dove (*Turtur turtur*)
A bird of passage that appears in the islands of the archipelago at various times of year, but is uncommon. It belongs to the family Columbidae.
Rolim
See Moura.
Kentish plover (*Charadrius alexandrinus*)

A small bird of the family Charadriidae that nests on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Its clutch consists of three yellowish or olive-coloured eggs, with blotches or streaks of another colour.
Ballad Collection of the Madeira Archipelago

In a volume of XXIV + 514 pages, published in this city in 1880, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo gathered a very large number of poetic compositions. He classified them systematically under the genres Stories, Tales and Games. The first comprised the kinds Sacred ballads (29 compositions), Secular ballads (22 compositions), *Xácaras* (19 compositions) and Cases (25 compositions); the second, the kinds Fairy tales (3 compositions), Allegorical tales (7 compositions), Children’s tales (3 compositions), *Lengas-lengas* (5 compositions) and Children’s *perlengas* (9 compositions); and the third, the kinds Children’s games (6 compositions) and Adult games (4 compositions).

For readers less versed in these matters, it may perhaps not be superfluous to say that, although these compositions were collected from local tradition and among the common people of the various parishes of this island, the great majority of them did not originate in this region. They were brought by the first settlers and by those who came here in succession to engage in trade and agriculture.

The illustrious collector of these poetic compositions does not state this categorically, nor does he refer in any detail to the influence that the environmental conditions of the time would have exerted on them. Yet it is impossible to accept that the origins of this popular poetry could lie in our own milieu. It is certain, however, that various causes would no doubt have modified the original works and also created new ones of a markedly local character and with features of their own, which today it would be impossible to determine even with approximate accuracy.

On the causes that contributed to the preservation of these compositions in local tradition, we shall transcribe some passages from the book’s interesting and valuable preface, which deserve to be placed on record here.
‘The historical and geographical conditions of this archipelago of Madeira explain how medieval narrative poetry came to it and has survived in it to this day.

‘Feudalism was succeeded by monarchism; the adventurous life of kings and noble lords at war gave way to the leisurely residence of both at court and in royal palaces; the rough customs and brutal sensuality of the Middle Ages gave way to the affected blandishments of urbane courtly libertinism. In the same way, in the sphere of literature, the narrative poetry of the ballads of those iron times was succeeded by the discursive poetry of Provençal-style songs – witty, erotic or critical – of palace cultism. The former, supplanted by the latter and modified in its language by the progress of the modern tongues, took refuge from the Castilian heights in the lower strata of the population; and there it has dwelt to this day as traditional poetry, more or less altered, more or less corrupted.

‘Now, this was the period when the islands of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and Madeira were discovered, in the first quarter of the 15th century. From then until past the middle of the 16th century, many settlers flocked here – nobles, merchants and commoners, Portuguese in the greater number, but not a few foreigners too: Spaniards, Italians, Flemings, Englishmen, Frenchmen and Germans – who, together with the still medieval ideas and customs of each country, brought their ancient poetry to these islands. Many Moors, captured on the opposite Moroccan coast and brought here, spread their tales and rigmaroles here. Finally, Philippine rule, besides the garrison of some four hundred Castilian soldiers it placed in this Archipelago, gave occasion for new peninsular inhabitants to emigrate here, and both groups inevitably brought with them some of those old ballads that so abound in their homeland. – This was the period of Madeiran progress and prosperity. The island of Madeira then became extremely rich through the sugar industry and its building timber; these two branches of trade and its geographical position raised it to an emporium of national and foreign shipping. And because it was the first and chief of the Portuguese colonies, it was made the diocesan metropolis of all our newly discovered overseas territories, from Brazil to Asia. All this contributed powerfully to attracting new settlers to this island and, with them, new examples of the narrative poetry of the Middle Ages. – From all these elements, the nucleus of the Madeiran population, one may deduce the provenance, variety and richness of the traditional narrative poetry of this archipelago.

‘Acquired in this way, that poetry took deep root in these islands. For, as we showed in another work (*Notas às Saudades da Terra*), medieval life and customs were implanted here; and when they were already declining on the mainland, they still flourished here, and became so thoroughly acclimatised that even now, despite so many innovations, they largely endure, especially in agriculture. – In these islands there persist, in name and in fact, the landlord, owner of the land, and the villein, who works it under a half-share tenancy (*colonato a meias*, sharecropping with half the produce to the landlord) by his own labour and that of his family, as a resident tenant (*caseiro*) or as a sharecropper (*meeiro*, without a house on the land) – that is, with or without residence – in the manner of the medieval tenant farmer (*colono*, under the *colonia* contract), bound or free, on the seigneurial land he cultivates. – And in such surroundings the narrative poetry of the Middle Ages, rejected by European palace cultism, settled in this Archipelago, living and dominant, like the almost suzerain power of its captains-donatary and the seigneurial rights of the local nobility, which, secured by the barrier of the sea and the delays of navigation, scoffed at royal power and municipal charters.

‘Once medieval narrative poetry had taken root in this way, causes no less particular kept it alive until now in the oral tradition of these islands. The island of Porto Santo, from the time it was discovered and settled, remained almost forgotten in its smallness and its poorer productive conditions; and its poetic tradition, scant but genuine, has lain there for almost four centuries, like its neglected population, geographically and socially isolated in the vastness of the Atlantic. The island of Madeira, supplanted in the sugar and timber industries by America and Africa, declined suddenly from the end of the 16th century. As a result of this, and of other causes, it lost its pre-eminence as a nautical emporium and its metropolitan crozier, and for almost two centuries it remained as if abandoned to misfortune in the solitude of the waters, until its precious wines restored it to wealth and to European society. Each of its larger or smaller centres of population, separated from one another by the deep basalt clefts of the land, converged on the parish community, within sight of each bell tower; there, in turn, each family of settlers or farmers, bound by the need for daily labour on the lord’s land that it made fruitful, toils and vegetates around the hearth, which is both its refuge and its prison. And the population, thus doubly isolated from outside contact by the sea and by adversity, and ever more inwardly concentrated by the ruggedness of the country and the servile condition of the farmer, has for that very reason preserved the medieval narrative poetry entrusted to its tradition: prosperity brought it, decline preserved it. In this lies the history of the Madeiran poetic tradition up to the middle of the 18th century. ‘And it was time to collect this tradition and preserve it in a book; for modern institutions and reforms, the new schools and better means of internal and external communication will produce their natural effects; and after another half-century, the new life to which civilisation calls these peoples will have diluted, if not entirely extinguished, the old traditional poetry in their memory.’ In a letter from Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo to the illustrious writer Teófilo Braga, in March 1880 (*Quarenta anos de vida literária*, page 118), the learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says: ‘Besides the *Romanceiro*, I have collected the *Cancioneiro Popular* of this archipelago in two volumes, still in draft. I consider it of no less value than the former. And, being unable to meet my friend’s request with any example of the ballad genre, which I do not have, because I included all of them in the *Romanceiro*, I offer you the whole *Cancioneiro*, for which purpose I shall set about putting it in order in good time.’ In a note to this letter, Dr Teófilo Braga reports that, unfortunately, this promise was never fulfilled. It is greatly to be regretted that the songbook collected by Dr Álvaro de Azevedo should have gone astray, if indeed it was ever sent to Dr Teófilo Braga. Or might it still be in the possession of his heirs? If so, it would be desirable to obtain a faithful copy of it and to entrust a competent person with overseeing its publication. We do not know what kinds of poetic composition make up the *Cancioneiro* referred to above. Notwithstanding the recognised authority of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo shown in his books of literary criticism, we wish to draw the attention of those who may be interested to an interesting article on the *Romanceiro* of Madeira written by that consummate master of these subjects, the notable philologist Dr Leite de Vasconcelos, published on pages 184–192 of volume XXXIII of the *Revista Lusitana*, which deserves to be read and considered. He disagrees with some of Dr Azevedo’s assertions, setting out the arguments he judged most compelling to prove his case, while paying the illustrious commentator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ the tribute of his highest esteem. The length of that article does not allow us to reproduce it in these pages.
Pilgrimage festivals

The country people of Madeira, generally cheerful and outgoing by nature, find in the pilgrimage festivals (*romarias*) one of their chief pastimes. Given over almost all year to work that demands a great expenditure of strength and energy, they seek in these amusements a way to forget the hardships of life and a few hours of delight for their spirit, which is untutored but generous and good.

At the time of the great feast-day gatherings (*arraiais*), numerous groups of men and women leave their homes for the places where these are held, sometimes covering great distances as they sing and dance to the sound of the *machetes* and *violas*, without showing any sign of fatigue from this rather strenuous exercise. Nor is it only the young men and women who give themselves over to such amusements: the old sometimes join in too, leaning on their staffs and improvising verses with which they beguile the weariness of the road and bring cheer to their fellow pilgrims.

It is said in Madeira ‘that the eves are better than the feasts’, and indeed it is on the day before any religious festival that the greatest joy and enthusiasm reign in the place where it is held. It is above all at night, when both the churchyard (*adro*) and the façade of the church are lit with coloured glasses and Venetian lanterns, that men and women give themselves up most fully to merrymaking, and that the character of popular amusements in Madeira can best be appreciated.

Although no feast-day gathering is held today without one or more brass bands, it is not the pieces they play that most hold the attention of the great majority of our country folk. Open-air songs, often sung as improvised contests, arouse far greater interest among country people. That is why the crowds are always densest and largest wherever there are young men ready to enjoy themselves and entertain others with their verses of intensely local flavour.

There are many similarities between the dances of our people and those of the black people of Africa, just as there are, and very remarkable ones, between certain songs peculiar to our countryside and Arab songs (see Music). The leaps and turns that characterise the island’s dances, often accompanied by shrieks, recall the African *batuques*, perhaps the chief pastime of black people on feast days when slavery existed here. The old Madeiran songs, for their part, reflect the monotony of the Arab chants so often heard with pleasure by the people in the times of colonisation.

Fireworks are a draw for the great majority of Madeiran feasts, and at times very large sums are spent on shells and rockets that might well be used to help the poor or for useful works in the parish (*freguesia*). Madeirans of the lowest social classes are generally thrilled by the deafening noise of certain exploding shells. That is why there is always a great abundance of these fireworks at every *arraial* (open-air popular festival at a church feast), and why the wildest follies are committed when it comes to setting them off. Nor is it only in the countryside that people are free to disturb those who do not enjoy the crack of bombs; in Funchal too the greatest abuses are committed in letting off rockets and shells, without the authorities seeking to bring those responsible into line.

After eleven o’clock or midnight, when the musicians are resting and most of the lights have gone out for lack of fuel, the site of the *arraiais* offers a spectacle at once curious and burlesque. Everywhere men and women can be seen lying about, overcome by weariness or drink. Those still on their feet remain so only to carry on long and tedious arguments with their companions, or to strike up one more song in a hoarse voice to earn yet another grog or glass of wine at the nearest tavern or stall.

Knife fights and serious disorders, so frequent at the *arraiais* of mainland Portugal, seldom occur in Madeira. Only now and then are there scuffles in which the combatants’ weapons are staves of heath or *folhado* (Clethra arborea, a native tree), and these are almost always caused by the copious libations in which the pilgrims indulge.

No family visits an *arraial* without a basket well stocked with food for the journey, and at the site of the feast there is always plenty of meat for the so-called *espetadas* that our country folk so enjoy. According to those who know, the skewer on which the meat for the *espetada* is threaded should be of laurel, and it is also advisable to feed the fire with branches of this tree so that the meat is tastier.

The leather bottle of wine or spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine) is the peasant’s inseparable companion at pilgrimages; the whole family drinks from it, as do any people he wishes to treat. A small gourd has become rare which, once dried and emptied of its seeds, was formerly much used by women and children to carry the drinks indispensable for the journey.

Among those who go on pilgrimage to places holding images to which the people are especially devoted, there are always some who take no part in the laughter and pagan merrymaking of their companions, and who show a religious feeling and a composure worthy of admiration. These are the pilgrims who have come to fulfil vows made in moments of anguish and who, faithful to their promises, bring their prayers to the altar together with the offerings owed to the image of their choice.

Free thought, always ridiculous and dangerous in educated men, has fortunately not yet reached the Madeiran countryside, and may it never do so, so that the people are not deprived of the consolations that religion offers in the sad events of life. Some of the religious customs of our people may contain a little superstition, but that is better than the absence of belief, which is the main cause of the anarchy and lack of morality recorded in many parts of the country.

It is at Monte, Ponta Delgada, Machico and Loreto that pilgrims fulfilling their vows appear in the greatest numbers. In the first of these parishes, says an author writing in 1880, ‘men are sometimes seen carrying heavy chains or iron bars, while women on bare knees drag themselves up over the sharp stones of the paved lane that leads to the steps climbing to the churchyard’.

Each of the pilgrimage festivals held in Madeira, says the Revd Father Eduardo C. Nunes Pereira, ‘is distinguished by a special attraction for pilgrims, drawn from its general religious motive, its topography or its particular secular character. At Ponta Delgada, Monte and Arco da Calheta it is the vows; at Machico and Santa Cruz the processions on the eve, with burning candles; at Caniço, rosaries of dried pears; at Ribeira Brava, the *império* of offerings and the fisherman’s little boat; at Caniçal, the procession of boats; at Camacha, São Vicente, Porto Moniz and Curral, the freedom of the countryside and the rustic character of the place’. Every parish has its religious festivities, those of the patron saint and of the Blessed Sacrament being especially splendid, but the ones that give rise to well-attended pilgrimage festivals are the following: Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*), on 15 August; the Lord Jesus (*Senhor Jesus*) of Ponta Delgada, on the first Sunday of September; Senhora do Loreto (Our Lady of Loreto), on 8 September; the Lord of Miracles (*Senhor dos Milagres*), at Machico, on 8 and 9 October; Piedade (Our Lady of Pity), at Caniçal, on the third Sunday of September; Nossa Senhora do Faial, on 8 September; Our Lady of Deliverance (*Nossa Senhora do Livramento*), at Caniço, on the second Sunday of September; Our Lady of Deliverance, at Curral, on the last Sunday of August; Our Lady of Remedies (*Nossa Senhora dos Remédios*), at Quinta Grande, on the second Sunday of September; that of Camacha, on the first octave day of Espírito Santo (the Holy Spirit, i.e. Pentecost); Santa Maria Madalena (St Mary Magdalene), at Porto Moniz, on 22 July; St Peter, at Ribeira Brava, on 29 June; St John, in Funchal, on 24 June; St Maurus, at Santa Cruz, on 15 January; and that of Santo António da Serra, on 13 June.

Some 40 to 50 years ago, a pilgrimage was made on the first Sunday of October to the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António da Serra to celebrate the end of the harvest, but this feast, which had an unusually savage character, has long since ceased to be held. While they stayed in that place, the pilgrims committed the wildest excesses, and on their return they paraded through the streets of the city carrying branches of trees and banners, preceded by a few men beating drums and playing stringed instruments (1921).

It would be interesting to know the origin of certain Madeiran popular feasts and the period in which they began to be held, but this is no easy matter, owing to the lack of material for any study one might wish to undertake on the subject. Tradition has preserved little or nothing, and the historian of the islands refers only to the pilgrimage festival of Nossa Senhora do Faial in the northern part of Madeira, saying that ‘on her day, which falls on 8 September, more than eight thousand souls gather on pilgrimage from all over the island, where a rich fair of provisions is to be seen, with much pork, beef and kid, which is an exceedingly tasty meat on that island, although in many lands and islands it is the worst of all’.

According to the same historian, the pilgrims often ‘stay two, three and more days at Nossa Senhora, resting from the toil of the journey, for they come ten and twelve *léguas* over very rugged country; and together they hold many festivities of plays, dances and music on many instruments – *violas*, guitars, flutes, rebecs and bagpipes – and along the slopes of the streams, which have great fields, on Our Lady’s day and during its octave, the pilgrims lodge in various bands, making great bonfires among those mountains’.
See Nossa Senhora do Monte, Ribeira Brava and pilgrims’ houses (*Casas de Romeiros*).
Pomegranate (Punica Granatum)

A small tree or shrub of the family Punicaceae, cultivated in São Martinho, Santo António and other parts of Madeira. An infusion of the unopened flowers or of the fruit rind of this species is used as a gargle against quinsy. The root bark of the pomegranate tree is one of the most effective vermifuges against tapeworm; the bark of the trunk and branches also has taenifuge properties, though weaker than those of the root.
Pilot fish (Naucrates ductor)

A fish of the family Scombridae that sometimes appears in the seas near the Madeira archipelago. It accompanies ships, floating timbers and even sharks, which, for all their voracity, spare their travelling companions. Its flesh is little prized.
Pilgrims’ houses
We know that houses were built to shelter pilgrims in the following places: Monte, Santo António da Serra and Piedade (Ponta de São Lourenço).

The pilgrims’ house at Monte (‘hill’) already existed between 1780 and 1790, and at a council meeting on 31 May 1822 it was declared to belong to the property of the municipality (*concelho*). Despite this, the Council resolved at its meeting of 18 November 1846 to have a building put up beside the church of Monte, ‘as a shelter for travellers and to house the beasts’; we do not know whether this building was ever actually constructed.

The pilgrims’ house at Santo António da Serra was built in 1808 at the expense of several British subjects, and is now in ruins. Until 1832 it was run by English committees, in which the names of Penfold, Selby, Leacock, Taylor and Gordon appear.

Of the house intended to lodge the devout who went on pilgrimage to the chapel of Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), no trace remains today.
Roncador (Pristipoma Bennettii)

A fish of the family Pristipomatidae found on stony bottoms, chiefly down to a depth of 30 *braças*. It is caught with hook and line or by means of a scoop net (*peneiro*) or a net. Its name comes from the noises it makes when caught.
Madeiran storm petrel (Oceanodroma Castro)

A small bird of the family Procellariidae, which spends part of its life on the high seas, sometimes ranging quite far from the coast. On dark nights it flies over the coastal rocks, uttering a cry that somewhat resembles the name by which it is known. It lays a single egg in a crevice in the rocks; the egg is white except at one end, where it bears reddish spots. It feeds on marine animals, which it shares with its chick, and the chick, when attacked in the nest, vomits an oil of a lovely wine-red colour and characteristic smell.
Rosa (José de Sousa)

He was military commander of Madeira when, by decree of 3 August 1917, he was appointed civil governor of the district, taking office on the 7th of the same month and year. He served until 28 September of that year. At the end of June 1918 he ceased to be military commander of the archipelago.
Róscio (Francisco João)
We know of this Madeiran from the extensive account Sousa Viterbo gives of him on pages 477 ff. of the *Diccionario Historico e Documental dos Architectos, Engenheiros e Construtores Portugueses*.

Francisco Róscio was born on this island around 1740, the son of Manuel Gonçalves Róscio, a native of Tenerife, and of Maria da Graça Rodrigues Jardim, a native of the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’). He studied at the Military Academy in Lisbon, and in 1762 was appointed infantry adjutant. He then served as a military engineer in the strongholds of Almeida and Elvas, showing remarkable competence, for which he was praised by the eminent engineer Jacques Funk, who had come from abroad expressly to direct the works on our fortifications. Róscio afterwards formed part of a commission of engineers sent to Brazil, where he again gave proof of his energy and knowledge. After 12 years away he returned to Portugal, then went back to Brazil to carry out the important mission of commissioner for the boundary demarcations in southern Brazil. He discharged it with the greatest zeal and competence, despite the enormous difficulties that arose at the time.

His energy and rare skill showed themselves brilliantly in São Pedro do Sul, as governor of that state, in the face of threats from the Spanish governor, the Marquis of Sobremontes: he halted the invading march of his troops and then succeeded in making peace, winning for Portugal some two hundred square *léguas* of territory.
He died in Brazil on 10 October 1805, after a very eventful life full of toil, having rendered his country the most distinguished services.
He left two manuscript works dealing chiefly with his scientific work and the commissions he carried out, of which Sousa Viterbo gives detailed accounts.
Rose

The only rose that grows wild in Madeira is *Rosa canina*, but gardens hold other species of rose, some truly remarkable for the size and colour of their flowers. *Rosa gallica*, *Rosa indica* and *Rosa damascena* are the species most cultivated in Funchal, but besides these many others are found in gardens, such as *Rosa moschata*, *Rosa Banksiae*, *Rosa centifolia*, *Rosa alba*, etc., etc.

In the hedges of São Martinho and Santo António *Rosa multiflora* is common, a species apparently naturalised that needs no care whatever from man. Essential oil of roses is extracted from the petals of *Rosa centifolia*, and the petals of *Rosa gallica* form the basis of conserve of roses, a remedy given with benefit in diarrhoea and tuberculosis. Remontant, or continuously flowering, roses are common in Madeira.
Rosmaninho

Madeirans give this name to *Santolina Chamaecyparissus*, a plant of the family Compositae grown in some gardens in Funchal, Camacha and Monte, and to *Lavandula pedunculata*, *L. viridis* and *L. dentata*, plants of the family Labiatae, the first two growing wild and the last cultivated and subspontaneous on the island. All these species are aromatic and can be used in baths and rubs; the flower heads of the santolina can be used as a tonic.
Ross (Dr Archibald Colquhoun)

An English physician who lived in Funchal for about 20 years. He had been in England since June 1856 when he learned that the cholera epidemic was raging on this island. He returned at once to Funchal to give the sick his medical services, was struck down by the disease on 5 September 1856 and died the following day. His death was deeply mourned by the whole population of Funchal, who had not failed to notice the act of self-sacrifice and courage performed by Dr Ross.
Ross (Sir James Clark)

He was the commander of the expedition that explored the Antarctic seas in the ships *Erebus* and *Terror* in 1840 and 1841. He was in Madeira in October 1839, where, with other officers, he measured Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’).
Rothschild (Baron Charles)

A wealthy English banker and distinguished entomologist, resident in London. He intends to study some of the insects of our archipelago and has already determined a species of flea found on the Cory’s shearwater (*cagarra*) by the Madeiran scientific expedition that visited the Selvagens in 1922, giving it the name *Xenopsylla gratiosa*.
Ruivinha (*Rubia peregrina* var. *angustifolia*)

A perennial plant of the family Rubiaceae, with rough linear-lanceolate or sublinear leaves and small flowers arranged in axillary cymes. Its roots are widely used in dyeing. When Madeirans wish to use them, they usually wash them first and then pound them with unripe blackberries. If the mixture is boiled together with the cloth to be dyed, the cloth takes on a beautiful red colour; it should then be boiled again with ash so that the colour does not fade.
The roots of the *ruivinha* are recommended for rickets, and they have the property of dyeing red the bones of people who take them internally.
Ruivo (peak)

This peak is very well known and is cited in countless Portuguese and foreign works, because it is the highest in Madeira and commands the widest panorama of the whole island. Its summit, or highest point, lies at the southern end of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’), while some of its spurs take in tracts of land within the boundaries of the parishes of Faial and São Jorge (‘St George’).

To reach this height, one must take the roads that lead there from the parishes of Santana or Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), the route from the latter of the two being preferable. By the first, the summit of the peak is reached by way of the Cumeada Alta (‘high ridge’); the whole route offers the finest viewpoints and passes close to the curious column of lava known as Homem em Pé (see that entry). By the second, one climbs the road of the Lombo Grande (‘great ridge’) and, at a certain height, comes upon a footpath that leads to the top of the lofty mountain. It can also be reached by setting out from Curral das Freiras and scaling the short cut known as the Lombo do Furão (‘ferret ridge’). However, besides being an extremely arduous ascent, this route is also full of dangers because of the ravines and precipices that flank it.

From the top of this height one can make out the orographic system of Madeira with relative precision, clearly distinguishing a considerable part of the highest mountains and the great gorges that surround them, almost always flanked by steep ravines and by the highest and most abrupt slopes. From that height the mountain range of endless peaks stands out, running lengthwise across Madeira from its westernmost to its easternmost point and forming the two well-defined slopes that make up the north coast and the south coast of the island.

Despite the difficulty of the ascent, many distinguished figures have visited this enchanting spot, some drawn by the dazzling, indescribable horizons it reveals, others attracted by the particular interest it holds for students of the physical and natural sciences.
The following list gives the results obtained by the various observers who have sought to measure the height of Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’).

The officers of the ships *Erebus* and *Terror* used the formulae of Gay-Lussac and of Rudberg to measure the peak, obtaining a height of 1858 metres by the first method and 1,860 metres by the second. One of Bowdich’s calculations is based on a trigonometric survey; all the other results were obtained by barometer, the late Colonel Eduardo Agostinho Pereira having used a barometer-altimeter for his measurement of the peak. The calculation by Colonel Alfredo Durão, which gives this mountain an altitude of 1861 metres, is considered one of the most accurate, since it was carried out under conditions particularly suited to obtaining a satisfactory result. This calculation was made in 1914.
The views from the top of the peak are magnificent, whichever way we turn our gaze.

Pico do Areeiro (‘sand pit’) with its reddish escarpments, the broad Pico das Torres (‘towers’), surrounded by several lesser summits, the highest of which is Pico do Gato, and the peaks of Canário, Cidrão, Grande and Santo António rise a short distance away, though separated from us by ravines of varying depth. Further off, to the west, one can make out the plateau of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), entirely bare of vegetation, and to the east the long, winding Ponta de São Lourenço. The parish (*freguesia*) of Santana, the verdant uplands of São Jorge and Boaventura, part of the Caminho do Poiso, Porto Santo and the three Desertas can all be seen from the top of the peak. The sea around the island is also visible from there, except in the direction of Pico das Torres, which is only a little lower than Pico Ruivo.

The spectacle to be seen from the top of the peak at sunrise deserves admiration for its fantastic and immensely beautiful quality. Seen from this summit, the sun, as it appears on the horizon, seems to tremble in its enlarged disc of a lovely golden colour. Yet this spectacle, although curious and worthy of attention, is far surpassed in beauty by the magnificent effects of light that the sun produces on the morning mists and the bare mountain summits as it rises.

Seven plant species have been found at the top of the peak, among them a small heath with pink or violet flowers (*Erica cinerea*). The *urze molar* grows almost to the summit, while the *urze durasia* goes no higher than halfway up the slope. The remains of a lava column covered with many olivine crystals are found on the upper part of the peak, and the surrounding ground consists of red scoria, lapilli and volcanic bombs.

According to a letter published in no. 355 of the *Correio de Madeira* of 21 June 1923, when the upland commons (montados) were divided, one part of Pico Ruivo, the eastern part, went to Faial, the northern part to Santana and the western part to São Jorge. The highest point of the mountain, the same letter states, belongs to Santana.

On one of the slopes of Pico Ruivo, not far from its summit, there is a cave or grotto known as Lapa da Cadela (‘bitch’s cave’), which gives shelter to visitors climbing this height when bad weather overtakes them in those sometimes inhospitable parts.

There was a pressing need to build a small mountain shelter nearby, but this was not achieved until 1939, to the great satisfaction of those who visit this picturesque spot and to the well-deserved credit of those who undertook this valuable improvement.

Countless compositions in prose and verse extol the marvellous beauty of those lofty parts, and countless too are the accounts, in Portuguese and in foreign languages, of the various excursions made there, many of which deserve to be read and duly appreciated. Among these we may mention that of the illustrious English naturalist and traveller T. E. Bowdich, in his interesting book *Excursions in Madeira and Porto Santo*, of which there is a French translation, and the one published in the issues of the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) of 2, 6 and 7 February 1912.
Sá
According to Dr Azevedo, this surname derives from Dona Guiomar de Sá, daughter of Henrique de Sá of Porto or, as some say, of João Rodrigues de Sá, who married Gaspar Bettencourt.

Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara, former owner of the Lombada (of Arco), was married to Dona Joana de Sá, chief lady of the bedchamber to the queen, and it is possible that some of his children, if he had any, took the surname of their mother's family.
Sá Cardoso (Alfredo Ernesto de)
He was civil governor of Madeira, appointed by decree of 20 March 1913, and took office on the 27th of the same month and year. In June 1919 he was prime minister.
Sá (José Correia de)

His appointment as governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira is dated 17 May 1758, and he took office on 27 May 1759. It was this governor who ordered the arrest and shipping out of the Jesuits on this island, and the sequestration and leasing of their property, in accordance with the orders issued by the Marquis of Pombal. He served until October 1767.
Sá Pereira (João António de)

He was appointed captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira in 1766, but did not take up the post until 9 December of the following year. His administration was a good one.

As we have already seen on page 101 of this volume, he sought to put an end to many abuses practised in Madeira, and for that reason his enemies celebrated his departure from this island with illuminations and fireworks. He left on 10 June 1777, after the fall of the Marquis of Pombal, to whom he was related. His services having been recognised by the new government, he was granted the title of Baron of Alverca.
Sabão (street)

It is one of the oldest streets in Funchal and links Rua do Comércio, or Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), with Rua da Alfândega. At a session of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) on 6 July 1922 it was given the somewhat vague name of ‘Rua 17 de Junho de 1922’, because that was the date on which the daring aviators Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral completed their flight between Lisbon and Rio de Janeiro.
Soap works

Frutuoso states in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) that Afonso V confirmed in 1469 the grant that Infante Ferdinand had made to Luís Gonçalves da Câmara of the black-soap works of the whole island of Madeira. The charter (foral) of the city of Funchal and of the towns of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Calheta (‘small cove’), dated 1515, records that black soap was to be sold at 10 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) the *arrátel* (old pound, about 459 g) and white soap at 12 *réis*.

In Madeira, as in Portugal, there was a soap monopoly lease (*contracto*), but the last one concluded ceased to be in force on 1 July 1858, and from then on the manufacture of and trade in this product were open to all. It was the law of 25 April 1857 that abolished the soap monopoly, which had brought so many hardships to the people of this island.
Madeiran elder (Sambucus maderensis)

A shrub or small tree with glabrous leaves of 5–7 oblong-lanceolate or lanceolate segments and yellowish or whitish flowers arranged in cymes. It is found at Ribeiro Frio, in Boaventura, Santana, etc., and is cultivated in Camacha and elsewhere in Madeira. Elder flowers, as an infusion, are used in gargles for inflammations of the throat, etc.
Sacred Heart (chapel)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Cardais (‘thistle patches’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Água de Pena, Canon Henrique Modesto de Bettencourt had a chapel dedicated to the Sacred Heart of Jesus built in 1907 on land he owned there.
A few years ago a chapel of this dedication was also founded in the parish of Monte (‘hill’) by Father Jorge de Faria e Castro.
Saião

The name of *Sempervivum glutinosum*, a sticky subshrubby member of the Crassulaceae, very common in Madeira. The juice of this plant is used internally and externally to treat injuries or wounds caused by falls, etc. It also serves to make the lines fishermen use tougher and more durable. There is another *saião*, *S. arboreum*, which is cultivated in gardens. The juice of the leaves of this species is recommended for corns.
See Farrobo (‘carob tree’).
Salt

Under the letters of grant of Prince Henry the Navigator, only the donataries could sell salt on this island and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). This privilege did not disappear when the donataries' captaincies of Madeira were turned into chief alcaideships, but it seems to have been little respected in later times. On 6 February 1769 an order was issued that the representative (*procurador*) of the Marquis of Castelo Melhor should not be obliged to supply the population with salt, and that anyone might unload and sell this commodity, as had been the practice before.
Salão
A reddish soil formed by the decomposition of volcanic material. It is not suited to growing vines, but potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word), etc., thrive in it.
Plant matter is absent from the composition of *salão* (reddish clay soil of volcanic origin), or present only in very small amounts.
The *salão* of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is an earth in which aluminium silicates predominate and which, because of its plastic properties, is commonly used to roof small houses and huts.
Wages

Because the cost of living has risen quite extraordinarily in recent times, all members of the working classes have been forced to demand better pay for their services, since they have no other way of maintaining their professional dignity and meeting their own most pressing needs and those of their families. Some workers now (1921) earn wages 20, 25 and 30 times higher than before the war. But if we consider that the price of all basic necessities has risen extraordinarily, as was shown on page 141 of this volume; that houses once let for 6 and 8 escudos (Portuguese currency from 1911, = 1,000 réis) a month can be had today only for 300 and 400 escudos; and that a suit or a pair of boots costs 18 and 20 times more today than formerly, etc., etc., then the demands of the working classes cease to cause surprise. We must acknowledge their right to improve their financial circumstances, so as to face the terrible crisis the country is going through, thanks to the errors and incompetence of our rulers (1921). Below we give as accurate a note as possible of what various classes of workers received before the war and receive today. It should be added that, despite the considerable differences between the old and the new wages, members of these classes never lack work on the terms they demand, whatever the nature of their occupations. This is due to various circumstances, and above all to the considerable change in recent times in the economic situation of a mainstay of the Madeiran population.
WAGES

Printers are usually paid monthly, compositors receiving 400 to 500 escudos and apprentices 150 to 200 escudos. Before the war, the latter received 4.50 to 7.00 escudos and the former 18.00 to 20.00 escudos a month. Owners of first-class barbershops charge 2.00 escudos for a haircut and 1.00 escudo for a shave, while those of second-class shops charge 1.50 escudos for a haircut and 75 centavos for a shave. Before the war, the same work cost 10 and 5 centavos in first-class barbershops and 5 and 3 centavos in second-class ones. A baker receives 70.00 escudos a week, whereas before the war his pay was about 30.00 escudos a month. A cook and a maid demand wages of around 100$000 and 60.00 escudos a month respectively, whereas before the war they received no more than 10.00 to 12.00 escudos and 3.00 to 5.00 escudos, also monthly.
What is set out in this article refers entirely to the situation preceding the year 1921.
Saldanha da Gama (Dom Manuel)
Dom Manuel Saldanha da Gama Melo e Torres was appointed Civil Governor of Madeira by decree of 12 June 1890, and took office on the 25th of that month.
By decree of 6 April 1893 he was appointed Civil Governor of this district for a second time, taking office on the 23rd of that month.
Saldanha da Gama (João)

He was appointed Governor and Captain-General (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of this archipelago on 4 May 1715 and took office on 27 June following. He was born in 1674 and died in 1754. We know little of his administration in Madeira, but he distinguished himself as a soldier in various campaigns and, as Viceroy of India, governed in exemplary fashion, rendering the most notable services to his country there.
Saldanha (Fernão)

This Governor-General of Madeira was appointed on 10 January 1625 and took office on 11 April of the same year. He died on this island on 10 August 1626, while serving here as Governor. On his death, Bishop Dom Jerónimo Fernando took over the duties of Governor.
Saldanha (Marquis of)
The Marquis, later Duke, of Saldanha was elected senator for Madeira for the legislative session of 1838 to 1840.
Salema (Box salpa)
A fish of the family Sparidae that frequently appears in Madeiran waters. It breeds in the coastal rock pools and lives in large shoals, travelling continually close to the shore.
Salema Vaz

Among the political deportees who came to this island in 1919 and were interned in the buildings of the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’) was the poet Salema Vaz. In 1921 he published in Lisbon, in a fine edition, a volume of verse entitled *Pão do Exílio, Escrito que foi durante o desterro e seu caminho da Ilha da Madeira, cidade do Funchal, no ano MCMXIX*, Lisbon, 1921, 134 pp. The poems in this volume were written from the voyage and departure from Lisbon for Madeira onwards and during the author’s exile on this island, and contain many references to various Madeiran people and things (1922).
Salt pans

There have been several attempts to establish the industry of extracting salt from sea water in the archipelago, but almost always with discouraging results. The earliest attempt dates from 1792, when the royal decree (*alvará*) of 20 November of that year permitted Tomás Watts, Francisco Martins da Luz and João José de Basto ‘to establish fisheries and salt works throughout the state of Madeira and at the beach called Formosa’. This attempt was followed by another from Francisco Vicente Espinosa da Câmara, who in 1823 applied for the exclusive right to make salt in Madeira for 30 years, setting out some means of obtaining this product on advantageous terms.

At Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’) there are traces of old installations for crystallising salt, probably built by the first people to try salt-making here. Very close to this locality (*sítio*), at Ponta da Cruz (‘point of the cross’), trials to produce salt were made about 15 years ago, but they came to nothing because the sea water had to be raised to a great height to get it into the reservoirs. It was José da Corte who tried to establish salt pans at Ponta da Cruz, but once the tuna-canning factory was set up, all attempts to extract salt at that locality ceased entirely.

Around 1865 Jacinto António de Sousa had salt pans built at Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’), in the localities of Lagoas (‘ponds’) and Serra da Cruz (‘upland of the cross’). These passed, we believe around 1878, into the possession of Filipe António Gonçalves. Some 15 to 20 years ago other salt pans were established near the old ones, owned by José Maurício Gomes, João Martins da Silva, José da Corte and Alexandre da Silva (1921). A great deal of salt, not always of poor quality, was made in both the new and the old salt pans, but this did not prevent both from being abandoned because they yielded little profit, or perhaps losses, to their owners. Clay was even imported from Portugal to line the floors and walls of the reservoirs of these later salt pans.

We also know of two other attempts to extract salt in Madeira, one at the locality of Fajã da Areia (‘sand flat’), in São Vicente, and the other in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniçal (‘reed bed’), neither of which produced encouraging results either. José Maurício Gomes and J. Pontes Leça set up and ran the Caniçal salt pans.

On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), too, there were some attempts to establish the industry of extracting salt from sea water. The earliest was that of Isidoro da Silva, who spent considerable capital building salt pans at the locality of Fontinha (‘little spring’). In 1890 and the years immediately following, Augusto de Nóbrega Noronha succeeded in extracting a great deal of salt from salt pans he had built at Serra de Fora (‘outer upland’), in the north of the island. Around 1903 further salt pans were established at the same locality, owned by Dr António Luís Pimenta; these, however, did not give satisfactory results, owing, it was said, to defects in the construction of the reservoirs meant to receive the water.

To operate salt pans in the archipelago, the water must be raised by machinery of some kind, since the shape of the coast means the reservoirs cannot lie below sea level. This circumstance on the one hand, and on the other a certain slowness in evaporation – because the sky is often overcast in summer and the atmosphere usually holds a large amount of water vapour – make salt-making more costly and difficult here than on the mainland. This does not mean that it cannot be carried on, perhaps even on advantageous terms, if certain rules are observed to which due attention has not always been paid until now.

The Paul do Mar salt pans did not give encouraging results because they were built in a spot little swept by the winds and steam engines were needed to raise the water. At Caniçal, however, there is reason to believe that salt extraction may yet prove profitable, provided care is taken to cement the reservoirs so that the product does not come out laden with impurities, as has already happened. There, as on Porto Santo, wind-driven pumps can be used to raise the water, a great saving in this operation. Indeed, it was with the help of one of these machines, and with reservoirs built as described above, that the late Augusto de Nóbrega Noronha obtained salt on that island as perfect as that which comes from Portugal.

The working of salt pans in this archipelago deserves special study, as it would soften the unfavourable impressions that have persisted here about the various failures surrounding this valued industry. To that end, we shall transcribe some passages from a fine article by the distinguished naval officer and academician Admiral Hugo de Lacerda, which contains valuable information on this important subject.

‘A simple comparison of the technical factors that may be considered fundamental to the question at hand, between those here and those on the Portuguese mainland, may, I believe, already shed some light. As is well known, mainland Portugal is one of the principal producers of salt: there are vast salt pans, or salt marshes, in the Ria de Aveiro, in the Mondego estuary, on the Tagus as far as Vila Franca and on the Ribatejo bank, on the River Sado as far as Alcácer do Sal, and also in the Algarve at Faro, Tavira and Portimão. Let us see. – As to the degree of salinity of the water and its purity, only advantages can be seen in this archipelago. The drawback I have heard mentioned, that salinity here is greater than on the mainland, can only hold in the opposite sense; besides, it is not because the mainland salt marshes are situated (with the exception of those at Faro) in river regions that they will receive less dense water, since they operate in the dry seasons. – With regard to the greater ease of filling the reservoirs, there can be no doubt that marked advantages exist on the mainland, where the flow of the highest tides alone is enough to let the water in freely; and the facilities are all the better given the greater stillness of river areas. The quantity of water to be treated is considerable, because each litre can yield only about twenty grams of sodium chloride; nevertheless, since the wind can be relied upon, the windmill can solve the difficulty more economically, all the more so as it can also be put to other uses. It should be noted that in Italy, also a great producer of salt, the Mediterranean tides rise at most 0.3 m above mean level, so it is only natural that recourse must be had there to more or less costly artificial processes. – As regards waterproofing the floors and walls of the reservoirs, which seems to have been the main cause of the failures mentioned, there is again no doubt about the advantages on the mainland. But if the lining, as was done on Porto Santo, cracked, cracks are less to be expected with modern reinforced-concrete methods, which in this case need not even allow for appreciable loads, a simple wire mesh perhaps sufficing as reinforcement; besides, good waterproofing processes already exist, the cracks themselves can be remedied, and one can count on the covering of liquid, at least in the season of highest temperatures in the sun. In Moçâmedes, I am told that the salt for curing the fish, so plentiful there, is made in reservoirs lined with concrete, naturally reinforced. The *Encyclopaedia Britannica* refers to reservoirs of this kind. – It is a condition that there be no rain during the production period, and this is identical and in practice met in both regions. – Heat is an important factor, the one to judge being above all direct solar radiation; as for heat in the shade, there should be some advantage here, but with regard to direct heat in the open sun there may be doubts, even in the coastal places relevant to the question, the sunniest, namely those of Porto Santo; nevertheless, one of the experiments has already shown that abundant salt could be obtained. – Capital importance must be attributed to the wind. In much of the south of Madeira relatively little action of this kind can be counted on; but on the north side, and on the south side from Machico eastwards, and above all on Porto Santo, judging by the winds that blow at Ponta de São Lourenço, the differences should not be so marked in relation to the strong northerlies of the mainland coast in the summer months. In this respect, too, that experiment which produced abundant salt (albeit of poor quality) must also be taken into consideration.

Lastly, there is the relative humidity of the atmosphere which, being considerable, must counteract the action of the sun and wind, reducing evaporation. This condition is exactly the same in the two regions considered in summer, because in winter (it is always worth repeating) the advantages here are considerably greater.

To sum up: as to technique, provided it is respected and the sites are well chosen, there seems no reason to think that good and abundant salt cannot be obtained here. The question is thus mainly a financial one, of reasonable profits: on one side the greater expense of lining the reservoirs and raising the water; on the other the cost of shipping salt from the mainland to here, and also the higher price of labour, both in the initial installation and in the production itself.

But this does not mean that there is no need to turn to a good expert, for both matters, assisted by staff trained in the work. And should a new, well-directed attempt perhaps be desired, would it not be possible to find a good printed guide, on both the technical and the financial side? The *Dicionário Português Ilustrado* refers to an article by a Portuguese engineer on the subject.

It must also be considered that Madeira may at any moment find itself isolated, or nearly so, and salt is among the first necessities, so much so that in some places it is a principal object of barter.’
Salmonete do alto (Polymixia nobilis)

A scombrid fish that lives at a relatively great depth and is generally caught with the *gorazeira* (deep-water longline for sea bream) or the *briqueira* (a Madeiran hand line for bottom fishing). Its excellent flavour makes it one of the most valuable species in the waters of Madeira.
Red mullet (Mullus surmuletus)

A fish of the family Mullidae that is not uncommon in Madeiran waters, also known as *salmonete de rolo*. It is caught in fish traps (*covos*) from the shore down to a depth of 60 *braças*, and is considered one of the finest fish of Madeira.
Parsley (Petroselinum hortense)
An umbellifer widely grown in the vegetable gardens of Madeira for its use in cookery. The crushed leaves of this plant are used as a resolvent on stings from wasps, bees and other insects.
Sage (Salvia officinalis)
A labiate with whitish, crenate, wrinkled leaves, grown in many parts of Madeira. It is a tonic and stomachic, and Madeirans also credit it with emmenagogue properties.
Salviati

This family surname, says the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), ‘derives from João Salviati, a native of Florence, who, being implicated in a conspiracy against the Medici, took refuge on the island of Madeira around 1478. Here he married Isabel Alvares de Abreu, and held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) at Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), above the Ribeira dos Socorridos, close to the sea. His descendants took the surname Florença’.
Sanatoria of Madeira

Prince Frederico Carlos de Hohenlohe asked the Portuguese Government for permission to establish seaside and mountain sanatoria in Madeira for the treatment of consumptives. For this purpose he was to organise a company under Portuguese law, and our government would have the right to dispose of a certain number of places for the treatment of poor patients. Permission was granted by ministerial dispatch of 9 June 1903, after a favourable opinion had been obtained from the National Assistance for Consumptives (*Assistência Nacional aos Tuberculosos*). A commission of German experts came to Madeira to choose the sites for the sanatoria, and our government appointed the physician Dom António de Lencastre to accompany that commission to this island.

Once the opinions of that physician, of the Higher Council of Public Hygiene (*Conselho Superior de Higiene Pública*) and of the Crown Attorney-General’s Office (*Procuradoria Geral da Coroa*) had been heard, the concession he had requested was definitively granted to the Prince of Hohenlohe. It required a substantial deposit to guarantee fulfilment of the clauses of the contract, among which was the right of the concessionaire to carry out expropriations in the public interest and to import, free of customs duties, the materials needed to build the sanatoria.

The Sanatoria company, or enterprise, had as its agent on this island the late commander Manuel Gonçalves, an intelligent and enterprising man. Immediately after its organisation the company acquired the *quintas* (country estates) Santana, Vigia (‘lookout’) and Bianchi. In August 1904 it received from abroad the first materials for the installations it was about to build in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), where it soon employed some 300 workers, not counting the technical staff who had come from Germany.

For some years the business of the Sanatoria Company on this island ran smoothly, despite the campaign waged against it by some English residents, who feared that the Hohenlohe concession might harm their interests. However, when the Company, relying on the privileges it enjoyed, sought to expropriate the Quinta Pavão, belonging to a British subject who had bought it shortly before from an Austrian, serious complications at once arose. These forced our government to open negotiations not only with the concessionary Company but also with the cabinets in London and Berlin, which were likewise interested in the matter.

When it proved impossible to reach an agreement with the concessionary Company, our government offered it three options: arbitration by the tribunal at The Hague, the choice of other land for building the sanatoria, or rescission of the contract. The Company preferred the last proposal as the most feasible, and perhaps as the one that brought the greatest profits and advantages to those interested in the business in question.

By the law of 3 November 1909 the Government was authorised to rescind the concession granted to the Prince of Hohenlohe by the ministerial dispatches of 9 June 1903 and 4 January 1904, and to buy back the buildings, installations and all the rights belonging to the concessionaire, on payment of 4,425,000 marks and the corresponding interest at 5 per cent from 20 August 1908, the date on which negotiations were concluded. General Parreira had come to Madeira, commissioned by the Government, to value the properties of the Sanatoria Company.

The ministerial order (*portaria*) of 18 November 1909 gave full powers to the Viscount of Geral de Lima, Treasury Delegate (*delegado do tesouro*), to accept the buyback of the concession. Shortly afterwards the Company’s movable and immovable property passed into the possession of the State. Since then it has been in the charge of the head of the district Revenue Office (*Repartição de Fazenda*), who is responsible for doing whatever is necessary for its upkeep and proper administration (1921).

The Sanatoria Company found in the former queen, Empress Amélie, one of its most devoted protectors. The late King Carlos I, on receiving Professor Pannwitz, one of the members of the commission that had come to Madeira in 1904 to choose the sites for the buildings intended for consumptives, spoke words of admiration and encouragement for the Prince of Hohenlohe’s initiative.

The properties that passed into the Government’s possession on rescission of the contract were the Quinta Santana, where one of the buildings intended to receive patients stands, the Quinta Vigia, the Quinta Bianchi, the Quinta Amélia, the Quinta dos Reis e Palmeira, and the land at Marmeleiros (‘quince trees’), where the so-called sanatorium for the poor stands (1921). The State also received a quantity of water from the Arrebentão that had been acquired to supply the Company’s buildings, as well as all the furniture in those buildings. For all this property it paid the sum of 4,753,354 marks, of which 328,541 marks were interest due.

Converted into Portuguese money, these amounts show that the Company received from the State the sum of 1,159,864,025 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), of which 1,079,700,000 *réis* was the value of the properties and 80,164,025 *réis* interest. At the time of the rescission the concessionaire was authorised to recover the deposit it had lodged to guarantee fulfilment of the clauses of the contract, which consisted of 725 bonds of the Portuguese foreign debt, each worth 20 pounds (1921).
We transcribe below two important documents that shed valuable light on the subject of this article:

From the *Diário do Governo* (‘Government Gazette’) of 29 October 1903: Directorate-General of Health and Public Welfare – 2nd Department. Informed by this knowledge, and after His Majesty’s Government had granted authorisation to build sanatoria there, the Prince of Hohenlohe organised a mission. Its medical side was represented by Professor Frankel of the Berlin Faculty, where his scientific authority is respected and enjoys the most glorious renown, and by Dr Pannwitz, secretary-general of the International Tuberculosis Bureau, who has so distinguished himself in directing various works in the fight against tuberculosis and in organising countless sanatoria. The mission’s aim was to choose sites on the island suitable for building sanatoria, some for those predisposed to tuberculosis, others for those infected with it. As the Prince wished a Portuguese physician to accompany the mission, Your Excellency’s generous goodwill saw fit to choose me, and it is with pleasure, and with the assurance of my gratitude, that I now report on my modest discharge of the honourable task I accepted.

We left on 2 September and returned to this capital on 7 October. We stayed on that island for ten very short days, and from our delightful excursions through that enchanting region, its villages, mountains and heights, we gathered the most pleasing impressions, though not without the light and shade that is the inescapable law of human contradictions.

From enjoying that matchless climate, and from the personal impression to which Sigismond Jaccoud – the great master of climatotherapy – attached such importance, and without so much as touching on the beauties to which artists surrender, seduced, we understood – I should say we felt – its incomparable physiology.

We felt its sedative effects, shown in the calm of the general circulation, the repose of the central nervous system and the lesser effort of inspiration, which bring patients the end of all excitement, the return of sleep, less coughing and a fuller satisfaction of the need to breathe. We felt too its tonic action, through the heightening of combustion within the organism and the quickening of the digestive functions, whose natural reward is better nutrition and a gain in weight.
The sad note, jarring in that glorious concert of nature, is the deplorable state of Madeira with regard to the very disease that people go there to cure.

And to one point I draw Your Excellency’s intelligent attention at once. Tuberculosis, like the splendid flora that has taken root there, has invaded the poor classes of the island, becoming there, as on the mainland, a popular disease. The mixing of sick and healthy in the hotels; the healthy succeeding the sick in their rooms without the slightest precaution or the most rudimentary disinfection; and the spread far beyond these centres of contagion, carried in dirty linen washed everywhere without prior treatment – these are serious causes of the propagation of tuberculosis. Its accomplices are the overwork (*surmenage*) of those who labour and the alcoholism of so many who deceive themselves with a momentary stimulation, vainly hoping to rebuild strength that only grows ever weaker.
It is this evil that must urgently be remedied. Certainly, the Prince of Hohenlohe’s enterprise meets one of the most essential requirements.

The immediate construction of sanatoria for rich and poor, run as closed establishments where the most meticulous disinfection is guaranteed, will surely transform the results that the immigration of consumptives has so far brought the island. The very grave drawback of the consumptive’s passage through the island disappears entirely, so that the benefit the patient seeks and obtains there brings it nothing but prosperity. In other words, building sanatoria prevents future invasions of Robert Koch’s bacillus. But what of the present evil? Part of it can be remedied by creating establishments for the poor; the rest will be met by enforcing the decree of 30 August 1902, which Your Excellency, with your lofty judgement, will know how to put into practice, providing Madeira with the equipment and staff indispensable for its defence. The law is certainly excellent, but ineffective and inapplicable without disinfection stations, etc., etc.
The work that the Prince of Hohenlohe intends to carry out is vast and complex. He wishes to make use of all the resources that the region offers.

Thus, on the coast he will set up cure hotels to treat the predisposed, the anaemic, the chlorotic, the lymphatic, the scrofulous, the exhausted and the neurasthenic. They will be equipped with all the modern apparatus that uses physical agents: heat, light, electricity, kinesitherapy and massage. He will build artificial beaches to complement thalassotherapy, etc.

In the mountains, below the fog zone, the general sanatoria for treating tuberculosis will be placed. Suitably wooded sites will be used, where large enclosed parks will be laid out for the patients’ enjoyment and for the open-air cure, which will be favoured by the nearness of superb pine woods.
The high altitudes will be reserved for more special indications, no doubt including the summer treatment of some forms of tuberculosis.

On the advice of the medical mission, as soon as the company begins its work two meteorological stations will be set up, one on the Arieiro at 1,700 metres and another on the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) at 1,500 metres, to judge reliably the winter weather conditions. The existing data, above all those presented by Mr João Tierno on the Paul, and the limited use made of the Arieiro for a few patients, admirable though they are, are not enough to form a scientific opinion.
