To take advantage of the Atlantic climate, the medical mission designated a strip of the coast of Funchal bay, and in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte it chose several sites, both for the sanatoria for the rich and for those for the poor, meeting the requirements of shelter and the other conditions that such establishments demand.
The first sanatorium for the poor, to be built immediately, will have forty beds in two pavilions, one for men and the other for women.

In closing, I must inform Your Excellency that the Government’s delegate owes as much gratitude for the distinguished manner in which he was received by the Prince of Hohenlohe and the whole mission, as all of us who have now visited *A Ilha da Madeira* (‘The Island of Madeira’) owe to the traditional courtesy with which the Portuguese authorities treated us.

God keep Your Excellency. To His Most Illustrious and Most Excellent Lordship the Minister of the Kingdom and President of the Council of Ministers. – Lisbon, 30 October 1903. – Dom António Maria de Lencastre.

From the *Diário do Governo* of 25 January 1914: ‘Until 12 noon on 27 February next, sealed tenders will be received at the Directorate-General of Public Finance, in the Ministry of Finance, for the lease, in a single lot, of the national properties specified below:

1. Quinta Bianchi, comprising a manor house, a lodge, stables, a belvedere (*mirante*), a garden, a vineyard and a cane field, served by water from the Arrebentão and from the Levada dos Piornais. It is bounded on the north by Rua Imperatriz Dona Amélia, where it has its main entrance, on the south by the cliff, on the east by Quinta Pavão (‘peacock estate’), and on the west by Carlos Bianchi and Luís Figueira da Silva, with a service door on that side.

2. Quinta Vigia, comprising a dwelling house, stables, various small houses, belvederes, gardens and orchards, served by water from the Arrebentão and the Levada dos Piornais. It is bounded on the north by Rua Imperatriz Dona Amélia, where it has its main entrance, by properties belonging to various persons, and also by the Beco das Angústias (‘sorrows’), onto which it has a door, and by the Quinta de Nossa Senhora das Angústias, and on the west by Quinta Pavão.

3. Quinta dos Reis e Palmeira, with a dwelling house, an orchard and a cane field, served by water from the Levada das Cales and by its own springs. It is bounded on the north by Carlos Augusto da Silva Carvalho, on the south by the Passeio da Quinta dos Reis and land belonging to Diogo António Ferreira, on the east by the Ribeiro da Quinta dos Reis and Baltasar Gonçalves, and on the west by the Caminho do Monte (‘Monte road’), onto which it has several doors. There are dwelling houses and other improvements (*benfeitorias*, tenant-made works on the land) belonging to the tenant farmers.

4. Quinta Sant’Ana, with a dwelling house, machinery for lighting, a laundry and ice-making, etc., storehouses, a pine wood, arable land, a vineyard and a cane field, served by water from the Arrebentão and the Levada das Cales. It is bounded on the north by the heirs of Vicente Cândido Machado, on the south by land belonging to Emília Augusta Figueira and Joaquim Ovídio de Jesus and by the Levada dos Flamengos, on the east by the Caminho do Monte, where it has its main entrance, and on the west by the road of the Monte Railway (*Caminho de Ferro do Monte*), the Caminho da Torrinha (‘little tower’), José Dias Ferreira and the said Emília Augusta Figueira.

5. Rural property in the locality (*sítio*) of Sant’Ana, with fruit trees and a tiled house, bounded on the north by Quinta Sant’Ana, on the south by Joaquim Ovídio de Jesus and the Azinhaga dos Ausentes, on the east by the said Ovídio and on the west by João Agostinho de Oliveira (now considered an annex of Quinta Sant’Ana).

6. Rural property in the locality of Torrinha, comprising arable land, fruit trees and a thatched hut, bounded on the north by the Levada do Flamengo, on the south and east by State land and on the west by the Monte Railway (now considered an annex of Quinta Sant’Ana).

7. Rural property in the locality of Livramento, land with a pool, bounded on the north, south and south-east by State land and on the west by the Monte Railway (now considered an annex of Quinta Sant’Ana).

8. Rural property in the locality of Livramento, with a tiled house, pine trees and a thatched hut, bounded on the north by Francisco Ferreira and Quinta Sant’Ana, on the south by João Agostinho de Oliveira, on the east by the said Quinta and the gully stream (*côrrego*), and on the west by the road of the Monte Railway (now considered an annex of Quinta Sant’Ana).

9. Rural property in the locality of Livramento, with fruit trees and a vineyard, bounded on the north by the heirs of Manuel de Freitas, on the south by land belonging to the Monte Railway Company, on the east by the gully stream and on the west by the road of the Monte Railway (now considered an annex of Quinta Sant’Ana).

10. The installation known as the Arrebentão Waters, which rises on the property described below and has its *terminus* at the Cais da Pontinha. It serves all the foregoing properties and also supplies shipping through the discharge outlet it has on the said quay. Its only obligation is to supply the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) with four *penas* of water for its public fountains on the Caminho do Monte.
11. Rural property in the locality of Arrebentão, with a pine wood, possessing excellent spring water captured to supply the above installation.

Tenders must be accompanied by a document proving that a provisional deposit of 10,000 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) has been made at the Caixa Geral dos Depósitos, in cash or in public debt securities; on the definitive award of the contract this will be raised to the sum corresponding to two years’ rent. In addition to the certification of the bidder’s signature, tenders must state the bidder’s profession and residence, and likewise those of the guarantor or guarantors offered, who must be Portuguese citizens with property or assets in Portugal.

The said properties go to auction unfurnished and will return to the possession of the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*) at the end of the contract, with all improvements made to them, without any right of retention or compensation for the tenant. The tenant is obliged to insure them in favour of the National Treasury against the risk of fire, and to compensate it for any damage not due to the normal use of the properties.
The monopoly lease (*contracto*) confers no exemptions of any kind, nor does it release the holder from compliance with the laws of the country, including tax and criminal law.

The building materials the State holds there do not form part of this monopoly lease, and the concessionaire is therefore obliged to keep them safe on the properties until the government disposes of them directly or at public auction.

On the said 27th, at twelve noon, in the Ministry of Finance, in the office of the Director-General of Public Finance, the Attorney General of the Republic and the Director-General of Customs will meet with him. Having examined the tenders submitted, they will draw up a ranking of them according to the rent and the other advantages offered, assessed as a whole. The government will award the concession to the most advantageous, while reserving the right to accept none if none suits it. If parliamentary approval is required for the definitive award of the contract, the government will submit the appropriate bill within 10 days.
3rd Department of the Directorate-General of Public Finance, 24 January 1914.’

The Head of Department, Augusto Correia da Silva Melo. After the failure of the company organised by the Prince of Hohenlohe, the task of building a sanatorium in Madeira passed to the ‘Assistência Nacional aos Tuberculosos’ (National Tuberculosis Assistance). The sanatorium would still not be a happy and eloquent reality had it not been for the benevolent efforts of Dr João Francisco de Almada, to whom this remarkable undertaking is chiefly owed, together with other indispensable improvements that are most closely bound up with it. Anyone wishing for detailed knowledge of the subject, which we cannot set out at length here, should read the interesting pamphlet *A Obra da A. N. T. na Madeira* by the distinguished writer Feliciano Soares, and the book *Dr. João Francisco de Almada*, produced under the chief editorship of the same writer. Its publication was due to the initiative of the present author, co-author of the *Elucidário Madeirense*.

The sanatorium was built on the former Quinta Santana, and its formal inauguration took place in 1941. It was given the name ‘Sanatório Doutor João Francisco de Almada’ as a most deserved tribute to the illustrious physician, who had died in this city on 14 June 1942.
Sanches (Afonso)

Closely related to the articles Columbus and Esmeraldo in this *Elucidário* are the following words, transcribed from the *Lello Universal* dictionary, about the Portuguese seaman Afonso Sanches: ‘... Portuguese pilot born in Cascais. Setting out in a caravel (*caravela*) for the East Indies in 1486, he was, some say, driven by a storm to America. There are others, however, who assert that he deliberately tried to reach India by crossing the Atlantic, and so arrived south-east of Florida, at the Lucayan Islands, recorded the island of São Salvador in his log and, on his way back to Lisbon, put in at the island of Madeira. Sanches died in the house of his friend and colleague Christopher Columbus, who had settled and married there.

Sanches’s log remained in Columbus’s possession. This assertion has been made by various writers, although it cannot be put forward as an undisputed truth. Of considerable interest on this subject is the note that the illustrious writer and academician Major J. Reis Gomes left in his book *A Filha de Tristão das Damas*, which we shall place on record here:

‘Linked with Columbus’s stay in Madeira and with his plan of sailing westwards is the tradition that he received from the hands of a dying pilot the chart on which the latter had marked what his eyes had seen during a tragic episode of forced navigation towards the west, carried along by stormy winds and seas.

This, in brief, is the story – disputed, it is true, but referred to by many authors, such as Frutuoso in Book I of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and Father Simão de Vasconcellos in his description of the *Descobrimento d’America*, besides the testimony of Friar António de São Romão, Garcilazo de la Vega, Pizarro e Araújo, Father Manoel Fialho, Friar Apollonio da Conceição, Mariz and others:

Afonso Sanches, pilot of a caravel from Cascais that carried sugar between Lisbon and Madeira, was caught by a violent storm that drove him, dismasted, westwards for many days (some put the length of this forced crossing at precisely 22 days). He discovered a new land (probably somewhere around the Gulf of Mexico), which he marked on his chart along with other details of the voyage, but he and his companions were so weak from hunger that he could not explore it. Anxious to save his life and mindful of the lack of provisions, he took advantage of favourable weather to make for the island of Madeira, where he found shelter in the house of Columbus, a pilot like himself and one of his acquaintances. But he arrived so worn out by hunger and hardship that he soon felt his last moments approaching. Seeing that he was dying, and that it was therefore impossible for him to attempt a fresh voyage and return with wealth and glory, he confided his secret in detail to Columbus in return for the hospitality he had received. He left him his annotated chart, which was for the Genoese the irrefutable proof of the soundness of his plans and the sure guide of his voyage to discover not the West Indies, as he himself supposed, but the New World.
Luciano Cordeiro also relates this tradition in his paper *L'Amerique et les Portugais*, which forms part of the *Compte rendu du Congrés Internacional des Americanistes – 1875*.
Spain, like us, also has its Afonso Sanchez. For that nation, the man who bequeathed his precious map to Columbus was an Andalusian.

Some scholars, among them the American Henry Harrisse, maintain that the whole affair is no more than a legend. So be it… Might the legend be seeking to embody in a single man all the longing that gripped most Madeiran seafarers of that time, who never tired of turning their hopeful eyes to the west, believing, though fearful?

None of them may have travelled on the wings of the storm until the ‘Indies’ came into view; but these, or rather America, would in a certain sense have come to them, borne on the ocean currents, setting before their astonished eyes exotic trees, timber carved in a barbarous and unknown style, and even corpses with truly strange faces. Seen in this light, the tradition, fabulous though it may be, has nonetheless given the fact a better explanation and a more picturesque character.
What does it matter whether the visionary was called Afonso Sanches, António do Leme, Pedro Correia, Vicente Dias or André Valente?
Sanches de Castro (Dr José Pereira)

He served as a district judge (*juiz de direito*) in Madeira. In 1855, as judge of the western judicial district (*comarca*), he sentenced Manuel Joaquim Fernandes to death for murdering Gerardo Pedro, of the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’). We believe that this Fernandes was the last Madeiran condemned to death by the courts, but we do not know whether he was actually executed.

Dr Sanches de Castro published a short work entitled *observações sobre o contrato de colónia na Madeira* (Funchal, 1857), on the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant). See Colonia.
Sancho (Dom)

A Castilian bishop who was in Madeira in 1548, having come from the Canary Islands. He consecrated the church of the monastery of São Francisco, and administered confirmation and conferred holy orders on the island. He sought to become Bishop of Madeira, and to that end ‘went to Lisbon, says Frutuoso, with the purpose of asking the King for that bishopric, citing in support what he had done there; but His Highness ordered that he be very well rewarded for his labours, and his petition was refused, since he was not a native, and there were many in the kingdom who deserved it’.
Sândalos

The vernacular name of *Mentha aquatica* and of a hybrid produced by crossing this species with *M. viridis*. *M. aquatica* is common in the beds of many streams, and both it and the said hybrid (the former *M. citrata*) are aromatic Labiatae, used, though only occasionally, in rural folk medicine. *M. aquatica* is also known by the name of *mentastro*.
Sanitation

Only from the last quarter of the 19th century did the sanitation of the city of Funchal – particularly the supply of drinking water and the laying of sewers – truly receive from the municipal council sessions the attention that the matter urgently demanded. A ministerial order (*portaria*) of 22 March 1897 instructed the Directorate of District Public Works (*Obras Públicas Distritais*) to carry out the studies needed for the supply of drinking water and the laying of sewers, and the law of 16 September of that year authorised the government to assist with the construction work. These two studies were carried out by the distinguished engineers Adriano Trigo and Aníbal Trigo, and earned the praise and full approval of the higher authorities. The study dealing specifically with the sewers was regarded as a valuable piece of work, and it has been of great help and a useful lesson for the works carried out later. It was published as a pamphlet of 95 pages. These important improvements, which form the chief foundation of public hygiene, have continued to be carried out, as the reputation our land enjoys as a privileged health resort requires. The most recent municipal council sessions have devoted the most careful attention to this important and pressing matter, to the general applause of all the townspeople.
The articles Water Supply and Levadas provide some essential further information on this subject.
Sanguinho (Rhamnus glandulosa)

A tree of the family Rhamnaceae with ovate or ovate-oblong serrated leaves, usually bearing 2 to 4 small glands or projections on the lower part of the upper surface. It has small greenish-yellow flowers arranged in short axillary clusters, and is found in the Serra do Seixal (‘pebble shore’) and between Lamaceiros (‘mud flats’) and Ribeiro Frio (‘cold brook’). It yields a pale, even-grained wood, formerly used for inlaid work (*embutidos*), but today unknown to the great majority of cabinetmakers, because it is very rare.
Sanha

This family surname, now extinct in Madeira, began with Manuel Afonso de Sanha, who founded the chapel of Bom Jesus (Good Jesus) at Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) and there established an entail (*morgado*) on the lands of Ribeiro do Peso (‘weighhouse brook’) and Ribeira do Inferno (‘hell’s stream’).
St Apollonia (chapel)

Near the former convent of St Francis in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), and belonging to it, there was a small chapel dedicated to Santa Apolónia (St Apollonia), which is today completely in ruins. It is the property of Pedro César de Brito (1921).
St Brigid (chapel)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’) there was a chapel dedicated to Santa Brígida (St Brigid), founded in 1668 by António Maciel de Afonseca Cerveira. Its site (*sítio*) is unknown. Religious services were held in it in 1754.
Santa Catarina Braga
See António Alfredo (I-72).
St Catherine (chapel)

In his quaint and picturesque manner of speech, Father Gaspar Frutuoso tells us ‘that Captain João Gonçalves… sheltering the ships by the islets, resolved to build his wooden residence on land, which he at once built close to the sea on a height, where the captain’s wife (*capitoa*, wife of the captain-donatary) Constança Rodrigues founded a church of Santa Catarina’. In that humble and obscure corner, later called Santa Catarina, the first stone was laid of the auspicious settlement of this archipelago, and therefore of the Portuguese colonisation that can never be praised enough. From the high, solitary rocky crest (*arrife*) the first donatary (*donatário*) directed the early work of this titanic task. The dense forest cover, the incredibly rugged terrain and the great shortage of labour made it extremely arduous and beset by insurmountable difficulties.

João Gonçalves Zarco, the first and foremost pioneer of the colonisation of Madeira, had his modest and earliest residence built there, commanding the whole vast amphitheatre of Funchal. Dona Constança de Almeida, his heroic and pious companion, had a small, devout chantry (capela) built close by, dedicated to St Catherine, the learned and glorious martyr of the city of Alexandria.

Although the historian of the islands emphatically calls it a ‘church’, it would have been only a poor and modest chapel of cramped dimensions, built of wood like the first dwellings of that period. The material was perhaps chosen from the fragrant cedars (*juniperus* or *oxycerbus*) that abounded throughout the island, for it is known that other chantries were built with the precious wood of these trees.

The exact time of its rebuilding, when all the timber of the original structure disappeared, is not known, but it is conjectured to have taken place in the third or last quarter of the 15th century. The present chantry was a further reconstruction which, as we have read somewhere, was carried out around the end of the 17th century, and it has received various repairs over time. The upper lintel of the portal still bears the date 1425, which attests to its antiquity; it is not known, however, whether this inscribed stone belonged to the first or the second reconstruction.

For Madeirans this old chapel is a true historic monument, an object of the highest and most respectful veneration. In its humility, its smallness and even its poverty, it is an immemorial commemorative pillar (*padrão*) that eloquently recalls the discovery of our archipelago and the beginning of the admirable work of its colonisation. As such it must be preserved with patriotic and religious care by rulers and ruled alike, showing our contemporaries and generations to come the devoted esteem with which we know how to preserve the glorious traditions of the past.

Yet another weighty reason counsels and urges this: its venerable antiquity. Contrary to what the author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) and his learned commentator asserted, when they named the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*) and the chapel of St Sebastian on the Largo do Chafariz (‘fountain square’) as the first chapels built on Madeira, it is now known, without fear of serious contradiction, that the little shrine of Santa Catarina was the first church raised on this island, as we already stated more than twenty years ago in the pages of the *Elucidário Madeirense*. This acknowledged priority should be regarded as yet another irrefutable claim on our heartfelt veneration and on our ardent support for the preservation and, where possible, the embellishment of so ancient and significant a monument. We believe that a stone inscription should be placed on one of the interior walls of the tiny church, bearing these or similar words: ‘This chapel, founded by the wife of João Gonçalves Zargo, was the first built on Madeira and recalls the discovery of this island and the beginning of its settlement.’

Since it is so closely related to what has been set out above, we cannot resist the wish to transcribe here the words we have already written elsewhere, which may perhaps be of some interest to the readers of this *Elucidário*:

‘Around 1425 Constança Rodrigues de Almeida, wife of João Gonçalves Zarco, founded the chapel of Santa Catarina, and “beside it,” says Frutuoso, “she built many houses to lodge women of good life, poor *mercieiras* (almswomen: poor women kept on alms in return for serving a chapel), to whom she left alms so that they should for ever take care to clean and serve that house (the chapel), as is still the custom today.” These words are commented on by Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo as follows: “The *Mercearia* of Santa Catharina... was a kind of hospice, where poor women of good morals lived on alms and were responsible for keeping the saint’s chapel clean. Both have been preserved to the present day. They are the property of the Count of Castello-Melhor.”’

We can add nothing to what has been transcribed, nor do we know whether Constança de Almeida’s foundation really survived until 1873, though doubtless in a form different from the original institution. What we can now affirm is that the institution disappeared long ago and that the houses and the chapel passed to other owners. This was certainly the first charitable institution in Madeira, and it lasted about four and a half centuries.

In the town (*vila*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), at the place still known today as Santa Catarina, stood the chapel of this dedication. We do not know when it was built or when it was demolished. We do know, however, that within the cemetery on the site of the old chapel a small chapel dedicated to the same saint was built, reserved solely for religious services in that cemetery. The image of St Catherine was greatly venerated by the inhabitants of Porto Santo. According to local tradition, Moorish pirates stole the image, and it was ransomed for a large sum and restored to worship in its chapel on that island.
The locality (*sítio*) of Santa Catarina, in the town of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), takes its name from the chapel of that dedication which Gonçalo de Freitas had built there in the 15th century.
In 1505 Rodrigo Enes founded the chapel of Santa Catarina in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), at the locality that still bears that name.
There was also a chapel of the same dedication in the parish of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’).
St Clare (church)

‘The captain, says Frutuoso, resolved to make his residence (as he did) on a height that stands above Funchal, and directly opposite his lodgings he founded a church of Our Lady of the Conception as his family vault (looking, most prudently, to the end at the very beginning), which is commonly called Nossa Senhora de Cima, because it is built above the town on a hillock at the foot of a peak...’

As is well known, and as the passage quoted shows, it was the discoverer of Madeira who founded the chantry (*capela*) of Our Lady known as Conceição de Cima, to distinguish it from Nossa Senhora da Conceição de Baixo (Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception ‘Below’) (volume II, page 451), and he intended it as the burial place of himself and his descendants. With the founding of the Convent of St Clare (volume I, page 309), adjoining the chapel of the Conceição, the church’s name gradually fell out of use and the convent’s name prevailed. Some years later it came to cover both buildings, so that the two shared a single name: the convent and church of St Clare.

Nothing of Zargo’s building survives today. The chapel underwent various alterations, and in the second half of the 17th century it was demolished when the present church was built. For Madeirans this church has great historical value, and it should command the deepest veneration from all. Within its walls lie the ashes of the discoverer of Madeira.

As patron of this church, João Gonçalves Zargo would no doubt have been buried in the chancel, beside the steps of the high altar of the old chapel. We read in an old manuscript ‘that the work was so arranged that Zarco’s grave lay in the middle of the chancel, with a stone tomb above it so tall that it makes it singularly venerable and worthy of respect. It is said that, many years later, the nuns obtained the removal of the imposing mausoleum, because it blocked their view of the altar, above all during the celebration of the divine offices.

The donataries of Funchal (see Donataries) ceased for good to reside on this island after the beginning of Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640). It must therefore be supposed that the removal of the discoverer’s mausoleum, or of a considerable part of it, took place after the year 1580, for we cannot accept that the captains-donatary would have permitted such a profanation of the sarcophagus of their predecessor, the founder of the house they represented.

It is a constant tradition that the remains of the illustrious discoverer of Madeira lie in the tomb at the far end of the church, beside the lower choir (coro de baixo). The tomb has been widely reproduced in engravings in many Portuguese and foreign works. It bears an inscription in Gothic lettering, now illegible, but on the adjacent floor the following words can be read:

Tomb of Captain Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcellos, which he had made for himself and his heirs on the removal of the first gravestone that was placed here, as a descendant of the first Martim Mendes de Vasconcellos, who lies here and who came to this island to marry Elena Gonçalves da Câmara, daughter of João Gonçalves Zarco, the discoverer of this island. It was made in the year 1710.

Does the Gothic inscription refer to Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, Zargo’s son-in-law, or to the discoverer himself, as someone has already claimed? It is our opinion that the inscription refers to the husband of Helena Gonçalves da Câmara.

And when did the translation of the remains take place? When the showy mausoleum was removed? When the church was rebuilt in the second half of the 17th century? When the body of Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcelos was laid in the grave? Or on some other occasion still? Nothing is known for certain on this matter, and there has been no lack of people who have asserted that the translation never took place, and that the discoverer’s ashes still lie beside the high altar, in the original place where they were laid. Nevertheless, it is not easy to overturn with a simple denial the unbroken tradition that holds the discoverer of Madeira to be buried in the tomb of his son-in-law Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos (see *Lápides* (‘Tablets’)).

In March 1919, while a floor was being laid in the chancel of this church, the gravestones covering the bones of the 2nd, 3rd and 5th donataries (*donatário*) of Funchal were discovered. In the centre, beside the steps of the high altar, lies a dark-coloured sepulchral slab bearing this epitaph: ‘Tomb of João Gonçalves da Câmara, second captain of this island.’ In the same chancel, on the Epistle side, another stone of the same colour was found, with the following inscription: ‘Tomb of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara....3rd captain of this island. Here lies Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, Count of Calheta (‘small cove’) and fifth captain of this island.’ We should note that on the stone bearing these last epitaphs two lines have been struck through, a circumstance for which we cannot offer any plausible explanation. No gravestone was found on the Gospel side. These tombs contain no reference whatever to the burial of the discoverer, which would be strange if his mortal remains had in fact stayed there. The third donatary, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, died in Matosinhos, but his remains were carried to Funchal and buried in the Convent of St Clare, as the epitaph transcribed above shows. João Gonçalves da Câmara, the 4th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*), died in Funchal and was buried in the Convent of St Clare, although no reference to his burial is to be found there.

The librarian of the Funchal Council, Adolfo César de Noronha, tried to found an art museum in the outbuildings of this church, making use of various paintings and other works of art that had belonged to several convents and were scattered about. Despite the praiseworthy and diligent efforts he made, his initiative met with not the slightest success.
Santa Cruz (cove, harbour, quay and stream)

The landing place of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) is formed by a cove of some size, which Frutuoso called a ‘beautiful cove’. It is partly lined by a stony beach where, in calm weather, small boats can easily come in. At the point in the bay where a reef (restinga) lies close to the shore, the reef was used to build a small landing place in 1845, which was improved in 1870. The present quay, larger and better suited to handling the traffic of the port, was built on the orders of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) in 1908-1909, making use of the works that had already been carried out earlier.
The town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz is crossed by the stream of the same name, which rises in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) and flows into the ocean.
Santa Cruz (parish)
We read in ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*):

‘Close by there stood a shady wood, where from an ancient fallen trunk a holy and precious gibbet [the Cross] was fashioned at Zargo’s command, and in the midst of the valley, then so fair, it was raised up by his Portuguese, so that, should a settlement be built there, it would keep the name of Santa Cruz [Holy Cross].’

The historian of the islands also says: ‘rounding a bend in the land, they entered a fine cove on the shore, where they saw a fair and delightful valley covered with trees set in order, and there on the ground they found some old stumps felled by time. From these the captain ordered a cross to be made, which he at once had raised on high on a tree, giving the place the name Sancta Cruz, where afterwards a noble town was founded...’

To commemorate the raising of the cross at the time of the discovery, a marble monumental cross was erected on the very spot, so tradition says. A storm blew it down in 1889, and it was rebuilt the following year. The old marble cross bore the arms of the Moniz family, and it was probably a member of this family who had it built. This fully explains the origin of the name of this parish (*freguesia*), which is one of the oldest and one of the places where the colonisation of Madeira began earliest.

The parish soon grew in importance and developed with remarkable speed. It quickly rivalled the neighbouring and rival settlement of Machico, which, according to some old documents, it soon came to surpass, except for the position Machico enjoyed as seat of the captaincy and residence of the donataries.

For the oldest parishes of this island, such as Machico, Santa Cruz, Câmara de Lobos, Ribeira Brava, etc., the year in which they were created is not known with complete precision. They were originally centres of population, or “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*), with their own chapels and private chaplains, as we have already noted with regard to the last of these parishes. Santa Cruz would have been created as an autonomous parish in the second quarter of the 15th century. The learned annotator of the *Saudades* says that ‘Santa Cruz was created shortly after Machico was constituted, the latter taking precedence solely because it was the head of the captaincy’. What we said elsewhere about the creation of the parish of Machico (volume II, page 294) applies here too: it is not very likely that this parish and that of Santa Cruz were created later than the parishes of Câmara de Lobos, Caniço and Ribeira Brava, as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo maintains.

The oldest document concerning this parish, cited in the *Indice Geral do Registo da Provedoria*, is the royal decree (alvará régio) of 5 December 1580, which fixed the vicar’s annual salary at 24,756 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). The royal decree of 9 July 1590 raised this to 15,000 *réis* in cash, 4 *moios* of wheat and 2 *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. A further 3,000 *réis* a year was added in 1600. The earliest parish priest known from the parish archive is Friar Hercules da Cunha, a native of Calheta (‘small cove’), who was already serving there in 1538. He was succeeded by João Drumond; around 1597 by the licentiate Belchior Rebelo (1604); then Francisco Duarte Morais (1622), António da Rocha (1637), Henrique Madureira de Figueiredo (1650), Tristão de Mendonça Vasconcelos (1674), Manuel Ferreira Teixeira (1687), the licentiate António Ferreira de Andrade (1693) and Estêvão Lomelino de Vasconcelos (1709).

A royal decree of 27 August 1589 established a curacy (*curato*) in this parish, with a stipend (*côngrua*) of 20$00 *réis* a year, to which the royal decree of 23 May 1747 added a further 40,000 *réis*, also annually.

We stated (volume II, page 294) that the collegiate church of Machico was established by the royal decree of 18 June 1572. In fact it already existed by then, as did that of Santa Cruz: the decree concerned the increase in the salary of the six beneficiaries of the two collegiate churches, which rose from 10$00 *réis* a year to 12,000 *réis*. The royal decrees of 9 July 1590 and 2 January 1610 raised these salaries, respectively, to 21,000 *réis* a year, and to 61,000 *réis* in cash, 2 *moios* of wheat and 1 *pipa* of wine, also annually.

The royal decree of 17 November 1557 created the post of preacher. Under the royal decree of 15 October 1644 this office was later entrusted to the guardian of the convent in the same parish, who performed it himself or through his friars, with a salary of 30,000 *réis* a year.
This collegiate church also had the post of organist, created before 6 February 1592, since a document of that date raises the organist’s salary to 6,000 *réis* a year.

The parish had its seat in a small chapel built there in the very first days of the colonisation, whose dedication was probably São Salvador, the present patron saint of the parish church. An old nobiliary tells us that this church was built in 1533 under the direction of João de Freitas (volume II, page 54), a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*). By a warrant (*provisão*) of 29 September of that year the king made him a royal grant of the chancel as a family vault for himself and his family, in recognition of the expense and labour the building had cost him. The church has undergone various repairs and restorations, and some have suggested that the side aisles are not part of the original building, which seems to us hardly admissible. It is the largest church outside Funchal and has three aisles, although one reads elsewhere that they are not three clearly defined aisles. It is in a fair state of repair and, says the annotator of the *Saudades*, contains ‘besides the altars, three further chapels, namely: the chancel, which the king granted to João de Freitas for his services, and especially for having given the land for the church and overseen its building; the chapel of São Tiago, now of the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*), founded by João de Morais; and that of the Almas, belonging to the Pereiras, who came from Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’)’.

The parish has the chapels of São Pedro, Santo Amaro, Our Lady of Remedies, Our Lady of Pity, Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception and St Elizabeth of Portugal. There were other chapels that the passage of time and human neglect have caused to disappear: those of Santa Catarina, São Lázaro, Our Lady of Grace, St Giles, São Francisco Xavier, Our Lady of the Peña de Francia, Jesus Cristo, Our Lady of the Rosary, St Joseph, São Fernando and St Sebastian. A brief account of these chapels will be given elsewhere in this work.

A large number of nobles and knights settled in this parish in the days of colonisation. Some of them founded entailed houses and became the founders of distinguished families. Among these we shall mention Antão Álvares de Carvalho, João Escórcio Drumond, João de Freitas (Volume II, page 54), Urbano and João Baptista Lomelino (Volume II, page 281), Pedro Álvares de Almadas Nuno da Costa, João Afonso Escudeiro (Volume I, page 136), Pedro Lopes de Figueiredo, Rui Gramacho, Lopo Lordelo, Antão Álvares de Sousa, etc.

Several members of the family of João de Freitas distinguished themselves heroically in our campaigns in Africa and Asia. The following passages, which we found in an old document, bear on the subject of this article: ‘Jordão de Freitas, whose deeds the historians of Asia describe at length, was born in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz and was captain of Moluco, lord of the islands of Ambon and Siam by grant of Dom Manuel, King of Ternate, in the year 1537, confirmed by King John III in the year 1543. Gonçalo de Freitas da Silva, his son and a native of the same town, served valiantly in India, where he held the same lordship, confirmed by King Sebastian in the year 1574. Jordão de Freitas da Silva, son of the latter, was sent as ambassador to France concerning the recovery of the artillery and other property of the fleet that was lost there in the year 1626; he died while pursuing this claim, and for this service his son Gonçalo de Freitas received the commandery of Santa Maria de Lisboa in the Order of Christ.’
We have already dealt in this work with the illustrious natives of Santa Cruz Friar Remígio da Assunção (volume I, page 101) and Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira (volume III, page 9).

The principal localities of this parish are: Vila, Serrado da Vila, Morena, Estreito, Espigão, São Fernando, Palmeira, Rego, Regadinhas, Lombo da Calçada, Fonte dos Almocreves, Eiras Velhas, Bom Jesus, Fazenda, Lombada, Dona Mécia, Fajocos, Ribeira de Santa Cruz, Águas Belas, Moinho da Serra, Levadas, Roma, Moreno, Eiras, Janeiro, Terça, Santa Catarina, Cano, São Sebastião, Calçada de São Gil, São Gil and Relação. The parish has 7,054 inhabitants (1921).
Santa Cruz (town and municipality)

The illustrious annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) is of the opinion that Machico was raised to the status of town (*vila*) at the same time as Funchal, that is, around 1452, although the royal diplomas granting these privileges and prerogatives to the two settlements are not to be found in the archives of their respective captaincies. Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), set within the captaincy of Machico, grew in importance soon after the discovery of Madeira. The increase in its population, together with its commercial and agricultural development, allowed it to rival its neighbour, so much so that its inhabitants asked for it to be granted the privileges of a town. Manuel I granted this by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 20 June 1515.

This letter, which is transcribed in full in the *Saudades*, on pages 505 ff., was presented at the seat of the captaincy of Machico on 17 July 1515 so that it could be put into immediate effect. Some councillors (*vereadores*) lodged objections to the creation of the new town, but these objections came to nothing, lacking both legal grounds and the support of the captain-donatary Tristão Vaz Teixeira. The rivalry between the two towns seems to date from this period; it has persisted through the centuries and even at present has not entirely faded.

When a new charter (foral) was granted to the city of Funchal in August 1515, the towns of Machico and Santa Cruz, forgetting their old rivalry for a moment, promptly asked jointly for a charter as well. It was granted to them, with various privileges and exemptions, by royal letter of 15 December 1515.

The town of Santa Cruz did not, however, free itself entirely from the tutelage of the captaincy of Machico, for its donataries continued to intervene in many matters of military and criminal jurisdiction. This tutelage came to a complete end only with the death of the last donatary of Machico. The very royal letter creating the town says: ‘. . . . e ho capitam da dita billa de Machiquo teraa na dita billa de Santa Cruz e seu termo asy ha cadeia e todallas outras liberdades que ateeaqui teue...’ (‘and the captain of the said town of Machico shall have in the said town of Santa Cruz and its *termo* [municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca] the gaol and all the other liberties that he has had hitherto’)

Especially from a commercial and industrial point of view, the town surpassed Machico in importance, and this led at once to the creation of a customs house, which we have already discussed at some length on page 43 of volume I of this work. From the many references we have found to this revenue house, from the number and standing of its officials, and from the records of various decrees entered in the books of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) of Funchal, we see that the customs house of the town of Santa Cruz was more important and busier than that of Machico, even though the latter stood at the seat of the captaincy.

The town had a charitable institution of some importance, its Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), of which an account has already been given in the article Misericórdias (volume II, page 376).

The municipality (*concelho*) of Santa Cruz is at present made up of the parishes (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz, Água de Pena (part), Santo da Serra (part), Gaula, Camacha and Caniço. The decree of 19 October 1852, which detached the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) from the municipality of Santana (‘St Anne’) and incorporated it into that of Machico, also separated some localities from the latter municipality and joined them to the municipality of Santa Cruz. This provoked vigorous protests from the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Machico and from various official bodies and private individuals of the same municipality. After a series of incidents that seemed endless, the secretary-general of the district, António Lopes Barbosa de Albuquerque, acting as civil governor, convened a meeting at the Casa dos Romeiros (‘pilgrims’ house’) in the parish of Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) on 11 September 1862. It brought together representatives of the Municipal Councils of Machico and Santa Cruz, the administrators of the municipalities, various public officials and other persons of standing. There a new municipal and parish division – the present one – was definitively agreed, and so the complaints and protests raised on both sides came to an end.

On more than one occasion the inhabitants of the parishes of Caniço and Camacha have petitioned the central government to have these parishes annexed to the municipality of Funchal, but the request was never granted. In March 1928 the building that housed the law courts and other municipal public offices caught fire. A large new building was then built to serve as the new town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) and also to accommodate the offices that had been housed in the burnt building; it was inaugurated at the beginning of 1933.
St Elizabeth (chapels)

The chapel of this dedication found in the building of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) in this city is handsome and spacious, and is reached through the building’s entrance hall. It must have been built at the beginning of the 18th century. The high altar, of gilt carved woodwork (*talha dourada*), is of great beauty, though perhaps with an excessive crowding of ornament. (1921)
Next to the hospital of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) there also stands a chapel dedicated to St Elizabeth of Portugal.
Santa Luzia (parish)

Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) is one of the four urban parishes (*freguesia*) of Funchal and forms part of the upper area of the city. It is the most recently created of the parishes of this municipality (*concelho*), and was formed from land belonging to the parishes of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) and of Nossa Senhora do Monte.

Once it was recognised that the Sé parish needed to be relieved of a considerable share of its households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths'), so that parish services could be better organised, the chapel of St Lucy, standing on a rise on the left bank of the stream of the same name, was chosen as the seat of the new parish, which had been created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 28 December 1676. The General Index of the Register of the Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) reads: ‘Decree of the Lord King Peter II, of 28 December 1676, empowering the bishop Dom Friar António da Silva Teles to create a parish in the Chapel of St Lucy, assigning to the vicar a stipend (*côngrua*) and a suitable territory, with part of the parish of the Sé outside the walls and part of that of Nossa Senhora do Monte, since the curates of the Sé had nearly 6,000 souls to attend to within the city’. The first vicar was Father Amaro de Atouguia, whose annual salary was set by the royal decree of 24 July 1681 at 21,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, 1 *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and one and a half *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat.
The same index cites the royal decree of 13 August 1745, which created a curacy (*curato*) in this parish with an annual salary of one and a half *pipas* of wine and one and a half *moios* of wheat.

The chapel of St Lucy was built at the end of the 15th century. Being in an advanced state of ruin, it collapsed in the first quarter of the 18th century, and the seat of the parish was provisionally moved to the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação, in the convent of the same name.

The royal decree of 9 September 1719 ordered a new church to be built, but it seems that construction did not begin at once, since warrants of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) dated 14 January, 13 February and 3 December 1740 authorised various payments to complete the works on the new church. It must be supposed that the work was only declared fully finished in 1741. This is the present church, which was built at a site somewhat removed from the old chapel, then known as Santa Luzia Velha.

This parish contained the chapels of São Francisco Xavier, Nossa Senhora da Boa Viagem, Nossa Senhora da Esperança, Nossa Senhora da Pena, Nossa Senhora do Vale, Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres, Our Lady of Consolation (*Nossa Senhora da Consolação*) and Nossa Senhora do Descanso (Our Lady of Rest), of which only the last two survive. We give an account of all of them elsewhere.

Within the bounds of this parish stood the convent of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação, which we have already discussed. In its convent grounds a large building was put up to serve as the Diocesan Seminary, and it is today the District General Council Palace (*Palácio da Junta Geral*) (see Seminary). Also in this parish is the Old People’s Home (*Asilo dos Velhinhos*), maintained by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) (see Asylums and Little Sisters of the Poor) (1921).

The central station of the Monte Railway (*Caminho de Ferro do Monte*) and its main installations are in this parish (volume I, page 221), as is the important industrial establishment known as the Fábrica do Torreão, to which we have already referred on page 394 of volume I of this work.

We have already dealt, in the article Levadas on page 235 of volume II, with the abundant and rich water source called the Levada de Santa Luzia, a levada (irrigation channel) whose important aqueduct crosses a considerable part of this parish. Alongside the levada runs an excellent road, which stretches from near the Santa Luzia stream to the northern end of the avenue of Pedro José d’Ornelas. It offers striking views over the bay, the city and its surroundings. It is one of the sections that are to make up the planned ring road of Funchal.
On 3 March 1898 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) granted permission to enlarge the old churchyard of Santa Luzia, and work began shortly afterwards.

According to the *Mappa alphabetico das ruas da Cidade*, approved by the civil governor on 5 October 1863, the boundaries of the parish of Santa Luzia were set as follows: the northern side of Rua do Carmo, between the bridge and the Vale brook; the eastern side of Rua das Hortas (Alferes Veiga Pestana) as far as Rua do Bom Jesus; this last street, on both sides, but only as far as Rua da Conceição (Correia Heredia); the Levadinha das Hortas; the part of Rua da Princesa (31 de Janeiro) that lies above the Ponte Nova (‘new bridge’) and adjoins it; and the start of the Calçada da Incarnação. Under the same map, the buildings on the northern side of Rua do Carmo but west of the Vale brook, Rua da Fábrica, Rua da Conceição, Rua da Ponte Nova and Rua da Princesa below the same bridge were assigned to the parish of the Sé, as was the part of Rua do Bom Jesus west of the said Rua da Conceição.

The parish priests of the Sé and of Santa Luzia include in the latter parish the eastern and western sides of Rua das Hortas below Rua do Bom Jesus, and the northern and southern sides of that street between Rua das Hortas and Rua da Conceição. Some public offices, however, regard the southern side of Rua do Bom Jesus as part of the parish of the Sé. Some also hold that the northern side of Rua do Carmo, between Rua das Hortas and the Vale brook, belongs to the parish of Santa Luzia rather than to that of the Sé.

To the east, the parish of Santa Luzia extends as far as the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’), and to the north it reaches above the Levada de Santa Luzia, without, however, reaching the Quinta da Paz on the Monte road.
Santa Maria (Dom Friar José de)

This pious bishop of Funchal was the son of Luís de Saldanha, steward (*viador*) of the household of Queen Luisa de Guzmán, and of Dona Violante de Mendonça. Embracing the monastic life, he entered the Capuchin order, where he was professor of arts and theology and held other important offices besides. Peter II appointed him bishop of this diocese in 1689, and he was confirmed by Pope Alexander VIII on 6 March 1690. On 25 November of that year he received episcopal consecration at the hands of Cardinal de Lencastre.

In March 1691 he entered his diocese and devoted himself entirely to the care of his flock. He visited the parishes of his bishopric several times, despite the roughness of the roads and the difficulty of transport and lodging in the places he travelled through. He was most zealous in ensuring that Christian doctrine was taught, and had a pastoral letter printed in which this matter was regulated and enforced with the utmost rigour. He convened a synod in the diocese, at which serious measures were taken on many points of ecclesiastical discipline that had long fallen into disuse.

Dom Friar José de Santa Maria was of a resigned and kindly disposition, and he bore with true Christian humility the high-handedness and vexations of the captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) Dom Rodrigo da Costa. Besides his irascible and despotic temperament, Dom Rodrigo enjoyed the open protection of his relatives, who belonged to the highest nobility and held the loftiest offices in the nation.

After a short episcopate of five years, he requested and obtained his transfer, and in recognition of his great merits and virtues he was placed in one of the principal sees of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). Transferred to the bishopric of Porto, he died there in the odour of sanctity on 26 October 1708, according to Dom António Caetano de Sousa.
He left Madeira on 15 September 1696, the day on which he relinquished the episcopal administration of this diocese.
St Mary Magdalene (chapels)

Anyone leaving Funchal along the Caminho de Santo António (‘St Anthony’) will come upon, at the roadside some two kilometres from the city centre, the ruins of an old, dilapidated chapel. From that heap of rubble the ruined façade still rises proudly, as if defying the fury of the centuries. Its pointed-arch doorway reveals its antiquity and the character of the buildings of an age of glory. It is one of the few vestiges of the Manueline style that still survive on this island.

This is the chapel of Santa Maria Madalena, which gave its name to the locality (*sítio*), more commonly known by the popular shortened form of Madalena (‘Magdalene’). After St Maurus, it is the oldest chapel in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António. We lack, however, the precise information needed to determine when it was founded, which does not seem to us to be later than the first quarter of the 16th century. The earliest reference to it that we have found dates from 1593, the year in which it received the grant of a quit-rent (*foro*). After the aforementioned chapel of St Maurus, it was also the most important in that parish for its antiquity, its size and its architectural style, and also for the devotion the faithful showed to its patron saint. It even came to own property of its own, of some importance, for the maintenance of its worship, something we are not aware that any other chapel in this parish possessed.

By a public deed of 11 March 1684, José Machado de Miranda took on the role of patron of this chapel. He had it rebuilt and endowed it with a quit-rent of four thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year, charged on the Quinta das Maravilhas. Major repairs were carried out on it in 1732, 1766 and 1773, but by 1820 it was already far gone in ruin.

In the locality (*sítio*) of Florenças, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’), there was a chapel of the same dedication, founded by João Portes Homem de El-Rei and his wife Dona Maria de Sousa in the year 1684. The chapel of Santa Maria Madalena in the parish of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) is one of the oldest in the north of Madeira. Over the years it has undergone various repairs and additions, and today it is a chapel of no small size. It was enlarged in 1789 and was extended once more only a few years ago. It once held a fine oil painting of its patron saint, which was not properly looked after and has been lost entirely. It may be said to be the seat of the parish’s curacy (*curato*), and beside the chapel stands a residence intended for the assistant priest (*coadjutor*) of the curacy. There is a cemetery close by.
It is the centre of an old and well-attended pilgrimage, held in July every year, and in former times a fair was held there at which a great deal of livestock was brought.
Santa Maria Maior (parish)
The parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) lies on the eastern side of the city of Funchal and is one of its four parishes.

It owes this name to the fact that its original parish church was larger than the chapel built by João Gonçalves Zarco on the site where the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) stands today, both being dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*). In former times it was also known as Conceição de Baixo (Lower Conceição), the other being called Conceição de Cima (Upper Conceição). It was likewise called Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), because it was built not far from the beach; this is the name that has lasted longest among the people, and it is still in use today. This parish became widely known, and still is at present, as the parish of Socorro (‘succour’), a name applied especially to the part of it lying between the parish church and the left bank of the Ribeira de João Gomes (‘João Gomes’s stream’). The name came from the image of Our Lady of Succour (*Nossa Senhora do Socorro*), which was venerated in the parish church and was in former times the object of fervent devotion among the inhabitants of Funchal.

We have already given an account of the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*) elsewhere (volume II, page 451), and we shall deal with the church of São Tiago (St James the Greater), to which the seat of the parish was transferred in 1803, at the appropriate place in this work.

On the creation of this parish we have said enough in the article Parishes (volume II, page 52), to which we refer the reader. It may be stated that this was the first parish of the archipelago and is at present the oldest.

When the magnificent church of the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) was built, the seat of the parish of Santa Maria Maior was transferred to the new and spacious church, around 1508. Some fifty years later, as the population kept on growing, the parish (*freguesia*) was divided by the royal decree (*alvará régio*) of 18 November 1557 into two independent parishes, with their respective seats in the Cathedral and in the church of Our Lady of Calhau.

After the Franciscan friars, it seems that Nuno Cão (see that entry) was one of the first priests to perform parish duties in this parish. He moved to the Cathedral in 1508 and in 1514 was raised to dean of that same Cathedral. When the parish was divided in 1537, the first vicar of Santa Maria Maior was the licentiate Antonio Mourão, to whom the royal decree of 23 February 1558 assigned an annual stipend of 20,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and two *moios* of wheat.
The curacy (*curato*) of this parish was created by royal decree of 27 August 1589, with an annual salary of 20,000 *réis*.

This church had a collegiate body, created by the royal decree of 18 November 1557. Besides the vicar and the curate, it comprised three further beneficiaries, whose number was later raised to six, together with a treasurer, a preacher and an organist.

This parish has the chapels of St Elmo, Our Lady of Good Success, Nossa Senhora do Faial (Our Lady of Faial) and Our Lady Mother of Mankind, as well as others that have since disappeared, of all of which we shall give a brief account.

Within this parish lie the former square (*campo*) of Carlos I, now named after Almirante Reis, the fortress of São Tiago (St James the Greater), the Campo da Barca (‘boat field’) or Campo de Miguel Bombarda, the Land Disinfection Station (*Posto de Desinfecção Terrestre*), the electric light works and other industrial establishments.

The parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior has a population of 7,823 inhabitants (1921). It begins at the Ribeira de João Gomes. Its eastern boundary is customarily taken to be the western or left-hand half of the Caminho do Palheiro and the Caminho da Terça (‘third part’), while the eastern or right-hand half belongs to the parish of São Gonçalo. It should be noted, however, that these boundaries do not agree with those marked in the *Mappa Alphabetico* of the city’s streets, approved by the civil governor on 15 December 1863. That map clearly states that the whole of the Rua do Palheiro, from the Quinta do Acciaioly or Quinta do Faial as far as the Rua Bela de São Tiago, belongs to the parish of Santa Maria Maior, and that this parish extends as far as the locality (*sítio*) of Louros (‘laurels’); the lane of Olaria, now the Travessa do Lazareto (‘quarantine hospital’), nevertheless lies in the parish of São Gonçalo. According to the same map, the area between the Rua Bela de São Tiago and the building of Tomás Teodoro, on the Calçada do Socorro (‘Succour causeway’), belongs on its northern side to Santa Maria Maior and on its southern side to São Gonçalo. The southern part of the Largo da Forca (‘gallows’) and of the Caminho do Lazareto, up to the point where the locality of Louros begins, must therefore be considered part of the latter parish.
See City boundaries, Parishes, Our Lady of Calhau, Académica (Praça), Cão (Nuno), Order of Christ, Carlos (Campo de D.) and Disinfection Station.
St Quiteria (chantries)

Writing about the chantry (capela) of this dedication, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states that it was founded by Simão de Nobrega in Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’), which is plainly a mistake. This chantry stood in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’) and was built by Second Lieutenant Simão de Nobrega e Sousa and his wife Maria Tavares de Sousa on the *quinta* (country estate) they owned in the locality (*sítio*) of Pico do Cardo (‘thistle peak’), in that parish. In Curral das Freiras there was only the chapel of St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*), which the nuns of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) had built. The chantry of Santa Quitéria was built in 1727, and its deed of endowment is dated 3 July of that year. By 1814 it had been deconsecrated, and divine worship had not been celebrated in it for many years. It gave its name to the locality in which it was built.

There was another chantry of the same dedication in the locality of Lombo da Estrela (‘ridge of the star’), in the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’), founded in 1724 by João Homem de Abreu and his wife Dona Ana Quitéria or Luzia. The deed of endowment is dated 30 May of that year.
A chantry of Santa Quitéria, founded by Father João da Silva Alves, once existed in the parish of Madalena do Mar (‘Magdalene by the sea’).
Santa Teresa (Friar Francisco de)
Carmelite friar, a native of Funchal, who died in 1698. Works: *Alphabetum Theologicum*.
Santana

The earliest known person to bear this surname was called Manuel de Santana e Vasconcelos and lived in the second half of the 18th century. According to the *Attestado Genealogico* of the Sant'Anna family, those who bear this surname descend from the Moniz de Bettencourt.
St Anne (chapels)
The chapel of St Anne in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Roque (‘St Roch’) was built by Francisco Dias in 1607. Services are still held there.

In the locality (*sítio*) of Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’), in the parish of São Martinho, at the place now called Santana (‘St Anne’), Agostinho Pedro de Vasconcelos Teixeira built a chapel of this dedication in 1780, on the *quinta* (country estate) he owned there; its deed of endowment is dated 22 April of the same year. It still exists, as does the house that adjoined it.

A chapel of the same dedication was built in the locality of Cruz do Carvalho (‘oak cross’), in the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), in 1790, by Dr António Dionísio da Silva Conde, judge of orphans (*juiz dos órfãos*) in Funchal.

A chapel of St Anne stands in ruins in the locality of Ribeira da Fernanda (‘Fernanda’s stream’), in the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’). It belonged to the Cardoso entail (*morgado*).
In the parish of Machico, on the Quinta Santana, there is a well-preserved chapel with this patron saint. We do not know the name of its founder or the year it was built.

There was a chapel of the same dedication in the locality of Fajã do Penedo (‘boulder flat’), in the parish of Boaventura (‘good fortune’), founded in 1768 by the holder of the entail António Francisco de Caires and his wife Teresa Maria de Barros; its deed of endowment is dated 20 April of that year. According to what we were told, it was demolished shortly after 1840.
Santana e Vasconcelos (Dona Maria do Monte)
See Bettencourt (Dona Maria do Monte de Santana e Vasconcelos Moniz de).
Santana e Vasconcelos (Henrique de)
He was born on this island and was a senior official of the customs houses (*Alfândegas*).

He represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislative session of 1884 to 1887. When Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira gave up his seat as deputy for this archipelago for the 1887 to 1889 legislature, Henrique de Santana was called to fill the vacancy, as the candidate with the most votes.
Santana e Vasconcelos (Jacinto de)
See Nogueiras (Viscount of).
Santana e Vasconcelos (João de)

He was born in Funchal in 1825 and began his public life as a primary schoolteacher on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). In 1856 he was appointed interim clerk (*escrivão*) of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), and was confirmed in the post by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 3 January 1859. He contributed to the Madeiran newspapers *A Discussão*, *A Madeira*, *O Semanário Official*, etc., publishing some interesting articles in the last of these on the *colonia* (Madeiran tenancy in which the landlord owns the land and the tenant the improvements, the produce being shared). He was a knight of the Order of the Tower and Sword for services rendered in Funchal during the cholera epidemic of 1856, and for many years he led the now defunct Regenerator party in Madeira. He died in Funchal on 27 December 1892.
Santana e Vasconcelos (Manuel de)

He was born in Funchal in 1798 and died in that city on 23 February 1851. He held the post of municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) and wrote *Clamor aos madeirenses* (Lisbon, 1835) and *Revista histórica do proselitismo anti-catholico na ilha Madeira pelo dr. Roberto Reid Kalley, medico escocez, desde 1838 até hoje* (Funchal, 1845).
Santana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Bettencourt (João de)

He was born in Funchal in 1806. On 9 August 1834 he was appointed superintendent (provedor) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), later becoming municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of the same island, a post he held for many years. He was also interim Civil Governor of the district of Funchal from 8 to 18 January 1862. He wrote the ‘Annals of the Municipality of Porto Santo’ (*Anais do Município do Porto Santo*), the original of which is held in the archive of that municipality, and he was one of the men who rendered the greatest services to that island. He died in Funchal on 22 June 1874.
Santana (parish)

This parish (*freguesia*) is, beyond any possible dispute, one of the most beautiful in Madeira and the most picturesque and enchanting in the whole north of the island. We shall not describe it from the point of view of its landscape and natural beauties. Our pen, after long and intimate contact with names, dates and facts, has grown barren and no longer lends itself to the literary genre in which the pompous finery of poetry adapts easily to the precision and rigour of description. Besides, this parish has been celebrated in prose and verse by so many brilliant and authoritative pens!

It is the parish of Madeira that bears the strongest resemblance to our picturesque province of Minho, the so-called Garden of Portugal. One detail, deserving the highest appreciation, should be stressed here: in spring and summer the most central roads of the parish of Santana (‘St Anne’) are transformed into the walks of a vast and enchanting *quinta* (country estate). They are lined with hedges of box, hydrangeas, ferns and fuchsias (*mimos*) which, mingled with a great profusion of flowers, give these roads a charm and an appeal that can be found nowhere else. It is a detail that deserves special mention, for it is unique in Madeira and is certainly not often met with elsewhere in the world...

We do not know when the clearing of the land in this parish began, and therefore when its colonisation and settlement started. Lopo Fernandes Pinto, who died in 1500, ‘held as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), says Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo, a good part of the parish of Santana, and the lands called “of the island”, from which two entails were formed...’ Among the early settlers we know of Jerónimo Cordeiro, Guterres Teixeira, Cristóvão Gomes, Manuel Gil, João Dias and Simão Álvares, who gave his name to a locality (*sítio*), etc. Gaspar Frutuoso, referring to this parish in 1590, says: ‘they are lands for tillage, with much grain and livestock; there are many chestnuts and walnuts, and plenty of water and fruit of every kind’. Very interesting, though somewhat hyperbolic, are the words that Father Fernando Vaz devotes to this parish when he seeks to justify the patron saint given to it, St Anne. Here they are: ‘St Anne suited it admirably as patron, for in the epistle of her feast it is sung *Non timebit domui suae a frigoribus nivis*, since in winter, we cannot deny it, it is one of the coldest parishes on the island, lying very high. From the same epistle the people of Santana seem to take the programme of their lives. They are dauntless workers, and so it may be said of those people: *Panem otiosa non comedit*. It is there that the finest and most famous linen cloths, called *favo* and *moio*, are woven: *Sindonem fecit et vendidit*. The spindle and the distaff, once handled by queens themselves, have not yet been cast aside there, so that these words fit: *Digiti ejus apprehenderunt fusum*. When morning has not even thought of dawning, the lamp inside the thatched huts already lights the first labours, so that once more the *Non extinguetur in nocte lucerna ejus* may prove true. Whenever the chance arises, the farmer buys the plot his parents tilled and where, as children, they were raised, to which this applies: *Consideravit agrum et emit eum*. The woman of Santana is not the frivolous, pert, extravagant woman, dressed in the latest and worst fashion, and so these words justly belong to her: *tu supergressa es universas*. Finally, before so much beauty and virtue, those born there cannot help rejoicing, counting themselves happy to have so honourable a cradle: *surrexerunt filii ejus et beatissimam praedicaverunt*.’

In the same article from which these passages were taken we read: ‘that the people of this parish, though hard-working and honest, are nonetheless distrustful and... sly. Where tributes, taxes and similar matters are concerned, they seem Azorean. Let the events speak for themselves: those over the parish councils (*juntas de paróquia*) (volume II, page 205), some 36 years ago, and over the tax registers, and others that caused public officials so many frights and gave rise to political reprisals and regrettable excesses’.

The lands that make up this parish (*freguesia*) originally belonged to the parish of São Jorge (‘St George’), from which they were separated around the middle of the 16th century. A small chapel dedicated to St Anne gave its name to the locality (*sítio*), to the surrounding lands and later to the whole parish. The same happened with every parish on this island that bears a name of a non-secular character, as we have pointed out elsewhere.

The annotator of the *Saudades* gives this parish as created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 4 June 1552. What this decree first created was a chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, which did not correspond to an autonomous parish. The first chaplain held this post together with that of parish priest of São Jorge. Under the said decree, this curate or chaplain had been allotted 8,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year for the parish duties of São Jorge, and a *moio* of wheat and a *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine for his service in Santana. The royal decrees of 16 February 1565, 1 March 1577 and 9 June 1581, which we have found cited in the *Índice Geral* of the Treasury Superintendency (Provedoria da Fazenda), always refer to the curate chaplain (*capelão-curado*) and set his emoluments at 12,000 *réis* in cash and a *moio* of wheat, at 20,000 *réis* and at 25,000 *réis* respectively. In the royal decree of 1 December 1588 the priest who performed the parish duties there is already called *vigário-curado* (curate vicar), and he was assigned an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine. It was perhaps from the date of this decree, or a little before, that Santana began to form a truly independent and autonomous parish.

As already stated, the first curate chaplain held the post together with that of parish priest of São Jorge for a period of 13 years. Around 1565 the parish had its own chaplain, Father Sebastião de Moraes, who served there for thirty years. He was succeeded by Cristóvão Pires, who was parish priest until 1632. We can record the following clergy who performed parish duties in this parish: Manuel Teixeira (1635–1671), Cosme Pais da Cunha (1672–1681), António Luís da Silva (1681–1690), Gabriel Pontes de Miranda (1694–1707), António Telo de Meneses (1707–1730), Inácio de Freitas Leal (1730–1743), António Teixeira (1744–1769), António Francisco da Cruz Pestana (1770–1777), Miguel Caetano Moniz (1777–1789), José Gomes de Andrade (1789–1799), João de Freitas Pestana (1799–1809), Jerónimo Álvares da Silva Pinheiro (1815–1829), Marcelino João da Silva (1835–1864), Hipólito Cassiano de Freitas, João Maurício Henriques, João Gomes, Alfredo de Paula Sardinha, João Quirino Gonçalves and Joaquim Fernandes, who is the present parish priest (1921) and has been since 1905.

The year in which the original chapel of Santana was built is not known. It was the seat of the chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, and later of the parish, and it underwent various alterations until it was demolished when the present church was built at the end of the 17th century. About this church we find the following information in an article by Father Fernando de Menezes Vaz, published in the *Correio da Madeira* (‘Madeira Courier’) of 10 April 1923: ‘It was built in 1698, the government spending the sum of 1,193,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), and it was repaired 36 years later. The sacristy, built on the north side, was later rebuilt, in 1745, on the south side, as this was the drier spot and the church furnishings and vestments kept better there. The bell-cote was also put up at that time. In the first quarter of the 19th century the church floor was badly damaged, or rather the church had no floor at all, and the people had to carry in bundles of myrtle, which they spread on the ground so that they could kneel. A committee was then formed, made up of Father Marcelino João da Silva, Carlos Frederico Accioli and Lieutenant Francisco António Jardim, to raise donations so that the floor could be laid anew, as was duly done. In the last few years the church has been re-lined, painted and re-floored, and its churchyard and surroundings have been embellished, thanks to the energy and initiative of its present, zealous parish priest, Joaquim Fernandes’.

In this parish (*freguesia*) there are the chapel of Santo António (St Anthony of Padua), in the locality (*sítio*) of the same name, which we shall deal with elsewhere, and a hotel that is very popular during the hot season.

Principal localities: Igreja, Parlatório, Barreiro, Serra de Água, Faias, Caminho Chão, Pico do Tanoeiro, Achada do Gramacho, Achada da Cruz, Fonte Grande, Pinheiro, Pico Silveira, Curral Velho, Fonte da Pedra, Serrado, Achada do Pampilar, Queimadas e Fontes, Pico de António Fernandes, Achada de Simão Alves, Lombo do Curral, Feiteira de Nuno, Feiteira de Cima, Lamaceiros, Ponte, Achada de Santo António, Vinhátego and Covas. It was on the islet near the locality that took the name of Rocha do Navio (‘ship cliff’) that, on 24 December 1860, during a violent storm, the Dutch galliot *Alfa*, bound from England for the island of Haiti, was wrecked; her crew of seven men were saved.

Among the many picturesque spots in this parish, the following deserve special mention and are worth a visit: Pico do Cortado, Achada de Santo António, Achada do Gramacho, Miradouro, Rocha do Navio, Cortado, Cumiada Altas Queimadas, Caldeirão Verde, Homem em Pé, Cova da Roda, etc.
The parish has two state schools and is the seat of a medical district covering all the parishes of the municipality (*concelho*). Its population is 3,107 inhabitants (1921).
Santana (islet)
It is also known as Rocha do Navio (‘ship cliff’) and lies off the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’). A Dutch ship was wrecked there in 1860.
Santana (municipality)

The municipality (*concelho*) of Santana (‘St Anne’) has its seat in the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name and was established in 1835. The municipalities of Câmara de Lobos, Santa Cruz, Porto Moniz and Santana were abolished by the decree of 10 December 1867, but this measure was never fully implemented, because those municipalities were restored shortly afterwards. From its creation the municipality of Santana comprised the parishes of Arco de São Jorge, São Jorge, Santana, Faial, São Roque and Porto da Cruz. However, the parish of Porto da Cruz was detached from it by the decree of 19 October 1852, and this parish then became part of the municipality of Machico.
St Maurus (chapels)

The chapel of Santo Amaro (‘St Maurus’), which stands in the locality (*sítio*) of the same name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António, is one of the oldest in the diocese. It is one of the few 15th-century buildings to have survived here in Madeira, although perhaps nothing remains of the original structure, given the far-reaching alterations made to it over the course of four and a half centuries.

Dr Álvaro R. de Azevedo, through an evident slip, places this chapel in the parish of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), when it has certainly always belonged to the parish of Santo António.
