The mistake may stem from the fact that its founder owned extensive lands in both these parishes, perhaps adjoining one another, so that at some time in the not-so-recent past the chapel may have been regarded as lying indifferently in one parish or the other. It was built at a spot on the boundary between the two parishes and, moreover, the main entrance of the *quinta* (country estate) that surrounded the chapel opened onto the road separating those parishes. These circumstances could easily have misled him and led him to suppose that the little church of Santo Amaro did not lie within the parish of Santo António.

Those even moderately read in the Madeiran chronicles know that four noblemen came to this island from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) with the express purpose of marrying the daughters of the discoverer of Madeira and first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal. The third of them, Dona Catarina da Câmara, married Garcia Homem de Sousa, who was the founder of this chapel. The annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states verbatim: ‘...Santo Amaro, which was founded by Garcia Homem de Souza, son-in-law of Zargo, in 1460 on the great settled estate (*fazenda povoada*) where he had a castellated dwelling.’ Elsewhere the *Saudades* also say of this same Garcia de Souza: ‘...he built the chapel, or strong or castellated house, to defend himself against his brothers-in-law; he was proud and violent’; and they add finally that ‘having quarrels with his brothers-in-law... he built a tower which stands near the Madre de Deus (‘Mother of God’)’.

What was the Madre de Deus? The original name of the chapel or locality of Santo Amaro? We cannot say. However, according to tradition, and as the learned annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ affirms, it was at Santo Amaro that Garcia Homem de Sousa built the castellated house mentioned in the old chronicles of this archipelago, to defend himself against his brothers-in-law in the bloody struggles he had with them. Indeed, some ruined houses of quite ancient construction still stand there, which are probably the remains of the fortress-like manor house that the proud and turbulent Garcia de Sousa built to shelter from the assaults of his enemies. A pointed-arch doorway of dressed stone (*cantaria*), still to be seen there and apparently bearing the stamp of Manueline-period buildings, ought to be carefully preserved. Traces of an old cistern also remain, and not many years ago the walls of an old tower could likewise still be seen there, all of it apparently of very early construction (1921).

There was a *quinta* there, within whose grounds stood the chapel and the probable building of Garcia de Sousa. Today only a gateway of some architectural pretension remains, which in former times also served as the entrance to the chapel.

Santo Amaro is one of the most important chapels in this bishopric, for its antiquity and historical traditions, for its size, and also for the crowds of worshippers who attend its patronal feast. It seems to us that little remains of its original structure, which underwent successive alterations over time. With the evident aim of isolating it from the rural and urban property within whose grounds it stood, a high wall was built in front of the façade, three or four metres away from it, and joined to the little church by a porch. All this greatly disfigured the front of the building and also considerably spoilt the beauty of the whole. It was probably from this time, which we cannot determine precisely, that the chapel began to be served exclusively through the present entrance, and the passage that opened onto the road to Tangue and Alecrins (‘rosemary bushes’) was closed off. We presume that the administrators of the chapel had relinquished their duties as patrons and left it to the care and management of the parish vestry, in whose charge it has been for many years, and in this way separated it from the rest of the *quinta* or estate on which it had been built.

This chapel always remained in the possession of the successors of Garcia Homem de Sousa, and we know that in 1700 the administrator of the entailed property of Santo Amaro was Filipe de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). His immediate successor was his son, José Joaquim de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, who passed it to his son, also named José Joaquim de Carvalhal Esmeraldo. He was succeeded in this entailed administration by his brother Francisco António de Bettencourt Carvalhal Esmeraldo, whose daughter, Dona Isabel Esmeraldo Barbosa de Matos e Câmara, inherited the property and chapel. She bequeathed it to her sister Dona Júlia Esmeraldo, who died on 14 September 1915.

The chapel as it stands today is a reconstruction dating from the second or third quarter of the 17th century. The little church has three altars and is of no mean size, but it contains nothing to catch the observer’s attention, for not even traces of the old, original building seem to be found there. In former times it was the centre of a well-attended pilgrimage.

Only a few years ago, beside the road leading to Lombada dos Esmeraldos (‘the Esmeraldos’ ridge’) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), could be seen the ruins of a chapel dedicated to St Maurus, said to have been built by João Esmeraldo at the end of the 15th century (see Lombada dos Esmeraldos).

Within the limits of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) stands a chapel dedicated to St Maurus, which was built by the people, though the year of its construction is unknown. Every year its patronal feast draws an extraordinary crowd from the surrounding parishes. It was rebuilt in 1922.
St Andrew Avellino (chapel)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas, stands the chapel of Santo André Avelino, founded in 1776 by Captain Carlos Nunes de Freitas da Silva and his wife, Dona Ana Guiomar de Moura Acciaioly Lomelino. It belonged to the house of the entail (*morgado*) of Nuno de Freitas Lomelino. On one of its walls is this inscription, placed there a few years ago: ‘Oferecida por Jacintho Fernandes e concluida por José dos Reis e Povo’ (‘Offered by Jacintho Fernandes and completed by José dos Reis and the People’). The dressed stone (*cantaria*) of the doorway bears the date 1774.
St Anthony (chapels)

The chapel of St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’) dates from the second quarter of the 16th century. It was not built in 1730, as Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo states, but rebuilt around that time. In 1729 the people asked the ecclesiastical authority for permission to reconstruct it, stating that it had been built by the parishioners roughly two centuries earlier. Its reconstruction was completed on 13 April 1730, the day it was inspected so that it could be blessed and then opened for worship.

On a property that the holder of the entail (*morgado*) João José de Bettencourt owned in the locality (*sítio*) of Adegas (‘wine cellars’), in the parish of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), the house had a small chapel or private oratory, whose dedication we do not know. António Gonçalves de Almeida bought the property and converted the oratory into a chapel with an outside door, dedicating it to St Anthony. The chapel was blessed on 13 June 1853.

In the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) there was a chapel dedicated to St Anthony, founded around 1682 on the entailed estate (*morgadio*) established by Captain António Teles de Meneses. We believe it to be the chapel whose ruins still stood a few years ago in the street that today keeps the name of Santo António or of the Hospital Velho.

In the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’) there is a chapel dedicated to St Anthony of the Miracles (*Santo António dos Milagres*), situated at Lombo do Salão (‘hall ridge’), where services are still held. It is the property of Juvenal R. de Vasconcelos (1921).

A chapel that once stood in the parish of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), founded by Henrique Brandão Henriques in 1696, was known as Santo António da Malvasia. Its deed of endowment is dated 13 August of the same year.

Yet another chapel dedicated to St Anthony stood in the parish of Ponta do Sol. It rose at the locality of Lugar de Baixo (see that entry) and belonged to the Carvalhal (‘oak grove’) family estate. When this property was sold some thirty years ago, its new owners demolished the house that stood there and the chapel of St Anthony attached to it. On the same site they built a handsome country house and, beside it, had the old chapel of St Anthony rebuilt. It was blessed by the diocesan prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto on 25 February 1906.

Within the courtyard of the Customs House (see that entry) there still stands a small chapel dedicated to St Anthony, built in 1714 by the superintendent (*provedor*) João de Aguiar. Above its portico is carved the inscription *Ad salem sol*.

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte, a short distance from the road that runs alongside the Levada de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’s channel’), stands a chapel dedicated to St Anthony, which Manuel Ferreira Frasão had built in 1718.
A chapel that Tristão de França Bettencourt had built in the parish of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) in 1727 was known as Santo António da Mouraria (‘Moorish quarter’).

The parish of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) belonged to the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), and the nuns built a chapel of St Anthony there, which had its own chaplain before the parish was created. It was an old building, dating perhaps from the end of the 16th century. When the parish of Curral das Freiras was created in 1790, its seat was established in the chapel of St Anthony, and it remained there for some years until the new parish church was built.

On the Quinta de Santo António, in the parish of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), stands a chapel with this dedication, built in 1705 by Inácio Viana do Rego. It belonged to Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) António Correia Herédia. It was bought some years ago by Francisco Pinto Correia and is today the property of his heirs (1921).
Captain António Espranger da Câmara built a chapel to St Anthony in the parish of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) in 1724; the deed of endowment is dated 4 June of that year.
There was once a chapel dedicated to St Anthony in the parish of Machico, whose founder and year of construction we do not know.
In the locality (*sítio*) of Pico (‘peak’), in the parish of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), there was a chapel with the same dedication, of which some ruins still remain.

There was also a chapel of this patron saint in the locality of Terra Batista (‘Batista’s land’), in the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), belonging to a family with the surname Nunes Caldeira.

On the Quinta do Pomar, in the parish of Quinta Grande (‘large estate’), next to the fine country house that stands there, the former vicar of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), António Silvino Gonçalves de Andrade, had a chapel dedicated to St Anthony built in 1883. This priest, who in his day enjoyed a reputation as a great preacher, was the brother of Dr Francisco Justino Gonçalves de Andrade and Dr João Jacinto Gonçalves de Andrade, whom we have discussed in this Elucidário (volume I, pages 69 and 66). This chapel of St Anthony is today the property of Dr João Francisco de Almada (1921).
In the former Rua da Laranjeira (see that entry), in the city of Funchal, there was a chapel of St Anthony, which the Council ordered to be demolished on 5 February 1836.
There is a chapel dedicated to St Anthony in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol.
Santo António da Serra (parish)

The parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António da Serra (‘St Anthony of the uplands’), or Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) as it is more commonly known, lies largely on a plateau overlooking the parishes of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) and Machico, at an average altitude of 700 metres above sea level. It is considered one of the most beautiful and enchanting resorts on this island. Although its winter season brings frequent rain and wind and marked drops in temperature, it is much sought after in the hot season for the freshness and mildness of its climate, together with the striking beauty of its admirable landscape. There are some excellent country houses there, where several families, especially from Santa Cruz and Machico, usually spend the hottest months of the year. In former times it was much visited by the English, who built several *quintas* here that still exist.

Like every part of the interior of Madeira, and particularly because of its climate and the dense mass of its woodland, Santo da Serra was not subject to any farming or attempt at colonisation in the earliest days of the settlement of our island. It is conjectured that land clearing began only in the first quarter of the 16th century, on the plateau where the parish church now stands or in its immediate surroundings. It is also supposed that at that time there were still no inhabitants with a fixed residence there.

‘Gil de Carvalho,’ says Father Fernando Augusto de Pontes, ‘originally built two chapels there. The first he never finished, at Alcoforado, the locality where he lived, which still bears the name Ermida (‘hermitage’). The second occupies the parish seat of this village.’ The same priest states, in his book *Excursões*, that Gil de Carvalho died in Santa Cruz in 1541, which would place the building of the chapels at an earlier date, for we are of the opinion that this construction would not have predated the last quarter of the 16th century. The one that was turned into the parish church already existed in 1612, since a royal decree (alvará régio) of 3 September of that year ordered the sum of 70,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) to be applied to the purchase of an altarpiece for that chapel. It may be supposed that by this time a population centre of some importance already existed there. This chapel had its own chaplain, and in 1790 he was permitted to administer the last sacraments in sudden cases.

The illustrious annotator of the *Saudades* writes: ‘The parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra was originally an old chapel subordinate to the vicar of Machico. Because he and the vicars of Santa Cruz and Água de Pena fiercely disputed possession of this chapel, Bishop Dom Friar Lourenço de Távora took it under his protection in 1612 and probably made it a curacy (*curato*). As time went on these disputes over jurisdiction continued, and later the same struggles broke out again over the boundaries of the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico. It was certainly from that period, that is, in the first quarter of the 17th century, that the chapel of Santo António da Serra came under the direct jurisdiction of the bishop, and that this prelate took under emphyteutic lease (*aforamento*, perpetual lease for an annual quit-rent) the lands surrounding the chapel, which were always regarded as belonging to the mitre of Funchal. By special concession of the diocesan bishops, these lands were later made available to the parish priests as part of their glebe (*passal*). The curacy, however, was only created in 1813. It was made up of the localities (*sítios*) of Preces, Ermida, Margaça and Madeira da Igreja, belonging to the parish of Machico; the localities of Mouro, Ameixieiras, João Ferino, Curral Velho, Ribeiro de João Gonçalves and Madre de Água, in the parish of Santa Cruz; and the locality of Achada do Barro (‘clay plateau’), in the parish of Água de Pena.’

While staying at Santo da Serra, the vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) and governor of the diocese (governador do bispado, administering the see in the bishop’s absence) António Alfredo de Santa Catarina Braga issued from there a warrant (*provisão*), dated 13 June 1836, abolishing the parish of Água de Pena and creating that of Santo – or rather, annexing the former to the curacy of Santo da Serra and making the latter the seat of the new parish, under the name of the parish of Santo da Serra e Água de Pena. The new parish did not last long, for the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 24 July 1848 restored the old parish of Água de Pena, which then lost the locality of Achada do Barro, incorporated into Santo da Serra. This place, which had been a curacy dependent on Machico, became an autonomous parish from 1848.

Various disagreements, lasting many years, arose between the municipal councils of Santa Cruz and Machico over the boundaries of their respective municipalities, each seeking to bring a considerable part of Santo da Serra under its own jurisdiction. These struggles ended in 1862, as already mentioned on page 299 of volume II, to which we refer the reader in order to avoid needless repetition.

The original chapel, which housed the seat of the curacy (*curato*) and the parish, must have been built towards the end of the 16th century or the beginning of the 17th. In 1612, as we have seen, it was granted the sum of 70,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for the making of its altarpiece. It no doubt underwent various repairs and may even have been enlarged, until around the middle of the 19th century it was completely rebuilt to the proportions it keeps today. In 1851 the government had the chancel and part of the parish house rebuilt, at a cost of about four *contos* (one million réis) *de réis*. The American consul João Howard March (volume II, page 339) built the body of the church and the walls surrounding the spacious churchyard at his own expense. He was commended by a ministerial order (*portaria*) of 3 July 1855 for the outstanding services he had rendered to this parish, and especially for building the church.

The solemn blessing of the new church took place on 23 August 1857 in the presence of the diocesan prelate, Dom Manuel Martins Manso. On that occasion the distinguished preacher Canon Francisco João de Freitas Ferraz delivered a notable sermon.

Opposite the parish residence, some British subjects had a house built to shelter those who came from distant parishes on pilgrimage to the small shrine dedicated to St Anthony, which was then a chapel of cramped dimensions. The house, built around 1808, was not small and had a certain architectural display. For some years it was managed by some English merchants, who saw to its upkeep and cleanliness, but it was later abandoned and within a few years was reduced to a shapeless heap of ruins. The neglect to which the house was left, and its rapid collapse, are owed to the public works department of this district, which had charge of the building, and also to some people of this parish.

In the article devoted to Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares, bishop of this diocese, we have already mentioned that this prelate lived for some months in this parish, serving a sentence of banishment imposed on him by the governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara (see volume III, page 216).

This was one of the parishes in which the Protestant proselytism begun and carried on by Dr Robert Kalley (volume II, page 208) put down the deepest roots and brought the greatest disturbance into the midst of Madeira’s peaceful population. Public order was disturbed here in 1844. Many arrests were made, inquiries and investigations were held in the seats of the municipalities of Santa Cruz and Machico, and various proceedings were brought against the rioters and some apostles of the new doctrines. The propagandists have not forgotten the original Calvinist evangelisation and have kept up their proselytising to the present day, though without appreciable results. It was Dr Kalley himself who, in this parish, at the *quinta* (country estate) of Serrado das Ameixieiras (‘plum-tree field’), led a large number of people to follow Calvinist ideas through his rare and overwhelming eloquence. We have already referred above to the striking landscape of this parish and the captivating panoramas to be enjoyed there, above all at the localities of Lamaceiros, Portela and Macelas. Father Fernando de Pontes, already cited, says: ‘At Portela, the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) lies at the spectator’s feet. At Lamaceiros there is not only the view of Porto da Cruz and Penha de Águia (‘eagle crag’), but also part of Faial and Santana, wrapped in the luxuriance of an opulent vegetation. At Macelas, there are the green-clad heights of the hills to the north, an immense expanse of verdure and countless cottages beneath one’s eyes; in the centre a stream winding and slipping away like ribbons of silver; down below, the gleaming white of many houses beside a church; further on, the wave breaking against the cliff; beyond, the sombre majesty of the cliffs of São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’) gazing at themselves in the sleeping waters, and the vastness of the ocean at the end...’.

What the *Annais do Porto Santo* tell us about the establishment of a settlement in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo da Serra, made up of inhabitants of that island, cannot pass without special mention. This interesting episode is related in the former *Heraldo da Madeira* in the following terms: ‘Maria I, moved to pity by the successive crises through which Porto Santo was passing, where hunger knocked at the doors of the less well-off despite the measures taken by the Marquis of Pombal, resolved to have some of these destitute people transported to Santo António da Serra. She provided them with everything they needed, spending much of her generosity, and 50,000 *cruzados* of public funds, on building a number of homesteads, which were distributed free of charge.

By royal decree (*alvará*) of 18 December 1768 Santo António da Serra came to be called the Aldeia da Rainha (the Queen’s Village), and Machico lost the lands north of the chapel, which were annexed to the new settlement.

The elements from which it was formed, however, were not such as could be consolidated on such auspicious foundations. With no aptitude for farming and an aversion to work, the emigrants from Porto Santo, beset by the winter cold and deep homesickness, gradually returned to their old homes, until in 1783 they abandoned the village altogether.

Poor administration and a lack of care for the property of the State have always been among the causes of our decline. There are disputes and quarrels over everything, on which rivers of money are spent.
The municipalities of Machico and Santa Cruz both wanted a say in the village. They went to law at length, and the former won when the village had all but ceased to exist.’

The principal localities of this parish are Ermida, Margaça, Madeira da Igreja, Fajã dos Rolos, Ribeira de Machico, Lombo das Faias, Fajã das Vacas, Lombo das Raizes, Casais Proximos, Achada do Barro, Poiso, Madre de Água, Serrado das Ameixieiras, Ribeira de João Gonçalves, Terra de Braga, João Ferino and Curral Velho. It has 2,130 inhabitants (1921).
See Craters and Geology.
Santo António (parish)

It is one of the five suburban parishes (*freguesia*) of Funchal and is bounded by the parishes of São Roque, São Pedro, São Martinho, Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos and Curral das Freiras.

The land that makes up this parish today originally belonged to the parish of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), which then extended its vast area as far as the foothills of the mountains encircling Curral das Freiras, which was separated from Santo António (‘St Anthony’) only in 1790.

As to its creation, Dr Álvaro de Azevedo tells us the following in one of his notes to the work of Gaspar Frutuoso: ‘The parish of Santo António, a suburb of Funchal, was probably created at the same time as that of São Pedro, in 1566, both having been separated from the Sé: it undoubtedly existed before 1574, because, as the royal decree (*alvará*) of 16 September of that year shows, the previous stipend (*côngrua*) of its vicar was increased’. Elsewhere, in another work, Dr Azevedo gives 1568 as the year of its creation.

We lack the necessary evidence to determine with absolute precision the year in which this parish was established, but it seems to us that its creation must date from an earlier period, at least as an autonomous curacy (*curato*), like others that existed in this diocese and that formed almost entirely independent parishes with their own civil and religious life. The oldest records we have found in its parish archive date from 1557, and from then on the entries of baptisms and marriages are kept regularly. This leads us to suppose that an autonomous curacy was created in precisely this year, and was later raised definitively to a parish in a year that can no longer be established. In this bishopric there were independent curacies and even chantries (capela) with altar dues *in solidum* and ‘curate chaplains’, which later became as many parishes, or rather were their true origin. Strong probabilities, then, not to say complete certainty, support our assertion, which places the creation of a curacy in 1557 and its definitive elevation to a parish around 1566.

The parish registers show that Father Gonçalo Jorge Rodrigues was the first priest to perform parish duties here, in the period from 1557 to 1559, although he never indicated the rank of the office he held. His successor, Francisco Afonso, from 1559 to 1569, always styled himself curate, as did others who followed him. It is very strange that, even after the creation of the parish, which beyond any doubt predates 1574, as a document of that year cited in several places shows, some of the priests who exercised the pastoral ministry here continued to style themselves curates, and others sometimes curates and sometimes vicars, as happened with Afonso Lopes, from 1585 to 1586.

The earliest parish priests of this parish were Gonçalo Jorge Rodrigues, Francisco Afonso, Miguel Rodrigues, Manuel Lopes, Vicente Afonso, Afonso de Leme, António Lopes, Domingos Fernandes and Fernão Gomes, all in the 16th century.

Only from 1574 onwards can we establish the amount of the respective stipends (*côngruas*), on the basis of the decrees we have found cited in the General Index of the former Treasury Superintendency (Provedoria da Fazenda) of the Royal Treasury (*Fazenda Real*) in this archipelago, to which we have referred on several occasions.

The oldest of these is the royal decree (alvará régio) of King Sebastian, dated 16 September 1574, issued in favour of the parish priest António de Lima and his successors. It raised the annual stipend, then 13,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), to 25,000 *réis*, likewise a year, since the parish had by then reached 120 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’). This stipend was increased again and again, doubtless in step with the ever-growing population, as the following decrees show: the royal decree of 17 July 1588, adding 30 *alqueires* of wheat to the previous stipend of 25,000 *réis*; the royal decree of 14 December of the same year, adding the sum of 4,000 *réis* a year for the Saturday masses for the souls of the royal princes (*infantes*); the royal decree of 26 August 1645, changing the form of payment of the stipend, which became 10,000 *réis* in cash and two and a half *pipas* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine; and finally the royal decree of 1 October 1775, adding two *moios* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat to the stipend fixed in the previous decree. The stipends of the parish priests of this parish (*freguesia*) underwent other changes, but we have no knowledge of them. The law (*carta de lei*) of 26 March 1845 altered the distribution of stipends in this diocese profoundly, though not equitably; the attached schedule, however, set no salary for the parish priest of Santo António, certainly through an oversight or inadvertent omission. The stipend, abolished by the decree of 20 April 1911, was two hundred thousand *réis* a year.

The growth of the population, and with it of parish duties, led the diocesan bishop, Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos, to petition for the establishment of a curacy (*curato*) in this parish. It was granted by the royal decree of Philip II of 29 October 1602, which authorised the creation of the post, and Father Domingos Brás was appointed to it. His salary was originally 20,000 *réis* a year in cash and one *pipa* of wine. This stipend was increased by one *moio* of wheat by the royal decree of 14 August 1609. The law of 26 March 1845, already cited, set the stipend of this parish’s curacy at 20,000 *réis* in cash, 1 *pipa* and 15 *almudes* of wine, and 1 *moio* and 30 *alqueires* of wheat. The decree of 20 April 1911 abolished the last stipend, which amounted to 130,620 *réis* a year.

We have reason to believe that at a certain period the curates were presented by the Crown, for we see that the curate Fernão Gomes signed himself ‘proprietary curate by the King’ and also ‘confirmed curate’, and we find cited the royal decree of John IV of 18 December 1648, by which Father Francisco de Gouveia was presented as curate of this parish.

It was in a chapel dedicated to St Anthony of Padua, which no doubt originally formed part of a settled estate (*fazenda povoada*), that the seat of this parish, or at least of an autonomous curacy (*curato*), was established around the middle of the 16th century, as stated above. It is possible that before the parish (*freguesia*) was created this chapel had its own chaplain, as generally happened in similar circumstances. The chapel gave its name to the locality (*sítio*) and later to the parish; the year of its construction is unknown.

Over the years it underwent some alterations and even additions. However, as it had become too small for the population, which was growing considerably, a church of larger proportions had to be built. The site chosen was the ground between the present parish house and the public road, which formed part of the glebe (*passal*) and was given for this purpose by the parish priest of the time, Father António Afonso de Faria; its construction dates from the first quarter of the 17th century. Between 1665 and 1682 the chancel was added and the chapels of the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*) and of the Almas (Holy Souls) were built, and other important improvements were also made. It was not a church of cramped dimensions, for it had 6 altars and its interior was finely decorated with gilt carved woodwork (*talha dourada*). A visitation decree (*provimento*) of 1756 calls it a ‘rich church’ as regards its decoration, but by then the ‘six altars were old and ill-proportioned’, in the words of the same decree.

We suppose that at the end of the 17th century or the beginning of the 18th important works of rebuilding or enlargement were carried out on the old church, for in the General Index of the register of the former Royal Treasury Office (*Provedoria da Real Fazenda*) on this island we find a reference to the royal decree (alvará régio) of 9 September 1711, which ordered the continuation of the works on the church of Santo António, estimated at 2,233,920 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis). We have no evidence to state that the works were completed in accordance with that estimate, but it is certain that major repairs were made to the old parish church at various times. With the building of the present church, demolition of the old one began in 1785, leaving standing the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament, which served as the parish seat until 1789. Next to the parish priest’s residence there still survives a stretch of wall which tradition says belonged to the old church.

The ever-growing population and the ruinous state in which the earthquake of 1748 had left the church at once made it advisable to build a new and larger church. A contemporary account of the earthquake says: ‘The church of Santo António has several cracks in its façade: the dressed stone (*cantaria*) of the main door is dislodged and the walls of the nave are broken in various places, as are those of the outbuildings, and what is felt most is the ceiling, which is badly damaged.’

Although the church had been so badly damaged, and despite the diligent efforts of its parish priest at the time, Dr António Pereira Borges, construction of the new church did not begin until 1783, that is, 35 years after that great earthquake. The site chosen was a plot of land almost adjoining the old church. Tradition records that, since the excavations found no ground firm enough to lay the foundations of the walls, large chestnut trunks were laid in the footings, and on them were set the first blocks of stone that served as the base for the walls of the new church. This may be a novelty for Madeira, where firm, secure ground is always found at a shallow depth, but not in other places, where the nature of the terrain makes it necessary to resort to these and similar methods.

The building took six years and was declared finished in 1789, although work on the interior ornamentation of the church, and especially of the altars, continued for some years. The guarantor and inspector of the works was Second Lieutenant António Francisco da Cruz Camacho, who died in the locality (*sítio*) of Ladeira (‘slope’) in this parish (*freguesia*) on 21 August 1815. He was buried beneath the arch of the chancel, and his tombstone bears this epitaph: ‘tomb of Second Lieutenant António Francisco da Cruz Camacho and of his wife and children and heirs, who was the guarantor and inspector of this church, which was begun in the year 1783 and completed in 1789’. He always showed the greatest dedication and selflessness in advancing the works, which at times proceeded very slowly, though for reasons beyond his control, and his memory deserves great gratitude for the unsurpassed zeal he displayed in bringing the new church to completion.

On the façade, above the main door, is a stone tablet bearing the following inscription: *Antonio Lusitanorum Protectori Templum Dedicat Aug. Reg. Maria Prima Illius Liberalitatem Efundentibus Suis In Hac Insula Ab Aerario Ad Ministris. Anno MDCCLXXXIII.* (To Anthony, protector of the Portuguese, the august Queen Maria I dedicates this church, her liberality being dispensed by her ministers of the treasury in this island. Year 1783.) Although religious services began to be held in the new church in 1789, its final interior completion took many more years. Work on the chapel of Nossa Senhora de Guadalupe was not declared finished until 1798; the chancel was still not entirely complete in 1801, and the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament was only finished at the beginning of the 19th century.

In 1880, when Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro was civil governor of this district, important works were carried out in this church on his orders. They consisted mainly of flooring the chancel, repairs to the walls and towers, re-roofing the whole church and other minor repairs. In 1852, too, some fairly significant repairs were made to the vestry washroom and other parts of the church.

The bell towers had never been completed, and it was in 1880 that Canon Feliciano Teixeira, deputy for Madeira, obtained from the central government the funds needed to raise the towers and finish them for good. The works were not carried out and completed until 1883. The spires of the towers were not built with the necessary solidity, for a stronger gust of wind brought down the southern one on 8 March 1899, and the northern one had to be taken down because it offered no guarantee of withstanding the weather.

In this parish church there is a chapel consecrated to Nossa Senhora de Guadalupe (Our Lady of Guadalupe), and the veneration of the Most Holy Virgin under that dedication in this parish is very old. The building of this chapel is due chiefly to the curate Manuel J. Pereira de Sousa, who not only adorned it with fine decorations but also obtained a papal brief dated 14 July 1805, granting a plenary indulgence to those who visit this church on the occasion of the feast of Nossa Senhora de Guadalupe.

This parish has the chapels of Santo Amaro, Our Lady of Prayers, Nossa Senhora do Pópulo, São João e Santana, Our Lady of Protection and the cemetery chapel, in all of which Mass is still celebrated. The chapel of St Philip (*São Filipe*) survives but has been deconsecrated, and that of Santa Maria Madalena is in ruins. No trace remains of the chapels of Nossa Senhora da Quietação, Santa Quitéria and Nossa Senhora das Brotas. We have dealt with each of these chapels elsewhere in this work. The chapel of Nossa Senhora do Pópulo, in the locality (*sítio*) of Pico do Cardo (‘thistle peak’), which belonged to the Jesuits, and the stay of Blessed Inácio de Azevedo in this parish, we have already discussed in volume I of the *Elucidário*, on page 110, and in volume II, on page 187.

The chapel of São João e Santana stands on the Quinta do Trapiche (‘sugar mill’), which has an excellent country house attached and was the property of Dona Maria Paula Rego, heiress of the old Gouveia Rego entailed estate (*morgadio*) to which this *quinta* (country estate) belonged. It served as the summer residence of the last prelates of this diocese, and a few years ago the diocesan seminary was temporarily housed there. Plans are under way to adapt this rural and urban property for a mental asylum, and some Brothers of St John of God have already begun the work (1921).

The main localities of this parish are: Casas Próximas, Romeiras, Courelas, Quinta das Freiras, Terra Chã, Jamboto, Fontes, Ladeira, Chamorra, Encruzilhadas, Vasco Gil, Casas, Casa Branca, Boliqueme, Barreira, Trapiche, Curral Velho, Laranjal, Lombo dos Aguiares, Pomar do Miradouro, Ribeira Grande, Lugar do Meio, Salão, Álamos, Penteada, Quinta do Leme, Madalena, Levada do Cavalo, Pilar, Pico dos Barcelos, Santo Amaro, Tanque, Alecrins, Preces, Pinheiro das Voltas, Santa Quitéria, Pico do Cardo, Três Paus, Viana, Ribeiro dos Socorridos and Fajã. Many of these localities command vast and striking views. Special mention is due to Pico dos Barcelos, which only a few years ago was almost entirely unknown to the great majority of the people of Funchal. Today, however, thanks to a recently built road (1921) giving easy access to the ridge of that peak, it has become an obligatory stop on every excursion made within the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal. Rarely a day passes, especially when tourists are visiting, without a considerable number of motor cars climbing that height, from which one enjoys one of the most marvellous stretches of the incomparable Madeiran landscape.

Besides some mobile schools, this parish has nine official primary schools, in the localities of Madalena, Casas Próximas, Salão, Terra Chã, Lombo dos Aguiares, Trapiche, Encruzilhadas, Chamorra and Romeiras. Santo António is the most populous parish on the island; the last published census gives it a total of 8,839 inhabitants (1921).

A major improvement carried out in this parish in recent years was the widening of the road leading from the Largo das Maravilhas to the parish church. The work began at the end of November 1914 and is still not fully finished (1921).
In March 1914 a small fortnightly magazine began to appear under the title *Paróquia de Santo António do Funchal*; 46 issues were published, containing a historical account of this parish.

We cannot fail to mention the important improvements made to the parish church between 1922 and 1928, on which more than three hundred *contos* (one million réis) de réis were spent, raised by public subscription among the parishioners. To these improvements was added the installation of a magnificent clock in one of the bell towers, a generous gift from the benevolent industrialist Henrique Hinton, which renders excellent service to this populous parish.

These notable improvements are described more fully in the book *Paroquia de Santo Antonio da Ilha da Madeira*, a volume of 230 pages containing a detailed historical monograph on the parish, written by one of the co-authors of this *Elucidário*.

In the local press and in the higher government of the district, the idea has arisen more than once of dividing the parish of Santo António into two autonomous parishes, in view of its continuous and growing population and the expansion of its territory, which stretches far across the mountainous heights surrounding it. They would bear the apt names of Santo António de Cima, with its seat in the locality of ‘Boliqueme’ or ‘Encruzilhadas’, and Santo António de Baixo, with its seat in the locality of ‘Casas Próximas’. The first would have a population of about 9,000 inhabitants and the second about 6,000. The greatest difficulty in carrying out this plan, which would bring undeniable advantages to the inhabitants, would be the building of a new parish church and of a presbytery, or residence for the clergy.
Santo António (peaks)
In the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’) there is a peak of the same name, 400 metres high, which stands a short distance from the parish church.
Overlooking the parish of Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’) rises a mountain height that reaches an altitude of 1740 metres, and from its summits vast panoramas unfold.
Holy Spirit (chapel)

This chapel, at the Lombada dos Esmeraldos (see that entry) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), was the seat of one of the two entailed estates (*morgadio*) founded there by the Fleming João Esmeraldo (see that entry); the other was known as the entailed estate of Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’). The chapel of Santo Espírito (‘Holy Spirit’), now called Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), was built at the beginning of the 16th century by this same João Esmeraldo. It was blessed, or rather consecrated, in 1508 by Bishop Dom João Lobo, who, before the diocese was created, had come to this island to exercise episcopal functions by order of the Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), to which the archipelago belonged in spiritual matters. The following inscription can still be read today on one of the inner walls of the church: ‘This church was consecrated by Dom João Lobo, Bishop of Taiere, on 27 August 1508.’ There is no doubt that the present church is not the original building. It was rebuilt around the middle of the 17th century on a larger scale than the first design. A few years ago it underwent further repairs and was blessed in 1904, as recorded by the following words found there: ‘This chapel, having been repaired, was blessed again on 10 June 1904, with the customary solemnities, by the diocesan prelate His Most Reverend Excellency Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto.’ It is the largest, most elegant and richest chapel in the whole diocese. The *azulejos* (painted glazed tiles) covering the lower walls of the nave and chancel are worthy of admiration; they depict the gifts and fruits of the Holy Spirit in symbolic figures. This chapel, which has five altars, contains some artistically and masterfully carved statues that at once catch the visitor’s attention. Near this church there still stands, though badly damaged, the large and imposing house of the administrators of this entailed estate, of which the 2nd Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’) was the last holder.

The Madeiran review *A Esperança* (‘Hope’), of 1 and 15 October 1920, contains an interesting description of this chapel from an artistic point of view, which deserves to be read despite whatever exaggeration it may contain. See the pamphlet *A Lombada dos Esmeraldos* by Father Fernando A. Silva.
Santo Servo de Deus
See Guarda (Friar Pedro da).
Santos (Octavio)

He was born in Funchal on 17 January 1900 and uses the pseudonym Octavio Marialva in his writings. Besides contributing to various newspapers and reviews, he has published many pamphlets in prose and verse, among which we may mention *Século 100*, *O Reino dos Génios*, *Sinfonia do Eu*, *Autoverdade*, *A Cortesã do Palácio Pitti*, *Policia Mental*, *O Verdadeiro Colombo*, *O Segredo dos Fakires*, *O Testamento de um Doido*, *Auto-Expressão*, *Divino Paraíso*, *Victoria de Samotracia*, *Iokannan*, *Cavalgada Heróica*, etc.
Sts Cosmas and Damian (chapel)

A chapel with this dedication once stood, though it disappeared long ago, in the locality (*sítio*) of Salão (‘hall’) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’). It was founded in 1681 by the surgeon António de França Gomes.
Santos (Dom Friar Miguel dos)

According to Henrique Henriques de Noronha in his respected ‘Secular and Ecclesiastical Memoirs’ (see 1-389), the friar Miguel dos Santos, a native of this island and son of Diogo Colaço de Abreu and Dona Maria Chamorra, was bishop of São Tomé de Meliapor. He gives no further details that would allow a fuller identification of this prelate.
Santos (Duarte Joaquim dos)

This distinguished musician and composer was born in Elvas, but lived for some years in Funchal and died here, aged 54, on 24 May 1855. (See the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) of 14 July 1910.)
Santos (Joaquim José de Faria)

He was born in Funchal on 21 January 1822 and held the post of clerk in the secretariat of the Council. He contributed to the *Archivista*, *Ordem*, *Baratissimo*, *Madeira* and *Verdade*, and died in this city on 12 April 1886.
Santos (Jorge)
See Rodrigues dos Santos (José Jorge).
Magi (chapel)

It stood near the old hospital of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood), when the hospital was housed in a building in the street known as Hospital Velho and later as Santo António. In 1514 King Manuel I gave it to the hospital of this city.

A chapel of the same name exists at the Quinta dos Reis (‘the kings’ estate’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’); it was built by order of Duarte Mendes de Vasconcelos in 1554. See Reis Magos (chapels).
Santos (Vitorino José dos)

He was born in Funchal on 29 December 1863, the son of Augusto César dos Santos and Dona Isabel de Ornelas Santos. He is a civil engineer, having studied at the former Polytechnic and Army schools in Lisbon. He was director of municipal public works in Luanda and section chief engineer of public works in the province of Angola, and after returning to Funchal he served here as municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) and police commissioner. He is director and teacher of the António Augusto de Aguiar Industrial School and head of the 6th District of the Technical Services of Industry in Funchal. In this last post he wrote several reports published in the *Boletim de Trabalho Industrial*; some of them, such as those on charitable institutions and trade associations, embroidery, handicrafts, wickerwork and inlaid work (*embutidos*), are thorough and highly valuable studies. He also published a book of verse entitled *Lágrimas*, which went through two editions, the first in Funchal in 1916, the second in Coimbra in 1918 (1921). He died on 1 October 1928.
St Bartholomew (church)

The old church of St Bartholomew (*São Bartolomeu*) was built in the Rua Direita (‘straight street’) of the early settlement of Funchal, a street that then ran along the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) as far as the vicinity of the present Ponte do Torreão (‘turret’). It was founded by Gonçalo Eanes de Velosa, and attached to it was a hospital or hospice (*albergaria*) intended to shelter poor and infirm clergy. In it he founded an entail with the obligation of having a Mass said there every Friday of the year for the soul of Infante Ferdinand. He was buried in this church, and according to what we have read in an old nobiliary, the following epitaph was carved on his tombstone: ‘Here lies Gonçalo Annes de Veloza, squire of Infante Ferdinand, whom God keeps, a native of Celorico, builder of this church of São Bartholomeu and hospital, who died in the era of 1497, on 1 August.’ The annotator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) says that this hospice was never occupied by poor clergy, as its founder had stipulated, and that it often served as lodging for missionaries who stopped in Funchal on their way to India.
It was in this hospice that the Jesuits settled in 1566, and they remained there until the church and college of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist) were built.
The church of St Bartholomew, long since deconsecrated, was demolished in the second quarter of the 19th century.
São Bartolomeu (stream and landing place)

The stream of this name rises on the plateau of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) and forms the boundary between the parishes of Calheta (‘small cove’) and Estreito da Calheta (‘the narrows of Calheta’) before flowing into the ocean. At its mouth there is an insignificant landing place, known as Porto da Ribeira (‘stream harbour’), not far from Ponta da Galé (‘galley point’).
St Bernardino (chapel)
See convent of St Bernardino (*São Bernardino*).
St Cajetan (chapel)

In 1780 António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo Alencastre, nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*), and his wife Dona Josefa Jacinta Betencourt Correia Henriques had a chapel dedicated to São Caetano (St Cajetan) built in the locality (*sítio*) of Terças (‘thirds’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), on the *quinta* (country estate) they owned there, which bore the same name as the chapel.
St Candidus (chapel)

In the locality (*sítio*) then called Fonte da Rocha (‘rock spring’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), Canon Francisco Cândido Correia Henriques built a chapel in 1732 dedicated to the martyr St Candidus, and provided it with a suitable endowment on 16 May of that year. It is in ruins (1921).
St Christopher (chapels)

This chapel, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, in the locality (*sítio*) that took its name from it, was built under a testamentary provision made in 1690 by Cristóvão Moniz de Meneses, ordering its construction. The date 1692 is carved on its portico.

In the parish of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), on land that today belongs to the parish of Boaventura (‘good fortune’), stood the chapel of São Cristóvão (‘St Christopher’). It was an old building, for the parish archive of the first of those parishes records that it was already in a poor state of repair in 1578, when Dona Maria de Leme was its administrator. It underwent various repairs and was demolished in 1748. It gave its name to the locality in which it had been built.
St Ferdinand (chapel)

In the locality (*sítio*) that still bears this name today, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), there once stood the chapel of São Fernando, whose founder and year of construction are unknown to us.
St Philip (chapel)

The Fleming António de Leme held land by *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), in the locality (*sítio*) still known today as Quinta do Leme (‘Leme’s estate’), and there he built a house and chapel, which the annotator of the *Saudades* dates to 1536. From documents we have had occasion to examine, we see that this chapel of St Philip (*São Filipe*) was rebuilt in 1654 by Inácio da Câmara Leme, the founder’s successor in the administration of this entail. The earthquake of 1748 left it badly ruined, and it was rebuilt once more in 1752 by its administrator, Francisco Aurélio da Câmara Leme.

In the locality that still bears the name of São Filipe (‘St Philip’), in the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), stands a chapel of this dedication, now deconsecrated and in an advanced state of ruin. It was built in 1562 by Filipe Gentil de Limoges and was the seat of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) he founded that year.

We have said elsewhere that not long ago the following inscription could still be read on a tombstone in this chapel: ‘Tomb of the innocents who were cruelly killed at the Achada (‘plateau’) of this city. 1621.’ We do not know the names of the persons to whom this inscription refers, nor the reasons for those deaths, but it may be supposed that they were members of the Limoges family, to whom the chapel belonged (1921).

Information gathered after that date allows us to state with certainty that the date inscribed on the tomb is 1666, and that the epitaph refers to the burial there of the bones of many children killed by the ‘foundling nurse’ (*ama dos expostos*) of that time. She took in the ‘foundlings’, killed them and buried them near her home in the well-known locality of Achada, in the parish of São Roque (‘St Roch’). This chapel, which was in an advanced state of ruin, was restored by its owner, the Countess of Torre Bela, and blessed by the diocesan prelate on 13 April 1925.
São Filipe (fort)

This fort, built, it seems, under Philippine rule (Spanish Habsburg rule over Portugal, 1580–1640), was entered from Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory square’) and stood between the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) and the Ribeira de João Gomes. It was ceded to the Council following a petition that the Council addressed to the Government on 27 February 1896, which was granted only much later. The large building housing the sugar-cane crushing mill on Largo do Pelourinho stands partly on the ground of the old fort of São Filipe (1921).
St Francis (chapels)

Ruined and long since withdrawn from worship, the chapel of São Francisco still stands in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’). It was the small church of the convent of Franciscan friars that once existed there. It belongs to Pedro César de Brito (1921).

In the parish of São Pedro, on the Caminho de Santo António (‘St Anthony’), there stood the chapel of São Francisco, better known as São Francisco das Furnas. It was founded by Canon Pedro Correia Barbosa in 1697. It belonged to the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Jérvis de Atouguia. In the house adjoining it the Viscount of Atouguia (see that entry) was born on 7 July 1797. Canon Pedro Correia Barbosa is the same man we referred to on page 126 of volume I of this *Elucidário*.
In 1675 Ambrósio Vieira de Andrade built a chapel dedicated to St Francis in the parish of Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’).
St Francis Borgia (chapel)

The chapel that Dom Francisco de Vasconcelos had built in 1760 in the locality (*sítio*) of Cruz da Guarda (‘cross of the guard’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), next to the houses he owned there, was dedicated to St Francis Borgia, not to St Francis Xavier, as the *Saudades* states. The deed is dated 2 May of that year.
São Francisco (street)

The street runs from Rua da Carreira (‘track’), or Rua do Dr Vieira, to Avenida do Dr Manuel de Arriaga. At a session of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) on 6 July 1922 it received the somewhat vague name of ‘Rua 22 de Março de 1921’, because on that date the daring Portuguese aviators Gago Coutinho and Sacadura Cabral made their flight between Lisbon and Madeira.

It would be good to restore the street’s old name, since the public is not prepared to recognise any other, and the Council has already honoured the two aviators by giving their glorious names to two streets of this city (1921).
St Francis Xavier (chapels)

In the locality (*sítio*) of Salão (‘hall’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), at the place called Cadeado (‘padlock’), stands a small chapel of this name, still used for worship. It was founded by Manuel da Silva Pinheiro in 1693, and its deed of endowment is dated 7 August of the same year. It belongs to the heirs of Dona Vicência Júlia de França Dória (1921).
João Vieira de Afonseca built a chapel with the same patron saint in the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) in 1684.

There was a chapel of the same dedication in the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), in the locality of Cruz da Guarda (‘cross of the guard’). Its founder is unknown; among its last owners were João Francisco Moniz de Meneses Cabral and his wife Dona Maria Isidora Álvares de Carvalho, who bequeathed it to their nephew, Father Francisco Xavier de Sousa e Castro.
St Giles (chapel)

On entailed lands (*terras vinculadas*) he owned in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), Antão Álvares de Carvalho founded a chapel dedicated to St Giles, in the locality (*sítio*) that bears this name.
São Gonçalo (parish)

At the eastern end of Funchal lies the parish (*freguesia*) of São Gonçalo (‘St Gonçalo’), one of the five suburban parishes of this municipality (*concelho*). It borders the parish of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) to the west and that of Caniço (‘reed’) to the east. Squeezed between these two parishes, it stretches from the edge of the ocean to the summits of the hills that enclose part of Funchal. The land that makes up this parish originally belonged to the parish of Santa Maria Maior. When that parish moved its seat to the church that later served as the Cathedral, the same land was incorporated into it as well, and it became part of the parish of Santa Maria Maior once again when Funchal was divided into two parishes, around 1558.

We have already given a brief account of the chapel of Our Lady of the Snows (*Nossa Senhora das Neves*), where the seat of the parish was established, on page 462 of volume II. It had its own chaplain, who performed some parochial duties, and it was later raised to the status of a curacy (*curato*) by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 7 March 1566, the curate receiving an annual salary of 12,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash and one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. The General Index of the Register of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*), which we have cited so often, mentions the following documents: a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 16 September 1574, awarding the curate 20,000 *réis* a year because the curacy had more than 100 households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’); a royal decree of 9 June 1581, setting this salary at 25,000 *réis*; a royal decree of 3 February 1589, adding thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine to the same salary; and a royal decree of 14 December 1592, fixing the corresponding stipend (*côngrua*) at 16,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. None of these documents speaks of a parish or a vicarage; they refer instead to a beneficed curate (*beneficiado curado*), albeit one with the duties of a parish priest. ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) states that the parish was created by the royal decree of 12 March 1574, yet the decree cited above, of 16 September 1574, which is later than that one, still refers expressly to a beneficed curate. From our examination and comparison of many documents concerning the creation of various ecclesiastical posts, we can state that the decrees cited in the General Index of the Crown Revenue Office are more reliable in their dates than those cited by the illustrious annotator of Gaspar Frutuoso. What seems most probable to us is that the beneficed curate created by the decree of 7 March 1566 corresponds to the creation of the parish, and that at that time the duties belonging to certain posts were confused with one another.

The chapel of Our Lady of the Snows, the original seat of the parish, dates from the 16th century, as we have already mentioned, and is among the oldest in this diocese. It underwent various alterations over the years, but by the beginning of the 17th century it was already too small for the population of the parish. Despite repeated efforts, it was only at the end of the 17th century that an order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*), dated 15 October 1697, directed that a new church be built. Construction began at the beginning of the 18th century.

This parish once had the chapels of Nossa Senhora da Incarnação (Our Lady of the Incarnation) and Our Lady of Pity, and those of Our Lady of the Snows and Nossa Senhora da Boa Nova (Our Lady of the Good News) still exist. We deal with them elsewhere.

The first settlement of this parish and the first farming in its area must, like those of the other parishes of this municipality (*concelho*), date from the colonisation and clearing of land that João Gonçalves Zarco began in Funchal immediately after the discovery and the fire that swept through the dense woods which no doubt covered the whole length of the valley. Of one early settler, the most distinguished of Zargo’s companions in the work of discovery, we know that he held extensive *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in this parish. They stretched from the right bank of the stream to which he gave his name as far as the Ribeira de João Gomes, and were bounded to the north by the ridges of the uplands. This was Gonçalo Aires, whom we have already discussed at some length on page 21 of volume II of this work. Within the bounds of this parish lie the magnificent *quinta* (country estate) of Palheiro (volume III, page 43) and the lazaretto of Gonçalo Aires, at the mouth of the stream of the same name (volume II, page 223 ff.). The principal localities are: Forca, Louros, Murteiras, São João de Latrão, Salões, Fonte, Boa Nova, Lombo da Quinta, Ribeira da Quinta, Palheiro do Ferreiro, Algarvio, Bica de Pau, Igreja, Ribeiro Seco, Neves and Cancela. It has 2,987 inhabitants (1921).
St John the Baptist (chapels)

More commonly known as São João da Ribeira (‘St John of the stream’), this chapel stands on the right bank of the westernmost stream of Funchal. Over time the stream has been called the Santa Catarina, São Paulo, São Lázaro, Santo António and São João stream, the last being the name it bears today. Some attribute the foundation of this chapel to João Gonçalves Zarco. It is undoubtedly one of the oldest in the diocese and one of the few from the 15th century still standing, although nothing of the original building survives. The Franciscan friars who accompanied the discoverer to this island built a small monastery beside the chapel and remained there until the Convent of St Francis was built in what was then the town (*vila*) of Funchal. Frutuoso says that, ‘the place being deserted, and a friar there… having hanged himself, these religious set up a house further down…’.

This account differs from that of the annotator of the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*), who states that the Franciscans ‘lived as hermits… and eleven years after the discovery, their number having increased… they gathered in community in the hospice (*hospício*) and chapel of St John the Baptist, which they began to build in 1432 with some alms and the labour of their own hands, without Zargo having founded the chapel…; in 1459 the friars left the hospice of St John the Baptist and set sail for Portugal…; fifteen years later Friar Rodrigo da Arruda arrived on the island…, and he re-established the community in the same hospice of St John the Baptist… Around 1476 the friars settled in St Francis’. This information from Dean Gonçalves de Andrade, which seems to us the most accurate, was drawn from the Franciscan chronicles, and he gives it as a refutation of the assertions of Father António Cordeiro.

At the beginning of the 18th century a violent flood of the stream destroyed the chapel and part of the adjoining hospice, and the National Treasury (*Fazenda Nacional*) rebuilt them in 1720. The flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803 also caused them considerable damage.

In 1762 the diocesan bishop, Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão, founded in this chapel a confraternity of St John the Baptist to maintain religious services there, but we believe it did not last long. Around the middle of the 19th century António Ferreira Nogueira and Manuel Fernandes Jardim carried out important repairs there at their own expense, restoring the chapel to worship. In former times it was the centre of a popular pilgrimage, with pilgrims coming from all over the island. Today the novenas and feast of the patron saint are celebrated with remarkable splendour and large crowds from the city and its surroundings. The *Serões* published an interesting and detailed article by the Madeiran writer João dos Reis Gomes describing the place, the chapel, the *arraial* (open-air popular festival at a church feast) and the festivities of the Espírito Santo (‘Holy Spirit’) that were once held there.

In the locality (*sítio*) of Lombo de São João (‘St John’s ridge’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), there is a chapel of the same dedication, whose date of construction we do not know. It belonged to the Viscount of São João.

In 1700, in the locality of Serrado da Adega (‘wine-cellar field’) in the parish of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), António Correia Henriques and his wife Dona Maria da Câmara founded the chapel of St John the Baptist, which they endowed by a notarial deed of 17 June of that year.

On the stream of Calheta (‘small cove’) stand the ruins of the chapel of St John the Baptist, built on the *quinta* (country estate) of São João, seat of the entailed estate (*vínculo*) established by Captain Manuel de Figueiroa, who founded this chapel in 1651. As it had fallen into serious disrepair, Dona Guiomar Quiteria Betencourt de Atouguia, widow of João Albuquerque e Freitas, rebuilt it in 1770, and a licence for its blessing was granted on 19 August of the same year.

In the parish of Campanário (‘bell tower’) there was a chapel dedicated to St John the Baptist, founded in 1728 by Father João Betencourt da Câmara. In 1813 it was administered by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Luís Sauvayre.
There was a chapel of the same dedication in the parish of Santana (‘St Anne’), built in 1660 by Canon Domingos Gonçalves de Alvarenga.

It seems that there was another chapel of St John the Baptist in the parish of Calheta, at Lombo do Atouguia (‘Atouguia’s ridge’). It still exists, but is known today as São Pedro de Alcântara. It may originally have had two dedications, which would not be a unique case on this island.
See Lombo do Atouguia.
St John of God (chapel)
The article ‘Mental Asylums’ gives an account of this chapel, which belongs to the Trapiche Nursing Home (*Casa de Saúde do Trapiche*), in Santo António.
St John Lateran (chapel)

This chapel, which was completely demolished some twenty years ago (1921) and had long before fallen into total ruin, stood in the locality (*sítio*) to which it gave its own name. It was built at the behest of Nuno Fernandes Cardoso and his wife Leonor Dias, who, by a will made in 1511, founded the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of São João de Latrão (‘St John Lateran’), which took its name from the chapel that served as its seat. Referring to this will, the annotator of the *Saudades* says: ‘This will, of which we have a copy, is a model of its kind, for the sound probity, simplicity of faith and virtuous pride that dictated it. The moral and historical justification of entails finds in that venerable document a most honourable commemorative pillar (padrão) in its favour. The pure type of entails (*instituições vinculares*) is there. Our age cannot accept them, that is evident. But the just and enlightened historian judges by a subtler and loftier standard than the mere comparison of the past with the present.’

The last representative of this entailed house (*casa vinculada*) was Nuno Fernandes Cardoso e Vasconcelos, grandfather of Luís Cardoso de Castro e Abreu, the present schoolteacher of the parish (*freguesia*) of Gaula (1921).
St John and St Anne (chapel)

This chapel, which stands in the locality (*sítio*) of Trapiche (‘sugar mill’) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), is known only by the name of the place where it was built. Sergeant-major (*sargento-mor*, a field officer ranking as major) João António de Gouveia Rego, owner of the *quinta* (country estate) of Trapiche, had a chapel dedicated to St John the Baptist and St Anne built there in 1814; it was blessed and the first Mass was celebrated on 14 August of the same year. Attached to it is an excellent country house, which for some time served as the seminary after that educational establishment ceased to operate in the Incarnação building (1921).
This house, the chapel and their surroundings underwent extensive alterations, as can be seen in the article asylums (*Manicómios*).
St John the Evangelist (college and church)

In the article Jesuits we have already given a brief account of the establishment of the Society of Jesus and of its presence on this island until it was expelled by order of the Marquis of Pombal, that is, from 1570 to 1760, a period of 190 years (volume II, page 186).

For some time the Jesuits lived in houses adjoining the chapel of St Sebastian, in the street of that name, now called Praça do Comércio (volume II, page 359). There they held divine worship and taught their courses in the humanities and theology. They later moved to the church and hospice (*albergaria*) of St Bartholomew (volume I, page 70), which stood in Rua Direita (‘straight street’), a street that then ran along the left bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) as far as the present-day Ponte do Torreão (‘turret’).

These religious acquired the open square where the College (*Colégio*) church and the barracks of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria n.º 27*) stand today (1921), and settled there in modest lodgings with a small church attached. We conjecture that they moved there in the last years of the 16th century. Construction of the great college and the magnificent church must have begun towards the end of the first quarter of the 17th century, as appears to follow from a manuscript of the mid-18th century. This agrees, moreover, with the following words of the learned annotator of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso: ‘We have searched in vain in the building and church of the Jesuit college in Funchal for an inscription recording when they were built: we found only, above the outer door of the classroom courtyard, which belongs to the same college... the date 1619... The vault of the chancel has traces of an architectural design that is still Manueline. The crossing, the nave and the carved woodwork of the chapels are in the bastard taste of the Renaissance. The building work was carried out, it seems, slowly and would only have been regarded as finished around the middle of the 17th century, apart from certain details of ornamentation that would have been definitively completed later still, such as the placing of the statues on the church façade, the decoration of some chapels, etc.

The Jesuits held this church and college until 16 July 1760, when, on the orders of the Marquis of Pombal, they left Madeira under arrest. For some years all the premises of the college and the church remained closed. Then, by a royal letter (*carta régia*) of 10 August 1787, Maria I ceded these buildings to the bishop, Dom José da Costa Tôrres, so that the Diocesan Seminary could be established there. This educational establishment was formally opened on 31 March 1788.

The Seminary did not remain there long, because the occupation of Madeira by British troops in 1801 forced that house of education to move to the old building in the New Convent (*Mosteiro Novo*) street. The Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*) was turned into barracks and occupied by part of the British garrison. When the British troops left, the College was vacated, and in 1803, at the time of the terrible flash flood (*aluvião*), it housed countless people who had been left homeless.

The College had also been occupied by some Portuguese military forces. The governor and captain-general, Dom José Manuel da Câmara, refused to withdraw them, as the bishop, Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares, demanded, so that the Diocesan Seminary could be reinstalled there. This refusal, together with other circumstances, gave rise in 1803 to a serious conflict between the governor and the prelate, as has already been briefly related on page 216 of this volume. Although the diocesan bishop emerged victorious from this conflict and his right to possession of the College and its premises was recognised, the Seminary certainly never returned there. The College continued to be used to quarter troops and to house various public offices.

From 1808 to 1814, during the second occupation of this island by British troops, the College once again served as their quarters, and for some time Major-General Beresford had the seat of his government of the island there. From that time to the present, the old Jesuit College has always served as barracks for the troops of this city’s garrison.

After the members of the Society of Jesus left this island in 1760, the church of São João Evangelista was closed to the public, and for many years no services were held in it. It is possible that while the Seminary occupied the building next to the church, the church was restored to religious use. We have seen it mentioned somewhere that the British troops attended Protestant services there, and that the church was placed under interdict as a result. We cannot state this with complete certainty.

When Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro took over the government of this district in 1847, the College church was in an advanced state of ruin, and Catholic worship had long since ceased there. It was solely thanks to his persistent efforts that the church underwent major repairs and was returned to religious service, which has continued without interruption to the present day.

A manuscript held in the Public Library of Porto, cited in the *Historia da Egreja em Portugal* by Fortunato de Almeida, contains some interesting information about the foundation of various colleges and churches established by the Jesuits. A distinguished friend of ours who lives in the city of Porto undertook to make some extracts from this manuscript relating to the college of São João Evangelista in Funchal, and we reproduce them below:

‘Its church is rich and majestic, adorned and furnished with precious ornaments in all its chapels and altars, with many pieces of the finest silver. It is 95 *palmos* long and 54 wide. The nave consists of four large chapels, which are 18 *palmos* deep and 21 wide; two of these, which lie beneath the choir, have the same depth and differ only in width, being just 15 *palmos* wide. It has its transept, which is 80 *palmos* long and 38 wide; the two chapels, or niches, beside the high altar are 10 *palmos* deep and the same in width; and the chancel is 32 deep and 23 wide. ‘All these chapels have their founders or confraternities, as follows. The niche on the Gospel side next to the chancel is consecrated to the Virgin Our Lady under the dedication of Nossa Senhora da Luz (Our Lady of Light). For this reason its feast and adornment were entrusted to the Confraternity of our Students, who attend or have attended those classes for some years, for this noble and devout brotherhood embraces all who studied in them. This most holy Lady is venerated and visited in her image by the whole of that city, being the object of very special devotion.’

‘The corresponding niche on the Epistle side is likewise dedicated to the same Lady, under the title of Succour. Its founders were Canon João de Saldanha and his brother, the beneficed cleric (*beneficiado*) Joseph de Saldanha, both most devoted to our Society and distinguished benefactors of that Royal College. On the two sides of the transept there are also two chapels facing each other. The one on the Gospel side is consecrated to Jesus Crucified and is cared for by the noble Brotherhood of the Stations of the Passion (*passos*, wayside oratories depicting scenes of Christ’s Passion) of the same Lord, which exists in that city. The corresponding one on the Epistle side is dedicated to Our Lady under the dedication which the city and island call ‘of the Second Condition’. ‘In the nave, the first chapel on the Gospel side is dedicated to the Holy Eleven Thousand Virgins; its founder was Simão Nunes Machado. The second, consecrated to the Archangel St Michael, was founded by the Reverend Father Miguel Pereyra, a very great benefactor of that college. On the Epistle side, the first is that of the Apostle of the East, St Francis Xavier, which was founded and endowed by the Licentiate Bento de Mattos. The second is that of St Anthony of Padua, and its founders were Doctor António Spínola, a famous physician in that city, and his wife Dona Francisca de São Paio, whom this college also counts among its distinguished benefactors. Of the two chapels beneath the choir, Father António Franco says that at the time he was writing they still had no founders, although they were adorned at the college’s expense. However, on enquiring of some religious who had lived in that college and celebrated Mass in its church, I learned that the chapel on the Epistle side was dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), and that its founder had been one António de Oliveyra, a native of this kingdom and of the town of Pombal, who had married Maria da Rocha on that island. Having no children, they founded the chapel and gave all their property to it. In one of the clauses of their joint will and grant, the said António de Oliveyra declared that, should he die before his wife, she would be bound on the day after his death to go and hear Mass for his soul in his aforesaid chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception; and he bound himself to do the same should his wife die first. He did and declared this in order to do away with the custom and abuse wrongly prevailing in that city, whereby those in mourning did not leave the house for a whole year, not even to hear Mass on feast days and holy days of obligation. Of the other chapel beneath the choir, facing this one, I am told that it is very well adorned, for the church has very sumptuous revenues; but when I wrote this I found no one who could tell me whether it had any founder or confraternity.’
