‘I wrote the account of this chapel according to the information given to me by Jesuits who had lived in that college; but afterwards I received the letter from Father José Lopes already mentioned, in which he tells me the following: “In a chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, which, although adorned by António de Oliveyra Baptista, has no founder, nor has it yet been purchased or endowed, even though the said man and his wife Maria da Rocha left it their thirds [of their estates], the amount of which is not yet known, since no inventory has been made.” After this was written, Father Lopes informed me in a letter of 10 March 1751 that the said chapel is consecrated to St Quiteria and has its own confraternity of that holy Virgin and Martyr. ‘The frontispiece and main façade of this church, which is magnificent and the finest on the whole island, was adorned with four marble statues of ordinary human size, representing St Ignatius, our founder and patriarch, St Francis Xavier, St Francis Borgia and St Stanislaus. The Reverend Father Manoel Lobo had them made by an expert sculptor at the Court in Lisbon; but they arrived on the island and were set in place after the rectorship of the Reverend Father José Lopes had already begun.’

‘The whole building of the College consists of five corridors, and the entire work is laid out in a magnificent quadrangle, which also takes in the Church. The corridor of the Porter’s Lodge is ninety-four *palmos* long; the one the College calls the Great Corridor, three hundred and fifty; that of the Library and the College’s inner Chapel, two hundred and twenty-eight; the Corridor known as the Eyrado [Terrace], one hundred and sixty-two; and that of the Lavatory, two hundred and forty-six. All of them are of the same width, sixteen and a half *palmos*, and twenty and a half in height. Many people of this Island have at various times granted great favours and donations to this our College, and so the number of its distinguished Benefactors is large. Dona Helena de Vasconcelos gave two *contos* for the building of the main Chapel, which she chose as her family vault and burial place, and that of her two cousins and sisters-in-law, Dona Brites da Silva and Dona Isabel da Silva, who gave the College more than four *contos* under the obligation of certain pious bequests. They also gave the sacristy of the Church various pieces of gold and silver. With this, and with the donations of the other benefactors of its Chapels, the Church became the best endowed of those we see in this Province, and so it is seen adorned with great richness and neatness. The dowry of this College was assigned by its most august Founder on the revenues of His Royal Customs House; but, as the years went by, it was changed to the Tithes of three parishes near Ribeira Brava, which are the most important share of its dowry and subsistence.’
To complete this information on the College of the Society of Jesus in Funchal, we transcribe the following notes, published in the former newspaper *A Justiça*:

‘The founder of the main chapel was Dona Helena de Bettencourt e Vasconcellos, wife of António de Andrade e Silva, and she endowed it with good revenues, as did her sisters-in-law Dona Brites and Dona Isabel da Silva, daughters of Martim Gonçalves de Andrade and Dona Maria de Brito. All three were buried in that chapel, and on the stone slab under which they rest one can still read today: Tomb of Dona Helena de Bettencourt, founder of this chapel, and of her cousins and sisters-in-law Dona Brites da Silva and Dona Isabel da Silva, distinguished benefactresses of this Church and College. In 1654 Simão Nunes Machado and his wife Dona Joana Telo made a grant of property to the chantry (*capela*) of the Eleven Thousand Virgins. In 1682 Father Miguel Pereira, who lies there, as can be seen from the inscription on his tombstone, also gave property to that of St Michael. Property was given to that of St Anthony by Dr António Spínola Teixeira and his wife Dona Francisca, a native of Coimbra. António de Oliveira, a native of Condeixa, and his wife Maria Rocha also gave property to that of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception.’

The Jesuits had taken possession of the chapel of St Sebastian and the adjoining houses, where they first settled, on 6 May, the day on which the Church commemorates the martyrdom inflicted on St John the Evangelist, from which he miraculously emerged unharmed. In memory of that fact, the religious gave the college and church the name of the exile of Patmos.
The architect and painter of the building was an Italian from Tuscany whose name we do not know, and the chief sculptor was called Brás Fernandes. See Município (square).
St John of Nepomuk (chapel)

João Nepomuceno de Freitas Leal had this chapel built in 1776 beside his residence in the locality (*sítio*) of Folhadal (‘folhado grove’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’). The deed of endowment of the chapel is dated 3 November of that year; the endowment was charged on an estate ‘at the place they call the friar’s gate, opposite the resting place, also opposite where the said friar Manuel de Gouveia lives, which he had from his father Pantaleão de Freitas Leal’, as can be read in the deed itself. A licence for it to be blessed was issued on 3 March 1786. By a papal brief dated the same year, the chapel was granted the faculty of a privileged altar.

When the curacy (*curato*) of Porto da Cruz was created in 1800, the curate was obliged to reside near this chapel and to celebrate divine service in it. It was placed under interdict from 1812 to 1822, because its administrator sought to remove it from parochial jurisdiction.

It always remained in the possession and administration of the Freitas Leal family. Dona Luzia Leal, niece of the founder, bequeathed the little church to Dona Augusta Lomelino de Freitas Leal, wife of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Dr João Baptista de Freitas Leal, and their nephews, António Lomelino Bianchi and his brothers, are its present owners (1921). The chapel is well preserved and services are held in it.
São João (stream)

It rises in the mountains of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’) and flows into the ocean at the locality (*sítio*) of São Lázaro, in the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), and is one of the three large streams that cross the city of Funchal. The stretch that runs through the parish of Santo António is called Ribeira Grande or Ribeira de Santo António. In former times it was also called St Francis, São Paulo, Santa Catarina and São Lázaro. All these names are found in old documents.
São Jorge (parish)

This parish (*freguesia*) was originally made up of the land that forms it today together with the land that now belongs to the parishes of Santana (‘St Anne’) and Arco de São Jorge (‘arc of São Jorge’). Santana soon broke away, having remained dependent on the mother parish for only a few years, and Arco de São Jorge became an autonomous parish in 1676.

It is no longer possible today to determine with complete precision when the colonisation and settlement of this parish began. One of its earliest *sesmeiros* (holders of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) was Lopo Fernandes Pinto, ‘who, says Dr Álvaro de Azevedo, came to live on this island around the middle of the 15th century and died in the year 1500: he held as a *sesmaria* a good part of the parish of Santana, and the lands called da Ilha (‘island’), from which two entails were formed, the one founded by his son Jorge Pinto and the entail of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’)’. These lands of Ilha lie in the interior of this parish. The last administrator (administrador do concelho, government-appointed head of the municipality) of the entailed estate founded by Jorge Pinto was the holder of the entail Falcão, an Azorean, who some years ago sold those lands to the tenant farmers who cultivated them.

Another early *sesmeiro* who held land in this parish was Pedro Gomes Galdo, whom we have found cited in various genealogies of the nobility and who, we conjecture, came to this island at the end of the 15th century. We have no knowledge of any other settlers who established themselves in this parish at the end of the 15th century or in the first half of the 16th.

The date that the annotator of the *Saudades* gives for the creation of this parish seems to us to be inaccurate. The year 1517, which he indicates as such, can only refer to the appointment of a chaplain of its own, who was given authority to perform certain parochial functions. The creation of São Jorge (‘St George’) as an autonomous parish must be contemporary with that of Faial, and perhaps even somewhat later, since it is certain that the latter parish was created in 1550, having had its own chaplain since 1519. The oldest document we have found cited concerning the parish of São Jorge is that of 4 June 1552, which increased the parish stipend (*côngrua*) and fixed it at one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat, one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and 8,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash; at that time the parish priest combined service in this parish with the chaplaincy with cure of souls (capelania-curada), not yet an autonomous parish, of Santana. We have reason to believe that the parish of São Jorge was created only a little before the date of that document. The royal decree (alvará régio) of 27 November 1572 granted the parish priest an annual salary of 25,000 *réis*, the parish then having 106 households (*fogos*, literally 'hearths'), and that of 20 April 1589 added to this salary a further thirty *alqueires* of wheat and a quarter of wine.

The new parish took its name from a chapel dedicated to St George, which later became the parish church. This chapel seems to have been built in the last quarter of the 15th century or the early 16th century. The parish church was built in the locality (*sítio*) of Calhau (‘pebble shore’), on one of the banks of the stream; we cannot at present say whether it stood on the same spot as the old chapel. Around 1660 the church was almost entirely destroyed by a flash flood (*aluvião*). It was then decided that the new church should be built on a safer and more sheltered site, one that would also be more convenient for the people, since the homesteads were spreading inland along the left bank of the stream.

The church built nearly a century later is the one that serves as the parish church today. Its construction must have begun towards the end of the second quarter of the 18th century, and the work was declared finished around the middle of the third quarter of the same century. Several orders of the Treasury Council (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 1747, 1751 and 1754 authorised the payment of certain sums for the work. The vicar Marques de Mendonça contributed greatly to the completion of the building and the embellishment of the church, not only with his zeal and dedication but also with his own private fortune.

The visitor’s eye is caught at once by the gilt carved woodwork (*talha dourada*) of the high altar and by the sacristy furniture made to hold the vestments and church furnishings. In several foreign works, especially in a piece by the Marquis Degli Albizzi, we find some references to these works of art. It is worth quoting here the words of Dr Alfredo Leal, recently (1921) published in a magazine of this city: ‘It is certainly one of the most beautiful churches in Madeira, above all for the richness of the gilt carved woodwork of the high altar, which is also the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament. It was in the sacristy, however, that I found an interesting feast for my eyes. The great table and the cupboards in til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) or Madeira mahogany (vinhático, Persea indica), with turned columns in the style the French call *rococo portugais*, which is found in all the carved woodwork of the 17th and 18th centuries in Portugal, are very artistically executed, without the gilding that has been and still is so abused in Portuguese churches. It is astonishing how, in that sacristy and in some others in Madeira, these lovely carvings have escaped the barbarous brush of the makers of false marble, which imitates bar soap more than marble, as has so unfortunately happened to the slender columns of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*). In the middle of the cupboards above the sacristy table, facing the place where the priest vests for the sacred mysteries of the altar, is a crucifix in which the body of Christ is perhaps a metre tall. It is one of the most beautiful wooden sculptures I have ever seen. It is a marvel in which anatomy and the expression of the face and gestures unite, producing a feeling that is tenderly grand.’

This church holds another artistic gem: a small image of the martyr St Sebastian, four to five decimetres tall, which is a true marvel of sculpture. It belonged to a chapel that once stood in this parish, of which no trace remains today.
The growth of the population brought this parish a curate, a post created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 11 February 1746.

Besides the chapel already mentioned, there was once that of Our Lady of the Rosary (*Nossa Senhora do Rosário*), in the locality (*sítio*) of Ilha, and that of St Peter still exists; we shall give a brief account of both elsewhere in this volume. Compared with other parishes of Madeira, this one has no great unevenness of terrain and is extremely picturesque. It offers the visitor beautiful and surprising panoramas and, like Santana, bears a strong resemblance to the enchanting landscapes of the Minho.

Principal localities: São Pedro, Achada Grande, Tanque, Farrobo, Ribeira Funda, Pico, Pé do Pico, Poço e Vale, Lombo do Cunha, Açougue Velho, Covas, Furna de Pedro Jorge, Lombo do Pico, Jogo da Bola, Pomar, Achada do Pico, Lanço, Fajã Alta, São Sebastião, Calhau, Pedra Mole, Loural, Tranquada, Banda do Sol and Ilha. In the locality of Ribeiro do Meio lies the well-known lignite deposit, which we have already discussed (volume II, page 271).
As for the Quinta de São Jorge, the property of the diocesan prelate, enough has already been said on page 13 of this volume. This parish has 2,142 inhabitants (1921).
São Jorge (islet, point, landing place and stream)
The small islet of São Jorge (‘St George’) lies close to the coast of the parish (*freguesia*) of the same name, almost opposite its landing place.

The projection on Madeira’s north coast that juts furthest out to sea is called Ponta de São Jorge (‘St George Point’) and lies on the coast of the parish of the same name. From the tip of this headland, at the spot known as the Vigia (‘lookout’), every twist and turn of the coastline can be seen, from the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) to that of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), and this village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) deserves a visit. At the spot known as Ponta Gorda (‘broad point’) a quay was built between 1904 and 1910; a footpath links it to the main road that connects the parishes of Santana (‘St Anne’) and São Jorge.

The stream rises near Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’) and crosses the parish of São Jorge, flowing into the sea at the landing place of the same name. Its tributaries are the Canário, Grande and Lombo da Furna brooks.
St Joseph (chapels)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), a short distance from the parish church, there stood a chapel dedicated to St Joseph which, according to the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), was founded by Luís Gonçalves da Silva in 1710. Around 1905 it was still standing, though in an advanced state of ruin, and bore the date 1709 above its doorway. On 15 April 1750 a licence was granted for it to be blessed, and its administrator at the time was Second Lieutenant Tomé João Pimentel. Was it only blessed in 1750, or was this a rebuilding? We do not know. It is certain, however, that the licence for the blessing was granted on 15 April 1750, as we were able to verify from an authentic document.

In the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’) there was a chapel dedicated to São José, whose founder and date we cannot determine. We do know, however, that the earthquake of 1748 left it badly damaged and that Francisco Agostinho de Figueiroa e Vasconcelos, its administrator and administrator of the entail attached to it, had it rebuilt in 1776, moving it to a safer site but close to the original building. So that services could be held in it, it was inspected by the ecclesiastical authorities on 3 June 1776.

In the same parish, and with the same dedication, there is today an elegant chapel built in 1915 in the locality (*sítio*) of Vale da Bica (‘spout valley’) by Dr Manuel dos Passos Freitas, beside the residence he owns there (1921).

On the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) there was a chapel dedicated to São José, founded in 1681 by Estêvão Bettencourt Perestrelo, governor of that island. The deed of endowment of this chapel is dated 7 July 1681.
In 1730 Father António Gonçalves Franco founded a chapel dedicated to São José in the parish of Machico; it is now in ruins.
In the parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) there was a chapel consecrated to São José, whose founder and date of construction are entirely unknown to us.
At the beginning of the second quarter of the 20th century, a chapel with the same dedication was built in the picturesque locality of Achada (‘plateau’), in the parish of Camacha.
São José (fort)

The fort of St Joseph on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) was built on the orders of the Marquis of Pombal and, in honour of the king’s name, was given that saint as its patron saint. It now belongs to the Águas do Porto Santo company, having been sold at auction for 52,250.00 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) on 18 May 1923 (1921).
St Lazarus (chapel)
There was a chapel with this dedication in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), founded by João Afonso Escudeiro at the beginning of the 16th century (see Bemposta).
The chapel of the former St Lazarus’s Hospital (*Hospital de São Lázaro*), now the civil gaol, has the same dedication (1921).
See St Lazarus’s Hospital.
St Lawrence (chapels)

In the Fort of São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’) there was a chapel dedicated to the martyr St Lawrence. It is quite old and already existed in 1566, the year in which French corsairs sacked the city. It had its own chaplain, and the oldest royal decree (*alvará*) we have found appointing that chaplain is dated 15 November 1641. We have seen somewhere that on 3 October 1846 Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro ordered an inventory of the silver objects belonging to this chapel, which weighed 36 pounds, and had them deposited in the Central Treasury. A new inventory was made on 3 December 1856, with further pieces added, the whole weighing 65 pounds of silver. In 1856 the chapel’s vestments were given to the church of Achadas da Cruz (see the São Lourenço Palace).

The chapel of St Lawrence in the locality (*sítio*) of the same name in the parish (*freguesia*) of Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) is quite old, for in the first years of the 16th century it was already the seat of a chaplaincy (capelania), which later became a parish. It served as the parish church until the middle of the 18th century, when the new church was built. An old tradition records that this chapel belonged to the Afonsos Jardins, who were among the earliest settlers there and owners of the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) on which the chapel stands.

In the parish of Camacha there was a chapel dedicated to St Lawrence, said to have been built by Francisco Gonçalves Salgado. It was of quite old construction, and in 1676 the seat of the new parish was established in it, so that it became the parish church; its patron saint is still that of the original chapel.
São Lourenço (fortress)

It was originally a simple bastion. Its construction seems to have begun in the time of the fourth donatary, João Gonçalves da Câmara, and the works continued by order of the king during the governorship of Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the fifth donatary, as the royal decree (*alvará*) of 11 September 1542 shows. When the French corsairs invaded in 1566, only the bastion existed, but by the reign of King Sebastian the fortress had been built, although it still looked different from how it appears today.

The São Lourenço fortress (*Fortaleza de São Lourenço*) displays on its east tower the arms of Portugal and the emblematic armillary sphere of Manuel I. When Dr Azevedo wrote his notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), the following inscription could still be seen above the door of the now destroyed chapel of the saint who gave his name to the fortification we are describing:
D. V. N. D. 16 3 S
According to Dr Azevedo, this inscription seems to mean: *DEO VOTA NOSTRO DOMINO*, 1635, that is, DEDICATED TO GOD OUR LORD, IN THE YEAR 1635.

The arms of Portugal and the sphere of Manuel I were removed from the fortress after the proclamation of the Republic, but some four years ago they were returned to their place, since it had been recognised, albeit belatedly, that there was no reason at all to hide them from public view. What could not be restored to the fortress was a statue of St Lawrence that stood in a niche above the main door, on the Largo da Restauração, for it was torn down and broken by some navy sailors who were in Funchal in 1911 (1921).
Near the spot where the meteorological station stands, there was for many years a chestnut tree that flowered and bore fruit every year and gave its name to one of the fortress’s bastions.
See Fortifications and the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’).
São Lourenço (point)
See Ponta de São Lourenço.
St Louis (chapels)

A chapel with this dedication once stood in the locality (*sítio*) of Diferença (‘difference’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Faial. It had been founded by Manuel de Carvalho Valdavesso, Judge of Orphans in Funchal, and his wife Dona Luísa Maria de Vasconcelos França e Noronha, daughter of Valentim de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, 7th holder of the entail (*morgado*) of Penha de Águia (‘eagle crag’). The deed of endowment, charged on a property in the parish of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), is dated 1 October 1725, so the chapel was built at approximately that time.

Beside the old bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*), Bishop Dom Luís Figueiredo de Lemos (volume II, page 30) built the chapel of São Luís, and he was buried there in 1608. It is said that his tomb was violated. When, around 1882, the chapel was converted to house a school, the ashes of this prelate were placed in the inner chapel of the bishop's palace, and some years later they were transferred to the Cathedral (Sé Catedral). Over them was laid the tombstone that had stood in the centre of the chapel where the prelate’s mortal remains had originally been buried. The chapel, which has a fine portal skilfully carved in *cantaria rija* (hard dressed stone of vesicular basalt), has been deconsecrated for many years.
São Martinho (parish)

In the early days of colonisation, before this parish (*freguesia*) was created, the lands that make it up today belonged to the parish of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*). They later became part of the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’), from which they were separated in 1579.

As we have already pointed out, the lands surrounding the first settlement that grew up in Funchal were immediately brought under cultivation. A number of “settled farmsteads” (*fazendas povoadas*) were organised, each with its own private chantry (capela), and these gave rise to the new parishes that followed.

So it was in São Martinho (‘St Martin’). There was an estate and a chantry of that name there, belonging to Afonso Anes, known as the Hortelão (the Gardener), according to the annotator of the *Saudades*. It was here that the seat of the parish was established, created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 3 March 1579.

By the same decree the parish priest was assigned an annual stipend (*côngrua*) of 11,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine. The decree of 16 July 1581 raised this to 16,000 *réis* in cash, one *moio* of wheat and half a *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. Some years later, the decree of 30 January 1589 added a further half *moio* of wheat and a quarter of wine to this salary.

Despite the growth in population, no curacy (*curato*) was created in this parish. Some years ago the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto appointed a curate to this parish on a provisional basis, dividing the stipend of one of the two parish priests of the Sé among the assistant priests of São Gonçalo, the Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) and São Martinho. These posts were created on an interim basis, but in this parish they have taken on a permanent character, in view of its population and activity (1921).

Nothing is known of the year in which the chapel of São Martinho was built, nor of the spot where it stood, though it is conjectured that it lay near the old parish church. Because the chapel was small, a parish church was built in the first or second quarter of the 17th century. Around 1735, however, this church was almost entirely rebuilt; it is the older of the two present parish churches.

The ever-growing population made the church too small for the services and activity of the parish, so an attempt was made to build a new church that would fully meet the needs of the faithful. The central government granted a fairly substantial sum for the new building, and the parishioners also gave generous donations, thanks mainly to the efforts and endeavours of the parish priest of the time, Father Manuel Pinto Correia. The foundation stone was laid and blessed with full solemnity on 8 July 1883. Work proceeded slowly, however, and for lack of funds it had to be halted within a short time.

Some thirty years later, building work resumed. On 2 August 1907 the benefactor José de Abreu, a parishioner, died in this parish, having left almost all of his fortune – a considerable one for the time – to the continuation of the work on the church. That sum could not cover all the heavy expenses still to be met, but the parish priest Teodoro João Henriques boldly took the initiative of pressing on with the work, trusting that the generosity of the parishioners would not allow the building to remain unfinished. And, happily, he was not mistaken. Around 1909 or 1910 the work, interrupted for more than twenty years, was vigorously resumed, and on 24 June 1918 the new church was consecrated with great splendour. It was opened for worship at once, while the decoration of the altars and side chapels and the final completion of other work continued.

This parish contains the chapels of Nossa Senhora da Vitória, Nossa Senhora da Ajuda, Nossa Senhora do Amparo, Nossa Senhora do Pilar, Nossa Senhora da Nazaré, Nossa Senhora das Virtudes and Santana. There were once also chapels of Nossa Senhora da Fé and Nossa Senhora de Jesus, which have been demolished. We give an account of some of these and others elsewhere in this work. In the article devoted to the chapel of Santo Amaro, we pointed out the error of the annotator of the *Saudades*, who placed in this parish the chapel of Santo Amaro and the castellated manor house of Garcia Homem de Sousa, both of which lie in the parish of Santo António.

The principal localities of this parish are: Pilar, Pico do Funcho, Lombada, Vitória, Quebradas, Areeiro, Ajuda, Piornais, Ribeiro Seco, Casa Branca, Nazaré, Amparo, Várzea da Igreja, Caminho Novo, Praia, Poço Borral, Pico de São Martinho and Virtudes.

The parish is bounded in part to the south by the so-called Praia Formosa (volume III, page 138) and to the west by the Ribeira dos Socorridos, which separates it from the parish of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). Near the Praia Formosa lies the Fojo (‘pit’), which we have already mentioned on page 230 of volume I of this work.

In this parish are the rifle range (*Carreira de Tiro*), of which we have already given an account (volume I, page 251), ‘Reid’s, Palace Hotel’ and its annexes, and the important fish cannery of Júdice Fialho, which we have also dealt with (volume II, page 161).

Of the so-called Estrada Monumental (‘monumental road’), which runs through a large part of this parish, and of the Ponte do Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook bridge’), where that road begins, we have already said what is necessary in volume I of this work, on page 416. On this subject the pamphlet *Collecção de documentos relativos á construção da Ponte do Ribeiro Secco*, published in 1848, may be consulted.

The land of this parish is watered by several levadas (irrigation channels), foremost among them the Levada dos Piornais (‘broom thickets’), one of the most important private levadas on the island, which we have already mentioned on page 256 of volume II.
The Bishop of Ceuta and Tangier, Dom Martinho de Aguiar, was born in São Martinho (volume I, page 28). The parish has 6,556 inhabitants (1921).
St Paul (chapels)

The chapel of this dedication on the Largo de São Paulo is one of the oldest on the island, and we believe it was the first to be built after that of St Catherine (see that entry). It was originally named after St Peter and St Paul (*São Pedro e São Paulo*). However, although the seat of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro was established there, it was the second name that endured through the ages and is still in use today. Above the portico one can still see the traditional keys, or papal arms, bearing witness to the chapel’s patron saint, or former dedication.

Its founder was João Gonçalves Zarco, who built his second residence beside it, said to have been the first stone house constructed in Funchal, and then moved there from Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’). See Moradias de Zargo (‘Zargo’s dwellings’).
The date 1426, which can be read above the outer gate leading into the small churchyard, evidently refers to the original building.
Over the centuries the small and modest church has undergone various repairs, and certainly nothing remains of the original building. In 1871 it was almost completely rebuilt.

Services in the chapel of St Paul were conducted by Franciscan friars until 1566, when the parish of São Pedro was created and its seat installed in this same chapel. The parish was abolished in 1579 and restored in 1586; it is not known whether the parish was installed for the second time in this chapel or in some other. In 1879 a confraternity bearing the name of the patron saint was organised there, and its statutes were approved by the highest authority of the district by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 13 March of that year.

It was beside this chapel that the building intended for the first hospital was erected, which had been donated for this purpose by the discoverer João Gonçalves Zargo, as already mentioned on page 366 of volume II.

There was once a chapel dedicated to St Paul in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), of which some ruins still remain. It was founded by Father Paulo Vieira Jardim, parish priest of that parish, who died there on 15 February 1776 and was buried in the chapel he had founded. It was also known as the chapel of St Paul and the Holy Souls (*São Paulo e Almas*).
São Paulo (street)
It ran between the Carreira (‘track’) gate and the Ribeira de São João (‘St John’s stream’), and is today part of Rua do Dr. Vieira, formerly Rua da Carreira.

Today the square in front of the chapel of St Paul (*São Paulo*) bears the name Largo de São Paulo, and the public way linking that square with Rua da Ribeira (‘stream’) is called Travessa de São Paulo. In former times the so-called ‘locality (*sítio*) of São Paulo’, which took in the surroundings of the chapel, extended as far as the bank of the Ribeira de São João.
São Pedro (Baron of)

To what we said about this fellow Madeiran of ours on page 261 of volume I of this work, it should be added that he wrote a pamphlet entitled *Do álcool e dos compostos alcoólicos em cirurgia*. He was the son-in-law of the 1st Baron of São Pedro (volume III, page 27) and the father of Dona Josefina de Castelo Branco Ribeiro da Cunha. As the wife of the civil governor José Ribeiro da Cunha, she rendered notable services to the destitute in this city, and her portrait is kept in the meeting room of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Misericórdia (Holy House of Mercy, a lay charitable brotherhood) of Funchal (1921).
St Peter (chapel)

At the western end of the south coast of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) stands a small chapel dedicated to St Peter, which once had a small pilgrims’ house attached to it. The annual feast of the patron saint is celebrated there, attended by large numbers of the island’s inhabitants.

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), west of the town (*vila*) and beside the road, stands the chapel of St Peter, founded by João Escorcio Drumond. It was razed by the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803 and rebuilt by the people some years later.

Near the parish church of the parish of São Jorge (‘St George’) there is a chapel dedicated to St Peter. It had fallen into ruin and was restored in 1901 by the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, who himself blessed it and returned it to worship on 7 August of the same year.
In the parish of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), at the place known as Terra de São Pedro (‘St Peter’s land’), there was once a small chapel dedicated to St Peter, of which not even traces remain.

In the locality (*sítio*) of Lamaceiros (‘mud flats’), in the same parish, there is a chapel consecrated to St Peter, to which the image of the saint from the other chapel of the same dedication was moved. It is not of recent construction, for as early as 1726 it was already in an advanced state of ruin. Some years later it was properly repaired through the efforts of Manuel Rodrigues Amarelo. The earthquake of 1748 caused it various kinds of damage, and it was promptly repaired. Only a few years ago important works were carried out on it. The chapel holds a greatly venerated image of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*).
The Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*) is always reserved in this chapel, and the doors of the little church stand open every day and all day long for anyone who wishes to visit it (1921).
St Peter of Alcantara (chapel)

This chapel stands in the locality (*sítio*) of Lombo do Atouguia (‘Atouguia’s ridge’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’). It was founded in 1783 by João Baptista Teixeira. The deed of endowment is dated 9 February 1783, and permission for the chapel to be blessed was granted on 13 October of the same year.
See chapel of St John the Baptist (*São João Baptista*).
São Pedro (fort)

It stood at the eastern end of the old Praça Académica (‘academic square’), and its demolition began on 20 September 1897, under an authorisation from the Ministry of War. Its construction was completed in 1707, according to an inscription that was on the gate of the fort and was transcribed on page 629 of the notes to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*).
The Fort of São Pedro was also known as the New Fort (*Forte Novo*).
São Pedro (parish)

São Pedro is the most populous and the most important of the four urban parishes (*freguesia*) of Funchal. It was within its bounds that the first colonisation and settlement began, because the discoverer Gonçalves Zarco himself made his first settlement there, on the height later called Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’). On the day the caravels first made for the bay that was to take the name of Funchal, they sought shelter by the islets lying to the west of that bay, as the day was already well advanced, and the captain decided that the discoverers should spend that night there. When they returned to this island from the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) a second time, to begin the work of colonisation in earnest, the ships again anchored in the shelter of the same islets. The first settlers took refuge aboard them for several days, when the fire raging fiercely through the woods forced them to leave the land scorched by the flames. These islets were later named the Ilhéus da Pontinha (‘little point’), and they lie within the parish of São Pedro.

‘The parish of São Pedro, in the city of Funchal,’ says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘had its origin in the chapel of St Paul (see that entry), founded by João Gonçalves Zarco, which was served by Franciscan friars and later by the curates of the Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), until it was separated from the latter and constituted a parish in its own right by the royal decree (*alvará*) of King Sebastian of 20 June 1566, with the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’) as its boundary to the east and the Ribeira dos Socorridos to the west. It was abolished by the royal decree of 3 March 1579 of the Cardinal-King Henry the Navigator, its urban part being reincorporated into that of the Sé, while from its suburban part the same decree created the parishes of São Roque and São Martinho; but a few years later, by the royal decree of Philip II of 14 August 1587, it was re-established with the boundaries it still has today.’

The frequently cited *Índice do Registo* of the former Crown Revenue Office (*Provedoria*) records that this parish was created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 20 July 1566, and not of 20 June 1566, as the annotator of the *Saudades* states. Its first parish priest was Gaspar Teixeira, whose annual stipend (*côngrua*) was fixed by the said decree of 20 July 1566 at 15,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and half a *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine. The royal decree of 20 August 1572 raised this to 25,000 *réis*, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine. The royal decrees of 8 May 1591, 17 May 1600, 19 August 1609 and 10 June 1749 raised the annual emoluments respectively to 26,700 *réis*, two *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine; 29,700 *réis*, two *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine; 30,000 *réis*, two *moios* of wheat and two *pipas* of wine; and 60,000 *réis*, two *moios* of wheat and two *pipas* of wine.

The curacy (*curato*) of this parish (*freguesia*) was created by the royal decree of 27 August 1589, which assigned the curate an annual stipend of 20,000 *réis*; the decree of 19 August 1609 added one *pipa* of wine to this.

This parish had a collegiate church, created by the decree of 26 May 1589, with two beneficed clerics (*beneficiado*) in addition to the vicar and the curate. The decree of 23 March 1590 gave this collegiate church another beneficed cleric, and that of 24 July of the same year created a fourth; under this last decree each received an annual salary of 6,000 *réis* in cash and one *moio* of wheat. The collegiate church also had a treasurer, a preacher and an organist.

The seat of this parish was established in the chapel of St Paul, which we have already described, and there is no doubt that when the parish was restored in 1587 this same chapel served as the parish church, despite its cramped dimensions. We do not know in what year the seat of the parish moved from the chapel of St Paul to the present parish church. Nor do we know when the new church was built. On this point the annotator of the *Saudades* gives the following information, which is the same as that supplied by the *Índice* of the Provedoria: ‘Under the decree of 15 June 1598 the fabric fund of the church received 4,000 *réis*, and by various orders of the Council of the Treasury the following sums were spent on it: in 1688, on works to the church, 900,000 *réis*; from 1737 to 1739, on the building of the new church, carried out under an award by public auction (*arrematação*), 6,742,000 *réis*; in 1742, for the casting of the bells, 217,000 *réis*; and in 1757, for repairing the damage caused by the earthquake of 1 April 1748, 3,029,730 *réis*. Also in 1742 the same Council ordered the churchyard, or paved area in front of the church, and the altarpiece of the high altar to be made, but it is not recorded how much was spent on these.’

The present head of state (1921), Mr Manuel Teixeira Gomes, on a visit to Madeira some years ago, discovered with his great learning and refined artistic taste the marvellous paintings in the sacristy of the church of São Pedro, which until then had gone unnoticed by everyone; he later revealed them to the wider public in his book *Cartas sem moral nenhuma*.

In this parish stand the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), which holds the tomb of João Gonçalves Zargo, and the chapels of São João da Ribeira, St Paul, St Catherine, Our Lady of the Peña de Francia (*Nossa Senhora da Penha de França*), Nossa Senhora das Angústias (see Lambert (quinta)), São Lázaro, Our Lady of Pity (*Nossa Senhora da Piedade*) (see Moradias de Zargo), Our Lady of Pity (see the Angústias Cemetery), Our Lady of Sorrows (*Nossa Senhora das Dores*) (see Princess Maria Amélia Hospice), Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) and Almas (see those entries). The chapels of Nossa Senhora das Maravilhas, Our Lady of Pity (Igrejinha), São Francisco das Furnas, Nossa Senhora da Salvação, Santa Brígida, Nossa Senhora da Vida, Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora and Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception no longer exist. The chapels of Nossa Senhora da Saúde and of São João, in the Fortress of the Pico (‘peak’), were deconsecrated long ago. We deal with all these chapels at greater length elsewhere.

Within this parish lie the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice, the Asylum for Beggars and Orphans (*Asilo da Mendicidade e Órfãos*), the Angústias Cemetery, the bishop’s palace with the Diocesan Chancery (*Câmara Eclesiástica*), the Milk Dispensary (*Lactário*), the Maternal Aid (*Auxílio Maternal*), the Theatre, the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’), the São Pedro Palace (‘St Peter’), the Fortress of the Pico, the British cemetery, the Anglican church, the English Telegraph Station, the Dona Maria Amélia Orphanage, the mole (breakwater) and road of the Pontinha, and the *quintas* (country estates) Vigia, Lambert, Bianchi, Cruzes, Favila, São João, etc., etc.

The parish of São Pedro extends westwards as far as the Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’) and northwards as far as the Azinhaga dos Ausentes, on the Santo António road, and the Travessa da Figueira Canhota, on the Achada road. The parish of São Pedro is further bounded by a part of the right bank of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia above the Largo do Torreão (‘turret’); the western half of the Rua dos Ferreiros (‘blacksmiths’), or do Comércio, between that square and the Rua dos Netos; the northern part of the latter street, bounded by the Rua dos Ferreiros and the Rua das Mercês; the Rua de São Pedro; the Rua das Pretas, or de Câmara Pestana, but only from the buildings numbered 70 and 47 onwards (1921); the western half of the Rua de São Francisco; and the Calçada de São Lourenço. The point where the Rua de São Francisco comes out into the Rua da Carreira (‘track’), or do Dr Vieira, marks the division between the parish of São Pedro and that of the Sé. The population of the parish of São Pedro is 7,061 inhabitants (1921).
St Peter González Telmo (chapel)
In the town (*vila*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), close to the beach, there once stood a chapel of this name.
See Corpo Santo (I-316).
São Pedro (lombada, stream and chapel)

In the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), not far from the town (*vila*) of the same name, lies the Lombada de São Pedro (‘St Peter’s ridge’), or Lombada de Santa Cruz. It is crossed by the stream likewise called São Pedro, more commonly known as the Ribeira da Boaventura (‘Boaventura stream’). In the early 16th century João Escorcio Drumond had a chapel built there, dedicated to the apostle St Peter. The great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803 razed it completely, and shortly afterwards it was rebuilt on a site less exposed to the violence of the current.
São Roque (waters)

In the article Machico (Health Resort), we have already referred to the waters of the springs of São Roque (‘St Roch’) in the town (*vila*) of Machico, which have remarkable therapeutic virtues, as is generally known and as many distinguished physicians affirm. Since the results of the analysis of these waters carried out by the illustrious chemist and analyst Charles Lapierre are hard to find today, we believe it of some interest to reproduce them here.

‘Having been commissioned by the Most Excellent Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Machico to examine, from the chemical and bacteriological point of view, the cold water of the “São Roque” spring, which is highly renowned and used as a therapeutic agent, I shall present the results of my experiments in the following report, which is divided into three parts: 1. Chemical analysis; 2. Bacteriological analysis; 3. General conclusions. 1. CHEMICAL ANALYSIS – The methods I followed are those most commonly used for this kind of work in official Portuguese and foreign laboratories. – A. Qualitative tests –

These tests showed that the water contained: many chlorides, a fair amount of sulphates, a fair amount of carbonates, a fair amount of lime and magnesia, and much sodium. B. – Quantitative tests (per litre). 1. Direct results of the analysis: residue at 180° 0.5324 grams; dissolved oxygen 6.3 cc; combined carbonic acid (from the carbonates) 0.0320 g; silica, iron oxide, alumina 0.0220; lime (CaO) 0.0288 g; magnesia (Mg.) 0.0397; sodium 0,1.460; sulphuric acid (SO3) 0.0222; total chlorine 0,2.485. Potassium nitrate 0.0030, or nitric nitrogen 0.42 mg.

Organic matter, acid and alkaline solution – nil; ammonia nil; nitrites nil. 2. Grouping of the elements (per litre): silica, iron oxide, alumina 0.0025; potassium nitrate 0.0030; magnesium sulphate 0.0423; calcium carbonate 0.0407; magnesium carbonate 0.0269; magnesium chloride 0.0305; sodium chloride 0.3717; sum of the elements 0.5377. Residue 0.5324.
Comparing the sum of the elements determined with the residue obtained directly by evaporation confirms the accuracy of the analysis.

II Bacteriological analysis – On the very day the water arrived in Coimbra, I made the necessary cultures in the various nutrient media in order to determine: 1. the number of bacteria present in one cubic centimetre of water; 2. the presence of bacteria of the coli-bacillus group, to which great importance is attached today.

1st Number of germs – I have not described the methods followed, having already done so in the report on the waters of Funchal that I addressed to the Municipal Council of that city, which was printed in *Coimbra Medica* and in Madeiran newspapers.

Nevertheless, I repeat that no great importance should be attached to the absolute value of the figures obtained, since the number of germs increases greatly whenever the water is subjected to changes in its medium, temperature, etc. Using the gelatine-plate method, with the plates examined 8 and 13 [days] after sowing, I found per cubic centimetre: 2,700 bacteria at 8 days and 3,060 at 13 days; fungi, 150 at 8 days and 160 at 13 days. According to Miguel’s classifications, it falls into the group of ‘Tolerable Water’.
The species that developed were all common saprophytes, none of them being regarded today as pathogenic.
2. Search for coliform species – The water, subjected simultaneously to the Elsner and Péré methods (see the Funchal report), showed no coliform species in the numerous plates sown.
Greater importance should be attached to this result than to the preceding one, based on the number of germs.

In the first few days two colonies appeared that were suspect because of their microscopic appearance; they fermented sugars but did not produce indole. After six days they liquefied the gelatine, so they were not bacteria of the coli bacillus group.

The absence of these species agrees with the chemical analysis and demonstrates that the water of the ‘São Roque’ spring is well captured and piped, with no communication between the spring and the nearby ground that could give rise to contamination affecting the purity of its water.
III CONCLUSION – The mineral-medicinal water of the ‘São Roque’ spring belongs to the class of hypothermal, hyposaline, sodium-chloride waters.

In its chemical composition it resembles, on the mainland, the waters of Amieira, analysed by Mr Santos e Silva, and the waters of Bicanho and of ‘Geiras’ (near ‘Amieira’) and of Fonte Nova (near Torres Vedras), which are also mineral-medicinal and which I have analysed.
Both my analyses and those of ‘Amieira’ were published in the *Coimbra Medica*.

By analogy with these waters, whose therapeutic effects are already known, it is natural that the water of the ‘São Roque’ spring should be suitable for the pathological cases in which the former give positive results, for example scrofula, skin complaints, gastric disorders, etc.

However, it is not for me to go into this matter further, since that is not the role of the chemist but of the physician, who, in the light of the water’s composition and the results obtained, could form a scientifically based opinion.
I may add that the bacteriological analysis indicates that the water appears to be in good condition at its source. Coimbra, 4 July 1896.
Charles Lepierre

Professor of chemistry at the Industrial School of Coimbra (*Escola Industrial de Coimbra*) and demonstrator at the Microbiology Laboratory (*Gabinete de Microbiologia*) of the University, corresponding member of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Lisbon (*Academia Real das Sciencias de Lisboa*), Officer of the Order of São Tiago, etc.’
St Roch (chapel)

On entering the small but beautiful bay of Machico, one sees on the left, leaning out over the ocean, a chapel dedicated to St Roch, at the foot of which lies the well-known spring of the same name. The present chapel is not the original one, which stood a short distance from it, roughly on the square that lies there, overlooking the sea. That building was old, but we do not know the year of its foundation. As it had fallen into an advanced state of ruin, its confraternity had it rebuilt in 1739, and it was then erected on the spot where it stands today. The licence granted for its blessing is dated 6 June of that year, but the date 1751 can be read on the high altar; this perhaps refers to the installation of that altar in place of another that may have stood there. Inside, the chapel is adorned with exquisite *azulejos* (painted glazed tiles) depicting the principal episodes in the life of the saint. They have been admired by Portuguese and foreigners alike, and they truly deserve a visit. A fine road leads from the centre of the town (*vila*) to the churchyard of the chapel; in the summer season it is much frequented by the holidaymakers who spend the hot months in Machico.
See São Roque (Águas de).
São Roque do Faial (parish)

São Roque do Faial was an integral part of the parish of Faial until it was separated from it and became an independent parish (*freguesia*) in 1848. Among its earliest known settlers were Brás Pereira da Silva, founder of the Pereira da Silva family of Faial, Jácome Nunes and several individuals with the surname Pires.
The parish takes its name from the chapel of St Roch, which has stood there since the middle of the 16th century.

The original chapel was founded by Cristóvão Pires, who had it built around 1551. He lived in the parish of Faial. On 6 August of that year, in the absence of the prelate, he declared before the cathedral chapter of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) that he had built that chapel at his own expense and suitably endowed it, and he asked for permission to celebrate divine services in it. It has undergone various repairs, and in 1889 it was considerably enlarged, when Father Casimiro Augusto de Freitas e Abreu was vice-vicar.

This chapel was cramped and its parts were out of proportion, which gave the whole a most unattractive appearance. It also stood in a dangerous position and was in an advanced state of ruin, so that a new church became absolutely necessary. The parish priest Daniel Nicolau de Sousa boldly took on this risky undertaking in a parish of limited population and scant resources. Through persistent and diligent efforts, he succeeded in building a new, larger church on a safer and more accessible site, thus endowing his parish with a remarkable and much-appreciated improvement. The site chosen lies in the locality (*sítio*) of Chão do Cedro Gordo (‘ground of the stout cedar’), and the new church was solemnly blessed by the diocesan prelate in December 1927.

A royal letter (*carta régia*) of 11 February 1746 created a curacy (*curato*) in the parish of Faial, obliging its curate to perform certain religious services in the chapel of St Roch. We have read somewhere that this curacy was created with its seat in that chapel, which seems to us to have no serious foundation, although the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) shares this opinion.

It was the law (*carta de lei*) of 24 July 1848 that truly established the independent parish, which was then given a parish priest, as it has always had ever since. Its first parish priests were Francisco José Nunes (1848–1865), who died there, Estevão Correia Bizarro (1865–1869), Caetano Velosa Castelo Branco (1869–1870), António Pereira (1870–1880), etc.

Principal localities: Terreiros, Cancela, Lombo dos Palheiros, Serradinho, Chão do Cedro Gordo, Pico do Cedro Gordo, Achada do Folhadal, Lombo Grande, Achada do Pau Bastião, Fajã do Cedro Gordo and Ribeiro Frio. The last of these localities is well worth a visit for the charm and picturesqueness of the spot and for the astonishing panoramas that open out from it.
The parish has a state school, founded in 1903, which at present operates in the locality of Chão do Cedro Gordo (1921). Its population is 956 inhabitants (1921).
São Roque (parish)

The lands that now make up this suburban parish (*freguesia*) of Funchal originally formed part of the parish of the Sé, Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and later belonged to the parish of São Pedro (‘St Peter’). The same happened with the parish of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), as has already been said elsewhere in this volume. The two parishes were separated from São Pedro in the same year, and the instrument that created them bears the same date.

The royal decree (alvará régio) of Cardinal Henry the Navigator, dated 3 March 1579, empowered the diocesan prelate Dom Jerónimo Barreto to create the parish of São Roque (‘St Roch’), and set the parish priest’s annual stipend (*côngrua*) at 14,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash, half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine. The royal decree of 16 January 1589 raised this salary to 19,000 *réis* in cash, half a *moio* of wheat and a quarter of wine, to which the decree of the 30th of the same month and year added a further 3,000 *réis* in cash and half a *moio* of wheat.

The parish (*freguesia*) took its name from the small chapel of St Roch that stood there, where the seat of the new parish was established. The chapel had been built by the inhabitants of the locality (*sítio*) in a year before the parish was created. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, basing himself on the order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 19 May 1704, which directed that the building of the new church and sacristy be put out to award by public auction (*arrematação*) for the sum of 795,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), appears to conclude that the present church was built in that year. This construction, or rather enlargement, was carried out on the chapel that stood in the locality still known today as Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’), which we believe to be the site of the original chapel of St Roch. The work seems to have been none too sound, for around 1790 the church collapsed and could no longer be used for worship. Religious services were then held in a small chapel whose dedication we do not know.

Work on the present church began at the start of the 19th century, but building was slow, and the works were declared complete only around the middle of that century. In the meantime, it had served as the parish church since the 1820s.

The parish has the chapels of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, Nossa Senhora da Alegria (Our Lady of Joy), Our Lady of the Rosary and St Anne; that of Nossa Senhora da Esperança (Our Lady of Hope) disappeared long ago. We give a brief account of each elsewhere.

The principal localities of this parish are: Achada, Muro da Coelha, Conceição, Fundoa, Igreja Velha, Calhau, Igreja Nova, Alegria, Bugiaria, Lombo Segundo, Lombo de João Boieiro and Santana. It has 3,289 inhabitants (1921).
St Sebastian (chapels)

The chapel of São Sebastião in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), an old building, belonged to the town’s Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). In 1734 it had been deconsecrated and was far gone in ruin, and it was entirely rebuilt at the expense of the same Council. It was inspected for the celebration of divine service on 20 November 1734.
On the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) there was a very old chapel dedicated to the martyr St Sebastian.
There was a chapel with the same dedication in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’); neither the year of its construction nor the name of its founder is known.

There was a chapel of São Sebastião in the parish of São Jorge (‘St George’), whose year of construction we do not know. We do know, however, that it was rebuilt by the parish priest Francisco Marques de Mendonça in 1765 and blessed on 11 September of the same year. The small image of the saint, a remarkable masterpiece of sculpture, is in the parish church.
See Market and chapel of São Sebastião, on page 359 of volume II.
St James the Less (chapel)

The chapel of São Tiago in the parish (*freguesia*) of Canhas is one of the oldest in the diocese and, according to Gaspar Frutuoso, it was João Gonçalves Zarco himself who planned it and chose the spot where it was to be built. The parish was established in it when it was created, around 1577. For other matters concerning this chapel, we refer the reader to the article on the parish of Canhas.
São Tiago (fortress)

‘This fortress,’ says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo in the notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), ‘stands on a point of solid rock that juts further into the waters of the harbour than the neighbouring beaches, so that it watches over and protects them on either side; it is, moreover, the end of the curtain wall that runs up to it along the Cabo do Calhau (‘end of the pebble shore’). The original building did not have the first battery that exists there now: the primitive portal lies inside this battery and bears at the top, in lettering of the period, the date 1614, which attests when the work was done.’

The fortress of São Tiago was rebuilt in 1767, as an inscription over the main gate, in the south-east corner of the entrance square, shows. The governor and captain-general José Correia de Sá had 50 pieces of artillery, with all their equipment, brought from London for its defence.
No. 3 Battery of Mountain Artillery is quartered in the fortress of São Tiago. See fortifications (*Fortificações*).
St James the Less (church)

The building of the church of São Tiago was decided by the solemn vow (see Vow to Saint James) that the authorities, clergy and people of Funchal made in 1523, when this island found itself ‘posta em muyta tempestade & tribulaçom de peste & fome & outros muytos trabalhos...’ (‘in great tempest and tribulation of plague and famine and many other hardships...’). On 21 July of that year the first stone of the building was laid. A contemporary document records the event, saying that on the ‘bymte & hun dias de julho lhe começarom a sua casa himdo a çidade e o cabido em proçisom solene descalçados & o Mestre schola Gonçalo Martim com o retábulo da imagem do bem auemturado apóstolo & deo a primeira enchadada no cunhall da capella da bamda do abamgelho, a qual casa se edificou em hua terra que Antonio Spindola deo para a dita casa...’ (‘twenty-first day of July they began his house, the city and the cathedral chapter going in solemn procession barefoot, and the Master of the School Gonçalo Martim with the altarpiece bearing the image of the blessed apostle, and he struck the first blow of the hoe at the corner of the chapel on the Gospel side; which house was built on a piece of land that António Espínola gave for the said house...’).

Of this António Espínola, the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) says that he was a native of Genoa and descended from the most ancient families of that city, and that he counted several Doges of that republic among his forebears. ‘King Manuel I granted him a coat of arms and the noble rank (*foro de fidalgo*) of his household. He held lands granted as *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) in Santiago and other places; and by a deed of 30 April 1524 he donated a small plot of land at the edge of the city, on which were built the chapel of Santiago, patron saint of the whole island, the sacristy and churchyard, on condition that members of his family should be buried there, and that the chaplain should ask for an Our Father and a Hail Mary for his soul. The deed was drawn up on parchment and is in the archive of the cathedral chapter (*Cabido*) of Funchal.’

The church of São Tiago, known today as the church of Socorro (‘succour’), where the seat of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) was installed in 1803, is not the original building. Nothing of that first structure remains at present, and it was much smaller than the present church. Some years later it underwent major repairs, and it was blessed by the diocesan bishop, Dom Jerónimo Fernando, on 25 July 1632. A century later, as the chapel had fallen into considerable disrepair, the Funchal Council decided to build a larger church. The old chapel was demolished in 1752, and the works were declared complete in 1768.

When the great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803 swept the church of Our Lady of Calhau (see that entry) into the sea, the Council gave the church of São Tiago to serve as the seat of the parish, on condition that the image of the patron saint and protector of the city should always be kept there. A stone tablet was then placed on the church’s façade, where it still remains, bearing the following inscription: *Hic lapis indicat liberalitatem senatus et populi hanc ecclesiam Fidelissimo Principi Regenti offerentium in locum parochiae per inundationem aquarum destructae Anno Domini MDCCCIII* (This stone records the generosity of the council and people, who offered this church to the Most Faithful Prince Regent in place of the parish church destroyed by the flood waters, in the year of Our Lord 1803). See Patron saints.
St Vincent (chapel)

On a solitary block of basalt at the mouth of the stream that crosses the town (*vila*) of São Vicente, the local people built a chapel in 1692, according to Dr Alvaro de Azevedo. It is dedicated to the martyr St Vincent of Saragossa, who is also the patron saint of the parish church, which stands a short distance away. This unusual little chapel is widely known through the engravings of it reproduced in various Portuguese and foreign works, and also through postcards.
São Vicente (parish)

It is unquestionably the most important, the most populous and the largest of all the parishes (*freguesia*) of northern Madeira. The only town (*vila*) established on the north coast of this island was the one created there around the middle of the 18th century; it has also been the seat of a municipality (*concelho*) since 1835 and of a judicial district (*comarca*) since 1875 (1921).

As with the great majority of the parishes of this archipelago, it is now impossible to determine with any approximate accuracy the year in which the settlement and colonisation of the lands that today make up this parish began. As is readily believed, farming and the clearing of the forests that went with it did not begin on the north coast in the years immediately following the discovery. In the south of the island the first settlers had more than enough land, more fertile and with milder climates, on which to exercise their energy and give free rein to their enterprising spirit. It was only when the colonists grew in number, drawn by the fame of the remarkable fertility of the soil and the abundance of its crops, when the grantees of land (*sesmeiros*) found in the African slave their chief helper in working the fields, and when sugar-making became a powerful source of wealth, that colonisation gradually spread out across the distant valleys, over the ridges and slopes of the inland mountains, and at times even into trackless and almost inaccessible places.

It is said that the first lands cultivated in the north of the island were those of Faial and Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), but it may be supposed that, at the same time, other lands were being worked at various points in the northern part, above all at Ponta Delgada, São Vicente, Seixal and Porto Moniz.

‘The parish of São Vicente,’ says the annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘is held, in the manuscripts we have consulted, to have been founded in 1440, which can be admissible only as regards the building of the first church and the institution of the chaplaincy; for the parish of Machico, the principal one of the captaincy, was constituted only in the year 1450: we therefore take the view that the parish of São Vicente dates from some years after this.’ There can be not the slightest doubt on this point if we carefully examine the dates on which the most important parishes in the south of this island were created. We are of the opinion that this parish was created only in the last quarter of the 15th century.

In 1590 Frutuoso wrote of this parish: ‘A league beyond Ponta Delgada lies the parish of São Vicente, of two hundred and fifty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), with large lands of grain crops and livestock; much fruit, of chestnut, walnut and other kinds; many vineyards and much water, and two water-powered sawmills.’ The royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 September 1575 assigned the parish priest an annual salary of 25,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), which was raised to 25,000 *réis*, half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine by the royal decree of 20 April 1589, and was further increased by a royal decree of the same month and year with half a *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine.

Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo is mistaken when he states that this parish had only a vicar. In fact the very *Memórias do Estado Eclesiástico* that he cites, and which we have now consulted, mention the royal decree of 2 January 1606 establishing the creation of the curacy (*curato*), a document also cited in the *Índice Geral da Provedoria*... to which we have so often turned. This decree fixes the curate’s annual stipend (*côngrua*) at 20,000 *réis*.

For the convenience of the people of the island, the parish of São Vicente became the seat of a vicariate forane (*vigairaria da vara*), that is, a deanery (*arciprestado*, group of parishes under an archpriest). It was created on 2 September 1812 by the diocesan prelate Dom Friar Joaquim de Meneses e Ataíde, and the first vicar forane or archpriest was Father Francisco Borges de Sousa e Melo, then parish priest of the parish, with jurisdiction ‘over all the parish priests, clergy and other persons of the said Town and its district’. By a warrant (*provisão*) of the vicar-general of 14 January 1814, this jurisdiction was extended to the parishes of Porto Moniz, Ribeira da Janela and Seixal, since he had learnt ‘that it is often better for them to go to the said Town than to that of Calheta (‘small cove’)’. We do not know what the powers of this vicar forane were, nor when the functions of the office ceased to be exercised, though it is certain that no such ecclesiastical authority has existed for some decades. Only very recently did the present diocesan prelate, within the powers conferred on him by the Code of Canon Law now in force, create the deaneries of Funchal, Calheta and São Jorge (1921).

A small chapel dedicated to St Vincent gave its name to the place where it had been built, and later to the new parish. We do not know the name of its founder or the year of its construction, but it must date from the time of the first agricultural settlement there. The seat of the parish was established in it when the parish was created in the last quarter of the 15th century. Over time it must have undergone various repairs and enlargements, as happened with all the chapels that were later turned into parish churches. An order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) dated 12 January 1664 directs that the sum of 560,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) be paid to the parish priest for the enlargement of the church, the document stating that the people should contribute whatever they could towards the same purpose. From this it seems that the present church was enlarged or underwent considerable repairs in the third quarter of the 17th century.
The parish has the chapels of Our Lady of the Rosary, Our Lady of Deliverance and São Vicente; that of Our Lady of Pity no longer exists. We have already given a brief account of them.

The main localities of this parish are Fajã da Areia, Vila, Terra-Chã, Fontinha, Poiso, Pé do Passo, Passo, Ribeira do Passo, Lanço, Feiteiras, Ginjas, Saramago, Loural, Vargem, Estreito da Vargem, Ribeira Grande, Achada do Til, Achada dos Judeus, Fajã dos Vinhaticos, Aviceiro, Ribeira do Rato, Lameiros, Cascalho, Limoeiro, Laranjal, Pé da Corrida and Cardais.

‘The parish of São Vicente,’ an educated person who has lived there for years tells us, ‘wedged at the foot of towering mountains, cut almost sheer, which surround it for dozens of kilometres like gigantic ramparts and leave it open only on the seaward side, is one of the loveliest places in Madeira, for its rugged look of grandly wild beauty. To the east it borders on Ponta Delgada; to the west its limits run as far as the Ribeira do Inferno (‘hell’s stream’), which nature thus sets between it and Seixal; to the north lies the sea; to the south stretches the plateau of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), which divides it from Serra Alva (‘white upland’), and, where the high backbone of the mountains dips, the gorge of the Encumeada (‘ridge pass’). Its lands are thick and dense, and in them abound the richest woods of leafy laurels, til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel), *vinhático* and heather, which at present are held, beyond dispute, to be the finest in Madeira.’

A kind of saying was once much in vogue here and is still known and quoted: ‘from São Vicente, neither donkey, nor wine, nor people’. It is not only a disparaging reference to that parish but also a glaring and grave injustice to the character, the sober ways and the open hospitality of its inhabitants, which it gives us great pleasure to emphasise here, as a well-deserved tribute to the truth. On this subject we may add that our great satirical poet Monteiro Teixeira (volume II, page 390) spent a fortnight in São Vicente in 1826 and wrote from there a letter in verse, published in the 2nd volume of his *Obras Poéticas*. In it, giving free rein to his poetic imagination and his marked leaning towards satire and epigram, he refers to this parish in terms that are not exactly flattering, but in which one clearly sees an itch to be witty rather than a wish to belittle or offend. This parish has 5,462 inhabitants (1921).

On 6 March 1929 this parish was the scene of a great tragedy that caused the deepest dismay throughout the island. After heavy rains, an extensive landslide took place, carrying away many dwelling houses in its fall, and thirty-two people met a terrible death. This great catastrophe occurred at localities not far from the chapel of Rosário, seat of the parish’s curacy (*curato*).
São Vicente (municipal court district)

The municipal court district (*julgado municipal*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), with its seat in the parish (*freguesia*) and town (*vila*) of the same name, was created by decree of 24 October 1931. It covers the parishes of São Vicente, Ponta Delgada and Boaventura, which make up the corresponding municipality (*concelho*). In 1926 the judicial district (*comarca*) of São Vicente had been abolished; it had been established by decree of 12 November 1875 and formally installed on 16 November 1876.
São Vicente (landing place and stream)

On the coast of the town (*vila*) of this name there is a small landing place where disembarking is difficult. The landing place at Fajã da Areia (see that entry), about two kilometres from the landing place of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), is preferable.

The waters of this stream rise in the mountains of the Encumeada de São Vicente (‘São Vicente ridge pass’) and, crossing the greater part of the parish (*freguesia*), flow out into the Ocean. At its mouth, in the middle of the stream bed, stands a solitary block of basalt bearing a small chapel dedicated to the martyr St Vincent, built by the people in the year 1692. Near the mouth of this stream there is a cave or chasm of some length, formed by an extinct lava channel.
São Vicente (town and municipality)

It is known that the towns (*vilas*) of Funchal, Machico and Porto Santo were created around the middle of the 15th century, and those of Santa Cruz, Ponta do Sol and Calheta at the beginning of the 16th century. No town at all was established in Madeira during the 17th century; that of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) was created in the second quarter of the 18th century.

The village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) of São Vicente, made a parish towards the end of the 15th century, was one of the parishes of northern Madeira that acquired the greatest importance from the earliest days of colonisation and where the population grew densest; even today it is the most populous of them all. It belonged to the captaincy of Machico, and the town of that name was the seat of all public administration. The people of the north of the island were therefore forced to make long and dangerous journeys to reach the capital of their captaincy whenever pressing circumstances obliged them to do so.

Because many parishes on the north coast had easier and more frequent communications with Funchal, the people of those parishes sought on several occasions to withdraw from the jurisdiction of the captaincy of Machico and be incorporated into that of Funchal, or else to obtain the creation of a municipality with its seat in São Vicente, covering this parish and other neighbouring ones.

This legitimate wish of the northern communities was fulfilled only in 1744, with the creation of the town of São Vicente. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo makes not the slightest reference to this event and was certainly unaware of the instrument that raised the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente to the rank of town. The royal decree (alvará régio) concerned, a lengthy and exceptionally interesting document, is dated 25 August 1744 and was first published in no. 14 and following issues of the newspaper *A Revista Madeirense* (‘Madeiran Review’) in 1902. With the establishment of constitutional government, the archipelago was divided into municipalities (*concelhos*), and the existing division into towns or municipalities was profoundly altered. The municipality of São Vicente was set up in 1835 and consisted, as it still does today, of the parishes of Boaventura, Ponta Delgada and São Vicente. The decree of 10 December 1867 abolished the municipality of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) and incorporated the parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela and Porto Moniz into that of São Vicente; shortly afterwards, however, the abolished municipality of Porto Moniz was restored. It was abolished again by the decree of 18 November 1895 and restored once more by the decree of 13 January 1898. During this short period the parishes of Seixal, Ribeira da Janela and Porto Moniz were once again part of the municipality of São Vicente.

Because the town of São Vicente lies in a confined site and has only a limited number of inhabitants, it has not enjoyed the growth and development befitting a place that was once the seat of a judicial district (*comarca*), enjoys the honours of a town, is the capital of a municipality and is the centre of a municipal court district (*julgado municipal*). It would therefore be advantageous to move it to a more spacious site, where a sizeable population could grow up around the municipal offices, as generally happens elsewhere. The idea of transferring the municipal seat to a locality (*sítio*) better suited to the purpose is not new. As recently as 1929 the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the municipality took up the matter with keen interest: a site was actually chosen and a plan for the future town was drafted. It may be presumed that the old judicial district will be restored, lending considerable importance to whatever settlement may come to be created.
Sapata (Centrophorus calceus)

A dogfish shark (Spinacidae), common at depths of between 350 and 700 *braças*. Although its flesh is not very tasty, it can be eaten, especially after being salted and dried in the sun. An oil considered to be of good quality is extracted from its liver.
Sapo (Tetrodon marmoratus)

A fish of the family Gymnodontes, which lives near the coast of Madeira and feeds on small crustaceans, crushing them with its powerful jaws. On muddy bottoms it is caught in large quantities with trawl nets. It has a large abdominal sac which sometimes swells excessively, forcing it to the surface, where it dies or is taken by seabirds.
Sack of Funchal by the French

One of the greatest calamities ever to strike this archipelago was the sack by the French Huguenots. The memory of the event no longer survives in local tradition, as do those of the floods of 1803 and the cholera of 1856, because it happened at a time very remote from our own. Yet the Madeiran chronicles and many historians of our country refer to it with genuine horror, painting it in the dark colours of the great tragedies and the most dreadful catastrophes.

The year was 1566.
