The fifth captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, was away in Lisbon, and the captaincy was governed by his uncle, Francisco Gonçalves da Câmara. The Portuguese Gaspar Caldeira was one of the many traders on the Gold Coast (*Costa da Mina*) who dealt in the gold and other goods that the natives traded on the African coast. Having abused the privileges granted to him by the royal regulations (*regimento*), Caldeira had to take refuge in France, and all his property was then confiscated. Deprived of these exemptions and privileges and forced to live outside his homeland, he neither acknowledged his error nor sought to justify himself; instead, he swore to wreak the most terrible vengeance and the vilest of reprisals on his fellow countrymen. He knew of Madeira’s prosperity and the importance of its great trade, and he was well aware how weak were the defences that could be mustered here against an attack by armed ships. So he conceived the plan of assaulting this island, thereby carrying out his dark revenge and making good the loss of the property that the confiscation had taken from him.

In Bertrand de Montluc he found an excellent instrument for his plans. Montluc was a gentleman of the household of King Charles IX and the son of Marshal de Montluc, who left his name in history for the acts of heroism he performed on the battlefield and also for the *Memoirs* of his life that he wrote, which went through several editions. It is impossible today to know whether Bertrand de Montluc was already preparing to roam the seas on risky ventures of privateering and piracy when he met Gaspar Caldeira, or whether it was Caldeira who, knowing the bold and adventurous spirit of the French *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility), led him to undertake that perilous enterprise.

Montluc had obtained Charles IX’s approval for the venture he had embarked on, but he concealed from the monarch his secret designs and the shady negotiations he had entered into with Gaspar Caldeira. He drew a considerable number of noblemen into his plans, chiefly from the old province of Guyenne. The Viscount of Jas was vice-admiral of this small pirate fleet, and also on board were Fabien de Montluc, a son of the Viscount of Pompadour, the Baron of Guitimeres, son of the viscount of the same title, and many other members of noble French families. They may not have known Montluc’s hidden aims, but it is quite certain that in those times robbery, depredation and plunder were fully justified in some European countries when crowned by acts of rare valour or by decisive strokes of daring.

In three large ships and eight smaller vessels, Montluc embarked about twelve hundred men, among them Gaspar Caldeira, Belchior Contreiras, António Luís and, it seems, other degenerate Portuguese as well. They left Bordeaux at the beginning of September 1566. According to Edmond Falgairolle, they were driven by a violent storm to put in at Madeira; but there is no doubt that their destination was this island and that their sole purpose was to rob and sack it, as indeed they did.

The author just cited says that Bertrand de Montluc, caring little for the leisure he enjoyed in France and weary of the intrigues of the court, had resolved to risk his life in African waters by attempting to found a fortress in East Africa, intended to protect French trade with those regions and with the countries of the East. He adds that when they reached Funchal and landed some men to take on water, they were met by the Portuguese with cannon fire, and that then ‘Montluc, carried away by his fervent enthusiasm and his great desire to make a name for himself, seized the opportunity to strike a real surprise blow and so affront the pride of Spain and Portugal, regarded at the time as the true masters of the seas’. The Madeiran chronicles and the Portuguese historians make not the slightest reference to any hostile reception of Charles IX’s subjects. Relations between France and our country were then quite friendly, and it is hard to believe that the Madeirans would have acted in that way, unless Montluc’s squadron appeared at Funchal in warlike array and with every appearance of true corsairs, as indeed they were. To understand the intentions of the pirate Montluc, it is enough to recall that on the eve of the day he assaulted Madeira he made a landing on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), unleashing all his fury on the defenceless inhabitants of that island. Moreover, the ferocious rage with which he attacked the city, the unheard-of cruelties he committed and, above all, the terrible sack to which he subjected Funchal, stripping it of its riches and loading them into eleven vessels, are eloquent and undisputed proof that this was an act of plain and simple piracy, and never a reprisal to avenge an injury received.

Gaspar Frutuoso devotes some forty pages to a detailed account of the many acts of violence and cruelty committed by the French during the sixteen days they remained in Funchal, in their terrible work of destruction and slaughter. Yet he does not give us a complete overall picture of that horrifying assault, in which human beasts gave free rein to their cannibal instincts, turning a rich city at the height of its prosperity into a field on which a bloody battle might have been fought, where nothing remained but the useless leavings of the plunder of an unbridled soldiery.

Without going on at excessive length, it is impossible for us to describe those Dantesque horrors, which, as the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) says, caused ‘more evils by deeds than men can imagine, or words can tell, or Christians can believe’.

The pirates landed at Praia Formosa (‘beautiful beach’) at about nine o’clock in the morning on 3 October and at once marched on the city, entering it at two different points. At the Portão de São Paulo (St Paul’s Gate) they met stubborn resistance, and several dozen men fell dead there on both sides. Having forced this entrance, they made for the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence), where the governor, with the forces at his disposal, resisted them bravely but had to yield to the seasoned strength and numbers of the attackers. Some pockets of resistance also formed in other parts of the city, but they proved entirely useless in the face of the fury and numbers of the pirates. Forces were organised in various parts of the island, ready to march on the city. However, persuaded by reports sent from Funchal that their presence would only further inflame the corsairs’ rage, they decided to turn back, leaving the corsairs complete masters of the situation.
In the assault on the Fort of São Lourenço, Bertrand de Montluc was mortally wounded. He was buried on the very spot where the fighting took place, and the Viscount of Jas succeeded him in command.

The sack followed, and for sixteen days the eleven ships were crammed with the richest and most varied spoils. Whatever they could not carry aboard was spoilt or destroyed. Thus they poured away thousands of *pipas* of wine and ruined thousands of *arrobas* of sugar. The contents of the wealthy houses, the silver of the churches and convents and the stocks of the great warehouses filled several ships. The damage those barbarians caused here is reckoned at some millions of *cruzados*.

The victims of the attackers’ fury are put at three hundred, some killed defending the city, but most of them savagely butchered by Montluc’s soldiery. Frutuoso says, and it is regarded as established fact, that a considerable part of the invaders were Huguenots. This readily explains the outrages and sacrileges they committed in the churches, not only sacking them and stripping them of all their riches, but also desecrating them, especially the images and objects used in worship.
From the fright and alarm caused by the arrival of the submarine in December 1916, one may fairly judge the panic and terror that spread among the population during the sack by the French.
By the time help arrived from Lisbon, the corsair ships had already weighed anchor and sailed for the Canary Islands, where they sold a considerable part of their abundant booty.

On 22 October 1566 our ambassador in France presented Charles IX with a forceful protest, demanding exemplary punishment of the culprits. Forquevaux, France’s representative in Lisbon, hastened to express his deep regret to our government, promising severe punishment of the criminals. Charles IX and the queen mother showed themselves extremely grieved by these most sorrowful events. Despite our ambassador’s efforts, however, those horrendous crimes went unpunished. Only the Portuguese Gaspar Caldeira was executed in Lisbon, because the same ambassador had managed to have him arrested in a fortress in Biscay, where he had been lured by deception. Some of Montluc’s companions were powerful and influential men in their own country, and many dozens of the attackers belonged to the most distinguished French families, which sufficiently explains their impunity.

The terrible sack that the people of Funchal suffered in 1566, briefly mentioned above on the basis of Gaspar Frutuoso’s narrative, is perhaps the greatest calamity ever to have befallen our city and some of its surroundings. It is regrettable that no rigorous and thorough study has yet been made of so sad and lamentable an event, as we have already noted elsewhere in this work. Simply as a contribution, we shall transcribe an interesting article by Stephens Gaselee, former director of the archives of the ‘Foreign Ofice’ in London, published in the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) of 9 February 1937, which is of some interest to this subject:

‘I recently had the good fortune to acquire a diplomatic document that relates to this incident, and I believe that an account and transcription of it may interest the readers of the *Diário da Madeira*. This document, written on a double sheet of quarto-sized paper, is addressed on the back “Ao muito honrrado embax(ad)or Do cristianissimo snnor “Rey de França em cortte de Castela” (To the most honourable ambassador of the Most Christian Lord King of France at the court of Castile).

This message, about which I have something more to say, was presumably endorsed by the recipient, and the date it bears is not entirely clear – “XVI J I an 1567”. It also bears the impressed seal of the Cardinal Regent of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), later the Cardinal-King Henrique of Portugal. The text is as follows:
Most honourable ambassador,

By the treasurer Le Fevre I received your letter of the 26th of last month, and from it I understood that, as soon as you learned of the outrages that Captain Montluc and those of his company committed on the island of Madeira, you informed the Most Christian Lord King of France of it by express courier, and of the sorrow this news caused him and of what he ordered on account of it, all of which I saw in the copies of the letters and papers you sent me. I thank you greatly for the affection and love you show towards my affairs and for the diligence with which you informed the Most Christian Lord King of France of what happened on the said island. For I trust and hold it certain that, just as he, even before learning in detail of the great and many outrages and excesses that the said Montluc and his vassals committed on the said island of Madeira, to the great disservice of Our Lord and contrary to what befitted so ancient a peace and friendship as the King my lord and the kings his predecessors have always had with the kings of France, wished to make known how much it displeased him that Montluc had not observed what he had prohibited and forbidden him, and judged him a rebel and disobedient; so likewise, after hearing João Pereira, formerly ambassador of the King my lord, he will make such a demonstration in this case that the King my lord may rightly be satisfied with it, and the world may know that the mind and intention of the said Lord King are what should be expected of him. Written in Lisbon on 16 December 1566. The Cardinal Infante Henrique.

The text of the message is written in a good chancery hand in the fashion of the period, and the signature on the document is in the Cardinal Regent’s own hand. As is apparent from the text, this was not really the beginning of the diplomatic correspondence. Father Fernando da Silva says: “On 22 October 1566 our ambassador in France presented Charles IX with a vigorous protest, demanding exemplary punishment of the guilty. Forquevaux, France’s representative in Lisbon, hastened to express his deep regret to our government, promising severe punishment of the criminals.” The letter transcribed above is presumably the official acknowledgement of Forquevaux’s note, expressing gratitude and the hope that the villains would in future be punished (which in fact never happened, for with the exception of Caldeira the other corsairs were never punished).

But was Forquevaux the French ambassador in Lisbon? I doubt that he was, because this letter was sent to him “at the court of Castile”. The reference books at my disposal did not enable me to resolve this doubt, so I consulted my friend the Count of Tovar, of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Lisbon, who is well known as a scholar of Portuguese diplomatic history and has published several books on the subject. I think I may venture to quote here two or three paragraphs of his prompt and kind reply:

“In April 1561 a gentleman of the court of Charles IX named Saint-Sulpice arrived in Lisbon as French ambassador. I do not know how long he remained in Portugal, but in the list of French ambassadors drawn up by Caix de Saint-Amour (*Recueil des Instructions, Portugal*, p. LIII) there is an entry that reads:

*1566 N., ambassadeur, envoyé par Charles IX.* (1566 N., ambassador, sent by Charles IX.) The author does not cite his source, but he evidently found somewhere the information that in that year, 1566, a French ambassador was sent to Lisbon. Might this ambassador not be Forquevaux, who was in Madrid as resident ambassador and may have been sent to Lisbon on some extraordinary mission? If so, the mission cannot have lasted long, because there is a letter from him to his government dated Madrid, 19 December 1566.

“The hypothesis that he was also and simultaneously accredited in Lisbon as resident ambassador does not seem acceptable to me, because I know of no example from that period that would support it. If Caix de Saint-Amour’s note refers to him, it is to be believed that he came as ambassador extraordinary on a special mission.”
And so I think the problem must be left, unless some expert on diplomatic history can shed further light on Forquevaux’s diplomatic activity in the latter part of 1566.
I intend to present the original document that gave me the subject of this article to the Regional Museum in the Palácio de São Pedro (St Peter Palace).’
Saque (Vergílio)
He was appointed civil governor of the district of Funchal at the end of October 1921, but never took up the post.
Saramago

The *saramago* of Madeira is *Raphanus raphanistrum*, with jointed silicles and white or yellow flowers; that of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) is *Brassica sinapistrum*, a plant known on Madeira as *mostarda* (mustard). Both plants belong to the family Cruciferae and are common on the two islands.
Sardinha
This family surname derives from Tomé Sardinha, who lived in a sumptuous house in Rua da Carreira (‘track’) and was married to an illegitimate daughter of João Gonçalves da Câmara.
Sardine

(*Clupea pilchardus*). A fish of the family Clupeidae, which appears chiefly during the winter, mixed with the mackerel, the horse mackerel and other species. It is caught in large quantities off the mouths of the streams after floods. Its breeding has been observed in the rock pools of the coast.
Sardinha (Dr Manuel)

He was born in Funchal on 20 September 1865 and qualified as a physician and surgeon at the now defunct Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica*) of this city. He served as municipal medical officer in Fajã da Ovelha (‘the ewe’s flat’) and Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). He was later appointed administrator of the Land Disinfection Station (*Posto de Desinfecção Terrestre*), run by the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), and is at present retired. He has contributed to various newspapers, was an editor of the *Diário de Notícias* and is the current director of the *Correio da Madeira* (1921). His contributions over several years to the *Almanach Bertrand*, as a solver of mathematical problems, are most valuable and have been highlighted there in a very honourable and exceptionally distinguished way for Dr Manuel Sardinha.
Sardinha (Father Alfredo de Paula)

He was born in Funchal on 2 April 1861 and died in the parish (*freguesia*) of Arco da Calheta (‘arc of Calheta’) on 23 May 1897. He studied at the Lyceum (*Liceu*) and the seminary (*Seminário*) of this city, and was ordained priest in 1885. He served as parish priest in the parishes of Santana, Faial, Fajã da Ovelha and Arco da Calheta.

He had shown a decided vocation for letters, in both prose and verse, but misfortune and illness sadly prevented him from devoting himself to sustained literary work, though much was to be expected of his undeniable talent and cultivated mind. He left various writings scattered through the newspapers, especially in *A Verdade*, of which he was an editor. He wrote many poems, some of which enjoyed great popularity and are still recited and sung today by some of his contemporaries.
He had remarkable gifts as an orator and in 1894 published the pamphlet *Discurso recitado na sala da Associação Católica do Funchal*....
Sargo (Sargus rondeletii)

A fish of the family Sparidae, common in the waters of the archipelago, which is caught by net, by line and by rod. Because it eagerly eats the faecal matter it finds, it is little recommended as a food fish. It has a shellfish-like flavour.
Sargo veado (Sargus cervinus)

A fish of the family Sparidae, which is taken with the net, the scoop net (*peneiro*), the line or the rod. It tastes of shellfish, because it feeds on molluscs, which it crushes with its strong teeth. The fishermen of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) usually call it *sargo breado*.
Sarmento (Alberto Artur)

He is the son of Artur Adolfo Sarmento and Dona Margarida Henriques Sarmento, and was born in Funchal on 7 July 1878. He attended the former Polytechnic School and Army School, and was commissioned as a second lieutenant of infantry on 25 October 1900. He is at present a lieutenant-colonel in the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria n.º 27*), in which he has served ever since he came to Madeira. Besides being an elegant and imaginative writer, as the many literary articles he has published in the Funchal newspapers show, notably in the *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’), of which he was one of the editors, he is also one of the Madeirans with the best knowledge of the history, geology and mineralogy of the archipelago, and he has published several valuable writings on the first of these subjects.

On a visit to Deserta Grande (‘great deserted island’) he made some botanical collections there, and his petrological collections from the archipelago are among the most complete known. The *Scirpus pungens*, variety *Sarmento*, was named after him: a wild sedge that grows near the chapel of St John the Baptist (*São João*) and is one of the rarest plants in Madeira.

Lieutenant-Colonel Sarmento is a temporary teacher at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) (1921), a knight of the Order of St James (*Ordem de São Tiago*), an auxiliary member of the former Geographical Society of Le Mans (France), and a corresponding member of the Lisbon Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*) and of other scientific and literary societies in Portugal and abroad (1921).

According to one of his most recently published works, he has brought out the following writings: *As Desertas*; *As Selvagens*; *O Funchal*; *Os alicerces para a história militar da Madeira*; *Ascendência, naturalidade e Mudança de nome de João Fernandes Vieira*; *As migalhas*; *Um ponto de História Pátria*; *História Militar da Madeira*; *Corografia elementar do arquipélago da Madeira–Noções mínimas*; *Homenagem a João Fernandes Vieira*; *Madeira–1801-02: 1807-1814*; *Um auto na Achada*; *Santo António de Lisboa bosquejado na Madeira*; *A Madeira e as Praças de Africa*; *As Freguesias da Madeira*; *Noticia histórico-militar sôbre a Ilha do Porto Santo*; *Ecos da «Maria da Fonte» na Madeira*; *Moedas, sêlos, Papel Selado e Medalhas na Madeira*; *Fasquias da Madeira*; *Os peixes dos mares da Madeira* (in collaboration with Adolfo César de Noronha); *As aves do arquipelago da Madeira*; *Mamíferos do arquipelago da Madeira*; *Subsidio para o estudo das Formigas da Madeira*; *Os escravos na Madeira*; *Lenda de pedra*; *Ensaios históricos da minha Terra*; *Ripas da Madeira*; *Répteis e Batráquios*; *Notas dos documentos sobre a epoca de D. João IV na Madeira*; *As pequenas indústrias da Madeira*; *Nossa Senhora da Esperança*; *Ensaios Históricos = Ilha da Madeira, Redemoinho de fôlhas*; *Santo António Pregador–Santo António Militar*; *A Princesa do Reino-Unido Portugal Brasil na Ilha da Madeira*; *Quadros sem aro*; *Vila e Freguesia de S. Vicente*; *A propósito do grande Brotero*; *Brotero dá parecer sôbre a estufa de Banger na ilha da Madeira*; *Sobremesa (A)*,–*Três frutos exóticos*.

Invited to contribute to the *Elucidário Madeirense*, he sent us only the articles ‘Doação da Ilha da Madeira’, ‘Donativo’, ‘Ex-libris’, ‘Ferro’, ‘Fortificações’, ‘Fotografia’, ‘Geologia’ and ‘João Fernandes Vieira’, which fill a dozen pages of this work. It is much to be regretted that his contribution was not larger, given the profound knowledge he possesses of every subject bearing on the life of our archipelago, and his highly esteemed merits as a notable writer.
Sarmento (José)

He was the son of José Sarmento and Dona Maria de Oliveira Sarmento, and died in Funchal, his native city, on 13 February 1905, aged 63. He was a celebrated pianist and organist at Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), and also held the post of music teacher at the Episcopal seminary (*Seminário*). He was a close friend of Platão de Vackcel, likewise a most distinguished musician, and contributed to various Funchal newspapers, his articles bearing witness to his considerable literary gifts.
Sarmiento (Dom Tomás Velazques)

He was the commander of the Castilian garrison in Madeira, made up of four companies of paid troops, when the revolution of 1 December 1640 broke out and gave the throne of Portugal to the Duke of Bragança. Although he could have opposed the recognition of John IV on this island, he did nothing to thwart the will of the Madeirans. He even attended the meeting at which the acclamation (*aclamação*, formal public proclamation of a new king) of the new monarch took place, and he left for his own country as soon as the opportunity arose, accompanied by the troops under his command.
Sarraut (Alberto)

Minister of the Colonies of the French Republic. He arrived in Madeira aboard the cruiser *Gueydon* on 17 October 1921 and landed at about 2 p.m., having been greeted on board by the civil governor, the harbour master and the military commander. The due military honours were paid to him at the quay, after which he went on to the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’), where he was received by the civil governor and the secretary-general (*secretário geral*). Accompanied by the civil and military authorities, he visited the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery and laid a wreath with a dedication on the tomb-monument of the sailors of the *Surprise*, who died when that ship was torpedoed inside the bay of Funchal. The governor also laid a wreath on the same monument, and speeches were given at the cemetery by M. Sarraut, the civil governor and the vice-president of the executive committee of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). An infantry detachment and a detachment of the Republican Guard paid military honours to M. Sarraut at the cemetery. The *Gueydon* left the port of Funchal for Brest on the 18th.
Sarsfield

This family surname is of Irish origin and seems to have been introduced into Madeira in the 18th century. In the first quarter of the 19th century Alexandre José Sarsfield lived in Funchal; he served more than once as treasurer of the *finto* (war tax apportioned among residents).
Sarsfield (Alexandre José)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Pedro (‘St Peter’) in this city on 17 September 1856, the son of Guilherme Henrique Sarsfield and Dona Cândida de Ornelas Sarsfield. He studied at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and at the Army School and followed a military career; for some years he has been a reserve colonel (1921).

As a captain he took part in the expedition sent in 1894 to our East Africa, and was present at the battle of Coolela and the capture of Manjacaze. He was head of the private office of the Ministry of War and military attaché to the Portuguese legation in Paris. In addition to various public-service commissions, both civil and military, he also served as civil governor of Guarda and as deputy for Madeira in the legislatures of 1902–1904, 1904 and 1906.

He has contributed widely to various newspapers and reviews, notably the *Revista de Educação e Ensino*, *Revista de Infantaria*, *Revista Militar*, *Revolução de Setembro*, *Primeiro de Janeiro* and *Diário de Notícias* of Lisbon. In recent years he has written extensively for the *Diario da Madeira*. He published several pamphlets on colonial and military subjects, and the books *Leitura para meus filhos* and *Educação*. He has two volumes ready for the press (1921).

He was prosecutor at the first court martial of the 1st Military Division (*Divisão Militar*, a territorial army command). He is an officer of the orders of the Tower and Sword, of St James, of St Benedict of Avis and of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*) of Vila Viçosa, and holds, among others, the silver medal for overseas service and the silver medal commemorating the expedition to Mozambique in 1894 and 1895. He also holds the 2nd-class cross of Military Merit of Spain, is a Grand Cross of the Order of Isabella the Catholic of the same country, and an officer of the Legion of Honour of France (1921). He died in December 1926.
Sarsfield (Eduardo da Rocha)

He is a native of Porto and the son of the Madeiran colonel Alexandre José Sarsfield. He was appointed civil governor of the district of Funchal by decree of 18 May 1922, taking up the post on the 28th of the same month and year.
Saudade (Scabiosa maritima)
A plant of the Dipsacaceae family, cultivated and naturalised in Madeira. Its flowers are fragrant and vary considerably in colour.
Longing for the Homeland

The celebrated work of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso is the richest and most abundant store of news and information that we possess about our archipelago. Were it not for this work, the history of Madeira in the 15th and 16th centuries would be reduced to the few pages left to us by a handful of old chroniclers and to the documents recorded in the municipal archive of this city. All who toil at the thankless task of gathering materials for the history of our land must draw on this abundant stream. It has defects and gaps, entirely excusable given the circumstances in which it was written, but it is unquestionably a work of the highest value, both for the copious and interesting information it provides and for the remarkable qualities as historian, man of letters and scholar that its author reveals in it.

It was in the peaceful retreat of the presbytery of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Grande, on the island of São Miguel, where he was parish priest, that Dr Gaspar Frutuoso (volume II, page 57) wrote the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*). It is a very extensive work, divided into six books, covering the history of the archipelagos of the Canary Islands, Cape Verde, Madeira and the Azores. In the second book, which deals with our archipelago, Dr Frutuoso refers in more than one place to Jerónimo Dias Leite (volume I, page 361), a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), who supplied him with much material for writing that book. In his own words: ‘And of Gonçalo Aires Ferreira, the root of these, they all say that he wrote the Discovery of the Island of Madeira, set down in truth, as I have said, on three sheets of paper; and the reverend Canon Jerónimo Dias Leite, no less learned than inquisitive, Chaplain to His Majesty, afterwards compiled it, enlarged it and polished it with his grave and refined style, written on eleven sheets of paper, and sent it to me when it was requested on my behalf, through the intercession of the noble Belchior Fernandes de Crasto, resident in the City of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), on this island where we are, and because the most magnificent Marcos Lopes, a wholesale merchant of great and honourable dealings who lived on this island of São Miguel, much esteemed and loved here for his good qualities and magnificent disposition, and now residing in Lisbon with a great house and a greater name, had it requested of him at my entreaty. From this writing, and from many other accounts that I sought from various persons of the island of Madeira and of other parts, all worthy of trust, and from other things that I saw and read, I gathered and composed this whole account of the discovery of the said Island, ordering, arranging, reducing, adding, and putting everything into chapters, in the manner in which I am telling it.’

This second book was published in 1873, with the following wording on its title page: *As Saudades da Terra pelo Doutor Gaspar Fructuoso. História das ilhas do Porto Sancto, Madeira, Desertas e Selvagens. Manuscripto do seculo XVI annotado por Alvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, bacharel formado em direito pela Universidade de Coimbra, professor de oratória, poetica e litteraria no lyceu nacional do Funchal, e advogado na Ilha da Madeira* Funchal. Typ. Funchalense. 1873. It has XI-920 pages: the first 310 contain the text of Dr Gaspar Frutuoso and the remainder the valuable annotations of Dr Álvaro de Azevedo. Printing began around the middle of 1870 and was completed on 16 April 1873. The title page of this volume does not say so, but the publication comprises only the second book of Frutuoso’s vast work.

The illustrious annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ describes how he acquired the manuscript used for the printing in the following terms: ‘We obtained our copy of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ from Mr João Diogo Pereira de Agrela da Câmara, of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), on this island of Madeira. In the first quarter of this century it was copied, at the order of Mr João Agostinho Pereira de Agrela da Câmara, holder of the entail (*morgado*), from the autograph which, for that purpose and as a most special favour, Mr André de Ponte do Quental, of the island of São Miguel, had brought to Madeira when he came here to marry Dona Carlota de Bettencourt e Freitas. – This was assured to us by Mr Pedro Agostinho Pereira de Agrela da Câmara and by the said Mr João Diogo, sons of the aforementioned João Agostinho, holder of the entail, whom we never came to know, but who we know was one of the most learned Madeirans of his time and a lover of good books, some of which we acquired from his library.’

On the last page of the book, Dr Azevedo advertises the sale of the manuscript ‘in two folio volumes of almost two thousand pages each’. On 23 January 1876, in a letter to the Azores addressed to Dr Ernesto do Canto, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo reported that he had sold the said manuscript to a lord, for the Royal Library of Edinburgh, where it should be at present.

In his *Bibliotheca Açoreana*, the illustrious native of São Miguel Dr Ernesto do Canto states that the copy used by Dr Álvaro de Azevedo ‘lacked the necessary accuracy’, which is much to be regretted. Dr Canto made a long and conscientious comparison between a printed copy of the work published by Dr Azevedo and Dr Gaspar Frutuoso’s own autograph. In that printed copy, which is today in the public library of Ponta Delgada, he entered ‘many important corrections and additions... resulting from the collation’, as we read in the introduction to Book 3 of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, published in 1922. In Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo’s edition Dr Frutuoso’s text fills 310 pages, but Dr Ernesto do Canto’s collation covers only the first 239.

If Dr Gaspar Frutuoso’s work is extremely valuable and deserves our greatest admiration and gratitude, it may be said that the learned and precious annotations with which Dr Álvaro de Azevedo so richly enhanced the text of the illustrious historian of the islands are of no less importance to Madeirans, and enjoy no less credit among us. We have referred to these most valuable notes so often in the course of this work, and drawn on them so frequently, that it would be unnecessary and superfluous to discuss them at greater length here.

The people of São Miguel wished to pay fitting tribute to their most illustrious fellow islander by marking the fourth centenary of his birth, which fell last year, 1922, with the publication of his celebrated work ‘Longing for the Homeland’. The first volume, containing the history of the island of Santa Maria, has already been printed, and three more volumes on the island of São Miguel are to follow. This first volume is preceded by several chapters, running to two hundred long pages, on Dr Gaspar Frutuoso and his vast and valuable work. They are thorough and complete studies, which set the figure of the historian of the islands in brilliant relief and assign him the true place he deserves in the history of Portuguese literature. They are remarkable works of research and criticism, which greatly honour and distinguish their authors and at the same time bring well-deserved fame and renown to the Azores. The introduction to this work contains various references to Madeira and to Book 2 of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, which deals with this archipelago, and every moderately educated Madeiran ought to own a copy of this book (1921).

Special mention must be made of the new edition of Book II of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, published in 1925, and of the first publication of Books I, III and IV, which had until then remained unpublished, carried out later in the city of Ponta Delgada. For this we shall draw on some passages from two articles on the subject that we published in the former *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’).

As is well known, the commentator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ did not confine himself to writing a few brief explanatory notes on the text, expanding or completing it. He also produced, in masterly fashion, a number of historical dissertations and studies that are bound to endure as a superior work of criticism and that at the same time reveal broad and solid learning. To cite only giants of unquestioned authority on the subject, we would recall that Camilo Castelo Branco, Pinheiro Chagas and Teófilo Braga referred to these works with the most fervent praise, and it is known that the first and the last were not in the habit of squandering their literary judgements on easy and commonplace compliments...

Madeirans of moderate culture, and especially those interested in the history of this archipelago, can accept the coexistence of the works of Frutuoso and Azevedo only by regarding them as indissolubly united and, if we may be permitted to say so, as two parts of the same whole.

A luxurious edition of the 2nd book of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ has just been produced in Porto (1925). It contains only the text of Gaspar Frutuoso, omitting the extensive and learned commentary of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo. The edition was ably directed by Dr Damião Peres, former rector of our lyceum (state secondary school) and now a distinguished professor at the University of Porto, who added some valuable, though not very numerous, annotations. It undoubtedly represents a good service to letters, but it will benefit above all scholars and those who devote themselves particularly to the study of our literature and its history in the period to which that work belongs.

The recent edition of the *Saudades* is not of prime importance to Madeirans, because it lacks what is regarded here as fundamental and of the greatest interest to all: Dr Azevedo’s Notes. Many people have consulted and know these commentaries, while few have taken the trouble to handle the archaic, though valuable, text of the historian of the islands. Hence the sincere regret, widely shared, that the work of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo was not now reproduced in full, that is, that Frutuoso’s work was not published with the annotations that accompanied it in the 1873 edition. In that way the service rendered to our land would have been of the very greatest value (1921).

Many years ago the illustrious Azorean Dr Ernesto do Canto pointed out that the manuscript used by Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo for the publication of the *Saudades* regrettably contained many errors and gaps, for which the distinguished commentator of Gaspar Frutuoso bears no blame whatsoever. As stated above, Dr Ernesto do Canto undertook the patient and conscientious task of collating the 1873 edition with the original, authentic text and of noting, in a copy held in the Public Library of Ponta Delgada, the omissions and deficiencies he found. He thus gave us the true historical narrative as it came from the pen of the illustrious Azorean chronicler. The printed part runs to 310 pages; Dr Canto collated it with the autograph up to page 239, so that only 71 pages remained to complete the comparison of the two texts.

It is clear that, despite the shortcoming mentioned, the text chosen for the present (1925) edition of the *Saudades* ought to have been the one in the Ponta Delgada library, with the corrections recorded in it by Dr Ernesto do Canto.

Instead, use was made of the codex in the Ajuda Library, which we had occasion to consult some years ago. Its age commends it, but since it has not been collated with the autograph, it leaves in our mind the doubt that it may be tainted by the errors that afflict so many other copies of the vast work of Father Gaspar Frutuoso.

The observations we make here in passing, without the slightest intention of any disparagement that might be misconstrued, do not seek to belittle the value of the recent edition of the *Saudades*, which we acknowledge to be great, and we take this opportunity to pay its illustrious author of the preface and annotator the sincere tribute of our heartfelt admiration (1925). As 1922 marked the fifth centenary of the birth of Doctor Gaspar Frutuoso, a committee was formed in the city of Ponta Delgada to commemorate the date fittingly, taking the opportunity to give due prominence to the eminent qualities as prose writer, historian and humanist that brought renown to that illustrious native of São Miguel. To the warmest applause of all, the committee organising the centenary decided that the greatest tribute that could be paid to the author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ would be the publication of his vast work in full, thereby strengthening his memory and making it endure through the ages, while at the same time giving his contemporaries and future generations knowledge of the history of the eastern group of the Azores in the 15th and 16th centuries. For weighty reasons, the committee did not carry out its original plan, but it succeeded in publishing the third and fourth books of the *Saudades*, which contain the history of the islands of São Miguel and Santa Maria, which form the administrative district of Ponta Delgada.

They make up four large volumes, whose value and interest are enriched by an extensive study of the historian of the islands, in which the subject is entirely exhausted, whatever the many aspects from which we might perhaps judge and assess him. The learned ‘Noticia Bibliográfica das Saudades da Terra’ by Mr João Simas, and most especially the biography and appraisal of Gaspar Frutuoso and his work by Mr Rodrigo Rodrigues, are studies that reveal not only patient and conscientious historical research combined with the most refined and rigorous critical spirit, but also a profound understanding of the gifts and qualities that should characterise the work of the writer, the scholar and the historian, taking into account the conditions of the time, the setting and the other special circumstances in which the work was produced. From Mr R. Rodrigues’s masterly study, chapter III deserves particular mention. Entitled ‘O Humanista, o Historiador, e o Valor da sua Obra’ (pages XXXIX–LV), it can, without any exaggeration, be placed on the same level as comparable works by Dona Carolina Michaelis, Teófilo Braga, Mendes dos Remédios and Fidelino de Figueiredo, the most authoritative masters of literary historiography in our country (1932).

In March 1937 Dr João Franco Machado gave a paper on ‘Longing for the Homeland’ at a session of the Portuguese Institute of Archaeology, History and Ethnography (*Instituto Português de Arqueologia, História e Etnografia*). Although we do not accept it in its entirety, we shall give a brief account of it, taken from a Lisbon newspaper, merely as information for those scholars who may perhaps find it of some interest.

‘…Dr João Franco Machado spoke on Gaspar Frutuoso and Jerónimo Dias Leite’, a subject of the greatest interest for the history of the island of Madeira. He stated that Gaspar Frutuoso, in book 2 of the ‘Saudades da Terra’, fell into many errors and shortcomings, and he reported on copies, almost all of them imperfect, of the manuscript that Frutuoso himself says he compiled from Jerónimo Dias Leite. One copy, however, made with great care, shows us that the strictly historical chapters of the ‘Saudades’ are a literal copy (today one would say plagiarism) of what Dias Leite (a canon of Funchal Cathedral) had written with such accuracy about the so-called account of Alcoforado and many documents in the Funchal archives.

Frutuoso performed a service by copying it, but in his work as copyist he made many slips, mangled names and dates and altered the logical sequence of facts established by Dias Leite. To the detriment of the truth, he transferred to the year in which he was writing (1590) statements that were accurate only for 1579, the date when Dias Leite’s manuscript was written.
The Institute decided to publish the whole of Jerónimo Dias Leite’s manuscript in volume II of the journal *Ethnos*, accompanied by the study by Dr Franco Machado’.

In 1939 it published ‘Book I’ of the *Saudades*, which deals with the archipelagos of the Canary Islands and Cape Verde, preceded by a long and expert study of the personality of Doctor Gaspar Frutuoso by the distinguished São Miguel writer Dr Manuel Monteiro Velho Arruda.
On all these editions, which comprise seven volumes, we published a series of articles in *O Jornal* in October and November 1943.

It will not be a needless repetition, for some readers of this *Elucidário*, to record here that Gaspar Frutuoso’s work entitled ‘Longing for the Homeland’ consists of the following volumes: Book I, which deals particularly with the archipelagos of the Canary Islands and Cape Verde, published in one volume in 1939 in the city of Ponta Delgada; Book II, the well-known work extensively annotated by Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, concerning Madeira and published in Funchal in one volume of VIII–917 pages in 1873, with a second edition in 1925 annotated by Dr Damião Peres; Book III, which deals with the island of Santa Maria, printed in one volume in the city of Ponta Delgada in 1922; Book IV, which deals with the island of São Miguel, in three volumes, also published in Ponta Delgada in 1924, 1926 and 1931. Book V and the little that he left written of Book VI remained unpublished, and no complete copies of them exist.

In appraising the value of Gaspar Frutuoso’s vast work, Dr João Cabral do Nascimento devoted several chapters of his interesting book *Apontamentos de Historia Insular*, which deserve to be read and appreciated, even though one may disagree with certain of the author’s assertions.
Saudades de Inverno (Chrysanthemum indicum)
A composite widely grown in Madeiran gardens. It produces numerous large flower heads, quite variable both in size and in the colour of the flowers. This plant is also called *despedidas de verão*.
Saúde (street)

This was the name, before 1838, of the old Entrada da Cidade (‘entrance to the city’). On 12 January 1838 the Ministry of Finance issued a ministerial order (*portaria*) authorising the Council to carry out works on the Saúde gate and street. It was to use part of the land belonging to the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’) and to demolish the wall that enclosed that land on the east side, as well as the gate itself.

Only on 8 February 1839 did the Council have the construction of the Entrada da Cidade put out to tender. The contract for the works was awarded on the 22nd of the same month and year, and building began shortly afterwards.

The public roads between Rua dos Álamos (‘poplars’) and the former Rua do Príncipe are known today as Rua da Saúde and Calçada da Saúde, because a chapel dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Saúde (Our Lady of Health) stands there.
Sauvaire
‘This family surname’, says the annotator of the *Saudades*, ‘derives from Honorato Sauvaire, a native of Marseilles, who came to this island of Madeira as consul of France around 1660.’

The *Biblioteca Açoreana* states that the work *Description Nautique des Açores*, by Charles Philipe de Kerhallet, published in Paris in 1865, cites the ‘Letter of 2 April 1721 on the volcanic island that then appeared near São Miguel, sighted by the commander of the English corvette *Richard e Izabel*, by Sauvaire, French consul general in Madeira.

Schmitz (Father Ernst)

This distinguished German priest was born in Rheydt on 18 May 1845, the son of Frederico Schmitz and Elizabeth Schmitz, and entered the Congregation of the Mission of St Vincent de Paul on 25 September 1864. In 1874 he served for a time as chaplain of the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*), but it was only in 1878 that he took up residence in Madeira. There he at first held that post again, and then, from 27 September 1881, that of vice-rector of the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*). In this latter office he rendered outstanding services to science and education, founding in 1882 a natural history museum that still exists today (see Seminary Museum), in which he succeeded in assembling the most varied specimens of the Madeiran fauna. In 1898 he withdrew to Theux, in Belgium, but at the end of 1902 he returned to the post he had left at the Funchal Seminary. He gave it up only on 7 July 1908 when, at the request of the Imperial German Government, he went to take charge of the hospice (*hospício*) of São Paulo in Jerusalem. In 1914 he moved to the German Hospice at Tabgha, on the shores of the Sea of Galilee (Lake Tiberias), and in the summer of 1920 he took over the direction of the Hospice of São Carlos in Haifa, where he died on 3 December 1922.

Father Ernst Schmitz was chiefly an ornithologist, but his studies and observations extended to several other branches of zoology, some of them unknown here in Madeira. Dr Auguste Forel’s work on the ants and Władysław Kulczyński’s on the arachnids of the archipelago are based on material collected by the Revd Schmitz. He also devoted great attention to the study of molluscs, both marine and terrestrial, of fishes, of some groups of insects, of corals, etc., etc. Although he was no student of botany, we nevertheless owe him a fine collection of marine algae, which was studied by Professor Schmitz, a German algologist. Among the species and varieties that recall the name of the former professor and vice-rector of the Funchal Seminary, we may cite *Motacilla boarula Schmitzii* and *Strix flammea Schmitzii* (birds), *Scopulus Schmitzii* (a fish), *Plagiolepsis pigmaea Schmitzii* (an ant), *Dienches Schmitzii* (a hemipteran), *Trochosa*, *Prosthesima*, *Lephthyphantes* and *Entelecara Schmitzii* (arachnids), *Pseudochelidura Schmitzii* (an earwig), *Sympherobius Schmitzii* (a neuropteran), *Cabralia Schmitzii* (a mollusc) and *Bystropogon madeirensis Schmitzii* (a plant of the family Labiatae).

In Portugal, Father Ernst Schmitz was a member of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Ciências de Lisboa*) and of the Portuguese Society of Natural Sciences (*Sociedade Portuguesa das Ciências Naturais*). He contributed to the *Annais de Sciencias Naturais* of Porto, the *Ornithological Jahrbuch* of Hallein (Austria), the *Ornithol. Monatsberichte* of Berlin, *Cosmos* of Paris, etc. The most valuable of his works is unquestionably the one entitled *Die Vogel Madeira's*, for it brings together everything that was known in 1899 about the ornithology of the Madeira archipelago.

Father Schmitz, who became a naturalised Portuguese citizen while living among us, often told his friends that what he loved best in the world was Madeira, in Madeira Funchal, and in Funchal the Seminary. He was indeed a great friend of our island, as he proved on many occasions. On 13 November 1922, already on the brink of the grave, he was still writing a letter to the editor of *A Esperança* (‘Hope’), which that newspaper published, declaring that his love of Madeira had never left him and that, since 1908, when he left for Palestine, he had not let a single day pass without offering a prayer to the Almighty for his many friends and acquaintances on this island.

In 1908 the students of the Diocesan Seminary published a pamphlet entitled *Preito e Homenagem* (‘Tribute and Homage’), which gave prominent and well-deserved emphasis to the high merits and virtues of this illustrious priest. The most cultivated and socially distinguished people of the whole archipelago contributed to the publication.

Funchal Cathedral (the Sé)

For the time and place in which it was built, our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*) is undoubtedly a magnificent and imposing church, not only in its architectural style but also for certain works of art it contains, which have caught the attention of many distinguished visitors. For this reason it is numbered among our national monuments.

When the plan for its construction was drawn up, the creation of the diocese was expected shortly, as indeed came to pass, and with it the elevation of this church to the rank of cathedral. This readily explains the proportions it was given and the air of grandeur apparent throughout the building. For a mere parish church, and in that period, it was an excessively grand construction, one that the circumstances of the time in no way permitted or warranted.

The names of the architect who drew up the plan of this work, and of any other artist who displayed his talent there, have remained unknown to us. Nowhere in the building is there a name, a date or an initial that might give us a useful lead for any research into the craftsmen who raised that majestic church. All that can be found are small marks on the dressed stones, which perhaps served to indicate conventional details of construction, as was common in former times on buildings that took many years to complete.

The manuscript *Noticia das cousas da Ilha da Madeira desde o seu segundo descobrimento pelo Zargo* states that our Cathedral was built to the measurements of the church of Carmo (Carmelite church), Lisbon, which, as is well known, was commissioned by Nuno Álvares Pereira. That magnificent church, one of the finest examples of Gothic architecture in Portugal, was destroyed by the earthquake of 1755. However, an old engraving, which Oliveira Martins reproduced in his work on Nuno Álvares, shows that its façade was very different from the frontage of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), except for the pointed portal with its archivolts and the rose window with its ornaments embroidered in stone. As for the interior, we can say nothing about any resemblance there may have been between the two churches, since we do not know any of the old chronicles dealing with Nuno Álvares and the Carmelite convent, where a description of its church will surely be found.

The earliest date known to us relating to the construction of our Cathedral is 5 June 1485. On that day Prince Manuel, Duke of Viseu and Grand Master of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*), by a letter signed at Santiago do Cacém, made a grant of land in the Campo do Duque (volume I, page 225) so that there might be built upon it ‘a church and square and churchyard and houses for the municipality (*concelho*)’. A letter from the same duke, dated 22 October 1488, granted half of the fines that ‘may be imposed on the island’ for ‘the making of the church which, God willing, I hope to have built in the said Funchal’.

Accounts of the year in which the work began are not entirely in agreement. Nevertheless, the most probable view to adopt is that of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, who states that the ‘building of the church began shortly after 1493, for in that year the Duke of Viseu, later King Manuel, ordered, by a letter registered on fol. 174 of volume I of the Archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal, that the revenue of the wine levy (imposição do vinho) be applied to that work.’ The annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) further adds: ‘…and by 1502 it was already under way, the proceeds of that levy then being assigned to it not only in the municipality of Funchal but also in those of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and Calheta (‘small cove’), as can be seen from the royal letter (*carta régia*) of the same King Manuel of that year 1502’. This letter is transcribed on page 488, not 503 as note XX states, and the following passages bear on the subject of this article: ‘Firstly, you ask us that the levy of the towns of Ponta do Sol and Calheta should always go to the works of the church of that town and of the municipality. To this we reply that it pleases us that, for as long as the works on the said church last, the levy of the aforesaid places be collected for them alone and for nothing else. Item, that the inhabitants of Ponta do Sol and Calheta should pay towards the church of that town whatever they are assessed until it is finished. To this we reply that it pleases us that each should pay what he is assessed according to his means’.

The letter cited clearly shows that the work was under way in 1502, which entirely invalidates the statement, found in many places, that construction of the Cathedral began in 1508. It is generally said that the building took a very long time, as almost always happened with buildings of that period, and to this was added the great shortage of resources of every kind in our community at the time. One can therefore easily judge that it would have been impossible to complete the building work between 1508 and 1516, or perhaps even before that latter year. What seems beyond doubt, in view of the above, is that construction began in the last decade of the 15th century, that is, shortly after 1493, as Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo states.

The main construction work on the Cathedral must have been finished by 1516, the year of its consecration, while the interior decoration and work on certain parts of the church continued slowly after that time. The distinguished annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ considers the church completed in 1508 and says it was consecrated in that year by Bishop Dom João Lobo, whereas Gaspar Frutuoso gives 16 October 1516 as the day of the consecration and states that the consecrating bishop was Dom Duarte. On this point we side with the author, not the annotator, of ‘Longing for the Homeland’. In various old manuscripts we have found the statement that our Cathedral was consecrated in 1516, and Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo is perhaps the only one to assert that it was in 1508. Moreover, all the old ecclesiastical chronicles we have been able to consult state that the consecration was performed by Bishop Dom Duarte, and there is not the slightest doubt that this prelate came to the island at the behest of the first bishop, Dom Diogo Pinheiro, appointed in 1514 when the bishopric was created.

After the consecration, as we have already said, work continued on the interior decoration, which was not yet finished, and over the course of time very important works were carried out there for the complete and final conclusion of the whole building. The order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 30 March 1560 directed that ‘the enclosure behind the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*) be built’, and that of 28 February 1635 ordered the completion of the works on the chancel, whose paintings were only placed there in the second quarter of the 18th century. The construction of the great sacristy and of the chapter house also dates from the second quarter of that century; these were let by award by public auction (*arrematação*) for 3,050,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in 1733. The present chapel of the Blessed Sacrament, which replaced the old one, began to be built around the middle of the 18th century. The altars in the side aisles were built at the beginning of the 19th century.

The description of the Cathedral that Gaspar Frutuoso wrote in 1590, which we transcribe below, is extremely picturesque: ‘… it is a much-frequented church, well shaded and cool, and it has a beautiful, very tall tower of dressed stone (*cantaria*), with a beautiful spire of *azulejos* (painted glazed tiles) which, when the rays of the Sun strike them, look like silver and gold. At the top of it hangs a clock bell so large that its hollow would hold thirty *alqueires* of wheat, and of so proud and great a sound that it is heard two *léguas* away; whenever it is rung, the people gather at any alarm of war. Further down the tower there are three windows, in which hang fifteen bells. The body of the church, which is subordinate to the tower, is large, with its churchyard, also spacious, enclosed in parts by a wall, and with ten steps leading up to it; outside it there is a square so large that bulls and horses are run in it, jousting with canes is held and other festivities take place. This church (whose dedication is to Nossa Senhora da Estrela) is laid out from East to West, with the main door facing the West and the two side doors from North to South. The altars (of which there are nine) are decorated in gold and blue, with three rich chantries (*capela*), where the choir lies within the arch, with its costly and finely worked seats of rich joinery; and at the crossing the Epistle and the Gospel are read.’
The Cathedral churchyard, once larger than it is today, was partly demolished in 1836, permission for the works having been granted by the civil governor on 29 December 1835.

Our Cathedral is a Gothic church with three naves, of rare and remarkable elegance, divided by tall, slender columns that spare it the heavy and gloomy appearance of many similar buildings. Above the naves rests the famous ceiling, made of native cedar wood in the Arabic style, with ivory inlays. Experts regard it as a work of rare value, and it never fails to arouse the greatest admiration among visitors. Emanuel Ribeiro says that ‘in it one admires the intricate music of Arabic interlacing, in which the geometer was able to discover a philosophy of form, harbouring strange sensations, at times of calm, serene and majestic feelings, at others steeped in a vague melancholy of mystery.

‘The apse is covered by a painted vault with strong ribs, finished with carved bosses. Surrounding those on the longitudinal axis, which represent the shield of the *quinas*, the Cross of the Knights of the Order of Christ and the armillary sphere, there are other interpretations of the native flora. The first are three fine symbols of our past History. In one beats the heart and soul of a free people; in another a generous faith, strong in hope; and in the others the laurel of glory gleams upon the trembling, curved wing of a sail, amid rough and foaming waves. ‘In Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) there are more than fifty canvases and panels on which the artist’s brush made the iridescent ranges of colour vibrate, in some of them beautifully. From the darkened backgrounds there sometimes emerges the pure outline of figures touched with such feeling and life, animated by such purity and tenderness, that they seem merely to rest in ecstatic and mystical contemplation, wrapped in gold-embroidered mantles which fall in long classical folds over bodies wasted by long and constant fasts of sacrifice.
‘Some of the panels, of the thirteen that adorn the altarpiece of the high altar in the chancel, deserve minutes of careful study.’

The chancel, which Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says bears the decadent, hybrid stamp of the 17th century, is entirely out of keeping with the dominant style of the whole church, as are the sacristy and the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament. The harmony of the original style was broken still further by the major repairs carried out after the earthquake of 1748, which caused considerable damage there, just as the French had already done irreparable harm in 1566. At the end of the 18th century, Canon João Paulo had several altars that were in an advanced state of ruin rebuilt at his own expense. He also had the present windows of the main façade opened; they contrast sharply with the pointed doorway and the rose window above, and robbed that frontispiece of the pure lines of the Manueline style that had been its own.
Then came the marbling on the slender columns, the coats of whitewash on the fine and distinctive frontage, and yet other artistic heresies that were perpetrated there with impunity…

The chapel of the Blessed Sacrament deserves special mention: taken as a whole, it is remarkably beautiful, with its very fine marbles and precious carving in gilded wood. Although small, it has such an air of grandeur and majesty that it makes a deep impression on the visitor.

This church holds one of the great marvels of 16th-century Portuguese goldsmiths’ work: a processional cross presented by King Manuel I to the first episcopal see founded in our overseas dominions. Although it is somewhat long, we cannot fail to transcribe here the description of it that Pinheiro Chagas gives in his *Historia de Portugal*: ‘This was one of the marvels of the Exhibition of Ornamental Art in Lisbon in 1882. It is of silver gilt, surrounded entirely by filigree or lacework of the most elegant workmanship. The arms of the cross each end in a closed panel, bounded by three semicircles on the upper arm and by four on the other three, and they show in relief Jesus Christ in the Garden, the Kiss of Judas, the Flagellation and the Ecce Homo. At the top, closing the upper panel from below, is the ribbon of the inscription. The figure of Christ, in high relief, rests against an elegant ornament of oak leaves, which ends at the sides and below near the hands and feet, and above reaches up to the inscription, forming there what look like two volutes. – On the back, which cannot be seen in the engraving, is the image of Christ standing, holding in his hand a globe surmounted by the cross. Four panels at the ends of the cross, corresponding to those on the front, appear on the back and represent the four Evangelists. At the lower end, before the knop, are the royal arms of Portugal, carved and held up by two angels. The whole moulding of the shaft is edged on the inside with a cord, which also surrounds the arms above and below, and the shaft rests on a hexagonal base, likewise ornamented on its outer edge with a cord. – Below everything is the foot of the cross, which serves to fit it onto a wooden staff. Between this and the base rises the most beautiful knop. From the foot spring oak branches, which seem to support the knop. The knop rises in the form of a Gothic temple in three storeys, profusely ornamented and surrounded by pinnacles, flying buttresses or buttresses, all furnished with statuettes under canopies of the most exquisite and graceful workmanship. – At the centre of each face and each storey of the knop there is a kind of door or window, all in floral decoration, each diminishing in height from the lowest to the highest. This whole body or knop is crowned on both faces, back and front, by the royal arms of Portugal held up by two angels, like the others already mentioned; on the two faces flanking the arms, armillary spheres stand out in high relief, and it can be seen that those of the back face are missing.

‘This wondrous artefact is somewhat damaged by mutilations caused by time. – The cross is evidently from the beginning of the 16th century and must have been given by Dom Manuel, as the arms and spheres clearly show, when in 1514 he had the bishopric of Funchal created. – The sculpting of the figures and a certain softness in the forms of the cross lead us to believe that, if the artefact did not come from abroad and was made in the country, foreign artists must have worked on it, from the vast pleiad of those who had settled here, drawn by its riches, and who even had many disputes with the native craftsmen.’

The great organ of our Cathedral, in the main choir, was commissioned by the diocesan bishop Dom Jerónimo Fernando, who headed this diocese from 1624 to 1641. For its time it was considered a very valuable instrument. Its design was drawn up by Father António Gonçalves, and it was built by a craftsman from Córdoba named João Manuel. The smaller organ, in the choir beside the chancel, was acquired in 1736; its purchase, transport and installation in its present position (1921) cost 1,100,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

For the Holy Week ceremonies, the so-called *camarim* (tiered throne erected for Holy Week), or throne, is set up in the chapel of the Lord Jesus; taken as a whole, it is of rare beauty and elegance. It is very tall and fills the whole of the chapel, which is quite spacious, and it is made up of hundreds of pieces, many of them in fine gilt carved woodwork (*talha dourada*). It dates from the first quarter of the 19th century.
As regards the clergy of the Cathedral, we have already said enough in the article cathedral chapter (volume I, page 179), to which we refer the reader. See Neale.

To this article, reproduced in full from the first edition of the *Elucidário*, it would be fitting to add new material on the history, architecture, works of art and precious liturgical objects of our Cathedral, and also to correct certain shortcomings of information to be found in it. The limited space available to us in these pages, however, has not allowed us to do so.

We take the liberty of referring the reader to the pamphlet we wrote, entitled *A Sé Catedral do Funchal* and published in 1936, in which we treated the subject at greater length, having gathered further notes from the various works we were able to consult in a brief study we carried out.
1485 – By a charter of 5 June of this year, Dom Manuel, Duke of Beja, as Grand Master of the Order of Christ, granted the land needed in the Campo do Duque for the building of the ‘Great Church’.
1488 – The royal decree (alvará régio) of 21 October authorised the collection of a tax, known as ‘penas’, intended for the new building.
1493 – Conjectural date for the start of the building works, which went on for a long time.

1493–1521 – Within this period, Dom Manuel, first as Grand Master of the Order of Christ and later as monarch, issued various instruments creating revenues and granting several ‘exemptions’ in favour of the future Cathedral. It is chiefly to him that its construction is owed.

1508 – The titular bishop Dom João Lobo blessed the new church, though its construction was still far from complete, and the seat of the parish, which until then had been in the church of Our Lady of Calhau, was transferred to it.
1516 – In 1514, with the creation of the diocese, the ‘Great Church’ became an episcopal cathedral. It was blessed by the titular Bishop of Dume, Dom Duarte, on 18 October 1516.
1518–1521 – The gift of the well-known and precious cross by King Manuel I, a marvel of 16th-century Portuguese goldsmithing, should be dated approximately to this period.
1533 – The archdiocese of Funchal is created, with four suffragan dioceses, and our Cathedral is raised to the rank of an archiepiscopal see. The archdiocese was abolished in 1551.
1566 – During the terrible sack by the French Huguenots, the Cathedral suffered many outrages and profanations, and various works of art were also seriously damaged.

1578 – The first diocesan synod was held in this church with remarkable splendour. It promulgated a set of ‘Constituições Diocesanas’ (diocesan constitutions), published in 1585 in a volume of XVI + 188 pages, which is today a great bibliographical rarity.

1608 – The prelate Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos dies and is buried in the Cathedral. The bishops Dom Gabriel de Almeida, who died in 1674, Dom Friar António Teles da Silva (1682), Dom Friar João do Nascimento (1753), Dom Gaspar Afonso da Costa Brandão (1784), Dom Luís Rodrigues de Vilares (1810) and Dom Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos (1880) also have their last resting place there.
1630 – Around this time work began on completing the chancel, with its fine panelling and interesting choir stalls.
1730–1740 – During this decade the main sacristy and the chapter house, with its outbuildings, were built.
1748 – The earthquake of this year caused considerable damage to the Cathedral building, especially to its tower and façade.
1755 – Around this time the chapel of the Blessed Sacrament was entirely rebuilt, the old one having been demolished.
1775 – A clock is installed in the Cathedral tower; in 1922 it was replaced by another, donated by a foreign national. The set of bells there was acquired in 1812.
1805 – The illustrious Portuguese painter Francisco Vieira, known as ‘Vieira Portuense’, is buried in this church, at a spot that is not known.
1940 – The ‘Museu Diocesano de Arte Sacra’ (Diocesan Museum of Sacred Art) is opened, housed in the rooms of the Chapter House.
Sé (parish)

As we have said elsewhere, the first parish (*freguesia*) created in Funchal was that of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), although in the very earliest days of colonisation parish functions were carried out simultaneously in various chapels and hermitages (volume II, page 52). This parish, created around 1438 and established in the church of Our Lady of Calhau (*Nossa Senhora do Calhau*), moved its seat to the new church that later became the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), some years before the diocese was instituted. The royal decree (alvará régio) of 18 November 1557 divided it into two separate parishes, with their seats in the Cathedral and in the church of Our Lady of Calhau. It was from the parish of the Sé that the parishes of São Pedro, Santo António, São Martinho, São Roque, Monte and, later, Santa Luzia were carved out.

Until 1562 parish duties were performed by the dean of the Sé. In that year the royal decree of 20 July created two curacies and relieved the most senior member of the cathedral chapter of those functions. The original stipend (*côngrua*) of each curate was 8,400 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year; the decree of 30 November 1563 raised it to 17,450 *réis*, and that of 21 February 1600 to 20,000 *réis*, likewise a year. The first curates, as the aforementioned founding decree states, were removable, but the post later became a collative benefice (*benefício colado*) like the others of its kind in this diocese. Roughly fifty years ago the prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto provisionally suppressed one of these curacies, creating at the same time an assistant priest (*coadjutor*) at the Sé and another in each of the parishes of São Gonçalo and São Martinho.
We shall not discuss here the church in which the seat of this parish was and still is housed, since we deal with it at some length elsewhere (see Sé Catedral).

Within this parish stand the church of the College (*Colégio*), the church of Carmo (Carmelite church), the church of Bom Jesus (Good Jesus) and the church of the Misericórdia (*Igreja da Misericórdia*). The chapels of St Sebastian, St Bartholomew, St Lawrence, Our Lady of Pity, Jesus Maria José, Our Lady of Grace, Our Lady of Deliverance and Nossa Senhora dos Varadouros (Our Lady of the Varadouros) no longer exist; we have referred to all of them elsewhere in this work. Inside the courtyard of the customs house there still survives, though now deconsecrated, a chapel whose dedication was to St Anthony.

It was also within this parish that, for several centuries, stood the house of João Esmeraldo, in which Christopher Columbus is said to have lived. It stood in the street that today bears the great navigator’s name, as may be seen in more detail in the article we devoted to him on page 286 of volume I of this *Elucidário*. Between the Rua da Alfândega and the Rua dos Murças, where the Largo da Sé continues, there once rose an old building that for many years served as the gaol and also as the town hall; we have already given an account of it elsewhere (volume I, page 183). We made the necessary reference to the Varadouros gate, the old entrance to the city, in the article Nossa Senhora dos Varadouros, on page 467 of volume II. The principal building in this parish is the Cathedral (the Sé), which is classified as a National Monument (*monumento nacional*) and is indeed a magnificent church, worthy of the highest esteem for its beautiful appearance and majesty.

The parish (*freguesia*) of the Sé occupies the most central part of the city, and it is here that the city’s main commercial, administrative and official activity takes place. Here are the most important commercial establishments, including all the banks, and most of the public offices, and here the commercial traffic of the city’s landing place and customs house is conducted. The number of its residents is falling considerably, because commercial activity keeps expanding and dwelling houses are steadily being turned into business premises.

According to the *Mappa Alphabetico* of the city’s streets, approved by the civil governor on 15 December 1863, the following belong to the parish, and in most cases form its limits: the south side of the Rua do Carmo (Costa Ferreira), from the bridge to the Vale stream; the north side of the same street, between that stream and the Rua das Hortas (Alferes Veiga Pestana); the western side of the latter street, below the Rua do Bom Jesus; the Rua da Conceição (Correia Heredia); the Rua da Ponte Nova; the part of the Rua do Bom Jesus between the Rua da Conceição and the Rua da Princesa (31 de Janeiro); the eastern side of the Rua dos Ferreiros, above the Rua dos Netos; the south side of this last street as far as the Rua do Castanheiro, and its north side from the bridge to the Rua dos Ferreiros; the Rua das Pretas (Câmara Pestana), at the points where the houses numbered 64 and 43 stand, belonging respectively to Dona Maria Camacho Teixeira de Sousa and José Teodoro Clerouin (1921); the part of the Rua da Carreira (Dr Vieira) bounded to the west by the Rua de São Francisco, and the eastern side of this street; the Fort of São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’); and finally the Rua do Anadia, from the pillory (*pelourinho*, stone column symbolising municipal jurisdiction) to the bridge opposite the Rua do Carmo. Some consider the whole of the Rua das Hortas as belonging to Santa Luzia, and the south side of the Rua do Bom Jesus, west of the Rua das Hortas, as belonging to the parish of the Sé. The parish of the Sé has 4,083 inhabitants (1921).
