Thyme (Thymus vulgaris)

A small woody plant of the Labiatae (mint family), widely grown in Madeiran kitchen gardens. Its sprigs, bearing small aromatic leaves, are much used as a seasoning in cooking. It is also called *cheiros*.
Seixal (parish)

We contend with a great scarcity of information about this parish, beginning with our uncertainty as to the most reliable spelling in which its name should be fixed. The difficulty is partly resolved by trying to discover exactly the origin of this word as applied to that parish (*freguesia*). Does the name come from *seixo*, meaning a stone or pebble, or did it take its origin from *seixo* denoting a plant species? The latter sense of the word is generally adopted, on the grounds that the former is very little known here, especially among the less educated classes. But would it have been so in the earliest days of colonisation? It is worth recalling in this connection that, on the day after the first landing at Machico, the discoverers gave the name *porto do Seixo* to a small beach that today belongs to the parish of Água de Pena, ‘because of what was found in it’, says the historian of the islands. Modern lexicographers write *seixo* in both the senses already indicated, but in older vocabularies one finds *seixo* for a pebble and *seiço* meaning a tree or plant. The word, as used for the parish with which we are dealing, is found written in various and even extravagant spellings: Seisal, Seiçal, Seissal, Ceisal, Ceixal and Seixal. Some of these spellings are plainly incorrect, but Seiçal is a correct, though antiquated, form, and it is also the most common in old documents. It would have been interesting and valuable for us to trace how this word changed in the registers of the parish archive over a long period of more than three centuries, but unfortunately we have not been able to do so. We are of the opinion that the name of this parish was taken from *seixo* or *seiço*, a small tree or shrub of the genus *Salix* and the family *Salicaceae* which, according to botanical publications, ‘is found in the beds of streams and on many damp rocks in Madeira’. It was probably spread in greater abundance over this island at the time of the discovery and the first settlements. We consider that the true spelling to adopt would be Seiçal, but since Seixal has been introduced and become general, it would perhaps be pointless today to fight against the commonly established usage, and to many the change might seem a pretentious and ridiculous innovation.

The land that today makes up the parish (*freguesia*) of Seixal originally belonged to the parish of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), when the latter was perhaps merely the seat of a simple chaplaincy (capelania) exercising parochial functions. Gaspar Frutuoso wrote in 1590: ‘Three leagues from São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) lies Seixal, which is a parish of up to twenty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’), with a church dedicated to São Brás. It has much land for rearing livestock, and the growing of grain and wine, and fruit of every kind.’ The present patron saint of its church is Santo Antão, and we believe it always was, and not São Brás, as we read in Frutuoso.

Both the annotator of the *Saudades*, who followed the information in the *Memórias... do Estudo Eclesiastico*, and the *Índice Geral da Provedoria...*, which we have cited so often, state that Seixal was made a parish by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 20 June 1553, so this is the date of its creation. The first parish priest was Father Francisco da Arca, who received as his annual stipend (*côngrua*) 7,400 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) in cash and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine, as fixed by the said founding decree. The royal decree of 10 February 1502 added one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. The decrees of 22 November 1575 and 9 June 1581 raised it to 20,000 and 25,000 *réis* a year respectively, and it was increased by half a *moio* of wheat and a quarter of wine by the royal decree of 10 September 1589. The decree of 15 December 1678 then reduced this salary to 19,000 *réis*, one and a half *moios* of wheat and one *pipa* of wine.
Main localities: Serra de Água, Portada, Penedo, Lombinho, Cova, Feiteiras, Farrobo, Ribeira da Lage, Fajã da Parreira and Ribeira Funda. It has 1203 inhabitants (1921).
Seixas

The first person of this surname of whom there is any record was José de Seixas, who married Dona Luísa de Mendonça. She outlived him and founded the chapel of Our Lady of Protection (*Nossa Senhora do Amparo*). This José de Seixas was Spanish consul in 1686.
Seixo (Salix canariensis)

A shrub or small tree with lanceolate, greyish leaves that are glaucous on the underside; the flowers are dioecious and borne in small catkins. It is common in stream beds and on many damp rocks in Madeira. The wood of this member of the Salicaceae is light and dull or reddish in colour; it is used for inlaid work (*embutidos*).
Selaginellaceae

These vascular cryptogams are represented in Madeira by the following species: *Selaginella kraussiana* and *S. denticulata*. The first is a naturalised plant; the second is native and very common almost everywhere.
Selvageira (Sideritis massoniana)

A whitish, tomentose labiate subshrub; the flowers are borne in racemes that are almost always panicled; the calyces are woolly; the corollas are very small and yellow. It is found in the ravines of the interior of Madeira, on the Ponta de São Lourenço, on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’). The Madeiran plants have larger leaves and a more branched inflorescence than the plants of the other islands. The *selvageira*, known in Madeira as *herva branca*, is a useful plant in the treatment of coughs, etc.
Savage Islands

The small group of the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*), which is politically part of the Madeira archipelago, lies between 30º and 30º 10' north latitude and 16°7, and 16°20' west longitude of the Greenwich meridian. It is made up of the following islets: Selvagem Grande (‘great wild island’), Selvagem Pequena (‘little wild island’) and Ilhéu de Fora (‘outer islet’). The second of these islets is also known as Ilhéu Grande and Pitão Grande (‘great peak islet’), and the last as Ilhéu Pequeno and Pitão Pequeno (‘little peak islet’).

In his pamphlet *As Selvagens*, Mr Alberto Artur Sarmento gives Selvagem Grande a length of 2.5 kilometres, a width of 2.2 kilometres and an area of some 5 square kilometres, adding that its coasts are steep and hard to approach because of the great number of rocks surrounding it. According to Mr Adolfo César de Noronha, the island’s sea cliffs can reach 100 metres in height, although the interior is more or less flat. The exceptions are the east, where Pico dos Tornozelos rises, and the west, where Pico da Atalaia (‘watchtower’) stands above the sea, its altitude estimated at about 150 metres. To the south there is also a small knoll, that of Inferno, about 115 metres above sea level.

Selvagem Grande lies 250 kilometres from Ponta da Agulha (‘needle point’) on Bugio, one of the three Desertas (‘deserted islands’), 280 from the port of Funchal, and 165 kilometres from Ponta do Hidalgo on Tenerife, so it is closer to the Canary Islands archipelago than to that of Madeira. Like the other two islets of the group, it is uninhabited, and its best anchorages are the cove of Pardelas, to the east, and another to the south, sheltered by the knoll of Inferno. At the locality (*sítio*) called Estancia, to the south-west, is the best landing place, which is why boats head there when they have people to put ashore. At that spot there is a shed and a cave with a wall and a door, where visitors can take shelter, and further inland there is a small hut roofed with zinc sheets, which can also shelter those who wish to spend the night in the central part of the island. Two cisterns have been built on Selvagem Grande, holding water all year round, and there are also three small springs – das Ovelhas, below Pico da Atalaia, the Salgada and das Galinhas – which yield some water for only part of the year. There are traces of some works having been carried out at the Galinhas spring, on the upper part of the island.

The Savage Islands are of volcanic origin. On Selvagem Grande, says Mr Alberto Sarmento, the porous, blackened scoriae of which it is formed have gradually broken apart under subaerial action, making the ground brittle, a surface of lapilli of vitrified mass and microlitic structure.

Dr Gagel, who studied some collections assembled by Mr Adolfo de Noronha, supposes that the Savage Islands must be formed essentially of phonolite, with a layer of more recent basaltic lavas, and with scoriae and small fossil deposits.

An extensive underground gallery, 150 metres long, Mr Sarmento also says, is rather curious, as it may have been formed by a volcanic channel or vent, in which prolonged infiltration later deposited a bed of calcium sulphate of saccharoidal crystallisation. It is interesting too for the coatings it forms on the rocks, a crust that crumbles easily and whose underside appears studded with brilliant white flakes.

Above Pardelas, on high ground, there is a Miocene shell deposit, and at the locality of Risco (‘cliff’), at a height of 90 to 100 metres, there is another Tertiary deposit. Near the sea and close to Cabeço do Inferno (‘hell’s knoll’) there are traces of subfossilised modern marine shells.
The summit of the peak of Tenerife can at times be seen from Selvagem Grande, and we have read somewhere that at no other point on the globe can land be made out at so great a distance.

Selvagem Pequena is low, flat and covered with calcareous sands which, says Mr Adolfo de Noronha, meet marine sands deposited at the bottom of bays formed by erosion platforms, set between points that jut out into the sea. According to Mr Sarmento, this islet measures 2 kilometres long and 1 wide, but Mr Noronha tells us that its shape is very poorly represented on the old charts, both French and English, so it is to be believed that these measurements are rather far from the truth.

There are neither springs nor cisterns on Selvagem Pequena, so visitors must bring water from Selvagem Grande, 15 kilometres away. On the island there are some walls, perhaps built in former times, which can be made into a shelter by laying a ship’s sail or some other covering over them. The only height on Selvagem Pequena is Pico do Veado, a rocky knoll 140 metres high.

Separated from Selvagem Pequena by an arm of the sea about a mile wide lies Ilhéu de Fora, also low and covered with sand, about 1200 metres long and at most 400 metres wide. It has no water and no height of any kind, and it abounds in *calcamares*, a seabird we have already mentioned in this work, which breeds in burrows or underground galleries. Similar burrows are found on Selvagem Grande, where the same bird is also very common.

Shearwaters (*cagarras*) are the chief wealth of the Savage Islands. Although some 20 to 22 thousand are caught every year, as the late Father Ernst Schmitz stated in 1901 in an article published in *Cosmos*, their numbers do not fall, which proves how dense the population is. They must therefore exceed a total of 60,000, because each shearwater lays only one egg, and there must be at least 40,000 for an annual breeding of 20 thousand. The Savage Islands, or rather Selvagem Grande, are visited every year, usually in September, by parties of hunters, who bring back many rabbits, shearwaters and salted fish, for which they always find buyers in Funchal. The shearwater lives on all three islands of the group, but the rabbit, which is a small breed like that of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), is found only on Selvagem Grande, where it has destroyed many plant species that once grew there. Selvagem Grande also supplies large quantities of limpets, salted or pickled in vinegar (1921).

Goats once lived on Selvagem Grande. Besides the animals already mentioned, there are now two species of rat (see that entry), the lizard (*lagartixa*), the gecko (*osga*) and various birds, among them the common tern (*garajau*), the kestrel (*francelho*), the *corre-caminho*, the *anjinho*, the gull and the *pintainho*. A leguminous plant peculiar to the three islets (*Lotus Paivae*) grows on all of them, and on the Ilhéu de Fora a variety of *Euphorbia obtusifolia* is abundant.

The Savage Islands group is surrounded by an extensive barrier of reefs that makes its coasts hard to approach. Landing on Selvagem Pequena, and above all on the Ilhéu de Fora, is much more difficult than on Selvagem Grande. Selvagem Pequena has beaches of rounded pebbles, as in Madeira, and platforms of marine erosion, and between it and the Ilhéu de Fora there are some rocks at the surface of the water and others under the sea. The Palheiros (‘barns’) are two rocks near Selvagem Grande, and to the north of the Ilhéu de Fora there are several reefs, two of which are known as the shoal of Sarmento (*baixa do Sarmento*) and the shoal of Noronha (*baixa do Noronha*).

It is believed that a rich treasure, taken in the plunder of three Mexican ships, was hidden on the Savage Islands by the crew of a Spanish vessel, and more than once the former holders of the entail (*morgado*) of those islands searched for it. In 1851 some Englishmen visited Selvagem Pequena and the Ilhéu de Fora in search of the same treasure, and the same men had made other searches in 1848, 1849 [and] 1850.

The Savage Islands were discovered by the navigators of Prince Henry the Navigator, and Diogo Gomes left a manuscript account of the main island of the group. In the 16th century, says Mr Alberto Sarmento, they belonged to a Madeiran family known as the Caiados. Around 1560 Canon Manuel Ferreira Teixeira, a descendant of these Caiados, gave them to his niece Dona Filipa Cabral de Vasconcelos, wife of José Ferreira de Noronha Franco, from whom descended João T. Cabral de Noronha, the last holder of the entail of the Savage Islands.
In 1904 the descendants of this holder of the entail sold the islands to the banker Luís da Rocha Machado. On his death they passed to his son, who is their present owner (1921).
Of particular relevance to this subject is an article published in the *Século* of Lisbon, from which we shall give some extracts.

‘Along the Portuguese coast, reefs made famous by tragedies rise from the sea; along our shipping lanes, fortresses of rock burst forth. On the route of three continents, between Europe, Africa and America, we have the barrier of reefs of the Desertas and the Savage Islands.
The *Carvalho Araujo*, on a research mission, recently set out for this group of rocks lost in the eternal solitude of the Atlantic.
Between Porto Santo, Madeira and the sixteen islands of the Canary archipelago lie the Desertas and the Savage Islands. The former lie close to Madeira.

The largest is fourteen kilometres long and two wide, with a hill of 480 metres. It is the only one where water is found, though brackish. It has never been inhabited. In the time of Prince Henry the Navigator there was a small chapel there to serve the men who went about the arduous work of hunting and fishing. They are called Deserta Grande, Ilhéu Chão and Bugio.

Further south, separated from the Desertas by an ocean abyss 4,512 metres deep, rises the islet of Selvagem. It lies 250 km from the last of those islands, 280 from Funchal, and 165 km from the nearest of the Canary Islands, Tenerife.
The Savage Islands group as a whole covers some eight miles. It consists of Selvagem Grande, Pitão Grande, Ilhéu Pequeno and a dozen or so further reefs.

Selvagens, the main islet, measures some 7½ kilometres in length by 2 in width. Its greatest height is 150 metres. Pitão Grande measures some two kilometres in length by 1 in width, with a central mass of rocks rising to 140 metres. Ilhéu Pequeno is 1,200 metres long by 400 wide; it is almost flat and made up more of sand than of rock.

Discovered in the time of Prince Henry, and found to be barren, they were taken over by donataries who exploited them for hunting, fishing and the gathering of orchil (a dye lichen), a dye plant highly prized in England and Flanders. Stocked with goats and rabbits on Prince Henry’s orders, they soon yielded a good profit, for the animals bred well.

In the 17th century the islets belonged to the Madeiran entail-holders the Teixeiras Caiados, and from them, through sales, they passed to the Rocha Machado family, also Madeiran, who now own the bulwarks of rock called the Savage Islands, rising on the shipping lane of three continents…

Ever since Prince Henry had goats and rabbits released on the Desertas and the Savage Islands, meat has been plentiful there, despite the lack of water. The animals slake their thirst by chewing a native plant heavily soaked in sap, which is a veritable store of drinkable liquid.

On these rugged rocks, full of shadowy hollows, live thousands of seabirds. If we are to believe an 18th-century writer, it was then impossible to walk on the Savage Islands without treading on nests. Even today, on the ledges of the cliff, among the stems of the tiny creeping plants, birds’ nests abound. The hunting of one species, the shearwater (*cagarra*), culls some 20,000 birds every year, and it is estimated that there are upwards of 60,000 on the islets.

The Savage Islands have their legend. Through the mists of time, belief grew in a treasure hidden on the largest island. For years the entail-holders of the Savage Islands searched doggedly for the pirates’ fortune concealed on the islet. The ground was dug over entirely, so much so that they later tried to cultivate it, so that the work done would not be wholly lost. But they lost heart at the lack of water and the absence of rain.

From 1847 to 1851, according to documents, seven Englishmen searched the Savage Islands for the treasure. They carried out excavations in four successive years, spending 2,500 pounds. The islands were dug over completely. The belief of this handful of adventurers rested on the confession of a dying man, who had told how he had been one of the crew of a pirate ship that plundered three Mexican vessels laden with gold during the war with the United States, and had then come to bury the treasure on a deserted island near Tenerife.

The treasure of the Savage Islands never appeared. Neither gold nor bread ever came from their bowels. Neither trees nor crops nor human lives seek out the crests of their rocks or the sandy soil of their flats. Only the goats raise their satanic heads against the outline of their peaks, and the birds wheel in their thousands near the nests hidden in their hollows. And, once a year, comes the hunt, the slaughter, of birds, goats, rabbits and fish.

Concerning the legendary report, mentioned above and discussed by several writers, of a ‘treasure’ buried on these islands, the following details, which we found in a Lisbon newspaper, are of some interest.
‘They lie in the open Atlantic, away from the shipping lane to South America, between the Canaries and Madeira, and they belong to a member of the Vieira de Castro family.

Nobody lives there. There is no water. They are bleak, bare rocks of volcanic origin, deeply gullied by the waves. In the season of bird migration the shearwaters (*cagarras*) alight there, resting for a few days from their Atlantic flight before heading for more pleasant parts.
Only the Spaniards of the Canaries know the Savage Islands, making frequent excursions there with the utmost disregard for our real sovereignty, which has no one to represent it.
The Savage Islands, however, have already aroused the greed of a famous Englishman, the explorer Shackleton, who died at the South Pole some years ago.
It is a curious and mysterious story, one well worth unravelling, for it would make any of us immensely rich. But it is better to tell it and savour it.

One day the owner of the Savage Islands was eating a hurried lunch with an English newspaper in front of him when a news item caught his attention. It said that Shackleton intended to explore those islets on his return from his voyage to the South Pole. Mere scientific curiosity? A base for long-range seaplanes? Geographical sentinels for England, mistress of the seas?

Nothing of the kind! Or rather, something much more and much better. Shackleton was going to the Savage Islands to find a fabulous treasure which a French privateer, wrecked there in the 18th century, had hidden in an unknown spot. The owner of the Savage Islands immediately telegraphed the explorer in London, forbidding him to make any searches on the islets.
And he thought no more about the matter. Months went by. The telegram received no reply. It was, naturally, thought the owner of the Savage Islands, a journalistic fantasy of no great consequence.
But he was mistaken. One day the famous Shackleton arrived in Funchal aboard his ship, fitted out and equipped for the expedition he was about to make to the South Pole.

The owner of the Savage Islands was astounded when the explorer, in that dry, direct language so characteristic of the English, asked his permission to search the islets for the treasure, which would be divided between the two of them. He agreed. On his return from the South Pole, Shackleton told him, he would go to England to fetch drilling machines, since he believed the treasure was buried beneath some rock, rockfalls being frequent there. When our compatriot expressed considerable surprise at the existence of the treasure, all the more so as he had never heard of it, Shackleton informed him that there was a document in the archives of the British Admiralty that proved it: the account of a sailor who had survived the wreck of the French privateer.

Twenty-four hours later Shackleton left for the South Pole, where he died. And with him died the idea of finding the treasure of the Savage Islands, which remains there still, hidden, mysterious and fabulous, guarded by the inscrutable rocks.’
Nettle tree (Celtis australis)

A tree of the family Urticaceae, grown in some *quintas* (country estates), squares and gardens of Funchal. It is native to Europe and has ovate-lanceolate, rough, serrated leaves and small drupes, which boys eat when they ripen, that is, in September.
Potato (semilha)

This name, given in Madeira to *Solanum tuberosum*, a plant of the family Solanaceae, derives from the Spanish word *semilla*. The word seems to have been written on a label that accompanied the first tubers brought to this island, imported from the Canary Islands, and was taken here for the name of the plant. The potato (Madeiran *semilha*) began to be cultivated in Madeira in 1760. It is propagated from cut pieces of its tubers, each piece having to contain a few eyes. The crop is harvested three or four months after the tubers have been planted.
Madeira produces some 25 million kilograms of potatoes (*semilhas*, the Madeiran word) a year, and the average yield per hectare may be reckoned at 10,000 kilograms (1921).
The potato is also grown on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it was introduced only a little after 1820.

This plant is native to the Andes, in South America, and was brought to Europe by the Spaniards shortly after the conquest of Peru. Combined with any other substance richer than itself in nitrogenous principles, it makes an excellent food for humans, and it can also be used, raw or cooked, as animal feed.
Seminary

The Council of Trent, held in the city from which it took its name, ordered that every diocese should create an establishment for religious instruction and education, intended for the ecclesiastical training of those who wished to become priests, and especially of those who would devote themselves to parish life. In fulfilment of that decree, King Sebastian created the Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*) by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 20 September 1566. The foundation took effect only later, in a year we cannot state precisely, but which fell within the period from 1573 to 1586. The establishment of this house of education is owed to the efforts of Bishop Dom Jerónimo Barreto, and he is rightly regarded as the founder of the Funchal Seminary.

It was first housed in a building on Rua Direita (‘straight street’), next to the dwelling of the prelate, who then had his residence there. At the end of the 16th century Bishop Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos built the old bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*), a considerable part of which still survives, together with the adjoining chapel, now deconsecrated. The Seminary moved to a building next to this palace and to its outbuildings at the end of that century or the beginning of the next.

The construction of the new residence of the prelates, the one that can still be seen today in the former Rua do Bispo, led to the Seminary's move to the house on Rua do Mosteiro Novo (‘the New Convent’). This had been intended for a convent of nuns (volume III, page 398), but was never put to the use for which it had been built. The earthquake of 1748 left this building so badly damaged that it had to be abandoned, and the establishment moved into another house or houses, whose location we do not know, remaining there until the year 1788.

It was Bishop Dom José da Costa Torres who obtained from the government in mainland Portugal the transfer of the former Jesuit College (*Colégio dos Jesuítas*) for use as a seminary. This was granted by royal letter of Maria I dated 10 August 1787, and the solemn opening in the new building took place on 31 March 1788. The Seminary did not stay there long, because the occupation of Madeira by British troops in 1801 forced it to move again, back to the old house on Rua do Mosteiro Novo, once this had been suitably repaired.

When the governor and captain-general Dom José Manuel da Câmara failed to have the College (*Colégio*) building vacated, a serious conflict arose between him and the diocesan bishop, as already mentioned on pages 216 and 266 of this volume.

In the article devoted to the late and illustrious Bishop Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto (volume I, page 130), we have already referred to the building raised within the convent grounds of the former Convento da Encarnação (Convent of the Incarnation) for the Diocesan Seminary. There the great prelate, spending his entire fortune, both inherited and acquired, endowed the diocese with a large and splendid building, which is one of the finest claims to glory of his episcopal administration. The Seminary began to operate in its new building in October 1909, but the law of 20 April 1911 suppressed the Seminary of this diocese, and the great building passed immediately into the possession of the State.

This institution of ecclesiastical instruction and education returned to its old house in Rua do Mosteiro Novo, where it operates at present. Before that it had spent some time in an annexe of our bishop’s palace, in Rua da Carreira (‘track’), and on a *quinta* (country estate) in the locality (*sítio*) of Trapiche, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (1921).

The royal letter of Sebastian of 20 September 1566, already cited, established the Seminary with twelve students and a rector, and gave it an endowment of 300,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) for its upkeep, plus 45,000 *réis* for the salary of the master of grammar and plainchant. It is presumed that the students attended the humanities classes that the Jesuits maintained in this city until 1759. From that year until the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city opened in 1837, where the seminarians began to attend the relevant classes, we do not know whether the Seminary’s pupils had their own courses within the Seminary building itself.

With the arrival in this bishopric of the eminent prelate Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto, the Seminary underwent a profound and radical transformation (volume I, page 130). In 1877 a complete preparatory course was created there, a larger number of pupils was admitted and the internal discipline was entirely reformed, so that the Seminary was placed on a par with the best-organised institutions of its kind.

From every point of view, the late Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto is the true reformer and restorer of the Funchal Seminary, and this institution ought to be given the name of that illustrious and benevolent prelate.

It would be a flagrant injustice not to say that, to the good reputation the Seminary enjoyed in moral, religious and scientific terms in the last years of its existence, no one contributed more than Father Ernst Schmitz, who was its teacher and director for thirty years. Among other important improvements, he was responsible for creating a natural history museum of regional character (volume II, page 414), which alone suffices to make his distinguished name undying here in Madeira, as we have already emphasised in the cited article devoted to Bishop Dom Manuel Agostinho Barreto. The decree of 25 April 1927 declared unlawful the transfer of the Incarnação building to the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), but only six years later, after a stubborn struggle, was the Diocesan Seminary installed there once more, beginning its work in October 1933.
Knotgrass (Polygonum aviculare)

A plant of the family Polygonaceae, with leaves that are generally lanceolate, sometimes wavy and crinkled, and small pink or white flowers arranged in clusters. It is common along paths and on uncultivated ground. An infusion of this plant is diuretic and is used in the treatment of rheumatism.
Sena Freitas (Canon José Joaquim)

This well-known writer and orator was born on the island of São Miguel in 1840 and died in the city of Rio de Janeiro on 22 December 1913. He visited Funchal many times and gave several speeches here, some of which are included in his work *Palavra do Semeador*. In the pamphlet *«As Novidades» no pelourinho* he deals with various matters concerning Madeira. Canon Sena Freitas wrote some fine descriptive articles about Funchal.

His mortal remains, brought from Brazil, lay for some days in the old chapel of St Elizabeth of Portugal (*Santa Isabel*) of the Funchal Misericórdia Hospital (*Hospital da Misericórdia do Funchal*), where solemn funeral rites were celebrated. On 2 March 1925 they were taken to the island of São Miguel, where they were buried.
Lord of Miracles
See Cristo (chapel) (volume I, page 332).
Sequeira

This family surname derives from Lopo Vaz de Sequeira, who held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) land at the Lombada da Ribeira Brava (‘ridge of Ribeira Brava’) and was married to Leonor Gonçalves do Pó.
Sequeira (Dr Maurício Augusto de)

He was born in Funchal on 17 July 1845 and died in the same city on 31 October 1911. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in philosophy and medicine from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and practised medicine in Funchal. Here he also taught at the now defunct Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica*) and held the chair of physics, chemistry and natural history at our lyceum (state secondary school). He wrote a physics textbook for use in secondary schools, which was never published. We believe this was because he lost his sight some years before his death and from then on abandoned the scientific studies to which he had devoted himself. See Mouraria (‘Moorish quarter’).
Sericulture

There were some attempts in former times to rear silkworms in Madeira, and in 1571 Dr Gaspar de Teive went so far as to make a contract with a silk manufacturer for the production of silk on the island. The Jesuits gave a certain impetus to sericulture, but we do not know whether any silk fabric was ever actually made in Madeira.

In 1877 the late Count of Canavial set up several installations at the Praça da Rainha (‘Queen’s Square’) for rearing silkworms, and planted large numbers of white mulberry trees there, though none of this work produced any results. Almost all the mulberry plantations were destroyed by the great gales at the beginning of 1881.

On this subject, the excellent article published in the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) of 13 October 1921 is of particular interest and may be of some real use, and we wish to preserve it in the columns of this *Elucidário*.

Among these initiatives, born of his soul and devised by his intelligence (the Count of Canavial), was the introduction to Madeira of sericulture or, perhaps more precisely, ‘sericiculture’: the combination of operations and processes involved in producing silk, and so covering both the rearing of the insects that produce it and the art of manufacturing silk. Popular leaflets distributed throughout the island then instructed the Madeiran people in how silk was made. These instructions, set out with great clarity and detail, ranged from the method of rearing the silkworm to a thorough description of all its metamorphoses and of how it should be treated at each stage of its life. The help of the civil and ecclesiastical authorities was sought, and the municipal councils were asked to cooperate in planting large numbers of the trees on which the insect feeds. Some trials were even made, but the fact is that, whether for lack of resources or for lack of perseverance, the initiative never became a reality.

And yet we remain convinced that the idea of developing a silk industry in Madeira is neither childish nor reckless, and still less a dream incapable of becoming fact in the realm of practical realities.

Indeed, the silk industry is thriving today in many countries that are far from possessing the natural conditions that distinguish Madeira. For that reason they make up for the lack of such conditions by using methods that make silk production costly, and smaller than what we could obtain on this island.

In the countries where the silk industry flourishes most, there is generally only one harvest a year, because the trees on which the insects feed grow poorly there. Moreover, the insects have to be reared in the heat of hothouses and stoves, so that they can withstand the almost always fatal consequences of great variations in the weather.

Madeira, however, thanks to the exceptional mildness of its climate, finds itself in far more favourable circumstances for the industry than those countries. Since mulberry trees grow more quickly here, two harvests a year could easily be obtained; and as for the insects, they could be reared naturally, without the use of artificial and always costly means to support their living conditions.

Furthermore, growing the particular trees that would need to be encouraged would not take the place of the other crops that we also need for our food and for the wealth of our economic balance. For this purpose, the spots where no other crop was possible, or where no other crop offered greater advantage, would be put to use with intelligence and care.

For these reasons we believe, even at this moment, that the idea we have outlined here well deserves analysis, study and consideration. In putting it forward we recall the figure of the Count of Canavial and some of the fruits of his investigative mind and patriotic soul.

And since, on this subject, we find ourselves today in the same situation as almost 50 years ago, when the idea was raised on this island, let us say, as the Count of Canavial did in 1874: ‘What, then, is to be done? To draw forcefully the attention of those who are in a position to exploit this new branch of industry; to instruct them in the practical means of achieving it, and moreover to point out to them, as an encouragement, the examples of other countries where, with fewer natural advantages, the most profitable results have been reaped from this same industry.’
Seringa (O)
The first issue of this newspaper appeared on 3 June 1918 and the twelfth, which we believe to have been the last, on 21 August of the same year.
Serpa Pinto (Alexandre Alberto da Rocha)

This well-known explorer of the Dark Continent was in Funchal around 1875, serving as a captain in the now disbanded 12th Battalion of Caçadores (Portuguese light infantry). He was a close friend of the late Major Daniel Simões Soares, also an officer of the same regiment, with whom he went so far as to plan a journey of exploration to Southern Africa, which never took place.
Serpa Pinto was born on 20 April 1846 and died on 28 December 1900. The account of his adventurous journey across the African continent is given in the book he wrote, entitled *A Carabina d'el-rei*.
Serpent moray (Muraena anatina)

A fish of the moray family, also known as the *moreia serpente* (serpent moray), which is rare off the coasts of the archipelago. Its bite is more dangerous than that of the other species of moray living in our waters, and can lead to serious accidents. It is prized for its delicate flavour.
Serra de Água (parish)

In the article Madeiras (volume II, page 323) we said that, after the great fire started by the first settlers, this island was quickly repopulated with tree species. Although that fire cost it the original, native abundance of its woodland, there can be no doubt that it was soon covered once more with extensive and plentiful forest vegetation. The timber trade and the export of wood were a logical consequence of the abundance of this luxuriant vegetation. Various mills and machines, built above all on the banks of the fastest-flowing streams to harness their motive power, went up in many parts of the island. These mechanical devices, certainly of very rudimentary construction, were given the name of water-powered sawmills (*serras de água*). Many places in Madeira still bear that name today, and in the parishes (*freguesias*) of Boaventura, Faial, Machico, Santana and Seixal there are inhabited localities (*sítios*) of some importance with the same name.

The parish of Serra de Água, which lies in the interior of the island, must have been, as can still be seen today, a centre of vast and rich woodland. Since it is crossed by a fast-flowing stream, it would have been relatively easy to set up a water-powered sawmill there, and the nearby landing place of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) invited the shipment of the timber. There was a locality of that name, which spread to the surrounding area and later to the parish. When the parish was created, that village (*lugar*, settlement rank below a town) was already known by the name of Serra de Água.

Much of this parish lies in a long, deep and narrow valley, encircled by towering, sheer mountains. It is surrounded by Pico da Cruz, Pico do Cedro, Pico Grande and other peaks, all of gigantic stature and of a wild and imposing magnificence.

The parish of Serra de Água was created by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 28 December 1676, and the diocesan prelate, Dom Friar António da Silva Teles, formally established it by an episcopal warrant (*provisão*) of 2 February 1678.

The seat of the new parish (*freguesia*) was set up in the small chapel of Our Lady of Help (*Nossa Senhora da Ajuda*), which already stood there; we do not know the year it was built or who founded it. It was considerably enlarged around 1699, after an order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) of 2 May 1698 directed that the works already begun be completed.

The royal decree of 5 March 1680 set the annual salary of the parish priest of the time, Father Manuel da Silva, at 12,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine and one *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat. This stipend (*côngrua*) was confirmed, without any increase, by the royal decree of 5 October 1749.

Serra de Água belonged to the municipality (*concelho*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) from the latter’s creation in 1835, and today forms part of the municipality of Ribeira Brava, which was created in 1914 and installed on 2 August of the same year. The principal localities are: Achada dos Aparícios, Boqueirão, Caminho do Matias, Eira da Moura, Fajã Redonda, Fajã dos Vinháticos, Lage, Passal, Pedra, Penedo, Pereira, Pinheiro, Poiso, Rocha Alta, Terra Grande and Travessa.
Its population is 1580 inhabitants (1921).
Serra e Moura (Tomás Nunes de)

He was appointed civil governor of Madeira by decree of 29 December 1883 and took office on 9 January 1884. As a sitting peer of the realm, he represented this archipelago in parliament during the legislative session of 1887 to 1889.
He died in Lisbon on 26 March 1917, a retired judge of the Supreme Court of Justice.
Water-powered sawmills

In the article on the parish (*freguesia*) of Serra de Água (‘water sawmill’) and in the article Timber (II-373) we have already dealt with the ‘machines’ or ‘mills’ built on the banks of the most abundant streams and used for sawing timber, especially timber destined for export to mainland Portugal and abroad. Interesting information on this subject, particularly on the legislation that regulated it, is given in a pamphlet, *Serras de Agua*, by the distinguished Madeiran Dr Jordão Apolinário de Freitas.
Agricultural Services

Madeira’s agricultural services were reorganised by Decree no. 8089 of 30 April 1922, which divided them, within the agricultural station of the 9th Region, into three groups: the group of physico-chemical and technological services; the group of cultivation and biological-agricultural services; and the group of services for the regime governing sugar, alcohol and spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine). The head of the agricultural station, who also directs one of the service groups, is an agronomist engineer, and the directors of the other two service groups are likewise agronomist engineers.

In addition to the three agronomist engineers, the station is to have two agricultural supervisors, an analyst and a laboratory assistant, so it will not be for want of technical staff that Madeiran agriculture fails to prosper. The agricultural station has autonomous administration under the decrees with force of law of 16 May 1911 and 14 December 1912.

The decree of 3 April 1922 retained, and placed under the agricultural station of the 9th Region, the following four experimental stations created by the former Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*): the stations of Louros (‘laurels’) and Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), in the low zone of the island; the Santo da Serra (‘the saint of the uplands’) station, in the middle zone; and the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’) station, in the high zone.
The agricultural station of the 9th Region is subordinate to the Directorate-General of Agricultural Services (*Serviços Agrícolas*). See Agricultural Region and Agricultural Syndicate of Madeira.
Forestry Services

Since 1897 these services have been in the charge of a department headed by a forestry officer (*regente florestal*). To date, it has confined itself to planting some exotic trees on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and promoting the sowing of maritime pine in the mountainous region of Madeira. Nothing has so far been done to conserve and propagate the native trees, and many of them may soon disappear because of the constant devastation wrought on them by woodcutters, charcoal burners and livestock (1921).

By the decree of 3 April 1922, the Forest Police (*Polícia Florestal*) services that had belonged to the former Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) were provisionally placed in the charge of the agricultural station of the 9th Region. Law no. 26 of 9 July 1913 created four forestry sections, which were divided into zones, that of Funchal being no. 25 and included in the fourth section, based in Lisbon. The decree of 8 May 1918 established eight forestry districts, with Funchal included in the sixth district, based in Lisbon, and eighteen forestry offices, that of Funchal being no. 18. See Afforestation, Livestock, Timber and Forest Police.
Sesmarias

In this archipelago the *sesmaria* laws preceded the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant) (volume I, page 290); or perhaps it would be more accurate and apt to say that the *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), evolving and adapting itself to local conditions, turned into the *colonia* contract. The account that Gama Barros gives in his monumental *Historia da Administração Publica em Portugal* of the *sesmaria* laws created in the reign of King Fernando shows that these laws were chiefly intended to make productive the lands that their owners kept abandoned, although the owners did not lose their right of ownership. In Madeira, it is known that the donataries, as the letters of grant from Prince Henry the Navigator allowed them, granted land in *sesmaria*, a practice carried out on a large scale throughout the island, in addition to the grants made directly by the monarchs. It is not known, however, whether the lands were granted free of any rent, pension or quit-rent (*foro*), and therefore with the *sesmeiro* (holder of a land grant, or *sesmaria*) holding absolute dominion over the land, or whether the land was subject to the payment of some contributions in favour of the Crown, the donataries or the Order of Christ. If such a levy ever existed, we have no knowledge of it today, and it could only have occurred in the earliest days of colonisation. From the time of the first entails (*instituições vinculares*), which date from the end of the 15th century, the *sesmeiro* was regarded as the absolute lord of his landholdings, disposing of them freely in creating countless entailed estates and in selling the lands and granting them on emphyteutic lease (*aforamento*, perpetual lease for an annual quit-rent).

Gaspar Frutuoso says ‘that when João Gonçalves arrived in Funchal, he began to lay out the town and to give out land in *sesmaria*, as he was instructed by the regulations (*regimento*) of Prince Henry . . ., and, in accordance with the said regulations, he gave for five years the lands that were not tilled, within which time the grantees were bound to make use of them and till them, on pain of having them taken away, should they fail to do so within this period, and given to whoever would make use of them’. No mention is made here of any charge weighing on the lands granted in *sesmaria*. Beyond what has been said, all that is known is that if the lands, after being brought into use, were abandoned by their cultivators, they could pass into the possession of third parties, when that abandonment lasted for more than five years.

As has already been said elsewhere, it was to Portuguese and foreign nobles, and to some prominent foreign merchants, that the donataries granted the land, and they found in the African slave their chief helper in clearing the ground. Many of these grantees (*sesmeiros*) grew rich and turned their lands into entailed estates. Contracting out the cultivation of those lands to free tenants in return for the half-share (*dimídia*, half of the harvest owed to the landlord), they gradually left the tilling and cultivation of the properties to them, and went off to enjoy the income of their fields and estates in the city or at court. Little by little the tenants freed themselves from the landowners’ tutelage. They farmed the *sesmaria* lands on their own account and burdened them with houses, walls and other improvements (*benfeitorias*, buildings and walls made by the tenant, which remained his property), to which ownership of the trees and plants themselves was later added. In this way they created a special situation that gave them almost the standing of co-owners of the land they tilled, while the former grantees, the true owners of the land, came to depend on them to a large extent. Here lies the true origin of the *colonia* contract (Madeiran sharecropping tenancy; produce divided, improvements owned by the tenant), which, as we said above, is simply a transformation of the old *sesmarias*. See Colonia, Old customs and Entails.
Sfenzel (Johs.)
Works: *Kreuz und Quer auf Madeira und den Canarischen Inseln*; Berlin, 1906.
Shackleton (Ernest)

This well-known English explorer was in Madeira from 16 to 19 October 1921, on his way to the Antarctic regions aboard the *Quest*. He died at the age of 47 on 5 January 1922, while his ship was off the island of South Georgia.
Silva (family)

This is a noble family surname. Gonçalo Denis da Silva founded the chapel of the Almas Pobres (Poor Souls in Purgatory) in Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), shortly after the foundation of the chantry (*capela*) of São Paulo (St Paul the Apostle). Jordão de Freitas da Silva, who lived in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) in 1618, was the grandson of Jordão de Freitas, of the household of the Infante Diogo, Duke of Viseu.
Silva (Clemente de Freitas da)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) on 25 November 1859 and died in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on 16 March 1917. He was secretary of the municipal councils of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) and Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), and secretary of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Ponta do Sol. He distinguished himself greatly as a solicitor (*solicitador*) and licensed advocate (*advogado provisionista*, practising by licence without a law degree), leaving valuable legal works that many distinguished jurists would not have disdained to sign. He contributed extensively to many newspapers and was the founder and editor of the *Brado d'Oeste* (‘Cry from the West’), which was published for many years in the town of Ponta do Sol.
Silva (Dona Mariana Xavier da)

This lady, a native of mainland Portugal, lived on this island for many years. In 1884 she published in Lisbon a book of pieces in prose and verse entitled *Na Madeira–Offerendas*, which contains various tales and narratives, some of them concerning this island, that make very interesting and pleasant reading. Judging by the dates of some of the articles and poems in this volume, Dona Mariana Xavier da Silva lived on this island during the years from 1872 to 1881.
Silva (Dr Américo Ciríaco Correia da)

He was appointed Civil Governor of the District by decree of 25 May 1918 and took up the post on 7 June. He is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and was born in Funchal on 16 March 1893.
Silva (Dr Cândido Joaquim da)

He was born in Funchal in 1806 and took his doctorate in medicine at the Montpellier faculty in 1830. Works: *Considérations générales sur la syphilis* (thesis). He died of a cerebral apoplexy on 8 February 1879. Here in Madeira he was known as Dr Silvado.
Silva (João Moniz da)

On the death of Dom Estêvão Brioso de Figueiredo, prelate of this diocese, the cleric João Moniz da Silva was presented as bishop of Funchal in 1689. He did not accept the mitre and was never confirmed, so his name is not included in the catalogue of the prelates of Funchal. Friar José de Santa Maria was appointed bishop in his place.
Silva (Manuel Lobo da)
He was appointed captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira on 21 October 1647 and took up the post in May of the following year.
Silva (Matias Figueira da)

He was born in Funchal in 1843, the son of José Figueira da Silva, and attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city. He then went to Coimbra, where he enrolled in the faculties of mathematics and philosophy of the University. Having fallen ill after a few months, he returned to Funchal, going back to Coimbra only the following year, not to continue the studies he had begun but to enrol in the Faculty of Law. He did not complete that course either, because his lung complaints worsened in that city. As his native air did not restore his health, he travelled to the United States, where he had an uncle of some means. He got on so well in that country that he decided to stay there, and some time later he enrolled in a school of medicine, completing the course with the highest distinction. For many years he practised his profession in the city of Brooklyn, where he was highly regarded for his learning and tact as a physician. He still lives there, although he gave up practice some years ago. He published various articles in American medical journals, especially in New York, and while he lived in Madeira he contributed to some local newspapers. He was also one of the authors of ‘The Guiana Epic’ (see that entry), a mock-heroic poem that was never printed, but of which copies are held by various people in Funchal.
Silva (Nicolau Francisco Xavier da)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’) in this city in the last years of the 17th century, the son of José da Silva Pimenta and Josefa Maria Teixeira, and died in Lisbon on 17 August 1754. He took his doctorate in the faculty of canon law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) in 1725 and taught there on an interim basis for some years. He settled in Lisbon, where he devoted himself with distinction to legal practice and to letters. He left several unpublished works and published the *Puro e affectuoso sacrificio* (Lisbon, 1724) and the *Oração de agradecimento à Academia Real*, printed in the *Colecção* of that Academy. He was a full member of the Royal Academy of History (*Academia Real de Historia*), which commissioned him to write the history of the inquiries (*inquirições*); he never completed it and it remained unpublished. He was considered one of the most learned men of his time. He assembled a choice library, which was bought by the monarch and formed the nucleus of the Ajuda Library (*Biblioteca da Ajuda*).
Silva (Father Júlio César Pereira da)

He was born on this island in 1845 and died in Lisbon on 19 April 1912. He was an army chaplain and honorary canon of Viseu Cathedral (Sé de Viseu), and had taught at the seminary and at the lyceum (state secondary school) of Beja. He contributed to various newspapers and published some of his addresses in several pamphlets.
Silva (Pedro da)

This governor-general of Madeira was known by the nickname of Mole (‘soft’). He was appointed on 30 May 1618 and took office on 6 July of the same year. He was later governor of India, and died there on 24 June 1639.
Silva Pinheiro (Canon Jerónimo Álvares da)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’) in 1770 and died in this city on 4 July 1861. He was ordained priest in 1795 and became a canon of our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*), holding high ecclesiastical offices such as those of vicar capitular (administrator of the vacant diocese elected by the chapter) and governor of this bishopric. He was a distinguished and vigorous journalist and, under the pseudonym Estrela do Norte, wrote many articles in *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’), the first newspaper published here in Madeira. He was imprisoned for supporting liberal ideas, but managed to escape from prison and leave for Brazil, where he remained until 1834. He always enjoyed great prestige and influence on this island.
Silva (Silvano Sátiro de)

He was born in Funchal on 12 January 1808 and attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of Funchal, later enrolling in the faculty of law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). He has contributed to various newspapers and wrote a pamphlet entitled *Rosario de Lágrimas* (1918).
Silva (Vasco Crispiniano da)

He is an infantry major and was born in Funchal on 3 May 1880. He was appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 29 April 1920 and was relieved of the post at his own request by decree of 1 October of the same year. He represented this archipelago in parliament as a senator, having been elected on 29 January 1922. He holds numerous Portuguese and foreign decorations.
Silva (Vicente Gomes da)

He was born in Funchal on 12 March 1827 and was one of the greatest artists Madeira has produced. Guided only by his talent and by some private study, he became a highly distinguished photographer, as well as a draughtsman, sculptor, engraver and founder worthy of the highest esteem. It was he who introduced photography and stereotyping to Madeira, and he was the first to make rubber stamps and to cast iron on this island, producing true marvels in all these fields. He worked with the daguerreotype and with wet collodion, leaving work more accomplished than that produced in the capital at the same time. The foundry he set up beside his house in the old Rua dos Pintos was a genuine success for Madeira, and the pieces that came out of it satisfied the most demanding customers through the artistry with which they were made. Vicente Gomes da Silva died in Funchal on 14 December 1906.

The now defunct *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’), in its issue of 13 December 1931, published an excellent article containing some biographical sketches of this distinguished artist, which deserve to be read and ought to be recorded here. We shall reproduce it in part in our columns:
‘Vicente Gomes da Silva was a striking figure of great prominence in our narrow artistic circles.

From an early age he showed enthusiasm for learning; and while still a schoolboy, on account of his fine handwriting, he was chosen by Luís Correia Aciaioli as an assistant at his well-regarded school at Socorro (‘succour’), where the Madeiran liberal class was educated, producing leading figures in the various branches of human knowledge.
He learnt French and English, which he handled with elegance and correctness, drawing from books, all of them foreign, the wealth of knowledge that so enlightened him.

With an instinctive skill, he captured on canvas admirable oil portraits of the most prominent figures of our society, painted watercolours of the landscapes of our land in vivid light, and painted marvellous miniature portraits on ivory plaques. Before long, foreigners were snapping up his works, on which he set little value, for, like most true artists, he did not appreciate the real worth of his fine work.
He went on to model with a simple burin, carving precisely in wood the characteristic types of the period, regional figures, with a realism and accuracy that caused astonishment.

When the partnership of Niépce and Daguerre presented its astonishing work in France, Vicente Gomes da Silva at once sent to Paris for books on the new science. Through great tenacity and study he succeeded in taking photographs on silvered copper plates – daguerreotypes – and then went on to making positives on glass. The public of Madeira thus had photographs some years before they were being made in Portugal.

Keeping step with the progress of the art, portraits in Madeira soon appeared on albumen paper, mounted on card. Vicente Gomes da Silva knew all the intricate chemistry of photography, preparing the collodion, the silver nitrate and the various darkroom reagents himself, without resorting to imported products.

The learned amateur photographer the Count of Torre Bela, frustrated by the demands on time and patience imposed by ‘wet collodion’, joined forces with his friend Vicente Gomes da Silva. After long nights of work they arrived at a more practical process – ‘dry collodion’ – which later came into general use and brought such progress to photography.
At the same time as working in photography, he engraved on copper plate, with rare perfection, coats of arms for wedding announcements, visiting cards, etc., besides other emblems.
Many years later Prince Nicholas of Oldenburg, struck by the fine finish of this artist’s engravings, had a great deal of silverware sent from Russia so that he could work it here.
Invited by the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) to go abroad to perfect his skills, he declined the honourable invitation, preferring to owe everything to himself.

In 1863 he travelled to France and England, acquainting himself with all the innovations of the day. On his return he opened an elegant and luxurious bazaar in the Largo da Sé (‘cathedral square’), where his most carefully finished photographic and engraving work was displayed alongside the latest novelties.

His photographic studio in the Rua dos Pintos – later incorporated into the Rua da Carreira (‘racecourse street’) – enjoyed great and well-deserved fame. It was surmounted by the imperial arms of Austria and stood under the patronage of the Dowager Empress of Brazil, Empress Amélie, who made him engraver to her household. Here the distinguished artist made rubber stamps for the first time in Portugal, and introduced stereotyping into Madeiran printing. He was never taught these two new graphic processes by any master, but simply gathered from foreign books and journals the instructions which he then tested and corrected’.
Brambles

Species of the genus *Rubus*, the commonest of which is *R. Ulmifolius*, Schott. The fruits of this *Rubus*, known as *amoras de silva* (blackberries), are edible and have a pleasant taste, but in large quantities they can cause colic. A decoction of the tender shoots and leaves of the bramble is used in gargles for diseases of the throat.
Silveira (António da)

He was captain of Diu and the 5th donatary of the captaincy of Machico, having succeeded Diogo Teixeira, who died without issue. In 1549 he sold the captaincy to Dom Afonso de Portugal, Count of Vimioso.
Silveira (António Roque da)
See Rabies (volume III, page 173).
Silveira (José Marciano da)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha in 1826 and died in Funchal on 8 July 1887. He worked as a primary schoolteacher in Machico, and at his death was a copying clerk in the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government's local civil office) of Funchal. For many years he edited the *Voz do Povo*, in which invective and diatribe were at times the main arguments of his polemics and press campaigns. He handled the scurrilous verse of the *gazetilha* (satirical verse column in a newspaper) with great ease, using it to wound and deride his opponents and adversaries. He did not spare even his own son-in-law, the journalist João Augusto de Ornelas, whom Silveira sought to wound and humiliate in *Filho do Ferreiro*, a pamphlet that has gone through several editions, intended especially for the Madeiran colonies in Demerara, Trinidad, etc. His journalistic output is vast, but his writings are generally modelled on the *Tripa Virada* and the *Besta Esfolada* of José Agostinho de Macedo. Some of his poems appear in ‘Flowers of Madeira’ (*Flores da Madeira*).
Simões Soares (Daniel Telo)

He is the son of the late lyceum (state secondary school) teacher Daniel Simões Soares and was born on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) on 23 May 1864. In 1875 he enrolled at the Military College (*Colégio Militar*), moving from there to the Funchal lyceum, where he completed his preparatory studies for the Army School (*Escola do Exército*). Posted overseas as a second lieutenant in 1885, he served in the province of Cape Verde, where, among other assignments, he held the Military Command (*Comando Militar*) on the island of Santo Antão. He was in Guinea in 1891, where he took part in the military operations against the Papel people. After retiring with the rank of general, he was president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Santa Catarina, on the island of Santiago, municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative), etc. He has lived in Funchal for some years, where he held the post of civil governor three times, taking office on 28 September 1917, 21 June 1919 and 17 November 1923. He was also municipal administrator of Funchal, police commissioner, a member of the now defunct Agricultural Council (*Junta Agrícola*) and senator for Madeira, having been elected on 13 June 1915. He is a member of the present District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) of Funchal and has already been president of this administrative body (1921).
Simon (E.)
Works: *Arachnides recueillis à l'ile Madère par M. A. Fauvel en 1896* (Bullet. Soc. Entomol. France, 1897).
Simon (Eug.)
Works: *Une asphodèle nouvelle: Asphodelus madeirensis, Simon* (Bull. Soc. Bot. des Deux-Sèvres, 1908–1909).
Madeira Agricultural Union

A newspaper of this city reported on 7 May 1922 that the Madeira Agricultural Union (*Sindicato Agrícola da Madeira*), having been duly approved, had just been installed, and it gave the list of the citizens elected to the syndicate’s general assembly, board of directors and supervisory board. The same newspaper added that the Syndicate had benefactor, founding, full and subscribing members. The first class comprised those who gave a sum of more than 100.00 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) or performed acts of recognised worth and usefulness; the second, those who paid the entrance fee of 10.00 escudos and the monthly subscription of 50 centavos; the third, those who paid the entrance fee of 5.00 escudos and were also liable for the subscription of 50 centavos; and the last, those who paid the annual subscription of 2.40 escudos in monthly instalments.

After the report we have mentioned, the Madeira Agricultural Union gave no further sign of life, although it has been represented on the administrative council of the station of the 9th Agricultural Region, in accordance with article 31 of the decree of 3 April 1922 (1922).
Estreito Agricultural Union

It was founded in 1918 in Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), and its statutes were published in the *Diário do Governo* (‘Government Gazette’) of 20 December of the same year. On 2 March 1919 it elected its governing bodies. Its purpose is to look after the agricultural interests of its members and to purchase fertilisers, seeds, machinery, insecticides, etc. (1921).
Syndic of the Senate

He had to be a law graduate, and his duty was to defend the interests of the Council in the courts. In the late 18th and early 19th centuries he often stood in for the clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*) when the latter was unavailable, drawing up and signing the minutes of the council sessions.
System of weights and measures

The system of weights and measures used in this archipelago was undoubtedly the same as that of mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), until the year in which the metric decimal system began to be adopted here. The *almude* (old liquid measure, about 17.5 litres), the canada (liquid measure, c. 1.4 litres), the *galão* (Portuguese gallon, about 3.16 litres), the *alqueire* (dry measure for grain; as a land measure c. 900 m²), the *arrátel* (old pound, about 459 g), the côvado (cubit, c. 66 cm), the *vara* (linear measure, c. 1.10 m), the *braça* (fathom, about 2.2 m), the foot and the *palmo* (span, about 22 cm), with their multiples and submultiples, were the types of weights and measures in use among us. They varied somewhat from parish (*freguesia*) to parish, as no doubt also happened on the mainland, from where they were brought to this island. For both weights and measures, the seats of the municipalities held standards that strictly governed the use of those types, though it is not known whether there was perfect uniformity between the standards of the various municipalities. A list of all these standards was drawn up in 1849 by a commission made up of Drs Manuel Joaquim Moniz, Luís da Costa Pereira and João Perestrelo de Vasconcelos, and published in no. 195 of the *Semanario Official*; however, it does not show the differences between the various standards, as would have been desirable. The list shows that these standards were very numerous, and some of them are of real interest for their careful workmanship and as documents for an archaeological study of the subject. In 1859 the central government sent the artillery officer Francisco de Paula Campos e Oliveira to Madeira, with the cavalry officer Fernando Seixas de Brito Bettencourt as his assistant, charged with introducing the new legal system of weights and measures into this archipelago. Campos e Oliveira travelled through every municipality and made a detailed study of the subject. On 28 August 1859 he sent an interesting and lengthy report to the Directorate-General of Commerce and Industry, which was published in nos 60 and 61 of the Funchal newspaper *A Reforma*, and from which we shall give some extracts.

‘The weights,’ says the said officer, ‘are some of iron, others of bronze. Some have the shape of a sphere set within circular hoops, also of iron, which cross at right angles and have a ring of the same metal where they meet; others have the shape of truncated cones or of quadrangular pyramids; and others, finally, are cylindrical, with or without a ring.

Among the bronze weights, the standard weights (*marcos*) of Funchal, Machico, Ponta do Sol and Calheta stand out, above all that of Funchal. This weight is of four *arrobas* and has the shape of a truncated cone. It is exquisitely worked and decorated with magnificent reliefs and openwork. The lid is adorned with three dragons or fabulous beasts in high relief, and beside them are two busts of knights in ancient armour. These busts support a handle whose ends pass through their backs and turn about them. The handle represents two men standing back to back, their hands raised above their heads, both holding up a small sphere in which the handle ends. On the lid is the following inscription: Conrad Mos Eych Master 1580.

The Machico weight bears this inscription on its outer surface: ‘The most high and most excellent King Dom Manuel, the First of Portugal, ordered me to be made in the year of the birth of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1499.’

‘The weights of Ponta do Sol and Calheta both bear inscriptions similar to that of Machico. Those of Calheta and Ponta do Sol, because they are better preserved, because they could easily be made complete, and because of the way they are made, deserve to be kept as monuments of our old standards of weights and measures. Far more worthy of archaeological consideration, however, is the four-*arroba* weight of Funchal; for besides being complete, I consider it an exquisite work of art of its kind.

‘In the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of Funchal I found a cubic box containing standards of linear measure, capacity and weight, all in brass, corresponding to the nine decimal measures but with a different nomenclature. All these standards bear the inscription: Arsenal do Exército, 1819., and the metre, the kilogram and the litre, which were called *vara*, *libra* (Portuguese pound, c. 459 g) and *canada* respectively, carry a further inscription which reads: King John VI established the uniformity of weights and measures throughout the United Kingdom by the decimal system, 1818: Arsenal do Exército 1819’

‘Because of old and widespread customs, the adoption of the new legal system of weights and measures met with stubborn resistance everywhere. In this archipelago, too, there were several riots in violent opposition to the system, which profoundly altered what had been practised for centuries in all kinds of commercial transactions. In the municipality (*concelho*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’) the rioters forced the authorities and the most prominent people to throw the weights and measures of the new system into the sea, and the same happened in the parish of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’); in Ponta do Sol the people set fire to the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*). In Santana (‘St Anne’) the people caused various disturbances, and in the town (*vila*) of São Vicente many documents of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government’s local civil office) were destroyed.

The new system was gradually introduced and became general here, and today its use presents not the slightest difficulty. Even so, it is still common today to speak of *almudes*, *galões*, *canadas* and *quartilhos* when measuring liquids; of *varas* and *côvados* when measuring cloth; of *braças* when measuring stone; of *moios* and *alqueires* when measuring cereals; and of *pés* (feet) when measuring timber.

The decimal metric system, decreed in Portugal on 13 December 1852, was ordered into effect by the decree of 20 June 1859: in Lisbon from 1 January 1860, and in the other towns and islands from 1 March, but only as regards the metre, or linear measure. For the other measures it was to be in force throughout the country in 1862.
