Sloane (Dr Hans)

English physician and naturalist, born in Ireland in 1660 and died in Chelsea in 1753. He was in Madeira from 21 to 23 October 1687, and recorded his impressions of our island in his work entitled *A Voyage to the Islands Madera Barbados, Jamaica, etc.* (London 1707-1725).
Smith (Chetien)
Norwegian botanist, born in October 1785 and died in the Congo on 21 September 1816. See Buch.
Smith (James)
English geologist who visited Madeira around 1840. Works: *On the geology of the island of Madeira* (*Proceedings of the Geol. Soc.*, vol. III, p. 351, 1840-41).
Smith (Ricardo Carlos)

English horticulturist who founded an acclimatisation garden in Funchal in 1757. It included a house with reading rooms stocked with Portuguese and English newspapers, and some French ones, as well as books on farming, chemistry, botany and agriculture. According to the newspapers of the time, the garden contained cotton from India and from New Orleans, groundnuts, cassava, collections of pineapples, orange trees, mango trees and other fruit-bearing species, the coconut palm, the oil palm and the sago palm, pines of various species, etc. *Musa textilis*, the paper mulberry (*Broussonetia*?) and sorghum also grew there; on this last plant Ricardo Smith published a work with the following title: *Instrucções theoricas e praticas sobre a cultura do Holcus saccharatus...* (Funchal, 1858, 62 pp.).
Smuts (General Jan Christaan)

This former Boer general arrived in Madeira aboard the British steamer *Arundel Castle* on 7 June 1921. He was greeted on board by the Civil Governor and the Military Commander, and military honours were rendered to him by an infantry detachment drawn up on Avenida Gonçalves Zarco.
General Smuts, who visited various parts of the city and its surroundings, among them Monte (‘hill’) and Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), left for England the same day.
Smyth (C. Piazzi)
See Piazzi Smyth.
Soares (family)

This family surname derives from Diogo Soares, who was donatary of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and from Manuel Soares, who in 1596 founded the chantry (capela) of Senhora da Boa Morte in the church of São Pedro (St Peter).
Soares (Dona Laura Veridiana de Castro e Almeida)

She is married to Feliciano Soares, a well-known man of letters from mainland Portugal, and was born in Funchal on 7 November 1870, the daughter of Dom Francisco de Castro e Almeida Pimentel de Sequeira e Abreu and Dona Maria Antónia de Bettencourt Pestana de Castro.

Under the pseudonym Dona Maria Francisca Teresa she published a book entitled *Em casa da avó – Na Ilha da Madeira* (Lisbon, 1923), and translated Hall Caine’s *The Eternal City* and *The Apostle* from English as *A Cidade Eterna* and *O Apóstolo*.
From her earliest years she showed a decided vocation for study, and she is one of the Madeiran women who have most distinguished themselves in the cultivation of letters.
Soares (Feliciano)

He was born in Aveiro on 14 October 1886 and is a junior customs officer (*aspirante da alfândega*) at the Funchal customs house. In this city he founded the Institute of Secondary and Commercial Education (*Instituto de Ensino Secundário e Comercial*) and the Antónia Georgina Scholarship Fund (*Bolsa de Estudos Antónia Georgina*), the latter intended to support poor students attending the country’s state schools. Works: *Crucificadas*, Funchal, 1915, 350 pp., and *O que eu vi e pensei*, Funchal, 1923, 267 pp. In collaboration with Emanuel Vitorino Ribeiro he published a pamphlet entitled *Terra! Terra!*, on the discovery of Madeira (1921).
Soares (João de Nóbrega)

He was born in this city on 11 June 1831. After attending the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) for some years, he travelled through Portuguese Africa and North America, returning to his homeland, where he settled, in 1855. He was a primary-school teacher, clerk (*escrivão*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*) and finally an employee of the tobacco inspectorate.

He devoted himself actively to letters and contributed very widely to many periodicals, especially on subjects of an essentially literary character. In poetry, drama, short stories, travel narratives, etc., he gave ample proof of his aptitude for these literary genres. He was director and editor of the *Revista Semanal*, the *Semanario Official* and the *Flor do Oceano*, and contributed to many newspapers, such as *A Pátria* (‘The Homeland’), *A Imprensa* (‘The Press’) and *O Funchalense*. When Canon Alfredo César de Oliveira founded *O Diário de Noticias* in this city in 1876, Nóbrega Soares was invited to be its editor and contributed actively to it for several years.

In separate volumes he published *Introducção à Geographia*, 1859; *Primeiras Noções de Moral*, 1861, with another edition in 1862; *Contos e Viagens*, 1867; *Scenas e Comedias*, 1865; *Scenas e Phantasias*, 1868; *Qual dos dois?*, 1862; *Um quarto com duas camas*, 1862; *Chorographia da Madeira*, 1862, of which two further editions were made; and *Grammatica da Lingua Portugueza*, 1884. He was preparing other literary works for the press that were never published, some of which are mentioned in the *Diccionario Bibliographico* of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva. He died in Funchal on 22 September 1890.
Soares (Father Caetano Alberto)

He was the son of António Soares Felgueiras and Dona Ana de Oliveira, and was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’) on 23 May 1790. He came to Funchal at a tender age to live in the house of his godfather, Canon Caetano Alberto de Araújo, and in this city he completed his preparatory studies in the humanities and the theology course at the Diocesan Seminary of Funchal (*Seminário Diocesano do Funchal*). He was ordained priest and went straight to Coimbra, where he enrolled in the faculty of law, graduating in 1820 or shortly afterwards. He was practising as a lawyer in Funchal and holding the chair of Latin when, in 1826, he was elected deputy for Madeira. He took his seat in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) and lived in Lisbon until 1828, when he left for Rio de Janeiro, fearing that he would fall victim to the persecution that the absolutist government was then beginning against supporters of liberal ideas.

Settling in the capital of Brazil, he became a naturalised Brazilian citizen and soon devoted himself to a legal career, earning a reputation there as a distinguished lawyer. He held various public posts, among them judge of orphans, counsel to the Imperial Household, president of the Institute of Lawyers, etc. When the Brazilian government offered a prize of one *conto* (one million réis) *de réis* to the author of the best draft civil code, Dr Caetano Alberto Soares was appointed a member of the committee charged with giving an opinion on the draft submitted.

Dr Soares had the misfortune to be struck by blindness, but he nevertheless continued to practise law, in which he achieved notable distinction. Because of this circumstance he left no printed works, apart from a memoir read at the Institute of Lawyers and published in 1848.
He died in Rio de Janeiro on 28 February 1867.
Soares (Urbano Canuto)

He was born in Funchal on 19 January 1894 and is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) of letters of the University of Lisbon (*Universidade de Lisboa*). He currently holds the post of full professor of the first group of the Faculty of Letters at the University of Porto. Works: *O Calão escolar da Casa Pia*, in collaboration with Dr Aurelio da Costa Ferreira (*Aguia*, 1914, and *Anais da Casa Pia*, 1915); *Linguagem e tradições populares do arquipélago da Madeira* (*Revista Lusitana*, 1915); *Epifanio Dias* (a speech delivered at the graveside of this professor, *Revista Lusitana*, 1917); and *Ensaios Filologicos, um manuscrito português do século XVI e o problema guanche* (*Revista da Faculdade de Letras do Porto*, 1920). He has several other works in preparation, among them a translation of Aristophanes’ *Clouds*, preceded by a study of Socrates.

On 19 April 1921, when the Faculty of Sciences of Porto conferred the degree of doctor on Marshal José Joffre, Generalissimo Armando Dias and General Horácio Smith Durrien, Dr Urbano Soares delivered an oration in Latin that was greatly admired by those versed in that language, and he drew up the doctoral diplomas of those military men (1921).
Madeiran Agricultural Society

The attempt to found an association to protect and develop Madeiran agriculture only became a reality during the administration of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) José Silvestre Ribeiro as civil governor of this district. Earlier efforts had always proved fruitless, and after that benevolent governor left Madeira the association led a very precarious existence, even ceasing to fulfil the obligations imposed on it.
As early as 1790 an attempt had been made here to establish an association of this kind, whose chief promoter at the time was Dr João Pedro de Freitas Drumond.

The formal inauguration of the Madeiran Agricultural Society (*Sociedade Agrícola Madeirense*) took place on 21 November 1849, attended by Prince Maximilian, Duke of Leuchtenberg, and by all the authorities and most prominent figures of our community. As can be seen in the *Epocha Administrativa*, the district’s highest authority gave the new association the most valuable support, recommending it most earnestly to all the authorities, to the administrative bodies and to the government of mainland Portugal.

The board (*mesa*) elected at that meeting drew up the statutes, which were approved by royal decree (alvará régio) of 30 August 1850. It entered into communication with other similar associations to guide its work better, and began publishing a newspaper entitled *O Agricultor Madeirense*, which was a reliable guide for farmers and warmly defended their interests. It acquired seeds, undertook the study and trial of new crops, dealt with livestock breeding, artificial pastures, the improvement of breeds, etc., and concerned itself with many matters of closest interest to the agriculture of this district. The reports of the society’s directorate and of its sub-committees, charged with studying the various questions most closely bound up with agriculture, reveal its zeal and interest in the affairs of this island. They give us eloquent testimony of what an association moved by the same aims and the same desires could achieve here.

The Sociedade Agrícola functioned regularly until 1858, having been re-established on different foundations in 1855. It suspended its sessions in 1860, and then functioned until 1864. It held a session in 1867 in order to consult the government on the introduction of wine from Portugal into Madeira, and was reorganised on 29 November 1876. From then until 1880, however, when it was finally dissolved, its work came to nothing.
Society for the Support of Primary Education

On 19 October 1858 a select assembly met in the São Lourenço Palace (‘St Lawrence’) to lay the foundations of an association whose special purpose was to promote and support primary education in this district, and several speakers addressed it on that occasion. The meeting was attended by the Infante Dom Luís, later King of Portugal, who there declared himself protector of the new association.
Funchal Building Cooperative Society
’. It was constituted by deed of 12 December 1901, its statutes having been approved at a session of the general assembly on 23 September 1900.

It was this society that had the buildings between Rua do Favila and the promenade and bridge of Ribeiro Seco (‘dry brook’) built. The plan and layout of the first houses erected there were approved by the Municipal Council of Funchal at its session of 10 October 1903.
Sociedade Cooperativa de Consumo e Credito do Funchal
See Cooperatives (*Cooperativas*).
Esperança Society

Its purpose was to establish a theatre in Funchal for the private entertainment of the members’ families and their acquaintances. Under the statutes it had 40 members, and could also have up to 5 honorary members. Ordinary members paid an entrance fee of 10,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) and a monthly subscription of 200 *réis*; honorary members paid the same monthly subscription but were exempt from the entrance fee.

The Esperança Society (*Sociedade Esperança*), constituted in 1858 with only 18 members at first, approved its statutes on 15 February 1860. They were signed by the interim directors Francisco Leandro Severim, João Maria da Silva Carvalho, Luís Alvares da Silva, Pedro Augusto da Silva Carvalho and João Alexandre de Carvalho. The decree approving these statutes is dated 10 May of the same year.

According to *O Direito* of 4 December 1858, the statutes were drafted by the member Nuno Dias de Vasconcelos. The founding members of the society also included Julio Galhardo de Freitas, who had already acted at the Teatro Concórdia, and Pedro de Alcantara Góis, who had made his debut in a performance staged at the Lancasterian School (*Escola Lancasteriana*). See Theatres.
Coimbra Academic Philanthropic Society

The initiative for founding this benevolent society, which has rendered so many services to poor students, is owed to Feliciano Augusto de Brito Correia, a law student and native of Madeira. The student meeting at which the organisation of the society was first discussed took place on 23 December 1849, and the same student was elected a member of the committee charged with presenting the outline of the statutes that were to govern the new association. The Sociedade Filantrópica Académica had its statutes approved by the government only on 26 May 1852.
Dr Feliciano Augusto de Brito Correia was deputy crown prosecutor in Funchal. He died on 9 January 1871, not quite 54 years old, having been born on 29 October 1817.
Funchal Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts

The society was founded in the Governor's Palace. Its first president was Dr João Pedro de Freitas Pereira Drumond and its first secretary Francisco Ferreira de Abreu. It had 28 full members and 24 honorary members, numbers that symbolised 24 August 1820, the day the revolution broke out in Porto, and 28 January 1821, the day Madeira followed suit. There were also corresponding members, 45 in number. The society's first public session took place on 23 August 1822.

The Funchal Society of Friends of the Sciences and Arts (*Sociedade Funchalense dos Amigos das Ciências e Artes*), modelled on the Royal Academy of Sciences of Lisbon (*Academia Real das Ciências de Lisboa*), was short-lived: it disappeared in 1823, with the restoration of absolute government on the island. Its statutes and regulations were printed in 1822 at the press of *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’).
Harmonia Society
In 1838 a society of this name existed in Funchal. Its main purpose was to organise gatherings for listening to fine pieces of music.
Humanitarian Society of the District of Funchal

A society under this name was founded in this city on 5 June 1858. According to the first article of its statutes, its purpose was ‘the rescue of persons in shipwrecks on the beaches of Funchal and their vicinity, and the rescue of persons in epidemics, fires and other similar calamities, in the city of Funchal and its surroundings’.
This society, whose statutes were approved by decree of 13 January 1862, was founded by a group of the most eminent people in Funchal. We believe that it was short-lived.
Patriotic Society
In 1821 there was a society of this name in Funchal, whose vice-president was Brigadier Jorge Frederico Lecor.
Patriotic and Economic Society of Commerce, Agriculture, Sciences and Arts

It was founded in Funchal in 1790, but we do not know how long it lasted. João José d'Orquigny (see that entry) delivered a speech at a general assembly of the Patriotic Society (*Sociedade Patriótica*) when taking his leave of it on 1 July 1790.
Madeiran Patriotic Society
In 1834 there was an association of this name in the city of Funchal, as can be seen from a pamphlet published that year, which contains a motion presented to the association by one of its members.
Society for the Protection of Domestic Animals

It was founded on 6 January 1897 and legalised by royal decree (*alvará*) of 6 May of the same year, and it was declared of public utility by decree of 16 March 1914. It has benefactor and subscribing members; the subscriptions, originally 10 centavos, have been raised to 50 centavos (1921).
There was another society of the same name, which was set up in the Hotel Miles, in Rua do Carmo (‘Carmel’), on 1 March 1880.
Thalia Society

Its purpose was to promote theatrical performances, and in 1858 it set itself up in a building on Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory’). The sergeants of the 16th Infantry gave a performance in a small theatre belonging to the society on 23 December 1858. The Tália society seems to have lasted only a few years.
Solander (Dr Daniel)
A distinguished Swedish naturalist and pupil of Linnaeus, born in Nordland on 28 February 1736, died in London on 16 May 1782. See Joseph Banks.
Unknown Soldier

Following the example of other countries, Portugal also wished to glorify the Unknown Soldiers who had given their lives for their homeland in the fight against the Germans. To this end, a programme of honours to be paid to these heroes was drawn up and published in the *Diário do Governo* (‘Government Gazette’), 2nd series, of 26 March 1921. As was to be expected of the well-proven patriotism of the Portuguese people, the programme was carried out with the greatest splendour and solemnity in all the country’s major centres. In accordance with the instructions of this programme, made public in Funchal by a public notice (*edital*) of the civil governor, the competent authorities had the national flags raised at midday on 7 April 1921 – the day chosen for the lying-in-state of the coffins of the Unknown Soldiers of France and of Africa in the Palace of National Sovereignty – on the fortresses, barracks and public buildings, where they remained until sunset on the 10th. At the same hour the infantry band played the national anthem and the salute march, and the church bells rang for 15 minutes.

Funchal paid homage to its immortal heroes on 7 to 10 April, the days set by the Government. The ceremonies held then, however, had neither the splendour nor the solemnity of those of 1 to 3 of the same month, on the occasion of the landing and embarkation of the urn containing the mortal remains of the Unknown Soldier who had fallen on the distant shores of Africa, in the struggle we waged there against the Germans.

As we have already said on page 110 of volume II of this work, the urn, brought by the steamer *Briton* of the Union Castle Mail, spent the night of 31 March to 1 April at the Maritime Disinfection Station (*Posto de Desinfecção Marítima*), which had been set up as a chapel of rest. It was brought ashore in the small steamer *Milano*, on which the authorities and other official figures had taken their places. When the urn was landed at the Pontinha (‘little point’) quay at about 9 o’clock at night, it received the due honours from an infantry detachment commanded by a captain, and the coffin was watched over through the night by officers of the garrison.

The cortège that accompanied the urn to the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) on 1 April was particularly imposing. It included the pupils and teachers of the primary, special and secondary schools of Funchal; the firemen, with the band of the ‘Artistas Funchalenses’; two patrols of scouts; the traffic staff of the Customs House and the Cabrestante (‘capstan’); various associations; the employees of the factory of W.m Hinton & Filhos; No. 1 Company of the Revenue Guard (*Guarda Fiscal*, customs and excise corps); naval forces and the civil police; the Syrian community; the director and staff of the ‘Western Telegraph Company’; representatives of the Masonic lodges; the Commercial Association; representatives of the banking houses; the press; the sergeants who had fought in Africa and France; the emigration police; the employees of the State Public Works; the directors and employees of the Customs House and the Post Office; the Protestant clergy; the director and staff of the Finance Department; the doctors, magistrates and lawyers; the Health Delegation; the Municipal Councils of the district; the District General Council (*Junta Geral*); the foreign officers resident in Funchal; the Portuguese officers; the families of Portuguese servicemen killed in the Great War; the civil and military authorities; the representatives of the Nation; the aide-de-camp of the Minister of the Navy; the consular corps; the general officers; a naval detachment from the cruiser *República*; the 27th Infantry Regiment; No. 3 Garrison Artillery Battery; the Republican Guard; and the philharmonic bands of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and the Artístico-Madeirense. The urn containing the mortal remains of the Unknown Soldier followed the Portuguese officers who had joined the cortège.

All the way from Pontinha to Avenida do Dr. Manuel de Arriaga, where an elegant catafalque had been erected, the cortège passed between two dense lines of people. The funeral urn, wrapped in the national flag, was carried on a gun carriage flanked by eight officers, some of them veterans of the Great War. Ahead of it went three other gun carriages bearing the many wreaths that had stood in the chapel of rest prepared the previous day at the Pontinha Disinfection Station (*Posto de Desinfecção*).

In front of the catafalque the highest-ranking civil and military dignitaries and the foreign officers formed a semicircle. The urn was taken from the gun carriage and placed on the plank bed, where it was guarded by the officers who had accompanied it there, four on each side. After a few minutes of silence Captain Américo Olavo de Azevedo, a veteran of the Great War, spoke. Although visibly unwell, he delivered a fine, patriotic speech that pleased everyone present.

The cortège then set off for the town hall by way of Rua João Tavira and Largo do Município. Foreign officers carried the coffin to the door of the building, and from there volunteer firemen carried it to the chapel of rest; their band played *A Portuguesa* as the funeral urn arrived. In the majestically decorated state room of the town hall, speeches were made by the President of the Council, Dr Teixeira Jardim; the civil governor, Rodrigues dos Santos; the British consul, Mr Staniford; the American consul, Mr Jenkins; the harbour master, Vital Gomes; the military commander, Colonel João M. Ferraz; and Senator Dr Manuel Augusto Martins. After the authorities who had joined the cortège had withdrawn, the room was visited by many thousands of people, who filed respectfully past the urn. It had been placed on a broad dais of five carpeted steps, with six large gilded torch-stands on each side, each ending in iron branches bearing five powerful electric lamps.

Before the cortège left Pontinha, the infantry officer Armando Pinto Correia, a veteran of the Great War, gave a brilliant address. It was followed by the minute of silence that those present were to observe, dedicated to all who had lost their lives on the battlefields in defence of the Fatherland, Liberty, Right and Justice.

When the steamer *Briton*, which, as we have said, carried the mortal remains of the Unknown Soldier, appeared on the horizon, the seaplane ‘F. 3’, which we mentioned in the article Aviation, flew out to meet it and circled the ship.

On 3 April, around midday, a new cortège formed, this time to accompany to the quay the remains of the Unknown Soldier, which were to be embarked on the cruiser *República*, charged with carrying them to Lisbon. The urn was borne by councillors (*vereadores*) from the chamber where it had lain in state to the door of the town hall. There it was handed over to the military detachment and placed on a gun carriage, the same councillors holding the tassels. In addition to the officers of the Funchal garrison, the foreign officers who had taken part in the cortège of the 1st joined the new procession.
As on the 1st, dense crowds lined the streets along which the cortège passed, and many people gathered on the quay and nearby to watch the embarkation ceremony.

The urn was carried from the beginning to the far end of the quay by the Civil Governor, the President of the Council, General Norton de Matos and the Military Commander. There it was handed over to a detachment of sailors from the cruiser *República*, and on that occasion the President of the Council and the French consul in Funchal gave speeches.

The urn was then transferred to a launch from the cruiser, in the middle of which stood a trophy made up of the flags of the Allied nations. The dignitaries who had borne the mortal remains of the Unknown Soldier to the end of the quay took their places in the same launch.
On arrival aboard the *República*, the urn was placed on a platform at the stern, with the wreaths arranged around it, and on that occasion General Norton de Matos and the cruiser’s commander spoke.

Moments later the cruiser left the harbour of Funchal for Lisbon, carrying on board the remains of the Unknown Soldier from Africa. A few days later they were to rest in the majestic Batalha Monastery, built by a valiant and patriotic king to commemorate one of the most glorious events in our history.
Flatfish (Rhombus madeirensis)

A fish of the family Pleuronectidae that lives on muddy or sandy bottoms close to the coast, where it is caught with trawl nets, sometimes in large quantities. It has a pleasant taste, but because of its small size it is a species of little commercial value.
Somerville (Captain B. T.)

Under the direction of Captain Somerville, the officers of the British ship *Argonaut* surveyed a chart of the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*), which bears the following title: *North Atlantic Salvage Islands. . . 1915.*
Alongside this chart there are two others, also surveyed by the same officers, with the following titles: *Piton Islands. . . 1915*, and *Great Salvage Island, 1915*.
Soundings

Madeira is surrounded by a fairly deep sea: the sounding line has descended to 4,205 metres 120 miles off the island’s north coast, and to 3,019 metres 50 miles off the same coast, in the direction of the Azores. Between Madeira and the Canary Islands the line went down to 4,392 metres, and between Madeira and the coast of Africa, a short distance from the island, to 4,071 metres. Between Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), depths of more than 2,000 metres have been recorded at some points, while between Madeira and the Azores the line has been seen to descend to 4,895 metres.

The results of the many soundings made in the seas around Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas are recorded in the geo-hydrographic charts published by the engineer António Pedro de Azevedo in 1877, 1879 and 1886.

In the waters off Ponta do Pargo (‘sea bream point’) there is a shoal about a mile and a half long, which coastal boats must keep clear of when the wind blows from the west. Between the point of São Lourenço and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’) there is a submarine bank whose middle part lies at a depth of 30 to 130 metres.
Sopa Económica
See Association for the Protection of the Poor (*Associação Protectora dos Pobres*). (I- 99).
Sorghum (Andropogon Sorghum)

A grass introduced to Madeira in 1856. It is native to tropical Asia and perhaps Africa, and was once widely grown in some parishes in the north of the island and in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), where the juice extracted from its stalks was used to make spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine). Sorghum, also known as *cana milho* and *canica*, is a good fodder, and its grain yields a flour that is used for human food in some countries.
Sousa

There are, it seems, two branches of this surname. One descends from Rui de Sousa, a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of the household of John II, who married on this island Constança Cabral, daughter of Diogo Cabral and of Brites Gonçalves da Câmara, Zarco’s daughter. The other derives from Antão Álvares de Sousa, a noble knight, who settled in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) around 1480.
Garcia Homem de Sousa, Zarco’s son-in-law, had a daughter named Leonor Homem, who married Duarte Pestana.
Sousa (Afonso Caminha de Vasconcelos)
He was Count of Calheta (‘small cove’) and 11th Donatary of Funchal, having received the captaincy in 1726.
Sousa (Bishop Dom José Xavier Cerveira e)
See Cerveira e Sousa. I-267.
Sousa Brasão (Manuel de)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente on 21 April 1884 and died at his residence in the Fort of São Lourenço (St Lawrence) on 21 December 1923. He was a captain in the Military Administration and served in southern Angola from 1914 to 1915, and in Mozambique from 1916 to 1917. He was elected deputy for Madeira on 10 July 1921 and contributed to various party newspapers.
Sousa (Dom Francisco)

His appointment as governor-general of Madeira dates from 18 January 1627, and he took office on 1 May 1628. After his departure, the diocesan bishop, Dom Jerónimo Fernando, took over the duties of governor-general.
Sousa (Dr Jacinto António de)

This distinguished professor at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) was born on this island on 3 January 1818, the son of Eugénio António de Sousa. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law and mathematics, and took his doctorate in the Faculty of Philosophy on 6 July 1858.

He held the chair of physics at the University and was one of the most eminent professors of his time. As director of the physics cabinet and the meteorological observatory, he rendered the most outstanding services to these scientific establishments, giving a new direction to the work carried out in them after a journey he made to various European countries.

Commissioned by the Portuguese government, he visited several foreign universities and observatories, and published notable reports on the observations and studies he carried out on his scientific missions. He was chosen as one of Portugal’s representatives to observe the solar eclipse in Spain in 1860, and Dr Simões de Carvalho says ‘that he performed this mission with great honour to his name, to the university and to the country’.

Among other works, he wrote: a report on a visit to the scientific establishments of Madrid, Paris, Brussels, London, Greenwich and Kew, 1862; *Observações meteorológicas feitas no observatório meteorologico e magnético da Universidade de Coimbra*, 1872; *Observações Meteorologicas...*, 1873; and *Additamento á Memoria Histórica da faculdade de philosophia...* 1873. He was director and editor of the scientific and literary review *O Instituto*, and a member of many scientific societies in Portugal and abroad. He died on 15 August 1880.
Sousa (Dr José de Barros e)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) on 1 March 1859. He was deputy crown prosecutor in the judicial district (*comarca*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and judge in the judicial district of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), and is today a judge of the High Court of Appeal (*Relação*) of Porto. He published a pamphlet, which has already run to three editions, entitled *Preceitos de Moral da Infância* (1921). He died in the city of Porto in December 1930.
Sousa e Silva (António Augusto de)
He was appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 26 April 1894 and took up the post on 17 May of the same year.

As inspector of works, he published *Relatório da inspecção às obras públicas do distrito do Funchal no anno de 1891...* Lisbon 1893, 41 pp. He published another detailed report on the same subject for the year 1892.
Sousa (Ernesto Venceslau de)

He was born in Funchal on 28 September 1879. He wrote the *Poema antipuniceo* (Funchal, 1904) and worked as a typographer while contributing to *A Cruz*, *A Esperança*, *A Voz do Operario* and *O Direito*. He usually signed his work with the pseudonym E. Tarolo. He died in the Princess Maria Amélia Hospice (*Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia*) on 25 December 1913.
Sousa (Francisco Clementino de)

He was born in this city on 26 February 1846, the son of the pharmacist Francisco Xavier de Sousa and Dona Virgínia Medina de Sousa. He completed the course of the Funchal Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica do Funchal*) in 1868 and on two occasions taught a chair there on an interim basis. For many years he held the post of sanitary inspector of the slaughterhouse of this municipality (*concelho*) and was treasurer of the former Banco Comercial da Madeira.

He contributed extensively and with distinction, in prose and verse, to the former newspaper *O Direito* (‘Law’), to the *Diário de Notícias* and to other periodicals. In defence of his father, and in a dispute with the Count of Canavial, he published an anonymous booklet in 1868 entitled *a questão entre o Dr. João da Câmara Leme. . . e o pharmaceutico Francisco Xavier de Sousa*, and in 1874 he published another pamphlet entitled *Resposta ao Sr. Acurcio Garcia Ramos*.

The hallmark of Francisco Clementino de Sousa’s writings, especially his poems, was satire and irony, handled with rare skill, exceptional talent and inimitable wit. His works were read with the greatest eagerness and always caused an extraordinary stir in our literary circles. It is no exaggeration to say that many of his poems rivalled those of Tolentino and of other poets who left a glorious name in our literature in the satirical genre. Had he lived in another milieu, he would easily have achieved great fame. Although a considerable part of his writings has lost its topicality, since it refers to people and events unknown to the present generation, these writings can still be read and enjoyed with great pleasure for the spontaneity, beauty of form and unsurpassed wit that shine through them. It would be a valuable service to letters to publish some of these works in a volume, saving from unjust and undeserved oblivion so many compositions that are true masterpieces of their kind. In many of his writings Francisco Clementino de Sousa adopted the pseudonym Faustino Brasão. He died in this city on 24 July 1896.
Sousa (Francisco de)

In 1877 a pamphlet was published in the city of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’) with the following title: *Tratado das Ilhas Novas e do descobrimento d'ellas e outras cousas feito por Francisco de Sousa, feitor d'el-rei Nosso Senhor na Capitania da cidade do Funchal na ilha da Madeira. . . e dos portugueses que forâo de Vianna e das ilhas dos Açores a povoar a terra nova do bacalhau. .. Anno do Senhor 1570*. A second edition of this booklet was produced in Ponta Delgada in 1884. The author of this pamphlet, a royal factor (*feitor*) in the captaincy of Funchal, was a native of this island.
Sousa (Garcia Homem de)

He was one of the *fidalgos* sent by the king to this island to marry the daughters of João Gonçalves Zarco, and he married Zarco’s third daughter, Catarina Gonçalves da Câmara. He held *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) lands in São Martinho (‘St Martin’) and Santo António, and built the fortified manor house of Santo Amaro (‘St Maurus’) to defend himself against his brothers-in-law, with whom he had quarrels for reasons that are not well known today. He was, says Dr Azevedo, a proud and violent man (see Santo Amaro (chapels)).
Henrique Henriques de Noronha says that Garcia Homem de Sousa was descended from Pedro Homem, one of the twelve knights who went to England.
Sousa (João Francisco de)

This Madeiran was born on 19 August 1868 and enlisted in the army on 22 January 1884, being commissioned second lieutenant of infantry on 15 March 1900. He was an officer risen from the ranks, but also a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), having completed his secondary studies at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school). He was senator for the constituency of Ponta Delgada (the Azores), and formed part of the column that left for southern Angola in 1915. He died, as a captain of the 17th Infantry, at the battle of the water-holes of Mangua (Cuanhama) on 19 August 1915, while going along the firing line encouraging the soldiers.

On the heroic part played by Captain Sousa in this Cuanhama campaign, one should read the notable article by Lieutenant-Colonel José de Oliveira Duarte published in the Funchal *Diario de Noticias* of 19 August 1945, on the thirtieth anniversary of the death of this distinguished Madeiran.
Sousa (José Caminha de Vasconcelos e)
He was Count and Marquis of Castelo Melhor and the last donatary of the captaincy of Funchal. By a deed of 9 September 1766 he ceded to the Crown most of his rights and prerogatives.
Sousa (Luís de Vasconcelos Câmara e)
See Câmara (Luís de Vasconcelos e).
Sousa (Manuel Alexandre de)

This infantry officer was born in Funchal on 2 February 1856 and died in Lisbon on 17 November 1903, then holding the rank of major. He was technical inspector of the Monte Railway Company (*Companhia do Caminho de Ferro do Monte*). Although some errors in building the line between Pombal and Atalhinho (‘little shortcut’) have been attributed to him, the fact is that his energy and acknowledged zeal did much to drive those works forward. He was also the concessionaire for the construction and operation of the Madeiran levadas (irrigation channels), as was seen on page 248 of this volume, and later director of the Limoeiro prison (*Cadeia do Limoeiro*). He carried on a lengthy controversy in the press with the engineer Adriano Augusto Trigo, and sought to install a lift between Largo de São Pedro and Caminho da Achada. (See II-248.)
Sousa Vaz (Dr F. de Assis)

Works: *De l'influence salutaire du climat de Madere dans le traitement de la phthisie pulmonaire, et de la superiorite de cette influence sur celle des climats du sud de la France et de l'Italie*, Paris, 1832. It is a short work, but in it the author, although he had no first-hand knowledge of Madeira, sets out the advantages of this island’s climate in the treatment of lung diseases.
Spencer Wells (Dr)

This distinguished English physician visited Madeira and published an article on the island in the *British Medical Journal* for May 1880, under the title *Notes of an easter holiday trip to Madeira*.
Spice (R. P.)
Works: *The Wanderings of the Hermit of Westminster on the Island of Madeira in 1883* (n.p., n.d.).
Spilsbury (F. B.)

He was surgeon of the *Favorita*, a British warship, and in the account he published of his voyage to the West Coast of Africa he refers to his stay in Madeira, where he remained from 12 to 19 October 1805. He speaks of the hospitality of the islanders, of leprosy, which he says was common, of the conical caps, of the flowers and fruits made by the nuns and of the thefts committed by the soldiers.
Sport

In the article we publish below, readers will find some materials for the history of sport in Madeira. It was written, at the request of one of the authors of this *Elucidário*, by a well-known journalist who is the sports editor of the *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’):

‘The sporting movement in Madeira may be described as remarkable, says the journalist in question. Among the various sports played in our community are the following: football, lawn tennis, billiards, table tennis, swimming and related events such as water polo, long-distance or endurance and sprint races, diving, rowing, yachting (sailing), croquet (on private grounds, especially at the *quintas* on the outskirts of the city), etc.

The most developed and best-loved sport in Madeira is, without doubt, football. On this island, as everywhere else, it went through an initial, preliminary phase in which it was played without any coordinating or educational body, the clubs arranging matches privately among themselves. In that early phase of football in Funchal many clubs were founded; some have since disappeared, while others still exist. Among those that have disappeared we still remember the Grupo Sportivo do Ateneu Comercial, the Grémio dos Empregados do Comércio (Shop Employees’ guild (*grémio*)), the Operário Funchalense, the Sporting Grupo do Funchal, the Continental Madeirense, the Académico, the Grupo Desportivo Insulano, etc.

Among the clubs founded at that time which are still active today are the following, in decreasing order of seniority: Grupo Sportivo Internacional, Club Sports da Madeira, Club Sport Marítimo, União Foot-ball Club (formerly União-Marítimo) and Clube Desportivo Nacional (formerly Nacional Sport Grupo).
In 1916, on the initiative of the União and Insulano clubs, the Associação de Foot-ball do Funchal (Funchal Football Association) was founded, and from then on the sport was properly organised.
Then began the second phase of football in Madeira, with regularly contested competitions.
In this second period the following were founded: Império Foot-ball Clube, Portugal F. C., Funchal F. C. and Ufania F. C., the last three short-lived and now defunct.

Once organised, the A. F. F. promoted the first Madeira Championship in the 1916–17 season, divided into two divisions. The winners were C. S. Marítimo in the 1st division and G. S. Internacional in the 2nd.

The following season (1917–18) the Madeira Championship was contested again, enlarged with a 3rd-division competition. The winners were C. S. Marítimo in the 1st division, União F. C. in the 2nd and C. S. Marítimo in the 3rd.
The activity of the Football Association, and consequently the Championship, was suspended during the 1918–19 and 1919–20 seasons.

In the 1920–21 season the Madeira Championship was held again, thanks to the strenuous efforts of Álvaro Reis Gomes, who, after a press campaign, succeeded in reviving the A. F. F. He worked devotedly on its reorganisation, assisted by Gonçalo de Ornelas, Luís da Costa and Anastácio do Nascimento. That season (1920–21) the winners were União F. C. in the 1st division – although C. S. Marítimo had won every match, it was disqualified for fielding a player not properly registered with the A. F. F. – União F. C. in the 2nd division and C. S. Marítimo in the 3rd.

In the 1921–22 season the Championship was won by C. S. Marítimo in the 1st division, C. S. Marítimo in the 2nd and C. S. Marítimo in the 3rd: the same club in every competition. In 1922–23 the result was the same: C. S. Marítimo, champion in all 3 divisions.
Besides its football champion, Madeira can take pride in other talents in various branches of sport, such as lawn tennis, sea diving, water-polo, billiards, etc. For example:

Lawn tennis: – António Vieira de Castro and Rui de Bianchi, the latter recently deceased in Switzerland. The survivor of this magnificent pair has already made his name on the mainland, competing against established players and winning a tournament held a few years ago at Caldas da Rainha. António Vieira de Castro is the tennis champion of Madeira and holds the corresponding prize: the ‘Strangers Club’ Cup. (1921)

Sea diving (high diving): – João de Sousa, António de Castro and others. They beat the Portuguese record, diving from 25 metres. Some people wrongly regard these men as professional divers, because they ply their trade aboard the liners, selling Madeiran handicrafts. But if their status raises doubts, we have a purely amateur young man (employed in commerce on land, just as the others are at sea) who dives from 18 metres, the record of the Liga M. D. Náuticos. His name is Ulrique Alves.

Water-polo: – The 1st championship of this aquatic sport held in Madeira (1922) by the L. M. D. N. was won by Império Foot-ball Clube in the first division. In the second division the winner was Clube Sport Marítimo.
A distinguished water-polo player, and the man who introduced the game here, was the late António Costa.

Billiards: – Alfredo Ferraz and Mário de Freitas, winners (1st and 2nd prizes respectively) of the Portuguese Billiards Championship, held in 1922 in Lisbon at the Grémio Lisbonense, at Arco do Bandeira, are Madeirans. Other distinguished billiard players: António Costa (died 1921) and José da Silva Coelho.

Table tennis: – The Madeirans Álvaro de Meneses Alves Reis Gomes and Manuel Pedro Nolasco de Pontes Leça won the Academic Championship held in Coimbra at the Centro Académico de Democracia Cristã in May 1921, taking the 1st and 2nd prizes respectively. An outstanding exponent of table tennis, and champion of the Madeira Sports Club (*Clube Sports da Madeira*), was the late Madeiran Arnaldo de Azevedo Ramos. The champion of Club Desportivo Nacional is the Madeiran João Crisóstomo Luís.
Sailing: – Afonso Coelho, Manuel Perestrelo and Humberto dos Passos Freitas.
Below we give various details about some of the sports associations in Funchal, two of which have already been noted on page 280 of volume I of the *Elucidário*, in the article Clubs (*Clubes*):

Club Sport Marítimo – Founded in September 1910, it adopted green and red as the colours of its banner and kit. Its members devote themselves to sporting exercise in general, and in particular to football and water sports.
It has carved a glorious name in the history of Madeiran football, having been regional champion in that popular sport from its introduction here down to the present day.

Its annals record countless victories over all the other Madeiran teams. It has never been beaten in Madeira except on one single occasion, by União Football Clube in 1919, when its ranks had been considerably weakened by the departure of some of its best players to that and other clubs. It also boasts most honourable results (wins and draws) against fine foreign teams that have called at our landing place aboard warships, training ships, transports, etc. In 1912, for example, it drew with the formidable German team of the cruiser *Pandora*.

Having brought to Funchal the powerful 1st eleven of Sport Lisboa e Bemfica, for many consecutive years champion of the capital, it inflicted two memorable defeats on it, on 9 and 13 April 1922, by 3–2 and 6–3 respectively.

C. S. Marítimo has made several tours to mainland Portugal and abroad (the Canary Islands). On 14 October 1922, in Porto, it beat Football Club do Porto, champions of Portugal, by 3–1, which earned it an enthusiastic welcome on its return to Madeira.

It holds the following trophies: the Madeira Championship Cup for 1st divisions; the same for 2nd divisions; the same for 3rd divisions; the ‘João Pimenta’ Cup; the ‘Champion 1910–1917’ Cup; the ‘Oscar Elsener’ Swiss Cup; the Portugal Cup; the Hinton Cup; the 2nd Swiss Cup; and the Association Bronze in football. It also holds the 2nd-division Cup of the Championship of the Liga Madeirense de Desportos Náuticos in water polo.
It is due to compete in the Championship of Portugal in football and then to visit the United States of America, having received an invitation to do so.
Its headquarters are at present at Rua de Santa Maria, 126, with windows overlooking the Campo do Almirante Reis (‘Admiral Reis field’), where the football matches are played.

Grupo Sportivo Internacional. – This is the oldest sports association in Madeira, founded in 1909. It adopted green and black as its colours. It won the 2nd-division championship in the first year it was contested. Its headquarters are at Rampa de Miguel Bombarda, no. 3.

Club Sports da Madeira. – Founded in March 1910, it adopted blue and white as its colours. During the early years of the Associação de Football do Funchal it was the chief rival of Club Sport Marítimo in the Madeira Championship, to which it lent much brilliance and excitement. In that period (1916–1918) its constant aim was to defeat C. S. Marítimo and wrest from it the title of regional champion. It never succeeded, however, although on several occasions it drew with its rival in fiercely contested matches that Madeiran sportsmen remember with nostalgia.

In the 1st year of the Swiss Cup (1918) it won the 2nd prize, a diploma. It also possesses several cups won in athletics, water sports and football. Outstanding among them is the monumental ‘America Cup’, won for this Club by Afonso Coelho in a sailing regatta.

Its football team has already travelled to the Canary Islands, where it drew with the best team there and brought back a commemorative trophy to Madeira. Its headquarters are at Rua de Hermenegildo Capelo, no. 11, opposite the Jardim Municipal (‘municipal garden’).
Liga Madeirense de Sports Náuticos. – Founded in 1922, in that same year it held the Madeira water-polo Championship, in two divisions, and organised other water events, such as races, diving, etc.
Madeira owes the organisation of this league to the initiative of Álvaro Reis Gomes, sports editor of the *Diário da Madeira*.
All the sports clubs of Funchal are affiliated to this federation (1921).

At the invitation of Club Sport Marítimo, the 1st team of Sporting Club de Portugal visited Funchal in 1924, and four matches were played, on 15, 18, 22 and 29 May. Sporting Club won every match. Its opponents were Club Sport Marítimo in the first, União Foot-Ball Club in the second, a team made up of players from Império, Madeira, União and Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) in the third, and Club Sport Marítimo again in the fourth. When the Sporting Club de Portugal players returned to Lisbon, they were accompanied by the 1st team of Club Sport Marítimo, which sought to contest there, for its club, the title of national champion, but without success’ (1924).

As a supplement to the article printed in the first edition, which is reproduced in full above, Dr Álvaro de Meneses Alves Reis Gomes and Mr Noé Pestana have supplied us with extensive and interesting information. It contains valuable material for the history of Madeiran sport, and we owe them our deeply grateful thanks.

‘An account of Madeiran sporting activities since the preceding article was written would provide material not for a short article – in keeping with the character of this publication – but for a book of many pages.

We must therefore try to condense the list of facts we are about to give, recording only the most important events. It is possible, however, that this brief account will contain some omissions, both because of the haste with which we are gathering these notes and because of the need to save space, so as not to become tedious.
To make our unpretentious work easier to consult, we shall divide it into sections and individual sports.
Cricket: – This is, strictly and truly, the oldest sport known to have been played in Madeira.

Since this is the national game of the English, cricket was introduced to the island by the British subjects living here. They were chiefly the sons of the wine merchants, and of those in other branches of trade and industry established here, on their return from their studies at schools in England, and also the employees of the ‘Brasilian Submarine Telegraph Co.’, which later gave way to ‘The Madeira Western Telegraph C.°’.

Organised play seems to date back to 1888, when the game was first played competitively by teams. That year also saw the founding of the first cricket organisation, called ‘The Madeira Cricket Club’, whose chief promoters were João Correia, F. C. Cornell and Mr H. P. Miles. The club rented the grounds of the field at the Achada (‘plateau’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha, from their owners, and played its inaugural match there on 20 March of the same year, between sides of bachelors and married men. Before then, however, the field, which until that date had been a sort of common land (*baldio*) used for grazing, had often been used for this and other sports.
On 1 January 1893 the ‘Excelsior Madeira Cricket Club’ was founded, and the original club later merged with it.

To give its members easier access to its principal sport – for it also promoted football, athletics, etc. – this new sporting body acquired a plot of land in São Martinho, at the locality (*sítio*) of Engenho Velho (‘old sugar mill’), which it converted into a sports ground. The ground was inaugurated on 19 April 1894 and later became known as Campo do Brás (‘Brás’s field’), after one of its former owners.

This club, which included some Madeirans among its members, played a number of hard-fought matches of cricket and other sports against teams from the ships of the naval squadrons that then called at Funchal, and against teams of employees of the Submarine Cable Company.

The ‘Excelsior’ was the first Madeiran sports club to carry the name of the Pearl of the Ocean abroad. On 10 May 1901 its cricket team sailed aboard the SS *Niger* for Las Palmas, where it played three matches, resulting in two victories for the neighbouring Spanish island and one for Madeira.
Further matches were played in succession by that team and others, until interest in cricket gradually waned, and our activity in the sport disappeared altogether around 1926.
Football: – The sport that won the most followers and supporters in Funchal was football, and in the golden age of the game our local scene was able to rank alongside the best on the mainland.

According to the journalist Mota de Vasconcelos, in his *Almanaque do Desportista Madeirense*, published in 1945, it was Mr Harry Hinton who, at the age of 18, in 1865, brought the first football to Madeira. This was also the first introduced into Portugal, since it was only in 1888 – 13 years after Madeira – that the same thing happened on the mainland, involving the three brethren Eduardo, Frederico and Guilherme Pinto Basto, well-known bankers, who are credited, in the same way as H. Hinton, with introducing football to mainland Portugal.

This Madeiran industrialist and former sportsman used that ball on the ground at Achada da Camacha (‘plateau of Camacha’), in games with other boys of his age, making the most of the weekends he spent there at the Quinta da Achadinha (‘little plateau estate’), his father’s property.

However, that first ball was ruined by the disorderly kicking of the group of young men among its owner’s acquaintances, and only some years later was the first match of association football played on this island between two properly organised sides, on the old Campo D. Carlos, today Almirante Reis. That first match must have taken place in 1894 or in 1895, according to the two versions known to us of the introduction of the popular English sport to Madeira.

In the first of these versions, according to the testimony of Mr H. A. Miles, a British subject who had lived in Madeira for more than 50 years, given when the ‘Album das Bodas de Prata da A. F. F.’ was being compiled, the first football match on the island must have taken place in 1894, between a ‘team’ of Englishmen living in our land and another made up of the crew of an English ship that lay at anchor in our harbour for three weeks undergoing repairs.

In the second version, gathered from the accounts of some old members of the seafaring class of the *bomboteiros* – a class closely linked with the introduction of football to Madeira – who lived near the old Campo D. Carlos already mentioned, the first match was played between two groups of crewmen from the English pleasure yacht (which they call ‘Lord’) named *Rhouma*, on her first voyage to Madeira, which has been established as taking place in 1895.

As for the introduction of the popular English game, these old seamen relate that on the second voyage of this vessel, which visited Madeira year after year for many years, a young seaman named João Viveiros, nicknamed ‘O Chicago’, persuaded the crew of the *Rhouma* to give him, on their departure, the ball they used for their amusement. He used it with other companions in disorderly games of kicking forward, mixed with plenty of running about.

As a curious note, we would point out that when the rubber of this ball wore out, João Viveiros filled it with an animal’s bladder and then began hiring it out at ten *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) an hour.

Enthusiasm for the game grew and, attempt by attempt, it made great progress around 1908 to 1910 with the return to Madeira of the late lamented sportsman Humberto dos Passos Freitas, back from his studies, who was a devoted promoter of this sport and perhaps its greatest driving force.

Madeiran football then acquired a life of its own, entering the phase already described in the previous article. From 1922 onwards it achieved its greatest renown, until in 1926 it reached its highest peak with the famous title of Champion of Portugal, won by Clube Sport Marítimo.

Thanks to the persistent efforts of the various leaders of the time, and in particular of Dr Álvaro dos Reis Gomes, former Secretary of the Portuguese Football Federation and delegate of the A. F. F. to that body, Madeira began in 1922–23 to take part in the highest football competition, then called the Championship of Portugal, sending a representative to the mainland every year.

In this competition, which from 1938–39 came to be called the ‘Taça de Portugal’, Madeira was represented 19 times, distributed as follows: Clube Sport Marítimo, 14 times; Clube Desportivo Nacional, 3 times; Clube de Futebol União, 2 times. Finally, in the 1941–42 season, when C. D. Nacional qualified as our representative, Madeira was eliminated from the competition because of difficulties created by the last world war.

In the various Madeira championships organised since the foundation of the A. F. F., in the first Honour categories, the winners were: Club Sport Marítimo, 17 times; C. D. Nacional, 6 times; C. F. União, 5 times. Various renowned clubs, both Portuguese and foreign, have visited Madeira, and our teams achieved the most flattering results. These gave Madeiran football a great reputation abroad, and led many of our best players to leave our island in search of other shores, lured by tempting promises.

Many of the leading clubs on the mainland have included several Madeiran players in their ranks, and the national team has already used the services of the following fellow islanders: José dos Ramos, Artur de Sousa (Pinga), Carlos Pereira and António Teixeira (Camarão). The following were also called up as reserves: José Rodrigues (Jusa), Jesuíno Gavião, Pedro de Sousa, Vasco Nunes and Rogério de Sousa. Of all these, Artur de Sousa, who was selected 21 times for international matches, achieved great fame both in Portugal and abroad, being the most outstanding Portuguese player of recent times. For this reason, in an article published in the Lisbon newspaper *A Bola*, the well-known sports journalist Cândido de Oliveira, a former national selector, set that Madeiran ‘ace’ alongside a mainland player of earlier times, Artur José Pereira, in a comparison to decide the best Portuguese player. The Madeiran journalist Noé Pestana replied to this article in the same newspaper with another, in which, supported by many authoritative opinions, he questioned whether Pinga was the best Madeiran player. For comparison he invoked the following players of the past: Moisés de Sousa, José Rodrigues (Jusa), António Alves, Manuel Ramos (Janota), José dos Ramos (José Pequeno) and Pedro de Sousa, concluding in favour of the last.

Not only did the best mainland clubs make use of Madeiran players, but so did some clubs in the Azores and in Africa, notably Lourenço Marques, where at one point almost the entire Madeiran representative side was to be found.

Madeira played the following inter-city matches: 1st Funchal–Porto, on 22/6/1930, in Porto, lost 1–3; 1st Funchal–Setúbal, on 29/6/1930, in Setúbal, lost 2–3; 2nd Funchal–Porto, on 13/7/1930, in Funchal, won 5–1; 1st Funchal–Las Palmas, on 14/4/1935, in Funchal, drawn 1–1; 1st Funchal–Lisbon, on 25/7/1937, in Funchal, drawn 3–3. Following this last encounter, another, unofficial match was played on 1 August of that same year, which Madeira won 1–0.

Several Madeiran clubs have travelled to the Canary Islands and the Azores, among them Club Sport Marítimo, C. D. Nacional, C. S. Madeira, Império F. Clube, União F. Club, G. S. Automobilista and Sporting Club da Madeira.

At present the following clubs are affiliated to the Funchal Football Association (*Associação de Futebol do Funchal*): Honour Division: Clube Sport Marítimo, Clube Desportivo Nacional, Clube de Futebol União and Sporting Club da Madeira; Promotion Division: Club Desportivo Barreirense, Clube de Futebol Andorinha, Club de Futebol Carvalheira, Clube de Futebol São João, Clube de Futebol Palmeira, Clube de Futebol Pátria and Grupo Desportivo da Segurança.

Owing to the constant departure of players from Madeira, and also to the lack of sports grounds, Madeiran football has entered a period of decline in recent years, and is currently going through a shortage of top-class players.

However, thanks to the ban on player transfers established by Decree-Law no. 32 946, and to the schools for young players set up by Clube Sport Marítimo, it is to be expected that in the near future our favourite sport will regain the front-rank position in Portuguese football to which its brilliant traditions entitle it.
Water sports: – Given the scant information at our disposal, it is difficult at present to fix an exact date or starting point for a historical account of Madeiran sporting activity on the water.

Madeira – an island with a coastline open on every side to a sea that is, on the whole, calm – is an ideal place for every kind of water sport. Only the inertia or indolence of its inhabitants, perhaps a fault of the climate, explains how little sport is practised in the bay, such as sailing and rowing, or indeed swimming and water-polo.

It is very likely that before 1910 – besides rowing contests between crews from ships anchored in our bay – some nautical events were held, for, as one would expect, people have always swum, at least on the beaches along the island’s coast, especially in summer. However, the first year in which we know that competitive events were organised is the one given above. For simplicity, we shall now summarise the main facts.

On 4 and 12 October 1913, to mark the 3rd anniversary of the proclamation of the Portuguese Republic, several nautical festivals were held, promoted by the newspaper *Athenista*, in which João Tiago de Castro, then an accomplished swimmer, distinguished himself.

In 1917 the Club Naval Madeirense was founded on the initiative of the late Viscount of Ribeira Brava, an enthusiastic sportsman. This began a phase of great activity: regattas with magnificent gigs, sailing races in graceful ‘monotypes’, and grand nautical festivals in which many Madeiran sportsmen stood out, such as Travassos Lopes, Humberto dos Passos Freitas, José Florêncio de Abreu, Afonso Coelho, Américo Patrício, Manuel Perestrelo, Dr João Miguel Rodrigues and others.

From then on, several nautical festivals were held every year at the Molhe da Pontinha, almost always for charitable purposes. Among the various sporting events, such as swimming races, the greasy pole, catching the duck, high dives (from the masts of anchored ships or from the islet), etc., games of water-polo were introduced, which found two great promoters in António Costa and Vasco Figueira.

In 1922 the Liga Madeirense de Desportos Náuticos (Madeiran Nautical Sports League) was founded. For some time it organised annual swimming events and the Madeira Water-polo Championship, the first champion of which was the now defunct Império Futebol Club.
On this League’s initiative, a team made up of the best swimmers from mainland Portugal came to Madeira in September 1924.

The Liga Madeirense de Desportos Náuticos ceased its activity in 1930. From then on, official swimming and water-polo competitions also ceased, and these sports were practised only at the occasional private festival organised at the ‘Lido’ swimming pool or at the bathing establishments on the beach of Campo Almirante Reis.

In 1940 the Associação de Natação do Funchal (Funchal Swimming Association) was founded, and the District Swimming Championships have been held every year. They have aroused little interest in recent years, however, for lack of the chief requirement for practising this sport in the manner of the great centres: a swimming pool or aquatic stadium.

Athletics: – Although athletics was practised in Madeira as early as 1899, at a festival organised by the Excelsior Madeira Cricket Club, the sport scarcely went beyond private events organised by newspapers or clubs, or the customary contests held at the ceremonies of swearing allegiance to the flag in our military units.
Of these private events, in which the clubs took part, the most important were the Funchal–Câmara de Lobos–Funchal marathons of 1911 and 1927, won respectively by Manuel Perestrelo and Alberto Malho.
In 1927 the Liga Madeirense de Sports Atléticos (Madeiran Athletic Sports League) was founded; it lasted no more than two or three years.

Tennis: – Tennis is the favourite sport of Madeira's sporting elite – as, indeed, it is almost everywhere – and it is so firmly established that countless *quintas* (country estates) of wealthy families, foreign or Madeiran, have courts laid out for playing it.
It is not easy at present to say exactly how long this splendid sport has been played here, for it goes back many years.

The chronicles record that during the visit of Their Majesties King Carlos I and Queen Empress Amélie to Madeira in 1901, several tennis matches were played at the Quinta do Palheiro, in which the King, a great sportsman, took part.
Many tennis tournaments have been organised here, from the earliest times to the present day, and the most valuable and splendid trophies have been contested.

The world's finest players have passed through Madeira, especially on pleasure trips. They have stayed here for many days, lodging in our best hotels, almost always during the winter season, and have taken part alongside our best players in various international tournaments and championships.
And because so very many talents have made their mark here in this fine sport, we refrain from mentioning any individual in this brief survey.
Miscellaneous: – Besides the sports mentioned above, many others have been practised in Madeira on a greater or lesser scale. Among them we shall mention the following:

Fencing and shooting: – If these were not introduced to Madeira by the late Viscount of Ribeira Brava – who practised fencing with every weapon with enthusiasm, dedication and acknowledged skill – this much-missed promoter of many sports was certainly one of their keenest champions, and he found a valuable collaborator in Carlos Nellis, from the mainland.
Nellis ran several fencing classes, and a number of tournaments were then held and contested with unusual interest.

Among his pupils, Jorge Gordon, Sotto Mayor, Humberto dos Passos Freitas, João de Oliveira Faria, António Vieira de Castro and Fernando Figueiredo stood out. Carlos Nellis had his pupils compete for the ‘Sebastião de Herédia’ cup (1920) – won two years running by Captain Raul Cohen – and the ‘Conde de Boussies’ cup (1920 to 1926), won in its first year by Raul Cohen, with António Vieira de Castro and Mr Hermos taking second places (with trophies). Fernando de Figueiredo also became a fine fencer; he kept the ‘Herédia’ cup for having won it three years running. He owns the cup that bears his name.

Another accomplished Madeiran fencer was Alberto Jardim, holder of the ‘Conde de Bousies’ cup, won after a hard-fought contest with Fernando de Figueiredo. Other Madeirans who also took an interest in this sport were Rui de Faria, Eduardo de Ascensão Velosa, José Ferreira Duarte Soares, Manuel Bianchi and Jorge Caldeira.

In the town (*vila*) of Ribeira Brava, during the lifetime of the titled nobleman of that name, several festivals were held in which the cream of the society of the day took part, and in which these sports featured prominently.
Table tennis: – This sport, widely known as ping-pong, was taken up in Madeira before it was in Lisbon.

This interesting sport was introduced here in 1917 by the late Arnaldo Azevedo Ramos, whose enthusiastic companions in the early days of the game were António Coutinho, António Mendes and João Crisóstomo Luís.
The sport grew and its followers and players increased, and from 1920 to 1925 every sports club on the island had suitable facilities for it; several inter-club tournaments were held at that time.
In 1936 the Madeira Ping-Pong Association (*Associação de Ping-Pong da Madeira*) was founded, and the sport then reached its greatest growth.
This body, however, was short-lived and soon disappeared, and today the sport is wholly without official support.
Motoring: – The first motor car arrived in Madeira on 30 December 1903, for Mr Harvey Foster; its owner took it with him when he returned to England the following year.

In 1907 another car arrived in Madeira, this one for the newly formed ‘Empresa Madeirense de Automóveis’. With it came a driver from the mainland named Francisco Franco, who stayed on our island for some time. Nine days after its arrival the car had an accident on the Caminho do Acioli, and all its passengers were injured.
The first Madeiran to drive motor vehicles was João Rodrigues (Morgado), who sat the ‘chauffeur’ examination on 11 February 1908.

As motoring developed on our island, excellent drivers emerged, and gymkhanas and other events were organised on several occasions, notably the 1st Barreiros Hill Climb in 1935, organised by the Automóvel Club de Portugal, in which some of the best amateur drivers from the mainland took part.

Cycling: – Although bicycles had fallen completely out of use in Madeira over the last ten to fifteen years, the sport had a great many followers here at the end of the 1800s and the dawn of the 1900s.

The first cycle race in Madeira dates from 1899, at a sports festival held by ‘The Madeira Cricket Club’, already mentioned. It was a comic event (a 100 m slow race), with R. Figueira placed 1st and C. Gomes 2nd.

In 1908 and 1911 several cycle rides were held from Funchal to Câmara de Lobos, as well as some town races (closed circuits), besides annual parades during the carnival festivities and various festivals in the Campo Almirante Reis.

But after cycling had vanished completely, so that for years not a single touring bicycle was to be seen in the streets of the city, it gradually reappeared. In 1938, on the initiative of the weekly *Comércio do Funchal*, then edited by Luís Quental, the 1st City Circuit was held; it aroused enormous enthusiasm and was won by Júlio Virissimo.
Since then several other races have been held with greater or lesser enthusiasm, the most important being the Funchal–Câmara de Lobos–Funchal race.

Basketball and volleyball: – These two sports also have their supporters here; the Funchal Basketball Association (*Associação de Basket-Ball do Funchal*) was founded in 1935 and the Volleyball Association (*Associação de Volley-Ball*) in 1945.
The former was active for about four years, and in recent years the sport has been left without any official organisation.

Stanford (Charles Thomas)

This distinguished British subject, who lived in Madeira for some years and held our island in the warmest affection, as he amply demonstrated in his exquisite books, was born in 1858 and died in England on 7 March 1932. His literary works include *Leaves from a Madeira Garden* and the engaging novel *Ace of Hearts*, whose plot unfolds on this island. He was a distinguished writer and a man of rare intellectual culture. He had been awarded the title of ‘Baronet of the United Kingdom’.
