Stuebel (Dr Alphons)

Through a simple oversight, no reference was made to the article written by Father Ernst Schmitz about Dr Alphons Stuebel when we dealt with the geology of Madeira. To what was said there must be added the authoritative opinion of that illustrious German naturalist, together with the no less judicious remarks, which accompany the said article, of the former professor of natural sciences at our Diocesan seminary (*Seminário*).

There is a wide divergence of opinion, at least on secondary questions, among the geologists who in the course of this century have studied the formation of the island of Madeira most closely. But just as the collision of bodies and their mutual friction often produce a spark and light, so it may be hoped that more light will also be shed on this question as competent men give their opinions after conscientious study, even if at first they reach differing results.

The opinions put forward by Luiz da S. Mousinho Albuquerque, by Dr J. Macaulay, Sir Charles Lyell, Dr Oswald Heer of Zurich and above all by Dr G. Hartung, who treated the subject more fully than any of them in his book *Madeira & Porto Santo*, etc., Leipzig, Engelmann, 1864, are fairly well known in Portugal. But very few of those interested in the geology of Portuguese lands will be aware of the painstaking and conscientious studies that Dr Alphons Stuebel of Dresden made of Madeira. He was in Madeira in 1862 and 1863, and after detailed and prolonged observation and exploration of the terrain he built the geological map of Madeira – not on a sheet of paper, but in relief, in modelling paste. On it every height and hollow, extinct crater, stream, levada (irrigation channel), settlement, etc., is shown with the greatest clarity, all on a scale of 1 to 55,000, so that it is more than a metre long, with a corresponding width.

This unique map of Madeira is in the Funchal Seminary Museum (*Museu do Seminário do Funchal*), and it admirably combines the gifts of science and art, all of which aim to facilitate and assist the study of geology, and of volcanology in particular.

Surely no little weight must be given to the opinion of a man whose whole life was devoted to volcanology, and whose ample fortune allowed him to go and study *de visu* the most interesting volcanic regions of our globe. We therefore believe we are doing a service in making better known this opinion of Dr Stuebel, which is set out in broad outline in his monumental work *Die Vulkanberge von Ecuador* and in the part of it *Ueber des Wesen des Vulkanismus*, published separately in Berlin, A. Asher & Co., 1897.

An example of the close union of two monogenetic volcanic elevations (that is, elevations due to a single volcanic cause, even if it manifests itself at long intervals of time) is provided, on a far larger scale than Pichincha on the Equator, by the island of Madeira. The whole mass of its mountains, which over a length of nearly 60 kilometres and a width of 15 to 20 rises to an altitude of 1,800 metres, was simply the product of two eruptive centres. And both of them, as can be concluded with great certainty from the way in which they are joined, were active at the same time.

‘The larger and higher of these two monogenetic structures is a caldera-shaped elevation that occupies more than two-thirds of the island. The caldera proper, which lies almost at the centre of the whole mass, is nearly 4 1/2 kilometres in diameter and 1,200 metres deep. A long valley (the former crater), which becomes very narrow in its lowest part and turns into a ravine, and which falls 600 metres over a length of 11 kilometres, drains the waters of this caldera, called Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’). Among the many peaks surrounding the caldera, the highest, and indeed the highest point on the island, is Pico Ruivo (1850) metres. From the rim of the caldera immense ridges stretch out in every direction, and although these differ greatly in length, structure and shape, the observer is left with the impression that this main part of the island is, in broad outline, a symmetrical structure produced by volcanic forces. ‘Very different is the second mass of the island, much smaller in extent, but only 300 metres lower than the first. It is a dome-shaped elevation, flattened at the top, where one would expect a crater; it forms a plateau more than 3 kilometres in diameter, called the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’).

The two eruptive centres, with their piled-up masses, lie so close to each other that their rocks not only touch but, to a certain extent, interlock. The boundary between the two masses is still clearly visible, marked by two very deep valleys running in opposite directions: one to the north, that of São Vicente, and the other to the south, that of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’). The headwater regions of these valleys, which erosion has widened and transformed into calderas with several branches, are separated only by a relatively very thin but high wall, a kind of crest bristling with peaks, which connects the plateau of the Paul da Serra with the western wall of the Curral das Freiras caldera.

‘Despite all the resemblance that the valleys of São Vicente and Ribeira Brava, with their caldera-shaped widenings, bear to the great caldera of Curral das Freiras, their significance for the geological structure of the island is essentially different. They are merely inter-hill spaces widened by erosion, whereas the valley of Curral das Freiras constitutes a true crater, and the stream of Curral, or of Socorridos, opens the way to this true eruptive centre.

‘We insist on this necessary distinction concerning the formation of these valleys precisely because Sir Charles Lyell, in his description of the island of Madeira (*Elements of Geology*), failed to make it.

‘While these two eruptive centres were piling up almost the entire mass of the island as it rose above sea level, it seems that some secondary centres, of which visible traces remain, were also active. This is evident above all on the high, steep northern coasts. In particular, we regard the Penha de Águia as an important remnant of an ancient destroyed crater.

‘In addition, the island, whose volcanic activity died out long ago, possesses a number of well-preserved crater formations, although they are small. Their position and their connection with the main mass of the island make it more than probable that the source of their scanty eruptive material must be placed within the mass of the island itself, and not in the immense depths beneath it from which the island itself took its origin. We may mention, for example, the shallow crater of the pond (*lagoa*) of the Serra de Santo António at the far eastern end of the island, as well as the small eruptive cones and lava flows that form the base of the plateau above Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) at the far north-western end of the island.

‘We do not wish to go into detail here about the tectonic structure of the volcanic mountains and their ramifications, but we should like to point out that the gradients of the mountain slopes and of the *lombos* show angles of inclination almost identical to those of the volcanic mountains of the Equator. As there, the spurs that radiate in all directions from the central mass remain fairly horizontal in their upper part, but descend in very steep slopes as they approach their bases.

‘This topographical and genetic description of Madeira, merely sketched here, is very well represented on the map that Jakob Melchior Ziegler drew on the basis of his own and others’ studies and drawings, and also on a relief map deposited at the Geological Institute of the University of Berlin.

‘All our theories on the nature of volcanism were first suggested to us by the geological examination of the island of Madeira, and soon afterwards confirmed by that of the Cape Verde islands. But we did not wish to publish them until we had also found them confirmed by the examination of other volcanic regions. We found this confirmation above all in South America. External circumstances long prevented the publication of the results of our studies. Today, after more than 20 years, we have resolved to publish them, at least in part.

The island of Tenerife bears a certain resemblance to Madeira in its configuration, although it is more than twice the size in area. This resemblance arises chiefly from the fact that Tenerife, too, is made up of two parts which must be distinguished genetically, even though tectonically they are joined and interlocked.

On Tenerife, too, we see the island’s caldera-shaped elevation joined to an extensive, flattened elevation without a crater. However, these two parts do not stand in the same relation to each other as, on Madeira, the caldera of the Curral does to the dome of the Paul da Serra. On Tenerife the part containing a caldera is so extensive and so high that the rest appears merely as a lateral appendage, a secondary member, which is not the case on Madeira.’
Sicilian sumac (Rhus Coriaria)

A shrub of the family Anacardiaceae, fully naturalised in Madeira. Its leaves have 4 to 7 pairs of ovate-lanceolate leaflets, sometimes reddish. The leaves and young shoots of this shrub are used for tanning leather. A certain quantity of sumac was once exported, but today this trade has come to a complete standstill.

Of this same shrub Gaspar Frutuoso says the following: ‘There is much sumac on this island of Madeira, which serves for tanning leather, especially cordovan, because it makes it very soft and white. This sumac is planted in small holes, as one plants roses and vines; its stem is like fennel, and its foliage resembles fennel too; it thrives on high, cool ground; it is harvested every year by cutting it level with the ground, so that the stock does not dry out and can sprout again, for it is a plant that lasts many years in the soil. It is a very profitable crop, because it multiplies so much that the fields fill with it, as with rose bushes, and the root spreads beneath the ground, and what grows on the island is very fine. Once the foliage, which is the said sumac, has been gathered, it is laid out in the sun, and when dry it is ground in a water mill (*engenho*), just as woad is ground on this island, and made into powder; and once ground it is shipped to various places in sacks and casks (*pipas*).’
Surface area

Estimates of the surface area of the whole archipelago, and especially of each of the islands that make it up, vary considerably. Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, who dealt with this subject at some length in his notable article in the *Dicionario Universal Portuguez Ilustrado*, says that some authors put the total area of the archipelago at more than a thousand square kilometres, and that it was later accepted that the area was around 800 kilometres. He ends by stating that the most recent calculations, which he considers closest to the truth, give the whole archipelago an area of 560 square kilometres: 500 kilometres for the island of Madeira, 50 for Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and 10 for the small group of the Desertas (‘deserted islands’).

Various official documents, and most recently the *Censo da População* published in the present year of 1934, state that the area of the island of Madeira is 740.62 square kilometres and that of Porto Santo 42,217. Apart from the cities of Lisbon and Porto, the Madeira archipelago is the region of our country with the highest population density, the *Censo* already cited giving a figure of 270 inhabitants per square kilometre for the present time.

Surdo (lane)

This lane links Rua do Dr. Vieira, or Rua da Carreira (‘track’), with Largo de São Pedro. On 24 April 1919, at the request of the Civil Registration Association (*Associação do Registo Civil*), it was given the name of the Madeiran Augusto José Vieira.
Augusto José Vieira, brother of Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira, was born in Funchal on 2 October 1861 and died in Lisbon on 27 December 1918.
Surprise

A French gunboat that was torpedoed by a German submarine in the harbour of Funchal on 3 December 1916, with the loss of 33 of her crew and 7 Portuguese, as related on page 159 of volume I of this work. When writing of General Mangin, we had occasion to say that the mortal remains of the French sailors that lay in the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery had been transferred on board the cruiser *Jules Michelet* on 28 November 1921. We must now add that a large procession was formed on that occasion, which accompanied the remains as far as the Pontinha (‘little point’).

The procession, which was about a kilometre long, was headed by a mounted detachment of the Republican Guard (*Guarda Republicana*). Behind it came the children of the schools and colleges with their teachers, the primary teaching body, the Funchal student body with its processional banner, the Banda Republicana Artístico Madeirense, the teachers of the lyceum (state secondary school), the scouts, chauffeurs, sports associations, the Banda dos Artistas Funchalenses, the firemen, various associations, the Red Cross (*Cruz Vermelha*), the crew of the Funchal lifeboat, the civil police and the Revenue Guard (*Guarda Fiscal*, customs and excise corps), the staff of the Harbour Master’s Office (*Capitania do Porto*), the junior staff of the customs house, the army sergeants, the ‘Grémio 5 de Outubro’, the English telegraph employees, the Commercial Association, the Press, the customs house officials, the District General Council (*Junta Geral*), the clergy, the Sisters of Charity, the doctors, the judiciary, the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), a naval contingent from the French cruiser *Cassiopée*, several English officers who had fought in the Great War, the officers of the garrison, three limbers bearing wreaths flanked by French sailors, two limbers carrying the coffins flanked by French petty officers, the French officers of the ships lying in the harbour, General Mangin, the civil governor, the secretary-general and the military governor, the diocesan prelate, Admiral Pugliesi-Conti, the consular corps, the brass band of the cruiser *Jules Michelet*, a naval detachment from the same ship, a detachment of the 27th Infantry with its band, and an infantry platoon of the Republican Guard.

Before the procession set off, speeches were made by Dr José Joaquim Teixeira Jardim, president of the Council, the consul of France, the military commander João Maria Ferraz, Major Artur Sarmento, the student José Duarte Soares, Admiral Conti and the harbour master Romano Vital Gomes. At the end of the speeches the band of the *Jules Michelet* played first *A Portuguesa* and then the *Marseillaise*.

The chapel of the Angústias cemetery, where the ten chestnut coffins holding the remains of the sailors of the *Surprise* lay, was draped in crape and brilliantly decorated with ferns and other plants. At the top of the façade hung the French flag, and below it the letters R. F. intertwined in red. Two lifebuoys hung on the walls, bearing the inscription: Surprise–3–12–916.

In the same chapel the diocesan prelate, Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, celebrated a mass attended by the senior authorities of the district, General Mangin, Admiral Conti, the officers of the Madeira military garrison, and the officers and sailors of the cruisers *Jules Michelet* and *Cassiopée*. During the ceremony the band of the first of these ships played Chopin’s funeral march, while a detachment of French sailors formed the guard of honour at the chapel door. The guard of honour at the cemetery gate was formed by an infantry detachment, with its band, and by another from the Republican Guard.

The 10 coffins with the mortal remains of the French sailors were carried to a launch of the *Jules Michelet*, while both the ship’s band and the band of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria n.° 27*) played the Marseillaise. General Mangin, Admiral Conti and other officers of the French navy boarded the same launch, and the Fort of São Tiago (St James the Greater) fired a salute.

At the moment of farewell, General Mangin and Admiral Conti once again expressed their gratitude to the civil, ecclesiastical and military authorities for the part they had taken in the tributes paid to the sailors of the *Surprise*.
The *Jules Michelet*, which carried the coffins with the remains of the French sailors, left the harbour of Funchal bound for Brest at half past seven in the evening of the said day, 28 November.

On 3 December 1921, five days after the tributes paid to the French sailors, the remains of the Madeirans killed in the torpedoing of the gunboat *Surprise* were borne to the tomb-monument that the wealthy banker Henrique Vieira de Castro had had built in the Angústias cemetery. These remains, kept in three urns, lay in the cemetery chapel, where at half past nine in the morning the diocesan prelate celebrated Mass, followed by the ritual absolution and the blessing of the grave. The decorations used for the tributes to the French sailors could still be seen in the chapel and along the cemetery avenue.

The procession formed at about 3 in the afternoon, in the following order: children of the Colégio Alexandre Herculano with their headmistress; girls from the orphanage of the Hospício (hospice (*hospício*)); a detachment of the Republican Guard; the sergeants of the Funchal garrison; representatives of the maritime staff of the Blandy firm; the students of Funchal; Sisters of St Vincent de Paul; the French community; representatives of the clergy; representatives of the embroidery houses; the guild (*grémio*) of commercial employees; doctors and lawyers; civil servants; ladies of the Red Cross; the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*); the urns, carried by volunteer firemen and flanked by councillors (*vereadores*); some women, relatives of the victims; the consular corps; the civil and military authorities and the diocesan prelate; officers of the garrison; and the band of the Artistas Funchalenses.

Speeches were made by the president of the Council, Dr Teixeira Jardim, Major Alberto Artur Sarmento and Commander Vital Gomes, after which the urns were carried to the monument and placed there. The Artistas band played *A Portuguesa* after each of the speeches delivered in the cemetery, and the national anthem was heard again, played by the same band and by that of the 27th Infantry Regiment (*regimento de infantaria 27*), as the urns were lowered into the tomb. At this solemn moment a detachment of infantry and another of the Republican Guard gave the military salute.

Throughout the day public buildings and consulates kept their flags at half-mast, and many shops half-closed their doors, shutting them completely while the ceremonies lasted. The same had been done during the ceremonies of 28 November, and it may be said without fear of contradiction that Madeira paid a fitting tribute both to the French and to the Portuguese who were treacherously killed in Funchal harbour on the morning of 3 December 1916. See Bombardment of Funchal, Angústias (cemetery) and Mangin (General).
T
Tobacco
A plant of the nightshade family (Solanaceae) native to America, whose leaves give off a strong, noxious smell when fresh. To make use of these leaves, they must be properly dried and fermented.

Tobacco growing has been free in the Adjacent Islands (*Ilhas Adjacentes*) since the publication of the law of 13 May 1864, whose provisions were maintained or extended by the law of 15 June 1882 and the decree of 8 October 1885.

While the monopoly was in force, Madeira had an administrator (*administrador do concelho*, government-appointed head of the municipality) of the tobacco contract and guards who enforced that same contract, and they often carried the strictness with which they performed their fiscal duties to extremes.

Between 1877 and 1882 some tobacco was planted in Madeira, chiefly in São Gonçalo and Santo António (‘St Anthony’). In 1907 the plant was cultivated on the island once again, but it never became widespread, even though it grows well in our soils when they are properly fertilised. *Nicotina Tabacum* was the dominant species in the plantings made in 1907 and the years that followed, but in some localities *Nicotina rústica* could also be seen. The first of these species grows naturalised on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and its cultivation is at present abandoned, or almost abandoned, throughout the archipelago.

In October 1877 the late Viscount of Monte Belo founded a factory for processing tobacco in Madeira. On 18 July 188? a second factory for the same purpose was set up; it lasted only a very short time, and its owner was the late João de Sales Caldeira. The first of these factories, after operating for some years on its owner’s account, was leased at the beginning of the 19th century to Francisco Gonçalves, who carried on the tobacco-processing industry on this island, at first alone and later in partnership with Nicásio de Azevedo Ramos and Abraão Adida.

In 1908 the ‘Companhia de Tabacos da Madeira’ was established in Funchal. It was wound up in 1912 and was succeeded by the ‘Empresa Madeirense de Tabacos, Lda’, founded on 1 October 1918, whose members were Leacock & C.ª, William Hinton & Filhos, Reid, Castro & C.ª and Rocha Machado & C.ª. The firms Reid, Castro & C.ª, Rocha Machado & C.ª and Hinton & Filhos gave up their rights – the first on 27 April 1914, the second on 26 January 1916 and the last on 28 April 1920 – and the tobacco business was left in the hands of the firm Leacock & C.ª. On 27 September 1920 this firm admitted Diogo Martinho de Freitas as a partner, and he is today the manager of the ‘Empresa Madeirense de Tabacos, Lda.’ (1921).

In 1922 this company imported 49,920 kilograms of leaf tobacco from the Azores, and in the same period 218,052 kilograms of processed tobacco arrived from the Azores and from abroad for various Funchal merchants. We have read somewhere that in 1914 the same company processed 40,918 kilograms of tobacco, 467 of them of Madeiran origin.

The defunct ‘Companhia de Tabacos da Madeira’ made use of the machinery of the Viscount of Monte Belo’s old factory, but the ‘Empresa Madeirense de Tabacos, Lda.’ has acquired various improved machines for its industry, and its products rival those that come from the Azores (1921).

On folio 232 of book VII of the ‘Arquivo da Câmara Municipal do Funchal’ a warrant (*provisão*) of 1698 is registered, which states that a new administration of tobacco in Madeira was to begin in the following year, 1699. In 1686 there was a judge-conservator (*juiz conservador*, judge protecting the monopoly’s privileges) of the state monopoly (*estanco*) on this island, an office that still existed in 1745, when it was held by the superintendent of the royal treasury (*provedor da fazenda*). The laws of 10 July 1919 and 22 January 1920 created a municipal tax of 50 centavos on every kilogram of tobacco cleared through the customs house. In 1922 this tax yielded the sum of 21,837.21 escudos (the Portuguese currency from 1911: 1 escudo = 100 centavos = 1,000 réis) for the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*).
Prickly pear (*Opuntia Turvei*)

A member of the cactus family native to tropical America, naturalised and cultivated in the lower zone (coastal belt) of Madeira. The berry-like fruits of the prickly pear (*tabaibeira*) are sweet and refreshing, and the fleshy, succulent, flattened and jointed branches of the plant (commonly called leaves) make good fodder for livestock once they have been cleaned of their spines.

The peel of the *tabaibos* (the fruits) is used to feed pigs. A few prickly pears grow at Campo de Baixo (‘lower field’) and Serra de Dentro (‘inner upland’) on the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Tide table
See Tides (II-324) and the harbour of Funchal (III-102).
Tábua (parish)

It seems that the origin of this parish’s name should be traced to a plant called *tábua*. The names Tabua and Tabuaço were given to places where that plant grew in abundance, and perhaps for the same reason the word Tábua appears several times in Brazilian chorography. Botany knows *Typha angustifolia* and *Typha latifolia*. Although these plants are not found on the island at present, the Madeiran flora has undergone appreciable changes, partly caused by man, so it is reasonable to suppose that in ancient times these plants, or one of them, grew within the area of this parish (*freguesia*). A species of *Typha* is found in the Canary Islands, so it would not be surprising if the genus had been represented in Madeira. In the locality (*sítio*) of Lugar de Baixo (‘lower place’) and at Tábua there grows a plant, *Cyperus laevigatus*, that is not found anywhere else in Madeira. Might the first settlers have confused this plant with the *tábua*, even though the two belong to species of different families? This too is possible, for it is reasonable to assume that Zarco and his companions were not distinguished for their learning in botanical matters.

In earlier times the word was spelt Atabua, as can be seen in many old documents and in the parish archive. It was from 1838 that Father António Francisco Drumond e Vasconcelos changed the original form of the word and began to write Tábua. His successors down to the present have adopted the new spelling, which is today generally followed by everyone.

The annotator of the *Saudades* gives 1586 as the year in which this parish was created. The oldest instrument cited in the *Índice Geral da Provedoria...* and in the *Memorias do Estado Eclesiástico...* is that of 1 March 1577, which added 8,700 *réis* to the original parish stipend (*côngrua*) of 11,300 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) a year. The same sources mention the royal decrees (alvará régio) of 15 December 1588, 15 November 1591 and 18 January 1654, which raised the parish priest’s annual salary respectively to 20,000 *réis*, half a *moio* (dry measure of grain, 60 *alqueires*) of wheat and a quarter of wine; to 16,000 *réis*, one *moio* of wheat and one *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) of wine; and to 19,000 *réis*, half a *moio* of wheat and a quarter of wine.
João Medeiros de Miranda, Manuel de Espínola, António Velho de Amil Luciano Espínola and Rui Gomes were the first priests to exercise parish duties in this parish.

The royal decree of 2 July 1743 established a curacy (*curato*) in this parish, the instrument stating that it ‘had been created at the request of the vicar António Miguel de Faria, because the said parish lies between two full-flowing streams and has more than a thousand parishioners’. The same decree set the curate’s annual stipend at one and a half *moios* of wheat and one and a half *pipas* of wine.

We do not know where the seat of the parish was established when it was created. We conjecture that a chapel of the Holy Trinity (*Santíssima Trindade*) already stood there and that the seat of the new parish (*freguesia*) was installed in it, as generally happened throughout the diocese in the early days of colonisation. It was no doubt a chapel of modest proportions, which must have undergone various repairs and perhaps enlargements until a church of more ample dimensions was built. The building that served as the parish church before the present one was destroyed by a flash flood (*aluvião*). It stood opposite the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*), and traces of the original building can still be seen on the site. An order of the Council of the Treasury (*Conselho da Fazenda*) dated 22 October 1675 decreed that a new church be built. However, it seems that the work either did not begin at once or proceeded very slowly, for on the façade of the church one reads the inscription ‘Rei Dom Pedro – 1696’ (King Dom Pedro), which is certainly the date of the building’s completion.

In an old document we read that in 1747 a request was made for a tabernacle with the Blessed Sacrament (*Santíssimo Sacramento*) in the parish church of Tábua, which had not previously existed, so that some of the faithful had died without receiving the Holy Viaticum.

This parish has the chapels of Madre de Deus (Mother of God) and of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, of which we have already given a brief account on pages 312 and 432 of volume II, and that of Nossa Senhora da Candelária (Our Lady of Candelaria), about which we know no particulars whatsoever.

Of this parish, Dr Gaspar Frutuoso wrote in 1590: ‘Half a *légua* from Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) lies Ribeira da Tábua, with a parish of almost thirty households (*fogos*, literally ‘hearths’). It once had two sugar mills and has many vineyards, canes and fruits, but its wine is like that of its neighbour Ribeira Brava. From this Ribeira da Tábua come the Medeiros, a noble and honourable people.’ The annotator of the *Saudades* rightly observes that at that time this parish had more than 100 households and not merely 30, as is clearly deduced from the royal decrees concerning the parish stipends which are cited there.

Regarding the Medeiros family, Dr Rodrigues de Azevedo says that ‘Rui Vaz de Medeiros was one of the first settlers who came to Madeira: he held as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) many lands in Atabua, from the stream towards the locality of Zimbreiro (‘juniper’)’. Another early settler of Tábua, Dr Azevedo also says, was the Frenchman Rui Vaz Urzel, who came to this island around 1480. Other early colonists and settlers there were Álvaro Martins, Jorge Lourenço, António Rodrigues, Manuel Rodrigues, António Luís, Diogo Fernandes, etc.
Several people from the parish of Tábua were involved in the popular riots that took place in the parish of Ribeira Brava and in the court cases that followed them (see page 385 of volume II).

The principal localities are: Praia, Lugares, Terça, Fajã, Ribeira, Boqueirão, Pico do Ferreiro, Bica de Pau, Corujeira, Zimbreiro, Massapés, Candelária, Ribeira da Caixa, Lugar da Serra and Barbuzano. When the municipality (*concelho*) of Ribeira Brava was created in 1914, the parish of Tábua became part of it, having then been detached from the municipality of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). This parish has 2,235 inhabitants (1921).
Tábua (stream)

The stream crosses the parish (*freguesia*) of Tábua from north to south and flows out on its coastline. It rises on the slopes of Pico das Pedras (‘peak of the stones’), at the edge of the Paul da Serra (‘upland marsh’), and receives the tributary brook of Barqueiro.
Grey mullet (Mugil corrugatus)

A fish of the family Mugilidae, today rare in the seas near the coast of Madeira because of the use of explosives to catch it. ‘The rational fishing of the grey mullet’, says Mr Adolfo de Noronha, ‘is done with the drag net or with the set net, especially in summer, when it comes into the shallow coastal waters. It is not caught on the hook, and can come to the rod only by accident, provided the hook used is of very small size.’

The grey mullet is a very tasty fish and therefore fetches a high price at market. Besides the species we have just described, *Mugil cephalus* and *M. auratus* also occur in Madeira, the latter known by the name of *tainha da moda*.

Fishermen often call grey mullets *mujas* (a corruption of *mugens*) and also *galinhas do mar* (‘sea hens’). The latter name is due to their ‘having a true crop that recalls that of the hen and is formed by the caecal stomach, lined internally by an extremely thick epithelium’.
Tamarisk (Tamarix gallica)

A tree or shrub of the family Tamaricaceae, widely cultivated on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it was introduced by João António Pedroso in 1834. A few tamarisks are also found in the *quintas* and gardens of Madeira.
Tams (Dr George)

Physician to a commercial expedition to the west coast of Africa organised by Ribeiro dos Santos, Portuguese consul in Altona. The expedition’s ships called at the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) in July 1841. Dr Tams wrote a work about the expedition in which he took part, with the following title: *Portugiesische Besitzungem in Sud West Afrika Mit einem Vorworte von Prof. Carl. Ritter*; Hamburg, 1845. This work has been translated into Portuguese and English.
Plantain

Two species are known by this name in Madeira: *Plantago lanceolada* and *P. major*. The first species has broadly ovate leaves with 5–7 veins. A decoction of the leaves of these two Plantaginaceae, both very common in Madeira, is widely used for diseases of the eyes.
Tangerine Tree, see Orange Tree
Tarolo (E.)
See Sousa (Ernesto Venceslau de).
Loggerhead turtle (Caouana Oaretta)

An amphibious reptile of the subclass Chelonia that appears in the seas near Madeira. Madeirans prize its meat, although it is less tasty than that of the tropical turtle. Its eggs have never been found on Madeira or Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and it is therefore supposed that the animal lays them in the sands of some of the Cape Verde islands.
Fishermen catch the turtle when they find it asleep on the surface of the ocean.
Tavares

Around the middle of the 15th century there lived in Madeira Joana Tavares, who was married to Vasco Esteves, nicknamed ‘o dos bons vinhos’ (he of the good wines). After 1580 Bernardo Tavares de Sousa, of noble origin, settled on this island. It is to be believed that the individuals with the surname Tavares who have lived here descend from these two stocks.
Tavares (Joaquim da Silva)

A distinguished Portuguese cecidologist who has done much to make known the zoocecidia of Portugal, Madeira and other countries. He is a member of the Society of Jesus and of the Lisbon Academy of Sciences (*Academia das Ciências de Lisboa*), and has taught in Portugal, Brazil and Spain. He wrote three contributions to the study of the zoocecidia of Madeira, all published in *Broteria*, the first in 1903, the second in 1905 and the last in 1914 (1921).
According to Father Tavares, of some 80 zoocecidia known in Madeira, most are the work of aphids or eriophyid mites.
Távora (Dom Álvaro José Xavier Botelho de)

Dom Álvaro Botelho de Távora was Count of São Miguel and was appointed governor and captain-general of Madeira on 21 July 1751, taking office on 27 August of the same year. He found many abuses in every branch of public administration, which he sought to correct and reform. He left the governorship on 6 May 1754 to take up the post of governor of the province of Goiás, in Brazil.
He died on 24 April 1789, having governed Madeira for less than three years.
Távora (Dom Fernando de)
He was the 5th bishop of this diocese, confirmed by Pope Pius V in the consistory of 14 November 1570.
He was a native of Santarém, the son of Fernão Cardoso and Dona Filipa de Brito, who belonged to the noblest and most distinguished families of that town (*vila*).

After taking his doctorate in theology at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), he entered the Order of St Dominic, in which he held important offices. He was a renowned preacher in his day and enjoyed a reputation as a man of rare talent and vast learning. He wrote a book of commentaries on the Gospel of St John and other works, which remained unpublished.

He enjoyed the particular esteem of King Sebastian, who in 1569 appointed him prelate of this diocese. He exercised the office through his vicars-general and never came to Madeira, out of the fear that the ocean crossing inspired in him. We know of no noteworthy event that marked his episcopal administration here.

Recognising that he could not take personal charge of his bishopric, he resigned the mitre in 1573 and was then appointed almoner (*esmoler*) to King Sebastian. He died in 1577 and was buried in the convent of São Domingos in Lisbon.
Távora (Dom Lourenço de)

This Funchal prelate left in the ecclesiastical chronicles of this bishopric an honourable memory of his episcopal administration. Brief though his time in this diocese was, he linked it to certain acts that justice requires us to mention specially in this place.

He belonged to one of the most distinguished families of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), being the son of Álvaro de Sousa and Dona Francisca de Távora. He was a nephew of the sadly notorious Dom Cristóvão de Moura, Marquis of Castelo Rodrigo, one of the Portuguese who did most to bring Portugal under Castilian rule.

Philip II went so far as to tear Friar Lourenço de Távora from the peace of the convent to which he had voluntarily withdrawn and where he had expected to spend his whole life. He was appointed prelate of Madeira in October 1609 and was consecrated bishop on 6 July 1610, taking charge of his bishopric the following year.

He convened a diocesan council, at which he promulgated several constitutions intended to correct the many abuses that had crept into ecclesiastical discipline. Under severe penalties, he compelled the administrators of chantries (capela) to fulfil the pious obligations to which they were bound and which had in large part already fallen into disuse. In the ordination of priests he was extremely scrupulous, conferring holy orders only on those he judged truly worthy of exercising the priestly ministry with the irreproachable conduct proper to that state. For some months he served on an interim basis as governor and captain-general of this archipelago, a post to which he had been appointed by royal decree (alvará régio) of 8 April 1614. After governing the diocese of Funchal for six years, he was transferred to the bishopric of Elvas, leaving Madeira on 7 October 1617.

In 1625 he resigned the episcopal see of Elvas and withdrew into the seclusion of his first convent, Santo António dos Capuchos (St Anthony of the Capuchins), in Lisbon. There, according to Jorge Cardoso, he died with a reputation for sanctity on 11 May 1629.

Before renouncing the mitre and retiring to his monastery, he gave the fabric of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) some dwelling houses that he owned in that city, with the obligation of celebrating a number of annual masses for the repose of his soul.
He was the eighth prelate of this diocese, having succeeded Dom Luís de Figueiredo e Lemos
Taylor (Helena MJ)

An Englishwoman who lived for many years in Madeira and died in England in October 1907, aged about 65. Works: *Madeira: its scenery, and how to see it* (London, 1882). This work contains a list of Madeiran ferns and another of Madeiran marine algae.
Theatre

The enthusiasm for theatrical performances here in Madeira probably followed the same phases as in the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). In churches and in the parlours of convents, *autos* and poems of a religious character were performed, in which the sanctity of the place was not always duly respected. The Constitutions of this bishopric, promulgated and approved in 1578, laid down ‘that no performances… be held in churches or chapels, by day or by night, without the special licence of the prelate, because of the many drawbacks and scandals that follow from them’.

We have found vague references to these performances in the churches and convents of this diocese, but we cannot determine precisely the nature of these spectacles or the way in which they were staged. We know that in 1622 a religious *auto* was performed in the church of São João Evangelista (St John the Evangelist), when solemn festivities were held there to mark the canonisation of St Francis Xavier. In the church or Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), the annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) tells us, there was a dramatic performance in 1718, when the governor and captain-general João de Saldanha da Gama left Madeira. It was written by Francisco de Vasconcelos Coutinho (volume I, page 315) and entitled *Residência do Governador e Capitão General*… and was performed by the nuns of the Convent of St Clare at his farewell; its characters were the Island, the Court, Longing, Religion and Fame. Before 1780 there was already a modest playhouse in Funchal, situated in the Rua das Fontes (‘springs’). This house, which at the beginning of the 19th century was called ‘da Comedia Velha’ (of the Old Comedy), collapsed on 19 March 1829, although its façade remained standing. In that year of 1780, it seems, the construction of the Teatro Grande (‘great theatre’) was completed; we devote a separate article to it.
Around 1820, or shortly before, and therefore while that theatre still existed (it was demolished in 1833), the Teatro do Bom Gosto was built; we also deal with it in another article.

When this theatre ceased to operate around 1838, steps were taken to convert the refectory and other quarters of the dissolved Convent of St Francis into a theatre, which was given the singular name of Prazer Regenerado and which did not last long. It opened on 20 December 1840.

At about this time or shortly afterwards the Concórdia dramatic society was formed. Around 1842 it had a small theatre of the same name built in Rua do Monteiro, where the distinguished performer Robio appeared before the public and where, in 1844, the drama *Amor e Pátria* by Sérvulo de Medina e Vasconcelos (volume II, page 336) was staged. A few performances were still given there in 1851. In 1856 the opening of the street between Ponte do Bettencourt and the church of Carmo (Carmelite church) led the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) to demolish the building in which that small theatre was housed.

José Silvestre Ribeiro, the most illustrious and public-spirited governor Madeira has had, sought to attend to and improve every branch of public administration and every local amenity, and he certainly could not neglect the establishment of a theatre in this city. If his diligent efforts and persevering initiative were not crowned with success, this was due solely to the insurmountable difficulties that arose and to the little zeal and commitment shown towards the undertaking by various private individuals, the administrative bodies, the deputies and the central government, as can be seen in volume 3 of the *Epocha Administrativa*. This took place in 1851 and 1852.

Around 1858 a dramatic society known as Talia was founded in Funchal. It gave a number of performances in various venues and later rented a house in Largo do Pelourinho (‘pillory’). We do not know when it ceased to exist, nor who its members and directors were, but it was still performing in public in 1859, after the Teatro Esperança had already opened.
We shall give a brief account of the latter in a separate article.

During the lifetime of the Teatro Esperança, and even before it, several dramatic societies were formed in this city, staging many dramas and comedies in various places. The Lancasterian School (*Escola Lancasteriana*) was at times used as a venue for concerts and for theatrical performances.

Between 1850 and 1880 various private and official attempts were made to provide this city with a theatre which, without being a grand playhouse, might nonetheless satisfy the wishes of the population and suit the conditions and circumstances of our community. All these efforts proved fruitless, however, until a bolder and more enterprising body of councillors resolved to build a theatre. It raised a loan for the purpose and at last gave Funchal an excellent playhouse, the present Teatro Manuel de Arriaga, which we shall discuss in another article of this work.
Besides the Teatro Manuel de Arriaga, Funchal today has the Teatro Circo and the Pavilhão Paris, the latter opened on 23 October 1909 and the former on 3 September 1911 (1921).

Several Madeirans have cultivated dramatic literature, writing plays of various genres for the stage. Among them we may mention Baltasar Dias, Francisco de Vasconcelos Coutinho, José Anselmo Correia Henriques, Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar, Sérvulo de Medina e Vasconcelos, João de Nóbrega Soares, Maximiliano de Azevedo, João de Freitas Branco, Luís António Gonçalves de Freitas, Dona Olímpia Fernandes, João dos Reis Gomes, José Jorge Rodrigues dos Santos, Jaime Câmara, Elmano Vieira, Alberto Figueira Jardim, etc., whose writings we mention in the articles devoted to these authors in this work.

Theatrical subjects were treated with great expertise by Luís da Costa Pereira, in the work *Rudimentos da Arte Dramática*, and by J. dos Reis Gomes in the books *O Teatro e o Actor*, which ran to two editions, and *A Música e o Teatro*.
Teatro de Bom Gosto

It seems that the existence in Funchal of the Teatro Grande (see that entry), a large and showy playhouse, did not justify the construction of a new theatre, which was given the name Teatro de Bom Gosto (‘good taste theatre’) and was built a few metres away from it. We do not know exactly when it was built, but we conjecture that it was between 1818 and 1820; it certainly already existed in 1821. It stood between Rua de São Francisco and the Misericórdia building (*Edifício da Misericórdia*) (1921), with access both to that street and to the side of the old Passeio Público (‘public promenade’). We do not know what led to the building of this new theatre, although some years ago we heard it said that it was chiefly owed to a whim of the 1st Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’).

We do not know whether that nobleman had it built, but we do know that it belonged to him and that, on returning from exile at the end of 1834, he had major repairs carried out there. It was then transformed into a respectable playhouse with 18 first-tier boxes and 6 second-tier boxes, 230 seats in the stalls and two galleries, one for men and the other for women. We have been told that it was larger than the old Teatro Esperança (‘Hope Theatre’) and that its interior was pleasant and attractive.

We do not know when it closed and ceased to host any theatrical performance. We know only that a show was still staged there in 1838, and it is said somewhere that by then it was already in an advanced state of ruin, which is difficult to reconcile with the repairs carried out there on the orders of the Count of Carvalhal, as mentioned above.
Teatro Esperança

Towards the end of 1858 a society of eighteen young men was formed in this city with the aim of staging some theatrical performances and building a small playhouse. This society, named Esperança, included among others Júlio Galhardo de Freitas and Pedro de Alcântara Góis, who had already shown their remarkable talent for the stage in several performances. The merchant João de Freitas Martins came to the aid of this worthy society by placing at its disposal an excellent warehouse he owned on Rua dos Aranhas. Conversion work began at once. The Council of Funchal contributed 200,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), and the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’) gave a similar sum and donated the scenery, this nobleman being the most devoted patron of the Esperança Society (*Sociedade Esperança*).

The formal opening took place on 10 March 1859 with performances of the plays *o Judeu* and *o Conde de Paragará*. António José de Sousa Almada (volume I, page 45), a dramatist and editor of a theatrical review who was then in Funchal, rendered the Esperança Society notable services in choosing, rehearsing and staging the plays.
When Rua 5 de Julho was opened, the Teatro Esperança was reduced to more cramped proportions, since the opening of that street required the demolition of some of the theatre’s outbuildings.
In 1887 it was acquired by the Count of Canavial and took that nobleman’s name. On 28 August 1915 it was sold to the builder João Pinto Correia, who demolished it shortly afterwards.
Until 1888, when the Teatro D. Maria Pia opened, the small Teatro Esperança was the only playhouse here, and various operetta and drama companies performed there.
Teatro Grande

The Teatro Grande (‘great theatre’) was the name by which people here knew the playhouse that stood opposite the Palácio de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence’) and occupied a large part of the square known as Largo da Restauração. It was built around 1780, and its demolition was ordered in 1833.

Miguel dos Santos Coimbra and José Rodrigues Pereira applied for the emphyteutic lease (*aforamento*, perpetual lease for an annual quit-rent) of a plot of land beside the fortress of São Lourenço, measuring 170 *palmos* in length and 60 in width, for the construction of the Casa da Ópera (opera house). The ‘master of works’ (*capitão-mestre*) reported that there was no objection to granting this concession. On 10 April 1776, therefore, a lease contract on the terms requested was concluded at the government secretariat, the grantees undertaking to pay an annual quit-rent (*foro*) of 5,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis).

The construction of this theatre was slow because of the great expense it entailed, due above all to the ample proportions given to it, although so vast a playhouse was hardly necessary in a place as small as Funchal. It was the largest theatre in Portugal after São Carlos, and its building cost around eighty *contos*, which 150 years ago was an enormous sum.

We do not know the exact year in which the building work on the theatre was declared finished, nor when the first performance was given there. We do know, however, that a few years after its completion, and after a good many performances had been given in it, it remained closed ‘for a long time owing to discord between impresarios and authors’, as the poet Francisco Manuel de Oliveira says in a note in his book of verse *Colecção Poética*. Oliveira further tells us that, after some repairs, it reopened on 29 January 1786. Among other pieces, a verse Prologue was performed, whose speakers were Discord, Funchal, Good Taste and Decency, from the pen of the same poet.

By a ministerial order (*portaria*) of the governor and captain-general, Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho, dated 1 July 1790, José Nicolau Teixeira de Vasconcelos e Câmara was appointed minister to the ‘Casa do Theatro’ at a time when a ‘Companhia Cómica’ (comic company) was performing there under the direction of the actor Pedro Baquino; this minister exercised very close superintendence and supervision over all the company’s activities. The theatre continued to operate for some years, until it fell prey to a fire that partly destroyed it on Maundy Thursday in one of the last years of the 18th century. When this island was occupied by British troops for the first time, from July 1801 to January 1802, the Teatro Grande served as a store for those troops’ provisions and equipment, by which time it was already in an advanced state of ruin.

‘It was later rebuilt,’ says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, ‘at the expense of the property owners and merchants, the government assisting them only by granting an annual lottery whose first prize was three *contos* (one million réis) de réis. When the royal family and the court fled to Brazil in 1807, a large part of the singing and dancing company that worked at the São Carlos theatre in Lisbon came to this island of Madeira under a three-year contract. The management was in the hands of the wealthy property owners Henrique Correia de Vilhena and Nuno de Freitas da Silva, who suffered losses of more than eighty *contos de réis*: the first went bankrupt as a result, and the second faced lawsuits and distraints. After its rebuilding this theatre had ninety boxes, forming four tiers, three hundred seats in the stalls and one hundred in the gallery.’

For many years various Portuguese and foreign companies performed there. In 1821, *O Patriota Funchalense* (‘The Funchal Patriot’) tells us, the ‘Companhia Grotesca’ of the Italian Fabri played at this theatre; it consisted of three men and women, who sang operettas and performed various ballets. The following year the same theatre held a gala performance at which a symphony composed by Father António Francisco Drumond was heard, and a drama in three acts entitled *A Festa do Olimpo*, by the distinguished Madeiran Manuel Caetano Pimenta de Aguiar, was staged.

Then came the turbulent times of our civil wars. The theatre was closed for long periods, and whenever it opened temporarily to the public, political demonstrations broke out at once, sometimes leading to disturbances of the peace in which armed troops had to intervene. In the end it was these displays of partisan factionalism that sealed the theatre’s fate.

The Teatro Grande was demolished in 1833, not in 1832 as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo states. It is much to be regretted that Funchal was thus deprived of a playhouse as vast and as finely decorated as this one was; the act can only be accepted and explained by the despotism then exercised by the absolutist government during the bloody civil war that was ravaging the country at the time. The reasons given for the demolition were that the theatre adjoined a fortress and hampered the defence of the city, that the street facing the governors’ palace needed widening, that the entrance to the palace should be embellished, etc. All of these make up a series of futile arguments, worthless as a justification for the violent and arbitrary measure of destroying a building of the importance and size of that magnificent playhouse. We have already given the true reason for the demolition elsewhere. On some performance nights, supporters of constitutional ideas took advantage of the large gathering of spectators to voice their liberal sentiments and spread the principles they professed, this propaganda spreading from the stage to the stalls, even though it amounted to a sacrilege against the established institutions.

The governor and captain-general of the time, Dom Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo, was moved by a spirit of rectitude and justice, and conciliatory tendencies could be seen in the acts of his administration. Even so, there came a moment when he let himself be carried away by the despotic demands of party politics. Yielding to the entreaties of his fellow partisans and bad advisers, he ordered the Teatro Grande to be razed to its foundations. It was the second largest playhouse in the country and had been built more than fifty years before. Simply closing the theatre would have saved it entirely from complete destruction.
Manuel de Arriaga Theatre

It was the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), under the presidency of João Sauvaire da Câmara, that began building our theatre, and the foundation stone was laid on 24 October 1884. The designs, plans and estimates were drawn up by the Porto engineer F. Soler, and all the building work was carried out under the direction of the master builder Manuel Pereira, a native of the city of Porto. The painting, the decoration and a considerable part of the scenery are the work of the Portuguese artist Eugénio Cotrim (1849-1937) and of the Italian Luigi Manini, who was born and died in Lisbon. All the work was declared complete in July 1887, and on the 27th of that month these artists, at a fine celebration held in the new theatre, formally handed this playhouse over to the Council. Its formal inauguration took place on 11 March 1888.

Despite the construction defects that can be seen in it and other shortcomings that would have been easy to correct, it is without doubt an excellent playhouse, and one of the finest our country possesses. At the formal inauguration the zarzuela *Las Dos Princesas* was staged by the Spanish company of José Zamorano. Since then various Portuguese and foreign companies have performed there, the principal ones being: the zarzuela companies of José Zamorano, Ramon Novarro Frederico Reparaz, Pablo Lopez and Ramon Santiago; the Italian opera company of maestro Patri; the operetta companies of Sousa Bastos, Stichini, Santos Júnior and Paquita Calvo – Fróis; the drama companies of Vitaliani Duse, Augusto Rosa, Joaquim de Almeida, Lucinda Simões, Taveira, Carlos de Oliveira, Ruas Ginásio and Ernesto do Vale; the concert performers Gabriela Reusser, the Pignateli quartet, the Júdice Costa quintet, Viana da Mota and Moreira de Sá Brindis de Salas and the Bensaúde quartet; and the conjurors and variety acts of J. C. Oliveira, the Companhia Russa, Francisco Franco, etc.

The Teatro Manuel de Arriaga (‘Manuel de Arriaga Theatre’) has 18 ground-floor boxes, 20 first-tier boxes, 21 second-tier boxes, 100 *fauteuils*, 160 seats and 200 places in the general gallery. The atrium is 34 metres long and 6 and a half wide, with 11 doors at the front and 2 on each side. On the upper floor there is a fine hall of the same dimensions with 15 windows. The theatre also has an excellent scene-painting room with a gallery running around it, from which there is a sweeping panorama.

Its first name was Teatro D. Maria Pia (‘Queen Maria Pia Theatre’), which the Municipal Council changed in November 1910 to Teatro Dr. Manuel de Arriaga (‘Dr Manuel de Arriaga Theatre’). However, this former deputy for Madeira flatly refused, in an official letter of 31 December, to allow his name to be given to the theatre. The Municipal Council therefore resolved, at its session of 12 January 1912, to name it Teatro Funchalense. On the death of Dr Manuel de Arriaga, whose name is bound up with the history of Madeira because of the way he championed the interests of this archipelago in parliament, the Council decided to perpetuate his name here in Madeira by calling our foremost theatre the Teatro Dr. Manuel de Arriaga (1921).
Teck (Prince and Princess of)

Prince Alexander of Teck and his wife, Princess Alice, called at Funchal on 8 January 1924 aboard the British steamer *Windsor Castle*, bound for the Cape of Good Hope. They were received with military honours. They went up to Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’), where they took an afternoon meal, then descended to Funchal in wicker toboggans (*carros de verga*), embarking shortly after midday.
Teijeira (*Arctium minus*)

A tubuliflorous composite that can grow to more than 1 metre in height, with wrinkled leaves, the lower ones sometimes very large, flower heads (*capítulos*) with an involucre of bracts ending in hooked, non-spiny tips, and purple flowers. It is found at Monte, at Ribeiro Frio, etc. An infusion of the leaves of this plant is widely used to treat skin diseases. See Dedaleira.
Teive (family)

The annotator of the *Saudades* and various books of genealogy state that this family surname ‘derives from Diogo de Teive, who in the year 1452 made a contract with Prince Henry the Navigator, in which he calls himself squire of the said Infante, and in which he undertook to build on the island of Madeira a sugar mill (engenho), the first there ever was here. He held much *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) land at Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and on the northern side, and there he founded an entailed estate (*morgadio*)’.

If the Teive family was illustrious for the lineage and ancestry of its forebears, it was no less so, and with ample reason, for counting among its members several men who distinguished themselves notably in arms and in letters, leaving a name crowned with glory in the history of this archipelago. We shall make brief mention of some of them. Diogo de Teive, the founder of the entailed estate, had several sons. He was succeeded in the administration of the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) by Gaspar de Teive, who held important court offices. He was accountant to Queen Catherine and master of the horse to Princess Maria, wife of Philip II, and to Dona Joana, mother of King Sebastian, whom he accompanied to Spain and where he died.

Gaspar de Teive left numerous descendants. Concerning his four sons, Diogo, Pantaleão, Aleixo and Gaspar, we transcribe word for word, leaving it all its old flavour, what we found in a piece of writing published some seventy years ago, which seems to us to date from the 18th century: ‘Dom Diogo de Teive, who was baptised in the same parish church of São Bento in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava in March 1540, was a page and then a gentleman of King Philip, with whom he took part in the expedition to England in the year 1544; and in Flanders he carried his helmet at the assault on Guintem. He went to Peru, whence he returned, serving the same king with that famous pearl kept in the Royal Treasury, called the Orphan because no equal to it has been found, of 89 carats. For this service the king granted him the royal grant of the staff of office of Chief Alguazil of Penama, with four thousand pesos of income for his life and that of his son, nine thousand *cruzados* towards his costs for the second expedition, and the corregidorship of Ariquipa, with two colleagues, in Peru, where he died, leaving distinguished descendants in Spain.','
‘Dom Pantaleão, his brother, was also a gentleman of the same kingdom, and the finest figure in Spain in his day; he died in Madrid, unmarried, of a lovesickness, in 1569.

‘Dom Aleixo de Teive, brother of the aforesaid, was page to Prince Carlos, whom he attended until the year 1668, when the death of that unfortunate prince took place; he was very valiant and, by order of the same King, it is said, he was found dead beneath the Ladies’ Balcony with 24 wounds, on the morning of 28 November 1573. ‘Dom Gaspar de Teive, another of his brothers, was brought up at the Paço (‘manor house’), where he was a *menino* of the prince and later page to Queen Isabel; he went to Germany in the year 1571 with the princes Ernest and Rudolf, and was a gentleman of the latter when he was emperor, and at his command came to Portugal to greet King Sebastian, whom he accompanied at the battle of Alcácer, and there he was killed on 4 August 1578.

‘António de Teive, his uncle, who was born in the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) of Ribeira Brava in the year 1516, served King John III at court and afterwards went to India, where he held various posts until he became overseer of the royal treasury (*vedor da fazenda*), independent of the viceroy. He was present at the sieges of Chaul and Goa. Finally, returning from that state, the carrack in which he was sailing disappeared. He left descendants in Portugal, from whom the lords of Bayan descend.

‘Friar António de Teive, says Henriques de Noronha in his *Nobiliário*, was a friar of the Order of St Augustine, a great theologian and preacher, prior (title of the parish priest) of Castelo Branco (‘white’) and Vila Viçosa. He was Definitor General of his province and visitor general (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) in India, where he died.

‘Baltazar de Teive, says the already cited Henriques de Noronha, was the son of Diogo de Teive and was born on this island in the year 1508. He studied in Paris and became a doctor of law, a man of great promise, all of which he cut short by marrying for love a kinswoman of his in Braga against the wishes of his parents, and he lived in poverty.’

Diogo Barbosa Machado, in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’), gives this Baltazar de Teive as a native of Braga. The genealogist Henriques de Noronha has him born on this island, without stating the place, and the distinguished Madeiran Agostinho de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, who carefully investigated the origins and descendants of the Teive family, states that he was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava, an opinion we can accept without rashness. The same Barbosa Machado says that he was a distinguished Latin poet and left some unpublished works. We cannot affirm it, but we have some reasons to believe, that the well-known Latin writer and jurist Diogo de Teive also belonged to this illustrious family. Those moderately versed in the literary history of our country know that this Diogo de Teive was, among us, one of the most celebrated writers in the Latin language of the 16th century. He was also a distinguished professor at the Faculty of Bordeaux and at our University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), to which John III expressly summoned him, and there he was one of the most brilliant ornaments of that institution of learning. We shall deal with the Madeiran Belchior de Teive, a distinguished member of this family, in a separate article.
Teive (Belchior de)

As we have already mentioned, Belchior de Teive belonged to a distinguished and noble family of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), whose members included several men who achieved real distinction in various fields of human endeavour.

We conjecture that he was born in the first years of the third quarter of the 16th century. He was the son of Gaspar de Teive and Dona Ana de Brito, the brother of Diogo, Pantaleão, Aleixo and Gaspar de Teive, whom we have dealt with in another article of this *Elucidário*, and the grandson of Diogo de Teive, the founder of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) of the Teives, which remained entailed in this family. According to a well-known genealogist, his parents had 25 children, and the subject of this biography was the last male of that distinguished and numerous progeny.

We know nothing of the particular circumstances of his life until 1581, by which time we find him a professor at the famous University of Salamanca, holding one of the chairs in the faculty of law. During his university studies he must certainly have given incontestable proof of rare talent and extraordinary learning to have been called, at the age of 26, to join the teaching staff of that famous institution, something quite unusual at the time. He was one of the most illustrious professors in the golden age of that university, then one of the most eminent and most frequented in all Europe. He also taught at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*).

His recognised merits and abilities naturally marked him out for other important and high offices. And so we see that in 1607 he gave up university teaching at the invitation of Philip II, in whose service he held posts of great responsibility and the highest trust. He became one of the four judges (*ouvidores*) of that sovereign’s Chamber (*Câmara*) and also one of his privy councillors.

We know that Belchior de Teive had a brilliant career in the offices and difficult missions entrusted to him, but we lack the necessary material to give a detailed account of all the posts he held and of how he conducted himself in them, setting out any facts or circumstances that would highlight the faculties of his gifted mind.

Relying on our scant notes, gathered piecemeal from the various printed and manuscript works we have been able to consult, we can say that Belchior de Teive, although he devoted himself to letters and taught at a university, also followed a military career. In those days such a career was considered almost obligatory, and always highly honourable, for all who did not dedicate themselves to the service of the Church. It was as a soldier that Philip appointed him general and adelantado (royal governor of a Castilian province) of Castile, a post equivalent to governor of that province and former kingdom, and one that then carried the widest powers. He was also general of the fleet and superintendent of its officers.

Belchior de Teive held important judicial offices, serving as criminal *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties) of the chancery of Valladolid and later as president of the Casa dos Alcaides.

In 1607 the government of Spain sent him to Portugal as superintendent general of the Public Treasury (*Fazenda Pública*), which seems to us to have been one of the highest-ranking and most responsible posts of the age.
As we have already noted, Belchior de Teive enjoyed the favour of Philip II, being one of the four *ouvidores* (judges) of his chamber and one of his privy councillors.

He was a prestigious and prominent figure in his time, owing to his extraordinary talent, the important offices he held and the influence he enjoyed among his fellow citizens. Diogo Barbosa Machado, in his *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’), says that he was a distinguished genealogist and that he left some unpublished works.

We do not know the year of his death, but in 1621 he was still a privy councillor of Philip II. He was undoubtedly a man of great stature, but his qualities of character leave much to be desired, for he sided with the enemies of his homeland and placed himself entirely at the service of the King of Spain.
Teixeira

Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the first captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico and Zarco’s companion in the colonisation of this archipelago, was married to Branca Teixeira, a noblewoman who, according to Frutuoso, came from the house of Vila Real. Their descendants adopted the mother’s surname, which became the surname of this family. They had four sons and eight daughters: Tristão Teixeira, who inherited the captaincy, Henrique Teixeira, João Teixeira, Lançarote Teixeira, Tristoa Teixeira, Isabel Teixeira, Branca Teixeira, Catarina Teixeira, Guiomar Teixeira Solanda Teixeira, Ana Teixeira and Catarina Teixeira.

Of João Teixeira, the third son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, the annotator of the *Saudades* says that ‘he was a great huntsman and fond of the chase, and for that reason he had in the town (*vila*) of Machico a hunting reserve (coutada) of his own at Caniçal (‘reed bed’), with so much game – rabbits, partridges, peacocks and many wild boar – that it is affirmed to have been the best hunting reserve in Portugal. This is borne out by a letter which is still today in the Council chamber of Machico, written by King Manuel I to its officers, in which he earnestly charges them to keep strict watch over the hunting reserve of the sons of the first captain, and to let no one enter it, because he had been told and assured that, should he chance to come to the island, there were no other lands where he could hunt and chase game but this one at Caniçal and the fields of Santa Catarina’.

Lançarote Teixeira, in the words of the same chronicler, ‘was one of the finest horsemen of the island; for besides being by inclination a very good rider, he had a great hand at breaking horses and was much given to it, so much so that in his time sixty knights of the golden spurs gathered in the town of Machico, very well turned out and mounted through the efforts of this Lançarote Teixeira. When the feast of St John or of Corpus Christi came round, there were so many horsemen for the jousts with canes and the skirmishes that it looked more like an army at war than a festive entertainment. And although all were very skilled in this art, he nonetheless stood out so far among them that it may rightly be said that he was the light and ornament of Machico. This Lançarote Teixeira was married to Beatriz de Góes’.
Teixeira (António)

He was the son of Lançarote Teixeira and Beatriz de Góis, and the grandson of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, first donatary (*donatário*) of Machico. He left his name in the old Madeiran books of nobility, where he was known as the Rei Pequeno (Little King). The following passages, taken from a piece by the learned genealogist Father Fernando de Meneses Vaz, are of interest:

‘The chronicles say that the surname came to him from the magnanimity of his person, from the generosity with which he shared out his revenues, and from the freedom with which he distributed them, both among those of his intimate circle and among the destitute and needy of the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish).

‘Nevertheless, since there is no beauty without a flaw, proud of his noble birth and savouring the good he lavished, he let himself be somewhat clouded by human vanity and pride. ‘Held to be great by men, he believed himself great before God as well.

‘He did not lack faith, it is true. He himself had built the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Piedade (Our Lady of Pity) at Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), as the seat of the entail (*morgado*) founded by his father, Lançarote Teixeira. Yet, full of himself, he would hear Mass, according to tradition, on horseback beside the main door of the church of Faial, making his mount kneel at the elevation of the Host, so as not to stand shoulder to shoulder with his slaves and servants, whose master he was. ‘But how often must the poor slave have wished to unseat him and whisper in his ear: before God we are all equal; God does not look at colour, only virtue distinguishes us?!... ‘Mortal like all men, though rich and great, António Teixeira departed this present life one day at a great age, and they buried him – without the horse, of course – in his family vault in the chancel of the old church of Faial, where he was left sleeping his final sleep.

‘The streams, however, did not wish him to hear the trumpets of the *venite ad judicium* there. They gathered there around 1699, entered the church and, with no other disrespect for the sanctuary, opened the family vault of the Rei Pequeno, carrying off his body as punishment for his arrogance in hearing Mass on horseback. And so down the stream went the holder of the entail (*morgado*), on foot, so many years after his death – he who in his lifetime had always gone about on horseback...

‘And what of the entailed estate (*vínculo*) of João Teixeira de Vasconcelos? – the reader will ask. It passed down through his descendants to Álvaro Teixeira de Orneias Saavedra, the last male of that dynasty of little kings, who, having no heir, left it to his sister Dona Maria Teodolinda.

‘The manor house of those noblemen stood at Banda dos Moinhos (‘side of the mills’), in Faial, and was swept into the sea in the flash flood (*aluvião*) of 1803. On that occasion the old holder of the entail, blind like old Aeneas, had left the house on a servant’s back, bound for Cruz, where he settled. That residence still exists, now without its entail holders, without the shade of the old oak trees, crumbling and falling down too...’
Teixeira (Canon Feliciano João)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on 2 January 1843, and was the brother of Dr João Augusto Teixeira and Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira, whom we have dealt with in this *Elucidário*. He was a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*) and a teacher at the seminary (*Seminário*), and in this city he carried out various public-service assignments. He represented Madeira in Parliament in the legislative sessions of 1880 to 1881 and of 1887 to 1889. Transferred to the archiepiscopal Cathedral of Évora, he died in that city on 2 May 1896. His mortal remains lie in the cemetery of the parish of Ponta do Sol.
Teixeira (Diogo)

He was the son of Tristão Teixeira and the 4th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico. Because he was mentally incapable, John III took the captaincy from him in 1538. When he died in 1540, he left no son or any other legitimate heir to succeed him in the captaincy, so in 1541 it was granted to António da Silveira, a former captain of Diu.
Teixeira (Dr João Augusto)
He was born in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on 25 July 1845 and died in Funchal on 21 March 1907.
The words we transcribe below come from the former newspaper *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’) and are from the pen of one of the authors of this work:

‘Dr João Teixeira distinguished himself chiefly as a physician and as a professor at our Medical-Surgical School, but he also displayed the remarkable gifts of his brilliant mind in other fields of human endeavour.

‘He was an eminent and deeply learned physician, and the vast and complex science of medicine seemed to hold no secrets for him. Among his colleagues he was regarded as a true master, and his advice was always heeded and listened to with the respect due to the great oracles of science.

‘In his last years he had almost given up his practice, which had once absorbed all his great energy. He devoted himself almost exclusively to teaching his chair, to hospital clinical work and to study, which he never abandoned.

‘As a professor he was among the most distinguished. To vast learning and clarity of exposition he added a brilliant and attractive style, which gave his lessons a particular distinction and charm and was the admiration of those who heard him. On several occasions the School was visited by distinguished physicians while Dr João Teixeira was lecturing to his students from the professor’s chair. The visitors were truly astonished at the breadth of his knowledge and at the expert and most distinguished way in which he conducted his teaching, and one of them declared, on hearing him, that no one at our university lectured better or with deeper knowledge of the subject.

‘Dr João Augusto Teixeira, who combined a most splendid talent with an astonishing memory, possessed immense erudition, gathered through his never-interrupted reading and his constant and diligent studies. No subject could be raised, however thorny and difficult, on which he could not discourse and converse with greater or lesser expertise.

‘He had a special fondness for the Latin language, which he always cultivated with particular care, coming to know it deeply and becoming a true master of it. Not long ago we heard him speak in particular of the Latin translation of *The Lusiads* (*Os Lusíadas*) by Father Francisco de Santo Agostinho de Macedo, a remarkable work that he had just reread, and which he discussed with his keen mind and special knowledge of the subject.

‘The illustrious deceased was always a most distinguished, prize-winning student, from primary school to the benches of the university. At Coimbra he revealed a superior intelligence, winning first prizes and leaving there a fine reputation for his application to study and for his real and undeniable talent. Even today his university contemporaries bear witness to this whenever Dr João Teixeira is mentioned, and among them must be counted Dr Bernardino Machado, his close friend and admirer. (1921).
‘Dr João Augusto Teixeira was a lifelong member of the Regenerator party. In 1901 he withdrew from politics, at the time of the events that then took place within that party.

‘In 1885 he was elected deputy for this island, and he defended Madeiran interests with ardent zeal. Particular mention should be made of a remarkable speech he gave in parliament on the wretched situation in which the neighbouring island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) then found itself. In parliament he met many of his former fellow students and contemporaries from university, who rejoiced that a man whose worth and merits they knew so well was taking his seat in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament). It was then that he received from Fontes Pereira de Melo, the glorious leader of the Regenerator party, tokens of great esteem and regard.

‘Despite the repeated entreaties of his political friends, Dr Teixeira refused to return to parliament. To draw him away from the tranquillity of his study and the comforts of his home, which he valued above all else, would have been to force on him a sacrifice that was beyond him.
