‘Among other public service appointments, the late doctor served as representative (*procurador*) to the former District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) and as a member of the central market delegation. ‘He was twice a teacher at our lyceum (state secondary school), a post he always filled with the competence that all acknowledged in him.

‘As a professor of our Medical School, he held for many years the post of director of the medical wards of the Hospital of St Elizabeth of Portugal (*Santa Isabel*), with great zeal and remarkable proficiency, the hallmarks of his austere character and his vast medical knowledge.

‘The illustrious deceased belonged to a family that produced a constellation of fine talents. Special mention is due to the late Canon Feliciano João Teixeira, Dr Manuel Joaquim Teixeira and Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira, professor at the Coimbra lyceum, all brothers of the man to whom we dedicate these lines; Dr João R. Passos, a United States citizen; Policarpo Passos Sousa, a distinguished poet; Dr Francisco dos Passos Sousa; Father João dos Passos Sousa, etc.’
Teixeira (Dr Nuno Silvestre)

He was born in the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on 31 December 1847, the son of Feliciano João Teixeira and Dona Joaquina Júlia dos Passos. In a piece of writing before us, one of his contemporaries at Coimbra, referring to 1877, when Dr Nuno Teixeira was a fifth-year student of medicine, says: ‘He was then held to be one of the most talented students of that academic generation: he was the top student in the Faculty of Medicine. Everyone supposed that, after the distinction awarded to him in the 5th year, as in earlier years, he would defend theses and join the university.’

It did not turn out that way. Dr Nuno Teixeira did indeed consider an academic career, and it seems he even prepared some scientific work with that aim. However, reasons unknown to us dissuaded him from this first intention, and he gave up a post that would have been a great honour for him and of considerable benefit to the University.

Here in Madeira Dr Nuno Teixeira has held the posts of teacher and rector of the Lyceum (*Liceu*), professor at the now defunct Medical School, health officer (*delegado de saúde*) of the district, municipal doctor (*médico do partido da Câmara*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this municipality (*concelho*), clinical director of the medical wards of the Holy House of Mercy (*Misericórdia*) of Funchal, municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative), etc.

He has contributed extensively and most valuably to several newspapers in this city, notably the *Diário de Notícias* (‘Daily News’), where for decades he has published popular science articles on Sundays, dealing with many points of medicine and hygiene in terms accessible to the general public. These articles stand out for their remarkably correct style and extraordinary clarity, which make them essential reading for a large proportion of that newspaper’s subscribers (1921).

In 1899 Dr Nuno Teixeira brought out a volume of 240 pages entitled *O Alcoolismo*, and he also published several pamphlets containing some of his reports as rector of the lyceum and as health officer (1921).
He died in Funchal on 28 February 1928.
Teixeira Jardim (Dr Arsénio)

He was born in Funchal on 3 August 1887 and qualified in medicine and surgery at the Lisbon Medical School. He practises in Monforte, in the Alentejo, and is well known both in Portugal and in Madeira as a specialist in diseases of the throat and ears. Works: *Breve noticia sobre dois casos de tétano chronico, um generalisado e outro localizado*, thesis, Lisboa, 1916, 42 pp.
Teixeira (João Maneio)

He was born on this island on 25 May 1839. In 1866 he completed the course in medicine and surgery at the Porto Medical School, where in the same year he defended his thesis *Das pseudarthroses resultantes de fracturas não consolidadas, e do seu tratamento*, which was published as a pamphlet.
Teixeira Júnior (José)
He was born in Funchal on 17 March 1889 and is pharmacist at the ‘Estefânia’ hospital in Lisbon. In 1889 he published a pamphlet of 65 pages entitled *Em Lisboa*.
Teixeira (Tristão)

Tristão Teixeira, or Tristão Teixeira das Damas as the chronicles call him, was the eldest son of Tristão Vaz Teixeira and the second captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico. He must have been born in mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), for Frutuoso says that the discoverer Tristão Vaz came to this island with his wife and children right at the beginning of the colonisation. He was called Tristão das Damas (‘Tristão of the Ladies’), says the historian of the islands, ‘because he was a great courtier and a great wit, composed many verses for the ladies, and was very eloquent in speech’.

The same chronicler says that a very grave accusation was made against Tristão Teixeira, which obliged the monarch to summon him to court, but that ‘after much trouble, spending much of his own, he nevertheless cleared himself very well and with great honour, clearing his good name’.
He died in Machico and lies there in the chapel of St John the Baptist (*São João*) in the parish church (volume II, page 284).
Tristão Teixeira is one of the main characters in the novel *A Filha de Tristão das Damas* by the Madeiran writer J. Reis Gomes.
Teixeira (Tristão)
He was the 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico, having inherited the captaincy from his father, Tristão Teixeira das Damas.
Yew (Taxus bacoata)

A tree or shrub of the family Taxaceae, now almost extinct in the mountains of Madeira. It has linear leaves, dioecious flowers and seeds with a fleshy scarlet aril. It yields reddish wood of good quality, but today this is almost unknown to the island’s cabinetmakers. The leaves of the yew are poisonous. See Cadamosto.
Telephones

The Funchal telephone network was opened on 5 October 1911. In 1908 the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) had laid down the conditions on which it allowed part of the tower of the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*) to be adapted as the central telephone exchange. The adaptation work did not begin until the following year. The late João Augusto Pereira, a former deputy for Madeira, contributed greatly to setting up Funchal’s telephone services.
On 6 August 1915 the Municipal Council resolved to petition the government to extend the telephone network to the whole island, but this improvement has not yet been granted to Madeira. (1921)
Wireless telegraphy

In the Funchal telegraph office building there is a wireless telegraphy station, opened on 2 June 1922; installing the apparatus took about 15 days. The first trial took place on 1 June, when contact was made with a British steamer 150 miles away and with a Portuguese steamer 400 miles away. Contact was also made with the station at Las Palmas, in the Canary Islands.

During the European war a wireless telegraphy station was operated on behalf of the British government at Quinta Santana (‘St Anne’), and the news it received from abroad was passed daily to the Funchal public through the newspapers. The Quinta Santana station ceased operating on 2 April 1919. By order of the Ministry of Finance, the installation of a radiotelegraph station at Quinta Santana was authorised on 12 December 1921, but it was never carried out.

In 1912 a contract was made with the Marconi Company to set up several wireless telegraphy stations in the country, one of them in Madeira. Nothing was done, however, because our government had failed to meet the obligations it had undertaken. In 1922 the same government was authorised by the Congress of the Republic to contract with the said Company for the establishment of a radiotelegraph network, under which the Company was first to install and operate at its own expense, at no cost to the State, wireless telegraphy stations in Lisbon, the Azores, Madeira, Cape Verde, Angola and Mozambique. (1921)
Submarine telegraph

Madeira is linked to Portugal (Carcavelos) by two cables of the ‘Western Telegraph Company’, and to São Vicente in Cape Verde by two cables of the same company and one of the ‘Eastern Telegraph Company’. This last cable comes directly from Great Britain and continues to South Africa, touching at São Vicente in Cape Verde, Ascension Island and St Helena.

The ‘Western Telegraph Company’ replaced the ‘Brazilian Telegraph Company’, which established the telegraph service between Madeira and the mainland in 1874, as stated on page 172 of volume I of this *Elucidário*, and which in 1883 or 1884 laid a second cable along the same route as the first. As for the submarine cable of the ‘Eastern Telegraph Company’, it was established under a contract signed on 21 September 1908. (1921) See Submarine cable.
Telegraphs

When the electric cable was established in Madeira, the following telegraphs existed here, communicating with one another by signals: that of Pico do Facho (‘beacon peak’), in Machico, that of Pico da Água, in Caniço (‘reed’), and Pico da Cruz (‘peak of the cross’), in São Martinho.
In earlier times, we know that telegraphs existed at Câmara de Lobos, at Ponta do Pargo and at Garajau, the last of these operating from 1839 to 1847.
Teles

It is a surname of good families, but it is not known who brought it to this island. In 1682 António Teles, or António Telo de Meneses, founder of the chapel of St Anthony of Padua in Santa Maria Maior (‘St Mary Major’), was living in Madeira.
The Teles de Meneses family descends from Vasco Moniz de Meneses and also, through illegitimacy, from the Counts of Vila Pouca.
Teles da Silva (Dom Friar António)

The prelate Dom Gabriel de Almeida, who died in this city in July 1674, was succeeded in this diocese by Dom Friar António Teles da Silva, the eleventh bishop of Funchal. The see was vacant only briefly, which did not always happen in the overseas bishoprics, since Dom António Teles da Silva was appointed, confirmed and consecrated immediately after his predecessor’s death.
His confirmation by Clement X is dated 16 December 1674; he received episcopal consecration the following January and took charge of his diocese on 25 April 1675.

He was the son of João Gomes da Silva, commander and *alcaide-mor* of Seiaz and *regedor* (parish administrative officer) of the Justices. He had taken vows in the Order of St Benedict and was a deputy of the tribunal of the Junta da Cruzada when the prince regent, later King Peter II, presented him as bishop of this diocese.

During his episcopate the parishes of Camacha, Serra de Água, Prazeres and Arco de São Jorge were created. He also obtained the creation of several curacies, under the prince regent’s resolution of 20 October 1676.

He enlarged the old bishop's palace (*Paço Episcopal*) and held a diocesan synod on 6 June 1680. He died in this city on 14 February 1682 and lies buried in the chancel of the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), having led this diocese for seven years.
We know nothing more of his episcopal administration, but Dom António Caetano de Sousa says of him that he ‘left an honoured memory of his name’.
Teles de Meneses (Guilherme)

He was born in Madeira around 1855, but has long lived in Portugal, and is at present a retired accountant of the former Court of Audit (*Tribunal de Contas*), today the Higher Council for the Financial Administration of the State. Having come to this island in 1894, he lived for some time in the house at Poiso (‘resting place’) and then in the one at Areeiro (‘sand pit’), making some meteorological observations at both, the results of which he later published. He was also municipal administrator (administrador do concelho, the government's representative) of the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal, but he did not remain long in this post because of a conflict with the governor, after he had forbidden the people, on 7 March 1896, to draw water from the fountains of João Denis (1921).

In the 15th series, no. 6 (1896) of the *Boletim da Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*, he published a paper entitled *A Madeira e o dr. Douglas*, a reply to what this physician had written in a pamphlet on the advantages of Las Palmas over Madeira as a health resort for consumptives. The Areeiro meteorological station, which never came into operation, and the adjoining house were built under the direction of Guilherme Teles de Meneses. (1921)
Telo de Meneses (Luís)
He was born in Madeira, the son of Gaspar Lopes Cortez. Having followed a military career, he was killed at the battle of Montijo on 26 May 1644. He was then a captain of infantry.
Boarfish (Capros aper)
A fish of the family Carangidae, uncommon in the seas of the archipelago. It is caught in waters of no great depth with hook and line, and it seems to have been common in other periods.
Tenerife visitors

In May 1922 a large number of Madeirans visited Santa Cruz de Tenerife, where both the authorities and the local people gave them a warm and splendid welcome. It was agreed that the people of Tenerife would make an excursion to Madeira to return the Madeirans’ visit, and this excursion took place at the end of December of the same year, during the celebrations of the fifth centenary of the discovery of our island.

The Tenerife party arrived at the landing place of Funchal on 28 December at about 1 p.m., aboard the steamer *Viera y Clavijo*. Various official figures and private individuals at once went on board to greet the excursionists, among whom was the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties), Don Andrés Orosco.

The party landed at the Cais da Pontinha (‘little point’) at about half past four in the afternoon. The first launch brought the *alcaide*, accompanied by the Spanish consul and the banker Henrique V. de Castro, while the other boats carried the rest of the excursionists, 76 in number, among them several ladies and girls. A little after 5 o’clock the procession set off. At its head went *A Academia* (‘The Academy’) with its processional banner, followed by the excursionists and those who had gone to receive them, including the president and councillors (*vereadores*) of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), and finally a long line of motor cars carrying many other people.

When they reached the avenue of João Gonçalves Zarco, the excursionists were greeted with the Spanish anthem, as they had been on landing. The same anthem was played again as they entered the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), where Dr Teixeira Jardim, the illustrious president of the Council, delivered a fine address, to which the distinguished Tenerife visitor Don Andrés Orosco replied.

The reception given to the Tenerife party at the palace of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) was equally splendid. Speeches were made by Dr Vasco Marques, Don Andrés Orosco and Dr Fernando Tolentino da Costa, the last of these when a glass of champagne was offered to our illustrious guests in one of the rooms of the palace. Not all the excursionists came on the steamer *Viera y Clavijo*: some had arrived on the 26th aboard the steamer *Andormha*, on its way to England.

The visitors from Tenerife were warmly received everywhere. On 3 January they were offered an afternoon meal at the Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’) and tea at Monte (‘hill’). They visited many places in Funchal and its surroundings, and some of them displayed their musical talents at the Dr Manuel de Arriaga theatre, where they were much appreciated and applauded.

They returned to Tenerife on the steamer *Viera y Clavijo* on 4 January 1923. On 4 February of the same year the *ayuntamiento* (Spanish municipal council) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) approved a proposal by the *alcaide* (town officer with police and jail duties), Don Andrés Orosco, to give the name of the island of Madeira to the Theatre square in that city, as a token of gratitude to the Madeirans for the way in which the excursionists had been treated here.

The plaque bearing this name was unveiled on 4 May. The ceremony was attended by the civil and military authorities, and also by the Portuguese consul in Tenerife, who represented the Municipality of Funchal. As the curtain covering the plaque was drawn back, the municipal band played the Spanish and Portuguese anthems, after which the consul and the *alcaide* Don Andrés Orosco gave speeches.

The Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) returned the honour paid to the Madeirans in the city of Santa Cruz de Tenerife by giving the name Praça de Tenerife (‘Tenerife Square’) to a considerable part of the old Campo da Barca (‘boat field’), after suitably adapting the site for that purpose.
Chaffinch (Fringilla tintillon)
A bird of the family Fringillidae, common in the wooded areas of the middle altitudes of Madeira, where it appears only occasionally.

It has handsome plumage and a pleasant song. It builds its nest from roots and the stalks of grasses or lichens, lining the inside with wool, hair or feathers. It lays a clutch of 4 eggs, whose colour may range from green or pale blue to reddish, by way of deep blue.
Terceira Lombada (peak)
). A mountain summit in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’), from which fine views can be enjoyed.
Terços

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’). In this locality stands the Quinta da Palmeira (‘palm-tree estate’), which is today the bishop’s residence. A chapel was recently built there, but we do not know its dedication.
Teresa (Maria Francisca)
See Soares (Dona Laura de Castro e Almeida).
Termo

In the days of absolute rule, this was a subdivision of the judicial district (*comarca*) and came under the jurisdiction of a judge who was at the same time president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). The *termo* (municipal jurisdictional district, a subdivision of the comarca) of Funchal, headed by a *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) appointed by the king, stretched from Caniço (‘reed’) to the stream of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) and took in 17 parishes.
Terra (A.)
The first issue of this twice-weekly newspaper appeared on 8 May 1922. It ran to 16 issues and is now suspended for lack of printing staff.
Terra do Baptista

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), with 105 *foros* and 651 inhabitants. There was once a chapel there dedicated to Nossa Senhora da Fé (Our Lady of Faith), founded in 1826 by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Diogo Dias de Orneias e Vasconcelos. There was also a chapel there dedicated to St Anthony of Padua (*Santo António*), belonging to the Nunes Caldeira family and founded around 1760. This locality belonged to the entailed estate (*morgadio*) founded by the Genoese João Baptista of the Italian Usodimare family, who married a child of the first donatary (*donatário*) of Machico, Tristão Vaz Teixeira; its last representative was João Bettencourt Baptista.
Terra (Ventura)

A Portuguese architect who drew up the plan of improvements that the city of Funchal needs, in accordance with the council resolutions of 21 November 1912 and 3 February 1913. The Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) and the Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) met the costs of this work, which the first of these bodies received on 19 November 1915, together with two copies, one of which was sent to the Agricultural Board.

It was the architect Ventura Terra, who died recently, who drew up the plan of the former Avenida Oeste, today Avenida do Dr Manuel de Arriaga. Among the improvements he proposed for the embellishment of the city was the construction of an avenue over the Ribeira de Santa Luzia. (1921)
Terreiro da Luta

The locality (*sítio*) of Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’) lies in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), 850 metres above sea level. It was there that a pious legend placed the apparition of the Blessed Virgin (*Santíssima Virgem*) to a poor and innocent little shepherdess, as briefly related on page 438 of the 2nd volume.
From this spot there open out vast horizons of unsurpassed and incomparable beauty.

These astonishing panoramas so captivated the distinguished Madeiran Commander Manuel Gonçalves, director of the Monte Railway Company (*Companhia do Caminho de Ferro do Monte*), that he conceived the idea of extending the railway line to that picturesque spot and of building a large restaurant high up on the steep mountainside, which would become an obligatory attraction for Portuguese and foreigners alike. The undertaking was difficult and risky, but Commander Gonçalves’s tenacity, talent and enterprising spirit overcame every setback that arose. In a short space of time some 1,400 metres of track were laid across extremely rugged ground, and the fine and imposing building now known as the Restaurante-Esplanada do Terreiro da Luta was erected. The formal inauguration of this section of the railway and of the restaurant took place on 24 June 1912. (1921).
A small illustrated promotional leaflet contains a fine description of the site, from the pen of an illustrious Madeiran writer, which deserves to be preserved in these pages:

‘The landscapes of Switzerland are famous, says the writer in question, for their heights and capricious relief, for their glaciers and exquisitely beautiful lakes; but the natural scenes of rugged Helvetia lack that majestic backdrop, full of grandeur, which leads us to the conception of immensity, the primordial source of life, in whose bosom life constantly multiplies and perpetuates itself: the mysterious ocean.

‘Around the “Terreiro da Luta”, very high mountains rise to the north, east and west, the site itself being a mountain plateau covered with dense, fragrant pine woods; to the south, however, the bay of Funchal opens out, vast and smiling, spreading in a gentle curve from the projection of the Balancal in the east to the abrupt cliff of the highest promontory in the world: the famous Cabo Girão. ‘The eye, gradually leaving behind the wilder aspects of this singular landscape – unexpected, deep abysses and astonishing rises of slope and height, all covered with intertwining vegetation – descends by imperceptible degrees along the valley that opens at our feet, the Curral Velho (‘old fold’), and, passing over the tall bell towers of the white church, links us to civilisation: it passes over the orderly houses of the city, stretches out over the harbour, where warships and towering transatlantic liners lose their unsettling size, and reaches beyond to the vastness of the horizon, blending on the dazzled retina the indigo of the waters with the luminous blue of the sky.

‘From this plateau one sees, to the east, the Pico do Infante, the Balancal, Choupana and São Gonçalo; to the south, Funchal and the broad harbour dotted with black by vessels of every kind; and, moving westwards, the parishes of São Martinho, São Roque, Santo António, Câmara de Lobos, Estreito and the Serras da Quinta Grande, whose ridge ends to the south in Cabo Girão and to the north in the Fontainhas, on the boundary of Câmara de Lobos.
‘From the parish of Estreito one can partly see the famous “Jardim da Serra” (‘upland garden’) and the locality known as the “Boca dos Namorados” (‘lovers’ pass’).

‘To the north the plateau falls away into a deep valley, the Curral do Leme (‘Leme’s fold’), followed by valley after valley, the ground rising little by little in folds covered with dense pine woods. On this side the “Terreiro da Luta” is surrounded, at the greatest heights, by the Serras do Monte, among them the Rebentão, at an altitude of 1,200 metres.

‘The sunset seen from this incomparable spot produces truly indescribable effects. The slanting rays bring out the capricious ruggedness of the forms, doubling them with their long shadows; they define the many valleys, in so many shades of green, that stretch towards Câmara de Lobos, give relief to the peaks and knolls rising on that side, and leave the gigantic Girão in black silhouette beneath a fiery sky, dusting everything with a purplish tone that gives the landscape a fantastic, eminently theatrical appearance...

‘It was at this enchanting spot, from which so many incomparable marvels may be enjoyed, that the Restaurante-Esplanada was built: a most elegant building in the style of the Swiss chalets, made entirely of reinforced concrete on the Hennebique system and measuring 37 metres in length by 16 in depth. To the south, in front of the building, stretches a covered terrace 46 metres long by 8 metres wide, where visitors, enjoying a panorama without rival, may take refreshment at the small tables scattered about it. Beyond the terrace lies the garden, spacious and planted with every specimen of the exuberant and varied ornamental flora that grows on this island.

‘The vast Restaurant Hall is on the first floor, which also has a room for private dinners or intimate celebrations. On this same floor is the Winter Garden, delightful for its comfort and charming for the arrangement of its plants and for the refined taste of all its decorative fittings, which were specially acquired abroad from among the most modern available in this field.

‘The Buffet and the American Bar each occupy spacious rooms on the first floor. ‘It is also in the corridor of this same floor that the “Lavatories and dressing rooms” are installed, meeting the refined and modern demands of comfort and hygiene.

‘In the cellars are the drink stores, a refrigerator, provision stores, etc., and the kitchen, with a central range, a special stove for the grill-room service, a stove for warming crockery, and a lavish set of cookware all in copper and nickel.
‘From the side tower, 10 metres high, the unequalled bird’s-eye view (*à vol d’oiseau*) enjoyed from the terrace or from any other point of the “Terreiro da Lucta” becomes even more striking.
‘The building has steam heating for cold days and numerous fans for hot ones, and it is lit throughout by electric light.

‘The installation of the Restaurante-Esplanada of Terreiro da Luta, due proportion being kept, was guided by the idea that it should in no case be inferior to the best and most modern establishments of its kind in Europe, with particular attention to the most scrupulous cleanliness and the utmost well-being of the visitor.’

The now defunct Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*) began to build a road intended to link Terreiro da Luta with Santo António da Serra (‘St Anthony of the uplands’). If this road is ever completed, it will allow Portuguese and foreigners alike to travel quickly to one of the most beautiful spots the island possesses. Had that body applied part of its substantial revenues to finishing the road, instead of acquiring upland commons (montados) and making other expenditure that was practically useless, we could today travel in about three hours to a place which, for its lovely landscapes and the freshness and greenness of its fields, fully deserves our admiration. (1921)

In a land such as Madeira, where nature everywhere appears to us in all its splendour, offering the visitor’s eyes panoramas whose description, as one writer put it, ‘is beyond the power of words and the vigour of the most skilful brush’, it is much to be regretted that roads are still so extremely backward, and that we can see and admire many of the chief natural beauties of our land only at the cost of danger and great sacrifice.

It is to Commander Manuel Gonçalves that we owe the inauguration of the first statue erected in Madeira. On climbing the short flight of steps leading to the Restaurant’s garden, one comes upon a fine bronze statue of João Gonçalves Zarco, showing the discoverer at the moment when, aboard the caravel under his command, he was approaching this then unknown island. This exquisite work is by the chisel of the award-winning artist Francisco Franco. (1921)

Someone had the happy idea of raising in this paradisiacal spot a grand monument in honour of Nossa Senhora da Paz (Our Lady of Peace). It consists of an exquisite marble statue set on a plinth flanked by artistic bronze bas-reliefs alluding to the traditional belief that the Most Holy Virgin appeared on that very spot. Attached to the monument stands a small, elegant chapel, where the holy sacrifice of the Mass and other acts of worship are frequently celebrated. The monument owes its erection to the ardent zeal and unremitting efforts of Father José Marques Jardim, who spared himself no sacrifice to give it the imposing and grand appearance that distinguishes it, even travelling abroad to raise donations so that the work could be carried out. The solemn inauguration, conducted with the greatest pomp and attended by thousands of people from every part of the island, took place under the presidency of the diocesan prelate on 14 August 1927. Because of the interest it adds to the account given in this article, we shall transcribe the record of the laying of the foundation stone, which was deposited in the cornerstone of the monument. ‘On the first day of the month of November in the year of Our Lord Jesus Christ one thousand nine hundred and twenty-three, in the pontificate of His Holiness Pius XI and the episcopate of His Most Reverend Excellency Dom António Manuel Pereira Ribeiro, His Excellency Mr Manuel Teixeira Gomes being President of the Portuguese Nation, and Mr Eduardo da Rocha Sarsfield Governor of this district of Funchal (*Distrito do Funchal*), at the locality (*sítio*) of Fonte da Telha (‘tile spring’), next to the Terreiro da Luta, the Foundation and Laying of the first stone of the Monument to Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*), Principal Patron of the city of Funchal and Secondary Patron of the whole Diocese, was carried out in the following manner:

After Mass had been celebrated at about nine in the morning in the Parish Church of Our Lady of the Mount, a grand procession was formed in the churchyard of that church. It was made up of the multitude of the faithful who, eager to glorify their heavenly Benefactress, had flocked from all over the Island, which is at once stirred whenever it is a matter of proclaiming the favour of Our Lady of the Mount.

Once they had set off in order, grouped by the various civil and religious associations, with groups of children from the schools and catechism classes bearing insignia, pennants and banners, it was wonderful to see them climbing the slope, singing hymns and prayers of thanksgiving for the countless favours that, in calamitous times, have always been promptly obtained through the intercession of the same Lady.

The miraculous Image, carried on its processional litter (andores) amid that whole multitude, thus made its triumphal ascent to the place where it had once regaled with sweets and heavenly fuchsias little Eva, the elder little sister of those girls who today come to recall, on this very spot, the scenes that took place here and which, who knows, they understand the better for their innocence.

Those who watched the Procession arrive at the *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) set aside for the monument, and who attended the open-air Mass, accompanied throughout by the solemn sounds of the music mingled with the singing of thousands of lips, felt themselves lifted from the earth and, on those heights, nearer to heaven!

It was nothing strange! It was the gratitude pent up for more than three centuries in the throbbing heart of the Madeiran People, still barely healed of continual ills and horrors, bursting forth swiftly from the depths of the soul.

The last war had left them drained by tears, hunger and cruel alarms. They had been ground beneath the sinister millstone of the bombardment. Their sons – good priests, spirited officers and dutiful soldiers – went off to the war. The black wing of death brushed close by them. Their eyes, in a pitiful grimace of supplication, turned upwards, and the Virgin of Monte heard their prayer.

With the peace, Portuguese arms were also glorified. Who could set a barrier against this free will of the people to glorify their heroes and leave a commemorative pillar (padrão) to the vitality of their race, which, if at times it knew fear, never knew cowardice! Our Lady of the Mount is their Patron. The soul of our people is made of a clod of the Homeland and a breath of Faith. To destroy the latter is to dissolve the former. That is why the festivals of Religion here among us are the apotheosis of our Homeland and the glory of our warriors.
The Monument to Our Lady of the Mount, on the summit of this mountain, will be the consecration of their religious faith through the sincere affirmation of love for their Homeland.

The Monument to Our Lady of the Mount, as well as being a vow for the Peace of the World, is an act of thanksgiving for all past blessings. It is not yet traced in stone, nor does it yet rise in all its moving majesty before the eyes of passers-by, but it lives, full of splendour, in the soul of every Madeiran who conceives it and who will lend it the effort of their will and the offering of their never-surpassed generosity.

And so, in the presence of His Most Reverend Excellency the Lord Bishop of Funchal, the Civil Corporations, Catholic Associations, the Academy, the Press, the Classes, the Schools and a great gathering of the People, at four o’clock in the afternoon the foundation stone was laid with the Blessing of the Roman Pontifical, the proper ceremonies being observed as is customary on such occasions. His Most Reverend Excellency the Bishop struck the ritual blows with the hammer; His Excellency Dr Manuel Pestana Reis, at the invitation of the parish priest and representing the city, handed the trowel; and His Excellency Dr Romano de Santa Clara Gomes, representing the Madeiran People, served with the float.

And for the record this minute was drawn up in duplicate. After being signed by those present, the original was placed in an iron casket, together with newspapers of the day and coins of the period, beneath the foundation stone, and the copy was handed to His Most Reverend Excellency the Bishop, to be kept in the archive of the Diocesan Chancery (*Câmara Eclesiástica*). Fonte da Telha, in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Monte (‘Our Lady of the Mount’), 1 November 1923.’
Earwig (Forficula auricularia)
An orthopteran insect that lives in gardens, especially in damp places. Its name comes from two small appendages resembling pincers or scissors (*tesoura*) at the lower end of its body.
Treasures
See the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*).
Thompson (I. C.)
He visited Madeira in the spring of 1887. Works: *Copepoda of Madeira and the Canary Islands* (*Linn. Journ. — Zoology*, vol. XX).
Thomson (Sir William)

This distinguished English man of science, who was given the title of Lord Kelvin in 1892, was in Madeira in 1874, when the island was linked to Brazil and Portugal by submarine telegraph. While here he married Miss Francis Ana Blandy, daughter of the English merchant Carlos Blandy. The wedding took place at the British consulate in Funchal on 24 June 1874; W. Thomson was then 49 years old and already a widower, and his bride was 36.
Thomson (W.)
See Scientific expeditions, on page 410 of volume 1.
Tiarks (Dr)
He came to Madeira in 1822, on the orders of the English government, to determine the difference in longitude between Greenwich and Funchal. He brought 14 chronometers in his baggage.
Tierno (João)

He was livestock intendant (*intendente de pecuária*) in Funchal, and in 1897 he published, in the *Boletim da Direcção Geral de Agricultura*, 6th year, no. 11, a work entitled *Relatório do Veterinário do Funchal*, in which he presents some meteorological, geological and botanical data, taken largely from the Portuguese and foreign works that deal with Madeira. In its distribution of plants by zones, the work contains errors that are hard to explain: it even names the *folhadeiro* as a characteristic species of the high Madeiran summits, when that species certainly does not grow beyond the interior valleys and is very common in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha. The meteorological observations that Mr Tierno reports as having been made at the shelter houses of Serra do Faial, Vale da Lapa and the Paul da Serra from 1888 to 1890 appear in no record whatsoever, and the keepers of those houses have told us that they knew nothing of them, which we find extraordinary. (1921)
Tigarro
On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) this name is given to *Scolymus maculatus*, a spiny composite that also grows on Madeira, near the coast.
Til (Ocotea foetens)

A member of the laurel family, 15–30 metres tall, with leathery, ovate, lanceolate or oblong leaves, hairy in the axils of the veins on the underside; small, usually hermaphrodite flowers gathered in clusters; a berry partly enclosed by a cup formed by the enlarged base of the perianth. The til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) is found in the forests of the interior and north of Madeira, and yields timber with clearly separated heartwood and sapwood, the latter white, the former black. When freshly cut, this wood has a strong and rather unpleasant smell, which disappears completely only after some years. *Til* wood is of excellent quality and much used for furniture and various other work. The cabinetmakers’ ‘white *til*’ comes from young trees or from the sapwood of old ones.
Blue shark (Carcharias glaucus)

). A fish of the family Carchariidae that occurs in our seas, where it is the true representative of the sharks. It has a bluish back, and for this reason it is known in some countries as the blue shark. Fishermen always try to kill it as soon as they spot it, for it is one of the most fearsome animals in our seas.
Its flesh, of poor quality, is seldom used.
Tintureira (Rhamnus latifolia)

A native tree of the buckthorn family (Rhamnaceae), now completely extinct in the uplands of Madeira. It is found in some *quintas* of Monte (‘hill’), and is recognised by its elliptic, acuminate, almost hairless leaves, with parallel, evenly spaced lateral veins, and by its small, yellowish, stalked, axillary flowers. It is also known as *ginjeira brava* and yields brownish or reddish wood, hard and even-grained.
Noble titles

The oldest noble title known to us relating to people of this archipelago is the one granted to Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, 5th captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, by royal decree (alvará régio) of 20 August 1576 (volume I, pages 180 and 198).

We know of no other title granted in the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries. In 1812, by decree of 17 December, the royal grant of Viscount of Torre Bela was conferred on the holder of the entail (*morgado*) Fernando José Correia Brandão Bettencourt de Noronha Henriques, who represented Portugal in Hamburg, Stockholm, Berlin, Vienna and Naples (see Torre Bela).

The statesman and diplomat António de Saldanha da Gama, who married Dona Antónia Basília Herédia de Bettencourt, representative and heir of the entailed house (*casa vinculada*) of the Herédias of this island, was granted the title of Count of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) by decree of 26 October 1823.
Charles Stuart, a British subject who represented his country at the court of Lisbon, held the title of Count of Machico, granted by decree of 22 November 1826 (see volume II, page 280).

The title of Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’) was granted by decree of 13 September 1835 to João Xavier de Carvalhal Esmeraldo Vasconcelos de Atouguia Bettencourt de Sá Machado, the wealthiest landowner on this island and one of the richest in the whole country (volume I, page 243 ff.). The illustrious Madeiran João Gualberto de Oliveira, statesman and parliamentarian, received the royal grant of Baron of Tojal by decree of 4 April 1838, and that of Count of the same title by decree of 17 September 1844 (see Tojal).
Dr Aires de Ornelas e Vasconcelos, peer of the realm, was honoured with the title of Baron of São Pedro by decree of 12 August 1845 (volume III, page 23).

On 15 October 1851 António Manuel de Noronha, a former governor and captain-general of this archipelago (volume II, page 427), was granted the title of Viscount of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), after the town (*vila*) of that name on this island.

The distinguished Madeiran António Aluísio Jervis de Atouguia (volume I, page 99) received the title of Viscount of Atouguia by decree of 15 March 1853. Fortunado Joaquim Figueira was granted the title of Baron of Conceição (‘Conception’) by decree of 11 September 1855. He was the father-in-law of the Viscount of Andaluz and of the lawyer Dr Nuno Ferreira Jardim, and the grandfather of Dr Alberto Figueira Jardim.

The title of Viscount of Nogueiras, granted by decree of 16 January 1867, was held by the Madeiran Jacinto de Santana e Vasconcelos Moniz de Bettencourt, husband of the Viscountess of Nogueiras (volume II, page 423) and father of the 2nd Viscount of Nogueiras (volume II, page 420).

By decree of 25 February 1871 the royal grant of Viscount of Calçada (‘paved way’) was bestowed on the holder of the entail (*morgado*) and great landowner Diogo de Orneias de França Carvalhal Frasão Figueiroa (volume I, page 179), who was later made Count of the same title. Diogo Berenguer de França, holder of an entail and landowner, received the title of Viscount of São João (‘St John’) by decree of 3 March 1871.
By the decree of 4 May 1871 Francisco Correia Herédia was granted the title of Viscount of Ribeira Brava (see that entry).
Dr João de Freitas da Silva was granted the title of Viscount of Monte Belo by decree of 24 March 1880 (volume II, page 53).
João Bettencourt de Araújo Carvalhal Esmeraldo (volume III, page 199) was granted the title of Viscount of Ribeiro Real by decree of 23 March 1882, and was later raised to Count of the same title.
Dr António Evaristo de Orneias received the royal grant of Baron of Orneias by decree of 14 October 1886 (volume III, page 20).

Of the titleholders whose decrees of grant are of unknown date to us, we shall mention the Count of Canavial (volume I, page 221), the Viscount of Gonçalves de Freitas (volume II, page 92), the Viscount of Casa Branca (General Alexandre César Mimoso), the Viscount of Bianchi (Augusto César de Bianchi), the Viscount of Vale Paraíso (João António Bianchi), the Baron of Jardim do Mar (Tristão Vaz Teixeira de Bettencourt e Câmara), the Baron of Uzel (Luís Augusto Ribeiro de Mendonça) and the Baron of Nora (Frederico Teles de Meneses).

Dom Álvaro da Costa de Sousa Macedo, governor and captain-general of this archipelago (volume II, page 276), held the title of Count of Madeira, and Domingos António de Sousa Coutinho that of Count and Marquis of Funchal (volume II, pages 56). To the same family belongs Agostinho de Sousa Coutinho, who also held the title of Marquis of Funchal and twice served as civil governor of this district (volume II, page 56).
Tojal (Count of)

João Gualberto de Oliveira, 1st Baron and 1st Count of Tojal, was born in this city on 12 July 1788. He was the son of the distinguished Madeiran João Francisco de Oliveira (volume III, page 11) and of Dona Maria Joaquina Farto de Oliveira.

He belonged to an old family of merchants and was himself a leading wine merchant in Funchal when he was elected deputy for Madeira to the legislative session that sat from 1834 to 1836. He was also elected senator for this archipelago in the legislatures of 1838 to 1840 and 1840 to 1842, and in 1843 he took his seat in the upper chamber as a full peer of the realm.

He held the Finance portfolio in 1837–1838, in 1841, from 1842 to 1846 and in 1847, and was Minister of Foreign Affairs from 1849 to 1851. He also served on an interim basis in charge of the portfolios of the Navy, of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) and of Justice, concurrently with that of Finance.

João de Oliveira stood out remarkably as a parliamentarian and statesman. The speeches he delivered in parliament earned him the standing of a distinguished political orator, revealing not only a notable correctness of form but above all a thorough knowledge of the matters he addressed.

It was as a statesman, directing the affairs of the Treasury, that he most distinguished himself. His name remains bound up (*vinculado*) with important reforms, and for that reason he holds a prominent place (*lugar*) in the history of our country’s public finances. His overhaul of many fiscal services – the collection and distribution of taxes, the drawing up of budgets, the contracts with foreign creditors, etc. – reveals his outstanding qualities as a financier and statesman. Even so, as happens to all who engage in party politics, his financial administration came under attack, chiefly from the deputy the Count of Podentes, who in parliament and in two pamphlets (*opúsculos*) openly criticised every act of João de Oliveira as Minister of Finance. The two volumes of the work entitled *Hontem, Hoje, e Amanhã* also devote a number of pages to his record as holder of the finance portfolio. The Count of Tojal published a booklet rebutting the accusations made against him, and also published in a pamphlet some of the speeches he had delivered in parliament.
On 4 April 1838 he received the royal grant (*mercê*) of the title of Baron of Tojal, and on 17 September 1844 that of Count of the same title.

He held many Portuguese and foreign decorations and served as inspector-general of the mails and posts of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal). He died on 9 February 1852 in Lisbon, where he had established himself as a merchant many years before.

On 27 March 1884 the title of Viscount (*visconde*) of Tojal was conferred on João Vicente de Oliveira, the relevant decree stating that this honour was granted ‘to perpetuate in his person the memory of the good services rendered to the country by his late cousin the Count of Tojal, of whom he is the only male representative’.
Tolentino da Costa (Dr Fernando)

Born in Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’) on 10 February 1873, he attended the lyceum (state secondary school) and the Medical-Surgical School of Funchal (*Escola Médico-Cirúrgica do Funchal*), completing his medical course in 1897. He served as a physician in São Tomé and at Trafaria, and as doctor on the Portuguese steamers of J. M. Andressen, of Porto. He sat on the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) during the government of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) João Franco. Later, after the Republic, he became president of the same Council, and it was on his initiative that the gaol building on the Largo da Sé was demolished, a step that the press and the people of Funchal had been demanding for more than half a century. He has been president of the executive committee of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*) and was a member of the former Agricultural Board (*Junta Agrícola*); it was owing to a proposal of his that this latter body had the *Flora do Archipelago da Madeira* published in 1914 (1921).
Tomás (Manuel)
According to the *Nobiliarchia Portuguesa*, volume 2, page 212, Manuel Tomás was born in Guimarães in 1585, the son of the physician Luís Gomes de Medeiros and Dona Gracia Vaz Barbosa.

We know nothing at all of the particular circumstances of his life before he settled in Madeira, nor of the reasons that led him to leave mainland Portugal, the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and make his permanent home in this city, where he remained until his death.

The distinguished annotator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) is inclined to suppose, on good grounds, that Manuel Tomás was a member of the chapter or even a dignitary of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*). He bases this on the reference made to him by the licentiate Bartolomeu do Vale Cabreira in his censor’s report on the poem ‘The Island Epic’ (*Insulana*), which says that ‘over the course of many years he acquired the benefice with which he is also endowed’.

We too have reason to accept the opinion of Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, who believed that the author of ‘The Island Epic’ and of the *Phenix da Lusitânia* was a canon of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé).

We know little of the life of this esteemed poet and respected writer. Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, following the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’), says ‘that he was murdered by the son of a farrier on 10 April 1665, when he was 80 years of age, although the motive that led the murderer to commit such an atrocity has not been revealed to us’.

Dr Azevedo says that Manuel Tomás, ‘having become involved in the dissensions from which the ecclesiastical sedition of 18 September 1668 later arose, was for that reason murdered on 10 April 1665 by the son of a farrier’.

We do not know on what grounds the distinguished professor based this assertion, nor how a man – and an octogenarian at that – could have been killed because of events that took place three and a half years after his murder. Manuel Tomás died on 10 April 1665, and the sedition broke out on 18 September 1668, as Dr Álvaro de Azevedo himself states and as can also be seen in the article ‘A deposição d’um governador’, published some years ago in the *Diário do Commercio* (‘Commercial Daily’).

It should be noted – and this is of the greatest importance in the present case – that the sedition was raised against the governor, Dom Francisco de Mascarenhas, over grievances, supposed or real, suffered at his hands. This governor and captain-general of Madeira took office on 28 November 1665, that is, seven months after the murder of Manuel Tomás.
It therefore seems to us very difficult to link the illustrious poet’s death to the sedition of 1668, unless historical evidence not yet known should come to change this opinion of ours.

The epic poem that bound Manuel Tomás to Madeiran history, and made him greatly loved by the sons of this archipelago, is well known, at least by name. With the fictions and hyperboles of poetry, and still more of the poetry of its time, it narrates the discovery of Madeira, which it attributes originally to Robert Machin, the island’s gradual development, the various phases of its history and, above all, the deeds and actions that brought renown to many Madeirans. Although it is a poem in which the author gave free rein to his imagination, it nonetheless contains some valuable and far from negligible information on the history of Madeira. The work, published in Flanders in 1635, enjoyed great popularity and for a long time was the favourite reading of all educated Madeirans. Quotations from it and references to it are very frequent in various manuscripts, memoirs, nobiliaries and many other writings dealing with Madeiran matters.
On the literary merits of Manuel Tomás and the value of his poem ‘The Island Epic’, let us hear the authoritative opinion of Inocêncio Francisco da Silva, who is not usually lavish with praise:

‘Manuel Thomaz was a poet of the Gongorist school, whose precepts he always followed as a fervent disciple. Although his style is, as befitted that school, turgid and emphatic, and abounds in hyperbolic ideas, amplifications and conceits, etc., he nonetheless possesses real merit, as a man endowed with a fertile wit and a lively imagination. Most of the defects noted in him are not his own, but those of the century in which he lived and of the poor doctrines in which he was schooled. The learned Francisco José Freire, in his *Arte Poética*, cites the *Insulana* with praise, and more than once, as one of our most notable epics; and indeed this appears to be Manuel Thomaz’s most valuable composition. Its greatest sin is perhaps its excessive length, for it could well have been reduced to five or six cantos, which would certainly have made it more balanced.’

Manuel Tomás also wrote the poem *Phenix da Lusitânia*, which deals with the liberation of Portugal from the Castilian yoke, as well as other writings listed in the *Diccionario Bibliographico Portuguez*.
Similar in subject to ‘The Island Epic’ is the poem ‘The Zarco Epic’ (*Zargueida*), published in 1806 and written by the Madeiran poet Francisco de Paula Medina, whom we have already discussed.
Tree tomato (Solanum insigne)

A small tree or shrub with oblong-ovate or ovate leaves, heart-shaped at the base, reddish-white flowers, and large, ovoid or elliptical orange berries. These berries are edible and can replace tomatoes in certain culinary uses.
Tomateiro do Diabo (Solanum sodomaeum)
). A spiny solanaceous shrub, naturalised at Caniço (‘reed’) and in some parts of Funchal. It has violet flowers and globose yellow berries.
Cape gooseberry (Physalis peruviana)
A solanaceous plant with heart-shaped leaves and globose berries enclosed in the calyces, thoroughly naturalised on Madeira. These berries are edible, and a very tasty preserve is made from them.
Tomato plant (Solanum lycopersicum)

A solanaceous plant widely grown on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) for its pleasantly acidic fruit, much used in cooking. The tomato plant is native to America and bears depressed, furrowed berries, globose or obovate in shape.
Toninha
The name given in Madeira to young individuals of two species of cetaceans: *Phocaena communis* and *Delphinus delphis*.
Tormentina (Torpedo hebetans)
A fish of the family Torpedinidae that occasionally appears in Madeiran waters.
Tornado (steamer)
The steamer was captured in Madeiran waters by the Spanish frigate *Gerona* on 22 August 1866 and was then taken to Cádiz.
Torre

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). Here stands the chapel of Nossa Senhora da Boa Hora, founded by the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António Correia Bettencourt Berenguer. It belonged to the house of the Counts of Torre Bela, who took the title of their countship from this locality. João Afonso Correia, one of Zargo’s companions, held extensive lands in Câmara de Lobos as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation), including the locality of Torre (‘tower’) and others, and is regarded as the founder of that distinguished and ancient Madeiran family.
Torre Bela (Viscount of)

). The 1st Viscount of Torre Bela was Fernando José Correia Brandão Bettencourt de Noronha Henriques, son of the holder of the entail (*morgado*) António João Correia Brandão Bettencourt Noronha Henriques and of Dona Ana Rosa de Vilhena. He was born on this island on 21 February 1768 and died in the city of Naples on 31 October 1821. He followed a diplomatic career and served as our country’s envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary in Hamburg, Stockholm, Berlin, Vienna and Naples. He was colonel of the Calheta (‘small cove’) regiment, Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) to John VI and commander of the Order of the Tower and Sword. He came of noble ancestry and represented the ancient house founded by João Afonso, a companion of Zargo, who held extensive lands on this island as a *sesmaria* (royal land grant to settlers on condition of cultivation) and served here as *almoxarife* (royal revenue officer and storekeeper) to Prince Henry the Navigator. Sanches de Baena states that the Viscount of Torre Bela was the 5th-generation grandson of António Correia Bettencourt and his wife Dona Joana Henriques, who were lords of Alcáçovas and descended from King Henry II of Castile.

The 1st Viscount of Torre Bela and his wife Dona Emília Henriqueta Pinto de Sousa, daughter of the Viscounts of Balsemão, had a son, João Correia Brandão de Bettencourt Henriques de Noronha, born in 1794. He was the second Viscount of Torre Bela and aide-de-camp to Miguel I, and died in 1875.

He married Dona Isabel Joaquina Correia de Atouguia e Vasconcelos, and from this marriage Dona Filomena Gabriela Correia Brandão Henriques de Noronha was born in Berlin in 1839. She married Russel Meneres Gordon, and they were the third Viscounts and first Counts of Torre Bela. The Countess of Torre Bela is the present representative of this family. (1921)

The son of these third Viscounts of Torre Bela was Diogo Murray Kenmure Correia, who served as attaché at the Portuguese legation in Berlin and held the title of 4th Viscount and 2nd Count of Torre Bela. He died a few years ago in Germany. (1921)
The title of first Viscount of Torre Bela was granted by decree of 17 December 1812.

Torreão

This is the name of the small square and of the bridge connected with it, although it is not a name known in Madeiran toponymy. On the spot now occupied by the Ponte do Torreão (‘turret bridge’), or perhaps very close by, there was a wooden bridge meeting the Caminho da Torrinha (‘little tower road’). Across it passed the numerous pilgrims making their way to the chapel – from 1565 the parish church – of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*). The present Caminho do Monte (‘Monte road’) was opened to the public, on the route it still follows, only at the beginning of the 19th century. Diogo Forjaz Coutinho, one of the most illustrious governors of Madeira, had a new and solid arched bridge of *alvenaria* (local name for compact basalt used as building stone) built there. On one of the parapets of its deck a curious and picturesque stone inscription was placed; it is now kept in the entrance hall of the Municipal Museum, and we transcribe it word for word:
Stop, traveller, stop, when you go up to Monte, and admire along the way the fine workmanship of this bridge, by the great Forjaz Coutinho, in the year 1787.
It was later widened, as the present traffic of passers-by and goods at this spot required.

Close by stands the well-known Fábrica do Torreão (‘turret factory’), the most important industrial establishment here in Madeira. It has always been a great source of prosperity for our agricultural industry, with a marked effect on every aspect of Madeiran life.
See the articles Sugar, Alcohol, Spirit, Sugar Cane, Hinton and Sugar Industry.
Torrend (Father Camilo)

A distinguished French mycologist, well known for his studies of the fungi of Portugal and Madeira. He is a member of the Society of Jesus and has taught in Lisbon, Belgium and Brazil. He wrote three contributions to the study of Madeiran fungi, published in volumes VIII, X and XI of *Broteria* (1909–1913).
Torres
This family surname descends from António de Sousa Torres, who in 1682 held the office of Spanish consul in Funchal.
Torres (peak)

The Pico das Torres (‘towers’) is made up of several steep rocky summits, the highest of which is the Pico do Gato. It lies a short distance from Pico Ruivo (‘russet peak’), though separated from it by a deep ravine. To reach it, one takes the *lombo* (ridge between valleys) of Furão and the Ribeira do Gato; the footpath, however, is dreadful and at times runs along the edge of fearsome precipices.

The Pico do Gato, the highest point of Madeira after Pico Ruivo, said to be about 1,830 metres high, is known, one may say, only to shepherds, for it is very hard to climb because of its sheer slopes, where there is not the slightest trace of a footpath. We heard from some men of the Curral, who accompanied us to Pico Ruivo and to the foot of the Pico das Torres, that an English lady once reached the top of the Pico do Gato. To get there she had to be roped and hauled up by cords at the steepest places by the Madeiran guides she had brought with her. A guide to Madeira written in German states that in 1905 the Pico do Gato was visited by two individuals of Russian origin, relatives of the author of that guide, but we know of no exploration of that high point of the island by scientists, Portuguese or foreign.
Torrinhas (pass)

It forms the pass between the uplands of Boa Ventura and the heights of Lombo Grande (‘great ridge’) in Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’). The surrounding hills are still covered with luxuriant vegetation, and on the Boa Ventura side there are also fine laurel woods, as well as numerous specimens of *Isoplexis sceptrum*, one of the loveliest shrubs in Madeira. (1921)

On the rocks flanking the Boca das Torrinhas (‘pass of the little towers’), *Sedum farinosum* grows in abundance: a small native member of the stonecrop family (Crassulaceae) that is not found in the low-lying parts of the island.
The Torrinhas (‘little towers’) lie 1,454 metres above sea level, 5 hours’ journey from Boa Ventura and 3 from Curral das Freiras.
Desert warbler (Sylvia deserti)
A small bird of passage in the Madeira archipelago that lives in the oases of the Sahara. Like the native blackcap, it belongs to the thrush family (Turdidae).
Blackcap (Sylvia atricapilla)
A bird of the thrush family (Turdidae), common in Madeira and often kept in cages for the beauty of its song.

The black colouring that normally covers the male’s head sometimes extends below the nape. Individuals showing this feature are called *toutinegras de capelo* (‘hooded blackcaps’), a trait that modern ornithologists regard as a case of melanism.
The hooded blackcap was formerly considered a distinct species (*Carruca Heinekeni*).
The blackcap builds a nest of interwoven roots in trees, in which it lays up to five eggs, whose colour varies in both the ground and the markings.

Portuguese labour

In several dozen articles scattered throughout this work, and especially in those found on pages 139 and 303 et seq. of volume II and the articles mentioned there, we have dealt at some length with the industries of this archipelago. These articles would have benefited from closer and more logical coordination, but pressing circumstances did not allow this to be done as would have been desirable.

Since it may shed some light on these subjects, we do not wish to omit mention of the pamphlet (*opúsculo*) by the writer and economist Peres Trancoso, *O Trabalho Português, I, Madeira* (‘Portuguese Labour, I, Madeira’), published in 1929, on the sources of the economic wealth and the industrial and commercial development of this archipelago, although we may disagree with several of the statements made in that work.

Forced labour

The penalty of forced labour on state works was imposed in certain cases on criminals who appeared before the Funchal courts. The convicts had iron chains fastened to their legs by a ring. These chains were made on the orders of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), as can be inferred from a resolution passed at its session of 9 November 1824.
Moths

Some species of the genus *Tinnea* (Lepidoptera) and *Demvetes vulpinus* (Coleoptera) attack upholstery and woollen fabrics, while in books it is the white larva of an *Anobium* (Coleoptera) that causes great devastation. A *lepisma* (Orthoptera), with an elongated, silvery body, also damages books and papers. To drive moths away from the furniture in which clothes are kept, Madeirans use peppers, the calyces and opercula of the eucalyptus, camphor and naphthalene.
Trachoma

This is the name given to certain whitish granulations that sometimes appear on the conjunctiva. These granulations, Dr Alfredo Ernesto Rodrigues, a specialist in diseases of the eye, tells us, occur very frequently among people from Paul do Mar (‘marsh by the sea’). Tragedy in Madeira (A)

by Albino de Meneses, Baptista Santos, Abel Rocha de Gouveia and Domingos dos Reis Costa, 1910, 189 pp. Regional dress. To shed further light on the subject treated in the article Indumentária (II-136), we transcribe the following interesting passages from the *Diário da Madeira* (March 1938):

‘Folklore studies of the dress peculiar to different regions have established conclusively that clothing, in its cut, arrangement and colouring, always corresponds to the way of life of the inhabitants and, above all, to the nature of the surroundings, through their climate, relief and the tones of the landscape. Where the landscape is richly flowered, splashed with many intense colours, dress – especially women’s dress – is equally colourful, so that the figure harmonises with and becomes part of the scene in which it lives and works. A Madeiran who visits the Minho at once finds there a landscape that recalls that of Madeira. And in the dress of the Minho woman he will recognise, in the bright, many-coloured stripes of the skirt, a close likeness to the dress of our own countrywomen. Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), luminous but colourless, has not given women’s dress – not even by imitation – the liveliness and hues that, in the eyes of Portuguese and foreigners alike, have made the charm of the peasant costume of this “Flower of the Atlantic”.
In the land of the Perestrelos, dress is as neutral as the tone of its fields and mountains.

Indeed, it all comes down to a formula of harmony imposed not by any rule of art but solely – rather as in mimicry – by instinctive conditions that are entirely unconscious. Within the many colours of Madeiran peasant dress there are variations from place to place or, at least, from municipality (*concelho*) to municipality.

Here striped skirts, elsewhere skirts entirely red; the same capes and bodices vary in colour; and the capes even differ in the tone of the edging on the points near the collar, and in the manner of throwing them or arranging them over the shoulders. It would be worth studying all this in the localities themselves, with information from the oldest people, the best keepers of traditional custom.

In the parishes (*freguesias*) or in the seats of the municipalities, as might be decided, the Tourism Delegation would arrange for dolls to be made and dressed by local ‘seamstresses’ according to the agreed model. Supervision would be entrusted to a committee of competent people in whom a regionalist sense was combined with an interest in this kind of folklore. It would be made up of Madeirans with a love of the subject and recognised good taste.

These small figures, classified by locality, municipality or parish – representing, of course, country people of both sexes – would form a permanent exhibition in a suitable place, which would certainly be of great interest to Portuguese and foreigners alike. It would be interesting for its picturesqueness, for its folkloric value and for recording the dress of the various localities, something that has still to be done in a definitive way.

We are inclined to believe that the study of our costumes and their recording in models – officially exhibited, let us say – could only benefit everyone interested in the folklore of Madeira as far as dress is concerned. If, alongside the accurately dressed figures, we added household objects and agricultural or other implements associated with the regions to which the garments belong, the exhibition would be more complete still and therefore more useful.

There are amateurs here of recognised talent, with proven skill in modelling clay, who, if entrusted with making the faces of the countrymen and countrywomen, would give them a local character and all the expressive force peculiar to our people.

Once the heads had been modelled and the body proportions set on a schematically made wooden frame, the rest would be up to the ‘seamstress’, we repeat, after the composition of the figure had been carefully studied.

We insist that the figure be dressed not in the city, which spoils everything with its fancies and inappropriate stylisations, but in the countryside, where people know the fabrics, how to cut and adorn them, and even how to sew them with precision.

At the same time, home weaving should be looked after with loving care, and the regional recipes of our dyeing, especially those for wool, which are based on vegetable colourings, should not be allowed to be lost.

At the Year-End Festivities, these little mannequins would serve as a model for the groups from each district that came to Funchal to take part in processions or other items on the programme. Contests would be held among them, intended solely to stimulate their love of their dress and customs, with prizes for their gallantry, the rhythm of their dances and, above all, the accuracy of their costume, everything always guided by a traditional spirit’.
Transport (means of)

In the articles Monte toboggans, Corsa, Palanquin and Hammock we gave some information on the means of conveyance and transport used on this island. To this we wish to add a few further details, taken from the pamphlet *Duas Palavras sobre a viação na Ilha da Madeira* by Joaquim Maria Fragoso, former director of Public Works of the District General Council (*Junta Geral*). Although they refer to the year 1905, they are still of particular interest to our subject:

‘In the streets of the city of Funchal, and on the roads that are paved like them, the commonest means of conveyance is the ox-drawn car. These cars consist of a body of wicker or wood, with an iron frame that supports an awning or roof from which curtains hang, and it rests on springs fixed to a kind of wooden sledge. It has no wheels and no front carriage, and it is drawn by oxen, which there are of a small breed but remarkably swift.

In front of these oxen walks a boy, whom they call the *candeeiro*, holding the yoke; and beside the car goes a man who goads the oxen and steers the car, taking hold of it and pulling it to one side or the other. For carrying loads they use *corsas* (wheelless wooden sledges) or *corsões* (large *corsas*), which consist of two parallel timbers joined together, from 1.6 m to 3 m long and 0.50 m wide.

To ease the friction and sliding of the cars and *corsas*, a cloth soaked in tallow is thrown on the ground in front of the car, which passes over it, leaving the runners of the sledge and the paving of the streets greased, even though a municipal by-law (*postura*) prohibits the use of tallow. So when a fine rain dampens the paving, it is extremely difficult to walk on it without slipping. Perhaps because of this greasing of the paving, and because of the nature of the stone and the slope of the streets, there is no dust in the city of Funchal, which is one more healthy condition to add to the many that that most gentle climate offers to the “invalids” who go there to recover their health.

In the rest of the island, people generally use the hammock (*rede*, slung from a pole and carried by two bearers), suspended from a pole that rests on the shoulders of two men. This way of travelling is very expensive, both because of the men’s day wages (three or four take turns to carry one person) and because they must frequently be given something to drink. They do not cover 3 kilometres without stopping at the taverns, which abound all over the island, to drink *poncha* (a mixture of spirit (*aguardente*, distilled from sugar cane or wine), water, sugar and lemon peel); and one cannot haggle over tips with those who hold one’s life in their hands. If one day you travel by hammock on the island of Madeira, I urge you to take the greatest care in choosing these men, who are often given to drunkenness and are therefore a real danger, to be added to the many others that these royal roads present.

People also travel on horseback, on *garranos* or ponies used to these tracks; and in Funchal there are even magnificent horses for hire, which is surprising, since here on the mainland hired horses are generally the most sluggish of beasts.

In Funchal there are already a few wheeled carriages (*char-à-bancs*), but there are few streets along which these vehicles can travel; and they can only run services to Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), along the monumental road of which I have already told you.

Above the city of Funchal, at an altitude of 595 metres, stands the church of Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*). Around it lie the most beautiful parks, as much for their vegetation, their abundant water and their mild summer temperature as for the lovely panorama to be enjoyed from there. It is the Sintra of

Madeira, with pretty chalets and magnificent hotels that offer visitors every comfort of modern luxury. To go to Madeira and not go to Monte (‘hill’) is, as the saying goes, to go to Rome and not see the Pope.

Between Funchal and Monte there is a railway on which a steam locomotive (with rack and pinion) makes that ascent in ten minutes, on a gradient that reaches 25 per cent. And since I am telling you about the means of transport in Madeira, I shall not fail to mention the so-called Monte carts or baskets, which most visitors use for the descent. They consist of a wicker platform mounted on two wooden runners greased with tallow, with a seat or settee with a back, also of wicker, which holds two or three people. At the front, on each side, two ropes are fastened, held by two men who walk behind and at the sides of the cart, and with these ropes they hold it back and steer it. The two men propel the carts down the slope by resting one foot on the cart and pressing the other against the paved lane (*calçada*) of the road. They are so skilled at this work, in which gravity serves as the motive force, that they steer the cart expertly and stop it whenever necessary. And so we came down from Monte by Royal Road no. 24 (*Estrada Real n.º 24*) in five minutes, over a distance of 4 kilometres, reaching a speed of 48 kilometres an hour!

As you see, some of these means of transport are so original that they are a real attraction. Together with the admirable climate of this island, its splendid panoramas and the curiosities of interest to the natural sciences, they do a very great deal to draw foreigners of social standing and wealth there. Give the island, if possible, a complete road system under normal conditions, cross it with railways, drive about it in coupés and victorias, and once the original means of transport it possesses today have entirely disappeared, the Island of Madeira will lose much of its originality.’ (1921). Closely related to the subject of this article is what we have said on page 417 of volume I, under the title *Estradas* (see Roads).
Trapiche

A locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), Funchal.
