Traste

The wall of earth or of stone and mortar that lines the levadas (irrigation channels), known today in Madeira also by the name of levada wall (*mainel*). The letter of King John II of 8 May 1493 refers to ‘terradas & trastes das levadas’, which shows that the term *traste* (earth or masonry wall lining a levada), in the sense of *mainel*, was once used in Portugal, where it now seems to be forgotten.
Honorific forms of address

Certain honorific forms of address used in society have become so extraordinarily widespread that it is hard to imagine how scrupulously their use was regulated in former times. Knowing how one should address people was almost a science, and the use of these forms varied considerably over time, for reasons that it is impossible to determine.

Madeira followed the example of mainland Portugal in the distinctions granted to people. Consequently, from the end of the 16th century to the beginning of the 18th century the governor and captain-general and the bishop of the diocese were addressed as *senhoria* (‘lordship’), while all other citizens received the address of *mercê* (‘grace’), with which they probably considered themselves greatly honoured.

For a long time the bishops were addressed as *mercê*, a form which in the first centuries of the monarchy had been granted only to kings. During the period of Castilian rule, however, they were already being addressed in Madeira as *senhoria ilustríssima* (‘most illustrious lordship’), as can be seen from documents recorded in the books of that time.

It was the law of 31 January 1739, recorded on folio 50 of Book 9 of the Archive of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), that laid down that the great churchmen should be addressed as *excelência* (‘excellency’). This form was also to be granted to governors holding the rank of captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira), but only while they were in the districts they governed. No other local authority was granted high honorific forms of address in the same law. This amounts to saying that the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate), the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), the customs judge (*juiz da alfândega*, head of the customs house) and other senior officials in Madeira continued, as before, to receive only the address of *mercê*.

At the end of the 18th century the Count of Castelo-Melhor and the Marquis of Valença – the latter *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) of Machico and the former of Funchal – were addressed as *excelência*, since both were grandees of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), whereas viscounts, barons and *moços fidalgos* were entitled only to *senhoria*. Later this last form was also given to the canons of Funchal Cathedral (the Sé) (*Sé do Funchal*), under the royal decree (alvará régio) of 15 November 1817, and to colonels commanding troops. All other officers received *mercê*, except marshals, lieutenant-generals and those of equivalent rank, who were entitled to *excelência*.

The governors and captains-general Dom Diogo Pereira Forjaz Coutinho and Dom José Manuel da Câmara were in the habit of addressing the Funchal Municipal Council as *senhoria* (lordship). This was contrary to law and established practice, and the latter was reprimanded for it by the government in mainland Portugal, which pointed out that the Council was entitled only to the form *mercê*. Only from 1834 onwards did the custom take hold – even then without legal authority – of the head of the district addressing the Municipal Councils and all authorities and heads of department (*repartição*) as *senhoria*.

Under the legislation in force until the establishment of the Republic, it was the governors and captains-general, and not the civil governors, who were entitled to the form *excelência* (excellency). Nevertheless, everyone considered it a duty to give this form of address to the representative of the central government in this district, and only the government itself sometimes denied it to him in the early constitutional period. On one occasion a judge of the Administrative Court addressed the civil governor of Funchal as *senhoria*, having been addressed in that way by the governor. The government, consulted on the matter, did not approve of the magistrate’s conduct, although it acknowledged that under the law the civil governor was not entitled to *excelência*.

It was customary to address the former commander of the 9th Military Division (*Divisão Militar*, a territorial army command), which had its headquarters in Funchal, as *excelência*, though sometimes unlawfully, since the post was not always held by general officers. From the commander of the Division, this form of address passed to the senior military authorities that later existed on the island.

The Funchal Municipal Council began to receive the form *excelência* from the civil governor only after its president was the Count of Carvalhal (‘oak grove’), a grandee of the realm. The municipal administrators (*administrador do concelho*, the government’s representative), by contrast, were always addressed as *senhoria* by the head of the district for as long as the monarchy lasted in the country. It was around 1872 that the Funchal Municipal Council began definitively to address the district judges as *excelência*, a form it later extended to the municipal administrator and, later still, to almost everyone.

To judge the importance that certain honorific forms of address had in the country in the 18th century and still at the beginning of the 19th, it is enough to say that the Dukes of Aveiro had to make the greatest efforts to obtain the form *excelência*, and that only in 1811 were the vice-rectors of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) granted the form *senhoria* – and this as a reward for the services rendered by the University in defence of the homeland during the French invasions!

At the beginning of the second quarter of the 14th century, when the great majority of men were addressed only as *mercê* or at most as *senhoria*, ladies in Madeira, following the practice in Portugal, were already almost always addressed as *excelência*. Not all ladies, however, were entitled to this deference from men, as is the case today, but only those who, by birth or by their husbands’ social position, formed a class worthy of particular consideration. The ladies to whom no one in former times dared deny the title of *dona* were those addressed as *excelência*, although by right this form belonged only to the wife of the captain-general and a few other ladies.

Today in Madeira the form *senhoria* is used only by the merchant class, and *mercê* by country people. *Vossemecê* and *amecê*, contractions of *vossa mercê*, are forms of address widely used among the lower classes of society, and also between illiterate superiors and inferiors, whereas *você* is used only between people who are friends; outside such relationships it is considered an offensive form of address.

Both works contain several references to Madeira, where the author lived as a child and to which he returned on the occasion of his visit to West Africa.
Travassos Valdez (José Lúcio)

This governor and captain-general (capitão-general, military governor of Madeira) of Madeira was appointed in March 1827 and arrived in Funchal on 27 April following, taking office on the 29th of the same month.

Despite his short administration, Travassos Valdez sought to be of use to this archipelago, informing the central government of the most urgent public needs that ought to be met without delay. He paid special attention to the construction of a quay and to the repairs to the forts and barracks, which had long been needed.

During his governorship Miguel I was proclaimed absolute king, in May 1828, but Valdez did not follow the movement in favour of absolutism that was under way in the country, and he prepared to defend Madeira against any attempted attack by the Miguelite (supporter of the absolutist King Miguel) troops. When, on 25 June 1828, the royalist frigate *Príncipe Real* appeared off our harbour carrying the new governor, José Maria Monteiro, Valdez prevented him from landing, and the frigate left our waters. As is well known, on 22 August 1828 the town (*vila*) of Machico was bombarded by the Miguelite squadron, and the island was then occupied by the invading forces; on 24 August Miguel was proclaimed and the new governor and captain-general, José Maria Monteiro, took office. As for Valdez’s actions on this occasion, which were very important, the reader is referred, to avoid needless repetition, to the article Occupation of Madeira by the Miguelite troops.

Travassos Valdez, who on 23 August 1828 had taken refuge with his wife and six children aboard the English corvette *Alligator*, left for England on the same ship, with other political exiles, on 6 September of that year.

José Lúcio Travassos Valdez had distinguished himself notably in the Peninsular Wars under the command of General Beresford, and later in the campaigns for liberty, soon rising to the highest ranks. He was later honoured with the title of Count of Bonfim and held the high offices of deputy, peer of the realm and minister of state, as well as carrying out other important public-service commissions. He was born on 23 February 1787 and died on 10 July 1862.
See *O conde de Bonfim, notícia dos seus principais feitos*, by G. N., 1860. This pamphlet deals at length with Travassos Valdez’s governorship in Madeira.
Travessa do Porto Santo

The stretch of channel or sea between the islands of Madeira (Ilhéu de Fora (‘outer islet’), off Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’)) and Porto Santo (Ilhéu de Baixo (‘lower islet’), or Ilhéu da Cal) is popularly known as the Travessa (‘crossing’). It is about 27 miles long. Violent storms often break out there, and the sea in these waters is generally rough.
White lupin (*Lupinus albus*)

A papilionaceous legume widely cultivated in Madeira. To rid the seeds of the white lupin of their bitterness, they must be boiled in water containing some ash and charcoal, and then steeped in water for about eight days, the water being changed twice a day. People also put the lupin seeds in sacks in the running water of streams, which considerably shortens the work of preparing them. The white lupin is much used to fertilise the land, and is often grown for that purpose alone.
Earthquakes

The list we publish below records the earthquakes that have occurred in Madeira and of which we have been able to obtain information. Only one of them caused damage of any real significance, yet no memory of the event survives in local tradition:

1748. On 31 March of this year, between one and two o’clock in the morning, a strong earthquake was felt in Madeira, followed by two further shocks. An account of the event written at the time, and reproduced on page 697 of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), states that some trustworthy persons claimed to have seen ‘towards the east of the said island a great band of fire rise into the air, and that shortly afterwards they observed a great glow of the colour of that same fire, which lasted for the space of a quarter of an hour, and it was felt that the air was unusually warm’.

On 1 April, by order of the prelate, solemn prayers were held in Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*), attended by the cathedral chapter, the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council), the officials, the nobility and the people. Afterwards the image of St James, patron saint of the city, was carried in procession to the altar of the Blessed Sacrament in the same Cathedral. The prayers continued, with the Blessed Sacrament exposed, until 9 April, ‘and these rogations’, says the same account, ‘were also made by all the other Religious Communities and all the Collegiate Churches of the City; but the inhabitants of the towns, villages and countryside practised, besides these, other exercises, as Catholic as they were spiritual.’

Penitential processions were held in Funchal on the nights of 2, 5 and 6 April. The first, in which almost everyone went barefoot, was joined by the prelate, the Chapter, the Senate, the friars of the convent of São Francisco, from which the procession set out, and a great many people, all going ‘in their places, and with such praiseworthy devotion that they moved the most impenitent creatures’.

On 9 April the last prayers were held in the Cathedral, where, at the prelate’s request, Father José de Figueiredo of the Society of Jesus preached, and ‘his sermon had such an effect on the whole congregation that many who for years had not availed themselves of the Sacrament of the Eucharist, laying aside their faults and confessing their errors, began a new life.’

From 1 April to 26 May further earthquakes were felt in Madeira on various days, but none of them reached the violence of the shock of 31 March, which caused considerable damage in many parts of the island. The Cathedral was left with several cracks and its façade leaning outwards, and the church tower also suffered badly. The same earthquake also caused considerable damage to the churches of Santa Maria Maior do Calhau, Santo António, São Gonçalo, Camacha, Machico, Caniçal, Porto Moniz, Prazeres, Paul, Arco da Calheta, Canhas, Serra de Água, Câmara de Lobos and Estreito de Nossa Senhora da Graça. The house in which the bishop lived was left uninhabitable, and the buildings of the Customs House (*Alfândega*) and the Contos, despite their very strong walls, were left with thirty-two cracks, besides other more or less notable damage.

Despite the violence of the earthquakes of 31 March 1748, there were only four victims: an old man, father of the vicar of Santo António (‘St Anthony’), a child and two women. The material damage, however, was considerable: according to the account we referred to above, there was not a building that escaped damage, however strong its walls. 1755. On 1 November of this year there was an earthquake in Madeira. In Funchal the sea rose 5 metres above high tide, and on the north of the island it drew back about 100 metres, leaving a great quantity of fish stranded. On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) the sea surged up the bed of the stream of the town (*vila*) for about a quarter of a mile, and as the water drained away the channel of the Ilhéu de Cima (‘upper islet’) was left almost dry (on this subject see *O Megasismo do 1.° de Novembro de 1755*, by Francisco Luís Pereira de Sousa, volume I, page 108).

1762. On 26 June there was an earthquake in Funchal, which caused no damage. 1768. On 5 November of this year the island of Madeira experienced a violent earthquake, but the documents of the period do not say whether it caused damage.
1804. On 24 April of this year there were three shocks during the night, at intervals of 8 to 10 minutes, all of them violent.
1813 and 1814. Thomas Edward Bowdich alludes to earthquakes felt in Madeira in 1813 and 1814, but without stating the days on which they occurred.

1816. Bowdich refers to an earthquake felt on 11 January of this year, which opened cracks in some houses in Funchal. Many people who were in the streets were thrown against the walls when the shock struck.

The *Anais de Machico* record that in the early hours of 2 February of the same year, while the people were hearing Mass in the mother church (*igreja matriz*), an extraordinary earthquake was felt, lasting for some time. The congregation rushed out of the church in a stampede, but no one was endangered and there was no significant damage.

This shock was also felt in other parts of the island, and the fright was so great that prayers and public processions were held in several churches. We have read somewhere that the procession of Christ Carrying the Cross (*Senhor dos Passos*) at Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’) was instituted on the occasion of the earthquake of 2 February 1816.
1842. The *Anais do Porto Santo* refer to a slight earthquake felt on that island on 24 October, but we have found no record that this shock was also noticed in Madeira.
1850. Dr Barrai, in the *Noticia sobre o clima do Funchal*, mentions an earthquake in the direction LW, felt at half past nine at night on 10 October, but which caused no damage whatsoever.
1883. On 23 July of this year, a strong earthquake was felt in Funchal at about two o'clock in the morning.

1884. On 13 February of this year, between 2 and 3 a.m., an earthquake accompanied by subterranean noise was felt in Funchal, and on 17 May, at about 3 a.m., there was a further, not very violent, shock.

On 22 December of the same year, at around 3 a.m., the inhabitants of Funchal felt two earth tremors. The first, the more violent, lasted about 20 seconds and the one that followed about 7 seconds. These shocks were also felt in Lisbon, at 3.29 a.m.

1886. On 21 January, at 8 a.m., a slight earth tremor lasting about 3 seconds was felt in Funchal. A woman from Água de Pena who was gathering limpets at the locality (*sítio*) of Queimada (‘burnt land’) fell into the sea at the moment of the shaking and died instantly.

1887. This year there were three earthquakes in Funchal: one on 7 January, at around half past ten at night, accompanied by subterranean noise; another on 27 January, at half past one in the morning; and the third on 6 August, at twenty past one in the morning.
1889. On 14 January of this year, at around half past five in the morning, a slight earthquake was felt in Funchal.

1910. On 24 November of this year, at around 9.20 p.m., an earthquake was felt in Funchal, accompanied by subterranean noise that seemed to come from the north-east. On the same day, two shocks were felt in Curral das Freiras (‘nuns’ fold’).
On the 26th of the same month there was another shock in Funchal, at 12.25 p.m. It lasted about 4 seconds and the movement seemed horizontal.
1914. At 4.45 a.m. on 27 December, a slight earthquake was felt in Funchal.

1918. The earthquake that occurred this year, at 4.23 a.m. on 25 July, was the most violent we have felt on this island. It was felt not only in Funchal but also at Monte (‘hill’), at Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’) and in the north of the island, and it damaged the plasterwork of some houses in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta Delgada. There were two shocks in quick succession, each lasting two seconds, and at the time a loud subterranean noise was heard.
1920. On 8 December of this year, at a quarter to six in the morning, a slight earthquake was felt in Funchal, which went unnoticed by many people.
1923. At 5.06 p.m. on 1 October, a slight earthquake lasting only 2 seconds was felt in Funchal. This shock was also felt in the parish of São Vicente and probably in other parts of the island.
Trevina (*Lotus glaucus*)

A perennial papilionaceous legume with trifoliate, glaucous leaves, leaf-like stipules and yellow or reddish-yellow flowers. It grows on coastal ground and is a good fodder plant. It is also found on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and the Desertas (‘deserted islands’).
Clover

This name is used for a large number of legumes with trifoliate leaves, belonging not only to the genus *Trifolium* but also to the genera *Ononis*, *Medicago* and *Melilotus*. *Trifolium repens*, *T. maritimum*, *T. pratense*, *T. incarnatum*, *T. agrarium*, *Medicago lupulina*, *Melilotus indica*, etc., etc., are plants very well suited to feeding livestock.
Tribuna (A)
A Funchal periodical of which twelve issues appeared, the first on 24 September 1864 and the twelfth on 21 December of the same year.
Tribuna Académica
It ran to 44 issues, the first on 4 February and the last on 16 December 1897.
Tribuna do Povo
The first issue of this weekly periodical appeared on 7 October 1922.
Administrative tribunal

The Administrative Tribunals were created by the code of 1886 and abolished by the decree of 21 April 1892. They replaced the District Councils, and each of these tribunals consisted of three magistrates appointed by government decree. Tribunal Secreto. This was the name of a Funchal periodical that was published clandestinely and had no fixed day of distribution. Twelve issues are known, all from 1844, but it seems to have first appeared in 1841.
Wheat

Wheat is grown in every parish of the archipelago, but its cultivation appears most important in the parishes of Santa Cruz, Calheta, Arco da Calheta, Ponta do Pargo, São Vicente, Porto Moniz and Porto da Cruz. It is almost always sown by hand, and it is harvested either by pulling it up or by cutting it with a sickle, the latter method being more common than the former. Threshing is done in one of three ways. It may take place on threshing floors, where the ears are trodden by oxen harnessed to a board with stones and pieces of iron fixed to its underside; or with hand-driven machines; or, finally, with flails, this last method being used only when the quantities of wheat harvested from a given plot are small.

The area under wheat in the whole archipelago is about 2,000 hectares, and production amounts to some 25,000 hectolitres a year. The yield per hectare varies considerably: on some land it may reach 30 hectolitres, while on other land it does not exceed 4 in years of little rain. The average yield on the island of Madeira must be 8 hectolitres per hectare, and in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal some 12 hectolitres.
Before the war Madeira imported about 7 million kilograms of wheat a year, and in 1919 it imported 4,511 tonnes of this cereal and 690 tonnes of flour (1921).

The richness of the soil in phosphoric acid and the island’s terrain, which lets the rain carry every year from higher ground to lower ground a certain quantity of the elements needed for plant nutrition, must be the reason why land remains productive even when the routine-bound, ignorant farmer devotes it to the uninterrupted cultivation of wheat and other cereals. Fertilising the land is of very little concern to the great majority of Madeira’s cereal growers. Some, however, do manure the ground destined for sowing with farmyard dung, and so obtain better harvests than those who do not. Wheat straw is used for thatching huts, for feeding livestock and sometimes also as bedding for stalled animals.

In wheat (*Triticum aestivum*) three types or sub-species are distinguished: soft wheat, turgid wheat and hard wheat. The first is characterised by a medium-sized caryopsis with a floury fracture and a completely hollow stem; the second by a large, thick, semi-soft caryopsis and a stem only partly hollow; and the third by a hard caryopsis with a hard fracture and a stem completely filled with pith.
In the following list we mention some of the varieties or sub-races grown in the archipelago. They are usually sown from December to March and harvested in June and July:
SOFT WHEATS
Trigo Alexandre

Ear square or nearly so in section, white, compact, with long awns that are more or less dark in the lower middle part. *Trigo branco* no. 1: ear white or with black spots, nearly square in section or somewhat flattened in profile, with a brittle rachis; awns white or black, rarely absent. It is also called *trigo ganil*.
Trigo amarelo
Like the preceding variety, but with yellowish, smooth glumes. It is also known by the names *trigo russo*, *trigo do Campanário*, *anafil* and *tangarola*.
Trigo americano
Long white ear, 10–15 cm long by 12–15 mm wide; lemmas sometimes bearing a short awn, those at the top in some cases long-awned. Similar to the preceding variety and perhaps merely a form of it.
TURGID WHEATS
Trigo anafil
It differs from *trigo barbela* only in its ears, which are sometimes darker or slightly violet. It is also called *trigo português*.
Trigo barbela
Narrow ear, 6–12 cm long, bearded, white or brownish, four-sided or slightly flattened on the face. It is also called *trigo do mato* and *trigo da serra*.
White wheat
Dense, white, glabrous ear, similar to that of red wheat; awns black at the base and divergent.

Hard wheats degenerate in Madeira. Unless care is taken to renew their seed, they readily take on the characters of turgid wheats. We have seen specimens of red and yellow wheat with somewhat divergent awns, more or less floury caryopses and hollow straw, except at the top, whereas none of the turgid and soft wheats found on the island loses the characteristics of the subspecies or cultivated types to which it belongs. (1921).

Besides *Triticum aestivum*, Madeira also has *T. polonicum*, characterised by very long, narrow caryopses with a hard fracture and by elongated glumes. For the time being, however, this species is little cultivated and is found only in the parish (*freguesia*) of Caniço (‘reed’).

In addition to the text transcribed verbatim from the first edition, the co-author of this work, Carlos Azevedo de Menezes, also published the following interesting information, which it is worth preserving here.

‘In a valuable study of the Portuguese varieties, published 40 years ago by the late professors Ferreira Lapa and Andrade Corvo in volume III, part II, of the *Memorias da Academia Real das Sciencias de Lisboa*, we find 29 different types of this cereal indicated and described: 26 from the mainland of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) and the Azores, and 3 from the Madeira archipelago. The Madeiran types are those still known in the archipelago today by the names *trigo mocho*, *trigo português* and *trigo Alexandre*, under which they were listed in that study. The first and second belong to *Triticum vulgare* and the last to *Triticum turgidum*, two races once regarded as distinct species, but which many botanists now include in the subspecies *tenax* of *Triticum sativum*, Lam.

Having had the opportunity to examine several samples of wheat gathered in different parts of Madeira in 1904 and 1905, we had no difficulty in recognising that the number of varieties on this island is greater than the number studied by the professors mentioned above. We further found that some of the old types, although similar to certain Portuguese types from which they may perhaps derive, nevertheless differ from them in noteworthy characters. The Madeiran varieties we were able to study all belong to the races *T. vulgare* and *T. turgidum*, known in the trade as soft wheats. We have never found *T. durum*, another race of *T. sativum*, on Madeira or on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and it may well not exist on these islands. The wheats that in Madeira are called ‘hard’ are, in our view, simply sub-races of *T. turgidum*, as can easily be recognised from the shape of their ears and glumes and from the consistency and arched shape of their grains. In true hard or durum wheats the grains are elongated, pointed and almost always vitreous, characters we did not observe in any of the Madeiran varieties.

As stated above, the area under wheat in the whole archipelago is about 2,000 hectares, and production amounts to some 25,000 hectolitres a year. The yield per hectare varies considerably: on some land it can reach 30 hectolitres, while on other land it does not exceed 4 in years of little rain. The average yield on the island of Madeira must be 8 hectolitres per hectare, and in the municipality (*concelho*) of Funchal 12 hectolitres.

The value of crop rotation is almost unknown to the people of Madeira, and there is land on which wheat is usually grown for 15 and 20 years in succession. Often this land is not even manured, and yet every year it produces a yield that the ignorant and perhaps unambitious farmer considers sufficient reward for his labour! Since the island’s soil is so fertile, it would be no surprise if its output tripled or quadrupled in a short time once it was subjected to more rational methods of cultivation.

All the varieties of wheat in Madeira are usually sown from December to March, and the harvest takes place in June and July. *T. turgidum* is grown more in the low-lying zone of the island than at higher elevations, the reverse of what happens with *T. vulgare*. The latter, which appears to be the oldest on the island, is found up to an altitude of 700 metres (1900).
Madeira imports about 7 million kilograms of foreign wheat every year, since local production is barely enough to meet consumption for 3 months.

Madeiran wheat is almost always sown by hand, and it is harvested either by pulling up the plants or by cutting them with a sickle. The latter method is far less common than the former. Threshing is done either on threshing floors, where the ears are trampled by oxen harnessed to a board with stones and pieces of iron fixed to its underside, or by hand-driven machines. Since threshing machines are now common across almost the whole island, the primitive method of having animals beat the ears is gradually falling out of use. People who own only small quantities of wheat usually thresh it with a flail (*malho*).
Wheat straw is used for thatching huts, as fodder for livestock and sometimes also as bedding for stalled animals.

The fertilisation of the land is a matter of very little concern to the great majority of Madeiran farmers. Some, however, manure the ground intended for sowing with dung from the fold (*curral*), and so obtain better harvests than those who do not manure. The richness of the soil in phosphoric acid and the configuration of the island’s terrain, which allows the rains to carry every year a certain quantity of elements necessary for plant nutrition from the higher ground to the lower, must be the reasons for the lasting productivity of the land that the ignorant, routine-bound farmer devotes to the uninterrupted cultivation of wheat and other cereals. To prevent the cultivated varieties from degenerating, farmers in the different parts of the island periodically exchange among themselves the wheat intended for sowing.

Madeirans credit local wheat with a higher nutritive value than imported wheat. The analyses carried out by the late Professor Ferreira Lapa on the three types referred to above confirm this opinion to some extent, since they showed, for those types, a proportion of protein matter equal to or even greater than that found in the best Portuguese varieties of soft wheat. Bread made from Madeiran flour is generally light and fluffy, brownish and tasty.’
Trigo branco no. 2
It differs from the preceding variety in having broader and more compressed ears.
DURUM WHEATS
Trigo canhoto

Similar to *trigo barbela* and *trigo de palha roxa*, differing from the latter in its yellowish colour and from the former in lacking awns, except sometimes at the top. It is also called *trigo canoco pelado*.
Trigo canoco
Very similar to the preceding, but with longer ears (5–6½ centimetres). It is also called *trigo pelado*, *rapado*, *anafil* and *canoquinho*.
Trigo de cabeça preta
Ears 6½ cm long by 2 cm wide, almost without awns and with dark spots.
Trigo de palha roxa
Ears 9–10 cm long by 8–15 mm wide, slightly violet or reddish, awnless or with the upper glumes bearing short awns. It is also called *trigo mouro*.
Trigo de Rieti

Similar to the preceding, from which it differs in its flatter ears, almost always white, and its more spreading awns. Trigo canoco burbudo. Bearded, whitish ears 4–6 cm long by 1½ to 2 cm wide, generally somewhat flattened.
Trigo mangalhão
Similar to the preceding, but with longer ears (12–15 centimetres).
Trigo mocho
Short, broad ear, somewhat flattened, 4½ to 5 cm long by 15–20 mm wide, without awns. It is also known as *trigo rapadinho*, *pelado*, *rapado* and *sem vergonha*.
Trigo vermelho
Ear 4½ to 7 cm long and 1½ to 2 cm wide, dense, usually somewhat flattened in profile; glumes downy; awns darker at the base. It is also called *trigo russo*.
Trigo (Adriano Augusto)

He was born in Moncorvo on 13 November 1862 and is an infantry colonel and civil engineer. He has served as section head and as director of Public Works of the district of Funchal (*Distrito do Funchal*). He contributed to several newspapers in this city, proving himself a writer and polemicist of merit. Among the works he has published, we shall mention the following: *A Iluminação da cidade do Funchal e o Diário de Noticias*, Funchal, 1895; *Levadas da Madeira. Relatório justificativo da proposta*, Lisbon, 1896; *Breves considerações sobre os melhoramentos de que carece o porto do Funchal*, Funchal, 1912; *Saneamento da cidade do Funchal...* (*Rev. O. Publicas e Minas*, XXX, 1899, nos 355 and 356); *Saneamento da cidade do Funchal, projecto de esgotos...*, Funchal, 1900; *Plano geral da distribuição e arrendamento das águas da levada da serra do Faial*, Lisbon, 1911; *Roteiro e guia do Funchal*, Funchal, 1910; and *Guide and plane of Funchal*, Funchal, 1910. His brother, the civil engineer Aníbal Augusto Trigo, collaborated on the last five of these works (1921).
Trigo (Aníbal Augusto)

The brother of the preceding, he was born in Moncorvo on 29 October 1865 and is also a civil engineer. He has served in the Directorate of Public Works of the district of Funchal (*Distrito do Funchal*), of which he is now director, and in the technical department of this city’s Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). He collaborated on some of the works mentioned in the previous article and, as municipal engineer, always gave the most eloquent proof of competence and of great austerity of character (1921). He died on 13 February 1944.
Trindade e Vasconcelos (Joaquim da)

He was born in the town (*vila*) of Machico in 1825 and died in Funchal on 14 April 1906. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law from the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) and for many years practised as a lawyer in the judicial district (*comarca*) of Funchal. He was also president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*). In 1867 he published a 40-page pamphlet entitled *Projecto de lei regulamentado contrato de colónia ou parceria agrícola na ilha da Madeira*, in which the late Dr José António de Almada collaborated.
Trip-Trap
An illustrated Funchal periodical of which seven issues appeared, the first on 9 January and the last on 22 February 1898.
Trombeta
See Ranhosa.
Angel’s trumpet (Datura suaveolens)

A tree-like member of the nightshade family, cultivated and naturalised in Madeira. It is native to Peru and for almost the whole year is covered with large, funnel-shaped, white and highly fragrant flowers.
Snipefish (Centriscus scolopax)

A small fish of the family Centriscidae, of no commercial value whatsoever. When a strong wind blows from the open sea, it appears in great numbers on the beach of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Trovisco
In Madeira this name is given to several species of the genus *Euphorbia*, the most common of which is *E. peplus*. The milky sap of this plant is used to treat skin diseases.
Truta (Ctenolabrus truta)
A fish of the wrasse family, rare in Madeiran waters but appearing fairly frequently in those of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Its flesh is tasty, though somewhat soft.
Truxillo (Dom Sancho)
See Sancho (Dom), on page 222 of this volume.
Tubarão (Carcharias microps)

A fish of the family Carcharidae, recorded in Madeiran seas. According to Richard Thomas Lowe, it is notable for the smallness of its eyes, and its teeth are weak in relation to its size; they are arranged in two rows, alike in both jaws. The specimens examined by that naturalist measured 8 feet and 5 or inches in length.

As Mr Adolfo César de Noronha informs us, the name *tubarão* given to the species in question is known today only to the fishermen of Caniçal (1921). Tuckey (T. K.). See Scientific expeditions, on page 410 of volume I of this *Elucidário*.
Tudesco (Adenocarpus complicatus)

A leguminous shrub with whitish branches, clustered trifoliate leaves and yellow flowers, found on the Caminho do Meio (‘middle road’) and at the locality (*sítio*) of Pasto (‘pasture’) near Choupana (‘hut’). *Tudesco* is a corruption of *codesso*.
Tomb Monument

This is the name of the monument erected within the Angústias (‘sorrows’) cemetery to the memory of those barbarously killed by the shells of a German submarine on 3 December 1916. We have already given a brief account of it on page 68 of volume I of this work, to which we refer the reader. It was handed over to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this municipality (*concelho*) on 15 December 1917. See Monuments (*Monumentos*).
Tombs

The churches of this diocese contain no tombs whose showy architecture, rich marbles or fine ornamentation would catch the visitor’s eye. Only on the side walls of the chancel of the church of Carmo (Carmelite church) are there two mausoleums which, without being grand or of remarkable artistic refinement, are nevertheless regarded as a work of value that deserves to be visited and duly appreciated. These tombs belong to the family of the church’s founder, and on two slabs of black marble the following epitaphs can be read: ‘Tomb of Pedro Gonçalves Brandão, and of his brother Manuel Martins Brandão and their heirs’ and ‘Tomb of António de Carvalhal Esmeraldo, *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) of His Majesty’s household, and of his wife Dona Maria Brandão’. In the church of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*) is the tomb of Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcelos, in which the discoverer Gonçalves Zargo is said to be buried (volume II, page 31).
Tuna of the University of Coimbra

This *tuna*, led by António Correia Caldeira Coelho, then a fifth-year law student, arrived in Funchal on 22 March 1913 and left for Lisbon on 3 April of the same year. It consisted of 45 students who, during their stay in Funchal, were lodged in the building of the former seminary at the start of the Caminho do Monte. The *tuna* was lavishly entertained in this city: on the day it landed, after a short visit to the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*), it was offered a reception at the residence of the Viscounts of Geraz de Lima. In its honour there were also a ball at the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), another at the ‘Grémio dos Empregados do Comércio’, a party at the Quinta da Choupana (‘hut’), and luncheons at the Casino Pavão (‘peacock casino’), the Terreiro da Luta (‘ground of the fight’) and the Monte Palace Hotel, etc. The students gave two performances at the theatre and visited Portela, Santa Cruz and Machico.
Turnbull
This English traveller visited Madeira in July 1800 during his voyage round the world. Here he found oranges, melons, sugar cane and bananas, as well as various tropical shrubs.
Tybumia (barque)

An English ship that entered the port of Funchal on 24 November 1884, with the purpose, as its captain declared, of taking on refreshments and allowing the passengers to get to know our island. Some days later the customs house learnt that aboard the *Tybumia* was a large cargo which it was intended to land without paying duties. The captain was therefore asked to present the ship’s manifest, and the vessel was closely watched with full fiscal rigour. These measures, however, only prevented the goods from being landed, for on the night of 2 December of that year the *Tybumia* weighed anchor and fled unexpectedly from our port, where it had lingered for some days awaiting the chance to carry out the smuggling. The Ilhéu fortress (*Fortaleza do Ilhéu*) fired several cannon shots at the smuggling ship to force it back to the anchorage, but the balls missed their target. Among the other passengers aboard the *Tybumia* were two women who, by their dress and refined manners, were at first taken by the inhabitants of Funchal for ladies of the highest English aristocracy!
U
União (A)
This newspaper, of the town (*vila*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), published its first issue on 31 January 1918.
Madeira Winegrowers’ Union

A company of this name was founded in early 1910 with a capital of 100 *contos* (one million réis) de réis, divided into shares of 20 thousand *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis), payable in instalments of 10 per cent over a period of 10 years. Its aim was to buy from its members Madeira wines as must, to keep them in store and improve them, and then to export them as a genuine product, free from the adulterations that have contributed so much to their discredit.

Although the founders of the União dos Viticultores each took 25 shares, worth 5 *contos* de réis, their example was not followed by others interested in raising the value of our wines, so the company was dissolved before it had rendered any service to our island.
Unification of the currency

Although Madeira was Portuguese territory, the gold and silver coin that once circulated here was foreign. Portuguese money was unknown to the great majority of people, and small traders often refused to accept it when someone from the mainland tried to use it to make a payment.

To put an end to a state of affairs that was not only humiliating for the country but also harmful to the population, Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Serpa Pimentel, Minister of Finance, proposed in parliament the unification of Madeira’s monetary system with that of Portugal. His proposal, presented in 1875, became law on 2 May 1879. This followed a petition addressed to the Government by the Funchal Commercial Association (*Associação Comercial do Funchal*), and speeches on the subject by Dr Agostinho de Orneias e Vasconcelos in the House of Peers and Dr Manuel José Vieira in the Chamber of Deputies, both of whom worked to secure the unification.

The speech delivered by the latter at the sitting of the Chamber of Deputies on 7 April 1879 became famous, and it drew the following words from the Minister of Finance: ‘I congratulate the Chamber on the speech it has just heard, and Madeira on the manner in which its interests are defended in this house’.

Some questioned the advantages of unifying Madeira’s monetary system with that of Portugal, but the fact is that unification put an end to many abuses. At the same time it averted the exchange crisis, whose consequences threatened to grow ever more serious for consumption in the district.

Many speculators made fortunes by buying, at a very low price on the English markets, the foreign coin that circulated on the island. As a result of this business, sometimes carried on on a large scale, commerce had latterly been unable to obtain bills of exchange at less than 42%, whereas in normal circumstances they were obtained at between 33 and 34%.

By the law of 2 May 1879, as has been said, the legal currency in the district of Funchal became the same as that of mainland Portugal. All payments made under contracts or agreements predating the enforcement of that law were to be made in strong currency (moeda forte, i.e. mainland coinage) with a discount of 1/16.

The period allowed for exchanging the coinage was two months, and the government was authorised to have silver coins of 500, 200, 100 and 50 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) minted, up to a total of 500,000,000 réis, for the needs of the district of Funchal.

Portuguese copper coin was already circulating in Madeira at the time of the currency unification law, alongside the so-called *pecunia madeirensis* (copper coins minted specially for Madeira), represented by coins of 20, 10 and 5 réis. In the issues of 1842, 1850 and 1852 these values appear between two vine branches, and not between a cana (land measure, c. 30 m²) and a vine branch, as was stated on page 360 of volume II through a slip that is hard to explain. See Currency.
Urgebão

Two plants of the Verbenaceae family are known by this name: *Verbena bonarbensis* and *V. officinalis*. The first, which is native to South America, has very rough, incised-serrate leaves and lilac flowers arranged in spikes that are short at first and later lengthen. The second, which is indigenous, has incised-serrate or pinnatifid leaves, sometimes glabrescent on the upper surface, and very small blue flowers arranged in narrow spikes that become filiform when fruiting. An infusion of the leaves of these plants is used for diseases of the liver and kidneys. *Jarvão* (popular name for vervain) is a corruption of *urgebão*.
Devil ray (Dicerobatis giornae)

A fish of the family Myliobatidae that sometimes appears near the coast of Madeira. It is the largest of the rays and can in some cases measure about 2 metres. Fishermen harpoon it whenever they can, because it is considered an animal harmful to man, although the misdeeds of which they accuse it lack confirmation. It is commonly held among fishermen that when a devil ray manages to catch a man, it pins him beneath its body and releases him only once he is dead.
Annual mercury (Mercurialis annua)
An annual member of the Euphorbiaceae, common on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It is a purgative plant.
Nettle (Urtica membranacea)
A plant of the Urticaceae family, very common in Madeira. Its stems and leaves are covered with hairs that secrete a caustic liquid. An infusion of nettles is recommended for skin diseases.
Heath

Of the three Ericaceae known by this name in Madeira, only two are of importance for their products: *Erica scoparia*, which is called *urze durasia* or broom heath, and *E. arborea*, known as *urze molar* or *betouro*. The latter has hairy leaves and branches; the former has them glabrous. The trunks, stumps and roots of these two species provide the best charcoal on the island, and their branches and twigs, once dried, are called ‘queima’ and are widely used as fuel. The *urze molar*, although almost always shrubby, can reach 8 to 10 metres in height, and in former times we knew some specimens whose trunks measured 1 to 2 metres in circumference. The wood of this species is hard, dense and dark brown, but it splits easily and is therefore little used in cabinetmaking. In the countryside it is sometimes used for troughs, spoons, etc. The stems that are not too thick make excellent walking staffs and hammock (*rede*, slung from a pole and carried by two bearers) poles. The *urze durasia* is almost always shrubby and only in some cases reaches 4 and 5 metres in height, when it has a small trunk 20 to 30 centimetres in diameter. Besides the uses mentioned, its branches serve for making brooms.
Urze de cheiro (Diosma ericoides)
A shrub of the Rutaceae family, cultivated in the gardens of Funchal. It is native to the Cape of Good Hope and has leaves similar to those of the heaths, but highly aromatic.
Orchil

Three lichens known by the name of orchil (a dye lichen) exist in the Madeira archipelago: *Nemaria fuciformis*, *N. rocella* and *N. fucoides*. These species, which contain a red colouring principle, were once exported in large quantities, but with the industrial processes for extracting aniline dyes their use in dyeing is today nil. *Nemaria rocella* and *N. fuciformis* were gathered mainly on the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), but both abound on the rocks of the north and south of Madeira.

Orchil was already being gathered in Madeira when Frutuoso wrote ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), and the trade in and export of this lichen lasted until the middle of the 19th century.
Uveira (Vaccinium maderense)

A shrub or small tree common in the mountains of Madeira, where it forms thickets, sometimes quite extensive. It has lanceolate leaves, often reddish, and globose-campanulate corollas spotted with red. The wood, which is quite hard, is used as fuel and for making charcoal, and from the [fruit] a preserve is made that is useful in treating coughs and colds.
Úzel
This family surname derives from Rui Vaz Uzel, who came to Madeira in 1480 and settled at Tábua.
Úzel (Baron of)

Luís Alexandre Ribeiro Mendonça, Baron of Úzel, was born in this city in 1839 and died on 2 June 1903. He was the son of Marcelino Ribeiro de Mendonça, whom we discussed on page 197 of this volume, and he held the posts of chief officer of a department of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) and teacher at our Lyceum (*Liceu*). He had a thorough knowledge of the French and English languages, and left some unpublished compositions in prose and verse in the former. He was a distinguished man of letters, and many of his writings are scattered through the newspapers. Some of his compositions are to be found in the ‘Flowers of Madeira’ (*Flores da Madeira*).
V
Vaccination

It seems that it was the court physician, Dr Domaire, who first carried out experiments in vaccination against smallpox in Madeira. He was followed by Dr Adams, to whom we have already referred on page 16 of volume I of this Elucidário. In a petition approved by the Governor and presented to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) at its session of 27 October 1802, Dr Adams asked that ‘every eight days they should send him four foundlings, on whom to test the vaccine against smallpox’. The same physician presented the results of the experiments he had carried out in a report written in English, which was translated by the interpreter major Francisco Manuel Patrone.

After Dr Adams, vaccinations were carried out by the Madeiran physician Dr António Caetano de Freitas, who also gave an account of what he had observed in two reports, one written in 1804 and the other in 1807.

In 1815, under a ministerial order (*portaria*) from the governor, the Council established that the foundlings should be vaccinated every month by the chief physician (*físico-mor*). At its session of 7 June 1823 the same body resolved to invite heads of families, by public notices, to send their children to be vaccinated at the hospital, where there was ‘a free establishment for that purpose, created last year through the efforts of the Council, in agreement with the chief health officers and the superintendent (*provedor*) of the same hospital.’

It seems, therefore, that the use of vaccination began to become general in Madeira only from 1822 or 1823 onwards. It is known, however, that the foundlings were vaccinated before then, and that in 1804, when many people still doubted the usefulness of inoculation, the governor Sequeira Freire was already recommending it to everyone as the only effective means of preventing the contagion and spread of smallpox.
Vahl (Dr Martin)

A Danish botanist who stayed in Madeira from 1901 to 1902 and from 1920 to 1921. On his second visit to this island he also visited Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). Works: *Madeiras Vegetation*, Copenhague, 1904, and *Ueber die Vegetation Madeiras* (*Engler's Botanische Jahrbuchn*, 1905).
Vaksel (Platão de)

He was born on the outskirts of Petrograd on 14 August 1844, the son of noble parents. He studied philosophy at the University of Leipzig, receiving his doctorate in 1874. He came to Madeira in November 1861 to accompany his sister, who was suffering from pulmonary tuberculosis and died here some months later. He stayed on the island for some time and made special studies of Madeiran music, on which he published an interesting article entitled *Alguns dados da historia da Musica na Madeira* in the *Gazeta da Madeira* in 1869; it was reproduced in the *Jornal do Comercio*.

Platão de Vaksel was also in Lisbon, to carry out historical and bibliographical research in the principal libraries, and afterwards returned to Madeira, where he had many friends. In June 1870 he went back to Russia, where he held the high office of director of the chancery in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of that empire. He was a member of the Instituto de Coimbra and of the Lisbon Geographical Society (*Sociedade de Geografia de Lisboa*). Besides the work already mentioned, he published many others, whose titles are listed in volume XVIII, page 295, of the *Diccionario Bibliographico Portuguez*; two of them, on music in Portugal, appeared in the *Gazeta da Madeira* in 1866 and 1868.

Platão de Vaksel was still alive when the war between Germany and Russia began, in which the latter country fought for some time alongside France and England, but after that no further news of him reached this island.
See Faria e Castro (José Carlos de).
Valadas (Colonel Manuel Raimundo de)
See Parish councils.
Valença (Marquises of)
See Vimioso (Counts of).
Valente (steamship)

The first steam vessel used in the coastal service of this island was the so-called *Vapor Valente*, which arrived in Funchal from England on 1 September 1872 and ran aground on 11 November 1876. It was imprudently left anchored close to the shore by the Ilhéu (‘islet’) just as a violent storm from the south was beginning to blow; it was driven against the coast below the Quinta Lambert, where it was completely destroyed.
Valleys

On this island, says the *Diccionario Universal Ilustrado Portuguez*, ‘there are valleys of indescribable scenery, in every variety of rustic beauty: everything there that is art, cultivation, the work of man, becomes incidental, paltry, almost nothing to the beholder, and nature alone displays her grandeur in the profusion of her spontaneous splendours. There the brush will fall from the hand, the string of the lyre will snap trembling, and the pen of the prose writer who attempts a description will exhaust itself in grandiloquent commonplaces, for only the power that produced these pictures with its creative *fiat*, taking volcanoes and the sea as its instruments, could render their lines and hues. Of these valleys we shall mention five. To the east, that of Machico. To the south, that of Funchal, including within it the Vale Formoso (‘beautiful valley’), the whole forming a vast amphitheatre-like panorama, the delight of every traveller who enters the bay and the most ample harbour that adorn its shores. Twelve and a half kilometres from here, in the high reaches of the parish (*freguesia*) of Estreito de Câmara de Lobos (‘the narrows of Câmara de Lobos’), the valley of Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’), rich in varied native vegetation, in the rugged recess of the wild mountains, dark green with untamed native woodland, which shelter it in an almost complete circle, leaving it open only to the south; in that direction, threaded by two streams that at last unite in a showy waterfall, it stretches with them down to the sea. To the north, the valley of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), where the little town stands, seat of the municipality (*concelho*) and judicial district (*comarca*) of that name: a broad valley, most pleasant in itself and striking for the contrast of the inaccessible, uncultivated mountains that, touching the clouds, surround it on all sides except the north, by the sea. And finally, towards the east, the encircled valley of Penha de Águia, a graceful name which in its sublime concision declares that there stands a very lofty promontory, dark green, towering over the surrounding land, majestic, a worthy throne for the queen of the air. This valley is formed by the parish of Faial and that of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’), and its setting, together with the crag that gave it its name, is so astonishingly beautiful that it has no rival to humble it among the Edens of Europe, perhaps of the world....’
Valhadolid (Father Francisco)

Whatever may be claimed to the contrary, the truth is that Madeira has not been the birthplace of anyone who has left a glorious name in the annals of music in our country. Only Father Francisco Valhadolid enjoyed great renown in his time. He is mentioned in most honourable terms by Diogo Barbosa Machado in the *Bibliotheca Lusitana* (‘Portuguese library’) and by Joaquim de Vasconcelos in his work *Os Músicos Portugueses*, and Ernesto Vieira probably deals with him in the *Dicionário dos Músicos Portugueses*, which we cannot verify at this moment.

We have seen doubts raised as to whether he was a native of this island, perhaps because of the unusual surname he bore. However, he lived for many years in Lisbon, in the parish of Santos-o-Velho, and died there, and his death record states that he was a native of Madeira. It is therefore reasonable to believe that the priest who drew up that record knew the birthplace of a colleague who had lived for many years within the bounds of his parish.

Valhadolid is said to have been born in 1640; he died in the parish of Santos on 17 July 1700 and lies buried in its parish church. Joaquim de Vasconcelos says that in Funchal he studied composition under Canon Manuel Fernandes, and in Lisbon counterpoint under the distinguished musician João Alves Frovo. He devoted himself to sacred music and left many compositions, which Vasconcelos lists and which were regarded in their time as works of great artistic value. He was working on a book entitled *Mistérios da música, assim pratica como especulativa* when death overtook him. He owned a rich music library, which seems to have been entirely lost.
He was a secular priest and for many years held the post of music teacher at the archiepiscopal seminary of Lisbon.
Steamship

The first steamship to visit the port of Funchal was the *Duke of York*, of the British merchant navy. It arrived here in the first half of May 1828, with a large number of passengers who visited various parts of the island.

The *Duke of York* also called at Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), arriving on 15 May with some 400-odd passengers, some of them people from Funchal. These passengers landed on that island at about 11 in the morning and, after seeing the principal sights, re-embarked at about 3 in the afternoon bound for Madeira.
Vapor

Almost opposite the old Rua das Dificuldades there once stood a most curious wooden building, known as the Vapor (‘steam’), whose ends rested on the two banks of the Ribeira de Santa Luzia (‘St Lucy’). It had a single storey and was painted red. It was originally intended as a café and bathhouse, and in its last years served as a residence for a few poor families. It was built in 1837 and demolished, we believe, in 1898, because it had fallen into serious disrepair. Many of the foreigners who spent the winter here could often be seen sketching or painting the extravagant structure that stood over the Ribeira de Santa Luzia.
Vara de salto (fishing pole)

A fishing implement consisting of a pole of Madeira mahogany (vinhático, *Persea indica*) or *folhado* (*Clethra arborea*, a native tree), with a line at its tip. At the end of the line is a wire about half a metre long, fitted with a hook. It is used to catch skipjack tuna (*gaiado*) and tuna: the hook is plain when intended for the first of these fish, and barbed when intended for tuna.
When the skipjack tuna takes the hook, it leaps and usually strikes the fisherman on the chest, and he then tears the hook from the fish with his teeth.
Varadouros (chapel and gate)
See Nossa Senhora dos Varadouros and Portas da cidade.
Varela

This family surname derives from Lopo Dias de Lira Varela, son of Afonso de Aragão, a Neapolitan knight. This Lopo Dias served in Africa, became a *moço fidalgo* (junior nobleman of the Royal Household) of the royal household in 1515, and was a professed knight of the Order of Christ (*Ordem de Cristo*).
Varela (Canon Dr António Vicente)

He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on 10 November 1854 and died in this city on 12 December 1903. He attended the lyceum (state secondary school) and seminary of Funchal and was ordained priest in 1881. In 1886 he completed his degree in theology at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*), and by royal letter (*carta régia*) of 29 March 1900 he was appointed canon of our Cathedral (*Sé Catedral*). He taught at Funchal Seminary (*Seminário do Funchal*), was deputy for this archipelago in the legislative session of 1892–1893 and president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Misericórdia*) of Funchal, and carried out other public service duties.

Dr Varela was a highly cultivated mind, a tireless worker and an ardent fighter, but also a restless and extremely impressionable spirit, at times violent and irascible, above all as a journalist. This earned him the ill will of many, so that he had to wage bitter campaigns and even suffer penalties imposed by his ecclesiastical superiors.

He founded several newspapers, almost all of them short-lived. Among them *O Latego* stands out for the violence of its language and its attacks on the ecclesiastical authorities, which Dr Varela later sincerely regretted.

Without being a remarkable journalist, he wrote with such astonishing ease that it amazed people. He published in book form: *A suspensão do professor da Escola Municipal da Ponta do Sol, Manuel José Varela*, 1888, 52 pp.; *Ultimas observações dum sentenciado. Resposta á critica do reverendo padre Pacheco...*, 1889, 127 pp.; *A guerra do Sr. D. Manuel Agostinho Barreto à confraria de Nª S.ª do Monte do Carmo*, 1891, 137 pp., which appeared anonymously; and *Victima da Rolha. A Decapitação do «Latego»...*, 1891, 282 pp., which was also published anonymously.
Varela (Dr José)

He was born in Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’) on 19 March 1874. He is a physician and surgeon, trained at the Medical-Surgical School of Lisbon (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica de Lisboa*), and a medical captain in the army, having enlisted with the rank of second lieutenant on 21 October 1903. He is a member of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*), and in 1921 he was elected senator for Madeira (1922).
Illustrious men

Under this title we shall present a survey of various men from this island who distinguished themselves notably away from their native soil, and particularly in our overseas campaigns. Many of them deserved fuller treatment in articles of their own, and some even a detailed biography. For some, however, we lack the essential information, while others were unintentionally omitted from the places they should have occupied in this work.

António Gonçalves da Câmara was a great-grandson of the discoverer João Gonçalves Zarco and the son of Dona Ana de Eça, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine. He was Master of the Hunt to King John III and held important offices at court, having earlier fought with outstanding valour in the lands of the East. He violently abducted Dona Isabel de Abreu, as is related at length on page 6 of volume I of this work.

Of João Rodrigues de Noronha, son of the 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, a chronicler says that he was a soldier of great renown in India, held the office of sea captain on the coast of Diu and later that of captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of Hormuz.
Manuel de Noronha, brother of the above, greatly distinguished himself in the Moroccan campaigns, serving as frontier captain (fronteiro) in Safi.
Rui Gonçalves da Câmara, captain-major of the Indian sea and captain of Barcelor and of Hormuz, left a name crowned with glory for the many exploits he performed.

Luís Gonçalves de Ataíde, lord of the Desertas (‘deserted islands’), fought in Africa as captain of the stronghold of Ceuta. He was the father of the Count of Atouguia and the forefather of the holders of that title.

Jordão de Freitas, of whom the chroniclers of India speak in highly laudatory terms, was born in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). He was captain of the Moluccas and lord of the islands of Amboíno and Siam, by a grant made by the King of Ternate and later confirmed by John III in 1543.

Gonçalo de Freitas da Silva, son of the above and likewise a native of Santa Cruz, served valiantly in Asia, where he held the same lordships as his father; these were confirmed by King Sebastian in 1574.

Jordão de Freitas da Silva, son of the above, who, a genealogist says, ‘was ambassador to France for the recovery of the artillery and other property lost there in the year 1626’, died while carrying out this mission. In reward for this service his son Gonçalo de Freitas was given the commandery of Santa Maria de Lisboa in the Order of Christ.

João de Freitas da Silva, a member of the same family, raised on this island in 1631 a company of 100 men, paid at his own expense, and went with it to fight in Pernambuco, where he was killed by the Dutch.

Diogo Cabral served with distinction in the East and was appointed by the king captain of the fleet intended to discover the Island of Gold, an enterprise that never took place because of the obstacles raised by the governor of India, Martim Afonso de Sousa. Lopo Mendes de Vasconcelos fought valiantly in India, having gone out to that state as captain of a carrack in the fleet commanded by Vasco da Gama, whose brother-in-law he was. This Madeiran returned to Asia once more as captain of a carrack.

Manuel de Vasconcelos, son of the above, was called ‘the one of India’ for his long service there, and was captain of the Moluccas and of Cannanore. He was the husband of the celebrated heroine Isabel da Veiga, who won such fame at the siege of Diu and whom all the chroniclers of our campaigns in Asia praise in the highest terms. Because she was married to a Madeiran, some have taken her for a native of this island, but she was born in mainland Portugal, of an illustrious family.

Manuel de Vasconcelos, of the same family, went out to India in 1613 as captain of a carrack, together with six sons, all of whom gave proof of great valour. As a result the eldest, António Mendes de Vasconcelos, received a commandery of the Order of Christ, which on his death passed to his brother Luís Mendes de Vasconcelos, commander of the fortress of Bassein. Another son of Manuel de Vasconcelos, named André de Vasconcelos, died heroically in the naval battle in the sea of Hormuz.
António Mialheiro, or Malheiro, took part in the capture of Azemmour as captain-major of four caravels and rendered notable services there. He was later governor of the castle of São Jorge da Mina.
Rui Dias de Aguiar the Elder died in the fortress of Cabo de Gué, in Africa, after valiantly defending it as its captain; a son of his of the same name also distinguished himself there.

Pedro Afonso de Aguiar, brother of the above, was chief outfitter of the fleets of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), superintendent (provedor) of the storehouses and commander of the Order of Christ. He went out to India as captain of a carrack in the armada of Lopo Soares, was with him at the destruction of Cranganore, and served as captain-major of the Southern Sea in the East. Later he was with Jaime, Duke of Braganza, at the conquest of Azemmour in Africa, where he was placed in charge of naval operations, in which he was highly skilled.

Luís de Noronha and João Fogaça de Eça, sons of Pedro Gonçalves da Câmara and Dona Joana de Eça, chief lady of the bedchamber to Queen Catherine, were the two captains of the fleet that, by order of the captain-donatary of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, sailed from this island to relieve the fortress of Santa Cruz at Cabo de Gué, in Africa, where they distinguished themselves by their valour and courage.

João Fernandes de Andrade, to whom we have already referred elsewhere (volume I, page 66), and his sons, born on this island, served valiantly in Africa, for which King John granted them their own coat of arms with the surname Arco. They were descendants of the Andrades of Galicia, Counts of Vilhalva. A son of João Fernandes de Andrade was Francisco de Andrade, who fought heroically in Morocco and who, having killed an ounce there, presented its skin to King Manuel I, who greatly prized it.

António Correia, whom his contemporaries called ‘the Great’, distinguished himself remarkably on many occasions in Africa and Asia, performing deeds of the utmost valour with the greatest selflessness and self-denial. He not only spent a considerable part of his fortune but also refused any reward for his services. For many years his descendants kept several letters that various monarchs had addressed to him, praising his valiant deeds and thanking him for the services he had selflessly rendered to his king and his country. Many years after his death, his great-grandson António Correia Henriques had restored to him the letter of nobility and the noble rank (*foro de fidalgo*) that António Correia had held in recognition of the great services he had rendered. His descendants Jorge Correia Betencourt, João Correia Betencourt and especially Gaspar Correia Betencourt also fought valiantly in Africa. The last of these was killed in Funchal in 1566, defending the city during the sack by French corsairs.
Manuel de Freitas Drumond was a great soldier in India, in the words of one chronicler, and was knighted at Mombasa during the siege laid to that city.
Lopo de Arouguia rendered great services in India and was appointed governor of the fortress of Daman.
Simão de Atouguia distinguished himself remarkably at Tangier, for which he was granted the commandery of São Pedro do Sul in the Order of Christ.
João de Betencourt de Vasconcelos went to India as captain of a carrack and there gave proof of great valour, holding various offices.
Matias de Andrade and his brother Manuel de Andrade Correia became well known in the Portuguese East for the posts they held and the acts of bravery they performed there.

Henrique Moniz de Meneses was awarded the Commandery of São Cosme in the Order of Christ in recognition of the outstanding services he rendered in Africa. His sons Vasco and Pedro Moniz also distinguished themselves in various campaigns; they drowned on the voyage they made to Maranhão in the fleet of Dom Luís de Melo, in the third quarter of the 16th century.
Tristão Teixeira, grandson of the first donatary (*donatário*) of Machico, distinguished himself so remarkably as a warrior in India that he was known as ‘the Reckless’.
Rafael Catanho, with whom several chroniclers deal, was famed as a great soldier in the lands of the East and went to India as captain of a carrack.
António de Andrade Couto was, says an old document, a famous captain in battles against the Persians, distinguished by the daring and composure with which he fought.
Belchior Berenguer was a brave and fearless soldier whose feats include having defeated in single combat ‘a proud Moor of great strength’.

Fernão Lopes de Freitas, of the Freitas family of Madalena (‘Magdalene’), served with distinction in India and then became *alcaide-mor* (royal governor of a castle and town) of Tangier, an office that passed down to his descendants.

Gaspar Vilela, says an old manuscript, was born in Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’) and was a valiant knight in the fortress of Cape Gué. When Safim was attacked and the Moors killed the captain and the *adail* of that stronghold, Gaspar Vilela took part in the expedition sent to relieve it, maintaining a number of men at his own expense. He remained there for some months, performing deeds of valour. He also accompanied the Infante Dom Luís on the expedition to Tunis.
António Espinola fought as a volunteer in India and was captain of a carrack at the taking of Mangalore, where he behaved like a hero.
Mem de Ornelas e Vasconcelos died at Chaul, where he distinguished himself as captain of a company. He had served in India for many years, always at his own expense and with great selflessness.
João de Ornelas de Vasconcelos, a close relative of the preceding, served for a long time in Morocco and became known for his acts of bravery at the taking of Safim and Azamor.

Francisco Figueiroa raised a *terço* on this island and served as its *mestre de campo* (colonel commanding a *terço*), taking it to fight in the wars against the Dutch in Brazil; he was one of the restorers of Pernambuco. He was later governor-general of the Cape Verde archipelago.

Manuel Dias de Andrade took part in the recapture of Bahia as captain of a carrack, and fought many times, with great heroism, in various fleets against the Turks and the Dutch. He died in Cape Verde while sailing in the fleet of Francisco de Melo to join the forces that were to attempt the recovery of Pernambuco.

António de Freitas da Silva served in the army that recaptured Bahia and was a fearless captain in the Pernambuco wars. He later distinguished himself in the campaigns of the Restoration against Spain, serving as military governor of Trás-os-Montes and as captain-major (*capitão-mor*, commander of the local militia) of a fleet.

João de Freitas da Silva, a relative of the preceding, raised a company of a hundred men on this island at his own expense and went to fight in the Pernambuco wars, where he distinguished himself and where he died at the hands of the Dutch.
Around the middle of the 17th century Francisco de Betencourt e Sá, after fighting heroically in Brazil, organised a *terço* in Madeira and went to serve in the wars of Flanders.

Diogo Vaz da Veiga, brother of Tristão Vaz da Veiga, spent two years in Asilah, says Gaspar Frutuoso, and afterwards served in various fleets, on several occasions as captain of a galley, ‘meeting with good fortune’. He died after being elected captain of Tangier.

Tristão de França, a knight of the Order of Christ and a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*), distinguished himself valiantly in the wars in Brazil, serving as captain of sea and war in the fleet in which António Teles de Meneses was general.

Francisco de França Barbosa, brother of the preceding, held the rank of captain of sea and war and later that of *mestre de campo* in Entre Douro e Minho, a province he governed during the wars of Restoration, in which he distinguished himself notably; the Count of Ericeira speaks of him in the most laudatory terms in *Portugal Restaurado*. Luís Telo de Meneses, a captain of infantry, died heroically at the battle of Montijo, one of the engagements in which Portuguese troops showed the greatest valour in the wars of Restoration.
Lúcio Betencourt de Vasconcelos was one of the brave soldiers of the wars of Restoration, in which he held the rank of captain of infantry.
Cristóvão de Ornelas de Abreu also served in the Restoration campaigns, in which he distinguished himself, and was later governor of the new colony of Buenos Aires.

Zenobio Acciaioli fought valiantly in the Pernambuco wars, where he was *mestre de campo*, winning fame as a doughty knight. João Baptista Acciaioli, his brother, likewise distinguished himself in the Pernambuco campaigns after the restoration of Portugal.

Francisco de Berenguer de Andrade, father-in-law of the illustrious João Fernandes Vieira, was one of the first to take part in the fighting that preceded the recovery of Pernambuco, showing remarkable intrepidity. António de Andrade Berenguer, Francisco Berenguer, Manuel Dias de Andrade and Agostinho César Berenguer, brothers-in-law of Fernandes Vieira, greatly distinguished themselves in the wars in Brazil and in those of the Restoration, but they were all born in Bahia.

Félix Ferreira served with dauntless courage in several engagements, and it is said that it was chiefly thanks to his bravery that most of the Portuguese were saved from the fleet that was wrecked off the coast of France in 1626.

Lourenço da Veiga, brother of Tristão Vaz da Veiga, of whom the *Saudades* say: ‘As a young man he served for some time in Asilah and in Tangier, where he was wounded. He sailed in several fleets as a soldier, and was captain-major of a squadron that hunted down a corsair and of others that went to Mina and to the Azores.’

We have dealt elsewhere in this work with the Madeirans João Fernandes Vieira and António de Abreu, and we have also sketched brief biographical notes on the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th donataries of Funchal, setting out the most important services they rendered to the country.
Varona (Friar Inácio José)

He belonged to the Carmelite order and preached in the church of the College (Igreja do Colégio, the Jesuit college church) during the splendid celebrations held there in thanksgiving for the Marquis of Pombal’s escape from the crime planned by the Genoese João Batista Pelle, who was executed on 11 October 1775. Friar Inácio’s address was published under the following title: *Oração na acção de graças que a Real Junta da Fazenda da ilha da Madeira fez celebrar pela prodigiosa conservação da muito necessária vida do Illustrissimo e Excelentissimo Senhor Marquez de Pombal Sebastião José de Carvalho e Mello na egreja de São João Evangelista da cidade do Funchal em 20 de Janeiro dirigida pelo seu presidente o Illustrissimo e Excellentissimo Senhor João Antonio de Sá Pereira, do concelho de S. M. Fidelissima, Senhor d'Alverca, Alcaide Mor de Monte Mor o Velho, Comendador da Ordem de Christo, Governador e Capitão General desta Ilha da Madeira*, Lisbon, 1776, 23 pp.
Vasconcelos

There are, it seems, four branches of this surname. One descends from Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos; another from Mem Rodrigues de Vasconcelos, who was married to Dona Catarina Furtado de Mendonça, eldest daughter of Bartolomeu Perestrelo, first donatary (*donatário*) of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’); another from Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcelos, who married a daughter of Tristão Vaz Teixeira; and the fourth from Fernão Tavares de Vasconcelos, a native of Freixo de Numão, who settled in Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) around 1540. See Ornelas.
Vasconcelos e Sá (João Augusto de)

He was born in this city on 9 July 1880, when his father was in command of the artillery battery quartered at São Tiago; he was the son of Luís Augusto de Vasconcelos e Sá, then a captain, and Dona Maria Algeraz de Vasconcelos e Sá. He is one of the most admired contemporary poets and the author of the verse collections *Um livro* and *Rimas pobres*. He wrote the celebrated song *Margarida vai á fonte*, which enjoyed extraordinary success.

João Augusto de Vasconcelos e Sá, a former cavalry officer, was one of the 289 political deportees who, after the Monsanto rising (*Jornada de Monsanto*), were held in the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’) in Funchal (vol. I, p. 350).
Vasconcelos e Sousa (Afonso and José de)
See Sousa (Afonso and José Caminha de Vasconcelos e).
Vaz
Besides the descendants of Tristão Vaz Teixeira, there were from the earliest times, says Dr Azevedo, craftsmen bearing this surname: in 1471 one Lopo Vaz was a goldsmith in Funchal.
Vaz

(Father Fernando Carlos de Meneses). He was born in the parish (*freguesia*) of Santana (‘St Anne’) on 1 February 1884. He studied at the seminary (*Seminário*) of this diocese and was ordained priest in 1909. He is at present parish priest of the parish of Porto da Cruz (‘harbour of the cross’). In the *Correio da Madeira* (‘Madeira Courier’) he published some well-crafted articles containing historical information on several parishes in the north of this island. In the parish archive of Faial he recently discovered the birth record of the illustrious Madeiran João Fernandes Vieira, whose native parish had until then been unknown, despite the painstaking research carried out to that end (1921).

Father Fernando Vaz, who devotes his leisure to various genealogical studies intended for publication, is the grandson of the distinguished Madeiran genealogist João Agostinho Pereira de Agrela (vol. I, p. 20 and vol. II, p. 435).
Vaz da Veiga (Tristão)

While Dom Francisco de Portugal, Count of Vimioso, was still alive and captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Machico, Philip II granted that captaincy to Tristão Vaz da Veiga on 25 February 1582.
