On 19 October 1585 he appointed him governor-general of this archipelago, and Vaz da Veiga took up the post on 22 November of the same year. It was the payment for the treason that Tristão Vaz da Veiga had committed against his homeland.

Gaspar Frutuoso says that heaven and earth are full of his ‘heroic deeds and glorious victories, from Japan to China, from Malacca to the Ganges, from the Ganges to the Tagus and from the Tagus to the ends of sea and land’. Many authors have written about Tristão da Veiga, and all are unanimous in extolling his martial valour and the heroic actions he performed; the author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) devotes fifty long pages to him in the warmest and loftiest panegyric. Yet after so many glorious exploits, which did so much to raise the prestige of the Portuguese name in the East, Tristão Vaz blackened the memory of his deeds. He went over to the enemies of his homeland and basely and treacherously surrendered the fortress of São Julião da Barra, which guarded the entrance to the harbour of Lisbon, thereby hastening the fall of Portugal under the Castilian yoke.

Pinheiro Chagas says that the ‘new governor, who had earlier sold his services to António, Prior of Crato, did not hesitate to hand over the maritime keys of Lisbon to the Spanish general for the modest reward of an annual income of three thousand *cruzados* and the town (*vila*) of Machico on the island of Madeira’.

This reward was increased, as has already been said, by the important post of governor-general of the Madeira archipelago, and we do not know whether he received any other payments for his most vile treason.

He was the third governor-general of this archipelago during the period of Spanish rule, and it must be admitted that in this office he rendered excellent service, above all in driving off, with prompt and vigorous relief, the attempts of various corsair ships that from time to time sought to attack this island.

Tristão Vaz da Veiga was a great-grandson of João Gonçalves Zarco and a grandson of Dona Beatriz Gonçalves da Câmara, the discoverer’s daughter, who married Diogo Cabral. He died in 1604 or shortly before, aged about 67.
Vaz (Tristão)

Tristão Vaz is the well-known and intrepid companion of João Gonçalves Zarco in the discovery of this archipelago. We share the opinion of the distinguished annotator of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) when he states that the surname Teixeira attached to the name of Tristão Vaz was an addition made by the chroniclers. This was certainly because the navigator’s descendants used that surname, which came from Branca (‘white’) Teixeira, Tristão Vaz’s wife. The letter of grant (*carta de doação*) of the captaincy of Machico (*Capitania de Machico*), dated 1440, says only Tristão, and that is also what he is called by Gomes Eanes de Zurara, the earliest chronicler to deal with our archipelago, who wrote his chronicle around 1453. João de Barros, in the mid-16th century, and Damião de Góis, at roughly the same period – that is, a century after the death of the illustrious discoverer – name him, the former Tristão Vaz and the latter Tristão Vaz Teixeira; this is the first occasion on which the surname Teixeira appears.

It is worth transcribing one of the notes to Frutuoso’s work on this subject: ‘Besides António Cordeiro and José Soares da Silva, Damião de Góis and António Galvão also gave the first captain-donatary of Machico the name Tristão Vaz Teixeira. We consider this a manifest error, arising from the same causes pointed out with reference to those first two writers. All four came after the adoption of the maternal surname Teixeira by the descendants of Tristão Vaz, which is spoken of in the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, and they confused him with those descendants. For that Tristão Vaz did not take the surname Teixeira, nor was he known by it, is proved by: 1. the letter of grant of the captaincy of Machico, which does not mention that surname; 2. the *Chronica de Guiné* by Gomes Eanes de Zurara, the only writer contemporary with Tristão Vaz, who calls him there only Tristão and Tristão da Ilha; 3. his will, cited by Frutuoso, in which the surname Teixeira likewise does not appear; and 4., finally, the customs of lineage, which would run counter to a husband adopting the surname of his wife’s family.

‘But suppose all these reasons were ineffective; suppose the word of Góis, Galvão, Cordeiro and Soares da Silva prevailed over that of Frutuoso, over the testimony of Zurara, over the authentic proof furnished by the letter of grant, and over the ideas and customs of the age; suppose the first donatary of Machico were called Tristão Vaz Teixeira: for that very reason the heading in the *Cancioneiro de Resende*, “Tristão Teixeira, captain of Machico”, would not refer to him. It lacks the Vaz, a surname that all the authorities favouring Teixeira place before it. None of them calls the first donatary of Machico Tristão Teixeira. This – not the addition but the substitution of a surname – appears only among the descendants of Tristão Vaz, as can be seen in the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, the ‘Island History’ (*Historia Insulana*) and the Madeiran *Nobiliarios*.

‘Therefore, and for the further reasons given in the places to which we append this addendum, we are convinced that Tristão Vaz, first donatary of Machico, did not take the surname Teixeira, and that the poet referred to in the heading of the *Cancioneiro de Resende* was Tristão Teixeira, “das Damas”, the second donatary.’

In the charter by which Prince Henry the Navigator grants a considerable part of Madeira to Tristão Vaz, he calls this navigator ‘knight of my household’. Azurara, in the *Chronica da Guiné*, says that the two discoverers of this archipelago were ‘noble squires brought up in that lord’s household, who asked him to provide for them as best he could, in keeping with their honour’. From these words, says Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, it follows ‘that Tristão was not a person of low condition, but a noble and honourable squire.’ A further presumption of Tristão Vaz’s nobility is that he married Branca Teixeira, a lady of one of the leading families of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), and that he came to the island of Madeira already married to her and with children, before he was given the captaincy of Machico. This shows that the marriage was not obtained on account of this royal grant.

‘This captain of Machico, Tristão, says Frutuoso, was so outstanding for his valour at the time when he served Prince Henry that he was commonly called Tristão, with no further surname, in honour of his knighthood. For the King, because he was such a man, gave him as arms of knighthood a phoenix on a blue field; and just as this bird is unique in the world, so he was the one and only knight of his name, Tristão. This was shown by many warrants and letters that the King and the Princes wrote to him, and they always named him Tristão da Ilha, Knight of their Household; and in his will he names himself thus, with no further adornment of surname. For in this way he was distinguished by his arms, which were (as I have said) a phoenix, which his descendants always bore in their arms, quartered with others that they added from the female line of the Teixeiras, namely a cross fleury and a fleur-de-lis, which are today carved on the arch of his chapel of São João Baptista in the main church of Machico.’

We must nevertheless recall here, as we have noted elsewhere, that in the old chronicles and the old Madeiran genealogies the name of João Gonçalves Zargo is always surrounded by an aura of greater prestige and higher regard than that of Tristão Vaz. This leads us to believe that the first discoverer, through his personal qualities, his social position or perhaps distinguished services rendered earlier, had won the rights of precedence and superiority that placed him above his companion in the discovery. Dr Gaspar Frutuoso writes: ‘The deed held by the heirs of João Gonçalves says that he was the principal in this feat (the discovery), naming Tristão Vaz as Tristão da Ilha, as the King and the Prince named him in their warrants and grants, as a less principal person, and not of such age or quality as João Gonçalves.’ And elsewhere the historian of the Islands says further, referring to the first colonisation: ‘he sent two captains with João Gonçalves, namely Bartolomeu Perestrelo, who was to remain on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), and Tristão, knight of the Prince’s household, both of whom came under the banner of the said João Gonçalves Zargo (although there is no lack of many who say otherwise)...’

Tristão Vaz is thought to have been born in the last years of the 14th century. He served in Africa, where he was knighted by Prince Henry the Navigator, to whose household he belonged as one of his noble squires, as already mentioned.

After the discovery of the island of Madeira, a brief account of which is given elsewhere, the author of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ states that Tristão Vaz settled on this island with his wife and children in May 1425. Madeira was then divided between him and Gonçalves Zargo into two captaincies, and the jurisdiction of the two captains-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) was defined, as already described in the articles Donataries, Captaincies, Captaincy of Machico and Ponta da Oliveira, to which we refer the reader to avoid needless repetition. In those articles we also briefly discussed Tristão Vaz’s administration as captain-donatary, which seems to have left a good deal to be desired.

For the punishment he inflicted on Diogo Barradas (volume I, page 128), he was summoned to court by the king and handed over to justice. He was sentenced to penal exile (degredo) on the island of São Tomé, where he remained for some time. His social standing, the services he had rendered and the influence exerted on his behalf restored him to possession of the captaincy of Machico.

‘On account of certain business he had in the Algarve,’ says Frutuoso, ‘this Tristão, the first captain, went to Silves, where he departed this present life, leaving his jurisdiction peopled with sons and daughters and with so noble a line as descended from him. He was more than eighty years of age, of which he would have governed some fifty, more or less.’
Veiga (Dr José Manuel da)
Dr José Manuel da Veiga was born in Funchal on 18 October 1794, the son of João Paulo da Veiga and Dona Jacinta Rosa Leça da Veiga.

In 1816 he enrolled in the faculty of canon law at the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*). After a brilliant course of study, in which he won first prize in every year, he received the doctoral hood (*capelo*) in 1822 and was then admitted to the teaching staff of that institution of higher education. During his studies he showed such extraordinary talent that his fellow students sought him out as their tutor and coach, and the professors admitted him into their intimate circle. This was remarkable at a time when the rigidity of university discipline did not allow such closeness between teachers and students. It seems that, while still a student at the University, he took holy orders and had even celebrated Mass, but he later abandoned his ecclesiastical career, to the great scandal of his contemporaries. On taking his doctorate he defended a thesis attacking a very important precept of Church discipline, which he published under the title *Memória sobre o celibato eclesiastico...* The volume was seized and ordered to be destroyed, and few copies circulated. In 1866, after his death, a second edition of this work appeared in a volume of two hundred and some pages.
After some years of teaching he gave up his professorial chair and set up practice as an advocate in Lisbon, where he had a large clientele and enjoyed the reputation of a distinguished lawyer.

Among the legal works that earned him standing as a notable jurist, the most outstanding is his *Código Penal da Nação Portuguesa*, published in 1837. Inocêncio Francisco da Silva’s *Diccionario Bibliographico* mentions other legal works by José Manuel da Veiga, which we omit for the sake of brevity.
He also courted the Muses, publishing a tragedy entitled *Medea* and a collection of assorted poems. He died in Lisbon on 26 September 1859.
Veiga Pestana (Second Lieutenant João Paulo da)

He was the son of João Pestana Santos and Dona Carlota Amália Drumond da Veiga Pestana, and was born in Funchal on 25 December 1895. Having completed his preparatory studies at the lyceum (state secondary school) of this city in 1913, he enrolled in the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*) to study civil engineering. However, when he was called up for the army in 1916, after Portugal entered the Great War, he was at once summoned to the school for militia officers on account of his scientific qualifications. He was posted as an officer cadet to the 30th Infantry Regiment (*infantaria 30*) on 1 May 1917 and commissioned second lieutenant on 5 September of the same year. Mobilised to serve with the Portuguese Expeditionary Corps (*C. E. P.*) in France, he left for that country on 11 September of the same year. There he met a glorious death at the Battle of the Lys on 9 April 1918, after spending seven months in the trenches and giving countless proofs of his military spirit and valour there. The Portuguese press wrote at length about the ill-fated officer João Paulo da Veiga Pestana, and the *Ilustração Portuguesa* published his portrait together with some biographical details.

At its session of 10 April 1919, the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) gave the name of Second Lieutenant Veiga Pestana to the old Rua das Hortas, this being ‘a simple but well-deserved tribute to the young officer who, when urged to flee as the danger drew nearest, replied, his eyes fixed on the Fatherland: Let whoever wishes flee; I stay to do my duty’.
Veitch (Henrique)

On 7 August 1857 the British subject Henrique Veitch died on this island, having served for many years as English consul here in Madeira. His name remains linked to the history of this archipelago, above all for the valuable protection he gave to many Madeirans when Miguelist troops seized Madeira, and again during the turbulent period of our civil wars. Henrique Veitch was appointed his country’s representative in Madeira during the second occupation of this island by British troops, in a year we cannot now state precisely, but which fell within the period from 1807 to 1814. Despite holding his post in so delicate a situation, he managed to conduct himself in such a way as to avoid conflict with the local authorities and not to stir up the ill will of the island’s inhabitants against him.

Henrique Veitch linked his name to Napoleon’s passage through Madeira on 23 August 1815, for, as is well known, he was the only person who went aboard the carrack *Northumberland* and spoke to the emperor. It is said that Napoleon received him and listened to him because Veitch addressed him as ‘Majesty’, whereas on board he could only be called by the plain name of General Bonaparte. When the English consul offered his services to Napoleon, the latter replied that he would be very glad to receive some books and fruit. Veitch very graciously obliged, sending him a magnificent gift of fruit, sweets and old wines. Napoleon sent Veitch some gold louis to pay for the boat that had carried the refreshments on board, and tradition has it that the consul placed them in the cornerstone of the Anglican church in Rua da Bela Vista when the foundations were dug for the building of that place of worship (see II-422).

Henrique Veitch was so fond of Madeira that he spent a considerable part of his fortune here buying a great deal of property and putting up several buildings. Outstanding among them is the house in Rua 5 de Outubro (‘5 October street’), between the Bom Jesus and Nova bridges, whose architecture is highly original for Madeira and at once catches the eye of any curious observer passing by. The houses in Rua das Queimadas de Baixo, in the locality (*sítio*) of Calassa and in the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos are also characteristic buildings. Special mention is due to the lovely residence at Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’), for the originality of its construction, for the pleasantness of the spot and also for the strange mausoleum that stands a short distance from the house, out in the open mountains, where the mortal remains of the English consul Henrique Veitch rest.

As we have already mentioned, the protection Veitch gave to many Madeirans during the turbulent period of our civil wars was invaluable. His houses served as a safe and hospitable refuge for many victims of political persecution. In 1828, when the absolutist troops occupied Madeira, he arranged the escape of many inhabitants of this island on board the frigate *Alligator*. Among them were the governor José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, the Count of Carvalhal and two of his nephews, the dean Januário Camacho, Colonel Albuquerque, the *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district), the *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) and many others.
Velosa

The surname Velosa (formerly Avelosa) descends from Gonçalo Anes de Velosa and a brother of his, natives of Celorico, who were among the first settlers of this island. Gonçalo Anes built the church of São Bartolomeu (St Bartholomew) in Funchal.
Velosa Castelo-Branco
Caetano Velosa Carvalhal Esmeraldo Castelo-Branco, holder of the entail (*morgado*), represented Madeira in parliament in the 1868–1869 legislature. He died on 12 June 1874.
Veloso de Oliveira (Dr António Rodrigues)
See Oliveira (Dr António Rodrigues).
Veloso (Dr Afonso de Melo Pinto)
This magistrate was appointed civil governor of this district by decree of 27 January 1910 and took office on 24 February of the same year. He served for only a few months.
Winds

Intensity and percentage frequency of the winds at Ponta de São Lourenço (‘St Lawrence Point’). From a study by the distinguished naval officer C. Pinto Basto Carreiro, we have taken the following interesting data:
PERCENTAGE INTENSITY OF THE WINDS OBSERVED AT SÃO LOURENÇO DURING THE YEARS 1930, 1931 AND 1932

The name trade winds (*alizados*) is given to the regular winds that blow steadily all year round on either side of the Equator, from the north-east towards the south-west in the northern hemisphere and from the south-east in the southern hemisphere.
In the North Atlantic the trade winds begin to be clearly felt on the island of Madeira, and sometimes even south of mainland Portugal. They blow steadily until close to the Equator.

Between the trade winds of the northern hemisphere and those of the southern hemisphere lies the zone of the equatorial calms. The counter-trade winds, or upper trade winds, blow in the high regions of the atmosphere in the opposite direction to the former.
Percentage of winds observed at São Lourenço during 1930, 1931 and 1932

The graph of the percentages of winds observed at São Lourenço shows that the prevailing winds are northerly, north-easterly and north-westerly. The least frequent winds are the ESE, SSE, WSW and WNW. The winds are observed at São Lourenço and not in Funchal, because the winds that affect the bay are not general, except when they belong to the southern quadrants. Of the southern quadrants, the most frequent winds are those from the SW and SE.
Intensity
The stormy winds are those of the southern quadrant, especially the S, SSW, SW and WSW. The greater percentage of these winds are strong.
The winds of the other quadrants are for the most part moderate. This is easily verified by looking at the attached scale’.
True Cross (Chapel of the)

‘João Gonsalves Zargo,’ says Frutuoso, ‘... passing further down to some very high mountains, there laid out another church of the Vera-Cruz...’. The idea of founding this chapel belongs to the discoverer, although it was built only later, in a year that is not known. It is nevertheless one of the oldest chapels in the diocese. Over time it has undergone various transformations, and nothing of the original building, certainly, survives there at present. It originally formed part of the parish of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’) or of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), and came to belong to the parish (*freguesia*) of Campanário (‘bell tower’) when the latter was created around the middle of the 16th century. Since 1848, when Quinta Grande (‘large estate’) became an independent parish, the old chapel of the Vera Cruz has belonged to that parish.

It stands in the locality (*sítio*) to which it gave its own name, and from there one enjoys a fine, wide panorama. It has sometimes served as the parish church, and the parish cemetery lies around it. The feast of its patron saint draws a considerable crowd, especially from the neighbouring parishes. (See Quinta Grande.)
Mullein

The plants known by this name in Madeira belong to the following species: *Verbascum thapsus*, *V. floccosum* and *V. sinuatum*. All these species are whitish and woolly (tomentose) and have large leaves, which are deeply cut in *V. sinuatum* and entire or merely toothed in *V. thapsus* and *V. floccosum*. The last of these is easily distinguished from the others by its very readily shed down. The yellow flowers and the leaves of the mulleins are emollient.
Verdade (A)
The first issue of this Catholic newspaper, which lasted for some years, appeared on 23 January 1875.
In 1915 another periodical of the same name appeared. Its first issue came out on 1 May, and it ended with no. 216 on 3 November 1919.
Vergasta (A)
The first issue of this newspaper appeared on 15 October 1873, and it ended with no. 60 on 6 December 1876.
Worms

Four terrestrial worms, says Johnson, have been recorded in Madeira, among them the earthworm. As for marine worms, more than 240 species are known, collected by Professor Paul Langerhans. This naturalist illustrated the new species well in the *Zeitschrift für wissenchaftliche Zoologie* (1879–1884).
The largest and most beautiful of the Madeiran marine worms is *Amphinone carunculata*, a species furnished with stinging bristles.
Electric traction

At the end of 1910 the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) tried to introduce electric traction in the city, going as far as awarding the contract for the work to the now defunct Empresa Madeirense de Automóveis. As this award was not approved by the higher authorities, the Council drew up new terms for the operation, and on 24 August 1911 it resolved to ask the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) for the permanent and free transfer of the national roads on which the electric lines would have to be laid. The General Council refused this transfer, on the grounds that it intended to put out to tender the work of establishing that system of traction on the roads in its charge. The Council then decided to abandon its plan to give the city the improvement we refer to, and to place the municipal roads at the disposal of the General Council so that it could carry it out on whatever terms it saw fit.

The General Council, as is well known, did nothing, and only in 1923 did it again take an interest in establishing electric traction on the island. An English company appears to be willing to undertake this improvement, if the conditions that the General Council sets in the tender to be opened suit it (1921).

In June 1917 an advertisement appeared in the Funchal newspapers inviting all those interested in establishing electric traction to state, at the offices of A. Georgi & C.ª or Reid Castro & C.ª, the sums they intended to subscribe towards this improvement. Nobody answered the call, because the promoter of the venture, although an honest man, offered no guarantee of providing sound management for the works he intended to carry out (1921).

Under Article 6 of the terms for the award of the contract for building and operating horse tramways (*caminhos de ferro americanos*) in Funchal, which accompanied the decree of 2 August 1902, the contractor was permitted to use electric traction on the lines he might build.
Viana
This family surname begins with Afonso de Viana, who settled in Caniço (‘reed’) around 1500.
Viana de Freitas (Manuel Luís)

He was born in Funchal on 28 May 1820 and died there on 29 May 1861. He was doorkeeper of the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) and a corresponding member of the Instituto Dramático de Coimbra. He contributed to several Funchal newspapers and wrote a drama entitled *D. Luiz d'Athayde*.
Viana (Francisco Eduardo Alves)

The remarkable cultural institution founded in the city of Rio de Janeiro by the Portuguese community in 1837 under the name of Gabinete Português de Leitura is well known. One of its founders was the Madeiran Francisco Eduardo Alves Viana, who served with the greatest dedication as secretary of the organising committee of that great undertaking. Its catalogue, published in 1906 in two volumes of 1400 pages, shows the merit of this foundation and the services it has rendered.
Vida (A)
It was published on 5 October 1912, producing a single issue.
Vida Académica (A)
This newspaper produced only two issues, published on 6 January and 1 February 1914.
Vida Diocesana
The first issue of this newspaper appeared on 3 July 1921.
Vidal (Captain A. T. E.)

He visited the Madeira archipelago in 1842 and 1843 aboard the steamer *Styx*, which he commanded. He was responsible for surveying a chart of the islands of Madeira, Porto Santo and the Desertas, published in 1843. Captain Vidal, of the British Royal Navy, was greatly assisted in his work by the engineer captain António Pedro de Azevedo. See Maps.
Birch

As an addition to what is set out in various places in this work on the forest cover of Madeira, and in particular on the afforestation of the neighbouring island of Porto Santo (III-120), we transcribe some passages from an article by the illustrious botanist Carlos de Meneses, published in the former *Diário do Comercio*, which is of particular interest on this much-debated and ever-pressing subject.
‘In 1910 a number of birch specimens were sent to Porto Santo to be planted there. They had been donated by a foreigner who takes a keen interest in the reafforestation of that island.

In the view of the experts, Porto Santo should be afforested with Madeiran or Mediterranean species, and never with species from central or northern Europe. These have climatic requirements that the island cannot satisfy, both because of its geographical position and because of the low altitude of its hills.

Even among the Madeiran species, it seems to us that choices must be made. It is not credible that the extremely dry and low-lying ground of Porto Santo would suit certain species that here in Madeira thrive only in the valleys and ravines of the interior, or else in the high, damp places on the southern and northern slopes of our island.

Madeira mahogany (*vinhático*, *Persea indica*), for example, is a species unsuited to the forest cover of Porto Santo. Although the specimens introduced there look healthy for the time being, thanks to the irrigation they have received, the time will come when they will wither and finally die, because they do not find in the soil and the atmosphere the conditions necessary for their existence.

Lack of rain and intense heat, with winter averages that are not very low, give the neighbouring island its climatic character. On its hills only certain species found in the lower zone of Madeira can be grown with advantage, such as the laurel, the til (*Ocotea foetens*, Madeiran laurel) and the *barbusano* (Apollonias barbujana, a laurel-forest tree). The Madeira mahogany (vinhático, Persea indica) is not among them, since it begins to appear with some frequency only above 400 or 500 metres and needs moisture to develop.

Now, if the Madeira mahogany, a Madeiran species, is unsuitable for afforesting Porto Santo, the birch is even more so. As is well known, this tree reaches its southern limit in the Alto Minho, Gerês, Marão and the Serra da Estrela, and forms significant stands only in the northern regions and in central Europe, where the cold is extremely intense in winter and the warm season is short.

Even if the birch were a Mediterranean species suited to cultivation on Porto Santo, we would still exclude it from the island’s forest cover, because trees with deciduous foliage are not very suitable for afforesting countries with hot climates.

What the neighbouring island needs is evergreen trees, as those of Madeira generally are, in order to protect the soil from evaporation as far as possible and so encourage springs to appear. A cover made up of deciduous species would do little to improve the condition of the land, since the influence of such a cover must necessarily be very limited in a country with winter averages that are not very low, such as the one of which we are speaking.’
Vieira

According to Frutuoso, it is the surname of a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) and noble family. In 1566 two members lived in Funchal: Manuel Vieira, syndic (síndico, lay agent managing a religious house's property) of the nuns of the Convent of St Clare (*Santa Clara*), and a certain Favila Vieira, whom Frutuoso describes as a *fidalgo*. At about the same time a *fidalgo* named António Vieira held the office of bailiff (meirinho) of the jurisdiction of Machico; he married a daughter of the donatary (*donatário*) Diogo Teixeira. There are other branches of the Vieira family, two of which came from the Azores. One of them appeared in Madeira in the second quarter of the 19th century; the other began with Manuel Vieira de Afonseca, a native of the island of Terceira, who was clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*) of Funchal.
Vieira (Augusto Elmano)

He was born in Funchal on 2 October 1892 and is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in Law of the University of Lisbon (*Universidade de Lisboa*), having completed his degree in 1920. As a student at our lyceum (state secondary school) he contributed to the *Primeiro de Dezembro* (‘First of December’) and the *Academico*, and later to *Século*, *Diário Nacional*, *Tempo*, *Diário da Tarde* (‘Evening Daily’), etc., of Lisbon, and to the *Diário de Noticias* and *Diário da Madeira* (‘Madeira Daily’) of Funchal. He was one of the leaders of the students’ strike of 1919.

He collaborated on the revue of Madeiran manners entitled *A Madeira por dentro*, which was staged at the Teatro Dr Manuel de Arriaga, and on the regional operetta *A Menina dos Bordados*, which was performed at the Paris pavilion. In 1915, when he began his law studies at the University of Lisbon, he wrote the dramatic episode *A Ultima Bênção*, which was published in Funchal in 1917.
Elmano Vieira practises as a lawyer in Funchal and is a member of the Funchal Municipal Council (1921).
Vieira (Augusto José)

He was born in Funchal on 2 October 1861 and died on 27 December 1918 in Lisbon, where he had lived for more than 40 years. He was the brother of Councillor (conselheiro, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira and of João José Vieira, of whom we shall speak below. He attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and enrolled at the Army School (*Escola do Exército*), but never completed the course. In this city he was editor of the newspaper *A Republica*, and in Lisbon he contributed to various newspapers, always championing the most advanced ideas. He was president of the Civil Registration Association (*Associação do Registo Civil*) and secretary of the Freethought Federation (*Federação do Livre Pensamento*). In 1909 he published the *Historia do Partido Republicano*, which remained unfinished and of which three volumes appeared.
Vieira Caetano (Father João)

He was born in the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) on 11 December 1884 and was ordained priest in June 1906. At present he serves as parish priest in the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’). He has contributed extensively and valuably to various newspapers. He was chief editor of *Brado de Oeste*, in which he published the historical novel *Da Choça ao Solar* (‘From Hut to Manor House’), whose plot unfolds on this island (1921).
Vieira (Councillor Manuel José)

He was one of the men who rendered the most distinguished services to Madeira, both as a parliamentarian and as a member of the various bodies to which he belonged. No one understood better than he the duties laid upon a citizen. He often went so far as to sacrifice not only his peace and well-being but even his own health in order to serve well in the unpaid offices with which politics or his friends invested him, to the applause of all the people of Funchal. He always placed his clear intelligence and organising spirit at the service of his country, and he worked with the most resolute goodwill to the end of his life, moved solely by the desire to be useful to his homeland and his fellow citizens.

Manuel José Vieira, son of Manuel José Vieira and Dona Luísa Correia Vieira, both natives of the Azores, was born in Funchal on 7 August 1836. He attended secondary school in this city and in 1855 left for Coimbra, where, after sitting the so-called maturity examination, he enrolled at the University, completing his degree in law in 1860. That same year he entered the competition for the post of teacher of geography and history at the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school). After brilliant examinations he was appointed to the post, which he held for about 40 years with the greatest competence and with a zeal that might be equalled but not surpassed. From 1864 to 1868 he was president of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), an office he held again from 1899 to 1908. In directing the affairs of the municipality he gave ample proof of his concern for the improvement of the city and of the conditions of those who live in it. Had he not left the presidency of the Council in 1908, the city might perhaps possess today a sewerage network and a good supply of drinking water, improvements in which, as is well known, he took a keen interest.

Dr Manuel José Vieira was deputy for Madeira in the legislatures of 1879, 1882–1884, 1884–1887, 1887–1889 and 1894–1895, and in 1889 he was elected peer of the realm for the district of Vila Real, although he never took his seat in that chamber. Among the benefits he obtained for Madeira as a deputy were the unification of the currency; the studies for the road around the island by the engineer Tellier, for which he secured a credit of 30 *contos* (1 conto = 1,000,000 réis, from 1911 1,000 escudos); the special legislation that gave the levadas (irrigation channels) of Madeira legal standing to safeguard their rights; the collection of the land on which the theatre and the municipal garden were built; the exemption from tonnage dues for steamers calling at the port of Funchal; the exemption from duties on the import of maize from 1882 to 1886; and the construction of the artificial harbour at the locality (*sítio*) of Pontinha (‘little point’), etc., etc.

Besides serving as deputy and as president of the Municipality, Dr Manuel José Vieira held many other offices. He was a district councillor, president of the former District General Council (*Junta Geral*), president of the Administrative Committee (*Comissão Administrativa*) of the Holy House of Mercy (*Santa Casa da Misericórdia*), a member of the Asylum committee, a member of the Anti-Phylloxera Committee, secretary and president of the Commercial Association, president of the general meeting and director of the Monte Railway (*Caminho de Ferro do Monte*) Company, president of the general meeting of the insurance company Madeiran Alliance (*Aliança Madeirense*), etc., etc. The former Funchal Beneficent Association owed him the most outstanding services. He was also a highly distinguished lawyer and a devoted protector of Madeiran agriculture.

Dr Manuel José Vieira held the title of Councillor (*carta de conselho*), and was later awarded the Grand Cross of the Order of Nossa Senhora da Conceição de Vila Viçosa for the truly remarkable way in which he represented the city during the visit that the former sovereigns King Carlos I and Empress Amélie made to this island in 1901. He was a member of the Coimbra Institute, the Association of Writers and Journalists and the Lisbon Geographical Society.

He was one of the editors of the *Revista Juridica*, a weekly publication that first appeared in this city on 19 October 1870, and he contributed to several Funchal newspapers, among them *O Direito* (‘Law’) and the *Diário Popular* (‘The People’s Daily’). Of his speeches, those he delivered in the Chamber of Deputies at the sittings of 7 May 1883, 13 February 1884 and 7 July 1888 (*Questão da propriedade na Madeira*) were reprinted as pamphlets. He died in Funchal on 12 June 1912. See Unificação da moeda and Rua da Carreira.
Vieira de Castro (Dr José Cardoso)

In sketching a brief biography of our illustrious fellow countryman Jaime Moniz, we referred to the supremely eloquent speech he delivered at the trial of Dr José Cardoso Vieira de Castro (volume II, page 382), after the lamentable tragedy that deprived the country of the services of this astonishing talent and distinguished parliamentarian. Dr Vieira de Castro passed through our port aboard the steamer *D. Antónia* in the first days of September 1871, bound for Luanda to serve the sentence passed by the court that had condemned him. Several people from this city went on board to pay their respects. The Madeiran journalist João Augusto de Ornelas (volume III, page 21) published a pamphlet entitled *A Coroa de Ouro, o que foi e o que é José Cardoso Vieira de Castro*, which we have never managed to see.
Dr José Cardoso Vieira de Castro was the uncle of Henrique Vieira de Castro, whom we discuss in this *Elucidário*.
Vieira de Castro (Dr Luís)

He was born in this city on 10 May 1898, the son of Henrique Augusto Vieira de Castro and Dona Alegria Adida Vieira de Castro. He attended the Funchal lyceum (state secondary school) and is a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law of the University of Coimbra (*Universidade de Coimbra*).

He began his literary career early, contributing to various newspapers and, while still attending our lyceum, publishing in book form some of the writings scattered through this city’s periodical press. He has already contributed widely to many newspapers and magazines, and in Coimbra he was an editor of, and a regular contributor to, several periodicals. At the end of 1923 he launched in this city a daily newspaper entitled *Jornal da Madeira*, of which he is director. He has published the following volumes: *Nebuloses*, Funchal, 1916; *Livro Extranho*, Porto, 1916; *Civilisados*, Coimbra, 1918; *A Hora Internacional e a Nacionalidade Portugueza*, Coimbra, 1919; and *a Europa e a Republica Portuguesa*, Coimbra, 1922 (1921).

After that date he published *O Mundo que finda e o mundo que começa*, 1936; *D. Carlos I*, 1936; *Limbo*, 1936; *Em Pé de Guerra*, 1937; *A Formação de Portugal*, 1938; *Pedra sobre Pedra*, 1942; and *Rumo à Vitoria*, 1943.
Vieira de Castro (Henrique Augusto)
He is the son of Luís Lopes Vieira de Castro and Dona Carolina Cândida Vieira de Castro, and was born in the city of Porto on 24 June 1869.

Towards the end of 1893 he settled in Funchal as director of the Bank of Portugal’s agency on this island, and he is currently managing partner of the important banking house Reid, Castro & C.ª. He is an intelligent, active and enterprising merchant and industrialist. To him is owed the growth of several Madeiran industries and also the notable development of various branches of local trade (1921).

Through his charitable acts, Henrique Vieira de Castro has rendered signal services to various charitable institutions and to the poor of our island. The founding of the School of Arts and Crafts (*Escola de Artes e Ofícios*), intended to support destitute children, is due in large part to him.

In the articles Angústias Cemetery (volume I, page 70), Escola Elementar do Comércio (volume I, page 398), Jardim Municipal (volume II, page 182) and Misericórdias (volume II, page 372) we have already referred specifically to some of the important services that Henrique Vieira de Castro has rendered to Madeira, which he regards as his true adopted homeland (1921).
Vieira (Dr Pedro Júlio)

He was a native of this city and a doctor of medicine of the Montpellier school, having completed his course there in 1852. He was president of the Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*), acting district physician of the same Council and physician at the Hospício da Princesa Dona Maria Amélia, the hospice (*hospício*) of Princess Maria Amélia. Works: *Etudes Médicales sur le Climat de Madère; thèse présentée et publiquement soutenue à la faculté de Médicine de Montpellier*; Montpellier, 1852, 91 pp. He died in Funchal, aged 70, on 28 October 1897.
Vieira (Francisco)

Madeiran poet who died in Funchal, aged about 40, on 13 November 1889. He contributed to several Madeiran newspapers, especially the periodical *A Verdade* (‘Truth’), and published the *Album Madeirense*, poems by various authors (Funchal, 1884), *Prelúdios poéticos* and *Petalas* (Funchal, 1887).
Vieira (João Fernandes)

To the article on this illustrious Madeiran on page 18 of volume II, we wish to add some further information that identifies him more clearly. We draw readers’ attention in particular to the valuable and exhaustive historical memoir by the academician Rodrigo de Lima Felner, *Nome verdadeiro do portuguez João Fernandes Vieira*, published in 1873, and to the fine study by Lieutenant-Colonel Alberto Artur Sarmento entitled *Ascendência, naturalidade e mudança de nome de João Fernandes Vieira*, printed in 1911. Drawing on these and other research works, the Brazilian writer Dr Mário de Melo published an excellent article, reprinted in the Funchal press, from which we shall extract a few passages that bear closely on our subject:

‘The Portuguese João Fernandes Vieira, who came to Brazil very young, was the most influential figure in the restoration of Pernambuco. He had blind panegyrists and has his detractors. The latter did not confine themselves to pointing out his errors, some of them amply documented, or his ambition, which may have been excessive – it is enough to note that, apart from the scientists brought by Maurice of Nassau and a few others, every European who came to Brazil had as his aim the accumulation of wealth.

Pereira da Costa and Alberto Lamego piled up document after document against the Madeiran. And to belittle him they began by casting doubt on his legitimate descent. They made him out to be now the bastard son of a Madeiran man of standing and a courtesan, now the son of a criminal and a mulatto woman. Viriato Corrêa and Paulo Setúbal took it upon themselves to spread the slander in popular books.

When the one and the other, in different years, spread this account, I protested, basing myself on what Adelino de Luna Freire had written. But my protest could not be forceful, given the scantiness of the documentation, for only recently was the baptismal certificate found of the man to whom the people of Pernambuco owe everything.

I knew that João Fernandes Vieira was the son of Francisco Dornelas and had changed his name on coming to Brazil, but according to my notes Francisco Dornelas’s wife was Teresa Mafra. Thus the stigma of being a bastard son hung over the liberator’s memory, and Antónia Mendes might well have been the courtesan spoken of by those who slandered his memory, or the real name of the “Benfeitinha”. Without losing any time, I wrote to Mr Alberto Sarmento asking him to tell me the name of Francisco Dornelas’s true wife.

In reply, he sent me an interesting monograph entitled “*Ascendencia, naturalidade & mudança de nome de João Fernandes Vieira*”, published in 1911 and therefore before the baptismal certificate came to light (found in the parish (*freguesia*) of Nossa Senhora do Faial, on the island of Madeira).

From this valuable piece of historical research, which confirms the findings of Adelino de Luna Freire, I see that the author, guided by a note written in the margin of the *Castrioto Lusitano*, found the following in the nobiliary (book of noble genealogies) of Caetano Velosa de Castelobranco, in a badly damaged manuscript: ‘§ 18 – Mendo d’Ornelas e Vasconcelos, son of Francisco Goes § 17 at fol. 40, married for the 1st time on 24 September 1559 in Machico to Helena Gomes, daughter of Pedro António, physician in Faial, and had: I – Francisco d’Ornelas no. 1. 2 – Aires d’Ornelas, who died in India. 3 – António d’Ornelas, who likewise died in India. 4 – Antónia d’Ornelas, wife of Simão de Vasconcelos, son of s. g. Married for the 2nd time to .... de Castro. 5 – Simão Fernandes § 21. Francisco d’Ornelas no. I married Antónia Mendes of the Lombada de Santa Cruz (‘ridge of Santa Cruz’), daughter of Jerónimo Mendes and of Bárbara Cristóvão, native of Faial, and had: 1 – Manuel de Ornelas, without issue. 2 – Francisco d’Ornelas, who later changed his name and was called João Fernandes Vieira, and follows. 3 – Antónia d’Ornelas, married to António Pires da Fra. of Faial, with issue. 4 – Helena d’Ornelas, wife of Pedro de Freitas Peixoto of Faial, son of c.....with issue. 5 – Maria d’Ornelas, wife of José Dias de Santana, with issue.

Francisco d’Ornelas fled to Brazil as a boy and there took the name João Fernandes Vieira. He became very rich, and with his wealth and valour he freed Pernambuco from the power of the Dutch for the Crown of Portugal. For these and many other services he was made a nobleman of the Royal Household (*fidalgo da Casa Real*) and a member of its Council of War; Alcaide-mor of the town of Pinhal; commander of the commanderies of the Order of Christ of São Pedro de Torradas and of Santa Eugénia d’Aula; superintendent of the fortifications of Pernambuco and of all the others of the State of Brazil to the north and pro.; Proclaimer of the Liberty and Restoration of Pernambuco.

The identification of João Fernandes Vieira is therefore confirmed. He had no reason to be ashamed of his ancestry. He was a *fidalgo* (nobleman of the lesser nobility) by his father’s blood and by his mother’s. The legend of his shameful illegitimacy and mixed race crumbles. He was a legitimate son, white, clean and pure. If that was so, why did he emigrate and change his name? He emigrated because of his adventurous temperament and because of the poverty which, together with the plague, was ravaging the island of Madeira. The legal system of the time was that of the entailed estate (*morgadio*). Only first-born sons had the right to the inheritance and its revenues, and the duty, together with the family name, of preserving the entail. ‘The brethren, starving, resentful of fortune but still blinded by the vanity of their name, would only submit to work in a foreign land.’

Francisco d’Ornelas, the second brother of Manuel d’Ornelas, understood early on that the whole of their father’s fortune would go to the latter. He heard the fantastic tales of the riches of Brazil, to which settlers were sailing on every ship. While still very young he ran away from his father’s house, joined a party of emigrants and sailed with it to try his luck through work. The first job he obtained in Pernambuco was as a servant. That was too humiliating for the lineage of the Dornelas. He changed his name. Even so, he took the surname Fernandes from his great-grandfather António Fernandes, of Covas (‘hollows’), in Faial, and the surname Vieira from his paternal great-great-grandfather Pedro Vieira, great holder of the entail (*morgado*) of the Ribeira de Machico (‘Machico stream’), on the island of Madeira, and joined them to the forename João, also from his maternal great-grandfather João Mendes. And so he created the full name of João Fernandes Vieira, under which he made his way in Brazil and passed into history, a name more dignified by his deeds than the one his parents had given him at the baptismal font’.

What has been transcribed above is fully confirmed by the extract from the baptismal certificate discovered by the distinguished genealogist Canon Fernando de Meneses Vaz, which was recorded on page 19 of volume II of this work. See Monuments (II-393).
Vieira (João José)

He was born in Funchal on 10 October 1844, the son of Manuel José Vieira and Dona Josefa Carolina do Nascimento Vieira. He attended the lyceum (state secondary school) of Funchal and the Medical-Surgical School (*Escola Médico-cirúrgica*), but did not complete the 1st-year course at the latter institution. He was a copying clerk and later secretary of the Municipal Administration (*Administração do Concelho*, the government’s local civil office) of Funchal. From a very early age he devoted himself to journalism: while still a student he contributed to the *Recreio* and the *Crepusculo*, and later to the *Fusão*, *Imprensa Livre*, *Povo*, *Diário Popular*, etc. He is a good poet, but his poems are either scattered through the old Funchal periodicals or were never printed, and are known only to a few friends. He was one of the authors of ‘The Guiana Epic’ (*Guyaneida*), a mock-heroic poem to which we referred on page 670 of the 1st volume of this *Elucidário*.

João José Vieira was treasurer and later president of the District General Council (*Junta Geral do Distrito*). Under the monarchy he was active in the Progressive Party, whose local leader was his brother, Councillor (*conselheiro*, honorary title of the royal council) Manuel José Vieira. He died in 1928.
Vieira Portuense

The distinguished painter Vieira Portuense came to this island seeking relief from his ailments and died in Funchal on 2 May 1805. His death record states that he died suddenly in the eating house of Maria Watror and that he was buried in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral).
Vicar general

Although the diocese of Funchal dates from 1514, the post of vicar general of the bishopric was created only in 1570. It was the royal decree (alvará régio) of King Sebastian of 30 August of that year that authorised Bishop Dom Jorge de Lemos to establish that ecclesiastical office, for which the same decree fixed an annual salary of fifty thousand réis.
Vigário (stream)

A watercourse that flows into the ocean west of the town (*vila*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). Near its mouth, on 4 March 1930, a great landslide occurred which violently drove the sea up the mouth of the stream; the backwash swept away about twenty people, who met a tragic death there. A considerable part of this stream is also known as the Ribeira da Caixa.
Vigia (quinta)

It is regarded as one of the most beautiful *quintas* (country estates) of Madeira, not so much for the sumptuousness of its residence and surrounding gardens as for its enviable position overlooking the sea, which recalls many of the rich and splendid villas of the famous Côte d’Azur. It belongs today to the State and was among the properties on this island owned by the former Sanatoria Company (*Empresa dos Sanatórios*), whose concessionaire was Prince Friedrich of Hohenlohe (see Sanatoria). Residents of this *quinta* included Queen Adelaide of England, Empress Elisabeth of Austria, the ill-fated Archduke Maximilian, later Emperor of Mexico, the Prince of Oldenburg, etc.

The Quinta Vigia housed the Republican Guard (*Guarda Republicana*) forces that were in Madeira until May 1922, and in August 1971 a bill was presented in parliament to hand over the same *quinta* as a house for journalists. The name of the *quinta* probably derives from the existence there of some watch-post (*vigia*), that is, some station intended to give the alarm of corsairs or any other enemy ships, and to prevent smuggling’.
The Quinta Vigia originally belonged to the wealthy Englishman Ricardo Davies, who came to Madeira at the end of the second quarter of the 19th century.
Lookouts

They were, says Dr Azevedo, ‘military and at the same time fiscal stations, which watched the sea, the coasts and beaches in order to give the alarm of corsairs or any other enemy ships, and to prevent smuggling. The watches were kept by the local people, in small fortified houses built on purpose to withstand the sea and prevent surprise attacks. King Sebastian gave them regulations (*regimento*) in 1567, which are recorded in volume V, fol. 105, of the *Archivo da Câmara do Funchal*, and by a royal decree (*alvará*) of 1569 he ordered that no one be exempt from this service’.

Vila (Calheta)

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Calheta (‘small cove’), comprising the town (*vila*) of the same name and its immediate surroundings. Here stand the building of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), various municipal offices, the Igreja Paroquial (‘parish church’) and the former Misericórdia of Calheta (*Casa da Misericórdia da Calheta*) with its adjoining chapel (see the articles under the heading Calheta).
Vila (Câmara de Lobos)

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), taking in part of the cluster of houses around the small cove. It is the seat of the municipality (*concelho*), and here are the town hall, various public offices, the post and telegraph office, the parish church and the chapel of Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception (*Nossa Senhora da Conceição*). This place was never raised to the rank of town (*vila*), although it is commonly called one, even in official documents (see the articles headed Câmara de Lobos).
Vila (Machico)
An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Machico, whose area extends beyond the town (*vila*) of that name (see Machico and the other articles under that heading).
Vila (Ponta do Sol)

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), comprising the town (*vila*) proper and some of its immediate surroundings. Here are the law court, the district-court (*comarca*) and municipal offices, the parish church and the chapels of St Sebastian (*São Sebastião*), which belongs to the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), and of St Anthony (see the articles headed Ponta do Sol).
Vila (Porto do Moniz)

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Porto Moniz (‘Moniz’s harbour’), improperly called Vila (‘town’), but which is the seat of the municipality (*concelho*) of that name. Here are the town hall and other municipal offices, the parish church, etc. It was never raised to the rank of town (*vila*). (See Porto Moniz.)
Vila (Porto Santo)
An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), taking in the town (*vila*) of the same name and its surroundings. (See the articles on Porto Santo and Baleira.)
Vila (Ribeira Brava)

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), which was known, and still is, by the name of Lugar (‘place’). With the creation of the municipality (*concelho*) in 1914 and of the town (*vila*) in 1928, it came to be called Vila, and the seat of the municipality was established there (see Ribeira Brava and the other articles under this heading).
Vila (Santa Cruz)

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’). It comprises the town (*vila*) of that name and its immediate surroundings (see Santa Cruz and the other articles under this heading).
Vila (São Vicente)

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) of the parish (*freguesia*) of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), taking in the small town (*vila*) of the same name and its surroundings (see the articles headed São Vicente).
Vila Mendo (Viscount of)
By decree of 12 April 1881 the Viscount of Vila Mendo was appointed civil governor of Funchal, taking up the post on 23 May of the same year. He served only a few months.
He was civil governor of this district a second time, appointed by decree of 10 November 1882 and taking office on the 16th of that month and year.
As an elective peer (*par electivo*), he represented Madeira in the Cortes (Portuguese parliament) in the legislative sessions of 1884 to 1887 and 1890 to 1892.

António de Gouveia Osório was granted the title of Viscount of Vila Mendo, a parish (*freguesia*) in the district of Viseu where he had a manor house and an entailed estate (*morgadio*) inherited from his forebears, and where he was born in 1826. He was a bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) in law and a member of the Court of Audit (*Tribunal de Contas*).
Vilão

This is the term generally used here to denote the country people of this island. The word almost always carries a pejorative sense, because the Funchal townsman regards the peasant as socially and mentally far beneath himself, although in most cases this is a flagrant injustice. The inhabitant of our countryside is ignorant, rough and superstitious, just as the inhabitant of the provinces of the mainland and of the Azorean islands is. And compared with the peasants of the suburban parishes and with a considerable number of the city’s own residents, he is in no way inferior to them, nor need he envy their degree of civilisation, except in his dress.

The rural inhabitants of Madeira, almost all of them illiterate, live in great isolation in homesteads scattered widely over the mountain slopes. Villages are unknown here, apart from small and thinly populated towns, so they are completely cut off from all social life and sheltered from the civilising influences of large centres of population. Their ignorance and the almost total isolation in which they live make them reserved and distrustful in their dealings with the landlords and the city folk. To this must be added a natural timidity, born largely of the absolute and at times despotic dependence in which for centuries they stood towards the holders of entails and the landlords, who came to own two-thirds of the arable land of Madeira. That is why our country folk are called crafty. As we have said elsewhere, it is generally acknowledged that the country people are of a peaceful and orderly disposition. The great majority are devoted to farm work, which in this region is very hard and toilsome owing to the particular nature of the terrain. They labour from daybreak until the shadows of night fall, generally carefree and indifferent to everything other than the unending toil of their laborious existence. Whether they live in straitened modesty or in reasonable sufficiency, their life passes serene and tranquil, and they are wholly resigned to their lot.
Towns

The first places in this archipelago to be raised to the rank of towns (*vila*), on account of their growth and because they served as the seats of the three captaincies, were Funchal (II-59), Machico (II-298) and Baleira (I-117). Despite his research, the learned commentator of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) was unable to discover the charters creating them, or even the precise dates on which this took place. He conjectures, however, with the strongest probability, that it happened around 1451, as has already been stated in the articles on those towns. Funchal, which thanks to its situation, climate, fertile soil, spacious harbour and other notable circumstances soon reached an unusual growth in population, was raised to the rank of city by the royal decree (alvará régio) of 21 August 1508, which is transcribed on page 61 of volume II of this work.

The royal decree (*alvará*) of 2 December 1501 created the town and municipality of Ponta do Sol (‘point of the sun’), whose area stretched from the parish (*freguesia*) of Tabua (‘bulrush’) to that of Achadas da Cruz (see III-99). It was soon reduced to much more limited proportions when the parish of Calheta (‘small cove’) was raised to the rank of town and municipality by the royal decree of 1 July 1502 (see I-191). The parish of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’), which soon rivalled that of Machico, became a municipality with the status of a town by the royal decree of 26 June 1515, despite the opposition raised by the judicial district (*comarca*) of Machico and by the head of that captaincy (see III-246).

The constant petitions of several parishes on the north coast of Madeira led to the creation of the town of São Vicente (‘St Vincent’), with its seat in the parish of that name, by the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 25 August 1744, although the municipality of Machico had raised serious obstacles to its creation (see III-282).

The municipality (*concelho*) of Ribeira Brava (‘wild river’), with its seat in this parish, was created by the decree of 6 May 1914, and the town itself by the decree of 26 March 1929. It was the eighth and last town established in this archipelago.
