By decree of 6 July 1900 he was appointed civil governor of Madeira, taking up the post on the 23rd of the same month and year.
Vilhena (Ernesto Jardim de)
He was a deputy for Madeira in the parliamentary session of 1908 to 1910.
Osier

The Madeiran osier appears to be the product of a cross between *Salix alba* and *S. fragilis*. It is a shrub or small tree with long, flexible branches and lanceolate leaves; the mature leaves are glabrous, while the young ones are somewhat satiny. Only female plants exist in Madeira, but these are extremely abundant and are propagated from cuttings with the greatest ease.

The longer shoots of the osier are used to make a great number of pieces of furniture and utensils, such as settees, chairs, tables, carts, baskets, etc., and the shorter ones for ties and straw bands, as well as for some of the small articles made on the island.

In 1912, 265,919 kilograms of worked wicker were exported abroad and to Lisbon, and 255,390 kilograms of raw wicker were exported abroad alone. England, the Canary Islands and the Cape of Good Hope were the chief importers of the unmanufactured wicker.

The wickerwork industry, which appears to have begun in the parish (*freguesia*) of Camacha around 1850, is in decline in Madeira today, according to the intelligent manufacturer Mr José Maria Teixeira. Meanwhile it is growing in other countries, above all in South Africa, to which the island exports its wicker. In the view of this well-informed manufacturer, the main causes of the industry’s loss of much of its former importance are several. The rising cost of the raw material prevents some manufacturers who are short of capital from buying it at the proper season. Many of the workers once employed in the industry have gone abroad, while others on the island have taken up more profitable work. Freight charges on finished wicker are heavier, because it takes up more space in ships’ holds. Finally, duties and local taxes weigh more heavily on wickerwork than on the raw material.

Madeira produces 700 to 800 tonnes of wicker a year, and perhaps half of this output leaves the island. At the Cape of Good Hope, once an important market for Madeiran wickerwork, many of the same articles are now made with wicker imported from our island, and the same is happening in Brazil. England is the country that at present imports large quantities of the wickerwork made in Madeira, and, we are told, it also receives large amounts of raw wicker (1921).

The osier is pruned from January to March. The wicker intended for working is gathered into bundles straight after cutting, and it is then customary to leave the lower ends of the bundles standing in water until the shoots begin to sprout. Once sprouting has begun, the wicker is peeled, taking care to cut off the part that has been under water.

Much of the wickerwork produced on the island is distinguished by the ingenuity, care and solidity of its workmanship. These qualities make it highly valued by Portuguese and foreigners alike, and at the same time show great skill and taste on the part of Madeiran craftsmen. Boaventura (‘good fortune’) and Camacha are the chief places where osier is produced, and it is from Camacha that most of the wickerwork exported or sold in Funchal comes.
Vimioso (Counts of)

They held the captaincy of Machico, which Dom Afonso de Portugal, 2nd Count, bought from António da Silveira for 35,000 *cruzados*, with the licence of John III. When this Dom Afonso de Portugal was given up for dead at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir, the captaincy was taken over by his son, Dom Francisco de Portugal. He is generally regarded as the 3rd Count of Vimioso, but he died before his father, in the naval battle of Vila Franca do Campo, and so never truly inherited the captaincy. In 1582 Philip II granted the captaincy of Machico to Tristão Vaz da Veiga. In 1604, however, Tristão Vaz having died, it passed into the possession of Dom Luís de Portugal, whom some consider the third and others the fourth Count of Vimioso. For reasons that are not well known, he later took religious vows, as did his wife, a daughter of the Count of Basto.

After this Dom Luís de Portugal, the donataries of Machico were: Dom Afonso de Portugal, 5th Count; Dom Luís de Portugal, 6th Count, who died by misadventure in a quarrel in 1656; Dom Miguel de Portugal, 7th Count, who died in 1687; Dom Francisco de Portugal e Castro, 8th Count and 2nd Marquis of Valença, who died in 1749; and Dom José Miguel de Portugal e Castro, 9th Count and 3rd Marquis of Valença, who died in 1775.

An old manuscript records that on 20 October 1767 the Treasury Council (*Conselho de Fazenda*) ordered the superintendent (*provedor*) to take possession of the donatary captaincy (*donataria*) of Machico in the name of the monarch, ‘since it has fallen vacant on the death of the 5th Count of Vimioso, Dom Martinho de Portugal, without a successor’. If such an order was indeed given, however, it seems not to have been carried out, for there are later documents referring to the chief castellanship (*alcaidaria-mor*) of Machico and to its holders, the Marquesses of Valença and Counts of Vimioso. It should also be noted that the 5th count, Dom Afonso and not Dom Martinho, died in the 17th century, and that the holder of the donatary captaincy of Machico at the time to which the said manuscript refers was Dom José Miguel de Portugal e Castro, 9th count, who was born in 1706 and died in 1775.

The donataries of Machico were also Marquesses of Valença from 10 March 1716, when King John V renewed this title, conferring it on Dom Francisco de Portugal, 8th Count of Vimioso, a sixth-generation descendant (*6.° neto*) of the Valença who died in 1460.
Vineyards

Vines were already being grown in Madeira in 1445, for Cadamosto, who visited the island that year, refers to ‘newly planted vineyards, among them Malmsey, brought from Candia’. According to Frutuoso, it was Henry the Navigator who introduced that grape variety to the island, and there is no reason to doubt this statement, even though Zurara, cited by Dr Azevedo, says nothing on the matter. The Italian navigator’s voyage took place before the *Chronica da conquista e descobrimento da Guiné* was written. Zurara’s ignorance of certain things about the island must therefore be put down either to vine-growing not yet being of great importance, or to his simply not mentioning wines in his work, as he did mention the ‘bread, and sugar, and honey, and wax, and timber’ of the flourishing Portuguese colony.

Dr Azevedo says that it is not only possible but natural that the Acciaioly family, of Florentine origin, brought the Malmsey vine with them when they settled in Madeira; this vine grows in the outskirts of the city of Napoli-di-Malvasia, on the island of Minoa. However, if it is true that Simão Acciaioly, who came here in 1515, was the founder of that family among us, he clearly cannot have introduced the vine to our land, since Cadamosto had already found it here seventy years earlier. It is most likely that the first settlers, on the instructions of Henry the Navigator, brought from Portugal some of the grape varieties grown there, preferring, of course, the most famous. Among these would have been the *malvasia candida*, originating in Candia and Minoa, which may well have been cultivated at that time in mainland Portugal, where it seems not to exist at present except as a mere curiosity.

Given that vine-growing in Madeira is as old, or almost as old, as the cultivation of sugar cane, and that already in Cadamosto’s time the island’s wines were *assai buonissimi*, it is strange, says Dr Azevedo, that in the 15th century the whole weight of seigneurial dues and demands fell on sugar, while wines were exempt from any heavy taxes, being subject only to payment of the tithe and of a municipal levy (*imposição*) established in 1485 ‘for the expenses of the council of the island’.

Dr Azevedo thinks that the unequal treatment given to wines and sugar in early times was a consequence of the low value and poor quality of the former. As is clear from what has been said above, however, this explanation cannot be accepted. It is more likely that the true reason our wines escaped the heavy taxes that burdened sugar in the first years of colonisation was the lack of foreign markets and the little demand for them in Portugal, itself a wine-producing country. To subject Madeiran wines to the same charges as sugar would have ruined viticulture at a time when it did not yet promise to become one of the island’s greatest sources of wealth.

Vine-growing received a certain impetus in the 16th century, when the sugar industry began to decline in Madeira (see Wines), but it was after 1640 that we see it expand more strongly. At that time the English, settling here in greater numbers than before to engage in the wine trade, became the chief promoters of the crop. Frutuoso refers in several places in ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*) to vine-growing in Madeira, but as regards grape varieties he mentions only Malmsey, which seems to have been the variety producing the island’s finest and most celebrated wines in the 16th century.

At the end of the 18th century many vines were planted in Madeira. Some time before, vine-growing had been introduced on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), on the land of Areias (‘sands’) and on other coastal ground: men maintained by the State were sent there to carry out the planting, which was done with cuttings supplied by the government.

Vine-growing flourished in Madeira until 1851, but in that year or the next *Oidium Tuckery* appeared on the island and destroyed the crop almost entirely (see Mangra). Once the disease had been overcome by the use of sulphur, vine-growing prospered here once more, until in 1871 or 1872 a new scourge, phylloxera (see that entry), harder to combat than *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium), came to devastate Madeira’s vineyards.

The introduction of foreign vines, onto which the old varieties of *Vitis vinifera* were grafted, made it possible to rebuild the island’s vineyards. Our viticulture is at present in a prosperous state, after passing through several crises that slowed its progress or even brought it within two steps of annihilation.

In the archipelago vines occupy an area of 1700 to 2,000 hectares, with an average yield of 6 to 7 *pipas* of wine per hectare. Ungrafted Madeiran vines are no longer found today, as they were before phylloxera appeared, but almost everywhere many of these vines have been successfully propagated by grafting them onto American vines or onto hybrids produced by crossing those vines with *Vitis vinifera*. There are also some direct-producer hybrids, such as Jacquez, Herbemont and Cunningham, the first being very common in Madeira.

Before the appearance of *mangra* (powdery mildew of the vine, oidium) (see that entry), it was the custom, chiefly in the north of the island, to use certain trees as supports for the vines, especially chestnuts (see Balseiras). That method of cultivation has been abandoned, however, and today the vines rest and spread over walkways or trellises made of poles or wicker, when they do not grow more or less flat on the ground (*vinhas de pé*) or supported by small stakes. The height of the trellises varies between 1.20 m and 3 metres.

European grape varieties are generally pruned by leaving on each arm of the stock a terminal cane with seven, eight and sometimes more buds, and one or more lateral shoots with two or three buds. If the stock or one of its arms is not very vigorous, the number of buds on the terminal cane may be reduced.
The principal grape varieties grown in Madeira, on account of the excellent wines they produce, are *malvasia candida*, Sercial (white grape variety), Verdelho, Boal and Tinta.

The first of these varieties can be recognised by its leaves, which are hairless on both surfaces and have 5 very deep, usually pointed lobes, and by its large bunches of elliptical or elliptical-globose berries, not very firm, greenish-yellow and finally golden. It is found in some gardens in Funchal, at Fajã dos Padres, in Câmara de Lobos, in Jardim do Mar, in Paul do Mar, etc. It produces the precious Malmsey wine, known for its sweetness and fragrance, and also gives good table grapes, although these are inferior to those of the other varieties on the island.

The second variety, which in Portugal is called *sercial*, *esgana*, *esgana-cão*, *esganinho* and *esganoso*, has medium-sized leaves, downy on the underside and almost hairless or pubescent on the upper side, with the three upper lobes clearly marked and the lower ones often merely suggested. Its bunches are usually small or medium-sized, with elliptical, greenish-yellow, sour and late-ripening berries. Its wine, once matured (before 8 to 10 years it is harsh and raw), is very dry and of excellent quality. Sercial is grown mainly at Fajã dos Padres, Ponta do Pargo and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos.

Verdelho, known in some parts of Portugal as *gouveio*, has medium-sized, rounded, wavy leaves, hairless or almost hairless on the upper surface and more or less downy on the underside, with shallow or merely suggested lobes. Its bunches are small or medium-sized, with very sweet berries, firm or fairly firm, elliptical or oblong, greenish-yellow and generally golden when ripe. Its grapes, somewhat strong in flavour, are very good to eat and produce a dry wine of pleasant taste, regarded as one of the finest in Madeira. Verdelho is grown in Funchal, Câmara de Lobos, Estreito de Câmara de Lobos, Porto Santo, etc.

Boal has medium-sized leaves, downy on the underside and almost hairless or pubescent on the upper side, with the upper lobes clearly marked, sometimes acuminate, and the lower ones usually only faintly suggested. Its bunches are large, dense and strongly winged, with berries that are almost always elliptical, firm, greenish-yellow, golden when ripe and very sweet. It is grown mainly in the municipalities of Funchal and Câmara de Lobos, and produces good table grapes and a highly prized wine.

Tinta can be recognised by its leaves, hairless or almost hairless on the upper surface and downy or cobwebby on the underside, often reddish when mature, with deep upper lobes, and by its small or medium-sized bunches of red-black berries, not very firm and very sweet, with pale or slightly coloured pulp. It is grown mainly in Câmara de Lobos, Estreito, São Martinho and Santo António, and yields excellent wine and good table grapes.

Besides the five varieties briefly described above, many others deserve appreciation, either for their use in winemaking or for the good table grapes they produce. Among the red varieties, the following seem to us worth mentioning: *listrão tinto*, from Porto Santo, with globose, firm berries; *negra mole* (*tinto molar* on Porto Santo), with globose or elliptical-globose berries, often uneven in size; *tinta do Porto Santo*, similar to *negra mole*; *negro* or *maroto*, with globose, firm berries, now grown only on Porto Santo; *castelão*, with berries somewhat firmer than those of *negra mole*, now grown only on the same island; *terrantês tinto*, with large, oval or subglobose, firm berries; *ferral*, with large, elliptical or oblong, firm berries and somewhat greenish pulp; and *barrete de padre*, with large, striped, firm berries. Among the white or violet varieties, the following deserve note: *malvasia roxa*, which differs from *malvasia candida* only in having violet or pinkish berries; *malvasião* or *malvasia babosa*, with soft and sometimes not very sweet berries, green or golden when ripe; *boal do Porto Santo*, with soft, ovoid or subglobose berries of the same colour as those of Madeira Boal; *cara de moça*, with large, firm, globose or elliptical-globose berries, golden or greenish; *cachudo*, very similar to Boal; *terrantês branco*, with globose, golden, very sweet berries, almost extinct in Madeira but grown on Porto Santo; *muscatel* and *moscatel do Porto Santo*, which differ from each other but both produce fragrant grapes of a special flavour; *málaga* or *alicante branco*, with globose, firm, sweet berries, golden when ripe; and the *listrão* of Madeira and that of Porto Santo, both with globose, firm and very tasty berries.

Isabella, or the American vine, a variety of *Vitis labrusca*, is widely grown in Madeira, where it was introduced shortly after 1840. *V. riparia*, known as *vinha de silvado*, is also common, but is used only as a grafting rootstock. Besides Jacquez, Herbemont and Cunningham (the Madeirans’ *canica*), which all seem to derive from crossing *Vitis aestivalis* with *V. vinifera*, other hybrids were introduced into Madeira after the phylloxera invasion, most of which are now extinct. Jacquez, grown as a direct producer, is also the vine generally preferred for grafting with the old *V. vinifera* varieties, because of its adaptation to the soils and its vigour and resistance to phylloxera.

The soils best suited to vine-growing are *pedra mole* ('soft stone': soft yellowish tuff and its soil) and gravel, the latter made up of basaltic particles and the former of red or yellowish tuffs. The hard clay soil known as *massapez* (heavy ferruginous clay soil) is the least suitable for viticulture.

The vineyards extend from the land near the coast up to 400 or 500 metres, and may even reach 600 and 700 metres in places less affected by mists. Vines are grown in the vicinity of Jardim da Serra (‘upland garden’), but the grapes ripen there much later than in Funchal.

Two articles on Madeiran vines were published in the now-defunct *Portugal Agrícola*, one written by the agronomist Mr Meneses Pimentel and the other by the present author. The *Estudos Ampelograficos* of the late João Marques Loureiro (Lisbon 1912) also list and describe in detail some of the most valuable grape varieties of our island. All these works can be consulted with profit by those who wish to acquire a broader knowledge of the subject.

We supplement the information in this article with the valuable material that its author (the distinguished botanist Carlos Azevedo de Meneses) set down in the review *Portugal agrícola* for April 1902, referred to above, from which some passages deserve to be transcribed:

‘As descriptions of the hybrids and American vines are of no great interest, since these stocks are well known in Portugal, we confine ourselves in the present article to the different forms of *Vitis vinifera* found in the archipelago, dividing them for this purpose into two large groups: red grape varieties and white or violet grape varieties.
RED GRAPE VARIETIES
Listrão

Leaves large or medium-sized, almost hairless on both faces or irregularly downy underneath; lobes 5, less often 3, nearly always acuminate, sometimes cleft, all of them, or at least the upper ones, well marked or deep; teeth triangular-lanceolate and acute, sometimes very large; petiolar sinus nearly always wide open, lateral sinuses slightly open or closed; bunches 18–30 centimetres long, cylindrical or conical, winged, very dense or somewhat loose; berries 16–20 millimetres, globose and firm, at first a light violet, finally almost black; pulp clear; pedicels reddish at the top. Grown on Porto Santo; it produces much-prized table grapes.
Tinta da Madeira

Leaves medium-sized, the veins and petioles often reddish, hairless on the upper surface or bearing some rather dense hairs near the veins and petiole, downy or cobwebby on the lower surface, the tomentum sometimes very sparse, in which case they appear somewhat glossy; upper lobes deep or well marked, the lower ones nearly always barely outlined; teeth ovate or ovate-triangular, obtuse, rarely subacute; lateral sinuses and petiolar sinus mostly closed because the lobes overlap; bunches winged or not, small or medium-sized (15–25 centimetres), nearly always dense; berries elliptic-globose or oblong, 15–23 millimetres, red, not very firm, very sweet, with clear or faintly coloured pulp. Stock tall and vigorous, of medium thickness; canes greyish-brown or reddish-brown, with short or medium internodes. It differs from the negra mole, with which it is generally confused, in having larger leaves with the sinuses nearly always more closed, and longer, larger berries. It is grown in Câmara de Lobos, in Estreito and in various spots in São Martinho and Santo António. It does not occur on Porto Santo. It yields excellent wine and good table grapes.
Negra mole

Leaves sometimes somewhat concave, generally medium-sized, more or less downy or cobwebby on the lower surface, almost hairless or slightly downy on the upper, sometimes with all the lobes well marked and the upper ones deep and acute or obtuse, at other times with all the lobes merely outlined; teeth ovate or triangular, acute or obtuse; lateral and petiolar sinuses open or closed; bunches small or medium-sized (15–20 centimetres), nearly always very dense, winged or not; berries globose or elliptic-globose, equal or unequal, 12–18 millimetres, soft or not very firm, red, very sweet, with clear pulp. Stock as in the preceding variety; canes light brown or reddish-brown, with short internodes. Mature leaves generally reddish. It differs from the bastardo in its berries, which are sometimes elliptic and always have clear pulp, and in its longer pedicels. It is found in the same places as the preceding variety, but is more abundant; it is also grown on Porto Santo, where it is known as tinta mollar. It yields excellent wine and good table grapes.
Tinta de Lisboa

It differs from the Madeiran tinta in having leaves that are nearly always whiter on the lower surface, and bunches that are usually smaller, with globose berries; and from the negra mole in its generally larger leaves, which are less inclined to turn reddish, and in its sinuses, which are nearly always more closed. It is found in some spots on the outskirts of Funchal; not common. It is little valued for wine; it gives good table grapes.
Bastardo tinto

Leaves medium-sized, downy on the lower face, the hairs sometimes flocculent and very irregularly arranged, hairless or slightly hairy on the upper; lobes shallow or merely outlined; teeth unequal, triangular or ovate-triangular, acute or subacute; petiolar sinus more or less open; bunches generally not exceeding 15 cm, cylindrical, cylindrical-conical or very short and broad, dense, sometimes winged; berries globose, very sweet, nearly equal or very unequal, 12–18 mm, at first somewhat firm, finally soft, red, with clear or faintly violet pulp; pedicels very short. Common on Porto Santo; on Madeira it is grown only in Estreito and Jardim da Serra. It produces good wine and good table grapes.
Tinta do Porto Santo

Leaves large or medium-sized, often reddish when mature; glabrous or subglabrous on the upper surface, somewhat downy or cobwebby on the underside, with 5 clearly marked lobes, acuminate, toothed or incised-toothed, the upper lobes fairly deep; teeth very unequal, triangular or triangular-lanceolate; petiolar sinus open; lateral sinuses open or closed. Bunches generally not exceeding 18 centimetres, cylindrical or cylindrical-conical, sometimes winged; berries globose or elliptical-globose, sweet, the same size as those of the *negra mole* but firmer, and with pulp that is always violet. – It is a very productive grape variety, and one that is now found only on Porto Santo.
Barrete de padre

Leaves medium-sized, glabrous on both surfaces, with 3–5 lobes, sometimes barely outlined, sometimes rather deep; terminal lobe sometimes divided into 3 secondary lobes; teeth generally short and broad, acute or obtuse; petiolar sinus slightly open or closed; bunches winged, usually large and loose; berries large or medium-sized, ellipsoid or ovate-subglobose, striped red, very firm. – It is grown around Funchal and also on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it is known by the name *barrete de frade*. It yields good table grapes.
Boal da Madeira

Leaves medium-sized, cottony on the underside, sub-glabrous or pubescent on the upper side, with the 3 upper lobes clearly visible, sometimes acuminate, the lower ones usually poorly defined; teeth unequal, generally sub-obtuse, less often acute; petiolar sinus closed or slightly open; upper lateral sinuses often barely visible because the lobes overlap; bunches large, strongly winged, dense; berries almost always elliptical, 15–22 millimetres, firm, greenish-yellow, turning golden when ripe, very sweet. Stock medium-sized; canes light brown, with short internodes. It is grown mainly in the municipalities of Funchal and Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’). It produces good table grapes and a highly prized dry wine.
Boal de cheiro

It differs from the local Boal in having leaves that are sometimes less cottony, petiolar sinuses generally more open, teeth almost always deeper and more acute, bunches less dense and berries less firm (sometimes soft), elliptical-globose or ovate. It is grown in São Gonçalo (Funchal). This may be the grape variety mentioned in Mr Pimentel’s article under the name *marôto*.
Boal do Porto Santo

It differs from the preceding variety in having more cottony leaves, lobes almost always acuminate and more closed petiolar sinuses; and from the Boal da Madeira in having soft or slightly firm berries, ovate or sub-globose. The differences between the Madeiran Boal and that of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) may perhaps be due simply to the influence of climate or soil, and the two varieties should perhaps be identified as one.
Cachudo

Very similar to the Boal da Madeira in the shape of its leaves and in other characters; it differs from it only in having bunches that are generally longer and narrower, and berries that are less firm and less flavoursome. It is a synonym of *babosa*. It produces a great deal of wine, but of inferior quality. Grown in São Martinho and Santo António.
Castellão

medium-sized or small, very similar to those of the *negra mole*, but with the lobes almost always clearly visible; bunches cylindrical or cylindrical-conical, usually winged, dense or fairly dense; berries globose, as a rule very unequal, somewhat firmer than in the *negra mole*, sometimes very small (8 millimetres), sometimes medium-sized (15–18 millimetres), red, with pale pulp, very sweet; pedicels regular. – It is a synonym of *tinta castellõa*, and probably also of *negrinho*. It is grown on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) and was once common on Madeira, where it seems to be extinct or almost extinct.
Chasellas

Leaves large, broad, glabrous, except on the veins of the lower surface, where they are slightly pubescent; lobes shallow, usually pointed; teeth very irregular, deep, usually acute; petiolar sinus more or less open; bunch compact, with very large, firm, elliptical-globose berries, almost red, greenish at the base. – It produces table grapes that are recommended more for their size than for their flavour, which is somewhat insipid. It is a grape variety of recent introduction, grown only around Funchal. It is a synonym of *uva franceza*.
WHITE OR VIOLET GRAPE VARIETIES
Ferral

Leaves glabrous on both surfaces, with 5 deep lobes, toothed or incised-toothed; teeth very unequal, triangular, acute or acuminate; lateral sinuses closed or slightly open, the petiolar sinus more or less open; bunches generally large and conical, dense or loose, winged; berries red, large, elliptical or oblong, firm, with a fairly tough skin and somewhat greenish pulp. Canes brownish. Average length of the berries: 35 millimetres. – It is grown in Funchal, in Seixal (‘pebble shore’) and in Ponta Delgada (‘slender point’). It produces very large and handsome table grapes, but of a rather coarse flavour. It was also formerly known by the names Alicante and Moscatel tinto.
Malmsey

A white grape variety which, it is claimed, seems to have been brought from the island of Crete around 1445. The Jesuits cultivated it carefully at the so-called Fajã dos Padres (‘the priests’ flat’), and it began to earn a great reputation at the end of the 16th century. It has a thick ‘stock’ and upright canes, with almost equal five-lobed leaves and large oblong bunches.

The distinguished writer and eminent agronomist Andrade Corvo states, in his *Memória sobre a «mangra» na Madeira*, that there are four kinds of Malmsey: the *candia* or *candel*, the purple Malmsey, the *babosa* and Malmsey proper. Of these varieties the *candia* is the principal one, and it is said to have been the first grape variety introduced into Madeira.

Dr Gaspar Frutuoso tells us that in the year 1590 ‘Malmsey wine is the best to be found in the world, and it is taken to India and to many parts of the world. And for these fruits the island is very famous everywhere’.

An official report for the year 1944 states that the ‘Malvasia Candia’ has almost completely disappeared, with only the odd farmer keeping a few vines as a relic of a bygone age. See Phylloxera, Mangra, Mildew and Wines.
Negro

large or medium-sized, sometimes reddish, cobwebby on the lower surface or covered here and there with floccose hairs, less tomentose or glabrous on the upper surface; all the lobes, or only the upper ones, clearly visible and pointed; middle lobe almost always larger than the lateral ones; teeth unequal, triangular or triangular-lanceolate, acute; petiolar sinus more or less open; upper lateral sinuses open or closed; bunches generally not exceeding 20 centimetres, cylindrical or cylindrical-conical, more or less dense, winged or not; berries slightly unequal, 12–18 millimetres, firm, sweet when ripe, globose, with pale or violet pulp and a fairly tough skin; pedicels regular. The stock is vigorous, with light-brown canes, sometimes striped; internodes elongated. It is a synonym of *marôto* and is grown on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’); it seems to be extinct on Madeira, where it was once abundant. It yields a great deal of wine, but of little esteem.
Sercial

Leaves medium-sized, downy on the lower surface, subglabrous or pubescent on the upper, with the 3 upper lobes clearly visible and the lower ones barely outlined; upper lobe almost always larger and more acute or acuminate than the lateral ones; teeth shallow, unequal; upper lateral sinuses and the petiolar sinus almost always open; bunches small or medium-sized, generally not exceeding 20 centimetres, dense, almost always winged; berries elliptical, 15–20 millimetres, greenish-yellow, slightly tart, fairly firm. The stock is vigorous; canes light greyish-brown, with short internodes. – This grape variety, which is now fairly rare in Madeira, is found at Fajã dos Padres, Ponta do Pargo and Estreito de Câmara de Lobos. When matured (before 10 years it is harsh and raw), its wine is very dry and of excellent quality. It is said that the Sercial (white grape variety) of Madeira is identical to the Esgana cão of Portugal.
Terrantez branco

Leaves medium-sized, tomentose on the underside, though with sparse tomentum, and on the upper side sub-glabrous, pubescent or scattered here and there with a few rather long hairs; upper lobes usually clearly visible and often pointed, the lower ones poorly defined or absent; teeth unequal, generally shallow, triangular, acute or sub-acute; petiolar sinus more or less open; lateral sinuses generally closed; bunches short, 10–15 centimetres, dense, cylindrical, sub-globose or cylindrical-conical, sometimes winged; berries globose, 12–20 millimetres, fairly firm, golden when ripe, very sweet. Canes brown or brownish-chestnut, with short internodes. Grown on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), it seems to be extinct or almost extinct on Madeira. It produces good wine and very tasty table grapes’.
Terrantez tinto

Leaves downy on the lower surface, rarely perfectly glabrous on the upper, with the 3 upper lobes visible or barely outlined; teeth very unequal and almost always rounded; petiolar sinus closed or slightly open; bunch generally winged, with red, large, oval or subglobose, firm berries; pedicels violet at the top. Mature leaves often reddish. – It is grown in some places around Funchal and on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). It produces highly prized table grapes.
Verdelho

Leaves medium-sized, rounded, wavy, glabrous or bearing a few hairs on the upper surface, downy on the lower, but with the indumentum sparse and irregularly distributed, sometimes almost absent over the whole blade or part of it; lobes very shallow or barely outlined, with obtuse or acute teeth; petiolar sinus usually very closed; bunches small or medium-sized (15–22 cm), generally winged and dense, cylindrical or cylindrical-conical; berries 15–20 millimetres, very sweet, firm or fairly firm, elliptical or oblong, greenish-yellow, generally golden when ripe. The stock is tall and very vigorous; canes greyish-brown or reddish greyish-brown, with short internodes. – It occurs in Funchal, in Câmara de Lobos and in Estreito de Nossa Senhora da Graça; it was once very common in both the north and the south of Madeira. It is also grown on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’). The rather strong grapes are very good for eating and produce a dry wine of pleasant flavour that is considered one of the finest in Madeira. The Madeiran Verdelho appears to be identical in its botanical characters to the *gouveio* of the Alto Douro.
Verdelho tinto

Leaves small or medium-sized, often with violet patches, downy on the lower surface, subglabrous or covered with a few hairs on the upper; upper lobes generally visible and acute, the lower ones barely outlined; teeth unequal, generally acute; petiolar sinus almost always open; lateral sinuses (where present) slightly open or closed. ‘Berries red, identical in shape to those of the white Verdelho.’
Vineyards and grapes of Porto Santo

– Special consideration is due to the interesting information supplied by the distinguished agricultural technician (*regente agrícola*) José Cruz Tavares on the cultivation of the vine and the production of grapes on the neighbouring island of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), even though one may perhaps disagree with some of the assertions contained in his articles on this important subject. We shall transcribe from them various passages that relate most particularly to the plan we have adopted here.
‘For a long time now I have thought that the farmers of the island of Porto Santo ought to seek to extend the area under vines, since this seems to me advantageous for the reasons I shall set out.

In the island’s poor and badly tilled soil, it is absolutely proven that the vine thrives better than any other crop. So much so that, despite its small extent, the economy of the 2,500 inhabitants who people the island, all or almost all of them farmers, rests mainly upon it. When the vine fails to produce, there is black poverty in the households, which are unambitious enough as it is.

Extending the cultivation of the vine would, in my view, be the most practical, viable and profitable way of partly promoting the afforestation of Porto Santo, an island that is today practically bare, and whose covering will not be easy without great expense on the part of the State and without the collaboration and goodwill of the whole population. Without trees the island is dry and its rainfall pattern completely disordered. If the winters are not very rainy, even drinking water runs short in summer. At other times torrential rains sweep the arable soil of the hills into the sea, leaving in its place gullies and fearsome ravines that hamper any and all tillage work that may be attempted.’

Let us first consider where the 250,000 kilos of grapes – an approximate estimate – that the island of Porto Santo produces on average at present have gone until now: to Funchal, as fruit. The rest is made into must, amounting to around 250 *pipas*. Part of this must is bought by the Madeira wine exporters, who fortify it before fermentation begins and take it to their Funchal lodges for blending and sweetening the fortified wines. The other part, about 200 *pipas*, ferments completely and is sold as table wine, chiefly in Madeira. Even so, not a single brand of table wine capable of making its name by its qualities or character is produced at present anywhere in the archipelago.

Madeira yields the celebrated fortified wines known throughout the world, but it cannot produce good table wines, given its very special agro-climatic conditions. On Porto Santo the situation is different. This island, lying only 40 miles north-east of the other, has entirely different soil and climatic conditions, closer to those of the mainland, though without losing their very *sui generis* character. The main difference between the musts produced on Porto Santo and those of Madeira lies in the relation between sugar content and total acidity.

The Delegation of the National Wine Board (*Junta Nacional do Vinho*) in the Madeira Wine Region, after the oenological trials it carried out, has already reached definitive conclusions about the nature and excellent quality of the table wines made from Porto Santo musts. Their acceptance by the Madeiran market also seems beyond doubt, both for their price and because they satisfy the most demanding palates. Nearly 200 *pipas* of mainland white and red wines are imported into Madeira every year; they are expensive, not always good, and many are of rather lower quality than that of Porto Santo. The latter could replace them, if not entirely then at least in large part. Moreover, consumption of Porto Santo wine on the Madeiran market could be greatly increased beyond its present level through well-judged publicity, which would not even be very costly. The question lies solely, and above all, in presenting it well made to the consumer, and in bringing out, through sound oenological technique, the exceptional qualities that undoubtedly distinguish it.

The consumption of fresh grapes could also be greatly expanded, provided that the trade were properly regulated so as to put an end to a number of abuses; some 100 tonnes are consumed amid the present disorder, which the administrative authority of Porto Santo, despite its very best intentions, has not managed to stop. Such regulation is no insurmountable task at present, thanks to the Corporative and Economic Coordination Bodies established in the archipelago.

The grapes grown on this island, above all white Listrão and Moscatel, are sweet, intensely fragrant and keep exceptionally well. They are certainly the first to ripen anywhere in metropolitan Portuguese territory, perhaps by a margin of nearly a month over the next. I believe that no serious attempt has yet been made to place Porto Santo grapes on the main markets of mainland Portugal, let alone on foreign markets. Since they are the first to appear, I think an experiment of this kind would give positive results.

Nor, as far as I know, has anyone thought of setting up a small raisin industry in Madeira, although raisins are much sought after today and sell at profitable prices. The grapes of Porto Santo, with their size, fragrance and richness in sugar, would naturally be the best suited. They lack nothing to rival the finest.

The technique of sweetening Madeira’s fortified wines with *jeropigas* and *abafados* from Porto Santo (*vinhos surdos*), used on a very small scale by the exporters, is imperfect, but it is nonetheless to be recommended where nothing better is available or possible. It is to be expected that, if the policy of quality in the production and trade of Portuguese wines continues to be followed, the Madeira wine exporters will turn more and more to the reserves of sugar that the musts of Porto Santo can supply. Everything suggests that this will happen, gradually, in the more or less near future. And if it does, nothing prevents me from thinking that this outlet could absorb more than ten times the present production.

These, then, are the reasons – not, however, free from certain conditions – that lead me to foresee, at a relatively early date, the improvement in value of the land of Porto Santo through the planting of vineyards, and to predict success for the farmers and landowners who take this path.’
Madeira mahogany (Persea indica)

A tree of the laurel family (Lauraceae), 10 to 25 metres tall, with oblong or oblong-lanceolate leaves that are light green or reddish, and small flowers gathered in axillary panicles. It grows in the forests and along the banks of streams, but on the south coast it does not thrive below 150 metres. It yields timber of a beautiful reddish colour, bearing a notable resemblance to that of mahogany (*Swietenia*), and much used for furniture and various other work. The bark of the Madeira mahogany (*vinhático*, *Persea indica*) is used for tanning. See Lauraceae.
Vinho de canteiro

In Madeira this is the name given to wine that does not go into the *estufa* (heated store for ageing Madeira wine) and instead undergoes its natural ageing in the cellar. It was to this wine, improved by the action of time, that the island owed its reputation as a wine-producing country. *Vinho de canteiro*, the wine of the canteiro system (natural ageing of the wine in casks on wooden supports, without artificial heating), is sometimes used in making other types of wine.
Vinho de roda

The merchants of Madeira in former times sometimes sent their wine on voyages across the Equator, receiving it back on its return improved by the high temperatures it endured in the ships’ holds. Wines that travelled to hot regions and came back to Madeira were called *vinhos de roda* (‘round-trip wines’). The *estufas* (heated stores for ageing Madeira wine) were created to give the wine a prolonged heat capable of producing effects similar to those produced by the heat of the ships’ holds. See Estufas.
Wines
We have already devoted some pages to this subject in the article Wine Industry (II-1545), to which we shall now add further essential information.

Many measures have been adopted and imposed by legislation to guarantee the genuineness of Madeira’s fortified wines. A detailed account of them is found in the esteemed work Navy and Overseas Archive (*Arquivo da Marinha e Ultramar*), of which a brief extract appears in the pamphlet *Vinhos da Madeira* by Nuno Simões, from which we transcribe the following illuminating passages:

‘On 23 December 1724 the merchants of Funchal addressed a petition bearing 38 signatures to the Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) concerning the wine trade and the prohibition on bringing in wines from the north of the island. The Senate established this prohibition by a municipal by-law (*postura*) of 9 January 1737. The merchant Francisco Teodoro submitted a petition on its disadvantages and advantages.

To prevent adulteration, the posts of *juiz de fora* (crown-appointed judge from outside the district) and President of the Residues were created in 1768. In that year Governor Sá Pereira issued by public proclamation (bando) an Order containing, in 13 articles, various measures to prevent the mixing of the wines of the South and the North, the latter being of inferior quality.

In a despatch of 30 August to Francisco Xavier de Mendonça Furtado, the same Governor expressly prohibited the blending of the two wines, as he had already ordered all the parishes and ports on 14 March.
None of these measures had their full effect, for on 16 August 1786 the Governor had to issue a new proclamation with severe penalties against offenders. The fraud was beginning to take new forms.

At the beginning of 1788, 19 Madeira wine merchants, most of them English, petitioned the Government against the fraud committed by some traders in the north of the island, who added the juice of black cherries to their wine to give it more colour and make it more like that of the south.

On 27 February of that year the Governor of the Island published a public notice (*edital*) ‘to eliminate the black cherry trees of this island, ordering that all those now existing be cut back to be grafted with red ones, and that all those which their owners will not uproot be pulled up by the roots’.

It also prohibited, ‘on pain of 6,000 *réis* (old Portuguese money of account; 1$000 = 1,000 réis, 1:000$000 = one conto = 1,000,000 réis) paid from gaol’, the replanting of black cherry trees, so as to prevent the adulteration ‘that the greed of some traffickers has attempted, to the grave discredit of the reputation of our wines and the ruin of their trade’. This Notice was not well received by those it threatened and affected. Petitions were submitted asking for its suspension. All were rejected, and one of their signatories, Canon Pedro Nicolau Acciaiuoli, was even arrested, an incident that Governor Dom Diogo Forjaz reported to the minister Martinho de Melo when informing him of the measures for the extermination of the black cherry trees.
Another form of fraud was denounced in 1791 in the petition of the English consul in Madeira to Luís Pinto de Sousa Coutinho, Secretary for Foreign Affairs.

Some merchants shipped Madeira wine to Tenerife and blended it there with very cheap local wine, in order to sell the whole as Madeira. The Archive holds the list of the ships that from 1784 to 1787 carried Madeira wines to Tenerife, where they were blended before being exported to Asia.

The decline in Madeira wine exports was attributed largely to these and other frauds, against which measures had to be taken in the early 19th century. There is no doubt that they contributed greatly to it.

Other and greater evils were, in the 19th century, to ruin Madeira’s principal product, which had been its greatest wealth ever since sugar, through competition from other countries, had lost first place in the Island’s economy.’

In 1914 the German chemists A. Kickton and R. Murdfield carried out an extensive and important analysis of Madeira fortified wines in the laboratories of the Hygiene Institute of the city of Hamburg. The *Revista de Chimica Pura e Applicada* published it in its issues of January to April 1916 under the title *Preparation, Composition et Apréciation du vin de Madere et de ses substituts*, a translation of the German original made by M. Eug. Ackermann. An offprint of it was issued as a pamphlet of 57 pages, which Dr Nuno Silvestre Teixeira rendered into our language in an excellent literal version and published in the Funchal *Diário de Notícias* (‘Daily News’) in November 1916. It is from the last of these articles that we take the following passages, because of their particular bearing on our subject.
‘I – Preparation
Madeira wine is a dessert wine of a particular character, prepared exclusively on the Portuguese island of Madeira by a method handed down from long ago.

Its special method of production consists in subjecting the must of fresh grapes (with whole bunches) to a very prolonged alcoholic fermentation. The base wines, once decanted or racked – generally well fermented, but sometimes also base wines still containing sugar – then have alcohol added (from wine or from sugar cane).

Sweetening is generally carried out by adding fortified must of fresh grapes (*geropigas*), and frequently also with cooked (caramelised) must, or else by using both these sweetening agents together, the second often serving chiefly for colouring.

In the products we examined, which may have been prepared before the Portuguese ban on sweetening of 1908 came into force, cane sugar was still very frequently used for sweetening. This sugar had been added partly as dry sugar and partly as syrup, and frequently also as a very dilute aqueous solution. Sweetening with cane sugar was generally accompanied by an addition of caramelised must. Only more rarely does sugar colouring appear to have been used for this purpose.

To hasten their maturing, and probably also to give them their special qualities, Madeira fortified wines are generally subjected to a heat treatment lasting months. This is almost always done in specially installed heated rooms (*estufas* (heated store for ageing Madeira wine)) brought to a temperature of roughly 50 °C; sometimes the wine, held in casks or glass bottles, is exposed to the rays of the sun. For the same purpose the wine is sometimes sent on a voyage to the tropics.

Madeira wine is often fortified again before export. The composition of Madeira wines is far from uniform across the various analytical results. This is due partly to the varying quantity of sugar in the different base wines, and above all to the differences in the sweetening agents used.

In general, the alcohol content of Madeira wines imported into Germany varies between 13.5 and 16 g per 100 cm³, corresponding roughly to 17 to 20% by volume. The proportion of extract (including sugar) varies between 5 and 8 g; that of acidity between 0.5 and 0.7 g; and that of sugar-free extract between 2 and 2.8 g per 100 cm³. For the last two components, the lower limit values have been set too low rather than too high, since samples that were entirely above any suspicion of blending by the addition of water show higher values, namely about 0.58 g for acidity and from 2.3 g upwards for sugar-free dry extract, per 100 cm³.

What is to some extent characteristic of Madeira wine is the ratio between the kinds of sugar, since the quantity of fructose is generally appreciably lower than that of glucose or, at most, equal to it; normally fructose makes up between 44 and 50% of the total sugar (as invert sugar). Exceptionally, Madeira wine also shows a predominance of fructose, but even then it is usually not very marked (up to about 52%).

As far as can be concluded from the analyses communicated to us, the content of Madeira wines is roughly 0.2 to 0.4 g of ash, 0.25 to 0,005 g of phosphoric acid, and 0.5 to 0.9 g of glycerine per 100 cm³.
III – Assessment

The provisions of the German wine law of 7 April 1909 have no objection to the method of preparing Madeira wine as practised in its country of origin, at least so long as cane sugar has not been used as a sweetening agent.

Under the German wine law, Madeira wines in which the presence of cane sugar can be shown may not be imported, nor may they circulate within the Empire, unless it is proved (as we explained above, such proof now seems very doubtful or difficult) that the products received their added sugar before the publication of the German wine law and before the Portuguese ban on sweetening of 1908 came into force. In any case, Madeira wines in which blending can be detected, as still very often happens, must be condemned.

Under the provisions of the commercial and maritime treaty between Germany and Portugal, and under the rules of the German wine law, the designations Madeira, Madeira Wine and similar word combinations are reserved, for circulation within the German Empire, to genuine fortified wines from the Funchal region that have not been blended with other wines.

Dessert wines from Madeira with an alcohol content below 17% by volume (or below roughly 13.5 g per 100 cm³) cannot be regarded as Madeira wines complying with Portuguese legal requirements and eligible for export to Germany, and consequently must not be admitted to domestic circulation under the designation ‘Madeira Wine’.
Imitations of Madeira wines
It is Spanish and often also Greek dessert wines that chiefly enter the trade as imitations of Madeira wines.

The Spanish and Greek imitations of Madeira wine often differ so greatly in composition from the chemical composition of genuine Madeira wines that chemical analysis can always detect the substitution of these products for the genuine wines.’

As is well known, the Junta Nacional do Vinho (National Wine Board) is an important national body whose purpose is to guide and protect viticulture and wine-making in the various regions of the country. The services it has already rendered, and will continue to render, to the cultivation of the vine and the trade in its rich products are very considerable. It was by the decree of 18 June 1940 that it extended its activity to the Madeiran archipelago, where its work has generally proved beneficial and produced appreciable results, despite the difficulties that always arise when a new means of protecting agriculture is introduced. The reports of the Junta Nacional do Vinho for the years 1940 and 1941 contain a great deal of data and information of particular interest to Madeira, but their considerable length does not allow us to reproduce them here.

Unfortunately, a complete monograph on the wines of Madeira has yet to be written, one that would trace their history, from the middle of the 15th century to the present day, in all the varied and interesting aspects it offers us.

This would require a broad descriptive work, carefully and thoroughly organised. Besides covering the various phases of the industry and the methods of wine-making, it should also provide reliable information on the proper choice of soil and the planting of vine cuttings, the effective treatment of the vines, the making and keeping of musts, the preparation of wines for shipment, their trade at home and abroad, the rigorous analysis of the so-called fortified wines and the careful preservation of the celebrated reputation they enjoy throughout the world. Each of these would be a subject of research and study in its own right, and for this it would be essential to make use of the valuable material scattered through various publications.

We shall give a brief account of some of them: *Memórias sobre as Ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo*, by João de Andrade Corvo, of which only Memória I was published, in 1855, with the subtitle ‘*A Mangra ou Doenças das Vinhas nas Ilhas da Madeira e Porto Santo*’, and which is considered a very important work, containing the most interesting and useful information; ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), 1873 edition, in the text and in the learned notes; *Os Vinhos da Madeira e o seu descrédito pelas estufas*, by the Count of Canavial, 1889; *Os Três Sistemas de Tratamento dos Vinhos da Madeira*, by the same author, 1900; *Noticia sobre o Vinho Canavial*, by the same author, 1882; *Acção Bactericida do Vinho Madeira*, by Dr Vicente Henriques de Gouveia, 1930; *Sur les vins de Madère*, by Dr Ferreira da Silva, 1896; *La vinification des vins de Madere et leur composition*, 1911, by the same author, studies published in the *Annales de falsifications*, pp. 4–59; *Préparation, composition et appréciation du vin de Madère et de ses substituts*, by A. Kickton and R. Murdfield, 1914, 57 pp., the notable study translated by Dr Nuno S. Teixeira and published in the *Diário de Noticias*, to which reference is made above; *Vinhos da Madeira*, by Nuno Simões, 1935, an offprint from the *Arquivo Financeiro e Segurador*; *O Vinho da Madeira – Como se prepara um nectar*, by J. Reis Gomes, 1937; *Informação Vinícola*, which contains valuable articles by the agricultural technician (*regente agrícola*) José Torres Tavares; the lengthy report (*Relatório*) of the inspector of the anti-phylloxera services, Almeida e Brito, for the year 1883; the reports (*Relatorios*) of the Junta Nacional do Vinho for the years 1940 and 1941; *O Arquipélago da Madeira na Legislação Portuguesa*, 1941, by Father Fernando Augusto da Silva, which mentions various decrees concerning the making of and trade in the wines of this archipelago; the *Elucidário Madeirense*, in various places and especially those mentioned in the articles ‘Vinhas’ and ‘Vinhos’; and *A Imprensa, As Colectividades do Distrito e o Projecção da Regulamentação da Produção, Fiscalização e Comercio dos Vinhos da Madeira*, 1916.

The article published in the newspaper *Informação Vinícola* of 20 September 1943, from the pen of the distinguished agricultural technician (*regente agrícola*) José da Cruz Tavares and entitled *Folclore do Vinho e da Vinha na Ilha da Madeira*, is not without originality and holds interest for the study of Madeiran ‘folklore’. We shall place it on record in these pages, and it will surely arouse the curiosity and interest of some readers of this work.
‘Madeira is a region rich in the folklore of the vine and of wine, richer perhaps than any other part of mainland Portugal.

The people sing of the grapes and the wine from the various varieties grown, but they single out those that give them the table wine they like best. They call this ‘dry wine’ because it undergoes no treatment, to distinguish it from ‘treated wine’ or ‘sweet wine’ – the fortified wine.

The Madeiran of the lower classes drinks it heartily, sometimes to excess, to the detriment of his own health and of the household budget. At the festivals and pilgrimages in which the region abounds, he goes along singing to the accompaniment of *rajões*, *machetes* and *braguinhas*. But for this he makes his worth felt in the following manner, especially when he has a good voice:
Whoever would like to hear me sing, Give me wine or give me money; For this little throat of mine Is not a blacksmith’s bellows.
Bring on the wine, bring on the wine! Bring another half *galão* (Portuguese gallon, about 3.16 litres)! Whoever wants to drink more wine, Put your mouth to the demijohn.
But little by little he grows more demanding:
Bring on the wine, bring on the wine! Bring on the salt cod as well! Bring bread with scabbard fish – All together it is not bad.

And things warm up, with *charambas* and *bailinhos*, amid banter and meaningful glances at the girls. The glasses are drained one after another, until matters may reach the raging paroxysm of the man who sang:
Lads: when I come to die, Bury me beside the wine! The *pipa* (wine cask and measure, c. 400–500 litres) for my pillow, The tap right at my snout.

In contrast to the barbarous materialism of this quatrain, admire the lyricism of this other one, in which the poet, lost in love, also gives his beloved the names of two commonly grown vines, among other pretty things he says to her:
O apple of my eye, My ‘tinta’, my ‘listrão’, Padlock of my breast, Key to my heart.
In Madeira the wine of the direct producers Jacquez, Isabella or ‘American’, Herbemont and Cunningham is much appreciated. But the ‘American’ or ‘scented wine’ is always the favourite:
The American wine Has always been more renowned; Because its grape is the plumpest It pushes the others aside
Whether you will or you will not, Tell me the truth now once and for all. You may drink as much as you please, For this is American wine.
He even goes so far as to credit it with certain medicinal virtues:
The American wine Is a wine of great renown. Whoever does not drink this wine Is always ailing.
This fine excuse and reason for drinking a little might well have been given to his sweetheart by the man who came to lament, or to mock, in this fashion:
My love does not want me to drink Either wine or spirit (aguardente, distilled from sugar cane or wine); For I am a young child And might die all of a sudden.
Of course, the people neither can nor know how to pronounce the tongue-twisting names of the other direct-producer varieties, and so they rendered them as best they could for their songs:
I like a pinch of snuff Because it smells to me of *rapé*; Let us drink this glass From the ‘jaqué’ vine.

It is clear enough what that glass of ‘jaqué’ was, with which the poet regaled himself, comparing it to the delights of a pinch of snuff. It will be harder, however, to make out what the treasure was made of that another balladeer sang of, forgoing the hundredfold reward God would send him:
To one who has a good heart God gives a hundred for the one he gives. Of this I give to no one, For it is my ‘armum’ wine.
For ‘armum’, or ‘armon’ and ‘armurio’ on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), is neither more nor less than the Herbemont.
Yet not everyone is content with badly made plonk of poor stock. There are still those who have good taste and can appreciate what will always be good in every age:
I am very fond of wine, But let it be old wine. I will tell you, gentlemen, That this is ‘verdelho’ wine.
And the singer was right! For Verdelho yields one of the finest and most fragrant fortified wines, when it is well tended and mellowed by the years.
If many people like wine, others prefer the grapes, although not everyone is able to grasp at once the longing of this poetess:
I am getting old now, I am quite worn out already. I no longer remember the taste Of the ‘caninha’ grape.
This ‘caninha’, like its synonym ‘canim’, is the vernacular rendering of the Cunningham direct producer, even though nobody says so.

In Madeira it is very common to make piquette (*água-pé*, thin drink made from pomace and water) from the pomace, which people either drink or leave to turn into vinegar. For want of anything better, the ‘peasant’ (*vilão*), the countryman, makes do with it:
O vine, give me a bunch, O bunch, give me a little grape! I want to make piquette, Since my father has no wine.
Makes do, so to speak... For there are crafty fellows who always have an easy resource and an expedient to hand, like the one who once came out with this:
This year I have no wine, I shall only make piquette. But I tell you, gentlemen, That my father-in-law has jaqué.

Worse off are those who have nothing but were used to having something. See the grim simplicity with which they nurse their longing for the good plant that produces the precious liquid which makes folk merry and also gives rich shade in front of their doors:
I have a barrel at home With neither wine nor piquette; Because the vine has withered, The jaqué vine I had.

The grape harvest, or ‘picking’ (*apanha*), begins in August in the most sheltered and sunniest localities: Of all the months in the year / I am very fond of August, / When the grapes are picked / And then the must is made.
It is done by men, women and children, by the household, neighbours, friends and guests, and while it lasts there is something of a festival, of merriment, with Cupid on the loose:
The world grumbles about everything, / Whether it is right or not. / Well, on the day of the grape harvest / I too want my share.
Farewell figs, farewell grapes, / Farewell, little fruit of summer; / Farewell, my love, farewell. / Until another time.
The grape harvests of Porto Santo seem also to hold a strong attraction for Madeirans, thanks to the splendid grapes grown there and the peaceful, healthy air one breathes:
I am growing very old, / Always sitting in a corner. / But I would still like to go / To the grape harvest on Porto Santo.
Porto Santo has lively festivals and a celebrated white table wine made almost exclusively from Listrão, which delighted a certain singer fond of revels and pilgrimages:
This year I am going to Monte, / Next year to Porto Santo; / If I like red wine, / I like white wine more.

Once picked, the grapes go in baskets to the wine presses, where the torment of the treading and the ‘second treading (*repisa*)’ awaits them. Treading is simply crushing by foot; but the second treading is an extremely violent operation to which the pomace is subjected after pressing, in order to extract a little more must from it when piquette is not to be made. While it lasts, the workers sing a song of its own, a traditional one, the ‘song of the second treading’, keeping time with the movement of jumping, feet together, with force and zest, on the spread-out pomace. It is a lengthy operation that must be done well if it is to be economical:
Since we are at the second treading, / Let us do it properly; / To the master’s content / And the mistress satisfied.
Nor do the popular quatrains dedicated in Madeira to the vine, the grape and wine end here’.
Vinte e Cinco Fontes

This is a delightful spot, visited by everyone who stays at the enchanting resort of Rabaçal (see that entry). Here countless springs gush from the sheer living rock of the cliff and plunge down from a considerable height. It lies about 3 kilometres from the Rabaçal houses.
Viola de arame

A musical instrument with wire strings, played only by country people. Its tuning, as we are informed by Captain Eduardo A. dos Santos Pereira, a distinguished amateur musician, is as follows: E (bass string), A, D, G, B, E (top string).

The *viola de arame* (wire-strung folk guitar) is an instrument much loved by country people and accompanies them on their journeys, but the sounds it produces are not very pleasing to the educated ear.
Violet (Viola adorata var. maderensis)

A perennial plant of the family Violaceae, common in the ravines of the interior of Madeira. Its gently scented flowers are emollient and diaphoretic. There is also on the island a violet with unscented flowers, whose botanical name is *Viola silvatica* var. *Riviniana*.
Turnstone
This name is given to *Strepsiles interpres*, a regular bird of passage, which, however, usually stays only a few days in the archipelago.
Virtudes

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), which took its name from the chapel of Nossa Senhora das Virtudes (Our Lady of Virtues) that stands there. It was built in 1661 at the behest of Francisco de Vasconcelos Bettencourt and rebuilt around the middle of the 19th century. In the same locality stands the chapel of St Anne (*Santana*), whose founder and year of construction we do not know.
Visco (Tolpis succulenta)

A subshrub 2 to 8 decimetres tall, with highly variable leaves (toothed, more or less cut, or linear and entire) and mediocre flower heads with yellow flowers. It belongs to the family Compositae, subfamily Liguliflorae. The milky sap that flows from the roots of the *visco*, once solid, has the elasticity and appearance of rubber, and can replace that substance for rubbing out pencil marks on paper. This is the only use of the Madeiran *visco*, nor can any other be found for it, since the quantity of sap produced by each plant is very small. The *visco* is a very common species in Madeira, and it has also been found on the Pico de Ana Ferreira (‘Ana Ferreira’s peak’), on Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Visconde do Ribeiro Real (square)

l (Largo do). It lies beside the Rua da Carreira (‘track’), or Rua do Dr. Vieira, at the point where the Rua Pimenta de Aguiar comes out. The bishop's palace has its main entrance on this square, which occupies the site of the old British cemetery, demolished in 1888. See Ribeiro Real (Count of).
Visit of the King and Queen of Portugal

On 22 June 1901 the cruisers *D. Carlos* and *S. Gabriel* and the royal yacht *D. Amélia* anchored in the harbour of Funchal, the first of them carrying King Carlos I and Queen Amélie. The monarchs were accompanied by the Minister of the Kingdom and President of the Council, Hintze Ribeiro; the Minister of the Navy, António Teixeira de Sousa; the Counts of Arnoso, Tarouca and Ribeira Grande; the Marquis of Faial; Vice-Admiral Brito Capelo; Dr Oliveira Feijão; and the queen’s lady-in-waiting, Dona Maria Francisca de Meneses.

The Portuguese sovereigns landed at the quay at the entrance to the city at about two in the afternoon. An imposing procession was at once formed and made its way to the Cathedral (Sé Catedral), where a solemn Te Deum was celebrated. The procession then headed for the Palácio de São Lourenço (St Lawrence Palace), which had been turned into a royal residence, and there the monarchs held a gala reception for the consular corps, the authorities, titled nobility and various official bodies.

Throughout the stay of the king and queen of Portugal on this island there was an unbroken series of festivities and enthusiastic demonstrations in their honour, of which we can give only a brief account. Special mention is due to the gala performance at the Theatre, so brilliantly described by the Count of Arnoso; the solemn session at the town hall (*Paços do Concelho*); the splendid entertainments given by Luís da Rocha Machado, the Viscount of Cacongo and João Blandy at their *quintas* (country estates) of Monte, Choupana and Palheiro do Ferreiro; the gala dinner at São Lourenço; the open-air Mass in the Praça Académica; the ball at Quinta Vigia; the industrial and agricultural exhibition, etc.
The monarchs visited the barracks, several charitable institutions and a number of public buildings.

The decorations on the quay, at the entrance to the city, in Praça da Constituição and along various streets and buildings were of unusual splendour. The illuminations were lavish and in the finest taste, and they were among the items on the programme of festivities that most aroused the interest and admiration of our visitors.

The grandeur of the reception given to the Portuguese monarchs, in which every social class enthusiastically joined, was owed above all to the civil governor, José Ribeiro da Cunha, and to the president of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*), Dr Manuel José Vieira. Before reaching Madeira, the cruiser *D. Carlos* stopped in the bay of Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’) to take on board the municipal council and authorities of that island, who went to pay their respects to the monarchs.
The King and Queen of Portugal embarked on 25 June, at about 6 in the evening, and sailed for the Azores, where they arrived on the morning of the 28th.

Anyone wishing for a more detailed account of all the festivities, the speeches delivered and various official documents relating to the royal visit should read the interesting book by Ciriaco de Brito Nobrega, entitled *a visita de suas majestades os reis de Portugal ao arquipélago madeirense*. It gives a complete description of everything that was done in Madeira to celebrate and solemnise the monarchs’ stay in this archipelago.
Visitação (Friar António da)

He was born in Madeira in 1546 and died on 13 October 1606. In 1568 he took the habit of the Carmelites, and he held very important offices in his order. He had a profound knowledge of Latin and was a celebrated preacher in his day. Diogo Barbosa Machado says that he left several *Poemas* and *Orações* (poems and orations), which remained unpublished.
Vitória

An inhabited locality (*sítio*) in the parish (*freguesia*) of São Martinho (‘St Martin’), where there is a chantry (capela) with the dedication of Nossa Senhora da Vitória (Our Lady of Victory). It was built in 1594 by Francisco de Betencourt on the lands of the entailed estate (*morgadio*) that he had founded there. It lies on the left bank of the Socorridos.
Vitória (Friar João Pinto da)

He was born on this island in the third quarter of the 16th century and died in Valencia, a city in Spain, in 1631. He entered the Carmelite order and went to Spain to complete his studies, remaining there until his death. He held the highest offices in his order, such as those ‘of provincial of Aragon and visitor (*visitador*, ecclesiastical inspector) of the province of Andalusia’. He was a writer esteemed in his day, and Diogo Barbosa Machado mentions the works *Vida del Fr. Juan Sanz*, Valência, 1612, and *Gerarchia Carmelitana*, Valência, 1616, both written in Spanish.
Nurseries and acclimatisation gardens

When the governor and captain-general of Madeira, Dom Diogo Forjaz Coutinho, proposed to the botanist Vandelli the creation of large plant nurseries on the island, intended to supply not only the Ajuda botanical garden but also, if need be, the gardens and hothouses of all Europe, the central authorities soon sent the civil government building (*Governo Civil*) of Funchal the authorisation needed to put the project into practice. On 6 May 1799, the said governor having already died, the provisional government ordered the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) José Maria de Afonseca to choose a suitable site for a plant nursery. On 9 August following, the same government stated in an official document that the land intended for growing northern species lay at the Lombada (‘long ridge’), in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), and that the southern species would be grown at whatever sites seemed most suitable until land of their own was assigned to them. Afonseca himself was put in charge of the nursery for northern species; if he was prevented, he could be replaced by José Joaquim de Vasconcelos, who would take charge of the nursery for southern species once it came to be established.

By 10 August 1823 the Monte nursery had distributed more than 20,000 trees to various places on Madeira and Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), according to a report on the work carried out for the benefit of the archipelago’s rural economy, submitted to the competent authorities by José Maria de Afonseca. The Monte nursery was abolished in 1828 by the government of Miguel I, and no one afterwards thought of restoring it. The decree of 4 January 1837 ordered the convent grounds of the former Convent of São Francisco (St Francis of Assisi) to be turned into a plant nursery, but it seems that nothing useful was done there to revive an undertaking that had already given such good results here in Madeira.

The land where the Monte nursery stood is still known today as the ‘Quinta do Jardim Botânico’ (‘botanical garden estate’). As for the nursery for southern species, we have no record that it was ever created.
What follows, written some years ago by one of the co-authors of this *Elucidário*, provides new information for the article ‘Acclimatisation Garden’ (*Jardim de Aclimação*) on page 178 of volume II.

‘In the locality (*sítio*) of Lombada, in the parish of Monte, there is a *quinta* known as the Botanic Garden (*Jardim Botânico*). Yet if we enter this *quinta* and closely examine the species that cover it, we find nothing that could in any way justify the name by which it is known. There is neither varied vegetation nor any rare species there; indeed, it may even be said that the Botanic Garden *quinta*, despite its name, is one of the properties in that parish that hold least interest for amateurs of botanical study.

Nevertheless, the name is not wholly inappropriate. If we consult old documents now unknown to the great majority of the people of Funchal, it is easy to see that on the spot where only common species now grow there was once an excellent nursery, which came to supply a large number of trees to various parts of the island.

The history of the nursery, or Botanic Garden, of Monte can be told in a few words. The Portuguese government learnt that the botanical explorations of Joseph Banks and Daniel Solander in 1768, and those of Francis Masson in 1776 and 1777, had led to the discovery of many valuable species in Madeira. This prompted the government to send an instruction to the governor and captain-general, Dom Diogo Forjaz Coutinho, to have gathered and sent to the botanic garden of Ajuda, then under the charge of Domingos Vandelli, not only all the recently discovered plants but also all those to which any economic or therapeutic value was attributed.

The request was carried out through the inspectors-general of agriculture. On that occasion the governor proposed to Vandelli the creation of large nurseries on the island, intended to supply not only the botanic garden of Ajuda but also, if need be, the gardens and hothouses of all Europe. Before long the central authorities sent down to the civil government of Funchal the authorisation needed to turn this idea into reality.

On 6 May 1799, Dom Diogo Forjaz Coutinho having by then died, the provisional government that had succeeded this governor ordered the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) José Maria d'Affonseca to choose a suitable site for a plant nursery. On 9 August following, the same government stated in another document that the land set aside for raising northern species lay in the Terra da Lombada, in the parish of Monte, and that the southern species would be grown in whatever places seemed most suitable until proper land was assigned to them. José Maria d'Affonseca himself was put in charge of the nursery for northern species; should he be unable to act, he could be replaced by José Joaquim de Vasconcellos, who was to have charge of the nursery for southern species, which, we believe, was never established.

As can be seen, the Monte nursery was already in existence in August 1799. It was an establishment of unquestionable usefulness, which prepared the island to receive the plant riches of various parts of the world. By 10 August 1823 the nursery had distributed more than 20,000 trees to various parts of Madeira and Porto Santo, according to a report on the work carried out for the benefit of the archipelago’s rural economy, submitted to the competent authorities by the aforementioned José Maria d'Affonseca.

The Monte nursery was abolished by the government of Miguel in 1828, and no one afterwards sought to re-establish it. The decree of 4 January 1837 ordered the convent grounds of the former convent of São Francisco to be used as a plant nursery but, it seems, nothing was done there either to revive an undertaking that had already produced such good results here in Madeira.

On acclimatisation gardens there is only one thing to record: the proposal made on 23 August 1852 by Dr Friedrich Welwitsch, the learned Austrian botanist, to the Portuguese government for the creation of two such establishments, one in São Paulo de Luanda and the other in Funchal. According to this botanist, the garden to be created in Funchal would be a subtropical garden. It would receive both tropical plants and those of cold countries, acclimatising them and, if possible, naturalising them, so that they could later be carried to other climates without harm.

Dr Welwitsch’s idea, although it won the approval of the Overseas Council (*Conselho Ultramarino*), was never put into practice, as is well known. We are left, however, with dozens of official letters recorded in the books of various public departments. They show that as early as the middle of the 19th century our official bodies spared neither paper nor ink when called upon to give an opinion on matters of which they understood nothing whatsoever.

Had things taken the same course at the end of the 18th century, the nursery or botanic garden of Monte would never have been established – the garden from which thousands of plants went out to repopulate a great many parts of the island (1921). See Agricultural Board, Passada da Novilha, Smith and Welwitsch.
