Flying fish (Exocoetus exiliens)

A teleost fish of the family Scombresocidae. The name *avoador*, or more properly *voador* (flyer), by which it is known comes from the flights it makes, using its pectoral fins, to escape its enemies in the water.
See Tuna.
Royal Volunteers of Dom Pedro

A battalion of this name existed in Funchal in the time of the governor José Lúcio Travassos Valdez, later Count of Bonfim. It consisted of 400 infantrymen, and enlistment began on 26 June 1828. Attached to the battalion was a cavalry company, which was supposed to have 64 men but only ever reached half that strength, and that only tolerably mounted. The Royal Volunteers of Dom Pedro dispersed when the Miguelist troops landed in Madeira.
Royalist Volunteers

The corps of Royalist Volunteers (*Voluntários Realistas*) Urban of Madeira was established in 1828 by the captain-general (*capitão-general*, military governor of Madeira) José Maria Monteiro. However, as can be seen from an official letter sent by Dom Álvaro da Costa de Macedo to the Count of Basto on 9 September 1831, this corps, which was meant to have 4 companies, only ever had one. For it, Dom Álvaro claimed the privileges and prerogatives granted to the Volunteers of the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal) by the decree of 26 September 1828.

Under captain-general Monteiro’s plan, the corps was to have a commanding major, and each company 1 lieutenant, 1 second lieutenant, 10 sergeants, 1 quartermaster-sergeant (*furriel*), 2 corporals, 2 lance corporals (*anspeçadas*) and 52 privates.
Vow to St James

– In the article Patron Saints (III-36) we have already dealt at some length with the apostle St James, chosen as patron saint of the Diocese of Funchal in the first quarter of the 16th century, and with the ‘vows’ solemnly made to him on that occasion. Foremost among these was the building of a church dedicated to his cult and to the celebration of the various religious ceremonies.

The passages from the records (*autos*) transcribed in that article were taken from the ‘Notes’ to ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), whose illustrious commentator tells us that he had copied them from an old and unknown ‘Miscellany’. Funchal Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal do Funchal*) rendered a valuable service by publishing, as a pamphlet, a complete facsimile copy of these important documents, following the originals entered in one of the books belonging to the Council’s old archive. The booklet bears the title ‘*Auto do Milagre do bem-aventurado Apostolo São Tiago Auto do Voto feito pela mesma Cidade do Funchal, ao mesmo Apostolo– 1521-1538*, extract from Volume I of the General Register of the Municipal Council of Funchal, deposited in the District Archive of Funchal’. It is preceded by an interesting ‘Introduction’ and closes with these words: ‘Introductory article, reading and conversion into modern language by the conservator, acting as Director of the District Archive, Alvaro Rogério Manso de Sousa’.

Because of the genuine authenticity of this publication, and the discrepancies between it and the transcription in ‘Longing for the Homeland’, we have decided to reproduce in full the text of these documents, which are most closely bound up with the subject of this article.

‘Record of the Miracle – In the year of the birth of Our Saviour Jesus Christ one thousand five hundred and twenty-one, on the seventeenth day of the month of March, Lazarus Sunday, in this city of Funchal, Doctor Pero Vaz being in it as *corregedor* (royal district magistrate) for the King Our Lord in this jurisdiction of Funchal, many were found sick of plague, and for days already people had been dying of the said illness without its being discovered. By means of guards and the regulations (*regimento*) of the land they set apart all those infected and removed them from the city; and notwithstanding the said separation the illness went on increasing, so much so that the Captain and the *corregedor* and officials and most of the people left the city. In the month of January of the year one thousand five hundred and twenty-three, the evil growing greatly, Captain Simão Gonçalves and the Judges and councillors (*vereadores*) and the people who were in the city gathered in council, and went to the choir of Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) of the said city, where they joined the dean and Chapter of the said Cathedral. And all, in praise of God, cast lots upon the twelve apostles, so that one of them should come forth as patron and advocate of this city; and at once, in the said choir, all being together, the lot fell upon the Blessed St James, whom they accepted as their defender and advocate. And all swore and promised that on his day they would hold a solemn procession for him and celebrate his feast, and that two councillors would always be stewards of the church of the said apostle, which was then newly built for him, and that the procurator of the city would be its clerk (*escrivão*), and that this ordinance should stand for ever. And from the said year of twenty-one until January of thirty-eight there were always Chief Guards, who had charge of the infected persons in the city and of sending them into penal exile (degredo); and in the meantime there were runners through the city, who every day went through the streets and learned of the sick in the city and reported them to the Chief Guards. And no master nor bloodletter let blood without licence from the said guards; and always, in the meantime, every year, there were infected persons in the said city, and the practice was always to set the infected apart and send them into exile outside the city, and for this purpose some houses were built on the islets, where the sick were washed. And with all these measures the plague never ceased; and in the year five hundred and thirty-eight, on the second day of January, the earth shook very greatly, and from then until the month of May many fell ill and died of the said evil, and the outbreak was so great that no year was worse. And throughout this time there were the said Chief Guards and men set apart to bury the dead who died of the said evil, whom they buried by night in the churchyards, it seeming to those who governed the land that, the evil being contagious, they did right to separate the sick from the healthy. And with all the separations the evil went on increasing; seeing which, the councillors of the said year five hundred and thirty-eight determined that from then onwards those who fell ill should be treated in their own houses and be buried by day, inside the churches, with the pomp that was fitting. And so, as this began to be relaxed, the evil began to diminish; and on the day of the Blessed Apostle, as the procession was about to set out, suddenly, not without divine permission, the hearts were touched of those who had charge of guarding the city, namely the Licentiate Gaspar da Nóbrega, who served as lieutenant of the Captain, and the Judges João Lourenço Leitão and Diogo Paes, and the councillors Manuel Afonso Ferreira Dromondo and Simão Darja and Heitor Homem de Sousa, and the municipal procurator (*procurador do concelho*) Manuel Carvalho. And all with one voice agreed that from that day onwards there should be no more guards in the city, and that those who fell ill of this evil should be treated as those with other illnesses are, and should be visited by whomever they wished, since in so long a time so many measures, at times very rigorous, had availed so little, which could well have remedied it had the remedy been a human one. But since that saying of the Blessed St James is true, that every good gift and every perfect gift always comes from Heaven, from the Father of Lights, so in this too it came to us from there, for all the aforesaid together recognised and confessed the truth: that the health of the city lay not in their guarding and rigour, but in the hands of the Lord God, to whom they commended themselves and from whom they hoped for the health of the city. And that from that day onwards they handed over the guarding of the city to the Blessed Apostle St James, Patron and Advocate of the said city, that he might be its guard and obtain from Our Lord health for it and for its people.’

And at once they set out with the said procession for the church of the Blessed Apostle, with all solemnity, where, as soon as they arrived, the councillors handed over the staffs of the Chief Guards and laid them on the altar, and there they remained and still are, in remembrance. And Father Licentiate Friar Vicente, preacher of the city, forthwith in his sermon publicly announced to all the people the decision of the governors, praising it greatly, together with the trust they had placed in the hands of the Lord God. This greatly pleased all the people, and they gave much praise to the Lord God for such a decision, which was not within their own power; and all, with one will and heart, at once held that the evil had been miraculously lifted by the Lord God and that health had been sent to the land. And the said governors at once ordered that all who were in exile might enter the city and their houses, and stay in them and go wherever they wished, which was carried out that very day. And all who were in exile, many with open sores and others with swellings not yet burst, came into the city and mingled with everyone; and from that day onwards the evil was miraculously lifted, the city was healthy, and there was never again any infection.
And the Lord God lifted the evil not only from the land but also from the hearts and mouths of men, for which we give Him many thanks and praises.

And so that so great a miracle and royal grant received from the Lord God should not be forgotten, since we had been freed from a plague no less than that of Pharaoh, the councillors of the said year had it written in this book of the register (*tombo*), to remain in memory for ever, together with the great debt we owe to our Patron and Advocate, through whose intercession we obtained so high a benefit and grant from the Lord God; and they signed here, with the judges and representative (*procurador*). And I, Simão Lopes, clerk of the Council (*escrivão da Câmara*), who wrote it.

‘Record of the Vow – In the year of the birth of Our Lord Jesus Christ one thousand five hundred and twenty-three, on Saturday the twenty-fourth day of the month of January, on the island of Madeira, in the Cathedral (the Sé) of the city of Funchal, in the choir of the said Cathedral, there appeared the Lord Captain Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, and the councillors (*vereadores*) and officers of the Council, citizens and guild representatives (*mesteres*) and many other people, and likewise the Lord Dean and Chapter with all the rest of the clergy (*clerezia*). And straightway it was set before them that on the eleventh day of the month of June of the year fifteen hundred and twenty-one, the said city being in great tempest and tribulation of plague and famine and many other hardships, it was agreed in the Council by the officers then serving, namely: João Correia, councillor, Vicente Gonçalves and Pero da Luz, judges, and the bachelor (*bacharel*, university graduate) João de Évora, representative, and the guild representatives, to take a roll of saints, namely: the name of Jesus Our Lord, and the Virgin Mary, Our Lady, and St John the Baptist and the twelve apostles, each by his own name. Of these they made fifteen slips, each with its own name, and cast them into a cap, and they were drawn by a boy named João, seven years of age, all first kneeling in prayer and promising to build a house in honour of whichever saint should come out by lot. And it pleased the Lord God that by lot there came out the blessed apostle St James the Less, in whose honour a feast was held throughout the city on that same day. On the twenty-first of July they began his house, the city and the said Chapter going in solemn procession, barefoot, with the schoolmaster Gonçalo Martins bearing the altarpiece (*retábulo*) with the image of the blessed apostle, and he struck the first blow of the hoe at the corner of the chantry (*capela*), on the Gospel side. This house was built on a piece of land that Antonio de Spinola gave for the said house. And because the said plague began once more to strike the said city somewhat, they, mindful of the foregoing, namely the Lord Captain and the officers of the Council and the guild representatives and citizens and people and the Dean and Chapter, resolved to have the said house finished at once, and from this day forward they took him as their protector and defender before Our Lord Jesus Christ, that he might be intercessor with the eternal God for the hardships of this people who commended themselves to him. And they vowed it, the Lord Captain as well as the officers of the Council and the guild representatives and the Lord Dean and Chapter, namely: the said Lord Captain in his own name and that of those descended from him, the officers of the Council in the name of the said City, and the said Lord Dean and Chapter in the name of all the clergy of the said Cathedral and city, forever, in every year of the world, to praise and celebrate the feast of the said glorious Saint, which is the first of May. For it they shall hold a solemn procession, which shall set out solemnly from the Cathedral of the said City and go to the said house of the said blessed saint, where they shall sing solemn vespers for him; and the same shall be done on the day itself, with solemn mass and procession, these processions to be held as on the very day of Corpus Christi. And it pleased the said Citizens to have the said saint painted in the Council chamber and on the banner and Seal of the City, just as St Vincent is borne on the banner of the City of Lisbon. And the aforesaid vowed this into the hands of the said Dean, to fulfil it all, for themselves and for their successors, and in witness and true faith thereof they signed it here. And I, António de Almada, notary public, now clerk (*escrivão*) of the Council, in the absence of Afonso Anes, wrote it. And likewise it pleased them to take as their protectors the blessed St Sebastian and St Roch, and to hold the said solemnity for them.’

On page 280 of this volume of the *Elucidário* there is a brief account of the church of St James the Less, today the parish church of Santa Maria Maior, to which we wish to add some further information.

The vow (*promessa*) was about to be fulfilled and the chapel dedicated to the patron saint built. Perhaps for lack of funds, or because the first enthusiasm shown at the time of the solemn ‘vow’ had cooled, the new church of the patron saint was in fact conceived on the most modest plan and built on very cramped proportions. It was no more than a poor, rustic chapel (*ermida*), like others scattered in various places on this island.

This regrettable failure, or mistaken understanding, of the obligations contracted in 1521 and 1538 was partly remedied in the second quarter of the 17th century with the construction of a new chapel, and later fully discharged when the present church was built, in the second half of the 18th century, as we shall see below.

In the first years of the second quarter of the 17th century, the Funchal Senate (*senado*, the municipal council) resolved to build a new chapel, in view of the smallness of the old chapel and the advanced state of ruin it was already in. Once the building was finished, the Council renewed, on 22 June 1632, the old commitments made by previous councillors (*vereações*), and on 25 July of the same year the diocesan bishop, Dom Jerónimo Fernando, gave the new chapel the ritual blessing with the greatest solemnity. The old fervour and veneration for the patron saint were reawakened, and the festivities then held in his honour were of great splendour and unusual brilliance, which lasted for many years.

At the council session (*vereação*) of 30 January 1754, the Funchal Senate took an important decision that seems to us somewhat strange today, since we do not know the reasons behind it: to demolish the chapel of São Tiago and build a church of larger proportions, more worthy of the purpose for which it was intended.

The image of the patron saint was taken to Funchal Cathedral (*Sé*) and the old chapel demolished, and construction of the new church began in that same year of 1754. The building work was slow: although it is stated somewhere that it was declared complete in 1768, the truth is that the venerable image was only transferred from the Cathedral to the new church in 1789, an act carried out with unusual solemnity and exceptional brilliance. It must be conjectured that the lengthy construction came to an end at approximately that time.

According to the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira* (1-4 ff.), the archive of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) holds the books *Reedificação da Igreja de São Tiago* and *Inventários e Rendas da Igreja de São Tiago*, which we have not had the opportunity to consult. They should contain some valuable information on the construction of the new church and on the weighty reasons that led the Senate to take this decision. It is to be presumed that the canonical blessing was given without much delay and that the church was at once handed over for worship.
Vow to the Blessed Virgin

The great flash flood (*aluvião*) of 9 October 1803, regarded as the greatest calamity ever to strike Madeira, of which we have already given a brief account (I-54 ff.), gave rise to the solemn ‘vow’ to place this island and the city of Funchal under the special protection of the Blessed Virgin (*Santíssima Virgem*), as recorded in the article Patron saints (III-36 ff.). It should be added that this ‘vow’ included in particular the clause choosing Our Lady of the Mount (*Nossa Senhora do Monte*) as special protectress of the city of Funchal. This was confirmed by an Apostolic Rescript of Pius VII dated 21 July 1804, and the feast of the Patronage of Our Lady of the Mount was then instituted, celebrated on 9 October each year with a solemn procession that went from the Cathedral to the parish church of Santa Maria Maior (St Mary Major). The ninth of October was formerly a holy day of obligation, preceded by its own vigil with fasting.
Voyages
*to the Madeira and Leward Caribbean Isles*, by Maria R... (Riddell); Edinburgh, 1792, 1 volume.
Voz da Madeira (A)
The first issue of this newspaper appeared in July 1908.
Voz do Operário (A)
The first issue of this newspaper appeared on 2 April 1899, and the last, no. 88, on 8 December 1900.
Voz do Povo (A)
This weekly, edited by José Marciano da Silveira, published its first issue on 17 May 1860 and ended with issue no. 1344 on 15 October 1877.
In 1911 another newspaper of the same name appeared; it published 59 issues, the first on 1 October and the last on 10 December.
Voz Publica (A)
This newspaper was published from 20 January to 6 September 1896, producing thirty-six issues.
Vues (Quelques)
*des Vendanges de 1891 à Madere, offertes par Blandy Frères & Cie.* It is a pamphlet with 8 plates and a short note on the island of Madeira and its wines.
Volcanism
See Stuebel (III-335 ff.).
Wallis (Samuel)
See Scientific expeditions (volume I, page 428).
Walsingham (Lord)
Works: *Catalogue of the Pterophoridae, Tortricidae and Tinidae of the Madeira Islands, with notes and descriptions of new species* (*Trans. Ent. Soc. Lond*, IV, 1894).
Waters (A. W.)

He mentions eight species of Madeiran membraniporids in his article entitled *Observations on the Membraniporidae* (*Linn. Societ Journ*, XXVI, 1898). He also wrote an article entitled *Bryzoa of Madeira* in the *Journal of the Royal Microscopical Society* (1899).
Watson (Robert Boog)

English doctor of laws and conchologist who, between 1864 and 1874, studied the marine shells of Madeira while serving as chaplain of one of the Protestant churches in Funchal. He is now deceased (1921). He wrote a work entitled *On the Marine Molusca of Madeira* (*Journ. Linn. Soc*, XXVI, 1897), having dealt with the same subject in 1873 in the *Proceedings of the Zoological Society of London*. In his work published in 1897, Watson mentions 382 species of marine molluscs, describing 35 that he considered new.

Like his compatriot Thomas Vernon Wollaston, Watson at times sought in his works to belittle other naturalists, which is unbecoming in a man of science and even more so in a clergyman, albeit a Protestant one.
Watson’s shells now belong to the English malacologist Tomlin, according to a letter sent to this city (1921).
Webb (Felipe Baker)

Distinguished English botanist, well known for his studies of the flora of the Canary Islands. He was born in Milford in 1793 and died in 1853. In 1828 he was in Madeira, where he stayed for some months to study the flora of this island. He also visited Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’).
Welwitsch (Dr Friedrich)

Austrian botanist, well known for his studies of the flora of Portugal and Angola. He was in Madeira in 1853, staying only a very short time. The year before, he had proposed to the government the creation of two acclimatisation gardens, one in São Paulo de Luanda and the other in Funchal, so that the latter would receive tropical plants destined to be taken to colder climates, and plants from those climates that it would be advantageous to grow in hot regions. Once such plants had adapted to our climate, it would then be easy to make them grow in countries colder or hotter than ours. The few plants collected by Welwitsch in Madeira in 1853 are in the herbarium of the Faculty of Sciences of the University of Lisbon (*Universidade de Lisboa*). Works: *Aforismos acerca da fundação dos jardins de aclimação na Ilha da Madeira e em Angola, na Africa Ocidental* (1921).
White (Roberto)

English subject who lived for some years in Madeira and who in 1851 wrote an interesting and valuable work entitled *Madeira, its climate and scenery*. In 1850 and 1851 he made meteorological observations in Funchal and Machico.
In 1857, during White’s lifetime, a second edition of his work appeared, edited and enlarged by James Yate Johnson (see that entry).
Wilkes
(Lieutenant Carlos). See Scientific expeditions (volume I, page 428).
Wilson (Miss Mary Jane)

This distinguished lady was born in Madras, in British India, on 3 October 1840. She settled in Madeira in 1880, and two years later she founded a school in the Palácio de São Pedro (‘St Peter’), which she named St. Georges High School and which was widely attended by girls from the best Funchal society. Having closed the school around 1892, she rebuilt the old hospital of the town (*vila*) of Santa Cruz (‘Holy Cross’) with money raised from alms. There she took in a number of patients and set up a pharmacy, rendering outstanding services to the sick and the poor of that municipality (*concelho*). She was the founder of a diocesan religious community which, through its hospital work and its teaching in many schools scattered across various parishes, earned the highest praise and the gratitude of the people of this island.

In 1907, during a smallpox epidemic, Miss Wilson took charge of the isolation hospital set up in the Lazareto de Gonçalo Aires (‘Gonçalo Aires quarantine hospital’). The circumstances were very grave, and the most lamentable consequences were feared. Yet so outstanding were the services that this illustrious lady rendered at the time that the groundless fears which had arisen in many minds, still under the impression of the unfortunate events of January 1905, were soon dispelled.
On this subject, one of the authors of the present work wrote in the former *Heraldo da Madeira* (‘Madeira Herald’):

‘Miss Wilson, devoting her boundless self-denial and her great and never-failing charity to the unfortunate smallpox patients, with no thought of the slightest gain or the most trifling reward, has placed herself on the same level as the great benefactors of humanity who, doing good purely for its own sake, aspire only to the approval of their own conscience and to the rewards of the life beyond the grave.

‘Alongside this incomparable charity, her kindly heart holds such treasures of tenderness, affection and gentleness that in the lazaretto she is the true providence of the sick, her brow always lit by the smile of hope and consolation.

‘The people, in their ignorance and excessive credulity, skilfully exploited by those who ought to have been their true mentors and guides, turned the lazaretto into a prison of Ugolino or a cave of Cacus, where the sick suffered the worst abuses, ranging from outrages against modesty to the most heinous murders. All this, which was nothing more than a legend and merely the object of wicked speculation, became for the general public an unshakeable belief, an axiomatic truth, which it would have been impossible to dispel or destroy.

Miss Wilson had to struggle stubbornly against these deep-rooted prejudices, superstitions and terrors. It was not without great fear that the first smallpox patients entered the isolation hospital. Before long, however, the spell was completely broken. Those fantastic horrors are gradually fading away, and in the lazaretto the patients found only the ardent flame of charity blazing intensely in a woman’s heart.
‘Today she is there the spirit of goodness, scattering blessings in abundance, a beacon of brilliant light illuminating so many minds, a rainbow of peace and hope comforting troubled hearts.’

With the establishment of the new political regime, Miss Wilson had to leave Madeira, but she returned to Funchal. She died in the house of the former convent of St Bernardino (*São Bernardino*), in Câmara de Lobos (‘seals’ den’), on 18 October 1916. On 15 April 1939 her remains were moved to the chapel of the building in Rua do Carmo (‘Carmel’) that houses the headquarters of the religious congregation she had founded.

As stated above, in 1884 Mary Jane Wilson founded a diocesan religious congregation, which she named the Franciscan Sisters of Our Lady of Victories (*Irmãs Franciscanas de Nossa Senhora das Vitórias*), and it received the full approval of the ecclesiastical authorities. This Congregation, which is devoted particularly to hospital work and to the elementary schooling of poor children, has rendered the most outstanding services here in Madeira, always with the greatest zeal and dedication, and these services are acknowledged by all without exception. Today its beneficent work in running the charitable institutions entrusted to it cannot be done without. A considerable number of its members already work selflessly in the evangelical missions of Portuguese Africa.
Winter (Dr Hermann)
A German bryologist who collected plants in Madeira at the beginning of 1912. Works: *Beitrage sur Kenntnis der Laubmoosflora von Madeira und Teneriffa* (*Hedwigia*, LV, 1914).
Wollaston (Thomas Vernon)

An English naturalist who visited our archipelago four times, the first in October 1847 and the last in the summer of 1855. He collected important zoological material on the various islands of the archipelago, especially in the fields of entomology and malacology. He also tried to visit the Savage Islands (*Selvagens*) aboard a pleasure yacht, but was unable to land there. Works: *Insecta Maderensia*, London, 1854; *Catalogue of the Coleopterous Insects of Madeira*, London, 1857; *Testacea Atlantica*, London, 1878; etc. This last work covers the molluscan fauna of the Azores, Madeira, the Selvagens, the Canary Islands, Cape Verde and St Helena.
As a malacologist, Wollaston falls far short of the Baron of Castelo de Paiva, Albers and others; as an entomologist, he is accused of having needlessly created many new species.

The zoological specimens that belonged to Thomas Vernon Wollaston are almost all held in the British Museum, although a collection of shells is in the possession of a certain Preston, a dealer in natural history objects (1921).
X
Wuellerstorf-Urbair (Commodore)

He commanded the Austrian frigate *Novara*, which made a voyage round the world in 1857, 1858 and 1859. The work entitled *Reise der Oesterreichischen Fregatte Novara um die Erde* (Vienna, 1861) contains a chapter in which Commodore Bernhard von Wüllerstorf-Urbair pays the well-deserved tribute of his admiration to the island of Madeira, where he stayed from 8 to 17 June 1857. The part of this chapter concerning our island was translated by João Félix Pereira and published in *Lampada* (nos 25 to 37, from 31 May to 10 September 1873). There is also a translation by the illustrious writer José Maria Latino Coelho, which appeared in the *Revista Contemporânea* and was reprinted in nos 2279 ff. of the now defunct *Diário do Comércio* (‘Commercial Daily’) of Funchal.
Xara

Madeirans give the name *xara branca* (white xara) to *Centrophorus squamosus* and *xara preta* (black xara) to *Centroscymnus coelolepis*. Both fish belong to the family *Espinacida* and can reach a length of 1 metre or a little more. According to the fishermen who have caught these species, the white xara is usually smaller than the black.
Xaras are eaten and have a flavour similar to that of salt cod. Fishermen sometimes sell the flesh of the blue shark (*Charcharias glaucus*) as xara.
Z
Zarco (João Gonçalves)

João Gonçalves Zarco was a Homeric figure at the dawn of our maritime ventures and voyages. He led the most important discovery made by Portuguese seamen in the first quarter of the 15th century, under the fruitful and glorious guidance of the Great Infante, Henry the Navigator. The discovery of Madeira is the great undying commemorative pillar (padrão) that truly marks the auspicious beginning of our odyssey as seafarers. It represents not only a notable territorial expansion of our dominions as a nation but, above all, our first great conquest as navigators and future masters of the seas.

The name of the illustrious navigator is inseparably bound up with this magnificent event in our history. The influence this great discovery had on the continuation of our maritime ventures has not been given due prominence, but there can be no doubt that it was exceptionally significant, and the discoverer and first coloniser of Madeira deserves a prominent place in the most brilliant pages of our maritime chronicles.

Gonçalo Velho Cabral, who discovered the islands of São Miguel and Santa Maria, won a more glorious name in history, because a distinguished biographer drew his portrait as a navigator in detail. He undertook extensive historical research with the meticulous care with which a descendant proud of his ancestral lineage extols the deeds of his forebears. João Gonçalves Zarco had no descendant to write his biography, nor has any research been done on him in the public archives, beyond the little that Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo found among the documents kept in the municipal registry of this city. The result is a marked scarcity of news and information about the great navigator, and it is extremely difficult to make even a modest biographical attempt in which the most characteristic features of his figure as warrior, navigator and coloniser are at least sketched in broad outline (1921).

Zarco or Zargo? [TN: The two spellings differ only in one consonant; the discussion concerns which form of the surname is correct.] This question is answered by the learned commentator of Frutuoso, who was also a distinguished philologist. He says that the first form is the more genuine way of writing this surname and has the best authors on its side, but that it became antiquated and usage adopted the second. We have consulted the oldest chroniclers and writers who dealt, if only briefly, with the discoverer of our archipelago, such as Gomes Eanes de Zurara, João de Barros and Damião de Góis, and found that all of them wrote Zarco. The accounts of the voyages made by Diogo Gomes, a contemporary of Prince Henry, and by Alvise Cadamosto (1450) adopt the same spelling. In a royal letter (*carta régia*) of Afonso V of the year 1449 we find the very antiquated form Zarquo, which corresponds to Zarco, the form adopted by our early chroniclers. The celebrated historian of the islands, who composed his work in the last quarter of the 16th century, uses the already modernised form Zargo. The spelling Zarco, found in two or three places in the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ (*Saudades da Terra*), must be considered a copyist’s slip or a printing error, since Gaspar Frutuoso certainly writes Zargo many dozens and perhaps hundreds of times. This was also the spelling always adopted by the annotator of that work. Every reason suggests that the spelling to follow today should be the one used by the illustrious author of ‘Longing for the Homeland’ and by his learned commentator.

What is the origin of the surname Zarco or Zargo, used by the illustrious discoverer of Madeira? João de Barros and later Damião de Góis, followed by the chronicler of the islands Gaspar Frutuoso, said that Zarco or Zargo was a nickname arising from a heroic deed performed by the navigator, and not a surname taken from his noble ancestry. The learned annotator of the *Saudades* does not share the opinion of those chroniclers. He says that the versions given by Frutuoso cannot be held to be true and are merely one more example of the general method followed in the invention of legends: to personify a proper name of unknown origin and break it down into a more or less plausible fable. In proof of his assertion he cites several old books of nobility in which the discoverer’s ancestry is recorded with the surname Zarco or Zargo.

It will not be entirely out of place to mention here, if only very briefly, the versions put forward by Gaspar Frutuoso that we noted above. In one of our encounters in Morocco, a Moor, a bold and skilful horseman, challenged one of the Portuguese warriors to a fierce combat. The Portuguese was defeated in the fight, paying heroically with his life for his extreme valour. Another Portuguese knight, and it seems several more, followed in the stubborn contest, all meeting the same unhappy fate, until the captain of our stronghold would not allow further lives to be sacrificed to the savage fury of the fiendish Moor. Then a knight who had not yet distinguished himself for his valour came forward, pleading and insisting with the utmost earnestness that he be allowed to charge the victorious Moor. Let us now hear the author of the *Saudades* in his naive and picturesque style: ‘And straightway the Soldier asked for the horse of a knight whom he chose for the purpose; and, mounting it with his shield on his arm and a piece of wood in his other hand, he advanced towards the Moor, who, seeing him skirmishing, came at him very haughtily. And every time he sought to strike the Christian, the latter did nothing but turn the Moor’s lance aside, which he did until, as soon as he saw the time and occasion, spurring his horse swiftly at the Moor, he dealt him so great a blow on an unguarded spot that, the Moor being stunned, he seized him by the hair and delivered him prisoner to the Captain; for which deed he was thenceforth known to the King. From this valiant Soldier, they say, João Gonçalves the Zargo descended, being his son or grandson; and others say that this feat of arms was performed by João Gonçalves himself; and because the Moor whom he, or his father, or grandfather killed was called Zargo, the same surname and name remained with them, or with him.’

Since our first African conquest took place in 1415 and Madeira was discovered four or five years later, it is hard to believe that the discoverer’s grandfather, who by then must certainly have been well on in years, could have been the hero of that exploit. It would be more credible to attribute it to his father, and far more credible still to the navigator himself. Yet it seems that not even the chronicler gave it much credence, for after recounting the episode he adds these words: ‘the information I have from the island of Madeira tells this beginning in another way:...’. Immediately afterwards he tells us that at the siege of Tangier ‘Zargo showed himself so knightly that he gave proof of his great valour, fighting bravely before the Infantes, who for this reason held him in high esteem. And in this place and combat he received a wound in one of his eyes from a crossbow bolt that the enemy shot at him, by which they destroyed one eye. And since in that time they called *zargo* anyone who had only one eye, the name remained with him as a badge and honour of his knighthood; for in it he gave such proofs and distinguished himself as so knightly that his valour and skill in war were of no small help in enabling Prince Henry the Navigator to escape and withdraw to the sea, at a time when Infante Ferdinand was already being left captive through treachery and cunning, as is related at length in the *Chronica d’El-Rey D. Duarte*’.

Friar Francisco Brandão says, in the *Monarchia Lusitana*: ‘There is no accepting the explanation that Doctor Gaspar Fructuoso gives in the history of the Islands, saying that he was called.... Zarco as a nickname because he was blind in one eye or because he had killed in Africa a Moor named Zarco....’.

Still on the origin of the discoverer’s surname, one of the notes to the ‘Longing for the Homeland’ transcribes the following passage from a genealogical work by José Freire Monterroio Mascarenhas: ‘The Zarco family is almost as old as the Kingdom (*reino*, i.e. mainland Portugal), for since the twelfth century records of it are found in its archives. Although we know that there is a *lugar* (settlement ranking between a town and a parish) in the province of Alentejo, near the town (*vila*) of Viana, with the name of Zarco, it has always seemed to us that the family did not take its surname from it, and that this derived not from a manor house but from a nickname; for this word Zarco, in the Castilian tongue as in the Portuguese, means a man who has greenish eyes, which Antonio de Nebrixa, in his Dictionary, explains in the Latin tongue with the word *glaucus*, and the same is said by Jeronymo Cardoso in his Vocabulary and by Ambrosio Calepino in his Dictionary; and so it was given as a nickname to one person, from whom it passed as a cognomen to his descendants’.

The name of João Gonçalves Zargo’s birthplace has remained unknown to us. Dr Álvaro de Azevedo says ‘that the authors are in doubt as to the place of his birth: some would have him a native of Tomar, because the Zarco family had an estate there, as the chronicler Brandão says; others of Lisbon; and some of Matosinhos or Porto, where Lousada says the Zarcos had a chapel.

Some of the old Madeiran books of nobility give Zargo as born in Matosinhos, and the writer Francisco Manuel de Melo, a descendant of the discoverer, also states that he was a native of that place. The third captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of Funchal, Simão Gonçalves da Câmara, the discoverer’s grandson, left his captaincy and settled in Matosinhos, where he died in 1530 (volume I, page 207). It is conjectured that his retirement to that part of the mainland may have been prompted by his family perhaps having originated there, by family traditions or by property the family owned in that place. None of these reasons constitutes conclusive proof that the great navigator was born in Matosinhos, but they are certainly presumptions worthy of the fullest consideration. It should be added that we were assured only recently that a tradition exists in that place that the discoverer of this archipelago was born there.

What was the precise date of his birth? One of the annotations to Frutuoso’s work reads: ‘it is not known for certain in what years João Gonçalves Zarco lived. From his being a young man in 1419, and from his eldest son, João Gonçalves da Câmara, having died aged eighty-seven in . . . March 1501, and therefore having been born in 1414, we infer that Zargo was born around 1395’. It seems to us that Zargo’s birth should be placed a little after 1390, so that he would have been between 25 and 30 years old at the time of the discovery. Some chroniclers regard him at that time as a young man, still of few years; yet we must not forget that he had already distinguished himself as a navigator and had conducted himself heroically at the second siege of Ceuta.

If we are to believe the genealogist Freire Mascarenhas, already cited, João Gonçalves Zarco was the son of Gonçalo Esteves Zarco and of Dona Brites, daughter of João Afonso of Santarém, overseer of the household of King John I. Gonçalo Esteves, who lived in the reigns of Afonso IV, Peter I and Ferdinand, was the son of Estêvão Pires Zarco, who was styled advocate in the King’s household and held important offices in the magistracy.

The name of the navigator Gonçalves Zargo gains no greater halo of glory from his having illustrious forebears and belonging to a family of noble traditions, though this was of capital importance at the time. Truth nevertheless requires us to say that the discoverer of the archipelago came of noble stock, and in that capacity frequented the household of Prince Henry the Navigator as a familiar (a member of his household). The old chroniclers Eanes de Azurara and João de Barros say so, the historian of the islands affirms it, and the same is found in the oldest and most reputable Madeiran genealogies. A book of nobility by José Freire Monterroio de Mascarenhas, cited above, whose manuscript is in the Public Library of Lisbon, contains a genealogy of Zargo tracing the illustrious navigator’s known ancestors back to the 12th century. In our view, one of the most conclusive proofs of his noble origin is his marriage to Dona Constança Rodrigues de Sá, daughter of Rodrigo Aires de Sá, who was Portugal’s representative in Rome and married there Dona Cecília Colonna, daughter of the marquis and prince of Colonna, one of the oldest, noblest and most esteemed families of the Roman patriciate. This has just been confirmed to us by a distinguished researcher on the mainland, after various searches in old and authoritative documents (1921). It should be noted that a marriage contracted at that time on such terms, when Zargo had not yet won fame as a celebrated discoverer and was not yet the wealthy captain-donatary of Funchal, could only have taken place if the spouse was a person of rank and proven noble ancestry. Aires de Sá, who misses no opportunity to extol hyperbolically the merits of the discoverer of the Azores, and who at times refers with manifest injustice to the discoverer of Madeira, says that João Gonçalves Zargo ‘was a man of modest origin . . . who managed to rise in the Household of Prince Henry and evolves into a settler’. The truth, however, is that he adduces no proof whatever for his assertion, which is moreover in flat contradiction with what the chroniclers, the books of nobility and the customs of the period tell us.

The genealogist Freire Monterroio, already cited, says that Gonçalves Zargo began ‘to serve Prince Henry the Navigator from a very young age’, and so served a long apprenticeship in the school of that illustrious and meritorious prince. Zargo distinguished himself as a navigator, making several voyages along the African coast, which was then the proven training ground, the arduous and well-tried course of our daring seafarers. Some writers, among them Francisco Manuel de Melo, assert that the illustrious navigator was the first to introduce firearms aboard his vessels, so that this improvement in the art of war waged on the ocean was owed to his inventive genius and martial ardour. He held the post of captain of the sea coasts of the Algarve and had several encounters at sea with Moors and Castilians, always giving proof of outstanding valour.

The discoverer of Madeira also distinguished himself as a brave and daring soldier, and the chronicles have left us highly laudatory references to his heroic conduct at Ceuta and at Tangier. In the first of these strongholds he was knighted, and in the disastrous action at Tangier he did much to ensure that Prince Henry could embark sheltered from the Moors’ assaults. Frutuoso says on this subject: ‘through the skill and effort of this knight João Gonçalves o Zargo, Prince Henry withdrew and embarked on the ships that were at sea for that purpose, Zarco remaining all the while on land, gathering in what men he could and valiantly withstanding the onslaught and weight of the Moors, who were coming upon him to get at the Prince. And after they had withdrawn, with the loss of many Portuguese, João Gonçalves withdrew badly wounded, with toil and danger, the Moors being countless. For this great service that this magnanimous João Gonçalves o Zargo did the Prince, and for others he had done the King, they held him in great esteem, and the King gave him offices of substance, in which he always showed himself a true knight’. His descendants continued their forefather’s glorious traditions, for many of them, and especially his successors in the captaincy, distinguished themselves valiantly in the strongholds of Africa, as we have already related in the articles we devoted to them in the first volume of this work (1921).

Shortly after the discovery of this archipelago and the division of the captaincies, Gonçalves Zargo settled in Funchal with his wife and children and began the work of peopling and colonising his donatary captaincy (*donataria*). ‘Captain João Gonçalves Zargo, say the *Saudades*. .. ., sheltering his ships by the islets that lie at the cape of this place, since there is a fine cove there, resolved to build on land his dwelling of wood, which he promptly built right by the sea on a high spot, where the captain’s wife (*capitoa*, wife of the captain-donatary) Constança Rodrigues later founded a church of Santa Catharina.’ It was beside this small church that Zargo had his first residence. It must without doubt have been a more than modest and uncomfortable dwelling built of wood, of a single storey and devoid of any architectural display, as were all the earliest houses built here in Madeira.

We have already said elsewhere that it was in the solitary retreat of Santa Catarina (‘St Catherine’) that Zargo directed the initial work of colonisation and laid the foundations of the future town, which progressed rapidly and reached a remarkable development within his lifetime. There, perhaps, he dreamed of the progress of the captaincy of which he was donatary (*donatário*) and of the aggrandisement of the house he had founded, glimpsing in the near future the honours and privileges that would be heaped upon his descendants and successors. Perhaps he had guessed that the monarch would reward him with the marks of nobility and the use of a coat of arms, already seeing his grandsons’ patents of nobility emblazoned with the coronet of count and of grandees of the Kingdom, in homage to the services rendered by their grandfather...

Some years later the discoverer moved his residence to the left bank of the stream, at the foot of the hill later called Pico dos Frias, near the chantry (capela) he had built there with the dedication to St Paul. It is said that this was the first residence built of stone to be raised in Funchal.

His definitive home, where he spent most of his life, was in the immediate vicinity of the site where he had the church of Conceição de Cima built. An old manuscript says: ‘he also resolved to build a dwelling for himself, as he did, on a height above the valley of Funchal, right opposite a church of Nossa Senhora da Conceição, as a family vault for himself and his kin’. This is the present church of the Convent of St Clare, and his residence is the old manor house of the Lomelino entailed estates, known today as the Quinta das Cruzes, as can be seen at greater length in the article Moradias de Zargo, on page 395 of volume II of this work, to which we refer the reader.

It is known that João Gonçalves Zarco devoted himself zealously to the colonisation of his captaincy, whose seat quickly grew in importance. A quarter of a century after settlement began, and while the discoverer was still alive, it was raised to the rank of town (*vila*), and roughly fifty years later it was granted the status of city by royal decree (alvará régio) of 21 August 1508. Little is known in any detail about the government of the first donatary, but nothing whatever is known to the discredit of the public administration of his captaincy. One accusation has been levelled against him: that he started the devouring fire which destroyed a considerable part of the original, luxuriant forest that covered this island from the edge of the ocean to the mountain crests. This event, narrated at some length on page 140 of the 2nd volume of the *Elucidário*, was certainly a risky act of daring, whose dire consequences the first settlers were perhaps unable to foresee. Yet it is equally certain that rapid and extensive colonisation made it imperative to destroy part of those dense and impenetrable thickets, which only a fire could reduce to the necessary proportions and so allow immediate agricultural use. According to João de Barros, it seems that this fire, because of the wide area over which it spread, caused serious losses and hindrances to the early colonisation; it is also beyond doubt that Madeira was quickly restocked with forest species and was soon covered with vast and abundant vegetation. The letter of grant (carta de doação) by which Henry the Navigator granted the captaincy of Funchal to João Gonçalves Zarco, to pass by the same letter to his direct successors, is dated 1 November 1450. This letter of the Infante was confirmed by royal letters of 25 November 1451 and 16 August 1461. The privileges and prerogatives conferred by these documents were essentially the same as those set out in the letters of grant made to the donataries Tristão Vaz Teixeira and Bartolomeu Perestrelo. The powers of the donataries were excessively broad and even extremely discretionary, for all civil and criminal jurisdiction lay with them, except for the imposition of the death penalty or the cutting off of a limb. They were lords of water and wind, that is, they alone could own mills or watermills, and they also held the rights to bake bread and to sell salt. In addition, they received a tenth of the revenues due to the Infante, together with the important prerogative of distributing uncultivated land. All this gave the captain-donataries of Funchal a very large annual income, making the house of the donataries of this captaincy one of the wealthiest in the country. Zarco’s 4th great-grandson and 5th donatary was made Count of Calheta and a grandee of the realm. The donataries of Funchal built a palace as their residence in Lisbon and lived in great splendour in the capital. We have no knowledge that Gonçalves Zarco reserved on this island, for himself or for his successors in the donatary captaincy, any land or real estate, but it is known that he granted vast territories to his other children and sons-in-law, such as the *lombada* (long ridge between valleys) at Ponta do Sol (volume II, page 277), and others besides.

Of the first donataries of Madeira, Zarco enjoyed the greatest prestige and influence. This was certainly owing to his personal qualities, and not merely to his being a person of higher rank than Tristão Vaz Teixeira, as Barros says in his first *Década*. The choice of captaincy itself seems to point to the superiority of the donatary of Funchal. The seat of his donatary captaincy enjoyed special advantages: its admirable situation, the ample space of the locality (*sítio*) for the growth of a populous settlement, the breadth of the harbour, the fertility of the soil, the picturesqueness of the place and the mildness of the climate. Set against the glaring inferiority of the other captaincy of Madeira in terms of soil, climate, lack of beaches and landing places, difficulty of communications, etc., these leave no doubt about the preference given to Gonçalves Zarco when the land found by the two navigators was divided. Later, with the rapid and remarkable growth of Funchal, the influence of the donataries of this captaincy kept increasing. At times they abused it, extending their jurisdiction over the other donatary captaincies and plainly encroaching on others’ powers, something to which the disastrous administration of the captain-donataries of Machico and Porto Santo contributed in large part. This was to some extent sanctioned by the governments of mainland Portugal, which did not curb these abuses and in official documents called the donatary of Funchal ‘the captain of the island’, as if the captaincy of Machico did not exist.

As mentioned above, João Gonçalves Zargo married Constança Rodrigues de Sá, or de Almeida, who according to the most authoritative genealogists was the daughter of Rodrigo Aires de Sá, Portugal’s ambassador in Rome, and of Cecília Colona, of the most noble Roman family of the marquises of Colona. A genealogical article says of this family: ‘A Roman patrician family whose origin goes back to Pietro de Colona, lord of a castle near Rome, who lived around 1100. His 3rd grandson, Seiarra de Colona, was raised to marquis in 1289, and his descendants were later made princes of Colona and of Palestrina and grandees of Spain; it is one of the Italian families of the loftiest lineage....’ In all likelihood, and according to the genealogies we have been able to consult, when the discoverer of our archipelago came to begin the work of colonisation he brought with him his wife Constança Rodrigues de Sá, his eldest son João Gonçalves da Câmara and his daughter Helena Gonçalves da Câmara. The third son, Luís Gonçalves da Câmara, 3rd captain-donatary (*capitão-donatário*) of the island of São Miguel, was very probably born in Madeira. In the article Sons and Sons-in-Law of Zargo (volume II, page 31) we have already dealt, if briefly, with the discoverer’s first descendants, and we refer our readers there. We need only correct here the information about Garcia Gonçalves da Câmara, who was the legitimate son of João Gonçalves Zargo and Constança Rodrigues, and not the natural son of the illustrious navigator, as stated there; that information came from a less authoritative source which we then held to be reliable. In the article Donataries we gave an account of the immediate succession of the captains-donatary of Funchal, descendants in the direct line of the discoverer down to the Philippine domination, and to each of them we devoted a fairly detailed special article on pages 201 ff. of the 1st volume of this work.

Zargo left a large and brilliant line of descendants, who spread through Madeira, the Azores, Brazil and mainland Portugal, and some of whom founded illustrious titled houses. One of his descendants, the great writer Francisco Manuel de Melo, says:

‘.... João Gonsalves Zarco, a man famous among us, for, not counting the more ancient houses, which are not recorded because they are uncertain, few men have we had in Portugal with such opulent lines of descent; three counts of this surname, Calheta, Vila Franca and Atouguia, owe him their male lineage..... And through marriages 21 titles of this kingdom descend from João Gonsalves.’ By a diploma of 4 July 1460, Afonso V granted the illustrious discoverer the use of a coat of arms, described in the same diploma as follows: ‘a black shield, and at its foot a green mountain upon which stands, firmly set, a silver tower between two golden wolves...’. In this royal letter (*carta régia*) the discoverer is named João Gonçalves de Câmara de Lobos, and his successors ought to have used that name, which in fact seems not to have happened, not even with Zargo himself. Of his coat of arms, of the historical error noticeable in it, of the surname Câmara used by his descendants, etc., we have already said enough in the article Câmara, on page 198 of volume I of this *Elucidário*.

Gonçalves Zargo died at a very advanced age. An old manuscript puts it picturesquely: ‘He reached such an old age that he had himself carried in men’s arms to sit in the sun, which greatly strengthened him. From there he ordered the affairs of his jurisdiction, governing and administering justice with his understanding wholly intact, never suffering the feebleness of a decrepit man.’ Some old books of genealogy give the navigator’s death as 1451, others as 1461, and yet another as 1471. Nothing definite is known on the matter. The year 1451 cannot be accepted, because the royal letter (*carta régia*) of 4 July 1460 shows that Zargo was still alive in that year. The date of 1461, held to be the most probable, is the one that best fits the 40 years of administration of the captaincy that the historian of the islands attributed to him. On the other hand, if we accept that he was born between 1390 and 1395, as we state above, we would have to suppose that he was between 66 and 71 years old at the time of his death. This certainly does not match the advanced age of which the chroniclers speak, especially for that period. If we accept 1471 as the year of his death and 1390 as that of his birth, he would have reached the age of 81, and the chroniclers’ unanimous statement about his decrepitude would then be fully justified. It may also be argued that he was perhaps born before 1390, in which case the dates of 1451 and 1461 would also have some possible justification. These are mere conjectures: there is at present no evidence that would allow us to fix precisely the year of the great discoverer’s death.

‘It pleased God to take him,’ says the manuscript already cited, ‘having governed the island.... not as its lord, but as father and companion to all its inhabitants.’ The mortal remains of the discoverer were buried in the church of Conceição de Cima, today the Convent of St Clare, which he had had built as a family vault for himself and his descendants. Zargo’s tomb lay in the chancel, as was indeed the general custom for the founders and patrons of churches. One reads somewhere ‘that the work was so arranged that the grave.... lay in the middle of the chancel, with a stone tomb above it so tall that it makes it singularly venerable and worthy of respect’. It is said that many years later the nuns succeeded in having the showy mausoleum removed, since it blocked their view of the altar. It was perhaps on that occasion that the ashes of the discoverer of Madeira were transferred to the family vault of his son-in-law Martins Mendes de Vasconcelos.

We are inclined to believe that this outrage – the removal of the mausoleum and the transfer of the discoverer’s remains, if it really took place – must have happened during the Philippine rule. At that time the donataries of Funchal no longer lived on this island and their role in government had become merely honorary, for it is hard to believe that they would have permitted such a profanation of the grave of their illustrious ancestor, the founder of the wealthy house they enjoyed. Frutuoso’s commentator says that the sarcophagus of Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos bears an inscription in Gothic capitals, illegible through wear, and that in the adjacent floor there is a large marble slab bearing the following epitaph:

Grave of Captain Gaspar Mendes de Vasconcelos, who had it made for himself and his heirs, the first slab laid here having been removed, as a descendant of the first Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos, who lies here and came to this island to marry Elena Gonçalves da Câmara, daughter of João Gonçalves Zarco, its discoverer. Made in the year 1710

This epitaph makes no reference to the discoverer’s ashes, and, according to what we heard from the person who tried to decipher it, the Gothic inscription does not seem to concern him either. Does it refer to Martim Mendes de Vasconcelos? Some have even supposed that the slab came from Portugal, where it covered the grave of an ancestor of Zargo’s son-in-law. When the floorboards of the chancel of the Convent of St Clare were lifted in March 1919, two tombstones were discovered there with epitaphs referring to the 2nd, 3rd and 5th captain-donataries of Funchal, as already related on p. 217 ff. of volume II of this work. Nothing relating to the discoverer was found there.

The chapel of St Catherine, the chapel of St Paul, the Quinta das Cruzes and above all the Convent of St Clare are modest but memorable monuments that eloquently recall the discoverer and the discovery of Madeira. These buildings deserve from the public authorities, and especially from the administrative bodies based in Funchal, the respect and veneration that are everywhere paid to objects and things closely bound up with the lives of illustrious men. They have the very grave duty of maintaining these buildings and of protecting them, as far as possible, from the ravages of time. And, as we have already said elsewhere in this book, this is a fitting occasion to make special mention of the two-handed sword (*montante*) of João Gonçalves Zargo. It was always kept in the house at Cruzes, and a constant tradition, handed down from generation to generation within the family that owned it, attributes it beyond doubt to the illustrious discoverer. It was always regarded as such, and the deep veneration paid to that relic there at all times confirms the truth of its origin still further. It is an old weapon, made to be wielded with both hands, and it is not distinguished by fine workmanship. It certainly has no intrinsic or artistic value, but it is worth a great deal for its five hundred and more years of existence and, above all, for having belonged to the great navigator who discovered this archipelago. It is perhaps the sword that Gonçalves Zargo wielded in Morocco in his charges against the Moors, winning fame as a brave and daring knight. This venerable relic is now in this city in the hands of a foreigner, who keeps it with the esteem it truly deserves. It ought, however, to be in the possession of the Municipal Council (*Câmara Municipal*) of this city. It is the duty of this administrative body to arrange its acquisition and to keep it religiously in its archives, until it can take its rightful place in the museum of art and antiquities that must one day be founded in this city (1921).

The idea of raising a monument in this city to the illustrious discoverer of Madeira is an old one, but no serious attempt was ever even sketched out to turn that idea into reality and so settle the outstanding debt to his glorious memory. It was in 1918 that the District General Council (*Junta Geral*) commissioned the maquette of the statue of Zargo, which is to stand on the Avenida do Dr. Manuel de Arriaga, as a continuation of the Entrada da Cidade. The maquette, the work of the distinguished Madeiran sculptor Francisco Franco, was exhibited at the Municipal Theatre (Teatro Municipal) on 2 March 1919. During the celebrations of the Fifth Centenary of Madeira the foundation stone of the monument was laid on that avenue, a ceremony of exceptional grandeur, as already described on page 163 of this volume (1921).

Outside the city, high in the mountains and overlooking the whole of Funchal, a bronze statue of João Gonçalves Zargo stands on the Terreiro da Luta. It shows the illustrious discoverer at the moment when the caravel under his command was approaching this then unknown island. This monument, from the chisel of the sculptor Francisco Franco, is due entirely to the initiative of the former merchant and distinguished Madeiran, Commander Manuel Gonçalves.

The Madeiran poet Francisco de Paula Medina e Vasconcelos published in Lisbon in 1806 a poem he called ‘The Zarco Epic’, of which, and of the *Georgeida*, Inocêncio Francisco da Silva says: ‘He sought to sound the epic trumpet, but one sees that this undertaking was far beyond his talent, and so in the two attempts he composed in that genre he never managed to rise above mediocrity. There are, however, in each of them, episodes that do no discredit to his muse and that can be read with pleasure’. Of Medina e Vasconcelos’s compositions, ‘The Zarco Epic’ brought him the greatest renown, and it is still today the best known of them all. It is an epic poem in *ottava rima*, modelled on the classical forms of the ancient epic. It is divided into ten cantos and contains more than five thousand lines. It deals with the discovery of Madeira by João Gonçalves Zargo, taking the discoverer’s surname for the poem’s title. It contains a series of interesting episodes with some happy poetic digressions, among which the legend of Robert Machin stands out. Only in Canto X is the discovery of this island described. The poem is preceded by a sonnet dedicated to Bocage, to which that eminent poet replies with another sonnet, undoubtedly the finest composition in the volume (1921).

The preceding passages on Gonçalves Zargo, transcribed word for word from the first edition of this work, should be compared with what is set out on pages 354 ff. of vol. I of the 1st edition, as a fuller clarification of the subject and also as a correction of some statements made at that time, especially the notes on the precise date of the discovery and on the names of those who carried out this chance or intentional undertaking (see I-355). Further new information, which we present below, is also of particular interest on this matter.

The article ‘Alguns Documentos do Mosteiro de Santa Clara do Funchal’, published on pages 171 ff. of volume IV of the *Arquivo Histórico da Madeira*, seeks to establish the true ‘spelling’ of the surname of the captain-donatary of Funchal, asserting that it should be written Zargo and not Zarco, as it is spelt in many places. It includes a document from the year 1447 in which that surname is reproduced, in facsimile, in the spelling Zargo. A question naturally arises: in the twenty-two years that passed between the start of settlement and the year 1447, would João Gonçalves always have written his surname with a g and never with a c? Such variations in names, surnames, family names and nicknames are not rare today, and they were even more frequent in past times. The document cited points to a presumption that should not be wholly rejected, but it does not establish an incontestable assertion that no one may legitimately doubt.

It should be noted that Gaspar Frutuoso, author of the ‘Longing for the Homeland’, Dr Álvaro Rodrigues de Azevedo, its illustrious commentator, and almost all the writers who have dealt with it used the spelling Zarco and not Zargo.

The conjectures about the probable year of João Gonçalves Zargo’s death were fully resolved by the information in the valuable piece published in the Funchal *Diário de Notícias* of 23 April 1927 by the distinguished writer João Cabral do Nascimento, which proves beyond doubt that he died in 1467. This is a significant contribution to Madeiran history.

The same *Arquivo Histórico*, in its volume for 1939, published a detailed article on the ‘two-handed sword’ of João Gonçalves Zargo discussed above. It sought to overturn the current opinion that the sword had belonged to the man to whom it has been attributed for centuries, but this was not proved incontestably. As is well known, this ‘two-handed sword’ was acquired by the public-spirited industrialist Henrique Hinton, who presented it to the Funchal Municipal Museum, where it is kept. Of particular interest on this subject is the article published in the *Diário da Madeira* of 16 November 1939, which readers wishing to learn more about the matter should consult.

The fitting tribute to the memory of João Gonçalves Zargo mentioned earlier was fully realised on 28 May 1934 with the solemn unveiling of the statue erected on Avenida Arriaga, as already described on page 394 of volume II of this *Elucidário*.
Zeolite
Sodium zeolite, or mesotype, has been found in the bed of the Ribeira dos Socorridos (‘stream of the rescued’), where it occurs as needle-like (acicular) crystals. It is a hydrated silicate.
Ziegler (J. M.)
He published the *Physical Map of the Island of Madeira* (1856), which is regarded as one of the best maps of our island to have appeared to date.
Phoenician juniper (Juniperus phoenicea)

A shrub, rarely a small tree, 1 to 5 metres tall, usually with a twisted trunk; the leaves are scale-like, imbricate and almost always appressed; the galbuli are subglobose and dark brown when ripe. This member of the Pinaceae has been found at Rocha do Navio, in Santana, on the Caminho de Larano (Porto da Cruz), etc. On Porto Santo (‘holy harbour’), where it was once very common, only a single specimen survived in 1903, on the slopes of Pico Branco (‘white peak’). It yields white or yellowish-white wood, much less aromatic than that of the cedar.

The localities of Zimbreiros at Paul do Mar and at Caniço, and of Zimbral de Areia and Zimbralinha on Porto Santo, probably take their names from the junipers (*zimbreiros*) that grew there in former times.
Zimmermann (Carlos)
A distinguished Swiss naturalist who studied Madeiran diatoms in volumes VIII and IX of *Broteria*. He is a member of the Society of Jesus and was a teacher at the now-closed college of São Fiel.
Zita (former Empress)

She arrived in Madeira with the former Emperor of Austria, Emperor Charles I, on 19 November 1921, at about half past ten in the morning, aboard the British cruiser *Cardiff*. The couple landed at the Pontinha (‘little point’) and went from there to the ‘Vila Vitoria’, where they took up residence. In January 1922 the former Empress left the island to fetch her children, who were being educated in Switzerland. She returned on 2 February with the princes Francisco Oto, Adelaide Maria, Roberto Carlos and Carlos Luís, and from the 18th of that month the whole family lived in the parish (*freguesia*) of Monte (‘hill’), at the *quinta* (country estate) of the banker Luís da Rocha Machado.

The former Emperor Charles died in the parish of Monte on 1 April 1922, and his body was laid in the parish church on the 5th of the same month. For this reason the former Empress decided to leave the island, which she did on 19 May of that year, aboard the liner *Infanta Isabel de Bourbon*, bound for Cádiz. Before leaving Monte, the former Empress prayed for a long time at her husband’s tomb; she had also attended the solemn funeral rites for the soul of the former Emperor, held in the Cathedral (Sé Catedral) on 27 April.
Vegetation zones

The article Flora (II-34) gave a brief account of the plant zones or regions found in Madeira, as in all mountainous countries, according to the varying conditions of climate. We wish to draw any interested reader’s attention to pages 216–222 of the *Flora do Arquipélago da Madeira* by the distinguished botanist Carlos de Azevedo de Meneses, where the subject is treated at greater length.
